In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat aliam partem constitutionis, in qua impugnatus respondet ad obiectionem in praecedenti capitulo recitatam, dicens quod illa verba Christi: Vae vobis legisperitis qui tulistis clauem scientiae &c. non sunt intelligenda de clauibus Ecclesiae, eo quod Christus ibidem loquitur scribis & Pharisaeis, quibus claues Ecclesiae datae non fuerunt. Ostendunt etiam, quomodo humilitas & fides possunt dici claues. In tertia parte impugnatores duo faciunt. Primo ostendunt, quod erroneum est dicere, quod clauis scientiae nullo modo est clauis Ecclesiae. Secundo ostendunt, quod per obiectionem impugnati non cassatur ratio appellantis. In quarta parte exponendo literam ostenditur, quomodo clauis scientiae dupliciter accipitur. Et alia multa de clauibus notantur, ostenditurque quod non derogat sacrae scripturae ponere plures claues, quam duas.
units.tr: Chapter 121. In the first two parts he recites and declares another part of the constitution, in which the one impugned answers the objection recited in the preceding chapter, saying that those words of Christ, Woe to you, lawyers, who have taken away the key of knowledge, etc., are not to be understood of the keys of the Church, because Christ there speaks to the scribes and Pharisees, to whom the keys of the Church were not given. They also show how humility and faith can be called keys. In the third part the impugners do two things. First they show that it is wrong to say that the key of knowledge is in no way a key of the Church. Second they show that the reasoning of the appellant is not overturned by the objection of the one impugned. In the fourth part, by explaining the letter, it is shown how the key of knowledge is taken in two ways. And many other things about keys are noted, and it is shown that it does not detract from Holy Scripture to posit more than two keys.

units.la: Cap. 122. In duabus primis partibus pertractat secundam assertionem, quam impugnat appellans, in qua impugnatus dicit sibi falsum impositum, videlicet quod dixisset, quod Papa in his quae ad fidem & mores pertinent, potest suorum praedecessorum diffinitiones revocare & contrarium statuere. In tertia parte id ipsum dixisse, nec falso impositum esse, ex dictis eius ostendunt, deinde inconvenientiam & perniciem illius erroris ostendunt. In quarta exponitur litera.
units.tr: Chapter 122. In the first two parts he treats the second assertion, which the appellant attacks, in which the one impugned says that something false was imputed to him, namely that he had said that the Pope, in matters pertaining to faith and morals, can revoke the definitions of his predecessors and establish the contrary. In the third part they show that he did say this, and that it was not falsely imputed, from his own words; then they show the inconvenience and the ruin of that error. In the fourth part the letter is explained.

units.la: Cap. 123. recitat & declarat, quomodo impugnatus sibi falsum impositum asserat, & obiectionem appellantis reiiciat. In tertia parte tria contra impugnatum affirmantur. Primum, ut dictum est, quod ex constitutionibus eius patenter infertur, quod Papae liceat praedecessorum suorum diffinitiones in dubium revocare & contrarium statuere. Pro quo improbando multa notatu digna adducuntur, praecipue quomodo diversimode aliqua diffiniuntur per clauem scientiae & per clauem potentiae ab ipso Papa. Et quomodo solus Papa potest diffinire, quamvis quivis peritus possit aliquid esse catholicum aut haereticum asserere & declarare. Secundum quod impugnatus de facto multa revocavit a praedecessoribus suis diffinita & per Ecclesiam approbata, ut patet revocando veritates Nicolai tertii contentas in decretali Exiit, & dogmatizando totidem haereses contrarias. Tertium est, quod ex dictis patere dicunt ad fidem catholicam pertinere, asserere quod Christus & Apostoli solum simplicem facti usum habuerunt in rebus temporalibus, abdicato omni dominio. In quarto notando verba textus ostenditur in solutione obiectionis, quod illa constituta per Iohannem 21. non sunt tenenda, quae constituit reiecta clave scientiae per prauitatem haereticam, per quam Papali dignitate privatum dicunt. Epilogando etiam ostenditur, in quibus locis scripturae habeatur; quod Christus & Apostoli omnium dominia abdicaverunt retento solo usu facti &c.
units.tr: Chapter 123. He recites and declares how the one impugned asserts that something false was imputed to him, and rejects the objection of the appellant. In the third part three things are affirmed against the one impugned. The first, as has been said, is that from his constitutions it is plainly inferred that it is lawful for the Pope to call into doubt the definitions of his predecessors and establish the contrary. In disproving this many noteworthy points are adduced, especially how some things are defined in different ways by the key of knowledge and by the key of power, by the Pope himself. And how the Pope alone can define, although any expert may assert and declare that something is Catholic or heretical. The second is that the one impugned has in fact revoked many things defined by his predecessors and approved by the Church, as is evident from his revoking the truths contained in the decretal Exiit of Nicholas III, and by teaching as dogma just as many contrary heresies. The third is that, from what has been said, they argue that it pertains to the Catholic faith to assert that Christ and the Apostles had only the simple use of fact in temporal things, with all dominion renounced. In the fourth part, by noting the words of the text, it is shown in the answer to the objection that those things established by John 21 are not to be held, which he established after rejecting the key of knowledge through heretical depravity, by which they say he was deprived of the papal dignity. In the epilogue it is also shown in which places of Scripture it is held that Christ and the Apostles renounced the dominion of all things, retaining only the use of fact, etc.

units.la: Cap. 124. & ultimum. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat conclusionem totius operis, in qua impugnatus ostendit causam constitutionum suarum, quas sigillo suo munitas validas haberi praecipit. In tertia parte impugnatores ex huiusmodi corroboratione eum pertinacem & haereticum manifestum esse concludunt. Unde quamplurima notatu dignissima differunt, utpote de duplici haeresi damnata explicite & implicite. Et utrius assertor debeat haereticus convinci & condemnari. Solvuntur item duae obiectiones, quarum prima est fratris Giraldi Odonis: quem impugnatores etiam haereticum affirmant & fautorem haereticae prauitatis: Colliguntque nouem conclusiones erroneas & haereticas ab eo assertas. In quarta parte notando literam ostenditur, quomodo pertinax debeat impugnatus convinci. Tandem ponitur peroratio autoris, hoc est Guilhelmi de Ockam, qui causam huiusmodi operis, quare ipsum compilaverit, & quare sic appellaverit, declarat. Admonens Lectores, si quid repugnans offenderint, diversis opinionibus diversorum, quas ipse duntaxat recitavit; adscribant. Haec sunt praecipue in hoc opusculo notanda. Praeter quae diligens lector multo plura comperiet, & sibi ut libuerit, annotabit.
units.tr: Chapter 124, and last. In the first two parts he recites and declares the conclusion of the whole work, in which the one impugned shows the cause of his constitutions, which he orders to be held valid, fortified by his seal. In the third part the impugners conclude from this confirmation that he is manifestly pertinacious and a heretic. Hence very many most noteworthy matters are discussed, namely about a double heresy, condemned explicitly and implicitly, and about how the asserter of either should be convicted and condemned as a heretic. Likewise two objections are solved, of which the first is that of Brother Giraldus Odo, whom the impugners also affirm to be a heretic and a supporter of heretical depravity. And they gather nine erroneous and heretical conclusions asserted by him. In the fourth part, by noting the letter, it is shown how the one impugned is to be convicted as pertinacious. Finally the author's peroration is set out, that is, of William of Ockham, who declares the reason for this work, why he compiled it, and why he so named it, admonishing readers that if they come upon anything inconsistent, they should ascribe it to the diverse opinions of diverse men, which he has merely recited. These are the things especially to be noted in this little work, besides which the diligent reader will discover much more, and will annotate as he pleases.

units.la: M. GVILHELMI OCKAMI OPVS NONAGINTA DIE- RVM, CONTRA ERRORES IOHANNIS XXII. PAPAE, DE VTILI DOMINIO REVM ECCLESIASTICARVM, ET ABDICATIONE BONORUM temporalium in perfectione status Mona- chorum & Clericorum.
units.tr: The Ninety Days' Work of Master William of Ockham, against the errors of Pope John XXII, concerning the useful dominion over ecclesiastical goods and the renunciation of temporal goods in the state of perfection of monks and clerics.

units.la: OPVS NONAGINTA DIERVM SEXTI
units.tr: The Ninety Days' Work, Sixth [Tractate]

units.la: Tractatus tertia partis Dialogi Magistri Guilhelmi Ockam: quem ideo Opus nonaginta dierum nuncupat, quod ipsum nonaginta dierum spatio compleuerit. In quo de gestis Fratris Michaelis de Cezena more recitatoris subtiliter pertractat, correspondenter ad id, quod sponderat se facturum in sexto tractatu tertia partis Dialogi.
units.tr: The treatise of the third part of the Dialogue of Master William Ockham, which he calls the Ninety Days' Work because he completed it within the space of ninety days. In it he treats, in the manner of a narrator, the deeds of Brother Michael of Cesena, in keeping with what he had promised to do in the sixth treatise of the third part of the Dialogue.

units.la: PROOEMIVM INCIPIT.
units.tr: THE PREFACE BEGINS.

units.la: DOctoris gentium & Magistri Beati Pauli irrefragibili authoritate decernitur, omnia esse probanda, id est, ratione discutienda, secundum Glossam. Quinimo iuxta illud Philosophi: Dubitare de singulis, non est inutile. Quia, sicut dicit quidam Sapientum non minimus: Non omne quod verisimile est, statim verum est. Sicut saepius, quod primum incredibile est, videmus non continuo falsum. Crebro siquidem faciem mendacii veritas retinet: crebro mendacium specie veritatis occultatur. Diligenter itaque examinanda sunt omnia & probanda, ne praecipitanter falsa pro veris a nimis credulis approbentur. Tunc autem efficacius examinantur omnia & probantur, exagitataque veritas magis splendescit in lucem, cum pro utraque parte contradictionis fortius & acutius allegatur. Proinde cum multa asserta in constitutione, Quia vir reprobus, (pro quibus in eadem constitutione multiplicius allegatum existit) nonnulli satagant impugnare: ideo ipsorum modus duxi praesentibus inserenda, ut utriusque partis allegationibus electis, ipsa veritas clarius elucescat. Ut autem apertius dictae constitutionis sciatur intentio, qualiterque contra ipsam obiectiones adversariorum procedant magis appareat. Ne quis dicat, quod verba, non mentem impugnant, tota constitutio per particulas cum reprobationibus est ponenda. Deinde obiectiones & responsiones impugnantium annectentur. Ad subiiciendas vero obiectiones (cum nesciam) minime respondebo. Sed quod constitutionis antedictae conditor respondeat, ardenter affecto. Oportet autem in primis materiam, intentionem & modum procedendi istius constitutionis exprimere. Est igitur materia istius constitutionis appellatio Fratris Michaelis de Cezena, quam reprobare & damnare molitur. Intentio vero est, Christianos a doctrina eiusdem Fratris penitus revocare. Modus autem procedendi ex divisione patebit. Dividitur vero haec constitutio in tres partes: videlicet in proemium seu prologum, Tractatum, & conclusionem. Prima pars incipit: Iohannes Episcopus seruus seruorum Dei. Quia vir reprobus. Secunda: In primis itaque, Tertia versus finem, ibi: Praemissa quoque.
units.tr: By the irrefragable authority of the teacher of the Gentiles, Master Paul, it is decreed that all things are to be proved, that is, to be examined by reason, according to the Gloss. Indeed, in line with the saying of the Philosopher: To doubt about single things is not useless. For, as one of the not least of the wise says: Not everything that is probable is at once true. Often we see that what at first seems incredible is not immediately false. Truth frequently wears the face of a lie, and a lie is frequently hidden under the appearance of truth. Therefore all things must be carefully examined and proved, lest the over-credulous too hastily approve false things as true. Moreover, all things are examined and proved more effectively, and the truth, once shaken, shines forth more brightly into the light, when arguments are advanced more strongly and sharply on both sides of the dispute. Accordingly, since many assertions in the constitution Quia vir reprobus (for which many arguments are adduced in that same constitution) are attacked by some who labour to refute them, I have thought it right to insert their method here, so that, with the arguments of both parties set out in selection, the truth itself may shine more clearly. Moreover, so that the intention of the said constitution may be known more openly, and so that it may appear more plainly how the objections of the adversaries proceed against it, lest anyone say that they attack the words and not the meaning, the whole constitution is to be set out piece by piece with its reprobations. Then the objections and replies of those who attack it will be appended. As for setting out the objections, I shall not respond, since I do not know them; but I eagerly desire that the author of the aforesaid constitution should reply. It is first necessary to express the matter, the intention and the method of proceeding of this constitution. The matter of this constitution, then, is the appeal of Brother Michael of Cesena, which it labours to reprove and condemn. The intention is to call Christians back entirely from the teaching of that same Brother. The method of proceeding will be clear from the division. This constitution is divided into three parts, namely the proem or prologue, the treatise, and the conclusion. The first part begins: John, bishop, servant of the servants of God. Because the reprobate man... The second: In the first place, then; the third, near the end, there: Moreover, the foregoing...

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Iohannes Episcopus seruus seruorum Dei ad perpetuam rei memoriam. Quia vir reprobus Michael de Cezena dudum Magister Generalis Ordinis Fratrum Minorum, qui suis excessibus exigentibus dicti ministerii status officio per nos de Fratrum nostrorum consilio priuatus & inhabilis redditus ad quaecunque dignitatis officia obtinenda fuerat, iustitia exigente, conuersus in vaniloquium, non intelligens quae loquitur, neque de quibus affirmant, in illum prorumpit insaniam, quod tres constitutiones nostras, videlicet illam constitutionem: Ad conditorem canonum: Cum inter: & Quia quorundam: misus est multipliciter impugnare, asserendo inter alia haereticum quod dicta constitutio cum inter, catholicum asserit: & catholicum, quod constitutio eadem haereticum declarauit. Et ut sua insania pluribus esset nota, libellos suos continens impugnationes praedictas ad diuersas mundi partes & studia destinare ac ipsos affigi in portis Ecclesiarum vel locis aliis publicis temeritate plebibili attentauit. Propter quae & plures ipsius excessus alios, fuerit de eorundem Fratrum consilio, fautor haereticorum & haereticus, exigente accidia, declaratus: prout in huiusmodi sententiis latius continetur. Licet impugnationes praedictae adeo sint insulsae, notoriae, quod sini responsione inligne: Quia tamen in ipsis impugnationibus arma sumit contra legem ex lege, ex Euangelium impugnat ex Euangelio: & de vero fingens mendacia, prout ad mendacium veritatem, ne simplicium corda possint inficere erronea ac haeretica sua dicta, succincte duximus suis oppositionibus (ut sequitur) respondendum.
units.tr: John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, for the perpetual memory of the matter. Because the reprobate man Michael of Cesena, formerly Minister General of the Order of Friars Minor, who, on account of his excesses, was by us, with the counsel of our brothers, deprived of the office of that ministry and made unfit to obtain any office of dignity, as justice required, has turned to vain talk, not understanding what he says nor the things about which they affirm, and has broken out into such madness that he has presumed to assail in many ways our three constitutions, namely that constitution Ad conditorem canonum, Cum inter, and Quia quorundam; asserting among other things, as heretical, that the constitution Cum inter is catholic, and, as catholic, that the same constitution declared heretical. And so that his madness might become known to many, he has rashly attempted to send his libels containing the aforesaid attacks to various parts of the world and places of learning, and to have them posted on the doors of churches or other public places, to the vexation of the common people. On account of these things, and of several other excesses of his, he was declared, with the counsel of the same Brothers, a favourer of heretics and a heretic, as the demands of the case required; as is set out more fully in such sentences. Although the aforesaid attacks are so foolish and notorious that they are unworthy of any reply, nevertheless, because in these attacks he takes up arms against the law from the law, and assails the Gospel from the Gospel, and, feigning falsehoods about the truth, as it were lying about the truth, we have thought it right to answer briefly, as follows, his objections, lest his erroneous and heretical statements infect the hearts of the simple.

units.la: ISta verba, quoad quatuor ab aduersariis impugnantur. Primo enim ostenditur, quod depositio Fratris Michaelis, de qua fit hæc mentio, nulla fuit: & quod de facto processit, & nullo modo de iure. Secundo ostenditur quod propter missionem libellorum suorum per mundum debet nullatenus reprobari. Tertio quod propter talem missionem libellorum, de quibus fit hic mentio, minime debet haereticus iudicari. Quarto quod impugnationes dictarum trium constitutionum Ad conditorem, Cum inter, & Quia quorundam: validæ sunt censendæ. Primum scilicet quod depositio Fratris Michaelis nulla fuit, & quod de facto processit, & nullo modo de iure, multis modis probare conantur.
units.tr: These words are attacked by the adversaries in four respects. First, they show that the deposition of Brother Michael, which is mentioned here, was no deposition at all, and that it proceeded only as a matter of fact and in no way by right. Second, they show that on account of the sending of his libels through the world he ought in no way to be reproved. Third, that on account of such sending of the libels, which are mentioned here, he ought by no means to be judged a heretic. Fourth, that the attacks on the three constitutions Ad conditorem, Cum inter and Quia quorundam are to be deemed valid. As to the first point, namely that the deposition of Brother Michael was no deposition, and that it proceeded only as a matter of fact and in no way by right, they try to prove it in many ways.

units.la: Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod sæpe dictus Frater Michael ante omnem depositionem & etiam latam contra ipsum à Præsidente, qui postea ipsum depositi, tanquam ab hæretico & pro causa hæresis legitime appellauit, licet occulte: quod secundum iura licet, quando aliter exspectatione mortis periculum immineret. In quo casu fuit Frater Michael antedictus, vel saltem hoc potuit probabiliter suspicari. Hoc viso duabus viis probare conantur, quod dicta depositio nulla fuit: & quod adhuc Frater Michael est verus Generalis Minister.
units.tr: To make this clear, they say that it must be understood that the often-mentioned Brother Michael, before any deposition, and even before the sentence pronounced against him by the President, who afterwards deposed him as a heretic and on account of heresy, lawfully appealed, although secretly; which the law permits when danger of death is imminent otherwise. In that case the aforesaid Brother Michael was, or at least could probably be suspected to be, in such danger. Seeing this, they try to prove in two ways that the said deposition was null, and that Brother Michael is still the true Minister General.

units.la: Prima via sic arguitur. Post appellationem vel prouocationem legitime interpositam non est aliquid innouandum: & per consequens, ille à quo appellatur vel prouocatur, non potest deponere appellantem vel prouocantem. Et si de facto deponit, depositio nulla est censenda. Frater autem Michael à Præsidente prædicto legitime appellauit seu prouocauit. Hanc probant, quia pro causa hæresis licet à Papa (etiam catholico) appellare seu prouocare: quamuis talis appellans seu prouocans, si causam, quam apponit, non probauerit, pœna debita sit plectendus. Ergo Frater Michael memoratus, qui legitime appellauit ab iurisdictione Præsidentis prædicti, appellatione præcedente fuit exceptus: & per consequens dicta depositio nulla fuit.
units.tr: The first way is argued thus. After a lawful appeal or provocation has been made, nothing is to be innovated; and consequently the one from whom the appeal or provocation is made cannot depose the appellant or the one who provokes. And if he does depose him in fact, the deposition is to be deemed null. But Brother Michael lawfully appealed or provoked from the aforesaid President. They prove this because, on account of heresy, it is lawful to appeal or provoke even from the Pope (even a catholic one), although such an appellant or provoker, if he has not proved the cause he alleges, is to be punished with the due penalty. Therefore Brother Michael, who lawfully appealed from the jurisdiction of the aforesaid President, was protected by a prior appeal; and consequently the said deposition was null.

units.la: Quod autem à Papa pro causa hæresis appellare vel prouocare cuilibet liceat Christiano, multi probare contendunt. Primo, quia ab omni habente superiorem in aliqua causa, licet pro eadem causa ad eundem superiorem iudicem appellare 2.q.6.placuit. Sed Papa in causa hæresis habet iudicem superiorem. Nam Papa potest pro hæresi iudicari. dist. 4. Si Papa. Imo sic notatur in Glossa, Papa non posset statuere, quod non posset de hæresi accusari: quia ex hoc periclitaretur tota Ecclesia. Qui autem potest de hæresi accusari: habet superiorem à quo poterit iudicari: ergo Papa habet in causa hæresis superiorem: quod Gloss. dist. 19. asserit manifeste dicens. Quod vbi de fide agitur Synodus est maior Papa: igitur à Papa pro causa hæresis est licitum appellare. Secundo probatur idem.
units.tr: That many contend a Christian may appeal or petition against the Pope on account of heresy is proved in several ways. First, because from anyone who has a superior in some matter it is lawful to appeal, for the same cause, to that same superior judge (2.q.6, "placuit"). But the Pope, in a case of heresy, has a superior judge. For the Pope can be judged for heresy (dist. 4, "Si Papa"). Indeed the Gloss notes this, saying the Pope could not lay down that he could not be accused of heresy, since in that case the whole Church would be imperilled. Whoever can be accused of heresy has a superior by whom he can be judged; therefore the Pope has a superior in a case of heresy. The Gloss on dist. 19 asserts this plainly, saying: "Where matters of faith are treated, a Synod is greater than the Pope." Therefore it is lawful to appeal from the Pope in a case of heresy. Second, the same point is proved thus.

units.la: Sicut ab aliquius communione & obedientia licet in aliquo casu recedere, ab eodem est licitum prouocare: quia maius est ab obedientia alicuius & communione recedere, quam ab eodem appellare, vel prouocare ab eodem. Sed pro causa hæresis licet à communione & obedientia Papæ recedere. Hoc exemplo & ratione probatur. Exemplo quidem: quia sicut habetur distinct. 19. multi clerici Romani à communione & obedientia Anastasii Papæ secundi, qui communicauit hæreticis, se laudabiliter abegerunt. Idem & ratione probatur: Quia non solum licet, sed etiam necessarium est ad salutem ab obedientia & communione excommunicatorum recedere, quando scilicet sciunt se excommunicationis sententiam incurrisse. Sed Papa si fiat hæreticus excommunicationis vinculo est ligatus, extra, de har. excommunicamus. Ergo qui sciunt eum talem, ipsum vitare tenentur. Patet igitur, quod pro causa hæresis licet ab obedientia & communione Papæ recedere. Ergo licitum est pro causa hæresis appellare seu prouocare. Multis aliis viis ostenduntur, quod in causa hæresis licitum est à Papa appellare vel prouocare. Ex quo concludunt quod Frater Michael propter appellationem interpositam ante decisionem causæ deponi non potuit: etiam supposito, quod ille à quo appellauit, in nullo in rei veritate à fide catholica deuiasset.
units.tr: Just as it is lawful in some case to withdraw from someone's communion and obedience, so it is lawful to petition against him; for it is a greater thing to withdraw from a person's obedience and communion than to appeal from him or petition against him. But in a case of heresy it is lawful to withdraw from the communion and obedience of the Pope. This is proved by example and by reason. By example: as is found in dist. 19, many Roman clergy commendably withdrew from the communion and obedience of Anastasius the Second, the Pope who communicated with heretics. It is proved by reason as well: it is not only lawful but even necessary for salvation to withdraw from the obedience and communion of excommunicated persons, when they know that they have incurred the sentence of excommunication. But if a Pope becomes a heretic, he is bound by the chain of excommunication (extra, de haereticis, "excommunicamus"). Therefore those who know him to be such are bound to avoid him. It is plain, then, that in a case of heresy it is lawful to withdraw from the obedience and communion of the Pope. Therefore it is lawful to appeal or petition against the Pope in a case of heresy. It is shown in many other ways that in a case of heresy it is lawful to appeal or petition against the Pope. From this they conclude that Brother Michael could not be deposed on account of an appeal lodged before the case was decided, even supposing that the one from whom he appealed had in truth not departed in any respect from the Catholic faith.

units.la: Secunda via sic arguitur. Hæreticus est omni potestate, auctoritate, & Ecclesiastica dignitate priuatus, etiâ si Papalis videatur præditus dignitate. Nam omnes hæretici quibuscunque nominibus censentur, iudicio & sententia generalis concilii sunt subiecti: imo etiâ Papa si efficiatur hæreticus, non solum sacris canonibus conciliorum, sed etiam canonibus summorum pontificum est subiectus, secundum notat Glo. 24.q.1.c.1. dicens: Hic est casus, quando scilicet aliquis in hæresim labitur, in quo Papa in canonem late sententiæ incidit. Nec obuiat ista regula: Quia par parem soluere vel ligare non potest. Quia si Papa hæreticus est, minor est quolibet catholico. Papa igitur si efficiatur hæreticus, sententiæ generalis concilii est subiectus. Sed per generale concilium sub Innoc. 3. celebratum omnes hæretici quibuscunque nominibus censentur, sunt excommunicati & damnati. Ergo omnes hæretici quibuscunque nominibus censentur, sunt omni potestate, auctoritate & Ecclesiastica dignitate priuati. Ergo nullum possunt prælatum deponere.
units.tr: The second line of argument runs thus. A heretic is stripped of all power, authority and ecclesiastical dignity, even if he appears to be endowed with papal dignity. For all heretics, under whatever names they are called, are subject to the judgement and sentence of a general council. Indeed, even the Pope, if he becomes a heretic, is subject not only to the sacred canons of the councils but also to the canons of the supreme pontiffs, as the Gloss notes on 24 q.1 c.1, saying: This is the case, namely when someone falls into heresy, in which the Pope incurs the sentence of excommunication latae sententiae. Nor does the rule stand in the way that an equal cannot dissolve or bind an equal. For if the Pope is a heretic, he is less than any Catholic. Therefore, if the Pope becomes a heretic, he is subject to the sentence of a general council. But by the general council celebrated under Innocent III, all heretics, under whatever names they are called, are excommunicated and condemned. Therefore all heretics, under whatever names they are called, are stripped of all power, authority and ecclesiastical dignity, and so they cannot depose any prelate.

units.la: Sed qui deposuit prædictum Fratrem Michaelem, vt isti impugnatores affirmât & multis modis ostendunt, sicut in eorum patet libris quampluribus, tunc fuit hæreticus manifestus. Ergo ipsum deponere nullo modo valebat. Et ex illo concludunt, quod etiam congregatio celebrata Parisiis ipsum nequiuit deponere. Tum quia dicta congregatio de mandato & in fauorem hæretici exitit celebrata. Tum quia multi veri Ministri, ad quos destitutio Generalis Ministri spectare dignoscitur, exclusi fuerunt. Tum quia multi, qui non fuerunt veri Ministri, admissi fuerunt. Tum quia dicta congregatio Parisiis non fuit secundum formam in regula traditam legitime convocata, & illa destitutio prædicti Fratris Michaelis nulla fuit. Ex quo sequitur, quod alterius institutio nulla fuit: & ita secundum istos sæpedictus Frater Michael verus Generalis Minister Ordinis Fratrum Minorum est censendus. De ista materia & contingentibus eam plures libri prolixi sunt conditi: in quibus prædicti impugnatores motiua adducunt quamplurima, obiectiones refellunt, & quæ possunt oriri dubia declarare nituntur. Quare quæ hic ex industria omittuntur, in operibus aliis requirantur. Secundo ex prædictis præfati impugnatores moliuntur à parte ostendere, quod prædicta missio libellorum per mundum est nullatenus reprobanda. Nam quod fit modo debito ad declarationem catholicæ veritatis, est minime reprobandum. Prædicti autem libelli fuerunt appellationes Fratris Michaelis pro fide catholica interiectæ. Ergo licitè publicatæ fuerunt: quia licitum est cuilibet appellationem seu provocationem legitimam publicare. Ergo prædicta missio debet nullatenus reprobari.
units.tr: But he who deposed the aforesaid Brother Michael, as these opponents assert and show in many ways, as is plain in many of their books, was then a manifest heretic. Therefore he could in no way depose him. From this they also conclude that the congregation held at Paris could not depose him either: first, because that congregation was convened at the command and in the favour of a heretic; second, because many true ministers, to whom the deposition of the Minister General is known to belong, were excluded; third, because many who were not true ministers were admitted; and fourth, because the said congregation at Paris was not lawfully convened according to the form laid down in the rule, so that the deposition of the aforesaid Brother Michael was null. From this it follows that the institution of his successor was null, and so, according to these men, the aforementioned Brother Michael is to be regarded as the true Minister General of the Order of Friars Minor. Many long books have been written on this matter and its circumstances, in which the aforesaid opponents adduce very many arguments, refute objections, and strive to explain the doubts that may arise. Therefore what is deliberately omitted here should be sought in their other works. Secondly, from what has been said, the aforesaid opponents undertake to show that the said dispatch of pamphlets throughout the world is by no means to be condemned. For what is done in the proper manner to declare Catholic truth is not to be condemned at all. Now the said pamphlets were appeals made by Brother Michael on behalf of the Catholic faith. Therefore they were lawfully published, because it is lawful for anyone to publish a lawful appeal or provocation. Therefore the said dispatch ought in no way to be condemned.

units.la: Tertio niduntur isti probare, quod propter talem missionem appellationum suarum non debuit ispe tactus Frater Michael hæreticus iudicari. Tum quia pro facto legitimo non debet aliquis hæreticus iudicari. Dicta autem divulgatio appellationum fuit legitima: quia pro fide defendenda catholica acceptata. Tum quia (quamuis erret etiam contra catholicam veritatem) paratus tamen est corrigi, si erraret, non est censendus hæreticus, cum non sit pertinax. Sic autem est hic: Quia præfatus Frater Michael in omni appellatione sua, sed omnia dicta sua correctioni sanctæ matris Ecclesiæ & concilii generalis subiecit & exposuit. Igitur etiam quamuis errasset in fide, non est hæreticus aliqualiter iudicandus. Et si dicatur, quod non est paratus corrigi, ex quo iudicium Papæ recusat, imo determinationem ipsius impugnat.
units.tr: Thirdly, these men strive to prove that on account of such a sending of his appeals the said Brother Michael ought not to have been judged a heretic. First, because no one ought to be judged a heretic for a lawful act. Now the said publication of the appeals was lawful, because it was undertaken in defence of the Catholic faith. Second, because a man who, although he may err even against Catholic truth, is nevertheless ready to be corrected if he errs, is not to be considered a heretic, since he is not obstinate. Now this is the case here: the aforesaid Brother Michael, in every appeal of his, submitted and exposed all his statements to the correction of holy mother Church and of a general council. Therefore, even if he had erred in faith, he is in no way to be judged a heretic. And if it is said that he is not ready to be corrected, since he refuses the judgement of the Pope, and indeed attacks his determination...

units.la: Ad hoc respondent defensores Fratris Michaelis, dicentes quod ex quo legitime appellavit, non debet se iudicio illus, à quo appellavit, submittere: imo ipsum debet publice recusare. Addunt autem quod prædictus Frater Michael debet apud omnes catholicos excusari: imo fidelis & catholicus reputari, pro eo quod in iudicio comparere legitime toto posse laborat. Ille autem à quo appellavit, tanquam suspectus ab omnibus reputandus, quia tanquam conscius suorum errorum (dicunt isti impugnatores) ad iudicium generalis concilii, à cuius iurisdictione in causa haeresis nullus nosciatur Christianus exemptus, venire recusat: imo quod generale concilium ad veritatem declarandam catholicam congregatur non permittit, in hoc reddens se suspectum, ut de ipso videatur impletum illud Salvatoris: Qui male agit, odit lucem: & non venit ad lucem, ut non arguantur opera eius.
units.tr: To this the defenders of Brother Michael reply, saying that since he appealed lawfully, he ought not to submit himself to the judgement of him from whom he appealed; indeed he ought to refuse it publicly. They add that the aforesaid Brother Michael ought to be excused before all Catholics, and indeed reckoned faithful and Catholic, because he labours with all his power to appear in judgement lawfully. But he from whom he appealed is to be regarded by everyone as suspect, because, as conscious of his errors (these opponents say), he refuses to come before the judgement of a general council, from whose jurisdiction no Christian in a case of heresy is known to be exempt. Indeed, he does not allow the general council to be convened to declare Catholic truth, thereby rendering himself suspect, so that in him is seen fulfilled that saying of the Saviour: Whoever does evil hates the light, and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved.

units.la: Hæc à me præscripta sunt breviter, eo quod de prædictis differere est extra intentionem meam in hoc opere principalem. De quarto, an scilicet impugnationes dictarum trium constitutionum, scilicet Ad conditorem: Cum inter: & Quia quorundam, sint validæ, ex sequentibus apparebit.
units.tr: I have set these things down briefly, since to discuss the aforesaid matters at length lies outside my principal purpose in this work. As to the fourth point, namely whether the impugnations of the said three constitutions, namely Ad conditorem, Cum inter, and Quia quorundam, are valid, this will appear from what follows.

units.la: His visis est ad literam accedendum. (Iohannes Episcopus) Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod damnabiliter retinet sibi hoc nomen (Dudum Minister Generalis) Dicunt quod ista privatio & inhabilitatio nulla est de iure. Quia per appellationem legitimam ab omni iurisdictione privantis fuit exemptus. Imo etiam dicunt, quod sine omni appellatione fuisset exemptus à iurisdictione eiusdem, quia ex quo lapsus fuit in haeresim, omni fuit potestate & auctoritate privatus. (Impugnare) Dicunt quod impugnare quascunque scripturas contra fidem orthodoxam est licitum. (Declarant) Dicunt quod erronee determinavit. Et ideo licitum est, quod est determinatum in ipsa, catholice reparare. (Attentant) Dicunt quod hoc fuit licitum, ex quo istæ appellationes nihil erroneum continebant. (Hæreticus) Dicunt quod non fuit hæreticus, etiam si erraret, quia paratus fuit corrigi. Qualiter cætera, quæ sequuntur, impugnant, in sequentibus apparebit. Unde sequitur:
units.tr: Having seen these things, we must now come to the text itself. (John, Bishop.) These opponents say that he damnably retains for himself this name (formerly Minister General). They say that this deprivation and disqualification is null in law, because by a lawful appeal he was exempted from the jurisdiction of the one who deprived him. Indeed they also say that even without any appeal he would have been exempted from that jurisdiction, since from the time he fell into heresy he was stripped of all power and authority. (To impugn.) They say that to impugn any writings whatever against the orthodox faith is lawful. (They declare.) They say that he determined erroneously, and therefore it is lawful to correct catholically what has been determined in it. (They attempt.) They say that this was lawful, since those appeals contained nothing erroneous. (Heretic.) They say that he was not a heretic, even if he erred, because he was ready to be corrected. How they oppose the rest that follows will appear in what follows. Whence it follows:

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: INprimis itaque hereticus istam constitutionem (Ad conditorem canonum) in eo nititur impugnare, quod dicta constitutio probat intendens, quod Fratres Minores sine proprio viuere profitentes in rebus, quæ usu consumuntur, non sunt censendi simplices usuarii, asserit, quæ sequuntur. Dicere scilicet quod in talibus rebus, scilicet quæ usu consumuntur, usus iuris vel facti separatus à proprietate rei seu dominio possit constitui repugnat iuri, obviat rationi. Et infra: In rebus usu consumptibilibus nec ius utendi nec usus facti separatur à rei proprietate, seu dominio possunt constitui, seu haberi.
units.tr: First, then, the heretic [Michael of Cesena's opponent] attempts to attack that constitution (Ad conditorem canonum) on the point that the said constitution, intending to prove that the Friars Minor, who profess to live without property in things consumed by use, are not to be regarded as mere users, asserts the following. Namely, that in such things, that is, things consumed by use, a right of use or a use in fact can be established separately from ownership of the thing or dominion, is contrary to law and opposed to reason. And below: In things consumed by use, neither a right to use nor a use in fact can be established or held separately from the ownership or dominion of the thing.

units.la: Hæc verba constitutionis prædictæ (ut dicit ipse hereticus) sacræ scripturæ, & sacris canonibus & definitionibus sanctorum, ac etiam determinationi sanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ obviant manifeste. Quod autem sacra scriptura repugnant per illud, quod legitur Actuum Apostolorum 2. & 4. capitulo aperte probatur, ut dicit. In secundo enim cap. dicitur sic: Omnes qui credebant, erant pariter, & habebant omnia communia: possessiones & substantias vendebant, & dividebant illas singulis, prout cuique opus erat. Quarto vero capitulo scribitur: Multitudinis credentium erat cor unum & anima una. Nec quisquam eorum, quæ possidebat, aliquid suum esse dicebat. Et paulo post: Nec quisquam egens erat inter eos. Quotquot enim erant possessores agrorum & domorum vendentes afferebant pretia eorum quæ vendebantur, & ponebant ante pedes Apostolorum. Dividebant autem singulis prout unicuique opus erat, & panem frangebant circa domum sumentes cibum cum exultatione. Hac ibi: Hoc autem vocabulum suum, ipsi exponunt sic: suum, id est, proprium, ut patet 12. quæst. 1. c. Scimus. & cap. Nobis. & ca. Non dicatis. Et per Augustinum circa principium Regulæ suæ & Glossam ordinariam super verbum habebant omnia communia, quæ dicit: Indicium fraterni amoris est omnia possidere, & nihil proprium habere. Ex quibus verbis (dicit ipse hereticus) insinuatur aperte, quod nullius rei temporalis, nec usu consumptibilis, nec non consumptibilis usu habebant credentes proprietatem: quia res consumptibiles usu, scilicet possessiones, agros, domos & substantias (Glossa 1. pecora) vendebant: & ipsa nec in speciali nec in eorum communitate retinebant. Illas autem res, quas lex, quæ in istis de usufructu constituitur, usu consumptibiles esse testatur, scilicet pecunias pro pretio rerum venditarum acceptas, & panes de quibus habetur ibi mentio specialis. in communi habebant & diuidebant singulis, prout cuiuscq; opus erat: & nullus ex eis aliquid suum, id est, proprium esse dicebat: sed tamen illi omnia communia: & sic quilibet eorum habebat vsum rerum vsu consumptibilium absque proprietate & dominio, à proprietate seu dominio separatum. Ex quibus concludit, quod dicta assertio & doctrina in dicta constitutione contenta obuiat Diuinae scripturae & omnem religionem habentem votum abdicationis proprietatis rerum temporalium destruit & confundit: quia secundum hoc quilibet religiosus, quando 5 veterem rebus vsu consumptibilibus, proprietarius censeretur. Hac sunt verba istius haretici: in quibus includit pre-culdubie multa falsa, ad quae, vt sequitur, respondemus.
units.tr: These words of the aforesaid constitution (as the heretic himself says) manifestly conflict with Holy Scripture, the sacred canons and the decrees of the saints, and also with the determination of the Holy Roman Church. He says that it is plainly shown to conflict with Scripture by what is read in Acts 2 and 4. In the second chapter it says: "All who believed were together, and had all things in common; they sold their possessions and goods, and divided them to all, as every man had need." In the fourth chapter it is written: "The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul. Neither did any of them say that any of the things which he possessed was his own." And a little later: "Neither was there any among them that lacked. For as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold, and laid them down at the feet of the apostles. And distribution was made to every man according as he had need; and they broke bread from house to house, and did eat their meat with gladness." Thus far there. They themselves explain this word "suum" (his own) as meaning "proprium" (proper), as is evident in 12 q. 1, c. Scimus, c. Nobis, and c. Non dicatis. And through Augustine near the beginning of his Rule, and the ordinary Gloss on the words "they had all things in common", which says: "It is a sign of brotherly love to possess everything and to have nothing proper to oneself." From these words (the heretic himself says) it is plainly implied that the believers had no ownership of any temporal thing, whether consumed by use or not consumed by use. For they sold things consumed by use, namely possessions, fields, houses and goods (the Gloss says: "flocks"), and they did not keep them either individually or in their community. But those things which the law, in the passages where usufruct is established, testifies to be consumed by use, namely the money received for the price of the things sold, and the bread which is specifically mentioned there, they held in common and divided to each as each had need; and none of them said that anything was his own, that is, proper to himself; but they all had all things in common. And so each of them had the use of things consumed by use without ownership and dominion, separated from ownership or dominion. From these points he concludes that the said assertion and doctrine contained in the said constitution opposes Divine Scripture, and destroys and confounds every religious order that has a vow of renouncing ownership of temporal things, since according to this, any religious, whenever he uses things consumed by use, would be judged a proprietor. These are the words of that heretic, in which he undoubtedly includes many falsehoods, to which, as follows, we reply.

units.la: IN ista parte incipit tractatus istius constitutionis, quae in tres partes principales diuiditur. Primo respondetur ad obiectiones contra constitutionem (Ad conditorem.) Secundo respondetur ab obiectionibus contra constitutionem (Cum inter.) Tertio ab obiectionibus contra constitutionem (Quia quorundam.) Secunda incipit ibi: Rursus iste haereticus, Cum inter nonnullos, satagit impugnare. Tertia pars incipit versus finem ibi: Adhuc iste haereticus constitutionem, Quia quorundam. 10
units.tr: In this part the treatment of that constitution begins, which is divided into three principal parts. First, objections against the constitution (Ad conditorem) are answered. Second, objections against the constitution (Cum inter) are answered. Third, objections against the constitution (Quia quorundam) are answered. The second begins where he says: "Again this heretic, Cum inter nonnullos, takes pains to attack." The third part begins near the end, where he says: "Still this heretic [attacks] the constitution Quia quorundam." 10

units.la: Prima pars diuiditur in quinque partes iuxta quinque contenta in dicta constitutione Ad conditorem, quae saepe dictus Frater Michael tanquam erronea reprobare conatur. Secunda pars incipit ibi: Adhuc dicit iste haereticus constitutionem praedictam. Tertia ibi: Rursus dictus haereticus ducit dictam constitutionem &c. Quarta ibi: Adhuc iste haereticus dictam constitutionem. Quinta ibi: Rursus dictus haereticus dictam constitutionem impugnare nititur. Prima pars adhuc diuiditur in septem partes, secundum quod ad septem obiectiones contra primam constitutionem istius acceptam de constitutione Ad conditorem canonum respondetur. Secunda pars incipit ibi: Item, ad probandum quod asserit. Tertia ibi: Adhuc iste veritatis. Quarta ibi: Rursus nititur: Quinta ibi: Praeterea dicit iste. Sexta ibi: Adhuc ad ostendendum. Septima ibi: Rursus dicit quod praedicta assertio. Prima pars adhuc diuiditur in duas partes. Primo enim ipsa impugnatio recitatur. Secundo respondetur ad ipsam partem immediate sequenti: Dicimus enim. 15
units.tr: The first part is divided into five parts according to the five contents of the said constitution Ad conditorem, which the often-mentioned Brother Michael tries to reject as erroneous. The second part begins where he says: "Still the aforesaid heretic says the aforesaid constitution." The third where: "Again the said heretic brings forward the said constitution, etc." The fourth where: "Still this heretic [attacks] the said constitution." The fifth where: "Again the said heretic strives to attack the said constitution." The first part is further divided into seven parts, according as replies are made to seven objections against the first constitution taken from the constitution Ad conditorem canonum. The second part begins where: "Likewise, to prove what he asserts." The third where: "Still this [heretic of the] truth." The fourth where: "Again he strives." The fifth where: "Moreover this man says." The sixth where: "Still, to show." The seventh where: "Again he says that the aforesaid assertion." The first part is further divided into two parts. For first the attack itself is recited; second, a reply is made to the part immediately following: "For we say." 15

units.la: In prima igitur parte ostendetur, quomodo nec vsus facti, nec vsus iuris in rebus vsu consumptibilibus possit a rei proprietate seu dominio separari: quod in constitutione Ad conditorem asserit impugnat, per illud Actuum 2. & 4. erant illis omnia communia. Quia dicit ipse, quod ex quo secundum veritatem scripturae omnia erant illis communia, nullius rei vsu consumptibilis proprietatem habebant. Et tamen constat, quod habebant vsum facti rerum vsu consumptibilium. Ergo in rebus vsu consumptibilibus potest vsus facti a proprietate & dominio separari. Haec est virtus impugnationis superius recitatae, quam impugnatores praedicti defensare nituntur. Dicunt autem, quod quia impugnatus sub multiplicitate vocabulorum errores conatur inducere, & molitur prosternere veritatem, ad euidentiam dicendorum quosdam terminos in hac constitutione saepe vitatos volunt exponere: considerando videlicet, quid sit vsus: quid vsus facti: quid vsus iuris: quid ius vtendi: qui sunt simplices vsuarii: quae sunt res vsu consumptibiles: & vocabula, meum, tuum, suum & huiusmodi. 30 35
units.tr: In the first part, therefore, it will be shown how neither a use in fact nor a use in law in things consumed by use can be separated from the ownership or dominion of the thing; this he attacks in the constitution Ad conditorem, asserting it, by the passage of Acts 2 and 4: "all things were common to them." For he says that since, according to the truth of Scripture, all things were common to them, they had no ownership of any thing consumed by use. And yet it is clear that they had a use in fact of things consumed by use. Therefore, in things consumed by use, a use in fact can be separated from ownership and dominion. This is the force of the attack recited above, which the aforesaid assailants strive to defend. They say, however, that since the opponent, under a multiplicity of words, tries to introduce errors and labours to overthrow the truth, they wish to explain certain terms, often avoided in this constitution, in order to make clear what is being said: namely, considering what is use, what is use in fact, what is use in law, what is the right of using, who are simple users, what are things consumed by use, and the words "mine", "yours", "his own" and the like. 30 35

units.la: Circa primum, quid sit vsus: dicunt quod hoc nomen vsus in scripturis variis modis quadruplicibus accipi potest. Vno modo accipitur secundum quod distinguitur a fruitione, secundum quod vsus & fruitio sunt actus voluntatis, quando aliquid assumitur in facultate voluntatis. Et sic raro vel nunquam accipitur vsus in scientia legali. Aliter secundo accipitur vsus pro actu vtendi re aliqua exteriori. Et sic accipitur vsus in omni facultate, quae vtitur hoc nomine vsus. Et isto modo accipitur vsus Iudicum 19. Habentes panem & vinum in meos, & ancillae tuae vsus. Tertio modo accipitur vsus pro consuetudine aliquid faciendi. Sic accipitur primo Regum 17. cap. cum dicit Dauid ai matus: Non possum sic incedere: quia nec vsum habeo. Sic etiam accipitur, dist. 11. ca. consuetudinis, & extra de consuet. cap. Cum consuetudine. Quarto modo accipitur vsus pro quodam iure speciali, quo quis valet vti rebus alienis, salua rerum substantia. Et isto modo accipitur vsus in scientiis legalibus & in scripturis, qui modos loquendi scientiarum legalium imitantur. Nec recolunt (vt asserunt) quod vsus hoc modo in Theologia vel Philosophia vnquam accipiatur. Sic ergo dicunt hoc nomen vsus his modis posse accipi: nec tamen negant quin alio modo accipiatur, siue inueniatur accep-tum. 40 45 50
units.tr: Concerning the first point, what is use: they say that the word "use" can be taken in four ways in the Scriptures. In one way it is taken as distinct from enjoyment, insofar as use and enjoyment are acts of the will, when something is taken up into the faculty of the will. And in this sense use is rarely or never taken in legal science. In another, secondly, use is taken for the act of using some external thing. And in this sense use is taken in every faculty which employs this word "use". And in this sense "use" is taken in Judges 19: "Having bread and wine for me, and for thy handmaid, and for the use [of the young man]..." Thirdly, use is taken for the custom of doing something. Thus it is taken in 1 Kings 17, when David, unaccustomed, says: "I cannot go thus, for I am not used to it." So too it is taken in dist. 11, c. Consuetudinis, and in extra de consuetudine, c. Cum consuetudine. Fourthly, use is taken for a certain special right by which one may use the things of another, the substance of the things being preserved. And in this sense use is taken in the legal sciences and in the Scriptures, which imitate the modes of speaking of the legal sciences. Nor do they recall (as they assert) that use is ever taken in this way in Theology or Philosophy. So they say that this word "use" can be taken in these ways; yet they do not deny that it may be taken in another way, or be found used otherwise. 40 45 50

units.la: De vsu facti dicunt, quod vsus facti est actus vtendi re aliqua exteriori: sicut inhabitare, comedere, bibere, equitare, vestem induere, & huiusmodi. Hoc pet scripturam Diuinam & perscriperius, Iudicum 19. Habentes panem & vinum in meos, & ancillae tuae vsus. Constat autem, quod isti vsuerant, comedere panem & bibere vinum. Igitur vsus pro actu comedendi & bibendi nonnullam accipitur. Item, Institut. de vsu & iure. §. 1. sic habetur: Qui fundi vsum nudum habet, nec vlterius habere intelligitur, quam vt oleribus, pomis, floribus, feno, stramento, ligno ad vsum quotidianum vtatur. In quibus verbis cum dicitur ad vsum quotidianum, vsus non accipitur pro iure, cum inconuenienter diceretur, ad ius quotidianum vtatur. Accipitur ergo vsus ibi pro actu vtendi, quo quis ius tale habet, quod vocatur vsus nudus, quo valet oleribus, pomis, & huiusmodi vti. Sed actus, quo quis vtitur oleribus & pomis, est actus comedendi. Ergo actus comedendi vocatur vsus etiam in iure. Et eadem ratione actus bibendi, & vestiendi, ac consimiles possunt vocari vsus. Item, quod actus comedendi vocatur vsus facti, etiam per dicta istius impugnati ostenditur. 55 60
units.tr: Concerning the use of a thing, they say that the use of a thing is an act of using some external object, such as dwelling in a house, eating, drinking, riding, putting on clothing, and the like. This is shown by Divine Scripture and by writers, Judges 19: "We have bread and wine for me and for thy handmaid." It is certain that those people were using, that is, eating bread and drinking wine. So use is taken in some sense for the act of eating and drinking. Likewise, Institutes, On Use and Right, §1, says: "One who has bare use of an estate is understood to have no more than the right to use vegetables, fruit, flowers, hay, straw and wood for daily use." In these words, when it says "for daily use," use is not taken for a right, since it would be improper to say "uses it for a daily right." So use is taken there for the act of using, by which one has a right of the kind called bare use, by which he may use vegetables, fruit and the like. But the act by which one uses vegetables and fruit is the act of eating. Therefore the act of eating is also called use in law. And by the same reasoning the acts of drinking, of clothing oneself, and similar acts may be called use. Furthermore, that the act of eating is called use of fact is also shown by the words of the author whom we are opposing.

units.la: 14 In hac enim constitutione, quia'vir reprobus, dicit in haec verba: vsus facti (supple est) vtentis proprius, quod non potest dici alterius, nec communicabilis. Datet enim quod actus comedendi Petri sic erat sibi proprius, quod non poterat dici alijs esse communis Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod hic actus comedendi vocatur vsus facti, & eadem ratione vocatur actus bibendi, & vestiendi, ac consimiles possunt vocari vsus facti. Si igitur omnis actus, quem exercet aliquis circa rem extrinsecam, scilicet comedendo, bibendo, vestiendo, legendo in libro, equitando & huiusmodi, vocatur vsus facti, & additur facti, ad differnendum talem vsum ab vsu iuris. Isti tamen non negant vsum facti posse accipi alio modo.
units.tr: For in that constitution, "the reprobate man" (vir reprobus) says in these words: the use of fact (understand "is") belongs to the one using, and cannot be called another's, nor communicable. For suppose the act of eating of Peter was so much his own that it could not be called common to others. From these words it is plainly clear that this act of eating is called use of fact, and by the same reasoning the act of drinking, of clothing oneself, and similar acts may be called use of fact. If, then, every act which a person performs on an external thing, namely eating, drinking, clothing, reading a book, riding and the like, is called use of fact, and fact is added to distinguish such use from use of right, nevertheless these people do not deny that use of fact can be taken in another way.

units.la: De vsu vero iuris dicunt, quod vsus iuris est quoddam ius positiuum determinatum, institutum ex ordinatione humana, qua quis habet licitam potestatem & auctoritatem vtendi rebus alienis, salua rerum substantia. Unde & sic diffinitur in iure: Vsus est ius vtendi rebus alienis salua rerum substantia. Vsus autem sic dictus dividi potest in nudum vsum & in vsumfructum. Naduusu est, cum quis habet ius vtendi re aliena, salua rerum substantia. Sed hoc ius non potest alteri vendere, nec locare, nec gratis concedere. Sed cum quis conducit domum, habet ius habitandi in domo cum 15 familia, sed hoc alteri vendere non potest, nec concedere nec locare. Similiter qui habet nudum vsum fundi, habet ius morandi in fundo, si voluerit, habet etiam ius percipiendi quosdam fructus crescentes in fundo secundum determinationem iuris ciuilis, sed tale ius alteri vendere, concedere, & locare non potest.
units.tr: Concerning use of right, they say that use of right is a certain determinate positive right, established by human ordinance, by which a person has a lawful power and authority to use the things of another, saving the substance of the things. Hence it is also defined in law: Use is the right of using the things of another, saving the substance of the things. Use so called may be divided into nudus usus and usufruct. Nudus usus is when one has the right to use another's thing, saving its substance. But this right cannot be sold to another, nor let, nor freely granted. Yet when someone hires a house, he has the right of dwelling in the house with his family, but he cannot sell, grant or let this to another. Similarly, one who has bare use of an estate has the right of staying on the estate if he wishes, and also the right of taking certain fruits growing on the estate according to the determination of civil law; but he cannot sell, grant or let such a right to another.

units.la: Vsufructus est pinguius ius in rebus alienis, salua rerum substantia, quia qui vsumfructum habet, non solum ipsa re vti potest, sed omne ius suum potest alteri vendere, concedere & locare. Sic igitur cum dicitur, vsus nudus, nudus additur ad differentiam vsusfructus. Unde & vsus iuris quandoque accipitur communiter: & sic est commune ad vsum nudum & vsumfructum. Quandoque vero accipitur magis specialiter; & sic accipitur pro vsu nudo, qui ab vsufructu distinguitur, quemadmodum hoc nomen consuetudo, quandoque accipitur communiter pro iure humano scripto & non scripto: quandoque specialiter pro iure humano non scripto, secundum quod ex decretis distinctione prima colligitur euidenter. Qualitercunque ergo accipiatur vsus iuris, semper est ius quoddam, & non est actus vtendi. Unde qui conducit domum ad habitandum, habet vsum iuris in domo, licet sit extra domum, & actu non inhabitet eam. Additur autem iuris, ad differentiam vsus facti, qui est actus quidam exercitus circa rem exercitam, secundum quod in iure accipitur: quaeliter etiam in Theologia saepe accipi inuenitur.
units.tr: Usufructus is a fuller right in the things of another, saving their substance, because one who has usufruct can not only use the thing itself, but can sell, grant and let all his right to another. So when it is said "bare use," nudus is added to distinguish it from usufruct. Hence use of right is sometimes taken in a general sense, and so it is common to bare use and usufruct. But sometimes it is taken more specially, and so it is taken for bare use, which is distinguished from usufruct, just as the word consuetudo (custom) is sometimes taken generally for written and unwritten human law, and sometimes specially for unwritten human law, as is clearly gathered from Decretum, distinction one. Therefore, however use of right is taken, it is always a certain right, and is not an act of using. Hence one who hires a house to live in has the use of right in the house, even though he is outside the house and does not actually dwell in it. But of right is added to distinguish it from use of fact, which is a certain act performed upon the thing used, as it is understood in law; and it is also often found so understood in Theology.

units.la: Quarto exponunt, quid est ius vtendi: dicentes, quod ius vtendi est potestas licita vtendi re extrinseca, qua quis sine culpa sua, & absque causa rationabili priuari non debet inuitus: & si priuatus fuerit, priuantem poterit in iudicio conuenire. Dicitur (Potestas licita) ad differentiam potestatis illicitae, qua fur saepe vtitur rebus alienis. Multi etiam alii frequenter per potestatem illicitam propriis rebus vtuntur. (Qua quis sine culpa sua) etiam ponitur ad differentiam gratiae, qua saepe alicui conceditur potestas licita vtendi re aliqua, qua tamen ad libitum concedentis (absque enim culpa sua & causa) licite priuari potest, solummodo, quia concedens concessam renocat potestatem: sic inuitati pauperes a diuite, habent licitam potestatem vtendi cibis & potibus positis ante se, quos tamen inuitans ad placitum suum poterit amouere: & si amouerit, non poterunt inuitati propter hoc inuitantem in iudicio conuenire, nec aliquam actionem habent contra ipsum, & talis potestas saepe vocatur gratia in iure. Unde notat Glossa ordinar. deci. quaestion. tert. Cauendum, quod si episcopus habet sumptus, unde possit expendere, non debet alios grauare. Nam potius videntur haec peti ex gratia, quam ex iure. Glossa etiam extra de potestatis, bona memoria, notat quod si aliqui vocantur ad aliquam electionem de gratia, tunc nec ius nec commodum sibi acquirunt: & ita inter ius & gratiam est discretio facienda. Ius igitur vtendi competit habenti vsumfructum, & non solum illis, sed saepe competit habenti dominium & proprietatem. Unde & in diffinitione vsus ponitur ius vtendi tanquam genus: cum dicitur, vsus est ius vtendi rebus alienis salua rerum substantia. Ex quo patet aperte, quod non omne ius vtendi est vsus: quia si omne ius vtendi esset vsus, prima particula diffinitionis vsus, quae ponitur loco generis, esset conuertibilis cum diffinito: & reliquae particulae essent superflluae, quamuis igitur omnis vsus iuris sit ius vtendi: non tamen omne ius vtendi est vsus iuris, qui distinguitur a dominio & proprietate. Sed omne ius vtendi rebus alienis, salua rerum substantia, est vsus. Et si dicatur, quod ius vtendi est seruitus: nullus autem habet in re propria seruitutem: ergo qui habet dominium rei non habet ius vtendi re illa, cuius habet dominium.
units.tr: Fourthly, they explain what the right of using is, saying that the right of using is a lawful power to use an external thing, from which a person ought not to be deprived against his will without his own fault and without a reasonable cause; and if he is deprived, he can bring the one depriving him to court. It is said (lawful power) to distinguish it from unlawful power, by which a thief often uses the things of others; many others also frequently use their own things by unlawful power. (by which a person, without his own fault) is also added to distinguish it from a favour, by which a lawful power to use some thing is often granted to someone, which, however, may lawfully be withdrawn at the pleasure of the granter (for without his own fault and without cause), simply because the granter revokes the power he has granted. Thus poor people invited by a rich man have a lawful power to use the food and drink set before them, which, however, the host may remove at his pleasure; and if he removes them, the invited guests cannot for this reason bring the host to court, nor have any action against him, and such a power is often called favour (gratia) in law. Hence the Ordinary Gloss notes, Decretum, causa 11 (?), Cauendum, that if a bishop has the means from which he can spend, he ought not to burden others; for these things seem to be asked for from favour rather than from right. The Gloss also, Extra, On Powers, Bona memoria, notes that if certain persons are called to some election by favour, then they acquire neither right nor advantage for themselves; and so a distinction must be made between right and favour. The right of using therefore belongs to one who has usufruct, and not only to such persons, but often belongs to one who has ownership and property. Hence also in the definition of use the right of using is placed as the genus, when it is said, Use is the right of using the things of another, saving the substance of the things. From this it is clearly evident that not every right of using is use: for if every right of using were use, the first part of the definition of use, which is placed in the position of genus, would be convertible with the thing defined, and the remaining parts would be superfluous. Therefore, although every use of right is a right of using, yet not every right of using is use of right, which is distinguished from dominion and property. But every right of using the things of another, saving their substance, is use. And if it is said that the right of using is a servitude, and no one has a servitude in his own property, then one who has ownership of a thing does not have the right of using that thing of which he has ownership.

units.la: Item, nonnunquam habet aliquis rei alicuius dominium & proprietatem, qua tamen licite vti non potest: sicut qui rem propriam alteri locauit, ipsa re vti non potest non illicite, igitur dominium rei seu proprietas non est ius vtendi. Ad primum istorum dicunt isti impugnatores: quod licet inueniatur in iure, quod omnis vsus est seruitus: & quod omnis seruitus est ius vtendi: forte tamen non inuenitur, quod omne ius vtendi est seruitus: & si hoc inueniretur, diceretur quod ius vtendi acciperetur magis stricte, & non communiter pro omni iure vtendi qualitercunque: nec esset hoc inconueniens; quia sicut beatus Augustinus multis exemplis ostendit decim. quint. de Trinitate, idem vocabulum aliquando generaliter, aliquando specialiter seu particulariter accipitur. Dicunt igitur isti, quod licet nullus iure proprio habeat seruitutem: tamen aliquis habet ius vtendi re propria.
units.tr: Again, someone sometimes has the dominion and property of a thing, which nevertheless he cannot use lawfully; as one who has let his own thing to another cannot use the thing itself without being unlawful. Therefore dominion or property of a thing is not the right of using. To the first of these points, these opponents say: although it is found in law that every use is a servitude, and that every servitude is a right of using, it may perhaps not be found that every right of using is a servitude; and if this were found, it would be said that the right of using is taken more strictly, and not generally for every right of using in whatever way; nor would this be inconvenient, because, as blessed Augustine shows by many examples, De Trinitate, book fifteen, the same word is sometimes taken generally and sometimes specially or particularly. These people therefore say that although no one has a servitude by his own right, nevertheless someone has a right of using his own property.

units.la: Non enim omnes, qui propriis rebus vtuntur, rebus illis vtuntur iniuste: nec etiam vtuntur eis semper de gratia alterius maioris, ergo de iure vtuntur eis: cum omnis, qui re vtitur aliqua, aut vtitur eadem iniuste & licite, aut de gratia alterius, aut de iure quod habet iure, sic igitur dominus rei, in qua alius nullum ius habet, cum non vtatur ipsa re iniuste & illicite, nec de gratia alterius, vtitur ipsa de iure quod habet in re, igitur habet in ista re ius vtendi: licet in illa re non habet seruitutem: quia non omne ius vtendi est seruitus: licet e contrario sit. Ad secundum dicunt, quod licet dominium rei non sit ius vtendi reipsa, quandocunque voluerit: saepe tamen habens dominium rei, habet simul cum dominio ius vtendi re, quando sibi placuerit: quandoque tamen retinet dominum, & ius vtendi concedit alteri, vel gratis vel pro pretio: & ita concessorquod dominium rei seu proprietatis non sit ius vtendi, non oportet concedere, quod qui habet dominium rei, non habet ius vtendi eadem re.
units.tr: For not all who use their own things use them unjustly, nor do they always use them by another's greater favour; therefore they use them by right. For every person who uses some thing does so either unjustly and unlawfully, or by another's favour, or by a right that he holds by right. So the owner of a thing in which no one else has any right, since he does not use that thing unjustly and unlawfully, nor by another's favour, uses it by the right he holds in the thing. Therefore he has a right to use that thing, though he does not have a servitude in it, because not every right to use is a servitude, although the converse holds. To the second point they say that although ownership of a thing is not a right to use the thing itself whenever one wishes, yet the person who has ownership of a thing often has, along with ownership, a right to use the thing when it pleases him. Sometimes, however, he keeps ownership and grants the right of use to another, either freely or for a price. And so, while it must be conceded that ownership of a thing, or property, is not a right to use it, it does not follow that the person who has ownership of a thing does not have a right to use that same thing.

units.la: Quinto declarant, quid intelligant per simplices vsuarios. Dicunt ergo, quod vsuarius fictum est ab hoc nomine vsus: ideo sicut hoc nomen vsus duplicyter accipitur, pro vsu iuris, & pro vsu facti: licet etiam aliis modis accipiatur. Ita hoc nomen [illegible, ~5 letters] duplicyter accipi potest. Vno modo, vt conueniat in significatione cum hoc nomine vsus, accipitur pro vsu iuris; vt ille dicatur vsuarius, qui habet vsum iuris, sed ille [illegible, ~4 letters] proprietarius, qui habet proprietatem rei, & tunc simplex vsuarius vocatur ille, qui habet [illegible, ~3 letters] vel saltem qui nullum ius habet praeter vsum iuris, & isto modo dicunt isti impugnatores, quod Fratres Minores sunt simplices vsuarii: quia neque isto modo sunt vsuarii, cum vsum, de quo est sermo in scientiis legalibus, & nunquam Theologia, non habeant. Aliter potest accipi hoc nomen vsuarius, vt in significatione conueniat cum hoc nomine vsus, secundum quod accipitur pro vsu facti: & sic dicitur vsuarius, qui habet vsum facti rei. Simplex autem vsuarius dicitur ille, qui habet vel habere potest vsum facti rei per carentiam omnis iuris, quo pro re vel vsu facti rei valet in iudicio vel nomine proprio vel nomine collegii litigare, & isto modo, dicunt isti, quod Fratres Minores sunt simplices vsuarii.
units.tr: Fifthly, they explain what they mean by simple usuaries. They say, then, that usuary is derived from the word use. Just as the word use is taken in two senses, for a right of use and for the actual use of a thing (though it is also taken in other ways), so this word usuary can be taken in two ways. In one way, so as to agree in meaning with the word use, it is taken for one who holds a right of use; thus he is called a usuary who has the right of use, but he who has the property of a thing is called a proprietor. In that case, a simple usuary is one who has the right of use alone, or at least has no right except the right of use. In this sense, these opponents say that the Friars Minor are simple usuaries, since in this sense they are not usuaries at all, because they do not have the use spoken of in the legal sciences, and never in theology. The word usuary can also be taken in another way, so as to agree in meaning with the word use as it is taken for the actual use of a thing; in this sense he is called a usuary who has the actual use of a thing. A simple usuary is then one who has, or can have, the actual use of a thing without any right by which he may sue in court, either in his own name or in the name of a corporate body, for the thing or its use. In this sense, they say, the Friars Minor are simple usuaries.

units.la: Sexto explanant, quae sunt res vsu consumptibiles; & quae non sunt vsu consumptibiles. Dicentes, quod res vsu consumptibiles sunt illae, quae ipso vsu, id est actu vtendi vel penitus consumuntur, quantum ad vtentem: vel vt communiter deteriorantur, & tandem consumuntur, huiusmodi sunt cibus & potus, medicinae, vnguenta, pecuniae, vestimenta, & similia. Pecunia enim quamuis quando de ea res emitur, quantum ad suam substantiam, minime consumatur, imo etiam nec deterioratur: tamen quantum ad em entem consumitur, hoc est totaliter cessat esse sua, & si in sua consumeretur substantia. Vestes etiam licet vsu facti primo nullatenus consumantur: tamen vt communiter deteriorari incipiunt; & tandem consumuntur. Aliae autem res, quibus vt contingit, vocantur res non consumptibiles vsu: sicut domus, quae ex inhabitatione non deteriatur, nisi forte per accidens, & aliae consimiles dicuntur non consumptibiles vsu. Et quia posset aliquis dicere, quod ille impugnatus accipit res vsu consumptibiles magis stricte, ideo secundum ipsum pecuniae & vestimenta non debent inter res vsu consumptibiles computari, ac de vestibus & pecuniis apparenter contra ipsum essent exclusae, ideo ostendunt impugnatores, quod ille impugnatus pecuniam atque vestes inter res vsu consumptibiles reputat computandas: & de vestimentis quidem exprimit manifeste. Nam in ista constitutione vir reprobus dicit in haec verba: Constat quod vestimenta quotidiana inter res vsu consumptibiles computantur. De pecunia etiam hoc idem insinuat, in responsione ad secundam obiectionem, sicut patebit ibidem. Vestes ergo & pecuniae etiam secundum istum impugnatum, sunt inter res vsu consumptibiles computandae.
units.tr: Sixthly, they explain which things are consumed by use and which are not. They say that things consumed by use are those which are wholly consumed by the very use, that is, by the act of using, so far as the user is concerned, or which commonly deteriorate and are at last consumed. Such are food and drink, medicines, ointments, money, clothing and the like. For although money, when a thing is bought with it, is not consumed in its own substance, nor even deteriorates, yet so far as the owner is concerned it is consumed, that is, it wholly ceases to be his, even if its own substance were not consumed. Clothes too, though by actual use they are at first in no way consumed, yet commonly begin to deteriorate and are at last consumed. Other things, which are of a different kind, are called things not consumed by use: such as a house, which does not deteriorate from being lived in, unless perhaps by accident, and other similar things are said not to be consumed by use. Since someone might say that the opponent takes things consumed by use in a narrower sense, so that according to him money and clothing ought not to be counted among things consumed by use, and so clothes and money would apparently be excluded by him, the opponents show that the opponent they attack does count money and clothes among things consumed by use. Of clothes he expresses this plainly. For in that constitution the reprobate man says in these words: It is agreed that everyday clothing is counted among things consumed by use. He also hints at the same about money in his reply to the second objection, as will be clear there. Therefore, even according to this opponent, clothes and money are to be counted among things consumed by use.

units.la: Septimo isti impugnatores, quid per dominium intelligi debeat, manifestant. Dicentes, quod huiusmodi nomina dominium, dominus, dominator, dominari, & huiusmodi, a diversis facultatibus aequivoce & variis modis accipiuntur. Aliter enim accipiuntur in philosophia morali, aliter in philosophia naturali, & aliter in modo loquendi vulgari, & aliter in scientia legali, & ideo cum secundum beatum Augustinum Theologia quodammodo omnes scientias apprehendat, talia nomina in diversis locis scripturae diuinae accipiuntur aequivoce. Hoc itaque nomen dominium saepe in philosophia morali accipitur pro potestate, qua quis libere potest in actus contrarios, & sic dicunt, quod homo est dominus; & habet dominium actuum suorum: bruta autem non habent dominium actuum suorum. Sic etiam accipitur dominari secundum vnam expositionem Genes. quart. cum dicit Dominus ad Cain: Sub te erit appetitus tuus, & tu dominaberis illum. Aliter accipiuntur talia vocabula pro habitu virtuali, quo quis secundum rationem rectam regit passiones suas, & sic dominari accipitur Prou. sext. cum dicitur: Melior est patiens viro forti: & qui dominatur animo suo, expugnatore vrbium. Aliter accipiuntur talia vocabula pro violento & vsurpato regimine super aliquos, quitah regimini non possunt vel non audent resistere, & tale dominium Petrus in epistola sua prima capit. quinto, senioribus interdicit dicens: Pascite qui est in vobis gregem Domini, prouidentes non coacte, sed spontanee secundum Deum; neque turpis lucri gratia, sed voluntarie, neque vt dominantes in clero, sed forma facti gregis ex animo. Sic etiam quandoque vulgariter dicitur, quod mulier dominatur viro suo, & seruus domino, & socius socio. Aliter accipiuntur huiusmodi vocabula pro potestate rem aliquam debito modo regendi, & sic nonnunquam dicitur puer dominari equo domini sui. Aliter accipiuntur aliqua talia vocabula in philosophia naturali pro potestate testate rem aliam corrumpendi, & sic dicitur, quod in omni mixto est aliquod elementum prædominans, tamen dicunt, quod non recolunt se legisse, quod hoc nomen dominus in tali significatione inueniatur.
units.tr: Seventhly, these opponents set out what ought to be understood by dominion. They say that such words as dominion, lord, ruler, to rule and the like are taken equivocally and in various ways from different disciplines. For they are taken one way in moral philosophy, another in natural philosophy, another in ordinary speech, and another in legal science. And so, since according to blessed Augustine theology in some way embraces all the sciences, such words are taken equivocally in various places of divine Scripture. Thus the word dominion is often taken in moral philosophy for the power by which someone can freely act in opposite ways; and so they say that man is lord and has dominion over his actions, whereas brute beasts do not have dominion over their actions.
