So too to rule is taken, according to one explanation, in Genesis 4, where the Lord says to Cain: Your desire shall be subject to you, and you shall rule over it. Other such words are taken for a virtual habit by which someone governs his passions according to right reason; and in this sense to rule is taken in Proverbs 16 where it is said: Better is the patient man than the strong, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes cities. Other such words are taken for a violent and usurped rule over certain people who cannot or dare not resist that rule; and Peter, in his first epistle, chapter 5, forbids such dominion to the elders, saying: Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight not by constraint but willingly, according to God; not for filthy lucre but with a ready mind; nor as lording it over the clergy, but being examples to the flock from the heart. So too it is sometimes said in ordinary speech that a wife rules her husband, a servant his master, and one partner his partner. Other such words are taken for the power of governing some thing in the proper way, and so it is sometimes said that a boy rules his master's horse. Other such words are taken in natural philosophy for the power of corrupting another thing; and so it is said that in every mixed body some element predominates. Yet they say that they do not recall having read that the word lord is found in this sense.

units.la: Aliter accipiuntur talia vocabula in scientia legali: scilicet pro potestate quadam speciali vendicandi rem temporalem aliquam, & defendendi, ac tenendi, & disponendi. Et dicunt potestate quadam speciali: quia licet aliqua potestas vendicandi rem temporalem, &c. Dominium appelletur in iure, non tamen omnis talis potestas vendicandi rem, &c. dominium nominatur. Qui enim domum conduxit, habet potestatem vendicandi domum, si expellatur illicite: & etiam defendendi, si aliquis eum domo spoliare tentauerit, habet etiam potestatem inhabitandi domum, & de domo aliqualiter disponendi: nec tamen propter hoc dominium habere dignoscitur. Non igitur omnis potestas vendicandi rem temporalem, &c. dominium nuncupatur, & tamen constat quod dominium est potestas vendicandi rem temporalem, &c. Oportet igitur diffinitionem propriam seu descriptionem domini, de quo in iure sæpe fit mentio, indagare. Dicunt autem isti impugnatores, quod diffinitionem propriam dominii non legerunt in aliqua scriptura autentica: & ideo volentes diffinitionem dominii assignare de dominio secundum quod accipitur in iure, distinguunt: Dicentes, quod dominiorum rerum temporalium, quoddam est dominium diuinum, de quo ad præsens non intendunt: aliud est dominium humanum; & illud est duplex. Quoddam enim competit hominibus in statu innocentiæ ex iure naturali vel diuino, de quo dicitur primis parentibus Genes. 1. Dominamini piscibus maris, & volatilibus cœli, & universis animantibus, quæ mouentur super terram. Aliud est, quod competit hominibus ex iure positiuo, vel ex institutione humana, & de isto dominio in iure ciuili & canonico sæpe fit mentio. Et dominium sic acceptum dupliciter accipi potest, communiter siue large, & specialiter siue stricte. Dominium communiter siue large isti impugnatores sic diffiniunt: Dominium est potestas humana principalis vendicandi & defendendi in humano iudicio rem aliquam temporalem. Et potestas humana separat hoc dominium à diuino dominio Principalis separat hoc dominium ab usu nudo, & usufructu, & ab omni alio iure, quod aliquis habet à dominio principali; & etiam à potestate procuratoris, qui habet potestatem rem aliquam nomine alterius vendicandi. Unde licet habens usum nudum, & usumfructum habeat potestatem vendicandi rem, & etiam defendendi illam: tamen potestatem habuit ab alio, qui sibi usum vel usumfructum concessit, iure primo sibi retento, absque acquisitione noui iuris. Sic etiam licet creditor habeat potestatem vendicandi rem impignoratam: imo etiam & nonnunquam hanc potestatem vendicandi rem & dominium transferendi: non tamen habet eiusdem rei dominium, quia illam habuit ab alio, qui iure primo retento, ius aliud minime acquisiuit. Hæc particula in humano iudicio separat hoc dominium à dominio, quod competit homini ex iure naturali, vel ex iure diuino primario.
units.tr: Other such words are taken in legal science, namely for a certain special power of claiming a temporal thing, of defending it, of holding it and of disposing of it. They say a certain special power, because although some power of claiming a temporal thing and so on is called dominion in law, not every such power of claiming a thing and so on is called dominion. For one who has hired a house has the power of claiming the house if he is unlawfully expelled, and also of defending it if someone tries to strip him of the house; he also has the power of living in the house and of disposing of it in some way; yet he is not on that account recognised as having dominion. Therefore not every power of claiming a temporal thing and so on is called dominion, and yet it is agreed that dominion is a power of claiming a temporal thing and so on. It is necessary, then, to investigate the proper definition or description of lordship, of which frequent mention is made in law. These opponents say that they have not read a proper definition of dominion in any authentic writing. Therefore, wishing to assign a definition of dominion as it is taken in law, they make distinctions. They say that of the dominions over temporal things, one is divine dominion, which they do not intend to discuss at present; the other is human dominion, and this is twofold. For one belongs to men in the state of innocence by natural or divine right, of which it is said to the first parents in Genesis 1: Have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the heavens, and over every living thing that moves upon the earth. The other belongs to men by positive right, or by human institution, and of this dominion there is frequent mention in civil and canon law. Dominion so understood can be taken in two ways: commonly or broadly, and specially or strictly. These opponents define dominion in the common or broad sense thus: Dominion is a principal human power of claiming and defending a temporal thing before a human judgment. The words human power separate this dominion from divine dominion. The word principal separates this dominion from bare use and usufruct, and from every other right that someone has from a principal owner, and also from the power of a procurator, who has power to claim some thing in another's name. Hence, although one who has bare use and usufruct has the power of claiming the thing and also of defending it, he had that power from another who granted him use or usufruct, the first owner retaining his right, without acquiring any new right. So too, although a creditor has the power of claiming a pledged thing, and indeed sometimes also the power of claiming it and transferring its dominion, he does not have dominion of that same thing, because he had it from another, who retained the first right and acquired no other right. The phrase before a human judgment separates this dominion from the dominion that belongs to a man by natural right or by primary divine right.

units.la: Separat etiam hoc dominium ab omni gratia & licentia vtendi re aliqua: licet etiam stricte accepto vocabulo gratiæ & licentiæ excludantur, cum dicitur, vendicandi, sic communiter accepto dominio, dicunt isti impugnatores, quod prælati & viri ecclesiastici habent dominium rerum ecclesiasticarum. Quod etiam sacris canonibus declarare nituntur. Nam beatus Gregorius, vt recitatur duodec. quæstion. secund. capit. Ecclesiasticis, ait: Quia igitur Theodorum virum eloquentissimum, consiliarium nostrum, mancipiorum cognoscimus ministerio destitutum: ideo puerum nomine Acefimum natione Siculum iuri dominioque suo dari tradique præcipimus, quem quoniam ex nostra auctoritate iam possidet, huius necesse fuit pro futuri testimonio temporis scripti ac robore largitatis auctoritate fulciri, quatenus Domino protegente secure eum semper sine ullius retractationis suspitione, vt dominus, valeat possidere. Ex his verbis apparet, quod ille Theodorus ius habuerit & dominium serui, quem possedit vt dominus: & eadem ratione clerici aliarum rerum ecclesiasticarum habent dominium. Hoc etiam idem Gregorius, prout legitur decim. sext. quæstion. quart. capitulo penultimo, insinuare videtur, qui scribens Petro Subdiacono ait: Volumus accedente te ad Panormitanam ciuitatem quæstionem ipsam tali ratione discutere, dominio rei apud possessorem, sicut hactenus possessum est, videlicet permanente. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod ecclesia rei, de qua agebatur, dominium possidebat.
units.tr: This dominion is also separated from every grace and permission to use any thing. Even if the words grace and permission are taken strictly and excluded, the term vendicandi (of claiming) remains, and in this sense dominion is commonly understood. These opponents say that prelates and churchmen have dominion over ecclesiastical goods, and they try to prove this from the sacred canons. For blessed Gregory, as cited in 12 quaest. 2, c. Ecclesiasticis, says: Since we know that Theodore, a most eloquent man and our counsellor, lacks the service of slaves, we therefore order that the boy named Acefimus, a Sicilian by birth, be given and handed over to his right and dominion. Since he already possesses him by our authority, it was necessary for this to be confirmed for the testimony and strength of future time by the authority of a written gift, so that, with the Lord protecting, he may possess him securely and always as owner, without any suspicion of challenge. From these words it appears that Theodore had the right and dominion over the slave whom he possessed as owner, and by the same reasoning clerics have dominion over other ecclesiastical goods. Gregory also seems to suggest this in 16 quaest. 4, the penultimate chapter, where, writing to the subdeacon Peter, he says: We wish, when you come to the city of Palermo, to examine the question itself in such a way that the dominion of the thing remains with the possessor, as it has been possessed until now. From these words it is understood that the Church held the dominion of the thing in question.

units.la: Amplius dicunt isti impugnatores, quod qui habet proprietatem rei, habet dominium rei. Prælati autem & viri ecclesiastici habent proprietatem rerum ecclesiasticarum, teste beato Gregorio, qui, vt recitatur 12. quæstion. cap. vltim. quandam domum, hortum & hospitia cuidam Religiosæ tradi præcepit iure proprietatis possidenda. Igitur illa Religiosa res temporales iure proprietatis possidere valebat. Episcopi etiam proprias ecclesias habere noscuntur, sicut patet 3. quæst. 1. cap. 1. & qu. 2. ca. Audiuimus, & in multis locis habetur, quod episcopi & monachi res proprias habent, ergo prælati & viri ecclesiastici habent dominium rerum ecclesiasticarum. Hoc etiam in decretali Nicolai Tertii Exiit qui seminat, habetur expresse, quod resonanes, quibus Fratres Minores vtuntur, in dominium & proprietatem ecclesiæ Romanæ receperunt. Hoc etiam ratione probatur. Nam constat per sacros canones, quod prælati & viri ecclesiastici ius habent in personalibus rebus, sed discurrendo per singula iura, quibus temporalia possidentur, in multis rebus nullum ius habent præter dominium, licet enim in aliquibus rebus habeant usumfructum, & in aliquibus usum: sicut ex verbis Augustini, quæ ponuntur 17. quæstion. vltima, cap. vltim. elici potest: tamen tale ius in multis aliis, quæ ab omni iure laicorum alienatæ noscuntur, nullatenus habent. Videtur igitur, quod in eis habent dominium. minium aliquale. Dicunt igitur isti impugnatores, quod multarum rerum habent prælati ecclesiæ & ecclesiastici viri dominium. Unde illarum rerum ecclesiasticarum, quæ libere absque conditione à fidelibus sunt donatæ ecclesiæ, Ecclesia in eis aliquo modo habet dominium: quia licet in talibus rebus non habeat ecclesia ita plenam potestatem dispensandi, sicut laici habent in suis: tamen ecclesiastici habent ita plenam potestatem nomine ecclesiæ in iudicio vendicandi; nec ipsi debent ecclesia absque causa priuari, sicut nec laici rebus suis: licet aliquæ personæ ecclesiasticorum valeant facilius rebus deputatis eis, ex causa priuari, & ita cum habeant hanc potestatem vendicandi & defendendi in iudicio res ecclesiæ: & talis potestas ad nullum spectat principalius quam ad episcopos: relinquitur quod habent aliquo modo dominium.
units.tr: Again, these opponents say that whoever has the ownership of a thing has its dominion. Prelates and churchmen have the ownership of ecclesiastical goods, as witnessed by blessed Gregory, who, as cited in 12 quaest., last chapter, ordered a certain house, garden and lodgings to be handed over to a certain religious woman, to be possessed by right of ownership. Therefore that religious woman could possess temporal goods by right of ownership. Bishops are also known to have their own churches, as is clear from 3 quaest. 1, c. 1, and quaest. 2, c. Audivimus, and in many places it is stated that bishops and monks have their own goods. Therefore prelates and churchmen have dominion over ecclesiastical goods. This is also expressly stated in the decretal of Nicholas III, Exiit qui seminat, that the revenues which the Friars Minor use were received into the dominion and ownership of the Roman Church. This is also proved by reason. For it is established by the sacred canons that prelates and churchmen have a right over personal goods, but when we run through the individual laws by which temporal goods are held, we find that in many things they have no right except dominion. For although in some things they have usufruct, and in some use, as can be drawn from the words of Augustine cited in 17 quaest. last, last chapter, yet they have no such right in many other things which are known to be wholly alienated from all lay right. It seems therefore that in these they have dominion. These opponents therefore say that prelates of the Church and churchmen have dominion over many goods. Hence, over those ecclesiastical goods which are given freely and without condition to the Church by the faithful, the Church in some way holds dominion. For although the Church does not have as full a power of disposing of such goods as laymen have over theirs, yet churchmen have, in the name of the Church, so full a power of claiming in court, and they themselves ought not to be deprived of the Church's goods without cause, any more than laymen of their own. Although some individual churchmen may more easily be deprived, for cause, of goods assigned to them, they nevertheless have this power of claiming and defending the Church's goods in court, and such power belongs most principally to bishops. It follows that they have dominion in some way.

units.la: Aliter accipitur humanum dominium magis stricte, vt isti impugnatores affirmant, & dominium stricte sumptum tali modo diffiniunt. Dominium est potestas humana principalis rem temporalem in iudicio vendicandi, & omni modo, qui non est à iure naturali prohibitus, pertractandi. Et per istam vltimam particulam excluditur ius, quod clerici in rebus temporalibus noscuntur habere: quia licet habeant potestatem principalem vendicandi, &c. non tamen possunt res ecclesiasticas ad suum libitum pertractare. Multisque modis possunt laici de suis temporalibus ordinare, qui clericis sunt penitus interdicti.
units.tr: These opponents affirm that human dominion is taken more strictly, and they define dominion, taken strictly, in this way: Dominion is the principal human power of claiming a temporal thing in court and of handling it in any way not prohibited by natural law. By this last clause, the right which clerics are known to have over temporal goods is excluded, because although they have the principal power of claiming, etc., yet they cannot handle ecclesiastical goods at their pleasure. Laymen can dispose of their temporal goods in many ways which are wholly forbidden to clerics.

units.la: Ista est diffinitio dominii stricte sumpti secundum istos: & quanto aliquo magis ab ista diffinitione recedit, tanto magis recedit à dominii plenitudine. Unde quanto aliqui magis vel minus artantur ad certos modos dispensandi & tractandi res suas: tanto magis vel minus dominium in rebus constat eos habere, propter quod idem homo sæpe pinguius dominium habet in quibusdam rebus suis: & in aliis habet minus pingue: sicut nonnulli pinguius dominium habent in rebus mobilibus, quas libere absque calumnia possunt dare, vendere, & legare: & in rebus suis immobilibus habent minus dominium, quia res illas non possunt vendere, dare, vel legare, cum hæredes suos de rebus immobilibus exhæredare non valeant. Forte autem ex ordinatione humana est rationabiliter institutum, quod tale dominium plenum nullus habeat in re sua quacunque; quin videlicet ex causa aliqui modi tractandi rem suam sibi valeant interdici: vt communiter cum dominium præcipue rerum mobilium (secundum quod frequentius & forte semper accipitur in iure ciuili, & vt communius accipitur in iure canonico) potestatem vendendi, dandi, & legandi includit. De potestate vendendi testatur Tharasius Constantinopolitanus episcopus, qui (vt habetur 1. quæst. 1. c. eos) ait: Omnis enim dominus, quod habet, si vult, vendit, siue seruum, siue aliud eorum quæ possidet. De potestate etiam legandi satis aperte canones Apostolorum insinuant, in quibus (vt habetur 12. quæstio. 1. cap. Sint manifeste) sic dicitur: Sint manifeste res proprie episcopi: si tamen habet res proprias & manifeste dominicas, vt potestatem habeat de propriis rebus moriens, sicut voluerit, & quibus voluerit derelinquere. De potestate etiam dandi, iura ciuilia & canonica manifeste loquuntur. Tale autem dominium non habent viri ecclesiastici in quibuscunque temporalibus, quæ Deo à fidelibus sunt oblata: quia omnes clerici ad certos modos dispensandi res ecclesiasticas sunt astricti in tantum, quod aliter dispensando vel tractando peccant mortaliter, nisi forte per ignorantiam vel modum alium valeant excusari, si etiam res ecclesiæ aliter dederint, legauerint vel alienauerint quocunque modo, quam est eis concessum, res illæ poterunt per iudicem reuocari. Et de tali dominio sæpe loquuntur iura canonica, quæ affirmant, quod clerici rerum ecclesiasticarum nequaquam sunt domini, sed procuratores vel dispensatores, secundum quod per plurimos sacros canones posset copiose probari: sed alias apparebit.
units.tr: This is the definition of dominion taken strictly, according to these men, and the further one departs from this definition, the further one departs from the fullness of dominion. Hence, the more or less one is bound to certain ways of disposing of and handling one's goods, the more or less dominion over the things one is found to have. For this reason the same man often has fuller dominion over some of his goods and less full dominion over others. Some have fuller dominion over movable goods, which they can freely give, sell and bequeath without challenge, and less dominion over their immovable goods, because they cannot sell, give or bequeath those, nor can they disinherit their heirs from immovable goods. Perhaps it has been reasonably established by human ordinance that no one has such full dominion over any of his goods, namely that for cause certain modes of handling one's own goods may be forbidden to him; since dominion, especially over movable goods (as it is most often, and perhaps always, understood in civil law, and more commonly in canon law), includes the power of selling, giving and bequeathing. Concerning the power of selling, Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople, bears witness, who (as found in 1 quaest. 1, c. Eos) says: Every owner, if he wishes, sells whatever he has, whether a slave or any other of the things he possesses. Concerning the power of bequeathing, the Canons of the Apostles indicate fairly clearly, where (as found in 12 quaest. 1, c. Sint manifeste) it is said: Let the goods of the bishop be clearly his own; if he has goods that are his own and clearly his by ownership, he may have the power, when dying, to leave his own goods as he wishes and to whom he wishes. Concerning the power of giving, civil and canon law speak plainly. Churchmen, however, do not have such dominion over any temporal goods which have been offered to God by the faithful, because all clerics are bound to certain fixed ways of disposing of ecclesiastical goods to such an extent that, if they dispose or handle them otherwise, they sin mortally, unless perhaps they can be excused through ignorance or some other way. And if they have given, bequeathed or alienated the Church's goods in any way other than is permitted to them, those goods can be recalled by a judge. Canon law often speaks of such dominion, affirming that clerics are by no means owners of ecclesiastical goods, but agents or stewards. This could be abundantly proved from many sacred canons, but it will appear elsewhere.

units.la: Octauo isti impugnatores ostendant, quid per proprietatem intelligunt. Dicunt enim, quod hæc nomina proprium & proprietas aliter accipiuntur in logica, & aliter in scientia legali; sed qualiter accipiantur in logica, non oportet in hoc opusculo pertractare. In legalibus autem scientiis, sc. in iure ciuili, & in iure canonico, sæpius proprietas accipitur pro dominio rei, vt idem sit proprietas & dominium: quamuis etiam forte aliter nonnunquam accipiatur, & ideo sicut dominium multipliciter accipitur; ita & proprietas dupliciter iuxta duos vltimos modos dominii.
units.tr: Eighthly, these opponents show what they understand by ownership. For they say that the words proprium and proprietas are understood in one way in logic and in another in legal science. But how they are understood in logic need not be treated in this little work. In the legal sciences, however, namely in civil and canon law, proprietas is often taken to mean the dominion of a thing, so that ownership and dominion are the same; although perhaps it is sometimes taken otherwise. Therefore, just as dominion is understood in many ways, so ownership is understood in two ways, according to the two last senses of dominion.

units.la: Nono dicunt, talia vocabula, meum, tuum, suum, habere in significatione conuenientiam cum eisdem, & in diuersis locis accipiuntur æquiuoce. Aliquando enim important dominium, & proprietatem etiam, prout ille impugnatus affirmat: & ideo hoc per exempla probare videtur superfluum. Aliter illa vocabula important licitam potestatem vtendi re aliqua, vel vsum rei ad hospitium vel deputationem alicuius rei ad vsum alicuius, sic dicitur vulgariter, quod inuitatus habet hospitium, & sæpe dicit, hoc est meum hospitium: cum tamen non habet hospitii proprietatem, & de isto modo accipiendi huiusmodi vocabula inferius, cum agetur de dominio & regno Christi, multa ponentur exempla, ideo ad præsens pertranseo. Aliis etiam modis, de quibus dicetur infetius, accipi possunt, & accipiuntur ista vocabula. Istas distinctiones ponunt isti impugnatores: quia, vt dicunt, per eas patebit, tam impugnati quam fratris Michaelis impugnantis intentio: & qualiter sub multiplicitate vocum iste impugnatus errores conatur deducere, qualiterque impugnati rationes facile improbantur: & impugnantis rationes insolubiles euidenter apparent. Dicunt etiam, quod aliqua prædictorum vocabulorum aliter accipi possunt: sed ista ad præsens eis sufficiunt.
units.tr: Ninthly, they say that such words as meum, tuum, suum have a correspondence of meaning with one another, and that they are taken equivocally in different places. For sometimes they signify ownership and property as well, as that opponent maintains; and so it seems superfluous to prove this by examples. Otherwise these words signify a lawful power of using some thing, or the use of a thing for lodging, or the assignment of some thing to the use of someone. Thus it is commonly said that the guest has his lodging, and often one says, "This is my lodging," although he does not have ownership of the lodging. Many examples of this way of taking such words will be set out below, when the lordship and kingdom of Christ are treated, so I pass over it for now. These words can also be taken in other ways, which will be described further on. Those opponents set out these distinctions, because, as they say, through them the intention both of the one opposed and of Brother Michael, the opponent, will become plain; and how this opponent tries to draw out his errors under a multiplicity of words, and how the arguments of the one opposed are easily refuted, while the arguments of the opponent are plainly seen to be insoluble. They also say that some of the aforesaid words can be taken in other ways, but for the present these suffice for them.

units.la: His visis dicunt isti impugnatores, quod ex præmissis euidenter concluditur, quod in verbis dictis, quæ impugnat, duo errores continentur aperte: quorum primus est, quod vsus facti a proprieproprietate rei seu dominio in rebus vsu consumptibilibus haberi non potest. Secundus est, quod in talibus rebus vsu consumptibilibus ius vtendi separatum a proprietate rei seu dominio haberi non potest. Verum quia haec duo, quae isti impugnatores putant erronea, iste impugnatus in ratione ad obiectionem superius recitatam asserit & confirmat: ideo impugnationes ipsorum vsque ad partem sequentem, in qua ponitur istius impugnati ratio, disterunt. Tertium autem, quod in verbis praemissis habetur, videlicet quod in quibusdam rebus vsu consumptibilibus non potest haberi vsus iuris a proprietate seu dominio separatus. Isti impugnatores concedunt proprie sumpto vsu iuris: quia dicunt, quod illa negatiua habet vnam causam veritatis veram, quae est ista: In talibus rebus vsu consumptibilibus non potest haberi vsus iuris: quia vsus iuris est ius vtendi rebus alienis, salua rerum substantia: & ideo proprie vsus iuris in multis rebus consumptibilibus vsu, non potest constitui vel haberi: & per consequens vsus iuris separatus a dominio seu proprietate non potest in talibus rebus haberi.
units.tr: Having seen these things, those opponents say that from what has been premised it is plainly concluded that two errors are openly contained in the words that he attacks. The first is that use of a fact cannot be had apart from the property of a thing, or ownership, in things consumed by use. The second is that in such things consumed by use, a right of using separated from the property of the thing or from ownership cannot be had. But because the author opposed asserts and confirms these two points, which those opponents consider erroneous, in his reply to the objection recited above, their refutations are deferred up to the following part, in which the reasoning of the same author is set out. The third point, which is found in the premises, namely that in certain things consumed by use a use of right separated from property or ownership cannot be had, those opponents grant in the proper sense of a use of right. For they say that this negative proposition has one true cause of its truth, which is this: in such things consumed by use, a use of right cannot be had, because a use of right is a right of using another's things, the substance of the things being preserved; and therefore, properly speaking, a use of right cannot be constituted or had in many things consumed by use, and consequently a use of right separated from ownership or property cannot be had in such things.

units.la: Ex quo dicunt, quod istam propositionem Fratres Minores in rebus, quae vsu consumuntur, non sunt censendi simplices vsuarii: non intendunt in omni sensu negare, nec eius oppositum in omni sensu concedere: quia, sicut dictum est, si hoc nomen vsuarii conueniat in significatione cum hoc nomine vsus, prout sumitur pro vsu iuris, sic concedunt quod Fratres Minores nec rebus, quae consumuntur vsu, sunt simplices vsuarii, quia nec in illis sunt vsuarii, eo quod in nullis rebus habent vsum iuris. Si autem nomen vsuarii conueniat in significatione cum hoc nomine vsus, vt accipitur pro vsu facti: sic concedunt, quod Fratres Minores sunt simplices vsuarii, hoc est, vtuntur rebus nullum habentes ius, per quod valeant in iudicio litigare.
units.tr: From this they say that the proposition that the Friars Minor are not to be counted as simple users in things that are consumed by use, they do not intend to deny in every sense, nor to grant its opposite in every sense. For, as has been said, if the word "user" agrees in meaning with the word "use" as it is taken for a use of right, then they grant that the Friars Minor are not simple users even of things consumed by use, because they are not users of them either, since they have no use of right in any things. But if the word "user" agrees in meaning with the word "use" as it is taken for a use of fact, then they grant that the Friars Minor are simple users, that is, they use things while holding no right by which they could litigate in court.

units.la: Postea videndum est de littera (Vsus iuris vel facti.) Ex hoc habetur aperte, quod etiam ille impugnatus distinguit inter vsum iuris & vsum facti. Explanet igitur, quis est vsus facti, quis non sit vsus iuris: & non poterit nisi dicendo, quod actus vtendi, sicut actus comedendi, bibendi, inhabitandi, equitandi, & huiusmodi sunt vsus facti. (Nec ius vtendi.) Hic deberet ostendere, quid est ius vtendi: quod ponitur in diffinitione vsus iuris. (Suum esse dicebat.) Hic hoc vocabulum suum accipitur secundum quod importat dominium seu proprietatem rei, licet alio modo accipi posset. (Sancti exponunt sic suum, id est proprium) verum est quod in illo loco ita exponunt: in quibusdam autem aliis locis aliter exponunt hoc vocabulum suum. (Absque proprietate & dominio) verum est de dominio, quod potestatem dandi, vendendi, & ligandi includit. Sequitur
units.tr: Next we must consider the phrase "use of right or of fact." From this it is plainly evident that the author opposed also distinguishes between use of right and use of fact. Let him therefore explain what use of fact is and what is not use of right; and he will be able to do so only by saying that acts of using, such as acts of eating, drinking, dwelling, riding, and such like, are uses of fact. "Nor a right of using": here he ought to show what the right of using is, which is set forth in the definition of use of right. "He used to say it was his own": here the word "his own" is taken insofar as it implies the ownership or property of the thing, although it could be taken in another way. "The saints explain 'his own' thus, that is, proper": it is true that in that passage they so explain it; in certain other passages, however, they explain this word "his own" differently. "Without property and ownership": it is true of ownership, which includes the power of giving, selling and binding. Follows...

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: Chapter III.

units.la: Dicimus enim & verum est, quod dicta constitutio docet & asserit, quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus nec ius vtendi, nec ipsum vti potest constitui vel haberi, licet nec ius vtendi, nec ipsum vti in rebus illis haberi possit vel constitui ipsis, tamen potest, sicut dicit dicta constitutio, quis abuti. Abuti autem, secundum eandem constitutionem (dum tractat de rebus vsu consumptibilibus) sumitur pro consumptione rei, & quod ius vtendi in talibus rebus non possit constitui, probat dicta constitutio ex diffinitione vsus, qui talis est: Vsus est ius vtendi alienis rebus salua rerum substantia, id est ius percipiendi fructus seu vtilitatem aliam in totum vel pro parte suo nomine, qui possunt ex re, in qua vsus constituitur, prouenire. Constat autem quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus, quamdiu earum substantia salua & integra permanet, nulla potest vtilitas prouenire, vt pote in pane & in vino, ex quibus nullus fructus vel vtilitas potest colligi seu haberi, substantia salua rei. Quare euidenter relinquitur, quod in rebus talibus vsu consumptibilibus ius vtendi separatum a proprietate seu dominio nequeat constitui seu haberi, & per hoc beatus Iohannes Chrysostomus rationem reddit, quare pecunia mutuata, vsura, sicut merces pro domo vel re alia vsu non consumptibili locata licite recipi nequaquam possit: dicens, quod in re vsu non consumptibili, vt in domo vel agro, habens ista non solum habet proprietatem seu dominium, sed ex illis salua rei substantia ac proprietate rei & dominio, fructum seu vtilitatem aliam percipit, vt patet in domo, in qua habitat: & sicut ex ea commodum inhabitationis habet sibi dominum saluo dominio remanente, sic ex agro quoque fructus recipit agri salua rei substantia, & dominio remanente. Et ideo quia locans fructus rei seu vtilitatem aliam prouenientem ex ea, retento sibi dominio, conductori concedit: nec illa sibi fructus seu vtilitatem domus vel agri finita locatione repetit, non est mirum si pro his precium recipere possit, mutuans autem pecuniam in eum, cui mutuat, pecunia transfert dominium, non fructum aliquem, nec vtilitatem aliam, qua ex ea salua rei substantia valeat peruenire: & tantundem ab eo cui mutuauit postea repetit, quare vltra illud, quod mutuauit, a recipiente mutuum licite recipere nequit, vt legitur octuagesimo octau. distinctione. cap. Eiiciens. Quod autem ipsum vti ab aliquo haberi nequeat, dicta constitutio, sequens Augustini sententiam positam in libro Confessionum clare probat: quia quod non est, haberi potest nequaquam, actus autem in rerum natura non est, nec antequam quis vtatur, nec postquam vsus est, nec dum est in actu vtendi, prout latius prosequitur dicta constitutio: quare relinquitur, quod haberi non potest.
units.tr: We say, and it is true, as the said constitution teaches and asserts, that in things consumable by use neither a right of using nor the using itself can be established or held. Yet although neither a right of using nor the using itself can be held or established in those things for them, one can, as the said constitution says, misuse them. Moreover, according to the same constitution (where it treats of things consumable by use), "to misuse" is taken to mean the consumption of the thing. The constitution proves that a right of using cannot be established in such things from the definition of use, which is this: "Use is the right of using another's things with the substance of the things preserved", that is, the right of taking, in whole or in part and in one's own name, the fruits or other advantage which can arise from the thing in which the use is established. It is clear that in things consumable by use, as long as their substance remains safe and whole, no advantage can arise from them, as in bread and wine, from which no fruit or advantage can be gathered or had while the substance of the thing is preserved. Hence it is evidently left that in such things consumable by use, a right of using separate from property or ownership cannot be established or held. By this, blessed John Chrysostom gives the reason why money lent cannot lawfully bring usury, and why the hire of a house or other thing not consumable by use cannot lawfully be received at all. He says that in a thing not consumable by use, such as a house or a field, one who has it not only has property or ownership, but from it, with the substance of the thing and its property and ownership preserved, receives fruit or other advantage. This is plain in a house in which one lives: just as one has the convenience of habitation from it while ownership remains with him, so from a field too he receives its produce, the substance of the field and his ownership remaining. And therefore, because the lessor, retaining ownership, grants the lessee the fruits of the thing or the other advantage arising from it, and after the lease ends does not reclaim from him the fruits or advantage of the house or field, it is no wonder that he may receive a price for them. But one who lends money transfers ownership of the money to the borrower, not any fruit or other advantage which could arise from it while its substance is preserved; and afterwards he reclaims from the one to whom he lent just the same sum. Therefore he cannot lawfully receive anything from the borrower beyond what he lent, as is read in distinction 88, chapter Eiiciens. That the using itself cannot be had by anyone, the said constitution clearly proves, following the opinion of Augustine set down in the book of the Confessions: what is not cannot be had at all; but an act is not in the nature of things, neither before someone uses, nor after use has occurred, nor while it is in the act of using. The constitution pursues this more fully. Therefore it is left that it cannot be had.

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnatus ad praesentem impugnationem nititur respondere. Et diuiditur ista pars in duas partes: quia primo circa illa, quae impugnat, suam explicat intentionem, & eandem probare conatur. Secundo ad illa, quae tangunt impugnationem praedictam, respondetur in parte immediate sequenti, cum dicit: Ad illud autem quod dicit, &c. In prima igitur parte primo tria proponit: quorum primum est, quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus non potest ius vtendi constitui vel haberi. Secundum est, quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus non potest ipsum vti, id est, actus vtendi, constitui vel haberi. Tertium est, quod licet in rebus vsu consumptibilib.non contingat vti: ipsis tamen contingit abuti, hoc est consumere: quia abuti re vsu consumptibili, accipitur pro consumptione rei. Deinde ibi: & quod ius vtendi, &c. pro tertia parte dicitur, quod ius vtendi in rebus vsu consumptibilibus non possit constitui vel haberi. Prima pars accipitur ex diffinitione vsus, qui talis est: Vsus est ius vtendi rebus alienis salua rerum substantia, id est ius percipiendi aliquam vtilitatem salua rei substantia, quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus reperiri non potest: quia salua substantia rerum vsu consumptibilium non potest ex eis vtilitas prouenire. Secundo probat idem per Iohannem Chrysost. qui per hoc reddit rationem, quare pro pecunia mutuata vsuram licite non conuenit accipere. Demum ibi, quod autem ipsum vti, &c. ostendit, quod ipsum vti, id est actus vtendi in rebus vsu consumptibilibus haberi non potest.
units.tr: In this part, the one attacked here strives to answer the present attack. The part is divided into two. First, he explains his own intention concerning the things he is attacked for and tries to prove it. Second, answers are given to the points that touch the aforesaid attack, in the part immediately following, where he says: "But as to what he says, etc." In the first part he first sets out three things. The first is that in things consumable by use a right of using cannot be established or had. The second is that in such things the using itself, that is the act of using, cannot be established or had. The third is that although one cannot use things consumable by use, one can misuse them, that is consume them, since "to misuse" a thing consumable by use is taken to mean its consumption. Then, with the words "and that a right of using", etc., he states the third point: that a right of using cannot be established or had in things consumable by use. The first point is taken from the definition of use, which is this: "Use is the right of using another's things with their substance preserved", that is, the right of taking some advantage while the substance of the thing is preserved. This cannot be found in things consumable by use, because with the substance of such things preserved no advantage can arise from them. Second, he proves the same point through John Chrysostom, who gives the reason why it is not right to take usury for money lent. Last, with the words "but as to the using itself", etc., he shows that the using itself, that is the act of using, cannot be had in things consumable by use.

units.la: Istum processum quo ad quatuor principaliter isti impugnatores satagunt improbare. Primo quo ad hoc quod dicit, quod ius vtendi in rebus vsu consumptibilibus haberi non potest. Secundo quantum ad hoc in persecutione dicit, quod in talibus rebus vsu consumptibilibus ius vtendi separatum a proprietate & dominio haberi non potest. Tertio quo ad hoc quod dicit, quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus actus vtendi haberi non potest. Quarto quo ad hoc dicit, quod rebus consumptibilibus non conuenit vti, sed abuti. Circa primum primo improbant ipsum dictum in se, secundo improbant vtramq; rationem, per quam ipsum dictum ostenditur. Ad euidentiam primi dicunt, quod duo sunt notanda: quorum primum est, quod principalis intentio istius impugnatin hac materia est damnare assertionem Fratrum Minorum, qui dicunt se habere in rebus vsu consumptibilib. simplicem facti vsum absq; omni iure vtendi, quemadmodum in decretali Nicolai III. quae incipit Exiit qui seminat, habetur. In dicta enim decre. Exiit, continetur expresse, quod Fratres Minores in omnib. rebus, quib. vtuntur, habent simplicem facti vsum nihil iuris, quod Fratres Minores dicunt sic debere intelligi: quod videl. rebus consumptibilibus vsu & rebus non consumptibilib. vsu de licentia seu gratia concedentis vtuntur absq; omni iure humano, quo pro se vel vsu rei valeant in iudicio litigare. Ex quo inferunt isti impugnatores, quod cum praesumendum sit, quod iste impugnatus assertione praedictam Fratrum Minorum ad rem & non ad nomen satagit improbare, ipse eodem modo & in eadem significatione vitur huiusmodi terminis, Ius vtendi, vsus facti, simplex facti vsus, & similibus quo modo & in qua significatione vtuntur praedicti Fratres Minores, praesertim cum huiusmodi terminis non vtantur in significatione extranea, sed modum suum loquendi ex auctoritate scripturae accipiant. Si enim iste in alia significatione terminos tales acciperet, quam Fratres Minores, ipsos ad rem nullatenus impugnaret, sed per aequiuocationem & sophistice ipsos velle, apud non intelligentes & simplices diffamare conuinceretur aperte. Quod vero in significatione extranea non vtantur huiusmodi terminis, probant ex hoc quod modum suum loquendi a decretali Exiit in corpore iuris inserta accipiunt. De hoc etiam postea plenius differetur. Secundo dicunt esse notandum, quod ius vtendi accipitur hic communius, quam pro vsu iuris, & ita licet aliquando ius vtendi inueniretur accipi specialiter pro vsu iuris, tamen non ita hic specialiter accipi poterit, sed accipitur magis communiter: quia, vt patet hic ex processu impugnati, ipse accipit ius vtendi, vt ponitur in diffinitione vsus. Vt autem ponitur in diffinitione vsus, accipitur communius, quam pro vsu tantum, ergo vt hic est sermo de iure vtendi, ius vtendi est ius communius quam vsus, cum ponitur in diffinitione vsus tanquam genus.
units.tr: The attackers set out to refute this line of argument chiefly in four respects. First, as to his claim that a right of using cannot be had in things consumable by use. Second, as to his claim in the course of the argument that in such things a right of using separate from property and ownership cannot be had. Third, as to his claim that the act of using cannot be had in things consumable by use. Fourth, as to his claim that it is not fitting to use things consumable by use, but only to misuse them. On the first point they first refute the statement itself, and second they refute both reasons by which it is shown. To make the first point clear, they say two things must be noted. The first is that the chief aim of this writer in this matter is to condemn the assertion of the Friars Minor, who say that in things consumable by use they have a simple factual use without any right of using, as is held in the decretal of Nicholas III that begins Exiit qui seminat. In that decretal Exiit it is expressly stated that the Friars Minor, in all the things they use, have a simple factual use and no right. The Friars Minor say this should be understood to mean that they use things consumable by use, and things not consumable by use, by the licence or favour of the grantor, without any human right by which they could go to law for themselves or for the use of the thing. From this the attackers infer that, since it must be presumed that the one attacked here is striving to refute the Friars Minor's assertion as to the matter and not merely the words, he uses such terms as "right of using", "factual use", "simple factual use", and similar ones in the same way and sense as the Friars Minor do. This is especially so because he does not use these terms in an alien sense, but takes his manner of speaking from the authority of Scripture. For if he took such terms in a different sense from the Friars Minor, he would not really attack them at all, but would be clearly shown to be trying to defame them by equivocation and sophistry before those who do not understand and before the simple. They prove that he does not use these terms in an alien sense from the fact that he takes his manner of speaking from the decretal Exiit, inserted in the body of the law. This will be discussed more fully later. Second, they say it must be noted that "right of using" is taken here more broadly than for the use of a right.

units.la: His visis, dicunt isti impugnatores, quod erroneum est dicere, ius vtendi in rebus vsu consumptibilibus non posse constitui vel haberi: sed probant sic. Habens potestatem & dominium rerum vsu consumptibilium: puta panis & vini, in quibus alius nullum ius habet, potest vti eis: quia potest manducare panem & bibere vinum, manducare autem panem & bibere vinum est vti pane & vino: quod non solum ex scripturis diuinis seu sanctorum, sed etiam ex iure ciuili, & ex dictis istius impugnati colligitur euidenter. Ait enim Apostolus prim. ad Tim. quint. Vtere modice vino, & Iosuae quinto sic legitur: Defecit manna, postquam comederunt de frugibus terrae: nec vsi sunt vltra cibo illo filii Israel. Et Augustinus, prout recitatur distinctione. quadragesim. prim. capitulo quisquis, loquens de cibis & aliis ait: Quisquis rebus praetereuntibus restrictius vtitur, quam sese habent mores eorum, cum quibus viuit: aut intemperans, aut superfluiosus est. Et, sicut adductum est prius, lex ciuilis ait: Qui fundi vsum nudum habet, nihil vlterius habere intelligitur, quam vt eleribus, pomis, floribus, foeno, stramentis, lignis ad vsum quotidianum vtatur, & iste impugnatus, sicut est superius recitatum, in ista constitutione, Quia vir reprobus, ait: Vsus facti sic est vtenti proprius, quod non potest dici alterius, nec communicabilis. Patet enim, quod actus comedendi Petri sic erat sibi proprius, quod non poterat dici aliis communis.
units.tr: Having established this, these opponents say that it is an error to claim that a right of use cannot be constituted or held in consumable goods. They prove it as follows. Someone who has the power and ownership of consumable goods, such as bread and wine, over which no one else has any right, can use them, because he can eat the bread and drink the wine, and to eat bread and drink wine is to use bread and wine. This is shown clearly not only from the divine Scriptures and the Fathers but also from civil law and from the words of this opponent himself. The Apostle says in 1 Tim. 5, Use a little wine, and Joshua 5 reads thus: The manna ceased after they had eaten of the fruits of the land, nor did the children of Israel make use of that food any more. And Augustine, as cited in distinction 41, chapter Quisquis, speaking of foods and other things, says: Whoever uses fleeting things more sparingly than the customs of those with whom he lives require is either intemperate or superstitious. And, as was cited earlier, civil law says: He who has the bare use of an estate is understood to have nothing further than to use the fallen fruit, apples, flowers, hay, straw and wood for daily use. This opponent himself, as was quoted above, in that constitution Quia vir reprobus, says: The use of a fact is so proper to the one who uses it that it cannot be called another's, nor is it communicable. For it is plain that Peter's act of eating was so much his own that it could not be called common to others.

units.la: Ex his & aliis quam pluribus patenter apparet, quod conuenit vti pane & vino & aliis comestibilibus: & quod actus comedendi vtendi. Negari ergo non potest, quin habens dominium & proprietatem panis & vini potest vti pane & vino, quare ergo si vtitur, aut vtitur iniuste pane, aut de gratia vel licentia alterius, aut de iure. Non potest dici quod iniuste: quia tunc, quandocunque comederet proprium panem & vinum proprium biberet, iniuste vteretur pane & vino. Ex quo sequitur manifeste, quod peccaret: quod erroneum est censendum. Nec potest dici, quod talis vtitur pane & vino de gratia vel licentia alterius: quia posipositum est, sicut saepe accidit, quod nullus alius habeat ius in tali pane & vino, cuius licentia requiratur ad hoc quod Dominus vtatur pane suo & vino. Si autem detur tertium, quod vtatur pane & vino suo de iure, igitur habet ius vtendi pane & vino, ergo in rebus vsu consumptibilibus potest ius vtendi constitui vel haberi. Et hoc ex dictis ipsius impugnati probatur aperte. Nam secundum ipsum omnis vsus facti iure vtendi est iniustus, sed non est necesse, quod omnis vtens pane & vino habeat vsum iniustum, igitur vtens pane & vino potest habere ius vtendi. Sed dicet aliquis, quod iste impugnatus non accipit vti pro actu comedendi vel bibendi aut consimili: quia actus comedendi non est actus vtendi secundum eum, sed est actus abutendi. Sed illud non valet: tum, quia ostensum est prius, quod actum comedendi vocat vsum facti: & vsum facti vocat actum vtendi, igitur actus comedendi est actus vtendi. Tum quia, si non vocaret actum comedendi, actum vtendi in nullo improbaret illos, quos redarguit, nisi sophistice & solummodo vocaliter, non ad mentem contradiceret eis: quia illi loquentes de actu vtendi, loquuntur de actu comedendi, bibendi, & huiusmodi, quem modum loquendi seruant iura diuina & humana, sicut ex praecedentibus patenter habetur, ergo si actum comedendi & bibendi non vocat actum vtendi, aequiuoce & per nouas impositiones vocum procedit contra ipsos. Per aequiuocationes autem & nouas impositiones vocum facile est omnia improbare. Tum quia, si actus comedendi potest vocari actus abutendi, multo fortius potest vocari actus vtendi: cum saepe scripturae loquentes de comestione vtantur verbo vtendi: & neque scripturae diuinae nec leges Canonicae vel ciuiles intendentes specialiter loqui de actu comedendi, vnquam vtantur verbo abutendi, secundum quod inferius apparebit: tum quia vocando actus comedendi, bibendi, vestiendi & huiusmodi actus abutendi tenet tota controuersia inter istum impugnatum & Fratres Minores: quia dicerent Fratres Minores, quod vocando actus comedendi, bibendi, vngendi, vestiendi & consimiles actus abutendi ipsi habent simplicem facti abusum, absque omni iure humano abutendi: & quod abusus facti potest in rebus vsu consumptibilibus a proprietate rei & dominio separari, & quod ecclesia Romana habet dominium & proprietatem in omnibus rebus vsu consumptibilibus, quibus vtuntur Fratres Minores, ipsis Fratribus Minoribus simplici abusu retento: & ita nihil ageret contra Fratres Minores, nisi quod deberent vti verbo abutendi, loquendo de rebus abusu consumptibilibus, quando vtuntur verbo vtendi. Patet ergo secundum istos, quod ius vtendi potest in rebus vsu consumptibilibus reperiri: hoc est, potest quis habere ius comedendi, bibendi, vestiendi.
units.tr: From these and many other passages it clearly appears that it is fitting to use bread, wine and other foodstuffs, and that the act of eating is using. Therefore it cannot be denied that one who has the dominion and ownership of bread and wine can use bread and wine. Why, then, when he does use them, does he use the bread unjustly, or by the grace or permission of another, or by right? It cannot be said that he uses it unjustly, for then whenever he ate his own bread and drank his own wine he would be using bread and wine unjustly. From this it plainly follows that he would be sinning, and that must be judged an error. Nor can it be said that such a person uses the bread and wine by the grace or permission of another, because it is assumed, as often happens, that no one else has any right in such bread and wine, whose permission would be required for the Lord to use his own bread and wine. If, then, the third option is granted, that he uses his own bread and wine by right, then he has a right of using bread and wine, and therefore a right of use can be constituted or held in consumable goods. This is clearly proved from the very words of this opponent. For according to him every use of a fact is use by right, and yet it is not necessary that everyone who uses bread and wine should have an unjust use. Therefore one who uses bread and wine can have a right of use. But someone may say that this opponent does not take use to mean the act of eating or drinking or the like, because for him the act of eating is not an act of using but of abusing. But that does not hold. First, because it was shown earlier that he calls the act of eating a use of fact, and he calls the use of fact an act of using; therefore the act of eating is an act of using. Second, because if he did not call the act of eating an act of using, he would not refute those whom he is confuting by the act of using at all, except sophistically and merely verbally, and not in their meaning. For those who speak of the act of using are speaking of the act of eating, drinking and the like, a way of speaking that divine and human law keeps, as is plainly seen from what precedes. Therefore, if he does not call the act of eating and drinking an act of using, he proceeds against them by equivocation and by new imposition of words. Yet all things can easily be refuted by equivocation and new imposition of words. Third, if the act of eating can be called an act of abusing, it can much more readily be called an act of using, since the Scriptures, when speaking of eating, often employ the verb to use, and neither the divine Scriptures nor the canon or civil laws, when intending to speak specifically of the act of eating, ever employ the verb to abuse, as will appear below. Fourth, the whole controversy between this opponent and the Friars Minor depends on calling the acts of eating, drinking, anointing, clothing and similar acts acts of abusing. For the Friars Minor would say that, in calling the acts of eating, drinking, anointing and clothing acts of abusing, they themselves have only a simple abuse of fact, without any human right of abusing; and that the abuse of fact in consumable goods can be separated from the property and dominion of the thing; and that the Roman Church has the dominion and ownership of all the consumable goods which the Friars Minor use, while the Friars Minor retain only a simple abuse. Thus he would accomplish nothing against the Friars Minor, except that they ought to use the verb to abuse when speaking of consumable goods, where they now use the verb to use. It appears, then, according to them, that a right of use can be found in consumable goods; that is, one can have a right to eat, drink and clothe oneself.

units.la: Secundo isti impugnatores reprobant vtramque rationem, per quam iste impugnatus conatur ostendere, quod ius vtendi non potest in rebus vsu consumptibilibus constitui vel haberi. Ad cuius euidentiam differentia tacta superius inter vsum & ius vtendi est ad memoriam reuocanda, cum enim ius vtendi ponatur in diffinitione vsus tanquam genus, constat quod aliqua differentia est inter vsum & ius vtendi: & quod ius vtendi est communius & generalius quam vsus, cum sit genus vel positum loco generis. Ex quo patenter apparet, quod per diffinitionem vsus inferri non potest, quod ius vtendi non potest in rebus vsu consumptibilibus constitui vel haberi: quia per diffinitionem inferioris non potest concludi aliquid a superiori negandum: sicut per diffinitionem hominis non potest inferri aliquid ab animali debere negari, sicut per diffinitionem hominis nullo modo couenit probare, quod nullum animal est irrationale: ita per diffinitionem vsus iuris, qui proprie sumptus non in omnibus rebus vsus consumptibilibus haberi potest, nullo modo probare conuenit, quod nullum ius vtendi potest in rebus vsu consumptibilibus constitui vel haberi.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents reject both arguments by which this opponent tries to show that a right of use cannot be constituted or held in consumable goods. To see this clearly, the distinction noted above between use and the right of use must be recalled. For since the right of use is placed in the definition of use as its genus, it is evident that there is some difference between use and the right of use, and that the right of use is more common and more general than use, since it is the genus or is put in the place of the genus. From this it plainly appears that it cannot be inferred from the definition of use that a right of use cannot be constituted or held in consumable goods. For by the definition of the lower term nothing can be concluded that must be denied of the higher term. Just as from the definition of man nothing can be inferred that must be denied of animal, and just as from the definition of man one cannot in any way prove that no animal is irrational, so from the definition of the right of use, which properly taken cannot be held in all consumable goods, one cannot in any way prove that no right of use can be constituted or held in consumable goods.

units.la: Forte autem aliquis puerliter cauillabit dicens, quod per diffinitionem inferioris conuenit aliquid negare a superiori particulariter sumpto: licet non vniuersaliter sumpto, ergo per diffinitionem vsus potest ostendi, quod aliquod ius vtendi non potest in rebus vsu consumptibilibus constitui vel haberi. Ad hoc impugnatores isti respondent dicentes: quod verum est, quod per diffinitionem vsus potest ostendi, quod aliquod ius vtendi non potest in omnibus rebus vsu consumptibilibus constitui vel haberi: quia illud ius vtendi, quod est vsus iuris proprie sumptus, non potest in omnibus rebus vsu consumptibilibus constitui vel haberi, & ideo concedunt, quod aliquod ius vtendi non potest quis habere in pane & in vino: quia non illud, quod est vsus proprie sumptus: aliquod tamen aliud ius vtendi potest quis habere in pane & in vino. Verum autem illud ius sit proprio nomine nominatum, vel sit innominatum, non est curandum ad praesens, sicut enim secundum iura plures sunt contractus innominati, ita forte sunt vel possunt esse plura iura innominata, hoc est non habentia propria nomina & vniuoca, sed communia tantum. Ius enim non scriptum non est proprio nomine nominatum: cum videatur solummodo nomine consuetudinis appellari. Consuetudo autem, sicut habetur in decretis dist. 1. nomen commune est ad ius scriptum, & non scriptum: licet, vt ibidem dicitur §. Cum itaque, Ius non scriptum generali nomine consuetudinis appelletur, sic igitur concedunt isti impugnatores, quod vsus iuris proprie sumptus & illud ius vtendi, quod est vsus iuris, non potest in omnibus rebus vsu consumptibilibus reperiri: nec vnquam Fratres Minores dixerunt se habere talem vsum: imo constanter negant se habere talem vsum. Aliud tamen ius vtendi potest in rebus huiusmodi constitui & haberi.
units.tr: Perhaps someone will childishly object that from the definition of a lower term it may be denied of a higher term, taken particularly though not universally, that something holds; therefore from the definition of use it can be shown that some right of use cannot be constituted or held in consumable goods. To this these opponents reply: it is true that from the definition of use it can be shown that some right of use cannot be constituted or held in all consumable goods, because that right of use which is the use of right, properly taken, cannot be constituted or held in all consumable goods. They therefore grant that a person cannot have a right of use in bread and in wine of that kind which is the proper use of right; yet some other right of use can be had in bread and wine. Whether that right is named by a proper name or is unnamed is not a concern for the present. For just as in law there are many unnamed contracts, so there are perhaps, or there may be, many unnamed rights, that is, rights not having proper and univocal names but only common ones. For an unwritten law is not called by a proper name, since it seems to be named only by the name of custom. Custom, however, as is stated in the Decretum, distinction 1, is a common name for written and unwritten law, although, as is said in the same place, §. Cum itaque, unwritten law is called by the general name of custom. So these opponents concede that the use of right, properly taken, and that right of use which is the use of right, cannot be found in all consumable goods; and the Friars Minor never said that they had such a use, but constantly deny that they have it. Yet another right of use can be constituted and held in goods of this kind.

units.la: Secundo isti impugnatores secundam rationem istius impugnati reprobare conantur, asserentes ipsum falsum assumere, cum dicit beatu Iohan. Chrysostomu per hoc, quod ius vtendi non potest in rebus vsu consumptibilibus constitui vel haberi, reddere rationem, quare pecunia mutuata non licet vsura recipere, quod vt euidenter ostendat, verba B. Ioh. Chrysostomi, in quibus se fundat iste impugnatus, adducunt in medium, quæ sunt hæc, ut habetur distin. 88. c. Eiiciens: Super omnes mercatores maledictus est plus usurarius. Ipse namque rem datam à Deo vendit, non comparatam ut mercator: post fœnus rem suam repetit, tollens aliena cum suis. Mercator autem non repetit rem venditam. Dicit aliquis: qui agrum locat, ut agrariam accipiat: aut domum, ut pensionem accipiat: non est similis ei, qui pecuniam dat ad usuram? absit. Primo quidem: quoniam pecunia non est disposita nisi ad emendum. Secundo quoniam agrum habens arando accipit ex eo fructum: & habens domum usum mansionis capit ex ea: & ideo qui locat domum vel agrum suum, usum dare videtur, & quodammodo mutare videtur cum lucro lucrum: ex pecunia reposita nullum usum capit. Tertio, ager vel domus veterascit. Pecunia spiritualiter homines intelliguntur. Hæc sunt verba beati Iohannis Chrysostomi, in quibus iste impugnatus se fundat. Ex quibus euidenter apparet, quod de iure utendi pecunia non loquitur, nisi per dominium pecuniæ intelligatur ius utendi pecunia, & ita constat aperte, quod per hoc, quod ius utendi in rebus usu consumptibilibus non potest constitui vel haberi, non reddit rationem, quare ex pecunia mutuata non licet usuram recipere: cum de hoc, scilicet an ius utendi in rebus usu consumptibilibus possit constitui vel haberi, nullam faciat penitus mentionem. Per aliud ergo reddit rationem Chrysostomus ibidem, quare peior est usurarius mercatore. Unde in illo capitulo Eiiciens, Iohannes Chrysostomus primo ostendit, quod omnis mercator tanquam malus est de ecclesia abiiciendus. Secundo dicit, quod usurarius est peior mercatore. Tertio assignat rationem, quare peior est usurarius mercatore. Quarto quæritur, an locans domum vel agrum debeat similis usurario reputari. Quinto assignat rationes, quare locans domum vel agrum non est similis usurario. Hæc quatuor ultima facit Iohannes Chrysostomus in verbis superius recitatis: Porro quia ex ratione, quam assignat beatus Iohannes Chrysostomus, quare usurarius peior est mercatore, habetur quæstionis fundamentum, quare locans domum vel agrum non debet usurario similis reputari: ideo illa ratio est videnda. Est autem ratio illa. Ille qui est transferens dominium alicuius rei in alterum: & postea eandem rem quantum ad valorem repetit, & aliquid ultra: peior est illo, qui transferens dominium alicuius rei non repetit eandem quantum ad valorem, & aliquam utilitatem. Sed mercator transferens dominium rei, quam vendit, accepto isto precio rei venditæ nihil repetit ultra, usurarius autem transfert dominium pecuniæ mutuatæ: & postea petit eandem pecuniam quantum ad valorem, & aliquid ultra, igitur usurarius peior est mercatore, & hoc intendit Iohannes Chrysostomus, cum dicit: Post fœnus rem suam quantum ad valorem repetit tollens aliena cum suis, hoc est aliquid ultra valorem rei suæ. Ex ista ratione patenter elicitur ista propositio, quod transferens dominium alicuius rei non debet petere pro eadem aliquid ultra valorem eiusdem rei, cuius transfert dominium. Et ista est ratio, quare pro pecunia mutuata non licet usuram recipere: quia mutuans pecuniam alteri transfert à se dominium pecuniæ, qui autem transfert dominium rei non debet pro eadem re petere aliquid ultra valorem eiusdem rei. Hoc accipi potest ex auctoritate Augustin. quæ ponitur 14. q. 3. Igitur mutuans pecuniam non debet aliquid petere ultra valorem pecuniæ: & per consequens pro pecunia mutuata non licet usuram recipere, & ista est una regula, quare pro pecunia mutuata non licet usuram recipere. Quæ ex verbis Iohannis Chrysostomi colligi potest, licet ille idem ipsam non assignaret, quare pro pecunia mutuata non licet usuram recipere: quia, sicut clare patet intuenti Chrysostomus in toto illo capitulo non intendit rationem istius veritatis assignare: sed intendit assignare rationem, quare peior est usurarius mercatore: & quare locans domum vel agrum non est similis usurario existimandus. Visa igitur ratione, quare pro pecunia mutuata non licet usuram accipere: quamuis ad eandem veritatem, dictam rationem Chrysostom. ibidem nequaquam assignet: consideranda sunt rationes Chrysostomi, quare locans domum vel agrum non est similis usurario iudicandus. Tres autem rationes assignare videtur, quare locans domum vel agrum non est similis usurario: quia mercator differt ab usurario in tribus. Primo in hoc quod pecunia non est ad aliud ordinata quam ad emendum, hoc est ad contractus humanos exercendos. Domus autem & ager sunt ad aliud ordinati: & ita qui locat domum vel agrum non est similis ei qui dat pecuniam, & ita per istam rationem non assignatur ratio: quare non licet pro pecunia mutuata usuram recipere: sed assignatur differentia inter usurarium & locantem domum vel agrum suum. Ex ista tamen differentia potest elici ratio, quare non licet pro pecunia mutuata usuram recipere: & tamen licet pro agro locato vel domo aliquid recipere. Nam ex quo pecunia non est disposita nisi ad emendum: qui dat pecuniam ad usuram, transfert à se dominium pecuniæ quare ultra valorem pecuniæ non licet sibi recipere: quia transferens dominium non debet exigere ultra valorem rei cuius transfert dominium à se. Locans autem agrum vel domum, non transfert à se dominium domus vel agri, quare domum vel agrum post tempus pro quo locauit potest repetere tanquam rem propriam: & quia à se transtulit potestatem utendi domo vel agro pro tempore isto, & eandem potestatem utendi domo vel agro non gratuito concessit illi cui locauit, pro translatione illius potestatis utendi domo potest aliquid petere. Et ex isto posset declarari, quod quemadmodum multi sunt contractus, qui ex forma non possunt censeri nomine usurarum, possunt tamen fieri in fraudem usurarum: sicut patet de venditione fundi ea lege, ut quandocunque soluitur pretium fundus, ad vendentem reuertatur. Ita locatio domus vel agri licet ex forma non sit contractus usurarius, posset tamen fieri in fraudem usurarum: puta si maius pretium, quam valeat domus vel ager, pro locatione reciperetur. Secunda differentia, quam assignat Chrysostomus inter usurarium & locantem domum vel agrum, est talis. Habens domum vel agrum, aliquam utilitatem habere potest ex domo vel agro: & ita qui locat alteri domum vel agrum sibi retento dominio concedit conductori potestatem recipiendi utilitatem ex domo vel agro, & ideo non transfert in eum dominium domus vel agri, sed transfert in eum talem potestatem recipiendi utilitatem ex domo: & priuat seipsum pro isto tempore tali potestate, igitur quodammodo mutat lucrum cum lucro, quare licite aliquid recipit pro translatione talis potestatis, sed ex pecunia reposita non recipit aliquam utilitatem (nisi forte per accidens) & ita non est simile de locante domum vel agrum, & de dante pecuniam ad vsuram, quare locans non transfert dominium rei locatae: sed potestatem recipiendi aliquam utilitatem ex re locata. Dans autem ad vsuram, transfert dominium pecuniae, & non transfert potestatem recipiendi utilitatem ex pecunia, retento sibi dominio pecuniae, ergo locans domum vel agrum non est similis vsurario: & tamen ex hoc patet, quare mutuans pecuniam no debet aliquid vltra valorem pecuniae exigere. Non enim potest pecuniam exigere tanquam rem propriam: quia translata fuit per mutuum proprietas pecuniae, ergo tantum exiget valorem pecuniae, ergo non potest vsuram exigere, quia vsura est aliquid vltra valorem pecuniae mutuatae, & ex isto patet, quare tradens pecuniam alteri ad pompam secundum leges potest aliquid recipere vltra pecuniam: quia tradens alteri non gratuito pecuniam ad pompam, non transfert dominium pecuniae, sed retinet sibi dominium pecuniae, quare pecuniam illam tanquam rem propriam licet repetere. Et quia tradens pecuniam ad pompam non gratuito, transtulit illam potestatem recipiendi aliquam utilitatem ex pecunia iudicio recipientis pecuniam ad pompam, potest pro translatione illius potestatis aliquid recipere. Et ex isto patet vlterius, quod licet talis traditio pecuniae ad pompam non sit ex forma contractus vsurarii, posset tamen fieri in fraudem vsurarum: & tunc non liceret vltra pecuniam traditam aliquid recipere. Nec obstat hoc, quod scilicet contingit transferre potestatem recipiendi utilitatem ex pecunia tradita ad pompam dicto Chrysostom. cum dicit, ex pecunia reposita nullum vsum capis: quia Chrysostomus loquitur de vsu, ad quem pecunia, in quantum pecunia, est principaliter ordinata.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents try to refute the second argument of the one they attack, claiming that he takes a false premise when he says, citing blessed John Chrysostom, that by the fact that a right of use cannot be established or held in things consumed by use, he gives the reason why interest may not be received on a loaned sum. To show this clearly, they bring forward the words of St John Chrysostom on which the attacked writer rests his case, which are these, as found in dist. 88, c. Eiiciens: Above all merchants is the usurer cursed. For he sells a thing given by God, not acquired as a merchant does: after the interest he takes back his own thing, taking what belongs to others along with his own. But the merchant does not take back the thing he sold. Someone says: is he who leases a field to receive its rent, or a house to receive its rent, not like one who gives money at interest? Far from it. First, because money is set aside only for buying. Second, because one who has a field takes fruit from it by ploughing, and one who has a house takes the use of living in it; so he who lets out his house or field seems to grant the use, and in a way seems to exchange gain for gain, whereas from money put aside he takes no use. Third, a field or house grows old, whereas money is understood spiritually for people. These are the words of blessed John Chrysostom on which the attacked writer rests his case. From them it is plainly evident that he is not speaking of a right to use money, unless by ownership of money one understands the right to use money. So it is clear that by the statement that a right of use in things consumed by use cannot be established or held, he does not give the reason why interest may not be received on a loaned sum, since he makes no mention at all of whether a right of use in things consumed by use can be established or held. Chrysostom therefore gives a different reason there, why the usurer is worse than the merchant. Hence, in that chapter Eiiciens, John Chrysostom first shows that every merchant, as a wicked man, is to be cast out of the Church. Second, he says that the usurer is worse than the merchant. Third, he assigns the reason why the usurer is worse than the merchant. Fourth, it is asked whether one who lets a house or field should be considered like a usurer. Fifth, he assigns reasons why one who lets a house or field is not like a usurer. Chrysostom makes these last four points in the words quoted above. Moreover, since from the reason that blessed John Chrysostom assigns, why the usurer is worse than the merchant, the ground of the question is obtained, namely why one who lets a house or field ought not to be counted like a usurer, that reason must be examined. It is this: he who transfers the ownership of a thing to another, and afterwards takes back the same thing in respect of its value, and something more, is worse than he who transfers the ownership of a thing and does not take back the same in respect of its value and some benefit. But the merchant, transferring the ownership of the goods he sells, takes back nothing more once he has received this price of the goods sold; the usurer, however, transfers the ownership of the money lent, and afterwards demands the same money in respect of its value, and something more. Therefore the usurer is worse than the merchant, and this is what John Chrysostom intends when he says: After the interest he takes back his own thing in respect of its value, taking what belongs to others along with his own, that is, something beyond the value of his own thing. From this reasoning there clearly follows the proposition that one who transfers the ownership of a thing ought not to ask for anything beyond the value of the same thing whose ownership he transfers. And this is the reason why it is not lawful to receive interest on a loaned sum: because one who lends money to another transfers from himself the ownership of the money, and one who transfers the ownership of a thing ought not to demand for the same thing anything beyond its value. This can be gathered from the authority of Augustine which is cited in 14. q. 3. Therefore one who lends money ought not to ask anything beyond the value of the money, and consequently it is not lawful to receive interest on a loaned sum; and this is one rule why interest may not be received on a loaned sum. This can be gathered from the words of John Chrysostom, although he himself did not state this reason why interest may not be received on a loaned sum: for, as is clear to anyone who considers it, Chrysostom in that whole chapter did not intend to assign the reason for this truth, but intended to assign the reason why the usurer is worse than the merchant, and why one who lets a house or field should not be judged like a usurer. So, although Chrysostom there by no means assigns this reason to the same truth, having seen the reason why interest may not be received on a loaned sum, we must consider Chrysostom's reasons why one who lets a house or field ought not to be judged like a usurer. He seems to assign three reasons why one who lets a house or field is not like a usurer: the merchant differs from the usurer in three respects. First, in that money is ordained for nothing but buying, that is, for carrying on human contracts. A house and a field, however, are ordained for another purpose; and so one who lets a house or field is not like one who gives money, and so by this reason no reason is assigned why interest may not be received on a loaned sum, but a difference is assigned between the usurer and one who lets his house or field. Yet from this difference a reason can be drawn why interest may not be received on a loaned sum, while it is lawful to receive something for a leased field or house. For since money is set aside only for buying, one who gives money at interest transfers from himself the ownership of the money, and therefore may not receive anything beyond the value of the money; because one who transfers ownership ought not to exact more than the value of the thing whose ownership he transfers from himself. But one who lets a field or house does not transfer from himself the ownership of the house or field, and therefore after the time for which he let it he may take back the house or field as his own property; and since he has transferred from himself the power of using the house or field for that time, and has granted that same power of using the house or field to the one to whom he let it, not gratuitously, he may ask something for the transfer of that power of using the house. And from this it could be shown that, just as there are many contracts which, by their form, cannot be counted as usury, yet can be made in fraud of usury, as is clear in the sale of an estate on the condition that, whenever the price is paid, the estate returns to the seller; so the letting of a house or field, although by its form it is not a usurious contract, could nevertheless be made in fraud of usury, for example if a greater price than the house or field is worth were received for the letting. The second difference that Chrysostom assigns between the usurer and one who lets a house or field is this. One who has a house or field can have some benefit from the house or field; and so one who lets a house or field to another, keeping the ownership for himself, grants to the lessee the power of receiving benefit from the house or field, and therefore does not transfer into him the ownership of the house or field, but transfers into him such a power of receiving benefit from the house; and for that time he deprives himself of such a power; therefore he in a way exchanges gain for gain, and so he lawfully receives something for the transfer of such a power. But from money put aside he receives no benefit (except perhaps incidentally). And so the case of one who lets a house or field is not like that of one who gives money at interest: the lessor does not transfer the ownership of the thing let, but the power of receiving some benefit from the thing let. But one who gives money at interest transfers the ownership of the money, and does not transfer the power of receiving benefit from the money, keeping the ownership of the money for himself. Therefore one who lets a house or field is not like a usurer. And yet from this it is clear why one who lends money ought not to exact anything beyond the value of the money. For he cannot exact the money as his own property, because the ownership of the money was transferred by the loan. Therefore he will exact only the value of the money, and so he cannot exact interest, because interest is something beyond the value of the money lent. And from this it is clear why one who hands over money to another for display according to the laws may receive something beyond the money: because one who hands over money for display, not gratuitously, does not transfer the ownership of the money, but keeps the ownership of the money for himself, and therefore may lawfully take back that money as his own property. And because one who hands over money for display, not gratuitously, has transferred to the other that power of receiving some benefit from the money at the discretion of the one receiving the money for display, he may receive something for the transfer of that power. And from this it further appears that, although such a handing over of money for display is not by its form a usurious contract, it could nevertheless be made in fraud of usury; and then it would not be lawful to receive anything beyond the money handed over. Nor does it stand in the way that it happens to transfer the power of receiving benefit from money handed over for display, which Chrysostom says in the words from money put aside he receives no use; for Chrysostom speaks of the use for which money, as money, is principally ordained.
