units.la: Tertia differentia, quam assignat Chrysostomus inter locantem domum vel agrum, & dantem ad vsuram, talis est. Ager vel domus veterascit: pecunia autem non veterascit, quare locans domum vel agrum, non est similis danti pecuniam ad vsuram: quia vnus accipit rem, quae veterascit: & alius, quae non veterascit. Est autem aduertendum, quod domus vel ager, si non saepius reparetur vel colitur, veterascit, quare vt non veterascat, oportet locantem expensas apponere, circa pecuniam autem vt non veterascat non oportet expensas apponere, quare cum locans domum vel agrum non transfert dominium domus vel agri: & conductor non tenetur domum vel agrum conseruare ad expensas suas: rationabiliter potest locans domum vel agrum ad conseruandum domum vel agrum a conductore ex domo vel agro aliquid recipere, non solum pro utilitate, quam habet conductor ex relocantis, sed etiam ad conseruandum seipsum indemnem, sed mutuans pecuniam, cum pecunia non veterascat, nec tales sumptus requirat, non debet ipse mutuans pro tali conseruatione indemnitatis suae aliquid recipere, & ita differentia est inter locantem domum vel agrum, & dantem pecuniam ad vsuram.
units.tr: The third difference that Chrysostom assigns between one who lets out a house or field and one who lends money at interest is this. A field or a house wears out, but money does not wear out. So the one who lets out a house or field is not like the one who lends money at interest, because one receives a thing that wears out, and the other a thing that does not. It must be noted, however, that a house or field, if it is not often repaired or tilled, wears out. So to keep it from wearing out, the lessor must bear the expenses. With money, by contrast, there is no need to bear expenses to keep it from wearing out. Since the lessor of a house or field does not transfer ownership of it, and the tenant is not bound to maintain the house or field at his own expense, the lessor of a house or field may reasonably take something from the tenant for keeping the house or field in repair. He may do so not only for the benefit the tenant derives from the lessor's property, but also to keep himself harmless. But the one who lends money, since money does not wear out and does not require such outlays, ought not to receive anything for the sake of preserving his own safety in this way. Thus there is a difference between one who lets out a house or field and one who lends money at interest.

units.la: Ex iis omnibus patet, quod in toto processu Chrysostomi nulla fit mentio de iure vtendi, an possit in rebus vsu consumptibilibus constitui vel haberi, an non possit: & quod principalis ratio, quare non licet pro pecunia mutuata vsuram recipere, est quia pro re cuius transfertur dominium non licet vltra valorem aliquid recipere. Qualiter autem debeat intelligi, quod dicunt leges, quod licet contrahentibus se inuicem decipere, ad praesens pro prolixitate vitanda est minime differendum. Ex praedictis inferunt isti impugnatores, quod per neutram rationem superius positam inferri potest, quod ius vtendi non potest in rebus vsu consumptibilibus constitui vel haberi.
units.tr: From all these things it is clear that in the whole argument of Chrysostom there is no mention of the right of use, whether it can or cannot be constituted or held in things consumed by use. It is also clear that the principal reason why it is not lawful to take interest on money lent is that it is not lawful to take anything beyond the value for a thing whose ownership is transferred. How the saying of the laws, that contracting parties may deceive one another, ought to be understood must not be discussed here, for the sake of brevity. From what has been said, these opponents infer that by neither of the reasons set out above can it be concluded that the right of use cannot be constituted or held in things consumed by use.

units.la: Deinde secundo isti impugnatores improbant praedicta principaliter, quo ad hoc quod dicitur, quod ius vtendi in rebus vsu consumptibilibus separatum a proprietate seu dominio non potest constitui vel haberi. Hoc enim (vt dicunt) iuri diuino, iuri naturali & humano aperte repugnat. Quod enim repugnet iuri diuino, ostendunt per illud Deuter. 23. c. Ingressus vineam proximi tui comede vuas quantum tibi placuerit: foras autem ne efferas tecum, si intraueris segetem amici tui, frangas spicas & manu conteres, falce autem non metes. Ex his verbis habetur aperte, quod Iudaei ex ordinatione diuina, & per consequens ex lege diuina, habebant ius comedendi vuas & grana spicarum: quorum tamen non habebant dominium & proprietatem: quia dominium vuarum & spicarum ad dominos agrorum & vinearum pertinebat, quod patet ex hoc, quia Domini agrorum & vinearum vuas & spicas colligere poterant, & collectas comedere, & gratis dare valebant: quod alii non poterant, ergo Domini agrorum & vinearum etiam vuarum & spicarum habuerunt dominium & proprietatem: licet etiam alii, antequam vuae & spicae colligerentur, haberent ius vtendi; hoc est ius comedendi vuas & grana spicarum. Sed forte diceret aliquis, quod alii non habebant ius comedendi vuas & grana spicarum, sed habebant tantum licentiam comedendi, quod per hoc posse probari videtur: quia Apostoli, sicut legitur Mat. 12. transeuntes per sata & esurientes coeperunt vellere spicas & manducare: & ita vtebantur licentia sibi a lege diuina concessa: & tamen non habebant in spicis ius vtendi, cum omni iuri renunciauerint, ergo illa licentia vtendi seu comedendi non erat ius vtendi seu comedendi.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents object to the above propositions chiefly on this point, namely that the right of use in things consumed by use cannot be constituted or held apart from property or ownership. For this (they say) openly conflicts with divine law, natural law and human law. That it conflicts with divine law they show from Deuteronomy 23: When you come into your neighbour's vineyard, you may eat grapes as much as you like, but you shall not put any in your vessel. When you come into your neighbour's standing corn, you may pluck the ears with your hand, but you shall not wield a sickle to it. From these words it plainly appears that the Jews, by divine ordinance and consequently by divine law, had the right to eat the grapes and the grain of the ears, yet they did not have the ownership and property of them. For the ownership of the grapes and ears belonged to the owners of the fields and vineyards. This is clear because the owners of the fields and vineyards could gather the grapes and ears, eat them when gathered, and give them freely, which others could not do. Therefore the owners of the fields and vineyards also had ownership and property of the grapes and ears. Yet others, before the grapes and ears were gathered, also had the right of use, that is, the right to eat the grapes and the grain of the ears. But perhaps someone would say that the others did not have the right to eat the grapes and grain of the ears, but only had permission to eat them. This seems to be proved by the fact that the apostles, as we read in Matt. 12., passing through the cornfields and being hungry, began to pluck the ears and eat them. Thus they used a permission granted them by divine law, and yet they did not have a right of use in the ears, since they had renounced every right. Therefore that permission to use or eat was not a right to use or eat.

units.la: Ad hoc isti impugnatores respondent, quod illa licentia erat ius quo ad illos, qui iuri illi renunciare nolebant, & quod licentia illa erat ius, patet: quia nullus per inferiorem Deo sine culpa & absque causa legitima tali licentia debuit priuari inuitus: imo si aliquis sine culpa sua & absque causa legitima tali licentia fuisset priuatus inuitus, habuisset actionem contra priuantem, & ideo illa licentia erat ius quoddam, & differebat à licentia, qua quis dat alicui licentiam vtendi veste sua cum potestate reuocandi, quandocunque sibi placuerit: quia illa licentia assimilatur priuilegiis, quae concedens quidocunque sibi placuerit, poterit reuocare: & tamen priuilegiatus contra alios priuare volentes haberet actionem, & ideo, sicut priuilegia leges sunt censendae, dist. 3. Priuilegia, ita illa licentia legis & ius nomine poterat appellari. Cum vero accipitur, quod Apostoli vtebantur illa licentia: & tamen non habebant ius vtendi. Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod Apostoli renunciauerunt illi licentiae: & ideo tunc non vtebantur illa licentia seu ordinatione diuina: sed vtebantur licentia iuris naturalis seu iure naturali, cui renunciare non poterant. Tempore enim necessitatis saltem extremae habet quilibet ex iure naturae potestatem vtendi illis, sine quibus sustentari non potest. Vnde & Christus ibidem probat ex Dauid, qui tempore necessitatis auctoritate iuris naturae comedit panes propositionis, quod discipuli licite in sabbatho etiam spicas, quae ad alienum pertinebant dominium, vellebant & manducabant: quia necessitas non habet legem.
units.tr: To this these opponents reply that the permission was a right with respect to those who were unwilling to renounce that right. That the permission was a right is clear, because no one below God ought to be deprived of such permission against his will, without fault and without a lawful cause. Indeed, if anyone had been deprived of such permission against his will, without fault of his own and without a lawful cause, he would have had an action against the one depriving him. So that permission was a kind of right, and it differed from the permission by which someone gives another leave to use his garment, with the power of revoking it whenever he pleases. For that permission is like the privileges which the one granting may revoke whenever he likes; yet the privileged person would still have an action against others who wished to deprive him. Therefore, just as privileges are to be counted as laws (dist. 3, Privilegia), so that permission could be called a right by the name of law. But when it is taken that the apostles used that permission, and yet did not have a right of use, these opponents say that the apostles renounced that permission. Therefore at that time they did not use it as a permission or ordinance of divine law, but used it by the permission of natural law, or by natural law, which they could not renounce. For at least in extreme necessity everyone has, by the law of nature, the power to use those things without which he cannot be sustained. Hence Christ in the same place also proves from David, who in a time of necessity by the authority of the law of nature ate the showbread, that the disciples lawfully on the Sabbath plucked and ate even the ears that belonged to another's ownership, because necessity has no law.

units.la: Secundo isti impugnatores moliuntur ostendere, quod praedicta assertio destruit ius naturale. Nam quilibet in extrema necessitate constitutus habet ius vtendi re vsu consumptibili, sine qua de hac vita migraret: & tamen dominium talis rei propter hoc non acquirit, quia nec Dominus retante consumptionem ipsius perdit dominium, nec indigens ea ipsius rei acquirit dominium, quod patet ex hoc, quod cessante necessitate extrema ante consumptionem rei, nec illi licet retinere rem talem, nec peccat Dominus eandem rem tanquam propriam repetendo. Hoc aperto declaratur exemplo. Nam si aliquis fuerit in tali articulo constitutus, quod nisi veste sibi praesente se cooperuerit, moretur: ille tunc habet ius cooperiendi se veste illa: nec aliquis licite absque peccato mortali ipsum poterit prohibere, nisi per alium modum eius necessitati succurreret. Si autem illa necessitas ante consumptionem vestis cessaret, ipse eam non potest inuito Domino retinere: & Dominus, sicut prius, potest de ea ad libitum suum ordinare, ergo stante necessitate iste habuit ius vtendi veste absque dominio & proprietate: & ita esto quod ius vtendi in rebus vsu consumptibilibus, quae statim actu vnico consumuntur, non posset a proprietate & dominio separari, sicut in cibo, potu, vnguentis, & huiusmodi: tamen in rebus, quae non statim consumuntur, sed multis durant temporibus, potest ius vtendi a proprietate & dominio separari. Constat enim, quod potest quis vestem conducere ad vtendum: qua conducta habet ius saltem ad tempus vtendi ipsa. Hoc etiam patet exemplo: quia hospites locant lectisternia sua hospitibus, & multa alia, quae tandem vsu consumuntur, quamuis non consumantur primo actu vtendi: & ita hospites habent in eis ius vtendi, in quibus tamen non habent dominium & proprietatem.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents labour to show that the aforesaid assertion destroys natural law. For anyone placed in extreme necessity has a right to use a thing consumed by use, without which he would depart from this life. And yet he does not acquire ownership of such a thing on that account. For neither does the owner, by withholding the consumption of it, lose ownership, nor does the one in need acquire ownership of it. This is clear from the fact that, once extreme necessity has ceased before the thing has been consumed, it is not lawful for him to keep the thing, nor does the owner sin if he demands the same thing back as his own. This is made plain by an example. Suppose someone is in such a situation that unless he covers himself with a garment that is present to him, he will die. Then he has a right to cover himself with that garment, and no one may lawfully forbid him without mortal sin, unless his need is met in some other way. But if that necessity ceased before the garment was used up, he cannot keep it against the owner's will, and the owner may, as before, dispose of it at his pleasure. Therefore, while the necessity lasted, this man had a right to use the garment without ownership and property. So even if the right of use in things consumed by use, which are consumed at once by a single act, such as food, drink, ointments and the like, could not be separated from property and ownership, yet in things that are not consumed at once but last for many periods of time, the right of use can be separated from property and ownership. For it is certain that someone may hire a garment for use, and having hired it he has a right at least for the time of using it. This is also shown by an example: innkeepers let out their couches and many other things to guests, which are finally consumed by use, though they are not consumed by the first act of using. So guests have a right of use in these things, though they do not have ownership and property of them.

units.la: Tertio isti impugnatores ostendunt, quod praedicta assertio repugnat iuri ciuili. Nam, sicut est saepe superius allegatum, lex dicit, quod qui fundi vsum nudum habet, nihil vlterius habere intelligitur, quam vt oleribus, pomis, floribus, feno, stramentis, lignis ad vsum quotidianum vtatur. Ex quibus verbis habetur aperte, quod qui fundi vsum iuris habet potestatem vtendi oleribus, pomis, floribus & huiusmodi quae inter res vsu consumptibiles computantur, aut ergo potestas vtendi huiusmodi rebus vsu consumptibilibus est licita, aut illicita, non potest dici quod illicita: quia tunc vtendo huiusmodi rebus peccaret, quod est omnino contrarium veritati. Si vero illa potestas vtendi est licita: aut igitur competit habenti nudum vsum solummodo de gratia aut de iure, non solummodo de gratia, consistat: quia saepe emitur vsus nudus fundi, & per consequens emitur potestas annexa vtendi huiusmodi rebus quae crescunt in fundo. Posset etiam habens vsum nudum, si tali potestate vtendi oleribus pomis &c. priuaretur inuitus, priuantem in iudicio conuenire, ergo non habet talem potestatem de gratia tantummodo. Competit ergo talis potestas sibi de iure: & per consequens talis potestas vtendi rebus vsu consumptibilibus est ius vtendi, vel saltem tali potestati est ius vtendi annexum, sed habens vsum nudum fundi, non habet olerum, pomorum, florum & huiusmodi rerum dominium & proprietatem: quia tales res non potest vendere, dare, nec legare: sed solummodo ipse potest vti eis cum sua familia, ergo in huiusmodi rebus ius vtendi est a proprietate & dominio separatum. Sed diceret aliquis, quod ex hoc sequeretur, quod rerum vsu consumptibilium esset proprie vsus iuris, quod isti impugnatores negant. Ad hoc dicunt isti impugnatores, quod rerum vsu consumptibilium saltem quae vnico actu consumuntur, non est proprie vsus iuris. Dicunt tamen, quod vsui iuris non nunquam est ius vtendi rebus consumptibilibus vsu annexum. Vnde dicunt quod quandoque vsus iuris non est annexum aliquod ius vtendi quacunque re vsu consumptibili: sicut cum quis habet nudum vsum domus, tali vsui iuris nullum ius vtendi rebus consumptibilibus vsu est annexum: quia habet solum potestatem inhabitandi domum & non plus, quandoque autem vsui iuris ex ordinatione humana, vel ex pacto est annexum ius vtendi rebus vsu consumptibilibus aliquibus vel omnibus, quae nascuntur in re, etiam habet vsum iuris, sicut est de vsu fundi, & ita ius vtendi huiusmodi rebus vsu consumptibilibus non est vsus iuris proprie, sed est vsui iuris annexum, & est forte ius innominatum nomine proprio: habet tamen hoc nomen commune eius vtendi.
units.tr: Third, these opponents show that the aforementioned assertion contradicts the civil law. For, as has often been cited above, the law says that he who has the bare use of an estate is understood to have nothing further than to use vegetables, fruit, flowers, hay, straw and wood for daily use. From these words it is clear that whoever has the legal use of an estate has the power to use vegetables, fruit, flowers and the like, which are counted among things consumed by use. Either this power to use such consumable things is lawful or it is unlawful. It cannot be called unlawful, for then he would sin by using such things, which is wholly contrary to the truth. If, however, that power of use is lawful, it must belong to the one who has the bare use either by grace alone or by right, not by grace alone. For the bare use of an estate is often bought, and with it there is bought, consequently, the power attached to using those things that grow on the estate. Moreover, if the holder of the bare use were deprived of such a power of using vegetables, fruit and so on against his will, he could sue the one who deprived him. Therefore he does not have this power merely by grace. Such a power therefore belongs to him by right, and consequently this power of using consumable things is a right of use, or at least a right of use is attached to such a power. But the holder of the bare use of an estate does not have ownership and property in the vegetables, fruit, flowers and the like, because he cannot sell, give or bequeath such things. He can only use them with his household. Therefore the right of use in such things is separated from property and ownership. But someone might say that it would follow from this that the use of consumable things would properly be a use of right, which these opponents deny. To this the opponents reply that the use of consumable things, at least those consumed by a single act, is not properly a use of right. They do say, however, that sometimes a right to use consumable things is attached to a use of right. So they say that sometimes a use of right has no right to use any consumable thing attached to it. Thus, when someone has the bare use of a house, no right to use consumable things is attached to that use of right, since he has only the power of living in the house and nothing more. But sometimes a right to use some or all consumable things that arise on the property is attached to a use of right, by human ordinance or by agreement, and then he also has a use of right, as is the case with the use of an estate. So the right to use such consumable things is not properly a use of right but is attached to a use of right. It is perhaps a right without a proper name of its own, though it has this common name for its use.

units.la: Tertio principaliter isti impugnatores hoc, quod dicitur in verbis istius constitutionis superius recitatis, scilicet quod actus vtendi in rebus vsu consumptibilibus haberi non potest, multipliciter improbare conantur, sed quia de hoc erit tractatus in sequentibus specialis: ideo hic vnica impugnatio breuiter adducetur, quae talis est. Si actus vtendi in rebus vsu consumptibilibus haberi non posset: hoc non est, nisi quia actus vtendi est successiuus & non totus simul. Vnde & hanc rationem istius assertionis tionis hic impugnatus assignat: sed hoc non potest impedire, quin actus habeatur: quia sicut actus est successivus, ita etiam annus est successivus: & tamen anni habentur, teste scriptura divina, quae 3. Reg. 1. ait: Rex David senuerat, habebatq; aetatis plurimos annos, ergo non obstante, quod actus utendi sit successivus, nihilominus haberi potest.
units.tr: Third, these opponents try to disprove in many ways the claim in the words of this constitution, cited above, that the act of using cannot be had in consumable things. But since there will be a special treatment of this later, the single objection will be briefly stated here, and it is this. If the act of using could not be had in consumable things, this would be only because the act of using is successive and not all at once. Hence the opponent also gives this reason for the assertion. But this cannot prevent the act from being had, for just as the act is successive, so too a year is successive, and yet years are had, as Scripture attests in 3 Reg. 1: King David had grown old and had many years of age. Therefore, although the act of using is successive, it can nonetheless be had.

units.la: Quarto principaliter impugnantes isti praedicta, quo ad hoc quod dicitur, quod rebus usu consumptibilibus non convenit uti, sed abuti, sed de illa fiet postea mentio specialis: ideo hic pertranseo.
units.tr: Fourth, these opponents chiefly dispute the aforementioned matter in respect of what is said, that it does not befit one to use consumable things but to abuse them. But a special mention of this will be made later, so I pass over it here.

units.la: His visis aliqua notabilia circa literam sunt videnda. (Docet & asserit) ex hoc notant isti impugnatores, quod ille impugnatus non est paratus corrigi, sed est errorum suorum defensor pertinax & assertor, (nec ipsum uti.) Ex hoc patet quod ipsum uti vocat usum facti: quia in impugnatione, ad quam iste impugnatus hic incipit respondere, non fit mentio de aliquo uti, nisi de usu facti, (potest constitui vel haberi.) De hoc in impugnatione nulla fit mentio: sed supponitur tanquam per scripturam sacram clarum & evidens, quod contingit uti rebus usu consumptibilibus, & probabatur, quod talis usus facti potest a proprietate & dominio separari, & ideo dicunt isti impugnatores, quod illud non est hic ad propositum, sed totaliter est impertinens reputandum. (Abuti) Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod ille modus loquendi de rebus usu consumptibilibus in scripturis divinis reperiri non potest: sed scriptura sacra loquendo de rebus usu consumptibilibus utitur verbo utendi, & non verbo abutendi, vel saltem non debemus utentes verbo utendi aliquatenus reprobare. (Ex diffinitione usus.)
units.tr: Having seen these things, some notable points about the wording must be considered. (Teaches and asserts) On this point the opponents note that the one they oppose is not ready to be corrected but is a stubborn defender and assertor of his errors. (Nor to use it.) From this it is clear that he calls to use it the use of fact, since in the objection to which he here begins to reply, there is no mention of any use except the use of fact. (Can be constituted or had.) No mention of this is made in the objection. Rather, it is assumed as clear and evident from Holy Scripture that it happens that things are used which are consumed by use, and it was argued that such a use of fact can be separated from property and ownership. Therefore these opponents say that this is not to the point but must be regarded as wholly irrelevant. (To abuse) The opponents say that this mode of speaking about consumable things cannot be found in the divine Scriptures. Holy Scripture, speaking of consumable things, uses the verb to use, not the verb to abuse, or at least we should not in any way condemn those who use the verb to use. (From the definition of use.)

units.la: Primo dicunt isti impugnatores, quod iste procedit sophistice, dum conatur aliquid a superiori negare per diffinitionem inferioris, (cum ius utendi sit communius quam usus: qui usus est ius utendi alienis rebus, salva rerum substantia.) Ex his verbis concedunt primo isti impugnatores, quod ius utendi sit communius quam usus, sicut dictum est prius. Secundo notant isti impugnatores, quod haec non est diffinitio usus universaliter sumpti: vel non est diffinitio usus in omni significatione huius nominis usus: tum quia usus rerum propriarum est usus ita proprie dictus, sicut usus rerum alienarum: tum quia usus rerum usu consumptibilium est proprius usus, sicut usus rerum quae non consumuntur usu.
units.tr: First, these opponents say that he proceeds sophistically when he tries to deny something of the higher kind by the definition of the lower. (Since the right of use is more common than use, which is the right to use other people's things with their substance preserved.) In these words the opponents first concede that the right of use is more common than use, as was said before. Second, the opponents note that this is not a definition of use taken universally, or at least not a definition of use in every sense of this word. For the use of one's own things is use in as proper a sense as the use of other people's things, and the use of consumable things is proper use just as the use of things not consumed by use is.

units.la: Ita enim proprie dicitur, ille habet usum cibi & potus: sicut, ille habet usum fundi. Igitur hic non diffinitur usus in omni significatione sua: sed in quadam significatione speciali, quae non est magis propria significatio quam alia. (Nulla potest utilitas provenire.) Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod hoc est falsum de multis rebus consumptibilibus usu: quia ex vestibus potest magna utilitas provenire salva rerum substantia, (utpote in pane & vino.) Dicunt quod exemplificat insufficienter: quia licet non proveniat utilitas ex pane & vino, dum integra manet eorum substantia: aliter tamen est de vestibus. Etiam causa est: quia panis & vinum actu unico consumuntur, multae autem vestes post plures actus integrae manent. (Quare evidenter relinquitur quod in rebus talibus usu consumptibilibus ius utendi separatum a proprietate seu dominio nequeat constitui seu haberi.) In illa illatione dicunt quod deficit: quia ex quo arguit per diffinitionem usus, debet illam conclusionem inferre: Usus in talibus rebus non potest constitui seu haberi, & illam conclusionem in uno sensu concedunt isti impugnatores: quia si accipiatur usus pro usu iuris stricte & proprissime sumpto, concedunt quod usus non potest in omnibus rebus usu consumptibilibus constitui vel haberi, sed ex hoc non sequitur, quod ius utendi non potest in talibus rebus constitui vel haberi: nec etiam sequitur, quod in talibus rebus non convenit uti.
units.tr: For one properly says, "He has the use of food and drink," just as one says, "He has the use of an estate." So use is not defined here in all its senses, but in a special sense, which is no more proper than the others. (No advantage can arise.) The opponents say this is false of many consumable things, since great advantage can arise from clothes while their substance is preserved. (As in bread and wine.) They say that the example is inadequate, since although no advantage arises from bread and wine while their substance remains whole, it is otherwise with clothes. The reason is also that bread and wine are consumed by a single act, whereas many garments remain whole after several acts. (Hence it clearly follows that in such consumable things a right of use separate from property or ownership cannot be constituted or had.) In this inference they say he fails, since from the definition of use he ought to draw the conclusion that use cannot be constituted or had in such things. The opponents concede this conclusion in one sense, for if use is taken as the use of right, strictly and most properly understood, they grant that use cannot be constituted or had in all consumable things. But it does not follow from this that a right of use cannot be constituted or had in such things, nor does it follow that one should not use consumable things.

units.la: Et si dicatur, quod ex hoc sequitur quod haec etiam est concedenda in aliquo sensu: Non conveniunt uti rebus consumptibilibus usu: quia hoc nomen usus, & hoc verbum uti in significatione conveniunt. Ad hoc respondent isti impugnatores, quod quamuis hoc sit concedendum in uno sensu: Nullus habet usum rerum consumptibilium: haec tamen in nullo sensu debet concedi: Nullus potest uti rebus usu consumptibilibus. Unde dicunt, quod talis argumentatio peccat: Nullus potest habere usum rerum usu consumptibilium: ergo nullus potest uti rebus usu consumptibilibus, quia antecedens potest habere sensum verum: & consequens nullum sensum habet verum. Causa autem, quare peccat talis consequentia, est, quia fundatur in una regula, quae habet multas instantias, & specialiter habet istam in opposito. Haec enim regula fallit, Nomen & verbum, quorum unum deriuatur ab alio, conveniunt in omni significatione, sicut & haec fallit, Duo nomina, quorum unum deriuatur ab alio, conveniunt in omni significatione. Exemplum primi accipitur ab Anselmo. De similitudinibus c. 1. qa secundum ipsum hoc nomen voluntas accipitur tripliciter: scil. instrumentum volendi, & affectio eiusdem instrumenti, & velle vel usus ipsius instrumenti: & tamen hoc verbum velle non accipitur unquam nisi pro actu ac usu instrumenti, saltem in creaturis. Non ergo hoc verbum velle habet tot significationes, quot habet hoc nomen voluntas: & ita non conveniunt in omni significatione. Exemplum secundi accipitur ex beato Hieronymo, & epistola Tharasi Constantinopolitani episcopi. Nam divinus & divinatio sunt duo nomina, quorum unum deriuatur ab alio: & tamen plures significationes habet hoc nomen divinus, quam hoc nomen divinatio. Nam secundum Tharasum Constantinopolitanum episcopum, ut habetur i.q.1.c. Eos qui, beatus Petrus potest dici divinus Apostolus: & ita hoc nomen divinus accipitur in bona significatione: & constat, quod accipitur saepe in mala significatione, ergo potest accipi in bona significatione & mala. Hoc autem nomen divinatio semper accipitur in mala significatione, nunquam in bona: teste Hieronymo, quod habetur i.q.1.c. Nunquam, ait: Nunquam divinatio in bonam partem accipitur, ergo haec duo nomina divinus & divinatio non in omni significatione conveniunt, & ideo non sequitur, beatus Petrus fuit divinus: ergo vtebatur divinatione: sicut nec sequitur, voluntas hominis est immutabilis & immortalis: ergo velle hominis est immutabile & immortale, sic etiam, quia hoc nomen usus & hoc verbum uti non conveniunt in omni significatione, eo quod hoc nomen usus habet plures significationes, quod hoc verbum uti.
units.tr: And if someone says that from this it follows that this proposition must also be granted in some sense, namely that it is not fitting to use consumable things by use, because the noun usus and the verb uti agree in meaning, these opponents reply that although it must be granted in one sense that no one has the use of consumable things, it must not be granted in any sense that no one can use consumable things by use. Hence they say that such an argument is faulty: no one can have the use of things consumed by use; therefore no one can use things consumed by use. The antecedent can have a true sense, while the consequent has no true sense. The reason such an inference fails is that it rests on a rule that has many exceptions, and especially on the opposite of this one. For this rule is false: a noun and a verb, one of which is derived from the other, agree in every meaning. So too this is false: two nouns, one derived from the other, agree in every meaning. An example of the first is taken from Anselm, De similitudinibus c. 1, since according to him the word voluntas (will) is taken in three ways: namely, the instrument of willing, the affection of that same instrument, and the act of willing or the use of the instrument itself. Yet the verb velle (to will) is never taken except for the act and use of the instrument, at least in creatures. So the verb velle does not have as many meanings as the noun voluntas has, and so they do not agree in every meaning. An example of the second is taken from blessed Jerome and from the letter of Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople. For divinus (divine) and divinatio (divination) are two nouns, one derived from the other, and yet the word divinus has more meanings than the word divinatio. For according to Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople, as it is found in i.q.1.c. Eos qui, blessed Peter may be called divinus Apostolus (a divine apostle), and so the word divinus is taken in a good sense. It is certain that it is often taken in a bad sense too, so it can be taken both in a good and in a bad sense. But the word divinatio is always taken in a bad sense and never in a good one, as Jerome attests, where it is found in i.q.1.c. Nunquam, saying: Nunquam divinatio in bonam partem accipitur (divination is never taken in a good sense). Therefore the two words divinus and divinatio do not agree in every meaning, and so it does not follow that Peter was divine, therefore he practised divination, just as it does not follow that the will of man is immutable and immortal, therefore the willing of man is immutable and immortal. Likewise, because the noun usus and the verb uti do not agree in every meaning, the noun usus has more meanings than the verb uti.

units.la: Nam hoc nomen usus quandoque significat actum utendi, quandoque quoddam ius determinatum, hoc autem verbum vti semper significat actum utendi, & nunquam nisi forte no[?] aliter sumptum significat tale ius, ideo non sequitur, nullus potest habere vsum rerum consumptibilium vsu: ergo non potest vti rebus consumptibilibus vsu, sicut non sequitur, nullus viator potest mutare voluntatem suam: ergo nullus viator potest mutare velle suum. Nec sequitur, nullus bonus vtitur diuinatione: ergo nullus bonus est diuinus. Causa autem, quare nulla consequentiarum praedicatarum valet, est: quia in qualibet consequentia illarum accipiuntur duo vocabula, quorum vnum deriuatur ab alio: & tamen vnum habet plures significationes quam aliud, & istius ignorantia, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, fecit illum impugnatum saepe ex auctoritatibus habentibus aliquem sensum verum inferre Sophistice consequentia nullum habentia sensum verum: & ita per aequiuocationes & multiplicitates conatus [illegible, ~3 letters] errores inducere. ( Et per hoc beatus Iohan. Chrysostomus rationem reddit &c.
units.tr: For the noun usus sometimes signifies the act of using, and sometimes a certain determinate right; but the verb uti always signifies the act of using, and never such a right, unless perhaps when taken otherwise. Therefore it does not follow that no one can have the use of consumable things by use, therefore no one can use consumable things by use; just as it does not follow that no wayfarer can change his will, therefore no wayfarer can change his willing; nor does it follow that no good man uses divination, therefore no good man is divine. The reason none of the inferences mentioned holds is that in each of them two words are taken, one derived from the other, and yet one has more meanings than the other. Their ignorance of this, as these opponents say, has often led that opponent, by citing authorities that have some true sense, to draw sophistical inferences having no true sense; and so by equivocations and multiple meanings he has tried to induce errors. (And through this blessed John Chrysostom gives his reason, etc.)

units.la: Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod falsum assumit, quia an ius vtendi possit in rebus vsu consumptibilibus constitui vel haberi: imo etiam an ius vtendi separatum a dominio seu proprietate possit in talibus rebus constitui vel haberi, Iohannes Chrysostomus, nullam penitus facit mentionem, sicut patet tenore allegati capituli intuenti. ( Iure vsus non consumptibili, vt in domo vel in agro ) vsque ibi ( Mutuans autem pecuniam ) hoc totum verum est, sed non est ad propositum, vt dicunt isti impugnatores. ( Pecuniam transfert dominium ) illud est ratio quare pro pecunia mutuata non licet vsuram recipere, quia scilicet mutuans transfert a se dominium pecuniae, & ideo non debet recipere vltra valorem pecuniae quam mutuauit.
units.tr: These opponents say that he assumes falsely, because John Chrysostom makes no mention at all of whether the right to use can be established or held in consumable things, or even whether the right to use separated from ownership or property can be established or held in such things; as is clear from the wording of the chapter cited, if one looks at it. The words "by the right of use of a non-consumable thing, as in a house or a field," down to "but he who lends money," are all true but not relevant to the point, as these opponents say. The words "money transfers ownership" give the reason why interest may not be received on money lent: namely, that the lender transfers ownership of the money from himself, and therefore ought not to receive more than the value of the money he lent.

units.la: Quod autem ius vtendi pecunia possit haberi vel non possit haberi: qua etiam ius vtendi pecunia separatum a dominio seu proprietate possit haberi, vel non possit haberi, hoc accidit: quia siue possit haberi, siue non, ex quo mutuans transfert dominium pecuniae, non potest iuste petere postea nisi valorem pecuniae, ergo nihil vltra potest recipere. Vnde sicut vendens domum propter hoc quod transfert a se dominium domus, non debet petere nisi valorem domus: licet emens domum non solum habeat dominium domus, sed etiam ius vtendi domo & etiam vtilitatem ex domo. Ita qui transfert a se dominium pecuniae licet recipiens postea dominium & proprietatem pecuniae haberet ius vtendi pecunia, & etiam vtilitatem ex pecunia, non debet transferens a se dominium pecuniae recipere aliquid vltra valorem pecuniae, & ita si pecunia sibi reddatur, non debet aliquid vltra exigere. ( Non fructum aliquem nec vtilitatem aliquam) illud nihil facit ad propositum, quia siue ille, qui recipit pecuniam mutuo, habeat aliquem fructum seu vtilitatem aliquam ex pecunia siue non habeat, mutuans pecuniam non debet exigere nisi valorem pecuniae in eadem specie, si vult, cuius translatum dominium, maxime cum contractus mutui debeat esse contractus gratuitus. Vnde sicut qui commodat alicui equum gratuite, non debet exigere nisi equum, quantumcunque; alius habuisset vtilitatem ex equo: ita mutuans pecuniam non debet exigere, nisi pecuniam, quantumcunque; alius habuisset vtilitatem ex pecunia, & ita cum ex pecunia non proveniat aliqua vtilitas (sicut vt communiter nulla vtilitas provenit ex pecunia reposita) in hoc differt vsurarius a mercatore secundum Chrysostomum. Ratio ergo, quare mutuans pecuniam non habet vsuram exigere, est quia mutuans pecuniam transfert le dominium pecuniae, sed quod ex pecunia proveniat vtilitas vel non proveniat, nihil facit ad hoc, quod etiam alio probatur exemplo. Vendens alterius equum non debet, nisi iustum pretium equi exigere: & tamen ex equo potest vtilitas provenire salua substantia equi. Vnde vendens alteri equum non potest equum exigere, & aliquid vltra propter vtilitatem, quam potuit habere ex equo: sed potest exigere iustum pretium equi: & hoc quia transtulit a se dominium equi, & ideo non potest exigere equum tanquam rem propriam: Sed locans domum vel agrum non transfert a se dominium domus vel agri, sed transfert a se potestatem recipiendi vtilitatem ex domo vel agro pro tempore locationis: & ideo domum vel agrum repetet tanquam rem propriam, & exiget aliquid propter potestatem recipiendi vtilitatem translatam in alium. Et ita, sicut non est simile de locante rem & de vendente rem, quia vendens transfert dominium, locans non transfert dominium: ita etiam propter idem non est simile de locante rem & de mutuante pecuniam: quia vnus transfert dominium rei, alius non. Et illa est causa, sicut dictum est, quare concedens pecuniam ad pompam potest repetere pecuniam & aliquid vltra. Potest enim repetere pecuniam tanquam rem propriam: & potest etiam recipere aliquid propter hoc, quod transtulit a se potestatem vtendi pecunia. Dicunt insuper isti impugnatores, quod esto quod ex pecunia non posset aliqua vtilitas salua substantia rei provenire: & propter hoc mutuans pecuniam non debet pro pecunia mutuata vsuram recipere: ex hoc tamen non sequitur, quod nullus potest habere ius vtendi pecunia: sicut nec ex hoc sequitur, quod nullus potest habere ius abutendi pecunia, sic etiam, sicut non sequitur: Nulla potest vtilitas ex pecunia salua substantia pecuniae provenire: ergo nullus potest habere ius abutendi pecunia separatum a dominio seu proprietate. Ita non sequitur, quod nullus potest habere ius abutendi pecunia a proprietate seu dominio separatum. Vnde totus processus istius impugnati ita concluderet de iure abutendi, sicut de iure vtendi, praesertim cum ius vtendi sit communius quam vsus iuris. ( Augustini sententiam.) Hic salsum imponit Augustino, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, quia dicunt, quod Augustinus in libro Confessionum dixit, & ideo dicunt, quod ille impugnatus verba Augustini non adduxit in mente, quia si adduxisset, vt dicunt, apparuisset omnibus, quod falso allegasset Augustinum. ( Actus autem vtendi in rerum natura non est.) Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod ista ratio est similis rationi quorundam Philosophorum antiquorum, propter quam negabant tempus & motum & omnia successiva quae in quarto physicorum habet dissolui, & non hic.
units.tr: Whether the right to use money can be held or cannot be held, and whether the right to use money separated from ownership or property can be held or cannot be held, this is beside the point: for whether it can be held or not, since the lender transfers ownership of the money, he cannot justly afterwards demand anything but the value of the money, and therefore can receive nothing more. Hence, just as a man who sells a house, because he transfers ownership of the house from himself, ought to ask only the value of the house, although the buyer of the house not only has ownership of the house but also the right to use the house and also the profit from the house; so too, one who transfers ownership of money from himself, although the recipient afterwards has ownership and property of the money and also the right to use the money and the profit from it, ought not to receive anything beyond the value of the money, and so if the money is returned to him, he ought not to demand anything more. (Not any fruit or any profit at all.) That has nothing to do with the point, because whether or not the one who receives money on loan has some fruit or profit from the money, the one lending money ought to demand nothing but the value of the money in the same kind, if he wishes, since ownership of it has passed to the borrower; especially since a contract of loan ought to be a gratuitous contract. Hence, just as one who lends a horse to someone freely ought to demand nothing but the horse, however much the other might have profited from the horse, so one who lends money ought to demand nothing but the money, however much the other might have profited from the money. And since no profit comes from money (as commonly no profit comes from money laid up), in this the usurer differs from the merchant, according to Chrysostom. The reason, therefore, why the lender of money may not demand interest is that the lender of money transfers the ownership of the money; but whether profit comes from the money or does not come, has nothing to do with this, which is also proved by another example. One who sells another's horse ought to demand only the just price of the horse, and yet profit can come from a horse while its substance is preserved. Hence the one who sells a horse to another cannot demand the horse, nor anything more on account of the profit he could have had from the horse; but he can demand the just price of the horse, and this because he has transferred ownership of the horse from himself, and therefore he cannot demand the horse as his own property. But one who lets a house or a field does not transfer ownership of the house or field from himself; he transfers from himself only the power of receiving profit from the house or field for the period of the letting. Therefore he will recover the house or field as his own property, and will demand something on account of the power of receiving profit transferred to another. And so, just as there is no likeness between one who lets a thing and one who sells a thing, because the seller transfers ownership and the lessor does not transfer ownership, so for the same reason there is no likeness between one who lets a thing and one who lends money, because the one transfers ownership of the thing and the other does not. And that is the reason, as has been said, why one who lends money for display may recover the money and something more. For he may recover the money as his own property, and he may also receive something on account of having transferred from himself the power of using the money. Moreover, these opponents say that even if no profit could come from money while its substance is preserved, and for this reason the lender of money ought not to receive interest on the money lent, it does not follow from this that no one can have the right to use money; just as it does not follow from this that no one can have the right to consume money, and so too, just as it does not follow that no profit can come from money while the substance of the money is preserved, therefore no one can have the right to consume money separated from ownership or property; so it does not follow that no one can have the right to consume money separated from ownership or property. Hence the whole argument of this opponent would conclude about the right to consume as much as about the right to use, especially since the right to use is more general than the use of a right. (The opinion of Augustine.) Here he falsely attributes something to Augustine, as these opponents say, because they say that Augustine in the book of his Confessions said it, and therefore they say that the opponent did not bring the words of Augustine to mind; for if he had brought them to mind, as they say, it would have appeared to everyone that he had cited Augustine falsely. (But the act of using is not in the nature of things.) These opponents say that this reasoning is similar to the reasoning of certain ancient philosophers, on account of which they denied time, motion, and all successive things, which are resolved in the fourth book of the Physics, and not here.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: ADillud autem, quod dicit: Ex prædictis scripturis sacris insinuatur aperte, quod nullius rei temporalis nec vsu consumptibilis, nec non consumptibilis vsu proprietatem credentes habebant: Dicimus, si intelligat, quod in speciali proprietatem non habebant credentes, verum esse quod dicit pro tempore illo primo, pro quo dicta scriptura loquitur, quia hic expresse scriptura prædicta dicit Actuum 4. ibi, cum dicit: Nec quisquam eorum quæ possidebat aliquid suum esse dicebat. Si autem intelligat, sicut & intelligo, vt per ea quæ proponit inferius clare patet, quod credentes nullius rei proprietatem habebant etiam in communi, scriptura prædicta contradixit expresse, cum dicat, quod ipsis (scilicet credentibus) omnia quæ possidebant erant communia inter eos, & quod illa communio quo ad dominium & proprietatem intelligi debeat, ex eo patet, quia illud, quod prius ante conuersionem Iudæorum ipsis fuerat proprium, postquam credentes effecti fuerunt, fuit inter eos communicatum. Constat autem, quod illa quæ possidebant ante conuersionem erant illi quantum ad dominium propria, alias enim illa communicare non poterant; quare sequitur, quod fuerunt quo ad proprietatem seu dominium inter eos communicata, quod de rebus non consumptibilibus vsu scriptura prædicta Actuum 4. aperte dicit, nisi violentia sibi fiat. Cum enim dixisset: nec quisquam eorum quæ possidebat aliquid suum esse dicebat: sed erant eis omnia communia, parum past sequitur: nec quisquam egens erat inter eos, & causam huius volens reddere subdit: Quotquot enim erant possessores agrorum & domorum vendentes pretia portabant ante pedes Apostolorum &c. Cum ergo prius dicat, quod inter credentes omnia erant communia: & post subiungat, quod agri vendebantur & domus, euidenter apparet quod illa erant effecta communia antequam venderentur. Alias enim sequeretur, quod remansissent istorum, quorum prius erant propria, & per consequens, quod ipsi ante ipsorum venditionem remansissent proprietarii, cuius tamen contrarium dicit scriptura prædicta, cum dicit, quod nec quisquam eorum qui possidebat, aliquid suum esse dicebat.
units.tr: As for what he says, that from the aforementioned holy Scriptures it is clearly indicated that believers had no ownership of any temporal thing, whether consumable by use or not consumable by use: I answer that, if he means that believers did not have private ownership, what he says is true for that first time to which the Scripture I have cited refers, since the Scripture expressly says in Acts 4: "Nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own." But if he means, as I do, and as is clear from what he sets out below, that believers had no ownership of anything even in common, the aforementioned Scripture expressly contradicts him, since it says that all that they possessed was held in common among them. That this communion must be understood with respect to ownership and property is clear from the fact that what had been their own before the Jews' conversion became shared among them after they became believers. It is certain that what they possessed before their conversion was their own as far as ownership went, for otherwise they could not have shared it. It follows that, as regards property or ownership, things were shared among them. Acts 4 says plainly that this holds for things not consumable by use, unless force is applied to them. For after saying, "Nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own, but everything was common to them," it adds, a little later, "Nor was there anyone needy among them," and, wishing to give the reason for this, it continues: "For as many as were owners of fields or houses sold them and brought the price and laid it at the feet of the apostles," and so on. Since it first says that all things were common among the believers, and then adds that fields and houses were sold, it is clearly evident that they had been made common before they were sold. Otherwise it would follow that the goods remained the property of those to whom they had previously belonged, and consequently that those people remained owners before they sold them, which is the opposite of what the aforementioned Scripture says when it states that none of those who possessed anything said it was his own.

units.la: Postquam in parte precedenti impugnatus circa illa quæ impugnabantur suam intentionem expressit, hoc ad illa quæ impugnas proposuit, nititur respondere. Et diuiditur illa pars in quinq; secundum quod ad quinq; tacta in illa impugnatione respondet. Secunda incipit in parte immediate sequente ibi: Ad illud autem quod voles. Tertia autem ibi: Ad id quod sequitur. Quarta autem ibi: Quantum autem ad illud. Quinta ibi: Ad vero quod dicit ille hereticus.
units.tr: Having, in the previous part, set out his own view on the points he was attacking, the critic now tries to answer the points he has raised against it. This part is divided into five, according to the five points touched on in that attack. The second begins in the next part, with the words "As for what you wished"; the third with "As for what follows"; the fourth with "As for what"; and the fifth with "As for what that heretic says."

units.la: In prima ergo parte respondet ad hanc propositionem, acceptam in appellatione impugnantis, & probatam ex scripturis: Credentes (de quibus fit mentio Actuum 2 & 4.) nullius rei temporalis nec vsu consumptibilis, nec rei non consumptibilis vsu proprietatem habebant, distinguens ipsam, quod potest habere duplicem intellectum: quia aut potest intelligi de proprietate in speciali, & sic exponit eam pro aliquo tempore: vel potest intelligi de proprietate in communi, quem intellectum appellanti imponit, & illum intellectum negat: quia dicit, quod scripturæ prædictæ repugnat, cum dicit, quod credentibus omnia quæ possidebant erant communia quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Et primo quidem ostendit in genere, quod omnia erant illis communia quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Secundo ostendit specialiter, quod res non consumptibiles vsu, vt puta domus, ager & huiusmodi, erant omnibus communes quo ad dominium & proprietatem, ibi quod de rebus non consumptibilibus vsu &c. Primum ostendit tali ratione, illa quæ ante conuersionem Iudæorum, de quibus ibi fit mentio, erant eis propria: post conuersionem erant eis effecta communia, sed ante conuersionem omnia erant eis propria quo ad dominium & proprietatem, ergo post conuersionem erant eis communia quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Maior illa videtur sibi manifesta, minorem probat per hoc, quod si ante conuersionem non fuissent bona eorum eis communia, non habuissent potestatem communicandi illa bona communitati credentium. Secundum scilicet quod res non consumptibiles vsu, sicut domus ager & huiusmodi erant toti communitati fidelium communes quo ad dominium & proprietatem, probat sic. Ager & domus vendebantur postquam omnia quæ credentes habebant erant facta communia toti communitati credentium. Hanc probat dupliciter. Primo sic ex ordinatione textus Actuum Apostolorum; quia primo dicitur, quod omnia erant illi communia: & postea dicitur quod nullus erat egens inter eos, cuius causa assignatur, quia quotquot erant possessores agrorum &c. ergo ante venditionem agrorum omnia erant communia.
units.tr: In the first part, he answers the proposition, taken from the wording of the critic and supported by Scripture, that believers (mentioned in Acts 2 and 4) had no ownership of any temporal thing, whether consumable by use or not consumable by use. He distinguishes it, pointing out that it can have two meanings: either it can be understood of private ownership, and in that case he explains it as applying to a certain time; or it can be understood of ownership in common. This second meaning he attributes to his opponent, and he denies it, because he says that it contradicts the Scripture, which says that for believers all that they possessed was common as regards ownership and property. First, he shows in general that everything was common to them as regards ownership and property. Second, he shows in particular that things not consumable by use, such as houses, fields and the like, were common to all as regards ownership and property, at the words "that as for things not consumable by use," and so on. He proves the first point by this argument: the things that before the Jews' conversion, which is mentioned there, were their own have become common to them after the conversion; but before the conversion everything was their own as regards ownership and property; therefore after the conversion it was common to them as regards ownership and property. He takes the major premise to be self-evident, and proves the minor by the fact that if their goods had not been common to them before the conversion, they would not have had the power to share those goods with the community of believers. As for the second point, namely that things not consumable by use, such as houses, fields and the like, were common to the whole community of the faithful as regards ownership and property, he proves it thus: fields and houses were sold after everything the believers had was made common to the whole community of believers. He proves this in two ways. First, from the order of the text of the Acts of the Apostles: for it is first said that everything was common to them, and afterwards it is said that there was no one needy among them, the reason given being that as many as were owners of fields and so on; therefore before the sale of the fields everything was common.

units.la: Secundo probat eadem ducens ad inconueniens: quia si ager & domus non fuissent effecti communes antequam venderent, ante venditionem remansissent proprii illorum, quorum fuerant ante conuersionem, ex quo sequitur, quod post conuersionem & ante venditionem domorum & agrorum ipsi fuissent proprietarii, quod repugnat scripturæ, cum dicit: Nec quisquam eorum quæ possidebat aliquid suum esse dicebat. Videtur ergo, quod domus, ager & huiusmodi res non consumptibiles vsu efficiebantur communes toti communitati credentium, antequam venderetur, sed res huiusmodi prius erant proprie quo ad dominium & proprietatem, ergo postea fuerunt communes quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Sic igitur impugnatus id quod dicitur in Actibus Apostolorum de communitate bonorum credentium, & de venditione domorum & agrorum & rerum non consumptibilium vsu: sic intelligit, quod videlicet illi Iudæi conuersi, de quibus ibi fit mentio, statim facta conuersione omnia quæ habebant mobilia & immobilia dederunt toti illi communitati credentium transferendo in totam communitatem illam id dominium quod prius ipsi habuerant, postea possessiones vendebant in nomine totius communitatis, & non nomine alicuius in speciali, quibus venditis pretium illarum rerum inter eos diuidebatur, & vnusquisq; habuit dominium & proprietatem possessionis sibi assignatæ.
units.tr: Second, he proves the same point by showing an absurdity: if the fields and houses had not been made common before they were sold, then before the sale they would have remained the property of those to whom they had belonged before the conversion. From this it follows that after the conversion, and before the sale of the houses and fields, those people would still have been owners, which contradicts Scripture when it says: "Nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own." It seems, then, that houses, fields and similar things not consumable by use became common to the whole community of believers before they were sold; but such things had previously been their own as regards ownership and property, therefore afterwards they were common as regards ownership and property. Thus the critic understands what is said in the Acts of the Apostles about the sharing of the goods of the believers, and about the sale of houses and fields and of things not consumable by use, in this way: that is, those converted Jews, mentioned there, as soon as they were converted gave all their movable and immovable goods to the whole community of believers, transferring to that entire community the ownership that they had previously held; afterwards they sold the properties in the name of the whole community and not in the name of any individual; when these were sold the price of those things was divided among them, and each one had ownership and property of the portion assigned to him.

units.la: Circa illa, quæ dicuntur hic, isti impugnatores sic procedunt. Primo enim eliciunt quædam notabilia, quę etiam iste impugnatus habet cōcedere. Secundo explicant intentionem appellantis circa illam ꝑpositionem, q̄ iste hic impugnat. Tertio plura quæ asserit hic iste impugnatus, reprobare conantur. Circa primū dicunt isti impugnatores, ꝓ ex dictis istius impugnati patet aperte, ꝓ etiam secundū eum duplex est ꝑprietas, scil. in speciali & in cōi, siue specialis & cōis. Ex quo sequitur vlterius secundum notabile, ꝓ dominium est duplex sc. in speciali & in cōi. Ex quo seqtur tertium notabile, ꝓ vsus facti, sicut actus comedendi & bibendi, potè à dominio in speciali separari. Quartū notabile, ꝓ elicitur ex dictis istius impugnati, est ꝓ dominiū, de quo loquitur iste impugnatus, in hoc casu mundanū & ciuile dominium est: quia est ptās vel habens annexam potestatem libere vendendi donandi, & sicut sibi placuerit disponendi res quarū habetur dominiū. Nam ipse vult, ꝓ illi conuersi de Iudęis quale dominiū spāle habuerant ante conuersionē, tale dominiū totī cōitati credentium conuersoꝛum dederunt, sed Iudæi conuersi ante conuersionē suam habuerunt in rebus suis ꝑdictum dominiū: sc. ciuile & mundanū, ꝓ est ptās vel habens annexā potātem vendendi &c. Nam Iudęi legibus Romanorū quantum ad res ꝑales subiecti fuerunt, & ita dominiū rerum ciuile & mundanū habebant, unde res suas ad placitum vendere poterant & dare, & de eis libere ordinare, ergo tale dominium ciuile & mundanū cōitati dederunt. Secundo isti impugnatores intentionē explicant appellantis, dicentes ꝓ appellans ibidē solummodo intendebat ꝑbare, ꝓ primi credentes nullius rei proprietate habebant in speciali, reputans certū ex hoc posse ꝑbari, quod vsus facti rerum consumptibiliū vsu, potè à proprietate & dominio etiā in communi separari. Vnde ad euidentiā intentionis appellatis faciunt duo. Primo enim ꝑbant, quod si vsus facti rerum consumptibilium vsu, scil. actus comedendi, bibendi, & induendi & huiusmodi potest separari à dominio in speciali, ꝓ etiam potest separari à proprietate & dominio in cōi. Secundo exponunt qualē proprietatem habebant primi credentes in rebus quas habebant: & qualem non. Ex hoc concludentes, ꝓ ille impugnatus solummodo sophistice reprobat appellantē. Ad euidentiā primi dicunt isti impugnatores esse sciendū, ꝓ prout ex diuersis assertionibus impugnati & appellantis euidenter apparet, ex hoc controuersia orta est inter ipsos: ꝓ appellans dicebat Ordinem Fratrum Minorū seu Fratres Minores habere vsum rerū vsu consumptibilium absq; ꝑprietate & dominio earundē, tam in speciali q̄ etiam in cōi: ita ꝓ nec Frater aliquis in speciali, nec totus Ordo in cōi habet dominiū vel proprietatē cuiuscunq; rei vsu consumptibilis, nolens per hoc excludere Fratres ab illo dominio, quod cōpetit toti generi humano, si aliquod est tale: nec volens excludere Fratres à dominio totius cōitatis fidelium, si dominiū commune alicuius rei temporalis habet tota cōitas fidelium: sed volebat excludere Fratres ab omni dominio, p quod possent in iudicio litigare ꝑprio Fratri vel toti Ordini fraterno. Ille autem impugnatus volebat ꝑbare p multas rationes, ꝓ in rebus vsu consumptibilibus vsus facti nō potest à tali dominio spāli & cōi separari, & contra illam assertionē ille appellans ꝑuocauit ostendens multis rationibus, ꝓ vsus facti in huiusmodi rebus potē ꝑprietate & dominio ciuile & mundano separari, tā in speciali q̄ in communi. Non omnes rationes tamen ꝑbant istam conclusionem æque directe & æque immediate, q̄uis ex qualibet ratione appellantis q̄busdā veris assumptis posset conclusio illa deduci. Vnde prima ratio appellantis primo & immediate concludit, ꝓ vsus facti in rebus consumptibilibus potè ꝑprietate & dominio speciali separari. Ex quo potest inferri vlterius, ꝓ vsus facti potè à proprietate & dominio cōi separari, ꝓ isti impugnatores ostendunt sic. Vsus facti non magis nec minus requirit dominiū commune q̄ speciale, sed vsus facti potest in huiusmodi rebus separari à dominio speciali, sicut ꝑbat prima ratio appellantis, ergo potest separari à dominio in cōi. Et qdem quod vsus facti possit separari à dominio cōi, est tam manifestum, quod negari non potest. Nam constat, quod ꝑprietarii habentes ꝑprietatē & dominium in speciali rerū vsu consumptibiliū habent vsum facti earundem rerum separatum à dominio cōi: quia illę res non sunt cōes, sed ꝑpriæ sibi. Sed quia forte dicet ille impugnatus, quod licet vsus facti in rebus vsu consumptibilibus possit separari à dominio spāli, sicut in reliquis habentibus vsū hmōi rerū absq; dominio spāli: & etiam à dominio cōi, sicut patet in laicis habentibus spāle dominium huiusmodi rerū, & ita vsus facti potest separari ab vtroq; dominio diuisim, non tamen ab vtroq; coniunctim sc. simul tā à dominio spāli quam communi. Vnde in laico vsus facti separatur à dominio communi, sed non à dominio in speciali, in Religioso vero separatur à dominio speciali, sed non à dominio communi, & propter hoc diceret forte, quod non potest separari ab vtroq; dominio simul & cōiunctim. Ideo isti impugnatores ostendunt, quod vsus facti in huiusmodi rebus potest separari ab vtroq; dominio simul, quemadmodū dicunt Fratres Minores, quod habent vsum facti huiusmodi rerū consumptibilium vsu: & tamen nō habent earundē dominium, nec in speciali nec in communi. Ex quo orta est tota discordia quantū ad separationē vsus facti in huiusmodi rebus à dominio & ꝑprietate inter istū impugnatum & appellantē. Porro quia vsus facti in hmōi rebus est duplex, sc. licitus & illicitus: ideo de vtroq; vsu facti ꝑbant, quod potest simul ab vtroq; dominio separari. De illicito videtur omnino certū. Nam fur, qui furatus est panē & vinum, si vtatur ipsis, non ꝑpter hoc acquirit dominium neq; speciale neq; cōis ipsorum, ergo ille vsus facti ab vtroq; dominio separatur, quod etiā vsus licitus potest ab vtroq; dominio separari, ostendunt rationibus & exēplis. Prima ratio talis est: ad hoc ꝓ vsus facti alicuius non sit illicitus, duo communiter videntur sufficere. Primum est, quod talis vsus facti nō sit volenti vti inhibitus. Secundum quod habeant licentiam vtendi ab illo, qui potest licentiam talem concedere, sed ista etiam possunt haberi absq; dominio speciali & cōi: sicut aliqs, cui non est inhibitum, seu prohibitum certam vestem induere, potest habere licentiā induendi talem vestem à dōo absque concessione dominii speciālis vel communis, ergo vsus licitus vestis potest ab vtroque dominio separari. Secunda ratio talis est: Sicut dominium commune non est magis inefficax ad faciendum vsum facti esse licitum, quam dominium speciale, quia ita licite vtitur aliquis re communi, si aliquid aliud speciale non obstat, sicut re propria, ita licita potestas vtendi non est magis inefficax ad faciendum vsum facti esse licitum quam dominium commune, ergo ad hoc quod vsus facti sit licitus, sufficit licita potestas vtendi communissima, ita quod dominium non requiritur, licet saepe ad aliud requiratur, sed licita potestas vtendi communissima est potestas vtendi, quam Deus in primis parentibus toti humano generi dedit post peccatum vel ante, ergo omni dominio amoto, & nullo alio obstante, stante tali potestate vtendi potest vsus facti esse licitus. Si ergo est aliqua res vsu consumptibilis, quae sub nullius est dominio, illa potestas vtendi communissima sufficit ad hoc, quod aliqs eadem relicite vtatur, si aliud non obstat, ergo talis rei vsus facti potest esse licitus absq; omni dominio: & per consequens vsus facti licitus rei vsu consumptibilis potest ab omni dominio speciali & communi separari. Illa ratio magis patebit, si declarata fuerit per exemplum. Ponatur igitur, quod sit aliqua res, puta vestis habita pro derelicta, quae in nullius bonis sit, nec ad alicuius speciem dominium neq; speciale neq; commune. Ista veste potest quis licite vti saltem in necessitate extrema: licet nolit acquirere dominium quodcunq; eiusdem vestis, non enim ad hoc, quod licite vtatur ipsa, est necesse quod acquirat dominium eius commune, nec etiam dominium eius speciale, igitur ad hoc, quod licite vtatur veste, sufficit potestas vtendi data a Deo: & ita licitus vsus facti vestis potest separari a dominio speciali & communi, licet non a potestate vtendi, cui nemo potest renunciare. Sed forte obiiciet aliquis contra hanc rationem dupliciter, primo, quia talis potestas vtendi data toti generi humano est quoddam dominium: & ita cum actus vtendi licitus non possit separari a tali potestate vtendi, non poterit separari ab omni dominio. Secundo, quia non videtur, quod sit talis licita potestas vtendi data toti humano generi, cui renunciari non possit: quia tunc fur haberet licitam potestatem vtendi re quam furatus est: quod videtur absurdum. Ad primam istorum dicunt, quod talis potestas vtendi non debet vocari dominium: sicut nec licita potestas vtendi dominio, quam habet conducens domum, debet vocari dominium domus: quia semper dominium, de quo in iure ciuili & canonico fit mentio, est aliquid aliud a potestate vtendi: ita quod sola potestas vtendi non est dominium. Si autem omnino contendas quod talis potestas vtendi data toti humano generi debet vocari dominium, dicunt quod de vocibus non intendunt contendere. Dicunt tamen, quod esto, quod talis potestas vtendi vocetur dominium, adhuc stat argumentum, quod licitus vsus facti potest separari in rebus consumptibilibus vsu, ab omni dominio speciali & communi, quod sit proprium alicui collegio speciali, quale est collegium Fratrum Minorum vel consimile, quod appellans solum modo probare volebat. Vnde loco istius termini licita potestas vtendi communissima, ponatur ille terminus dominium communissimum: & arguatur sic: sicut dominium commune non est magis efficax ad faciendum vsum facti esse licitum quam dominium speciale: ita dominium communissimum, quod datum fuit toti generi humano, non est magis efficax ad faciendum vsum facti esse licitum, quam dominium speciale minus commune. Et fiat vlterius argumentum de dominio communissimo, sicut prius argutum est de licita potestate vtendi communissima: & concludatur, quod vsus facti huiusmodi potest esse licitus absq; dominio speciali & communi, quod sit proprium alicui collegio speciali.
units.tr: Concerning what is said here, these opponents proceed as follows. First, they draw out certain notable points, which the one under attack must also concede. Second, they explain the intention of the appellant regarding that proposition which the one under attack opposes here. Third, they try to refute several claims which the one under attack asserts here. On the first point, these opponents say that it is clear from the statements of the one under attack that, according to him, ownership is twofold, namely special and common. From this follows a second notable point: dominion is twofold, special and common. From this follows a third notable point: the use of a thing in fact, such as the act of eating and drinking, can be separated from special dominion. A fourth notable point, drawn from the statements of the one under attack, is that the dominion he is speaking of in this case is worldly and civil dominion. For a property holder, or one who has attached to it the power to sell, give and dispose freely of the things he owns, as he pleases, is such a dominion. He holds that the converted Jews gave to the whole community of believing converts the same special dominion they had held before their conversion. But the Jews, before their conversion, had in their own goods this civil and worldly dominion, which is the property or possession with the power of selling, and so on. For under Roman law the Jews were subject to the Romans as regards their property, and so they held civil and worldly dominion over their goods. Hence they could sell and give their goods at will and dispose of them freely. Therefore they gave this civil and worldly dominion to the community. Second, these opponents explain the intention of the appellant, saying that in that place the appellant only meant to prove that the first believers had no ownership of anything in particular. He thought this could be proved from the fact that the use of a thing in fact, in the case of consumable things, can be separated from ownership and dominion even in common. Accordingly, two things serve to make the appellant's intention clear. First, he proves that if the use in fact of consumable things, namely the acts of eating, drinking, clothing oneself and the like, can be separated from special dominion, then it can also be separated from ownership and dominion in common. Second, he sets out what kind of ownership the first believers had in the things they possessed, and what kind they did not have. From this they conclude that the one under attack refutes the appellant only by sophistry. To make the first point clear, these opponents say that it must be understood that the dispute between them arose from the differing assertions of the one attacked and the appellant, as is evident. The appellant said that the Order of Friars Minor, or the Friars Minor, have the use of consumable things without ownership or dominion over them, both in particular and in common. So neither any friar in particular nor the whole Order in common has dominion or ownership of any consumable thing. He did not wish by this to exclude the friars from that dominion which belongs to the whole human race, if there is any such dominion. Nor did he wish to exclude the friars from the dominion of the whole community of the faithful, if the whole community of the faithful has a common dominion over some temporal thing. He wished rather to exclude the friars from every dominion by which they could go to law against a particular friar or against the whole fraternal Order. The one under attack, however, wished to prove by many arguments that in consumable things the use in fact cannot be separated from such special and common dominion. Against that assertion the appellant contended, showing by many arguments that the use in fact of such things can be separated from ownership and from civil and worldly dominion, both in particular and in common. Yet not all his arguments proved this conclusion equally directly and equally immediately, although from each of the appellant's arguments that conclusion could be deduced from certain true assumptions. Hence the appellant's first argument concludes primarily and immediately that the use in fact of consumable things can be separated from ownership and special dominion. From this it can further be inferred that the use in fact can be separated from common ownership and dominion, as these opponents show thus: the use in fact requires common dominion no more and no less than special dominion; but the use in fact can in such things be separated from special dominion, as the appellant's first argument proves; therefore it can be separated from common dominion. And indeed that the use in fact can be separated from common dominion is so manifest that it cannot be denied. For it is plain that proprietors who have ownership and dominion in particular over consumable things have the use in fact of those same things separated from common dominion, because those things are not common but are their own. But perhaps the one under attack will say that, although the use in fact of consumable things can be separated from special dominion, as it is in others who have the use of such things without special dominion, and also from common dominion, as is evident in laymen who have special dominion over such things, and so the use in fact can be separated from each dominion separately, yet it cannot be separated from both dominions together, that is, at once from special and from common dominion. Thus in a layman the use in fact is separated from common dominion but not from special dominion, while in a religious it is separated from special dominion but not from common dominion, and for this reason he might perhaps say that it cannot be separated from both dominions at once and together. Therefore these opponents show that the use in fact of such things can be separated from both dominions at once, just as the Friars Minor say that they have the use in fact of consumable things by using them, and yet they have no dominion over them, neither in particular nor in common. From this the whole disagreement arose, between the one under attack and the appellant, concerning the separation of the use in fact of such things from dominion and ownership. Moreover, since the use in fact of such things is twofold, namely lawful and unlawful, they therefore prove that of both kinds of use in fact it can be separated at once from both dominions. Concerning the unlawful use, the matter seems entirely certain. For a thief who has stolen bread and wine, if he uses them, does not on that account acquire dominion over them, either special or common. Therefore that use in fact is separated from both dominions. That even lawful use can be separated from both dominions, they show by arguments and examples. The first argument runs thus: for the use in fact of anything not to be unlawful, two things commonly seem sufficient. The first is that such use in fact is not forbidden to one who wishes to use it. The second is that one has permission to use it from the one who can grant such permission. But these two things can also be had without special and common dominion. For example, someone to whom it is not forbidden or prohibited to wear a certain garment can have permission from the lord to wear such a garment without any grant of special or common dominion. Therefore the lawful use of a garment can be separated from both dominions. The second argument runs thus: just as common dominion is no less effective than special dominion in making the use in fact lawful, since someone uses a common thing lawfully, provided nothing else special stands in the way, just as he uses his own thing, so the lawful power of using is no less effective than common dominion in making the use in fact lawful. Therefore, for the use in fact to be lawful, the most common lawful power of using is sufficient, so that dominion is not required, although it is often required for something else. But the most common lawful power of using is the power of using which God gave to the whole human race in the first parents, either before or after the fall. Therefore, with all dominion removed and nothing else standing in the way, while such a power of using remains, the use in fact can be lawful. If, then, there is some consumable thing which is under no one's dominion, that most common power of using is sufficient for anyone to use it lawfully, if nothing else stands in the way. Therefore the use in fact of such a thing can be lawful without any dominion. Consequently the lawful use in fact of a consumable thing can be separated from all special and common dominion. This argument will become clearer if it is explained by an example. Let it be supposed, then, that there is some thing, say a garment, regarded as abandoned, which belongs to no one's goods, and over which there is no dominion, special or common, of anyone. Someone can use that garment lawfully, at least in extreme necessity, even if he is unwilling to acquire any ownership of it. For in order to use it lawfully it is not necessary that he acquire common dominion over it, nor even special dominion over it. Therefore, to use the garment lawfully, the power of using given by God is sufficient. And so the lawful use in fact of the garment can be separated from special and common dominion, although not from the power of using, which no one can renounce. But perhaps someone will object to this argument in two ways. First, because such a power of using given to the whole human race is a kind of dominion; and so, since lawful use cannot be separated from such a power of using, it cannot be separated from every dominion. Second, because it does not seem that such a lawful power of using given to the whole human race can be renounced; for then a thief would have a lawful power of using the thing he has stolen, which seems absurd. To the first objection they answer that such a power of using ought not to be called dominion, just as the lawful power of using which a tenant has in a house ought not to be called dominion of the house.
