For the dominion of which mention is made in civil and canon law is always something other than the power of using, so that the power of using alone is not dominion. But if you insist altogether that such a power of using given to the whole human race ought to be called dominion, they say that they do not intend to contend about words. Yet they say that, even granting that such a power of using is called dominion, the argument still stands: that the lawful use in fact in consumable things can be separated from every special and common dominion, which is proper to some particular college, such as the college of the Friars Minor or something similar, which the appellant wished only to prove. Therefore, in place of this term "most common lawful power of using," let the term "most common dominion" be put, and let the argument run thus: just as common dominion is no more effective than special dominion in making the use in fact lawful, so the most common dominion, which was given to the whole human race, is no more effective in making the use in fact lawful than a less common special dominion. Let the argument about most common dominion be developed further, just as it was argued before about the most common lawful power of using. And let it be concluded that this kind of use in fact can be lawful without special and common dominion, which is proper to some particular college.

units.la: Ad secundum dicunt, quod fur habet licitam potestatem vtendi communissimam respectu rei, quam furatus est, sed aliquid aliud obstat, quare tunc non potest licite vti, quia scilicet res est appropriata alteri, qui non dedit specialem potestatem vtendi furi, & ideo illa potestas communissima quasi ligata est, ne possit in actum, nisi tempore necessitatis extremae deduci, sic ergo patet secundum istos, quod licitus vsus facti potest esse in rebus vsu consumptibilibus absq; omni dominio speciali & communi, quod sit proprium alicui collegio speciali. Ex praedictis dicunt isti patere, quod ille impugnatus solum sophistice reprobat appellantem. Nam intentio appellantis est loqui de dominio inuento humanitus, per quod potest quis in iudicio pro rebus temporalibus litigare. Loquendo autem de tali dominio constat, quod qua ratione vsus facti in rebus vsu consumptibilibus potest separari ab vno dominio: eadem ratione potest separari ab omni dominio inuento humanitus. Et ita ostendere quod vsus facti non fuit separatus in primis credentibus a dominio communi, sed a dominio speciali, non est ad rem, nec appellantem vere sed sophistice reprobare. Et ex isto patet, quod licet impugnatio appellantis non concludat, quod quilibet illorum habeat vsum facti rerum consumptibilium vsu, ab omni dominio humanitus inuento speciali & communi separatum: tamen concludit directe, quod Apostoli habuerunt vsum facti rerum consumptibilium vsu a dominio speciali & communi: quod esset proprium Apostolorum collegio separatum. Et ex hoc & praedictis patet, quod tres conclusiones ex ratione appellantis sequuntur. Prima est, quod quilibet istorum scilicet conuersorum & Apostolorum ac discipulorum ipsorum Apostolorum habuerit vsum facti rerum consumptibilium vsu, ab omni dominio speciali & communi pleno & libero, quod vocatur dominium ciuile & mundanum, separatum. Secunda: quod quilibet illorum habuit vsum facti rerum consumptibilium vsu ab omni dominio speciali separatum. Tertia: quod quilibet Apostolorum habuit vsum facti vsu consumptibilium ab omni dominio speciali & communi: quod esset proprium collegio Apostolorum separatum. Istam conclusionem eandem probant isti impugnatores per exempla quam plurima. Primum exemplum accipitur ex dictis istius impugnati. Nam secundum ipsum (sicut patet in verbis superius recitatis) pro aliquo tempore omnia erant Apostolorum lis & primis credentibus communia. Sed constat, quod Apostoli pro illo tempore non erant omnino nudi, ergo pro primo tempore vtebantur vestibus, quæ pertinebant ad dominium totius communitatis, ergo vsus illarum vestium separatus fuit à dominio speciali cuiuscunque Apostoli, & à dominio communi totius collegii Apostolorum: & ita eadem ratione vsus facti huiusmodi rerum, quibus Fratres Minores vtuntur, potest separari à dominio speciali cuiuscunque Fratris Minoris, & à dominio communi totius ordinis eorundem Fratrum. Secundum exemplum est de habente vsum fundi, qui habet licitum vsum pomorum, olerum, florum, & huiusmodi: quorum tamen non habet dominium & proprietatem, neque in speciali neque in communi. Tertium exemplum est de Iudæis tempore veteris legis, qui licitum vsum facti vuarum & spicarum habere poterant in agris & vineis alienis, vt patet Deuteronom. 23. quorum tamen non habebat proprietatem & dominium neque in speciali neque in communi. Quartum exemplum est de hospitibus, qui licite vtuntur cibis, potibus, mappis, lectisterniis, & multis aliis vsu consumptibilibus absq; dominio communi & speciali. Quintum exemplum est de servis, qui licite vtuntur rebus vsu consumptibilibus dominorum suorum, quorum non habent dominium neque speciale neque commune. Sextum exemplum est de filiofamilias, qui vtitur rebus, quorum non habet dominium nec speciale nec commune. Septimum est de sacerdotibus, qui sæpe vtuntur vestimentis diuino cultui deputatis, quorum non habent dominium neque in speciali neque in communi. Octauum exemplum de celebrante, qui vtitur speciebus panis & vini, quæ tamen ad eius non spectant dominium neque speciale neque commune. Sic igitur patet, quod ex hoc, quod per primam rationem appellantis ostenditur, quod vsus facti fuit separatus in primis credentibus quo ad res vsu consumptibiles à dominio speciali, potest probari quibusdã veris coassumptis, quod vsus facti in huiusmodi rebus potest à dominio speciali & cõi separari.
units.tr: To the second point, they say that a thief has a lawful power of using, in the most general sense, the thing he has stolen. But something else stands in the way, so that he cannot lawfully use it: namely, the thing belongs to another, who has not given the thief any specific power of using it. That general power is therefore as it were bound, so that it cannot be put into act except in a time of extreme necessity. So, according to these men, it is plain that a lawful use of fact can exist in things consumed by use, without any specific or common ownership that belongs to some particular corporate body. From what has been said, these men argue, it is clear that the one attacked refutes the appellant only sophistically. For the appellant's intention is to speak of ownership devised by human law, through which a person may sue in court for temporal goods. Speaking of such ownership, it is evident that by the same reasoning by which the use of fact in consumable goods can be separated from one kind of ownership, it can be separated from every kind of ownership devised by human law. And so to show that the use of fact was not separated from common ownership in the first believers, but from specific ownership, is beside the point, and does not truly refute the appellant but only sophistically. And from this it is plain that, although the attack on the appellant does not prove that each of them had the use of fact in consumable goods separated from every specific and common ownership devised by human law, it does directly prove that the Apostles had the use of fact in consumable goods separated from specific and common ownership, which would be proper to the college of Apostles. And from this and what was said before, it is clear that three conclusions follow from the appellant's argument. The first is that each of these, namely the converts, the Apostles and the disciples of the Apostles themselves, had the use of fact in consumable goods separated from every specific and common ownership, full and free, which is called civil and worldly ownership. The second: that each of them had the use of fact in consumable goods separated from every specific ownership. The third: that each of the Apostles had the use of fact in consumable goods separated from every specific and common ownership, which would be proper to the college of Apostles. These same opponents prove this same conclusion by very many examples. The first example is taken from the words of this man under attack. For according to him (as is plain from the words quoted above), for some time all things were common to the Apostles and the first believers. But it is certain that the Apostles, for that time, were not altogether naked; therefore in that first time they used clothes which belonged to the ownership of the whole community. Therefore the use of those clothes was separated from the specific ownership of any Apostle, and from the common ownership of the whole college of Apostles. And so by the same reasoning, the use of fact in such things as the Friars Minor use can be separated from the specific ownership of any Friar Minor, and from the common ownership of the whole order of those Friars. The second example is of a person who has the use of a field, and who has the lawful use of apples, herbs, flowers and the like, of which, however, he has neither ownership nor property, either specific or common. The third example is of the Jews in the time of the old law, who could have the lawful use of fact of grapes and ears of grain in other people's fields and vineyards, as is plain from Deuteronomy 23, and yet they had no property or ownership of them, either specific or common. The fourth example is of guests, who lawfully use food, drink, napkins, bedding and many other things consumed by use, without common or specific ownership. The fifth example is of servants, who lawfully use the consumable goods of their masters, of which they have neither specific nor common ownership. The sixth example is of the son under his father's authority, who uses things of which he has neither specific nor common ownership. The seventh is of priests, who often use vestments set apart for divine worship, of which they have neither specific nor common ownership. The eighth example is of the celebrant, who uses the species of bread and wine, which nonetheless do not belong to him by either specific or common ownership. Thus it is plain that from what is shown by the appellant's first argument, namely that the use of fact in the first believers was separated from specific ownership as regards consumable goods, it can be proved, with some true premises added, that the use of fact in such goods can be separated from specific and common ownership.

units.la: Secundo circa explicationem intentionis appellantis isti impugnatores exponunt, qualem proprietatem habuerunt primi credentes in rebus, quas habebant postquam omnia facta fuerunt communia, dicentes quod (sicut tactum est prius.) proprietas est duplex, quemadmodum dominium est duplex, quoddam enim dominium est ciuile & mundanum, quod est potestas rem in iudicio vendicandi & de re ad libitum disponendi, & hoc vocatur à nonnullis dominium liberum & absolutum, ab aliquibus vocatur plenum dominium. Aliud est dominium, quod est potestas principalis vendicandi rem in iudicio, quale dominium, sicut ostensum est prius, habet nunc de facto clerici in rebus ecclesiæ: tamen pro cautillationibus amouendis dicunt isti impugnatores, q; potestatum principalium vendicandi rem in iudicio, quædam est principalis, quædam principalior, & quædam principalissima. De membris istius distinctionis non duxi exemplificandum ad præsens, per ipsam tamen multæ obiectiones possibiles fieri possunt excludi. Dicunt igitur isti impugnatores, quod primum dominium vel proprietatem non habebant primi credentes in rebus, quas habebant: quia ex ordinatione ipsorum, quam forte mutare non poterant, ita fuit constitutum inter eos, vt de rebus, quas habebant omnes de communitate illa, sustentaretur vnusquisque secundum quod indigeret, nec poterant res illas in alios vsus conuertere, nec per modum alium alienare, & ita non habebant dominium liberum siue plenum in illis rebus. Dominium secundo modo dictum, quod fuit dominium simile Dominio, quod habent nunc clerici in rebus ecclesiæ, habuerunt secundum aliquos primi credentes, & hoc vel tota communitas omnium ibidem fidelium, vel communitas illorum qui non erant Apostoli. Non enim videtur verisimile, si infideles res illas abstulissent, quin aliq fideles habuissent potestatem easdem res in iudicio repetendi. Nec videtur fuisse vtile & expediens, q; tota communitas fidelium tali potestate se priuasset inter tot infideles & cupidos constituta. Videtur ergo, quod in rebus istis talem potestatem in communi habuerunt primi credentes: & hoc vel tota communitas, vel aliqua pars communitatis, Apostoli tamen, vt dicunt, non habuerunt talem proprietatem nec in speciali nec in communi: sic quod talis proprietas competiisset soli collegio Apostolorum, vt postea patebit.
units.tr: Secondly, in explaining the appellant's intention, these opponents set out what kind of property the first believers had in the goods they possessed after all things had been made common. They say that (as was said before) property is twofold, just as ownership is twofold. For one kind of ownership is civil and worldly, which is the power of claiming a thing in court and disposing of it at will; some call this free and absolute ownership, and some call it full ownership. The other kind is the power of principal claim to a thing in court, which kind of ownership, as was shown earlier, the clergy now in fact have in the goods of the Church. Yet, to remove quibbles, these opponents say that among the powers of principal claim to a thing in court, one is principal, another more principal, and another most principal. I have not thought it necessary to give examples of the members of this distinction at present, but through it many possible objections can be excluded. These opponents therefore say that the first believers did not have the first kind of ownership or property in the goods they possessed, because by their own arrangement, which perhaps they could not change, it was established among them that each member of that community should be supported according to his need from the goods all of them held; nor could they turn those goods to other uses or alienate them in any other way. And so they did not have free or full ownership of those goods. The second kind of ownership, which was like the ownership the clergy now have in the goods of the Church, the first believers had, according to some, and this was held either by the whole community of the faithful there, or by the community of those who were not Apostles. For it does not seem likely that, if unbelievers had carried off those goods, some of the faithful would not have had the power to reclaim the same goods in court. Nor does it seem to have been useful and expedient that the whole community of the faithful should have deprived itself of such a power, when it was set among so many unbelievers and covetous men. It seems therefore that the first believers had such a power over those goods in common, and this was held either by the whole community or by some part of the community; but the Apostles, as they say, did not have such property either specifically or in common, so that such property belonged to the college of Apostles alone, as will be shown later.

units.la: Circa tertium principale istius totius partis dicunt isti impugnatores, q; in responsione istius impugnati superius recitata duo errores principaliter continentur. Primus est, quod omnia, quæ erant communia primis credentibus, erant communia quo ad dominium tale, quale in ipsis bonis ante suam conuersionem habuerant. Secundus est, q; domus, ager & huiusmodi immobilia erant communia toti communitati, quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Primum errorem impugnant per hoc, q; scripturæ sacræ repugnat. Ad cuius evidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod Iudæi conuersi ante conuersionem suam tale dominium habuerunt in bonis suis, q; de eis poterant libere ordinare vendendo, donando, ac etiam vni dare plus, alteri minus ad suæ placitum voluntatis. Vnde dominium liberum habuerunt in ipsis bonis suis, sed postquam conuersi fuerunt ad fidem, & bona sua credentium communitati dederunt: communitas illa non habuit tale dominium in bonis ipsis: quia illa communitas non habuit potestatem vendendi aliquam rem datam, nisi pro aliquo sustentando de communitate. Iterum, illa communitas non habebat potestatem donandi plus minus indigenti, & minus magis indigenti: imo etiam non habebat potestatem dandi multum minus indigenti, & nihil penitus magis indigenti, ergo communitas illa non habuit tale dominium in bonis illis, quale habuerunt Iudæi ante conuersionem suam. Iterum, quilibet Iudæus ante conuersionem suam habuit potestatem transferendi dominium rei suæ in liberum dominium alterius, ita quod poterat sic rem suam dare alteri, q; alter haberet potestatem dandi, vendendi & legendi eandem rem ad suæ libitum voluntatis, sed talem potestatem non habuit illa communitas in rebus temporalibus sibi à Iudæis conuersis collatis: & per consequens illa communitas non habebat tale dominium seu proprietatem, quale habuerunt Iudæi ante conuersionem suam, quod enim tale dominium non habuit illa communitas, expresse probatur per illud Actuum 2. cap. Diuidebant illa omnibus, prout cuique opus erat, & per illud eodem capitulo: diuidebant singulis prout cuique opus erat, vbi dicit Glosa ordinaria: non secundum personas & munera, sed secundum indigentiam. Ex quibus verbis euidenter colligitur, quod illa communitas non poterat licite secundum placitum suae voluntatis res illas collatas dispensare, nec plus dare minus indigenti, & minus magis indigenti: nec poterat illa bona diuidere secundum dignitatem personarum, nec secundum munera oblata, vt plus daret illi qui plura & maiora dedit, & minus illi, qui nihil vel minora communitati dedit, sed tenebatur distribuere illa bona secundum indigentiam personarum, vt magis indigenti plus daret, & minus indigenti minus daret, & ideo quantum ad haec communitas illa magis potestatem dispensandi modo limitato, quem transgredi non licebat, quam dominium in illis bonis videbatur habere. Tamen quantum ad potestatem vendicandi, si iniuste ablata fuisset, videtur in istis bonis aliquale dominium habuisse: sed non tale, quale habuerunt Iudaei, qui bona sua communitati dederunt, antequam conuerterentur ad fidem, & ideo dicunt isti impugnatores, quod scripturae diuinae repugnat de communitate credentium habuisse tale dominium in rebus datis sibi a fidelibus, quale habuerunt dantes antequam conuerterentur ad fidem. Sed quia diceret aliquis, quod iste impugnatus non intendit, quod omnino tale dominium habuerit communitas illa, quale habuerunt Iudaei ante conuersionem. Ideo probant isti impugnatores, quod ratio sua, per quam probat, quod communitas illa habuerit dominium illorum bonorum, aeque concludit de tali dominio, quale habuerunt Iudaei ante conuersionem suam, sicut de alio qualicunque. Nam eadem facilitate, qua dicis, quod illud, quod primo proprium ante conuersionem postea fuit communicatum inter eos, & tamen non habuerunt post dominium tale, quale prius habuerant: eadem facilitate dicetur, quod illud quod erat primo proprium, postea fuit communicatum absque omni proprietate & dominio, quia aliquid potest esse commune multis, quamuis non sit eis commune quantum ad dominium seu proprietatem, sicut per leges imperiales & diuersorum regnorum mores ac consuetudines diuersarum regionum, ac per iura canonica posset copiose probari. Potest enim aliquid esse commune multis per licitam potestatem vtendi vel abutendi absque omni dominio & proprietate, sicut in veteri lege vuae & granaspicarum erant communes quantum ad licitam potestatem comedendi in agro & vinea aliena, quamen non erant communes quantum ad dominium & proprietatem, & ita ex hoc, quod aliquid primo est proprium, & postea commune, aeque potest probari, quod communitas habet dominium tale quale habuerit ille, cuius res fuit propria, sicut potest probari, quod habuerit qualecunque dominium.
units.tr: Concerning the third main point of this whole part, these opponents say that the response of the author under attack, quoted above, contains two main errors. The first is that everything that belonged to the first believers was held in common in the sense of the same ownership that they had in their goods before their conversion. The second is that houses, fields and similar immovable property were held in common by the whole community, as regards ownership and property. They attack the first error on the ground that it contradicts Holy Scripture. To make this clear, they say, it must be understood that Jewish converts, before their conversion, had such ownership of their goods that they could freely dispose of them by selling or giving them away, and could even give more to one person and less to another as they pleased. Thus they had free ownership of their goods. But after they were converted to the faith and gave their goods to the community of believers, that community did not have such ownership of those goods. For the community had no power to sell any thing given to it, except to support someone from the community. Again, the community had no power to give more to one who was less needy and less to one who was more needy; indeed it did not even have the power to give much less to one who was less needy and nothing at all to one who was more needy. Therefore that community did not have over those goods the ownership that the Jews had before their conversion. Again, every Jew before his conversion had the power to transfer the ownership of his property into the free ownership of another, so that he could give his property to someone else in such a way that the other could give, sell and use the same thing at his pleasure. But that community did not have such power over the temporal goods brought to it by the converted Jews. Consequently that community did not have such ownership or property as the Jews had before their conversion. That the community did not have such ownership is clearly proved by the passage in Acts 2, they distributed those things to all, as each had need, and by the same chapter, they distributed to each one as each had need, where the Ordinary Gloss says: not according to persons and offices, but according to need. From these words it is plainly gathered that that community could not lawfully dispense those gifts according to the pleasure of its will, nor give more to the less needy and less to the more needy. Nor could it divide those goods according to the dignity of persons, or according to the gifts offered, so that it would give more to the one who had given more and greater things, and less to the one who had given nothing or lesser things to the community. Rather it was bound to distribute those goods according to the need of persons, giving more to the more needy and less to the less needy. Therefore, in this respect, that community had a power of dispensing, under a fixed limit that it was not lawful to exceed, rather than the ownership it seemed to have in those goods. Yet, as regards the power of recovering them if they had been unjustly taken away, it seems to have had some kind of ownership in those goods, but not such as the Jews had who gave their goods to the community before they were converted to the faith. And so these opponents say that it contradicts divine Scripture to hold that the community of believers had over the things given to it by the faithful such ownership as those who gave them had before they were converted to the faith. But because someone might say that the one under attack did not mean that the community had entirely the same ownership as the Jews had before their conversion, these opponents prove that his argument, by which he proves that the community had ownership of those goods, applies equally to such ownership as the Jews had before their conversion as to any other kind. For with the same ease with which you say that what was first owned privately before conversion was afterwards shared among them, and yet they did not afterwards have the same ownership they had before, with the same ease it may be said that what was first private was afterwards shared without any property or ownership at all. For something can be common to many without their holding it in common as regards ownership or property, as could be amply proved from the imperial laws, the customs of various kingdoms and the usages of different regions, and from the canon law. For something can be common to many through a lawful power of using or consuming it without any ownership or property. Thus in the old law grapes and ears of grain were common, as regards the lawful right to eat them in another's field and vineyard, yet they were not common as regards ownership and property. And so from the fact that something was first private and afterwards common, it can equally be proved that the community has such ownership as he had whose property it was, as it can be proved that it had some kind of ownership at all.

units.la: Secundus error contentus in verbis praedictis, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, est, quod domus, agri, pecunia, & omnia immobilia, erant communia toti communitati credentium quo ad dominium & proprietatem, ita quod nullus post conuersionem suam de illa multitudine habebat alicuius talis rei dominium & proprietatem in speciali, sed iste error, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, scripturae sacrae repugnat. Nam sicut legitur Actuum quinto, Petrus dixit Ananiae vni de numero credentium post venditionem agri: Nonne manens tibi manebat & venundatum in tua erat potestate? Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod ager ante venditionem erat ipsius Ananiae, quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Aliter enim falsum dixisset beatus Petrus: Manens tibi manebat, hoc est, poteras libere tibi agrum retinere, nec tenebaris eum vendere, sed libere poteras eum vendere vel tenere, ergo ager ille nunquam fuit totius communitatis quantum ad dominium & proprietatem. Amplius, Actuum 4. sic loquitur: quotquot enim erant possessores agrorum aut domorum vendentes afferebant pretia eorum & ponebant ante pedes Apostolorum. Et postea subditur: Ioseph autem, qui cognominatus est Barsabas ab Apostolis, quod est interpretatum, filius consolationis, Leuites, Cyprius genere, cum haberet agrum, vendidit illum & attulit pretium, & posuit ante pedes Apostolorum. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod possessores domorum & agrorum nomine proprio, & ex propria voluntate huiusmodi agros & domos vendebant: nec vnquam legitur, quod ex ordinatione vel mandato communitatis vendebant huiusmodi res, ergo semper ante venditionem earum fuerunt vendentium quo ad dominium & proprietatem in speciali. Rursus hoc auctoritate Gregorii probatur aperte. Gregorius enim, vt habetur 17.q.1.ca. Ananias Deo pecunias vouerat, quas post Diaboli persuasione subtraxit. Ex quibus verbis habetur expresse, quod Ananias vouit Deo pecunias, quas pro vendito agro recepit, sed nullus vouet Deo rem alienam, neque rem communitatis, sed rem propriam, igitur istae pecuniae, antequam Ananias voueret Deo, fuerunt ipsius Ananiae. Aliter enim ipse non habuisset potestatem vouendi illas pecunias Deo plus, quam quicunque alius de communitate, ergo illae pecuniae fuerunt ipsius Ananiae post venditionem agri. Ex quo sequitur, quod ager ante venditionem fuit ipsius Ananiae & non communitatis, erroneum igitur est dicere, vt asserunt isti impugnatores, quod domus, ager & huiusmodi erant totius communitatis quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Ad rationem vero, quam probatur, respondent faciliter dicentes: quod saepe scriptura diuina non seruat ordinem rei gestae. Nam tentator semel tantum Christum assumpsit in sanctam ciuitatem, & semel tantum in montem excelsum. Et tamen Matthaeus Euangelista primo narrat, quod Diabolus eum in sanctam ciuitatem & postea narrat, quod assumpsit eum in montem excelsum, sicut patet Matth. 4. Lucas vero c.4. istas duas assumptiones recitat ordine contrario, ergo alter istorum in scribendo non seruauit ordinem rei gestae. Alia exempla innumera in scriptura possent adduci: sed illud vnum tam apertum sufficiat. Non ergo ordo rei gestae ex ordine scribendi potest semper sufficienter probari. Vnde & saepe factum posterius praemittitur, & postmodum facta priora ad declarationem facti posteriori, de quo sermo praecesserat, subsubdu̅atur, sicut enim beatus Matthæus primo dicit Christum natum de virgine, & postea volens declarare qualiter natus est, narrauit quomodo antequam nasceretur de vtero mater eius inuenta est à Ioseph habens in vtero de Spiritu san�to: & tamen habuit in vtero de san�to Spiritu antequam Christus ex eius vtero nasceretur: & ita factum posterius prius narratur. Ordo igitur rei gestæ non semper ex ordine scribendi, sed sæpe ex diuersis locis scripturæ, & sæpe ex ratione colligi debet. Unde & seriò 5 Regum 2. c. narratur, quod Roboam filius regnauit, & postea 14. e. narratur, quæ fuit mater eius. Ex tamen per rationem colligi debet, quod priusquam regnaret, habuit matrem. Sic igitur in præsenti, quamuis primo dicatur Actuum 4. Nec quisquam eorum quæ possidebant aliquid suum esse dicebat: sed erant eis omnia communia: & postea dicatur: neque enim eorum quisquam egens erat inter illos. Quotquot enim possessores agrorum ac domorum erant, vendentes afferebant pretia eorum &c. tamen ille non fuit ordo rei gestæ, sed primo vendebantur possessiones & substantiæ; quibus venditis, vendentes ponebant pretia ante pedes Apostolorum, vouentes & offerentes Deo pretia communia. Unde primo præmittitur, quod omnia erant communia: sed postea narratur modus per quem facta fuerunt communia, quia præ-ditionem possessionum & substantiarum & oblationem pretii rerum venditarum factam sponte Deo. Et ꝯ iste fuerit ordo rei gestæ, ex diuersis locis textus, & ex auctoritate beati Gregorii testantis, quod 15 Ananias Deo voluit petunias, quas ꝑ agro suo receperat, colligitur euidenter, sicut ostensum est priùs & tamen in ratione accipitur, quod nisi illa vendita fuissent communitatis quo ad dominium & ꝑprietatem, illi quorum fuerunt ante conuersionem, remansissent ꝑprietarii. Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod proprietarii fuerunt ante venditionem & ante oblationem pecuniarum Deo: & cum dicitur, quod hoc repugnat scripturæ dicenti: Nec quisquam eorum quæ possidebat aliquid suum esse dicebat. Dicunt, quod si ille impugnatus sciret distinguere tempora, posset concordare scripturas; alio tempore dicitur: Nec quisquam eorum quæ habebat aliquid suum esse dicebat: & postea dicitur ꝯ possessores agrorum & domorum vendentes afferebant &c. Nec est verum, quod tempore prius fuerunt proprietarii. Ex cuius verbis colligi potest, ꝯ secundum ipsum primi credentes maiore diligentia sui temporalis ordinandis, ꝗ de fide discenda, & vita sua quo ad spiritualia ordinanda: qa si fidem addiscendam & vitā suam quo ad spiritualia ordinandam (puta quod diligerent Deum diligere, seruireq; eidē, & placere) præposuissent ordinationi temporalium, si tempore priori, ipsis temporalium suorum ꝑprietas & dominium remansisset: & ita pro-pore fuissent proprietarii, ꝯ ille negat: & tamen quod hoc fuerit verum declaratur: quia soli, qui doctores erant & patres primoꝰ credentium, nequaquam doctrinam magistri sui si tradiderint, ꝗ ait: Primum quaerite regnum Dei & iustitiam eius: & hæc omnia adiicientur vobis. Nec se-dū, ꝗ Apostoli primo credentes informauerint ad dandum temporalia sua communicari eos induxerint ad fidem verā addiscendam, & quo deberent vitā suam quo ad spiritualia naremo si hoc fecissent credentibus occasionē suspicandi dedissent, ꝯ eorum tempor sent, & ꝑpter hoc eis fidē prædicassent: ꝯ minime est credendum. Primo ergo B. Petrus corde ex verbis suis de fide & sacramento baptismi suscipiendo & aliis spiritualibus, cū dixit formauit: & postmodū ipsi credentes bona sua vendebant, & pretiū ad communem substantiam omnium sponte offerebant, & ita toto tempore, quo ante venditionē rei circa spirituales fuerunt, reī suarū ꝑprietarii remanserunt. Quod autē primo circa spiritualia fuerunt occupati textu Actuū Apostolorum patenter elicitur, vbi post sermonē B. Petri de credentibus sic (scil. verbis B. Petri) auditi compuncti sunt corde & dixerunt ad Petrū & reliquos Apostolos: quid faciemus fratres? Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, ꝯ isti prompti erant informationem Petri & aliorum tenere & seq. Qualem autem informationem B. Petrus eisdem tradidit, ibidē subiungitur, Petrus vero ait ad illos, Pœnitentiam agite, & baptizetur vnusquisque vestrum in nomine Ihesu Christi in remissionem peccatorum vestrorum, & accipietis donum Spiritus sancti, vobis enim est hæc repromissio vestris, & omnibus qui longe sunt, quoscunq; aduocauerit Dominus Deus noster. Aliis etiā verbis plurimis contestatus est, & exhortabatur eos dicens: saluamini à generatione illa prava, in illa informatione suæ de ordinatione bonorū suorū nulla fit mentio secundū B. Petrum meminit. Similiter Marci vltimo: Euntes in mundū vniuersum, prædicate Euangelium omni creaturæ, qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, hic saluus erit: qui vero non crediderit, condemnabitur. In qua de temporalibus mentio non habetur, postq; Iudæos de fide Christi instruxerat, querentes quid agere debeant de pœnitentia agenda, de suscipiendo baptismo, de dono Spiritus S. recipiendo si non sint in infidelitate, non de temporalibus informauit: cuius doctrinā recipientes spiritualibus instruntur. Unde ibidē immediate subiungitur: Qui ergo receperunt sermones eius, baptizati sunt & appositæ sunt in anima circiter tria millia. Erant autē perseuerantes in doctrina Apostolorū, & communicatione suorum temporalium: sed à baptismo & aliis spiritualibus inceperunt, ergo illi proprietarii remanserunt, non enim est credibile, quod postquam crediderunt, sua temporalia communitati dederunt, proprietarii ergo remanserunt.
units.tr: The second error contained in the words above, as these opponents say, is that houses, fields, money and all immovable property were held in common by the whole body of believers as regards ownership and property, so that after their conversion no one in that multitude had ownership or property of any such thing in particular. But, as these opponents say, this error contradicts Holy Scripture. For we read in Acts 5 that Peter said to Ananias, one of the number of believers, after the sale of his field: Did not the land, while it remained unsold, remain yours? And after it was sold, was it not in your power? From these words it is plainly gathered that the field, before it was sold, belonged to Ananias himself as regards ownership and property. Otherwise blessed Peter would have spoken falsely in saying: While it remained, it remained yours, that is, you could freely keep the field and were not obliged to sell it, but you could freely either sell it or keep it. Therefore that field never belonged to the whole community as regards ownership and property. Further, Acts 4 speaks thus: For as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them and brought the prices of them and laid them down at the Apostles' feet. And afterwards it is added: Now Joseph, who was surnamed Barnabas by the Apostles, which is being interpreted the son of consolation, a Levite and a Cypriot by birth, having a field, sold it and brought the price and laid it at the Apostles' feet. From these words it is made clear that the possessors of houses and fields sold such fields and houses in their own name and by their own will. Nowhere is it read that they sold such things by the decree or command of the community. Therefore, before the sale, these things always belonged to the sellers as regards ownership and property in particular. Again, this is clearly proved by the authority of Gregory. For Gregory, as is found in 17 q. 1, ca. Ananias had vowed money to God, which he afterwards withdrew at the persuasion of the Devil. From these words it is expressly stated that Ananias vowed to God the money which he received for the field he had sold. But no one vows to God another's property, nor the property of the community, but his own property. Therefore that money, before Ananias vowed it to God, belonged to Ananias himself. Otherwise he would not have had the power to vow that money to God any more than any other member of the community. Therefore that money belonged to Ananias after the sale of the field. From this it follows that the field, before its sale, belonged to Ananias and not to the community. It is therefore wrong, as these opponents assert, to say that houses, fields and the like belonged to the whole community as regards ownership and property. As for the argument they press, they answer it easily, saying that Holy Scripture often does not keep the order of the events it relates. For the tempter took Christ into the holy city only once, and only once onto the high mountain. Yet Matthew the Evangelist first relates that the Devil took him into the holy city, and afterwards relates that he took him onto the high mountain, as is seen in Matth. 4. Luke, however, in chapter 4 recounts these two takings in the opposite order. Therefore one of them, in writing, did not keep the order of the events. Countless other examples could be brought from Scripture, but this one so plain is enough. Therefore the order of events cannot always be sufficiently proved from the order of writing. Hence it often happens that a later event is placed first, and afterwards earlier events are brought in to explain the later event under discussion. For just as blessed Matthew first says that Christ was born of a virgin, and afterwards, wishing to explain how he was born, related how, before he was born from her womb, his mother was found by Joseph to have a child in her womb of the Holy Spirit; yet she had the child in her womb of the Holy Spirit before Christ was born from her womb. Thus a later event is narrated first. The order of events, therefore, is to be gathered not always from the order of writing, but often from different passages of Scripture, and often from reason. Hence also in 2 Kings 2 it is related that Rehoboam, the son, reigned, and afterwards in chapter 14 it is related who was his mother. Yet from reason it must be gathered that before he reigned he had a mother. So also in the present case, although it is first said in Acts 4: Nor did any of them say that anything they possessed was his own, but all things were common to them; and afterwards it is said: Neither was there anyone among them in want. For as many as were possessors of fields or houses sold them and brought the prices of them, etc., that was not the order of events. Rather, first the possessions and goods were sold, and when they were sold, the sellers laid the prices at the Apostles' feet, vowing and offering the prices to God for the common fund. Hence it is first stated that all things were common, but afterwards the manner by which they were made common is related, namely by the sale of possessions and goods and the voluntary offering to God of the price of the things sold. That this was the order of events is clearly gathered from the different passages of the text, and from the authority of blessed Gregory, who testifies that Ananias vowed to God the money he had received for his field, as has been shown before. Yet it is also understood by reason that, if those sold things had not belonged to the community as regards ownership and property, those who owned them before their conversion would have remained the owners. These opponents say that they were owners before the sale and before the offering of the money to God. And when it is said that this contradicts the Scripture which says: Nor did anyone say that anything he possessed was his own, they reply that if the one whom they attack knew how to distinguish times, he could reconcile the Scriptures. At one time it is said: Nor did anyone say that anything he had was his own; and afterwards it is said that the possessors of fields and houses sold them, etc. Nor is it true that they were owners at an earlier time. From these words it may be gathered that, according to the same passage, the first believers were more diligent in ordering their temporal affairs than in learning the faith and in ordering their life as regards spiritual things. For if they had put the learning of the faith and the ordering of their life as regards spiritual things (namely, that they should love God, serve him and please him) before the ordering of temporal things, then, at an earlier time, the ownership and property of their temporal goods would have remained with them, and so they would have been owners at an earlier time, which he denies. Yet that this was not so is made clear, because those who were the teachers and first Fathers of the believers did not hand down the teaching of their Master, who says: Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you. Nor is it likely that the Apostles, having first instructed the believers to share their temporal goods in common, led them to learn the true faith and how they ought to order their life as regards spiritual things. If they had done this, they would have given the believers occasion to suspect that they preached the faith to them for the sake of temporal gain; and that is by no means to be believed. Therefore blessed Peter first instructed them in the faith and in receiving the sacrament of baptism and other spiritual matters, when he said: Repent; and afterwards the believers themselves sold their goods and voluntarily offered the price for the common fund of all. Thus throughout the whole time during which they were occupied with spiritual things before the sale of their property, they remained owners of their goods. That they were first occupied with spiritual matters is plainly drawn from the text of the Acts of the Apostles, where, after blessed Peter's sermon, those who heard it (namely, the words of blessed Peter) were pricked in heart and said to Peter and the other Apostles: What shall we do, brethren? From these words it is understood that they were ready to hold to and follow the instruction of Peter and the others. What instruction blessed Peter gave them is added in the same place: Peter said to them, Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of your sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is to you and to your children, and to all who are far off, whom the Lord our God shall call. He also testified with very many other words and exhorted them, saying: Save yourselves from this crooked generation. In that instruction of his there is no mention, according to blessed Peter, of the ordering of their goods. Similarly, at the end of Mark: Go into all the world, preach the gospel to every creature; he who believes and is baptized shall be saved, but he who does not believe shall be condemned. In which there is no mention of temporal matters. After he had instructed the Jews in the faith of Christ, when they asked what they should do about repentance, about receiving baptism, and about receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit if they were not in unbelief, he did not instruct them about temporal things. Those who receive his teaching are instructed in spiritual things. Hence immediately after it is added in the same place: Those then who received his word were baptized, and there were added about three thousand souls. They were also persevering in the doctrine of the Apostles and in the sharing of their temporal goods; but they began with baptism and other spiritual things. Therefore those owners remained owners. For it is not credible that, after they had believed, they gave their temporal goods to the community. Therefore they remained owners.

units.la: Post hoc circa literā aliqua sunt notanda. (proprietatē) illud est verbū appellans, ꝯ dicunt principaliter debere sumi hic ꝑprietate spāli ciuili & mundana, quale sanctorum & sacros canones clerici & religiosi non hāt in rebus ecclesiæ. Unde dicitur est duplex: vna est communis, alia est specialis. Communis adhuc est duplex, & specialis. Vna qua potest proprietarius, siue sit persona singularis siue communitas, de rebus vendendo, donando, legando, alienando, & vtendo ac consumendo, si est res vsu consumpta. ad suæ libitū voluntatis, & illo modo, vt prius, accipitur proprietas in iure canonico & in iure ciuili, &talè proprietatem nec cōmunem nec specialè habet religiosi in quibuscunq; rebus temporalibus: nec clerici in rebus ecclesiæ: quia temporalia ad certos vsus & certum modum disponendi sunt eis concessa, & propter hoc sæpe absolute & sine distinctione dicitur, quod nō habent proprietatem in huiusmodi rebus: & quod non sunt domini huiusmodi rerum, teste Alexandro III. ext. de donationib. & fraternitate, dicens: Cum episcopus & quilibet prælatus ecclesiasticarū rerum sit procurator, non dominus, &c. & Aug. vt habetur 12. q. 1. c. vlt. idem dicit: talem proprietatem non habuerūt primi credentes in rebus communib. ideo absolute dicit appellans, quod primi credentes nullius rei neq; vsu cōsumptibilis, neq; non cōsumptibilis vsu, postquam sc. omnia fuerant facta cōmunia, proprietatem habebant: quia proprietatē nec specialē, nec cōmunem habebant. Alia est proprietas non tā specialis q; communis, quæ est potestas rem vendicandi in iudicio; licet nō sit potestas de re libere disponendi vendēdo, donādo, legādo, alienando, & vtendo ad libitū, & talem proprietatē non specialē, sed cōmunem habebant primi credentes, & hoc vel tota cōmunitas secundum aliquos, vel altera pars cōmunitatis, sc. illa à qua erat cōmunitas specialis, sc. Apostolorū distincta pro tempore illo, q; tempus nō incepit ab initio cōuersionis primorū credentium, sed incepit postq; baptizati & in fide instructi inceperunt confirmare necessitatē multorum credentiū, qui non habebant, vnde poterant ex propriis sustentari (nullius rei proprietatē habebant) illud verū est accipiendo proprietatē primo modo dicta. (Omnia quæ possidebant erant cōmunia inter eos) verū est, q; erant cōmunia quantum ad potestatē vtendi & sustentandi se: sed nō erat cōmunia quantū ad proprietatē primo modo dicta secundum q; intendit ille impugnatus (& q; illa cōmunia, &c.) Hic incipit prima ratio ad probandū, q; omnia erant cōmunia quantum ad proprietatē primo modo dicta (illud quod prius ante conuersionē Iudæorum ipsis fuit proprium, postquam credentes effecti fuerunt, fuit inter eos cōmunicatum.) Illa est maior rationis suæ, in qua, sicut patet, nō ponitur dominiū, nec proprietas, nec aliqua talis declaratio quo ad dominiū & proprietatem, & ideo secūdum rectam formā arguendi non deberet poni in cōclusione. Et ideo ex illa maiori conclusio sua nō deberet inferri: sed solūmodo deberet illā conclusionem inferre; omnia fuerunt inter eos cōmunicata: & nō illa, q; infertur: quia semper ex forma est fallacia secundū quid ad simpliciter, quin in tali modo arguēdi altera determinatio ponitur in minori & in conclusione, quæ nō ponitur in maiori, sicut hic: omne currēs est animal: homo nunc primo est currens: ergo homo nunc primo est animal, quia hæc determinatio nunc primo ponitur in minori & in cōclusione, sed non ponitur in maiori: imo maior accipit sine determinatione tali. Consimiliter est hic talis fallacia: illud q; prius ante cōuersionem ipsis fuerat proprium, postq; credentes effecti fuerunt, fuit inter eos cōmunicatum: sed illa quæ poterant ante conuersionem fuerunt eis propria quo ad potestatem dandi plus minus indigenti: & minus vel nihil plus magis indigenti: ergo postquam fuerunt conuersi, illa, quæ posse desunt, fuerunt inter eos communicata, quo ad potestatem dandi plus minus indigenti; & minus vel nihil magis, plus indigenti, & consimilis fallacia ex forma est in argumento suo: quia hæc determinatio quo ad dominium & proprietatem accipitur in minori & consequentia, & non in maiori. Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod ille impugnatus accepit maiorem suam sub hoc sensu: Illud quod prius ante conuersionem Iudaorum ipsis fuerat proprium, postquam credentes effecti fuerunt, fuit eodem modo, quo primo fuerat proprium, inter eos communicatum, & tunc bene sequitur conclusio: quia eadem determinatio, quæ ponitur in minori & in conclusione, subintelligitur virtualiter in maiori. Ad hoc dicunt isti impugnatores, quod maior sub illo sensu est falsa, imo dicunt, quod sic intellecta est erronea reputanda: quia bona Iudæorum ante conuersionem illo modo fuerunt propria eius, quod poterant libere eā dare suis consanguineis, nihil vel parum dando extraneis, illo autem modo non erant communia communitati credentium: sicut nec illo modo bona ecclesiæ sunt modo communia. Multiet iam modis aliis erant illa bona propria Iudæis ante conuersionem, quibus non erant communicata postea inter eos: quod ex præcedentibus colligitur euidenter, & ita patet clare, quod ille sophistice arguit (vt dicunt isti impugnatores) dicentes, quod si modos arguendi sciuisset, nunquam per illud sophisma nec per consimilia, quæ frequenter adducit, veritatem catholicam impugnasset. (Constat aut, quod illa quæ possidebant ante conuersionem, erant illis quantum ad dominium propria.) Illa est minor rationis suæ, in qua ponitur hæc determinatio quantum ad dominium, quæ in maiori minime posita fuit: etiā ita sophistice arguit (quare sequitur quod fuerunt, quo ad proprietatem seu dominium inter eos communicata) hæc est conclusio rationis suæ, circa quam isti impugnatores duo notant. Primum est, quod in hac conclusione ponitur hæc determinatio quo ad proprietatem seu dominiū, quæ nequaquam fuit posita in maiori, & ideo sophistice infertur illa conclusio. Sicut posito, quod aliquis volens intrare religionem conserat alicui monasterio monachorum omnia bona sua, quorum prius habuit dominium libere, sic q; potuit illa dare, vendere & legare, ac etiam alienare ad libitum, & arguatur sic: Illa quæ erant isti propria, postea omnibus de monasterio, quod intrauit, sunt communicata, sed prius erant propria, quo ad potestatem dandi vel vendendi, legandi, & quomodolibet alienandi, igitur postea sunt communicata, quo ad potestatem dandi, vendendi, legandi, & quomodolibet alienandi, certum est, quod arguitur sophistice: quia constat, quod conclusio secundum sacros canones falsa est, & præmissæ sunt veræ, igitur dicunt, q; argumentatio istius est sophistica reputāda. Secundo notāt isti impugnatores, quod cum iidem termini nō debeant accipi æquiuoce in præmissa & conclusione: dominium, q; ponit hoc tā in minori q; in cōclusione, nō accipitur æquiuoce, sed in minori accipitur dominiū, p dominio simili & mudano, q; est potestas alienādi, vendēdi, donādi, legādi, & vēdi re ad placitū, q; secundū iura ciuilia rerum suarum vnusquisque est moderator & arbiter, ergo eodem modo accipitur dominium hoc in conclusione, cum dicitur quod illa bona Iudaeorum fuerunt communicata quo ad dominium: & ita secundum illum impugnatum communitas fidelium credentium habebat dominium ciuile & mundanum, quod est potestas dandi, vendendi, &c. (In rebus illis communibus) quod est omnino falsum & erroneum: quia tenebantur credentes de illis temporalibus sustentare, & non poterant ea alienare ad libitum (quod de rebus non consumptibilibus vsu, &c.) illud dicunt isti impugnatores omnino esse falsum, sicut ex praecedentibus patet aperte (nisi violentia sibi fiat.) Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod violetia fieret scripturae, si diceretur, quod immobilia erant communicata credentibus, quo ad dominium & proprietatem: quia sicut ex scriptura patet, ipsi spontanee vendebant huiusmodi res: & ita illae semper ante venditionem erant suae propriae, & non communes. (Cum ergo prius dicat, quod inter credentes erant omnia communia) male arguit. Prius scribit: ergo prius fuit factum: quia, sicut ostensum est, ordo scripturae non semper sequitur rei gestae ordinem. (Ipsi ante venditionem illorum remansissent proprietarii) illud, quod ille impugnatus habet pro vltimo incommenienti, habent isti impugnatores pro vero. Cum dicit (nec quisquam eorum quae possidebant, &c.) illud dicit scriptura pro tempore post venditionem omnium & allationem pretiorum: & ita illi, quod dicitur, quod ante venditionem proprietarii remanserunt, nullatenus aduersatur.
units.tr: After this, some things about the wording should be noted. The term "property" (proprietas) is used here, they say, principally in the secular, civil and worldly sense, the kind that the holy canons say clerics and religious do not have in the goods of the Church. Hence property is said to be twofold: one kind is common, the other special. The common kind is again twofold, as is the special. The first is the power of an owner, whether a single person or a community, to sell, give, bequeath and alienate goods, and to use and consume them, if the thing is consumed by use, at his own pleasure. It is in this sense that property is taken in canon law and in civil law, and clerics and religious have neither this common nor this special property in any temporal goods. Clerics have no such property in the goods of the Church, because temporal goods have been granted to them for certain uses and in a certain manner of disposal. For this reason it is often said absolutely, without distinction, that they have no property in such goods and are not their owners. Alexander III testifies to this in ext. de donationib. & fraternitate, saying: Since a bishop and every prelate is the steward, not the owner, of ecclesiastical goods, and so on. Augustine, as found in 12. q. 1. c. vlt., says the same: The first believers did not have such property in common goods. So the objector says absolutely that the first believers, when everything had been made common, had property in no thing, whether consumable by use or not consumable by use, because they had neither special nor common property. The other kind of property is not so much special as common: it is the power to claim a thing in court, although it is not the power to dispose of the thing freely by selling, giving, bequeathing, alienating and using it at will. The first believers had this common, not special, property, and according to some this belonged either to the whole community or to another part of the community, namely to that part from which the special community, that is the Apostles, was distinct at that time. This time did not begin at the start of the conversion of the first believers, but began after they were baptized and instructed in the faith and began to meet the need of the many believers who had nothing and so could not be supported by their own means. (They had property in no thing) is true, if property is taken in the first sense mentioned. (All that they possessed was common among them) is true in that they were common as to the power of using and supporting themselves, but they were not common as to property in the first sense, as the objector who is being attacked intends (and that those common goods, and so on). Here begins the first argument to prove that all things were common as to property in the first sense: (what before the conversion of the Jews was their own, after they became believers, was shared among them). This is the major premise of his argument, and in it, as is plain, neither dominion, nor property, nor any such statement about dominion and property is set down. So, according to the correct form of arguing, it should not have been put in the conclusion. And so the conclusion should not be drawn from that major premise; rather he should have drawn only this conclusion: all things were shared among them, and not the one he infers, because in the form of such an argument there is always a fallacy of the qualified to the unqualified, when another qualification is placed in the minor premise and in the conclusion but not in the major premise, as here: everything running is an animal; a man is now running for the first time; therefore a man is now an animal for the first time. This is a fallacy, because the qualification now for the first time is placed in the minor premise and in the conclusion but not in the major premise; indeed the major premise is taken without such a qualification. A similar fallacy of form is present here: what before the conversion was their own, after they became believers was shared among them; but those things which they could have before the conversion were theirs as to the power of giving to those more or less in need, and less or nothing to those more in need; therefore after they were converted, those things which were lacking were shared among them as to the power of giving to those more or less in need, and less or nothing to those more in need. The qualification as to dominion and property is taken in the minor premise and in the consequent, and not in the major premise. But perhaps someone will say that the objector took his major premise in this sense: what before the conversion of the Jews was their own, after the believers became such, was shared among them in the same way in which it had first been their own, and then the conclusion follows well, because the same qualification which is placed in the minor and in the conclusion is virtually understood in the major. To this these objectors reply that the major premise in that sense is false; indeed they say that, so understood, it must be regarded as erroneous, because the goods of the Jews before the conversion were their own in the sense that they could freely give them to their kinsmen, giving little or nothing to strangers; but in that sense they were not common to the community of believers, just as the goods of the Church are not now common in that sense. Those goods were in many other ways the Jews' own before the conversion, in ways in which they were not afterwards shared among them, as is clearly gathered from what precedes, and so it is plain that he argues sophistically (as these objectors say), saying that if he had known the forms of argument he would never have attacked Catholic truth by that sophism or by similar ones, which he often brings forward. (It is certain, however, that the things they possessed before the conversion were their own as to dominion.) This is the minor premise of his argument, in which the qualification as to dominion is set down, which was in no way set down in the major premise. He argues sophistically in this way too, (wherefore it follows that they were shared among them as to property or dominion). This is the conclusion of his argument, about which these objectors note two things. First, that in this conclusion the qualification as to property or dominion is set down, which was not set down at all in the major premise, and so the conclusion is inferred sophistically. Suppose that someone entering a religious order gives to a monastery of monks all his goods, over which he had free dominion, so that he could give, sell and bequeath them and alienate them at will, and let it be argued thus: what was his is now shared among all in the monastery he has entered; but before it was his to give, sell, bequeath and alienate in any way; therefore it is now shared as to the power of giving, selling, bequeathing and alienating in any way. It is certain that this is argued sophistically, because it is clear that the conclusion is false according to the holy canons and the premises are true. Therefore, they say, his argument must be regarded as sophistical. Secondly, these objectors note that since the same terms ought not to be taken equivocally in premise and conclusion, dominion, which he places in both the minor and the conclusion, is not taken equivocally; but in the minor it is taken as dominion in the sense of a similar and worldly kind, which is the power of alienating, selling, giving, bequeathing and selling a thing at pleasure, since according to civil law each person is the manager and arbiter of his own goods. Therefore dominion is taken in the same way in the conclusion, when it is said that those goods of the Jews were shared as to dominion. And so, according to the objector he attacks, the community of believing faithful had civil and worldly dominion, which is the power of giving, selling, and so on (in those common goods). This is wholly false and erroneous, because the believers were bound to support themselves from those temporal goods, and could not alienate them at will (which of things not consumed by use, and so on). These objectors say that this is entirely false, as is plain from what has gone before (unless violence is done to it). These objectors say that violence would be done to Scripture if it were said that immovable goods were shared among the believers as to dominion and property, because, as is clear from Scripture, they sold such things of their own accord, and so those things were always their own before the sale and not common. (Since, therefore, he first says that all things were common among the believers) he argues badly. He writes first: therefore it was done first. For, as has been shown, the order of Scripture does not always follow the order of events. (They would have remained owners before the sale of those things): what the objector he attacks holds as the last absurdity, these objectors hold to be true. When he says (nor did anyone of those things which they possessed, and so on), Scripture says this of the time after the sale of everything and the handing over of the prices, and so what is said, that before the sale they remained owners, is in no way contrary to it.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: AD illud autem, quod volens probare, quod rerum vsu non consumptibilium credentes non habuerunt dominium etiam in communi, subiungit: sc. quia res non consumptibiles vsu vendebant: & ipsas nec in speciali, nec in eorum communitate retinebant, dicimus, quod ex hoc non sequitur, quod ante venditionem illarum rerum non habuerunt dominium: sed bene sequitur, quod post venditionem illud non retinuerint: & hoc est verum, per venditionem n. perfectam in ementes transtulerunt dominium, quia illud sibi non retinuerunt, & si quaeratur, quare Apostoli agros & domos non retinuerunt in Iudaea, sed potius illis venditis habuerunt precia eorum in communi. Respondet Melchiades Papa dicens: futuram (id est transiturreturn) ecclesiam in gentibus (id est ad gentes) Apostoli providebant: ideo praedia in Iudaea minime sunt adepti. Et si dicatur, quod Melchiades videtur supponere, quod credentes etiam ante venditionem praediorum illa nequaquam habuerunt in communi, cum dicat, quod illa in Iudaea minime sunt adepti: dicimus quod Melchiades pro tanto dixit Apostolos in Iudaea non fuisse adeptos praedia, quia nihil sic adepti fuerant, vt illa sibi intenderent retinere: & ideo non videbantur ea fuisse adepti: cum, quisquam adipisceretur, vt eam in continenti a se abdicare debeat, adeptus proprie non dicatur. Ex praedictis patet, quod Apostoli fuit licitum in Iudaea, si voluissent, retinere praedia, nec voto compulsi sunt, quia non retinuerunt voce propria, quia se non contractuos moram inibi, sed transituros se praevidebant ad gentes.
units.tr: As for his claim that the believers did not have ownership even in common of things that are not consumed by use, the opponent adds that they sold things not consumed by use, and kept them neither individually nor in their common fund. We reply that it does not follow from this that they did not own those things before they were sold. What does follow is that they did not keep ownership after the sale. And this is true: by a completed sale they transferred ownership to the buyers, since they did not keep it for themselves. If it is asked why the Apostles did not keep the fields and houses in Judea, but rather had the price of them in common after they were sold, Pope Melchiades answers that the Apostles foresaw that the Church would be about to pass (that is, to the Gentiles). Therefore they did not acquire estates in Judea at all. And if it is said that Melchiades seems to assume that the believers did not hold those estates in common even before they were sold, since he says that the Apostles did not acquire them in Judea, we reply that Melchiades said the Apostles did not acquire estates in Judea for this reason: they had not acquired them in such a way as to intend to keep them. Therefore they did not seem to have acquired them. For someone who acquires a thing with the obligation to renounce it at once is not properly said to have acquired it. From what has been said it is clear that the Apostles were permitted to keep estates in Judea if they wished. They were not compelled by a vow, because they did not keep them, in the proper sense, since they did not intend to remain there, but foresaw that they would pass on to the Gentiles.

units.la: In illa parte respondet ad secundam, quod accepit appellans, quod videlicet primi credentes non retinuerunt res non consumptibiles vsu, nec in speciali nec in communi, & circa hoc duo facit. Primo enim respondet per distinctionem distinguens duo tempora, sc. tempus ante venditionem, & post venditionem: unde dicit, quod post venditionem non retinuerunt dominium, sed ante venditionem bene habuerunt dominium huiusmodi rerum in communi. Et secundo ibi (si quaeratur) mouet quaestionem, quare Apostoli domos & agros in Iudaea non retinuerunt. Ad quam respondet secundum Melchiadem Papam, quia sc. sciuerunt ecclesiam transituram ad gentes. Tertio ibi (Et si dicatur) obiiciendo contra praedictam responsionem, respondet, vt plane habetur in litera. Vltimo ibi (Ex praedictis patet) concludit ex praedictis, quod licitum fuit Apostolis habere in Iudaea praedia.
units.tr: In that part he answers the second point, namely what the questioner assumed: that the first believers did not keep things not consumed by use, either individually or in common. On this he does two things. First, he answers by a distinction, separating two times: the time before the sale and the time after the sale. So he says that after the sale they did not keep ownership, but before the sale they did indeed hold ownership of such things in common. Second, at if it be asked he raises the question why the Apostles did not keep houses and fields in Judea, and he answers it according to Pope Melchiades: namely, because they knew the Church would pass to the Gentiles. Third, at And if it be said he objects against the preceding answer and replies, as is plainly stated in the text. Last, at From what has been said it is evident he concludes from what has been said that it was lawful for the Apostles to hold estates in Judea.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, in istis verbis quatuor contineri errores. Quorum primus est, quod communitas credentium habuit domos & agros, quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Secundus est, quod Apostoli habuerunt praedia in Iudaea. Tertius est, quod Apostoli ideo non retinuerant praedia, quae habebant in Iudaea, quia transituri fuerunt ad gentes. Quartus est, quod Apostolis licuit in Iudaea, & inter gentes praedia possidere. De primo errore dictum est in parte praecedenti, vbi ostensum est, quod Iudaei conuersi domos & agros non dederunt communitati, sed tanquam res proprias vendiderunt, & postea pretium sponte obtulerunt communitati.
units.tr: But these opponents say that four errors are contained in these words. The first is that the community of believers had houses and fields as far as ownership and property are concerned. The second is that the Apostles held estates in Judea. The third is that the Apostles did not keep the estates they had in Judea because they were going to pass to the Gentiles. The fourth is that the Apostles were permitted to possess estates in Judea and among the Gentiles. The first error was dealt with in the earlier part, where it was shown that the Jewish converts did not give their houses and fields to the community, but sold them as their own property, and afterwards offered the price freely to the community.

units.la: Secundus error hic contentus, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, est quod Apostoli habuerunt praedia in Iudaea, q; hoc dicat ille impugnatus, patet aperte, ait enim: dicimus quod Melchiades pro tanto dicit Apostolos in Iudaea non fuisse adeptos praedia, quia non sic adepti fuerunt ea, quod illa sibi intenderent retinere. Ex quibus verbis clare colligitur, q; Apostoli in Iudaea praedia habuerunt, quamuis illa intenderent minime retinere. At hoc isti impugnatores reprobare nituntur, primo sic: Constat quod Apostoli nō habuerunt in Iudaea aliqua praedia, praeter praedia conuersorum ad fidem. Vnde & de illis praediis videtur ille impugnatus intendere, sed ostensum est prius, quod illa praedia semper ante venditionem ipsorum remanserunt propria illorum, quorum prius fuerunt: ergo illa praedia ante venditionem ipsorum ad proprietatem & dominium Apostolorum minime pertinebat, nec pertinebant ad eorum dominium post venditionē, ergo Apostoli post passionē Christi in Iudaea praedia minime habuerunt. Secundo sic: Apostoli quantum ad consilium paupertatis imitatores Christi fuerunt, sed Christus, non obstante, q; non erat de Iudaea regulariter transiturus, ante mortē suam in Iudaea praedia non recepit, cū ipse dicat Matt. 8. Vulpes foueas habent & volucres caeli nidos: filius autem hominis non habet vbi caput suum reclinet, ergo nec Apostoli in Iudaea receperunt. Ex hoc patet, quod praedia Iudaeorum conuersorum nequaquam in totius communitatis dominium transierunt. Cum sit igitur verisimile, q; Apostoli sequerentur vitā Christi & modū viuendi eiusdē, sed Christus nullū praedium pro se vel suo collegio speciali recepit; sed tū sustinuit, q; mulieres sibi & suis discipulis de suis facultatibus ministrarent, sicut patet Luc.8. & quod loculi pauperibus indigentibus portarentur: ita Apostoli pro se prædia minime receperunt, sed permiserunt fideles de precio suorum bonorum Apostolorum & aliorum indigentias subleuarent. Tertio illud sic ostenditur, summi sacerdotes sequentes Apostolos non fuerunt pauperiores ipsis Apostolis, sed plures summi sacerdotes post Apostolos prædia à fidelibus minime receperunt, licet prædiorum pretia reciperent, ergo multo magis Apostoli prædia conuersorum in Iudæa minime receperunt. Maior est manifesta, & inferius multis modis probabitur. Minor probatur auctoritate Urbani Papæ, qui, ut habetur 12. q. 1. c. videntes, ait: Videntes autem summi sacerdotes & alii atque Levitæ, & reliqui fideles plus utilitatis posse conferre, si hereditates & agros, quos vendebant, ecclesiis, quibus præsidebant, episcopi traderent: eo quod ex sumptibus eorum tam præsentibus quam futuris temporibus plura & elegantiora possent ministrare fidelibus communem vitam deducentibus, quam ex precio ipsorum, coeperunt prædia & agros, quos vendere solebant, matricib. ecclesiis tradere & ex sumptibus eorum viuere. Ex quibus verbis euidenter colligitur, quod in primitiua ecclesia & diu post, talis fuit consuetudo, quod fideles, qui alios fideles vitam communem ducere cupientes de bonis suis sustentare volebant, ipsis prædia non dederunt, sed prædia vendiderunt & ex precio vitam communem ducentibus necessaria ministrarunt. Postea autem coeperunt (sicut Urbanus Papa dicit) prædia & agros matricibus ecclesiis tradere, nequaquam ergo Iudæi conuersi sua prædia dederunt Apostolis: sed, sicut textus Actuum Apostolorum eloquitur manifeste, ipsi sua prædia vendiderunt, & precium ante pedes Apostolorum pro sustentandis fidelib. posuerunt. Sed contra illa obiici potest, primo per capitulum allegatum Melchiadis Papæ, qui insinuare videtur, quod ecclesia inter gentes prædia magna obtinuit, ergo fideles non vendiderunt prædia, sed ecclesiæ tradiderunt. Secundo quia posteriores Apostolis non erant sapientiores, neq; maiorem curam habentes de fidelib. sustentandis quam Apostoli, si ergo sicut dicit Urbanus Papa, Episcopi posteriores ordinauerunt pro utilitate communem vitam ducentium, quod non precia, sed prædia ecclesiis traderentur: Videtur multo magis hoc ordinauerunt Apostoli. Ad primum illorum isti impugnatores respondent, dicentes quod Melchiades nequaquam dicit, quod ecclesia, hoc est collegium communem vitam ducentiu, prædia tempore Apostolorum obtinuit: sed explicat manifeste, quod tempore Constantini imperatoris prædia sunt adepta. Aliter dicunt, responsioni prædictæ non obuiat, quod in Iudæa pro tempore Apostolorum, nec ecclesia, quæ est congregatio illorum, qui diuino cultui sunt specialiter deputati, nec tota congregatio fidelium, nec aliqua pars illius congregationis prædia sibi retinuit, inter gentes autem tempore Apostolorum, licet congregatio illorum, qui erant diuino cultui specialiter deputati: & ita congregatio communem vitam ducentium in communi prædia non haberet, sed de precio prædiorum & eleemosynis sustentaretur: multi tamen erant fideles inter gentes, qui prædia habuerunt & retinuerunt; & ita inter fideles in Iudæa, & inter fideles inter gentes tempore Apostolorum fuit differentia manifesta, quo ad retentationem prædiorum. Ad secundum dicunt isti impugnatores, quod aliquid est expediens pro uno tempore, quod pro alio minus expediens, imo aliquando nocivum dignoscitur, & ideo quamuis Apostoli fuerunt sapientiores & maiorem sollicitudinem de communi utilitate gerentes, quam sequentes eos: ipsi tamen vitam Christi sequentes nec prædia habere volebant, nec quod congregatio vitam communem ducentium haberet prædia ordinauerunt: quia tunc non erat ita necessarium, sicut postea fuit. Christiani etiam qui fuerunt vicini Apostolis, hoc non seruabant: & tamen non fuerunt minoris sapientiæ, nec minoris feruoris ad communem bonum quam posteriores, & hoc quia tunc non ita expediebat. Quarto probatur, quod Apostoli in Iudæa prædia minime habuerunt per hoc, quod Apostoli omnia temporalia abdicauerunt, quo ad dominium & proprietatem sicut per Scripturam sacram, doctrinam sanctorum & determinationem ecclesiæ constat aperte: sed de illa materia erit postea sermo prolixus: ideo ad præsens transeo.
units.tr: The second error, as these opponents say, is contained here: that the Apostles held estates in Judea. That the opponent asserts this is clear, for he says: We reply that Melchiades for this reason says that the Apostles did not acquire estates in Judea, because they did not so acquire them that they intended to keep them. From these words it is clearly inferred that the Apostles did hold estates in Judea, although they did not at all intend to keep them. But these opponents try to refute this, first thus: It is certain that the Apostles had no estates in Judea apart from the estates of those converted to the faith. And it seems that the opponent intends these very estates. But it has been shown before that those estates always remained the property of those to whom they had belonged before the sale. Therefore those estates did not belong to the ownership or property of the Apostles before they were sold, nor did they belong to their ownership after the sale. Therefore the Apostles did not hold estates in Judea after Christ's passion. Second, thus: The Apostles, so far as the counsel of poverty goes, were imitators of Christ. But Christ, although he was not to pass regularly out of Judea, did not receive any estates in Judea before his death, since he himself says in Matt. 8: The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head. Therefore neither did the Apostles receive any in Judea. From this it is clear that the estates of the Jewish converts by no means passed into the ownership of the whole community. Since it is therefore probable that the Apostles followed the life of Christ and his manner of living, but Christ received no estate for himself or for his own special company, yet he allowed women to minister to him and his disciples from their means, as is clear from Luke 8, and that purses were carried for the needy poor, so the Apostles likewise did not receive estates for themselves, but allowed the faithful to relieve their own needs and those of others from the price of their goods. Third, this is shown thus: the high priests who followed the Apostles were not poorer than the Apostles themselves, yet the high priests after the Apostles did not receive estates from the faithful, although they did receive the price of estates. Therefore much more the Apostles did not receive the estates of the converts in Judea. The major premise is obvious, and will be proved below in many ways. The minor premise is proved by the authority of Pope Urban, who, as is found in 12. q. 1. c. videntes, says: "When the high priests and the others, the Levites and the remaining faithful, saw that more usefulness could be provided if the bishops handed over to the churches to which they presided the inheritances and fields which they were selling, because from their revenues, both present and future, they could supply more and finer things to the faithful who lived the common life than from the price of them, they began to hand over the estates and fields which they used to sell to the mother churches and to live on their revenues." From these words it is clearly gathered that in the primitive Church, and long after, the custom was such that the faithful who wished to support other faithful living the common life from their goods did not give them estates, but sold the estates and supplied from the price what was necessary for those living in common. Afterwards, however (as Pope Urban says), they began to hand over estates and fields to the mother churches. Therefore the Jewish converts did not give their estates to the Apostles at all; but, as the text of the Acts of the Apostles plainly says, they sold their estates and laid the price at the feet of the Apostles to support the faithful. But against these things it may be objected, first, by the chapter cited from Pope Melchiades, who seems to hint that the Church among the Gentiles obtained great estates. Therefore the faithful did not sell their estates, but handed them over to the Church. Second, because those who came after the Apostles were not wiser, nor had greater care for supporting the faithful, than the Apostles. If therefore, as Pope Urban says, the later bishops ordained for the benefit of those living in common that estates should be handed over to the churches, not the price, it seems that the Apostles ordained this much more. To the first of these the opponents reply, saying that Melchiades does not at all say that the Church, that is the community of those living in common, obtained estates in the time of the Apostles, but explains plainly that estates were acquired in the time of the emperor Constantine. Otherwise they say that the aforesaid answer is not contradicted by the fact that in Judea, in the time of the Apostles, neither the Church, which is the assembly of those specially set apart for divine worship, nor the whole assembly of the faithful, nor any part of that assembly, kept estates for itself; but among the Gentiles in the time of the Apostles, although the assembly of those specially set apart for divine worship, and so the assembly of those living in common, did not hold estates in common but was supported from the price of estates and alms, there were nevertheless many faithful among the Gentiles who held and kept estates. And so among the faithful in Judea and among the faithful among the Gentiles in the time of the Apostles there was a clear difference as regards the keeping of estates.
