To the second they say that something may be expedient at one time which is less expedient at another, indeed is sometimes recognised as harmful; and therefore, although the Apostles were wiser and bore greater concern for the common good than those who followed them, they nevertheless, following the life of Christ, neither wished to have estates, nor did they ordain that the assembly of those living in common should have estates, because at that time it was not as necessary as it later became. Christians too who lived near the Apostles did not observe this, and yet they were not less wise, nor less fervent for the common good, than those who came later; and this was because at that time it was not so expedient. Fourth, it is proved that the Apostles held no estates in Judea because the Apostles renounced all temporal things as far as ownership and property are concerned, as is plainly established by Holy Scripture, the teaching of the saints and the determination of the Church. But there will be a lengthy discussion of that matter later, so for now I pass over it.

units.la: Tertius error, ut dicunt isti impugnatores, hic continetur est quod Apostoli ideo non retinuerunt prædia quæ habebant in Iudæa: quia transituri fuerunt ad gentes. Hoc dicunt isti impugnatores esse erroneum pro eo, quod in his verbis insinuat impugnatus Apostolos inter gentes prædia habuisse & retinuisse. Si enim propter hoc tantummodo Apostoli prædia, quæ in Iudæa habebant, non retinuerunt, quia transituri erant ad gentes, igitur quando venturi erant ad gentes, si gentes eis prædia offerre volebant, ipsi retinere oblata prædia intendebant. Constat autem, quod multi fideles inter gentes Apostolis prædia obtulerunt, ergo Apostoli oblata prædia receperunt & retinuerunt, sed hoc constat esse falsum: quia nusquam legitur, quod Apostoli inter gentes prædia receperunt. Unde & Apostolus Paulus, qui erat doctor gentium & magister, etiam sæpe sumptus a gentibus recipere recusauit, quia pro victu suo manibus propriis laborauit, & prim. Timoth. sext. ait: Habentes autem alimenta & quibus tegamur his contenti simus. Ex quibus patet, quod Paulus inter gentes prædia non recepit, & idem constat de Apostolis aliis.
units.tr: This third error, as these opponents say, is contained here: that the Apostles did not keep the estates they had in Judea because they were about to go to the Gentiles. These opponents say this is mistaken, since in these words the one being attacked implies that the Apostles had and kept estates among the Gentiles. For if the Apostles gave up the estates they had in Judea only because they were about to go to the Gentiles, then when they were to go to the Gentiles, they intended to keep any estates the Gentiles offered them. But it is clear that many faithful Gentiles offered estates to the Apostles, so the Apostles must have accepted and kept what was offered. This, however, is plainly false, since nowhere is it read that the Apostles accepted estates among the Gentiles. Indeed, the Apostle Paul, who was the teacher and master of the Gentiles, often refused to accept support even when it was offered by the Gentiles, because he labored with his own hands for his living, and in 1 Tim. 6 he says: "And having food and raiment, let us be therewith content." From this it is evident that Paul did not receive estates among the Gentiles, and the same holds for the other Apostles.

units.la: Quartus error (ut dicunt isti impugnatores) est, quod Apostolis licuit in Iudæa & inter gentes prædia possidere, sed illud, ut dicunt isti impugnatores, scripturæ diuinæ repugnat. Nam quibus interdicitur congregare thesauros, eisdem interdicitur prædia possidere. Nam de prædiis thesauri congregantur & sæpe expedit & est rectæ consonum rationi prædia possidentes congregare thesauros eo, quod sæpe absque thesauro rite coli, conseruari & defendi non possunt. Christus autem congregare thesauros Apostolis interdixit, dicens Matthæi sexto. Nolite thesaurizare vobis thesauros in terra, ubi erugo & tinea demolitur, & ubi fures effodiunt furantur, ergo Christus Apostolis interdixit prædia possidere, vel saltem ne possiderent consuluit Apostolis, ergo doctrinam & consimilia sui magistri sequentibus prædia minime licuit possidere.
units.tr: The fourth error (as these opponents say) is that the Apostles were permitted to possess estates both in Judea and among the Gentiles, but this, as these opponents say, contradicts divine Scripture. For those who are forbidden to gather treasures are likewise forbidden to possess estates. For treasures are gathered from estates, and it is often expedient, and agreeable to right reason, for those who possess estates to gather treasure, since estates often cannot be properly cultivated, preserved, and defended without treasure. But Christ forbade the Apostles to gather treasures, saying in Matthew 6: "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal." Therefore Christ forbade the Apostles to possess estates, or at least advised the Apostles not to possess them. Therefore it was not permitted for those who follow the teaching and the like precepts of their Master to possess estates.

units.la: Amplius, quibus interdicitur sollicitudo de crastino, ipsis interdicitur prædiorum possessio: quia prędia possidentes per se vel per alios de prædiis futuris temporibus disponendis sollicitudinem magnam oportet habere. Christus autem sollicitudinem de crastino interdixit, dicens Matthæi sexto. Nolite solliciti esse in crastinum, ergo eis interdicta fuit prædiorum possessio: & per consequens eis non licuit prædia possidere. Rursus, ea quæ ad pericula spiritualia & peccata inclinant, sine quibus vitam conuenienter transigere contingit, Apostoli reliquerunt. Aliter enim de placendo Deo minus fuissent solliciti, sed prædia, sicut & diuitiæ, ad spiritualia pericula & peccata inclinant, teste Apostolo, qui prim. ad Timo. sext. ait: Qui volunt diuites fieri, incidunt in tentationem & laqueum diaboli, & desideria multa & inutilia & nociua, quæ mergunt hominem in perditionem & interitum, ergo Apostoli prædia reliquerunt. Sed forte diceret ille impugnatus, quod Christus noluit Apostolos, dum esset cum eis, prædia possidere: quin tamen post eius abscessum prædia possiderent, minime interdixit. Sed hoc dicunt isti impugnatores stare non posse. Nam non est perfectorum de maiore perfectione ne ad imperfectionem vel minorem perfectionem transfire. Apostoli autem saltem post aduentum Spiritus sancti, perfecti fuerunt, ergo nullam perfectionem, quam a Christo acceperant, & secum seruauerant, relinquere debuerunt. Sed dum erant cum Christo, prædia minime habuerunt, nec habere voluerunt, vt Christo perfectius adhærerent, ergo post aduentum Spiritus sancti multo magis prædia habere non debebant. Unde si Apostoli, qui non erant omnino perfecti, imo prædia, perfectionis amore minime habuerunt: multo magis post aduentum Spiritus sancti, quando erant in omni perfectione magis quam antea radicati, & ad quos tunc principaliter in terris gubernatio spectabat fidelium perfectionis amore, &, vt exemplum darent fidelibus, omnia debuerunt propter Deum relinquere, & vt suspitionem tollerent, quod propter temporalia prædicarent, nenequaquam prædia debuerunt habere. Ad hæc nulla religio est perfectior in paupertate, Apostolica paupertate. Multi autem sunt religiosi, qui prædia non solum in speciali, sed etiam in communi habere recusant. Patet de Fratribus Prædicatoribus & aliis Mendicantibus, ergo multo magis Apostoli nequaquam prædia debuerunt habere.
units.tr: Furthermore, those who are forbidden to be anxious about tomorrow are forbidden to possess estates, because those who possess estates must, either themselves or through others, have great anxiety about arranging their estates for future times. But Christ forbade anxiety about tomorrow, saying in Matthew 6: Be not anxious for the morrow. Therefore the possession of estates was forbidden to them, and consequently it was not permitted for them to possess estates. Again, the Apostles left behind those things which incline toward spiritual dangers and sins, and without which it is possible to live life fittingly. For otherwise they would have been less anxious about pleasing God. But estates, like riches, incline toward spiritual dangers and sins, as the Apostle witnesses, who says in 1 Tim. 6: They that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare of the devil, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. Therefore the Apostles left behind estates. But perhaps that man under attack would say that Christ, while he was with them, did not want the Apostles to possess estates, yet he did not forbid them to possess estates after his departure. But these opponents say this cannot stand. For it is not for the perfect to pass from a greater perfection to imperfection or to a lesser perfection. The Apostles, however, were perfect at least after the coming of the Holy Spirit; therefore they ought not to have abandoned any perfection that they had received from Christ and kept with them. But while they were with Christ they had no estates, nor did they wish to have them, so that they might cleave more perfectly to Christ. Therefore, after the coming of the Holy Spirit, they ought much more not to have estates. Hence, if the Apostles, who were not altogether perfect, and indeed for the love of perfection did not have estates, then much more after the coming of the Holy Spirit, when they were rooted in all perfection more than before, and when the governance of the faithful in the world principally belonged to them, they ought, for the love of perfection and to give an example to the faithful, to leave everything for God's sake, and in order to remove the suspicion that they preached for the sake of temporal things, they ought by no means to have had estates. Moreover, no religious order is more perfect in poverty than the Apostolic poverty. Many religious, however, refuse to have estates not only individually but even in common. This is evident of the Friars Preachers and the other Mendicants. Therefore much more the Apostles ought by no means to have had estates.

units.la: Porro quia ille impugnatus, quantum ad istas quatuor assertiones de prædiis Apostolorum, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, doctrinæ Fratrum Prædicatorum obuiat & repugnat, primo ordinem eorum destruit & confundit manifeste insinuans, quod paupertatem Apostolicam nullatenus imitantur proprietatem prædiorum a se penitus abdicando, ideo pro ipsis & eorum doctrinam sequentibus, quid de illa materia sentiat Thomas doctor eorum adducunt. In libro itaque contra doctrinam retrahentium a religione prim. capit. decim. quint. ait: Manifestum est igitur secundum expositiones præmissas, Apostolis interdictum fuisse, ne agros vel vineas, vel alia huiusmodi bona immobilia possiderent. Quis autem dicat, nisi hæreticus patens, diuinissimam instructionem a Christo perfectioni euangelicæ derogare ? Ex quibus verbis euidenter habetur, quod interdictum fuit a Christo Apostolis, ne prædia possiderent: & quod sapit hæresim secundum illum dicere, quod possessionum carentia derogat euangelicæ perfectioni, & ita cum Apostoli euangelicam perfectionem nequaquam reliquerint, constat eos prædia minime possedisse. Item illud in eodem capitulo dicit: Est autem vlterius considerandum, qualiter præmissa Domini præcepta, scilicet nolite possidere aurum, fuerunt ab Apostolis obseruata. Et infra: quod autem nihil temporalium possiderent, aut etiam in via deferrent, ante tempus passionis aperte ostenditur ex hoc, quod legitur Lucæ vigesimo secundo, vbi Dominus discipulis suis dicit: quando misi vos sine sacculo & pera & calceamentis, nunquid aliquid defuit vobis ? at illi dixerunt: nihil. Sed quia ibi subdit: dixit ergo eis, sed nunc qui habet sacculum tollat, similiter & peram, posset alicui videri, quod Dominus totaliter præcepta priora relaxauerit: sed hanc relaxationem quantum ad personas Apostolorum imminentis persecutionis tempore, referendam apparet ex verbis Bedæ, qui dicit: Non eadem viuendi regula persecutionis & pacis tempore discipulos informat. Misit quidem discipulis ad prædicandum, quid tollerent in via præcepit: mortis vero instante periculo & tota simul gente pastorem gregemque persequente, congruam ipsis regulam decernit, permittens vt tollant victui necessaria, donec sopita insania persecutorum, tempus euangelizandi redeat. Et subdit: vbi nobis quoque dat exemplum ex iusta nonnunquam causa instante, quædam de nostri propositi rigore posse sine culpa intermitti. Hæc verba Bedæ. Ex quibus concludit Thomas, & ex quo etiam apparet, ad rigorem euangelicæ disciplinæ pertinere, quod aliquis careat omni possessione terrena. Quid autem super hoc Apostoli post passionem seruauerunt, & seruandum tradiderunt, aperte in Actibus Apostolorum docetur. Legitur enim Actuum quarto, quod multitudinis credentium erat cor vnum & anima vna: nec quisquam eorum, quæ possidebat, aliquid suum esse dicebat, sed erant istis omnia communia. Et ne aliquis dicat, eos habuisse possessiones communes: puta agros & vineas, aut aliquid huiusmodi: hoc per sequentia excluditur. Sequitur enim: quotquot possessores domorum ac agrorum erant vendentes afferebant pretia eorum, quæ vendebantur, & ponebant ante pedes Apostolorum. Ex quo patet hanc esse euangelicam vitæ obseruantiam ab Apostolis obseruatam, vt ea quæ ad necessitatem vitæ pertinent, possideantur communiter, possessionibus omnino abdicatis. Ex his verbis colligitur euidenter, quod Thomas in quatuor obuiat manifeste isti impugnato: quorum primum est, quod omnia præcepta Christi data Apostolis & discipulis de obseruantia paupertatis, sicut quod non possiderent aurum, &c. & consimilia, nunquam nisi dispensatiue ad tempus relaxata fuerunt. Cuius oppositum tenet ille impugnatus, sicut postea apparebit. Secundum est, quod ad euangelicae vitae obseruantiam spectat possessionibus etiam carere in communi. Tertium est, quod Apostoli nec in Iudaea nec inter gentes possessiones, nec in communi nec in speciali habuerunt, nec licuit eis habere. Ex quo sequitur, sicut postea ostendetur, quod Apostoli voluerant omnibus possessionibus in speciali & in communi carere. Quartum est, quod possessiones, de quibus fit mentio Actuum 4. capit. quas vendebant, non erant communes, sed erant propriae ante venditionem, & precia earum communicata fuerunt. In istis, & in his quae sequuntur ex eis, ille impugnatus doctrinae Thomae contradicit aperte. Unde idem Thomas contra quosdam Magistros Parisienses destruentes euangelicam paupertatem, capitulo sexto, multis modis conatur ostendere, quod actualis paupertas, quae est per abdicationem proprietatis omnium temporalium, ad euangelicam pertinet paupertatem, quam & Apostoli seruauerunt. Unde, sicut arguit, euangelica perfectio maxime in Apostolis claruit, sed ipsi paupertatem actualem habuerunt sua omnia relinquentes, & infra sic ait: Vlterius ostendamus, quod illa perfectio, quae aliquid propria reliquit, non requirat possessionem diuitiarum in communi. Primordium enim huius perfectionis in Christo & in Apostolis fuit: sed ipsi non leguntur sua relinquentes aliquas possessiones habuisse in communi: imo potius legitur, quod nec etiam domum habebant ad manendum, ut satis probatum est. Et infra: Item Augustinus dicit in tertio libro de doctrina Christiana: quod illi, qui conuersi ex Iudaeis fuerunt ad Christum, in primitiva ecclesia, quia proximi spiritualibus fuerunt, tam capaces extiterunt Spiritus sancto, ut venderent omnia, eorumque precium indigentibus distribuendum ante pedes Apostolorum ponerent. & infra: Non enim hoc vllas ecclesias gentium fecisse scriptum est: quia non tam proprie inuenti erant, qui simulacra manu facta Deos habebant. hoc Augustinus, ex quibus infert Thomas: Ex quo patet, quod Augustinus praefert perfectionem ecclesiae primitiuae Iudaeorum perfectioni ecclesiae ex gentibus, in hoc, quod omnia sua vendiderunt pauperibus distribuendo: sed ipsi ita vendiderunt propria, quod nullas possessiones in communi seruauerunt sibi. Ex his colligitur euidenter, quod secundum illum Apostoli nullas possessiones habuerunt, nec habere licite potuerunt. Et quod illi, de quibus fit mentio in Actibus, possessiones suas non tanquam communes, sed tanquam proprias vendiderunt, dicit enim quod vendiderunt propria: & ita illae possessiones nunquam communes fuerunt. Ex hoc dicit infra expresse in haec verba: Apostoli reseruabant pecunias & etiam colligebant, vt sanctis pauperibus, qui praedia sua vendiderant propter Christum, necessaria ministrarent, nec tamen illas pecunias habebant de aliquibus possessionibus, sed ex eleemosynis fidelium. Apostoli igitur illas possessiones habuerunt. Et si dicas, quod saltem habebant pecunias, & seruabant secundum Thomam. Dicendum quod vel Thomas sibiipsi contradicit in hoc, quod prius dixerat, quod praeceptum de pecuniis non portandis non fuerat nisi dispensatum ad tempus: vel loquitur illo modo loquendi, quo dicitur, quod qui per alium facit, per seipsum facere videtur, vt dicatur, quod Apostoli reseruabant pecunias, quia ordinauerunt quod alii reseruarent.
units.tr: Now, since that opponent, in respect of these four assertions about the Apostles' estates, as these objectors say, runs counter to and contradicts the teaching of the Friars Preachers, he first attacks and confounds their order, plainly implying that they do not at all imitate Apostolic poverty by completely renouncing ownership of property. Therefore, on behalf of them and of those who follow their teaching, they cite what their teacher Thomas thinks about this matter. In his book Against the doctrine of those who withdraw from religion, chapter fifteen, he says: It is therefore clear, according to the explanations set out above, that the Apostles were forbidden to possess fields, vineyards, or other such immovable goods. But who would say, unless he were an open heretic, that the most divine instruction of Christ detracts from evangelical perfection? From these words it is evident that Christ forbade the Apostles to possess estates, and that, according to him, to say that the lack of possessions detracts from evangelical perfection savours of heresy. Since the Apostles did not abandon evangelical perfection, it follows that they certainly did not possess estates. Likewise, in the same chapter he says: Further, we must consider how the Lord's precepts just stated, namely, "Do not possess gold," were observed by the Apostles. And below: That they possessed nothing temporal, or even carried anything on the road, before the time of the Passion, is clearly shown by what we read in Luke chapter twenty-two, where the Lord says to his disciples: "When I sent you without purse, bag, or sandals, did you lack anything?" And they said: "Nothing." But because he adds there: "He said to them, but now let him who has a purse take it, and likewise a bag," someone might think that the Lord had altogether relaxed his earlier precepts. But this relaxation, as far as the persons of the Apostles are concerned, must be referred to the time of the impending persecution, as appears from the words of Bede, who says: "The same rule of living does not form the disciples in a time of persecution as in a time of peace. He sent the disciples to preach, and commanded them what to take on the road; but when danger of death was imminent, and the whole nation was persecuting the shepherd and the flock, he laid down a rule suited to them, allowing them to take what was necessary for sustenance until the madness of the persecutors subsided and the time for evangelising returned." And he adds: "Here he also gives us an example that, when a just cause presses, some things may be relinquished without fault from the rigour of our own purpose." These are Bede's words. From them Thomas concludes, and it also appears from them, that it belongs to the rigour of evangelical discipline that someone should lack all earthly possession. What the Apostles did about this after the Passion, and what they handed down to be kept, is clearly taught in the Acts of the Apostles. For we read in Acts chapter four that the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and that none of them said that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them. And lest anyone say that they had common possessions, such as fields and vineyards or something of that kind, this is excluded by what follows: For as many as were possessors of houses or lands sold them and brought the prices of what was sold and laid them at the Apostles' feet. From this it is clear that the evangelical manner of life observed by the Apostles was this: that those things which pertain to the necessities of life were held in common, with possessions utterly renounced. From these words it is evidently gathered that Thomas opposes that opponent in four points. The first is that all the precepts of Christ given to the Apostles and disciples about observing poverty, such as that they should not possess gold, and similar ones, were never relaxed except by dispensation for a time. The opponent holds the opposite, as will appear later. The second is that it pertains to the observance of the evangelical life to lack possessions even in common. The third is that the Apostles had no possessions, either in common or individually, neither in Judaea nor among the Gentiles, nor were they permitted to have any. From this it follows, as will be shown later, that the Apostles wished to be without all possessions, both individual and common. The fourth is that the possessions mentioned in Acts chapter four, which they sold, were not common, but were their own before the sale, and their prices were shared. In these points, and in what follows from them, that opponent plainly contradicts the teaching of Thomas. Hence the same Thomas, against certain Parisian masters who destroyed evangelical poverty, in chapter six, tries in many ways to show that actual poverty, which consists in renouncing ownership of all temporal goods, belongs to evangelical poverty, which the Apostles also kept. Thus, as he argues, evangelical perfection shone especially in the Apostles, but they had actual poverty, leaving all their own things; and below he says: Let us further show that that perfection which left something of its own does not require the possession of riches in common. For the beginning of this perfection was in Christ and in the Apostles, but we do not read that they, leaving their own things, had any possessions in common; rather we read that they did not even have a house to dwell in, as has been sufficiently proved. And below: Likewise Augustine says in the third book of On Christian Doctrine that those who were converted from the Jews to Christ in the primitive Church, because they were near to spiritual things, were so capable of the Holy Spirit that they sold everything and placed the price at the feet of the Apostles to be distributed to the needy. And below: For it is not written that the churches of the Gentiles did this, because they were not so fit, who had gods made by hand as idols. This is Augustine's; from which Thomas infers: From this it is clear that Augustine prefers the perfection of the primitive Church of the Jews to the perfection of the Church from the Gentiles, in that they sold all their goods and distributed them to the poor; but they sold their own property in such a way that they kept no possessions in common for themselves. From these things it is evidently gathered that, according to him, the Apostles had no possessions, nor could they lawfully have them. And that those mentioned in the Acts did not sell their possessions as common, but as their own, for he says they sold their own property; and so those possessions were never common. From this he says expressly, in these words: The Apostles kept money and also collected it, so that they might supply the necessities of the holy poor, who had sold their estates for Christ; yet they did not have that money from any possessions, but from the alms of the faithful. Therefore the Apostles had those possessions. And if you say that at least they had money and kept it, according to Thomas: it must be said either that Thomas contradicts himself in this, since he had earlier said that the precept about not carrying money was dispensed with only for a time; or he speaks in that manner of speaking by which it is said that one who acts through another seems to act himself, so that it is said that the Apostles kept money because they ordered that others should keep it.

units.la: His visis, est ad litteram transeundum. (Vendebant) sc. illi quorum erant. (Nec in eorum communitate retinebant) quia res, quas vendebant, ad communitatis dominium minime pertinebant. (Ex hoc nosequitur, quod ante venditionem illarum rerum non habuerunt dominium.) Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod ex hoc quod illi, quorum erant ante conuersionem, vendebant illas res tanquam proprias, sicut ex textu Actuum Apostolorum bene colligitur. (Unde sequitur quod communitas illa, rerum illarum non habuit dominium: quia Apostoli domos & agros non retinebant in Iudaea.) Causa est, quia non retinebant illa, quae non habebant: praedia autem non habebant in Iudaea illo tempore, nec vnquam, ideo non retinebant. (Respondet Melchiades Papa.) Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod Melchiades non respondet ad illam quaestionem; quare Apostoli domos & agros non retinebant in Iudaea. Sed potest dici, quod respondet ad illam quaestionem, quare nulli fideles illo tempore domos retinebant in Iudaea: sicut postquam gentes conuersi fuerunt, multi fideles inter ipsos praedia retinebant. Unde illa videtur fuisse intentio Melchiadis Papae: quod quia Apostoli praeuidebant, quod fideles de Iudaeis conuersi, qui praedia habuerunt, vel omnes vel plures ex eis, transituri erant ad gentes, consuluerunt eis Apostoli, quod omnia praedia sua distraherent, & pro salute animarum suarum de precio debite ordinarent, & quod nulli communitati communem vitam ducentium aliqua praedia darent. Causa autem, quare consuluerunt omnibus, quod praedia sua distraherent, cum tamen forte non omnes praedia possidentes ad gentes fuerunt transituri, potuit esse illa, quia Apostoli ignorabant vel si per reuelationem Spiritus sancti sciuerunt, dicere noluerunt, qui erant transituri ad gentes, & qui non, & ideo voluerunt omnes esse paratos, & secundum illam explanationem textus Melchiadis sic debet legi. Apostoli praeuidebant futuram ecclesiam in gentibus (hoc est, multos de ecclesia transituros ad gentes) idcirco communem vitam ducentes in Iudaea praedia minime sunt adepti, etiam pro breuissimo tempore, & tunc littera est plana, & sensus apertus.
units.tr: Having seen these things, we must now pass to the letter. (They sold), that is, those to whom the things belonged. (Nor did they retain it in the common possession of that community), because the things they sold did not at all belong to the ownership of the community. (From this it does not follow that they had no ownership of those things before the sale.) These objectors say that from the fact that those to whom the things belonged before their conversion sold them as their own, as is rightly gathered from the text of the Acts of the Apostles. (Hence it follows that that community did not have ownership of those things, because the Apostles did not retain houses and fields in Judaea.) The reason is that they did not retain what they did not have; and they did not have estates in Judaea at that time, nor ever, therefore they did not retain them. (Melchiades the Pope answers.) These objectors say that Melchiades does not answer that question, namely why the Apostles did not retain houses and fields in Judaea. But it can be said that he does answer that question, namely why no faithful at that time retained houses in Judaea, just as after the Gentiles were converted many of the faithful among them retained estates. Hence this seems to have been the intention of Pope Melchiades: that since the Apostles foresaw that the faithful converted from the Jews who had estates, either all or most of them, would be going over to the Gentiles, the Apostles advised them to sell all their estates and to dispose of the price for the salvation of their souls, and that they should give no estates to any community that lived a common life. The reason why they advised all to sell their estates, although perhaps not all who held estates were going to go over to the Gentiles, may have been that the Apostles did not know, or if they knew by revelation of the Holy Spirit, were unwilling to say, who were going to go to the Gentiles and who not; and so they wished all to be ready. And according to that explanation the text of Melchiades should be read thus: The Apostles foresaw the future Church among the Gentiles (that is, that many from the Church would be going over to the Gentiles); therefore, living a common life in Judaea, they did not acquire estates at all, not even for a very short time. And then the letter is plain and the sense open.

units.la: Est tamen aduertendum, quod vnius rei possunt esse multae causae: quarum quaelibet aliquando est causa sufficiens, aliquando vero nulla est causa sufficiens, & ideo quamuis fuerit vna causa, quam assignat Melchiades, quare communem vitam ducentes in Iudaea praedia minime sunt adepti: haec tamen forte non fuit praecisa causa, quamuis forte fuerit causa sufficiens, & ideo propter aliam causam poterant etiam inter gentes esse aliqui communem vitam ducentes, qui praedia minime sunt adepti. Aliter potest dici, quod Melchiades non intendit causam assignare, quare Apostoli non retinebant praedia in Iudaea pro seipsis: sed quia non recipiebant nec retinebant praedia pro aliis, puta pro subditis suis. (Quia non sic adepti fuerunt, &c.) Hoc dicunt isti impugnatores nullo modo continere veritatem : quia Melchiades absolute dicit sine omni determinatione: minime sint adepti. ( Cum qui sic rem adipiscitur, vt eam in continenti à se abdicare debeat, adeptus proprie non dicatur. ) Illud dicunt à veritate penitus alienum. Quia constat, quod mercator emens rem, vt eam statim vendat, adipiscitur ipsam : quia qui acquirit liberum dominium alicuius rei, proprie eam adipiscitur, maxime si obtinet liberam possessionem eius. ( Apostolis licitum fuit in Iudaea, si voluissent, retinere praedia. ) Hic dicunt isti impugnatores duos errores obuiantes persectioni Apostolicae contineri. Quorum primus est, quod Apostoli praedia in Iudaea habuerunt. Secundus, quod licuit eis habita praedia retinere. ( Nec voto compulsi sunt ) hic est, vt dicunt, alius error, scilicet quod votum dimittendi vel non habendi praedia minime emiserunt, sed voluntate propria, illud posset habere vnum sensum verum, scilicet quod spontanee praedia dimiserunt: sed intendit ibi ille impugnatus omnem obligationem spontaneam praecedentem excludere, & ideo dicunt isti impugnatores secundum mentem istius hic errorem includi. ( Quia se non contractaturos morar) haec non est causa, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, sed quia proprietatem omnium temporalium prius per votum reliquerant.
units.tr: It should be noted, however, that one thing can have many causes. Any one of them is sometimes a sufficient cause, and sometimes none is. So although the one cause that Melchiades assigns, why those living a common life in Judaea did not acquire estates, was perhaps not the exact cause, it may well have been a sufficient one. For that reason, others living a common life among the Gentiles might also have failed to acquire estates for some other cause. Another way to put it is that Melchiades did not intend to give the cause why the Apostles did not keep estates in Judaea for themselves, but rather why they neither received nor kept estates for others, for example for their own subjects. (Quia non sic adepti fuerunt, &c.) Those opponents say this in no way contains the truth, because Melchiades speaks absolutely, without any qualification: minime sint adepti ("they did not acquire at all"). (Cum qui sic rem adipiscitur, vt eam in continenti à se abdicare debeat, adeptus proprie non dicatur.) They say this is wholly foreign to the truth. For it is plain that a merchant who buys a thing in order to sell it at once does acquire it, since whoever gains free ownership of a thing properly acquires it, especially if he holds free possession of it. (Apostolis licitum fuit in Iudaea, si voluissent, retinere praedia.) Here, say those opponents, two errors are contained that stand in the way of Apostolic perfection. The first is that the Apostles had estates in Judaea. The second is that they were permitted to keep the estates they had. (Nec voto compulsi sunt) This, they say, is another error, namely that they did not make a vow to give up or not to have estates, but acted of their own will. That could have one true sense, namely that they voluntarily gave up their estates. But the man being attacked intends there to exclude every prior voluntary obligation, and so those opponents say that by his meaning this error is included. (Quia se non contractaturos morar) This, those opponents say, is not the reason, but rather that they had earlier surrendered the ownership of all temporal goods by a vow.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: ADillud autem, quod subsequenter dicit, quod res vsu consumptibiles in communi credentes habebant: & sic quilibet eorum habebat rerum vsu consumptibilium vsum facti, dicimus quod si intelligat, quod erant eis communia, quo ad proprietatem seu dominium, verum dicit. Si vero intelligat, quod non fuerunt quo ad proprietatem seu dominium, sed tantum quo ad simplicem facti vsum, eum errare dicimus, & Scriptura sacra contradicit supradicta, & quod scriptura illa determinatiue supponat res vsu consumptibiles, quo ad proprietatem seu dominium credentibus fuisse communes, patet: dicit enim, omnia istis, sc. credentibus, fuisse communia: & quia qui omne dicit, nihil excludit, sequitur quod dictum illud etiam res vsu consumptibiles comprehendit. Quaero ergo, quo ad quid erant ista communia bona illa, aut dicet ille haereticus, quod erant communia, quo ad vsum facti: aut quo ad ius vtendi seu vsum fructum seu possessionem: aut quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, hoc enim secundum decretalem illam Exiit, in rebus temporalibus reperiri consueuerunt: quod tamen verum est in rebus non consumptibilibus vsu, quantum autem ad simplicem vsum facti, quod res illa, scilicet vsu consumptibiles, communes fuerint, dici nequaquam potest, primo quidem, quia in reb. talibus, scilicet vsu consumptibilibus, vsus facti iumendo vsum proprie, locum habere non potest. Vsus enim sumptus proprie requirit, quod cum ipso vsu substantia rei remaneat salua, vt ex praedictis patet, quod in rebus consumptibilibus nequit esse. Item, quia vsus facti sic est vtentis proprius, quod non potest dici alterius, nec communicabilis sibi, patet enim, quod actus comedendi Petri sic erat sibi proprius, quod non poterat dici alii esse communis. Quare communio praedicta non potest intelligi, quo ad simplicem vsum facti. Rursus, quia vsus facti communitati non conuenit, cum talis vsus personam veram exigat: quam non gerit communitas, sed potius imaginariam seu repraesentatam. Ad haec, non potest dici, quod respectu iuris vtendi seu vsus fructus dicta communio possit dici: cum in rebus talibus, scilicet vsu consumptibilibus, iura praedicta, scilicet ius vtendi seu vsus fructus, constitui nequeant, vt ex eorum diffinitionibus, quas ponit dicta constitutio, Ad conditorem canonum, patet. Item, nec quo ad possessionem dicta communio potest dici: quia si loquamur de possessione, quae ius est, illa communio inter credentes secundum eum esse non potuit, cum ipse asserat Apostolos nullum ius habuisse in istis temporalibus, sed tantum simplicem vsum facti, si autem loquamur de possessione quae facti est, illa sic est cuius, et possidentis propria, quod non est communis alicui, nec etiam communicabilis, sicut de vsu facti dictum est supra, quare sequitur, quod res illa vsu consumptibiles, quae inter ipsos erant effecta communes, quo ad proprietatem & dominium, sint communes inter ipsos effecta.
units.tr: As for what he goes on to say, that the believers held goods consumed by use in common, so that each of them had the use in fact of those goods: if he means that they were common to them as regards ownership or dominion, he speaks the truth. But if he means that they were not common as regards ownership or dominion, but only as regards the simple use in fact, we say he is wrong, and holy Scripture contradicts what was said above. That this Scripture clearly assumes that goods consumed by use were common to the believers as regards ownership and dominion is plain: for it says that all things were common to them, that is, to the believers; and because whoever says "all" excludes nothing, it follows that this saying also covers goods consumed by use. I ask, then, in respect of what those common goods were. Will that heretic say that they were common as regards the use in fact, or as regards the right of using or usufruct, or as regards possession, or as regards dominion and ownership? For these are what, according to that decretal Exiit, are usually found in temporal things. This is true of things not consumed by use; but as to the simple use in fact, it can by no means be said that those things, namely goods consumed by use, were common. First, because in such things, namely goods consumed by use, the use in fact, taking "use" properly, cannot occur. For use properly taken requires that the substance of the thing remain intact along with the use, which, as is clear from what has been said, cannot happen in consumable things. Again, because the use in fact belongs so properly to the one using that it cannot be called another's or communicable to someone else: for it is clear that Peter's act of eating was so his own that it could not be called common to another. So the said communion cannot be understood as regards the simple use in fact. Furthermore, use in fact does not suit a community, since such use requires a real person, which a community is not, but rather an imaginary or represented one. Besides, it cannot be said that the said communion holds with respect to the right of using or of usufruct, since in such things, namely goods consumed by use, the aforesaid rights, namely the right of using and usufruct, cannot be established, as is clear from their definitions, which the said constitution Ad conditorem canonum sets out. Nor, again, can the said communion be called one as regards possession: for if we speak of possession, which is a right, that communion among the believers could not, on his view, have existed, since he himself asserts that the Apostles had no right in these temporal things, but only the simple use in fact; and if we speak of possession which is a matter of fact, that is so much the possessor's own and proper that it is common to no one, nor even communicable, as was said above of the use in fact. Hence it follows that those things consumed by use, which among them had been made common as regards ownership and dominion, were made common among them.

units.la: In illa parte respondet ad tertium, quod in impugnatione tangitur appellantis, accepit enim appellans, quod credentes res vsu consumptibiles habebant in communi. Ad illud respondet ille impugnatus, dicens quod illa propositio potest habere duplicem intellectum, vnus intellectus est, quod credentes illi habebant res vsu consumptibiles quo ad dominium & proprietatem, & illum intellectum dicit esse verum, sed est contra appellantem. Alius intellectus potest esse ille, credentes habebant res vsu consumptibiles in communi, quo ad simplicem facti vsum, & illum intellectum dicit esse falsum, quem attribuit appellanti. Secundo ibi ( & quod scriptura illa, &c.) probat, quod credentes habebant in communi res vsu consumptibiles, quo ad dominium & proprietatem per locum a diuisione, sic, quia constat quod primi credentes habuerunt res vsu consumptibiles in communi, ita quod res illae erat omnib. communes, aut ergo fuerunt quo ad vsum facti: aut quo ad ius vtendi seu vsum fructum: vel quo ad possessionem: vel quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Illam diuisionem esse sufficientem per decretalem Exiit, probat, quae ponit praedicta in rebus temporalibus reperiri, sed illae res vsu consumptibiles non fuerunt communes credentibus, quo ad simplicem vsum facti, quod rationib. probare conatur. Primo sic. In rebus vsu consumptibilibus simplex vsus facti proprie sumedo reperiri non potest, ergo illae res vsu consumptibiles non fuerunt communes credentibus, quantum ad simplicem vsum facti. Secundo sic: vsus facti sic est proprius vtentis, quod alteri communicari non potest, patet de actu comedendi, ergo illae res vsu consumptibiles non fuerunt communes quantum ad simplicem facti vsum. Tertio sic: vsus facti communitati conuenire non potest: quia vsus facti exigit veram personam, qualis non est communitas, ergo illae res non fuerunt communes, quantum ad simplicem facti vsum. Secundo probat secundam partem diuisionis praedictae, sc. quod illæ res vsu consumptibiles non fuerunt communes credentibus quantum ad ius vtendi seu vsumfructum: quia in talibus rebus prædicta iura, sc. ius vtendi & vsusfructus, nequeunt reperiri. Tertio probat tertiam partem, sc. quod illæ res vsu consumptibiles non fuerunt cómunes quantum ad possessionem: quia si sic; aut ergo quantum ad possessionem, quæ est iuris; aut quantum ad possessione, quæ est facti. Primum non potest dici secundum appellantem: quia secundum eum, vt dicit ille impugnatus, primi credentes non habuerunt in temporalibus aliquod ius, sed tantum simplicem facti vsum. Secundum etiam dari non potest: quia possessio quæ est facti non potest esse communis, sicut nec vsus facti. Relinquitur ergo, sicut dicit ille impugnatus, quod illæ res erant communes, quantum ad dominium & proprietatem.
units.tr: In that part he answers the third point, which the refuter touches on in the appellant's argument. For the appellant took it that the believers held goods consumed by use in common. To this the refuted party replies, saying that the proposition can have a twofold meaning. One meaning is that those believers held goods consumed by use in common as regards dominion and ownership; this meaning he says is true, but it is against the appellant. The other meaning could be that the believers held goods consumed by use in common as regards the simple use in fact; this meaning he says is false, and he attributes it to the appellant. Second, there (and that Scripture, &c.) he proves that the believers held goods consumed by use in common as regards dominion and ownership, by an argument from division, thus: it is agreed that the first believers held goods consumed by use in common, so that those things were common to all; therefore they were common either as regards the use in fact, or as regards the right of using or usufruct, or as regards possession, or as regards dominion and ownership. That this division is sufficient, according to the decretal Exiit, which states that these things are found in temporal goods, he proves; but those goods consumed by use were not common to the believers as regards the simple use in fact, which he tries to prove by reasons. First, thus: in goods consumed by use, the simple use in fact, properly taken, cannot be found; therefore those goods consumed by use were not common to the believers as regards the simple use in fact. Second, thus: the use in fact is so proper to the one using that it cannot be communicated to another, as is plain from the act of eating; therefore those goods consumed by use were not common as regards the simple use in fact. Third, thus: use in fact cannot belong to a community, since use in fact requires a real person, and a community is not such; therefore those goods were not common as regards the simple use in fact. Second, he proves the second part of the aforesaid division, namely that those goods consumed by use were not common to the believers as regards the right of using or usufruct: because in such things the aforesaid rights, namely the right of using and usufruct, cannot be found. Third, he proves the third part, namely that those goods consumed by use were not common as regards possession: because if they were, then either as regards possession which is a right, or as regards possession which is of fact. The first cannot be said, according to the appellant, since, as the refuted party says, the first believers had no right in temporal things, but only the simple use in fact. The second cannot be granted either, since possession of fact cannot be common, any more than use in fact. It remains, therefore, as the refuted party says, that those things were common as regards dominion and ownership.

units.la: Circa illam partem misti impugnatores sic procedunt. Primo enim explicant rationem appellantis. Secundo ostendunt, quod ratio istius impugnati, per quam probat, quod illæ res erant com-munes, quantum ad dominium & proprietatem, non concludit. Circa primum dicunt, quod intentio appellantis est dicere, quod res vsu consumptibiles fuerunt communes primis credentibus, quantum ad potestatem releuandi suas indigentias mediate vel immediate per ipsas. Ad cuius euidentiam est sciendum, quod illarum rerum consumptibilium vsu quædam erant pecuniæ, & quædam erant aliæ res, quæ in cibo & potu consistebant. Et forte fuerunt adhuc aliquæ aliæ. Aliis rebus à pecunia licebat forte omnibus vti, sed pecunia vti fuit quibusdam licitum, & quibusdam non fuit licitum, sicut Apostolis non fuit licitum, & tamen per illas pecunias poterant Apostoli aliquomodo suas indigentias releuare in quantum alii poterant necessaria ad victum de pecuniis emere, & Apostolis assignare. Et ita licet Apostoli non reciperent pecuniam per se vel per interpositam personam: tamen quodammodo mediate per pecuniam suas indigentias subleuabant, inquantum alii emebant illa, quæ erant necessaria Apostolis ad suas indigentias subleuandas, & ita omnia illo modo erant communia omnibus quantum ad potestatem, scilicet supradictam. Et secundo erant omnia communia omnibus, quantum ad potestatem petendi suas indigentias subleuari per res illas. Tertio erant communes vel omnibus vel aliis omnibus præterquam Apostolis, quantum ad ius vendendi & repetendi si iniuste ablatæ fuissent: & quantum ad ius etiam defendedi in iudicio, si aliquis eas à fidelibus indebite petiuisset. Et ita accipiendo dominium & proprietatem communiter, sicut distinctum est prius, illæ res fuerunt communes vel simpliciter omnibus, vel omnibus, exceptis Apostolis, quantum ad tale dominium & proprietatem in communi. Sed non erant communes quibuscunque credentibus, quantum ad dominium ciuile & mundanum, quo possent res illas ad placitum dispensare, aut etiam libere vendere & donare, & de tali dominio & proprietate loquitur ille impugnatus, & ideo dicunt, quod hic aperte errat dogmatizando, quod res vsu consumptibiles erant communes illis credentibus, quantum ad tale dominium & proprietatem, sicut ostensum est prius. Et ex illo concludunt isti impugnatores, quod Apostoli non habuerunt dominium & proprietatem in speciali: nec etiam in communi, quantum ad speciale ipsorum collegium illarum rerum vsu consumptibilium: quia res communes non sunt proprie alicuius, nec aliquibus de illa communitate: sed res illæ vsu consumptibiles fuerunt communes omnibus credentibus, ergo non fuerunt proprie alicui Apostolo, nec toti collegio Apostolorum: & tamen habuerunt vsum facti illarum rerum, ergo habuerunt vsum facti à proprietate & dominio separatum, & de hoc superius patuit, & infra patebit.
units.tr: On that part the mixed refuters proceed thus. First they explain the appellant's argument; second, they show that the reasoning of this refuted party, by which he tries to prove that those things were common as regards dominion and ownership, does not follow. On the first point they say that the appellant's intention is to say that goods consumed by use were common to the first believers as regards the power of relieving their needs, directly or indirectly, through them. To make this clear, it must be known that some of those goods consumed by use were money, and others were things which consisted in food and drink; and perhaps there were still others. For some of the other things it was perhaps lawful for all to use, but to use money was lawful for some and not for others, as it was not lawful for the Apostles; yet through that money the Apostles could in some way relieve their needs, insofar as others could buy with the money the things necessary for food and hand them over to the Apostles. And so, although the Apostles did not receive money either themselves or through an intermediary, nevertheless in a certain way they relieved their needs indirectly through money, insofar as others bought those things which were necessary for the Apostles to relieve their needs; and so all things were in that way common to all as regards the aforesaid power. Second, all things were common to all as regards the power of asking that their needs be relieved through those things. Third, they were common either to all or to all except the Apostles, as regards the right of selling and of recovering them if they had been unjustly taken away, and also as regards the right of defending them in court if anyone had unduly sought them from the faithful. And so, taking dominion and ownership in the common sense, as was distinguished before, those things were common either absolutely to all, or to all except the Apostles, as regards such dominion and ownership held in common. But they were not common to any believers at all as regards civil and worldly dominion, by which they could dispense those things at pleasure, or even sell and give them freely; and it is of such dominion and ownership that the refuted party speaks. Therefore, they say, he plainly errs in teaching that goods consumed by use were common to those believers as regards such dominion and ownership, as was shown before. And from this these refuters conclude that the Apostles had neither dominion nor ownership in particular, nor even in common, as regards the special collective body of the Apostles of those goods consumed by use: for common things do not properly belong to anyone, nor to some of that community; but those goods consumed by use were common to all believers, therefore they did not properly belong to any single Apostle, nor to the whole college of the Apostles; and yet they had the use in fact of those things; therefore they had the use in fact separated from ownership and dominion, as was shown above and will be shown below.

units.la: Secundo ostendunt isti impugnatores, quod ratio, per quam ille impugnatus probare conatur, quod res illæ vsu consumptibiles fuerunt communes, quantum ad dominium & proprietatem, accipiendo dominium, sicut ille accepit, sc. pro dominio quod est potestas libere dispensandi & ordinandi de re ad illius placitum voluntatis, cuius est dominiü, non concludit: imo etiam de nullo dominio concludit. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod ille impugnatus vtitur hic istis terminis vsus facti, ius vtendi, vsusfructus, possessio, proprietas eodem modo, quo vtitur ipsis Nicolaus Tertius in decretali Exiit. Unde & hic ille impugnatus per distam decretalem Exiit, suam diuisionem esse sufficientem probare molitur, cum dicit: hæc enim secundum decretalem illam Exiit, in rebus temporalibus re-periri consueuerunt, in dicta autem particula illius decretalis Exiit ius vtendi non accipitur communissime pro quocunque iure vtendi: sed accipitur pro iure vtendi quo valet aliquis pro vsu rei in iudicio litigare, & vsum a iudice petere si negatur. Quod enim ibidem ius vtendi non accipiatur communissime, patet aperte. Nam secundum ipsum Fratres in rebus, quibus vtuntur, nihil iuris habent. Alibi tamen dicit, quod Fratres in extremæ necessitatis articulo constituti possunt iure poli sustentationi naturæ prouidere. Et ita aliquod ius vtendi rebus, quibus natura sustentetur, possunt habere Fratres, non ergo Fratres Minores carent omni iure, nomine iuris communissime sumpto, oportet ergo cum Nicolaus dicit Fratres in rebus, quibus vtuntur, nihil iuris habere: & per consequens nō ha-bent ius vtendi, quod ius vtendi ibidem strictius accipiatur. Accipit ergo ius vtendi pro iure, quo habens ius potest in iudicio pro vsu rei litigare. Hoc etiam patet ex alio, quia secundum eundem Nicolaum in eadem decretali Exiit, vsus facti quo Fratres Minores rebus vtuntur, facti tantummodo nomen habens quod facti est in vtendo tantum, præbet vtentibus nihil iuris. Et postea subdit: rebus Fratres vti licite possunt durante concedentis licentia. Ex his verbis euidenter colligitur, quod Nicolaus Tertius inter ius & licentiam manifeste distinguit, & quod licentiam negat esse ius: & tamen communissime accipiendo ius pro omni licita potestate, licentia posset vocari ius, sed licentia talis, de qua loquitur Nicolaus Tertius, quæ nullam dat actionem, non potest vocari ius, quo potest quis pro re vel vsu rerum in iudicio litigare.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents show that the argument by which that opponent tries to prove that the consumable goods were held in common, as regards dominion and property, taking dominion in the sense he gives it, namely the power to dispose of and order a thing freely at the pleasure of the will of its owner, does not conclude. Indeed, it concludes nothing about any dominion at all. To make this clear, they say it must be understood that this opponent uses the terms "use of fact", "right of use", "usufruct", "possession" and "property" in the same way that Nicholas III uses them in the decretal Exiit. So here too the opponent, through that decretal Exiit, labours to prove that his division is sufficient, when he says: "for according to that decretal Exiit, these things are usually found in temporal matters." In the passage of that decretal Exiit, however, "right of use" is not taken in the most general sense of any right of use, but in the sense of a right by which a person can sue in court for the use of a thing, and ask a judge for that use if it is refused. That "right of use" is not used there in the most general sense is plain enough. For according to the same Nicholas, the Friars have no right in the things they use. Elsewhere, however, he says that Friars who are in the extreme article of necessity may provide for the sustenance of nature by right. So the Friars can have some right of use in the things by which nature is sustained; therefore the Friars Minor do not lack every right, taking "right" in the most general sense. It follows that when Nicholas says the Friars have no right in the things they use, and consequently no right of use, "right of use" is there taken in a stricter sense. He therefore takes "right of use" to mean the right by which a person who has it can sue in court for the use of a thing. This is also clear from another point: according to the same Nicholas in the same decretal Exiit, the use of fact by which the Friars Minor use things, which has only the name of fact because it consists only in using, gives the users no right at all. And he adds afterwards: "The Friars may lawfully use things for as long as the grantor's permission lasts." From these words it is evident that Nicholas III clearly distinguishes right from permission, and denies that permission is a right. Yet if "right" is taken in its most general sense as any lawful power, permission could be called a right; but a permission of the kind Nicholas III speaks of, which gives no action at law, cannot be called a right by which a person may sue in court for a thing or for the use of things.

units.la: Et in hoc secutus fuit Isidorum, qui, vt habetur distinct. i. cap. omnes, ait: transfer per agrum alienum fas est: ius non est, vbi dicit Glossa: licet sit aquum iure diuino: tamen non est ius, id est non dat ciuilem actionem. Ex his manifeste colligitur, quod nonnunquam accipitur ius pro iure, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare, & ita accipit Nicolaus Tertius ius vtendi, pro iure, quo valet quis pro visu rei in iudicio litigare, cum ergo ille impugnatus hic allegat Nicolaum, debet eodem modo accipere ius vtendi, quomodo accipit Nicolaus Tertius. Secundo dicunt isti impugnatores, quod visus facti potest dupliciter accipi, scilicet pro actu vtendi, vt pro actu comedendi, bibendi, vestiendi, &c. Aliter potest accipi pro potestate licita talem actum eliciendi.
units.tr: Here he followed Isidore, who, as is found in distinct. i. cap. omnes, says: it is lawful to pass through another's field, but it is not a right; where the Gloss says: although it is just by divine law, it is nonetheless not a right, that is, it does not give a civil action. From these words it is clearly gathered that "right" is sometimes taken to mean a right by which a person can sue in court, and in this way Nicholas III takes "right of use" to mean the right by which a person can sue in court for the use of a thing. Since this opponent here cites Nicholas, he ought to take "right of use" in the same way that Nicholas III takes it. Secondly, these opponents say that "use of fact" can be understood in two ways: either as the act of using, such as the act of eating, drinking, clothing oneself and so on, or as the lawful power of performing such an act.

units.la: His visis dicunt, quod ratio non concludit, imo ex ipsa sequeretur, quod Fratres Minores res multas haberent quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Nam constat, quod res multae concessae sunt Fratribus in communi, & nulli Fratri in speciali, etiam res visu consumptibiles, & per consequens tales res etiam visu consumptibiles sunt communes Fratribus Minoribus, aut ergo communes sunt Fratrib. quantum ad visum facti, & hoc non secundum illum, quia visus facti est cuilibet proprius secundum ipsum, aut quo ad ius vtendi seu visum fructum: quod non potest dici, quia fratres talia iura habere non possunt secundum Nicolaum III. aut quo ad possessionem, & tunc aut quo ad possessionem, quae est ius, & hoc dici non potest, quia Fratres non habent tale ius secundum Nicolaum III. aut quo ad possessionem, quae est facti, & hoc dici non potest, quia possessio facti est cuilibet propria & nulli communicabilis, relinquitur ergo quod sunt communes quantum ad proprietatem & dominium, & ita clare patet, quae propositio istius impugnati aequaliter probat de Fratribus Minoribus, quod habent res communes non solum visu consumptibiles, sed etiam non consumptibiles visu, quantum ad dominium & proprietatem, sicut probat de primis credentibus, quod res non consumptibiles visu erant eis communes ad dominium & proprietatem. Quare cum hoc non sit concedendum de Fratrib. etiam secundum illum impugnatum, qui dicit solos Fratres Minores profiteri viuere sine proprio: & per consequens Fratres Minores nullas res habent communes quantum ad dominium & proprietatem, sicut habent alii Religiosi. Euidenter ergo concluditur, quod ratio praedicta de primis credentibus non conuenit, sicut nec Fratribus Minoribus, licet secundum rei veritatem non sit omnino simile de primis credentibus & de Fratribus, sicut nec est simile de tota communitate fidelium, & de vna communitate partiali & speciali. Nam sicut non est expediens, quod tota communitas fidelium quantum ad omnem sui partem voto castitatis se astringat, & tamen est expediens, quod aliqua communitas partialis fidelium voueat castitatem: ita licet sit conueniens, quod vna religio partialis abdicet a se omne ius vtendi, quo valeat pro temporalibus in iudicio litigare, tamen non est conueniens, quod tota congregatio fidelium omne tale ius a se abdicet: quia expedit, quod aliqui fideles potestatem habeant bona fidelium defendendi, illo autem tempore, quo credentes omnia sua fecerunt communia, ipsi erant vel tota communitas fidelium, vel fere tota: ita quod pauci vel nulli praeter ipsos erant tunc fideles, & ideo non videtur fuisse conueniens, quod a se abdicauerit omne ius in temporalibus, quae habebant.
units.tr: Having seen this, they say that the argument does not conclude; indeed, it would follow from it that the Friars Minor have many things as regards dominion and property. For it is certain that many things have been granted to the Friars in common and to no Friar in particular, including things consumable by use; and consequently such things, even those consumable by use, are common to the Friars Minor. Either they are common to the Friars as regards use of fact (but not in the sense that use of fact, according to him, belongs to each person and is his own); or as regards the right of use or usufruct (which cannot be said, because the Friars cannot have such rights according to Nicholas III); or as regards possession. If as regards possession, either the possession that is a right is meant (which cannot be said, because the Friars do not have such a right according to Nicholas III), or the possession that is a fact is meant (which cannot be said either, because the possession of fact belongs to each person and cannot be shared with anyone). It remains that they are common as regards property and dominion. And so it is quite plain that this opponent's proposition proves equally of the Friars Minor that they hold things in common not only if they are consumable by use but also if they are not consumable by use, as regards dominion and property; just as he proves of the first believers that things not consumable by use were common to them as regards dominion and property. Since this must not be conceded of the Friars, even according to that opponent, who says that only the Friars Minor profess to live without property, it follows that the Friars Minor have no things in common as regards dominion and property, as other religious orders have. It is therefore clearly concluded that the aforesaid argument about the first believers does not apply, nor does it apply to the Friars Minor, although in truth the first believers and the Friars are not altogether alike, just as the whole community of the faithful is not like one partial and special community. For just as it is not expedient for the whole community of the faithful to bind itself by a vow of chastity in every part, yet it is expedient for some partial community of the faithful to vow chastity, so it may be fitting for one partial religious order to renounce every right of use by which it might sue in court for temporal things, but it is not fitting for the whole congregation of the faithful to renounce every such right, because it is expedient that some of the faithful have power to defend the goods of the faithful. But at the time when the believers made all their goods common, they were either the whole community of the faithful or nearly the whole; so that few or none beyond them were then faithful. Therefore it does not seem to have been fitting that they should have renounced every right in the temporal goods they had.

units.la: Per hoc patet responsio ad rationem istius impugnati: quia si intelligat per visum facti, sicut intelligit solummodo actum vtendi, sicut actum comedendi, bibendi & huiusmodi: sic est diuisio sua insufficiens, si ius vtendi accipiatur, sicut accipitur in decretali Exiit, quam allegat: quia sicut aliquid potest esse multis commune, quod non est commune nec quo ad ius facti, qui est actus vtendi: nec quo ad ius vtendi, quo valet quis pro visu rei in iudicio litigare: nec quo ad visum fructum: nec quo ad possessionem: nec quo ad dominium seu proprietatem. Hoc multis probatur exemplis. Primum est de Fratribus Minoribus, qui saepe multas res habent communes: & tamen nullo praedictorum modorum, sed sunt eis communes quantum ad licitam potestatem vtendi, quamdiu durat licentia concedentis. Secundum exemplum est de inuitatis ad mensam alicuius, quibus illa, quae apponuntur coram omnibus, simul & coram nullo determinatae, sunt eis communia, antequam incipiant actualiter vti ipsis: & tamen nullo praedictorum modorum sunt eis communia, sed sunt eis communia quo ad licitam potestatem vtendi. Diceret aliquis forte ad illud exemplum, quod illa sunt eis communia, quo ad possessionem facti, sed non excludit exemplum, quin etiam vocando talem praesentiam rerum possessionem facti possint aliqua fieri communia absque omni possessione tali: puta si aliquis diues daret aliquibus pauperibus licentiam intrandi domum suam, & vtendi omnibus, quae inuenirent in mensa apposita: illa tunc per talem licentiam effecta essent communia, quantum ad licitam potestatem vtendi ante verum actum vtendi, & absque omni iure vtendi, quo valerent visum in iudicio vendicare, si concedens suam licentiam reuocaret: & sine omni visufructu & sine dominio & proprietate, & sine possessione etiam tali, quae esset rerum praesentia, & ita aliquid est commune, & tamen nullo praedictorum modorum. Tertium exemplum de seruis & famulis, qui habent communem licentiam vtendi ad necessitatem aliquibus rebus domini sui, quibus nulla est certa portio assignata in illis, illa enim sunt communia, & tamen nullo praedictorum modorum, patet per membra singula discurrendo, sunt ergo communia alio modo: quia quantum ad licitam potestatem vtendi pro suis necessitatibus subleuandis, quousque dominus ordinaret. Posset enim eis per modum alium prouidere.
units.tr: This gives the answer to this opponent's argument. If he understands "use of fact" as meaning only the act of using, such as the act of eating, drinking and the like, then his division is insufficient, if "right of use" is taken as it is in the decretal Exiit which he cites. For just as something can be common to many people without being common either as regards the right of fact, which is the act of using, or as regards the right of use by which a person can sue in court for the use of a thing, or as regards usufruct, or as regards possession, or as regards dominion or property. This is proved by many examples. The first is the Friars Minor, who often have many things in common, and yet not in any of the aforesaid ways; they are common to them as regards the lawful power of using, for as long as the grantor's permission lasts. The second example is of guests invited to someone's table, for whom the dishes set out before everyone together, and before no one in particular, are common, before they actually begin to use them; and yet they are common to them in none of the aforesaid ways, but only as regards the lawful power of using. Perhaps someone might say, in answer to this example, that those things are common to them as regards possession of fact; but the example does not exclude that, even if we call such presence of things possession, some things may become common without any such possession. Suppose a rich man gave some poor people permission to enter his house and use everything they found on the table set out: by such permission those things would then be made common, as regards the lawful power of using, before any actual use, and without any right of use by which they could claim the use in court if the grantor revoked his permission; and without any usufruct, without dominion and property, and without even such possession as would be the presence of things. Thus something is common, and yet in none of the aforesaid ways. The third example is of servants and household slaves, who have a common permission to use some of their master's things for their necessities, for which no fixed portion is assigned to them. Those things are common to them, and yet in none of the aforesaid ways, as can be seen by going through each member separately. They are therefore common in another way: as regards the lawful power of using them to relieve their needs, until the master should decide otherwise, for he could provide for them in another way.

units.la: Multa alia exempla possent adduci, sed illa ad praesens sufficiant: quia per illa, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, patet expresse, quod diuisio sua, sicut ipse eam intelligit, est insufficiens reputanda. Cum vero allegatur Nicolaus, dicunt quod Nicolaus Tertius magis communiter accepit visum facti quam ille: quia Nicolaus Tertius non solum accepit visum facti pro actu vtendi sicut pro actu comedendi, bibendi & inhabitandi & huiusmodi: sed accepit etiam vsum facti pro licita potestate vtendi, quomodo accepit vsum beatus Clemens, prout recitatur duodecim. quaestion. 1. cap. dilectissimus, cum dicit: Communis enim vsus omnium, quae sunt in hoc mundo omnibus esse hominibus debuit, &c. vbi non accipitur vsus pro actu vtendi, nec pro vsu qui est vsus iuris nudus, & pro vsu fructu, sed accipitur pro licita potestate vtendi, & sic accipit vsum facti Nicolaus, vnde simplicem vsum facti vocat licitam potestatem vtendi, cui non est necessario annexum ius, quo vsum valeat in iudicio vendicare, nonnunquam tamen vsus facti vocat actum vtendi.
units.tr: Many other examples could be adduced, but let these suffice for the present: for by these, as those opponents say, it is clearly shown that his division, as he himself understands it, must be regarded as insufficient. When Nicholas is cited, they say that Nicholas the Third took the phrase "use of fact" more broadly than he does: for Nicholas the Third took "use of fact" not only for the act of using, such as the act of eating, drinking, inhabiting and the like, but also took "use of fact" for the lawful power of using, in the way blessed Clement took "use," as it is recited in Dist. 12, c. Dilectissimus, where he says: "For common use of all the things that are in this world ought to be for all men," etc. Here "use" is not taken for the act of using, nor for use which is bare right of use, nor for usufruct, but for the lawful power of using. Thus Nicholas takes "use of fact," and so he calls the lawful power of using "simple use of fact," to which a right by which one may claim the use in court is not necessarily attached; yet sometimes he calls the act of using "use of fact."

units.la: Sed forte aliquis dubitaret circa praedicta, an licentia debeat ius vocari? Ad hoc dici potest ad praesens, quod an licentia possit vocari ius communissime accepto nomine iuris, est inferius indagandum. Ad praesens autem sufficit, quod non debet vocari ius, quo valeat quis rem vel vsum rei in iudicio vendicare vel defendere quo quomodo. Sed adhuc quaereret aliquis, quomodo accepit Nicolaus Tertius ius vtendi? Ad hoc potest dici, salvo meliori iudicio, quod licet ius vtendi communiter, & tamen proprie sumptum communius sit, quam vsusfructus & nudus vsus, tamen stricte sumptum est idem quod nudus vsus. Et sic Nicolaus Tertius in decretali Exiit videtur accipere ius vtendi, & sic accepto iure vtendi, an Nicolaus Tertius, cum dicit: cum in rebus temporalibus sit considerare praecipuum proprietatem, possessionem, vsumfructum, ius vtendi & simplicem facti vsum, & alterius, &c. sufficienter enumeret omnia, quae possunt in rebus temporalibus reperiri vel non, ad praesens est nullatenus inquirendum, praesertim cum Nicolaus Tertius enumerauit illa, quae ad suum intentum sufficiunt.
units.tr: But perhaps someone might doubt about what has been said, whether a "license" ought to be called a right? To this it can be said, for the present, that whether a license can be called a right in the most general sense of the word "right" is to be investigated further on. For the present, it is enough that it ought not to be called a right by which one may in any way claim or defend a thing, or the use of a thing, in court. But someone would still ask, how did Nicholas the Third take "right of use"? To this it can be said, with better judgment reserved, that although "right of use" is more common when taken properly, and is more general than usufruct and bare use, yet taken strictly it is the same as bare use. And so Nicholas the Third in the decretal Exiit seems to take "right of use," and with "right of use" so taken, whether Nicholas the Third, when he says: "since in temporal things one must consider chiefly ownership, possession, usufruct, right of use and simple use of fact, and of another," etc., sufficiently enumerates all that can or cannot be found in temporal things, is in no way to be inquired into at present, especially since Nicholas the Third listed those things which suffice for his purpose.

units.la: Viso, quomodo diuisio istius impugnati, vt eam intelligit, est insufficiens, & ita quantum ad formam arguendi ratio sua est soluta, tamen illa solutio ad primos credentes, de quibus facta est ratio, applicetur. Et vt videatur, quomodo erant omnia istis communia, est per membra singula discurrendum. Cum igitur primo accipitur, quod illae res non erat communes omnibus credentibus, quantum ad simplicem facti vsum. Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod illa potest concedi, si simplex facti vsus excludat omne ius, quia dicunt, quod inter illos credentes erant aliqui, qui vel gerentes vicem totius communitatis, vel alicuius congregationis partialis, poterant res illas, si ablatae fuissent ab infidelibus, in iudicio vendicare, & ita vel tota communitas, vel aliqua pars communitatis ius habebat in rebus communibus, quo valebant in iudicio litigare. Communitas tamen specialis Apostolorum nullo modo tale ius habebat, & ita Apostoli vtendo aliquibus rebus communibus habebant actum vtendi separatum ab omni dominio speciali & communi proprio collegio Apostolorum. Sic igitur accepto simplici vsu facti, non solum pro actu vtendi, sed etiam pro licita potestate vtendi separata ab omni iure, quo quis valeat in iudicio litigare, concedi potest quod res illae non erant communes omnibus, quantum ad simplicem vsu facti, nec appellans vnquam dixit, quod erant communes omnibus, quantum ad simplicem vsum facti, sic accepto simplici vsu facti. Si autem simplex vsus facti accipitur pro licita potestate vtendi, cui non necessario est annexum ius, quo quis valeat litigare in iudicio: sic fuerunt omnia communia quantum ad simplicem facti vsum, hoc tamen propter Apostolos intelligendum est sane, quibus non erat licitum vti pecunia; sed tantum licitum erat eis vtiliis, quae de pecunia emebantur, & licet hoc sit verum secundum impugnatores, tamen rationes suae, vt dicunt, non concludunt. Vnde dicunt, quod prima ratio sua accepit errorem apertum, cum dicitur, quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus vsus facti sumendo vsum proprie, locum habere non potest, hoc enim vt dicunt, erroneum esset censendum.
units.tr: Having seen how the division of this opponent, as he understands it, is insufficient, and so as far as the form of arguing goes his reasoning is refuted, nevertheless that solution is to be applied to the first believers, of whom the argument was made. And so that it may be seen how all things were common to them, we must go through each part separately. When it is first assumed that those things were not common to all believers as regards the simple use of fact, these opponents say that this may be granted if simple use of fact excludes every right: for they say that among those believers there were some who, acting on behalf of the whole community or of some partial assembly, could claim those things in court if they had been taken by unbelievers; and so either the whole community or some part of the community had a right in common things by which they could litigate in court. Yet the special community of the Apostles in no way had such a right, and so the Apostles, in using some common things, had an act of using separate from every special ownership and from what was common to the proper college of the Apostles. Thus, taking "simple use of fact" not only for the act of using but also for the lawful power of using, separated from every right by which one may litigate in court, it can be granted that those things were not common to all as regards simple use of fact, and the appellant never said that they were common to all as regards simple use of fact, taking simple use of fact in this sense. But if "simple use of fact" is taken for the lawful power of using, to which a right by which one may litigate in court is not necessarily attached, then all things were common as regards simple use of fact; yet this must be understood with care concerning the Apostles, to whom it was not lawful to use money, but only lawful for them to use the things that were bought with money. And although this is true according to the opponents, nevertheless, as they say, their arguments do not conclude. Hence they say that his first argument rests on a manifest error, when it is said that in things consumed by use, the use of fact, taking "use" properly, cannot have a place; for this, they say, would be judged erroneous.

units.la: Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod aliquod nomen vel vocabulum habet saepe plures significationes, quarum quaelibet est propria. Vnde dicunt, quod semper in primo modo aequiuocationis quaelibet significatio est propria, licet in secundo modo, si vna sibi principalis & communior sit propria, & secundaria aut minus communis sit impropria. Nunc autem ita est, quod hoc nomen vsus habet plures significationes: quia aliquando accipitur pro actu vtendi, aliquando pro quodam iure determinato, quo quis determinato modo vellet vti rebus alienis. Prima autem significatio huius nominis vsus est principalior & communior: tum quia prius inventa, tum quia in pluribus scientis & modo loquendi vulgari saepius vsitata. Nam hoc nomine vsus in prima significatione vtuntur omnes scientiae, quae vtuntur hoc nomine vsus. Sic enim Theologia, Philosophia moralis, medicina, & legales scientiae vtuntur hoc nomine vsus. Et modus etiam loquendi vulgaris in eadem significatione vtitur hoc nomine vsus, sed alia significatione eius non vtuntur nec Theologia, nec moralis Philosophia, nec medicina, nec vulgaris modus loquendi, sed solummodo legales scientiae & scripturae, quae modum loquendi scientiarum legalium imitantur, vtuntur hoc nomine vsus in secunda significatione, hoc auctoritatibus innumeris manifeste posset probari: sed propter prolixitate vitanda minime adducuntur.
units.tr: To make this clear, they say it must be known that a name or term often has several meanings, each of which is proper. Hence they say that in the first kind of equivocation every meaning is proper, whereas in the second kind, if one meaning is principal and more common, it is proper, and the secondary or less common meaning is improper. Now it is the case that this word "use" has several meanings: for sometimes it is taken for the act of using, and sometimes for a certain determinate right by which someone would wish to use another's things in a determinate way. The first meaning of this word "use" is, however, the principal and more common one, both because it was discovered first and because it is more often used in many sciences and in ordinary speech. For all the sciences that use the word "use" use it in the first sense. Thus theology, moral philosophy, medicine and the legal sciences use the word "use" in this way. And ordinary speech also uses the word "use" in this same sense; but neither theology, nor moral philosophy, nor medicine, nor ordinary speech uses its other meaning; only the legal sciences and the writings which imitate the manner of speaking of the legal sciences use the word "use" in the second sense. This could be clearly proved by countless authorities, but they are not cited, to avoid prolixity.

units.la: Prima ergo significatio vsus, secundum quod accipitur pro actu vtendi, est principalis & communior significatio huius nominis vsus, nec est a significatione alia deriuata vel accepta, ergo illa est propria significatio eius, licet etiam forte alia sit propria.
