Cum igitur actus comedendi, bibendi & huiusmodi in Theologia, Philosophia morali, medicina, vulgari modo loquendi & in scientiis legalibus vocentur actus vtendi & vsus, sicut per innumeras auctoritates posset ostendi, constat quod actus comedendi & bibendi & huiusmodi est proprie vsus. Ex quo patenter infertur, quod vsusfacti, qui proprie vocatur actus vtendi, proprie in rebus vsu consumptibilibus reperitur, & quamuis vsus facti proprie reperiatur in rebus vsu consumptibilibus, tamen vsus iuris non reperitur proprie in omnibus rebus vsu consumptibilibus. Vnde ille terminus vsus iuris habet duas significationes, vnam propriam: & secundum illam concedendum est, quod vsus iuris reperitur in rebus non consumptibilibus vsu. Aliam habet significationem impropriam: & secundum illam conceditur, quod vsus iuris reperitur in quibusdam rebus vsu consumptibilibus, nullo tamen modo debet negari vsum facti 5 in rebus vsu consumptibilibus reperiri proprie sumpto vsu. Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod tales distinctiones multiplicitatum vocabulorum, & declarationes vocabulorum, ad scientias spectantes sermocinales, non ad scientias reales, nec ad scripturas de rebus: & ita cum tractatur de rebus, sicut in proposito tractatur de rebus & non de sermonibus, talia minime sunt adducenda. Ad hoc isti impugnatores respondent dicentes, quod in omnibus scripturis & argumentationibus impugnantibus veritatem defectus, qui admittuntur in ipsis debet veritatis amator patentius explicare, ne in errorem simplices inducantur, iste autem impugnatus, ut dicunt isti impugnatores, per multiplicitates terminorum & nominum & abusiuos & extraneos modos loquendi, prophanas vocum novitates & modorum loquendi communium reprobationem molitur errores inducere, prosternere veritatem, Scripturas sacras ad falsum trahere intellectum, doctrinam sanctorum subuertere, determinationem ecclesiae reprobare, decretales summorum Pontificum annullare, haereticare catholicos innocentes, & religiones confundere, ac fidem destruere orthodoxam, ideo dicunt, quod huiusmodi multiplicitates & modos loquendi oportet euidentius explanare: quia ipsis declaratis expressius omni intelligenti patebit, quod doctrina istius impugnati ab omni veritate est vacua, plena erroribus, nullam habens apparentiam, vel colorem; imo existimant, quod si illa, quae ad sermocinales spectant scientias, didicisset & intellexisset: etsi non veritatis amore, tamen ex timore verecundiae scripturas suas nullatenus publicasset, quantae autem utilitatis pro intelligendis scripturis, imo quantae necessitatis sint sermocinales scientiae, sancti canonicae scripturae tractatores euidenter exponunt.
units.tr: The first meaning of "use," therefore, insofar as it is taken for the act of using, is the principal and more common meaning of the word "use," and it is not derived or received from another meaning; therefore it is its proper meaning, although perhaps another is also proper. Since, then, the acts of eating, drinking and the like are called "acts of using" and "use" in theology, moral philosophy, medicine, ordinary speech and the legal sciences, as could be shown by innumerable authorities, it is established that the acts of eating, drinking and the like are properly "use." From this it is plainly inferred that "use of fact," which is properly called the act of using, is properly found in things consumed by use; and although use of fact is properly found in things consumed by use, yet right of use is not properly found in all things consumed by use. Hence that term "right of use" has two meanings: one proper, and according to it it must be granted that right of use is found in things not consumed by use; another improper, and according to it it is granted that right of use is found in certain things consumed by use. Yet it must in no way be denied that use of fact is found in things consumed by use, taking "use" properly. But perhaps someone will say that such distinctions of many-meaning words, and explanations of words, belong to the sciences that deal with speech, not to the real sciences, nor to writings about things; and so, when things are treated, as in the present matter things and not words are treated, such things are not to be brought forward at all. To this these opponents reply, saying that in all writings and arguments which attack the truth, the defects which are admitted in them ought to be explained more openly by a lover of truth, lest simple people be led into error. But this opponent, as these opponents say, by the multiplicity of terms and names, and by abusive and foreign modes of speech, labours to introduce errors, overthrow the truth, twist the Holy Scriptures to a false sense, subvert the teaching of the saints, reject the determination of the Church, annul the decretals of the supreme Pontiffs, brand innocent Catholics as heretics, confound the religious orders, and destroy the orthodox faith through profane novelties of words and the rejection of common modes of speech. Therefore they say that such multiplicities and modes of speech must be explained more clearly, because once they are explained it will be plainer to every intelligent person that the teaching of this opponent is empty of all truth, full of errors, and has no appearance or colour at all. Indeed they think that if he had learned and understood the things pertaining to the sciences of speech, then, even if not from love of truth, yet from fear of shame he would never have published his writings; and how great is the usefulness, indeed the necessity, of the sciences of speech for understanding the Scriptures, the holy expositors of the canonical Scriptures clearly set out.

units.la: Augustinus enim in libro secundo de ordine rerum asseruit manifeste, quod ad quaestiones difficiles Theologiae tractandas nullus debet sine scientia disputandi accedere. Anselmus etiam docet, vnumquemque Theologiam volentem addiscere prius in rudimentis grammaticae & logicae fundari debere, & Hieronymus, vt recitatur distinction. trigesim. tert. capitulo, si quis, ait: Si quis grammaticam artem nouerit, vel dialecticam recte loquendi rationem habeat, & inter vera & falsa diiudicet, non improbamus. Quia ergo ille impugnatus, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, propter ignorantiam multiplicitatis vocum & modorum per diuersa sophismatum diuerticula in multas incidit falsitates, ad suas clarius manifestandas multiplicitates vocum & fallacias, per quas sua peccant sophismata, patenter oportet detegere: quia aliter sua sophismata insoluta manebunt.
units.tr: For Augustine clearly asserts in the second book of de ordine rerum that no one should approach the difficult questions of theology without the skill of disputation. Anselm also teaches that anyone who wishes to learn theology must first be grounded in the rudiments of grammar and logic. And Jerome, as quoted in distinction. trigesim. tert. capitulo, si quis, says: If anyone has learned the art of grammar, or has the method of speaking correctly from dialectic, and can distinguish true from false, we do not disapprove. Since, then, that man who was attacked, as these opponents say, through ignorance of the multiplicity of words and modes, fell into many falsehoods through the various side-paths of sophisms, it is necessary to expose plainly the multiple meanings of words and the fallacies by which his sophisms go wrong, so that his sophisms, once made clear, may be shown to be unsound. Otherwise his sophisms will remain unrefuted.

units.la: Prima itaque ratio sua falsum assumit, cum dicit, quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus vsus facti proprie sumendo, locum habere non potest, quia vsus facti, sicut dictum est, proprie significat actum comedendi, bibendi, & huiusmodi. Cum vero probat, quod vsus proprie sumptus requirit, quod cum ipso remaneat rei substantia salua: illa si habet veritatem, debet intelligi de vsu iuris, non de vsu facti. Et ita per eam probatur, quod vsus iuris in omnibus rebus vsu consumptibilibus proprie locum habere non potest, sed ex hoc non sequitur, quod vsus facti in ipsis proprie habere locum non potest: & ita prima ratio errorem accipit apertum, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, hoc tamen non obstante, illam debet concedere, quod illae res erant communes omnibus quantum ad vsum facti, & hoc accipiendo vsum facti, quantum ad licitam potestatem vtendi ipsis rebus communibus, vel aliquib. emptis de aliis rebus communibus, quod dicunt propter Apostolos, quibus non licebat vti pecunia, quae tamen debet inter res illas vsu consumptibiles computari.
units.tr: His first argument, then, assumes something false when it says that in things consumed by use use of fact, taken in its proper sense, cannot apply, because use of fact, as has been said, properly signifies the act of eating, drinking and the like. When he proves that use taken properly requires that the substance of the thing remain intact with it, that proof, if it has any truth, must be understood of use in law, not of use in fact. And so it is proved through that argument that use in law cannot properly apply to all things consumed by use; but it does not follow from this that use in fact cannot properly apply to them. Thus the first argument, as these opponents say, takes an obvious error. Nevertheless, he must concede this, that those things were common to all as regards the use of fact, and this taking the use of fact as the lawful power of using those common things, or some things bought from other common goods, which they say was for the sake of the Apostles, who were not allowed to use money, though this must be counted among those things consumed by use.

units.la: Secunda etiam ratio non concludit, quia procedit de vsu facti, qui est actus vtendi, & non de potestate vtendi modo praedicto.
units.tr: The second argument also does not conclude, because it proceeds from use of fact, which is the act of using, and not from the power of using in the manner just described.

units.la: Tertia ratio, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, assumit quaedam erronea, quae sunt ita ridiculosa, vt nequaquam improbatione, sed derisu indigeant. Primum est, quod vsus facti communitati non conuenit, illud, quod dicunt isti impugnatores, esse erroneum, quia scripturae diuinae repugnat. Populus enim est quaedam communitas, & tamen populo conuenit vsus facti. Ait enim Apostolus 1.Cor.4. Sedit populus manducare & bibere, & illud habetur Exod. 32. In aliis etiam locis scripturae patenter vsus facti populo, plebi turbae & ita communitatibus multis tribuitur. Secundum erroneum in ratione praedicta contentum, vt dicunt, est, quod communitas gerit personam imaginariam seu repraesentatam, hoc enim videtur contrarium veritati, etiam repraesentata nequeunt agere realiter, sed ecclesia est quaedam communitas, quae multos potestatus reales exercere, habet enim ecclesia iurisdictionem magnam, per quam potest iudicare inter litigantes, res ecclesiae defensare, & multa alia facere, quae nequeunt personae imaginariae repraesentatae conuenire. Hoc per multas auctoritates scripturae diuinae, & per sacros canones multipliciter posset ostendi, sicut dicunt isti impugnatores, quod est tam derisorium, quod non oportet rationibus vel auctoritatibus improbare, hoc etiam, vt dicunt, dicta istius impugnati repugnat.
units.tr: The third argument, as these opponents say, assumes certain erroneous things which are so ridiculous that they need not refutation but derision. The first is that use of fact does not belong to a community; this, these opponents say, is false, because it contradicts the divine Scripture. For the people is a certain community, and yet use of fact belongs to the people. For the Apostle says, 1 Cor. 4: The people sat down to eat and drink, and it is found in Exod. 32. Also in other places Scripture plainly attributes use of fact to the people, the multitude, the crowd, and thus to many communities. The second error contained in the aforesaid argument, they say, is that a community bears an imaginary or represented person. This seems contrary to the truth: even represented persons cannot act in reality, but the Church is a certain community which can exercise many real powers. For the Church has great jurisdiction, by which it can judge between litigants, defend the property of the Church, and do many other things which cannot belong to a represented imaginary person. This could be shown in many ways by many authorities of divine Scripture and by the sacred canons, as these opponents say; but this is so absurd that it need not be refuted by reasons or authorities. This too, they say, contradicts the statements of the man who was attacked.

units.la: Nam in constitutione sua (quia quorundam) asserit manifeste, quod Ordo Minorum non est persona imaginaria & repraesentata; & eadem ratione, alia communitas non est persona imaginaria & repraesentata. Ad rationem igitur dicit isti impugnatores: coitati potest vsus facti conuenire: quia potest maducare & bibere & vestiri, & cum dicitur, talis vsus vnam & verae personam exigit. Dicunt, quod interdum vsus facti, sicut vnus actus comedendi & bibendi, requirit vnicam personam, licet aliquis sit alius actus, qui non requirit vnicam personam, sed plures personas, sicut de tractu navis, qui non vnicam personam, sed multas personas veras requirit, & ita omnis actus requirit veram personam: & hoc vel vnam vel plures. Cum vero dicit, quod communitas non gerit veram personam, dicunt, quod communitas non est vna vera persona, sed est plures verae personae. Unde populus est multi homines congregati in vnum, sicut communitas fidelium est multi fideles profitentes. Et ideo cum dicit, quod communitas gerit personam imaginariam seu repraesentatam, dicunt, quod illud est ridiculosum: quia communitas non est aliquid fantasticum nec imaginarium, sed verae personae: sicut grex porcorum non est aliquid fantasticum: nec civitas est aliquid fantasticum aut fictum, sed est verae res plures, non unica.
units.tr: For in his constitution (Quia quorundam) he plainly asserts that the Order of Minors is not an imaginary and represented person; and by the same reasoning another community is not an imaginary and represented person. To the argument, then, these opponents reply: use of fact can belong to a community, because it can eat, drink and clothe itself; and when it is said that such a use requires one true person, they say that sometimes use of fact, such as a single act of eating and drinking, requires one single person, though there is another kind of act which does not require one single person but several persons, as with the hauling of a ship, which requires not one single person but many true persons; and so every act requires a true person, either one or several. When he says that a community does not bear a true person, they say that a community is not one true person but several true persons. Hence a people is many men gathered into one, just as the community of the faithful is many faithful who profess the faith. And so when he says that a community bears an imaginary or represented person, they say that this is ridiculous: for a community is not something fantastic or imaginary, but true persons; just as a herd of pigs is not something fantastic, nor is a city something fantastic or fictitious, but are many true things, not a single one.

units.la: Deinde isti impugnatores respondent ad illud membrum, quod res vsu consumptibiles non fuerunt communes credentibus, quantum ad ius utendi seu usumfructum: dicentes, quod accipiendo ius utendi stricte, sicut in decretali Exiit, illae res non fuerunt communes credentibus, neque quo ad ius utendi, neque quo ad usumfructum: quia illae res non fuerunt alicuius alterius, quam illorum credentium, & ideo non habebant in eis tale ius utendi, id est nudum usum iuris, neque usumfructum. Accipiendo tamen ius utendi communius, sic fuerunt illae res communes vel omnibus credentibus, vel aliquibus quo ad ius utendi.
units.tr: Then these opponents reply to that clause, that things consumed by use were not common to believers as regards the right of use or usufruct, saying that taking the right of use strictly, as in the decretal Exiit, those things were not common to believers, neither as regards the right of use nor as regards usufruct, because those things belonged to no one other than those believers, and therefore they did not have in them such a right of use, that is, the bare use of right, nor usufruct. Yet taking right of use more broadly, those things were common either to all believers or to some as regards the right of use.

units.la: Et quia dicitur, fuerunt communes omnibus credentibus, vel aliquibus quo ad ius utendi sumptum communiter propter Apostolos: inde intentio istorum quantum ad Apostolos est hic aliqualiter declaranda. Dicunt igitur isti impugnatores, quod nec est intentio appellantis, nec ipsorum in suis traditionibus indagare, an Apostoli habuerunt in temporalibus aliquod ius utendi, imo etiam aliquale dominium & proprietatem communem collegio suo speciali & toti residuo communitatis fidelium, vel illorum qui bona communia ecclesiae expensanda receperunt: sed intentio eorum est, quod Apostoli in rebus temporalibus non habuerunt dominium, vel proprietatem, nec aliquod ius utendi, etiam communiter accepto iure utendi pro iure, quod actione dat civilem, proprium collegio Apostolorum, quemadmodum nolunt discutere, an Fratres Minores nunc habeant ius vel dominium communiter accepto dominio in rebus communibus totius ecclesiae, in quibus, sicut ostensum est, prius vel tota communitas omnium fidelium, vel communitas aliquorum fidelium, non omnium habet aliquale dominium: sed intendunt asserere, quod nec totus ordo Fratrum Minorum: nec aliqua pars Ordinis habet aliquod dominium vel ius, quo possit quis in iudicio litigare, quod sit proprium toti Ordini vel alicui parti eius, & propter hoc saepe vtuntur tali modo loquendi: tota communitas credentium, vel aliqua pars habuit ius aliquod in rebus communibus, quia si Apostoli habuerunt ius commune collegio suo & aliis, etiam debet dici, quod tota communitas habebat ius in huiusmodi rebus. Si autem Apostoli non habebant ius commune sibi & aliis, cum certum sit quod non habuerunt proprium, nec aliquib. Apostolis, nec alicui Apostolo, neque toti collegio Apostolorum: tunc debet dici, quod altera pars communitatis omnium fidelium, qui tunc erat; aliquod ius habuit in huiusmodi rebus. Apostoli autem secundum illum modum habebat tantum modo licita potestate utendi reb. emptis de pecunia quae erat communis, & etiam habebat licitam potestatem utendi rebus aliis post distributionem factam per illos ad quos distribuere pertinebat.
units.tr: And because it is said that they were common to all believers, or to some as regards the right of use, taken in common with regard to the Apostles, the intention of these men concerning the Apostles must here be explained in some measure. These opponents therefore say that it is neither the intention of the appellant, nor of themselves in their treatises, to inquire whether the Apostles had in temporal matters any right of use, or indeed any common dominion and property, shared by their special college and the whole remainder of the community of the faithful, or of those who received common goods of the Church to be spent. Rather, their intention is that the Apostles had no dominion or property in temporal things, nor any right of use, even taking the right of use in the common sense of a right which gives a civil action, belonging to the college of the Apostles. In the same way they are unwilling to examine whether the Friars Minor now have a right or dominion, taking dominion in the common sense, in the common goods of the whole Church; in which, as has been shown, either the whole community of all the faithful, or the community of some of the faithful, not all, has some kind of dominion. Rather, they intend to assert that neither the whole Order of Friars Minor nor any part of the Order has any dominion or right by which one could litigate in court, which belongs to the whole Order or to some part of it; and for this reason they often use this manner of speaking: the whole community of believers, or some part, had some right in common goods. For if the Apostles had a right common to their college and to others, it must also be said that the whole community had a right in such things. But if the Apostles did not have a right common to themselves and to others, since it is certain that they had no right of their own, neither as individual Apostles nor as a single Apostle, nor to the whole college of Apostles, then it must be said that the other part of the community of all the faithful who then existed had some right in such things. In this manner the Apostles had only the lawful power of using goods bought with the money which was common, and also had lawful power of using other things after the distribution made by those to whom it belonged to distribute.

units.la: Et ad illud, quod de possessione, dicunt quod illae res communes fuerunt vel omnibus credentibus vel aliquibus quantum ad possessionem, quae est ius possidendi seu detinendi, nec hoc negat appellans, licet dicat Apostolos nullum ius proprium Apostolis vel eorum collegio in illis temporalibus habuisse, sed tantum simplicem facti usum, per exclusionem omnis iuris proprii collegio Apostolorum & cuilibet Apostolo.
units.tr: And as to what they say about possession, that those goods were common either to all believers or to some of them as regards possession, which is the right of possessing or holding, the appellant does not deny this, although he says that the Apostles, or their college, had no proper right over those temporal goods, but only the simple use in fact, with every proper right excluded from the college of Apostles and from each Apostle.

units.la: Ad conclusionem autem, quam vltimo infert, quod illae res erant effectae communes quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Dicunt quod erant communes vel toti communitati, vel alicui parti communitatis, quo ad aliquale dominium seu proprietatem: sed non ad tale dominium, quale iste impugnatus ipsos asserit habuisse.
units.tr: As to the conclusion which he finally draws, that those goods had been made common as regards ownership and property: they say that they were common either to the whole community or to some part of the community, as regards some kind of ownership or property, but not to that kind of ownership which this man under attack claims they had.

units.la: Circa literam aliqua sunt notanda. (Si vero intelligat quod non erant eis communia quo ad proprietatem seu dominium) hic recitat verba appellantis, quod licet intelligat, quod non erant eis communia quo ad proprietatem seu dominium illo modo, quo accepit ille impugnatus proprietatem seu dominium, puta accipiendo dominium pro dominio quod nonnulli vocant dominium liberum, quomodo res ecclesiae non sunt communes, quo ad proprietatem seu dominium. Diceret tamen appellans, quod erant communes omnibus vel aliquibus quo ad dominium, alio modo accipiendo dominium, sicut tactum est prius (sed tantum quo ad simplicem facti usum.) Hic falsum imponit appellanti, ut dicunt, quia sicut patet in tota illa impugnatione, de simplici facti usu, praecipue cum dictione exclusiva, nullam facit penitus mentionem (Aut quo ad ius utendi seu usumfructum.) Hic innuit quod pro eodem accipiatur ius utendi & usufructus, quod non est verum. Caetera patent per ea, quae dicta sunt superius.
units.tr: Some points must be noted about the wording. (But if he understands that they were not common to them as regards property or ownership) here he recites the appellant's words, which, although he understands that they were not common to them as regards property or ownership in the sense in which that man under attack took property or ownership, namely taking ownership in the sense that some call free ownership, in which way the goods of the church are not common as regards property or ownership. The appellant would nevertheless say that they were common to all or some as regards ownership, taking ownership in another sense, as was said before (but only as regards the simple use in fact.) Here, as they say, he falsely imputes to the appellant, because, as is plain throughout that whole refutation, he makes no mention at all of simple use in fact, especially with the exclusive word, (or as regards the right of use or usufruct.) Here he hints that the right of use and usufruct are taken as the same thing, which is not true. The rest is clear from what has been said above.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAP. VII.

units.la: Quantum autem ad illud, quod postea haereticus dicit, videlicet: Et sic quilibet eorum habebat usum rerum usu consumptibilium absque dominio & proprietate, siue a proprietate & dominio separatum: dicimus, quod illud infert ex falsa suppositione, quam fecerat prius. Dixerat enim quod res usu consumptibiles inter credentes erant communes tantum, quo ad simplicem usum facti. Et ex hoc concludit, quod quilibet eorum absque absque dominio & proprietate habeat rerum vsu consumptibilium vsum facti, unde cum primum sit falsum, scilicet quod res vsu consumptibiles essent communes inter credentes tantum quo ad simplicem vsum facti: imo erant communes quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, vt superius est probatum, patet illud, quod ex eo concluditur, esse falsum, sc. quod quilibet haberet in rebus talibus simplicem vsum facti. Praeterea patet alia ratione esse falsum: quia vsus facti habere nequit ab aliquo, vt superius est ostensum.
units.tr: As for what the heretic says next, namely: "And so each of them had the use of consumable goods without dominion and ownership, that is, separated from ownership and dominion," we reply that he draws this inference from a false assumption he had made earlier. For he had said that consumable goods were common among the believers only as to the simple use of the fact. From this he concludes that each of them, without dominion and ownership, has the use of the fact of consumable goods. Since the first point is false, namely that consumable goods were common among the believers only as to the simple use of the fact, but in fact they were common as to dominion or ownership, as was proved above, what he concludes from it is clearly false, namely that each would have a simple use of the fact in such goods. Moreover, it is false for another reason: the use of the fact cannot be had from anyone, as was shown above.

units.la: In ista parte respondet impugnatus ad quartum, quod appellans tangit in impugnatione superius recitata. Inferebat enim appellans, quod quilibet eorum (scilicet credentium) habebat vsum rerum vsu consumptibilium absque proprietate & dominio, siue à proprietate seu dominio separatum. Ad quod ille impugnatus respondet, dicens quod illud infert appellans ex falsa suppositione, sc. quod res erant communes inter credentes, tantum quo ad simplicem facti vsum, quod (vt dicit) patet esse falsum ex praecedentibus: quia ostensum est, quod illae res erant communes, quo ad dominium seu proprietatē. Secundo dicit conclusionē illatā esse falsam: quia vsus facti nequit habere.
units.tr: In this part the one attacked replies to the fourth point, which the appellant touches on in the objection recited above. For the appellant inferred that each of them (namely the believers) had the use of consumable goods without ownership and dominion, that is, separated from ownership or dominion. To this the one attacked replies, saying that the appellant infers this from a false assumption, namely that the goods were common among the believers only as to the simple use of the fact. As he says, this is clearly false from what came before, since it has been shown that those goods were common as to dominion or ownership. Second, he says the conclusion drawn is false, because the use of the fact cannot be had.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores illa, quae hic dicuntur, impugnant duplicitep. Primo quia appellanti salsum imponit, cum asserit ipsum dixisse res vsu consumptibiles fuisse communes credentibus, tantum quo ad simplicem facti vsum: quia, sicut patet intuenti, de simplici facti vsu in tota illa impugnatione appellantis nulla fit mentio, & ideo appellans non inferebat, quod quilibet eorum habebat tantum simplicem facti vsum rerum vsu consumptibilium à dominio separatum, sed inferebat, quod quilibet habebat vsum rerum vsu consumptibilium à proprietate seu dominio separatum. Intendens loqui de dominio speciali, & de dominio communi civili & mundano: quod dominium liberum appellatur. Secundo impugnant isti praedicta quo ad hoc, quod dicit, quod vsus facti habere nequit ab aliquo. Hoc enim multis modis conantur ostendere erroneum, sicut postea apparebit.
units.tr: But these objectors attack what is said here in two ways. First, they falsely charge the appellant, when he asserts that the appellant said consumable goods were common to the believers only as to the simple use of the fact. For, as anyone can see, the simple use of the fact is not mentioned anywhere in the whole of the appellant's objection. The appellant therefore did not infer that each of them had merely the simple use of the fact of consumable goods separated from dominion; he inferred that each had the use of consumable goods separated from ownership or dominion. He meant to speak of special dominion, and of civil and worldly common dominion, which is called free ownership. Second, these objectors attack the above on the ground that he says the use of the fact cannot be had from anyone. For they try in many ways to show this to be an error, as will appear later.

units.la: Nunc ad literam accedatur, (Habebit vsum) dicit appellans vsum: & non dicit tamen simplicē vsum facti, (absq; dominio) sc. speciali, & absq; dominio communi civili & mundano, quo potest dominus res suas prout voluerit ordinare (dixerat enim superius, &c.) Patet clare, quod nunquam hoc dixerat (ex hoc concludit, &c.) Falsum est secundum istos, quia nec concludit illud, quod ille impugnatus dicit, nec illud ex quo dicit eum concludere, & ita in toto isto processu usque ibi: Praeterea, appellanti falsum imponit (vsus facti habere nequit) de hoc inferius disseretur.
units.tr: Now let us come to the letter. (He will have the use) the appellant says "use," but he does not say "simple use of the fact," (apart from dominion), that is, special dominion, and apart from common civil and worldly dominion, by which an owner may dispose of his goods as he wishes (for he had said above, etc.). It is plain that he never said this (he concludes from this, etc.). According to these men it is false, because he draws neither the conclusion the one attacked states nor the premise from which he says he draws it; and so throughout this whole passage up to the words Moreover, he falsely charges the appellant (the use of the fact cannot be had). This will be discussed further below.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Ad illud vero, quod dicit ille haeretic, quod dicta doctrina, sc. quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus vsus iuris vel facti à proprietate seu dominio separatus non potest constitui nec haberi, omnem religionem habentem votum abdicationis proprietatis rerum temporalium destruit & confundit: quia secundum hoc quilibet religiosus, quando vtitur rebus vsu consumptibilibus proprietarius censetur, dicimus, quod mentitur aperte. Omnes enim religiones, praeterquam beati Francisci, quorum professores ad viuendum sine proprio astringuntur, confitentur se habere posse secundum suas Regulas, & habere etiam tam res vsu consumptibiles, quam non vsu consumptibiles, quo ad proprietatem & dominium in communi, licet aliquid per statuta super additā Regulis, quantum ad aliqua immobilia suas Regulas duxerint restringendas, quare professores dicti non possunt vti rebus, si vsus proprie sumatur, vt superius est probatum: possent tamen res huiusmodi consumere, vt potè panem comedendo & vinum bibendo & sic de aliis, sed per actum consumendi talia non sunt censendi proprietarii, cum ipsa non vt propria consumere, sed vt communia sunt censenda. Actusque consumēdi res huiusmodi nequaquam ab ipso communi dominio separatur, sicut si duo habentes panem communem, illum indiuisim comederent, neuter propter hoc panis, quem comederent, proprietarius fieret, nec diceretur comedisse panem proprium, sed communem.
units.tr: As to what that heretic says, namely that the said doctrine (that in consumable things the use of right or of fact cannot be constituted or held separately from ownership or dominion) destroys and confounds every religion that has a vow of renouncing the ownership of temporal goods, because according to this any religious, when he uses consumable things, is considered a proprietor: we say he plainly lies. For all religious orders, except that of blessed Francis, whose members are bound to live without property, confess that by their Rules they may have, both as to ownership and dominion in common, consumable and non-consumable things, although by statutes added to their Rules they have chosen to restrict some immovable things under their Rules. Wherefore the said members cannot use things, if use is properly taken, as has been proved above; yet they can consume such things, as by eating bread and drinking wine and so on. But by the act of consuming such things they are not to be considered proprietors, since they do not consume them as their own, but are to be regarded as common. And the act of consuming such things is in no way separated from the common ownership itself, just as if two men who had common bread ate it undivided, neither would become a proprietor of the bread they ate because of this, nor would it be said that they had eaten their own bread, but common bread.

units.la: In ista parte ille impugnatus respondet ad quintum, quod in impugnatione tangitur appellantis, quod videlicet doctrina istius impugnati omnem religionem habentem votum abdicationis proprietatis omnium temporalium destruit & confundit, & diuiditur in duas partes, quia primo ad hoc directe respondet. Secundo suam intentionem circa praecedentia magis expresse declarat in parte immediate sequenti: Videtur etiam quod probabiliter. Respondet ergo ad quintum superius tactum, dicens quod doctrina sua non confundit omnem religionem, quia omnes religiones, praeterquam B. Francisci, fatentur se habere res vsu consumptibiles, & non consumptibiles, quo ad dominium seu proprietatem in communi, & ideo non sunt censendi proprietarii: quia actus eorum circa res huiusmodi vsu consumptibiles à communi dominio separantur.
units.tr: In this part the impugned man answers the fifth point, which the appellant touches on in the impugnation, namely that the doctrine of this impugned man destroys and confounds every religion having a vow of renouncing all temporal goods. The answer is divided into two parts: first he answers this directly; second he declares his intention concerning the preceding points more clearly in the part immediately following: It also seems that probably. So he answers the fifth point mentioned above, saying that his doctrine does not confound every religion, because all religions, except that of blessed Francis, confess that they have consumable and non-consumable things as regards dominion or ownership in common, and therefore they are not to be considered proprietors, since their acts concerning such consumable things are separated from common dominion.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores circa illam partem sic procedunt. Primo n. ostendunt, quod omnem religionem habentem votum abdicationis proprietatis omnium temporaliū ille impugnatus destruit & confundit. Secundo ostendunt quod specialiter destruit & confundit religionem B. Francisci. Tertio ostendunt, quod vsus facti respectu rerum vsu consumptibilium potest à dominio speciali & communi separari. Quarto ex dicendis intentionem appellantis in hac parte declarant.
units.tr: But these impugners proceed on that part as follows. First, they show that the impugned man destroys and confounds every religion having a vow of renouncing all temporal goods. Second, they show that he particularly destroys and confounds the religion of blessed Francis. Third, they show that the use of fact in regard to consumable things can be separated from special and common dominion. Fourth, from what follows they make clear the appellant's intention on this point.

units.la: Primo ergo ostendunt, quod ille impugnatus omnem talem religionem destruit & confundit: quia ex doctrina sua sequitur euidenter, vt dicunt, quod omnis religiosus habet vel licite habere potest dominium rerum vsu consumptibilium in speciali, quod probant sic, si vsus facti huiusmodi rerum vsu consumptibilium non potest à dominio seu à proprietate tam communi, quam speciali separari, ergo qui habet vsum facti huiusmodi rerum, & non habet earundem rerum dominium commune, habet earundem rerum dominium speciale, sed quilibet talis religiosus, sicut quilibet monachus & Frater Praedicatorū, ac quilibet alius potest habere vsū facti hmōi reī ū absq; dominio cōmuni, sicut si aliquis dat vni soli praedicatori, vel vni soli monacho licentiā vtendi aliqua veste vel alia re vsu consumptibili, ipse licite potest uti retali usu consumptibili, sed non habet in re illa dominium commune sibi & aliis Fratribus suis: quia intentio concedentis fuit concedere licentiam utendi uni soli, & per consequens non habet in re illa dominium commune, & tamen habet usum facti, & per illum impugnatum usus facti non potest ab omni dominio separari, ergo tunc habet dominium speciale. Ex quo sequitur manifeste, quilibet religiosus utendo rebus usu consumptibilibus potest licite fieri proprietarius in speciali: quod est omnem religionem confundere & destruere. Sed forte diceret aliqs, quod talis acquirit dominium commune, non speciale, quia monachus quicquid acquirit monasterio acquirit, & eadem ratione quicquid Frater praedicator vel alius religiosus acquirit, Ordini suo acquirit.
units.tr: First, then, they show that the impugned man destroys and confounds every such religion, because from his doctrine it evidently follows, as they say, that every religious has, or can lawfully have, dominion over consumable things in particular. They prove it thus: if the use of fact of such consumable things cannot be separated from dominion or ownership, whether common or particular, then whoever has the use of fact of such things and does not have common dominion of those same things, has particular dominion of them. But any such religious, such as any monk or Friar Preacher or any other, can have the use of fact of such a thing without common dominion. For example, if someone gives to one preacher alone, or to one monk alone, permission to use some garment or other consumable thing, he can lawfully use that consumable thing, yet he does not have common dominion of that thing with his other brothers, because the intention of the giver was to grant permission to use it to one alone, and consequently he does not have common dominion over that thing. And yet he has the use of fact, and according to that impugned man the use of fact cannot be separated from all dominion; therefore he then has special dominion. From this it manifestly follows that any religious, by using consumable things, can lawfully become a proprietor in particular, which is to confound and destroy every religion. But perhaps someone would say that such a person acquires common, not special, dominion, because whatever a monk acquires, he acquires for the monastery, and by the same reasoning whatever a Friar Preacher or other religious acquires, he acquires for his Order.

units.la: Sed, ut dicunt isti impugnatores, hoc non concludit, quia, cum dicitur: quicquid monachus acquirit, monasterio acquirit, non debet universaliter intelligi de omni re, quae acquiritur alicui monacho quo ad licitam potestatem utendi. Si enim aliquis accommodat uni monacho equum suum ad equitandum, non propter hoc aliquis alius de monasterio habet potestatem equitandi equum. Similiter si aliquis invitat monachum ad comedendum, non propter hoc intelligitur alios monachos invitare. Illud ergo, quicquid monachus acquirit monasterio acquirit, debet intelligi de illis, quae monachus acquirit quo ad dominium, quale est possibile monacho convenire, quando scilicet ille, a quo acquirit rem, dominium eiusdem rei a se intendit transferre. De illis autem, quae monachus acquirit quo ad licitam potestatem utendi tantummodo, non habet universaliter veritatem. Et causa differentiae est: quia monachus non potest habere cuiuscunque rei dominium speciale qualecunque: sed potest habere licitam potestatem utendi aliqua re usu consumptibili & non consumptibili specialem. Secundo ostendunt, quod ille impugnatus specialiter destruit & confundit religionem beati Francisci: quia secundum ipsum haec religio beati Francisci caret omni dominio seu proprietate speciali & communi, sed usus facti secundum eundem in rebus usu consumptibilibus non potest ab omni dominio speciali & communi separari, ergo religio beati Francisci debet omni usu facti in rebus usu consumptibilibus carere, sed talis religio, quae aliquem obligaret ad carendum omni usu facti in huiusmodi rebus, est illicita: quia inobservabilis, ergo religio beati Francisci est illicita reputanda, & ita religionem illam destruit & confundit.
units.tr: But, as these impugners say, this does not follow, because when it is said whatever a monk acquires, he acquires for the monastery, it must not be understood universally of every thing that is acquired by some monk as regards the lawful power of using it. For if someone lends his horse to one monk to ride, it does not follow that any other monk of the monastery has the power of riding the horse. Likewise, if someone invites a monk to eat, it is not understood that he invites the other monks. Therefore, whatever a monk acquires, he acquires for the monastery, must be understood of those things which the monk acquires as regards dominion, such as it is possible for a monk to have, namely when he from whom the thing is acquired intends to transfer the dominion of that same thing from himself. But of those things which a monk acquires only as regards the lawful power of using, it is not universally true. And the reason for the difference is this: a monk cannot have dominion of any thing whatever in particular, but he can have a lawful power of using some consumable and non-consumable thing in particular. Second, they show that the impugned man particularly destroys and confounds the religion of blessed Francis, because according to him this religion of blessed Francis lacks all dominion or ownership, particular and common; but according to the same man the use of fact in consumable things cannot be separated from all particular and common dominion; therefore the religion of blessed Francis must lack every use of fact in consumable things; but such a religion, which would bind someone to lack every use of fact in such things, is unlawful, because it cannot be observed; therefore the religion of blessed Francis must be considered unlawful, and so he destroys and confounds that religion.

units.la: Tertio ostendunt, quod usus facti in huiusmodi rebus usu consumptibilibus potest ab omni speciali dominio & etiam communi separari, & hoc quidem ex dictis istius impugnati infertur aperte. Nam secundum eum Fratres Minores non habent dominium rerum quarumcunque; nec in speciali nec in communi: & tamen habent usum huiusmodi rerum, igitur &c. Quarto isti impugnatores ex praedictis intentionem appellantis in hac parte declarant dicentes: quod appellans intentione istius impugnati ex diversis dictis & rationibus eiusdem concepit.
units.tr: Third, they show that the use of fact in such consumable things can be separated from all particular and even common dominion; and this is plainly inferred from the statements of this impugned man. For according to him the Friars Minor have no dominion of any things whatever, neither particular nor common; and yet they have the use of such things; therefore etc. Fourth, these impugners, from what has been said, declare the intention of the appellant on this point, saying that the appellant, from the various statements and arguments of the same man, conceived the intention of the impugned man.

units.la: Ex rationibus autem eius sequitur evidenter, quod usus facti in rebus usu consumptibilibus non potest a proprietate seu dominio speciali aliqualiter separari, & ut hoc pateat, est una ratio ipsius breviter pertractanda. Ille enim impugnatus ideo ponit usum facti non posse a proprietate seu dominio in rebus usu consumptibilibus separari: quia per usum facti substantia rei consumptibilis usu consumitur, & per consequens usus facti non potest in huiusmodi rebus a proprietate seu dominio separari, sed ex illa ratione sequitur, quod usus facti in huiusmodi rebus non potest a proprietate seu dominio speciali separari, quia si ideo non potest in huiusmodi rebus usus facti a proprietate seu dominio separari, quia per talem usum facti substantia rerum non consumitur, & dominium principaliter consumitur per usum facti, quia dominium esse non ita directe consumitur per usum facti alicuius, sicut dominium speciale, ergo per illam rationem usus facti in huiusmodi rebus non potest separari a dominio speciali.
units.tr: Now from his arguments it evidently follows that the use of fact in consumable things cannot be separated in any way from particular ownership or dominion; and to make this clear, one of his arguments must be briefly examined. For the impugned man holds that the use of fact cannot be separated from ownership or dominion in consumable things because by the use of fact the substance of a consumable thing is used up, and consequently the use of fact in such things cannot be separated from ownership or dominion. But from that reason it follows that the use of fact in such things cannot be separated from particular dominion. For if the use of fact in such things cannot be separated from ownership or dominion because by such a use of fact the substance of the things is not consumed, while dominion is principally consumed by the use of fact (since dominion is not consumed by someone's use of fact so directly as particular dominion is), then by that reasoning the use of fact in such things cannot be separated from particular dominion.

units.la: Appellans ergo volens illum impugnare ad mentem magis quam ad verba, habuit, quod usus facti potest in huiusmodi rebus separari a dominio speciali, & quod qui ponit (sicut ille) quod usus facti non potest in huiusmodi rebus a speciali dominio separari, omnem religionem habentem votum abdicationis proprietatis omnium temporalium destruit & confundit, quia si usus facti non potest in huiusmodi rebus separari a dominio speciali, ergo religiosi comedendo, bibendo, sunt proprietarii reputandi.
units.tr: The appellant, therefore, wishing to attack him, aimed at his meaning rather than his words, and held that the use of fact can in such things be separated from special ownership; and that whoever holds (as he does) that the use of fact cannot in such things be separated from special ownership, destroys and confounds every religious order that has a vow of renouncing property in all temporal goods, because if the use of fact cannot in such things be separated from special ownership, then religious who eat and drink must be reckoned as proprietors.

units.la: Sed forte dicet aliqs, quod ille impugnatus concedit, quod usus facti in huiusmodi rebus potest a dominio speciali separari. Dicit enim quod aliquis potest comedere panem, non ut proprium, sed ut coem. Ad hoc dicunt isti impugnatores, quod in hoc sibi ipsi contradicit, quia ex aliis dictis eius sequitur, quod usus facti in huiusmodi rebus non potest separari a dominio speciali. Unde & propter hoc, sicut patebit inserius, dicit quod votum utendi sine proprio ad res huiusmodi minime se extendit.
units.tr: But perhaps someone will say that the author attacked concedes that the use of fact in such things can be separated from special ownership. For he says that a person may eat bread not as his own, but as common. To this those who attack him reply that in this he contradicts himself, because it follows from his other statements that the use of fact in such things cannot be separated from special ownership. Hence also, as will become clear below, he says that the vow of using without property does not extend at all to things of this kind.

units.la: Ex quo patet, quod religiosi secundum ipsum habent dominium speciale in huiusmodi rebus, quod non potest, nisi quia secundum ipsum usus facti non potest in huiusmodi rebus separari a dominio speciali. Ad hoc aliter isti impugnatores declarant intentionem appellantis, dicentes quod ille impugnatus, cum loquitur de dominio, quod habebant primi credentes in rebus usu consumptibilibus, & a quo dicit usum facti in rebus huiusmodi separari non posse, est dominium liberum civile & mundanum, tale autem dominium est quodammodo dominium speciale, & ita ille impugnatus habet dicere, quod usus facti in huiusmodi rebus non potest separari a dominio speciali, & ex hoc sequitur manifeste, quod opinio eius omnem religionem habentem votum abdicationis proprietatis destruit & confundit.
units.tr: From this it is plain that, according to him, religious have special ownership in such things, which could not be the case unless, according to him, the use of fact cannot in such things be separated from special ownership. Those who attack him explain the appellant's intention otherwise, saying that the author attacked, when he speaks of the ownership which the first believers had in consumable goods, and from which he says the use of fact cannot be separated in such things, means free civil and worldly ownership; and such ownership is in a certain way special ownership. So the author attacked must be saying that the use of fact in such things cannot be separated from special ownership, and from this it clearly follows that his opinion destroys and confounds every religious order that has a vow of renouncing property.

units.la: Post haec est ad literam accedendum, (praeterquam beati Francisci.) Hic aperte concedit, quod religio beati Francisci caret omni proprietate & dominio communi & speciali, & ita vel illa religio est inobservabilis & illicita: vel usus facti potest ab omni dominio speciali & communi in rebus usu consumptibilibus separari, (quo ad proprietatem & dominium in communi) hoc de dominio libero, quae est potestas de rebus libere ordinandi, non habet veritatem de alio dominio, de quo dictum est prius, potest concedi, dici tamen possunt uti rebus consumptibilibus usu, si usus proprie sumatur, hoc dicunt isti impugnatores omni veritate carere: quia sicut propria locutio est, cum dicimus, aliquos vti huiusmodi rebus consumptibilibus vsu, talis enim modus loquendi vsitatus fuit in Theologia, & in aliis scientiis, ac etiam in vulgari locutione, antequam scientiae legales essent inventae. Et ita propter modum loquendi scientiarum legalium posteriorem non debet prior modus loquendi improprius reputari. Unde vt proprie sumptum est commune ad actum consumendi & ad multos alios actus, qui non sunt actus consumendi. Potest tamen dici, quod vsus iuris, quae est vna significatio specialis huius nominis vsus, non potest proprie in rebus, quae actu vnico consumuntur, aliqualiter reperiri, sed de tali vsu non intendit appellans, unde quantum ad intentionem appellantis ita sufficit sibi, quod actus consumendi res consumptibiles vsu potest ab omni proprietate & dominio speciali & communi separari, sicut vsus facti potest taliter separari, & ita dicunt isti impugnatores, quod ille impugnatus mentem appellantis non tangit in aliquo, sed verba eius per quaedam nouas impositiones vocum calumniari molitur, ( cum ipsa non vt propria consumere, sed vt communia sunt censenda ) hoc secundum illum non habet veritatem de Fratribus Minoribus, ergo Fratres Minores consumunt res, neq; vt proprias neq; vt communes, ergo actus consumendi huiusmodi res potest ab omni dominio speciali & communi separari: quae est principalis conclusio appellantis in hac parte. ( Actusque consumendi res nequaquam a communi dominio separatur. ) Illud potest habere verum sensum de aliis religiosis a Fratribus Minoribus, sicut ex praedictis apparet: & tamen si intelligeretur de omnibus religiosis, esset omnino falsum.
units.tr: After these things we must come to the letter (except the blessed Francis). Here he plainly concedes that the religion of blessed Francis lacks all property and both common and special ownership; and so either that religion is unobservable and unlawful, or the use of fact can be separated from all special and common ownership in consumable goods (as regards property and ownership in common). That this is true of free ownership, which is the power of freely disposing of goods, may be granted; but of the other ownership, of which we spoke earlier, it may be said that people use consumable goods by use, if "use" is taken properly. Those who attack him say this has no truth at all, because it is a proper way of speaking when we say that some people use such consumable goods by use; for this manner of speaking was customary in theology and in the other sciences, and also in ordinary speech, before the legal sciences were invented. And so, because of the later manner of speaking of the legal sciences, the earlier, improper manner of speaking ought not to be counted as improper. Hence, taken properly, "common" applies to the act of consuming and to many other acts which are not acts of consuming. It may however be said that the use of right, which is one special meaning of this word "use", cannot properly be found in things which are consumed by a single act; but the appellant does not intend such use, and so, as far as the appellant's intention goes, it is enough for him that the act of consuming consumable goods by use can be separated from all property and special and common ownership, just as the use of fact can be so separated. And so those who attack him say that the author attacked does not touch the appellant's meaning at all, but strives to slander his words by some new impositions of terms (since these things are not consumed as proper goods but must be regarded as common). According to him this is not true of the Friars Minor; therefore the Friars Minor consume goods neither as proper nor as common, and therefore the act of consuming such things can be separated from all special and common ownership: which is the appellant's principal conclusion on this point. (And the act of consuming things is by no means separated from common ownership.) That might have a true sense concerning religious other than the Friars Minor, as appears from what has been said; yet if it were understood of all religious, it would be wholly false.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: Chapter IX.

units.la: Videtur etiam quod probabiliter possit dici, quod post distributionem bonorum vsu consumptibilium, quae fiebat inter Apostolos & credentes alios, vt dicitur Act. 2. & 4. quilibet portionis sibi assignatae proprietarius & dominus posset dici. Et hoc scriptura praedicta Act. 4. videtur expresse supponere, cum dicit: nec etiam quisquam egrat egens inter ipsos, & quare hoc, reddit rationem subiungens: Quotquot enim possessores agrorum & domorum erant vendentes afferebant pretia eorum quae vendebantur & ponebant ante pedes Apostolorum, Diuidebant autem singulis prout cuiq; opus erat. Cum ergo dicat, quod nullus egens erat, pro eo quod vnicuiq; diuidebatur prout opus erat, supponit aperte, quod illud quod vnicuiq; dabatur diuisum, cuilibet erat proprium. Diuidere enim est diuisim aliquibus diuersas partes rei alicuius dare. Cum igitur daretur ab istis, qui dare poterant scilicet Apostolis: & illis qui recipere poterant ea quae ad vitae humanae sustentationem pertinebant: videtur, quod Dominus quilibet fuerit eius portionis, quae sibi fuerat assignata. Alias non videretur verum, quod dicitur, quod egentes non essent, nisi plus post diuisionem haberent in assignata sibi portione, quam ante. Prima confirmat, quod vestimenta quotidiana inter res vsu consumptibiles computantur, post communionem autem praedictam, de qua fit mentio in praeallegato ca. Actor. 4. in Actibus legitur quod Angelus Petro dixit ei: praecingere & calcia te caligas tuas. Item dixit ei: circunda tibi vestimentum tuum &c. vbi clare supponit Angelus, quod caligae & vestimentum assignata Petro, propriae quo ad dominium erant Petri, quare videtur quod pecunia, panis, vinum & res alia vsu consumptibiles sibi diuisim pro vita sustentatione assignatae, similiter eius essent. Nec vetum vinendi finem videtur, quod se extendat ad talia, quibus necessario eget vita humana. Preterea ex illo capitulo Actor. 4. probari non potest, quin credentes de bonis istis communibus ex diuisione Apostolorum licite recipere potuerint, & vt proprium obtinere. Scriptura enim praedicta quantum ad hoc nihil aliud adducit, nisi quod sequitur: Multitudinis credentium erat cor vnum & anima vna, nec quisquam eorum quae possidebat, aliquod suum esse dicebat, sed erant illis omnia communia. Per verba autem illa videntur isti omnia, quae poss. debant, a se dominium abdicasse, & illud transtulisse in communitatem. Non autem videntur se astrinxisse, quin si detur eis de bonis illis communibus, quo ad sustentationem vitae suae possint licite recipere, & vt propria retinere: imo hoc scriptura praedicta sacra supponit aperte, cum dicit: diuidebantur autem cuique prout opus erat. Diuidere autem est, sicut praedictum est, alterius rei diuisas partes aliquibus dare.
units.tr: It also seems that it can probably be said that, after the distribution of goods for consumption that was made among the Apostles and the other believers, as is reported in Acts 2 and 4, each person became the proprietor and lord of the portion assigned to him. The Scripture cited above, Acts 4, seems to presuppose this clearly when it says: "Neither was there any among them that lacked." It gives the reason for this in the following words: "For as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold, and laid them down at the Apostles' feet; and distribution was made unto every man according as he had need." Since it says that no one was in need, because distribution was made to each one as he had need, it plainly implies that what was given to each person in distribution belonged to each person as his own. To distribute is to give separate parts of some thing to different people. Since these things were given by those who could give, namely the Apostles, and were received by those who could receive what pertains to the sustenance of human life, it seems that each person was the lord of the portion assigned to him. Otherwise it would not be true that they were not needy unless they had more after the distribution in the portion assigned to them than before. The first point is confirmed by the fact that everyday clothing is counted among things consumed by use. After the aforementioned fellowship, mentioned in the chapter of Acts 4 cited above, we read in the Acts that the angel said to Peter: "Gird thyself, and bind on thy sandals" (Acts 12). Likewise he said to him: "Cast thy garment about thee," etc. Here the angel clearly presupposes that the sandals and garment assigned to Peter were his own as to ownership. Therefore it seems that money, bread, wine, and other things consumed by use, assigned to him separately for the sustenance of life, were likewise his. Nor does the vow of living without property seem to extend to such things as human life necessarily needs. Moreover, it cannot be proved from that chapter, Acts 4, that believers could not lawfully receive from these common goods, by the distribution of the Apostles, and hold them as their own. For the aforesaid Scripture adduces nothing else on this point except what follows: "The multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul; neither said any of them that aught of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common." By these words it seems that they renounced ownership of all their possessions and transferred it to the community. But they do not seem to have bound themselves so that, if they were given something from those common goods for the support of their lives, they could not lawfully receive it and keep it as their own. Indeed, the holy Scripture aforesaid presupposes this plainly when it says: "distribution was made unto every man as he had need." To distribute, as has been said, is to give separate parts of another thing to some people.

units.la: In parte ista intentione suam circa praecedentia specialiter quantum ad diuisionem bonorum, quae rata facta inter Apostolos & alios credentes, expressius manifestat, dicens primo, quilibet Apostolorum & aliorum credentium post distributionem illam, de qua fit mentio Actor. 2. & 4. dominus fuit & proprietarius portionis sibi assignatae. Secundo ibi (& hoc scriptura) probat pluribus rationibus, quilibet eorum erat proprietarius portionis sibi assignatae. Ratio autem prima potest sic formari. Ille qui non est egens, pro eo quod sibi datur illud quod sibi opus est, est proprietarius & dominus illius quod sibi datur, sed inter Apostolos & credentes alios nullus erat egens pro eo quod vnicuiq; dabatur prout opus erat, sicut Act. 4. habetur, ergo vnusquisque eorum fuit proprietarius & dominus portionis sibi assignatae. Secunda ratio potest sic formari, quando aliquid inter aliquos diuiditur, vnusquisq; est proprietarius & Dominus portionis sibi assignatae: quia diuidere est diuisim aliquas partes diuersas diuersis dare. Illud autem quod alicui datur, fit ei proprium, sed illa cōia diuidebantur inter Apostolos & alios credentes, igitur quilibet eorum post diuisionem fuit proprietarius & dominus portionis sibi assignatae. Tertia ratio potest similiter formari. Illud quod datur ab illo qui potest dare, & datur illi qui potest recipere fit proprium illiuscui datur, sed necessaria ad vitae sustentationem dabantur ab istis qui poterant dare scilicet ab Apostolis, & dabantur illis qui poterant recipere, ergo quilibet eorum fuerat proprietarius & dominus portionis sibi assignatae. Quarta ratio potest sic formari. Ille qui ante diuisionem habet rem aliquam in communi, & qui post diuisionem illius rei habet in portione sibi assignata plusq; habebat ante diuisionem, habet in portione sibi assignata proprietatem & dominium in speciali: sed credentes post diuisionem communiter habebant plus in portionibus suis quam ante: quia aliter non fuisset verum, quod non erant egentes, ergo quilibet eorum fuit proprietarius & Dominus portionis sibi assignatæ. Tertio principaliter ibi (Preterea constat) probat specialiter de beato Petro, & eadem ratione de aliis Apostolis, quod erat proprietarius & dominus portionis sibi assignatæ, & hoc probat duabus auctoritatibus, vt patet in litera. Ex quibus infert, q; eadé ratione Petrus erat proprietarius & dominus pecuniæ, panis & vini, & cuiuslibet alterius rei, quæ sibi p diuisionem extitit assignata. Quarto ibi (Nec votum vinendi &c.) cuidam tacitæ obiectioni respondet, posset enim aliqs dicere, q; per rationes prædictas quilibet religiosus post diuisionem panis & vini & huiusmodi rerum vsu consumptibilium quilibet eorum est proprietarius & dominus portionis sibi assignatæ. Ad hoc respondet dicens, q; votum viuendi sine proprio non se extendit ad illa, quibus necessario eget vita humana, ex hoc insinuans esse concedendum, q; quilibet religiosus post diuisionem factam inter eos est proprietarius & Dominus portionis sibi assignatæ. Quinto ibi (Preterea ex illo capitulo) ostendit quod per librum Actuum Apostolorum probari non potest, quin credentes poterant de bonis communibus recipere & vt proprium retinere, & quia non aliud dicitur nisi q; multitudinis credentium erat cor vnum &c. per quæ verba licet possit ostendi, quod primo omnia bona sua communitati dederunt, tamen probari non potest, quod non poterant postea de illis aliquid proprium recipere & tenere, imo potest ostendi quod poterant: quia scriptura testatur, quod illa diuidebantur. Diuidere autem est alicuius rei diuisas partes aliquibus dare, quod autem datur, fit proprium eius cui datur, ergo quilibet eorum habuit proprium.
units.tr: In this part he more expressly sets out his intention concerning the preceding matters, especially as to the distribution of goods that was made among the Apostles and the other believers. He says first that each of the Apostles and of the other believers, after that distribution mentioned in Acts 2 and 4, was the lord and proprietor of the portion assigned to him. Second, at the words "and this Scripture," he proves by several arguments that each of them was the proprietor of the portion assigned to him. The first argument may be formed thus: he who is not needy, because there is given to him what he needs, is the proprietor and lord of what is given to him. But among the Apostles and the other believers no one was needy, because to each was given as he had need, as is found in Acts 4. Therefore each of them was the proprietor and lord of the portion assigned to him. The second argument may be formed thus: when something is divided among some people, each of them is the proprietor and lord of the portion assigned to him, because to divide is to give separate parts to different people separately. But what is given to someone becomes his own. But those common goods were divided among the Apostles and the other believers. Therefore each of them after the distribution was the proprietor and lord of the portion assigned to him. The third argument may be formed similarly. What is given by one who can give, and given to one who can receive, becomes the property of the person to whom it is given. But the necessities of life were given by those who could give, namely the Apostles, and were given to those who could receive. Therefore each of them had been the proprietor and lord of the portion assigned to him. The fourth argument may be formed thus: he who before the distribution has a thing in common, and who after the distribution of that thing has more in his assigned portion than he had before the distribution, has ownership and lordship in particular in the portion assigned to him. But the believers after the distribution generally had more in their portions than before, because otherwise it would not have been true that they were not needy. Therefore each of them was the proprietor and lord of the portion assigned to him. Third, chiefly, at the words "Moreover it is evident," he proves specifically concerning the blessed Peter, and by the same reasoning concerning the other Apostles, that he was the proprietor and lord of the portion assigned to him. He proves this by two authorities, as appears in the text. From these he infers that by the same reasoning Peter was the proprietor and lord of the money, bread, and wine, and of any other thing that was assigned to him by the distribution. Fourth, at the words "Nor does the vow of living," etc., he answers a certain tacit objection. For someone might say that by the aforesaid arguments every religious, after the distribution of bread, wine, and such things consumed by use, is the proprietor and lord of the portion assigned to him. To this he answers that the vow of living without property does not extend to those things which human life necessarily needs. By this he hints that it must be conceded that every religious, after the distribution made among them, is the proprietor and lord of the portion assigned to him. Fifth, at the words "Moreover from that chapter," he shows that from the book of the Acts of the Apostles it cannot be proved that believers could not receive from the common goods and keep them as their own. And since nothing else is said except that "the multitude of believers was of one heart," etc., although by these words it can be shown that at first they gave all their goods to the community, yet it cannot be proved that afterwards they could not receive and hold anything of those goods as their own. Indeed it can be shown that they could, because Scripture testifies that those goods were distributed. But to distribute is to give separate parts of a thing to some people, and what is given becomes the property of the one to whom it is given. Therefore each of them had property of his own.

units.la: Sed impugnatores dicunt, in verbis præmissis plures contineri errores. Quorum primus est, quod quilibet Apostolorum erat proprietarius & Dominus portionis sibi assignatæ. Secundus est quod quilibet alius de numero credentium erat proprietarius & Dominus portionis sibi assignatæ. Tertius est quod votum viuendi sine proprio non extendit se ad ea, quibus necessario eget vita humana. Alios plures errores minus principales, de quibus in responsione ad rationes illius impugnati circa literam apparebit prædictis verbis asserunt contineri. Dicunt autem isti impugnatores, quod quia ille impugnatus in hac parte non vadit ad verba, sed ad mentem suam de Apostolis & religiosis, quasi totum venenum suum effundens explicatur manifeste, ideo circa premissa diligentius volunt insistere, dicunt itaq;, quod primus error sapit hæresim manifestam.
units.tr: But the opponents say that many errors are contained in the words quoted above. The first of these is that each of the Apostles was the proprietor and lord of the portion assigned to him. The second is that each of the other believers was the proprietor and lord of the portion assigned to him. The third is that the vow of living without property does not extend to those things which human life necessarily needs. They assert that several other, less important errors will appear in the reply to the arguments of that opponent concerning the text, and that they are contained in the aforesaid words. These opponents also say that, because the author attacked in this part does not go by the words but by his own opinion about the Apostles and the religious, pouring out, as it were, his whole poison, it is clearly explained; therefore they wish to insist more carefully on the matters set out above. They therefore say that the first error savours of manifest heresy.

units.la: Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt primo esse notandum, quod in illo errore sc. quod quilibet Apostolus habebat dominium rerum in speciali, religiosis omnibus aduersatur, licet enim fuerint quidam Fratres Prædicatores & nonnulli de quibusdam aliis Ordinibus, qui dixerunt Apostolos habuisse dominium & proprietatem aliquarum rerum in communi: omnes tamen vsq; ad tempora istius impugnati dixerunt, q; Apostoli nullius rei temporalis dominium vel proprietatem habuerunt in speciali: & in hoc dixerunt se vitam Apostolicam imitari habendo sc. aliqua in communi quantum ad aliquale dominium vel proprietatem: & nihil habendo penitus in spali quoad dominium seu proprietatem, iste autem omnibus contradicit asserens, quod habuerunt proprietatem & dominium in speciali. Sed quod hoc sit erroneum, isti impugnatores multis modis ostendere moliuntur. Et qa quodammodo expressius determinatio ecclesiæ & doctrina sanctorum isti errori contradicunt & obuiant: ideo a determinatione & auctoritatibus sanctorum incipiunt in scriptura diuina postmodum se fundantes, q; enim prædicta assertio, determinationi ecclesiæ obuiet & repugnet, ostendunt. Ait enim Nicolaus papa in decretali Exiit per vniuersale ecclesiam hactenus approbata: Dicimus quod abdicatio proprietatis huiusmodi rerum tam in speciali quam etiam in communi propter Deum meritoria est & sancta: quā & Christus viam perfectionis ostendens, verbo docuit, & exemplo firmauit, quamque primi fundatores militantis ecclesiæ, prout abipso fonte hauserant, in volentes perfecte viuere, per doctrina ac vita ipsorum alueos deriuarunt.
units.tr: To make this plain, they say that first it must be noted that the error in question, namely that every Apostle had lordship over things individually, is opposed to all religious orders. There were some Friars Preachers and some from certain other orders who said that the Apostles had dominion and ownership of some things in common. Yet all of them, up to the time of this man attacked, said that the Apostles had no temporal dominion or ownership individually. In this they said they imitated the apostolic life: they had some things in common, with some kind of dominion or ownership, and individually they had nothing at all in the way of dominion or ownership. This man, however, contradicts them all, asserting that the Apostles had ownership and dominion individually. These opponents labour to show in many ways that this is erroneous. Because the determination of the Church and the teaching of the saints contradict and oppose this error in a more explicit way, they begin with the determination and the authorities of the saints, and afterwards base themselves on divine Scripture. They show that the aforesaid assertion conflicts with and opposes the determination of the Church. For Pope Nicholas says in the decretal Exiit, which the universal Church has so far approved: "We say that renunciation of the ownership of such things, both individually and in common, for God's sake, is meritorious and holy. Christ, showing the way of perfection, taught this by word and confirmed it by example, and the first founders of the militant Church, drawing it from the very source, passed it on to those who wished to live perfectly, by their teaching and life, as from channels."

units.la: His expressius dici non posset, quod Apostoli proprietatem omnium rerum temporalium abdicarunt: & ita nullius proprietatem habuerunt in speciali. Sed dicit ille impugnatus, q; illa decretalis Exiit non fuit per vniuersalem ecclesiam approbata, hoc autem, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, isti impugnatum nequaquam excusat. Tum quia illa decretalis Exiit, ex quo nullus catholicus sibi multis temporibus contradixit, per taciturnitatem fuit ab omnibus approbata: quia sicut error, cui non resistitur, approbatur dist. 83. c. Error: ita veritas catholica, cui non resistitur, debet pro approbata censeri, tum quia esto, quod non fuit ab vniuersali ecclesia approbata, tamen ex hoc, quod ille impugnatus assertionem dictæ decretalis impugnat, assertionem contrariam esse catholicam diffinitiue & solenniter approbando. Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod siue vna assertio fuerit hæretica, siue alia, se demonstratiue probare, quod ille impugnatus modo non est papa. Est autem eorum ratio talis: aut assertio Nicolai tertii, quod Apostoli omnis rei temporalis proprietatem abdicauerunt, est hæretica: Aut assertio contraria istius impugnati, quod Apostoli habuerunt proprietatem etiam in speciali, est hæretica.
units.tr: Nothing could be said more explicitly than this: that the Apostles renounced ownership of all temporal things, and so had no ownership individually. But the man attacked says that the decretal Exiit was not approved by the universal Church. As these opponents say, this in no way excuses him. For that decretal, since no Catholic has contradicted it for many ages, has been approved by all through silence. Just as an error that is not resisted is approved (dist. 83, c. Error), so a Catholic truth that is not resisted ought to be regarded as approved. And even if it was not approved by the universal Church, by the fact that the man attacked assails the assertion of that decretal, he is by defining and solemnly approving the contrary assertion as Catholic. These opponents say that whether the one assertion or the other is heretical, they can demonstrate that the man attacked is not now pope. Their argument runs thus: either the assertion of Nicholas III, that the Apostles renounced ownership of every temporal thing, is heretical; or the contrary assertion of this man attacked, that the Apostles had ownership even individually, is heretical.

units.la: Hanc oportet necessario illum impugnatum concedere, quia secundum ipsum altera istarum, imo sua assertio in scriptura sacra est fundata. Si assertio prædicta istius impugnati est hæretica, cum sit eiusdem pertinax defensator, q; probatur ex sua determinatione solenni & ultimata, & ex sententiis & pœnis, quas negantibus & resistentibus in sua constitutione infligit, ex persecutione, quam appellantibus & defensoribus assertionis contrariæ inferre non cessat, ex coactione, qua alios ad assertionem suam irreuocabiliter defendenda iurare compellit, ex abiuratione, qua cogit multos assertionem contrariam abiurare, ex recusatione, qua de veritate renuit: informari sequitur, vt dicunt, demonstratiue, quod ipse est hæreticus reputandus. Si autem est hæreticus, non est verus papa: quia nullus hæreticus est verus papa, sicut in aliis allegationibus quamplurimis rationibus & auctoritatibus probare conantur.
units.tr: The man attacked must necessarily concede this, since according to him one or other of these assertions, indeed his own, is founded in holy Scripture. If the aforesaid assertion of this man attacked is heretical, then, since he is its obstinate defender (as is proved from his solemn and final determination, from the sentences and penalties he inflicts in his constitution on those who deny and resist it, from the persecution he never ceases to bring upon those who appeal against and defend the contrary assertion, from the compulsion by which he forces others to swear that they will defend his assertion irrevocably, from the abjuration by which he compels many to abjure the contrary assertion, and from the refusal by which he declines to acknowledge the truth), it follows, they say, that he is to be demonstrably reckoned a heretic. And if he is a heretic, he is not a true pope, since no heretic is a true pope. In their other allegations they try to prove this by many arguments and authorities.

units.la: Sian. Si autem assertio Nicolai tertii fuit hæretica: ipsemet Nicolaus tertius fuit hæreticus reputandus. Hanc conditionalem probant: quia si Nicolaus tertius in prædicta assertione errauit, cū ipsam diffinitiue ptulerit, omnibusq; Christianis tenendā sub comminatione pœnarū tradiderit. Sequitur euidēter, q eidem assertioni hæretice firmiter & irreuocabiliter adhærebat. Ex quo pateterinfertur, q nō fuit paratus corrigi, si autē non fuit paratus corrigi fuit inter hæreticos cōputandus, & si sic r.ō fuit verus papa, & si non fuit verus papa, veros Cardinales nullo modo creauit. Et p consequens Cardinales creati p ipsum, verū papa eligere minime potuerunt. Et ita posteriores summi pontifices nō fuerunt veri summi pontifices: nec p consequens veros Cardinales creauerunt. Ex quo sequitur, q ille ab illis, qui non fuerunt veri Cardinales, electus nunq̄ fuit verus papa. Sed quia forte diceret aliquis, quod Nicolaus tertius erat hæreticus: & ideo veros Cardinales non creauit, & tamen summi pontifices sequentes fuerunt veri pontifices summi, quia ab aliis Cardinalibus, qui creati fuerunt à prædecessoribus Nicolai tertii, extiterunt electi. Sed illa esset friuola & vana euasio: quia si Nicolaus tertius fuit hæreticus propter dictam assertionem, sequitur necessario, quod Nicolaus quartus, & Bonifacius octauus, & Benedictus secundus, & Clemens quintus, qui eandem assertionem Nicolai tertii in suis constitutionibus asseruerunt & approbauerunt, fuerunt hæretici, sed omnes, qui elegerunt illum impugnatum in summum pontificem, fuerunt creati à Nicolao tertio, vel Nicolao quarto, vel Bonifacio octauo, vel Benedicto II. vel Clemente quinto, ergo non fuit à veris electoribus aliquo modo legitime & rite electus: & per consequens nunquam fuit verus papa.
