Illam rationem dicunt isti impugnatores esse demonstratiuam & insolubilem ad probandum, quod ille impugnatus, siue sit hæreticus siue non sit hæreticus, non est modo verus papa, &, vt dicunt, omnes cauillationes, quæ possent contra ipsam adduci, aliis in allegationibus euidenter excludunt.
units.tr: Suppose the assertion of Nicholas III was heretical; then Nicholas III himself must be reckoned a heretic. They prove this conditional: if Nicholas III erred in that assertion, since he pronounced it definitively and handed it down to be held by all Christians under threat of penalties, it clearly follows that he adhered firmly and irrevocably to that heretical assertion. From this it plainly follows that he was not prepared to be corrected. And if he was not prepared to be corrected, he must be counted among the heretics; and if so, he was not a true pope; and if he was not a true pope, he in no way created true cardinals. Consequently, the cardinals created by him could not elect a true pope. And so the later supreme pontiffs were not true supreme pontiffs, nor, consequently, did they create true cardinals. From this it follows that the man attacked, having been elected by those who were not true cardinals, was never a true pope. But perhaps someone would say that Nicholas III was a heretic and therefore did not create true cardinals, yet the following supreme pontiffs were true supreme pontiffs because they were elected by other cardinals, who had been created by predecessors of Nicholas III. That, however, would be a frivolous and empty escape. For if Nicholas III was a heretic because of the said assertion, it necessarily follows that Nicholas IV, Boniface VIII, Benedict II and Clement V, who in their constitutions asserted and approved the same assertion of Nicholas III, were heretics as well. But all who elected the man attacked as supreme pontiff were created by Nicholas III, or Nicholas IV, or Boniface VIII, or Benedict II, or Clement V. Therefore he was not lawfully and duly elected in any way by true electors, and consequently was never a true pope. These opponents say that this argument is demonstrative and insoluble for proving that the man attacked, whether or not he is a heretic, is not now a true pope; and, as they say, it clearly excludes in the other allegations all the cavils that could be brought against it.

units.la: Amplius isti impugnatores per auctoritatem sanctorum dictam assertionem improbare nituntur. Ait enim Hieronymus in epistola ad Exuperantium: Nemo Apostolis pauperior fuit: & nemo tantum pro Domino de reliquit, ergo Apostoli fuerunt pauperrimi, sed illi qui retinent rerum dominium in speciali non sunt pauperrimi, ergo Apostoli non habuerunt rerum dominium in speciali. Item Augustinus super secundam epistolam ad Corinth. ait: Hoc fuit Apostolis gloriosum: quod sine sollicitudine ac nomine possidenti non solum ea quæ in possessionibus erant, sed etiam ipsos earum dominos possidebant. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod Apostoli nihil habebant nomine possidendi, & per consequens multo magis nihil habebant iure dominii in speciali. Item Hieronymus ad Demetriadem virginem ait: Apostolici fastigii perfecta, virtutis est omnia vendere & pauperibus distribuere, & sic leuem atq; expeditum cum Christo ad cœlestia subuolare. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod ad Apostolicum spectat fastigium omnia vendere & pauperibus distribuere, qui autem omnia vendit & pauperibus distribuit, nullius rei dominium habet saltem in speciali, ergo ad Apostolicum fastigium spectat nullius rei dominium habere in speciali. Item Hieronymus ad Elbediam ait: Si vis esse perfecta, & stare in primo fastigio pauperta-tis, fac quo fecerunt Apostoli. Vende omnia quæ habens & da pauperibus, & sequere Saluatorem, & nudam solamque crucem nuda sequaris. Ex his verbis colligitur euidenter, quod Apostoli nullius rei dominium retinuerunt saltem in speciali. His concordat beatus Gregorius super Euangelia, qui exponens illud Matth. 4. Relictis retibus secuti sunt eum, ait: Ad vnius iussionis vocem Petrus & Andreas relicture- tibus secuti sunt Saluatorem, ad vnum domini preceptum hoc quod habere videbantur obliti sunt, & infra: sed forte aliquis tacitu cogitationibus dicit: Sed quid aut quantum vtique ille piscator ad vocem Dominicam dimisit, qui pene nihil habuit? Sed in hac re affectum potius debemus considerare quam censum, multum reliquit qui nihil sibi retinuit: multum reliquit qui quantum libet parum totum deseruit: qui cum re possessa etiam concupiscentia habendi renunciauit. A sequentibus ergo tanta dimissa sunt, quanta à non sequentibus concupisci potuerunt. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod Apostoli nihil retinuerunt quo ad dominium & proprietatem saltem in speciali. Ex his aliisq; quampluribus auctoritatibus, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, euidenter apparet Apostolos nullius rei proprietatem habuisse in speciali. Istam autem doctrinam sanctorum & ecclesiæ dicunt in scriptura diuina fundari, quod probant primo specialiter de pecunia: quia beatus Petrus pecuniæ in speciali proprietatem nō habuit, cuius contrarium ille impugnatus asserit manifeste. Ait enim beatus Petrus: Argentum & aurum non est mihi: quod autem habeo, hoc tibi do, in nomine Iesu Christi Nazareni surge & ambula. Ex quibus verbis euidenter colligitur, quod beatus Petrus pecuniam non habebat. Sed forte dicet ille impugnatus, quod beatus Petrus tunc pecuniam non habebat, quia pecuniam, quæ sibi fuerat assignata, expenderat vel dederat pauperibus, sed sic exponere scripturam est ipsam, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, peruertere. Nam secundum doctrinam sanctorum, ideo beatus Petrus carebat pecunia, non quia pecuniam sibi assignatam expenderat, sed vt præceptum sui magistri de non habenda pecunia custodiret, hoc expresse Chrysostomus testari videtur. Ait enim Omelia vltima super Matthæum: Si bonum esset aurum habere hoc, vtique dedisset Christus Apostolis, qui ineffabilia eis bona tribuit. Nunc autem non solum non dedit, sed habere prohibuit. Ideoque Petrus non solum non verecundatur, sed decoratur in paupertate, dicens: Argentum & aurum non est mihi. Et Ambrosius super Lucam, ait: Apostolus Petrus primus dominica sententia executor ostendens, non esse in vacuum effusa Domini præcepta, cum posceretur à paupere, vt ei aliquid pecuniæ largiretur, ait: Argentum & aurum non habeo: ta- men non tam in hoc gloriatur Petrus, quod argentum & aurum non habeat: quam quod seruet Dei mandatum, qui præcepit: Nolite possidere aurum, hoc est dicere: Vides me Christi discipulum & aurum à me requiris? Aliud multo pretiosius auro nobis donauit. Et Bernardus ad Eugenium papam libro 2. ait: Nec locus, inquit, ocio, vbi sedula vrget sollicitudo omnium ecclesiarum. Nam quid aliud dimisit tibi sanctus Apostolus? quod habe, inquit, hoc tibi do, quid illud vnum? Sed nec aurum nec argentum, cum ipse dicat, argentum & aurum non est mihi, & infra esto quod alia quacunq; ratione hoc vendices, sed non Apostolico iure, nec enim ille tibi dare potuit, quod non habuit. Ex his patet aperte, quod beatus Petrus non ideo non habuit pecuniam, quia pecuniam sibi assignatam expenderat: sed quia Domini praeceptum seruare volebat, quod Glossa super illud verbum Petri: Argentum & aurum &c. asserit manifeste, dicens: memor illius praecepti: Nolite possidere aurum nec argentum, pecuniam, quae ad pedes Apostolorum ponebatur, non sibi retinebat, sed ad vsus pauperum, qui sua patrimonia reliquerant, reseruabat, hoc est reseruari mandabat. Non enim ipsemet beatus Petrus custodiuit pecuniam, sed quia custodiret, ordinauit.
units.tr: Furthermore, these opponents try to refute the assertion by the authority of the saints. For Jerome says in his letter to Exuperantius: No one was poorer than the Apostles, and no one left so much for the Lord; therefore the Apostles were most poor. But those who retain ownership of goods in particular are not most poor; therefore the Apostles did not have ownership of goods in particular. Likewise Augustine, on the second letter to the Corinthians, says: It was glorious for the Apostles that, without anxiety and without the name of possessor, they possessed not only the things that were in their possessions, but even were the lords of those things. From these words it is clearly gathered that the Apostles had nothing in the sense of possessing, and consequently much less did they have ownership of anything in particular. Likewise Jerome, writing to the virgin Demetrias, says: It is the mark of perfect apostolic virtue to sell everything and distribute it to the poor, and so to fly light and unencumbered with Christ to heavenly things. From these words it is plainly held that it belongs to the apostolic height to sell everything and distribute it to the poor; but whoever sells everything and distributes it to the poor has no ownership of any thing, at least in particular; therefore it belongs to the apostolic height to have no ownership of anything in particular. Likewise Jerome, writing to Eustochium, says: If you wish to be perfect and to stand on the first height of poverty, do what the Apostles did. Sell all that you have and give to the poor, and follow the Saviour, and naked follow the naked cross alone. From these words it is clearly gathered that the Apostles retained ownership of nothing, at least in particular. Blessed Gregory agrees with this in his homilies on the Gospels, where, expounding that passage of Matthew 4, Leaving their nets they followed him, he says: At the voice of a single command Peter and Andrew, leaving the nets, followed the Saviour; at the one word of the Lord they forgot what they seemed to have. And a little further: But perhaps someone thinks in silence: What, or how much, did that fisherman leave at the Lord's call, who had almost nothing? But in this matter we ought to consider the disposition rather than the wealth. He left much who kept nothing for himself; he left much who gave up wholly however little he had; who renounced even the desire of having along with the thing possessed. So much was left by those who followed as could have been desired by those who did not follow. From these words it is given to understand that the Apostles retained nothing as regards ownership and property, at least in particular. From these and many other authorities, as these opponents say, it clearly appears that the Apostles had no property in anything in particular. They say, moreover, that this doctrine of the saints and of the Church is founded in divine Scripture, which they prove first specially with regard to money: because blessed Peter had no property in money in particular, whereas that opponent manifestly asserts the contrary. For blessed Peter says: Silver and gold I have not; but what I have, that I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk. From these words it is clearly gathered that blessed Peter had no money. But perhaps that opponent will say that blessed Peter then had no money because he had spent or given to the poor the money that had been assigned to him; but to explain Scripture in this way is, as these opponents say, to pervert it. For according to the doctrine of the saints, blessed Peter lacked money not because he had spent the money assigned to him, but in order to keep the command of his Master not to have money; Chrysostom seems to attest this expressly. For he says in his last homily on Matthew: If it were good to have gold, Christ would surely have given it to the Apostles, to whom he gave ineffable goods. But now he not only did not give it, but forbade them to have it. Therefore Peter not only is not ashamed, but is adorned in poverty, saying: Silver and gold I have not. And Ambrose, on Luke, says: The Apostle Peter, the first executor of the Lord's sentence, showing that the Lord's precepts were not poured out in vain, when a poor man asked him to give him some money, said: Silver and gold I have not. Yet Peter does not glory so much in this, that he has no silver and gold, as that he keeps God's command, who commanded: Do not possess gold. That is to say: You see me a disciple of Christ, and you ask me for gold? He has given us something much more precious than gold. And Bernard, in the second book to Pope Eugenius, says: Nor is there leisure, he says, where the anxious care of all the churches presses. For what else did the holy Apostle leave you? What I have, he says, that I give you. What is that one thing? But neither gold nor silver, since he himself says: Silver and gold I have not. And a little further: Suppose you sell this by whatever other means, but not by apostolic right; for he could not give you what he did not have. From these things it is plain that blessed Peter did not lack money because he had spent the money assigned to him; but because he wished to keep the Lord's command. The Gloss on those words of Peter, Silver and gold, etc., asserts this plainly, saying: Mindful of that precept, Do not possess gold nor silver, he did not keep for himself the money that was laid at the feet of the Apostles, but reserved it for the use of the poor, who had left their patrimonies; that is, he ordered it to be reserved. For blessed Peter himself did not keep the money, but ordained that it be kept.

units.la: Secundo ostendunt eandem conclusionem isti impugnatores, sic, sicut Apostoli seruabant consilium Christi de castitate & obedientia, ita etiam seruabant consilium Christi de paupertate, sed Christus docuit & consuluit abdicationem proprietatis omnium temporalium in speciali, igitur Apostoli seruabant idem consilium. Maior videtur aperta. Minorem probant per illud consilium, quod dedit Christus adolescenti quaerenti, quid sibi deesset, ex quo mandata seruauerat, Matth. 19. dicens: Si vis perfectus esse, vade, vende omnia quae habes & da pauperibus, & habebis thesaurum in caelo, & veni & sequere me. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod Christus consuluit abdicationem proprietatis omnium temporalium: quia per venditionem omnium & largitionem eorum factam pauperibus constat proprietatem auferri, sequitur ergo quod Apostoli nullius rei proprietatem habebant in speciali. Ex quo ille adolescens, si voluisset fuisse perfectus, nullius rei proprietatem in speciali habuisset. Sed diceres, videtur posse probari, quod illa auctoritas non concludat. Primo quia non est verisimile, quod Christus consuluerit tibi, quod vestimenta sua vederet, & ad eum non vestitus, sed nudus veniret, & ita illa verba Christi licet generaliter prolata sint: tamen non sunt ita generaliter intelligenda, quin aliquarum rerum poterat proprietatem & dominium retinere. Secundo quia per hanc auctoritatem non probatur, quod postea non debuit proprietatem habere: sed pro tunc debeat a se proprietatem abdicare. Unde non dixit sibi Christus: vade & vende omnia quae habes & da pauperibus: & nunquam alicuius rei de catero proprietatem acquiras, ergo Christus ei potestatem acquirendi proprietatem rerum in speciali minime dissuasit. Sed illae obiectiones non concludunt. Nam licet Christus in suo consilio principaliter intendebat proprietatem omnium temporalium abdicare: vnicum tamen modum abdicandi proprietatem temporalium (qui forte illi adolescenti erat conueniens) expressit vocaliter.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents show the same conclusion thus: just as the Apostles observed Christ's counsel concerning chastity and obedience, so they also observed Christ's counsel concerning poverty; but Christ taught and counselled the renunciation of ownership of all temporal goods in particular; therefore the Apostles observed the same counsel. The major premise is plain. They prove the minor by that counsel which Christ gave to the young man who asked what was still lacking to him, since he had kept the commandments, Matthew 19, saying: If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come and follow me. From these words it is given to understand that Christ counselled the renunciation of ownership of all temporal goods, because by selling all and giving it to the poor it is evident that ownership is taken away; it follows, therefore, that the Apostles had no ownership of anything in particular. From this, that young man, if he had wished to be perfect, would have had no ownership of anything in particular. But you may say that it seems possible to prove that this authority does not conclude. First, because it is not likely that Christ counselled him to sell his garments and come to him not clothed but naked; and so those words of Christ, though spoken generally, are not to be understood so generally that he could not keep ownership and dominion of some things. Second, because this authority does not prove that he ought not afterwards to have ownership, but that for the time being he ought to renounce ownership. Hence Christ did not say to him: Go and sell all that you have and give to the poor, and never acquire ownership of anything again; therefore Christ by no means dissuaded him from the power of acquiring ownership of things in particular. But those objections do not conclude. For although Christ in his counsel principally intended the renunciation of ownership of all temporal goods, he expressed vocally only one way of renouncing ownership of temporal goods (which perhaps was suitable for that young man).

units.la: Ad cuius euidentiam est sciendum, quod quadruplex est modus temporalia abdicandi a sanctis hactenus vsitatus. Vnus est temporalia dando pauperibus, & ille modus aliquando absq; venditione, & aliquando per venditionem congrue exercetur. Nam absq; venditione pecuniae ea quae in cibo & potu consistunt, ac vestes aliquae, & nonnullae res aliae conuenienter distribuuntur pauperibus, possessiones autem magnae, villae, ciuitates & castra, vasa pretiosa, & etiam vestes pretiosae, & res aliae multae absq; venditione nequaquam datur conuenienter pauperibus: quia eleemosynae sunt faciendae pauperibus, vt sustententur, non vt ditentur. Alius modus abdicandi temporalia est relinquendo parentibus, sicut enim qui naturaliter moritur, nonnulla bona sua parentibus ordinare relinquit: ita etiam qui moritur morte ciuili propter Deum, omnia dimittendo & religionem intrando, saepe tenetur secundum Deum aliqua bona sua parentibus reliquisse. Tertius modus relinquendi proprietatem temporalium est conferendo bona sua ecclesiae, per quem modum primi credentes possessionibus suis vel substantiis venditis pretia communitati credentium conferebant. De istis tribus modis abdicandi proprietatem temporalium legitur in libro Prosperi, sicut recitatur 1. q. 2. c. sacerdos, vbi sic scribitur: Sacerdos, cui dispensationis cura commissa est, non solum sine cupiditate, sed etiam cum laude pietatis accipit a populo dispensanda: & fideliter dispensat accepta, quia omnia sua aut reliquit pauperibus, aut eis distribuit, aut ecclesiae rebus adiunxit. Quartus modus abdicandi proprietatem temporalium est sua pro derelictis habendo, & ille modus absq; causa speciali seruari non debet: quia communitati fidelium expedit, quod vnusquisq; de rebus suis recte disponat, & illo modo loquitur beatus Hieronymus ad Paulinum dicens: Si habes in potestate rem tuam, vende, si non habes, proiice, vbi sic ex praecedentibus & sequentibus patet aperte, quod beatus Hieronymus Paulino suadet, ne propter ordinationem rerum suarum conuersionem suam procrastinet. Christus ergo ad abdicationem proprietatis omnium temporalium adolescentem exhortans, vnum modum expressit, alios modos insinuans, vt ille sit sensus: Si vis perfectus esse, vade & vende omnia quae habes, quae sc. non expedit parentibus tuis relinquere, nec est necesse tecum ad vsum facti afferre, & quae non conuenienter, nisi vendantur, dantur pauperibus, & hoc, si ipsa habes in tua potestate, non enim Saluator volebat, quod ille adolescens pecunias, si quas haberet, primo venderet, & postea daret pauperibus, nec volebat, quod si de iure aliqua parentibus relinquere tenebatur, quod illa vederet & daret pauperibus, nec etiam consulebat, si aliquas possessiones suas in sua potestate non habebat, sed oportuisset, quod eas longo tempore per iudicium acquisset, quod primo eas recuperaret & venderet, & tandem daret pauperibus, & demum ad Christi sequelam veniret, nec etiam hortabatur, quod vestes, quibus induebatur, si Apostoli non habuerunt habitum distinctum, & omnes res alias venderet & daret pauperibus, vt sic non vestitus veniret ad ipsum, sed perfectionem euangelicam adolescenti declarans voluit, quod rebus, quas in sua potestate habebat, recte dispositis & omnibus abdicatis quo ad proprietatem ad sequelam sui veniret. Et ita, sicut ille potuit, non obstante consilio Christi de venditione omnium pecunias, si quas habebat sine omnium venditione pecuniarum praevia, statim dare pauperibus, ita si tenebatur potuit aliqua parentibus suis reliquisse, sicut etiam implendo mentem Christi potuit, si Apostoli & discipuli non haberent distinctum habitum, vestes aliquas secum ad vsum, non ad proprietatem afferre.
units.tr: To make this clear, it must be understood that there are four ways of giving up temporal goods that the saints have hitherto used. The first is by giving temporal goods to the poor, and this is sometimes done without selling and sometimes by selling, as is fitting. Without selling, money, food and drink, certain clothes, and some other things may suitably be distributed to the poor. But large estates, farms, cities and castles, precious vessels, costly clothes and many other things can by no means be suitably given to the poor without being sold, because alms are to be given to the poor so that they may be sustained, not so that they may be enriched. The second way of giving up temporal goods is by leaving them to parents. Just as a person who dies a natural death commonly leaves some of his goods to his parents by arrangement, so too a person who dies a civil death for God's sake, by giving up everything and entering religious life, is often bound, according to God, to have left some of his goods to his parents. The third way of giving up ownership of temporal goods is by conferring one's goods on the Church, which is how the first believers, having sold their estates or substance, brought the proceeds to the community of believers. These three ways of giving up ownership of temporal goods are read in the book of Prosper, as cited in 1. q. 2. c. sacerdos, where it is written thus: A priest, to whom the care of the distribution has been committed, receives from the people what is to be distributed, not only without covetousness but even with praise for his piety; and he distributes faithfully what he has received, because he has either left all his own goods to the poor, or distributed them to them, or added them to the property of the Church. The fourth way of giving up ownership of temporal goods is to regard one's own goods as abandoned, and this way ought not to be followed without a special cause, because it is expedient for the community of the faithful that each person should dispose of his own goods rightly. In this sense blessed Jerome speaks to Paulinus, saying: If you have your property in your power, sell it; if you do not have it, cast it away; where it is plainly clear from what goes before and after that blessed Jerome persuades Paulinus not to delay his conversion on account of the disposal of his goods. Therefore, in exhorting the young man to give up ownership of all temporal goods, Christ expressed one way and hinted at the others, so that the meaning is this: If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, that is, what it is not fitting to leave to your parents, what you need not carry with you for use, and what cannot suitably be given to the poor unless it is sold; and this only if you have these things in your own power. For the Saviour did not wish that this young man should first sell whatever money he might have and afterwards give it to the poor; nor did he wish that, if he was bound by law to leave something to his parents, he should sell that and give it to the poor; nor did he advise that, if he did not have some of his possessions in his power, but would have to acquire them by a lengthy legal process, he should first recover them, sell them, give them to the poor, and only then come to follow Christ. Nor did he urge him to sell the clothes he wore, although the Apostles did not have a distinct habit, and to sell all other goods and give them to the poor, so that he would come to him naked. Rather, declaring the evangelical perfection to the young man, he wished that, once the things he had in his power were rightly disposed of and all ownership of them given up, he should come to follow him. And so, just as the young man could, without violating Christ's counsel to sell everything, give at once to the poor whatever money he had, without first selling all his money, so, if he was bound, he could leave something to his parents; and likewise, in fulfilling Christ's intention, the Apostles and disciples, since they did not have a distinct habit, could bring some clothes with them for use, not as property.

units.la: Ad secundam obiectionem isti impugnatores respondent, quod iuxta sententiam Christi dicentis: Nemo mittens manum suam ad aratrum & respiciens retro aptus est regno Dei: perfectio semel assumpta absq; imperfectione relinqui non potest, nisi forte in casu necessitatis, vel ex alia causa rationabili & urgente, ipsam quis saltem ad tempus relinquere cogeretur. Cum ergo Christus abdicationem proprietatis omnium temporalium tanq; ad perfectionem pertinentem consuluerit adolescentibus abdicatio talis semel assumpta absq; imperfectione relinqui non potest, & ita Christus dans consilium persectionis, manifeste consuluit omnia temporalia pro omni tempore abdicare quo ad proprietatem. Quarto eandem veritatem, ut dicunt isti impugnatores, ostendunt per verba Christi, qui, ut habetur Lucae 14. ait: Sic ergo ex vobis qui non renunciat omnibus quae possidet, non potest meus esse discipulus. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod volentes Christi esse perfecti discipuli, omnibus quae possidebant, renunciabant, non autem renunciabant omnibus quantum ad usum facti, ergo renunciabant quantum ad proprietatem, saltem in speciali.
units.tr: In answer to the second objection, these opponents reply that, according to the saying of Christ: No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God, once perfection has been taken up it cannot be given up without imperfection, unless perhaps in a case of necessity, or for some other reasonable and pressing cause which compels someone to give it up at least for a time. Since therefore Christ advised the young men to give up ownership of all temporal goods as belonging to perfection, such a renunciation, once taken up, cannot be given up without imperfection; and thus Christ, in giving the counsel of perfection, plainly advised giving up all temporal goods, as far as ownership goes, for every time. Fourthly, these opponents say, the same truth is shown by the words of Christ, who says, as found in Luke 14: So therefore whoever of you does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple. From these words it is to be understood that those who wished to be perfect disciples of Christ renounced all that they possessed, and did not renounce all only as to use, so they renounced it as to ownership, at least in particular.

units.la: Et quod verba Christi praedicta debeant intelligi de renunciatione omnium quatum ad proprietatem, auctoritatibus sanctorum patenter videtur posse probari. Beatus enim Gregorius super Evangelia, dicta verba pertractans ait: Certe cum sequentibus nova mandata proponeret, dixit: Nisi quis renunciaverit omnibus quae possidet, non potest meus esse discipulus. Ac si aperte dicat: qui per vitam veterem alienam concupiscentiis, per novam conversationis studium & viam largiamini, per largitatem autem proprietas abdicatur, ergo verba Christi secundum beatum Gregorium de renunciatione, quae est abdicatio proprietatis, debent intelligi.
units.tr: And that the words of Christ quoted above must be understood of renunciation of all things as to ownership can plainly be proved by the authority of the saints. For blessed Gregory, treating these words in his homilies on the Gospels, says: Surely, when he was setting out the new commands, he said: Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple. As if he were plainly saying: those who through the old life are given over to foreign desires, let them, through the new life and way of conversion, be generous; and through generosity ownership is given up. Therefore, according to blessed Gregory, the words of Christ must be understood of renunciation, which is the giving up of ownership.

units.la: Item Ambrosius Homelia 16. super Genesim ait: Christus Dominus noster sacerdotibus suis, quid praeceperit audiamus: qui non renunciaverit omnibus quae possidet, non potest meus esse discipulus, & infra: Negat Christus suum esse discipulum, quem viderit aliquid esse possidentem: & eum qui non renunciat omnibus quae possidet, & infra: Festinemus transfire a sacerdotibus Pharaonis, quibus terrena possessio est, ad sacerdotes Domini, quibus in terra pars non est, quibus portio Dominus est, talis enim erat & ille, qui ducebat tanquam egentes & multos locupletantes, ut nihil habentes & omnia possidentes.
units.tr: Likewise Ambrose, in Homily 16 on Genesis, says: Let us hear what Christ our Lord commanded his priests: whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple; and below: Christ denies that he is his disciple who is seen to possess anything; and he who does not renounce all that he possesses; and below: Let us hasten to pass from the priests of Pharaoh, who have earthly possession, to the priests of the Lord, who have no part in the land, for whom the Lord is their portion. For such was also that man who treated as needy those who were rich, and as rich those who had nothing and possessed everything.

units.la: Ex his verbis clare datur intelligi, quod qui persecte verbum implet Christi praedictum: Nisi quis renunciaverit: sunt tales, quibus in terra pars non est: & quibus portio Dominus est, tales autem sunt, qui nullius rei proprietatem habent in speciali. Apostoli autem cupiebant verba Christi implere perfecte, & non minus perfecte, quam alii, ergo ipsi omnibus renunciaverunt quantum ad proprietatem saltem in speciali. Alias auctoritates scripturae divinae quamplurimas contra assertionem praefatam adducunt, quas causa brevitatis omitto.
units.tr: From these words it is clearly to be understood that those who perfectly fulfil the aforesaid word of Christ, "Unless someone renounces," are such as have no part in the land, and for whom the Lord is their portion; and such are those who have ownership of no particular thing. But the Apostles desired to fulfil the words of Christ perfectly, and no less perfectly than others; therefore they renounced all things as to ownership, at least in particular. They bring forward very many other passages of divine Scripture against the aforesaid assertion, which I omit for the sake of brevity.

units.la: Ad haec, isti impugnatores quinto per rationes in scripturis fundatas autenticis praedictam assertionem satagunt reprobare. Est autem prima ratio talis, paupertas Apostolorum non fuit minor nec imperfectior quam paupertas monachorum & aliorum Religiosorum Mendicantium & non mendicantium, sed monachi & alii Religiosi vouent paupertatem, quae est abdicatio paupertatis omnium temporalium in speciali, ergo & paupertas Apostolica abdicationem proprietatis omnium temporalium in speciali includebat. Haec ratio confirmatur auctoritate beati Gregorii, qui, ut habetur 16. q. 1. cap. Ex auctoritate, asserit monachos figuram Apostolorum tenere, non autem monachi, eo quod monachi, tenent figuram Apostolorum, quo ad officii dignitatem, nec quo ad sacramentorum dispensationem, ergo tenent figuram Apostolorum quo ad propriorum renunciationem, quod expresse notat Glossa 12. q. 1. c. videntes, dicens: Episcopi tenent locum Apostolorum, ut hic scilicet quo ad dignitatem: monachi quo ad renunciationem proprietorum & communem vitam. Ex quo sequitur, quod Apostoli propriis renunciaverunt quo ad proprietatem saltem in speciali, hoc etiam auctoritate beati Hieronymi supra allegata, qui ait: Apostolis nemo fuit pauperior &c. probatur manifeste &c.
units.tr: Besides these things, these opponents, fifthly, through reasons founded on the authentic Scriptures, labour to refute the aforesaid assertion. The first reason is this: the poverty of the Apostles was neither less nor more imperfect than the poverty of monks and other religious, both mendicant and non-mendicant; but monks and other religious vow poverty, which is the renunciation of ownership of all temporal goods in particular; therefore the apostolic poverty also included renunciation of ownership of all temporal goods in particular. This reasoning is confirmed by the authority of blessed Gregory, who, as found in 16. q. 1. cap. Ex auctoritate, asserts that monks hold the figure of the Apostles, but not the monks in the sense that they hold the figure of the Apostles as to the dignity of office, nor as to the dispensing of the sacraments; therefore they hold the figure of the Apostles as to the renunciation of their own goods. This the Gloss expressly notes on 12. q. 1. c. videntes, saying: Bishops hold the place of the Apostles, namely here as to dignity; monks as to the renunciation of their own goods and common life. From this it follows that the Apostles renounced their own goods as to ownership, at least in particular; this is also clearly proved by the authority of blessed Jerome cited above, who says: No one was poorer than the Apostles etc.

units.la: Secunda ratio talis est. Fratres Praedicatores & Minores non perfectius perfectionem Evangelicam imitantur, quam Apostoli, sed Fratres Praedicatores & etiam Minores per abdicationem proprietatis omnium temporalium in speciali perfectionem Evangelicam imitantur, unde & de Fratribus Praedicatoribus simul & de Fratribus Minoribus, ut ille impugnatus in sua constitutione, Quia quorundam, affirmat Alexander quartus in Condemnatione libelli contra statum praedicatorum & Minorum editum, dicit in haec verba: Cum insuper iidem Fratres propter Deum omnia reliquerint, exilia vitae subsidia mendicantes, Christumque imitentur pauperem, perfectionem evangelicam amplexando, propter quod evidenter apparet eos in statu non solum salvandorum existere, sed etiam perfectorum, & per sua religionis observantiam, quae quidem ipsius perfectionis evangelicae tenet firmam in aeterna retributionis praemio praecellentem gloriam promereri. Ex quibus verbis colligitur evidenter, quod Fratres Praedicatores & Minores propter Deum omnia quo ad proprietatem in speciali relinquentes, perfectionem Evangelicam amplexantur, & perfectionis Evangelicae tenent formam, ergo & Apostoli, qui non imperfectius perfectionem Evangelicam imitati fuerunt, nullius rei proprietate in speciali habuerunt.
units.tr: The second argument runs as follows. The Preaching Friars and the Minor Friars do not imitate evangelical perfection more perfectly than the Apostles did. But the Preaching Friars and the Minor Friars imitate evangelical perfection by renouncing ownership of all temporal goods individually. Hence, concerning both the Preaching Friars and the Minor Friars, Alexander IV affirms, in his constitution Quia quorundam, which was issued in the Condemnation of the book against the state of the Preachers and Minors, and which attacked that author, he says in these words: Since moreover these same Friars, for God's sake, have left all things, begging for the necessities of life and imitating Christ in poverty, embracing evangelical perfection, it is therefore evident that they stand not only in the state of those who are to be saved but also of the perfect, and through the observance of their religion, which holds firm the form of this very evangelical perfection, they merit a glory surpassing in the reward of eternal retribution. From these words it is clearly gathered that the Preaching and Minor Friars, who for God's sake leave all things as regards individual ownership, embrace evangelical perfection and hold the form of evangelical perfection. Therefore the Apostles, who did not imitate evangelical perfection less perfectly, had ownership of nothing individually.

units.la: Postremo propter eos, qui dicta Thomae recipiunt, isti impugnatores ostendunt, quod praedicta assertio sententiae Thomae penitus adversatur. Unde in libro suo contra Magistros Parisienses c. 6. ait: Multo est laudabilius, quod aliquis omnibus suis datis, etiam seipsum Deo det, quod ad Apostolicam perfectionem pertinet. Unde dicit Hieronymus ad Lucinum haereticum: Seipsum offerre Deo proprium Christianorum est & Apostolorum, qua totum censum, quem habuerant, Domino tradiderunt. Item in eodem capitulo, sicut adductum est prius, ait: Evangelica perfectio maxime in Apostolis claruit: sed ipsi actualem paupertatem habuerunt sua omnia relinquentes. Unde Petrus dixit Mat. 19. Ecce nos reliquimus omnia. Et Hieronymus dicit ad Ebidiam: si vis esse perfectus &c. Ex quibus concludunt: Ergo actualis paupertas ad Evangelicam perfectionem pertinet. Ex his clare patet, quod Apostoli sua omnia reliquerunt, nec valet dicere, quod reliquerunt omnia, licet non quo ad proprietatem neq; in speciali neq; in communi: secundum quod dicit ille impugnatus.
units.tr: Finally, on account of those who accept the statements of Thomas, these opponents show that the aforesaid assertion is utterly opposed to the opinion of Thomas. Hence in his book against the Parisian Masters, chapter 6, he says: It is much more praiseworthy that someone, giving all his goods, also gives himself to God, which pertains to apostolic perfection. Hence Jerome says to Lucinus the heretic: To offer oneself to God is proper to Christians and to the Apostles, who handed over to the Lord all the wealth they had. Likewise in the same chapter, as was cited before, he says: Evangelical perfection shone most in the Apostles; but they had actual poverty, leaving all their goods. Hence Peter said in Matth. 19., Behold, we have left all things. And Jerome says to Ebidia: If you wish to be perfect, and so on. From these they conclude: therefore actual poverty pertains to evangelical perfection. From this it is clear that the Apostles left all their goods. Nor is it valid to say that they left all things, though not as regards ownership, either individually or in common, as that attacked author says.

units.la: Nam secundum Thomam, Euangelica perfectio maxime in Apostolis claruit. Sed ad perfectionem Euangelicā pertinet omnia reliquisse quo ad proprietatem saltem in speciali. Ergo Apostoli omnia reliquerunt secundum eum, quo ad proprietatem in speciali. Quod autem secundum Thomam reliquisse omnia quo ad proprietatē in speciali, ad Euangelicā perfectionem pertineat, patenter in multis locis affirmat. Vnde in libro suo contra quosdam Magistros Parisienses ab Alexandro 4. condemnatos, ipsorū de paupertate recitans opinionē 6. ait: Asserunt etiam paupertatem laudari in scripturis non actualem, qua aliquis rebus temporalibus se exspoliat, sed habitualem, qua aliquis rem temporalem contemnit corde, etiam si res possideat. Ad destructionem huius erroris hoc modo procedemus. Primo ostendemus ad perfectionem Euangelicam pertinere non solum paupertatem habitualem, sed etiam actualem, quae fit per abiectionem temporalium. Ex his verbis clare patet, quod secundum istū abdicatio omnium temporalium quo ad proprietatē in speciali ad Euangelicā pertinet perfectionē. Quia ipse loquitur de abdicatione illa quā vocat paupertatem actualē, quae à religiosis Mendicantibus omnia quo ad proprietatem in speciali dimittentibus propter Deū, assumitur: quā illam prędicti Magistri Parisiensis impugnare volebāt, & ille eā in libro illo defendit. Nullū est ergo dubiū, quin ille Doctor loquatur de actuali paupertate, quae est abdicatio omnium temporalium quo ad proprietatē in speciali secundū ipsum. Et quod actualis paupertas ad Euangelicam perfectionem pertineat, probat ipse vbi prius 19. rationibus in auctoritatibus sanctorū fundatis.
units.tr: For according to Thomas, evangelical perfection shone most in the Apostles. But to evangelical perfection belongs leaving all things, at least as regards individual ownership. Therefore, according to him, the Apostles left all things as regards individual ownership. That, according to Thomas, leaving all things as regards individual ownership pertains to evangelical perfection, he affirms clearly in many places. Hence, in his book against certain Parisian Masters condemned by Alexander IV, reciting their sixth opinion on poverty, he says: They also assert that the poverty praised in the Scriptures is not actual, by which someone strips himself of temporal things, but habitual, by which someone despises a temporal thing in his heart, even if he possesses it. To destroy this error we shall proceed in this way. First we shall show that not only habitual poverty but also actual poverty, which comes about through the casting off of temporal things, pertains to evangelical perfection. From these words it is clear that, according to this author, the renunciation of all temporal goods as regards individual ownership pertains to evangelical perfection. For he speaks of that renunciation which he calls actual poverty, which is taken up by the religious Mendicants who, for God's sake, give up everything as regards individual ownership. This the said Parisian Master wished to attack, and Thomas defends it in that book. There is therefore no doubt that this Doctor speaks of actual poverty, which, according to him, is the renunciation of all temporal goods as regards individual ownership. And that actual poverty pertains to evangelical perfection he proves himself, in the place cited before, with nineteen reasons founded on the authorities of the saints.

units.la: Secundo isti impugnatores alium errorem in verbis praemissis istius impugnati asserunt contineri: quod videlicet quilibet alius de numero credentium post diuisionem facta erat proprietarius & dominus portionis sibi assignatę. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendū, quod illa communitas credentiū non durabat vna die tantū, neq; duobus tantū, imo nec tantū paucis diebus: sed tempore multo durauit, quod ex diuersis scripturis autenticis dicunt posse probari. Hoc supposito ex textu Actuum Apostolorum ostendunt, quod illa bona post diuisionē factam nō erant propria illis, quibus dabantur quo ad dominium & proprietatem in speciali. Nam illa diuisio non fiebat nisi ad credentiū indigentias subleuandas. Vnde in textu habetur sic: Erant eis omnia communia. Et sequitur: Neq; eorum quisquā egens erat inter illos. Quotquot enim possessores agrorum ac domorum erant, vendentes afferebant pretia eorum quae vendebant & ponebant ante pedes Apostolorum & diuidebant singulis prout cuiq; opus erat. Ex his verbis euidenter colligitur, quod illa bonorum diuisio ex charitate Fraternitatis processit, qua cupiebant singulorum indigentias releuare. Sed illa diuisio bonorum temporalium inter aliquos, quae fit solum modo ad indigentias singulorum releuandas, dat cuilibet facultatem vtendi siue consumendi secundum modum istius loquendi illa, quae sic sunt necessaria, & nullam proprietatem tribuit singulis in speciali: tum quia absq; tali proprietate in speciali vita humana congrue sustentatur: tum quia si quilibet fieret proprietarius & Dominus in speciali portionis sibi assignatę, principalis intentio diuidentis facilIter posset frustrari. Possent enim aliqui illorum, quibus esset facta diuisio, si fierēt proprietarii & Domini portionū suarum in speciali, portiones suas alteri dare vel aliis extra communitatē vendere vel donare. Quod si darent extra communitatem, vel necesse esset eorū indigentias minime releuare, vel ab aliis aliquā partem portionis suae subtrahere, quorū vtrumq; esset intentionem principalē diuidentis frustrare. Nullus ergo credentium in Ecclesia fuit proprietarius & Dominus in speciali portionis sibi assignatę: sed tamen fuerunt illae portiones sibi assignatę, non ad dandum nec vendendū, sed tantum ad suas indigentias releuandas. Si enim quilibet illorum habuisset potestatē dandi vel vendi portionem sibi assignatā, cito potuisset frustrari tota & principalis intentio illorum: sed rebus suis venditis eorum pretia communitati dederunt. Nam si aliqui illorum prima die dedissent aliis vel in communitate vel extra communitatem portiones suas, aliqui fuissent multum ditati, & aliqui multū egentes: & ita frustrata fuisset eorū intentio, per quā quantum in eis fuit optabant, quo nullus egens esset inter eos. Ex his, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, patenter habetur, quod illa verba: Erant eis omnia communia, non dicebantur pro vna die tantū: quamtamen oporteret secundū ipsum impugnatū. Nā si duobus diebus fuerunt eis communia omnia: In istis duobus diebus nullus manducauit, neq; bibit, quia nullus manducauit aut bibit, nisi portionē sibi assignatā, aut cibū vel potū emptū de portione sibi assignata. Sed in illis duobus diebus nulla fuit eis portio assignata, si nulla portio fuit communis. Ergo in illis duobus diebus nullus manducauit neq; bibit. Quod non continet veritatē. Constat ergo quod illa communio omnū non durauit vna die, nec vna hora diei, sed multis diebus durauit: & tamen constat, quod in istis diebus portiones singulis assignabantur. Ergo nullus eorū fuit proprietarius & Dominus in speciali portionis sibi assignatę. Secundo isti impugnatores sic arguunt: communē vitā ducere nō est, ī vna hora omnia habere communia, quemadmodū hęredes alicuius ipso mortuo habent omnia communia, qui postea statim diuidunt inter se: sed communē vitā ducere est de communibus sustentari. Qui ergo communē vitā ducit, de bonis communibus sustentatur, sicut ex auctoritate Beati Gregor. quae ponitur 12. q. 1. t. Quintus, & ex auctoritate Vrbani eiusdem 12. & q. 2. Scimus, colligitur euidenter. Sed primi credentes communem vitam duxerunt, teste Clemente, qui, vt habetur 12. c. 1. Dilectissimus, ait: Istius enim consuetudinis mōre retento, etiam Apostoli eorum, discipuli, vt praedictum est, vna nobiscum & vobiscum communem vitam duxerunt. Ergo de bonis omnibus sustentari fuerunt omnes. Ergo portiones singulis assignatę communes erant, non proprię, quoad dominium in speciali, quemadmodū nec portiones monachis assignatae sunt eis propriae, ita quod ipsarum habeant dominium in speciali. Dicet autem aliquis forte ignarus, quod sustentati fuerunt de bonis, quae prius fuerunt communia: & tali modo communē vitam duxerunt. Sed hoc friuolū est. Nam si duo fratres diuidant hereditatem communē, & postea vterq; viuat de portione sua, nō dicuntur propterea communē vitā ducere. Ergo consimiliter si illi credentes in primitiva Ecclesia diuserunt bona communia quo ad proprietatem & quilibet postea vixit de portione sibi assignata, nullatenus duxerunt communem vitam. Tertio sic arguunt. Regulae sanctorum, scilicet Basilii, Benedicti, & Augustini, quas suis fratribus tradiderunt, quo ad abdicationem rerum temporalium ex modo viuendi credentium in primitiva Ecclesia acceptae fuerunt. Unde Greg. 12. q. 1. c. quia tua, scribens Augustino monacho Anglorum Episcopo ait: Quia tua fraternitas monasterii regulu erudita seor sum no debet fieri a clericis suis in Ecclesia Anglorum, quae auctore Deo nuper ad fide perducta est. Hanc debet instruere conuersatione, qua initio fuit pluribus nostris, in quibus nullus eorum ex his q possidebant proprium habebat, sed erat illis omnia communia. In hoc concordat beat. Basil. qui quaerentibus fratribus suis, utrum liceret habere aliquod proprium, respondit in haec verba: hoc est contrarium testimonio, q in Actibus Apostolorum de isto, q quaerebantur, prius scriptum est. Ibi enim ita dicitur: quia nemo ex bonis suis quicquam proprium esse dicebat, sed erant illis omnia communia. Et Augustin. in Regula sua ait: Nō dicatis aliquid proprium, sed sint vobis omnia communia. Sic enim legitur in Actibus Apostolorum, & in Regula beati Bened. habetur. Ex quibus patet, q ad exemplar modi viuendi credentium, de quibus in Actibus Apostolorum fit mentio, religiones instituerunt. Sed mandatum est, & infra pbatur, q religiosi sanctorum pdictorum Regulas profitentes non sint Domini & proprietarii in speciali portionum quae eis assignantur. Ergo nec illi credentes erant Domini & proprietarii in speciali portionum sibi assignatarum. Quarto sic arguunt. Perfectioni credentium in primitiva Ecclesia est minime detrahendum. Sed dicere, q ipsi primo omnia propria diuiserunt, statim proprietatem sumserunt, est eorum perfectioni detrahere. Ergo hoc minime est dicendum. Vltimo isti impugnatores propter eos, q dicta Thomae sequuntur, verba ipsius adducunt, q in libro contra retrahentium a religione, c. 15. contra seipsum obiiciens p decretum Melchiadis Papae, ad illud decretum respondet in haec verba: Sed si quis recte consideret, haec praemissa non contrariantur. Ecclesia enim in sui primordio in omnibus suis membris talis fuit, qualis postmodum vix apud perfectos quosq; inuenitur. Sicut enim natura, sic & gratia debuit a perfectis initio sumere. Et ideo Apostoli secundum ipsum statum fidelium vita ordinauerunt perfectam conuenientem. Unde dicit Hier. in libro de Illustribus viris: Apparet primum talem Christo fuisse Ecclesiam, quales nunc monachi esse nituntur & cupiunt, ut nihil cuiusquam proprium sit, nullus inter eos diues nec pauper: patrimonia egentibus diuidantur, ut oratione vacent & psalmis, de doctrina quoq; ac continentia. Hic autem modus viuendi perfectioni congruus fuit apud primos credentes, non solum in Iudaea sub Apostolis, sed etiam apud Aegyptum sub Marco Euangelista, ut ibidem Hier. ostendit, & in secundo libro Ecclesiasticae historiae narratur. Processu vero temporis multi in Ecclesiam erant intraturi, qui hac perfectione deficerent: q non erat futurum ante Iudaeorum excidium, sed Ecclesia apud gentes multiplicata. Quod postquam contigit, vtile iudicauerunt Ecclesias uplati, ut praedia & agri Ecclesiis conferrentur, non propter perfectiores quosq;, sed propter infirmiores, qui ad priorum fidelium perfectionem accedere non valerent. Ex his patenter habetur, & quod secundum illum Doctorem primi credentes perfectius reliquerunt temporalia quam posteriores. Et quam monachi eorum paupertatem imitantur, quamuis non omnes id ipsum attingant, quia omnes, qui possessiones habent in communi, ab eorum perfectione deficiunt. Et ita nullius proprietatem habuerunt in speciali: sicut & monachi nunc habere noscuntur.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents assert that another error is contained in the words of the man they attack: namely, that every other one of the believers, after the division was made, became an owner and proprietor of the portion assigned to him. To make this clear, they say it must be understood that that community of believers did not last one day only, nor two, nor even a few days, but lasted a long time, which they say can be proved from various authentic Scriptures. On this assumption they show from the text of the Acts of the Apostles that those goods, after the division, were not the property of those to whom they were given, as regards ownership and proprietorship in particular. For the division was made only to relieve the needs of the believers. Hence the text reads: They had all things in common. And it continues: Neither was there any among them that lacked. For as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold, and laid them down at the Apostles' feet; and distribution was made to every man according as he had need. From these words it is clearly gathered that this division of goods proceeded from the charity of the brotherhood, by which they desired to relieve the needs of each. But a division of temporal goods among certain persons, made only to relieve the needs of individuals, gives each one the faculty of using, or consuming, in the sense of that phrase, those things which are so necessary, and it grants no proprietorship to each individual in particular: first, because human life is suitably sustained without such particular proprietorship; second, because if each one became owner and proprietor in particular of the portion assigned to him, the chief intention of the one dividing could easily be frustrated. For some of those to whom the division had been made, if they became owners and proprietors in particular of their portions, could give their portions to another, or sell or give them to others outside the community. And if they gave them outside the community, it would either be necessary that their needs were not relieved at all, or that part of their portion were taken away from others; and either of these would frustrate the principal intention of the one dividing. Therefore no believer in the Church was owner and proprietor in particular of the portion assigned to him; yet those portions were assigned to them not for giving or selling, but only to relieve their needs. For if each one of them had the power to give or sell the portion assigned to him, the whole and principal intention of them all could soon have been frustrated; but having sold their goods, they gave the prices to the community. For if some of them had on the first day given their portions to others, either within the community or outside it, some would have become very rich and some very needy; and thus their intention, by which, as far as lay in them, they desired that no one among them should be needy, would have been frustrated. From these things, as these opponents say, it is plainly evident that the words They had all things in common were not said of one day only; yet they would have to be, according to the man they attack. For if all things were common to them for two days, then in those two days no one ate or drank, because no one ate or drank except from the portion assigned to him, or from food or drink bought from the portion assigned to him. But in those two days no portion was assigned to them, if no portion was common. Therefore in those two days no one ate or drank. This is not true. It is clear, then, that this community of all things did not last one day, nor one hour of a day, but lasted for many days; and yet it is clear that in those days portions were assigned to each person. Therefore none of them was owner and proprietor in particular of the portion assigned to him. Secondly, these opponents argue thus: to lead a common life is not to have all things in common for one hour, as the heirs of someone who has died have all things in common, and then immediately divide them among themselves; but to lead a common life is to be sustained by common goods. Therefore whoever leads a common life is sustained by common goods, as is clearly gathered from the authority of Blessed Gregory, which is cited in 12, q. 1, Quintus, and from the authority of Urban in the same place, 12, q. 2, Scimus. But the first believers led a common life, as witnessed by Clement, who, as is found in 12, c. 1, Dilectissimus, says: For by keeping the custom of this manner of life, their Apostles, disciples, as has been said, also led a common life with us and with you. Therefore all were sustained by all the goods. Therefore the portions assigned to each were common, not proper as regards ownership in particular, just as the portions assigned to monks are not proper to them, so that they have ownership of them in particular. But someone perhaps, being ignorant, will say that they were sustained by goods which had previously been common, and in that way they led a common life. But this is frivolous. For if two brothers divide a common inheritance, and afterwards each lives on his own portion, they are not on that account said to lead a common life. Therefore, similarly, if those believers in the primitive Church divided common goods as regards ownership, and each afterwards lived on the portion assigned to him, they did not lead a common life in any way. Thirdly, they argue thus. The rules of the saints, namely of Basil, Benedict, and Augustine, which they handed down to their brothers, were received, as regards the renunciation of temporal goods, from the way of life of the believers in the primitive Church. Hence Gregory, in 12, q. 1, c. Quia tua, writing to Augustine, monk and bishop of the English, says: Since your brotherhood, trained in the rule of the monastery, ought not to be set apart from your clergy in the Church of the English, which by God's authority has lately been brought to the faith, let it instruct them by that manner of life which at the beginning was practised by many of our people, among whom none of them claimed anything as his own among the things he possessed, but all things were common to them. In this Basil agrees, who, when his brothers asked whether it was lawful to have anything as one's own, answered in these words: This is contrary to the testimony which is written earlier in the Acts of the Apostles about those who were asking. For there it is said: since no one called anything of his own goods his own, but all things were common to them. And Augustine in his Rule says: Do not call anything your own, but let all things be common to you. For so it is read in the Acts of the Apostles, and it is contained in the Rule of Blessed Benedict. From these things it is evident that the religious orders were instituted on the pattern of the way of life of the believers mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles. But it has been commanded, and is proved below, that religious who profess the aforesaid rules of the saints are not owners and proprietors in particular of the portions assigned to them. Therefore neither were those believers owners and proprietors in particular of the portions assigned to them. Fourthly, they argue thus. The perfection of the believers in the primitive Church must by no means be detracted from. But to say that they first divided all their possessions, and at once took ownership, is to detract from their perfection. Therefore this must by no means be said. Lastly, these opponents, for the sake of those who follow the sayings of Thomas, cite his words, which in the book Against those who withdraw from religion, chapter 15, objecting against himself by the decree of Pope Melchiades, he answers in these words: But if anyone considers rightly, these premises do not contradict one another. For the Church at its beginning was, in all its members, such as hardly anywhere is found among the most perfect afterwards. For just as nature, so grace ought to have begun from the perfect. And therefore the Apostles arranged a perfect and fitting way of life according to the very state of the faithful. Hence Jerome says in the book On Illustrious Men: It appears that the Church was at first such as monks now strive and desire to be, so that nothing of anyone's is his own, no one among them is rich or poor, their patrimonies are divided to the needy, that they may be free for prayer and psalms, and also for teaching and continence. Now this manner of life was fitting to perfection among the first believers, not only in Judaea under the Apostles, but also in Egypt under Mark the Evangelist, as Jerome there shows, and as is told in the second book of the Ecclesiastical History. But in process of time many were to enter the Church who would fall short of this perfection; this was not to happen before the destruction of the Jews, but the Church was multiplied among the Gentiles. When this happened, the prelates judged it useful that farms and fields be conferred on the churches, not on account of the more perfect, but on account of the weaker, who could not attain to the perfection of the earlier faithful. From these things it is plainly evident both that, according to that Doctor, the first believers relinquished temporal goods more perfectly than the later ones, and that monks imitate their poverty, although not all of them attain the same thing, because all who have possessions in common fall short of their perfection. And thus they had ownership of nothing in particular, just as monks are now known to have none.

units.la: Tertius error, vt isti impugnatores affirmant, contentus in verbis praedictis est, q votu viuendi sine proprio, ad ea quibus necessario eget vita humana, minime se extendit. Illa assertio efficacius quam per regulas profitentium viuere sine proprio improbari non potest. Ideo primo ad reprobandum assertionem praefatam verba Regularum adducunt. In regula autem Beati Benedicti sic scribitur: Nē aliquis praesumat aliquid dare aut accipere, nec aliquid habere proprium, nullam omnino rem, neq; codicem, neque tabulas, neq; graffinium: sed nihil omnino, quippe quibus nec corda sua, nec voluntas licet habere in propria potestate. Omnia vero necessaria a patre monasterii sperare, nec quicquam habere, quod Abbas non dederit, aut permiserit. Omniaq; sint omnibus communia, vt scriptum est: nec quisquam aliquid suum esse dicat aut praesumat. Et alibi in eadem Regula sic dicitur: vestimenta fratribus secundum locorum qualitatem, vbi habitant, vel aeris temperiem dentur. Et infra: Accipientes noua, vetera semper reddant, in praesenti reponenda vestiario, propter pauperes, & pedules. Et quodcunq; est vestimentum, dum accipiunt nouum, reddant. Femoralia hi, qui in via diriguntur, de vestiario accipiant: qui reuertentes lota ibi restituant. Ex his aliisq; quamplurimis verbis Beati Benedicti claret aperte, quod monachi eiusdem Regulae professores nullius omnino rei debent habere proprietatem in speciali. In qua etiam de vestimentis, quibus necessario vita eget humana, fit mentio specialis. Ergo votum viuendi sine proprio ad ea quibus eget vita humana se extendit. Item, Augustin. in Regula sua ait: Non dicatis aliquid proprium, sed sint vobis omnia communia. Et infra: Vestras vestes in vnum beatu sub vno custode vel duobus vel quot sufficere possint ad eas exequendas, ne tinea ledantur. Et sicut pascimini vno cellario, sic induamini ex vno vestiario, si fieri potest. Ad vos non pertineat, quod vobis indumentum pro temporum congruentia proferatur: vtrum hoc recipiat vnusquisq; quod deposuerat, an aliud quod alter habuerat. Ex his patet, quod secundum Regulam Beati Augustini nullus debeat habere proprietatem in speciali cuiuscunque rei, & de vestimentis est hic specialiter interdictum, cum tamen constet quod vestimentis necessario eget vita humana. Item, in Regula Beati Francisci continetur expresse, quod Fratres sibi nihil appropriant nec domum, nec locum, nec aliquam rem. Ex quo patet, quod votum Fratrum Minorum viuendi sine proprio ad res, quibus necessario vita eget humana, se extendat. Ista impugnatores ratione probare conantur: Est autem prima ratio talis: qui non est in propria potestate, sed in potestate alterius, nullius rei proprietatem in speciali potest habere. Haec enim est ratio, quare seruus nihil possidet proprium, quia est res Domini sui. Et ita omnis res, qua vtitur, & non est aliena, est Domini sui. Sed religiosi vouentes viuere sine proprio non sunt in propria potestate, sed in potestate illius, cui obedientiam promiserunt. Ergo nullius rei possunt habere proprietatem in speciali. Confirmatur. Nulla res quantumcunq; ipsa egeat vita humana, potest esse magis in potestate alicuius, quam proprium corpus & propria voluntas. Sed nec proprium corpus nec propria voluntas religiosi volentis viuere sine proprio est in potestate ipsius. Ergo multo magis nulla res est sic in potestate ipsius, vt ipsius proprietatem habeat in speciali. Haec ratio per auctoritates, quibus asseritur, quod seruus nihil possidet, & quod qui ab alio possideturipse nihil possidet, & quod monachus est seruus, & quod monachus non habet liberum arbitrium, & quod non habet velle nec nolle, & quod abnegauerit semetipsum & propriam voluntatem: posset confirmari, sed causa prolixitatis vitandę minime adducuntur.
units.tr: The third error, as these opponents claim, is contained in the words quoted above: that the vow of living without property does not extend to the things that human life necessarily requires. That assertion cannot be refuted more effectively than by the rules of those who profess to live without property. So first, to refute the assertion, they cite the words of the Rules. In the Rule of Blessed Benedict it is written: Let no one presume to give or receive anything without the abbot's leave, or to have anything as his own, nothing at all: no book, no tablets, no stylus, nothing whatever, since they may not have their bodies or their wills in their own power. They are to expect all necessities from the father of the monastery, and to have nothing that the abbot has not given or allowed. Let all things be common to all, as it is written, and let no one say or presume that anything is his own. And elsewhere in the same Rule it is said: Clothing is to be given to the brothers according to the nature of the places where they live or the temperature of the air. And below: When they receive new garments, they are always to return the old ones, to be stored in the wardrobe for the poor. Whatever garment they receive new, they must return the old. Those who are sent on a journey are to take breeches from the wardrobe, and on returning are to wash them and give them back there. From these and many other words of Blessed Benedict it is clear that the monks who profess this Rule ought to have no property at all in particular. In this Rule, too, special mention is made of clothing, which human life necessarily requires. Therefore the vow of living without property does extend to the things that human life requires. Likewise Augustine says in his Rule: Do not call anything your own, but let all things be common to you. And below: Let your garments be gathered together in one place under one or two keepers, or as many as are needed to air them, lest they be damaged by moths. And just as you are fed from one storeroom, so you are to be clothed from one wardrobe, if possible. It is not for you to concern yourselves with what clothing is brought out for you according to the season, whether each one receives back what he had laid down or something another had worn. From these words it is plain that according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine no one ought to have property in particular in any thing whatever, and clothing is here specifically forbidden, although human life plainly needs clothing. Likewise, the Rule of Blessed Francis expressly states that the brothers appropriate nothing to themselves, neither house, nor place, nor any thing. From this it is clear that the vow of the Friars Minor, to live without property, extends to the things that human life necessarily requires. These opponents try to prove this by reason. The first reason is this: whoever is not in his own power, but in the power of another, can have no property in any particular thing. For this is the reason why a slave owns nothing as his own: he is his master's possession. And so every thing he uses, which is not his own, belongs to his master. But religious who vow to live without property are not in their own power, but in the power of him to whom they have promised obedience. Therefore they can have no property in any particular thing. Confirmation: no thing, however much human life needs it, can be more in the power of someone than one's own body and one's own will. But neither the body nor the will of a religious who vows to live without property is in his own power. Therefore much less is any thing so in his power that he has property of it in particular. This reasoning could be confirmed by authorities, which assert that a slave owns nothing, that one who is possessed by another owns nothing himself, that a monk is a slave, that a monk has no free will, that he has neither will nor refusal, and that he has denied himself and his own will. But for the sake of brevity these are not cited.

units.la: Secunda ratio talis est: si votum viuendi sine proprio ad ea, quibus necessario vita eget humana, minime se extendit: ergo licet monachis & aliis religiosis proprietatem & dominium in speciali panis & vini, vestimentorum & huiusmodi possidere: quia istis necessario vita eget humana. Sed hoc est inconueniens, tum quia tunc praelatus eorum non posset de huiusmodi rebus, postquam eis essent assignatae, aliqualiter ordinare, ipsis inuitis. Quia praelatus religiosorum de rebus alienis intromittere se non debet. Et ita si praeciperent eis praelati quod res huiusmodi communicarent aliis, obedire nullatenus tenerentur: & per consequens illa assertio aufert a religiosis obedientiam manifeste. Tum quia tunc possent res huiusmodi eis assignatas dare, vendere & legare ad suae placitum voluntatis. Et ita religiosi de rebus huiusmodi condere testamenta, quemadmodum Episcopi & alii clerici habentes res proprias praeter res communes Ecclesiae, de rebus propriis possunt condere testamenta. Imo sequeretur magis absurdum, videlicet quod religiosis liceret proprietatem pecuniarum in speciali habere. Quia quibus licet rem propriam vendere eidem licet habere in speciali pretium eiusdem rei. Sed per praedictam assertionem licet religiosis habere proprietatem in speciali huiusmodi rerum. Ergo licet eis vendere eadem. Et per consequens licet pecuniam, pro qua res venduntur huiusmodi habere in speciali: quod est inconueniens, & decretali Innocentii tertii extra, de sta. mo. Cum ad monasterium, repugnat aperte.
units.tr: The second reason is this: if the vow of living without property does not extend to the things that human life necessarily requires, then monks and other religious may have property and ownership in particular of bread and wine, clothing and such things, because human life necessarily requires these. But this is absurd, first because their superior could not then order anything about such things, once they had been assigned to them, against their will. For the superior of religious ought not to meddle with other people's things. And so, if their superiors ordered them to share such things with others, they would not be bound to obey at all; and consequently that assertion manifestly takes obedience away from religious. Second, because they could then give, sell and bequeath such assigned things at their pleasure. And so religious could make wills concerning such things, just as bishops and other clergy who have their own property, apart from the common goods of the Church, can make wills concerning their own property. Indeed, something even more absurd would follow, namely that religious would be allowed to have property in money in particular. For whoever is allowed to sell his own thing is also allowed to have the price of that thing in particular. But by the aforesaid assertion religious are allowed to have property in particular in such things. Therefore they are allowed to sell them. And consequently they are allowed to have in particular the money for which such things are sold; and this is absurd, and openly contradicts the decretal of Innocent III, Extra, de statu monachorum, Cum ad monasterium.

units.la: Tribus praedictis assertionibus, quas isti impugnatores erroneas reputant improbatis: ad rationes adductas in litera respondere nituntur. Ad quas, vt dicunt, manifestius dissoluendas, dicunt quod verbum dandi & verbum diuidendi saepe in scripturis accipiuntur aequiuoce. De verbo dandi patet: quia dare aliquando rem alteri, est facere rem esse accipientis quo ad dominium & proprietatem, maxime in speciali. Hanc significationem non oportet per auctoritates ostendere. Aliquando vero rem dare alteri, non est facere rem esse accipientis quo ad dominium & proprietatem, maxime in speciali: sed dare est rem assignare vel tradere. Sic accipitur Gen. 3. cum dicitur de muliere: Tulit de fructu illius & comedit, dedit{a} viro suo: quae tamen non fecit fructum illum esse viri sui quo ad proprietatem & dominium in speciali. Sic etiam accipitur Matth. 9. cum dicitur de Saluatore: Accepit quinque panibus & duobus piscibus aspiciens in caelum benedixit & fregit & dedit discipulis: quibus tamen Saluator non dedit panes & pisces quo ad dominium & proprietatem in speciali, sed tradidit eis ad distribuendum turbis. Sic etiam accipitur Matth. 25. vbi sic dicitur, Homo peregre proficiscens vocauit seruos suos, & tradidit illis bona sua, & vni dedit quinque talenta &c. Vbi dicunt isti, quod verbum dandi accipitur pro verbo tradendi: quia seruis, de quibus ibi fit mentio, non fuerunt data bona illa, vt fierent eorum quo ad dominium eorum in speciali, sed erant tradita eis vt lucrarentur in eis. Secundo dicunt, quod etiam verbum diuidendi accipitur dupliciter. Aliquando enim quod diuiditur, fit illorum quibus diuiditur quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Sic inter fratres diuiditur hereditas: quia quilibet eorum fit proprietarius & Dominus portionis sibi assignatae. Sic accipitur Lucae 12. cum quidam de turba dixit Christo: Magister dic fratri meo vt diuidat mecum hereditatem. Aliquando autem diuidere non est facere portiones diuisas esse illorum, quibus assignantur quo ad dominium & proprietatem: sed diuidere est certas portiones aliquibus assignare & tradere. Et sic accipitur Numeri 4. cap. cum dicitur Aaron & filii eius intrabunt ipsique disponent onera singulorum & diuident quid portare quis debeat. Illa tamen portanda diuisa Leuitis nequaquam fiebant eorum quoad proprietatem seu dominium neque in speciali neq; in communi. His visis dicunt isti, quod ille impugnatus praedictos errores sub multiplicitate vocum conatur adducere: quia, vt dicunt, rationes eius vocibus vtuntur aequiuocis. Unde ad primam rationem dicunt, quod maior est falsa, accipiendo verbum diuidendi pro verbo tradendi & deputandi rem ad vsum alicuius: quia inter monachos multorum monasteriorum nullus inuenitur egens pro eo quod cuilibet datur, hoc est assignatur, illud quod sibi opus est. Et tamen nullus eorum est proprietarius & Dominus portionis sibi assignatae. Minor vero est vera accipiendo verbum diuidendi pro verbo assignandi vel tradendi ad vsum. Eadem responsio daretur ad illam rationem, si tam in maiore quam in minore acciperetur praecise verbum dandi, vel praecise verbum diuidendi. Ad secundam rationem dicunt quod maior est erronea, accepto verbo diuidendi illo modo, quo accipitur in Actibus Apostolorum. Quia ibi accipitur verbum diuidendi pro verbo assignandi diuisa ad vsum. Et ita dicunt, quod in illa ratione additur nouus error, scilicet quod accipiendo verbum diuidendi pro verbo assignandi vel deputandi diuisa aliquibus ad vsum aliquem, quando aliquid diuiditur inter aliquos, quilibet eorum fit proprietarius & Dominus portionis sibi assignatae. Sic enim quando res religiosorum diuiduntur inter eos, & certae partes assignantur diuersis, quilibet fieret Dominus & proprietarius portionis suae. Quare quilibet monachus esset proprietarius & Dominus in speciali cellae sibi assignatae & lecti atq; equi, si diuersi equi diuersis monachis assignantur ad equitandum. Sic ergo, vt dicunt isti, maior illius secundae rationis est falsa. Cum vero probatur, quod diuidere est diuisim aliquas
units.tr: Against the three aforesaid assertions, which these opponents judge to be erroneous and refuted, they strive to answer the reasons adduced in the text. To dissolve these more clearly, as they say, they claim that the word giving and the word dividing are often taken equivocally in Scripture. As for the word giving, it is clear: sometimes to give a thing to another is to make the thing belong to the recipient with respect to ownership and property, especially in particular. This meaning need not be shown by authorities. But sometimes to give a thing to another does not make the thing belong to the recipient with respect to ownership and property, especially in particular; rather, to give is to assign or hand over the thing. So it is taken in Genesis 3, where it is said of the woman: She took of its fruit and ate, and gave to her husband; yet she did not make that fruit her husband's with respect to property and ownership in particular. So also it is taken in Matthew 9, where it is said of the Saviour: He took five loaves and two fishes, and looking up to heaven he blessed and broke, and gave them to the disciples; yet the Saviour did not give the loaves and fishes to them as their property in particular, but handed them over to them to distribute to the crowds. So also it is taken in Matthew 25, where it is said: A man going on a journey called his servants and handed over his goods to them, and to one he gave five talents, etc. Here these opponents say that the word giving is taken for the word handing over, because those goods were not given to the servants so that they might become their property in particular, but were handed to them so that they might trade with them. Second, they say that the word dividing is also taken in two ways. For sometimes what is divided becomes the property and ownership of those to whom it is divided. Thus an inheritance is divided among brothers, because each of them becomes the owner and proprietor of the portion assigned to him. So it is taken in Luke 12, when a man from the crowd said to Christ: Master, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me. But sometimes dividing does not make the divided portions belong to those to whom they are assigned, with respect to ownership and property; rather, dividing is assigning and handing over certain portions to certain people. So it is taken in Numbers 4, where it is said: Aaron and his sons shall go in, and they shall appoint the burdens of each one, and divide what each one is to carry. Yet those burdens divided to the Levites did not in any way become theirs as property or ownership, either in particular or in common. Having seen this, these opponents say that the author whom they refute tries to bring in the aforesaid errors under cover of ambiguous words, because, as they say, his reasons use equivocal terms. Hence, to the first reason they say that the major premise is false, if the word dividing is taken for the word handing over and assigning a thing to someone's use; for among the monks of many monasteries no one is found lacking what is necessary to him, because whatever is given, that is, assigned, to each one is what he needs. And yet none of them is the owner and proprietor of the portion assigned to him. The minor premise, however, is true if the word dividing is taken for the word assigning or handing over for use. The same answer would be given to that reason if, in both the major and the minor premise, the word giving or the word dividing were taken precisely. To the second reason they say that the major premise is erroneous, if the word dividing is taken in the way it is used in the Acts of the Apostles. For there the word dividing is taken for assigning divided portions for use. And so they say that in that reason a new error is added, namely that, when the word dividing is taken for assigning or designating divided portions to some people for some use, whenever something is divided among several people, each of them becomes the owner and proprietor of the portion assigned to him. For thus, when the goods of religious are divided among them and definite parts are assigned to different people, each would become the lord and proprietor of his own portion. Therefore every monk would be the owner and proprietor in particular of the cell assigned to him, and of his bed and horse, if different horses were assigned to different monks for riding.
