Thus, as these men say, the major premise of that second reason is false. When it is proved that to divide is to give separate parts to separate people...

units.la: {a} Gen. 3. aliquas partes diuersas diuersis dare. Dicunt, quod accipiendo dividere in prima significatione, & dare in prima, concedunt. Accipiendo autem dividere in secunda significatione, & dare in prima, falsum est. Et cum dicitur, quod datur alicui fit ei proprium: negatur accipiendo dare in secunda significatione sua. Et illo modo conceditur, quod bona illa distribuebantur Apostolis & aliis credentibus, & non aliter. Per idem respondent ad tertiam rationem, quod accipiendo dare in prima significatione concedunt maiorem: in secunda significatione negant maiorem: in secunda significatione negant maiorem. Et sic accipi debet in minori, si minor habet aliquo modo veritatem. Ad quartam rationem, quae maiorem apparentiam videtur habere, dicunt quod maior est erronea, cum dicitur: omnis qui post divisionem alicuius rei habet in portione sibi assignata plus quam habebat ante divisionem, habet in portione sibi assignata proprietatem & dominium in speciali: quia cellulae & lecti ac vestes & aliae res dividuntur inter monachos, ita quod cuilibet assignatur certa cella, lectus, vestes & res alia, quilibet illorum habet in re sibi assignata plus quam ante: quia habet licitam potestatem vendi, quia antea non habebat: & tamen nullus eorum habet in eadem dominium & proprietatem in speciali. Sic fuit de primis credentibus, quod quilibet eorum habuit post divisionem licitam potestatem vtendi portione sibi assignata absq; alia divisione, qualem potestatem antea non habuit. Sicut diversi venientes ad aliquam civitatem, postquam ad diversa hospitia sunt charitative recepti, quilibet in hospitio sibi gratis concesso habet aliquid plusquam prius: quia habet licitam potestatem manendi in ipso absq; alia concessione, quam ante concessionem non habuit: & tamen in hospitio non habet proprietatem & dominium neq; in speciali neq; in communi.
units.tr: {a} Gen. 3. aliquas partes diuersas diuersis dare. They say that if divide is taken in its first sense and give in its first sense, they grant the point. But if divide is taken in its second sense and give in its first, the claim is false. And when it is said that what is given to someone becomes his own, they deny this, taking give in its second sense. In that sense they concede that those goods were distributed to the Apostles and the other believers, and in no other way. In the same manner they answer the third argument: taking give in its first sense, they grant the major premise; in its second sense, they deny the major premise; in its second sense, they deny the major premise. The minor premise must be taken in the same way, if it has some truth. To the fourth argument, which seems to have the greater plausibility, they reply that the major premise is erroneous, when it is said: everyone who, after the division of something, has in the portion assigned to him more than he had before the division, has in that assigned portion ownership and proprietorship in the particular sense. For cells, beds, clothes and other things are divided among monks, so that a particular cell, bed, clothing and other item is assigned to each, and each of them has in the thing assigned to him more than before, because he has the lawful power of selling it, which he did not have before; and yet none of them has ownership and proprietorship of it in the particular sense. So it was with the first believers: after the division, each of them had the lawful power of using the portion assigned to him without any further division, a power he did not have before. It is like people arriving at some city who, after being received charitably into different lodgings, each has something more in the lodging freely granted to him than before, because he has the lawful power of staying in it without any further grant, which he did not have before the grant; and yet he has no ownership or proprietorship in the lodging, either in the particular or in the common sense.

units.la: Ad auctoritates, quibus postea probat, quod Petrus fuit proprietarius & dominus caligarum & vestimentorum: Respondent, quod illa non erant Petro quo ad dominium & proprietatem saltem in speciali, sed quo ad vsum. Et de hoc magis patebit super litera. Cum vero vltimo dicit ille impugnatus, quod per illa verba, multitudinis credentium &c. non potest probari, quod non poterant postea recipere de istis communibus, & vt propria retinere. Respondent isti impugnatores, quod per illa verba & sequentia, sicut deducitur contra secundam assertionem, potest probari, quod ideo dederunt pretia rerum suarum communicati, ne aliquis quantum supperet eis facultas essent egens inter eos. Et ideo ne aliquis eorum extra communitatem daret vel venderet aliquam portionem, ac etiam daret alteri intra communitatem, & ita vnus multum abundaret, & alter egeret: ordinauerunt, quod portiones illae assignarentur ad eorum indigentias releuandas, & non ad dominium vel proprietatem in speciali. Et quod hoc fuerit eorum intentio, ex textu & expositionibus sanctorum, vt dicunt isti, constat aperte.
units.tr: As to the authorities by which he afterwards proves that Peter was the owner and proprietor of the sandals and garments, they reply that these things belonged to Peter not as to ownership and proprietorship, at least in the particular sense, but as to use. This will become clearer on the passage itself. As for the last point, where that opponent says that from the words of the multitude of believers, etc., it cannot be proved that they could not afterwards take from these common goods and keep them as their own, these opponents reply that from those words and what follows, as is drawn out against the second assertion, it can be proved that they gave the prices of their goods in common so that none among them, however much his means abounded, would be needy among them. Therefore, lest any of them should give or sell a portion outside the community, or also give it to another within the community, and so one should have much in abundance while another was in need, they ordained that those portions should be assigned to relieve their needs, and not for ownership or proprietorship in the particular sense. And that this was their intention, as they say, is plainly evident from the text and from the explanations of the saints.

units.la: His visis aliqua circa literam sunt notanda (Videtur etiam) quamuis hoc non videatur asserere illa quae sequuntur: omnia tamen postea diffinitiue & assertiue determinant. (Proprietarius & Dominus). Ex his verbis isti impugnatores elicuunt duas primas assertiones principales, quas asserunt esse erroneas. (egens) Id est, mendicus, quod veritatem habuit pro aliquo tempore, quis forte non pro omni tempore sequenti. Sed ex hoc non potest concludi, quod aliquis eorum erat proprietarius, sicut saepe monachi, servi filiifamilias, & alii multi non sunt egentes, id est, mendici, sed quo ad vsum abundant, & tamen non sunt proprietarii. (Afferebant pretia eorum quae vendebant) Hic notant quod possessiones nunquam fuerunt communes tantummodo pretia facta fuerunt communia. (Dividebant) Hoc est assignabant, sicut inter monachos cuilibet assignatur portio sua. Inter quos etiam saepe res immobiles & aliae non consumptibiles vsu dividuntur: (prout cuiq; opus erat) Ex hoc colligitur, quod nulli fuit aliqua portio assignata ad dividendum vel vendendum aut legandum, sed tantummodo ad suam indigentiam subleuandam, & ad se sustentandum. Et ita nulli fuit aliqua portio assignata, vt esset eius quo ad dominium seu proprietatem in speciali. (Supponit aperte quod illud quod vnicuique dabatur divisim cuiuslibet erat proprium) Hoc negant, imo dicunt, quod eo quod dicitur prout vnicuique opus erat, supponit, quod non dabatur nisi ad releuandum indigentiam cuiuslibet: quod verum est, considerata serie tota textus ibidem. (Dividere enim est divisim &c.) Dicunt quod dividere, vt accipitur in Actibus Apostolorum, vbi de praedicta divisione fit mentio, est dare, accipiendo dare pro verbo mandendi vel assignandi ad vsum, non accipiendo dare pro facere rem esse accipientis, quo ad dominium seu proprietatem in speciali. (Cum ergo daretur ab illis qui dare poterant, scilicet Apostolis) Ex his verbis isti impugnatores imponunt impugnato nouum errorem. Quia cum in toto isto processu accipit dare pro transferre dominium ab vno in alium, sequitur quod Apostoli dando illa bona singulis dominium illorum a se in alios transtulerunt. Et ita secundum ipsum ista bona prius erant Apostolorum quantum ad dominium & proprietatem in speciali, sicut post divisionem facta sunt singulorum quo ad proprietatem seu dominium in speciali. Et ex isto errore, vt dicunt, sequitur aliud errorem, scilicet quod illa bona diuisa nunquam fuerunt communia credentibus: quia si ante divisionem fuerunt propria Apostolorum, ex quo Apostoli poterant dare illa bona: & post divisionem suerunt propria singulorum, nunquam fuerunt communia credentibus, quamuis posset dicere, quod fuerunt communia collegio Apostolorum, & illis qui recipere poterant quo ad vsum, sed non quo ad dominium seu proprietatem in speciali. (sustentationem) tantummodo non ad vendendum nec dandum. (Videtur quod quilibet fuerit Dominus &c.) male infert, sed deberet inferre, quod quilibet habuerit potestatem vtendi portione sibi assignata, qualem ante divisionem non habuit. (Alias non videretur verum, quod dicitur, quod egentes non essent) Illa ratio est ad oppositum. Ideo enim illa erant divisa inter eos quo ad dividendi potestatem portionibus sibi assignatis, non quo ad dominium seu proprietatem in speciali, ne essent egentes.
units.tr: Having considered these things, some points must be noted about the text. (Videtur etiam) Although this does not seem to assert what follows, nevertheless they afterwards determine all these things definitively and assertively. (Proprietarius & Dominus) From these words those opponents draw the first two principal assertions, which they affirm to be erroneous. (egens) That is, a beggar, which was true for some time, though perhaps not for every later time. But from this it cannot be concluded that any of them was an owner, just as monks, sons under the authority of a father, and many others are often not needy, that is, beggars, but abound in use, and yet are not owners. (Afferebant pretia eorum quae vendebant) Here they note that the possessions were never held in common, only the prices were made common. (Dividebant) That is, they assigned, as among monks each is assigned his own portion. Among whom also immovable and other non-consumable things are often divided for use. (prout cuiq; opus erat) From this it is gathered that no portion was assigned to anyone to divide, sell or bequeath, but only to relieve his need and to sustain himself. And so no portion was assigned to anyone so that it would be his as to ownership or proprietorship in the particular sense. (Supponit aperte quod illud quod vnicuique dabatur divisim cuiuslibet erat proprium) This they deny; indeed they say that from the words as each had need it is supposed that nothing was given except to relieve each one's need, which is true, when the whole sequence of the text there is considered. (Dividere enim est divisim &c.) They say that divide, as it is used in the Acts of the Apostles, where mention is made of the aforesaid division, means to give, taking give for the verb of committing or assigning for use, not taking give as making a thing belong to the recipient as to ownership or proprietorship in the particular sense. (Cum ergo daretur ab illis qui dare poterant, scilicet Apostolis) From these words those opponents attribute a new error to the one they oppose. For since in this whole argument he takes give to mean transferring ownership from one to another, it follows that the Apostles, by giving those goods to individuals, transferred their ownership from themselves to others. And so, according to him, those goods were previously the Apostles' as to ownership and proprietorship in the particular sense, just as after the division they became each person's as to proprietorship or ownership in the particular sense. And from this error, as they say, another error follows, namely that those divided goods were never held in common by the believers: for if before the division they were the Apostles' own, since the Apostles could give those goods, and after the division they were each person's own, they were never common to the believers, although one could say that they were common to the college of Apostles and to those who could receive them as to use, but not as to ownership or proprietorship in the particular sense. (sustentationem) only, not for selling or giving. (Videtur quod quilibet fuerit Dominus &c.) He draws the inference wrongly; he ought to have inferred that each had the power of using the portion assigned to him, a power he did not have before the division. (Alias non videretur verum, quod dicitur, quod egentes non essent) That reasoning is against the opposing view. For those goods were divided among them as to the power of dividing the portions assigned to them, not as to ownership or proprietorship in the particular sense, so that they would not be needy.

units.la: Quia facilius possunt aliqui fieri egentes, quando aliqua bona diuiduntur inter eos quo ad proprietatem in speciali, vt libere possint ea vendere & donare, quam quando diuiduntur inter eos ad vsum sine potestate vendendi & dandi. Qui enim aliquam portionem recipit quo ad dominium seu proprietatem in speciali, statim potest rem dare & reddere se egentem. Non sic ille, qui portionem suam recipit tantum modo ad vtendum. Et ideo ne essent egentes, ordinatum fuit inter credentes, ne aliquis posset dare portionem suam: sicut nunc inter monachos ordinatum est, ne aliquis vendat vel det absque licentia superioris rem aliquam. Et propter hoc conseruantur, ne sint egentes. Nam monachi & alii religiosi possent dare & vendere portiones suas, saepe efficerentur egentes, qui nunc abundant. Sed forte videbitur alicui, quod secundum istos impugnatores primi credentes habuerunt in portionibus sibi assignatis simplicem vsum facti. Ex quo dicunt, quod dictae portiones non erant eis assignatae, nisi ad vtendum tantum modo. Ad hoc dicunt, quod illi credentes non habuerunt tantum simplicem vsum facti: quia licet per diuisionem non erant portiones assignatae, nisi ad vtendum: tamen ante illam diuisionem habuerunt in eis ius quoddam commune, per diuisionem minime perdiderunt. Et ita semper vltra vsum facti ius aliquod habuerunt. (nisi pauci diuisionem plus haberent.) Illud est verum. Sed illud plus non est dominium seu proprietas in speciali, est licita potestas vtendi, quam habuerunt per diuisionem: quemadmodum monachus habet licitam potestatem dormiendi in camera aliqua, antequam sibi per superiorem fuerit assignata. (Praeterea constat quod vestimenta quotidiana &c.) ex hoc notant isti impugnatores, quod secundum impugnatum nullus potest vti vestibus quibuscunque; absque dominio & proprietate, ex quo dicit vestes inter res vsu consumptibiles computandas: & secundum ipsum nullus potest vti rebus vsu consumptibilibus absque dominio & proprietate. (Caligas tuas) Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod ille impugnat per multiplicitatem & aequiuocationem talium vocabulorum meum, tuum, eius, ipsius, huiusmodi conatur simplices in errores inducere, quod credent Apostolos habuisse dominium & proprietatem in speciali, & quod Christus habuit dominium in speciali & alios plures errores per multiplicitatem talium vocabulorum satagit palliare, & puritatem corrumpere fidei orthodoxae. Et ideo dicunt, quod talia vocabula meum, tuum, suum, nostrum, vestrum, eius, ipsius, habere, & huiusmodi in scripturis, variis modis & aequuoce accipiuntur. Aliquando enim denotant dominium & proprietatem in speciali: sicut accipitur in Actibus, cum dicitur: nec quisquam eorum quae possidebat aliquid suum esse dicebat &c. Et etiam Genes. 14. dixit Abraham ad regem Sodomorum: Non accipiam ex omnibus quae tua sunt. Aliquando important curam & custodiam. Et sic dicitur Iohan. 19. de Beato Iohanne: Accepit eam (scilicet virginem Mariam) in suam: quae tamen non fuit sua quo ad dominium seu proprietatem. Sic etiam dicit saepe vulgariter famulus de equo Domini sui: Ille est equus meus, quia sibi est ad custodiam deputatus. Aliquando important vsum facti & licitam potestatem vtendi: sicut peregrini & alii saepe dicunt se habere hospitium. Et vnus dicit, hic est hospitium meum: alius, hic est hospitium meum: quorum tamen non habent dominium & proprietatem, sed licitam potestatem vtendi, scilicet in habitandi. Sicut dicitur primo Maccabeorum 12. ca. vbi habetur quod Spartiatae scripserunt Iudaeis in haec verba: Pecora nostra & possessiones nostrae vestrae sunt: & vestra nostra. Quod non debet intelligi quo ad dominium & proprietatem, sed quo ad licitam potestatem vtendi, & in tempore necessitatis. Sic etiam in Regula Fratrum Minorum, quod habeant duas tunicas, vnam cum caputio & aliam sine caputio, quae voluerint habere, scilicet ad vsum, non quo ad proprietatem. Aliquando important locum originis. Sicut Luc. 4. Nemo Propheta acceptus est in patria sua. Aliquando consuetudinem habitandi, iuxta illud Matth. 9. Venit in ciuitatem suam: quae non erat sua quo ad dominium & proprietatem, sed quia ibi consueuerat habitare. Aliquando important sanguinis propinquitatem: sicut ille est pater meus: Ille est filius tuus. Aliquando important totum vel partem; sicut, ille habet manus suas. Aliquando important praelationem aut dominationem: sicut, Ille est Episcopus meus: Ille est Archidiaconus eius: Ille est rex tuus. Multis aliis modis accipiuntur huiusmodi vocabula. Et ideo dicunt, quod cum dixit Angelus Petro: calciate caligas tuas: illae caligae non erant Petro quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, sed erant suae quo ad licitam potestatem vtendi vel calciandi. Et si quaeras, cuius fuerunt quo ad dominium seu proprietatem? dicunt isti impugnatores, quod postea respondebunt, vbi tractabitur, an Apostoli habuerunt aliquius rei dominium in communi. (Vestimentum tuum) dicunt quod vestimentum erat Petro quo ad licitam potestatem vtendi, non quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, sed in speciali. Vbi clare supponit Angelus quod caligae & vestimentum assignata Petro propriae erant quo ad dominium Petri. Hic primo notant isti impugnatores, quod quicquid prius videbatur dixisse subsibio, hic asserit manifeste. Secundo dicunt quod angelus hic non supponit, quod caligae & vestimenta erant propriae Petro: sed supponit, quod ipse habuit potestatem vtendi eis. (Quare videtur quod pecunia) quod hic specialiter dicit Petrum habuisse pecuniam quo ad proprietatem & dominium in speciali, inferius tractabitur. (Nec votum vtendi sine proprio) In hoc isti impugnato Thomas contradicit expresse in libro suo contra doctrinam detrahentium, vbi dicit: Ea quibus vtuntur religiosi ad sustentationem vitae non sunt eorum quantum ad proprietatem dominii. Sed dispensantur ad vsum necessitatis ipsorum ab his, qui horum dominium habent quicunque sint illi. Haec ille. Vbi de Fratribus Minoribus loqui videtur: quia respondet ad obiectionem illorum, quidicebant esse impossibile, quod aliquis nihil in communi vel proprio possideat: quia necesse est quod comedant & bibant & induantur, quod facere non possunt, si nihil haberent. Ad quam obiectionem per verba superius recitata respondet. Ex quibus, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, clare patet, quod
units.tr: Some people can more easily be made needy when goods are divided among them as their own property, so that they may freely sell and give them away, than when they are divided among them for use only, without the power to sell or give. For a man who receives a portion as his own property can at once give the thing away and make himself needy. It is not so with one who receives his portion only for use. Therefore, so that they might not become needy, it was ordained among the believers that no one could give away his portion, just as now among monks it is ordained that no one may sell or give anything without the leave of a superior. For this reason they are kept from becoming needy. For monks and other religious, if they could give away and sell their portions, would often become needy, as some now abound. But perhaps someone will think that, according to these opponents, the first believers had in their assigned portions only the simple use of the fact. From this they say that those portions were assigned to them only for use. To this they reply that those believers did not have merely the simple use of the fact. For although the portions were assigned by the division only for use, nevertheless before that division they had in them a certain common right, which they did not lose by the division at all. And so they always had some right beyond the use of the fact. (Except that a few had more through the division.) That is true. But that "more" is not dominion or property in particular. It is the lawful power of using, which they had through the division, just as a monk has the lawful power of sleeping in some room before it is assigned to him by the superior. (Moreover it is clear that daily garments etc.) From this these opponents note that, according to the one attacked, no one can use any clothes without dominion and property, since he says clothes are to be counted among things consumed by use; and according to him no one can use things consumed by use without dominion and property. (Your sandals.) These opponents say that the one attacked, through the multiplicity and equivocation of such words as mine, yours, his, its, of this kind, tries to lead simple people into errors: that they will believe the Apostles had dominion and property in particular, and that Christ had dominion in particular; and he labours to disguise many other errors through the multiplicity of such words and to corrupt the purity of the orthodox faith. And so they say that such words as mine, yours, his, ours, yours, its, to have, and the like, are taken in Scripture in various ways and equivocally. For sometimes they denote dominion and property in particular, as is taken in Acts, when it is said: nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own, etc. And in Genesis 14 Abraham said to the king of Sodom: I will not take anything from all that is yours. Sometimes they signify care and custody. So it is said in John 19 of the blessed John: He took her (namely the Virgin Mary) into his keeping, which nevertheless was not his as regards dominion or property. So too a servant often says in common speech of his lord's horse: That is my horse, because it has been assigned to him for its keeping. Sometimes they signify the use of the fact and the lawful power of using, as travellers and others often say that they have a lodging. One says, this is my lodging; another, this is my lodging. Yet they have no dominion or property in it, only the lawful power of using it, namely for dwelling. As it is said in 1 Maccabees chapter 12, where it is recorded that the Spartans wrote to the Jews in these words: Our flocks and our possessions are yours, and yours are ours. This must not be understood as regards dominion and property, but as regards the lawful power of using, and in time of need. So too in the Rule of the Friars Minor, that they may have two tunics, one with a hood and another without a hood, which they wish to have, namely for use, not as property. Sometimes they signify the place of origin, as in Luke 4: No prophet is accepted in his own country. Sometimes they signify the custom of dwelling, according to Matthew 9: He came into his own city, which was not his as regards dominion and property, but because he had been accustomed to live there. Sometimes they signify blood kinship: that man is my father; that one is your son. Sometimes they signify a whole or a part: he has his hands. Sometimes they signify precedence or lordship: that is my bishop; that is his archdeacon; that is your king. These words are taken in many other ways. And so they say that when the angel said to Peter: gird on your sandals, those sandals were not Peter's as regards dominion or property, but were his as regards the lawful power of using or putting them on. And if you ask whose they were as regards dominion or property, these opponents say that they will answer afterwards, where it will be treated whether the Apostles had dominion of any thing in common. (Your garment.) They say that the garment was Peter's as regards the lawful power of using, not as regards dominion or property in particular. Here the angel clearly presupposes that the sandals and garment assigned to Peter were Peter's own as regards dominion. Here these opponents first note that whatever Thomas seemed earlier to have said in passing, here he asserts plainly. Secondly they say that the angel here does not presuppose that the sandals and garments were Peter's own, but presupposes only that he had the power of using them. (Why it seems that money…) That he here specifically says Peter had money as regards property and dominion in particular will be treated below. (Nor a vow of using without one's own.) Thomas expressly contradicts this opponent in his book against the doctrine of detractors, where he says: The things which religious use for the sustenance of life are not theirs as regards ownership of property. But they are dispensed for the use of their necessity by those who have the dominion of these, whoever they are. Thus he. Here he seems to be speaking of the Friars Minor, because he is answering the objection of those who said it was impossible for anyone to possess nothing either in common or as his own, since it is necessary to eat, drink and clothe oneself, which they cannot do if they have nothing. To this objection he replies in the words recited above. From these, as these opponents say, it is clearly evident that

units.la: Sss 3 (signature) quod secundum Thomam in rebus vsu consumptibilibus vsus potest à proprietate & dominio separari. (Praeterea ex illo capitulo Act. 4. non potest probari quin credentes &c.) Hoc negant isti, sicut superius est deductum. (Scriptura enim praedicta aliquid ad hoc nihil aliud dixit nisi quod sequitur; multitudinis credentium &c.) Dicunt hoc esse falsum: quia praeter verba hic recitata, Scriptura praedicta dicit: Neque enim quisquam eorum egens erat inter illos. Ex quibus verbis & verbis hic recitatis concluditur, quod divisio illa fuit tantummodo ad sustentandum omnes: & non quod aliquis haberet potestatem dandi vel vendendi portionem suam. Et ita nullus eorum habuit proprietatem portionis suae in speciali. Ad cuius evidentiam dicunt isti impugnatores, quod ex duabus causis credentes in primitiva Ecclesia voluerunt omnia esse communia, & nihil habere proprium in speciali, nec ante divisionem: nec post, scilicet ex perfectionis amore, & ut nullus esset egens inter eos. Et ex utraque causa sequitur quod nullus eorum habuit proprietatem in speciali portionis suae post divisionem. Si enim habuissent proprietatem in speciali portionis suae ad perfectionem religiosorum posterioris temporis, qui nullius rei proprietatem habuerunt in speciali, minime pervenissent: cum tamen sancti dicant, eos fuisse perfectiores. Unde & ex perfectionis amore dicunt eos omnes possessiones in communi reliquisse. Et ita ex perfectionis amore, qui vigebat in eis, apparet quod nullius rei proprietatem in speciali post divisionem habuerunt. Ex secunda causa, quare omnia voluerunt esse communia, patet idem: quia aliter forte cito fuissent aliqui egentes inter ipsos. (Non autem videntur se astrinxisse &c.) Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod se astrinxerunt, ne perfectionem priorem dimitterent: & ne aliquis esset egens inter ipsos. (Imo hoc scriptura praedicta sacra supponit aperte.) Hic asserit manifeste, ut isti dicunt, quod prius videbatur absque assertione proferre. (Dividere autem est sicut praedictum est aliquam rei divisae partes aliquibus dare) Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod hoc est verum accipiendo verbum dandi pro verbo tradendi seu assignandi vel deputandi. Et sic nihil facit ad propositum istius: quia dare non est facere rem esse accipientis quo ad dominium seu proprietatem.
units.tr: Sss 3 (signature) that, according to Thomas, in things consumed by use, use can be separated from property and dominion. (Moreover, it cannot be proved from that chapter, Acts 4, that the believers etc.) These opponents deny this, as has been deduced above. (For the aforesaid Scripture said nothing else to this effect except what follows: the multitude of believers etc.) They say this is false, for besides the words recited here, the aforesaid Scripture says: "Nor was any of them needy among them." From these words and the words recited here it is concluded that that division was made only to sustain everyone, and not so that anyone would have the power of giving or selling his portion. And so none of them had property in his portion in particular. To make this evident, these opponents say that for two reasons the believers in the primitive Church wished all things to be common and to have nothing as their own in particular, neither before the division nor after it: namely from love of perfection, and so that no one would be needy among them. And from each reason it follows that none of them had property in his portion in particular after the division. For if they had property in particular in their portions, they would never have attained the perfection of the religious of later times, who had property in nothing in particular; yet the saints say that they were more perfect. Hence, also from love of perfection, they say that they all left their possessions in common. And so, from the love of perfection which flourished among them, it appears that after the division they had property in nothing in particular. From the second reason why they wished all things to be common, the same appears, because otherwise some of them might quickly have become needy. (But they do not seem to have bound themselves etc.) These opponents say that they bound themselves so that they would not give up their earlier perfection, and so that no one would be needy among them. (Indeed the aforesaid sacred Scripture plainly presupposes this.) Here he asserts plainly, as these opponents say, what before seemed to be put forward without assertion. (To divide, however, as has been said, is to give some parts of a divided thing to some persons.) These opponents say that this is true if the word "give" is taken to mean "hand over," "assign" or "appoint." And so it does nothing for his proposition, for to give is not to make a thing belong to the recipient as regards dominion or property.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: ITem, ad probandum, quod asserere, quomodo in rebus, quae vsu consumuntur, non possit haberi vsus à dominio separatus, obuiet scriptura sacra: adducit illud, quod Petrus Domino dixit Matth. 19. Ecce nos reliquimus omnia & secuti sumus te. Quod secundum eum non potest intelligi, quod Apostoli reliquerunt omnia quantum ad vsum: quia constat ex scriptura sacra, quod postea rebus vsu consumptibilibus vtebantur. Igitur reliquerunt omnia tam consumptibilia quam non consumptibilia vsu quantum ad dominium & proprietatem, vt probatur, sicut ipse dicit 12. q. 1. c. dilectissimis. Quia qui dicit omnia, nihil excipit. Et sanctus Gregorius super illo relictis rebus, dicit, quod multum reliquit, qui nihil sibi retinuit: qui quantumlibet parum, totum deserit. Ergo dicere quod vsus rerum consumptibilium non potest separari à proprietate & dominio, sacra scriptura obviat & repugnat. Et confirmat hoc, sicut dicit, quod Apostoli abdicationem omnium rerum voluerunt secundum Augustinum 17. de ciuitate Dei. Ad quorum exemplar religiosi, qui figuram Apostolorum tenent, vt dicitur 19. q. 1. c. Ex auctoritate, volunt abdicationem omnium rerum vsu consumptibilium, non tamen quantum ad vsum. Quare sequitur secundum eum, quod Apostoli voluerunt, & religiosi volunt abdicationem dominii & proprietatis omnium rerum vsu consumptibilium & non consumptibilium vsu. Haec dicta eius.
units.tr: Likewise, to prove that in things which are consumed by use, the use cannot be had separate from ownership, he brings forward Holy Scripture. He cites what Peter said to the Lord in Matthew 19: "Behold, we have left all and followed you." According to him, this cannot be understood to mean that the Apostles left everything as regards use, because Scripture plainly shows that they afterwards used consumable goods. Therefore they left all things, both consumable and non-consumable, as regards ownership and property, as he proves, just as he says in 12 q. 1, c. Dilectissimis. For whoever says "all" excludes nothing. And St. Gregory, commenting on the words "they left their things," says that he has left much who has kept nothing for himself, and that he who gives up even the smallest part gives up the whole. Therefore, to say that the use of consumable goods cannot be separated from property and ownership is contrary to, and opposed by, Holy Scripture. He confirms this by saying that the Apostles wished for the renunciation of all things, according to Augustine, De Civitate Dei, book 17. The religious, who hold the figure of the Apostles, as is said in 19 q. 1, c. Ex auctoritate, follow their example and wish to renounce all consumable goods, but not as regards use. Hence it follows, according to him, that the Apostles wished, and religious men now wish, the renunciation of ownership and property of all consumable and non-consumable goods as regards use. These are his words.

units.la: POstquam in parte praecedenti ille impugnatus respondit ad primam obiectionem appellantis: Hic ad secundam respondet. Et diuiditur in duas partes: quia primo obiectionem recitat appellantis: Secundo respondet ad ipsam in parte immediate sequenti. Est autem obiectio talis. Apostoli diuiserunt proprietatem omnium rerum consumptibilium vsu & non consumptibilium vsu: & diuiserunt vsum facti rerum consumptibilium vsu. Igitur vsus facti in rebus huiusmodi potest à proprietate & dominio separari. Confirmatur: quia Apostoli voluerunt & religiosi volunt abdicationem omnium temporalium: sed non volunt abdicationem vsus facti in rebus vsu consumptibilibus. Ergo voluerunt Apostoli & volunt religiosi abdicationem dominii huiusmodi rerum.
units.tr: After the accused party in the preceding part answered the first objection of the appellant, here he answers the second. This section is divided into two parts: first he recites the objection of the appellant, and second he answers it in the part immediately following. The objection is as follows. The Apostles divided the property of all consumable and non-consumable goods, and they divided the actual use of consumable goods. Therefore the actual use of such goods can be separated from property and ownership. It is confirmed thus: the Apostles wished, and the religious now wish, the renunciation of all temporal goods, but they do not wish the renunciation of the actual use of consumable goods. Therefore the Apostles wished, and the religious now wish, the renunciation of the ownership of such goods.

units.la: Ad euidentiam istius obiectionis dicunt isti impugnatores, esse sciendum, quod licet illa obiectio primo & directe ex forma verborum probet, quod vsus facti potest separari à proprietate & dominio in speciali: tamen secundario suppositis quibusdam veritatibus, quae licite negari non possunt, probat quod vsus facti potest separari ab omni dominio in speciali & in communi, quo valeat aliquis pro re vel vsu rei in iudicio litigare. Confirmatio autem non probat tantum, nisi per consequentiam: sicut aliqualiter patet ex praecedentibus, & magis ex sequentibus apparebit.
units.tr: To make this objection clear, these opponents say that it must be understood that, although the objection proves first and directly, from the form of the words, that the actual use can be separated from property and ownership in a particular sense, yet secondarily, given certain truths which cannot lawfully be denied, it proves that the actual use can be separated from every ownership, both particular and general, so that someone could go to law over a thing or over the use of a thing. The confirmation, however, proves this only by inference, as is somewhat clear from what has gone before and will become clearer from what follows.

units.la: Sed accedamus ad textum (Ecce nos reliquimus omnia) debet intelligi quod reliquerunt omne dominium rerum temporalium, quod esset proprium cuicunque Apostolo vel toti collegio Apostolorum, quantum ad dominium & proprietatem, qua valerent in iudicio litigare. (Voluerunt) hoc licet in scripturis diuinis vocaliter non legatur, tamen ex scripturis & expositionibus sanctorum colligitur, vt dicunt isti. (Figuram Apostolorum tenent) non tamen omnes secundum omnem gradum perfectionis Apostolos imitantur: sed in aliquo gradu imitantur, & in aliquo deficiunt. (Volunt abdicationem temporalium, quantum ad omnem proprietatem in speciali: & quantum ad omnem proprietatem etiam in communi: Habent tamen vnam proprietatem, quae est potestas de re libere disponendi. Talem enim proprietatem in nulla re temporali habent monachi neque in speciali, neque in communi. Habent tamen vnam proprietatem in communi communiter dictam, qua possunt rem nomine communitatis suae specialis vendicare in iudicio, & etiam defensare. Sed Apostoli etiam talem proprietatem in quacunque re temporali minime habuerunt.
units.tr: But let us come to the text ("Behold, we have left all"). It must be understood that they left every ownership of temporal goods which might belong to any Apostle, or to the whole college of Apostles, as regards ownership and property, by which they might be able to litigate in court. ("They wished") this, although it is not read in so many words in the divine Scriptures, is nevertheless gathered from the Scriptures and the expositions of the saints, as these men say. ("They hold the figure of the Apostles") yet they do not imitate the Apostles in every degree of perfection, but imitate them in some degree and fall short in another. ("They wish the renunciation of temporal goods, as regards every particular property, and as regards every property even in common.") They nevertheless have one property, which is the power of freely disposing of a thing. Monks have no such property in any temporal thing, either particular or common. Yet they have one property in common, commonly so called, by which they can claim in court, and even defend, a thing in the name of their particular community. But the Apostles never had such a property in any temporal thing whatsoever.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Ad hoc dicendum, quod per verba illa: Ecce nos reliquimus &c. non potest concludi, quod quo ad dominium seu proprietatem reliquerint ea. Reperimus enim haec verba dicta de Petro, Iacobo, & Iohanne Luc. 5. vbi dicitur, quod subductis ad terram navibus, relictis omnibus secuti sunt eum. Et tamen post verba illa legitur Matth. 4. quod Iesus ambulans iuxta mare Galilaeae vidit Petrum & Andream mittentes retia in mare, quibus ait: venite post me, faciam vos fieri piscatores hominum. Qui continuo relictis retibus secuti sunt eum. Et quod illud, quod dictum est Luc. 5. praecesserit illud quod dictum est Matth. 4. dicit Augustinus in libro de concordia Euangelistarum expresse. Item post illud, quod legitur Matth. 8. habetur Matth. 8. quod venit Iesus in domum Petri. Ergo domus adhuc remanserat Petri. Item Matth. 26. legitur quod, vnus ex his qui erant cum Iesu (videlicet Petrus, vt dicitur Iohan. 18.) exemit gladium & percutiens seruum pontificis amputauit auriculam eius. Cui Iesus ait: Conuerte gladium tuum in locum suum. Ergo gladius erat Petri. Item Luc. 22. dictum est Petro & alio Apostolo: qui habet sacculum, tollat similiter & peram: & qui non habet (scilicet gladium) vendat tunicam suam & emat gladium. Item Actor. 12. dixit Angelus Petro: praecingere & calcia te caligas tuas. Item dixit ei: circunda tibi vestimentum tuum & sequere me. In quibus sacra scriptura evidenter supponit, quod post illa verba posita Luca 5. de Petro & Iacobo & Iohanne: Relictis omnibus secuti sunt eum, scripturae sacrae praedicta supponunt eum habuisse & retia & domum. Et post illa verba Petri: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, etiam notatur gladium & vestes habuisse, vt sua. Quare relinquitur, quod per verba illa; Relictis omnibus secuti sunt eum, non potest concludi Apostolos a se dominium omnium temporalium abdicasse. Item de Matthaeo legitur Luc. 5. quod cum Iesus dixisset Matthaeo, sequere me: quod ipse surgens relictis omnibus secutus est eum. Erstatim sequitur, quod Matthaeus, qui & Levi dicebatur, fecit ei magnum conuiuium in domo sua. Vnde patet, quod quantumcunque de eo dicat scriptura, quod relictis omnibus secutus est eum, non sequitur quod, quo ad Dominium reliquerit ea, eum statim subdatur, quod in domo sua fecerit sibi conuiuium magnum.
units.tr: To this I answer that the words, "Behold, we have left all, etc.," cannot prove that they gave up ownership or property in those things. For we find these words said of Peter, James, and John in Luke 5, where it is said that, when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him. Yet after those words we read in Matthew 4 that Jesus, walking by the Sea of Galilee, saw Peter and Andrew casting their nets into the sea, and said to them, "Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men." And they immediately left their nets and followed him. Augustine expressly states, in his book on the harmony of the Evangelists, that what is said in Luke 5 came before what is said in Matthew 4. Again, after what is read in Matthew 8, we find in Matthew 8 that Jesus came into Peter's house. So Peter's house still remained his. Again, Matthew 26 reads that one of those who were with Jesus (namely Peter, as John 18 says) drew a sword and, striking the servant of the high priest, cut off his ear. Jesus said to him, "Put your sword back into its place." So the sword was Peter's. Again, Luke 22 says to Peter and another Apostle: "He who has a purse, let him take it, and likewise a bag; and he who has no sword, let him sell his coat and buy one." Again, Acts 12 says the angel said to Peter, "Gird yourself and put on your sandals." He also said to him, "Wrap your cloak around you and follow me." In these passages Scripture clearly presupposes that, after the words in Luke 5 about Peter, James, and John, "When they had left everything, they followed him," the same Scriptures suggest that he had both nets and a house. And after Peter's words, "Behold, we have left everything," it is also noted that he had a sword and clothes, as his own. Therefore it follows that by the words, "When they had left everything, they followed him," it cannot be concluded that the Apostles renounced the ownership of all temporal things. Again, of Matthew it is read in Luke 5 that when Jesus had said to Matthew, "Follow me," he rose and, leaving everything, followed him. Immediately after, it follows that Matthew, who was also called Levi, made him a great feast in his own house. Hence it is plain that, however much Scripture says of him that he left everything and followed him, it does not follow that, as to ownership, he gave those things up, since he at once is shown to have held a great feast in his own house.

units.la: In ista parte ille impugnatus ad praedicam obiectionem respondet. Et diuiditur in quinque partes. In prima respondet ad auctoritatem illam: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia &c. In secunda ad capitulum Clementis 12. q. 1. dilectissimi. Tertio ad illud quod dicitur Apostolos post illa verba: Ecce nos &c. habuisse vsum rerum vsu consumptibilium. Quarto ad illud, quod tangitur de voto Apostolorum. Quinto ad illud, quod adducitur de monachis tenentibus figuram Apostolorum. Secunda pars incipit ibi: Item non obstat. Tertio ibi: Item in eodem quod dicit quod Apostolu. Quarta ibi: in eo quod dicit. Quinta ibi: Item non obstat c. illud 18. q. 1. Prima diuiditur in tres. Primo enim ad illam auctoritatem respondet, ostendens quod non debet intelligi, quod Apostoli reliquerunt omnia quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Secundo declarat, quod est alius modus relinquendi ibi & propter hoc. Tertio redit ad ostendendum propositum principale ibi: de Iacobo autem. In prima igitur parte dicit, quod per illa verba Petri: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, non potest ostendi, quod reliquerint omnia quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Nam post consimilia verba dicta de Petro, Iacobo & Iohanne legitur aliqua habuisse quo ad dominium & proprietatem, scil. tam mobilia quam immobilia. Sed post verba praedicta Petri legitur Petrus aliqua habuisse quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Ac post verba de beato Matthaeo ipse legitur aliqua habuisse. Et per talia verba: Nos reliquimus omnia &c. & aequipollenter non potest concludi, quod omnia reliquerint quo ad dominium seu proprietatem. Et ad hoc probandum septem auctoritates scripturae adducit.
units.tr: In this part, the man attacked answers the aforesaid objection. The answer is divided into five parts. In the first he answers that authority, "Behold, we have left all, etc." In the second, he answers the chapter of Clement, 12 q. 1, "Dilectissimi." Third, he answers what is said, that after those words, "Behold, we, etc.," the Apostles had the use of things consumable by use. Fourth, he answers what is touched on concerning the vow of the Apostles. Fifth, he answers what is adduced concerning the monks who hold the figure of the Apostles. The second part begins there: "Likewise, it is no objection." The third there: "Likewise, in the same place, where it says that the Apostles." The fourth there: "In that which it says." The fifth there: "Likewise, it is no objection, the chapter 'Illud,' 18 q. 1." The first part is divided into three. For first he answers that authority, showing that it must not be understood to mean that the Apostles left everything as to ownership and property. Second, he explains that there is another way of leaving, there and on account of this. Third, he returns to show the principal proposition, there: "But as for James." In the first part, then, he says that by the words of Peter, "Behold, we have left everything," it cannot be shown that they left everything as to ownership and property. For after similar words spoken of Peter, James, and John, we read that they had some things as to ownership and property, both movable and immovable. But after the aforesaid words of Peter, we read that Peter had some things as to ownership and property. And after the words about the blessed Matthew, he is likewise read to have had some things. And by such words as "We have left everything, etc.," and words of equivalent force, it cannot be concluded that they gave up everything as to ownership or property. To prove this he adduces seven passages of Scripture.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores illa reprobare conantur. Procedunt autem sic. Primo eius assertionem impugnant: Secundo ad auctoritates, quas ille allegat pro se respondent. Ad euidentiam primi dicunt esse sciendum, quod sicut teste Clemente, vt habetur distinct. 27. c. Relatum, multa verba sunt in scripturis diuinis, quae possunt trahi ad eum sensum, quem sibi sponte vnusquisque praesumpserit: sed non oportet. Ita verba beati Petri, cum dixit Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, nude accepta, & non vt relata ad antecedentia & consequentia & alia loca scripturae diuinae, posset quis ad eum sensum trahere, vt aliter quam quo ad dominium & proprietatem dicat beatus Petrus se & alios Apostolos omnia reliquisse. Sed non debemus talem sensum contra veritatem scripturarum accipere: sed ex ipsis scripturis sensum oportet capere veritatis. Et ideo ex sacrarum serie scripturarum conantur ostendere, quod cum beatus Petrus dixit: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia: intellexit de modo relinquendi omnia quo ad dominium seu proprietatem. Et hoc tam in speciali quam in generali quo ad communitatem ipsorum Apostolorum. Et hoc loquendo de dominio seu proprietate, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare, aut etiam auctoritate propria vel suae communitatis rem aliquam dare vel vendere aut locare aut circa rem aliquam contractum exercere: quia de tali dominio loquitur ille impugnatus. Primo autem probant isti impugnatores, quod Apostoli reliquerunt omnes possessiones quo ad proprietatem seu dominium tam in speciali quam in communi. Secundo probant, quod vniuersaliter omnia reliquerunt quo ad proprietatem seu dominium tam in speciali quam in communi. Primam conclusionem, cuius contrarium dicit ille impugnatus, probant primo sic. Non imperfectionem modum relinquendi possessiones tradidit Christus Apostolis sub praecepto vel consilio, quam consuluit illi adolescenti, occasione cuius dixit beatus Petrus verba praedicta: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia. Sed illi adolescenti praedicto consuluit relinquere omnes possessiones tam in speciali quam in communi, dicens ei: Si vis perfectus esse, vade & vende omnia quae habes & da pauperibus quæ verba secundum omnes de vendendis possessionibus debent intelligi. Quod ex ipso textu colligitur euidenter, vt scribitur: Cum audisset adolescens verba hæc, abiit tristis. Erat enim habens multa possessiones. Vendita autem & data pauperibus nec in speciali nec in communi habentur. Ergo consuluit Christus adolescenti prædicto omnes possessiones relinquere tam in speciali quam in communi. Ergo eundem modum relinquendi omnia indixit Apostolis sub consilio vel præcepto. Constat autem quod Apostoli præcepta Christi & consilia impleuerunt. Ergo Apostoli omnes possessiones in communi & in speciali reliquerunt. Secundo ficarguunt. Primo, Petro dicente: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia: quæ verba secundum omnes debent intelligi de omnibus possessionibus, licet secundum aliquos non debeant intelligi de omnibus mobilibus Quia, sicut dicitur, vestes suas minime reliquerunt. Quærunt isti impugnatores, aut intellexit de modo relinquendi cum intentione redeundi seu reassumendi possessiones relictas? aut cum intentione minime reassumendi & nunquam habendi? Primum non potest dici: quia de eodem modo relinquendi omnia locutus est Petrus, quando dixit: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia. Et Christus, quando dixit ibidem subiungens Omnis qui reliquerit domum vel fratres aut sorores, aut patrem aut matrem, aut uxorem aut filios aut agros propter nomen meum, centuplum accipiet &c. Sed Christus locutus est de modo relinquendi cum intentione minime reassumendi: quia reliquisse domum aut agros cum intentione reassumendi, non est opus magnæ perfectionis. Christus autem ex magno præmio, quod relinquenti domum aut agros promisit, ostenditur de opere magnæ perfectionis locutus fuisse. Igitur loquitur de modo relinquendi cum intentione non assumendi. Ergo de eodem modo relinquendi intellexit verba sua Petrus, cum dixit: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia. Qui autem relinquit aliquas possessiones cum intentione nunquam rehabendi; relinquit eas quantum ad dominium & proprietatem: tum quia frustra sibi proprietatem & dominium retineret: tum quia qui relinquit bona temporalia cum intentione nunquam rehabendi, vel de eisdem recte disponit, scil. vendendo vel dando ac legando: vel ipsa habet pro derelictis. Et sive vno sive alio prædictorum modorum relinquat bona quæcunque, ipse reliquit quo ad dominium & proprietatem: quia vendentes, dantes & legantes post confirmationem testamenti: & similiter habentes bona pro derelictis relinquunt ipsa quantum ad dominium & proprietatem. Relinquitur ergo quod Apostoli omnes possessiones, de quibus nullo contradicente verba Petri prædicta debent intelligi, reliquerunt quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Tertio sic arguunt: paupertas Apostolica non fuit minor nec imperfectior paupertate Religiosorum sequentium ipsos. Hæc ex dictis & probatis cap. tulo nono præcedenti colligitur euidenter. Sed plures sunt Religiosi Mendicantes, nullas possessiones habentes in communi. Ergo multo magis Apostoli non habuerunt possessiones in communi. Et si dicat aliquis, quod nulla est religio habentium quecunque in communi, quin etiam aliqua immobilia habeant in communi: quia habent domos & hortos in communi. Et ita per hanc rationem non probatur, quia Apostoli aliqua immobilia habuerint in communi, licet non amplas possessiones. Sed isti impugnatores dicunt hoc non valere: quia dicunt, quod causa, quare tales religiosi habent aliqua immobilia in communi, est quia simul conuersantur & morantur. Et ideo conueniens est, quod domos & hortos habeant in communi, sicut quædam mobilia habent in communi. Sed Apostoli nequaquam simul manebant, nisi aliquando ad breue tempus aliqui eorum simul morabantur. Et ideo sicut possessiones non habuerunt in communi, ita etiam domibus & hortis caruerunt in communi. Quarto ficarguunt. Paupertas Apostolica paupertati Christi debuit esse conformis. Sed Christus non habuit possessiones etiam in communi, quia habens possessiones etiam in communi habet vbi caput suum reclinet, & vbi moretur. Christus autem non habuit vbi caput suum reclinaret, ipso testante Matth. 8 qui ait: Vulpes foueas habent & volucres cœli nidos: filius autem hominis non habet vbi caput suum reclinet. Ergo etiam Apostoli possessiones & domos quascunque in communi min. me habuerunt. Porro quia illa communio hactenus paucos habuerit contradictores, & multos habuerit defensores: quia omnes Religiosi mendicantes & Doctores eorum, vsque ad tempora istius impugnati, ipsam firmiter tenuerunt, & in scriptis reliquerunt, sicut de Thoma patet in speciali supra capitulo sexto. Ideo secundam conclusionem, scil. quod Apostoli omnia mobilia & immobilia, consumptibilia vsu & non consumptibilia vsu, reliquerunt quantum ad dominium & proprietatem, tam in speciali quam etiam in communi, fortius isti impugnatores probare conantur. Hanc enim multi religiosi mendicantes, & quidam alii consueuerunt impugnare. Sed quod Apostoli reliquerunt omnia tam in speciali quam etiam in communi, isti impugnatores ostendunt, & quia plures summi pontifices hanc assertionem non solum sententialiter sed etiam vocaliter diffinierunt, & firmiter tenuerunt. Ideo illam assertionem primo per sententiam plurimorum pontificum satagunt confirmare, dicentes, sicut allegatum est supra capitulo 9. Nicolaus tertius sententialiter & vocaliter diffiniuit censin hæc verba: Dicimus quod abdicatio proprietatis huiusmodi omnium rerum tam in speciali quam etiam in communi propter Deum, meritoria est & sancta: quam & Christus viam perfectionis ostendens verbo docuit & exemplo firmauit: quamque primi fundatores militantis ecclesiæ prout ab ipso hauserant, in volentes perfectæ viuere per doctrinam ac vitam ipsorum aluerunt. Ex his verbis quatuor colliguntur aperte. Primum est, quod abdicatio proprietatum omnium rerum tam in speciali quam etiam in communi spectat ad perfectionem. Secundum est quod Apostoli hanc abdicationem ab ipso Christo acceperunt & dicerunt. Tertium est quod Apostoli hanc abdicationem in se seruauerunt. Quartum est quod Apostoli hanc abdicationem aliis seruandam exemplo & doctrina tradiderunt. Et ita clarius dici non posset, quod Apostoli omnia reliquerunt quo ad dominium & proprietatem tam in speciali, quam etiam in communi. Istam eandem sententiam tenuit postea Bonifacius octauus, qui eadem verba Sext. 6. decretalium compilato, per ipsum inseruit, & ita per solennem approbationem, illam sententiam fecit suam. Clemens etiam quintus decreta Exiit, in qua verba continentur prędicta, approbans eandem sententiam fecit suam. Et ita patet aperte, quod plures summi pontifices hanc assertionem firmiter & irrevocabiliter tenuerunt. Propter quod isti impugnatores putant demonstratiue per hoc se probare, quod ille impugnatus modo non est verus Papa: quam probationem hic non replico, quia posita est superius cap. 9. Viso autem quod haec assertio est per plures Romanos pontifices solenniter diffinita & determinata, ostendunt isti impugnatores; quod haec diffinitio Romanorum pontificum in scripturis diuinis & doctrina sanctorum patenter est fundata. Et secundum quod quatuor in praedictis verbis Nicolai tertii continentur, ut dictum est, quatuor conclusiones probare nituntur. Quarum prima est, quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium rerum tam in speciali quam etiam in communi propter Deum ad perfectionem spectat. Secunda est quod Christus talem abdicationem docuit. Tertia quod Apostoli abdicationem huiusmodi seruauerunt. Quarta quod talem abdicationem alios docuerunt.
units.tr: But these opponents try to refute those points. They proceed in this way. First they attack his assertion; second they answer the authorities which he cites in its support. To make the first point clear, they say that one must know that, as Clement testifies (as found in dist. 27, c. Relatum), there are many words in the divine Scriptures which can be drawn to whatever sense each person spontaneously presumes for himself, but this should not be done. So the words of blessed Peter, when he said "Behold, we have left all things," taken bare and not related to what comes before and after and to other passages of divine Scripture, could be drawn by someone to a sense in which blessed Peter says that he and the other Apostles left all things in some way other than as to dominion and ownership. But we must not take such a sense against the truth of the Scriptures; we must rather draw the sense of the truth from the Scriptures themselves. And so from the sequence of the sacred Scriptures they try to show that when blessed Peter said, "Behold, we have left all things," he meant a way of leaving all things as to dominion or ownership. This holds both specifically and generally, with respect to the community of the Apostles themselves. And this is said of dominion or ownership in the sense in which one may bring a lawsuit in court, or even, by one's own authority or that of one's community, give, sell or let some thing, or enter into a contract concerning some thing; for it is of such dominion that the man they oppose is speaking. Now these opponents first prove that the Apostles left all their possessions as to ownership or dominion, both specifically and in common. They first prove the first conclusion, the contrary of which the man they oppose maintains, in this way. Christ did not give the Apostles an imperfect manner of leaving possessions under precept or counsel, the one he counselled to that young man, on whose occasion blessed Peter spoke the words above: "Behold, we have left all things." But Christ counselled that young man to leave all possessions, both specifically and in common, saying to him: "If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have and give to the poor"; and these words, according to everyone, must be understood of selling possessions. This is clearly gathered from the text itself, as it is written: When the young man heard these words, he went away sad. For he had many possessions. But things sold and given to the poor are considered neither specifically nor in common. Therefore Christ counselled the aforesaid young man to leave all possessions, both specifically and in common. Therefore he likewise commanded the Apostles, under counsel or precept, the same manner of leaving all things. It is certain, however, that the Apostles fulfilled the precepts and counsels of Christ. Therefore the Apostles left all possessions both in common and specifically. Secondly, they argue as follows. First, Peter speaking: Behold, we have left all things: words which, according to everyone, must be understood of all possessions, although according to some they need not be understood of all movables, because, as it is said, they did not leave their clothes. These opponents ask: did he mean the manner of leaving with the intention of returning to or taking back the possessions left? Or with the intention of never taking them back and never having them again? The first cannot be said, because Peter spoke of the same manner of leaving all things when he said, Behold, we have left all things. And Christ, when he said there, adding: Everyone who has left house, or brothers or sisters, or father or mother, or wife or children or fields for my name's sake, shall receive a hundredfold, etc. But Christ spoke of the manner of leaving with the intention of never taking back: because leaving a house or fields with the intention of taking them back is not a work of great perfection. Christ, however, from the great reward he promised to one who leaves house or fields, is shown to have spoken of a work of great perfection. Therefore he speaks of leaving with the intention of not taking back. Therefore Peter understood his words in the same manner of leaving, when he said, Behold, we have left all things. Now whoever leaves some possessions with the intention of never reclaiming them, leaves them as to dominion and ownership: both because he would retain ownership and dominion in vain otherwise, and because whoever leaves temporal goods with the intention of never reclaiming them either disposes of them rightly, namely by selling, giving or bequeathing, or regards them as abandoned. And whether he leaves any goods by one or other of these ways, he leaves them as to dominion and ownership: because those who sell, give or bequeath (after the testament is confirmed), and likewise those who regard goods as abandoned, leave them as to dominion and ownership. It follows, then, that the Apostles left all possessions, about which blessed Peter's words must be understood without anyone contradicting, as to dominion and ownership. Thirdly, they argue thus: the poverty of the Apostles was neither less nor more imperfect than the poverty of the religious orders who follow them. This is clearly gathered from what was said and proved in the preceding ninth chapter. But there are many mendicant religious who have no possessions in common. Therefore much more the Apostles did not have possessions in common. And if someone says that there is no order of those having anything at all in common, since they even have some immovables in common, because they have houses and gardens in common, then by this argument it is not proved that the Apostles had any immovables in common, although not extensive possessions. But these opponents say this does not hold, because they say that the reason why such religious have some immovables in common is that they live and dwell together; and therefore it is fitting that they have houses and gardens in common, just as they have certain movables in common. But the Apostles by no means lived together, except that sometimes for a short time some of them dwelt together. And therefore, just as they did not have possessions in common, so also they lacked houses and gardens in common. Fourthly, they argue. The poverty of the Apostles ought to have been conformed to the poverty of Christ. But Christ did not have possessions even in common, because one who has possessions even in common has where to lay his head and where to dwell. Christ, however, had nowhere to lay his head, as he himself testifies in Matthew 8, who says: Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests: but the Son of man has not where to lay his head. Therefore the Apostles too had no possessions or houses of any kind in common, not even a little. Moreover, since that community has hitherto had few opponents and many defenders, because all the mendicant religious and their teachers, up to the time of this man they oppose, firmly held it and left it in writing, as is clear of Thomas in particular above in the sixth chapter, therefore these opponents try more strongly to prove the second conclusion, namely that the Apostles left all movables and immovables, consumable by use and not consumable by use, as to dominion and ownership, both specifically and also in common. For many mendicant religious and certain others have been accustomed to attack this. But these opponents show that the Apostles left all things both specifically and also in common, and that many supreme pontiffs not only in sentence but also expressly defined and firmly held this assertion. Therefore they strive first to confirm that assertion by the judgment of many pontiffs, saying, as was alleged above in the ninth chapter, that Nicholas III in sentence and expressly defined in these words: "We say that the renunciation of ownership of all things of this kind, both specifically and also in common, for God's sake, is meritorious and holy; which Christ also taught by word, showing it as the way of perfection, and confirmed by example; and which the first founders of the militant Church, as they had drawn it from him, nourished by their teaching and life in those who wished to live perfectly." From these words four things are plainly gathered. The first is that the renunciation of ownership of all things, both specifically and also in common, pertains to perfection. The second is that the Apostles received this renunciation from Christ himself and taught it. The third is that the Apostles themselves kept this renunciation. The fourth is that the Apostles handed it on by example and teaching to others to be kept. And so it could not be said more clearly that the Apostles left all things as to dominion and ownership, both specifically and also in common. The same judgment was afterwards held by Boniface VIII, who inserted these same words into the Sixth Book of the Decretals, and so by solemn approval made that judgment his own. Clement V also, approving the same judgment, made it his own in the decree Exiit, in which the aforesaid words are contained. And so it is clearly evident that many supreme pontiffs firmly and irrevocably held this assertion. On account of this, these opponents think they demonstratively prove that the man they oppose is not now a true Pope; this proof I do not repeat here, since it was set out above in chapter 9. Having seen that this assertion has been solemnly defined and determined by many Roman pontiffs, these opponents show that this definition of the Roman pontiffs is plainly founded in the divine Scriptures and the teaching of the saints. And, according to the four things contained in the aforesaid words of Nicholas III, as has been said, they strive to prove four conclusions. The first of these is that the renunciation of ownership of all things, both specifically and also in common, for God's sake, pertains to perfection. The second is that Christ taught such a renunciation. The third is that the Apostles kept such a renunciation. The fourth is that they taught others such a renunciation.

units.la: Quod autem talis abdicatio proprietatis omnium rerum tam in speciali quam etiam in communi propter Deum ad perfectionem spectet, multis modis ostendere moliuntur. Primo sic: Omnis abdicatio superfluitatis rerum temporalium ad perfectionem spectat. Hoc videtur tam euidens quod probatione non indiget. Sed retentio proprietatis siue in speciali siue in communi est quaedam superfluitas temporalium rerum: quia omnia in rebus temporalibus quae non sunt necessaria ad sustentationem licitam humanae naturae, sunt inter superflua computanda. Natura autem ita licite sustentatur in temporalibus sine retentione proprietatis siue in communi siue in speciali, sicut cum retentione talis proprietatis: E. omnis retentio proprietatis siue in communi siue in speciali est quaedam superfluitas temporalium rerum. E. abdicatio omnis talis proprietatis ad perfectionem spectat. Contra illam rationem obiici potest. Nam non videtur, quod omnis retentio vel habitio proprietatis rerum in communi sit inter superflua computanda: quia omnis superfluitas est vitiosa. Et per consequens omnes retinentes superflua sunt vitiosi. Ex quo sequitur, quod omnes habentes proprietatem quarumcunque rerum in communi sunt vitiosi: quod non est aliqualiter concedendum. Ad hoc isti impugnatores respondent dicentes, quod aliquid dicitur esse superfluum triplíciter. Vel quia vitiosum & nociuum, sicut comestio dicitur esse superflua, quia nocet naturae & generat morbum. Aliter dicitur superfluum, quod de se est nocumenti occasio, sicut cum aliquis comedit quod de se nocere non potest, potest tamen esse nocendi occasio. Tertio dicitur aliquid superfluum quod nec est nociuum nec nocendi occasio, non est tamen necessarium, sicut saepe comedere unam fabam, neque est nociuum nec posset nocere, esset tamen inutile & non necessarium. Ad propositum dicunt, quod retentio proprietatis quarumcunque rerum in communi vel in speciali est superflua tertio modo: quia non est necessaria, cum sine ea possit sustentari natura humana: imo etiam sine ipsa contingit exercere alia, quae ad distincta spectant officia, sicut studere, legere, cantare, scribere & alia quae ad reliqua spectant officia. Retentio etiam proprietatis rerum in communi est superflua secundo modo, quia est nocendi occasio, cum enim vnusquisque vt communiter magis amet rem, cuius habet proprietatem in communi, magisque sollicitetur circa ipsam, quam circa rem, in qua penitus nullam habet proprietatem, retentio proprietatis rerum in communi amoris superflui & nociui, ac etiam sollicitudinis superfluae & nociuae potest esse occasio. Et ideo talis retentio est superflua secundo modo. Primo vero modo nec retentio proprietatis rerum in communi, nec retentio proprietatis etiam maximarum diuitiarum in speciali est de se superflua, quia non est de se nociua: imo in casu potest vtraque esse meritoria. Ad formam igitur obiectionis respondent, quod omnis superfluitas primo modo dicta est vitiosa. Sed non omnis superfluitas secundo modo & tertio modo dicta est vitiosa. Sed omnis talis superfluitas in diuitiis potest esse vitiosa. Sed forte obiiciet aliquis, quia etiam abdicatio proprietatis omnium rerum in communi potest esse vitiosa: quia potest esse nocumenti occasio.
units.tr: That such renunciation of all ownership of goods, both individually and in common, for God's sake pertains to perfection, these opponents try to show in many ways. First, thus: every renunciation of the superfluity of temporal goods pertains to perfection. This seems so evident that it needs no proof. But the retention of ownership, whether individual or common, is a certain superfluity of temporal goods, because everything in temporal goods that is not necessary for the lawful sustenance of human nature is to be counted among superfluities. Yet nature is lawfully sustained in temporal things without retaining ownership, whether common or individual, just as it is with such ownership retained. Therefore every retention of ownership, whether common or individual, is a certain superfluity of temporal goods. Therefore the renunciation of every such ownership pertains to perfection. An objection can be raised against this argument. For it does not seem that every retention or possession of ownership of goods in common is to be counted among superfluities, since every superfluity is vicious. Consequently, all who retain superfluities are vicious. From this it follows that all who have ownership of any goods in common are vicious, which by no means ought to be conceded. To this, these opponents reply, saying that something is called superfluous in three ways. Either because it is vicious and harmful, as eating is called superfluous when it harms the nature and produces disease. Otherwise something is called superfluous which is in itself an occasion of harm, as when someone eats what in itself cannot harm but can be an occasion of harm. Thirdly, something is called superfluous which is neither harmful nor an occasion of harm, yet is not necessary, as to eat one bean often: it is neither harmful nor could it harm, but it would be useless and unnecessary. As to the matter at hand, they say that the retention of ownership of any goods in common or individually is superfluous in the third way, because it is not necessary, since human nature can be sustained without it. Indeed, without it one can also engage in other activities that belong to distinct duties, such as studying, reading, singing, writing, and the others that belong to the remaining duties. The retention of ownership of goods in common is also superfluous in the second way, because it is an occasion of harm: since each person commonly loves more the thing of which he has common ownership, and is more anxious about it than about a thing of which he has no ownership at all, the retention of common ownership can be an occasion of superfluous and harmful love and of superfluous and harmful anxiety. And therefore such retention is superfluous in the second way. But in the first way, neither the retention of ownership of goods in common nor the retention of ownership, even of very great riches, individually, is superfluous in itself, because it is not harmful in itself; indeed, in some cases either can be meritorious. Therefore, in answer to the form of the objection, they say that every superfluity in the first sense is vicious, but not every superfluity in the second and third senses is vicious. But every such superfluity in riches can be vicious. But perhaps someone will object that the renunciation of ownership of all goods in common can also be vicious, since it can be an occasion of harm.

units.la: Ad hoc respondent, quod talis abdicatio non est de se occasio nocumenti vel mali: & ideo non minus spectat ad perfectionem. Quia non omne quod potest esse occasio mali, deficit a perfectione. Corpus enim Christi ab aliquo sumptum indigne est occasio mali sumentis, nec tamen deficit a perfectione. Sed illud quod de se & communiter est occasio mali, ad perfectionem non pertinet. Retentio autem proprietatis rerum etiam in communi inclinat ad amorem & sollicitudinem nociuam circa temporalia. Et ideo ad perfectionem non pertinet. Et si dicatur, quod tunc religiosi retinentes proprietatem rerum in communi non essent perfecti, nec essent in statu perfectionis.
units.tr: To this they reply that such renunciation is not in itself an occasion of harm or evil, and therefore it pertains no less to perfection. For not everything that can be an occasion of evil falls short of perfection. Thus the body of Christ, when received unworthily by someone, is an occasion of evil to the one who receives it, yet it does not fall short of perfection. But what in itself and commonly is an occasion of evil does not pertain to perfection. The retention of ownership of goods, even in common, however, inclines toward a harmful love and anxiety about temporal things. Therefore it does not pertain to perfection. And if it is said that then religious who retain ownership of goods in common would not be perfect, nor be in a state of perfection—

units.la: Ad hoc respondent dicentes, quod religiosi retinentes proprietatem rerum possunt esse perfecti, sicut habentes proprietatem magnarum diuitiarum, possunt esse perfecti. Unde reges & principes retinentes suas diuitias in speciali possunt esse perfecti: tamen talis retentio non pertinet ad statum perfectionis. Sed nunquid sunt religiosi retinentes proprietatem rerum in communi in statu perfectionis?
units.tr: To this they reply, saying that religious who retain ownership of goods can be perfect, just as those who have ownership of great riches can be perfect. Hence kings and princes who retain their riches individually can be perfect; yet such retention does not pertain to the state of perfection. But are religious who retain ownership of goods in common in the state of perfection?

units.la: Ad hoc respondent, quod tales sunt in statu perfectionis, non propter retentionem proprietatis rerum in communi, sed propter abdicationem proprietatis rerum in speciali propter Deum. Et ita abdicatio eorum ad perfectionem spectat. Sed retentio proprietatis in communi non spectat ad perfectionem. Et ideo licet sint in statu perfectionis, non tamen sunt in statu maximæ perfectionis: sed à maxima perfectione quantum ad hoc deficiunt. Secundo isti impugnatores sic arguunt. Sollicitudo circa temporalia est impedimentum caritatis & perfectionis, ipsa veritate testante, quæ Matth. 6. ait: Qui autem seminatus est in spinis, hic est qui verbum Dei audit & sollicitudo istius seculi & fallacia diuitiarum suffocat verbum & sine fructu efficitur. Sollicitudo ergo temporalium fructum impedit (spiritualium. Licitum ergo & bonum quanto magis tollit sollicitudinem huius seculi & temporalium, tanto magis ad perfectionem spectat. Sed abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium in communi est licita & bona; sicut inferius ostendetur, & magis tollit sollicitudinem circa temporalia, quam abdicatio proprietatis in speciali tantum: quia quamuis interdum aliquis ex bona causa vel mala sollicitudinem tantam adhibeat circa temporalia, quorum non habet proprietatem nec in speciali nec in communi: sicut aliquis circa temporalia, quorum habet proprietatem in communi: tamen vt communiter & quantum ad inclinationem quam ingerunt temporalia maiorem sollicitudinem adhibent homines circa communia bona, quam circa illa quæ nec sunt propria nec communia, quemadmodum licet interdum aliquis sit magis sollicitus circa communia quam circa propria. Vnde legimus multos propria propter communia neglexisse. Tamen vt communiter homines sunt magis circa propria quam circa communia solliciti. Homines etiam quorum natura corrupta ad cupiditatem est prona, quanto magis aliqua bona temporalia spectant ad ipsos, tanto circa illa sunt magis solliciti. Sed bona temporalia magis spectant ad illos, quibus sunt communia quantum ad dominium & proprietatem in communi, quam ad illos quorum non sunt quantum ad dominium & proprietatem in communi neque in speciali. Ergo homines ex ipsis bonis communibus inclinantur ad maiorem sollicitudinem exhibendam circa ipsa, quam si non essent communia. Et ita manifeste patet, quod abdicatio proprietatis in speciali & in communi ex natura sua magis tollit sollicitudinem circa temporalia, quam abdicatio proprietatis in speciali tantum. Ergo magis spectat ad perfectionem. Tertio sic arguunt. Quod ex magnitudine amoris diuini procedit, ad perfectionem spectat. Sed abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium in communi & in speciali propter Deum ex magnitudine amoris diuini procedit. Qui enim omnia abdicat tam in communi quam in speciali, propter aliquem finem hoc facit. Aut ergo propter Deum, aut propter aliquod temporale. Non propter aliquod temporale: quia talis stultus esset censendus, præsertim cum per talem abdicationem non posset consequi aliquod temporale, nisi forte à casu. Si autem abdicat omnia in speciali, & etiam in communi propter Deum: Ergo talis abdicatio ex amore diuino procedit, & ita ad perfectionem spectat. De illa conclusione fiet postea tractatus specialis. Quia ipsam specialiter reprobat iste impugnatus, vt in sequentibus apparebit.
units.tr: To this they reply that such people are in the state of perfection, not because of the retention of ownership of goods in common, but because of the renunciation of ownership of goods individually for God's sake. And so their renunciation pertains to perfection. But the retention of ownership in common does not pertain to perfection. And therefore, although they are in a state of perfection, they are not in the state of the greatest perfection, but fall short of the greatest perfection in this respect. Secondly, these opponents argue thus: anxiety about temporal things is an impediment to charity and perfection, as the truth itself testifies, which says in Matt. 6: "He who is sown among thorns is the one who hears the word of God, and the care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful." Therefore anxiety about temporal things hinders the fruit of spiritual things.
