Therefore whatever is lawful and good, the more it removes anxiety about this world and temporal things, the more it pertains to perfection. But the renunciation of ownership of all temporal goods in common is lawful and good, as will be shown below, and it removes anxiety about temporal things more than renunciation of ownership individually alone does. For although at times someone, from a good or bad cause, applies such great anxiety to temporal things of which he has no ownership, either individually or in common, as someone does about temporal things of which he has ownership in common, nevertheless, as a general rule and as far as the inclination that temporal things produce goes, people apply greater anxiety to common goods than to those that are neither their own nor common, just as, although at times someone is more anxious about common goods than about his own. Hence we read that many have neglected their own things on account of common ones. Yet as a general rule people are more anxious about their own things than about common ones. Also, people whose corrupt nature is prone to covetousness, the more certain temporal goods belong to them, the more anxious they are about those things. But temporal goods belong more to those for whom they are common in dominion and ownership in common, than to those for whom they are neither common nor individual in dominion and ownership. Therefore people are inclined, by the very common goods, to show greater anxiety about them than if they were not common. And so it is clearly evident that renunciation of ownership both individually and in common, by its very nature, removes anxiety about temporal things more than renunciation of ownership individually alone. Therefore it pertains more to perfection. Thirdly, they argue thus: what proceeds from the greatness of divine love pertains to perfection. But the renunciation of ownership of all temporal goods, in common and individually, for God's sake, proceeds from the greatness of divine love. For one who renounces everything, both in common and individually, does so for some end. Either for God's sake, or for some temporal thing. Not for some temporal thing, since such a person would be judged a fool, especially since by such renunciation he could not obtain any temporal thing, except perhaps by chance. But if he renounces everything individually, and also in common, for God's sake, then such renunciation proceeds from divine love, and so pertains to perfection. A special treatise will be devoted to this conclusion later, because this opponent specifically rejects it, as will appear in what follows.

units.la: Secunda conclusio hic probanda est, quod Christus docuit prædictam abdicationem proprietatis omnium temporalium in communi. Quam rem isti impugnatores ostendunt. Primo sic: Quicquid Christus consuluit, ipse docuit (Consulere enim in Christo fuit docere) sed Christus consuluit omnia relinquenda quantum ad dominium & proprietatem, tam in speciali quam etiam in communi. Quia cuidam principi interroganti, quid faciendo vitam æternam possidebo, vltimate respondit dicens, Luc. 18. Omnia quæcunq; habes vende & da pauperibus. Ex qua responsione euidenter colligitur, quod consuluit abdicationem proprietatis omnium quæ habebat tam in speciali quam etiam in communi: quia exprimendo modum, per quem illa quæ abdicantur, omnino abdicantur quantum ad omnem proprietatem in communi & in speciali, venditionem videlicet, cum dixit: Omnia quæcunq; habes vende. Insinuauit aperte, quod si oportuisset illum principem ad sustentationem naturæ aliquid retinere, puta cibum, aut potum, vel vestem, illud non debuit, si volebat Christi consilium adimplere, quo ad proprietatem in speciali vel in communi aliqualiter retinere, sed ad sustentandum naturam tantummodo. Fuit ergo hæc intentio Christi, cum dixit: Omnia quæ habes, vende, hoc est, omnium quæcunq; habes, ita à te proprietatem abiicias, ac si essent vendita, vt quæ potes conuenienter vendere, vendas. Quæ vero vendi non possunt, sicut sunt pecuniæ, illas nihilominus à te alienes, dando pauperibus vel quibus teneris. Si autem aliqua habes, quibus pro sustentanda natura carere non potes, vel quia nullus est, qui necessaria tibi ministret, vel ex aliqua alia rationabili causa, illorum nihilominus proprietate ita à te abiicias, ac si essent vendita vsu tantummodo licito tibi retento. Et ita constat secundum istos, quod Christus in verbis prædictis consuluit talem abdicationem omnium temporalium, qualis per venditionem rerum, & erogationem factam pauperibus habetur. Constat autem, quod res, quæ venduntur & dantur pauperibus, quo ad omnem proprietatem in speciali & in communi penitus abdicantur. Ergo talem abdicationem Christus consuluit. Secundo sic arguunt. Christus Matth. 6. indixit Apostolis sub consilio vel præcepto amotionem omnis sollicitudinis, quæ non est necessaria, dicens: Dico vobis ne solliciti sitis anime quid manducetis, neque corpori vestro quid induamini. Et post: Nolite ergo solliciti esse dicentes: quid manducabimus? aut quid bibemus? aut quo operiemur? Et post: Nolite ergo sollicit esse de crastino. Ex quibus verbis patenter colligitur, quod omnem sollicitudinem etiam circa illa, quæ in cibo, & potu, & vestimentis consistunt, sine quibus vita humana sustentari non potest, quæ non est necessaria, & sine qua contingit sustentari naturam, & ea quæ ad officium cuiuslibet pertinent exercere, Christus præcepit vel consuluit amouendam. Et ille intellectus verborum Christi ex sententia Augustini patenter habetur. Unde super verba predicta dicit in sermone Domini in monte: non hoc dicit, ut illa non prosint, quantum necessitas est, sed ut non illa faciant quicquid evangelii predicatione iubentur. Ex quibus verbis Augustini datur intelligi, quod omnem sollicitudinem, quae non est necessitatis, Christus ab Apostolis voluit amouere, solummodo sollicitudinem, quae necessitatis est, relinquendo eisdem. Sed proprietas rerum temporalium in communi non est necessitatis: nec etiam solicitudo de tali proprietate acquirenda vel conseruanda est necessitatis. Ergo Christus omnem proprietatem temporalium in communi, & omnem sollicitudinem de proprietate tali a perfecte ipsum sequi volentibus [illegible, ~3 letters] amouendas. Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod habere sollicitudinem de proprietate rerum in communi habenda, est necessitatis: quia qui abdicat omnem proprietatem in speciali & in communi, fami & periculo se exponit. Quod non licet, quamdiu homo habet quod faciat. Ergo retinere proprietatem rerum saltem in communi est necessitatis. Ad hoc dicunt isti impugnatores, quod talis nequaquam famis periculo se exponit, sicut nec religiosi mendicantes habentes aliqua in communi, quae eis ad naturam sustentandam non sufficiunt, nisi aliqua de novo mendicent. Unde sicut illi religiosi mendicant res ad proprietatem in communi, ita possunt alii mendicare res consimiles ad licitum usum absque omni proprietate in communi. Nec secundi plus quam primi se exponunt periculo: quia natura ita sustentatur per licitum usum absque omni proprietate in speciali & in communi, sicut per licitum usum cum omni proprietate in communi. Et idem est de aliis actibus, qui debent per temporalia exercere. Ita enim celebrat aliquis missam in vestimentis, quorum non habet proprietatem neque in speciali, neque in communi, sicut in vestimentis, quorum habet proprietatem in speciali vel in communi. Igitur talis proprietas non est necessitatis. Ergo Christus eam consuluit abdicandam. De aliis verbis Christi, quibus idem consuluit in diversis locis occasione sumpta ex assertionibus istius impugnati patebit.
units.tr: The second conclusion to be proved here is that Christ taught the aforesaid renunciation of all temporal property in common. The opponents show this thing. First, as follows: whatever Christ advised, he taught (for to advise in Christ was to teach). But Christ advised that everything be given up as to ownership and property, both individually and in common. When a certain ruler asked him what he must do to possess eternal life, he finally answered, Luke 18: Sell all that you have and give to the poor. From this answer it is clearly gathered that he advised the renunciation of ownership of all that the man possessed, both individually and in common, because by stating the manner in which the things to be renounced are wholly given up as to all property, both in common and individually, namely by sale, he said: Sell all that you have. He plainly implied that if the ruler had needed to keep something for the support of nature, such as food, drink or clothing, he should not, if he wished to fulfil Christ's counsel, keep anything as property individually or in common, but only for sustaining nature. So this was Christ's meaning when he said Sell all that you have: that you should cast off ownership of all that you have, as if it were sold, so that you sell what can properly be sold; but what cannot be sold, such as money, you should nonetheless alienate by giving it to the poor or to those to whom you are bound. If, however, you have some things without which you cannot go on sustaining nature, either because there is no one to supply your needs or for some other reasonable cause, you should nonetheless cast off ownership of these as if they were sold, keeping for yourself only their lawful use. Thus it is evident, according to these men, that in the words quoted Christ advised such a renunciation of all temporal goods as is achieved by selling things and distributing them to the poor. And it is clear that things which are sold and given to the poor are wholly renounced as to all property, both individually and in common. Therefore Christ advised such a renunciation. Second, they argue thus. In Matthew 6 Christ enjoined on the apostles, as counsel or precept, the removal of all anxiety that is not necessary, saying: I tell you, do not be anxious for your life, what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall put on. And afterwards: Do not be anxious, therefore, saying: What shall we eat? or what shall we drink? or with what shall we be clothed? And afterwards: Do not be anxious, therefore, for tomorrow. From these words it is plainly gathered that Christ commanded or advised that be removed every anxiety that is not necessary, even about those things which consist in food, drink and clothing, without which human life cannot be sustained, and without which nature may be sustained and the duties belonging to anyone's office can be performed. And this sense of Christ's words is plainly found in Augustine. For on the aforesaid words in the Sermon on the Mount he says: He does not say this so that those things would be of no use, as far as necessity requires, but so that they would not do whatever the preaching of the gospel commands. From these words of Augustine it is given to understand that Christ wished the apostles to remove all anxiety that is not of necessity, leaving to them only the anxiety that is of necessity. But ownership of temporal goods in common is not a matter of necessity; nor is anxiety about acquiring or keeping such ownership a matter of necessity. Therefore Christ advised that all ownership of temporal goods in common, and all anxiety about such ownership, be removed from those who wish to follow him perfectly. But perhaps someone will say that to be anxious about having ownership of goods in common is a matter of necessity, because whoever renounces all ownership, individually and in common, exposes himself to hunger and danger. This is not lawful, as long as a man has something to do. Therefore to retain ownership of goods, at least in common, is a matter of necessity. To this the opponents reply that such a man in no way exposes himself to the danger of hunger, any more than mendicant religious who have some things in common which are not enough for them to sustain nature, unless they beg some new things. Thus, just as those religious beg goods for common ownership, so others may beg similar goods for lawful use without any common ownership. Nor do the latter expose themselves to any greater danger than the former, because nature is sustained by lawful use without any ownership, individually or in common, just as it is by lawful use with common ownership. The same holds for other acts which must be performed by means of temporal goods. Thus a man celebrates Mass in vestments of which he has no ownership, either individually or in common, just as he does in vestments of which he has ownership individually or in common. Therefore such ownership is not a matter of necessity. Therefore Christ advised that it be renounced. About the other words of Christ, in which he gave the same advice in various places, occasioned by the assertions of this opponent, it will be made clear later.

units.la: Tertia conclusio hic probanda est, quod Apostoli abdicationem huiusmodi seruauerunt, quam isti impugnatores ostendunt primo sic. Apostoli Christi seruauerunt eius consilia. Sed Christus consuluit omnem proprietatem rerum in speciali & in communi abdicandam, sicut ostensum est. Ergo Apostoli abdicationem huiusmodi seruauerunt. Secundo sic: paupertas nullorum post Apostolos fuit maior nec perfectior paupertate Apostolorum. Hoc auctoritate Hieronymi superius allegata patet expresse: qui asserit, neminem fuisse pauperiorem Apostolis. Hoc est etiam consonum rationi. Per Apostolos enim post Christum fundata fuit religio Christiana. Religio autem Christiana maxime docet rerum temporalium contemptum. Igitur & perfectissimam paupertatem. Igitur perfectissima paupertas in Apostolis debuit relucere. Sed aliqui post Apostolos omnem proprietatem rerum temporalium in speciali & in communi reliquerunt. E. & Apostoli abdicatione huiusmodi seruauerunt. Tertio sic: Apoli temporalia non quaerebant, nisi ad necessitate tantum modo: quia ultra necessitate quaerere est quodammodo superflue quaerere. Quaerere a superflue est aliquomodo a perfectione deficere. Quod de Apostolis in hoc casu est nullatenus presumendum. Sed proprietas rerum sive in speciali sive in communi non est necessitatis: quia sine ea valet quis omnia quae ad ipsam pertinent exercere. E. Apostoli in rebus nullam proprietatem habuerunt. Quarto sic: Qui in rebus temporalibus non quaerunt nec habent nisi visum, non habent in eisdem proprietate neque in communi neque in speciali. Sed Apostoli in rebus temporalibus non habuerunt nisi visum. Unde Apostolus ad Philip. ultimo: semel & bis in usum mihi misistis. Ubi dicit Glossa ab Augustino accipitur in usum praeter quem nihil est quaerendum. Et Hieron. super illud Apostoli, 1. Thim. 6. Habentes alimenta & quibus tegamur; dicit sic: habentes alimenta & quibus tegamur, ut ostenderet non quaerere nisi usum. Apostoli ergo non quaerebant in rebus temporalibus nisi usum. Usus autem post haberi sine omni proprietate in speciali & in communi. Ergo Apostoli nullam proprietatem quaerebant in rebus temporalibus. Sed dicet ille impugnatus, quod usus non potest in multis rebus a proprietate separari. Et ita in istis Apostoli quaerentes usum quaerebat & proprietatem sal e in communi. Hoc refellunt isti impugnatores dicentes, quod esto quod usus iuris, de quo loquuntur Iuristae, non possit a proprietate separari, tamen usus, de quo loquitur Apostolus in auctoritate praedicta, & de quo loquuntur auctoritates Augustini & Hieronymi, sive debeant vocari proprie usus sive abusus secundum modum istius impugnati loquendi, potest a proprietate in communi & in speciali separari. Quia auctoritates predicte loquuntur de visu, qui est actus comedendi & bibendi & huiusmodi, aut licita potestas actus huiusmodi exercendi. Constat autem, quod huiusmodi actus & licita potestas actus huiusmodi exercendi, possunt a proprietate communi & speciali separari, sicut probatum est prius, & amplius inferius ostendetur. Ergo usus sive sit proprie usus, sive non sit proprie usus, de quo loquuntur auctoritates, potest a proprietate communi & speciali separari. Apostoli autem talem usum solummodo, de quo loquuntur auctoritates praedictae, quaerebant. Ergo nullam proprietatem communem nec specialem quaerebant.
units.tr: The third conclusion to be proved here is that the apostles kept this kind of renunciation, which the opponents show first as follows. The apostles of Christ kept his counsels. But Christ advised that all ownership of goods, individually and in common, be renounced, as has been shown. Therefore the apostles kept this kind of renunciation. Second, thus: no one after the apostles had greater or more perfect poverty than the poverty of the apostles. This is plainly shown by the authority of Jerome cited above, who asserts that no one was poorer than the apostles. This also agrees with reason. For the Christian religion was founded after Christ through the apostles. But the Christian religion above all teaches contempt for temporal goods. Therefore it also teaches the most perfect poverty. Therefore the most perfect poverty ought to have shone forth in the apostles. But some after the apostles gave up all ownership of temporal goods, individually and in common. Therefore the apostles also kept this renunciation. Third, thus: the apostles sought temporal goods only as far as necessity required, because to seek beyond necessity is in some sense to seek superfluously. To seek superfluously is in some way to fall short of perfection. This must in no way be presumed of the apostles in this case. But ownership of goods, whether individually or in common, is not a matter of necessity, because without it a person can carry out all the things that belong to it. Therefore the apostles had no ownership of goods. Fourth, thus: those who do not seek or have in temporal goods anything but use have no ownership of them, either in common or individually. But the apostles had in temporal goods nothing but use. Hence the Apostle to the Philippians, at the end: Once and again you sent to me for my use. Where the Gloss, taken from Augustine, says: for use, beyond which nothing is to be sought. And Jerome, on that saying of the Apostle, 1 Timothy 6: Having food and wherewith to be covered, says: Having food and wherewith to be covered, so that he might show that they sought nothing but use. Therefore the apostles sought in temporal goods nothing but use. But use can be had without any ownership, individually or in common. Therefore the apostles sought no ownership in temporal goods. But the man under attack will say that use cannot be separated from ownership in many things, and so in these the apostles, seeking use, were also seeking ownership, at least in common. The opponents refute this by saying that, even granting that the use of law, of which the jurists speak, cannot be separated from ownership, nevertheless the use of which the Apostle speaks in the aforesaid authority, and of which the authorities of Augustine and Jerome speak, whether it ought properly to be called use or abuse according to the manner of speaking of this opponent, can be separated from common and individual ownership. For the aforesaid authorities speak of eating, which is the act of eating and drinking and the like, or of the lawful power of exercising such an act. But it is clear that such an act and the lawful power of exercising it can be separated from common and individual ownership, as was proved before and will be shown more fully below. Therefore whether the use is properly use or not, of which the authorities speak, it can be separated from common and individual ownership. The apostles, however, sought only that kind of use of which the aforesaid authorities speak. Therefore they sought no common or individual ownership.

units.la: Quarta conclusio, quam isti impugnatores probare conantur, est quod Apostoli abdicationem huiusmodi alios docuerunt. Quod probatur per hoc, quod omne doctrinam, quam a Christo acceperat, alios docuerunt, iuxta illud Matth. ultimo: Euntes igitur docete omnes gentes baptizantes eos in nomine Patris & Filii & Spiritus sancti, docentes eos seruare omnia quaecunque mandaui vobis. Sed Apostoli a Christo acceperant, quod ad perfectionem spectat vitae Christianae omnium rerum temporalium proprietatem in speciali & in communi abdicare. Ergo etiam hoc alios docuerunt. Sed hoc videtur contrarium veritati: quia si Apostoli docuissent abdicare omnium temporalium proprietatem in speciali vel in communi; hoc maxime docuissent primos credentes, dicentes, quod, sicut iuxta verba beati Petri, quae ponuntur s. q. i. c. Oportet. Oportet etiam quod docet, & instruit animas rudes, esse talem, vt pro ingenio discentium posset semetipsum aptare. Ita etiam oportet eum, qui docet esse talem, vt pro necessitate temporum & personarum, & aliarum circumstantiarum qualitate, semetipsum aptare possit. Respondeti potest, quod in ecclesia primitiva, quando multitudo infidelium catholicos persequentium abundabat, & tamen per potestates etiam infideles, aliqualis fidelibus fiebat interdum iustitia, erat conueniens, vt primi conuersi ex Iudaeis omnem proprietatem in communi, etiam & in speciali, qua liberè, sicut ante conuersionem valerent de rebus temporalibus ordinare, à se penitus abdicarent, quodam nouo modo proprietatis retum in communi, & ante illa tempora forsitan inaudito modo vsu retento, quo res, quae prius erant propriae, pro derelictis nequaquam haberent, nec talem proprietatem, qualem prius habuerant, in personam aliam vel communitatem transferrent, & tamen pro eis, si ab infidelibus detentae fuissent aut ablatae, vel vendicatae, potuissent in iudicio coram infidelibus litigare. Et ideo hoc eos Apostoli docuerunt, quia pensata conditione personarum, inter quas mulieres, etiam simplices habentes paruulos nutriendos, exiterunt, fuit conueniens vt aliqualem proprietatem, quae raro vel nunquam in iure vocatur proprietas, retinerent. Postmodum vero Apostoli altiorem paupertatem aliis docuerunt. Et quamuis hoc nō legeretur, nihil tamen esset negandum: quia multa docuerunt Apostoli, quae non scripserunt. Et de multis est absque dubio concedendum, quod docuerint fideles, quamuis in scripturis autenticis minime habeantur: secundum quod per exempla de diuersis Apostolis posset aperte probari. Ex his, isti impugnatores nituntur concludere, quod verba Petri, cum dixit: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, de abdicatione proprietatis omnium in speciali & in communi debent intelligi. Quia illa verba fuerunt beati Petri, postquam fuit ad Apostolatum sumptus & ad praedicandum missus, & de praedicatione reuersus, sicut habetur Luc. 9. Et postquam doctrinam Christi de sollicitudine necessariorum ad victum & vestitum non habendum audierat, & postquam consilium Christi de venditione omnium temporalium datam adolescenti audierat. Quare cum non sit aliquatenus praesumendum, quod Petrus volebat Christum per aequiuocationem vel ambiguum modum loquendi aut verba duplicia aliquo modo decipere, constat quod Petrus de illo modo relinquendi omnia intellexit, quomodo Christus omnem sollicitudinem circa temporalia abiiciendam docuerat. Et quomodo, quando Apostolos ad praedicandum misit, eos docuerat aurum, argentum, pecuniam non possidere. Et quomodo docuerat adolescentem omnia abdicare. Sed Christus sollicitudinem temporalium dissuadendo proprietatem specialem & communem temporalium dissuasit, sicut ostensum est, interdicendo etiam Matth. 10. possessionem auri & argenti & pecuniae, proprietatem specialem & communem rerum huiusmodi interdixit. Consulendo etiam adolescenti omnium abdicationem, proprietatem & communionem omnium abdicandam admonuit. Ergo etiam Petrus volens sub verbis ambiguis vel multiplicibus se iactare, cum dixit: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia. Et de modo relinquendi omnia, quae Christus prius docuerat & suaserat, & confirmauerat, intellexit. Quasi diceret beatus Petrus: Ecce fecimus quemadmodum docuisti. Docuisti enim omnem sollicitudinem, quae non est necessitatis, penitus deserendam. Et per consequens omnem proprietatem in speciali & in communi, cum non sit necessitatis, omnino cauendam. Docuisti etiam aurum & argentum & pecuniam in speciali vel in communi minime possidenda. Insuper docuisti, quod omnia quae conuenienter vendi possunt, sunt vendenda & pauperibus eroganda: & eadem ratione omnem proprietatem in speciali & in communi omnium temporalium abdicandam. Et ideo nos tuis doctrinis & monitis adhaerentes reliquimus omnia, omnem proprietatem specialem & communem omnium temporalium abdicando. Quia talem modum abdicandi omnia docuisti. Et ideo sciens Petrus se & alios Apostolos omnia reliquisse eo modo, quo Christus docuerat omnia relinquenda, confidenter & cum audacia magna quaesiuit, quid ergo erit nobis? quasi diceret: Et omnia relinquendo & te sequendo fecimus, sicut nos & alios docuisti. Quid ergo erit nobis praemii?
units.tr: The fourth conclusion, which these opponents try to prove, is that the Apostles taught others to renounce such things. This is proved from the fact that they taught others all the doctrine they had received from Christ, according to the words of Matthew's last chapter: "Going therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you" (Matt. 28). But the Apostles had received from Christ that, for the perfection of the Christian life, one must renounce ownership of all temporal goods, both individually and in common. Therefore they also taught others this. But this seems contrary to the truth. For if the Apostles had taught the renunciation of all ownership of temporal goods, individually or in common, they would have taught it above all to the first believers. Here the words of St Peter, quoted in the Decretum (dist. 1, c. "Oportet"), apply: "It is necessary that the one who teaches and instructs simple souls be such that he can adapt himself to the capacity of his learners. So too it is necessary that the one who teaches be such that he can adapt himself to the necessity of the times and persons and the quality of other circumstances." It may be answered that in the primitive Church, when there was a great multitude of unbelievers persecuting Catholics, and when justice was sometimes obtained for the faithful even through the powers, though they were unbelievers, it was fitting that the first converts from among the Jews should renounce completely from themselves every ownership in common, and also individually, by which, as before their conversion, they were free to dispose of temporal goods. They did so in a new manner of holding goods in common, a manner perhaps unheard of before those times, retaining a use by which the things that had previously been their own were in no way regarded as abandoned, and they did not transfer such ownership as they had before to another person or community. Yet, if these goods had been held or taken by unbelievers, or claimed, they could still have pursued the matter at law before unbelievers. Therefore the Apostles taught them this, because, having weighed the condition of the persons among whom were women, even simple women with small children to nourish, it was fitting that they should retain a certain ownership, which is seldom or never called ownership in law. Afterwards, however, the Apostles taught others a higher poverty. And although this is not read, nothing should be denied on that account, since the Apostles taught many things that they did not write down. And about many things it must undoubtedly be conceded that they taught the faithful, although they are by no means contained in the authentic Scriptures, as could be clearly proved by examples concerning various Apostles. From these points these opponents strive to conclude that the words of Peter, when he said, "Behold, we have left all things" (Matt. 19; Luke 18), must be understood of the renunciation of all ownership, individually and in common. For those words were spoken by St Peter after he had been taken up into the apostolate and sent to preach, and after he had returned from preaching, as is recorded in Luke 9. And after he had heard Christ's teaching not to be anxious about food and clothing, and after he had heard Christ's counsel given to the young man to sell all temporal goods. Therefore, since it is in no way to be presumed that Peter wished to deceive Christ by equivocation, or by an ambiguous manner of speaking or double words, it is clear that Peter understood the manner of leaving everything in the sense in which Christ had taught that all anxiety about temporal things was to be cast off. And as when he sent the Apostles to preach, he had taught them not to possess gold, silver or money. And as he had taught the young man to renounce everything. But Christ, by dissuading anxiety about temporal things, dissuaded individual and common ownership of temporal things, as has been shown; by forbidding in Matthew 10 also the possession of gold and silver and money, he forbade individual and common ownership of such goods. By advising the young man to renounce everything, he admonished that all ownership and community of goods was to be renounced. Therefore Peter also, wishing to boast in ambiguous or manifold words when he said, "Behold, we have left all things," meant the manner of leaving everything that Christ had previously taught, advised and confirmed. As if St Peter were saying: "Behold, we have done as you taught. For you taught that all anxiety that is not of necessity is to be wholly abandoned, and consequently all ownership, individually and in common, since it is not necessary, is to be wholly avoided. You also taught that gold and silver and money, individually or in common, are not to be possessed. Moreover, you taught that all things that can suitably be sold are to be sold and given to the poor, and by the same reasoning all ownership of all temporal goods, individually and in common, is to be renounced. And so we, adhering to your teachings and admonitions, have left all things, renouncing all individual and common ownership of all temporal goods, because you taught this manner of renouncing all things." And therefore Peter, knowing that he and the other Apostles had left all things in the manner in which Christ had taught that all things were to be left, asked confidently and with great boldness: "What then shall we have?" As if he said: "By leaving all things and following you we have done as you taught us and the others. What reward, then, shall we have?"

units.la: Post praedicta isti impugnatores ad auctoritates, quas ipse impugnat, in fulcimentum suae assertionis adducit. Respondent dicentes: quod in omnibus per aequiuocationes & multiplicitates vocum procedit. Quia, sicut dictum est cap. 9. talia vocabula meum, tuum, suum, nostrum, vestrum, eorum, ipsius, & huiusmodi in diuersis locis accipiuntur aequiuoce, sicut ibidem declaratum extitit. Ad primam igitur auctoritatem acceptam ex euangelio Lucae concedunt, quod ex illis verbis, relictis omnibus secuti sunt eum: non potest inferri: quod tunc omnia reliquerint quo ad proprietatem in speciali & communi, quia pene sunt diuersi modi relinquendi omnia. Et ideo dicunt, quod ex verbis Petri, cum dixit: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, non posset inferri, quod intellexerit de modo relinquendi omnia quo ad proprietatem in speciali & communi, nisi ille intellectus ex aliis verbis scripturae eliceretur. Quia igitur ex diuersis locis scripturae patenter elicitur, quod Petrus loquitur de primo modo relinquendi, quem Christus prius docuerat. Et Christus prius docuerat modum relinquendi omnia quo ad proprietatem in speciali & in communi. Ideo concedi debet, quod Petrus de tali modo relinquendi intellexit. Sed cum dicit Lucas de modo relinquendi omnia quo ad proprietatem in speciali & in communi, praesertim cum Petrus Iacobus & Iohannes non fuerint tunc ad Apostolatum assumpti. Quod patet ex Glossa ibidem, quae super illo verbo: Ex hoc iam eris homines capiens, ait: Nondum electus in Apostolum, sed praedicitur ei quod est aliquando eligendus. Et ita patet, quod ille impugnatus non potest plus concludere, nisi quod ex istis verbis Petri: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, non habendo respectum ad praecedentia & sequentia & alia loca scripturae, non potest concludi quod reliquerunt omnia quo ad proprietatem in speciali & in communi. Et hoc concedunt. Existimant tamen verbis & aliis concluditur intentum eorum, vt dicunt, & hoc sufficit: quia principaliter probare conantur, quod dicere Apostolos non reliquisse proprietatem in speciali & in communi scripturæ sacræ repugnat. Cum vero dicit, quod reperimus post idem dictum Lucæ 5. Relictis omnibus secutis sunt eum, scil. Petrus, Iacobus & Iohannes. Et tamen postea dicitur de Petro & Andrea, vt legitur Matth. 9. Relictis retibus secuti sunt eum, concedunt isti impugnatores, quod Lucas non intellexit de modo relinquendi omnia quo ad proprietatem speciale & communem. Sed ex hoc non sequitur quod Petrus non intellexerit de tali modo relinquendi. Quia sæpe vnum vocabulum in diversis locis scripturæ æquivoce & diversis modis accipitur. Et tunc quare vno modo accipitur in vno loco, & alio modo in alio ex diversis locis, & ex antecedentibus & sequentibus, ac etiam ex ratione interdum colligere oportet. Cum autem secundo dicit, quod post illud Matth. 4. legitur Matth. 8. quod venit Iesus in domum Petri. Ergo domus adhuc remanserat Petri. Dicunt isti, quod intelligendo, quod domus illa erat Petri quod ad proprietatem, errat aperte. Quia secundum ipsum illud, quod dicitur Matth. 4. Relictis retibus &c. præcessit illud, quod dicitur Matth. 8. quod Iesus venit in domum Petri. Sed secundum Glossam super illud Matth. 4. Relictis retibus &c. secuti sunt eum: sic quod amplius ad propria non reuersi. Igitur si Petrus postea ad domum, quam prius habuerat, fuit reuersus, non fuit reuersus ad eam sicut ad propriam. Et ita tunc non erat propria Petri. Quod etiam testatur Gregor. dicens super illud Matth. 4. Relictis retibus secuti sunt eum. Tanta a sequentibus dimissa sunt, quanta a non sequentibus concupiscere potuerunt. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod Petrus tunc nullam domum quo ad proprietatem sibi retinuit. Dicunt ergo, quod illa domus dicebatur Petri, non quo ad proprietatem, sed quo ad consuetudinem habitandi. Quia Petrus ibi consuevit habitare. Illo enim modo dicit viator etiam peregrinus aliquam ciuitatem interdum ingredientis: illud est hospitium meum: quia ibi consueuerat habitare. Vnde sicut Bethsaida dicebatur ciuitas Andreæ & Petri, vt legitur Ioh. 1. tamen non erat ipsorum quo ad proprietatem: quia tunc pauperes non fuissent: sed erat ipsorum quo ad originem. Et Nazareth dicebatur Mariæ & Ioseph, Luc. 2. quæ tamen non erat ipsorum quo ad proprietatem & dominium, sed quo ad consuetudinem ibidem manendi. Ita ista domus poterat dici Petri, quia ibi consueuerat habitare. Potuit etiam dici Petri domus, si aliquando fuit Petri. Unde & sæpe res vendita vel donata vocatur illius, qui eam vendidit vel donauit. Sic etiam Bethlehem dicebatur ciuitas Dauidis, sicut patet Luc. 2. Natus est Iesus in Bethlehem Iuda ciuitate Dauid; quæ tamen tunc non erat Dauid: sed ideo illo tempore vocabatur ciuitas Dauid, quia aliquando fuerat eius. Modi ergo loquendi in scripturis sunt sollicite attendendi: quia scriptura diuina modos loquendi communes & vulgares non abjicit. Et propter hoc multa verba scripturæ possunt aliquis ad suam trahere voluntatem. Sed non oportet: quia non sensum semper, quem possunt verba sonare, sed quem series scripturarum prætendit debet extrahere orthodoxus. Quod vero tertio dicit de gladio, quem Petrus exemit, non concludit, quia ille gladius potuit dici Petri, alio modo quam quo ad proprietatem. Potuit enim dici Petri quantum ad consuetudinem vel actum portandi, iuxta quem modum loquendi dicit aliquis de gladio, quem consueuit portare, quamuis sit domini sui, Iste est gladius meus. Sicut famulus dicit de equo domini sui, quem consueuit equitare: Ille est equus meus. Ad auctoritatem vero Lucæ 22. super literam apparebit. Ad illud vero de libro actuum: Calcia te caligas tuas & circumda tibi vestimentum tuum, dicunt, sicut responderunt prius cap. 9. Ad vltimum de Matthæo concedunt, quod per illa verba non potest concludi, quod Matthæus tunc reliquerit omnia quo ad proprietatem: sed dicunt quod non est simile de illis verbis dictis de Matthæo, & de verbis Petri propter eam, quæ est dicta prius de verbis dictis Lucæ 5. de Petro, Iacobo & Iohanne.
units.tr: After these points, the opponents bring forward, in support of their assertion, the authorities that he himself attacks. They reply that in all of these things the argument proceeds through equivocations and the many senses of words. For, as was said in chapter 9, such words as my, thy, his, our, your, their, of him, and the like, are taken equivocally in different places, as was shown there. So, to the first authority, taken from the Gospel of Luke, they concede that from the words having left all things, they followed him, it cannot be inferred that they then left everything as to property, both particular and common, since there are almost as many ways of leaving everything as there are of holding it. Accordingly, they say that from Peter's words when he said Behold, we have left all things, it could not be inferred that he meant the manner of leaving everything as to particular and common property, unless that sense were drawn out from other words of Scripture. Since it is plainly drawn from various passages of Scripture that Peter speaks of the first way of leaving all things, which Christ had earlier taught, and since Christ had earlier taught the way of leaving all things as to particular and common property, it must be conceded that Peter meant that way of leaving. But when Luke says of the way of leaving all things as to particular and common property, especially since Peter, James and John had not yet been taken up into the apostleship at that time, this is clear from the Gloss on the same passage, which, on the words From now on you will be catching men, says: He was not yet chosen as an apostle, but it is foretold to him that he will someday be chosen. And so it is plain that the opponent cannot conclude more than this: that from those words of Peter, Behold, we have left all things, taken without regard to what precedes and follows and to other passages of Scripture, it cannot be concluded that they left everything as to particular and common property. This they concede. Yet they think that their purpose is reached from the words and other passages, as they say, and that this is enough, because they are chiefly trying to prove that to say the apostles did not leave property, particular or common, contradicts Scripture. As for the passage which he finds after the same words of Luke 5, having left all things they followed him, namely Peter, James and John, and then it is said of Peter and Andrew, as we read in Matthew 9, having left their nets they followed him, these opponents concede that Luke did not mean the way of leaving everything as to particular and common property. But it does not follow from this that Peter did not mean that way of leaving. For one word is often taken equivocally and in different ways in different passages of Scripture, and so one must sometimes gather from the context, from what precedes and follows, and also from reason, why it is taken in one way in one place and in another way elsewhere. As for the second point, that after Matthew 4 we read in Matthew 8 that Jesus came into the house of Peter, and therefore the house still remained Peter's, these opponents say that to understand that this house was Peter's as to property is an obvious error. For, according to him, what is said in Matthew 4, having left their nets etc., came before what is said in Matthew 8, that Jesus came into the house of Peter. But according to the Gloss on having left their nets etc., they followed him, they did not return to their possessions any more. Therefore, if Peter afterwards returned to the house he had before, he did not return to it as to his own. And so it was not then Peter's property. Gregory also testifies to this, saying on the words of Matthew 4, having left their nets they followed him: So much was left by those who followed as those who did not follow could desire. From these words it is given to understand that Peter then kept no house for himself as property. They say, therefore, that the house was called Peter's not as to property but as to the custom of dwelling there, because Peter used to live there. For in that way a traveller, even a foreigner, sometimes says of a city that he enters, that is my lodging, because he used to stay there. Hence, just as Bethsaida was called the city of Andrew and Peter, as we read in John 1, yet it was not theirs as to property, for then they would not have been poor, but it was theirs as to origin; and Nazareth was called the town of Mary and Joseph, Luke 2, which was nevertheless not theirs as to property and ownership, but as to the custom of staying there. So that house could be called Peter's because he used to live there. It could also be called Peter's house if it had once been Peter's. Hence too a thing that has been sold or given is often called the property of the one who sold or gave it. So also Bethlehem was called the city of David, as is clear from Luke 2, Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea, the city of David; yet at that time it was not David's, but it was then called the city of David because it had once been his. The ways of speaking in Scripture must therefore be carefully attended to, for divine Scripture does not reject common and ordinary ways of speaking. And for this reason one can bend many words of Scripture to his own will. But one ought not to do so, for the orthodox reader must draw out not the sense that the words may sound, but the sense which the connected course of Scripture sets forth. As for what he says thirdly about the sword that Peter drew, it does not conclude, because that sword could be called Peter's in a way other than as to property. It could be called Peter's as to the custom or act of carrying it, according to which way of speaking someone says of a sword he is accustomed to carry, although it belongs to his lord, This is my sword. Just as a servant says of his lord's horse, which he is accustomed to ride, That is my horse. As for the authority of Luke 22, it will become clear from the text itself. As for that passage from the book of Acts, Gird up your loins and put on your garment, they say, as they answered earlier in chapter 9. Finally, concerning Matthew, they concede that from those words it cannot be concluded that Matthew then left everything as to property. But they say that the words said of Matthew are not like the words said of Peter, because of what was said earlier about the words of Luke 5 concerning Peter, James and John.

units.la: Nunc etiam per literam transcurrendum. (Per illa verba: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, &c. non potest concludi &c.) Isti impugnatores concedunt, sicut dictum est, quod per illa verba præcise non relata ad antecedentia & consequentia, & ad alia loca scripturæ, non potest concludi &c. & hoc sufficit appellanti. (in domum Petri) hoc est in domum, in qua Petrus consuevrat habitare: quia forte Petrus & Andreas erant ita pauperes, quod ante vocationem primam non habebant domum, nisi conducam: vel in domum Petri, quæ aliquando fuerat Petri. (Ergo domus adhuc remansrat Petri) Male infert, sicut ex ostensis apparet. Ex hoc notant isti impugnatores, quod secundum illum impugnatum Apostoli nec mobilia nec immobilia reliquerunt quo ad dominium & proprietatem. (Exemit gladium suum) Quia scilicet consueuit ipsum portare: vel quia tunc actu portabat. Et si quæras, cuius fuit gladius ille quo ad dominium & proprietatem? Ad hoc dicunt isti impugnatores, quod hoc ad eos non pertinet indagare: quia secundum beatum Hieronymum in multis melius est dubitare, quam aliquid temere diffinire. Sicut etiam dicit Origenes, quod ignoratur, quando Iesus venit in domum Simonis, de quo dictum est prius. Si tamen dicerent, quod ille gladius erat alicuius alterius, a quo eum accepefat ad portandum, hoc improbari non posset, vt dicunt. (In loco suum) Ex hoc posset argui, quod ille locus erat gladii quo ad dominium & proprietatem, si hoc vocabulum suum semper notaret dominium & proprietatem. Et ideo dicunt, quod suum, meum, tuum & huiusmodi accipiuntur æquiuoce: quia ex eis præcise non potest probari aliquid esse alicuius quo ad dominium & proprietatem, nec non esse. Tollat similiter & peram) hoc dictum fuit dispensatiue secundum Bedam: per illam tamen dispensationem non concedebatur, quod haberent dominium & proprietatem sacculi & peræ, sed quod portarent. Vnde cum Christus dixisset discipulis suis Luc. 10. Nolite portare sacculum neque peram &c. duo interdixit eis, scil. proprietatem huiusmodi rerum & facultatem vel actum portandi huiusmodi. Passione autem imminente dispensatio cum eis quantum ad secundum, non quantum ad primum, sicut tempore necessitatis extremæ licitum est tollere etiam aliena ad vendum.
units.tr: Now we must also go through the text word by word. (By those words, Behold, we have left all things, etc., it cannot be concluded, etc.) These opponents concede, as has been said, that by those words taken on their own, not related to what precedes and follows and to other passages of Scripture, it cannot be concluded, etc., and that this is enough for the one who appeals. (into the house of Peter) that is, into the house in which Peter used to live; for perhaps Peter and Andrew were so poor that before their first calling they had no house except a rented one, or into the house of Peter which had once been Peter's. (Therefore the house still remained Peter's) He infers badly, as appears from what has been shown. From this, these opponents note that according to the opponent the apostles left neither movable nor immovable goods as to ownership and property. (He drew his sword) Because, namely, he used to carry it, or because then he was actually carrying it. And if you ask whose that sword was as to ownership and property? To this these opponents say that it is not their business to inquire into this, because according to the blessed Jerome it is better in many things to doubt than to define anything rashly. Just as Origen also says that it is not known when Jesus came into the house of Simon, which was mentioned before. Yet if they should say that the sword belonged to someone else, from whom he had received it to carry, this, they say, could not be disproved. (In his place, his own) From this it could be argued that this place was the sword's as to ownership and property, if this word his own always signified ownership and property. And so they say that his own, mine, thine and the like are taken equivocally, because from them alone it cannot be proved that anything belongs to someone as to ownership and property, nor that it does not. (Let him likewise take also his purse) This was said by way of dispensation, according to Bede. Yet by that dispensation it was not granted that they should have ownership and property of the bag and purse, but that they should carry them. Hence, when Christ had said to his disciples, Luke 10, Do not carry a bag or a purse, etc., he forbade them two things: namely, the ownership of such things, and the power or act of carrying such things. But when the Passion was at hand, the dispensation with them was concerning the second, not the first, just as in a time of extreme necessity it is lawful even to take what belongs to others in order to sell it.

units.la: Non autem est licitum proprietatem tei alienæ sibi aliqualiter vendicare. (Venditio & emptio) hoc potest fieri tempore necessitatis extremæ absque dominio & proprietate: sicut si aliquis haberet tunicam alienam esset in articulo necessitatis extremæ, quod si non venderet tunicam & emeret sibi necessaria, moreretur: ipse tunc haberet licitam potestatem vendendi tunicam, cuius tamen propter hoc non haberet dominium & proprietatem; sicut creditor in multis casibus potest vendere rem impignoratam, cuius tamen non acquisivit dominium & proprietatem. (Emat gladium) hoc secundum nonnullos doctores mystice, non ad litteram debet intelligi. Unde Basilius prædicta verba pertractans ait: Non iubet Dominus portare marsupium & peram, & emere gladium, sed prædicta futurum, quod (scil. Apostoli) oblito tempore passionis dominum & legis Domini auderent sumere gladium. Sepe enim scriptura vitatur imperatiua sermonis specie loco prophetiæ. In pluribus tamen libris non invenitur accipiat, tollat vel emat: sed tollet vel emet. (Habuisse.) Uno modo vel alio, scil. vel quo ad proprietatem & dominium, vel quo ad licitam facultatem vtendi, vel quo ad actum vtendi, vel per alium modum. Unde habere in diuersis locis accipitur æquiuoce. Quandoque enim importat dominium & proprietatem: quandoque potestatem vtendi: quandoque actum vtendi: quandoque originem: quandoque consuetudinem habitandi vel aliquid faciendi per aliud: & quandoque quis dicitur habere partem, sicut etiam totum habet partes, & partes habent totum, & prælatus habet subditos, & subditi habent prælatum. Unde modos accipiendi habere, est difficile enumerare quia licet quidam Sapiens in quodam loco ponat octo modos, quibus dicitur habere, tamen præter illos sunt multo plures. Ex diuersis igitur locis scripturæ qualiter vnum dictum interdum debet intelligi, oportet accipere. (Per verba illa, relictis omnibus secuti sunt eum, non potest concludi &c.) Hoc conceditur: & tamen per illa verba Petri habito respectu ad antecedentia, & consequentia, potest hoc concludi. ) Quantumcunque de eo dicat scriptura, quod relictis omnibus secutus est eum, non sequitur, quod quo ad dominium reliquit ea.) Concedunt: quia per alia loca scripturæ non potest haberi, quod illa verba debeant intelligi de modo relinquendi omnia quo ad dominium & proprietatem: sicut est de illis verbis Petri: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, sicut ostensum est prius.
units.tr: It is not lawful to claim for oneself in any way the ownership of another's property. (Sale and purchase) This can be done in a time of extreme necessity without dominion and ownership. For example, if someone who had another man's tunic were at the point of extreme necessity, and if he did not sell the tunic and buy what he needed, he would die. In that case he would have a lawful power to sell the tunic, yet he would not thereby have dominion and ownership of it, just as a creditor in many cases may sell a pledged thing without having acquired dominion and ownership of it. (Let him buy a sword) According to some teachers, this must be understood mystically, not literally. So Basil, treating these words, says: The Lord does not command them to carry a purse and a bag, and to buy a sword, but by these words he foretells that the apostles, forgetting the time of the passion, would dare to take up the sword against the Lord and the law of the Lord. Scripture often avoids the imperative form of speech in place of prophecy. In many books, however, one does not find let him take, let him carry or let him buy, but he will take or he will buy. (To have.) In one way or another, that is, either with respect to ownership and dominion, or with respect to the lawful power of using, or with respect to the act of using, or in some other way. So to have is taken equivocally in different places. Sometimes it signifies dominion and ownership, sometimes the power of using, sometimes the act of using, sometimes origin, sometimes the habit of dwelling or of doing something through another; and sometimes one is said to have a part, just as a whole has its parts, parts have the whole, a prelate has subjects, and subjects have a prelate. Hence it is difficult to enumerate the ways in which to have is taken, for although a certain wise man in one place sets down eight senses in which one is said to have, there are in fact many more besides these. It is therefore necessary to take from the different places of Scripture how one statement must sometimes be understood. (From those words, "they left all and followed him," it cannot be concluded, etc.) This is granted; and yet from those words of Peter, when they are considered in relation to what goes before and what follows, this can be concluded. (However much Scripture says of him that they left all and followed him, it does not follow that as to ownership they left them.) They grant it, because from other passages of Scripture it cannot be held that those words must be understood of the manner of leaving all as to ownership and property, as is the case with those words of Peter: Behold, we have left all, as has been shown before.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Sed propter hoc Petrus Matth. 19. cum Dominus dixisset uni, qui non erat de discipulis: Si vis perfectus esse, vende omnia quæ habes, & da pauperibus, & habebis thesaurum in cælo: & veni & sequere me. Petrus dixit: Ecce reliquimus omnia &c. Non dixit, vendidimus omnia & dedimus pauperibus: sed dixit: Nos reliquimus omnia. Possunt enim res temporales quæ ad curam & affectionem illarum sine dominii abdicatione relinqui. Vel, reliquimus omnia, scil. præter illa, sine quibus potest hæc vita transiri, sicut sunt alimenta, vel pro alimentis necessaria, quibus non est verisimile quod ipsis renunciarent, vt probant scripturæ prædictæ, & alia multa, de quibus dicetur latius infra in obiectionibus, quas ille hereticus facit contra constitutionem: Cum inter.
units.tr: But on account of this, Peter (Matt. 19) answered the Lord, who had said to one who was not among the disciples: "If you want to be perfect, sell all that you have and give it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me." Peter said: "Behold, we have left all things," etc. He did not say, "We have sold everything and given it to the poor," but said, "We have left all things." For temporal goods can be left in respect of care and affection without renouncing ownership. Or, "we have left all things," namely, except those things without which this life cannot be got through, such as food, or what is necessary for food, which it is not likely they renounced, as the aforesaid Scriptures prove, and many others, which will be discussed more fully below in the objections that that heretic raises against the thesis, beginning "Cum inter."

units.la: Postquam in parte præcedenti ille impugnatus ostendit, quod per verba Petri non potest ostendi, quod Apostoli reliquerint omnia quo ad dominium & proprietatem: hic amplius hoc declarans, ostendit quod est alius modus relinquendi omnia, quam quo ad dominium seu proprietatem ostendens quod duobus modis omnia reliquerunt quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, unus modus est, quod Apostoli omnia reliquerunt quo affectionem & curam. Alius modus reliquerunt omnia præter illa, sine quibus non potest hæc vita transiri, cuiusmodi sunt alimenta pro alimentis necessaria.
units.tr: After the one under attack showed in the previous part that the words of Peter cannot prove that the Apostles left all things in respect of ownership and property, here, declaring this more fully, he shows that there is another way of leaving all things than in respect of ownership or property. He shows that they left all things in two ways in respect of ownership or property. One way is that the Apostles left all things in respect of affection and care. The other way is that they left all things except those without which this life cannot be got through, such as food, or what is necessary for food.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores impugnant prædicta quantum ad duo principaliter. Ostendendo videlicet primo, quod Apostoli omnia reliquerunt, non solum quo ad affectionem & curam, sed etiam quo ad dominium seu proprietatem. Secundo ostendunt, quod etiam reliquerunt omnia, sine quibus non potest hæc vita transiri quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Primum ostendunt primo sic: Perfectius est relinquere temporalia quo ad affectionem & curam: & etiam quo ad dominium & proprietatem, quam quo ad affectionem & curam tantummodo. Aliter enim omnes religiosi frustra relinquerent omnia quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Sed Apostoli perfectissime omnia reliquerunt. Ergo non solum omnia reliquerunt quo ad affectionem & curam: sed etiam quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Secundo sic arguunt: qui relinquunt actu omnia & etiam voluntatem habendi, non relinquunt solummodo omnia quo ad dominium & proprietatem: quia qui retinet dominium & proprietatem, non abdicat voluntatem habendi: imo etiam non abdicat principale modum habendi, qui est habere iure dominii & proprietatis. Apostoli autem reliquerunt voluntate habendi omnia temporalia, teste Glossa Luc. 18. quæ sup illa verba Petri: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, ait: setia voluntate habendi. Et eadem verba dicit Glossa sup illa verba Petri Matt. 19. Ecce nos reliquimus omnia. Et hoc testatur Greg. qui, sicut allegatum est prius, sup illa verba Matt. 4: Relictis retibus secuti sunt eum ait: Multum. {Multum} reliquit, qui quantumlibet parum, totum deseruit, qui cum re possessa etiam concupiscentiæ habendi renunciauit. Qui autem possessa deserit, & concupiscentiæ habendi renunciat, dominium abdicat & proprietatem. Hoc autem fecerunt Apostoli secundum Gregor. Ergo reliquerunt omnium dominium & proprietatem. Tertio sic arguunt: Relinquere aliqua dupliciter potest intelligi: quia relinquere vno modo, idem est, quod prius habitum dimittere. Sicut dicitur Iohan. 4. Reliquit igitur mulier hydriam suam, & abiit in ciuitatem. Sic etiam accipitur Matth. 4. cum dicitur: Relictis retibus secuti sunt eum: Quamuis aliter accipiatur relinquere in prima auctoritate, & aliter in secunda. Quia mulier sic reliquit hydriam suam, quæ tamen forte non erat accommodata sibi, & ideo forte dicebatur sua: non tamen reliquit voluntatem habendi ipsam. Petrus autem & Andreas sic reliquerunt retia, quæ prius habuerant, quod reliquerunt voluntatem habendi. Aliter relinquere aliqua accipitur pro nolle habere ipsa. Non enim sic dicit Petrus: Nos reliquimus omnia, ipse intellexit omnia habuisse & omnia dimisisse. Hoc enim fallum fuisset: quia pauperes erant Apostoli. Intellexit ergo: Relinquimus omnia id est, Nolumus aliqua habere: & ita reliquerunt voluntatem habendi quæcunq;. Qui autem relinquit voluntatem habendi quæcunq;, relinquit dominium & proprietatem quorumcunq;. Et ita Apostoli quo ad dominium & proprietatem omnia reliquerunt.
units.tr: But these opponents attack the aforesaid points chiefly on two grounds. Namely, first, they show that the Apostles left all things not only in respect of affection and care, but also in respect of ownership or property. Second, they show that they also left all things, without which this life cannot be got through, in respect of ownership and property. They argue the first point in this way. It is more perfect to leave temporal goods in respect of affection and care and also in respect of ownership and property than in respect of affection and care alone. Otherwise all religious would leave all things in vain in respect of ownership and property. But the Apostles left all things most perfectly. Therefore they left all things not only in respect of affection and care, but also in respect of ownership and property. Second, they argue thus: those who actually leave everything, and also the will to have, do not merely leave all things in respect of ownership and property, because whoever retains ownership and property does not renounce the will to have; indeed, he does not even renounce the chief mode of having, which is to have by the right of ownership and property. But the Apostles left all temporal things with the will to have them, as the Gloss witnesses on Luke 18, where, on those words of Peter, "Behold, we have left all things," it says: "Behold, we have left all things," it says, with the will to have set aside. And the Gloss says the same words on Peter's words in Matt. 19, "Behold, we have left all things." Gregory also testifies to this, who, as was cited earlier on the words of Matt. 4, "Forthwith they left their nets and followed him," says: "He who left much, or however little, has left everything, who, together with the thing possessed, has also renounced the desire to have." But whoever gives up what he possesses and renounces the desire to have, gives up ownership and property. Now the Apostles did this, according to Gregory. Therefore they left the ownership and property of all things. Third, they argue thus: leaving something can be understood in two ways. For leaving, in one sense, is the same as giving up what was previously held, as it is said in John 4: "The woman therefore left her waterpot and went away into the city." So also it is taken in Matt. 4 when it is said: "Forthwith they left their nets and followed him." Although "to leave" is taken in one way in the first authority and in another in the second. For the woman left her waterpot in such a way that, though perhaps it was not suited to her and so perhaps was called hers, she did not leave the will to have it. But Peter and Andrew left their nets, which they had previously had, in such a way that they left the will to have them. In another sense, "to leave" something is taken as being unwilling to have it. For Peter did not say, "We have left all things," as if he understood that they had had everything and had let it all go. For that would have been false, since the Apostles were poor. He understood, therefore: "We leave all things," that is, we are unwilling to have anything; and so they left the will to have whatever things. But whoever leaves the will to have whatever things, leaves the ownership and property of whatever things. And so the Apostles left all things in respect of ownership and property.

units.la: Quarto sic arguunt, Si Apostoli reliquerunt omnia quo ad affectionem: aut reliquerunt omnia quo ad omnem affectionem, scil. illam, quæ est necessitatis & illam quæ non est necessitatis. Cum enim nullus in hac vita possit sine temporalibus sustentari; necesse est quod vnusquisq; naturam suam cupiens sustentare aliquam affectionem habeat ad temporalia: & ita aliqua affectio est necessitatis, & aliqua non est necessitatis. Aut Apostoli reliquerunt omnia quo ad omnem affectionem, quæ est necessitatis: aut quo ad aliquam affectionem, quæ non est necessitatis. Primum dici non potest, quia in hoc fuissent Apostoli vitiosi censendi. Nec secundum dici potest, quia hoc est de necessitate salutis. Et ita Petrus dicens: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, nihil ad supererogatione pertinens expressisset. Intellexit ergo beatus Petrus, quod omnia reliquerunt quo ad omnem affectionem, quæ non est necessitatis. Qui autem relinquit omnia quo ad omnem affectionem, quæ non est necessitatis, relinquit affectionem habendi proprietatem temporalium: quia illa non est necessitatis.
units.tr: Fourth, they argue thus: if the Apostles left all things in respect of affection, they left either all affection, namely that which is necessary and that which is not necessary, or else all affection that is necessary, or else affection that is not necessary. For since no one in this life can be sustained without temporal things, it is necessary that each person who wishes to sustain his nature should have some affection for temporal things; and so some affection is necessary, and some is not necessary. Either the Apostles left all things in respect of all the affection that is necessary, or in respect of some affection that is not necessary. The first cannot be said, because in that case the Apostles would have to be judged faulty. Nor can the second be said, because that is necessary for salvation. And so Peter, saying, "Behold, we have left all things," would not have expressed anything pertaining to supererogation. Therefore blessed Peter understood that they left all things in respect of all affection that is not necessary. But whoever leaves all things in respect of all affection that is not necessary, leaves the affection for having the ownership of temporal things, because that is not necessary.

units.la: Quinto sic arguunt: Si Apostoli reliquerunt omnia quo ad curam, aut quo ad curam quæ est necessitatis, quod dici non potest. Omnis enim in hac vita degens oportet quod aliquam curam habeat de temporalibus aut reliquerunt omnia quo ad curam, quæ non est necessitatis. Et si hoc: aut ergo reliquerunt omnia quo ad talem curam actualem: & hoc non fuisset magnæ virtutis in Apostolis. Sic enim omnes boni & mali relinquunt omnia quo ad cura actualem. Aut relinquunt omnia quod ad curam quæ non est necessitatis, non solum abdicando curam actualem, sed etiam relinquendo voluntatem habendi curam, quæ non est necessitatis. Et ex hoc sequitur, quod Apostoli omnia reliquerunt quo ad dominium & proprietatem: quia qui relinquit aliqua nolendo habere curam de ipsis, quæ non est necessitatis: aut ipsa habet pro derelictis, vt concedantur occupanti. Et sic relinquit dominium & proprietatem. Aut ipsa dat, vel vendit, aut alicui alienat à se: & sic adhuc relinquit dominium & proprietatem. Aut relinquit voluntatem habendi curam de ipsis retinendo proprietatem vt nullus habeat curam de ipsis. Et hoc est de rebus suis male disponere, quod vitio carere non potest. Et ideo quod Apostoli tali modo reliquerunt omnia quo ad curam, est minime concedendum.
units.tr: Fifth, they argue thus: if the Apostles left all things in respect of care, they left either all care that is necessary, or care that is not necessary. The first cannot be said, for everyone living in this life must have some care for temporal things. Or else they left all things in respect of care that is not necessary. And if this is so, then either they left all things in respect of such actual care, and this would not have been any great virtue in the Apostles, for thus all good and bad people alike leave all things in respect of actual care; or else they left all things in respect of care that is not necessary, not only by giving up actual care, but also by leaving the will to have care that is not necessary. And from this it follows that the Apostles left all things in respect of ownership and property. For whoever leaves some things, being unwilling to have care of them that is not necessary, either holds them as abandoned, so that they are granted to whoever takes them, and so he leaves ownership and property; or he gives or sells them, or alienates them from himself, and so again he leaves ownership and property; or he leaves the will to have care of them while retaining ownership, so that no one has care of them. And this is to manage one's own goods badly, which cannot be free from fault. Therefore it must by no means be granted that the Apostles left all things in respect of care in such a way.

units.la: Sexto sic arguunt, aut Apostoli habuerunt intentionem resumendi ea, quæ reliquerunt, aut non habebant intentionem resumendi, si habebat intentionem resumendi beatus Petrus dicebat: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, de parua perfectione se iactasset. Si a non habebant intentionem resumendi, vel igitur de rebus suis quantumcunq; parvis communiter ordinauerunt ipsa dando, aut vendendo, aut aliter à se dominium abdicando. Vel si non poterant vel non expediebat de eis ordinare, ipsa pro derelictis habebant: & ita proprietatem & dominium reliquerunt. Nullo enim modo est virtuosi taliter res suas negligere, vt ipsa velit quo ad proprietatem & dominium retinere, & tamen non eas congrue moderari: quia hoc reipublicæ est nociuum. Dicunt igitur isti impugnatores, quod Apostoli reliquerunt omnia, non in principio, sed postquam fuerunt ad apostolatum assumpti, quo ad perfectionem & curam, quæ non est necessitatis. Et propter eandem rationem reliquerunt omnia quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Quæ proprietas non est necessitatis. Nec videtur aliqua ratio, qua reliquerunt omnia quo ad affectionem & curam; quia reliquerint illa quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Tum quia sicut cura & affectio non sunt necessitatis, ita proprietas non est necessitatis. Tum quia retentio proprietatis non debet esse sine cura: quia hoc reipublicæ est nociuum. Et ideo retinere proprietatem rerum, & nolle curam habere de eis nec per se, nec per alium, non laudabile, sed vituperabile est censendum. Sequitur ergo, quod cum Apostoli reliquerint omnia quo ad affectionem & curam propter Deum omnia reliquerunt quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Causa autem, quare Petrus dixit, reliquimus omnia, & non, vendidimus omnia, super literam apparebit.
units.tr: Sixth, they argue thus: either the Apostles had the intention of taking back what they left, or they had no such intention. If they had the intention of taking it back, blessed Peter would have boasted of a small perfection when he said, "Behold, we have left all things." If they had no intention of taking it back, then either they arranged their goods, however small, in a general way, by giving them, or selling them, or otherwise renouncing ownership of them; or, if they could not or it was not expedient to arrange them, they held them as abandoned, and so they left the property and ownership. For it is in no way virtuous to neglect one's goods in such a way that one wishes to retain them as property and ownership, and yet not manage them properly, because this is harmful to the commonwealth. Therefore these opponents say that the Apostles left all things, not at the beginning, but after they had been taken up into the apostolate, in respect of perfection and care that is not necessary. And for the same reason they left all things in respect of ownership and property, which is not necessary. Nor does any reason appear why they left all things in respect of affection and care, but not in respect of ownership and property. Both because just as care and affection are not necessary, so property is not necessary; and because the retention of property must not be without care, since this is harmful to the commonwealth. And so to retain the property of things, and to be unwilling to have care of them either personally or through another, is to be judged not praiseworthy but blameworthy. It follows, then, that since the Apostles left all things in respect of affection and care for God's sake, they left all things in respect of ownership and property. The reason why Peter said, "we have left all things," and not, "we have sold all things," will appear from the letter.

units.la: Secundo isti impugnatores conantur ostendere, quod Apostoli illa, sine quibus non potest hæc vita transiri, reliquerunt quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Quod probant primo sic. Non minus sub verbis Petri, cum dixit: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, comprehenduntur illa, sine quibus non potest hæc vita transiri, quam sub voto religiosorum, qui cupientes paupertatem Apostolicam imitari, viuere sine proprio profitentur. Sed sub voto talium religiosorum comprehenduntur illa, sine quibus hæc vita transiri non potest, sicut ostensum est prius. Igitur sub verbis Petri comprehenduntur illa, sine quibus haec vita transiri non potest. Apostoli igitur vitae necessa[illegible, ~6 letters] religiosi. Sed non reliquerunt ea quo ad facultatem & actum vtendi. Ergo reliquerunt ea quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Secundo sic. Non magis generaliter dicitur in Actibus Apostolorum de primis credentibus, quod erant eis omnia communia, quam Petrus dixit de se & compostolis suis: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia: quia non magis generaliter sunt praedicta verba in Actibus quam verba Petri. Sed ille impugnatus propter illa verba in Actibus concedit quod non solum illa, sine quibus potest haec vita transiri: sed etiam illa, sine quibus non potest transiri vita, illa fuerunt eis communia eadem ratione propter generalitatem verborum Petri concedi, quod Apostoli reliquerunt etiam illa, sine quibus non potest haec vita transiri, sed non reliquerunt illa quo ad facultatem & actum vtendi. Igitur reliquerunt illa quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Confirmatur haec ratio: quia abdicatio primorum credentium non erat verisimilis, quam abdicatio Apostolorum: sed per illum impugnatum primi credentes reliquerunt omnia, sine quibus non potest haec vita transiri quo ad proprietatem in speciali. Ergo & Apostoli reliquerunt omnia, sine quibus non potest haec vita transiri quo ad proprietatem saltem in speciali. Et ita verba Petri ad illa, sine quibus non potest haec vita transiri, debent extendi.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents try to show that the Apostles left those things without which this life cannot be got through, as to ownership and property. They prove this first as follows. Peter's words, when he said Behold, we have left all things, cover no less those things without which this life cannot be got through than the vow of religious men do, who, wishing to imitate apostolic poverty, profess to live without property. But the vow of such religious men covers those things without which this life cannot be got through, as has been shown above. Therefore Peter's words cover those things without which this life cannot be got through. So the Apostles [part of the text is illegible in the scan] religious. But they did not leave those things as to the faculty and act of using them. Therefore they left them as to ownership and property. Secondly, it is stated in general terms in the Acts of the Apostles about the first believers that they had all things in common, and no more generally than Peter said of himself and his fellow apostles, Behold, we have left all things. For the words in Acts are no more general than Peter's words. But that opponent, because of those words in Acts, concedes that the first believers had in common not only those things without which this life can be got through, but also those without which it cannot be got through. By the same reasoning, because of the generality of Peter's words, it must be conceded that the Apostles left even those things without which this life cannot be got through, though not as to the faculty and act of using them. Therefore they left them as to ownership and property. This argument is confirmed: the renunciation of the first believers was no less likely than that of the Apostles. But, according to that opponent, the first believers left all things without which this life cannot be got through, at least as to property in particular. Therefore the Apostles too left all things without which this life cannot be got through, at least as to property in particular. And so Peter's words must be extended to those things without which this life cannot be got through.

units.la: Tertio arguunt sic. Verba Petri praedicta: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, extendi debent ad illa, de quibus Christus antea locutus fuerat: quia occasione Christi ad adolescentem, & de adolescente, cui dixerat: Si vis perfectus esse vade & vende &c. dixit Petrus verba praedicta. Sed Christus antea locutus fuerat de pecunia. Quia, vt habetur Luc. 18. Christus videns illum tristem factum, dixit, quam difficile qui pecuniam habent, in regnum coelorum introbunt. Ergo & verba Petri ad pecuniam debent extendi. & tamen saepe pecuniae pro alimentis sunt necessariae. Ergo verba Petri ad necessaria vitae debent extendi. Confirmatur haec ratio: quia secundum Augustinum de doctrina Christiana, & ponitur i.q.i. Totum quicquid homines habent in terra, omnia quorum domini sunt, pecunia vocatur, servus, vas, ager, arbor, pecus, quicquid horum est pecunia dicitur. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod omnia quae pecunia vendi possunt & emi, debent sub nomine pecuniae comprehendi. Alimenta autem & alia sine quibus haec vita transiri non potest, vendi possunt & emi. Ergo possunt nomine pecuniae comprehendi. Sed ostensum est, quod verba Petri ad pecuniam debent extendi. Ergo etiam ad illa, sine quibus haec vita transiri non potest, debent extendi.
units.tr: Thirdly, they argue thus. Peter's words above, Behold, we have left all things, must be extended to those things about which Christ had spoken earlier, because Peter uttered those words on the occasion of Christ's words to the young man, and about him, to whom he had said, If you wish to be perfect, go and sell, and so on. But Christ had earlier spoken about money, since, as we find in Luke 18, Christ, seeing him made sad, said, how hard it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of heaven. Therefore Peter's words must also be extended to money. Yet money is often necessary for food. Therefore Peter's words must be extended to the necessities of life. This argument is confirmed: according to Augustine in On Christian Doctrine, which is also cited in Dist. 1, q. 1, Whatever men have on earth, everything of which they are the owners, is called money: slave, vessel, field, tree, cattle, whatever of these is, is called money. From these words it can be understood that everything that can be sold and bought for money must be comprehended under the name of money. Food and other things without which this life cannot be got through can be sold and bought. Therefore they can be comprehended under the name of money. But it has been shown that Peter's words must be extended to money. Therefore they must also be extended to those things without which this life cannot be got through.

units.la: Nunc ad literam accedamus. (Sed propter hoc) scil. contigit reliquisse omnia, dominium & proprietatem minime abdicando. (Cum Petrus dixit: Ecce nos &c.) Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod hoc falsum est. Quia non propter illam causam dixit: sed dixit hoc, ecce &c. vt declararet se & suos discipulos fecisse, quod audiuit tunc Christum adolescenti consulere. Et ideo sequitur, quod intellexit de modo relinquendi omnia quo ad proprietatem. (non dixit, nos vendidimus omnia) quia falsum dixisset. Quamuis enim vendidissent omnia sua, non propter hoc vendidissent omnia, quia multa erant, quae non erant sua, quae non poterant vendere. Vt igitur Petrus omnia comprehenderet & sua, & non sua, non dixit, vendidimus omnia: quia falsum dixisset: sed dixit, reliquimus omnia, hoc est nostra, abiiciendo proprietatem ipsorum: & reliquimus aliena, nolendo neq; dono neq; emptione, neque aliquo alio quouismodo vnquam habere proprietatem ipsorum, sicut quodammodo relinquuntur aliena, dum potestas habendi proprietatem ipsorum penitus abdicatur. Et isto modo verba Petri generalissime de omnibus temporalibus propriis & alienis debent intelligi. Dicunt tamen isti impugnatores, quod licet Petrus non dixerit, vendidimus omnia nostra: non tamen hoc negauit, nec ex scriptura potest probari, quod sua nequaquam vendidit. Imo multae auctoritates Hieronymi sonare videntur, quod sua vendiderit. Nam, sicut allegatum est supra, Hieronymus ad Ebidiam ait: Si vis esse perfecta, & in primo stare fastigio dignitatis, fac quod fecerunt Apostoli: Vende omnia quae habes &c. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, vt videtur, quod Apostoli omnia sua vendiderunt. Dedimus pauperibus) Petrus hoc non dixit: non tamen negauit se aliqua dedisse pauperibus. (Possunt enim res temporales relinqui quo ad curam &c.) hoc verum est: sed locum in Apostolis, postquam fuerint ad Apostolatum assumpti, non habuit. Et ideo concedunt, quod ex istis verbis solummodo non potest concludi, quod Apostoli omnia reliquerint quo ad dominium. Ex intellectu tamen illorum verborum, qui debet colligi ex serie scripturarum, hoc concluditur evidenter, vt dicunt. Appellans autem magis voluit arguere ex intellectu verborum, quam ex ipsis verbis. Ideo, vt dicunt, habent intentum. (Vel reliquimus omnia praeter illa sine quibus haec vita transiri non potest) Dicunt quod talis exceptio non potest colligi ex scripturis, sed oppositum ex scripturis patenter habetur. Ideo talis exceptiua concedi non debet.
