(Quibus non est verisimile quod renunciauerint) verum est quo ad licitam potestatem vtendi: tamen verisimile est, vt ex scripturis elicitur, quod istis renunciauerint quo ad proprietatem & dominium. (Hoc probant scriptura praedicta) Dicunt quod illae probationes per aequiuocationem procedunt. Et ideo nullae sunt censendae. Et alia multa ad quibus dicitur &c. vbi isti impugnatores respondebunt ad eas, & quomodo per aequiuocationem procedunt ostendere conabuntur.
units.tr: Now let us come to the letter of the text. (But on account of this), namely, that it happened that they left all things, not by renouncing ownership and property at all. (When Peter said: Behold, we, etc.) These opponents say that this is false, because he did not say it for that reason. He said this, behold, etc., to make clear that he and his disciples had done what they heard Christ then advise the young man to do. Hence it follows that he meant the manner of leaving all things as regards property. (He did not say, we have sold all things) because he would have spoken falsely. For although they had sold all their goods, they would not on that account have sold all things, since there were many things which were not theirs and which they could not sell. So that Peter might include all things, both their own and not their own, he did not say, we have sold all things, because that would have been false; but he said, we have left all things, that is, our own things, by casting off their ownership; and we have left others' things, by being unwilling ever to have their ownership, neither by gift, nor by purchase, nor in any other way whatever, just as others' things are in some sense left when the power of holding their ownership is wholly renounced. And in this way Peter's words must be understood most generally of all temporal goods, both one's own and others'. Yet these opponents say that although Peter did not say, we have sold all our things, he did not deny it either, nor can it be proved from Scripture that he in no way sold his own things. Indeed, many statements of Jerome seem to say that he did sell his own things. For, as was cited above, Jerome says to Ebidia: If you wish to be perfect, and to stand at the first height of dignity, do what the Apostles did: sell all that you have, and so on. From these words it can be understood, as it seems, that the Apostles sold all their own things. (We have given to the poor) Peter did not say this; yet he did not deny that he had given something to the poor. (For temporal goods can be left as to care, etc.) This is true, but it had no place among the Apostles after they had been taken up to the apostolate. And so they concede that from these words alone it cannot be concluded that the Apostles left all things as to ownership. Yet, they say, it is clearly concluded from the sense of those words, which must be gathered from the sequence of the Scriptures. But the one who makes the appeal wished to argue from the sense of the words rather than from the words themselves. Therefore, as they say, they have their aim. (Or we have left all things except those without which this life cannot be got through) They say that such an exception cannot be gathered from the Scriptures, but the opposite is plainly found in the Scriptures. Therefore such an exception ought not to be granted. (It is not likely that they renounced those things) This is true as regards the lawful power of using them; yet it is likely, as is drawn from the Scriptures, that they renounced them as regards property and ownership. (The aforesaid Scripture proves this) They say that those proofs proceed by equivocation, and therefore are to be counted as nothing. (And many other things to which it is replied, etc.) Here these opponents will reply to them, and will try to show how they proceed by equivocation.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: DE Iacobo autem & Iohanne dicitur Matth. 4. quod relicto patre suo Zebedeo in naui cum mercenariis secutisunt eum. Certe patrem non reliquerunt, vt eo renunciarent, & postea non habuerint eum, imo eius filii remanserunt: quia illa verba non concludunt, quod per verba illa, nos reliquimus omnia, intelligantur a fortiori omnia temporalia saltem illa de quibus sacra scriptura dicit contrarium, quo ad proprietatem & dominium abdicasse.
units.tr: Concerning James and John, it is said in Matthew 4 that, having left their father Zebedee in the ship with the hired servants, they followed him. Certainly they did not leave their father so as to renounce him and thereafter not have him; rather, his sons remained with him. For those words do not prove that by the words "we have left all," all temporal things are to be understood a fortiori, at least those concerning which Holy Scripture says the contrary, that they renounced them as to ownership and dominion.

units.la: A Signatis duobus modis relinquendi, quibus ille impugnatus asserit Apostolos omnia reliquisse: hic redit ad propositum, ostendens quod per illa verba, Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, non potest concludi, quod omnia quo ad dominium reliquerunt, simul cum hoc insinuans vnum alium modum salutis verba Petri absq; hoc quod omnia reliquerit quo ad proprietatem: dicens quod sicut per illa verba Matthaei 4. dicta de Iacobo & Iohanne, relicto patre suo Zebedeo &c. non potest concludi, quod non amplius habuerunt eum pro patre: ita ex illis verbis Petri, Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, non potest concludi quod reliquerint quo ad proprietatem: quia licet reliquissent aliqua quo ad dominium, non tamen illa de quibus dicit scriptura contrarium, vt verba Petri, Reliquimus omnia, intelligantur cum illa exceptione, praeter illa de quibus scriptura dicit contrarium.
units.tr: Having set out the two ways of leaving by which that opponent claims the Apostles left everything, the author now returns to his purpose. He shows that from the words Behold, we have left all, it cannot be concluded that they left everything as to ownership. At the same time he suggests another way of understanding Peter's words, one that does not require that he left everything as to property. He says that just as from the words of Matthew 4 about James and John, having left their father Zebedee, etc., it cannot be concluded that they no longer regarded him as their father, so from Peter's words, Behold, we have left all, it cannot be concluded that they left things as to property. For although they left some things as to ownership, they did not leave those things about which Scripture says the contrary. Thus Peter's words, We have left all, are to be understood with the exception: except those things about which Scripture says the contrary.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt illam responsionem non valere: & quod insuper errorem includit. Quod probatio non valeat, ostendunt: quia omnis modus relinquendi, qui competebat Apostolis ex doctrina Christi, fuit possibilis, conueniens & laudabilis atque virtuosus. Sed modus relinquendi patrem non erat possibilis, neque conueniens neque laudabilis. Modus autem relinquendi patrem, quantum ad assistentiam seu praesentiam & obsequium corporale propter seruitium Christi est conueniens & laudabilis. Ergo verba dicta de Iacobo & Iohanne, cum dicitur, relicto patre suo &c. de tali modo relinquendi debent intelligi. Et ita consimiliter verba Petri de modo relinquendi laudabili & perfecto debent intelligi. Talis est modus relinquendi omnia quo ad dominium & proprietatem: ideo &c. Error qui, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, continetur in verbis praedictis, est quod Apostoli postquam fuerunt ad apostolatum assumpti, & etiam post missionem Spiritus sancti, habuerunt proprietatem rerum in speciali: quia illae res, quas dicit scriptura Apostolos habuisse, non dicit fuisse Apostolorum, sed alicuius vnius Apostoli. Patet de singulis, de quibus impugnatus exemplificat, sicut de domo Petri, tunica, caligis, vestimento & huiusmodi. Ergo Apostolorum fuit proprietarius in speciali: quod improbatum est prius. Et contra hoc etiam inferius arguitur.
units.tr: But these opponents say that this answer is not valid, and that moreover it contains an error. They show that the proof is not valid, because every way of leaving that was open to the Apostles from the teaching of Christ was possible, fitting, praiseworthy and virtuous. But the way of leaving a father was not possible, nor fitting, nor praiseworthy. Yet the way of leaving a father, as to attendance or bodily presence and service for the sake of Christ's service, is fitting and praiseworthy. Therefore the words said of James and John, when it is said having left their father, etc., must be understood of this kind of leaving. And likewise Peter's words must be understood of the praiseworthy and perfect way of leaving. Such is the way of leaving all things as to ownership and property; therefore, etc. The error that, as these opponents say, is contained in the aforesaid words is this: that the Apostles, after they were taken up into the apostolate, and even after the mission of the Holy Spirit, had property in particular things. For the things which Scripture says the Apostles had are not said to have belonged to the Apostles in common, but to some one Apostle. This is plain in each case that the opponent gives as an example, such as Peter's house, tunic, sandals, clothing and the like. Therefore the Apostles were, in particular, owners of property; which has been refuted above. And it is argued against this further on as well.

units.la: Nunc accedatur ad textum: (Relictio) quantum ad praesentiam corporalem, (vt propatre postea non habuerunt eum) quia hoc non fuisset laudabile, sed dissonum rationi. (Verba illa non concludunt &c.) Concediturquod per verba illa nude accepta, cum sint de se multos sensus habentia, nullum sensum determinatum ex his praecise absque aliis contingit concludere: sed ex intellectu illorum, qui ex aliis locis elicitur bene concludit intentum suum appellans, vt dicunt isti impugnatores. (Saltem illa &c.) hic elicitur assertio praedicta, scil. quod Apostoli habuerunt in speciali proprietatem illarum rerum, quas scriptura asserit eos habuisse: quam esse erroneam isti impugnatores affirmat. (Scriptura dicit contrarium.) Dicunt quod scriptura nunquam dicit contrarium. Quamuis scriptura dicat alia verba, quae scripturarum ignari possunt trahere ad contrarium.
units.tr: Now let us come to the text. (Leaving) as to bodily presence; (so that they afterwards did not have him as father) because this would not have been praiseworthy but contrary to reason. (Those words do not prove, etc.) It is granted that words taken bare in this way, since they have many senses in themselves, cannot by themselves necessarily establish any one determinate sense; but from their meaning, which is drawn from other passages, they do well to prove the point the author intends, as these opponents say. (At least those, etc.) Here the aforesaid assertion is drawn out, namely that the Apostles had property in particular in those things which Scripture states they had; these opponents affirm that this is erroneous. (Scripture says the contrary.) They say that Scripture never says the contrary. Although Scripture uses other words, which those ignorant of the Scriptures may twist to mean the contrary.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: ITEM non obstat capitulum dilectissimis 12. q. 1. quod pro se dictus haereticus induxit, in quo beatus Clemens scribens discipulis suis Hierosolymis habitantibus cum beato Iacobo episcopo Hierosolymitano, aequiparat statum Apostolorum & ipsorum discipulorum ac Iudaeorum Hierosolymis post missionem Sancti Spiritus conuersionem, quantum ad modum habendi illa temporalia statui primorum parentum in statu innocentiae constitutorum. Et dicit ibi: Quantum ad statum praedictum primorum parentum, quod communis vsus omnium, quae sunt in hoc mundo, omnibus hominibus esse debuit. Sed per iniquitatem alius dixit, hoc esse suum, & alius illud. Et sic inter mortales facta est diuisio. Proculdubio illa scriptura supponit, quod si primi parentes non peccassent, omnia communia fuissent quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Quod patet in eo, quod dicit, quod per iniquitatem id est, per peccatum primorum parentum, alius dixit hoc esse suum: & alius illud. Et sic inter mortales facta est diuisio. Haec autem diuisio facta fuit eius rei, cuius prius erat communio. Diuisio autem facta est rerum, & non vsus simplicis facti, vt patet, quia alius dicebat hoc suum esse: & alius illud. Non dicit, quod ipsum diceret vsum huius rei suum esse, & alius alterius: sed dicebat vnus rem aliquam, & alius aliam suam. Sicq; patet, quod rerum dominia, non quo ad vsum diuisio fuit facta. Et per consequens sequitur, quod ante diuisionem quo ad rerum dominia: communio erat. Et hoc clarius sequentia patet in eodem capitulo, vbi sequitur: & sic non potest diuidi aer: neque splendor solis, ita nec reliqua quae communiter data sunt omnibus hominibus ad habendum. Vbi manifeste dicit, omnia temporalia communiter data fuisse omnibus hominibus ad habendum: non dicit, quod ad facti vsum, sed dicit ad habendum, quia vsus facti haberi nullatenus potest, vt superius est probatum. Ergo si data fuerunt eis, & ab illo (scilicet Deo, qui dare potuit, dicendum est, quod Domini fuerunt effecti. Quia dare est accipientis rem facere.
units.tr: ITEM, the chapter of Clement cited by the heretic in his own favour (12. q. 1, Dilectissimis) is no obstacle. In it the blessed Clement, writing to his disciples living at Jerusalem with the blessed James, bishop of Jerusalem, equates the state of the Apostles and their disciples, and of the Jews converted at Jerusalem after the mission of the Holy Spirit, with the state of the first parents established in innocence, as regards the manner of holding temporal goods. And there he says: "As to the aforesaid state of the first parents, the common use of all the things that are in this world ought to have belonged to all men. But through iniquity one man said, 'This is mine,' and another, 'That is mine,' and so division arose among mortals." That writing undoubtedly supposes that, if the first parents had not sinned, all things would have been common as regards ownership and property. This is plain from the words that through iniquity, that is, through the sin of the first parents, one man said, "This is mine," and another, "That is mine," and so division arose among mortals. Now this division was made of that thing which had previously been held in common. Moreover, the division was of things, and not merely of the simple fact of use, as is plain, because one man said that this was his, and another that that was his. He does not say that one called the use of this thing his, and another the use of another thing; rather, one said that a certain thing was his, and another said that a different thing was his. So it is clear that the division was made as to the ownership of things, not as to their use. And consequently it follows that, before the division, there was community as regards the ownership of things. This is made clearer still by what follows in the same chapter, where it continues: "And so the air cannot be divided, nor the light of the sun, nor the other things which are given in common to all men to hold." There he plainly says that all temporal goods were given in common to all men to hold. He does not say to use as a matter of fact; he says to hold, because the mere use of a thing cannot in any way be held, as was proved above. Therefore, if they were given to them by him who could give (namely God), it must be said that they became their lords. For to give is to make the thing the recipient's.

units.la: POstquam ille impugnatus respondit ad illa verba Petri Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, hic respondet ad capitulum Clementis, Dilectissimi: quod ad probandum vsum posse separari a proprietate & dominio appellans inducit. Et diuiditur in duo: quia primo ostendere conatur, quod per illud capitulum Clementis non potest ostendi, quod in statu innocentiae fuisset vsus facti separatus a dominio vel proprietate. Ostendens, quod si primi parentes non peccassent, omnia quibus vsi fuissent, fuissent eis communia quo ad dominium. Secundo per illud capitulum Clementis probare molitur, quod Apostoli & eorum discipuli ante conuersionem eorum de quibus ibidem fit mentio, aliqua possidebant, quae postea communicauerunt Iudaeis conuersis. Primum dupliciter conatur ostendere. Primo sic: illa fuissent vel fuerunt communia quo ad dominium seu proprietatem in statu innocentiae: quae postea diuisa fuerunt quo ad dominium: sed res ipsae fuerunt diuisae, quo ad dominium post peccatum primorum parentum. Ergo res ipsae fuerunt vel fuissent communes quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, si primi parentes non peccassent: & ita ibi non fuisset vsus a proprietate & dominio separatus. Secundo ibi (& hoc clarius) probat secundo modo, quod omnia ibi fuerunt communia quo ad dominium. Quia illud, quod datur aliquibus ab illo qui potest dare, datur eis quo ad dominium: ita quod Domini efficiuntur illorum quae dantur. Sed res erant datae a Deo omnibus hominibus ad habendum, igitur domini efficiebantur: & per consequens in statu innocentiae fuisset vsus a proprietate seu dominio non separatus.
units.tr: AFTER that opponent replied to the words of Peter, "Behold, we have left all things," here he replies to Clement's chapter, "Dilectissimi," which he cites in order to prove that use can be separated from property and ownership. And this is divided into two parts. First, he tries to show that from that chapter of Clement it cannot be shown that in the state of innocence there would have been a use of things separated from ownership or property, showing that if the first parents had not sinned, all the things they had used would have been common to them as regards ownership. Second, he labours to prove from that chapter of Clement that the Apostles and their disciples, before the conversion of those of whom mention is made there, possessed certain things, which they afterwards shared with the converted Jews. He tries to show the first point in two ways. First, thus: those things would have been or were common as regards ownership or property in the state of innocence, which were afterwards divided as regards ownership; but the things themselves were divided as regards ownership after the sin of the first parents. Therefore the things themselves were, or would have been, common as regards ownership or property, if the first parents had not sinned; and so there would not have been a use separated from property and ownership. Second, there (and this more clearly) he proves in a second way that all things there were common as regards ownership. For what is given to some by him who can give is given to them as regards ownership, so that they become the owners of the things that are given. But the things were given by God to all men to hold; therefore they became owners; and consequently in the state of innocence there would have been a use not separated from property or ownership.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, quod ille in omnibus non solum erronee, sed etiam cauillose & sub vocum multiplicitate procedit. Vnde dicunt, quod licet verbis praemissis multi continentur errores, de quibus super literam apparebit: tamen est vnus error principalis, quem per duas rationes praedictas probare molitur. Scilicet quod tale dominium rerum temporalium haberent primi parentes, & habuissent si non peccassent, quale nunc habent illi qui habent dominia rerum. Ille error, vt dicunt, patenter elicitur ex hoc, quod dicit, beatum Clementem non solum comparare, sed etiam aequiparare statum Apostolorum & ipsorum discipulorum ac Iudaeorum Hierosolymis post missionem Spiritus sancti conuersorum; quantum ad modum habendi illa temporalia primorum parentum in statu innocentiae constitutorum. Cum igitur secundum illum impugnatum, vt prius, patuit, Apostoli & eorum discipuli ac ibi Iudaei conuersi habuerunt tale dominium, quale Iudaei conuersi habuerunt ante conuersionem ipsorum. Sequitur, quod tale fuit dominium primorum parentum, quale est nunc dominium mundanorum. Quia dominium primorum parentum fuit tale, quale fuit dominium Apostolorum & praedictorum: & aequiparat Clemens secundum ipsum statum istorum statui illorum, quantum ad modum habendi temporalia. Et dominium Apostolorum & praedictorum fuit tale, quale fuit Iudaeorum conuersorum ante ipsorum conuersionem. Et illud fuit dominium mundanorum. Igitur dominium primorum parentum fuit tale, quale est dominium mundanorum. Sed hoc dicunt isti impugnatores esse erroneum. Ad cuius evidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod dominium temporalium datum primis parentibus fuit potestas rationabiliter regendi ac gubernandi temporalia absque eorum resistentia violenta, ita quod domini violentiam vel nocumentum inferre non poterant. Vnde quantum ad talem potestatem super terrena & specialiter super animalia, dicitur Eccles. 18. Dominus Deus de terra creavit homines. Et post: Dedit illi potestatem eorum, quae sunt super terram, posuit timorem illius super omnem carnem, & dominatus est bestiarum & volatilium. De potestate autem regendi & gubernandi, aut ordinandi & disponendi quaedam alia dicitur Gen. 2. Tulit ergo Dominus Deus hominem & posuit eum in paradiso voluptatis vt operaretur & custodiret illum. Ex quibus verbis recte intellectis datur intelligi, quod in rebus, quarum primi parentes gubernationem habebant, nihil contra eorum voluntatem accidisset: & ita talis perfecta potestas regendi & disponendi temporalia fuit dominium, quod datum fuit primis parentibus. Propter quod dixit eis Deus Genes. 1. Replete terram, & subiicite eam, hoc est ad placitum vestrum regite & disponite eam: & dominamini piscibus maris & volatilibus caeli, hoc est perfectam potestatem, cui non potuerunt resistere habete super pisces maris & volatilia caeli & universa animantia, quae mouentur super terram. Praeter illud autem dominium data fuit ipsis & animantibus terrae potestas vtendi quibusdam rebus determinatis: ita quod aliquibus vti poterant, & non aliis. Vnde Genes. 1. postquam Deus dederat primis parentibus potestatem subiiciendi terram & dominium omnium animalium, sic scribitur: Dixitque Deus: Ecce dedi vobis omnem herbam afferentem semen super terram & vniuersa ligna quae habent in semetipsis sementem generis sui, vt sint vobis in escam & cunctis animantibus terrae, omnique volucri caeli & vniuersis quae mouentur in terra & in quibus est anima viuens, vt habeant ad vescendum. Ex his verbis datur intelligi, quod herbae & ligna huiusmodi data erant communiter hominibus & aliis animalibus ad vescendum. Vnum autem lignum, non obstante generali potestate vescendi homini data erat exceptum, vt habetur Genes. 2. cum dicitur, ex omni ligno Paradisi comede; de ligno autem scientiae boni & mali ne comedas. In quacunque die comederis ex eo, morte morieris. Secundo isti impugnatores dicunt esse notandum: quod diuersarum rerum diuersi sunt modi vtendi. Vnde alius est vsus illorum quae manducari non debent: & illorum quae manducari licet. Eiusdem etiam rei sunt diuersi modi vtendi: quia eadem re diuersis modis vti contingit, sicut pecunia contingit vti ad pompam, & etiam ad aliam rem emendam. Sic pane contingit vti comedendo, & ipsum pro alia re permutando. Tertio dicunt, quod licet primis parentibus fuerit data potestas vtendi omnibus temporalibus vno modo vel alio: Illa tamen potestas vtendi non erat dominium, quod a Deo fuit ipsis collatum: tum quia habuerunt potestatem vtendi angelis, non quidem coactiue, sed per alium modum, quod ex verbis Beati Augustini super illud 1. Corinth. 3. Omnia enim vestra sunt, colligitur manifeste. Et tamen super Angelos non receperunt dominium: tum quia cessante illo dominio non cessauit omnis potestas vtendi. Aliqua tamen potestas vtendi rebus, quarum eis fuit datum dominium, à dominio illo minime differebat. Gubernare enim & disponere est quidam actus vtendi. Et ideo potestas taliter disponendi fuit potestas vtendi. Et ita fuit dominium: non tamen ex hoc sequitur, quod omnis potestas vtendi fuerit tale dominium. Illa enim potestas data fuit aliis animalibus, quibus non fuit datum dominium. Ex his arguunt isti impugnatores contra assertionem praedictam: scilicet quod dominium primorum parentum fuit tale, quale est dominium mundanorum.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he proceeds in everything not only erroneously but also captiously, and under a multiplicity of words. Hence they say that although many errors are contained in the words quoted, which will appear from the letter itself, there is nevertheless one principal error, which he tries to prove by the two arguments mentioned above: namely, that the first parents had and would have had, had they not sinned, such ownership of temporal goods as those who now hold ownership of things have. That error, they say, is plainly drawn from his saying that the blessed Clement not only compares but even equates the state of the Apostles and their disciples, and of the Jews converted at Jerusalem after the mission of the Holy Spirit, with the first parents established in innocence, as regards the manner of holding temporal goods. Since, therefore, according to that opponent, as was shown before, the Apostles and their disciples, and the converted Jews there, had such ownership as the converted Jews had before their conversion, it follows that the ownership of the first parents was such as the ownership of worldly men now is. For the ownership of the first parents was of the same kind as that of the Apostles and the aforesaid persons, and Clement equates the state of these with the state of those as regards the manner of holding temporal goods. And the ownership of the Apostles and the aforesaid persons was of the same kind as that of the Jews converted before their conversion. And that was the ownership of worldly men. Therefore the ownership of the first parents was of the same kind as the ownership of worldly men is now. But these opponents say this is erroneous. To make this evident, they say it must be known that the ownership of temporal things given to the first parents was the power of ruling and governing temporal things reasonably, without violent resistance on their part, so that the things could not inflict violence or harm on their lord. Hence, as to such power over earthly things, and especially over the animals, it is said in Ecclesiasticus 18: "The Lord God created men out of the earth." And after: "He gave them power over the things that are upon the earth, he set the fear of them upon all flesh, and they have dominion over beasts and birds." Concerning the power of ruling and governing, or of ordering and disposing, something else is said in Genesis 2: "The Lord God took the man and put him into the garden of pleasure to dress it and to keep it." From these words, rightly understood, it is shown that in the things over which the first parents had government nothing would have happened contrary to their will; and so such perfect power to rule and dispose of temporal things was the ownership that was given to the first parents. On account of this God said to them in Genesis 1: "Fill the earth and subdue it," that is, rule and dispose of it at your pleasure; "and have dominion over the fishes of the sea and the birds of the heaven," that is, have perfect power, which they could not resist, over the fishes of the sea, the birds of the heaven, and all living creatures that move upon the earth. Besides that ownership, however, there was given to them and to the living creatures of the earth a power of using certain determined things, so that some things they could use and others not. Hence in Genesis 1, after God had given the first parents power to subdue the earth and dominion over all the animals, it is written thus: "And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed upon the earth, and all trees which have in themselves the seed of their kind, to be meat for you and for all the beasts of the earth, and for every fowl of the heaven, and for all things that move upon the earth, and in which there is living soul, that they may have to eat." From these words it is understood that herbs and trees of this kind were given in common to men and to the other animals for food. But one tree, notwithstanding the general power of eating given to man, was excepted, as is found in Genesis 2, where it is said: "Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil thou shalt not eat; for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die." Secondly, these opponents say that it must be noted that different things have different modes of use. Hence the use of things that ought not to be eaten is one thing, and the use of things that may be eaten is another. Moreover, the same thing has different modes of use, because one may use the same thing in different ways: money may be used for display, and also for buying another thing; bread may be used by eating it, and also by exchanging it for another thing. Thirdly, they say that although the first parents were given power to use all temporal things in one way or another, that power of using was not the ownership which was conferred on them by God; both because they had power to use the angels, not indeed by coercion, but in another way, which is clearly gathered from the words of the blessed Augustine on 1 Corinthians 3: "For all things are yours"; and yet they did not receive ownership over the angels; and because when that ownership ceased, not all power of using ceased. Nevertheless, some power of using things, of which ownership had been given to them, did not differ at all from that ownership. For to govern and to dispose is a certain act of using. And so the power of so disposing was a power of using, and thus it was ownership. Yet it does not follow from this that every power of using was such ownership. For that power was given to other animals too, to which ownership was not given. From these points these opponents argue against the aforesaid assertion, namely that the ownership of the first parents was of the same kind as the ownership of worldly men is now.

units.la: Quia dominium primorum patentum fuit potestas ad libitum disponendi de temporalibus, quorum habuerunt dominium, secundum quod patet per auctoritates superius allegatas. Sed dominium mundanorum, & etiam dominium quod secundum illum impugnatum habuerunt Apostoli, & eorum Discipuli, ac etiam dominium quod habuerunt Iudaei conuersi in temporalibus istis, non fuit talis perfecta potestas de rebus ad libitum disponendi & regendi: quia si illud dominium habuissent, habuissent etiam ipsum in pecora, & alia animalia, quae tamen non ita obediebant eis, sicut obediussent hominibus, si in statu innocentiae permansissent. Et ita illud dominium istorum non fuit tale, quale fuit primorum parentum, vt dicunt isti impugnatores: quia illa potestas, quam dedit Christus discipulis suis, dicens Lucae 10. Ecce dedi vobis potestatem calcandi super serpentes & scorpiones & super omnem virtutem inimici & nihil vobis nocebit. Et similiter illa, quae dixit Marcus recitans verba Christi: In nomine meo daemonia eiicient, serpentes tollent, & si mortiferum quid biberint, non eis nocebit. Et vniuersaliter potestas faciendi miracula multo magis assimilatur dominio dato primis parentibus, quam dominium mundanorum vel aliorum in rebus temporalibus, quod habent quicunque ex ordinatione humana. Imo dicunt, quod dominium, quo dicitur de puero vel famulo, quod dominatur e quo domini sui: quia potest regere ad suae placitum voluntatis: & vniuersaliter omnis potestas violenta, cui resisti non potest, quantum ad aliquas conditiones morales, magis assimilatur dominio primorum parentum quam dominium quod habent quicunque in rebus temporalibus ex pacto humano praeter dominium naturale. Dominium ergo quod fuit Apostolorum & Discipulorum ipsorum ac Iudaeorum conuersorum, non fuit tale dominium, quale fuit dominium primorum parentum.
units.tr: Because the dominion of the first parents was a power, at their pleasure, to dispose of the temporal goods of which they held dominion, as is evident from the authorities cited above. But the dominion of worldly men, and also the dominion which, according to that opponent, the Apostles and their disciples had, and likewise the dominion which the converted Jews had in these temporal goods, was not such a perfect power of disposing and ruling things at will. For if they had had that dominion, they would also have had it over sheep and other animals, which nevertheless did not obey them as they would have obeyed men had they remained in the state of innocence. And so the dominion of these men was not such as that of the first parents, as these opponents say, because of the power which Christ gave to his disciples, saying (Luke 10): "Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you." Likewise is that which Mark, reporting the words of Christ, says: "In my name they shall cast out devils, they shall take up serpents, and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them." And in general the power of working miracles is much more like the dominion given to the first parents than the dominion which worldly men, or others, have over temporal things by human ordinance. Indeed they say that the dominion by which a boy or servant is said to rule over his masters, since he can direct them at his pleasure, and in general every violent power which cannot be resisted, in respect of certain moral conditions, is more like the dominion of the first parents than the dominion which all men have in temporal things by human agreement, apart from natural dominion. Therefore the dominion of the Apostles and their disciples and of the converted Jews was not such a dominion as that of the first parents.

units.la: Amplius, aut dominium primorum parentum fuit naturale: aut aliquid superadditum naturae. Si fuit naturale: tunc non fuit nisi potestas naturalis corporis & sapientiae naturalis, qua volebant omnia absque ipsorum resistentia gubernare. Ad talem autem potestatem constat, quod non reducti erant illi, de quibus in actibus fit mentio: quia natura in eis, quantum ad defectus naturales, fuit minime reparata. Si autem dominium fuit aliquid superadditum naturae: constat quod fuit aliquid absolutum: quia aliter animalia habuissent aequalem potestatem resistendi habenti tale dominium; sicut non habenti: sicut hunc habent aequalem virtutem resistendi, postquam aliquis effectus est eorum Dominus, sicut ante. Tale autem absolutum super naturale non fuit in illis, de quibus fit in actibus mentio. Ergo non habuerunt tale dominium, quale habuerunt primi parentes.
units.tr: Furthermore, the dominion of the first parents was either natural or something added to nature. If it was natural, then it was only a natural power of the body and a natural wisdom, by which they could govern all things without resistance from them. But it is certain that those of whom mention is made in the Acts were not restored to such a power, since nature in them was by no means repaired as regards its natural defects. But if the dominion was something added to nature, it is certain that it was something absolute; for otherwise the animals would have had an equal power of resisting one who held such a dominion as one who did not, just as they now have an equal power of resisting, after someone has become their lord, as before. Now such an absolute, supernatural dominion was not in those of whom mention is made in the Acts. Therefore they did not have such a dominion as the first parents had.

units.la: Ad rationem primam istius impugnati respondent, quod aliquarum rerum, quarum primo fuit communio, postea facta fuit diuisio, sed tamen non omnino eodem modo: quia alio modo fuerunt communia, & postea propria; sicut econuerso saepe alio modo aliqua sunt propria, & postea alio modo fiunt communia. Vnde primo aliqua sunt propria quo ad dominium liberum siue plenum: postea vero fiunt communia absque tali dominio libero siue pleno: sicut patet de intrantibus monasteria, & conferentibus bona sua eisdem monasteriis. Sed forte instabit ille impugnatus, quod praeter dominium quod fuit talis perfecta potestas subiiciendi & regendi, & quasi vincendi seu superandi quod habuerunt primi parentes in statu innocentiae, habuerunt dominium quod per peccatum minime perdiderunt, quamuis perderent primum. Nam nulli possunt inter se diuidere aliqua bona quo ad distincta dominia; nisi prius habeant dominium commune in diuidendis. Sed primi parentes vel filii eorum diu post peccatum diuiserunt inter se bona temporalia quo ad distincta dominia. Ergo post peccatum habuerunt commune dominium. Sed illud non acquisierunt per peccatum. Ergo ante peccatum habuerunt dominium commune. Ad hoc dicunt isti impugnatores, quod primi parentes post peccatum non habuerunt dominium commune omnium temporalium proprie loquendo de dominio: sed habebant potestatem appropriandi sibi, & etiam acquirendi commune dominium: quia quae in nullius bonis sunt, occupanti concedantur. Et ideo illa proprietas non fuit proprie dominium commune, sicut nec modo potestas appropriandi seu acquirendi illa, quae caelo terra mariq; capiuntur, est proprie dominium commune. Quia si esset proprie commune dominium nullus deberet sibi appropriare aliqua ipsorum absq; communitatis consensu. Et ideo si concedatur, quod illa potestas appropriandi fuit commune dominium, dicunt isti impugnatores, quod tale dominium non fuisset in statu innocentiae, si primi parentes non peccassent, quia ibi non fuisset potestas appropriandi. Et si quaeratur, vnde igitur habuerunt primi parentes talem potestatem appropriandi res temporales, quam non habuerunt ante peccatum? Dicunt isti, quod habuerunt illam potestatem ex natura corrupta, quia ex dictamine rationis naturalis coniuncitur, quod expedit posse peccantibus, quod etiam habent potestatem appropriandi sibi aliqua, nisi eorum aliqui eadem potestate sponte se priuent, ita quod nullus debet in principio cogi talem potestatem dimittere,
units.tr: To the first argument of this opponent they reply that, of some things of which there was at first common possession, a division was afterwards made, but not altogether in the same way: for they were held in common in one way and afterwards as private property in another; just as, conversely, some things are often held as private property in one way and afterwards become common in another way. Hence some things are at first private as to free or full dominion, but afterwards become common without such free or full dominion; as is evident in the case of those who enter monasteries and confer their goods upon those same monasteries. But perhaps this opponent will insist that, besides the dominion which was a perfect power of subjecting and ruling, and as it were of conquering or overcoming, which the first parents had in the state of innocence, they had a dominion which they did not lose through sin, although they lost the first. For no persons can divide goods among themselves as to distinct dominions unless they first have a common dominion over the things to be divided. But the first parents, or their sons, long after the sin, divided temporal goods among themselves as to distinct dominions. Therefore after the sin they had a common dominion. But they did not acquire this through sin. Therefore before the sin they had a common dominion. To this these opponents reply that the first parents after the sin did not have a common dominion over all temporal things, properly speaking of dominion; but they had the power of appropriating things to themselves, and also of acquiring a common dominion, since things which belong to no one are granted to whoever takes them into possession. And therefore that power was not properly a common dominion, just as neither is the power of appropriating or acquiring those things which are taken by sea, land and air, now properly a common dominion. For if it were properly a common dominion, no one ought to appropriate any of those things to himself without the consent of the community. And so, if it is granted that this power of appropriating was a common dominion, these opponents say that such a dominion would not have existed in the state of innocence if the first parents had not sinned, because there would not have been a power of appropriating there. And if it is asked, then whence did the first parents have such a power of appropriating temporal things, which they did not have before the sin? These men say that they had that power from corrupt nature, because it follows from the dictate of natural reason that it is expedient for sinners to be able, also, to appropriate some things to themselves, unless some of them of their own accord deprive themselves of that power; so that no one ought at the beginning to be compelled to give up such a power.

units.la: Ex isto patet, quod esto quod in primis parentibus in principio non fuerit vsus facti abomni dominio separatus quod ad res consumptibiles, tamen in utroq; ipsorum, talis vsus fuisset ab omni proprietate separatus: quia licet uterq; habuisset dominium tale, neuter tamen habuit proprietatem. Quia illa res temporalis dicitur propria, quae ita est unius, quod non est alterius hominis. Et ideo modo certum est, quod nulla fuit proprietas. Et ex illo sequitur, quod quodlibet dominium ex iure positivo introductum sit idem quod proprietas. Dominium tamen si debet vocare dominium, q; competit absq; omni iure positivo diuino & humano, non est idem quod proprietas. Patet etiam ex predictis, quod in statu innocentiae fuisset actus utendi separatus a rebus vsu consumptibilibus nó a dominio, quod est perfecta potestas subiiciendi & regendi, sed ab omni dominio, q; inter mortales est inuentu. Clare insuper ex praedictis, quod Apostoli & eorum Discipuli ac Iudaei conuersi, nec habuerunt tale dominium, quale habuerunt primi parentes ante peccatum: nec habuerunt tale dominium, si tamen vocari debet dominiu, quale habuerunt primi parentes ante diuisionem rerum: quia illi habuerunt potestatem appropriandi sibi illa quorum habuerunt tale dominium. Apostoli autem & discipuli ac Iudaei conuersi non habuerunt talem potestatem appropriandi sibi communia, sicut probatum est prius.
units.tr: From this it is clear that, even if in the first parents at the beginning there had been no use of things consumable separated from all dominion, nevertheless in each of them such a use would have been separated from all property; for although each would have had such a dominion, neither would have had property. For a temporal thing is called one's own when it so belongs to one that it does not belong to another man. And therefore it is now certain that there was no property then. And from this it follows that any dominion introduced by positive law is the same as property. Yet dominion, if it ought to be called dominion, which belongs without any positive law, divine or human, is not the same as property. It is also clear from what has been said that in the state of innocence there would have been an act of using, separated from things consumable by use, not from dominion, which is a perfect power of subjecting and ruling, but from all dominion such as is found among mortals. It is clear further from what has been said that the Apostles and their disciples and the converted Jews had neither such a dominion as the first parents had before the sin, nor such a dominion (if indeed it ought to be called dominion) as the first parents had before the division of things; for those men had the power of appropriating to themselves the things of which they had such dominion. But the Apostles and disciples and converted Jews did not have such a power of appropriating to themselves common goods, as has been proved before.

units.la: Ad secundam rationem respondent isti impugnatores, quod illud argumentum non concludit de dominio; quale habuerunt mortales post peccatum. Si autem intelligatur de alio dominio, non est ad propositum.
units.tr: To the second argument these opponents reply that the argument does not conclude about the dominion which mortals have after the sin. But if it is understood of another dominion, it is not to the point.

units.la: His dictis circa literam aliqua sunt notanda. (Equiparat statum Apostolorum &c.) Hoc dicunt esse falsum: quia Beatus Clemens comparat & non æquiparat: licet aliquo modo assimilet, quantum ad modum habendi illa temporalia. Illud potest aliquo modo concedi sic, scilicet quod Beatus Clemens assimilet vnum statum alteri quantum ad modum habendi temporalia quo ad vsum facti, non quantum ad modum habendi quo ad dominium: quia nunquam aliqui mortales habuerunt tale dominium temporalium, quale habuerunt primi parentes in statu innocentiae. Imo illud ipsimet primi parentes perdiderunt: quia primis parentibus inobedientibus Deo, omnia eis inobedientia sunt effecta. Vnde & de terra dixit sibi Deus: Spinas & tribulos germinabit tibi. Verum tamen sicut natura non fuit omnino destructa, ita nec illud dominium fuit omnino destructum, ita tamen fuit diminutum & deterioratum, quod nomine dominii non debuit appellari. Propter quod Deus benedicens Noe & filiis eius, sicut patet Genes. nono, licet potestatem prius habitam in statu innocentiae insinuaret, non esse destructam, dicens: Terror vester ac tremor sit super cuncta animalia terrae &c. tamen talem potestatem dominii nomine nullatenus appellauit. (Communis vsus) Hoc est, similis potestas vt dicum debitis circumstantiis absque omni appropriatione. (Sed per iniquitatem autem alias dixit hoc esse fiem &c.) Verum est quod si nunquam fuisset iniquitas, nunquam fuisset appropriatio talis. Et sicut mortales post peccatum facta est diuisio quantum ad dominium & proprietatem. (Omnia communia fuissent quantum ad dominium) Hoc est verum quo ad perfectam potestatem subiiciendi: quia quilibet saltem cum peruenisset ad perfectam aetatem, habuisset talem potestatem seu proprietatem. Hic insinuat & loquitur de proprietate, qualis est inter mortales. Et talis non fuisset in statu innocentiae, nec vnquam de tali proprietate loquitur scriptura, cum loquitur de dominio primorum parentum ante peccatum. Vnde proprietas secundum quod hoc nomine scientiae legales vtuntur, licet significet idem, quod dominium, accipiendo dominium, quod competit ex iure positivo, non tamen significat idem, quod dominium, accipiendo dominium secundum alias significationes, de quibus dictum est in principio istius opusculi. Vnde quamuis dicatur, ille dominatur animo suo: non propter hoc dicitur, quod ille habet proprietatem animi sui, quia secundum illum modum loquendi, tunc maxime dominatur quis voluntati suae, quando relinquit propriam voluntatem; & committit se voluntati alterius, & promptè facit, quicquid alius sibi suadet & imponit: sic etiam licet dicatur de famulo, quod dominatur equo Domini sui, non propter hoc dicitur, quod habet proprietatem equi. Et ita plures significationes habet hoc nomen dominium, quam hoc nomen proprietas. Et propter hoc dicunt isti impugnatores, quod ille impugnatus in toto illo processu sub verbis ambiguis & obscuris ac cauillose procedit. (quod patet) dicunt isti, quod illa quae sequuntur nullo modo faciunt patere illud, quod intendit. (Haec autem diuisio facta a fuit eius rei, cuius prius erat commune) Hic dicunt isti impugnatores, q; illa diuisio fuit eiusdem, cuius prius erat communio. Sed non eodem modo fuit res diuisa, quo prius fuerit communis, & ideo ex hoc, quod postea fuit propria quo ad dominium, non potest concludi, quod prius erat communis quo ad dominium. Et quia ille impugnatus hic & alibi fundat se in virtute talis propositionis: Quando aliqua communia diuiduntur, illa eodem modo sunt propria, quo prius fuerunt communia, & econuerso: quia illa negata processus diuersi nullum habent colorem. Ideo isti impugnatores plura adducunt exempla ad probandum falsitatem dictae propositionis & cuiuslibet consimilis. Primum exemplum inexpugnabile eis appareret, & est de creditoribus habentibus communia pignora aliquorum collegiorum, vel etiam aliquarum singularium personarum. Nam constat per iura, quod isti creditores habentes pignora communia in casu licite possunt vendere quibuscunq;, qui non sunt prohibiti emere ista pignora communia. Vendant ergo vnum pignus vni mercatori, & aliud alii, & aliud tertio. Hoc posito hec est diuisio illorum, quae prius erant communia: & tamen non eodem modo sunt diuisa, quo prius erant communia. Nunc enim sunt diuisa & propria quo ad dominium & proprietatem: quae tamen non erant prius communia quo ad dominium & proprietatem: quia creditores dominium & proprietatem minime habuerunt. Item, si aliqui habentes communes pecunias partem pecuniarum diuidant tidant inter mercatores & partem inter monasteria, dominium à se totaliter transferendo, pecuniæ datæ monasteriis non eodem modo fiunt propriæ monasteriis, quo pecuniæ datæ mercatoribus fiunt propriæ ipsis, & ita non eodem modo fiunt illæ pecuniæ proprię monasteriis, quo prius fuerant communes dantibus eas.
units.tr: Having said this, a few points about the text need noting. (He makes the state of the Apostles equal, etc.) They say this is false, because Blessed Clement compares rather than equates: although in some way he likens them, as far as the manner of holding those temporal goods is concerned. This can be conceded in some sense, namely that Blessed Clement likens one state to the other as regards the manner of holding temporal goods in respect of use in fact, not as regards the manner of holding in respect of ownership: because no mortals ever had such ownership of temporal goods as the first parents had in the state of innocence. Indeed, the first parents themselves lost that very thing: for when the first parents disobeyed God, all things became disobedient to them. Hence God also said to the earth: Thorns and thistles shall it bring forth to you. Yet, just as nature was not wholly destroyed, so that dominion was not wholly destroyed either; but it was diminished and debased to such an extent that it ought not to be called dominion by name. For this reason God, blessing Noah and his sons, as is clear from Genesis 9, while hinting that the power held earlier in the state of innocence was not destroyed, saying: Let the fear and dread of you be upon all the beasts of the earth, etc., nevertheless by no means called such power dominion by name. (Common use) That is, a similar power, used in due circumstances, without any appropriation. (But they say that this came to be through iniquity, etc.) It is true that if there had never been iniquity, there would never have been such appropriation. And just as after sin a division came among mortals as regards dominion and property. (All things would have been common as regards dominion) This is true as regards the perfect power of subjecting: because each person, at least once he had reached full age, would have had such power or property. Here he hints at and speaks of property such as exists among mortals. And such property did not exist in the state of innocence, nor does Scripture ever speak of such property when it speaks of the dominion of the first parents before sin. Hence property, in the sense in which the legal scholars use this name, although it signifies the same as dominion when dominion is taken as the right that arises from positive law, does not signify the same as dominion when dominion is taken in its other senses, which were spoken of at the beginning of this little work. Thus, although it is said, "he rules over his own mind," it is not for this reason said that he has the property of his own mind; because in that way of speaking, a man rules over his own will most fully when he gives up his own will, commits himself to the will of another, and readily does whatever another persuades and imposes on him. So too, although it is said of a servant that he rules his master's horse, it is not for this reason said that he has property in the horse. And so the word dominion has more meanings than the word property. And for this reason those opponents say that the author, throughout that whole argument, proceeds with ambiguous and obscure words and in a captious way. (which is evident) Those opponents say that what follows does nothing to make clear what he intends. (But this division was made of that thing of which previously there was a common holding) Here those opponents say that the division was of the very thing of which there had previously been common holding. But the thing was not divided in the same way as it had previously been common; and therefore, from the fact that it was afterwards the proper possession of someone as regards dominion, it cannot be concluded that it was previously common as regards dominion. And because the author under attack here and elsewhere founds himself on the force of this proposition: when some common things are divided, they are proper in the same way as they were previously common, and conversely: since, when this is denied, the different processes have no plausibility. Therefore those opponents adduce several examples to prove the falsity of that proposition and of any like it. The first example seems to them unanswerable, and it concerns creditors holding common pledges of some colleges, or even of some individual persons. For it is established by law that these creditors holding common pledges may in a lawful case sell them to whomever they like, provided they are not forbidden to buy those common pledges. Let them then sell one pledge to one merchant, another to another, and a third to a third. Given this, there is a division of those things which were previously common; and yet they have not been divided in the same way as they were previously common. For now they are divided and proper as regards dominion and property, which nevertheless were not previously common as regards dominion and property, since the creditors had no dominion or property at all. Likewise, if some persons holding common money divide part of the money among merchants and part among monasteries, wholly transferring dominion from themselves, the money given to the monasteries does not become the monasteries' own in the same way as the money given to the merchants becomes their own, and so that money does not become the monasteries' own in the same way as it was previously common to the givers.

units.la: Tertium exemplum est de abbate vel alia reuerenda persona dante Eleemosynam de bonis communibus pauperibus secularibus: quia illæ Eleemosynæ datæ fiunt propriæ quo ad liberam potestatem dandi, vendendi & alicui alienandi ac legandi: & tamen illo modo non fuerunt communes. Ergo illa diuisa non eodem modo fiunt propria, quo fuerunt prius communia. Quartum exemplum est de confetente bona aliqua alicui monasterio: quia illa fiunt communia, quæ prius fuerunt propria: non tamen eodem modo sunt factæ communia, quo prius erant propria. Modo enim non sunt communia quo ad liberum seu plenum dominium: neq; quo ad potestatem libere dandi, vendendi & alicui alienandi: & tamen illo modo prius erant propria. Et ita secundum istos paret aperte, quod licet aliqua diuidantur, quæ prius erant communia, non est necesse, quod eodem modo fiant propria, quo prius suerunt communia, nec econuerso. (Diuisio autem facta est rerum) hoc conceditur. (& non vsus simplicis facti) Hoc etiam conced— tamen si intelligatur cum dictione excludente pro illo tempore, quo primum facta est rerum diuisio. Tamen sæpe postea fit inter multos diuisio, tantum quo ad potestatem habendi simplicem vsum facti, sicut patet de Fratribus Minoribus, quibus diuiduntur cellæ & aliæ res multæ. Idem est de seruis & inuitatis sæpe ad mensam alicuius. (Non dicit quod vnus diceret vsum rei suæ esse: & alius alterius) Verum est, quod hoc non dicit: & tamen hoc non negauit. Unde prima diuisio rerum facta inter mortales fuit, & quo ad dominium & quo ad potestatem vtendi: quia regulariter, nisi in certis casibus, qui habet dominium rei, habet potestatem vtendi re: licet aliquando aliquis habeat dominium rei, & tamen careat potestate vtendi re, saltem ad tempus. Patet de rebus ignoratis: & ita inter dominium rei & licitam potestatem vtendi re, est differentia manifesta. (Sicque patet, quod rerum quo ad dominia, non quo ad vsum fuit facta diuisio) Hoc consequens secundum istos includit duas partes; vnam affirmatiuam, quod, scilicet quo ad dominia fuit facta diuisio, & illa est vera. Aliam negatiuam, quod, scilicet non fuit diuisio facta quo ad vsum: & hæc est falsa, accipiendo vsum pro potestate vtendi, quo modo accipit Clemens in prædicto capitulo Dilectissimi: quia particulariter facta fuit diuisio quo ad dominia: ex hac sequebatur diuisio quo ad potestatem vtendi. Tamen licet ita fuerit inter illos, qui res primitus diuiserunt: tamen inter quosdam alios posteriores sæpe facta est alio modo diuisio: quia sæpe quo ad potestatem vtendi tantummodo. (Et per consequens sequitur quod ante diuisionem quo ad rerum dominia communio erat) Istud secundum eos nullo modo sequitur, etiam licet consequens esset verum: non tamen sequeretur ex præmissis, quia, sicut ostensum est, licet aliquæ res inter aliquos diuidantur, non tamen oportet, quod isto modo fiant propriæ, quo prius fuerant communes, patet de vendentibus pignora communia mercatoribus. Dicunt tamen isti impugnatores, quod licet in propositio gratia materiæ non vi argumenti concederetur, quod ante primam diuisionem rerum res fuerint isto modo quo ad dominium, quo nunc omnes res, quæ in nullius bonis sunt, quæ occupanti conceduntur, sunt quodammodo communes quo ad dominium omnibus hominibus, vel saltem illis qui tali dominio non renunciauerunt in quantum habent potestatem diuidendi & appropriandi sibi ista quæ capiunt. Tale tamen dominium non fuit primorum parentum ante peccatum, nec fuisset in statu innocentiæ, si non peccassent, sed ante peccatum habuerunt tantummodo dominium, quod est perfecta potestas subiiciendi & regendi aliqua temporalia, & potestatem vtendi huiusmodi rebus, non autem tunc habuerunt dominium quod est potestas appropriandi & diuidendi res inter se quo ad dominia, sed tale dominium habuerunt post peccatum ante diuisionem rerum, quia in tempore medio inter tempus innocentiæ & primam diuisionem rerum habuerunt potestatem diuidendi res inter se & appropriandi sibi eas. Et ita fuit triplex tempus, scil. ante peccatum, in quo tempore habuerunt dominium, quale nunquam aliq; postea habuerit. Secundum tempus fuit post peccatum, & ante diuisionem rerum. Et in isto tempore habuerunt potestatem diuidendi & appropriandi sibi res. Et si talis potestas vocetur dominium, potest concedi, quod habuerunt dominium commune rerum. Tertium tempus fuit post diuisionem rerum. Et tunc inceperunt dominia propria, qualia nunc sunt mundanorum. (Et hoc clarius) Dicut isti quod nullo modo patet intelligenti: (Communiter data sunt) hoc est concessa sunt. Unde & verbum dandi nonnunquam accipitur pro verbo concedendi. Unde sæpe quis dat, quod non habet, quia concedit quod non habet. (Ad habendum) habere, sicut dictum est prius multipliciter accipitur. Unde & vnus modus habendi est habere quo ad licitam potestatem vtendi, & ita data sunt ad habendum, quo ad licitam potestatem vtendi, & etiam quo ad dominium ante peccatum, quod est potestas perfecta regendi &c. & post peccatum quo ad dominium, quod est potestas diuidendi inter se & appropriandi sibi: si tamen debet vocari dominium ista potestas. (Non dicit quo ad vsum facti) verum est, quod non dicit verbaliter, non tamen negauit, neq; verbaliter neq; sententialiter. Sed sententialiter dixit accipiendo vsum facti pro licita potestate vtendi: quia cum dixit: data sunt ad habendum, debet intelligi, sicut dictum est, quod data sunt ad habendum quo ad licitam potestatem vtendi. (Vsus facti habeni nullatenus potest) hoc, dicunt isti impugnatores, est erroneum, de quo inferius disseretur. (Domini fuerunt effecti.) Concedi potest vno modo accipiendo dominium, sed non accipiendo dominium pro tali dominio, quale est dominium mundanorum, vel quale fuit dominium primorum credentium, si tamen dominium appellari debet. (Dare est accipientis facere) Sicut verbum dandi accipitur multipliciter, secundum quod declaratum est prius: ita etiā verbum accipiendi accipitur multipliciter. Aliquandō enim importat dominium; aliquando importat vsum vel potestate vtendi, aliquando importat custodiam; & aliis modis accipi potest. Similiter facere esse accipientis, æquiuoce accipitur: vel quod faciat rem esse accipientis quo ad dominium: vel quo ad potestatem vtendi: vel quo ad custodiam, & multis aliis modis. Vnde sicut aliquid dicitur esse alicuius multipliciter vel quo ad dominium, vel 5 quo ad potestatem vtendi, vel quo ad custodiam, vel quo ad originem, & aliis modis quasi innumeris: ita etiam facere rem esse accipientis multipliciter dicitur, & non semper importat dominium. Propter quod etiam sic dare rem, vt sit aliquo modo accipientis, non semper importat dominium: imo aliquando nec importat dominium, nec potestatem vtendi. Et ita dicunt isti impugnatores, quod iste impugnatus per verba multiplicia errores conatur inducere. 10
units.tr: The third example concerns an abbot or other reverend person giving alms from common goods to secular poor: those alms become proper as regards the free power of giving, selling, alienating to anyone, and bequeathing, and yet in that way they were not common. Therefore that divided thing does not become proper in the same way as it was previously common. The fourth example concerns someone who grants certain goods to a monastery: those things become common which were previously proper, yet they have not become common in the same way as they were previously proper. For now they are not common as regards full or free dominion, nor as regards the power of freely giving, selling, or alienating to anyone, and yet previously they were proper in that way. So, according to these men, it is plainly evident that although some things are divided which were previously common, it is not necessary that they become proper in the same way as they were previously common, nor conversely. (The division of things was indeed made) this is conceded. (and not the simple use of fact) This too is conceded, provided it is understood with the excluding phrase "for that time," namely the time when the first division of things was made. Yet often afterwards a division is made among many people only as regards the power of having simple use of the fact, as is clear of the Friars Minor, among whom cells and many other things are divided. The same holds of servants and of those often invited to someone's table. (It does not say that one would say the use of his own thing is his, and another's of another's) It is true that it does not say this, yet it did not deny it. Hence the first division of things made among mortals was both as regards dominion and as regards the power of using, for as a rule, except in certain cases, whoever has dominion of a thing has the power of using it, although sometimes someone has dominion of a thing and yet lacks the power of using it, at least for a time. This is clear of things unknown to their owner; and so between dominion of a thing and lawful power of using it there is a manifest difference. (And so it is plain that the division of things was made as regards dominions, not as regards use) This consequence, according to these men, contains two parts: one affirmative, that the division was made as regards dominions, and this is true; the other negative, that the division was not made as regards use, and this is false, taking use to mean the power of using, as Clement takes it in the aforesaid chapter Dilectissimi. For in particular the division was made as regards dominions, and from this followed division as regards the power of using. Yet although it was so among those who first divided the things, among certain later persons a division has often been made in another way, namely often as regards the power of using only. (And consequently it follows that before the division there was common ownership as regards the dominions of things) According to these men this does not follow in any way, even if the consequent were true; nor would it follow from the premises, because, as has been shown, although some things are divided among some persons, it is not necessary that they become proper in the same way as they were previously common, as is clear of those who sell common pledges to merchants. These opponents, however, say that although in the proposition, for the sake of the matter and not by force of argument, it might be conceded that before the first division of things, things were in that way as regards dominion, in which all things that belong to no one's goods, and which are granted to whoever takes them, are in some sense common to all men as regards dominion, or at least to those who have not renounced such dominion, insofar as they have the power of dividing and appropriating to themselves what they take. Yet such dominion did not belong to the first parents before sin, nor would it have belonged to them in the state of innocence had they not sinned. Before sin they had only dominion, which is the complete power of subjecting and governing temporal things, and the power of using such things; they did not then have the dominion which is the power of appropriating and dividing things among themselves as regards dominions. They had that dominion after sin and before the division of things, because in the interval between the time of innocence and the first division of things they had the power of dividing things among themselves and appropriating them to themselves. Thus there were three times: before sin, in which they had a dominion such as no one has had since; the second time, after sin and before the division of things, in which they had the power of dividing and appropriating things to themselves; and if such a power is to be called dominion, it may be conceded that they had a common dominion of things; the third time, after the division of things, when proper dominions began, such as worldly people now have. (And this more clearly) These men say what in no way is plain to an intelligent reader. (Commonly given) that is, granted; hence the verb "to give" is sometimes taken for the verb "to grant," and so someone often gives what he does not have, because he grants what he does not have. (To have) having, as was said before, is taken in many ways. Hence one way of having is to have as regards lawful power of using, and so things are given to be had, as regards lawful power of using, and also as regards dominion before sin, which is the complete power of governing, and after sin as regards dominion, which is the power of dividing among themselves and appropriating to themselves, if indeed this power ought to be called dominion. (He does not say as regards use of fact) It is true that he does not say it in words, yet he did not deny it, neither in words nor in sense. But he said it in sense, taking use of fact to mean lawful power of using, for when he said given to be had, it must be understood, as was said, that they are given to be had as regards lawful power of using. (Use of fact can in no way be had) This, say these opponents, is erroneous, and it will be discussed below. (They were made owners) This can be conceded in one sense of dominion, but not if dominion is taken as the dominion of worldly people, or as the dominion of the first believers, if indeed it ought to be called dominion. (To give is to make it the receiver's) Just as the verb "to give" is taken in many ways, as was explained before, so also the verb "to receive" is taken in many ways. For sometimes it implies dominion, sometimes it implies use or power of using, sometimes it implies custody, and it can be taken in other ways. Likewise "to make something be the receiver's" is ambiguous: either that one makes the thing the receiver's as regards dominion, or as regards power of using, or as regards custody, and in many other ways. Therefore, just as something is said to belong to someone in many ways, either as regards dominion, or as regards power of using, or as regards custody, or as regards origin, and in almost countless other ways, so also to make a thing belong to the receiver is said in many ways, and does not always imply dominion. For which reason also to give a thing so that it is in some way the receiver's does not always imply dominion; indeed sometimes it implies neither dominion nor power of using. And so these opponents say that this man, by many words, tries to induce errors.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAP. XV.

units.la: DEinde subiungit Beatus Clemens sic: Istius enim consuetudinis morte retento, Apostoli eorumq; discipuli vna nobiscum & vobiscum communem vitam duxerunt. Vt enim bene nostis, erat multitudinis credentium cor vnum, & anima vna. Nec quisquam eorum aut nostrum de his quae possidebat esse dicebat aliquid suum, sed omnia nobis & istis erant communia. In quibus verbis supponit Beatus Clemens aperte, quod ante conuersionem illorum Iudaeorum, de qua mentio habetur Act. 2. & 4. ca. Apostoli & eorum discipuli aliqua possidebant ibi, cum dicit: Apostoli eorumq; discipuli, vna nobiscum & vobiscum: Et loquitur de Iudeis conuersis, qui communem vitam duxerunt. Et in quo erat illa communis vita, declarat, dicens: erat enim multitudinis credentium cor vnum, & anima vna. Nec quisquam eorum (scilicet Apostolorum: & ipsorum discipulorum, de quibus locutus est supra) aut nostrum (scilicet Iudaeorum conuersorum) de his quae possidebat. Ecce aperte dicit, quod Apostoli & discipuli aliqua possidebant ante. Sequitur: aliquid suum esse dicebat, (scilicet conversis) & istis (scilicet Apostolis) & eorum discipulis erant communia. Sic quod per praedictum capitulum clare patet, quod ante conuersionem Iudaeorum praedicta Apostoli & eorum discipuli aliqua habebant: & quod ista communicauerunt Iudeis conuersis: & quod Iudei conversi communicauerunt Apostolis & discipulis eorum similiter qua habebant. Ita quod quisquam eorum, scilicet Apostolorum & discipulorum ac Iudaeorum conversorum, eorum quae possidebat, nihil esse suum dicebat, sed omnia erant communia inter ipsos. 15 20 25
units.tr: Next Blessed Clement adds this: "For, the custom of that life being maintained, the Apostles and their disciples lived a common life with us and with you. For, as you well know, the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul. Nor did any of them, whether of them or of us, say that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to us and to them." In these words Blessed Clement clearly assumes that, before the conversion of those Jews mentioned in Acts 2 and 4, the Apostles and their disciples possessed some things. When he says "the Apostles and their disciples, with us and with you," he is speaking of the converted Jews, who lived a common life. He explains in what that common life consisted, saying: "For the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul. Nor did any of them" (namely of the Apostles and of their disciples, of whom he spoke above) "or of us" (namely of the converted Jews) "possessed anything." Here he plainly says that the Apostles and disciples possessed some things before. He goes on: "said that anything was his own" (namely the converts), "and to them" (namely the Apostles) "and their disciples, all things were common." So the passage clearly shows that before the conversion of the Jews the Apostles and their disciples had some things, that they shared these with the converted Jews, and that the converted Jews shared likewise what they had with the Apostles and disciples. So none of them, that is of the Apostles and disciples and converted Jews, said that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common among them.

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnatus per praedictum capitulum Clementis conatur ostendere, quod Apostoli & Discipuli, ante conuersionem Iudaeorum, de quibus in Actibus fit mentio, aliqua possidebant: quia dicit, quod ex dicto capitulo colligitur, quod Apostoli & eorum discipuli communicauerunt Iudeis conversis illa quae habebant: & econuerso. Igitur ante dictam conuersionem aliqua possidebant. 30
units.tr: In this part, the author under attack tries to show from this chapter of Clement that the Apostles and disciples, before the conversion of the Jews mentioned in the Acts, possessed some things, because he says that it follows from that chapter that the Apostles and their disciples shared what they had with the converted Jews, and conversely. Therefore, before that conversion, they possessed some things.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores magis volentes, vt asserunt, impugnare mentem quam verba, dicunt quod licet verba praedicta istius impugnati extense accepto vocabulo possidendi sensum verum possent habere: tamen accipiendo vocabulum possidendi magis stricte pro eo quod possidetur iure proprietatis & dominii, sicut accipit ille impugnatus, verba illa erronea sunt censenda, quantum ad hoc quod asserunt Apostolos ante conuersionem dictorum Iudaeorum aliqua iure proprietatis & dominii posscdisse, & illa communitati credentium contulisse: quia vt dicunt, & probatum est prius, & inferius amplius ostendetur, Apostoli postquam fuerunt ad Apostolatum assumpti, nihil iure proprietatis & dominii possidebant, hoc est detinebant ad vsum vel facultatem vtendi. 35 40
units.tr: But these opponents, who, as they assert, wish to attack the meaning rather than the words, say that although the words of the author under attack could have a true sense if the word "possess" is taken broadly, yet if the word "possess" is taken more strictly for what is held by the right of ownership and dominion, as that author takes it, those words must be judged erroneous, insofar as they assert that the Apostles, before the conversion of those Jews, possessed some things by right of ownership and dominion and contributed them to the community of believers. For, as they say, and it has been proved already and will be shown further below, the Apostles, after they were called to the apostolate, possessed nothing by right of ownership and dominion; that is, they held nothing for use or for the faculty of using it.

units.la: Quod vt appareat videamus literam. (Istius enim consuetudinis) scilicet communem vitam ducendi. Communem vitam duxerunt, viuendo videlicet de communibus. Non enim hic vita accipitur pro primo actu animae: sed accipitur pro sustentari, vt dicatur communem vitam ducere, qui de communibus sustentatur. Et ideo, quando communia diuiduntur inter ducentes communem vitam, adhuc remanent aliquo modo communia, sicut prius: sed diuiduntur, vt pro illo tempore quilibet licite vtatur portione sibi assignata. Et ideo quandocunq; credentes sustentabantur de diuisis, adhuc erant communia. (Quae possidebat) Super hoc dicit Glossa in decretis sic: dic possidebat, id est, detinebat, sicut superius dicitur possidere. Ex illa Glossa clare patet, quod in Actibus & in ca. praedicta Clementis verbum possidendi accipitur pro verbo detinendi: illo modo super dicitur possidere, id est, detinere: qui tamen nullum habet dominium in his, quae possidet seu detinet. Et ita ex isto toto capitulo non 45 50 poterit concludi, nisi forte quod Apostoli aliqua detinebant antea vel cum dominio vel sine dominio. Aliud notant isti impugnatores, quod cum dicitur, quae possidebat, debet referri ad tempus illud, quo erant communia, non ad tempus praecedens: quia dicitur possidebat, quod est verbum temporis imperfecti: non possederat, quod est verbum temporis plusquamperfecti. Et ideo necesse est, quod ibi accipiatur verbum possidendi pro verbo detinendi, & non pro habere dominium. Quia aliter esset oppositio in adiecto: Nec quisquam eorum, quae possidebat aliquid suum esse dicebat: quia ille esset sensus, nec quisquam eorum, quorum tunc habebat dominium, aliquid suum esse dicebat. (Omnia nobis & istis erant communia) scilicet quo ad potestatem sustentandi per illa vno modo vel alio: & secundum istos ex hoc non potest probari, quod erant omnibus Apostolis & aliis communia, quoad dominium etiam tale, quale conuersi, & forte aliqui Discipuli Apostolorum habuerunt. Ad cuius 55 60 euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum: quod de discipulis Apostolorum erant aliqui, qui ante dictam communitatem credentium poterant habere in speciali, & in communi, sicut inferius declarare nitentur. (Supponit Beatus Clemens aperte quod ante conuersionem &c.) Dicunt quod accipiendo verbum possidendi pro verbo detinendi, nec aperte supponit nec negat. Tamé est verum, siue supponatur, siue Non. Sed accipiendo verbum possidendi pro habere iure proprietatis & dominii: sic est omnino contra intentionem Clementis. (Communem vsum duxerunt.) Expositum est prius. (Apostoli & Discipuli aliqua possidebant ante.) Verum est quo ad Apostolos, quod aliqua possidebant ad facultatem vel actum vtendi. (Erant communia &c.) Ad sustentandum omnes, scilicet Apostolos, & alios. Ad hoc enim erant, vt scilicet omnes sustentarentur. (Aliqua habebant) ad vsum. (Illa communicauerunt Iudaei conuersi.) Volendo scilicet quod Iudaei conuersi vterentur eis, si indigerent. (Communicauerunt Apostoli.) Non dando eis proprietatem ipsorum, sed volendo quod Apostoli sustentarentur de eis, si indigerent. (Quae possidebant.) Detinebant, sicut prius. (Suum) id est, proprium.
units.tr: Let us look at the text to see this. ("For the custom of that life," namely of living a common life.) They led a common life, that is, living on common goods. For here "life" is not taken for the first act of the soul, but for sustenance, so that one who is sustained from common goods is said to lead a common life. And so, when common goods are divided among those who lead a common life, they still remain common in some sense, as before, but they are divided so that for that time each may lawfully use the portion assigned to him. Therefore, whenever the believers were sustained from what was divided, the goods were still common. ("What he possessed.") On this the Gloss on the Decretum says: "Say 'possessed,' that is, held, as above it is said 'to possess.'" From that Gloss it is clear that in Acts and in the aforementioned chapter of Clement the word "possess" is taken for the word "hold," in the same way as above "to possess" means "to hold," though such a person has no dominion over what he possesses or holds. And so from this whole chapter nothing can be concluded, except perhaps that the Apostles previously held some things, either with dominion or without dominion. These opponents also note that when it says "what he possessed," it must be referred to the time when they were common, not to the earlier time, because it says "possessed," which is a verb of the imperfect tense, not "had possessed," which is a verb of the pluperfect tense. Therefore it is necessary that the word "possess" be taken there for "hold," and not for "have dominion." Otherwise there would be a contradiction in the terms: "Nor did any of them say that anything which he possessed was his own," since the sense would be: "nor did any of them say that anything over which he then had dominion was his own." ("All things were common to us and to them.") Namely as regards the power of sustaining oneself by these in one way or another; and according to these opponents, it cannot be proved from this that all the Apostles and others had common goods even in the sense of dominion of the kind the converts had, and perhaps some disciples of the Apostles had such.
