For clarity on this, they say it must be known that among the disciples of the Apostles there were some who, before the said community of believers, could have things individually and in common, as they will try to declare below. ("Blessed Clement clearly assumes that before the conversion," etc.) They say that, taking the word "possess" for the word "hold," he neither clearly assumes nor denies it. Still it is true, whether it is assumed or not. But taking the word "possess" for "have by right of ownership and dominion," this is wholly contrary to Clement's intention. ("They led a common use.") This has been explained before. ("The Apostles and disciples possessed some things before.") It is true, as regards the Apostles, that they possessed some things for the faculty or act of using them. ("Were common, etc.") For sustaining all, namely the Apostles and others. For this was the purpose, that all should be sustained. ("Had some things") for use. ("The converted Jews shared those things.") Namely by intending that the converted Jews should use them if they were in need. ("The Apostles shared.") Not by giving them their own property, but by intending that the Apostles should be sustained from them if they were in need. ("What they possessed.") They held, as before. ("Suum") that is, their own.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAP. XVI.

units.la: Item in eo, quod dicit, quod Apostoli post Petri verba illa: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia &c. vsi sunt rebus consumptibilibus vsu: dicimus esse falsum: quia in rebus vsu consumptibilibus, vsus proprie sumptus haberi nequit, nec ipsis aliquis potest vti, vt superius est ostensum.
units.tr: Likewise, as to what he says, that after Peter's words, "Behold, we have left all things," etc., the Apostles used consumable things by use: we say this is false, because in consumable things, use taken properly cannot be had, nor can anyone make use of them, as was shown above.

units.la: In illa parte respondet ad illud, quod assumpsit appellans, quod Apostoli post verba Petri: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, rebus vsu consumptibilibus vtebantur, dicens hoc esse falsum: quia in talibus rebus, vsus proprie sumptus haberi non potest.
units.tr: In that part he answers what the objector assumed, that after Peter's words, "Behold, we have left all things," the Apostles used consumable things. He says this is false, because in such things use taken properly cannot be had.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, quod in his verbis tres dogmatizat errores: & praeter hoc intentionem appellauit, & rationem minime tangit. Primus error, vt dicunt, hic contentus est, quod Apostoli post illa verba Petri: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, rebus vsu consumptibilibus minime vtebantur. Secundus est, quod in rebus consumptibilibus vsus proprie sumptus haberi non potest. Tertius est, quod talibus rebus non potest vti. Primum, vt dicunt, est omnino erroneum: quia contra scripturas diuinam in multis locis, quae Apostolos asserit post verba Petri praedicta coenasse cum Christo & comedisse ac bibisse. Secundum improbatum est prius, vbi ostensum est, quod vsus proprie sumptus in talibus rebus potest haberi. Et de tertio etiam dictum est prius. Secundo dicunt isti impugnatores, quod iste impugnatus intentionem appellantis minime tangit. Appellans enim non plus probare intendit, nisi quod potest quis manducare & bibere, & vestibus indui, ac actus consimiles circa res vsu consumptibiles exercere, absque eorum dominio seu proprietate. Vtitur autem talibus vocabulis vsus, vti & consimilibus: quia talibus vtitur scriptura diuina, cuius modum loquendi nemini est licitum reprobare. Unde quantum ad mentem appellantis sufficit ostendere, quod actus consumendi res vsu consumptibiles, siue consumptio huiusmodi rerum, potest a proprietate & dominio separari. Cum igitur constet, quod Apostoli consumpserint res vsu consumptibiles post illa verba Petri: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, in istis rebus non habuerunt dominium seu proprietatem; Appellans habet intentum scilicet quod actus consumendi res vsu consumptibiles potest a proprietate & dominio separari: quia quantum ad mentem appellantis tantum valet dicere actus consumendi potest in huiusmodi rebus a proprietate seu dominio separari, sicut quod vsus potest in huiusmodi rebus a proprietate seu dominio separari.
units.tr: But these opponents say that in these words he teaches three errors, and besides this he has missed the objector's intention and does not touch the argument at all. The first error, as they say, is contained in this, that the Apostles after those words of Peter, "Behold, we have left all things," did not use consumable things at all. The second is that in consumable things use taken properly cannot be had. The third is that one cannot make use of such things. The first, they say, is altogether erroneous, because it is contrary to divine Scripture in many places, which states that the Apostles, after the words of Peter mentioned, dined with Christ and ate and drank. The second has been refuted before, where it was shown that use taken properly can be had in such things. Of the third too it was said before. Secondly, these opponents say that this refuter does not touch the objector's intention. For the objector intends to prove no more than that a person can eat and drink, be clothed, and perform similar acts with consumable things, without ownership or property of them. He uses such words as "use," "to use," and similar, because divine Scripture uses such words, and no one is permitted to reject its manner of speaking. Hence, as far as the objector's meaning goes, it is enough to show that the act of consuming consumable things, or the consumption of such things, can be separated from property and ownership. Since it is established that the Apostles consumed consumable things after Peter's words, "Behold, we have left all things," they had no ownership or property in these things. The objector's point is that the act of consuming consumable things can be separated from property and ownership. For, as far as the objector's meaning goes, to say that the act of consuming can be separated from property or ownership in such things is worth just as much as to say that use can be separated from property or ownership in such things.

units.la: Explicemus itaque literam. (Vsi sunt) Hic est modus loquendi scripturae Diuinae. Unde Iosue 5. Desecit manna postquam comederunt de frugibus terrae: nec vsi sunt vltra cibo illo filii Israel. Et ita appellans serviit manna, postquam comederunt de frugibus terrae: nec vsi sunt vltra cibo illo filii Israel. (Dicimus esse falsum.) Hic dicunt isti impugnatores, quod hoc Diuinae scripturae repugnat. Quia sicut patet per auctoritatem praeallegatam sumptam ex Iosue 5. Qui manducat res vsu consumptibiles, vtitur eis. Certum autem est, quod manducauerunt res vsu consumptibiles, vtitur eis. Unde dicunt, quod licet assertio istius, cum dicit quod Apostoli nec vsi fuerunt eis. Igitur vsi fuerunt rebus consumptibilibus vsu, sit tam ridiculosa & puerilis, vt qui non viderunt quam vsi fuerunt rebus consumptibilibus vsu, vix credere possint, quod hoc asserat, & videatur multis quod intellectus, qui proscripturas ipsius, vix credere possint, quod hoc asserat, & videatur multis quod intellectus, qui prior ex verbis istius colligitur, nulli homini, qui habet vsum rationis, debet imponi, sed tantummodo ex verbis istius colligitur, nulli homini, qui habet vsum rationis, debet imponi, sed tantummodo isti impugnatores in hoc & in consimilibus ignorantiam modorum loquendi, & conatus errores inducendi per nouas vocum impositiones &c. deberet ascribi. Et tamen propter hoc nequit de haeresi excusari: quia secundum Beatum Hieronymum ex verbis inordinate prolatis incurritur haeresis excusari. (In rebus vsu consumptibilibus vsus proprie sumptus haberi nequit.) Illud dicunt omnino esse erroneum. (In rebus vsu consumptibilibus, vsus iuris proprie sumptus habere nequit: haec tamen, in huiusmodi rebus vsus proprie sumptus haberi nequit, est nullatenus concedendum. Haec tamen, in huiusmodi rebus vsus proprie sumptus haberi nequit: haec tamen, quia scriptura dicit, & aliae scientiae proprie loquendo concedunt, quod contingit habere vsum rerum vsu consumptibilium: sed non concedunt, quod proprie loquendo contingit habere vsum iuris talium rerum. Imo nullae scientiae nisi legales vtuntur vocabulo vsus in tali significatione. (Nec istius aliquis potest vti.) Illud dicunt esse omnino erroneum, sicut inferius ostendetur. (Vt superius est ostensum) scilicet sophistice, vt dicunt isti.
units.tr: Let us then explain the letter. "They used" (vsi sunt): this is the manner of speaking of divine Scripture. Hence Joshua 5: "The manna ceased after they had eaten of the fruits of the land; nor did the children of Israel use that food any longer." And so the objector follows this, saying that the manna ceased after they ate of the fruits of the land, and the children of Israel no longer used that food. "We say this is false": here these opponents say that this contradicts divine Scripture. For, as is plain from the authority cited above, taken from Joshua 5, whoever eats consumable things uses them. It is certain that they ate consumable things, and so they used them. Hence they say that the assertion of this man, that the Apostles did not use them, is so ridiculous and childish that those who have not seen it can hardly believe he asserts it, and it seems to many that the meaning which is gathered first from his words should not be imputed to any man who has the use of reason; rather, the ignorance of modes of speech, and the attempt to induce errors through new impositions of words, should be ascribed to these opponents in this and similar matters. Yet on account of this he cannot be excused from heresy, because according to Blessed Jerome, heresy is incurred from words carelessly uttered. (In consumable things use taken properly cannot be had.) They say this is altogether erroneous. (In consumable things, the use of right taken properly cannot be had; yet this, that in such things use taken properly cannot be had, is by no means to be conceded.) Yet this, that in such things use taken properly cannot be had, is conceded because Scripture says so and other disciplines, speaking properly, concede that one may have the use of consumable things; but they do not concede that, properly speaking, one may have the right of use of such things. Indeed, no disciplines except legal ones use the word "use" in that sense. (Nor can anyone make use of such things.) They say this is altogether erroneous, as will be shown below. (As was shown above.) Namely, sophistically, as these men say.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: Item in eo, quod dicit Beatum Augustinum dixisse, voluisse rerum omnium abdicationem, dicit falsum. Hoc enim Beatus Augustinus non dixit: sed cum recitasset, Apostolos dixisse: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, & secuti fumus te, subiunxit: Hoc votum potissime vouerant. Dic mihi, quid est illud votum quod vouerunt? Certe dicit non potest, quod votum illud esset abdicationis dominii, seu proprietatis omnium temporalium rerum: cum de hoc in praecedentibus, seu subsequentibus nullam fecerit mentionem. Quid igitur est illud votum? Certe videtur quod voluerant se Dominum secuturos: de quo immediate mentio habita erat ibi, secuti fumus te. Et si dicatur, quod imo voluerant sereliquturos omnia, & Dominum secuturos: quia praecesserant verba illa, tamen dixisset: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, & secuti sumus te. Dicimus, quod non est verisimile, quod Beatus Augustinus intellexerit, quod in voto huiusmodi, scilicet quod reliquimus omnia, intelligantur illa comprehensa, quae Scriptura sacra postea asserit eos habuisse: sicut sunt, qua ipsos habuisse superius est probatum. Item, non est intelligendum, quod Beatus Augustinus intellexerit, quod ipsi Apostoli voluerunt nihil habere aliud in communi: cum intendens iuxta vitam Apostolicam suam religionem fundare, loquens suis fratribus sic dixerit in Regula sua: sit anima una, & cor unum in Domino, & non dicatis aliquid proprium: sed sint vobis omnia communia: & distribuatur unicuique vestrum, prout opus erit. Et sequitur: sic enim legistis in Actibus Apostolorum, quia erant omnia communia: & distribuebantur unicuique prout opus erat. Cum igitur Beatus Augustinus, & eius fratres, res habuerint, & habeant in communi: non est revocandum in dubium, quin Beatus Augustinus Apostolos habuisse supposuerit in communi. Quare per auctoritatem praedictam Augustini, iste haereticus nequaquam potest concludere, quod Apostoli voto abdicaverunt omnium rerum dominium, nec quod illud abdicaverunt in proprio & in communi.
units.tr: Likewise, in saying that Blessed Augustine said he willed the renunciation of all things, he speaks falsely. For Blessed Augustine did not say this. After reciting that the Apostles said, "Behold, we have left all things, and have followed you," he added: "They had especially vowed this vow." Tell me, what is that vow they vowed? Surely he cannot say that this vow was the renunciation of ownership, or of the property of all temporal things, since he made no mention of this in what precedes or follows. What then is that vow? Surely it seems that they had vowed to follow the Lord, which was mentioned immediately before: "we have followed you." And if it is said that, on the contrary, they had vowed to leave all things and to follow the Lord, because those words had gone before, yet he would have said: "Behold, we have left all things, and have followed you." We say that it is not likely that Blessed Augustine understood that in a vow of this kind, namely that we have left all things, those things were included which Holy Scripture afterwards asserts they had, as it has been proved above that they had them. Likewise, it is not to be understood that Blessed Augustine meant that the Apostles themselves wished to have nothing in common, since, intending to found his religious community on the apostolic life, he spoke thus to his brothers in his Rule: "Let there be one soul and one heart in the Lord, and do not call anything your own, but let all things be common to you, and let distribution be made to each of you as need requires." And it follows: "For thus you have read in the Acts of the Apostles, that all things were common, and distribution was made to each as he had need." Since therefore Blessed Augustine and his brothers have had, and do have, things in common, it is not to be doubted that Blessed Augustine supposed the Apostles to have had things in common. Wherefore, by the aforesaid authority of Augustine, this heretic can by no means conclude that the Apostles by vow renounced ownership of all things, nor that they renounced it both individually and in common.

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnatus respondet ad illud, quod de voto Apostolorum in obiectione praemissa tangit appellans. Dicens primo quod Beatus Augustinus non dicit Apostolos voluisse abdicationem omnium rerum. Secundo dicit, quod fuit illud votum, de quo loquitur Augustinus, ibi: Quidigitur &c. dicens, quod voluerunt sequi Dominum. Tertio ibi: Et si dicatur, obiicit contra se. Quarto ibi: Dicimus, respondet primo dicens: quod Augustinus sub primo voto comprehendit illa, quae scriptura Apostolos asserit habuisse. Secundo ibi: Item non est, dicit quod Augustinus non intellexit, quod Apostoli abdicaverunt omnia in communi. Quod conatur probare per hoc, quod regula Beati Augustini est fundata iuxta vitam Apostolicam: & tamen fratres sui habent aliquid in communi. Ultimo ibi, quare per auctoritatem, concludit per auctoritate Beati August. non potest concludi, quod Apostoli abdicaverunt dominium omnium rerum: nec illud abdicaverunt in proprio & in communi.
units.tr: In this part, the man attacked replies to what the objector touches on concerning the vow of the Apostles in the preceding objection. First, he says that Blessed Augustine does not say that the Apostles wished the renunciation of all things. Second, he says what that vow was, of which Augustine speaks, at "Quid igitur etc.", saying that they wished to follow the Lord. Third, at "Et si dicatur", he raises an objection against himself. Fourth, at "Dicimus", he answers, first saying that Augustine included under the first vow those things which Scripture asserts the Apostles had. Second, at "Item non est", he says that Augustine did not understand that the Apostles renounced all things in common. He tries to prove this by the fact that Blessed Augustine's Rule is founded on the apostolic life, and yet his brothers have something in common. Last, at "Quare per auctoritatem", he concludes that by the authority of Blessed Augustine it cannot be concluded that the Apostles renounced ownership of all things, nor that they renounced it individually and in common.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores impugnat praedicta quantum ad sex. In primo enim ostendunt, quod Apostoli voluerunt abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum in speciali. Secundo quod voluerunt abdicationem proprietatis omnium in speciali & in communi. Tertio quod Augustinus hoc sensit. Quarto quod specialiter probant, quod voluerunt abdicationem dominii illarum rerum, quas Scriptura asserit eos aliquo modo habuisse. Quinto quod licet Regula Beati Augustini iuxta vitam Apostolicam sit fundata: tamen non tangat ad ultimam perfectionem vitae Apostolicae. Sexto quod medium per quod probat Apostolos habuisse dominium aliquarum rerum in communi, non concludit.
units.tr: But these attackers assail the aforesaid points in six ways. In the first, they show that the Apostles willed the renunciation of ownership of all temporal things individually. Second, that they willed the renunciation of ownership of all things both individually and in common. Third, that Augustine thought this. Fourth, that they prove specifically that they willed the renunciation of ownership of those things which Scripture asserts they had in some way. Fifth, that although Blessed Augustine's Rule is founded on the apostolic life, it does not reach the ultimate perfection of the apostolic life. Sixth, that the means by which he proves that the Apostles had ownership of some things in common does not conclude.

units.la: Primum, scilicet quod Apostoli voluerunt abdicationem proprietatis omnium temporalium in speciali, ostendunt primo sic. Ad perfectionem vitae Apostolicae pertinebat perfectionem sciendi assumptam postea nequaquam relinquere, iuxta illud Saluatoris Lucae 9. Nemo mittens manum suam ad aratrum & aspiciens retro aptus est regno Dei. Ad quem autem pertinet perfectionem assumptam non quaquam relinquere, ad eundem pertinet se in eadem perfectione voto firmare. Ad perfectionem igitur vitae Apostolicae pertinebat se in assumpta perfectione voto firmare. Sed teste Beato Petro, cum dicit: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, Apostoli proprietatem omnium temporalium abiecerunt sicut ostensum est prius, & inferius amplius ostendetur. Igitur Apostoli se in dicta temporalium abiectione voto firmaverunt, & per consequens voluerunt abdicationem proprietatis omnium temporalium saltem in speciali. Secundo sic arguunt. Votum religiosorum profitentium regulam beati Augustini, vel regulam beati Benedicti, non est perfectius voto Apostolorum de eodem. Sed Apostoli voluerunt aliquam paupertatem, & dicti religiosi etiam vouent paupertatem. Ergo votum paupertatis praedictorum religiosorum non est perfectius, quam fuerit votum paupertatis Apostolorum. Dicti autem religiosi vouent abdicationem proprietatis omnium temporalium in speciali. Ergo Apostoli voluerunt abdicationem proprietatis omnium temporalium saltem in speciali. Tertio sic: sicut qui aliquam rem perfecte relinquit, ipsam non potest resumere: sic qui perfecte relinquit voluntatem habendi, non potest voluntatem habendi resumere. Unde perfecte relinquere voluntatem habendi, non est a voluntate habendi desistere. Tunc enim quilibet quando dormiret relinqueret voluntatem habendi. Sed ad laudem Apostolorum, dicit Glossa super illud Matth. 19. Ecce nos reliquimus omnia: quod ipsi reliquerunt voluntatem habendi. Et Gregorius dicit, quod Petrus & Andreas dimiserunt desideria habendi. Ergo voluntatem habendi non potuerunt resumere. Sed qui sic relinquit voluntatem habendi, quod eam resumere nequit, vouet non habere. Si enim non voueret, posset resumere, sicut prius. Apostoli ergo voluerunt non habere temporalia. Quod debet intelligi quantum ad proprietatem & dominium: ita voluerunt abdicationem proprietatis omnium temporalium saltem in communi. Quarto sic: Apostoli non imperfectius seruauerunt consilia Euangelica, quam Pharisaei, scribae & alii sub lege veteri constituti, seruauerunt consilia legis veteris. Non enim obliti fuerunt verborum sui Magistri dicentis Matth. 5. Dico autem vobis, quia nisi abundaverit iustitia vestra plusquam Scribarum & Pharisaeorum non intrabitis in regnum caelorum. Audistis quia dictum est antiquis &c. vbi Christus in sinuauit aperte, quod legem Euangelicam debuerunt Apostoli perfectius seruare, quam antiqui seruauerunt legem Mosaicam. Et ideo non imperfectius debuerunt seruare consilia Euangelica, quam illi seruauerint consilia veteris legis. Sed nonnulli Pharisaei & Scribae ac alii sub lege veteri constituti, nonnulla consilia legis veteris sub voto seruauerunt. Patet de Nazareis Numer. 6. & tert. cap. vbi scribitur: Hoc offeretis Domino in solennitatibus vestris praeter vota & oblationes spontaneas. Et
units.tr: The first point, namely that the Apostles willed the renunciation of ownership of all temporal things individually, they show first as follows. It belonged to the perfection of the apostolic life never afterwards to abandon the perfection once undertaken, according to that saying of the Saviour in Luke 9: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God." Now whoever belongs to not abandoning afterwards the perfection undertaken, belongs also to binding himself by vow to that same perfection. Therefore it belonged to the perfection of the apostolic life to bind themselves by vow to the perfection undertaken. But by the testimony of Blessed Peter, when he says, "Behold, we have left all things," the Apostles renounced the ownership of all temporal things, as was shown before and will be shown more fully below. Therefore the Apostles bound themselves by vow to that renunciation of temporal things, and consequently they willed the renunciation of ownership of all temporal things at least individually. Secondly, they argue thus. The vow of religious professing the Rule of Blessed Augustine or the Rule of Blessed Benedict is not more perfect than the vow of the Apostles concerning the same matter. But the Apostles willed a certain poverty, and the said religious also vow poverty. Therefore the vow of poverty of the said religious is not more perfect than the vow of poverty of the Apostles was. But the said religious vow the renunciation of ownership of all temporal things individually. Therefore the Apostles willed the renunciation of ownership of all temporal things at least individually. Thirdly, thus: just as one who perfectly relinquishes some thing cannot take it up again, so one who perfectly relinquishes the will to have cannot resume the will to have. Hence to relinquish perfectly the will to have is not to cease from the will to have. For then anyone who was asleep would relinquish the will to have. But to the praise of the Apostles, the Gloss on that passage of Matthew 19, "Behold, we have left all things," says that they relinquished the will to have. And Gregory says that Peter and Andrew put aside the desires of having. Therefore they could not resume the will to have. But one who so relinquishes the will to have that he cannot resume it, vows not to have. For if he did not vow, he could resume it, as before. Therefore the Apostles willed not to have temporal things. This must be understood with respect to ownership and dominion: thus they willed the renunciation of ownership of all temporal things at least in common. Fourthly, thus: the Apostles did not observe the evangelical counsels more imperfectly than the Pharisees, scribes and others living under the old law observed the counsels of the old law. For they had not forgotten the words of their Master, who says in Matthew 5: "But I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter into the kingdom of heaven. You have heard that it was said to the ancients," etc., where Christ plainly indicated that the Apostles ought to observe the Gospel law more perfectly than the ancients observed the Mosaic law. And therefore they ought not to observe the evangelical counsels more imperfectly than those observed the counsels of the old law. But some Pharisees and scribes and others living under the old law observed certain counsels of the old law under vow. This is clear from the Nazirites, Numbers 6, and in the third chapter, where it is written: "You shall offer this to the Lord in your solemnities, besides vows and voluntary offerings. And"

units.la: Sequitur: Si quis virorum votum domino vouerit, &c. Ex quibus aliisque quamplurimis colligitur euidenter, quod antiqui in veteri lege multa voauerunt, ad quae alias minime tenebantur. & in hoc, quod se voto astrinxerunt perfectius fecerunt: quia idem opus factum cum voto melius est ceteris paribus quam sine voto, secundum quod postea ostendetur, ergo apostoli multo magis quam illi consilia euangelica seruare voluerunt. Sed abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium est consilium euangelicum, teste ipsa veritate, quae ait: Si vis perfectus esse, vade & vende omnia quae habes, & da pauperibus, &c. ergo apostoli talem abdicationem sub voto seruauerunt.
units.tr: It follows: If any man vow a vow to the Lord, etc. From these and very many other passages it is clearly gathered that the ancients in the old law vowed many things to which otherwise they were not bound, and in this, that they bound themselves by vow, they did more perfectly; because the same work done with a vow is better, other things being equal, than without a vow, as will be shown afterwards. Therefore the Apostles much more wished to observe the evangelical counsels than those did. But the renunciation of ownership of all temporal things is an evangelical counsel, by the testimony of the truth itself, which says: If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, and give to the poor, etc. Therefore the Apostles observed such renunciation under vow.

units.la: Secundo isti impugnatores ostendunt, quod apostoli etiam voluerunt abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum in speciali & in communi. Nam votum apostolorum paupertatis non fuit imperfectius voto paupertatis quorumcunque religiosorum eos sequentium. Sed nonnulli religiosi, puta Fratres Minores, vouent abdicationem proprietatis omnium in speciali & in communi, sicut postea ostendetur. ergo & apostoli votum huiusmodi emiserunt. Confirmatur, quia omnis religio quantum ad tria vota principalia in religione, scilicet obedientiae, paupertatis, & castitatis, a vita apostolica sumpsit originem, fuitque vita apostolica forma & exemplar omnium religionum quantum ad illa tria vota. igitur conueniens fuit, ut nulla religio sequens in aliquo istorum trium votorum apostolicam vitam excederet: sed, sicut dictum est, religio Fratrum Minorum vouet abdicationem proprietatis omnium in speciali & etiam in communi. igitur & vita apostolica idem votum emisit.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents show that the apostles also willed the renunciation of ownership of all things, both individually and in common. For the apostles' vow of poverty was no less perfect than the vow of poverty made by any religious who follow them. But some religious, namely the Friars Minor, vow the renunciation of ownership of everything, both individually and in common, as will be shown later. Therefore the apostles also made a vow of this kind. This is confirmed, because every religious order, as regards the three principal vows in religion, namely obedience, poverty and chastity, took its origin from the apostolic life, and the apostolic life was the form and pattern of all religious orders as regards those three vows. Therefore it was fitting that no later order should in any of these three vows go beyond the apostolic life. But, as has been said, the order of the Friars Minor vows the renunciation of ownership of everything, both individually and in common. Therefore the apostolic life also made this same vow.

units.la: Tertio isti impugnatores ostendunt, hanc fuisse intentionem B. Augustini; quia cum dicit beatus Augustinus, hoc votum potentissime vouerant; aut debet referri ad totum, cum dicit apostolos dixisse, ecce nos dimisimus omnia & secuti sumus te: aut debet referri ad vltimam partem, scilicet, quod voluerunt sequi Christum. Si detur primum, habetur propositum, scilicet quod voluerunt relinquere seu dimittere omnia tam in speciali quam in communi, quia apostoli dicentes; ecce nos dimisimus omnia, locuti sunt de isto modo dimittendi omnia, quo Christus viam perfectionis docens consuluit omnia dimittenda, cum dixit cuidam: Si vis perfectus esse, vade & vende omnia quae habes, & da pauperibus: sed tunc docuit omnia dimittenda tam in speciali quam in communi: quia quae venduntur & pauperibus erogantur, tam in speciali quam in communi dimittuntur. Igitur si votum apostolorum debet intelligi de vtroque, sc. de dimittendo omnia, & de sequendo Christum, sequitur quod sub voto omnia dimiserunt tam in speciali quam in communi. Si autem detur secundum, scilicet, quod voluerunt tantummodo sequi Christum, quaerunt isti impugnatores, si apostoli voluerunt sequi Christum, aut voluerunt eum sequi corporaliter tantum, aut spiritualiter, eius videlicet implendo consilia & praecepta. Primum non potest dici, quia sic nullius fuisset persectionis illud votum. Multi enim Christum corporaliter sequebantur sine omni virtute. hoc etiam est contra Glossam Mat. 4. super illud: Relictis omnibus secuti sunt eum, quae ait: Inessu pedum, sed magis obedientia & affectu, amplius ad propria non reuersuri. Ex quib. verbis patenter habetur, quod licet apostoli incessu pedum Christum secuti fuerint: magis tamen obedientia & affectu ipsum sunt secuti. Si detur secundum, scilicet quod voluerunt sequi Christum spiritualiter eius praecepta & consilia adimplendo. igitur magis principalia eius consilia magis voluerunt. consilia autem principalia Christi fuerunt obedientiae, castitatis & paupertatis. ergo sicut apostoli voluerunt obedientiam, quam docuit Christus, cum dixit: Si quis vult venire post me, abneget semetipsum: ita voluerunt paupertatem, quam Christus docuit, cum dixit: Si vis perfectus esse, vade & vende omnia quae habes & da pauperibus. Sed tunc Christus docuit abdicationem omnium in speciali & in communi. ergo apostoli secundum intentionem B. August. omnium abdicationem in speciali & in communi voluerunt. Amplius, si apostoli non tantum sequebantur Christum, sed etiam voluerunt sequi Christum, hoc fuit, quod sequi Christum ex voto est perfectius & deo gratius, quam sequi Christum sine voto. Alia n. causa, ut videtur, assignari non potest: sed vbi est eadem causa, debet esse idem effectus; sicut vbi est eadem ratio, debet esse idem ius. ergo si sequi Christum ex voto est perfectius, quam sine voto, & dimittere omnia ex voto est perfectius quam sine voto: ergo si apostoli ex voto secuti sunt Christum, ex voto omnia dimiserunt. Sed instabit aliquis contra praedicta dicens, quod illae rationes non concludunt: quia si concluderent, sequeretur quod voluissent omnia consilia Christi, cum nequaquam specificetur votum ipsorum, & non magis potest concludi, quod unum consilium Christi voluerunt quam aliud. Sequeretur etiam, quod omnia quaecunque fecerunt, ex voto fecerunt. Cum omne bonum factum ex voto sit perfectius quam sine voto. Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, quod illa non concludunt. Dicunt enim ad primum, quod quamuis votum apostolorum minime specificaretur, tamen ex quo voluerunt, rationabiliter concedi debet quod illa voluerint potissime, quae Christus artius consulebat, & quae inter opera exteriora ad fidem veram suscipiendam infidelbus maxime poterant prouocare. Ex quo ipsi in voto & aliis operibus suis doctrinam Christi tenere, & ad eandem doctrinam alios prouocare verbis & factis principaliter studebant. Sed inter consilia Christi, consilia paupertatis, castitatis, & obedientiae, videntur a Christo strictius imposita & edocta. Per ista etiam maxime prouocari poterant infideles ad doctrinam Christi suscipiendam. Vnde apostoli per paupertatem specialiter reddiderunt se non suspectos, ne quis crederet ipsos propter aliquod temporale, doctrinam euangelicam praedicare: vt sic nullus eos mala intentione veritates inauditas docere putaret. & ita relinquitur, quod apostoli specialiter seruare paupertatem assumptam voluere debebant. Aliter a praedictis minime discordando. Dido. Dicunt quod votum apostolorum specificatur quantum ad paupertatem, cum Augustinus loquens de paupertate apostolorum & sequela Christi statim dicat, hoc votum potissime vouerunt. Ad secundum dicunt isti impugnatores, quod bona, quae faciunt sancti, sunt in triplici differentia: quaedam enim proponunt perpetuo custodire, quaedam sunt quae licet non proponant nec expediat in perpetuum observare, tamen firmiter & irrevocabiliter ex magna deliberatione tenaces proponunt, quaedam vero sunt, quae faciunt sancti cauta deliberatione, & diligenter advertunt, quod in voluntate faciendi talia debent se minime firmare. Prima & secunda decet, & expedit voto firmare, sed non tertia. Nunc autem apostoli paupertatem perpetuo seruare voluerunt: & ideo vouerunt eandem. Alia autem quae vouere non fuit expediens, sine voto fecerunt. Unde quamuis specialiter bonum opus factum ex voto, quando vouere est licitum & expediens, sit perfectius ceteris paribus, quam sine voto: tamen vouere non est semper expediens neque licitum: imo est interdum illicitum, quia non semper debet quis se firmare in isto, quod facere mente proponit.
units.tr: Thirdly, these opponents show that this was the intention of the blessed Augustine. For when the blessed Augustine says, they made this vow most strongly, the words must refer either to the whole statement, where he says that the apostles said, behold, we have left all things and followed you, or to the last part, namely that they wished to follow Christ. If the first is granted, the point is established, namely that they willed to leave or give up all things, both individually and in common. For when the apostles said, behold, we have left all things, they spoke of that manner of giving up all things in which Christ, teaching the way of perfection, counselled that all things be given up, when he said to a certain man: If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, and give to the poor. Then he taught that all things should be given up, both individually and in common, for what is sold and distributed to the poor is given up both individually and in common. Therefore, if the apostles' vow must be understood of both, namely of giving up all things and of following Christ, it follows that under the vow they gave up all things, both individually and in common. If, however, the second is granted, namely that they willed only to follow Christ, these opponents ask whether the apostles willed to follow Christ bodily only, or spiritually, that is, by fulfilling his counsels and precepts. The first cannot be said, for then that vow would have been of no perfection at all. For many followed Christ bodily without any virtue. This is also contrary to the Gloss on Matt. 4, on the words: they left all things and followed him, which says: by the step of their feet, but more by obedience and affection, not intending to return any more to their own things. From these words it is plainly clear that, although the apostles followed Christ by the step of their feet, they followed him rather by obedience and affection. If the second is granted, namely that they willed to follow Christ spiritually by fulfilling his precepts and counsels, then they willed his principal counsels more than others. The principal counsels of Christ were those of obedience, chastity and poverty. Therefore, just as the apostles willed the obedience Christ taught when he said: If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, so they willed the poverty Christ taught when he said: If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have and give to the poor. But then Christ taught the renunciation of all things, both individually and in common. Therefore, according to the intention of the blessed Augustine, the apostles willed the renunciation of all things, both individually and in common. Furthermore, if the apostles not only followed Christ but also willed to follow him, this was because to follow Christ by a vow is more perfect and more pleasing to God than to follow Christ without a vow. For no other cause, it seems, can be assigned; and where the cause is the same, the effect must be the same, just as where the reason is the same, the right must be the same. Therefore, if to follow Christ by a vow is more perfect than without a vow, and to give up all things by a vow is more perfect than without a vow, then, if the apostles followed Christ by a vow, they gave up all things by a vow. But someone will object to what has been said, claiming that these arguments do not prove the point: for if they did, it would follow that they willed all the counsels of Christ, since their vow is not specified at all, and it cannot be concluded any more that they willed one counsel of Christ rather than another. It would also follow that whatever they did, they did by a vow, since every good work done by a vow is more perfect than one done without a vow. But these opponents say that those arguments do not conclude. To the first they reply that although the apostles' vow was not specified in detail, nevertheless, since they willed, it ought reasonably to be granted that they willed most of all those things which Christ urged more strictly, and which among outward works could most of all move unbelievers to receive the true faith. For by their vow and their other works they chiefly strove to hold to the teaching of Christ, and to move others to the same teaching by word and deed. But among the counsels of Christ, the counsels of poverty, chastity and obedience appear to have been imposed and taught by Christ more strictly. By these especially unbelievers could be moved to receive the teaching of Christ. Hence the apostles, through poverty, made themselves especially free from suspicion, lest anyone believe that they preached the gospel for the sake of some temporal gain; and so no one would think that they taught unheard-of truths with an evil intention. And thus it follows that the apostles ought specially to have kept the poverty they had undertaken. Otherwise, without departing at all from what has been said. I reply: these opponents say that the apostles' vow is specified as regards poverty, since Augustine, speaking of the poverty of the apostles and the following of Christ, immediately says: they made this vow most strongly. To the second, these opponents say that the good works which saints do are of three kinds. For some they propose to keep perpetually; some, although it is not fitting or expedient to observe them in perpetuity, nevertheless they firmly and irrevocably propose to hold to after great deliberation; and some are those which saints do after careful deliberation, and diligently take note that they must in no way bind themselves to the will to do such things. The first and second kinds it is fitting and expedient to confirm by a vow, but not the third. Now the apostles willed to keep poverty perpetually, and therefore they vowed it. Other things, which it was not expedient to vow, they did without a vow. Hence, although a good work done specifically by a vow, when it is lawful and expedient to vow, is more perfect than one done without a vow, other things being equal, nevertheless vowing is not always expedient or lawful; indeed it is sometimes unlawful, because one ought not always to bind oneself to what one has intended in mind to do.

units.la: Quarto specialiter probant isti impugnatores: quod apostoli vouerunt abdicationem proprietatis illarum rerum, qua scriptura sacra eos aliquomodo asseruit habuisse: cuiusmodi fuerunt caligae, vestimentum, tunica, gladius, & huiusmodi. Hoc probant sic: Votum religiosorum se extendit ad talia, sed votum paupertatis apostolorum non fuit minus utile quam votum paupertatis religiosorum quorumcunque. Ergo votum paupertatis apostolorum ad huiusmodi se extendit. De hoc dictum est superius, & magis dicetur inferius: ideo hic breviius pertransitur.
units.tr: Fourthly, these opponents specifically prove that the apostles vowed the renunciation of ownership of those things which Holy Scripture states they in some way had: such as sandals, clothing, a tunic, a sword and things of that kind. They prove it thus: the vow of religious extends to such things, but the vow of poverty of the apostles was not less useful than the vow of poverty of any religious. Therefore the vow of poverty of the apostles extends to things of this kind. This has been said above and will be said more below, so it is passed over here more briefly.

units.la: Quinto isti impugnatores probare nituntur: quia licet regula beati Augustini sit fundata iuxta apostolicam vitam; tamen non attingit ad ultimam perfectionem apostolicae vitae. Quod probant primo sic: carere possessionibus in communi ad perfectionem spectat, alioquin omnes religiosi mendicantes frustra possessiones in communi abiecerunt. Sed apostoli non poterant habere possessiones in communi, sicut vouentes illam regulam B. Augustini possunt habere possessiones in communi. Ergo ad ultimam perfectionem paupertatis apostolicae nequaquam attingunt. Secundo sic: ad perfectionem apostolicae paupertatis pertinebat pecuniam minime possidere, sicut patet: Matth. 10. vbi sic dicitur: Nolite possidere neque aurum, neque argentum neque pecuniam, in zonis vestris. Ad hoc autem vouentes regulam B. Augustini minime astringuntur, ergo ad ultimam perfectionem paupertatis apostolicae non attingunt. Sexto conantur ostendere, quod medium per quod probat apostolos habuisse dominium & proprietatem aliquarum rerum in communi, non concludit; sed concludit, quod non habuerunt proprietatem cuiuscunque rei in speciali, quia quando aliqua regula iuxta aliam, ad quam nequaquam attingit, est fundata ex defectu persectionis in secunda regula, non potest ostendi idem defectus in prima; sicut ex carentia alicuius perfectionis in imperfectiori non potest argui catentia eiusdem perfectionis in perfectiori. Non enim sequitur: imperfectius caret hac perfectione, ergo perfectius caret eadem. Sed regula beati Augustini, sicut dictum est, licet sit fundata iuxta regulam apostolicae vitae, tamen ad ultimam perfectionem eiusdem non attingit. Habere autem aliquarum rerum dominium in communi est quidam defectus perfectionis, non quidem essentialis, sed paupertatis. Ergo ex hoc quod ista persectio non est de essentia regulae beati Augustini, non potest inferri, quod non fuerit de substantia apostolicae vitae. Quod autem medium supradictum concludat apostolos non habuisse quarumcunque rerum proprietatem & dominium in speciali, ostendunt sic: quando aliqua regula iuxta aliam est fundata, ad cuius ultimam perfectionem nequaquam attingit, quicquid perfectionis reperitur in regula secunda, reperitur in prima. Sed regula beati Augustini est fundata iuxta regulam apostolorum, & perfectionis est abdicare proprietatem & dominium omnium in speciali: & hoc faciunt vouentes regulam beati Augustini. Ergo multo perfectius hoc fecerunt apostoli. Et ita apostoli nullius rei habuerunt proprietatem & dominium saltem in speciali.
units.tr: Fifthly, these opponents try to prove that, although the rule of the blessed Augustine is founded upon the apostolic life, it does not reach the final perfection of the apostolic life. They prove this first thus: to be without possessions in common pertains to perfection, otherwise all the mendicant religious have cast off common possessions in vain. But the apostles could not have possessions in common, as those who vow the rule of the blessed Augustine can have possessions in common. Therefore they do not attain to the final perfection of apostolic poverty. Second, thus: it pertained to the perfection of apostolic poverty not to possess money at all, as is plain from Matt. 10, where it is said: Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts. But those who vow the rule of the blessed Augustine are not bound to this. Therefore they do not attain to the final perfection of apostolic poverty. Sixthly, they try to show that the middle term by which they prove that the apostles had lordship and ownership of some things in common does not conclude; rather it concludes that they had no ownership of any thing individually. For when one rule is founded upon another, to whose final perfection it in no way attains, owing to a lack of perfection in the second rule, the same defect cannot be shown in the first; just as from the absence of some perfection in the less perfect cannot be argued the absence of the same perfection in the more perfect. For it does not follow: the less perfect lacks this perfection, therefore the more perfect lacks the same. But the rule of the blessed Augustine, as has been said, although it is founded upon the rule of the apostolic life, nevertheless does not attain to its final perfection. Now to have lordship of some things in common is a certain defect of perfection, not indeed essential but of poverty. Therefore from the fact that this perfection is not of the essence of the rule of the blessed Augustine, it cannot be inferred that it was not of the substance of the apostolic life. That the aforesaid middle term concludes that the apostles did not have ownership and lordship of any things individually, they show thus: when one rule is founded upon another, to whose final perfection it in no way attains, whatever perfection is found in the second rule is found in the first. But the rule of the blessed Augustine is founded upon the rule of the apostles, and it is a perfection to renounce ownership and lordship of all things individually, and those who vow the rule of the blessed Augustine do this. Therefore the apostles did this much more perfectly. And so the apostles had no ownership and lordship of anything, at least individually.

units.la: Circa literam vero notanda sunt plura [hoc enim beatus Augustinus non dixit.] Dicunt isti quod hic aperte verba beati Augustini peruertit, quod, vt dicunt, apparet ex serie verborum Augustini, quae sunt haec: De terra ergo sufficiatus est ille supra omnes diuites pauper: & de illo stercore erectus supra omnes populos opulentos: ille inops vt sederet cum potentibus populi, quibus aut: sedebitis super sedes duodecim & sedem gloriae hereditate dabis eis, dixerant enim potentes illi: Ecce dimisimus omnia, & secuti sumus te. hoc votum potentissime vouerunt, sed unde hoc eis nisi ab illo de quo continuo dictum est. Dns votum vouentis? haec Augustinus. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod votum, de quo posterius loquitur Augustinus ad totum praecedens debet referri, vt asseratur ipsos vouisse etiam abdicationem omnium, cum dixerunt: Ecce nos dimisimus omnia: & obedientiam, cum dixerunt, & secuti sumus te. [Dici non potest quod votum illud esset abdicationis dominii, &c.] Dicunt quod illud votum comprehendit abdicationem dominii & proprietatis omnium temporalium, & etiam sequelam Christi, quae in perfecta observantia praeceptorum & consiliorum Christi consistit, quae etiam votum abdicationis proprietatis omnium rerum includit. & ita aperte insinuat Augustinus, quod apostoli vouerunt abdicationem proprietatis omnium tam in specie ipsam abdicationem specificando: Ecce nos dimisimus omnia, quam etiam in genere perfectam observantiam praeceptorum & consiliorum Christi promittendo, ibi, & secuti sumus te. [cum de hoc in praecedentibus seu subsequentibus nullam fecit mentionem.] dicunt quod licet de voto non fecerit vocalitem mentionem: tamen deillo, quod eadebat sub voto, fecit in præcedentibus mentionem expressam, cum dicit: Dixerant enim potentes illi. Ecce nos dimisimus omnia, & secuti sumus te. propter quod cum immediate subiunxit, hoc votum potentissime vouerant: per hoc propositum hanc completam sententiam immediate ante prolatam intelligit. Et ita constat, quod de abdicatione proprietatis omnium temporalium fecit in præcedentibus mentionem: & postea asseruit, quod non solum abdicauerunt omnia, sed quod ad talem abdicationem seruandam se voto astrinxerunt. [videtur quod vouerant se Dominum secuturos] hoc est verum præcipue de sequela spirituali per obseruationem mandatorum & consiliorum ipsorum: & ita ex hoc ipso, vt dicunt isti, quod vouerant se dominum secuturos, potest concludi quod vouerant abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum. quia hoc ad perfectam sequelam Christi pertinebat. [de quo immediate mentio erat ibi, secuti sumus te] non solum de hoc erat mentio: sed etiam specialiter erat mentio de abdicatione proprietatis omnium, ibi: Ecce nos dimisimus omnia. [Non est verisimile quod B. Augustinus intellexerit, quod in voto huiusmodi, scilicet quod reliquimus omnia, intelligantur illa comprehensa quæ sacra scriptura eos postea asserit habuisse.] Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod in hoc sibiipsi contradicit: quia in his verbis concedit illud quod in obiectione præmissa, ad quam hic respondet, fuit acceptum, scilicet quod vouerant se reliquros omnia, & dominum secuturos: cum tamen antea dixerit manifeste, quod dici non potest, quod votum illud esset abdicationis dominii, seu proprietatis omnium rerum temporalium. Secundo dicunt, quod hic omnino loquitur irrationabiliter: quia sicut constat, quod B. August. in voto abdicationis, quæ in sua regula continetur, comprehendit illa quæ asserit postea fratres suos posse habere illa, verisimile est quod in voto huiusmodi apostolorum: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, intelligat illa esse comprehensa, quæ tamen eos scriptura sacra asseruit habuisse. & hoc quia voto abdicationis proprietatis omnium rerum non obuiat habere aliqua quoad facultatem vtendi, & quoad actum vtendi, & aliomodo quam quoad facultatem vtendi & actum vtendi, apostoli res quascunque habuerint non legitur. & ideo sicut non obstante voto abdicationis proprietatis omnium in speciali, de quo dicit August. in Regula sua: non dicatis vos habere aliquod proprium: sed sint vobis omnia communia, possunt fratres sui aliquid habere. Unde postea dicit: certum est eos nihil habere, possidere, dare, vel accipere, sine superioris licentia debere. quod si propinquus, vel amicus, vel quilibet fratrum cuiquam aliquid offerre voluerit, primo quidem priori insinuetur: & sic suscipiatur, si ipse mandauerit: de quo tamen nil fiat aliud, nisi quod prioris placuerit. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi: quod non obstante voto abdicationis proprietatis, Augustinus voluit quod aliqua susciperent & haberent, quæ tamen essent sub voto comprehensa: quia voluit quod non reciperentur vt propria. ita verisimile est quod beatus August. intellexerit, quod in voto huiusmodi apostolorum: Reliquimus omnia, intelligantur omnia comprehensa, quæ sacra scriptura eos postea asserit habuisse: quia non habuerunt ipsa vt propria, sed habebant ipsa tantummodo quoad licitam potestatem vtendi & quo ad actum vtendi. [Quae ipsos habuisse] Verum est quo ad licitam potestatem vtendi, non quo ad dominium & proprietatem. [Item non est intelligendum quod beatus Augustinus intellexerit, quod ipsi apostoli vouerunt non habere aliquid in communi.] Hoc isti negant, quia dicunt, quod Augustinus intellexerit ipsos non habere aliquid quomodo Christus consuluit adolescenti dimittere omnia, cum dixit: Si vis perfectus esse vade & vende omnia quæ habes, & da pauperibus. quia occasione illius dixit Petrus in persona omnium apostolorum: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia. sed Christus consuluit adolescenti dimittere omnia in speciali & in communi: quia vendita & data pauperibus dimittuntur in speciali & in communi. ergo apostoli sic vouerunt non habere aliquid, nec in speciali nec in communi. quod debet intelligi quo ad proprietatem & dominium, quia nō habere aliquid et in speciali quo ad vsum facti nulli est licitum, iuxta vitam apostolicam. Conuenienter dicitur iuxta vitam apostolicam: quia Regula beati Augustini in pluribus distat à vita apostolica: & tamen in multis imitatur ipsam. & ideo non est simpliciter vita apostolica, sed iuxta eam est fundata. [Cum igitur beatus Augustinus, & eius Fratres res habuerint, vel habeant in communi, non est reuocandum in dubium, quin beatus Augustinus apostolos habuisse supposuerit in communi.] Dicunt isti quod male infert, quia ex hoc quod regula beati Augustini est fundata iuxta vitam apostolicam: & in multis distat ab ipsa: quicquid perfectionis est in regula beati Augustini, quoad essentialia, religioni debet attribui apostolicæ vitæ. & ideo ex hoc quod Fratres sancti Augustini nullius rei proprietatem habent in speciali, debet inferri quod apostoli nullius rei proprietatem habuerint, saltem in speciali: quia hoc pertinet ad votum paupertatis: quod est essentiale omni religioni perfectæ. Sed habere proprietatem rerum in communi, non pertinet ad perfectionem paupertatis religiosorum: imo deficit ab vltimo gradu perfectissimæ paupertatis. ergo ex hoc, quod inuenitur in Fratribus sancti Augustini, non debet argui quod vitæ apostolicæ competebat: sicut ex hoc, quod habere possessiones magnas in communi, nō obuiat Regulæ beati Augustini: non potest concludi quod apostoli poterant habere magnas possessiones in communi. [Quare per auctoritatem prædictam Augustini iste hereticus nequaquam poterit concludere, quod apostoli voto abdicauerint omnium rerum dominium.] Dicunt isti primo, quod mendaciter vocat appellantem hæreticum. Secundo dicunt, quod per auctoritatem Augustini potest concludere, quod apostoli omnium rerum dominium abdicauerunt: cum super abdicatione dominii omnium rerum votum emiserunt. [Nec quod id abdicauerint in proprio & communi.] Magis proprie dixisset in speciali & communi, quia conuenienter dicitur, quod proprium potest haberi in speciali vel in conuenientia secundum ipsum. non sic autem conuenienter dicitur, quod proprium potest haberi in proprio & communi. Dicunt etiam, quod ex processu Augustini & diuersis assertionibus eius potest concludi, quod apostoli abdicauerint omnium rerum dominium in speciali & communi: & de hoc latius dicetur inferius.
units.tr: Regarding the wording itself, several points must be noted [for Blessed Augustine did not say this.]. These people say that here he plainly distorts the words of Augustine, as they claim is evident from the sequence of Augustine's words, which are these: Therefore that poor man was raised up from the earth above all the rich, and from that dung he was lifted up above all the wealthy peoples, that he might sit with the princes of the people, to whom it is said, you shall sit upon twelve thrones and you shall give them a seat of glory by inheritance. For those powerful men had said: Behold, we have left all things and followed you. They vowed this most powerfully, but whence did they have it, unless from him of whom it was said immediately: the Lord is the vow of the one who vows? Thus Augustine. From these words it is to be understood that the vow of which Augustine speaks afterwards must be referred to the whole preceding passage, so that it is asserted that they had vowed also the renunciation of everything, when they said: Behold, we have left all things, and obedience, when they said and have followed you. [It cannot be said that that vow was a renunciation of ownership, etc.] These men say that the vow includes the renunciation of ownership and of the property of all temporal things, and also the following of Christ, which consists in the perfect observance of the precepts and counsels of Christ, and this also includes a vow to renounce the property of all things. And so Augustine plainly implies that the apostles vowed the renunciation of the property of all things, both specifically, naming the renunciation itself, Behold, we have left all things, and generally, by promising the perfect observance of the precepts and counsels of Christ, there, and have followed you. [although he made no mention of this either in what precedes or in what follows.] They say that although he did not make a vocal mention of the vow, nevertheless he did make an express mention, in the preceding words, of that which fell under the vow, when he says: For those powerful men had said: Behold, we have left all things and followed you. For this reason, when he immediately adds, they vowed this most powerfully, by this word he understands the complete sentence just stated immediately before. And so it is clear that he made mention in the preceding words of the renunciation of the property of all temporal things, and afterwards asserted that they had not only given up everything, but had bound themselves by vow to keep such a renunciation. [it seems that they had vowed to follow the Lord] This is true especially of the spiritual following through the observance of his commands and counsels; and so from this very fact, as these men say, that they vowed to follow the Lord, it can be concluded that they vowed the renunciation of the property of all things, because this pertained to the perfect following of Christ. [of which there was immediate mention there, and have followed you] Not only was there mention of this, but there was also a special mention of the renunciation of the property of all things, there: Behold, we have left all things. [It is not likely that Blessed Augustine understood that in a vow of this kind, namely that we have left all things, those things are understood to be included which holy Scripture afterwards asserts they had.] These opponents say that in this he contradicts himself, because in these words he concedes what was accepted in the objection stated above, to which he here replies, namely that they had vowed to leave all things and to follow the Lord; yet before this he had clearly said that it cannot be said that that vow was a renunciation of ownership, or of the property of all temporal things. Secondly, they say that here he speaks altogether irrationally, because just as it is agreed that Blessed Augustine, in the vow of renunciation contained in his rule, included those things which he asserts his brethren could afterwards have, so it is likely that in the vow of the apostles, Behold, we have left all things, he understands that those things are included which holy Scripture asserts they had. And this is so because the vow of renouncing the property of all things does not stand in the way of having some things as to the faculty of using and as to the act of using, and in no other way than as to the faculty of using and the act of using; nowhere is it read that the apostles had any things otherwise. And therefore, just as, notwithstanding the vow of renouncing the property of all things in particular, of which Augustine speaks in his Rule: Do not say that you have anything of your own, but let all things be common to you, his brethren can have something. Hence he says afterwards: It is certain that they ought to have, possess, give or receive nothing without the permission of the superior. But if a relative, or a friend, or any of the brethren wishes to offer something to anyone, let it first be reported to the prior, and so let it be received if he commands it; yet nothing else shall be done with it than what the prior has pleased. From these words it is to be understood that, notwithstanding the vow of renouncing property, Augustine wished that they should receive and have some things, which nevertheless were included under the vow, because he wished that they should not be received as their own. So it is likely that Blessed Augustine understood that in a vow of this kind of the apostles, We have left all things, all those things are understood to be included which holy Scripture afterwards asserts they had, because they did not have them as their own, but had them only as to the lawful power of using and as to the act of using. [That they had] This is true as to the lawful power of using, but not as to ownership and property. [Likewise it is not to be understood that Blessed Augustine understood that the apostles themselves vowed not to have anything in common.] The opponents deny this, because they say that Augustine understood that they did not have anything in the way that Christ counselled the young man to give up all things, when he said: If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, and give to the poor. On the occasion of this, Peter said in the name of all the apostles: Behold, we have left all things. But Christ counselled the young man to give up all things both in particular and in common, because things sold and given to the poor are given up both in particular and in common. Therefore the apostles vowed in this way not to have anything, neither in particular nor in common. This must be understood as to property and ownership, because not to have anything in particular, as to the actual use, is lawful for no one, according to the apostolic life. It is fittingly said according to the apostolic life, because the Rule of Blessed Augustine differs from the apostolic life in many respects, and yet in many things imitates it. And so it is not simply the apostolic life, but it is founded upon it. [Since therefore Blessed Augustine and his brethren have, or hold, things in common, it is not to be called into doubt that Blessed Augustine supposed that the apostles had things in common.] These men say that he draws a false inference, because from the fact that the Rule of Blessed Augustine is founded upon the apostolic life, and differs from it in many respects, whatever perfection there is in the Rule of Blessed Augustine, as to its essentials, must be attributed to the apostolic life of religion. And therefore, from the fact that the brethren of Saint Augustine have no ownership of anything in particular, it must be inferred that the apostles had no ownership of anything, at least in particular; for this pertains to the vow of poverty, which is essential to every perfect religion. But to have ownership of things in common does not pertain to the perfection of the poverty of religious men; indeed it falls short of the last degree of most perfect poverty. Therefore from what is found among the brethren of Saint Augustine it should not be argued that it belonged to the apostolic life; just as, from the fact that having great possessions in common does not conflict with the Rule of Blessed Augustine, it cannot be concluded that the apostles could have had great possessions in common. [Wherefore by the aforesaid authority of Augustine this heretic can by no means conclude that the apostles by vow renounced the ownership of all things.] These men say, first, that he falsely calls the appellant a heretic. Secondly, they say that from the authority of Augustine it can be concluded that the apostles renounced the ownership of all things, since they made a vow concerning the renunciation of ownership of all things. [Nor that they renounced it in what is their own and in common.] He would have spoken more properly of in particular and in common, because it is fittingly said that what is one's own can be held in particular or, according to him, in a suitable manner. But it is not fittingly said that what is one's own can be held in what is one's own and in common. They also say that from the course of Augustine's argument and his various assertions it can be concluded that the apostles renounced the ownership of all things, both in particular and in common; and this will be discussed more fully below.

units.la: CAP. XVIII
units.tr: CAP. XVIII

units.la: Item non obstat capitulum illud 16. q. 1. cap. Ex auctoritate, per ipsum superius allegatum: imo facit potius contra ipsum. Loquitur enim de monachis, qui vt dicitur ibi, figuram apostolorum tenent. Constat autem quod monachi habent mobilia & immobilia quoad proprietatem & dominium in communi, vt probatur 18. q. 2. c. In nullo. quare videtur quod & apostoli habuerint seu potuerint habere talia in communi. Verum est tamen, quod in Iudaea non retinuerunt immobilia, sed potius vendiderunt: quia providebant ad gentes ecclesiam transfituram, vt probatur Act. 2. & 4. ca. & 12. q. 1. ca. futuram.
units.tr: Likewise, the chapter 16 q. 1, c. Ex auctoritate, cited above by the same author, does not stand in the way; indeed it rather tells against him. For it speaks of monks, who, as it says there, hold the figure of the apostles. But it is clear that monks have movables and immovables in common as to ownership and dominion, as is proved in 18 q. 2, c. In nullo. Hence it seems that the apostles also had, or could have had, such things in common. It is true, however, that in Judaea they did not keep immovable property but rather sold it, because they foresaw that the church would pass to the Gentiles, as is proved Act. 2 and 4 ch., and 12 q. 1, c. futuram.

units.la: In ista parte respondet iste impugnatus ad illud, quod in obiectione praemissa tangit appellans de religiosis, figuram tenentibus apostolorum, dicens: quod illud capitulum de religiosis non facit pro appellante, sed contra ipsum: quia illud capitulum loquitur de monachis, qui possunt habere mobilia & immobilia in communi. ergo & apostoli potuerunt, non tamen retinuerunt in Iudaea, quia praevidebant ad gentes ecclesiam transituram.
units.tr: In this part the impugned author answers what the appellant touched on in the objection above, about religious men who hold the figure of the apostles. He says that this chapter about religious men does not favour the appellant but tells against him, because that chapter speaks of monks, who may have movables and immovables in common. Therefore the apostles could also have had them, but they did not retain them in Judaea, because they foresaw that the church would pass to the Gentiles.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt hic tres errores improbatos superius replicari: quorum primus est, quod apostoli semper potuerunt habere dominium & proprietatem possessionum in communi. Secundus est quod in Iudaea tales possessiones habuerunt post missionem Spiritus sancti. Tertius est quod possessiones huiusmodi vendiderunt. Secundo dicunt, quod medium per quod primum errorem probare conatur, non habet apparentiam nec colorem. De praedictis tribus assertionibus dictum est prius, & postea diffuse dicetur. Ideo probant quod medium suum primam assertionem non probat. Nam licet monachi figuram teneant apostolorum quantum ad renunciationem proprietatis, status tamen monachorum possessiones habentium in communi non est omnino idem cum statu apostolorum, nec ad perfectionem status apostolorum attingit: sed in parte, non totaliter imitatur. Ex quo colligitur evidenter, quod nihil quod ad perfectionem non pertinet, ex hoc quod reperitur in statu monachorum, potest de statu apostolorum inferri. sed habere immobilia seu possessiones in communi, licet nequaquam perfectioni essentiali repugnet, tamen ad perfectionem non pertinet: imo altissimae perfectioni paupertatis obviat manifeste, quia ad paupertatem altissimam nequaquam attingit, imo repugnat altissimae paupertati. ergo ex hoc, quod habere possessiones in communi competit statui monachorum, nequaquam concludi potest, quod apostolis competebat. Sed forte obiiciet aliquis contra praedicta dicens, quod secundum sententiam Prosperi, vt habetur. 12. q. 1. ca. Expedit, facto Paulini ostenditur, quod propria debent propter perfectionem contemni, & sine impedimento perfectionis posse facultates ecclesiae, quasi iam pro facto communi possideri. Ex quibus verbis aperte colligitur, quod possidere possessiones in communi, perfectioni impedimentum non praestat: & ita non repugnat altissimae paupertati. Ad hoc respondent isti impugnatores, distinguendo tam de perfectione quam de impedimento perfectionis, dicentes quod perfectio, de qua nunc loquimur, est duplex: quaedam, scilicet essentialis, quae reddit hominem perfectum: ita est charitas perfecta, qua habita perfecte est homo perfectus quantumcunque; caret aliis secundum actum, licet aliis virtutibus sante illa charitate perfecta secundum praeparationem animi carere non possit. Alia est perfectio quasi essentialis vel secundaria, quae in aliis virtutibus a charitate inuenitur: sicut si dicatur paupertas perfecta vel castitas perfecta, & sic de aliis. Secundo distinguunt de impedimento perfectionis, dicentes quod aliquid dicitur impedimentum perfectionis, quia perfectioni repugnat aut de perfectione diminuit. Secundo dicitur impedimentum perfectionis, quod communiter & quasi ex natura sua in hominibus ad vitia inclinatis est occasio diminutionis perfectionis: non tamen semper ex ipso sequitur diminutio perfectionis. Secundum hoc dicunt ad praemissam obiectionem, quod possidere quoad dominium & proprietatem facultates ecclesiae non est impedimentum primo modo perfectionis primo modo dictae: quia potest quis esse perfectus in charitate absque diminutione charitatis perfectae, quae potest haberi in via, licet facultates ecclesiae possideat. sed possidere dicto modo facultates ecclesiae, est impedimentum primo modo dictum perfectionis secundo modo dictae, quia de virtute paupertatis diminuit. Non enim perfectissimus gradus paupertatis stat cum tali possessione facultatum ecclesiae. Unde ita est de tali possessione ecclesiae respectu perfectionis primo modo dictae & secundo modo dictae, sicut est de castitate coniugali respectu castitatis & virginitatis. Castitas enim coniugalis non necessario diminuit aliquid de perfectione castitatis. Quia ita potest esse perfecta charitas in vtente coniugio, sicut in virgine: charitas tamen vtentis coniugio necessario diminuit de perfectissimo gradu castitatis, quia ad virginitatem nequaquam attingit: nec quantumcunque sit perfectior virgine in charitate aureolam virginitati debitam consequetur. Sic licet quis possidens possessiones ecclesiae sit ita perfectus in charitate, sicut caretis eis, non ta
units.tr: But these opponents say that three errors already refuted above are being repeated here. The first is that the apostles could always have had dominion and ownership of possessions in common. The second is that they had such possessions in Judaea after the mission of the Holy Spirit. The third is that they sold such possessions. Secondly, they say that the means by which he tries to prove the first error has neither appearance nor colour. These three assertions have been discussed before, and will be discussed at length later. So they prove that his means does not prove his first assertion. For although monks hold the figure of the apostles as regards renunciation of ownership, the state of monks who have possessions in common is not wholly the same as the state of the apostles, nor does it attain to the perfection of the apostles' state; it imitates it only in part, not totally. From this it is evident that nothing which does not pertain to perfection can be inferred about the state of the apostles from what is found in the state of monks. But to have immovables or possessions in common, although it by no means conflicts with essential perfection, nevertheless does not pertain to perfection; indeed it plainly stands in the way of the highest perfection of poverty, since it by no means reaches the highest poverty but rather conflicts with it. Therefore, from the fact that having possessions in common befits the state of monks, it can by no means be concluded that it befitted the apostles. But perhaps someone will object to what has been said, that according to the opinion of Prosper, as found in 12 q. 1, c. Expedit, "the case of Paulinus shows that private things ought to be despised for the sake of perfection, and that the goods of the church may be possessed without hindrance to perfection, as if already held in common." From these words it is plainly gathered that possessing possessions in common is no impediment to perfection, and so does not conflict with the highest poverty. To this these opponents reply by distinguishing both concerning perfection and concerning the impediment to perfection. They say that the perfection we are now speaking of is twofold: one is essential, which makes a man perfect; such is perfect charity, by which, once it is had perfectly, a man is perfect however much he lacks other things in act, although he cannot lack the other virtues in the preparation of the mind without that perfect charity. The other is perfection that is, as it were, essential or secondary, which is found in the other virtues apart from charity; as when one speaks of perfect poverty or perfect chastity, and so on with the others. Secondly, they distinguish concerning the impediment to perfection, saying that something is called an impediment to perfection in two ways: either because it conflicts with perfection or diminishes it; or because it commonly, and as it were by its nature, is an occasion of diminishing perfection in men inclined to vices, although it does not always necessarily result in a diminution of perfection. In accordance with this they answer the objection put forward, that to possess the goods of the church as to dominion and ownership is not an impediment to perfection in the first sense of the first kind, since a man can be perfect in charity without any diminution of the perfect charity that can be had in this life, even though he possesses the goods of the church. But to possess the goods of the church in that way is an impediment to perfection in the first sense of the second kind, since it diminishes the virtue of poverty. For the most perfect degree of poverty does not stand with such possession of the goods of the church. So the situation with such possession of the church's goods, with respect to perfection in the first and second senses, is as with conjugal chastity with respect to chastity and virginity. For conjugal chastity does not necessarily diminish anything of the perfection of chastity; for charity can be as perfect in one who uses marriage as in a virgin. Yet the charity of one who uses marriage necessarily diminishes the most perfect degree of chastity, since it by no means reaches virginity; nor, however much more perfect in charity he is than a virgin, will he obtain the reward of a crown due to virginity. So, although a man who possesses the goods of the church may be as perfect in charity as one who lacks them,

Sic licet possessio facultatu ecclesiæ non sit impedimentum primo modo dictum perfectionis primo modo dictæ; est tamen impedimentum illius perfectionis, scilicet charitatis accipiendo impedimentum secundo modo, quia quasi ex sua natura est occasio minus diligendi Deum & nimiæ sollicitudinis circa temporalia. Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod secundum ista esset per omnia eodem modo impedimentum perfectionis possessio communium, sicut possessio propriorum: quia possessio propriorum non necessario diminuit de caritate, licet possit esse occasio diminutionis caritatis vel diminutionis actus caritatis: necessario tamen de paupertate diminuit; & ita sine impedimento perfectionis possunt possideri propria, sicut communia. Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod possibile est, quod sine diminutione caritatis & per consequens perfectionis primo modo dictæ, possideantur propria in speciali. Et ita quantum ad multa simile est de possessione propriorum & de possessione communium. Est tamen in multis aliis differentia. Primo quia, ut communiter propriorum possessio magis inclinat ad amorem & sollicitudinem circa temporalia quam possessio communium. Secundo quia plus distat à gradu perfectissimo paupertatis. Unde & habentes propria quodammodo ditiores sunt habentibus communia. Et carentes propriis sunt quodammodo pauperiores, quam habentes propria. Tertio quia non est tanta necessitas & utilitas boni communis & pauperum possidere propria, sicut possidere communia. Et propter istam causam, sicut tangit Prosper in prædallegato capitulo; Viri perfecti perfectionis amore debent propria contemnere, quia raro aut nunquam retentio propriorum ex charitate proximorum & zelo communis boni procedit: & tamen viri perfecti absque impedimento perfectionis primo modo dictæ possunt communia possidere: quia charitas proximorum & zelus communis charitatis hoc sæpe requirunt. Et ideo secundum Gregorium, ut habetur 8. q. 1. In scripturis: Sicut toto desiderio debemus occupationem fugere: ita si desit qui prædicet onus occupationis libenti necesse est humero subire. Sic viri perfecti toto desiderio possessionum communium dispensationem fugiunt: & tamen si desit qui communia rite dispenset, possessionum communium onus amore proximorum libenter suscipiunt. Et ex hoc, ut dicunt, euidenter colligitur, quod quemadmodum occupatio vitæ actiuæ sæpe est occasio diminutionis actus diligendi Deum; ita possessio communium sæpe est occasio minoris feruoris & amoris diuini, & ideo sicut licet vita contemplatiua secundum se sit excellentior quam vita actiua, tamen nonnunquam propter utilitatem communem vita contemplatiua intermittitur: & vitæ actiuæ insistitur à perfectis; ita licet carentia possessionum in communi secundum se sit melior quam habere possessiones in communi, tamen aliquando propter utilitatem communem perfecti absque impedimento perfectionis, hoc est absque omni diminutione charitatis, imo ex abundantia charitatis communia ad dispensandum suscipiunt. In hoc tamen aliquem gradum paupertatis quamuis meritoriæ secundum actum dimittunt: quamuis secundum præparationem animi altissimam paupertatem retineant. sic etiam posset aliquis absque impedimento perfectionis, hoc est, absque diminutione charitatis totius mundi dominium retinere.
units.tr: yet he will not be as poor. So, although the possession of the goods of the church is not an impediment to perfection in the first sense of the first kind, it is nevertheless an impediment to that perfection, namely charity, taking impediment in the second sense, since it is by its nature almost an occasion of loving God less and of excessive anxiety about temporal things. But perhaps someone will say that, according to these distinctions, possession of things in common would be in every way an impediment to perfection in the same way as possession of private property; for possession of private property does not necessarily diminish charity, although it may be an occasion of diminishing charity or of diminishing the act of charity; yet it necessarily diminishes poverty; and so private property can be possessed without impediment to perfection, just as common property can. These opponents say that it is possible that private property held individually can be possessed without diminution of charity, and consequently without diminution of perfection in the first sense. And so in many respects the possession of private property and of common property is alike. There is, however, a difference in many other things. First, because, as a rule, possession of private property inclines more to love of and anxiety about temporal things than possession of common property does. Second, because it is further removed from the most perfect degree of poverty; hence those who have private property are in a sense richer than those who have common property, and those who lack private property are in a sense poorer than those who have it.
