Third, because there is not so great a need and usefulness for the good of the community and of the poor to possess private property as there is to possess common property. And for this reason, as Prosper touches on in the chapter cited above, "men of perfection ought to despise private property out of love of perfection," because retention of private property rarely or never proceeds from love of neighbours and zeal for the common good; whereas men of perfection can possess common goods without impediment to perfection in the first sense, since love of neighbours and zeal for the common charity often require this. And therefore, according to Gregory, as found in 8 q. 1, In scripturis: "Just as we ought to flee occupation with all our desire, so, if there is no one to undertake the burden of occupation, it is necessary to take it up willingly on the shoulder." So men of perfection flee the stewardship of common possessions with all their desire; yet if there is no one to dispense the common goods duly, they willingly take up the burden of common possessions out of love for their neighbours. And from this, they say, it is clearly gathered that just as the occupation of the active life is often an occasion of diminishing the act of loving God, so the possession of common goods is often an occasion of less fervour and less divine love; and therefore, just as the contemplative life, although in itself more excellent than the active life, is nevertheless sometimes interrupted for the common good, and the perfect devote themselves to the active life; so, although lacking possessions in common is in itself better than having possessions in common, yet sometimes for the common good the perfect, without impediment to perfection, that is, without any diminution of charity, or rather out of abundance of charity, take common goods upon themselves to dispense. In this, however, they give up some degree of poverty, meritorious in act, although in the preparation of the mind they retain the highest poverty. So too one might, without impediment to perfection, that is, without diminution of charity, retain dominion over the whole world.

units.la: Est tamen differentia inter possessionem propriorum & communium, sicut tactum est: quia necesse est ad possidendum communia viros bonos eligere; & ideo necesse est viros bonos se multis periculis etiam spiritualibus exponendo communium possessionem suscipere. sed non sic est necesse eligere aliquos ad propria possidendum. Ex prædictis igitur apparet, quod habere possessiones in communi licet non de charitate, sed de altissima paupertate diminuit.
units.tr: There is, however, a difference between the possession of private goods and of common goods, as has been said. For good men must be chosen to hold common goods, so good men who take on the possession of common goods expose themselves to many dangers, even spiritual ones. But no one needs to be chosen to possess private goods. From what has been said, then, it is clear that having possessions in common, although it does not diminish charity, does diminish the highest poverty.

units.la: Apostoli autem non solum in charitate, sed etiam in paupertate fuerunt perfectissimi, quod non solum decens, imo etiam necessarium videtur fuisse; ut scilicet tanquam primi fundatores post Christum nouæ ecclesiæ, non solum doctrina, sed etiam vita ad perfectissimum mundi contemptum alios inuitarent. Perfectissimus autem mundi contemptus est perabdicationem propriorum & communium ergo & apostoli talem abdicationem seruare debuerunt.
units.tr: The apostles, however, were most perfect not only in charity but also in poverty, which seems not only fitting but even necessary. As the first founders of the new Church after Christ, they were to invite others, by their way of life as well as by their teaching, to the most perfect contempt of the world. But the most perfect contempt of the world is the complete renunciation of private and common goods. Therefore the apostles too must have observed such renunciation.

units.la: Nunc textum more solito declaramus. [Facit potius contra ipsum.] Dicunt quod facit pro ipso: quia sicut non solum perfectior charitas non reperitur in monachis quam in apostolis; sed etiam nec maior obedientia, nec maior castitas, quantum ad animam reperitur in monachis quam in apostolis. ita nec maior paupertas reperitur in monachis quam in Apostolis. sed monachi nullius rei proprietatem etiam vsu consumtibilis habent in speciali. ergo apostoli nullius rei vsu consumptibilis proprietatem habuerunt in speciali; & tamen constat quod apostoli habuerunt vsum facti rerum consumptibilium vsu. ergo vsus facti in huiusmodi rebus potest à proprietate & dominio in speciali separari. sed non est maior ratio quod possit separari à dominio in speciali quam à dominio in communi; imo ex hoc quod potest separari à dominio in speciali, poterit etiam separari ab omni dominio. & hæc est principalis conclusio appellantis, scilicet quod vsus facti respectu rerum vsu consumptibilium potest à proprietate & dominio separari. [Figuram apostolorum tenent.] Non tamen ad perfectionem eorum attingunt; sed in pluribus non in omnibus imitantur. & ideo licet ex hoc, quod monachi carent omni proprietate in speciali, argui possit, quod apostoli cauerunt omni proprietate in speciali, non tamen ex hoc quod monachi habent immobilia, vel etiam mobilia in communi, argui potest quod apostoli habuerunt aliqua in communi. [Quoad proprietatem & dominium in communi.] Hoc potest concedi de dominio, quod est potestas vendicandi in iudicio rem, quae non est alterius quoad dominium. non est autem verum de dominio, quod est potestas de re ad libitum disponendi. [Quare videtur quod & apostoli habuerunt, &c.] Dicunt quod male infert, quod monachi habent mobilia & immobilia in communi. ergo & apostoli habuerunt vel habere potuerunt: quia habere huiusmodi diminuit de gradu altissimae paupertatis. & ideo ex hoc, quod monachi ab illo gradu deficiunt, non potest argui, quod apostoli in hoc defecerunt. [In Iudaea non retinuerunt immobilia.] Verum est: quia non habuerunt. [quia potius vendiderunt.] Hoc dicunt omnino esse erroneum: quia tantum possessiones & praedia vendiderunt, sicut patet in Actibus. [Ideo apostoli quia praevidebant ad gentes ecclesiam transituram.] Haec non fuit causa, quare apostoli vendiderunt, quia apostoli post missionem Spiritus sancti nullam possessionem vendiderunt: sed haec fuit causa una, quare de consilio apostolorum suas possessiones vendiderunt: huius tamen fuerunt aliae causae. [Ut probatur Act. 1. & 4.] Hocibi non probatur, sed ostenditur, quod possessiones suas conuersi vendiderunt, non apostoli [& 12. q. 1. ca. futuram.] ibi de venditione apostolorum nulla fit mentio, ut patet intuenti.
units.tr: Now we explain the text in the usual way. It rather works against him. They say it supports him. For just as monks are found to have no more perfect charity than the apostles, and no greater obedience or greater chastity of soul than the apostles, so monks are found to have no greater poverty than the apostles. But monks have no ownership in particular of any thing, not even of things consumed by use. Therefore the apostles had no ownership in particular of any thing consumed by use. Yet it is agreed that the apostles did have the actual use of consumable things. Therefore the actual use of such things can be separated from ownership in particular. But there is no greater reason why it could be separated from ownership in particular than from ownership in common. Indeed, if it can be separated from ownership in particular, it could also be separated from all ownership. And this is the main conclusion of the appellant, namely that the actual use of consumable things can be separated from ownership and dominion. They keep to the figure of the apostles. Yet they do not attain to the apostles' perfection; they imitate them in many respects, though not in all. So although it may be argued from the fact that monks lack all ownership in particular that the apostles avoided all ownership in particular, it cannot be argued from the fact that monks hold immovables, or even movables, in common that the apostles had any things in common. As regards ownership and dominion in common. This may be conceded of dominion, which is the power of claiming a thing in court when it is not another's as regards ownership. But it is not true of dominion, which is the power of disposing of a thing at will. Why it seems that the apostles also had them, etc. They say he infers wrongly that monks hold movables and immovables in common, and therefore the apostles had them, or could have had them, because holding such things diminishes the degree of the highest poverty. So from the fact that monks fall short of that degree, it cannot be argued that the apostles fell short in this. In Judaea they did not keep immovables. True, because they did not have them. But rather sold them. They say this is wholly mistaken, for they sold only estates and lands, as is plain in the Acts. Therefore the apostles, because they foresaw that the Church would pass to the Gentiles. This was not the reason the apostles sold; for after the mission of the Holy Spirit the apostles sold no possessions. But this was one reason why, on the counsel of the apostles, they sold their possessions; there were other reasons too. As is proved in Acts 1 and 4. Nothing is proved there; it is shown that the converts sold their possessions, not the apostles. And 12 q. 1, c. futuram. There is no mention there of the apostles' selling, as is plain to anyone who looks.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAP. XIX.

units.la: ADhuc iste veritatis & fidei inimicus ad probandum, quod in rebus, quae usu consumuntur, potest haberi usus a dominio separatus, arguit sic. Omnes decimae terrae sive de frugibus sive de pomis arborum domini sunt, ut habetur Levitici vlt. Usus autem decimarum tantum est Levitarum, ut habetur Numeri 18. Constat autem, quod illae decimae sunt de frugibus & pomis, quae sunt res consumptibiles usu. quare cum dominium decimarum sit domini, & usus earum sit Levitarum: Sequitur quod in rebus usu consumptibilibus haberi potest usus a dominio separatus.
units.tr: Still this enemy of truth and of the faith, to prove that in things consumed by use, use can be had separately from ownership, argues thus. All tithes of the land, whether of crops or of the fruit of trees, belong to the Lord, as is found at the end of Leviticus. But the use of the tithes belongs only to the Levites, as is found in Numbers 18. It is agreed that those tithes are of crops and fruits, which are things consumed by use. Therefore, since the ownership of the tithes is the Lord's and their use belongs to the Levites, it follows that in things consumed by use, use can be had separately from ownership.

units.la: Hic iste impugnatus nititur respondere ad tertiam obiectionem appellantis. & primo ipsa obiectio recitari videtur. Secundo respondetur ad ipsam in parte immediate sequenti.
units.tr: Here the one attacked seeks to answer the third objection of the appellant. First, the objection itself seems to be recited; second, it is answered in the part immediately following.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, quod ille impugnatus male & peruerse recitat hic obiectionem appellantis. Nam verba appellantis sunt haec. Tertio ostenditur quod dicta assertio scripturae divinae repugnat. Nam sicut habetur Numeri 18. Leviticii vlt. Dominium decimarum sive de pomis sive de frugibus terra, quae res usu consumptibiles esse constat, fuit & est Dei, dominium ecclesia est Dei: sed usus illarum fuit & est ministrorum Dei. ergo usus rerum usu consumptibilium potest a proprietate & dominio separari, & eius oppositum manifeste obviat scripturae divinae. Ex his patet, quod obiectio non est subeisdem verbis, ut superius, recitata. qualiter autem in sententia differat, super literam apparebit.
units.tr: But these attackers say that the one attacked recites the appellant's objection wrongly and perversely here. For the appellant's words are these: Thirdly it is shown that the said assertion contradicts divine Scripture. For as is found in Numbers 18 and at the end of Leviticus, the ownership of the tithes, whether of the fruit of trees or of the crops of the land, which are plainly things consumed by use, was and is God's; the ownership of the Church is God's; but the use of them was and is the ministers of God's. Therefore the use of things consumed by use can be separated from ownership and dominion, and the opposite of this plainly runs counter to divine Scripture. From this it is clear that the objection is not recited in the same words as above. How it differs in sense will appear from the wording.

units.la: Est autem, ut dicunt, intentio appellantis, quod dominium quod est potestas de re ad libitum ordinandi quantum ad multa, quae sacerdotibus & Levitis legis veteris competebant, ipsi Levitae & sacerdotes nequaquam habebant; usum tamen illarum rerum habebant. Ex quo volebat appellans concludere, quod in huiusmodi rebus consumptibilibus usu, usus potest a tali dominio separari. & eadem ratione potest usus in huiusmodi rebus ab omni dominio separari: quia dicunt, ut patebit inferius, omnes rationes istius impugnati aeque concludere de uno dominio & de alio; & ita si usus huiusmodi rerum potest a tali dominio, quod est potestas de re libere ordinandi, separari: sequitur per consequentiam, quod usus huiusmodi rerum potest ab omni dominio separari.
units.tr: The intention of the appellant, as they say, is that ownership, meaning the power of freely disposing of a thing in many matters that belonged to the priests and Levites of the old law, the Levites and priests themselves did not have at all, yet they had the use of those things. From this the appellant wished to conclude that in such consumable things, use can be separated from such ownership. And by the same reasoning the use of such things can be separated from all ownership. For they say, as will become clear below, that all the arguments of this attacked writer conclude equally about one ownership and about the other. So if the use of such things can be separated from such ownership, which is the power of freely disposing of a thing, it follows by consequence that the use of such things can be separated from all ownership.

units.la: Sed paucis exponamus textum. [Domini sunt.] id est domino principaliter offeruntur, nec dabantur Levitis nisi propter dominum. [usus autem decimarum tantum est Levitarum] in verbis appellantis haec dictio tantum minime invenitur, sicut patet intuenti verba superius recitata. & ideo in hoc in sententia verba, quae imponit iste impugnatus, distant a verbis appellantis.
units.tr: But let us explain the text briefly. They are the Lord's. That is, they are offered principally to the Lord, and were given to the Levites only on account of the Lord. But the use of the tithes belongs only to the Levites. In the appellant's words the word "only" (tantum) is not found at all, as is plain to anyone who looks at the words recited above. So in this sense the words the attacked writer imposes differ from the appellant's words.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: AD hoc dicendum, quod iste arguit evidenter ex falsis. quod enim dicit Levitas habuisse usum tantum decimarum: falsum dicit, ut probatur Num. 18. ca. per eum in contrarium allegato. ubi Dominus sic dicit: Filiis Levi dedi omnes decimas Israel in possessionem pro ministerio, quo serviunt mihi in tabernaculo foederis. Ex quibus patet, quod Levita non tantum usum in decimis, sed etiam dominium habuerunt.
units.tr: To this I answer that the objector argues clearly from false premises. For his claim that the Levites had only the use of the tithes is false, as is shown in Num. 18, the chapter he cites against us. There the Lord says: "I have given to the sons of Levi all the tithes of Israel for an inheritance, in return for the service they perform for me in the tabernacle of the covenant." From this it is clear that the Levites had not only the use of the tithes but also ownership.

units.la: Nec obstat, quod in eodem capitulo dicitur, quod in usus Levitarum & necessaria dominus decimas separavit. Aliud est enim alicui in usum rem aliquam dare: & aliud alicui dare usum alicuius rei. Ubi enim usus rei indivisibilis conceditur alicui, usus tantum rei & non dominium sibi intelligitur esse datus. sed ubi alicui res datur in usum nedum usus rei, sed & dominium intelligitur esse datum.
units.tr: Nor does it stand in the way that the same chapter says the Lord set apart the tithes for the use and needs of the Levites. It is one thing to give someone a thing for use, and another to give someone the use of a thing. Where the use of an indivisible thing is granted to someone, only the use and not the ownership is understood to have been given. But where a thing is given to someone for use, it is understood that not only the use but also the ownership has been given.

units.la: Unde cum dicitur in praeallegato capitulo: quod in usus Levitarum & necessaria Dominus separavit, declaravit Dominus, ad quid vel propter quid Levitis decimas dedit, quia enim de frugibus & fructibus duplisiter nos vivimus; uno modo comedendo, ad quod primo & principaliter sunt concessi, iuxta illud Gen. 1. Ecce dedi vobis omnem herbam & universa ligna, quae habent in semetipsis sementem generis sui, ut sint vobis in escam. verum quia nonnunquam qui abundat in talibus deficit in aliis necessariis ad vitam humanam, voluit dominus, quod Levitae possent non solum de frugibus illis comedere, sed de illis quoad alia vitae necessaria vendendo & permutando sibi providere. & ideo dicit in usus & necessaria. & ita dicendum est de verbis illis in eodem ca. contentis ad Aaron prolatis, ubi dominus sic dixit: universa frugum initia quae offeruntur, ..., portantur, cedent in usus tuos. Illarum autem rerum dominium concessit illis dominus ... Dominus ad Aaron loquens sic dixit: Omnis oblatio & sacrificium, & quicquid pro peccato offeretur ... mihi, & erit in sancta sanctorum, tuum erit & filiorum tuorum sequitur: primitias autem quas voluerunt & obtulerunt filii Israel, dedi tibi & filiis & filiabus tuis iure perpetuo. Ex quibus patet quod non solum in decimis, nec in aliis praedictis alia, Aaron & Levita usum, sed & dominium habuerunt.
units.tr: So when it is said in the chapter already cited that the Lord set them apart for the use and needs of the Levites, the Lord declared to what end, or for what reason, he gave the tithes to the Levites. For we live on the fruits and produce in two ways: first by eating, which is the primary and principal purpose, according to Gen. 1: "Behold, I have given you every herb and all the trees which have seed of their own kind in themselves, to be meat for you." But since whoever has plenty of such things often lacks other necessities of human life, the Lord willed that the Levites should be able not only to eat of those fruits but also, by selling and exchanging them, to provide for themselves the other necessities of life. That is why he says "for use and necessities." The same must be said of the words in the same chapter addressed to Aaron, where the Lord spoke thus: "All the firstfruits of the grain that are offered... are brought, shall be yours for your use. But the ownership of those things the Lord granted to them..." The Lord, speaking to Aaron, said: "Every offering and sacrifice, and whatever is offered for sin... shall be mine, and shall be in the holy of holies; it shall be yours and your sons'. Then follows: But the firstfruits which the children of Israel will and offer, I have given to you and to your sons and daughters by a perpetual right. From these words it is clear that Aaron and the Levites had not only the use but also the ownership, not only of the tithes but also of the other things mentioned.

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnatus ad praedictam obiectionem nititur respondere. Dicens, quod ex falsis procedit, cum assumit Levitas habuisse usum tantum decimarum. quod esse falsum ostendit per capitulum allegatum Numeri 18. Secundo ibi: nec obstat, respondet quibusdam verbis eiusdem capituli, quae contrarium sonare videntur: dicens quod aliud est dare alicui usum rei, & dare alicui aliquid in usum. Qui enim dat usum, non dat dominium. Sed qui dat in usum, rem aliquam dat eiusdem rei dominium. Et ideo cum dicitur in eodem capitulo. In usu Levitarum &c. ostendit, quod Dominus dederit Levitis dominium decimarum. Tertio ibi: quia enim de frugibus, assignat causam, quare Dominus dedit Levitis dominium decimarum, ut scilicet ex eis acquirerent alia necessaria vitae vendendo & permutando. Quarto ibi, & idem dicendum est, respondet ad alia verba eiusdem capituli, quae videntur esse contra ipsum, ostendens per verba eiusdem capituli, quod illarum rerum dedit Dominus dominium Aaron & Levitis.
units.tr: On this point the objector sets out to answer the above objection. He says that it proceeds from false premises, since it assumes that the Levites had only the use of the tithes. He shows that this is false by the chapter cited from Num. 18. Second, where he says nec obstat ("nor does it stand in the way"), he answers certain words of the same chapter which seem to sound the opposite, saying that it is one thing to give someone the use of a thing and another to give someone something for use. For one who gives the use does not give ownership, but one who gives something for use gives ownership of that very thing. Therefore when it is said in the same chapter, In usu Levitarum ("for the use of the Levites"), etc., he shows that the Lord gave the Levites ownership of the tithes. Third, where he says quia enim de frugibus ("for since we live on the fruits"), he gives the reason why the Lord gave the Levites ownership of the tithes, namely that they might acquire from them the other necessities of life by selling and exchanging. Fourth, where he says & idem dicendum est ("and the same must be said"), he answers the other words of the same chapter which seem to be against him, showing from the same chapter that the Lord gave ownership of those things to Aaron and the Levites.

units.la: Circa istam partem isti impugnatores sic procedunt. Primo enim ostendunt, quod iste impugnatus appellanti falsum imponit. Secundo declarat intentionem auctoritatum, quibus probare molitur, quod Levitae habuerunt dominium decimarum & aliarum oblationum & sacrificiorum. Tertio explicant mentem appellantis. Circa primum dicunt, quod iste impugnatus imponit appellanti, quod secundum eum Levitae habuerunt tantum usum decimarum: cum tamen istam exclusivam nusquam ponat. Et ita dicunt, quod falsum sibi imponit. Circa secundum dicunt, quod quaedam distinctio tacta superius est ad memoriam revocanda, scil. quod dominium est duplex. quoddam enim est dominium, quod est potestas principalis, quamvis non semper principalissima, vendicandi rem in iudicio ac etiam defendendi. Aliud est dominium, quod supra dictam potestatem addit potestatem de re libere ordinandi. Dominium primo modo dictum videntur sacerdotes & Levitae in omnibus rebus eis ex divina ordinatione vel sponte oblatus a populo habuisse. Nam si aliquis decimas, primitias, partem sacrificiorum, quae sacerdotibus debebantur, & etiam panes propositionis furatus fuisset, ipsi habuissent potestatem vendicandi in iudicio, sicut modo episcopi, & personae ecclesiae habent potestatem vendicandi ius ecclesiae in iudicio, si fuerint ablatae vel iniuste detentae. Et ideo sicut aliquo modo conceditur, quod viri ecclesiae habent dominium rerum ecclesiasticarum: ita potest concedi, quod sacerdotes & Levitae veteris legis habuerunt aliquo modo dominium decimarum & aliarum rerum sibi a Deo concessarum. Non enim videtur, quod a rebus temporalibus magis fuerunt expropriati, quam ministri ecclesiae in nova lege. Sed dominium secundo modo dictum non habuerunt sacerdotes & Levitae in omnibus rebus eis assignatis: & tamen in multis earum ius habebant & potestatem vendi.
units.tr: On this point these objectors proceed as follows. First, they show that the objector imposes a falsehood on his opponent. Second, they explain the meaning of the authorities by which he labours to prove that the Levites had ownership of the tithes and of the other offerings and sacrifices. Third, they explain the mind of the objector. On the first point they say that the objector charges his opponent with holding that, in his view, the Levites had only the use of the tithes, when he never states this exclusively. Thus they say he falsely imputes this to him. On the second point they say that a distinction touched on above must be recalled to mind, namely that ownership is twofold. For there is one kind of ownership, which is a principal power, though not always the most principal, of claiming a thing in court and also of defending it. Another kind of ownership adds to that power the power of freely disposing of the thing. The priests and Levites seem to have had ownership in the first sense of all the things given to them by divine ordinance or offered willingly by the people. For if anyone had stolen the tithes, the firstfruits, the portion of the sacrifices that was due to the priests, and even the showbread, they would have had the power to claim them in court, just as now bishops and the persons of the Church have the power to claim the right of the Church in court if it has been taken away or unjustly held. And so, just as it is in some sense conceded that the men of the Church have ownership of ecclesiastical goods, so it may be conceded that the priests and Levites of the old law had in some sense ownership of the tithes and other things granted to them by God. For they do not seem to have been more stripped of temporal things than the ministers of the Church in the new law. But the priests and Levites did not have ownership in the second sense in all the things assigned to them, though in many of them they had the right and power of selling.

units.la: Potestas tamen vendi respectu aliquarum rerum magis distabat ab isto dominio, & respectu aliarum minus distabat a dominio, isto modo, dicto. Nam respectu aliquarum rerum habebant potestatem vendi absque omni potestate vendendi, donandi, permutandi aut quomodolibet alienandi, vel de eis disponendi, sicut fuit de panibus propositionum, quos soli sacerdotes in loco sancto debebant comedere. Aliquas autem res familiae suae dare poterant ad vescendum. Unde Numeri 18. scribitur: Primitias autem quas voluerunt & obtulerunt filii Israel tibi dedi & filiis ac filiabus tuis iure perpetuo: qui mundus est in domo tua vescetur ex eis. Ex his dicitur, quod auctoritates, quas iste adduxit ad probandum, habebant dominium oblationum sacrificiorum & huiusmodi, non concludunt de dominio secundo modo dicto; sed videntur concludere de dominio primo modo dicto. Tertio isti impugnatores explicant mentem appellantis dicentes, appellans per rationem praedictam intendebat directe concludere, quod usus facti in rebus usu consumptibilibus potest separari a dominio, est libera potestas vendendi, donandi rem, & de illa ad libitum disponendi, supponens tanquam certum, quod si usus facti in huiusmodi rebus potest a tali dominio separari, & usus facti in huiusmodi rebus potest ob omni dominio separari. Et de hoc patebit inferius. Quod a ratio sua probet, quod usus facti in huiusmodi rebus potest a tali dominio separari, videtur eis apertum. Nam de plurimis decimis & oblationib. & sacrificiis sacerdotes & Levitae non habebant aliquam potestatem quomodolibet disponendi, nisi potestate comedendi tantummodo. Unde Deut. 26. sic legitur. Quando conpleveris decimam cunctarum frugum tuarum, anno decimarum tertio dabis Levitae & advenae & pupillo & viduae, & comedant intra portas tuas & saturentur. Ex his verbis datur intelligi, quod quemadmodum advenae & pupilli non habebant nisi tantum modo potestate comedendi de huiusmodi decimis, ita nec Levitae habebant potestate aliter disponendi de huiusmodi decimis, quia tantum modo comedendo: & ita dominium liberum, proprie dictum nullatenus habuerunt, & tamen habuerunt usum facti. Ergo in decimis huiusmodi fuit usus facti a tali dominio separatus. & item Levitae. sic legitur: Omnis qui habuerit maculam de semine Aaron sacerdotis, non accedet offerre hostias domino, nec panes Deo suo: vescetur tamen panib. qui offeruntur in sanctuario. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod talis poterat uti panibus, in quibus tamen nullum habebat dominium saltem quod est potestas vendendi &c. Nec solum est verum de sacerdotib. & Levitis quod habebat usum facti a tali dominio separatus: imo et alii saepe habebat usum facti in huiusmodi rebus a tali dominio separatus. Nam de nonnullis oblatis & sacrificiis Deo habebat potestatem vtendi, sc. comedendi, de quib. aliud nihil facere potuerunt. Unde Deut. 12. sic habetur: Ad locum quem elegerit Dominus Deus vester de cunctis tribubus vestris, ut ponat nomen suum ibi, & habitet in eo, veniens venietis & offeretis in illo loco holocausta & victimas vestras, decimas & primitias manuum vestrarum, & vota atq; donaria, primogenita boum & ouium, & comedetis in conspectu domini Dei vestri. & post: Illic ergo ... quae praecipio conferetis holocausta & hostias & primitias manuum vestrarum & quicquid praecipuum est in muneribus quae votistis Deo: ibi epulabimini coram domino Deo vestro: vos ac filii & filiae vestrae, famuli ac famulae, atq; Leuitae, qui in vestris urbibus commorantur. Et infra: Non poteris comedere in oppidis tuis decimas frumenti, vini & olei tui: primogenita armentorum & pecorum, & omnia quae voveris & sponte offerre volueris & primitias manuum tuarum, sed coram domino Deo tuo comedes ea in loco quem elegerit dominus Deus tuus, tu & filia, servus ac famula atq; Leuita qui manent in urbibus tuis. Et infra: Quod autem sacrificaveris & voveris domino, tolles & venies ad locum, quem elegerit dominus, & offeres oblationes tuas: carnem & sanguinem super altare domini Dei tui, sanguinem hostiarum fundens in altari: carnibus autem ipse vescaris. Ex his verbis aliisq; quamplurimis consideranter datur intelligi, quod sanctificata & oblata domino, comedendi potestatem habebant, sed non de eis aliquid aliud ordinandi. & ita habuerunt usum facti a tali domino separatum. imo videtur, quod in talibus nullum dominium habuerunt: quia illa simpliciter erant oblata & sanctificata Deo: & eis erat concessa potestas tantummodo comedendi. Esto etiam, quod offerentes habuissent dominium, quod est potestas vendicadi rem in iudicio: filii tui & filiae, servi & famulae tale potestatem minime habuerunt, & tamen habuerunt usum facti. ergo usus facti quo ad illos in huiusmodi rebus fuit ab omni dominio separatus.
units.tr: Yet the power of selling was further removed from that ownership with respect to some things, and less far removed with respect to others, in the sense just described. For with respect to some things they had the power of selling without any power of giving, exchanging, alienating in any way, or disposing of them, as was the case with the showbread, which only the priests were to eat in the holy place. But some things they could give to their household to eat. So Num. 18 says: "The firstfruits which the children of Israel will and offer, I have given to you and to your sons and daughters by a perpetual right: whoever is clean in your house shall eat of them." From this it is said that the authorities which the objector brought to prove that the priests had ownership of the offerings, sacrifices and the like do not conclude about ownership in the second sense, but seem to conclude about ownership in the first sense. Third, these objectors explain the mind of the objector, saying that the objector, by the argument mentioned, intended directly to conclude that the use of a thing consumed in use can be separated from ownership, that ownership is the free power of selling or giving the thing and of disposing of it at will. He assumes as certain that if the use of such things can be separated from such ownership, then the use of such things can be separated from every ownership. It will be shown further below. That his argument proves that the use of such things can be separated from such ownership seems plain to them. For concerning most of the tithes, offerings and sacrifices, the priests and Levites had no power of disposing of them in any way except the power of eating them. Hence Deut. 26 reads thus: "When you have finished paying the tithe of all your fruits, in the third year of tithes you shall give it to the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow, and they shall eat within your gates and be filled." From these words it is to be understood that just as strangers and fatherless had no power but only the power of eating of such tithes, so neither did the Levites have power to dispose of such tithes otherwise than by eating them. So they did not in any way have free ownership, properly so called, and yet they had the use of the thing. Therefore in such tithes the use of the thing was separated from ownership. Likewise with the Levites. It reads thus: "Whoever has a blemish of the seed of Aaron the priest shall not come to offer sacrifices to the Lord, nor bread to his God; yet he may eat of the bread which is offered in the sanctuary." From these words it is to be understood that such a man could use the bread, though he had no ownership of it, at least in the sense of the power of selling, etc. Nor is it true only of priests and Levites that they had the use of a thing separated from such ownership; indeed others often had the use of such things separated from such ownership. For concerning some offerings and sacrifices to God they had the power of using, that is, of eating, and of nothing else. Hence Deut. 12 reads: "To the place which the Lord your God shall choose out of all your tribes, to put his name there and dwell there, you shall come and offer in that place your burnt offerings and victims, the tithes and firstfruits of your hands, and vows and gifts, the firstborn of oxen and sheep, and you shall eat in the sight of the Lord your God." And after: "There therefore... you shall bring your burnt offerings and sacrifices and the firstfruits of your hands and whatever is most excellent among the gifts which you have vowed to God; there you shall feast before the Lord your God, you and your sons and daughters, your menservants and maidservants, and the Levites who dwell in your cities." And below: "You cannot eat in your towns the tithes of your corn, wine and oil, the firstborn of your herds and flocks, and all that you have vowed and willingly offer, and the firstfruits of your hands; but before the Lord your God you shall eat them in the place which the Lord your God shall choose, you and your daughter, your manservant and maidservant, and the Levite who dwells in your cities." And below: "What you sacrifice and vow to the Lord, you shall take and go to the place which the Lord shall choose, and offer your oblations: the flesh and blood upon the altar of the Lord your God, pouring the blood of the victims upon the altar; but you may eat the flesh yourself." From these words and from very many others it is to be understood with careful consideration that, once sanctified and offered to the Lord, they had the power of eating, but not of ordaining anything else concerning them. So they had the use of the thing separated from such ownership. Indeed it seems that in such things they had no ownership at all, because those things were simply offered and sanctified to God, and to them was granted only the power of eating. Even granting that the offerers had ownership, which is the power of claiming the thing in court, the sons and daughters, menservants and maidservants had no such power at all, and yet they had the use of the thing. Therefore with respect to them the use of such things was separated from all ownership.

units.la: Sequitur videre aliqua circa literam. [Iste arguit evidenter ex falsis] hoc negant. [Quod enim dicit Leuitas habuisse usum tantum decimarum] dicuntur quod appellanti falsum imponit. [Dedi omnes decimas Israel in possessionem &c. Ex quibus patet, quod Leuita non tantum usum in decimis, sed etiam dominium habuerunt.] Dicunt quod hoc non patet ex verbis scripturae praemissae: licet ex istis & aliis patere posset, quod Leuitae in quibusdam decimis habuerunt ius comedendi, non tamen habuerunt in omnibus dominium, quo valerent de decimis ad suum libitum ordinare: quia, sicut ostensum est prius, dare non semper accipitur pro conferre dominium rei datae. [Nec obstat quod in eodem ca. dicitur quod in usus Leuitarum & necessaria dominus decimas separavit] illud obstat, ut dicunt isti: quia aliquarum decimarum habebant usum & potestatem vendi absque omni potestate de eis aliter disponendi: & ita habuerunt usum absque dominio libero & proprietate, quae est potestas de re ad libitum disponendi. [Aliud est enim alicui in usum rem aliquam dare, & aliud dare alicui usum alicuius rei.] Ista assertio continet duas particulas, in quarum utraque ponitur hoc nomen usus, sicut de se patet. Et si quidem in utraque particula accipiatur usus univoce, & eodem modo, dicunt isti quod est omnino irrationabiliter dictum: quia si in utraque particula accipiatur usus pro iure quodam determinato vendi, constat quod non est aliud secundum rem dare rem aliquam in usum talem, & dare alicui talem usum iuris rei. Si etiam accipitur in utraque particula pro potestate vendi: constat quod non est aliud, sicut non est aliud alicui in potestate vendi rem aliquam dare, & dare alicui potestatem vendi eadem re. Sicut si accipiatur pro actu vendi non est aliud: quia non est aliud dare alicui rem in actum vendi, & dare sibi actum vendi: nisi forte dicas, quod dare in actum vendi est dare potestatem vendi: sed tunc non acciperetur usus uniformiter in utraque particula, nec esset sicad propositum istius. Si autem hoc vocabulum usus aequivoce & differenter accipiatur in una particula, & in alia, sic potest concedi. Unde si in prima particula hoc nomen accipiatur pro potestate vendi, & in secunda pro usu iuris determinati, sic potest concedi: sicut aliud est dare alicui rem aliquam in potestatem vendi, & dare usum rei qui est iuris quoddam civile. Unde nonnunquam dat aliquis alicui potestatem equitandi equum suum: cui tamen non confert tale ius civile vendi. Sed isto modo nihil facit ad intentionem istius impugnati. [Ubi enim usus alicuius rei immisibili conceditur: usus tantum rei & non dominium sibi intelligitur datum esse.] Si hoc vocabulum usus accipitur pro usu determinato iuris civilis, quod est quoddam iuris distinctum a dominio & usufructu, continet veritatem. Sed isto modo in tota obiectione praemissa non accipit usum appellans: nec sic unquam accipitur nomen usus in scriptura divina. Si vero nomen usus in verbis praemissis accipitur pro potestate vendi: sic aliquin continet veritatem, & aliquando falsitatem: quia qui dat sic potestatem vendi, ut a se transferat dominium, si alius est capax, & vult recipere, dat etiam dominium: quandoque autem dat potestatem vendi dominio sibi retento. Idem potest dici de illo, qui dat usum accepto vocabulo usus pro actu vendi. [sed ubi alicui resultat in usum, nedum usus rei, sed etiam dominium intelligitur esse datum.] Si hoc vocabulo usus accipiatur pro usu determinato, opponitur. Dicunt isti, quod est simpliciter salsum, quia implicat contradictionem: scilicet quod aliquis haberet tale usum alicuius rei, & dominium eiusdem: quia sequeretur, quod esset res aliena & propria. Si accipitur vocabulum usus pro potestate vendi, sic adhuc est falsum, ut dicunt: quia saepe datur alicui hospitium vel res alia in potestate vendi, non tamen propter hoc intelligitur dominium esse datum. Et quia iste impugnatus hoc dictum suum neque ratione neque auctoritate probat, eadem facilitate contemnitur qua probatur. [cum dicitur in praellegato ca. quod in usus Leuitarum & necessaria dominus separavit. Declarauit dominus ad quid vel propter quid Leuitis decimas dedit.] hoc concedunt isti. [quia enim de frugibus &c.] hoc non impugnant. [Voluit dominus quod Leuitae possent non solum de frugibus illis comedere, sed etiam de illis quo ad alia vitae necessaria vendendo vel permutando sibi providere.] Hic dicunt istum impugnatum contra sacra scriptura errare: quia, sicut patet Leuitici 27: Fruges, de quibus est sermo, sanctificabantur domino. Unde Leuit. 27: sic habetur: Omnes decimae terrae sive de frugibus, sive de pomis arborum, domini sunt & illi sanctificatur. Sed sanctificata domino, vendere non licebat: imo nec licebat sanctificata domino, omnibus dare indifferenter ad vescendum. Unde Leuiti.
units.tr: It follows that we should look at some points concerning the letter. [This man argues plainly from falsehoods]. They deny this. [For what he says, that the Levites had only the use of the tithes]: they say he wrongly charges his opponent with this. [I have given all the tithes of Israel into possession, etc. From these words it is plain that the Levites had not only the use of the tithes, but also ownership.] They say this does not follow from the words of Scripture quoted above. From these and other passages it could be shown that the Levites had a right to eat some of the tithes, but they did not have ownership of all of them, by which they could dispose of the tithes as they pleased, because, as was shown earlier, to give does not always mean to confer ownership of the thing given. [Nor does it stand in the way that in the same chapter it is said that the Lord set apart the tithes for the uses and needs of the Levites]: this does not stand in the way, as they say, because the Levites had the use of some tithes and the power to sell them, without any power of disposing of them otherwise. So they had the use without free ownership and property, which is the power to dispose of a thing as one pleases. [For it is one thing to give someone a thing for use, and another to give someone the use of a thing.] This statement contains two clauses, and in each of them the word use occurs, as is obvious. If the word use is taken univocally, and in the same sense in both clauses, they say the statement is utterly irrational. For if in both clauses use means some determinate legal right to sell, it is clear that, in substance, to give someone a thing for such a use is no different from giving him such a use-right in the thing. If it is taken in both clauses as the power to sell, it is clear there is no difference, just as there is no difference between giving someone a thing into his power to sell and giving him the power to sell the same thing. Likewise if it is taken as the act of selling, there is no difference, because giving someone a thing for the act of selling is no different from giving him the act of selling. Unless perhaps you say that to give for the act of selling is to give the power of selling; but then use would not be taken uniformly in both clauses, and it would not serve the purpose of this argument. If, however, this word use is taken equivocally and in different senses in the one clause and the other, then the statement can be granted. So if in the first clause the word is taken for the power to sell, and in the second for a determinate legal use, the statement can be granted, just as it is one thing to give someone a thing into his power to sell and another to give him the use of a thing, which is a certain civil right. Thus sometimes a man gives someone the power to ride his horse, yet does not confer on him the civil right to sell it. But in this sense the statement has nothing to do with the purpose of the author being attacked. [For where the use of a thing is granted to someone in a determinate way, only the use of the thing and not ownership is understood to have been given.] If the word use is taken for a determinate use of civil law, which is a right distinct from ownership and usufruct, the statement contains truth. But in this sense the one making the objection does not take use in the whole of the objection quoted above, nor is the word use ever taken in this sense in Holy Scripture. If, however, the word use in the words quoted above is taken for the power to sell, then the statement sometimes contains truth and sometimes falsehood, because whoever gives the power to sell in such a way as to transfer ownership from himself, if another is capable and willing to receive it, also gives ownership; but sometimes he gives the power to sell while keeping ownership for himself. The same can be said of one who gives the use, if the word use is taken for the act of selling. [But where the use of a thing is conferred on someone, not only the use of the thing but also ownership is understood to have been given.] If the word use is taken for a determinate use, it is opposed. They say this is simply false, because it implies a contradiction: namely, that someone should have such a use of a thing and ownership of the same thing, since it would follow that the thing would be both another's and one's own. If the word use is taken for the power to sell, it is still false, as they say, because lodging or some other thing is often given to someone with the power to sell, yet it is not therefore understood that ownership has been given. And since the author under attack does not prove this statement of his either by reason or by authority, it is despised with the same ease with which it is asserted. [When it is said in the chapter cited above that the Lord set apart the tithes for the uses and needs of the Levites]: they grant this. [For as to the fruits, etc.] They do not dispute this. [The Lord willed that the Levites could not only eat of those fruits, but also, by selling or exchanging them, provide for themselves the other necessities of life.] Here they say that the author under attack errs against Holy Scripture, because, as is plain from Leviticus 27, the fruits in question were consecrated to the Lord. For Leviticus 27 reads thus: All the tithes of the land, whether of the fruits or of the fruit of the trees, are the Lord's, and are consecrated to him. But what is consecrated to the Lord could not be sold; indeed, what was consecrated to the Lord could not even be given indiscriminately to everyone to eat. Hence Leviticus.

units.la: Leuit. 22. ca. sic scribitur: Homo de semine Aaron, qui fuerit leprosus, aut patiens fluxum seminis, non vescetur de his, quæ sanctificata sunt mihi, donec sanetur. Omnis alienigena non comedet de sanctificatis: inquilinus sacerdotis, & mercenarius non comedet ex eis. & infra: Si filia sacerdotis cuilibet ex populo nupta fuerit, de his quæ sanctificata sunt, & de primitiis non vescetur. Ex his aliisq; quampluribus colligitur evidenter, quod non licebat sacerdotibus, & Leuitis dare sanctificata indifferenter omnibus ad vescendum: & per consequens multo magis non licebat vendere ipsa vel permutare: & ita non omnia quæ dabantur eis, ad hoc dabantur eis, ut vendendo, ac permutando sibi prouidere liceret. Quia de sanctificatis nullatenus hoc licebat. & ideo dixit, in usu & necessaria: patet quod non ideo dixit, quia nonnullis tantum uti debebant & vendere aut permutare minime poterant. [Et idem dicendum est de illo verbo in eodem capitulo contento, ad Aaron prolatis: ubi Dominus sic dixit, primitiarum frugum initia &c.] Hic etiam dicunt isti, quod errat: quia, ut dicunt, nō licebat sacerdotibus vendere primitias, aut etiam permutare. Vnde dicunt quod esto, quod cum dicit Leuitas & sacerdotes habuisse dominium decimarum, primitiarum, oblationum, sacrificiorum, & huiusmodi: per æquivocationē huius vocabuli dominium posset aliqualiter glosari: tamen cum dicit eos potuisse vendere, & permutare huiusmodi, nullo modo potest excusari: & specialiter de initiis frugum, de quibus hoc sit mentio, quod ex verbis scripturæ colligitur evidenter. Nam post verba prædicta sequitur immediate: qui mundus est in domo tua, vescetur ex eis. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod immundi in domo sacerdotis talibus frugum initiis vesci non poterant. ergo multo magis non debuerunt vendi, aut etiam permutari. Debebat ergo sacerdos, & qui mundi erant, in domo sua vesci huiusmodi frugum initiis. & per consequens non licebat sibi ea vendere, vel permutare. & ideo dicunt, quod iste errat, cum dicit. [Et idem dicendum est &c.] Secundo isti impugnatores notant ex istis verbis & prædictis, eum dixit. [Volvit Dominus &c.] Quia in tota ista serie verborum, per dominium intelligit potestatem, qua potest quis tem vendere & permutare, & de ea sibi necessaria prouidere. Quare dicunt, quod accipiendo dominium, sicut ipse accipit, omnino erroneum est, quod sacerdotes & Leuitæ in omnibus huiusmodi rebus habuerunt dominium. [Domino deportantur.] Quia Domino principaliter offeruntur. [Cedent in usus tuos.] Hoc est, dabuntur tibi ad vtendum. scilicet ad comedendum, vel aliquo alio modo conuenienti vtendum. Et de istis constat, quia non poterat ea vendere, nec permutare. [Illarum autem rerum dominium accessit illi Dominus.] Hoc dicunt omnino esse falsum, accipiendo dominium, sicut iste intelligit. s. pro potestate vendendi & permutandi. [& in eodem cap. patet.] Dicunt quod in eodem cap. patet contrarium sicut ostendent statim post. [Reddetur tibi.] Dicunt hic isti impugnatores, quod aliquid reddere Deo non est aliud quam dominium rei relinquere, & diuinis vsibus applicare. hoc autem sunt in triplici doctrina. quædam n. ex speciali ordinatione Dei diuinis vsib. applicantur, quia per ipsa colitur Deus, sicut fuerunt in veteri lege templū, vestes, vasa & huiusmodi. & ista solùmodo ad dominium Dei pertinere videntur, ita q; in nulli' bonis sunt nec tñ pro derelictis habetur, nec occupanti concedentur, sed diuino cultui deputatur. talia fuerūt multa in lege veteri, quę vendere aut permutare aut quomodolibet alienare nulli licebat. & ideo ad nullius hominis dominiū pertinebāt: & si ablata fuissent, aut iniuste detenta, nullus habuisset potestatē tanq; sua, sed tanquā Dei in iudicio vendicandi. Talia fuerūt arca Dei, mēsa propositionis, vestes quas fecit Moyses Aaron fratri suo & filiis eius ad vtendū, sicut habetur Exo. 28. & alia multa, q; nō poterat aliquo modo alienare. & ideo multis talib. vtebatur, in quib. nullū habebant dominiū. Aliqua vero sunt diuino cultui deputata ex generali ordinatione Dei, & speciali ordinatione humana, sicut sunt vestes, quib. multi vtuntur sacerdotes, & multa alia quę in ecclesiis reperiuntur. & ista aliquomodo ad dominiū humanū pertinere videtur; in quantū homines habēt potestatē ipsa vel in propria forma vel in alia forma alienādi & vendēdi & ad aliorū vsū & liberū dominiū transferendi & vendendi. Tertia sunt, quę nequaq; diuino cultui deputātur, sed ad sustentandū seruientes Deo specialiter assignātur. & de talib. potest, vt videtur, concedi, q; aliqualiter ministri Dei habēt eorū dominiū, in quantū habet potestatē ipsa tanquā sua vsui suo applicādi, & in iudicio vēdicandi, vel defendendi cōtra vēdicantes iniuste. De istis tñ quedam fuerunt in veteri lege, quæ ministri Dei nō poterant aliquo modo alienare, sed tñ cōsumere. [tuū eris & filiorū tuorū] non quantū ad potestate vendēdi & permutandi, sicut intelligit iste impugnat: sed quantū ad potestate comedendi, q; per verba immediate sequentia declaratur aperte, cū dicitur: in sanctuario comedetis illud mares tantū comedent ex eo, quia consecratū est domino. Ex quib. verbis datur intelligi, q; illud erat Aaron & filiorū eius quantū ad licita potestate comedendi, non ad aliū vsum nec quantū ad potestate vendēdi & permutādi: & ita tunc vsus facti separabatur à dominio tali, q; est potestas de re libere ordinandi. [Dedi tibi & filiis tuis &c.] non quantū ad potestatē vendēdi & permutādi: sed quantū ad potestatē comedēdi, q; ex verbis immediate sequētib. euidēter apparet, quib. dicitur: Qui mundus est in domo tua, vescetur ex eo. Ex quib. verbis colligitur, q; non alia potestate vrendi habebat, nisi comedendi tantumodo. [Ex quib. patet, q; nō solū in decimis, nec in reb. prædictis Aaron & Leuita vsi, sed dominiū habuerunt.] Contrariū sequitur omnino accipiēdo dominiū, sicut accipit iste. s. pro potestate vendendi, permutandi &c. qa res pdictas nō poterāt vendere, nec et pmutare. C A P. XXI.
units.tr: Leviticus 22: "A man of the seed of Aaron who is a leper, or who suffers an issue of seed, shall not eat of the things that are sanctified to me, until he is cleansed. Every stranger shall not eat of the holy things, a sojourner of the priest, or a hired servant, shall not eat of them." And further: "If the priest's daughter is married to any man of the people, she shall not eat of the holy things, or of the firstfruits." From these and many other passages it is clearly gathered that the priests and Levites were not permitted to give the sacred things indiscriminately to all to eat, and consequently much less were they permitted to sell or exchange them. So not everything that was given to them was given so that they might provide for themselves by selling and exchanging, since this was in no way allowed with things that were sanctified. Therefore when it says "in use and necessity," it is plain that it did not say this because they were to use only some things and could not sell or exchange them. [And the same must be said of that word in the same chapter, spoken to Aaron, where the Lord said: "the first-fruits of the fruits, the beginnings," etc.] Here too these men say he is wrong, because, as they say, the priests were not permitted to sell the firstfruits, or even to exchange them. Hence they say that, granted that when he speaks of the Levites and priests having ownership of the tithes, firstfruits, offerings, sacrifices, and such like, the ownership could be somehow explained by an equivocation of the word "ownership"; yet when he says they could sell and exchange such things, this cannot be excused in any way, and especially in the case of the beginnings of the fruits, which are the subject here, as is clearly gathered from the words of Scripture. For immediately after the aforesaid words there follows: "he who is clean in your house shall eat of them." From these words it is made clear that the unclean in a priest's house could not eat of such firstfruits. Therefore much more they ought not to have been sold or exchanged. The priest, and those who were clean, were therefore obliged to eat such firstfruits in his house; and consequently it was not permitted to him to sell or exchange them. And so they say that he is wrong when he says [And the same must be said, etc.]. Secondly, these opponents note from these words and the preceding ones, when he said [The Lord has willed, etc.], that in this whole series of words he understands by ownership the power by which one can sell and exchange, and so provide for oneself what is necessary. Wherefore they say that, taking ownership as he takes it, it is wholly erroneous that priests and Levites had ownership of all such things. [Are carried to the Lord.] Because they are offered principally to the Lord. [They shall pass into your use.] That is, they shall be given to you for use, namely for eating, or for use in some other suitable way. And from these things it is plain that they could not sell or exchange them. [But the ownership of those things passed to him, the Lord.] They say this is altogether false, taking ownership as he understands it, that is, as the power of selling and exchanging. [And in the same chapter it is clear.] They say that in the same chapter the contrary is clear, as they will show immediately after. [It shall be rendered to you.] Here these opponents say that to render something to God is nothing other than to leave the ownership of a thing and dedicate it to divine uses. Now such things are of a threefold kind. For some things, by a special ordinance of God, are dedicated to divine uses, because God is worshipped through them, as in the old law were the temple, vestments, vessels and such like. These seem to pertain to the ownership of God alone, so that they are in no one's goods, nor are they regarded as abandoned, nor are they granted to an occupier, but are assigned to divine worship. Many such things existed in the old law, which no one was permitted to sell or exchange or in any way alienate. And therefore they did not pertain to the ownership of any man; and if they had been taken away or unjustly withheld, no one would have had power over them as his own, but only as God's, to claim in judgment. Such were the ark of God, the table of showbread, the garments which Moses made for Aaron his brother and his sons to use, as is found in Exodus 28, and many other things which could in no way be alienated. And therefore they used many such things in which they had no ownership. Others, however, are assigned to divine worship by a general ordinance of God and a special human ordinance, such as the vestments which many priests use, and many other things found in the churches. These seem in some way to pertain to human ownership, insofar as men have the power to alienate and sell them, either in their own form or in another form, and to transfer and sell them to the use and free ownership of others. The third kind are those which are not at all assigned to divine worship, but are specially designated for the support of those who serve God. And of such things it may, as it seems, be granted that the ministers of God have ownership of them in some way, insofar as they have the power to apply them to their own use, and to claim them in judgment, or to defend them against those who unjustly claim them. Yet of these there were some in the old law which the ministers of God could in no way alienate, but only consume. [Yours shall be, and your sons'.] This is not as regards the power of selling and exchanging, as this opponent understands it, but as regards the power of eating, which is plainly declared by the words immediately following, where it says: "In the sanctuary you shall eat it; only the males shall eat of it, because it is consecrated to the Lord." From these words it is understood that it belonged to Aaron and his sons as regards the lawful power of eating, not for any other use, nor as regards the power of selling and exchanging; and so then the use of the thing was separated from such ownership, which is the power of freely disposing of the thing. [I have given to you and your sons, etc.] Not as regards the power of selling and exchanging, but as regards the power of eating, which is evident from the words immediately following, where it says: "He who is clean in your house shall eat of it." From these words it is gathered that they had no other power of using it than eating only. [From which it is clear that Aaron and the Levites did not only use the tithes and the aforesaid things, but had ownership of them.] The contrary follows altogether if ownership is taken as he takes it, namely as the power of selling, exchanging, etc., since they could not sell or exchange the aforesaid things. CAP. XXI.

units.la: Rūrsus nititur ostendere, quod dicere, quod simplex vsus facti nō possit haberi in reb. vsu consumptibilibus à dominio separatis, est vitā Christi & apostolorū eius impugnare, quia perfectio paupertatis, sicut & alia perfectiones consiliorū euangelicorū fuerunt in Christo & in apostolis perfectissime. & ideo est secundum eum, quod paupertas evangelica excludit sollicitudinē, quā requirit proprietas seu dominiū temporaliū rerum. Ex quo sequitur secundū eum, quod vsus rerum vsu cōsumptibilium potest à proprietate & earum dominio separari.
units.tr: Again he strives to show that to say that simple use of fact cannot be had in things consumed by use, separated from ownership, is to attack the life of Christ and of his apostles. For the perfection of poverty, as also the other perfections of the evangelical counsels, were in Christ and in the apostles most perfectly. And therefore, according to him, evangelical poverty excludes the anxiety which the property or ownership of temporal things requires. From this it follows, according to him, that the use of things consumed by use can be separated from property and from the ownership of them.

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnatus respondet ad quartam obiectionem appellantis contra primam assertionem impugnati. Et primo recitat obiectionem. Secundo suam ponit rationem in parte immediate sequenti ibi: ad hoc dicendum. Est autem obiectio talis. Christus & apostoli perfectissime seruauerunt euangelicam paupertatem. sed euangelica paupertas excludit omne dominium. ergo nullius rei habuerunt dominium: & tamen habuerunt vsum rerum vsu consumptibilium. ergo in rebus vsu consumptibilibus potest vsus facti a proprietate & dominio separari.
units.tr: In this part this opponent responds to the fourth objection of the appellant against the first assertion of the impugned party. And first he recites the objection; secondly he sets out his own reasoning in the part immediately following, where he says: ad hoc dicendum. The objection is this: Christ and the apostles most perfectly observed evangelical poverty. But evangelical poverty excludes all ownership. Therefore they had no ownership of any thing; and yet they had the use of things consumed by use. Therefore, in things consumed by use, the use of fact can be separated from property and ownership.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, quod truncate obiectionem recitat supradictam. vnde in appellatione Minorum haec obiectio ponitur sub his verbis: Quarto ostenditur, quod dicta assertio vitae Christi & apostolorum eius impugnat. quia perfectio paupertatis sicut & perfectiones aliae consiliorum euangelicorum, fuit in Christo & apostolis perfectissime. & constat quod paupertas euangelica proprietatem & dominium rerum vsu consumptibilium excludit. quia excludit sollicitudinem, quam requirit proprietas seu dominium rerum, sicut plane probant auctoritates in appellatione prolixa inductae. sed paupertas euangelica non excludit vsum rerum vsu consumptibilium. ergo vsus rerum consumptibilium potest a proprietate earum & dominio separari. haec verba Appellationis, quae aliqualiter, quamuis non multum in sententia, distant a verbis superius recitatis.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he recites the aforesaid objection in truncated form. In the Appeal of the Minorites, this objection is put in these words: Fourthly, it is shown that the said assertion impugns the life of Christ and his apostles, because the perfection of poverty, as also the other perfections of the evangelical counsels, was in Christ and the apostles most perfectly. And it is plain that evangelical poverty excludes ownership and dominion over things consumable by use, because it excludes the anxiety which ownership or dominion over things requires, as the authorities cited at length in the Appeal plainly prove. But evangelical poverty does not exclude the use of things consumable by use. Therefore the use of consumable things can be separated from their ownership and dominion. These are the words of the Appeal, which differ somewhat from the words recited above, though not much in sense.

units.la: Quae vt clariora sunt, declaremus. [quod vsus simplex facti] dicunt quod de hoc in verbis praedictis nulla fit mentio: licet hoc intendat appellans [fuerunt in Christo & apostolis perfectissime] non solum secundum praeparationem animi, sed etiam secundum opus exterius, sicut isti ostendere molintur. [excludit sollicitudinem] non tamen omnem, quia non necessaria.
units.tr: So that these points may be clearer, let us explain them. [that simple use of fact] they say there is no mention of this in the aforesaid words, although the appellant intends [were in Christ and the apostles most perfectly] not only according to preparation of mind but also according to outward work, as these men labour to show. [excludes anxiety] not, however, all of it, since it is not necessary.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: AD hoc dicendum, quod concedimus, quod perfectio paupertatis in Christo & apostolis perfectissime fuit: persectio siquidem paupertatis euangelicae plus consistit in animo, vt scil. animus amore istius temporalibus non adhaereat, quam in carentia temporalium rerum. Hanc autem paupertatem perfectissime habuit Christus, & post eum apostoli eius. & per consequens perfectionem paupertatis euangelicae habuerunt.
units.tr: As to this, it must be said that we concede that the perfection of poverty was in Christ and the apostles most perfectly. For the perfection of evangelical poverty consists more in the mind, namely that the mind does not cling to such temporal things through love of them, than in the lack of temporal things. Christ had this poverty most perfectly, and after him his apostles. And consequently they had the perfection of evangelical poverty.

units.la: In parte ista ad obiectionem praemissam nititur respondere. & diuiditur in tres partes, scil. quod ad tria tacta in dicta obiectione respondet. secunda pars incipit in parte immediate sequenti ibi: Ad illud autem. Tertia ibi, ad illud autem quod dicit. dicit ergo quod perfectio paupertatis euangelicae perfectissime fuit in Christo & apostolis. sed illa magis consistit in animo, quam in carentia rerum temporalium: & illam habuerunt perfectissime.
units.tr: In this part he tries to answer the aforesaid objection. It is divided into three parts, namely he answers the three points touched on in the objection. The second part begins in the next part, at As to that. The third begins at as to that which he says. He says, therefore, that the perfection of evangelical poverty was in Christ and the apostles most perfectly. But that perfection consists more in the mind than in the lack of temporal things, and they had it most perfectly.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod licet verba praedicta pure affirmatiue accepta, nullum videantur continere errorem: tamen si secundum intentionem dicentis intelligantur negatiue. sc. quod paupertas euangelica fuit perfectissime in Christo & in apostolis quantum ad praeparationem animi & non quantum ad carentiam rerum temporalium. Dicunt, quod talis intellectus est omnino erroneus. veruntamen quia hoc ex istis verbis praecise colligi nequaquam potest: ideo de hoc ad praesens minime disseretur, sed postea de hoc in loco suo prolixe tractabitur.
units.tr: But these opponents say that, although the words above, taken purely affirmatively, seem to contain no error, yet if they are understood according to the intention of the speaker in a negative sense, namely that evangelical poverty was most perfect in Christ and the apostles as regards preparation of mind and not as regards lack of temporal things, then such a meaning is wholly erroneous. However, because this cannot be gathered precisely from these words, it will not be discussed at present, but it will be treated at length later, in its proper place.

units.la: Nunc satis est verba textus explanasse [plus consistit in animo] hoc verum est: tamen consistit etiam in carentia rerum. [& per consequens perfectionem paupertatis euangelicae habuerunt] dicunt isti, quod licet antecedens fuerit verum, & similiter consequens: tamen consequentia nulla est. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quando aliqua duo sunt de essentia alicuius, quorum vnum est persectius, & aliud minus perfectum, ex hoc quod habetur magis perfectum, non potest inferri quod perfectio totius habetur. sicut ex hoc, quod anima est in coelo, non potest concludi, quod pedes homo sit in coelo. sed ad essentiam euangelicae paupertatis pertinent duo. sc. non adhaerere temporalibus nimio amore, & carere temporalibus. ergo ex hoc, quod apostoli habuerunt primum, non potest inferri quod habuerunt perfectionem euangelicae paupertatis. Quod autem ad essentiam euangelicae paupertatis pertineat carentia rerum temporalium, in parte sequenti conabuntur ostendere.
units.tr: For now it is enough to have explained the words of the text. [plus consistit in animo] This is true; yet it also consists in lack of things. [and consequently they had the perfection of evangelical poverty] These men say that although the antecedent is true, and likewise the consequent, the consequence is nonetheless invalid. To make this clear, they say, one should know that when two things belong to the essence of something, one of which is more perfect and the other less so, it cannot be inferred from the fact that the more perfect one is had that the perfection of the whole is had. Just as from the fact that the soul is in heaven, it cannot be concluded that the man's feet are in heaven. But two things belong to the essence of evangelical poverty: not to cling to temporal things with excessive love, and to lack temporal things. Therefore, from the fact that the apostles had the first, it cannot be inferred that they had the perfection of evangelical poverty. That the lack of temporal things pertains to the essence of evangelical poverty, they will try to show in the following part.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: AD illud autem, quod dicit: Paupertas euangelica rerum vsu consumptibilium dominium & proprietatem excludit. dicimus, quod est falsum, imo illarum rerum supponit scriptura sacra ipsos apostolos ad minus in communi habuisse proprietatem & dominium, vt probatur act. cap. 4. vt est superius ostensum.
units.tr: As to what he says: evangelical poverty excludes ownership and property of things consumable by use. We say that this is false. Indeed, Holy Scripture presupposes that the apostles themselves had ownership and property of those things, at least in common, as is proved in Acts 4, as has been shown above.

units.la: Hic respondet ad secundum, quod in obiectione praemissa tangebatur. sc. quod paupertas euangelica proprietatem excludit: dicens hoc esse falsum, quia apostoli habuerunt aliquarum rerum proprietatem & dominium, saltem in communi.
units.tr: Here he answers the second point touched on in the aforesaid objection, namely that evangelical poverty excludes ownership and property. He says this is false, because the apostles had ownership and property of some things, at least in common.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt hic duos errores includi. quorum primus est, quod paupertas euangelica rerum dominium & proprietate non excludit. Secundus est quod apostoli habuerunt aliquarum rerum in communi. Quod primum sit erroneum, probare conantur. Primo sic. illa paupertas est praecipue euangelica reputanda, quae singulariter in euangelio edocetur, & volentibus doctrinam euangelicam perfecte sequi iniungitur. Non n. videtur quod propter aliam rationem aliqua paupertas debeat euangelica nuncupari, sicut illa, nec aliqua paupertas debet apostolica appellari, nisi quam apostoli docuerunt vel facto seruauerunt. sed paupertas quae in euangelio singulariter edocetur, omne dominium & proprietatem excludit. Nam in nullo loco euangelii paupertas, quod Christus docuit, magis explicari videtur, quam quando Christus viam perfectionis quaerenti respondit: Si vis perfectus esse, vade & vende omnia quae habes, & da pauperib. qui autem omnia vendit, & dat pauperib. omne dominium, proprium, & comune relinquit. ergo paupertas euangelica omne dominium & proprietate excludit. Secundo sic arguunt. Paupertas euangelica non est minor paupertate quae quorumcunq; religiosorū.sed pauptas aliquorū religiosorū, puta Fratrū Minorum, omne dominium & pprietatem excludit,sicut inferius ostendetur.ergo & paupertas euangelica omne dominium& pprietatem excludit.Tertio sic: cuiuslibet doctrinæ pfectæ moralis est docere, qualiter tam actus interiores quā exteriores virtuosus debeat exercere.sed doctrina euangelica,prout tractat de pauptate,est doctrina perfecta moralis.ergo non tm docet, qualiter qs debeat esse pauper quantū ad actū interiorē.s.quantū ad præparationē animi:sed et quantū ad opus exterius.s.quantum ad carentiā temporaliū rerū. Sed abdicare omnium tēporaliū rerum dominium & pro-prietatem propter Deū,est opʾ virtuosūm pauperta-tis: quia secundū Nicolaum tertiū in decretali.Exiit talis abdicatio propter Deū meritoria est & sancta.ergo ad doctrinā euangelicā spectat ab-dicationē huiusmodi suadere.Ex quo sequitur,q talis abdicatio, paupertas euāgelica est cēsenda.
units.tr: But these opponents say that two errors are included here. The first is that evangelical poverty does not exclude ownership and property of things. The second is that the apostles had some things in common. They try to prove that the first is erroneous. First, thus: that poverty is rightly regarded as evangelical which is taught singularly in the gospel and is enjoined on those who wish to follow the evangelical doctrine perfectly. For it does not seem that any poverty ought to be called evangelical for another reason, nor should any poverty be called apostolic, except that which the apostles taught or kept in deed. But the poverty which is taught singularly in the gospel excludes all ownership and property. For in no passage of the gospel is the poverty that Christ taught more clearly explained than where Christ answered the one seeking the way of perfection: "If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, and give to the poor." But he who sells all and gives to the poor leaves behind all ownership, private and common. Therefore evangelical poverty excludes all ownership and property. Secondly, they argue thus: evangelical poverty is not less than the poverty of any religious order. But the poverty of some religious, namely of the Friars Minor, excludes all ownership and property, as will be shown below. Therefore evangelical poverty also excludes all ownership and property. Thirdly, thus: it is the task of every perfect moral doctrine to teach how both inner and outer acts ought to be exercised virtuously. But evangelical doctrine, insofar as it treats of poverty, is a perfect moral doctrine. Therefore it teaches how one ought to be poor not only as regards the inner act, namely the preparation of mind, but also as regards outward work, namely the lack of temporal things. But to renounce the ownership and property of all temporal things for God's sake is a virtuous work of poverty, because according to Pope Nicholas III in the decretal Exiit, such renunciation made for God's sake is meritorious and holy. Therefore it pertains to evangelical doctrine to persuade such renunciation. From this it follows that such renunciation is to be counted as evangelical poverty.

units.la: Dicunt igitur isti impugnatores, q paupertas euangelica illa vocatur, q singulariter in euangelio explicite traditur & docetur:& q omne dominiū & proprietatem,quo videl.quis in iudicio valet litigare,excludit.Hęc n. paupertas licet in veteri lege cōtineatur implicite, sicut & oēs perfectiones consiliorū euangelicorū:in ipsa tm minime explicatur propter q necaliqs legitur tunc ipsam seruasse.Vnde & ex hoc quarto ostendunt,q paupertas euangelica omne dominiū & proprietatē excludit. nam sicut lex euangelica est quodāmodo pfectior veteri lege, ita paupertas euangelica aliquid pfectiōis addit vltra perfectionē paupertatis antiquorū patrum.hæc de se videtur patēs: & tm probatur auctoritate Greg.qui primo libro Moraliū ait:Nec du precepti virtus emicuerat,quā omnia relinqui præceperat.sed tamē beatus Iob eandē preceptionis vim in corde seruabat: quia nimirū substantia suā reliquerat mente,qua sine delectatione possidebat. Ex quib. verbis clare datur intelligi, q licet beatus Iob totam substantiā suam mente reliqrit:quia tm substantiam suam actualiter retinebat,virtus ṗceptiomnia relinquendi nondū pfectissime,quātum ad omnem perfectionē, q in euangelio suadetur, emicuit.& ita paupertas,q in euāgelio docetur explicite,aliquid perfectionis addit vltra paupertatem,q sancti patres seruabant.sed ipsi omnia reliquerunt secundū præparationem animi,& nōnulli etiam quantum ad affectionem & curam, teste apostolo ad Hebr.11. qui de quibusdam ait: Circuierunt in melotis,in pellibus caprinis, egentes, angustiati,afflicti:quibus dignus non erat mundus, in solitudi-nibus errantes,in montibus,in spelunciis & in cauernis terrae.ergo ad euangelicā paupertatē pertinet actua-lis abdicatio omnis dominii & proprietatis omnium rerum temporaliū.Quinto sic arguunt.lex euangelica est perfectissima ergo docet extremos gradus virtutum. Extremus autem gradus paupertatis est abdicatio omnis dominii & proprietatis. ergo lex euangelica talem docet paupertatē. & per consequens talis abdicatio ad euangelicam pertinet paupertatem.
units.tr: These opponents therefore say that evangelical poverty is that which is explicitly delivered and taught singularly in the gospel, and which excludes all ownership and property by which one may contend in judgment. For this poverty, although contained implicitly in the old law, as are all the perfections of the evangelical counsels, is not at all explained there, on account of which it is not read that anyone then kept it. Hence they show from this, fourthly, that evangelical poverty excludes all ownership and property. For just as the evangelical law is in some way more perfect than the old law, so evangelical poverty adds something of perfection beyond the perfection of poverty of the ancient fathers. This seems plain in itself, and it is proved by the authority of Gregory, who in the first book of the Moralia says: "Nor had the virtue of the precept shone forth, which had commanded that all things be relinquished. But blessed Job kept the same force of the precept in his heart, because he had indeed relinquished his substance in mind, which he possessed without delight." From these words it is clearly to be understood that, although blessed Job relinquished his whole substance in mind, because he still actually retained his substance, the virtue of relinquishing all had not yet shone forth most perfectly, as to every perfection which is urged in the gospel. And so the poverty taught explicitly in the gospel adds something of perfection beyond the poverty which the holy fathers kept. But they relinquished all according to preparation of mind, and some also as regards affection and care, the apostle bearing witness in Hebrews 11, who says of certain ones: "They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, in want, distressed, afflicted, of whom the world was not worthy, wandering in deserts, in mountains, in caves and in the holes of the earth." Therefore the actual abdication of all ownership and property of all temporal things pertains to evangelical poverty. Fifthly, they argue thus: the evangelical law is most perfect; therefore it teaches the extreme degrees of the virtues. But the extreme degree of poverty is the abdication of all ownership and property. Therefore the evangelical law teaches such poverty, and consequently such abdication pertains to evangelical poverty.

units.la: Quia vero isti impugnatores asserunt manifeste, q ista assertio istius impugnati est error quorundam Magistrorum Parisiensis olim per Alexand. 4. condemnatus: & per Doctores Ordinum Prædicatorum & Minorum multipliciter reprobatus.ideo dicunt isti, q iste impugnatus hic incidit in errorem per Romanos pontifices.s.Alex. 4:& Innoc. 4. condemnatum. Quod autem magis appareant,verba prædicti Alexandri quarti in quadam decretali eius, q incipit: non sine multa, adducunt. Ait autem sic:Cum insuper iidem Fratres omnia reliquerint propter Deū, exilia vita subsidia men-dicantes, Christumq; pauperem imitentur perfectionē euangelicā amplexando: propter q cuiderter apparet,eos nō solum in statu saluandorū existere,sed etiam perfectorū per sua religionis obseruantiā, qua quidē ipsum perfectionis euangelicæ tenet formā in aeterna retributionis primo præcellentem gloriā promereri.
