Et infra : Volumus, & per apostolica scripta mandamus,quatenus singuli vestrū omnes Magistros, Doctores, & alios, quisque in scholis, siue in prædicationibus,seu alibi contra præmissa vel aliquid ipsorum attentauerint, vel in posterum attentabunt, ex parte nostra monere studeatis. Et infra:Cerni terminum præfigendū eisdem dictu suum reuocent publice, male se dixisse fatentes,illaq; detestentur penitus & retractent afferendo contrarium, & illudetiam fideliter prædicando. Et infra: Nos nihilominus auctoritate præsentium districtius inhibemus,ne quisquam prasmissa vel aliquod præmissorū per-tinaciter astruere,vel quomodolibet defensare præsumat. quicunq; id præsumpserit; tanquam contumax, & ecclesiæ Romanæ rebellis ab omnibus fidelibus habeatur. Ex his verbis colligunt isti tria. Primum est, quod ad euangelicam paupertatem spectat abdicatio omnis proprietatis in speciali & communi.Secundū est,quod constitutionibus istius impugnati nulla est fides penitus adhibenda. Tertium est,quod omnes tenentes assertionem prædictam tanquam contumaces & rebelles Romanæ ecclesiæ sunt censendi. Primum declarant sic. Illa abdicatio, quæ perfectionem euangelicam amplexatur & perfectionis tenet formam, ad euangelicam pertinet paupertatem.sed abdicatio proprietatis omnium rerum in speciali & in communi perfectionem euangelicam amplexatur, & perfectionis euangelicæ tenet formam.cum Alexander prædictus de Fratribus Minoribus,qui talem abdicationem vouent in verbis præmissis asserat manifeste:ergo huiusmodi abdicatio ad euangelicam pertinet paupertatem.
units.tr: But since these opponents state plainly that this assertion of the man they attack is the error of certain masters of Paris, once condemned by Alexander IV and repudiated in many ways by the doctors of the Orders of Preachers and Minors, these men say that the man under attack here has fallen into an error condemned by Roman pontiffs, namely Alexander IV and Innocent IV. To make this clearer, they cite the words of the said Alexander IV in a certain decretal of his that begins "Non sine multa." He says: "Since moreover the same Brothers have left all things for God's sake, living on alms and begging, and imitate Christ the poor man by embracing evangelical perfection, it is therefore clearly evident that they not only exist in the state of those who are to be saved, but also of the perfect, since through the observance of their religion, which indeed holds the very form of evangelical perfection, they merit a glory that surpasses all others in the eternal reward." And further: "We will, and by apostolic writings we command, that each of you take care to warn all masters, teachers and others, whoever in the schools, or in sermons, or elsewhere, have attempted or in future attempt anything contrary to the premises or to any of them." And further: "Let a time limit be set for them, within which they publicly revoke what they have said, confessing that they spoke badly, and utterly detest and retract those things, asserting the contrary and also preaching that faithfully." And further: "We moreover, by the authority of these presents, more strictly forbid anyone to presume to assert obstinately, or in any way to defend, the premises or any of the premises. Whoever shall presume to do so, let him be regarded by all the faithful as stubborn and a rebel against the Roman Church." From these words they draw three conclusions. The first is that the renunciation of all ownership, both in particular and in common, belongs to evangelical poverty. The second is that no faith at all is to be given to the constitutions of this man under attack. The third is that all who hold the said assertion are to be judged stubborn and rebels against the Roman Church. They establish the first thus. That renunciation which embraces evangelical perfection and holds the form of perfection belongs to evangelical poverty. But renunciation of the ownership of all things, both in particular and in common, embraces evangelical perfection and holds the form of evangelical perfection, since Alexander, said above, plainly states this of the Brothers Minor, who vow such renunciation in the words quoted. Therefore such renunciation belongs to evangelical poverty.

units.la: Nec valet dicere, quod Alexander ibidem loquitur de Fratribus Prædicatoribus & Minoribus: & tamen Fratres Prædicatores habent aliquarum rerum dominium in communi. Nam licet loquatur de vtrisque: tamen loquens de paupertate eorum affirmat aperte, quod Fratres Minores, qui huiusmodi abdicationem vouent, perfectionem euangelicam amplexantur, & persectionis euangelicæ tenent formam. ergo abdicatio ad euangelicam pertinet paupertate. unde licet eos coniungat, tamen intendit, quod vtrorumque paupertas ad euangelicam paupertatem pertinet; quamuis paupertas illorum quantum ad aliquem gradum sit perfectio paupep-tate illorum. Vnde paupertas euangelica vltra omnem paupertatem praecedentium patrum addit duos gradus. s. in abdicatione proprietatis omnium in speciali se voto firmare, & in abdicatione omnium tam in speciali quam etiam in communi se voto firmare. & ita utrorumque paupertas ad euangelicam pertinet paupertatem: imo etiam paupertas monachorum magnas possessiones habentium in communi a paupertate euangelica non debet excludi, quamuis ipsam non ita perfecte imitetur, sicut paupertas eorum qui non habent possessiones etiam in communi. Secundo colligunt isti ex praedictis, & constitutionibus istius impugnati nulla est fides penitus adhibenda: quia non maioris auctoritatis est iste, quam fuerit Alexander quartus. Sed secundum istum decretalipdictae Alexandri quarti, fides est minime adhibenda, cum doctrinam falsam secundum istum contineat. falsae autem doctrinae nulla debet fides adhiberi, ergo nec constitutionibus istius est fides aliqualiter adhibenda. Unde dicunt isti, quod iste reprobando doctrinam summorum pontificum ostendit omni auctoritate carere, quare & doctrinae suae nullus cogitur adhaerere, & si de facto alios cogit suam doctrinam defendere, facto sibiipsi contrarius inuenitur. Tertio concludunt isti ex praemissis, quod ostenentes assertionem istius impugnati contumaces & rebelles Romanae ecclesiae sunt censendi. Nam ex quo constitutionibus istius impugnati est minime adhaerendum, sicut ostensum est prius, decretali praedicta Alexandri quarti omnes tenentes abdicationem Fratrum Minorum, s. perfectionem euangelicam minime amplexari & perfectionis euangelicae formam non tenere, sunt contumaces & rebelles ratione ecclesiae iudicati. hoc autem tenent ostes, q dicunt, euangelicam paupertatem dominium rerum & proprietatem nequaquam excludere. ergo ostes dictam assertionem tenentes contumaces & rebelles Romanae ecclesiae sunt censendi. Ex quo inferunt quod omnes consentientes vel approbantes constitutiones istius de hac materia, ac eas tanquam approbandas, legentes, approbantes, exponentes, scribentes, praedicantes vel eis quomodolibet adhaerentes, sunt contumaces & rebelles Romanae ecclesiae reputandi. Insuper isti impugnatores propter eos, qui doctrinam Thomae sequuntur, verba eiusdem praedictam assertionem tanquam erroneam reprobantis adducunt. Dicit enim, quod in libro suo, quem edidit contra praedictos Magistros Parisienses, ca. 6. pertractans, & p rubrica praemittens: Utrum religioso liceat omnia sua relinquere, ita quod nihil sibi possidendum remaneat nec in proprio nec in communi, assertive pronuntiat verba, quae sequuntur, dicens: Praedictis autem non contenti aduersarii veritatis religionum omnium fundamentum ab ipso domino firmiter collocatum nituntur evertere, videl. paupertatem, dicentes illicitum fore omnibus suis dimissis pauperem religionem ingredi, qua possessiones ac redditus non habeat. Et infra loquens de Vigilantio haeretico, ait: Nec solum totentus fuit Iouinianum imitari, consilium de virginitate euacuans, sed super addere ausus est, ut etiam consilium de paupertate seruanda omnino destrueret. Unde Hieronymus de eo dicit, quod autem asserit eos melius facere, qui vtuntur rebus suis & paulatim fructus possessionum pauperibus diuidunt, quam illos qui possessionibus venundatis semel omnia largiuntur, non a me ei, sed a Deo respondebitur: Si vis esse perfectus, vade & vende omnia quae habes, & da pauperibus, & veni sequere me. Matt. 19. Hic autem error per successiones errantium vsq; ad hodierna tempora peruenit, & in haereticis quibusdam, qui Cathari nominantur, permansit & adhuc permanet, sicut patet in quodam tractatu cuiusdam defidei Heresiarchae Lombardi nostri temporis, quem edidit contra catholicam veritatem: in quo inter catera condemnat statum eorum, qui relictis omnibus igere volunt cum Christo. Nuper autem (quod est horribile) antiquus error renouatus est ab hiis, qui fidem defendere videbantur, & more errantium in pejus procedentes, non sunt contenti diuitias paupertati aequare, vt Iouinianus: vel diuitias paupertati praeferre, vt Vigilantius: sed paupertatem totaliter condemnare, dicentes non esse licitum omnia sua pro Christo relinquere, nisi talem religionem intret, quae possessionem habeat: vel nisi talis de labore manuum viuere intendat. Asserunt etiam paupertatem laudari in scripturis non actualem, qua scilicet aliquis rebus temporalibus se expoliat, sed habitualem, qua aliquis rem temporalem contemnit corde, & si res possideat. Hic explicat sententialiter assertionem praedictam istius impugnati, qui ponit quam euangelica paupertas omnium rerum temporalium dominium & paupertatem nequaquam excludit, quia euangelica paupertas maxime laudatur in scripturis. & ideo si euangelica paupertas non excludit omnem dominium temporalium, actualis paupertas, quae excludit omnem dominium, non maxime laudatur in scripturis, vt dicunt praedicti aristes secundum Thomam.
units.tr: Nor is it valid to say that Alexander is speaking there of the Brothers Preachers and Minors together, and yet the Brothers Preachers hold some things in common as ownership. For although he speaks of both, nevertheless, speaking of their poverty, he openly affirms that the Brothers Minor, who vow such renunciation, embrace evangelical perfection and hold the form of evangelical perfection. Therefore renunciation belongs to evangelical poverty. Hence, although he joins them, he intends that the poverty of both belongs to evangelical poverty, although the poverty of the one is, in some degree, more perfect than the poverty of the other. Thus evangelical poverty, beyond all the poverty of the earlier Fathers, adds two degrees: namely, to bind oneself by vow to renounce all things in particular, and to bind oneself by vow to renounce all things both in particular and in common. And so the poverty of both belongs to evangelical poverty. Indeed, even the poverty of monks who hold large possessions in common ought not to be excluded from evangelical poverty, although they do not imitate it as perfectly as those who have no possessions even in common. Secondly, these men conclude from the foregoing, and from the constitutions of this man under attack, that no faith at all is to be given to them: because this man is of no greater authority than Alexander IV was. But according to the said decretal of Alexander IV, faith is by no means to be given, since it contains, according to this man, false doctrine; and no faith ought to be given to false doctrine. Therefore neither is faith in any way to be given to this man's constitutions. Hence these men say that this man, by rejecting the doctrine of the supreme pontiffs, shows that he lacks all authority, so that no one is bound to adhere to his doctrine; and if he in fact compels others to defend his doctrine, he is found to be contrary to himself. Thirdly, these men conclude from the premises that those who uphold the assertion of this man under attack are to be judged stubborn and rebels against the Roman Church. For since one must by no means adhere to this man's constitutions, as has been shown before, all who hold the renunciation of the Brothers Minor, namely that they do not embrace evangelical perfection and do not hold the form of evangelical perfection, are judged by the Church to be stubborn and rebels, according to the aforesaid decretal of Alexander IV. But these men hold, who say that evangelical poverty by no means excludes ownership of things and property. Therefore these men who hold the said assertion are to be judged stubborn and rebels against the Roman Church. From this they infer that all who consent to or approve the constitutions of this man on this matter, and who read, approve, expound, write, preach or in any way adhere to them as things to be approved, are to be reckoned stubborn and rebels against the Roman Church. Moreover, these opponents, on account of those who follow the doctrine of Thomas, cite the words by which he rejects the said assertion as erroneous. For he says, in his book which he published against the said Masters of Paris, chapter 6, treating of the question, with the heading placed before it, "Whether it is lawful for a religious to give up all his goods, so that nothing remains to be possessed either in private or in common," he asserts the following words, saying: "But the adversaries of the truth, not content with these things, strive to overthrow the foundation of all religious orders, firmly laid by the Lord himself, namely poverty, saying that it is unlawful for anyone, having dismissed all his goods, to enter a poor religion, which has no possessions or revenues." And further, speaking of the heretic Vigilantius, he says: "Nor was he content merely to imitate Jovinian, emptying the counsel concerning virginity, but dared moreover to add that he would utterly destroy the counsel to keep poverty. Hence Jerome says of him that, as for his claim that those do better who use their goods and gradually distribute the fruits of their possessions to the poor, rather than those who sell their possessions and give everything away at once, he will not answer to me but to God: 'If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and come, follow me.' Matt. 19." This error has come down through successions of erring men to the present day, and has persisted and still persists among certain heretics called Cathars, as is evident from a treatise of a certain heresiarch of Lombardy of our own time, which he published against Catholic truth, in which, among other things, he condemns the state of those who, having left everything, wish to go with Christ. Recently, however (which is horrible), the ancient error has been renewed by those who seemed to defend the faith, and, proceeding worse in the manner of erring men, they are not content to equate riches with poverty, as Jovinian did, or to prefer riches to poverty, as Vigilantius did, but totally condemn poverty, saying that it is not lawful to give up all one's goods for Christ unless one enters such a religion as has possessions, or unless one intends to live by the labour of one's hands. They also assert that poverty is praised in the Scriptures not as actual poverty, by which one strips oneself of temporal goods, but as habitual poverty, by which one despises temporal things in the heart even while possessing them. Here he sets out in summary form the assertion of this man under attack, who holds that evangelical poverty by no means excludes ownership and possession of all temporal things, because evangelical poverty is most praised in the Scriptures; and therefore, if evangelical poverty does not exclude all ownership of temporal things, actual poverty, which excludes all ownership, is not most praised in the Scriptures, as the aforesaid critics say following Thomas.

units.la: Sed istum errorem Thomas multis rationibus reprobare conatur: quarum plures, vt isti impugnatores dicunt, contra assertionem praedictam sunt euidentes: & auctoritates assumunt saepe dictam assertionem apertissime conuincentes. Et ideo dictarum seriem rationum duxi praesentibus inserendam. post verba itaque supradicta subiungit immediate Thomas dicens: ad destructionem huius erroris hoc modo procedemus. Primo ostendemus ad perfectionem euangelicam pertinere, non solum paupertatem habitualem, sed etiam actualem, quae fit per abiectionem temporalium rerum. Secundo ostendemus, quod haec perfectio manet, etiam si possessiones in communi non habeantur. Tertio quod haec perfectio etiam in his qui possessionibus carent non semper requirit manuum laborem. Quarto soluemus ea quae pro se inducunt. Ad ostendendum autem paupertatem actualem ad euangelicam perfectionem pertinere, assumatur primo quod dicitur Matth. 19. Si vis perfectus esse vade & vende omnia quae habes & da pauperib. sed ille, qui sua vendit & pauperib. tribuit, non solum habitualem paupertatem elegit, sed actualem. ergo actualis paupertas ad euangelicam perfectionem pertinet. Item, persectio euangelica consistit imitatione Christi. sed Christus non solum voluntate, sed etiam realiter pauper fuit. Unde dicitur Matt. 17. super illud, Vade ad mare: Glossa Dominus tanta paupertatis fuit, vt vnde tributum solueret, non haberet. & Luce 9. vulpes foueas habent &c. Dicit Glossa: ego sum tanta paupertatis, vt nec hospitium quidem habeam, nec meo vtar tecto. & per multas alias auctoritates de facili hoc probari potest. ergo actualis paupertas ad persectionem euangelicam pertinet. Item, euangelica perfectio maxime in apostolis claruit. sed ipsi actualem paupertatem babuhabuerint sua omnia relinquentes. Vnde Petrus dixit Matth. 19. Ecce nos reliquimus omnia &c. & Hiero. ad Elbidium. Si vis esse perfecta & in primo stare fastigio dignitatis, fac quod fecerunt apostoli, vende omnia quae habes & da pauperibus, & nuda sequeris crucem virtute nuda sequaris & sola. ergo actualis paupertas ad evangelicam perfectionem pertinet. Item Marci 10. super illud: quam difficile qui pecunias habet &c. Glos. aliud est pecunias habere, aliud amare. Multi habent & non amant: multi non habent, & amant. Item alii habent & amant: alii vero nec habere nec amare se gaudent. qui tutiores sunt: qui cum apostolo dicere possunt: Mihi mundus crucifixus est & ego mundo. ergo actualis paupertas & habitualis sic praeferenda est habitualii paupertati. Item idem potest haberi Mat. 19. per Glossam super illud: Dives difficile intrabit in regnum coelorum. Glossa, de omnib. tutius est, nec habere nec amare divitias. Item Iacobi secundo. Nonne Deus elegit pauperes in hoc mundo. Gloss. inopes rerum temporalium. hoc autem non est nisi per actualem paupertatem. ergo actualiter pauperes electi sunt a Deo. Item Lucae 14. Nisi quis renunciaverit omnib. quae possidet. Glossa, hoc dicitur inter renunciare omnib. & reliquisse omnia: quia renunciare conuenit omnibus, qui ita licite vtitur mundanis, quae possident, ut tamen mente tendat ad aeterna. Reliquisse est tantummodo perfectorum, qui omnia temporalia postponunt & solis aeternis inhaerent. Ergo relinquere, quod pertinet ad actualem paupertatem, est evangelica perfectionis: sed renunciare, quod pertinet ad habitualem, secundum Glossam praedictam, est de necessitate salutis.
units.tr: But Thomas tries to refute this error with many arguments. Several of them, as these opponents say, plainly contradict the assertion above, and they cite authorities that very clearly refute it. So I have thought it right to set out the series of those arguments here. Immediately after the words quoted above, Thomas goes on: We shall proceed to destroy this error in the following way. First, we will show that evangelical perfection involves not only habitual poverty but also actual poverty, which comes about through the renunciation of temporal goods. Second, we will show that this perfection remains even if possessions are not held in common. Third, that this perfection, even in those who lack possessions, does not always require manual labour. Fourth, we will answer the arguments they put forward for themselves. To show that actual poverty pertains to evangelical perfection, let us first assume what is said in Matthew 19: "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor." But one who sells his goods and gives them to the poor has chosen not only habitual poverty but actual poverty. Therefore actual poverty pertains to evangelical perfection. Likewise, evangelical perfection consists in the imitation of Christ. But Christ was poor not only in will but also in reality. Hence on Matthew 17, "Go to the sea," the Gloss says: the Lord was so poor that he had nothing from which to pay the tax. And Luke 9: "Foxes have holes," and so on. The Gloss says: I am of such poverty that I do not even have a lodging nor use a roof of my own. And this can easily be proved by many other authorities. Therefore actual poverty pertains to evangelical perfection. Likewise, evangelical perfection shone most clearly in the apostles. But they had actual poverty, since they left all their goods behind. Hence Peter said in Matthew 19: "Behold, we have left all things," and so on. And Jerome to Elbidius: "If you wish to be perfect and to stand on the first height of dignity, do what the apostles did: sell all that you have and give to the poor, and follow the naked cross, naked and alone." Therefore actual poverty pertains to evangelical perfection. Likewise, on Mark 10, "How hard it is for those who have money," and so on, the Gloss says: it is one thing to have money, another to love it. Many have and do not love; many do not have and do love; others both have and love; others rejoice neither to have nor to love. Those are safest who can say with the apostle: "The world is crucified to me and I to the world." Therefore actual poverty is to be preferred to habitual poverty in this way. Likewise the same can be had from Matthew 19 through the Gloss on the words "A rich man will hardly enter the kingdom of heaven": the Gloss says, it is safest of all neither to have nor to love riches. Likewise, James 2: "Has not God chosen the poor in this world?" The Gloss: those lacking temporal goods. But this is only through actual poverty. Therefore those chosen by God are actually poor. Likewise, Luke 14: "Unless a man renounces all that he possesses." The Gloss: this is said to distinguish renouncing all from leaving all behind. For renouncing belongs to all who use worldly goods lawfully, which they possess, yet in mind strive toward eternal things. Leaving behind belongs only to the perfect, who put all temporal things second and cleave only to eternal things. Therefore leaving behind, which pertains to actual poverty, belongs to evangelical perfection; but renouncing, which pertains to habitual poverty, according to the Gloss just cited, is necessary for salvation.

units.la: Item Hieronymus in epistola contra Vigilantium post verba supra inducta subiungit: Ad eum loquitur (sc. Domi-nus) dicens: Si vis perfectus esse &c. qui vult esse perfectus, quia cum apostolis patrem, naviculam & retia dimisit, ille, quem tu laudas, secundus ascensus gradus est, sc. qui fructuum possessionum dat pauperibus quem & nos recipimus, dummodo sciamus primam, secundis & tertiis esse praeferenda. ergo patet, quod praeferendi sunt, qui omnia sua dimittunt illis, qui de fructibus possessionum, quas retinent, pauperibus dividunt. Item Hieronymus in epistola ad Rusticum monachum: Si habes substantiam unde, & da pauperibus: si non habes, grande onere liberatus es, nudus Christum nudus sequere: durum, grande, difficile, sed magna sunt pramia. & multa alia huiusmodi ex epistola Hiero-nymi accipi possunt, quae de actuali paupertate necesse est ut intelligantur, quae causa brevitatis dimittuntur ad praesens. Item August. dicit in libro de ecclesiasticis dogmatibus: Bonum est facultates cum dispensatione pauperibus erogare: melius est per intentionem sequendo dominum simul donare & absolutum a sollicitudinibus egere cum Christo, & sic idem quod primum. Item Ambrosius in libro de Officiis: Nullum adminiculum praestant divitiae ad vitam beatam, quod evidenter Dominus notat in evangelio dicens: Beati pauperes, quoniam vestrum est regnum coelorum. Itaque paupertatem, famem, dolorem, quae putantur mala, non solum impedimento non esse ad vitam beatam, sed adiumento esse evidentissime probant. sed hoc non potest intelligi de paupertate habituali, qua homo divitias subiicit: quia haec a nullo putatur impedimento beatitudinis. ergo oportet quod intelligitur de paupertate actuali, qua omnia abiicit. Item Gregorius dicit in homil. 8. secundae partis super ezechielem: Cum quis aliquid suum vovet Deo, & aliquid non vovet, sacrificium est: cum vero omne quod habet, omne quod vivit, omne quod sapit, omnipotenti Deo vivit, holocaustum est. sed holocaustum erat dignissimum sacrificium. ergo perfectissimum opus est omnia sua propter Deum dimittere. Item Greg. in prologo Moralium: Cum enim adhuc me cogeret animus praesenti mundo quasi spem tenus deservire, ceperunt multa contra me ex eiusdem mundi cura surgere, ut in eo iam non spem, sed quod est graviter mente retinerer, quae tandem cuncta sollicite fugiens portum monasterii petit, & relicta, quae sunt mundi, ex huius mundi naufragio solus evasi. Ex quo patet, quod periculosum est res mundi possidere: quia earum possessio periculo-se mentem retinet: & ideo laudabilius est possessionem rerum temporalium a se abiicere per actualem paupertatem, ut mens a cura divitiarum liberetur. Item Chrysost. dicit in libro qui dicitur, nemo laeditur nisi a semetipso: quid apostolos penuria rerum corporalium laesit? nonne in fame & siti & nuditate degebant? & pro his clari, maximi & magnifici habebantur, atque ingentem per hoc fiduciam quaesierant apud Deum? Ex quo patet, quod actualis paupertas, quae in penuria rerum consistit, ad apostolicam perfectionem pertinet. Item Bernardus dicit ad Senon. Archiepiscopum: Felix qui nihil sibi iuretur ex omnibus, quae habet, non foveā, ut vulpes, non tanquam volucres nidum, non locules quomodo ludas, non domos sicut nec. Maria locum in diversorio, imitatus profecto illum qui non habebat ubi reclinare caput. Ex quo patet, quod nihil omnino possidere in mundo ad Christianam perfectionem pertinet. Item 1. q. 2. c. Si quis: Profecto perfectior est ille, qui se rebus mundi expoliat, aut qui cum nihil habuerit, nec habere desiderat: quam ille, qui ex multis quae possidet aliquid ecclesiae praestiterit. Ex quo patet, quod nihil possidere ad perfectionem Christianam pertinet. Item cum, qui vacat contemplationi divinae, magis opus esse a rebus mundanis liberum, quam eos qui contemplationi philosophicae vacabant. Sed philosophi, ut libere philosophiae vacarent, laudabiliter mundi substantiam abiiciebant. unde Hieronymus dicit ad Paulinum presbyterum de institutione monachorum: Socrates ille Thebanus homo quondam dives, cum ad philosophandum Athenas pergeret, magnum auri pondus abiecit: nec putavit se posse: & virtutes simul & divitias possidere. ergo multo magis ad vacandum contemplationi divinae laudabilius relinquere. Unde super illud Matth. 19. Si vis perfectus esse &c. dicit Glossa interlinearis: Ecce con-templativa, quae ad evangelium pertinet. Item praemium excellens non debetur, nisi merito excellenti, sed praemium excellens, s. iudiciaria potestas debetur actuali paupertati, sicut patet Mat. 19. super illud. Vos qui reliquistis omnia & secuti estis, domini, hi iudices erunt: qui licita habentes renunciaverunt. Dicit Glossa. Qui reliquerunt omnia, paupertate meritum excellens consistit. Item 1. Cor. 7. Apostolus consilium dans de virginitate servanda rationem assignat, ut s. sine sollicitudine sint, sed abiectio divitiarum maxime facit hominem sine sollicitudine: quia divitiae possessoribus de necessitate multas sollicitudines inferunt. unde Luc. 8. Divitiae per spinas significantur, quae verbum sua sol-licitudine suffocant in cordibus auditorum. ergo sicut virginitas, ita & actualis paupertas ad evangelicam perfectionem pertinet. Ex his verbis (ut dicunt isti) colliguntur octo, quorum doctrinae istius impugnati aperte repugnat. quorum primum est, quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium in speciali & in communi propter Deum perfectionem spectat: quia de illa abdicatione loquitur iste Doctor in cap. quod ex rubrica, quam toti capitulo praemittit, ex pluribus rationibus supradictis, quae de illa abdicatione concludunt, patenter apparet. Secundum est, quod perfectior est talis abdicatio proprie-tatis tatis paupertate, q; in sola præparatione animi seu voluntate consistit. Tertium est quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium rerum ad evangelicam pertinet paupertatem: quia paupertas q; pertinet ad evangelicam perfectionem, pertinet ad evangelicam paupertatem: quia paupertas ad nullam evangelicam perfectionem potest immediatius pertinere, quam ad evangelicam paupertatem. talis autem abdicatio, q; est actualis paupertas, quam Christus consuluit, cum iuveni dixit: Si vis perfectus esse, vade & vende omnia quae habes & da pauperibus: ad evangelicam perfectionem pertinet, sicut iste Doctor in multis locis concludit. ergo ad evangelica ptinet paupertate. Quartum est, q; Christus non solum fuit pauper voluntarius, sed et realiter per carentiam pprietatis omnium temporaliu. Quintum est, quod apostoli quo ad proprietatem omnia reliquerunt. Sextum est q; actualis paupertas, quae in penuria rerum consistit, ad apostolicam perfectionem ptinet. Septimum est, quod illa praeferenda est habituali paupertati, sicut virginitas castitati coniugali. Octavum est q; actuali paupertati debetur iudiciaria paupertas. Multa alia ex praedictis verbis istius Doctoris colligi possunt, quae doctrinae istius impugnati omnino repugnant.
units.tr: Likewise Jerome, in his letter against Vigilantius, after the words quoted above, adds: He speaks to him (that is, the Lord) saying, "If you wish to be perfect," and so on. He who wishes to be perfect, because with the apostles he left behind his father, his little boat and his nets, is the second step of ascent, namely he who gives the fruits of his possessions to the poor, whom we too receive, provided we know that the first is to be preferred to the second and third. Therefore it is clear that those who give up all their goods are to be preferred to those who divide among the poor the fruits of the possessions they keep. Likewise Jerome, in his letter to the monk Rusticus: "If you have substance, from which you may give to the poor; if you have none, you are released from a great burden. Naked, follow the naked Christ: it is hard, great, difficult, but the rewards are great." Many other things of this kind can be taken from Jerome's letter, which must be understood of actual poverty, but for the sake of brevity are passed over for now. Likewise Augustine says in the book On Ecclesiastical Dogmas: "It is good to distribute one's resources to the poor with good management; it is better, by intention, following the Lord, to give them away at once and, free from anxieties, to be poor with Christ, and so the same as the first." Likewise Ambrose in the book On Duties: "Riches furnish no aid to the blessed life, which the Lord plainly points out in the Gospel, saying: 'Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of heaven.' Thus poverty, hunger and pain, which are thought to be evils, are shown most evidently not only not to be a hindrance to the blessed life but a help to it." But this cannot be understood of habitual poverty, by which a man makes riches subject to himself, for that is thought by no one to be a hindrance to blessedness. Therefore it must be understood of actual poverty, by which one casts off everything. Likewise Gregory says in the eighth homily of the second part on Ezekiel: "When someone vows something of his to God and does not vow something else, it is a sacrifice; but when he vows all that he has, all that he lives by, all that he knows, to almighty God, it is a burnt offering." But the burnt offering was the most worthy sacrifice. Therefore it is the most perfect work to give up all one's goods for God's sake. Likewise Gregory in the prologue to the Moralia: "For while my mind was still forced to serve the present world, as it were up to a point, many cares of this same world began to rise against me, so that I was held by them in my mind not as a hope but as a grave burden; at last, fleeing all these things with care, I sought the harbour of the monastery, and, leaving behind what belongs to the world, I alone escaped from the shipwreck of this world." From this it is clear that it is dangerous to possess the things of the world, because their possession dangerously holds the mind; and therefore it is more praiseworthy to cast off from oneself the possession of temporal goods through actual poverty, so that the mind may be freed from the care of riches. Likewise Chrysostom says in the book which is called "No one is harmed except by himself": what harmed the apostles by the lack of bodily goods? Did they not live in hunger, thirst and nakedness? And for this they were held famous, great and magnificent, and by this they had won immense confidence before God. From this it is clear that actual poverty, which consists in lack of material goods, pertains to apostolic perfection. Likewise Bernard says to the Archbishop of Sens: "Happy is he who claims nothing for himself from all that he has: he does not dig a hole like a fox, nor a nest like a bird, nor keep purses like Judas, nor houses like...; nor a place in an inn like Mary, truly imitating him who had nowhere to lay his head." From this it is clear that to possess nothing at all in the world pertains to Christian perfection. Likewise, Causa 1, q. 2, c. "Si quis": Truly he is more perfect who strips himself of worldly things, or who, having nothing, does not even desire to have anything, than he who gives something to the Church out of the many things he possesses. From this it is clear that to possess nothing pertains to Christian perfection. Likewise, one who is free for the contemplation of God needs to be freer from worldly things than those who were devoted to philosophical contemplation. But the philosophers, in order to be free for philosophy, praiseworthily cast away their material substance. Hence Jerome says to Paulinus the presbyter, on the education of monks: "That Socrates of Thebes, once a rich man, when he went to Athens to philosophize, threw away a great weight of gold, and did not think that he could possess both virtues and riches at once." Therefore it is much more praiseworthy to leave all behind in order to devote oneself to the contemplation of God. Hence on Matthew 19, "If you wish to be perfect," the interlinear Gloss says: Behold the contemplative life, which belongs to the Gospel. Likewise, an excellent reward is due only to excellent merit; but an excellent reward, namely judicial power, is owed to actual poverty, as is clear from Matthew 19 on the words "You who have left all things and followed me, you will be judges"; those who renounced what was lawful to them. The Gloss says: those who left all behind; excellent merit consists in poverty. Likewise, 1 Corinthians 7: the apostle, giving counsel on keeping virginity, assigns this reason, that they may be without anxiety; but the renunciation of riches especially makes a man free from anxiety, because riches necessarily bring many anxieties to their possessors. Hence Luke 8: riches are signified by the thorns, which choke the word with their anxiety in the hearts of the hearers. Therefore, just as virginity, so also actual poverty pertains to evangelical perfection. From these words (as they say) eight points are gathered, to which the doctrine of this opponent is plainly contrary. (1) The first is that the renunciation of ownership of all temporal goods, both individually and in common, for God's sake, concerns perfection; for this teacher speaks of that renunciation in the chapter "Quod ex," which he prefaces to the whole chapter, and from the many reasons above, which conclude about that renunciation, it clearly appears. (2) The second is that such a renunciation of ownership is more perfect than poverty, which consists only in the preparation of mind or will. (3) The third is that the renunciation of ownership of all things pertains to evangelical poverty, because poverty which pertains to evangelical perfection pertains to evangelical poverty; for poverty cannot pertain to any evangelical perfection more immediately than to evangelical poverty. Such a renunciation, which is actual poverty, which Christ advised when he said to the young man, "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor," pertains to evangelical perfection, as this teacher concludes in many places. Therefore it pertains to evangelical poverty. (4) The fourth is that Christ was not only a voluntary poor man, but also really poor through the lack of ownership of all temporal goods. (5) The fifth is that the apostles left all things as regards ownership. (6) The sixth is that actual poverty, which consists in lack of goods, pertains to apostolic perfection. (7) The seventh is that it is to be preferred to habitual poverty, as virginity is preferred to marital chastity. (8) The eighth is that judicial power is owed to actual poverty. Many other things can be gathered from the aforesaid words of this teacher, which are entirely opposed to the doctrine of this opponent.

units.la: Secunda assertio in supradictis verbis contenta, quam isti impugnatores dicunt esse erroneam, est quod apostoli habuerunt aliquarum rerum dominium in communi. de quo dictum est prius, & ostensum, quod apostoli omnium rerum in communi abdicaverunt dominium: ita quod collegium apostolorum nullius rei habebat dominium pprium illi collegio: q; adhuc conatur ostendere. Primo sic: Paupertatem evangelicam apostoli perfectissime servaverunt. sed ad pauptarem evangelicam spectat abdicatio pprietatis omnium rerum in speciali & in communi, sicut ostensum est prius. ergo apostoli tale abdicationem servaverunt: & ita nullius pprietatem habuerunt in communi, ita q; nulla res erat propria cuicunq; apostolo vel soli collegio apostolorum. Secundo sic: apostoli persectione evangelica essentialem alicui religioni pfecte semel assumpta, nisi forte tempore necessitatis, q; legem non habet, nullatenus dimiserunt. sed secundum istum & secundu veritatem, post conversionem primorum credentium, qn omnia fuerunt communia, nec aliquis apostolus, nec totu collegium apostolorum habuit aliq; rem sibi ppriam: quia quilibet fuit communis aliis et secundum istum abdicatio autem pprietatis huiusmodi est essentialis alicui religioni perfecte, & ad evangelicam pertinet perfectione. ergo apostoli istam perfectionem, postquam eam assumpserunt, nullatenus dimiserunt. ergo saltem post tempus conversionis dictorum credentium apostoli nullius rei proprietate habuerunt, q; essent propria alicui apostolo, vel toti apostolorum collegio. Tertio sic: apostoli debuerunt quantum poterant tollere illis, quibus pdicabant omne occasionem suspicandi, quod propter temporalia pdicarent. Unde & propter hoc Beatus Paulus ab illis, quibus pdicabat, sumptus necessarios nolebat recipere. sed qn temporalia a pdicantibus tam in speciali quam etiam in communi quo ad pprietate & dominium respuuntur, magis tollitur occasio suspicandi, q; propter temporalia praedicant, q; qn recipiuntur in communi quo ad dominium. ergo apostoli cupientes quantum poterant omne huiusmodi suspitione auferre, nec in speciali, nec in communi pprietatem & dominium rerum temporalium receperunt. Ideo dicunt isti impugnatores, q; propter 4. rationes apostoli, qd quid in rebus temporalib. no fuit eis necessarium ad sustentationem vitae & executionem sui officii, dimiserunt. Primo. s. ut vitae & doctrinae Christi se perfectius conformarent. Secundo ut fidelib. & infidelib. exemplariores se praeberet, ac per hoc ad fidem & vitam bonam efficacius provocaret. Tertio ut omne sollicitudine praeter necessaria circa temporalia deuitaret, ac p hoc peccandi occasiones auferret, & contemplationi, praedicationi, & aliis bonis spiritualib. operae daret liberius. Quarto, ut mundu esse calcandu apertius demonstrarent, si sine retentione dominii in communi poterat sustentari in communi, & actus ptinetes ad suu officiu exercere. nec n. cibi & pot. pter retentionem dominii, in communi, melius nutriunt: nec pter tale dominium act, q; p res temporales exercetur, sunt aliquasiter meliores. ergo apostoli omne dominium pprii ipsorum collegio, reliquerunt. Nunc textu, ut instituim, declaremus [Paupertas evangelica rerum usu consumptibilium dominium & proprietate excludit.] Si intelligatur de gradu perfectissimo evangelicæ paupertatis, sic excludit dominium in speciali & in communi. Sed si intelligatur de gradu non perfectissimo evangelicæ paupertatis, sed minus perfecto, sic excludit dominium & proprietate libera, q; est potestas de re ad libitu ordinadi, alia pprietate salte communé, q; est minus potestas dicandi in iudicio, non excludit. Unde dicitur esse sciendum, q; ante tempora Christi non fuit potestas ... communitate, q; duceret communē vitā, ita q; oes res usu consumptibiles & non congruit fuisse aliq; communes. sed Christ' docuit apostolos ducere vitā communē, ut omnia essent eis consumptibiles essent communia proprietate & dominio proprio, ipsorum collegio: das in hoc forma viuedi communia ab omni pp. si q nollet oem pprietate penit' abdicare. & sic pter hoc pecuniā muniter cū aliquali pprietate, oem proprietate & dominiū abdicare, communē vitam du voluit in locutis reseruari, ut q nolle' nullā proprietate in locutis reseruauit, & ita communē ecret aliqualē proprietate reseruado. Ch... atē in speciali & in communi, siue aliqualem promune vitā ducentes siue abiiciāt omnē proprie...tur. [Illarū rerū supponit scriptura sacra &c.] hoc prietatē retinēat, pauperatem euangelicam imitari. dicunt prius probatum esse falsum.
units.tr: The second assertion contained in the words above, which these opponents say is erroneous, is that the apostles held lordship over some things in common. This was discussed earlier and shown: the apostles renounced lordship over all things, both individually and in common, so that the college of apostles had no proper lordship over anything belonging to that college. He still tries to show this. First, thus: the apostles observed evangelical poverty most perfectly. But renunciation of all ownership of things, both individually and in common, belongs to evangelical poverty, as was shown earlier. Therefore the apostles observed such renunciation, and so they had no ownership in common, such that no thing was the property of any apostle or of the whole college of apostles. Second, thus: the apostles never abandoned the essentials of evangelical perfection, once they had fully embraced it, except perhaps in a time of necessity, which has no law. But according to this view, and according to the truth, after the conversion of the first believers, when all things were held in common, neither any apostle nor the whole college of apostles had any thing as their own, since each was common to the others. Renunciation of this kind of ownership is essential to a religious life lived perfectly, and it belongs to evangelical perfection. Therefore the apostles never abandoned this perfection once they had taken it up. Therefore, at least after the time of the conversion of those believers, the apostles had no ownership of any thing that was the property of any apostle or of the whole college of apostles. Third, thus: the apostles ought, as far as they could, to remove from those to whom they preached every occasion of suspecting that they preached for the sake of temporal things. For this reason the blessed Paul would not receive the necessary support from those to whom he preached. But when temporal goods are refused by those who preach, both individually and in common, as regards ownership and lordship, the occasion for suspicion that they preach for temporal gain is removed more than when they are received in common as regards lordship. Therefore the apostles, desiring as far as they could to remove all such suspicion, received neither individually nor in common the ownership and lordship of temporal goods. Hence these opponents say that for four reasons the apostles gave up whatever in temporal things was not necessary for them for sustaining life and performing their office. First, so that they might conform themselves more perfectly to the life and teaching of Christ. Second, so that they might present themselves as a more striking example to believers and unbelievers, and thereby more effectively move them to faith and good living. Third, so that they might avoid all anxiety about temporal things beyond what was necessary, and thereby remove occasions of sin, and devote themselves more freely to contemplation, preaching and other spiritual goods. Fourth, so that they might demonstrate more clearly that the world is to be trampled underfoot, if they could be sustained in common without retaining lordship in common and could exercise the acts belonging to their office; for food and drink are not better for nourishment because of retained lordship in common, nor is an act performed through such lordship over temporal things any better. Therefore the apostles left behind all lordship of their own to their college. Now let us explain the text, as we have proposed: Evangelical poverty excludes lordship and ownership over things consumed by use. If this is understood of the most perfect degree of evangelical poverty, it excludes lordship both individually and in common. But if it is understood of a degree that is not most perfect but less perfect, it excludes free ownership, which is the power to dispose of a thing at will, but it does not exclude some other ownership, at least a common one, which is less than the power of claiming in court. Hence it is said that one must know that before the time of Christ there was no ... communal life, which would lead to a common life, so that all things consumed by use were not fitting to be held in common. But Christ taught the apostles to lead a common life, so that all things consumed by use would be common to them, with no ownership or lordship of their own belonging to any one of them, but belonging to their college; he gave them a form of living in common free from all private ownership, if he did not wish them to renounce all ownership entirely. And so, because of this, though he wished the common life to be led with some money and some ownership, he reserved the complete renunciation of all ownership and lordship for those who wished it, so that they might retain some ownership in the common life, whether leading a common life in some measure or renouncing all private ownership. Holy Scripture presupposes these things, etc. They say that what was previously proved to be false is that they imitate evangelical poverty.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CHAP. XXIV.

units.la: Ad illud 2.q; dicit, quod abdicatio proprietatis & dominii sollicitudinē excludit, dicimus similiter q; est falsum. & quod talis abdicatio nō excludat sollicitudinē, patet. Cōstat enim quod si Dominus seruo coedat peculium, quam proprietas seu dominium peculii in seruum non cadat, non propterea seruus a sollicitudine est immunis. Alias inutiliter ebendisset Dominus seruum negligentem, de quo agitur Luc. 19 quia pecuniam a domino sibi trade ... dit ... ad vsuras. & hoc videmus ad sensum, quod ille, ad quem rei vtilitas pertinet sine dominio, magis est circa rem illam sollicitudinem habens, quam sit nudus Dominus eius. [illegible, ~20 letters] in fratribus Minoribus, qui nudum vsum facti se habere in talibus asserunt, qui circa illa magis sunt solliciti, quam Romana ecclesia, ad quam illarum rerum dominium asserunt pertinere.
units.tr: As to his second point, that renunciation of ownership and dominion excludes care, we likewise say that this is false, and it is plain that such renunciation does not exclude care. For it is established that if the Lord grants a slave a peculium, ownership or dominion of the peculium does not pass to the slave, yet the slave is not on that account free from care. Otherwise the Lord would have rebuked the negligent servant in Luke 19 to no purpose, the one who had been handed money by his lord and had not put it out at interest. We also see in practice that the one to whom the usefulness of a thing belongs, without dominion, is more anxious about that thing than its bare lord is. [illegible, ~20 letters] among the Friars Minor, who claim that they have only the bare use of fact in such things, and who are more anxious about them than the Roman church, to which they assert the dominion of those things belongs.

units.la: Hic iste impugnatus respondet ad tertium, quod in praemissa obiectione tangebatur. Sabdicatio dominii & proprietatis, sollicitudinem excludit, dicens hoc esse falsum. Cuius falsitatem per duo exempla. S. de seruo, cui Dominus concedit peculiũ, & de Fratrib. Minorib. probare molitur.
units.tr: Here this opponent answers the third point, which was touched on in the foregoing objection: that the renunciation of dominion and ownership excludes care, saying that this is false. He tries to prove its falsity by two examples: the slave to whom the Lord grants a peculium, and the Friars Minor.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt: quod hic cauillose procedit, nec metem nec verba tangit appellantis. Nam appellans non dicit, quod abdicatio huiusmodi excludit omnem sollicitudinem: sed dicit, quod excludit sollicitudinem, quam requirit prophetas seu dominium rerum. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod sollicitudo multiplex inuenitur. Est enim sollicitudo naturalis necessitatis, qua quilibet de natura sustentanda tenetur aliquomodo esse sollicitus. Istam sollicitudinem abdicatio proprietatis omnium rerum nequaquam excludit. Alia est sollicitudo seruilitatis, qua seruus vel famulus ac mercenarius de his, quae sibi a Domino committuntur, debet esse sollicitus, & hanc sollicitudinem voluntaria abdicatio huiusmodi proprietatis excludit. Unde nec serui, nec obligati Romano imperio, nec manentes tali sollicitudini obligati recipiendi sunt ad religionem. Alia est sollicitudo compassiuae pietatis, qua quis ad releuandam proximi indigentiam est sollicitus: sicut sunt illi, qui faciunt eleemosynas & tenent hospitalitatem. Hanc sollicitudinem ut plurimum abdicatio proprietatis omnium rerum in speciali & communi excludit. non tamen omnem sollicitudinem talem abdicatio ista excludit in omni casu: quia in aliquo casu huiusmodi abdicantes proximo subuenire tenentur. Sed abdicatio proprietatis in speciali non in communi, sollicitudinem istam non excludit. Nam multi religiosi obligati ad hospitalitatem, hanc sollicitudinem habere tenentur. Alia est sollicitudo potestatiuae auctoritatis: qua potest quis temporalia in iudicio vendicare, & per eis diuersimode litigare. & hanc sollicitudinem requirit proprietas rerum seu dominium. Istam vero excludit paupertas euangelica in suo perfectissimo gradu, quia qui caret rei proprietate in speciali & in communi, non potest pro re, nomine proprio vel suae communitatis in iudicio litigare. Primam sollicitudinem paupertas euangelica non excludit: sed quarta, quae est ad propositum: quia non est necessaria viris perfectis. & ita apparet quod dictum appellantis, cum dicit, quod paupertas euangelica excludit sollicitudinem, quam requirit proprietas seu dominium rerum, continet veritatem: quia intelligit de euangelica paupertate in suo perfectissimo gradu, & de sollicitudine potestatiua, qua potest quis pro temporalib. in iudicio litigare. Ex istis apparet, quod exempla istius impugnati de seruo & Fratribus Minoribus pro ipso non faciunt. Nam licet seruus habeat sollicitudinem seruilitatis, non tamen habet illam quam requirit proprietas seu dominium rerum: nec tamen ipse seruat euangelicam paupertatem, quia ... sua non est voluntaria, sed coacta. Fratres vero Minores licet aliquam sollicitudinem habeant, quia naturalis necessitatis, non tamen habent illam, quam requirit proprietas seu dominium rerum. Non enim possunt pro rebus in iudicio quomodolibet litigare: quod tamen potest ecclesia Romana saltem per pastores suos. Ad illud autem, quod dicit, quod abdicatio proprietatis & dominii sollicitudinem excludit, dicunt isti: quod iste impugnatus truncate recitat verba appellantis. Quia appellans dicit, quod excludit sollicitudinem, quam requirit proprietas seu dominium rerum. & istud est in calumniabile: quia manifestum est, quod sollicitudinem illam excludit. Unde abdicatio proprietatis & dominii in communi & in speciali excludit sollicitudinem, quam requirit proprietas & dominium rerum in speciali, vt. S. nomine proprio non possit pro re in iudicio litigare. Abdicatio vero proprietatis & dominii in communi & in speciali excludit illam sollicitudinem, quam requirit proprietas & dominium rerum in speciali vel in communi. quia nec nomine proprio, nec nomine suae communitatis potest pro re in iudicio litigare. Hanc sollicitudinem requirit talis proprietas: licet et plures sollicitudines saepe requirat, quae ad sollicitudinem est quarto modo dicta possunt aliquomodo reduci. Verum quid textus dicat, videamus. [Dicimus similiter quod est falsum.] Dicunt isti, quae ex praedictis patenter constat, quod hic dicit verum esse falsum. [Talis abdicatio non excludit sollicitudinem.] Dicunt isti, quod si dixisset quod non excludit omnem sollicitudinem, verum dixisset: quia non excludit sollicitudinem naturalis necessitatis, & et compassiuae pietatis; sub sollicitudine minime comprehenduntur. Unde Chrysost. super illud Matt. Nolite possidere aurum neque argentum &c. Ait: Ex hoc patet quod eos angelos, vt ita dicam, constituit ab omni eos soluens vita huius sollicitudine, vt vna detinerentur cura, quae est doctrina ecclesiae. quod Chrysost. dicens, apostolos ab omni huius vitae sollicitudine absolutos, sollicitudinem naturalis necessitatis sub vocabulo sollicitudinis minime comprehendit. Quamuis ergo appellans dixisset euangelicam paupertatem omnem sollicitudinem excludere, deberet nullatenus reprehendi, sed sane intelligi cum modo loquendi sanctorum imitatus fuisset. tamen hoc non dixit, sed dixit quod excludit sollicitudinem, quam requirit proprietas &c. Dicunt praeterea, quod cum iste dicit, quod talis abdicatio non excludit sollicitudinem, errat a parte; quia constat quod illa sollicitudinem, qua qs nomine proprio vel sui collegii litigat in iudicio pro rebus excludit. [Non propterea seruus a sollicitudine est immunis.] Verum est quod non est immunis ab omni sollicitudine, est tamen immunis ab illa sollicitudine, quae requirit proprietas, seu dominium. [Pecunia sibi a Domino tradita non tradiderat ad vsuras.] Ex hoc patet, quod seruus ille aliquam sollicitudinem debebat habere; non tamen illam, quam requirit proprietas. [Ille ad quae rei vtilitas pertinet, sine dominio magis est circa illam rem sollicitus quam sit studio Dominus eius.] Dicunt quod istud non est ad propositum, nec continet veritatem, quod non sit ad propositum. patet, quia talis non habet illam sollicitudinem, quam requirit proprietas, licet habeat aliam; nec continet veritatem, quia saepe ille, ad quam vtilitas rei pertinet de reparatione
units.tr: But these opponents say that he proceeds here captiously and touches neither the meaning nor the words of the appellant. For the appellant does not say that such renunciation excludes all care, but says that it excludes the care which ownership or dominion of things requires. To make this clear, they say it must be understood that care is found in many forms. There is the care of natural necessity, by which everyone is bound to be somewhat anxious about sustaining his nature. Renunciation of ownership of all things by no means excludes this care. There is another care, that of servitude, which a slave, servant or hired man must have about what is committed to him by his lord, and this care is excluded by such voluntary renunciation of ownership. Hence neither slaves, nor those bound to the Roman empire, nor those remaining bound to such care, are to be admitted into the religious orders. There is another care, that of compassionate piety, by which one is anxious to relieve the need of a neighbour, as are those who give alms and keep hospitality. Renunciation of ownership of all things, both in particular and in common, for the most part excludes this care; yet that renunciation does not exclude every such care in every case, because in some cases those who renounce are bound to help their neighbour. But renunciation of ownership in particular, not in common, does not exclude this care, for many religious who are bound to hospitality are obliged to have this care. There is another care, that of power and authority, by which one can claim temporal goods in judgment and litigate over them in various ways. It is this care that ownership or dominion of things requires. Evangelical poverty in its most perfect degree excludes this care, because one who lacks ownership of a thing, both in particular and in common, cannot litigate in court over that thing in his own name or in the name of his community. Evangelical poverty does not exclude the first care; but the fourth kind, which is the one at issue, is not necessary for perfect men. And so it appears that the appellant's statement, when he says that evangelical poverty excludes the care which the ownership or dominion of things requires, contains the truth, because he means evangelical poverty in its most perfect degree, and the power-based care by which one may litigate over temporal goods in court. From these points it is clear that the examples of this opponent, the slave and the Friars Minor, do not help his case. For although the slave has the care of servitude, he does not have that which ownership or dominion of things requires; nor does he keep evangelical poverty, because his ... is not voluntary but compelled. The Friars Minor, although they have some care, because of natural necessity, do not have that which ownership or dominion of things requires. For they cannot litigate in any way over things in court; yet the Roman church can do so, at least through its ministers. As for his claim that renunciation of ownership and dominion excludes care, these opponents say that this opponent quotes the appellant's words in a truncated form. For the appellant says that it "excludes the care which the ownership or dominion of things requires." And this is blameless, because it is manifest that it excludes that care. Hence renunciation of ownership and dominion, both in common and in particular, excludes the care which ownership and dominion of things require in particular, so that one cannot litigate in court over a thing in his own name. Renunciation of ownership and dominion in common and in particular excludes that care which ownership and dominion of things require in particular or in common, because one can litigate over a thing in court neither in his own name nor in the name of his community. Such ownership requires this care, although it often requires several cares, which can in some way be reduced to the care spoken of in the fourth sense. But let us see what the text itself says. [We likewise say that this is false.] These opponents say that it is plain from what has been said that what he states here as true is false. [Such renunciation does not exclude care.] These opponents say that if he had said that it does not exclude all care, he would have spoken truly, because the care of natural necessity and of compassionate piety is not at all included under care. Hence Chrysostom, on the words of Matthew, Do not possess gold or silver, etc., says: From this it is clear that he set those men, so to speak, as angels, freeing them from all anxiety of this life, so that they were occupied with one care, which is the teaching of the Church. When Chrysostom says that the apostles were freed from all anxiety of this life, he by no means includes the care of natural necessity under the word anxiety. Therefore, although the appellant could have said that evangelical poverty excludes all care, he should not be blamed at all, but understood in the sense of the saints' manner of speaking, had he imitated it. Yet he did not say this; he said that it excludes the care which ownership requires, etc. These opponents further say that when this opponent says that such renunciation does not exclude care, he is wrong in this respect, because it is established that the care by which someone litigates over things in his own name or that of his college is excluded. [Nor on that account is the slave free from care.] It is true that he is not free from all care, but he is free from that care which ownership or dominion requires. [The money handed to him by his lord he had not handed over to be put out at interest.] From this it is clear that that slave ought to have some care, but not that which ownership requires. [He to whom the usefulness of a thing belongs, without dominion, is more anxious about that thing than its lord is.] These opponents say that this is not to the point, and that it does not contain the truth, which is why it is not to the point. This is evident, because such a person does not have that care which ownership requires, although he has another; nor does it contain the truth, because often he to whom the usefulness of a thing belongs is by no means anxious about the repair and preservation of the thing

[Vt ad sensum videri potest in Fratrib. Minoribus, qui nudū vsum facti se habere in talib. asserent.] Sed nudus vsus facti posset accipi pro vsu iuris, qui sic diffinitur: Vsus est ius utendi rebus alienis &c. Dicunt isti, q̄ Fratres Minores non haberent nudum vsum facti: quia dicunt, se nullum ius habere. [circa secunda magis sunt solliciti] dicunt q̄ loquēdo de sollicitudine, q̄ requirit rerum proprietas, Fratres Minores circa res istas nullo modo sunt solliciti: quia nullatenus litigant pro rebus in iudicio. Et de ista sollicitudine loquitur est appellans. Et si dicas, q̄ aliqui Fratres in iudicio litigant pro rebus illis, dicunt isti, quod illi pseudo Fratres sunt censendi [quam Romana ecclesia] Dicunt isti, q̄ hoc est falsum, quia Romana ecclesia procuratores suos & officiales instituit, qui de rebus fratrum vsibus deputatis debent esse solliciti: eas, si iniuste ablatae fuerint vel detentae, in iudicio repetendo nomine Romanae ecclesiae: & eas, si quis vendicauerit indebite, defendendo. haec ante sollicitudo Fratrib. Minoribus non potest competere. hoc dicunt isti, specialiter patet p priuilegium Martini papae, qui de talibus procuratoribus constituendis prouide ordinauit. & ita Romana ecclesia circa res Fratrum vsibus deputatas, sollicitudinem sufficientem adhibuit, quam Fratres Minores exercere non valent.
units.tr: [illegible, ~3 letters] Digitized by Google watermark omitted. and preservation of the thing. This is plain of those who hire houses, horses and many other things, whose usefulness they have, but for whose preservation and repair they take little trouble; rather, the owners must apply care to them. [As can be seen in practice among the Friars Minor, who claim that they have only the bare use of fact in such things.] But bare use of fact could be taken for use of right, which is defined thus: Use is the right of using another's things, etc. These opponents say that the Friars Minor would not have bare use of fact, because they say they have no right at all. [are more anxious about the second things] These opponents say that, speaking of the care which ownership of things requires, the Friars Minor are in no way anxious about those things, because they never litigate over things in court. And it is of this care that the appellant speaks. And if you say that some friars do litigate in court over those things, these opponents say that those are to be counted pseudo-friars. [than the Roman church] These opponents say that this is false, because the Roman church appoints its procurators and officials, who ought to be anxious about the things assigned to the friars' use, and who, if they have been taken away or detained unjustly, must recover them in court in the name of the Roman church, and defend them if anyone claims them wrongly. This care cannot belong to the Friars Minor. These opponents say this is especially evident from the privilege of Pope Martin, who made careful provision for appointing such procurators. And so the Roman church has applied sufficient care to the things assigned to the friars' use, which the Friars Minor are not able to exercise.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: Praeterea dicit iste haereticus, quod vitae apostolorum repugnat doctrinae predictae: quia secundum eam quantum ad abdicationem proprietatis rerum temporalium fuerunt apostoli secundū beatū Remigiū ad dignitatē primi hominis reuocati. sed primus homo & eius posteri, si stetissent in originali iustitia, habuissent vsum rerum vsu consumptibilium sine proprietate & dominio earundem, secundum beatum Clementem (vt dicit) ad quod probandum induxit 12. q. 1. c. dilectissimis: quare dicere, quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus non potest vsus a proprietate & dominio separari, est vt dicit vitam apostolorum & religiosorum apostoles in abdicatione proprietatis omnium rerum imitantium impugnare.
units.tr: Furthermore, this heretic says that the life of the apostles is at odds with the doctrine described above. For according to that doctrine, as far as the renunciation of ownership of temporal goods is concerned, the apostles were restored, according to blessed Remigius, to the dignity of the first man. But the first man and his posterity, had they remained in original righteousness, would have had the use of consumable goods without ownership or dominion over them, according to blessed Clement (as he says), whom he cites to prove this in 12. q. 1. c. dilectissimis. Therefore, to say that in consumable goods use cannot be separated from ownership and dominion is, as he says, to attack the life of the apostles and of the religious who imitate the apostles in renouncing ownership of all things.

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnatus respondet ad quintam obiectionē appellantis, q̄ est talis. Apostoli secundū beatū Remigiū quantū ad abdicationē temporalium fuerūt ad dignitatē primi hominis reuocati. sed in statu innocentiae fuisset vsus rerum consumptibilium vsu absq; proprietate & dominio. ergo vitae apostolorum repugnat doctrina predicta. Ex hoc patet, quod iste appellans non intendit p obiectionē istam primo probare, q̄ in rebus vsu consumptibilibus potest vsus facti a proprietate & dominio separari: sed intendit principaliter & directe probare, quod apostoli habuerunt vsum facti a proprietate & dominio separatū. Sed textū breuiter videamus. [Ex quo sequitur conclusio prima secundū beatū Remigium.] Auctoritas beati Remigii in appellatione breui non ponitur, sed in maiori: q̄, vt magis pateat obiectio appellantis, est praesentibus inserenda. Dicit itaq; sic beatus Remigius super illud Mat. 10. Nolite possidere aurum &c. Ostendit Dominus in his verbis q̄ sancti praedicatores reuocati sunt ad primi hominis dignitatē: quia quamdiu caelestes possident thesauros. ista non concupiunt: sed mox vt peccata illa admisit, ista desiderare coepit. [habuissent vsum rerum vsu consumptibilium sine proprietate & dominio earū] quia nulla fuisset inter eos quantū ad dominium appropriatio rerū. [vitā apostolorū] qui nulla rem sibi appropriare volebant.
units.tr: In this part, the man being attacked answers the fifth objection of the appellant, which is as follows. According to blessed Remigius, the apostles were recalled to the dignity of the first man so far as renouncing temporal goods is concerned. But in the state of innocence there would have been the use of things consumable by use, without property and ownership. Therefore the life of the apostles contradicts the aforesaid doctrine. From this it is clear that this appellant does not intend, by this objection, first to prove that in things consumable by use the use of a thing can be separated from property and ownership; rather, he principally and directly intends to prove that the apostles had the use of a thing separated from property and ownership. But let us look briefly at the text. From this follows the first conclusion, according to blessed Remigius. The authority of blessed Remigius is not given in brief in the appeal, but in fuller form, which is to be inserted here so that the objection of the appellant may be clearer. He speaks thus, then, on that verse of Matthew 10, Possess no gold, etc.: The Lord shows in these words that the holy preachers were recalled to the dignity of the first man, because as long as they possess heavenly treasures, they do not covet these things; but as soon as he [man] began to commit those sins, he began to desire them. [would have had the use of things consumable by use, without property and ownership of them], because there would have been among them no appropriation of things as to ownership. [the life of the apostles], who wished to appropriate nothing to themselves.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: AD quod dicendū, quod illud, quod ipse dicit, quod primi parentes in statu innocentiae in nullo habuerūt dominium, sed tantū simplicem facti vsum, ad minus post illā benedictionē Crescite &c. Scriptura sacre contradicit expresse. Legitur n. Gen. 1. c. quod Dominus primus parentib. dixit: Crescite & multiplicamini, & replete terrā & subiicite eā. Alia litera loco eius, quod supra dicitur, & subiicite eam, habet & dominamini ei. & illā p sequitur Aug. in lib. super Gen. ad litera, & in libro de ciuitate lib. 14. c. 21. & sequitur: Et dominamini piscib. maris & volatilib. caeli & vniuersis animantibus, q̄ mouentur super terram. Ex quib. euidenter appareret, primos parentes post benedictionem praedictā, & terra & piscib. maris, ac volatilium caeli & vniuersorum animantium, quae mouentur super terram, dominium in statu innocentiae habuisse.
units.tr: To this it must be said that what he states, namely, that the first parents in the state of innocence had no ownership in any respect, but only the simple use of a thing, is expressly contradicted by Holy Scripture, at least after that blessing, Increase, etc. For it is read in Genesis 1 that the Lord said to the first parents: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it. Another reading, instead of what is said above, and subdue it, has and have dominion over it; and Augustine follows this in his book on Genesis according to the letter, and in the City of God, book 14, chapter 21, and it continues: And have dominion over the fish of the sea and the birds of the heaven and all living things that move upon the earth. From these words it appears plainly that the first parents, after the aforesaid blessing, had ownership in the state of innocence both of the earth and of the fish of the sea, and of the birds of the heaven and of all living things that move upon the earth.

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnat ad obiectionē praemissam nititur respondere. & primo respondet ad illud, q̄ accepit de statu innocentiae, quod primi parentes habuissent vsum rerum consumptibilium vsu, absq; dominio & proprietate earundē. Secundo ad capitul. Clementis ibi: Nec obstat. Prima pars diuiditur in duas: q̄a primo ondit, quod primi parentes habuerunt in statu innocentiae temporaliū rerū dominiū huiusmodi rerū. Secunda ibi: Et si quaeratur. Primo ergo respondendo ad obiectionē dicit, q̄ primi parentes sahē post illā benedictionē Crescite &c. habuerūt rerū dominium, q̄ probat p verba Gen. superius recitata. Sed isti impugnatores dicūt, istū impugnatū hic cauillose procedere: necad mēte vadit appellatis, quia appellas intēdit loqui de dominio proprio alicui personae, vel collegio speciali. Ad q̄ insinuandū aperte semp vel frequenter cū loquitur de dominio, vocabulū proprietatis adiungit, tali modo vel æquiualenti; dominium seu proprietas: vt p hoc det intelligere, q̄ loquitur de dominio, q̄ in scientiis legalib. vocatur proprietas. Illud a. dominiū, q̄ in scientiis legalib. & in scripturis modū loqndi scientiarū legalū seruantib. vocatur proprietas, et proprium alicui personę singulari, vel collegio speciali, virtute cui° contra aliā personā vel collegiū, si re cuius habet tale dominiū vēdicauerit vel detinuerit, pōt in iudicio litigare, agēdo vel defendendo. Et q̄ dominium, q̄ vocatur proprietas vel proprium, sit tale dominiū, probare nituntur. Ad cuius euidentiā dicuntēsse sciendum, quod sicut omne q̄ dicitur proprii, conuenit alicui homini & non alii, vel aliis: sicut etiam de proprietate, quod ideo proprietas appellatur, quia conuenit alicui vel aliquibus, & non alii vel aliis. Dominiū igitur, quod vocatur proprietas: aut ideo dicitur proprietas, quia conuenit homini vel hominibus, & nō alii hominī, vel aliis hominib. Aut dicitur proprietas hominis vel hominibus, & nulli alteri, vel aliis extra genus humanū. Si detur primum, habetur intentum. quod dominium de quo loquitur appellans est proprium vni persona singulari, vel alicui collegio speciali. Secundum dici non potest: quia nullius rei habet homo dominium, quin eiusdem rei habeat aliquis extra genus humanum dominium. & de Deo quidem est certum: quia Domini est terra plenitudo eius. de angelis etiam extendendo nomen domini, ad tale dominium, quale habuerunt primi parentes in statu innocentiae, videtur habere veritatem. Non n. minus sunt subiecti universae aliae creaturae nunc angelis, quam tunc fuerunt primis parentibus. Dominium ergo illud, quod vocatur proprietas, nullomodo fuit in statu innocentiae: nec fuisset unquam, si primi parentes non peccassent, quia nulla res taliter alicui personae singulari, vel collegio speciali appropriata fuisset & ita nam dominium, quod competit primis parentibus, aequivoce sit dicendum dominium, respectu dominii, de quo locutus est appellans, & de quo iura loquuntur, patet quod iste cavillose contra ipsum procedit, nec in aliquo haberet mente eius. Concedendum est igitur, quod primi parentes habuerunt dominium temporalium: sicut & potest dici, quod angeli habent dominium daemoniorum, & rerum temporalium: quia daemones & res temporales angelis subiiciuntur, & ipsi dominantur eis. sed de tali dominio non est sermo in appellatione appellantis.
units.tr: In this part, the man being attacked tries to answer the objection stated above. And first he answers what was taken from the state of innocence, namely, that the first parents would have had the use of things consumable by use without ownership and property of them. Second, he answers the chapter of Clement, there: Nor is it an obstacle. The first part is divided into two: first, he says that the first parents in the state of innocence had ownership of temporal goods of this kind; the second, there: And if it is asked. First, then, answering the objection, he says that the first parents, after that blessing, Increase, etc., had ownership of goods, which he proves by the words of Genesis cited above. But these attackers say that the man being attacked here proceeds captiously, and that he does not follow the intention of the appellant, because the appellant intends to speak of ownership belonging to some particular person or special body. To make this clear, the appellant always, or frequently, when he speaks of ownership, adds the word property in this way or its equivalent: ownership or property, so that he may make it understood that he is speaking of ownership, which in legal sciences is called property. Now that ownership which in legal sciences, and in writings that keep the manner of speaking of legal sciences, is called property, and which belongs to some single person or special body, by virtue of which it can litigate in court, by suing or defending, against another person or body, if it has claimed or detained a thing of which it holds such ownership. And they try to prove that the ownership which is called property or one's own is of this kind. To make this evident, they say that it must be known that just as everything that is said to be one's own belongs to one man and not to another or others, so also property is so called because it belongs to someone or some persons and not to another or others. Therefore, ownership which is called property is either called property because it belongs to one man or to men and not to another man or others; or it is called the property of a man or men and of no other, or of others outside the human race. If the first is granted, the point is established: the ownership of which the appellant speaks is proper to one single person or to some special body. The second cannot be said, because a man has no ownership of anything without some being outside the human race also having ownership of the same thing. This is certainly true of God, for the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof. Also of the angels, if the name of lord is extended to such ownership as the first parents had in the state of innocence, it seems to be true; for the other creatures are no less subject to the angels now than they were then to the first parents. Therefore that ownership which is called property was in no way in the state of innocence, nor would it ever have been, had the first parents not sinned, because no thing would have been appropriated in such a way to any single person or special body. And so, since the ownership which belonged to the first parents must be called equivocally ownership, in relation to the ownership of which the appellant spoke and of which the laws speak, it is clear that this man proceeds captiously against him, and that he did not have his meaning in mind. It must therefore be conceded that the first parents had ownership of temporal goods, just as it can also be said that the angels have ownership of demons and of temporal goods, because demons and temporal goods are subject to the angels, and the angels rule over them. But of such ownership there is no discussion in the appellant's appeal.

units.la: Nunc ad explanationem literalem. [Primi parentes in statu innocentia in nullo habuerunt dominium.] Quamuis hoc habeat unum sensum verum: quia verum est secundum istos, accepto vocabulo dominii, pro dominio, ex quo opponuntur contractus humani, & etiam actiones in iudicio. quia nullum tale dominium habuerunt primi parentes. Non enim tales contractus, sicut emptio, venditio, donatio, conductio, mutuum, & huiusmodi aliae actiones in iudicio fuissent in statu innocentiae: ideo nullum tale dominium habuerunt: cum hoc appellans sub verbis praedictis non dicat. sed dicit: primus homo & posteri eius, si stetissent, habuissent usum rerum usu consumptibilium, sine proprietate & dominio earundem. In quibus verbis evidenter insinuat, quod loquitur de dominio, quod in iure vocatur proprietas: & nullum tale dominium habuerunt primi parentes in statu innocentiae. Unde quamuis concedendum sit in aliquo sensu, quod primi parentes habuerunt dominium in statu innocentiae rerum temporalium, non tamen est concedendum, quod habuerunt tunc proprietatem rerum temporalium. & hoc, quia hoc nomen dominium habet aliquas significationes, quas non habet hoc nomen proprietas: sicut e contrario hoc nomen proprietas habet aliquas significationes, quas non habet hoc nomen dominium, licet forte in scientiis legalibus nunquam accipiatur in illis significationibus hoc nomen proprietas [sed tantum simplicem facti usum.] De hoc appellans hic nullam penitus facit mentionem, quamuis habeat veritatem: secundum simplex usus facti excludit omne ius, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare. tale enim ius in statu innocentiae non fuisset.
