[Scriptura sacra contradicit expresse.] Dicunt isti, quod nulla est contradictio: quia contradictio est oppositio unius & eiusdem, non nominis tantum, sed rei & nominis, iuxta sententiam sapientis. Aliter autem accipit appellans dominium & scriptura divina in illo loco Gen. 1. licet in multis aliis locis utatur scriptura dominio nomine dominii, quomodo utitur hic appellans: & ita licitum fuit sibi illo modo uti vocabulo dominii, ex quo scriptura sacra & scientiae legales sic utuntur. Dominamini: hoc est, potestatiue vtimini eis. [dominium in statu innocentia habuisse] hoc verum est de dominio, quod est vigor potestatiuus regendi & utendi eis ad solatium, & aliis modis licitis. sed tale dominium non habent ullo modo mortales in multis rebus temporalibus. De dominio autem, quod vocatur proprietas temporalium, non habet veritatem: quia tale dominium tunc non fuit.
units.tr: Now to the literal explanation. [The first parents in the state of innocence had no ownership in any respect.] Although this has one true sense, namely that it is true according to them, if the word ownership is taken for that ownership to which human contracts and also actions in court are opposed, because the first parents had no such ownership. For such contracts as buying, selling, giving, hiring, lending, and other such actions in court would not have existed in the state of innocence; therefore they had no such ownership, since the appellant does not say this in the aforesaid words. But he says: the first man and his posterity, had they stood, would have had the use of things consumable by use, without property and ownership of them. In which words he clearly implies that he is speaking of ownership which in law is called property; and the first parents had no such ownership in the state of innocence. Hence, although it must be conceded in some sense that the first parents had ownership of temporal goods in the state of innocence, it must not be conceded that they then had property in temporal goods. This is because the name ownership has some meanings which the name property does not have, just as, conversely, the name property has some meanings which the name ownership does not have, although perhaps in legal sciences the name property is never taken in those meanings. [But only the simple use of a thing.] Of this the appellant makes no mention here at all, although it is true: the simple use of a thing excludes every right by which someone can litigate in court; for such a right would not have existed in the state of innocence. [Holy Scripture expressly contradicts.] These men say that there is no contradiction, because a contradiction is an opposition of one and the same, not only of name but of thing and name, according to the saying of the wise man. But the appellant and divine Scripture understand ownership differently in that passage of Genesis 1, although Scripture in many other places uses the word ownership in the sense in which the appellant uses it here; and so it was lawful for him to use the word ownership in that way, since Holy Scripture and the legal sciences use it so. Have dominion: that is, use them with power. [had dominion in the state of innocence] This is true of that ownership which is the power of ruling and using things for comfort and for other lawful purposes; but mortals in no way have such ownership over many temporal things. But as to the ownership of temporal goods which is called property, it is not true, because such ownership did not then exist.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Et si quaeratur, utrum illud dominium proprium fuerit vel commune, videtur dicendum, quod si tempore benedictionis praedicta solus Adam formatus erat, & non Eua, sicut ordo scripturae sacra evidenter innuit: cum illa benedictio fuerit data Adam extra paradisum existente; Eua vero formata fuerit, ipso Adam in paradisum translato, ut patet Gen. 1. c. & 2. videtur, quod ante formationem Eua dominium temporale Adae proprium fuerit, non commune. Commune quidem esse non potuit: cum solus pro tempore illo fuerit: & respectu unius, qui nunquam alios socios habuit, nihil commune dici potest. Et videtur hoc expresse dici Eccl. 17. c. vbi dicit sic. Deus creavit de terra hominem & secundum imaginem suam fecit illum. Et sequitur: Dedit illi potestatem eorum, quae sunt super terram, & posuit timorem illius super omnem carnem, & dominatus est bestiarum & volatilium. Ex quibus patet, quod solus dominatus fuit. Ex quo sequitur ipsum solum pro illo tempore dominium habuisse: quia secundum Dionysium de divinis nominibus c. 12. A dominio dicitur Dominus, dominans & dominator. Unde cum de solo Adam dicatur, quod dominatus est bestiarum & volatilium: sequitur, quod & solus Dominus fuit. & quod Eua tunc formata non esset, patet: quia statim post illa verba: & dominatus est bestiarum & volatilium, sequitur. Creavit ex ipso adiutorium simile sibi. Hoc idem videtur sentire Damascenus 1. c. vbi loquens de primo parente sic dicit: Hunc igitur hominem condidit masculum constituxit: statuit & tribuit ei suiipsius divinam gratiam: & in gratia & in communione eius per hanc ipsam fecit. Unde & animalium nominatorem prophetica, ut suorum donorum dominator effecit. Alia litera habet, ut suorum servorum dominator fecit; & sequitur: Fecit ex ipso auxiliatricem ipsius &c.
units.tr: And if it is asked whether that dominion was proper or common, it seems we must say that, if Adam alone had been formed at the time of the aforesaid blessing, and not Eve, as the order of sacred Scripture clearly indicates (since that blessing was given while Adam was still outside paradise, and Eve was formed after Adam had been brought into paradise, as Gen. 1. c. & 2. makes plain), then before Eve was formed, Adam's temporal dominion was proper to him and not common. Indeed it could not have been common, since he was alone at that time, and nothing can be called common with respect to one who never had any companions. This seems to be stated expressly in Eccl. 17. c., where it says: God created man from the earth and made him after his own image. And it goes on: He gave him power over the things that are upon the earth, and set the fear of him over all flesh, and he had dominion over the beasts and the birds. From these words it is clear that he alone had dominion. From this it follows that he alone had dominion for that time, because, according to Dionysius, On the Divine Names, c. 12, from "dominion" comes "Lord," "ruling," and "ruler." Therefore, since it is said of Adam alone that he had dominion over the beasts and the birds, it follows that he alone was Lord; and that Eve was not yet formed at that time is clear, because immediately after those words, that he had dominion over the beasts and the birds, it follows: He made for himself a helper like himself. Damascene seems to hold the same view, c. 1, where, speaking of the first parent, he says: Therefore he fashioned this man, male, and established him, and bestowed on him his own divine grace; and in grace and in fellowship with him he made him through this very grace. Whence also, as a prophet, he made him the namer of the animals, so that he became the lord of his gifts. Another reading has: so that he became the lord of his servants; and it continues: He made from him a helper like himself, etc.

units.la: Ostenso secundum istum impugnatu, quod primi parentes habuerunt in statu innocentiae dominium & proprietatem rerum temporalium. Hic quaeritur, quale fuit illud dominium, proprium sc. an commune. & determinat, quod Adam habuit primo dominium proprium omnium temporalium. probat tali ratione: Dominium, quod competit uni soli, & nunquam habuit socios, est dominium proprium. sed Adam habuit dominium ante formationem Eua. Hoc probat auctoritate Eccl. 17. c. & auctoritate Iohannis Damasceni. ergo Adam habuit dominium proprium temporalium. Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, in verbis praemissis duos errores principaliter contineri: quorum primus est, quod illa benedictio Crescite &c. fuerit data Adę extra paradisum ante formationē Eųę. Secund⁹ est, ꝙ Adam ante formationē Euæ habuit dominiū ᵱprium temporaliū. Quod primū sit erroneū reputandū, ex serie text. Gen. 1. conātur ostendere. ibi n. sic scribitur: Creauit Deus hominē ad imaginē suam: ad imaginē Dei creauit illū, masculū & feminā creauit eos: benedixit q⁊ illis Deus, & ait: Crescite & multiplicamini & replete terram & subiicite eam: & dominamini piscib. maris, & volatilib. cœli, & vniuersis animantibus, quæ mouentur super terrā. Ex quib. verbis clare patet, ꝙ Deus masculū & feminam creauit, quib. benedixit. unde & oēs particulæ benedictionis eiusdē in plurali, nō in singulari numero, ᵱferuntur. ergo illa benedictio post illā formationē Euæ data fuit: & ꝙ hoc congruū fuerit, rōne ᵱbatur. Nā in illa benedictione ᵱceptū de prole multiplicāda cōtinetur. proles a ᵱ virū absq; muliere multiplicari non potuit. ergo congruū fuit, ꝙ post formationē mulieris idē ᵱceptum imponeretur: & ita benedictio illa ante formationē Euæ data non fuit. Secundus error, vt dicunt isti, est ꝙ Adā ante formationē Euę habuit dominiū ᵱprium temporaliū rerum. Ad cuius euidentiā dicunt esse sciendū, ꝙ dominiū non dicitur esse ᵱprium: quia de facto cōuenit vni soli. Tunc n. si oēs monachi vnius abbatiæ morerētur vel occiderentur ᵱter vnum: ille vnus haberet dominiū proprium omnium bonorū eiusdem abbatiæ, & esset tunc ᵱprietarius reputādus: ꝙ omnino falsum est censendū. Nō ergo dicitur dominium proprium, qā de facto cōuenit vni soli: sed dicitur ᵱprium, qñ ita appropriatur vni, quod absq; vnius donatione vel venditione, aut legatione, aut aliquo alio humano contractu, quo dominium rei transfertur in aliquē, vel saltē sine aliquo actu vel morte illius, alteri nō potest cōpetere. Propter quod si aliquis fundaret aliquod monasteriū, & multis bonis dotaret: primus q efficeretur monachus in eodē monasterio nō haberet dominiū proprium illorum bonorum, nec esset tunc ᵱprietarius reputandus: quia absq; eius donatione & venditione & omni alio humano contractu, quo dominium rei transfertur in aliquē; & absq; omni actu eius & morte, si alius fiat monachus in eodē monasterio, secundus haberet earundē rerum dominiū aliquale sicut primus. Ex hoc concludunt isti, ꝙ posito ꝙ Adam habuerit dominiū rerum temporalium aliquale; non tale, quale modo habēt homines, ante formationē Euæ; non propter hoc habuit dominiū proprium earundē, quia dominiū rerum, ꝙ absq; omni donatione, venditione, & alia humana ordinatione, qua rerum dominiū transfertur in aliquē, & actu & morte illius potest ad alium puenire, non est proprium alicui. sed dominiū temporaliū rerū ad Euā absq; omni ordinatione Adæ & actu & morte eius poterat puenire; imo in statu innocentiæ nunq; p ordinationē ipsius puenisset ad ipsum; qā in statu innocentiæ nunq; vnus de se in alterū alicuius rei transtulisset dominiū, sed qlibet vbicunq; tem inuenisset sibi ad vtendū vel ět ad solatiū oportunum ipsam absq; ordinatione alterius accepisset. ergo Adā dominiū ᵱprium nō habuit ante formationē Euæ. Hęc ratio cōfirmatur; quia Adā absq; culpa sua nullo debuit ᵱprio priuari; & p consequens ante formationē Euæ nō habuit proprium dominiū, qā si habuisset formata Eua, eodē dominio ᵱprio fuisset absq; culpa sua priuatus. sed Eua formata ita habuit dominiū omniū, sicut Adā. ergo Adā Eua tunc formata, nō habuit dominiū ᵱprium. Sic igitur dicunt isti, ꝙ esto ꝙ dominiū rerum fuerit datū Adæ ante formationem Euæ; nō tn habuit tunc dominiū ᵱprium; qā illud dominiū nō fuit sibi datum ᵱ se solo, sed pro se & muliere formāda de ipso, ac ᵱ omnib. posteris eorundē; nec ad ipsum pertinebat Eua formata sibi aliq; cōferre dominiū. ¶ Illa a. q̄ iste adducit ᵱ assertionib. supradictis, super litera dissoluentur. [Videtur dicendū] licet hic videatur loq minime assertiue; tn postea hoc asserit manifeste. [tēpore benedictionis prædictæ] sc. Crescite & c. multiplicamini &c. qa de nulla alia benedictione prī fecerat mentionē. [Solus Adā formatus erat] hoc dicunt esse erroneū, sicut ostensum est prius [hoc ordo scriptura euidenter innuit] hic notāt duo. Primo, ꝙ hic asserit manifeste, ꝙ prī videbatur nō sub assertione, sed cōditionaliter protulisse; qā dicere ordinē scripturę aliqd euidenter innuere, est eidē firmiter inhærere, si, ꝙ hoc dicit, de veritate scripturę nō dubitat. Secundo notāt hoc dictū suū esse aperte falsū, cum ordo scripturę hoc nō innuat; & verba scripturę oppositū aperte demonstrent, sicut per verba benedictionis prędictę clare patet. Et si dicatur, ꝙ ordo scripturę innuit, ꝙ benedictio illa fuerit data ante formationē Euæ; tum qa illa benedictio ante ponitur in scriptura, q̄ mod⁹ formationis Euæ describatur; qā illa benedictio ponitur Gen. 1. c. Formatio a. Euę describitur in 2. c. Tū quia illa benedictio fuit data ante præceptum de comedendo ex omni ligno paradisi, & ante præceptum de non comedendo ex ligno scientię boni & mali. sed illud præceptū fuit datum soli Adæ ante formationem Euæ. ergo illa benedictio fuit data ante formationem Euæ. Ad primum istorum dicunt, quod sicut illa benedictio ponitur in textu, antequam describatur modus formationis Euæ; ita etiam antequam describatur modus formationis Euæ, dicitur masculū & feminam creauit eos. Et tn constat, quod Dominus ante formationē Euæ feminam non creauit, quia Eua fuit prima femina a Deo creata. & ideo sicut anteq describatur modus formationis Euę, per anticipationem dicitur Deum creasse feminam. Ita per anticipationem dicitur Deum masculo & feminæ benedixisse. Ad secundam videtur nonnullis dicendum, quod illa benedictio non fuit data ante præceptum de comedendo &c. licet dominium ante fuerit datum; quia videtur eis, quod istud dominium non fuit nisi naturale vel concreata potestas potenter vtendi & gubernandi res, quarum habebant dominium; & ita a principio habuit Adam tale dominium, propter quod videtur eis, quod cum Dominus dixit; Dominamini piscibus maris &c. magis fuit ᵱceptum exercendi dominium, quam collatio dominii. sicut cum dixit Multiplicamini, non conferebat potestatem multiplicandi prolē: sed de exeundo in actū potestatis prius collatę dedit ᵱceptum. & ita quicquid sit de tēpore collationis dominii, constat ꝙ benedictio illa fuit data post formationē Euæ. [cū illa benedictio fueris data Adæ extra paradisum existente. ] Hoc dicunt omni veritate carere; quia illa benedictio nō fuit data ante præceptū de comedendo; & tamen illud præceptum fuit datū Adam in paradiso existente. Nec obstat, quod prius fit mentio de benedictione illa, quam de prædicto præcepto: quia sicut ostensum est prius & postea amplius ostendetur, ordo literæ non semper sequitur ordinem rei gestæ. [ Videtur quod ante formationem Euæ dominium temporalium Adæ proprium fuerit, non commune ] hoc non sequitur ex prædictis, etiam posito, quod antea habuerit dominiū [Commune quidem esse non potuit, &c.] Hic dicunt, quod aliquando aliquid dicitur commune, quia communicandum. Unde dicit Glo. dist. 1. dic communia, id est, communicanda tempore necessitatis. Aliter dicitur commune, quod de facto conuenit pluribus. Primo modo fuit illud dominium commune, etiam posito quod ante formationem Euæ Adam habuerit dominium, quia illud dominiū communicandum fuit Euæ, nō ab Adā, sed à Deo: nec Adam illud sibi appropriare valebat. & ideo commune fuit, hoc est, communicandum: & commune sic sumptum extra tempus necessitatis, distinguitur contra proprium, secundum quod commune & proprium diuidunt dominium. Et ideo quod de facto & actu conueniat pluribus, vel non conueniat, hoc accidit. sed si extra tempus necessitatis ad dominium est communicandum, non ex contractu humano habentis dominium, dicitur commune, secundum quod commune distinguitur contra proprium. [Respectu vnius quæ nunquam aliquos socios habuerit, nihil commune dici possit.] Istud est falsum de illo, quod dicitur commune, quia communicandum. Unde sicut aliquid potest dici commune, quod competit vni, qui de facto nullos socios habet, sicut patet, si vnus solus monachus de aliquo monasterio remaneret superstes, qui propter hoc non esset proprietarius, ita potest aliquid dici commune respectu vnius, qui nunquam de facto habuit socios. & hoc quia communicandum est aliis. nec aliis aduenientibus valet illud ipsis appropriare. [Dedit eis potestatem] Scilicet vtendi ad libitū, & regendi seu ordinādi. [Et dominatus est bestiarum, &c.] Hoc est potestatem habuit bestias & volatilia cœli ad placitum ordinandi. [Ex quib. patet quod solus dominator fuit.] Dicunt hic isti, quod de facto solus tunc fuit actualiter dominator. Ex hoc tamen non sequitur, quod habuit tunc dominium proprium, quia dominium proprium importat, quod res, cuius est dominium proprium, non sit alteri communicanda modo superius dicto. videtur tamē nonnullis, quod tunc non fuerit Adam dominator. Quia illud, quod dicitur ibi in Ecclesiaste. per anticipationē dicitur. [Ex quo sequitur ipsum solū pro illo tempore dominiū habuisse.] Dicunt, q quamuis concederetur, quod ipse tunc solus habuit dnium actu, ex hoc tn non sequitur, quod habuit dnium proprium: sicut ex hoc non sequitur, quod fuit proprietarius. Quemadmodū non sequitur, vnus solus monachus aliis mortuis, habet actu dnium rerū monasterii determinate: ergo ipse est proprietarius. [Cum de solo Adam dicitur, quod dominatus est bestiarū & volatiliū, sequitur quod et solus dominus suis] Male arguit, vt isti dicunt: quia sæpe aliquid in vno loco dicitur de vno solo, nec tamen propter hoc negatur ab aliis. De solo n. Iesu dicitur Mat. 23. Relictis illis abiit foras extra ciuitatem in Bethania. Nec tn ex hoc sequitur, quod ipse solus sine discipulis abiit extra ciuitatē. Et de hoc sunt exempla innumera, q aliquid dicitur de vno solo, nec tn propter hoc negatur de aliis. [Et q Eua tunc formata nō esset: patet quia statim post illa verba: & dominatus est bestiarū & volatiliū: sequitur, creauit ex ipso adiutorium simile sibi.] Hic dicit q male arguit, quia arguit virtute isti medii, hoc est posterius scriptu; ergo fuit posterius facta: q infinitas capit instantias: qa nō semp ordo scripturæ sequitur ordine rei gestæ, q per illud Ecclesiastici supra allegatū: euidenter ostendunt. Nam ibi sic scribitur Deus de terra creauit hominē: & secundū imaginem suam fecit illum, & iterū: cōuertit illū in ipsum: & secundū se vestiuit illū, &c. & sequitur: Et dedit illi potestate eorū quæ sunt super terrā. Posuit timorē illius super omē carnē, & dominatus est bestiarum & volatiliū. Creauit ex ipso adiutorium simile sibi: cōsilium & lingua, & oculos & aures, & cor dedit illis. In quib. verbis constat, q sapiēs ordinem rei gestæ q̄tum ad oīa nequaquam seruat. Prius n. narrat, quod dominus dedit hoī numerum dierum & tēpus, antequam de muliere faciat mentionem: & tn constat quod Eua, antequam Adam numerum dierum haberet, formata fuit; qa eadē die, qua Adā creatus erat, ipsa fuit formata. sic ergo ordo scripturæ nō semper sequitur ordinē rei gestæ. & hoc ēt exemplo. 1. Mach. 3. c. euidenter ostēditur, vbi sic legitur; Et surrexit Iudas qui vocabatur Machabeus, filius eius, pro eo & adiuuabant eum ēs fratres eius, & vniuersi qui se coniunxerant patrius: & præliabatur prælium Israel cum lætitia, & dilatauit gloriam populo suo, & induit se loricam sicut gygas, & succinxit se arma bellica sua in prælis, & protegebat castra gladio suo. Vbi constat, quod ordo rei gestæ non in omnib. conseruatur. Non n. prius præliabatur Israel cum lætitia, & postea Iudas se armauit. Constat ergo, quod in scripturis non semper ordo rei gestæ seruatur; & ideo ex hoc, quod post illa verba & dominarus est bestiarum & volatilia cœli: subditur, Et creauit ex ipso adiutorium simile sibi: sic probari non potest, quod Adam ante formationem Euæ habuit dominium rerum; quamuis hoc nonnulli concedāt, dicentes tn, quod illud dominium non fuit proprium reputandum; quia non pro se solummodo, sed & pro aliis quodammodo recepit. [Hoc idē videtur sentire Damascenus] dicūt quod Damascenus hoc nō sensit. [Alium nominatorem prophetice, vt suorum donorum dominator effecit.] Dicūt per anticipationem esse dictum; quidam tamen concedunt, quod tunc habuit dominium, sed non erat dominium proprium, sed commune, hoc est communicandum, & nullo modo appropriandum. [& sequitur fecit ex ipso auxiliatricem ipsius.] Dicunt quidam, hoc fuisse antea factum, licet hic posterius à Damasceno narretur.
units.tr: Having shown, against this opponent, that our first parents possessed dominion and ownership of temporal things in the state of innocence, the question now is what kind of dominion it was: whether it was proper (that is, private) or common. The author determines that Adam first had proper dominion over all temporal things. He proves this by the following reasoning: dominion that belongs to one alone, and never had companions, is proper dominion. But Adam had dominion before Eve was formed. This is proved by the authority of Ecclesiasticus 17 and the authority of John Damascene. Therefore Adam had proper dominion over temporal things. But these opponents say that two errors are chiefly contained in the foregoing statements. The first is that the blessing "Increase and multiply" etc. was given to Adam outside paradise, before Eve was formed. The second is that Adam had proper dominion over temporal things before Eve was formed. They try to show from the sequence of the text of Genesis 1 that the first claim should be regarded as erroneous. For the Scripture is written thus: God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. God also blessed them, and said: Increase and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it; and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth. From these words it is clearly evident that God created male and female, and it was to them that he gave the blessing. Hence all the parts of the same blessing are expressed in the plural, not in the singular. Therefore that blessing was given after the formation of Eve. And they prove that this was fitting by reason: for that blessing contains the command to multiply offspring. Offspring could not be multiplied by a man without a woman. Therefore it was fitting that the same command should be laid down after the formation of the woman, and so that blessing was not given before the formation of Eve. The second error, as they say, is that Adam before the formation of Eve had proper dominion over temporal things. To make this evident, they say that one must know that dominion is not called proper because it in fact belongs to one alone. For if all the monks of one abbey were to die or be killed except one, that one would have proper dominion over all the goods of that abbey and would then have to be reckoned its owner; which is wholly false to suppose. Dominion is therefore not called proper because it in fact belongs to one alone, but it is called proper when it is so appropriated to one that, apart from that one's gift or sale, or bequest, or some other human contract by which the ownership of a thing is transferred to another, or at least apart from some act or death of that one, it cannot belong to another. For this reason, if someone were to found a monastery and endow it with many goods, the first man who became a monk in that monastery would not have proper dominion over those goods, nor would he then be reckoned their owner. For without his gift, sale, or any other human contract by which ownership of a thing passes to another, and without any act or death of his, if another became a monk in the same monastery, the second would have a dominion over the same goods of some kind, just as the first did. From this they conclude that, granting that Adam had dominion over temporal things of some kind, though not of the kind men now have, before Eve was formed, it does not follow that he had proper dominion over them. For dominion over things that can pass to another without any gift, sale, or other human arrangement by which ownership is transferred, and without the act or death of the owner, is not proper to anyone. But dominion over temporal things could come to Eve without any arrangement of Adam, and without his act or death. Indeed, in the state of innocence it would never have come to her through his arrangement, since in the state of innocence no one would ever have transferred ownership of a thing from himself to another; rather, each, wherever he found something at the proper time for use or even for comfort, would have taken it without any arrangement by another. Therefore Adam did not have proper dominion before Eve was formed. This reasoning is confirmed, because Adam, without his own fault, ought not to have been deprived of anything that was his own; and consequently before Eve was formed he did not have proper dominion, for if he had had it, then once Eve was formed he would have been deprived of that same proper dominion without any fault of his own. But once formed, Eve had dominion over all things just as Adam did. Therefore, once Eve was formed, Adam did not have proper dominion. Thus these men say: granted that dominion over things was given to Adam before the formation of Eve, he did not then have proper dominion, because that dominion was not given to him for himself alone, but for himself and the woman to be formed from him, and for all their posterity; nor did it belong to him to confer any dominion on Eve once she was formed. ¶ The assertions which this author adduces above will be answered by the text itself. [It seems to be said] although here it seems that he speaks in no way assertively, yet afterwards he asserts this plainly. [at the time of the aforesaid blessing] namely, Increase and multiply etc., because he had made no mention of any other blessing earlier. [Adam alone had been formed] they say this is erroneous, as was shown before. [the order of Scripture evidently suggests this] here he notes two things. First, that he here asserts plainly that the author seemed to have put forward the claim not as an assertion but conditionally; for to say that the order of Scripture evidently suggests something is to cling firmly to it, if he who says this does not doubt the truth of Scripture. Second, he notes that this statement of his is manifestly false, since the order of Scripture does not suggest it, and the words of Scripture clearly demonstrate the opposite, as is plain from the words of the blessing above. And if it is said that the order of Scripture suggests that the blessing was given before the formation of Eve, both because that blessing is placed in Scripture before the mode of Eve's formation is described (for the blessing is placed in Genesis 1, while the formation of Eve is described in chapter 2), and because that blessing was given before the command about eating from every tree of paradise, and before the command not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, but that command was given to Adam alone before the formation of Eve; therefore that blessing was given before the formation of Eve. To the first of these they reply that just as the blessing is placed in the text before the mode of Eve's formation is described, so too, before the mode of her formation is described, it is said male and female he created them. And yet it is certain that the Lord did not create the woman before Eve was formed, since Eve was the first woman created by God. And so, just as before the mode of Eve's formation is described it is said by anticipation that God created a woman, so by anticipation it is said that God blessed male and female. To the second, some think it should be said that the blessing was not given before the command about eating etc., although the dominion was given earlier; for it seems to them that this dominion was nothing but a natural or innate power of using and governing the things over which they had dominion, and so from the beginning Adam had such dominion. Hence it seems to them that when the Lord said have dominion over the fish of the sea etc., it was rather a command to exercise dominion than a conferring of dominion; just as when he said multiply, he did not confer the power of multiplying offspring, but by commanding them to go into the act of a power previously conferred, he gave a command. And so, whatever may be the time of the conferring of dominion, it is certain that the blessing was given after the formation of Eve. [when that blessing was given to Adam while he was outside paradise] They say this lacks all truth, because that blessing was not given before the command about eating; and yet that command was given to Adam while he was in paradise. Nor does it matter that mention is made of that blessing before the aforesaid command, because, as was shown before and will be shown more fully later, the order of the text does not always follow the order of the events narrated. [It seems that before the formation of Eve, Adam's dominion over temporal things was proper, not common] this does not follow from what was said above, even granting that he had dominion earlier. [Indeed it could not be common, etc.] Here they say that sometimes something is called common because it is to be shared. Hence the Gloss on dist. 1 says: call them common, that is, to be shared in time of need. In another sense a thing is called common when in fact it belongs to several. In the first sense, that dominion was common even granting that Adam had dominion before Eve was formed, because that dominion was to be shared with Eve, not by Adam but by God; nor could Adam appropriate it to himself. And so it was common, that is, to be shared; and common so understood, outside a time of need, is distinguished from proper, according to the way common and proper divide dominion. And so whether it in fact belongs to several or not is accidental. But if, outside a time of need, dominion is to be shared, and not by a human contract on the part of the one who holds the dominion, it is called common, in the sense in which common is distinguished from proper. [With respect to one who never had any companions, nothing can be called common] This is false of that which is called common because it is to be shared. Hence, just as something can be called common which belongs to one who in fact has no companions (as is plain if one lone monk of some monastery remained alive, who for that reason would not be an owner, so something can be called common with respect to one who never in fact had companions), this is because it is to be shared with others, and when others arrive it cannot be appropriated to them. [He gave them power] namely, to use at will and to govern or arrange. [And he had dominion over the beasts, etc.] That is, he had power to arrange the beasts and the birds of the air at his pleasure. [From which it is plain that he was the sole ruler.] Here they say that in fact he alone was then actually the ruler. Yet it does not follow from this that he then had proper dominion, because proper dominion implies that the thing of which there is proper dominion is not to be shared with another in the manner stated above. Yet it seems to some that Adam was not then a ruler at all, because what is said there in Ecclesiastes is said by anticipation. [From which it follows that he alone had dominion for that time.] They say that even if it were granted that he alone then actually had dominion, it still does not follow that he had proper dominion, just as it does not follow that he was an owner. As it does not follow, when all other monks are dead and one monk alone is actually in possession of the goods of the monastery, that he is therefore the owner. [Since it is said of Adam alone that he had dominion over the beasts and birds, it follows that he alone was lord over his sons] This is a bad inference, as they say, because it is often said of one alone something that happens in one place, and yet it is not on that account denied of others. For it is said of Jesus alone in Matthew 23: Leaving them, he went out of the city into Bethany. Yet it does not follow from this that he went out of the city alone, without his disciples. And there are countless examples where something is said of one alone, and yet is not on that account denied of others. [And that Eve was not then formed is plain, because immediately after those words, and he had dominion over the beasts and birds, it follows: he created from him a helper like himself.] Here they say the argument is bad, because it infers from the force of the intervening statement, namely that it was written later, that it was made later. This has infinite exceptions, because the order of Scripture does not always follow the order of the events, as is clearly shown by the passage of Ecclesiasticus cited above. For there it is written thus: God created man of the earth, and made him after his own image, and turned him back into it, and clothed him with strength according to himself, etc., and it follows: And he gave him power over the things that are upon the earth. He put the fear of him upon all flesh, and he had dominion over the beasts and birds. He created from him a helper like himself, counsel and tongue, and eyes and ears, and gave them a heart. In these words it is clear that the wise man by no means keeps the order of the events in every respect. For first he tells that the Lord gave man the number of his days and a time, before he makes mention of the woman. And yet it is certain that Eve was formed before Adam had the number of his days, since on the same day on which Adam was created, she too was formed. So the order of Scripture does not always follow the order of events. This is also shown clearly by the example of 1 Maccabees 3, where it is read thus: And Judas, who was called Maccabeus, his son, rose up in his place, and his brothers helped him, and all who had joined themselves to his father; and Israel fought the battle with gladness, and he enlarged the glory of his people, and put on a breastplate like a giant, and girded on his warlike arms in battles, and protected the camp with his sword. Here it is plain that the order of events is not kept in every case. For Israel did not first fight the battle with gladness, and afterwards Judas arm himself. It is therefore clear that in the Scriptures the order of events is not always kept; and so it cannot be proved from the fact that after the words and he had dominion over the beasts and birds of the air it is added, and he created from him a helper like himself, that Adam had dominion over things before the formation of Eve; although some grant this, saying nonetheless that this dominion was not to be reckoned proper, because he received it not for himself alone but in some way for others too. [Damascene seems to hold the same view] they say that Damascene did not hold this. [He made him a namer of the animals, as a prophetic ruler of his gifts.] They say it is said by anticipation; some, however, grant that he then had dominion, but it was not proper dominion; it was common, that is, to be shared, and in no way to be appropriated. [and it follows, he made from him a helper for him.] Some say this was done earlier, although here it is told by Damascene later.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: Nec obstat capitulū dilectissimis in cōtrariū allegatū. Per illud n. concludi nō pot, q primi parentes temporalium dominium non habuerunt, sed quod illud non habuerint diuisim: imo ex auctoritate philosophi, quam B. Clemens ineo{n}in eodem capitulo addu-cit, concludit euidenter ipsos habuisse dominium in commune. Ipse tamen non potest diuidi aer, neque splendor solis, ita nec reliqua, quae communiter data sunt ad habendum, diuidi debent. Ex quibus verbis clare patet, quod temporalia fuisse data communiter omnibus: et ideo facta fuerunt ab illo, qui dedit potestatem, videlicet Deus, et ei qui tapax fuit, sicut homo, sequitur dominium sui-bum fuisse. Nec Philosophus nihil comparationem aeris et splendoris solis respectu dominii, ut sicut non habebant dominium aeris et splendoris solis, sic nec habebant dominium temporalium rerum, sed respectu indiuisionis rerum illam comparationem induxit: sicut enim non potest diuidi aer nec splendor solis, ita nec reliqua, quae communiter data sunt hominibus ad habendum, diuidi debent, sed communia sunt habenda. De aere tamen beatus Augustinus, quod ego reddidero, possim reducere: illud tamen non poteris. Quae reddi potest. Nam ex ueribus alimenta nos capere meditari dicunt: quod resumendo possumus reficere, ut ad te ductum naribus consentatur.
units.tr: Nor does the chapter that the most beloved (opponent) cites to the contrary stand in the way. It cannot be concluded from that passage that the first parents had no dominion over temporal things, but only that they did not have it divided. Indeed, from the authority of the philosopher, which blessed Clement adduces in the same chapter, he plainly concludes that they had dominion in common. Air cannot be divided, nor can the light of the sun, and so the rest of the things given in common for use ought not to be divided either. From these words it is clear that temporal things were given in common to all, and therefore they were made over by him who gave the power, namely God, to him who is capable, as man is, and it follows that dominion was theirs. Nor did the Philosopher make that comparison of air and sunlight with respect to dominion, so that just as they had no dominion over air and sunlight, neither had they dominion over temporal things. He introduced the comparison with respect to the indivisibility of things: just as air cannot be divided, nor sunlight, so the rest of the things given in common to men for use cannot be divided, but must be held in common. Yet concerning the air, blessed Augustine's words, which I shall render, may be brought back; but you will not be able to do that, which can be given back. For they say that we take nourishment from the air, which, when taken in again, we can restore, so that it agrees with the nostrils as it is led to you.

units.la: In ista parte iste impugnatus respondet ad capitulum Clementis per quod barbare volebat, quod primus homo et posteriores, si in statu innocentiae perstitissent, sum rerum usu consumptibilium absque proprietate et dominio carendum. Dicens per illud capitulum potest concludi, quod primi parentes habuerunt dominium in communi: quia auctoritas philosophi, quam beatus Clemens inducit, ostendit, quod temporalia data sunt hominibus ad habendum: et per consequens ad eorum spectant dominium. Secundo, Nec philosophus, soluit quandam obiectionem. Potest aliquis dicere, quod philosophus comparat aerem et splendorem solis ad temporalia. Ergo sicut aer et splendor solis non ... ad dominium mortalium, ita etiam non deberent habere dominium temporalium. Ad quod respondet dicens, quod philosophus non inducit illam comparationem respectu dominii, sed respectu indiuisionis.
units.tr: In this part, the opponent answers the chapter of Clement, by which he crudely meant that the first man and his descendants, had they remained in the state of innocence, would have to do without property and dominion in the use of consumable things. He says that from that chapter it can be concluded that the first parents had dominion in common, because the authority of the philosopher which blessed Clement introduces shows that temporal things were given to men to be had, and consequently belong to them as dominion. Second, the Philosopher does not answer a certain objection. Someone may say that the philosopher compares air and sunlight to temporal things. Therefore, just as air and sunlight do not ... belong to the dominion of mortals, so neither ought men to have dominion over temporal things. To this he replies that the philosopher does not introduce that comparison with respect to dominion, but with respect to indivisibility.

units.la: Tertio ibi: de aere tamen, inducit auctoritatem Augustini, per quam probare videtur, quod aeris quantum ad aliquam partem habet unusquisque dominium proprium. Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod hic, sicut in aliis, cauillose procedit. Non enim appellans negat in omni sensu primos parentes in statu innocentiae dominium temporalium habuisse, sed negat ipsos habuisse dominium quod vocatur proprietas, quo valet quis dicere. Hoc ita est meum, quod non est tuum: et illud ita est tuum, quod non est meum. Et ita loquitur de mente beati Clementis, qui ait: Communis enim usus omnium, quae sunt in hoc mundo, omnibus hominibus esse debuit: sed per iniquitatem alius dixit hoc esse suum: et alius illud. Ex his verbis euidenter datur intelligi, quod ante iniquitatem non debuit unus dicere, hoc esse suum, et alius illud: sed haec verba meum et suum, quamuis semper spectent ad dominium (quod vocatur proprietas) ergo ante iniquitatem non habuit aliquis dominium, quod vocatur proprietas. Et ista est intentio appellantis: qui non intendebat plus probare, nisi quod usus facti in rebus usu consumptibilibus potest ab omni dominio, quod vocatur proprietas, separari.
units.tr: Third, there, concerning the air, he introduces the authority of Augustine, by which he seems to prove that each person has his own dominion over some part of the air. But those opponents say that here, as elsewhere, he proceeds sophistically. For the one who appeals does not deny in every sense that the first parents in the state of innocence had dominion over temporal things, but denies that they had that dominion which is called property, by which one can say: "This is mine, which is not yours, and that is yours, which is not mine." And so he speaks in the mind of blessed Clement, who says: "For common use of all the things that are in this world ought to have belonged to all men, but through iniquity one man said that this was his, and another that was his." From these words it is clearly intimated that before iniquity one man ought not to have said that this was his and another that was his. But these words "mine" and "yours," although they always pertain to dominion (which is called property), therefore before iniquity no one had dominion which is called property. And this is the intention of the one who appeals, who did not mean to prove more than that the use of a fact in consumable things can be separated from all dominion which is called property.

units.la: Dominium autem, quod habuerunt primi parentes in statu innocentiae, est totaliter alterius rationis ab isto dominio. Nec illud dominium videtur fuisse proprium primis parentibus, sicut videtur fuisse commune illis et angelis. Si enim iuxta sententiam Salthoris diabolus princeps huius mundi vocatur propter potestatem, quam usurpatiue exercet in hoc mundo: videtur quod multo magis angeli principes et domini istorum temporalium poterunt appellari propter potestatem quam super ea obtinere noscuntur. Nec videtur, quod minorem potestatem habeant super ea, quam habuerunt primi parentes in statu innocentiae, et quam eorum posteri habuissent, si in statu innocentiae perstitissent. Licet angeli non ita eis indigeant, sicut ipsi indigunt, sed aliquo indigere, dominium non requirit: quia Deus, qui nullo modo indiget, perfectissimus vniuersorum est Dominus. Constat igitur, quod appellans loquitur de dominio, quod vocatur proprietas: et de illo verum est secundum istos, quod usus facti in rebus usu consumptibilibus, potest ab omni dominio separari. De aliis dicetur super literam.
units.tr: But the dominion which the first parents had in the state of innocence is entirely of a different kind from that dominion. Nor does that dominion seem to have been proper to the first parents, just as it seems to have been common to them and to the angels. For if, according to the opinion of Salthorus, the devil is called "prince of this world" because of the power which he exercises usurpingly in this world, it seems much more likely that the angels may be called princes and lords of these temporal things because of the power which they are known to hold over them. Nor does it seem that they have less power over them than the first parents had in the state of innocence, and than their descendants would have had had they remained in the state of innocence. Although the angels do not need them in the same way that men need them, yet dominion does not require needing something, because God, who needs nothing whatever, is the most perfect Lord of all things. It is plain, then, that the one who appeals speaks of the dominion which is called property, and concerning that it is true, according to these men, that the use of a fact in consumable things can be separated from all dominion. Of other matters it will be said on the letter (of the text).

units.la: [Per illud enim concludi non potest, quod primi parentes temporalium dominium non habuerunt.] Illud non habet veritatem, ut dicunt de dominio, quod vocatur proprietas, de quo locutus est appellans. De alio autem dominio, quale habent angeli, et habuerunt commune cum hominibus, potest concedi, sed tunc non est ad propositum. Sed quod illud non habuerunt diuisim hoc concedunt quia necessarium est. [Imo ex auctoritate philosophi, quam beatus Clemens eodem capitulo addueit, concluditur euidenter ipsos habuisse dominium in communi.] Nullo modo concluditur ibidem de dominio, quod habuerunt primi parentes in statu innocentiae: sed concluditur de dominio, quod est potestas diuidendi, et appropriandi res temporales, quod habuerunt primi parentes post peccatum ante diuisionem rerum, licet philosophus hoc nescierit. Sed de tali dominio non est locutus appellans. [Sicut non potest diuidi aer, nec splendor solis, ita nec reliqua, quae communiter data sunt ad habendum, diuidi debent.] Ex his verbis clare patet (ut dicunt isti) quod philosophus non loquitur de alio dominio, quam de illo dominio, quod est potestas diuidendi et appropriandi. Tale autem dominium non fuit in statu innocentiae nec fuisset, si stetisset, quod totum genus humanum non habuisset in illo statu potestate diuidendi et appropriandi res temporales. Et ita non loquitur de dominio, quod fuit in statu innocentiae. [Fuisse data communiter omnibus ad ha[illegible, ~6 letters]. Verum est: & ideo post peccatum habuerunt potestatem vtendi omnibus, sicut coms muribus, absque omni appropriatione. [Sed licet semel dare illi qui potest, vt pote Deo, & in quo capax sit, sicut homo: sequitur quod eorum dominium factum sit [illegible, ~10 letters] conclusio vera sensu, tamen male arguit: quia aliquando accipiendo verbum [illegible, ~4 letters] significatione, non sequitur: hoc datum ab eo, qui dare potest, scilicet qui capax dominus efficitur. Saepe enim aliquis dat alteri hospitium, hoc est concedit hospitium alterius morandum ad tempus, & tamen ille non efficitur dominus licet sit capax domini. Dicunt igitur, quod iste vocabulis vtens aequivocis hic & saepe alibi in suis argumentationibus fallaciam aequivocationis committit, non est ad eam aliter respondendum, quia ad sophismata per aequivocationem peccantia est recta responsio vocum multiplicitatem [illegible, ~5 letters]. [Sicut non habebant dominium aeris & splendoris solis, sicut nec habuerunt dominium temporalium.] Dominium aeris, splendoris solis primi parentes minime habuerunt; habebant tamen dominium aliarum rerum, licet non dominium quod vocatur proprietas. [sed respectu admissionis tantum illam comparationem indicit.] Istud nonnulli concedunt, quia sicut non poterant dividere aerem & appropriare sibi, aere in suo loco manente, nec splendorem solis: ita non debebant, si omnes [illegible, ~3 letters] boni, dividere temporalia & appropriare sibi. Post peccatum tamen poterant dividere temporalia & appropriare sibi; & ita aliquod dominium habuerunt super temporalia, quale non habuerunt super aerem & splendorem solis. [Si aliquid aeris quod ego reddidero, &c.] Augustinus intendit, quod aer manens in loco suo extra corpus humanum appropriari non potest; aer tamen in alimentum receptus quodammodo appropriatur, sicut & cetera alimenta.
units.tr: [For it cannot be concluded from that that the first parents had no temporal dominion.] This is not true, as they say, of the dominion which is called property, about which the one who appeals spoke. But concerning another dominion, such as angels have, and which they shared in common with men, it can be conceded, but then it is not to the point. But that they did not have it divided, they concede, because it was necessary. [Indeed, from the authority of the philosopher, which blessed Clement adduces in the same chapter, it is clearly concluded that they had dominion in common.] It is in no way concluded there about the dominion which the first parents had in the state of innocence, but it is concluded about the dominion which is the power of dividing and appropriating temporal things, which the first parents had after sin and before the division of things, although the philosopher did not know this. But the one who appeals did not speak of such dominion. [Just as air cannot be divided, nor can the light of the sun, so neither should the rest of the things which are given in common to be had be divided.] From these words it is clearly evident (as they say) that the philosopher does not speak of any other dominion than that which is the power of dividing and appropriating. But such dominion did not exist in the state of innocence, nor would it have existed had they stood fast, for the whole human race would not have had in that state the power of dividing and appropriating temporal things. And so he does not speak of the dominion which existed in the state of innocence. [Given in common to all for having ...] This is true; and therefore after sin they had the power of using all things, as if in common, without any appropriation. [But although it is once given by him who can give, as God, and to him in whom it is capable, as man, it follows that their dominion has been made ...] The conclusion is true in sense, yet the argument is badly made, because when a word is taken in a certain meaning, it does not follow that what is given by him who can give, namely who makes the one capable into lord. For often someone gives another lodging, that is, grants lodging to another to stay for a time, and yet that person does not become lord, though he is capable of being lord. They say, therefore, that this man, using equivocal terms here and often elsewhere in his arguments, commits the fallacy of equivocation. It is not to be answered otherwise, because the right answer to sophisms committing fallacy through equivocation is to point out the multiplicity of the terms. [Just as they had no dominion over air and sunlight, so neither did they have dominion over temporal things.] The first parents by no means had dominion over air and sunlight; yet they had dominion over other things, although not the dominion which is called property. [but he introduced that comparison only with respect to admission.] Some concede this, because just as they could not divide the air and appropriate it to themselves, the air remaining in its place, nor the light of the sun, so neither ought they, if all were good, to divide temporal things and appropriate them to themselves. After sin, however, they could divide temporal things and appropriate them to themselves; and so they had some dominion over temporal things, of a kind they did not have over air and sunlight. [If some of the air which I shall return, etc.] Augustine means that air remaining in its place outside the human body cannot be appropriated; yet air taken in as nourishment is in some way appropriated, as are other foods.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX.

units.la: Adhuc ad ostendendum, quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus vsus facti possit a dominio separari, adducit quod legitur Luca. 19. vbi dominus seruo, cui pecuniam ad negociandum tradiderat, & eam tenerat otiosam, dixit: Serue nequam; quare non dedisti pecuniam meam & ego veniens eum vsuris exegissem? Ex qua authoritate patet, vt dicit, quod in pecunia predicta seruus vsum habebat actualiter, & dominus proprietatem eiusdem, quare cum pecuniam ipsa de rebus vsu consumptibilibus lex praeallegata testetur expresse secundum eum, predicta doctrina sancto evangelio contradicit.
units.tr: Further, to show that in things consumable by use the use of a thing can be separated from ownership, he cites what is read in Luke 19, where the lord said to the servant to whom he had entrusted money to trade, and who had kept it idle: "Wicked servant, why did you not give my money, so that when I came I might have exacted it with interest?" From this authority, he says, it is plain that the servant actually had the use of the money, while the lord held its ownership; therefore, since the aforementioned law expressly says that money is among things consumable by use, the doctrine mentioned contradicts the holy Gospel.

units.la: Hic iste impugnatus recitat obiectionem appellantis; quae est quod secundum euangelium seruus potest vti pecunia domini sui absque dominio & proprietate. Cuius responsionem capitulo sequenti videbimus: nunc literam declaremus.
units.tr: Here the man under attack recites the objection of his opponent, which is that according to the Gospel a servant may use his lord's money without dominion and ownership. We shall see his answer to this in the following chapter; for now let us explain the text.

units.la: [Quare non dedisti.] Ex hoc patet quod aliquis potest dare illud, cuius non habet dominium & proprietatem: quia seruus non habuit dominium & proprietatem pecuniae, quam tamen dare debuit; verbum igitur dandi aequivoce in diversis locis accipitur. [Pecuniam meam.] Ex hoc notant isti quod quando actualiter seruus debebat vti pecunia, illa pecunia erat domini. & ita vsus pecuniae fuisset a proprietate & dominio separatus. [Predicta doctrina sancto evangelio contradicit] quia secundum euangelium seruus potest vti pecunia domini sui: quamuis pecuniae eiusdem non habeat dominium & proprietatem; quod negat doctrina praedicta.
units.tr: ["Why did you not give."] From this it is clear that someone can give what he has no dominion and ownership over, since the servant did not have dominion and ownership of the money, which nevertheless he ought to have given; the verb "to give" is therefore taken equivocally in different places. ["My money."] From this they note that when the servant was actually obliged to use the money, that money belonged to the lord, and so the use of the money would have been separated from ownership and dominion. ["The aforementioned doctrine contradicts the holy Gospel"], because according to the Gospel a servant may use his lord's money, although he has no dominion and ownership of that money; which the aforementioned doctrine denies.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: Adhoc dicendum, quod sicut probatum est supra, impossibile est in rebus vsu consumptibilibus quenquam vsum habere vel simplicem vsum facti. Nec obstat scriptura praedicta. Vsus enim pecuniae imo potius abusus non est simpliciter alicui tradere; sed taliter tradere, quod consumpta quoad dominium censeatur. Vnde licet seruus actualiter pecuniam mutuando tradat, per translationem solam sine translatione domini nequaquam vsus, sed abusus potius fuisse pecuniae potest dici. Sed per translationem domini habetur pro consumpta pecunia: quam quidem translationem, non seruus sed dominus, cuius nomine fiebat, mutuum fecit. Vnde cum seruus nomine domini mutuasset, ipse dominus videtur vsus, imo abusus potius fuisse pecuniae, & non seruus. Praeterea seruus, qui iussu domini per unitatem mutuat, non debet dici habere vsum seu abusum simplicem facti, cui ius habuerit per concessionem huiusmodi mutuandi.
units.tr: To this it must be said that, as has been proved above, it is impossible for anyone to have the use, or simple use of fact, in things consumable by use. Nor does the aforementioned Scripture stand in the way. For to hand over money is not simply a use of it; or rather it is an abuse, unless it is handed over in such a way that it is counted as consumed as regards ownership. Hence, although the servant actually hands the money over by lending it, it can be said that by the transfer alone, without transfer of ownership, there was by no means a use of the money, but rather an abuse. But by the transfer of ownership the money is held as consumed; and this transfer was made not by the servant but by the lord, in whose name it was done. Hence, since the servant lent in the name of the lord, the lord himself seems to have used, or rather abused, the money, and not the servant. Moreover, a servant who by his lord's command lends money in this way ought not to be said to have simple use or abuse of fact, since he has the right to lend by such a concession.

units.la: In ista parte iste impugnatus ad praemissam obiectionem respondet; & videt duplicitet. Primo seruus non vtitur nec abutitur pecunia domini sui mutuando: quia non facit translationem domini, sed dominus vtitur seu abutitur potius pecunia, cuius nomine fit translatio domini. Secundo respondet, seruus in tali pecunia non habet simplicem vsum facti, cum habeat ius mutuandi.
units.tr: On this point the man under attack answers the aforementioned objection, and he sees it in two ways. First, the servant does not use or abuse his lord's money by lending it, because he does not effect a transfer of the lord's ownership; rather the lord uses, or rather abuses, the money, in whose name the transfer of ownership is made. Second, he answers that the servant in such money does not have simple use of fact, since he has the right to lend.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod hoc est isti impugnato omnino concludum; & ideo dicunt, quod eiusdem quaestionem quam friuolam, quod improbatione non indiget. Contra ipsum tamen propter simpliciores (ut asserunt) volunt arguere ostendendo, quod seruus ille, si dedisset mutuum pecunia vsus fuisset, licet nomine domini sui. Nam qui tradit pecuniam, & transfert dominium eiusdem pecuniae nomine alterius, vtitur pecunia nomine alterius. Sed seruus, de quo fit mentio in euangelio supradicto, si fecisset iuxta voluntatem domini sui, sicut alii servi eius, tradidisset pecuniam domini suae ad mensam; & eiusdem nomine transtulisset dominium, sicut alii servi transtulerunt dominium pecuniae traditae sibi. Ergo vere pecunia vsus fuisset, licet nomine domini sui. Ex quo sequitur, quod habuisset vsum abusum dominio, & proprietate speciali, & in communi separatum. Amplius, non minus vtitur pecunia, qui nomine alterius mutuat pecuniam, quam qui nomine alterius emit rem aliquam de pecunia ipsius. Sed qui emit alterius nomine vere vtitur pecunia; quia omnis emptio sit quidam contractus humanus factus per pecuniam; qui vere emit, vere vtitur, vel abutitur pecunia. Sed aliquis vere emit rem vel emere potest de pecunia alterius: quod non solum experientia quotidie docet, sed etiam scriptura divina testatur. 3. enim Regum cap. 10. scribitur: Educebantur equi Salomonis monie de Ægypto & de Choa. Negociatores enim regis emebant de Choa & statuto precio per dutebant. Ex ijs verbis colligitur, quod negociatores Salomonis vere emebant equos de pecunia Salomonis. ergo vere vtebantur, vel abutebantur secundum modum istius loquendi ineptum (vt dicunt) pecunia. Ergo consimiliter, qui vere mutuat pecuniam nomine alterius, vere vtitur vel abutitur ea: & ita potest quis habere vsum vel abusum ab omni proprietate & dominio separatum. Rursum, seruus secundum istum potest nomine domini mutuare pecuniam. Ponatur ergo quod mutuet pecuniā nomine domini, tunc quæritur aut tantum modo tradit pecuniam nomine domini, aut cum traditione pecuniæ transfert dominium. Primum non potest dici, quia nomine domini potest seruus tradere pecuniam domini sui alicui, quamuis non mutuet nam nomine domini: sicut potest eam penes aliquem deponere nomine domini sui non mutuando eam eidem. Si detur secundum, habetur propositum: quia qui tradit pecuniam & transfert dominium in eundem nomine alterius vtitur vel abutitur ipsa nomine alterius: sicut qui nomine proprio tradit alicui pecuniam & transfert dominium in eundem, & non donat eam nomine proprio, vtitur ea. Sic ergo patet quod seruus potest vti vel abuti pecunia domini sui, qui autem vtitur nomine alterius, vtitur. ergo seruus potest vti pecunia domini sui. Item non minus vtitur pecunia, qui mutuat pecuniam: quam qui expendit pecuniam. sed aliquis expendendo pecuniam domini sui vere vtitur ipsa licet domini sui sit. Confirmantur rationes prædictæ: quia non minus exercet aliquem actum, qui exercet ipsum nomine alterius, quam qui exercet aliquem actum de mandato alterius. sed qui exercet aliquem actum de mandato alterius, vere exercet actum illum: sicut qui manducat de mandato alterius vere manducat: & qui occidit alium de mandato alterius, vere occidit. ergo qui exercet actum aliquem nomine alterius, vere exercet actum illum. sed sicut actus comedendi cibum est actus vtendi cibo vel abutendi cibo: & actus bibendi vinum est actus vtendi vel abutendi vino: ita actus mutuandi pecuniam est actus vtendi pecunia: & actus emendi rem de pecunia est actus vtendi pecunia: & actus expendendi pecuniam est actus vtendi pecunia. Sicut igitur qui manducat & bibit de mandato alterius, vere & realiter vtitur vel abutitur cibo & potu: ita qui mutuat pecuniam, & emit rem de pecunia, & expedit pecuniam nomine alterius, vere & realiter vtitur vel abutitur pecunia. sed experientia quotidiana & scriptura diuina testantur, quod aliquis potest mutuare pecuniam, emere de pecunia, & expendere pecuniam alienam nomine alterius, ergo per experientiam & scripturam diuinam constat, quod vere & realiter contingit vti vel abuti pecunia aliena. & ita vsus facti potest in pecunia à proprietate & dominio separari. Notant igitur isti impugnatores, quod licet aliquæ obiectiones appellantis directe & primo excludant tantum modo, quod vsus facti in rebus vsu consumptibilibus potest separari à proprietate & dominio specialiter: & per consequentiam concludant, quod potest separari ab omni dominio & proprietate communi & speciali. Ista tamen ratio (vt dicunt) demonstratiue & directe concludit, quod vsus facti quantum ad pecuniam potest ab omni dominio seu proprietate communi & speciali separari: quia seruus in pecunia domini quam mutuat vel expendit, nullum habet dominium seu proprietatem neque specialem neque communem. Cum igitur secundum venerabilem Anselm. li. r. Cur Deus homo: Sue vno siue pluribus argumentis veritas inexpugnabilis monstretur æqualiter ab omni dubitatione defenditur: & quia veritas prædicta, vt dicunt, quod in rebus vsu consumptibilib. vsus facti potest ab omni proprietate seu dominio separari, hoc argumento inexpugnabiliter demonstratur, ipsa est absque omni dubitatione tenenda, etiam si alia argumenta ipsam minime demonstrarent. Secundo isti impugnatores dicunt secunda ratione istius impugnationis esse ad propositum. Quod de simplici vsu facti, & an seruus habeat ius mutuandi pecuniam, in obiectione præmissa nulla fit mentio. & ideo ad præsens de illa ratione eius nullatenus differetur: quia inferius conuenientiorem locum habebit. Nunc paucis textum prosequamur. [Impossibile est in rebus vsu consumptibilibus quenquam vsum habere.] Dicunt isti, quod hic replicat errorē sæpius recitatum, de quo post tractabitur. [vel simplicem vsum facti] Dicunt quod hoc erroneum: & tamē de hoc in obiectione præfata nulla fit mentio [vsus enim pecunia, imo potius abusus] Dicunt quod magis proprie dicitur vsus pecuniæ, quam abusus pecuniæ, nisi quando quis male vtitur pecunia: sicut magis proprie dicitur vsus cibi & potus, quam abusus cibi & potus, nisi quis male vtatur cibo & potu: quia scriptura diuina, philosophia & medicina, cum de cibo & potu fit mentio, nunquam vtuntur verbo abutendi, nisi in mala significatione. sc. pro male vti, sed semper vtuntur vel verbo vtendi. [Sed taliter tradere, quod consumpta quoad dominium censeatur] hoc potest facere seruus, licet dominus suus dormiat, & nullum actum tunc neque interiorem neque exteriorem circa eum exerceat: imo etiam si licet actum vtendi, qui est mutuare pecuniam, tunc haberet dummodo hoc seruo nequaquam constiterit: & ideo dominus tunc non dicitur vti pecunia vel abuti, nisi quia præcepit aliquando vti pecunia: & ita cum secundum istum vsus pecuniæ vel abusus sit eam tradere taliter, quod consumpta quoad dominium censeatur: & hoc facit realiter seruus, licet de mandato domini; sequitur quod seruus vere & realiter vtitur vel abutitur pecunia. & ideo dicunt isti, quod iste hic sibi ipsi contradicit aperte. [Per translationem domini, habetur pro consumpta pecunia] hoc concedunt isti [quidem translationem non seruus, sed dominus, cuius nomine fiebat mutuum, facit.] Hanc dicunt esse falsam: quia seruus facit illam translationem, licet de mandato domini. & ideo quamuis concedi debeat sub aliquo sensu: sed dominus facit illam translationem: quia qui per alium facit, per seipsum facere videtur: sicut dicimur posse, quod per amicos possumus: non tamen debet negari, quod seruus uas facit: quia uterq; quodammodo illam translationem facit, sed unus de mandato alterius. & ideo vere facit, quia qui facit aliquid de mandato alterius, vere facit: nec propter hoc minus facit q de mandato alterius facit, licet propter hoc aliquando minus ascribatur vel imputetur eidem. [Vi- de cum servus nomine domini mutuasset] ex hoc patet, quod secundum illum servus potest mutuare pe- cuniā nomine domini. sed mutuare pecuniam est uti pecunia, sicut equitare equum est uti equo: & inhabitare domum est uti domo. ergo servus potest uti pecunia domini sui licet nomine domini sui [ipse dominus videtur uti.] hoc tamen aliquo sensu concedi potest: sicut praecipiens aliquem occidi, aliquomodo dicitur ipsum occidere. Alius tamen qui de praecepto occidit, vere occidit. [& non servus] dicunt quod ista negativa ex affirmativa praemissa non sequitur, sicut pater per exemplum de occidente aliquem de mandato alterius. [servus qui iussu domini mutuat non debet dici habere usum vel abusum simplicem facti.] Hanc negant: & quod sit neganda in simili postea conabuntur ostendere. [cum sus habuit per concessionem huiusmodi mutuandi] dicunt quod iussio vel concessio talis ius nullum dat.
units.tr: But these opponents say that this is entirely settled against him, and so they call the question trivial and in no need of refutation. Nevertheless, for the sake of simpler readers (as they put it), they want to argue against him by showing that if that servant had lent the money, he would have used it, though in his master's name. For whoever hands over money and transfers its ownership in another's name uses the money in that other's name. But the servant mentioned in the gospel above, if he had acted according to his master's will, as the other servants did, would have handed the money over to the table and transferred ownership in his master's name, just as the other servants transferred ownership of the money entrusted to them. Therefore he would truly have used the money, though in his master's name. From this it follows that he would have had the use of the money, abused it, and held it with a special and separate ownership. Further, whoever lends money in another's name uses the money no less than whoever buys something with another's money in that person's name. But whoever buys in another's name truly uses the money, since every purchase is a human contract made with money, and whoever truly buys truly uses or abuses the money. Yet someone truly buys, or can buy, a thing with another's money; experience teaches this every day, and divine Scripture attests it too. For in Educebantur equi Salomonis (3 Reg. 10.) it is written: "The horses of Solomon were brought out of Egypt and from Choa. For the king's merchants bought them from Choa and brought them at a fixed price." From these words it is gathered that Solomon's merchants truly bought horses with Solomon's money; therefore they truly used, or (to use the inept phrase of these men) abused, the money. Likewise, then, whoever truly lends money in another's name truly uses or abuses it; and so a person can have the use or abuse of something entirely separated from all property and ownership. Again, according to this man, the servant can lend money in his master's name. Suppose then that he lends money in his master's name; the question is whether he merely hands the money over in his master's name, or whether by handing it over he transfers ownership. The first cannot be said, since a servant can hand his master's money to someone in his master's name without lending it, just as he can deposit it with someone in his master's name without lending it to that person. If the second is granted, our proposition follows: for whoever hands money over and transfers ownership of it to the same person in another's name uses or abuses it in that other's name, just as whoever hands money to someone in his own name and transfers ownership to that person, without giving it in his own name, uses it. Thus it is plain that a servant can use or abuse his master's money, and whoever uses in another's name does use. Therefore a servant can use his master's money. Likewise, whoever lends money uses it no less than whoever spends it; but someone who spends his master's money truly uses it, even though it belongs to his master. The foregoing arguments are confirmed as follows: whoever performs some act in another's name performs it no less than whoever performs an act by another's command. But whoever performs an act by another's command truly performs that act; as whoever eats by another's command truly eats, and whoever kills another by command truly kills. Therefore whoever performs some act in another's name truly performs that act. Now as the act of eating food is an act of using or abusing food, and the act of drinking wine is an act of using or abusing wine, so the act of lending money is an act of using money, the act of buying a thing with money is an act of using money, and the act of spending money is an act of using money. Just as whoever eats and drinks by another's command truly and really uses or abuses food and drink, so whoever lends money, buys a thing with money, or spends money in another's name truly and really uses or abuses the money. But daily experience and divine Scripture attest that someone can lend money, buy with money, and spend another's money in another's name; therefore experience and divine Scripture establish that it truly and really happens that another's money is used or abused. And so the use of fact can be separated from property and ownership in money. These opponents therefore observe that although some of the appellant's objections, taken directly and in the first place, exclude only that the use of fact in consumable things can be separated specially from property and ownership, and by inference conclude that it can be separated from all ownership and property, both common and special; yet this argument (as they say) demonstrates directly and conclusively that the use of fact, as regards money, can be separated from all ownership or property, both common and special, because the servant has no ownership or property in his master's money that he lends or spends, neither special nor common. Since therefore, according to the venerable Anselm (Cur Deus homo, bk. 1), a truth that cannot be overthrown is shown equally free from all doubt whether by one argument or by several, and since this truth, as they say, that in consumable things the use of fact can be separated from all property or ownership, is inexpugnably demonstrated by this argument, it must be held without any doubt, even if other arguments did not demonstrate it. Secondly, these opponents say that the second argument of this refutation is beside the point. For the objection above makes no mention of simple use of fact, or of whether the servant has the right to lend money; and so for the present nothing will be said about that argument, since it will have a more suitable place further on. Now let us briefly follow the text. [It is impossible for anyone to have the use of consumable things.] These men say that here he repeats the error often recited, which will be treated later. [or simple use of fact] They say this is an error; yet no mention of it is made in the aforesaid objection. [for the use of money, or rather abuse] They say that "use of money" is more properly said than "abuse of money," unless someone uses money badly; just as "use of food and drink" is more properly said than "abuse of food and drink," unless someone uses food and drink badly. For divine Scripture, philosophy and medicine, when speaking of food and drink, never use the word "abuse" except in a bad sense, that is, to use badly; they always use the word "use." [But to hand over in such a way that, as far as ownership goes, it is considered consumed] the servant can do this even though his master is asleep and at that time performs no act, either inward or outward, concerning it; indeed, even if the master had the right to perform the act of using, which is lending money, he would not have it, provided this were never agreed with the servant. Therefore the master is then not said to use or abuse the money, except in that he once ordered its use. And so, since on this view the use or abuse of money is to hand it over in such a way that, as far as ownership goes, it is considered consumed, and the servant does this really, though by his master's command, it follows that the servant truly and really uses or abuses the money. And so these men say that this author here plainly contradicts himself. [By the transfer of the master, it is held that the money is consumed] these men grant this, [indeed the transfer is made not by the servant but by the master, in whose name the loan was made.] They say this is false, for the servant makes that transfer, though by his master's command. So although it must be conceded in some sense that the master makes the transfer, since whoever acts through another seems to act himself (as we are said to be able to do things through friends), yet it must not be denied that the servant does make it, since each in a way makes that transfer, one at the other's command. He truly makes it, since whoever does something by another's command truly does it; nor does he do it any less because he does it by another's command, though for that reason the act may sometimes be ascribed or imputed to him less. [See, when the servant had lent in his master's name] from this it is plain that, according to him, the servant can lend money in his master's name. But to lend money is to use money, just as to ride a horse is to use a horse, and to live in a house is to use a house. Therefore the servant can use his master's money, though in his master's name [the master himself seems to use it.] This may be granted in some sense, just as one who orders someone killed is in a way said to kill him; yet the one who kills by command truly kills. [and not the servant] they say that this negative does not follow from the affirmative premise, just as the father, by the example of killing someone by another's command, shows. [A servant who lends by his master's order ought not to be said to have the simple use or abuse of fact.] This they deny, and they will later try to show that it must be denied in a similar case. [since the master had, by the grant of such lending] they say that an order or such a grant gives no right.

units.la: CAP. XXXI.
units.tr: CAP. XXXI.

units.la: Rursus dicit, quod predicta assertio determinationi sanctae Romanae ecclesiae obviat & repugnat: quia in decretali, quae incipit (Exiit qui seminat,) per universalem ecclesiam (ut dicit) approbata, & in concilio Viennensi confirmata, diffinitur quod Fratres Minores habent usum facti omnium rerum, quibus utuntur, absque omni dominio & proprietate. de quo usu sic dixit: qui usus non iuris sed facti tantummodo nomen habens, quod facti est tantum in utendo praebet utentibus nihil iuris. Manifestum est autem (ut dicit) quod Fratres Minores habent usum facti rerum usu consumptibilium. ergo in rebus usu consumptibilibus potest usus facti a proprietate & dominio separari.
units.tr: Again he says that the aforesaid assertion opposes and contradicts the determination of the holy Roman Church. In the decretal that begins "Exiit qui seminat," which is (as he says) approved by the universal Church and confirmed in the Council of Vienne, it is defined that the Friars Minor have the use of fact of all the things they use, without any dominion or property. Of this use he said: "This use, which has the name of use not of right but of fact only, which is only of fact in using, gives the users no right at all." It is clear (as he says) that the Friars Minor have the use of fact of things consumed by use. Therefore, in things consumed by use, the use of fact can be separated from property and dominion.

units.la: In parte ista impugnatus respondet ad aliam obiectionem appellantis contra primam assertionem de constitutione Ad conditorem, acceptam. Et primo obiectionem ponit. Secundo responder in parte immediate sequenti. Est autem obiectio talis secundum Nicolaum tertium in decretali Exiit: Fratres Minores habent usum facti omnium rerum, quib. utuntur, & tamen non habet dominium seu proprietatem. ergo in rebus usu consumptibilibus potest usus facti a proprietate & dominio separari. Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod iste impugnatus hic omittit aliqua exempla, per quae assertionem praedictam appellans nititur probare. unde immediate post obiectionem praemissam subiungit appellans haec verba: Allegationes autem ad auctoritates pro praedictis rationibus in appellatione prolixae perfectissime continentur. Ista eadem conclusio, scilicet quod usus facti in rebus usu consumptibilibus potest a proprietate & dominio separari, declaratur in Appellatione ea- dem per iura canonica & civilia copiose, & etiam per multa exempla, scilicet de servo, filiofamilias, religiosis, nunciis dominorum, & habente vestem accommodatam, qui habent usum rerum usu consumptibilium sine proprietate & dominio earundem. Haec verba appellantis, quae iste nec recitat nec ad ipsa respondet: quia (ut dicunt) ad exempla de servo, filiofamilias & nunciis dominorum & habente vestem accommodatam, nullam responsionem poterit invenire. servus enim cum sit possessio domini sui, proprietatem vestis, qua utitur, nequaquam habet. filiusfamilias et, cum sit in potestate patris, vestis, qua induitur, non habet proprietatem. Idem ius est de multis, quib. utuntur nuncii dominorum. qui etiam vestitur veste accommodata, non habet proprietatem eiusdem: & ita omnes praedicti habent usum facti rerum consumptibilium usu proprietate speciali & communi separatum. [Qui usus non iuris] sc. quo valeat pro re vel usu rei in iudicio litigare. [sed facti tantummodo nomen habens] hoc est, vocatur usus facti, & non usus iuris [Nihil iuris] quo valeat in iudicio litigare.
units.tr: In this part, the one attacked answers another objection of the appellant against the first assertion, which was taken from the constitution "Ad conditorem." First he sets out the objection; second he replies in the part immediately following. The objection, according to Nicholas III in the decretal "Exiit," runs as follows: the Friars Minor have the use of fact of all the things they use, and yet they have no dominion or property. Therefore, in things consumed by use, the use of fact can be separated from property and dominion. His opponents say that this author omits some examples by which the appellant tries to prove the aforesaid assertion.
