So, immediately after the objection given above, the appellant adds these words: "The allegations supporting the aforesaid reasons are fully set out at length in the appeal. This same conclusion, namely that the use of fact in things consumed by use can be separated from property and dominion, is declared at length in the same appeal, by canon and civil law, and also by many examples: concerning the slave, the son under power, religious, the messengers of lords, and the man who has borrowed clothing, who have the use of things consumed by use without property and dominion over them." His opponents say that this author neither quotes these words of the appellant nor replies to them, because (as they say) he cannot find any answer to the examples of the slave, the son under power, the messengers of lords and the man with borrowed clothing. For a slave, since he is the possession of his lord, certainly has no property in the clothing he uses. A son under his father's power likewise has no property in the clothing he wears. The same law applies to many things used by the messengers of lords. The man who is dressed in borrowed clothing also has no property in it. And so all the aforesaid persons have the use of fact of things consumed by use, separated from special and common property. ["Qui usus non iuris"], that is, by which one can go to law in court over a thing or the use of a thing. ["sed facti tantummodo nomen habens"], that is, it is called the use of fact and not the use of right. ["Nihil iuris"], by which one can go to law in court.

units.la: CAP. XXXII.
units.tr: CAP. XXXII.

units.la: Ad hoc dicendum, quod, sicut dicit dicta constitutio Ad conditorem canonum verba praedicta intellexit, conditor illius canonis Exiit, de reb. quae non consumuntur usu, quod per praecedentia & sequentia probatur satis clare. Ante enim praeposuerat, quae sequuntur: Cum in rebus temporalibus sit considerare praecipue proprietatem, possessionem, usum fructum, & simplicem facti usum, &c. Et post sequitur: Condecens fuit ei professioni, quae profiteri denotat Christum pauperem in tanta paupertate sectari necessario usu facti fore contentam. Cum autem praedicta, sc. proprietas, usufructus, ius utendi, & usus facti sumptus proprie nequeat in rebus usu consumptibilibus reperiri: sed proprietas tantum ut patet ex diffinitionibus usufructus & usus: apparet quod de rebus usu consumptibilibus in quibus praemissa nequeunt reperiri, non intellexit conditor canonis verba illa. Hoc etiam apparet per ea, quae in eadem constitutione postea subsequuntur. Sequitur enim, quod praedictis (sc. quod Fratres sint usu facti contenti) non obviat quod civilis providentia in humanis rebus constituit: videlicet non posse usum vel usufructum a dominio perpetuo separari, ne dominium semper abscedente ab eo usufructu dominus inutile redderetur: quae quidem lex de rebus illis intelligitur, quarum penes unum usus rei, & penes alium dominium potest sc. inutile remanere: quod nequaquam in rebus usu consumptibilibus potest esse, cum in illis per usum seu abusum usuarii, substantia talis rei esse desinat: & per consequens, proprietas etiam inutilis non subsistat: sicut dicitur in constitutione Ad conditorem canonum supradicta. Si autem velit iste haereticus, quod dicta constitutio Exiit, diffinerit, quod Fratres Minores in rebus usu consumptibilibus habeant simplicem usum facti, dicimus quod diffinivit impossibile: & per consequens diffinitio de iure non teneret. Cum enim sit impossibile in rebus usu consumptibilibus usum iuris vel facti habere a dominio separatum: cum hoc rationi obviet & iuri repugnet statutum a quocunque factum in contrarium non te- neat. Item in hoc, quod dicit, quod dicta constitutio fuit per universalem ecclesiam approbata, dicimus quod quantum ad hoc, sc. quod Fratres Minores in rebus usu consumptibilibus habeant usum facti, numquam fuit per universalem ecclesiam approbata. Dicimus etiam, quod non fuit in Viennensi concilio confirmata. Nec hoc potuit per constitutionem aliquam vel alterum approbare: imo nec de Fratrum consilio fuit promulgata.
units.tr: To this it must be said that, just as the said constitution "Ad conditorem canonum" understood the aforesaid words, so the author of that canon "Exiit" meant them of things that are not consumed by use. This is shown quite clearly by what comes before and after. For he had earlier set down the following: "Since in temporal things one must consider chiefly property, possession, usufruct, and the simple use of fact, etc." And afterwards it follows: "It was fitting for that profession, which signifies that Christ in such poverty was pursued as poor, that those who profess it should of necessity be content with the use of fact." But since the aforesaid things, namely property, usufruct, the right of use, and the use of fact, can properly be found in things consumed by use only as property (as is clear from the definitions of usufruct and use), it appears that the author of the canon did not mean those words of things consumed by use, in which the aforesaid things cannot be found. This also appears from what follows in the same constitution. For it goes on to say that the civil provision made for human things, namely that use or usufruct cannot be permanently separated from dominion, lest, with dominion always departing from that usufruct, the owner be made useless, does not oppose the aforesaid claim (that the Friars are content with the use of fact). This law is understood to apply to those things in which the use of the thing may be in one person and the dominion, which may remain useless, in another. This cannot possibly be the case in things consumed by use, since in them the substance of such a thing ceases to exist through the use or abuse of the user, and consequently the property, which would then be useless, does not subsist either, as is said in the constitution "Ad conditorem canonum" cited above. But if this heretic wishes that the said constitution "Exiit" defined that the Friars Minor have the simple use of fact in things consumed by use, we say that it defined something impossible, and consequently the definition would not hold in law. For since it is impossible to have the use of right or of fact in things consumed by use separated from dominion, and since this is contrary to reason and opposed to law, a statute made by anyone to the contrary does not hold. Likewise, as to his claim that the said constitution was approved by the universal Church, we say that, as far as this goes, namely that the Friars Minor have the use of fact in things consumed by use, it was never approved by the universal Church. We also say that it was not confirmed at the Council of Vienne. Nor could it have been approved by any constitution or other means: indeed, it was not even promulgated with the advice of the Friars.

units.la: Hic ad supra positam obiectionem respondet, dicens primo, quod decretalis Exiit, debet intelligi de rebus, quae non consumuntur usu: quod per duo dicta decretalis in ipsa conatur ostendere. Secundo quod si intelligatur de rebus usu consumptibilibus, non tenet. Tertio quod dicta decretalis quoad hoc quod Fratres Minores in rebus usu consumptibilibus habeant usum facti, nunquam fuit per universalem ecclesiam approbata. Quarto quod non fuit in Viennensi concilio confirmata. Quinto quod non fuit de Fratrum consilio promulgata.
units.tr: Here, in reply to the objection set out above, he says, first, that the decretal "Exiit" must be understood of things that are not consumed by use, which he tries to show from two statements in the decretal itself. Second, that if it is understood of things consumed by use, it does not hold. Third, that the said decretal, as far as this goes, that the Friars Minor have the use of fact in things consumed by use, was never approved by the universal Church. Fourth, that it was not confirmed at the Council of Vienne. Fifth, that it was not promulgated with the advice of the Friars.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, istum errasse quoad octo. Primo in hoc quod dicit Nicolaum tertium non debere intelligi de rebus, quae consumuntur usu. Secundo quantum ad hoc, quod dicit, quod proprietas tantum potest in rebus usu consumptibilibus reperiri, non possessio, nec ius utendi, nec usus facti. Tertio quantum ad hoc, quod dicit, quod in rebus usu consumptibilis non potest penes unum usus rei, et penes alium dominium remanere. Quarto quantum ad hoc, quod dicit quod in omnibus rebus usu consumptibilibus per usum, sive abusum vitae substantia rei definitur esse. Quinto quantum ad hoc, quod dicit, quod si diffinitio Nicolai intelligatur de rebus usu consumptibilibus, ipsa non tenet. Sexto quod dicta decretalis, quoad hoc, non fuit per universalem ecclesiam approbata. Septimo quod non fuit in Viennensi concilio confirmata. Octavo, quod non fuit de Fratrum consilio promulgata.
units.tr: But his opponents say that he has gone wrong in eight respects. First, in saying that Nicholas III ought not to be understood of things consumed by use. Second, as to his statement that in things consumed by use only property can be found, and not possession, nor the right of use, nor the use of fact. Third, as to his statement that in things consumed by use the use of a thing cannot remain with one person and dominion with another. Fourth, as to his statement that in all things consumed by use the substance of the thing is defined to be ended by the use or abuse of life. Fifth, as to his statement that if Nicholas's definition is understood of things consumed by use, it does not hold. Sixth, that the said decretal, in this respect, was not approved by the universal Church. Seventh, that it was not confirmed at the Council of Vienne. Eighth, that it was not promulgated with the advice of the Friars.

units.la: Primo itaque, isti impugnatores nituntur probare istum errare in hoc, quod dicit decretalis Exiit, de rebus consumptibilibus non debere intelligi. Primo sic: ait namque Nicolaus tertius: porro cum ipsa regula expresse contineat, quod Fratres nihil sibi approprient nec dominium, nec locum, nec aliquam rem, sitque declaratum per eundem praedecessorem Greg. 9, et nonnullos alios hoc servare debere, tam in speciali quam in communi, quam sic artam abdicationem venenosis obtrectationibus allorum insensata depravavit astutia, ne Fratrum eorundem perfectionis claritas, talium imperitis sermonibus lacteretur. Dicimus quod abdicatio proprietatis huiusmodi omnium rerum tam in speciali quam etiam in communi, propter Deum meritoria est, et sancta: quam etiam viam perfectionis Christus ostendens, verbo docuit, et exemplo firmavit. Ex his verbis clare datur intelligi, quod Fratres Minores nullius rei proprietatem debent habere, nec in speciali nec in communi; et tamen secundum Nicolaum tertium possunt uti rebus consumptibilibus usu, ergo in eis potest secundum Nicolaum usus facti a proprietate et dominio separari; et ita de huiusmodi rebus debet intelligi. Item infra dicit idem sic. Nec quisquam ex his insurgat errone: quod taliter propter Deum proprietatem omnium abdicantes tanquam homicidae sui, vel temptatores Dei, viventi diffidentia se committant. Sic enim ipsos committunt divinae providentiae in vivendo, ut viam non contemnant providonis humanae, quin vel de his quae offeruntur liberaliter, vel de his quae mendicant, vel de his quae conquiruntur per laborem suum sustentantur. Ex his verbis colligitur evidenter, quod Fratres Minores illarum rerum abdicant proprietatem, de quibus sustentantur. Sed certum est, quod de rebus usu consumptibilibus sustentantur. Ergo rerum usu consumptibilium abdicant proprietatem.
units.tr: First, then, his opponents try to prove that he is wrong in holding that the decretal "Exiit" must not be understood of consumable things. First, as follows. Nicholas III says: "Moreover, since the rule itself expressly contains that the Friars shall appropriate to themselves nothing, neither dominion, nor place, nor any thing, and since it has been declared by the same predecessor Gregory IX, and by several others, that they must observe this both in particular and in common, which foolish cunning has so perversely attacked with poisonous detraction from others, lest the clear perfection of those same Friars be sullied by the unlearned talk of such people..." We say that the renunciation of property of this kind, of all things both in particular and in common, is meritorious and holy for God's sake; Christ, showing this as the way of perfection, taught it in words and confirmed it by example. From these words it is clearly to be understood that the Friars Minor ought to have no property in any thing, either in particular or in common; and yet, according to Nicholas III, they may use consumable things by use. Therefore, according to Nicholas, the use of fact in them can be separated from property and dominion, and so it ought to be understood of such things. Likewise, a little further on, he says the same thing: "Nor let anyone rise up with this error: that those who renounce all property for God's sake, like murderers of themselves or tempters of God, commit themselves to living by a despairing trust. For they commit themselves to divine providence in living in such a way that they do not disregard the means of human provision, but are sustained either by what is offered freely, or by what they beg, or by what they gain by their own labour." From these words it is plainly gathered that the Friars Minor renounce property in those things by which they are sustained. But it is certain that they are sustained by things consumed by use. Therefore they renounce property in things consumed by use.

units.la: Ex quo sequitur, quod cum dicit Nicolaus: qui inquam usus non iuris, sed facti tantum modo nomen habens, quod facti est tantummodo in utendo praebet utentibus nihil iuris, non tantum de rebus non consumptibilibus usu, sed etiam consumptibilium usu intelligit. Item infra dicit idem et quidem ibi quod non est aliqualiter praesumendum, quod haec cuncta deficerent, sicut nec ceteris, sicut nec ipsis Fratribus iure polleat extremae necessitatis articulo, ad providendum sustentationi naturae, via omnibus extrema necessitate detentis concessa praeluditur. Ex his patet, quod Nicolaus de omnibus, quibus sustentari potest humana natura, intelligit; et ita intelligit de rebus consumptibilibus usu, quibus natura potissime sustentatur. Item infra dicit: Ne autem talis abdicatio proprietatis omnimodo renunciationem usus rerum cuiquam videatur inducere. Nam cum in reb. temporalibus sit considerare praecipuum, proprietatem possessionem, usufructum, ius utendi et simplicem usum facti, et ultimo tanquam necessario egeat, licet primis carere possit vita mortalium, nulla prorsus potest esse professio, quae a se usum necessariae sustentationi excludat. Ex his patenter habetur, quod secundum Nicolaum Fratres Minores vouent abdicationem proprietatis omnimodae. Ergo vouent abdicationem proprietatis usu consumptibilium: quia si retinerent proprietatem rerum usu consumptibilium, non vouerent abdicationem proprietatis omnimodae: quinimo possent esse ditiores multis castra et civitates habentibus. Saepe enim divitiae rerum usu consumptibilium, sicut vini, frumenti, olei et huiusmodi, divitias possidentium castra et civitates excedunt. Si ergo Fratres non vouerunt abdicationem proprietatis huiusmodi rerum usu consumptibilium, non vouerant abdicationem proprietatis omnimodae. Item ex eisdem verbis colligitur, quod Nicolaus intelligit de rebus, quae ad sustentationem necessariam requiruntur. Tales autem sunt res usu consumptibiles. Ergo secundum eum talis abdicatio non excludit simplicem facti usum rerum usu consumptibilium. Ergo contingit habere simplicem facti usum rerum consumptibilium usu, et carentiam proprietatis earum. Item subiungit idem sic; Verum condecens fuit eis professioni, quae ipsi ante devovit Christum pauperem in tanta paupertate sectari omnium abdicare dominium, et rerum sibi concessarum necessario usu fore contentam. Ex his clare patet, quod secundum Nicolaum Fratres omnium abdicant dominium; et per consequens abdicant dominium rerum usu consumptibilium. Item dicit, quod rerum concessarum necessario usu sunt contenti. Ergo ex hoc sequitur quod omnibus rebus sibi concessis licite uti possunt, sed res usu consumptibiles sunt eis concessae. Ergo huiusmodi rebus possunt uti; quod iste negat. Item idem subdit Nicolaus: Nec per hoc, quod proprietatem usus et rei cuiuscumque dominium a se abdicasse videntur, simplici usui omnis rei nunciatum esse convincitur: qui inquam usus non iuris, sed facti tantum modo nomen habens, quod facti est tantum, in utendo praebet utentibus nihil iuris: quinimo necessariarum rerum ad vitam tam sustentationem, quam ad officiorum sui status exerccunctentur: accepto quod de pecunia infra subiungitur, moderatus usus secundum eorum regulam & veritatem omnimodam concessus est Fratribus: quibus rebus Fratres licite uti possunt durante concedentis licentia. Ex his verbis patet expresse, quod Nicolaus de omnibus rebus concessis fratribus non consumptibilibus usu, & consumptibilibus usu intelligit: quia ipsemet explicans intentionem suam dicit expresse, quod moderatus usus rerum necessariarum ad vitæ sustentationem, & ad officiorum sui status executionem Fratribus est concessus. Constat autem quod res usu consumptibiles sunt fratribus necessariæ ad vitæ sustentationem. ergo moderatus usus rerum usu consumptibilium fratribus est concessus. ergo verba prædicta cum dicit, qui inquam usus non iuris, &c. de omnibus rebus consumptibilibus & non consumptibilibus necessariis fratribus debent intelligi. Et infra dicit sic: Profecto non fuit confessoris Christi regulam constituentis intentio: quinimo contrarium in ipsa conscripsit, contrarium in vivendo servavit: & cum ipse temporalibus ad necessitatem usu fuerit, & in pluribus locis in regula, usum tale licere fratribus manifestat. Dicit namque in regula: quod clerici faciant divinum officium, ex quo habere reperserunt Breviaria. Ex quo patenter insinuat, quod fratres sui habituri essent usum Breviariorum & librorum, qui sunt ad divinum officium opportuni. In alio quoque capitulo dicitur, quod ministri & custodes pro necessitatibus infirmorum & aliis Fratribus inducendis per amicos spirituales sollicitam curam gerant secundum loca & tempora diversitatem regionis. Alibi etiam exhortans fratres per congruum laboris exercitium, ad otium evitandum dicit, quod de mercede laboris prose & suis fratribus corporis necessaria recipiant. In alio quoque capitulo continetur, quod Fratres vadant pro eleemosyna confidenter. Et infra: Ex quibus omnibus satis claret ex regula, ad victum, vestitum divinum cultum, & sapientiale studium necessariarum rerum usum fratribus esse concessum. Ex quibus verbis patenter habent, quod Nicolaus intelligit de rebus necessariis ad victum & vestitum. Tales autem res necessariæ ad victum & vestitum sunt res usu consumptibiles: & ita constat, quod ubicunque loquitur Nicolaus de abdicatione omnium, quam Fratres vovent: & de usu rerum eis concessarum res usu consumptibiles comprehendit. Ex prædictis concludunt isti, quod secundum Nicolaum tertium Fratres Minores res nullius rei consumptibilis habent dominium, neque in speciali neque in communi: & tamen secundum ipsum Fratres Minores habent usum facti rerum usu consumptibilium. ergo usus facti rerum usu consumptibilium potest ab omni proprietate speciali & communi separari. Secundo concludunt quod contingit habere simplicem facti usum rerum usu consumptibilium: quia dicit Nicolaus tertius. Cum in rebus temporalibus sit considerare principalem proprietatem, possessionem, usum, fructum, ius utendi, & simplicem facti usum, & ultimo tanquam necessario egeat, licet primis carere possit vita mortalium, nulla prorsus pate esse professio, quæ à se usum necessariæ sustentationis excludat. Ex quib. verbis clare colligitur, quod usus necessariæ sustentationis pertinet ad simplicem usum facti, sed usus necessariæ sustentationis est respectu rerum consumptibilium usu. ergo contingit habere simplicem usum facti respectu rerum consumptibilium usu. Secundo isti impugnatores moliuntur ostendere, quod iste errat, cum asserit, quod prædicta, scilicet possessio, usufructus, ius utendi, & usus facti in rebus usu consumptibilibus nequeunt reperiri, sed proprietas tantum. Primo quia secundum prædicta in rebus usu consumptibilibus potest usus facti reperiri. ergo non reperitur in eis tantum proprietas. Secundo quia potest quis conducere vestem ad vendum per diem. ergo talis habet ius utendi & tamen tunc non habet proprietatem. ergo in veste non tantum reperitur proprietas. Pecunia etiam, quæ inter res usu consumptibiles computatur, dari potest ad pompam, cum non sit mutuum, sed potius commodatum, seu locatio, secundum Glossam eadem. conducens pecuniam ad pompam habet ius utendi pecunia ad pompam: & tamen non habet proprietatem eius: quia conducens rem non habet proprietatem rei conductæ. ergo in pecunia non solum proprietas, sed etiam ius utendi poterit reperiri. Quia etiam in rebus usu consumptibilibus possit haberi ius utendi sine proprietate, probatum est supra cap 3. Tertio isti impugnatores probant istum errare in hoc, quod dicit, quod in rebus usu consumptibilibus non potest usus rei penes unum: & dominium penes alium remanere; quod dicunt esse salsum. Primo de famulo expendente pecuniam domini sui: & de eo, qui vitur pecunia ad pompam: & de emente res diversas de pecunia domini sui: & de servo vtente veste domini sui: & de fratribus vtentibus rebus alienis de licentia concedentium, & de ventente veste locata seu conducta. Quarto isti impugnatores asserunt istum errare, cum dicit, quod in rebus usu consumptibilibus per usum seu abusum vsuarii, substantia talis rei esse desinit, contrarium istius ad sensum apparet. Constat enim, quod nec per usum, nec abusum pecuniæ, substantia pecuniæ desinit esse, licet nonnunquam dominium pecuniæ præcedens usum pecuniæ nec substantia nec dominium pecuniæ desinit esse: sicut cum quis vitur pecunia ad pompam. Item manifestum est, quod sæpe nec per usum nec per abusum vestis substantia vestis non desinit esse. tunc enim non posset quis sæpius uti eadem veste: quod sacræ scripturæ repugnat aperte. Exodi enim 28. sic scribitur: Facies & feminalia linea, ut operiant carnem turpitudinis suæ, a renibus usque ad femora: & utentur eis Aaron & filii eius, quando ingredientur tabernaculum testimonii. In quibus verbis insinuatur aperte, quod post usum feminalium ipsorum, substantia remanebat. hoc idem insinuatur in Actibus, cum angelus dixit Petro: Calcia te calceamentis tuis, & circunda tibi vestimentum tuum. Item sicut traditio pecuniæ cum translatione dominii, est usus vel abusus pecuniæ secundum istum, sicut patuit supra capitulo 19, ita traditio vini, panis & aliarum rerum usu consumptibilium cum translatione earundem est quoque usus vel abusus, & per consequens venditio & simplex permutatio rerum usu consumptibilium ptibilum potest esse vsus vel abusus earum. sed per venditionem vel per mutationem eth substantiá rei nequaquam definit esse: ergo non semper per vsum vel abusum rei vsu consumptibilibus substantia rei definit esse.
units.tr: From this it follows that when Nicholas says, "which use, I say, is not a right but has only the name of a fact, and so offers the users nothing of right in using," he means not only the use of non-consumable things but also the use of consumable things. Again, a little further on he says the same, and indeed there, that it must not be presumed in any way that all these things would fail, just as the Friars themselves may not claim any right in the extremity of necessity; the way to providing for the support of nature is blocked to all who are held by extreme necessity. From these words it is clear that Nicholas means all the things by which human nature can be sustained, and so he means especially the things that nature is chiefly sustained by, namely consumable things. Again he says further on: "Lest such a renunciation of ownership should seem to bring with it a renunciation of the use of things altogether. For since in temporal things one must consider the chief elements, ownership, possession, usufruct, the right of use and the simple use of fact, and since the last of these is needed as necessary, although the life of mortals can do without the first, no profession can be made at all that excludes from itself the use needed for sustenance." From these words it is plainly held that, according to Nicholas, the Friars Minor vow the renunciation of all ownership whatever. Therefore they vow the renunciation of ownership of consumable things, because if they retained ownership of consumable things, they would not have vowed the renunciation of all ownership; indeed they could be richer than many who hold castles and cities. For often the wealth of consumable things, such as wine, grain, oil and the like, exceeds the wealth of those who possess castles and cities. So if the Friars did not vow the renunciation of ownership of such consumable things, they did not vow the renunciation of all ownership. Again, from the same words it is gathered that Nicholas means things that are required for necessary sustenance. Such things, however, are consumable things. Therefore, according to him, such a renunciation does not exclude the simple use of fact in consumable things. Therefore it is possible to have the simple use of fact of consumable things, and a lack of ownership of them. Again the same man adds: "Yet it was fitting for them to profess that they would follow Christ, who was poor, in such great poverty, to renounce the lordship of all things, and to be content with the necessary use of the things granted to them." From these words it is clearly evident that, according to Nicholas, the Friars renounce the lordship of all things, and consequently renounce the lordship of consumable things. Again he says that they are content with the necessary use of things granted to them. Therefore it follows from this that they can use lawfully all the things granted to them, but consumable things are granted to them. Therefore they can use such things, which this man denies. Again Nicholas adds the same: "Nor is it shown by the fact that they seem to have renounced ownership of use and lordship of any thing that the simple use of any thing has been wholly denied; which use, I say, is not a right but has only the name of a fact, and so offers the users nothing of right in using. Rather, the things necessary for life are to be enjoyed, both for sustenance and for the performance of the duties of their state." After the words that follow concerning money: "A moderate use, according to their rule and the full truth, is granted to the Friars; with these things the Friars may use lawfully while the licence of the granter lasts." From these words it is expressly clear that Nicholas means all things granted to the friars, whether non-consumable or consumable in use, because he himself, explaining his intention, expressly says that a moderate use of things necessary for the sustenance of life and for the performance of the duties of their state has been granted to the Friars. It is certain, however, that consumable things are necessary to the Friars for sustaining life. Therefore a moderate use of consumable things has been granted to the Friars. Therefore the aforesaid words, when he says "which use, I say, is not a right," etc., must be understood of all consumable and non-consumable things necessary to the Friars. And further on he says thus: "Surely it was not the intention of the confessor of Christ who drew up the rule; rather he wrote the contrary in it and observed the contrary in living; and since he himself made use of temporal things as necessity required, and in many places in the rule he makes clear that such use is lawful for the Friars." For he says in the rule that the clerics are to perform the divine office, for which they have received breviaries. From this he plainly hints that his Friars would have the use of breviaries and books which are suited to the divine office. In another chapter too it is said that the ministers and guardians are to take anxious care, according to the places and times and the diversity of the region, for the needs of the sick and for others to be brought in through spiritual friends. Elsewhere too, exhorting the friars by a fitting exercise of labour to avoid idleness, he says that they are to receive from the wages of their labour what is necessary for the body, for themselves and for their brothers. In another chapter it is contained that the Friars should go confidently for alms. And further on: "From all these things it is sufficiently clear from the rule that the use of necessary things for food, clothing, divine worship and studies of wisdom is granted to the Friars." From these words it is plainly had that Nicholas means things necessary for food and clothing. Such things necessary for food and clothing, however, are consumable things; and so it is established that wherever Nicholas speaks of the renunciation of all things that the Friars vow, and of the use of things granted to them, he includes consumable things. From the foregoing these men conclude that, according to Nicholas the third, the Friars Minor have no lordship of any consumable thing, neither particular nor common; and yet, according to him, the Friars Minor have the simple use of fact of consumable things. Therefore the simple use of fact of consumable things can be separated from all particular and common ownership. Secondly, they conclude that it is possible to have the simple use of fact of consumable things, because Nicholas the third says: "Since in temporal things one must consider the principal ownership, possession, use, usufruct, the right of using, and the simple use of fact, and since the last of these is needed as necessary, although the life of mortals can do without the first, no profession at all can be made that excludes from itself the use needed for sustenance." From these words it is clearly gathered that the use needed for sustenance belongs to the simple use of fact, but the use needed for sustenance relates to consumable things. Therefore it is possible to have the simple use of fact in relation to consumable things. Secondly, these opponents labour to show that this man is wrong when he asserts that the aforesaid things, namely possession, usufruct, the right of use and the use of fact, cannot be found in consumable things, but only ownership. First, because according to what has been said, the use of fact can be found in consumable things; therefore ownership alone is not found in them. Secondly, because someone can hire a garment for use for a day; therefore he has the right of use, and yet then he does not have ownership; therefore in a garment ownership alone is not found. Money too, which is counted among consumable things, can be given for display, since it is not a loan but rather a commodatum or a lease, according to the same Gloss. One who hires money for display has the right of using money for display, and yet he does not have its ownership, because one who hires a thing does not have ownership of the thing hired; therefore in money there can be found not only ownership but also the right of use. Also, that in consumable things a right of use can be had without ownership has been proved above in chapter 3. Thirdly, these opponents prove that this man is wrong in what he says, that in consumable things the use of a thing cannot remain with one and the ownership with another, which they say is false. First, in the case of a servant spending his master's money; and of one who spends money for display; and of one who buys different things with his master's money; and of a servant using his master's garment; and of friars using things belonging to others with the licence of those who grant it; and of one who uses a garment that is hired or leased. Fourthly, these opponents assert that he is wrong when he says that in consumable things the substance of such a thing ceases to be through the use or abuse of the user; the opposite of this appears to the senses. For it is plain that neither by the use nor the abuse of money does the substance of money cease to be, although sometimes the ownership of money that precedes its use neither the substance nor the ownership of the money ceases to be, as when someone spends money for display. Again it is evident that often neither through use nor through abuse does the substance of a garment cease to be; for otherwise one could not use the same garment many times, which plainly contradicts Holy Scripture. For Exodus 28 is written thus: "Make also linen breeches to cover the flesh of their nakedness, from the loins even to the thighs; and Aaron and his sons shall wear them when they go into the tabernacle of the testimony." In these words it is plainly hinted that after the use of those breeches the substance remained. The same is hinted in the Acts, when the angel said to Peter: "Gird yourself and put on your sandals, and wrap your garment about you." Again, just as the handing over of money with the transfer of ownership is, according to this man, a use or abuse of money, as was shown above in chapter 19, so the handing over of wine, bread and other consumable things with the transfer of the same is likewise a use or abuse; and consequently sale and simple exchange of consumable things can be a use or abuse of them. But by sale or by exchange the substance of the thing by no means ceases to be; therefore it is not always through the use or abuse of a consumable thing that its substance ceases to be.

units.la: Quinto dicunt eum errare, cum dicit, quod si Nicolaus intellexit de rebus vsu consumptibilibus, diffinitio sua non tenet. Nam cum constet (vt dicunt) quod iste intellexit de rebus vsu consumptibilibus, & non consumptibilibus vsu, si diffinitio sua non tenet. Eadem ratione non teneret diffinitio Greg. noni, Alexan. quarti, Innocen. quarti, & Clementis quinti: quotomnes idem quoad abdicationem Fratrum Minorum, cum Nicolao tertio diffinierunt: determinantes, quod Fratres Minores nullius rei temporalis debent proprietatem seruare. Vnde Greg. 9. in declaratione sua sic ait: Praeterea cum in ipsa regula contineatur expressè, quod Fratres nihil sibi approprient, nec dominium, nec locum, nec aliquam rem ac ipsi processu temporis contaminari timeant ordinis potestatem praesertim cum iam dixerint aliqui proprietatem mobilium pertinere ad totum ordinem in communi: nobis fuit humiliter supplicatum, vt in hoc & animarum dignaremur prouidere periculis, & totius ordinis potestati. Dicimus itaque quod nec in communi nec in speciali debent proprietatem, sed vtensilium & librorum & eorum mobilium; quae licet habere, ordo vsum habeat, &c. Item Alexander quartus & Innocentius quartus sic diffiniunt: Dicimus quod nec in speciali nec in communi debent habere: sed loca & domorum ac vtensilium & librorum & eorum, quae licet habere, ordo vsum habeat, &c. Et Clemens quintus in decretali. Exiuit de paradiso, ait: Proinde cum vir sanctus paupertatis promissa in regula modum exprimens, dicit in eadem: Fratres sibi nihil appropriant, nec domum, nec locum, nec aliquam rem, sed tanquam peregrini & aduenae in hoc seculo in paupertate & humilitate domino famulantes vadant pro eleemosyna confidenter: sic quod deo laratum est per nullos praedecessores Romanos pontifices hanc expropriationem debere intelligi tam in speciali quam in communi: propter quod, & rerum omnium oblatarum concessarum & donatarum fratribus quasdam vsum facti, scilicet ordini, vel ipsis fratribus licet habere, proprietatem & dominium in se & Romanam ecclesiam receperunt, dimisso scilicet ipsis fratribus in eis tantum modo simplici facti vsu. Et infra: Dicti ordinis professores pro nulla re temporali possunt in iudicio experiri. Ex his euidenter apparet, quod praedicti summi pontificis diffinitionem, Fratres Minores nullius rei proprietatem habere neq; in speciali neq; in communi. & per consequens secundum istos nullius rei vsu consumptibilis habent proprietatem: & tamen secundum ipsos habent vsum huiusmodi rerum. ergo secundum ipsos in huiusmodi rebus potest vsus à dominio & proprietate separari. Ex quo sequitur, quod si diffinitio Nicolai non tenet, nec istorum diffinitio tenet: & ita omnes isti errasent; quod est temerarium reputandum.
units.tr: Fifthly, they say he is wrong when he says that if Nicholas meant things consumed by use, his definition does not hold. For since it is agreed (as they say) that he meant things consumed by use, and not things not consumed by use, then if his definition does not hold, the same reasoning would mean that the definitions of Gregory IX, Alexander IV, Innocent IV and Clement V do not hold either. All of them defined the renunciation of the Friars Minor in the same way as Nicholas III, determining that the Friars Minor must keep no ownership of any temporal thing. Hence Gregory IX, in his declaration, says: "Moreover, since the rule itself expressly states that the Friars shall appropriate nothing to themselves, neither dominion, nor place, nor any thing, and since they fear that over time they may be contaminated by the power of the Order, especially since some have already said that ownership of movable goods belongs to the whole Order in common, we have been humbly asked to provide, in this matter also, for the dangers to souls and for the power of the whole Order. We say therefore that they must have ownership neither in common nor in particular, but only the use of the utensils and books and those movable goods which the Order is permitted to have, etc." Likewise Alexander IV and Innocent IV define thus: "We say that they must have neither in particular nor in common, but the Order shall have the use of places and houses and of utensils and books and those things which it is permitted to have, etc." And Clement V in the decretal Exiit qui seminat, says: "Accordingly, since the holy man, in expressing in the rule the promise of poverty, says in the same place: 'The Friars shall appropriate nothing to themselves, neither house, nor place, nor any thing, but as pilgrims and strangers in this world, serving the Lord in poverty and humility, shall go confidently for alms,' it has been declared by God that this expropriation must be understood by no previous Roman pontiffs, either in particular or in common. For this reason, and because of all the things offered, granted and given to the friars, they have received for themselves and the Roman Church the ownership and dominion, certain things being in use as a matter of fact, namely for the Order, or which the friars themselves are permitted to have, leaving to the friars only the simple use in fact." And below: "The professed members of the said Order cannot sue in court for any temporal thing." From these things it is evident that the definition of the aforesaid supreme pontiff, that the Friars Minor have ownership of nothing either in particular or in common, and consequently, according to them, have ownership of no consumable thing, is nevertheless, according to them, a use of such things. Therefore, according to them, in such things use can be separated from dominion and ownership. From this it follows that if Nicholas's definition does not hold, neither does theirs, and so all of them would have erred, which must be regarded as rash.

units.la: Sexto dicunt eum errare, cum dicit, quod decretalis Exiit, quoad praedictam assertionem, non est per vniuersalem ecclesiam approbata. Nam omnis assertio publice per vniuersam ecclesiam promulgata, si per nullum catholicum reprobatur, per vniuersalem ecclesiam approbatur. Nam si talis assertio est catholica & fidelis, constat quod vniuersalis ecclesia ipsam nullatenus reprobando noscitur approbare. Si autem est erronea, & teste Innocentio, vt habetur dist. 93. Error: Error: cui non resistitur, approbatur: si nullus catholicus talem assertionem erroneam reprobat, vniuersalis ecclesia ipsam conuincitur approbare. Cum ergo ante tempora istius impugnati nullus fuerit inuentus catholicus, qui reprobauerit dictam assertionem in decretali praefata contentam: sequitur quod ipsam vniuersalis ecclesia approbauit. Amplius: Vniversalis ecclesia dictam decretalem Exiit, approbauit, nihil in ea penitus reprobando. qui autem aliquid absolute approbat, nullam partem reprobando omnem partialem approbare conuincitur. Aliter posset aliquis licite omnia scripta haereticorum abque periculo approbare: quia nullum inuenitur scriptum cuiuscunque haeretici, quin multas contineat veritates. relinquitur igitur, quod vniuersalis ecclesia omnem assertionem contentam in decretali Exiit, approbauit: & ita praedictam assertionem approbauit. Septimo dicunt eum errare, cum dicit istam decretalem non fuisse Vienensi concilio confirmatam: quia de ista assertione fiebat in praedicto concilio examinatio specialis, quae in constitutione edita tempore concilii & per concilium confirmata est in serta. ergo ista assertio est in generali concilio confirmata.
units.tr: Sixthly, they say he is wrong when he says that the decretal Exiit, with regard to the aforesaid assertion, has not been approved by the universal Church. For every assertion publicly promulgated throughout the universal Church, if it is not rejected by any Catholic, is approved by the universal Church. For if such an assertion is Catholic and faithful, it is clear that the universal Church is known to approve it by not rejecting it at all. But if it is erroneous, then, as Innocent testifies, as is found in Dist. 93, "Error: Error, which is not resisted, is approved." If no Catholic rejects such an erroneous assertion, the universal Church is shown to approve it. Since therefore, before the times of this opponent, no Catholic was found who rejected the said assertion contained in the aforesaid decretal, it follows that the universal Church approved it. Furthermore: the universal Church approved the said decretal Exiit, rejecting nothing in it at all. But whoever approves something absolutely is shown to approve every part of it, rejecting no part. Otherwise anyone could safely approve all the writings of heretics without danger, since no writing of any heretic is found that does not contain many truths. It remains, therefore, that the universal Church approved every assertion contained in the decretal Exiit, and so it approved the aforesaid assertion. Seventhly, they say he is wrong when he says that this decretal was not confirmed by the Council of Vienne, because a special examination of this assertion was made in the said council, and it was confirmed by the council in a constitution issued at the time of the council, and it is set down in the Sext. Therefore this assertion has been confirmed by a general council.

units.la: Octavo dicunt eum errare, cum dicit, quod haec constitutio non de Fratrum concilio promulgata: quia non est verisimile, quod constitutio cum tanta maturitate digesta super tanto negocio absque Fratrum concilio emanasset: nec ipse ponit, quod de Fratrum concilio non fuerit promulgata. Nunc accedatur ad literam [Verba praedicta intellexit condutor illius canonis Exiit, de rebus quae consumuntur vsu.] Istud dicunt esse omnino erroneum, & contra mentem dictae constitutionis: quia de omnib. rebus, quibus Fratres vtuntur, intellexit. [cum in rebus temporalib. fit consideratio.] Istud habet veritatem: non tamen in omni re temporali est omnino ista consideratio, sed in aliquibus est omnia illa considerare, & non in omnibus. [sed proprietas tantum] hoc dicunt esse erroneum: quia simplex vsus facti reperitur in rebus vsu consumptibilibus: quia nullomodo potest negari accipiendo simplicem vsum facti, sicut Nicolaus tertius accipit in dicta decretali Exiit. Nam ipse accipit simplicem vsum facti, p actu vtendi, cui non est annexum necessario aliquod ius, quo valet quis rem vel vsum rei in iudicio vendicare. Ex quo non potest carere vita mortalium. talis actus est actus comedendi, bibendi, induendi & huiusmodi & ita accipit vsum facti pro manducare & bibere, ac alios actus circa eas exerceri. ergo in talib. reb. conuenit reperire simplicem facti vsum. Quod vero Nicolaus tertius accipiat simplice vsum facti, & vsum facti ac etiam necessarium vsum pro actu comedendi, bibendi, &c. patet. Nam cum dixisset; cum in rebus temporalib. fit consideratio. darè præcipuè, proprietatè, possessionè, vsufructu, ius vtendi & simplicem vsum facti, immediatè subiunxit: licet primis carere possit vita mortalium, nulla prorsus potest esse prof. sio. quarei vsum necessariæ sustentationis excludat. Ex quibus verbis apparet, quod simplicem vsum facti vocat vsum necessariæ sustentationis. Constat autem quod vsus necessariæ sustentationis est huiusmodi, quibus homo sustentatur. Item postea concludit Nicolaus tertius: Ex quibus omnibus satis claret ex regula ad victum, vestitum, dominicum cultum, sapientiale studium, necessarium rerum vsum, fratribus esse concessum. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod necessarius vsus illarum rerum, quæ ad victum & vestitum spectant, fratribus est concessus. tunc quæritur, quis est ille necessarius vsus: Aut est actus comedendi, bibendi, & induendi: aut aliquis alius vsus? Si detur primum, habetur intentum, quod Nicolaus tertius vocat necessarium vsum, actum comedendi, bibendi & huiusmodi. Secundum non potest dari: quia ille vsus non esset, nisi vsus, qui vocatur vsus iuris, qui inuentus est à iuristis, quem fratres secundum Nicolaum tertium non habent, cum vsus facti, quem habent, nihil tribuat eis. & ita constat, quod Nicolaus vocat simplicem facti vsum, necessarium vsu, & dicitur necessarius, quia requiritur ad sustentandum naturam, vel ad aliquid aliud faciendum: quod necesse est fieri. Simplicem autem facti vsum, vocat actum, qui non habet necessario annexum ius quodcunq;, quo quis valeat in iudicio litigare. huiusmodi est actus comedendi, bibendi & huiusmodi: quia licet interdum actus comedendi habeat tale ius annexum: hoc tamen accidit: & ideo vocatur simplex vsus. [vt patet ex diffinitionibus vsufructus & vsus.] Dicunt quod istud non est ad propositum. Nam vsus, qui diffinitur sic; Vsus est ius utendi rebus alienis, &c. est vsus iuris, & nō est simplex facti vsus, de quo loquitur Nicolaus. & ita per illam diffinitionem non pōt concludi, quod simplex facti vsus, de quo loquitur Nicolaus, nequit in reb. vsu consumptibilibus reperiri. [Apparet quod de rebus vsu consumptibilib. &c.] Dicunt, quod male infert, quia Nicolaus intelligit de rebus in quibus proprietas & simplex vsus facti possunt inueniri. & huiusmodi sunt res vsu consumptibiles, in quib. præmissa tñ aliqua præmissorum possunt in rebus vsu consumptibilibus reperiri. & hoc sufficit ad hoc ꝙ de eis intelligat Nicolaus. [In rebus humanis constituit.] Ex hoc apparet, ꝙ non est ex natura rei, sed ex constitutione humana. quare non repugnat naturæ rei perpetuo vsum à dominio separari: sed repugnat iuri positiuo ciuili. [Quæ quidem lex de reb. illis intelligitur, quarum penes vnum vsu rei, &c.] Hoc concedunt. [Quod nequaquam in rebus vsu consumptibilibus potest esse.] Hoc negant. patet in vestibus. imo in cibo & potu, in seruo qui habet vsum, & dominus suus habet dominium, tamen non habet illum vsum, de quo loquitur lex illa: quia illa lex loquitur de vsu iuris, quem non habet seruus, sed habet vsum facti. [Cum in iuris per vsum seu abusum vsuarii, substantia talis rei esse desinat.] hoc in quibusdam est verum, & in quibusdam falsum: sicut est ostensum superius secundum istos. [Dicimus quod quantum ad hoc, scilicet, quod Fratres Minores habeant in rebus vsu consumptibilibus vsum facti, nunquam fuit per vniuersalem ecclesiam approbata.] Constat, quod accipiendo vsum facti, sicut accipit Nicolaus, etiam secundum istum, sicut patebit inferius, scilicet pro actu comedendi, bibendi, &c. ista assertio fuit per vniuersalem ecclesiam approbata, siue Nicolaus tertius loquitur proprie siue improprie, de quo posterius differetur.
units.tr: Eighthly, they say he is wrong when he says that this constitution was not promulgated with the Friars' council, because it is not likely that a constitution so maturely composed on so great a matter would have been issued without the Friars' council; nor does he himself assert that it was not promulgated with the Friars' council. Now let us turn to the text: [The author of that canon Exiit understood the aforesaid words of things that are consumed by use.] They say this is entirely erroneous and contrary to the intention of the said constitution, because it understood them of all things which the Friars use. [Consideration is given to temporal things.] This is true; yet with every temporal thing such consideration is not wholly made, but with some things it is right to consider all those points, and not with all. [But only ownership.] They say this is erroneous, because simple use in fact is found in things consumed by use, since it can in no way be denied, if we take simple use in fact, as Nicholas III takes it in the said decretal Exiit. For he takes simple use in fact to mean the act of using, to which there is not necessarily annexed any right by which one may claim the thing or the use of the thing in court. Such an act cannot be lacking in mortal life. Such an act is the act of eating, drinking, clothing and the like; and so he takes use in fact to mean eating and drinking, and other acts exercised about these things. Therefore in such things it is fitting to find simple use in fact. That Nicholas III takes simple use in fact, and use in fact and also necessary use, to mean the act of eating, drinking, etc., is clear. For when he had said, "Consideration is given to temporal things," he at once added, principally, ownership, possession, usufruct, the right of use and simple use in fact: "Although the first may be lacking to mortal life, nothing at all can be a profession which excludes the use of necessary sustenance." From these words it appears that he calls simple use in fact the use of necessary sustenance. It is certain, moreover, that the use of necessary sustenance is of the kind by which a man is sustained. Next, Nicholas III concludes: "From all these things it is sufficiently clear that by the rule the necessary use of things is granted to the friars for food, clothing, divine worship, and the study of wisdom." From these words it is to be understood that the necessary use of those things which pertain to food and clothing has been granted to the friars. Then the question is asked: what is that necessary use? Is it the act of eating, drinking and clothing, or some other use? If the first is given, the point is granted, that Nicholas III calls the act of eating, drinking and the like necessary use. The second cannot be given, because that use would be nothing but the use called use of right, which was invented by the jurists, and which the friars, according to Nicholas III, do not have, since the use in fact which they have grants them nothing. And so it is clear that Nicholas calls simple use in fact necessary use, and it is called necessary because it is required for sustaining nature, or for doing something else which must be done. But simple use in fact he calls an act which has no necessarily annexed right by which one may be able to litigate in court. Such is the act of eating, drinking and the like, because although the act of eating sometimes has such a right annexed, this happens by accident, and therefore it is called simple use. [As is evident from the definitions of usufruct and use.] They say this is not to the point. For use, which is defined thus, "Use is the right to use another's things," etc., is use of right, and is not the simple use in fact of which Nicholas speaks. And so by that definition it cannot be concluded that the simple use in fact of which Nicholas speaks cannot be found in things consumed by use. [It appears that concerning things consumed by use, etc.] They say he infers badly, because Nicholas understands it of things in which ownership and simple use in fact can be found, and such are things consumed by use, in which some of the aforesaid things can be found. And this is enough for Nicholas to be understood as speaking of them. [He established it in human affairs.] From this it appears that it is not from the nature of the thing, but from human constitution. Therefore it is not contrary to the nature of a thing that use be perpetually separated from dominion; but it is contrary to positive civil law. [Which law indeed is understood of those things of which one, in the use of a thing, etc.] They concede this. [Which can in no way be in things consumed by use.] They deny this. It is plain in clothes; indeed in food and drink, in a slave who has use and whose master has dominion, yet he does not have that use of which that law speaks, because that law speaks of use of right, which the slave does not have, but he has use in fact. [Since by the use or abuse of a usuary the substance of such a thing ceases to be.] This is true in some cases and false in others, as has been shown above according to them. [We say that as to this, namely, that the Friars Minor have use in fact in things consumed by use, it was never approved by the universal Church.] It is certain that, taking use in fact as Nicholas takes it, even according to this opponent, as will appear below, namely for the act of eating, drinking, etc., this assertion was approved by the universal Church, whether Nicholas III speaks properly or improperly, which will be treated later.

units.la: CAP. XXXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIII.

units.la: ADhuc dicit iste hæreticus constitutionem prædictam Ad conditorem canonum, errorem alium continere, in eo quod continet, qua sequuntur: Rursus non simplex vsus facti, qui neque seruitus, nec pro illo competit iis vtendi, in talibus rebus, (scilicet vsu consumptibilibus,) potest constitui vel haberi. cum enim vti re aliqua, nihil aliud sit proprie quam fructus rei seu vtilitatem aliquam in solidum vel pro parte recipere, quæ ex ea possunt salua rei substantia prouenire, restat quod re illa vti quis nequeat, ex qua salua substantia, nulla potest sibi prouenire vtilitas, quales res vsu consumptibiles esse constat. Ex quibus patet, quod hic vsus quiett seruitus personalis, nec ius vtendi, quod non est seruitus, sed mere ius personale, nec actus ipse vtendi sine iure aliquo, possunt in rebus vsu consumptibilibus constitui vel haberi: cum quodlibet præmissorum exigat, quod ex re ipsa, salua rei substantia possit habenti ius vtendorum, seu vtendi ex re ipsa vtilitas aliqua prouenire. quod vtique in rebus nequit vsu consumptibilibus reperiri. & inf. a: Licet autem in rebus vsu consumptibilibus, nec ius vtendi, nec ipsum vti possit constitui vel haberi, ipsis tamen poterit quis abuti. Aputi autem dum tractatur de rebus vsu consumptibilibus pro rei consumptione sumitur, quod ei opponitur, quod est vti. Vti quidem supponit, quod cum vsu salua rei substantia manent: sed abutis exigit, quod cum actu huiusmodi rei substantia consumatur, cum abuti nihil aliud, quam contra naturam vsus vti in hac materia proprie dici possit.
units.tr: Furthermore, this heretic claims that the aforesaid constitution, Ad conditorem canonum, contains another error, in what it says as follows: "Again, a mere use of fact, which belongs neither to servitude nor to a right of using, cannot be established or held in such things (namely, things consumable by use). For to use some thing is properly nothing other than to receive the fruit of a thing, or some benefit from it, wholly or in part, which can arise from it while its substance remains intact. It follows that one cannot use a thing from which no benefit can arise to him while its substance remains intact, which is evidently the case with things consumable by use. From this it is plain that in things consumable by use neither this use, which is personal servitude, nor the right of using, which is not servitude but purely a personal right, nor the act of using itself without some right, can be established or held. For each of the things set out requires that some benefit of using can arise to the one who has the right of using, or to the one using, from the thing itself while its substance remains intact; and this cannot be found in things consumable by use." And further on: "Although in things consumable by use neither the right of using nor the using itself can be established or held, yet one can abuse them. But 'abuse,' when things consumable by use are under discussion, is taken for the consuming of the thing, which is the opposite of 'use.' For use presupposes that the substance of the thing remains intact along with the use, but abuse requires that the substance of such a thing be consumed by the act; since abuse, in this matter, can properly mean nothing other than to use contrary to the nature of use."

units.la: Postquam iste impugnarus respondit ad obiectiones appellantis contra primam assertionem: Hic incipit respondere ad obiectiones eiusdem contra secundam assertionem impugnatam. & diuiditur in tres partes, secundum quod ad hoc, quæ tangit appellans, respondit, partes patebunt in prosequendo. Circa primam partem primo ponit assertionem impugnatam. Secundo impugnationem in parte immediate sequenti. Tertio ad obiectionem nititur respondere, ibi Ad hoc dicendum.
units.tr: After this opponent has replied to the objections of the appellant against the first assertion, he now begins to answer the appellant's objections against the second assertion, which he attacks. This is divided into three parts, and the parts will become clear as we proceed, according to how he answers what the appellant touches on. In the first part he first sets out the assertion under attack; second, he attacks it in the part immediately following; third, he tries to answer the objection, at the words "To this it must be said."

units.la: Assertio autem hic impugnata principaliter est, quod non contingit vti rebus consumptibilibus vsu. [Simplex vsus facti] secundum istos illi primo inuenerunt vti hoc modo loquendi, acceperunt simplicem vsum facti pro actu circa rem exteriorem exercito: qui non requirit in exercente ius aliud, quo pro tali actu exercendo quis valeat in iudicio litigare. &isto modo actus comedendi est simplex vsus facti: quia istum actum potest quis exercere, licet nullum ius habeat exercendi eundem actum, quo iure si impediretur, valeret impediente in iudicio conuenire. Cum vti realire aliqua nihil aliud sit proprie, &c. Dicunt istam diffinitionem in nullo authentico inueniri: & si esset diffinitio ipsius vti, non esset diffinitio eius in omni sua propria significatione, sed in aliqua significatione speciali: quia tunc hoc vocabulum vti esset æquiuocum: sicut hoc nomen vsus est æquiuocum, habens plures significationes, quarum multæ sunt propriæ. Unde significatio huius nominis vsus, secundum quod accipitur pro actu comedendi, bibendi & huiusmodi, non est minus propria quam quæcunq; alia. [Restat quod re illa vti quis nequeat, &c.] Dicunt, quod infert fallum ex fallo: [quales res vsu consumptibiles esse constat] dicunt, quod nunquam vel vix potest aliqua res vsu consumptibilis reperiri, quin ex ipsa substantia salua possit mediante aliquo actu vtendi aliqua vtilitas prouenire licet sint multæ res, circa quas si quis exerceat actum vtendi, ad quem principaliter ordinantur, nulla vel parua potest vtilitas prouenire, salua ipsarum substantia, sicut sunt illa quæ in cibo & potu, & multa quæ in medicinis consistunt. multæ vero sunt res vsu consumptibiles, ex quibus deterioratis potest vtilitas prouenire, salua ipsarum substantia: licet quis circa eas exerceat actum ad quem principaliter ordinantur, sicut vestes. Aliqui vero sunt, quarum nec substantia deteriorat proueniente vtilitate ex ipsis, sicut pecuniæ: quia licet sæpe dominium pecuniæ consumatur tamen, substantia pecuniæ manet salua [Nec ius vtendi, quod non est seruitus, sed mere personale, nec actus vtendi sine iure aliquo possunt in rebus vsu consumptibilibus constitui vel haberi.] Vtrumque dicunt esse erroneum. de iure vtendi probatum est: quia actus vtendi sine iure aliquo non potest esse, nisi sicut actus comedendi, vel bibendi, aut huiusmodi: qui, vt constat, potest in rebus vsu consumptibilibus reperiri. [Cum quidem licet præmissorum exigat, quod ex re ipsa salua rei substantia, &c.] Hoc negant: ipsis tamen poterit quis abuti, licet abuti in vna significatione sit idem, quod valde vti secundum grammaticos. & sic posset concedi, quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus contingit abuti: ex quo sequitur quod eis contingit vti, tamen abuti nunquam in tali significatione, cum de rebus vsu consumptibilibus fit mentio, in scriptura sacra accipitur. [Abuti autem dum tractatur de rebus vsu consumptibilibus pro rei consumptione sumitur.] In theologia & philosophia non sic accipitur. [Vti quidem præsupponit quod cum vsu salua rei substantia manebat.] Hoc dicunt omnino falsum, accipiendo vti, sicut in theologia accipitur. Unde cum dixit Paulus vere modico vino: non præsuppositit quod substantia vini remaneret salua. [Sed abuti exigit quod cum actu huius rei substantia consumatur.] Hoc dicunt omnino erroneum de pecunia, qua contingit abuti secundum istum: & tamen substantia pecuniæ non consumitur. licet nonnunquam dominium pecuniæ consumatur. [Cum abuti nihil aliud quam contra naturam vsus vti, in hac materia proprie posset dici.] Hic dicunt isti, quod iste ignorat propriam vocem: quia concedit expresse illud, quod improbare intendit: quia concedit, quod abuti est proprie contra naturam vsus vti. ergo aliud est proprie vti: quia contra naturam vsus vti est vti. ergo qui abutitur rebus vsu consumptibilibus, proprie vtitur rebus vsu consumptibilibus. & ita contingit vti rebus consumptibilibus vsu: quia tamen negat.
units.tr: The assertion attacked here is principally this: that it is not possible to use things consumable by use. [Simple use of fact] According to these men, those who first devised this way of speaking took "simple use of fact" to mean an act performed upon an external thing, which does not require in the one performing it any further right by which, for performing such an act, he would be able to sue in court. In this sense the act of eating is a simple use of fact, because a person can perform this act even though he has no right to perform it, and if he were prevented by a right, he could bring the one preventing him to court. As for "since to use some thing is properly nothing other than, etc.," they say this definition is not found in any authoritative source; and even if it were a definition of use itself, it would not be a definition of it in every proper sense, but in some special sense only, since the word "use" would then be equivocal, just as the term "use" is equivocal, having several meanings, many of which are proper. Hence the sense of this term "use," as it is taken for the act of eating, drinking and the like, is no less proper than any other. [It follows that one cannot use that thing, etc.] They say he infers falsehood from falsehood. [Which things consumable by use are evidently such] They say that a thing consumable by use can never, or hardly ever, be found from which some benefit cannot arise, through some act of using, while its substance remains intact. For there are many things on which, if one performs the act of using to which they are principally ordained, either no benefit or only a slight one can arise while their substance remains intact, such as those things that consist in food and drink, and many that consist in medicines. Yet there are many things consumable by use from which a benefit can arise, their substance remaining intact, even though one performs upon them the act to which they are principally ordained, such as clothes. And there are some whose substance does not deteriorate although a benefit arises from them, such as money: for although the ownership of money is often consumed, the substance of the money remains intact. [Nor a right of using, which is not servitude but purely personal, nor the act of using, can be established or held without some right, in things consumable by use.] They say both of these are erroneous. As to the right of using, it has been proved that the act of using cannot exist without some right, except as the act of eating, drinking or the like, which, as is evident, can be found in things consumable by use. [For although each of the things set out requires that from the thing itself, its substance remaining intact, etc.] This they deny, since one may abuse them, although to abuse in one sense is the same as to use excessively according to the grammarians. And so it could be conceded that in things consumable by use it is possible to abuse them; from this it follows that it is possible to use them, though abuse, in that sense, is never taken, when things consumable by use are mentioned, in Holy Scripture. [But abuse, when things consumable by use are treated, is taken for the consuming of the thing.] In theology and philosophy it is not so understood. [For use presupposes that the substance of the thing remains intact along with the use.] They say this is wholly false, if use is taken as it is understood in theology. Hence when Paul said "a little wine," he did not presuppose that the substance of the wine would remain intact. [But abuse requires that the substance of the thing be consumed by the act.] They say this is wholly erroneous concerning money, which, according to him, can be abused, and yet the substance of money is not consumed, although sometimes the ownership of money is consumed. [Since abuse, in this matter, could properly mean nothing other than to use contrary to the nature of use.] Here they say this man does not understand the proper term, because he expressly concedes what he intends to disprove: he concedes that to abuse is properly to use contrary to the nature of use. Therefore to use properly is something else, since to use contrary to the nature of use is to use. Therefore whoever abuses things consumable by use properly uses things consumable by use; and so it is possible to use things consumable by use. Yet he denies this.

units.la: CAP. XXXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIV.

units.la: HÆc verba constitutionis. Ex quibus apparere dicit hereticus supradictus, quod dicta constitutio in eo quod dogmatizat, quod nec vsus facti nec actus vtendi haberi potest in rebus consumptibilibus vsu: quod nullus huiusmodi rebus vsu consumptibilibus vti potest, quamuis eis abuti possit: abusu, qui contra naturam vsus existit, sacræ scripturæ obuiat manifeste. Ad quod probandum inducit illud Leuit. 27. vbi dicitur, quod omnes decimæ terræ siue de fructibus, siue de pomis arborum domini sunt. & Num. 18. dicitur de Leuitis, quod nihil aliud possidebunt decimarum oblationes ceterenti quas in vsu eorum & necessaria separaui. ex quibus liquet (vt dicit) quod vsus in rebus vsu consumptibilibus ex Dei statuto habetur.
units.tr: These are the words of the constitution. From them the aforesaid heretic says it appears that the said constitution, in what it teaches as doctrine, holds that neither the use in fact nor the act of using can be had in consumable things: that no one can use things consumed by use, although he can abuse them; and that abuse, which exists contrary to the nature of use, manifestly opposes Holy Scripture. To prove this he brings forward Leviticus 27, where it is said that all the tithes of the land, whether of the fruits or of the fruit of the trees, belong to the Lord. And Numbers 18 says of the Levites that the tithe-offerings which they set apart for their use and necessities would be all they possessed. From these things it is clear (he says) that use in consumable things is had by God's appointment.

units.la: Hic contra præmissam assertionem primam obiectionem subiicit appellantis, quæ in hoc consistit, quod Num. 18. habetur, quod Deus dedit decimas rerum vsu consumptibilium in vsum Leitarum. ergo poterant habere vsum rerum consumptibilium vsu.
units.tr: Here, against the assertion first stated, the appellant's first objection is brought forward, which consists in this: Numbers 18 says that God gave the tithes of consumable things to the Levites for their use. Therefore they were able to have the use of consumable things by consuming them.

units.la: [Nec vsus facti nec actus vtendi.] Sæpe vsus facti, & actus vtendi accipiuntur pro eodem. potest tamen vsus facti accipi pro potestate vtendi, vt distinguitur etiam ab actu vtendi. [Nihil aliud possidebunt] sc. ex prima diuisione terræ promissionis [in vsus eorum] hoc est ad vtendum eis.
units.tr: [Neither the use in fact nor the act of using.] The use in fact and the act of using are often taken for the same thing. Yet the use in fact can be taken as the power of using, as it is also distinguished from the act of using. [They will possess nothing else] namely, from the first division of the land of promise; [for their use] that is, for them to use.

units.la: CAP XXXV.
units.tr: CHAP. XXXV.

units.la: AD hoc dicendum quod iste in praedictis manifeste sefundat in falsis. quod enim Leuitæ in decimis tantum habuerunt simpliciter facti vsum, falsum est: & qui dixit expresse illo capitulo Num. 18. peripsum allegato: vbi sic dominus dicit: Filiis Leui dedi omnes decimas Israel in possessionem pro ministerio quo seruiunt mihi in tabernaculo fœderis. Ex quo patet, quod Leuitæ non tantum vsum in decimis sed etiam dominium habuerunt. nec obstat, quod in eodem capitulo dicitur quod in vsu Leuitarum & necessaria dominus decimas separauit. Aliud est enim alicui dare in re aliqua vsum facti, & aliud rem alicui in vsus eius & necessaria dare, vt superius est est visum. Ad illud autem quod dicit, quod vsus in rebus vsu consumptibilibus ex Dei statuto habetur dicimus quod est falsum: qui a in tota scriptura sacra non habetur mentio de simplici vsu facti.
units.tr: To this I answer that he manifestly founds himself on falsehoods in what he has said above. It is false that the Levites had only the simple use of the tithes. The man who makes this claim expressly appeals to Num. 18, where the Lord speaks thus: "I have given to the sons of Levi all the tithes of Israel as an inheritance, in return for the ministry by which they serve me in the tabernacle of the covenant." From this it is plain that the Levites had not merely the use of the tithes but also ownership of them. Nor does it stand in the way that in the same chapter it is said that the Lord set the tithes apart for the use and needs of the Levites. For it is one thing to give someone the use of a thing, and another to give a thing to someone for his use and needs, as was shown above. As for his claim that use of consumable goods is granted by God's decree, we say that this is false, since there is no mention anywhere in Holy Scripture of the simple use of a thing.

units.la: Hic ad præmissam obiectionem respondet dicens, quod Leuitæ non habuerunt in decimis tantum simplicem facti vsum sed etiam dominium: & quod est aliud dare rem in vsum, & dare alicui vsum facti: & quod ex Dei statuto non habetur vsus in rebus vsu consumptibilibus, quia de simplici vsu facti in scriptura sacra nulla fit mentio.
units.tr: Here he answers the previous objection, saying that the Levites had not only the simple use of the tithes but also ownership; that giving a thing for use is different from giving someone the use of a thing; and that by God's decree no use of consumable goods is granted, because Scripture makes no mention of the simple use of a thing.

units.la: Sed dicunt primo isti impugnatores quod iste appellanti falsum imponit. Secundo quod obiectione non tangit, & concedit propositum. Tertio quod aperte errat cum dicit, in vsum rebus vsu consumptibilibus ex Dei statuto non haberi. Dicunt itaque; primo, quod iste appellanti falsum imponit, cum asserit aßerit eum dixisse Leuitas in decimis tantum habuisse simplicem facti vsum. hoc enim non dicit, sed tantum modo dicit, quod habuerunt vsum in huiusmodi rebus, cum quo stat quod habuerit ius vtendi huiusmodi rebus: imo ex hoc quod habuerunt vsum in huiusmodi rebus, non sequitur quod non habuerunt dominium in eisdem. Secundo dicunt quod obiectionem non tangit, & tamen concedit propositum. nam cui datur aliquid in vsum, ille potest habere vsum eiusdem rei, quae sibi data est in vsum. sed decimae multarum rerum vsu consumptibilium fuerunt datae Leuitis in vsum etiam secundum istum. ergo Leuitae poterant habere vsum earundem decimarum. Minorem ipse concedit: maior probatur per eum. nam sicut patuit supra capitulo 10. ipse dicit, quod vbi aliquid alicui datur in vsum, nedum vsus rei sed & dominium intelligitur esse datum. ergo quando aliquid datur in vsum, tam vsus quam dominium datur. Sed cui datur vsus rei, ille potest habere vsum rei. ergo quando aliqua res datur in vsum, ille potest habere vsum rei. & ita cum decimis aliquarum rerum vsu consumptibilium datae fuerint Leuitis in vsum, secundum istum Leuitae potuerunt habere vsum earundem: & ita dicunt, quod iste expresse concedit propositum appellantis, cum dicit quod decimae fuerunt datae Leuitis in vsum. Tertio dicunt, quod errat aperte, cum dicit vsum in rebus vsu consumptibilibus ex Dei statuto non haberi. nam in illis rebus habetur vsus ex Dei statuto, quae ex Dei statuto datae sunt in vsum. sed multae res vsu consumptibiles datae sunt in vsum ex Dei statuto. Patet de decimis in auctoritate praeallegata: & de frugum initiis ibidem, cum dicitur: Vniuersa frugum initia, quae gignit humus, & domino deportantur, cedent in vsus tuos. Et Deuteronom. 24. Si vindemiaueris vineam tuam, non colliges temerantes racemos, sed cedent in vsus advenae, pupilliac viduae. Ex his patenter colligitur, quod nonnullae res vsu consumptibiles datae sunt in vsum, ex Dei statuto. Ergo in huiusmodi rebus habetur vsus ex Dei statuto. constitutur ergo: si huiusmodi res ex Dei statuto datae sunt in vsum, datae sunt in vsum iuris aut in vsum facti, non in vsum iuris: quia tunc Leuitae & sacerdotes & advenae, pupilli, ac viduae habuissent vsum, & alii dominium: quod est contra veritatem, & contra istum. ergo huiusmodi res vsu consumptibiles datae sunt in vsum facti. & per consequens vsus facti potest in rebus huiusmodi reperiri: quod iste negat. Ratio vero, per quam dictam assertionem provocare conatur, non valet (vt isti dicunt) quia quamuis de simplici vsu facti sub istis vocibus vel aggregatis mentio in sacra scriptura minime habeatur, tn de re non habetur mentio in scriptura: quia per simplicem vsum facti, non intelligit appellans nisi vsum, cui non est necessario annexum ius, quo quis valeat in iudicio litigare. & talis vsus est actus comedendi, bibendi, & huiusmodi, de quibus actibus saepe fiat mentio in scriptura. [In praedictis manifeste se fundat in falsis.] Dicunt quod hoc est scripturae sacrae falsitatem imponere, cum in praedictis non se fundet nisi auctoritate scripturae: sicut patet per verba obiectionis praemissae. [Quod enim Leuita in decimis tantum habuerint simplicem vsum facti.] Hoc non dixit appellans, qui in tota illa parte non intendit probare, nisi quod Leuitae habuerunt vsum in rebus consumptibilibus vsu. [Sed etiam dominium habuerunt.] Potest concedi & habuerunt dominium, sed non plenum. [Et aliud rem alicui in vsus eius.] Ex hoc sequitur, quod cui datur res in vsum, ille vsum rei potest habere: & ita si decimae fuerunt datae Leuitis in vsus, potuerunt habere vsum eorum. cetera sunt impugnata per istos, in isto & aliis capitulis.
units.tr: But first, these opponents say, he falsely charges the appellant. Second, he does not touch the objection and grants the point at issue. Third, he plainly errs when he says that no use of consumable goods is granted by God's decree. So, first, they say that he falsely charges the appellant when he asserts that the appellant said the Levites had only the simple use of the tithes. The appellant does not say this, but only that they had the use of such things, which is consistent with their having the right to use them. Indeed, from the fact that they had the use of such things it does not follow that they did not have ownership of them. Second, they say that he does not touch the objection, yet he concedes the point. For whoever is given something for use can have the use of that very thing given to him for use. But tithes of many consumable goods were given to the Levites for use, even according to him. Therefore the Levites could have had the use of those same tithes. The minor premise he grants himself; the major is proved by his own words. For, as appeared above in chapter 10, he says that where something is given to someone for use, not only the use of the thing but also ownership is understood to be given. Therefore when something is given for use, both use and ownership are given. But to whom the use of a thing is given, he can have the use of the thing. Therefore when a thing is given for use, he can have the use of the thing. And so, since tithes of certain consumable goods were given to the Levites for use, according to him the Levites could have had the use of the same goods. So they say he expressly concedes the appellant's point when he says that the tithes were given to the Levites for use. Third, they say he plainly errs when he says that no use of consumable goods is granted by God's decree. For use is granted by God's decree in those things which were given for use by God's decree. But many consumable goods were given for use by God's decree. This is clear about the tithes in the passage already cited, and about the firstfruits of the crops in the same place, where it says: "All the firstfruits of the crops which the ground yields, and which are brought to the Lord, shall go to your use." And in Deut. 24: "When you reap your vineyard, you shall not gather the bruised clusters; they shall go to the use of the stranger, the fatherless and the widow." From these passages it is plainly gathered that some consumable goods were given for use by God's decree. Therefore use of such goods is granted by God's decree. It follows, then: if such goods were given for use by God's decree, they were given either for use in law or for use in fact, not for use in law, because then the Levites, the priests, the strangers, the fatherless and the widows would have had use, and others ownership, which is contrary to the truth and to him. Therefore such consumable goods were given for use in fact. And consequently the use of fact can be found in such goods, which he denies. The argument by which he tries to provoke the said assertion does not hold (as these men say), because although no mention of the simple use of fact is found in Holy Scripture under these words or phrases, yet the thing itself is mentioned in Scripture. For by the simple use of fact the appellant understands nothing but a use to which the right by which one may litigate in court is not necessarily attached. Such a use is the act of eating, drinking and the like, and such acts are often mentioned in Scripture. [He manifestly founds himself on falsehoods.] They say that this is to charge Holy Scripture with falsehood, since in what he has said above he founds himself on nothing but the authority of Scripture, as is clear from the words of the objection given above. [For it is false that the Levites had only the simple use of fact in the tithes.] The appellant did not say this, since in that whole part he intends to prove nothing except that the Levites had the use of consumable goods. [But they also had ownership.] It may be conceded that they had ownership, but not full ownership.
