[And to give a thing to someone for his use.] From this it follows that whoever is given a thing for use can have the use of it; and so, if the tithes were given to the Levites for their use, they could have had the use of them. The rest is refuted by these men, in this and other chapters.

units.la: CAP. XXXVI.
units.tr: CAP. XXXVI.

units.la: Adhuc dicit haereticus praedictum, quod vbicunque, sacra scriptura de vsu rerum consumptibilium vsu loquitur: semper manifestat, quod quis rebus vsu consumptibilibus potest vti, sicut patet. 1. ad Tim. 5. Vbi apostolus dicit: Vtere modico vino. Et secundi Reg. 13. ibi. Filiae regis virgines vestimentis huiusmodi vtebantur. Et Num. 18. ibi: Vniuersa frugum initia quae domino deportantur, cedent in vsus tuos. Et parum post: Carnes vero in vsu tuo cedent. Et iud. 19. ibi. Habentes panem & vinum in tuos, & ancillae tuae vsus. Et Deut. 24. infine, & Iosue 5. ibi: Nec vsi sunt vestimenta, &c. Et Leuit. 7. ibi: In vsus varios, &c. & Hest. 5. & Exod. 28. Item et patet (secundum eum) per auctoritates sancti Clementis 11. q. 1. c. dilectissimis, & sancti Aug. dist 41. In ista parte nititur respondere ad quasdam auctoritates scripturae, quas pro se inducit appellans. & primo recitat eas: secundo respondet ad ipsas in parte immediate sequenti. Auctoritates patent de se. [Quod proprie conuenit & veraciter eis vti.] quia talis locutio aliquis potest vti rebus consumptibilibus vsu est propria & vera [cedent in vsus tuos] hoc est, ea vteris eis. CAP. XXXVII.
units.tr: The heretic further says the aforesaid: wherever Holy Scripture speaks of the use of consumable things, it always shows that someone can use consumable things, as is plain from 1 Tim. 5, where the apostle says: Use a little wine. And 2 Kings 13, there: The king's virgin daughters used garments of this kind. And Num. 18, there: All the first fruits of the crops that are brought to the Lord shall pass to your use. And a little after: But the flesh shall pass into your use. And Judg. 19, there: Having bread and wine for yourself and for the use of your maidservant. And Deut. 24 at the end, and Josh. 5, there: Nor did they use the garments, etc. And Lev. 7, there: For various uses, etc., and Esth. 5 and Exod. 28. Likewise it is also clear (according to him) from the authorities of St Clement, 11 q. 1 c. dilectissimis, and St Augustine, dist. 41. In this part he labours to answer certain passages of Scripture which he brings forward in his own support, citing them. First he recites them; second, in the part immediately following, he replies to them. The passages are clear in themselves. That it fits properly and truly to use them, because such an expression, that someone can use consumable things, is proper and true. Shall pass into your use, that is, you use them. CAP. XXXVII.

units.la: CAP. XXXVII.
units.tr: CAP. XXXVII.

units.la: Adhos dicendum, quod constitutio praedicta ad conditorem canonum, loquitur de vsu & de vti secundum quod diuiditur vsus contra dominium & proprietatem & contra vsum fructum & ius vtendi, secundum decretalem illam Exiit, qua dicit ista scilicet vsumfructum, proprietatem & ius vtendi ac simplicem vsum facti in temporalibus reperiri: cuius gratia dicta constitutio ad conditorem canonum fuit facta.
units.tr: To these things it must be said that the aforesaid constitution, addressed to the author of the canons, speaks of use and of using as it is divided against ownership and property, and against usufruct and the right of using, according to that decretal Exiit, which says that usufruct, property, and the right of use, and simple use of fact, are found in temporal things; for the sake of which that constitution was made for the author of the canons.

units.la: Hic ad praedicta respondet insinuans, quod aliter loquitur de vsu & vti, quam auctoritates scripturae superius allegatae.
units.tr: Here he responds to the aforesaid points, hinting that he speaks of use and of using in a different sense from the passages of Scripture cited above.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod hoc concedit iterum appellantis: & tamen ad obiectionem non respondet. Quod concedat intentum, patet, quia si iste accipit vsum & vti, secundum quod Nicolaus rectius accipit in decretali praedicta: & nihilominus ille, sicut ostensum est capitulo 32. concedit & dicit, quod Fratres habent vsum rerum consumptibilium vsu, scilicet alimentorum & vestimentorum. ergo ipse debet concedere, quod contingit vti rebus consumptibilibus vsu. Amplius, vsus diuisus contra proprietatem & dominium & contra vsumfructum & contra ius, non est nisi actus comedendi, bibendi vel huiusmodi, & facultas actus huiusmodi exercendi: quia vsus iuris non diuiditur contra ius vtendi, cum vsus iuris sit ius vtendi reb. alienis, &c. ergo si accipit vsum & vti secundum quod diuiditur contra prædicta, debet concedere quod rebus vsu consumptibilibus contingit vti. Secundo dicit, quod ad obiectionem appellantis non respondet, quia obiectio illa fundatur in hoc, quod scriptura sacra dicens quod talibus rebus consumptibilibus vsu contingit vti: & quod contra vsum earum vere & proprie loquitur. Ad hoc autem iste non respondet. Ex his etiam concludunt, quod sub abusu vocum introducere conatur errores. Error n. vt dicunt, quem principaliter in hac parte intendit inducere, est quod Fratres Minores non possunt manducare & bibere, & indui vestimentis, nisi habeant proprietatem & dominium earundem rerum. Si autem veteretur visitato modo loquendi in theologia & in scientiis philosophiæ, ad errorem prædictum nullum posset inuenire colorem. & ideo vtitur hoc nomine vsus in vna significatione, quæ non inuenitur nisi solummodo in scientiis legalib. in qua significatione accepto hoc nomine vsus simpliciter concedi debet, quod Fratres Minores non habent vsum rerum consumptibilium vsu: quia in illa significatione simpliciter debet concedi, quod nullarum rerum nec consumptibilium vsu nec non consumptibilium vsu habent vsum: quia non habent tale ius vtendi rebus alienis, &c. q; vocatur vsus: & ex hoc colorem inuenit ad concludendum, quod Fratres Minores nō habent vsum rerum vsu consumptibilium à proprietate & dominio separatum. Ex hoc concludens sophisticè, quod Fratres Minores non possunt manducare & bibere, & aliis reb. vsu consumptibilib. vti, nisi habeant proprietatem & dominium earundem rerum. quia vero ex æquiuocatione huius nominis vsus ita colorem inuenit ad persuadendum, licet sophisticè, prædictum errorem, vt isti dicunt. Ideo explicare nituntur, quæ positiones in hac materia dñt concedi in quo sensu, & quæ negari. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod cum ablative dicitur rerum consumptibilium vsu, semper iste ablatiuus vsu coniunctus cum verbo vel nomine consumendi sic dicendo res consumptibiles vsu vel reb. consumptibilib. vsu, vel in alio casu: vel sic, res quæ consumuntur vsu: Iste ablatiuus vsu accipitur pro comestione, inductione, bibitione vel aliquo alio tali actu, quo res consumitur. Nam cum panis consumitur vsu, nullus vsus potest dari, quo consumatur nisi comestio vel aliquis alius actus, qui non magis proprie potest vocari vsus, quam comestio. Et ita constat, quod iste ablatiuus vsu accipit pro comestione bibiti. ne & huiusmodi actib quib. res consumitur. Hoc visio dicunt, quod si in ista Fratres Minores non habent vsum rerum consumptibilium vsu: iste accusatiuus vsum accipiatur pro eadem significatione, in qua accipitur iste ablatiuus vsu: ista esset simpliciter neganda in illo sensu. Si vero iste accusatiuus vsum accipiatur pro alia significatione, puta pro vsu iuris, qui sic diffinitur: Vsus est ius vtendi rebus alienis: & sic dicunt quod est concedenda. Similiter eodem modo accipiendo vsum, hæc est concedenda: Fratres Minores non habent vsum rerum consumptibilium vsu à proprietate & dominio separatum. Aliter accipiendo vsum, ista debet negari, sicut in eadem significatione accipiendo vsum hæc est concedenda: Fratres Minores non habent vsum rerum consumptibilium vsu à proprietate seu dominio separatum: quia nullius rei habent talem vsum, sed quamuis tales negatiuæ in aliquo sensu concedantur: tamen affirmatiuæ, quæ eis contradicere secundum vocem videntur, non dñt absolute sine distinctione negari. Quamuis in vno sensu possint negari, & in alio concedi & minus necessarium est eas distinguere concedendo, quam negando, pro eo quod ex scriptura diuina, quæ maioris est auctoritatis, quam quæcunque legalis scia, absolute accipiuntur: quæ scriptura diuina nunquam vtitur hoc nomine vsus in illa significatione, in qua debent negari. Ex isto dicunt, quod theologi & philosophi, qui de scientiis legalibus se nullatenus intromittunt, absolute dñt concedere, quod aliquis potest habere vsum rerum consumptibilium vsu: & sine distinctione negare, quod nullus potest habere vsum rerum consumptibilium vsu, & quia de alia significatione vsus in qua affirmatiua potest habere vnum sensum salsum, & negatiua vnum sensum verum, se minime intromittunt. qui autem peritus est in scientiis legalibus nec affirmatiuam, nec negatiuam debet concedere vel negare, nisi præsuppositia distinctione huius nois vsus: cum in scientiis legalib. hoc nomen vsus in vtraq; significatione accipiatur, sc. pro vsu iuris, qui est ius vtendi reb. alienis, &c. & pro comestione, & bibitione & aliis actibus circa res temporales exercitis. & ita dicendum est de illis, qui hoc nomine vsus tam secundum q accipitur in theologia & philosophia, quam secundum q accipitur in scientiis legalibus, vti proponunt. Quia ergo iste impugnatus absolute negat, quod aliquis potest habere vsum rerum consumptibilium vsu, q scriptura diuina absolute determinat, quamuis non sub eadem serie verborum, dicunt quod erroneus, imo hæreticus est censendus: quia secundum B. Hiero. Ex verbis inordinate prolatis incurritur hæresis. Sicut quamuis posset credi, q licet diceret, q nullus posset manducare vel bibere, q hoc non sentiret: tamen si hoc diceret & pertinaciter defensaret, esset hæreticus reputandus, cum hoc scripturæ diuinæ, quæ est regula fidei, aduersetur aperte. Per prædictam et patet, quod purus theologus, & similiter purus philosophus absolute debet concedere, quod contingit vti reb.consumptibilib.vsu: & absolute negare, quod non contingit vti reb.consumptibilibus vsu, & idem videtur de iuristis: quia licet in iure hoc nomen vsus habeat tales duas significationes, de quibus dictum est prius, tamen forte non inuenitur in iure, quod hoc verbum vsu acceptum verbaliter vnquam accipiatur nisi pro actu qualis est comestio, bibitio, inhabitatio, equitatio, emptio, & hmoi, de quib. actib. non est æquiuocum sed vniuocū: & ideo dñt absolute concedere, q reb. vsu consumptibilib. contingit vti & absolute negare, q reb. vsu consumptibilib. non contingit vti. Si tñ inueniretur iure, q hoc verbum vti acceptū verbaliter nō p ise accipieretur pro tali actu circa rem temporalem exercito, sed et denotaret vel importaret vsum, qui est ius, quoddam positivum determinatum, de quo dictum est supra: sic cum distinctione deberent concedere, quod contingit uti omnibus rebus usu consumptibilibus: & quod non contingit uti omnibus rebus consumptibilibus usu: & eodem modo propositis cum distinctione deberent utramque negare: quia utraque haberet unum sensum verum & unum sensum falsum. Ex istis dicunt isti patere, quod quicquid sit de propositionibus, in quibus ponitur hoc nomen usus, & hoc verbum uti, nullo modo debet negari, quin Fratres Minores possint manducare & bibere & vestibus indui absque omni dominio & proprietate rerum. Et ita iste nihil habet de intento principali. Principalis intentio appellantis in hac parte est probare, quod contingit manducare, bibere, indui alios actus circa res usu consumptibiles exercere, abiique proprietate & domino earundem [Loquitur de usu & uti secundum quod dividitur &c.] & ita accipitur pro actu vendi, qualis est inhabitatio, comestio &c. quia sic non accipitur pro iure. Ergo accipitur pro actu circa rem temporale exercito. [Ac simplicem usum facti.] hic simplex usus facti, accipitur pro actu circa rem temporale exercito, quod hoc ut fiat non requirit, quod exercens ipsum habeat proprietatem eiusdem rei, nec posse dissensione quod est ius, nec usufructum, nec ius vendi, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare. Talis est actus comestio, induitio, inhabitatio. Potest n. aliquis etiam licite de licentia alterius inhabitare domum, & manducare, ac bibere, & actus huiusmodi exercere: licet non habeat aliquod praedictorum, & tunc habet tantum simplicem usum facti qui autem habet aliquod praedictorum, potest habere simplicem usum facti. Sed praeter simplicem usum facti, habet aliquid aliud, puta proprietatem, vel ius vendi, vel aliquid aliud [cuius gratia] scilicet ad replicandum secundum istos.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he again concedes what the appellant says, and yet he does not answer the objection. That he concedes the point is clear. If he takes use and to use in the sense in which Nicholas more correctly takes them in the decretal cited above, and nonetheless, as was shown in chapter 32, he concedes and says that the Friars have use of consumable things by use, namely of food and clothing, then he himself must concede that it is possible to use consumable things by use. Furthermore, use taken as divided off from property and dominion, and from usufruct and right, is nothing but the act of eating, drinking or the like, and the faculty of exercising such an act. For the use of right is not divided off from the right of using, since the use of right is the right of using another's goods, and so on. Therefore, if he takes use and to use as divided off from the things aforesaid, he must concede that consumable things can be used by use. Second, he says that he does not answer the appellant's objection, because that objection rests on this: that Holy Scripture, saying that it is possible to use such consumable things by use, speaks truly and properly against their use. But this man does not answer that. From these points they also conclude that he tries to introduce errors under an abuse of words. For the error, as they say, which he principally intends to induce in this part, is that the Friars Minor cannot eat and drink and clothe themselves with garments unless they have property and dominion over the same things. But if he kept to the customary way of speaking in theology and in the sciences of philosophy, he could find no colour for that error. And so he uses the word use in one meaning, which is found only in the legal sciences. In that meaning, if the word use is taken simply, it must be conceded that the Friars Minor do not have the use of consumable things by use, because in that meaning it must simply be conceded that they have the use of no things, neither consumable nor non-consumable, because they do not have such a right of using another's goods, and so on, which is called use. From this he finds a colour for concluding that the Friars Minor do not have the use of consumable things by use separated from property and dominion. Reasoning from this in a sophistical way, he concludes that the Friars Minor cannot eat and drink, and use other consumable things by use, unless they have property and dominion of the same things. Because, through the equivocation of this word use, he finds a colour for persuading, though sophistically, the aforesaid error, as these men say, they therefore strive to explain in what sense the propositions in this matter are to be conceded, and in what sense denied. To make this clear, they say it must be known that when the ablative is said by use of consumable things, that ablative by use is always joined with the verb or noun to consume, as in saying things consumable by use or consumable things by use, or in another case; or thus, things which are consumed by use. This ablative by use is taken for eating, drinking, or any other such act by which the thing is consumed. For when bread is consumed by use, no use can be given by which it is consumed except eating or some other act, which is not more properly called use than eating is. And so it is clear that this ablative by use is taken for the eating and drinking of food and for such acts by which things are consumed. They say that if, in the proposition that the Friars Minor do not have the use of consumable things by use, that accusative use is taken in the same meaning in which that ablative by use is taken, the proposition must simply be denied in that sense. But if that accusative use is taken in another meaning, namely for the use of right, which is defined thus: Use is the right of using another's things, then they say it is to be conceded. Likewise, taking use in the same way, this is to be conceded: the Friars Minor do not have the use of consumable things by use separated from property or dominion. Taking use in another way, this must be denied, just as, taking use in the same meaning, this is to be conceded: the Friars Minor do not have the use of consumable things by use separated from property or dominion, because they have no such use of any thing. But although such negative propositions are conceded in some sense, the affirmative propositions, which seem to contradict them according to the wording, must not simply be denied without distinction. Although they can be denied in one sense and conceded in another, it is less necessary to distinguish them by conceding than by denying, because they are taken absolutely from Holy Scripture, which has greater authority than any legal science; and Holy Scripture never uses this word use in that meaning in which they must be denied. From this they say that theologians and philosophers, who in no way meddle with the legal sciences, must simply concede that someone can have the use of consumable things by use, and must deny without distinction that no one can have the use of consumable things by use. And because they do not meddle with the other meaning of use, in which an affirmative proposition may have one false sense and a negative one a true sense, they do not meddle with it at all. But one who is skilled in the legal sciences must neither concede nor deny either the affirmative or the negative proposition, unless the distinction of this word use has first been made; since in the legal sciences this word use is taken in both meanings, namely for the use of right, which is the right of using another's things, and so on, and for eating, drinking and other acts exercised upon temporal things. And so it must be said of those who propose these things, taking this word use both in the sense in which it is taken in theology and philosophy and in the sense in which it is taken in the legal sciences. Therefore, since this opponent absolutely denies that anyone can have the use of consumable things by use, which Holy Scripture absolutely determines, although not in the same order of words, they say he is to be judged erroneous, indeed heretical; for according to Blessed Jerome, heresy is incurred by words uttered without order. Just as, although it might be believed that someone who said that no one could eat or drink did not mean it, yet if he said this and stubbornly defended it, he would have to be reckoned a heretic, since this openly contradicts Holy Scripture, which is the rule of faith. By the aforesaid it is clear that a pure theologian, and likewise a pure philosopher, must absolutely concede that it is possible to use consumable things by use, and absolutely deny that it is not possible to use consumable things by use. The same seems to hold for the jurists. For although in law this word use has the two meanings already mentioned, yet perhaps it is not found in law that this word use, when taken verbally, is ever taken except for an act such as eating, drinking, dwelling, riding, buying and the like; and concerning such acts it is not equivocal but univocal. And so they must absolutely concede that it is possible to use consumable things by use, and absolutely deny that it is not possible to use consumable things by use. Yet if it were found in law that this word to use, taken verbally, did not in itself signify such an act exercised upon a temporal thing, but rather denoted or implied the use which is a certain positive and determined right, of which it was said above, then they would have to concede with a distinction that it is possible to use all consumable things by use, and that it is not possible to use all consumable things by use; and likewise, with propositions so framed, they would have to deny both with a distinction, since each would have one true sense and one false sense. From these things they say it is clear that, whatever is the case with the propositions in which this word use and this verb to use occur, they must in no way be denied, so that the Friars Minor could not eat and drink and clothe themselves with garments without any dominion or property of things. And so this opponent has nothing to do with the principal intention. The principal intention of the appellant in this part is to prove that it is possible to eat, drink, dress and exercise other acts upon consumable things, without property and dominion of the same things. [He speaks of use and to use as they are divided, etc.] and so it is taken for an act of using, such as dwelling, eating, etc., because it is not taken in that way for a right. Therefore it is taken for an act exercised upon a temporal thing. [And the simple use of fact.] Here the simple use of fact is taken for an act exercised upon a temporal thing, which, in order to be done, does not require that the one exercising it have property of the same thing, nor a right of usufruct, nor the right of using by which one may sue in court. Such an act is eating, dressing, dwelling. For someone may lawfully, with another's permission, dwell in a house, eat and drink, and exercise acts of this kind, even though he has none of the aforesaid rights; and then he has only the simple use of fact. But one who has any of the aforesaid rights may have the simple use of fact too. Yet besides the simple use of fact he has something else, namely property, or the right of using, or something else [for the sake of which], namely, as these men say, to reply.

units.la: CAP. XXXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVIII.

units.la: Stetetiam haereticus ad ostendendum, quod pecunia inter res usu consumptibiles numeretur, allegat legem, quae expredictis patet.
units.tr: The heretic also, to show that money is counted among things consumed by use, cites the law which is set out above.

units.la: Hic recitat unam obiectionem de pecunia, qua conuenit uti: & tamen inter res usu consumptibiles numeratur. Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod de hoc in obiectionibus contra istam assertionem, quod non conuenit uti rebus consumptibilibus usu, nulla fit mentio.
units.tr: Here he recites one objection about money: it is fitting to use money, and yet it is counted among things consumed by use. But these opponents say that nothing is mentioned, in the objections against this assertion, about whether it is fitting to use consumable things by use. ## CHAPTER XXXIX.

units.la: CAP. XXXIX.

Constat autem quod secundum leges in rebus usu consumptibilibus, neque usufructus, neque ius vendi quod est seruitus, nec etiam ius vendi, quod non est seruitus, sed mere ius personale, potest cor stitus vel haberi, ut probatur. ff. de usufructu earum rerum, quae usu consumuntur l. 1. & l. 2. & ff. de iureiu. l. Sed & si possessori §. sed si rerum, cum multis similibus.
units.tr: It is established, however, that according to the laws, in things consumed by use, neither usufruct, nor the right of sale which is a servitude, nor even the right of sale which is not a servitude but purely a personal right, can be constituted or held. This is proved in ff. de usufructu earum rerum, quae usu consumuntur, l. 1 and l. 2, and ff. de iureiurando, l. Sed & si possessori, §. sed si rerum, with many similar passages.

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnatus redit ad declarandum intentionem suam, & ad completius respondendum auctoritatibus superius allegatis. Et primo ostendit, quod in rebus usu consumptibilibus neque usufructus, neque ius vendi, quod est seruitus, neque ius vendi quod non est seruitus, poterit reperiri, accipiendo usum & uti, ut leges accipiunt. Secundo conatur ostendere, quod nemo potest uti rebus consumptibilibus usu: & hoc in parte immediate sequeti. Tertio ostendit, quod consumptio potest in rebus huiusmodi reperiri, ibi: Licet autem in rebus. Quarto quasi dicta recapitulat ibi: Dicimus ergo. Quinto ad auctoritates inductas respondet ibi: Licet autem, ut praedictum est. Dicit ergo quod secundum leges, neque usufructus, neque ius vendi, quod est seruitus, neque ius vendi, quod non est seruitus, potest in rebus usu consumptibilibus reperiri. Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, ita non esse ad propositum sed istum cauillose procedere: quia ex hoc, quod usufructus non potest in omnibus rebus usu consumptibilibus reperiri: & ex hoc, quod est aliquod ius vendi speciale quod est seruitus. & aliquod quod non est seruitus, non potest in rebus usu consumptibilibus reperiri, non potest inferri, quod nullum ius vendi potest in rebus usu consumptibilibus reperiri. & ideo esto, quod leges dicant aliquod ius vendi non reperiri in omnibus rebus consumptibilibus usu, nihilominus concedendum est, quod aliquod ius potest in rebus talibus inueniri, sicut per iura diuina & humana superius est ostensum. [In rebus usu consumptibilibus] forte in aliquibus rebus usu consumptibilibus potest usufructus, vel saltem usus reperiri, sed non in omnibus. Aliquae enim res usu consumptibiles, sicut vestes & multae aliae locari possunt saltem ad tempus.
units.tr: In this part the opponent returns to explain his intention and to answer more fully the authorities cited above. First, he shows that in things consumed by use neither usufruct, nor the right of sale which is a servitude, nor the right of sale which is not a servitude, can be found, taking use and to use as the laws take them. Second, he tries to show that no one can use consumable things by use, and he pursues this in the part immediately following. Third, he shows that consumption can be found in things of this kind, there: Although in things. Fourth, he recapitulates what has been said, as it were, there: Therefore we say. Fifth, he answers the authorities introduced, there: Although, however, as has been said. He says therefore that according to the laws neither usufruct, nor the right of sale which is a servitude, nor the right of sale which is not a servitude, can be found in things consumed by use. But these opponents say that this is not to the point, and that he proceeds sophistically. For from the fact that usufruct cannot be found in all things consumed by use, and from the fact that there is some special right of sale which is a servitude and some which is not, which cannot be found in things consumed by use, it cannot be inferred that no right of sale can be found in things consumed by use. And so, even granting that the laws say a right of sale is not found in all consumable things, it must nevertheless be conceded that some right can be found in such things, as has been shown above by divine and human law. [In things consumed by use] perhaps usufruct, or at least use, can be found in some things consumed by use, but not in all. For some things consumed by use, such as clothes and many others, can be let out, at least for a time. ## CHAPTER XL.

units.la: CAP. XL.

Item nec quisquam uti talib. rebus potest, sumendo proprie uti. Usus enim seu uti si sumatur proprie secundum leges requirit quod ex re illa, in qua usum habere se asserit, vel qua vult uti, possit fructus vel utilitatem aliquam assequi, substantia salua rei: quod non potest in rebus usu consumptibilibus reperiri. Et ex hoc beatus Ioan. Chrysost. rationem reddit, quare mutuans pecuniam pro mercede pecuniam recipere nequeat licite: cum locans agrum vel domum hanc licite recipere possit, vt dictum est supra. Ex quibus patet, quod in rebus usu consumptibilibus usu habere nequeat: nec quis ipsis etiam uti possit, cum hoc iuri repugnet, & obuiet rationi.
units.tr: Likewise no one can use such things, if "to use" is taken in the proper sense. For use, or to use, if taken properly according to the laws, requires that from the thing in which one claims to have use, or which one wishes to use, one can obtain some fruit or advantage while the substance of the thing remains safe; and this cannot be found in things consumed by use. From this, blessed John Chrysostom gives the reason why one who lends money cannot lawfully receive money as payment, whereas one who lets out a field or a house can lawfully receive payment, as was said above. From these things it is clear that one cannot have use in things consumed by use, nor can anyone use them, since this is repugnant to law and opposed to reason.

units.la: Hic conatur ostendere, quod nemo potest uti rebus usu consumptibilibus: quia nullus potest habere fructum vel utilitatem aliquam ex huiusmodi rebus, salua rerum substantia: & hoc (dicit) est ratio, quare Chrysostomus dicit, quod non licet recipere mercedem pro pecunia mutuata.
units.tr: Here he tries to show that no one can use things consumed by use, because no one can have any fruit or advantage from such things while their substance remains safe. And this (he says) is the reason why Chrysostom says it is not lawful to receive payment for money lent.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod verba istius praedicta continent quatuor errores. Primus, quod non contingit uti rebus consumptibilibus usu proprie sumendo uti. Secundus est, quod qui vtitur proprie re aliqua, habet fructum vel utilitatem ex re, salua rei substantia. Tertius est, quod ex nulla re usu consumptibili potest quis habere fructu vel utilitate salua rei substantia.
units.tr: But these opponents say that the words of this passage contain four errors. The first is that it does not happen that one uses consumable things by use, taking "to use" in the proper sense. The second is that one who uses a thing properly has fruit or advantage from the thing while the substance of the thing remains. The third is that from no thing consumed by use can one have fruit or advantage while the substance of the thing remains.

units.la: Quartus quod per hoc, quod ex pecunia non potest quis habere vtilitatem, salua rei substantia, reddit rationem Chrysostomus, quare pro pecunia mutuata non licet mercedem recipere. Quod primum sit erroneum, ex his quae dicta sunt supra cap. 6. principaliter & communior & magis vsitata est significatio huius nominis vsus secundum quod accipitur pro comestione & actib. exercitis circa res temporales: Si illa significatio, secundum quam accipitur secundum iuristas pro quodam iure determinato, non minus proprie accipitur in illa significatione, quam in alia, ergo locutio scripturae sacrae, cum dicit aliquem habere vsum rerum consumptibilium vsu, non est minus proprie, quam locutio scientiarum legalium, cum dicunt aliquem habere vsum fundi, vel domus. Et confirmatur, quia scriptura diuina processit legales scientias: & per consequens ante fuit scriptura diuina, quia hoc nomen vsus acceptum pro tali iure: quia nunquam inuenitur, quod aliquis vsus fuerit hoc nomine vsus in illa significatione, antequam legales scientiae scriberentur. Scriptura ergo diuina, quae incepit a Moyse, precessit illam significationem huius nominis vsus. Quaeritur ergo, cum Moyses dixit Exo. 28. Faciès & feminalia lineà, vt operiat carnem verpitudinis suae a renibus vsque ad femora, & vtentur ea Aaron & filii eius. Et eum dixerit Num. 18. Vniuersa frugum initia, quae gignit humus, & quae Domino deportantur, cedent in vsum tuum. & post: Carnis vero in vsum tuum cedent. aut loquebatur proprie, aut loquebatur improprie. Si tunc loquebatur proprie: ergo semper postea talis modus loquendi fuit proprius, quia propter nouam significationem alicuius vocabuli superuenientem, non debet modus loquendi scripturae diuinae mutari, primo fuit proprius, postea censeri improprius. Ergo improprie dicitur. Adhuc quod hic vsus nominis significat ratione, scilicet foeminalibus, & carnibus, & similibus consumptibus vti. Si dicas: quod Moyses tunc loquebatur proprie hoc sine ratione dicis, quia tunc haec vocabula vsus & vti, non habebant significationem magis propriam, quam illa esset, qua vtebatur Moyses. Dicunt igitur isti, quod talis modus loquendi est proprius: nec vnquam fuit Doctor, vel expositor scripturae diuinae, qui dixerit quod locutio talis est proprie sumendo vti vere dicitur, quod quis potest vti rebus consumptibilibus, vt dicunt isti, contentus in verbis suis est, quod quia ut ita proprie loquendo, aliquis habet vsum ex re salua rei substantia, quod non hoc est ex vsu (vt dicunt isti) loquitur ex predictis: quia aliquis proprie loquendo vti, potest habere ex eis vtilitatem, salua eorum substantia. Talis enim, quod nullus ex re vsu consumptibili potest habere vsum vel vtilitatem, nisi ea consumat, sicut dicunt. Ideo pecunia capit in substantia de pecunia: quia substantia pecuniae per vsum consumitur, ideo pecunia non manet saluum vtenti. Falsum est, vt dicunt isti, quod sicut etiam sensui patet.
units.tr: The fourth is that by saying one cannot get advantage from money while its substance remains, Chrysostom gives the reason why it is not lawful to receive payment for money lent. That the first is erroneous follows from what was said above in chap. 6.: the principal, more common and more usual meaning of the word use is that which is taken for eating and for actions performed on temporal things. If that meaning, according to which the jurists take it for a certain determinate right, is no less properly taken in that sense than in another, then the language of Holy Scripture, when it says that someone has the use of consumable things by use, is no less proper than the language of the legal sciences when they say that someone has the use of a field or a house. This is confirmed, because Holy Scripture preceded the legal sciences; and consequently Holy Scripture existed before this word use was taken for such a right, since it is never found that any use had this meaning of the word before the legal sciences were written. Holy Scripture, therefore, which began with Moses, preceded that meaning of the word use. The question then is this: when Moses said in Exod. 28, "You shall make them linen breeches to cover the nakedness of their flesh, from the loins even to the thighs, and Aaron and his sons shall wear them," and when he said in Num. 18, "All the first fruits of the earth which they bring to the LORD shall be for your use," and afterwards, "the flesh of the wave offering shall be for your use," did he speak properly or improperly? If he then spoke properly, then such a manner of speaking was always proper afterwards, since on account of a new meaning of a word arising later, the manner of speaking of Holy Scripture ought not to change; what was first proper is not to be counted improper later. Therefore it is used improperly. Moreover, this use of the word signifies, by reason, that one may use linen breeches, flesh and similar consumables. If you say that Moses then spoke properly, you say this without reason, because at that time the words use and to use did not have a more proper meaning than the one Moses used. Therefore these opponents say that such a manner of speaking is proper, and no teacher or expositor of Holy Scripture has ever said otherwise. The opponent is content with his words, that because, speaking properly, someone has use from a thing while its substance remains safe, it does not follow from use (as these men say) that he speaks of the foregoing. For one who uses a thing properly can have advantage from it while its substance remains. For it is such that no one can have use or advantage from a thing consumed by use unless he consumes it, as they say. Hence money is consumed in its substance, because the substance of money is used up by use, and so money does not remain safe for the one using it. This is false, as these men say, and as even the senses show.

units.la: Quartus error secundum eos, quod loquendo, quare pro pecunia mutuata non licet mercedem recipere, quia illa ... evidenter.
units.tr: The fourth error, according to them, is this: in speaking, why it is not lawful to receive a reward for money lent, because that ... clearly.

units.la: Sed ratio est: quia per mutuum transfertur dominium pecuniae, quod non licet recipere vltra valorem rei, quod proprie habet valorem rei: propter quod pro vno pane, de cuius valore constat, non licet minus accipere vltra valorem panis, quando venditur panis. Vbi a non est notus valor rei, licet contrahentibus, secundum leges se decipere: quamuis apud Deum ille, cui notus est valor rei, si decipit alium, non sit innocens a peccato. Valor autem pecuniae notus est: & ideo quia transfert dominium pecuniae, nihil debet recipere vltra valorem pecuniae. & istam rationem tangit Glossa, 14. q. 2. c. Si fenerauerit, quia in illis quae consistunt in numero, pondere & mensura, transfertur dominium. In equo autem & domo non transfertur dominium: ideo pro equo & domo potest quis licite recipere, non autem pro his, quorum transfertur dominium vltra quid potest recipere. Sed forte dices, si locans domum vel equum potest recipere vltra valorem domus & equi, quia potest recipere domum & equum & aliquid vltra: quare etiam mutuans pecuniam non potest recipere, vltra valorem pecuniae, s. pecunia & aliquid vltra? Dicunt isti, quod locans domum vel equum retinet dominium domus & equi: & ideo potest repetere dominium & equum tanquam rem propriam: & pro illo quod concessit alteri, potest aliquid recipere, quia sic nunquam recipit valorem illius quod transtulit in alium. Sed mutuans pecuniam non potest repetere pecuniam tanquam rem propriam, quia tamen dominium pecuniae transtulit potest petere valorem pecuniae, sed non plus.
units.tr: But the reason is this: through a loan the ownership of the money is transferred, and it is not lawful to receive anything beyond the value of the thing, since money properly has the value of the thing. For this reason, when bread is sold, it is not lawful to take less than the value of the bread, for a single loaf whose value is known. Where the value of a thing is not known, the contracting parties are permitted by the laws to deceive one another, although before God he who knows the value of the thing is not innocent of sin if he deceives another. But the value of money is known, and so, because it transfers the ownership of the money, one ought to receive nothing beyond the value of the money. The Gloss touches on this reasoning at 14. q. 2. c. Si fenerauerit, because ownership is transferred in those things which consist in number, weight and measure. In a horse or a house, however, ownership is not transferred, and so one may lawfully receive payment for a horse or a house, but not for those things whose ownership is transferred; beyond the thing itself one may receive nothing. But perhaps you will say: if one who lets a house or a horse may receive more than the value of the house and the horse, because he may receive the house and the horse and something more besides, why should one who lends money not be able to receive, beyond the value of the money, the money and something more? They reply that the one who lets a house or a horse retains the ownership of the house and the horse, and so he may reclaim the ownership and the horse as his own property; and for what he has granted to another he may receive something, since in this way he never receives the value of what he has transferred to another. But one who lends money cannot reclaim the money as his own property, because he has transferred the ownership of the money; he may claim the value of the money, but no more.

units.la: [Vsus enim seu vti si sumatur proprie secundum leges requirit, &c.] Istud dicunt esse falsum; quia leges hoc non dicunt de vsu in omni significatione propria huius nominis vsus; quia si hoc dicerent, reprobarent modum loquendi scripturae diuinae; & per consequens non essent approbandae. Volunt tamen leges quod vsus iuris non inuenitur proprie in omnibus rebus consumptibilibus vsu. sed cum hoc stat, quod alius vsus quod vsus iuris inueniatur proprie in rebus consumptibilibus vsu. [quod non potest in rebus vsu consumptibilibus reperiri,] hoc dicunt esse falsum, sicut ostensum est. [Chrysost. rationem reddit &c.] Dicunt hoc esse falsum, sicut dictum est. [cum locans agrum vel domum &c.] Ratio, quare potest recipere mercedem, est: quia repetit domum vel agrum tanquam rem propriam. Pro potestate vero recipiendi vtilitatem ex agro vel domo recipit aliquid; non tamen valorem agri vel domus sed sed valorem illius potestatis, quam alteri concessit. [in rebus usu consumptibilibus haberi usus nequeat] hoc de quibusdam rebus usu consumptibilibus habet unum sensum verum, & alium falsum: quorum utrumque est proprius, quia utraque significatio usus est propria. [Nec quia ipsis etiam vti possit] dicunt: quod hoc nullum sensum verum habet: quia hoc verbum vti verbaliter sumptum non habet tot significationes, quod habet hoc nomen usus. Si tamen inveniretur quod haberet aliquem sensum verum, non propter hoc esset negandum ipsam habere sensum falsum.
units.tr: [For use, or to use, if taken properly, requires according to the laws, etc.] They say this is false, because the laws do not say this of use in every proper meaning of the word use; for if they did say so, they would reject the manner of speaking of divine Scripture, and consequently they would not be worthy of approval. They do, however, want it to be the case that the use of right is not found properly in all things consumed by use; but this is consistent with another use, namely that the use of right is found properly in things consumed by use. [which cannot be found in things consumed by use] they say this is false, as has been shown. [Chrysostom gives the reason, etc.] They say this is false, as has been said. [when one lets a field or a house, etc.] The reason why he may receive a reward is that he reclaims the house or field as his own property. For the power of receiving the benefit from the field or house, however, he receives something; yet not the value of the field or house, but the value of that power which he has granted to another. [that in things consumed by use no use can be had] this has one true sense concerning certain things consumed by use, and another false sense; both are proper, since both meanings of use are proper. [Nor because one can also use them] they say this has no true sense at all, since the verb to use, taken verbally, does not have as many meanings as the noun use. If, however, it were found to have some true sense, this would not on that account have to be denied to have a false sense as well.

units.la: CAP. XLV.
units.tr: CAP. XLV.

units.la: Licet autem in rebus talibus sc. usu consumptibilibus, usus vesti locum sibi proprie non vendicent. consumptio tamen & actus consumendi locum habet, ut dicit constitutio adducta: quae tamen non possunt dici simplicia: nec a rei quae consumitur, dominio separata, cum ipsa rei consumptione eius dominium pereat, & prorsus diffinat esse, ut probat dicta constitutio. Ad conditorem canonum, quae sic dicit. Praeterea si in rebus usu consumptibilibus posset usus constitui vel haberi, nequaquam simplex, nec a rei substantia proprietate seu dominio separatus, usus huiusmodi posset dici: cum per talem usum i.e. utendi actum, & in ipso actu, & cum ipso actu, res consumatur huiusmodi: nec actus sine ipsius rei consumptione esse valeat usus talis. Ex quo patet, quod usus talis nec simplex nec separatus a dominio potest dici: & hoc patet, cum per talem facti usum, proprietas & dominium ipsius rei perire noscitur.
units.tr: But although in such things, that is, things consumed by use, the use of the thing does not properly claim a place for itself, consumption and the act of consuming nonetheless have a place, as the cited constitution says; yet these cannot be called simple, nor separated from the ownership of the thing that is consumed, since with the very consumption of the thing its ownership perishes, and it wholly ceases to exist, as the said constitution proves. To the compiler of the canons, who says thus: Moreover, if in things consumed by use a use could be established or had, such a use could by no means be called simple, nor separated from the substance or property or ownership of the thing; since through such a use, that is, the act of using, and in the act itself and together with the act itself, things of this kind are consumed; nor can an act be a use of this kind without the consumption of the thing itself. From this it is clear that such a use cannot be called either simple or separate from ownership; and this is clear, since through such a use of the thing its property and ownership are known to perish.

units.la: In parte ista dicit, quod licet usus non possit in rebus usu consumptibilibus reperiri, in ipsis consumptio, & etiam actus consumendi poterit reperiri. & tamen actus consumendi in talibus non erit a proprietate seu dominio separatus: quod dicit esse probatum in constitutione. Ad conditorem, in qua ad hoc probandum, talem innuit rationem: Actus consumendi non separatur ab illo, quod per ipsum actum consumitur: sed dominium rerum usu consumptibilium consumitur per actum consumendi: ergo actus consumendi a dominio minime separatur.
units.tr: In this part he says that although use cannot be found in things consumed by use, consumption and also the act of consuming can be found in them. Yet the act of consuming in such things will not be separated from property or ownership, which he says has been proved in the constitution Ad conditorem, in which, to prove this, he suggests the following reasoning: the act of consuming is not separated from that which is consumed through that very act; but the ownership of things consumed by use is consumed through the act of consuming; therefore the act of consuming is in no way separated from ownership.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores circa praedicta tria facere moliuntur. Primo enim declarare conantur, quod ex illis, quae hic dicit iste impugnatus, apparet quod illa, quod dixit superius de usu & usu, impertinentia ad propositum sunt. Secundo ostendunt ipsum errare, cum dicit, quod actus consumendi in rebus usu consumptibilibus, non potest dici simplex, nec a proprietate seu dominio separatus. Tertio ratio, per quam praedictam assertionem probare conatur, multipliciter deficiat, nituntur ostendere. Quod igitur illa, quae superius iste impugnatus dixit de usu & usui impertinentia ad propositum sunt censenda, ostendunt. Nam principalis intentio appellatis est ostendere, quod actus comedendi, bibendi, induendi, & huiusmodi circa res consumptibiles usu, sive vocentur actus utendi, sive actus consumendi, sive actus abutendi, sive aliter quomodocunque; possunt a proprietate & dominio separari, & quod fratres Minores habent huiusmodi actus, qualitercunque vocentur absque dominio seu proprietate rerum circa res tales actus exercent. Tota igitur praecedens disputatio de usu & usu, an possint in rebus usu consumptibilibus reperiri, fuit impertinens. Nec iste impugnatus per ipsam intentionem appellantis evacuavit, sed ex ipsa in plures errores & abusus modos loquendi incidit manifeste (ut dicunt) quia cum hic dicat, quod actus consumendi non potest a proprietate seu dominio separari: ad ea rationes & exempla, quibus probat appellas, quod actus comedendi, bibendi, induendi & huiusmodi possunt a proprietate & dominio separari, sibi restat respondere. Secundo isti impugnatores ostendunt istum errare, cum dicit, quod actus consumendi in rebus usu consumptibilibus non potest a proprietate & dominio separari.
units.tr: But these opponents set themselves to attack the aforesaid three points. First they try to show that from what this author, whom they are attacking, says here, it appears that what he said earlier about use and use is irrelevant to the matter at hand. Second, they show that he errs when he says that the act of consuming in things consumed by use cannot be called simple, nor separated from property or ownership. Third, they try to show that the reasoning by which he attempts to prove the said assertion is faulty in many ways. That, then, what this author whom they attack said earlier about use and use is to be judged irrelevant to the matter, they demonstrate as follows. For the principal intention of the appellant is to show that the acts of eating, drinking, clothing, and the like, with respect to things consumed by use, whether they are called acts of using, acts of consuming, acts of misusing, or however else, can be separated from property and ownership; and that the Friars Minor have such acts, however they are named, and exercise such acts upon such things without ownership or property of the things. The whole preceding dispute about use and use, whether they can be found in things consumed by use, was therefore irrelevant. Nor has this author whom they attack refuted the appellant's intention itself; rather, from that very intention he has manifestly fallen (so they say) into many errors and abusive modes of speaking. For since he here says that the act of consuming cannot be separated from property or ownership, it remains for him to answer the reasons and examples by which the appellant proves that the acts of eating, drinking, clothing and the like can be separated from property and ownership. Second, these opponents show that he errs when he says that the act of consuming in things consumed by use cannot be separated from property and ownership.

units.la: Ad cuius evidentiam dicitur esse sciendum, quod actus consumendi quidam est illicitus & iniustus, & quidam est licitus, & quidam neque est iustus neque iniustus: & de quolibet istorum ostenditur, quod potest a proprietate & dominio separari. De iniusto quidem patet aperte. Nam si fur furatur panem & vinum, & consumit ea: talis habet actum consumendi iniustum absque dominio & proprietate: quia per hoc quod consumit panem & vinum, non acquirit dominium panis & vini.
units.tr: To make this clear, it must be understood that an act of consuming is sometimes unlawful and unjust, sometimes lawful, and sometimes neither just nor unjust; and of each of these kinds it is shown that it can be separated from property and ownership. Of the unjust kind this is plainly evident. For if a thief steals bread and wine and consumes them, he has an unjust act of consuming without ownership and property, because by consuming the bread and wine he does not acquire ownership of the bread and wine.

units.la: Similiter si creditor vestem impignoratam consumit, actus ille consumendi vestem est a proprietate & dominio separatus, & ita actus consumendi iniustus potest a proprietate & dominio separari. De secundo etiam ostenditur, scil. quod actus licitus consumendi potest a proprietate & dominio separari. Hoc patet per exempla inducta superius capitul. 4. de apostolis & habente usum fundi, ut comedentibus vuas & grana spicarum in agris & vineis alienis, tempore veteris legis: & de hospitibus, & de servis, & filiofamilias, & de sacerdotib. celebrantibus & consumentibus species sacramenti altaris: qui ea habent licitum actum consumendi res consumptibiles usu, quarum tamen non habent dominium & proprietatem. Tertio ostenditur idem de actu consumendi, quod neque est iustus neque iniustus. Nam bruta animalia habent actus consumendi res usu consumptibiles, quarum tamen non habent dominium & proprietatem. Similiter si etiam alienati a sensu consumant res alienas, ipsi habent actum consumendi neque iustum neque iniustum: quia talis actus non imputatur eis neque ad laudem, neque ad vituperium; & tamen per talem actum consumendi, proprietatem seu dominium non acquirunt. Verumetiam ante usum rationis saepe habent actum consumendi absque dominio seu proprietate. Tertio principaliter institutur ostendere, quod ratio, per quam probat, quod actus consumendi a proprietate seu dominio minime separatur, multipliciter deficit; imo erronea est censenda. Ad cuius evidentiam dicitur esse sciendum, quod aliquid consumi per aliquem actum potest multipliciter intelligi. Uno modo, quod aliqua res absoluta per actum aliquem desinat esse, sicut per digestionem cibi, & potus, cibus enim & potus vere desinunt, & per actionem ignis in res quas cohurit, illae res desinunt esse. Alio modo dicitur aliquid consumi per aliquem actum, quia per aliquem actum aliqua res absoluta desinit habere respectum vel appellationem aliquam respectivam. Sic dicitur pecunia consumi quādo expenditur: quia definit esse illius, cuius prius fuit: & tñ nulla res ibi aboletur. Definit esse, nec corrumpitur. Tertio dicitur aliquid consumi per aliquem actum, qui ad aliquem respectus vel appellatio respectiua definit inhaerere alicui vel verificari de aliquo. Et ideo non dicitur dominium alicuius consumi: imo sic dominium Dei respectu alicuius rei potest consumi. Deus definit esse Dominus illius rei, per hoc quod ipsa res consumitur: licet ipse Deus non desinat esse. Sed iste modus quantum ad rem non multum differt a secundo & primo, quia non potest reperiri sine secundo & primo simul. Dicunt etiam quod forte sunt alii modi, quibus potest aliquid consumi per aliquem actum: sed isti eis sufficiunt. Secundo dicunt esse notandum, quod aliquid dicitur esse separatum ab alio: quia alteri non vnitur, siue aliud sit in rerum natura, siue non. Sic dicuntur liquae substantiae separatae à materia: quia non vniuntur materiae: & non minus separatae essent à materia, si nulla materia esset in rerum natura. Sic etiam anima post mortem dicitur separata à corpore: quia non vnitur corpori vt forma: & non minus dicitur separata à corpore, post complatam incinerationem, & destructionem corporis quam ante. Ex his arguunt contra praedictam opinionem istius: & primo contra minorem, quam ponit explicite, cum asserit, quod ipsa rei consumptio reddit dominium perit: & p consequens consumitur. quia aut intendit, quod dominium consumitur per ipsam consumptionem, aut intendit quod dominium alicuius alterius perit ipsa consumptio. Primum, accipit quod debeat probare. Deberet enim probare, quod semper consumens habet aliquod dominium rei, quam consumit: quod non probat, sed accipit sine probatione. Vnde dicunt illi, quod saepe per actum consumendi nullum dominium consumentis perit, nec consumitur. Quando enim fur furatur panem & vinum, & consumit ipsa, nullum dominium furis perit, vel consumitur per actum consumendi illius. Ita est de seruis consumentibus res dominorum suorum, & de Fratribus Minoribus, qui consumendo res eis concessas, nullum dominium ipsorum Fratrum perit vel consumitur; quia in illis rebus nullum dominium habent. Si autem intendit, quod per actum consumendi perit & consumitur dominium alicuius alterius, quod non est consumens; nihil potest ex ipsa concludere; quia tunc maior esset falsa, virtute cuius deberet arguere. s. quod actus consumendi non separatur ab illo, quod per actum consumitur; quia accipiendo consumi per aliquem actum tertio modo, sic per actum consumendi consumitur vel perit. Accipiendo perire pro consumi, dominium actuale Dei perit in re illa, quae consumitur; hoc est per actum consumendi Deus desinit esse dominus actualiter rei consumptae secundum Augustinum, & tñ actus consumendi est separatus à dominio Dei; sicut per actum consumendi seruorum consumitur dominium dominorum, & tñ actus consumendi seruorum est separatus à dominio dominorum; similiter per actum consumendi subditorum consumitur dominium generale & mediatum, quod habent reges & principes; consumptis per actus subditorum; & tñ actus consumendi in subditis est separatus à dominio regum & principum. Patet ergo per hoc, quod dominium alterius consumentis perit vel consumitur per actum consumendi, non potest probari quod actus consumentis non est à proprietate dominio separatus. Nec valet dicere, quod ideo actus consumendi non est separatus à dominio, qa dominium rei consumptae non est, & nihil separatur ab eo quod non est. Hoc non valet, quia dum durat actus consumendi, durat dominium; & ideo licet actus consumendi non sit separatus à dominio post consumptionem, est tñ separatus à dominio ante consumptionis, quamdiu durat actus consumendi; tum quia licet dominium non esset, adhuc esset actus separatus à dominio; sicut anima dicitur separata à corpore, postquam corpus desinit esse, quia non est vnita corpori; ita ille actus diceretur separatus à dominio, quia nō est vnitus dominio. Sed adhuc forte dicet, sicut innuit, quod ideo actus consumendi non est à rei dominio separatus, quia substantia rei perit per actum consumendi. Sed dicunt isti, quod hoc non valet; quia per hoc quod substantia perit per actum consumendi, & substantia rei non est in alio, quam sit actus consumendi, bene potest probari quod actus consumendi non est separatus à substantia rei; sed ex hoc non sequitur, quod non sit separatus à dominio, quia nullum dominium rei est in consumente, & aliquod dominium est extra consumentem. Porro quia vt isti dicunt, ultima actio istius est, quod actus consumendi non est nec esse potest in rerum natura. & illud quod non est, non est separatum ab aliquo, ex quo sequitur quod actus consumendi non est separatus à dominio rei: ideo ipsi ostendunt, quod actus consumendi est in rerum natura; & per consequens si non est cum dominio rei, est separatus à dominio rei. Quod a. actus consumendi sit in rerum natura, ostendunt ad psens per dicta istius. Primo quia illud, quod nō est in rerū natura, nō habet locū in rebus vsu consumptibilibus; quia illud, quod non est, nusquam habet locum. sed secundum istū actus consumendi habet locū in rebus consumptibilibus vsu. ergo actus cōsumendi est in rerum natura. Item illud, per quod vera substantia perit vel consumitur, est vel fuit in rerum natura. sed secundum istum, per actum consumendi substantia rei desinit esse, & perit seu consumitur. ergo est vel fuit in rerum natura. Actus consumendi est in rerum natura; vel est coniunctus cum dominio, vel separatus à dominio; sed sape non est coniunctus dominio; ergo saepe est à dominio separatus. Consumptio tñ & actus consumendi locum habet. ergo actus consumendi est in rerum natura. Istis sic visis paucis verbis texte explicemus. [Quaedam non possunt dici simplicia] hoc, vt dicunt isti, sine ratione asserunt; quia secundum Nicolaum terminum aliquis est simplex vsus facti. ergo & aliquis est simplex actus consumendi; cum actum consumendi vocet Nicolaus vsum facti, sicut ostensum est prius; quia omnis actus consumendi est vsus facti, sed nō econuerso. & nō est maior ratio, quod aliquis vsus facti possit dici. dei simplex, q; actus consumendi. Vnde iste impugnatus deberet exprimere, quis visus est simplex visus facti. sed hoc (vt isti dicunt) non facit: quia hoc faciendo esset sibiipsi contrarius. [Nec à rei quae consumitur dominio separata] hoc improbatum est prius [cum ipsa rei consumptione eius dominium pereat] si loquitur de dominio consumptibilis, dicunt isti, quod saepe est falsum. Si loquitur de dominio alterius, non est ad propositum [si in rebus visu consumptibilibus &c.] hoc negant [cum per talem visum i.e. vtendi actum &c.] Ex hoc sequitur, q; actus vtendi est in rerum natura: quia per illud, q; nihil est, nihil perit [res consumatur huiusmodi.] Ex hoc & alio vero, sc. quod res non distat ab actu, potest inferri, q; actus non est separatus à substantia rei: sed ex hoc non sequitur, q; non est separatus à dominio rei. [Ex quo patet, quod visus talis &c.] dicunt quod hoc nullo modo patet [cum per talē facti visum proprietas & dominii ipsius rei perire noscatur.] Si loquitur de dominio consumentis, falsum est, propter falsam implicationem: quia implicat consumentem habere dominium rei, quod saepe est falsum. Si loquitur de dominio alterius, patet quod nihil concludit.
units.tr: Similarly, if a creditor consumes a garment given in pledge, that act of consuming the garment is separated from ownership and dominion, and so an unjust act of consuming can be separated from ownership and dominion. The second point is also shown, namely that a lawful act of consuming can be separated from ownership and dominion. This is clear from the examples cited above in chapter 4: the apostles and one who has the use of a field, who eat grapes and ears of grain in other people's fields and vineyards in the time of the old law; guests, servants, and sons under their father's authority; and priests who celebrate and consume the elements of the altar sacrament. These have the lawful act of consuming things that are consumed by use, though they do not have dominion and ownership of them. Third, it is shown of the act of consuming that it is neither just nor unjust. For brute animals have the act of consuming things that are consumed by use, though they do not have dominion and ownership of them. Likewise, if people who have lost their senses consume other people's goods, they have an act of consuming that is neither just nor unjust, because such an act is not imputed to them either as praise or as blame; and yet through such an act of consuming they do not acquire ownership or dominion. Indeed, even before the use of reason, children often have an act of consuming without dominion or ownership. Third, and chiefly, it is my intention to show that the reasoning by which they prove that the act of consuming is never separated from ownership or dominion fails in many ways; indeed it should be judged erroneous. To make this clear, it must be understood that something being consumed by some act can be understood in several ways. In one way, some absolute thing ceases to exist through some act, as food and drink cease to exist through digestion, and things that fire burns up cease to exist through the action of the fire. In another way, something is said to be consumed by some act when, through that act, an absolute thing ceases to have some relation or relative designation. Thus money is said to be consumed when it is spent, because it ceases to belong to the person to whom it previously belonged; yet no thing is destroyed there. It ceases to belong to him, but it is not corrupted. In a third way, something is said to be consumed by some act when, through that act, it ceases to inhere in something or to be true of something in respect of some relation or relative designation. And so the dominion of someone is not said to be consumed; rather, God's dominion over a thing can be consumed in this sense. God ceases to be the Lord of that thing when the thing itself is consumed, although God himself does not cease to exist. But this mode, as far as the thing is concerned, does not differ much from the second and first, because it cannot be found without the second and first at the same time. They also say that there are perhaps other modes by which something can be consumed by some act, but these are enough for them. Second, they say it must be noted that something is said to be separated from another when it is not united to it, whether or not the other thing exists in nature. Thus pure substances are said to be separated from matter, because they are not united to matter; and they would be no less separated from matter if no matter existed in nature. So too the soul after death is said to be separated from the body, because it is not united to the body as form; and it is no less said to be separated from the body after the body has been reduced to ashes and destroyed than it was before. From these points they argue against the aforesaid opinion of that man. First, they argue against the minor premise, which he states explicitly when he asserts that the very consumption of a thing causes the ownership to perish, and consequently it is consumed. For he means either that the ownership is consumed by the very consumption, or that the ownership of someone else perishes by the consumption. The first he takes for granted, when he ought to prove it. For he would have to prove that the consumer always has some ownership of the thing he consumes; this he does not prove but assumes without proof. Hence they say that often, by the act of consuming, no ownership of the consumer perishes or is consumed. For when a thief steals bread and wine and consumes them, no ownership of the thief perishes or is consumed by his act of consuming. So it is with servants consuming the goods of their masters, and with the Friars Minor, who, by consuming the goods granted to them, lose or consume no ownership of their own, because they have no ownership in those goods. If, however, he means that by the act of consuming the ownership of someone other than the consumer perishes and is consumed, nothing can be concluded from this; for then the major premise would be false, by whose force he ought to argue, namely that the act of consuming is not separated from that which is consumed by the act. For if we take "consumed by some act" in the third sense, then by the act of consuming something is consumed or perishes. If we take "perish" to mean "be consumed," God's actual dominion over that thing which is consumed perishes; that is, by the act of consuming, God ceases to be actually the lord of the consumed thing, according to Augustine. And yet the act of consuming is separated from God's dominion; just as by the act of consuming servants the dominion of masters is consumed, and yet the act of servants' consuming is separated from the dominion of masters. Likewise, by the act of consuming of subjects the general and mediate dominion that kings and princes have is consumed, being used up by the acts of the subjects; and yet the act of consuming in the subjects is separated from the dominion of kings and princes. It is therefore clear from this that, because the ownership of another consumer perishes or is consumed by the act of consuming, it cannot be proved that the act of the consumer is not separated from ownership and dominion. Nor is it valid to say that the act of consuming is not separated from dominion because the dominion of the consumed thing no longer exists, and nothing is separated from what does not exist. This is not valid, because while the act of consuming lasts, the dominion lasts; and so, although the act of consuming is not separated from dominion after the consumption, it is nevertheless separated from dominion before the consumption, as long as the act of consuming lasts. For even if the dominion did not exist, the act would still be separated from dominion, just as the soul is said to be separated from the body after the body ceases to exist, because it is not united to the body; so that act would be said to be separated from dominion, because it is not united to dominion. But perhaps he will still say, as he hints, that the act of consuming is not separated from the dominion of the thing because the substance of the thing perishes by the act of consuming. But these men say that this is not valid; because, from the fact that the substance perishes by the act of consuming, and the substance of the thing is not in anything other than the act of consuming, it can well be proved that the act of consuming is not separated from the substance of the thing; but it does not follow from this that it is not separated from the dominion, since no dominion over the thing is in the consumer, and some dominion lies outside the consumer. Moreover, since, as they say, the final point of his argument is that the act of consuming is not and cannot be in the nature of things, and what is not is not separated from anything, it follows that the act of consuming is not separated from the dominion of the thing; therefore they show that the act of consuming is in the nature of things, and consequently, if it is not with the dominion of the thing, it is separated from the dominion of the thing. That the act of consuming exists in the nature of things they show at present from his own statements. First, because what is not in the nature of things has no place in things consumed by use; for what is not has no place anywhere. But according to him the act of consuming has a place in things consumed by use. Therefore the act of consuming is in the nature of things. Again, that by which a true substance perishes or is consumed is or was in the nature of things. But according to him, by the act of consuming the substance of the thing ceases to exist, and perishes or is consumed. Therefore it is or was in the nature of things. The act of consuming is in the nature of things; it is either joined with dominion or separated from dominion; but it is often not joined with dominion; therefore it is often separated from dominion. Yet consumption and the act of consuming do have a place. Therefore the act of consuming is in the nature of things. Having seen these points, let us explain the text in a few words. [Some things cannot be called simple:] they assert this, as these men say, without reason; for according to Nicolaus, a term is "a simple use of a fact." Therefore some act of consuming is also a simple act, since Nicolaus calls the act of consuming a use of a fact, as was shown before; for every act of consuming is a use of a fact, but not conversely. Nor is there any greater reason why some use of a fact could be called simple than an act of consuming. Hence the author under attack ought to state which sight is a simple sight of a fact. But this (as these men say) he does not do, because by doing so he would be contrary to himself. [Nor is it separated from the dominion of the thing consumed:] this has been disproved before. [since the very consumption of the thing causes its ownership to perish:] if he speaks of the ownership of the consumable thing, these men say that this is often false. If he speaks of the ownership of another, it is not to the point. [if in things consumed by use etc.:] this they deny. [since by such a use, that is, the act of using etc.:] From this it follows that the act of using is in the nature of things, because by that which is nothing nothing perishes. [the thing is consumed in this way.] From this and another truth, namely that the thing does not differ from the act, it can be inferred that the act is not separated from the substance of the thing; but it does not follow from this that it is not separated from the dominion of the thing. [From which it is clear that such a sight etc.:] they say that this is clear in no way [since by such a sight of the fact the ownership and dominion of the thing itself is known to perish.] If he speaks of the dominion of the consumer, it is false, on account of the false implication: for it implies that the consumer has dominion over the thing, which is often false. If he speaks of the dominion of another, it is clear that he concludes nothing.

units.la: CAP. XLII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLII.

units.la: Dicimus ergo, quod decretalis Ad conditorem canonum de visu & vti loquitur, sicut decretalis Exiit loquebatur qua de ipsis loquitur secundum quod leges loquuntur, secundum quas impossibile est loquendo de illa proprie, sicut dicta decretalis Ad conditorem loquitur, & dicit expressè in §. Rursus nec simplex visus facti, ibi, cum dicit. Cum enim vti re aliqua nihil sit aliud proprie &c. Locum habeant in rebus consumptibilibus visu: sed in ipsis consumptio & consumendi actus locum habent, vt probatur ff. de usufructu earum rerum quae visu consumuntur. l. hoc senatus. §. 1. & §. 2. ff. de iureiurando. l. sed & si possessori §. sed si rerum.
units.tr: We say, then, that the decretal Ad conditorem canonum speaks of use and usufruct as the decretal Exiit did, in which those things are spoken of according to the way the laws speak, according to which it is impossible to speak of them properly, as the said decretal Ad conditorem speaks, and states expressly in §. Rursus nec simplex visus facti, where it says: "For since to use a thing is properly nothing other than..." They have a place in consumable things through usufruct; but in such things consumption and the act of consuming take place, as is proved in the Digest on the usufruct of those things which are consumed by use: l. hoc senatus §1 and §2 ff. de iureiurando; l. sed & si possessori §. sed si rerum.

units.la: Hic epilogat vel explicat quaedam dicta prius, dicens quod constitutio Ad conditorem loquitur, sicut decretalis Exiit: & ita loquitur sicut leges loquuntur, secundum quas visus & vti proprie sumendo non habet locum in rebus consumptibilibus visu, sed consumptio & actus consumedi.
units.tr: Here he sums up or explains some things said earlier, saying that the constitution Ad conditorem speaks as the decretal Exiit does, and speaks as the laws speak, according to which use and usufruct, taken properly, do not apply to things consumed by use, but consumption and the act of consuming do.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, ipsum falsum asserere cum dicit quod secundum leges visus & vti proprie sumendo non habent locum in rebus visu consumptibilibus: quod ad praesens per unicam legem saepe allegatam ostendunt. Dicit enim lex, q; qui fundi visum nudum habet, nihil ulterius habere intelligitur quam vt oleribus, pomis, floribus, faeno, stramentis, lignu ad visum quotidianum utatur. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod oleribus, pomis, floribus & huiusmodi, quae sunt res visu consumptibiles, secundum leges contingit vti, & quod in illis visus & vti proprie locum habent: cum dicit, ad visum quotidianum utatur. l. oleribus, pomis &c. Nec lex loquitur ibi improprie, cum ibi utatur visu & vti in significatione communi, & quam primo habebant haec vocabula, & in quo visitantur in omni facultate, quae utitur istis vocabulis.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he asserts what is false when he says that, according to the laws, use and usufruct taken properly do not apply to things consumed by use. For the present they show this by a single law, often cited. For the law says that whoever has a bare use of an estate is understood to have nothing more than the right to use the herbs, fruit, flowers, hay, straw and wood for his daily needs. From these words it is clearly gathered that, according to the laws, one may use herbs, fruit, flowers and such things, which are consumable by use, and that in these use and usufruct properly taken do have application, since the law says "may use for daily needs." l. oleribus, pomis etc. Nor does the law speak improperly there, since it uses use and usufruct in their common meaning, the meaning these words first had, and as they are found in every field that employs these words.

units.la: Istis sic visis paucis verbis textum explicemus. [Loquendo de illis proprie] etiam proprie loquendo visus & vti habent locum in rebus consumptibilibus visu.
units.tr: Having looked at these matters, let us briefly explain the text. Speaking of those things properly, even speaking properly, use and usufruct have application to things consumable by use.

units.la: CAP. XLIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLIII.

units.la: Licet autem, vt praedictum est, in rebus visu proprie loquendo locum non habeat: tamen frequenter dicitur, quod quis in illis visum habeat vel eis utatur: sed quoties hoc contingit, visus vel vti pro rei consumptione debent sumi. Sic dicimus, quod quoties sacra scriptura visum in talibus rebus visu consumptibilib. attribuit, pro rei consumptione ipsum sumit. vt patet in illa auctoritate, Vtere modico vino. Sumitur enim vti pro consumere, id est pro bibere. Constat enim vinum bibendo consumi: & per hoc patet responsio ad alias auctoritates inductas. Hoc saluo, quod illa Numeri 18. capitulo, vbi dicitur, Vniuersa frugum initia quae domino deportantur, cedent in visus tuos, falso modo inducitur, vt superius est ostensum.
units.tr: Although, as has been said, use in the strict sense has no place in things, nevertheless it is often said that someone has or uses them. But whenever this happens, "have" or "use" must be taken to mean the consumption of the thing. So we say that whenever Sacred Scripture attributes the use of consumable things to someone, it takes the word in the sense of consuming the thing, as is clear from the passage, "Use a little wine" (1 Tim. 5). For "use" is taken there to mean "consume", that is, "drink", since wine is plainly consumed by drinking. By this the answer to the other passages cited is also clear, except that the passage in Numbers 18, where it says, "All the firstfruits of the grain which are brought to the Lord shall be yours to use," is wrongly cited, as was shown above.

units.la: Hic ad auctoritates inductas supra capitul. 36. expressius, quam ante, respondet dicens, quod omnes illae auctoritates accipiunt visum & vti pro rei consumptione: & ita improprie.
units.tr: Here, in answer to the passages cited above in chapter 36, he replies more explicitly than before, saying that all those passages take "use" and "have" to mean the consumption of the thing, and so improperly.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod hic modos loquendi destruit approbatos, quos negando nititur seminare. Nunquam enim aliquis ante istum ausus fuit dicere, quod scriptura sacra asserens visum in rebus visu consumptibilibus reperiri, & quod huiusmodi rebus contingit vti, loqueretur improprie. Eadem enim facilitate, qua iste dicit, quod scriptura sacra loquitur impropre de visu, & quod hoc nomen visus habet aliam significationem secundum leges, quam sit illa secundum quam accipitur in scriptura diuina: posset dici, quod scriptura sacra loquitur semper improprie, quandocunq; vtitur aliquo vocabulo, quod in aliqua alia facultate inuenitur aliam significationem habere: & ita scriptura diuina loqueretur improprie dicens, quod Deus creauit coelum & terram: quia ibi aliter accipitur verbum creandi, quam in iure canonico, vbi capitur scilicet pro promouere ad aliquam dignitatem: sicut dicitur, papa creare cardinales. Loqueretur etiam scriptura improprie dicens: In principio erat verbum, quia principium saepe accipitur pro principio magnitudinis, secundum quam significationem non habet veritatem dictum Euangelistae. Manifeste igitur decorat scripturae diuinae, qui dicit, quod scriptura diuina loquens de visu rerum consumptibilium, loquitur improprie, quia quandoque leges aliter accipiunt visum: cum citius deberet dici e conuerso, quod leges loquuntur improprie, vbi accipiunt visum in alia significatione, quam in accipitur in scriptura diuina.
units.tr: But these opponents say that this man destroys approved modes of speech, which he tries to sow by denying them. For no one before him has ever dared to say that when Sacred Scripture asserts that use is found in things consumed by use, and that it happens to be used with such things, it speaks improperly. For with the same ease with which he says that Scripture speaks improperly of use, and that this word "use" has a different meaning in the law from that in which it is taken in divine Scripture, one could say that Scripture always speaks improperly whenever it uses any word that has a different meaning in some other discipline. Thus divine Scripture would speak improperly in saying that God created heaven and earth, since the verb "create" is taken there differently from its sense in canon law, where it means to promote someone to a dignity, as when we say that the pope creates cardinals. Scripture would also speak improperly in saying, "In the beginning was the Word," since "beginning" is often taken to mean the beginning of magnitude, and in that sense the statement of the Evangelist would not be true.
