Clearly, then, he does a disservice to divine Scripture who says that Scripture, speaking of the use of consumable things, speaks improperly because at times the laws take "use" differently. It would have been far more fitting to say the reverse: that the laws speak improperly where they take "use" in a different sense from that in which it is taken in divine Scripture.

units.la: Nam saepe qn vocabulum transfertur, sicut homo, primo significat animal rationale, de qua significatione transfertur ad significandum hominem pictum: & ista significatio, qua significat hominem pictum, dicitur significatio hominis impropria. Prima a significatio hominis dicitur propria: & ita est de aliis. Sed hoc vocabulum vsus non transferebatur de significatione, secundum quam accipiunt leges, vbi loquuntur de vsu iuris, aliter quam loquitur scriptura diuina ad significationem illam secundum quam accipitur in scriptura sacra. Nequaquam enim scriptura sacra accepit vocabula quaecunque a legibus: sed forte e contrario conditores legum hoc vocabulum vsus a significatione prima, quae est eadem in scriptura sacra, & in medicina, scientia morali, ac vulgari modo loquendi, in quibus conditores legum periti fuerunt, saltem in morali scientia & vulgari modo loquendi, transferendo propter aliquam similitudinem, vel aliquam aliam causam ad quandam aliam significationem, secundum quam accipitur in legibus, & non in scriptura sacra. Ergo significatio secundum quam accipitur hoc vocabulum vsus in legibus & non alibi, ante deberet dici impropria, quam significatio secundum quam accipitur in scriptura sacra, & ita ante deberet dici, quod leges loquuntur improprie, cum in significatione secunda vtuntur vocabulo vsus, quam scriptura sacra, quae vtitur eodem vocabulo vsus in significatione, de qua ad aliam vocabulum vsus est translatum. Ex eodem patet, quod cum leges vtuntur vocabulo in significatione vsus in vtraque significatione: secundum quod accipitur in sacra scriptura, & secundum quod tantummodo accipitur in legibus: citius deberet dici, quod leges ipsae loquuntur improprie, qui accipiunt vsum illo modo, quo nequit in omnibus rebus vsu consumptibilibus reperiri: quando accipitur vsus pro rei consumptione, quia qui accipiunt vsum pro rei consumptione, accipiunt vsum, sicut accipiunt vsum, qui loquuntur in scriptura sacra. Est tamen aduertendum, quod vsus in scriptura sacra non solum accipitur pro rei consumptione, sed etiam pro aliis actibus, qui non sunt rei consumptiones: quia vsus est nomen commune vel vniuocum vel aequiuocum ad consumptionem rei, & ad alios actus, qui non sunt consumptiui. Ex his dicunt isti patere, quod modos loquendi destruit approbatos: quibus destructis manifestos errores, s. quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus non contingit vti, quod nullus potest habere vsum facti rerum vsu consumptibilium a dominio separatum, & alios multos conatur inducere. Quare dicunt, quod et si sensum verum haberet, sicut non habet, secundum quod alibi est monstratum, doctrina sua tanquam scripturae sacrae non congruens, sed aduersans, esset minime sustinenda.
units.tr: For often, when a word is transferred, as "man" first signifies a rational animal, and from that meaning it is transferred to signify a painted man, the latter meaning is called the improper meaning of "man". The first meaning of "man" is called the proper meaning, and so it is with other words. But this word use was not transferred from the meaning in which the laws take it, when they speak of the use of law, differently from the way Scripture speaks of it, to that sense in which it is taken in Sacred Scripture. For Sacred Scripture by no means takes whatever words it uses from the laws. Rather, on the contrary, the framers of the laws, who were skilled in medicine, in moral science and in common speech (in which the framers of the laws were skilled, at least in moral science and common speech), perhaps took this word use from its first meaning, which is the same in Sacred Scripture, in medicine, and in ordinary speech, and transferred it, on account of some likeness or some other cause, to another meaning in which it is taken in the laws and not in Sacred Scripture. Therefore the meaning in which this word use is taken in the laws and nowhere else ought to be called improper before the meaning in which it is taken in Sacred Scripture. And so it ought first to be said that the laws speak improperly, since in the second sense they employ the word use, whereas Sacred Scripture employs the same word use in the sense from which the word use was transferred to another meaning. From the same it is clear that when the laws use the word in the sense of use, in both senses, that in which it is taken in Sacred Scripture and that in which it is taken only in the laws, it ought rather to be said that the laws themselves speak improperly, since they take use in that way in which it cannot be found in all things consumed by use. This is so when use is taken to mean the consumption of a thing, because those who take use to mean the consumption of a thing take use just as those who speak in Sacred Scripture take it. It must be noted, however, that use in Sacred Scripture is taken not only for the consumption of a thing but also for other acts which are not consumptions of a thing, since use is a common name, either univocal or equivocal, for the consumption of a thing and for other acts that do not consume. From these points, these men say, it is clear that he destroys approved modes of speech, and that once these are destroyed he tries to introduce manifest errors: namely, that one cannot use things consumed by use, and that no one can have the use of the fact of things consumed by use separated from ownership. And he tries to introduce many others. Therefore they say that even if his doctrine had a true sense, which it does not, as has been shown elsewhere, it would be by no means to be upheld, since it does not agree with Sacred Scripture but opposes it.

units.la: [Quoties hoc contingit vsus vel vti pro rei consumptione deberet sumi.] Dicunt isti, quod consumptio dupliciter accipi potest: uno modo pro consumpto esse, alio modo pro motu seu alteratione praecedente consumptum esse. Si accipiatur primo modo hic consumptio, dicunt illum eriare cum dicit, quod quotiens hoc contingit &c. quia sic scriptura sacra vtitur vsu & vti aliter, quasi pro tali significatione i.e. pro consumpto esse, sicut patet Exod. 18. ibi: Vtetur eis. (sc. foeminalibus.) Aaron & filii eius. & 29. ibi, Vestem autem sanctam, quam vtetur Aaron, habebunt filii eius post eum. Et 39. ibi; Vestes quoque, quib. sacerdotes vtuntur &c. Et Deut. 22. ibi; Nec vir vtetur veste foeminea. Secundo Reg. 13. ibi; Huiusmodi enim filiae regis virgines vestibus vtebantur, & in multis aliis locis. Accipiendo autem consumptionem pro motu vel alteratione praecedente, adhuc non est verum, accipiendo consumi in prima significatione, de qua dictum est supra c. 7. quia saepe dicitur, quod vtitur quis pecunia, quae tamen illo modo nequaquam consumitur.
units.tr: [Whenever this happens, "use" or "to use" must be taken to mean the consumption of the thing.] These men say that consumption can be understood in two ways: in one way as the state of having been consumed, and in another as the motion or alteration that precedes the state of having been consumed. If "consumption" is taken here in the first sense, they say he is mistaken when he says, "whenever this happens, etc.", since Scripture uses use and to use otherwise, as if in such a sense, that is, in the sense of having been consumed. This is clear from Exodus 28, "Aaron and his sons shall use them," and Exodus 29, "The holy garment which Aaron shall use shall belong to his sons after him," and Exodus 39, "The garments also which the priests use, etc." Also Deuteronomy 22, "A man shall not use a woman's garment." And 2 Kings 13, "For the king's virgin daughters wore such garments," and in many other places. But if "consumption" is taken to mean a motion or alteration that precedes it, it is still not true, if "consume" is taken in the first sense, which was discussed above in chapter 7, since it is often said that someone uses money, which nevertheless is not consumed in that way at all.

units.la: [Quotiens sacra scriptura vsum in talibus rebus vsu consumptibilibus attribuit pro rei consumptione ipsum sumit.] falsum est accipiendo consumptionem primo modo, sicut patet per auctoritates prius inductas: & forte secundo modo etiam accipiendo est falsum. Sed de hoc est ad praesens minime differendum. [Vt patet in illa auctoritate, vtere modico vino: sumitur enim vtere pro consume.] Scilicet secundo modo accipiendo consumere. [Constat enim vinum bibendo consumi] secundo modo accipiendo consumi [falso modo inducitur.] Dicunt quod recte inducitur: quia per eam probatur aperte, quod contingit carnium vsum habere, quae inter res vsu consumptibiles computantur.
units.tr: [Whenever Sacred Scripture attributes use to such consumable things, it takes it to mean the consumption of the thing.] This is false if "consumption" is taken in the first sense, as is clear from the passages cited earlier, and perhaps it is also false if taken in the second sense. But this is not to be discussed at present. [As is clear from that passage, "use a little wine": for "use" is taken to mean "consume".] That is, taking "consume" in the second sense. [For it is plain that wine is consumed by drinking.] Taking "consumed" in the second sense. [Wrongly cited.] They say that it is rightly cited, because through it is openly proved that it is possible to have the use of meats, which are counted among things consumed by use.

units.la: CAP. XLIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLIV.

units.la: Adhuc iste haereticus dicit, quod dicere quod sunt aliquae res vsu consumptibiles, & tamen non contingit illis vti, contradictionem implicat manifestam.
units.tr: Furthermore, this heretic says that to say there are some things consumable by use, and yet it is not possible to use them, implies a manifest contradiction.

units.la: Hic respondet ad aliam obiectionem, quam tangit appellans, & primo ponit eam: secundo respondet in parte sequenti. Obiectio autem de se patet.
units.tr: Here he answers another objection, which the appellant touches on. He first sets it out and then answers it in the following part. The objection is clear in itself.

units.la: Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt isti impugnatores, quod quando quis absolute sine omni distinctione negat aliquam propositionem multiplicem habentem diuersos sensus, intelligitur negare omnem sensum eiusdem, nisi consuetum sit talem propositionem accipi in uno sensu & non in alio. Tunc enim propter consuetudinem accipiendi propositionem multiplicem in uno sensu & non in alio, intelligitur saepe negare sensum consuetum, & non aliam. Sed ista propositio non contingit vti rebus vsu consumptibilibus: vel habet unum sensum tantum, vel si habet plures, ille sensus in quo accipitur vti illo modo quo accipitur in scriptura sacra est magis consuetus, vel non minus vsitatus quam alius. Ergo qui negat istam propositionem absolute sine distinctione intelligitur omnem sensum, vel saltem communem sensum negare. Sed iste impugnatus propositionem illam: contingit vti rebus consumptibilibus vsu: absolute sine omni distinctione saepe negauit. Ergo potuit merito appellans sibi imponere, quod ipsam negauit vniuersaliter: & sic accepto vsu, sicut in sacra scriptura accipitur, quia sic accipitur magis communiter. Sed sic contradictionem implicat manifestam dicere, quod sint aliquae res vsu consumptibiles, & tamen non contingit illis vti: quia nullae res dicuntur vsu consumptibiles, nisi quia contingit illis vti. Ergo si sunt res vsu consumptibiles, & non contingit illis vti, contingit illis vti, & non contingit illis vti. [Contradictionem implicat] hoc est verum accipiendo vsum & vti, vt accipiuntur in theologia, qui est consuetus modus accipiendi praedicta vocabula.
units.tr: To make this plain, these opponents say that when someone absolutely, without any distinction, denies a proposition that has several senses, he is understood to deny every sense of it, unless it is customary to take such a proposition in one sense and not in another. For then, because of the custom of taking a proposition in one sense and not in another, he is often understood to deny the customary sense and not the others. But the proposition "it is possible to use things consumable by use" either has only one sense, or, if it has several, the sense in which "use" is taken as it is taken in Holy Scripture is more customary, or is no less in use than another. Therefore whoever denies that proposition absolutely, without distinction, is understood to deny every sense, or at least the common sense. But this opponent has often denied that proposition, "it is possible to use consumable things by use," absolutely and without any distinction. Therefore the appellant could rightly impute to him that he denied it universally, taking "use" as it is taken in Holy Scripture, because it is taken there more commonly. But to say that there are some things consumable by use and yet it is not possible to use them implies a manifest contradiction, because no things are called consumable by use except because it is possible to use them. Therefore, if there are things consumable by use and it is not possible to use them, then it is possible to use them and it is not possible to use them. [It implies a contradiction.] This is true, taking "use" and "to use" as they are taken in theology, which is the customary way of taking the aforementioned words.

units.la: CAP. XLV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLV.

units.la: Refectio per hoc, vt ignarus & inscius, legislatorem arguit, qui rubricam posuit de vsufructu earum rerum quæ vsu consumuntur. Vnde constitutio loquitur secundum quod legislator & leges plerunq; loquuntur, sumendo vsum pro abusu, i.e. pro consumptione rei: quia nec alius vsus, nisi videl. consumptio in rebus vsu consumptibilibus esse potest. & ideo dicit lex. ff. de iureiur. d. etiam possessionis. §. sed si rerum: Sed si rerum, in quibus vsufructus constitui non potest, propter abusum, i.e. propter rei consumptionem &c. & glossa super rubr. ff. de vsufructu earum rerum, quæ vsu consumuntur, super illo verbo vsu, quæ dicit, i.e. quasi vsu. Expresse ibi innuit, quod vsus ibi ponitur improprie.
units.tr: The refutation, on the ground that he is ignorant and unaware, accuses the lawgiver who placed the title on the usufruct of those things which are consumed by use. Hence the constitution speaks as the lawgiver and the laws generally speak, taking use for abuse, that is, for the consumption of a thing, since there can be no other use in things consumed by use than their consumption. And so the law says in Dig. de iureiur., l. etiam possessionis, §. sed si rerum: "But if things are such that a usufruct cannot be established in them, because of abuse, that is, because of the consumption of the thing," etc. And the gloss on the title Dig. de usufructu earum rerum, quae usu consumuntur, on the word usu, which says "i.e. as if by use," there clearly hints that use is here taken improperly.

units.la: Hic respondet ad obiectionem, dicens: quod ex ipsa sequitur, quod legislator male posuit rubricam de vsufructu &c.
units.tr: Here he answers the objection, saying that it follows from the thing itself that the lawgiver wrongly placed the title on the usufruct, etc.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod ipse non euadit, quin ex verbis suis, quæ asserit in constitutione ad conditorem, negando simpliciter posse aliquem vti rebus consumptibilib. vsu: sequitur quod contradictionem includit aliquas res esse vsu consumptibiles: & tamen non contingit illis vtaquia tamen quantum ad hanc materiam magis est disputatio ad nomen, quam ad rem, ipsam aliis derelinquunt.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he cannot escape the conclusion that, from his own words, which he asserts in the constitution to the founder, flatly denying that anyone can use things consumed by use, it follows that he includes a contradiction in saying that some things are consumed by use, and yet it is not possible to use them. But as far as this matter goes, the dispute is about the name rather than the thing, and they leave the matter itself to others.

units.la: [Vt ignarus & insciens.] Ista sunt vocabula contumeliosa, quæ, vt dicunt isti, à veritatis amatoribus sunt vitanda. [Legislatorem arguit] dicunt, quod non arguit legislatorem: quia non imponit legislatori, quod dixerit aliquas res esse vsu consumptibiles: & tn non contingit illis vti, quia nec intelligitur quod legislator dixerit, q; nemo potest vti rebus consumptibilibus vsu. [Rubricam posuit de vsufructu &c.] Dicunt isti, q; sæpe ponitur ab auctoribus rubrica de his quæ contradictionem includunt. Exempla multa sunt ad hoc. Ponitur n. rubrica de vacuo in philosophia, & tn vacuum esse secundum philosophiam contradictionem includit. Ponitur etiam rubrica de infinito etiam secundum magnitudinem & tamen secundum philosophiam aliquid esse infinitam magnitudine molis contradictionem includit. Alia multa exempla possent adduci: sed ista sufficiant. Ratio autem, quare ponuntur tales rubricæ, quia rubricæ sæpe ponuntur, non vt illa ostendantur esse, q; importantur per rubricas, sed vt ostendantur non esse: & q; non sunt monstretur. & ideo esto, q; illa rubrica includeret contradictionem de vsufructu earum rerum quæ vsu consumuntur: ex hoc legislator argui nequaquam posset, nisi postea legislator in tractatu asseret hoc esse possibile. [sumendo vsum pro abusu, i.e. pro consumptione rei] leges sumunt vsum, etiam pro consumptione rei & aliter. [Nec alius vsus nisi videl. consumptio in rebus vsu consumptibilib. esse potest.] Hoc dicunt esse ei roneu: tum quia contingit vti rebus vsu consumptibilibus illo vsu, q distinguitur contra fruitionem, de quo loquitur Augustinus dicens, q vti est sumere aliquid in facultatem voluntatis, & tamen ille vsus non est consumptio: tum quia ligna sunt res vsu consumptibiles: quia combustione consumuntur, & tn alius vsus quā consumptio in ipsis poterit reperiri: tum quia contingit vti pecunia ad pompam, & tn ille vsus non est consumptio: imo nulla est res, qua non contingat vti absq; consumptione. [Vsufructus constitui non potest.] Differentia est inter vsum & inter vsufructum, sicut patet ex his q dicta sunt secundo capit. Et ideo licet vsufructus non posset constitui in rebus vsu consumptibilibus: ex hoc non sequitur, quod vsus non potest habere de eis: & maxime accipiendo vsum, sicut in theologia accipitur. [quasi vsu, expresse ibi innuit q vsus ponitur ibi improprie.] Dicunt q quasi non est semp nota improprietatis. Nam dicit apostolus: quasi tristes, semper autem gaudentes: & tn tristes, non accipitur ibi improprie: quia vere & proprie opus fideles in hac misera vita esse tristes, quamuis de multis etiam gaudere conveniat. & ideo ex hoc, quod dicitur quasi vsu, non potest argui, quod vsus ibi accipiatur improprie.
units.tr: [Clumsy and unaware.] These are insulting words, which, they say, should be avoided by lovers of the truth. [He accuses the lawgiver.] They say that he does not accuse the lawgiver, since he does not charge the lawgiver with having said that some things are consumed by use, and yet it is not possible to use them; for it is not understood that the lawgiver said that no one can use things consumable by use. [He placed a title on usufruct, etc.] These opponents say that authors often place a title on matters which involve a contradiction. There are many examples of this. For a title is placed on the void in philosophy, and yet, according to philosophy, the void involves a contradiction. A title is also placed on the infinite, even in magnitude, and yet, according to philosophy, something infinite in the magnitude of its mass involves a contradiction. Many other examples could be brought forward, but these are enough. The reason why such titles are placed is that titles are often placed not to show that the things they name exist, but to show that they do not exist, and that they are not shown to exist. And so, even if that title included a contradiction about the usufruct of those things which are consumed by use, the lawgiver could in no way be accused on this ground, unless the lawgiver afterwards asserted in the treatise that this is possible. [Taking use for abuse, that is, for the consumption of a thing.] The laws take use also for the consumption of a thing, and in other senses. [There can be no other use than consumption in things consumed by use.] They say this is false, because it is possible to use things consumed by use in that sense of use which is distinguished from enjoyment, of which Augustine speaks, saying that to use is to take something into the power of the will; and yet that use is not consumption. Also, because wood is consumed by use, since it is consumed by burning, and yet another use than consumption can be found in it. Also, because it is possible to use money for display, and yet that use is not consumption; indeed, there is no thing which cannot be used without consumption. [A usufruct cannot be established.] There is a difference between use and usufruct, as is clear from what was said in the second chapter. And so, although a usufruct could not be established in things consumed by use, it does not follow from this that use cannot be had of them, especially if use is taken as it is taken in theology. [As if by use: he clearly hints that use is here taken improperly.] They say that "as if" is not always a sign of impropriety. For the apostle says, "as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing" (2 Cor. 6.), and yet "sorrowful" is not taken there improperly, since it truly and properly belongs to the faithful to be sorrowful in this wretched life, although it is also fitting for them to rejoice in many things. And so from the fact that it is said "as if by use," it cannot be argued that use is taken improperly there.

units.la: CAP. XLVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLVI.

units.la: Adhuc dicit hereticus, quod cum secundum Aug. lib. 1. de doctrina Christiana: abusus fit illicitus vsus, ex prædictis sequi videtur, quod Christus & apostoli & alii sancti viri, quoties actus comedendi, bibendi & induendi exercuerunt, totiens rebus huiusmodi sunt abusi: quod sentire vel dicere impium est & blasphemum.
units.tr: The heretic further says that, since according to Augustine in the first book of De doctrina Christiana, abuse is illicit use, it seems to follow from the above that Christ, the apostles and other holy men, whenever they performed the acts of eating, drinking and clothing themselves, thereby abused such things. To think or say this is impious and blasphemous.

units.la: Hic respondet ad aliam obiectionem appellantis, quam primo recitat: secundo soluit in parte sequenti. Obiectio est satis patens, licet sit recitata truncate.
units.tr: Here he replies to another objection of the appellant, which he first recites and then resolves in the following part. The objection is fairly plain, although it has been recited in truncated form.

units.la: [Abusus fit illicitus vsus] hoc est verum de abusu, quo creaturæ rationales abutuntur rebus, secundum quod theologia loquitur de abusu. [Sunt abusi quod sentire &c.] hoc est verum accipiendo abuti, sed quod in scriptura sacra accipitur abuti respectu rerum consumptibilium vsu.
units.tr: That "abuse is illicit use" is true of abuse as rational creatures abuse things, in the sense in which theology speaks of abuse. That "they are abusers" is true if "to abuse" is taken in that sense, but in Holy Scripture "to abuse" is used with respect to the use of consumable things.

units.la: CAP. XLVII.
units.tr: CAP. XLVII.

units.la: Ad quod dicimus, quod Christus & apostoli & alii sancti viri panem comedendo & vinum bibendo abusi sunt rebus illis, sicut abusus in constitutione prædicta sumitur: in qua pro rei consumptione accipitur, sicut ex eius serie manifeste patet.
units.tr: To this we reply that Christ, and the apostles, and other holy men, in eating bread and drinking wine, did abuse those things, in the sense in which "abuse" is taken in the aforesaid definition, where it means the consumption of a thing; this is clear from the sequence of that very passage.

units.la: Hic ad primam obiectionem respondet concedendo conclusionem illatam. Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod quia iste impugnatus facit hic difficultatem de significatione eius termini abusi, & voces sunt significativæ ad placitum; ideo nolunt hic multum insistere. Dicunt tn, q appellans, quia Doctor sacræ theologiæ vsus est termino abutendi, secundum q in scriptura sacra, quæ de rebus consumptibilib. vsu fit mentio, accipitur; & secundum quod in aliis scietiis & originalib. sanctorum ac in vulgari & in communi modo loquendi accipitur; & ideo loquendo secundum q catholici fideles loquuntur communiter; nõ unmerito habuit pimpio & blasphemo dicere, quod Christus & apostoli ac alii sancti viri, comedendo, bibendo & inducendo abutuntur rebus maxime cum modu loquendi Augustini servaverit. Unde si Augustinus dixit, quod abusus est illicitus vsus, potuit appellans dicere, quod dicere Christum & apostolos abusos fuisse rebus est impium & blasphemum. Ad Augustinum autem iste non respondet: & ideo dicunt, quod obiectionem non soluit.
units.tr: Here he answers the first objection by granting the conclusion drawn. But these opponents say that, since the man they attack makes difficulty here about the meaning of the term "abuse," and words signify by convention, therefore they do not wish to dwell on this point at length. They say, however, that the appellant, because he is a Doctor of sacred theology, has used the term "to abuse" in the sense in which it is taken in Holy Scripture, where mention is made of the use of consumable things, and in the sense in which it is taken in other sciences and in the original languages of the saints, and in the vulgar and common manner of speaking; and therefore, speaking in the way that Catholic faithful commonly speak, he was not undeservedly held to have said, impiously and blasphemously, that Christ and the apostles and other holy men abused things by eating, drinking and using them, especially since he has kept to the manner of speaking of Augustine. Hence, if Augustine said that abuse is illicit use, the appellant could say that to say that Christ and the apostles abused things is impious and blasphemous. But this man does not answer Augustine; and therefore they say that he does not resolve the objection.

units.la: CAP. XLVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLVIII.

units.la: Sed contra hoc dicit haereticus supradictus, quod hoc, videl. quod abusi sumitur pro consumptione rei, non valet: tum quia quod sic debeat accipi, nec ratione nec auctoritate probatur: tum quia abusi re non voce semper in mala significatione sumitur: sicut patet Gen. 34. & Hester. ultimo: & 1. Cor. 9. & aliis pluribus locis.
units.tr: But the aforementioned heretic says against this that the point, namely that abusus is taken for the consumption of a thing, does not hold: first, because it is proved neither by reason nor by authority that it ought to be understood this way; second, because abusus, in respect of the thing and not the word, is always taken in a bad sense, as is clear from Gen. 34, Esther last chapter, 1 Cor. 9, and many other places.

units.la: Hic recitat obiectionem aliam appellantis, quae patet de se. [Quod abusi sumitur pro consumptione rei] appellans intelligit, quod consumptio rei non est una significatio adaequata huius nominis abusus, licet aliquis abusus sit consumptio rei: sicut rationale non est una significatio adaequata animalis, licet aliquod animal sit rationale: vel sub aliis verbis intelligit, quod abusus & consumptio rei non sint convertibilia, licet aliquis abusus sit consumptio rei: quia nec omnis abusus est consumptio rei, nec omnis consumptio rei est abusus [quod sic debeat accipi] scil. quod omnis abusus sit consumptio rei. [Abusi re non voce semper in mala significatione accipitur] hoc est, abusus secundum quod accipitur in scriptura & in philosophia, & in communi modo loquendi, semper significat malum, etiam culpae vel in abutente, vel in illo quo abutens abutitur, sicut inferius ostendetur.
units.tr: Here he recites another objection of the appellant, which is clear enough in itself. The appellant understands "that abusus is taken for the consumption of a thing" to mean that the consumption of a thing is not one adequate signification of the word abusus, although some abuse is a consumption of a thing, just as rational is not one adequate signification of animal, although some animal is rational. Or, in other words, he means that abusus and consumption of a thing are not convertible terms, although some abuse is a consumption of a thing, since not every abuse is a consumption of a thing, and not every consumption of a thing is an abuse. "That it ought to be understood in this way", namely, that every abuse is a consumption of a thing. "Abusus is taken in a bad sense always by the thing, not by the word", that is, abusus, as it is taken in Scripture, in philosophy and in common speech, always signifies evil, whether the fault lies in the one who abuses or in that by which the abuser abuses, as will be shown below.

units.la: CAP. XLIX.
units.tr: CHAP. XLIX.

units.la: Ad hoc dicimus, quod illud, quod dicit, nec ratione nec auctoritate probari, quod verbum abutipro rei consumptione sumatur, evidenter est falsum. ff. de usufr. earum rerum quae usu consumuntur. l. hoc senatus. §. Si pecuniae, dicitur sic: si pecuniae sit usufructus legatus, vel earum rerum, quae in abusu consistunt, nec cautio interveniat, videndum finito usufructu, an pecunia quae data sit vel caeterae res quae in absumptione consistunt, condici possint. Ubi patet, quod legislator in rebus, quae usu consumuntur, promiscue utitur verbo abusu videl. & consumptione & eadem lege. §. ubi dicitur sic: Quae in usufructu pecuniae diximus vel caeterarum rerum, quae sunt in abusu, eadem et in usu dicenda sunt. Item ff. de iureiurando. l. sed & si possessori. §. sed si rerum usufructus propter abusum i.e. propter rei consumptionem constituí non potest &c. Ubi aperte abusum pro consumptione recipit legislator. Ex quib. patet, quod legislatores loquentes proprie de rebus, quae usu consumuntur, negant usum in illis habere locum, & abusum locum habere concedunt. Qui quidem abusus i.e. rei consumptio, si fiat ab eo, cuius ius abutendi i.e. consumendi competit, erit licitus: si vero ab eo, cui ius non competit, illicitus est censendus.
units.tr: To this we reply that the claim that the word abuti cannot be shown, either by reason or by authority, to be used for the consumption of a thing is plainly false. In the Digest, under de usufructu earum rerum quae usu consumuntur, the law Hoc senatus, §. Si pecuniae, says: "If the usufruct of money, or of those things which consist in abuse, is bequeathed, and no security is given, it must be considered, when the usufruct has ended, whether the money that was given, or the other things which consist in consumption, can be claimed back." Here it is clear that the lawmaker, speaking of things which are used up, uses the word abusus, that is, consumptio, interchangeably, and in the same law, §. where it says: "What we have said of the usufruct of money or of other things which are in abuse, must likewise be said of their use." Likewise in the Digest, de iureiurando, the law Sed et si possessori, §. Sed si rerum: "the usufruct of things cannot be established on account of abuse, that is, on account of the consumption of the thing," and so on. Here the lawmaker plainly takes abusus for consumptio. From these passages it is clear that the lawmakers, speaking properly of things which are used up, deny that use has a place in them, and grant that abuse has a place. This abuse, that is, the consumption of the thing, will be lawful if it is done by the one whose right of abusing, that is, of consuming, belongs to him; but if it is done by one to whom the right does not belong, it is to be judged unlawful.

units.la: Hic iste impugnatus ad praemissam obiectionem respondet. & potest dividi in quatuor partes. Primo enim ostendit, quod abuti potest sumi pro rei consumptione per auctoritates. Secundo per rationem in parte sequenti. Tertio ostendit, quod abusus potest sumi in bona significatione legib. imperator ibi, Palsum insuper dicit. Quarto ostendit idem auctoritate scripturae divinae ibi, adhuc reperimus. In hoc ergo textu, primo ostendit quod abuti sumatur pro rei consumptione. secundo ibi: Ex quibus patet &c. infert quod legislatores negant proprie usum in rebus consumptibilibus usu. tertio ibi: qui quidem abusus, declarat quis abusus est licitus? quia ille cui competit ius abutendi & quis est illicitus? quia ille qui fit ab eo qui non habet ius abutendi.
units.tr: Here this author, who is under attack, answers the preceding objection, and his answer can be divided into four parts. First, he shows that to abuse can be taken to mean the consumption of a thing, by means of authorities. Second, by reason, in the following part. Third, he shows that abuse can be taken in a good sense in the laws, where the emperor says, "Moreover he says falsely." Fourth, he shows the same from the authority of divine Scripture, where he says, "Still we find." In this text, first, he shows that to abuse is taken for the consumption of a thing. Second, where he says, "From these things it is evident," he infers that the lawgivers strictly deny that use applies to things consumed by use. Third, where he says, "Which abuse," he explains what abuse is lawful, namely that which is done by the one who has the right to abuse, and what is unlawful, namely that which is done by one who does not have the right to abuse.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores circa hoc tria conantur ostendere. Primum est, quod non respondet ad mentem appellantis. Secundum est quod falsum dicit, cum asserit, quod legislatores loquentes proprie de rebus, quae usu consumuntur, negant usum in illis locum habere. Tertius est quod errat aperte dicens, quod ille abusus accipiendo abusum, ut ille accipit, est illicitus, cui non competit ius abutendi.
units.tr: But these opponents try to show three things about this. The first is that he does not answer the mind of the appellant. The second is that he says what is false when he asserts that lawgivers, speaking strictly of things consumed by use, deny that use has a place in them. The third is that he clearly errs in saying that that abuse, taking abuse as he takes it, is unlawful for one who does not have the right to abuse.

units.la: Circa primum dicunt, quod non est intentio appellantis dicere, quod nunc abusus accipiatur pro consumptione rei quoquomodo. Nam si fur furatur panem & manducat eum, potest dici quod abutitur pane: vel si qs aliter utitur pane, manducando ipsum aliter quam convenit, potest dici quod abutitur pane, & tunc consumit panem. Sed intentio eius est, quod abusus & consumptio rei non convertuntur: & quod abusus secundum quod accipitur in scriptura sacra & in philosophia & communi modo loquendi, non plus accipitur pro consumptione rei quam usus. Sed sicut usus est, quod commune ad aliquam consumptionem rei & alios actus videndi, ita et abusus est quod commune ad aliquam consumptionem rei & aliquos alios actus.
units.tr: As to the first, they say that it is not the intention of the appellant to say that abuse is now taken for the consumption of a thing in any way whatever. For if a thief steals bread and eats it, it can be said that he abuses the bread; or if someone uses bread otherwise, eating it in a way other than is fitting, it can be said that he abuses the bread, and then he consumes the bread. But his intention is that abuse and the consumption of a thing are not convertible, and that abuse, as it is taken in Holy Scripture, in philosophy and in common speech, is no more taken for the consumption of a thing than use is. For just as use is something common to some consumption of a thing and to other acts of seeing, so abuse is something common to some consumption of a thing and to some other acts.

units.la: Ex hoc patet, quod leges non sunt contra appellantes: quia leges aliter loquuntur, quam philosophia & theologia & vulgaris modus loquendi. Nec plus sunt contra appellantes, quam contra scripturam divinam: quia appellans utitur terminis illis in eadem significatione, in qua utitur scriptura divina. Ex hoc concludit isti impugnatores, quod iste impugnat potius debuerat negare modum loquendi scripturae legum, dicendo quod non est abutendum rebus consumptibilibus usu, quia modum loquendi divinae. dicendo, quod non convenit uti rebus consumptibilibus usu quia utitur duabus sciētiis. Supiori & inferiori: et vult reputari peritus in eis: citius debet negare modum loquendi scientiae inferioris, quam scientiae superioris. Sed iste impugnator utitur theologia & scientiis legalibus, & peritus vult reputari in eis. imo, ut dicunt isti quis nunquam theologiam didicerit, vult esse Doctor Doctorum theologiae, & oēs quaestiones theologiae intricatissimas subito diffinire. Constat autem, quod theologia est superior omni legali scientia. ergo citius deberet negare modum loquendi legalis scientiae, dicendo quod non est abutendum rebus consumptibilibus usu; quia modum loquendi theologiae, dicendo quod non contingit uti rebus consumptibilibus usu; cum theologia in plerisque locis absolute affirmet, quod rebus talibus contingit uti. Secundo dicitur, quod falsum dicit, asserens quod legislatores loquentes proprie de rebus, quae usu consumuntur, negant usum in omni significatione sua, proprie in illis locum habere. Dicunt enim quod legislatores loquentes proprie de rebus consumptibilibus usu, asserunt usum in aliqua significatione proprie in illis locum habere, sicut ostensum est supra cap. 42. Sciendum est igitur secundum istos, quod leges proprie loquendo concedunt usum in rebus consumptibilibus vsu:quia concedunt in eis proprie loquendo vsum facti, nec vnq; dicunt tales locutiones esse improprias:Iste vtitur cibo,& potu:iste vtitur veste: ille vtitur pecunia, tñ proprie loquendo negant vsum iuris in eis. Vnde secundū leges vsus iuris dupliciter accipi potest, sc. proprie & improprie, si proprie accipiatur:non est ponendus in rebus consumptibilibus vsu, Improprie vero sumptus potest concedi in eis.Dicunt igitur isti,q; quia iste impugnatus nesciit distinguere inter magis cōmunē & minus commune:& ignorat quod aliqñ nomen minus commune impropriè dicitur de aliquo,de quo tamē magis commune pprie dicitur:sicut homo pictus improprie dicitur,& tamē proprie vocatur corpus.ideo putat,quod illud,q; leges dicunt de vsu iuris. sc. quod improprie,nō proprie in rebus vsu consumptibilibus inuenitur, dicitur de vsu, quod est nomen magis cōmune, quam sit vsus iuris. (quod vsus non inueniatur pprie dici de rebus consumptibilibus vsu. Veruntamen propter illos,qui in fundamentis communib. omnium scientiarum sunt minus instructi, dicunt esse sciendum:q; sicut vocabulū æquiuocū potest de eodē affirmari & negari propter multitudinem significationum:ita idem vocabulū æquiuocum potest de eodem dici proprie & improprie ,pter diuersitatem significationum,ex quibus oriūtur diuersi sensus propositionum. sed tamen tunc non debet negari illud vocabulum æquiuocum dici proprie. sed est concedendum,q; dicitur proprie & improprie.Sic dicunt esse de legibus: quod quamuis inueniretur asserere,quod vsus improprie reperitur in rebus vsu consumptibilibus vsu, quia tunc acciperent vsum pro vsu iuris:tamen non negant vsum dici proprie de rebus consumptibilibus vsu, quia constat secundum leges quod vsu proprie sumptus inueniatur in rebus consumptibilibus vsu.
units.tr: From this it is clear that the laws are not against the appellants, because the laws speak differently from philosophy, theology and common usage. Nor are they more against the appellants than they are against divine Scripture, because the appellant uses those terms in the same sense in which divine Scripture uses them. From this, these opponents conclude that the author who is attacked ought rather to have denied the manner of speaking of the law of Scripture, saying that things consumed by use should not be abused, because of the manner of speaking of divine law, saying that it is not fitting to use things consumed by use, since [the law] uses two sciences, the higher and the lower, and wishes to be reputed skilled in both. He ought sooner to deny the manner of speaking of the lower science than that of the higher science. But this opponent uses theology and legal sciences, and wishes to be reputed skilled in them. Indeed, as these men say, though he has never learned theology, he wishes to be the Doctor of Doctors of theology and to define at once all the most intricate questions of theology. Yet it is agreed that theology is superior to every legal science. Therefore he ought sooner to deny the manner of speaking of legal science, saying that things consumed by use should not be abused, than to deny the manner of speaking of theology, saying that it is not possible to use things consumed by use, since theology in many places affirms absolutely that it is possible to use such things. Secondly, they say that he speaks falsely in asserting that lawgivers, speaking strictly of things consumed by use, deny that use has a place in them in every sense. For they say that lawgivers, speaking strictly of things consumed by use, assert that use has a place in them strictly in some sense, as was shown above in chapter 42. So it must be understood, according to these men, that the laws, speaking strictly, concede use in things consumed by use, because they strictly concede in them the use of fact, and they never say that such expressions are improper: "This man uses food and drink; this man uses clothing; that man uses money." Yet strictly speaking they deny the use of right in them. Hence, according to the laws, the use of right can be taken in two ways, namely strictly and improperly. If it is taken strictly, it is not to be attributed to things consumed by use; but taken improperly, it can be conceded in them. These men therefore say that this author who is attacked did not know how to distinguish between the more common and the less common, and does not know that sometimes a less common name is said improperly of something of which the more common is said properly, as a painted man is said improperly to be a man, and yet is properly called a body. So he thinks that what the laws say about the use of right, namely that it is found improperly and not strictly in things consumed by use, is said of use, which is the more common name, than is the use of right. (That use is not found strictly said of things consumed by use.) Nevertheless, for the sake of those who are less instructed in the common foundations of all sciences, they say that it must be understood that just as an equivocal word can be affirmed and denied of the same thing because of the multitude of its meanings, so the same equivocal word can be said of the same thing both strictly and improperly, because of the diversity of meanings from which diverse senses of propositions arise. But then that equivocal word must not be denied to be said strictly; rather it must be conceded that it is said both strictly and improperly. They say the same is true of the laws: although one might find them asserting that use is found improperly in things consumed by use, because then they would be taking use for the use of right, yet they do not deny that use is said strictly of things consumed by use, because it is established by the laws that use taken strictly is found in things consumed by use.

units.la: Tertio dicunt istum errare,cum dicit quod ille abusus est illicitus, cui non competit ius utendi,accipiendo abusum,sicut accipit iste. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum,quod iste accipit hic ius abutendi non pro iure naturali:quia illud competit omnibus & essent tunc falsum , quod dicit,quod si fiat ab eo cui competit ius abutendi,actus est licitus:quia ius naturæ competit omnib. non tamē omnes qui abutuntur secundū modum istius loquendi licite abutuntur.fures enim sepe abutuntur rebus illicite,& tñ omne ius naturale competit:licet tale ius naturale non semper faciat actum abutendi esse licitum. Accipit ergo ius abutendi pro iure positiuo: quia omne ius vel est ius naturæ vel ius positiuum.sed accipiendo ius abutendi pro iure positiuo dicunt, quod erroneum est,quod actus,qui fit ab eo cui non competit ius est illicitus:quia ex hoc sequeretur,quod omnes Fratres Minores vtendo vel abutendo rebus haberent actus illicitos, cum non habeant in rebus ius positiuū,quod sufficiat ad licitū actum vtendi vel abutendi:& ita status fratrum Minorum esset status illicitus & erraret vniuersalis ecclesia statū huiusmodi approbando seu acceptādo Beatus etiā Franciscus & alii sancti eiusdē Ordinis decessissent in peccato mortali. Ex pdicta etiam assertione sequretur,quod qcunq; facit aliquid de gratia non de iure, haberet actū illicitum. & ita q; de gratia aliquorū electorū interesset electioni alicuius plati, non de iure, peccaret: quod est salsum manifeste.quod hoc sequatur patet:qa qua ratione posset aliquis interesse electioni alicuius prælati de gratia nō de iure:eadē ratione posset quis vti veste alterius de gratia non de iure.
units.tr: Thirdly, they say that he errs when he says that that abuse is unlawful for which the right of using does not belong, taking abuse as he takes it. To make this evident, they say it must be understood that he takes here the right of abusing not as the natural right, because that belongs to all, and then it would be false that he says that if an act is done by one to whom the right of abusing belongs, it is lawful; for the natural right belongs to all, yet not all who abuse, in the sense of this way of speaking, abuse lawfully. For thieves often abuse things unlawfully, and yet all natural right belongs to them, although such natural right does not always make the act of abusing lawful. He therefore takes the right of abusing as positive right, because every right is either natural right or positive right. But taking the right of abusing as positive right, they say it is erroneous to hold that an act done by one to whom the right does not belong is unlawful; for from this it would follow that all Friars Minor, in using or abusing things, would have unlawful acts, since they do not have in things a positive right sufficient for a lawful act of using or abusing; and thus the state of the Friars Minor would be an unlawful state, and the universal Church would have erred in approving or accepting a state of this kind. Also blessed Francis and other saints of the same Order would have died in mortal sin. From the same assertion it would also follow that whoever does something by grace and not by right would have an unlawful act; and so that some of the elect who took part in the election of some prelate by grace and not by right would sin, which is manifestly false. That this follows is clear: for by the same reasoning by which someone could take part in the election of a prelate by grace and not by right, someone could likewise wear another's clothing by grace and not by right.

units.la: [Quia verbum abuti pro rei consumptione sumatur] scil.sicut conuertibile cum ipso: & hoc secundum quod accipitur in theologia & philosophia ac cōmuni & vulgari modo loqndi[si pecunia sit vsufructus legatus.]Ex hoc patet,quod non solū vsus,sed et vsufructus in rebus vsu consumptibilib. reperitur:tñ potest dici,quod vsufructus improprie sumptus,& nō proprie in rebus vsu consumptibilibus reperitur. Vsus vero pter diuersas significationes, quas non oēs habet vsufructus tam pprie sumptus q; improprie sumptus,potest in rebus vsu consumptibilib.reperiri: quia vna significatio pria huius nominis vsus,q; est cōmunis ad actus circa res temporales exercitos:proprie habet locū in rebus vsu cōsumptibilibus. Alia vero habet significatione impropria, q; est significatio impropria vsus iuris:& secundū illam et in rebus vsu consumptibilib.reperitur, tales autē duas significationes non habet vsufructus.& ideo licet vsufructus pprie sumptus non reperiatur in rebus consumptibilib.vsu:vsus tñ pprie sumpt9 poterit repiri;quia vsus habet plures significationes pprias,sicut innuunt isti c.2,& secundū vna reperitur in rebus consumptibilib. vsu, secundū vero alia non reperitur in eis.[In abusu consistunt]sic nō accipitur abusus in theologia, nec in pphetia,nec in vulgari modo loqndi[permisceri vtitur] si intelligat, quod vtitur eis legislator, sicut conuertibilibus,negandū est;quia nō omnis cōsumptio rei est abusus; si intelligat quod sic vtitur eis, quod vnum potest verificari de alio, saltē particulariter cōcedunt: qa aliqs abusus est consumptio rei; & aliqua cōsumptio rei est abusus.Esto etiā,quod legislator humanus vteretur eis,sic quod secundū eum omnis abusus esset cōsumptio rei,tamē non sic vtitur legislator diuinus, cuius modū loqndi imitatur appellans,& consimiliter dicunt ad alias auctoritates legū inductas.[Ex quibus patet &c.] Dicunt quod male infert;quia non sequitur,legislatores concedunt abusum in rebus consumptibilibus;ergo negant proprie vsum in eis; imo sicut ostenderur in sequēti capitulo per verba istius ex hoc ipso,quod concedunt in eis abusum proprie sicut iste dicit,concedunt in eis proprie vsum. vnde ex forma propositionum ista stant simul,quod sit in eis proprie abusus & proprie vsus; quia abusus sic sumptus & vsus non opponuntur.[Si vero ab eo, cuius non competit, illicitum est censendum] dicunt esse falsum; quia potest fieri licite ab eo, qui habet licentiam vtendi,licet ius non habeat.
units.tr: Because the word "to abuse" is taken for the consumption of a thing, namely as convertible with it, and this in the sense in which it is taken in theology, philosophy, and common everyday speech, if money is bequeathed as a usufruct. From this it is clear that not only use but also usufruct is found in things consumed by use. Yet it can be said that usufruct is found in such things only improperly, not properly. Use, however, because it has various meanings, not all of which usufruct has, whether taken properly or improperly, can be found in things consumed by use. For the first meaning of this word "use," which is common to acts performed on temporal things, applies properly to things consumed by use. Another meaning is improper, namely the improper sense of use in law, and in that sense too it is found in things consumed by use. Usufruct has neither of these two meanings. Therefore, although usufruct taken properly is not found in things consumed by use, use taken properly can be found there, since use has several proper meanings, as these authorities in chapter 2 hint: in one sense it is found in things consumed by use, and in another sense it is not. They consist in abuse: abuse is not understood this way in theology, nor in prophecy, nor in everyday speech. Is accustomed to be mixed up: if he means that the lawgiver uses these terms as convertible, this must be denied, for not every consumption of a thing is abuse. If he means that he uses them so that one can be predicated of the other, they grant it at least in part, since some abuse is a consumption of a thing and some consumption of a thing is abuse. Grant also that a human lawgiver used them so that, in his usage, every abuse would be a consumption of a thing; still, the divine lawgiver does not use them so, and the one making the appeal imitates his manner of speaking. They reply in the same way to the other authorities of the laws cited. From which it is clear, etc. They say he infers wrongly, for it does not follow that because lawgivers concede abuse in things consumed by use, they therefore deny use properly in them. Indeed, as will be shown in the following chapter from this man's own words, the very fact that they concede abuse in such things properly, as he says, shows that they concede use properly in them. Hence, from the form of the propositions, it stands that there is both proper abuse and proper use in them, since abuse so taken and use are not opposed. But if it is done by one to whom it does not belong, it must be judged unlawful: they say this is false, since it can be done lawfully by one who has permission to use, even if he has no right to it.

units.la: CAP. L.
units.tr: CAP. L.

units.la: Item quod abusus pro consumptione ponitur, congruit rationi, praepositio enim sensum dictionis, cui per compositionem praeponitur, augere vel diminuere consueuit. Unde patet, quod rationi congruit, quod per illam praepositionem ab sensu huius dictionis vsus, cui per compositionem praeponitur, augeatur.
units.tr: Likewise, that abuse is used for consumption agrees with reason. For the preposition usually increases or diminishes the sense of the word to which it is prefixed by composition. Hence it is clear that it agrees with reason that by this preposition the sense of the word use, to which it is prefixed, is increased.

units.la: Hic ostendit per rationem, quod abusus pro consumptione rei sumitur: quia haec praepositio ab auget sensum dictionis, cui per compositionem praeponitur.
units.tr: Here he shows by reasoning that abuse is taken for the consumption of a thing, because this preposition ab increases the sense of the word to which it is prefixed by composition.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores hic faciunt tria. Primo enim concedunt, quod conclusio quam ultimo infert, est vera. Secundo ostendunt quod quis ipsa sit vera, tamen ratio per quam iste probat eam, non valet. Tertio ostendunt quod ex ipsa sequitur, quod ita proprie debet cedere vsum in rebus vsu consumptibilibus, sicut abusum. Dicunt ergo primo, concedendo quod haec praepositio ab sensum dictionis vsus auget; quia secundum grammaticos vna significatio huiusmodi verbi abuti est valde vti: haec tamen significatio in theologia non est in vsu: imo videtur omnino recessisse ab vsu. Secundo dicunt, quod licet haec sit vera: tamen ratio, per quam probat ipsam, non valet. quamuis enim haec praepositio ab aliquando augeat sensum dictionis, cui per compositionem praeponitur: non tamen semper auget sensum huius dictionis vsus: sed est fallacia consequentis arguendo a particulari ad singulare determinata. quod autem haec praepositio ab non semper augeat sensum dictionis, cui per compositionem praeponitur, patet per exempla innumera, sicut de abducere, ablactare, absistere & aliis multis. Tertio dicunt, quod ex istis verbis suis sequitur, quod vsus proprie inuenitur in rebus consumptibilibus vsu. Nam vbi sensus dictionis per dictionem augetur, a dictione composita ad simplicem est consequentia bona: & vbi proprie habet locum dictio composita, ibi habet proprie locum dictio simplex. Sicut sequitur, ille absorbet; ergo sorbet: & vbi habet locum proprie absorbere, ibi habet locum proprie sorbere: sicut illud quod est proprie album, per augmentum est albū proprie. Si ergo haec praepositio ab auget sensum huius dictionis vsus, cum dicitur abusus: vbi proprie inuenitur abusus, ibi etiā proprie inuenitur vsus: quia si non inueniretur proprie vsus, sensus huius dictionis vsus non esset auctus, sed magis diminutus vel destructus. Et ex isto sequitur, quod si abusus est proprie consumptio rei, quod et vsus est proprie consumptio rei: quia omnis abusus est vsus secundum istū: quia omne quod est aliquale, per augmentum est tale: & quod augetur secundum aliquid, non desinit esse quale prius fuit per adventum illius quod auget ipsum. Auget itaque aliquando & aliquando non.
units.tr: But these opponents do three things here. First, they grant that the conclusion he finally draws is true. Second, they show that although it is true, the reasoning by which he proves it is not valid. Third, they show that it follows from it that use must be taken properly in things consumed by use, just as abuse is. So first, granting that this preposition ab increases the sense of the word use, they say that according to the grammarians one meaning of this kind of verb abuti is "to use up" [to abuse]; yet this meaning is not in use in theology, indeed it seems to have fallen entirely out of use. Second, they say that although this is true, the reasoning by which he proves it is not valid. For although this preposition ab sometimes increases the sense of the word to which it is prefixed by composition, it does not always increase the sense of this word use. This is a fallacy of the consequent, arguing from the particular to the singular determinate. That this preposition ab does not always increase the sense of the word to which it is prefixed by composition is plain from countless examples, such as abducere [to lead away], ablactare [to wean], absistere [to desist], and many others. Third, they say that from these words of his it follows that use is properly found in things consumed by use. For where the sense of a word is increased by a prefix, the inference from the compound word to the simple one is good; and where the compound word properly applies, the simple word also properly applies. Thus it follows: he absorbs, therefore he sips; and where to absorb properly applies, to sip properly applies too, just as what is properly white becomes properly whiter by augmentation. If therefore this preposition ab increases the sense of this word use, when it is said abuse, then where abuse is properly found, use is also properly found there. For if use were not properly found, the sense of the word use would not be increased but rather diminished or destroyed. And from this it follows that if abuse is properly the consumption of a thing, then use is also properly the consumption of a thing, since, according to him, every abuse is a use; for whatever is of some quality becomes, by augmentation, of that quality, and what is increased in some respect does not cease to be what it was before by the addition of that which increases it. So it sometimes increases and sometimes does not.

units.la: [Rationi congruit quod per illam praepositionem ab &c.] Dicunt, quod non congruit rationi, sed congruit voluntati instituentium. Unde significata vocabulorum non per rationem, sed per vsum loquentium & auctores probari debent.
units.tr: [That by this preposition ab, etc., agrees with reason] They say that it does not agree with reason but agrees with the will of those who established the language. Hence the meanings of words are to be proved not by reason but by the usage of speakers and by authors.

units.la: CAP. LI.
units.tr: CAP. LI.

units.la: Falsum insuper dicit in eo, quod dicit, quod abusus quotiens re, non voce dicitur, accipitur in mala significatione. In legibus enim imperatorum abusus cum de rebus vsu consumptibilibus vsu agitur, in bona parte communiter sumitur, vt superius est probatum.
units.tr: Moreover, he says falsely in what he states, that abuse, whenever it is taken in regard to a thing and not to a word, is understood in a bad sense. For in the laws of the emperors, when abuse is spoken of in relation to things consumed by use, it is commonly taken in a good sense, as was shown above.

units.la: Hic concludit, quod abusus in legibus imperatorum in bona significatione accipitur.
units.tr: Here he concludes that abuse in the laws of the emperors is taken in a good sense.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, quod non vadit ad mentem appellantis: qa appellas sumit abusum, vt sumitur in theologia: & sic accipitur semp in mala significatione, cum de rebus vsu consumptibilibus fit mentio. [Quotiens re non voce accipitur in mala significatione] hoc est, vt in theologia & philosophia naturali accipitur: vel in mala significatione, quia significat malum culpae abutentis, vt illo modo, quo quis abutitur in theologia.
units.tr: But these opponents say that this does not go to the mind of the appellant: for the appellant takes abuse as it is taken in theology, and so it is always taken in a bad sense when mention is made of things consumed by use. [Whenever it is taken in regard to a thing and not to a word, it is taken in a bad sense] that is, as it is taken in theology and natural philosophy; or in a bad sense, because it signifies the evil of the fault of the one who abuses, in the way in which someone abuses in theology.

units.la: CAP. LII.
units.tr: CAP. LII.

units.la: Adhuc reperimus, quod in scriptura sacra abusus in bona significatione sumitur. Unde Hiere. 18. propheta Deus loquens dicebat sic: Fiant corruentes in conspectum tuo in tempore furoris tui abutere eis: vbi abutere non pro actu illicito, sed pro licito debet sumi cum in Deo abusus in mala parte sumptus non cadat, tamen autem valet dicere, abutere eis, ac si diceret, consume: sicq; patet quod abusus etiam in scriptura sacra pro consumptione sumitur, & in significatione bona.
units.tr: We find further that in Holy Scripture "abuse" is used in a good sense. So in Jeremiah 18 God speaks through the prophet: "Let them fall before your face in the time of your anger; abuse them." Here "abuse" must be taken not in an unlawful sense but in a lawful one, since abuse in a bad sense cannot apply to God. Nevertheless, "abuse them" can be read as if he said "consume them." So it is clear that "abuse" in Holy Scripture is also used for consuming, and in a good sense.

units.la: Hic ostendit, quod abusus in scriptura sacra accipitur in significatione bona, sicut patet Hier. 18. Sed isti impugnatores dicunt istam obiectionem contra appellantem non valere: tum quia scriptura loquitur ibi improprie, loquendo autem improprie, non est inconveniens aliquid attribuere alicui, & tamen proprie loquendo hoc ab eo negare: tum quia etiā ibi potest dici, quod abutere accipitur aliquo modo in mala significatione. Primū declarant, quia abuti proprie secundū quod in theologia accipitur est perversum ad finem consonum naturae rei vti. hoc declarari posset per auctoritates Bibliae, in quib. de abuti fit mentio: quia Deus saepe creaturas rationales earum exigentibus culpis ad finem dissonum naturę earū adducit; & tunc Deus dici potest improprie abuti huiusmodi rationalib. creaturis; & ideo quadmodū furor, ira & huiusmodi improprie attribuitur Deo; ita et abuti improprie attribuitur Deo; & ita patet quod ista obiectio non est contra appellantem; qa nusquam inuenitur, quod abuti proprie sumptum accipiatur in bona significatione in scriptura diuina. Secundo dicunt, quod ibi potest dici, quod aburi potest accipi in mala significatione. Ad cuius evidentiam decernere esse sciendum, quod saepe vocabulum significat vnum principaliter, & aliud secundario. saepe etiā significat vnū in recto, & aliud in obliquo; & p consequens vtrumq; pertinet aliquo modo ad significationem eius. Ex hoc dicunt ad propositum, quod abuti secundum quod accipitur a Hieremia, licet non significet malum culpae in Deo, connotat tamen vel importat, & p consequens significat aliquo modo malum culpę in illis, quibus optabat Deum abuti. Et ita ibi accipitur in mala significatione non ex parte Dei, sed ex parte aliorum. Dicunt vltra, quod ibi non accipitur vt pro consumptione rei: tum quia homines non vocantur res vsu consumptibiles: tum quia non optabat propheta, quod Deus consumeret eos, sed magis quia humiliaret eos, & ad bonum conuerteret.
units.tr: Here he shows that abuse is used in Holy Scripture in a good sense, as Jeremiah 18 makes plain. But these opponents say that this objection against the appellant does not hold: first, because Scripture there speaks improperly, and when one speaks improperly it is not wrong to attribute something to someone which, speaking properly, one denies of him; second, because there too abuse can be said to be taken in some bad sense. They explain the first point thus: to abuse, properly as it is taken in theology, is to turn a thing to an end that does not agree with its nature. This could be shown from passages of the Bible where abuse is mentioned, because God often leads rational creatures, on account of their deserved guilt, to an end that does not suit their nature. Then God can be said improperly to abuse such rational creatures. Just as wrath, anger and the like are improperly attributed to God, so to abuse is improperly attributed to him. So it is clear that this objection is not against the appellant, since nowhere in divine Scripture is to abuse found taken properly in a good sense. Second, they say that there it can be said that "abuse" can be taken in a bad sense. To make this clear, one must know that a word often signifies one thing principally and another secondarily, and often signifies one thing directly and another indirectly; consequently both pertain in some way to its meaning. From this they argue for their case: to abuse, as Jeremiah uses it, although it does not signify the guilt of evil in God, nevertheless connotes or implies it, and consequently in some way signifies the guilt of evil in those whom he wished God to abuse. So it is taken there in a bad sense not on God's side but on the side of others. They add further that it is not taken there to mean consuming a thing: first, because men are not called consumable things; second, because the prophet did not wish God to destroy them but rather to humble them and turn them to good.

units.la: [In scriptura sacra abusus in bona significatione sumitur] sed improprie. [Furere tui] hic furer accipitur improprie [abutere eis asi diceret, consumeos] dicunt, quod male exponit scripturam: quia dicit abutere eis, hoc est puni & humilia ac confunde eos [pro consumptione sumitur] dicunt quod falsum est: sed pro punitione & humiliatione sumitur & in significatione bona, sed improprie.
units.tr: [In Holy Scripture "abuse" is taken in a good sense] but improperly. [Let them fall before your face] here "fall" is taken improperly. [Abuse them, as if he said, consume them] they say this explains Scripture badly, because it says "abuse them," that is, punish, humble and confound them. [Taken for consuming] they say this is false; it is taken for punishing and humbling, and in a good sense, but improperly.

units.la: CAP. LIII.
units.tr: CAP. LIII.

units.la: ADhuc dicit iste haereticus, quod illa diffinitio, quam dat de vti dicta constitutio, non est vera diffinitio, neque consona diffinitionibus, quas dant Sancti.
units.tr: Again this heretic says that the definition of use given in the aforesaid constitution is not a true definition, nor agreeable to the definitions given by the Saints.

units.la: Hic respondet ad aliam obiectionem appellantis: & primo recitat ipsam: secundo soluit in parte sequenti. Obiectio patet de se. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt isti impugnatores, q sicut non est licitum cuicunq; voces de novo imponere. si enim liceret alicui voces nouiter instituere, posset talis haeresim quamcunq; dogmatizare: & postea significationes vocu ad suum placitu explicare: & ita posset docere, q Christus non est Deus & homo: & quod non fuit natus de virgine, & postea se exponere: sic non est licitum cuicunque diffinitiones nouas non consonas, sed dissonas distinctionibus maiorū vocabulis assignare: cum diffinitiones, vt saepe, exprimant, quid vocabula significent. Ex hoc dicit, quod cum diffinitio, quam iste dat de vti, sit dissona diffinitionibus sanctorum & maiorum, ipsa est merito reprobanda. Necest vera diffinitio: quia nusquam inuenitur, quod vti acceptum verbaliter sit conuertibile cum illa diffinitione.
units.tr: Here he answers another objection of the appellant. First he recites it; second he resolves it in the following part. The objection is clear in itself. To make it plain, these opponents say that just as it is not lawful for anyone to impose new words, so it is not lawful for anyone to assign new definitions, not agreeing with but differing from the distinctions of the greater authorities. For if anyone were allowed to introduce new words, such a person could teach any heresy whatever, and afterwards explain the meanings of the words to suit himself, and so could teach that Christ is not God and man, and that he was not born of a virgin, and then explain himself away. Thus it is not lawful for anyone to assign new definitions not agreeing with the distinctions of greater authorities, since definitions usually express what words mean. From this they say that, since the definition this man gives of use differs from the definitions of the saints and greater authorities, it is rightly to be rejected. Nor is it a true definition, because nowhere is it found that the word use, taken verbally, is convertible with that definition.

units.la: CAP. LIV.
units.tr: CAP. LIV.

units.la: AD hoc dicimus, quod illa diffinitio, descriptio seu notificatio, quam dat dicta constitutio de vti, conueniens est & vera. Ducet enim, quod vti re aliqua nihil aliud est quam fructus rei seu vtilitatem aliam in solidum vti pro parte recipere, qui ex ea possunt salua rei substantia prouenire. & quod sit conueniens patet. Vsus enim diffinitur sic: Vsus est ius vtendi rebus alienis salua substantia rei. Ex quo sequitur, quod vti proprie loquendo requirit, quod cum ipso vsu remaneat substantia salua rei: & quod ex ea posit vtendi vtilitas aliqua prouenire.
units.tr: To this we say that the definition, description or notification of use which the said constitution gives is suitable and true. For it says that to use some thing is nothing other than to take the fruit of the thing, or some other usefulness of it, wholly or in part, which can come from it while the substance of the thing is preserved. And that it is suitable is clear. For use is defined thus: Use is the right of using another's things while the substance of the thing is preserved. From this it follows that to use, speaking properly, requires that with the use itself the substance of the thing remain intact, and that some usefulness of using can come from it.

units.la: Hic ad praemissam, obiectionem respondet: & diuiditur in tres partes. Primo conatur ostendere, quod diffinitio sua de vti est conueniens. Secundo respondet ad hoc, q tangit appellans, q diffinitio sua non est consona dictis sanctorum in parte immediate sequenti. Tertio reprehendit modum loquendi appellantis ibi: praeterea iste haereticus. Dicit ergo, quod diffinitio sua est vera, quod ostendit per diffinitionem vsus, quae habetur consimilis. Sed dicut isti impugnatores, quod hic est ad memoriā reuocandum, quod dictū est supra, s. quod hoc verbum vti acceptū verbaliter non habet tot significationes, quod habet hoc nomē vsus. hoc verbum enim vti sumptū verbaliter, semp notat actum: hoc nomen vero vsus significat actum eundem, quem significat hoc verbū vti. & praeter actum significat ius quoddā, quod potest dici haberi sine actu. sicut enim multi habent dominiū rei sine actu exercito circa rem: ita multi habent vsum, quod est ius quoddā vtendi rebus alienis &c. absq; omni actu, sicut aliquis habet vsum domus, licet ipsam actualiter nequaq; inhabitet. & potest quis habere vsum fundi, licet sit extra fundū, & nullū fructū actu ex fundo recipiat. Ex isto dicunt patere, q licet vsus in vna significatione sic diffiniatur: Vsus est ius vtendi rebus alienis, salua rerum substantia: Vti tamen non debet sic diffiniri: Vti nil aliud est proprie quam fructus rei seu vtilitatem aliā &c. & hoc, quia hoc verbum vti non conuenit cum hoc nomine vsus in illa significatione, sed in alia: & hoc per exemplum declarant. Nam sicut vsus se habet ad vti, sic se habet voluntas ad velle: & tñ quia voluntas habet plures significationes quam hoc verbum velle: ideo licet voluntas sic diffinitur: Voluntas est potentia qua primo & libere valet ad oppositū: non tamen Velle posset sic diffiniri: Velle est ferri primo & libere in oppositū: & licet voluntas sic diffiniretur: Voluntas est potentia incorporalis potens ferri in oppositā: non tamen velle posset sic diffiniri: Velle est actus incorporalis qui fertur in oppositā: & ita est de multis aliis: quod saepe duo vocabula sic se habent, quod vnum deriuatur ab alio: & tñ quia vnum habet plures significationes, potest habere aliquam diffinitionē, qualem pportionaliter aliunde habere non potest, sicut patet de diuino & diuinatione & multis aliis. ita dicunt esse in ppositū, quod vsus habet aliquam diffinitionem, qualem proportionabiliter vti habere non potest: sed praeter illā diffinitionem vsus potest habere aliam, & illi proportionabiliter consimilem potest hoc verbum vti habere: quia si diffiniatur vsus, vt significat actum vtendi, vti aliquo modo cōsimiliter diffinietur, imo eadem erit diffinitio vtriusque. Secundo dicunt, quod esto, quod vti in vna significatione diffiniretur modo praedicto: ex hoc tamen non sequitur, quod non potest aliter proprie diffiniri. Quia, sicut iste insinuat, eiusdem vocabuli aequiuoci possunt esse plures diffinitiones, quarum vtraque sit aeque propria, sicut significationes sunt aeque propriae. Constat autem quod hoc verbum vti proprie in vna significatione importat actum comedendi, bibendi, vestiendi, & huiusmodi. ergo illa poterit aliqua diffinitio ipsius vti competere. & ita esto, quod praedicto modo diffinietur, ad hoc tamen potest aliter proprie diffiniri: quia illa non esset sola diffinitio propria ipsius vti. Vnde dicunt, quod quamuis multa verba circa hanc materiam possent exponi; in hoc tamen erat aperte scripturam reprobando dixisse, quod dicit neminem posse vti rebus consumptibilibus vsu proprie loquendo; & quod proprie loquendo vti nihil est aliud quam fructus rei &c. [Nihil est aliud proprie &c.] sed hoc additum proprie nullo modo potest bene exponi ad intellectum istius, vt dicunt impugnatores isti, nec vti posset omni modo diffiniri sicut vsu. [Ex quo sequitur quod vti proprie loquendo requirit quod cum ipso vsu &c.] Hoc non sequitur: quia vti non conuenit cum vsu in illa significatione: & esto quod vti in vna significatione propria hoc requireret: ex hoc non sequitur, quod non habet aliam significationem propriam, in qua hoc nũ requirat. & ita stat appellantis intentum, quod proprie loquendo rebus vsu consumptibilib. contingit vti.
units.tr: Here he answers the foregoing objection, and it is divided into three parts. First he tries to show that his definition of use is suitable. Second he answers what the appellant touches on, that his definition does not agree with the words of the saints, in the immediately following part. Third he rebukes the appellant's manner of speaking, there: moreover this heretic. He says, therefore, that his definition is true, which he shows by the definition of use, which is found to be similar. But these opponents say that here we must recall what was said above, namely that the verb to use, taken verbally, does not have as many meanings as the noun use has. For the verb to use, taken verbally, always denotes an act; the noun use signifies the same act that the verb to use signifies, and besides the act it signifies a certain right which can be said to be held without the act. Just as many hold ownership of a thing without exercising any act concerning it, so many hold use, which is a certain right of using another's things, etc., without any act at all; as someone holds the use of a house although he does not actually live in it, and someone may have the use of a field though he is outside it and actually receives no fruit from it. From this they say it is clear that although use in one sense is defined thus, Use is the right of using another's things, the substance of the things being preserved, the verb to use ought not to be defined in this way: To use is properly nothing other than to take the fruit of a thing or some other usefulness of it, etc. And this is because the verb to use does not agree with the noun use in that sense, but in another. They illustrate this with an example. For as use stands to to use, so will stands to to will. Since the will has more meanings than the verb to will, it can be defined thus: The will is the faculty by which one freely and primarily can act toward opposites; but to will cannot be defined thus: To will is to be borne freely and primarily toward opposites. And although the will may be defined thus: The will is an incorporeal faculty able to be borne toward opposites, yet to will cannot be defined thus: To will is an incorporeal act which is borne toward opposites. And so it is with many other words: often two words stand in such a relation that one is derived from the other, and yet since one has several meanings, it can have a definition which the other cannot have in proportion, as is clear of divine and divination and many others. So they say that it is in point here that use has a definition which to use cannot have in proportion; but besides that definition, use may have another, and the verb to use can have a definition proportionally similar to it, since if use is defined as signifying the act of using, to use will be defined in a similar way in some sense; indeed the definition of each will be the same. Second, they say that even if to use were defined in one sense in the way described, it does not follow from this that it cannot be properly defined otherwise. For, as this man hints, one and the same ambiguous word can have several definitions, each of which is equally proper, just as its meanings are equally proper. It is certain that the verb to use, properly in one sense, implies the act of eating, drinking, clothing and the like; therefore that can be some definition belonging to to use. So even if it were defined in the aforesaid way, it can still be properly defined otherwise, since that would not be the only proper definition of to use. Hence they say that although many words on this subject could be explained in various ways, in this matter he plainly, by rejecting Scripture, said that no one can use consumable things in the proper sense of use, and that properly speaking to use is nothing other than the fruit of a thing, etc. [Nothing else properly, etc.] But this added word properly cannot in any way be well explained, as these opponents say, to make sense; nor can to use be defined in every way as use can. [From this it follows that to use, speaking properly, requires that with the use itself etc.] This does not follow, since to use does not agree with use in that sense; and even if to use, in one proper sense, required this, it does not follow that it lacks another proper sense in which the noun requires it. And so the appellant's intention stands: that, speaking properly, it is possible to use consumable things.

units.la: CAP. LV.
units.tr: CHAP. LV.

units.la: ADillud autem, quod dicit, quod dicta diffinitio non est consona diffinitionibus, quas dant sancti: dicimus quod non est inconueniens, quod eiusdem rei diuersimode considerata dentur diffinitiones diuersae. Sancti autem qui ipsum vti diffiniunt, ipsum vti sumunt aliter, quam sumat constitutio antedicta. respectu enim finis ipsum vti accipiunt, videl. ad quem finem res, quibus vtuntur, ordinentur. & secundum hoc Aug. dicit, quod vti est res, quae in vsum veniunt, referre ad ea, quibus est fruendum. Decretalis autem Exiit (cuius occasione constitutio Ad conditorem canonum facta fuit) de vsu loquitur, non prout res ad finem est ordinabilis, sed prout contra dominium seu contra proprietatem ac vsumfructum, ac ius vtendi diuiditur. & ideo non est mirum, si per sanctos aliae diffinitiones de vsu data fuerint: cum ipsum vti aliter sumpserit, quam sumat constitutio antedicta.
units.tr: As for what he says, that the said definition does not agree with the definitions that the saints give, we answer that it is not inappropriate for different definitions of the same thing to be given when it is considered in different ways.
