The saints who define use (vti) take it differently from how the aforesaid constitution takes it. For they understand use with respect to its end, namely the end to which the things we use are ordered, and according to this Augustine says that use is the referring of those things which come into use to those things which are to be enjoyed. But the decretal Exiit (on whose account the constitution Ad conditorem was made) speaks of use not as a thing is ordinable to an end, but as use is divided against dominion, or against ownership and usufruct, and against the right of using. Therefore it is no wonder if other definitions of use have been given by the saints, since use itself is understood differently from how the aforesaid constitution understands it.

units.la: Hic respondet ad hoc, quod accepit appellans, quod diffinitio sua non est consona diffinitionibus sanctorum: dicens, quod non est inconueniens, quod eiusdem rei sint plures diffinitiones. & ideo non est absurdum, quod vti diffiniatur aliter quam sancti diffiniunt: quia aliter accipitur a sanctis, & aliter in decre. Exiit & in constitutione Ad conditorem.
units.tr: Here he replies to what the appellant objected, that his definition does not agree with the definitions of the saints, saying that it is not inappropriate for one thing to have several definitions. Therefore it is not absurd that use is defined differently from how the saints define it, because it is taken differently by the saints and differently in the decretal Exiit and in the constitution Ad conditorem.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod hic deficit in duobus. Primo quia ad mentem appellantis nequaquam respondet. Secundo, quia sibiipsi contradicit. Quod ad mentem appellantis nequaquam respondeat, conantur ostendere: non enim appellans negare volebat eiusdem rei posse esse diffinitiones diuersas: imo concederet, quod vti posset diuersimode diffiniri: sed supposuit tanquam certum, quod sancti, & maxime Augustinus, qui de vti multum exquisite tractauit in diuersis locis, non loquuntur de vti semper improprie: imo proprie loquebantur. Cum igitur diffinitio istius impugnati de vti non sit consona, nec eadem in sententia cum diffinitionibus sanctorum de vti, sequitur manifeste, quod non solum diffinitio istius de vti non est propria, imo siue ista sit propria, siue impropria, siue nulla, aliqua alia ab ista est propria diffinitio ipsius vti & ita male dicit affirmas, quod sola sua diffinitio de vti est propria, cum diffinitio sanctorum de vti sit propria. Ex quo sequitur, quod cum diffinitio sanctorum de vti conueniat nobis respectu rerum consumptibilium vsu rebus consumptibilibus proprie vti contingit: quod iste negat. Secundo dicunt, quod iste contradicit sibiipsi, cum dicit, quod decre. Exiit, & sua Ad conditorem loquitur de vsu, prout diuiditur contra dominium seu proprietatem & vsumfructum ac ius vtendi: tum quia constat quod decretalis Exiit loquitur de vsu, qui est actus comedendi, bibendi, induendi & huiusmodi, qui proprie possunt in rebus consumptibilibus reperiri: quod iste negat. tñ quia vsus distinctus contra ius vtendi non est ille vsus, qui sic diffinitur: vsus est ius vtendi rebus alienis: ergo loquitur de alio vsu, quam sit ille vsus: alius est vsus facti. vsus autem facti etiam secundum istum, sicut ostensum est supra, comprehendit actum bibendi, comedendi &c. ergo ille vsus, qui distinguitur contra ius vtendi in rebus vsu consumptibilibus, proprie reperitur.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he fails here in two respects. First, because he does not answer the appellant's meaning at all. Second, because he contradicts himself. That he does not answer the appellant's meaning they try to show. For the appellant did not wish to deny that one thing can have different definitions; indeed he would concede that use can be defined in different ways. But he assumed as certain that the saints, and above all Augustine, who treated use very carefully in various places, do not always speak of use improperly, but indeed speak of it properly. Since, then, the definition of this man concerning use does not agree, nor is it the same in meaning, with the definitions of the saints concerning use, it clearly follows not only that this man's definition of use is not proper, but also that, whether that definition is proper, improper or nothing, some other definition than this is the proper definition of use itself. And so he wrongly affirms that his definition alone of use is proper, when the saints' definition of use is proper. From this it follows that, since the saints' definition of use applies to us with respect to consumable things, it is possible to use consumable things properly, which this man denies. Second, they say that he contradicts himself when he says that the decretal Exiit, and his own Ad conditorem, speak of use as it is divided against dominion or ownership and usufruct and the right of using. This is so because it is certain that the decretal Exiit speaks of use, which is the act of eating, drinking, clothing and the like, which can properly be found in consumable things; this man denies it. Moreover, use distinguished against the right of using is not that use which is defined thus: "use is the right of using another's things." Therefore he speaks of a different use from that use. The other is the use of fact (vsus facti). But the use of fact, even according to him, as has been shown above, includes the act of drinking, eating and so on. Therefore that use which is distinguished against the right of using in consumable things is properly found.

units.la: [Ipsum vti sumunt aliter &c.] tamen proprie sumunt, & proprie loquebantur aliter sumendo ipsum vti. [Vti est res quae in vsum veniunt referre ad ea quibus fruendum est.] hic licet sit diffinitio seu notificatio Augustini, tamen propria est. Ex qua sequitur, ex quo est propria, quod rebus vsu consumptibilibus conuenit proprie vti: quia proprie conuenit referre res vlu consumptibiles ad ea quibus fruendum est. [cuius occasione &c.] sc. ad reprobandum ipsam [ac ius vtendi diuiditur] ille est vsus facti [si per sanctos aliae diffinitiones] tamen proprie [cum ipsum vti aliter sumpserit] sed proprie. [quam sumat constitutio antedicta] quae aliter accepit vti secundum istos, quam aliquis vnquam ante ipsum.
units.tr: [They understand use differently, etc.] Yet they understand it properly, and they spoke properly when understanding use in another way. [Use is the referring of those things which come into use to those things which are to be enjoyed.] Here, although it is the definition or notification of Augustine, it is nevertheless proper. From this it follows, since it is proper, that it belongs properly to consumable things to be used, because it belongs properly to refer consumable things to those things which are to be enjoyed. [on whose account, etc.] namely, to reprobate it. [and it is divided against the right of using] that is the use of fact. [if other definitions have been given by the saints] yet properly. [since use itself has been understood otherwise] but properly. [than the aforesaid constitution takes it] which, according to them, has understood use differently from anyone before it.

units.la: CAP. LVI.
units.tr: CHAP. LVI.

units.la: PRaterea iste haereticus loquendo de vsu & de vti extra modum loquendi scripturae sacrae & sanctorum seponit. dicit enim in rebus vsu consumptibilibus locum habere absque iure aliquo simplicem vsum facti. profecto modus iste loquendi nec in nouo testamento, neque in veteri, neque in scripturis sanctorum aliquibus, sicut credimus, poterit reperiri. Praeterea aduertat iste haereticus, si Augustini diffinitio conueniat dictis suis, ipse dicit, quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus potest haberi vsus simplex a dominio separatus. Aug. autem dicit, quod vti est res quae in vsu veniunt referre ad ea quibus est fruendum. Proculdubio dicta diffinitio eius dictis non conuenit, cum de rebus loquatur dicta diffinitio: & ipse de simplici vsu facti dicendo: Vti est res quae in vsum &c.
units.tr: Moreover, this heretic, in speaking of use and of using, departs from the manner of speaking of Holy Scripture and of the saints. For he says that in consumable things a simple use of fact takes place without any right. Surely this manner of speaking cannot be found, as we believe, either in the New Testament or in the Old, or in any writings of the saints. Furthermore, let this heretic notice that if Augustine's definition agrees with his statements, he says that in consumable things there can be a simple use separated from dominion. But Augustine says that use is the referring of those things which come into use to those things which are to be enjoyed. Undoubtedly that definition does not agree with his statements, since the definition speaks of things, and he speaks of the simple use of fact, saying: "Use is the referring of those things which come into use," etc.

units.la: Hic reprehendit appellantem, quantum ad modum loquendi, quo ad hoc quod ponit simplicem vsum facti in rebus: tum quia talis modus in Biblia vel in libris Sanctorum minime reperitur: tum quia talis modus loquendi non conuenit cum diffinitione, quam ponit Augustinus de vti.
units.tr: Here he rebukes the appellant as to his manner of speaking, in that he posits a simple use of fact in things; both because such a manner is nowhere found in the Bible or in the books of the saints, and because such a manner of speaking does not agree with the definition of use which Augustine gives.

units.la: Sed impugnatores dicunt, quod iste reprehendit hic appellantem iniuste. Primo qa licet iste modus loquendi sub eisdem vocibus simul iunctis non inueniatur in nouo nec in veteri testamento, nec in libris sanctorum dogmatizatorum ab ecclesia: inuenitur tn in scripturis authenticis summorum pontificum. Isto n. modo loquendi utitur Nicolaus tertius in decretali Exiit cum dicit: Cum in reb. temporalibus sit considerare praecipuum proprietatem, possessionem, vsumfructum, ius utendi & simplicem facti vsum, & infra: Nec per hoc, quod proprietatem vsus & rei cuiuscunque a se dominium abdicasse videantur, simplici vsui renunciasse esse conuincitur. & Clemens quintus in decretali Exiui, ait: quas & quarum vsus facti licet habere, dimisso ipsis fratribus tantummodo simplici vsu facti. & ita reprehendere appellantem propter istum modum loquendi est reprehendere modum loquendi summorum pontificum. Secundo quod iniuste reprehendat eum, patet, quia modus loquendi, qui non inueniatur modo loquendi scripturae diuinae contrarius, sed congruens, est nullatenus arguendus. Nam secundum Glossam primam Thy. n. vlr. Non omnes, sed prophanae solum vocum nouitates sunt vitandae. Sunt enim doctrinae religiosae congruentes, verborum quaedam nouitates. Licet igitur iste modus loquendi esset nouus cum tamen sit a multis temporibus vlitatus, siue sit congruens scripturae diuinae, est minime arguendus. quod vero sit congruens scripturae diuinae, ostenditur, quia per simplicem facti vlum non intelligit appellans, nisi vsum facti quae non necessario habet ius annexum, quo valeat quis pro vsu rei in iudicio litigare. sed multos habuisse talem vsum ex scriptura diuina conuincitur, sicut superius patet, & posterius amplius ostendetur, ergo iste modus loquendi est congruus ad exprimendum, qualem vsum contingit habere in rebus, secundum quod scriptura diuina sumit vsum. Tertio dicunt, quod reprehendit eum iniuste, cum intendit eum reprehendere, quia diffinitio Augustini non conuenit cum dictis suis, propter hoc n. est minime arguendus: quia quando voces sunt aequiuocae, licet vt illis vocibus non solum in vna significatione, sed etiam in alia. Vsus autem aequiuoce accipitur in diuersis locis. & ideo licet vti hoc nomine alio modo, quam in determinato loco loquitur Augustinus, praesertim cum Augustinus alibi vtatur eodem modo hoc vocabulo vsus [Extra modum loquendi scripturae sacrae & sanctorum seponit] verum est, dicunt isti vocaliter: modo tamen loquendi eorum minime aduersatur. Nec etiam negat modum eorum loquendi, sed virtualiter ex scriptura diuina & libris sanctorum accipitur. Sed modus loquendi istius impugnati modo loquendi Bibliae aduersatur, cum neget modum loquendi Bibliae, & sanctorum, dicens, quod rebus vsu consumptibilibus non contingit vti absq; iure. Aliqn n. est absq; iure. constat n. quod fur comedendo panem, quem furatus est, habet simplicem facti vsum, quia habet actum comedendi panem: & in sine iure, imo contra ius. Aliqn vero inuenitur sine iure, sed non sine licentia. Aliquotiens inuenitur cum iure, accipiendo simplicem facti vsum in vna significatione eius, [Profecto iste modus loquendi, &c.] verum est q nō inuenitur vocaliter: sicut nec ille, res vsu consumptibiles: neutiquam modus loquendi est a sapientibus reprobandus: quia vtrumque scripturae sacrae est congruens. [Si Augustini diffinitio conueniat dictis suis] nec repugnat nec conuenit: quia aliter accipit vsum ibi Augustinus, & aliter appellans. Alibi tamen realiter conuenit modus loquendi Augustini cum dictis appellantis. [cum de rebus loquatur dicta diffinitio] principaliter loquitur ibi Augustinus de actu, qui est vti, & secundario de rebus. Diffinit enim vti: & ita principaliter loquitur de vti: ipse de simplici vsu facti. ita principaliter: & tamen nihilominus loquitur de rebus, respectu quarum potest esse simplex vsus facti.
units.tr: But the opponents say that he rebukes the appellant here unjustly. First, because although this manner of speaking, with these same words joined together, is not found in the New or the Old Testament, nor in the books of the saints approved by the Church, it is nevertheless found in the authentic writings of the supreme pontiffs. For Nicholas III uses this manner of speaking in the decretal Exiit when he says: Since in temporal goods one must consider chiefly the ownership, the possession, the usufruct, the right of using and the simple use of fact, and below: Nor is it proved, by the fact that they seem to have renounced the ownership of use and of any thing whatever, that they have renounced simple use. And Clement V in the decretal Exivi says: whose simple use of fact it is lawful to have, the brothers having been left only with simple use of fact. Therefore to rebuke the appellant for this manner of speaking is to rebuke the manner of speaking of the supreme pontiffs. Second, that he rebukes him unjustly is clear, because a manner of speaking which is not contrary to the manner of speaking of Holy Scripture, but agrees with it, ought in no way to be censured. For according to the first Gloss on 1 Tim. 6: "Not all novelties of words, but only profane ones, are to be avoided. For there are religious doctrines, and some novelties of words which agree." Although this manner of speaking would therefore be new, since it has been in use for many ages, if it agrees with Holy Scripture it is by no means to be censured. That it does agree with Holy Scripture is shown by this: the appellant understands by simple use of fact nothing other than the use of fact which does not necessarily have a right annexed to it, by which one may plead in court for the use of a thing. But it is shown from Holy Scripture that many have had such a use, as is clear above and will be shown more fully later. Therefore this manner of speaking is suitable for expressing what kind of use it is possible to have in things, according as Holy Scripture takes use. Third, they say that he rebukes him unjustly, since he intends to rebuke him because Augustine's definition does not agree with his statements. For on that account he is by no means to be censured, because when words are equivocal they may be taken not only in one sense but also in another. And use is taken equivocally in different places. Therefore, although this word is used in a different way from how Augustine speaks in a certain place, especially since Augustine elsewhere uses this same word "use" in the same way. [He departs from the manner of speaking of Holy Scripture and of the saints] It is true, these opponents say, in words; yet it is not contrary to their manner of speaking. Nor does he deny their manner of speaking, but it is virtually taken from Holy Scripture and the books of the saints. But the manner of speaking of this opponent is contrary to the manner of speaking of the Bible, since he denies the manner of speaking of the Bible and of the saints, saying that it is not possible to use consumable things without a right. For sometimes there is use without right: it is clear that a thief who eats the bread he has stolen has a simple use of fact, because he has the act of eating bread, and without right, indeed against right. Sometimes, however, it is found without right but not without permission. Sometimes it is found with right, taking simple use of fact in one of its senses. [Surely this manner of speaking, etc.] It is true that it is not found in these words, just as neither is the phrase "consumable things"; by no means is this manner of speaking to be rejected by the wise, because both are suitable to Holy Scripture. [If Augustine's definition agrees with his statements] It neither conflicts nor agrees, because Augustine understands use there in one way and the appellant in another. Elsewhere, however, Augustine's manner of speaking agrees in fact with the statements of the appellant. [since the definition speaks of things] Augustine there speaks chiefly of the act, which is use, and secondarily of things. For he defines use, and so speaks chiefly of use; he (the appellant) speaks of simple use of fact. So chiefly; and yet nonetheless he speaks of things, with respect to which there can be simple use of fact.

units.la: CAP. LVII.
units.tr: CAP. LVII.

units.la: Adhuc dicit iste haereticus, quod predicta assertio determinationi sanctae Romanae ecclesiae obuiat in sapedicta decretali Exiit, dicente sic. In his quae ad victum & vestitum & diuinum cultum ac sapientiale studium pertinent, necessarium vsum rerum fratribus esse concessum. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod contingit vti rebus pertinentibus ad victum & vestitum, quas constat, esse res consumptibiles vsu.
units.tr: This heretic further says that the aforesaid assertion runs counter to the determination of the holy Roman Church in the aforementioned decretal Exiit, which speaks thus: In those things which pertain to food and clothing and divine worship and the study of wisdom, the use of things is granted to the brothers as necessary. From these words it is clearly gathered that it is possible to use things pertaining to food and clothing, which are plainly things consumed by use.

units.la: Hic respondet ad vltimam obiectionem appellantis contra assertionem praedictam. & post recitat ipsam. Secundo soluit in parte immediate sequenti. Obiectio patens est de se.
units.tr: Here he replies to the last objection of the appellant against the aforesaid assertion, and afterwards recites it. Secondly, he answers in the part immediately following. The objection is clear enough in itself.

units.la: Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod iste impugnatus vnam obiectionem positam in appellatione dimittit, quae talis est: Praeterea quibus vti non contingit, non contingit abuti: quia cum vti & abuti sint contraria nata sunt fieri circa idem. si ergo non contingit vti rebus consumptibilibus: eis non contingit abuti. ¶[Necessarium vsum.] Necessarium vsum vocat actum circa rem exteriorem temporalem, sine quo non potest conseruari natura.
units.tr: Those opponents say that this man under attack omits one objection put forward in the appeal, which is as follows: Moreover, those things which we cannot use, we cannot abuse, since use and abuse are contraries and are by nature concerned with the same thing. If therefore it is not possible to use consumable things, it is not possible to abuse them. ¶ [Necessarium vsum.] By "necessary use" he means an act concerning an external temporal thing, without which nature cannot be preserved.

units.la: CAP. LVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER LVIII.

units.la: Dicimus quod per verba illa non concessit fratribus simplicem vsum facti: imo hoc ipso, quod ipsis vsum concessit, si concessio valuit ius ipsis vtendi concessit: & sic in illum non habuit simplicem vsum facti. Et si dicas, quod imo nullum ius concessit. Dicimus, quod quantum ad res vsu consumptibiles posuit vsum improprie, pro rei consumptione. nec est nouum, quod idem verbum ponatur improprie, & proprie respectu diuersorum. Praeterea decretalis praedictam dicit, necessarium vsum rerum in his quae ad victum & vestitum pertinent fratribus esse concessum. Non dicit, vsum facti. & sic nihil facit pro eo: & si omnino dicas, quod conditor canonis intellexit de vsu facti, sumendo vsum, proprie dicimus quod cum in talibus rebus vsus constitui nequeat neque haberi, vt probat dicta constitutio, & est probatum supra in articulo primo: Dicta constitutio contineret quantum ad hoc impossibile: & per consequens cum constitutio possibilis esse debeat, non valeret: non tamen illa fuit conditoris intentio, vt probat constitutio ad conditorem canonum antedicta.
units.tr: We say that by those words he did not grant the friars a simple use of fact. Indeed, by the very fact that he granted them the use, if the grant was valid, he granted them the right of using, and so in that respect he did not grant a simple use of fact. And if you say that he granted no right at all, we answer that, as regards things consumed by use, he used the word "use" improperly, to mean the consumption of the thing. Nor is it new for the same word to be used improperly in one case and properly in relation to others. Moreover, the decretal says that the necessary use of things in those matters which pertain to food and clothing has been granted to the friars. It does not say "use of fact," and so it does nothing to support that view. And if you should altogether maintain that the author of the canon meant use of fact, taking "use" in that sense, we say plainly that since in such things use can neither be established nor held, as the said constitution proves, and as has been proved above in article one, the said constitution would, as far as this goes, contain something impossible; and consequently, since a constitution ought to be possible, it would not be valid. Yet that was not the intention of the author, as the constitution cited above, addressed to the author of the canons, proves.

units.la: In parte ista ad obiectionem praemissam respondet. Et quatuor ponit rationes. Prima est quod per verba illa decretalis Exiit, non habetur, quod concessit fratribus simplicem facti vsum. Se-cunda cunda est, quod Nicolaus accepit ibi vsum improprie, & illa ponitur ibi: & si dicat. Tertia, quod decretalis Exiit non loquitur ibi de vsu facti, & ponitur ibi pretextu. Quarta quod si decretalis Exiit loquitur de vsu facti, proprie ipsa est impossibilis, & non tenenda, & illa ponitur ibi; & si omnino
units.tr: In this part he replies to the objection set out above, and he gives four reasons. The first is that the words of the decretal Exiit do not show that he granted the friars the simple use of fact. The second is that Nicholas there took "use" improperly, and this is stated there; and if he says... The third is that the decretal Exiit does not speak there of use of fact, and it is stated there under the pretext. The fourth is that if the decretal Exiit speaks of use of fact, then it is in itself impossible and not to be upheld, and this is stated there; and if absolutely

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt praedicta verba continere quatuor falsa: primum est, quod dominus Nicolaus per illa verba non concessit simplicem vsum facti. Secundum est quod Nicolaus quo ad res vsu consumptibiles accepit vsum improprie. Tertium est quod non concessit eis vsum facti. Quarto, si decretalis Exiit, intellexerit de vsu facti proprie loquendo, non valeret, quia esset impossibilis. Quod autem primum, sc. quod Nicolaus non concessit fratribus simplicem facti vsum sit falsum, probare conantur. Nicolaus n. dicit in dicta decretali Exiit, in haec verba: non talis abdicatio proprietatis omnimoda renunciatio rerum vsus cuiquam videatur inducere. Nam in rebus temporalibus sit considerare praecipuum proprietatem, possessionem, vsum fructum, ius vtendi & simplicem facti vsum, & vltimo tanquam necessarium egeat licet primis carere possit vita mortalium, nulla prorsus poterit esse professio, quae a se vsum necessariae sustentationis excludat. Ex quibus verbis colligun-tur duo: quorum primum est, quod Nicolaus Fratribus tribuit simplicem facti vsum. Nam illum vsum, quo necessarie eget vita mortalium, tribuit Fratribus, sed simplici vsu facti necessario eget vita mortalium secundum Nicolaum, cum dicat, licet primis carere possit. Ex quo sequitur, quod vltimo sc. simplici vsu facti necessario eget vita mortalium: ergo attribuit Fratribus simplicem facti vsum. Secundum quod colligitur ex praedictis est, quod Nicolaus tertius per simplicem vsum facti intelligit vsum necessariae sustentationis comprehendit sub simplici vsu, dicit: licet primis carere possit vita mortalium, nulla prorsus poterit esse professio, quae a se vsum necessariae sustentationis excludat. Quae verba essent penitus inconnexa, nisi per vltimum, sc. simplicem facti vsum, intelligeret vel comprehenderet vsum necessariae sustentationis. Constat ergo quod Nicolaus per simplicem facti vsum vel intelligit vsum necessariae sustentationis, vel sub simplici facti vsu vsum necessariae sustentationis comprehendit. Et ex isto sequitur evidenter, quod Nicolaus tertius tribuit & concedit Fratribus simplicem facti vsum ex quo concedit eis vsum necessariae sustentationis. Item idem Nicolaus sic dicit: Verum concedens fuit ei professioni, quae se ipsam devovit Christum pauperem in tanta paupertate secutari omnium abdicare dominium & rerum sibi concessarum necessario vsu fore contentam. Vbi per hoc proprietatem vsus & rei cuiuscunque dominium a se abdicasse videtur simplici vsui omnis rei renunciatum esse convincitur. Ex his verbis patet, quod per vsum necessariae sustentationis simplicem facti vsum intelligit. Et si diceret forsitan impugnatus, q per vsum necessariae sustentationis intelligit simplicem vsum, non simplicem vsum facti. Vn dicit, simplici vsui omnis rei, &c. Nō dicit, simplici vsui facti dicitur, q nō est verū. Nā q p simplicē vsū intelligat simplicem vsum facti, patet p ilia, q post verba praemissa immediate sequuntur. Ait n. qui inquā vsus non iuris sed facti tantum modo nomē habens &c. Ex quib. clare patet q loquitur de simplici vsu facti, & ita per vsum necessariae sustentationis intelligit simplicem vsum facti, vel econuerso, & quodcunq; horum detur, sequitur sicut tribuit Nicolaus Fratribus vsum necessariae sustentationis, ita tribuit eis simplicem vsum facti. Ex hoc sequitur, quod tribuit Fratribus simplicem facti vsum respectu rerum consumptibilium vsu. Nam vsus necessariae sustentationis est respectu rerum vsu consumptibilium: quod ex verbis Nicolai colligitur, cum ait, Quamvis necessarium rerum tam ad vitā sustentationem quam etiam efficiens sui status executionem, excepto de pecunia infra subiungitur, moderatus vsus secundum eorum regulam & veritate omnimodam, concessus est Fratribus, quib. reb. Fratres licite vti possunt. Ex quib. verbis patet, quod distinguit res necessarias ad vitae sustentationem ab aliis rebus: & non nisi sicut res vsu consumptibiles, à reb. non consumptibilib. vsu. ergo vsus necessariae sustentationis est respectu rerum vsu consumptibilium. & ois vsus sustentationis est simplex vsus facti: ergo aliquis simplex vsus facti est respectum rerum consumptibilium vsu secundum Nico. Ex praedictis potest colligi, vt videtur, quod non sp simplex vsus secundum Nicolaum excludit ius & proprietatem: tū quia tunc simplici vsu facti non necessario egeret vita mortalium: quia vita mortalium non necessario egetaliquo, quod necessario excludit ius & proprietatem. Multi n. diuites substentantur sine omni vsu excludente ius & proprietatem: cum multi sp vtantur rebus propriis & non alienis, tum quia vsus necessariae sustentationis est simplex vsus facti. Vsus aut necessariae sustentationis non semper excludit ius & proprietatem, sicut dictum est de multis diuitib. ergo nec simplex vsus facti sp excludit ius & proprietatem. Et si dicatur, quod hoc est contra Nico. tertium, qui loquens de vsu necessariae sustentationis ait: qui inquā, vsus non iuris sed facti tantum modo nomē habens, q facti est tantū in vsu dicitur præbet vtentib. nihil iuris. Ex quib. verbis videtur, q vsus necessariae sustentationis excludit omne ius positiuum, & per consequens proprietatem. Adhuc dicunt isti, q Nicolaus non loquitur ibi de vsu necessariae sustentationis sed loquitur determinate de vsu necessariae sustentationis Fratrum Minorum. Et verum est, q aliqs vsus necessariae sustentationis, licet non qa est vsus necessariae sustentationis, sed propter abdicationē ois iuris annexā excludit omne ius & proprietatem. & sic dicendum est conf-militer de simplici vsu, q aliqs simplex vsus facti, propter abdicationem ois iuris annexa excludit omne ius positiuum. sed non ois simplex vsus facti excludit omne ius: quia in vna significatione ois simplex vsus facti excludat ius & proprietatem. Ex praedictis colligitur evidenter, q ois vsus necessariae sustentationis est simplex vsus facti in vna significatione, non econuerso. Secundo colligitur q ois vtens re quacunq; vsu consumptibili vsu, vel non consumptibili vsu, habet simplicē vsum facti: hoc est, habeta liquē actu vtendi qui potest separari ab oi iure licet non sp separetur ab oi iure. Omnis n. actus exterior vtendi re temporali, de quo nunc est sermo, est indifferens ad actum licitū. illicitum: & ita omnis talis est simplex vsus facti hoc est, est vsus, qui potest esse sine omni iure inio potest esse contra ius & illicitus. quod ergo dicunt Fratres Minores singulariter habere vsum simplicem facti, debet intelligi cum dictione exclusiva vel æquipollenti, sic: Fratres Minores habent in rebus, quibus vtuntur tantum simplicem vsum facti, vel non habent ius, sed simplicem vsum facti. Et si quæratur: ad quid ergo additur simplex, cum sufficeret dicere, habent, tantum vsum facti. Dicunt quod additur simplex ad insinuandum, quod talis vsus facti non necessario habet annexum quodcunq; ius. hoc autem non insinuatur ita sine hac dictione simplex: cum dicitur, vsus facti: sicut cum dicitur, simplex vsus facti. Secundo dicunt isti impugnatores, quod aliud falsum continent verba prædicta, quod Nicolaus videlicet in verbis præmissis accepit vsum improprie. quod enim hoc sit falsum, ostendunt: quia Nicolaus accepit ibi vsum, sicut accipitur in scriptura sacra & in doctrina sanctorum & in medicina, & in philosophia morali & naturali, ac etiam in vulgari modo loquendi. Sed scriptura sacra, ac philosophia, & vulgaris modus loquendi sic loquendo de vsu non loquuntur improprie: nec vnquam auditum est, quod aliquis intelligens dixerit talem modum loquendi: ista vitur cibo & potu, vel consimili, esse improprium. ergo Nicolaus sequens modum loquendi scripturæ diuinæ, & philosophiæ, & vulgaris locutionis accepit proprie vsum. Tertium falsum contentum in verbis prædictis secundum istos, est quod Nicolaus tertius non concessit Fratribus vsum, quo necessario eget vita mortalium. talis est simplex vsus facti, sicut patet ibi: Cum in rebus temporalibus, &c. Sed simplex vsus facti, est vsus facti. ergo concessit eis vsum facti. hoc non solum sententialiter, sed etiam vocaliter explicat manifeste. Nam loquens de vsu concesso Fratrib. ait: qui inquam vsus non iuris, sed facti tantum modo nomen habens, quod facti est tantum, in vtendo præbet vtentibus nil iuris. Ex quibus verbis patet indubie, quod vsus facti concessit Fratribus. Ex quo patet vltetius: quod vsus facti distinguitur ab vsu iuris: & quod potest esse sine vsu iuris. Quartum falsum est, quod si decretalis Exiit intellexerit de vsu facti in loquendo, non valeret: quia esset de impossibili. quod n. hoc debeat reputari falsum, patet, quia constat quod Nicolaus intelligit de vsu facti, sicut ostensum est: sed vsum facti respicit in his, quæ pertinent ad victum & vestitum, non est impossibile, sicut ostensum est. ergo proprie hoc non debet iudicari decretalis Exiit, non valere. [Per verba illa non concessit Fratribus simplicem vsum facti.] Hoc patet esse falsum, quia concessit eis necessarium vsum. sed vsus necessarius est simplex vsus facti, sicut ostensum est: ergo &c. [Si concessio valuit iuxta ipsis vtendi concessit.] Hoc est falsum & contrarium isti impugnatori (vt dicunt isti.) quod sit falsum patet, quia aliquid conceditur absq; iure. quod sit contrarium impugnatori patet, quia secundum eum in huiusmodi rebus, quæ ad victum pertinent & vestitum, non potest habere ius vtendi, sed bene proprietas: & tamen possunt concedi. ergo possunt concedi sine iure vtendi. [Et sic in illis non habent simplicem vsum facti.] Male infert secundum istos: quia simplex vsus facti potest esse cum iure vtendi, quamuis non necessario requirat ius vtendi: sicut actus comedendi potest esse cum iure comedendi, licet non requirat necessario ius comedendi ad hoc quod sit in serum natura [potuit vsum improprie pro rei consumptione.] Innuit, quod consumptio rei sit vsus improprie: quod falsum est, imo aliqua consumptio rei est proprie vsus. Non omnis tamen consumptio est proprie vsus. [non dicit vsum facti.] verum est, quod ibi non dicit vocaliter vsum facti, sed supra dixit simplicem vsum facti. & ex verbis decretalis Exiit, pateter habetur, quod vsus necessarius est vsus facti; quia vsus necessarius non est vsus iuris, quia multi sustentantur & sua officia exequuntur absq; vsu iuris, sicut patet de Fratribus Minoribus, & etiam de illis qui in rebus, quibus vtuntur, non habent dominium & proprietatem qui sustentantur & sua officia exequuntur absq; vsu iuris. Vsus ergo iuris non est necessarius ad victum & vestitum & diuinum cultum ac sapientiale studium. ille ergo vsus qui est necessarius ad prædictam, est vsus facti, & per consequens qui loquitur de vsu necessario ad prædicta, loquitur de vsu facti sententialiter, quamuis non semper vocaliter. [dicta constitutio continuaret quantum ad hoc impossibile.] hoc & illa quæ immediate præcedunt dicunt esse falsa [non tamen illa fuit conditoris intentio] hoc dicunt esse contra intellectum etiam omnium æmulorum, qui ante ipsum fuerunt [vt probat constitutio ad conditorem.] dicunt quod sophistice probat & male.
units.tr: But these opponents say that the aforementioned words contain four falsehoods. The first is that Lord Nicholas, by those words, did not grant the simple use of fact. The second is that Nicholas, with respect to consumable goods, took "use" improperly. The third is that he did not grant them the use of fact. The fourth is that, if the decretal Exiit is understood to speak of the use of fact in the proper sense, it would not be valid, because it would be impossible. As to the first, namely that Nicholas did not grant the friars the simple use of fact, they try to prove it false. For Nicholas says in that decretal Exiit, in these words: such a renunciation of ownership does not seem to bring with it an absolute surrender of the use of things. For in temporal things one must consider the chief elements: ownership, possession, usufruct, the right of use, and the simple use of fact; and though the last is needed only as a necessity, while the first may be lacking to mortal life, no profession at all could exclude from itself the use of necessary sustenance. Two things are gathered from these words. The first is that Nicholas grants the friars the simple use of fact. For he grants the friars the use which mortal life necessarily needs, but according to Nicholas mortal life necessarily needs the simple use of fact, since he says though the first may be lacking. From this it follows that mortal life necessarily needs the last, namely the simple use of fact; therefore he attributes the simple use of fact to the friars. The second thing gathered from the foregoing is that Nicholas III, by the simple use of fact, understands the use of necessary sustenance, or comprehends the use of necessary sustenance under the simple use. He says: though the first may be lacking to mortal life, no profession at all could exclude from itself the use of necessary sustenance. These words would be wholly disconnected unless by the last, namely the simple use of fact, he understood or included the use of necessary sustenance. It is clear, then, that Nicholas by the simple use of fact either means the use of necessary sustenance, or under the simple use of fact comprehends the use of necessary sustenance. And from this it evidently follows that Nicholas III grants and concedes to the friars the simple use of fact, since he concedes to them the use of necessary sustenance. Again, the same Nicholas says: But he concedes to that profession which has devoted itself to follow Christ the poor in such great poverty, to renounce all ownership, and to be content with the necessary use of the things granted to it. Where by this he seems to have renounced from himself the ownership of the use and of any thing, it is shown that the simple use of every thing has been renounced. From these words it is plain that by the use of necessary sustenance he means the simple use of fact. And if the opponent should perhaps say that by the use of necessary sustenance he means simple use, not simple use of fact, the answer is: he says simple use of every thing, etc.; he does not say simple use of fact, which is not true. That by simple use he means simple use of fact is plain from what immediately follows the words quoted. For he says: which use, I say, is not of right but bears only the name of fact, etc. From these words it is clearly evident that he is speaking of the simple use of fact; and so by the use of necessary sustenance he means the simple use of fact, or the reverse. And whichever of these holds, it follows that just as Nicholas grants the friars the use of necessary sustenance, so he grants them the simple use of fact. From this it follows that he grants the friars the simple use of fact with respect to consumable goods. For the use of necessary sustenance is with respect to goods consumed in use. This is gathered from the words of Nicholas, when he says: Although the necessary things, both for sustenance of life and for carrying out the execution of their state, except money, are subjoined below, a moderate use according to their rule and the full truth is granted to the friars, with which things the friars may lawfully use. From these words it is plain that he distinguishes the things necessary for sustenance of life from other things, and that these are used only as things consumed by use, not as things not consumed by use. Therefore the use of necessary sustenance is with respect to things consumed by use; and every use of sustenance is simple use of fact. Therefore some simple use of fact is with respect to things consumed by use, according to Nicholas. From what has been said it can seem to follow that the simple use according to Nicholas does not always exclude right and ownership; for then the simple use of fact would not be necessary to mortal life, because mortal life does not necessarily need anything that necessarily excludes right and ownership. For many rich men are sustained without any use excluding right and ownership, since many always use things that are their own and not another's; and because the use of necessary sustenance is simple use of fact. But the use of necessary sustenance does not always exclude right and ownership, as has been said of many rich men; therefore neither does simple use of fact always exclude right and ownership. And if it is said that this is against Nicholas III, who, speaking of the use of necessary sustenance, says: which use, I say, is not of right but bears only the name of fact, which, being only of fact, in use gives those who use it no right at all, from these words it seems that the use of necessary sustenance excludes all positive right, and consequently ownership. Further, these opponents say that Nicholas is not speaking there of the use of necessary sustenance in general, but speaks specifically of the use of necessary sustenance of the Friars Minor. And it is true that some use of necessary sustenance, although it is not such because it is use of necessary sustenance, but on account of the renunciation of all right annexed to it, excludes all right and ownership. And so it must be said in like manner of simple use: that some simple use of fact, on account of the renunciation of all right annexed to it, excludes all positive right. But not every simple use of fact excludes all right, because in one sense every simple use of fact excludes right and ownership. From what has been said it is evidently gathered that every use of necessary sustenance is simple use of fact in one sense, but not conversely. Secondly, it is gathered that every one who uses any thing whatever, whether by a consumable use or a non-consumable use, has a simple use of fact: that is, has a bare actual power of using, which can be separated from every right, although it is not always separated from every right. For every outward act of using a temporal thing, which is what we are now discussing, is indifferent to lawful and unlawful action; and so every such act is simple use of fact, that is, it is a use which can be without any right, indeed can be against right and unlawful. Therefore what the Friars Minor say, that they have simple use of fact alone, must be understood with an exclusive or equivalent word, thus: the Friars Minor have in the things they use only simple use of fact, or they have no right, but only simple use of fact. And if it is asked: why then is simple added, since it would suffice to say they have only use of fact? They reply that simple is added to indicate that such use of fact does not necessarily have any right annexed to it; and this is not indicated so without the word simple, when one says use of fact, as it is when one says simple use of fact. Secondly, these opponents say that the aforesaid words contain another falsehood, namely that Nicholas in the words above took use improperly. That this is false they show: because Nicholas there takes use as it is taken in Holy Scripture, in the doctrine of the saints, in medicine, in moral and natural philosophy, and also in common speech. But Holy Scripture, philosophy and common speech, speaking so of use, do not speak improperly; nor has it ever been heard that any intelligent person has said that such a way of speaking, that someone uses food and drink or the like, is improper. Therefore Nicholas, following the manner of speaking of divine Scripture, of philosophy and of ordinary speech, took use in the proper sense. The third falsehood contained in the aforesaid words, according to these men, is that Nicholas III did not grant the friars the use which mortal life necessarily needs. Such is simple use of fact, as is plain there: Since in temporal things, etc. But simple use of fact is use of fact; therefore he granted them use of fact. This he explains clearly not only in meaning but also in words. For speaking of the use granted to the friars, he says: which use, I say, is not of right but bears only the name of fact, which, being only of fact, in use gives those who use it no right at all. From these words it is indubitably plain that he granted the friars use of fact. From this it further appears that use of fact is distinguished from use of right, and that it can exist without use of right. The fourth falsehood is that if the decretal Exiit is understood to speak of use of fact in the proper sense, it would not be valid, because it would be impossible. That this must be regarded as false is plain, because it is established that Nicholas means use of fact, as has been shown; but he regards use of fact in those things which pertain to food and clothing, and this is not impossible, as has been shown. Therefore the decretal Exiit should not properly be judged invalid. [By the words, "he did not grant the friars the simple use of fact."] This is plainly false, because he granted them necessary use; but necessary use is simple use of fact, as has been shown; therefore etc. [If the concession was valid according to them, he conceded the use of it.] This is false and contrary to the opponent (as they say). That it is false is plain, because something is conceded without right. That it is contrary to the opponent is plain, because according to him in such things as pertain to food and clothing one cannot have a right of use, but only ownership; and yet they can be granted. Therefore they can be granted without a right of use. [And so in those things they do not have simple use of fact.] According to these men, this is wrongly inferred: because simple use of fact can exist together with a right of use, although it does not necessarily require a right of use; just as the act of eating can exist together with a right to eat, although it does not necessarily require a right to eat in order to be in its nature. [He could use use improperly for consumption of a thing.] He hints that the consumption of a thing is use in an improper sense; which is false, indeed some consumption of a thing is use in the proper sense. Yet not every consumption is use in the proper sense. [He does not say use of fact.] It is true that there he does not expressly say use of fact, but above he said simple use of fact. And from the words of the decretal Exiit it is plainly held that necessary use is use of fact; because necessary use is not use of right, since many are sustained and carry out their duties without use of right, as is plain of the Friars Minor, and also of those who, in the things they use, do not have dominion and ownership, yet are sustained and carry out their duties without use of right. Use of right is therefore not necessary for food and clothing and divine worship and wise study. That use, therefore, which is necessary for the aforesaid things is use of fact; and consequently he who speaks of use necessary for the aforesaid things speaks of use of fact in meaning, although not always in words. [The said constitution would continue impossible as to this.] These men say this and what immediately precedes it is false. [Yet that was not the intention of the founder.] They say this is contrary to the meaning of all the rivals who came before him. [As the constitution proves to the founder.] They say it is sophistically and badly proved.

units.la: CAP. LIX.
units.tr: CHAP. LIX.

units.la: Virsus dictus hereticus dicit dictam constitutionem Ad conditorem canonum, errorem alium continere in eo quod continet quæ sequuntur: Præterea, inquit, si simplex facti vsus absq; iure vtendi haberi posset ab aliquo constat quod non iustus esset actus vtendi huiusmodi reputandus: cum ille vsu fuerit, cui ius non competebat vtendi. talis autem vsus, sc. non iustus, ad perfectionis statum nequaquam pertinet, nec perfectioni aliquid adiicit: sed potius sibi repugnare, ac detrahere noscitur manifeste: & infra, loquens de vsu facti concesso Fratribus secundum quod in decretalis Exiit continetur, sic dicit: Ex quo sequitur, quod vsus facti, de quo ordinate loquitur, de tali intelligi debeat, qui iustus sit & pro quo competat ius vtendi.
units.tr: Virsus, the so-called heretic, says that the constitution Ad conditorem canonum contains another error, in what follows: "Moreover," he says, "if a simple use of fact could be had by someone without a right to use, it is clear that an act of such use would not be reckoned just, since it would be a use for which there was no right to use. Such a use, namely one that is not just, does not pertain at all to the state of perfection, nor does it add anything to perfection, but rather is known to be plainly repugnant to it and to detract from it." And further on, speaking of the use of fact granted to the Friars according to what is contained in the decretal Exiit, he says: "From this it follows that the use of fact, of which he speaks in order, ought to be understood of such a use as is just and for which the right to use is available."

units.la: Postquam in parte præcedenti iste impugnatus respondit ad obiectiones appellantis contrarias secundam assertionem suam: hic respondet ad obiectiones appellatis contra tertiam assertionem, quod reputat appellans erroneam. Et diuiditur in tres partes. Primo recitat suam assertionem. Secundo recitat obiectiones appellatis immediate ipse sequeti. Tertio rrndet ad obiectiones ibi: ad hoc dicimus. Est igitur assertio hæc recitata, quod impugnare intedit appellas, quod nulla actus vtendi potest esse licitus absq; iure vtendi. [Nō iustus esset actus vtendi huiusmodi reputandus.] Hæc est affirmatiua de termino infinito, quæ non est ibi necessario infinitans, vt ille sit sensus, actus vtendi huiusmodi esset reputandus non iustus [Talis autem vsus, sc. non iustus ad perfectionis statum nequaquam pertinet.] hæc habet vnum sensum falsum, sicut patebit inferius, siue hæc sensum verum, siue non. [Sed potius sibi repugnare ac detrahere noscitur manifeste] hæc est habet sensum falsum. [Qui iustus sit & pro quo competat ius vtendi] hoc includit falsum, vt patebit.
units.tr: After the opponent in the previous part answered the objections of the appellant against his second assertion, here he answers the objections the appellant raised against his third assertion, which the appellant considers erroneous. It is divided into three parts. First, he recites his assertion. Second, he recites the objections of the appellant that immediately follow. Third, he replies to the objections, at "To this we say." The assertion, then, is recited as follows, and the appellant intends to attack it: that no act of using can be lawful without a right to use. [That such an act of using would not be reckoned just.] This is an affirmative proposition with an infinite term, which is not necessarily infinitating there, so that the sense is: an act of using of this kind would be reckoned not just. [Such a use, namely not just, does not pertain at all to the state of perfection.] This has one false sense, as will become clear below, whether or not it also has a true sense. [But rather is known to be plainly repugnant to it and to detract from it.] This has a false sense. [Which is just and for which the right to use is available.] This includes a falsehood, as will be shown.

units.la: CAP. LX.
units.tr: CHAPTER LX.

units.la: ISte haereticus volens imponere constitutioni, quod non dicit, quod praedicta constitutio intelligis loqui de iure rerum ciuili & mundano, quod est ius proprium, pro quo datur actio in iudicio, sicut patet in hac constitutione Ad conditorem & in constitutione, quae incipit: Quia quorundam, in qua hic, vt dicit, manifestat aperte, de qua asserit inferius se dicturum. Hac autem asserit obuiare sacrae scripturae dicenti Mat. 19. in persona apostolorum. Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, &c. Ex quo, vt dicit, per doctores catholicos patet, quod reliquerunt ius agendi in iudicio: quod non fiat cum tali perfectione superrogationis, quae implicat aliquod peccatum, sicut probat apostolus 1. ad Corinth. 3. dicens: Iam quidem omnino delictum est in verbo, quia iudicia habetis inter vos. & ideo (ut dicit Christus iniunxit perfectis vt non litigent neque contendant in iudicio Matth. 5. & Luc. 6.
units.tr: This heretic, wishing to impose on the constitution something it does not say, claims that the said constitution is to be understood as speaking of civil and worldly right over things, which is proper right, the right for which an action is given in court, as is plain in this constitution Ad conditorem and in the constitution beginning Quia quorundam, in which (as he says) it is openly made clear here, and about which he asserts he will speak further below. He asserts that this is opposed to Holy Scripture, which says in Matthew 19, in the person of the apostles: "Behold, we have left all things," etc. From this, as he says, it is clear through the Catholic teachers that they gave up the right of suing in court, and that this was not done with such a perfection of supererogation as implies some sin. The apostle proves this in 1 Corinthians 6, saying: "Now indeed there is altogether a fault among you, because you have lawsuits with one another." And therefore, as Christ says, he enjoined on the perfect that they should not go to law nor contend in court (Matthew 5 and Luke 6).

units.la: Hic iste impugnatus recitat obiectionem appellantis contra assertionem praedictam, quam reputat erroneam: quae consistit in hoc, quod impugnatus loquitur de iure ciuili & mundano, per quod datur actio in iudicio. De tali autem iure dicit appellans, quod apostoli non habuerunt tale ius: & tamen habuerunt licitum usum multarum rerum. Ad euidentiam praedictae obiectionis & aliarum isti impugnatores faciunt quinque: Primo n. adducunt obiectiones alias appellantis contra praedictam assertionem, quas iste ex scientia certa dimittit. Secundo notant de quo usu fit hoc sermo. Tertio declarant de quo iure locutus est appellans & etiam impugnatus. Quarto ostendunt differentiam inter usum iustum & licitum. Quinto explicant intentionem appellantis quantum ad obiectionem praemissam. Dicunt igitur isti impugnatores, quod appellans post verba, quae recitat iste, vt suam magnam intentionem exprimeret, immediate subiunxit dicens: Praeterea nullus de multitudine credentium aliquod ius proprium habebat, vt dicitur Act. 4. Tunc constat quod quilibet apostolorum & illorum de multitudine credentium habebat usu rerum usu consumptibilium & non habebat ius ciuile & mundanum. ergo dicere, quod non possit haberi usus facti absque tali iure vtendi contradicit scripturae sacrae. Praeterea et talis assertio diffinitioni sanctae Romanae ecclesiae obuiat manifeste quod patet ex pluribus. Primo ex eo quod dicta decretalis Exiit dicit, quod in reb. temporalib. est considerare proprietatem, possessionem, vsumfructum, ius vtendi, & simplicem facti vsum, & quod vltimo tanquam necessario egeat, licet primum carere possit vita mortalium, nulla prorsus potest esse professio, quae a se vsum necessaria sustentationis excludat. Ex quibus verbis clare patet, quod vita mortalium potest licite carere proprietate, possessione, vsufructu, & iure vtendi: & contenta esse simplici vsu facti rerum necessariarum ad vitam. & ita potest haberi vsus simplex facti absque iure vtendi, secundum ecclesiae determinationem. Secundo ex eo, quod in eadem diffinitione ecclesia insinuatur, quod nec per hoc quod proprietatem vsus & rei cuiuslibet dominium abdicasse videtur, simplici vsui renunciatum esse comimcitur. Ex quibus verbis clare patet, quod dicta professio Fratrum Minorum ius proprium abdicauit: & per consequens ius vtendi ciuile, quod est ius proprium & sic habent vsum facti simplicem, absque tamen iure vtendi. Tertio ex eo, quod eadem decretalis dicit sic: Quis inquam vsus non iuris, sed facti tantummodo nomen habens quod facti est tantum in vtendo, praebet vtentibus nihil iuris. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod licet habere licitum vsum absque iure vtendi. Item vsus facti licitus fuisset in statu innocentiae, in quo non fuisset ius vtendi ciuile per leges introductum: ergo vsus facti licitus potest a tali iure vtendi ciuili (de quo iste loquitur) separari: Haec verba appellationis praedictae. Post quae quibusdam interpositionis, quae iste impugnatus inferius recitabit, concludit appellans dicens: Ex praedictis patet, quod ipse errat, cum dicit, quod ordinatio domini Nicolai debet intelligi de vsu, pro quo competit ius vtendi, quia non debet intelligi de vsu, pro quo competit ius vtendi, sed de vsu pro quo competit licentia vtendi. Haec verba Appellationis, quvt dicunt isti impugnatores impugnatus omisit propter duo. Primo quia ad ipsa nesciunt rationem quacunque habente apparentiam inuenire. Secundo ne ex ipsis pateret expressius, quomodo obiectiones & aliae appellantis rationes insolubiles persequerentur. Secundo isti impugnatores notant, de quo vsu fit hic sermo, dicentes: quod hoc non fit sermo de vsu rerum consumptibilium tantum: sed de vsu facti quarumcunque rerum respectu quarum contingit habere vsum facti & ideo dicunt quod iste impugnatus non poterit recurrere ad illam miseram fugam, dicendo quod alii sumunt vsum improprie, & ipse proprie, sicut fecit respondendo ad obiectiones contra secundam assertionem. Tertio isti impugnatores declarant de quo iure vtendi locutus est appellans, & etiam impugnatus, dicentes quod appellans & impugnatus locuti sunt de iure vtendi, secundum quod loquitur decretalis Exiit. quod appellans taliter locutus sit de iure vtendi, ex eo patet, quod ad defensionem dictae decretalis Exiit, animam & corpus exponit, quod autem iste impugnatus locutus fuerit sic de iure vtendi patet nam ipse expresse supra capitulo 37. 42. & 55. dicit constitutione Ad conditorem fuisse factam gratia decretalis Exiit. & ideo loquitur de vti & vsu, sicut loquitur decretalis Exiit. ergo eadem ratione loquitur de iure vtendi sicut loquitur decretalis Exiit. Ad sciendum ergo quomodo iste appellans & iste impugnatus loquuntur de iure vtendi, videndum est, quomodo decretalis Exiit, occasione cuius orta est inter praedictos appellantem & impugnantum controuersia, accepit ius vtendi, & quantum ad hoc dicunt isti impugnatores, quod decretalis Exiit, sumit ius vtendi pro iure humanitus instituto seu humanitus acquisito vel inuento, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare & quod sic accipiat dicta decretalis, probare conantur. Omne enim ius vtendi aut est ius naturale aut ius positiuum sed Nicolaus non accepit ius vtendi pro iure naturali: tum quia dicit, quod iure vtendi potest carere vita mortalium, ibi: licet primis (sc. proprietate possessionum, vsufructu & iure vtendi) carere possit vita mortalium, &c. Iure autem naturali non potest carere vita mortalium: quia tali iuri nullus renunciare potest. ergo non accepit ius vtendi pro iure naturali: tum quia secundum Nicolaum Fratres Minores nullum ius vtendi habent in temporalibus, sicut ex praecedentibus patet aperte: sed secundum eum habent ius utendi naturale, cum dicat, ipsis iure poli ad providendum sustentationi naturae viam non esse conclusam. ergo nō accepit ius utendi pro iure naturali. Sumit ergo ius utendi pro iure positivo. ius autem positivum utendi qualitercunque accipiatur, vel est humanum vel diuinum. sed Nicolaus in decretali Exiit, non accepit ius utendi pro iure diuino positivo: quia iure diuino positivo nihil in his temporalibus possidetur. licet enim Iudæi & aliqui alii, sicut habetur Deut. 2. aliqua possederunt iure diuino positivo, nunc tamen nullus possidet aliquid iure positivo diuino. Accepit ergo Nicolaus tertius ius utendi pro iure diuino positivo humano. illud non potest intelligi, nisi duplex: vel illud quod quis absque culpa & causa priuari non debet, quo potest aliquid in iudicio experiri, vel illud quod competit solummodo ex gratia & licentia, quo non potest quis contra quemcunque in iudicio experiri. sed Nicolaus tertius in decretali Exiit, non accepit ius utendi secundo modo. quia cum dicat expresse, quod vsus Fratrum Minorum est absque omni iure utendi: & tamen secundum eum non est sine licentia; constat quod ius utendi distinguitur a licentia. Nicolaus tertius ibi accipit ius utendi pro iure, quo valet quis pro usu rei iudicio experiri. & sic semper loquitur appellans de iure utendi, licet aliquando etiam strictius, & non solum isto modo loquatur de iure utendi.
units.tr: Here this man under attack recites the objection of the appellant against the aforesaid assertion, which he considers erroneous. It consists in this: that the man under attack speaks of civil and worldly right, through which an action is given in court. The appellant, however, says of such a right that the apostles did not have it, and yet they had the lawful use of many things. To make clear this objection and others, these critics do five things. First, they set out the other objections of the appellant against the said assertion, which this man dismisses as already known. Second, they note what kind of use this discussion concerns. Third, they declare what right the appellant and also the man under attack spoke of. Fourth, they show the difference between just use and lawful use. Fifth, they explain the intention of the appellant as regards the objection set out above. These critics therefore say that the appellant, after the words this man recites, in order to express his great purpose, immediately added: "Moreover, none of the multitude of believers had any proper right, as is said in Acts 4." Then it is evident that each of the apostles and of those of the multitude of believers had the use of things, consumable things, and did not have civil and worldly right. Therefore to say that a use of fact cannot be had without such a right of using contradicts holy Scripture. Moreover, such an assertion plainly opposes the definition of the holy Roman Church, as is clear from several points. First, from the fact that the said decretal Exiit says that in temporal matters one must consider ownership, possession, usufruct, the right of using, and the simple use of fact, and that the last is needed as necessary, although the first can be lacking in mortal life; and that no profession at all can be one which excludes from itself the use necessary for sustenance. From these words it is clear that mortal life can lawfully lack ownership, possession, usufruct, and the right of using, and be content with the simple use of fact of things necessary for life. And so, according to the Church's determination, a simple use of fact can be had without the right of using. Second, from the fact that in the same definition the Church hints that a renunciation of simple use is not implied by the fact that one seems to have given up the ownership of property and the dominion of any thing. From these words it is clear that the said profession of the Friars Minor gave up proper right, and consequently the civil right of using, which is proper right; and so they have the simple use of fact, but without the right of using. Third, from the fact that the same decretal says: "What use, I say, which bears the name not of right but only of fact, and which is only in the using, gives those who use it no right." From these words it is clear that one may lawfully have a lawful use without the right of using. Likewise, a lawful use of fact would have existed in the state of innocence, in which civil right of using, introduced by laws, would not have existed; therefore a lawful use of fact can be separated from such a civil right of using (which this man speaks of). These are the words of the said appeal. After certain interpolations, which this man under attack will recite below, the appellant concludes, saying: "From what has been said it is clear that he errs when he says that the ordinance of Lord Nicholas ought to be understood of a use for which the right of using is due, because it ought not to be understood of a use for which the right of using is due, but of a use for which there is a licence of using." The critics say that the man under attack omitted these words of the appeal for two reasons. First, because he could find no reason at all with any appearance of truth for them. Second, lest it should appear more clearly from them how the objections and other unanswerable arguments of the appellant pursue him. Second, these critics note what use this discussion concerns, saying that this discussion is not only about the use of consumable things, but about the use of fact of whatever things it happens to have use of fact. Therefore they say that this man under attack will not be able to take refuge in that wretched evasion of saying that others take "use" improperly and he himself properly, as he did in answering the objections against the second assertion. Third, these critics declare what right of using the appellant spoke of, and also the man under attack, saying that the appellant and the man under attack spoke of the right of using as the decretal Exiit speaks of it. That the appellant spoke in this way of the right of using is clear from the fact that in defending the said decretal Exiit he sets out soul and body. That this man under attack also spoke thus of the right of using is clear, for he himself expressly says, above in chapters 37, 42 and 55, that the constitution Ad conditorem was made for the sake of the decretal Exiit. And so he speaks of "use" and "using" as the decretal Exiit speaks. Therefore, for the same reason, he speaks of the right of using as the decretal Exiit speaks. To know, then, how this appellant and this man under attack speak of the right of using, we must see how the decretal Exiit, on whose account the controversy between the said appellant and the man under attack arose, takes the right of using. On this point these critics say that the decretal Exiit takes the right of using to mean a right instituted by human authority, or acquired or discovered by human means, by which a person may litigate in court; and they try to prove that the said decretal takes it in this sense. For every right of using is either a natural right or a positive right; but Nicholas did not take the right of using as a natural right, first because he says that mortal life can lack the right of using, namely: "although the first (that is, ownership of possessions, usufruct and the right of using) mortal life can lack," etc. But mortal life cannot lack a natural right, because no one can renounce such a right. Therefore he did not take the right of using as a natural right. Second, because according to Nicholas the Friars Minor have no right of using in temporal things, as is plainly clear from what precedes; but according to him they have a natural right of using, since he says: the way to provide for the sustenance of nature is not closed to them by the right of heaven. Therefore he did not take the right of using as a natural right. He therefore takes the right of using as a positive right. But a positive right of using, however it is understood, is either human or divine. But Nicholas, in the decretal Exiit, did not take the right of using as a positive divine right, because nothing in these temporal matters is possessed by positive divine right. For although Jews and some others, as is found in Deuteronomy 2, once possessed some things by positive divine right, yet now no one possesses anything by positive divine right. Nicholas therefore took the right of using as a positive human right, or a divine right instituted by man. That can be understood in only two ways: either as that which a person must not be deprived of without fault and without cause, by which one can bring a claim in court; or as that which belongs only by grace and licence, by which a person cannot sue anyone in court. But Nicholas III, in the decretal Exiit, did not take the right of using in the second sense; for since he expressly says that the use of the Friars Minor is without any right of using, and yet according to him it is not without licence, it is plain that the right of using is distinguished from licence. Nicholas III there takes the right of using as the right by which a person may litigate in court for the use of a thing. And so the appellant always speaks of the right of using, though sometimes more strictly, and he does not speak of the right of using only in this way.

units.la: Quarto isti impugnatores ostendunt differentiam inter vsum iustum & vsum licitum. Ad cuius euidentiam est sciendum, quod nomen iustitiæ triplociter accipi potest uno modo accipitur, pro quadam virtute particulari distincta ab aliis tribus virtutibus cardinalib. habente materiam specialem distinctam a materia cuiuslibet alterius virtutis cardinalis, secundum quam homo iuste operatur ad alterum. Secundo accipitur iustitia pro quadam virtute cardinali, quæ vocatur iustitia legalis, quæ omnes actus virtutum ordinat ad bonum commune. Tertio accipitur iustitia pro debita ordinatione actus ad rationem, vel aliam operationem: & ita secundum quosdam vocatur iustitia metaphorice sumpta. & istius opinionis fuit Thomas. 2.2. q. 56. articulo secundo, vbi ait: Iustitia ergo proprie dicta requirit diuersitatem suppositorum. Ideo non est nisi vnius hominis ad alterum. sed secundum similitudinem accipiuntur in vno & eodem homine diuersa principia actionum quasi diuersa agentia, sicut ratio irascibilis & concupiscibilis: & ideo metaphorice in vno & eodem homine dicitur iustitia esse. secundum quod ratio imperat irascibili & concupiscibili: & secundum quod hoc obediunt rationi, & vniuersaliter secundum quod vnicuique parti hominis attribuitur, quod ei conuenit. Unde philosophus in 5. Ethicorum, hanc iustitiam appellat secundum metaphoram dictam. & post dicit, quod iustitia quæ fit per fidem in nobis, est per quam iustificatur ipsius, quæ quidem in ipso debita ordinatione partium animæ consistit. Hoc autem pertinet ad iustitiam metaphorice dictam, quæ potest inuenire in aliquo solitariam vitam agente. Ex his patet, quod actus potest dici tripliciter iustus, vel quia est actus elicitus a iustitia particulari: & sic sunt multi actus humani licite, non iusti: sicut actus castitatis, fortitudinis, misericordiæ, & liberalitatis, et alii multi. Aliter dicitur actus iustus, qui elicitur vel imperatur a iustitia legali, qua vult aliquis legem seruare. Et sic secundum philosophiam moralem Aristotelis multi sunt actus aliarum virtutum etiam exteriores in comparatione ad alterum, qui licet possint esse iusti, quia possunt imperari a iustitia legali, possunt tamen non esse iusti ipsis existentibus virtuosis: quia possibile est, quod de illis nulla sit lex humana pœnit institua. Aliter dicitur actus iustus a iustitia, tertio modo dictus, siue illa iustitia debeat metaphorice vocari iustitia, siue etiam proprie. & isto modo omnis actus licitus est iustus, quia est bonus & vere consonus rationi. etiam sic patet differentia inter vsum licitum & vsum iustum, quia accipiendo iustum primo modo & secundo modo, sicut proportionaliter accipitur iustitia. multi sunt vsus liciti, qui non sunt iusti. Tertio modo accipiendo iustum, omnis actus licitus est iustus secundum eos, qui ponunt quod omnis actus humanus est bonus vel malus moraliter.
units.tr: Fourthly, these opponents show the difference between just use and lawful use. To make this clear, it must be understood that the word "justice" can be taken in three ways. In the first, it means a particular virtue, distinct from the other three cardinal virtues, with a special matter of its own, different from the matter of any other cardinal virtue, by which a man acts justly toward another. In the second, "justice" means a cardinal virtue called legal justice, which directs the acts of all the virtues to the common good. In the third, "justice" means the due ordering of an act to reason or to some other operation, and so according to some it is called justice in a metaphorical sense. Thomas held this opinion, 2.2 q. 56 art. 2, where he says: "Justice properly so called requires a diversity of persons. Therefore it exists only between one man and another. But by way of likeness, diverse principles of action are found in one and the same man, as if they were diverse agents, such as the irascible and the concupiscible reason; and so in one and the same man justice is said metaphorically to exist, insofar as reason commands the irascible and concupiscible powers, and insofar as these obey reason, and generally insofar as each part of the man is given what is fitting to it." Hence the Philosopher in the fifth book of the Ethics calls this justice the justice spoken of by metaphor. And afterwards he says that "the justice which is effected in us through faith is that by which a man is justified, and which indeed consists in the due ordering of the parts of the soul." This pertains to justice metaphorically so called, which can be found in someone living a solitary life. From these things it is clear that an act can be called just in three ways. It may be called just because it is an act elicited by particular justice; and in this sense there are many acts that are lawful but not just, such as the acts of chastity, fortitude, mercy, liberality, and many others. Otherwise an act is called just when it is elicited or commanded by legal justice, by which someone wishes to keep the law. And so, according to Aristotle's moral philosophy, many acts of the other virtues, even external acts in relation to another, although they can be just because they can be commanded by legal justice, may nevertheless not be just while the persons are virtuous, because it is possible that no human law has been instituted concerning them. Otherwise an act is called just from justice in the third sense, whether that justice ought to be called justice metaphorically or also properly. And in this way every lawful act is just, because it is good and truly agreeable to reason. In this way too the difference between lawful use and just use is evident, because, taking "just" in the first and second senses, as justice is proportionally understood, there are many lawful uses which are not just. Taking "just" in the third sense, every lawful act is just according to those who hold that every human act is morally good or bad.

units.la: Quinto ex prædictis isti impugnatores explicant intentionem appellantis, dicentes quod appellans intendit concludere, quod potest quis habere vsum licitum & iustum tertio modo rerum consumptibilium vsu & non consumptibilium vsu absque iure utendi, quo quis valeat in iudicio litigare licet non possit habere vsum iustum primo modo dictum absque iure utendi tali.
units.tr: Fifthly, from what has been said, these opponents explain the intention of the appellant, saying that the appellant means to conclude that a man can have a lawful and just use, in the third sense, of consumable and of non-consumable things without a right of using by which he may litigate in court, although he cannot have a just use in the first sense without such a right of using.

units.la: [quod non dicit], verum est quod non dicit vocaliter sub eisdem verbis: hoc tamen dicit sententialiter, vt inferius ostendetur. [intendit loqui de iure utendi ciuili & mundano.] hoc isti impugnatores postea probare nitentur. [Reliquerunt ius agendi in iudicio] quia apostoli reliquerunt omnia, quæ in rebus temporalibus non erant necessitatis nec utilitatis pro tempore illo cuiusmodi fuit ius agendi in iudicio, quantum ad ipsos apostolos, licet vtile tunc fuerit, quod aliqui alii fides habere ius agendi in iudicio pro temporalibus rebus. [non stat cum tali perfectione supererogationis] licet posset stare cum perfectione caritatis, sicut licet actus coniugalis non stet cum illa perfectione supererogationis, quæ est virginitas, stat tamen cum perfectione caritatis [Christus iniunxit perfectis, vt non litigent &c.] hoc Christus iniunxit volentibus perfectissimam paupertatem exteriorem seruare: & tamen possibile est sine diminutione charitatis in iudicio litigare.
units.tr: [that he does not say]: It is true that he does not say it in the same words, but he says it in substance, as will be shown below. [He means to speak of the civil and worldly right of using.] These opponents will afterwards try to prove this. [They left the right of acting in court] because the apostles left all things which were not necessary or useful in temporal matters for that time; such a right of acting in court, so far as the apostles themselves were concerned, although it was then useful that some others should have a right of acting in court for temporal things. [It does not agree with such perfection of supererogation] although it could agree with the perfection of charity, just as the conjugal act, although it does not agree with that perfection of supererogation which is virginity, nevertheless agrees with the perfection of charity. [Christ enjoined on the perfect that they should not go to law, etc.] Christ enjoined this on those who wished to keep the most perfect outward poverty; and yet it is possible to litigate in court without any diminution of charity.

units.la: CAP. LXI.
units.tr: CAP. LXI.

units.la: ADhæc dicimus, quod dicta constitutio aperte & expresse loquitur de vsu, pro quo competit ius utendi: quod est aliud a iure agendi. potest enim alicui competere ius utendi, cui non competit ius agendi. quare dicimus, quod imponit constitutioni, quod nec intellexit nec dixit. Verum autem tale ius sit mundanum & ciuile: & an pro illo apostolis competierit ius agendi dicetur inferius in his, quæ opponit iste hæreticus contra constitutionem: Cum autem
units.tr: Here we say that the said constitution speaks clearly and expressly of use, for which the right of using belongs, and this is something other than the right of acting. For a right of using can belong to someone to whom the right of acting does not belong. Therefore we say that he imputes to the constitution what it neither understood nor said. Whether that right is worldly and civil, and whether the apostles had a right of acting in regard to it, will be said below, in the things this heretic objects against the constitution, beginning "But when."

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnatus respondet ad obiectiones appellantis praemissas. & diuiditur in duas partes: quia primo ad pmissa respondet. secundo quandā responsione appellantis ad rationem istius impugnati, quae supra c. 59. innuitur, conatur excludere, ibi: Item dicit dictus haereticus. prima in duas diuiditur. Primo dicit, quod constitutio Ad conditorem loquitur de usu, pro quo competit ius utendi. Secundo ostendit, quod constitutio, quia quorundā non loquitur de iure, quod est proprium in parte immediate sequenti. Dicit ergo primo, q appellans falsum imponit, quia constitutio Ad conditorem loquitur de usu pro quo competit ius utendi, quod est aliud a iure agendi.
units.tr: In this part, this opponent replies to the appellant's objections stated above. It is divided into two parts. First he replies to the premises; second he tries to exclude an answer of the appellant to the argument of this opponent, which is hinted at above in chapter 59, beginning "Likewise the said heretic says." The first part is divided into two. First he says that the constitution "Ad conditorem" speaks of use, for which the right of using belongs. Second he shows that the constitution "quia quorundam" does not speak of right, which is the subject of the immediately following part. He says, therefore, first, that the appellant falsely imputes, because the constitution "Ad conditorem" speaks of use for which the right of using belongs, which is different from the right of acting.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores circa praedicta sic procedunt. Primo enim declarat intentionem impugnati in hac parte. Tertio haec dicta improbare conantur. Quantum ad primum, dicunt quod iste impugnatus ponit hic ius utendi esse licentiam utendi, seu licitam potestatem utendi, vel talem licentiam non posse esse sine iure utendi, quod ex verbis eiusdem ostendunt. Nam cito post praemissa dicit in haec verba: Sed hic iste haereticus inter ius & licentiam videtur facere differentiam, supponens, quod aliquis habeat licentiam utendi ab eo, qui eam potest concedere, & quod non habeat ius utendi quod tamen evidenter est falsum. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod licentia utendi est ius utendi secundum istum: vel non est sine iure utendi imo sequitur q ipsa licentia utendi est ius utendi secundum ipsum, quia potest quis dare alicui licentiam utendi nihil aliud sibi concedendo.
