units.tr: But these opponents proceed on the above as follows. For first they declare the intention of the one attacked in this part; third, they try to disprove these statements. As to the first, they say that this opponent holds here that the right of using is the licence of using, or a lawful power of using, or that such a licence cannot exist without a right of using, which they show from his own words. For soon after the premises he says in these words: "But here this heretic seems to make a difference between right and licence, supposing that someone has licence to use from the one who can grant it, and yet does not have a right of using, which is evidently false." From these words it is gathered that, in his view, the licence of using is a right of using, or else it does not exist without a right of using; indeed it follows that, according to him, the licence itself is a right of using, because someone can give another a licence to use by granting him nothing else.

units.la: Secundo isti impugnatores praedictam assertionem improbare conantur. Ad cuius evidentiam primo distinguit de iure utendi. secundo distinguunt de licentia. tertio assertionem praedictam impugnant. Circa primum dicunt, quod ius utendi est duplex. quoddam enim ius utendi naturale: aliud est ius utendi positiuum. ius utendi naturale commune est omnibus hominibus: quia ex natura, non ex aliqua constitutione superueniente habetur. Verum tamen licet omnis homo habeat omni tempore tale ius utendi, non tamen habet tale ius utendi rebus pro omni tempore. illi enim, qui nullas res proprias habent, neq; communes, licet habeant ius utendi rebus alienis, non tamen habet ius utendi rebus alienis, nisi pro tempore necessitatis extremae. in quo tempore virtute iuris naturae omni re praesente, sine qua vita eorum saluari non posset, licite uti possunt. Alio autem tempore, auctoritate illius iuris rebus alienis uti non possunt. Aliud est ius utendi positiuum, quod ex constitutione aliqua vel humana pactione habetur & de isto iure utendi dictum est prius. 1. ca. 2. Unde istud ius utendi non est aliud quam quaedam licita potestas exercendi actum aliquem circa rem temporalem extrinsecam, qua quis absque culpa rationabili priuari non debet inuitus: & si priuatus fuerit priuantem iniuste, poterit in iudicio conuenire. Quod enim ius utendi positiuum sit talis licita potestas, patet, quia nullum illicitum debet ius aliqualiter reputari, cum dicat Isidorus (ut habetur dist. 1.) ius autem est dictum, quia iustum est. quod autem etiam tali iure utendi nullus sine culpa & absque causa rationabili debeat priuari inuitus, patet. Nam omne ius utendi est ius. nullus autem sine culpa & absq; causa rationabili debet suo iure priuari, ut notat Glossa extra de constitutionibus c. 1. & extra de eo qui cognouit consanguineam uxoris suae. c. ultimo & 22. dist. ca. renouantes, & ex sacris canonibus colligitur manifeste. ergo iure utendi absque causa rationabili & sine culpa nullus priuari debet. quod etiam priuatus iniuste priuantem possit in iudicio conuenire, patet ex hoc, quod quilibet ius suum positiuum in iudicio prosequi potest. necalicui facit iniuriam, qui ius suum prosequitur. qui ergo tali iure utendi priuatur iniuste, potest priuante in iudicio conuenire. rursus, ille cui fit iniuria potest iniuriantem coram iudice conuenire: maxime si tali actioni minime renunciauit. sed illi qui priuatur tali iure utendi sine culpa & absque rationabili causa, fit iniuria. ergo potest iniuriantem in iudicio conuenire, si tali actione non renunciauerit & ita qui habet ius utendi tale, potest priuantem iniuste in iudicio conuenire. Sed contra praedicta obiici pōt, nam aliquis pōt a iure suo priuari absque causa & sine culpa: quia priuilegia sunt iura quaedam teste Isidoro, qui ut habetur dist. 3. ait: Priuilegia sunt leges priuatorum. quasi priuatae leges. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod priuilegia sunt leges quaedam: & per consequens potestas concessa per priuilegium ius censetur. sed concedens priuilegium potest ad placitum sine culpa & absq; causa priuilegiatos priuilegio concesso priuare ergo potest priuilegiatus absque causa & sine culpa iure suo priuari. Ad hoc dici potest, quod sicut princeps legibus suis non astringitur: imo suis legibus est solutus: & ideo respectu ipsius quodammodo leges non sunt: sic etiam princeps priuilegiis suis non subditur. & ideo potestas priuilegiatis concessa respectu principis quodammodo nome iuris amittit, ut respectu ipsius, potiꝰ gratia q ius dicatur: respectu tñ aliorū proprie dicitur ius & ideo concedens priuilegiū, pōt ad placitum priuilegiatos priuare. Alii autē nō pōt. nemo ergo iure suo ab illo respectu cuius nō gratia, sed ius proprie dicitur, debet sine culpa, & absq; causa priuari. Ab alio vero respectu cuius gratia dicitur, pōt priuari gratia sibi concessa, sine culpa & absque causa. Secundo distinguunt de licentia, quia quaedam est licentia, quae reuocari a concedente non potest, sicut cum praelatus religiosus dat subdito suo licentiam ordinem alium intrandi, quem postea reuocare non potest. Et per talem licentiam ius quoddam acquiritur. Alia est licentia, quae ad placitum concedentis reuocari potest: & per talem licentiam nullum ius videtur acquiri.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents try to disprove the aforesaid assertion. To make this clear, they first distinguish the right of use, then distinguish the licence, and third, they attack the aforesaid assertion. On the first point they say that the right of use is twofold. For there is a natural right of use, and there is a positive right of use. The natural right of use is common to all men, because it arises from nature, not from some later enactment. Yet although every man has such a right of use at all times, he does not have it over things at all times. Those who have no property of their own, nor any held in common, though they have a right of use over other people's goods, have that right only in a time of extreme necessity. In such a time, by virtue of the natural right, they may lawfully use any thing, present or absent, without which their life could not be preserved. At other times, they cannot use another's goods by the authority of that right. The positive right of use is different. It arises from some enactment or from human agreement, and we spoke of this right of use earlier, in Book 1, chapter 2. This right of use is therefore nothing other than a lawful power to exercise some act concerning an external temporal thing, from which no one should be deprived against his will without a reasonable fault on his part. If he is deprived by someone acting unjustly, he may bring that person to court. That the positive right of use is such a lawful power is clear, because no unlawful thing should be regarded as a right in any sense, since Isidore says (as is found in dist. 1): ius autem est dictum, quia iustum est ("a right is so called because it is just"). That no one should be deprived of this right of use against his will without fault and without a reasonable cause is also clear. For every right of use is a right, and no one should be deprived of his right without fault and without a reasonable cause, as the Gloss notes in extra de constitutionibus c. 1, and extra de eo qui cognouit consanguineam uxoris suae, c. ultimo, and 22 dist., c. renouantes, and as is manifestly gathered from the sacred canons. Therefore no one should be deprived of a right of use without a reasonable cause and without fault. That a man unjustly deprived may bring the one who deprives him to court is clear from this, that anyone may pursue in court his positive right. Nor does he who pursues his own right do wrong to anyone. Therefore whoever is unjustly deprived of such a right of use may sue the one who deprives him. Again, one who is wronged may bring the wrongdoer before a judge, especially if he has not renounced such an action. But a man who is deprived of such a right of use without fault and without a reasonable cause is wronged. Therefore he may bring the wrongdoer to court, if he has not renounced such an action; and so whoever has such a right of use may sue the one who unjustly deprives him. But it may be objected against what has been said that a man can be deprived of his right without cause and without fault, because privileges are certain rights, as Isidore testifies, who says (as is found in dist. 3): Priuilegia sunt leges priuatorum, quasi priuatae leges ("Privileges are the laws of private persons, as if private laws"). From these words it is gathered that privileges are certain laws, and consequently a power granted by privilege is counted as a right. But the one granting a privilege may at his pleasure, without fault and without cause, deprive the privileged person of the privilege granted. Therefore the privileged person may be deprived of his right without cause and without fault. To this it may be replied that just as a prince is not bound by his own laws, but is released from them, and so in relation to him laws are in a sense not laws, so also a prince is not subject to his own privileges. Therefore the power granted to privileged persons, in relation to the prince, in a sense loses the name of right, and is better called a favour (gratia) than a right. In relation to others, however, it is properly called a right. Hence the one granting a privilege can, at his pleasure, deprive the privileged persons of it, but others cannot. No one, therefore, should be deprived without fault and without cause of his right in relation to that party in relation to whom it is properly a right, and not a favour. In relation to another party, in relation to whom it is called a favour, he may be deprived of the favour granted to him, without fault and without cause. Secondly, they distinguish the licence, because there is a licence that cannot be revoked by the one who grants it, as when a religious superior gives his subject a licence to enter another order, which he cannot afterwards revoke. And through such a licence some right is acquired. There is another licence which may be revoked at the pleasure of the one granting it, and through such a licence no right seems to be acquired.

units.la: Tertio isti impugnatores assertionem istius impugnati, cum insinuat, quod aliquis potest habere ius utendi, q est licentia utendi absq; iure agendi, impugnat, ostendentes primo, quod non omnis licentia utendi, est ius utendi. Secundo quod qui habet ius utendi aliqua re determinata, habet ius agendi. Primum ostendunt primo secundum Nicolaum tertium in decretali 1. Exiit Fratres Minores utentes rebus à fidelibus eis concessis, nullum habent ius utendi eis pro illo tempore: & tamen habent licentiam utendi eisdem pro illo tempore, quo utuntur, ergo licentia utendi non est ius utendi, antecedens patet per Nicolaum supradictum, qui ait: nec per hoc, quod proprietatem usus & rei cuiuscunque dominium a se abdicasse videntur, simplici usui omnis rei renunciatum esse concinnitur, qui inquam usus non iuris, sed facti tantummodo nomen habens, quod facti est tantum in utendo praebet utentibus nihil iuris: quinimo necessariarum rerum, tam ad vitae sustentationem, quam ad officiorum sui status executionem, excepto quod de pecunia infra subiungitur, moderatus usus secundum eorum regulam & veritatem omnimodam concessus est Fratribus, quibus rebus Fratres licite uti possunt, durante concedentis licentia. Ex quibus verbis colligitur evidenter: quod concedens Fratribus licentiam utendi rebus, nihil iuris tribuit eis, & per consequens nec licentia utendi est ius utendi: nec necessario ipsa concessa tribuitur ius utendi. Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod praedicta verba Nicolai nullatenus continent veritatem, etiam secundum ipsum. Nam secundum praedicta, & secundum ipsum Fratres habent ius utendi rebus, quibus utuntur: quia iuri utendi naturali renunciare non possunt, cum ipse dicat, quod ipsis Fratribus iure poli in extremae necessitatis articulo ad prouidendum sustentationi naturae, via nequaquam praecluditur, falsum ergo videtur, quod Fratres in huiusmodi rebus nihil iuris habent. Ad hoc dicunt isti, quod licet Fratres Minores in rebus, quibus utuntur, non habeant aliquod ius positiuum: habent tamen aliquod ius utendi in eis scilicet ius naturale, licet non semper pro illo tempore, quo utuntur, & ideo Nicolaus non dicit, quod Fratres in huiusmodi rebus nihil iuris habent: sed dicit, quod usus, quem habent Fratres in rebus, nihil iuris tribuit eis, unde dicit, qui inquam usus non iuris sed facti tantummodo nomen habens, quod facti est tantum in utendo praebet utentibus nihil iuris. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod ex hoc quod Fratres utuntur modo communi rebus nihil iuris eis tribuitur, cum quo tamen stat, quod aliunde habeant ius aliquod scilicet ius naturale, sed illud ius non habent nisi tantummodo pro tempore necessitatis extremae. Ex istis patet, quod licentia utendi non est ius utendi: quia Fratres habent licentiam utendi rebus pro alio tempore, quam pro tempore necessitatis extremae: sed non habent quodcunq; ius utendi, nisi pro tempore extremae necessitatis, ergo licentia utendi non est ius utendi. Ex praedictis notant isti impugnatores, quod signanter Nicolaus tertius asserit Fratres Minores proprietatem omnium & dominium abdicare: sed nusquam dicit eos commune ius omnium abdicare: quia proprietati & potestati appropriandi licet renunciare: sed iuri utendi naturali nulli renunciare licet: quia quilibet omni tempore habet ius utendi ex iure naturali, sed non quilibet habet illud ius pro omni tempore, sed pro tempore necessitatis extremae. Secundo probant isti impugnatores eandem conclusionem sic: si licentia utendi est ius utendi: ergo quicunq; habet speciale licentiam utendi, habet ius speciale utendi, sed quilibet religiosus habet specialem licentiam utendi rebus multis, qua omnis alius caret, ergo quilibet habet ius speciale, ius autem speciale, quod competit uni soli, est ius proprium, ergo quilibet religiosus habet ius proprium: & ita quilibet religiosus est proprietarius reputandus. Tertio sic: leruus habet licentiam utendi rebus domini sui: & tamen non habet ius utendi eisdem rebus, ergo non omnis licentia utendi est ius utendi. Quarto sic: Nemo priuandus est iure suo absq; causa & sine culpa, sed licentia utendi potest quis saepe priuari licite sine culpa & sine causa, ergo non omnis licentia utendi est ius utendi. Item post ea isti impugnatores ostendunt, quod qui habet ius utendi positiuum re determinata habet ius agendi, & primo sic: qui potest repetere suum, habet ius agendi: quia repetitio iudicialis sine iure agendi esse non potest, sed qui habet ius utendi aliquo, si ablatum fuerit, potest illud repetere. Vnicuiq; enim licet sua repetere, saltem cum debitis circumstantiis. Unde etiam clerici & monachi, bona communia saltem de licentia superioris repetere possunt, & sicut res suas communes repetere possunt, ita etiam iura sua repetere possunt, ergo quicunq; habet ius utendi re determinata, saltem positiuum, habet ius agendi, & ratio confirmatur per beatum Augustinum, qui ut habetur 14.q.i.c.quod debetur, ait: Quod debetur & benigne remittitur, non tamen inique repetitur. Ex quibus verbis euidenter colligitur, quod omne, quod debetur, absq; inquitate repeti potest, si ergo ius utendi alicui debetur, absq; iniquitate repeti potest: & per consequens cui debetur ius utendi, habet ius agendi: quia sine iure agendi nihil quod debetur licite repeti potest.
units.tr: Thirdly, these opponents attack the assertion of the author under discussion, where he suggests that someone can have a right to use something, which is a licence to use without a right to act. They show, first, that not every licence to use is a right to use. Second, that whoever has a right to use some specific thing has a right to act. They prove the first point, first, from Nicholas III in the decretal Exiit, under the title "Of the Friars Minor": the Friars Minor, using things given to them by the faithful, have no right to use them for that time, and yet they have a licence to use them for the time they are using them. Therefore a licence to use is not a right to use. The antecedent is plain from Nicholas, who says: "Nor, because they seem to have renounced the ownership of use and the dominion of any thing, is it to be concluded that the bare use of every thing has been given up. This use, I say, which has the name not of right but only of fact, and which, being of fact only, gives the users no right in using, but rather a moderate use of necessary things, both for sustaining life and for performing the duties of their state, is granted to the Friars, according to their rule and in full truth, except for money, which is dealt with below. The Friars may lawfully use these things for as long as the licence of the grantor lasts." From these words it is clearly gathered that whoever grants the Friars a licence to use things gives them no right, and consequently a licence to use is not a right to use, nor is a right to use necessarily given by the licence itself. But perhaps someone will say that these words of Nicholas do not contain the truth even according to his own view. For according to them, and according to Nicholas himself, the Friars have a right to use the things they use, because they cannot renounce the natural right to use, since he himself says that by divine law the way is in no way closed to the Friars themselves, in the extreme article of necessity, for providing for the sustenance of nature. It therefore seems false that the Friars have no right in such things. To this these men reply that although the Friars Minor have no positive right in the things they use, they nevertheless have some right of use in them, namely a natural right, though not at all times when they are using them. So Nicholas does not say that the Friars have no right whatever in such things. He says that the use the Friars have in things gives them no right, and so he says: "This use, I say, which has the name not of right but only of fact, and which, being of fact only, gives the users no right in using." From these words it is gathered that, because the Friars use things in the common manner, no right is given them by it. Yet it is consistent with this that they have some right from elsewhere, namely a natural right, but they have that right only for the time of extreme necessity. From these points it is plain that a licence to use is not a right to use, because the Friars have a licence to use things at other times than the time of extreme necessity, but they have no right to use at all except in the time of extreme necessity. Therefore a licence to use is not a right to use. From what has been said, these opponents note that Nicholas III pointedly asserts that the Friars Minor renounce the ownership and dominion of all things, but nowhere says that they renounce the common right of all things. For it is lawful to renounce property and the power of appropriating, but no one may renounce the natural right to use: everyone at all times has a right to use by natural law, but not everyone has that right at all times, only in the time of extreme necessity. Secondly, these opponents prove the same conclusion thus: if a licence to use is a right to use, then whoever has a special licence to use has a special right to use. But every religious has a special licence to use many things, which every other person lacks. Therefore every religious has a special right, and a special right, which belongs to one person alone, is a proper right. Therefore every religious has a proper right, and so every religious is to be regarded as a holder of property. Thirdly: a slave has a licence to use the things of his master, and yet he has no right to use those same things. Therefore not every licence to use is a right to use. Fourthly: no one is to be deprived of his right without cause and without fault. But a person can often be lawfully deprived of a licence to use, without fault and without cause. Therefore not every licence to use is a right to use. Next, these opponents show that whoever has a positive right to use a specific thing has a right to act. They show this first thus: whoever can recover what is his has a right to act, since a judicial recovery cannot take place without a right to act. But whoever has a right to use something, if it has been taken away, can recover it. For it is lawful for each person to recover his own, at least with due circumstances. Hence clerics and monks too can recover common goods, at least with the licence of a superior, and just as they can recover their common things, so they can recover their rights. Therefore whoever has a right to use a specific thing, at least a positive one, has a right to act. This reasoning is confirmed by the blessed Augustine, who, as is found in 14 q. 1 c. Quod debetur, says: "What is owed, and is kindly remitted, may nevertheless not be unjustly recovered." From these words it is plainly gathered that whatever is owed can be recovered without wrong. If, then, a right to use is owed to someone, it can be recovered without wrong, and consequently the one to whom a right to use is owed has a right to act, since without a right to act nothing that is owed can be lawfully recovered.

units.la: (Loquitur de usu pro quo competit ius utendi) & ideo male: quia de tali usu non loquitur decretalis Exiit: cuius tamen occasione, ut iste dicit, facta fuit constitutio, Ad conditorem, (potest enim alicui competere ius utendi, cui non competit ius agendi) hoc saltem non est verum de iure utendi positiuo, quidquid sit de iure utendi naturali, (imponit constitutioni quod nec intelligit nec dicit) hoc dicunt esse falsum: quia constitutio sententialiter dicit hoc, (vtrum autem tale ius sit mundanum & ciuile) tale ius humanum est, hoc est positiuum & ciuile est, secundum quod omne ius, quod non est naturale & ius gentium, dicitur ciuile. (An pro illo Apostolus competierit ius agendi) iste tenet quod sic, sicut inferius ostendetur.
units.tr: (He speaks of use, for which the right of use is competent) And so wrongly: for the decretal Exiit does not speak of such use, though on its occasion, as this writer says, the constitution Ad conditorem was made. (For a right of use may belong to someone to whom the right of action does not belong.) At least this is not true of positive right of use, whatever may be said of natural right of use. (He charges the constitution with saying what it neither understands nor says.) They say this is false, because the constitution states this in its sentence. (Whether such a right is worldly and civil) it is human, that is, positive and civil, since every right that is not natural or the law of nations is called civil. (Whether the Apostle had a right of action with respect to it) this writer holds that he did, as will be shown below.

units.la: CAP. LXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXII.

units.la: Item in hoc, quod dicit, quod constitutio Quia quorundam continet manifeste, quod intelligitur de iure ciuili & mundano, quod est proprium, mentitur aperte: imo dicta constitutio dicit clare, quod ius utendi communitatis Fratrum existit. Cum enim Innocentius & Alexand. in suis declarationibus Regulae Fratrum Minorum dixerint, quod locorum, domorum, utensilium & librorum, quae licet habere ordini, habeat ordo usum, dicta constitutio Quia quorundam, volens probare, quod illud de usu iuris intelligi debeat, sic subiunxit: cum enim dicatur in declara-tionibus tionibus supradictis, quod ordo vsum rerum habeat premissarum, ad vsum iuris necesse est hoc referre: facta quidem quae singulorum sunt personam veram exigunt & requirunt. Ordo autem vera persona non est, sed representata & imaginaria potius est censenda, quare quae facti sunt sibi vere conuenire nequeunt, licet ei possint congruere quae sunt iuris. Ex quibus patet, quod dicta constitutio ius vtendi non dicit esse proprium, sed toti vniuersitati commune.
units.tr: Likewise, when he says that the constitution Quia quorundam clearly contains a statement about civil and temporal right, which is a matter of ownership, he lies outright. On the contrary, that constitution plainly says that the right of using belongs to the common community of the Friars. For when Innocent and Alexander, in their declarations on the Rule of the Friars Minor, said that the order has the use of places, houses, utensils and books, which the order is allowed to have, the constitution Quia quorundam, wishing to prove that this must be understood of the right of use, added this: since it is said in the aforesaid declarations that the order has the use of the aforesaid things, this must necessarily be referred to the right of use. Facts, indeed, which belong to individuals, require and demand a real person. But the order is not a real person; it should rather be regarded as represented and imaginary. Therefore what pertains to facts cannot properly apply to it, although what pertains to right can suit it. From these things it is clear that the said constitution does not say that the right of using is private, but that it is common to the whole community.

units.la: Hic impugnatus iste conatur ostendere, quod constitutio quia quorundam non loquitur de iure vtendi, quod est proprium, quod tamen, vt dicit, sibi imponit appellans, hoc autem sic ostenditur, constitutio quia quorundam loquitur de iure illo vtendi, de quo loquitur Innocentius & Alexander in suis declarationibus Regulae Fratrum Minorum, sed ipsi loquuntur de iure vtendi, quod est commune, & non de iure vtendi quod est proprium: ergo &c.
units.tr: Here this opponent tries to show that the constitution Quia quorundam does not speak of the right of using that is private, which, as he says, he falsely attributes to it by calling it so. He shows this as follows: the constitution Quia quorundam speaks of that right of using of which Innocent and Alexander speak in their declarations on the Rule of the Friars Minor; but they speak of the right of using that is common, and not of the right of using that is private; therefore etc.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores contra iplum tria nituntur ostendere, quorum primum est, quod constitutio quia quorundam loquitur de iure contentioso & litigioso: ex quo concludunt, quod constitutio ad conditorem loquitur de iure agendi. Secundum est, quod eadem constitutio quia quorundam, loquitur de iure proprio, non solum collegio, sed etiam personae. Tertium quod verba quae recitat hic de constitutione quia quorundam plures errores ridiculosos includunt. Primum videlicet, quod constitutio quia quorundam loquitur de iure contentioso & litigioso, sic ostendunt: impugnans aliquam assertionem seu aliquas assertiones eodem modo debet intelligi vti vocabulis, quo vtitur assertio impugnata: aliter non ad rem, sed ad nomen & sophistice impugnaret, sed assertio, quam constitutio quia quorundam impugnat, loquitur tantum modo de iure contentioso & litigio: quod ex verbis, quae recitat constitutio supradicta quia quorundam, euidenter apparet. Ait enim sic: rursus asseruisse dicuntur publice huiusmodi assertores: quod abdicatio iuris in cuiuscunque rei proprietate & in vsu eius, est sancta & meritoria propter Deum, & a Christo in seipso seruata Apostolisque impositae, & ab ipsis sub voto assumpta, nec per hoc vsus facti ad sustentationem naturae in Christo & Apostolis coniunctur esse non iustus, sed tanto iustior atque perfectior & Deo acceptior, & mundo exemplarior, quanto plenius renunciatum fuerit omni iuri, per quod potest sic vtens pro huiusmodi quomodolibet contendere vel in iudicio litigare. Haec verba assertionis, quam constitutio praedicta quia quorundam impugnat. Ex quibus patenter colligitur, quod assertio praedicta loquitur de iure contentioso & litigioso, cum dicat aperte: quanto plenius renunciatum fuerit omni iuri, per quod potest sic vtens pro iure huiusmodi quomodolibet contendere vel in iudicio litigare.
units.tr: But these opponents try to show three things against him. The first is that the constitution Quia quorundam speaks of a right that is contentious and litigious; from this they conclude that the constitution Ad conditorem speaks of the right of acting. The second is that the same constitution Quia quorundam speaks of a right that belongs not only to the college but also to the person. The third is that the words which he here quotes from the constitution Quia quorundam contain several ridiculous errors. The first, namely that the constitution Quia quorundam speaks of a contentious and litigious right, they show as follows: one who attacks an assertion, or several assertions, must understand the words in the same way as the assertion he attacks uses them; otherwise he would attack not the thing but the word, and would argue sophistically. But the assertion which the constitution Quia quorundam attacks speaks only of a contentious and litigious right, which clearly appears from the words that the aforesaid constitution Quia quorundam quotes. For it says thus: Moreover, such assertors are said to have publicly asserted that the renunciation of right in the ownership of any thing and in its use is holy and meritorious before God, and was observed by Christ in himself and imposed on the Apostles, and was taken up by them under a vow; and that by this the use of the thing for sustaining nature is not unjust in Christ and the Apostles, but is so much more just, more perfect, more acceptable to God, and a better example to the world, as the renunciation of every right by which one using in this way may in any manner contend or litigate in court is more complete. These are the words of the assertion which the aforesaid constitution Quia quorundam attacks. From them it is plainly gathered that the aforesaid assertion speaks of a contentious and litigious right, since it openly says: as the renunciation of every right by which one using in this way may in any manner contend or litigate in court is more complete.

units.la: Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod licet dicta assertio in fine loquitur de iure vtendi contentioso & litigioso, tamen in principio magis generaliter loquitur de iure, cum dicit, quod abdicatio iuris in cuiuscunque rei proprietate & in vsu eius est sancta &c. Ibi enim nequaquam specificatur ius, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare.
units.tr: But perhaps someone will say that although the said assertion at its end speaks of a contentious and litigious right of using, yet at its beginning it speaks more generally of right, since it says that the renunciation of right in the ownership of any thing and in its use is holy, etc. For there the right by which someone may litigate in court is in no way specified.

units.la: Sed ista obiectio (vt dicunt) non valet propter duo: tum quia licet in principio nequaquam specificetur ius: tamen in fine assertionis specificatur: tum quia dicta constitutio quia quorundam, non tantum impugnat primam partem praedictae assertionis, sed etiam vltimam in qua specificatur ius per ius, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare. Ad euidentiam primi dicunt esse sciendum, quod per sequentia saepe antecedentia debent intelligi. Secundo dicunt esse notandum, quod saepe verbum indiffinite prolatum nequaquam vniuersaliter debet intelligi, sicut prius est ostensum. Ex his dicunt patere, quod prima particula assertionis praefatae tantum pro iure, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare, debet intelligi: quia cum non dicatur abdicatio omnis iuris in cuiuscunque rei proprietate &c. Sed abdicatio iuris, ex sequentibus, in quibus aperte cum specificatione dicitur, quanto plenius renunciatum fuerit omni iuri, per quod potest sic vtens pro iure quomodolibet contendere &c. manifeste claret, quod prima particula de iure, quo potest quis in iudicio litigare, debet intelligi, & ideo non dicit, quod abdicatio omnis iuris in cuiuscunque rei proprietate & in vsu eius est sancta &c.
units.tr: But this objection (as they say) does not hold, for two reasons: first, because although the right is in no way specified at the beginning, it is specified at the end of the assertion; second, because the said constitution Quia quorundam attacks not only the first part of the aforesaid assertion but also the last, in which the right is specified as the right by which someone may litigate in court. To make the first point clear, they say it must be known that what goes before should often be understood in light of what follows. Second, they say it must be noted that a word spoken indefinitely should by no means be understood universally, as was shown before. From these points they say it is plain that the first clause of the aforesaid assertion must be understood only of the right by which one may litigate in court; for since it is not said the renunciation of every right in the ownership of any thing etc., but the renunciation of right, the following words, in which it is openly and specifically said, as the renunciation of every right by which one using in this way may in any manner contend etc., make it manifestly clear that the first clause about right must be understood of the right by which one may litigate in court; and therefore it does not say that the renunciation of every right in the ownership of any thing and in its use is holy, etc.

units.la: Hoc enim falsum est etiam secundum istos assertores: quia dicunt quod abdicatio iuris naturalis in vsu rei non est sancta, cum illi iuri nemini liceat renunciare, qui enim tali iure renunciaret, non posset in articulo necessitatis extremae de re aliena sine licentia alterius conseruare vitam suam: quod falsum est. Sed assertio praedicta dixit, quod abdicatio iuris: hoc est alicuius iuris in cuiuscunque rei proprietate & in vsu eius est sancta &c. vt sit sensus: Abdicatio alicuius iuris quantum ad proprietatem & vsum cuiuscunque rei est sancta &c. ideo postea cuidam tacitae obiectioni respondens, de quo iure intellexerit expressit, dicens: Nec propter hoc vsus facti ad sustentationem naturae in Christo & Apostolis coniunctur esse non iustus: sed tanto iustior atque perfectior & Deo acceptior & mundo exemplarior: quanto plenius renunciatum fuerit omni iuri, per quod potest sic vtens pro iure huiusmodi quomodolibet contendere vel in iudicio litigare. Quasi diceret, si aliquis dixerit, quod si Christus & Apostoli abdicauerunt omne ius in rebus, actus eorum fuisset iniustus, dicendum est, quod non abdicauerunt omne ius, quia non ius naturale: sed abdicarunt omne ius, per quod potest quis in iudicio litigare, & ideo vsus eorum non fuit non iustus &c.
units.tr: For this is false even according to these assertors, because they say that the renunciation of natural right in the use of a thing is not holy, since no one may renounce that right; for one who renounced such a right would not be able, in a case of extreme necessity, to preserve his life from another's property without the other's permission; which is false. But the aforesaid assertion said that the renunciation of right, that is, of some right, in the ownership of any thing and in its use is holy, etc., so that the sense is: the renunciation of some right as regards the ownership and use of any thing is holy, etc. Therefore, afterwards, answering a certain unspoken objection, it expressed which right it meant, saying: Nor on this account is the use of the thing for sustaining nature not just in Christ and the Apostles; but it is so much more just, more perfect, more acceptable to God, and a better example to the world, as the renunciation of every right by which one using in this way may in any manner contend or litigate in court is more complete. As if it were saying: if someone should say that, if Christ and the Apostles renounced every right in things, their acts would have been unjust, it must be replied that they did not renounce every right, because they did not renounce natural right, but they renounced every right by which one may litigate in court; and therefore their use was not unjust, etc.

units.la: Sic ergo patet, quod licet dicta assertio in prima particula non specificet, de quo iure loquatur: tamen in fine specificat manifeste: & ita praemissa obiectio non procedit: quia prima particula de iure, quo potest quis in iudicio litigare, debet intelligi: & sic intelligunt & intellexerunt a principio omnes, qui cum isto appellante concordauerunt & concordant, vbicunque enim dixerunt vel dicunt, quod Fratres Minores non habent ius vtendi in rebus & consimilia, semper loquebantur & loquuntur de iure, quo quis valet in iudicio litigare.
units.tr: Thus it is plain that, although the said assertion in its first clause does not specify which right it speaks of, yet at its end it clearly specifies it; and so the aforesaid objection does not hold, because the first clause must be understood of the right by which one may litigate in court. And so all those who agreed, and agree, with this appellant have understood and do understand it from the beginning; for wherever they have said or say that the Friars Minor have no right of using things, and similar things, they have always spoken and do speak of the right by which one may litigate in court.

units.la: Secundo dicunt isti, quod praemissa obiectio non procedit, quia constitutio, quia quorundam, non solum impugnat primam particulam assertionis memoratae: sed etiam impugnat vltimam particulam assertionis eiusdem: & ita cum illa particula de iure vtendi, quo potest quis litigare non solum sententialiter, sed etiam vocaliter aperte loquatur, constat quod constitutio quia quorundam de eodem iure debet intelligi. Quod vero dicta constitutio quia quorundam non solum primam partem sed etiam vltimam assertionis eiusdem impugnet, patet, cum post dictam assertionem immediate subiungat: qua quidem assertio continet multa falsa, cum Christum expropriationem praedictam omnis iuris in cuiuscunque rei proprietate, & in eius vsu in se seruasse, nec eam imposuisse Apostolis, nec sub voto ab ipsis fuisse receptam Euangelica seu Apostolica doceat historia: sed contrarium euidentius manifestat. Quod autem in praedicta assertione adiicitur, quod per abdicationem iuris praedicti, videlicet proprietatis & eius vsus, vsus facti ad sustentationem in Christo & Apostolis non committitur esse non iustus, sed tanto iustior &c. & impossibilitatem inducit & errorem dictum huiusmodi euidenter. Ex his verbis colligitur euidenter, quod constitutio quia quorundam non solum impugnat seu reprobat primam particulam assertionis praedictae: sed etiam vltimam illam, scilicet sed tanto iustior &c. In qua expresse fit mentio de iure, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare, ergo praedicta constitutio, quia quorundam, loquitur de eodem iure, quo quis videlicet valet in iudicio litigare. Aliter enim sophistice praedictam particulam impugnaret. Vt autem appareat, quod constitutio quia quorundam nequaquam sufficienter praedictam assertionem impugnat, isti impugnatores ad impugnationes in ea contentas, respondere conantur.
units.tr: Secondly, these men say that the aforesaid objection does not hold, because the constitution Quia quorundam attacks not only the first clause of the said assertion but also attacks the last clause of the same assertion; and so, since that clause plainly speaks of the right of using by which one may litigate, not only in sense but also in words, it is established that the constitution Quia quorundam must be understood of the same right. That the said constitution Quia quorundam attacks not only the first part but also the last part of the same assertion is clear, since immediately after the said assertion it adds: which assertion contains many false things, since the Gospel or Apostolic history teaches that Christ did not renounce in himself the aforesaid renunciation of every right in the ownership of any thing and in its use, nor imposed it on the Apostles, nor was it received by them under a vow; but history rather shows the contrary very clearly. And what is added in the aforesaid assertion, that through the renunciation of the aforesaid right, namely of ownership and its use, the use of the thing for sustaining nature in Christ and the Apostles is not held to be unjust, but so much more just, etc., brings in an impossibility and plainly an error of this kind. From these words it is clearly gathered that the constitution Quia quorundam not only attacks or rejects the first clause of the aforesaid assertion, but also that last one, namely but so much more just etc., in which mention is expressly made of the right by which one may litigate in court. Therefore the aforesaid constitution Quia quorundam speaks of the same right, namely that by which one may litigate in court. Otherwise it would attack the aforesaid clause sophistically. But so that it may appear that the constitution Quia quorundam by no means sufficiently attacks the aforesaid assertion, these opponents try to answer the objections contained in it.

units.la: Ad impugnationem autem dictae primae particulae dicunt, quod dicta constitutio quia quorundam eidem particulae falsum imponit, videlicet quod Christus & Apostoli omne ius in omnis rei & proprietate & eius vsu abdicauit dicens, cum Christum ex propriationem praedictam omnis iuris &c. Hoc enim non dicit praedicta assertio, sed tantum vsa est verbo indiffinite prolato, dicens quod abdicatio iuris &c. non dixit, omnis iuris. Secundo respondent ad impugnationes secundae particulae, quae sunt ite: impossibile est enim actum humanum extrinsecum esse iustum: si exercens actum ipsum nullum ius habeat exercendi: imo non iustus, sed iniustus committitur talis vsus. Item est absurdum & erroneum, quod actus aliquis non habentis ius actum huiusmodi faciendi fit iustior & Deo acceptior, quam habentis cum concludit actum iniustum iustiorem & Deo acceptiorem existere quam sit iustus. Istae sunt duae impugnationes vltimae particulae praedictae assertionis. In quibus oportet accipere ius pro iure, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare, cum taliter etiam & vocaliter accipiatur ius in praefata particula impugnata. Sed dicunt isti, quod istae impugnationes sunt sophisticae: & quod ex ignorantia aequiuocationis istorum nominum iustus & iniustus procedunt, quod praedictae impugnationes per distinctiones de iustitia & iusto superius c. 60. expositas dissoluuntur.
units.tr: As for the objection to the first part of that proposition, they say that the constitution Quia quorundam imposes a falsehood on that part, namely that Christ and the Apostles renounced all right in every thing, both its ownership and its use, saying: since Christ renounced the aforesaid ownership of all right, etc. The aforesaid assertion does not say this; it merely uses an indefinite word, saying that the renunciation of right, etc., and does not say "of all right." Secondly, they reply to the objections to the second part, which are these: for it is impossible that a human act outwardly performed should be just if the one performing the act has no right to perform it; indeed such use is committed not as just but as unjust. Likewise it is absurd and erroneous that an act of one who has no right to perform such an act should be more just and more acceptable to God than that of one who has the right; it concludes that an unjust act is more just and more acceptable to God than what is just. These are the two last objections against the aforesaid assertion. In them ius must be taken as the right by which a person is entitled to sue in court, since the word ius in the part objected to is likewise taken in this way and in this sense. But these men say that these objections are sophistical, and that they arise from ignorance of the equivocation of the terms just and unjust, and that the aforesaid objections are dissolved by the distinctions concerning justice and the just which were explained above in chapter 60.

units.la: Vnde ad primam dicunt, quod accipiendo actum iustum pro actu a iustitia, quae est virtus particularis distincta contra alias virtutes elicitum possset concedi: quod actus non esset sic iustus sine iure tali: sed accipiendo actum iustum pro actu elicito a iustitia tertio modo dicta, quae secundum Thomam est iustitia metaphorice dicta, sic potest actus esse iustus sine iure, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare. Sic enim actus castitatis est iustus, imo quilibet actus bonus est isto modo iustus, & tamen multi actus boni multarum virtutum eliciuntur sine iure, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare. Per idem respondet ad secundum, quod licet esset inconueniens, quod actus non habentis ius esset iustior, secundum quod actus dicitur iustus: quia elicitur a iustitia, quae est virtus particularis distincta contra alias virtutes sine iure, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare: non tamen est inconueniens, quod aliquis actus sit iustior secundum quod actus dicitur iustus a iustitia tertio modo dicta sine tali iure, quia sit actus alius habentis tale ius, unde sic actus diligendi Deum est iustus & iustior, quia melior quam actus mercenarii recipientis mercedem pro labore suo. Et cum innuitur, quod tunc actus iniustus esset iustior & Deo acceptior, quam actus iustus. Dicunt, quod hoc non sequitur: quia non omnis actus exercitus sine iure, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare, est actus iniustus accipiendo enim actum iniustum, put opponitur actui iusto elicito a iustitia particulari, multi sunt actus, qui nec sunt iusti nec iniusti. Actus enim temperantiae, fortitudinis, prudentiae, misericordiae, liberalitatis, & aliarum virtutum illo modo non sunt iusti nec iniusti: accipiendo actum iniustum, vt opponitur actui iusto tertio modo dicto, sic actus talis non est iniustus, sed iustus: & tamen sine iure quo valet quis in iudicio litigare: sed non sine rone recta, & de hoc amplius patebit inferius. Ex praedictis concludunt isti impugnatores, quod constitutio Ad conditorem loquitur de iure agendi. Nam constitutio Ad conditorem loquitur de eode iure, de quo loquitur constitutio quia quorunda sed constitutio quia quorunda loquitur de iure agendi: cum sicut ostensum est, loquatur de iure, quo valet aliquis in iudicio litigare, ergo constitutio Ad conditorem loquitur de iure agendi: & ita secundum illam constitutionem ius vtendi est ius agendi. Quod confirmatur, quia secundum istum in principio istius constitutionis, quia vir reprobus, ius vtendi est vsus iuris ciuilis, sed vsus iuris ciuilis est ius agendi, ergo ius vtendi secundum istum est ius agendi. Dicunt igitur, quod cum dicit ius vtendi posse competere alicui, cui non competit ius agendi, sibi ipsi contrarius inuenitur.
units.tr: Hence to the first they say that, taking a just act as an act elicited by justice, which is a particular virtue distinct from the other virtues, one could concede that the act would not be just without such a right; but taking a just act as an act elicited by justice in the third sense mentioned, which according to Thomas is justice in a metaphorical sense, then an act can be just without the right by which a person is entitled to sue in court. For thus an act of chastity is just, indeed every good act is just in this way, and yet many good acts of many virtues are elicited without the right by which a person is entitled to sue in court. In the same way they answer the second point: although it would be inconvenient for an act of one who has no right to be more just, insofar as an act is called just because it is elicited by justice, which is a particular virtue distinct from the other virtues, without the right by which a person is entitled to sue in court, nevertheless it is not inconvenient that some act should be more just, insofar as it is called just by justice in the third sense mentioned, without such a right, because it is the act of another who has such a right; thus the act of loving God is just and more just, because it is better than the act of a hired servant who receives wages for his labour. And when it is implied that then an unjust act would be more just and more acceptable to God than a just act, they say this does not follow: for not every act performed without the right by which a person is entitled to sue in court is an unjust act. For taking an unjust act as opposed to a just act elicited by particular justice, there are many acts which are neither just nor unjust. For the acts of temperance, fortitude, prudence, mercy, liberality and the other virtues are in that sense neither just nor unjust; taking an unjust act as opposed to a just act in the third sense mentioned, such an act is not unjust but just, and yet it is done without the right by which a person is entitled to sue in court, though not without right reason; and this will be made clearer further below. From the foregoing these objectors conclude that the constitution Ad conditorem speaks of the right to act. For the constitution Ad conditorem speaks of the same right of which the constitution Quia quorundam speaks, but the constitution Quia quorundam speaks of the right to act, since, as has been shown, it speaks of the right by which a person is entitled to sue in court; therefore the constitution Ad conditorem speaks of the right to act, and so according to that constitution the right to use is the right to act. This is confirmed, because according to the same author at the beginning of that constitution, quia vir reprobus, the right to use is the use of civil right, but the use of civil right is the right to act; therefore the right to use, according to him, is the right to act. They say, therefore, that when he says that the right to use can belong to someone to whom the right to act does not belong, he is found to be self-contradictory.

units.la: Secundo isti impugnatores conantur ostendere, quod constitutio quia quorundam loquitur de iure vtendi, proprio, non solum collegio, sed etiam personae. Nam sicut patet p rationes, quibus probare conantur, quod actus est iniustus, si exercens ipsum actu non habet ius faciendi: ipse loquitur de iure sine quo actus est iniustus, & p quae actus est iustus, sed tale ius secundum eum non est ius commune communitati. Nam ad hoc, quod aliquis actus sit iustus, ius commune communitati non sufficit, sicut nec sufficit ad hoc quod actus sit licitus. Vnde ad hoc, quod monachus licite aliquam cellam inhibiter, vel equum equitaret, nō sufficitius commune suo collegio: sed requiritur quod ipse in speciali habeat licentiam à superiori ad actus tales exercendos. Licentia autem secundū istum est ius vtendi, ergo ad hoc, q; tales actus sint liciti & iusti, requiritur ius vtendi proprium, præter ius vtendi commune, & de illo iure, quod facit actum esse iustum, loquitur constitutio, quia quorundam, ergo loquitur de iure vtendi proprio.
units.tr: Secondly, these objectors try to show that the constitution Quia quorundam speaks of the right of use proper not only to the community but also to the person. For as is evident from the arguments by which they try to prove that an act is unjust if the one performing it has no right to do it, he speaks of the right without which an act is unjust, and by which an act is just; but such a right, according to him, is not a right common to the community. For for an act to be just, a right common to the community is not sufficient, just as it is not sufficient for an act to be lawful. Hence, for a monk to lawfully inhabit some cell or ride a horse, it is not sufficient for the common right of his community; rather it is required that he himself have in particular a licence from his superior to perform such acts. But a licence, according to him, is the right to use; therefore, for such acts to be lawful and just, a proper right of use is required, over and above the common right of use; and the constitution Quia quorundam speaks of that right which makes the act just; therefore it speaks of the proper right of use.

units.la: Tertio isti impugnatores ostendunt, quod verba, quæ hic recitantur ad constitutionem, quæ quarundam, plures errores ridiculosos includunt. Quorum primus est: quod Ordo Fratrū Minorum habet vsum iuris in rebus, quibus vtitur, quod enim hoc sit erroneum, patet, quia omnis vsus iuris est vsus nudus vel vsusfructus, sed Ordo Fratrum Minorum non habet vsum nudum iuris in rebus, nec vsum fructū, quia omnis habens talem ius, potest pro vsu rei in iudicio litigare: q; secundum Clementē quintū Fratribus Minoribus convenire non pōt, ergo ordo Fratrum Minorū non habet vsum iuris.
units.tr: Thirdly, these objectors show that the words which are here quoted from the constitution Quia quorundam contain several ridiculous errors. The first of these is that the Order of Friars Minor has the use of right in the things which it uses. That this is erroneous is evident, because every use of right is either bare use or usufruct; but the Order of Friars Minor has neither bare use nor usufruct of right in things, because everyone having such a right can sue in court for the use of the thing; and according to Clement V the Friars Minor cannot be sued; therefore the Order of Friars Minor does not have a use of right.

units.la: Secundus error ibi contentus, vt dicunt, est quod ordo Fratrum Minorum est persona repræsentata & imaginaria, q; enim hoc sit erroneum, ostendunt: quia si ordo Fratrum Minorum est persona repræsentata & imaginaria, eadem ratione ecclesia, & quælibet communitas esset persona repræsentata & imaginaria: q; est absurdum, q; enim est tantum repræsentatum & imaginarium, est fantasticum: & non est in re extra animā, sed ecclesia non est quid fantasticum non existens extra animam, ergo non est persona repræsentata & imaginaria. Confirmatur, qa aut ecclesia est extra animā, aut in anima tantum, aut quid compositum ex ente in anima & ente extra animam, si est in anima tantum, vel aliquid compositum ex ente in anima & ente extra animā: ergo nullū reale nec iurisdictionem potest habere: quæ dicere de ecclesia est impium & blasphemum, si autem ecclesia est extra animam: vel ergo est vna res vel plures: & siue sit vna siue plures, non est persona repræsentata & imaginaria, ecclesia ergo non est persona repræsentata & imaginaria, & eadem ratione ordo Fratrum Minorum non est persona repræsentata & imaginaria.
units.tr: The second error contained there, they say, is that the Order of Friars Minor is a represented and imaginary person. They show that this is erroneous: because if the Order of Friars Minor is a represented and imaginary person, for the same reason the Church and every community would be a represented and imaginary person; which is absurd, for what is merely represented and imaginary is fantastical, and does not exist outside the soul; but the Church is not something fantastical not existing outside the soul; therefore it is not a represented and imaginary person. It is confirmed thus: either the Church is outside the soul, or in the soul only, or something compounded of a being in the soul and a being outside the soul; if it is in the soul only, or something compounded of a being in the soul and a being outside the soul, then it can have nothing real nor any jurisdiction; which to say of the Church is impious and blasphemous. If, however, the Church is outside the soul, then either it is one thing or several things; and whether it is one or several, it is not a represented and imaginary person; therefore the Church is not a represented and imaginary person, and for the same reason the Order of Friars Minor is not a represented and imaginary person.

units.la: Tertius error (vt dicunt) est, quod quæ facti sunt, Ordini vere nequeunt cōuenire, quod enim hoc sit erroneum probare conantur: quia si ea quæ sunt facti, Ordini nequeunt convenire, eadem ratione ea quę sunt facti nulli communitati vel collegio possunt convenire: & per consequens ea quę sunt facti, nec ecclesiæ, nec concilio generali, nec congregationi fidelium, nec populo, nec turbæ, nec plebi, neq; ciuitati, regno, vel cuicunq; alii vniuersitati, aut cōmunitati poterunt convenire: q; scripturę sacræ, & sacris canonibus, ac doctrinæ sanctorum noscitur repugnare. Luc. enim 1. sic legitur: Omnis multitudo populi erat erans foris hora incensi: & inde erat plebs expectans Zachariam: & mirabantur quod tardaret ipse in templo. & Matth. 22. sic scribitur, & cum intrasset (sc. Iesus,) Hierosolymā, commota est vniuersa ciuitas, dicens, quis est hic? & Act. 15. Ibi igitur deducti ab ecclesia transibant Phœnicem &c. & infra: Placuit Apostolis & senioribus, cum omni ecclesia eligere viros ex eis, & mittere Antiochiam cum Paulo & Barnaba &c. Item Greg. vt habetur 12. q. 3. c. Sicut, ait: Sicut ecclesia proprias res amittere non debet: ita eam rapacitatis ardore habere alienas non oportet. Item vniuersalis ecclesia approbat constituta synodi, vt habetur 25. q. 1. confidimus, & Gelasius papa di. 16. c. sancta, ait: sancta Romana ecclesia post illas nouī & veteris testamenti scripturas, quas regulariter suscipimus, & has suscipi non prohibet, sanctam synodum Nicenam &c. Et Greg. eadē di. c. sicut ait: Cunctas vero quas prefata veneranda concilia personas respuunt respuo. Et Isidorus eadem di. c. 1. ait: Consubstantialem Deo patri Dei filiū eadem sancta synodus per symbolum diffiniuit, & extra de sponsalibus & matrimonio c. 1. sic habetur, diffiniuit super hoc sancta synodus &c. & extra de summa trinitate & fide catholica c. damnamus ait Innocentius: Nos autem sacro approbante concilio credimus &c. Ex his aliisq; innumeris auctoritatibus & sacris canonibus luce clarius constat, quod ea quæ facti sunt, possunt ecclesiæ, concilio, synodo, populo, multitudini, communitati & collegiis convenire.
units.tr: The third error (as they call it) is that what are matters of fact cannot truly belong to an Order. They try to prove that this is erroneous: for if matters of fact cannot belong to an Order, then by the same reasoning they cannot belong to any community or college; and consequently matters of fact could belong neither to the Church, nor to a general council, nor to a gathering of the faithful, nor to a people, nor to a crowd, nor to the common folk, nor to a city, kingdom, or any other corporate body or community. This is known to contradict Holy Scripture, the sacred canons and the teaching of the saints. For Luke 1 reads thus: "The whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense; and the common folk were waiting for Zechariah, and they marvelled that he tarried in the temple." And Matthew 22 is written thus: "And when he (that is, Jesus) entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred, saying, Who is this?" And Acts 15: "Being therefore brought on their way by the Church, they passed through Phoenicia, etc." and further: "It seemed good to the apostles and elders, with the whole Church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas, etc." Likewise Gregory, as is found in 12 q. 3, c. Sicut, says: "As the Church ought not to lose its own goods, so it ought not to hold other people's goods out of a greed for plunder." Likewise the universal Church approves what a synod has decreed, as is found in 25 q. 1, Confidimus; and Pope Gelasius, in d. 16, c. Sancta, says: "The holy Roman Church, after those Scriptures of the New and Old Testament which we regularly receive, and does not forbid these to be received, the holy Nicene Synod, etc." And Gregory in the same distinction, c. Sicut, says: "All those persons whom the aforesaid venerable councils reject, I too reject." And Isidore in the same distinction, c. 1, says: "The same holy synod defined by the creed that the Son of God is consubstantial with God the Father"; and in Extra, de sponsalibus et matrimonio, c. 1, it is found thus: "the holy synod defined on this point, etc."; and in Extra, de summa trinitate et fide catholica, c. Damnamus, Innocent says: "We, however, with the approval of the holy council, believe, etc." From these and other countless authorities and sacred canons it is clearer than daylight that matters of fact can belong to the Church, to a council, to a synod, to a people, to a multitude, to a community and to colleges.

units.la: Quartus error (vt dicunt) est, quod licet ordini non possint convenire ea quæ sunt facti: ei tamen convenire possunt ea quæ sunt iuris, hoc ergo dicunt esse erroneum: quia omne ius ad aliquem attinet ordinatur, cui ergo illud q; facti est convenire non potest, nec illud quod iuris est, eidem poterit convenire. Item, nulli quod est solum imaginarium potest ius aliquod convenire: sed ordo secundum istum est solum modo quid imaginarium: ergo ei non potest ius convenire.
units.tr: The fourth error (as they call it) is that although matters of fact cannot belong to an Order, matters of right can belong to it. They say this is erroneous, because every right is ordered to some person to whom it belongs; so what is a matter of fact cannot belong to that person, and neither can what is a matter of right belong to him. Likewise, no right can belong to something which is merely imaginary; but according to them an Order is merely something imaginary; therefore no right can belong to it.

units.la: (Item intelligitur de iure mundano & ciuili quod est proprium) hoc probatum est quo ad vtramq; particulam (ius vtendi communitatis fratrum existit) hoc falsum est de iure vtendi humanitus instituto & directe decretali Exiit obuiat & repugnat, (ordo vsum habeat) hoc est Fratres vsum habeant: quia Fratres sunt Ordo, sicut enim secundum Apostolum ad Hebræos 3. fideles sunt domus Dei, loquens enim de domo Dei: qua domus sumus nos, si fiduciam & gloriam spei vsq; ad finem firmi retineamus: ita Fratres sunt ordo, & ordo est Fratres. Ex quo sequitur euidenter, q; ordo non est persona imaginaria & repræsentata: sed ordo est vere persona reales, (dicta constitutio quia quorundam volens probare q; illud de vsu iuris debeat intelligi) & male: quia dictū Innoc. & Alex. quarti debet intelligi de vsu facti, non de vsu iuris. (Ad vsum iuris necesse est hoc referre) dicunt isti, q; male dicit, quia debet referri ad vsum facti. (Facta quedam quę singulorū sunt personam veram exigunt & requirunt) hoc verum est, sed nō semper exigunt vnam personam veram, sed aliquando exigunt plures veras personas. (Ordo autem vera persona non est) verū est quod ordo non est vnica vera persona, sed est verę personę, sicut populus non est vnus hō, sed est plures homines, (sed repræsentata & imaginaria potius est censenda) hoc dicunt fantastice dictū: quia ordo est verę plonæ, sicut ecclesiæ est verę plonæ, (quæ facti sunt, sibi convenire nequeunt) hoc est erroneū sicut est erroneū dicere, q; illa q facti sunt ecclesiæ nequeunt convenire, (licet possint ei congruere, quæ sunt iuris) hoc innuitur, q; plonæ imaginariæ possunt congruere ea q sunt iuris, q; est ridiculosum secundum istos. (Ex quibus patet, q; dicta constitutio ius vtendi non dicit esse proprium) verum est, q; hoc non dicit vocaliter, tamen hoc sequitur ex dictis ibidem. Et qui vnum dicit, dicit omnia quae sequuntur ex illo, ideo vere potest dici, quod hic dicit. (Sed toti vniuersitati communi) dicunt quod utrumq; dicit, vnum vocaliter & aliud sententialiter, & ideo sibiipsi contradicit.
units.tr: (Likewise it is understood of worldly and civil right, which is proper.) This has been proved as to both parts. (The right of using belongs to the community of the brothers.) This is false, and it is opposed and contradicted by the decretal Exiit concerning the right of use instituted by human authority. (The Order has the use.) That is, the Brothers have the use; for the Brothers are the Order, just as, according to the Apostle to the Hebrews 3, the faithful are the house of God: for speaking of the house of God, he says, "whose house we are, if we hold fast the confidence and the glory of hope firm to the end." So the Brothers are the Order, and the Order is the Brothers. From which it follows plainly that the Order is not an imaginary and represented person, but the Order is truly a real person. (The said constitution, because it wished to prove something of certain persons, that that must be understood of the use of right.) And wrongly so, because the statement of Innocent and Alexander IV ought to be understood of the use of fact, not of the use of right. (It is necessary to refer this to the use of right.) They say this, and speak wrongly, because it ought to be referred to the use of fact. (Certain facts which belong to individuals demand and require a true person.) This is true, but they do not always demand one true person; sometimes they demand several true persons. (But the Order is not a true person.) It is true that the Order is not a single true person, but it is true persons, just as a people is not one man but several men. (But it is to be regarded rather as represented and imaginary.) They say this as a fanciful statement, because the Order is of true persons, just as the Church is of true persons. (Matters of fact cannot belong to it.) This is erroneous, just as it is erroneous to say that the things which are matters of fact cannot belong to the Church. (Although matters of right may befit it.) This is hinted, because imaginary persons can befit matters of right, which is ridiculous according to them. (From which it is evident that the said constitution does not say that the right of using is proper.) It is true that it does not say this in words; nevertheless it follows from what is said there. And he who says one thing says all that follows from it; therefore it can truly be said that this is what it says. (But to the whole community in common.) They say that it says both things, one in words and the other in sense, and so it contradicts itself.

units.la: CAP. LXIII.
units.tr: CAP. LXIII.

units.la: Recte dicit dictus haereticus, quod si vsus posset separari a iure vtendi, vsus a iure vtendi separatus non esset iniustus, quia aliud est habere ius vtendi, & aliud licentiam vtendi, & ideo quamuis vsus absq; omni iure & licentia vtendi esset illicitus vsus: tamen absq; iure vtendi cum licentia tamen vtendi nequaquam illicitus esse censendus.
units.tr: The aforesaid heretic rightly says that if use could be separated from the right to use, then use separated from the right to use would not be unjust, because having a right to use is one thing, and having a licence to use is another; and so, although use without any right and licence to use would be unlawful use, yet use without the right to use, but with licence to use, is by no means to be considered unlawful.

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnatus quandam responsionem appellantis ad rationem istius impugnati, quae innuitur supra capit. 59. reprobare conatur, & diuiditur in duas partes, quia primo recitat dictam responsionem: secundo eam impugnat in parte immediate sequenti.
units.tr: In this part, the one who is attacked here tries to refute a certain reply of the appellant to the argument of this opponent, which is hinted at above in chapter 59., and it is divided into two parts: first he recites the said reply, and secondly he attacks it in the part immediately following.

units.la: Ad euidentiam primae partis est sciendum, quod supra capitulo 59. innuitur talis ratio ad probandum, quod vsus concessus Fratribus Minoribus non est sine iure vtendi: quia aliter esset illicitus. Et ad hoc hic respondet appellans dicens, quod vsus, qui non est sine iure vtendi, & sine licentia vtendi, qualis non est vsus Fratrum, non est illicitus.
units.tr: To make clear the first part, it should be known that above, in chapter 59., an argument is hinted at for proving that the use granted to the Friars Minor is not without the right to use, because otherwise it would be unlawful. And to this the appellant here replies, saying that use which is not without the right to use and without licence to use, such as the use of the Friars is not, is not unlawful.

units.la: (Vsus a iure vtendi separatus, non esset iniustus) Etiam esto, quod non esset iustus, secundum quod aliquis actus dicitur iustus propter iustitiam particularem contra alias virtutes distinctam: quia sic accipiendo actum iustum, multi sunt actus, qui nec sunt iusti, nec iniusti: qui tamen sunt boni vel mali. (Aliud est habere ius vtendi & aliud licentiam vtendi) hoc continet omnimodam veritatem de iure, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare, de quo loquitur constitutio quia quorundam: sicut ostensum est in capitulo praecedenti.
units.tr: (Use separated from the right to use would not be unjust) Even granting that it would not be just, in the sense in which an action is called just on account of particular justice, which is distinguished from the other virtues: for taking a just action in this sense, there are many actions which are neither just nor unjust, yet which are good or bad. (Having a right to use is one thing, and having a licence to use another) This contains the entire truth about that right by which a person may litigate in court, of which the constitution Quia quorundam speaks, as has been shown in the preceding chapter.

units.la: CAP. LXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXIV.

units.la: Secundum hoc iste haereticus inter ius & licentiam videtur facere differentiam, supponens quod aliquis habeat vtendi licentiam ab eo, qui potest eam concedere & quod non habeat ius vtendi: quod tamen euidenter est falsum. Si enim aliquis licentiam concedat alii vtendi re sua visibili: ita quod licentia teneat, constat quod ille habet ius vtendi re illa, cui licentia est concessa, hinc est quod religiosus in concordia extra suum monasterium electus sine sui superioris licentia ius consentiendi non habet: obtenta tamen licentia ius habet consentiendi. Extra de electione quam sic. li. 6. & c. si religiosus: cum similibus multis.
units.tr: Accordingly, this heretic seems to draw a distinction between right and licence, supposing that someone may have licence to use a thing from one who can grant it, and yet not have a right to use it. This is plainly false. For if someone grants another licence to use his visible property, so that the licence holds, it is clear that the one to whom the licence is granted has a right to use that thing. Hence a religious, elected in a chapter outside his monastery without the licence of his superior, has no right to consent; yet once licence is obtained, he has the right to consent. Extra, De electione, Quam sic, Book 6, and c. Si religiosus, with many similar passages.

units.la: In ista parte iste impugnatus praedictam responsionem improbare conatur. Et diuiditur in duas partes, secundum quod duas rationes adducit, secunda incipit in parte immediate sequenti. Dicit ergo primo: quod secundum praedictam responsionem sic differt licentia a iure, quod aliquis potest habere licentiam sine iure: quod tamen est falsum: quia si aliquis concedit alicui licentiam vtendi, sic quod licentia teneat, ille habet ius vtendi: quod probat per exemplum de religioso: cui si conceditur licentia consentiendi in electionem de se factam, ipse habet ius consentiendi.
units.tr: In this part, the one under attack tries to refute the aforesaid answer. The passage is divided into two parts, according to the two arguments he brings forward; the second begins in the part immediately following. He says first that, according to the aforesaid answer, licence differs from right in such a way that someone can have a licence without a right. This is false, he argues, because if someone grants another licence to use, so that the licence holds, that person has the right to use. He proves this by the example of the religious: if licence is granted to a religious to consent to his election, he himself has the right to consent.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, quod ratio non probat. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod appellans non intendit asserere, quod omnis, qui habet licentiam, non habet ius: sed aliquis potest habere licentiam, licet ex hoc ius non habeat. Nam, sicut dictum est supra cap. 61. aliquando concessa licentia ius quoddam acquiritur: aliquando non, quando enim obtenta licentia non potest ad libitum reuocari, ius quoddam acquiritur: quando vero ad libitum potest reuocari, nec virtute licentiae potest, habens eam in iudicio litigare, nullum ius acquiritur. Nunc autem aliquando datur licentia vtendi rebus, quae potest ad libitum reuocari: sicut concedentibus Fratribus Minoribus licentiam habitandi in locis suis possunt illam licentiam ad libitum reuocare. Nec Fratres virtute talis licentiae possunt in habitatione locorum huiusmodi in iudicio litigare: ideo ipsis per licentiam huiusmodi nullum ius acquiritur. Aliquando autem datur licentia vtendi rebus, quae non potest ad libitum reuocari, sicut patet in commodato secundum iura ciuilia & canonica de commodato loquuntur: sicut patet extra de commodato, precarium, licet enim possit quandoq; reuocari commodatum: tamen ante vsum expletum, ad quem concedunt, reuocari non potest, & ideo concessa licentia vtendi commodato ius quoddam acquiritur. Per hoc patet quod ratio praedicta istius impugnati vel probat: quod non super licentia obtenta acquiritur ius: licet quandoq; hoc sit verum. Ex quo patet quod per exemplum de religioso etiam esto quod sit verum: conclusio intenta non probatur, quia per vnum exemplum vniuersalis probari non potest.
units.tr: But these opponents say that the argument does not prove it. To make this clear, they say it must be understood that the appellant does not mean to assert that everyone who has a licence lacks a right, but that someone may have a licence even though he does not thereby have a right. For, as was said above at chap. 61, sometimes a certain right is acquired by a granted licence, and sometimes not. When the licence, once obtained, cannot be revoked at will, a certain right is acquired. But when it can be revoked at will, the holder cannot litigate in court by virtue of the licence, and no right is acquired. Now sometimes a licence to use things is given which can be revoked at will: as when the Friars Minor are granted licence to dwell in their places, the grantors can revoke that licence at will. Nor can the Friars, by virtue of such a licence, litigate in court concerning their dwelling in such places; so no right is acquired for them through such a licence. Sometimes, however, a licence to use things is given which cannot be revoked at will. This is clear in loan for use (commodatum), of which the civil and canon laws speak, as is clear in Extra, De commodato, precario. For although a loan for use can sometimes be revoked, it cannot be revoked before the use for which it was granted is completed; and so, with licence to use the loan granted, a certain right is acquired. From this it is clear that the aforesaid argument of this opponent proves only that no right is acquired from a licence obtained, although this is sometimes true. Hence, by the example of the religious, even if it were true, the intended conclusion is not proved, because a universal cannot be proved by one example.

units.la: (Supponens quod aliquis habeat vtendi licentiam ab eo qui eam possit concedere: & quod non habeat ius vtendi) si intelligatur particulariter, hoc est de intentione appellantis: sed vniuersaliter intellectum non est de intentione sua. Ad intentionem autem suam habendam sufficit, quod particulariter intelligitur (quod enim euidenter est falsum) particulariter intellectum est verum euidenter, sicut probatum est supra cap. 61.) Constat quod ille habet ius vtendi re illa cui licentia est concessa) hoc non habet veritatem de licentia, quae potest ad libitum reuocari: & quia non potest quis in iudicio litigare, (obtenta tamen licentia: ius habent consentiendi extr. de electis c. quam sic. li. 6. & c. si religiosus) siue sit verum siue falsum, quod religiosus obtenta licentia habet ius consentiendi: hoc non dicitur in capitulis allegatis quia de iure consentiendi nulla ibi fit mentio. Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod si aliqua licentia potest dici ius: & omnis licentia poterit dicitur, quia non est ratio quare vna licentia debeat vocari ius magis quam alia. Ad hoc dici potest secundum praedicta, quod ratio est quare vna licentia potest vocari ius, & non alia: quia scilicet vna potest ad libitum reuocari & alia non, vnde licentia, quae non potest ad libitum reuocari, ideo potest vocari ius: quia illa licentia non debet licentiatus sine culpa & absq; causa priuari. Potest nihilominus vocari licentia, quia licentiatus illa vti non tenetur: sed quaedam alia licentia tantum licentia, & non ius vocari debet.
units.tr: (Supposing that someone has licence to use from one who can grant it, and yet has no right to use it) if this is taken particularly, it is the appellant's intention; but taken universally, it is not his intention. To hold his intention, it is enough that it is understood particularly, (for what is manifestly false) when taken particularly, is manifestly true, as proved above at chap. 61. It is clear that that person has the right to use the thing to which licence has been granted) this does not hold true of a licence which can be revoked at will; and since one cannot litigate in court (yet once licence is obtained, they have the right to consent: Extra, De electis, c. Quam sic, Book 6, and c. Si religiosus) whether it is true or false that a religious, once licence is obtained, has the right to consent, this is not stated in the chapters cited, because no mention of a right to consent is made there. But perhaps someone will say: if any licence can be called a right, then every licence could be called one, since there is no reason why one licence should be called a right rather than another. To this it can be replied, in line with what has been said, that there is a reason why one licence can be called a right and another cannot: namely, one can be revoked at will and another cannot. A licence which cannot be revoked at will may therefore be called a right, because the licensee ought not to be deprived of it without fault and without cause. Nevertheless, it may also be called a licence, because the licensee is not bound to use it; but some other licence should be called merely a licence, and not a right.

units.la: CAP. LXV.
units.tr: Chapter 65.

units.la: PRaterea autem iste haereticus dicit, quod iste cui vtendi re aliqua licentia est concessa, iuste re illa vtitur, aut quod iniuste, aut quod nec iuste re illa vtitur nec iniuste, si dicat quod iniuste: concordat vtiq; cum constitutione praedicta, qua vult, quod qui sine iure vtitur, vtatur iniuste, si dicat quod iuste vtitur, sequitur per consequens, quod & iure, quia quod iuste fit, & fit iure, extr. de verborum significatione ca. ius dictum 14. q. 3. qd dicam. Si autem dicat, quod ille cui est licentia vtendi concessa, nec iuste vtatur nec iniuste: hoc est falsum. Impossibile est enim actu humanum indifferentem esse, id est nec bonum nec malum: nec iustum nec iniustum. Cum enim actus humanus dicatur, qui ex deliberata voluntate procedit: & per consequens qui est propter aliquem finem, qui quidem obiectum noscitur voluntatis, oportet quod si finis actus sit bonus, quod & ipse actus sit bonus, si vero finis sit malus, oportet quod actus sit malus: quia, sicut Aug. in lib. de moribus ecclesiae dicit: secundum quod finis est culpabilis vel laudabilis, secundum hoc laudabilia vel culpabilia sunt opera nostra.
units.tr: Moreover, this heretic says that a person to whom a licence to use some thing has been granted either uses that thing justly, or unjustly, or neither justly nor unjustly. If he says unjustly, he certainly agrees with the aforesaid constitution, which holds that whoever uses without right uses unjustly. If he says justly, it follows that he also uses it by right, because what is done justly is done by right (extr. de verborum significatione, c. Ius dictum; 14 q. 3, Quod dicam). But if he says that the one to whom the licence was granted uses it neither justly nor unjustly, this is false.
