For a human act cannot be indifferent, that is, neither good nor bad, neither just nor unjust. A human act is that which proceeds from deliberate will, and so is for some end. Since that end is known to be the object of the will, it follows that if the end of the act is good, the act itself is good, and if the end is bad, the act must be bad. For, as Augustine says in the book On the Morals of the Church, our works are blameworthy or praiseworthy according as their end is blameworthy or praiseworthy.

units.la: In parte ista secunda rationem adducit ad probandum, quod qui habet licetiam vtendi re aliqua, habet ius vtendi eadem re: & primo probat ipsam: secundo ad quandam obiectionem, quae contra ipsam posset adduci, respondet parte sequenti. Est ergo ratio talis. Qui vtitur re aliqua de licentia alterius sine iure, aut vtitur iuste, aut iniuste, aut neq; iuste neq; iniuste, si iniuste, concordat cum constitutione Ad conditorem, si iuste: ergo iure, extr. de verborum significatione c. ius dictum est, & 14. q. 4. quid dicam, si neq; iuste neq; iniuste, hoc dici non potest, quia omnis actus humanus est iustus vel iniustus.
units.tr: In this second part he gives an argument to prove that whoever has a licence to use some thing has the right to use the same thing. First he proves the point itself, and second, in the following part, he answers an objection that might be brought against it. The argument runs thus. Whoever uses a thing by another's licence without right either uses it justly, or unjustly, or neither justly nor unjustly. If unjustly, he agrees with the constitution Ad conditorem. If justly, then he uses it by right (extr. de verborum significatione, c. Ius dictum est; and 14 q. 4, Quid dicam). If neither justly nor unjustly, this cannot be said, because every human act is either just or unjust.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod iste cauillose procedens sub aequiuocatione vocum veritatis amatores catholicos nititur reprobare. Vnde ad huius argumenti dissolutionem primo distinguitur de iure: secundo ostendunt de quo iure appellans & iste impugnatus locuti sunt prius. Tertio ostendunt quomodo res temporales dicuntur diuersimode esse diuersorum: & quomodo diuersi diuersimode dicuntur temporalia possidere. Quarto replicant breuiter distinctionem de iusto & iustitia ac iuste. Quinto respondent ad formam argumenti praecedentis,
units.tr: But these opponents say that he, proceeding sophistically through an equivocation of words, seeks to discredit the Catholic lovers of truth. So, to dissolve this argument, they proceed as follows. First, they make a distinction about right. Second, they show which right the appellant and the man attacked were speaking of earlier. Third, they show how temporal things are said in different ways to belong to different people, and how different people are said to possess temporal goods in different ways. Fourth, they briefly repeat the distinction between the just, justice and justly. Fifth, they answer the form of the preceding argument.

units.la: Circa primum dicunt, quod hoc nomen ius aliquando accipitur pro iure fori: Aliquando pro iure poli. Ista distinctio colligitur ex verbis Augustini de vita clericorum, quae ponuntur 17. q. 4. ca. vltim. q. ait: In potestate habebat episcopus nec reddere: sed iure fori non iure poli. Et ex eisdem ca & quaest. §. notandum, habetur eadem distinctione. Ad istius autem distinctionis euidentia est sciendum, quod ius fori vocatur iustum, quod ex pactione seu ordinatione humana vel diuina explicita constituitur, vnde & ius fori ius consuetudinis large sumpto vocabulo consuetudinis poterit appellari, & de isto iure dicitur in decretali distinctio. 6. ius vero consuetudinis post naturale legem exordium habuit, ex quo homines conuenientes in vnum coeperunt simul habitare. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod istud ius per pactionem seu ordinationem humanam constituitur, postquam pactionem seu ordinationem consuetudine aut lege firmatam violari ad placitum cuiuscunq; non debet, teste Aug. lib. 2. confessionum, put habetur di. 8. c. quae contra. qui ait: Quae contra mores sunt hominum flagitia, pro morum diuersitate sunt vitanda, vt pactu inter se gentis, aut ciuitatu consuetudine, vel lege firmatum, nulla ciuis aut peregrini libidine violetur. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod ius pactione humana institutum violari ad placitum cuiuscunq; non debet, quis in nonnullis casibus auctoritate superioris contra tale ius aliqd licite fieri possit, sicut Aug. declarat ibidem, quod etiam ius humanitus constitutum non debeat ad libitum violari ostenditur: a secundum Isidorum, vt habetur in decretis di. 1. Omne ius legibus & moribus constat, sed leges & mores no debent ad placitum violari, ergo ius humanitus institutum non licet absq; auctoritate superioris ad placitum violare. Quod enim mores non liceat ad placitum violare, patet per capitulum Augustini superius allegatum, Quae contra. De legibus etiam patet idem p eundem Augustinum de vera religione, qui vt legitur di. 4. c. 3. in isti, ait: In istis temporalibus legibus quanquam de iis homines iudicent, cum eas instituunt: tamen cum fuerunt instituta ac firmata, non licebit iudici de ipsis iudicare, sed secundu ipsas. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod leges humanitus institutae non sunt ad placitum etiam aliquorum iudicum violandae: & ita etiam iura humanitus instituta non sunt ad placitum violanda. Ex quo sequitur vlterius, quod licentia, quae iure fori potest a concedente ad placitum reuocari, est de iure fori minime repudianda quod praecipue noscitur veritate habere, quado concedes licentia non est superior illo, cui licentia est concessa, quod dicitur propter concedente aliqui priuilegiu, quod potest ad libitum reuocare: quod tamen licet no respectu principis, sed respectu subditorum cotinet vim legis. Ius aut e poli vocatur aequitas naturalis, quae absq; omni ordinatione humana & etiam diuina pure positiua est consona rationi rectae: siue sit consona rationi rectae pure naturali, siue sit consona rationi rectae acceptae ex illis quae sunt nobis diuinitus reuelata: pter quod hoc ius aliquado vocatur ius naturale: quia omne ius naturale pertinet ad ius poli. Aliquando vocatur ius diuinum: quia multa sunt consona rationi rectae iure naturali & iure diuino: sicut consonum est rationi rectae acceptae ex credibilibus, quod Euangelii praedicantes saltem qui no habent vnde sustententur aliunde, de bonis illorum quibus praedicant sustententur, hoc tamen per rationem pure naturale probari no potest: sicut p tale rationem probari sufficienter non potest, quod illa quae praedicant, sunt vera vtilia & necessaria illis quibus praedicat.
units.tr: On the first point, they say that the word ius is sometimes taken for the right of the forum (ius fori), and sometimes for the right of heaven (ius poli). This distinction is drawn from the words of Augustine in On the Life of Clerics, which are placed in 17 q. 4, c. ult., q. Ait: "The bishop had the power not to give back, but by the right of the forum, not by the right of heaven." The same distinction is found in the same chapter and question, §. Notandum. To make this distinction clear, it must be known that the right of the forum is called that which is established by explicit human or divine agreement or ordinance. Hence the right of the forum may also be called the right of custom, taking the word custom broadly, and the decretal Distinctio 6 speaks of this right. The right of custom, however, had its beginning after natural law, from the time when men, coming together, began to live in one place. From these words it is understood that this right is established by human agreement or ordinance, and that once an agreement or ordinance has been confirmed by custom or law, it ought not to be violated at the pleasure of anyone. Augustine witnesses this in book 2 of the Confessions, as found in D. 8, c. Quae contra, where he says: "The crimes that are against men's customs are to be avoided according to the diversity of customs, so that what has been confirmed among a people by mutual agreement, or by the custom or law of a state, is not violated by the lust of any citizen or stranger." From these words it is understood that a right established by human agreement ought not to be violated at the pleasure of anyone, although, as Augustine explains in the same place, in some cases something may lawfully be done against such a right by the authority of a superior. That even a right constituted by men may not be violated at will is also shown by Isidore, as found in the Decretum, D. 1: "All right consists of laws and customs." But laws and customs ought not to be violated at pleasure. Therefore a right instituted by men may not lawfully be violated at pleasure without the authority of a superior. That customs may not lawfully be violated at pleasure is clear from the chapter of Augustine cited above, Quae contra. The same holds of laws, as is clear from the same Augustine in On True Religion, who, as is read in D. 4, c. 3, says: "In these temporal laws, although men judge about them when they establish them, yet once they have been instituted and confirmed, it is not lawful for a judge to judge about them, but according to them." From these words it is understood that laws instituted by men may not be violated at the pleasure even of some judges; and so too rights instituted by men may not be violated at pleasure. From this it further follows that a licence which, under the right of the forum, can be revoked at will by the one who grants it, is by no means to be rejected under the right of the forum. This is especially known to hold true when the one granting the licence is not superior to the one to whom it is granted. This is said of a grant made by one who may revoke a privilege at will; which, although it does not bind the prince, nevertheless with respect to subjects has the force of law. The right of heaven, however, is called natural equity, which, apart from any human and even any divine positive ordinance, agrees with right reason: whether it agrees with right reason purely natural, or with right reason received from those things which have been revealed to us by God. For this reason this right is sometimes called natural right, since all natural right belongs to the right of heaven. Sometimes it is called divine right, because many things agree with right reason both by natural right and by divine right. Thus it agrees with right reason, received from things to be believed, that preachers of the Gospel, at least those who have no other means of support, be sustained by the goods of those to whom they preach. Yet this cannot be proved by reason purely natural, just as it cannot be sufficiently proved by such reason that what they preach is true, useful and necessary to those to whom they preach.

units.la: Secundo dicunt isti, quod appellans & iste impugnatus, cum altercantur an vsus rerum absq; iure vtendi posset esse licitus? loquuntur de iure fori, quod enim sic loquatur appellans, constat: & ipse concedit, quod vero sic loquatur iste impugnatus, constat ex hoc, quod ipse loquitur in hac parte de iure vtendi illo modo, quo loquitur Nicolaus tertius in decretali sua Exiit: cum dicit, quod in rebus temporalibus est considerare proproprietatem, possessionem, vsumfructum, ius utendi, & simplicem facti vsum, & cum dicit: qui inquâ vsus nõ iuris, sed facti tantùmodo nomen habens: quod facti est tantùmodo in vtendo prabet vtentib. nihil iuris, quod n. sic loquatur, sicut prædicti, manifeste patet exc. 61. & 60. & 31. & 32. & 37. & 41. & 55. & 58. & 69. sed prædicti loquuntur de iure utendi, quod est de iure fori. Quod n. impugnatores prædicti istius loquântur de tali iure, constat aperte: quia loquuntur de iure, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare, tale autem ius est de iure fori, ergo &c. quod etiâ Nicolaus loquatur de tali iure in prædictis verbis patet: quia negàs Fratrib. ius utendi, non negat eis iuspoli: sed expressè côcedit, ergo ibi non loquitur de iure poli, sed de iure fori. Constat ergo quod verba istius impugnati de iure fori debent intelligi. Neq; n. aliter impugnatores, quibus respondet in constitutione quia quorundam, neq; appellante praefatum, neq; Fratres Minores dicentes se nihil iuris habere in his, quibus vtuntur, nisi sophistice, reprobare: quia omnes prædicti intelligunt de iure utendi, quod ad ius fori pertinere dignoscitur.
units.tr: Second, they say that the appellant and the man attacked, when they dispute whether the use of things could be lawful without a right of use, speak of the right of the forum. That the appellant speaks so is plain, and he himself concedes it. That the man attacked speaks so is clear from the fact that in this part he speaks of the right of use in the sense in which Nicholas III speaks in his decretal Exiit, when he says that in temporal things one must consider ownership, possession, usufruct, the right of use, and the simple use of fact, and when he says: "that use which bears only the name of fact, not of right, which in using gives nothing of right to those who use it." That the aforesaid speak in this way is clearly shown in exc. 61. & 60. & 31. & 32. & 37. & 41. & 55. & 58. & 69. But the aforesaid speak of the right of use, which belongs to the right of the forum. That the opponents speak of such a right is plain, because they speak of the right by which one may litigate in court, and such a right belongs to the right of the forum. That Nicholas too speaks of such a right in the aforesaid words is shown by the fact that, in denying the Friars the right of use, he does not deny them the right of heaven but expressly concedes it. Therefore there he speaks not of the right of heaven but of the right of the forum. It is therefore clear that the words of this man attacked must be understood of the right of the forum. For otherwise the opponents, to whom he replies in the constitution Quia quorundam, would not refute either the appellant or the Friars Minor, who say that they have no right in those things they use, except sophistically. All the aforesaid understand it of the right of use, which is known to pertain to the right of the forum.

units.la: Tertio ostendunt, quomodo res temporales dicuntur diuersimode esse diuersorum, dicentes, quod res temporales dicuntur esse aliquorum ex meriti dignitate: & isto modo omnia sunt iustorum: hoc est iusti digni sunt omnia possidere: & isto modo nulla res temporalis est impii: quia impius nõ est dignus etiâ pane quo vescitur: & ideo quia Deus ola fecit propter iustos, dicitur qp aliquo mô ola sunt iusto. ú ex iure diuino, sicut dicit August. ad Vincentium, ut habetur 24. q. 7. c. 1. quamuis res quaecunque terrena non recte à quoquam possideri possit, nisi vel iure diuino quo cuncta sunt, &c. hoc est, quib. iusti sunt soli digni. Aliter dicunt temporalia esse aliquorum ex debiti necessitate vel etiâ honestate, quia sc. eis ex ratione recta debentur, & isto modo superflua diuitum sunt pauperum & indigentium: quia sc. diuites tenentur eis superflua elargiri, & sic intelligenda sunt verba Ambrosii, quae ponuntur 67. di. c. sicut ii, cum dicit: Esurientium panis est quem tu detines: nudorum vestimentum est, quod tu recludis: miserorû redemptio est pecunia quam tu in terra defodis. In his verbis etiam bona ecclesiae dicuntur esse pauperum, & quę sic dicuntur esse aliquorum, possunt dici eorum ex iure diuino: quia per ius diuinum tenentur eorum possessores ea talib. indigentibus exhibere. Tertio dicuntur temporalia esse aliquorum iure poli, & simul quandoq; iure fori & côscientia bona, & sic res, quib. quis vitur in articulo necessitatis extremae, sunt illius siue sint illius iure fori, siue non. Quarto dicuntur res esse aliquorum sinceritate conscientiae: & sic res temporales dicuntur esse illorum, qui non ex auaritia, nec intentione mala, sed ratione moti res tales habere noscuntur, nõ sunt aũt illorum isto modo, qui eas ex auaritia vel mala intentione detinent: & sic dicit Ambros. vbi prius: Sed ait auarus, quid iniustum est, si cum aliena non inuadam, propria diligentius seruo? O impudens, dic tu, quid propria dicis, quae ex quibus reconditis in hunc mundum detulisti? & infra. Proprium nemo dicat, quod est commune: plus sufficeret sumptui, & violenter obtentum est, & infra: quis tam iniustus, tam auarus, quam qui multorum alimenta non suum vsum sed abundantiam & delitias facit? Quinto dicuntur aliqua temporalia esse aliquorum ex iure fori tantummodo, & iste modus in multos diuiditur: quia aliqua ex iure fori sunt aliquorum vel quo ad proprietatem & dominium, vel quo ad vsum nudum, vel quo ad vsumfructum vel forsitan aliis modis, & isto modo possunt aliqua esse aliquorum, licet non sint illorum aliquo quatuor prædictorum modorum, unde & auari multa habet iure fori, quibus sunt indigni, nec eis debentur, sed aliis, & quae non ex conscientia recta, sed auaritia sola sibi retentant. Ex his patet, quod diuersi diuersimode noscuntur temporalia possidere, quidam enim possident temporalia iure fori: sicut illi, qui tempore necessitatis extremę res possident temporales, quibus vtuntur: quidam possident conscientia bona: quidam autem nullo iure, nec conscientia bona possident temporalia, sicut tyranni, vsurarii, & alii iniuste temporalia possidentes.
units.tr: Thirdly, they show how temporal goods are said to belong to different people in different ways. Some say that temporal goods belong to certain people by reason of the worth of their merit, and in this sense all things belong to the just: that is, the just alone are worthy to possess everything. In this sense no temporal good belongs to the impious, since the impious man is not worthy even of the bread he eats. And because God made all things for the sake of the just, all things are said in some way to belong to the just, and this by divine right, as Augustine says to Vincentius, as found in 24. q. 7. c. 1: although no earthly thing can rightly be possessed by anyone, unless either by divine right, by which all things are, etc.; that is, the just alone are worthy of them. In another way, temporal goods are said to belong to certain people by the necessity of debt or even of decency, because they are due to them by right reason, and in this sense the superfluous goods of the rich belong to the poor and the needy, since the rich are bound to hand over their superfluities to them. In this way the words of Ambrose, found in 67. d. c. Sicut ii, are to be understood, where he says: The bread that you hold back belongs to the hungry; the clothing that you lock away belongs to the naked; the money that you bury in the earth is the ransom of the wretched. In these words the goods of the Church are also said to be the poor's, and things said in this way to belong to certain people can be said to be theirs by divine right, because by divine right their possessors are bound to supply them to such needy people. Thirdly, temporal goods are said to belong to certain people by the right of heaven, and at the same time sometimes by the right of the forum and by a good conscience; and so the goods which a person uses in the article of extreme necessity are his, whether or not they are his by the right of the forum. Fourthly, things are said to belong to certain people by the sincerity of conscience; and in this sense temporal goods are said to belong to those who hold such things not from avarice or evil intent, but moved by reason; they do not belong in this sense to those who hold them from avarice or evil intent. So Ambrose says in the place cited above: But the avaricious man says, what is unjust about it, if I do not invade what belongs to others, but take more careful care of what is my own? O shameless man, tell me, what do you call your own? What did you bring into this world from the hidden places? And below: Let no one call his own what is common; it would have sufficed for expense, and it has been seized by force; and below: who is so unjust, so avaricious, as the one who makes the sustenance of many not his use but his abundance and luxuries? Fifthly, some temporal goods are said to belong to certain people by the right of the forum alone, and this mode divides into many kinds: for some things belong by the right of the forum to certain people either as to ownership and dominion, or as to bare use, or as to usufruct, or perhaps in other ways; and in this sense some things can belong to certain people even though they are not theirs in any of the four aforesaid ways. Hence the avaricious man also holds many things by the right of the forum, for which he is unworthy and which are not due to him but to others, and which he keeps for himself not from right conscience but from avarice alone. From these things it is clear that different people hold temporal goods in different ways: some possess temporal goods by the right of the forum, such as those who in a time of extreme necessity possess the temporal goods which they use; some possess them with a good conscience; but some possess temporal goods by no right and with no good conscience, such as tyrants, usurers, and others who possess temporal goods unjustly.

units.la: Quarto replicant distinctionem quandam de iustitia & iusto & iuste, quia quaedam est iustitia particularis distincta contra alias virtutes: quaedam est iustitia legalis: alia est iustitia qua operatio recta rationi conformatur, & sic dicitur proportionabiliter actus iustus vel iniustus tripliciter: & aliquid dicitur tripliciter iniuste fieri vel etiam iuste.
units.tr: Fourthly, they repeat a certain distinction concerning justice, the just, and justly: for there is a particular justice, distinct from the other virtues; there is legal justice; and there is another justice, by which an action is conformed to right reason. And thus an act is called just or unjust in three ways, and something is said to be done unjustly or even justly in three ways.

units.la: Quinto per prædicta isti impugnatores respondent ad formã argumenti istius impugnati dicentes, quod cum accipitur haec propositio: Iste cui vtendi re aliqua licentia est concessa (quia scilicet non est ius) aut iuste vtitur, aut iniuste, aut neque iuste, neque iniuste. Dicunt, quod si accipiatur primo modo, secundum quod aliquid dicitur fieri iuste, quia sit à iustitia particulari, quae est distincta virtus contra alias virtutes: sic neque vtitur iuste neque iniuste: quia sic accipiendo iustitiam & iustum multi sunt actus etiam meritorii & demeritorii, qui nec sunt iusti vel iniusti: licet sint boni vel mali, & laudabiles vel vituperabiles: quia etiam actus castitatis sic neque est iustus, neq; iniustus. Si autem accipiatur iuste tertio modo, sic dicunt, quod vtitur iuste re, cuius habet licentiam vtendi, quia vtitur conformiter rationi rectae, & ideo concedunt quod vtitur iure: non quidem iure fori, sed iure poli. Qu'a omne quod rede absq; iure fori fit, iure poli fit, vnde sic iure facere, nõ est aliud quam bene moraliter facere. Et iure vti est bene moraliter vti, sicut iure possidere est bene moraliter possidere. Sed forte dicet aliquis, qp talis non vtitur iure poli re sibi concessa, sicut nec possidet iure poli: quia nemo vtitur re aliqua iure poli, nisi qui re tali vtitur tempore necessitatis extremae, quod Nicolaus Tertius videtur innuere, cum dicit in decretali Exiit: Et quidem vbi dicit, quod non est aliqualiter praesumendum, quod haec cuncta deficerent, sicut nec caeteris, sic nec ipsis Fratribus iure poli in extrema necessitatis articulo, ad providendum sustentationi naturae via extrema necessitate detentis concessa non praecluditur. Ex quibus verbis insinuari videtur, quod nemini licet vti rebus iure poli, nisi sit in extremae necessitatis articulo constitutus. Ad hoc dicunt, quod licet Nicolaus dicat, quod licet omnibus in extremae necessitatis articulo constitutis vti rebus necessariis ad sustentationem naturæ iure poli: non tamen negat aliquos posse in aliis casibus uti rebus iure poli. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, uti cp temporalibus rebus pertinet ad ius naturæ, cui nemo licite renunciare potest: non tamen sic pertinet ad ius naturale, quin possit in multis casibus limitari, & quodammodo coartari, & ne in actum licite exeat impediri: quemadmodum secundum Isidorum, ut habetur distinction. prim. ius naturale, communis omnium possessio & omnium una libertas ad ius pertinet naturale: & tamen istud ius quodammodo coartatur: quia & temporalia appropriantur, & multi seruituti subduntur: non tamen istud ius naturale potest taliter euacuari, quia nunquam sic possunt temporalia appropriari, quin tempore necessitatis debeant esse communia: sic posse uti temporalib. potest per legem humanam & voluntatem propriam liberi hominis quodammodo coartari, & aliqui ne in actum utendi exeat impediri, sic n. potest aliquis voto firmare, quod à carnib. abstinebit: sicut etiam homines prohibentur uti rebus alienis: posse tñ uti temporalib. temporaliter euelli nō potest. & ideo iure poli potest quilibet uti re temporali quacunque, qua uti neq; iure naturæ, neq; iure humano, neq; iure diuino, neq; facto proprio prohibetur, & ideo tempore necessitatis extremæ potest quilibet iure poli uti qualibet re temporali, qñ aliter vitam suā conseruare non posset: quia ad non utendū re temporali in hoc casu neq; iure quocunq; neq; facto proprio obligatur, vbi aūt uti aliqua re temporali determinata aliquis p hoc solummodo impeditur, quia res illa est aliena, eo cp nullus re aliena, in qua nullū ius habet præter ius naturale, extra casum necessitatis extremæ uti debet, ipso inuito, cuius est res illa: sola pmissio illius, cuius est res, quæ p licentiā declaratur, sufficit ad hoc, cp iure poli utatur eadē re. Per permissionē aūt, & p consequens per licentiā solummō remouetur impedimentū prohibens habeti ius naturale utendi, ne exeat in actū utendi, & nullū ius nouum sibi cōfert, ergo talis sic permissus seu licentiatus iure poli poterit uti re illa, quæ est aliena. Illud etiā, sc. cp tali licentiato nullū ius nouum confertur, tali ratione probatur. Omne ius vel est diuinū vel humanum. Et si humanū, vel est naturale & poli, vel est ius positiuū & fori, sed per talem permissionē seu licentiam constat, cp non cōfertur ius diuinū, nec ius poli siue naturale, ergo si cōfertur aliquod ius habenti licentiā, tale ius pertinet ad ius fori, ergo talis vteretur re illa iure fori: cp constat esse falsum. Quia p omne ius fori potest quis in iudicio litigare, talis aūt nō habet aliquod ius, quo valeat in iudicio litigare, ergo non vtitur re illa iure fori, vtitur ergo solūmodo iure poli. Tunc tñ primo, qñ licentiatus seu permissus vtitur licite iure poli tali re & nō prius: quia modo est amotū prohibens ius naturale: ne exiret in actū utendi, cp ante amotum minime fuit. Et ex quo patet, cp Fratres Minores, si non habēt ius positiuum in reb. cōmune sibi & omnibus aliis fidelibus quibuscunq; reb. licite vtuntur iure poli: & non iure fori, vtuntur quantumcunq; sint extra articulū necessitatis extremæ: quia iure utendi naturali renunciare non possunt, possunt n. voto firmare, cp nullam rem propriā nec aliquod ius proprium in temporalib. volunt habere. Et ideo iure fori nulla re uti possunt, quia si re aliena uti debeat, oportet remouere prohibens quod per permissionē seu licentiam ius, ad quem spectat permittere vel dare licentiam, amouetur: quo amoto, iure poli possunt in actum. Si autem vtuntur re aliqua, quæ occupanti conceditur, vel pro derelicta habentur, vtuntur ipsa iure poli: quia respectu talis rei nullum est impedimentum prohibens ne ius naturale utendi in eis exiret in actum utendi.
units.tr: Fifthly, by these things the aforesaid opponents answer the form of the argument of this opponent, saying that when this proposition is taken: He to whom permission to use some thing has been granted (since it is not a right) either uses it justly, or unjustly, or neither justly nor unjustly. They say that if it is taken in the first sense, according to which something is said to be done justly because it proceeds from particular justice, which is a virtue distinct from the other virtues, then he uses it neither justly nor unjustly; for taking justice and the just in this way, there are many acts, even meritorious and demeritorious ones, which are neither just nor unjust, though they may be good or evil, and praiseworthy or blameworthy; for even an act of chastity is in this way neither just nor unjust. But if it is taken in the third sense, that he uses justly, they say that he uses justly the thing for which he has permission to use, because he uses it in conformity with right reason; and so they concede that he uses it by right, not indeed by the right of the forum, but by the right of heaven. For whatever is done rightly, apart from the right of the forum, is done by the right of heaven; so to act by right is nothing other than to act well morally; and to use by right is to use well morally, just as to possess by right is to possess well morally. But perhaps someone will say that such a person does not use by the right of heaven the thing granted to him, any more than he possesses it by the right of heaven: since no one uses any thing by the right of heaven unless he uses such a thing in a time of extreme necessity, which Pope Nicholas III seems to hint at when he says in the decretal Exiit: and indeed where he says that it is not to be presumed in any way that all these things would fail, just as they would not fail for the others, so neither is the way of extreme necessity, granted to the Friars by the right of heaven in the article of extreme necessity to provide for the sustenance of nature, shut off to them. From these words it seems to be implied that no one is permitted to use things by the right of heaven unless he is placed in the article of extreme necessity. To this they reply that although Nicholas says that all who are placed in the article of extreme necessity may use things necessary for the sustenance of nature by the right of heaven, he does not deny that some may use things by the right of heaven in other cases. To make this clear, they say it must be known that temporal things belong to the natural law, from which no one can lawfully renounce; yet they do not so belong to the natural law that in many cases they cannot be limited and in some measure restricted, and prevented from lawfully passing into act: just as, according to Isidore, as found in Dist. 1, Ius naturale, the common possession of all and the one freedom of all belong to the natural law; and yet that right is in some measure restricted, because temporal goods are appropriated and many are subjected to servitude; yet that natural right cannot be so emptied out, because temporal goods can never be appropriated in such a way that in a time of necessity they do not have to be common. So too the power to use temporal goods can be in some measure restricted by human law and the free man's own will, and some are prevented from passing into the act of using; for a man may bind himself by vow that he will abstain from meat, just as men are forbidden to use the goods of others; but the power to use temporal goods cannot be utterly uprooted. Therefore by the right of heaven anyone may use any temporal thing whatever, which he is forbidden to use neither by natural right, nor by human right, nor by divine right, nor by his own act; and so in a time of extreme necessity anyone may use by the right of heaven any temporal thing whatever, when he could not otherwise preserve his life; for in this case he is bound by no right whatever, nor by his own act, not to use a temporal thing. But where someone is prevented from using a particular temporal thing only for this reason, that the thing is another's, since no one should use a thing belonging to another, over which he has no right except natural right, outside the case of extreme necessity, against the will of its owner, the permission of the owner alone, declared by licence, suffices for him to use the same thing by the right of heaven. Now permission, and consequently licence, removes only the impediment preventing the natural right to use from passing into the act of using, and it confers no new right; therefore one so permitted or licensed will be able to use by the right of heaven that thing which belongs to another. That to the licensed person no new right is conferred is proved by this reasoning: every right is either divine or human; and if human, it is either natural and of heaven, or it is positive and of the forum; but it is evident from such permission or licence that neither divine right nor the right of heaven, that is natural right, is conferred; therefore if some right is conferred on the one who has licence, that right belongs to the right of the forum, and therefore he would use that thing by the right of the forum; which is manifestly false. For by any right of the forum one can litigate in court; but such a person has no right by which he can litigate in court; therefore he does not use that thing by the right of the forum, but only by the right of heaven. Yet he uses it lawfully by the right of heaven only from the first moment when the licensed or permitted person uses such a thing, and not before; for only now has the impediment preventing natural right from passing into the act of using been removed, which it was not before. And from this it is clear that the Friars Minor, if they have no positive right in things common to them and to all other faithful, lawfully use all things by the right of heaven and not by the right of the forum, and they use them however far they are from the article of extreme necessity; for they cannot renounce the natural right of using, since they can bind themselves by vow that they wish to have no private thing nor any private right in temporal goods. Therefore they can use no thing by the right of the forum; for if they ought to use a thing belonging to another, it is necessary to remove the impediment, namely the right by which permission or licence is given, to which it belongs to permit or grant licence, and when that is removed, they can pass into the act by the right of heaven. But if they use some thing which is granted to an occupant, or is held to be abandoned, they use it by the right of heaven; for with respect to such a thing there is no impediment preventing the natural right to use from passing into the act of using.

units.la: (Qui sine iure vtitur iuste vtitur.) Hic supponit iste impugnatus, quod aliquis potest uti re aliqua sine iure, quod de iure fori debet intelligi: quia sine iure omni naturali non potest uti re aliqua, cum ius naturale omnib. sit commune di.1. ius naturale. Et ita constat, cp iste impugnatus loquitur de iure fori (si dicat cp iuste vtatur sequitur per consequens quod & iure) verū est, cp sequitur, cp vtitur iure poli vel iure fori (quia quod iuste fit, fit & iure) verum est, quod fit iure poli vel iure fori, sed non oportet, cp semper fiat iure fori (ext. de verborū significatione c. Ius dictum est & 14. q. 4. c. quid dicam.) Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod quia verba in prædictis capitulis, in quibus iste se fundat, obscura videtur, volunt ea adducere in medium, & qualiter debent intelligi explicare, quæ sunt hæc. Hoc enim iure possidetur, quod iuste: hoc iuste, quod bene. Ex quibus verbis insinuatur duæ propositiones videl. quod omne quod bene possidetur, iuste possidetur: & omne quod iuste possidetur, iure possidetur, ex quib. sequi videtur, cp omnis, qui bene vtitur re aliqua, iure vtitur eadē re: & ita bonus usus utendi à iure utendi separari nō potest, sed dicunt isti, cp prædicta capitula loquuntur disiunctiue vel æquipollenter de iure poli & de iure fori. Ius aūt poli nō est aliud, q̄ potestas conformis rationi rectæ; absq; pactione. Ius fori est potestas ex pactione, aliqn conformi rationi rectæ: & aliquando discordanti. Nullus autem bene possidet rem aliq̄, nisi secundum rationem rectam eam possideat, & ita qui possidet bene iure poli vel iure fori possidet, sed non omnis qui iure fori possidet, bene possidet. Ex quo sequitur, quod prędicta verba de iure fori non possunt intelligi, quia multa possidentur iure fori, quæ nō bene possidentur, & multa possidentur bene, quæ nō possidentur iure fori. Quod n. multa posideantur iure fori, quæ nō bene posidentur, patet de multis, quę iure posidētur, quibus tñ male vtuntur: & p consequēs nō bene posident, teste Aug. qui i. c. allegato, quid dicā, ait: Male aūt possidet, qui male vtitur, & Isidor. i. c. allegato iu dictū, ait: Male aūt possidet qui vel suis male vtitur, vel aliena præsumit. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod nonnulli propriā rem male possident: & per consequens multa posidentur iure fori, quæ tñ male possidentur. Quod etiā multa bene posideantur, quæ iure fori minime posidentur, patet, quia qui legitime præscribit rem alienā, ante præscriptionem cōpletam bene posidet: & tñ ante præscriptionem cōpletam nullo iure fori posidet, ergo multa bene posidētur, quę tamen nullo iure fori posidentur, non ergo prædicta capitula loquuntur tñ de iure fori, sed etiā de iure poli, & ita ex eis concludi nō potest, quod qui vtitur re aliena licentia alterius, vtitur iure fori, sed sufficit quod vtatur iure poli. Appellans autem probans, quod vsus licitus potest à iure vtendi separari, non loquitur de iure poli, sed de iure fori, sicut saepe explicat manifeste, quare argumentum praedictum contra appellantem in nihilo concludit (nec iuste vtatur nec iniuste.) Sed iuste & iniuste accipiatur primo modo, non est inconveniens, unde sic accipiendo qui dat alicui rem aliquam ex libertate non ex debito aliquo, nec dat iuste nec iniuste: quia non tenetur sibi dare: & ideo non exercet actu iustitiae particularis sed liberalitatis: nec tenetur non dare: & ideo non dat iuste. Accipiendo tamen iuste & iniuste tertio modo, sic non est concedendum, quod nec vtatur iuste nec iniuste (nec bonum nec malum) hoc concedunt sine distinctione (nec iustum nec iniustum) hoc concedunt in uno sensu, & in alio negant: sicut ex praedictis apparet. (Oportet quod si finis actus sit bonus, quod & ipse actus sit bonus.) Dicunt isti, quod quia iste in difficultatibus Theologicis minime est instructus, de quibus tamen se temerarie intromittit: ideo de hoc dicto eius, & de hoc quod dicit de obiecto voluntatis pertranseunt.
units.tr: (He who uses without right uses justly.) Here the author under attack assumes that someone can use a thing without right, which must be understood of right in the sense of civil law (ius fori): for without any natural right one cannot use a thing at all, since natural right is common to all (Distinction 1, "ius naturale"). It is thus plain that the author under attack speaks of right in the sense of civil law. (If he says that one uses justly, it follows consequently that one uses by right too.) It is true that whatever is done justly is done by right, whether by natural right or by civil right; but it does not follow that it is always done by civil right (Extra, "De verborum significatione," chapter "Ius dictum est"; and 14, q. 4, chapter "Quid dicam"). These objectors say that, because the words in the aforesaid chapters, on which he rests his case, seem obscure, they wish to bring them into the open and explain how they should be understood. They are these: "For that is held by right which is held justly; that is held justly which is held well." From these words two propositions are implied: first, that everything held well is held justly; and second, that everything held justly is held by right. From these it seems to follow that everyone who uses a thing well uses that same thing by right; and so good use cannot be separated from the right of using. But these objectors say that the aforesaid chapters speak disjunctively, or equivalently, of natural right and of civil right. Now natural right is nothing other than a power in accordance with right reason, apart from any agreement; civil right is a power arising from agreement, sometimes in accordance with right reason, and sometimes at odds with it. No one holds a thing well unless he holds it in accordance with right reason; so whoever holds it well holds it by natural right or by civil right, but not everyone who holds it by civil right holds it well. From this it follows that the aforesaid words cannot be understood of civil right, since many things are held by civil right that are not held well, and many things are held well that are not held by civil right. That many things are held by civil right which are not held well is plain from many things that are held by right, yet are used badly, and so are not held well; as Augustine, in the chapter cited, "Quid dicam," says: "He who uses badly holds badly"; and Isidore, in the chapter cited above, says: "He holds badly who either uses his own things badly or presumes upon what is another's." From these words it is clearly gathered that some men hold their own property badly; and consequently many things are held by civil right which are nonetheless held badly. That also many things are held well which are not held at all by civil right is plain, because one who lawfully prescribes another's property holds it well before the prescription is complete, and yet before the prescription is complete he holds it by no civil right; therefore many things are held well which nonetheless are held by no civil right. The aforesaid chapters, then, do not speak only of civil right but also of natural right, and so it cannot be concluded from them that one who uses another's property with another's permission uses it by civil right; it is enough that he uses it by natural right. But the appellant, in proving that lawful use can be separated from the right of using, does not speak of natural right but of civil right, as he often explains plainly; wherefore the aforesaid argument against the appellant concludes nothing. (Neither does he use justly nor unjustly.) But if "just" and "unjust" are taken in the first sense, there is no inconsistency: taking them so, one who gives someone a thing out of liberality, and not from any debt, neither gives justly nor unjustly; for he is not bound to give it to him, and so he does not exercise the act of particular justice but of liberality; nor is he bound not to give, and so he does not give unjustly. Taking "just" and "unjust" in the third sense, however, it must not be conceded that he uses neither justly nor unjustly. (Neither good nor evil.) These they concede without distinction. (Neither just nor unjust.) These they concede in one sense and deny in the other, as appears from what has been said. (It must be that if the end of an act is good, the act itself is good too.) These objectors say that, since he is not at all instructed in theological difficulties, in which he nonetheless rashly meddles, they pass over this saying of his, and what he says about the object of the will.

units.la: CAP. LXVI.
units.tr: CHAP. LXVI.

units.la: NEc obstat, si dicatur, quod imo Isidorus inter iustum & iniustum ponere medium fas videtur, dicens quod ire per agrum alienum fas est: ius non est. Isidorus enim divisit legem in divinam & humanam: & imposuerat nomina istis legibus dicens: quod fas lex divina est, ius lex humana. Unde volens de his exemplum dare, subiunxit: ire per agrum alienum fas est, id est de iure divino licitum est: ius non est: id est de iure humano non licet: ut patet dist. 1. c. omnes leges. Non ergo voluit Isidorus inter iustum & iniustum, fas pro medio ponere: sed declarare, quod aliquid de iure divino licet, quod de iure humano non licet.
units.tr: Nor is it an objection if someone says that Isidore does seem to place something between the just and the unjust, when he says that it is fas to go through another's field, but it is not ius. For Isidore divided law into divine and human, and he gave these laws names, saying that fas is divine law and ius is human law. So, wishing to give an example of these, he added: it is fas to go through another's field, that is, it is permitted by divine law; it is not ius, that is, it is not allowed by human law. See dist. 1, c. Omnes leges. Isidore therefore did not mean to set fas as a mean between the just and the unjust, but to show that something is permitted by divine law which is not permitted by human law.

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnatus respondet ad quandam obiectionem, quae posset fieri contra rationem praedictam: contra hoc quod sc. accipit, quod non est medium inter actum iustum & iniustum: & est talis. Secundum Isidor. transfire per agrum alienum fas est, ius non est: ergo nec est iustum, quia ius non est: nec est iniustum, quia fas est: & ita est aliquod medium inter iustum & iniustum. Ad quam respondet dicens, quod Isidor. per verba illa non intendit dicere, quod aliquis actus est medius inter iustum & iniustum: sed quod aliquid est licitum de iure divino, quod non est licitum de iure humano.
units.tr: In this part the author under attack answers an objection that could be raised against the foregoing argument, namely against his claim that there is no mean between a just and an unjust act. The objection runs as follows: according to Isidore, to pass through another's field is fas, it is not ius. Therefore it is not just, because it is not ius, and it is not unjust, because it is fas; and so there is some mean between the just and the unjust. To this he replies that Isidore did not intend by those words to say that some act is intermediate between the just and the unjust, but that something is permitted by divine law which is not permitted by human law.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores, quia hanc obiectionem ad istam quaestionem non faciunt, circa ipsam non multum instant. Dicunt tamen, quod per verba Isidori praedicta bene probatur, quod accipiendo ius, sicut appellans accepit, cum dicit, vsum licitum posse separari à iure vtendi: quia ipse accepit ibi ius vtendi pro iure fori, aliquis actus est bonus & licitus sine iure tali: quia transire per agrum alienum non est ius: & tamen est licitum, ergo aliquis actus est licitus sine iure tali: & eadem ratione potest actus vtendi esse licitus sine iure vtendi.
units.tr: But these critics, since the objection does not bear on the present question, do not press it much. Yet they say that the words of Isidore cited above do prove well that, taking ius in the sense in which the appellant took it when he said a lawful use can be separated from the right of using, an act can be good and lawful without such a right. For he there took the right of using to mean the right of the court; passing through another's field is not a ius, and yet it is lawful; therefore some act is lawful without such a right; and by the same reasoning an act of using can be lawful without a right of using.

units.la: (Inter iustum & iniustum ponere medium fas videtur.) Dicunt isti, quod fas non est medium inter iustum & iniustum, etiam primo modo accipiendo iustum & iniustum: quia saepe fas est iustum etiam primo modo accipiendo iustum. Nam multa sunt iusta iure fori: tamen inter iustum & iniustum illo modo accepta, est aliquod aliud medium, saltem per abnegationem, quia actus aliarum virtutum & aliorum vitiorum ab iniustitia oppositá iustitiae particulari nec sunt iusti nec iniusti: illo modo inter iustum etiam & iniustum tertio modo dicta est medium per abnegationem, licet n. omnis actus vel malus vel bonus necessario comprehenditur sub iusto vel iniusto illo modo dictis: tamen quidam alii actus nec sunt iusti nec iniusti. Nam actus non vtentium ratione nec sunt iusti nec iniusti & tertio modo accipiendo iustum & iniustum. (Ire per agrum alienum fas est.) Proprie loquendo aliud est ire per agrum alienum, aliud non prohibere aliquem ire per agrum: & utrumque; in casu sub fas poterit comprehendi: & tamen utrumque potest ad iustitiam etiam particularem spectare (fas lex divina est) Isidorus dicit, quod omne, quod fas est, nomine divinae vel naturalis legis accipiatur. Omne tamen quod fas est, etiam lex divina poterit appellari, inquantum per legem divinam, omne quod fas est saltem in genere fieri mandatur (fas est) id est de iure divino licitum est: imo praeceptum, si innoxius est transitus quia de iure naturali, quod est immutabile, est quod vbi aliquid mihi prodest, & alteri non nocet, aequum est, ut me non prohibeas: licet ius fori ibi deficiat, nec per legem humanam potest statui contrarium, quod lex iniqua esset, & contra ordinem caritatis & contra doctrinam Christi dicentis Matth. 7. Omnia ergo quaecunque vultis ut faciant vobis homines: ita & vos facite illis, hoc est enim lex & prophetae, verumtamen multa videntur in multis casibus non nocere alicui & alicui prodesse, quae per legem humanam expedit prohiberi: quia si non prohiberentur saepe & communitati & personis obessent, talibus tamen prohibitis generaliter vtendum est saepe (Aliquid de iure divino licet, quod de iure humano non licet.) Magis proprie dixisset, aliquid non est de iure divino illicitum, quod est de iure humano illicitum, refert enim dicere affirmatiue aliquid de iure divino, licet & dicere negatiue: aliquid non est de iure divino illicitum, quod est illicitum de iure humano, sed quia, ut dicunt isti impugnatores, iste impugnatus diversitatem modorum loquendi ignorat, sicut & quamplurimi alii, ideo circa hoc diutius nolunt insistere.
units.tr: (It seems that fas is a mean between the just and the unjust.) These critics say that fas is not a mean between the just and the unjust, even taking the just and the unjust in the first sense, because very often what is fas is just even when the just is taken in the first sense. For many things are just by the right of the court; yet between the just and the unjust, taken in that sense, there is some other mean, at least by negation, since acts of the other virtues and of the other vices, which are opposed to particular justice as injustice, are neither just nor unjust. In that way too, between the just and the unjust taken in a third sense, there is a mean by negation; for although every act, whether good or bad, is necessarily included under the just or unjust in the senses mentioned, yet some other acts are neither just nor unjust. For acts of those who do not use reason are neither just nor unjust, taking the just and the unjust in the third sense. (To go through another's field is fas.) Properly speaking, it is one thing to go through another's field, and another not to forbid someone to go through the field; both can, in the case, come under fas, and yet both can relate even to particular justice. (Fas is divine law.) Isidore says that whatever is fas is understood under the name of divine or natural law. Yet whatever is fas may also be called divine law, insofar as by divine law whatever is fas is commanded to be done at least in general. (Fas is) that is, it is permitted by divine law; indeed it is even commanded, if the passage is harmless. For by natural law, which is unchangeable, it is fair that where something benefits me and does no harm to another, you do not forbid me; although the right of the court fails there, and no contrary can be established by human law, since such a law would be unjust and against the order of charity and against the teaching of Christ, who says in Matt. 7: Therefore whatever you want men to do to you, do so to them, for this is the law and the prophets. Yet in many cases it often seems that many things do no harm to one person and benefit another, though human law finds it expedient to forbid them; for if they were not forbidden, they would often be harmful both to the community and to individuals; yet with such things forbidden, one must often generally refrain. (Something is permitted by divine law which is not permitted by human law.) The author would have spoken more properly if he had said: something that is unlawful by human law is not unlawful by divine law; for it makes a difference whether one says affirmatively that something is permitted by divine law, or says negatively that something is not unlawful by divine law though it is unlawful by human law. But because, as these critics say, the author under attack is ignorant of the difference between modes of speaking, as are very many others, they are unwilling to dwell on this point at greater length.

units.la: CAP. LXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXVII.

units.la: ADhuc iste haereticus dictam constitutionem satagit impugnare in eo, quod probare intendens, quod simplex vsus, id est sine iure vtendi à proprietate seu dominio separatus in re vsu consumptibili haberi non potest, sic dicit: Praeterea quod simplex vsus, id est sine iure vtendi à proprietate seu dominio separatus in re vsu consumptibilium habere nequeat, sic probatur, si enim haberi posset vsus talis, aut ante ipsum actum, aut in ipso actu, aut post actum completum huiusmodi haberetur, quod autem fieri nequeat, ex hoc patet, quia quod non est, nequaquam haberi potest. Patet aut, quod actus ipse antequam exerceatur, aut etiam dum exercetur, aut postquam perfectus est in rerum natura non est, ex quo sequitur quod haberi minime potest. Licet enim ante actum ipsum, quis facultatem habeat ipsum exercendi: per hoc tamen actus ipse in rerum natura, nisi in potentia, non existit, cum autem actus est in fieri, nec adhuc est in rerum natura, cum esse rem perfectam significet: quod quamdiu est in fieri, non potest actui convenire. Quod enim de actu, qui est in fieri, praeteriit, iam non est, quod autem fit, instantaneum seu momentaneum est: & tale quod magis intellectu percipi potest, quam sensu, adhuc post actum completum. licet si ex ipso facto producta res aliqua fuerit, res ipsa haberi valeat: factum tamen ipsum quod iam transiit non habetur.
units.tr: Furthermore, this heretic tries to attack the said constitution on the point where, in order to prove that simple use, that is, use separated from ownership or dominion and from the right of using, cannot be had in a consumable thing, he says: "Moreover, that simple use, that is, use separated from ownership or dominion and from the right of using, cannot be had in consumable things, is proved thus. For if such a use could be had, it would be had either before the act itself, or in the act itself, or after the act has been completed. But that this cannot happen is clear from this, that what does not exist can in no way be had. It is plain that the act itself, before it is exercised, or while it is being exercised, or after it has been completed, is not in the nature of things, and it follows that it can by no means be had. For although someone may have the ability to perform the act before it occurs, the act itself does not exist in the nature of things except potentially. And when the act is in process of becoming, it does not yet exist in the nature of things, since to exist signifies a completed thing; and what is still in process of becoming cannot belong to the act. For what has passed of an act that is in process of becoming no longer exists, and what is done is instantaneous or momentary, and such a thing is perceived more by the intellect than by the senses, even after the act has been completed. Although, if some thing has been produced by the deed itself, that thing can be had, the deed itself, which has already passed, is not had."

units.la: Postquam in parte praecedenti ille impugnatus respondit ad obiectiones appellantis contra tertiam assertionem ipsius: hic respondet ad obiectiones eiusdem appellantis contra quartam assertionem impugnati, quam reputat appellans erroneam. Et dividitur in tres partes: quia primo ponit assertionem impugnatam. Secundo ponit impugnationes eiusdem assertionis. Tertio ad ipsas impugnationes respondet. Secunda pars incipit in parte immediate sequenti. Tertia ibi: Proculdubio ista consequentia. Est igitur assertio impugnata, quod actus vtendi re vsu consumptibili separatus à iure vtendi haberi non potest: quia non potest esse in rerum natura, eo quod nullus actus vtendi potest esse in rerum natura: quia nec ante actum, nec quando actus exercetur, nec post actum completum.
units.tr: After the previous part, that author answered the objections of the appellant against his third assertion; here he answers the appellant's objections against the fourth assertion of the attacked author, which the appellant regards as erroneous. It is divided into three parts: first it sets out the assertion under attack; second, it sets out the objections to that assertion; third, it answers those objections. The second part begins in the immediately following part, and the third there: Doubtless this consequence. The assertion under attack is therefore that the act of using a consumable thing, separated from the right of using, cannot be had, because it cannot exist in the nature of things, since no act of using can exist in the nature of things: neither before the act, nor while the act is being exercised, nor after the act has been completed.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt hic plures errores contineri, quos non solum sicut appellans: sed etiam multis aliis modis satagunt reprobare, & ideo eorum motiva praesentibus duxi inserenda. Dicunt igitur, quod in verbis praemissis quinque continentur errores: quorum primus est, quod simplex vsus, id est sine iure vtendi, à proprietate seu dominio separatus in re vsu consumptibili haberi non possit. Secundus est quod actus ipse, dum exercetur, in rerum natura non est. Tertius est quod actus haberi non potest. Quartus est quod esse solummodo rem perfectam significat. Quintus est quod factum haberi non potest.
units.tr: But these opponents say that several errors are contained in the words quoted, which the appellant and many others try to refute in various ways, and so I have thought fit to insert their arguments here. They say, then, that five errors are contained in the words cited. The first is that simple use, that is, use without the right of using, separated from ownership or dominion, cannot be had in a consumable thing. The second is that the act itself, while it is being exercised, is not in the nature of things. The third is that the act cannot be had. The fourth is that "to be" signifies only a completed thing. The fifth is that the deed cannot be had.

units.la: De primo errore dictum est prius: & etiam quod hoc sit erroneum, ex consequentibus apparebit, ut isti dicunt.
units.tr: Of the first error something has been said already, and it will appear from what follows, as these men say, that this is erroneous.

units.la: Secundus error, ut dicunt, est, quod actus ipse dum exercetur in rerum natura non est, quod autem secundum sit erroneum, multipliciter probare conantur, & primo sic: Si actus dum exercetur non est in rerum natura, hoc non est, nisi quia actus, sc. est successivus, quia hoc sua ratio manifeste declarat. Nam per rationem suam aequaliter oppositum, nullum successivum esse in rerum natura, quod est erroneum, & manifeste Scripturae sacrae repugnat, ergo dicere, quod actus vtendi dum exercetur non est in rerum natura, est erroneum reputandum. Quod autem nullum successivum esse in rerum natura, obviat scripturae divinae: patet aperte. Nam tempus, annus, dies, hora, & huiusmodi sunt successiva: & tamen sunt in rerum natura, scribitur enim Ioh. 13. Cum ergo accepisset ille buccellam, exiit continuo: erat autem nox. Ex quibus verbis constat, quod nox fuit aliquando in rerum natura: & tn nox est quoddam successivum, ergo successivum potest esse in rerum natura. Item quod erit, poterit esse in rerum natura, sed aliquando fuit, & adhuc est verum dicere quod tempus erit. Dicit n. Apostolus 2. Tim. 4. Erit n. tempus, cum sanam doctrinam non sustinebunt, ergo tempus potest esse in rerum natura: & tn est successivum. Item idem Apost. ead. epist. c. 3. ait: In novissimis diebus instabunt tempora periculosa: & per consequens tempora possunt esse in rerum natura. Item Ioh. 10. scribitur: Facta sunt autem encaenia Hierosolymis, & hyems erat. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod hyems aliquando fuit: & per consequens successiva possunt esse in rerum natura, & ita actus potest esse in rerum natura, quia non est maior ratio, quare unum successivum possit esse in rerum natura quam aliud. Item Luc. vlt. dicitur: Super hoc omnia tertia dies est hodie, ergo tertia dies tunc fuit, & ita aliquod successivum potest esse in rerum natura. Item Exo. 12. dicitur: Est enim phase, id est transitus Domini. Iste ergo transitus fuit in rerum natura: & tamen non fuit momentaneus, sed successivus. Non enim omnes primogeniti Aegypti in instanti occidebantur, sed in tempore. Item Cantic. 7. sic dicitur: Quam pulchri sunt gressus tui in calciamentis filia principis. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod gressus etiam corporales pulchri sunt censendi, sed illa, quae non sunt, nec esse possunt, non sunt pulchra, ergo gressus possunt esse in rerum natura: & tamen sunt successivi. Item Gen. 27. dixit Isaac: Vox quidem vox Iacob est, &c. ergo illa vox fuit in rerum natura: & tamen vox est quoddam successivum, ergo successiva possunt esse in rerum natura. Vnde quod successiva fuerunt, sunt, & erunt, & possunt esse in rerum natura, ex locis innumeris scripturae divinae colligitur euidenter, sicut 4. Regum 6. vbi dicitur: Ecce enim sonitus pedum eius post eum est, & 3. Reg. 8. scribitur: Sint sermones mei: isti, &c. & 1. Reg. 20. Ecce Kalendae sunt in crastino, & Ioha. 6. Erat proximum pascha dies festus Iudaeorum. Et quint. cap. Post hoc erat dies festus Iudaeorum, & septim. capitulo. Tempus meum nondum aduenit, tempus autem vestrum semper paratum est, & Matthaei 8. Ecce motus magnus factus est in mari. & Luc. 13. Ecce anni tres sunt, ex quo venio, &c. & Num. 10. Quando autem congregandus est populus, simplex tubarum clangor erit. Ex his aliisque quam pluribus patenter habetur: quod successiva, sicut tempus, motus, voces, sermones, anni, dies, soni, & huiusmodi possunt esse in rerum natura. Secundo per scripturam diuinam probant specialiter, quod actus vtendi, sicut actus comedendi, & huiusmodi possunt esse in rerum natura, nam quod potest dari, potest esse in rerum natura: quia illud, quod nihil est nec esse potest, dari non potest: sed actus vtendi potest dari: teste Moyse, qui, ut habetur Num.11. Num. 11. ait ad Dominum: Sexcenta millia peditum populi huius sunt: & tu dicis, dabo eis esum carnium mense integro. Ex quib. verbis habetur, quod Deus promisit dare populo esum carnis, ergo esus carnium pot esse in rerum natura, hoc confirmatur per istum: quia secundum eum in plurib. locis superius visus potest dari, accipiendo visum etiam pro actu vtendi, ergo visus potest esse in rerum natura. Item Prou. 23. scribitur, noli esse in conuiuiis potatorum nec in comessationib. eorum. Ex quib. verbis colligitur, quod aliquis potest esse in comessationib. potatorum: sed illis quae non possunt esse in rerum natura, non potest aliquis interesse: quia aut interesset eis antequam sint, aut dum sunt, aut postquam sunt per rationem suam. Non antequam sint, nec postquam sunt, certum est: nec dum sunt, quia non sunt secundum istum, ergo illis quae non sunt nec esse possunt, non pot aliquis interesse. Cum ergo aliquis pot interesse comessationib. potatorum, sequitur quod comessationes potatorum possunt esse in rerum natura, sed comessatio intercludit actum comedendi ergo actus coedendi pot esse in rerum natura, hoc etiam eodem modo probat per illud Apost. ad Rom. 13. Non in comessationib. & ebrietatibus.
units.tr: The second error, as they say, is that the act itself, while it is being exercised, is not in the nature of things. They try to prove in many ways that this second point is erroneous, and first as follows: If the act, while it is being exercised, is not in the nature of things, this is so only because the act, namely, is successive, as its very definition plainly declares. For by its definition, the opposite is equally true: that nothing successive can be in the nature of things; and this is erroneous and manifestly contrary to holy Scripture. Therefore to say that the act of using, while it is being exercised, is not in the nature of things must be reckoned erroneous. That nothing successive can be in the nature of things conflicts with divine Scripture is clear enough. For time, year, day, hour and such things are successive, and yet they are in the nature of things, for it is written in John 13: "When therefore he had received the sop, he went out immediately; and it was night." From these words it is clear that night was at some time in the nature of things, and yet night is something successive; therefore something successive can be in the nature of things. Likewise, what will be can be in the nature of things; but it has been and still is true to say that a time will come. For the Apostle says in 2 Tim. 4: "For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine"; therefore time can be in the nature of things, and yet it is successive. Likewise the same Apostle, in the same epistle, chapter 3, says: "In the last days perilous times shall come"; and consequently times can be in the nature of things. Likewise John 10 says: "And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter." From these words it is gathered that winter was at some time; and consequently successive things can be in the nature of things, and so an act can be in the nature of things, since there is no greater reason why one successive thing should be able to be in the nature of things rather than another. Likewise Luke 24 (last chapter) says: "Today is the third day since these things were done," therefore the third day then was, and so some successive thing can be in the nature of things. Likewise Exodus 12 says: "For it is the Passover, that is, the passing over of the Lord." That passing over was therefore in the nature of things, and yet it was not momentary but successive; for not all the firstborn of Egypt were killed in an instant, but over a period of time. Likewise Song of Songs 7 says: "How beautiful are your feet in sandals, O prince's daughter!" From these words it is held that even bodily steps are to be considered beautiful; but things that are not, and cannot be, are not beautiful; therefore steps can be in the nature of things, and yet they are successive. Likewise Genesis 27: Isaac said: "The voice is indeed the voice of Jacob," etc.; therefore that voice was in the nature of things, and yet a voice is something successive; therefore successive things can be in the nature of things. Hence it is clearly gathered from countless passages of divine Scripture that things which were successive, are, and will be, and can be in the nature of things: as in 2 Kings 6, where it is said: "Behold, the sound of his feet is behind him"; and 1 Kings 8 is written: "Let my words be these," etc.; and 1 Kings 20: "Behold, tomorrow is the new moon"; and John 6: "The Passover, a feast of the Jews, was near"; and in chapter 5: "After this there was a feast of the Jews"; and in chapter 7: "My time is not yet come, but your time is always ready"; and Matthew 8: "Behold, there arose a great tempest in the sea"; and Luke 13: "Behold, these three years I have come," etc.; and Numbers 10: "When the people are to be gathered, the sound of the trumpets shall be a simple blast." From these and very many other passages it is plainly held that successive things, such as time, motion, voices, words, years, days, sounds and the like, can be in the nature of things. Secondly, they prove specially from divine Scripture that the act of using, like the act of eating, and such things, can be in the nature of things; for what can be given can be in the nature of things, since what is nothing and cannot be cannot be given. But the act of using can be given, as Moses bears witness, who, as is recorded in Num. 11. Num. 11., said to the Lord: "The people among whom I am are six hundred thousand footmen; and thou sayest, I will give them flesh to eat for a whole month." From these words it is held that God promised to give the people the eating of flesh; therefore the eating of flesh can be in the nature of things. This is confirmed by the following: because, according to him, sight can be given in many places above, taking sight also for the act of using; therefore sight can be in the nature of things. Likewise Prov. 23 is written: "Do not be among the drinkers of wine, nor among those who riot with them." From these words it is gathered that someone can be among the drinking-bouts of drunkards; but one cannot take part in things that cannot be in the nature of things, because one would take part in them either before they exist, or while they exist, or after they exist, by his reasoning. Not before they exist, nor after they exist, is certain; nor while they exist, because according to him they do not exist; therefore no one can take part in things that are not and cannot be. Since therefore someone can take part in the drinking-bouts of drunkards, it follows that drinking-bouts can be in the nature of things; but a drinking-bout excludes the act of eating; therefore the act of eating can be in the nature of things. He proves this in the same way from the Apostle's words to the Romans 13: "Not in revelling and drunkenness."

units.la: Tertio sic arguunt: Si actus vtendi non est in rerum natura; ergo vtens non est in rerum natura: sicut si albedo non est in rerum natura, sequitur quod album non est in rerum natura. Tales n. propositiones, Vtens est in rerum natura: Album est in rerum natura: Musicum est in rerum natura, & consimiles, falsae sunt, siue subiecta non sint in rerum natura siue formae quae denotantur subiectis competere, non sint in rerum natura, unde siue homo, siue musica non sit in rerum natura, haec est falsa, Musicum est in rerum natura, ergo siue ille qui vtitur, siue actus vtendi non sit in rerum natura, haec erit falsa: vtens est in rerum natura, sed secundum istum nullus actus vtendi est in rerum natura, ergo haec est falsa: vtens est in rerum natura, & per consequens sua contradictoria est vera: nullus vtens est in rerum natura. Quarto probat, quod includit contradictionem, actu exerceri, & non esse in rerum natura: quia quod nihil est, non exercetur, sed actus per istum nihil est: ergo non exercetur. Item, aliter se habet actus ad esse, qui est in fieri, & antequam sit infieri, sed actus secundum istum est in fieri, ergo actus tunc est in rerum natura. Item, quod aliquid existitin potentia, potest aliquid existere in actu: licet tunc non existat in actu, qui existit in potentia, sed secundum istum ante ipsum actum non existit nisi in potentia, vt dicit hic, ergo tunc existit in potentia, ergo aliquid potest existere in actu. Confirmatur, quia illud quod non pot esse in rerum natura, nec existit in actu nec in potentia, sed actus existit in potentia secundum istum, ergo pot esse in rerum natura. Item, aut actus, qui exercetur, est aliquid, aut nihil, non pot dici quod sit nihil: quia tunc os successiuum esset nihil: quod est incoueniens: si est aliquid: ergo habet aliquid esse, & non habet tunc tunc esse in potentia: quia antequam exercereatur, fuit in potentia, ergo tunc habet aliquid esse in actu, ergo tunc est & ita dicunt isti, quod dicere actu qui exerceretur non esse in rerum natura, & quod actus non potest esse in rerum natura, est erroneum, imo haereticum reputandum. Tertius error, vt dicunt isti, contentus in praedictis verbis est, quod actus haberi non potest, quod est erroneum, quia si actus haberi non potest, eadem ratione nullum successiuum potest haberi: ita tempus, dies, & anni, motus, verba & sermones, & alia successiua haberi non possent: quod sacrae Scripturae obuiat manifeste. Ait enim Apostol. ad Gal. 6. Dum tempus habemus, operemur bonum ad omnes, & Eccles. 3. Omnia tempus habent, & Ioh. 9. Ætatem habet ipse, prosé loquatur. Et 3. Reg. 1. Rex David senuerat, habebatque aetatis plurimos dies, & Ioh. 5. Erat autem ibi quidam homo 38. annos & octo habens in infirmitate sua, & Ioh. 6. Domine verba vitae aeternae habes. Ex quibus authoritatibus, aliisque quampluribus colligitur euidenter, quod successiua possunt haberi: & per consequens actus potest haberi, hoc etiam patet: quia illud, quod potest dari, potest haberi, ab illo cui potest dari, tempus aut actus edendi possunt dari. De actu edendi ostensum est prius per illud Num. 11. Dabo eis esum carnium. De tempore patet per illud Apoc. 3. Dedit illi tempus ut paenitentiam ageret, ergo possunt haberi. Quartus error hic contentus (vt dicunt) est, quod esse solummodo rem perfectam significat. Quod enim hoc intendat, patet per hoc, quod ipse probare conatur, quod actus non est in rerum natura: quia esse significat rem perfectam, quae probatio nullo modo concluderet, si esse significaret indifferenter rem perfectam vel imperfectam. Intendit ergo quod esse significat solummodo rem perfectam, sed hoc dicunt esse erroneum. Tum quia nulla successiua essent: tunc quia tunc nullae partes entis perfecti separatae essent, & ita nulla anima separata esset: nullum etiam corpus esset, quando anima esset separata: nec aliquod ens imperfectum esset in rerum natura: quae omnia sunt absurda. Quintus error (vt dicunt) est quod factum haberi non potest, quod secundum vnum intellectum, etiam dictis istius impugnati repugnat. Nam proprie factum est res facta, sed res facta potest haberi (vt ipse dicit) ergo factum potest haberi, si autem per factum intelligat rem successiuam, adhuc potest haberi: quia successiua possunt haberi, sicut ostensum est prius. His visis dicunt isti impugnatores, quod indubitanter est tenendum, quod successiua possunt esse in rerum natura, & quod possunt haberi: & ideo actus vtendi pot esse in rerum natura: & potest haberi. Circa solutionem aut rationis sophisticae, quam adducit, nolunt multum insistere: quia illa ratio ab exponentibus quartum librum physicorum dissoluitur, & ideo secundum quod exponentes circa naturam turpis, & aliorum successiuorum diuersimode opinantur, secundum hoc diuersimode ad rationem praedictam respondent. Aliter n. respondent illi, qui dicunt quod successiua aliquam rem distinctam ab ea re permanenti significant. Aliter illi, qui dicunt, quod nomina successiua nullam rem, praeter permanentes, importat, licet importent plures res permanentes diuersimode: quia aliquas affirmatiue, & aliquas negatiue, sed distorum opinantium rationes pertractare, & quae illarum sit probabilior indagare ad praesens non expedit, sed hoc in quo praedicti opinantes concordant cum scriptura diuina, scilicet quod successiua sunt in rerum natura, & quod possunt haberi, fideliter est fatendum.
units.tr: Thirdly, they argue thus: if the act of using is not in the nature of things, then the one who uses is not in the nature of things, just as, if whiteness is not in the nature of things, it follows that the white thing is not in the nature of things. For propositions such as The one who uses is in the nature of things: The white thing is in the nature of things: The musical thing is in the nature of things, and similar ones, are false, whether the subjects are not in the nature of things or the forms denoted by the subjects do not belong to them. So if either the man or music is not in the nature of things, the proposition "The musical thing is in the nature of things" is false. Likewise, if either the one who uses or the act of using is not in the nature of things, the proposition "The one who uses is in the nature of things" will be false. But according to him no act of using is in the nature of things; therefore the proposition "The one who uses is in the nature of things" is false, and consequently its contradictory is true: no one who uses is in the nature of things. Fourthly, he proves what involves a contradiction: to be exercised in act and yet not to be in the nature of things. For what is nothing is not exercised, but by his account the act is nothing; therefore it is not exercised. Again, an act stands in a different relation to being, since it is in becoming, and before it is in becoming; but according to him the act is in becoming, therefore the act is then in the nature of things. Again, whatever exists in potency, something can exist in act, though what exists in potency does not then exist in act; but according to him, before the act itself, it exists only in potency, as he says here; therefore it then exists in potency, and therefore something can exist in act. This is confirmed: that which cannot be in the nature of things exists neither in act nor in potency; but according to him the act exists in potency; therefore it can be in the nature of things. Again, either the act which is exercised is something or it is nothing. It cannot be said to be nothing, for then the successive act would be nothing, which is absurd. If it is something, then it has some being, and does not then have being only in potency, since before it was exercised it was in potency; therefore it then has some being in act, and so it is then. And so those men say that to say the act which is being exercised is not in the nature of things, and that an act cannot be in the nature of things, is erroneous, indeed to be regarded as heretical. The third error, as they say, contained in the aforesaid words is that an act cannot be had, which is erroneous, because if an act cannot be had, by the same reasoning no successive thing can be had: thus time, days and years, motion, words and speeches, and other successive things could not be had, which plainly contradicts holy Scripture. For the Apostle says in Galatians 6: While we have time, let us work good toward all; and Ecclesiastes 3: All things have their time; and John 9: He is of age; let him speak for himself; and 1 Kings 1: King David had grown old and had many days of age; and John 5: Now there was a certain man there who had been ill for thirty-eight years; and John 6: Lord, you have the words of eternal life. From these and many other authorities it is clearly gathered that successive things can be had, and consequently an act can be had. This too is evident, because what can be given can be had by the one to whom it can be given; time or the act of eating can be given. Concerning the act of eating it was shown before, from Numbers 11: I will give them flesh to eat. Concerning time it is clear from Revelation 3: He gave her time to repent, therefore they can be had. The fourth error, as they say, contained here is that being signifies only a perfect thing. That he means this is clear from what he tries to prove, that an act is not in the nature of things, because being signifies a perfect thing; and that proof would in no way conclude if being signified indifferently either a perfect or an imperfect thing. He therefore intends that being signifies only a perfect thing, but they say this is erroneous: both because then there would be no successive things; and because then no separate parts of a perfect being would exist, and so no separated soul would exist; also no body would exist when the soul was separated, and no imperfect being would exist in the nature of things. All of these are absurd. The fifth error, as they say, is that what has been made cannot be had, which, in one sense, even by the statements of the man they attack, is contradictory. For properly the made thing (factum) is a thing that has been made, but a made thing can be had (as he himself says); therefore the made thing can be had. If, however, by factum he means a successive thing, it can still be had, because successive things can be had, as was shown before. Having seen these things, these opponents say that it must be held without doubt that successive things can be in the nature of things and can be had; and therefore the act of using can be in the nature of things and can be had.
