As for the solution of the sophistical argument which he adduces, they are unwilling to dwell on it at length, because that argument is resolved by the commentators on the fourth book of the Physics; and so, since those expositors on the nature of time and other successive things hold diverse opinions, they answer the aforesaid argument in diverse ways accordingly. Those who say that successive terms signify some thing distinct from the permanent thing answer otherwise, and so do those who say that successive names import no thing besides permanent things, though they import several permanent things in different ways, some affirmatively and some negatively. But to go through the arguments of those holding these opinions, and to inquire which is the more probable, is not expedient at present. What the aforesaid opinions agree on with divine Scripture, namely that successive things are in the nature of things and that they can be had, must faithfully be confessed. Dedit

units.la: (Quod simplex vsus, id est sine iure vtendi a proprietate seu dominio separatus in re vsu consumptibili haberi non possit.) possit) omnia verba præter ista, quod vsus haberi non possit, videntur superflua: quia ista est conclusio, q̄ intendit hic probare, sc. quod vsus, id est actus vtendi haberi non potest: & nō plus probat de simplici vsu, quam de alio: ne plus de vsu sine iure vtendi, quam de vsu cum iure vtedi: nec plus de vsu à proprietate seu dominio separato, quam de vsu cum dominio seu proprietate cõiuncto, sicut istemet fatetur. (Quod non est, nequaquã haberi potest) verum est, dum non est: tñ illud quod modo non est, postea potest haberi (aut etiam dũ exercetur) sc. non est, secundum istum: sed hoc dicunt isti esse falsum, quia actus dum exercetur est (per hoc tamen actus ipse in rerũ natura nisi in potentia non existit.) Ex hoc arguũt isti, q̄ secundum istum actus antequã exercetur est in potentia: ergo potest esse in actu: quia omne q̄ est in potentia potest esse in actu. (Cum aut actus est in fieri, nec adhuc in rerũ natura est.) Hoc negat isti, quia eoipso, quod est in fieri, est in rerum natura illo modo, quo cõpetit successiuis esse in rerum natura, vnde licet quãdo per actum aliqua res permanens fieri debet, illa res non sit in rerum natura, quando actus est in fieri: ipse tamen actus tunc est in rerum natura (cum esse rem perfectam significet) verum est quod esse rem perfectã, nõ tñ significat rem perfectã (sicut iste putat) sed etiã significat rem imperfectã, quia oẽm rem significat perfectã vel imperfectã: quia significat totũ & partes: permanetia & successiua: perfectibilia & perfectiones eorũ (q̄ quamdiu est in fieri non potest actui conuenire. Sic dicat, q̄ esse perfectũ permanens nõ potest conuenire actui, dũ est in fieri, concedunt si intelligat, q̄ nullũ esse sibi possit conuenire, dum est in fieri, negant (quod aut fit instantaneũ seu momentaneum est) istud diuersimode dicunt esse verũ, qui circa naturã temporis & aliorum successiuorũ diuersimode opinantur: sicut circa instãs & mutatũ esse diuersimode opinantur. Ex hoc tñ non sequitur, q̄ tempus & motus non sunt: sed sequitur q̄ non quicquid quocunq; modo importatur p tempus & motũ est: & sic proportionabiliter est dicendũ de actu (& talè q̄ magis intellectu quã sensu percipi potest) dicunt, q̄ liect secundũ vnã opinionem illud, q̄ secundum se totũ est de actu magis intellectu q̄ sensu percipi potest. Ex hoc tñ non sequitur, q̄ actus non est: sed sequitur, q̄ non quaelibet pars actus est. Alii dicunt, quod illud, q̄ est de actu etiam secundũ se totũ p sensum percipi potest: sed quomodo hoc intelligunt, nõ posset breuiter declarari: ideo ad præsens omittitur (si ex ipso facto produ&tares aliqua fuerit) ipsum factũ est ipsa res produ&ta proprie loquendo: & etiã actus pot vocari factũ, sicut dicitur, scio facta tua proprie (factũ tamen ipsũ quod iam transiit nõ habet) ipsum factũ, q̄ est res facta, non transiit, licet actus transierit. Vltimo isti impugnatores, ne philosophiæ ignari credant istã rationẽ esse nouam, & aliquid veritatis habere, manifestare conatur, q̄ ista ratio est quorundã antiquorũ philosophorum, propter q̄ negabant tempus, & motũ dicentes nullũ esse tẽpus, & q̄ nihil potest moueri, quos Aristot. in lib. physicor. reprobat multis modis. Fuit enim inter alias vna ratio ipsorum ista, quod præteriit de tempore siue de motu nõ est: quod futurum est, nondum est, quod autem nunc est, instantaneum est & momentaneum: q̄ nõ est pars temporis, neq; motus, ergo nec tẽpus est, nec motus. Et istud argumentũ realiter est idẽ cũ argumento istius. Vnde p rationẽ istius ita probatur: q̄ neq; motus, neq; tempus est, sicut quod actus vtendi nõ est: sic arguendo, motus nec anteq̃ aliquid moueatur, nec dum aliquid mouetur, nec postquam motum est, est in rerum natura, quia licet antequam aliquid moueatur, habeat facultatem vt moueatur, tñ motus tunc in rerum natura nisi in potentia nõ existit, cum aut aliquid mouetur: nec adhuc motus est in rerum natura, cũ esse rem perfectã significet: quod q̃ diu mobile mouetur, motui conuenire nõ potest, quod n. de motu præteriit, iam non est, quod aut est, instantaneum seu momentaneum est, est tale quod magis intellectu q̃ sensu percipi potest, ergo tunc non est: & certũ est, quod post motum cõpletum motus non est, ergo motus non potest esse in rerũ natura. Et consimiliter põt argui, quod tẽpus non est, & quod dies non est: quia dies nõ est ante diem: nec post cõpletam diẽ: nec dum dies durat: quia quod præteriit de die, iam non est: illud quod est de die instantaneum & momẽ-taneum est, ergo dies non est, & simpliciter potest probari, quod anni, voces, soni, cursus, incensus, & huiusmodi, non possunt esse in rerum natura, & quod haberi non possunt: quæ sacræ Scripturæ repugnant aperte, quare præditta ratio, per quam tam manifesti errores sophistice concluduntur, est hæreticalis censenda: nec ab aliquo ad aliquid probandum, aliqualiter adducenda.
units.tr: (That simple use, that is, use separated from the right of using and from ownership or dominion, cannot be had in a consumable thing.) All the words except this one, that use cannot be had, seem superfluous, because this is the conclusion he intends to prove here, namely that use, that is, the act of using, cannot be had. It proves no more about simple use than about any other use: not more about use without the right of using than about use with the right of using, nor more about use separated from ownership or dominion than about use joined to ownership or dominion, as he himself admits. (What is not cannot by any means be had) is true while it is not; but what now is not can afterwards be had (or even while it is being exercised), namely it is not, according to him. But these men say this is false, because the act, while it is being exercised, (yet by this the act itself does not exist in the nature of things except in potency). From this these men argue that, according to him, the act before it is exercised is in potency; therefore it can be in act, because whatever is in potency can be in act. (But when the act is in process of becoming, it is not yet in the nature of things.) These men deny this, because by the very fact that it is in process of becoming, it is in the nature of things in that way which belongs to successive things. Hence, although when a permanent thing is to be made through the act, that thing is not in the nature of things while the act is in process of becoming, yet the act itself is then in the nature of things (since it signifies a thing perfected). It is true that it signifies a perfected thing, but not only a perfected thing, as he thinks; it also signifies an imperfect thing, since it signifies every thing as either perfect or imperfect, because it signifies the whole and the parts, the permanent and the successive, the perfectible and their perfections (which, as long as it is in process of becoming, cannot belong to the act). Thus, if he means that the perfect permanent being cannot belong to the act while it is in process of becoming, they concede it; if he means that no being can belong to it while it is becoming, they deny it. (But whatever is produced is instantaneous or momentary): these men say this is true in different ways, since they hold different opinions about the nature of time and other successive things, just as they differ about the instant and change of being. From this, however, it does not follow that time and motion are not; it follows only that not whatever is signified in any way by time and motion is. So, proportionately, must be said of the act (and such that it can be perceived more by the intellect than by the sense). They say that, according to one opinion, that which belongs to the act as a whole in itself can be perceived more by the intellect than by the sense. From this, however, it does not follow that the act is not; it follows only that not every part of the act is. Others say that what belongs to the act, even as a whole in itself, can be perceived by the sense; but how they understand this could not be briefly explained, so for the present it is omitted. (if some product has come from the very deed). The deed itself is, properly speaking, the thing produced, and the act too can be called a deed, as we properly say "I know your deeds." (Yet the deed itself, which has already passed away, does not have) the deed itself, which is the thing done, has not passed away, although the act has passed away. Lastly, these opponents, lest those ignorant of philosophy believe this argument is new and has some truth, try to show that it belongs to certain ancient philosophers, on account of whom they denied time and motion, saying there is no time and nothing can be moved; Aristotle refutes them in many ways in the Physics. For among their arguments was this one: what has passed of time or motion is not; what is future is not yet; but what now is, is instantaneous and momentary, and is not a part of time or motion; therefore neither time nor motion exists. And this argument is really the same as the argument of this man. By his reasoning it is proved thus: neither motion nor time is, just as the act of using is not. Arguing so: motion is not in the nature of things before something is moved, nor while something is moved, nor after it has been moved. For although before something is moved it has the capacity to be moved, yet motion then exists in the nature of things only in potency; when something is being moved, motion is not yet in the nature of things, since it signifies a perfected thing. (As long as a mobile thing is being moved, this cannot belong to motion), for what of motion has passed is no longer; and what is, is instantaneous or momentary, and such that it can be perceived more by the intellect than by the sense; therefore then it is not. And it is certain that after the motion is completed, the motion is not; therefore motion cannot be in the nature of things. Similarly it can be argued that time is not, and that a day is not: a day is not before the day, nor after the completed day, nor while the day lasts, because what of the day has passed is no longer, and what is of the day is instantaneous and momentary; therefore the day is not. Simply put, it can be proved that years, voices, sounds, courses, incense-burnings, and such things cannot be in the nature of things and cannot be had; and these openly contradict Holy Scripture. Wherefore the aforesaid argument, by which such manifest errors are sophistically concluded, is to be judged heretical, and it is not to be brought forward by anyone to prove anything whatever.

units.la: CAP. LXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 68.

units.la: HAEc verba ipsius constitutionis. Ex quibus concludere nititur dictus hereticus, quod predicta probatio gesta Christi, & Apostolorum eius destruit, quæ sacra Scriptura eos fecisse testatur, scil. quod si actus vtendi haberi non possit, quia in rerum natura non est, neque antequam fiat, neque dum fit, nec postquam perfectus fuerit: per consequens sequitur, quod neque aliquid fieri possit, cum factum antequam fiat in rerum natura non sit: nec dum fit, nisi per instans, neque postquam fuerit perfectum.
units.tr: These are the words of the constitution itself. From them the said heretic tries to conclude that the aforesaid proof destroys the deeds of Christ and of his Apostles, which Holy Scripture testifies that they performed: namely, that if the act of using cannot be had, because it is not in the nature of things, neither before it is done, nor while it is being done, nor after it has been completed, then by consequence it follows that nothing can be done, since what is done before it is done is not in the nature of things, and while it is being done exists only in the instant, and not after it has been completed.

units.la: Hic iste impugnatus ad obiectiones appellantis respondet. Et primo respondet ad obiectiones hic recitatas. Secundo ad quasdam alias rationes, quæ contra quandam assertionem prædictæ annexam adduci videntur ibi: Preterea dicit iste. Prima in duas diuiditur: sc. quod ad duo, quæ tangit appellans, respondet, secunda ibi: Rursus dicit iste. Prima in duas: quia primo recitat obiectionem appellantis. Secundo respondet in parte immediate sequenti. Dic ergo quod appellans ex verbis superius recitatis infert, quod dicta verba destruunt gesta Christi & Apostolorum eius. Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod truncate recitat verba appellantis. Nã verba appellantis sunt hæc, quæ sequuntur: In quibus verbis (sc. præmissis) istius impugnati includitur dictũ & ratio dicti, dictũ sc. quod simplex vsus, id est sine iure vtendi à proprietate seu dominio separatus in re vsu consumptibili haberi non potest, quod constat esse hæreticũ, per rationes contra primũ errorem & tertiũ introductas. Ratio aut dicti destruit gesta Christi & Apostolorũ, quæ Scri-ptura prura sacra eos fecisse testatur: ac etiam gesta fidelium: quia si ista ratio concluderet, sequeretur quod Christus nec comedit nec bibit, nec praedicavit, nec pedes discipulorum lavit, quia per eandem rationem dicetur: si aliquid istorum fecit aut ante actum, aut post actum, aut in ipso actu, secundum dictam rationem non ante actum, quia ante actu nullum istorum fuit, quia ante actum comedendi, bibendi, praedicandi, ambulandi & eundi actus ipsi in rerum natura, nisi in potentia, non existebant, unde ante actum comedendi, bibendi, praedicandi, &c. nec comedit, nec bibit, nec praedicavit, &c. nec post actu completum: quia post actum nullum istorum exercuit, nec in ipso actu: quia pars istorum, quae praeterierant, iam non erat; pars quae futura erat, nondum erat: illud aut quod erat in instanti, non erat aliquod istorum actu, sed potentia, quod magis intelligitur intellectu quam sensu: quia comedere & bibere, &c. non sunt in instanti, sed in tempore. Similiter omnia gesta Christi non fuerunt in instanti, sed in tempore, ergo si dicta ratio concluderet, sequeretur, quod Christus nihil gessit corpore aliter in hoc mundo, de hiis quae S. Scriptura eum gessisse testatur. Eodem modo sequitur de omnibus Apostolis & aliis sanctis fidelibus, quod dicere vel sentire est haereticum & insanum, unde ad talem sophisticam rationem non oportet aliter respondere, nisi, sicut respondetur 4. physicor. ad rationes sophisticas probantes non esse tempus, nec motum: quia haec sophistica ratio est. Ex his patet, quod obiectiones appellantis sunt truncate superius recitatae. (Cum factum antequam fiat in rerum natura non sit,) quamvis hoc sit verum: tamen hoc non accepit appellans, maxime accipiendo factum, sicut accipit iste impugnatus.
units.tr: Here the one who is attacked answers the objections of the appellant. And first he answers the objections recited here; second, to certain other arguments which seem to be brought against a certain assertion annexed to the aforesaid, there: Furthermore this man says. The first is divided into two: namely, that he answers the two points which the appellant touches upon; the second there: Again this man says. The first is divided into two, because first he recites the objection of the appellant, and second he answers in the part immediately following. Say therefore that the appellant infers from the words recited above that these words destroy the deeds of Christ and of his Apostles. But those attackers say that he recites the words of the appellant in a truncated way. For the words of the appellant are these, which follow: In these words (namely those premised) of this attacked man is contained both the statement and the reason for the statement: the statement, namely, that simple use, that is, use separated from ownership or dominion and from the right of using, in a consumable thing cannot be had, which is clearly heretical, by the arguments introduced against the first and third error. The reason for the statement destroys the deeds of Christ and of his Apostles, which Scripture testifies that they performed; and also the deeds of the faithful: for if this reasoning were conclusive, it would follow that Christ neither ate nor drank, nor preached, nor washed the feet of the disciples; for by the same reasoning it would be said: if he did any of these things either before the act, or after the act, or in the act itself, then according to the said reasoning not before the act, because before the act none of these existed, since before the act of eating, drinking, preaching, walking and going, those acts did not exist in the nature of things, except in potency; whence before the act of eating, drinking, preaching, etc., he neither ate, nor drank, nor preached, etc.; nor after the act was completed, because after the act he exercised none of them; nor in the act itself, because the part of these acts that had already passed was no longer there, and the part that was to come was not yet there; and that which was in the instant was not any of these acts in actuality, but in potency, which is grasped more by the intellect than by the senses, because to eat and to drink, etc., are not in an instant but in time. Likewise all the deeds of Christ were not in an instant but in time; therefore if the said reasoning were conclusive, it would follow that Christ did nothing in the body in this world of those things which Holy Scripture testifies he did. In the same way it follows of all the Apostles and other holy faithful that to say or think this is heretical and insane; whence it is not necessary to answer such a sophistical argument otherwise than as is answered in the fourth book of the Physics to the sophistical arguments proving that there is no time and no motion: because this is a sophistical argument. From these things it is evident that the objections of the appellant are recited above in a truncated form. (Since what is done before it is done is not in the nature of things,) although this is true; yet the appellant did not take it in this sense, especially taking "done" as the attacked man takes it.

units.la: CAP. LXIX.
units.tr: CHAP. LXIX.

units.la: Proculdubio ista consequentia est falsa: & est potius totum contrarium concludendum, videlicet quod si actus vtendi quia in rerum natura non est, haberi non poterit, concludi debet, quod quia factum in rerum natura non est fieri potest, sicut enim quod non est haberi non poterit: sic quod est factum fieri nequit, unde si actus vtendi haberi non possit, quia in rerum natura non est, sequitur quod factum, quia in rerum natura non est, fieri possit.
units.tr: Undoubtedly this inference is false. Rather, the opposite should be concluded: if the act of using cannot be had because it is not in the nature of things, it must be concluded that what has been made cannot be made because it is not in the nature of things. For just as what is not cannot be had, so what is made cannot be made. Hence, if the act of using cannot be had because it is not in the nature of things, it follows that what is made, because it is not in the nature of things, can be made.

units.la: Hic iste impugnatus ad praedictam obiectionem appellantis nititur respondere, dicens quod ista consequentia non valet: actus vtendi, quia in rerum natura non est, non potest haberi, ergo factum, quia in rerum natura non est, non potest fieri, sed oppositum sequitur sic: actus vtendi, quia in rerum natura non est, non potest haberi, ergo factum, quia in rerum natura non est, potest fieri: quia sicut non est, non potest haberi, ita quod factum est fieri nequit. Sed isti impugnatores dicunt primo, quod iste impugnatus non respondet ad obiectiones appellantis, secundo dicunt, quod verba praedicta multa irrationabilia & fantastica continent manifeste. Quod vero iste impugnatus hic ad praemissas obiectiones appellantis nequaquam respondeat, dicunt isti omni intuenti verba appellantis, & ista verba hic posita aperte patere. Nam appellans nullam talem consequentiam facit: quia actus vtendi in rerum natura non est, haberi non potest, ergo quod factum in rerum natura non est, non potest fieri, sed fundavit se in hoc: quod si actus vtendi non potest esse in rerum natura, quia nec ante actum, nec dum actus exercetur, nec post actum completum: ergo consimiliter, si Christus non comedit ante actu, nec dum actus exercebatur, nec post actum Christus non comedit: & eadem ratione, nec bibit nec ambulavit, nec praedicavit, nec orauit.
units.tr: Here this author under attack tries to answer the appellant's objection just mentioned, saying that the inference does not hold: the act of using, because it is not in the nature of things, cannot be had; therefore what is made, because it is not in the nature of things, cannot be made. But the opposite follows thus: the act of using, because it is not in the nature of things, cannot be had; therefore what is made, because it is not in the nature of things, can be made, since just as what is not cannot be had, so what is made cannot be made. But these attackers say, first, that this author does not answer the appellant's objections, and second, that the words quoted contain many manifestly irrational and fanciful claims. That this author in no way answers the appellant's objections above, these men say, is plain to anyone who reads the appellant's words and the words quoted here. For the appellant makes no such inference, that because the act of using is not in the nature of things it cannot be had, and therefore what is not in the nature of things cannot be made. He rests instead on this: if the act of using cannot be in the nature of things, because it is not there before the act, nor while the act is being exercised, nor after the act is completed, then similarly, if Christ did not eat before the act, nor while the act of eating was being exercised, nor after the act, Christ did not eat; and by the same reasoning he neither drank, walked, preached, nor prayed.

units.la: Quod vero Christus non comedit ante actu, nec dum actus comedi exercebatur, nec post actum comedendi completum, probatur p rationem istius sic: ante actum comedendi Christus non comedit, quia tunc actus comedendi non existebat, nec in potentia, nec comedit dum actus exercebatur, quia dum actus exercebatur secundum istum non fuit nisi aliquid instantaneum seu momentaneum, quod magis intellectu quam sensu percipitur: ergo tunc Christus non comedit in instanti, sed in tempore, nec Christus comedit, certum est post actum comedendi completum: ergo nunquam comedit, & ita est de verbis, quae iste ponit in responsione sua, & ad quae respondet in verbis appellantis: &ita est de aliis. Dicunt igitur isti: quod quia ad rationes appellantis nesciunt rationem rationabilem invenire, finxit quaedam alia verba non intelligibilia, ad quae nituntur respondere, p hoc cupiens coram simplicib. se iactare, quasi rationes appellantis dissoluisset. Secundo dicunt isti, quod verba praedicta plura continent irrationabilia & fantastica, quorum primum est, quod actus vtendi non est in rerum natura, secundum quod actus vtendi haberi non potest. Tertium est, quod factum in rerum natura non est. Et quartum est, quod illud quod est factum fieri nequit. Quintum quod factum, quia in rerum natura non est, fieri potest. De primis duobus dictum est supra c. 67. Tertium, quod factum in rerum natura non est, est erroneum secundum istos: quia factum non potest accipi nisi pro actu vel pro reproducta per actum, si accipiatur pro actu: sic est error, sicut est error, quod actus non est in rerum natura, si accipiatur pro re producta: sic etiam est erroneum, quod constat quod res producta per actum est in rerum natura. Quartum, sc. quod illud quod est factum fieri nequit, si accipiatur pro re producta, sic potest concedi, quod illud quod est factum nequit fieri a creatura, quia iam factum est, si accipiatur pro actu: sic est falsum, quia actus fit & est in fieri. Quintum, scil. quod factum, quia in rerum natura non est, fieri potest, videtur erroneum: implicat enim quod ideo factum fieri potest, quia non est in rerum natura, sed hoc est falsum: quia tunc chimera posset fieri, quia non est in rerum natura.
units.tr: That Christ did not eat before the act, nor while the act of eating was being exercised, nor after the act of eating was completed, is proved by this reasoning: before the act of eating Christ did not eat, because the act of eating did not then exist, not even in potency; nor did he eat while the act was being exercised, because while the act was being exercised, on this view, there was only something instantaneous or momentary, perceived by the intellect rather than by the senses. Therefore Christ did not eat then in an instant but in time. Nor, it is certain, did Christ eat after the act of eating was completed. Therefore he never ate. And so it is with the words he puts in his answer, to which he responds in the words of the appellant, and so it is with the rest. These men therefore say that, since he could not find a reasonable answer to the appellant's arguments, he invented certain unintelligible words to which he tries to respond, wishing thereby to boast before simple people as if he had dissolved the appellant's arguments. Secondly, these men say that the words quoted contain many irrational and fanciful claims. The first is that the act of using is not in the nature of things, insofar as the act of using cannot be had. The third is that what is made is not in the nature of things. The fourth is that what is made cannot be made. The fifth is that what is made, because it is not in the nature of things, can be made. Of the first two, it was said above in chapter 67. The third, that what is made is not in the nature of things, is erroneous by their account, because "made" can be taken only for the act or for the thing produced by the act. If it is taken for the act, the claim is an error, just as it is an error to say that the act is not in the nature of things if "made" is taken for the thing produced. It is likewise erroneous, since it is plain that the thing produced by the act is in the nature of things. The fourth, that what is made cannot be made, may be granted if "made" is taken for the thing produced, namely that what has been made cannot be made by a creature, since it is already made; but if it is taken for the act, it is false, since the act is made and is in the process of being made. The fifth, that what is made, because it is not in the nature of things, can be made, seems erroneous. For it implies that a thing can be made because it is not in the nature of things, and this is false, since then a chimera could be made because it is not in the nature of things.

units.la: (Ita consequentia est falsa.) Istam consequentiam non facit appellans. (Si actus vtendi: quia in rerum natura non est haberi non potest, concludi debeat: quod quia factum in rerum natura non est fieri non possit.) Istam consequentiam: vel conditionalem verius, non facit appellans, nec de ipsa facit aliquam mentionem. (Sicut enim quod non est haberi non potest) verum est dum non est (sic quod est factum fieri nequit) falsum est respectu Dei: quia Deus posset iterum illa facere, quae sunt, & etiam ipsos actus iterum facere posset. (Si actus vtendi haberi non possit: quia in rerum natura non est, sequitur quod factum, quia in rerum natura
units.tr: (Thus the inference is false.) The appellant does not make this inference. (If the act of using cannot be had because it is not in the nature of things, it must be concluded that what has been made cannot be made, because it is not in the nature of things.) The appellant does not make this inference, or rather conditional, nor does he mention it at all. (For just as what is not cannot be had) is true while it is not; (so what has been made cannot be made) is false with respect to God, since God could make again the things that exist, and could also make the acts themselves again. (If the act of using cannot be had because it is not in the nature of things, it follows that what is made, because it is not in the nature of things

units.la: {y} Cum factum antequam fiat in rerum natura non sit. natura non est, fieri posset.) Istam consequentiam negant, quamuis nihil faciat contra intentionem appellantis: nec iste probat eam: & ideo eadem facilitate contemnitur, qua probatur.
units.tr: {y} (Since what, before it is made, is not in the nature of things.) is not in nature, could be made.) They deny this inference, although it does nothing against the appellant's intention, nor does this author prove it. Therefore it is dismissed with the same ease with which it is asserted.

units.la: CAP. LXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER 70.

units.la: Rursus dicit iste haereticus, quod per rationem praedictam sequeretur, quod nec usus rerum usu consumptibilium etiam coniunctus cum proprietate seu dominio haberi posset, quod de usu facti utique nos fatemur: & idem dicimus de rebus non consumptibilibus usu. Licet enim iste quis de facto uti valeat, habere tamen nequit in talibus usum facti, ut ex praedictis patet.
units.tr: Again, this heretic says that by the reasoning stated above it would follow that not even the use of consumable things, joined with ownership or dominion, could be had; and indeed we admit this concerning the use of fact, and we say the same of non-consumable things by use. For although a person may be able to use something as a matter of fact, yet in such things he cannot have the use of fact, as is clear from what has been said above.

units.la: In parte ista respondet ad secundam obiectionem appellantis, quae fuit, quod per rationem suam nullus posset habere usum consumptibilium usu, ad quam respondet concedendo conclusionem loquendo de usu facti. Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, quod conclusio, quam concedit, est erronea: quia eadem ratione, qua nullus posset habere usum facti rerum consumptibilium usu: Eadem ratione nullum successivum posset haberi, quod scripturae divinae repugnat aperte, sicut ostensum est cap. 67. Secundo dicunt, quod ex his dictis patet, quod illa ratio in vanum adducta fuit ad probandum, quod simplex usus facti sine iure a proprietate seu dominio separatus in re usu consumptibili haberi non potest: quia per illa aequaliter probatur quod usus facti sine iure, proprietate seu dominio separatus in re non consumptibili usu haberi non potest, & quod usus coniunctus iuri utendi vel dominio seu proprietati haberi non potest, (quod de usu facti, &c.) hic respondet ad rationem praetactam concedendo conclusionem. (Licet enim illi quis de facto uti valeat: habere tamen nequit in talib. usum facti) hoc est irrationabiliter dictum: quia qua ratione potest concedi, quod aliquis potest uti rebus, poterit concedi quod aliquis potest habere usum rei: sicut quia concedit ur, quod aliquis vixit multis annis: ideo conced\itur quod habet multos annos: & ita patet, quod tota difficultas, q; iste facit de hac materia, est de hoc verbo est: & de hoc verbo habere: an. sc. sicut conceditur quod aliquis utitur re. ita debeat concedi, quod usus est, & quod aliquis habet actum utendi: sicut an debeat concedi, actus comedendi est, & aliquis habet actum edendi, quemadmodum conceditur quod aliquis comedit: & ita difficultate vocali & fantastica, ut dicunt, replet quaternos suos: & sub talibus difficultatibus frivolis & fantasticis nititur errores inducere contra catholicam veritatem.
units.tr: In this part he answers the second objection of the appellant, which was that by his reasoning no one could have the use of consumable things by use; to which he replies by granting the conclusion, speaking of the use of fact. But these opponents say that the conclusion he grants is erroneous: for by the same reasoning by which no one could have the use of fact of consumable things by use, by the same reasoning no successive thing could be had, which plainly contradicts Scripture, as was shown in chapter 67. Secondly, they say that from what has been said it is clear that that argument was brought in vain to prove that simple use of fact, separated from right, ownership or dominion, cannot be had in a consumable thing by use; for by the same reasoning it is equally proved that use of fact, separated from right, ownership or dominion, cannot be had in a non-consumable thing by use, and that use joined to the right of using, or to dominion or ownership, cannot be had (as to use of fact, etc.). Here he replies to the aforementioned argument by granting the conclusion (For although a person may be able to use something as a matter of fact, yet in such things he cannot have the use of fact). This is said unreasonably: for by whatever reasoning it may be granted that someone can use things, it may be granted that someone can have the use of a thing; just as, because it is granted that someone has lived many years, it is therefore granted that he has many years. And so it is clear that the whole difficulty this man makes about this matter lies in this word "is" and in this word "have": namely, whether, just as it is granted that someone uses a thing, it ought likewise to be granted that it is a use, and that someone has the act of using; just as whether it ought to be granted that the act of eating is, and that someone has the act of eating, in the way it is granted that someone eats. And so with a verbal and imaginary difficulty, as they call it, he fills his notebooks, and under such frivolous and imaginary difficulties he strives to induce errors against Catholic truth.

units.la: CAP. LXXI.
units.tr: Chapter 71.

units.la: Praeterea dicit iste haereticus, quod dicta constitutio falsum includit in eo, quod dicit, quod in rebus usu consumptibilibus possit usus constitui vel haberi, nequaquam simplex nec separatus a proprietate seu dominio usus huiusmodi posset dici: cum per talem usum, id est utendi actum, & in ipso actu & cum ipso actu res huiusmodi consumatur, in ipsiusque rei exerceatur substantia, nec sine ipsius rei consumptione esse valeat usus talis.
units.tr: Furthermore, this heretic says that the said constitution contains a falsehood in saying that use can be established or held in things consumed by use. Such a use could by no means be called simple, or separate from the property or ownership of the thing, since through such a use, that is, through the act of using, and in and with that very act, the thing is consumed and its substance is spent. Nor can such a use exist without the consumption of the thing itself.

units.la: In ista parte respondet ad quandam obiectionem: quae contra quandam assertionem istius impugnati praedictae annexam adduci videtur. Et haec pars dividitur in tres: quia primo ponit assertionem. Secundo recitat impugnationem appellantis. Tertio respondet ad dictam impugnationem. Secunda pars incipit immediate post verba hic recitata. Tertia ibi: Ad hoc dicendum est. Dicit ergo primo: quod adhuc appellans praedictam constitutionem impugnat in hoc, quod ponit, quod si in rebus usu consumptibilibus, usus posset constitui vel haberi, ille tamen usus non esset simplex, nec a proprietate seu dominio separatus, cuius rationem assignat: quia per talem actum utendi, & in ipso actu, & cum ipso actu huiusmodi res consumitur.
units.tr: In this part he answers a certain objection, which seems to be brought against one assertion of the constitution under attack, one that is attached to the passage just quoted. The part is divided into three. First he states the assertion; second he recites the appellant's objection; third he answers that objection. The second part begins immediately after the words quoted here, and the third at "Ad hoc dicendum est." He says first, then, that the appellant, still attacking the aforesaid constitution, objects to its claim that if a use could be established or held in things consumed by use, that use would nonetheless not be simple, nor separated from property or ownership. He gives the reason: through such an act of using, and in and with that very act, the thing is consumed.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod dictum in se est erroneum: & ratio, per quam probatur, plures includit errores. Dictum in se est tale: quod videlicet si in rebus usu consumptibilibus potest usus constitui vel haberi: talis usus nec est simplex nec est a proprietate seu dominio separatus, & ita hoc dictum duas partes includit, quarum utraque est erronea, & ideo primo probant, quod talis usus posse esse simplex, secundo probant, quod poteset esse a proprietate seu dominio separatus. Ad evidentiam primi dicunt esse sciendum: quod talia nomina simplex, simplicitas, simpliciter, in diversis scientiis & vulgari modo loquendi accipiuntur aequivoce. Unde in philosophia naturali, simplex, duplicter accipitur. Uno modo, ut distinguitur contra compositum. Alio modo contra secundum quid: quod quidam dicit quod quaedam est generatio simplex, quaedam secundum quid, in Logica etiam accipiuntur aequivoce, quia aliter accipiuntur, cum dicitur, suppositionum alia est simplex, alia est personalis, & aliter cum dicitur, consequentiarum alia est simplex, alia ut nunc, aliter cum dicitur, propositio quaedam est de inesse simpliciter, quaedam de inesse ut nunc, & cum dicitur, quaedam propositio convertitur simpliciter, quaedam per accidens, quaedam per contrapositionem, & aliter, cum una fallacia assignatur secundum quid & simpliciter. Distinctione vero praedictarum significationum non oportet eos in praesentibus declarare. Aliter accipiuntur huiusmodi vocabula in Theologia, & in scientiis legalibus, & in vulgari locutione. Unde simpliciter uno modo opponitur dolositati: & sic accipitur Iob primo, cum dicitur: Et erat vir ille simplex, & rectus & timens Deum, & prim. Paralipomen. ultim. dicit Dauid: Scio Domine Deus, quod probes corda & simplices diligis, & ego in simplicitate cordis mei laetus obtuli universa haec. Et Sapientiae primo. In simplicitate cordis quaerite illum, & Matthaei decimo. Estote prudentes sicut serpentes, & simplices sicut columba. Et Anterius Papa, ut habetur sex. quaestion. prim. Ex merito, ait: Habeant omnes simplicitatem columbae, nec cuiquam inchinas. obtinentur dolos: & serpentis astutiam, ne aliorum supplantentur insidiis. Aliter simplicitas accipitur pro stultitia vel ignorantia seu indiscretione vel imperitia, & sic dicunt iura, quod parcendum est simplicitati, vt habetur extra de rerum permutatione, cum vniuersorum, & ext. de haereticis, super literis, & de consecr. distin. 2. Scriptura dicit, & ext. de translat. inter corporalia, vbi dicit Innocentius III. veniam erroris dedimus, quia non ex malignitate, sed ex simplicitate peccarunt, & extra de haeretic. cum ex iniuncto, vbi sic dicitur: Non est tamen simplicibus sacerdotibus a scholasticis detrahendum, & sic etiam accipitur in decr. dist. 36. §. 1. cum dicitur, oportet etiam ordinantem esse prudentem, quod contra eos notandum est, qui sub nomine simplicitatis excusant stultitiam sacerdotum. Sic etiam accipitur simplex dist. 39. ca. Petrus, vbi Glossa notat duplicem simplicitatem vnam, quae est contraria dolo, alia quae est negligentia siue stultitia.
units.tr: But these opponents say that the statement is erroneous in itself, and that the reasoning by which it is proved contains several errors. The statement in itself is this: if a use can be established or held in things consumed by use, such a use is neither simple nor separated from property or ownership. The statement therefore contains two parts, each of which is erroneous. So first they prove that such a use can be simple, and second that it can be separated from property or ownership. To make the first clear, they say we must know that such terms as simple, simplicity and simply are used equivocally in different sciences and in ordinary speech. Thus in natural philosophy "simple" is taken in two ways: in one way as opposed to compound, and in another as opposed to "in a certain respect" (secundum quid). Some say there is a simple generation and some a generation in a certain respect. In logic too the terms are taken equivocally. They are used one way when one says that of suppositions one kind is simple and another personal; another way when one speaks of consequences, one kind being simple and another "as now" (ut nunc); another way when one speaks of a proposition de inesse simpliciter and another de inesse ut nunc; and again when one says that one proposition is converted simply, another by accident, another by contraposition; and differently again when a fallacy is assigned "in a certain respect" and "simply." There is no need, in the present matter, for them to explain the distinction between these meanings. In theology, in the legal sciences and in ordinary speech these words are used otherwise. Thus "simply" in one sense is opposed to deceit, as in Job 1, where it says, "And that man was simple, and upright, and feared God." And David says in the last chapter of the first book of Paralipomenon: "I know, Lord God, that thou triest the heart and lovest the simple; and I, in the simplicity of my heart, have joyfully offered all these things." And Wisdom 1: "Seek him in simplicity of heart." And Matthew 10: "Be ye wise as serpents, and simple as doves." Pope Anterus, as is found in C. 6 q. 1, Ex merito, says: "Let all have the simplicity of the dove, and let them not be taken in by deceits; and let them have the cunning of the serpent, lest they be overthrown by the snares of others." In another sense "simplicity" is taken for foolishness, or ignorance, or indiscretion, or inexperience. So the laws say that simplicity must be pardoned, as is found in Extra, De rerum permutatione, Cum universorum; Extra, De haereticis, Super literis; De consecr. dist. 2, Scriptura dicit; and Extra, De translatione, Inter corporalia, where Innocent III says: "We have granted pardon for error, because they sinned not from malice but from simplicity." Also Extra, De haereticis, Cum ex iniuncto, where it is said: "Nevertheless simple priests are not to be disparaged by the scholastics." It is taken the same way in Dist. 36 §1, where it is said: "It is also necessary that the one ordaining be prudent," which must be noted against those who, under the name of simplicity, excuse the foolishness of priests. "Simple" is likewise taken in Dist. 39, c. Petrus, where the Gloss notes a twofold simplicity: one which is contrary to guile, and another which is negligence or foolishness.

units.la: Aliter dicitur simplex, idem quod perfectum, & sic loquitur Anselmus Monologion capit. 28. vbi dicit, quod solum esse Dei dicitur simplex perfectum & absolutum. Aliter distinguitur simplex contra solenne, & sic dicitur votum simplex, quod non est solenne, vt habetur: ext. qui clerici vel volentes matrimonium contrahere possunt c. cōsuluit, & c.
units.tr: In another sense "simple" means the same as perfect, as Anselm speaks of it in Monologion, chapter 28, where he says that "the being of God alone is called simple, perfect and absolute." In another sense "simple" is distinguished from solemn, and so we speak of a "simple vow," which is not solemn, as is found in Extra, Qui clerici vel volentes matrimonium contrahere possunt, c. Consuluit, and elsewhere.

units.la: Rursus. Aliquando dicitur simplex, quod adiuncto caret, & sic loquitur Anselmus de simplicibus, vbi ostendit, quod declarationis gratia, quedam sunt simplicia, quedam duplicia, &c. Aliter accipitur simplex, Num. 10. cum dicitur: quando autem congregandus est populus, simplex clangor tubarum erit, vbi simplex contra concisum distinguitur. Aliter accipitur simplex in vulgari locutione: quia quod notat carentia maioris dignitatis: sicut cum dicitur: iste est simplex sacerdos: denotatur quod est sacerdos, & non habet maiorem dignitatem, quam sacerdotium, sicut dicitur aliquis esse simplex miles: quia dignitatem maiorem militia non habet, & sic etiam aliquis dicitur esse simplex monachus: quia in quo vnus monachus praefertur alteri caret, sicut accipitur ext. de sent. excommun. Nuper, vbi dicitur, aliquos posse absolui a simplici sacerdote: & in multis aliis locis sic accipitur.
units.tr: Again, sometimes "simple" is said of what lacks an addition. So Anselm speaks of simple things, where he shows that, for the sake of explanation, some things are simple and some double, and so on. In Numbers 10 "simple" is taken where it says: "When the people are to be gathered, the sound of the trumpets shall be simple," where "simple" is distinguished from "divided." In ordinary speech "simple" is taken to denote the lack of greater dignity. When one says, "He is a simple priest," it is meant that he is a priest and has no dignity greater than the priesthood. So one is said to be a "simple soldier" because soldiering gives him no greater dignity, and someone is called a "simple monk" because in him no monk is preferred to another. This is the sense in Extra, De sententia excommunicationis, Nuper, where it is said that some may be absolved by a simple priest. It is taken in this way in many other places.

units.la: Aliquando vero dicitur simplex, quod conditione, specificatione, modificationem, aut abdicationem aliquam includit, sic illud quod per se ponitur, sine addito vel sine determinatione quacunque, dicitur simpliciter poni: & sic aliquid dicitur simpliciter aliquale, quia est veraciter tale. Ex his patenter apparet, quod simplex multis modis accipitur, etiam quod actus vtendi potest multipliciter dici simplex. Nam secundum multos dicitur simplex: secundum philosophiam naturalem, quia non componitur ex materia & forma: secundum etiam Theologiam potest dici simplex, sicut potest dici bonus. Sicut ideo dicitur bonus, quia bono modo & bene elicitur: ita potest etiam dici simplex, quia a simplici, & sine dolo elicitur, vel etiam exercetur. Potest etiam dici simplex, sicut potest dici stultus vel indiscretus: quia a stulto vel indiscreto exercetur, potest etiam dici simplex: quia est sine alio actu vtendi. Sicut secundum Anselmum quandoque aliqua declaratio dicitur simplex, quia est sine alia declaratione. Aliis modis potest dici simplex, sicut post patebit.
units.tr: Sometimes, however, "simple" is said of what includes no condition, specification, modification or qualification. So what is put by itself, without any addition or determination whatever, is said to be "simply put," and something is said to be "simply such" because it is truly such. From these things it is plainly evident that "simple" is taken in many ways, and that the act of using can be called simple in many ways. For according to many it is called simple: according to natural philosophy, because it is not composed of matter and form. In theology too it can be called simple, just as it can be called good. Just as it is called good because it is elicited in a good manner and well, so it can also be called simple, because it is elicited, or exercised, by a simple person and without guile. It can also be called simple as it can be called foolish or indiscreet: because it is exercised by a foolish or indiscreet person, it can also be called simple, because it is without another act of using. So, according to Anselm, a declaration is sometimes called simple because it is without another declaration. It can be called simple in other ways too, as will be shown afterwards.

units.la: Ex quo concludunt, quod hic iste impugnatus cum sine distinctione negauerit actu posse esse simplicem, qui tot modis potest esse simplex, ostendit a pte se grammaticae, logicae, rhetoricae ignarus, nec tamen propter dictatum ignorantiam facultatum ipsum reprehensibile arbitrantur: sed in hoc damnabiliter deliquit (vt dicunt) quod sic philosophiae & Theologiae ignarus, vtpote qui earum nunc fuit discipulus, sed a pueritia baratator existens, tumultibus seculi intendebat, quaestiones Theologiae difficiles determinare praesumit: & ideo magister errorum existit, qui nunc fuit discipulus veritatis. Nullus n. (vt dicunt) est quaestionum intricatarum Theologicae facultatis determinator idoneus, nisi fuerit in grammatica, maxime quantum ad tropos, figuratiuas locutiones, quae docentur in ea & in logica, ac metaphysica & Theologia perfectus.
units.tr: From this they conclude that this man under attack, by denying without distinction that an act can be simple, when it can be simple in so many ways, shows himself ignorant of grammar, logic and rhetoric. Yet they do not think he is to be blamed for lacking these arts. Rather, he sinned damnably in this, as they say: being ignorant of philosophy and theology, having once been their pupil, but from boyhood a swindler and intent on the tumults of the world, he presumes to determine difficult questions of theology. Thus he is a master of errors who was once a disciple of truth. For no one (as they say) is a fit determiner of intricate questions of the theological faculty unless he is first accomplished in grammar, especially as regards tropes and figurative expressions, which are taught in grammar and in logic, and then perfected in metaphysics and theology.

units.la: Aliae n. summe prosunt, sed parum respectu praedicatorum. Ad propositum inducitur, quod duo sunt modi, quib. actus vtendi dicitur simplex: & illi ad intentum istorum sufficiunt, dicitur n. vsus facti vno modo simplex: quia quod sibi ius aliquod sit annexum vel adiunctum, non requirit, & sic actus comedendi dicitur actus vtendi simplex: quia accidit actui comedendi, quod comedens ius habeat comedendi, & sic aliquo videtur loqui Nicolaus III. de simplici vsu. Secundo dicitur actus vtendi simplex, qui est sine iure vtendi: sicut illud votum dicitur simplex, quod solennitate caret: & ille dicitur simplex sacerdos, qui maiori dignitate ecclesiastica caret.
units.tr: Other points are very useful, but of little use for the preachers. The matter is brought in to the point that there are two ways in which an act of using is called simple. These two are enough for the purpose here. In the first sense, the use of a fact is called simple because it does not require that some right be attached to or joined with it. In this way the act of eating is called a simple act of using, because it happens to the one eating that he has the right to eat. In this sense Nicholas III seems to speak of simple use. Secondly, a simple act of using is one that is without a right of using, just as a vow is called simple when it lacks solemnity, and a priest is called simple when he lacks higher ecclesiastical dignity.

units.la: Primo modo accipiendo simplicem actum vtendi, sic omnis vere vtens habet simplicem actum vtendi: & isto modo aliquid dicitur simpliciter aliquale, quod sine addito praedicatur, sic dicendo: hoc est album: sed illud, de quo non dicitur album, nisi cum addito, non est simpliciter album: propter quod licet album cum addito praedicat de Aethiope sic dicendo: Aethiops est albus secundum dentes: non dicitur tamen simpliciter albus, quia haec non est vera: Aethiops est albus, & isto modo videtur concedendum, quod quilibet vtens habet simplicem actum vtendi: quia habet actum vtendi, qui non requirit de se necessarium ius vtendi, loquendo de iure fori. Aliter potest dici simplex actus vtendi ille actus, quia de facto non habet ius tale vtendi annexum, & iste potest vocari nudus actus vtendi: sicut nuda promissio vocatur, quae non est iuratoria, &c. &nudus vsus iuris vocatur, vsus iuris qui non est vsufructus.
units.tr: If we take a simple act of using in the first sense, then every person who truly uses has a simple act of using. In this way something is said to be simply such-and-such when it is predicated without an addition, as in saying "this is white." But that which is called white only with an addition is not simply white. For this reason, although "white" may be predicated with an addition of an Ethiopian, saying "the Ethiopian is white as to his teeth," he is not called simply white, because the statement "the Ethiopian is white" is not true. In this sense it seems necessary to concede that every user has a simple act of using, because he has an act of using which does not of itself require a necessary right of using, speaking of the right of the court. In another sense, that act may be called a simple act of using which, in fact, has no such right of using attached to it. This may be called a bare act of using, just as a promise is called "bare" when it is not sworn, and a use of right is called "bare" when it is a use of right which is not usufruct.

units.la: Restat probare, contra istum impugnatum, quod talis vsus potest esse simplex, quod per Nicolaum III. aperte ostenditur, qui in decretali Exiit, ait: Cum in rebus temporalibus sit considerare praecipuum proprietatem, possessionem, vsumfructum, ius vtendi, & simplicem vsum facti: liset primis possit carere vita mortali, nulla prorsus potest esse professio, quae a se vsum necessarium sustentationis excludat. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod vsus necessariae sustentationis est simplex vsus facti, sed in rebus consumptibilibus vsu reperitur vsus necessariae sustentationis, ergo in eis reperitur simplex vsus facti. Secundo probatur, quod talis actus vtendi potest esse a proprietate seu dominio separatus: quia Fratres Minores habent vsum huiusmodi rerum, & tamen nullius rei talis habent dominium seu proprietatem, ergo vsus earum est a proprietate seu dominio separatus. Quod vero Fratres vtantur huiusmodi reb. patet ad sensum, quod etiam nullius rei habeat dominium seu proprietatem, probatur per assertiones diuersorum summorum Pontificum. Hoc enim expresse diffinit Greg. IX. & Nicolaus III. & Clemens
units.tr: It remains to prove, against this opponent, that such a use can be simple. This is clearly shown by Nicholas III, who in the decretal Exiit says: "Since in temporal things one must consider ownership, possession, usufruct, the right of using, and simple use of fact, although in the first three a mortal life may do without, there can be no profession at all which excludes from itself the necessary use of sustenance." From these words it is gathered that the use of necessary sustenance is a simple use of fact; but in consumable things the use of necessary sustenance is found; therefore in them is found a simple use of fact. Secondly, it is proved that such an act of using can be separated from ownership or dominion, because the Lesser Brothers have the use of such things, and yet they have no ownership or property of any such thing; therefore their use of them is separated from ownership or dominion. That the Brothers use such things is plain to the senses; that they have no dominion or property of anything is proved by the assertions of various supreme Pontiffs. For Gregory IX, Nicholas III and Clement

units.la: Bbbbb 2 V.vc V. vt patet sup. c. 32. hoc Innocen. IV. & Alexan. IV. in suis declarationib. aperte testantur, qui dicunt: Dicitur insuper, quod cum in ipsa regula cōtineatur expresse, quod Fratres nihil sibi approprient, nec domum, nec locum, nec aliquam rem: quia nec in cōmuni nec in speciali debet proprietatem habere: sed locorum & domorum & vtensilium ac librorū & eorum mobilium (qua licet habere) ordo vsum habeat; & Fratres secundū quod generales & prouinciales Ministri duxerint ordinandū, hiis vtantur. Et Clemens IV. in quodā priuilegio ait: Cū dilecti filii Fratres Minores ex professione sua voto adeo se voluntaria submiserint paupertati, vt nec diuisim, nec cōmuniter aliquid proprii valeant obtinere: sed omnia quae ipsis in eleemosynam erogantur, seu alias eorū contemplatione prouenient, iuri ac proprietati ecclesiæ Romanæ ac crescere dignoscantur, &c. Et Greg. IV. in quodā priuilegio dicit: Ordo Fratrum Minorū humilitati deditus paupertatis, & rem & nomen appropriatis abiecit: & quicquid ei obuenire dignoscitur, ipso facto in nostrum & ecclesiæ Romanæ dominiū transfire perhibetur. & Martinus Papa IV. in priuilegio qp incipit, Exultantes, ait: sidem q Fratres qui pro nulla re temporali possunt in iudicio experiri: exclusiq; quibuslibet sollicitudinib. liberum & quietum diuinis vacent obsequiis, & offerentium donantium concedentiū, aut in ultima voluntate relinquentium ordini predicto vel fratrib. aliquid propter Deum, pia intentio non fraudetur: ficq; nos sollicitudini, qua predictum ordo pro suis necessitatibus, quotiens ingrueret necessitas, vel vtilitas suaderet, recurrere ad Romanam ecclesiam cogetur, ad quam omnium rerum mobilium & immobilium, quibus fratres vti possunt, quib. proprietas & dominium nullo modo spectat, &c. Ex his aliisq; quam pluribus assertionibus summorum Pontificum liquet aperte: quod Fratres Minores nullius rei vsu consumptibilis habent dominium seu proprietatem: & tā vtuntur rebus vsu consumptibilibus, ergo vsus eorum in huiusmodi reb. à proprietate seu dominio est separatus. Secundo dicunt impugnatores, quod ratio istius, per quam praedicta assertionem probare molitur, plures includit errores. Quorum primus est, quod p talem actum & in ipso actu & cum ipso actu res huiusmodi conseruatur. Secundus, quod actus huiusmodi in ipsius rei exercetur substantia: tertius quod huiusmodi actus sine rei consumptione esse non valet, omnes isti errores, vt dicunt, vnico improbantur exemplo. Nam quādo quis expendit pecuniam, & emit de pecunia rem aliquam: nec per huiusmodi actum, nec in ipso actu, nec cum ipso actu pecunia, quantum ad substantiam suam consumitur: nec huiusmodi actus in ipsius pecuniæ substantia exercetur: & sine consumptione huius rei potest esse talis actus. Idem posset per alia multa exempla probari. Ad rationem autem in re dicunt isti, quod fundatur in falso. Fundatur n. in isto medio: nullus actus vtendi re aliqua est à proprietate seu dominio separatus, quando res per actum & in actum & cū ipso actu consumitur, sed ista probatio est falsa: nec aliq; apparentiam habet secundum istos. Nam consumptio rei non plus facit, quod actus non potest separari ab vno dominio quam ab alio, si ergo propter consumptionē rei vsus non potest separari à dominio vtentis: eadem ratione nō posset separari à quocunq; dominio, & ita non posset separari à dominio Dei, nec à dominio regum, nec ab aliquo alio dominio. (Cum per talem vsum, id est vtendi actum.) Hic concedit vtendi actum, qui est vsus, reperiri in rebus consumptibilib. (& ipso actu, & cum ipso actu) isti duo modi loquendi nō important aliud in propósito, quam primus modus loquendi, cum dicitur per actum. (In ipsius q rei exerceatur substantia) oppositum patet de vsu pecuniæ. (Nec sine rei consumptione esse valeat vsus talis) contrarium patet de vsu vestium & pecuniarum & multarum aliarum rerum consumptibilium (res huiusmodi insinuatur.) Istud est falsum: siue intelligatur de consumptione rei quantum ad substantiam, siue de consumptione quantum ad dominium, patet quando aliquis vtitur ad pompam pecunia.
units.tr: Clement V, as is clear above in chapter 32, expressly defines this; and Innocent IV and Alexander IV bear clear witness in their declarations, who say: "It is further said that, since the rule itself expressly contains that the Brothers appropriate nothing to themselves, neither house, nor place, nor any thing, because they ought to have no property either in common or in particular, but the order has the use of places, houses, utensils, books, and their movable goods (which they are allowed to have), and the Brothers use these as the general and provincial ministers shall have decided to be arranged." And Clement IV, in a certain privilege, says: "Since our beloved sons the Lesser Brothers, by the vow of their profession, have so voluntarily submitted themselves to poverty that they can obtain nothing of their own, either separately or in common, but all things which are bestowed on them as alms, or otherwise come to them through regard for them, are known to fall under the right and property of the Church of Rome," etc. And Gregory IV, in a certain privilege, says: "The Order of Brothers, devoted to the humility of poverty, has cast off both the thing and the name of appropriation; and whatever is known to come to it is said, by the very fact, to pass into our dominion and that of the Church of Rome." And Pope Martin IV, in the privilege which begins Exultantes, says: "Since the Brothers, who cannot be sued in court for any temporal thing, and with all anxieties set aside, may devote themselves freely and quietly to divine services, and the pious intention of those offering, giving, granting, or leaving anything in their last will to the said order or the brothers for God's sake is not defrauded; so that we are not burdened with the anxiety which the said order, as often as necessity presses or advantage suggests, is compelled to have recourse to the Church of Rome for its needs, to which belong, in no way, ownership and dominion of all movable and immovable things which the brothers may use," etc. From these and many other assertions of the supreme Pontiffs it is clearly evident that the Lesser Brothers have no dominion or ownership of anything consumable which they use; and yet they use consumable things; therefore their use of such things is separated from ownership or dominion. Secondly, the opponents say that the reasoning by which the author tries to prove the aforesaid assertion includes several errors. The first of these is that through such an act, and in the act itself and together with the act, such a thing is preserved. The second is that an act of this kind is exercised upon the very substance of the thing. The third is that such an act cannot exist without the consumption of the thing. The opponents say all these errors are refuted by a single example. For when someone spends money and buys something with the money, the money is not consumed as to its substance either through such an act, or in the act itself, or together with the act; nor is such an act exercised upon the substance of the money itself; and such an act can exist without the consumption of this thing. The same could be proved by many other examples. But as to the reasoning, these opponents say it is founded on something false. For it is founded on this middle term: no act of using any thing is separated from ownership or dominion when the thing is consumed by the act, in the act, and together with the act. But this proof is false, and by their account it has not even the appearance of truth. For the consumption of a thing does no more make the act unable to be separated from one dominion than from another. If, therefore, on account of the consumption of the thing the use cannot be separated from the dominion of the user, then by the same reasoning it could not be separated from any dominion whatever, and so it could not be separated from the dominion of God, nor from the dominion of kings, nor from any other dominion. (Since through such a use, that is, the act of using.) Here he concedes that the act of using, which is use, is found in consumable things. (And in the act itself, and together with the act.) These two modes of speaking do not mean anything else in the matter than the first mode of speaking, when it is said "through the act." (That the substance of the thing itself is exercised.) The opposite is plain of the use of money. (Nor can such a use exist without the consumption of the thing.) The contrary is plain of the use of clothes, money, and many other consumable things. (Such a thing is insinuated.) This is false, whether it is understood of the consumption of the thing as to its substance, or of its consumption as to dominion; this is plain when someone uses money for display.

units.la: CAP. LXXXII.
units.tr: CAP. LXXXII.

units.la: Dicit enim quod predicta constitutio intelligit, quod statim & vltimate in actu vtendi res huiusmodi consumatur, cum manifestum sit quod vestes non statim in primo actu vtendi vltimate & omnino consumantur: sicut & panis non statim in principio actus consumitur, & sic non est inconueniens, quod Dominus habeat dominium cibi vel panis existentis in ore serui.
units.tr: For he says that the aforesaid constitution means that such things are consumed immediately and ultimately in the act of using them, since it is plain that clothes are not at once and wholly consumed in the first act of using them, just as bread is not consumed at once at the beginning of eating it; and so it is no absurdity that the lord should have ownership of the food or bread that is in the mouth of his servant.

units.la: Hic recitat obiectionem appellantis contra assertionem praedictam, quae duas obiectiones includit: quarum prima est: Quod nec vestes semper consumuntur: nec panis consumitur in principio actus, secunda est, quod sicut quis habet dominium serui sui, ita habet dominium panis existentis in ore serui. (Praedicta constitutio intelligit quod statim & vltimate, &c.) quia aliter non est ad propositum, vt post patebit (ita non est inconueniens quod Dominus habeat dominium cibi, &c.) Ad hoc iste impugnatus non respondet.
units.tr: Here he recites the objection of the appellant against the aforesaid assertion, which includes two objections. The first is: that clothes are not always consumed, nor is bread consumed at the beginning of the act; the second is: that just as someone has ownership of his servant, so he has ownership of the bread that is in the servant's mouth. (The aforesaid constitution means that immediately and ultimately, etc.) This is because otherwise it is not to the point, as will become clear later. (So it is no absurdity that the lord should have ownership of the food, etc.) The one who is attacked does not answer this.

units.la: CAP. LXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 63.

units.la: Ad hoc dicendum est, quod iste haereticus imponit constitutioni, quod nec intellexit nec dixit, videl. quod in primo actu vtendi vltimate & omnino res vsu consumptibiles consumantur: sed intellexit & euidenter expressit, quod per vsum vtendi perfectum, per quem res dicuntur vsu consumptibiles, consumantur: dixit enim, quod per talem vsum, id est vtendi actum & in ipso, & cum ipso actu res huiusmodi consumuntur. Posuit enim copulatiue vtendi actum & in ipso actu & cum ipso actu, unde satis expressit, quod non per ipsius actus principium consumantur res huiusmodi, sed per actum perfectum. Item subiunxit, quod actus vtendi in ipsius rei consumptibilis vsu exercetur substantia: nec sine ipsius rei consumptione esse valeat vsus talis. Unde cum dicat, quod sine rei consumptione esse non valeat vsus talis, satis euidenter expressit, quod de vsu illo, per quem res consumitur, non de eius principio, intellexit.
units.tr: To this it must be said that this heretic imputes to the constitution what he neither understood nor said, namely that in the first act of using, things consumed by use are wholly and ultimately consumed. Rather, he understood and plainly expressed that things consumable by use are consumed through the perfect use by which they are called consumable by use. For he said that such things are consumed by such use, that is, by the act of using and in it, and together with the act itself. For he joined by "and" the act of using, "in it" and "together with the act itself," so that he sufficiently expressed that such things are not consumed through the beginning of the act itself, but through the completed act. Moreover, he added that the act of using is carried out in the substance of the thing's use as consumable, and that such use cannot exist without the consumption of the thing itself. Therefore, since he says that such use cannot exist without the consumption of the thing, he has quite clearly expressed that he meant by that use, through which the thing is consumed, not its beginning.

units.la: Hic ad obiectionem respondet, qp appellans constitutioni falsum imponit. Ad qp probandū innuit vnā distinctionē de vsu, qp videl. quidā est vsus perfectus, & quidā est vsus imperfectus, p quem respondet. det dicens: quod appellans imponit constitutioni, quod intelligat, quod per primum actum vtedi res consumatur, quod falsum est (vt dicit) quia constitutio intellexit de actu perfecto, per quem res consumitur: quod dupliciter per verba ipsius constitutionis probare conatur, vt patet in litera.
units.tr: Here he answers the objection by saying that the appellant falsely imputes to the constitution. To prove this he suggests a distinction concerning use, namely that some use is perfect and some use is imperfect, by which he replies. He says that the appellant imputes to the constitution that it means that the thing is consumed by the first act of using, which is false (as he says), because the constitution understood it of the perfect act by which the thing is consumed. He tries to prove this in two ways from the words of the constitution itself, as is evident in the text.

units.la: Sed impugnatores dicunt, quod in nullo respondet ad obiectionem appellantis. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt primo, esse sciendum quod actus vtendi non potest intelligi esse perfectus, nisi tripliciter. Primo quia nihil deficit actui, quod requiritur ad esse vel bene esse actus: sicut homo dicitur perfectus, quia nihil deficit homini, quod requiritur ad esse vel bene esse hominis, & iste modus duos modos perfecti includit. Secundo dicitur actus perfectus, quia finitus vel completus: sicut motus dicitur perfectus, quia finitur vel completur. Tertio potest intelligi perfectus, quia per ipsum deuenitur ad illud, & per ipsum intendebatur, sicut aedificatio domus dicitur perfecta, quando domus est facta, hoc est, aedificans intendebat.
units.tr: But the opponents say that he does not answer the objection of the appellant in any way. To make this clear they say, first, that it must be known that an act of using cannot be understood as perfect except in three ways. First, because nothing is lacking to the act that is required for the being or well-being of the act; just as a man is said to be perfect because nothing is lacking to him that is required for the being or well-being of a man, and this way includes two modes of perfection. Second, an act is said to be perfect because it is finished or completed; just as a motion is said to be perfect because it is finished or completed. Third, it can be understood as perfect because by it one arrives at that thing and it was intended by it; just as the building of a house is said to be perfect when the house has been made, that is, when the builder intended it.

units.la: Secundo dicunt esse sciendum, quod appellans nunc intendebat probare, quod actus vtendi in rebus vsu consumptibilibus, qui est finitus & completus, est a proprietate seu dominio separatus: quia tunc non est separatus, nec coniunctus, eo quod tunc non est, sed intendebat probare, quod actus vtendi in rebus huiusmodi, dum durat seu exercetur, potest a proprietate seu dominio separari. Per haec patet, quod ratio appellantis est irrevocata penitus & insoluta. Nam si tu dicis, quod res consumitur per actum perfectum, aut intelligis de actu perfecto primo modo, secundo vel tertio modo. Si primo modo, sic stat ratio appellantis, quia quantumcunque induitio vestis sit perfecta primo modo, & quantumcunque esset comestio panis consumpti: imo si panis esset tunc consumptus, ipsa comestio minime exercetur secundum modum istius loquendi. Si intelligis de actu perfecto secundo modo, vel tertio, sic planum est: quod talis actus non est a proprietate seu dominio separatus, sed hoc non est: quia res est consumpta per talem actum: sed quia talis actus non est: quia successiuum quando finitur seu completur, tunc non est, propter quod talis actus non est separatus a dominio seu proprietate. Hoc etiam patet: quia talis actus perfectus secundo modo vel tertio non plus potest esse separatus in rebus non consumptibilibus vsu a proprietate seu dominio, quam in rebus consumptibilibus vsu.
units.tr: Second, they say it must be known that the appellant was now intending to prove that the act of using things consumable by use, which is finished and completed, is separated from ownership or dominion; for then it is not separated, nor joined, because then it is not. Rather, he intended to prove that the act of using such things, while it lasts or is carried on, can be separated from ownership or dominion. From these things it is clear that the appellant's argument is wholly unrefuted and unanswered. For if you say that a thing is consumed by a perfect act, you mean either the perfect act in the first, the second or the third sense. If in the first sense, the appellant's argument stands, because however perfect the wearing of a garment is in the first sense, and however much the eating of bread is consumed; indeed, if the bread were then consumed, the eating itself is in no way carried on according to the manner of speaking. If you mean a perfect act in the second or third sense, then it is plain that such an act is not separated from ownership or dominion; but this is not the point, because the thing is consumed by such an act. Yet such an act is not, because a successive act, when it is finished or completed, then is not; on account of which such an act is not separated from ownership or property. This is also clear, because a perfect act in the second or third sense can no more be separated from ownership or property in things not consumable by use than in things consumable by use.

units.la: Constat n. quod actus inhabitandi domum, qui est completus & finitus, non est separatus a proprietate domus: quia tunc cessat, nec est tunc, nec etiam exercetur tunc: & ita est de omni actu alio perfecto secundo modo, vel tertio modo, ergo actus inhabitandi domum perfectus non potest separari a dominio, & per consequens quod res consumatur nihil facit ad hoc, quod actus possit a proprietate seu dominio separari, vel non possit separari: quia domus non consumitur per actum inhabitandi perfectum, & tamen actus inhabitandi domum perfectus, id est finitus & completus, non est a proprietate domus, seu dominio separatus, & ideo ratio istius impugnati non plus probat, quod actus vtendi in rebus consumptibilibus vsu non potest a proprietate seu dominio separari, quam quod actus vtendi in rebus non consumptibilib. vsu non potest a proprietate seu dominio separari, quare sicut absolute sine distinctione concedit & asserit, quod actus vtendi non potest in rebus consumptibilibus vsu a proprietate & dominio separari: ita deberet absolute, & sine distinctione concedere, quod actus vtendi non potest in rebus non consumptibilibus vsu a proprietate & dominio separari, & ex hoc etiam patet, quod sicut per rationem praecedentem positam supra, concedit & asserit quod simplex vsus, id est sine iure vtendi a proprietate seu dominio separatus, in re vsu consumptibili haberi non potest: ita absolute & sine distinctione, propter eandem rationem debet concedere, quod simplex vsus, id est sine iure vtendi a proprietate seu dominio separatus, in re non consumptibili vsu haberi non potest: quia illa ratio non plus concludit de vsu rei consumptibilis vsu, quam de vsu rei non consumptibilis vsu: imo quicquid dicit de inseparabilitate vsus rei consumptibilis vsu a iure vtendi, & a proprietate seu dominio, deberet similiter dicere de inseparabilitate vsus rei non consumptibilis vsu a iure vtedi, & a proprietate seu dominio. Item contra praedicta arguunt sic: aut per actum vtendi non perfectum vel principium actus, per quem vel per quod nequaquam res consumitur, necessario acquiritur dominium rei seu proprietas, si antea minime habebatur: aut non necessario acquiritur, etiam licet prius habitum non fuisset.
units.tr: For it is certain that the act of inhabiting a house, which is complete and finished, is not separated from the ownership of the house; because then it ceases, and it neither is nor is carried on then. And so it is with every other act perfect in the second or third sense. Therefore the perfect act of inhabiting cannot be separated from dominion; and consequently that the thing is consumed contributes nothing to whether the act can or cannot be separated from ownership or dominion, because the house is not consumed by the perfect act of inhabiting, and yet the perfect act of inhabiting the house, that is, finished and completed, is not separated from the ownership or dominion of the house. Hence this opponent's argument proves no more that the act of using things consumable by use cannot be separated from ownership or dominion than that the act of using things not consumable by use cannot be separated from ownership or dominion. Therefore, just as he absolutely and without distinction concedes and asserts that the act of using things consumable by use cannot be separated from ownership and dominion, he ought absolutely and without distinction to concede that the act of using things not consumable by use cannot be separated from ownership and dominion. And from this it is also clear that, just as by the preceding argument set out above he concedes and asserts that simple use, that is, use separated from the right of using and from ownership or dominion, cannot be had in a thing consumable by use, so absolutely and without distinction, for the same reason, he ought to concede that simple use, that is, use separated from the right of using and from ownership or dominion, cannot be had in a thing not consumable by use. For that argument concludes no more about the use of a thing consumable by use than about the use of a thing not consumable by use. Indeed, whatever he says about the inseparability of the use of a consumable thing from the right of using and from ownership or dominion, he ought similarly to say about the inseparability of the use of a non-consumable thing from the right of using and from ownership or dominion. Again, they argue against what has been said thus: either by an act of using that is not perfect, or by the beginning of an act, by which or through which the thing is in no way consumed, ownership or property of the thing is necessarily acquired, if it was not previously had at all; or it is not necessarily acquired, even if it was not previously had.

units.la: Si detur primum, ergo sicut actus perfectus non potest esse a dominio separatus in re consumptibili vsu, ita etiam actus alius qui non est perfectus secundum istum, non potest in re consumptibili vsu a proprietate seu dominio separari, & per consequens absq; rei consumptione non potest in rebus vsu consumptibilib. actus vtendi a proprietate seu dominio separari. Si detur secundum, habetur propositio appellantis, quod sc. aliquis potest vti re vsu consumptibili absq; dominio seu proprietate in primo actu vtendi vltimate & omnino res vsu consumptibiles consumantur, quia aliter non probaretur per rationem illam, quod actus vtendi non potest a proprietate seu dominio separari, imo non obstante illa ratione: multi actus vtendi eadem re possent a proprietate & dominio separari: & omnis actus talis vsque ad finem actus posset a proprietate seu dominio separari: quia vsque ad finem actus vtendi res minime est consumpta.
