units.tr: If the first is granted, then just as a perfect act cannot be separated from dominion in a thing consumable by use, so too another act which is not perfect according to him cannot be separated from property or dominion in a thing consumable by use; and consequently, without consumption of the thing, the act of using things consumable by use cannot be separated from property or dominion. If the second is granted, the appellant's proposition is had, namely that someone can use a thing consumable by use without dominion or property in the first act of using, and that things consumable by use are wholly and ultimately consumed; for otherwise it would not be proved by that argument that the act of using cannot be separated from property or dominion. Indeed, notwithstanding that argument, many acts of using with the same thing could be separated from property and dominion, and every such act up to the end of the act could be separated from property or dominion, because up to the end of the act of using the thing is in no way consumed.

units.la: (Euidenter expressit quod per actum vtendi.) De actu vtendi perfecto nunquam prius fecerat mentionem, sed absolute vsus fuerat actu vtedi, nunquam distinguens inter actum vtendi perfectum & imperfectum, vocatur autem hic actus vtendi perfectus, actus vtendi finitus & consummatus, & verum est quod tunc actus non est separatus a dominio rei sine res fuerit consumptibilis vsu, siue non fuerit consumptibilis vsu: quia tunc actus non est, nec etiam exercetur. (Dixit enim quod per talem vsum, id est vtendi actum, &c.) Hic ponitur vna probatio, per quam conatur ostendere quod intellexit de actu vtendi perfecto. (Posuit enim copulatiue vtendi actum & in ipso actu, & cum ipso actu.) Hoc est contra ipsum: quia ex copulatiua sequitur, quaelibet pars copulatiue, & ita ex quo concedit copulatiuam, oportet eum concedere quamlibet partem eius per se positam. Sicut si Paulus est homo, & Martinus est homo: sequitur quod Paulus est homo. (Unde satis expressit, quod non per ipsum actum principium consumantur res huiusmodi) male infert. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum: quod differentia est inter consumi & consumptum esse: sicut inter moueri & motum esse: & inter alterari & alteratum esse: & ideo licet expressisset, quod per ipsius actus principium res non consumeretur, quia sicut motus & alteratio non sunt in instanti, sed in tempore, ita etiam consumi non est in instanti, sed in tempore. (Sed per actum perfectum) verum est, quod per actum perfectum, hoc est finitum & completum, aliqua res est consumpta, tamen in principio actus res incipit consumi. Saepe tamen sunt actus vtendi plures perfecti, respectu eiusdem rei vsu consumptibilis, per quos tamen res minime est consumpta, patet de vestibus. (Item subiunxit quod actus vtendi in ipsius rei consumptibilis exercetur facto.) Hic incipit alia probatio ad idem: sc. quod intellexit de actu vtendi perfecto, sed dicunt, quod illud quod hic accipit, & prius asseruit, falsum est: quia vsus pecuniae non exercetur in substantia pecuniae: quia substantia pecuniae p vsum non variatur nec alteratur in aliquo, nisi forte aliquando per accidens. (Nec sine rei consumptione esse valeat vsus talis) hoc etiam falsum est, sicut prius est ostensum (de vsu illo, per quem res consumitur non de eius principio intellexit.) Ex hoc sequitur, quod per dicta rationem nullo modo probatur, quod comedens panem & bibens vinum ac vtens aliis rebus consumptibilibus, dum comedit & bibit & vitur aliis rebus, habet dominium & proprietatem rei talis, & ita non obstante ratione praedicta potest quis comedere panem, cuius non habet dominium: & bibere vinum, cuius non ipse, sed alius habet dominium, & hoc solum hic intendit appellans.
units.tr: (Clearly he expressed that by the act of using.) He had never before mentioned a perfect act of using. He had simply used "act of using" without ever distinguishing between a perfect and an imperfect act. Here, however, this act is called perfect, finished and completed. It is true that the act is not separated from ownership of the thing, whether or not the thing is consumable by use, since then the act does not exist and is not even exercised. (For he said that through such use, that is, the act of using, etc.) Here one proof is offered by which he tries to show that he meant a perfect act of using. (For he put the act of using conjunctively, both in the act itself and with the act itself.) This tells against him, for from a conjunctive statement it follows that each part of the conjunction holds. So once he concedes the conjunction, he must concede each part of it taken by itself, as when Paul is a man and Martin is a man, and it follows that Paul is a man. (Hence he has sufficiently made clear that such things are not consumed by the beginning of the act itself) he infers wrongly. To make this evident, they say one must know that there is a difference between to be consumed and to have been consumed, just as between to be moved and to have been moved, and between to be altered and to have been altered. So although he had said that the thing is not consumed by the beginning of the act, motion and alteration are not in an instant but in time, and so too being consumed is not in an instant but in time. (But through a perfect act) it is true that through a perfect act, that is a finished and complete one, some thing has been consumed. Yet at the beginning of the act the thing begins to be consumed. Often, however, there are several perfect acts of using with respect to the same thing consumable by use, through which the thing is nevertheless not at all consumed. This is evident in the case of clothes. (Likewise he added that the act of using is exercised on the very thing consumed by the using.) Here begins another proof of the same point, namely that he meant a perfect act of using. But they say that what he takes here, and had asserted before, is false, because the use of money is not exercised on the substance of money. The substance of money is not varied or altered in any way by use, except perhaps sometimes accidentally. (Nor can such use exist without consumption of the thing) this too is false, as was shown before. (He understood that use by which the thing is consumed, not its beginning.) From this it follows that by the said argument it is in no way proved that one who eats bread, drinks wine and uses other consumable things, while he eats, drinks and uses those things, has ownership and property of such a thing. So, notwithstanding the aforesaid argument, a man may eat bread of which he has no ownership, and drink wine of which he himself does not have ownership but another does. This alone is what the appellant here intends. ## CHAPTER LXXIV.

units.la: CAP. LXXIV.

Rursus dictus haereticus dictam assertionem impugnare nititur in eo, quod dicit, quod retentio dominii quam summus Pontifex fecit in rebus, quae ad Fratres Minores obuenerant, vel inposterum obuenirent, dictis fratribus quantum ad statum perfectionis nequaquam profuit, quantum ad hoc quod propter carentiam talis dominii se pauperiores dicere valeant, quam si res illas cum illo, quo carere se dicunt dominio obtinerent, & infra: Talis enim carentia re in praesenti ac spe in futurum omni commodo denudati pauperiorem non efficit non habentem, & infra: Nolentes in posterum, quod sub pretextu seu pallio talis dominii verbalis, nudi & aenigmatici fomentum quantum malis, quantum precedunt ex simulatione huiusmodi ministretur, sancimus, &c.
units.tr: Again the said heretic strives to impugn that assertion in that he says that the retention of ownership which the supreme Pontiff made in the things that had come, or would in future come, to the Friars Minor did not in any way benefit the friars as regards the state of perfection, so that by reason of the lack of such ownership they could call themselves poorer than if they obtained those things with that ownership of which they say they are bereft; and below: For such a lack, stripped of every advantage in present things and in hope for the future, does not make the one who does not have them poorer; and below: Wishing that in future, under the pretext or cloak of such verbal, bare and enigmatic ownership, no nourishment of evils, however great, arising from such pretence be supplied, we decree, etc.

units.la: Postquam iste impugnatus in parte praecedenti respondit ad obiectiones appellantis contra quartam assertionem eiusdem: hic incipit respondere ad obiectiones appellantis contra quintam assertionem istius impugnati, quam reputat appellans haereticam, & diuiditur in tres partes; quia primo replicat ipsam assertionem impugnatam, secundo recitat ipsam impugnationem, tertio ad impugnationem respondet. Secunda pars incipit in parte immediate sequenti. Tertia ibi: Profecto est haereticum. Dicta autem assertio continet tres partes: quarum prima est, quod carentia dominii in rebus quibus Fratres Minores vtuntur, non prodest fratribus quantum ad statum perfectionis, vt per talem carentiam se valeant dicere pauperiores. Secunda est, quod carentia dominii omni temporali commodo denudati pauperiorem non efficit non habentem: tertia est quod tale dominium est verbale, nudum, aenigmaticum: & de istis patebit inferius. (Retentio dominii.) Intendit quod carentia dominii seu expropriatio huiusmodi non profuit fratribus sicut ex consequentibus apparebit (quo carere se dicunt dominio) inuit, quod in rei veritate Fratres non carent dominio huiusmodi rerum: licet dicant falso se carere tali dominio (omni commodo denudati) dicunt quod tale dominium non est ab omni commodo spirituali denudatum, sicut postea ostendetur (pauperiorem non efficit non habentem) hoc probabunt irrationabiliter omnino dici.
units.tr: After this man, who was impugned in the preceding part, answered the appellant's objections to the fourth assertion of the same author, here he begins to answer the appellant's objections to the fifth assertion of this impugned author, which the appellant considers heretical. It is divided into three parts: first he restates the impugned assertion itself, second he recites the impugning, and third he answers the impugning. The second part begins in the immediately following part, and the third there: Assuredly it is heretical. The said assertion contains three parts. The first is that the lack of ownership in the things the Friars Minor use does not benefit the friars as regards the state of perfection, so that through such a lack they could call themselves poorer. The second is that a lack of ownership, stripped of every temporal advantage, does not make one who lacks it poorer. The third is that such ownership is verbal, bare and enigmatic. About these things it will become clear further below. (The retention of ownership.) He means that the lack of ownership, or expropriation of this kind, did not benefit the friars, as will appear from what follows. (From which they say they are bereft of ownership.) He implies that in the truth of the matter the friars do not lack ownership of such things, although they falsely say they lack such ownership. (Stripped of every advantage.) They say that such ownership is not stripped of every spiritual advantage, as will be shown later. (Does not make the one who lacks it poorer.) This they will prove to be said quite unreasonably.

units.la: CAP. LXXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXV.

units.la: Praedicta verba secundum ipsum haereticum S. Scriptura ac doctrina euangelica & Apostolica & sancta matri ecclesia obuiant & repugnant. Nam ex scriptura diuina superius (vt asserit) est ostensum, quod Apostoli & eos sequentes viri perfecti ex consilio Christi proprietatem & dominium rerum temporalium omnium reliquerunt vsu rerum necessariarum ad vitam humanam sustentationem, cui non est licitum renunciare, contenti. Constat (secundum ipsum) quod dominium quod Apostoli in rebus omnibus temporalibus, quarum vsum habebant ex Christi consilio reliquerunt, fuit omni temporali commodo vsu, scil. vtili denudatum, sicut manifeste patet in rebus, quorum proprietatem & dominium vsu retento, prout euangelica testatur historia, reliquerunt, cum in consilio Christi dato de rebus temporalibus abdicandis abdicatio proprietatis & dominii earum rerum & non vsus, vt superius ostenditur, includatur. Si ergo carentia talis dominii ad perfectionem non pertinet, nec pauperiorem efficit non habentem, sicut dicta constitutio dogmatizat: Sequitur quod Christus simulatam & fallacem doctrinam tribuit volentibus ad persectionem attingere consulendo, quod omnia temporalia quae ad proprietatem & dominium relinqueret. Et quod Augustin. & Hieronymus doctores ecclesiae, & alii sancti patres institutores religionum erraverunt, qui dictum Christi consilium sequi volentes abdicationem proprietatis & dominii rerum omnium sunt professi.
units.tr: According to the heretic himself, the words quoted above are opposed to and contrary to Holy Scripture, the Gospel and Apostolic doctrine, and the holy mother Church. For, as he asserts above, it has been shown from divine Scripture that the Apostles, and the men who followed them as perfect men, by Christ's counsel gave up the ownership and dominion of all temporal goods, while content with the use of the things necessary for sustaining human life, and it is not lawful to renounce that use. It follows (according to him) that the dominion which the Apostles gave up over all temporal goods, the use of which they had by Christ's counsel, was stripped of every temporal benefit of use, that is, of useful use. This is plainly evident in the things whose ownership and dominion they gave up while keeping the use of them, as the Gospel history bears witness; since in Christ's counsel on giving up temporal goods, the renunciation of the ownership and dominion of those things, and not of their use, is included, as is shown above. If, therefore, the lack of such dominion does not pertain to perfection, and does not make the one who lacks it poorer, as the said constitution dogmatizes, it follows that Christ offered a feigned and deceptive doctrine to those who wished to attain perfection by counsel, namely that they should give up all temporal goods which they would retain as ownership and dominion. And that Augustine and Jerome, teachers of the Church, and the other holy Fathers, who founded religious orders, erred, since, wishing to follow Christ's counsel, they professed the renunciation of ownership and dominion over all things.

units.la: Hic impugnatus recitat obiectiones appellantis contra assertionem praedictam, quae consistit in hoc, quod Christus talem abdicationem talis dominii consuluit, & Apostoli tale dominium reliquerunt: & similiter sancti patres religionum institutores vsu rerum necessariarum vitae humanae sustentatione, cui non est licitum renunciare contenti, iuxta illud Apostoli: habentes alimenta & quibus tegamur, his contenti simus.
units.tr: Here the one under attack recites the objections of the appellant against the aforesaid assertion. These consist in this: that Christ counselled such a renunciation of such dominion, and that the Apostles gave up such dominion, and likewise that the holy Fathers who founded religious orders, content with the use of the things necessary for sustaining human life, which it is not lawful to renounce, act according to the Apostle's words: having food and covering, with these let us be content.

units.la: (Fuit enim temporali commodo vsu scilicet vtili denudatum) scilicet illo tempore quo Apostoli habuerunt vsum & alii dominium.
units.tr: (For it was stripped of every temporal benefit of use, that is, of useful use), namely at that time when the Apostles had the use and others had the ownership.

units.la: CAP. LXXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXVI.

units.la: PRefecto iste haereticus, vt praevaricator legis, notorie verba constitutionis praedictae truncate recitat illa, quae eius defectum manifeste insinuant, omittendo. Intendit enim probare dicta constitutio, quod retentio dominii praedicta facta per summum pontificem, quantum ad statum perfectionis nequaquam praedictis Fratribus profuit, quam probationem omittit haereticus supradictus, quae talis est, vt ex dicta constitutionis tenore manifestius liquet. Quod enim inquit, quantum ad statum perfectionis profuerit retentio dominii supradictae, patet, cum enim perfectio vitae Christianae principaliter & essentialiter in caritate consistat, quae ab Apostolo vinculum perfectionis dicitur: & quae vnit seu iungit aliqualiter in via hominem suo fini. Ad quam per contemptum bonorum temporalium & ipsorum expropriationem via disponitur: per hoc praecipue quod sollicitudo, quam ipsa temporalia in acquirendo, conseruando, & dispensando exigunt quamplurimum ab actu caritatis retrahens amputatur. Restat, quod si sollicitudo eadem post expropriationem huiusmodi, quae ante ipsam inerat, perseueret, ad perfectionem huiusmodi, talis expropriatio valeat nil conferre. Constat autem, quod post ordinationem praedictam non fuerunt in acquirendis aut conseruandis bonis praedictis in iudicio & extra minus solliciti, quam ante illam fuerant Fratres ipsi, qua quod sint Religiosi Mendicantes, alii habentes aliqua in communi. Credimus vtiq; quod nullus sapiens probationem huiusmodi reprobabit, propter quod ipsam haereticus non expressit.
units.tr: This heretic, like a prevaricator of the law, obviously recites the words of the aforementioned constitution in a truncated form, omitting those that clearly expose its weakness. For the constitution intends to prove that the retention of ownership made by the supreme pontiff did not in the least benefit the aforesaid Brothers as regards the state of perfection. The heretic leaves out the proof on which this rests, and it is as follows, as is clearer from the tenor of the constitution. For what it says, that the aforesaid retention of ownership benefited the state of perfection, is evident. Since the perfection of the Christian life consists chiefly and essentially in charity, which the Apostle calls the bond of perfection, and which in some measure joins a man to his end while he is on the way, the way to it is prepared by contempt of temporal goods and their renunciation, chiefly in that the anxiety which temporal goods demand in acquiring, keeping and dispensing them is cut off, drawing one away from the act of charity. It follows that if this same anxiety remains after such renunciation as was there before it, such renunciation can contribute nothing to that perfection. It is certain, however, that after the aforesaid ordinance the Brothers themselves were no less anxious, in judgment and outside it, about acquiring or keeping those goods than they had been before, since they are mendicant religious, while others have some things in common. We believe, at any rate, that no wise person will reject this proof, and the heretic therefore has not stated it.

units.la: Hic impugnatus ad obiectiones appellantis contra praedictam assertionem respondet. Et diuiditur in duas partes: quia primo respondet ad obiectiones in praecedenti capitulo recitatas. Secundo respondet ad quasdam alias tacitas in appellatione appellantis. Secunda ibi: Ad illud autem quod induxit. Prima diuiditur in tres, secundum quod ad tria tacta in obiectionibus praedictis respondet. Secunda ibi: Ad hoc autem quod ipse dicit. Tertia ibi: Ad illud autem quod dicit. Prima adhuc in duas diuiditur, secundum quod duo dicta in constitutione Ad conditorem replicat, ad ostendendum quod appellans truncate recitat illa, quae in dicta constitutione Ad conditorem habentur, per quae, vt dicit, defectus appellantis ostenditur. Secunda pars incipit in parte immediate sequenti ibi: Item intendit. In prima igitur parte dicit, quod appellans truncate recitat verba constitutionis Ad conditorem: quia omittit rationem, per quam probatur quod talis retentio dominii facta per summum pontificem nequaquam profuit Fratribus quantum ad statum perfectionis. Est autem ratio talis Perfectio vitae Christianae essentialiter consistit in caritate, ad quam per contemptum temporalium praecipue via disponitur, per hoc quod sollicitudo circa temporalia amputatur, ergo si sollicitudo sit eadem post expropriationem huiusmodi, quae fuit ante expropriationem: huiusmodi expropriatio ad perfectionem nihil confert, sed Fratres Minores fuerunt aeque solliciti circa temporalia post expropriationem huiusmodi, sicut ante & sicut aliireligiosi mendicantes: quia fuerunt aeque solliciti circa temporalia post ordinationem Nicolai tertii de retentione dominii sicut ante, ergo talis expropriatio ad perfectionem nihil contulit eis.
units.tr: Here the author, having been attacked, replies to the objections of the appellant against the aforesaid assertion. The reply is divided into two parts: first he answers the objections recited in the preceding chapter, and second he answers certain other objections implied in the appellant's appeal. The second part begins at "Now as to what he has brought forward." The first part is divided into three, according to the three points touched upon in those objections that he answers. The second begins at "But as to what he himself says." The third begins at "But as to what he says." The first part is further divided into two, since he replies to two statements in the constitution Ad conditorem, to show that the appellant recites in truncated form the things that are contained in that constitution Ad conditorem, through which, as he says, the appellant's defect is shown. The second part begins in the immediately following section, at "Furthermore he intends." In the first part, then, he says that the appellant recites the words of the constitution Ad conditorem in truncated form, because he omits the reasoning by which it is proved that such retention of ownership made by the supreme pontiff in no way benefited the Brothers as regards the state of perfection. The reasoning is as follows: the perfection of the Christian life consists essentially in charity, and the way to it is prepared chiefly by the contempt of temporal things, in that anxiety about temporal things is cut off. Therefore, if the anxiety after such renunciation is the same as it was before, such renunciation contributes nothing to perfection. But the Friars Minor were equally anxious about temporal things after this renunciation as before, and as the other mendicant religious are. For they were equally anxious about temporal things after the ordinance of Nicholas III on the retention of ownership as before. Therefore such renunciation contributed nothing to their perfection.

units.la: Sed impugnatores probare conantur, quod in ista ratione hic adducta, quam omisit appellans, plures errores & mendacia Fratrum diffamatoria continentur. Ex quibus reprobatae impugnationes appellantis fortiores intelligentibus apparebunt. Primus autem error hic contentus, vt dicunt, est quod expropriatio siue abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium in speciali & in communi ad statum perfectionis non pertinet. Secundus est quod ad caritatem per contemptum bonorum temporalium & expropriationem ipsorum via disponitur. Per hoc praecipue quod sollicitudo quam ipsa temporalia in acquirendo & conseruando exigunt amputatur. Tertius est quod si manet eadem sollicitudo ante expropriationem omnium temporalium, quae fuit ante dictam expropriationem, talis expropriatio ad perfectionem valet nil conferre, primum vero mendacium diffamatorium hic contentum est, quod post expropriationem huiusmodi Fratres Minores non minus fuerunt circa temporalia solliciti in iudicio & extra quam ante fuerant. Secundum est quod Fratres Minores non sunt minus solliciti circa temporalia, quam alii religiosi Mendicantes. Si autem intelligeret, quod Fratribus praedicta duo competerent ex statu suo, essent erronea reputanda.
units.tr: But the opponents try to prove that this argument, which the appellant omitted, contains several errors and defamatory lies against the Brothers. From these the rebuttals of the appellant's attacks will appear the stronger to those who understand them. The first error contained here, as they say, is that the renunciation or abdication of ownership of all temporal goods, both individually and in common, does not pertain to the state of perfection. The second is that the way to charity is prepared chiefly by contempt of temporal goods and their renunciation, in that the anxiety which temporal goods demand in acquiring and keeping them is cut off. The third is that if the same anxiety remains after the renunciation of all temporal goods as was there before that renunciation, such renunciation contributes nothing to perfection. The first defamatory lie contained here is that after such renunciation the Friars Minor were no less anxious about temporal things, in judgment and outside it, than they had been before. The second is that the Friars Minor are no less anxious about temporal things than the other mendicant religious. But if he understood that the two aforesaid points belonged to the Brothers by reason of their state, they would have to be regarded as erroneous.

units.la: Primus igitur error, vt dicunt isti, contentus in verbis praedictis, est quod expropriatio siue abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium in speciali & in communi ad statum perfectionis non pertinet. Quod enim hoc intendat, patet aperte. Nam dicit, quod retentio dominii supradicta Fratribus non profuit ad perfectionis statum, per retentionem autem dominii intelligit expropriationem praedictam. Nam praemissa ista conclusione probanda, quantum ad statum perfectionis nequaquam eis profuit retentio dominii supradicta: Postea in ratione, per quam istam conclusionem probare conatur, de retentione dominii nulla fit mentio, sed tantum modo de expropriatione, quare cum praemisit, quod retentio dominii eis non profuit de expropriatione intellexit. Vel si voluit distinguere inter retentionem dominii & expropriationem: oportet quod per rationem suam primo probet istam conclusionem. Expropriatio supradicta non profuit Fratribus quantum ad statum perfectionis. Et ex ista infert istam: Retentio dominii non profuit eis: & ita manifeste patet ratione suam, qui intendit, quod expropriatio omnium temporalium ad statum perfectionis non prodest. Sed hoc sit erroneum reputandum isti impugnatores multipliciter probare conantur. Dicunt enim primo, quod deterdeterminationi ecclesiæ Romanæ contradicit, quod per Nicolaum tertium, vt dicunt, aperte demonstratur. Ait enim Nicolaus tertius in decretali Exiit, sicut ostensum superius est c. 9. Dicimus quod abdicatio proprietatis huiusmodi rerum omnium temporalium tam in speciali quam etiam in communi propter Deum meritoria est & sancta: quam & Christus viam perfectionis aspiciens verbo docuit & exemplo firmauit, quamque primi fundatores militantis ecclesiæ prout ab ipso fonte hauserant, in volentes perfecte viuere per doctrinas ac vitæ ipsorum alueos deriuarunt. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod huiusmodi abdicatio seu expropriatio spectat ad viam perfectionis. Aliter enim Christus ipsam verbo docendo & exemplo firmando viam perfectionis minime ostendisset: Apostoli etiam per doctrinas & vitæ ipsorum alueos viam perfectionis in volentes perfecte viuere nullatenus deriuassent. Amplius, illa abdicatio seu expropriatio, quæ est ardua, difficilis propter Deum, quæ meritoria est & sancta, ad viam perfectionis spectat, sed expropriatio supradicta meritoria est & sancta secundum verba Nicolai prædicta, ergo ad viam perfectionis spectat, & ita prodesse Fratribus potuit ad statum perfectionis. Secundo sic arguunt, illud quod à Christo consulitur volenti viam perfectionis arripere, ad statum perfectionis spectat, sed Christus abdicationem omnium temporalium consuluit viam perfectionis volenti arripere, cum dicit Matth. 19. Si vis perfectus esse vade & vende omnia quæ habes & da pauperibus, ergo huiusmodi abdicatio ad statum perfectionis spectat. Tertio sic: Paupertas Euangelica ad statum perfectionis spectat, sed abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium ad Euangelicam pertinet paupertatem, hæc ostensa est supra capit. 13. ergo talis abdicatio ad statum perfectionis spectat. Quarto sic: Illud quod tollit impedimentum perfectionis, aliquo modo ad persectionem spectat, sed voluntaria abdicatio proprietatis possessionum omnium temporalium in speciali & in communi tollit impedimentum perfectionis scilicet amoris diuini, in quo consistit persectio: quia tollit amorem temporalium, qui est impedimentum amoris diuini, ergo abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium in speciali & in communi ad perfectionem spectat. Circa istam rationem suppositia maiore tanquam certa sunt duo probanda: quorum primum est, quod voluntaria abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium tollit vel diminuit amorem eorum.
units.tr: The first error, then, as they say, contained in the aforesaid words is that the renunciation or abdication of ownership of all temporal goods, both individually and in common, does not pertain to the state of perfection. That he means this is plain. For he says that the aforesaid retention of ownership did not benefit the Brothers as regards the state of perfection; by retention of ownership, however, he means the aforesaid renunciation. For after stating the conclusion to be proved, that the aforesaid retention of ownership in no way benefited them as regards the state of perfection, in the reasoning by which he tries to prove this conclusion no mention is made of retention of ownership, but only of renunciation. Hence, when he put forward that retention of ownership did not benefit them, he understood renunciation. Or, if he wished to distinguish between retention of ownership and renunciation, he ought first to prove this conclusion in his reasoning: the aforesaid renunciation did not benefit the Brothers as regards the state of perfection; and from this he infers the other: retention of ownership did not benefit them. And so it is clearly evident from his reasoning that he means that the renunciation of all temporal goods does not serve the state of perfection. But these opponents try in many ways to prove that this is to be regarded as erroneous. For they say first that it contradicts the determination of the Roman Church, which, as they say, is clearly shown by Nicholas III. For Nicholas III says in the decretal Exiit, as was shown above in chapter 9: We say that the abdication of ownership of all such temporal goods, both individually and in common, is meritorious and holy for God's sake; Christ, looking to the way of perfection, taught it by word and confirmed it by example, and the first founders of the militant Church, drawing it from its very source, derived it into the channels of their teaching and their lives for those who wished to live perfectly. From these words it is plainly gathered that such abdication or renunciation pertains to the way of perfection. For otherwise Christ, by teaching it in word and confirming it by example, would not have shown the way of perfection at all; nor would the Apostles, through their teaching and their lives, have derived the way of perfection into the channels for those wishing to live perfectly. Furthermore, that abdication or renunciation which is arduous and difficult for God's sake, which is meritorious and holy, pertains to the way of perfection; but the aforesaid renunciation is meritorious and holy according to the words of Nicholas cited above; therefore it pertains to the way of perfection, and so it could benefit the Brothers as regards the state of perfection. Secondly, they argue thus: that which Christ counsels to one wishing to take up the way of perfection pertains to the state of perfection; but Christ counselled the abdication of all temporal goods to one wishing to take up the way of perfection, when he says in Matt. 19: If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have and give to the poor; therefore such abdication pertains to the state of perfection. Thirdly, thus: Evangelical poverty pertains to the state of perfection; but the abdication of ownership of all temporal goods pertains to Evangelical poverty; this was shown above in chapter 13; therefore such abdication pertains to the state of perfection. Fourthly, thus: that which removes an impediment to perfection pertains to perfection in some way; but voluntary abdication of ownership of all possessions and temporal goods, both individually and in common, removes an impediment to perfection, namely to divine love, in which perfection consists, for it removes love of temporal things, which is an impediment to divine love; therefore abdication of ownership of all temporal goods, both individually and in common, pertains to perfection. In regard to this argument, with the major premise supposed as certain, two things must be proved. The first is that voluntary abdication of ownership of all temporal goods removes or diminishes love of them.

units.la: Secundum est, quod amor temporalium est impedimentum amoris diuini, primum probatur, nam amor temporalium ex proprietate rerum temporalium tam in speciali quam etiam in communi nascitur & augetur, testante beato Hieronymo, qui ait super Matth. 19. quia diuitiæ habitæ dissicile contemnuntur: non dicit Dominus impossibile est diuitem intrare in regnum cælorum, sed difficile. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod diuitiæ habitæ difficile contemnuntur: & per consequens diuitiæ habitæ facile diliguntur: quia quod cum difficultate contemnitur, facile amatur. Ex proprietate igitur temporalium amor eorum nascitur vel augetur, hoc etiam beatus Bernardus de colloquio Simonis & Iesu testatur dicens: hæc fugiendarum diuitiarum precipua causa est: quia vix aut nunquam sine amore valent possideri: siquidem glutinosa nimis non modo exterior, verum etiam interior substantia nostra videtur: & facile cor humanum omnibus, qua frequentat, adhaeret. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi quod sine amore temporalia difficile possidentur.
units.tr: The second point is that love of temporal things is an impediment to the love of God. The first part is proved as follows. The love of temporal things arises and grows from the possession of temporal things, both individually and in common, as blessed Jerome attests in his comment on Matthew 19: riches once possessed are with difficulty despised; the Lord does not say it is impossible for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven, but difficult. From these words it is clear that riches once possessed are with difficulty despised, and consequently that riches possessed are easily loved, because what is despised with difficulty is easily loved. Love of temporal things therefore arises or grows from their possession. Blessed Bernard also bears witness to this in his colloquy of Simon and Jesus, saying: this is the chief reason for fleeing riches: because they can scarcely or never be possessed without love, since our substance, not only outward but also inward, seems very sticky, and the human heart easily clings to all the things it frequents. From these words we are given to understand that temporal things are possessed with difficulty without love.

units.la: His concordat beatus Augustin. qui in epistola ad Paulinum & Thearsiam ait: Terrena diliguntur artius adepta quam concupita. Nam unde iuuenis ille tristis discessit, nisi quia magnas habebat diuitias. Aliud est enim nolle incorporare illa quæ desunt, aliud iam incorporata diuellere: illa velut extranea repudiantur, ista velut membra præscinduntur. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod ex possessione temporalium amor eorum augetur.
units.tr: Blessed Augustine agrees with this, who in his letter to Paulinus and Therasia says: Earthly things are clung to more tightly when acquired than when desired. For why did that rich young man go away sad, unless because he had great riches? For it is one thing not to wish to take in what we lack, and another to tear away what has already been taken in: the former are rejected as foreign, the latter are cut off as limbs. From these words it is plainly held that love of temporal things grows out of their possession.

units.la: Hoc etiam Chrysostomus asserit manifeste: qui super Matth. ait: Appositio diuitiarum maiorem accendit flammam, & vehementior fit cupido. Ex his colligitur euidenter, quod ex possessione temporalium amor eorum nascitur vel augetur, aut etiam retinetur. Ex quo manifeste infertur, quod illud, quod tollit possessionem temporalium, tollit amorem eorum, vel diminuit, cum ergo voluntaria abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium in speciali & in communi, tollat possessionem temporalium, sequitur euidenter, quod tollit vel diminuit amorem temporalium rerum, & ita probatum est primum præmissorum.
units.tr: Chrysostom also asserts this clearly, who on Matthew says: The addition of riches kindles a greater flame, and desire becomes more vehement. From this it is evidently gathered that love of temporal things arises or grows from their possession, or is at least retained by it. From this it is clearly inferred that whatever removes the possession of temporal things removes or diminishes love of them. Since voluntary renunciation of ownership of all temporal things, individually and in common, removes the possession of temporal things, it evidently follows that it removes or diminishes love of temporal things. And so the first of the premises is proved.

units.la: Secundo probandum est, quod amor temporalium est impedimentum amoris diuini, hoc autem testatur beatus Augustin. qui 10. lib. confessionum loquens ad Deum ait: Minus te amat, qui te cum aliquid amat, quod propter te non amat, sed amor qui ex possessione temporalium nascitur vel augetur non est propter Deum, si enim esset tantummodo propter Deum, non esset maior, quando possiderentur, quam quando non possiderentur, ille igitur amor est impedimentum amoris Dei: quia diminuit vel tollit amorem Dei.
units.tr: Second, it must be proved that love of temporal things is an impediment to the love of God. Blessed Augustine testifies to this, who in book 10 of the Confessions, speaking to God, says: He loves you less who loves something along with you that he does not love for your sake. But love which arises or grows from the possession of temporal things is not for God's sake; for if it were only for God's sake, it would not be greater when things are possessed than when they are not. That love, therefore, is an impediment to the love of God, because it diminishes or takes away the love of God.

units.la: Item idem Augustinus lib. 83. Quæstion. hoc aperte insinuat dicens: quod nutrimentum caritatis est minutio cupiditatis, ergo augmentatio cupiditatis quæ fit per amorem temporalium est impedimentum caritatis.
units.tr: Likewise the same Augustine, in his 83 Questions, clearly hints at this when he says that the nourishment of charity is the lessening of desire. Therefore the increase of desire which comes through love of temporal things is an impediment to charity.

units.la: Item Augustinus eodem lib. ait: Caritatis venenum est spes adipiscendorum temporalium, ergo multo magis adeptio temporalium est caritatis venenum. Ex quo sequitur, quod multo fortius amor temporalium est venenum caritatis: & per consequens est impedimentum amoris diuini.
units.tr: Likewise Augustine, in the same book, says: The hope of obtaining temporal things is the poison of charity. Therefore much more the actual obtaining of temporal things is the poison of charity. From this it follows that much more strongly the love of temporal things is the poison of charity, and consequently an impediment to the love of God.

units.la: Item Hieronymus, vt habetur 12. q. 1. c. Clericus, ait: Si quispiam aliquid habuerit præter Dominum, pars eius non erit Dominus, hoc autem potissime debet intelligi de habere per amorem, qui non est propter Dominum. Ex quo patenter infertur, quod amor temporalium impedit habere Dominum: & per consequens impedit amorem Domini, quia Dominus per amorem habetur.
units.tr: Likewise Jerome, as is found in 12 q. 1 c. Clericus, says: If anyone has anything besides the Lord, the Lord will not be his portion. This ought especially to be understood of having something through love, which is not for the Lord's sake. From this it is plainly inferred that love of temporal things hinders our having the Lord, and consequently hinders the love of the Lord, because the Lord is had through love.

units.la: Quinto tandem conclusionem, scilicet quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium ad perfectionem spectat, sic ostendunt: illud quod disponit ad perfectionem & contrariatur occasioni peccatorum, per quae perfectio tollitur, ad perfectionem spectat, sed abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium disponit ad perfectionem, & contrariatur possessioni temporalium, quae est occasio peccatorum, per quae perfectio tollitur, ergo abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium ad perfectionem spectat.
units.tr: Fifthly and finally, they show that renunciation of ownership of all temporal things pertains to perfection in this way: that which disposes to perfection and is opposed to the occasions of sin, through which perfection is lost, pertains to perfection. But renunciation of ownership of all temporal things disposes to perfection and is opposed to the possession of temporal things, which is an occasion of sins through which perfection is lost. Therefore renunciation of ownership of all temporal things pertains to perfection.

units.la: Circa illam rationem sunt duo probanda: quorum primum est, quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium disponit ad perfectionem. Secundum est quod possessio temporalium, cui contrariatur abdicatio supradicta, est occasio peccatorum per quae perfectio tollitur, primum probatur auctoritate Gregor. qui quarto Moralium ait: Sunt nonnulli iustorum, qui ad apprehendendum culmen perfectionis accincti, dum altiora interius appetunt, exterius cuncta derelinquunt. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod cuncta derelinquere ad perfectionem disponit, imo quasi exigitur, hoc etiam testatur Ambros. qui primo lib. de Officiis ait: non potest quis premium accipere, nisi legitime certauerit, neque gloriosa victoria vbi non fuerunt laboriosa certamina, ideo Dominus in Euangelio: Beati pauperes spiritu: quoniam ipsorum est regnum caelorum: non dicit, beati divites, sed pauperes, inde enim incipitur beatitudo diuino iudicio, vbi aerumna aestimatur humano. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod paupertas: & per consequens abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium est via ad beatitudinem in ista vita. De qua loquitur Saluator Matt. 6. sed illa est perfectio, vel non sine perfectione, ergo paupertas vel est perfectio vel ad perfectionem disponit. Secundo probandum est quod possessio temporalium, cui contrariatur abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium, est occasio peccatorum, per quae perfectio tollitur, hoc enim testatur Greg. 4. li. Moralium dicens: Rarum valde est, vt qui possident aurum ad requiem tendant: cum persemetipsam veritas dicat, quod difficile, qui pecunias habent, intrabunt in regnum caelorum. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod diuitiarum possessio impedit intendere ad regnum caelorum, sed hoc non fit, nisi inclinando ad peccata, ergo est occasio peccatorum, hoc etiam Aug. de verbis Domini aperte insinuat, specialiter explicans quod est causa superbiae dicens: nihil est quod sic generent diuitiae, quam superbiam, omne pomum, omne granum, omne frumentum, omne lignum, omne germen habet vermem suum, vermis diuitiarum superbia. Et idem de Lapsu mundi ait: In diuitiis nil tam cauendum est quam superbia morbus. Possessio igitur diuitiarum est occasio superbiae, quod etiam sit occasio aliorum vitiorum, testatur idem Augustinus, de Lapsu mundi ait: Diuitiae ipsae quae putatis plenae esse delitiarum, plenioresque sunt periculorum: & per consequens sunt occasiones peccatorum. Hoc etiam testatur Greg. qui super illud Euangelii Exiit, qui seminat, ait: Quis enim mihi vnquam crederet, si spinas diuitias interpretari voluissem: maxime cum illa pungat, ista delectet, & tamen spinae sunt, quia cogitationum suarum punctionibus mentem lacerant: & cum vsq; ad peccatum pertrahunt, quasi infligto vulnere cruentant, & ideo primo Moralium ait: Solet rerum abundantia tanto a timore diuino mentem soluere, quanto hanc exigit diuersa cogitare, nam dum foris per multa spargitur, stare in intimis fixa prohibetur.
units.tr: For this argument two things must be proved. The first is that renunciation of ownership of all temporal things disposes to perfection. The second is that the possession of temporal things, to which the aforesaid renunciation is opposed, is an occasion of sins through which perfection is lost. The first is proved by the authority of Gregory, who in the fourth book of the Moralia says: There are some of the just who, girding themselves to grasp the summit of perfection, while they desire higher things inwardly, leave all things outwardly. From these words we are given to understand that to leave all things disposes to perfection, indeed is almost required for it. Blessed Ambrose also testifies to this, who in the first book of On Duties says: No one can receive the prize unless he has struggled lawfully, nor is a victory glorious where there were no laborious contests. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. He does not say, blessed are the rich, but the poor; for blessedness begins there by divine judgment, where hardship is esteemed by human judgment. From these words we are given to understand that poverty, and consequently renunciation of ownership of all temporal things, is the way to blessedness in this life, of which the Saviour speaks in Matt. 6. But that is perfection, or not without perfection; therefore poverty is either perfection or disposes to perfection. Secondly, it must be proved that the possession of temporal things, to which renunciation of ownership of all temporal things is opposed, is an occasion of sins through which perfection is lost. Gregory says this in the fourth book of the Moralia: It is very rare that those who possess gold strive for rest, since Truth himself says that those who have money will with difficulty enter the kingdom of heaven. From these words it is gathered that the possession of riches hinders striving for the kingdom of heaven. But this does not happen unless one is inclined to sins; therefore riches are an occasion of sins. Augustine also clearly hints at this in On the Words of the Lord, explaining specifically what causes pride, when he says: Nothing is so productive of pride as riches. Every apple, every grain, every wheat, every wood, every shoot has its worm; the worm of riches is pride. And in his On the Fall of the World he says: In riches nothing is so to be guarded against as the disease of pride. That the possession of riches is an occasion of pride, and that it is also an occasion of other vices, the same Augustine testifies. In the same work he says: The riches themselves, which you think are full of delights, are fuller of dangers, and consequently they are occasions of sins. Gregory also testifies to this, who on the Gospel words A sower went out says: Who would ever believe me if I wished to interpret the thorns as riches, especially since the one pricks and the other delights? Yet they are thorns, because with the stings of their cares they lacerate the mind, and when they draw it as far as sin, they make it bleed as if a wound had been inflicted. And so in the first book of the Moralia he says: the abundance of things is accustomed to loosen the mind from the fear of God in proportion as it demands that it think of diverse things; for while it is scattered abroad outwardly among many things, it is prevented from remaining fixed in its inner depths.

units.la: Ex his aliisq; copluribus sanctorum testimoniis euidenter apparet, diuitias occasionem peccandi praestare, & plenas esse periculis, quod testimonio Apostolico confirmatur, q primae Tim. 6. ait: Qui volunt diuites fieri, incidunt in tentationem & in laqueum Diaboli & desideria multa & nociua quae mergunt hominem in interitum & perditionem. Vltimo, quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium ad perfectionem pertineat, sanctorum auctoritatibus conantur ostendere. Hoc enim auctoritate B. Hieronymi probant, qui ad Rusticum monachum ait: Si perfectus esse desideras, exi cum Abraham de patria & de cognatione tua, si habes substantiam, vende & da pauperibus: si non habes, grandi onere liberatus es, nudum Christum nudus sequere: durum, grande, difficile, sed magna sunt praemia. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod qui perfectus esse desiderat, debet omnia vendere, & dare pauperibus: & per consequens proprietatem omnium abdicare. Item, illud quod est melius, ad perfectionem spectat, sed omnia dimittere est melius quam aliqua retinere: teste beato Augustino de Bono coniugali, quod ait: Bonum erat quod faciebant qui de substantia sua Christo & eius discipulis ministrabant: sed melius qui omnem substantiam dimiserunt vt Christum Dominum expeditius sequerentur, ergo omnia dimittere ad perfectionem spectat. Item his concordat Ambros. qui li. 1. de officiis ait: Officium omne aut medium aut perfectum, quod aeque scripturarum auctoritate probare possumus, habemus enim in euangelio dixisse Dominum: Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serua mandata: non homicidium facies: non adulterabis: haec media sunt officia, quibus aliquid deest, ideo sequitur: si vis perfectus esse, vade & vende omnia quae habes & da pauperibus & sequere me, hoc est igitur perfectum officium. Ex his verbis datur intelligi quod vendere omnia & dare pauperibus ad perfectionem spectat. Idem Beda super illud Marci 2. Reliquit omnibus secutus est eum, ait: Persectam nobis abrenunciationis seculi formam tribuit, dum non solum lucra reliquit vectigalium, sed & pericula contempsit. Lucra igitur & pericula mundana contemnere: & per consequens omnium abdicare proprietatem, ad perfectionem spectat. Item beatus Bernar. ait: habetur in euangelio & perfectionis consilium & remedium infirmitatis. Nolite thesaurizare vobis thesauros in terra, hac perfectio est. Si igitur non thesaurizare thesauros in terra perfectionis est, multo fortius abdicatio proprietatis omnium deberet perfectio reputari. Ex his aliisq; quam pluribus apparet (vt dicunt isti) quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium ad perfectionem spectat.
units.tr: From these and many other testimonies of the saints it clearly appears that riches offer an occasion of sinning and are full of dangers. This is confirmed by the testimony of the Apostle, who says in 1 Tim. 6: Those who want to become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the Devil, and into many foolish and harmful desires, which drown men in destruction and perdition. Lastly, they try to show from the authority of the saints that renunciation of ownership of all temporal things pertains to perfection. They prove this by the authority of blessed Jerome, who says to the monk Rusticus: If you desire to be perfect, go out with Abraham from your country and your kindred; if you have substance, sell it and give to the poor; if you do not have it, you are freed from a great burden. Naked, follow the naked Christ. It is hard, great and difficult, but the rewards are great. From these words we are given to understand that whoever desires to be perfect must sell everything and give it to the poor, and consequently renounce ownership of everything. Likewise, what is better pertains to perfection; but to give up everything is better than to keep some things. Blessed Augustine bears witness to this in On the Good of Marriage, where he says: It was good what those did who ministered to Christ and his disciples from their substance; but better were those who gave up all their substance so as to follow the Lord Christ more freely. Therefore to give up everything pertains to perfection. Likewise Ambrose agrees with these, who in the first book of On Duties says: Every duty is either middling or perfect, which we can prove equally by the authority of the Scriptures. For we have in the Gospel the Lord saying: If you want to enter into life, keep the commandments: you shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery. These are middle duties, in which something is lacking. Therefore it follows: If you want to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and follow me. This, therefore, is the perfect duty. From these words we are given to understand that to sell everything and give to the poor pertains to perfection. Bede, on the words of Mark 2, He left all and followed him, also says: He gave us the perfect form of renunciation of the world, since he left not only the gains of the tax office but also despised its dangers. Therefore to despise worldly gains and dangers, and consequently to renounce ownership of everything, pertains to perfection. Likewise blessed Bernard says: The Gospel contains both a counsel of perfection and a remedy for weakness. Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth: this is perfection. If, therefore, not storing up treasures on earth is perfection, much more should the renunciation of ownership of everything be counted as perfection. From these and many more it appears (as they say) that renunciation of ownership of everything pertains to perfection.

units.la: Porro quia solutio dubiorum est manifestatio veritatis: Ideo contra praedicta obiiciunt, vt ipsa plenius valeant declarare. Primo igitur ostendunt, quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporaliū in speciali & in communi, ad statū perfectionis non spectat, & primo sic: statuus episcoporū est perfectior statu quorumcunq; religiosorū: ergo est perfectior statu illorū quod abdicant praedicto modo omnium proprietate, sed episcopi nō abdicant omnium proprietate: ergo talis abdicatio ad perfectionem non pertinet. Secundo sic: illud sine quo potest quis esse perfectus, ad statū perfectionis non pertinet: sicut illud sine quo potest quis esse homo, ad naturam hominis minime spectat, sed aliquis potest esse perfectus sine abdicatione huiusmodi, patet de patribus veteris testamenti, qui sine abdicatione perfecti fuerunt, multi etiam religiosi sunt in statu perfectionis absq; abdicatione huiusmodi. Tertio sic: in Collationibus patrum dicit Abbas Moyses: ieiunia, vigilias, meditatio scripturarum, nuditas ac privatio omnium facultatum non perfectio, sed perfectionis instrumenta sunt. Ex quibus verbis patet quod abdicatio temporalium est tantum modo instrumentum perfectionis, sed sicut abdicatio omnium temporalium est instrumentum perfectionis, ita etiam possessio divitiarum est instrumentum perfectionis, est enim instrumentum caritatis, quo caritas Christi per opera misericordiae indigentiis subuenit proximorum: sicut patet de Thobia qui de facultatibus suis ex perfectione caritatis esurientes alebat, nudisq; vestimenta praebebat, & mortuis atq; occisis sepulturam sollicitus exhibebat, imo dividebat unicuique prout poterat de facultatibus suis Thobi. 1. Item patet de Iob & aliis patribus veteris testamenti. Idem etiam patet de multis in novo testamento, non ergo plus pertinet ad statum perfectionis abdicatio omnium temporalium, quam divitiarum possessio. Quarto specialiter ostenditur, quod rationes non concludunt, nam auctoritates adductae non loquuntur de rebus paruis necessariis sustentationi humanae: sed tantum modo de possessione magnarum divitiarum, ergo per eas probari non potest, quod abdicatio omnium rerum temporalium privatarum & magnarum ad statum perfectionis spectat. Item non loquitur de abdicatione divitiarum in communi: sed tantum modo in speciali, ergo probari non potest, quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium in speciali & in communi ad statum perfectionis spectat, hoc confirmatur: quia bona communia pertinent ad perfectionem caritatis, quae omnia faciunt communia, ergo abdicare proprietatem communium, non facit ad perfectionem. Ad euidentiam solutionis istorum dicunt isti esse sciendum, quod aliquid pertinere ad perfectionem quadrupliciter potest intelligi, uno enim modo pertinet aliquid ad perfectionem: quia est de se perfectio essentialiter, & isto modo caritas & actus meritorius diligendi Deum ad perfectionem spectant. Secundo modo pertinet aliquid ad perfectionem: quia est arduum quid & difficile, impedimenta perfectionis primo modo dictae tollens vel diminuens & ad ipsam disponens, & isto modo abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium in speciali & in communi & graves vigiliae, perpetua continentia, singularia ieiunia, abdicatio propriae voluntatis & huiusmodi ad perfectionem spectant. Tertio modo potest intelligi aliquid ad perfectionem spectare: quia ex magna perfectione procedit, sive sit difficile & arduum, sive non sit difficile: sicut multi sancti viri ex perfectione magna, dispensationem rerum ecclesiarum communium & episcopatus, ac dignitates alias receperunt: quia ex perfectione caritatis curas huiusmodi non ex ambitione vel auaritia susceperunt, imo quantum licuit renuerunt, & tales praecipue sunt idonei ad regendum, teste Augustino, qui, ut habetur 8 q.1. cap. qui episcopatum, ait: Otium sanctum quaerit caritas veritatis, negotium iustum suscipit necessitas caritatis: quam sarcinam si nullus imponit percipienda atq; intuenda veritati vacandum est, si autem imponitur, suscipienda est propter caritatis necessitatem. Huic etiam concordat Grego. in Registro, ut habetur eisdem causa & quaestione c. in scriptura.
units.tr: Since the resolution of doubts is the manifestation of truth, they raise objections against the foregoing, so that they may be able to explain them more fully. First, then, they show that the renunciation of all temporal property, both in particular and in common, does not pertain to the state of perfection; and first thus: the state of bishops is more perfect than the state of any religious; therefore it is more perfect than the state of those who renounce all property in the aforesaid manner; but bishops do not renounce all property; therefore such renunciation does not pertain to perfection. Second, thus: that without which a man can be perfect does not pertain to the state of perfection; just as that without which a man can be a man does not belong at all to human nature. But someone can be perfect without such renunciation; this is plain from the Fathers of the Old Testament, who were perfect without renunciation, and many religious are also in the state of perfection without such renunciation. Third, thus: in the Conferences of the Fathers Abbot Moses says: fasting, vigils, meditation on the Scriptures, nakedness and the deprivation of all means are not perfection, but instruments of perfection. From these words it is plain that the renunciation of temporal goods is only an instrument of perfection; but just as the renunciation of all temporal goods is an instrument of perfection, so also the possession of riches is an instrument of perfection, for it is an instrument of charity, by which the love of Christ, through works of mercy, comes to the aid of the needs of neighbours; as is plain of Tobit, who out of the perfection of charity fed the hungry from his means, gave clothing to the naked, and was careful to provide burial for the dead and slain, indeed divided his means to each as he was able Tob. 1. Likewise it is plain of Job and other Fathers of the Old Testament. The same is plain of many in the New Testament. Therefore the renunciation of all temporal goods pertains no more to the state of perfection than the possession of riches does. Fourth, it is specially shown that the arguments do not conclude, for the authorities adduced do not speak of small things necessary for human sustenance, but only of the possession of great riches; therefore it cannot be proved by them that the renunciation of all temporal goods, both private and great, pertains to the state of perfection. Likewise it does not speak of the renunciation of riches in common, but only in particular; therefore it cannot be proved that the renunciation of property, both in particular and in common, pertains to the state of perfection. This is confirmed, because common goods pertain to the perfection of charity, which make all things common; therefore renouncing the property of common goods does not contribute to perfection. For the clear resolution of these points, they say it must be known that something can be understood to pertain to perfection in four ways. In one way something pertains to perfection because it is in itself perfection essentially; and in this way charity and the meritorious act of loving God pertain to perfection. In a second way something pertains to perfection because it is something arduous and difficult, removing or diminishing the impediments of perfection in the first sense and disposing towards it; and in this way the renunciation of property of all temporal goods, both in particular and in common, and severe vigils, perpetual continence, singular fasts, the renunciation of one's own will and the like pertain to perfection. In a third way it may be understood that something pertains to perfection because it proceeds from great perfection, whether it is difficult and arduous or not difficult: just as many holy men, out of great perfection, received the stewardship of the common goods of the churches and bishoprics and other dignities; because out of the perfection of charity they undertook such cares not from ambition or avarice, but indeed refused them as far as was permitted; and such men are especially fit to rule, as Augustine testifies, who, as is found in 8 q.1. cap. qui episcopatum, says: Holy leisure is sought by the love of truth; just business is undertaken by the necessity of love. If no one lays this burden upon us, we must devote ourselves to receiving and contemplating the truth; but if it is laid upon us, it must be accepted on account of the necessity of love. Gregory in his Register also agrees with this, as is found in the same causa et quaestione, c. in scriptura.

units.la: Est autem aduertendum, quod iste modus non in omnibus differt a secundo, in hoc enim quodam modo conuenit cum secundo, quod utrobique illud, quod ad perfectionem pertinere dicitur, est quodammodo difficile: sed diuersimode, quia in secundo modo hoc, quod ad perfectionem pertinet, est difficile naturae corruptae. Sicut naturae corruptae & hominibus suas passiones sequentibus est difficile omnia dimittere, saepe ieiunare, perpetuo continere, & alterius se subiicere voluntati: sed illud quod ad perfectionem pertinet tertio modo, est facile naturae corruptae & hominibus secundum inclinationem passionum viuentibus: sed hominibus in diuino amore fundatis est difficile: sicut magnas recipere dignitates, hominibus suas sequentibus passiones est facile, hominibus tamen perfectis considerantibus tales dignitates esse plenas periculis spiritualibus est difficile, propter quod sancti viri antiquitus cum magno timore & tremore ac difficultate maxima huiusmodi officia receperunt. Quarto modo potest aliquid intelligi ad perfectionem pertinere: quia potest qualitercunq; ad perfectionem disponere, & isto modo omnis actus bonus siue fit facilis siue dissicilis, potest dici ad perfectionem pertinere, & sic aliquid pertinet ad perfectionem in uno, & eius contrarium pertinet ad perfectionem in alio: quia diuersi diuersimode & saepe per contraria ad perfectionem disponuntur. Secundum dicunt esse sciendum, quod illa, quae dicuntur pertinere ad persectionem secundo modo, dicuntur pertinere ad statum perfectionis secundum quod modo loquimur de pertinentibus ad statum perfectionis: an autem omnes alii modi vel aliqui, aut quis tantum modo pertineant vel pertineat ad statum perfectionis dicunt ad praesens esse minime indagandum. Tertio dicunt esse sciendum, quod status perfectionis vocatur ille status, qui supra obligationem ad perfectionem habendam primo modo dictam, ad quam omnes obligantur, obligat assumentes ad aliqua ad perfectionem secundo modo pertinere noscuntur: quia obligat ad aliqua ardua & difficilia naturae corruptae & hominibus suas sequentibus passiones. Quarto dicunt esse sciendum: quod diversi status non ad omnia eadem ardua & difficilia secundo modo obligant assumentes: & ideo non est inconueniens, quod unus status excedat alium in uno, & excedatur ab eodem in alio. Secundo praedicta ad praeactas obiectiones respondere nituntur, unde ad primam dicunt: quod licet status episcoporum sit multis perfectior statu religiosorum abdicantium proprietatem omnium in communi & in speciali: in hoc tamen non est perfectior scil. quantum ad esse in actuali paupertate, in quo non est perfectior quacunq; religione votum paupertatis habente, similiter etiam quantum ad abstinentiam & multa alia non est perfectior statu religiosorum. Ad secundam dicunt, quod licet illud sine quo potest aliquis esse perfectus, non sit perfectio primo modo dicta: potest tamen ad statum perfectionis spectare: quia multa spectant ad statum perfectionis, quae non sunt perfectio primo modo dicta: sed sufficit quod sint perfectiones secundo modo dictae: & quod assumentes talem statum ad ipsas obligentur. Unde sicut aliqua pertinent ad perfectionem hominis dupliciter: quia quaedam sunt, sine quibus non est homo completus scilicet omnia membra, quaedam sunt sine quibus non est homo perfectus perfectione secunda, cuiusmodi sunt scientiae, pulchritudo, fortitudo, virtutes & huiusmodi: ita aliquid pertinet ad perfectionem Christiani catholici, sine quo non est perfectus Christianus catholicus perfectione prima: & tale est principaliter charitas, & minus principaliter fides & spes. Aliquid autem quasi secundario pertinet ad perfectionem Christiani catholici, sine quo non est perfectus omni perfectione secundaria, sicut virginitas, & tale quid est proprietatem omnium abdicare in speciali & in communi: sine hoc tamen in actu potest aliquis esse perfectus, sed non potest esse perfectus in summo, sine tali abdicatione, secundum praeparationem animi, & isto modo sancti patres in veteri testamento & perfectissimi religiosi obtinent abdicationem secundum praeparationem animi: non tamen habuerunt in actu omnem perfectionem secundariam. Ad tertia dicunt: quod verum est, quod huiusmodi abdicatio est instrumentum perfectionis primo modo dicta, sicut nec abdicatio proprietatis omnium in speciali est perfectio primo modo dicta. Perfectio enim primo modo dicta non potest male haberi nec fieri vel assumi, sed abdicatio proprietatis omnium sive in speciali tantum, sive in speciali & in communi, potest male assumi, quia malo sine: quemadmodum hypocritae multa ardua & difficilia faciunt, ut ab hominibus videantur. Cum vero dicitur, quod sicut abdicatio proprietatis omnium est instrumentum perfectionis: ita etiam diuitiarum possessio est instrumentum perfectionis. Dicunt isti: quod verum est, quod tam abdicatio omnium diuitiarum, quam earum possessio potest esse instrumentum perfectionis: sed aliter & aliter, nam abdicatio omnium est instrumentum arduum & difficile fragilitati humanae; diuitiarum autem possessio non est instrumentum arduum neq; difficile fragilitati humanae, cum sit appetibilis secundum naturam corruptam viuentibus, secundo quia licet abdicatio omnium postquam facta esset inuoluntaria & coacta, posset esse radix aliquorum malorum: hoc tamen non esset nisi in quantum quodammodo esset mutata in possessionem diuitiarum secundum desiderium animi, & propter hoc non ita est occasio peccatorum, sicut est diuitiarum possessio, propter quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium in speciali & etiam in communi pertinet ad perfectionem secundo modo, sed possessio diuitiarum potest dici pertinere ad perfectionem tertio modo, sed communiter loquendo illa quae pertinent ad perfectionem, tertio modo, magis dicuntur pertinere ad imperfectionem quam ad perfectionem: quia secundum se quodammodo sunt imperfecta, licet ex aliqua circumstantia, vel circumstantiis possint in casu esse perfecta, vel ex perfectione procedere, & ideo nonnunquam dicuntur pertinere ad statum perfectionis: quia ardua & difficilia ad statum perfectionis pertinere noscuntur. Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod non solum ardua & difficilia ad statum perfectionis spectant, sed etiam quaedam alia spectant ad statum perfectionis: sicut ad statum praelatorum, qui est status perfectionis, spectat docere, corrigere, punire & huiusmodi, ergo licet possessio diuitiarum non sit quid arduum & difficile: tamen poterit spectare ad statum perfectionis: & videtur quod specialiter spectet ad statum praelatorum, qui est status perfectionis. Nam de statu praelatorum spectat punire delinquentes, delinquentes autem sine potentia puniri non possunt, potentia autem sine diuitiis non habetur, ergo sine possessione diuitiarum praelati delinquentes conuenienter punire non possunt, ergo possessio diuitiarum ad statum pertinet praelatorum. Ad hoc dicunt isti, quod aliqua esse difficilia duplicifer potest intelligi, uno modo, quia cum difficultate, rite & legitime exercentur & sic docere, regere, corrigere & huiusmodi, quae ad statum pertinent praelatorum, possunt inter difficilia computari. Aliter possunt aliqua intelligi difficilia, quia a suas passiones sequentibus cum difficultate appetuntur: & sic docere, regere, punire, & huiusmodi non sunt difficilia reputanda, propter quod concedunt, quod aliqua, quae non sunt illo modo difficilia, hoc est difficiliter & raro a suas passiones sequentibus appetita, pertinent ad statum perfectionis, & maxime praelatorum: sicut docere, regere, iudicium facere, corrigere, punire & huiusmodi: tamen dicunt quod possessio diuitiarum non per se pertinet ad statum praelatorum: quia possessio diuitiarum, tum propter sollicitudinem quam requirit, tum propter amorem inordinatum & alia vitia, quae saepe nascuntur ex ipsa retrahit ab aliis, quae per se ad statum pertinent praelatorum, propter quod Apostoli non solum possessionem & proprietatem diuitiarum, sed etiam dispensationem ipsarum, absque omni proprietate, quemadmodum aliqui Fratres Minores, modo res quibus vruntur Fratribus suis dispensandas penitus reliquerunt: & ad huiusmodi dispensationem faciendam septem diaconos elegerunt, sicut patet Act. 7. Cum igitur nunquam fuerunt perfectiores praelati quam fuerunt Apostoli, neque quo ad vitam, neque quo ad statum: sequitur, quod diuitiarum possessio ad statum praelatorum nequaquam per se poterit pertinere.
units.tr: Now it must be noted that this third mode does not differ from the second in every respect. In one way it agrees with the second, in that under both the thing said to pertain to perfection is somewhat difficult. But the difficulty is of different kinds. In the second mode, what pertains to perfection is difficult for corrupt nature: for those who are corrupt and follow their passions, it is hard to give up everything, to fast often, to abstain perpetually, and to submit themselves to another's will. But what pertains to perfection in the third mode is easy for corrupt nature and for those who live according to the inclination of their passions, while it is difficult for those who are grounded in divine love. So, for example, to receive great dignities is easy for those who follow their passions, but for perfect people, who consider that such dignities are full of spiritual dangers, it is difficult. For this reason, holy men of old received such offices with great fear and trembling and the utmost difficulty. In the fourth mode, something can be understood to pertain to perfection because it disposes toward perfection in any way at all. In this sense every good act, whether it is easy or difficult, can be said to pertain to perfection, and so one and the same thing may pertain to perfection in one person while its contrary pertains to perfection in another, because different people are disposed to perfection in different ways, and often by contraries. Secondly, they say that it must be known that the things said to pertain to perfection in the second mode are said to pertain to the state of perfection, in the sense in which we are now speaking of things pertaining to the state of perfection. But whether all the other modes, or some of them, or only one of them, pertain to the state of perfection, they say that this is by no means to be inquired into at present. Thirdly, they say that it must be known that the state of perfection is that state which, over and above the obligation to have perfection in the first sense (to which all are bound), binds those who take it on to certain things known to pertain to perfection in the second sense, because it binds them to certain arduous and difficult things, difficult for corrupt nature and for those who follow their passions. Fourthly, they say that it must be known that the different states do not bind those who take them on to all the same arduous and difficult things of the second sense. Therefore it is not inconsistent that one state should surpass another in one respect, and be surpassed by the same state in another. Secondly, they try to answer the aforementioned objections with the points just set out. As to the first, they say that although the state of bishops is in many respects more perfect than the state of religious who renounce ownership of all things, both in common and individually, yet it is not more perfect in this respect, namely as regards actual poverty. In this respect it is not more perfect than any religious order that has a vow of poverty. Likewise, as regards abstinence and many other things, it is not more perfect than the state of religious. As to the second, they say that although that without which someone cannot be perfect is not perfection in the first sense, it can nevertheless belong to the state of perfection. Many things belong to the state of perfection that are not perfection in the first sense; it is enough that they are perfections in the second sense, and that those who assume such a state are bound to them. Thus, just as some things pertain to human perfection in two ways (for some are such that without them a man is not complete, namely all the limbs; others are such that without them a man is not perfect with second perfection, such as knowledge, beauty, strength, the virtues and the like), so some things pertain to the perfection of the catholic Christian without which he is not a perfect catholic Christian with first perfection. Chief among these is love, and less principally faith and hope. But some things pertain, as it were secondarily, to the perfection of the catholic Christian, without which he is not perfect in every secondary perfection. Such is virginity, and such is the renunciation of all property, both individually and in common. Yet without this one can be perfect in act, but one cannot be perfect in the highest degree without such renunciation, in respect of the preparation of the mind. In this sense the holy fathers under the Old Testament and the most perfect religious have renunciation in respect of the preparation of the mind, although they did not actually possess every secondary perfection. As to the third, they say that it is true that such renunciation is an instrument of perfection in the first sense, just as the renunciation of individual ownership is not perfection in the first sense. For perfection in the first sense cannot be had or made or assumed badly, but the renunciation of all property, whether only individual or both individual and common, can be assumed badly, because it is done with a bad purpose, just as hypocrites do many arduous and difficult things so that they may be seen by men. But when it is said that just as the renunciation of all property is an instrument of perfection, so too the possession of riches is an instrument of perfection, they reply: it is true that both the renunciation of all riches and their possession can be an instrument of perfection, but in different ways. For renunciation of all things is an instrument that is arduous and difficult for human frailty, whereas the possession of riches is not an arduous or difficult instrument for human frailty, since it is desirable to those who live according to corrupt nature. Secondly, although renunciation of all things, once it had become involuntary and forced, could be the root of certain evils, this would happen only insofar as it had in some way been turned into possession of riches through the desire of the mind. For this reason it is not as much an occasion of sins as the possession of riches is. Therefore the renunciation of property, both individually and also in common, pertains to perfection in the second sense, whereas the possession of riches may be said to pertain to perfection in the third sense. But, speaking in general, those things which pertain to perfection in the third sense are said to pertain more to imperfection than to perfection, because in themselves they are in some way imperfect, although in some case, by some circumstance or circumstances, they may be perfect, or may proceed from perfection. Therefore they are sometimes said to pertain to the state of perfection, because arduous and difficult things are known to pertain to the state of perfection. But perhaps someone will say that not only arduous and difficult things pertain to the state of perfection, but also certain other things do: for example, to the state of prelates, which is a state of perfection, belong teaching, correcting, punishing and the like. Therefore, although the possession of riches is not something arduous and difficult, it may still pertain to the state of perfection, and it seems that it especially pertains to the state of prelates, which is a state of perfection. For it belongs to the state of prelates to punish offenders, and offenders cannot be punished without power, and power is not had without riches. Therefore, without the possession of riches, prelates cannot properly punish offenders, and so the possession of riches pertains to the state of prelates. To this they reply that something can be understood as difficult in two ways. In one way, because it is exercised with difficulty, rightly and lawfully; and in this sense teaching, governing, correcting and the like, which belong to the state of prelates, may be counted among difficult things. In another way, things may be understood as difficult because they are sought with difficulty by those who follow their passions; and in this sense teaching, governing, punishing and the like are not to be reckoned difficult. Therefore they concede that some things which are not difficult in that sense (that is, things which are sought with difficulty and rarely by those who follow their passions) pertain to the state of perfection, and especially to the state of prelates: such as teaching, governing, judging, correcting, punishing and the like. Nevertheless, they say that the possession of riches does not in itself pertain to the state of prelates, because the possession of riches, both on account of the anxiety it requires and on account of inordinate love and other vices which often arise from it, draws prelates away from those things which in themselves belong to the state of prelates. For this reason the apostles not only renounced the possession and ownership of riches, but also left entirely to others, without any ownership, the distribution of them. Just as some Friars Minor now leave the goods which they use to be distributed by their brethren entirely to others, so the apostles chose seven deacons to carry out this distribution, as is clear from Acts 7. Therefore, since prelates were never more perfect than the apostles were, neither in life nor in state, it follows that the possession of riches can by no means in itself pertain to the state of prelates.
