units.la: Veruntamen dicunt esse sciendum, quod aliquid pertinere ad statum praelatorum duplicifer potest intelligi, scilicet vel per se & essentialiter, sicut paupertas, castitas, & obedientia per se & essentialiter pertinent ad statum religiosorum perfectorum. Aliter aliquid potest pertinere ad statum praelatorum, quasi per accidens, propter defectum vel neglinegligentiam aliorum: sicut dicunt Iuristae, quod ad prælatum sæpe pertinet supplere negligentiam iudicis secularis. Primo modo possessio diuitiarum neque communium, neque speciialium pertinet ad prælatos. Secundo modo possessio diuitiarum maxime communium ad prælatos poterit pertinere: sicut antiquitus prælati communia possidebant, hoc est dedinebant & dispensabant. Quia enim tunc temporis prælati alios, scientia, fide, sanctitate & industria præcellebant: imo alii erant quasi oues respectu ipsorum, expediens communitati fidelium existebat, quod prælati bona communia suscuperent dispensanda, si autem postea prælati fuissent, vel nunc essent auaritia & aliis viciis magis quam laici irretiti: expediret communitati fidelium bona communia committere laicis iustis, bonis & industriis dispensanda.
units.tr: Yet they say it must be understood that something can pertain to the state of prelates in two ways. Either it pertains through itself and essentially, as poverty, chastity and obedience pertain through themselves and essentially to the state of perfect religious. Or something can pertain to the state of prelates as it were per accidens, on account of the defect or negligence of others. Thus the jurists say that it often falls to a prelate to supply the negligence of a secular judge. In the first way, possession of riches, whether common or special, does not pertain to prelates. In the second way, possession of riches, especially common riches, can pertain to prelates. Formerly prelates held common goods, that is, they distributed and dispensed them. For since at that time the prelates surpassed others in learning, faith, holiness and diligence, and others were like sheep in comparison with them, it was expedient for the community of the faithful that the prelates should take up common goods to dispense. But if afterwards the prelates were, or now are, ensnared by avarice and other vices more than laymen, it would be expedient to commit common goods to just, good and diligent laymen to dispense.

units.la: Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod bona ecclesiæ pertinent ad proprietatem & dominium ecclesiæ, ergo contra prælatorum voluntatem non debent committi aliis quibuscunque.
units.tr: But perhaps someone will say that the goods of the Church belong to the property and dominion of the Church, and therefore they ought not to be committed to anyone whatsoever against the will of the prelates.

units.la: Ad hoc dicunt nonnulli, quod bona communia, quæ vocantur, & quodammodo sunt ecclesiæ quo ad dominium & proprietatem, primo & principalissime post Deum, sunt totius communitatis fidelium quo ad dominium & proprietatem, vel illius partis totius communitatis, quæ ab aliis distinguitur, quæ etiam omni dominio & communitati etiam qualicunque fidelium respectu bonorum communium renunciauerunt: si tamen sunt aliqui tales, communia enim bona a fidelibus oblata Deo ad duo principaliter ordinantur, scilicet ad Deum honorandum, & ad fidelium indigentias releuandas. Ordinantur enim ad Deum honorandum, vt fiant ecclesiæ libri, ornamenta, & alia quibus Deus specialiter honoratur & colitur. Ordinantur etiam ad fidelium indigentias releuandas: sed fidelium, sicut testatur Hieronym. vt habetur 12. quæst. 1. duo sunt genera: vnum quod diuino officio mancipatur, sicut sunt religiosi & alii ecclesiastici viri. Aliud est illorum, qui non sic diuino officio mancipantur, sicut sunt laici. Primis dispensanda sunt bona communia, etiam si propria habeant ad se sustentandum: quia nemo tenetur suis stipendiis militare, seruis non sunt bona communia conferenda, nisi propria bona deficiant, tunc enim sunt bona communia quibuscunque fidelibus, si sufficiunt erogända: & ideo bona communia omnibus fidelibus communia quodammodo sunt censenda. Omnibus enim fidelibus vel omnibus, exceptis illis qui bonorum communium ecclesiæ dominio renunciauerunt: si qui sunt tales, sunt communia quo ad dominium & proprietatem aliqualem, quæ scilicet est potestas vendicandi rem, seu pro re in iudicio litigandi. Quantum etiam ad facultatem per ipsa suas indigentias releuandi, sunt omnia omnibus communia, sed diuersimode: quia omnia omnibus sunt communicanda, licet aliter & aliter.
units.tr: To this some say that common goods, which are called and in a certain way are the Church's, with respect to dominion and property, belong first and most principally, after God, to the whole community of the faithful, or to that part of the whole community which is distinguished from the others, and which has also renounced all dominion and all share in common goods, whatever their status among the faithful. If there are any such people, for common goods offered by the faithful to God are principally ordained to two ends: to honour God, and to relieve the needs of the faithful. They are ordained to honour God so that they may become books, ornaments and other things by which God is especially honoured and worshipped. They are also ordained to relieve the needs of the faithful. But the faithful, as Jerome testifies (see 12, q. 1), are of two kinds: one that is devoted to the divine office, such as religious and other ecclesiastical men; the other that is not so devoted to the divine office, such as laymen. Common goods are to be dispensed to the first kind even if they have property of their own to support themselves, because no one is bound to serve as a soldier at his own expense. Common goods are not to be conferred on the second kind unless their own goods fail; then common goods belong to all the faithful, if they suffice for distribution. Therefore common goods must in a certain way be regarded as common to all the faithful. For they are common to all the faithful, or to all except those who have renounced dominion over the Church's goods (if there are any such), and they are common with respect to dominion and a certain property, namely the power of claiming a thing, or of contending in court on account of a thing. As far as the faculty of relieving their needs through them is concerned, all things are common to all, but in different ways, since all things are to be shared with all, although in different manners.

units.la: Primo enim generi fidelium sunt communicanda, licet ipsi habeant propria, quibus valeant suis necessitatibus subuenire. Aliis, nisi deficientibus propriis, sunt minime communicanda: sicut si sunt pauperes non habentes victum & vestitum, vel captiui vnde possint se redimere non habentes: & consimiliter de aliis in quibuscunque necessitatis articulis constitutis est dicendum, hoc per sacros canones posset copiose probari: sicut patet 12. q. 4. cap. aurum & c. sicut omnino, & multis aliis locis, & ita bona ecclesiæ sunt quodammodo communia omnibus: & in hoc communitas fidelium ecclesiam primitiuam quodammodo imitatur, licet enim non imitetur in hoc, quod nullus illorum habuit aliquid proprium: in hoc tamen imitatur, quod sicut illis omnia erant communia, ita modo omnibus fidelibus aliqua, non omnia sunt communia. Sed quæret aliquis, quomodo ergo ista bona dicuntur ecclesiæ, ex quo sunt communitatis fidelium? Ad hoc dicunt, quod sicut bona vnius monasterii, vel vnius episcopatus, aut ecclesiæ alterius collegialis, vel etiam non collegialis, dicuntur bona talis episcopi vel decani, aut talis monasterii vel ecclesiæ: & tamen principalius sunt bona tota totius ecclesiæ: & principalius sunt bona capitis clericorum, quam clericorum quorumcunque. Ita etiam oblata Deo dicuntur bona ecclesiæ vel clericorū, & tamen sunt principalius bona communitatis fidelium. Quia sicut non obstante episcopus bona sibi deputata pōt in iudicio vendicare & agere pro eis: papa nihilominus omnem talem potestatem principalius noscitur obtinere, si per communitatem fidelium est tota potestas clericorum super communia oblata Deo tributa papæ, non tamen sic, quin illam posset communitas fidelium reuocare: sic non obstante, quod communitas clericorum habet aliquale dominium in bonis communibus, tamen communitas fidelium principaliorem potestatem habet in eisdem: imo principalissimam habet post Deum. Ex his igitur patet, vt dicunt, quod possessio diuitiarum nequaquam per se pertinet ad prælatos, cum igitur dicitur, quod ipsi habent corrigere & punire, dicunt quod ad ipsos pertinet corrigere & punire pœna spirituali, scilicet excommunicatione. Pœna vero corporali: puta incarceratione, exilio vel huiusmodi pertinet ad eos punire inuocato auxilio brachii secularis.
units.tr: For to the first kind of the faithful they are to be shared even when they have their own goods by which they can relieve their needs. To others they are by no means to be shared, unless their own goods fail, as when they are poor and lack food and clothing, or are captives lacking the means by which they could redeem themselves. And the same is to be said of others placed in any articles of necessity. This could be copiously proved from the sacred canons, as is evident in 12, q. 4, cap. Aurum, and cap. Sicut omnino, and in many other places. And so the goods of the Church are in a certain way common to all, and in this the community of the faithful in some measure imitates the primitive Church. For although it does not imitate it in this, that none of them had anything of their own, it does imitate it in this: as all things were common to them, so now some things, though not all things, are common to all the faithful. But someone will ask how these goods are then called the Church's, since they belong to the community of the faithful. To this they answer that just as the goods of one monastery, or of one bishopric, or of another collegiate church, or even of a non-collegiate one, are called the goods of this or that bishop or dean, or of this or that monastery or church, and yet are principally the goods of the whole Church, and are principally the goods of the head of the clergy rather than of any clerics whatever, so also goods offered to God are called the goods of the Church or of the clergy, and yet they are principally the goods of the community of the faithful. For just as, notwithstanding that a bishop can claim in court and sue for the goods assigned to him, the pope nevertheless is known to hold every such power more principally; so, if the whole power of the clergy over common goods offered to God is by the community of the faithful granted to the pope, yet not in such a way that the community of the faithful could not revoke it, then notwithstanding that the community of the clergy has some dominion over common goods, the community of the faithful nevertheless has the more principal power over the same, and indeed the most principal power after God. From these things, they say, it is clear that possession of riches does not pertain of itself to prelates. Therefore, when it is said that they have to correct and punish, they say that it pertains to them to correct and punish with spiritual penalty, namely excommunication. But to punish with corporal penalty, such as imprisonment, exile or the like, pertains to them only by calling upon the arm of the secular power.

units.la: Si vero deficeret eis brachium seculare: tunc propter defectum vel negligentiam brachii secularis possent per se vti aliquali potentia ad crimina delinquentium corrigenda, quemadmodum multi sancti episcopi propter defectum bonitatis iustitiae & industriae in secularibus dispensationem bonorum communium susceperunt, propter quod dicunt nonnulli, quod si laici essent ratione bonitatis industriæ & zeli boni communis ita sufficientes, sicut prælati: melius esset & magis consonum scripturæ diuinæ dicenti: Nemo militans Deo implicat se negotiis secularibus: quod prælati prædicationi, orationi & officio diuino intenderent: & laici dispensationi bonorum communiismunit implicaretur: sicut si clerici inferiores essent æqui boni, iusti & industrii, æque bonum cömune zelantes, melius esset exemplo Apostolorū, q oratioini & ministerio verbi intendere satagentes sepe Diaconos elegerūt, q cömunia dispensarent, q clerici inferiores ad cōmunia dispensandū idonei, cōmunia possiderent: q plati spiritualibus tota mente incumberent: & tunc plati, qn inuenirent seculares volūtarios ad iustitiā faciendā, non indigerent potentia ad puniendos malos: vbi vero laici inuocati negligerent, vtile esset platos habere potentiam impios coercendi. Et ideo in tali casu vtile esset prælatos vel clericos obedientes platis, bonorū cömunium possessionē habere, imo posset esse casus, q laici omnia bona Ecclesiæ possiderent. Si enim omnes clerici fierent hæretici, omnia bona eorū essent ad laicos devoluta, non quo ad proprietatem, sed quo ad licitā detentionem. Quamdiu postea non inuenirentur clerici, nisi fures, adulteri, percussores, gulosi, ebriosi, discordias seminantes, & vitiis aliis inuoluti, congrueret q bona communia per laicos bonos & industrios dispensarentur. Ad quartam obiectionem dicunt isti: quod quædam auctoritates loquuntur de omnibus rebus temporalibus parvis & magnis: quædā vero licet loquantur primo & vocaliter de magnis divitiis, tamen p- portionabiliter de parvis debent intelligi: qa quantū ad hoc, idē est iudicium de toto & de parte: & de magno & parvo. Et ideo sicut abdicatio magnarum divitiarum ad statū perfectionis spectat: ita etiam abdicatio parvarū ad statum perfectionis spectat. Sed dicet aliquis q non est simile de magnis divitiis & de parvis. Primo quia amor divitiarum, superbia & alia vitia non sequuntur parvas divitias, sed solummodo abundantes. Ergo abdicare parvas divitias ad statum perfectionis non pertinet. Ite, id non pertinet ad statum perfectionis, cuius contrarium ex charitate procedit. Sed habere divitias cōmunes ex charitate procedit, quia charitas non quærit quæ sunt sua, icd magis intendit cōmunibus. Ergo carere cōmunibus divitiis ad statum perfectionis non pertinet. Ad primam istorum dicunt isti, q licet parvas divitias non sequatur tantus amor temporalium, neq; superbia tanta, neq; etiam vitia alia ita gravia in eadem specie, sicut sequuntur divitias abundantes, tamen alia amor & aliqua superbia & alia vitia sequuntur ex parvis divitiis. Quod patet, quia illud, q sine dolore nequaq; amittitur, sine amore minime possidetur. Sed parvæ divitiæ nequaq; amittuntur sine dolore. Ergo sine amore nullatenus possidentur. Item, vnusquisq; plus diligit re propria quantumcunq; parua q alienam. Ergo aliqs amor sequitur possessionē rerum parvarū: & consimiliter est de alienis vitiis. Ad secundum dicunt, q cum aliquis facit res suas esse cōmunes, duo ibi intelliguntur. Nam talis res aliquas cōmunicat alius: & nihilominus res eadē quantū ad dominium & aliqualē proprietatē quodā modo retinet sibi, scil. in cōmuni. Primū a charitate procedit: secundū vt cōmuniter ab amore sui procedit: multo fortius qn aliqs non facit res suas cōmunes, sed res alienas acquirit in cōmuni, q uis ad statū perfectionis pertinet nolle habere res proprias in speciali, tamen velle habere rerū dominiū in cōmuni ad statum perfectionis pertinet. Nec hoc p se regulariter ex charitate procedit: quis non sit impossibile q ex charitate procedat: sicut nec impossibile q retentio divitiarū propriarū ex charitate procedat. Cū igitur dicitur, charitas non quærit quæ sua sunt: hoc est dictū Apostolicum plenum veritate: sed cū dicitur, intedit cömunibus, hoc verum est, quemadmodū largiri Eleemosynā, & divitias proprias dispensare ex charitate procedit. Cū hoc tamen stat, q sicut melius est omnia dare & cū Christo egere, q divitias dispensare: ita melius esset omnia relinquere & cum Christo omni proprietate speciali & cōmuni carere: qui tamen habet res cōmunes, nec vult eas dimittere, si conuenienter & cum debitis circumstantiis intendit istis communibus poterit esse in statu perfectionis, sed non in statu altissimæ paupertatis.
units.tr: But if the secular arm should fail them, then, on account of the failure or negligence of the secular arm, they could themselves use some measure of power to correct the crimes of offenders, just as many holy bishops, because of the lack of goodness, justice and diligence in secular men, undertook the administration of common goods. For this reason some say that if laymen were, by reason of goodness, diligence and zeal for the common good, as sufficient as prelates, it would be better and more in harmony with the divine Scripture, which says: "No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs" (2 Tim. 2), that the prelates should devote themselves to preaching, prayer and the divine office, and the laymen should be engaged in the administration of common goods. Likewise, if inferior clerics were equally good, just and diligent, equally zealous for the common good, it would be better, after the example of the Apostles, who, eager to devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the Word, often chose deacons to dispense common goods, that the inferior clerics, being fit to dispense common goods, should possess them, and that the prelates should devote themselves wholly to spiritual things. Then the prelates, when they found secular men willing to do justice, would not need power to punish the wicked; but where laymen who were called upon were negligent, it would be useful for the prelates to have power to restrain the impious. Therefore in such a case it would be useful for prelates, or clerics obedient to prelates, to have possession of common goods; indeed, there could be a case in which laymen possessed all the goods of the Church. For if all clerics became heretics, all their goods would devolve upon the laymen, not as to property, but as to lawful possession. As long as afterwards no clerics were to be found except thieves, adulterers, murderers, gluttons, drunkards, sowers of discord, and men involved in other vices, it would be fitting that common goods be dispensed by good and diligent laymen. To the fourth objection these men reply that some authorities speak of all temporal goods, small and great, but others, although they speak primarily and expressly of great riches, must nevertheless be understood proportionally of small ones, since in this respect the judgment about the whole and about the part is the same, and about the great and the small. Therefore, just as renunciation of great riches belongs to the state of perfection, so also renunciation of small riches belongs to the state of perfection. But someone will say that the case of great riches is not like that of small ones. First, because the love of riches, pride and other vices do not follow small riches, but only abundant ones; therefore renouncing small riches does not pertain to the state of perfection. Next, that which does not pertain to the state of perfection is what proceeds from the contrary of charity; but having common riches proceeds from charity, because charity does not seek its own things but rather intends common things; therefore lacking common riches does not pertain to the state of perfection. To the first of these, these men reply that although so great a love of temporal things, so great a pride, and other vices of the same kind as grave, do not follow small riches as they follow abundant ones, nevertheless some love, some pride and other vices do follow from small riches. This is evident, because what is not lost without grief is not possessed without love; but small riches are never lost without grief; therefore they are never possessed without love. Again, each person loves what is his own, however small, more than what belongs to another. Therefore some love follows the possession of small riches, and it is similar with the vices of others. To the second they say that when someone makes his goods common, two things are understood there. For another shares such goods in common, and yet the same goods, as to dominion and a certain property, are still retained by him for himself, namely in common. The first proceeds from charity; the second proceeds, as commonly happens, from self-love. Much more so, when someone does not make his own goods common but acquires other people's goods in common, although it pertains to the state of perfection not to want to have one's own goods individually, yet to want to have dominion over goods in common does pertain to the state of perfection. Nor does this proceed of itself regularly from charity, although it is not impossible that it proceeds from charity, just as it is not impossible that the retention of one's own riches proceeds from charity. Therefore, when it is said that charity does not seek its own things, that is an apostolic saying full of truth; but when it is said that it intends common things, this is true, just as bestowing alms and dispensing one's own riches proceed from charity. Yet it remains the case that, just as it is better to give everything and to be in want with Christ than to dispense riches, so it would be better to leave everything and, with Christ, to be without any special or common property. Nevertheless, one who has common goods and is not willing to relinquish them can be in the state of perfection, if he intends those common goods suitably and with due circumstances; but not in the state of the most exalted poverty.

units.la: Secundus error (vt dicitur) contentus in verbis istius impugnati superius recitatis, est: quod ad charitatem per contemptum bonorum temporalium & expropriationem ipsorum via disponitur per hoc precipue, q sollicitudo q ipsa temporalia in acquirendo, conservando, & dispensando exigit, amputatur. Hoc enim esse erroneū probare nituntur. Primo sic: ille q caret amore temporaliū, magis disponitur ad charitatē, q ille qui caret sollicitudine temporalium: quia amor temporaliū est plurim̃ malorum occasio, & magis obuians amori diuino, q sollicitudo circa temporalia. Ergo magis disponitur via ad charitatē per amputationem amoris inordinati temporalium, quam per amputationē sollicitudinis circa temporalia: & ita falsum est, q via precipue disponitur ad charitatem per amputationē sollicitudinis circa temporalia. Secundo sic: sicut vnusquisq; magis disponitur ad charitatē p bonā affectionē interiorem, quā p opus exterius. Ita vnusquisq; magis disponitur ad charitatem per amputationem malæ affectionis interioris, quam p amputationem operis exterioris, cum opus exterius non sit bonum vel malum, nisi propter actū interiore. Cum ergo amor inordinatus temporaliū sit affectio interior, & sollicitudo sit exterior: magis disponitur via ad charitatē per amputationem amoris, quam per amputationē sollicitudinis. Tertio sic: magis disponitur via ad charitatem per amputationem impedimenti, q directe tollit vel diminuit actum charitatis, quam per amputationem illius, q non ita tollit vel diminuit actum charitatis. Sed amor inordinatus temporalium directe tollit vel diminuit actum charitatis vt ex præcedentibus euidenter apparet. Sollicitudo autem, quam exigunt temporalia, non ita tollit vel diminuit actum charitatis: quia licet sollicitudo, ad quam inclinant temporalia, mediante amore, ad quem primo inclinant, tollat vel diminuat actum charitatis: tamen sollicitudo quam exigunt temporalia, non ita tollit vel diminuit actum charitatis, cum talis sollicitudo possit ex charitate procedere. Unde multi retinentes divitias proprias vel communes sæpe ex charitate, vt eas dispensent vtiliter in operibus misericordiæ ex charitate moventur: & per consequens sollicitudo non ita tollit vel diminuit actum charitatis, sicut amor temporalium inordinatus. Præcipue ergo via disponitur ad charitatem per amputationem amoris inordinati temporalium. Quarto sic: AmAmputatio sollicitudinis, quam exigunt temporalia, sæpe ex stultitia uenit. Vnde Prou. 24. sic scribitur: Per agrum hominis pigri pertransiui, & per [illegible, ~20 letters] tum repleuerant vrtica, operuerant superficiem eius spine, & maceria lapidum destructa [illegible, ~10 letters] colligitur, quod carentia sollicitudinis, quam exiguunt agri & vineæ, non [illegible, ~10 letters] gritia prouenit. Ergo carentia vel amputatio sollicitudinis non præcipue ad [illegible, ~10 letters] cut nec stultitia nec pigritia ad charitatem disponit.
units.tr: The second error (as it is said), contained in the words of this opponent recited above, is that the way to charity is prepared chiefly by contempt of temporal goods and their expropriation, namely by cutting off the anxiety that temporal things themselves demand in acquiring, preserving and dispensing them. They strive to prove that this is erroneous. First, thus: he who lacks love of temporal things is more disposed to charity than he who lacks anxiety about temporal things, because love of temporal things is very often the occasion of evils and is more opposed to divine love than anxiety about temporal things is. Therefore the way to charity is prepared more by cutting off disordered love of temporal things than by cutting off anxiety about them. So it is false that the way is chiefly prepared to charity by cutting off anxiety about temporal things. Second, thus: just as each person is more disposed to charity by good inner affection than by an outward work, so each person is more disposed to charity by cutting off bad inner affection than by cutting off an outward work, since an outward work is good or bad only on account of the inner act. Since, then, disordered love of temporal things is an inner affection, and anxiety is outward, the way to charity is prepared more by the cutting off of love than by the cutting off of anxiety. Third, thus: the way to charity is prepared more by removing an impediment that directly takes away or diminishes the act of charity than by removing one that does not so take away or diminish it. But disordered love of temporal things directly takes away or diminishes the act of charity, as is plainly evident from what has gone before. The anxiety that temporal things demand, however, does not take away or diminish the act of charity in this way. For although the anxiety to which temporal things incline, through the love to which they first incline, does take away or diminish the act of charity, the anxiety that temporal things demand does not do so, since such anxiety can proceed from charity. Hence many who keep their own or common riches, often moved by charity, so that they may spend them usefully in works of mercy, are moved by charity; and consequently anxiety does not take away or diminish the act of charity as disordered love of temporal things does. The way to charity is therefore prepared chiefly by the cutting off of disordered love of temporal things. Fourth, thus: the cutting off of the anxiety that temporal things demand often comes from folly. Hence Proverbs 24 is written thus: "I passed by the field of the sluggard, and by the vineyard of the foolish man; and lo, it was all overgrown with nettles, its surface covered with thorns, and its stone wall broken down." From this it is gathered that the lack of anxiety which fields and vineyards demand does not come from virtue but from folly. Therefore the lack or cutting off of anxiety does not chiefly dispose to charity, and neither folly nor sloth disposes to charity.

units.la: Tertius error, vt dicunt, contentus in verbis prædictis, est quod si manet eadem [illegible, ~15 letters] dictam expropriationem, quæ ante ipsam inerat, talis expropriatio ad perfectionem [illegible, ~10 letters] re. Quod enim hoc sit erroneum, probare conantur. Primo ducendo ad hæresim [illegible, ~10 letters] si manente eadem sollicitudine expropriatio temporalium ad perfectionem valet nil expropriatio temporalium fiat per votum paupertatis, sequitur quod si manet eadem sollicitudo circa temporalia post votum, quæ fuit ante votum, votum paupertatis ad perfectionem valet nil cõferre. Sed qua ratione votum paupertatis manente eadem sollicitudine ad perfectionem valet nil conferre, eadem ratione votum castitatis manente eadem castitate, & eadem ratione votum obedientiæ, si alius quis non plus obediret post votum quam ante, sicut sæpe accidit, ad perfectionem valeret nil conferre, & per consequens eadem ratione omne votum supra bonum quod vouetur ad perfectionem vel bonitatem conferret, quod est erroneum manifeste. Constat enim, quod consilium datur de voto. Ait enim Propheta: Vouete & reddite. Consilium autem est de meliori vel saltem de bono. Ergo vouere est bonum. Vbi autem bonum additur bono finito, totum reddituir melius. Ergo manente eadem sollicitudine ipsa expropriatio per votum paupertatis ad perfectionem aliquid confert. Prætea virtus est circa arduum & difficile. Sed actus vouendi paupertatem est magis arduus & magis difficilis, quam amputare sollicitudinem circa temporalia. Ergo ille actus magis virtuosus. Ex quo sequitur, quod manente eadem sollicitudine, ipse actus vouendi ad perfectionem aliquid confert: imo ma- gis confert ad perfectionem & ad statum perfectionis, quam amputatio sollicitudinis, quia per votum paupertatis firmatur quis in statu perfectionis, puta in religione: non autem per amputationem sollicitudinis. Ergo magis confert ad statum perfectionis, quam amputatio sollicitudinis. Et ita per tale votum magis disponitur via ad charitatem, quam per amputationem sollicitudinis, quod est contra primam assertionem superius impugnatam. Amplius, professio religionis in rite profitentibus aliquid confert ad perfectionem. Sed sæpe eadem sollicitudo & etiam maior sine peccato: imo meritorie manet post professionem in multis religiosis, quam ante in nouitiatu inerat. Sæpe enim professi ex merito obedientiæ laudabiliter sunt magis sollicti circa temporalia acquirenda, cõseruanda, & dispensanda, quam fuerunt dum erant nouitii. Ergo manente eadem sollicitudine professio ad perfectionem aliquid confert: & per consequens quamuis maneret eadem sollicitudo circa temporalia, sicut sæpe eadem, vel maior est in Fratribus Minoribus post expropriationem, quam ante inerat, quia illa expropriatio fit, quando profitentur, tamen ipsa expropriatio ad perfectionem valet aliqd conferre. Impugnatus assertionibus supradictis, quas isti reputant erroneas, mendacia diffamatoria quæ (vt dicunt) continentur in verbis prædictis, conantur detegere. Dicentes, primum mendacium esse, quod Fratres Minores post expropriationem huiusmodi non fuerunt minus sollicitiin iudicio & extra, circa temporalia, quā fuerant ante: quia secundū eum Fratres Minores non fuerunt expropriati ante ordinationem Nicolai tertii, & secundū ipsum non fuerunt dicto modo minus solliciti post ordinationem quam ante. Ergo non fuerunt minus sollicti post expropriationem quam ante. Sed hoc constat esse falsum, vt dicunt, quia ante expropriationem prædicta poterat habere dominium & proprietatem rerum, & pro ipsis in iudicio litigare, quæ post minime facere poterant quam ante dicta expropriationem fuerunt seculares vel nouitii, & tam seculares quam nouitii poterant habere, & nonnulli habuerunt rerum dominium & proprietatem. Nonnunquam etiam aliqui nouitii aliter fuerunt de rebus suis solliciti ante expropriationem, quam post expropriationem. Ergo non est generaliter verum, quod nō minus fuerunt solliciti post expropriationem quam ante. Secundum mendacium est, vt dicunt, quod Fratres Minores non sunt minus sollicíti circa temporalia in iudicio & extra, quā sint alii religiosi mendicantes, quod constat esse falsum. Quia nulla sollicitudo circa temporalia est aliis religiosis mendicantibus interdicta, quin eadem sit æque districte Fratribus Minoribus interdicta. Multæ autem sollicitudines circa temporalia sunt Fratribus Minoribus interdictæ, quæ aliis nullatenus interdicuntur. Patet de pertractatione pecuniæ, imo etiam de receptione pecuniæ, quia pecuniam non possunt, nec per se, nec per interpositam personam recipere. Et constat quod sæpe de facto Fratres perdunt vtilitatem, quæ ex pecunia poterit prouenire propter hoc, quod per se ipsos pecuniam nequaq; recipere possunt. Pro nulla etiam re valent in iudicio litigare, nec de facto litigant. Si enim de facto pro- merent p rebus temporalibus litigare, sicut faciunt sæpe alii religiosi mendicantes, constat quod nec religiosi alii, nec clerici, nec laici sunt eis ita fauorabiles, quin contra eos excipiendo, quod non possunt in iudicio litigare, ipsos omni modo impedirent ab actione sua. Et ita constat, quod de facto nec in iudicio nec extra sunt sollicit circa temporalia, sicut Religiosi alii mendicantes.
units.tr: The third error, as they say, contained in the foregoing words, is that if the same anxiety remains after the said expropriation as was there before it, such expropriation does nothing to advance perfection. They try to prove that this is erroneous. First, by leading to the heresy: if, with the same anxiety remaining, the expropriation of temporal things is of no value for perfection, provided it is made by a vow of poverty, it follows that if the same anxiety about temporal things remains after the vow as was there before the vow, the vow of poverty contributes nothing to perfection. But for the same reason that the vow of poverty contributes nothing to perfection while the same anxiety remains, the vow of chastity would contribute nothing while the same chastity remains, and likewise the vow of obedience, if someone did not obey more after the vow than before, as often happens. By the same reasoning, every vow would contribute nothing to the perfection or goodness of the good that is vowed, which is plainly erroneous. For it is clear that counsel is given about the vow. The Prophet says: "Vow and pay" (Ps. 76:12). Counsel, however, concerns what is better, or at least what is good. Therefore to vow is good; and where a good is added to a finite good, the whole becomes better. Therefore, with the same anxiety remaining, the expropriation itself by a vow of poverty contributes something to perfection. Moreover, virtue is concerned with what is arduous and difficult. But the act of vowing poverty is more arduous and more difficult than cutting off anxiety about temporal things. Therefore that act is more virtuous. From this it follows that, with the same anxiety remaining, the act of vowing itself contributes something to perfection; indeed it contributes more to perfection and to the state of perfection than the cutting off of anxiety does, because by the vow of poverty a person is confirmed in the state of perfection, for example in a religious order, whereas this is not so by the cutting off of anxiety. Therefore it contributes more to the state of perfection than the cutting off of anxiety does. And so by such a vow the way to charity is prepared more than by the cutting off of anxiety, which is contrary to the first assertion impugned above. Furthermore, profession in a religious order contributes something to perfection in those who profess it rightly. But often the same anxiety, and even a greater one, without sin, indeed meritoriously, remains after profession in many religious, as was there before, in the novitiate. For often those who have professed, from the merit of obedience, are laudably more anxious about acquiring, preserving and dispensing temporal things than they were while they were novices. Therefore, with the same anxiety remaining, profession contributes something to perfection; and consequently, even though the same anxiety about temporal things might remain, as is often the same or even greater among the Friars Minor after expropriation as it was before, nevertheless that expropriation, which takes place when they profess, does contribute something to perfection. Having impugned the assertions above, which these men judge erroneous, they try to expose the defamatory lies which (as they say) are contained in the words quoted. They say the first lie is that the Friars Minor, after such expropriation, were not less anxious in court and out of it about temporal things than they had been before. For, according to him, the Friars Minor were not expropriated before the ordinance of Nicholas III, and according to that same ordinance they were not, in the said manner, less anxious after it than before. Therefore they were not less anxious after expropriation than before. But this, they say, is plainly false, because before the said expropriation they could have ownership and property of things, and could litigate in court for them; which they could scarcely do afterwards. Those who were secular or novices before the expropriation could hold, and some did hold, ownership and property of things, both secular and novices alike. Sometimes too some novices were more anxious about their possessions before the expropriation than after it. Therefore it is not generally true that they were not less anxious after expropriation than before. The second lie, they say, is that the Friars Minor are not less anxious about temporal things, in court and out of it, than the other mendicant religious are. This plainly is false. For no anxiety about temporal things is forbidden to the other mendicant religious which is not equally and strictly forbidden to the Friars Minor, whereas many anxieties about temporal things are forbidden to the Friars Minor which are in no way forbidden to the others. This is clear regarding the handling of money, indeed even regarding the receiving of money, since they can receive money neither personally nor through an intervening person. And it is plain that the Friars often in fact forgo the benefit that could come from money, precisely because they cannot in any way receive money in person. Nor are they able to litigate in court for any property, and in fact they do not litigate. For if they were in fact to try to litigate for temporal things, as the other mendicant religious often do, it is clear that neither other religious, nor clergy, nor laity would be so favourable to them that they would not, by objecting that they cannot litigate in court, impede them in every way from their action. And so it is plain that, in fact, the Friars Minor are neither in court nor out of it anxious about temporal things as the other mendicant religious are.

units.la: (Verba constitutionis prædictæ truncate recitat.) Verum est, quod nō recitat omnia verba: tamen recitat illa, quæ sibi sufficiunt. (Illa quæ eius defectum manifeste insinuant omittendo) Imo dicunt isti, sicut stensum est, omittendo illa quæ intentionem ipsius appellantis declarant, & quæ istum impugnat in multis errare, quæ appellans non tetigit manifestant. (Retentio dominii) intendit per retentionem dominii expropriationem omnium temporalium. (Via per hoc disponitur.) Per amputationem scil. {a}licet amoris inordinati temporalium, & etiam per votum paupertatis. (Restat quod si sollicitudo eadem posset expropriationem huiusmodi quae ante ipsum inerat perficere ad perfectionem huiusmodi talis expropriatio valeat subsequi.) Istud dicunt esse falsum, & intertur ex falso, ut ostensum est, & nihilominus dicunt quod sophistice ex falsis antecedentibus concladitur: quia quando plura disponunt ut ad aliquid unum quanto plura & alia minus ex carentia minus disponentis in summo gradu, non potest argui quod alia nihil disponunt. Et ideo esse quod amputatio sollicitudinis circa temporalia praecipue disponeret ad charitatem, ex hoc non sequeretur, quamvis sollicitudo non esset totaliter amputata: sed manet eadem quae prius, quod alia nihil conferrent ad charitatem: imo possent multum conferre, quia non tantum sicut illud quod summe disponeret. (Post ordinationem praedictam.) Hoc insinuat quod ista expropriatio Fratrum Minorum, scilicet abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium in speciali & in communi non fuerit ante ordinationem Nicolai tertii, id est manifeste falsum: quia istam abdicationem vovit Beatus Franciscus, & omnes Fratres sequentes usque ad tempus praesens. (Quamvis sint religiosi mendicantes alii.) Hoc dicunt esse falsum, ut probatum est. (Credimus utique quod nullus sapiens probatione huiusmodi reprobabit.) Dicunt quod omnis sapiens probatione huiusmodi reprobabit: quia, ut dicunt, in extraordinariis erroribus fermentatur (Propter quod ipsam haereticus non expressit.) Dicunt quod appellans Doctor Theologiae sacrae solennis, quem iste idiota praelumit temerarie haereticum appellare; non propter efficaciam rationis praedictae ipsam omisit exprimere, cum pecce aperte tam in materia quam in forma, sicut evidenter probatum existit: sed ipsam non expressit, quia causa brevitatis pro tunc dimisit errores contentos in ipsa indiscussos.
units.tr: (He recites the words of the aforesaid constitution in truncated form.) It is true that he does not recite all the words, but he recites those that suffice for him. (By omitting those words which clearly point to its defect) Indeed, as has been shown, they say, he omits those things which declare the intention of the appellant, and which show that the appellant, in attacking him, did not touch on the many errors he commits. (Retention of ownership) He means by the retention of ownership the renunciation of all temporal goods. (The way is prepared by this.) That is, by the cutting away of the disordered love of temporal things, and also by the vow of poverty. (It remains that if the same anxiety could bring about expropriation of the kind that was present before, such expropriation could follow to bring about perfection of this kind.) They say this is false, and it is inferred from a falsehood, as has been shown; and nevertheless they say that it is sophistically concluded from false antecedents. For when several things dispose toward one thing, the more so and the others less, from the deficiency of the less disposing thing at the highest degree, it cannot be argued that the others do nothing to dispose toward it. And so, even if the cutting away of anxiety about temporal things especially disposed toward charity, it would not follow from this, although the anxiety were not wholly cut away, that the rest contribute nothing to charity. The position remains the same as before: the others could contribute much, since they do not contribute merely as that which disposes in the highest degree. (After the aforesaid ordinance.) This suggests that the expropriation of the Friars Minor, namely the renunciation of ownership of all temporal goods, both individually and in common, did not exist before the ordinance of Nicholas III; which is manifestly false, because Blessed Francis vowed this renunciation, and all the friars following him to the present time have observed it. (Although there are other mendicant religious.) They say this is false, as has been proved. (We certainly believe that no wise man will reprove this by such proof.) They say that every wise man will reprove it by such proof, because, as they say, it ferments in extraordinary errors. (On account of which the heretic did not express it.) They say that the appellant, a solemn Doctor of sacred Theology, whom this idiot rashly presumes to call a heretic, did not omit to express that argument of the aforesaid kind on account of its lack of force, since he clearly sins both in matter and in form, as has been plainly proved; but he did not express it because, for the sake of brevity, he then passed over the errors contained in it without discussion.

units.la: CAP. LXXVII.
units.tr: CHAP. LXXVII.

units.la: {b}Item, intendit probare dicta constitutio, quod quantum ad hoc quod propter carentiam talis dominii, se pauperiores Fratres ipsi dicere valeant: quam si res ipsas cum illo, quo carere se dicunt, dominio obtinerent: non profuit retentio dominii supradicta. Quod (ut sequitur) probat. Licet enim praedecessor noster praedictus Dominium earum rerum, quae ipsis Fratribus offerri seu conferri, aut alias obvenire contingeret: quarum tamen usum facti haberet, licet ordini vel Fratribus antedictis usu simplici facti praedicta Fratribus reservato, in se & Romanam Ecclesiam recipiendum duxerit, ac libere pertinere decreverit, ut superius est expressum: attento tamen ipsorum Fratrum vendi modo, & eius effectu, & patientia, circa modum Romanae Ecclesiae subsecuta, non ipse usus Fratrum dici debet: sed potius Romana Ecclesia dominium esse simplex. Quia enim simplicem usuarium dicere poterit, cui rem usuariam licet permutare, vendere, aut donare, praeculdubio hae naturae repugnant usuario, nec ad usuarium pertinens, quamtum de rebus mobilibus antedictis faciunt Fratres ipsi. Quod autem dominium Romanae Ecclesiae reservatum simplex conferri debeat, ex hoc patet, quod ex illo nullo eidem Ecclesiae temporale obvenit hactenus commodum, nec speratur quod obvenire debeat in futurum: tum nec intentio reservandi, ipsorum Fratrum fuerit, quod ad quemcumque alium quam ad Fratres dictarum rerum peveniret compendium: quod praeculdubio modus ipsorum Fratrum, & Romana Ecclesia subsecuta patientia evidentius declaravit. Et quod talis fuerit intentio ordinati, etiam ex hoc patet: quod illarum rerum sibi & Ecclesiae Romanae dominium danitas et retinuit, quarum usum facti licet habere Ordini & Fratribus antedictis. Talis autem dominii carentia re in praesenti, despe in futurum omni commodo denudati, quo ad paupertatem temporalem, quam altioris pro mendicitate alii in testimonii habentibus sibi vindicant dicti Fratres, pauperitatem non efficit non habentem. Ex praedictis probatum evidenter credimus, quod attento usu dictorum Fratrum rerum, in quibus usum facti simplicem afferunt se habere & patientia Apostolicae Sedis, eos pauperiores carentia talis dominii non effecit.
units.tr: Likewise, the said constitution intends to prove that, as to the claim that the friars can call themselves poorer because they lack such ownership, retaining that ownership would not have helped them if they obtained the things themselves with the ownership they say they lack. It proves this as follows. Although our predecessor mentioned above decided to receive into himself and the Roman Church, and declared to belong freely to them, the ownership of those things which were offered or conferred on the friars themselves, or otherwise came to them, of which they nonetheless had the simple use of fact, the aforesaid simple use of fact being reserved to the Order or to the friars mentioned above, as stated above; yet, in view of the manner in which the friars themselves sell, its effect, and the forbearance of the Roman Church that followed concerning that manner, that use should not be called the friars' use. Rather, the ownership of the Roman Church should be called simple. For one who may be called a simple usuary, to whom it is permitted to exchange, sell, or give away the usufructuary thing, is certainly not a usuary, since these acts are repugnant to a usuary and do not belong to one, yet this is what the friars themselves do with the aforesaid movable things. That the reserved ownership of the Roman Church ought to be conferred as simple is clear from this: no temporal advantage has so far come to that Church from it, nor is it hoped that any will come in future. Nor was it the intention of the one reserving it that any gain from those things should come to anyone other than the friars, which the manner of the friars themselves and the forbearance of the Roman Church that followed have more clearly declared. That this was the intention of the ordinance is also evident from this: he granted and retained for himself and the Roman Church the ownership of those things of which the Order and the aforesaid friars may have the simple use of fact. Lack of such ownership, stripped now of every advantage and in future of every hope, does not make one who lacks it poor in temporal poverty, which the said friars claim for themselves as a higher testimony of their mendicancy. From the foregoing we firmly believe it has been clearly proved that, in view of the friars' use of things, over which they claim to have the simple use of fact, and with the forbearance of the Apostolic See, their lack of such ownership has not made them poorer.

units.la: In parte ista impugnatus replicat rationem factam in constitutione Ad conditorem: per quam probatur, quod carentia dominii, quo carent Fratres Minores, non reddit eos pauperiores, quam si tale haberetur dominium: quam rationem omisit appellans. Dicit ergo, quod retentio dominii quia carent Fratres, non profuit ipsis, ut per eam essent pauperiores. Quod probatur: quia licet Romanus pontifex dominium rerum, quibus utuntur Fratres sibi retinuerit, attentis tamen Fratrum vendi modo, & circa eundem modum patientia Romanae Ecclesiae subsecuta, usus Fratrum non debet dici simplex, sed dominium Romanae Ecclesiae debet dici simplex. Haec ratio continet duas partes quarum primam probat ibi: Quia enim simplicem quam probat sic. Ille non est simplex usuarius, cui licet rem usuariam permutare, vendere, & donare. Hoc faciunt Fratres de rebus, quibus utuntur. Ergo non sunt simplices usuarii: & per consequens usus eorum non est simplex. Postea ibi: quod autem dominium, probat secundam partem, scilicet quod dominium Romanae Ecclesiae est simplex, ex quo habentur nullum provenit commodum temporale, nec speratur quod provenire debeat in futurum. Sed tale est dominium rerum, quibus Fratres Minores utuntur: quia nec fuit intentio reservantis, nec intentio Fratrum, quod ex illis rebus alicui alteri temporale commodum proveniret. Ergo dominium Romanae Ecclesiae est simplex. Sed propter carentiam dominii omni temporali commodo denudati, quale est dominium simplex, non est carens pauperior. Ergo propter carentiam talis dominii non sunt Fratres pauperiores.
units.tr: In answer to this part, the opponent repeats the argument made in the constitution Ad conditorem, by which it is proved that the lack of ownership which the Friars Minor have does not make them poorer than if they held such ownership. The appellant left this argument out. He therefore says that retaining ownership, because the friars lack it, did not benefit them so as to make them poorer. This is proved as follows: although the Roman pontiff retained for himself the ownership of the things the friars use, nevertheless, in view of the friars' manner of selling and the forbearance of the Roman Church that followed concerning that manner, the friars' use should not be called simple, but the ownership of the Roman Church should be called simple. This argument has two parts. The first he proves where he says, "For one who...", as follows: one is not a simple usuary to whom it is permitted to exchange, sell, and give away the usufructuary thing. The friars do this with the things they use. Therefore they are not simple usuaries, and consequently their use is not simple. Then, where he says, "that the ownership...", he proves the second part, namely that the ownership of the Roman Church is simple, since no temporal advantage has come from it, nor is it hoped that any will come in future. But such is the ownership of the things the Friars Minor use, since it was neither the intention of the one reserving it nor the intention of the friars that any temporal advantage should come to anyone else from those things. Therefore the ownership of the Roman Church is simple. But one who lacks ownership stripped of all temporal advantage, which is simple ownership, is not made poorer by lacking it. Therefore the friars are not made poorer by their lack of such ownership.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, haec verba plures continere errores. Ad cuius evidentiam dicunt primo esse videndum, quod dominium vocat dominium simplex; dicentes: quod dominium simplex vocat dominium simpliciter inutile, quod non est verum dominium, sed dominium solummodo nuncupatur, non est dominium. Hoc ex dictis suis probatur expresse. Nam constat, quod dominium simulatum verbale, nudum & aenigmaticum est dominium inutile, spiritualiter praecipue, cum simulata sint inutilia reputanda, quamvis temporaliter inveniantur talia. Dominium etiam simulatum non est verum dominium. Dominium vero verbale, nudum & aenigmaticum solo nomine dominium reputatur. Sed praedictum dominium Romanae Ecclesiae est simulatum, verbale, nudum & aenigmaticum secundum istum: cum aperte dicat in constitutione Ad conditorem: Nolentes, in posterum sub pretexta seu pallio talis dominii verbalis, nudi et aenigmatici tanta bona, quanta a dictis Fratribus faciunt infigi, ac semetipsum tantum malis, quanta procedunt ex simulatione huiusmodi ministrare. Ex quibus verbis non solum modo patet, quod dictum dominium est simulatum, verbale, nudum & aenigmaticum: sed etiam ex eis colligitur evidenter, quod secundum istum tale dominium est inutile, imo nocivum, cum dicto dominio multa bona infici, & multis malis ministrari fomentum. Et ita patet quod dominium simplex vocat hoc dominium inutile, fictum, & nocivum. Hoc viso dicunt isti, quod in praedictis verbis quatuor principaliter continentur errores. Quorum primus est, quod per carentiam dominii Romanae Ecclesiae reservati Fratres Minores non possunt dici pauperiores. Secundus est quod dominium rerum, quibus Fratres Minores utuntur, Romanae Ecclesiae reservatum est simplex praedicto modo accipiendo simplex. Tertius est quod dominium omni temporali commodo denudatum est inutile. Quartus est quod carentia dominii omni commodo temporali denudati non efficit pauperem non habentem seu carentem tali dominio. Alios errores, mendacia & contradictiones dicunt isti contineri in verbis praedictis, de quibus super literam apparebit.
units.tr: But these opponents say that these words contain several errors. To make this clear, they say that one must first see what he means by "simple ownership". They say: "simple ownership" means ownership that is simply useless, which is not true ownership but is only named ownership, and is not ownership at all. They prove this expressly from his own words. For it is agreed that feigned, verbal, bare and enigmatic ownership is useless ownership, especially in the spiritual sense, since feigned things are to be considered useless, even if they are found to be such temporally. Feigned ownership is also not true ownership, while verbal, bare and enigmatic ownership is considered ownership in name only. But the aforesaid ownership of the Roman Church is, according to him, feigned, verbal, bare and enigmatic, since he plainly says in the constitution Ad conditorem: Wishing, in future, not to furnish under the pretext or cloak of such verbal, bare and enigmatic ownership as many goods as the said friars make to be inflicted, and to supply to themselves only as many evils as proceed from feigning of this kind. From these words it is clear not only that the said ownership is feigned, verbal, bare and enigmatic, but also that, according to him, such ownership is useless, indeed harmful, since many goods are infected by it and fuel is supplied to many evils. And so it is plain that he calls this ownership, which is feigned, useless and harmful, "simple ownership." Having seen this, they say that four main errors are contained in the aforesaid words. The first is that through lack of the ownership reserved by the Roman Church the Friars Minor cannot be called poorer. The second is that the ownership of the things the Friars Minor use, reserved to the Roman Church, is simple, taking "simple" in the sense just described. The third is that ownership stripped of all temporal advantage is useless. The fourth is that lack of ownership stripped of all temporal advantage does not make poor one who does not have or lacks such ownership. They say that other errors, lies and contradictions are contained in the aforesaid words, which will become apparent from the text itself.

units.la: Est igitur primus error hic contentus, quod propter carentiam dominii Romanae Ecclesiae reservati Fratres Minores non possunt dici pauperiores. Quod enim hoc sit erroneum, multipliciter probare conantur. Primo sic. Sicut per adeptionem veri dominii aliquis dicitur dicitor, ita per carentiam dominii veri aliquis dicitur pauper. Sed dominium rerum, quibus utuntur Fratres Romanae Ecclesiae reservatum est verum dominium. Illud enim dominium, quod alicui tribuit potestatem agendi, vel defendendi, actetiam vtendi & dispensandi est verum dominium. Propter hoc enim & similia dicitur aliquod dominium esse verum dominium. Sed dominium Romanae Ecclesiae reservatum in huiusmodi rebus est tale: quod per ipsum poterit alicui competere potestas agendi & defendendi in iudicio: ac etiam utendi & dispensandi: quae si illud dominium reservatum Romanae Ecclesiae dimitteretur Fratribus, haec omnia competerent Fratribus Minoribus, sicut haec omnia competunt aliis religiosis mendicantibus, & aliis respectu rerum quibus utuntur, & quarum habent aliquale dominium. Ergo tale dominium est verum dominium: licet non sit ita plenum dominium, sicut dominium, quod habent laici in rebus suis. Sicut igitur per adeptionem talis dominii dicitur aliquis dicitor: ita per carentiam eiusdem dominii dicetur aliquis pauperior: & per consequens Fratres Minores per carentiam talis dominii vere dicuntur pauperiores.
units.tr: The first error contained here, then, is that through lack of the ownership reserved to the Roman Church the Friars Minor cannot be called poorer. They try to prove in many ways that this is erroneous. First, as follows. Just as someone is called richer by acquiring true ownership, so someone is called poorer by lacking true ownership. But the ownership of the things the friars use, reserved to the Roman Church, is true ownership. For that ownership which grants someone the power of acting or defending, and also of using and dispensing, is true ownership. It is for this and similar reasons that some ownership is called true ownership. But the ownership reserved to the Roman Church in such things is of this kind: through it there may belong to someone the power of acting and defending in court, as well as of using and dispensing. If that reserved ownership were handed over by the Roman Church to the friars, all these powers would belong to the Friars Minor, just as they belong to other mendicant religious and to others with respect to the things they use and over which they have some kind of ownership. Therefore such ownership is true ownership, although it is not as full as the ownership that laymen have in their own goods. Thus, just as someone is called richer by acquiring such ownership, so someone will be called poorer by lacking the same ownership; and consequently the Friars Minor are truly called poorer through their lack of such ownership.

units.la: Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod propter adeptionem talis dominii non dicitur quis ditior. Nam Papa propter adeptionem talis dominii non est ditior: & per consequens Fratres propter carentiam talis dominii non sunt pauperiores: quia si propter alicuius dominii adeptionem non est quis ditior, nec propter eiusdem dominii carentiam est quis pauperior. Quod autem Papa propter adeptionem talis dominii non fit ditior, ostenditur. Nam per illud dominium, per quod habenti nulla potestas acquiritur specialis, sed omnis potestas agendi, defendendi, vtendi, dispensandi, & similia faciendi, habet quis sine tali dominio, sicut cum tali dominio non fit ditior. Papa autem absque reservatione talis dominii haberet in rebus, quibus Fratres Minores utuntur, omnem potestatem praedictam & consimilia faciendi, quae habet cum reservatione talis dominii. Ergo Papa propter reservationem talis dominii non fit ditior. Et per consequens Fratres propter carentiam eiusdem dominii non sunt pauperiores.
units.tr: But perhaps someone will say that a person does not become richer by acquiring such ownership. For the Pope does not become richer by acquiring such ownership, and so, consequently, the friars do not become poorer by lacking it, because if someone does not become richer by acquiring a given ownership, neither does he become poorer by lacking that same ownership. That the Pope does not become richer by acquiring such ownership is shown as follows. A person has, without such ownership, whatever power is conferred by an ownership through which no special power is acquired but only the power to act, defend, use, dispense and do similar things, and he does not become richer by having it. The Pope, however, without the reservation of such ownership, would have over the things the Friars Minor use all the aforesaid power and the power to do similar things that he has with the reservation of such ownership. Therefore the Pope does not become richer through the reservation of such ownership, and consequently the friars are not poorer through lacking the same ownership.

units.la: Ad solvendum plene istam obiectionem dicunt isti impugnatores quod oportet inquirere quale potestatem habet Papa super res aliorum religiosorum & clericorum. Ad hoc enim sunt diversae opiniones. Quidam enim dicunt, quod ex intentione fidelium, diversae res diversis sunt Ecclesiis, monasteriis, & aliis collegiis assignatae, a quibus sine culpa, & absque causa sufficienti & rationabili, etiam manifesta auferri non debent. Dicunt enim, quod in traditione rei suae quilibet potest imponere legem, quam vult, maxime quae non est legibus improbata. Cum igitur Ecclesiae & collegia aliqua ex donatione fidelium sint ditata & dotata, potuerunt fideles ditando, & dotando Ecclesias talem legem imponere, quod a nullo viuente, nec etiam a Papa tollerentur bona collata Ecclesiis sine culpa earum, & absque causa rationabili sufficienti & manifesta: tales enim leges, conditiones, aut pacta non videntur legibus reprobata: imo nec videtur, quod possent iustis legibus reprobari. Et haec videtur fuisse intentio regum & principum, quando Ecclesias construxerunt, & monasteria, quae & multis diuitiis dotaverunt. Propter quod de facto, quando Papa de bonis Templariorum post cassationem eorum voluit ordinare, plures patroni seu fundatores locorum ipsorum in multis partibus restituerunt expresse dicentes, quod intentio progenitorum & antecessorum eorum fuit solummodo bona illa Templariis pro defensione fidei assignare. Et ideo ipsis destructis bona ipsorum ad successores dantium fuerunt legitime devoluta: & sic dicta bona occupant usque ad praesentem diem. Alii dicunt, quod Papa in omnibus bonis Ecclesiae habet plenitudinem potestatis, sic quod potest ipse in iudicio vindicare & defendere, & ad quoscunque usus, ad quos data sunt converti. Et secundum istam opinionem secundam distinguendum est de rebus, quibus Fratres utuntur. Quaedam enim eis dantur vel offeruntur a viris Ecclesiasticis de bonis Ecclesiae: & illarum Papa non acquirit de novo quodcunque dominium, sed dominium sibi reservat, in quantum nullum dominium Fratribus ipsis concedit: nec efferentes vel dantes aliquod in Fratres transferunt dominium. Et quantum ad istas res distinguendum est, inter adeptionem dominii & reservationem seu retentionem dominii: quia istarum rerum Papa, per hoc quod Fratribus offeruntur vel dantur, nullum acquirat dominium, sed dominium quod prius habuit retinet sibi nullum
units.tr: To resolve this objection fully, these opponents say one must inquire what power the Pope has over the goods of other religious orders and of clergy. On this there are different opinions. Some hold that, by the intention of the faithful, different goods are assigned to different churches, monasteries and other colleges, and these may not be taken from them without fault, without a sufficient and reasonable cause, even a manifest one. For they say that in handing over his own property anyone may impose whatever law he wishes, especially one not forbidden by law. Since therefore churches and colleges have been enriched and endowed by the gifts of the faithful, the faithful, in enriching and endowing the churches, could have imposed such a law that the goods conferred on the churches could not be taken away by anyone living, not even by the Pope, without fault on their part and without a reasonable, sufficient and manifest cause. For such laws, conditions or agreements do not seem to be reprobated by law; indeed it does not even seem that they could be reprobated by just laws. And this seems to have been the intention of the kings and princes who built churches and monasteries and endowed them with great riches. Hence, in fact, when the Pope wished to dispose of the goods of the Templars after their suppression, many patrons or founders of those places in many regions restored them, expressly saying that the intention of their forefathers and predecessors had been to assign those goods to the Templars solely for the defence of the faith. And so, with the Templars destroyed, their goods lawfully passed back to the successors of the donors, and those goods are still held by them today. Others say that the Pope has fullness of power over all the goods of the Church, so that he can himself in judgement claim and defend them and convert them to whatever uses they were given for. According to this second opinion, one must distinguish concerning the things the Friars use. For some of these are given or offered to them by churchmen out of the goods of the Church. Of these the Pope acquires no new dominion, but keeps for himself the dominion he already had, since he grants no dominion to the Friars; nor do those who offer or give anything transfer dominion to the Friars. And regarding these things one must distinguish between acquiring dominion and reserving or retaining dominion, because the Pope, by the fact that these things are offered or given to the Friars, acquires no dominion over them, but retains for himself the dominion he previously had, granting none to the Friars.

units.la: nullum {a}ullam dominium Fratribus concededo. Sic non est de aliis religiosis: quia etiam talium rerum quàm-uis secundum istam opinionem nullum dominium Papæ depereat, tamen aliquod dominium religiosi aliis concedunt: quemadmodum qui accommodat seu concedit alii vestem suam, cum potestate eam retinendi quamdiu cunq; sibi placuerit, nihil amittit. Ita enim potest libere facere de veste, quod placet, & tamen alius acquirit potestatem vtendi veste, quam prius non habuit. Aliæ sunt res, quæ de bonis propriis à laicis vel clericis sunt oblatæ vel datæ. Et illarum Papa acquirit dominium tale, quale habet in bonis communibus. Intentio enim dantium seu offerentium, nisi secus exprimant, est q; hoc fiat de rebus illis, quomodo Fratrum statui competit, sicut Ecclesia ordinauit. Fratrum autem statui competit, quod illarum rerum Fratribus non acquiratur dominium. Ecclesia autem ordinauit, quod dictarum rerum in Ecclesiam transferatur dominium: & quod Fratres licite vtantur eisdem, quàdiu Papæ placuerit. Et propter illas res Papa fit ditior tunc, quando res huiusmodi taliter Fratribus concedantur. Propter primas autem Papa non fit ditior, qñ Fratribus Minoribus conceduntur: sed factus fuit ditior propter eas, qñ primò oblatæ fuerunt Ecclesiæ. Et ita stat argumentum: q ex quo p adeptione talis dominii, habens dominium tale est ditior. Sequitur quod Fratres carentes tali dominio sunt vere & realiter pauperiores: quam si tale dominium obtinerent. Secundo sic arguunt: Fratres Minores sunt pauperiores propter carentiam dominii, quod retinent seculares in quibusdam rebus, quibus vtuntur, scil. in quibusdam locis quæ inhabitant. Ergo à simili sunt pauperiores propter carentiam dominii, q in aliis rebus quibus vtuntur retinet sibi Romana Ecclesia: q a qua ratione carentia dominii quarundâ rerum facit eos pauperiores, carentia dominii aliarû rerum facit eos pauperiores.
units.tr: Not so with other religious orders. Even though, on this opinion, the Pope loses no dominion over such things, they nevertheless grant some dominion to their members. It is like someone who lends or gives his cloak to another, with the power of keeping it for as long as he pleases: he loses nothing. He may freely do with the cloak whatever he likes, and yet the other acquires a power of using the cloak which he did not have before. There are other things which are offered or given to the Friars from the private property of laymen or clergy, and of these the Pope acquires dominion of the same kind as he has over common goods. For the intention of the givers or offerers, unless they express otherwise, is that this be done with those things in the way that befits the state of the Friars, as the Church has ordained. It befits the state of the Friars that no dominion over those things be acquired for the Friars themselves. The Church has ordained that dominion over those things be transferred to the Church, and that the Friars may lawfully use them for as long as it pleases the Pope. And because of those things the Pope becomes richer when such things are granted to the Friars in this way. But because of the first kind the Pope does not become richer when they are granted to the Friars Minor; he became richer because of them when they were first offered to the Church. And so the argument stands: since by the acquisition of such dominion one who has it becomes richer, it follows that the Friars who lack such dominion are truly and really poorer than they would be if they had it. Secondly, they argue thus: the Friars Minor are poorer because of their lack of the dominion which secular people retain over certain things the Friars use, namely certain places they inhabit. Therefore, by parity, they are poorer because of their lack of the dominion over other things they use, which the Roman Church retains for itself. For whatever reason the lack of dominion over some things makes them poorer, the lack of dominion over other things makes them poorer too.

units.la: Antecedens probatur. Nâ constat q ille à quo res ptiosæ licite & ad libitû alterius possunt ab eo auferri, est pauperior, quam si haberet dominium quo posset res illas retinere contra voluntatem alterius & eas in iudicio defendere. Sed si Fratres haberent dominium locorum, quæ patroni seu fundatores aut dantes sibi reseruant, possent ea contra eorum voluntatem tenere, nec patroni seu dantes possent Fratres licite ad libitum suum expellere; sicut nunc possunt eos ad libitum licite, etiam aliq; causa expellere. Ergo Fratres propter carentiam talis dominii in illis rebus sunt pauperiores. Amplius, carentia dominii, quod potest care vendi, reddit carentem pauperiorem. Sed dominium locorum & aliarum rerum, quibus vtuntur Fratres, quod sibi retinent concedentes, potest care vendi. Multi enim inuenirentur mercatores, qui pro illo dominio magnam darent pecuniam. Auari enim & Fratribus indeuouri, qui nullum ius suum dimitterent pro tali dominio: ex quo per illud dominium possent sibi res retinere, & si deinerentur per iudicium recuperare non modicam libenter offerrent pecuniam, & emerent dominium supradictum. Quo empto Fratres expellerent, nec Fratres nec alius nomine cuiusquam possent tales emptores propter retentionem rerum huiusmodi infestare. Ergo carentia dominii talis reddit Fratres ipsos pauperiores. Rursus, Fratres vtentes locis & domibus ac aliis rebus, quarum dominium sibi retinent concedentes, non sunt ditiores propter huiusmodi, quam sunt alii quibus precarium vel commodatum conceditur. Et ita constat, quod Fratres propter carentiam talis dominii pauperiores sunt censendi. Confirmatur, quia constat quod qui habent vsum iuris vel vsumfructum, plus iuris habet in rebus, quarum habent vsum iuris & vsumfructum, quam habeant Fratres Minores in rebus quarum dominium sibi retinent laici concedentes casde. Sed tales vsuarii & vsufructuarii sunt pauperiores, quam si illarum rerum haberent dominium, & nullus alius haberet vsum iuris, nec vsumfructum ipsarum. Ergo multo fortius Fratres sunt pauperiores, quam si haberent dominium talium rerum, quibus vtuntur quod sibi retinent concedentes, & per consequens ratione eadem sunt pauperiores propter carentiam dominii quod sibi Ecclesia Romana reseruat. Tertio sic arguunt: Expropriati sunt pauperes. Ergo magis expropriati sunt magis pauperes. Sed qui carent quocunq; dominio vero sunt magis expropriati, quam illi qui habent tale verum dominium. Vnde autem dominium quo valet quis pro temporalibus nomine proprio vel sui collegii in iudicio litigare, est verum dominium, non falsum neq; fictum. Ergo qui carent omni dominio, quo valet quis in iudicio litigare, sunt magis expropriati, quam si tale dominium haberent. Ex quo sequitur, q sunt magis pauperes. Sed Fratres propter carentiam dominii Romanæ Ecclesiæ reseruati non possunt pro rebus illis in iudicio litigare. Ergo propter carentiam talis dominii sunt magis expropriati: & per consequens pauperiores. Quarto sic arguunt: Illi qui realiter magis à temporalibus elongantur, sunt pauperiores. Sed Fratres Minores secundum Nicolaum tertium in decretali Exiit, propter carentiam omnis dominii in speciali & in communi, magis à temporalibus elongantur. Ergo propter carentiam talis dominii sunt pauperiores. Quinto sic: Illi qui habent altissimâ paupertate, sunt pauperiores quam illi, qui non habent eam. Illi autem, quia carent tali dominio, habent altissimam paupertatem. Qui autem habent tale dominium, non habent altissimâ paupertatem. Hoc patet per Innocentium 5. qui dicit, altam paupertatem esse, habere pauca propria propter Deum: altiorem quæ nulla habet propria, habet tamen in communi: altissimam, quæ nihil habet in hoc mundo, nec in proprio nec in communi. Ergo q carent tali dominio, propter talem carentiam sunt pauperiores. Sed ad hoc iste impugnatus respondet in constitutione, quia quorundâ dicens, quod Innocent. 5. hoc dixit non vt Papa, sed vt frater Petrus de Tharentasia in quadam Postilla sua. Licet hæc responsio sua sit colorata: quia non omnia dicta summorum pontificum, præcipue quæ non solenniter auctoritate Papali diffiniunt, sunt autentica reputanda: tamen ratio stat, quia constat, quod illa paupertas est altior, quæ caret aliquo, quod pertinet ad diuitias, quam illa quę habet illud. Sed dominium commune aliquo modo ad dominium spectat. Aliter enim religiosi magnas possessiones habentes nullo modo essent ditiores, quam reli-
units.tr: The antecedent is proved. It is plain that one from whom valuable things may lawfully be taken at another's pleasure is poorer than he would be if he had a dominion by which he could keep those things against another's will and defend them in court. But if the Friars had dominion over the places which patrons, founders or donors reserve for themselves, they could hold them against the will of those patrons or donors, and the patrons or donors could not lawfully expel the Friars at their pleasure, as they now can lawfully expel them at pleasure, even without any cause. Therefore the Friars, through lack of such dominion over those things, are poorer. Further, the lack of a dominion which can be sold makes one poorer. But the dominion over the places and other things the Friars use, which the granting laymen keep for themselves, can be sold. For many merchants would be found who would give a large sum of money for that dominion. There would be greedy men, enemies of the Friars, who would not give up any right of theirs for such a dominion, since through it they could keep the things for themselves; and if they were deprived of them by judgement, they would gladly offer no small sum of money and buy the aforesaid dominion. Once it was bought, they would expel the Friars, and neither the Friars nor anyone else on behalf of anyone could harass such buyers on account of keeping such things. Therefore the lack of such dominion makes the Friars themselves poorer. Again, Friars who use places, houses and other things, the dominion of which the granting laymen keep for themselves, are not richer because of this than others to whom a precarious or loaned use is granted. And so it is plain that the Friars are to be judged poorer because of their lack of such dominion. It is confirmed, because it is plain that those who have the use of a right or the usufruct have more right in those things, of which they have the use of right and the usufruct, than the Friars Minor have in the things of which the laymen granting them keep the dominion for themselves. But such users and usufructuaries are poorer than if they had dominion over those things, and no one else had the use of right or the usufruct of them. Therefore the Friars are much more poor than if they had dominion over such things as they use, which the granting laymen keep for themselves, and consequently, for the same reason, they are poorer because of their lack of the dominion which the Roman Church reserves for itself. Thirdly, they argue thus: the destitute are poor; therefore those who are more stripped are more poor. But those who lack any dominion whatever are more stripped than those who have such true dominion. Now dominion by which someone can litigate in court over temporal things, in his own name or in the name of his college, is true dominion, not false or fictitious. Therefore those who lack all dominion by which one can litigate in court are more stripped than if they had such dominion. From which it follows that they are more poor. But the Friars, because of their lack of the dominion reserved by the Roman Church, cannot litigate in court over those things. Therefore, through lack of such dominion, they are more stripped, and consequently poorer. Fourthly, they argue thus: those who are really further removed from temporal things are poorer. But the Friars Minor, according to Nicholas III in the decretal Exiit, because of their lack of all dominion, both individual and common, are further removed from temporal things. Therefore, because of their lack of such dominion, they are poorer. Fifthly, thus: those who have the highest poverty are poorer than those who do not have it. But those who lack such dominion have the highest poverty, whereas those who have such dominion do not have the highest poverty. This is plain from Innocent V, who says: high poverty is to have few possessions for God's sake; higher is that which has no possessions of its own but has them in common; highest is that which has nothing in this world, neither as its own nor in common. Therefore those who lack such dominion are poorer because of that lack. But this opponent replies to this in the constitution Quia quorundam, saying that Innocent V said this not as Pope but as Brother Peter of Tarentaise, in a certain Postil of his. Although this answer of his is specious, since not all the sayings of the supreme pontiffs, especially those not solemnly defined by papal authority, are to be regarded as authoritative, nevertheless the reasoning holds, because it is plain that that poverty is higher which lacks something that belongs to riches than the poverty which has it. But common dominion pertains in some way to dominion. Otherwise religious who have great possessions would in no way be richer than the mendicant religious. Therefore that poverty is higher which lacks common dominion than that which has common dominion.

units.tr: {a} The printed line at the head of the page is cut and partly illegible; the first words are read from the fragments shown. mendicant religious. Therefore that poverty is higher which lacks common ownership, than that which has common ownership, other things being equal.

units.la: Secundus error (vt dicunt) contentus in verbis praedictis est, quod dominium rerum, quibus Fratres Minores vtuntur, Romanae Ecclesiae reseruatum est simplex: hoc est, verbale, nudum, aenigmaticum & simulatum. Quod enim hoc sit erroneum, probare nituntur primo sic. Dominium verum non est dominium verbale, nudum, aenigmaticum & simulatum. Sed dominium huiusmodi rerum est verum dominium. Igitur non est verbale, nudum & aenigmaticum & simulatum. Maior est manifesta de se. Minor probata est prius, scil. contra assertionem praedecessorem.
