Secundo sic: Illud cuius carentia pertinet ad substantiam Regulae a Romana Ecclesia approbatae, non est nudum, verbale, aenigmaticum & simulatum, maxime si non est malum, nec aliquid negatiuum. Sed dominium Romanae Ecclesiae reseruatum, non est quid negatiuum vel priuatiuum, nec est peccatum, & carentia eius pertinet ad substantiam Regulae Beati Francisci a Romana Ecclesia approbatae. Ergo non est verbale, nudum, aenigmaticum & simulatum. Tertio sic: qui tanquam perfectionem aggrediens abdicat aliquid: quod est verbale, nudum, aenigmaticum & simulatum, est simulator & fictus. Sed Beatus Franciscus tanquam viam perfectionis aggrediens, abdicauit dominium rerum, quod sibi Ecclesia Romana reseruat. Ergo Beatus Franciscus fuit simulator & fictus. Sed hoc est impium cogitare.
units.tr: The second error (as they say) contained in the aforesaid words is that the ownership of the things which the Friars Minor use is reserved to the Roman Church in a bare sense: that is, verbal, naked, enigmatic and pretended. They try to prove that this is erroneous, first thus: true ownership is not verbal, naked, enigmatic and pretended ownership. But ownership of this kind of things is true ownership. Therefore it is not verbal, naked, enigmatic and pretended. The major premise is evident in itself. The minor was proved earlier, namely against the assertion of the predecessor. Second, thus: that whose lack pertains to the substance of a Rule approved by the Roman Church is not naked, verbal, enigmatic and pretended, especially if it is not evil and is not something negative. But the ownership reserved to the Roman Church is not something negative or privative, nor is it a sin, and its lack pertains to the substance of the Rule of Blessed Francis approved by the Roman Church. Therefore it is not verbal, naked, enigmatic and pretended. Third, thus: one who, setting out as if upon a way of perfection, renounces something which is verbal, naked, enigmatic and pretended, is a pretender and a feigner. But Blessed Francis, setting out as if upon the way of perfection, renounced the ownership of things which the Roman Church reserves to itself. Therefore Blessed Francis was a pretender and a feigner. But to think this is impious.

units.la: Tertius error, vt dicunt isti, contentus verbis praedictis est, quod dominium omni temporali commodo denudatum est inutile, quia verbale, nudum, aenigmaticum & simulatum. Hoc enim esse erroneum & haeresim sapere manifestam, probare conantur. Nam si aliquod dominium ideo est inutile, quia est omni temporali commodo denudatum: Ergo non est aliquod commodum spirituale: quia si ex dominio posset haberi commodum spirituale, propter commodum spirituale posset esse vtile. Si autem non est commodum spirituale, non est vita beata futura: nec erit generalis resurrectio mortuorum. Sed ista sunt haeretica manifesta. Ergo haereticum est dicere, quod omne dominium temporali commodo denudatum est inutile: quamuis veritatem contineat, quod omne dominium temporali & spirituali commodo denudatum est inutile. Amplius, si dominium aliquod ideo est inutile: quia temporali commodo denudatum. Ergo omnia alia eadem ratione, quae sunt temporali commodo denudata, inutilia sunt censenda. Sed opera misericordiae, sicut hospitalitatis, Eleemosynae, captiuorum redemptio, orationes etiam & ieiunia, meditatio scripturarum, & alia opera bona quamplurima sunt saepe omni temporali commodo denudata. Ergo omnia talia essent nunc inutilia reputanda: quod esse haereticum nullus fidelis ignorat.
units.tr: The third error, as those men say, contained in the aforesaid words is that ownership stripped of every temporal advantage is useless, because it is verbal, naked, enigmatic and pretended. They try to prove that this is erroneous and savours manifestly of heresy. For if some ownership is therefore useless because it is stripped of every temporal advantage, then there is no spiritual advantage either: for if a spiritual advantage could be had from ownership, the ownership could be useful for the sake of a spiritual advantage. But if there is no spiritual advantage, there is no blessed life to come, and there will be no general resurrection of the dead. But these are manifest heresies. Therefore it is heretical to say that all ownership stripped of temporal advantage is useless, although it contains the truth that all ownership stripped of both temporal and spiritual advantage is useless. Furthermore, if some ownership is therefore useless because it is stripped of temporal advantage, then by the same reasoning all other things which are stripped of temporal advantage must be judged useless. But works of mercy, such as hospitality, almsgiving, the ransoming of captives, also prayers and fasts, the meditation of the Scriptures, and very many other good works, are often stripped of every temporal advantage. Therefore all such things would now have to be judged useless, which no faithful person is ignorant to be heretical.

units.la: Quartus error (vt dicunt) est, quod carentia dominii omni temporali commodo denudati non reddit pauperiorē nō habentē siue carentem tali dominio. Ex hoc enim sequeretur, quod Fratres Minores propter carentia dominii in rebus, quarum dominium sibi retinent laici concedentes eis vsum earundem rerum, non essent pauperiores: quod ostensum est esse falsum contra primam assertionem in isto capitulo impugnatam. Sequeretur etiam quod serui vtentes rebus dominorum, quorum dominium saepe est omni temporali commodo denudatum, non essent propter carentiam talis dominii pauperiores: quod constat esse falsum, quia si tale haberent dominium, quale habent Domini, essent ditiores. Ergo propter carentiam talis dominii sunt pauperiores.
units.tr: The fourth error (as they say) is that the lack of ownership stripped of every temporal advantage does not make poorer one who does not have, or lacks, such ownership. For it would follow from this that the Friars Minor, because of their lack of ownership of things whose ownership the laity retain while granting them the use of those same things, would not be poorer: which has been shown to be false, against the first assertion attacked in this chapter. It would also follow that servants who use the goods of their masters, whose ownership is often stripped of every temporal advantage, would not be poorer on account of their lack of such ownership: which is plainly false, since if they had such ownership as their masters have, they would be richer. Therefore on account of the lack of such ownership they are poorer.

units.la: (Vsu simplici facti praedicto fratribus reseruato) Hic notant isti duo. Primum est, quod secundum istum Nicolaus tertius vsus est tali modo loquendi, simplex vsus facti.
units.tr: (The simple use of fact, reserved to the friars as above) Here these two men note the following. The first is that, according to this man, Nicholas III used this way of speaking, the simple use of fact.

units.la: Ergo talis modus loquendi non est per appellantem inuentus, nec est reprobandus, si vtitur tali modo loquendi: quem tamen prosunt simplice vsum facti: quia Fratres possunt habere illud, quod eis reseruatur secundum istum: sed secundum istum simplex vsus facti fratribus reseruatur. Ergo possunt habere simplicem vsum facti. Quod iste prius negauit dicens: quod & vsus facti neq; in rebus consumptibilibus vsu neq; in rebus non consumptibilibus vsu habere non potest. Sed dicet, quod aliquid potest reseruari quod tamen haberi non potest: & ideo licet simplex vsus facti possit reseruari, non tamen potest haberi. Sed hoc friuolum est: quia per eandem rationem, per quam probatur, quod vsus facti haberi non potest, qa scil. illud quod non potest esse in rerum natura, non potest haberi, potest etiam probari, quod vsus facti non potest reseruari: qa quod non potest esse in rerum natura, reseruari non potest. Illud enim quod non potest esse in rerum natura, nihil est, nec potest esse. Quod autem nihil est nec potest esse aliquid, non potest reseruari. Quod ergo non potest esse in rerum natura, non potest reseruari. Sed vsus facti (secundum istum) non potest esse in rerum natura. Ergo non potest reseruari. Vel si potest reseruari eadem ratione potest haberi.
units.tr: Therefore this way of speaking was not invented by the appellant, nor is it to be condemned if he uses it; yet the Papists nonetheless prefer the simple use of fact, because the Friars can have what is reserved to them according to this man; but according to this man the simple use of fact is reserved to the friars. Therefore they can have the simple use of fact. This man denied that earlier, saying that the use of fact can be had neither in consumable things nor in non-consumable things. But he will say that something can be reserved which nonetheless cannot be had, and so, although the simple use of fact can be reserved, it cannot be had. But this is frivolous: for by the same reasoning by which it is proved that the use of fact cannot be had, namely that what cannot exist in the nature of things cannot be had, it can also be proved that the use of fact cannot be reserved, because what cannot exist in the nature of things cannot be reserved. For what cannot exist in the nature of things is nothing, nor can it be anything. But what is nothing and cannot be anything cannot be reserved. Therefore what cannot exist in the nature of things cannot be reserved. But the use of fact (according to this man) cannot exist in the nature of things. Therefore it cannot be reserved. Or if it can be reserved, by the same reasoning it can be had.

units.la: (In fide Romana Ecclesiam recipiendum duxerit.) Quantum ad res, quarum vsum Fratres ante decretalem Exiit, habuerunt, debet intelligi. (Recipiendum) hoc est, fuisse receptum manifestandum: quia illae res iam antea in dominium Romanae Ecclesiae transferant, quantum ad res, quas Fratres erant post Decretalem Exiit, habituri, debet intelligi: quia tunc ordinauit vel magis ordinationem, qualem fecerant praedecessores sui, renouauit, quod tales res in quibus dantes non retinerent dominium. Ad cuius euidentiam dicitur esse sciendum, quod de substantia regulae beati Francisci est, quod Fratres nec in speciali nec in communi habeant cuiuscunq; rei dominium, quo in iudicio agendo vel defendendo valeant litigare. Quod autem rerum dominium, quibus vtuntur, sit Romanae Ecclesiae vel non sit Romanae Ecclesiae, hoc accidit regulae supradictae. Unde & aliquarum rerum quibus Fratres vtuntur dominium spectat ad Romanam Ecclesiam: & aliquarum rerum dominium spectat ad alios. Et ita quod si Romanae Ecclesia non haberet dictarum rerum dominium, statui Fratrum nullatenus repugnaret: imo quod res, quibus Fratres vtuntur, sub nullius essent dominio, sed habitae per derelictis, seu concederentur occupati, qui esset capax dominii, in nullo Fratrum statui obuiaret: hoc tamen reipublicę minime expediret. Et ideo quod ecclesia rerum multarum, quibus Fratres vtuntur, habet dominium, hoc de voluntate dantium vel non contra voluntatem ipsorum per ecclesiam ordinatum existit, quae est causa hoc potuit ordinare. Et ideo licet a principio Ordinis ecclesia Romana nullarum rerum, quibus vtebantur Fratres, habuisset dominium, sicut postea noscitur habuisse: status Fratrum propter hoc in nullo fuisset mutatus. An autem a principio Ordinis Romana ecclesia habuit vel non habuit dictarum rerum dominium, nolunt isti ad praesens inquirere. (Ac libere pertinere decreuerit) Dicunt isti, quod nullae res ecclesiae, quae sunt communes, ita libere pertinent ad Papam, sicut multae res libere pertinent ad laicos multos: quia, vt dicunt, Papa non habet plenum dominium super res quascunque ecclesiae, nec potest de eis aliter ordinare, quam ipsas ad honorandum Deum vel ad reuelandas necessitates fidelium dispensando. Et ideo dicunt, quod peccat mortaliter parentes vel alios aliter, quam ordinatum est de voluntate dantium per sanctos patres de communibus bonis ditando: & ipsi ditati de necessitate salutis restituere eadem bona tenentur, & ipse bona alienata vel successor suus, si ipse non fecerit, repetere obligatur, in tantum quod si non fecerit, quilibet fidelis potest iudicare absque omni temeritate Papam ditantem & alios ditatos in peccato mortali existere.
units.tr: (Has judged that the Church is to be received in the Roman faith.) This must be understood as regards the things whose use the Friars had before the decretal Exiit. (To be received) that is, to have been received, is to be made clear; because those things were already previously transferred into the ownership of the Roman Church. As regards the things which the Friars were to have after the decretal Exiit, it must be understood that then it ordained, or rather renewed the ordinance such as its predecessors had made, that such things be held in which the donors would not retain ownership. For the clear understanding of this it is said that it must be known that it is of the substance of the rule of Blessed Francis that the Friars should have no ownership of any thing, either individually or in common, by which they could litigate in bringing or defending a suit. But whether the ownership of the things which they use belongs to the Roman Church or does not belong to it, this is an accident of the aforesaid rule. Hence the ownership of some of the things which the Friars use belongs to the Roman Church, and the ownership of other things belongs to others. And so, if the Roman Church did not have ownership of the said things, this would by no means conflict with the state of the Friars; indeed, if the things which the Friars use were under no one's ownership, but were held as derelict, or were granted to whoever was occupying them and was capable of ownership, this would conflict in no way with the state of the Friars; yet this would be by no means expedient for the commonwealth. And therefore the fact that the Church has ownership of many of the things which the Friars use exists by ordinance of the Church, made with the will of the donors, or not against their will, and this is the reason it could ordain this. And so, although from the beginning of the Order the Roman Church had no ownership of any of the things which the Friars used, as it is later known to have had, the state of the Friars would not on that account have been changed in any respect. But whether from the beginning of the Order the Roman Church had or did not have ownership of the said things, these men are unwilling to inquire into at present. (And has decided that they pertain freely) These men say that none of the Church's common goods pertain so freely to the Pope as many goods pertain freely to many laymen: because, as they say, the Pope does not have full ownership over any goods of the Church, nor can he ordain concerning them otherwise than by dispensing them to honour God or to relieve the necessities of the faithful. And therefore they say that parents, or others, who enrich themselves from common goods otherwise than has been ordained, by the holy Fathers, with the will of the donors, sin mortally; and those so enriched are bound by necessity of salvation to restore those same goods, and the Pope himself, or his successor, if he has not done so, is bound to reclaim the goods alienated; to such an extent that if he does not do so, any faithful person may judge, without any rashness, that the Pope who enriches and the others who are enriched are in mortal sin.

units.la: Cum igitur dicitur, tales res ad Romanam ecclesiam libere pertinere: debet intelligi, quod ita libere pertinent res huiusmodi ad dominium Romanae ecclesiae, sicut quaecunque aliae res ecclesiae, quas sibi soli reseruat, & no committit aliis dispensandas. (Attento tamen ipsorum Fratrum Minorum vtendi modo.) Istud dicunt isti non esse additum, nisi ad diffamandum: quasi modus vtendi Fratrum non esset consonus dictis eorum, cum dicunt se omni carere dominio: vel quasi non esset consonus regulae, quam ipsi vouent, vel declarationibus summorum pontificum. Nam modus vtendi Fratrum in nullo vari at naturam dominii, quo carent Fratres: nec modus vtendi ipsorum facit ipsos ditiores, etiam si esset modus vtendi illicitus. Unde etiam fur, qui vtitur rebus pretiosis furtim sublatis, non est propter hoc realiter ditior reputandus. Ergo consimiliter, licet Fratres vterentur rebus illicite, non essent propter hoc veraciter ditiores: quia per talem vsum illicitum nec dominium nec ius aliquod in rebus acquirerent. (Et patientia citra modum Romana ecclesia subsecuta.) Hoc etiam dicitur friuole (vt dicunt isti) quia patientia Romanae ecclesiae non mutat in aliquo naturam dominii. (Non ipse vsum Fratrum dici debet, scilicet simplex.) Hic aperte contradicit Nicolao tertio, qui asserit talem vsum dici simplicem. (Sed potius Romana ecclesia, dominium esse simplex.) Hoc probatum est esse falsum: quia illud dominium est verum dominium, quo valet Romana ecclesia res Fratrum in iudicio vendicare, & eas a Fratribus auferre, & alius elargiri. (Quis enim simplicem vsuarium dicere potest, cui rem vsuariam licet permutare, vendere, aut donare.) Dicunt isti, quod hic videtur vocare simplicem vsuarium habentem vsum rei absque omni iure vtendi: & sic accipiendo dicunt, quod licere alicui rem permutare, vendere, & donare potest intelligi dupliciter, scil. auctoritate propria, vel sui collegii, aut auctoritate alterius. Primo non licet simplici vsuario rem vsuariam dicto modo permutare, vendere vel donare. Secundo modo licet, sicut seruo & famulo licet auctoritate domini equum permutare, vendere, & donare, si Dominus ei dederit talem potestatem, quod facere potest, nullum dando ei dominium: sicut etiam famuli mercatorum nonnullas res dominorum suorum permutant, vendunt, & quandoque donant vel dant. (Haec natura repugnant vsuarii.) Dicunt quod haec non repugnant naturae vsuarii, licet non necessario competant vsuario. (Nec ad vsuarium pertinent.) Verum est in quantum vsurius est: tamen sibi non repugnant: Et ideo possunt sibi competere per licentiam aliam specialem. (Quatamen de rebus mobilibus antedictis faciunt Fratres ipsi.) Verum est: non tamen auctoritate propria, sed auctoritate summi pontificis. Et ideo de rebus etiam immobilibus, quarum dominium sibi laici reseruant, non possent hoc facere, si ipsi laici Fratribus haec duxerint interdicenda: de licentia autem ipsorum bene possent. (Quod autem dominium Romana ecclesiae reseruatum simplex censeri debeat.) Hic notant quidam istorum duo. Primum est, quod Papa & clerici dicuntur aliquomodo habere dominium seu proprietatem rerum ecclesiasticarum: q nonnulli pertinaciter negant, quamuis hoc supra cap. 2. probatum extiterit. Hoc tamen sicaliis auctoritatibus satagunt confirmare, vt habetur extra de praescriptionibus cap. si diligenti, ait: Cum iudicatus Calaritanus ad ius & proprietatem beati Petri pertineat &c. & 10. q. 2. c. si aeconomus: sicut habetur post statutum aut tempus & placitum reddituum ipsorum proprietate ad ius & dominium ecclesiasticum, recurrente firmiter, sine completo vno spacio, quod inter eos fuerit constitutum, seu mortis sua tempore, si hoc quoq; contigerit, is qui possessionem ecclesiasticam & ecclesiasticorum reddituum vsufructum habendi gratia pacto interueniente susceperat, non minus quam alterius tanta quantitatis quanta acceperat redditus, cum ipsorum praediorum dominus in rebus immobilibus eorum colonis & mancipiis ecclesiae derelinquat. Et Gregorius, vt habetur 12. q. 2. cap. sicut ecclesia, ait: Sicut ecclesia propriias res amittere non debet &c. Ex his aliisq; verbis quam pluribus patet aperte, quod aliquo modo Papa & alii clerici habent dominium & proprietatem ecclesiasticarum rerum. Nec obstat quod dicit Alexan. 4. vt habetur extra de donationibus c. fraternitatem, quod scil. episcopus & quilibet praelatus, ecclesiasticarum rerum est procurator, non Dominus: quia ibi accipitur Dominus pro illo, qui habet dominium plenum, ita q potest de re ad libitum ordinare: & si alienauerit, alienatio per alium reuocari non potest. Et isto modo etiam Papa non est Dominus ecclesiasticarum rerum, quia ei non licet de rebus ecclesiae facere quod sibi placuerit, sed tenetur de ipsis certis modis & non aliis ordinare. Haec Papa Symachus testatur aperte, vt habetur 12. quaest. 2. non liceat Papa praedia ecclesia alienare aliquo modo pro aliqua necessitate &c. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod non licet Papae praedia ad libitum alienare, & per consequens ratione consimili non licet Papae de aliis rebus ecclesiae ad libitum ordinare. Non enim tunc Symachus voluit legem successori suo potestatiue imponere, quia hoc non potuit, cum non habeat imperium par in parem: sed quid non liceret Papae, voluit declarare. Secundo notanti isti, quod istud dominium non est simplex, vt iste vocat simplex, licet posset dici simplex aliquo modo, sed tunc non esset ad propositum istius in aliquo (Ex hoc patet quod ex illo nullum eidem ecclesia temporale obuenit hactenus commodum nec speratur quod obuenire debeat in futurum) Ex hoc notant isti, quod iste ponit pro causa, quare dominium supradictum est simplex, id est, verbale, nudum & aenigmaticum & simulatum, quia scil. ex illo nullum obuenit commodum temporale, nec speratur quod obuenire debeat in futurum. Ex quo concludunt isti, quod iste nullum reputat commodum spirituale. (Cum nec intentio referentis nec ipsorum fratrum fuerit quod ad quemcunque alium quam ad fratres dictarum rerum proueniret compendium) Dicunt quod ex hoc in nullo variatur dominium, nec propter hoc debet dici tale dominium verbale & aenigmaticum, praesertim cum Papae liceat dictam intentionem mutare, quandocunque sibi placuerit, sicut dominium regis in aliqua ciuitate vel castro in nullo mutatur, licet intendat quod alius seruiens sibi recipiat eiusdem compendium, etiam si promisisset alicui dare aliquod castrum. Adhuc non esset eiusdem dominium variatum in aliquo. Ergo multo magis propter talem intentionem non variatur rei dominium. (Quod proculdubio modus ipsorum & Romana ecclesia subiecta patientia euidentius declarauit.) Scilicet talem fuisse intentionem sed non declarauit, quin Papa alius posset dictam intentionem mutare. (Quarum vsum facti licet habere ordini & fratribus antedictis.) Hic expresse contradicit etiam vocaliter his, quae saepe & multis modis conatus est defendere & probare. Quia saepe asseruit, quod vsus facti quarumcunq; rerum siue consumptibilium vsu siue non consumptibilium vsu haberi non potest: quia non potest esse in rerum natura. Hic autem dicit sententialiter & vocaliter, quod licet fratribus habere vsum facti. (Talis autem dominii carentia &c.) Hoc totum improbatum est prius. (At saepe in hoc futurum) hoc non impedit veritatem dominii nisi carentia illius spei esset ex necessitate, non ex libera voluntate, cum potestate ad placitum dimittendi carentiam illam. (sibi vendicant.) Quia secundum istum fratres Minores non sunt realiter pauperiores, quam religiosi alii mendicantes, sed solo nomine sine re sunt pauperiores (Pauperiorem non efficit non habentem.) Dicunt isti, quod sicut aliquis non dicitur diues, vel ditior propter actualem actum vtendi: quia tunc rex esset ditior, quando vteretur vestibus pretiosis, quam si vestibus vilibus vteretur: sed dicitur aliquis ditior propter dominium & alia iura, quae habet in rebus siue vtatur siue non; siue etiam intendat vti, siue non intendat vti; siue etiam intendat sibi retinere, siue intendat aliis erogare: quia vsus actualis & intentio vtendi in futurum: non faciunt aliquem ditiorem. Sic etiam non dicitur aliquis pauperior propter vsum viliorum rerum: nec propter intentionem vtendi vilioribus: sed dicitur quis pauperior vel minus pauper propter carentiam dominii & aliorum iuium in temporalibus maiorem vel minorem: & propter hoc carentes tali dominio sunt pauperiores, quam si dictum haberent dominium. Alias enim ecclesia magno tempore oberrasset tale dominium inutiliter retinendo. (Attento vsu dictorum Fratrum.) Hoc calumniose & diffamatorie additur, vt dicunt isti: quia hoc nihil facit ad hoc, quod fratres Minores pauperiores vel minus pauperes sunt censendi. (Vsum facti simplicem asserunt se habere.) Ex hoc notant isti, quod iste realiter imponit, quicquid imponit de simplici vsu facti communitati Ordinis, & appellanti. Et ita patet, & dicunt esse certum, quod appellans nullam dicit nouitatem: sed persequerat tantum modo in assertione, quam totus Ordo a principio defensauit.
units.tr: When it is said that such goods belong freely to the Roman Church, it must be understood that goods of this kind pertain to the dominion of the Roman Church just as freely as any other goods of the Church, which it reserves to itself alone and does not commit to others to dispense. (Provided, however, that the manner of using of the Friars Minor themselves is observed.) These men say this was added only to defame them, as if the Friars' manner of use were not consistent with their own statements that they lack all dominion, or as if it were not consistent with the rule they vow, or with the declarations of the supreme pontiffs. For the Friars' manner of use in no way alters the nature of the dominion they lack, nor does their manner of use make them richer, even if it were an unlawful manner of use. Hence a thief who uses precious things he has stolen is not, for that reason, to be regarded as really richer. Likewise, even if the Friars used goods unlawfully, they would not for that reason truly be richer, because by such unlawful use they would acquire neither dominion nor any right in the goods. (And the Roman Church's forbearance, which followed without limit.) This too is said to be frivolous (as they say), because the Roman Church's forbearance does not in any way change the nature of dominion. (That the use of the Friars themselves should not be called simple.) Here he plainly contradicts Nicholas III, who asserts that such use is called simple. (But rather that the dominion of the Roman Church is simple.) This has been proved false, because that dominion is true dominion, by which the Roman Church can claim the Friars' goods in court, take them away from the Friars, and bestow them on others. (For who can call a simple user one to whom it is lawful to exchange, sell, or give away the thing in use?) These men say that here he seems to call a simple user one who has the use of a thing without any right of using it. Taking it in this sense, they say that a person's being allowed to exchange, sell, or give away a thing can be understood in two ways: by his own authority or that of his college, or by the authority of another. First, a simple user may not exchange, sell, or give away the thing in use in the said manner. Second, it is lawful in the second way: just as a servant or attendant may, by his master's authority, exchange, sell, or give away a horse, if the master has given him such power, without giving him dominion; just as merchants' servants also exchange, sell, and sometimes give away or hand over certain goods of their masters. (These are repugnant to the nature of a user.) They say these do not conflict with the nature of a user, although they do not necessarily belong to the user. (Nor do they pertain to the user.) It is true insofar as he is a user; yet they do not conflict with him, and so they can belong to him by some other special license. (Yet the Friars themselves do this with the aforesaid movable goods.) True; yet not by their own authority, but by the authority of the supreme pontiff. And therefore, as to immovable goods whose dominion the laity reserve to themselves, they could not do this if the laity had judged such things to be forbidden to the Friars; but with the laity's license they certainly could. (That the dominion reserved by the Roman Church ought to be considered simple.) Here some of these men note two things. The first is that the Pope and the clergy are said in some way to have dominion or ownership of ecclesiastical goods, which some stubbornly deny, although this was proved above in chapter 2. Yet they take pains to confirm it by other authorities, as found in Extra, De praescriptionibus, chapter si diligenti, which says: "Since the judgment of Cagliari pertains to the right and property of blessed Peter, etc.," and in 10 q. 2, c. si aeconomus, where it is found that after the term or the time and agreement of the revenues, with the ownership of their property returning firmly to ecclesiastical right and dominion once the agreed period has been completed, or at the time of his death should this also happen, he who received the ecclesiastical possession and the usufruct of the ecclesiastical revenues by agreement must restore not less than another such quantity of revenue as he had received, since the lord of those estates leaves the immovable things to the church's tenants and serfs. And Gregory, as found in 12 q. 2, c. sicut ecclesia, says: "Just as the Church ought not to lose its own goods, etc." From these and many other words it is plainly evident that in some way the Pope and the other clergy have dominion and ownership of ecclesiastical goods. Nor is it an obstacle that Alexander IV, as found in Extra, De donationibus, c. fraternitatem, says that a bishop and any prelate is the steward, not the lord, of ecclesiastical goods; for there "lord" is taken to mean one who has full dominion, so that he may dispose of the thing at will, and if he alienates it, the alienation cannot be revoked by another. In this sense too the Pope is not lord of ecclesiastical goods, since it is not lawful for him to do with the Church's goods whatever he pleases; he is bound to dispose of them in certain ways and not others. Pope Symmachus openly testifies to this, as found in 12 q. 2: "It is not lawful for the Pope to alienate the estates of the Church in any way for any necessity, etc." From these words it is gathered that the Pope may not alienate estates at will, and consequently, by similar reasoning, the Pope may not dispose of other goods of the Church at will. For Symmachus did not then wish to impose a law on his successor by authority, since he could not do so, having no power over an equal; he wished rather to declare what would not be lawful for the Pope. Secondly, these men note that this dominion is not simple in the sense he calls simple, although it could be called simple in some way; but then it would not serve his purpose at all. (From this it is evident that no temporal advantage has so far accrued to the same Church from that, nor is it hoped that any should accrue in future.) From this these men note that he gives as the reason why the aforesaid dominion is simple, that is, verbal, bare, enigmatic and feigned, namely that no temporal advantage comes from it, nor is it hoped that any should come in future. From this they conclude that he regards no spiritual advantage as such. (Since it was the intention neither of the one reporting nor of the friars themselves that any profit from the said goods should come to anyone other than the friars.) They say that dominion is in no way altered by this, nor for this reason ought such dominion to be called verbal and enigmatic, especially since the Pope may change that intention whenever it pleases him. Just as the king's dominion over some city or castle is in no way changed, even if he intends that another servant of his should receive its profit, or even if he had promised to give someone some castle, the dominion would still not be altered in any respect. Therefore, much more, the dominion of a thing is not changed by such an intention. (Which without doubt the friars' manner and the Roman Church's submissive forbearance declared more clearly.) That is, that such was the intention, but he did not declare that another Pope could not change that intention. (Of which it is lawful for the Order and the aforesaid friars to have the factual use.) Here he also expressly and verbally contradicts what he has often and in many ways tried to defend and prove. For he often asserted that the factual use of any things, whether consumable or non-consumable, cannot be had, because it cannot exist in the nature of things. Here, however, he states both in his judgment and verbally that the friars may have factual use. (But the lack of such dominion, etc.) All this has been refuted before. (But often in the future in this respect) This does not hinder the truth of dominion, unless the lack of that hope were from necessity and not from free will, since there is power at pleasure to give up that lack. (They claim for themselves.) Because according to him the Friars Minor are not really poorer than other mendicant religious, but are poorer only in name and not in fact. (Not having does not make one poorer.) These men say that just as someone is not called rich or richer on account of the actual act of using, since then a king would be richer when he wore precious clothes than when he wore cheap ones, but someone is called richer on account of the dominion and other rights he has in things, whether he uses them or not, whether he intends to use them or not, and whether he intends to keep them or to distribute them to others: for actual use and the intention to use in future do not make anyone richer. So too no one is called poorer on account of the use of cheaper things, nor on account of the intention to use cheaper things; but someone is called poorer or less poor on account of a greater or lesser lack of dominion and other rights in temporal goods; and for this reason those lacking such dominion are poorer than if they had that dominion. Otherwise the Church would for a long time have erred by uselessly retaining such dominion. (Considering the use of the said friars.) This is added calumniously and defamatorily, as these men say, since it has nothing to do with whether the Friars Minor are to be judged poorer or less poor. (They assert they have simple factual use.) From this these men note that he really imposes whatever he imposes about simple factual use on the community of the Order and on the appellant. And so it is plain, and they say it is certain, that the appellant puts forward no novelty, but merely pursues the assertion which the whole Order has defended from the beginning.

units.la: CAP. LXXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXVIII.

units.la: AD hoc autem quod ipse dicit, quod ex hoc sequitur, quod Christus simulatam & fallacem doctrinam tribuit volentibus ad perfectionem attingere, quod omnia temporalia quo ad proprietatem & dominium relinquerent consulendo. Dicimus falsum esse, quod hoc consuluit Apostolis nec discipulis suis ad minus quod non haberent in communi: & de hoc dicetur Latius in obiectionibus contra constitutionem, Cum inter, per ipsum haereticum factus.
units.tr: As for what he says next, that it follows that Christ gave a feigned and fallacious teaching to those who wished to attain perfection, by advising them to give up all temporal goods as to ownership and dominion: we say this is false, and that he did not advise this to the Apostles or to his disciples, at least not that they should not hold things in common. This will be discussed more fully in the objections against the constitution Cum inter, made by the heretic himself.

units.la: In ista parte respondet ad secundum, quod in praedicta obiectione tangit appellans, scilicet quod Christus tribuisset simulatam & fallacem doctrinam volentibus ad perfectionem attingere, scilicet quod omnia relinquerent consulendo, dicens: quod hoc est falsum, quia hoc non consuluit Apostolis nec discipulis, saltem quod non haberent in communi.
units.tr: In this part he answers the second point, which the appellant touches on in the aforesaid objection, namely that Christ would have given a feigned and fallacious teaching to those who wished to attain perfection, namely that they should give up everything by counsel. He says that this is false, because he did not counsel this to the Apostles or to the disciples, at least that they should not hold things in common.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod hoc errorem asserit manifestum, etiam praeter hoc ad rationem appellantis non respondet. Quod asserat manifestum errorem, dicunt esse patens: cum dicat, quod Christus non consuluit Apostolis, nec discipulis, quod omnia relinquerent quo ad dominium & proprietatem: de quo dictum est prius, & amplius inferius inquiretur. Secundo dicunt, quod ad obiectionem appellantis non respondet, cum appellans de Apostolis & discipulis Christi nullam ibi specialem faciat penitus mentionem: sed absolute sine alia modificatione accipiat, quod Christus consuluit volentibus ad perfectionem attingere, quod omnia relinquerent, quo ad dominium & proprietatem in communi: quod ex Euangelio constat esse certissimum, etiam licet hoc consilium Apostolis & suis discipulis non dedisset. Nam constat Christum dixisse petenti, quae esset via perfectionis: Si vis perfectus esse vade & vende omnia quae habes & da pauperibus. Vbi Christus in persona illius interrogantis omnibus volentibus ad perfectionem attingere consuluit, quod omnia relinquerent, quo ad dominium & proprietatem, tam in speciali quam etiam in communi: quia qui omnia vendit & dat pauperibus, omnia relinquit etiam tam in speciali quam in communi, sicut su-
units.tr: But these opponents say that this asserts a manifest error, and moreover that it does not answer the appellant's argument. They say it is plain that it asserts a manifest error, since it says that Christ did not counsel the Apostles or the disciples to give up everything as to dominion and ownership. This has been discussed above, and will be inquired into further below. Secondly, they say it does not answer the appellant's objection, since the appellant makes no special mention of the Apostles or disciples of Christ there at all, but takes it absolutely and without any other qualification, that Christ counselled those who wished to attain perfection to give up everything, as to dominion and ownership in common. They say this is certain from the Gospel, even if he had not given this counsel to the Apostles and his disciples. For it is established that Christ said to the man who asked him what the way of perfection was: If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, and give it to the poor. Here Christ, in the person of that questioner, counselled all who wished to attain perfection to give up everything as to dominion and ownership, both in particular and in common, because whoever sells all and gives to the poor gives up everything, both in particular and in common, as was deduced above.

units.la: pra fa deductum existit. Et ex hoc posset inferri, quod Christus hoc consuluit Apostolis & suis discipulis, si ipsi volebant ad perfectionem attingere: nisi diceretur, quod Christus eos plusquam aliosab illa generalitate specialiter non excepit: quod probabilitatem non habet. ( Simulatam & falsam doctrinam tribuis &c. ) Si abdicatio talis dominii non est nisi quid simulatum, vt ipse dicit. (Dominus quod falsum est quod hoc consuluit apostolis. ) Hoc non accepit appellans: sed accepit, quod hoc Christus consuluit volentibus attingere ad perfectissimam paupertatem realiter, & non solum secundum praeparationem animi: tamen verum est, q hoc consuluit Apostolis, sicut post ostendetur. (Ad minus quod non habeant in communi.) Hoc dicunt esse falsum: quia per donationem factam pauperibus omnia dimittuntur etiam in communi.
units.tr: Hence it could be inferred that Christ gave this counsel to the Apostles and his disciples, if they wished to attain perfection, unless it were said that Christ did not specially except them from that general rule more than others. This has no probability. ("You attribute a feigned and false teaching, etc.") If such renunciation of dominion is nothing but something feigned, as he says. ("He says it is false that he advised this to the apostles.") The appellant did not take it this way. He took it that Christ counselled this to those wishing to attain the most perfect poverty in fact, and not only in preparation of mind. Yet it is true that he advised this to the Apostles, as will be shown afterwards. ("At least that they should not have in common.") They say this is false, because by the gift made to the poor, everything is given up, even in common.

units.la: CAP. LXXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXIX.

units.la: Ad illud quod dicit, quod etiam ex praedictis sequitur, quod Augustinus & Hieronymus, & alii sancti patres religionum institutores erraverunt: qui dictum Christi consilium sequi volentes abdicationem proprietatis & dominii rerum omnium sunt professi. Dicimus quod mentitur aperte: quia nullus illorum exceptis fratribus Minoribus abdicavit a se, nec suis Fratribus res quantum ad proprietatem & dominium in communi, imo eis secundum suas regulas licet & licuit habere etiam res immobiles in communi.
units.tr: To what he says, which also follows from the foregoing, that Augustine and Jerome and the other holy Fathers, the founders of religious orders, erred, since, wishing to follow Christ's counsel, they professed the renunciation of all ownership and dominion over things: we say that he plainly lies. For none of them, except the Friars Minor, renounced for himself, or for his brothers, the ownership and dominion of goods in common. Indeed, according to their rules, it is and was lawful for them to hold even immovable goods in common.

units.la: Hic respondet ad tertium, quod in praedicta obiectione tangit appellans, quod scilicet sancti religionum institutores errassent sequendo consilium Christi supradictum dicens, quod falsum est, quia nullus illorum praeter Fratres Minores abdicat proprietatem & dominium in communi.
units.tr: Here he answers the third point, which the appellant touches on in the objection above, namely that the holy founders of religious orders erred by following the counsel of Christ mentioned above. He says this is false, because none of them, apart from the Friars Minor, renounces ownership and dominion in common.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti, quod iste non respondet ad rem, sed evasiones frivolas nititur invenire: quia ad medium, in quo fundatur consequentia appellantis, non respondet. Fundatur enim illatio appellantis in hoc medio, quod qua ratione carentia dominii in communi non efficit carentem pauperiorem, consimili ratione carentia dominii in speciali non reddit carentem pauperiorem: quia sicut propter dominium speciale dicitur quis dicitur aliquo modo: quamvis non ita dives propter dominium commune, sicut propter dominium speciale. Si igitur propter carentiam dominii in communi non dicitur quis pauperior: sequitur necessario, quod etiam propter carentiam dominii in speciali non dicetur quis pauperior. Cum igitur sancti patres religionum aliarum, quam Fratrum Minorum institutores abdicaverunt proprietatem omnium in speciali intendentes per hoc consilium Christi imitari praedictum, quamvis non in tem omnium in speciali intendentes per hoc consilium Christi imitari praedictum, quamvis non in supremo gradu dicti consilii, cupientesq; sic imitando dictum Christi consilium pauperiores existere, sequitur quod erraverunt aperte, si propter carentiam dominii non sunt carentes pauperiores. Quod sequitur necessario, si propter carentiam dominii communis non sit quis pauperior. Nequaquam igitur appellans supposuit, quod sancti praedicti omnia abdicaverunt in communi: sed supposuit medium memoratum, quo concesso sequitur conclusio, quam intulit. Dicunt tamen isti, quod non intendunt, quod per omnia sit simile de carentia dominii specialis & communis: sed quantum ad hoc est simile, quod si carentia dominii communis non reddit carentem pauperiorem, nec carentia dominii specialis reddit carentem pauperiorem. Nec est inconveniens, quod diversae causae habeant eundem effectum, & tamen q vna illarum causet effectum intensiorem, & alia minus intensum. Et p hoc vt dicunt possunt solui cavillationes, quas posset quis proferre contra praedictam rationem adducere (Sequi volentes) quantum ad abdicationem proprietatis omnium in speciali. (Exceptis Fratribus Minoribus) Hic patet, quod etiam secundum ipsum Fratres Minores abdicant proprietatem omnium in communi, & ita vel Regula Fratrum Minorum est illicita, vel hoc est licitum reputandum.
units.tr: But these men say that he does not answer the point, and that he strives to find frivolous escapes, since he does not answer the middle term on which the appellant's inference rests. For the appellant's inference rests on this middle term: by the same reasoning by which lacking dominion in common does not make a man poorer, lacking dominion in particular does not make a man poorer. For just as a person is said to be in some way richer on account of particular dominion, though not so rich on account of common dominion as on account of particular dominion. If therefore a man is not said to be poorer on account of lacking dominion in common, it necessarily follows that he will not be said to be poorer on account of lacking dominion in particular either. Therefore, since the holy Fathers of the other religious orders, other than the founders of the Friars Minor, renounced the ownership of all things in particular, intending by this to imitate the aforesaid counsel of Christ, although not on the highest level of that counsel, and desiring by so imitating the counsel of Christ to become poorer, it follows that they plainly erred, if they are not made poorer by lacking dominion. And this necessarily follows, if a man is not made poorer by lacking common dominion. So the appellant by no means assumed that the aforesaid saints renounced all things in common; rather, he assumed the middle term mentioned, and once this is granted, the conclusion he drew follows. Yet these men say that they do not mean that the case of lacking particular dominion is in every respect like that of lacking common dominion; but it is alike in this respect: if lacking common dominion does not make a man poorer, neither does lacking particular dominion make a man poorer. Nor is it absurd that different causes should have the same effect, while one of them produces the effect more intensely and the other less intensely. And by this, as they say, the quibbles that someone might bring against the aforesaid argument can be resolved. (Wishing to follow) with respect to renouncing the ownership of all things in particular. (Except the Friars Minor.) Here it is clear that, even according to him, the Friars Minor renounce the ownership of all things in common; so either the Rule of the Friars Minor is unlawful, or this must be judged lawful.

units.la: CAP. LXXX.
units.tr: CHAP. LXXX.

units.la: Ad illud autem quod inducitur Levitici ultimo, vbi dicitur, quod omnes decima terrae sive de frugibus, sive de pomis arborum Domini sunt & illi sanctificantur. Et quod Num. 18. loquens de perfectione Levitarum Dominus dicit: nihil aliud possidebunt decimarum oblatione contenti: quas in vsus eorum & necessaria separavit. In vsu, inquit, idem haereticus, non in dominium dicit.
units.tr: As for what is brought forward from the last chapter of Leviticus, where it is said that all the tithe of the land, whether of the fruits or of the fruit of the trees, belongs to the Lord and is holy to him; and from Numbers 18, where the Lord, speaking of the Levites' perfection, says: "They shall possess nothing else, content with the offering of the tithes, which I have set apart for their use and needs." "For use," he says, this heretic, "not for ownership," he says.

units.la: In ista parte iste impugnatus ad quaedam alia, quae obiecit appellans, nititur respondere. Et dividitur in duas partes, secundum quae ad duo respondet. Secunda pars ibi: Ad illud quod dicit. Prima in duas dividitur: quia primo ponit obiectionem. Secundo sumit subdit rationem in parte immediate sequenti. Est autem obiectio de Levitis, q Levitae habuerunt vsum rerum, quarum Deus habuit dominium.
units.tr: In this part, the one attacked here tries to answer certain other points that the appellant raised. The reply is divided into two parts, according to the two matters to which he responds. The second part begins at "As for what he says." The first part is divided into two, because he first sets out the objection and then, in the immediately following part, adds his own reasoning. The objection concerns the Levites: that the Levites had the use of things over which God had ownership.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod iste impugnatus, ad obiectiones appellantis respondere verba appellantis trifariam recitat: ea per quae evidenter convincitur astute propter simplices decipiendos omittens. Ad cuius evidentiam verba ponunt integre appellantis: quae in sequentibus caput luculenter exaudient. Verba autem appellantis sunt haec: Praeterea scriptura sacra Levitici ultimo dicit, quod omnes decima terrae sive de frugibus sive de pomis arborum Domini sunt & illi sanctificantur, & Num. 18. loquens de perfectione Levitarum dicit: Nihil aliud possidebunt decimarum oblatione contenti, quas in vsus eorum & necessaria separavi. In vsu, inquit, non in dominium. Ex qua scriptura sacra patet, quod dominium omnium decimarum sive de pomis sive de frugibus terrae, quae res de sui consumptibiles esse constat, est Dei, & vsus mimistrorum ipsius: & licuit q tale dominium Dei est omnino temporaliter donatum. Et secundum hanc haereticam doctrinam dominii Dei verbale, aenigmaticum & simulatum est dicendum: q dicere vel sentire est haereticum & insanum.
units.tr: But these opponents say that the one attacked, in answering the appellant's objections, cites the appellant's words in three parts, leaving out those by which he is clearly and cunningly refuted, so as to deceive the simple. To make this plain, they set out the appellant's words in full, which the following chapter will make clear. The appellant's words are these: "Moreover, Holy Scripture says in the last chapter of Leviticus that all the tithe of the land, whether of the fruits or of the fruit of the trees, is the Lord's and is holy to him; and in Numbers 18, speaking of the perfection of the Levites, it says: 'They shall possess nothing else, content with the offering of the tithes, which I have set apart for their use and needs.' 'For use,' he says, 'not for ownership.' From this Holy Scripture it is evident that the ownership of all tithes, whether of the fruit of the trees or of the fruits of the earth, which are plainly things that are consumed, belongs to God, and the use of them to his ministers; and that such ownership of God has been wholly given over in temporal matters. And according to this heretical doctrine, the ownership of God must be called verbal, enigmatic and feigned; to say or think so is heretical and mad."

units.la: Praeterea
units.tr: Moreover

units.la: Praterea ecclesia Romana in sacris canonibus docet de rebus ecclesia quod dominium rerum est Dei siue corporis eius mystici, quod est ecclesia: & visus & dispensatio earum est prelatorum ecclesie. Et August. in libr. de facultatibus ecclesie dicit: quod Dei sunt ea, quae ecclesia conferuntur: & quod ipsa res, siue sint vestes siue aliqua vasa, sunt ad visum ministrorum eius. Romani etiam pontifices, qui hactenus fuerunt, in rebus temporalibus visu consumptibilibus & non consumptibilibus, quae fratribus Minoribus offeruntur, dantur vel conceduntur, dominium ecclesie seruauerunt & retinuerunt, visu tantummodo simplicis facti ipsis Fratribus derelicto: diffinientes, quod carentia talis dominii est meritoria, sancta & perfecta: & quod Christus & Apostoli viam perfectionis ostendentes abdicationem huius dominii docuerunt, & quod retentio siue reseruatio talis dominii omni temporali commodo denudati cum concessione visus, facta a pauperibus non est fructuosa domino, cum sit meritoria ad aeterna, & professioni pauperum opportuna, quod tanto censetur vtilior, quanto commutat temporalia pro aeternis: sicut clare patet in decretali predicta, Exiit qui seminat. Ex predicto igitur errore sequitur, quod ecclesia catholica in predictis erravit: ac per consequens in articulum fidei: Et vnam sanctam catholicam & apostolicam ecclesiam, sub quo continetur, quod ecclesia catholica errare non potest in fide vel moribus, error predictus vehementer impingit. Vnde dicta doctrina est haeretica merito iudicanda: tum quia scripturae sacrae per quam fidei probantur articuli, contradicit; tum quia errorem ecclesie catholice imponit, & eius doctrine & determinationibus manifeste repugnat. Et hic articulus valde diffuse in appellatione prolixa clarius continetur. Haec sunt verba appellationis ad quae vt isti dicunt, iste impugnatus nescivit responsionem rationabilem inuenire, & ideo noluit recitare.
units.tr: Moreover, the Roman Church teaches in the sacred canons concerning the goods of the Church that the ownership of the goods belongs to God, or to his mystical body, which is the Church, and that the use and disposal of them belongs to the prelates of the Church. Augustine also, in his book on the property of the Church, says that those things which are given to the Church belong to God, and that the goods themselves, whether they are garments or some vessels, are for the use of his ministers. Moreover, the Roman pontiffs who have hitherto held office have kept and retained the ownership of the Church over temporal goods, both those consumed by use and those not consumed, which are offered, given or granted to the Friars Minor, leaving to the Friars themselves only the simple fact of use. They have defined that the lack of such ownership is meritorious, holy and perfect, and that Christ and the Apostles, showing the way of perfection, taught the renunciation of this ownership; and that the retention or reservation of such ownership, when the person is stripped of all temporal advantage and is granted only use, made by the poor, is not profitable to the lord, since it is meritorious for eternal things and suited to the profession of poverty, and is judged all the more useful as it exchanges temporal things for eternal ones; as is plainly seen in the aforementioned decretal, Exiit qui seminat. From the aforesaid error it follows that the Catholic Church has erred in these matters, and consequently in an article of faith; and the aforesaid error strongly strikes at the article in which we confess one holy, catholic and apostolic Church, under which is contained that the Catholic Church cannot err in faith or morals. Hence the said doctrine must rightly be judged heretical, both because it contradicts Holy Scripture, through which the articles of faith are proved, and because it imputes error to the Catholic Church and plainly conflicts with her teaching and determinations. This article is set out more fully and clearly in the long appeal. These are the words of the appeal, to which, as these men say, the one attacked did not know how to find a reasonable answer, and therefore did not wish to quote them.

units.la: CAP. LXXXI.
units.tr: Chapter LXXXI.

units.la: Profecto per hoc se praevaricatorem legis manifestum ostendit, in illo enim cap. Num. 18. expresse dicitur quod Dominus dedit Leuitis dominium decimarum: & ad quid daret eis declarauit dicens quod in visum eorum & necessaria decimas huiusmodi separauit. Non autem dixit quod visu facti Leuitae essent contenti: multum autem refert vtrum res aliqua aliquibus detur in visum & necessaria: an visus in re aliqua seu rei alicuius a cui concedatur: sicut plenius & latius est superius vbi adduxit eadem capitula declaratum. Ad illud quod dicit quod hoc est contradictionem ecclesie factam in c. Exiit: superius saepius est responsum.
units.tr: Certainly by this he shows himself a manifest transgressor of the law. For in that chapter, Num. 18, it is expressly said that the Lord gave the Levites dominion over the tithes, and he declared for what purpose he gave them, saying that he set apart such tithes for their use and needs. But he did not say that the Levites were content with the mere use of the thing. Yet it matters greatly whether a thing is given to some for use and needs, or whether the use of some thing is granted to someone, as has been explained more fully and at greater length above, where he cited the same chapters. As to his claim that this is contrary to the determination of the Church in c. Exiit, this has been answered many times above.

units.la: Hic ad praedicta iste impugnatus nititur respondere dicens, quod Num. 18. dicitur expresse, quod Dominus dedit Leuitis dominium decimarum, quia ipsas in visus eorum & necessaria separauit. Ad illud de determinatione ecclesiae dicitur: quod saepe superius est responsum.
units.tr: Here, in reply to the foregoing, this opponent tries to answer, saying that Num. 18 expressly states that the Lord gave the Levites dominion over the tithes, because he set them apart for their use and needs. As to the point about the determination of the Church, it is said that this has often been answered above.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod ad neutrum illorum, quae accipit de appellante respondet. Non enim respondet ad primum: quia non est intentio appellantis, quod Leuitae in nullis decimis habeant dominium qualitercunque acceptum: quia in omnibus decimis habent aliquale dominium, sed non habent in omnibus decimis plenum dominium, quia aliquas non poterant vendere nec donare ad libitum. Sed intentio appellantis est probare, quod non omne dominium omni temporali commodo denudatum est verbale, nudum, aenigmaticum & simulatum, sicut iste dicit: quia omnium decimarum Deus habet plenum dominium. Dominium autem Domini est omni commodo temporali denudatum: nec tamen est verbale, nudum, aenigmaticum & simulatum. Sed dicit aliquis: quod ista ratio aeque concludit de rebus quorumcumque, sicut de decimis Leuitarum. Iterum, dominium Dei est alterius rationis a dominio humano. Ergo ex hoc, quod dominium Dei omni temporali commodo denudatum non est verbale, nudum & aenigmaticum & simulatum, probari non potest quod dominium humanum omni temporali commodo denudatum est verbale, nudum, aenigmaticum & simulatum. Ad primum istorum concedunt isti, quod ratio appellantis concludit de rebus quorumcunque: quia Deus est omnium Dominus: & tamen dominium Dei respectu quarumcunque rerum omni temporali commodo denudatum non est verbale, nudum aenigmaticum & simulatum. Fecit tamen appellans specialiter obiectionem praedictam de decimis Leuitarum: quia illas habent ex speciali dono Dei: & quia non habent isti plenum dominium in multis decimis, sicut multi laici habent in rebus suis. Ad secundum dicunt: quod licet dominium Dei sit alterius rationis a dominio humano: tamen contingit saepe arguere ab vno ad aliud. Et ita est in proposito: quia nulla apparet ratio, si dominium Dei omni temporali commodo denudatum non est verbale, nudum, aenigmaticum & simulatum: quin dominium humanum omni temporali commodo denudatum poterit non esse verbale, nudum aenigmaticum & simulatum. Ad secundum etiam de determinatione ecclesiae dicunt isti, quod non respondet. Nam licet saepe, quamuis male & erronee, vt dicunt isti, ad dictam determinationem responderit: tamen in quantum ad conclusionem, quam hic intendit appellans, scilicet quod non omne dominium omni temporali commodo denudatum est verbale, nudum, aenigmaticum & simulatum, adducitur, nusquam respondit, nec respondere potest: nisi dictam determinationem ecclesiae, aut dictum proprium reprobando, sicut intuenti verba appellantis, si est intelligens, euidenter apparet.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he does not answer either of the points which he takes from the appellant. For he does not answer the first. It is not the appellant's intention that the Levites have no dominion over any tithes whatever, in whatever sense it is taken. For they have some kind of dominion over all tithes, but they do not have full dominion over all tithes, since some they could not sell or give away at will. The appellant's intention is to prove that not every dominion stripped of all temporal benefit is merely verbal, bare, enigmatic and feigned, as this man claims, since God has full dominion over all tithes. Yet the dominion of the Lord is stripped of all temporal benefit, and nevertheless it is not verbal, bare, enigmatic and feigned. But someone says: this argument concludes just as much about the things of anyone as about the tithes of the Levites. Again, the dominion of God is of a different kind from human dominion. Therefore, from the fact that the dominion of God, stripped of all temporal benefit, is not verbal, bare, enigmatic and feigned, it cannot be proved that human dominion stripped of all temporal benefit is verbal, bare, enigmatic and feigned. To the first of these points, the opponents concede that the appellant's argument concludes about the things of anyone, since God is the Lord of all; and yet the dominion of God with respect to any things whatever, stripped of all temporal benefit, is not verbal, bare, enigmatic and feigned. The appellant, however, made the aforesaid objection specifically about the tithes of the Levites, because they have them by a special gift of God, and because these men do not have full dominion over many tithes, as many laymen have over their own goods. To the second point they say that, although the dominion of God is of a different kind from human dominion, it often happens that one argues from the one to the other. And so it is in the present case, for there appears to be no reason why human dominion stripped of all temporal benefit could not be non-verbal, bare, enigmatic and feigned, if the dominion of God stripped of all temporal benefit is not verbal, bare, enigmatic and feigned. To the second point too, concerning the determination of the Church, these men say that he does not answer. For although he has often replied to that determination, though badly and erroneously, as they say, yet as regards the conclusion which the appellant intends here, namely that not every dominion stripped of all temporal benefit is verbal, bare, enigmatic and feigned, which is adduced, he has nowhere answered, nor can he answer, except by rejecting the said determination of the Church or his own said statement. This is evident to anyone who is intelligent and reads the appellant's words.

units.la: In illo enim c. Num. 18. expresse dicitur quod Dominus dedit Leuitis dominium decimarum.) Hoc dicunt isti esse falsum: quia expressa mentio de dominio nulla fit illo cap. Tamen esto, quod ita esset, argumentum staret: quia per dominium humanum Dominus nunquam priuatur dominio suo. Ergo quamuis Leuitae habeant dominium decimarum, Deus tamen nihilominus habet dominium eorundem, sed dominium Dei est omni temporali commodo denudatum: quia Deus bonorum nostrorum Eorum non eget, & non est verbale, nudum &c. Ergo non omne dominium omni temporali commodo denudatum est verbale, nudum &c. Et ita appellans habet intentum, etiam dato quod Levitae habebant dominium decimarum. (In usu eorum & necessaria decimae huiusmodi separauit) Hoc verum est de aliquibus decimis, & de aliquibus est falsum: quia aliquas decimas Dominus separauit in usum eorum tantummodo, & non in alia necessaria, sicut patet supra cap. 70. (non autem dixit quod usu facti Levitae essent contenti) verum est, quia aliquale dominium & ius habuerunt in decimis: tamen vltra ius quod habebant debebant quantum ad aliquas vsu facti esse contenti, quantum ad aliquas non. (Multum autem refert verum res aliqua aliquibus detur in usum & necessaria, an usu in re aliqua seu rei alicuius alicui concedatur) Istud est verum propter hoc, quod dicitur in usum necessaria: quia aliquid potest concedi in vsum, quamuis non concedatur in necessaria. Patet secundum iura de commodato, quod conceditur ad certum vsum, non tamen conceditur in necessaria. Et ita refert, an aliquid concedatur in vsum, & an concedatur in necessaria & propter hoc refert, an aliquid concedatur in necessaria, & an alicui concedatur vsus: sed non refert an aliquid concedatur in vsum, & an alicui concedatur vsus. (Sicut plenius & latius est superius, vbi adduxit eadem capitula, declaratum.) Dicunt isti, quod hoc est manifeste falsum: quia de hoc ibi nulla fit mentio. Sed iste nititur declarare ibidem: quod refert an aliquid concedatur in vsum, & an alicui concedatur vsus alicuius rei, nequaquam erraffet.) Superius saepius est responsum. Dicunt quod non, applicando ad conclusionem, quam hic intendit appellans: quia nec de illa conclusione mentio fuit antea facta.
units.tr: In that chapter, Num. 18, it is expressly said that the Lord gave the Levites dominion over the tithes. These men say this is false, since no express mention of dominion is made in that chapter. Yet even granting that it were so, the argument would stand, because through human dominion the Lord is never deprived of his own dominion. Therefore, although the Levites have dominion over the tithes, God nevertheless has dominion over the same tithes. But the dominion of God is stripped of all temporal benefit, because God has no need of our goods, and it is not verbal, bare, etc. Therefore not every dominion stripped of all temporal benefit is verbal, bare, etc. And so the appellant attains his aim, even granting that the Levites had dominion over the tithes. (For their use and needs he set apart such tithes.) This is true of some tithes and false of others, because he set apart some tithes for their use alone and not for other needs, as is clear above in chapter 70. (But he did not say that the Levites were content with the mere use of the thing.) This is true, because they had some dominion and right over the tithes; yet beyond the right they had, they were to be content with mere use in some cases and not in others. (It matters greatly whether a thing is given to some for use and needs, or whether the use of some thing is granted to someone.) This is true because of the words for use and needs, since something can be granted for use without being granted for needs. As the law of loan (commodatum) makes clear, something is granted for a certain use and yet not granted for needs. And so it matters whether something is granted for use and whether it is granted for needs, and for this reason it matters whether something is granted for needs and whether use is granted to someone; but it does not matter whether something is granted for use and whether use is granted to someone. (As has been explained more fully and at greater length above, where he cited the same chapters.) These men say this is manifestly false, because nothing is said about this there. But he tries to explain there that it matters whether something is granted for use and whether the use of some thing is granted to someone, and he nowhere went wrong. Above it has often been answered. They say it has not, when applied to the conclusion which the appellant intends here, since no mention of that conclusion was made before either.

units.la: SECVNDA PARS PRINCIPALIS OPE- RIS NONAGINTA DIERVM.
units.tr: SECOND PART OF THE PRINCIPAL WORK OF NINETY DAYS.

units.la: CAP. LXXXII.
units.tr: CHAP. LXXXII.

units.la: RVrsus iste haereticus constitutionem, Cum inter nullos, satagit impugnare, dicens quod dicta constitutio declarat fore censendum haereticum affirmare deinceps Dominum nostrum Iesum, eiusq. Apostolos non habuisse aliquid in speciali nec in communi: & insuper haereticum fore dicit censendum affirmare Christo & eius Apostolis, in bis quae eos habuisse sacra scriptura testatur, non compositisse ius vtendi, nec illa vendendi seu donandi ius habuisse, aut ex ipsis alia acquirendi.
units.tr: Again, this heretic labours to refute the constitution Cum inter nullos, saying that the said constitution declares that it is to be counted heretical from now on to affirm that our Lord Jesus Christ and his Apostles had nothing, either individually or in common. He further says that it is to be counted heretical to affirm of Christ and his Apostles, in those things which holy Scripture testifies they had, that they did not have the right of use, and that they did not have the right to sell or give them away, or to acquire other things from them.

units.la: Postquam iste impugnatus respondit ad obiectiones contra constitutionem Ad condictorem: hic incipit respondere ad obiectiones appellantis contra constitutionem Cum inter. Et diuiditur in quinq; partes: quia primo ponit verba constitutionis Cum inter, vt appellans recitat ipsa. Secundo ostendit, quod appellans verba constitutionis recitat imperfecte. Tertio explicat intellectum, quem constitutioni praefatae appellans imponit. Quarto conatur ostendere, quod appellans imponit constitutioni, quod ipsa non dicit. Quinto, ad alia quae obiiciuntur respondet. Secunda pars incipit ibi: Dicimus quod haereticus iste. Tertia ibi: Dicit ergo. Quarta ibi: profecto iste haereticus. Quinta ibi: proculdubio dicta ipsius. In prima igitur parte ponit duo dicta constitutionis, Cum inter, vt appellans recitat ea, & est sensus literae planus.
units.tr: After this opponent replied to the objections against the constitution Ad condictorem, here he begins to answer the appellant's objections against the constitution Cum inter. The passage is divided into five parts. First, he sets out the words of the constitution Cum inter, as the appellant quotes them. Second, he shows that the appellant quotes the words of the constitution imperfectly. Third, he explains the meaning which the appellant attaches to the said constitution. Fourth, he tries to show that the appellant imposes on the constitution something it does not say. Fifth, he replies to the other objections. The second part begins at: We say that this heretic. The third at: He says therefore. The fourth at: Certainly this heretic. The fifth at: Undoubtedly his words. In the first part, then, he sets out the two statements of the constitution Cum inter, as the appellant quotes them, and the plain sense of the letter is clear.

units.la: (Affirmare deinceps) Subintelligitur, pertinaciter: quia de assertione pertinaci loquitur constitutio manifeste. Et si argumentum a contrario sensu valet, hoc, vt dicunt isti impugnatores, includitur error apertus: quod videlicet aliquid scripturae diuinae contrarium potest fieri de nouo haereticum, quod est erroneum manifeste. Nam omne quod aduersatur scripturae diuinae semper est haereticum: quia quod aliquid sit haereticum non dependet ex voluntate humana, sicut nec ex voluntate humana dependet, quod aliqua veritas sit catholica. Si enim aliqua veritas siue explicite siue implicite in scriptura diuina contenta fieret catholica voluntate humana, fides nostra in sapientia hominum consisteret: quod sententiae Apostoli contradicit aperte; cum dicit primae ad Corinth. 2. fides vestra non sit in sapientia hominum, sed in virtute Dei. Nulla igitur veritas in scriptura diuina etiam implicite contenta potest fieri catholica per sapientiam aut voluntatem humanam. Ergo nec aliqua falsitas scripturae diuinae contraria fieri potest haeretica per sapientiam aut voluntatem humanam. Et ita si pertinax assertio, quod Christus & Apostoli non habuerunt aliquid nec in speciali nec in communi, est modo haeretica, prius fuit haeretica. Et ideo dicere & deinceps est haeretica, si argumentum a contrario sensu valet, est patenter errare. Nec praedictis obsistit, quod legitur in Decretis aliquas haereses esse nouas. Quia haereses illae non dicebantur nouae pro eo, quod prius non erant veraciter haereses: sed dicebantur nouae haereses, quia erant nouiter dogmatizatae, & tamen in rei veritate prius erant haereses. (Non habuisse aliquid in speciali nec in communi) Hoc non potest intelligi negando omnem modum habendi: quia hoc nequaquam fuit inter scholasticos in dubium reuocatum. Intelligitur ergo de aliquo speciali modo habendi. Et discurrendo per singulos non potest intelligi, nisi de modo habendi iure proprietatis & dominii.
units.tr: (Affirm from now on) It is to be understood as "obstinately", because the constitution clearly speaks of an obstinate assertion. If the argument from the contrary sense holds, then, as these opponents say, there is included a plain error: namely, that something contrary to divine Scripture can newly become heretical, which is manifestly false. For whatever opposes divine Scripture is always heretical, since whether something is heretical does not depend on human will, just as whether some truth is catholic does not depend on human will. For if any truth contained in divine Scripture, whether explicitly or implicitly, were made catholic by human will, our faith would rest on the wisdom of men, which openly contradicts the words of the Apostle when he says in 1 Cor. 2: your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God. No truth contained in divine Scripture, even implicitly, can therefore be made catholic by human wisdom or will. Therefore neither can any falsehood contrary to divine Scripture be made heretical by human wisdom or will. And so, if the obstinate assertion that Christ and the Apostles had nothing, either individually or in common, is heretical now, it was heretical before. Therefore to say "from now on it is heretical" is, if the argument from the contrary sense holds, to err plainly. Nor does what is read in the Decretals, that some heresies are new, stand against this. Those heresies were not called new because they had not previously been truly heresies, but they were called new heresies because they had only recently been taught, and yet in the truth of the matter they had been heresies before. (Not to have had anything, either individually or in common) This cannot be understood as denying every mode of having, since that has never been called into doubt among the schoolmen. It is therefore understood of a particular mode of having. And, going through the cases one by one, it can only be understood of the mode of having by the right of ownership and dominion.

units.la: CAP. LXXXIII.
units.tr: CHAP. LXXXIII.

units.la: Dicimus quod haereticus iste constitutionem imperfecte recitat, quantum ad vltimam partem eius: quia post illud verbum; nequaquam ipsis ius vtendi, omittendi, seu conseruandi, quod immediate sequitur ibi. Item post verbum, aut ex ipsis acquirendi, omittit quae sequuntur, scil. quae tamen ipsos de praemissis fecisse sacra scriptura testatur seu ipsos potuisse facere supponit aperte. Vnde vt melius eius fraus & malitia detegatur, textus dicta constitutionis partis vltima noscitur esse talis; rursusque in posterum pertinaciter affirmare quod redemptori nostro prædicto eiusq; Apostolis his quæ eos habuisse sacra scriptura testatur, quamquam ius ipsis vtendi seu consumendi competierit, nec illa vendendi seu donandi et ius ex ipsis alia acquirendi: quæ tamen ipsos de præmissis fecisse scriptura sacra tacet, se facere supponit aperte: cum talis assertio ipsorum vsum & gesta evidenter includit, quod vtiq; de vsu gestis seu factis redemptoris nostri Dei filii sentire nephas est & scripturæ sacræ contrariari, sanctæ catholicæ inimicum, assertionem ipsam pertinacem de fratrum eorundem consilio deinceps vt hæreticam condemnandam merito & hæreticam declaramus &c.
units.tr: We say that this heretic quotes the constitution imperfectly, as regards its final part. For after the words nequaquam ipsis ius vtendi, he omits what immediately follows there, namely omittendi, seu conseruandi. Also, after the words aut ex ipsis acquirendi, he omits what follows: namely, that although holy Scripture testifies that they did these things, or clearly assumes that they could have done them, [the constitution says that they had them]. So that his fraud and malice may be better exposed, the text of the final part of the said constitution is known to read thus: "And again, to affirm obstinately in future that our aforesaid Redeemer and his Apostles, in those things which holy Scripture testifies they had, although the right of using or consuming them belonged to them, did not have the right of selling or giving them away, nor the right to acquire other things from them: whereas holy Scripture is silent that they did these things, and clearly assumes that they did them: since such an assertion of theirs clearly includes their use and deeds, which it is wicked to think of the use and deeds or actions of our Redeemer, the Son of God, and which is contrary to holy Scripture, hostile to the holy catholic [Church], we rightly declare that the assertion itself, made obstinately, is to be condemned from now on as heretical, on the advice of the same brothers, etc."

units.la: Hic ostendit quod appellans verba constitutionis recitat imperfecte, sicut plane patet.
units.tr: Here he shows that the appellant quotes the words of the constitution imperfectly, as is plainly evident.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod iste in hoc suum errorem amplius, quam appellans narrat, manifestat. Unde dicunt, quod appellans studens brevitati plures errores istius impugnati in discussos omisit, quos etiam minime recitavit. Plures etiam in appellatione prolixa pertractat, quos pertransit in breui: quia in breui succinctius recitat, & discutit in prolixa. Unde & totam seriem constitutionis Cum inter: quo ad secundam partem, sicut iste hic replicat, in prolixa appellatione ponit appellans, in qua serie, vt dicunt isti, iste impugnatus errorem alium in prædictis implicat manifeste. Ex quo etiam expositiones, quæ pro aliis saluandis erroribus adduci poterant, excluduntur.
units.tr: But these opponents say that this man, in this matter, makes his error plainer than the appellant relates. They say that the appellant, aiming at brevity, omitted several of this opponent's errors which he discussed, and did not even mention them. The appellant also treats several at length in his lengthy appeal which he passes over briefly, since in the brief passage he recites more concisely and discusses at length. Hence the appellant, in his lengthy appeal, sets out the whole sequence of the constitution Cum inter as regards the second part, as this man here repeats it; in that sequence, these opponents say, this opponent plainly involves another error in what has been said. From this also are excluded the explanations which could have been brought forward to save the other errors.

units.la: Est autem error talis, vt dicunt. Qui vtitur re aliqua vel consumit, habet ius vtendi vel consumendi, ac etiam ius vendendi seu donandi, & ex ipsa re alia acquirendi, alioquin vsus est iniustus. Quod enim iste error ex verbis superius recitatis colligatur, patet aperte. Nam iste probat, quod Christus & Apostoli habuerunt in rebus, quas eos scriptura sacra habuisse testatur, ius vtendi seu consumendi, ac etiam ius vendendi seu donandi, & ex ipsis alia acquirendi: quæ aliter vsus eorum, & gesta fuisset iniusta.
units.tr: The error is, as they say, of this kind: whoever uses a thing or consumes it has the right to use or consume it, and also the right to sell or give it away, and to acquire other things from the thing itself; otherwise the use is unjust. For that this error is gathered from the words recited above is plain. For this man proves that Christ and the Apostles had, in the things which holy Scripture testifies they had, the right to use or consume them, and also the right to sell or give them away, and to acquire other things from them; otherwise their use and deeds would have been unjust.

units.la: Ex qua ratione colligitur evidenter, quod qui vtitur re aliqua vel consumit habet ius vtendi seu consumendi, ac etiam ius vendendi seu donandi, & ex ipsa re alia acquirendi, alioquin vsus est iniustus.
units.tr: From this reasoning it is clearly gathered that whoever uses a thing or consumes it has the right to use or consume it, and also the right to sell or give it away, and to acquire other things from the thing itself; otherwise the use is unjust.
