units.la: Sed quod hoc sit erroneum, probare conantur. Primo: quia scripturæ diuinæ contradicit aperte. Nam sacerdotes & eorum familiæ aliiq; fideles in veteri lege pluribus rebus oblatis Deo licite vtebantur, quibus tamen ius vtendi aut ex ipsis alia acquirendi minime habuerunt: licet nonnulli eorum habuerunt ius vtendi seu consumendi. Ergo per hoc, quod aliquis non habet omnia ista iura in rebus, quibus vtitur, scilicet ius vtendi seu consumendi, ius vendendi seu donandi, & ius ipsis alia acquirendam, probari non potest, quod vsus eius sit iniustus.
units.tr: But they try to prove that this is erroneous. First, because it openly contradicts divine Scripture. For priests and their households and other faithful people in the old law used many things offered to God lawfully, yet they had by no means the right to use them or to acquire other things from them, although some of them had the right to use or consume them. Therefore, by the fact that someone does not have all these rights in the things he uses, namely the right to use or consume them, the right to sell or give them away, and the right to acquire other things from them, it cannot be proved that his use is unjust.

units.la: Assumptum manifeste probatur per scripturam sacram assumat vicinum suum, qui iunctus est domui eius iuxta numerum animarum, quæ sufficere possint ad esum agni. Et post ea dicitur: nec comedetis ex eo crudum quid, nec coctum aliquid, sed assum igni tantum, caput cum pedibus & intestinis vorabitis: nec remanebit ex eo quicquam vsque mane. Si quid residuum fuerit, igni comburetis.
units.tr: The assumption is plainly proved from holy Scripture: let him take his neighbour, who is joined to his house, according to the number of souls which may suffice for eating the lamb. And afterwards it is said: You shall not eat of it raw, nor boiled at all, but roasted with fire only: you shall eat the head with the feet and the entrails, and nothing of it shall remain until morning. If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire.

units.la: Ex his verbis colligitur evidenter, quod Iudæi agnum paschalem & hœdum non poterant vendere, nec donare, nec aliquid aliud ex ipsis acquirere, sed tantum modo manducare, & partem residuam igni cremare: & tamen actus eorum non fuit illicitus reputandus. Ergo similiter poterant Christus & Apostoli actum licitum habere: sed falsa esset ista copulatiua: Christus & Apostoli habuerunt ius vtendi seu consumendi, & ius vendendi seu donandi, & ius alia acquirendi ex rebus quas ipsos sacra scriptura habuisse testatur.
units.tr: From these words it is clearly gathered that the Jews could not sell or give away the paschal lamb and the kid, nor acquire anything else from them, but could only eat them and burn the remainder with fire; and yet their act was not to be reckoned unlawful. Therefore Christ and the Apostles could likewise have had a lawful act; but that conjunctive proposition would be false: Christ and the Apostles had the right to use or consume, and the right to sell or give away, and the right to acquire other things from the things which holy Scripture testifies they had.

units.la: Item vt habetur Leuitici 24. Sacerdotes poterant licite manducare, panes propositionis: & tamen non habebant ius vendendi eos nec donandi, nec ex ipsis alia acquirendi. Ergo absque talibus iuribus potest esse licitus vsus, vel licita consumptio. Deut. 12. & multis aliis locis scripturæ diuinæ habetur aperte, quod Iudæi quasdam decimas, & oblata sanctificata Deo habebant potestatem licite comedendi & consumendi.
units.tr: Likewise, as is found in Leviticus 24, the priests could lawfully eat the bread of the Presence, yet they had no right to sell or give it away, nor to acquire anything else from it. Therefore lawful use or lawful consumption can exist without such rights. Deut. 12. and many other passages of divine Scripture clearly show that the Jews had the power to lawfully eat and consume certain tithes and offerings consecrated to God.

units.la: In quibus tamen ius vendendi, donandi, & ex ipsis alia acquirendi nullatenus habuerunt. Ergo absque talibus iuribus poterant vsus & gesta Christi Apostolorumque eius esse licita. Secundo dicunt isti, quod error prædicta quotidianæ experientiæ contradicit, quia quotidie videmus multos licite vti vel consumere ea, quæ in cibo & potu consistunt, in quibus tamen non habent ius donandi, vendendi & ex ipsis alia acquirendi.
units.tr: Yet in these things they had no right whatever to sell, give away, or acquire anything else from them. Therefore, without such rights, the uses and deeds of Christ and of his Apostles could be lawful. Secondly, these people say that the error I have described contradicts daily experience, because every day we see many people lawfully using or consuming the things that consist in food and drink, although they have no right to give or sell them, or to acquire anything else from them.

units.la: Patet de inuitatis, religiosis & seruis & aliis multis. Dicunt igitur, quod esto, quod nullus possit licite vti rebus, nisi habeat ius vtendi, si licentia vtendi vocetur ius vtendi: tamen potest tam notum, quod probatione non indiget. Quilibet enim laicus habens vsum rationis, hoc advertit. Et ita ex hoc, quod Christus & Apostoli non habuerunt prædicta, non potest inferri, quod vsus & gesta eorum fuerunt iniusta.
units.tr: This is plain in the case of invited guests, members of religious orders, servants, and many others. They therefore say that, even granting that no one may lawfully use things unless he has the right to use them, if the permission to use is called a right to use, this is so well known that it needs no proof. For every layman who has the use of reason notices it. And so from the fact that Christ and the Apostles did not have the aforesaid rights, it cannot be inferred that their use and their deeds were unjust.

units.la: Imperfecte recitat verum est; tamen illud, quod recitat, sufficit ad probandum istum impugnatum errare. (Omittit quæ sequuntur) verum est in breui appellatione, sed non in prolixa. (Unde ut melius eius fraus & malitia detegatur) Dicunt isti, quod per verba sequentia intentio & veritas, ac innocentia appellantis detegitur, & istius impugnati malitia & perfidia declaratur aperte. (Quae eos habuisse scriptura sacra testatur.) Ex his verbis patet, quod iste impugnatus intendit, quod Christus & Apostoli habuerunt iura prædicta in his rebus solummodo, quas ipsos habuisse scriptura sacra testatur. Quare patet aperte, quod non loquitur de iure naturali, cui nemo renunciare potest, quod habet quilibet in rebus etiam alienis: sed loquitur de iure positivo. (Nequaquam ius ipsis vtendi.) Hic ostensum est, non accipit ius vtendi pro iure naturali, sicut aliqui ignari conantur ostendere, sed pro iure positivo, & non diuino, vt constat. Ergo humano & de tali iure non potest dictum fuisse saluari, nisi ius humanum vocaretur licentia vtendi: nec illa vendendi seu donandi ius habuerunt, acaccipiendo ius pro iure positiuo. Christus & Apostoli non habuerunt in rebus, quibus vtebantur, nec ius vendendi nec ius donandi. Si autem acciperetur ius pro iure naturali, sic posset concedi, quod habuerunt ius vendendi, scil. in articulo necessitatis extremæ: sed non ius donandi etiam in articulo necessitatis cuiuscunque: licet si vidissent alium in extrema necessitatis articulo constitutum habuisset ius tradendi, & ita ius donandi accipiendo verbum dandi pro verbo tradendi: sed verbum donandi hic & forte nunquam accipitur pro verbo tradendi, aut ex ipsis alia acquirendi: tale ius positiuum minime habuerunt: licet non solum in rebus, quas eos scriptura sacra habuisse testatur, sed etiam in quibuscunque aliis habuerint ius naturale alia ex ipsis acquirendi, scil. in necessitate extrema. (quæ tamen ipsos de præmissis fecisse scriptura sacra testatur) licet aliqua de præmissis eos fecisse scriptura sacra testetur, quia testatur eos aliquibus vsos fuisse & consumpsisse: non tamen testatur eos ipsas res vendidisse, donasse & ex eis alia acquisisse: quod de Christo inquantum fuit homo, constat aperte. Nec obstat quod Christus pluribus millibus hominum legitur panes dedisse & pisces, quia potest dici, quod sicut inquantum Deus multiplicauit dictos panes & pisces, ita inquantum Deus dedit eos turbis sequentibus manducandos. Aliter potest dici & priori responsioni non obuiat, quod Christus inquantum homo non donauit dictos panes & pisces, vt hoc verbum dandi accipitur: sed dedit turbis dictos panes & pisces, hoc est per Apostolos tradidit comedendos. Quod autem Christus rem aliquam vendiderit, vel ex re vna aliam acquisierit, nusquam habetur. De Apostolis vero videtur scriptura diuina testari ipsos res emisse. Sed ad hoc est facile respondere: quia hoc fecerunt vel nomine aliorum, vel tempore necessitatis extremæ, scil. quando aliter necessaria vitæ acquirere nequiuerunt. Et in hoc casu licitum est cuilibet de pecunia aliena, si aliter vitam suam sustentare non potest, rem emere necessariam sustentationi humanæ. (Seu potuisse facere supponit aperte) Hoc per scripturam probari non potest: quia ex nullo loco scripturæ colligi potest, quod Christus inquantum homo extra tempus necessitatis extremæ potuit de rebus, quas habuit, res alias emere & alias acquirere ipsasq; donare. Idem patet de Apostolis. (Cum talis assertio ipsorum visum & gesta euidenter includat in præmissu non insta.) Hoc dicunt esse erroneum: quia contingit vti licite re absque iure retinendi, vendendi, donandi & ex ipsa alia acquirendi: quia licentia alterius conuenit licite vti re aliena, secundum quod ex decretali Exiit, patentur habetur, vt superius est probatum.
units.tr: The opponent recites the truth imperfectly, yet what he recites is enough to prove that the man he attacks is in error. (He omits what follows.) What he says is true in a brief statement, but not in a lengthy one. (So that his deceit and malice may be better exposed.) They say that through the words that follow, the intention, truth and innocence of the speaker are revealed, and the malice and treachery of the man he attacks are plainly declared. (Which holy Scripture testifies they had.) From these words it is clear that the man attacked intends that Christ and the Apostles had the aforesaid rights only in those things which holy Scripture testifies they had. Hence it is plain that he is not speaking of natural right, which no one can renounce and which everyone has even in things belonging to others, but of positive right. (By no means a right for them to use.) Here it is shown that he does not take "right to use" as natural right, as some ignorant people try to show, but as positive right, and not divine, as is evident. Therefore it cannot be said to be saved in a human sense, and of such a right, unless human right were called permission to use. Nor did they have a right to sell or to give, taking "right" as positive right. Christ and the Apostles had, in the things they used, neither a right to sell nor a right to give. But if "right" were taken as natural right, then it could be granted that they had the right to sell, namely in a case of extreme necessity; but not the right to give, even in a case of any necessity whatever. Although, if they had seen another placed in the extremity of necessity, they would have had the right to transfer, and so the right to give, taking "give" for "transfer"; but the word "give" here is perhaps never taken to mean "transfer", or "acquire other things from them". They did not have such a positive right at all, although they had natural right, not only in the things which holy Scripture testifies they had, but also in whatever other things, to acquire other things from them, namely in extreme necessity. (Which nevertheless holy Scripture testifies they did with the aforesaid things.) Although holy Scripture testifies that they did some of the aforesaid things, since it testifies that they used and consumed some things, yet it does not testify that they sold those things, gave them away, and acquired other things from them. This is plainly true of Christ insofar as he was man. Nor does it stand in the way that Christ is read to have given bread and fish to several thousand people, because it can be said that just as, insofar as he was God, he multiplied the said bread and fish, so insofar as he was God he gave them to the following crowds to eat. It can also be said otherwise, and this does not oppose the former answer: that Christ insofar as man did not give the said bread and fish in the sense of this word "give", but gave the crowds the said bread and fish, that is, handed them through the Apostles to be eaten. But that Christ sold anything, or acquired another thing from one thing, is nowhere found. Of the Apostles, indeed, divine Scripture seems to testify that they bought things. But this is easy to answer: they did it either in the name of others, or in a time of extreme necessity, namely when they could not otherwise acquire the necessities of life. And in this case it is lawful for anyone, with another's money, if he cannot otherwise sustain his life, to buy a thing necessary for human sustenance. (Or it supposes that they could have done this clearly.) This cannot be proved by Scripture, because from no passage of Scripture can it be gathered that Christ insofar as man, outside a time of extreme necessity, could from the things he had buy other things, acquire others, and give them away. The same is plain of the Apostles. (Since such an assertion of theirs evidently includes the sight and deeds in an unjust premise.) They say this is erroneous, because it happens that one may use a thing lawfully without the right to keep it, sell it, give it away, and acquire other things from it; for the permission of another suits lawful use of another's property, as is evident from the decretal Exiit, as was proved above.

units.la: CAP. LXXXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER 84.

units.la: Dicit ergo iste hereticus, quod dicta constitutio, cum de habere & competere loquitur, intelligit de habere seu competere iure proprietatis seu dominii ciuilis & mundani, per quod contenditur & in iudicio litigatur. Et quod de tali intellexerit, patet, vt dicit: quia dicta constitutio euidenter includit, quod Christus & Apostoli in his rebus, quas eos habuisse sacra scriptura testatur, im vendendi & donandi, & alia ex ipsis acquirendi habuerint: quod ius a iure humano fuisse introductum, manifestum.
units.tr: The heretic therefore says that the said constitution, when it speaks of having and belonging, understands it of having or belonging by the right of ownership or civil and worldly dominion, by which claims are made and disputes are brought in court. And that he understood it so is clear, as he says: because the said constitution plainly implies that Christ and the Apostles, in those things which holy Scripture testifies they had, had the right of selling, giving away, and acquiring other things from them; which right, that it was introduced by human law, is manifest.

units.la: In ista parte exprimit intellectum, quem appellans dictæ constitutioni imponit, dicens: quod secundum appellantem dicta constitutio loquitur de habere iure proprietatis seu dominii ciuilis & mundani.
units.tr: In this part he sets out the meaning which the appellant places on the said constitution, saying that, according to the appellant, the said constitution speaks of having by the right of ownership or civil and worldly dominion.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod hic truncate recitat verba appellantis, vt in sequenti capitulo apparebit.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he recites the appellant's words here in a truncated form, as will appear in the following chapter.

units.la: (Intelligit de habere seu competere iure proprietatis &c.) hoc in sequentibus ostendetur. (Quod ius a iure humano fuisse introductum) de hoc postea differetur.
units.tr: (He understands it of having or belonging by the right of ownership, etc.) This will be shown in what follows. (That this right was introduced by human law) this will be deferred to later.

units.la: CAP. LXXXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXXV.

units.la: Profecto iste hereticus imponit constitutioni, quod ipsa non dicit. Constitutio enim dicit, quod pertinaciter affirmare Christum & Apostolos in his quæ habuisse sacra scriptura, ius ipsis vtendi seu consumendi non competit, vel illa vendendi seu donandi ius non habuerit, aut ex ipsis alia acquirendi, quia tamen ipsos de præmissu fecisse scriptura sacra testatur, seu ipsos facere potuisse supponit aperte hereticum est censendum. Et tamen licet de iure dominii seu proprietatis nullam fecerit mentionem, ipse tamen imponit ei, quod intellexerit loqui de iure proprietatis & dominii ciuilis & mundani, per quod contenditur, & in iudicio litigatur. Hoc ex eo, quia ius emendi & donandi, quod dicta constitutio Christum & Apostolos asserit habuisse, ab humano iure introductum fuisse manifestum existit. Et idea dicit, quod dicta constitutio intellexit, quod Christus & Apostoli non solum in communi, sed etiam in speciali proprietatem & dominium rerum temporalium habuerunt: quod dictum secundum eum omnem religionem, quæ volens vitam & doctrinam Apostolorum sequi volens viuere sine proprio, destruit & confundit: & omnes religiosos facit proprietarios, etiam in speciali, & sui voti per consequens transgressores, & doctrinæ euangelicæ & Apostolicæ ac sedi sanctæ Romanæ ecclesiæ, & omnium doctorum ecclesiæ sanctorum patrum institutorum religionum, obuiat manifeste.
units.tr: Surely this heretic imputes to the constitution what it does not say. For the constitution says that to affirm obstinately that Christ and the Apostles did not have the right to use or consume the things which holy Scripture records they possessed, or did not have the right to sell or give them away, or to acquire other things from them, since holy Scripture testifies that they did these things beforehand, or implies that they were able to do them, is plainly to be judged heretical. And although it makes no mention of the right of lordship or ownership, he nevertheless imputes to it that it meant to speak of the right of ownership and of civil and worldly lordship, by which claims are made and disputes are litigated in court. This is because the right to buy and to give, which the said constitution asserts Christ and the Apostles had, is manifestly shown to have been introduced by human law. And so he says that the said constitution meant that Christ and the Apostles had ownership and lordship over temporal goods not only in common but also individually. According to him, this assertion destroys and confounds every religious order which, wishing to follow the life and teaching of the Apostles, wants to live without property, and it makes all religious proprietors, even individually, and consequently transgressors of their vow; and it manifestly opposes the evangelical and apostolic doctrine, the see of the holy Roman Church, and the institutions of the religious orders as taught by all the holy Fathers and teachers of the Church.

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnatus conatur ostendere, quod appellans imponit constitutioni, quod ipsa non dicit: dicens, quod appellans imponit constitutioni, quod loquitur de iure proprietatis & dominii, quod tamen non dicit, cum de iure proprietatis & dominii nullam faciat mentionem.
units.tr: In this part, the opponent here impugned tries to show that the appellant imputes to the constitution what it does not say, namely that the appellant imputes to the constitution that it speaks of the right of ownership and lordship, which however it does not say, since it makes no mention at all of the right of ownership and lordship.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod licet constitutio vocalem non faciat de iure dominii mentionem: tamen tam constitutio ipsa, quam conditor eius, intelligit de illo iure, quorum vtrumque probat appellans. Vnde aliquæ rationes eius probant, quod constitutio Cum inter, debet intelligi de iure proprieproprietatis & dominii. Alia vero eiusdem probant, quod cum conditor dictæ constitutionis sūæ in illa constitutione sue in aliis dicit Christum & Apostolos res aliquas habuisse, ipse intelligit de habere iure proprietatis & dominii. Quod, vt ostendatur apertius, & simul cum hoc manifestetur omnibus, quod iste impugnatus truncate recitat obiectiones appellantis, illas, quæ ipsum aperte convincunt, omittens, verba appellantis sunt præsentibus inserenda, quæ sunt hæc. Sextus error sumitur in dicto statuto, Cum inter, ex eo quod ipse pronunciavit siue declaravit hereticum fore censendum affirmare deinceps dominum Iesum eiusq; Apostolos non habuisse aliqua in speciali nec etiam in communi. Insuper hereticum fore censendum affirmare Christo & eius Apostolis in his, quæ eos habuisse sacra scriptura testatur, non competisse ius vendi, nec illa vendendi, seu donandi, seu ex ipsis alia acquirendi: quæ quidem doctrina de habere & competere iure proprietatis & dominii civilis & mundani, per quod contenditur & in iudicio litigatur, se intellexisse ex pluribus manifestat: tum quia in dicto statuto, Quia quorundam, expresse improbat sensum eorum asserentium, quod abdicatio iuris in vsufructu, rei proprietate & in eius vsu, per quod potest sic vtens pro vsu huiusmodi contendere vel in iudicio litigare, est meritoria & sancta & à Christo in seipso seruata, Apostolisq; impositta, & ab ipsis sub voto assumpta & pertinaciter asserit in eodem hac verba appellantis. Ex quibus clarét, quod iste truncate recitat obiectiones eius, & quod ad ipsas respondere non potest. Et ideo, vt dicunt isti, ipsa cautelose, vt decipiat simplices, scienter omittit.
units.tr: But these opponents say that although the constitution does not mention the right of lordship in words, yet both the constitution itself and its author mean that right, and the appellant proves both. Hence some of his arguments prove that the constitution Cum inter must be understood of the right of property and lordship; others of his prove that when the author of that constitution says, in that and in other constitutions, that Christ and the Apostles had certain things, he means that they had them by the right of property and lordship. But so that this may be shown more clearly, and at the same time made plain to all, that this opponent recites the appellant's objections in a truncated form, omitting those which clearly convict him, the appellant's own words must be inserted here, and they are these: The sixth error is drawn from the said statute, Cum inter, from the fact that it pronounced, or declared, that it is to be judged heretical to affirm henceforth that the Lord Jesus and his Apostles had nothing, either in particular or in common. Moreover, it is to be judged heretical to affirm that to Christ and his Apostles, in those things which holy Scripture testifies they had, there did not belong the right to sell them, nor to sell, give away, or acquire other things from them. That this doctrine concerns having and holding by right of civil and worldly ownership, by which claims are made and disputes litigated in court, the author has shown himself to have understood from several things: partly because in the said statute, Quia quorundam, he expressly disapproves the sense of those who assert that renunciation of the right in the usufruct, of the property of a thing and of its use, by which one who uses it in this way may claim or litigate in court for such use, is meritorious and holy, and was observed by Christ in himself, imposed on the Apostles, and by them taken up under vow; and he obstinately asserts in the same place these words of the appellant. From these it is clear that he recites the appellant's objections in a truncated form, and that he cannot answer them. And so, as these men say, he cunningly and knowingly omits them, in order to deceive the simple.

units.la: (Imponit constitutioni, quod ipsa constitutio non dicit) Verum est, quod constitutio non dicit hoc vocaliter: dicit tamen sententialiter. Im ipsis vtendi siue consumendi non competierit vel illa vendendi seu donandi im non habuerit, aut vt ipsis alia acquirendi. (Hic volens recitare sententiam constitutionis, Cum inter, quoad vnam partem eius mutat notam copulationis in notam disiunctionis: Ex quo patet euidenter, quod ipse intendit in dicta constitutione; Cum inter, quod Christus & Apostoli habuerunt ius vtendi, vendendi donandi & ex rebus alia acquirendi: & quod aliter vsus & gesta eorum fuissent non iusta. Licet de iure dominii seu proprietatis nullam fecerim mentionem.) Verum est vocalem: tamen ex hoc non potest concludi, quod non intellexerit de tali iure, quemadmodum secundum istu, vt patet supra cap. 81. Numeri cap. 18. de dominio nulla vocalis fit mentio: & tamen dicit iste, quod ibi expresse dicitur, quod Dominus dedit Leuitis dominium decimarum: ita quamquis in constitutione, Cum inter, de dominio non fiat mentio vocalis, tamen intelligit de dominio: & hoc ex eo verum est, sed non ex eo solo, sed ex eo & multis aliis, ad quæ iste respondere nequaquam quia nescit attentat, ideo dicit quod constitutio intellexit, quod Christus & Apostoli non solum in communi, sed etiam in speciali proprietatem & dominium rerum temporalium habuerunt, verum est secundum istos; quod dicta constitutio hoc intellexerit, licet ipsa hoc vocaliter nequaquam expresserit: verumtamen conditor eius in ista constitutione, quia vir reprobus, hoc vocaliter & sententialiter asserit manifeste: sicut ex superioribus patet & ex sequentibus apparebit.
units.tr: (He imputes to the constitution what the constitution does not say.) It is true that the constitution does not say this in words; yet it says it in sense: that it would not belong to them to use or consume them, or that it did not have the right to sell or give them, or to acquire other things from them. (Here, wishing to recite the sense of the constitution Cum inter, as regards one part of it, he changes the conjunction into a disjunction. From this it is evident that he intends in the said constitution Cum inter that Christ and the Apostles had the right to use, sell, give, and acquire other things from goods, and that otherwise their practice and deeds would not have been just.) Although I have made no mention of the right of lordship or ownership. It is true in words; yet it cannot be concluded from this that it did not mean such a right. According to this man, as appears above in chapter 81, and Numbers chapter 18, no word of lordship is made; and yet he says that there it is expressly stated that the Lord gave the Levites the lordship of the tithes. So although in the constitution Cum inter no word of lordship is spoken, yet it means lordship. And this is true, not from this alone, but from this and many other things, to which this man in no way answers, because he does not know how to attempt it. Therefore he says that the constitution meant that Christ and the Apostles had property and lordship over temporal things not only in common but also individually. It is true, according to them, that the said constitution meant this, although it did not express it in words at all; but its author, in this constitution, being a reprobate man, asserts this clearly both in words and in sense, as appears from what precedes and will appear from what follows.

units.la: CAP. LXXXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER 86.

units.la: Præculdubio dicti ipsius hæretici possent vno verbo repelli, scil. quod falsum imponit constitutioni imponendo ei, quod intellexerit loqui de iure domini seu proprietatis, cum nulla in ea habeatur de dominio mentio, vt patere potest cuilibet intuenti.
units.tr: Doubtless the said heretic's objections could be refuted with a single word, namely, that he falsely charges the constitution with meaning that it spoke of right of lordship or ownership, since there is no mention of lordship in it, as anyone looking at it can see.

units.la: In ista parte iste impugnatus ad obiectiones appellantis nititur respondere. Et diuiditur in duas partes: quia primo ponit vnam responsionem generalem. Secundo assertionem principalem appellantis pertractat: quasi pro solutione obiectionis sufficiat ostendere eandem assertionem esse falsam. Secunda pars incipit in parte immediate sequenti. Dicit ergo, quod omnes obiectiones appellantis possent vnico verbo repelli, dicendo, scil. quod constitutio non facit mentionem de dominio.
units.tr: In this part the one attacked tries to answer the objections of the appellant. It is divided into two parts: first he offers one general answer; second he deals with the appellant's principal assertion, as though it were enough to answer the objection to show that the same assertion is false. The second part begins in the part immediately following. He says, then, that all the appellant's objections could be refuted with one word, namely by saying that the constitution makes no mention of lordship.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti, quod iste respondet ad conclusionem, & non ad probationes, per quas probatur conclusio: quia sæpe verba intelliguntur de aliquo, quod vocaliter nequaquam exprimitur. Licet ergo de dominio non fiat mentio vocalis: tamen appellans probat, quod de dominio debet intelligi: & ita per dictam responsionem obiectiones sunt minime repelluntur: quia etiam non tanguntur. (Falsum imponit constitutioni &c.) Hoc deberet iste ostendere ad obiectiones respondendo. (Cum nulla in ea habeatur de dominio mentio) verum est vocalis: sed ex hoc non sequitur, quod de dominio non debet intelligi.
units.tr: But these men say that he answers the conclusion and not the proofs by which the conclusion is established, since words are often understood of something that is not expressed in words at all. Although, then, no spoken mention of lordship is made, the appellant proves that it ought to be understood of lordship; and so the objections are by no means refuted by that answer, since they are not even touched. (He falsely charges the constitution, etc.) He ought to show this by answering the objections. (Since there is no mention of lordship in it) It is true as to the spoken words; but it does not follow from this that it ought not to be understood of lordship.

units.la: CAP. LXXXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXXVII.

units.la: Sed quia iste hereticus pertinaciter asserit Christum & Apostolos nullius rei temporalis proprietatem seu dominium in communi vel proprio habuisse, videndum est vtrum eius assertio possit stare: & quia ipse dicit in præcedentibus, & hoc etiam supponit, quod dominium proprium de iure humano est introductum. Primo, quia si quæritur quo iure sit ius proprietatis seu dominii introductum? Ad hoc dicit iste hereticus, quod à iure humano & ciuili. Ad quod probandum inducit 8. dist. c. quo iure, vbi dicitur, quod iure humano dicitur: hic villa mea est: hic seruus meus est; hac domus mea est. Item inducit dictum Clementis quod recitatur 12. q. 1. c. dilectissimis, vbi sic dicitur: communis vsus omnium quæ sunt in mundo, omnibus hominibus esse debuit: sed per iniquitatem alius hoc dicit esse suum & alius illud, & sic inter mortales facta est diuisio & intelligit per illud, quod dicit per iniquitatem debere intelligi iuu humanum.
units.tr: But because this heretic obstinately asserts that Christ and the Apostles had no ownership or dominion over any temporal thing, either in common or as private property, we must consider whether his assertion can stand. He says in what precedes, and also assumes, that private dominion was introduced by human law. First, if it is asked by what law the right of property or dominion was introduced, this heretic answers that it was by human and civil law. To prove this he cites distinction 8, chapter "quo iure," where it is said that by human law one says: this estate is mine, this servant is mine, this house is mine. He also cites the words of Clement, recited in 12, question 1, chapter "dilectissimis," where it is said: the common use of all things that are in the world ought to have belonged to all men; but through iniquity one man says this is his and another that, and so division has come about among mortals. By "iniquity" he understands human law.

units.la: In ista parte pertractat iste assertionem principalem appellantis, scilicet Christus & Apostoli nullius rei temporalis proprietatem habuerunt, nec in communi nec speciali. Et diuiditur in duas partes: primo pertractat quandam quæstionem aliam incidentalem. Secundo pertractat quæstionem principalem, ibi; secundo quaeritur. Prima in tres: quia primo proponit duas quæstiones, quas intendit pertractare. Secundo ponit assertionem appellantis circa quæstionem incidentalem ibi scriptura sacra. Litera plana est.
units.tr: In this part he treats the principal assertion of the appellant, namely that Christ and the Apostles had no ownership of any temporal thing, neither in common nor individually. The section is divided into two parts. First he treats another, incidental question; second he treats the principal question, at "secondly it is asked." The first part has three divisions: first he proposes the two questions he intends to treat; second he sets out the appellant's assertion on the incidental question, at "Holy Scripture." The wording is plain.

units.la: (Pertinaciter asserit) Hoc dicunt isti esse falsum propter duo. Primo quia veritatis assertio non est pertinax sed fidelis. Secundo quia esto, quod assertio esset falsa: tamen appellans non esset pertinax, cum paratus sit corrigi in omnibus, si erraret, per concilium generale. (Dominium proprium &c.) Bene dicitur dominium proprium: quia dominium, quod non est proprium, non est de iure humano introductum. (Ius proprietatis seu dominii.) Ex hoc patet aperte, quod iste loquitur tantum in ista conclusione de dominio, quod est proprietas. (A iure humano) generaliter dicit, a iure humano, non a iure regum, secundum quod modo vocantur reges: quia ante reges fuit dominium, quod est proprietas. (Et intelligit illud quod dicit per iniquitatem, debere intelligi ius humanum.) Hoc accepit a Glossa 12. q. 1. cap. dilectissimis, quæ super verbum per iniquitatem, dicit, id est, per consuetudinem iuris gentium, æquitati naturali contrariam.
units.tr: (Obstinately asserts) These men say this is false for two reasons. First, the assertion of truth is not obstinate but faithful. Second, even if the assertion were false, the appellant would not be obstinate, since he is ready to be corrected in all things, should he err, by a general council. (Private dominion, etc.) It is rightly said private dominion, because dominion that is not private was not introduced by human law. (The right of property or dominion.) From this it is plainly clear that he speaks in this conclusion only of dominion that is property. (By human law) he says generally by human law, not by the law of kings in the sense in which kings are now so called, because there was dominion, that is, property, before kings. (And he understands by what he calls iniquity human law.) He takes this from the Gloss on 12, question 1, chapter dilectissimis, which, on the words through iniquity, says: that is, through custom of the law of nations, contrary to natural equity.

units.la: CAP. LXXXVIII.
units.tr: Chapter 88

units.la: Scriptura sacra dicit contrarium euidenter, scilicet quod imo iure diuino non humano fuerit dominium introductum. Ius enim diuinum est, quod in scripturis diuinis habemus, vt legitur 8. dist. c. quo iure, in principio. Vbi dicitur, quod ius diuinum est quod in scripturis diuinis habemus. Humanum ius, quod in legibus regum. In scripturis autem diuinis habemus, quod antequam leges regum, imo etiam antequam reges essent, res aliqua alicuius erant. Ergo iure diuino aliquis dicere poterat, aliquid suum esse. Maior patet per cap. quo iure praeallegatum. Minor autem probatur etiam pro innocentia statu. Videtur enim quod Adam in statu innocentiae antequam Eua formaretur, solus dominium habuit rerum temporalium. Commune enim dominium, cum solus esset pro illo tempore habere non potuit: cum communio plures requirere dignoscatur. Et quod Dominus fuerit antequam Eua formaretur, Eccles. 17. probari videtur expresse. Ibi enim dicitur sic: Deus de terra creauit hominem. Et sequitur: posuit timorem illius super omnem carnem: & dominatus est bestiarum & volatilium. Dicit ergo quod dominatus fuit. Ex quo sequitur, quod dominium habuit. A dominio enim secundum Dionysium d. dist. no. c. 12. dicitur Dominus, dominator & dominans. Ex quo sequitur, quod ex quo dominatus est, quod dominium habuit. Quod autem tunc formata Eua non esset, patet: quia statim post illa verba; & dominatus est bestiarum & volatilium: sequitur, creauit ex eo (scil. Adam) adiutorium simile sibi scil. Euam. Ad idem facit Sapientia 9. vbi dicitur sic: Deus Patrum nostrorum & dominus misericordiae qui fecisti omnia verbo tuo, & sapientia tua constituisti hominem vt dominaretur creaturae tuae quae a te facta est &c. Et hoc expresse dicit Damascenus lib. 2. c. 8. vt dictum est supra. Item post lapsum primorum parentum ante diluuium & antequam essent reges, potuit aliquis dicere: hoc est meum. Probatur Gen. 3. vbi Deus ad Adam dixit: In sudore vultus tui vescieris pane tuo. Ergo patet quod Adam tunc potuit dicere, panem suum: & tamen tunc non erant reges, imo nec homines alii, nisi soli primi parentes. De Abel quoq; qui fuit secundo genitus primorum parentum, dicitur Gen. 4. quod Abel obtulit de primogenitis gregis sui. Ex quo patet, quod Abel potuit dicere, iste grex est meus. Item quod post diluuium sine iure regum potuerit aliquis dicere suum, patet. Legitur enim Gen. 9. & Noe vineam plantauit, & vinum ex ea productum bibit. Puto, quod nullus sapiens negabit, quin vinea dominus fuerit & etiam vini: & tunc non legimus regem aliquem extitisse. Item Gen. 12. dicit Dominus ad Abraham existentem in terra Chanaan; Semini tuo dabo terram hanc: quod & fecit. Constat autem quod illi de semine suo potuerunt dicere: terra ista nostra est: & hoc non per iura regum, quia eam ex collatione Dei habuerunt, non regu. Item Gen. 26. Cum descendisset Isaac in Gerara, dixit Dominus ei: Tibi & semini tuo dabo vniuersas regiones has. Quarum regionum dominium semen eius non ex iure regum, sed ex collatione Dei habuit. Praeterea Num. 31. dicitur, quod vnius cuiusque quod in praeda rapuerat, suum erat. Quod non erat per iura regum: cum ille populus Israeliticus tunc regem non haberet, sed dux Moyses eius tantum esset. Item Num. 33. Dominus ad Moysem dicit: Praecipe filiis Israel & dic ad eos: Quando transieritis Iordanem intrantes in terram Chanaam, dispergite cunctos habitatores terrae illius. Ego enim dedi vobis illam in possessionem, quam diuidetis vobis sorte. Quod & fecerunt, vt legitur Iosue 13. Quilibet ergo istorum post diuisionem terrae illius portionem illam, quae ad eum obuenit, potuit dicere suam esse: & hoc non iure regum, sed diuino, cum tunc temporis (vt dictum est) regibus non regeretur populus ille. Item Num. 35. Dominus ad Moysem dicit: Praecipe filiis Israel, vt dent Leuitis de possessionibus suis vrbes ad habitandum & suburbana per circuitum, vt ipsi in vrbibus maneant & suburbana sint pro pecoribus & iumentis. Quod etiam fecerunt, vt legitur Iosue 14. Ex quibus patet, quod cum Dominus praecepit filiis Israel dare Leuitis de possessionibus suis, quod filii Israel antequam darent possessiones illas, poterant dicere suas esse, & etiam Leuita ex quo sibi fuerunt data: & hoc non per iura regum, cum reges non haberent, sed per ordinationem diuinam. Ex quibus omnibus patet, quod in scripturis sacris habemus, quod aliquis in statu innocentiae & post lapsum primorum parentum, & ante diluuium & post diluuium, dicere poterat sine iure regum aliquid esse suum. Et quod de iure diuino sint dominia aliqua, probatur 23. q. 2. cap. 1.
units.tr: Holy Scripture plainly says the opposite, namely that dominion was introduced by divine right, not by human right. For divine right is what we have in the divine Scriptures, as is read in dist. 8, c. quo iure, at the beginning, where it is said that divine right is what we have in the divine Scriptures, and human right is what is in the laws of kings. Now in the divine Scriptures we have that, before there were laws of kings, or even before there were kings, some things belonged to someone. Therefore by divine right someone could say that something was his. The major premise is clear from the chapter quo iure cited above. The minor premise is also proved from the state of innocence. For it seems that Adam, in the state of innocence before Eve was formed, alone had dominion over temporal things. Common dominion could not exist when he was alone at that time, since community is known to require several persons. And that the Lord existed before Eve was formed seems to be expressly proved by Ecclesiasticus 17. For there it is said: "God created man out of the earth," and it follows: "He set the fear of him over all flesh, and he had dominion over the beasts and the birds." So it says that he had dominion. From this it follows that he had dominion. For, according to Dionysius, dist. [?] no., c. 12, "Lord," "ruler" and "lording it" derive from "dominion." Hence it follows that, since he ruled, he had dominion. That Eve had not yet been formed at that time is clear, because immediately after the words "and he had dominion over the beasts and the birds" there follows: "He created out of him (that is, Adam) a helper like himself, namely Eve." To the same effect is Wisdom 9, where it is said: "O God of our fathers and Lord of mercy, who hast made all things by thy word, and by thy wisdom hast ordained man that he should have dominion over thy creature which was made by thee," and so on. Damascene expressly says this in book 2, c. 8, as was said above. Likewise, after the fall of our first parents, before the flood and before there were kings, someone could say: "This is mine." This is proved from Genesis 3, where God said to Adam: "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat thy bread." Therefore it is clear that Adam could then say "my bread," and yet at that time there were no kings, nor indeed any other men except the first parents alone. Also of Abel, who was the second-born of our first parents, it is said in Genesis 4 that Abel offered of the firstlings of his flock. From this it is clear that Abel could say: "This flock is mine." Likewise, that after the flood someone could call something his without the right of kings is clear. For we read in Genesis 9 that Noah planted a vineyard and drank the wine made from it. I think no wise man will deny that he was the owner of the vineyard and also of the wine, and at that time we do not read that any king existed. Again, in Genesis 12 the Lord says to Abraham, who was in the land of Canaan: "To thy seed I will give this land," and he did so. It is certain that those of his seed could say: "This land is ours," and they had it not by the laws of kings, but from God's grant, not from a king. Again, in Genesis 26, when Isaac had gone down to Gerar, the Lord said to him: "To thee and to thy seed I will give all these regions." The dominion of these regions his seed had not by the right of kings, but from God's grant. Moreover, Numbers 31 says that what each one had seized in the spoil was his own. This was not by the laws of kings, since that Israelite people then had no king, but only Moses as its leader. Again, in Numbers 33 the Lord says to Moses: "Command the sons of Israel and say to them: When you have crossed the Jordan and entered the land of Canaan, drive out all the inhabitants of that land. For I have given it to you in possession, and you shall divide it by lot." And they did this, as is read in Joshua 13. Therefore each of them, after the division of that land, could say that the portion which fell to him was his own, and this not by the right of kings, but by divine right, since at that time, as has been said, that people was not ruled by kings. Again, in Numbers 35 the Lord says to Moses: "Command the sons of Israel that they give to the Levites, out of their possessions, cities to dwell in and pasture lands round about, so that they may dwell in the cities and the pasture lands may be for their flocks and herds." This they also did, as is read in Joshua 14. From these passages it is clear that, when the Lord commanded the sons of Israel to give to the Levites from their possessions, the sons of Israel, before they gave those possessions, could say that they were their own, and the Levites too, from the time they were given to them; and this not by the laws of kings, since they had no kings, but by divine ordinance. From all these things it is clear that we have in the holy Scriptures that someone, in the state of innocence and after the fall of our first parents, both before and after the flood, could say without the right of kings that something was his own. And that some dominions are by divine right is proved in 23 q. 2, c. 1.

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnatus circa praedictam quaestionem improbando assertionem appellantis suam ponit sententiam. Et diuiditur in duas partes: quia primo ponit suam assertionem. Secundo ad auctoritates pro assertione contraria allegatas respondet ibi; Ex praedictis itaq. Prima in tres diuididiuiditur. Quia primo ostendit, quod dominium rerum temporalium non iure humano, sed diuino extitit introductum. Secundo ostendit, quod dominium rerum temporalium non potuit dari hominibus iure humano, sed diuino tantummodo. Tertio ostendit: quid circa dominium rerum temporalium iure humano est inductum. Secunda ibi: Adhuc & nullo iure. Tertia ibi: Verum est 14-meh. In prima igitur parte primam conclusionem probat tali ratione: Ius diuinum est quod in scripturis diuinis habemus. Ius humanum quod in legibus regum. Sed in scripturis diuinis habemus quod antequam essent reges, temporalia ad aliquorum dominium pertinebant. Ergo iure diuino, non iure humano, rerum dominium extitit introductum. Maiorem ostendit per auctoritatem Augustini, quae ponitur dist. 8. cap. quo iure. Circa probationem minoris primo ostendit per tres auctoritates, quod dominium proprium rerum in statu innocentiae fuit inductum: & non per reges. Constat ergo quod a Deo. Secundo: Item quod post lapsum, probat per duas auctoritates, quod dominium temporalium post lapsum ante diluuium absque legibus regum fuit inductum. Tertio ibi: Item quod post diluuium, probat vna auctoritate, quod post diluuium dominium rerum fuit inductum absque legibus regum. Quarto ibi: Item Gen. 12. Probat per duas auctoritates, quod aliquarum rerum dominium fuit inductum absque legibus regum. Sexto ibi: Item Numeri 33. probat per tres auctoritates, quod aliquarum rerum dominium fuit inductum immediate a Deo.
units.tr: In this part, this author, when refuting the said question and disproving the assertion of the appellant, sets out his own opinion. And it is divided into two parts: first he sets out his own assertion; second, he answers the authorities alleged for the contrary assertion, there, "From what has been said, therefore." The first part is divided into three. First he shows that dominion over temporal things was introduced by divine right, not by human right. Second he shows that dominion over temporal things could not be given to men by human right, but by divine right only. Third he shows what has been introduced by human right concerning dominion over temporal things. The second part begins there: Yet also by no right. The third begins there: It is true. In the first part, then, he proves the first conclusion by this argument: divine right is what we have in the divine Scriptures; human right is what is in the laws of kings. But in the divine Scriptures we have that, before there were kings, temporal things belonged to the dominion of certain persons. Therefore dominion was introduced by divine right, not by human right. He shows the major premise by the authority of Augustine, which is cited in dist. 8, c. quo iure. Concerning the proof of the minor premise, he first shows by three authorities that proper dominion over things was introduced in the state of innocence, and not by kings. Therefore it is clear that it was from God. Second, with "Likewise, that after the fall," he proves by two authorities that dominion over temporal things was introduced after the fall and before the flood, without the laws of kings. Third, with "Likewise, that after the flood," he proves by one authority that after the flood dominion over things was introduced without the laws of kings. Fourth, with "Likewise Genesis 12," he proves by two authorities that dominion over certain things was introduced without the laws of kings. Sixth, with "Likewise Numbers 33," he proves by three authorities that dominion over certain things was introduced immediately by God.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores plura hic dicta reputantes erronea sic procedunt. Primo enim quinque conclusiones, quas putant catholicas, improbare conantur. Secundo nituntur ostendere, quod plures errores in hac serie continentur. Tertio discurrendo per litteram ad auctoritates singulas satagunt respondere. Circa primum primo dicunt, quod in statu innocentiae nullum fuit dominium proprium. Haec conclusio tractata est supra cap. 26. 27. & 28. Ideo de ipsa pertransitur ad praesens. Secunda conclusio, quam probant, est quod primum dominium temporalium proprium post lapsum fuit iure humano, seu ordinatione aut voluntate humana inductum. Hanc probant sic. Prima diuisio dominiorum, quae legitur in scriptura, fuit inter Abel & Cain. Sic enim legitur Gen. 4. Fuit autem Abel Pastor ouium: & Cain agricola. Factum autem post multos dies, vt offerret Cain de fructibus terrae munera Deo: Abel quoque obtulit de primogenitis gregis sui, & de adipibus eorum, & respexit Dominus ad Abel, & ad munera eius: ad Cain autem ad munera eius non respexit. Ex his verbis colligitur, quod isti duo habuerunt rerum diuersarum distincta dominia: sed non legitur quod ista diuisio fuit facta praecepto diuino. Ergo voluntate humana fuit prima dominiorum diuisio introducta. Sed forte obiiciet aliquis contra hoc dupliciter. Primo quia antequam nasceretur Cain vel Abel dixit Dominus ad Adam: In sudore vultus tui vesceris pane tuo, sicut habetur Gen. 3. Ergo Adam habebat panem ante filios. Item in eodem c. legitur; fecit quoque Dominus Deus Adae & uxori eius tunicas pelliceas & induit eos. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod vterque; de dono Dei habuit propriam pelliceam. E non solum ante nativitatem Cain & Abel fuit dominiorum distinctio sed etiam immediate a Deo fuit dominiorum distinctio introducta. Sed ad vtramque istarum obiectionum respondent isti, quod licet inter primos parentes fuerit rerum diuisio quantum ad vsum omnes tamen fuerunt communes quantum ad aliquale dominium, quod propter vinculum matrimonii ac concordiam & amorem inter ipsos satis videtur probabile. Stante enim amore & concordia inter ipsos non videtur, quod debuerunt aliqua ratione moueri ad dividendum temporalia inter se quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Dicunt etiam quod esto, quod diuisissent inter se res temporales quo ad dominium, & prima dominiorum diuisio non fuisset inter Cain & Abel: tamen adhuc voluntate humana prima dominiorum diuisio fuisset inducta. Nam antequam Adam panē vesceretur, & antequam eis Deus daret pelliceas, legitur, quod cum cognouissent se esse nudos conseruerunt folia ficus; & fecerunt sibi perizomata. Non apparet autem, quod plus appropriauerint sibi pelliceas, quam perizomata. Ergo si pelliceae & aliae res fuerunt diuersae inter eos quo ad dominium: sequitur quod perizomata fuerunt diuersa inter eos quo ad dominium, & non ex speciali praecepto diuino, sed voluntate humana. Ergo voluntate humana fuit prima dominiorum distinctio introducta. Tertia conclusio est, quod iure humano absque legibus Regum secundum & Reges contra Duces, Comites, Barones & alios seculares principes diuiduntur multarum rerum distincta dominia & diuersis temporib' introducta fuerunt. Hoc patet aperte de diuisione facta inter filios filiorum Noe, Gen. 10. de quib' dicitur; ab hiis diuisae sunt insulae gentium in regionibus suis. Multa alia de diuisione terrarum subduntur ibi. Quae diuisio voluntate & ordinatione humana facta fuit. Quarta conclusio est, quod aliquarum rerum temporalium diuersa & distincta dominia immediata ordinatione diuina introducta fuerunt. Quod per plures auctoritates allegatas ab isto aperte probatur. Hoc non ex Deut. 2. patenter ostenditur, vbi Dominus ad Moysem: Transibitis per terminos fratrum vestrorum filiorum Esau, qui habitant in Seir, & timebunt vos. Videte ergo diligenter ne moueamini contra eos. Neque enim dabo vobis de terra eorum quantum petest vnius pedis calcare vestigium, quia in possessionem dedi Esau montem Seyr. Et post: nec pugnate contra Moabitas, nec iniras aduersus eos prelium. Non n. dabo tibi quicquam de terra eorum, quia filiis Lot tradidi ar in possessione. Ex his patet, quod praedictorum regionum Seir & Ar dominia ex speciali ordinatione diuina filiis Esau & Moab data fuerunt. Et si diceretur, quod hoc non fuit nisi per inspirationem vel approbationem occultam, non per speciale praeceptum, hoc de quibusdam aliis dici non potest. Nam vt habetur Exod. 12. filii Israel in exitu de Aegypto, de praecepto Domini spoliauerunt Aegyptios: & ita de speciali ordinatione & praecepto diuino spoliorum acquisierunt dominium: & ita iure diuino aliquarum rerum dominium extitit introductum. Quod per alias auctoritates scripturae diuinae posset copiose probari, sed praeficiunt.
units.tr: But these opponents, judging that many of the points stated here are mistaken, proceed as follows. First, they try to disprove the five conclusions that they think are Catholic. Second, they undertake to show that several errors are contained in this series. Third, going through the text passage by passage, they labour to answer each of the authorities. As to the first point, they say first that in the state of innocence there was no private dominion. This conclusion was treated above in chapters 26, 27 and 28, so I pass over it here. The second conclusion they try to prove is that the first private dominion over temporal goods after the Fall was introduced by human law, that is, by human ordinance or will. They prove it thus. The first division of possessions that is read of in Scripture was between Abel and Cain. For Genesis 4 reads: Now Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground. And in process of time it came to pass that Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering unto the Lord. And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the Lord had respect unto Abel and to his offering: but unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect. From these words it is gathered that these two had distinct dominions over different things. But it is not read that this division was made by divine command. Therefore the first division of dominions was introduced by human will. But perhaps someone will object to this in two ways. First, because before Cain or Abel was born, the Lord said to Adam: In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, as is found in Genesis 3. Therefore Adam had bread before his sons. Likewise, in the same chapter it is read: Unto Adam also and to his wife did the Lord God make coats of skins, and clothed them. From these words it is given to understand that each of them had a skin coat of their own, as a gift of God. And so the distinction of dominions existed not only before the birth of Cain and Abel, but was also introduced immediately by God. But to both these objections these men reply that although there was a division of things among the first parents as to use, yet all things were common as to some kind of dominion, which seems sufficiently probable on account of the bond of marriage and the concord and love between them. For while love and concord prevailed between them, it does not seem that they ought for any reason to have been moved to divide temporal things between themselves as to dominion and property. They also say that even if they had divided temporal things between themselves as to dominion, the first division of dominions would not have been between Cain and Abel; yet even so the first division of dominions would have been introduced by human will. For before Adam ate bread, and before God gave them skins, it is read that when they knew they were naked they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves aprons. But it does not appear that they claimed more for themselves in the skins than in the aprons. Therefore, if the skins and other things were distinct between them as to dominion, it follows that the aprons were distinct between them as to dominion too, and this not by a special divine command but by human will. Therefore the first distinction of dominions was introduced by human will. The third conclusion is that distinct dominions over many things were introduced at different times by human law, without the laws of kings, both by the second kings and against dukes, counts, barons and other secular princes. This is clear from the division made among the sons of the sons of Noah, Genesis 10, of whom it is said: By these were the isles of the Gentiles divided in their lands. Many other things about the division of lands are added there. That division was made by human will and ordinance. The fourth conclusion is that distinct and separate dominions over certain temporal things were introduced by immediate divine ordinance. This is openly proved by the many authorities that they cite. It is plainly shown from Deuteronomy 2, where the Lord said to Moses: You shall pass through the coast of your brethren the children of Esau, which dwell in Seir; and they shall be afraid of you: take ye good heed therefore unto yourselves: meddle not with them; for I will not give you of their land, no, not so much as a foot breadth; because I have given mount Seir unto Esau for a possession. And afterwards: Distress not the Moabites, neither contend with them in battle; for I will not give thee of their land any possession, because I have given Ar unto the children of Lot for a possession. From these it is clear that the dominions of the aforesaid regions, Seir and Ar, were given to the sons of Esau and Moab by a special divine ordinance. And if it were said that this was only by secret inspiration or approval, not by a special command, that cannot be said of certain other things. For as is found in Exodus 12, the sons of Israel, at their going out of Egypt, by the command of the Lord spoiled the Egyptians; and so by a special divine ordinance and command they acquired dominion over the spoils; and thus dominion over certain things was introduced by divine law. This could be copiously proved by other authorities of divine Scripture, but I omit them.

units.la: Quinta
units.tr: Fifth

units.la: Tertia conclusio est, quod post promulgationem euangelii & euacuationem legalium omnium temporalium propria dominia noua à iure humano fuerunt, & non à iure diuino, neque ex aliqua collatione Dei speciali. Hoc probatur: Nam ab illo tempore, neque Iudæi, neque Christiani, neque Pagani aliquid iure diuino nouiter possidebant. Ergo ex tunc nullum fuit nouum dominium iure diuino, cum omnes tunc fuerunt Iudæi, Christiani & Pagani; Quod Iudæi tunc non possidebant aliquid nouiter iure diuino, patet; quia de iure diuino non possidebantur nouiter alia à Iudæis, quam illa quæ ex præcepto scripturæ diuinæ acquirebant: sed illa præcepta iam cessauerant. Ergo iure diuino nihil nouiter possidebant. Quod etiam Christiani non possidebant aliquid nouiter iure diuino, patet quia nullius rei dominium in speciali ex collatione Dei speciali acquisierunt: quia in toto nouo testamento non legitur, quod Deus rem aliquam temporalem dederit Christianis quo ad dominium speciale: nisi dicas, quod Christus pauerit turbas. Sed ex hoc non sequitur, quod post promulgationem euangelii & euacuationem legalium aliquid specialiter dederit Christianis. Ex hoc etiam quod pauit turbas, non sequitur quod dederit eis dominium panum & piscium, quia dictos panes & pisces non dedit eis nisi ad comedendum. Sed forte dices, quod clerici acquirunt dominia rerum iure diuino; quia ex nouo testamento eis debentur stipendia, dicente Christo Luc. 10. Dignus est operarius mercede sua. Et 1. Corinth. 9. dicit Apostolus: Quis militat suis stipendiis unquam? Et ibidem: Qui altari deseruiunt, cum altari participant. Ita & Deus ordinauit his, qui euangelium annunciant, de euangelio viuere. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod ex ordinatione diuina annunciantibus euangelium temporalia debentur stipendia. Ergo temporalia possidebant iure diuino. Ad hoc dicunt, quod ista ordinatio Dei est ordinatio generalis nullam rem temporalem speciale determinans: & imo propter talem ordinationem generalem non dicuntur aliqua possideri iure diuino, prout nunc loquimur. Quemadmodum enim quamuis ex ordinatione Dei generali diuites debeant dare eleemosynas pauperibus: & tamen eleemosynæ datæ pauperibus non dicuntur possideri iure diuino, sed iure humano: quia in ordinatione dicta Dei generali nulla res temporalis specificatur: sic licet ex ordinatione Dei generali teneantur fideles tribuere necessaria annunciantibus euangelium & aliis clericis officio diuino insistentibus: tamen propter hoc illa quæ dantur eis, non dicuntur possideri iure diuino, sed iure humano: quia ex voluntate humana processit quod ista temporalia & non alia ipsis data fuerunt. Et ita talia possidentur à clericis iure humano. Iterum licet ex ordinatione Dei teneantur fideles annunciantibus euangelium & aliis clericis necessaria ministrare: non tamen tenentur eis temporalium conferre dominium, sed sufficeret eis ad implendum dictum præceptum diuinum eis absq; dominio necessaria elargiri. Quod autem in eos temporalium translulerunt aliquale dominium, hoc in principio ex voluntate conferentium dependebat: & post quantum ad aliquas res temporales ex iure humano summorum pontificum & generalium conciliorum extitit institutum. Et ita clerici quicquid possident, iure humano possident: quia Deus nec in speciali nec in communi dedit vllum denarium clericis, licet ordinauerit quod fideles eis debeant necessaria ministrare. Est tamen sciendum, quod sicut dicit Glossa dist. 8. cap. quo iure, ius diuinum quandoq; sumitur pro iure canonico: & sic concedendum est, quod aliquid possidetur à clericis iure diuino: sed sic modo non loquimur in iure diuino, quo etiam Pagani possederint, ab illo tempore iure diuino, sed humano, quarumcunq; rerum dominium, non est necesse probare, cum non appareat, quod Deus aliquid dederit eis in speciali, nisi sicut solem suum oriri facit super bonos & malos. Patet ergo quod post promulgationem euangelii & euacuationem legalium omnia noua temporalia dominia à iure humano fuerunt, & non à iure diuino; nisi sicut omnia dominia sunt à iure diuino: quia omne ius humanum in præceptis diuinis generalibus continetur.
units.tr: The third conclusion is that after the promulgation of the gospel and the abrogation of all the legal provisions, new private dominions over temporal goods came by human law and not by divine law, nor by any special bestowal of God. This is proved thus. From that time neither Jews, nor Christians, nor pagans possessed anything newly by divine law. Therefore from then on there was no new dominion by divine law, since all were then Jews, Christians or pagans. That the Jews did not then newly possess anything by divine law is clear, because no possessions were newly held by divine law by the Jews other than those acquired by the command of divine Scripture; but those commands had already ceased. Therefore they newly possessed nothing by divine law. That the Christians also did not newly possess anything by divine law is clear, because they acquired dominion over no particular thing by a special bestowal of God, since in the whole New Testament it is not read that God gave any temporal thing to Christians as a particular dominion, unless you say that Christ fed the crowds. But from this it does not follow that after the promulgation of the gospel and the abrogation of the legal provisions He gave anything specially to Christians. Nor from the fact that He fed the crowds does it follow that He gave them dominion over the loaves and fishes, since He gave them the said loaves and fishes only to eat. But perhaps you will say that clerics acquire dominion over things by divine law, because stipends are due to them from the New Testament, Christ saying in Luke 10: The labourer is worthy of his hire. And the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 9: Who goeth a warfare any time at his own charges? And in the same place: They which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar. Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel. From these words it is given to understand that by divine ordinance temporal stipends are due to those who proclaim the gospel. Therefore they possessed temporal things by divine law. To this they reply that this ordinance of God is a general ordinance, determining no particular temporal thing; and indeed, because of such a general ordinance, things are not said to be possessed by divine law, in the sense in which we are now speaking. For just as, although by the general ordinance of God the rich ought to give alms to the poor, yet the alms given to the poor are not said to be possessed by divine law but by human law, because in that general ordinance of God no temporal thing is specified: so, although by the general ordinance of God the faithful are bound to furnish necessities to those who proclaim the gospel and to other clerics devoted to divine office, yet on account of this the things given to them are not said to be possessed by divine law but by human law, because it came from human will that these temporal things and no others were given to them. And so such things are possessed by clerics by human law. Again, although by the ordinance of God the faithful are bound to supply necessities to those who proclaim the gospel and to other clerics, yet they are not bound to confer on them dominion over temporal things; rather, to fulfil the said divine precept it would suffice to bestow on them the necessities without dominion. As for the fact that the givers transferred some kind of dominion over temporal things to them, this at the beginning depended on the will of the givers; and afterwards, as to certain temporal things, it was established by the human law of the supreme pontiffs and of general councils. And so whatever clerics possess, they possess by human law, because God has given no penny to clerics, either particularly or in general, although He ordained that the faithful should supply them with necessities. It must be known, however, that, as the Gloss says in dist. 8, cap. quo iure, divine law is sometimes taken to mean canon law; and so it must be granted that something is possessed by clerics by divine law; but in this sense we are not now speaking of divine law. As for what the pagans possessed, from that time, by divine law, but by human law, of whatever things the dominion was, it is not necessary to prove, since it does not appear that God gave them anything in particular, except as He makes His sun rise on the good and the evil. It is clear, therefore, that after the promulgation of the gospel and the abrogation of the legal provisions, all new temporal dominions came by human law and not by divine law; unless, indeed, all dominions come by divine law, because all human law is contained in the general divine precepts.

units.la: Secundo ex prædictis dicunt isti impugnatores, quod quatuor errores in præmissa serie continentur. Quorum primus est, quod omne ius humanum quo temporalium dominia possidebantur, regum legibus continetur: secundum quod reges contra publicas alias potestates & rectores aliquid distinguuntur. Quod enim hoc dicat, patet expresse: cum per hoc, quod ante diluuium & post diluuium in populo Israelitico non fuerunt tales reges, probare nituntur: quod illa quæ tunc habebant & non possidebant iure humano, sed diuino. Sed quod hoc sit erroneum, patet aperte, quia illa sola dominia fuerunt à iure diuino, & non ab humano, quæ ex dono Dei speciali per specialem revelationem manifeste possessa fuerunt; sicut patet de spoliis, quæ de Ægyptiis tulerunt Hebræi, & de mulieribus aliis, de quibus in scriptura diuina fit mentio. Sed manifestum est quod Hebrei & alii multorum dominia iuste possederunt: quæ tamen ex dono Dei per specialem revelationem manifesto multiplicata possiderunt. Patet de Abel & Cain Gen. 4. Et de Abraham, qui iure emptionis possedit speluncam, in qua sepelivit uxorem suam. Iacob etiam per laborem suum & industriam multa acquisivit, ut patet Gen. 17. 30. 31. Hoc idem de Isaac, Ioseph aliisq; patribus veteris testamenti: & de paganis multis posset per scripturam diuinam copiose probari. Ergo ipsi talia possederunt iure humano: & tamen illa intra non continebantur in legibus regum. Ergo non omnia iura humana, quibus possidebantur temporalia continebantur in legibus regum. Secundus error est, quod omnia dominia, de quibus in sacra scriptura fit mentio, fuerunt à iure diuino, & non à iure humano. Quod enim hoc intelligatur, patet aperte, cum per hoc probetur aliqua possideri iure diuino, quia ius diuinum in scripturis sacris habemus, & in scripturis sacris habemus, quod aliqua possidebantur. Ex quo sequitur secundum eum, quod omnia dominia, de quibus in scriptura sacris fit mentio, fuerunt à iure diuino, non ab humano. Sed quod hoc sit erroneum, patet, quia de dominio Romanorum, & aliorum multo-tum rum paganorum in scriptura sacra fit mentio, & tamen eorum dominia fuerunt à iure humano, non diuino. Qualiter autem debeat auctoritas Augustini intelligi, quam ipse pro se allegat; super literam apparebit. Tertius error est, quod Adam antequam Eua formaretur, habuit dominium rerum temporalium, quod est proprietas, siue proprium. De isto errore dictum est supra cap. 26. & 27. & 28. Quartus error est, quod Adam antequam filios procrearet, habuit proprium dominium panis, quo vescebatur. Hoc probabiliter putant isti erroneum: quamuis hoc sufficienter nesciant demonstrare. Probabiliter tamen hoc tenent pro eo, quod non apparet ratio, quae potuisset mouere Adam ad appropriandum sibi panem, quo vescebatur, quo ad dominium: cum raro vel nunquam inter virum & vxorem, inter quos est saepe minor dilectio & concordia, quam fuerit inter Adam & Euam, talis appropriatio panis quo ad dominium fiat: & ita non videtur, quod Adam appropriauerit panem quo vescebatur, quo ad dominium, Euam ab eodem dominio excludendo. Tertio discarendo per litteram ad singulas auctoritates inductas respondent.
units.tr: Secondly, from the foregoing, these opponents say that four errors are contained in the above sequence. The first is that all human right by which temporal dominions were possessed is contained in the laws of kings, so that kings are distinguished from other public powers and rulers. That they say this is plain, since they try to prove, from the fact that there were no such kings among the people of Israel before or after the flood, that what they then held they possessed by divine right and not by human right. But that this is an error is clear, because only those dominions were from divine right and not from human right which were manifestly possessed through a special gift of God and a special revelation, as is plain of the spoils the Hebrews took from the Egyptians, and of the other women mentioned in Holy Scripture. Yet it is evident that the Hebrews and many others possessed dominions justly, which they nevertheless held, manifestly increased, through the gift of God by special revelation. This is plain of Abel and Cain, Gen. 4. And of Abraham, who possessed by right of purchase the cave in which he buried his wife. Jacob also acquired much by his labour and industry, as is plain from Gen. 17. 30. 31. The same holds of Isaac, Joseph and the other fathers of the Old Testament, and of many pagans, which could be proved at length from Holy Scripture. Therefore they possessed such things by human right, and yet those things were not contained in the laws of kings. Therefore not all human rights by which temporal goods were possessed are contained in the laws of kings. The second error is that all dominions mentioned in Holy Scripture were from divine right and not from human right. That this is what they mean is plain, since by this they prove that something is possessed by divine right, because we have divine right in the sacred Scriptures, and in the sacred Scriptures we have that certain things were possessed. From this it follows, according to them, that all dominions mentioned in Holy Scripture were from divine right and not from human. But that this is an error is clear, because Holy Scripture mentions the dominion of the Romans and of many other pagans, and yet their dominions were from human right and not divine. How the authority of Augustine, which they themselves allege, ought to be understood will become clear from the letter. The third error is that Adam, before Eve was formed, had dominion over temporal goods, which is property, or ownership. Concerning this error it was said above in chaps. 26, 27 and 28. The fourth error is that Adam, before he begat children, had proper dominion over the bread on which he fed. These men think this probably erroneous, although they do not know how to demonstrate it sufficiently. Yet they hold it probable, because there appears no reason that could have moved Adam to appropriate to himself as a matter of dominion the bread on which he fed, since such an appropriation of bread as dominion rarely or never happens between husband and wife, among whom there is often less love and harmony than there was between Adam and Eve; and so it does not seem that Adam appropriated the bread on which he fed as dominion, thereby excluding Eve from the same dominion. Thirdly, I answer by the letter to each of the authorities adduced.

units.la: (Quinimo iure diuino) Concedi potest sub uno sensu: quod omne dominium, iure diuino extitit introductum illomodo loquendo, quo dicit Apostolus Rom. 13. Non est potestas nisi à Deo. Sic nullum est dominium, nisi aliquomodo à iure diuino: quia à Deo est omne dominium. Sed sic non loquitur iste, cum distinguit inter dominia, quae sunt à iure diuino, & quae sunt à iure humano. Et ideo, quemadmodum dictum est, illud dominium dicitur hic esse à iure diuino, quod ex dono Dei per specialem reuelationem manifeste diuinam possidetur. Et sic non omnia dominia sunt à iure diuino. (Non humano fuerit dominium introductum) Ista negatiua est in omni sensu falsa, sicut probatum est supra: quia dominium proprium iure humano extitit primitus introductum. Unde qui tenet doctrinam Thomae, quid ipse dicat, aduertat. Ait enim, secunda secundae quaestione 44. Ar. 2. Secundum ius naturale non est distinctio possessionum, sed secundum humanum conditum, quod pertinet ad institutum, vt supra dictum est. Unde proprietas possessionum non est contra ius naturale, sed iuri naturali superadditur per inuentionem rationis humanae. Ergo secundum istum proprietas dominiorum per inuentionem rationis humanae extitit introducta. Ius enim diuinum est quod in scripturis diuinis habetur.) Non tamen omne ius, de quo in scripturis diuinis fit mentio, est ius diuinum: nisi sicut omnia iura diuina sunt, quia omne iustum est à Deo immediate vel mediate. (Vt legitur 8. dist. 6. quo iure) His ita respondetur: licet in lege & euangelio ius naturale contineatur, non tamen quaecunque in lege & euangelio continentur, naturali iuri cohaerere probantur. (Et humanum ius, quod in legibus regum) Istud fuit verum pro tempore Augustini, pro quo ipse contra haereticos sui temporis loquebatur: quia pro tempore illo cunctae nationes regibus subiectae fuerunt à nomine regum Imperatores nullatenus excludendo. Et ideo illo tempore omnia dominia temporalia iure Imperatorum vel regum possidebantur: sed pro multis aliis temporibus non habuit veritatem, nisi extendendo nomen regum ad omnes, qui super alios aliquam obtinent potestatem. Quod tamen forte in prima rerum diuisione non habuit veritatem: quia forte Cain & Abel absque auctoritate prioris, propria auctoritate inter se res aliquas diuiserunt, quemadmodum Abraham & Loth propria auctoritate, vt habetur Gen. 13. regiones inter se diuisisse videntur. Quod enim sic accipiendo stricte nomen Regum, humanum ius non semper fuerit in legibus regum, claret aperte: quia vnusquisque populus & ciuitas, vt habetur in decretis dist. 1. potest sibi ius proprium constituere. E. abeq; regibus possunt populi & ciuitates ac aliae communitates sibi iura humana constituere, constat multos populos & ciuitates fecisse. Unde & Romani aliquando regibus caruerunt; & tamen humanis legibus vtebantur: & etiam leges tunc secerunt humanas: & tunc eorum legib' aliqua possidebantur. (In scripturis autem diuinis habetur, quod antequam leges regum, imo etiam ante reges essent, res aliqua alicuius erat) Istud habet veritatem: quia ante tempora regum possidebantur aliqua res iure diuino, & aliqua iure humano, quaedam non iure regum. (E iure diuino aliquid dicere poterat aliquid suum esse) hoc est concedendum quis ex antecedente praecise sumpto non sequatur. Sed ex illa affirmatiua non sequitur ista negatiua: nihil tunc possidebatur iure humano. (Maior patet &c.) Ex maiore, cum vtraque sit affirmatiua, non sequitur haec negatiua: ante reges non fuit dominium introductum iure humano: nec etiam ex vi formae arguendi sequitur haec affirmatiua: ante reges poterat aliquis dicere aliquid esse suum iure diuino: quia praemissae non disponuntur in modo & figura, nec in aliqua forma debita arguendi: sicut exercitatis in principiis Dialecticis claret aperte. Quia tamen conclusio, quam vocaliter explicat, bene intellecta est vera, non oportet defectum argumenti exponere. (Solus fuit Adam dominium habuit.) Quamuis solus ante formationem Euae habuisset dominium, non tamen propter hoc fuisset proprium: sicut si omnes monachi alicuius monasterii morerentur praeter vnum, ipse solus tunc haberet dominium bonorum monasterii: & tamen illud dominium non esset proprium, sed commune, hoc est communicandum: nec ipse tunc esset proprietarius, sicut dictum est supra cap. 27. cum communio plures requirere dignoscatur, nisi à casu accidat impedimentum. Quod autem tunc formata Eua non esset, hoc dictum est supra cap. 27.) Constituit eum hominem vt dominaretur creaturae tuae &c.) Ibi accipitur homo tam pro masculo quam pro foemina: & ita ex illa auctoritate concludi non potest, quod Adam ante formationem Euae habuit dominium temporalium: & licet habuisset tunc dominium, tamen non habuisset tunc dominium, quod est proprietas.) Et hoc expresse dixit Damascenus) Ad hoc dictum est capitulo 27.) quod post lapsum primorum parentum ante diluuium & antequam essent reges potuit aliquis dicere hoc est meum) hoc est concedendum: sed ex hoc non sequitur, quod illud dominium non erat introductum iure humano, licet sequatur, quod introductum iure regum: nec appellans dicit, quod dominium erat primo introductum iure regum, sed quod erat introductum iure humano. Multa a . facerunt [illegible, ~6 letters] iure humano, quae non fuerunt iure regum. (Vesceris pane tuo) iste potius fuit Adae quo ad vsum & quo ad dominium commune aliquo modo: licet non quo ad dominium proprium sibi. (Obedite de primogenito ...) Iste gtex erat suus iure humano: licet non iure regum. (Quod post diluvium sine iure regum potuerit aliquis dicere suum) Hoc concedendum est: quia tunc etiam iure humano poterat aliquis dicere aliquid esse suum.
