(Noe vineam plantavit: illa vinea erat Noe) Licet forte non propria sibi sine iure regum, & forte sine iure humano: cum hoc tamen stat, quod prima dominiorum divisio fuit facta voluntate humana. (Semini tuo dabo terram hanc) Ex quo sequitur evidenter, quod dominium aliquarum rerum temporalium iure Divino absq; iure humano extitit introductum, sed illud non erat primum dominium proprium. (Tibi & semini tuo dabo universas regiones has) Ad istam auctoritatem respondetur, sicut ad priorem. (Uniuscuiusq; quod in praeda raperat suum erat) Ex hoc bene sequitur, quod illa dominia non erant per iura regum. (Ego dedi vobis in possessionem quam dissidetis vobis forte) Sicut in praecedente concedendum est, quod illa dominia non erant per iura regum. (Dent Levitis de possessionibus suis) Conceditur, quod illae possessiones non possidebantur legibus regum: cum hoc tamen stat, quod prima dominiorum divisio iure humano extitit introducta. (Ex quibus omnibus patet, quod in scripturis sacris habemus quod aliquis & in statu innocentiae & post lapsum primorum parentum: & post diluvium dicere poterat sine iure regum aliquid esse suum) Ista conclusio habet sensum verum, quia in statu innocentiae poterat Adam dicere, sine iure regum aliquid esse suum, quo ad potestatem vendi, & quo ad dominium. Post peccatum vero primorum parentum sine iure regum poterat aliquis dicere aliquid esse suum quo ad usum & quo ad dominium aliquo modo commune, scilicet tam Adam quam Eus. Alius vero sine iure regum poterat dicere aliquid esse suum quo ad dominium proprium iure humano introductum. Post diluvium aliqui poterant sine iure regum dicere res aliquas esse suas iure divino: & aliqui poterant dicere res aliquas esse suas iure humano, & tamen sine iure regum. Et ita patet, quod ista conclusio in nihilo assertioni derogat appellantis: quia ipse non intendit, quod omnis dominiorum divisio fuit introducta iure regum, ut reges contra potestatis alias distinguuntur. Sed intendit, quod prima dominiorum divisio fuit introducta iure humano sive iure regum sic nomine sumpto. Postea vero aliqua dominia iure divino introducta fuerunt. Tempore vero Beati Augustini omnia dominia fuerunt a iure regum comprehendendo Imperatores sub nomine regum. Et tunc omnes regiones regibus subiectae fuerunt. Et ita si iste sciret dominia & tempora distinguere, posset concordare scripturas. (Quod de iure Divino sint dominia aliqua probatur 23. q. 7. c. 1.) Dictum capitulum hic male allegatur. Verba enim dicti capituli, ex quibus poterat accipi assertio supradicta, sunt haec: Quaecunque res quaecunque, terrena non ratione a quoquam possideri possunt nisi vel iure divino, quae cuncta iustorum sunt: vel iure humano, quod in potestate est regum. In his autem verbis non habetur, quod aliqua dominia sint iure Divino: quia tunc secundum verba praedicta cuncta essent iustorum quo ad dominium, quod tamen falsum est, quia si cuncta essent iustorum, quoad dominium, alii non haberent in his iustum dominium: quod falsum est. Non ergo intendit Augustinus, quod iure Divino cuncta sint iustorum quo ad dominium: sed intendit quod iure Divino cuncta sunt iustorum, quo ad dignitatem habendi. Hoc est, iusti digni sunt omnibus: impii nullis rebus sunt digni, licet multarum rerum habeant verum & iustum dominium, quo tamen iusto dominio sunt indigni.
units.tr: (Indeed, by divine right) This may be granted in one sense: every lordship has been introduced by divine right, speaking in the way the Apostle does in Rom. 13, There is no power but of God. In that sense there is no lordship that does not in some way come from divine right, because all lordship is from God. But this author does not speak in that sense when he distinguishes between lordships that are from divine right and those that are from human right. So, as has been said, the lordship here called one from divine right is the one that is held through a gift of God, by a special and manifestly divine revelation. Not all lordships are therefore from divine right. (It was not introduced by human right) This negative is false in every sense, as was proved above, because private lordship was first introduced by human right. Whoever holds the teaching of Thomas should note what he himself says, in secunda secundae, question 44, article 2: By the natural law there is no distinction of possessions, but it arises from human convention, which belongs to institution, as was said above. So the ownership of possessions is not against the natural law, but is added to the natural law by the invention of human reason. Therefore, according to him, the ownership of lordships was introduced by the invention of human reason. (For divine law is what is contained in the divine Scriptures.) Yet not every law that is mentioned in the divine Scriptures is divine law, except in the sense that all divine laws are such because all that is just is from God, immediately or mediately. (As is read in dist. 6, quo iure) To this it is answered: although the natural law is contained in the law and the gospel, not everything contained in the law and the gospel is shown to belong to the natural law. (And human law, which is in the laws of kings) This was true in the time of Augustine, for whom he himself was speaking against the heretics of his time, since in that time all nations were subject to kings, without excluding emperors under the name of kings. So in that time all temporal lordships were possessed by the right of emperors or kings. But for many other times it was not true, unless the name of kings is extended to all who hold some power over others. Yet perhaps even this was not true in the first division of things, since perhaps Cain and Abel divided some things between themselves on their own authority, without the authority of a superior, just as Abraham and Lot seem, on their own authority, to have divided the regions between themselves, as is recorded in Gen. 13. That, taking the name of kings strictly, human law has not always been in the laws of kings, is clear: for every people and city, as is found in dist. 1 of the Decretals, can establish its own law. Therefore peoples, cities and other communities can establish human laws for themselves without kings; it is established that many peoples and cities have done so. Hence the Romans too were at times without kings, and yet they used human laws, and they then made human laws, and some things were then possessed under their laws. (But in the divine Scriptures it is found that before the laws of kings, indeed even before there were kings, some thing belonged to someone) This is true, for before the time of kings some things were possessed by divine right, and some by human right, and some not by the right of kings. (From divine right one could say that something was one's own) This must be granted, provided one does not infer from the antecedent taken alone. But from that affirmative the negative does not follow: that nothing was then possessed by human right. (The major is clear, etc.) From the major premise, since both are affirmative, this negative does not follow: that before the kings no lordship was introduced by human right. Nor, from the force of the form of argument, does this affirmative follow: that before the kings someone could say that something was his by divine right, because the premises are not arranged in the right mode and figure, nor in any proper form of argument, as is clear to those practised in the principles of dialectic. Yet because the conclusion which he expresses in words is true when rightly understood, there is no need to expose the defect of the argument. (Adam alone had lordship) Although before the forming of Eve Adam alone would have had lordship, it would not for that reason have been private. It would be like this: if all the monks of a monastery died except one, he alone would then hold the lordship of the goods of the monastery; yet that lordship would not be private but common, that is, to be shared, and he himself would then not be a proprietor, as was said above in chapter 27, since community is known to require several persons, unless an accident prevents it. That Eve was not yet formed at that time was said above in chapter 27. (He appointed him man to have dominion over your creatures, etc.) Here "man" is taken both for the male and for the female. So from that authority it cannot be concluded that Adam had lordship over temporal things before Eve was formed; and even if he had lordship at that time, he would not then have had lordship that is ownership. (And Damascene expressly said this) To this it was answered in chapter 27. (that after the fall of our first parents, before the flood and before there were kings, someone could say, this is mine) This must be granted; but it does not follow from this that that lordship was not introduced by human right, although it does follow that it was not introduced by the right of kings. Nor does the appellant say that lordship was first introduced by the right of kings, but that it was introduced by human right. Many things were made [illegible] by human right which were not by the right of kings. (Eat of your bread) This rather belonged to Adam in use, and in some way in common lordship, though not as private lordship to himself. (Obey the firstborn ...) This flock was his by human right, though not by the right of kings. (That after the flood someone could call something his without the right of kings) This must be granted, because then also by human right someone could call something his. (Noah planted a vineyard: that vineyard was Noah's) Perhaps it was not his as private property without the right of kings, and perhaps not without human right; yet it is consistent with this that the first division of lordships was made by human will. (To your seed I will give this land) From this it evidently follows that lordship over some temporal things was introduced by divine right without human right, but that was not the first private lordship. (To you and your seed I will give all these regions) To this authority the answer is the same as to the earlier one. (What each man seized in the spoil was his) From this it rightly follows that those lordships were not by the laws of kings. (I have given you a possession which you did not labour for) As in the preceding case, it must be granted that those lordships were not by the laws of kings. (Let them give to the Levites from their own possessions) It is granted that those possessions were not held by the laws of kings, though it is consistent with this that the first division of lordships was introduced by human right. (From all these things it is clear that in the sacred Scriptures we have that someone, both in the state of innocence and after the fall of our first parents, and after the flood, could say without the right of kings that something was his) This conclusion has a true sense, for in the state of innocence Adam could say, without the right of kings, that something was his, as to the power of selling and as to lordship. But after the sin of our first parents, without the right of kings someone could say that something was his as to use and as to lordship held in some way in common, namely both Adam and Eve. Another, without the right of kings, could say that something was his as to private lordship introduced by human right. After the flood some could say without the right of kings that certain things were theirs by divine right, and some could say that certain things were theirs by human right, and yet without the right of kings. So it is clear that this conclusion in no way detracts from the appellant's assertion, for he does not mean that every division of lordships was introduced by the right of kings, as kings are distinguished from other powers. But he means that the first division of lordships was introduced by human right, or by the right of kings, taking the name in that sense. Later, however, some lordships were introduced by divine right. In the time of Blessed Augustine all lordships were by the right of kings, including emperors under the name of kings; and then all regions were subject to kings. So if this man knew how to distinguish lordships and times, he could agree with the Scriptures. (That some lordships are by divine right is proved in 23, q. 7, c. 1.) The cited chapter is wrongly alleged here. For the words of that chapter, from which the above assertion could be taken, are these: Whatever thing, whatever earthly thing, can be possessed by anyone not by reason, except either by divine right, which all belong to the just, or by human right, which is in the power of kings. But in these words it is not said that some lordships are by divine right, for then according to the words quoted everything would belong to the just as regards lordship; which is false, for if everything belonged to the just as regards lordship, others would not have just lordship over these things, which is false. Augustine therefore did not mean that by divine right everything belongs to the just as regards lordship, but he meant that by divine right everything belongs to the just as regards the worthiness of having. That is, the just are worthy of all things; the impious are worthy of no things, although they have true and just lordship over many things, yet they are unworthy of that just lordship.

units.la: CAP. LXXXIX.
units.tr: CHAP. LXXXIX.

units.la: ADhuc quod nullo iure humano, sed solum Divino dominium temporalium rerum potuerit hominibus dari, patet. Constat enim quod rem aliquam aliquis dare non potest, nisi cuius est, vel alius eius voluntate. Nec est dubium, quin Deus omnium temporalium, vel iure creationis (quia ille e nihilo creavit) vel iure factionis, quia de sua materia illa fecerat, dominus esset. Ergo nullus rex de illarum dominio, nisi de voluntate Dei, potuit ordinare. Unde patet, quod nec, iure naturali primaevo, si ponatur pro illo iure, quod omnibus animantibus est commune, tamen illud non nihil statuat, sed inclinat, seu dirigat ad alia omnibus animantibus communia facienda. Nec iure gentium, nec iure regum seu Imperatorum fuit dominium temporalium rerum introductum: sed per dominium, quia erat & earum rerum dominus, fuit collatum primis parentibus, ut patet Genes. 1. Quarum rerum Adam quamdiu solus fuit, id est, antequam Eva formaretur, solus, ut videtur, Dominus extitit, ut superius est ostensum.
units.tr: That dominion over temporal things could be given to men by no human right, but by Divine right alone, is also clear. For it is established that no one can give a thing unless it belongs to him, or unless another gives it with his will. And there is no doubt that God was lord of all temporal things, either by the right of creation (since he created them out of nothing) or by the right of making (since he had made them from his own matter). Therefore no king could ordain anything concerning their dominion except by the will of God. Hence it is clear that not even by the primeval natural right, if that right is taken to be the one common to all living creatures, does it establish that, but rather it inclines or directs them toward doing other things common to all living creatures. Dominion over temporal things was introduced neither by the law of nations nor by the right of kings or emperors. Rather, dominion was conferred on our first parents, because God himself was also lord of those things, as is clear from Gen. 1. While Adam was alone, that is, before Eve was formed, he alone, as it seems, remained lord of those things, as was shown above.

units.la: In parte ista ostendit, quod rerum dominium temporalium nullo iure humano potuit dari hominibus, sed iure Divino tantum modo. Et est ratio talis: Deus est Dominus omnium rerum: ergo solus Deus vel aliquis de voluntate eius potuit dominium temporalium dare hominibus.
units.tr: In this part he shows that dominion over temporal things could not be given to men by any human right, but only by Divine right. The argument is this: God is the lord of all things; therefore God alone, or someone by his will, could give dominion over temporal things to men.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, quod iste hic caquillose procedit, & in nihilo tangit mentem appellantis: quia non intendit appellans, quod dominium temporale commune primo fuit a iure humano, sed intendit quod prima dominiorum divisio est a iure humano. Ratio autem istius procedit de dominio communi primo dato hominibus, & ita nullatenus est contra appellantem.
units.tr: But these opponents say that this argument proceeds in a captious manner and touches nothing in the mind of the appellant. For the appellant does not mean that common dominion over temporal things was first derived from human right, but that the first division of dominions was derived from human right. The argument, however, concerns the common dominion first given to men, and so it is in no way against the appellant.

units.la: (Solum Divino, scilicet iure dominium temporalium rerum potuerit hominibus dari) Istud non habet veritatem de omni dominio: quia tunc modo, nullus posset licite transferre dominium alicuius vel in alium, nisi sibi Deus revelaret, quod hoc sibi placeret, quod est erroneum. Si ergo habet veritatem de dominio primo dato hominibus debet intelligi: sed illud dominium fuit commune, non proprium. (Confiteatur enim quod rem aliquam aliquis dare non potest, nisi cuius est.)
units.tr: (That dominion over temporal things could be given to men by Divine right alone.) This is not true of every dominion, for then no one could lawfully transfer the dominion of anything to himself or to another, unless God revealed to him that this pleased him, which is erroneous. If therefore it is true of the first dominion given to men, it must be understood thus: but that dominion was common, not private. (For it is granted that no one can give a thing unless it is his.)

units.la: {y} marginal line numbers 5 to 60 printed in left margin. Hoc verum est, quando vnus solus est dominus rei: sed quando plures sunt domini, licet vnus principalis, & alius minus principalis seu secundarius, non est verum. Et ideo quando solus Deus erat rerum temporalium Dominus, nullus potuit eas dare hominibus, nisi Deus vel voluntate Dei: sed postquam homines primi effecti fuerunt aliquo modo domini in communi temporalium rerum, potuerunt post peccatum illas res dare & inter se diuidere. Et ita prima collatio temporalium facta hominibus fuit a solo Deo: sed diuisio earundem quo ad dominia fuit a iure humano. (Vel alium eius voluntate) hic innuit, quod aliquis potest dare rem, cuius non habet dominium. Ex quo sequitur, quod aliquis potest dare pecuniam, cuius non habet dominium: & per consequens potest uti pecunia, cuius non habet dominium: quod alibi negat. (Ergo nullus rex de illarum dominio nisi de voluntate Dei potuit ordinare.) Verum est, quod omnia fiunt de voluntate Dei iubente vel permittente: sed non est ad propositum. (Nec iure gentium nec iure regum, seu imperatorum fuit dominium verum temporalium introductum.) Istud verum de communi dominio, quod datum fuit omnibus in primis parentibus: de dominiis propriis non est verum, nec sequitur nisi sophistice ex praemissis. (Solus, ut videtur, Dominus existit) Hoc non probat sufficienter. (Ut superius est ostensum) sed sophistice.
units.tr: {y} Marginal line numbers 5 to 60 are printed in the left margin. This is true when one person alone is the lord of a thing; but when there are several lords, although one is principal and another less principal or secondary, it is not true. And therefore, when God alone was lord of temporal things, no one could give them to men except God or by the will of God; but after the first men had become in some way lords in common of temporal things, they could, after sin, give those things and divide them among themselves. And so the first conferring of temporal things on men was made by God alone, but the division of them as to dominions was by human right. (Or by another with his will.) Here he hints that someone can give a thing of which he has no dominion. From this it follows that someone can give money of which he has no dominion, and consequently can use money of which he has no dominion, which he denies elsewhere. (Therefore no king could ordain concerning their dominion except by the will of God.) It is true that all things happen by the will of God commanding or permitting, but this is not to the point. (Nor by the law of nations, nor by the right of kings or emperors, was true temporal dominion introduced.) This is true of the common dominion which was given to all in the first parents; it is not true of private dominions, nor does it follow except sophistically from the premises. (Only, as it seems, the Lord exists.) This does not prove sufficiently, but sophistically. (As was shown above.)

units.la: CAP. XC.
units.tr: CAP. XC.

units.la: VErum est tamen, quod de iure gentium multi modi acquirendi dominium, & nonnulli per iura civilia seu Imperialia fuerunt introducti. Item, modus agendi pro istis rebus temporalibus in iudicio, id est, forma certa proponendi ius suum in iudicio, fuit per iura civilia introductum.
units.tr: It is true, however, that by the law of nations many modes of acquiring dominion were introduced, and some by civil or imperial law. Likewise, the manner of proceeding in court for these temporal things, that is, a fixed form of setting out one's right in judgment, was introduced by civil law.

units.la: In parte ista ostenditur, quid per ius humanum circa rerum dominium est introductum: dicens, quod modi acquirendi dominium, & modus agendi pro temporalibus in iudicio humano inducti fuerunt.
units.tr: In this part it is shown what has been introduced by human law concerning the dominion of things, saying that the modes of acquiring dominion, and the modes of pleading for temporal things in human judgment, were brought in.

units.la: Omnia quae hic dicuntur, sunt pure affirmativa, & pure affirmatiue intellecta continent veritatem: licet si intelligentur negative, essent erronea iudicanda. Ideo isti impugnatores ista hoc nequaquam repugnant.
units.tr: All the things said here are purely affirmative, and, understood purely affirmatively, they contain the truth, although, if they were understood negatively, they would have to be judged erroneous. Therefore these opponents by no means contradict them.

units.la: (Multi modi acquirendi dominium: & nonnulli per iura civilia seu Imperialia fuerunt inducti.) Ex hoc patet, quod ius civile aliud quam formulas agendi in iudicio introduxit: cuius oppositum iste dicet in parte sequenti: cum extra iudicium multis modis per ius civile inductis rerum acquiratur dominium. Nam per usucapionem & praescriptionem per ius civile inductas ante omne iudicium acquiritur dominium temporalium rerum: & ita iste sibiipsi contradicit aperte.
units.tr: (Many modes of acquiring dominion, and some were introduced by civil or imperial law.) From this it is plain that civil law introduced something other than mere forms of proceeding in court, the opposite of which this man will say in the following part, since dominion over things is acquired outside of judgment by many modes introduced by civil law. For dominion over temporal things is acquired before any judgment, through usucapion and prescription, which are introduced by civil law; and so this man openly contradicts himself.

units.la: CAP. XCI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XCI.

units.la: EX praedictis itaque patet, quod non obstat capitulum Quo iure, in contrarium allegatum. Loquitur enim de iure agendi in iudicio, cuius formulas civile ius, & non aliud introduxit. Et hoc voluit dicere Augustinus in cap. Quo iure, quando dixit: Tolle iura Imperatorum: & quid debet dicere: haec villa mea est: meus est iste servus: mea est haec domus? quasi diceret, nullus potest in iudicio proponere hoc, nisi per Imperatoria iura: quod ius actionum formulas introduxit. Vel potest dici, quod hoc dicebat Augustinus cum haereticis disputando, non quod hoc pro veritate teneret, scilicet quod dominium de iure Diuino non esset. Et quod ita sit, patet. Quia 22. quaest. 7. cap. 1. ipse idem Augustinus contrarium dixit expresse, vbi sic dicit: Quamuis res quaecunque terrena non recte a quocunque possideri possit, nisi vel iure Diuino, quo cuncta iustorum sunt: vel iure humano, quod in potestate est regum terrae &c.
units.tr: From what has been said it follows that the chapter Quo iure, cited against us, is no obstacle. For it speaks of the right of bringing an action in court, whose forms civil law, and nothing else, introduced. This is what Augustine meant in chap. Quo iure, when he said: Take away the laws of the Emperors: and what should one say: this farm is mine, this slave is mine, this house is mine? As if he were saying that no one can put this forward in court except by Imperial laws, which introduced the forms of actions. Or it can be said that Augustine said this in disputing with heretics, not because he held it to be true, namely that dominion is not by divine right. That this is so is clear. For in 22. quaest. 7. cap. 1. the same Augustine expressly said the contrary, where he writes: Although no earthly thing can rightly be possessed by anyone, unless either by divine right, by which all things belong to the just, or by human right, which is in the power of the kings of the earth, etc.

units.la: In ista parte respondet ad authoritates pro assertione contraria allegatas. Et primo ad primam. Secundo ad secundam in parte immediate sequenti: Item, non obstat. Prima potest diuidi in duas, scilicet cum dum quod duas responsiones ponit. Secunda ibi: Vel potest dici. Est autem prima responsio haec: quod Augustinus loquitur de iure agendi, cuius formulas ius civile, & non aliud introduxit. Secunda est, quod Augustinus loquitur tantummodo disputando, & non secundum intentionem.
units.tr: In this part he answers the authorities alleged for the contrary assertion. First he answers the first, and secondly the second, in the part immediately following: Likewise, it is no obstacle. The first can be divided into two, since he gives two answers. The second begins at: Or it can be said. The first answer is this: that Augustine speaks of the right of acting in court, whose forms civil law, and nothing else, introduced. The second is that Augustine speaks only by way of dispute, and not according to his own intention.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, quod iste dupliciter errat. Primo in hoc, quod dicit ius civile formulas actionum, & non aliud induxisse. Secundo in hoc, quod dicit Augustinum praedicta verba non dixisse tanquam vera. Quod enim primum sit erroneum, manifeste ostenditur. Ad cuius evidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod ius civile, ut notat Glossa di. 1. & ius civile, multipliciter accipitur: quia quandoque dicitur ius civile, illud ius, quod non est naturale, vel ius gentium: sed hoc modo ius canonicum dicitur ius civile. Secundo modo dicitur ius civile, omne illud quod non est ius canonicum. Tertio modo ius civile, dicitur ius 12. tabularum. Quarto modo dicitur ius civile, ad differentiam iuris praetorii. Licet autem accipitur ius civile pro iure humano, quod non est canonicum, quamuis appellans, si diceret dominium esse a iure civili, acciperet magis large ius civile, scilicet pro iure humano. Sic ergo accipiendo ius civile, scilicet pro iure humano, quamuis non sit canonicum, erroneum est dicere, quod ius civile nihil nisi formulas actionum induxit: quod scripturae Diuinae contradicit aperte. Nam primo Regum cap. 30. sic habetur: Aequa enim pars erit descendentis ad proelium & remanentis ad sarcinas, & similiter diuident. Et factum est hoc ex illa die: & deinceps constitutum est & praefinitum, & quasi lex in Israel usque ad diem hanc. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod per illius praedictum constitutum a Dauid remanentibus ad sarcinas portio praedae exiit acquisita. Ergo non tantum formulae actionum, sed etiam rerum diuisio per ius civile, quod Dauid rex constituit, fuit inducta. Item, Gen. 47. sic scribitur: Ex eo enim tempore vsq; in praesentem diem in vsuer sa terra Aegypti regibus quinta pars soluitur, & factum est quasi in legem, absq; terra sacerdotali, qua libera ab hac conditione fuit. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod per legem institutam ex ordinatione & sapientia Ioseph Regibus Aegypti quinta pars acquirebatur. Ergo lex illa non tantum formulas actionum, sed etiam dominium quintae partis induxit. Quod rerum dominia etiam extra iudicium iure humano acquirantur, testatur expresse Isidorus: qui, vt habetur in decretis dist. 1. ait: Ius gentium est sedium occupatio, aedificatio, munitio, bella, captiuitates, seruitutes, postliminia. Ex quibus verbis habetur, q iure gentiu non solum formulae actionu, sed etiam sedium occupationes, seruitutes & postliminia sunt inducta. Item, vt ibidem habetur, idem Isidorus ait: Ius militare est belli inferendi solemnitas. Et infra: Item, praeda diuisio & pro personarum laboribus & qualitatibus ipsa diuisio, ac principis portio. Ergo iure militari, quod est ius humanum, non tantum formulae actionum, sed etiam praedae diuisio & portio principis sunt inducta. Item, sicut dictum est supra, vsucapiones & praescriptiones per iura ciuilia sunt inducta. Sed per vsucapiones, & praescriptiones rerum dominia acquiruntur. Ergo per iura ciuilia aliud quam formulas actionum inducitur.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he errs in two ways. First in saying that civil law introduced only the forms of actions and nothing else. Secondly in saying that Augustine did not say those words as true. That the first point is mistaken is plainly shown. For its clarity they say it must be known that civil law, as the Gloss notes on dist. 1, and civil law, is taken in several senses. Sometimes civil law means that law which is not natural law or the law of nations; and in this sense canon law is called civil law. In a second sense, civil law means everything that is not canon law. In a third sense, civil law means the law of the Twelve Tables. In a fourth sense, civil law is contrasted with praetorian law. Now if civil law is taken for human law which is not canonical, then, although one who says that dominion comes from civil law would be using the term more broadly, namely for human law, it is nonetheless mistaken, when civil law is so taken, to say that civil law introduced nothing but the forms of actions. This clearly contradicts Divine Scripture. For in 1 Kings 30 it is written thus: For as his part is that goes down to the battle, so shall his part be that tarrieth by the stuff: they shall share alike. And it was so from that day forward; he made it a statute and an ordinance for Israel, and it has continued to this day. From these words it is evident that by that ordinance made by David, the portion of the spoil was acquired by those who remained with the baggage. Therefore not only the forms of actions but also the division of goods was introduced by the civil law which King David established. Likewise Genesis 47 is written thus: For from that time until this day, in the land of Egypt, a fifth part is paid to the kings, and it became a law, except the land of the priests, which was free from this condition. From these words it is plainly had that by the law instituted through the ordinance and wisdom of Joseph, a fifth part was acquired by the kings of Egypt. Therefore that law introduced not only the forms of actions but also the dominion of the fifth part. That rights of dominion are acquired even outside court by human law is expressly attested by Isidore, who, as is found in the Decretum dist. 1, says: The law of nations is the occupation of places, building, fortification, wars, captivities, servitudes, and rights of return. From these words it is had that by the law of nations not only the forms of actions but also the occupation of places, servitudes and rights of return were introduced. Likewise, as is found in the same place, Isidore says: Military law is the solemnity of waging war. And below: Likewise, the division of booty, and the division itself according to the labours and qualities of persons, and the portion of the prince. Therefore by military law, which is human law, not only the forms of actions but also the division of booty and the portion of the prince were introduced. Likewise, as was said above, usucaptions and prescriptions were introduced by civil laws. But by usucaptions and prescriptions the dominion of things is acquired. Therefore through civil laws something other than the forms of actions is introduced.

units.la: Secundo dicunt, quod errat, cum dicit Augustinum dixisse verba praedicta non quod ea pro veritate teneret, sed tantum modo cum haereticis disputando: Nam si Augustinus dixit illa verba cum haereticis disputando: aut accipit ipsa tanquam falsa simpliciter, aut tanquam vera, aut tanquam falsa tamen ab eis concessa, aut tanquam dubia. Si accepit ipsa contra haereticos tanquam falsa simpliciter, per ipsa non potuit eos convincere: & ita inaniter laborauit. Si accepit ea tanquam vera, habetur intentum: quod dicat ea tanquam tenens ipsa pro veris. Si accepit ea tanquam falsa, tamen concessa ab haereticis, hoc est omnino falsum: quia haeretici contra quos disputauit Augustinus, ipsa non reputauerunt vera, cum ipsi dixerunt, vt recitat Augustinus ibidem: Quid nobis & Imperatori? quasi dicerent, res nostras ab Imperatoribus non tenemur: Ergo ipsi illa verba minime concedebant. Nec accepit ea Augustinus tanquam dubia: quia tunc per ipsa haereticos minime conuincisset, sed inaniter laborasset, & ita Augustinus verba praedicta tanquam vera, cum ipsa acceperit, non tanquam dicta ab aliis recitando, sed simpliciter asserendo.
units.tr: Secondly they say that he errs when he says that Augustine spoke the aforesaid words not because he held them to be true, but only in disputing with heretics. For if Augustine said those words in disputing with heretics, he either took them simply as false, or as true, or as false yet conceded by them, or as doubtful. If he took them against the heretics simply as false, he could not have convinced them by them, and so he would have laboured in vain. If he took them as true, the point is gained: that he says them as one holding them to be true. If he took them as false yet conceded by the heretics, this is wholly false, because the heretics against whom Augustine disputed did not regard them as true, since they said, as Augustine recites in the same place: What have we to do with the Emperor? as if to say, we do not hold our goods from the Emperors. Therefore they by no means granted those words. Nor did Augustine take them as doubtful, for then he would not have convicted the heretics by them at all, but would have laboured in vain. And so Augustine, having taken the aforesaid words as true, did not state them as things said by others, but asserted them simply in his own voice.

units.la: (Loquitur enim de iure agendi in iudicio.) Verum est, quod loquitur de iure agendi, cum dicit, Quo iure defendis villas Ecclesiae? Et etiam loquitur de iure possidendi, cum dicit, unde quisque possidet quod possidet: nonne iure humano? (Cuius formulas in ciuile, & non aliud introduxit.) Affirmatiua est vera: sed negatiua est erronea, quia ius ciuile etiam rerum dominia introduxit. (Quis audet dicere.) Scilicet in iudicio, vel extra iudicium, quasi diceret, nullus: quia, tolle iura Imperatoris: & quis (ex conscientia extra iudicium) audeat dicere hoc villa mea est? quasi dicat, nullus potest in iudicio proponere hoc, nisi per Imperatoria iura. Ex ista negatiua sequitur alia negatiua, scilicet quod nullus potest extra iudicium veraciter dicere: Hoc est meum, quo ad dominium, nisi per iura Imperatoria. Et ita per iura Imperatoria, non tantum formulae actionum, sed etiam vera dominia inducta fuerunt. (Quod ius gentium introduxit.) Ista affirmatiua est vera: & etiam ista, quod ius multarum rerum dominia introduxit. (Non quod hoc pro veritate teneret.) Ista negatiua est falsa, sicut ostensum est. (Quod dominium de iure diuino non esset.) Istam negatiuam Augustinus non dixit, cum haereticis vt iste dicit, sicut expresse patet in 1. cap. Quo iure, sed dixit istam affirmatiuam iure Diuino: Dominii est terra &c. Et affirmatiue dixit omnia possideri iure humano: & ista affirmatiua; omnia possidentur iure humano, vera fuit tempore Augustini. Sed ante natiuitatem Christi non semper fuit vera: quia aliquando multa possidebantur iure diuino, & non iure humano. Ista autem negatiua, dominium non est de iure Diuino, tempore Augustini habuit vnum sensum verum, & alium falsum. Si enim intelligatur, quod dominium fuerit praecise a iure humano & nullo modo, nec mediate nec immediate a iure diuino, erronea est. Si autem intelligatur, quod dominium proprium alicuius rei non est a iure Diuino, hoc est, non habetur ex speciali dono Dei per reuelationem specialem manifestato: sic est modo verum, & fuit tempore Augustini, quod dominium non est sic iure a Diuino. Aliquando autem fuit hoc falsum. (Ipse idem Augustin. contrarium dicit expresse.) Falsum est, quia Augustin. ibidem de dominio nullam facit mentionem. (Non recte a quocunque possit possideri, nisi vel iure diuino.) Signanter loquitur Augustin. cum nota possibilitatis, nec ex verbis suis aliquis concluderet, quod de facto aliqua possidentur iure Diuino, non illo modo quo omnia a quocunque possidentur, iure Diuino possidentur, quo cuncta iustorum sunt: vnde dixit, sunt, & non dixit, possidentur. Si enim dixisset, quod cuncta possidentur a iustis, non esset ita apparens dictum Augustini, imo falsum. Nam omnia dicuntur esse iustorum, quia iusti digni (sunt omnibus) licet non omnia possideant: nec omnia sunt iustorum quo ad dominium & proprietatem, sed quo ad dignitatem habendi. Et ita Augustin. cum dixit, cuncta iustorum sunt, de dominio non loquitur. (Vel iure humano quod in potestate est regum terra &c.) quod tempore Augustini habuit veritatem, secundum mentem Augustini.
units.tr: (For he speaks of the right of acting in court.) It is true that he speaks of the right of acting, when he says: By what right do you defend the farms of the Church? And he also speaks of the right of possessing, when he says: Whence does each one possess what he possesses? Is it not by human right? (Whose forms civil law, and nothing else, introduced.) The affirmative is true, but the negative is mistaken, because civil law also introduced the dominion of things. (Who dares to say?) That is, in court or outside court, as if to say, no one: because, take away the laws of the Emperor, and who (in conscience, outside court) would dare to say, this farm is mine? As if to say, no one can put this forward in court except by Imperial laws. From this negative there follows another negative, namely that no one outside court can truly say, This is mine, as to dominion, except by Imperial laws. And so by Imperial laws not only the forms of actions but also true dominions were introduced. (Which the law of nations introduced.) This affirmative is true, and so is this, that human law introduced dominions over many things. (Not because he held this to be true.) This negative is false, as has been shown. (That dominion would not be by divine right.) Augustine did not say this negative to the heretics, as the opponent says, as is plainly clear in the first chapter, Quo iure; but he said this affirmative: The earth is the Lord's, etc., by divine right. And he affirmed that all things are possessed by human right; and this affirmative, that all things are possessed by human right, was true in Augustine's time. But before the birth of Christ it was not always true, since at times many things were possessed by divine right and not by human right. But this negative, that dominion is not by divine right, had one true sense and another false in Augustine's time. For if it is understood that dominion came solely from human right and in no way, neither mediately nor immediately, from divine right, it is mistaken. But if it is understood that the proper dominion of some thing is not from divine right, that is, is not had by special gift of God made manifest by special revelation, then it is now true, and was true in Augustine's time, that dominion is not so by divine right. At other times, however, this was false. (The same Augustine expressly says the contrary.) This is false, because Augustine in that place makes no mention of dominion at all. (Cannot rightly be possessed by anyone, unless either by divine right.) Augustine speaks pointedly with a mark of possibility, and no one could conclude from his words that some things are in fact possessed by divine right, not in that way in which all things are possessed by anyone by divine right, by which all things belong to the just. Hence he said are, and did not say are possessed. For if he had said that all things are possessed by the just, the words of Augustine would not appear so, but would indeed be false. For all things are said to belong to the just, because the just are worthy of all things (are worthy) although they do not possess all things; nor do all things belong to the just as to dominion and ownership, but as to the worthiness of having. And so Augustine, when he said all things belong to the just, is not speaking of dominion. (Or by human right, which is in the power of the kings of the earth, etc.) This, according to Augustine's meaning, had truth in Augustine's time.

units.la: CAP. XCII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XCII.

units.la: Item, non obstat 12. q. 1. c. dilectissimis, vbi dicitur sic: Communia vsus omnium, quae sunt in hoc mundo, omnibus esse hominibus debuit: sed per iniquitatem alius dixit hoc esse suum, alius istud. Et sic inter mortales facta est diuisio. Ex hoc dicit ipse, quod diuisio temporalium est facta per ius humanum, quod dicitur iniquum & contra aequitatem iuris naturalis. Dicimus quod hoc est falsum: quia per iniquitatem non intellexit ius gentium, cum sit aequum, sed intellexit peccatum primorum parentum, per quod natura corrupta fuit, & post non fuit contenta communibus, sed sibi propria voluit possidere.
units.tr: Likewise, the decree at 12 q. 1, c. dilectissimis, does not stand in the way, where it says: "The use of all things that are in this world ought to have been common to all men; but through iniquity one said that this was his, another that was his. And so division arose among mortals." From this he says that the division of temporal goods was made by human law, which is called unjust and contrary to the equity of natural law. We say that this is false, because by "iniquity" he did not mean the law of nations, since that is equitable, but the sin of our first parents, through which nature was corrupted, and afterwards was not content with things held in common but wished to possess things as its own.

units.la: Hic respondet ad secundam auctoritatem inductam pro assertione contraria, dicens quod per iniquitatem non intelligitur ius gentium, sed peccatum primorum parentum, postquam homines voluerunt sibi propria possidere.
units.tr: Here he answers the second authority cited for the opposite view, saying that by iniquity is meant not the law of nations but the sin of our first parents, after men wished to possess things as their own.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, quod hic per propria verba convincitur: quia si post peccatum primorum parentum homines, scil. primi parentes, vel alii, non fuerint contenti communibus, sed voluerunt sibi propria possidere: ergo per adinuentionem humanam, & per consequens iure humano est dominiorum diuisio introducta.
units.tr: But these opponents say that this is refuted by his own words. For if after the sin of our first parents, men (namely the first parents themselves, or others) were not content with things held in common but wished to possess things as their own, then the division of ownership was introduced by human invention, and consequently by human law.

units.la: (Communis vsus omnium) Id est, potestas cuiuscunq; cum debitis circumstantiis vtendi omnibus esse debuit, scil. in statu innocentiæ: & adhuc deberet, si non esset pronitas hominum ad dissentiendum & male agendum. (Sed per iniquitatem) hoc Glossa 12. q. 1. c. dilectissimis, exponit dupliciter. Vno modo sic, per iniquitatem, id est, per consuetudinem iuris gentium aequitati naturali contrariam. Id est, quae consuetudo est contraria illi æquitati naturali, quae fuisset in statu innocentiæ, & etiam illi æquitati naturali, quæ debet esse inter homines in omnibus sequentibus rationem. Æquitati autem naturali, quæ est inter homines pronos ad dissentiendum & male agendum, non est contraria ista consuetudo, & ita contrarietas est secundum genus naturæ, & non est secundum genus morum: quia talis consuetudo non est iniqua neq; mala.
units.tr: (Communis usus omnium) That is, the power of each person to use all things with due circumstances ought to have belonged to everyone, namely in the state of innocence; and it would still do so, were it not for the propensity of men to dissent and to act wickedly. (Sed per iniquitatem) The Gloss on 12 q. 1 c. dilectissimis explains this in two ways. In one way, thus: through iniquity, that is, through a custom of the law of nations contrary to natural equity. That is, the custom is contrary to that natural equity which would have existed in the state of innocence, and also to that natural equity which ought to exist among men in all matters following reason. But this custom is not contrary to the natural equity which exists among men who are prone to dissent and to act wickedly; so the contrariness is according to the kind of nature, and not according to the kind of morals, because such a custom is neither iniquitous nor evil.

units.la: Ista expositionem Glossæ secutus est appellans. Aliter exponit sic, per iniquitatem, id est, per sollicitudinem, vt ibi: Facite amicos vobis de mammona iniquitatis, id est, quae per sollicitudinem est quaesita. Et ita secundum Glossam iniquitas accipitur pro iure gentium & pro sollicitudine: & vtroq; modo exponendo per iniquitatem accipitur quodammodo causaliter, & tam ius gentium q; sollicitudo humana fit causa diuisionis dominiorum factæ inter mortales.
units.tr: The appellant followed this explanation of the Gloss. He explains it differently, thus: through iniquity, that is, through anxious care, as in: Make friends for yourselves by means of the mammon of iniquity, that is, what is acquired through anxious care. And so, according to the Gloss, iniquity is taken both for the law of nations and for anxious care; and in either way of explaining, through iniquity is taken in some sense causally, and both the law of nations and human anxiety become the cause of the division of dominions made among mortals.

units.la: Tertio modo potest exponi, sicut iste exponit, vt iniquitas accipiatur ibi pro peccato primorum parentum. Et tunc per iniquitatem non accipitur proprie causaliter, sed accipitur occasionaliter: quia iniquitas primorum parentum fuit occasio diuisionis dominiorum. Si enim no peccassent, nunquam fuisset diuisio, & tamen no fuit causa diuisionis, sed voluntas humana sequens fuit causa diuisionis dominiorum prima. Aliquorum autem dominiorum voluntas diuina sola fuit causa. Et sic aliqui alio modo facta fuit aliqui inter mortales diuisio, scil. per specialem ordinationem diuinam (speciali revelatione manifestatam. (Ex hoc dicit ipse q diuisio temporalium est facta per ius humanum, quod dicitur iniquum, & contra aequitatem iuris naturalis.) Hic appellanti falsum imponit, quia nunquam dicit, ius humanum esse iniquum: licet dicat, q est æquitati naturali contrarium. Sed quomodo hoc debeat intelligi, patet ex prædictis. (Quia per iniquitatem non intellexit ius gentium.) Hoc contradicit Glossæ prædictæ. (Cum sit aequum.) Proprie loquendo verum est, quod est æquum. Et tamen aliter accipiendo vocabulum, & forte improprie, potest vocari aliquo modo iniquitas, & dici quod non est æquum.
units.tr: It can be explained in a third way, as this author explains it, so that iniquity is taken there for the sin of the first parents. Then through iniquity is not taken properly as a cause, but as an occasion, because the iniquity of the first parents was the occasion of the division of dominions. For if they had not sinned, there would never have been a division; and yet it was not the cause of the division, but the human will following on it was the first cause of the division of dominions. Of some dominions, however, the divine will alone was the cause. And thus, in another way, a division was made among mortals of some things, namely by a special divine ordinance (made known by special revelation). (From this he says that the division of temporal goods was made by human law, which is called iniquitous and contrary to the equity of natural law.) Here he falsely charges the appellant, for he never says that human law is iniquitous, although he says it is contrary to natural equity. But how this ought to be understood is clear from what has been said above. (Because by iniquity he did not understand the law of nations.) This contradicts the Gloss cited above. (Since it is equitable.) Properly speaking, it is true that what is equitable is equitable. Yet, taking the word otherwise, and perhaps improperly, it can in some sense be called iniquity, and be said not to be equitable.

units.la: Sic enim loquitur Glossa di. 1. ius generale, dicens: Quandoq; tamen est aliquod ius, quod non est aequum, nec iustum: vt si alicuius vxor adultera &c. Et imprudenter inducitur quandoq; rigor contra naturalem æquitatem. Qualiter autem verba hæc possunt intelligi, patere potest ex prædictis. (Sed intellexit peccatum primorum parentum.) Concedit ur, quod sic potest intelligi: cum hoc tamen stat, quod etiam aliter possit intelligi. (Posit non fuit contenta communibus, sed sibi propria voluit possidere.) Hic, sicut dictum est, clare concedit, quod per voluntatem humanam facta est dominiorum diuisio, & ita sibiipsi contrarius inuenitur.
units.tr: For thus the Gloss speaks on di. 1, ius generale, saying: Sometimes, however, there is a law which is neither equitable nor just, as when someone's wife is an adulteress, etc. And harshness is sometimes imprudently brought in against natural equity. How these words can be understood can be seen from what has been said above. (But he understood the sin of the first parents.) It is granted that it can be understood thus; yet it also stands that it can be understood otherwise. (Since they were not content with things held in common, but wished to possess things as their own.) Here, as has been said, he clearly concedes that the division of dominions was made by human will, and so he is found to be contrary to himself.

units.la: CAP. XCIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XCIII.

units.la: SEcundo quaeritur, vtrum Christus alicuius rei temporalis dominium habuerit & quale. Quod autem dominium rerum temporalium habuerit, sacra Scriptura, tam in Testamento Veteri quam in Nouo in multis locis testatur. Multi quidem Prophetae eum regem populi Israelitici, & per consequens habere regni dominium prophetauerunt. Esaias quidem de eo prophetizauit, Esa. 33. sic dicens: Ecce Dominus iudex noster, Dominus legifer, Dominus rex: ipse veniet & saluabit nos. Et per os Hieremiae Prophetae, Dominus Hieremiae 23. ita dicit: Suscitabo Dauid germen iustum, & regnabit rex, & sapiens erit. Et sequitur: Et hoc est nomen, quod vocabunt eum, Dominus iustus noster. Iste enim est lapis abscissus de monte sine manibus, cui Deus cœli dedit regnum, quod in aeternum non dissipabitur, vt habetur Daniel. 2. Item, Zachariae 9. de eo dicitur sic: Exulta satis filia Hierusalem, iubila filia Hierusalem. Ecce rex tuus veniet, iustus & Saluator ipse pauper & ascendens super asinam, & super pullum filium asinae. De hoc Dauid in multis locis prophetauit. Vnde in quodam loco in persona eius sic dicit: Ecce constitutus sum rex ab eo super Sion &c. eumq; futurum in multis aliis locis prophetauit. Vnde totus ille Psalmus, Erutauit, loquitur de rege isto & ipsa eius, scil. Ecclesia. Et multi alii Psalmi loquuntur de rege huiusmodi satis clare. De hoc etiam Salomon Canticorum 3. sic dixit: Egredimini filiae Sion, & videte regem Salomonem &c. De hoc etiam antequam conciperetur, Gabriel Archangelus, vt legitur Luc. 1. dixit: Dabit illi Dominus sedem Dauid patris eius, & regnabit &c. Item, & eo nato Angelus ad pastores Luc. 2. dixit: Natus est vobis hodie Saluator, qui est Christus Dominus, id est, Rex & Dominus. Huic etiam nato illi tres Magi Euangelici Matth. 2. perhibuerunt testimonium, sic dicentes: Vbi est qui natus est Rex Iudaeorum. Item, ille Nathanael verus Israelita, in quo dolus non erat, dixit ei Iohan. 1. Rabbi tu es filius Dei: tu es Rex Israel. Pilatus quoq; insuperscriptione scripsit: Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum. Et reclamantes, Noli scribere Rex Iudaeorum: sed quia dixit se regem Iudeorum audire noluit, sed respondit, quod scripsi scripsi. Hoc etiam Saluator nosier confessus fuit, Iohan. 18. Cum enim Pilatus interrogaret eum, vtrum esset Rex Iudaeorum, respondit ei: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. Ex quo Pilatus concludens dixit: ergo Rex es tu. Iesus vero respondit: Regnum meum non est hinc: non dixit, non est hic: sed dixit, non est hinc, quasi diceret, regnum meum à mundo non habeo, sicut nec habebat, imo à Deo, sicut Angelus genitrici praedixerat, dicens Luca primo. Dabit ei Dominus sedem David &c. Etiam hoc Beatus Petrus Apostolus secundo expresse testatur, dicens: Certissime sciat omnis domus Israel: quia & Dominum eum Christum fecit Deus hunc Iesum, quem vos crucifixistis. In quibus verbis satis clare Petrus concludit duo de Domino nostro Iesu: videlicet quod regnum suum à mundo non habuerit, sed à Deo, ex eo quod dicit, quod Iesum fecit Dominum Christum. Per Christum enim regem intelligimus: quia Christus interpretatur unctus. Et quia reges inungi consueverunt, per Christum intelligimus regem. Unde Rabanus ibidem: Manifeste Petrus ex hoc verbo regnum Christi non terrenum, sed caeleste ostendit esse. Item, concludit Petrus ex verbis praedictis, quod Christus inquantum homo subsistens in divina suppositio factus est Dominus & rex factus. Constat enim quod inquantum erat Deus, crucifixus non fuit, sed inquantum homo. Et ideo cum rex & Dominus fuerat factus inquantum crucifixus: & crucifixus fuit inquantum homo: sequitur quod & regnum & dominium tanquam homini Deus ei concessit. Hoc etiam suppone Angelus eo nato pastoribus, dicens: Hodie natus est Salvator, qui est Christus Dominus in civitate David, id est, Rex & Dominus. Ubi advertendum, quod illud, quod Gabriel Archangelus Christo nondum nato dixerat de futuro, dicens Maria: Dabit ei Dominus sedem David patris eius &c. Angelus ipse eo nato dixit pastoribus per verba de praesenti dicens: Hodie natus est Salvator, qui est Christus Dominus. Hoc Augustinus in libro de Concordia Evangelistarum, in proemio expresse testatur dicens: Dominus Iesus Christus unus verus rex & unus verus sacerdos est. Et paulo post dicit sic: Secundum hominem quippe Christus & rex & sacerdos effectus est, cui dedit Deus sedem David patris sui, & regni eius non erit finis. Item, quod Salvator fuerit Dominus omnium temporalium videtur. Deo enim dicitur Isaiae decimo sexto: Emitte agnum Domine dominatorem &c. Item Micheae quinto de eodem dicitur sic: Et tu Bethlehem Ephrata parvulus es in millibus Iuda. Ex te enim egredietur, qui sit dominator in Israel, & egressus eius ab initio à diebus aeternitatis. Malachias vero cap. de eo dicitur sic: Statim veniet ad templum sanctum suum dominator, quem vos quaeritis, & angelus testamenti quem vos vultis. Idem, Iohannes decimo tertio, ipsa veritas dixit: Vos vocatis me magister &c. Item Matthaei vigesimo primo dicit discipulis: Ite in castellum quod contra vos est, & statim invenietis asinam alligatam & pullum cum ea: solvite & adducite mihi. Et si quis vobis aliquid dixerit, dicite: quia Dominus his opus habet, & confestim dimittet eos. Hoc quoque Beatus Iohannes, Apocalypsis decimo nono, cap. testatur, dicens: habet scriptum in vestimento suo, rex regum & Dominus dominantium. Hoc insuper Apostoli in suo Symbolo confitentur dicentes: Et in Iesum Christum filium eius unicum Dominum nostrum qui conceptus est. Hoc etiam sancti patres in Symbolo, quod cantatur in Missa, protestantur expresse ibi: Et in Iesum Christum filium eius unicum Dominum nostrum &c. Premissa autem, scilicet regnum & universale dominium, habuit Iesus inquantum Deus ab aeterno, eo ipso, quia Deus pater genuit eum, & inquantum homo ex tempore, scilicet ab instanti conceptionis suae ex Dei datione, ut patet ex praedictis.
units.tr: Second, it is asked whether Christ held any dominion over temporal things, and of what kind. That he did hold dominion over temporal things, Holy Scripture attests in many places in both the Old and the New Testament. Many prophets foretold that he would be the king of the people of Israel and, consequently, would have dominion over the kingdom. Isaiah prophesied of him, Isa. 33: "Behold, the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king: he will come and save us." Through the mouth of the prophet Jeremiah, the Lord says, Jer. 23: "I will raise up to David a righteous branch, and a king shall reign, and he shall be wise." And it continues: "And this is the name by which they will call him: The Lord our righteousness." For he is the stone cut out of the mountain without hands, to whom the God of heaven has given a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed, as is found in Daniel 2. Likewise, Zechariah 9 says of him: "Rejoice greatly, daughter of Jerusalem; shout, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king comes, just and a Saviour, himself poor and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt, the foal of an ass." David prophesied of him in many places. Hence in one passage he speaks in his person: "Behold, I have been set as king by him over Zion," etc. He also prophesied that he would be so in many other places. Hence that whole psalm, "Be exalted," speaks of this king and of his own, that is, the Church. And many other psalms speak quite clearly of a king of this kind. Solomon too said of him, Song of Songs 3: "Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon," etc. Before he was conceived, the archangel Gabriel said to Mary, as we read in Luke 1: "The Lord will give him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign," etc. Likewise, after he was born, the angel said to the shepherds, Luke 2: "A Saviour is born to you today, who is Christ the Lord," that is, King and Lord. Also, to this newborn child the three Magi of the Gospel bore witness, Matt. 2, saying: "Where is he who is born King of the Jews?" Likewise, that Nathanael, a true Israelite in whom there was no guile, said to him, John 1: "Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel." Pilate too wrote on the inscription: "Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews." And when the chief priests objected, "Do not write, The King of the Jews," he would not change it, but answered, "What I have written, I have written." Our Saviour also confessed this, John 18. When Pilate asked him whether he was King of the Jews, he answered him: "My kingdom is not of this world." From this Pilate concluded: "So you are a king?" But Jesus answered: "My kingdom is not from here." He did not say "is not here," but said, "is not from here," as if to say, "I do not have my kingdom from the world, just as I did not have it," but rather from God, as the angel had foretold to his mother, saying in Luke 1: "The Lord will give him the throne of David," etc. The blessed apostle Peter also testifies clearly to this in the second chapter, saying: "Let all the house of Israel know most certainly that God has made this same Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ." In these words Peter clearly concludes two things about our Lord Jesus: namely, that he did not have his kingdom from the world, but from God, from the fact that he says that God made Jesus Lord and Christ. For by Christ we understand king, since Christ means "anointed," and since kings were customarily anointed. Hence Rabanus on this passage: "Peter shows plainly from this word that the kingdom of Christ is not earthly but heavenly." Likewise, Peter concludes from the words cited that Christ, insofar as he is man, subsisting in the divine person, was made Lord and king. For it is certain that insofar as he was God he was not crucified, but insofar as he was man. And therefore, since he had been made king and Lord insofar as he was crucified, and he was crucified insofar as he was man, it follows that both kingdom and dominion were given him by God as to a man. The angel also signified this when he was born and spoke to the shepherds: "Today a Saviour is born in the city of David, who is Christ the Lord," that is, King and Lord. Here it should be noted that what the archangel Gabriel said to Mary about the future, before Christ was born, "The Lord will give him the throne of David his father," etc., the angel himself, after he was born, expressed to the shepherds in the present tense, saying: "Today a Saviour is born, who is Christ the Lord." Augustine in his book on the Harmony of the Evangelists clearly testifies to this in the preface, saying: "The Lord Jesus Christ is the one true king and the one true priest." And a little after he says: "Christ was made both king and priest according to his humanity, to whom God gave the throne of his father David, and of his kingdom there will be no end." Likewise, that the Saviour was Lord of all temporal things appears. For it is said of him by God in Isaiah 16: "Send forth, O Lord, the lamb, the ruler," etc. Likewise, Micah 5 says of him: "But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are little among the thousands of Judah, out of you shall come forth one who will be ruler in Israel, and his goings forth are from of old, from everlasting." Malachi says of him in the chapter: "The ruler whom you seek will suddenly come to his holy temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire." Likewise, John 13, the truth itself said: "You call me Teacher," etc. Also, Matthew 21 says to the disciples: "Go into the village that is over against you, and straightway you will find an ass tied and a colt with her: loose them and bring them to me. And if anyone says anything to you, say that the Lord has need of them, and immediately he will send them." The blessed John also testifies to this, Revelation 19, saying: "He has written on his garment and on his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords." Moreover, the apostles confess this in their creed, saying: "And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was conceived," etc. The holy Fathers also expressly profess this in the creed that is sung at Mass: "And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord," etc. The premises, namely the kingdom and universal dominion, Jesus had as God from eternity, by the very fact that God the Father begot him; and as man from time, namely from the moment of his conception, by the gift of God, as is clear from what has been said above.

units.la: Postquam in parte praecedenti disseruit, quo iure sit rerum dominium introductum: hic ad quaestionem principalem accedit, inquirens, an Christus & Apostoli alicuius rei temporalis habuerunt dominium. Et dividitur in duas partes: quia primo tractat praedictam materiam de Christo. Secundo de Apostolis, ibi: Nunc autem de Apostolis videndum. Prima dividitur in duas: quia primo ostendit, quod Christus inquantum homo habuit regnum & universale dominium rerum temporalium. Secundo ostendit, quomodo hoc non obstante Christus fuit pauper. Secunda ibi: sed dicit iste haereticus. Prima in tres: quia primo ostendit, quod Christus ab instanti suae conceptionis habuit regnum & universale dominium omnium temporalium ex Dei datione.
units.tr: After discussing in the preceding part by what right the dominion of things was introduced, he now comes to the principal question, inquiring whether Christ and the apostles held dominion over any temporal thing. It is divided into two parts: first he treats this matter concerning Christ, and second concerning the apostles, where he says: "Now, however, we must consider the apostles." The first part is divided into two: first he shows that Christ, insofar as he is man, had a kingdom and universal dominion over temporal things; second, he shows how, notwithstanding this, Christ was poor. The second begins: "But this heretic says." The first part has three divisions: first he shows that Christ, from the moment of his conception, had a kingdom and universal dominion over all temporal things by the gift of God.

units.la: Secundo ostendit, quod non ab instanti suae conceptionis, sed postea quorundam rerum per alios modos acquisitis dominium.
units.tr: Secondly, he shows that Christ did not acquire dominion from the moment of his conception, but later, by other means, of certain things.

units.la: Tertio ostendit, quod Christus regno & universali dominio nunquam renunciavit. Secunda ibi: Et nihilominus habuit dominium. Tertia ibi: Et si velut dicere. Prima poterit dividi in tres partes: quia primo ostendit per 15. auctoritates, quod Christus inquantum homo fuit rex in temporalibus. Secundo ostendit per octo auctoritates, quod Christus inquantum homo fuit Dominus omnium temporalium, ibi: Item, quod Salvator fuit Dominus omnium. Tertio determinat, quando Christus habuit regnum & dominium omnium ibi: premissa autem. Primo autem quaerit quaestionem. Secundo determinat ostendemus, quod Christus habuit dominium omnium temporalium, quod fuit rex, quod per ista auctoritates ostendit.
units.tr: Thirdly, he shows that Christ never renounced his kingdom and universal dominion. The second part begins with And nevertheless he had dominion. The third begins with And if, as it were, one should say. The first part can be divided into three parts. First, he shows by fifteen authorities that Christ, as man, was king in temporal affairs. Secondly, he shows by eight authorities that Christ, as man, was Lord of all temporal things, at Likewise, that the Saviour was Lord of all. Thirdly, he determines when Christ had the kingdom and dominion of all things, at But the premises. He first raises the question, and secondly he determines it. We will show that Christ had dominion over all temporal things and that he was king, which he shows by these authorities.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt hic contineri duas haereses manifestas. Quarum prima est, quod Christus inquantum viator, fuit rex in temporalibus. Secunda est, quod Christus inquantum homo viator ab instanti conceptionis suae fuit Dominus temporalium omnium. Ut autem apertius convincant haereses supradictas, sic procedunt. Primo aequivocationes istorum nominum rex & Dominus declarare nituntur. Secundo circa praedicta quam suam reputant, explicant veritatem. Tertio duas assertiones praedictas haeresim sapere manifestam probare conantur.
units.tr: But these opponents say that two manifest heresies are contained here. The first is that Christ, as a wayfarer, was king in temporal affairs. The second is that Christ, as a mortal man on the way, was from the moment of his conception Lord of all temporal things. To prove these heresies more clearly, they proceed thus. First, they try to explain the ambiguities of the names king and lord. Secondly, they set out the truth as they understand it concerning the matters mentioned. Thirdly, they try to prove that the two assertions mentioned above plainly savour of heresy.

units.la: Circa primum dicunt, quod hoc nomen rex, cum dicatur à regendo, secundum varios modos reginimis, potest aliquis rex modis variis appellari. Unde ut de divino regimine, & angelorum, & etiam de regimine quale invenitur in rebus irrationabilibus taceatur: Inter homines praeter modos alios, triplex regimen reperitur. Unum est, quo aliquos alios regit temporaliter, quantum scilicet ad temporalia & actiones quae temporalia dignoscuntur respicere:
units.tr: On the first point they say that the word king, since it is derived from ruling, can be applied to someone in various ways, according to the various modes of ruling. So, leaving aside the divine government, that of the angels, and also the kind of rule found among irrational creatures, they say that among men there is, besides other modes, a threefold rule. The first is that by which someone rules others in temporal matters, that is, as far as temporal things and the actions which pertain to temporal things are concerned:

units.la: & & isto modo largissime accepto nomine Regis, Imperatores, Reges, Duces, Comites, & Barones & Patresfamilias possent vocari reges. Unde & nonnunquam vulgariter dicitur, quod quilibet Pater familias est rex in domo sua. Secundum tamen modum communem loquendi illi soli ab isto modo regendi appellantur reges, qui supremum modum regendi huiusmodi obtinere noscuntur. In quo tamen modo aliqui possunt esse gradus, & sic Reges a Ducibus, Baronibus, & aliis Potestatibus secularibus distinguuntur. Aliud est regimen spirituale, quo quis alios circa spiritualia regit. Et isto modo Papa & quilibet praelatus potest rex vocari. Si enim, sicut post patebit, qui motus & passiones suas sensuales per rationem regit, rex poterit appellari: multo magis qui alios circa spiritualia regit, regis nomen poterit obtinere. Aliud est regimen, quo quis seipsum, ac motus & actus suos ratione recta regit. Et ab isto regimine quilibet rationabiliter viuens poterit rex nuncupari. Unde & propter hoc Beatus Remigius omnes Christi electos asserit esse reges.
units.tr: and in this very broad sense of the name king, emperors, kings, dukes, counts, barons and heads of households could be called kings. Hence it is sometimes commonly said that every head of a household is king in his own house. Yet according to the common manner of speaking, only those are called kings by this mode of ruling who are known to hold the highest form of such rule. Within this mode, however, there can be degrees, and so kings are distinguished from dukes, barons and other secular powers. Another is spiritual government, by which someone rules others in spiritual things. In this way the Pope and any prelate can be called king. For if, as will be shown later, one who governs his sensual motions and passions by reason can be called king, much more can one who rules others in spiritual matters obtain the name of king. Another is the rule by which someone governs himself and his own motions and acts by right reason. By this rule any man who lives reasonably can be called king. For this reason also Blessed Remigius asserts that all the elect of Christ are kings.

units.la: Exponens enim illa verba Apocalypsis prim. Fecit nos regnum & sacerdotes Deo patri suo, ait: Per hanc sententiam omnes sacerdotes demonstrantur, qui supra reges fuerant appellati. Quia enim caput Dei filius rex & sacerdos, congruenter & membra capitis reges & sacerdotes vocantur, quibus per Petrum dicitur: Vos estis genus electum regale sacerdotium. Ipsi enim sunt reges, ipsi & sacerdotes & sacrificium, & altare. Quia & tumultus carnalium voluptatum contra se insurgentes, ut reges, refrenant, sacrificium laudis & mortificationis Deo immolant, corpusque suum a praesentis seculi cupiditatibus mortificant, ut bestia viva fiant. Ipse itaque vnigenitus prius rex & sacerdos, fecit nos suos electos & sacerdotes, quos reges terra constituit, & ipso tempore sacerdotes monstrantur. Ex his clare monstratur, quod aliquis a regendo proprias cupiditates & motus sensuales poterit rex vocari, & ita in scripturis hoc nomen rex variis modis accipitur.
units.tr: For in explaining those words of Revelation 1, He has made us a kingdom and priests to God his Father, he says: By this sentence all priests are shown, who were called kings above. For since the Son of God, the king and priest, is the head, the members of the head are fittingly called kings and priests, to whom it is said through Peter: You are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9). They are themselves kings, themselves priests, sacrifice and altar. For they also, as kings, restrain the tumults of carnal desires rising against them, offer to God the sacrifice of praise and mortification, and mortify their body from the lusts of the present age, so that they become a living sacrifice. Thus the only-begotten himself, first king and priest, made us his elect and priests, whom the kings of the earth have appointed, and at the same time they are shown to be priests. From these things it is clearly shown that one who, by ruling his own desires and sensual motions, can be called king; and so in the Scriptures this name king is taken in various ways.

units.la: Secundo dicunt, quod hoc nomen Dominus aequivoce in scripturis accipitur. Vno enim modo dicitur aliquis Dominus, propter aliquam potestatem, quam noscitur obtinere. Et iste modus in multis diuiditur, de quibus dictum est supra 2. cap. Alio modo dicitur aliquis Dominus propter praerogatiuam sanctitatis, virtutis, vel sapientiae, aut diuitiarum, vel alicuius alterius excellentiae. Sic enim diuites & potentes, ac domini magni, sacerdotes & religiosos, ac alios multos, saepenumero Dominos appellant: propter praerogatiuam sanctitatis, religionis, aut ordinis, vel sapientiae, & alicuius excellentiae, quam in eis considerant, vel in eis reputant praeeminere. Sic etiam multi diuites vocant aliquos Dominos, quibus tamen non reputant se subiectos. Et iste modus loquendi non solum in vulgari locutione, sed in scripturis Diuinis habetur: Abdias enim, vt supra habetur 3. Regum decim. septim. dixit Heliae Prophetae: Nunquid indicatum est tibi a Domino meo quid fecerit? Vbi Abdias Heliam dominum suum vocauit propter praerogatiuam prophetiae & sanctitatis, quam sciunt in ipso. Sic mulier Sunamitis, quae Elisaeo fecerat coenaculum, propter praerogatiuam sanctitatis dominum appellauit, vt habetur 4. Regum quart. cap. dicens: Noli quaeso Domine mi vir Dei, noli mentiri ancilla tua. Et post: Nunquam petiui filium a Domino meo. Et ita haec mulier Elisaeum Dominum appellauit, cui tamen temporaliter subiecta non fuit.
units.tr: Secondly, they say that the name Lord is used ambiguously in the Scriptures. For in one way someone is called lord on account of some power which he is known to hold. And this mode is divided into many kinds, of which it was said above, chapter 2. In another way someone is called lord on account of a pre-eminence of holiness, virtue, wisdom, riches, or some other excellence. For in this way the rich and powerful, great lords, priests and religious, and many others, very often call people Lords, on account of the pre-eminence of holiness, religion, or office, or wisdom, and of some excellence which they see in them or think to be pre-eminent in them. So too many rich men call some people lords, although they do not consider themselves subject to them. And this manner of speaking is found not only in common speech but in the divine Scriptures: for Obadiah, as is recorded in 1 Kings 18, said to the prophet Elijah: Has it not been told to my lord what he has done? Here Obadiah called Elijah his lord on account of the pre-eminence of prophecy and holiness which they knew in him. So the Shunammite woman, who had made a room for Elisha, called him lord on account of the pre-eminence of holiness, as is recorded in 2 Kings 4, saying: Do not, I beg you, my lord, man of God, do not deceive your handmaid. And after: Did I ever ask a son of my lord? And so this woman called Elisha lord, although she was not subject to him temporally.

units.la: Secundo principaliter isti impugnatores circa paupertatem Christi suam, quam reputant, exprimunt veritatem, dicentes, quod Christus inquantum Deus fuit rex omnium, sicut & pater rex est omnium: & eodem regimine, quo pater omnia regit. Secundo dicunt, quod Christus inquantum homo mortalis, non erat rex a regendo temporaliter, & secundum quod aliquis dicitur rex, propter supremum modum regendi temporaliter alios: licet fuerit rex temporaliter a regendo aliquo modo temporaliter Apostolos, qui cum eo quasi conuersabantur continue.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents, concerning the poverty of Christ, set forth the truth as they understand it, saying that Christ, as God, was king of all, just as God the Father is king of all, and by the same government by which the Father rules all things. Secondly, they say that Christ, as a mortal man, was not king by ruling temporally, nor in the sense in which someone is called king by the highest mode of ruling others temporally, although he was in some way a temporal ruler, ruling temporally the Apostles, who were continually with him as companions.

units.la: Tertio dicunt, quod Christus fuit rex a spirituali regimine: quia ad hoc venit in mundum, vt scilicet fideles sibi credentes quantum ad spiritualia gubernaret.
units.tr: Thirdly, they say that Christ was king by spiritual rule, because he came into the world for this purpose, namely to govern, as far as spiritual things are concerned, the faithful who believe in him.

units.la: Quarto dicunt, quod Christus inquantum Deus, fuit Dominus omnium, sicut Deus pater est Deus omnium.
units.tr: Fourthly, they say that Christ, as God, was Lord of all, just as God the Father is God of all.

units.la: Quinto dicunt, quod Christus inquantum homo mortalis, non erat Dominus omnium temporalium dominio proprio sibi, licet fuisset Dominus omnium dominio communi, quod secundum multos datum fuit a Deo toti generi humano: & hoc si nulli licet renunciare tali dominio.
units.tr: Fifthly, they say that Christ, as a mortal man, was not Lord of all temporal things by his own proper dominion, although he was Lord of all by common dominion, which according to many was given by God to the whole human race; and this holds if no one may renounce such dominion.

units.la: Sexto dicunt, quod licet Christus inquantum homo mortalis, nullius rei habuit dominium: quod in scripturis vocatur proprietas. Poterat tamen antonomastice propter praerogatiuam vnionis naturae humanae in ipso ad diuinam, sanctitatis a aliarum gratiarum dominus appellari. Ex his dicunt isti patere, quod iste impugnatus nominum aequiuocatione deceptus in haeresis incidit supradictas.
units.tr: Sixthly, they say that although Christ, as a mortal man, had dominion over nothing, which in the Scriptures is called ownership, nevertheless he could, by a figure of speech, be called Lord of holiness and of other graces, on account of the pre-eminence of the union of his human nature with the divine. From these things they say it is clear that this opponent, deceived by the ambiguity of the names, has fallen into the heresies mentioned above.

units.la: Tertio igitur principaliter duas assertiones praedictas sapere haeresim manifestam probare nituntur. Ad cuius euidentiam, primo explicant intentionem istius impugnati, dicentes: quod iste non solum intendit, quod Christus inquantum homo mortalis, fuerit rex propter regimen temporale, non propter quemcunque modum regendi temporaliter, sed propter potestatem regendi supremo modo regendi temporaliter: ita quod non solum inquantum Deus, sed etiam inquantum homo mortalis ex officio sibi commisso pertinebat ad ipsum de temporalibus iudicare, haereditates diuidere, leges condere seculares, homicidas, latrones & malefactores alios debitae subdere vltioni, peregrino, pupillo, & viduae, cum opprimerentur a potentibus, temporale exhibere auxilium, & alia quae ad regum secularium officium pertinent, exercere.
