Nec etiam intendit solummodo, quod Christus fuit Dominus omnium illo modo quo quilibet est quodammodo Dominus omnium, sicut totum genus humanum habet omnium commune dominium; sed etiam intendit, quod ita vel verius omnia erant Christi inquantum fuit homo mortalis, quo civitates & castra sunt aliquius regis; ita quod habuit dominium in speciali, & non solum in communi.
units.tr: Thirdly, then, they chiefly try to prove that the two assertions mentioned above plainly savour of manifest heresy. To make this clear, they first explain the intention of this opponent, saying: that he means not only that Christ, as a mortal man, was king by temporal government, not by any kind of temporal ruling, but by the power of ruling in the highest mode of temporal ruling; so that not only as God, but also as a mortal man, by the office committed to him, it belonged to him to judge temporal matters, to divide inheritances, to enact secular laws, to hand over murderers, robbers and other evildoers to due punishment, to give temporal help to the stranger, the orphan and the widow when they were oppressed by the powerful, and to exercise the other things which pertain to the office of secular kings. Nor does he intend merely that Christ was Lord of all in the way that anyone is in some sense Lord of all, just as the whole human race has a common dominion over all things; but he intends also that all things were Christ's, in the same way or more truly, as a mortal man, as cities and fortresses belong to some king; so that he had dominion in the particular sense, and not only in the common sense.

units.la: Hoc viso primo probant isti, quod Christus inquantum homo mortalis, non erat rex in temporalibus, à supremo modo regendi temporaliter. Secundo ostendunt, quod non fuit Dominus praedicto modo omnium rerum temporalium. Primum ostendunt primo auctoritatibus; secundo rationibus. Est autem prima auctoritas, per quam ostendunt, quod Christus non fuit praedicto modo rex, ipsius Christi dicentis Iohan. 18. Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod regnum Christi inquantum homo, non fuit regnum temporale. Sed ad hoc respondet iste impugnatus dicens, quod Christus non intendebat negare regnum suum esse temporale & mundanum: sed intendebat dicere, quod regnum suum non habebat à mundo, sed à Deo: quia mundus non sibi reddit regnum, nec eligit eum in regem, sed Deus. Unde, sicut patet supra, iste impugnatus hanc auctoritatem pro sua assertione adduxit, probans per eam, quod Christus fuit rex, quamvis non habuerit regnum à mundo, sed à Deo. Unde propter hoc dixit Christus, ut dicit: Regnum meum non est hinc: & non dixit, non est hic. Ex hoc dans intelligere, quod regnum non habebat à mundo, sed à Deo. Sed dicunt isti, quod hic scripturam Divinam aliter intelligit, quam sensus Spiritus sancti effl agitat, ad suum sensum scripturam trahens apertissime repugnantem. Nam quod Christus per verba praedicta intendebat asserere, quod non habuit regnum temporale, nec talie, qualia mundani niti untur acquirere, per seriem Evangelii etiam patet aperte. Nam, sicut in textu Evangelico constat, praecipua accusatio, quam Iudaei proponebant coram Pilato contra Christum, & per quam volebant maxime provocare Pilatum contra Christum, imo per quam ultimo coegerunt quodammodo Pilatum dare sententiam contra Christum, fuit de regno Christi, dicentes, quod Christus se asseruit Regem Iudaeorum. Unde Lucae vigesimo tertio sic scribitur de Iudaeis:
units.tr: Having seen this, these men first prove that Christ, as a mortal man, was not a king in temporal affairs, in the supreme sense of ruling temporally. Second, they show that he was not, in the aforesaid sense, the Lord of all temporal things. They show the first point first by authorities and second by reasons. The first authority, by which they show that Christ was not a king in the aforesaid way, is the saying of Christ himself in John 18: My kingdom is not of this world. From these words it follows that Christ's kingdom, as man, was not a temporal kingdom. But the opponent answers this, saying that Christ did not mean to deny that his kingdom was temporal and worldly. He meant rather that his kingdom did not have its origin from the world but from God, because the world does not give him the kingdom or choose him as king, but God does. Hence, as appears above, this opponent cited this authority for his assertion, proving by it that Christ was a king even though he had his kingdom not from the world but from God. On this account Christ said, as he says: My kingdom is not from here, and did not say, is not here. From this he gives us to understand that he did not have the kingdom from the world but from God. But these men say that here he understands Divine Scripture otherwise than the sense which the Holy Spirit demands, dragging Scripture to his own sense, which is most plainly contrary to it. For that Christ, by the aforesaid words, intended to assert that he did not have a temporal kingdom, nor one such as worldly men strive to acquire, is also clearly evident from the course of the Gospel. For, as the Gospel text makes plain, the chief accusation which the Jews brought before Pilate against Christ, and by which they most wanted to provoke Pilate against him, indeed by which at last they more or less forced Pilate to pass sentence against Christ, concerned Christ's kingdom, for they said that Christ had claimed to be King of the Jews. So Luke 23 writes of the Jews:

units.la: Coeperunt autem illum accusare, dicentes, hunc inuenimus subuertentem gentem nostram, & prohibentem tributa dare Caesari, & dicentem se Christum regem esse. Iohan. decimo non. sic habetur: Quaerebat Pilatus dimittere eum. Iudaei autem clamabant dicentes: Si hunc dimittis, non es amicus Caesaris. Omnis enim, qui se regem facit, contradicit Caesari. Et post dixit eis Pilatus: Regem vestrum crucifigam? Responderunt pontifices: Non habemus regem, nisi Caesarem. Tunc ergo tradidit eis illum ut crucifigeretur. Ex quibus verbis colligitur evidenter, quod Iudaei principaliter accusaverunt Christum, quod regem se fecerit, loquentes de rege temporali, qualem regem Caesar noluit sustinere, ne recognosceret regnum ab ipso. Propter quod dixerunt, Omnis qui se regem facit, contradicit Caesari. Et per hanc accusationem vltimo coegerunt quodammodo Pilatum in necessitatem dandi sententiam mortis contra Christum, sicut patet per verba praeallegata.
units.tr: They began to accuse him, saying, We found this fellow perverting our nation, and forbidding to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ a king. John 19 has it thus: Pilate sought to release him. But the Jews cried out, saying: If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend. For everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar. And afterwards Pilate said to them: Shall I crucify your king? The chief priests answered: We have no king but Caesar. Then therefore he delivered him to them to be crucified. From these words it is clearly gathered that the Jews principally accused Christ of making himself king, speaking of a temporal king, such as Caesar would not allow to be recognised as ruling in his own right. On this account they said, Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar. And by this accusation they at last more or less forced Pilate into the necessity of passing a sentence of death against Christ, as the words quoted above make plain.

units.la: Sed Christus non negavit se regem, imo asseruit, & tamen accusationem Iudaeorum sufficienter excludit coram Pilato, qui nullum voluit sustinere regem Iudaeorum praeter Caesarem, illo modo appellando regem, quo Iudaei accusantes Christum loquebantur de rege. Ergo manifeste patet, quod Christus declaraverit coram Pilato aliter se esse regem, quam Iudaei loquebantur de rege, & quod non erat rex illo modo, quo Iudaei loquebantur de rege. Cum ergo illi intellexerint de rege temporali regnante vel temporaliter regnare volente, sequitur quod Christus dicens: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo: ostendit se non esse regem temporaliter, nec regnum terrenum habentem.
units.tr: But Christ did not deny that he was a king; indeed he affirmed it. Yet he sufficiently removed the Jews' accusation before Pilate, who would not tolerate any king of the Jews except Caesar, understanding the word "king" in the sense in which the Jews who accused Christ spoke of a king. It is therefore manifest that Christ made clear to Pilate that he was a king in a different way from that in which the Jews spoke of a king, and that he was not a king in the way the Jews meant. Since they understood it of a temporal king, one who reigns temporally or wishes to reign temporally, it follows that Christ, in saying, My kingdom is not of this world, showed that he was not a king in temporal affairs, nor one who held an earthly kingdom.

units.la: Hic oportet tria probare. Primum est, quod Iudaei accusantes Christum intelligebant de rege temporaliter regnante, vel temporaliter regnare volente. Secundum est, quod Pilatus nullum praeter Caesarem volebat esse regem Iudaeorum, illo modo loquendo de rege, quomodo intelligebant Iudaei. Tertium est, quod Christus Pilato satisfecit accusationem Iudaeorum sufficienter & apte excludendo. Ex quibus patenter concluditur, quod Christus aliter loquebatur de rege & de regno, quam Iudaei: & per consequens non asseruit se regem in temporalibus, sed alio modo. Primum est satis apertum: quia aliter per dictam accusationem Pilatum contra Christum minime provocassent. Romani enim & nuntii eorum de his, quae pertinebant ad legem Iudaeorum, tunc temporum curare videbantur: Nec propter transgressionem legis aliquem dignum morte iudicabant. Unde, sic habetur Actuum vigesimo tertio. Lisias tribunus mittens beatum Paulum ad Felicem praesidem, scripsit in haec verba: Quem (scilicet Paulum) invenի accusari de quaestionibus legis eorum, nihil vero dignum morte aut vinculis habentem crimen. Et, sicut legitur cap. vigesimo quinto, Pontius Festus de Paulo loquens dixit: De quo cum stetissent accusatores, nullam causam defferebant, de quibus suspicabar malam: quaestiones vero quasdam de sua superstitione habebant adversus eum, de quodam Iesu defuncto, quem affirmabat Paulus viuere. Et post: Ego vero comperi nihil dignum morte eum admisisse. Et cap. vigesimo sexto sic legitur: Et surrexit Rex, & Praeses & Berenice, & qui assistebant eis. Et cum secessissent, loquebantur ad invicem dicentes, quia nihil morte aut vinculis dignum quid fecit homo iste. Ex his verbis colligitur evidenter, quod Romani tunc temporis propter diversas & adversas assertiones legis Iudaicae, etiam si dixissent aliquem hominem esse Deum, cum Paulus fateretur Iesum Christum esse Deum, nullum dignum morte ac vinculis reputabant. Ergo quantumcunque Iudaei accusassent Christum Pilato, quod dixisset se esse Deum vel regem, alio modo quam temporaliter; & non in praeiudicium regni temporalis Caesaris, Pilatum contra Christum minime provocassent, sed Pilatus eorum accusationem friuolam. lam reputasset, quia non reputaret eam contra Caesarem, aut contra pacem publicam temporalem. Ergo Iudaei loquebantur de rege temporali.
units.tr: Here three things must be proved. The first is that the Jews, in accusing Christ, understood a king who reigns temporally, or who wishes to reign temporally. The second is that Pilate would not have any king of the Jews except Caesar, speaking of a king in the sense in which the Jews understood it. The third is that Christ satisfied Pilate, sufficiently and aptly removing the Jews' accusation. From these points it is plainly concluded that Christ spoke of king and kingdom differently from the Jews, and consequently did not claim to be a king in temporal affairs, but in another way. The first is quite evident, since otherwise the Jews would not have provoked Pilate against Christ by that accusation. For the Romans, and their envoys, seemed at that time not to concern themselves with matters that belonged to the law of the Jews, nor did they judge anyone worthy of death for breaking the law. So Acts 23 has it: Lysias the tribune, sending the blessed Paul to Felix the governor, wrote in these words: Whom (namely Paul) I found to be accused concerning questions of their law, but having nothing worthy of death or of bonds. And as is read in chapter 25, Porcius Festus, speaking of Paul, said: Concerning whom, when the accusers stood up, they brought no charge of such evil as I supposed; but they had certain questions against him about their own superstition, and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive. And after: But I found that he had done nothing worthy of death. And in chapter 26 it is read thus: And the king rose up, and the governor, and Bernice, and those who sat with them. And when they had withdrawn, they talked among themselves, saying, This man has done nothing worthy of death or of bonds. From these words it is evident that the Romans at that time, because of the various and opposing assertions of the Jewish law, did not regard anyone as worthy of death or bonds even if he had said that a man was God; for Paul confessed that Jesus Christ was God. Therefore, however much the Jews had accused Christ before Pilate of saying that he was God or king in some way other than temporally, and not to the prejudice of Caesar's temporal kingdom, they would not have provoked Pilate against Christ. Pilate would have already reckoned their accusation frivolous, since he would not regard it as against Caesar or against the public temporal peace. Therefore the Jews were speaking of a temporal king.

units.la: Secundum etiam, scilicet quod Pilatus nullum praeter Caesarem esse volebat regem temporalem Iudaeorum, est manifestum: quod ipse sciebat Caesarem vendicare sibi dominium omnium regnorum, & ita nolebat aliquem esse regem Iudaeorum, nec ab ipso recognoscere regnum.
units.tr: The second point, that Pilate would not have any temporal king of the Jews except Caesar, is also manifest, because he knew that Caesar claimed for himself dominion over all kingdoms, and so he was unwilling for anyone to be king of the Jews or to be recognised by him as holding a kingdom.

units.la: Tertium, scilicet quod Christus Pilato satisfecit dictam accusationem Iudaeorum sufficienter & aperte excludendo, per textum Euangelicum patenter ostenditur. Nam post dictam accusationem Iudaeorum, & responsionem Christi, qua concesserat se esse regem, & quo modo esset rex expresserat. Dixit Pilatus, sicut habetur Iohan. decim. octau. Ego nullam in eo inuenio causam. Et cap. decim. non. dixit Pilatus: Ecce adduco eum foras ut cognoscatis, quia eo in nullam causam inuenio. Et post: Accipite eum & crucifigite eum. Ego non inuenio in eo causam. Ex quibus verbis clare patet, quod Pilatus reputabat accusationem Iudaeorum per responsionem Christi sufficienter exclusam. Quia cum Iudaei Christum coram Pilato accusassent, quod ipse diceret se regem Iudaeorum. Quod sine dubio ipsi de rege temporaliter regente aut volente regere intelligebant, quia aliter nullo modo fuisset in praeiudicium Caesaris. Quod tamen ipsi manifestissime praetendebant, dicentes: Omnis qui se regem facit, contradicit Caesari. Et cum Christus per responsionem suam insinuasset manifestissime, quod non vendicare intendebat sibi regnum temporale, quod de hoc mundo esset: sed aliud spirituale, de quo prius dictum est. Et ita clarissime demonstrasset Pilato multiplicitatem & aequivocationem huius nominis regis: & per consequens, quod dixisset se regem longe alio modo, quam intellexerunt Iudaei in accusatione.
units.tr: The third point, that Christ sufficiently and plainly removed the Jews' aforesaid accusation and satisfied Pilate, is clearly shown by the Gospel text. For after the Jews' accusation and Christ's answer, in which he had conceded that he was a king and had explained in what way he was king, Pilate said, as John 18 has it: I find no fault in him. And in chapter 19 Pilate said: Behold, I bring him out to you, that you may know that I find no fault in him. And afterwards: Take him and crucify him, for I find no fault in him. From these words it is clear that Pilate considered the Jews' accusation sufficiently removed by Christ's answer. For when the Jews had accused Christ before Pilate of saying that he was king of the Jews, they undoubtedly understood this of a king who reigns temporally or wishes to reign temporally, since otherwise it could in no way have been to the prejudice of Caesar. And they most openly alleged this, saying: Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar. But Christ, by his answer, had most clearly hinted that he did not intend to claim a temporal kingdom which was of this world, but another, spiritual kingdom, of which he had spoken before. Thus he had most clearly shown Pilate the multiple meanings and ambiguity of this word "king", and consequently that he had called himself king in a quite different sense from that which the Jews understood in their accusation.

units.la: Et cum Pilatus vidisset, quod Iudaei probare non poterant, quod Christus dixisset se regem in praeiudicium Caesaris, ipse Pilatus accusationem eorum friuolam reputabat: quia, sicut testatur Matth. cap. vigesim. septim. sciebat quod per inuidiam tradidissent eum. Propter quod sic habetur ibidem: Accepta aqua lauit manus coram populo, dicens: Innocens ego sum a sanguine iusti huius. Et Marci decimo quint. sic legitur dixisse Pilatus: Vultis dimittam vobis regem Iudaeorum? Sciebat enim quod per inuidiam tradidissent eum. Ex quibus verbis patenter colligitur, quod Pilatus intellexit aperte, quod Iudaei accusantes Christum, quod dixerat se regem Iudaeorum: & Christus concedens se regem Iudaeorum, accipiebant nomen regis aequivoce. Nam si Christus dixisset se regem illo modo, quo accipiebant Iudaei accusantes ipsum, Pilatus reputasset dignum morte, tanquam in iudicio confessum de crimine dignissimo morte, usurpando scilicet regnum temporale praeter Caesaris voluntatem. Sed quaereret aliquis, unde aduertit Pilatus, quod Christus se aliter intelligebat esse regem, quam Iudaei accusantes? Dicendum est, quod hoc aduertit ex verbis Christi, cum dixit: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo: quia si ex hoc mundo esset regnum meum, ministri mei utique decertarent, ut non traderer Iudaeis. Nunc autem regnum meum non est hinc. Ex quibus verbis dedit intelligere, quod non habebat tale regnum, de quali accusabant Iudaei: quia si habuisset tale regnum, ministri sui decertassent pro eo, ut non traderetur Iudaeis. Sed adhuc ex istis verbis non videtur Pilatus plane intellexisse, an Christus fateretur se esse regem hic vel alibi, nec quale regnum haberet: & ideo quasi admirando intulit: Ergo rex es tu? & quasi diceret: Ergo tu concedis te esse regem, quamuis non talem regem, sicut dicunt Iudaei. Vbi est ergo regnum tuum? & quale regnum habes? Ad istas quaestiones, quas aliquo modo videbatur cogitare Pilatus, respondit Christus declarans, vbi & quale esset regnum suum, dicens: Tu dicis quod rex sum ego. Ego in hoc natus sum, & ad hoc veni in mundum, ut testimonium perhibeam veritati: & omnis qui est ex veritate, audit vocem meam. Vbi Christus primo fatetur se regem dicens: Rex sum ego. Secundo ostendit, vbi est regnum suum, quia hic, cum dicit: in hoc natus sum & ad hoc veni in mundum: quasi diceret, natus sum ut regnem in hoc mundo. Tertio ostendit, quale suit regnum suum, & qualiter regnare venerat dicens: Ut testimonium perhibeam veritati, quasi diceret, veni regnare, sed non veni regnare temporaliter, sed spiritualiter perhibendo testimonium veritati. Quarto ostendit, quae pertinebant ad regnum suum: quia credentes in eum. Et ideo dicit: Omnis qui est ex veritate, audit vocem meam: quasi diceret, Omnes qui credunt veritati, pertinent ad regnum meum.
units.tr: When Pilate saw that the Jews could not prove that Christ had called himself king to the prejudice of Caesar, he himself regarded their accusation as frivolous, because, as Matthew 27 testifies, he knew that they had handed him over out of envy. For this reason it is written there: Taking water, he washed his hands before the people, saying: I am innocent of the blood of this just man. And Mark 15 records Pilate saying: Do you want me to release to you the king of the Jews? For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy. From these words it is plainly gathered that Pilate clearly understood that, when the Jews accused Christ of having said that he was king of the Jews, and Christ, while admitting he was king of the Jews, they were taking the word "king" equivocally. For if Christ had called himself king in the sense in which the Jews, who accused him, understood it, Pilate would have judged him worthy of death, as one who had confessed in court a crime deserving death, namely, claiming a temporal kingdom against Caesar's will. But someone might ask: how did Pilate perceive that Christ understood himself to be king in a different sense from the accusing Jews? The answer is that he perceived this from Christ's words when he said: My kingdom is not of this world; for if my kingdom were of this world, my ministers would surely fight, so that I should not be handed over to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from here. By these words he made it understood that he did not have the kind of kingdom of which the Jews accused him; for if he had such a kingdom, his ministers would have fought for it, so that he would not be handed over to the Jews. Yet from these words it does not seem that Pilate had plainly understood whether Christ would confess that he was king here or elsewhere, or what kind of kingdom he had. And so, as if in wonder, he asked: So you are a king? as if to say: so you concede that you are a king, though not such a king as the Jews say. Where then is your kingdom, and what kind of kingdom do you have? To these questions, which Pilate seemed in some way to be pondering, Christ replied, declaring where and of what kind his kingdom was, saying: You say that I am a king. For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, that I should bear witness to the truth; and everyone who is of the truth hears my voice. Here Christ first confesses that he is king, saying: I am a king. Second, he shows where his kingdom is, namely here, when he says: for this I was born and for this I came into the world, as if to say: I was born to reign in this world. Third, he shows what sort of kingdom his was, and in what way he had come to reign, saying: that I should bear witness to the truth, as if to say: I came to reign, but not to reign temporally; I came to reign spiritually, by bearing witness to the truth. Fourth, he shows who belongs to his kingdom: those who believe in him. Therefore he says: everyone who is of the truth hears my voice, as if to say: all who believe the truth belong to my kingdom.

units.la: Et ita ex his verbis fuit Pilatus plene informatus, quod quamvis Christus reputasset se regem hic, non tamen reputauit se regem temporalem. Et ideo Pilatus non reputauit Christum in aliquo Caesari, qui quaerebat regna temporalia, aduersari. Quare ipsum reputauit innocentem, qui aliter intellexit se regem, quam Iudaei. Et ista veritas sic per seriem Euangelicam declarata, scilicet quod Christus aliter fuit rex, quam intellexerant Iudaei accusantes ipsum, sanctorum auctoritatibus confirmatur. Vnde Augustinus super Iohannem ait: Fideles Christiani sunt regnum eius: quod non tollitur, imo emitur sanguine Christi. Ergo tempore Pilati solum modo Christiani pertinebant ad regnum Christi. Sed si Christus fuisset rex illo modo, quo Iudaei loquebantur de rege accusantes Christum, non solum Christiani, sed omnes Iudaei in regno Iudaeorum constituti pertinuissent ad regnum Christi, quod falsum est secundum Augustinum. Ergo secundum Augustinum aliter Christus fuit rex, quam intelligebant Iudaei. Hoc etiam testatur Chrysostomus super illud, regnum meum non est hinc, dicens: Non priuat mundum a sua prouidentia & prelatione: sed ostendit regnum suum non esse humanum neque temporale. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod Christus non habebat regnum tale, quale est regnum humanum & mundanum: & ita non fuit illo modo rex, quo intelligebant Iudaei. Ex hoc aperte docet Augustinus super Iohannem cap. 19. dicens sic: Audite Iudaei & Gentes, audi circumcisio, audi praeputium. præceptium, audite omnia regna terrena: non impedio dominationem vestram in hoc mundo, quia regnum meum non est de hoc mundo: nolite metuere metu vanissimo, quo ille Herodes maior expavit, & tot infantes occidit timendo potius quam irascendo crudelior. Regnum, inquit, meum non est de hoc mundo: quid amplius? vultis venire ad regnum, quod non est de hoc mundo? Venite credendo, & nolite servire metuendo. Dicit quidem in Prophetia de Deo patre: Ego autem constitutus sum rex ab eo super Sion montem sanctum eius, prædicans præceptum eius. Sed Sion & mons ille non est de hoc mundo. Quod enim est regnum eius, nisi credentes? quibus dicitur: De hoc mundo non estis, sicut ego non sum de hoc mundo, quamvis eos vellet esse in hoc mundo. Propter quod de istis dixit ad patrem: Non rogo ut tollas eos de mundo, sed ut serues eos à malo. Unde & hic non ait: regnum meum non est in hoc mundo: sed, non est de hoc mundo: cum hoc probaret, dicens: Si regnum meum esset de hoc mundo, ministri mei utique decertarent, ut non traderer Iudæis. Nunc autem regnum meum non est hinc: non ait, non est hic: sed non est hinc. Hic enim est regnum eius usque in finem seculi habens inter se commixta zizania usque ad messem. Messis enim est finis seculi, quando messores venient, id est, angeli, & colligent de regno omnia scandala. Quod utique non fieret, si regnum suum non esset hic: sed tamen non est hinc, quia peregrinatur in mundo. Hæc Augustinus. Ex quibus tria colliguntur aperte. Quorum primum est, quod modus regiminis Christi dominationem terrenam & terrenorum nullatenus impediuit. Ex quo sequitur, quod Christus non veniet regnare temporaliter siue seculariter, sed spiritualiter solum: quia si de regimine seculari se intromisisset, dominationem secularium impediuisset, ipsosque maxime provocasset. Secundum est: quod ad regnum Christi non peruenitur per secularem subiectionem, sed per fidem, quia credendo. Et per consequens regnum Christi non est seculare seculariter gubernatum, sed spiritualiter spiritualiter gubernatum. Tertium est, quod credentes sunt regnum Christi: quia Ecclesia est regnum Christi. Unde sicut Christus est rex & sponsus, ita Ecclesia est regnum & sponsa. Et propter hoc sæpe Ecclesia Christi præsens in hoc mundo regnum cœlorum in hoc Evangelio appellatur, teste Gregor. qui in Homelia De communi virginum, ait: Sciendum vobis est, quod sape in sacro eloquio regnum cœlorum præsens Ecclesia dicitur: de quo in alio loco Dominus dicit: Mittet filius hominis Angelos suos, & colligent de regno eius omnia scandala. Illud ergo regnum, de quo Christus dicit, Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo, est Ecclesia sua, credentes comprehendens bonos & malos. Unde & illud regnum cœlorum vocatur. Ex prædictis patet aperte, quod Regnum Christi non fuit Iudæa, secundum quod Iudæa comprehendit omnes Iudæos constitutos ibidem, sicut intellexerunt Iudæi accusantes Christum, quod diceret se regem Iudæorum: sed regnum Christi fuit Ecclesia Christi, comprehendens solummodo credentes in Christum. Et ita Regnum Christi non fuit regnum seculare; sed fuit regnum spirituale: hoc est, fuit Ecclesia Christianorum ab eo spiritualiter gubernanda.
units.tr: Thus from these words Pilate was fully informed that, although Christ regarded himself as a king here, he did not regard himself as a temporal king. Therefore Pilate did not consider that Christ was in any way opposed to Caesar, who sought temporal kingdoms; so he judged him innocent, since Christ understood himself to be king in a different sense from the Jews. And this truth, thus declared through the sequence of the Gospel, namely that Christ was king otherwise than the Jews who accused him had understood, is confirmed by the authority of the saints. Hence Augustine on John says: The faithful Christians are his kingdom, which is not taken away, but rather bought with the blood of Christ. Therefore in Pilate's time only Christians belonged to Christ's kingdom. But if Christ had been king in the sense in which the Jews spoke of a king when they accused Christ, not only Christians but all Jews established in the kingdom of the Jews would have belonged to Christ's kingdom, which is false according to Augustine. Therefore, according to Augustine, Christ was king in a different sense from what the Jews understood. Chrysostom also testifies to this on the words my kingdom is not from here, saying: He does not deprive the world of his providence and pre-eminence, but shows that his kingdom is neither human nor temporal. From these words it is plainly held that Christ did not have a kingdom such as human and worldly kingdoms are; and so he was not king in the sense in which the Jews understood. Augustine clearly teaches this on John 19, saying thus: Hear, Jews and Gentiles; hear, circumcision and uncircumcision; hear, all earthly kingdoms: I do not hinder your dominion in this world, for my kingdom is not of this world. Do not fear with that most vain fear with which that Herod the Elder was terrified, and who killed so many infants, being more cruel through fear than through anger. My kingdom, he says, is not of this world: what more? Do you wish to come to a kingdom which is not of this world? Come by believing, and do not serve out of fear. Indeed, in the prophecy about God the Father it is said: "But I have been established king by him over Sion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his commandment." But Sion and that mountain are not of this world. For what is his kingdom, if not the believers? To them it is said: "You are not of this world, as I am not of this world," although he wished them to be in this world. Therefore concerning these he said to the Father: "I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from evil." Hence here too he does not say: my kingdom is not in this world, but: it is not of this world; proving this, he says: "If my kingdom were of this world, my ministers would surely fight, so that I should not be handed over to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from here." He does not say: it is not here; but: it is not from here. For his kingdom is here until the end of the age, having tares mixed among it up to the harvest. For the harvest is the end of the age, when the reapers, that is, the angels, will come and gather out of his kingdom all the stumbling-blocks. This certainly would not happen if his kingdom were not here; yet it is not from here, because it is a pilgrim in the world. So Augustine. From these words three things are clearly gathered. The first is that the manner of Christ's rule did not in any way hinder earthly dominion and earthly affairs. From this it follows that Christ will not come to reign temporally or secularly, but spiritually alone; for if he had intruded into secular government, he would have hindered secular dominion and would above all have provoked those who held it. The second is that one does not come to Christ's kingdom through secular submission, but through faith, by believing. And consequently Christ's kingdom is not governed secularly in a secular way, but spiritually in a spiritual way. The third is that believers are Christ's kingdom, because the Church is Christ's kingdom. Hence, just as Christ is king and bridegroom, so the Church is kingdom and bride. And for this reason the Church of Christ present in this world is often called in this Gospel the kingdom of heaven, as Gregory testifies in his Homily on the common (state) of virgins, where he says: You must know that in sacred speech the present Church is often called the kingdom of heaven; of which the Lord says in another place: "The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all stumbling-blocks." That kingdom therefore of which Christ says, "My kingdom is not of this world," is his Church, comprising good and bad believers; and for this reason it is also called the kingdom of heaven. From what has been said it is plainly evident that the kingdom of Christ was not Judea, insofar as Judea comprises all the Jews established there, as the Jews who accused Christ understood when they said he called himself king of the Jews; but the kingdom of Christ was the Church of Christ, comprising only those who believe in Christ. And so the kingdom of Christ was not a secular kingdom, but a spiritual kingdom: that is, it was the Church of Christians to be governed spiritually by him.

units.la: Secunda auctoritas principalis, ex qua probatur, quod Christus non fuit rex in secularibus, ex Evangelio Luc. cap. prim. accipitur, vbi Angelus regni eius modum regnandi describens ait: Dabit ei Dominus sedem Dauid patris eius, & regnabit in æternum; & regni eius non erit finis. Ex quibus datur intelligi, quod illo modo & non alio Christus erat rex futurus, quomodo erat in domo Iacob regnaturus. Sed Christus inquantum hoc, quamdiu fuit victurus hac vita mortali, non erat regnaturus seculariter, sed tantum modo spiritualiter. Ergo non erat rex futurus quantum ad secularia, sed quantum ad spiritualia tantum.
units.tr: The second principal authority, by which it is proved that Christ was not a king in secular matters, is taken from the Gospel of Luke, chapter 1, where the angel, describing the manner of his kingdom, says: "The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end" (Luke 1). From these words it is understood that Christ was to be king in that way and in no other, namely as he was to reign over the house of Jacob. But Christ, as long as he was to live this mortal life, was not going to reign in a secular manner, but only in a spiritual manner. Therefore he was not going to be king in secular things, but only in spiritual things.

units.la: Hic videtur probandum, quod Christus inquantum homo mortalis, non regnauit secularier, sed spiritualiter tantum. Sed hoc probatione non indiget. Nam Christus de regimine seculari, maxime de supremo regimine seculari, a quo dicitur aliquis rex, secundum quod nunc loquimur de rege, de temporalibus se nunquam intromisit: quia per Parlamenta & curias, neq; per rebus temporalibus iudicabat, neq; de malefactoribus iustitiam faciebat, neq; expugnauit hostes, neq; militibus stipendia tribuebat, nec alia quæ ad regimen pertinent seculare aliqualiter exercebat. Regnum ergo Christi non seculare, sed spirituale fuit.
units.tr: Here it seems necessary to prove that Christ, as a mortal man, reigned not in a secular manner but only in a spiritual manner. But this needs no proof. For Christ never meddled with secular government, especially the supreme secular government from which one is called a king, which is what we are now speaking of when we speak of a king. He did not judge in parliaments and courts, nor did he decide temporal matters, nor did he do justice upon wrongdoers, nor did he overcome enemies, nor did he pay wages to soldiers, nor did he in any way exercise the other things that pertain to secular rule. Therefore the kingdom of Christ was not secular but spiritual.

units.la: Hoc aperte Glossa super verba prædicta testatur, quæ ait: Dabit illi Dominus Deus sedem Dauid patris eius, id est, Israeliticam plebem, cui Dauid, & filii eius temporalis regni gubernacula prabuere: huiusmodi regnum spirituale datum est à Christo, quando dispositum est à Deo, ut de semine Dauid incarnaretur gentem imperpetuum vocaret regnum, & non solum in illa gente Iudæorum, sed regnabit in æternum, id est, in tota Ecclesia, quæ per fidem & confessionem Christi ad patriarcharum pertinet sortem: sicut in illis, qui de patriarcharum sorte nati sunt in hiis, qui de oleastro exscissi in oliuam bonam sunt inserti. Ex quibus verbis clare patet, quod regnum Christi non erat seculare, sed spirituale, ad quod soli credentes, sive de Iudæis, sive de gentibus, pertinebant.
units.tr: The Gloss on the words quoted clearly bears witness to this, when it says: "The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father," that is, the Israelite people, over whom David and his sons held the reins of temporal rule. A kingdom of this kind, spiritual, was given by Christ when it was ordained by God that he should be incarnate of the seed of David; and it calls the nation "for ever," not only in that nation of the Jews, but "he will reign for ever," that is, in the whole Church, which through faith and confession of Christ belongs to the lot of the patriarchs, just as those who were born of the lot of the patriarchs belong to those who were cut off from the wild olive and grafted into the good olive. From these words it is plainly evident that the kingdom of Christ was not secular but spiritual, and that only believers, whether from the Jews or from the Gentiles, belonged to it.

units.la: Item, quod regnum Christi non fuerit terrenum, seculare siue mundanum, Beda testatur, & poniturin Glossa super illud Matthæi vigesim. prim. Benedictus qui venit: Venit regnum patris nostri Dauid. Atenim secundum Iohannem, cum turba eum rapere vellent, & facere regem, fugit & regnum adhuc victurus noluit. Nunc autem iam passurus regnum non refugit, sed dici modo hymnos fidei filio Dei & rege dignos non eos reprimit, qui regnum Dauid in eo restaurandum & perfectam benedictionis dona continent: quia scilicet non temporalis & terreni, sed æterni in cœlis rex esset imperii, ad quod qui perceperunt gloriam resurrectionis & triumphum ascensionis peruenirent. Unde discipulis post propositionem ait: Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo, & in terra. Ex his patet, quod regnum Christi non erat terrenum & temporale. Huic concordat Leo Papa in sermone de Epiphania, sic dicens: Herodes vero audiens Iudæorum principem natum, successorem suspicatus expauit. Et paruum post: O cæca stulta æmulationis impietas, quæ perturbandum putat diuinum tuo furore consilium. Dominus mundi temporale non quærit regnum, qui præstat æternum.
units.tr: Likewise, that the kingdom of Christ was not earthly, secular or worldly, is attested by Bede, and it is set down in the Gloss on Matthew 21, "Blessed is he who comes: the kingdom of our father David comes" (Matt. 21). But according to John, when the crowd wanted to seize him and make him king, he fled and would not accept a kingdom while he was still to live. Now, however, when he was about to suffer, he did not refuse a kingdom, and he did not rebuke those who now sang hymns of faith, fitting for the Son of God and a king, who expected that the kingdom of David would be restored in him together with the full gifts of blessing. For he would be a king of an empire not temporal and earthly but eternal in heaven, to which those who had received the glory of the resurrection and the triumph of the ascension would attain. Hence after the resurrection he said to the disciples: "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth" (Matt. 28). From this it is evident that the kingdom of Christ was not earthly and temporal. Pope Leo agrees with this in his sermon on the Epiphany, saying thus: "Herod, hearing that the prince of the Jews was born, suspected a successor and was terrified." And a little later: "O blind, foolish impiety of rivalry, which thinks that the divine counsel can be disturbed by your rage! The Lord of the world does not seek a temporal kingdom, he who bestows an eternal one."

units.la: Eccee num. Ex his colligitur, quod Christus in quantum homo, regnum temporale non habuit. Item, sanctus Fulgentius in Sermone de Epiphania dicit: Munus vero auri regem demonstrat Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, non vtique talem regem, qui suam imaginem in solidis accipit, sed qui suam imaginem in ipsis hominibus quærit. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod Christus non erat talis rex, quales sunt reges, quia suas imagines in nummis quærunt; & ita in temporalibus nequaquam fuit rex censendus. Hoc idem testatur Rabanus, vt iste allegat, sicut superius apparebit.
units.tr: Behold, then. From these things it is gathered that Christ, as a man, did not have a temporal kingdom. Likewise, Saint Fulgentius in his sermon on the Epiphany says: The gift of gold indeed shows our Lord Jesus Christ to be a king, not indeed such a king as receives his image on solid coins, but one who seeks his image in men themselves. From these words it is plainly held that Christ was not the kind of king that kings are, since they seek their images on coins; and so he is by no means to be counted a king in temporal matters. Rabanus bears witness to the same thing, as this writer cites, as will appear above.

units.la: Restat nunc eandem assertionem ostendere per rationes sacris auctoritatibus roboratas. Est autem prima ratio talis, qui non est iudex litium secularium, nec diuisor hereditatum & facultatum, non est rex in temporalibus.
units.tr: It remains now to show the same assertion by reasons strengthened by sacred authorities. The first reason is this: whoever is not a judge of secular lawsuits, nor a divider of inheritances and property, is not a king in temporal matters.

units.la: Prædicta enim ad regis officium pertinere noscuntur. Sed Christus non fuit iudex litium, nec diuisor hereditatum & terrenarum facultatum. Ergo Christus non fuit rex in temporalibus seu secularibus & terrenis. Maior est nota. Minor auctoritate Christi & Beati Ambrosii manifeste probatur. Cum enim, vt legitur Lucæ duodecimo, quidam de turba diceret Christo: Magister dic fratri meo vt diuidat mecum hereditatem. Christus respondit: Homo, quis me constituit iudicem, aut diuisorem super vos? quasi diceret, nullus. Ergo Christus non erat iudex litium, nec diuisor hereditatum. Quod Beatus Ambrosius ibidem asserit manifeste dicens: Bene ergo terrena declinat, qui propter diuina descenderat. Nec iudex dignatur esse litium & arbiter facultatum, viuorum habens mortuorumque iudicium, arbitrium quæ meritorum. Et parum post: Vnde merito refutatur hic frater, qui dispensatorem cælestium gestiebat terrena occupare. His clarius dici non potest, quod Christus nequaquam fuit iudex litium secularium, nec terrenarum arbiter facultatum; & per consequens non fuit rex in secularibus reputandus.
units.tr: For the things just mentioned are known to belong to the office of a king. But Christ was not a judge of lawsuits, nor a divider of inheritances and earthly property. Therefore Christ was not a king in temporal or secular and earthly matters. The major premise is well known. The minor is plainly proved by the authority of Christ and of Blessed Ambrose. For when, as we read in Luke 12, a certain man from the crowd said to Christ, Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me, Christ answered, Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you? as if to say, no one. Therefore Christ was not a judge of lawsuits, nor a divider of inheritances. Blessed Ambrose plainly asserts this in the same place, saying: Rightly, then, he avoids earthly things, who came down for divine things. Nor does he deign to be a judge of lawsuits and an arbiter of property, he who holds the judgment of the living and the dead, the arbitration of merits. And a little later: Hence this brother is rightly rejected, who desired to take over earthly affairs, the steward of heavenly things. Nothing could be said more clearly than this: Christ was by no means a judge of secular lawsuits, nor an arbiter of earthly property; and consequently he is not to be regarded as a king in secular matters.

units.la: Secunda ratio pro eadem assertione est hæc: Qui verbo & exemplo docuit regna temporalia contemnenda, non debet rex in temporalibus reputari. Sed Christus verbo & exemplo docuit regna temporalia contemnenda. Quod enim verbo docuit, principatus & regna temporalia contemni debere, patet aperte per illud Matth. vigesimo: Iesus autem vocavit ad se, & ait: Scitis quia principes gentium dominantur eorum, & qui maiores sunt, potestatem exercent in eos; non ita erit inter vos, sed quicunque voluerit inter vos maior esse, sit vester minister. &c. Ex quibus verbis patenter elicitur, quod Christus principatus & potestatem temporalem super alios, & per consequens temporalia regna verbo docuit contemni debere. Quod etiam regna temporalia exemplo docuerit contemnenda, patet clare per illud Iohan. sexto: Iesus ergo cum cognovisset, quia venturi essent, vt raperent eum & facerent eum regem, fugit iterum in montem. Vbi Chrysostomus ait: Propheta iam erat apud eos, & regem eum intronizare volebant propter gulam, quia, scilicet pauerat eos. Christus autem fugit, erudiens nos mundanas fugere dignitates: & per consequens instruxit nos exemplo mundana contemnere regna. Ergo Christus nequaquam rex fuit in temporalibus: quia aliter tam in verbis, quam in factis sibiipsi fuisset contrarius, vnum dicens verbo & aliud faciens exemplo.
units.tr: The second reason for the same assertion is this: whoever taught by word and example that temporal kingdoms are to be despised ought not to be regarded as a king in temporal matters. But Christ taught by word and example that temporal kingdoms are to be despised. That he taught by word that principalities and temporal kingdoms ought to be despised is plain from Matthew 20: But Jesus called them to himself and said: You know that the princes of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise power over them; it shall not be so among you, but whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him be your minister, and so on. From these words it is clearly drawn that Christ taught by word that principality and temporal power over others, and consequently temporal kingdoms, ought to be despised. That he also taught by example that kingdoms are to be despised is clear from John 6: Jesus therefore, when he knew that they were going to come and seize him and make him king, fled again into the mountain. Where Chrysostom says: He was already a prophet among them, and they wanted to enthrone him as king because of their belly, because, namely, he had fed them. But Christ fled, teaching us to flee worldly dignities, and consequently he instructed us by example to despise worldly kingdoms. Therefore Christ was by no means a king in temporal matters; for otherwise he would have been contrary to himself, both in words and in deeds, saying one thing in word and doing another by example.

units.la: Tertia ratio est hæc: Qui regnum suscepit gubernandum & de regimine ipsius se nullatenus intromittit, quamuis possit, de malitia & nequitia vel negligentia merito est arguendus, quia talis vult habere nomen regis & officium, & quæ regis sunt minime exercere, quod malitiæ vel negligentiæ est penitus abscindendum. Sed Christus de singulari regimine cuiuscunq; regni se nullatenus intromisit. Ergo vel non suscepit regnum gubernandum: nec fuit rex per consequens, vel fuit de malitia & negligentia arguendus: sed neq; malitia neq; negligentia sibi debet imponi. Ergo secundum est, quod inquantum homo mortalis, nullum regnum suscepit regendum: & per consequens nec rem nec nomen regis secularis obtinuit.
units.tr: The third reason is this: whoever has received a kingdom to govern and in no way meddles with its government, although he could, ought rightly to be accused of malice, or negligence. For such a person wants to have the name and office of king, and yet does not exercise the things that belong to a king; and this must be utterly cut away as malice or negligence. But Christ in no way meddled with the particular government of any kingdom whatever. Therefore either he did not receive a kingdom to govern, and so was not a king, or he ought to be accused of malice and negligence; but neither malice nor negligence can be imputed to him. Therefore the second alternative holds: as a mortal man he received no kingdom to rule, and consequently he obtained neither the reality nor the name of a secular king.

units.la: Quarta ratio est hæc: In eodem regno seculari non possunt esse plures veri reges non habentes regnum pro indiuiso, quorum neuter recognoscit regnum ab altero. Sed Imperator Romanorum tempore Christi fuit verus rex Iudææ, quamuis fuisset rex aliorum regnorum, & constat quod Christus & Imperator non tenebant regnum Iudææ pro indiuiso, nec Christus recognoscebat regnum Iudææ ab Imperatore, nec Imperator a Christo. Ergo Christus non fuit verus rex secularis Iudææ, & per consequens a simili non fuit verus rex secularis cuiuscunq; alterius regni.
units.tr: The fourth reason is this: in the same secular kingdom there cannot be several true kings who do not hold the kingdom undivided, and neither of whom acknowledges the kingdom from the other. But the Emperor of the Romans at the time of Christ was the true king of Judea, although he was also king of other kingdoms. It is clear that Christ and the Emperor did not hold the kingdom of Judea undivided, that Christ did not acknowledge the kingdom of Judea from the Emperor, and that the Emperor did not acknowledge it from Christ. Therefore Christ was not a true secular king of Judea, and by similar reasoning he was not a true secular king of any other kingdom.

units.la: Hic videntur tria probanda. Primum est, quod Cæsar seu Imperator fuit rex Iudææ. Hoc ex Euangelio elicitur euidenter, Christo dicente: Reddite quæ sunt Cæsaris Cæsari. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod illa quæ Cæsar vendicauit in Iudæa, vere erant sua. Sed Cæsar tanquam rex Iudææ & Dominus vendicauit tributum. Ergo tributum erat ipsius, tanquam regis & Domini. Ergo ipse vere fuit rex. Secundum hic probandum est, quod Cæsar non recognoscebat regnum a Christo, nec recognoscere tenebatur. Nam ante natiuitatem Christi Cæsar fuit rex verus: sed post natiuitatem Christi regnum Cæsaris non fuit in aliquo diminutum, nec immutatum, nec in aliquam subiectionem redactum. Ergo sicut ante natiuitatem Christi non tenebatur ab aliquo homine recognoscere regnum quodcunq;: ita post natiuitatem non tenebatur ab homine in quantum homo recognoscere regnum: & ita non tenebatur recognoscere a Christo regnum in quantum erat homo. Tertium, quod videtur probandum est, quod Christus non recognoscebat regnum a Cæsare. Sed hoc probatione non indiget, cum regnum aliquod nunquam vendicauerat, sed rex fieri recusabat, & fugit ne sublimaretur in regem, sicut patet Ioh. 6.
units.tr: Three things seem to need proof here. The first is that Caesar, or the Emperor, was king of Judea. This is plainly drawn from the Gospel, where Christ says: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's." From these words it is gathered that what Caesar claimed in Judea truly belonged to him. But Caesar claimed tribute as king and lord of Judea. Therefore the tribute was his, as king and lord. Therefore he truly was king. The second thing to be proved is that Caesar did not acknowledge his kingdom from Christ, nor was he bound to do so. For before the birth of Christ Caesar was a true king; but after the birth of Christ Caesar's kingdom was not diminished in any way, nor changed, nor brought under any subjection. Therefore, just as before the birth of Christ he was not bound to acknowledge any kingdom from any man, so after that birth he was not bound, as a man, to acknowledge a kingdom from a man; and thus he was not bound to acknowledge his kingdom from Christ insofar as Christ was a man. The third thing that seems to need proof is that Christ did not acknowledge the kingdom from Caesar. But this needs no proof, since Christ never claimed any kingdom; rather, he refused to become king and fled lest he be raised up as king, as appears in John 6.

units.la: Quinta ratio est: Si Christus fuit rex alicuius regni temporalis, non est maior ratio, quare fuerat rex vnius regni temporalis, quam alterius, nisi quis dicat quod quia filius Dauid, specialiter fuerit rex Iudææ: sequitur quod fuerit rex omnium regnorum, vel specialiter Iudææ. Sed neutrum potest dici: quia sive fuerit rex omnium regnorum, sive specialiter Iudaeorum: omnes Iudaei saltem in Iudaea constituti pertinuissent ad regnum eius. Sed non omnes Iudaei in Iudaea constituti pertinebant ad regnum eius. Ergo non fuit rex temporalis Iudaeorum: & per consequens multo magis non fuit rex temporalis alterius regni. Hic probandum est, quod non omnes Iudaei etiam in Iudaea constituti pertinebant ad regnum Christi, inquantum erat homo mortalis, licet omnes pertineant ad regnum eius inquantum erat Deus: per Glossam super Ioh. 19. Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum, probatur aperte, cum ait: corde, non carne. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod Christus erat tantum modo Rex Iudaeorum, qui erant Iudaei corde; quales fuerunt fideles, & non carne tantum modo, quales fuerunt infideles. Ergo Iudaei non credentes in Christum non pertinebant ad regnum Christi inquantum fuit homo. Hoc etiam patet, quia regnum Christi erat Ecclesia Christi: cum secundum Gregor. ut allegatum est supra, regnum coelorum, quod est regnum Christi, sit Ecclesia praesentis temporis. Sed Iudaei non credentes in Christum non pertinebant ad Ecclesiam Christi. Ergo non pertinebant ad regnum Christi. Hoc etiam tertio patet: quia sicut idem Christus fuit & est sponsus, rex & pastor: ita eadem congregatio fuit sponsa Christi, regnum & ovile. Sed ad ovile Christi non pertinebant Iudaei non credentes, nec credituri in Christum, ipso Christo testante, qui Ioh. 10. ait: Ego sum pastor & cognosco oves meas & cognoscunt me meae. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod omnes oves Christi cognoverunt Christum per fidem. Ergo Iudaei non credentes non fuerunt oves Christi, & per consequens non pertinebant ad ovile Christi. Ex quo sequitur, quod non pertinebant ad regnum. Hoc etiam per plures auctoritates superius allegatas, quibus asseritur, quod credentes erant regnum Christi, patet aperte: & ita Christus non fuit rex in saecularibus.
units.tr: The fifth reason is this: if Christ was king of some temporal kingdom, there is no greater reason why he should have been king of one temporal kingdom rather than another, unless someone says that, because he was the son of David, he was king of Judea in particular. Then it follows that he was king of all kingdoms, or king of Judea in particular. But neither can be said. For whether he was king of all kingdoms or king of the Jews in particular, all Jews, at least those established in Judea, would have belonged to his kingdom. But not all Jews established in Judea belonged to his kingdom. Therefore he was not a temporal king of the Jews, and consequently much less was he a temporal king of any other kingdom. Here it must be proved that not all Jews, even those established in Judea, belonged to the kingdom of Christ insofar as he was a mortal man, although all belong to his kingdom insofar as he was God. This is shown by the Gloss on John 19, "Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews," where it is plainly proved, since it says "by heart, not by flesh." From these words it is held that Christ was King of the Jews only in the case of those who were Jews in heart, such as the faithful, and not merely Jews in flesh, such as the unbelieving. Therefore Jews who did not believe in Christ did not belong to Christ's kingdom insofar as he was a man. This is also evident because the kingdom of Christ was the Church of Christ, since according to Gregory, as was alleged above, the kingdom of heaven, which is the kingdom of Christ, is the Church of the present time. But Jews who did not believe in Christ did not belong to the Church of Christ. Therefore they did not belong to the kingdom of Christ. This is shown a third way as well: just as the same Christ was and is bridegroom, king and shepherd, so the same congregation was the bride, the kingdom and the flock of Christ. But unbelieving Jews did not belong to the fold of Christ, nor were they to belong to it, Christ himself testifying, who says in John 10: "I am the shepherd, and I know my sheep, and my sheep know me." From these words it is gathered that all the sheep of Christ knew Christ through faith. Therefore unbelieving Jews were not sheep of Christ, and consequently did not belong to his fold. From this it follows that they did not belong to the kingdom. This is also plainly shown by the many authorities cited above, by which it is asserted that believers were the kingdom of Christ. And so Christ was not a king in secular affairs.

units.la: Sexta ratio est haec: illud fuit regnum Christi, de quo prophetaverunt Prophetae. Sed Prophetae prophetantes de regno Christi futuro, non prophetaverunt de regno aliquo temporali. Ergo nec regnum aliquod temporale fuit regnum Christi. Maior est clara. Minor probatur: quia regnum Christi, de quo prophetaverunt Prophetae, erat per Christum reparandum & restaurandum, teste Esaia, qui c. 9. ait: Parvulus enim natus est nobis & factus est principatus super humerum eius, & vocabitur nomen eius admirabilis, Deus, fortis, pater futuri saeculi, princeps pacis, multiplicabitur eius imperium, & pacis non erit finis. Super solium David, & super regnum eius sedebit, ut confirmet illud & corroboret illud in iudicio & iustitia a modo & usque in sempiternum. Ex quibus verbis clare colligitur, quod regnum Christi, de quo prophetavit Esaias, erat per ipsum confirmandum & corroborandum: & per consequens reparandum & restaurandum. Hier. 23. prophetavit Hieremias de Christo dicens: Ecce dies veniunt, dicit Dominus: & suscitabo David germen iustum, & regnabit rex & sapiens erit, & faciet iudicium & iustitiam in terra. In diebus illis salvabitur Iuda & Israel habitabit confidenter: & hoc nomen, quod vocabunt eum, Dominus iustus noster. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod qui erant futuri de regno Christi, erant saluandi & habituri confidenter. Ergo regnum coelorum, de quo prophetavit Hieremias in verbis praedictis, erat reparandum per Christum. Sed regnum Iudaeae temporale non extitit per Christum reparatum, nec etiam restauratum; sed potius dissipatum: quia propter peccata, quae commiserunt in Christum, fuit destructum. Unde & eversionem Hierusalem, quae erat metropolis in regno Iudaeae, ipse praedixit, ut habetur Lucae 19. ubi sic legitur: ut appropinquavit, videns civitatem fleuit super eam, dicens: quia si cognovisses & tu. Et quidem in hac die tua, quae ad pacem tibi. Nunc autem abscondita sunt ab oculis tuis. Quia venient dies in te & circumdabunt te inimici tui vallo, & circumdabunt te, & coangustabunt te undique, & ad terram prosternent te, & filios tuos qui in te sunt: & non derelinquent lapidem super lapidem, eo quod non cognoveris tempus visitationis tuae. Ex quibus verbis colligitur evidenter, quod regnum Iudaeae per Christum non fuit temporaliter reparatum, sed postea: quia tempus visitationis suae spiritualis non cognovit, sed Christum persequebatur ad mortem, extitit dissipatum. Regnum ergo Christi, de quo prodixerunt Prophetae, non fuit regnum temporale. Nec prosperitas quam tunc Prophetae prophetaverunt futuram debet intelligi temporalis, sed spiritualis propter abundantiam gratiarum & spiritualium charismatum, quibus Christus in se credentes, qui erant regnum, affluentissime honorauit, confirmavit & corroboravit & saluavit, ac inter mundi aduersitates confidentes reddidit & securos.
units.tr: The sixth reason is this: that was the kingdom of Christ of which the prophets prophesied. But the prophets, prophesying of the future kingdom of Christ, did not prophesy of any temporal kingdom. Therefore no temporal kingdom was the kingdom of Christ. The major premise is clear. The minor is proved because the kingdom of Christ, of which the prophets prophesied, was to be repaired and restored by Christ, as Isaiah witnesses, who says in chapter 9: "For unto us a child is born, and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace. Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom, to order it, and to establish it with judgment and with justice from henceforth even for ever." From these words it is clearly gathered that the kingdom of Christ, of which Isaiah prophesied, was to be confirmed and strengthened by him, and consequently repaired and restored. Jeremiah prophesied of Christ in Jeremiah 23, saying: "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely; and this is his name whereby he shall be called, The Lord our righteousness." From these words it is gathered that those who were to be of the kingdom of Christ were to be saved and to dwell securely. Therefore the kingdom of heaven, of which Jeremiah prophesied in the words cited, was to be repaired by Christ. But the temporal kingdom of Judea was not repaired or restored by Christ; rather it was scattered, since it was destroyed because of the sins they committed against Christ. Hence he himself also foretold the overthrow of Jerusalem, which was the metropolis in the kingdom of Judea, as is found in Luke 19, where it is read thus: "And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it, saying, If thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace! but now they are hid from thine eyes. For the days shall come upon thee, that thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side, and shall lay thee even with the ground, and thy children within thee; and they shall not leave in thee one stone upon another; because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation." From these words it is evidently gathered that the kingdom of Judea was not repaired temporally by Christ, but afterwards, because it did not recognise the time of its spiritual visitation, but persecuted Christ to death, it was scattered. The kingdom of Christ, of which the prophets spoke, was therefore not a temporal kingdom. Nor should the prosperity which the prophets then foretold be understood as temporal, but as spiritual, on account of the abundance of graces and spiritual gifts with which Christ most richly honoured, confirmed, strengthened and saved those who believed in him, who were the kingdom, and made them confident and secure amid the adversities of the world.

units.la: Septima ratio est haec: Christus non decetnens inter vnum officium sibi commissum & aliud, beatum Petrum vicarium suum instituit, dicens: Pasce oves meas. Ergo Christus quantum ad omne officium, quod habuit inquantum homo, respectu subditorum suorum beatum Petrum vicarium suum instituit. Sed beatus Petrus non fuit vicarius Christi quantum ad officium regni temporalis. Ergo nec Christus habuit officium regni temporalis: & per consequens regnum Christi non fuit temporale, sed spirituale; quale regnum beato Petro commisit, cum dixit: Pasce oves meas. Et prius promiserat dicens: Et tibi dabo claves regni coelorum.
units.tr: The seventh reason is this: Christ, who did not divide himself between one office committed to him and another, appointed his vicar, the blessed Peter, saying: "Feed my sheep." Therefore Christ appointed the blessed Peter as his vicar with respect to every office he held as man, in relation to his subjects. But the blessed Peter was not Christ's vicar with respect to the office of a temporal kingdom. Therefore Christ did not hold the office of a temporal kingdom either, and consequently the kingdom of Christ was not temporal but spiritual. It was this kind of kingdom that he committed to the blessed Peter when he said, "Feed my sheep." He had earlier promised it, saying: "And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven."

units.la: Hic oportet probare, quod Beatus Petrus non fuit vicarius Christi quantum ad officium regni temporalis, nec etiam in temporalibus quibuscunque. Hoc autem probatur primo sic. Si Beatus Petrus fuisset vicarius Christi quantum ad officium regni temporalis in aliquo regno temporali, Beatus Petrus habuisset potestatem iudicandi omnes, & de omnibus, non solum credentibus, sed etiam non credentibus constitutis in regno sibi subiecto. Sed Beatus Petrus de infidelibus, qui nunquam fidem Christi suscepterunt, habuit minime iudicare, teste Apostolo, qui imperia omnium praelatorum Ecclesiae dixit, 1. Corinth. 5. Quid mihi de his qui foris sunt iudicare? Ergo Beatus Petrus de his, qui foris erant in quocunque regno non habuit iudicare: & ita non fuit vicarius Christi in quocunque regno temporali. Secundo sic: qui est vicarius generalis alicuius regis temporalis in aliquo regno non habentis superiorem, habet iurisdictionem temporalem super omnes constitutos in regno, qui per regem minime sunt exempti. Sed Christus instituendo beatum Petrum vicarium, nullum exemit a iurisdictione Beati Petri. Ergo Beatus Petrus habuit iurisdictionem temporalem super omnes constitutos in regno. Ita cum regnum ipsi non plus fuerit vnum quam aliud: sequitur, quod Beatus Petrus habuit iurisdictionem super imperatorem, & omnes alios reges. Ex quo sequitur, quod cum Romanus pontifex sit successor Beati Petri sibi aequalis in potestate a Christo sibi concessa, quilibet Romanus pontifex habuit iurisdictionem temporalem super Imperatorem Romanorum & omnes alios reges mundi, quod sacris canonibus repugnat aperte. Vnde Nicolaus Papa, vt habetur dist. 96. cap. cum ad verum, sic ait: Cum ad verum ventum est, vltra sibi nec Imperatoris iura pontificatus arripuit, nec pontifex nomen Imperatoris vsurpauit, quoniam idem mediator Dei & hominum Christus Iesus actibus propriis & dignitatibus distinctis officia potestatis virtusque discreuit. Ex his datur intelligi, quod Romanus Episcopus ex successione Beati Petri non habet iurisdictionem temporalem super Imperatorem. Quod etiam Papa non habeat iurisdictionem super alios reges, testari videtur Innocentius tertius, qui, vt habetur extra de iudiciis, cap. 13. ait: non putet aliquis quod iurisdictionem illustris regis Francorum perturbare aut minuere intendamus &c. Non ergo Papa super regem Francorum iurisdictionem obtinet temporalem. Item, si Papa haberet ex successione Beati Petri iurisdictionem temporalem super reges, multo magis ex eadem successione haberet iurisdictionem temporalem super possessiones eorum & aliorum. Cuius contrarium asserit Bernhardus aperte, qui scribens ad Eugenium ait lib. 1. cap. quint. Ergo in criminibus non in possessionibus potestas vestra. Propter illa siquidem, & non propter has, accepistis claues regni coelorum. Praevaricatores itaque excludi non possessiones, vt sciatis, ait, quia filius hominis habet potestatem in terra dimittendi peccata. Et infra subdit: Quae nam tibi videtur maior dignitas & potestas, dimittendi peccata, aut pradia diuidendi? habent haec infima & terrena iudicis suos reges, & principes terra. Quid fines alienos invaditis? quid falcem vestram in alienam messem extenditis? Ex quibus veribus patet, quod Papa per potestatem sibi datam a Christo super possessiones iurisdictionem non obtinet. Ex his aliisque quamplurimis patet quod Beatus Petrus iurisdictionem temporalem super Imperatorem & reges non habuit: & ita non fuit vicarius Christi in aliquo regno temporali. Sed forte aliquis praedictis obiiciet. Primo per auctoritatem Nicolai Papae, quae ponitur dist. vigesim. secund. cap. prim. vbi sic legitur: Illam vero solus fundauit ipse & super petram fidei mox nascentis extitit, qui Beato Petro aeterna vita claujgero aeterni simul & coelestis Imperii iura commisit. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod Beatus Petrus iura obtinuit terreni Imperii, & per consequens iurisdictiones habuit super terrenum Imperatorem. Quod etiam successores Beati Petri iurisdictione habeant super Imperatores & reges, probatur.
units.tr: Here it must be proved that the blessed Peter was not Christ's vicar with respect to the office of a temporal kingdom, nor in any temporal matters whatever. This is first proved as follows. If the blessed Peter had been Christ's vicar with respect to the office of a temporal kingdom in some temporal realm, the blessed Peter would have had power to judge all men, and about all matters, not only over believers but also over unbelievers living in the kingdom subject to him. But the blessed Peter had no right to judge unbelievers, who had never received the faith of Christ, as the Apostle testifies, who spoke of the judgment of all prelates of the Church, saying, 1 Corinthians 5: "What have I to do with judging those who are outside?" Therefore the blessed Peter had no right to judge those who were outside any kingdom, and so he was not Christ's vicar in any temporal kingdom. Second, as follows: whoever is the general vicar of some temporal king in a kingdom having no superior has temporal jurisdiction over all who live in the kingdom and who are not exempted by the king. But Christ, in appointing the blessed Peter as vicar, exempted no one from the jurisdiction of the blessed Peter. Therefore the blessed Peter had temporal jurisdiction over all who lived in the kingdom. Since the kingdom was no more one thing to him than another, it follows that the blessed Peter had jurisdiction over the emperor and all other kings. From this it follows that, since the Roman pontiff is the successor of the blessed Peter, equal to him in the power granted to him by Christ, every Roman pontiff would have temporal jurisdiction over the Emperor of the Romans and all other kings of the world. This plainly contradicts the sacred canons. Hence Pope Nicholas, as found in dist. 96, cap. "Cum ad verum," says: "When it came to the truth, the pontificate neither seized the rights of the Emperor any further, nor did the pontiff usurp the name of Emperor, since the same mediator between God and men, Christ Jesus, by his own acts and distinct dignities, separated the offices of each power." From these things it can be understood that the Roman bishop, by succession from the blessed Peter, does not have temporal jurisdiction over the Emperor. That the Pope does not have jurisdiction over other kings also seems to be attested by Innocent III, who, as found in Extra de iudiciis, cap. 13, says: "let no one think that we intend to disturb or diminish the jurisdiction of the illustrious king of the Franks, etc." Therefore the Pope does not hold temporal jurisdiction over the king of the Franks. Likewise, if the Pope had temporal jurisdiction over kings by succession from the blessed Peter, he would far more by the same succession have temporal jurisdiction over their possessions and those of others. The opposite is plainly asserted by Bernard, who, writing to Eugenius, says in book 1, chapter 5: "Your power, then, is over crimes, not over possessions. For it is on account of those that you have received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, not on account of these. Therefore, so that you may know, he says, that the transgressors are excluded, not the possessions, because the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins." And below he adds: "What greater dignity and power do you think there is, to forgive sins, or to divide estates? These lowly and earthly things have their own judges, the kings and princes of the earth. Why do you invade other people's boundaries? Why do you stretch your sickle into another's harvest?" From these words it is clear that the Pope, by the power given him by Christ, does not hold jurisdiction over possessions. From these and very many other things it is clear that the blessed Peter had no temporal jurisdiction over the Emperor and kings, and so he was not Christ's vicar in any temporal kingdom. But perhaps someone will object to the foregoing, first by the authority of Pope Nicholas, which is set out in dist. 22, cap. 1, where it is read thus: "He alone founded that Church and it stood upon the rock of the newly born faith, he who entrusted to the blessed Peter, keeper of eternal life, the rights of both the eternal and the heavenly empire." From these words it is clear that the blessed Peter obtained the rights of an earthly empire, and consequently had jurisdiction over the earthly Emperor. That the successors of the blessed Peter also have jurisdiction over emperors and kings is proved as follows.

units.la: Primo: quia deponit Imperatores & reges, vt patet 15. q. 6. ca. alius. Item, Romanum transfert Imperium, extra de electione. cap. venerabilem. Ergo super Imperium iurisdictionem nobis citur obtinere. Item, Imperator praestat ei iuramentum fidelitatis: ergo sibi in temporalibus est subiectus. Item, quod Papa Romanus iurisdictionem habeat temporalem, videmus ad sensum. Sed Papa non est maioris potestatis, quam fuerit Beatus Petrus. Ergo & Beatus Petrus iurisdictionem huiusmodi temporalem: sed non habuit iurisdictionem huiusmodi temporalem limitatam. Ergo reges & alii sibi temporaliter subiecti fuerunt.
units.tr: First: because he deposes emperors and kings, as is clear from 15 q. 6, cap. "Alius." Likewise, he transfers the Roman Empire, Extra de electione, cap. "Venerabilem." Therefore we seem to hold jurisdiction over the Empire. Likewise, the Emperor swears an oath of fealty to him; therefore he is subject to him in temporal matters. Likewise, we see with our own senses that the Roman Pope has temporal jurisdiction. But the Pope is not of greater power than the blessed Peter was. Therefore the blessed Peter also had such temporal jurisdiction; but he did not have such temporal jurisdiction limited. Therefore kings and others were subject to him temporally.

units.la: Ad primum istorum dicunt aliqui istorum impugnatorum, quod per Imperium terrenum & coelestem intellexit Nicolaus Papa bonos & malos in Ecclesia militante: & ita per terrenum Imperium non intellexit dignitatem imperialem terrenam. Hoc declarant sic: per imperium coeleste non potest Nicolaus Papa intelligere aliud, quam bonos in Ecclesia militante: quia per Imperium coeleste non potest intelligere bonos existentes in Ecclesia triumphante, cum super illos Petrus nullam iurisdictionem habuerit. Ergo consimiliter per terrenum imperium intelligit Nicolaus Papa malos in Ecclesia militante, & ita per dictam auctoritatem non potest concludi, quod Beatus Petrus super Imperatorem iurisdictionem habuerit temporalem, sed quod super bonos & malos in Ecclesia militante iurisdictionem habuerit temporalem. Ad quintum dicunt, quod Papa Romanus illam iurisdictionem temporalem, quam noscitur obtinere, non habuerit ex successione Beati Petri, quia tunc non haberet maiorem iurisdictionem temporalem in vna regione, quam in alia, sicut nec Beatus Petrus, quod tamen noscitur esse falsum. Non ergo ratione successionis, sed collatione fidelium, Papa habuit iurisdictionem in diuersis regionibus temporalem. Et haec est sententia Bernhardi, vt adductum est alibi. Et cum dicitur, quod Papa non est maioris potestatis quam fuerit Beatus Petrus. Dicunt, quod quo ad spiritualia Papa non est maioris potestatis quam fuerit Beatus Petrus: sed quo ad temporalia, maiorem habet potestatem, sicut ditior est quam fuerit Beatus Petrus. Ad secundum dicunt dupliciter. Vno modo, quod ratione criminis Imperator Christianus subest Papae, & idem dicitur de aliis regibus. Et ita Papa super reges ratione criminis & Imperatores iurisdictionem habet spiritualem, & non temporalem. Aliter dicunt, quod licet Papa habeat iurisdictionem temporalem super Imperatorem & reges alios, tamen talem iurisdictionem temporalem habere sibi non repugnat. Et ideo Papa tam Romanus quam alius iurisdictionem super Imperatorem quam super regem non habet in personam superiorem, qui in casu noscitur obtinere, potest in persona Papae transferre, & etiam auctoritate Papae potest Imperatorem vel regem deponere. Et sic legitur deposuisse regem Franciae 15. q. 6. c. alius, vbi super illo verbo deposuit, dicit Glossa, dicitur deposuisse, quia deponentibus consensit, hoc est auctoritate Papae reputantis regem deponendum, eundem regem deposuerunt. Et illo modo posset archiepiscopus vel episcopus aliquem regem deponere. re, non ratione officii specialis, sed auctoritate Papæ sibi potestatem huiusmodi conferentis. Ad tertiam dicunt nonnulli, quod Papa transfert Romanum Imperium, non in quantum successor beati Petri, sed auctoritate Romanorum, qui sibi potestatem huiusmodi concesserunt. Ad quartam dicunt aliqui, quod Imperator, qui primus iurauit Papæ ex devotione vel humilitate aut ex ordinatione Romanorum sibi iurauit: & ideo alii prædecessores ipsius, qui sibi minime iurauerunt, vel sibi debitum ex successione beati Petri aliqualiter subtraxerunt, sibi iurare nullatenus tenebantur. Ex prædictis colligitur, quod beatus Petrus huiusmodi regnum temporale suscepit à Christo. Quare nec Christus regnum aliquod habuit temporale.
units.tr: To the first of these, some of these opponents reply that by the earthly and heavenly empire Pope Nicholas meant the good and the wicked in the Church militant, and so by the earthly empire he did not mean the earthly imperial dignity. They explain this as follows: by the heavenly empire Pope Nicholas can mean nothing other than the good in the Church militant, because by the heavenly empire one cannot mean the good existing in the Church triumphant, since Peter had no jurisdiction over them. Therefore, in the same way, by the earthly empire Pope Nicholas means the wicked in the Church militant, and so from the said authority it cannot be concluded that the blessed Peter had temporal jurisdiction over the Emperor, but only that he had temporal jurisdiction over the good and the wicked in the Church militant. To the fifth argument they say that the Roman Pope did not have that temporal jurisdiction which he is known to hold by succession from the blessed Peter, because then he would not have greater temporal jurisdiction in one region than in another, just as Peter did not; which, however, is known to be false. Therefore the Pope held temporal jurisdiction in different regions not by succession but by the gift of the faithful. This is also the view of Bernard, as cited elsewhere. And when it is said that the Pope is not of greater power than the blessed Peter, they reply that as regards spiritual matters the Pope is not of greater power than the blessed Peter, but as regards temporal matters he has greater power, just as he is richer than the blessed Peter was. To the second argument they reply in two ways. In one way, that by reason of crime a Christian emperor is subject to the Pope, and the same is said of other kings; and so the Pope has spiritual jurisdiction over kings and emperors by reason of crime, and not temporal jurisdiction. In another way they say that although the Pope has temporal jurisdiction over the Emperor and other kings, it is nonetheless not inconsistent for him to have such temporal jurisdiction. And therefore the Pope, whether Roman or any other, does not have jurisdiction over the Emperor or over a king in the way that a superior person has it; whatever is known to be held in such a case may be transferred to the person of the Pope, and by the authority of the Pope the Emperor or a king may also be deposed. And thus it is read that he deposed the king of France, 15 q. 6, cap. "Alius," where, on the words "he deposed," the Gloss says: "he is said to have deposed him, because he consented to those who deposed him; that is, by the authority of the Pope, who judged the king ought to be deposed, they deposed that same king." In that way an archbishop or bishop could depose some king, not by reason of a special office, but by the authority of the Pope who confers such power on them.
