To the third argument some reply that the Pope transfers the Roman Empire not as successor of the blessed Peter but by the authority of the Romans, who granted him such power. To the fourth argument some reply that the Emperor who first swore to the Pope did so out of devotion or humility, or by the arrangement of the Romans; and therefore his other predecessors, who did not swear to him or in some way withheld what was owed to him by succession from the blessed Peter, were in no way bound to swear to him. From these things it is gathered that the blessed Peter received such a temporal kingdom from Christ. Therefore Christ did not hold any temporal kingdom either.

units.la: Octaua ratio pro prædicta assertione talis est: Christus fuit forma & exemplar totius perfectionis Christianæ. Quicquid enim perfectionis est & vtile fuit fidelibus, Christus exercuit. Sed reliquisse regnum temporale, perfectionis est, sicut & fugere ecclesiasticas dignitates, perfectionis est. Quia appetere dignitates seculares vel ecclesiasticas ad imperfectionem noscitur pertinere. Vtile autem fuit fidelibus, quod Christus omnem secularem contemneret dignitatem. Ergo Christus nullam secularem habuit dignitatem vel regiam vel aliam. Ergo Christus non fuit rex in temporalibus.
units.tr: The eighth argument for the aforesaid assertion runs as follows. Christ was the form and exemplar of all Christian perfection. Whatever is perfect and useful to the faithful, Christ practised. But to have relinquished a temporal kingdom is perfection, just as fleeing ecclesiastical dignities is perfection, since seeking secular or ecclesiastical dignities is known to belong to imperfection. Yet it was useful to the faithful that Christ should despise every secular dignity. Therefore Christ had no secular dignity, regal or otherwise. Therefore Christ was not a king in temporal affairs.

units.la: Sed forte aliquis contra prædictam rationem obiiciet, quod Christus non omnia, quæ perfecta sunt, exercuit. Nam sicut dictum est, fugere ecclesiasticas dignitates ad perfectionem humilitatis noscitur pertinere in tantum, quod soli fugientes ecclesiasticas dignitates eisdem dignitatibus dignè habentur, teste beato Greg. qui vt habetur 8. q. 1. c. 5. in scriptura, ait: Sicut locus regiminis desiderantibus tenendus est, ita fugientibus offerendus est. Et tamen Christus locum regiminis minime reculauit. E. Christus non omnia, quæ sunt perfectionis, exercuit. Ergo per hoc, quod perfectionis est temporalia regna reliquisse, non potest concludi, quod Christus non fuerit rex secularis siue in secularib'. Sed illa obiectio exclusa est, cum in assumpta propositione additur, & vtile fuit fidelibus. Nam ea quæ perfectionis & vtilitatis sunt, quæ docuit alios, Christus fecit. Christus aut reliquisse locum regiminis spiritualis, nullius fuit vtilitatis: sed fidelibus nocuisset & Christus retinere locum regiminis spiritualis magnæ fuit vtilitatis.
units.tr: But perhaps someone will object to this argument that Christ did not practise everything that is perfect. For, as has been said, fleeing ecclesiastical dignities is known to belong to the perfection of humility, to such an extent that only those who flee ecclesiastical dignities are rightly held worthy of those same dignities, as the blessed Gregory testifies, who says, as is found in 8. q. 1. c. 5. in scriptura: As the place of rule is to be kept for those who desire it, so it is to be offered to those who flee it. And yet Christ did not refuse the place of rule. Therefore Christ did not practise everything that belongs to perfection. Therefore it cannot be concluded from the fact that relinquishing temporal kingdoms belongs to perfection that Christ was not a secular king, whether in secular matters. But that objection is answered by the addition in the minor premise, "and was useful to the faithful." For Christ did what was both perfect and useful, the things he taught others. But for Christ to have relinquished the place of spiritual rule would have been of no use to anyone; indeed it would have harmed the faithful, whereas for Christ to retain the place of spiritual rule was of great use.

units.la: Christum a. habere regnum temporale, & de regno temporali se intromittere, nullius fuisset vtilitatis. quare conueniens fuit, quod Christus locum spiritualis regiminis retineret, & regno temporali careret. Et ita liquet, quod Christus regnum temporale non habuit. Porro inter regere & dominari sine dominium & proprietate temporalium rerum habere, differentia inuenitur. Ostenso autem, quod Christus non fuit rex in temporalib' secundum quod aliquis dicitur rex à supremo modo regendi temporaliter. Secundo isti impugnatores conantur ostendere, quod Christus inquantum homo mortalis, non fuit Dominus hab eis dominium & proprietatem omnium temporalium rerum. Primo quidem auctoritates: secundo per rationes. Primo igitur hoc ostenduntur auctoritate ipsius Christi dicentis Matth. 8. Vulpes foueas habent, volucres cæli nidos: filius autem hominis non habet vbi caput suum reclinet. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod Christus non habuit proprium hospitium: & per consequens non habuit proprietatem & dominium omnium. Si d forte dicet aliquis, quod ex verbis prædictis concludi non potest, quod Christus non habuerit hospitium quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Quod sic ostenditur. Nam eodem modo accepit Christus habere cum dixit affirmatiue, vulpes foueas habent &c. & cum negatiue dicit: filius autem hominis non habet vbi caput suum reclinet: alioquin in eadem sententia Christus acciperet idem verbum æquiuoce. Sed cum dicitur, vulpes foueas habent: ibi non accipitur pro modo habendi, quo ad dominium & proprietatem sed pro modo habendi, quo ad morandi seu manendi seu quiescendi consuetudinem. E cum dicit filius hominis non habet vbi caput suum reclinet, non accipitur habere pro habere quo ad dominium seu proprietate, sed quo ad consuetudinem manendi vel quiescendi, hoc est, filius hominis non habet hospitium, in quo ex consuetudine commoretur, sicut vulpes habent foueas, in quib' ex consuetudine commorantur.
units.tr: For Christ to have a temporal kingdom, and to meddle in temporal government, would have been of no use. Hence it was fitting that Christ should retain the place of spiritual rule and go without a temporal kingdom. And so it is clear that Christ did not have a temporal kingdom. Moreover, a difference is found between ruling and lording it, and between having dominion and ownership of temporal goods. Having shown, then, that Christ was not a king in temporal matters in the sense that someone is called a king by the highest mode of ruling in temporal affairs, these opponents secondly try to show that Christ, as a mortal man, was not the lord, having dominion and ownership, of all temporal things. They do this first by authorities and second by reasons. First, then, they show it by the authority of Christ himself, who says in Matt. 8: Foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests, but the Son of man has not where to lay his head. From these words it is clearly gathered that Christ had no proper lodging, and consequently had no ownership or dominion over all things. If anyone should perhaps say that it cannot be concluded from these words that Christ had no lodging with respect to dominion and ownership, this is shown as follows. Christ used the verb have in the same way when he said affirmatively, foxes have holes, etc., and when he says negatively, the Son of man has not where to lay his head; otherwise, within the same sentence, Christ would be using the same word equivocally. But when it is said, foxes have holes, have is not taken in the sense of having by ownership or property, but in the sense of having by the custom of dwelling, staying or resting. And when it says the Son of man has not where to lay his head, have is not taken as having with respect to dominion or property, but with respect to the custom of dwelling or resting; that is, the Son of man has no lodging in which he customarily dwells, just as foxes have holes in which they customarily dwell.

units.la: Sed ista obiectio non procedit secundum istos: quia secundum traditiones sanctorum, & specialiter sanctis Clementis, vt habetur Dist. 37. c. relatum, Scriptura sic est intelligenda, vt à sanctis patribus est exposita. Sed secundum expositionem sanctorum, cum Christus dixit, filius h. hominis non habet vbi caput suum reclinet: ipse loquebatur de modo habendi quo ad dominium siue ad proprietatem, Glos. testatur, quod ibidem ait in persona Christi: Ego sum tanta pauperitatis, vt nec hospitium quidem habeam, nec meo vtar tecto. Ex quibus verbis patenter colligitur, quod ex paupertate fuit, quod hospitium non habebat. Sed non habere hospitium quo ad consuetudinem habitandi non necessario et paupertate procedit. Quemadmodum diuites peregrini peregrinatione hospitium non habent quo ad consuetudinem habitandi, ex quo vagi sunt, & tamen habent multas diuitias. Cum ergo ratione paupertatis Christus dixerit verba prædicta, sequitur quod intellexit se non habere hospitium quo ad dominium seu proprietatem. Item quauis rex ex consuetudine circuiens regnum, peragens de loco ad locum posset dicere, quod non haberet hospitium quo ad consuetudinem: non tamen posset dicere, quod tecto vteretur alieno. Sed secundum Glosam Christus vtebatur tecto alieno, ergo tectum, quo vtebatur Christus, non fuit suum quo ad dominium seu proprietatem. Et cum dicitur, quod tunc Christus in eadem sententia vsus fuisset eodem vocabulo æquiuoce. Dicunt isti, quod hoc sæpe facit scriptura, secundum quod probat Innoc. 3. extr. de summa trinitate & fide catholica c. damnamus, per illas duas auctoritates: volo vt ipsi sint vnu in nobis, sicut & nos vnu sumus, Et, estote perfecti, sicut & pater vester cœlestis est perfectus: in quarum prima vnum bis sumptu æquiuoce accipitur: & in secunda nomè perfecti. Secunda auctoritas, qua ostenditur Christi pauptas, sumitur Zach. 9. vbi dicitur: Ipse pauper ascendes super asinam & super pullum filium asinæ. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod licet Christus fuerit rex, non quidem in temporalib' sed in spiritualib. tñ pauper erat, & per consequens non habuit dominium & proprietatem omnium temporalium: qua si habuisset in speciali dominium & proprietatem omnium rerum temporalium, suis let set ditior homo, qui vnquam fuit. Tertia auctoritas accipitur ex epistola secunda beati Pauli ad Corinth. 8. cap. vbi sic scribitur: Scitis enim gratiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi: quoniam propter vos egenus factus est, cum esset dives, vt illius inopia vos diuites efficeretis. Et consilium in hoc do &c. Ex quibus verbis habetur aperte, quod Christus propter nos factus est inops & egenus. Qui autem est Dominus omnium temporalium iure proprietatis in speciali, non est inops & egenus. Ergo Christus non fuit Dominus omnium temporalium rerum. Hoc etiam Augustus super dicto verbo Apostoli asserit manifeste dicens: Factus est, inquit, egenus in tantum, vt non haberet quod habent vulpes. Quia & Bernhardus pertractans verba praedicta ad Fratres de Monte Dei dicit: cum dives esset, pauper pro nobis factus est, & qui voluntaria paupertatis dedit praeceptum, in semetipso formam dignatus est demonstrare. Ex quibus verbis liquet, quod illius voluntariae paupertatis, cuius Christus dedit praeceptum, ipse in semetipso formam demonstrauit. Sed ipse dedit praeceptum voluntariae paupertatis, qui carentiam dominii & proprietatis in semetipso decreuit. Ex quo sequitur euidenter, quod non erat Dominus omnium temporalium iure proprietatis. Quarta auctoritas accipitur ex Psalmista, qui in persona Christi ait: Ego autem mendicus sum & pauper. Vbi dicit Glossa. Hoc Christus dicit de se ex forma Ierusalem, ne quis gloriam praedicta laetitia sibi arroget. Christus igitur inquantum homo fuit pauper: & per consequens non habuit vniuersale temporalium rerum dominium. Quinta auctoritas accipitur Trenorum tertio cap. vbi Hieremias in persona Christi ait: Ego vir videns paupertatem meam. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod Christus fuit pauper: & per consequens non habuit vniuersale rerum temporalium dominium. Et quod Hieremias verba praedicta dixerit in persona Christi, patet per Glossam ibidem, quae ait: licet omnibus conuenire videatur, excellentius de ipso intelligitur, in quo sicut excellunt omnia, ita & visio illa. Et infra: Sicut gloriosior est paupertas Christi, ita hac visio paupertatis profundior. Verba ergo praedicta dixit Hieremias in persona Christi, ostendens eius maximam paupertatem. Sexta auctoritas accipitur ex determinatione ecclesiae quae ponitur in decretali Exiit: in qua sic scribit diffinitve Papa dicens, quod abdicatio proprietatis huiusmodi omnium rerum tam in speciali quam etiam in communi, propter Deum meritoria est & sancta, quam & Christus viam perfectionis ostendens verbo docuit, & exemplo firmavit. His verbis apertissime asseritur, quod Christus exemplo firmauit abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum: & ita omnium rerum abdicauit proprietatem: & per consequens non habuit vniuersale omnium rerum dominium. Et ex his, sicut tactum est cap. 9. concluduntur isti impugnatores, quod vel ille est haereticus, vel Nicolaus tertius est haereticus. Et si ille est haereticus, non est verus Papa. Si autem Nicolaus tertius fuit haereticus, ille nunquam fuit verus Papa. Et per consequens sive iste sit haereticus sive catholicus, non est modo verus Papa. Alia auctoritas accipitur ex epistola beati Hieronymi ad Nepotianum, qui ait: Turpe est ante fores sacerdotes Domini crucifixi & pauperis, qui sibi quoque vescebatur alieno, litteres consulum & militum excubare. Ex quibus verbis clare patet, quod Christus erat pauper & cibo vescens alieno: & per consequens non habuit dominium omnium temporalium vniuersale. Octava est eiusdem ad Eliodorum, qui ait: Affatim dives est, qui cum Christo pauper est. Christus ergo fuit pauper. Nona est Gregorii Nazianzeni, qui ait: Vestigiis illius incedam, qui propter nos pauper factus est, cum esset dives. Christus ergo ex quo fuit pauper, non habuit rerum temporalium vniuersale dominium. Decima est Chrysostomi, qui super Epistolam ad Hebraeos ait: Nemo causetur de paupertate, tanquam causa sit multorum malorum, neque obloquatur de Christo, qui dixit illam perfectionem. Si vis perfectus esse &c. Hoc enim & verbis ipse dixit, & operibus ostendit, & per discipulos suos docuit. Christus igitur secundum istum pauper fuit. Undecima est eiusdem, vbi prius, qui ait: vis audire paupertatis praedicata, ipsam professus est Christus & dixit: filius hominis non habet, vbi caput suum reclinet. Ex his verbis patet, quod Christus non habuit omnium rerum dominium. Duodecima est eiusdem super verba Christi, Matth. 6. Filius hominis non habet &c. Aspice quomodo paupertatem, quam Dominus docuerat, per opera demonstrat. Non erat ei mensa, nec candelabrum, nec domus, nec quicquam aliud talium. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod Christus erat tantae paupertatis, quod non habuit mensam, nec candelabrum, nec domum &c. Ex quo sequitur euidenter, quod non habuit vniuersale omnium rerum temporalium dominium. Tertiadecima est beati Bernhardi super illud Lucae: Cum factus esset Iesus annorum 12. qui ait; vt te Domine per omnia nostra paupertati conformares, quasi vnus in turba pauperum stipem per ostia mendicabas. Christus ergo ex voluntaria paupertate stipem per ostia mendicabat: & per consequens non habuit omnium rerum vniuersale dominium. Quartadecima est Anshelmi de Sacris, qui ait: Pauper ita fuit Christus, vt veniens in mundum non in sua, sed in aliena domo nasceretur: & natus propter inopiam loci in praesepio brutorum animalium poneretur, vt veniens in mundo non haberet vbi caput suum reclinaret, nec moriens vnde nuditatem suam tegeret, nec mortuus vnde inuolueretur, nec sepulcrum aut locum vbi corpus mortuum locaretur. Ex his euidenter habetur, quod Christus non habuit omnium temporalium rerum dominium & proprietatem: quia si sic, natus in domo propria fuisset viuens, quia in mundo multa hospitia, imo propria habuisset, vbi caput reclinasset moriens: quia habuisset vnde propriam nuditatem texisset, nec alibi corpus mortuum quam in sepulchro, & in loco proprio Christi locatum fuisset. His igitur auctoritatibus & aliis quasi innumeris, quas causa breuitatis omitto, euidenter ostenditur, quod Christus inquantum homo mortalis, non habuit ab instanti suae conceptionis vniuersale rerum dominium.
units.tr: But this objection does not hold according to these men, because according to the traditions of the saints, and especially of holy Clement, as is found in Dist. 37. c. relatum, Scripture is to be understood as the holy Fathers have expounded it. According to the exposition of the saints, when Christ said the Son of man has not where to lay his head, he was speaking of the manner of having as regards dominion or ownership. The Gloss bears witness to this, where it says in the person of Christ: I am of such poverty that I do not even have a lodging, nor do I use a roof of my own. From these words it is plainly gathered that it was from poverty that he had no lodging. But not having a lodging as regards the custom of dwelling does not necessarily arise from poverty. Thus rich travellers have no lodging as regards the custom of dwelling, since they are wanderers, and yet they have great riches. Since, then, Christ spoke the aforesaid words on account of poverty, it follows that he meant he had no lodging as regards dominion or ownership. Again, although a king, going about his realm and travelling from place to place, could say that he had no lodging as regards custom, he could not say that he used a roof belonging to another. But according to the Gloss Christ used a roof belonging to another; therefore the roof which Christ used was not his own as regards dominion or ownership. And when it is objected that Christ in the same sentence would then have used the same word equivocally, these men reply that Scripture often does this, as Innocent III proves in extr. de summa trinitate & fide catholica c. damnamus, by those two passages: I will that they may be one in us, as we also are one, and be perfect, as also your heavenly Father is perfect. In the first of these the word "one" is taken equivocally twice, and in the second the word "perfect." The second authority, by which Christ's poverty is shown, is taken from Zechariah 9, where it is said: He, poor, rides upon an ass and upon a colt, the foal of an ass. From these words it is clear that although Christ was a king, not indeed in temporal matters but in spiritual, yet he was poor, and consequently he did not have dominion and ownership of all temporal things. For if he had possessed in particular dominion and ownership of all temporal things, he would have been the richest man who ever lived. The third authority is taken from the Second Epistle of Blessed Paul to the Corinthians, chapter 8, where it is written thus: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich. And in this I give counsel, etc. From these words it is clearly held that Christ for our sakes became needy and poor. But he who is Lord of all temporal things by the right of particular ownership is not needy and poor. Therefore Christ was not Lord of all temporal things. Augustine also asserts this plainly on the saying of the Apostle, saying: He became poor, he says, to such a degree that he had not what the foxes have. Blessed Bernard too, treating the aforesaid words, says to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu: though he was rich, yet he became poor for us, and he who gave the precept of voluntary poverty deigned to show the pattern in himself. From these words it is evident that of that voluntary poverty, of which Christ gave the precept, he himself showed the pattern in himself. But he gave the precept of voluntary poverty who decreed in himself the lack of dominion and ownership. From this it clearly follows that he was not Lord of all temporal things by the right of ownership. The fourth authority is taken from the Psalmist, who says in the person of Christ: But I am needy and poor. Here the Gloss says: Christ says this of himself in the figure of Jerusalem, lest anyone claim for himself the glory of the aforesaid joy. Christ, therefore, as man was poor, and consequently did not have universal dominion over temporal things. The fifth authority is taken from Lamentations, chapter 3, where Jeremiah says in the person of Christ: I am the man who has seen my poverty. From these words it is plain that Christ was poor, and consequently did not have universal dominion over temporal things. That Jeremiah spoke the aforesaid words in the person of Christ is shown by the Gloss on the same place, which says: although it may seem to apply to all, it is understood more excellently of him, in whom, as all things excel, so also does that sight. And below: As the poverty of Christ is more glorious, so this sight of poverty is more profound. Jeremiah therefore spoke the aforesaid words in the person of Christ, showing his supreme poverty. The sixth authority is taken from the determination of the Church which is set down in the decretal Exiit, in which the Pope writes definitively, saying that the renunciation of ownership of such all things, both in particular and also in common, is meritorious and holy for God's sake, which Christ also taught in words, showing the way of perfection, and confirmed by example. By these words it is most plainly asserted that Christ by example confirmed the renunciation of ownership of all things, and so he renounced ownership of all things, and consequently did not have universal dominion over all things. And from these things, as was touched on in chapter 9, these opponents conclude that either that man is a heretic, or Nicholas III is a heretic. And if that man is a heretic, he is not a true Pope. But if Nicholas III was a heretic, that man never was a true Pope. And consequently, whether this man is a heretic or a Catholic, he is not now a true Pope. Another authority is taken from the letter of Blessed Jerome to Nepotian, who says: It is shameful that the priests of the crucified and poor Lord should keep watch before the doors, as letters of consuls and soldiers, he who also ate food belonging to another. From these words it is clearly plain that Christ was poor and ate food belonging to another, and consequently he did not have universal dominion over all temporal things. The eighth is from the same writer to Heliodorus, who says: He is abundantly rich who is poor with Christ. Christ therefore was poor. The ninth is from Gregory Nazianzen, who says: I will walk in the footsteps of him who, though he was rich, became poor for our sakes. Christ therefore, since he was poor, did not have universal dominion over temporal things. The tenth is from Chrysostom, who, on the Epistle to the Hebrews, says: Let no one complain of poverty as if it were the cause of many evils, nor speak against Christ, who named that perfection: If you wish to be perfect, etc. For he both said it in words, and showed it in deeds, and taught it through his disciples. Christ, therefore, according to this writer, was poor. The eleventh is from the same, in the place mentioned before, who says: Do you wish to hear the praise of poverty? Christ himself professed it and said: the Son of man has not where to lay his head. From these words it is plain that Christ did not have dominion over all things. The twelfth is from the same, on the words of Christ in Matthew 6: The Son of man has not, etc. Look how he shows by his works the poverty which the Lord had taught. He had no table, nor lampstand, nor house, nor anything else of the kind. From these words it is plain that Christ was of such poverty that he had no table, nor lampstand, nor house, etc. From this it clearly follows that he did not have universal dominion over all temporal things. The thirteenth is from Blessed Bernard on that passage of Luke: When Jesus was made twelve years old, who says: that you might conform yourself, Lord, in all things to our poverty, you begged alms at the doors like one of the crowd of the poor. Christ therefore, by voluntary poverty, begged alms at the doors, and consequently did not have universal dominion over all things. The fourteenth is from Anselm of Sacris, who says: Christ was so poor that, coming into the world, he was born not in his own house but in another's; and because of the lack of room he was laid, when born, in the manger of brute animals, so that, coming into the world, he had no place where to lay his head, nor, dying, anything with which to cover his nakedness, nor, when dead, anything in which to be wrapped, nor a tomb or a place where his dead body might be laid. From these things it is plainly held that Christ did not have dominion and ownership of all temporal things. For if it were so, had he been born in a house of his own, he would have lived in a house of his own, since in the world there are many lodgings, indeed he would have had his own, where he might have laid his head in death; since he would have had something with which to cover his own nakedness, and he would not have been laid dead anywhere but in a tomb, and in a place belonging to Christ. Therefore, from these authorities and others almost countless, which I omit for the sake of brevity, it is plainly shown that Christ, as mortal man, from the moment of his conception did not have universal dominion over temporal things.

units.la: Secundo haec eadem assertio per rationes in scripturis diuinis & auctoritatibus sanctorum patrum fundatas aperte probatur. Est autem prima ratio talis. Omnia ad perfectionem & fidelium vtilitatem spectantia, quae Christus docuit, ipse fecit. Sed abdicare temporalium diutiarum dominium & proprietatem, ad perfectionem & fidelium utilitatem spectabat: & hanc abdicationem Christus docuit. Ergo ipse hanc abdicationem seruauit, & per consequens non habuit omnium diuitiarum dominium & proprietatem. Maior probatur multipliciter. Primo auctoritate Lucae Actuum 1. qui ait: Primum quidem sermonem feci de omnibus, O Theophile, quae coepit Iesus facere & docere. Ergo Christus fecit, quae docuit. Item Matth. 5. dicit ipse Christus: Qui ergo soluerit unum de mandatis istis minimis & docuerit sic homines, minimus vocabitur in regno caelorum. Sed Christus non fuit minimus in regno caelorum, sed maximus. Ergo non soluit illa, quae docuit. Item, Christus non fecit aliquid, de quo alios reprehendit: alioquin conuenienter intelligenda fuisset de eo sapientis auctoritas, qua dicitur:
units.tr: Second, this same assertion is clearly proved by arguments grounded in the divine Scriptures and in the authority of the holy Fathers. The first argument runs as follows. Christ himself did everything that he taught that pertains to the perfection and benefit of the faithful. But giving up the dominion and ownership of temporal riches pertained to the perfection and benefit of the faithful, and Christ taught this renunciation. Therefore he himself observed this renunciation, and consequently he did not have dominion and ownership of all riches. The major premise is proved in several ways. First, by the authority of Luke in Acts 1, who says: The first account I made, O Theophilus, concerned all that Jesus began to do and to teach. So Christ did what he taught. Likewise, Christ himself says in Matthew 5: Whoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But Christ was not least in the kingdom of heaven, but greatest. Therefore he did not break those things that he taught. Likewise, Christ did not do anything for which he rebuked others; otherwise the saying of the wise man would have to be understood of him, which says:

units.la: Turpe est doctori, cum culpa redarguit ipsum.
units.tr: It is shameful for a teacher when he is rebuked for his own fault.

units.la: Sed Christus redarguit Pharisaeos, quia non fecerunt illa, quae docuerunt, dicens in reprehensione eorum: Dicunt enim & non faciunt. Ergo Christus fecit ea, quae docuit. Quod etiam Christus specialiter illa, quae docuit de paupertate, fecit, asserit manifeste Chrysostomus in auctoritate decima addutta superius, & similiter 12. Hoc idem testatur Bernhard. sicut patet prius in prosecutione tertiae auctoritatis. Sic ergo probata est maior. Minor continet tres partes. Quarum prima est, quod abdicare diuitiarum dominium & proprietatem, ad perfectionem spectat. Secunda est, quod vtile fuit fidelibus Christum diuitiarum proprietatem & dominium abdicare. Tertia est, quod Christus docuit abdicationem huiusmodi diuitiarum.
units.tr: But Christ rebuked the Pharisees because they did not do what they taught, saying in their reproof: For they say and do not. Therefore Christ did the things that he taught. That Christ in particular did the things he taught about poverty is clearly asserted by Chrysostom in the tenth authority adduced above, and similarly in the twelfth. Bernard bears the same witness, as is evident earlier in the pursuit of the third authority. So the major premise is proved. The minor premise contains three parts. The first is that giving up dominion and ownership of riches pertains to perfection. The second is that it was useful to the faithful that Christ gave up dominion and ownership of riches. The third is that Christ taught the renunciation of riches of this kind.

units.la: Prima pars patet, tu quia Christus dixit: Si vis perfectus esse vade & vende omnia quae habes, & da pauperibus. Igitur diuitiarum abdicare dominium propter Deum, ad perfectionem spectat: tum quia omnibus votorum essentialium religionibus profectis ad perfectionem spectat. Et votum paupertatis ad perfectionem spectat. Et per consequens diuitiarum abdicare dominium propter Deum ad perfectionem spectat.
units.tr: The first part is evident, since Christ said: If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, and give to the poor. Therefore, giving up dominion of riches for God's sake pertains to perfection; both because all the essential vows of the religious orders, when professed, pertain to perfection, and the vow of poverty pertains to perfection. And consequently, giving up dominion of riches for God's sake pertains to perfection.

units.la: Secunda pars, scil. quod vtile fuit fidelibus Christum abdicare dominium & proprietatem, patet aperte. Nam per hoc praebuit aperte efficacia exempla fidelibus temporalia contemnendi. Ex retentione autem diuitiarum nullam auctoritatem spiritualem fideles consecuti fuissent. Ergo vtile & exemplare fuit fidelibus Christum abdicare dominium. Et per hoc soluitur obiectio, si quis obiiceret, quod Christus praelationem & summum sacerdotium minime abdicauit neq; fugit: & tamen fugere ecclesiasticas dignitates, etiam Papatum, ad perfectionem spectat: & Christus docuit huiusmodi fugere dignitates, cum dixit Matth. 18. Nisi conuersi fueritis & efficiamini sicut parvuli, non intrabitis in regnum caelorum. Et Matth. 23. Qui se humiliauerit, exaltabitur. Igitur Christus non omnia fecit, quae docuit, & ad perfectionem spectant. Ad hanc obiectionem obliquam est facile respondere. Nam sicut Christus venit propter salutem nostram, ita fecit illa quae erant nostrae saluti vtila. Vtile autem fuit nostrae saluti, quod Christus omnium diuitiarum abdicaret dominium: & non fuit vtile, quod summum sacerdotium & omnem praelationem abdicaret: & ideo vnum fecit, & non aliud.
units.tr: The second part, namely that it was useful to the faithful that Christ gave up dominion and ownership, is plainly evident. For by this he clearly provided the faithful with effective examples of despising temporal things. Yet from the retention of riches the faithful would have gained no spiritual authority. Therefore it was useful and exemplary for the faithful that Christ gave up dominion. And by this the objection is resolved, should someone object that Christ by no means gave up preeminence and the supreme priesthood, nor did he flee from them; and yet fleeing ecclesiastical dignities, even the papacy, pertains to perfection, and Christ taught such fleeing of dignities when he said in Matthew 18: Unless you are converted and become as little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven. And in Matthew 23: Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted. Therefore Christ did not do all that he taught and that pertains to perfection. It is easy to answer this objection indirectly. For just as Christ came for our salvation, so he did those things that were useful to our salvation. But it was useful to our salvation that Christ give up dominion of all riches; and it was not useful that he give up the supreme priesthood and all preeminence. Therefore he did the one and not the other.

units.la: Tertia pars, scil. quod Christus docuit diuitiarum abdicare dominium & proprietatem, patet aperte Christo dicente cuidam adolescenti, Matth. 19. Si vis perfectus esse vade & vende omnia quae habes & da pauperibus: & veni, & sequere me. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod Christus docuit diuitias vendere, & dare pauperibus. Diuitiae autem venditae & pauperibus erogatae quoad proprietatem & dominium abdicantur. Igitur Christus docuit diuitiarum abdicare dominium. Item ibidem dixit Christus Apostolis: Amen dico vobis, quod vos qui reliquistis omnia & secuti estis me, in regeneratione cum sederit filius hominis in sede maiestatis suae, sedebitis & vos. Vbi Christus explicite approbando & laudando modum Apostolorum omnia relinquendi docuit eum modum omnia relinquendi. Sed Apostoli reliquerunt ea, quae reliquerant quod ad dominium & proprietatem. Igitur Christus docuit rerum temporalium abdicare dominium & proprietatem. Item Matth. 10. dixit Christus Apostolis: Nolite possidere aurum neq; argentum &c. Vbi expresse auri & argenti atq; pecuniae docuit abdicare dominium. Item Matth. 6. dixit discipulis: Nolite thesaurizare vobis thesauros in terra: vbi thesaurorum docuit abdicare dominium. In multis aliis quoq; locis Christus docuit mundum contemnere, & diuitiarum abdicare dominium. Esto igitur, quod non docuisset omnium temporalium abdicare dominium; quod tamen non est verum: & tamen certum est, quod thesaurorum, auri & argenti, & amplarum diuitiarum docuit abdicare dominium. Ex quo & maiore accepta sequitur euidenter, quod Christus saltem amplarum diuitiarum abdicauit dominium & proprietatem: & per consequens non habuit omnium temporalium vniuersale dominium.
units.tr: The third part, namely that Christ taught the renunciation of dominion and ownership of riches, is clearly shown by Christ saying to a certain young man, in Matthew 19: If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, and give to the poor; and come, and follow me. From these words it is clearly gathered that Christ taught to sell riches and give them to the poor. But riches that are sold and distributed to the poor are renounced as regards ownership and dominion. Therefore Christ taught the renunciation of dominion of riches. Likewise, in the same place Christ said to the Apostles: Truly I say to you, that you who have left all and followed me, in the regeneration when the Son of man shall sit on the seat of his majesty, you also shall sit. Here Christ, explicitly approving and praising the manner in which the Apostles left everything, taught that very manner of leaving everything. But the Apostles left those things which they had left, as far as dominion and ownership go. Therefore Christ taught the renunciation of dominion and ownership of temporal things. Likewise, in Matthew 10 Christ said to the Apostles: Do not possess gold nor silver, etc. Here he expressly taught the renunciation of dominion over gold, silver and money. Likewise, in Matthew 6 he said to his disciples: Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth; here he taught the renunciation of dominion over treasures. In many other places too Christ taught that the world is to be despised and dominion over riches renounced. Grant, then, that he had not taught the renunciation of dominion over all temporal things, which is nevertheless not true; still it is certain that he taught the renunciation of dominion over treasures, gold and silver, and large riches. From this, and from the greater premise being accepted, it evidently follows that Christ at least renounced dominion and ownership of large riches, and consequently he did not have universal dominion over all temporal things.

units.la: Secunda ratio pro eadem assertione est haec. Paupertas religiosorum non est maior necaliquor nec perfectior paupertate Christi. Sed religiosi abdicant dominium & proprietatem diuitiarum, saltem in speciali: ergo Christus saltem in speciali diuitiarum abdicauit dominium. Et constat, quod nullus alius a Christo habuit dominium temporalium omnium commune cum Christo. Ergo Christus nec in speciali nec in communi habuit temporalem vniuersale dominium. Maior est manifesta. Nam omnes religiosi imitantur Christum in paupertate: E. nulli religiosi sunt pauperiores Christo. Minora probatione non indiget.
units.tr: The second argument for the same assertion is this. The poverty of the religious is not greater than, nor more perfect than, the poverty of Christ. But the religious renounce dominion and ownership of riches, at least in particular; therefore Christ at least in particular renounced dominion of riches. And it is agreed that no one other than Christ had dominion of all temporal things in common with Christ. Therefore Christ had universal temporal dominion neither in particular nor in common. The major premise is obvious. For all religious imitate Christ in poverty; therefore no religious are poorer than Christ. The minor premise needs no proof.

units.la: Tertia ratio est hoc. Christus instituendo beatu Petru vicariu suu, dicendo; Pasce oues meas: omnia pertinentia ad Christum, quae erant ad pascendas oues necessaria, eidem beato Petro commisit. Cum ergo ad oues pascendas sint temporalia oportuna: si Christus habuit dominium & paupertatem omnium temporalium: sequitur quod Christus omnia temporalia dispositioni & ordinationi beati Petri commisit. Ex quo sequitur, quod omnia temporalia ad dispositionem & ordinationem beati Petri spectabat: quod est absurdum. Tunc n. ad Romanum pontificem successione beati Petri temporalia pertinerent: quod nescitur esse fallum.
units.tr: The third argument is this. In instituting blessed Peter as his vicar, saying: Feed my sheep, Christ entrusted to the same blessed Peter all the things belonging to Christ that were necessary for feeding the sheep. Since, then, temporal goods are suitable for feeding the sheep, if Christ had dominion and ownership of all temporal goods, it follows that Christ entrusted all temporal goods to the disposition and ordering of blessed Peter. From this it follows that all temporal goods pertained to the disposition and ordering of blessed Peter, which is absurd. For then temporal goods would pertain to the Roman pontiff by succession from blessed Peter, which is not known to be false.

units.la: Hic restat duo probare. Primum est, quod non omnia temporalia pertinebant ad dispositionem seu ordinationem beati Petri: secundum quod non omnia temporalia pertinent seu pertinebant ad dispositionem, seu dispensationem, vel ordinationem successorum beati Petri. Primum probatur aperte. Primo per illud Ambrof. in lib. de ossi. qui Apostolos sine auro misit, ecclesias sine auro congregauit. Ex quo datur intelligi, quod ad illos, qui primo virtute assistente diuina, ecclesias congregabant, aurum minime pertinebat. Et per consequens aurum ad beatum Petrum, qui erat principalis congregator ecclesiarum, non spectabat. Hoc ipsemet Petrus testatur dicens: argentum & aurum non est mihi. Ex quibus verbis patenter colligitur, quod dispensatio omnium ad ipsum minime pertinebat. Item, si omnia temporalia ex commissione Christi pertinuissent ad beatum Petrum: & secundum istum post conuersionem Iudaeorum, de quibus Act. 2. fit mentio, Apostoli omnia quae habebant communicabant Iudaeis conuersis; & e converso: & sic omnia fiebant communia: Ergo beatus Petrus omnia temporalia communicauit Iudaeis, & aliis. Et per consequens omnia temporalia etiam infidelium fuerunt eis tunc communia: quod est absurdum. Item, si omnia temporalia beato Petro commissa erant a Christo: aut ergo quantum ad temporalia erat superior Caesare & aliis regibus & principibus, ac etiam quibuscunque habentibus proprium: aut erat inferior: aut par. Si erat in temporalibus superior: Ergo omnes, qui non recognouerunt temporalia sua a beato Petro, erant temporalium iniusti detentores. Et ita Caesar & omnes homines mundi habentes proprium, non recognoscentes temporalia sua a beato Petro, fuissent iniusti detentores, quod est absurdum, praecipue de fidelibus, qui erant subiecti beato Petro, & tamen temporalia sua a beato Petro minime recognouerunt. Nec potest dici, quod beatus Petrus fuit in temporalibus inferior omnibus habentibus proprium: quia tunc vel Christus fuisset omnibus inferior in temporalibus: vel beatum Petrum omnibus habentibus proprium in temporalibus subdidisset: quorum utrumque est absurdum. Nec potest dici, quod beatus Petrus fuit par omnibus habentibus proprium, quia tunc nullus habuisset licitam potestatem vendere & alienare res suas, absque expresso consensu beati Petri, nec econuerso: quia si duo habent aequale ius in re aliqua, vnus non vendit licite rem illam sine voluntate alterius. Patet ergo, quod nequaquam omnia temporalia pertinebant ad dispositionem vel dispensationem beati Petri. Secundum, scilicet quod nequaquam omnia temporalia pertineant ad dispositionem seu dispensationem successorum beati Petri, inquantum scil. sunt successores beati Petri, probatur. Nam hoc beatus Bernh. testatur expresse in lib. de consideratione ad Eugenium Papam, dicens in haec verba: Nam quid aliud sanctus dimisit Apostolus? quod habeo, inquit, hoc tibi do. Quid est illud vnum scio, non est aurum neque argentum: cum dicat ipse, argentum & aurum non est mihi. Et infra: Esto vt alia quacunque ratione hoc tibi vendices: sed non Apostolico iure. Ex quibus verbis habetur aperte, quod Papa Apostolico iure, scil. inquantum successor beati Petri auri & argenti aliarumque diuitiarum dispensationem minime habet. A quo autem Papa abundantiam diuitiarum habuit, declaratidem in eodem libro: Petrus hic est, qui nescitur processisse aliquando vel gemmis ornatus, vel sericis, nec tectus auro, nec vectus equo albo, nec stipatus milite, nec circumstrepentibus septus ministris; absque his cum credidit satis posse impleri salutare mandatum: si amas me, pasce oues meas. In his enim successisti non Petro, sed Constantino. Ex his verbis colligitur, quod Papa in abundantia diuitiarum non beato Petro, sed Constantino successit. Et quo concluditur, quod Papa in quibuscunque temporalibus non est vicarius Christi: quia nulla inueniuntur temporalia, in quibus possit dici magis esse vicarius Christi quam in aliis: & ita vel in omnibus vel in nullis temporalibus est vicarius Christi in omnibus temporalibus, sicut ostensum est. Ergo in nullis temporalibus est Christi vicarius. Ex quo sequitur, quod Christus inquantum homo non habebat omnium temporalium dominium & proprietatem. Et illae rationes pro assertione praedicta ad praesens sufficiant: quia postea ostendetur, quod Christus inquantum homo nullius rei temporalis habebat dominium & proprietatem.
units.tr: Two things remain to be proved here. The first is that not all temporal goods belonged to the disposal or ordering of blessed Peter; the second is that not all temporal goods belong, or belonged, to the disposal, dispensation or ordering of the successors of blessed Peter. The first is proved plainly. First, by Ambrose's saying in his book De officiis: He sent out the Apostles without gold; without gold he gathered the churches. From this we are given to understand that gold did not belong at all to those who, with divine power assisting them, first gathered the churches. Consequently gold did not belong to blessed Peter, who was the principal gatherer of the churches. Peter himself testifies to this, saying: Silver and gold I have none. From these words it is plainly gathered that the dispensation of all goods did not belong to him at all. Again, if all temporal goods had belonged to blessed Peter by the commission of Christ, then, on this view, after the conversion of the Jews mentioned in Acts 2, the Apostles would have shared all that they had with the converted Jews, and conversely, and so all things would have become common. Therefore blessed Peter shared all temporal goods with the Jews and others; and consequently all temporal goods, even those of unbelievers, would then have been common to them. This is absurd. Again, if all temporal goods had been committed to blessed Peter by Christ, then either in temporal matters he was superior to Caesar and other kings and princes, and to all who held property, or he was inferior, or equal. If he was superior in temporal matters, then all who did not acknowledge their temporal goods as held from blessed Peter were unjust holders of those goods. So Caesar and all men of the world who held property, not acknowledging their temporal goods from blessed Peter, would have been unjust holders. This is absurd, especially of the faithful, who were subject to blessed Peter and yet did not acknowledge their temporal goods from him at all. Nor can it be said that blessed Peter was inferior to all who held property in temporal matters, for then either Christ would have been inferior to all in temporal matters, or Peter would have subjected himself in temporal matters to all who held property. Each of these is absurd. Nor can it be said that blessed Peter was equal to all who held property, for then no one would have had a lawful power to sell and alienate his goods without the express consent of blessed Peter, nor conversely; for if two have an equal right in some thing, one does not lawfully sell that thing without the will of the other. It is therefore clear that not all temporal goods belonged in any way to the disposal or dispensation of blessed Peter. The second point, that not all temporal goods belong to the disposal or dispensation of the successors of blessed Peter, insofar as they are successors of blessed Peter, is proved as follows. Blessed Bernard states this expressly in his book De consideratione addressed to Pope Eugenius, saying in these words: For what else did the holy Apostle leave behind? "What I have," he says, "that I give to you." What is that one thing I know? It is not gold nor silver, since he himself says: silver and gold I have none. And a little further on: Grant that you claim these things by some other right whatever; but not by the Apostolic right. From these words it is plainly held that the Pope, by the Apostolic right, that is, insofar as he is successor of blessed Peter, has no dispensation of gold, silver and other riches. From whom the Pope had his abundance of riches, the same book makes clear: This is Peter, who is not known ever to have gone forth adorned either with jewels or silks, nor covered with gold, nor carried on a white horse, nor surrounded by soldiers, nor attended by a crowd of ministers; without these things he believed that the saving command could be fulfilled well enough: "If you love me, feed my sheep." For in these things you have succeeded not Peter but Constantine. From these words it is gathered that the Pope, in his abundance of riches, succeeded not blessed Peter but Constantine. And from this it follows that the Pope in no temporal matters is the vicar of Christ, since no temporal matters can be found in which he may be said to be the vicar of Christ more than in others; so either in all or in no temporal matters he is the vicar of Christ. He is not the vicar of Christ in all temporal matters, as has been shown. Therefore he is the vicar of Christ in no temporal matters. From this it follows that Christ, as man, did not have dominion and ownership of all temporal goods. These arguments are enough for the present in support of the aforesaid assertion, since it will be shown later that Christ, as man, had dominion and ownership of no temporal thing.

units.la: Restat ergo discurrendo per literam ad singulas auctoritates inductas pro assertione contraria respondere, Quod autem dominium rerum temporalium habuit) hic accipit dominium pro dominio quod est proprietas: quae proprietas post peccatum primorum parentum exitit introducta. Non enim accipit dominium pro dominio generi humano collato, quia tunc Christus non aliter fuisset Dominus omnium temporalium, quam quilibet alius a Christo, quod negare intendit. (In multis locis testatur) imo in nullo loco testatur. (Multi quidem Prophetaeum regem futurum populi Israelitici prophetauerunt.) Verum est, quod multi prophetauerunt regem futurum non solum populi Israelitici, sed etiam omnium gentium, quae creditura erant in ipsum. Vnde & Dauid dixit: Dicite in gentibus, quia Dominus regnauit. Vnde isti dicunt esse sciendum, quod Christus secundum deitatem rex fuit omnium bonorum & malorum, secundum humanitatem autem rex fuit credentium, siue credentes essent Iudaei secundum carnem, siue gentiles, qui tamen credentes omnes, & soli Iudaei erant secundum spiritum, & per consequens prophetarunt ipsum habere regni dominium quodammodo, scilicet spirituale, non seculare, nec temporale. (Ecce Dominus iudex vester, Dominus legifer vester, Dominus rex vester, ipse veniet & saluabit vos.) Illa auctoritas est contra ipsum, quia ipsa neq; de iudice seculari seu temporali, neq; de legifero temporali seu seculari, neq; de saluatione temporali seu seculari, potest intelligi, cum dicitur: Dominus iudex vester, aperte probatum est supra auctoritate Luc. 12. cum dixit Christus: Quis me constituit iudicem ac diuisorem super vos? Nusquam n. legitur, quod Christus de temporalibus iudicauerit. E. non erat iudex in temporalibus. Nec etiam cum dicit Esaias: Dominus legifer, videtur de legifero temporali posse intelligi, quia nusquam legitur, quod leges de temporalibus quibuscunq; statuerit, nisi forte dicas, quod legem de temporalibus rebus statuerit docens ipsas penitus concontemnendas. Sed talis lex non temporalis, sed spiritualis est censenda. Nec etiam cum dicitur, ipse veniet & salvabit vos, potest de temporali salvatione intelligi, cum dixerit suis, vt habetur Matth. 24. Tradent vos in tribulatione & occident vos. Non venit igitur Christus saluare temporaliter Iudaeos, neq; credentes, neq; non credentes. Non credentes, cum credentes omnem tribulationem & mulki mortem pro ipso sustinuerunt temporalem. Neque non credentes, cum propter peccata commissa in ipsum destructi fuerint per Romanos. Cum igitur auctoritas Esaiae, neque de iudice temporali, neque de legifero temporali, neque de salvatione temporali possit intelligi: nullomodo per ipsam potest ostendi, quod Esaias prophetauerit Christum regem temporalem futurum: sed sicut Christus est iudex spiritualiter, & legifer spiritualiter, & spiritualiter saluauit credentes, sic spiritualiter fuit rex super credentes in ipsum. (Et regnabit rex) Illa etiam verba Hieremiae non debent de rege temporali intelligi: sicut nec intellexit Hieremias, quod Christus erat temporaliter regnaturus, cum dixit (regnabit) nulla enim apparet ratio, quod Hieremias dicendo regnabit rex, plus intellexerit, quod Christus erat futurus rex temporalis, quam quod erat regnaturus temporaliter.
units.tr: It remains, therefore, to go through the text and answer each of the authorities brought forward for the opposite assertion. But he had dominion over temporal things: here he takes dominion for dominion that is ownership, which ownership was introduced after the sin of our first parents. For he does not take dominion in the sense of dominion conferred on the human race, since then Christ would not have been Lord of all temporal things in any other way than any other person apart from Christ, which he intends to deny. (He bears witness in many places), indeed in no place does he bear witness. (Many prophets foretold that a king would come for the people of Israel.) It is true that many prophets foretold a king to come not only for the people of Israel but for all the nations who were to believe in him. Hence David also said: Say among the nations, the Lord hath reigned. Hence these men say that it must be understood that Christ was king of all, good and bad, according to his deity, but according to his humanity he was king of believers, whether the believers were Jews according to the flesh or Gentiles; yet all believers, and only the Jews, were so according to the spirit. Consequently the prophets foretold that he would have dominion of the kingdom in a certain way, namely spiritual, not secular or temporal. (Behold, the Lord your judge, the Lord your lawgiver, the Lord your king; he will come and save you.) That passage is against him, because it cannot be understood of a secular or temporal judge, nor of a temporal or secular lawgiver, nor of a temporal or secular salvation, when it says: the Lord your judge. It has been plainly proved above by the authority of Luke 12, when Christ said: Who made me a judge or divider over you? For nowhere is it read that Christ judged in temporal matters. Therefore he was not a judge in temporal matters. Nor, when Isaiah says the Lord lawgiver, can it seem to be understood of a temporal lawgiver, since nowhere is it read that he laid down laws concerning any temporal things, unless perhaps you say that he laid down a law concerning temporal things, teaching that they must be utterly despised. But such a law is to be judged not temporal but spiritual. Nor, when it is said he will come and save you, can it be understood of temporal salvation, since he said to his followers, as in Matthew 24: They will deliver you up to tribulation and will kill you. Christ therefore did not come to save the Jews temporally, neither the believers nor the unbelievers. Not the unbelievers, since the believers endured every tribulation and many died temporally for him; nor the unbelievers, since on account of the sins committed against him they were destroyed by the Romans. Since therefore the authority of Isaiah can be understood neither of a temporal judge, nor of a temporal lawgiver, nor of a temporal salvation, it cannot in any way be shown by it that Isaiah prophesied Christ would be a temporal king. But just as Christ is judge spiritually and lawgiver spiritually, and spiritually saved believers, so he was spiritually king over those who believe in him. (And a king shall reign): those words of Jeremiah also ought not to be understood of a temporal king, just as Jeremiah did not understand that Christ was to reign temporally when he said shall reign. For there appears no reason why Jeremiah, in saying a king shall reign, should have understood more that Christ was to be a temporal king than that he was to reign temporally.

units.la: (Et hoc est nomen quod vocabunt eum, Dominus iustus noster) Hic accipitur Dominus loquendo de Christo inquantum erat homo mortalis, non pro Domino rerum temporalium, sed pro Domino propter praerogatiuam vnionis naturae humanae ad diuinum suppositum, & auctoritatis specialis ac sanctitatis aliarum gratiarum. (Cui Deus coeli dedit regnum quod in aeternum non dissipabitur) Ista verba Danielis non possunt intelligi de regno temporali, quia omne tale regnum dissipabitur: sed debent intelligi de regno spirituali, hoc est de ecclesia Christi, quae nunquam dissipabitur, sed in fine mundi omnibus exclusis pestiferis perficietur, confirmabitur, corroborabitur, & stabilietur. (Ecce rex tuus veniet iustus &c. Hic loquitur propheta Zacharias de rege spirituali: quod ostendit cum subdit; Ipse pauper &c. Per quod claret aperte, quod non erat rex in temporalibus: quoniam sine diuitiis regnum temporale bene regi non potest. (Ego autem constitutus sum rex ab eo.) Hoc dicit Dauid in persona Christi spiritualiter loquens de rege: quod bene ostendit declarans modum regendi, cum subdit; Praedicans praeceptum eius. Praedicando ergo & docendo, ac sacramenta instituendo, non temporaliter Christus regnauit: & ita spiritualiter fuit rex, non in temporalibus. (Totus ille psalmus Eructauit, loquitur de rege illo) constat quod ille psalmus non potest ad litteram de Christo inquantum fuit homo, intelligi.
units.tr: (And this is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord our just one) Here Lord is taken of Christ as he was a mortal man, not as Lord of temporal things, but as Lord on account of the pre-eminence of the union of the human nature with the divine person, and of his special authority and the holiness of his other graces. (To whom God of heaven has given a kingdom which shall never be destroyed) These words of Daniel cannot be understood of a temporal kingdom, because every such kingdom will be destroyed. They must be understood of a spiritual kingdom, that is, of the Church of Christ, which will never be destroyed but, at the end of the world, with all the pestilent ones excluded, will be perfected, confirmed, strengthened and established. (Behold, your king comes to you, just etc.) Here the prophet Zechariah speaks of a spiritual king, as he shows when he adds: He is poor etc. From this it is plain that he was not a king in temporal affairs, since a temporal kingdom cannot be well governed without riches. (But I have been established king by him) David says this in the person of Christ, speaking spiritually of the king, as he shows well when he declares the manner of his rule, adding: Proclaiming his decree. Therefore by preaching and teaching, and by instituting the sacraments, Christ did not reign temporally; and so he was king spiritually, not in temporal matters. (The whole of that psalm, My heart has uttered, speaks of that king) It is agreed that this psalm cannot be understood literally of Christ as he was man.

units.la: Cum enim dicitur; Accingere gladio tuo super femur tuum potentissime, intende prospere, procede & regna. Sagittae tuae acutae, populi sub te cadent, sedes tua in seculum seculi, vnxit te Deus Deus tuus. Myrrha & gutta & casia a vestimentis tuis a domibus eburneis, a quibus delectauerunt te filiae regum in honore tuo. Astitit regina a dextris tuis in vestitu deaurato. Pro patribus tuis nati sunt tibi filii: constitues eos principes super omnem terram. &c. Non potest exponi ad litteram, vt de gladio materiali, prosperitate temporali, modo regnandi temporali, sagittis materialibus, sede materiali, vnctione corporali, vestimentis corporalibus, filiabus regum carnalibus, regina carnali, filiisque carnalibus, & principibus temporalibus debeant praedicta verba intelligi. Et per consequens psalmus ille de rege temporali non loquitur. Et cum de sponsa eius ecclesia psalmus ille loquatur: non loquitur de sponsa Christi carnali, sed spirituali. Ergo similiter loquitur de rege non temporali, sed spirituali. Item Glossa dicit ecclesiam esse sponsam, de qua loquitur psalmus praedictus. Sed illa sponsa est regina. Sed non est regina temporaliter. Ergo spiritualiter tantum est regina. Ergo & rex, de quo loquitur, non temporaliter, sed spiritualiter est rex censendus. (Et alii multi psalmi loquuntur de rege huiusmodi) Sicut alii Psalmi loquuntur de rege Christo, ita loquuntur de eius regimine, ipsum regnare dicentes: sed alii Psalmi non loquuntur de regimine Christi temporali, sed spirituali, nec dicunt ipsum regnare temporaliter. Igitur per alios Psalmos concludi non potest, quod Christus rex fuerit temporalis. Hoc enim posset ostendi discurrendo per Psalmos de Christo rege loquentes. Sed ipse concedit, quod Christus non regnauit temporaliter, nisi in valde paucis, de quo inferius disseretur. Ideo ad praesens de hoc non dicetur.
units.tr: For when it is said: Gird your sword upon your thigh, most mighty one; press on prosperously, proceed and reign. Your sharp arrows, the peoples shall fall under you; your throne is for ever and ever; God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows. Myrrh and stacte and cassia are from your garments, from ivory palaces, from which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honour. The queen stood at your right hand in a golden robe. Instead of your fathers sons have been born to you; you shall make them princes over all the earth etc., it cannot be expounded literally, so that these words should be understood of a material sword, of temporal prosperity, of a temporal manner of reigning, of material arrows, of a material throne, of bodily anointing, of bodily garments, of carnal daughters of kings, of a carnal queen, of carnal sons and of temporal princes. And consequently that psalm does not speak of a temporal king. And since that psalm speaks of his bride, the Church, it does not speak of a carnal bride of Christ but of a spiritual one. Therefore it likewise speaks of a king who is not temporal but spiritual. Again, the Gloss says that the Church is the bride of whom the aforesaid psalm speaks. But that bride is a queen. But she is not a queen temporally. Therefore she is a queen only spiritually. Therefore the king of whom it speaks is to be judged king not temporally but spiritually. (And many other psalms speak of a king of this kind) Just as other psalms speak of Christ as king, so they speak of his rule, saying that he reigns; but other psalms do not speak of Christ's rule as temporal but as spiritual, nor do they say that he reigns temporally. Therefore it cannot be concluded from other psalms that Christ was a temporal king. For this could be shown by going through the psalms that speak of Christ the king. But he himself concedes that Christ did not reign temporally, except in very few matters, which will be discussed below. So for the present nothing more will be said on this.

units.la: (Videte regem Salomonem &c.) Illa verba intellecta de Christo spiritualiter de rege debent intelligi, quemadmodum verba quae sequuntur, cum dicitur: in diademate quo coronauit eum mater sua in die desponsationis illius & in die laetitiae cordis eius, non debent intelligi de diademate materiali, neq; coronatione materiali, neq; de desponsatione carnali, neque de mundana laetitia. (Dabit ei Dominus Deus sedem Dauid patris eius & regnabit &c.) Ista verba sic non intelliguntur de sede materiali, quia CHRISTUS nunquam in sede materiali Dauid sedit: ita non debent intelligi de regno temporali, nec de modo regendi temporaliter.
units.tr: (Behold King Solomon etc.) Those words, when understood spiritually of Christ, must be understood of a king, just as the words that follow, when it is said: with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his espousal and on the day of the gladness of his heart, must not be understood of a material crown, nor of a material coronation, nor of a carnal espousal, nor of worldly gladness. (The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign etc.) Those words are not understood of a material throne, because Christ never sat on the material throne of David; so they must not be understood of a temporal kingdom, nor of a temporal manner of ruling.

units.la: Vnde dicunt isti, quod ex intellectu istius impugnati circa verba praedicta sequitur, quod regnum temporale sit in perpetuum duraturum: cum ibidem dicatur expresse: regnabit in domo Iacob in aeternum, & regni eius non erit finis. Si ergo regnum Christi fuit temporale; & regni eius non erit finis: ergo aliquod regnum temporale non habebit finem: & per consequens nunquam erit generalis resurrectio mortuorum: quod quia falsum est, verba praedicta debent intelligi de regno spirituali, quod est ecclesia, quae nunquam habebit finem: sed in die iudicii coronabitur & inperpetuum feliciter permanebit. (Natus est nobis Saluator qui est Christus Dominus, id est, rex & Dominus) conceditur hoc de rege (spiritualiter intellecto: & de dominio propter praerogatiuas maximas, non propter dominium temporale. (Vbi est qui natus est rex Iudaeorum) licet illi tres Magi, qui non plene instructi explicite de modo regnandi Christi, intellexissent de rege temporali: tamen verba ista de rege spirituali secundum rei veritatem debent intelligi. (Tu es filius Dei: tu es rex Israel) Prima particula intelligitur de Christo secundum deitatem: & secunda etiam post intelligi de Christo secundum deitatem: quae nihilominus potest de ipso intelligi secundum humanitatem: sed tunc loquitur de rege spiritualiter, non temporaliter intellecto. (Iesus Nazarenus rex Iudaeorum.) Sicut illa verba secundum veritatem non debent intelligi de his, qui erant Iudaei carnaliter, sed spiritualiter secundum Glossam: ita debent intelligi de rege spirituali non temporali. Hoc etiam Saluator noster confessus fuit. Iohan. 18. Dicunt isti, quod Saluator non absolute confessus est se regem: sed cum quadam modificatione, scil. non illo modo, quo intellexerunt Iudaei, sed aliter. Ideo dixit Christus respondens Pilato: Tu dicis quia rex sum ego. Ego in hoc natus sum & ad hoc veni in mundum ut testimonium perhibeam veritati. Vbi declarauit se regem esse aliter, quam intellexerunt accusantes. Hoc probant isti auctoritate beati Augustini, quae praedictam sententiam aperte videtur afferre super illud: Tu dicis quia rex sum ego. Dicens in haec verba: Non quia regem se timuit confiteri, sed ita libratum est, ut neque se regem neget, neque regem talem se fateatur, cuius regnum putetur esse de hoc mundo. (Regnum meum non est hoc de mundo.) Hoc modo secundum istos dicunt verba illa intelligi, sicut verba Christi Ioh. 15. cum dixit Apostolis, De mundo non estis: sed ego elegi vos de mundo. Et cap. 17. de eis dicit: De mundo non sunt. Quae verba non debent intelligi, quod Apostoli non fuissent ab hominibus huius mundi progeniti. Sed sicut Apostoli dicuntur non esse de mundo, quia non sunt mundani conuersantes mundane: ita regnum Christi non erat de hoc mundo, hoc est non erat mundanum mundane regendum.
units.tr: Hence these men say that from the understanding of this opposed view of the aforesaid words it follows that a temporal kingdom would endure for ever, since it is expressly said in the same place: He shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end. If therefore Christ's kingdom was temporal, and of his kingdom there shall be no end, then some temporal kingdom will have no end; and consequently there will never be a general resurrection of the dead. Since that is false, the aforesaid words must be understood of a spiritual kingdom, which is the Church, which will never have an end, but on the day of judgement will be crowned and will remain happily for ever. (Our Saviour has been born to us, who is Christ the Lord, that is, king and lord) This is granted of a king understood spiritually, and of dominion on account of his very great prerogatives, not on account of temporal dominion. (Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?) Although those three Magi, who were not fully instructed and did not explicitly know the manner of Christ's reign, understood it of a temporal king, nevertheless these words must be understood, according to the truth of the matter, of a spiritual king. (You are the Son of God; you are the king of Israel) The first clause is understood of Christ according to his deity; and the second, too, is understood afterwards of Christ according to his deity, which nevertheless can be understood of him according to his humanity; but then it speaks of a king understood spiritually, not temporally. (Jesus of Nazareth, king of the Jews) Just as those words, according to the truth, must not be understood of those who were Jews carnally, but spiritually, according to the Gloss, so they must be understood of a spiritual king, not a temporal one. Our Saviour himself also confessed this. John 18. These men say that the Saviour did not confess absolutely that he was a king, but with a certain qualification, namely, not in the way in which the Jews understood it, but otherwise. Therefore Christ, answering Pilate, said: You say that I am a king. For this I was born and for this I came into the world, that I should bear witness to the truth. There he declared that he was king in a different way from what his accusers understood. These men prove this by the authority of blessed Augustine, which seems plainly to bring forward the aforesaid opinion on that text: You say that I am a king. He says in these words: Not because he feared to confess that he was a king, but it was so balanced that he neither denies that he is a king nor confesses himself to be such a king whose kingdom is thought to be of this world. (My kingdom is not of this world.) In this way, according to these men, those words are to be understood, just as the words of Christ, John 15, when he said to the Apostles: You are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world. And in chapter 17 he says of them: They are not of the world. Those words must not be understood as meaning that the Apostles were not born of the men of this world. But just as the Apostles are said not to be of the world, because they are not worldly, living worldly lives, so the kingdom of Christ was not of this world, that is, it was not a worldly kingdom to be governed worldly.

units.la: Ex quo Pilatus concludens dixit: (Igitur rex es tu.) Dicunt isti, quod Pilatus non concluisit ex illo, regnum meum non est de hoc mundo, sicut infra patebit. Iesus vero respondit, regnum meum non est hinc. Dicunt isti, quod hic falso recitat verba Euangelistae. Iesus enim propter praedictam quaestionem Pilati: Ergo rex es tu, non respondit, Regnum meum non est hinc. Sed respondit, tu dicis: quia rex sum ego. Ego in hoc natus sum &c. Vnde ut sciatur, quod ille falso recitat verba Euangelistae: ponatur series textus, quae talis est: quid fecisti? Respondit Iesus: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo quia si ex hoc mundo esset regnum meum, ministri mei utique decertarent, ut non traderer Iudaeis. Nunc autem regnum meum non est hinc. Dixit itaque ei Pilatus, ergo rex es tu. Respondit Iesus: Tu dicis, quia rex sum ego. Ego natus sum in hoc &c. Patet ergo quod ex verbis his, Regnum meum non est hinc, conclusit Pilatus: ergo rex es tu.
units.tr: From this Pilate, drawing a conclusion, said: (Are you then a king?) These men say that Pilate did not conclude from that, my kingdom is not of this world, as will be made clear below. But Jesus answered, my kingdom is not from hence. These men say that here the words of the Evangelist are wrongly quoted. For Jesus, on account of the aforesaid question of Pilate, Are you then a king?, did not answer, My kingdom is not from hence. But he answered, You say that I am a king. For this I was born etc. So that it may be known that he wrongly quotes the words of the Evangelist, let the sequence of the text be set out, which is this: What have you done? Jesus answered: My kingdom is not of this world; for if my kingdom were of this world, my ministers would surely have fought that I should not be delivered to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from hence. Pilate therefore said to him, Are you then a king? Jesus answered: You say that I am a king. For this I was born etc. It is plain, then, that from these words, My kingdom is not from hence, Pilate concluded: Are you then a king?

units.la: Et ideo ex his verbis, regnum meum non est de hoc mundo: regnum meum non est hinc, non fuit plene satisfactum Pilato de accusatione Iudaeorum dicentium Christum fecisse se regem in iniuriam Caesaris. Dicente Augustino, ut prius dictum est: Tu dicis, ac si diceret, carnaliter carnaliter dicis: propter quod postquam Pilatus conclusit dicens: Ergo rex es tu, carnaliter intelligens, Christus plenius informauit Pilatum; quomodo erat rex, non in iniuriam Caesaris dicens: tu dicis carnaliter intelligens: quia rex sum ego. Ego in hoc natus sum &c. quasi diceret, verum est, quia rex sum, sed non carnaliter, sicut tu carnaliter intelligis: quia non sum rex temporaliter in iniuriam Caesaris, sicut falso imponunt mihi Iudaei, sed rex sum spiritualiter: quia ego in hoc natus sum, & ad hoc veni in mundum, ut testimonium perhibeam veritati. Quasi diceret, non veni ut regnarem temporaliter: sed veni ut testimonium perhiberem veritati, docens homines conuerti ad veritatem.
units.tr: And so, from these words, my kingdom is not of this world: my kingdom is not from here, Pilate was not fully satisfied about the accusation of the Jews, who said that Christ had made himself king against Caesar. As Augustine said earlier, You say it, as if he said, you say it carnally. Therefore, when Pilate concluded, saying, So you are a king, understanding it carnally, Christ instructed Pilate more fully: he was king, but not against Caesar, saying, you understand carnally, that I am a king. For this I was born, etc. As if he said: it is true that I am a king, but not in the carnal sense you understand. For I am not a temporal king to Caesar's injury, as the Jews falsely charge me, but I am a spiritual king: for I was born for this, and came into the world for this, that I should bear witness to the truth. As if he said: I did not come to reign temporally, but I came to bear witness to the truth, teaching men to turn to the truth.

units.la: Propter quam responsionem Christi Pilatus interrogans, quid est veritas, & responsionem Christi non expectans, exiit ad Iudaeos, & dixit eis, ego nullam in eo inuenio causam, quasi diceret ipsum interrogans, & diligenter examinans negat se esse regem temporaliter in iniuriam Caesaris, sed dicit, aliter se esse regem, nec vos probare potestis, quod regem se fecerit temporalem in iniuriam Caesaris. Ideo dico vobis, quod nullam in eo inuenio causam. (Regnum meum non est hinc.) Hoc est, regnum meum non pertinet ad mundanos. (Non dixit, non est hic.) Verum mundo non habeo, sicut nec habebat, imo a Deo. Iste videtur fuisse intellectus Pilati, quem habuit, an Christus fecisset se regem in iniuriam Caesaris, quia si Christus fecisset se regem temporalem, quamvis dixisset le regnum habuisse a Deo, Pilatus non minus, imo forte magis reputaslet Christum iniuriatum fuisse Caesari, quam si dixisset se habuisse regnum temporale a mundo. Et ideo volens amplius informari de intentione Christi, intulit, Ergo rex es tu. Quasi diceret, quid ad me, a quo dicas te habuisse regnum? Dic mihi an reputes te habere regnum temporale in praeiudicium Caesaris condemnabo. Propter quod Christus amplius declarans quomodo erat rex, dicit, Ego in hoc natus sum &c. Et ex tunc Pilatus praedicto modo verba praemissa minime intellexerit. Intellexit verba angeli ad genitricem Christi, ut declaratum est prius. (Dominum eum & CHRISTVM fecit DEVS hunc IESVM.) Dominum eum vocat Petrus propter praerogatiuam unionis, sanctitatis & auctoritatis spiritualis, ac aliarum gratiarum. CHRISTVM vero vocat propter unctionem spiritualem, non corporalem. (Quod regnum suum a mundo non non habuerit: sed à Deo.) Hoc verum est de regno spirituali, non temporali, Iesum fecit Dominum Christum id est regem, de rege spiritualiter, non temporaliter intellecto, concedi potest. (Per Christum enim regem intelligimus) Per Christum in scriptura non solum intelligimus regem temporalem, sed etiam regem spiritualiter, & etiam sacerdotes. Unde cum dicit propheta in persona Dei: Nolite tangere Christos meos, per Christos ibi non intelliguntur solummodo reges temporales, sed etiam alii sancti Dei. (Quia reges in ungi consueuerunt.) Verum est, quod inungi consueuerunt corporaliter reges temporales: & ideo cum Christus non fuerit inunctus in regem corporaliter, nō potest concludi ex hoc, quod dicitur vnctus, quod rex fuerit temporalis, sacerdotes etiam & prophetæ consueuerunt inungi. De vnctione sacerdotum habetur in multis locis scripturæ diuinæ. De vnctione vero prophetarum habetur 4. Reg.19. vbi dixit Deus ad Heliam: Helisæum filium Saphat, qui est de Abelmeula, vnges prophetam pro te. Ex hoc ergo, quod reges consueuerunt inungi, & Iesus fuit inunctus, non potest concludi, quod rex fuerit temporaliter. (Regnum Christi non terrenum, sed cœleste ostendit esse.) Hic Rabanus vocat regnum cœleste credentes in Christum, credentes cœlestia. (Item concludit Petrus ex verbis praditis, quod Christus inquantum homo subsistens in diuino supposito fuerit dominus & rex factus.) Hoc concedi potest intelligendo eum dominum propter prærogatiuam gratiarum, & regem spiritualiter non temporaliter (cum rex & dominus fuerit factus inquantum crucifixus.) Hic ille est sibi ipsi contrarius: quia ipse dicet postea, quod Christus habuit regnum & vniuersale dominium ab instanti suæ conceptionis, hic autem dicit, quod fuit factus Rex & Dominus inquantum crucifixus, quæ duo repugnant aperte, nam si factus fuit rex & dominus inquantum crucifixus: ergo antequam esset crucifixus, non fuit rex & dominus. Sicut sequitur: Christus fuit factus homo inquantum incarnatus: ergo ante incarnationem non fuit homo. Sicut etiam sequitur: Petrus inquantum homo factus est rationalis: ergo antequam factus esset homo, non fuit rationalis. (Regnum & dominium tanquam homini Deus sibi cessit.) Hoc potest concedi intelligendo regnum spiritualiter, & dominium pro prærogatiua gratiarum. (Christus Dominus, id est Rex & Dominus) quamuis possit concedi secundum bonum intellectum, quod Christus fuerit Rex & Dominus: non tamen ex hoc, quod quicunque est Christus, concludi potest quod sit Rex, maxime temporalis: quia multi fuerunt Christi, qui non fuerunt reges: quod probatione non indiget propter euidentiam eius. (Illud quod Gabriel Angelus, &c.) Hoc totum potest concedi, si bene intelligatur de regno, sc. spirituali. (Dominus Iesus Christus vnus verus Rex & vnus verus sacerdos est.) Hoc dictum angelus intelligit spiritualiter loquendo de rege (secundum hominem, quippe Christus & rex & sacerdos effectus est, cui dedit Deus sedem Patris sui & regni eius non erit finis.) Sicut hic angelus non loquitur de sede Dauid materiali, nec intendit, quod alicuius regni temporalis non erit finis: ita non intelligit de rege temporali. (Item quod Saluator Dominus omnium temporalium) hoc potest concedi secundum Deitatem, non secundum humanitatem, accipiendo sicut accipit ille. (Emitte Domine dominatorem terræ.) Illa verba Esaiæ non possunt intelligi de Christo secundum humanitatem, secundum quod dominator dicitur à dominando temporaliter. Nam sicut non dicitur creator antequam creet, ita non dicitur quis dominator antequam dominetur: sed manifestum est & ille concedit (sicut post patebit) quod Christus secundum humanitatem nō dominabatur terræ, licet secundum illum in quibusdam paucis gesserit se pro Domino. Verba igitur intelligenda sunt de Christo secundū Deitatem. (Ex te mihi egredietur qui sit dominator in Israel.) Hæc verba Michææ intelligenda sunt de Christo secundū Deitatē, sicut & verba sequētia, cū dicitur: & egressus eius ab initio æternitatis, nō possunt de Christo intelligi, nisi secundū Deitatem. (Dominator quæ vos quæritis.) Illa etiā verba intelligēda sunt de Christo secundum formā Deitatis. (Vos vocatis me magister & domine.) Dominus dicitur non solū secundū Deitatem, sed etiā secundum humanitatē: non propter dominium temporaliū ante passionē, sed propter prærogatiuā cōplurium gratiarum, sic etiā milites & alii vocāt Fratres Minores dominos propter prærogatiuā religionis, qui tn nullius rei temporalis habent dominiū. (Dominus opus his habet.) Hic dicitur Dominus secundū Deitatem, vnde Gloss. ibid. Dominus simpliciter omnium rerum, cui seruire debet creatura. Potest etiā dici Dominus secundum humanitatē, propter prærogatiuā gratiarum. (Rex regū & dominus dominantiū.)
