Ista verba intelligi possunt de Christo secundum Deitatem, vel secundum aliquos intelliguntur de Christo secundum humanitatē, post resurrectionē, qñ data fuit sibi omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra, sicut per seriem textus ostendunt. (Et in Iesum Christum filium eius vnicum Dominum nostrum.) Illa verba intelliguntur de Christo secundum Deitatem: vel intelliguntur secundū humanitatem propter prærogatiuā gratiarum: eodē modo dicitur ad verba symboli, quod cātatur in Missa. (Præmissa aut, sc. regnum & vniuersale dominium habuit Iesus inquantum Dominus ab æterno.) Illa verba sunt erronea: quia ex his sequitur, quod Iesus inquantum Deus fuisset rex & Dominus ab æterno: & ita mundus fuisset ab æterno, quod est hæreticum. Dicendū est igitur, quod sicut Deus pater non habuit seruum ab æterno, ita non fuit Dominus, nec etiam rex ab æterno: sed ex tempore per creationem rex absq; sui mutatione vel mutabilitate factus est rex & Dominus: ita etiam Iesus inquantum Deus non habuit regnum, & vniuersale dominium ab æterno, sed cum tempore post consubstantialitatem eius cum patre. (Et inquantum homo ex tempore, scil. ab instanti sua conceptionis ex Dei datione.) Hoc improbatum est supra.
units.tr: Pilate, questioning Christ after this answer, asked What is truth? and, not waiting for Christ's reply, went out to the Jews and said to them, I find no cause in him. It is as if, questioning him and examining him carefully, he denied that Christ was a temporal king to Caesar's injury, but said that he was a king in another way, and that they could not prove that he had made himself a temporal king to Caesar's injury. Therefore I tell you that I find no cause in him. (My kingdom is not from here.) That is, my kingdom does not belong to worldly people. (He did not say, it is not here.) Indeed, I do not have it from the world, just as he did not have it, but from God. This seems to have been Pilate's understanding, as he took it, whether Christ had made himself king against Caesar. For if Christ had made himself a temporal king, then even though he had said that he had his kingdom from God, Pilate would no less, or perhaps even more, have judged Christ to have wronged Caesar than if he had said he had a temporal kingdom from the world. And so, wishing to be better informed about Christ's intention, he added, So you are a king. It is as if he said: what is it to me, from whom you say you have a kingdom? Tell me whether you think you have a temporal kingdom; I will condemn you to Caesar's detriment. Therefore Christ, declaring more fully how he was a king, says, For this I was born, etc. And from then on Pilate did not understand the words said above in that way. He understood the words of the angel to Christ's mother, as was explained earlier. (God made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus.) Peter calls him Lord on account of the pre-eminence of union, of holiness and of spiritual authority, and of other graces. He calls him Christ on account of a spiritual anointing, not a bodily one. (That he did not have his kingdom from the world, but from God.) This is true of a spiritual kingdom, not a temporal one. (Jesus made Lord and Christ), that is, king, can be granted if it is understood of a king in the spiritual sense, not the temporal. (For by Christ we understand a king.) In Scripture, by Christ we understand not only a temporal king but also a spiritual king, and also priests. Hence when the prophet speaks in the person of God, Touch not my Christs, by Christs are meant there not only temporal kings but also other saints of God. (Because kings were accustomed to be anointed.) It is true that temporal kings were customarily anointed bodily. Therefore, since Christ was not anointed as king bodily, it cannot be concluded from the fact that he is called anointed that he was a temporal king; priests and prophets also were accustomed to be anointed. The anointing of priests is found in many places of divine Scripture. The anointing of prophets is found in 4 Reg. 19, where God said to Elijah: Elisha the son of Shaphat, who is of Abelmeholah, you shall anoint as prophet in your place. Therefore from the fact that kings were accustomed to be anointed, and Jesus was anointed, it cannot be concluded that he was a temporal king. (He shows that Christ's kingdom is not earthly but heavenly.) Here Rabanus calls the heavenly kingdom the believers in Christ, believers in heavenly things. (Peter also concludes from the words cited that Christ, as man subsisting in the divine person, was made Lord and king.) This may be granted if one understands him as Lord on account of the pre-eminence of graces, and as king spiritually, not temporally. (Since he was made king and Lord insofar as he was crucified.) Here this writer contradicts himself, because he will say afterwards that Christ had a kingdom and universal dominion from the moment of his conception, but here he says that he was made King and Lord insofar as he was crucified. These two claims clearly contradict each other: for if he was made king and Lord insofar as he was crucified, then before he was crucified he was not king and Lord. It follows as: Christ was made man insofar as he was incarnate; therefore before the incarnation he was not man. It also follows as: Peter, insofar as he was made a man, became rational; therefore before he was made a man, he was not rational. (God ceded kingdom and dominion to him as to a man.) This may be granted if the kingdom is understood spiritually and the dominion as the pre-eminence of graces. (Christ the Lord, that is, King and Lord) may be granted in a good sense, that Christ was Lord and King; yet from the fact that whoever is Christ, it cannot be concluded that he is king, especially a temporal king, for there were many Christs who were not kings, which needs no proof because it is evident. (That which the angel Gabriel, etc.) All of this can be granted if it is rightly understood of the spiritual kingdom. (The Lord Jesus Christ is the one true King and the one true priest.) The angel understands this statement spiritually, speaking of the king (according to the man, for Christ was made both king and priest, to whom God gave the throne of his father, and of his kingdom there will be no end.) Just as this angel does not speak of David's material throne, nor intend that there will be no end of some temporal kingdom, so he does not understand it of a temporal king. (Likewise, that the Saviour is Lord of all temporal things) may be granted according to the Godhead, not according to the manhood, understanding it as he understands it. (Send, O Lord, the ruler of the earth.) Those words of Isaiah cannot be understood of Christ according to his humanity, insofar as a ruler is so called from ruling temporally. For just as one is not called a creator before he creates, so one is not called a ruler before he rules; but it is clear, and he grants it (as will appear afterwards), that Christ according to his humanity did not rule the earth, although according to that nature he conducted himself as Lord in a few particular instances. The words therefore must be understood of Christ according to the Godhead. (Out of you shall come forth to me one who is to be ruler in Israel.) These words of Micah must be understood of Christ according to the Godhead, and likewise the following words, when it is said: and his going forth is from the beginning, from eternity; these cannot be understood of Christ except according to the Godhead. (Whom do you seek, ruler?) Those words also are to be understood of Christ according to the form of the Godhead. (You call me teacher and Lord.) Lord is said not only according to the Godhead but also according to the humanity: not on account of temporal dominion before the passion, but on account of the pre-eminence of many graces; so also soldiers and others call the Lesser Brothers lords on account of the pre-eminence of their religious life, though they have no temporal dominion over anything. (The Lord has need of these.) Here Lord is said according to the Godhead, whence the Gloss on the same passage: Lord simply of all things, whom creation ought to serve. It can also be said of Christ as Lord according to the humanity, on account of the pre-eminence of graces. (King of kings and Lord of lords.) These words may be understood of Christ according to the Godhead, or, according to some, they are understood of Christ according to the humanity after the resurrection, when all power in heaven and on earth was given to him, as the sequence of the text shows. (And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.) Those words are understood of Christ according to the Godhead, or they are understood according to the humanity on account of the pre-eminence of graces; in the same way it is said of the words of the creed that is sung at Mass. (But the foregoing, namely that Jesus had kingdom and universal dominion as Lord from eternity.) Those words are erroneous, because from them it follows that Jesus, insofar as he is God, would have been king and Lord from eternity, and so the world would have existed from eternity, which is heretical. It must therefore be said that just as God the Father did not have a servant from eternity, so he was not Lord, nor king, from eternity; but from time, through creation, he was made king and Lord without any change or mutability in himself. So also Jesus, insofar as he is God, did not have a kingdom and universal dominion from eternity, but in time, after his consubstantiality with the Father. (And insofar as he is man, from time, namely from the moment of his conception, by God's gift.) This has been disproved above.

units.la: CAP. XCIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XCIV.

units.la: ENTi bilominus habuit dominium aliquarum rerum temporalium non ab instanti suæ conceptionis, sed postea successiue modis aliis: vtpote ex collatione fidelium, vel emptione acquisitarum: & quæ sunt illæ, videamus.
units.tr: Nevertheless, he had dominion over certain temporal things, not from the moment of his conception but afterwards, successively, by other means: namely, by the gifts of the faithful, or by things acquired through purchase. Let us see what these were.

units.la: Nullus autem de hiis potest melius testimonium perhibere, quam Apostoli & discipuli eius, videamus ergo quid super hoc ipsi dicant specialiter a tempore, quo coepit miracula facere & praedicare, certe narrant ipsum habuisse aliqua, licet pauca, habuit itaque vestimenta. Unde legitur Matth. 17. in transfiguratione sua vestimenta eius facta esse alba, sicut nix. Item Ioh. 13. dicitur de eo sic: Surgit a coena & ponit vestimenta sua, &c. Item Ioh. 19 in persona eius legitur: Partiti sunt vestimenta mea sibi & in vestem meam miserunt sortem, & ad idem facit Matthei 27. Item Iohannes Baptista videtur supponere, quod habuit calciamenta. Legitur enim Matth. 3. quod beatus Iohannes Baptista loquens de eo dixit: Cuius non sum dignus calciamenta portare. Marc. prim. recitatur ipsum dixisse: Cuius non sum dignus procumbens solvere corrigiam calciamentorum eius. Iste Iohannes supponit ipsum loculos habuisse, in quibus Iudas quae mittebantur portabat, unde Ioh. 13. cum dixisset Iudas Iesus: Quod facis, fac citius. Quidam putaverunt, quia loculos habebat Iudas, quod dixisset ei Iesus: Eme eo, quae opus nobis sunt ad diem festum: aut ut egenis aliquid daret, & quod loculi essent Iesu, patet per Augustinum dicentem: Habebat Dominus loculos a fidelibus oblata conservans, & suorum necessitatibus aliisque indigentibus tribuebat, ut habetur 12. quaest. 1. cap. habebat, & patet per illud, quod in eius persona Psalmista dicit: Qui manducat meum panem, levabit calcaneum suum contra me, & recitatur Iohan. 13. Quod autem vinum interdum habuit, patet quod ad minus in coena illa habuit, in qua eucharistiam instituit sacramentum. De quo habetur Matth. 26. Marc. 14. & Luc. 22. Iste ergo haereticus dicendo Christum Iesum Dominum nostrum non habuisse dominium aliquod temporalium, scripturis praedictis Veteris & Novi Testamenti contradicit expresse.
units.tr: No one can bear better witness to these matters than the Apostles and his disciples. Let us see, then, what they themselves say about this, especially from the time when he began to work miracles and to preach. They certainly report that he had some things, though few. He therefore had clothing. Hence it is read in Matt. 17 that at his transfiguration his garments became white as snow. Likewise John 13 says of him: "He rises from supper and lays aside his garments," etc. Likewise John 19 reads in his person: "They have divided my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture," and Matt. 27 agrees with this. Again, John the Baptist seems to assume that he had shoes. For Matt. 3 reads that the blessed John the Baptist, speaking of him, said: "Whose shoes I am not worthy to carry." Mark 1 relates that he said: "Whose shoes' thongs I am not worthy, stooping down, to loose." This John assumes that he had a purse, in which Judas carried the things that were sent. Hence John 13, when Judas had said, "Jesus said to him, What you do, do quickly." Some thought that, because Judas had the purse, Jesus had said to him, "Buy those things we need for the feast," or that he should give something to the poor; and that the purse was Jesus' own is clear from Augustine saying: "The Lord had a purse, keeping the offerings made by the faithful, and gave them to the needs of his own and to other needy people," as is found in 12 q. 1 c. "habebat." It is also clear from what the Psalmist says in his person: "He who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me," and it is recited in John 13. That he at times had wine is clear, since at least at that supper, in which he instituted the sacrament of the Eucharist, he had it, as is recorded in Matt. 26, Mark 14 and Luke 22. This heretic, therefore, by saying that Christ Jesus our Lord had no dominion over any temporal things, expressly contradicts the aforesaid Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments.

units.la: Postquam in parte praecedenti ille impugnatus ostendit, quod Christus ab instanti suae conceptionis habuit ex Dei datione regnum & universale omnium temporalium rerum dominium; hic conatur ostendere, quod praeter illud universale dominium non ab instanti suae conceptionis, sed post quaedam rerum temporalium per modos, scilicet emptione vel collatione fidelium, acquisivit dominium. Et posset haec pars dividi in tres. Prior enim proponit conclusionem, quam intendit probare. Secundo probat eam. Tertio ibi; Iste ergo haereticus, &c. concludit quod appellans scripturae divinae contradicit. Secunda pars posset dividi in quinque partes, secundum quod primo probat per tres auctoritates, quod Christus habuit dominium vestimentorum, secundo probat per tres auctoritates, quod habuit dominium calciamentorum: ibi. Item B. Iohan. tertio per duas auctoritates ostendit, quod habuit dominium loculorum, ibi: Item Ioh. supponit, quarto unica auctoritate, quod habuit dominium panis, ibi: Et patet per illud, quinto unica auctoritate, quod habuit dominium vini ibi; Quod autem vinum.
units.tr: After the opponent was refuted in the preceding part by showing that Christ, from the moment of his conception, had the kingdom and universal dominion over all temporal things by God's gift, here he tries to show that, apart from that universal dominion, he acquired dominion, not from the moment of his conception but after certain temporal things, by means, namely purchase or the gifts of the faithful. This part can be divided into three. The first proposes the conclusion he intends to prove. Second, he proves it. Third, at "This heretic therefore," etc., he concludes that the opponent contradicts divine Scripture. The second part can be divided into five sections: first, he proves by three authorities that Christ had dominion over garments; second, by three authorities, that he had dominion over shoes, at "Likewise St. John the Baptist"; third, by two authorities, he shows that he had dominion over purses, at "Likewise John supposes"; fourth, by a single authority, that he had dominion over bread, at "And it is clear from that"; fifth, by a single authority, that he had dominion over wine, at "That he at times had wine."

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores contra praedicta quatuor probare conantur. Primo generaliter, quod Christus nullius rei temporalis habuit dominium temporale. Secundo quod Christus non habuit calciamenta, etiam quantum ad usum. Tertio specialiter, quod Christus non habuit proprietatem & dominium loculorum. Quarto declarant, quomodo Christus aliquas res habuit absque dominio & proprietate. Primum igitur, sc. quod Christus nullius rei habuit dominium & proprietatem, sed quod od dominium & proprietatem cuiuslibet rei temporalis abdicaverit. Primo ostendunt per determinationem ecclesiae. Secundo probat eandem determinationem ecclesiae in scripturis divinis, & sanctorum auctoritatib. esse fundatam. Quod autem ex determinatione ecclesiae habeant, quod Christus omnem proprietatem cuiuslibet rei temporalis abdicaverit, dicunt esse tam apertum, quod nullus legens eandem determinationem, de hoc poterit dubitare. In decretali enim Exiit, sicut saepe extitit allegatum, continentur haec verba: Omnis abdicatio proprietatis huiusmodi rerum tam in speciali quam in communi propter Deum meritoria est, & sancta: quam & Christus viam perfectionis ostendens verbo docuit, & exemplo firmavit. Quibus verbis patenter asseritur, quod Christus omnium temporalium abdicavit dominium & proprietatem tam in speciali, quam etiam in communi, ergo nullius rei temporalis habuit dominium seu proprietatem, neque in speciali, neque etiam in communi, ergo per collationem fidelium & emptionem non acquisivit rerum dominium. Ista verba supra pertractata sunt c. 9. & ideo illa quae hic desunt, ibi quaerantur. Secundo isti impugnatores ostendunt, quod praedicta de terminatio ecclesiae in scripturis divinis & sanctorum auctoritatib. est fundata. Quod probant primo sic. Illud quod Christus docuit Apostolos & alios facere: & Christus hoc facere fuit vile fidelibus, hoc ipsemet Christus fecit, sed Christus docuit Apostolos & alios omnium rerum temporalium abdicare dominium, tam in speciali quam etiam in communi: & Christus hoc facere fuit vile fidelibus, igitur Christus hoc fecit. Et ita Christus omnium temporalium abdicavit dominium, tam in speciali, quam etiam in communi. Quomodo illa ratio ex scripturis divinis capiat fulcimentum, qualiterque confirmari ac roborari valeat, & defendi, ex his quae dicta sunt c. 9. & 11. & 92. aperte patet. Et ideo si quis de ipsa dubitaverit, videat illa quae in dictis capitulis differuntur. Secundo sic arguunt: Paupertas Apostolica non fuit maior, nec altior paupertate Christi, sed Apostoli reliquerunt proprietatem & dominium omnium temporalium, tam in speciali, quam etiam in communi, igitur & Christus omnium proprietatem & dominium abdicavit. Maior ex his, quae dicta sunt capitulo praecedenti evidenter colligitur: quia in nulla perfectione, quae ad utilitatem spectabat credentium, aliquis unquam Christum expressit, igitur Apostoli in virtute paupertatis non solum interiori, sed etiam exteriori Christi minime excesserunt, minor ex his quae probata sunt c. 2. sufficienter apparet, ibi enim probatum est, quod Apostoli abdicatione proprietatis omnium temporalium, tam in speciali, quam etiam in communi servaverunt, & de hoc inferius disseretur. Sequitur igitur, quod Christus omnium rerum tam in speciali quam etiam in communi abdicavit dominium & proprietatem. Tertio sic: Paupertas quorumcunque religiosorum non est maior, nec altior paupertate Christi, sed aliqui religiosi, scilicet Fratres Minores, vovent abdicationem proprietatis cuiuslibet rei temporalis, ergo Christus proprietate omnium temporalium abdicauit tam in speciali quam etiam in communi. Maior videtur manifesta, & ex praecedentibus colligitur evidenter: tum quia Christus fuit exemplar omnis perfectionis & veritatis, tum quia Christus fecit ea, quae docuit, docuit autem illam paupertatem, quam religiosi seruant, igitur paupertas illorum religiosorum non est altior paupertate Christi, minor euidenter colligitur ex rescriptis & decretalib. summorum Pontificum, quae recitata sunt in hoc opere c. 32. & 71. Quarto sic: Paupertas euangelica perfectissime relucebat in Christo, sicut & aliae virtutes euangelicae perfectissime fuerunt in ipso, sed ad perfectionem euangelicae paupertatis spectat abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium in speciali & in communi. Haec ex c. 13. probatur aperte, ergo Christus omnium temporalium proprietatem & dominium abdicauit. Ex his patet manifeste, quod Christus nullius rei temporalis habuit dominium per proprietatem in speciali: quod insuper ex alio ostenditur. Ex hoc videl. quod omnes religiosi imitantur paupertatem Christi, religiosi autem non habent proprietatem alicuius in speciali, ergo nec Christus habuit proprietatem cuiuscunque rei temporalis in speciali. Item Christus non fuit magis proprietarius, quam illi, de quibus dicitur Act. 2. & 4. Multitudinis credentium erat cor vnum, &c. sed nullus eorum habuit proprietatem alicuius rei in speciali, ergo nec Christus habuit alicuius rei proprietatem in speciali.
units.tr: But these opponents try to prove the contrary of the four points above. First, in general, that Christ had no temporal dominion over any temporal thing. Second, that Christ did not have shoes, even as to use. Third, in particular, that Christ did not have ownership and dominion of purses. Fourth, they explain how Christ had some things without dominion and ownership. Take the first, namely that Christ had no dominion and ownership of any thing, but that he renounced dominion and ownership of every temporal thing. First they show this by the determination of the Church. Second, they prove that this same determination of the Church is grounded in divine Scripture and the authorities of the saints. That they hold from the determination of the Church that Christ renounced all ownership of any temporal thing, they say is so plain that no one reading that determination could doubt it. For in the decretal Exiit, as has often been cited, these words are contained: "Every renunciation of ownership of things of this kind, both in particular and in common, is meritorious and holy for God's sake; which Christ also, showing the way of perfection, taught by word and confirmed by example." By these words it is plainly asserted that Christ renounced dominion and ownership of all temporal things, both in particular and also in common. Therefore he had no dominion or ownership of any temporal thing, neither in particular nor in common; therefore by the gift of the faithful and by purchase he did not acquire dominion over things. These words were treated above in chapter 9, and so what is lacking here is to be sought there. Second, these opponents show that the aforesaid determination of the Church is founded in divine Scripture and the authorities of the saints. They prove this first thus: That which Christ taught the Apostles and others to do, and which it was fitting for the faithful to do, Christ himself did. But Christ taught the Apostles and others to renounce dominion over all temporal things, both in particular and in common; and it was fitting for the faithful to do this. Therefore Christ himself did this. And so Christ renounced dominion over all temporal things, both in particular and in common. How that argument draws support from divine Scripture, and how it can be confirmed, strengthened and defended, is clearly seen from what was said in chapters 9, 11 and 92. And so if anyone doubts it, let him look at what is discussed in those chapters. Second, they argue thus: The poverty of the Apostles was not greater or higher than the poverty of Christ; but the Apostles left ownership and dominion of all temporal things, both in particular and in common; therefore Christ also renounced all ownership and dominion. The major premise is clearly inferred from what was said in the previous chapter, since no one ever expressed Christ in any perfection that pertained to the benefit of believers; therefore the Apostles, in the virtue of poverty, not only inwardly but also outwardly, did not in any way go beyond Christ. The minor premise is sufficiently evident from what was proved in chapter 2, for there it was proved that the Apostles preserved, by renouncing ownership of all temporal things, both in particular and in common, and this will be discussed further below. It follows, then, that Christ renounced dominion and ownership of all things, both in particular and in common. Third, thus: The poverty of any religious orders is not greater or higher than the poverty of Christ; but certain religious, namely the Friars Minor, vow the renunciation of ownership of any temporal thing; therefore Christ renounced ownership of all temporal things, both in particular and in common. The major premise seems manifest and is clearly inferred from what precedes: both because Christ was the exemplar of all perfection and truth, and because Christ did the things he taught; and he taught that poverty which religious keep. Therefore the poverty of those religious is not higher than Christ's poverty. The minor premise is clearly inferred from the rescripts and decretals of the supreme Pontiffs, which are recited in this work in chapters 32 and 71. Fourth, thus: Evangelical poverty shone most perfectly in Christ, just as the other evangelical virtues were in him most perfectly; but to the perfection of evangelical poverty belongs the renunciation of ownership of all temporal things, both in particular and in common. This is plainly proved from chapter 13; therefore Christ renounced ownership and dominion of all temporal things. From these things it is clear that Christ had no dominion of any temporal thing through ownership in particular. This is further shown from another argument: that all religious imitate the poverty of Christ; but religious have no ownership of anything in particular; therefore neither did Christ have ownership of any temporal thing in particular. Again, Christ was no more an owner than those of whom it is said in Acts 2 and 4: "The multitude of believers had one heart," etc. But none of them had ownership of any thing in particular; therefore neither did Christ have ownership of any thing in particular.

units.la: Secundo ostenduntur isti impugnatores, quod Christus non habuit calciamenta etiam quo ad visum: quod ratione in scriptura diuina considerata probare conantur. Est autem ratio talis. Christus fuit forma & exemplar vitae, quam tradidit Apostolis & discipulis aliis obseruandam, ipso attestante, qui Ioh. 13. ait: Exemplum dedi vobis, vt quemadmodum ego feci vobis, ita & vos faciatis. Hoc etiam B. Petrus asserit manifeste in canonica sua prima c. 2. dicens: Christus passus est pro nobis, vobis relinquens exemplum vt sequamini vestigia eius. Sed Christus praecepit Apostolis, aliisq; discipulis, vt calciamentis minime vterentur, vnde Matth. 10. sic legitur: Hos duodecim misit praecipiens eis, &c. & post: Nolite possidere aurum neque argentum neque pecuniam in zonis vestris, nec peram in via, neque duas tunicas, neque calciamenta, & Marc. 6. sic legitur: Conuocauit duodecim & coepit eos mittere binos: & dabat ipsis potestatem immundorum spirituum, & praecepit illis ne quid tollerent in via, nisi virgam tantum: non peram, non panem, neque in zonis aes, sed calciatos sandaliis, & Luc. 10. sic habetur: Post hae autem designauit Dominus & alios 72. & misit illos binos, &c. & post: Nolite portare sacculum, neque peram, neque calciamenta. Ergo Christus vsum calciamentorum Apostolis & nonnullis aliis discipulis interdixit. Quod etiam sanctorum auctoritates testantur expresse. Vnde Ambros. in lib. de Fuga seculi ait: Iesus discipulos sine calciamentis & pecunia misit. Item Hieronymus ad Eustochium ait: Moyses & Iesus Naue nudis in terra pedibus iubentur incedere: & discipuli sine calciamentorum onere & vinculis pellium nudi ad praecepta noui euangelii destinantur: & milites vestimentis in sorte diuisis caligas non habebant, quas tollerent, nec habere poterat Dominus, quod prohibuerat in seruis. Item Iohannes Chrysostomus vltima homil. super Matth. dicit: Apostoli vna tunica induti & discalceati omnes superauerunt, & idem homel. 32. dicit sic: Christus Apostolis dixit: nunquid aliquid defuit vobis, quando misi vos nudos & discalceatos? Item Bernard. de septem horis, tertia hora ait: Postea cogita, quomodo habebat illes suos sanctissimos pedes confractos, quia cum festinatione duxerunt eum & reduxerunt: nec credas quod esset calciatus: quia nec ipse nec discipuli eius calciamentis vtebantur. Item Glossa super illud Matth. decim. Nolite possidere aurum, &c. ait: Propemodum necessaria vitae amputauit, ne curent de crastino, qui docet omnia regi a Deo: nec ipsa necessaria, nec cellarium secum vebant, nihil praeter vestimentum, nec etiam minima: ergo nec habuerunt calciamenta. Ex his aliisque compluribus constat aperte, quod Christus prohibuit ne Apostoli aliiue eius discipuli calciamenta portarent, ergo & ipse vsum calciamentorum abiecit. Tertio isti specialiter probare conantur, quod Christus non habuit proprietatem & dominium loculorum, quod probant primo sic. Christus nullius rei temporalis habuit proprietatem, saltem in speciali, ergo nec loculorum proprietatem habuit saltem in speciali. Antecedens probatum est prius: & adhuc amplius potest ostendi, hoc enim Glossa ad Hebr. testari videtur, quae ait: Succincti & expediti currimus sine dubitatione ad certamen martyrii, aspicientes in auctorem: qui ideo bona terra contempsit, vt contemnenda monstraret, sed si aliquid contempsit vt contemnere monstraret, sequitur quod proprietatem omnium abdicauit, vt proprietatem omnium abdicandam monstraret. Aliter enim non dedisset exemplum abdicationis omnium, quantum ad proprietatem in speciali: & per consequens nequaquam omnia contempsisset perfecte. Secundo sic arguunt. Christus seruauit formam viuendi, quam Apostolis instituit obseruandam, sed Christus praecepit Apostolis & euangelizantibus verbum Dei, quod non haberent proprietatem pecuniae, ergo nec ipse proprietatem habuit loculorum. Maior probata est prius: & similiter minor, quae adhuc sanctorum testimoniis declaratur. Ait enim Chrysostomus super illud Matth. 10. Nolite possidere aurum neque argentum, &c. Intende qualiter omnibus eos denudans omnia eis dedit: permittens in domibus eorum, quae docentur, manere nihil habentes. Si autem qui in aliena patri existentes & apud ignotos abeuntes, nihil aliud oportet portare a quotidiano cibo, multo magis domi manentes. Et Rabanus idem ait: Consequenter hoc praecepit euangelizatoribus veritatis, quibus ante dixit: Gratis accepistis gratis date. Si enim sic praedicant, vt pretium non accipiant, superflua est auri & argenti nummorum possessio. Nam si cumulassent aurum & argentum, viderentur non causa hominum, sed causa lucri praedicare. Item Ambrosius super illud Lucae: Nihil tuleritis in via, ait: Qualiesse debeat, qui euangelizat regnum Dei, praeceptis euangelicis designatur, vt sine virga, sine pera, sine calciamentis, id est subsidii temporalis adminicula non requirens fidei, qua tutus putet sibi quo minus ea requirit magis posse suppetere. Item Hieronymus ad Hiesemiam ait: Apostoli toto orbe peregrini non as in zona, non virgam in manu, non caligas habere finguntur in pedibus. Ex his aliisque compluribus patet aperte, quod Christus Apostolis & aliis euangelizatoribus veritatis praecepit, ne pecuniam possiderent, & quod ipsi peregrinando per mundum pecuniam minime possiderent, ergo multo magis Christus euangelizans per mundum proprietatem non habuit pecuniae vel loculorum. Tertio sic probant assertionem eandem: Christus non habuit proprietatem in speciali illorum quae erant communia: sed illa quae portabantur in loculis, erant communia, teste Gloss. super illud Matth. 17. Vade ad mare, &c. quae ait: Dominum tanta paupertatis fuit, ut unde tributum daret non haberet. Iudas quidem habebat communia in loculis: sed res pauperum in usus suos convertere nefas duxit ipsum dans exemplum nobis, ergo Christus non habuit proprietatem loculorum in speciali. Sed dicet aliquis, quod secundum praedicta Christus habuit proprietatem loculorum saltem in communi: quia hic dicuntur illa, quae erant in loculis, facta communia. Ad hoc dici potest dupliciter. Dicunt n. quidam, quod ea quae portabantur in loculis, erant communia, quo ad aliquale proprietatem extenso modo accepto nomine proprietatis toti communitati fidelium, & ideo pertinebant ad proprietatem Christi in speciali: nec ad proprietatem Christi & Apostolici collegii secundum dictum collegium distinguebatur a communitate fidelium, sicut pars a toto. Et aliter dicitur, quod illa quae erat communia, non Christo & Apostolis tm, sed etiam aliis pauperibus & indigentibus, quo ad licitam potestatem utendi ipsis, pro suis necessitatibus subleuandis, & ideo non erant communia eis quo ad dominium & proprietatem: sicut modo bona ecclesiae dicuntur esse pauperum, non quo ad dominium & proprietatem, sed quia deputata sunt ordinata ad pauperes sustinendos: ita illa quae portabantur in loculis deputata erant ad releuandas indigentias Christi & discipulorum suorum, ac pauperum aliorum, & tali modo erant eis communia, non quo ad dominium & proprietatem, & intellectus tam ex euangelio quam ex sanctorum auctoritatibus colligitur euidenter. Unde Ioh. 12. sic scribitur de Iuda dicente: Quare hoc unguentum non veniit trecentis argenteis, & datum est egenis? Dixit autem hoc, non quia de egenis pertinebat ad eum, sed quia fur erat & loculos habens ea, quae mittebantur portabat, & ut legitur Matthaei 26. Discipuli alii dixerunt: Ut quid perditio haec? Potuit enim venundari multo & dari pauperibus. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod illa quae portabantur in loculis, custodiebantur pauperibus & egenis, quod Glossa Iohannis duodecim testatur dicens: Cui angeli ministrabant, loculos habebat in sumptus pauperum condescendens infirmis, quod etiam Iohannes Euangelista aperte insinuat dicens capitulo decimo tertio. Quidam autem putabant, quia loculos habebat Iudas, quod dixisset ei Iesus: eme ea quae opus sunt nobis ad diem festum, aut ut egenis aliquid daret. Ex quibus insinuatur aperte, quod ea quae portabantur in loculis ad releuandas indigentias Christi & aliorum pauperum deputata fuerunt, quod Glossa ibidem asserit manifeste dicens: Quia loculos in quibus oblata seruabantur habebat suorum necessitatibus & aliis indigentibus, in quo forma ecclesiae seruandi necessaria est instituta, qua iubentur non cogitare de crastino, ne pro terrenis seruiat vel timore inopia iustitiam deferat. Item Augustinus ibidem ait: Habebat enim Dominus loculos a fidelibus oblata obseruans, & suorum necessitatibus & aliis indigentibus tribuebat: tunc primum ecclesiastica pecunia forma est instituta.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents are shown that Christ did not have shoes, not even for appearance's sake; they try to prove this from a consideration of divine Scripture. The argument runs as follows. Christ was the form and pattern of the life which he handed on to the Apostles and his other disciples to be observed, as he himself testifies in John 13: "I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you also should do." The blessed Peter also asserts this plainly in his first canonical epistle, chapter 2: "Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example that you should follow his steps." But Christ commanded the Apostles and the other disciples not to use shoes at all. Thus Matthew 10 reads: "These twelve he sent out, charging them," etc.; and afterwards: "Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your purses, nor a scrip for the way, nor two coats, nor shoes." And Mark 6 reads thus: "He called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them power over unclean spirits, and charged them to take nothing for the way except a staff only: no scrip, no bread, nor money in their purses, but to be shod with sandals." And Luke 10 has it: "After these things the Lord also appointed seventy-two others, and sent them two by two," etc.; and afterwards: "Do not carry a purse, nor a scrip, nor shoes." Therefore Christ forbade the Apostles and some other disciples the use of shoes. The authority of the saints also testifies to this expressly. Hence Ambrose in his book On Flight from the World says: "Jesus sent the disciples without shoes and without money." Likewise Jerome, writing to Eustochium, says: "Moses and Joshua the son of Nun are commanded to walk barefoot on the earth; and the disciples are sent out, without the burden of shoes and the bonds of skins, barefoot to the precepts of the new gospel; and the soldiers, when the garments were divided by lot, had no boots which they might take away, nor could the Lord have them, since he had forbidden them to his servants." Likewise John Chrysostom, in the last homily on Matthew, says: "The Apostles, clothed in one tunic and barefoot, surpassed everyone." And in homily 32 he says thus: "Christ said to the Apostles: Did anything fail you when I sent you out naked and barefoot?" Likewise Bernard, in On the Seven Hours, the third hour, says: "Afterwards consider how his most holy feet were bruised, because they led him and brought him back in haste; and do not believe that he was shod, for neither he nor his disciples used shoes." Likewise the Gloss on that passage of Matthew 10, "Do not possess gold," etc., says: "He cut away almost the necessities of life, so that they should not worry about tomorrow, he who teaches that all things are governed by God; they carried with them neither the necessities nor a store-room, nothing but a garment, not even the smallest thing; therefore they did not have shoes either." From these and many other passages it is plainly established that Christ forbade the Apostles and his other disciples to carry shoes, and therefore he himself rejected the use of shoes. Thirdly, these men try especially to prove that Christ did not have ownership and possession of the purse, which they prove first thus. Christ had no ownership of any temporal thing, at least not in particular; therefore neither did he have ownership of the purse, at least not in particular. The antecedent has been proved before, and it can be shown further still; for the Gloss on Hebrews seems to bear witness to this, which says: "Girded and ready, we run without doubt to the contest of martyrdom, looking to the author, who therefore despised good earthly things, that he might show that things to be despised are to be despised." But if he despised something in order to show that it is to be despised, it follows that he renounced ownership of all things, that he might show that ownership of all things is to be renounced. For otherwise he would not have given an example of renouncing all things as regards ownership in particular; and consequently he would not have despised all things perfectly. Secondly, they argue thus. Christ kept the form of living which he instituted for the Apostles to observe; but Christ commanded the Apostles and those preaching the word of God that they should not have ownership of money; therefore neither did he himself have ownership of the purse. The major premise has been proved before, and the minor likewise, which is further declared by the testimonies of the saints. For Chrysostom says on that passage of Matthew 10, "Do not possess gold nor silver," etc.: "Observe how, stripping them of everything, he gave them everything: allowing them, when they teach in the houses of others, to remain having nothing. For if those who stay in a foreign land and go among strangers must carry nothing else but daily food, much more should those who remain at home." And Rabanus says the same: "Consequently he commanded this to the preachers of the truth, to whom he had said before: Freely you have received, freely give. For if they preach in such a way that they take no reward, the possession of superfluous gold and silver coins is unnecessary. For if they had heaped up gold and silver, they would seem to preach not for the sake of men, but for the sake of gain." Likewise Ambrose, on the saying of Luke, "Take nothing for the way," says: "What kind of man ought to be he who preaches the kingdom of God is shown by the evangelical precepts: that without a staff, without a scrip, without shoes, that is, not seeking the aids of temporal support, he should trust in faith, by which he thinks that what he does not seek will the more surely be at hand for him." Likewise Jerome, writing to Hiesemia, says: "The Apostles, wandering as strangers through the whole world, are not imagined to have a farthing in the girdle, a staff in the hand, or boots on the feet." From these and many other passages it is clearly evident that Christ commanded the Apostles and the other preachers of the truth not to possess money, and that they, travelling about the world, did not possess money at all; therefore much more did Christ, preaching through the world, have no ownership of money or of the purse. Thirdly, they prove the same assertion thus: Christ did not have ownership in particular of those things which were common; but those things which were carried in the purse were common, as the Gloss on Matthew 17, "Go to the sea," etc., testifies, which says: "The Lord was of such poverty that he had nothing from which he might pay the tribute. Judas indeed had the common funds in the purse, but he thought it wicked to turn the goods of the poor to his own uses, setting an example for us," therefore Christ did not have ownership of the purse in particular. But someone will say that according to what has been said Christ had ownership of the purse at least in common, because here those things which were in the purse are said to have been made common. To this it can be answered in two ways. Some say that those things which were carried in the purse were common, in an extended sense of the word "ownership," to the whole community of the faithful, and therefore they belonged to Christ's ownership in particular; nor to the ownership of Christ and of the apostolic college, since that college was distinguished from the community of the faithful as a part from the whole. And another view is that what was common was common not only to Christ and the Apostles, but also to other poor and needy people, as regards the lawful power of using it for relieving their necessities; and therefore it was not common to them as regards dominion and ownership: just as now the goods of the Church are said to belong to the poor, not as regards dominion and ownership, but because they are set aside and ordained to support the poor; so those things which were carried in the purse were set aside to relieve the needs of Christ and his disciples and of other poor people, and in this way they were common to them, not as regards dominion and ownership; and this meaning is clearly gathered both from the gospel and from the authorities of the saints. Hence it is written in John 12 of Judas speaking: "Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred pence and given to the poor?" And he said this not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief, and having the purse he carried what was put into it; and as is read in Matthew 26, the other disciples said: "Why this waste? For it could have been sold for much and given to the poor." From these words it is gathered that what was carried in the purse was kept for the poor and needy, which the Gloss on John 12 bears witness to, saying: "He to whom angels ministered had a purse for the expenses of the poor, condescending to the weak." John the Evangelist also plainly hints at this in chapter 13, saying: "Some thought, because Judas had the purse, that Jesus had said to him: Buy those things which we need for the festival, or that he should give something to the needy." From these it is plainly suggested that what was carried in the purse was appointed to relieve the needs of Christ and of other poor people, which the Gloss on the same place clearly asserts, saying: "Because he had the purse in which the offerings were kept, for the needs of his own people and others in want, in which the form of the Church's keeping of necessities was instituted, by which they are commanded not to take thought for tomorrow, lest they serve for earthly things or, through fear of want, neglect justice." Likewise Augustine says in the same place: "For the Lord had a purse, keeping the offerings made by the faithful, and gave them to his own needs and to others in want: then for the first time the form of ecclesiastical money was instituted."

units.la: Item Hieronymus super illud Matthaei decimo septimo. Vade ad mare & primum piscem, &c. ait: Dominum tanta fuisse paupertatis, ut unde tributa pro se & Apostolis solueret, non haberet. Quod si quis obiicere voluerit, quomodo in loculis Iudas portabat pecuniam? Respondebimus, res pauperum in usus suos convertere nefas putauit.
units.tr: Likewise Jerome, on that passage of Matthew 17, Go to the sea and cast in the first fish, etc., says: The Lord was in such poverty that he did not have what he needed to pay the tribute for himself and the apostles. But if anyone wishes to object, how did Judas carry money in the money-box? We reply: he thought it wrong to turn the goods of the poor to his own use.

units.la: Item Chrysostomus super istis verbis Iohan. 13. quia loculos habebat Iudas, &c. ait: & nimirum nullum discipulorum pecunias deferebat: sed per hoc, quod dicit, occulte insinuat, quod quadam mulieres eum de suis facultatibus nutriebant, qui autem non virgam, non peram, non aes iubet deferre, loculos ferebat ad inopum ministerium: ut discas quoniam valde pauperem & mundo crucifixum huius oportet partis multam facere procurationem, multa enim ad nostram doctrinam dispensans agebat. Ex praedictis liquet aperte, quod illa quae portabantur in loculis, non erant deputata, nisi ad sustentationem Christi & discipulorum & pauperum aliorum. Sed quaeret aliquis, ad cuius dominium pertinebant illae pecuniae? & non videtur quod poterant pertinere nisi ad dominium Christi vel Apostolorum, quod Augustin. insinuare videtur, cum dicit, quod tunc primum ecclesiastica pecunia forma est instituta. Ex quo ecclesiastice videtur concludi, quod cum praelati ecclesiae habeant aliquale dominium pecuniae, quod Christus tunc habuit aliquale dominium illius pecuniae, cum ipse solus fuerit tunc praelatus fidelis. Ad istud dicunt aliqui, quod dominium illius pecuniae non plenum nec ita liberum, quale in rebus suis habet mundani, sed aliquale, quo videlicet poterat aliquis propter ista in iudicio litigare, pertinebat ad communitatem fidelium, quae includebat Christum & Apostolos ac omnes fideles. Alii dicunt, quod illarum pecuniarum dominium pertinebat ad dantes: quia ipsi tantummodo deponebant pecuniam de voluntate Christi pro indigentium necessitatibus releuandis praesens sibi dominium retinentes. Unde dicunt, quod pro magna parte ista erat pecunia mulierum, quae sequebantur Christum & ministrabant ei de facultatibus suis, ut habetur Lucae 8. Quarto isti declarare nituntur, quomodo Christus aliquas res habuit absque earum dominio & proprietate dicentes quod, sicut ostensum est supra ca. 2. huiusmodi vocabula meum, tuum, suum, eius, ipsius, habere, & huiusmodi, in significatione multipliciter accipiuntur in scripturis. Aliquando enim important dominium & proprietatem: aliquando usum facti: aliquando licitam potestatem utendi: aliquando consuetudinem utendi: aliquando custodiam, & aliis variis modis quasi innumerabilibus accipi possunt. Quare concedi potest, quod Christus res varias habuit quantum ad usum, & quantum ad licitam potestatem utendi, & quantum ad consuetudinem utendi, & quantum ad dispensationem aliqualem seu dispensationem: licet non habuit dominium & proprietatem.
units.tr: Likewise Chrysostom, on those words of John 13, because Judas had the money-box, etc., says: And surely none of the disciples carried money. But by what he says he secretly hints that certain women were supporting him from their own means. He who bids them carry no staff, no bag, no money, carried a money-box for the ministry to the poor, so that you may learn that one who is very poor and crucified to the world must make much provision for this part, for in dispensing much for our teaching he was doing many things. From the above it is clear that the things carried in the money-box were set aside only for the support of Christ, of the disciples and of the other poor. But someone will ask: to whose ownership did those moneys belong? It seems they could belong only to the ownership of Christ or of the apostles, which Augustine seems to suggest when he says that then for the first time the church's money system was instituted. From this it seems to follow that, since the prelates of the Church have some kind of ownership of money, Christ too then had some kind of ownership of that money, since he alone was then the faithful prelate. To this some reply that the ownership of that money was not full, nor as free as worldly men have in their own things, but of some kind, by which one could for those reasons go to law in court; it belonged to the community of the faithful, which included Christ, the apostles and all the faithful. Others say that the ownership of those moneys belonged to the givers, because they merely deposited the money by Christ's will to relieve the needs of the needy, while keeping ownership for themselves. Hence they say that for the most part this money belonged to the women who followed Christ and ministered to him from their means, as is found in Luke 8. Fourthly, these men try to explain how Christ had some things without ownership and property. They say that, as was shown above in chapter 2, words such as mine, yours, his, of him, own, to have and the like are taken in many senses in the Scriptures. For sometimes they signify ownership and property; sometimes actual use; sometimes lawful power of using; sometimes customary use; sometimes custody; and they can be taken in other varied ways, almost innumerable. Hence it may be conceded that Christ had various things as regards use, as regards lawful power of using, as regards customary use, and as regards some administration or stewardship, although he did not have ownership and property.

units.la: His visis super litteram aliqua sunt notanda, & auctoritates inductæ sunt soluendæ. (Et nihilominus habuit dominium aliquarum rerum temporalium non ab instanti suæ conceptionis.) Ista verba contradicunt aliis dictis suis: quia dicit, quod ab instanti suæ conceptionis habuit vniuersale dominium omnium rerum temporalium: & quia tali dominio renunciare non potuit, ergo nullæ res fuerunt tempore Christi, quarum non habuit dominium ab instanti suæ conceptionis: nisi dicas, quod non habuit illarum rerum dominium ab instanti conceptionis suæ, quæ tempore conceptionis suæ non fuerunt in rerum natura, quarum etiam rerum Deus non habuit tunc dominium, quia tunc non erant, sed de talibus rebus iste non loquitur: quia forte pecuniæ quas dicit Christus postea habuisse, & non ab instanti suæ conceptionis, tunc fuerunt: & ita fuerunt forte nonnullæ aliæ res.
units.tr: Having considered the text, some points must be noted, and the authorities cited must be resolved. (And nevertheless he had ownership of some temporal things, not from the instant of his conception.) These words contradict his other statements. For he says that from the instant of his conception he had universal ownership of all temporal things; and since he could not renounce such ownership, there were therefore no things in Christ's time of which he did not have ownership from the instant of his conception. Unless you say that he did not have ownership, from the instant of his conception, of those things which at that time did not exist in nature, and of which God too then had no ownership, since they did not yet exist. But this author is not speaking of such things. Perhaps the moneys which he says Christ later had, and not from the instant of his conception, then existed, and so perhaps some other things existed too.

units.la: Nec posset ista contradictio saluari, nisi quis æquiuocatione dominiorum vel modorum habendi dominium assignaret; quod ille non pot (sed postea successiue modis aliis: vtpote ex collatione fidelium vel emptione acquisitarum) si Christus postea acquisiuit aliquarum rerum dominium, aut acquisiuit dominium proprium, aut commune, non commune, quia perdidisset dominium proprium, quod habuerat primum; quod ille negat, nec dominium proprium, quia tunc in eisdem reb. habuisset duo dominia propria: sc. primum ab instanti suæ conceptionis, & aliud postea acquisiuit: quod est inconueniens. Nec potest quis assignare differentiam talium duorum dominiorum in eadem re (narrant ipsum habuisse aliqua, licet pauca) sed de dominio & proprietate nullam penitus faciunt mentionem: & per consequens de dominio nouiter acquisito nullam faciunt mentionem, & ita esto, quod habuisset omnium vniuersale dominium, per dicta Apostolorum & discipulorum non posset inferri quod habuisset aliquarum rerum dominium post conceptionem Christi nouiter acquisitum: sed tam facile dicent, qui vellent, quod habuit dominium illarum rerum ab instanti suæ conceptionis, sicut aliarum. (Habuit itaq; vestimenta) verum est, quantum ad vsum, sed quæreret aliquis, cuius fuerunt vestimenta quantum ad dominium & proprietatem? Et dicunt isti, quod quantum ad veritatem euangelii nō referret cuius fuerint quo ad dominium, dummodo non fuerint Christi quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Dicunt tamen quidam illorum, quod quemadmodum templum & nonnulla vasa in templo in Veteri Testam. fuerūt solius Dei quo ad dominium, & ministrorum templi quo ad vsum: ita vestimenta Christi erant solius Dei quo ad dominium, & Christi inquantum erat homo quo ad vsum. Aliqui vero dicunt, quod erant dantium: aliqui etiam dicunt, quod in nullius hominis erat dominio. (Et vestimenta eius.) Ex hoc quod erant eius nō potest concludi, quod erant sua quo ad dominium: sicut nec ex hoc quod Nazareth erat ciuitas Mariæ & Ioseph, cum dicatur de eis Luc. 2. Reuersi sunt in Galilæam in ciuitatem suam Nazareth, potest concludi, quod Nazareth erat Mariæ & Ioseph quo ad dominium & proprietatem: sed sicut ibi Nazareth erat ciuitas Mariæ & Ioseph, quo ad consuetudinem habitandi, ita illa vestimenta erant Christi quo ad consuetudinem vtendi. (Ponit vestimenta sua) quo ad consuetudinem vtendi (partiti sunt vestimenta mea, &c.) sicut prius erant Christi quo ad consuetudinem portandi. (Quod habuit calciamenta.) Hoc improbatum est prius (non sum dignus calciamenta portare) hoc ad literam exponi potest dupliciter, vno modo, vt intelligatur conditionaliter: hoc est, si haberet calciamenta, non essem dignus calciamenta portare, aliter, quod per calciamenta intelligantur sandalia, quibus vsus fuit Christus (soluere corrigiam calciamentorum) sicut prius, vt soluam corrigiam calciamenti, sicut ad primam istarum. (Item Iohannes supponit ipsum loculos habuisse) hoc verum est, quantum ad aliqualem dispensationem: sicut etiam multi fratres Cistertienses habent aliqualem dispensationem in rebus, in quibus tamen non habent dominium seu proprietatem (in quibus Iudas quæ mittebantur portabat.) Quæret aliquis, quomodo Christo permittente & consentiente Iudas portabat pecuniam: cum Christus sibi, sicut aliis Apostolis, interdixerit portare pecuniam? Dupliciter dici potest, vno modo, quod Christus, qui erat supra omnem legem positiuam, dispensauit cum eo, alio modo, quod hæc fecerit tempore necessitatis, quæ legem non habet, aliis autem temporibus non portauit. (Loculos habebat Iudas.) Arguat hic ille impugnatus, quod Iudas, non Christus habuit proprietatem loculorum: quia hic dicitur Iudas loculos habuisse. In tota autem sacra Scriptura non inuenitur vocaliter dictum, quod Christus habuit loculos, si ergo non obstante, quod dicatur Iudam loculos habuisse, non potest inferri, quod habuit proprietatem in loculis: sequitur quod nec ex scripturis potest inferri, quod Christus habuit proprietatem in loculis. (Habebat Dominus loculos.) Ista sunt verba Augustini, non Euangelistæ, quæ recte sunt intelligenda, scilicet quod Dominus habebat loculos, scilicet quantum ad aliqualem dispensationem absque dominio & proprietate (tribuebat) hoc est, ordinabat tribuendum. (Qui manducat meum panem) quantum ad aliqualem dispensationem. (Quod ad minus in cœna ista habuit scil. vinum) habuit vinum tunc, quantum ad vsum, vinum, in quo instituit sacramentum, non fecit suum inquantum erat homo quo ad dominium: sicut sæpe vinum, in quo sacerdos conficit, non est suum quo ad dominium, postquam autem confecerat, species vini erant specialiter Dei quo ad dominium (scripturis prædictis Veteris & Noui Testamenti contradicit expresse.) Patet per prædicta, vt isti dicunt, quod non contradicit, sed concordat.
units.tr: This contradiction could not be resolved unless someone assigned an equivocation in the ownerships or in the modes of having ownership: (but afterwards successively by other means, namely acquired by the gifts of the faithful or by purchase). If Christ afterwards acquired ownership of some things, he either acquired proper ownership or common ownership, not common, because he would have lost the proper ownership he had at first. This he denies. Nor was it proper ownership, because then he would have had two proper ownerships of the same things: first, from the instant of his conception, and another which he later acquired; and this is absurd. Nor can anyone assign a difference between two such ownerships of the same thing (they relate that he had some things, though few), but they make no mention at all of ownership and property. Consequently they make no mention of newly acquired ownership either. And so, even granting that he had universal ownership of all things, it cannot be inferred from the sayings of the apostles and disciples that he had ownership of some things acquired anew after the conception of Christ. But those who wish will just as easily say that he had ownership of those things from the instant of his conception, as of the others. (Therefore he had garments) It is true as regards use, but someone would ask: to whom did the garments belong as regards ownership and property? And these men say that, as regards the truth of the Gospel, it would not matter to whom they belonged as regards ownership, provided they were not Christ's as regards ownership and property. Some of them, however, say that just as the temple and some vessels in the temple in the Old Testament belonged to God alone as regards ownership, and to the ministers of the temple as regards use, so Christ's garments belonged to God alone as regards ownership, and to Christ insofar as he was man as regards use. Others say that they belonged to the givers; some even say that they were under no man's ownership. (And his garments.) From the fact that they were his, it cannot be concluded that they were his as regards ownership, just as from the fact that Nazareth was the city of Mary and Joseph, since it is said of them in Luke 2, They returned into Galilee, to their own city Nazareth, it cannot be concluded that Nazareth belonged to Mary and Joseph as regards ownership and property. But just as there Nazareth was the city of Mary and Joseph as regards the custom of dwelling, so those garments were Christ's as regards the custom of using. (He lays down his garments) as regards the custom of using (they divided my garments, etc.), just as before they were Christ's as regards the custom of carrying. (That he had sandals.) This was rejected before (I am not worthy to bear his sandals). This can be explained literally in two ways: in one way, so that it is understood conditionally, that is, if he had sandals, I would not be worthy to carry his sandals; in another, that by sandals are understood the sandals which Christ used (to loose the thong of his sandals), as before, that I may loose the thong of the sandal, as to the first of these. (Likewise John supposes that he had the money-box.) This is true as regards some stewardship, just as many Cistercian brothers also have some stewardship over things of which, nevertheless, they have no ownership or property. (In which Judas carried what was sent.) Someone will ask how Judas carried the money with Christ's permission and consent, since Christ had forbidden him, as he had the other apostles, to carry money. It can be said in two ways: in one way, that Christ, who was above every positive law, dispensed with him; in another, that he did this in a time of necessity, which has no law, but at other times he did not carry it. (Judas had the money-box.) Here the man being attacked may argue that it was Judas, not Christ, who had the ownership of the money-box, because here it is said that Judas had the money-box. But in the whole of Holy Scripture it is not found said in words that Christ had a money-box. So if, notwithstanding that it is said that Judas had the money-box, it cannot be inferred that he had ownership of the money-box, it follows that nor can it be inferred from the Scriptures that Christ had ownership of the money-box. (The Lord had the money-box.) These are the words of Augustine, not of the evangelist, and they are rightly understood to mean that the Lord had a money-box, that is, as regards some stewardship without dominion and property (he distributed), that is, he ordered that it be distributed. (He who eats my bread) as regards some stewardship. (That in this supper at least he had wine.) He had wine then as regards use. The wine in which he instituted the sacrament he did not make his own, insofar as he was man, as regards ownership; just as often the wine in which the priest consecrates is not his own as regards ownership, but after he has consecrated it, the species of wine are specially God's as regards ownership. (He expressly contradicts the aforesaid Scriptures of the Old and New Testament.) It is clear from what has been said, as these men claim, that it does not contradict but agrees.

units.la: CAP. XCV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XCV.

units.la: Etsi velit dicere, quod illi regno & dominio renunciauit expresse, ostendat illud si sciat: quod tamen, vt credimus, per sacram Scripturam non poterit: imo contrarium sacra Scriptura exponit expresse: qua suppo-nis nit eum non longe à passione sua dixisse: Vos vocatis me magistcr & domine, & bene dicitis, sum etenim. Item istud Matt. 21. vbi Dominus duobus discipulis dixit: Ite in castellum quod contra vos est: & statim inuenietis asinam alligatam & pullum cum ea: soluite & adducite mihi: & si quis vobis aliquid dixerit: dicite quia Dominus his opus habet. Ite tempore passionis se regem recognouit, vt probatum est supra. Item David in persona eius legitur dixisse, etiam pro tempore passionis eius: Diuiserunt sibi vestimenta mea: & super vestem meam miserunt sortem. Et recitatur Matt. 27. Ex quibus euidenter apparet ipsum regno & dominio non renunciasse praedictis: imo videtur quod nec potuerit renunciare: & si fecisset, contra ordinationem patris fecisset. Dicit enim Daniel. 2. vbi de eius regno fit mentio, sic: Suscitabit Deus coeli regnum, quod in aeternum non dissipabitur: & regnum eius alteri non tradetur. Item Daniel. 7. dicitur sic: Dedit ei potestatem & honorem & regnum, & omnes populi, tribus & linguae ipsi seruient. Potestas eius potestas aeterna, quae non auferetur, & regnum eius non corrumpetur.
units.tr: Even if the opponent wishes to say that Christ expressly renounced the kingdom and dominion, let him show it, if he knows it. Yet, as we believe, he will not be able to do so from holy Scripture. Indeed, holy Scripture expressly teaches the contrary, and it supposes that Christ, not long before his passion, said: "You call me Master and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am." Likewise, in Matthew 21, where the Lord said to two disciples: "Go into the village that is over against you, and immediately you will find an ass tied and a colt with her; loose them and bring them to me; and if anyone says anything to you, say that the Lord has need of them." At the time of his passion he acknowledged himself to be king, as has been proved above. Likewise David is read to have spoken in his person, also for the time of his passion: "They part my garments among them, and upon my vesture they cast lots." And this is recited in Matthew 27. From these passages it clearly appears that he did not renounce the aforesaid kingdom and dominion. Indeed, it seems that he could not even have renounced them, and if he had done so, he would have acted against the ordinance of the Father. For Daniel 2, where mention is made of his kingdom, says: "The God of heaven will set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, and its kingdom shall not be left to another." Likewise Daniel 7 says: "He was given power, and honour, and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes and tongues shall serve him. His power is an everlasting power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be corrupted."

units.la: In parte ista ostendere nititur, quod Christus regno & vniuersali dominio nequaquam renunciauit. Primo autem dicit, quod appellans non potest probare per Scripturam S. quod renunciauit regno & vniuersali dominio. Secundo ibi: imo contrarium, probatur per tres auctoritates, quod Christus non renunciauit regno & dominio, sed ipse retinuit. Tertio ibi: imo videtur, probatur, quod Christus non potuit renunciare regno & dominio, tali ratione: Christus non potuit facere contra ordinationem Patris, sed Pater ordinauit, quod regnum Christi duraret in perpetuum, ergo Christus regno & dominio renunciare non potuit, maiorem supponit tanquam certam habens pro impossibili, quod Christus fecisset contra ordinationem Patris, maiorem probat duabus auctoritatibus Daniel.
units.tr: In this part the author seeks to show that Christ by no means renounced the kingdom and universal dominion. First, he says that the appellant cannot prove from holy Scripture that Christ renounced the kingdom and universal dominion. Second, at the words "indeed the contrary", he proves by three authorities that Christ did not renounce the kingdom and dominion, but kept them. Third, at the words "indeed it seems", he proves that Christ could not renounce the kingdom and dominion, by this reasoning: Christ could not act against the ordinance of the Father, but the Father ordained that the kingdom of Christ should last for ever; therefore Christ could not renounce the kingdom and dominion. He takes the major premise as certain, holding it to be impossible that Christ should have acted against the ordinance of the Father, and he proves the major premise by two authorities from Daniel.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores, licet concedant, quod Christus non renunciauit regno & dominio proprie loquendo: quia ei, quod non est, renunciare non potest. Christus autem ante passionem suam nunquam habuit inquantum homo regnum temporale & dominium, seu proprietatem omnium temporalium, & per consequens eidem minime renunciauit, loquendo proprie, tamen dicunt istum impugnatum hic in duobus errare. Quorum primum est, quod Christus non longe ante passionem habuit regnum temporale & dominium seu proprietatem temporalium rerum. Secundum est, quod ideo Christus nullo modo potuerit renunciare regno & dominio: quia si fecisset, contra ordinationem Patris fecisset. Primum improbatum est prius: vbi ostensum est, quod Christus inquantum homo mortalis nunquam habuit regnum temporale & vniuersale rerum dominium seu proprietatem; & per consequens multo magis ex quo coepit praedicare, non habuit regnum & dominium supradicta. Et quod tunc non habuit regnum & dominium memorata facile posset ostendi. Quod autem non habuit vniuersale dominium omnium in sequenti cap. patebit. Hic vero probabitur, quod regnum non habuit temporale. Hoc enim B. Augustinus in quodam sermone de Innocentibus testatur expresse, qui loquens de regno Christi ait: Putabat se infelix tyrannus Domini Saluatoris aduentu regali solio detrudendum: sed non ita est. Non ad hoc venerat Christus, vt alienam gloriam inuaderet, sed vt suam donaret. Non, inquam, ad hoc venerat, vt regnum terrestre praeriperet, sed vt coeleste donaret. Non venerat ad potestates dignitatesque rapiendas, sed ad contumelias & iniurias perferendas. Non ad hoc venerat, vt sacrum illud caput ad diadema gemmatum, sed ad coronam spineam prapararet. Non inquam ad hoc venerat, vt constitueretur supra sceptra magnificus, sed vt crucifigeretur illusus. Item Leo Papa in quodam sermone de Epiphania, ait: Sed apparet illos (scilicet Iudaeos) carnaliter cum Herode sapuisse, & regnum Christi cum huius mundi potestatibus aestimasse, vt & isti temporalem sperarent ducem, & terrenum metuerent illum consortem. Ex his verbis clare patet, quod regnum Christi non fuit tale, quale est regnum terrenorum: nec Christus fuit Dux temporalis: & per consequens Rex fuit minime temporalis. Item Augustinus in epistola ad Manducantes, ait: Itaque non Christus regno decoratus, nec Christus terrenis opibus diues, nec Christus vlla terrena felicitate prefulgens: sed Christus crucifixus per totum terrarum orbem praedicatur. Item Gregorius in Pastorali ait: Ipse Dei & hominum mediator regnum percipere vitauit in terris, qui supernorum spirituum scientiam, sensumque transcendens ante saecula regnat in coelis, qui enim idcirco in carne venerat, vt non solum populum redimeret, verum etiam per suam conuersationem doceret exempla sequentibus praebens rex fieri noluit. Ad crucis vero patibulum sponte peruenit, oblatam gloriam culminis fugit, poenam probrosae mortis expetiit, vt membra eius discerent fauores fugere, terrores minime timere, pro veritate aduersa diligere, prospera formidando declinare. Item Augustinus super illud Iohan. prim. Ergo cum cognouisset quia venturi essent, &c. ait: Putare ipsum regnare tunc, quemadmodum turba putabant, erat eum rapere, id est indebite trahere, ac de ipso aestimare. Ex his claret, quod qui putabant Christum regnare temporaliter, trahebant Christum indebite, ac de ipso etiam indebite aestimabat. Sed dicet aliquis, quod Christus fuit rex temporalis, quamuis temporaliter non regnaret, sed istam obiectionem confutat beatus Augustinus super illud Iohannis; Abiit Iesus trans mare Galilea, qui ait: Venit ipse vnus vtraque personam in se portans, sacerdotis & regis, sacerdotis per victimam, quam seipsum obtulit pro nobis Deo, regis, quia regimur ab eo. Ex quibus verbis constat aperte, quod Christus non dicebatur rex, nisi quia rexit, & per consequens quia regnauit, sed non regnauit temporaliter: ergo non fuit rex temporalis. Item Glosla super illud Iohan. decim. octau. Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo, ait: hoc est regnum, quod nos scire noluit, si quod prius vicisset interrogando, ostendere voluit: quia & de suo regno hominum esset opinio Iudaeorum, gentium, qua ostensa apertius vtrisque respondetur, Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. Decepti estis: non enim impedio dominationem vestram in mundo, ne vane timeatis & saluatis: sed ad regnum coeleste credendo venite. His concordat Ambrosius in hymno Epiphaniae dicens:
units.tr: But these opponents, although they grant that Christ did not renounce the kingdom and dominion, speaking properly, because one cannot renounce what one does not have, nevertheless say that our author errs here in two points. Christ, as man, never had a temporal kingdom, dominion, or ownership of all temporal things before his passion, and consequently he never renounced them, speaking properly. The first error is that Christ did not, not long before his passion, have a temporal kingdom, dominion, or ownership of temporal things. The second is that for this reason Christ could in no way have renounced the kingdom and dominion, because if he had done so he would have acted against the ordinance of the Father. The first has been refuted before, where it was shown that Christ, as mortal man, never had a temporal kingdom or universal dominion or ownership of things; and consequently, much more so from the time he began to preach, he did not have the aforesaid kingdom and dominion. That he did not then have the kingdom and dominion mentioned could easily be shown. That he did not have universal dominion over all things will become clear in the following chapter. Here, however, it will be proved that he did not have a temporal kingdom. For Blessed Augustine expressly testifies to this in a certain sermon on the Holy Innocents, where, speaking of the kingdom of Christ, he says: "The unhappy tyrant thought that at the coming of the Lord and Saviour he would be thrust down from his royal throne, but it is not so. Christ did not come to seize another's glory, but to give his own. I say, he did not come to snatch away an earthly kingdom, but to give a heavenly one. He did not come to seize powers and dignities, but to endure insults and injuries. He did not come to prepare that holy head for a jewelled diadem, but for a crown of thorns. I say, he did not come to be made magnificent above sceptres, but to be crucified, mocked." Likewise Pope Leo, in a certain sermon on the Epiphany, says: "But it appears that those (namely the Jews) were carnally wise with Herod, and esteemed the kingdom of Christ as one of the powers of this world, so that they hoped for a temporal leader, and feared him as an earthly rival." From these words it is clear that the kingdom of Christ was not such as the kingdom of earthly rulers is, nor was Christ a temporal leader; and consequently he was by no means a temporal king. Likewise Augustine, in his letter to the Manducantes, says: "Christ is not therefore proclaimed as adorned with a kingdom, nor as rich in earthly wealth, nor as shining with any earthly happiness, but as crucified, throughout the whole world." Likewise Gregory, in the Pastoral Rule, says: "The Mediator between God and men avoided receiving a kingdom on earth, he who, surpassing the knowledge and understanding of the supernal spirits, reigns in heaven before the ages. For he had come in the flesh so that he would not only redeem the people, but also by his conduct teach them and offer examples to those who follow; he refused to become king. Indeed he went voluntarily to the gibbet of the cross; he fled the offered glory of rule; he sought the punishment of a shameful death, so that his members might learn to flee favours, to fear terrors in no way, to love adversity for the truth, and to avoid prosperity by dreading it." Likewise Augustine, on the words of John 1, "Therefore when he perceived that they would come," etc., says: "To think that he was then reigning, as the crowd thought, was to seize him, that is, to drag him undeservedly, and to form an unworthy judgement of him." From this it is clear that those who thought Christ reigned temporally were dragging Christ undeservedly, and were also judging him undeservedly. But someone will say that Christ was a temporal king, although he did not reign temporally; but the blessed Augustine refutes this objection on the words of John: "Jesus went away beyond the sea of Galilee," where he says: "He came himself, bearing in himself both persons, of priest and of king: of priest, through the victim which he offered himself for us to God; of king, because we are ruled by him." From these words it is plainly established that Christ was called king only because he ruled, and consequently because he reigned, but he did not reign temporally; therefore he was not a temporal king. Likewise the Gloss on the words of John 18: "My kingdom is not of this world," says: "This is the kingdom which he was unwilling to make known to us, but wished to show by first asking, if they had been conquered: for the opinion of the Jews and of the Gentiles about his kingdom was that it was of men. This being shown, he answers both more plainly: 'My kingdom is not of this world.' You are deceived: for I do not hinder your dominion in the world, so that you may not fear in vain and be saved, but come believing to the heavenly kingdom."

units.la: Hostis Herodes impie, Christum venisse quid times, Non arripit mortalia, Qui regna dat coelestia.
units.tr: Wicked Herod, why do you fear that Christ has come? He does not seize mortal kingdoms; he gives heavenly kingdoms.

units.la: Item consimiliter sonat Glossa in principio libri proverbiorum, dicens: parabola Graece, Latine similitudines: quod vocabulum ideo Salomon huic operi imposuit, ut non iuxta literam intelligamus, quae dicit, in quo Dominum parabolica turbis loquentem signat, sicut nomine suo & regno pacificato regnum Christi multiplicabitur eius imperium, de quo dictum est: Et regni eius non erit finis. Et, super solium eius sedebit. Ipse etiam Christus super David & rex spiritualis Israel. Ex his aliisque quamplurimis colligitur evidenter, quod Christus non venit regnum temporale suscitare, nec rex fieri voluit temporalis, neque dignitates assumere temporales: sed rex extitit spiritualis Israel. Quomodo autem tempore passionis recognovit le regem non temporaliter, sed spiritualiter, est in praecedentibus declaratum.
units.tr: In the same way the Gloss on the beginning of the Book of Proverbs says: "Parable" in Greek, "similitudes" in Latin. Solomon gave this word to the work so that we should not understand it according to the letter, which says that the Lord, speaking in parables to the crowds, signifies that, just as the kingdom of Christ is multiplied by his name and his peaceful reign, so his empire will be multiplied, of which it is said: "And of his kingdom there shall be no end." And: "He shall sit upon his throne." Christ himself is also over David and the spiritual king of Israel. From these and very many other passages it is clearly gathered that Christ did not come to restore a temporal kingdom, nor did he wish to become a temporal king or to assume temporal dignities; he was the spiritual king of Israel. How he acknowledged himself to be king at the time of his passion, not in a temporal but in a spiritual sense, has been declared in what precedes.

units.la: Secundum, in quo dicunt istum errare, est, quod ideo Christus nullo modo potuit renuntiare regno & dominio supradictis: quia si fecisset, contra ordinationem patris fecisset. Ad cuius intellectum dicunt esse sciendum, quod iste opinatur, quod omnia de necessitate eveniunt, ita quod contradictionem includit quaecunque evenire aliter quam eveniunt, cum ratio fundamentalis est, quia Deus omnia ab aeterno quomodo debeant fieri ordinavit: contradictionem autem includit, quod ordinatio divina impediatur, ergo contradictionem includit, quod quaecunque aliter eveniant, quae eveniunt. Istam rationem generalem ad probandum, quod omnia de necessitate eveniunt, ipse hic applicat ad materiam specialem: scilicet quod Christus non potuit renunciare regno & dominio supradictis: quia Deus pater ab aeterno ordinavit, quod Christus non renunciaret regno & dominio, sed contradictionem includit, quod ordinatio divina impediatur: & per consequens contradictionem includit, quod Christus faceret contra ordinationem patris, ergo contradictionem includit, quod Christus renunciaverit regno & dominio supradictis. Nec valet dicere ad excusationem ipsius, quod per potentiam Dei ordinatam non potuit fieri, quod Christus renunciaverit regno & dominio, & sicut intellectus illius habet: hoc tamen potuit fieri per Dei potentiam absolutam, quae potest in omne illud, quod nequaquam contradictionem includit.
