Quia iste impugnatus, ut quidam istorum impugnatorum dicunt se audivisse ab ore eius, & ipse postea in sermonibus suis declaravit, negat illam distinctionem Theologorum de potentia Dei ordinata & absoluta, intendens multis rationibus ostendere, quod quicquid potest Deus de potentia absoluta, potest etiam de potentia ordinata, & quicquid non potest de potentia ordinata, non potest de potentia absoluta. Unde & quidam istorum impugnatorum propter illam distinctionem, & illa quae sequuntur ex ipsa principaliter, acerbe prosequuntur.
units.tr: The second point in which they say this man errs is that Christ could in no way have renounced the kingdom and dominion mentioned above, because if he had done so he would have acted against the ordinance of the Father. To understand this, they say, one must know that this man holds that all things happen of necessity, so that whatever happens otherwise than it does happen involves a contradiction, since the fundamental principle is that God has ordained from eternity how all things are to be done. But it involves a contradiction that the divine ordinance should be hindered; therefore it involves a contradiction that anything should happen otherwise than it does. This general argument, to prove that all things happen of necessity, he here applies to a particular matter: namely, that Christ could not renounce the kingdom and dominion mentioned above, because God the Father ordained from eternity that Christ should not renounce kingdom and dominion; but it involves a contradiction that the divine ordinance be hindered, and consequently it involves a contradiction that Christ should act against the Father's ordinance; therefore it involves a contradiction that Christ should have renounced the kingdom and dominion mentioned above. Nor is it valid to say in his defence that, by the ordained power of God, it could not have come about that Christ renounced kingdom and dominion, and so on in the sense in which his words are taken; for this could have come about by the absolute power of God, which can do anything that does not involve a contradiction. For this man who is attacked, as some of his attackers say they heard from his own mouth, and as he afterwards explained in his sermons, denies that distinction of the theologians between the ordained and the absolute power of God. He intends to show by many arguments that whatever God can do by absolute power he can also do by ordained power, and whatever he cannot do by ordained power he cannot do by absolute power. Hence some of his attackers, on account of that distinction and the consequences that follow from it chiefly, pursue him bitterly.

units.la: Principalis autem ratio, quare negat istam distinctionem de potentia absoluta & ordinata, est, quia Deus aliquid faceret de potentia absoluta, quod non facit de potentia ordinata, Deus posset aliquid facere quod non ordinavit se facturum: & ita Deus esset mutabilis. Alia ratio sua est: quia in Deo idem est essentia & potentia, sed in Deo non sunt duae essentiae: ergo nec duae potentiae. His visis dicunt isti, quod iste hic dogmatizat implicite haeresim detestandam: scilicet quod omnia de necessitate eveniunt, ideo sic contra istum procedunt. Primo probant, quod non omnia de necessitate eveniunt. Secundo ostendunt, quod nulla quantum ad divinam potentiam de necessitate eveniunt. Tertio moliuntur ostendere specialiter, quod si Christus habuit regnum & dominium supradicta, ipse potuit absolute renunciare eisdem. Quarto declarant, quomodo debet intelligi, quod in Deo est duplex potentia, scilicet absoluta & ordinata: & quomodo Deus potest aliqua facere de potentia absoluta, quae non facit de potentia ordinata. Quinto ad rationes, quae pro haeresi sua tanguntur, respondent.
units.tr: The principal reason why he denies that distinction between absolute and ordained power is that God would then do by absolute power something that he does not do by ordained power, so God could do something that he has not ordained that he will do; and thus God would be changeable. His other reason is that in God essence and power are the same, but in God there are not two essences; therefore neither are there two powers. Having seen this, they say that this man here implicitly teaches the detestable heresy that all things happen of necessity, and so they proceed against him in the following way. First they prove that not all things happen of necessity. Second, they show that, as far as divine power is concerned, nothing happens of necessity. Third, they labour to show particularly that, if Christ had the kingdom and dominion mentioned above, he could absolutely have renounced them. Fourth, they explain how it must be understood that there is a twofold power in God, namely absolute and ordained, and how God can do some things by absolute power that he does not do by ordained power. Fifth, they answer the arguments that are brought forward in support of his heresy.

units.la: Primo ergo probare conantur, quod non omnia de necessitate eveniunt, sed quod aliqua possent aliter evenire, & primo sic: Deus potuit & potest multa facere, quae non fecit nec facit: & posset multa non facere, quae facit, ergo multa potuerunt & possent aliter evenire, quod eveniunt & euenerunt, & per consequens non omnia de necessitate eveniunt, sed plura contingenter. Antecedens probatur auctoritatibus manifestis. Nam, ut habetur Matth. 3. Iohannes Baptista ait: Potens est Deus de lapidibus istis suscitare filios Abrahae, & idem recitatur Lucae 3. Ex quibus verbis, quae non solum mystice, sed etiam ad literam debent intelligi, patet quod Deus potuit de lapidibus suscitare filios Abrahae: quod tamen nequaquam fecit. Secunda auctoritas habetur lib. Sap. c. 11. vbi sic scribitur. Quoniam quidem errantes colebant mutos serpentes & bestias superuacuas, immisisti illis multitudinem mutorum animalium in vindictam, ut scirent quia per quae peccat quis, per haec & torquetur. Non enim impossibilis erat omnipotens manus tua, quae creauit orbem terrarum ex materia inuisa, immittere illis multitudinem vrsorum, aut audaces leones, aut nouos generis ira plenas & ignotas bestias, aut vaporem igneum spirantes, aut odorem fumi proferentes, aut horrendas ab oculis scintillas emittentes, quarum non solum laesura poterat illes exterminare, sed & aspectu pertimorem occidere. Nam & sine his vno spiritu occidi poterant. His verbis patenter asseritur, quod Deus modis multis poterat malos occidere & punire, quibus tamen eos minime molestauit. Poterat ergo multa facere, quae non fecit. Item, sicut legitur Danielis 3. capit. Sydrac, Mysac & Abdenago dixerunt ad regem Nabuchodonosor: Ecce enim Deus noster, quem colimus, potest eripere nos de camino ignis ardentis, & de manibus tuis, O rex, liberare: quod si noluerit, notum sit tibi
units.tr: First, then, they try to prove that not all things happen of necessity, but that some things could happen otherwise; and they argue first in this way. God could and can do many things that he has not done and does not do, and he could leave undone many things that he does; therefore many things could have happened and could happen otherwise than they do and have happened, and consequently not all things happen of necessity, but many happen contingently. The antecedent is proved by plain authorities. For in Matthew 3 John the Baptist says: "God is able of these stones to raise up children to Abraham," and the same is related in Luke 3. From these words, which must be understood not only mystically but also literally, it is clear that God could have raised up children to Abraham from stones, which nevertheless he did not do at all. The second authority is in the Book of Wisdom, chapter 11, where it is written thus: "Because those who went astray worshipped mute serpents and worthless beasts, you sent upon them a multitude of mute animals as punishment, so that they might know that by what a man sins, by the same he is tormented. For your almighty hand, which created the world from formless matter, was not unable to send upon them a multitude of bears, or bold lions, or new and unknown beasts full of rage, or beasts breathing fiery vapour, or emitting a stench of smoke, or sending out terrible sparks from their eyes, which could not only harm them but also kill them by their very look. For even without these they could be killed by a single breath." By these words it is plainly asserted that God could in many ways have destroyed and punished the wicked, yet he did not at all trouble them in those ways. Therefore he could do many things that he did not do. Likewise, as we read in Daniel 3, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego said to King Nebuchadnezzar: "For behold, our God, whom we worship, is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace and out of your hand, O king, to rescue us; but if he will not, be it known to you, O king, that we do not worship your gods." From these words it is clearly gathered that these three faithful, catholic and holy men firmly believed that God could deliver them from the furnace of fire, and yet they did not know whether he would wish to deliver them, and...

units.la: Ffff 4 tibi rex, quia Deos tuos non colimus. Ex his verbis colligitur euidenter, quod isti tres viri fideles catholici atque sancti firmiter crediderunt, quod Deus eos potuit liberare de camino ignis, & tamen nesciebant, an eos voluerit liberare, & per consequens ignorabant an eos esset liberaturus, ergo firmiter crediderunt, quod Deus eos potuit liberare, esto quod non esset eos liberaturus. Ex quo sequitur euidenter, quod crediderunt Deum posse facere aliqua, quae non facit. Item, sicut legitur Luc. 1. dixit Angelus ad Mariam: Non erit impossibile apud Deum omne verbum. Volens per hoc persuadere possibilitatem incarnationis: quae persuasio nullam haberet apparentiam, nisi Deus posset facere aliqua, quae non facit. Si enim Deus non posset facere alia, quam facit, & faciet: quantum ad rem, non esset differentia inter propositionem de futuro, & propositionem de possibili. Sed dicere, Deus potest incarnari, tantum valeret, ac si diceret, Deus incarnabitur: & ita sicut per illam: non est possibile apud Deum omne verbum, non poterit probari, quod Deus incarnabitur: ita per ipsam non posset probari, quod Deus potest incarnari, quare ad persuadendum possibilitatem incarnationis haec propositio: Non est impossibile apud Deum omne verbum, esset inutilis. Patet ergo, quod Deus potest facere multa, quae non facit. Quod etiam ratione probatur. Nam qui est omnipotens, potest facere multa, quae non facit, non enim dicitur aliquis omnipotens, qui facit omnia quae facit: sed qui sive faciat sive non faciat, omnia potest. Deus autem est omnipotens, sicut per scripturam sacram & Symbolum Apostolorum, ac etiam per Symbolum quod cantatur in Missa, patet aperte, ergo Deus potest facere multa, quae non facit. Item, quod Deus posset facere multa, quae non facit, probat Magister Sententiarum lib. 1. di. 43. auctoritate Salvatoris, Mat. 26. An putas, quia non possum &c. sic dicens: ut certius firmiusque teneatur, scriptura testimonii asseramus, Deum aliter facere posse quam faciat, veritas ipsa ait: An putas quia non possum rogare patrem & exhibebit mihi plusquam duodecim legiones Angelorum? Ex quibus verbis patenter innuitur, quod & filius poterat rogare quod non rogabat, & pater poterat exhibere quod non exhibebat, utrumque igitur poterat facere, quod non faciebat. Item Augustinus in Enchiridion, & Magister Sententiarum allegat ibidem, ait: Omnipotens voluntas multa potest facere quae non vult facere, nec facit. Item Augustinus in eodem, ut Magister allegat ubi supra, ait: Cur apud quosdam non sancta sint virtutes, quae si sancta fuissent, egissent illi homines poenitentiam: & sancta sint apud eos, qui non erant credituri: tunc non latebit quod nunc latet. Nec utique Deus iniuste noluit salvos fieri, cum possent salvi esse, si vellet. Tunc in clarissima sapientia luce videbitur, quod nunc pierum fides habet, antequam manifesta contemplatione videatur, quam certa & incommutabilis & efficacissima sit voluntas Dei, quae praesit & non velit: nihil autem quod non possit, velit. Item Idem, ut recitatur ibidem, ait sic: Dominus Lazarum suscitavit in corpore: nunquid dicendum est, non potuit Iudam suscitare in mente? Potuit quidem: sed noluit. Item Augustinus super Genesi, & Magister recitat dist. 44. dicit sic: Talem potuit Deus hominem fecisse, qui nec peccare posset, nec vellet, & tamen talem non fecit, ergo Deus potuit facere, quod non fecit. Unde & de istis, qui dicunt, Deum non posse facere aliud quam facit, dicit Magister Sententiarum lib. 1. distin. 43. in haec verba: Quidam tamen de suo sensu gloriantes Dei potentiam cogitare sub mensura conati sunt. Cum enim dicunt, hucusque potest Deus, & non amplius, quid est hoc aliud quam eius potentiam, quae infinita est, conducere & restringere ad mensuram? Aiunt enim: Non potest aliud Deus facere quam facit: nec melius facere id quod facit: nec aliquid praetermittere de his quae facit. Ex his verbis constat aperte, quod secundum Magistrum Sententiarum, qui dicunt Deum non posse facere aliud quam facit, divinam potentiam infinitam ad mensuram conantur restringere: & per consequens in articulum fidei de omnipotentia Dei impudenter impingunt. Unde pro illis, qui sequuntur doctrinam Thomae, quod ipse hic tenuerit, scilicet Deum posse aliqua facere, quae non facit, est monstrandum, qui lib. 2. contra Gentiles cap. 23. probat ex intentione, quod Deus non agit de necessitate naturae in creaturis, sed per arbitrium voluntatis. Item cap. 26. probat, quod divinus intellectus ad certos effectus non coartatur. Unde in illis capitulis dixit: sciendum tamen, quod quamuis divinus intellectus ad certos effectus non coartetur, ipse tamen statuit sibi determinatos effectus, quos per suam sapientiam ordinatam producat. Item cap. 27. probat, quod nec voluntas Dei coartatur ad determinatos effectus, unde in fine concludit dicens: Non igitur ex necessitate divinae voluntatis aliqui effectus procedunt: sed ex eius libera dispositione. Item cap. 28. dicit: per hoc autem excluditur quorundam error probare nitentium, quod Deus non potest facere nisi quod facit: quia non potest facere nisi quod debet, & post dicit sic: Non est autem necessarium, si Deus suam bonitatem vult esse, quod Deus vult alia a se produci, & post: ostensum est quod Deus produxit res in esse non ex necessitate naturae, neque ex necessitate scientiae, neque voluntatis, neque iustitiae, nullo igitur modo divinae bonitati est debitum, quod res in esse producuntur. Item lib. 3. c. 9. ait: Nihil igitur Deus facere potest, quin sub ordine suae providentiae cadat: sicut non potest aliquid facere, quod eius operationi non subdatur: potest tamen alia facere, quam ea quae subduntur eius providentiae vel operationi, si absolute consideretur eius potestas, sed nec potest facere aliqua, quae sub ordine providentiae ipsius ab aeterno non fuerunt, eo quod mutabilis esse non potest. Hanc autem dispositionem quidam non considerantes in diversos errores inciderunt, quidam enim immobilitatem divini ordinis ad res ipsas, quae ordini subduntur, ostendere conati sunt dicentes: quod omnia necessario esse, in tantum quod quidam dixerunt quod Deus non potest facere alia quam quae facit. Contra quod est illud quod habetur Matth. 26. An non possum rogare patrem, & exhibebit mihi plusquam duodecim legiones Angelorum? Ex his aliisque quamplurimis, quae prima parte Summa, & super librum primum Sententiarum, & aliis locis diversis, iste Doctor determinat, patet expresse, quod ipse erroneum putat dicere, quod Deus non potest alia facere quam facit, vel quod omnia de necessitate eveniunt.
units.tr: Ffff 4 tibi rex, quia Deos tuos non colimus. From these words it is clearly gathered that these three faithful, catholic and holy men firmly believed that God was able to deliver them from the furnace of fire, and yet they did not know whether He would wish to deliver them, and consequently they did not know whether He would deliver them. Therefore they firmly believed that God could deliver them, even though He was not going to deliver them. From this it follows plainly that they believed God could do some things which He does not do. Likewise, as is read in Luke 1, the angel said to Mary: Non erit impossibile apud Deum omne verbum ("with God nothing will be impossible"), wishing by this to persuade the possibility of the incarnation; and this persuasion would have no appearance of force unless God could do some things which He does not do. For if God could not do other things than what He does and will do, then in substance there would be no difference between a proposition about the future and a proposition about the possible. But to say "God can be incarnate" would mean no more than to say "God will be incarnate"; and so, just as by the words "nothing is impossible with God" it could not be proved that God will be incarnate, so by the same words it could not be proved that God can be incarnate; hence, to persuade the possibility of the incarnation, this proposition, "Nothing is impossible with God," would be useless. It is therefore evident that God can do many things which He does not do. This is also proved by reason. For he who is omnipotent can do many things which he does not do; for one is not called omnipotent who does only what he does, but he who, whether he acts or does not act, is able to do all things. But God is omnipotent, as is plainly shown by Holy Scripture, by the Apostles' Creed, and also by the creed which is sung in the Mass; therefore God can do many things which He does not do. Again, that God could do many things which He does not do is proved by the Master of the Sentences, book 1, distinction 43, on the authority of the Saviour, Matthew 26: An putas, quia non possum &c. (“Do you think that I cannot ask the Father?”), speaking thus: "That it may be held more certainly and firmly, we assert by the testimony of Scripture that God can act otherwise than He does; the truth itself says: Do you think that I cannot ask the Father, and He will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?" From these words it is plainly implied that the Son could ask what He did not ask, and the Father could provide what He did not provide; therefore both could do what they did not do. Likewise Augustine in the Enchiridion, which the Master of the Sentences also cites in the same place, says: "Almighty will can do many things which it does not wish to do, nor does it do." Likewise Augustine in the same work, as the Master cites above, says: "Why are the powers not holy among some, which, had they been holy, those men would have done penance, and which are holy among those who were not going to believe? Then what is now hidden will not remain hidden." Nor indeed did God unjustly refuse to have them saved, since they could have been saved had He willed it. Then, in the most clear light of wisdom, it will be seen what the faithful now hold by faith, before it is seen by manifest contemplation: how certain, unchangeable and most effective the will of God is, which governs and does not will; for He wills nothing which He cannot do. Likewise the same, as is quoted in the same place, says thus: "The Lord raised Lazarus in the body: must it be said that He could not raise Judas in the mind? He could indeed, but He did not will to." Likewise Augustine on Genesis, which the Master cites in distinction 44, says: "God could have made such a man as could neither sin nor wish to, and yet He did not make such a man"; therefore God could do what He did not do. Hence also, concerning those who say that God cannot do otherwise than what He does, the Master of the Sentences, book 1, distinction 43, speaks in these words: "Some, however, glorying in their own opinion, have tried to measure the power of God by a standard. For when they say, 'God can do this far and no further,' what else is this than to bring His power, which is infinite, under and restrict it to a measure? For they say: God cannot do otherwise than He does, nor do better what He does, nor leave out anything of what He does." From these words it is plainly evident that, according to the Master of the Sentences, those who say that God cannot do otherwise than He does try to restrict the infinite divine power to a measure, and consequently rashly strike against the article of faith concerning the omnipotence of God. Therefore, to show that Thomas, who follows this doctrine, held here that God can do some things which He does not do, we must point to book 2 against the Gentiles, chapter 23, where he proves from the intention that God does not act in creatures by the necessity of nature, but by the choice of His will. Again, chapter 26, he proves that the divine intellect is not confined to certain effects. Hence in those chapters he said: "It must be understood, however, that although the divine intellect is not confined to certain effects, yet it has set for itself determined effects which it produces in an ordered way through its wisdom." Again, chapter 27, he proves that the will of God is not confined to determined effects, and in the end he concludes, saying: "Therefore certain effects do not proceed from the necessity of the divine will, but from its free disposition." Again, chapter 28 says: "By this, however, is excluded the error of certain men who strive to prove that God cannot do anything but what He does, because He cannot do anything but what He ought"; and afterwards he says thus: "It is not necessary, if God wills His goodness to be, that God wills other things to be produced apart from Himself"; and afterwards: "It has been shown that God produced things into being not from the necessity of nature, nor from the necessity of knowledge, nor of will, nor of justice; therefore it is in no way owed to the divine goodness that things are brought into being." Again, book 3, chapter 9, he says: "God therefore can do nothing which does not fall under the order of His providence, just as He cannot do anything which is not subject to His operation; yet He can do other things than those which are subject to His providence or operation, if His power is considered absolutely; but He cannot do those things which, under the order of His providence, have not been from eternity, because that order cannot be changed." Some, however, not considering this disposition, have fallen into various errors; for some have tried to show the immutability of the divine order in the very things which are subject to that order, saying that all things exist of necessity, to such an extent that some have said that God cannot do other things than those which He does. Against this is what is found in Matthew 26: "Do you think that I cannot ask the Father, and He will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?" From these and very many other passages, which this Doctor determines in the First Part of the Summa, and on the first book of the Sentences, and in various other places, it is plainly clear that he himself thought it erroneous to say that God cannot do other things than what He does, or that all things happen of necessity.

units.la: Secundo eandem conclusionem, quod non omnia de necessitate eveniunt, probant praedicti impugnatores, sic. Creaturae rationales multa non faciunt, quae possent facere, ergo non omnia de necessitate eueniunt: Consequentia est euidens, antecedens authoritate & ratione probatur. Authoritate primo sic. 2. Mach. 6. Eleazarus, qui pro diuinis legibus mortem sustinuit, cum plagis perimeretur, dixit: Domine qui habes sanctam scientiam manifeste: tu scis quia cum à morte possem liberari, duros corporis sustineo dolores, secundum animam vero propter timorem tuum libenter haec patior. Ex quibus verbis euidenter colligitur, quod ille vir sanctus potuisset infidelibus consentire: & sic à morte liberari: & tamen non consensit. Potuit ergo facere aliquid, quod non fecit. Item Ecclesiastici 30. de beato diuite sic scribitur: Beatus diues qui potuit transgredi, & non transgressus: & facere mala & non fecit. His verbis clarius dici non posset, quod potest quis facere aliquid quod non facit. Item, sicut habetur Matth. 26. & Marci 14. Discipuli Christi dixerunt: vt quid perditio ista unguenti facta est? Poterat enim unguentum istud venundari plusquam trecentis denariis, & dari pauperibus, & tamen non fuit venundatum, nec datum pauperibus, ergo aliquid potuit fieri, quod tamen non fiebat. Nec enim Christus de hoc, quod asseruerunt illud unguentum potuisse venundari & dari pauperibus, ipsos aliqualiter reprehendit: sed de indignatione ipsorum, de effusione unguenti super caput ipsius. Item Matth. 20. cum Christus interrogaret Iacobum & Iohannem: potestis bibere calicem, quem bibiturus sum? Responderunt, possumus. Non dixerunt, bibemus. Ex quo patet, quod sciuerunt se posse bibere calicem Christi, nesciuerunt tamen, an essent bibituri. Item Genes. 31. dixit Laban ad Iacob: & nunc valet quidem manus mea reddere tibi malum: sed Deus patris tui heri dixit mihi: caue ne loquaris cum Iacob quicquam durius. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Laban potuit reddere malum Iacob: & tamen non fecit, ergo potuit aliquid facere, quod minime fecit.
units.tr: Secondly, the aforementioned opponents prove the same conclusion, that not all things happen by necessity, in the following way. Rational creatures do not do many things which they could do; therefore not all things happen of necessity. The consequence is evident, and the antecedent is proved by authority and by reason. First, by authority, thus. In 2 Mach. 6, Eleazar, who endured death for the divine laws, said when he was being killed with blows: Lord, who hast manifest holy knowledge, thou knowest that whereas I might be delivered from death, I endure hard pains in body, but in soul I suffer these things gladly for fear of thee. From these words it is clearly gathered that this holy man could have consented to the unbelievers and so been delivered from death, and yet he did not consent. He could therefore do something which he did not do. Likewise, Ecclesiasticus 30 is written of the blessed rich man: Blessed is the rich man who could have transgressed and did not transgress, and could do evil and did not. More clearly than these words, it could not be said that a man can do something which he does not do. Again, as is found in Matt. 26 and Mark 14, the disciples of Christ said: Why was this waste of the ointment made? For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred pence and given to the poor, and yet it was not sold, nor given to the poor. Therefore something could be done which was nevertheless not being done. For Christ did not rebuke them in any way for saying that the ointment could have been sold and given to the poor, but for their indignation at the pouring of the ointment upon his head. Again, in Matt. 20, when Christ asked James and John: Are you able to drink the cup that I am to drink? they answered: We are able. They did not say: We will drink. From this it is plain that they knew they were able to drink Christ's cup, yet they did not know whether they were going to drink it. Again, in Gen. 31, Laban said to Jacob: It is in the power of my hand to do you harm; but the God of your father spoke to me yesterday, saying, Take heed that you speak nothing harsher to Jacob. From these words it is gathered that Laban could have done Jacob harm, and yet he did not; therefore he could do something which he in no way did.

units.la: Hoc etiam ratione secunda probatur. Nam qui potest mereri & demereri, potest facere aliquid, quod non facit, nam si non posset aliter facere, non esset in potestate eius aliter facere, sed per illud, quod non est in potestate alicuius in se, non meretur, nec demeretur, sed homo potest mereri & demereri, ergo potest aliter facere, & aliud quam facit. Haec ratio confirmatur: quia omne meritum est laudabile: & omne demeritum est vituperabile, sed illud quod non est in nostra potestate, vt possimus illud facere, & non facere, non est laudabile, neque vituperabile, ergo omne meritum & demeritum est in nostra potestate, vt possimus illud facere, & non facere, maior est euidens, minor probatur authoritate Augustini 3. de Libero arbitrio, qui ait: motus quo huc, atque illuc voluntas convertitur, nisi esset voluntarius, atque in nostra potestate, neque laudandus, cum ad superiora, neque culpandus homo esset, cum ad inferiora detorqueret, quasi quandam cardinem voluntatis. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod illud, quod non est in potestate nostra, & tamen facimus, non est laudabile, nec vituperabile.
units.tr: This is also proved by a second argument. For whoever can merit and demerit can do something he does not do; for if he could not act otherwise, it would not be in his power to act otherwise. But what is not in a person's power in himself, he neither merits nor demerits. Man, however, can merit and demerit; therefore he can act otherwise and do something other than what he does. This argument is confirmed thus: every merit is praiseworthy and every demerit blameworthy, but what is not in our power, so that we could do it or not do it, is neither praiseworthy nor blameworthy. Therefore every merit and demerit is in our power, so that we could do it or not do it. The major is evident; the minor is proved by the authority of Augustine, On Free Choice of the Will, book 3, who says: "The motion by which the will is turned this way or that would not be voluntary and in our power, and man would be neither to be praised when it turns to higher things nor to be blamed when it turns to lower things, were it not, as it were, a kind of hinge of the will." From these words it is clearly gathered that what is not in our power, and yet we do it, is neither praiseworthy nor blameworthy.

units.la: His concordat Sapiens mundi 3. Ethicorum, vbi probat, quod propter ista quae non sunt in potestate nostra, neque laudamur neque vituperamur. Patet ergo quod omne meritum & demeritum est in potestate nostra: & per consequens possumus multa non facere, quae facimus: & multa facere, quae non facimus, quare concludit euidenter, quod non omnia de necessitate eueniunt. Aliter enim, vt probat Philosophus, non oporteret negotiari neq; consiliari, quia de istis quae de necessitate eueniunt, non oportet negotiari neq; consiliari.
units.tr: The wise man of the world agrees with this in the third book of the Ethics, where he proves that for those things which are not in our power we are neither praised nor blamed. It is plain, then, that every merit and demerit is in our power; and consequently we are able not to do many things that we do, and to do many things that we do not do. Hence he rightly concludes that not all things come to pass of necessity. For otherwise, as the Philosopher proves, there would be no need to deliberate or take counsel, since one does not need to deliberate or take counsel about those things which come to pass of necessity.

units.la: Ostenso, quod non omnia de necessitate eueniunt, isti probare nituntur, quod nulla de necessitate eueniunt quantum ad diuinam potentiam, quin Deus posset omnia impedire. Nam potentia Dei non plus artatur ad istos effectus, quam ad illos, neque enim propter scientiam, neque per aeternam ordinationem, neque per mutationem ipsius, neque per aliquid quod est idem cum Deo, neque per aliquid quod non est Deus, potest Deus plus artari ad istos effectus producendos & conseruandos, quam ad illos, cum ergo ostensum sit, quod aliqua non eueniunt de necessitate, sequitur quod nulla in quantum fiunt à Deo, de necessitate eueniunt.
units.tr: Having shown that not all things come to pass of necessity, these men strive to prove that nothing comes to pass of necessity with respect to divine power, so that God could not hinder all things. For the power of God is no more restricted to those effects than to those others. For neither by his knowledge, nor by his eternal ordination, nor by his change, nor by anything that is the same as God, nor by anything that is not God, can God be more restricted to producing and preserving these effects than those. Since, therefore, it has been shown that some things do not come to pass of necessity, it follows that nothing, in so far as it comes to be, comes to pass of necessity from God.

units.la: Pro illis autem, qui doctrinam Thomae tenent, ostendunt aperte, quod haec sit intentio Thomae, qui lib. 1. contra Gentiles c. 81. ait sic: Voluntas non ex necessitate fertur ad ea quae sunt ad finem, si finis sine hoc esse possit, & post: cum ergo diuina voluntas possit sine alio esse, quinimo nec per alia aliquid perfectionis ei accrescat: nulla inest ei necessitas, vt alia velit ex hoc quod vult suam voluntatem: & per consequens nulla inest ei necessitas, vt quacunque alia producat vel conseruet, & infra sic dicit: Solum igitur illud bonum voluntas secundum suam rationem non potest velle non esse, quo non existente tollitur totaliter tota ratio boni, tale autem nullum est prater Deum, potest igitur voluntas secundum suam rationem velle non esse quodcunque prater Deum. Ex his sequitur, quod Deus potest destruere omnem rem aliam à se: & per consequens respectu Dei nihil euenit de necessitate. Item prima parte Summae quaestione 19. articulo 3. dicit sic: Cum voluntas Dei sit possit esse perfecta sine aliis, cum nihil ei perfectionis eius aliis accrescat, sequitur quod alia à se eum velle non sit necessarium absolute, ergo contingenter vult quaecunque alia à se, & ita omnia alia à Deo contingenter eueniunt: & per consequens nulla de necessitate eueniunt secundum istum Doctorem.
units.tr: As for those who hold the doctrine of Thomas, they clearly show that this was Thomas's meaning, who in book 1 against the Gentiles, chapter 81, says thus: "The will is not carried of necessity toward those things which are for the end, if the end can be without them." And afterwards: "Since, therefore, the divine will can be without another, nay, nothing of perfection accrues to it through other things, there is in it no necessity to will other things because it wills its own will; and consequently there is in it no necessity to produce or preserve whatever other things." And below he says thus: "The will, according to its own nature, cannot will not to be only that good, in whose absence the whole nature of good is totally taken away; such a good, however, is none apart from God. The will, therefore, according to its own nature, can will not to be whatever is apart from God." From these things it follows that God can destroy every thing other than himself; and consequently, with respect to God, nothing comes to pass of necessity. Likewise, in the first part of the Summa, question 19, article 3, he says thus: "Since the will of God can be perfect without others, since nothing of perfection accrues to it from others, it follows that his willing other things besides himself is not absolutely necessary; therefore he wills whatever is other than himself contingently, and so all things other than God come to pass contingently; and consequently, according to this teacher, nothing comes to pass of necessity."

units.la: Tertio isti impugnatores probare conantur, quod si Christus habuit regnum & dominium temporale, ipse potuit absolute renunciare eisdem. Hoc autem vnica ratione ad praesens nituntur ostendere, quae talis est. Non magis artabatur Christus ad habendum regnum temporale, & dominium vniuersale temporalium rerum: quam ad redimendum genus humanum per passionem suam, sed Christus non artabatur, neque necessitabatur ad saluandum genus humanum per passionem suam, ergo non artabatur neque necessitabatur habere regnum & dominium antedicta. cta. Ex quo sequitur, quod si habuit regnum & dominium antedicta, ipse potuit absolute, ita quod contradictionem minime includebat, renunciare eisdem. Maior est evidens: minor probatur auctoritate Augustini, qui lib.13. de Trinitate cap.10. vt recitat Magister Sententiarum li.1.dist.44. dicit, quod fuit & alius modus nostrae liberationis possibilis Deo, qui omnia potest: sed nullus alius nostrae miseriae succurrere fuit convenientior. Hoc idem asserit manifeste idem Magister lib.3.di.20. Nequaquam igitur necessitabatur Christus dicta regnum & dominium retinere, si ipsa habuit.
units.tr: Thirdly, these opponents try to prove that if Christ had a kingdom and temporal dominion, he could absolutely have renounced them. They rest this, for the present, on a single argument, which is this. Christ was no more constrained to have a temporal kingdom and universal dominion over temporal things than to redeem the human race by his passion; but Christ was not constrained or necessitated to save the human race by his passion; therefore he was not constrained or necessitated to have the aforesaid kingdom and dominion. From this it follows that if he had the aforesaid kingdom and dominion, he could absolutely, so that it did not involve any contradiction, have renounced them. The major is evident. The minor is proved by the authority of Augustine, who in book 13 of On the Trinity, chapter 10, as the Master of the Sentences, book 1, distinction 44, quotes, says that "there was also another possible way of our deliverance for God, who can do all things; but no other way was more fitting to succour our misery." The same Master asserts this plainly in book 3, distinction 20. Christ was therefore by no means necessitated to retain the said kingdom and dominion, if he had them.

units.la: Quarto declarant, quomodo debet intelligi distinctio Theologorum, dicentium in Deo esse duplicem potentiam (i. absolutam & ordinatam: & quomodo Deus potest aliqua facere de potentia absoluta, & non potest de potentia ordinata: dicentes, quod non est intelligenda distinctio dicta, sicut quidam ignari putant, quod realiter in Deo sit duplex potentia, quarum una est absoluta, & alia ordinata: quia unica potentia est in Deo: imo ipsa unica potentia est unica essentia: sed, sicut secundum Magistrum Sententiarum lib.1. dist.45. Sacra scriptura de voluntate Dei variis modis loqui consuevit, & non Dei voluntas diversa, sed locutio diversa est; ita scriptura divina sanctorum patrum de potentia Dei variis modis loqui consuevit: & tamen non est diversa potentia Dei, sed locutio est diversa: quia scilicet cum per talia vocabula potest, possibile, potentia, & consimilia in significatione conuenienti scripturae loquuntur de Deo, huiusmodi vocabula in diversis locis accipiuntur aequivoce. Unde in quibusdam locis denotant vel importunt omnia ista, quae non repugnant Deo facere, sic accipitur hoc verbum potest in auctoritatibus prius allegatis, & in multis aliis locis: sicut etiam accipitur hoc nomen omnipotens, Genes. 17. cum dicit Dominus ad Abraham: Ego Deus omnipotens, & in Symbolo Apostolorum: & in Symbolo quod cantatur in Missa, cum dicitur: Credo in unum Deum patrem omnipotentem &c. Aliter huiusmodi vocabula importunt vel connotant solummodo illa, quae ordinavit se facturum: & non omnia illa, quae potuit & posset ordinare se facturum. Sic accipitur Gen. 18. vbi dixit Dominus: Num celare potero Abraham, quae gesturus sum? quasi diceret, non, & tamen constat quod Deus non necessitabatur revelare Abraham, quae erat facturus: sed ideo dixit: Num celare potero &c. quia ordinavit se revelaturum Abraham quae facturus erat, sic etiam accipitur Genes. 19. cum Dominus dixit ad Loth: Festina & salvare ibi, quia non potero facere quicquam donec ingrediaris illuc. Hoc est, non faciam quicquam donec ingrediaris illuc. Sic etiam accipitur Marci. 6. cum dicitur de Salvatore nostro: Non poterat ibi virtutem ullam facere, nisi paucos infirmos impositis manibus curavit: & mirabatur propter incredulitatem illorum: & tamen constat quod Christo in quantum erat Deus, non erat absolute impossibile facere ibi virtutem: sed dicitur, quod non poterat ibi facere virtutem ullam, quia propter incredulitatem & indignitatem istorum noluit ibi facere virtutem, sic ergo hoc verbum potest accipitur aequivoce in scripturis de Deo loquentibus, quemadmodum idem verbum cum loquimur de hominibus, accipitur aequivoce, vno enim modo dicimur illa posse, quae de iure possumus: & illud dicitur posse fieri, quod licite & debite fieri potest, sic accipitur Gen. 39. cum dicit Ioseph ad Aegyptiam: Quomodo ergo possum hoc malum facere, quasi diceret: Licite & de iure non possum. Aliter dicimus posse illa, quae absolute possumus sive bene sive male. Aliter enim nequaquam peccare possemus, sic ergo hoc verbum posse accipitur aequivoce in scripturis, cum loquitur de Deo, vnica communis potentia realiter est in Deo, sed locutio est diversa: & propter istam diversam locutionem dicitur, quod Deus potest aliqua de potentia absoluta, quae non potest de potentia ordinata: hoc est, Deus potest aliqua accipiendo verbum posse secundum primam significationem eius, quae tamen non potest de potentia ordinata, haec est concedenda, Deus non potest illa, accipiendo hoc verbum posse in secunda significatione eius: & ita dicere, quod Deus potest aliqua de potentia absoluta, quae non potest de potentia ordinata, non est aliud secundum intellectum recte intelligentium, quam dicere quod Deus aliqua potest, quae tamen minime ordinavit se facturum: quae tamen si faceret, de potentia ordinata faceret ipsa: quia si faceret ea, ordinaret se facturum ipsa. Quia igitur, vt dicunt isti, iste impugnatus nescivit videre aequivocationem huius verbi potest, ideo male intellexit istam distinctionem Theologorum de potentia Dei absoluta & ordinata: & tamen dicunt, quod licet ipsam ad intellectum recte intelligentium intellexisset, ipsam nihilominus probasset respectu Dei, quia imaginatur, quod sic Deus omnia de necessitate ordinavit, & de necessitate absoluta oportet eum facere illa: ita quod ipsum non facere ipsa contradictionem includit: quod in suis sermonibus probare rationibus conatur.
units.tr: Fourthly, they explain how the distinction of the theologians must be understood, who say that there is a twofold power in God, namely absolute and ordained, and how God can do some things by absolute power which he cannot do by ordained power. They say that the said distinction is not to be understood as some ignorant people suppose, that in God there is really a twofold power, one absolute and the other ordained; for there is one power in God, indeed that one power is the one essence. Rather, just as, according to the Master of the Sentences, book 1, distinction 45, Holy Scripture is accustomed to speak of the will of God in various ways, and it is not that the will of God is diverse, but the manner of speaking is diverse, so the divine Scripture and the holy Fathers are accustomed to speak of the power of God in various ways, and yet the power of God is not diverse, but the manner of speaking is diverse. That is to say, when Scripture speaks of God by such words as "can," "possible," "power," and the like, in a meaning suited to the passage, these words are taken equivocally in different places. Hence in some places they denote or imply all those things which it is not contrary to God to do. So the word "can" is taken in the authorities cited above and in many other places; and so also the name "almighty" is taken in Genesis 17, where the Lord says to Abraham, "I am God Almighty," and in the Apostles' Creed, and in the creed which is sung at Mass, where it is said, "I believe in one God, the Father almighty," etc. In another way such words imply or connote only those things which he has ordained that he will do, and not all those things which he was able and could ordain that he would do. So it is taken in Genesis 18, where the Lord said: "Shall I be able to hide from Abraham what I am about to do?" as if he were saying "no"; and yet it is certain that God was not constrained to reveal to Abraham what he was about to do; but he said, "Shall I be able to hide," etc., because he had ordained that he would reveal to Abraham what he was about to do. So also it is taken in Genesis 19, when the Lord said to Lot: "Hurry and save yourself there, for I cannot do anything until you enter there." That is, "I will do nothing until you enter there." So also it is taken in Mark 6, where it is said of our Saviour: "He could there do no mighty work, except that he laid his hands on a few sick folk and healed them; and he marvelled because of their unbelief." And yet it is certain that for Christ, insofar as he was God, it was not absolutely impossible to work a miracle there; but it is said that he could do no mighty work there, because on account of their unbelief and unworthiness he was unwilling to work a miracle there. Thus the word "can" is taken equivocally in Scriptures speaking of God, just as the same word is taken equivocally when we speak of men. For in one sense we are said to be able to do those things which we may do by right; and that is said to be possible which may be done lawfully and rightly. So it is taken in Genesis 39, when Joseph says to the Egyptian woman: "How then can I do this great evil?", as if he were saying: "I cannot lawfully and by right." In another sense we say that we can do those things which we are able to do absolutely, whether well or ill; for otherwise we could never sin. So the word "can" is taken equivocally in Scripture when it speaks of God. There is one common power really in God, but the manner of speaking is diverse; and on account of this diverse manner of speaking it is said that God can do some things by absolute power which he cannot do by ordained power. That is, God can do some things, taking the word "can" in its first signification, which yet he cannot do by ordained power; this is to be conceded, that God cannot do those things, taking the word "can" in its second signification. And so to say that God can do some things by absolute power which he cannot do by ordained power is nothing else, according to the understanding of those who rightly understand, than to say that God can do some things which yet he has not ordained that he will do; and yet if he were to do them, he would do them by ordained power, for if he did them, he would thereby ordain that he would do them. Therefore, as these men say, because this opponent did not know how to see the equivocation of this word "can," he misunderstood the theologians' distinction concerning the absolute and ordained power of God. Yet they say that even if he had understood it according to the sense of those who understand it rightly, he would nevertheless have proved it with respect to God, because he imagines that God has ordained all things of necessity, and that it is of absolute necessity that he must do them, so that his not doing them involves a contradiction; and he tries to prove this in his discourses by arguments.

units.la: Quinto isti respondent ad rationem fundamentalem istius, quam hic ad materiam applicat specialem, dicentes quod istud argumentum est omnino simile argumento, quod recitat Magister Sententiarum lib.1. di.38. per quod aliqui nitebantur probare, quod si aliquid posset aliter fieri quam fit, praescientia Dei posset falli. Est etiam simile argumento, quod recitatur dist.14. per quod aliqui conati sunt probare, quod numerus electorum non potest augeri vel minui: & ideo similem habet solutionem, quomodo argumentum istius solui debeat in libro praedicto Sententiarum & in scripturis doctorum super Sententias studiosus poterit invenire, & super literam aliqualiter apparebit. Rationes vero per quas probare conatur, quod praemissa distinctio de potentia Dei absoluta & ordinata non est approbanda, facile dissoluuntur. Prima enim ex falso intellectu procedit, quod hoc esset possibile secundum distinguentes, Deus aliqua facit de potentia absoluta, quae non facit de potentia ordinata, hoc enim de inesse secundum eos est impossibile, & contradictionem includit: quia eo ipso, quod Deus aliquid faceret, quod non faciet ipse, illud faceret de potentia ordinata, haec tamen de impossibili, Deus potest aliquid facere de potentia absoluta, quod nunquam faciet de potentia ordinata, in sensu divisionis accepta vera est, quemadmodum ista de possibili, ille qui est praedestinatus potest damnari, vera est in sensu divisionis: & tamen ista de inesse, praedestinatus damnatur, est impossibilis, & contradictionem includit, haec virtualiter est sententia Magistri Sententiarum lib. 1. dist. 41. quae respondens obiectioni quorundam probare nitentium, quod numerus electorum non potest augeri nec minui, sic ait: quibus respondemus ex ea ratione dictum esse & verum esse numerum electorum non posse augeri vel minui: quia non potest verumque simile esse, scilicet ut aliquis salvetur & non fit praedestinatus: vel ut aliquis praedestinatus fit & damnetur, intelligentia enim conditionis implicita veritatem facit in dicto & impossibilitatem. Si vero simpliciter intelligatur, impossibilitas non admittitur: ut cum dicitur, praedestinatus potest vel non potest damnari: & reprobus potest vel non potest salvari. In his enim & huiusmodi locutionibus ex ratione dicti dividenda est sententia dictionis. Alia namque fit intelligentia, si per coniunctionem haec accipiantur dicta, atque alia, si per disiunctionem, ut supra cum de praescientia agebatur, praetactum est. Si enim cum dicu, praedestinatus non potest damnari, intelligis ita, id est non potest esse, ut praedestinatus fit & damnetur: verum dicis, quia coniunctim intelligis: falsum autem intelligas disiunctim, ut si intelligas, istum non posse damnari, quem dico praedestinatum: potuit enim non esse praedestinatus, & ita damnaretur. Ex his evidenter apparet, quod secundum Magistrum sententiarum haec est impossibilis, praedestinatus damnatur: haec tamen habet unum sensum verum, praedestinatus potest damnari: ita haec est impossibilis, aliquid fit a Deo & non de potentia ordinata: hoc tamen habet unum sensum verum, aliquid potest fieri a Deo quod non fiat de potentia ordinata, & tamen si fieret, de potentia ordinata fieret, sic ergo ista de possibili in uno sensu est vera: & tamen ista de inesse de eisdem terminis est impossibilis, nec debet aliquis de hoc mirari, quia etiam de creaturis loquendo invenitur veritatem habere, haec enim habet unum sensum verum, album potest esse nigrum, haec tamen est impossibilis album est nigrum, haec etiam habet unum sensum verum, non album potest esse album: haec tamen est impossibilis, non album est album. Qui igitur in hac materia catholice & secure loqui voluerit, necesse est inter propositiones de possibili, de impossibili, & de necessario, ac de inesse, & etiam inter diversos sensus illarum de modo sciat distinguere, aliter enim faciliter ponet vel negabit unam pro alia, & incidet in errorem: quia omni homini, qui non est in Logica & Theologia excellenter instructus, expedit in hac materia magis tacere, quam loqui, praeter illa quae in scripturis reperiuntur expressa. Secunda ratio contra praedicta ex salso etiam intellectu procedit, sicut tactum est supra, concedendum est enim, quod non sunt in Deo duae potentiae, quarum una sit absoluta, & alia ordinata: tamen hoc verbum potest, cum loquimur de Deo, accipi potest, sicut supra declaratum existit.
units.tr: Fifthly, they answer the fundamental argument of this man, which he applies here to the particular matter. They say that this argument is wholly similar to the argument which the Master of the Sentences recites in Sentences, book 1, dist. 38., by which some strove to prove that if anything could be done otherwise than it is done, God's foreknowledge could be false. It is also similar to the argument recited in dist. 14., by which some tried to prove that the number of the elect can be neither increased nor diminished. So it has a similar solution. How the argument of that man ought to be solved, a diligent reader can find in the aforesaid book of the Sentences and in the writings of the teachers on the Sentences, and it will appear in some measure from the text itself. The reasons by which he tries to prove that the aforesaid distinction between God's absolute and ordained power is not to be approved are easily dissolved. The first proceeds from a false understanding: that, according to the distinguishers, God does some things by absolute power which he does not do by ordained power. For this, according to them, is impossible in the present tense (de inesse) and includes a contradiction, because by the very fact that God would do something which he himself will not do, he would be doing it by ordained power. Yet "God can do by absolute power something which he will never do by ordained power" is true when taken in the sense of division, just as "the one who is predestined can be damned" is true in the sense of division. Yet "the predestined man is damned," in the present tense, is impossible and includes a contradiction. This is virtually the opinion of the Master of the Sentences, book 1, dist. 41., who, answering the objection of certain men trying to prove that the number of the elect can be neither increased nor diminished, says: "To them we reply that what has been said is true, namely that the number of the elect cannot be increased or diminished, because the two things cannot both be: that someone is saved and not predestined, or that someone is predestined and damned. For the understanding of the implied condition makes the statement true, and the impossibility lies in the saying. But if it is understood absolutely, the impossibility is not admitted, as when it is said that the predestined can or cannot be damned, and the reprobate can or cannot be saved. For in these and similar expressions the sense of the statement must be divided according to the way it is put. The understanding is different if the statements are taken conjunctively, and different if taken disjunctively, as was noted above when foreknowledge was under discussion. If when you say 'the predestined cannot be damned' you mean it thus, that it cannot be that he is predestined and damned, you speak truly, because you understand it conjunctively. But you understand falsely if you understand it disjunctively, that this man whom I call predestined cannot be damned; for he could have not been predestined, and so would be damned." From these things it is evident that, according to the Master of the Sentences, "the predestined is damned" is impossible, yet it has one true sense: "the predestined can be damned." Likewise, "something is done by God and not by ordained power" is impossible, yet it has one true sense: "something can be done by God which is not done by ordained power, and yet if it were done, it would be done by ordained power." So this statement about the possible is true in one sense, while the statement in the present tense, with the same terms, is impossible. Nor should anyone wonder at this, since it is found to hold even when speaking of creatures. "White can be black" has one true sense, yet "white is black" is impossible. "Not-white can be white" also has one true sense, yet "not-white is white" is impossible. Therefore whoever wishes to speak in this matter catholically and securely must know how to distinguish between propositions of the possible, of the impossible, of the necessary, and of the present tense (de inesse), and also between the different senses of these modal forms. Otherwise he will easily affirm one for another and fall into error. For any man who is not excellently instructed in Logic and Theology had better be silent in this matter rather than speak, except for those things which are expressly found in Scripture. The second reason against the aforesaid also proceeds from a false understanding, as was touched on above. For it must be conceded that there are not in God two powers, one absolute and the other ordained. Yet this word "can," when we speak of God, can be taken in the way explained above.

units.la: Nunc ad literam. (Si velit dicere quod illi regno & dominio renunciavit.) Dicunt isti, quod appellans non vult dicere, quod Christus renunciavit illi regno & dominio, (saltem proprie accipiendo verbum renunciandi) quia nunquam ante passionem suam habuit illa regnum & dominium: ideo non renunciavit eisdem. (Ostendas illam si sciat) ipse non vult eam ostendere: sed vult ostendere, quod non habuit ante mortem regnum & dominium temporale (imo contrarium sacra scriptura supponit expresse.) Dicunt quod hoc falsum est, & ad omnes auctoritates, quas ad hoc probandum hic adducit, responsum est supra, ideo hic ad ipsas non expedit respondere (imo videtur quod nec potuerit renunciare.) Ista in sensu divisionis falsa est: sicut ista est falsa in sensu divisionis secundum Magistrum Sententiarum: praedestinatus non potest damnari. Potuisset enim Christus habuisse regnum & dominium, & postea renunciasse eisdem, (si fecisset, contra ordinationem patris fecisset.) Ista falsa est secundum istos: quia sicut si Christus per alium modum quam per mortem suam liberasset genus humanum, non fecisset contra ordinationem patris, imo secundum ordinationem patris: quia si Christus aliter liberasset genus humanum, pater aliter ordinasset. Ita si Christus renunciasset regno & dominio, non fecisset contra ordinationem patris: imo fecisset ordinationem patris: quia si Christus renunciasset, pater talem renunciationem ordinasset, & ita haec est impossibilis: Christus facit contra ordinationem patris: sicut haec est impossibilis, aliquis condemnatur contra praedestinationem Dei: & haec sunt similes, aliquid fit contra praescientiam Dei. De istis tamen propositionibus de possibili: Christus potest facere contra ordinationem patris: Aliquis potest damnari contra praedestinationem Dei, aliquid potest fieri contra praescientiam Dei: & consimilibus, non est per eundem modum dicendum, sicut de istis de inesse correspondentibus ipsis, sicut ex superioribus potest aliqualiter intelligentibus apparere. Auctoritates vero, quas iste adducit, sunt de inesse, & non de impossibili: & ideo in nullo probant negatiuam de possibili, qualiter autem intelligendae sunt, patet supra cap. 93. ideo hic replicare nequaquam oportet.
units.tr: Now to the letter. (If he wishes to say that he renounced that kingdom and dominion.) These men say that the appellant does not mean that Christ renounced that kingdom and dominion (at least taking the word "renounce" properly), because he never had that kingdom and dominion before his passion, and therefore did not renounce them. (Show it, if he knows it.) He himself does not wish to show it, but wishes to show that he did not have a temporal kingdom and dominion before death (indeed Sacred Scripture expressly presupposes the contrary). They say this is false, and the answer to all the authorities which he adduces here to prove it has been given above, so there is no need to reply to them here. (Indeed it seems he could not even have renounced it.) This, taken in the sense of division, is false, just as the statement "the predestined cannot be damned" is false in the sense of division according to the Master of the Sentences. For Christ could have had a kingdom and dominion and afterwards renounced them. (If he had done so, he would have acted against the ordination of the Father.) This is false according to these men. For just as, if Christ had freed the human race by some means other than his death, he would not have acted against the ordination of the Father but in accordance with it, since if Christ had freed the human race otherwise, the Father would have ordained otherwise, so too, if Christ had renounced the kingdom and dominion, he would not have acted against the ordination of the Father but would have fulfilled it, since if Christ had renounced them, the Father would have ordained such a renunciation. And so "Christ acts against the ordination of the Father" is impossible, just as "someone is condemned against the predestination of God" is impossible, and "something happens against the foreknowledge of God" is similar. Yet these propositions of the possible, "Christ can act against the ordination of the Father," "someone can be condemned against the predestination of God," "something can happen against the foreknowledge of God," and similar ones, are not to be understood in the same way as the corresponding propositions in the present tense, as can appear to those who understand the above in some measure. The authorities which this man adduces, however, are in the present tense and not of the impossible, and so they in no way prove a negative of the possible. How they are to be understood is clear above in chapter 93, so there is no need at all to repeat it here.

units.la: CAP. XCVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XCVI.

units.la: Sed dicit iste haereticus, quod hoc est contra sacram scripturam, quae in pluribus locis dicit, Christum fuisse pauperem & egenum. Ad quod dicendum, quod appellans falsum assumit, cum in tot locis sacra scriptura ostendat fuisse regem & Dominum. Cuius contrarium afferere, est dicere contra sacram scripturam: & mendaces reddere Prophetas, Angelum, & Apostolos, ac ipsum Dominum nostrum, ut visum est. Ad illud autem quod dicitur, quod fuisse egenum & pauperem scriptura in pluribus locis testatur: Dicendum est, quod non carentia Dominii facit eum pauperem & egenum, sed potius carentia perceptionis fructus & obventionis rerum, quarum Dominus erat. Nudum enim dominium separatum in perpetuum ab omni perceptione commodi rei habentem non facit divitem, cum sit inutile reputandum. Unde habens tale dominium potest egenus & pauper merito reputari: quod patet ad sensum. Si enim rex Francia non renunciando regno se absentaret a regno: & post lapsum temporis alicuius incogniti redire ad illud, si se pro rege non gereret, hoc autem reliqua emolumenta perciperet dicti regni, sed in domo regia distribueret ei vnus alius ex gratia necessaria vitae suae: talis vtique licet rex esset & Dominus, posset mendicus & pauper merito reputari. Hinc est, quod Apostolus ad Galat. 4. dicit: Quod haeres quamdiu est parvulus, non differt a seruo, cum tamen sit Dominus omnium. Sic Christus rex regum & Dominus dominantium quo ad perceptionem fructuum regni & rerum temporalium, nisi in valde paucis, pro rege vel Domino se non gessit: propter quod merito pauper dici potuit voluntarius & egenus, non propter dominii carentiam sive regni, sed propter hoc, quia se eorum fructibus & proventibus non iuuabat.
units.tr: But that heretic says that this is contrary to Holy Scripture, which in many places says that Christ was poor and needy. To this I reply that the objector assumes something false, since Holy Scripture shows in so many places that he was king and Lord. To assert the opposite is to speak against Holy Scripture and to make the Prophets, the Angel, the Apostles, and our Lord himself liars, as has been shown. As for the claim that Scripture testifies in many places that he was needy and poor, the answer is that it is not the lack of lordship that makes him poor and needy, but rather the lack of receiving the fruit and produce of the things of which he was Lord. For bare lordship, cut off forever from any enjoyment of the benefit of the thing, does not make a man rich, since it must be regarded as useless. So one who has such lordship can rightly be regarded as needy and poor, as is plain to common sense. Suppose the king of France, without renouncing the kingdom, were to withdraw himself from the kingdom, and after some unknown lapse of time were to return to it, but did not act as king, while someone else received the remaining revenues of that kingdom and gave him from the royal household what was necessary for his life. Then, even though he was king and Lord, he could rightly be regarded as a beggar and a poor man. Hence the Apostle says in Galatians 4: that the heir, as long as he is a child, differs in no way from a servant, although he is Lord of all. So Christ, king of kings and Lord of lords, as to the enjoyment of the fruits of the kingdom and of temporal goods, did not act as king or Lord, except in very few matters. For this reason he could rightly be called a poor and needy man by his own choice, not because of lack of lordship or kingdom, but because he did not help himself with the fruits and revenues of these things.

units.la: Postquam in parte praecedenti iste ostendit, quod Christus habuit regnum temporale, & vniuersale dominium omnium rerum: Hic nititur declarare, quod hoc non obstante, Christus fuit pauper & egenus, & primo tangit obiectionem appellantis, dicentis scripturam sacram asserere Christum fuisse pauperem & egenum. Secundo ibi, ad quod Dauid, respondet quod appellans falsum assumit. Tertio ibi, ad illud autem quod dicitur, declarat, quo modo Christus fuit pauper & egenus: quia non propter carentiam dominii & regni, sed propter carentiam perceptionis fructuum. Quarto ibi, Nudum enim dominium, probat tripliciter, quod aliquis potest dici egenus & pauper propter carentiam perceptionis fructuum, licet non careat dominio: & hoc primo ratione: secundo per exemplum ibi, quod patet ad sensum: tertio auctoritate ibi; sic Christus rex regum, infert & explicat conclusionem suam principaliter hic intentam, scilicet quomodo Christus fuit pauper: licet fuerit rex & Dominus omnium temporalium rerum.
units.tr: After showing in the previous part that Christ had a temporal kingdom and universal lordship over all things, here he undertakes to declare that, notwithstanding this, Christ was poor and needy. First he touches on the objection of the opponent, who says that Holy Scripture asserts that Christ was poor and needy. Second, at to which, he replies that the objector assumes something false. Third, at as for the claim, he explains in what sense Christ was poor and needy: not because of lack of lordship and kingdom, but because of lack of enjoyment of the fruits. Fourth, at For bare lordship, he proves in three ways that someone can be called needy and poor because of lack of enjoyment of the fruits, although he does not lack lordship: first by reason; second by example, at as is plain to common sense; third by authority, at so Christ, king of kings. Then he draws and explains his conclusion, which is the main point here, namely how Christ was poor, although he was king and Lord of all temporal things.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores praedicta quo ad quatuor satagunt reprobare. Primo enim ostendunt ipsum errare cum dicit, quod Christus fuit pauper propter carentiam perceptionis fructuum rerum: & non propter carentiam dominii. Secundo probant ipsum errare cum dicit, quod nudum dominium separatum in perpetuum ab omni perceptione commodi rei habentem non facit diuitem. Tertio in hoc quod dicit, quod omne tale dominium ab omni perceptione commodi separatum, est inutile reputandum. Quarto cum innuit, quod Christus in quantum homo, in quibusdam paucis pro rege se gessit, vel pro Domino.
units.tr: But these opponents of the above labour to refute it in four points. First, they show that he is wrong when he says that Christ was poor because of lack of enjoyment of the fruits of things, and not because of lack of lordship. Second, they prove that he is wrong when he says that bare lordship, cut off forever from any enjoyment of the benefit of the thing, does not make a man rich. Third, in what he says, that every such lordship separated from all enjoyment of benefit must be regarded as useless. Fourth, when he hints that Christ, as man, acted as king or Lord in a few matters.

units.la: Primo ergo conantur ostendere istum errare: cum dicit, Christum non fuisse pauperem propter carentiam dominii, sed propter carentiam perceptionis fructuum & obuentionis rerum, quarum erat Dominus. Hoc enim scripturae sacrae, vt dicunt, repugnat: quia licet propter aequiuocationem huiusmodi nominum pauper & egenus, inops, mendicus, & similium in significatione conuenientium aliqua verba scripturae diuinae asserentia Christum fuisse pauperem & egenum nude accepta ad talem sensum intelligi possent, quod Christus diceretur pauper propter carentiam perceptionis fructuum: quia teste Clemente, vt habetur 37. c. Relatum, sunt multa verba in scripturis diuinis, quae trahi possunt ad eum sensum, quem sibi sponte vnusquisque praesumpsit: tamen inspecta serie scripturarum patet aperte, quod Christus secundum scripturas diuinas fuit pauper propter carentiam, & non solum propter carentiam perceptionis fructuum. Si enim, sicut ostensum est supra capitulo, quia Christus fecit ista quae docuit: & Christus docuit paupertatem: non solum illam, quae est per carentiam perceptionis fructuum, sed etiam istam quae est per carentiam dominii, sicut ostensum est supra. Constat quod Christus tenuit paupertatem, quae fit per carentiam dominii: quod etiam multae rationes in diuinis scripturis fundatae, prout ex praecedentibus colligitur, euidenter & patenter ostendunt. Hoc etiam aliter adhuc quam prius ratione & auctoritate probatur. Est autem prima ratio talis. Christus abdicauit omnem superfluitatem temporalium rerum, sed habere dominium temporalium rerum ad superfluitatem spectat, sicut ex praecedentibus patet, ergo Christus dominium rerum temporalium abdicauit. Secunda ratio est haec secundum Magistrum Sententiarum lib. 3. dist. 3: Christus omnes defectus nostros suscepit praeter peccatum, quos ei conueniebat suscipere, & nobis expediebat, sed carentia dominii & proprietatis temporalium rerum est defectus quidam: & talem carentiam conueniebat Christum suscipere: & hoc nobis expediebat, ergo Christus carentiam dominii & proprietatis rerum suscepit. Maior habetur a Magistro Sententiarum: ipse eam ab auctoritatibus sanctorum accepit. Minor etiam quo ad omnes partes eius probatur: carentia dominii temporalium rerum sit defectus quidam, quamuis non vitiosus, pa quia est priuatio dominii. Priuatio autem rei positiuae in defectum sonat. Secunda pars, scilicet quod Christum conueniebat suscipere defectum huiusmodi, patet, nam conueniebat Christum suscipere illa, quae fuissent in statu innocentiae, & nostram informationem minime impediebant, sed carentia dominii proprii fuisset in statu innocentiae, ergo talem carentiam Christus assumpsit, licet enim in statu innocentiae non fuisset fames, sitis & huiusmodi nonnulli defectus afflictiui, non tamen carentiam huiusmodi defectuum, sed ipsos defectus Christus accepit: quia eorum carentia nostram informationem impediuisset. Per hoc enim & huiusmodi se assumpsisse veram carnem passibilem & mortalem ostendit, sed carentia dominii, quod est proprietas, fuisset in statu innocentiae, & assumptio talis carentiae nostram informationem minime impediuit, ergo conueniebat Christum talem carentiam dominii assumere. Item, conueniebat Christum suscipere illud, per quod maxime mirabilis & magnus ad nostram vtilitatem appareret, sed per paupertatem, quae est contemptus omnis dominii temporalium maxime quis mirabilis atque magnus apparet, teste Chrysostom. homel. 46. super Matthaeum, qui ait: Si autem homines duodecim orbem terrarum conuerterant: excogita, quanta est nostra malitia, cum tanti existentes eos qui reguntur non possumus corrigere, quos decem millibus mundi oportebat sufficere & esse fermentum. Sed signa, ait, habebant, sed non signa eos mirabiles fecerunt. Multi enim & daemones proiicient. ni, quae iniquitatem operati sunt, non sunt facti mirabiles, sed puniti, sed quid est, inquam, quod eos magnos ostendit? pecuniarum contemptus, gloria despectus, ab omnibus vitae huius negotiis ereptio: qui si non hoc habuissent, etsi decem millia mortuos suscitassent, non solum non profecissent, sed vt seductores aestimati essent. Ex his verbis euidenter ostenditur, quod pecuniarum contemptus aliquem esse magnum ostendit, ergo maior pecuniarum & diuitiarum contemptus ostendit aliquem esse magis magnum, sed contemnere non solum perceptionem fructus pecuniarum & diuitiarum, sed etiam dominium, est maior contemptus pecuniarum & diuitiarum, quam contemnere solum perceptionem fructus earum, ergo magis magnum ostendit. Nam qui contemneret solum perceptionem fructus pecuniarum, & sibi dominium retineret, redderet se suspectum, quod non perfecte contemneret pecunias, sed amaret: & quod in futurum vellet etiam fructum diuitarum percipere: & ita pro summe magno minime haberetur, cum ergo Christus deberet summe magnus haberi, conueniebat ipsum non solum perceptionem fructus diuitiarum, sed etiam dominium contemnere & penitus abdicare. Tertia pars, scilicet quod Christum abdicare dominium temporalium nobis expediebat, patet aperte: quia per hoc maxime ad contemptum dominii diuitiarum & temporalium rerum inducimur.
units.tr: First, then, they try to show that he is wrong when he says that Christ was not poor because of lack of lordship, but because of lack of enjoyment of the fruits and produce of the things of which he was Lord. For, they say, this contradicts Holy Scripture. Although, because of the ambiguity of such names as poor and needy, destitute, beggar, and similar words that agree in meaning, some words of divine Scripture asserting that Christ was poor and needy could be taken in a bare sense and understood to mean that Christ was called poor because of lack of enjoyment of the fruits, since, as Clement testifies in Decretum 37, c. Relatum, there are many words in the divine Scriptures that can be drawn to whatever sense each one has freely presumed for himself, nevertheless, on looking at the sequence of the Scriptures, it is clear that Christ, according to the divine Scriptures, was poor by lack, and not only by lack of enjoyment of the fruits. For if, as was shown above in the chapter, Christ did the things he taught, and Christ taught poverty, not only that which consists in lack of enjoyment of the fruits, but also that which consists in lack of lordship, as was shown above, then it is certain that Christ held to the poverty that comes through lack of lordship. This many reasons grounded in the divine Scriptures, as may be gathered from what precedes, plainly and openly show. This is also proved in another way, by reason and authority, besides the earlier one. The first reason is this: Christ renounced every superfluity of temporal things; but to have lordship over temporal things belongs to superfluity, as is plain from what precedes; therefore Christ renounced lordship over temporal things. The second reason is this, according to the Master of the Sentences, Book 3, distinction 3: Christ took upon himself all our defects except sin, those which it was fitting for him to take and which were expedient for us; but lack of lordship and of ownership of temporal things is a certain defect; and it was fitting for Christ to take such a lack, and this was expedient for us; therefore Christ took upon himself the lack of lordship and of ownership of things. The major premise is held by the Master of the Sentences; he took it from the authorities of the saints. The minor premise is proved in all its parts: that lack of lordship over temporal things is a certain defect, although not a vicious one, because it is a privation of lordship; and a privation of a positive thing signifies a defect. The second part, namely that it was fitting for Christ to take on such a defect, is plain, for it was fitting for Christ to take those things which would have existed in the state of innocence and did not in the least hinder our formation. But lack of proper lordship would have existed in the state of innocence; therefore Christ assumed such a lack. For although in the state of innocence there would have been no hunger, thirst, and similar afflicting defects, Christ did not take on the lack of such defects, but the defects themselves; because their absence would have hindered our formation. For by this and similar things he showed that he had assumed true flesh, capable of suffering and mortal. But lack of lordship, which is a property, would have existed in the state of innocence, and the assumption of such a lack did not in the least hinder our formation; therefore it was fitting for Christ to assume such a lack of lordship. Again, it was fitting for Christ to take on that by which he would most appear wonderful and great for our benefit. But through poverty, which is the contempt of all lordship over temporal things, a man appears most wonderful and great, as Chrysostom witnesses in homily 46 on Matthew, who says: "But if twelve men had turned the world upside down, consider how great our wickedness is, since, being so great, we cannot correct those who are ruled, when we ought to suffice for ten thousand of the world and be the leaven. But, he says, they had signs, yet it was not the signs that made them wonderful. For many also who worked iniquity cast out demons, yet they were not made wonderful but punished. But what, I ask, is it that showed them to be great? Contempt of money, disdain of glory, removal from all the business of this life; and if they had not had this, even if they had raised ten thousand dead, they would not only not have made progress, but would have been thought deceivers." From these words it is plainly shown that contempt of money shows a man to be great; therefore greater contempt of money and riches shows a man to be greater; but to despise not only the enjoyment of the fruit of money and riches, but also the lordship, is a greater contempt of money and riches than to despise only the enjoyment of their fruit; therefore it shows greater greatness. For one who despised only the enjoyment of the fruit of money, and kept lordship for himself, would make himself suspected of not despising money perfectly, but of loving it, and of wishing in the future to enjoy the fruit of riches as well; and so he would not be held in the highest esteem. Since, then, Christ ought to be held in the highest esteem, it was fitting for him to despise and wholly renounce not only the enjoyment of the fruit of riches, but also lordship. The third part, namely that it was expedient for us that Christ should renounce lordship over temporal things, is plain: for by this we are led most of all to contempt of lordship over riches and temporal things.

units.la: Patet ergo, quod Christus inter caeteros nostros defectus carentiam dominii & proprietatis diuitiarum suscepit: quia hoc sibi conueniebat, & nobis expediebat. Sed forte aliquis contra rationem praedictam obiiciet dicens, quod carentia dominii, quod est proprietas, non est defectus: quia fuisset in statu innocentiae, in quo nullus fuisset defectus, ergo Christus non debuit carentiam talem suscipere. Sed ad istam obiectionem est facile respondere. Multa enim habent rationem defectuum, & quodammodo naturalium in statu naturae destitutae, quae non habent rationem defectuum in statu naturae institutae, nec etiam in statu glorioso. Nuditas enim in statu naturae institutae non fuit defectus, quod Gen. primo insinuatur aperte, cum dicitur: Erat autem uterque nudus (Adam scilicet & uxor eius) & non erubescebant: & tamen nuditas est quidam defectus in statu naturae destitutae. Sic etiam carentia dominii, quae est proprietas, non fuisset defectus in statu naturae bene institutae: sicut nec est defectus in statu gloriae: est tamen defectus quidam in statu naturae destitutae, licet non sit defectus vitiosus. Est autem defectus in statu naturae destitutae: quia per ipsam contingit aliquem impediri ab his, quae sibi necessaria dignoscuntur, hoc autem in statu innocentiae minime contigisset, ideo ibi non fuisset defectus, secundum quod nunc loquimur de defectu. Secundo auctoritate: quia Christus fuit pauper per carentiam dominii. Hoc enim Glossa Luc. 24. sicut adductum est supra, testatur aperte, cum dicit: Ego sum tanta paupertatis, vt nec hospitium quidem habeam, nec meos vtar tecto. Hoc enim falsum fuisset, si habuisset dominium tecti, quo vrebatur, quia tecto proprio vsus fuisset: licet forte hoc alii nesciuissent.
