Ad hoc etiam sunt multae aliae auctoritates, quae de carentia dominii aperte debent intelligi, sicut in capitulo 92. patenter est ostensum.
units.tr: It is therefore plain that Christ took upon himself, among our other defects, the lack of ownership and property of riches, because this befitted him and was profitable for us. But perhaps someone will object to the foregoing reasoning, saying that lack of ownership, which is property, is not a defect, since it would have existed in the state of innocence, in which there was no defect; therefore Christ ought not to have taken upon himself such a lack. This objection is easy to answer. Many things have the character of defects, and in a sense are natural, in the state of corrupt nature, which do not have the character of defects in the state of nature as instituted, nor in the glorious state. For nakedness in the state of nature as instituted was not a defect, as Genesis 1 plainly hints when it says: Now both of them, the man and his wife, were naked, and were not ashamed; and yet nakedness is a certain defect in the state of corrupt nature. So too lack of ownership, which is property, would not have been a defect in the state of well-instituted nature, just as it is not a defect in the state of glory; yet it is a certain defect in the state of corrupt nature, though not a vicious defect. And it is a defect in the state of corrupt nature because through it a person is impeded from those things which are recognised as necessary to him; but this would in no way have happened in the state of innocence, so there would not have been a defect there, in the sense in which we now speak of defect. Second, by authority: for Christ was poor through lack of ownership. The Gloss on Luke 24, as was cited above, plainly bears witness to this when it says: I am of such poverty that I do not even have a lodging, nor do I use a roof of my own. For this would have been false if he had possessed ownership of the roof under which he dwelt, since he would have used a roof of his own; although perhaps others did not know this. There are also many other authorities to this effect, which must plainly be understood of lack of ownership, as was clearly shown in chapter 92.

units.la: Secundo dicunt istum errare cum dicit, quod nudum dominium separatum in perpetuum ab omni perceptione commodi rei, habentem non facit diuitem, quod enim hoc sit erroneum dicunt aperte patere recte sapientibus ex his, quae dicta sunt supra cap. 77. Vbi ostensum est multis rationibus, quod Fratres Minores sunt pauperiores propter carentiam dominii, quod in rebus, quibus vtuntur Romana sibi reseruat ecclesia, & per consequens habens tale dominium, quamuis esset in perpetuum ab omni perceptione commodi separatum, habentem faceret ditiorem. Hoc enim ratio de aperta probatur. Nam ad hoc, quod aliquis sit vere diues, non requiritur actualis perceptio commodi rei: quia tunc quando aliquis dormiret, & non perciperet actualiter commodum villarum suarum & castrorum, non esset propter dominium illorum magis diues, quam si illorum nō haberet dominium: quod est absurdum, nec requiritur voluntas seu propositum percipiendi commodum ex rebus suis: qa tunc si quis diues proponeret omnia bona sua dare pauperibus, vel monasteriis, seu alii cuicunq;, statim propter tale propositum non esset diues: quod etiam est absurdum: quia tunc millesies in die sola voluntate posset quis effici diues & pauper, vt volendo, non volendo de bonis suis vnquam percipere commodum temporale: quod est absurdum, nec dicitur quis diues propter perceptionem commodi futuram: quia illud, quod futurum est, non facit aliquem nunc diuitem vel pauperem. Dicitur ergo aliquis diues propter dominium rerum quod habet: siue intendat de istis percipere commodum temporale, siue intendat nunquam in perpetuum percipere commodum temporale, quod veritatem maxime habet, quando habet liberam potestatem percipiendi commodum de rebus ipsis, si sibi placuerit. Quod enim talis sit diues, quamuis non intendat percipere de rebus commodum, patet: quia qui habet liberam potestatem percipiendi commodum de rebus, ac ipsas vendendi, donandi, dispensandi, & ad libitum ordinandi, est diues propter huiusmodi res, sed habens dominium plenum & liberum, licet non intendat vnquam aliquod commodum percipere de rebus suis, habet potestatem percipiendi commodum ex ipsis: habet etiam potestatem vendendi, donandi, & ad libitum ordinandi de ipsis, ergo debet dines merito reputari. Dominium ergo nudum, licet in perpetuum ab omni perceptione commodi separetur, tamen habentem facit diuitem: quia habens ipsum habet potestatem commodum percipiendi, si voluerit, habet etiam potestatem ex ipsis acquirendi & vendendi, donandi & ad libitum disponendi, diues igitur merito est censendus.
units.tr: Secondly, they say that he errs when he asserts that bare ownership, separated for ever from every enjoyment of the benefit of a thing, does not make the one who has it rich. That this is erroneous, they say, is plain to those who are rightly wise from what was said above in chapter 77, where it was shown by many arguments that the Friars Minor are poorer because of their lack of ownership, since the Roman Church reserves to itself ownership of the things they use; and consequently such ownership, even if it were for ever separated from every enjoyment of benefit, would make the one who has it richer. This is proved by a clear argument. For to be truly rich, actual enjoyment of the benefit of a thing is not required: for when a man is asleep and does not actually enjoy the benefit of his farms and castles, he would not on account of his ownership of them be richer than if he had no ownership of them, which is absurd. Nor is the will or purpose of drawing benefit from one's goods required: for then if a rich man should propose to give all his goods to the poor, or to monasteries, or to anyone else, he would not at once for that reason cease to be rich, which is also absurd; for then a man could be made rich and poor a thousand times a day by will alone, by willing and not willing ever to draw temporal benefit from his goods, which is absurd. Nor is someone called rich on account of future enjoyment of benefit, since what is future does not make anyone rich or poor now. Someone is therefore called rich on account of the ownership of the things he has, whether he intends to draw temporal benefit from them or intends never for ever to draw temporal benefit; and this holds most of all when he has free power to draw benefit from the things themselves, if he pleases. That such a person is rich, even though he does not intend to draw benefit from the things, is plain: for whoever has free power to draw benefit from things, and to sell them, give them away, dispense them and dispose of them as he wishes, is rich on account of such things. But one who has full and free ownership, even if he never intends to draw any benefit from his goods, has the power to draw benefit from them; he also has the power to sell, give away and dispose of them as he wishes; therefore he ought rightly to be counted rich. Bare ownership, then, even if it were separated for ever from every enjoyment of benefit, nevertheless makes the one who has it rich: for the one who has it has the power, if he wills, to draw benefit, and also has the power to acquire, sell, give away and dispose of things from it; therefore he is rightly to be judged rich.

units.la: Tertio dicunt istum errare cum asserit, quod omne dominium a perceptione commodi temporalis in perpetuum separatum est inutile reputandum. Hoc enim sapit haeresim manifestam, scilicet quod non sit aliquod commodum spirituale, propter quod tale dominium possit vtile reputari, quod est tam aperte haereticum, quod probatione non indiget, sicut enim elemosyna omnium carê commodo temporali non debet inutilis, sed vtilis reputaritita dominium rei ab omni commodo separatum potest vtile reputari, si habens dominium concedat vtilitatem aliis ex ipsis rebus propter Deum. Sed forte dices, quod iste non intellexit, quod tale dominium sit reputandum inutile spiritualiter: sed quod est inutile temporaliter. Sed ista excusatio non valet: quia per hoc, quod secundum ipsum tale dominium est inutile reputandum, probat ipse quod habens tale dominium non est diues propter ipsum, quae probatio nulla esset, nisi intelligeret, quod tale dominium est inutile omni carens vtilitate, tam spirituali quam temporali: quia si aliquis potest dici diues propter diuitias ex perceptione commodi temporalis: multo magis diceretur diues propter diuitias temporales, si habens eas ex ipsis commodum percipiat spirituale, cum commodum spirituale maius sit, quam commodum temporale. Non est ergo tale dominium inutile reputandum.
units.tr: Thirdly, they say he errs when he asserts that all ownership separated for ever from the enjoyment of temporal benefit must be reckoned useless. For this savours of manifest heresy, namely that there is no spiritual benefit on account of which such ownership might be reckoned useful; and this is so plainly heretical that it needs no proof. For just as almsgiving, which is entirely without temporal benefit, is not to be reckoned useless but useful, so too ownership of a thing separated from every benefit may be reckoned useful if the owner grants the usefulness of the things to others for God's sake. But perhaps you will say that this man did not mean that such ownership is to be reckoned spiritually useless, but that it is useless temporally. But this excuse does not hold: for by the fact that, in his view, such ownership must be reckoned useless, he proves that one who has such ownership is not rich on account of it; and this proof would be worthless unless he meant that such ownership is useless, lacking every benefit, both spiritual and temporal. For if someone can be called rich on account of riches from the enjoyment of temporal benefit, he would be called rich all the more on account of temporal riches if, having them, he draws spiritual benefit from them, since spiritual benefit is greater than temporal benefit. Such ownership is therefore not to be reckoned useless.

units.la: Quarto dicunt eum errare, dum dogmatizat Christum in quantum erat homo in quibusdam paucis pro rege vel Domino se gessisse. Nam nusquam legitur, quod in quantum homo se gessit pro rege vel Domino, praesertim cum rex non fuerit in quantum homo neq; Dominus. Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod dominium istius in hac parte Glossa dist. 4. c. quoniam idem, notat aperte dicens, quod Christus quadam fecit sicut imperator, cum vendentes & ementes de templo frangendo eiecit, vt 1. q. 3. c. ex multis. Ad hoc dicunt isti, quod si Glossa praedicta est toleranda, vel ba ista debent intelligi de Christo in quantum erat Deus, non in quantum erat homo. Nam Christus in quantum erat homo eiiciens frangendo vendentes & ementes de templo, vt habetur ca. pradutto scilicet 1. q. 3. ca. Ex multis, non gessit officium imperatoris temporalis, sed magis gessit officium ostiarii, secundum Magistrum Sententiarum: qui maioris auctoritatis dignoscitur, quam Glossator praedictus. Ait enim Magister Sententiarum lib. 4. dist. 23. Hoc officium (scilicet ostiariorum) Dominus in sua persona suscepit, quando flagello de funiculis facto vendentes & ementes de templo eiecit. Ipse enim ostiarium se signans dicit: ego sum ostium, per me si quis introierit &c. Ex his verbis patenter habetur, quod Christus in facto praedicto officium ostiarii, non imperatoris, in quantum homo suscepit. Constat autem quod in his, quae fidei sunt, magis standum est Theologorum sententiae, q; iuristarum. Sententia ergo Magistri Sententiarum praedictae Glossae, si sibi contrariatur, est merito praeferenda. Iuristae enim se intromittendo de Theologicis difficultatibus vltra verba, quae a Theologia recipiunt, falcem suam nosc untur in messem mittere alienam, & ideo si in illis de suo aliquid proferre praesumpserint, facile incident in errorem.
units.tr: Fourthly, they say he errs when he teaches that Christ, in so far as he was man, in certain few matters acted as king or lord. For nowhere is it read that in so far as he was man he acted as king or lord, especially since a king is not a king in so far as he is man, nor a lord. But perhaps someone will say that the Gloss on dist. 4, c. quoniam idem, plainly indicates this lordship in this part, saying that Christ did some things as an emperor, when he cast out from the temple those who bought and sold, by breaking [a whip], as in 1 q. 3, c. Ex multis. To this these men reply that, if the aforesaid Gloss is to be tolerated, these words must be understood of Christ in so far as he was God, not in so far as he was man. For Christ, in so far as he was man, when he cast out by breaking those who bought and sold from the temple, as is found in the chapter cited, 1 q. 3, c. Ex multis, did not perform the office of a temporal emperor, but rather performed the office of a doorkeeper, according to the Master of the Sentences, who is recognised as of greater authority than the aforesaid Glossator. For the Master of the Sentences says in book 4, dist. 23: The Lord in his own person took up this office (namely of doorkeepers), when with a scourge made of cords he cast out those who bought and sold from the temple. For he himself, marking himself as a doorkeeper, says: I am the door; if anyone enters by me etc. From these words it is plainly clear that Christ, in the aforesaid deed, took up the office of a doorkeeper, not of an emperor, in so far as he was man. It is agreed, however, that in matters which belong to faith, one must rather abide by the opinion of the theologians than of the jurists. Therefore the opinion of the Master of the Sentences, if it conflicts with the aforesaid Gloss, is rightly to be preferred. For jurists, by meddling in theological difficulties beyond the words they receive from theology, are known to put their sickle into another's harvest; and so if they presume to put forward anything of their own on such matters, they will easily fall into error.

units.la: (Dicit Christum fuisse pauperem & egenam.) Dicunt isti, quod sacra scriptura non solum dicit verbaliter Christum fuisse pauperem & egenum: sed etiam quomodo fuit pauper & egenus scil. per carentiam dominii manifestat. (In tot locis sacra scriptura aperte ostendat scilicet Christum fuisse regem & Dominum.) Dicunt isti, quod sacra scriptura testatur Christum fuisse regem & Dominum, & ideo qui negaret in omni sensu Christum fuisse regem & Dominum, scripturae diuinae contradiceret, sed qui concedit Christum fuisse regem & Dominum spiritualem: & negat ipsum in quantum erat homo fuisse regem & Dominum temporalem: scripturae diuinae minime contradicit. Sed e contra dicunt isti, quod hoc ex multis patet esse falsum, (non carentia dominii fecit eum pauperem & egenum) hoc ostensum est esse falsum. (Sed potius carentia perceptionis fructuum & obuentionum rerum) verum est, quod huiusmodi carentia fecit eum pauperem, quia pauper vixit, carentia tamen dominii magis fecit eum pauperem, q; carentia perceptionis praedictae: q a nullius rei habuit dominium, sed aliquarum rerum percepit fructum, (quarum erat Dominus) hoc omnino dicunt esse falsum, in quantum Christus erat homo mortalis. (Nudum enim dominium &c.) Hoc enim veritate caret: q a quamuis tale dominium faceret aliquem esse pauperem aliquo modo, tamen facit eum etiam esse divitem aliquo modo. Nam pauptas & abundantia diuitiarum non sunt in omni significatione oppositae: quinimo ide potest esse diues & pauper secundum diuersas significationes istorum nominum diues & pauper, unde q habet copiam diuitiarum: & tamen nullum commodum percipit ex ipsis: potest dici diues & etiam pauper aliquo modo, q enim talis, qui habet rerum dominium ab omni perceptione commodi in perpetuum separatum possit vocari diues, ex scriptura diuina colligitur manifeste. Nam Saluator, vt legitur Luc. 12. Hominis cuiusdam diuitis uberes fructus ager attulit, & post dicit autem illi Deus, stulte hac nocte repetent animam tuam a te: quae autem parasti, cuius erunt?
units.tr: (He says that Christ was poor and needy.) These men say that Holy Scripture not only states in words that Christ was poor and needy, but also shows how he was poor and needy, namely through lack of lordship. (In so many places Holy Scripture plainly shows that Christ was king and Lord.) These men say that Holy Scripture testifies that Christ was king and Lord, so whoever denied that Christ was king and Lord in every sense would contradict divine Scripture. But whoever concedes that Christ was a spiritual king and Lord, and denies that he, as a mortal man, was a temporal king and Lord, does not in the least contradict divine Scripture. On the contrary, these men say that this is shown to be false from many considerations. (The lack of lordship did not make him poor and needy) this has been shown to be false. (But rather the lack of receiving the fruits and revenues of things) it is true that such a lack made him poor, since he lived as a poor man. Yet the lack of lordship made him poor more than the lack of that receipt did, since he had lordship over nothing and received the fruit of some things (of which he was Lord). These men say this is altogether false, insofar as Christ was a mortal man. (For bare lordship etc.) This lacks truth, because although such lordship would make someone poor in some way, it also makes him rich in some way. For poverty and abundance of riches are not opposites in every sense. Indeed, the same person can be both rich and poor according to the different senses of these words rich and poor: one who has an abundance of riches but gets no benefit from them can be called rich and also poor in some way. That one who has lordship of goods, cut off forever from every benefit of the thing, can be called rich is clearly gathered from divine Scripture. For the Saviour, as we read in Luke 12: The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully. And afterwards God said to him: Fool, this night they will require your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?

units.la: Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, q ille erat diues: & tamen de bonis suis nunq erat aliquod commodum perceptrurus. Item, q est locuples, potest dici diues merito appellari, sed scriptura diuina vocat locupletem aliquem, quis de bonis suis sit commodum minime percepturus, unde Eccl. 11. sic scribitur: Est q locupletatur parte agendo, & hac pars merces diei illius in eo, quod dicit, inueni requiem mihi, & nunc manducabo de bonis meis solus: & nescit quod tempus praetereat illum, & mors appropinquet, & relinquat omnia aliis & moritur. Ex his datur intelligi, quod quis quandoque locupletatur: & tamen de bonis suis nullum commodum est in perpetuum percepturus. Potest ergo quis appellari diues, quamuis de bonis suis nunquam sit aliquod commodum percepturus, & per consequens erit diues, quis habeat dominium ab omni commodo in perpetuum separatum. Quod etiam talis aliquo modo possit vocari pauper concedit ille impugnatus, & in hoc scripturae sacrae minime contradicit. Nam de tali videtur loqui Salomon Prouerbior. 13. dicens: Est quasi pauper, cum in multis diuitiis fit, qui enim in multis diuitiis consistit, & non percipit fructum ex eis, potest pauper quodammodo appellari, nec mirum cum omnis auarus quantumcunque abundet diuitiis, pauper & egens possit censeri, teste Hieronym. qui in prologo Bibliae ait: Antiquum dictum est, auaro tam deesse, quod habet, quam quod non habet. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod auaro quodammodo omnia desunt, cui autem desunt omnia, paup poterit appellari, ergo omnis auarus pot vocari paup: & eadem ratione habens dominium tpalium & nullum commodum percipit ex eis, potest vocari pauper. Similiter abundantes diuitiis fructumque ex eis tam spiritualem quam temporalem capientes, sed eas nequaquam amantes, pauperes quandoque vocantur, ergo multo fortius, qui ex ipsis nullum fructum percipiunt, neque spirituale neque temporalem, possunt pauperes quodammodo reputari. Propter diuersas igitur significationes & diuersos modos accipiendi haec nomina diues & pauper, qui habet dominium diuitiarum, & nullum commodum ex ipsis percipit, potest dici pauper & diues, & ita nudum dominium separatum in perpetuum ab omni perceptione commodi rei, vere facit habentem diuitem: & contrarium dicere est contra scripturam sacram aperte, sicut ostensum est, (cum sit inutile reputandum) hoc est contrarium catholicae veritati, sicut ostensum est, quia poterit esse vtile sibi, vel quia sui, puta serui, vel aliqui amici ex ipso dominio percipiunt commodum temporale: vel quia ipsemet ex ipsis rebus commodum percipit spirituale. Et si dicas, quod hoc dicunt leges, dicendum est, testante Nicolao papa, sicut legitur distin. 10. c. 1. leges imperatorum inueniuntur euangelicae atque canonicae sanctioni aliquoties obuiare. Leges etiam quandoque solum considerant vtilitatem temporalem, qui autem tractat de his, quae fidei sunt, magis debet attendere vtilitatem spiritualem, (vnde non habens tale dominium potest egenus & pauper merito reputari.) Ista possunt concedi in aliquo sensu, secundum quod Dauid dicit: Diuites eguerunt: imo etiam omnes diuites possunt aliquo modo egeni & pauperes reputari: sicut omnes auari possunt aliquo modo egentes & pauperes, reputari: & tamen reputandi sunt diuites. Ita habens tale dominium, licet possit quodammodo reputari pauper & egenus, secundum modum Theologorum loquendi, debet nihilominus diues reputari. Et ideo si Christus habuisset tale dominium, quamuis fuisset aliquo modo pauper, fuisset nihilominus vere diues. (Talis vtique licet rex esset & Dominus posset mendicus & pauper merito reputari) Ista posset secundum aliquem modum loquendi concedi: & tamen hoc non obstante propter regnum Franciae, & propter potestatem libere gubernandi regnum Franciae & disponendi de bonis regni, si sibi, placeret, esset vere diues, quamuis pro diuite nequaquam se gereret. Sed propter hoc, quod aliquis non gerit se pro diuite, non est dicendum quod non est vere diues (heres quamdiu parvulus est &c.) dici potest, quod in multis differt a seruo, cum ipse non sit seruus: tamen quantum ad potentiam disponendi bona, & regendi, non differt, & ita auctoritas ista ad propositum istius nihil facit, (quo ad perceptionem fructuum regni & rerum temporalium, nisi in valde paucis, pro rege vel Domino se non gessit) quamuis Christus percepit fructus temporalium aliquorum, tamen in perceptione illorum pro rege vel domino se non gessit, sed tanquam pauper necessaria vitae recepit, secundum quod ex auctoritatibus superius allegatis, & multis aliis patet expresse (non propter dominii carentiam sive regni.) Istud est superius improbatum.
units.tr: From these words it is evidently gathered that that man was rich, and yet he was never going to receive any benefit from his goods. Likewise, one who is locuples (wealthy) can rightly be called rich, but divine Scripture calls someone locuples who will never receive any benefit from his goods. So Ecclesiastes 11 is written thus: There is one who grows rich by working, and his reward for that day is in what he says: I have found rest for myself, and now I will eat of my goods alone; and he does not know that time passes him by, and death draws near, and he leaves everything to others and dies. From these words it is understood that someone sometimes grows rich, and yet will never receive any benefit from his goods in perpetuity. So someone can be called rich even though he will never receive any benefit from his goods, and consequently he will be rich who has lordship cut off forever from every benefit. That such a person can in some way also be called poor, this man under attack concedes, and in this he does not contradict holy Scripture. For Solomon seems to speak of such a person in Proverbs 13, saying: He is like a poor man, when he is in great riches. For one who is in great riches but does not receive fruit from them can in some way be called poor, and it is no wonder, since every miser, however much he abounds in riches, can be judged poor and needy, as Jerome testifies in the prologue to the Bible: It is an old saying that the miser lacks as much what he has as what he does not have. From these words it is understood that in some way all things are lacking to the miser, and one to whom all things are lacking may be called poor; therefore every miser can be called poor. By the same reasoning, one who has lordship of temporal goods and receives no benefit from them can be called poor. Likewise, those who abound in riches and take fruit from them, both spiritual and temporal, yet do not love them at all, are sometimes called poor; therefore much more so those who receive no fruit from them, neither spiritual nor temporal, can in some way be regarded as poor. Therefore, because of the different meanings and different ways of taking these words rich and poor, one who has lordship of riches and receives no benefit from them can be called both poor and rich, and so bare lordship cut off forever from every receipt of benefit from a thing truly makes its holder rich. To say the contrary is plainly against holy Scripture, as has been shown. (Since it is to be reckoned useless) this is contrary to Catholic truth, as has been shown, because it may be useful to him, or because his servants or some friends receive temporal benefit from that lordship, or because he himself receives spiritual benefit from those things. And if you say that the laws say this, it must be answered, as Pope Nicholas testifies, as is read in Dist. 10, c. 1: the laws of emperors are found at times to oppose the evangelical and canonical sanction. Laws also sometimes consider only temporal usefulness, but one who treats of the things of faith ought rather to attend to spiritual usefulness. (Hence one not having such lordship can rightly be reckoned needy and poor.) These things may be conceded in a certain sense, according to what David says: The rich have become needy. Indeed, all the rich can in some way be reckoned needy and poor, just as all misers can in some way be reckoned needy and poor, and yet they are to be reckoned rich. So one having such lordship, although he may in some way be reckoned poor and needy according to the way of speaking of theologians, must nonetheless be reckoned rich. And therefore, if Christ had had such lordship, although he would have been poor in some way, he would nonetheless have been truly rich. (Such a one, even if he were king and Lord, could rightly be reckoned a beggar and poor) These things may be conceded according to some manner of speaking; yet notwithstanding this, on account of the kingdom of France, and the power of freely governing the kingdom of France and disposing of the goods of the kingdom as he pleased, he would truly be rich, even though he did not conduct himself as a rich man. But because someone does not conduct himself as rich, it must not be said that he is not truly rich. (An heir, as long as he is a child, etc.) It can be said that he differs in many respects from a servant, since he is not a servant; yet as regards the power of disposing of goods and ruling, he does not differ, and so that authority does nothing for the argument here. (As to receiving the fruits of the kingdom and temporal things, except in very few cases, he did not conduct himself as king or Lord) although Christ received the fruits of some temporal things, yet in receiving them he did not conduct himself as king or Lord, but as a poor man he received what was necessary for life, as is clearly shown by the authorities alleged above and by many others (not on account of the lack of lordship or of kingdom). This has been refuted above.

units.la: CAP. XCVII.
units.tr: CAP. XCVII.

units.la: NVnc autem de Apostolis est videndum: vtrum habuerint dominium aliquarum rerum temporalium in proprio vel communi. In quaestione ista videtur distinguendum inter tempus, quo Apostoli fuerunt cum Redemptore nostro dum viueret: & tempus post eius mortem, si quaeratur, vtrum tempore, quo cum Redemptore nostro fuerunt, habuerint aliqua: videtur adhuc distinguendum inter tempus antequam ad predicandum mitterentur, & tempus missionis, & quo in praedicatione fuerunt, & tempus postquam sunt a praedicatione reuersi.
units.tr: Now we must consider the Apostles: whether they held dominion over any temporal things, either as their own or in common. In this question it seems necessary to distinguish between the time when the Apostles were with our Redeemer while he lived, and the time after his death. If the question is whether they had anything at the time they were with our Redeemer, it still seems necessary to distinguish between the time before they were sent out to preach, the time of their mission and of their preaching, and the time after they had returned from preaching.

units.la: Postquam ille impugnatus in parte praecedenti disseruit, an Christus alicuius rei temporalis habuit dominium: Hic inquirit, an Apostoli habuerunt rerum dominium & proprietatem. Secundo inquirit, an Apostolis licuit pro temporalibus litigare, secunda ibi: tertio videndum est vtrum pro rebus &c. Prima pars diuiditur in duas: quia primo proponit quaestionem & duas distinctiones, vt videtur sibi, necessarias ad quaestionem propositam diffiniendam, secundo, prosequitur membra illarum distinctionum. Secunda pars incipit immediate post verba praescripta, ibi, si consideretur. Litera est plana: & isti impugnatores ipsum quo ad praedicta, nequaquam impugnant: quia hic nihil diffinitiue dicit.
units.tr: Having argued in the preceding part whether Christ held dominion over any temporal thing, this part inquires whether the Apostles held dominion and ownership of things. Second, it inquires whether the Apostles were permitted to litigate over temporal things; the second part begins at the words "thirdly, it must be considered whether for things etc." The first part is divided into two: first, he proposes the question and two distinctions, which seem to him necessary for settling the question proposed; second, he pursues the members of those distinctions. The second part begins immediately after the words prescribed above, at "if it is considered." The text is plain, and these opponents do not attack it at all on the points stated, since here he says nothing in a definitive way.

units.la: (In ista quaestione.) Hic ponit primam distinctionem. (Si quaeratur &c.) Hic ponit secundam distinctionem, quae est subdistinctio primae distinctionis.
units.tr: (In this question.) Here he sets out the first distinction. (If it is asked, etc.) Here he sets out the second distinction, which is a subdistinction of the first.

units.la: CAP. XCVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 98.

units.la: SI consideretur primum tempus, scilicet tempus antequam ad praedicandum mitterentur, non videtur, quod eis habere aliqua, praesertim ad vitae sustentationem pertinentia, fuerit interdictum: quod apparet ex forma vocationis eorum. Cum ad discipulatum vocati fuerunt, forma vocationis Petri & Andreae, vt patet Matth. 4. fuit haec: Venite post me, & faciam vos fieri piscatores hominum, & sequitur: At illi relictis retibus continuo secuti sunt eum. De Iacobo autem & Iohanne in eodem capitulo non dicitur aliquid, nisi quod vocauit eos, & sequitur: Et illi statim relictis retibus & patre secuti sunt eum. Forma autem vocationis Matthaei fuit haec: Sequere me, & sequitur, Quod relictis omnibus surgens secutus est eum. Forma autem vocationis Philippi, nosciture fuisse talis: Sequere me: vt habetur Iohan. 1. Ex forma autem vocationum praedicatorum, nec ex his quae ipsi fecisse tunc leguntur, non apparet quod ipsi renunciauerint omnibus suis. De Petro enim & Andrea non legitur quod tunc reliquerint nisi retia sua, & tamen legitur Marci 1. & Matthei 8. quod post praedicta Iesu egrediens de synagoga venit in domum Simonis & Andreae cum Iacobo & Iohanne, vbi cuiusdam socrum Petri
units.tr: If we consider the first time, namely the time before they were sent out to preach, it does not appear that they were forbidden to have any possessions, especially those pertaining to the sustenance of life. This is clear from the form of their calling. When Peter and Andrew were called to discipleship, the form of the call, as is plain from Matt. 4, was this: "Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men." And it follows: "And they immediately left their nets and followed him." Concerning James and John, in the same chapter, nothing is said except that he called them, and it follows: "And they immediately left the nets and their father and followed him." The form of Matthew's call was: "Follow me," and it follows: "He rose, left everything, and followed him." The form of Philip's call is known to have been: "Follow me," as is found in John 1. From the form of the calls of these preachers, and from what they are then read to have done, it does not appear that they renounced all their possessions. For concerning Peter and Andrew it is read only that they then left their nets, and yet it is read in Mark 1 and Matthew 8 that, after the things mentioned, Jesus, going out of the synagogue, came into the house of Simon and Andrew with James and John, where he healed Peter's mother-in-law of a fever.

units.la: Gggg 2 Petri de febre. De Iacobo autem & Iohanne, non legitur quod tunc reliquerunt nisi retia & patrem, quae quidem retia videntur fuisse patris, qui viuebat, potius quam ipsorum. De Philippo autem non legitur, quod tunc reliquerit aliquid. De Matthaeo autem legitur, quod relictis omnibus secutus est eum, & tamen statim sequitur, postquam dictum est quod omnia reliquit, & secutus est eum, quod fecit sibi Leui, (id est Matthaeus) magnum conuiuium in domo sua, ergo per istam generalitatem non deserat domum illam esse suam.
units.tr: Gggg 2 Concerning James and John, it is not read that they then left anything except their nets and their father; and those nets seem to have been their father's, who was still alive, rather than their own. Concerning Philip, it is not read that he then left anything. Concerning Matthew, it is read that he left everything and followed him; and yet it immediately follows, after it has been said that he left everything and followed him, that Levi (that is, Matthew) made a great feast in his own house. Therefore, by this general statement, it does not follow that the house was not his own.

units.la: In parte ista iuxta membra praedictarum distinctionum propositam quaestionem determinat. Et diuiditur ista pars: quia primo determinat dictam quaestionem, iuxta membra secundae distinctionis, quae est subdistinctio distinctionis primae, & in hoc cap. determinat eandem quaestionem, quantum ad vnum membrum distinctionis primae. Secundo determinat eandem quaestionem, quantum ad aliud membrum primae distinctionis, secunda pars ibi: Si autem quaeratur de tempore post mortem Christi &c. Prima adhuc diuiditur in tres, secundum tria membra secundae distinctionis, secunda pars ibi: Si vero consideretur tempus, quo missi fuerunt &c. Tertia ibi: Si autem consideretur tempus post resurrectionem &c. Prima pars diuidirur in quatuor partes, secundum quod quadrupliciter probare conatur, quod Apostolis ante missionem ipsorum ad praedicandum, nulla temporalia interdicta fuerunt. Secunda ponitur immediate post verba praemissa ibi: Praeterea cum &c. Tertia ibi: De discipulis autem constat. Quarta ibi: Item nec cum ipsos. In prima parte vna ratione conatur ostendere, quod Apostolis antequam mitterentur ad praedicandum, nulla temporalia interdicta fuerunt. Quia non est dicendum, quod eis aliquid interdictum fuerit, nisi quantum ex forma vocationis eorum: vel ex his, quae fecisse leguntur, apparet, sed neque ex forma vocationis Apostolorum, neque ex his quae fecisse leguntur apparet, quod omnia temporalia reliquerint: sed magis econuerso: ergo non est dicendum, quod eis aliqua temporalia interdicta fuerunt: vel quod omnia sua temporalia reliquerunt. Maior videtur euidens: quia ipse eam subintelligit. Minorem probat per formam vocationum sex Apostolorum: & per illa quae illi fecisse leguntur, quia de vocatione aliorum sex Apostolorum in scripturis nulla fit mentio.
units.tr: In this part, according to the members of the aforementioned distinctions, he settles the question proposed. And this part is divided: first, he settles the said question according to the members of the second distinction, which is a subdistinction of the first distinction, and in this chapter he settles the same question as far as one member of the first distinction is concerned. Second, he settles the same question as far as the other member of the first distinction is concerned; the second part begins: "But if it is asked concerning the time after the death of Christ, etc." The first part is further divided into three, according to the three members of the second distinction; the second part begins: "But if the time at which they were sent is considered, etc." The third begins: "But if the time after the resurrection is considered, etc." The first part is divided into four parts, according to the fourfold way in which he tries to prove that no temporal things were forbidden to the Apostles before their being sent out to preach. The second is set down immediately after the words quoted above, beginning: "Moreover, since, etc." The third begins: "But it is certain concerning the disciples." The fourth begins: "Likewise, nor with them." In the first part he tries, by one argument, to show that nothing temporal was forbidden to the Apostles before they were sent out to preach. For it is not to be said that anything was forbidden to them except as far as it appears from the form of their calling, or from the things they are read to have done. But it appears neither from the form of the Apostles' calling nor from the things they are read to have done that they left all their temporal goods; rather the contrary. Therefore it is not to be said that any temporal things were forbidden to them, or that they left all their temporal goods. The major premise seems evident, because he himself takes it for granted. He proves the minor from the form of the calls of six Apostles and from those things which they are read to have done, because there is no mention in the Scriptures of the calling of the other six Apostles.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt istum periculose errare, cum asserit quod Apostoli antequam mitterentur ad praedicandum, nullius rei temporalis reliquerunt dominium seu proprietatem, licet enim vt dicunt, ad probandum quasdam verisimilitudines ex scripturis contingat accipere: Ex ipsis tamen scripturis vt a maioribus expositae dignoscuntur, contrarium manifeste accipitur, quod pluribus rationibus ex scripturis autenticis trahentibus auctoritatem & fulcimentum probare nituntur. Est autem eorum prima ratio talis. Quando Christus fecit Apostolis sermonem in monte, de quo legitur Matt. 5. & quando fecit ipsis & turbis sermonem in loco campestri, de quo habetur Luc. 6. siue fuerit idem termo siue alius, Christus Apostolis aliqua tempora sub praecepto vel consilio interdixit, & ipsi eadem temporalia reliquerunt, sed sermo praedictus de quo habetur Mat. 5. 6. & 7. & etiam ille de quo habetur Luc 6. praecessit missionem Apostolorum ad praedicandum, ergo aliqua temporalia Apostolis antequam mitterentur ad praedicandum, sub praecepto vel consilio interdicta fuerunt: & per consequens ipsi aliqua, antequam mitterentur ad praedicandum reliquerunt. Maior quo ad vtramque partem ex euangelio patenter habetur. Nam in eodem sermone Mat. 6. dicit Christus Apostolis: Nolite thesaurizare vobis thesauros in terra, vbi aerugo vel tinea demolitur, & vbi fures effodiunt & furantur. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod Christus thesaurorum possessionem Apostolis interdixit, ex ratione autem interdictionis huiusmodi, quam insinuat Christus, cum dicit: vbi aerugo &c. apparet, quod omnem superfluitatem temporalium interdixit eisdem. Si enim ideo thesauri sunt in terra minime congregandi, quia aerugo & tinea demolitur in terra: & similiter fures effodiunt & furantur: per huiusmodi autem aerugo, tineam atque fures intelliguntur omnia quae temporalia possunt auferre. Videtur quod omnia quae in terra possunt auferri, & non sunt necessaria, nullatenus sint congreganda. Omnis igitur superfluitas temporalium in verbis praedictis, Apostolis extitit interdicta. Omne autem dominium seu proprietas temporalium debet inter superflua reputari, cum sine proprietate seu dominio contingat vitam sustentare humanam, & officia ecclesiastica exercere, ergo in verbis praemissis Saluator sub praecepto vel consilio omne dominium seu proprietatem temporaliu interdixit. Iterum in eodem sermone sollicitudinem de crastino Apostolis interdixit. Ex quo sequitur, quod magnarum diuitiarum possessionem interdixit eisdem, & ita patet, quod aliqua temporalia eisdem explicite interdicta fuerunt. Quod etiam eis temporaliu possessio quo ad dominium & proprietatem implicite fuerit interdicta, patet per illud eiusdem sermonis c. 7. Intrate per angustam portam. Porta autem angusta, de qua intendebat Christus, comprehendit voluntariam & euangelicam paupertatem, ergo eis pauptatem euangelicam implicite sub praecepto vel consilio imponebat. Pauptas autem euangelica temporaliu abdicationem includit, ergo tunc aliqua eis temporalia interdicta fuerunt. Ex quo sequitur, tunc aliqua temporalia reliquerunt. Nullo enim modo est censendum probabile, quod illi, quos ita extulit Christus, vt eos lucem mundi & sal terrae diceret, praecepta Christi & consilia non impleuerunt. Constat igitur, quod Apostoli tunc praecepta Christi & consilia impleuerunt: & per consequens temporalia reliquerunt. Minor probatione non indiget, ipsa tamen & nonnulla istam rationem contingentia in sequentibus amplius apparebunt. Secunda ratio talis est. Non imperfectiorem regulam viuendi tradidit Christus Apostolis, anteq mitteret ad praedicandum eosdem, quod aliis qui busque discipulis, sed cuidam discipulo domesticarum rerum dominium interdixit implicite, ergo multo magis Apostolis dominium temporalium, antequam eos ad praedicandum mitteret, interdixit. Maior est euidens. Minorem ostendunt: quia magis distrahit a sequela Christi rerum domesticarum dominium, quod paterni funeris sepultura: cum paterni funeris sepultura pietatis officium sit censendum, Christus autem cuidam discipulo sepulturam paterni funeris interdixit. Nam sicut legitur Matth. 8. cum diceret redemptori nostro quidam de discipulis eius: Domine permitte me primum ire & sepelire patrem meum. Iesus ait illi: Sequere me, & dimitte mortuos sepelire mortuos. Ergo multo magis domesticarum rerum dominium implicite interdixit eisdem, & per consequens multo magis Apostolis, antequam ad praedicandum mitterentur, aliqua temporalia interdicta fuerunt. Tertia ratio eorum est haec. Apostoli etiam antequam ad praedicandum mitterentur, non ad imperfectiorem statum vocati fuerunt, quam fuit ille iuvenis, cui dixit Christus, Si vis perfectus esse vade & vende omnia quae habes &c. Hoc patet ex commendatione, qua Christus extulit Apostolos, cum dixit Matth. 5. Vos estis lux mundi &c. Sed ille vocatus fuit ad abdicationem dominii omnium temporalium: licet terrenis illectus ipsam noluerit assumere, ergo multo magis & Apostoli etiam antequam ad praedicandum mitterentur, ad huiusmodi statum vocati fuerunt. Talem autem vocationem nullatenus renuerunt, ergo talem statum voluntarie assumpserunt. Quarta ratio est haec. Qui nihil sibi retinent, sed totum deserunt, relinquunt omnia quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, sed Apostoli antequam ad praedicandum mitterentur, nihil sibi retinuerunt, sed totum deseruerunt, teste beato Gregorio, qui loquens de Petro & Andrea super illud Matt. 4. Relictis retibus secuti sunt eum, ait: Ad vnius iussionis vocem Petrus & Andreas secuti sunt redemptorem, & infra: In hac re fratres carissimi, affectum potius debemus pensare quam censum. Multum reliquit, qui nihil sibi retinuit. Multum reliquit, qui quantumlibet parum totum deserit. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod Petrus & Andreas nihil sibi retinuerunt, sed totum deseruerunt in illa vocatione, de qua fit mentio Matth. 4. quae praecessit missionem Apostolorum ad praedicandum, ergo & omnes alii Apostoli ad eundem statum assumpti antequam ad praedicandum mitterentur, nihil retinuerunt, sed totum deseruerunt: & per consequens omnia reliquerunt quo ad dominium seu proprietatem.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he errs dangerously when he asserts that the Apostles, before they were sent out to preach, left no ownership or property of any temporal thing at all. For although, as they say, it may be possible to take some probable indications from the Scriptures to prove certain points, nevertheless, when the Scriptures are understood as explained by the greater authorities, the contrary is clearly seen; and they strive to prove this by several arguments drawn from authentic Scripture, which carry authority and support. Their first argument is of this kind. When Christ delivered the sermon to the Apostles on the mount, which is read of in Matt. 5, and when he delivered a sermon to the Apostles and the crowds in a level place, which is found in Luke 6, whether it was the same discourse or a different one, Christ forbade the Apostles certain goods, under precept or counsel, and they left those same temporal goods. But the aforementioned sermon, which is found in Matt. 5, 6 and 7, and also that in Luke 6, preceded the sending of the Apostles to preach. Therefore, certain temporal goods were forbidden to the Apostles, under precept or counsel, before they were sent out to preach; and consequently they left some things before they were sent out to preach. The major premise, with respect to both parts, is plainly found in the Gospel. For in the same sermon, Matt. 6, Christ says to the Apostles: "Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where rust or moth destroys, and where thieves dig through and steal." From these words it is plainly seen that Christ forbade the Apostles the possession of treasures; and from the reason for such a prohibition, which Christ suggests when he says "where rust, etc.," it appears that he forbade them every superfluity of temporal goods. For if treasures are not to be gathered on earth precisely because rust and moth destroy on earth, and likewise thieves dig through and steal, then by "rust," "moth," and "thieves" are understood all those things which can take away temporal goods. It seems that whatever can be taken away on earth, and is not necessary, is by no means to be gathered. Therefore, all superfluity of temporal goods was forbidden to the Apostles in the words quoted. But all ownership or property of temporal goods must be counted among superfluities, since human life can be sustained and ecclesiastical offices exercised without property or ownership. Therefore, in the words quoted, the Savior forbade, under precept or counsel, all ownership or property of temporal goods. Again, in the same sermon he forbade the Apostles anxiety about tomorrow. From this it follows that he forbade them the possession of great riches; and thus it is plain that certain temporal goods were explicitly forbidden to them. That the possession of temporal goods was also implicitly forbidden to them, as regards ownership and property, is clear from that passage of the same sermon, chapter 7: "Enter by the narrow gate." The narrow gate of which Christ was speaking includes voluntary and evangelical poverty; therefore he imposed evangelical poverty on them implicitly, under precept or counsel. But evangelical poverty includes the renunciation of temporal goods; therefore at that time certain temporal goods were forbidden to them. From this it follows that at that time they left certain temporal goods. For in no way is it to be considered probable that those whom Christ so exalted, calling them the light of the world and the salt of the earth, did not fulfill the precepts and counsels of Christ. It is therefore evident that the Apostles then fulfilled the precepts and counsels of Christ, and consequently left temporal goods. The minor premise needs no proof; yet it and some things pertaining to this argument will appear more clearly in what follows. The second argument is this. Christ did not give the Apostles, before he sent them out to preach, a less perfect rule of life than he gave to the other disciples; but he implicitly forbade one disciple the ownership of his household goods. Therefore, much more, before he sent the Apostles out to preach, he forbade them the ownership of temporal goods. The major premise is evident. The minor is shown thus: ownership of household goods distracts a person from following Christ more than the burial of a father; and the burial of a father is to be regarded as a duty of piety; yet Christ forbade a certain disciple the burial of his father. For, as is read in Matt. 8, when one of his disciples said to our Redeemer, "Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father," Jesus said to him, "Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their dead." Therefore, much more, he implicitly forbade them ownership of household goods; and consequently, much more, certain temporal goods were forbidden to the Apostles before they were sent out to preach. Their third argument is this. The Apostles, even before they were sent out to preach, were not called to a less perfect state than that of the young man to whom Christ said, "If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, etc." This is clear from the commendation with which Christ exalted the Apostles when he said in Matt. 5, "You are the light of the world, etc." But that man was called to the renunciation of ownership of all temporal goods, although, enticed by earthly things, he was unwilling to take it up. Therefore, much more, the Apostles also, even before they were sent out to preach, were called to such a state. They in no way refused such a calling; therefore they voluntarily took up such a state. Their fourth argument is this. Those who retain nothing for themselves but give up everything, leave all things as regards ownership or property. But the Apostles, before they were sent out to preach, retained nothing for themselves but gave up everything, as the blessed Gregory testifies, who, speaking of Peter and Andrew on that text of Matt. 4, "Having left their nets, they followed him," says: "At the voice of one command, Peter and Andrew followed the Redeemer," and below: "In this matter, dearest brethren, we ought to weigh the affection rather than the wealth. He who has retained nothing for himself has left much. He who gives up everything, however little, has left much." From these words it is made clear that Peter and Andrew retained nothing for themselves but gave up everything in that calling mentioned in Matt. 4, which preceded the sending of the Apostles to preach. Therefore all the other Apostles also, taken up into the same state before they were sent out to preach, retained nothing but gave up everything; and consequently they left all things as regards ownership or property.

units.la: (Non videtur quod eis habere aliqua praesertim ad vitae sustentationem pertinentia fuerit interdictum.) Oppositum est ostensum per hoc, quod non debebant de crastino cogitare, per hoc enim nouit Christus omnem superfluitatem, non sollicitudinem, quae est necessitatis naturalis interdicere Apostolis, cum ergo dominium etiam eorum, quae pertinent ad sustentationem vitae, inter superflua debeat aestimari: sequitur quod Christus tale dominium eorum, quae sunt necessaria vitae Apostolis interdixit, & ideo non interdixit eis habere aliqua quo ad usum: sed quo ad dominium seu proprietatem (quod apparet ex forma vocationis eorum.) Dicunt isti, quod rectus sensus scripturae loquentis de istis, quae Apostolis interdicta fuerunt, non tantum ex forma vocationis Apostolorum, sed etiam ex aliis locis colligi debet, & idcirco licet per formam vocationis Apostolorum non posset ostendi, quod Apostolis habere temporalia quo ad dominium erat interdictum, non tamen esset propter hoc negandum, sufficit enim ad hoc tenendum, quod ex scriptura alibi ostendatur, (cum enim ad discipulatum vocati fuerunt &c. Hic etiam insufficienter arguit: non reliquerunt omnia quo ad dominium, quando ad discipulatum vocati fuerunt: ergo non reliquerunt omnia antequam ad praedicandum mitterentur. Poterant enim omnia relinquere, quando ad Apostolatum vocati fuerunt: quod nonnullis videtur probabile. Tunc enim Christus formam viuendi & regulam eis tradidisse videtur. Alii autem dicunt, quod Apostoli in vltima vocatione sua ad discipulatum omnia quo ad proprietatem & dominium reliquerunt, (relictis retibus continuo secuti sunt eum) vbi dicit Glossa: Incessu pedum, sed magis obedientia & affectu amplius ad propria non reuertuntur. Ex qua Glos. colligitur, quod ex tunc dominium & proprietatem omnium reliquerunt. (Ex forma autem vocationum praedictarum, nec ex his quae ipsi fecisse tunc leguntur, non apparet quod ipsi renunciauerunt omnibus bonis suis.) Esto quod hoc totum esset verum, tamen ex hoc non potest concludi, quod non renunciauerunt omnibus bonis suis: cum ex aliis locis scripturae hoc patenter appareat, veruntamen ex forma vocationum praedictarum apparet, quod ipsi tunc renunciauerunt omnibus bonis suis. Nam de Matthaeo dicit: Relictis omnibus surgens secutus est eum. Ex quibus verbis apparet, quod omnia tunc reliquerit quo ad dominium & proprietatem, quod Glossa accepta de Ambrosio ibidem sentire videtur. Ait enim: reliquit propria, qui rapiebat aliena, nec solum lucra vectigalium reliquit, sed & periculum contemnit, quod poterat timere a principibus saeculi, quia rationes vectigalium incompositas relinqueret. Et quia in nullo prorsus huius vitae respectum vel cogitationem sibi reservauit dominicorum talentorum, fidelis dispensator esse meruit. Ex his colligitur, quod beatus Matthaeus propria reliquit: sed non fuit ratio, quod magis reliquisset ista propria, quam illa, ergo omnia propria reliquit. Et ex hoc concluditur, quod cum de Matthaeo dicitur, quod relictis omnibus surgens secutus est eum: haec verba non debent intelligi tantum modo de theloneo, & his quae erant in theloneo: quia illa non erant propria eius, sed erant propria Caesaris vel alterius principis, cuius erat theloneum. Debent ergo verba praedicta intelligi, & de theloneo quo ad congregationem & conservationem, & custodiam ipsorum: ac etiam de omnibus propriis quo ad dominium seu proprietatem (relictis secutus est eum.) Iterum secundum Glossam Matthaeus in nullo prorsus huius vitae respectum vel cogitationem sibi reservauit, ergo nec alicuius rei dominium sibi reservauit. Hoc etiam beatus Ambrosius sentire videtur, qui in quadam homelia ait: Mystica vocatio publicani, quam sequi iubet non corporis gressu (supple tantum modo) mentis affectu. Itaque ille auarus de mercedibus dura, de laboribus periculosa, nautarum emolumenta cōuertens verbo vocatus propria derelinquit, qui rapiebat aliena: ac illud vile sedile destituens, toto post Dominum vestigio mentis incedit. Ex his verbis manifeste colligitur, quod beatus Matthaeus, non solum vectigalium lucra, quae sua non erant, sed etiam proPropria dereliquit. Cum ergo dicatur omnia reliquisse, sequitur quod omnia propria dereliquit, ergo nihil sibi retinuit, quo ad dominium seu proprietatem. Ex quo concluditur, quod cum omnes Apostoli eiusdem fuerint professionis, omnes Apostoli omnem proprietatem temporalium reliquerunt (De Petro enim & Andrea, non legitur quod tunc reliquerunt nisi sua retia.) Dicunt isti, quod quamuis ibidem non fiat mentio explicita, nisi de rebus: tamen ex diversis locis scripturae elicitur, quod tunc, vel quando ad Apostolatum electi fuerunt, sicut habetur Luc. 6. & Christus regulam, & formam viuendi, quae habetur in isto sermone, qui ponitur Matth. 5. 6. & 7. exposuit, omnia reliquerunt, quo ad dominium & proprietatem. (Et tamen legitur Marci 1. & Matth. 8. quod post praedicta ille egrediens de synagoga venit in domum Simonis & Andreae, cum Iacobo & Iohanne, ubi curauit socrum Petri de febre.) Dicunt isti, quod quamuis post praedicta legatur Marci 1. & Matth. 8. quod ille egrediens de synagoga &c. Tamen nec Marci 1. nec Matth. 8. legitur, quod post praedicta ille egrediens de synagoga venit in domum Simonis &c. Et ideo hoc falsum scripturae imponit, quia quamuis Marcus & Matthaeus posterius narrent, quod ille ingrediens de synagoga venit in domum Simonis, modo tamen narrant, quod hoc fuit posterius factum: nec semper ex ordine scripturae potest concludi ordo rei gestae. Dicunt ergo quod potuit fieri quod Christus egrediens de synagoga veniret in domum Simonis ante dictam vocationem Petri & Andreae. Unde & beatus Lucas prius narrat illum ingressum in domum Simonis & Andreae, quam narret penultimam vocationem Petri & Andreae. Aliter dicunt, quod ille aduentus potuit esse inter dictam vocationem Petri & Andreae, & electionem ipsorum ad Apostolatum, & ita si ante electionem ad Apostolatum non reliquerunt proprietatem omnium, potuit tunc illa domus esse eorum quoad proprietatem. Tertio dicunt, quod illa domus tunc potuit dici Petri & Andreae, non quia tunc erat ipsorum quo ad dominium & proprietatem, sed quia aliquando fuit eorum quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Saepe enim aliqua dicuntur esse aliquorum, non quia tunc sint eorum quo ad dominium & proprietatem: sed quia aliquando fuerant ipsorum quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, & de tali modo loquendi inueniuntur exempla plura in scripturis, patet de Bethlehem, quae post mortem Danid adhuc vocabatur ciuitas Danid, Luc. 1. & de Sion, quae tempore Machabaeorum vocabatur ciuitas Dauid, 1. Mach. 1. & gladius Goliath post mortem eius vocabatur gladius Goliath, quia fuerat eius, 1. Reg. 21. & tabernaculum Sarae, etiam post mortem Sarae vocabatur tabernaculum Sarae, Gen. 24. Sic domus praedicta potuit vocari domus Petri & Andreae, quia fuerat aliquando eorum quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Quarto dicunt, quod licet dicta domus non fuisset vnq; Petri & Andreae quo ad dominium, sicut forte nunq; fuit, quia fortassis non fuerunt ita diuites, quod domum propriam, sed solum conductam habarent: tamen potuit dici domus Petri & Andreae propter consuetudinem habitandi in ipsa: quemadmodum Nazareth dicebatur ciuitas Mariae & Ioseph, quae tamen non erat ipsorum quo ad dominium seu proprietatem: sed solum quo ad consuetudinem manendi ibidem. Patet ergo, ut isti dicunt, quod ille impugnatus ex scripturis male intellectis, & sub multiplicitate vocum opiniones erroneas contra doctrinam sanctorum patrum conatur inducere. (De Iacobo autem & Iohanne non legitur quod tunc reliquerunt nisi retia & patrem: quae quidem retia videtur fuisse patris (qui viuebat) potius quam ipsorum.) Ex hoc non potest concludi, quod non reliquerint omnia quo ad dominium seu proprietatem: quia quod omnia reliquerint modo praedicto ex aliis scripturis colligitur: & etiam ex illo loco scripturae videtur rationabiliter posse inferri. Si enim amore sequendi Christum patrem, cui ex lege naturae obligati fuerunt, quo ad praesentiam corporalem, & corporale obsequium, reliquerunt, videtur quod multo fortius temporalium rerum proprietatem & dominium reliquerunt, vel relinquere parati fuerunt. Ex quo colligitur, quod saltem quando Christus de contemptu mundi & sollicitudine temporalium abiiciendam in monte eis explicite praedicauit, omnia quo ad dominium & proprietatem reliquerunt, si prius minime reliquerunt. (De Philippo autem minime legitur quod tunc reliquerit aliquid) quamuis tunc non legatur explicite, quod Philippus reliquerit aliquid. Ex hoc tamen non sequitur, quod nihil reliquit, & maxime non sequitur, quod nec tunc nec quando fuit ad Apostolatum assumptus, nihil reliquit (statim sequitur, postquam dictum est quod reliquit omnia & secutus est eum, quod fecit sibi Leui, id est, Matthaeus magnum conuiuium in domo sua: ergo per istam generalitatem non desierat domus esse sua.) Dicunt quod non sequitur, quin desierit ista domus esse sua quo ad proprietatem, licet quo ad appellationem non desierit esse sua: quia postea vocabatur domus sua. Aliter dicunt, quod illud conuiuium fuit factum in domo Matthaei ante vocationem, de qua prius fuit mentio facta, licet narretur posterius. Tertio dicunt aliqui, quod tunc Matthaeus non reliquerat omnia quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, sed quando fuit ad Apostolatum assumptus, & regulam viuendi a Christo accepit audiendo scilicet sermonem Christi in monte, omnia quo ad proprietatem seu dominium dereliquit. Vnde dicunt, quod istum processum circa Apostolos Christus seruauit. Primo vocauit eos vltimate: & tunc non reliquerant omnia quo ad dominium seu proprietatem: quia animo illa esset voluntas Christi nescicbant: sed tunc parati erant Christo perfecte & in omnibus obedire, & quam formam viuendi eis vellet tradere obseruare, postea ducens eos in montem duodecim ad Apostolatum assumpsit: & eis regulam & formam viuendi, quam eos voluit seruare, exposuit: in qua interdicendo eis thesaurizationem & contentionem in iudicio, & omnem sollicitudinem superfluam, insinuauit aperte quod omnium temporalium abdicarent dominium. Quod & ipsos tunc fecisse, quamuis non legatur explicite, est credendum: quia aliter non fuissent ad Apostolatum idonei, eo quod non fuissent parati in omnibus voluntati Christi parere. Postmodum vero ipsos ad Apostolatum probatos ad praedicandum transmisit: & tunc eis quasdam speciales circumstantias circa abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum iniunxit, sicut inferius ostendetur.
units.tr: (It does not seem that they were forbidden to have anything, especially things pertaining to the sustenance of life.) The opposite is shown by the fact that they were not to take thought for the morrow. By this Christ forbade the Apostles every superfluity, though not the anxiety that concerns natural necessity. Since ownership even of what pertains to the sustenance of life must be counted among superfluities, it follows that Christ forbade the Apostles such ownership of what is necessary for life. He therefore did not forbid them to have anything as regards use, but as regards ownership or property (which appears from the form of their calling). Those people say that the right sense of Scripture about what was forbidden to the Apostles must be gathered not only from the form of the Apostles' calling but also from other passages. Therefore, although it could not be shown from the form of their calling that the Apostles were forbidden to hold temporal goods as regards ownership, this should not on that account be denied. To maintain it, it is enough that it is shown elsewhere in Scripture (for when they were called to discipleship etc.). Here too he argues insufficiently: they did not leave all things as regards ownership when they were called to discipleship; therefore they did not leave all things before they were sent to preach. For they could have left all things when they were called to the apostleship, which seems probable to some. For then Christ seems to have handed on to them the form of living and the rule. Others, however, say that the Apostles in their final calling to discipleship left all things as regards property and ownership (leaving the nets, they followed him at once). Here the Gloss says: By the going of their feet, but more by obedience and affection they did not return any more to their own things. From this Gloss it is gathered that from then on they left the ownership and property of all things. (From the form of the aforesaid callings, however, and from what is read they then did, it does not appear that they renounced all their goods.) Even granting that all this were true, it cannot be concluded from it that they did not renounce all their goods, since this clearly appears from other passages of Scripture. Indeed, from the form of the aforesaid callings it appears that they then renounced all their goods. For of Matthew it says: Leaving all, he rose and followed him. From these words it appears that he then left all things as regards ownership and property, which the Gloss, taken from Ambrose, seems to think in the same place. For he says: He left his own things, he who was robbing others' goods. He left not only the gains of the tolls but also despised the danger he could fear from the princes of the world, since he would leave the unsettled toll accounts. And because he reserved for himself absolutely no regard or thought for anything in this life of the Lord's talents, he deserved to be a faithful steward. From this it is gathered that blessed Matthew left his own things, but there was no reason why he should have left those own things rather than the others; therefore he left all his own things. And from this it is concluded that when it is said of Matthew that leaving all, he rose and followed him, these words must not be understood only of the toll-booth and what was in it, because those were not his own but belonged to Caesar or another prince, whose toll it was. The aforesaid words must therefore be understood both of the toll-booth as to the gathering, keeping and custody of it, and also of all his own things as to ownership or property (left, he followed him). Again, according to the Gloss, Matthew reserved for himself absolutely no regard or thought for anything in this life; therefore he did not reserve for himself ownership of anything either. Blessed Ambrose also seems to think this, for in a certain homily he says: The mystical calling of the publican, which bids him follow not with the step of the body (understand: only) but with the affection of the mind. Thus that greedy man, turning the hard wages, the dangerous labours and the profits of the sailors into a word, was called and left his own things, he who was robbing others' goods; and leaving that base seat, he walked with his whole footstep of mind after the Lord. From these words it is clearly gathered that blessed Matthew left not only the gains of the tolls, which were not his own, but also his own things. Since, therefore, he is said to have left all, it follows that he left all his own things, and so kept nothing for himself as regards ownership or property. From this it is concluded that, since all the Apostles were of the same profession, all the Apostles left all ownership of temporal goods (For of Peter and Andrew it is not read that they then left anything but their nets.) Those people say that although no explicit mention is made there except of things, it is drawn from various passages of Scripture that then, or when they were chosen to the apostleship, as is found in Luc. 6., and when Christ expounded the rule and form of living contained in that sermon set down in Matth. 5. 6. & 7., they left all things as regards ownership and property. (And yet it is read in Marci 1. and Matth. 8. that after the aforesaid things he, going out of the synagogue, came into the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John, where he healed Simon's mother-in-law of fever.) Those people say that although it is read after the aforesaid things in Marci 1. & Matth. 8. that he went out of the synagogue etc., neither in Marci 1. nor in Matth. 8. is it read that after the aforesaid things he, going out of the synagogue, came into the house of Simon etc. So this falsely imposes on Scripture. Although Mark and Matthew relate afterwards that he came from the synagogue into Simon's house, they now relate that this was done later, and the order of events cannot always be concluded from the order of Scripture. They say, therefore, that it could have happened that Christ, going out of the synagogue, came into Simon's house before the said calling of Peter and Andrew. Hence blessed Luke also first relates that entry into the house of Simon and Andrew before he relates the penultimate calling of Peter and Andrew. Others say otherwise: that that coming could have been between the said calling of Peter and Andrew and their choice to the apostleship, and so, if they had not left the property of all things before the choice to the apostleship, that house could then have been theirs as regards property. Thirdly, they say that the house could then be called Peter's and Andrew's, not because it was then theirs as regards ownership and property, but because at some time it had been theirs as regards ownership and property. For often some things are said to be of certain people not because they are theirs at that time as regards ownership and property, but because they once were. Many examples of this manner of speaking are found in Scripture: Bethlehem, which after David's death was still called the city of David (Luc. 1.); Zion, which in the time of the Maccabees was called the city of David (1. Mach. 1.); Goliath's sword, which after his death was called Goliath's sword because it had been his (1. Reg. 21.); and Sarah's tent, which even after Sarah's death was called Sarah's tent (Gen. 24.). So the aforesaid house could be called the house of Peter and Andrew, because at some time it had been theirs as regards ownership and property. Fourthly, they say that although the said house had never been Peter's and Andrew's as regards ownership, as perhaps it never was, since perhaps they were not so rich as to have a house of their own but only rented one, it could still be called the house of Peter and Andrew on account of their custom of living in it. Just as Nazareth was called the city of Mary and Joseph, which nevertheless was not theirs as regards ownership or property but only by their custom of staying there. It is clear, then, as they say, that this man, attacking from badly understood Scriptures, and hiding behind a multiplicity of words, tries to introduce erroneous opinions against the doctrine of the holy Fathers. (Of James and John, however, it is not read that they then left anything but the nets and their father; and those nets seem to have been the father's, who was still alive, rather than their own.) From this it cannot be concluded that they did not leave all things as regards ownership or property. That they left all in the aforesaid manner is gathered from other Scriptures, and it can also reasonably be inferred from that passage. For if out of love of following Christ they left their father, to whom they were bound by the law of nature, as regards bodily presence and bodily service, it seems much more likely that they left, or were ready to leave, ownership and property of temporal things. From this it is gathered that, at least when Christ openly preached to them on the mountain that they must cast off contempt of the world and anxiety about temporal things, they left all things as regards ownership and property, if they had not left them before. (Of Philip, however, it is not read at all that he then left anything), although it is not then read explicitly that Philip left anything. From this, however, it does not follow that he left nothing, and especially it does not follow that neither then nor when he was taken up to the apostleship did he leave anything. (It immediately follows, after it is said that he left all and followed him, that Levi, that is Matthew, made a great feast in his house; therefore by that generality the house had not ceased to be his.) They say that it does not follow that the house ceased to be his as regards property, although as regards its name it did not cease to be his, since afterwards it was called his house. Others say otherwise: that that feast was made in Matthew's house before the calling mentioned earlier, although it is narrated later. Thirdly, some say that Matthew had not then left all things as regards ownership or property, but when he was taken up to the apostleship and received the rule of living from Christ, namely by hearing Christ's sermon on the mountain, he left all things as regards property or ownership. Whence they say that Christ observed this order with the Apostles. First he called them at the last, and then they had not left all things as regards ownership or property, because they did not know what Christ's will in the matter was; but they were then ready to obey Christ perfectly and in all things, and to keep whatever form of living he wished to hand on to them. Afterwards, leading the twelve up the mountain, he took them to the apostleship, and set out for them the rule and form of living which he wished them to keep. In it, by forbidding them hoarding, contention in judgement and all superfluous anxiety, he plainly intimated that they should renounce ownership of all temporal things. That they too then did this, although it is not read explicitly, must be believed; for otherwise they would not have been fit for the apostleship, since they would not have been ready to obey Christ's will in all things. Afterwards, having proved them fit for the apostleship, he sent them out to preach, and then he enjoined on them certain special circumstances concerning the renunciation of ownership of all things, as will be shown below.

units.la: CAP. XCIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XCIX.

units.la: Praeterea cum ille misit duodecim, quos & Apostolos vocauerat, legimus eis interdixisse aliqua, videl. vt non possiderent aurum, neque argentum, neque as in zonis suis, & alia nonnulla. Ex quibus patet, quod ante missionem illa ipsis interdicta non erant: alias frustra in missione fuissent eis talia interdicta, vt patet Matth.10. Marc.6. & Luc.9. Eodem modo 70. discipulis dum eos misit, aliqua interdixit, vt patet Luc.10. Ex quo sequitur, quod ante illa ipsis non fuerant interdicta.
units.tr: Moreover, when he sent out the twelve, whom he had also called Apostles, we read that he forbade them certain things, namely that they should not possess gold, or silver, or money in their belts, and some other things. From this it is clear that these things had not been forbidden them before the mission; otherwise such prohibitions in the mission would have been pointless, as is clear from Matt. 10, Mark 6 and Luke 9. In the same way, when he sent out the seventy disciples, he forbade them certain things, as is clear from Luke 10. From this it follows that these things had not been forbidden them before.

units.la: Hic ponit secundam rationem ad probandum, quod Apostolis antequam ad praedicandum mitterentur, nulla temporalia interdicta fuerunt, quia quando eos ad praedicandum misit, aliqua interdixit, sc. quod non possiderent aurum, &c. ergo antea ipsis minime talia interdixit: & per consequens antea ipsis licuit talia quo ad dominium possidere: & ita antea non omnia quo ad dominium reliquerunt.
units.tr: Here he gives a second argument to prove that, before the Apostles were sent out to preach, no temporal things were forbidden them. For when he sent them to preach, he forbade them some things, namely that they should not possess gold, and so on. Therefore he had not forbidden them such things before. Consequently, it was lawful for them before to possess such things as property, and so before they had not given up everything as to ownership.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, istam rationem omni colore carere. Ad cuius evidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod licet sub generali speciale contineri noscatur; interdicto tamen aliquo generaliter, non frustra postea interdicitur specialiter: quemadmodum aliquid generaliter imperatum, nō frustra postea specialiter iniungitur: quia, teste Innocentio Tertio, vt habetur ext. de haeret. c.fi aduers. Plus timeri solet quod specialiter iniungitur, quam quod generaliter imperatur, & in hoc concordat concilio Toletano, quod, vt habetur dist.23.c. Quanquam, ait: Solet enim plus timeri quod singulariter pollicetur: quam quod generali sponsione concluditur. Vbi Glossa notat multa specialia plus valere quam generalia: sicut plus valet specialis cautio quam generalis: & plus valet specialis confirmatio quam generalis: & plus specialis appellatio quam generalis: & similiter specialis delegatio quam generalis: & specialis subscriptio quam generalis: & plus valet speciale mandatum quam generale. Ex his dicunt isti aperte patere, quod ratio praedicta apparentia est nudata: quia non sequitur; Christus quando misit Apostolos ad praedicandum eis, ne aurum vel argentum aut pecuniam possiderent, quo ad dominium specialiter interdixit: ergo prius ne possiderent quaecunque temporalia quo ad dominium generaliter nequaquam iniunxit: cum saepe plus valeat mandatum speciale quam generale.
units.tr: But these opponents say that this argument has no colour at all. To make this clear, they say that it must be understood that although the special is known to be contained in the general, yet when something has been forbidden in general, it is not pointless to forbid it specifically afterwards; just as something commanded in general is not pointlessly enjoined specifically afterwards. For, as Innocent III is found to say in ext. de haeret. c. fin. aduers.: What is specifically enjoined is usually feared more than what is commanded in general, and the Council of Toledo agrees, which, as is found in dist. 23, c. Quanquam, says: For what is promised singly is usually feared more than what is concluded by a general pledge. Here the Gloss notes that many special things are worth more than general ones: a special caution is worth more than a general one, a special confirmation more than a general one, a special appeal more than a general one, likewise a special delegation more than a general one, a special subscription more than a general one, and a special command is worth more than a general one. From these points, they say, it is plainly evident that the aforesaid argument is stripped of its appearance. For it does not follow that, because Christ, when he sent the Apostles to preach, specifically forbade them to possess gold, silver or money as ownership, he therefore had earlier in general not enjoined that they should not possess any temporal things as ownership; since a special command is often worth more than a general one.

units.la: Item apparet ex scriptura idem praeceptum non inutiliter replicari, quod diversis modis contingit. Quandoque enim idem praeceptum sub eadem forma in diversis locis replicatur. Unde & praecepta Decalogi Exod. vigesim. capit. describuntur, quae tamen Deuteronom. quint. cap. replicantur. Quandoque vero non sub eadem forma idem praeceptum penitus replicatur. Unde Matth. quinto, ponitur praeceptum de dilectione proximi inquantum iubentur omnes inimicos diligere: & tamen Christus in coena dixit Apostolis: Mandatum novum do vobis vt diligatis invicem. Ex diversis ergo causis praecepta saepius replicantur, & ea quae primo generaliter imperantur, postea specialiter iniunguntur: & ita fuit de Christo & Apostolis.
units.tr: It also appears from Scripture that the same precept is not uselessly repeated, and this happens in different ways. For sometimes the same precept is repeated under the same form in different places. Hence the precepts of the Decalogue are described in Exod. chap. 20, and yet they are repeated in Deut. chap. 5. Sometimes, however, the same precept is repeated in quite a different form. Hence Matt. 5 sets down the precept about love of neighbour, in that all are commanded to love their enemies; and yet Christ said to the Apostles at supper: A new commandment I give you, that you love one another. Therefore precepts are repeated often for different causes, and those things which are first commanded in general are afterwards enjoined specifically; and so it was with Christ and the Apostles.
