units.la: Primo enim cum Christus in monte explicite interdixit Apostolis repetitionem temporalium, & contentionem pro eisdem in iudicio: ac omnem thesaurizationem in terra, pro eo quod in terra aerugo & tinea demolitur, & fures effodiunt & furantur; & etiam omnem sollicitudinem circa temporalia superfluam: tunc eisdem generaliter interdixit possessionem auri, argenti & pecuniae, quo ad dominium & proprietatem, quando misit eos ad praedicandum possessionem huiusmodi specialiter interdixit, iniungens ipsis nihilominus ne talia etiam portare absque dominio & proprietate praesumerent: sicut ex Marc.6. & Lu.9. colligitur evidenter. Quod autem dixit de 70. discipulis patet, quod non concludit: quia per hoc non probatur, quod ante dictam missionem ipsis nō fuerunt aliqua interdicta, sed tamen an eis fuerint aliqua interdicta, non est ad praesens inquirendum. (Cum ille misit duodecim quos & Apostolos vocauerat.) Hic aperte insinuat, quod Christus praedictos duodecim ante fecerat Apostolos, quam eos ad praedicandum transmitteret: cuius contrarium asserit postea manifeste: & ita sibiipsi contradicit aperte. (Legimus eis interdixisse aliqua) specialiter, quae prius indixerat generaliter (videl. vt non possiderent aurum, &c.) De his in sermone in monte, quando Christus Apostolis proprietatem temporalium generaliter interdixit, non fiebat mentio specialis. (Ex quibus patet, quod ante missionem iflam eis interdicta non erant.) Male arguit: ac si argueret: Deus praecepit filiis Israel, vt legitur Exodi vigesimo. Non occides: Non moechaberis: Non furtum facies. ergo haec eis prius praecepta non erant. Constat enim, quod in lege naturae aute legem Mosaicam haec erant praecepta. Moyses etiam in Deuteronomio haec eadem praecepta, imo fere omnia alia praecepta, contenta in Exodo, Leuitico & Numeris, replicavit: quia, teste Hieronymo in prologo Bibliae, Deuteronomium sic ea habet quae priora sunt, vt tamen nova sint omnia de veteribus. Et tamen haec ante librum Deuteronomii praecepta fuerunt.
units.tr: First, when Christ on the mountain expressly forbade the Apostles the pursuit of temporal things and contention over them in judgement, and all hoarding on earth, because rust and moth destroy on earth, and thieves dig through and steal; and also every superfluous anxiety about temporal things, then he forbade them in general the possession of gold, silver and money, as to ownership and property. When he sent them to preach, he forbade such possession specifically, enjoining on them nonetheless that they should not presume to carry such things even without ownership and property; as is clearly gathered from Mark 6 and Luke 9. As for what he said about the seventy disciples, it is plain that this proves nothing: for it is not proved by this that nothing had been forbidden them before that sending. But whether anything had been forbidden them is not to be inquired into at present. (When he sent out the twelve, whom he had also called Apostles.) Here he plainly implies that Christ had made the aforesaid twelve Apostles before he sent them out to preach; yet he afterwards clearly asserts the contrary, and so openly contradicts himself. (We read that he forbade them certain things) specifically, which he had earlier forbidden in general (namely that they should not possess gold, etc.). Of these there was no specific mention in the sermon on the mount, when Christ forbade the Apostles in general the ownership of temporal things. (From which it is clear that these things had not been forbidden them before that mission.) He argues badly, as if one were to argue: God commanded the sons of Israel, as we read in Exodus 20: You shall not kill; You shall not commit adultery; You shall not steal. Therefore these precepts had not been given them before. For it is certain that these were precepts in the law of nature before the Mosaic law. Moses also repeated these same precepts in Deuteronomy, indeed almost all the other precepts contained in Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers; because, as Jerome says in the prologue to the Bible, Deuteronomy has those things which were earlier in such a way that yet all are new from the old. And yet these precepts existed before the book of Deuteronomy.

units.la: (Alias frustra in missione fuissent eis talia interdicta.) Ex praecedentibus patet hanc esse falsam. Unde frustra fuerunt eis in missione talia specialiter interdicta: quia iniuncta specialiter plus movent & cordi fortius imprimuntur: & priora generalia aptius explicantur, & nonnunquam bonum obedientiae adaugetur, multae aliae etiam causae possent assignari, quare eadem saepius replicantur: & quae generaliter fuerant imperata, specialiter iniunguntur. (Eodem modo septuaginta discipulis) melius dixisset septuag.duob. (dum eos misit aliqua interdixit) hoc verum est. Ex quo sequitur, quod ante illa ipsis non fuerant interdicta) siue quod hic infert fuerit verum siue falsum, argumentum suum non valet: quia sicut ostensum est, talis consequentia non valet: Talia fuerant ab eis interdicta, quando missi fuerunt; ergo prius non fuerunt eis interdicta: quia ex tali affirmatiua, negatiua infertur sophistice.
units.tr: (Otherwise such things would have been pointlessly forbidden them in the mission.) From what has gone before it is clear that this is false. Hence such things specifically forbidden them in the mission were not pointless: for things enjoined specifically move the mind more and are impressed more strongly on the heart; earlier general precepts are also more aptly explained, and sometimes the merit of obedience is increased. Many other causes could also be given why the same things are often repeated, and why what has been commanded in general is enjoined specifically. (In the same way to the seventy disciples) he would better have said seventy-two. (when he sent them, he forbade them certain things) this is true. (From this it follows that these things had not been forbidden them before) whether what he infers is true or false, his argument does not hold: for, as has been shown, such a consequence is not valid. Such things had been forbidden them when they were sent; therefore they had not been forbidden them before: for from such an affirmative a negative is inferred sophistically.

units.la: CAP. C.
units.tr: CAP. C.

units.la: DE discipulis autem constat, quod habuerunt aliqui multa. De Ioseph ab Arimathia, legitur Iohannis 19. quod erat discipulus Iesu. Matthaei autem 27. dicitur quod erat dines homo, & discipulus Iesu. Iterum constat, quod Simon leprosus erat de discipulis Iesu: & tamen legitur Matth. 26. quod ille erat in Bethania in domo eius. Item Lazarus, Martha & Maria Magdalena, qui erant eius discipuli, erant multa bona habentes. Deinde legitur de eis Ioh. 11. quod castrum dictum Bethania erat Maria Magdalena & Martha: & quod in Bethania secerunt ei coenam magnam, in qua Martha ministrabat. Lazarus autem erat unus ex discumbentibus cum eo. Maria vero accepta libra unguenti nardipistici pretiosi unxit pedes Iesu, & extersit capillis suis pedes eius. De Tabitha quoque, quae interpretatur Dorcas, quam Petrus suscitauit a mortuis, legitur Act. 9. quod erat discipula & plena operibus bonis & eleemosynis, quas faciebat: & quod omnes viduae flentes ostenderunt Petro tunicas & vestes, quas faciebat eis Dorcas. Ex quibus patet, quod & ista non obstante discipulatu temporalia habebat, de quibus faciebat eleemosynas praedictas: nec reperimus quod Dominus noster aliam legem viuendi discipulis dederit, & aliam Apostolis suis: imo beatus Clemens in quadam Epistola sua, cuius pars recitatur 12. quaest. 1. capit. Dilectissimis, exprese supponit, quod eadem erat Apostolorum & discipulorum vita dicens: communis vita omnibus est necessaria, & maxime his, qui vitam Apostolorum eorumque discipulorum imitari volunt.
units.tr: Concerning the disciples, it is clear that some of them had many possessions. Of Joseph of Arimathea we read in John 19 that he was a disciple of Jesus. Matthew 27 says he was a rich man and a disciple of Jesus. Again, it is clear that Simon the leper was one of the disciples of Jesus, and yet Matthew 26 reads that he was in Bethany, in his house. Likewise Lazarus, Martha and Mary Magdalene, who were his disciples, had many good things. Then we read of them in John 11 that the village called Bethany belonged to Mary Magdalene and Martha, and that in Bethany they made him a great supper, at which Martha served. Lazarus was one of those reclining with him. Mary, taking a pound of precious spikenard ointment, anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. Of Tabitha, also called Dorcas, whom Peter raised from the dead, we read in Acts 9 that she was a disciple, full of good works and of the alms she gave; and that all the widows, weeping, showed Peter the tunics and garments that Dorcas had made for them. From these things it is plain that she, notwithstanding her discipleship, had temporal goods, out of which she gave those alms. Nor do we find that our Lord gave one rule of living to the disciples and another to his Apostles. Indeed, the blessed Clement, in one of his letters, part of which is quoted in 12 q. 1, c. Dilectissimis, expressly supposes that the life of the Apostles and of the disciples was the same, saying: a common life is necessary for all, and especially for those who wish to imitate the life of the Apostles and of their disciples.

units.la: Hic ponit tertiam rationem ad ostendendum, quod Apostolis antequam ad praedicandum mitterentur, nulla temporalia interdicta fuerunt. Est autem ratio talis. Christus non dedit aliam legem viuendi Apostolis & aliis discipulis, hanc probat auctoritate Clementis, quae ponitur 12. quaest. 1. capitu. Dilectissimis, quae supponit, quod eadem fuit vita Apostolorum & discipulorum, sed aliis discipulis habere temporalia fuit minime interdictum: quia temporalia habuerunt, secundum quod probat per quatuor exempla, quorum primum est de Ioseph ab Arimathia, secundum de Simone leproso, tertium de Lazaro, Martha, & Maria Magdalena, quartum de Dorca, ergo, &c. Circa istam rationem primo ponit minorem cum declaratione sua, secundo ibi: Nec reperimus: Ponit maiorem cum sua probatione.
units.tr: Here he gives a third reason to show that no temporal goods were forbidden to the Apostles before they were sent out to preach. The reasoning is this. Christ did not give one rule of living to the Apostles and another to the other disciples. He proves this by the authority of Clement, quoted in 12 q. 1, c. Dilectissimis, which supposes that the life of the Apostles and of the disciples was the same; but it was in no way forbidden to the other disciples to have temporal goods, since they did have them, as he proves by four examples: the first of Joseph of Arimathea, the second of Simon the leper, the third of Lazarus, Martha and Mary Magdalene, and the fourth of Dorcas. Therefore, etc. In regard to this argument, he first puts forward the minor premise with its explanation, and secondly, at "Nor do we find," he puts forward the major premise with its proof.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores hic duabus viis principaliter improbare nituntur. Primo enim ostendunt, quod licet ista ratio sit inducta ad probandum, quod Apostolis antequam mitterentur ad praedicandum, non fuerunt aliqua temporalia interdicta: tamen ipsaeque concludit, quod nunc vel saltem non post reuersionem de praedicatione fuit eis habere quaecunque temporalia in speciali, quo ad dominium & proprietatem interdictum a Christo. Secundo probare conantur, quod errorem continet manifestum, cum accipit, quod non reperitur Christum dedisse aliam legem viuendi Apostolis & aliis discipulis. Ad intelligentiam autem dicendorum praemittunt, quod ipse hic accipit generaliter nomen discipuli pro omnibus Christianis: & inter istos & illos discipulos Christi non distinguens. Nam sub nomine discipuli comprehendit diuites & pauperes, viros & mulieres: sicut exemplia sua testantur aperte: & ita vocat ibi discipulos omnes Christianos. Ex isto dicunt isti primum probandum aperte patere. Nam iste sub eadem lege viuendi constituit Apostolos & alios discipulos, qui post reuersionem eorum de praedicatione conuersi fuerunt: & quando alii discipuli propria possidebant. Nam ipse constituit sub eadem lege viuendi Apostolos & Ioseph ab Arimathia, quando legitur fuisse dites, & nobilis decurio, & Dorcam, quando eleemosynas faciebat: volens probare, quod Apostolis temporalia possidere minime extitit interdictum: per hoc quod praedicti temporalia possidebant, sed praedicti, scilicet Ioseph & Dorcas, & similiter leprosus & Lazarus & Martha & Magdalena, temporalia possederunt, postquam Apostoli de praedicatione reuersi fuerunt, ergo secundum istum temporalia possidere postquam Apostoli de praedicatione reuersi fuerunt, eis nullatenus extitit interdictum: quod esse erroneum isti impugnatores in sequentibus ostendere conabuntur.
units.tr: But these opponents set out to refute this by two main lines of attack. First, they show that although this argument is brought forward to prove that no temporal goods were forbidden to the Apostles before they were sent out to preach, yet it itself concludes that now, or at least not after their return from preaching, it was forbidden to them by Christ to have any temporal goods in particular, as to ownership and property. Secondly, they try to prove that it contains a plain error, when it takes it that Christ is not found to have given the Apostles and the other disciples different rules of living. To understand what follows, they first point out that he here takes the name "disciple" in a general sense for all Christians, and does not distinguish between those disciples of Christ and those others. For under the name of disciple he includes rich and poor, men and women, as his examples clearly testify; and so he calls all Christians disciples there. From this, these men say, the first point to be proved is plainly evident. For he places the Apostles and the other disciples, who were converted after the Apostles' return from preaching, under the same rule of living, and at a time when the other disciples possessed property of their own. For he places the Apostles and Joseph of Arimathea under the same rule of living, when he is said to have been rich and a noble councillor, and Dorcas, when she gave alms; wishing to prove that it was in no way forbidden to the Apostles to possess temporal goods, because the aforesaid men possessed temporal goods. But the aforesaid men, namely Joseph and Dorcas, and likewise the leper, Lazarus, Martha and Magdalene, possessed temporal goods after the Apostles had returned from preaching. Therefore, according to him, to possess temporal goods after the Apostles had returned from preaching was in no way forbidden to them. The opponents will try in what follows to show that this is erroneous.

units.la: Secundo dicunt ipsum dogmatizare errorem apertum, cum asserit, Christum non aliam legem viuendi dedisse Apostolis, quam aliis discipulis, per alios discipulos intelligens omnes Christianos, & specialiter Ioseph de Arimathia, & Dorcam & Simonem leprosum, ac Lazarum & sorores eius. Hoc autem ostendunt esse erroneum. Primo sic: Christus praecepit Apostolis non possidere aurum, neque argentum, neque pecuniam, & non portare calciamenta, ac etiam non habere duas tunicas: sed talia non praecepit omnibus aliis discipulis: & specialiter non praecepit ista praedictis Ioseph & aliis, ergo aliam legem viuendi dedit Apostolis, quam nonnullis aliis discipulis. Secundo sic: Christus non latiorem legem viuendi tradidit Apostolis, etiam post reuersionem de praedicatione, quam suasit illi, cui dixit: Si vis perfectus esse vade vende omnia quae habes, &c. Sed illi suasit strictiorem legem viuendi, praesertim quo ad paupertatem, quam imposuerit Ioseph ab Arimathia, & aliis discipulis supradictis, strictiorem ergo legem viuendi tradidit Christus Apostolis, quam aliis multis discipulis suis. Minor est euidens: & posset etiam per ista, quae ille allegat de Ioseph & aliis praenominatis, patenter ostendi. Maior etiam videtur clara: quia tunc Apostoli fuerunt primi fundatores datores militantis ecclesiæ post Christum, ergo non debuerunt lautius viuere, quam ille, cui dixit Christus: Si vis perfectus esse, &c. si conuersus fuisset ad Christum. Tertio sic arguunt: Christus imposuit Apostolis continentiam à carnali concubitu: quod satis innuitur Matth. 19. cum dicit Christus: Sunt eunuchi qui castrauerunt seipsos propter regnum cœlorum: qui potest capere capiat, vbi dicit Hieronymus: Domini vox est, milites suos ad pudicitiæ premium concitantis, quasi dicens: qui potest pugnare pugnet, & superet ac triumphet. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod Christus continentiam suadebat: & per consequens ipsam maxime Apostolis tradidit obseruandam, sed continentiam aliis supranominatis, nec etiam omnibus Christianis non imposuit. Ergo aliam legem viuendi tradidit Christus Apostolis, quam multis aliis discipulis. Ad illa vero, quæ iste pro sua assertione adducit, super litera respondebitur.
units.tr: Secondly, they say that he is teaching an open error when he asserts that Christ gave the Apostles no other rule of living than he gave the other disciples, understanding by the other disciples all Christians, and specially Joseph of Arimathea, Dorcas, Simon the leper, and Lazarus and his sisters. They show that this is erroneous. First, thus: Christ commanded the Apostles not to possess gold, silver or money, nor to carry shoes, nor even to have two tunics; but he did not command such things to all the other disciples, and in particular he did not command them to the aforesaid Joseph and the others. Therefore he gave the Apostles a different rule of living from that given to some of the other disciples. Secondly, thus: Christ did not give the Apostles a looser rule of living, even after their return from preaching, than he urged on the one to whom he said: If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, etc. But he urged on that man a stricter rule of living, especially as regards poverty, than he imposed on Joseph of Arimathea and the other disciples mentioned above. Therefore Christ gave the Apostles a stricter rule of living than he gave to many of his other disciples. The minor premise is evident, and it could also be plainly shown from what he cites about Joseph and the others named before. The major premise also seems clear, because the Apostles were then the first founders and givers of the militant Church after Christ; therefore they ought not to have lived more luxuriously than the one to whom Christ said: If you wish to be perfect, etc., even if he had been converted to Christ. Thirdly, they argue thus: Christ imposed on the Apostles continence from carnal intercourse, which is sufficiently indicated in Matthew 19, where Christ says: There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. He who can receive it, let him receive it, where Jerome says: It is the voice of the Lord, rousing his soldiers to the prize of chastity, as if saying: let him who can fight, fight, and overcome, and triumph. From these words it is clear that Christ urged continence, and consequently gave it especially to the Apostles to be observed, but he did not impose continence on the other disciples mentioned above, nor on all Christians. Therefore Christ gave the Apostles a different rule of living from that given to many of his other disciples. As for the things this man adduces in support of his assertion, they will be answered word by word.

units.la: (De discipulis autem constat quod habuerunt aliqui multa.) Dicunt isti, quod in triplici differentia fuerunt discipuli, quidam enim erant Apostoli: quidam vero præter Apostolos ad prædicandum fidem Christi fuerunt à Christo specialiter deputati, de quibus habetur Lucæ decim. capitulo. Tertii erant simpliciter conuersi ad fidem, sed officium prædicationis à Christo minime susceperunt. Primi & secundi non habebant temporalia quo ad dominium & proprietatem: sed tertii poterant habere quæcunque temporalia quo ad dominium & proprietatem, quæ tamen retinere minime artabantur, sed ad suum libitum relinquere poterant propter Deum: & de istis tertiis multi habebant multa. Inter istos vero fuerunt illi, quos iste enumerat, saltem illo tempore, quo fit de eis mentio in euangelio, & ideo exempla illa in nullo concludunt intentum istius. (De Ioseph, &c.) Ista vera sunt de eo, quia ante mortem Christi prædicationis officium nequaquam susceperat. (Castrum dictum Bethania erat Maria Magdalena & Martha) quod suerit earum quo ad dominium & proprietatem Euangelista non exprimit, nec tamen negat: sed siue fuerit earum, quo ad dominium & proprietatem, siue fuerit earum, quo ad originem vel mansionem, quemadmodum Bethsaida Iohannis primo dicitur ciuitas Andreæ & Petri, istud exemplum non est ad propositum: quia Maria & Martha non erant tunc de annunciantibus publice ex officio sibi commisso à Christo euangelicam veritatem. (De Tabitha quoque quæ interpretatur Dorcas.) Ex isto exemplo patet, quod ille intendit, quod Apostoli etiam post missionem Spiritus sancti, saltem post recessum eorum à multitudine credentium conuersorum ex Iudæis non dimiserunt proprietatem temporalium: quia ista Dorcas tempore illo fuit, & illo tempore eleemosynas faciebat: quod isti postea improbabunt. (Ista discipulatu non obstante temporalia habebat.) Ista bene poterat habere temporalia, quia votum non emiserat paupertatis, sicut Apostoli. (Nec reperimus, &c.) Istud dicunt erroneum, sicut ostensum est supra. Et si quæras, quando dedit eis aliam legem, dicunt, quod Matthæi decimo, & Marci sexto, & Lucæ nono, & etiam Matthæi quinto, sexto & septimo, de quo postea disseretur. (Eadem erat Apostolorum, & discipulorum vita.) Concedunt aliqui, quod eadem erat vita Apostolorum & aliquorum discipulorum, scilicet septuaginta duorum, & forte quorundam aliorum, qui eorum vitam imitari volebant: sed non erat eadem vita Apostolorum, & omnium discipulorum Christi. (Qui vitam Apostolorum eorumque discipulorum imitari volunt.) Potest dici, quod beatus Clemens per discipulos non intelligit omnes Christianos, sed quoldam qui specialiter vitam Apostolorum imitati fuerunt. Et ex isto plane patet, quod non eandem legem viuendi seruabant Apostoli, & omnes alii Christiani: quia ex verbis prædictis Clementis euidenter colligitur, quod Apostoli vitam communem semel acceptam nunquam postea dimiserunt, & tamen multi Christiani non seruabant tempore beati Clementis vitam communem, ergo aliam legem viuendi tenuerant Apostoli, & multi alii Christiani.
units.tr: (Concerning the disciples, it is clear that some of them had many possessions.) These men say that the disciples were of three kinds. For some were Apostles; others, besides the Apostles, were specially appointed by Christ to preach the faith of Christ, of whom we read in Luke, chapter ten. The third kind were simply converted to the faith, but did not receive the office of preaching from Christ. The first and second kinds had no temporal goods as regards ownership and property; but the third kind could have any temporal goods as regards ownership and property, which they were not bound to keep, but could give up at their pleasure for God's sake; and many of these third kind had many possessions. Among these were those whom he lists, at least at the time when they are mentioned in the Gospel, and so those examples in no way prove his point. (Of Joseph, etc.) These things are true of him, because before the death of Christ he had by no means taken up the office of preaching. (The village called Bethany belonged to Mary Magdalene and Martha.) The Evangelist does not state, but also does not deny, that it was theirs as regards ownership and property. But whether it was theirs as regards ownership and property, or theirs as regards origin or residence, just as Bethsaida is called in John, chapter one, the city of Andrew and Peter, this example is not to the point; for Mary and Martha were not then among those publicly proclaiming the gospel truth from an office committed to them by Christ. (Of Tabitha also, who is called Dorcas.) From this example it is plain that he means that the Apostles, even after the sending of the Holy Spirit, at least after their withdrawal from the multitude of believers converted from the Jews, did not give up ownership of temporal goods; for this Dorcas was alive at that time and gave alms at that time; which these men will afterwards refute. (Notwithstanding discipleship, she had temporal goods.) She could well have temporal goods, because she had not made a vow of poverty, as the Apostles had. (Nor do we find, etc.) They call this erroneous, as has been shown above. And if you ask when he gave them another rule, they say: Matthew, chapter ten, and Mark, chapter six, and Luke, chapter nine, and also Matthew, chapters five, six and seven, which will be discussed later. (The life of the Apostles and of the disciples was the same.) Some concede that the life of the Apostles and of some disciples, namely the seventy-two, and perhaps of certain others who wished to imitate their life, was the same; but the life of the Apostles and of all Christ's disciples was not the same. (Who wish to imitate the life of the Apostles and of their disciples.) It can be said that the blessed Clement does not mean by disciples all Christians, but certain ones who specially imitated the life of the Apostles. And from this it is quite plain that the Apostles did not observe the same rule of living as all other Christians; for from the words of Clement quoted above it is clearly gathered that the Apostles never afterwards gave up the common life once they had accepted it; and yet many Christians in the time of the blessed Clement did not keep a common life; therefore the Apostles and many other Christians held to different rules of living.

units.la: CAP. CI.
units.tr: CHAPTER CI.

units.la: Item nec cum ipsos Apostolos ex discipulis fecit, videtur eis indixisse aliam vitam, quam prius habuerant, sed potestatem eis aliquam tribuisse. Unde cum eos Apostolos ordinauit, legitur Matt. 10. sic dixisse: Et conuocatis duodecim Apostolis suis dedit illis potestatem spirituum immundorum, vt eiicerent eos, & curarent omnem languorem & omnem infirmitatem.
units.tr: Likewise, when he made the Apostles out of his disciples, he does not seem to have imposed on them a different way of life from the one they had before, but rather to have given them some authority. Hence when he ordained them Apostles, Matthew 10 reads that he said: "And when he had called his twelve Apostles, he gave them power over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every sickness and every infirmity."

units.la: Hic ponit quartam rationem pro assertione prædicta: quæ potest sic formari. Christus non indixit Apostolis aliam vitam, quando fecit eos Apostolos, quam prius habuerant, sed antequam essent Apostoli, non dimiserunt omnia temporalia, ergo nec quando fuerunt ad Apostolatum assumpti omnia temporalia reliquerunt: & per consequens antequam ad prædicandum mitterentur, neque quaquam omnia temporalia dimiserunt.
units.tr: Here he gives a fourth reason for the aforesaid assertion, which can be framed thus: Christ did not impose on the Apostles a different way of life when he made them Apostles from the one they had before; but before they were Apostles they had not given up all their temporal goods; therefore neither when they were taken up into the apostleship did they give up all their temporal goods. Consequently, before they were sent out to preach, they had by no means given up all their temporal goods.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores prædicta reputant insufficienter dicta. Primo quia ex scripturæ testimoniis minime probat, quod Christus, cum ex discipulis fecit Apostolos, ipsis vitam aliam non indixit. Secundo quia insinuat, quod tunc Christus eos Apostolos ordinauit, quando misit eos ad prædicandum: quia dicit, quod Matthæi decimo legitur de eorum ordinatione. Totum autem illud capitulum videtur loqui de missione Apostolorum ad prædicandum, & de informatione eorum de actione officii prædicationis iniuncti. Et si dicatur, quod quamuis in eodem capitulo simul legantur dicta ordinatio Apostolorum & missio ad prædicandum: tamen prius ordinauit eos Apostolos, & postea ad prædicandum misit. Eadem facilitate dicetur sibi quod si illud capitulum Matthæi decimi rememorat ordinationem Apostolorum: ex hoc concludi non potest, quod eis viam aliam non indixit, sæpe enim aliquis rememorat aliquod factum succincte, non omnia illud factum contingentia explicans. explicando. Dicunt igitur quod Matth.10. non loquitur de ordinatione Apostolorum: cum de ordinatione ipsorum nulla penitus mentio fiat ibidem. Unde dicit ibi sic: Convocatis duodecim discipulis suis dedit illis potestatem spirituum immundorum, ut eiicerent eos & curarent omnem languorem & omnem infirmitatem. Duodecim autem Apostolorum nomina sunt haec: Primus Simon, &c. Et post expressionem nominum Apostolorum, sequitur immediate: Hos duodecim misit sic praecipiens eis, &c. In his autem verbis de ordinatione Apostolorum nulla fit mentio: sed magis cum dicit in principio: Convocatis duodecim discipulis suis, eos quasi antonomatice discipulos appellando, supponit eos fuisse prius Apostolos ordinatos: & quia Matthaeus nomina ipsorum Apostolorum antea nequaquam expresserat: ideo supponens eos fuisse iam Apostolos ordinatos, nomina eorum explicat dicens: Duodecim autem Apostolorum nomina sunt haec, &c. Non igitur eos, ut videtur, tunc Apostolos ordinavit: sed eos iam ordinatos Apostolos tunc ad praedicandum transmisit. Unde videtur, quod ante sermonem, quem fecit Christus in monte, de quo habetur Matthei quinto, sexto & septimo, ipsos Apostolos ordinavit, quod ex Evangelio Lucae, qui magis explicite ordinationem ipsorum prosequitur, colligitur, ut videtur, aperte. Nam sicut patet Lucae sexto. Christus ipsos ordinavit Apostolos, antequam sermonem faceret, qui in eodem capitulo recitatur. Ibi enim sic legitur: Factum est autem in illis diebus: Exiit in montem orare, & erat pernoctans in oratione Dei: & cum dies factus esset, vocavit discipulos suos, & elegit duodecim ex ipsis, quos & Apostolos nominavit: Simonem quem cognominavit Petrum, &c. & sequitur: Et descendens cum illis stetit in loco campestri: & turba discipulorum eius & multitudo copiosa plebis, &c. Et post: Et ipse elevatis oculis in discipulos suos dicebat: Beati pauperes quia vestrum est regnum Dei, &c. Ex his verbis colligitur evidenter, quod ipsos ordinavit Apostolos antequam faceret praedictum sermonem ad turbas, sed sermo qui recitatur Matt. quinto, sexto & septimo, vel fuit idem cum sermone qui recitatur Lucae sexto capitulo, vel praecessit illum eadem die, sequebatur tamen ordinationem Apostolorum, quod Glossa Matthaei quinto testatur sic dicens: Huic rei consentit Lucas ita dicens: factum est autem in illis diebus, Exiit in montem orare: & erat pernoctans in oratione Dei: & cum dies factus esset, vocavit discipulos suos, & elegit duodecim ex ipsis, quos & Apostolos nominavit, sed Lucas dicit post descensum de monte in loco campestri eundem sermonem turbis praedicasse stando: quem Matthaeus dicit habitum discipulis in monte sedendo, potuit enim esse, ut in monte duodecim eligeret, quod Matthaeus tacet, Lucas dicit, & electis sermonem illum tunc haberet, quod Matthaeus dicit, Lucas praeterit, & postquam descendit, alterum sermonem illi simile turbis faceret, de quo Matthaeus tacet, Lucas dicit. Vel potuit Dominus primo esse cum solis discipulis in eminentia montis, quando ex eis duodecim elegit. Deinde cum eis descendisset in aliquam aequalitatem, quae tamen in monte esset, & multas capere turbas posset: & ibi stetisse, donec turba congregarentur, & post cum sedisset, discipulis propius venisse: & ita illis & ceteris unum sermonem habuisse, quem dicunt Matthaeus & Lucas diverso narrandi modo, sed eadem veritate rerum. Ex his verbis datur intelligi, quod sive fuerit idem sermo, sive alius, ordinatio Apostolorum praecessit utrumque: & ita fuerunt ordinati Apostoli ante sermonem, qui ponitur Matthei quinto, sexto & septimo, quod etiam alia Glossa Matthaei quinto super illud: accesserunt ad eum discipuli eius, asserit manifeste dicens: Quos ibi constituit duodecim. Item alia Glossa idem ait: Apostolos praeeminentius abducit, ut a monte prius montes suscipiant pacem populo. Ex his patet, quod Apostoli ordinati fuerunt ante sermonem, qui recitatur Matthei quinto, sexto & septimo, eadem tamen die.
units.tr: But these opponents think the aforesaid points are insufficiently stated. First, because from the testimonies of Scripture it by no means proves that Christ, when he made Apostles out of his disciples, did not impose on them another way of life. Second, because it implies that Christ ordained them Apostles at the time he sent them out to preach, since it says that in Matthew 10 their ordination is read. Yet that whole chapter seems to speak of the sending of the Apostles to preach and of their instruction in carrying out the office of preaching laid upon them. And if it is said that, although the ordination of the Apostles and the sending out to preach are read together in the same chapter, nevertheless he first ordained them Apostles and afterwards sent them out to preach, then with equal ease it may be replied that if that chapter of Matthew 10 recalls the ordination of the Apostles, it cannot be concluded from this that he did not impose on them another way of life; for someone often recalls an event briefly, without explaining everything that pertains to that event. These men therefore say that Matt. 10 does not speak of the ordination of the Apostles, since no mention at all is made there of their ordination. Hence it says there: When he had called his twelve disciples, he gave them power over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every sickness and every infirmity. Now the names of the twelve Apostles are these: First Simon, etc. And immediately after the naming of the Apostles it follows: These twelve he sent out, instructing them thus, etc. In these words there is no mention of the ordination of the Apostles. Rather, when it says at the beginning: When he had called his twelve disciples, calling them disciples almost as a title, it presupposes that they had previously been ordained Apostles; and since Matthew had not earlier stated the names of these Apostles, he, presupposing that they had already been ordained Apostles, now sets out their names, saying: Now the names of the twelve Apostles are these, etc. Therefore, as it seems, he did not then ordain them Apostles, but sent them out to preach as Apostles already ordained. Hence it seems that Christ ordained the Apostles before the sermon he gave on the mount, recorded in Matthew 5, 6 and 7; this is clearly gathered, as it seems, from the Gospel of Luke, who more explicitly follows up their ordination. For, as is evident from Luke 6, Christ ordained them Apostles before he gave the sermon recited in that same chapter. There it is read thus: And it came to pass in those days that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God; and when it was day, he called his disciples, and of them he chose twelve, whom also he named Apostles: Simon, whom he surnamed Peter, etc. And it follows: And he came down with them and stood in a level place: and the company of his disciples and a great multitude of people, etc. And after: And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples and said: Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of God, etc. From these words it is clearly gathered that he ordained them Apostles before he gave the aforesaid sermon to the crowds; but the sermon recited in Matthew 5, 6 and 7 was either the same as the sermon recited in Luke 6, or came before it on the same day, yet it followed the ordination of the Apostles. The Gloss on Matthew 5 bears witness to this, saying: Luke agrees with this thing, saying: "And it came to pass in those days that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God; and when it was day, he called his disciples, and of them he chose twelve, whom also he named Apostles." But Luke says that after coming down from the mountain, in a level place, he preached the same sermon to the crowds standing; which Matthew says was delivered to the disciples while sitting on the mountain. For it may be that on the mountain he chose the twelve, which Matthew passes over and Luke states; and having chosen them, he then gave that sermon, which Matthew states and Luke passes over; and after he came down, he gave another sermon similar to it to the crowds, of which Matthew says nothing and Luke does. Or the Lord may first have been with the disciples alone on the height of the mountain, when he chose the twelve from them; then, having come down with them to some level ground, which nevertheless was on the mountain and could hold many crowds, he stood there until the crowds gathered; and afterwards, when he had sat down, the disciples came nearer; and thus he delivered one sermon to them and to the others, which Matthew and Luke relate in different manners of narration but with the same truth of the facts. From these words it is understood that whether it was the same sermon or another, the ordination of the Apostles came before both; and so the Apostles were ordained before the sermon recorded in Matthew 5, 6 and 7. Another Gloss on Matthew 5, on the words his disciples came to him, asserts this plainly, saying: Those whom he appointed there, twelve. Another Gloss likewise says: He leads the Apostles aside more eminently, so that from the mountain they might first receive peace for the people. From these things it is evident that the Apostles were ordained before the sermon recited in Matthew 5, 6 and 7, yet on the same day.

units.la: Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod tunc Matthaeus non fuit Apostolus, quia ipse postea fuit electus, sicut patet Matthei octavo.
units.tr: But perhaps someone will say that Matthew was not then an Apostle, because he was chosen afterwards, as is clear from Matthew 8.

units.la: Ad hoc respondet Glossa super illud Matth. octau. Vidit hominem sedentem in telonio, dicens: Hinc probabilius videtur, quod praemissa memorat, cum duodecim elegerit ante sermonem, licet ergo vocatio Matthaei post sermonem istum narretur, tamen in re praecessit sermonem eundem. (Nec cum ipsos Apostolos ex discipulis fecit, videtur eis indixisse aliam vitam quam prius habuerant.) Dicunt isti, quod vel tunc vel ante, aliam vitam eis indixit, sicut ex praecedentibus colligitur manifeste (sed potestatem eis aliquam tribuisse) non legitur, quod Salvator ante dederit praeceptum Apostolis miracula faciendi, quam indixit eis aliam vitam: nec inuenitur explicitum in euangelio, quod tunc, quando Christus ordinavit Apostolos, ipsis dederit potestatem miracula faciendi: quia quamvis Marci tertio sic legitur: Et fecit ut essent duodecim cum illo: & ut mitteret eos praedicare: & dedit illis potestatem curandi infirmos, & eiiciendi daemonia: tamen ibi minime explicatur, quod quando elegit eos in Apostolos, ipsis praedictam contulit potestatem: & tamen potuit esse, quod quando ordinavit eos Apostolos, & ut eis aliam vitam indiceret & potestatem tribueret miracula faciendi, (cum eos Apostolos ordinavit, legitur Matthei decimo sic dixisse.) Hic dicunt istum dupliciter deficere. Primo quia Matthei decimo de ordinatione Apostolorum nulla fit mentio, secundo quod errat asserens Christum dixisse verba quae sequuntur, scilicet & convocatis discipulis suis, &c. Ista enim non fuerunt verba Christi, sed Matthaei Evangelistae. (Dedit illis potestatem spirituum immundorum) quamvis tunc dederit, tamen potuit esse quod prius dedisset, unde & Marci tam 3. quam 6. narratur quod dedit illis talem potestatem (ut eiicerent) textus habet, ut eiicerent.
units.tr: To this the Gloss on the words He saw a man sitting at the receipt of custom in Matthew 8 replies, saying: It seems more probable from this that he recorded earlier matters when he chose the twelve before the sermon; so although the calling of Matthew is narrated after that sermon, nevertheless in fact it came before the same sermon. (Nor, when he made the Apostles out of his disciples, does he seem to have imposed on them a different way of life from the one they had before.) These men say that either then or earlier he imposed on them another way of life, as is clearly gathered from what has gone before. (But to have given them some authority) is not read: that the Saviour gave the Apostles the command to work miracles before he imposed on them another way of life. Nor is it found explicitly in the Gospel that when Christ ordained the Apostles, he then gave them the power to work miracles. For although Mark 3 reads thus: And he made that they should be twelve with him, and that he might send them out to preach; and he gave them power to heal the sick and to cast out devils, yet it is in no way explained there that when he chose them as Apostles he conferred that power on them. And yet it could be that when he ordained them Apostles, and in order to impose on them another way of life and to give them the power to work miracles, (when he ordained them Apostles, Matthew 10 reads that he said thus). Here they say this is faulty in two ways. First, because Matthew 10 makes no mention of the ordination of the Apostles; second, because it is wrong to assert that Christ said the words that follow, namely and when he had called his disciples, etc. For these were not the words of Christ but of the Evangelist Matthew. (He gave them power over unclean spirits), although he then gave it, it could have been that he had given it earlier; hence Mark, both in chapter 3 and in chapter 6, relates that he gave them such power (to cast them out); the text has to cast them out.

units.la: CAP. CII.
units.tr: CHAP. CII.

units.la: SI vero consideretur tempus, quo missi fuerunt ad praedicandum, videtur pro illo tempore, quod aliqua fuerint eis habere interdicta. Legitur enim Matth. 10. quod istos duodecim Apostolos misit praecipiens eis dicens: Nolite possidere aurum neque argentum, neque pecuniam in zonis vestris: non peram in via: neque duas tunicas, neque calciamenta, neque virgam. Marci vero sexto legitur sic dixisse: Et vocavit duodecim, & coepit eos mittere binos: & praecepit eis ne quid tollerent in via nisi virgam tantum: non peram: neque in zona aes: sed calceatos sandaliis & ne induerentur duabus tunicis. Luca vero nono legitur sic dixisse: Misit illos (scilicet duodecim Apostolos) praedicare regnum Dei & sanare infirmos, & ait ad illos: Nihil tuleritis in via neque virgam: neque peram: neque panem: neque pecuniam: neque duas tunicas habeatis. Ex quibus verbis videtur, quod pro tempore viae praedictae tantum praedicta eis fuerint interdicta. Augustinus tamen dicit expresse libro de concordia Evangelistarum, quod illud non fuit praeceptum, sed potestas data recipiendi necessaria ab eis, quibus evangelium praedicabant: quam servare Apostolis licuit, vel etiam non servare, alias autem Apostolus Paulus transgressor praecepti huius extitisset: quia plerumque ab illis, quibus praedicabat, non recipiebat necessaria, sed illa vel recipiebat ab aliis vel ea suis manibus acquirebat, sicut patet prima ad Corinth. non. ad Philippens. quart. ad Thessalonien. 4. & Actuum vigesimo, ubi dicitur: Argentum autem & aurum aut vestimenta nullius concupiui, sicut ipsi scitis, quoniam ad ea, quae mihi opus erant, & his qui mecum sunt, ministraverunt manus istae. Praeterea quod illud praeceptum fuerit temporale, satis innuitur Lucae vigesimo secundo, ubi Dominus Apostolis dixit: Quando misi vos sine pera & sacculo: nunquid aliquid defuit vobis? Et praeterea discipulis 72. quando misit eos dixit: Nolite portare sacculum, in quo pecunia consueuit portari: neque peram, in qua consueuerunt alimenta portari: neque calciamenta: & tamen de illis certum est, quod multi ex discipulis erant multa habentes, ut patet ex praedictis.
units.tr: If, however, we consider the time when they were sent out to preach, it appears that certain things were forbidden to them for that time. For Matthew 10 reads that Christ sent out these twelve Apostles, giving them this charge: "Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts; no bag for the road, nor two tunics, nor shoes, nor a staff." But Mark 6 reads that he said: "And he called the twelve, and began to send them out two by two, and commanded them to take nothing for the road except a staff only: no bag, no bread, and no money in their belts; but to go shod with sandals and not to wear two tunics." Luke 9 reads that he said: "He sent them (namely the twelve Apostles) to preach the kingdom of God and to heal the sick, and said to them: Take nothing for the road, neither staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money, nor have two tunics." From these words it seems that the foregoing prohibitions applied only to the time of that journey. Augustine, however, states expressly in his book on the harmony of the Evangelists that this was not a command but a permission to receive necessities from those to whom they preached, which the Apostles might observe or not observe as they chose; otherwise the Apostle Paul would have been a transgressor of this command, since he often did not receive necessities from those to whom he preached, but received them from others or earned them with his own hands, as is clear from 1 Cor. 9., Phil. 4., 1 Thess. 4., and Acts 20, where it says: "I have coveted no one's silver or gold or clothing, as you yourselves know; these hands ministered to my needs and to those who were with me." Moreover, that this command was temporary is sufficiently indicated in Luke 22, where the Lord said to the Apostles: "When I sent you without bag or purse, did you lack anything?" And besides, when he sent out the seventy-two disciples he said: "Do not carry a purse in which money is usually carried, nor a bag in which food is usually carried, nor shoes." And yet it is certain that many of those disciples had many possessions, as is clear from what has been said.

units.la: Postquam in parte praecedenti iste respondit ad quaestionem propositam de Apostolis iuxta primum membrum secundae distinctionis: Hic respondet ad eam iuxta secundum membrum distinctionis eiusdem, ostendens primo, quod Apostolis pro tempore, quo ad praedicandum mittebantur, aliqua temporalia interdicta fuerunt. Quod tribus auctoritatibus probat. Secundo ibi: Ex quibus videtur, concludit, quod talia eis interdicta non fuerunt, nisi pro tempore viae praedictae tantummodo. Tertio ibi: Augustinus respondet, quod Augustinus vult, quod illud non fuit praeceptum Apostolis. Quarto ibi: Praeterea quod illud, probat, quod illud fuit temporale praeceptum, scilicet pro tempore viae praedictae tantum modo, quod primo probat auctoritate Christi. Secundo ibi: Praeterea discipulis 72. Probat idem per simile de 70. discipulis, quibus erat datum a Christo praeceptum consimile: & tamen respectu eorum fuit praeceptum temporale, ergo & respectu Apostolorum praeceptum extitit temporale.
units.tr: After the preceding part, he answered the question proposed about the Apostles according to the first member of the second distinction. Here he answers it according to the second member of the same distinction, showing first that certain temporal things were forbidden to the Apostles for the time when they were sent out to preach. He proves this by three authorities. Second, at "From these words it seems," he concludes that such things were forbidden to them only for the time of the aforesaid journey. Third, at "Augustine answers," he shows what Augustine means, namely that this was not a command to the Apostles. Fourth, at "Moreover, that this command," he proves that the command was temporary, namely only for the time of the aforesaid journey; he proves this first by the authority of Christ, and second, at "Moreover, when he sent out the seventy-two," he proves the same by analogy with the seventy disciples, to whom Christ gave a similar command, and yet for them the command was temporary; therefore for the Apostles too the command was temporary.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt, quod in verbis praemissis quadrupliciter errat. Primo cum dicit, praeceptum de non possidendo aurum, &c. fuisse temporale pro tempore viae praedictae tantum modo. Secundo cum imponit beato Augustino, quod dicat illud non fuisse praeceptum. Tertio cum dicit, quod praeceptum datum septuaginta de non portando sacculum, & aliis non portandis fuit temporale. Quarto cum asserit aliquos de illis multa habuisse, quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Quod primum sit erroneum reputandum, multipliciter probre conantur. Primo sic: qui perfectionem aliquam pro omni tempore profitetur, pro omni tempore ad eandem perfectionem nocitur obligatus, sed beatus Petrus, & eadem ratione alii Apostoli paupertatem, quae est carentia auri & argenti, & aliarum divitiarum, profitebatur pro omni tempore, ergo ad talem perfectionem remansit omni tempore obligatus. Ex quo sequitur, quod illud Domini praeceptum: Nolite possidere aurum, &c. non extitit temporale obligans solummodo pro via praedicta. Maior est manifesta, minor euidenter ostenditur, per beatum Augustinum, qui in libro de Mirabilibus sacrae Scripturae ait: In excusatione eleemosynae & pauperta-tis professione, Petrus paralytico ait: Surge & ambula, illud magistri praeceptum seruans: Nolite possidere aurum neque argentum. Ex his verbis euidenter colligitur, quod Petrus professus fuerat paupertatem: & quod tunc praedictum Domini praeceptum seruabat, ergo illud praeceptum non extitit temporale modo praedicto. Secundo sic: Praeceptum negativum nullum tempus specificans obligat pro omni tempore, quo illud expedit obseruari, sed praedictum praeceptum est negativum, nullum tempus specificans, cum sine temporis specificatione dicatur: Nolite possidere aurum neque argentum, neque pecuniam in zonis vestris, & expediebat Apostolis & etiam aliis illud obseruare, non solum pro tempore viae praedictae: sed etiam pro aliis temporibus, ergo pro aliis temporibus obligabat.
units.tr: But these assailants say that in the words quoted above the author errs in four respects. First, when he says that the command not to possess gold, and so on, was temporary, applying only to the time of the aforesaid journey. Second, when he charges Blessed Augustine with saying that it was not a command. Third, when he says that the command given to the seventy not to carry a purse, and the other prohibitions, were temporary. Fourth, when he asserts that some of them had many possessions as to ownership and property. That the first point is to be regarded as false they try to prove in many ways. First, thus: whoever professes some perfection for all time is bound to that same perfection for all time; but Blessed Peter, and by the same reasoning the other Apostles, professed poverty, which is the lack of gold and silver and other riches, for all time; therefore they remained bound to such perfection at all times. From this it follows that the Lord's command, "Do not possess gold," and so on, was not a temporary obligation binding only for the aforesaid journey. The major premise is manifest; the minor is clearly shown by Blessed Augustine, who in his book On the Wonders of Holy Scripture says: "In the excuse for alms and the profession of poverty, Peter said to the paralytic: Rise and walk, keeping that command of the Master: Do not possess gold or silver." From these words it is clearly gathered that Peter had professed poverty, and that at that time he was keeping the aforesaid command of the Lord; therefore that command was not temporary in the aforesaid sense. Second, thus: a negative command that specifies no time binds for all time in which it is expedient to observe it; but the aforesaid command is negative and specifies no time, since it is stated without any specification of time: "Do not possess gold or silver, nor money in your belts"; and it was expedient for the Apostles and for others to observe it not only during the aforesaid journey but also at other times; therefore it bound them at other times.

units.la: Hic restat probare, quod non solum pro tempore viae praedictae, sed etiam pro aliis temporibus expediebat Apostolis & aliis seruare praedictum praeceptum. Hoc autem expresse asserit Chrysostomus, qui super illud Match. Nolite possidere aurum, &c. ait: Multa per hoc vnum commendabat. Primum quidem non suspectos faciens Apostolos. Secundo autem ab omni eos eruens sollicitudine, ut vacationem omnem sermoni tribuerent. Tertio docens eos suam virtutem. Hoc nempe eis & postea dicit: Nunquid aliquid defuit vobis, quando misi vos nudos & discalceatos? Ex his verbis patet, quod Apostolis & auditoribus eorundem expediebat, quod Apostoli aurum & argentum ac pecuniam minime possidebant aliis temporibus, quam tempore viae praedictae: quia per illud praeceptum, sicut dicit Chrysostomus, non suspecti fiebant, & ab omni sollicitudine eruti erant, ut praedicationi vacarent, ac etiam Christi virtutem cognoscebant, sed ita aliis temporibus, sicut tempore viae praedictae, expediebat Apostolis & aliis, ut fierent non suspecti, ab omni sollicitudine eruerentur, & ut praedicationi vacarent, & Christi virtutem cognoscerent, ergo ita pro aliis temporibus, sicut pro via prædicta, dictum præceptum Apostolos obligabat. Sed forte dicet ille, quod dictum præceptum tempus viæ prædictæ spectat: tum quia ibi antedictum præceptum habetur: hos duodecim misit, &c. tum quia ibidem subiungitur; non peram in via neque duas tunicas, &c. tum quia Marc. 6. datur ibi idem præceptum, ubi tamen specificatur tempus viæ prædictæ, cum dicitur, & præcepit eis, ne quid tulerent in via, nisi virgam tantum: non peram, non panem, neque in zona aës: tum quia Lucæ 9. ubi de eodem præcepto fit mentio, Christus viam specificat supradictam, unde dixit Christus ad Apostolos: Nihil tuleritis in via neque virgam, neque peram, neque panem, neque pecuniam. Pecuniam autem, aurum & argentum videtur intelligi. Sed ad ista tripliciter respondetur; primo quia, sicut sæpe unus Evangelista aliquid dicit, quod alius tacet: ita quandoque unus dicit idem & alius, sed alio modo: & tunc cum illi modo non repugnent, illud debet utroque modo intelligi, & ideo esto, ut unus Evangelista vel plures specificet vel specificent viam prædictam in dicto præcepto de non possidendo auro & argento & pecunia: non propter hoc potest concludi, quod non debeat absolute pro omni tempore expediente intelligi. Ex quo unus Evangelista idem sine omni specificatione temporis ponit præceptum: cum ista duo, scilicet non possidere pecuniam pro via prædicta & non possidere pecuniam, neque pro ista via neque pro alio tempore, nullam repugnantiam inter se noscantur habere, quare cum Matthæus recitet absolute sine omni specificatione viæ vel temporis memoratum præceptum absolute pro omni tempore debet intelligi. Secundo respondetur, quod ex hoc quod præceptum datur de non possidendo auro & argento, &c. pro via prædicta, intelligitur idem præceptum etiam pro aliis temporibus esse datum: quia ubi est eadem ratio, vel fortior, debet esse idem ius, sed eadem est ratio dicti præcepti pro illo tempore illius viæ, & pro aliis temporibus quibus erant Apostoli prædicaturi, ergo illud præceptum datum fuit eis non solum pro via prædicta, sed etiam pro aliis temporibus.
units.tr: Here it remains to prove that it was expedient for the Apostles and others to observe the aforesaid command not only during the aforesaid journey but also at other times. This Chrysostom expressly asserts, who, commenting on the words of Matthew, "Do not possess gold," and so on, says: "By this one command he commended many things. First, by making the Apostles not open to suspicion. Second, by freeing them from all anxiety, so that they might devote all their leisure to preaching. Third, by teaching them his power. For he says to them afterwards as well: Did you lack anything when I sent you naked and barefoot?" From these words it is clear that it was expedient for the Apostles and their hearers that the Apostles did not possess gold, silver, or money at times other than the time of the aforesaid journey; for by that command, as Chrysostom says, they were made not open to suspicion, were freed from all anxiety so that they might devote themselves to preaching, and also came to know Christ's power. But it was expedient for the Apostles and others in the same way at other times as during the aforesaid journey, that they should become not open to suspicion, be freed from all anxiety, devote themselves to preaching, and know Christ's power; therefore the said command bound the Apostles at other times in the same way as for the aforesaid journey. But perhaps he will say that the said command concerns the time of the aforesaid journey, because the previously mentioned command is found there: "He sent these twelve," and so on; because immediately after it is added: "no bag for the road, nor two tunics," and so on; because Mark 6 gives the same command there, where the time of the aforesaid journey is specified when it says: "and he commanded them to take nothing for the road except a staff only: no bag, no bread, no money in their belts"; and because in Luke 9, where mention is made of the same command, Christ specifies the aforesaid journey, whence Christ said to the Apostles: "Take nothing for the road, neither staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money." But by "money" gold and silver seem to be meant. To these things, however, a threefold answer is given. First, because just as often one Evangelist says something which another passes over, so sometimes one says the same thing as another but in a different way; and when these ways are not contradictory, the thing ought to be understood in both ways. And so, even if one Evangelist or several specify the aforesaid journey in the said command about not possessing gold, silver, and money, it cannot on that account be concluded that it ought not to be understood absolutely for all time when it is expedient. For since Matthew sets down the same command without any specification of time, these two things, namely not to possess money for the aforesaid journey and not to possess money either for that journey or for any other time, are known to have no contradiction between them; therefore, since Matthew recites the aforesaid command absolutely, without any specification of journey or time, it ought to be understood absolutely for all time. Second, it is answered that from the fact that the command not to possess gold, silver, and so on, is given for the aforesaid journey, it is understood that the same command was also given for other times; because where there is the same reason, or a stronger one, there ought to be the same law; but the reason for the said command during that time of the journey is the same as for the other times when the Apostles were going to preach; therefore that command was given to them not only for the aforesaid journey but also for other times.

units.la: Tertio respondetur, quod licet Christus miserit tunc Apostolos ad prædicandum: tamen in præcipiendo eis non possidere aurum neque argentum, neque pecuniam, secundum nullum Evangelistam tempus illius viæ specificauit: sed absolute præcepit eis, quod in via non ferrent pecuniam, intendens quod quandocunque irent ad prædicandum, non tollerent pecuniam, unde Matthæus non dicit: Non peram in hac via, qua nunc ituri estis: sed absolute dixit: non peram in via, nec Marcus dixit: Ne quid tollerent in illa via, qua tunc ituri erant: sed absolute dixit: Ne quid tollerent in via, &c. neque Lucas dixit: Nihil tuleritis in hac via, qua nunc ituri estis: sed absolute dixit: Nihil tuleritis in via.
units.tr: Thirdly, it is answered that although Christ then sent the Apostles to preach, yet in commanding them not to possess gold, silver or money, no Evangelist specified the time of that journey. Rather, he commanded them absolutely that they should not carry money on the way, meaning that whenever they went out to preach they should not take money with them. Hence Matthew does not say, "Do not possess a purse on this journey on which you are now about to go," but absolutely says, "Do not possess a purse on the way." Nor does Mark say, "Let them take nothing on that journey on which they were then about to go," but absolutely says, "Let them take nothing on the way," etc. Nor does Luke say, "Take nothing on this journey on which you are now about to go," but absolutely says, "Take nothing on the way."

units.la: Et ita dictum præceptum Christi de omni via, qua ituri erant ad prædicandum debet intelligi, si autem non debebant possidere aurum, &c. in via: multo fortius nec extra viam, scilicet ante terminum viæ, nec in termino viæ, secundum quod arguit Chrysostomus super illud: Nolite possidere, &c. dicens: Intende qualiter eos omnibus denudans omnia eis dedit, permittens in domibus eorum, qui docentur manere & nihil habentes introire. Si autem in aliena patria existentes, & apud ignotos abeuntes nihil aliud oportet petere quotidiano cibo: multo magis domi manentes. Ex quibus verbis habetur aperte, quod secundum Chrysostomum, si non debebant inter ignotos possidere pecuniam: multo magis nec domi inter notos, & eadem ratione postquam inter ignotos manere inciperent, non deberent pecuniam possidere.
units.tr: And so the said precept of Christ must be understood as applying to every journey on which they were about to go to preach; and if they were not to possess gold, etc. on the way, much more so not outside the way, that is, before the end of the journey, nor at its end. This is what Chrysostom argues on the words "Do not possess...", saying: "Consider how he, stripping them of everything, gave them all things, permitting them, when they were taught, to stay in their houses and to enter with nothing. But if, being in a foreign country and going among strangers, they ought to ask for nothing beyond their daily food, much more so when remaining at home." From these words it is clearly held that, according to Chrysostom, if they were not to possess money among strangers, much more so not at home among acquaintances; and by the same reasoning, once they began to remain among strangers, they ought not to possess money.

units.la: Quare sequitur manifeste, quod nec pro via aliqua, nec in termino viæ debebant pecuniam possidere, quando carere pecunia fuit expediens, & ita manifeste patet, quod stat ratio supradicta, scilicet quod illud præceptum Christi fuit datum Apostolis pro omni tempore, quo expediebat Apostolis dictum præceptum seruare: & non pro tempore viæ prædictæ solummodo.
units.tr: Hence it clearly follows that they were not to possess money either for any journey or at the end of a journey, whenever it was expedient to be without money. And so it is plainly evident that the above reasoning holds: namely, that this precept of Christ was given to the Apostles for every time in which it was expedient for them to observe the said precept, and not for the time of the aforesaid journey only.

units.la: Tertio sic arguunt: Ubi est eadem ratio, debet esse idem ius: quia de similibus simile iudicium est habendum: sed eadem fuit ratio, sicut tactum est, quare Apostoli non deberent aurum neque argentum, neque pecuniam possidere pro tempore viæ prædictæ: & pro omni alio tempore, quo prædicaturi erant; ergo præceptum, quod ratio iuris obtinet, æqualiter obligabat ipsos pro tempore viæ prædictæ, & pro omni alio tempore, quo prædicaturi erant. Maior est manifesta. Minor auctoritatibus sanctorum Patrum probatur aperte. Nam una ratio, quare Christus noluit Apostolos pro tempore illius viæ possidere prædicta fuit, ut qui docere debebant omnia divina providentia gubernari, ostenderent seipsos nihil de crastino cogitare. Hanc rationem assignat Rabanus super illud Matthæi decimo: Nolite possidere aurum, &c. dicens: Qui divitias detruncaverat, propemodum necessaria vitæ amputavit, ut Apostoli, doctores verae religionis, qui docebant divina providentia gubernari, seipsos ostenderent nihil cogitare de crastino, sed hæc ratio ita respiciebat omnia alia tempora, quibus debebant populis prædicare, sicut tempus viæ prædictæ, ergo æqualiter obligabat eos præceptum præfatum pro tempore viæ prædictæ, & pro aliis temporibus, quibus prædicaturi erant.
units.tr: Thirdly, they argue thus: where there is the same reason, there must be the same law, because like judgment is to be given in like cases. But the reason was the same, as has been touched upon, why the Apostles should not possess gold, silver or money for the time of the aforesaid journey, and for every other time when they were about to preach. Therefore the precept, which the force of law maintains, equally obliged them for the time of the aforesaid journey and for every other time when they were about to preach. The major premise is evident. The minor is plainly proved by the authority of the holy Fathers. For one reason why Christ did not want the Apostles to possess the aforesaid things during that journey was that, since they were to teach that all things are governed by divine providence, they should show themselves to think nothing of tomorrow. Rabanus assigns this reason on the words of Matthew 10: "Do not possess gold, etc.", saying: "He who had cut off riches nearly cut off the necessities of life, so that the Apostles, teachers of true religion, who taught that all things are governed by divine providence, might show themselves to take no thought for tomorrow." But this reason applied to all other times when they were to preach to the people just as it applied to the time of the aforesaid journey. Therefore the aforesaid precept equally obliged them for the time of the aforesaid journey and for other times when they were about to preach.

units.la: Item alia ratio secundum Chrysostomum, quare Apostoli pro via prædicta non debuerunt talia possidere, fuit (sicut allegatum est prius) ut Apostoli per contemptum divitiarum magni & mirabiles apparerent. (Auctoritatem, quam hic insinuant, quære supra capitulo nonagesimo quinto) sed ita debebant Apostoli apparere magni & mirabiles pro aliis temporibus, sicut pro tempore viæ prædictæ, ergo ita debuerunt catere prædictis pro aliis temporibus, quibus prædicaturi erant, sicut pro tempore viæ prædictæ, & sic discurrendo per omnes rationes, quæ pro prædicto præcepto potuerunt assignari, constat quod æqualiter debebant mouere Apostolos ad non possidendum huiusmodi bona pro tempore viæ prædictæ, & pro omnibus aliis temporibus, quibus prædicaturi erant, ergo præceptum obligabat ipsos, pro aliis temporibus, sicut pro illo.
units.tr: Again, another reason, according to Chrysostom, why the Apostles ought not to possess such things during the aforesaid journey was (as was said before) so that by contempt of riches they might appear great and wonderful. (For the authority they here suggest, see above in chapter ninety-five.) But the Apostles ought to appear great and wonderful at other times just as they did during the aforesaid journey. Therefore they ought to be without such things at other times when they were about to preach, just as during the aforesaid journey. And so, by running through all the reasons that could be assigned for the said precept, it is established that they equally ought to move the Apostles not to possess such goods during the aforesaid journey and for all other times when they were about to preach. Therefore the precept obliged them at other times just as at that time.

units.la: Quarto sic arguunt: Non debuerunt Apostoli aliquam perfectionem semel assumptam, quamdiu utile esset Apostolis & aliis eandem perfectionem seruare, dimittere, teste Saluatore, qui Lucæ nono ait: Nemo mittens manum ad aratrum, & respiciens retro, aptus est regno Dei. Hoc etiam ratio persuadet. Nam si talem perfectionem semel assumptam sine communi utilitate sua & aliorum pro aliquo tempore dimisissent: non utique profecissent, sed turpiter defecissent, sed Apostoli non debuerunt deficere, sed magis proficere, ergo perfectionem assumptam, quamdiu utile esset ipsis & aliis seruare, eandem dimittere minime debuerunt, sed non possidere aurum neque argentum, neque pecuniam propter Deum ad perfectionem noscitur pertinere: & non possidere huiusmodi fuit utile Apostolis & aliis non solum pro tempore viæ prædictæ, sed etiam pro aliis temporibus, quibus prædicaturi erant, sicut auctoritates sanctorum protestantur aperte, de quibus aliquæ sunt superius allegatæ, & nonnullæ inferius adducentur, ergo Apostoli non debuerunt huiusmodi possidere, non solum pro tempore viæ prædictæ, sed etiam pro aliis temporibus, quibus prædicaturi erant.
units.tr: Fourthly, they argue thus: The Apostles ought not, once they had taken up some perfection, to lay it aside, as long as it was useful for the Apostles and others to keep the same perfection, the Saviour bearing witness, who says in Luke 9: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God." Reason also persuades this. For if they had once taken up such perfection and, without common benefit to themselves and others, had laid it aside for some time, they would not have made progress but would have shamefully fallen away. But the Apostles ought not to fall away but rather to make progress. Therefore they ought in no way to lay aside the perfection they had taken up, as long as it was useful for themselves and others to keep it. But not to possess gold, silver or money for God's sake is known to pertain to perfection; and not to possess such things was useful for the Apostles and others not only for the time of the aforesaid journey but also for other times when they were about to preach, as the authorities of the holy Fathers plainly attest, some of which have been cited above and some of which will be adduced below. Therefore the Apostles ought not to possess such things not only for the time of the aforesaid journey but also for other times when they were about to preach.

units.la: Quinto sic arguunt: Non debuerunt Apostoli, qui post Christum erant primi prædicatores Euangelicæ veritatis, illa perfectione carere, quæ decet communiter prædicatores veritatis eiusdem: quia Apostoli, qui immediatè à Christo instructi fuerunt, sicut non debuerunt esse inferiores aliis prædicatoribus doctrina, ita non debuerunt esse inferiores vita exemplari, sed prædicatores communiter euangelicæ veritatis decet omni tempore, quo prædicationis exercent officium: imo etiam omni tempore carere huiusmodi, quo ad dominium & proprietatem propter Deum, ergo & Apostoli non solum pro tempore viæ prædictæ, sed etiam pro omni tempore, quo prædicaturi & inter populos conuersaturi erant, debebant proprietatem huiusmodi rerum propter Deum abdicare. Maior est manifesta. Minor probatur auctoritatibus aperte. Unde Beda super illud Marci sexto. Præcepit eis, ne quid tollerent, loquens communiter de prædicatoribus veritatis, ait: Tanta prædicatori debet esse fiducia in Deo, ut præsentis vitæ sumptus, quamuis non prouideat, tamen sibi eos non defuisse certissime sciat: ne dum mens eius occupatur ad temporalia, minus aliis prouideat æterna. Item Ambrosius super illud Lucæ: Nihil tuleritis in via, loquens de prædicatoribus in communi ait: Qualis debeat esse, qui euangelizat regnum Dei, præceptis euangelicis designatur, ut sine virga, sine pera, sine calciamentis, id est subsidiis temporalis adminicula non requirens fidei, qua tutum putet sibi quo ea minus requirit magis posse suppetere.
units.tr: Fifthly, they argue thus: The Apostles, who after Christ were the first preachers of the Gospel truth, ought not to lack that perfection which commonly befits the preachers of that same truth. For the Apostles, who were instructed immediately by Christ, just as they ought not to be inferior to other preachers in teaching, so they ought not to be inferior in exemplary life. But preachers of the Gospel truth commonly ought, at every time when they exercise the office of preaching, and indeed at all times, to be without such things as regards lordship and ownership for God's sake. Therefore the Apostles too, not only for the time of the aforesaid journey but for every time when they were about to preach and live among the peoples, ought to renounce ownership of such things for God's sake. The major is evident. The minor is plainly proved by authorities. Thus Bede, on the words of Mark 6: "He commanded them that they should take nothing," speaking commonly of preachers of the truth, says: "A preacher ought to have such confidence in God that, though he does not provide for the expenses of the present life, he may know most certainly that they will not be lacking to him, lest, while his mind is occupied with temporal things, he provide less for eternal things for others." Likewise Ambrose, on the words of Luke: "Take nothing on the way," speaking of preachers in general, says: "What sort of person he who preaches the kingdom of God ought to be is set out in the evangelical precepts: without a staff, without a purse, without sandals, that is, not requiring the aids of temporal supports, but trusting in faith, by which he thinks it safer to have what he requires less."

units.la: Item Glossa super illud Deuteronomii: Non alligabitis os bouì trituranti, ait: Occupati in doctrina non possunt sibi prouidere necessaria. Item Chrysostomus homel. decim. quint. super Matth. ait: Talis est luminis virtus, ut non solum luceat, sed & illuc ducat illos, qui sequuntur. Cum enim viderint omnia præsentia nos contemnentes ad futura præparatos, ante omnem sermonem operibus nostris crederent. Quis enim ita est amens, ut videns eum qui heri lasciuiebat & ditabatur omnia exutum, famem & inopiam & duram vitam & periculA & sanguinem & occisionem & omnia, quæ videntur periculosa, tolerare præparatum: non manifestam accipiat hinc futurorum demonstrationem? Si autem præsentibus nos implicuerimus & immiscuerimus, qualiter poterit credere, quod ad possessionem aliquam festinemus? Ex his aliisque quam pluribus auctoritatibus colligitur euidenter, quod communiter prædicatores decet euangelicæ paupertatis non solum aurum, argentum & pecuniam: sed etiam omnia temporalia contemnere propter Deum, & omnium proprietate carere: licet non omnes ad hoc teneantur inuiti, & ita constat, quod Apostoli pro omni tempore, quo prædicabant & conuersabantur inter populos, post prædictam perfectionem semel impositam huiusmodi minime possidebant, quo ad dominium seu proprietatem.
units.tr: Likewise the Gloss on the words of Deuteronomy: "You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain," says: "Those occupied in teaching cannot provide for their necessities for themselves." Likewise Chrysostom, Homily 15 on Matthew, says: "Such is the power of light that it not only shines but also leads those who follow it there. For when they see us, despising all present things, prepared for future things, they would believe our works before any sermon. For who is so foolish that, seeing one who yesterday was wanton and rich stripped of everything, prepared to endure hunger and poverty and a hard life and danger and blood and slaughter and all things which seem perilous, does not take from this a clear demonstration of things to come? But if we entangle and mix ourselves with present things, how will they be able to believe that we hasten to any possession?" From these and many other authorities it is clearly gathered that preachers commonly ought, in evangelical poverty, to despise not only gold, silver and money but all temporal things for God's sake, and to be without ownership of all things; although not all are bound to this against their will. And so it is established that the Apostles, at all times when they preached and lived among the peoples, after the aforesaid perfection was once imposed, did not possess such things as regards lordship or ownership.

units.la: Sexto sic arguunt: Semel prohibita, quorum quædam pro tempore necessitatis tantummodo videntur esse concessa, pro omni tempore intelliguntur esse prohibita: exemptis illis pro tempore necessitatis, quæ pro necessitate supplenda necessaria dignoscuntur, sed possidere prædicta, scilicet aurum, argentum, pecuniam, saeculum, peram, & huiusmodi, semel fuit prohibitum: & possidere aliquid horum, scilicet aurum, argentum, pecuniam & res alias, quo ad dominium & proprietatem in tempore necessitatis non est necessarium pro necessitate subleuanda, ergo possidere huiusmodi, quo ad dominium & proprietatem pro omni tempore erat prohibitum: licet pro causa necessitatis portare huiusmodi & vti eis legatur fuisse concessum, maior est manifesta: minor probatur.
units.tr: Sixthly, they argue as follows. What has once been forbidden, and of which some things seem to have been permitted only for a time of necessity, is understood to be forbidden for all time, except those things which in a time of necessity are recognized as needed to meet the need. But to possess the things named, namely gold, silver, money, the purse, the wallet and the like, was once forbidden. And to possess any of these, namely gold, silver, money or other goods, as to ownership and property, is not necessary in a time of necessity to relieve need. Therefore to possess such things as to ownership and property was forbidden for all time. That it is read that carrying such things and using them for the sake of necessity was permitted, the major premise is evident. The minor is proved.

units.la: Primo auctoritate Christi dicentis Lucæ duodecimo. Quando misi vos sine sacculo, pera & calciamentis, nunquid aliquid defuit vobis? at illi dixerunt, nihil. Ipse vero ait illis: Nunc si quis habet sacculum tollat: similiter & peram: & qui non habet gladium, vendat tunicam suam & gladium emat. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod Christus solummodo pro tempore necessitatis quædam prædicatoribus, quæ interdixerat prius, tunc concessit, quia dixit: Nunc, hoc est tempore tantæ persecutionis, quod est tempus necessitatis, qui habet sacculum, tollat: similiter & peram, &c. hoc est, tollat omnia, quæ pro tali tempore opportuna noscuntur. Alia igitur, quæ pro tali tempore non erant necessaria, nequaquam concessit, sed interdicta (sicut antea) remanserunt. His concordat Beda super prædicta verba Christi dicens: Non enim eadem viuendi regula persecutionis, quapacis tempore discipulas informat. Misfis quidem discipulis ad praedicandum, ne quid tollerent in via, praecepit, ordinans scilicet, vt qui euangelium annunciant, de euangelio viuant, instante vero mortis articulo, & contra illa gente pastorem & gregem persequente, congruam Christus regulam decreuit permittens vt tollant victui necessaria, donec sopita persecutorum insania tempus euangelizandi redeat, in hoc quoque nobis datur exemplum; vt iusta nonnunquam causa instante, quadam de nostri rigoris proposito posse sine culpa intermitti. Ex his verbis habetur euidenter, quod Christus illa, quae prius interdixerat, tunc solum concessit propter persecutionem instantem, concedendo necessaria tantum, & non alia, possessio autem auri & argenti & pecuniae quo ad dominium & proprietatem nunquam est necessaria, quin sine illa potest necessitas subleuari: ergo, &c. Potest enim quis tempore necessitatis alienam pecuniam etiam absque licentia, & multo fortius de licentia portare & tractare, & de ipsa rem emere necessariam, & absque eius dominio & proprietate: quia non semper emens rem de pecunia aliqua habet eius dominium & proprietatem, sicut enim potest quis tem vendere licite, & eius transferre dominium in alium, cum tamen non habet dominium & proprietatem.
