units.tr: First, by the authority of Christ, who says in Luke chapter twelve: "When I sent you out without purse, wallet and shoes, did you lack anything? And they said, Nothing. But he said to them: Now, if anyone has a purse, let him take it; likewise also a wallet; and let him who has no sword sell his tunic and buy a sword." From these words it is clearly gathered that Christ granted to the preachers, only for a time of necessity, certain things which he had forbidden before. For he said: "Now, that is, in this time of such great persecution, which is a time of necessity, let him who has a purse take it, likewise also a wallet, etc.," that is, let him take everything that is known to be suitable for such a time. Other things, which were not necessary for such a time, he by no means granted, but they remained forbidden as before. Bede agrees with this on the same words of Christ, saying: "The rule of living in a time of persecution is not the same as that which forms the disciples in a time of peace. When he sent the disciples to preach, he commanded them to take nothing on the way, ordaining, that is, that those who announce the gospel should live from the gospel. But when the hour of death approaches, and the people persecute shepherd and flock, Christ decreed a suitable rule, permitting them to take the things necessary for sustenance, until the madness of the persecutors subsides and the time for preaching the gospel returns. In this also an example is given to us: that when a just cause presses, some part of the strictness of our purpose may be set aside without fault." From these words it is clearly seen that Christ granted those things which he had previously forbidden only because of the impending persecution, granting necessities only and not other things. But the possession of gold, silver and money, as to ownership and property, is never necessary, since need can be relieved without it. Therefore, etc. For in a time of necessity a person may carry and handle another's money even without permission, and much more so with permission, and may buy a necessary thing with it without having its ownership and property. For one who buys a thing with some money does not always have the ownership and property of that money, just as one can lawfully sell a thing and transfer its ownership to another although one does not have ownership and property of it.

units.la: Ita potest quis in casu rem aliquam emere de pecunia, cuius non habet dominium & proprietatem. Christus igitur quantum ad omnia, quae prius interdixerat, solummodo relaxauit ista, quae pro tempore persecutionis necessaria erant, & ita constat, quod dictum praeceptum: Nolite possidere aurum, &c. non solum obligabat Apostolos pro omni tempore, quo ad hoc, quod non possidentes huiusmodi, quo ad dominium & proprietatem: sed etiam obligabat eos pro omni tempore extra tempus necessitatis quo ad hoc, quod non portarent pecuniam, & ita praedictum praeceptum non fuit temporale pro tempore viae praedictae solummodo.
units.tr: So, in a case, one may buy some thing with money of which one does not have ownership and property. Christ therefore, with regard to all the things he had previously forbidden, relaxed only those which were necessary for the time of persecution. And so it is clear that the said precept, "Do not possess gold," etc., bound the Apostles not only at all times, so that they should not possess such things as to ownership and property, but also bound them at all times outside the time of necessity, so that they should not carry money. Thus the said precept was not temporary, valid only for the time of the aforesaid journey.

units.la: Secundo dicunt isti impugnatores istum errare, cum imponit beato Augustino, quod dicat illud non fuisse praeceptum. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod Christus mittens Apostolos ad praedicandum, aliqua eis praecepit, & aliqua permisit, nonnulla vero praedixit. Illa enim per quae praedicatio eorum fieret magis credibilis, & per quae audientes magis prouocarentur ad credendum, praecepit Apostolis, vt Apostoli non solum auditores doctrinae instruerent, sed etiam exemplis allicerent, huiusmodi fuerunt illa, per quae debebant perfectum mundi contemptum ostendere, inter quae non minimum locum tenet nolle pecuniam, neque portare, neque quo ad dominium possidere, & ideo omnia quae ad abdicationem pecuniae pertinebant, sub praecepto cadebant. Quaedam vero Christus permisit Apostolis, illa scil. quae pro sustentatione eorum oportuna fuerunt, sicut ab auditoribus sumptus accipere: & illud non praecepit Christus Apostolis, nisi in casu, quando scilicet non possent aliunde necessaria vitae acquirere. Et de isto loquitur Augustinus, cum dicit, illud non fuisse eis praeceptum, sed permissum, quod expresse Augustinus manifestat, cum in libro de concordia Euangelistarum ait: cum secundum Matthaeum Dominus subiecerit: Dignus est enim operarius cibo suo, satis ostendit, cur eos possidere hoc, aut afferre noluerit: non quod necessaria non sint sustentationi huiusmodi vitae, sed quod sic eos mittebat, vt eis ista deberi determinaret ab his, quibus credentibus Euangelium praedicabant. Alioqui contra hoc praeceptum fecit Apostolus, qui victulum quotidianum de labore manuum suarum transfigebat, sed dedisse eis potestatem, in qua fore scirent ista sibi deberi. Ex quibus verbis ostenditur, quod recipere sumptus ab auditoribus non erat praeceptum Apostolis; quod etiam idem Augustinus de opere monachorum explicat manifeste dicens: Permisit enim Dominus, sed non iussit accipere necessaria a subditis, vt quisquis vellet, eo uteretur, quod sibi liceret ex Domini institutione, si quis uti nollet, contra iussum non faceret, sed de suo iure cederet. Potestas tamen est, non iussio Domini, accipere sumptus. Ex his verbis habetur aperte, quod accipere sumptus non fuit praeceptum.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents say that he errs in attributing to St Augustine the claim that this was not commanded. To make this clear, they say, it must be known that Christ, sending the Apostles to preach, commanded them some things, permitted some, and foretold some. For those things by which their preaching would become more credible, and by which hearers would be more provoked to believe, he commanded the Apostles, so that they should not only instruct the hearers in the doctrine but also draw them on by examples. Of this kind were those by which they were to show a perfect contempt for the world. Among these, not least place is held by not wishing to have money, nor to carry it, nor to possess it as to ownership. And therefore all things pertaining to the renunciation of money fell under the precept. Some things, however, Christ permitted to the Apostles, namely those fitting for their sustenance, such as receiving provisions from their hearers. Christ did not command this to the Apostles except in the case when they could not otherwise acquire the necessities of life. And it is of this that Augustine speaks when he says that it was not commanded to them but permitted. Augustine makes this expressly clear when, in the book On the Harmony of the Evangelists, he says: "When the Lord added, according to Matthew, 'For the labourer is worthy of his food,' he sufficiently showed why he was unwilling that they should possess or carry this. Not that these things are not necessary for the sustenance of such a life, but that he sent them in such a way that he determined these things to be owed to them by those to whom, believing, they preached the gospel." Otherwise, the Apostle Paul acted against this precept, since he earned his daily bread by the labour of his own hands; but he had been given the power by which they would know that these things were owed to them. From these words it is shown that receiving provisions from hearers was not a precept for the Apostles. Augustine also explains this clearly in On the Work of Monks, saying: "For the Lord permitted, but did not command, that necessities be received from subjects, so that whoever wished might use what was lawful for him by the Lord's institution. If anyone did not wish to use it, he would not act against a command, but would give up his right. Receiving provisions is a permission of the Lord, not a command." From these words it is plainly had that receiving provisions was not a precept.

units.la: Possidere tamen pecuniam fuit absolute prohibitum, sicut etiam tollere peram, & sacculum, fuit prohibitum: quorum vtrumque Gregorius concordans cum Augustino asserit manifeste, dicens homelia decimfeptima super Euangelia: Ecce autem qui peram & sacculum portare prohibuit, sumptus & alimenta ex ipsa praedicatione concedit. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod secundum Gregorium licet portare sacculum & peram fuerit prohibitum: & per consequens multo fortius possidere pecuniam erat prohibitum: tamen sumptus accipere non erat praeceptum, sed concessum, & ita patet aperte hic, quod dictum est prius, scil. quod Christus mittens discipulos ad praedicandum aliqua praecepit, & quaedam concessit, non praecepit: & ita sophistice de falsitate arguit Augustinum imponens ei, quod ipsum dixisse minime inuenitur.
units.tr: Yet to possess money was absolutely forbidden, just as carrying a wallet and a purse was forbidden. Gregory, agreeing with Augustine, clearly asserts both of these, saying in his seventeenth homily on the Gospels: "Behold, he who forbade carrying purse and wallet grants provisions and food from the preaching itself." From these words it is plain that, according to Gregory, carrying purse and wallet was forbidden, and consequently possessing money was forbidden much more strongly; yet receiving provisions was not commanded but permitted. So it is plainly shown here what was said before, namely that Christ, sending the disciples to preach, commanded some things and permitted some, and did not command others. And so these opponents argue sophistically against Augustine, charging him with having said what is by no means found in him.

units.la: Tertio isti impugnatores dicunt istum errare, cum asserit, quod praeceptum datum septuaginta duob. discipulis de sacculo & aliis non portandis extitit temporale, datum scilicet tantummodo pro tempore viae illius: quod ostendunt sic Discipuli septuag. duo, qui post Apostolos errant primi praedicatores euangelicae veritatis, perfectionem semel assumptam, quam eos seruare, tam pro aliis temporibus, quam pro tempore viae praedictae fuit vtile eis & aliis, minime dimiserunt: quia si dimisissent, apti regno Dei non fuissent, iuxta illud Saluatoris: Nemo mittens manum ad aratrum, &c. aptus est regno Dei, sed seruare illa aliis temporibus, quae Christus imposuit septuag. duob. discipulis, quando misit eos ad praedicandum, fuit vtile ipsis, & auditoribus eorundem: sicut ex superioribus colligitur euidenter, ergo praeceptum illud non fuit temporale solummodo pro illa via, sed etiam ipsos pro aliis temporibus, quibus praedicaturi erant, aptabat.
units.tr: Thirdly, these opponents say he errs when he asserts that the precept given to the seventy-two disciples, about not carrying a purse and not carrying other things, was temporary and given only for the time of that journey. They show it thus: the seventy-two disciples, who after the Apostles were the first preachers of the evangelical truth, did not at all give up the perfection once undertaken, which it was useful for them and for others to keep both at other times and during the time of the said journey. For if they had given it up, they would not have been fit for the kingdom of God, according to the saying of the Saviour: "No one who puts his hand to the plough... is fit for the kingdom of God." But to keep at other times those things which Christ imposed on the seventy-two disciples when he sent them to preach was useful to themselves and to their hearers, as is clearly gathered from what was said above. Therefore that precept was not temporary for that journey only, but also bound them for the other times in which they were to preach.

units.la: Quarto dicunt eum errare, cum dixit, patere ex dictis suis prioribus, quod aliqui de istis septuaginta duob. multa habuerunt. Hoc enim videtur manifestam falsitatem habere. Nam ipse probat solummodo de Ioseph ab Arimathia, Simone leproso, Lazaro, Maria Magdalena, Martha, & Dorca, quod habuerunt multa; sed nullus istorum fuit de illis 72. vel saltem non probat, quod aliquis illorum fuerit de ipsis, ergo non patet, quod aliquis de illis 72. habuit multa, postquam ad praedicandum fuit missus: nec de aliquo illorum in aliqua scriptura autentica potuit reperiri, quod multa habuit.
units.tr: Fourthly, they say he is wrong when he said, as is clear from his earlier statements, that some of those seventy-two had many possessions. For this seems to be plainly false. He proves only that Joseph of Arimathea, Simon the leper, Lazarus, Mary Magdalene, Martha and Dorcas had many possessions; but none of these was one of the seventy-two, and he does not prove that any of them was among those seventy-two. So it is not clear that any of the seventy-two had many possessions after he was sent to preach; nor can it be found in any authentic Scripture that any one of them had many possessions.

units.la: (Videtur pro illo tempore, quod aliqua fuerit eis habere interdicta:) Si dicat, videtur, dubitando, erratapertè. (Nolite possidere aurum, &c.) Hoc interdixit eis non solum habere aurum & argentum & pecuniam, quo ad proprietatem, sed etiam illa portare. Prius enim Christus, dum sermones faceret in monte, possessionem auri, argenti, & pecuniae, sicut aliarum rerum, quo ad proprietatem & dominium, interdixit: sed portare huiusmodi, tunc nullatenus interdixit. Possunt enim multi portare pecuniam, cuius non habent dominium & proprietatem, fuit autem rationabile non solum interdicere eis possessionem pecuniae, quo ad dominium & proprietatem: sed etiam portare pecuniam, ut per hoc Christus omnino auditoribus redderet ipsos non suspectos, quod propter divitias praedicarent, formam & regulam viuendi etiam operibus ostendendo (non peram in via) hic specialiter viam specificat, quia pera nisi in via necessaria non videtur (neque calciamenta) si interdixit eis calciamenta in via, quando magis indigent eis: multo magis in domo, quando minus indigerent ipsis (ne quid tollerent in via.) Ex hoc non sequitur, quod extra viam liceret eis tollere illa: quia argumentum a contrario sensu saepe fallit in Theologia.
units.tr: (It seems that for that time some things were forbidden them.) If he says, "it seems," doubting, he errs openly. (Possess no gold, etc.) This forbade them not only to have gold, silver and money as property, but also to carry them. For earlier, when Christ was preaching on the mount, he forbade possession of gold, silver and money, as of other things, as to ownership and dominion; but he did not at all forbid carrying such things at that time. For many can carry money of which they have no ownership or property. It was reasonable, then, not only to forbid them to possess money as to ownership and property, but also to forbid them to carry money, so that by this Christ would altogether show the hearers that the preachers were not suspected of preaching for the sake of riches, displaying the form and rule of living also by their works. (Not a bag on the way.) Here he specifies the way in particular, because a bag seems necessary only on a journey. (Nor shoes.) If he forbade them shoes on the way, when they most needed them, much more at home, when they would need them less (lest they take anything on the way). It does not follow from this that outside the journey it would be allowed them to take those things, for an argument from the contrary sense often fails in theology.

units.la: (Sed calciatos scandalis) Ex hoc patet, quod sandalia possunt calciamenta vocari: quia absque calciamentis nemo est calciatus, quare verba beati Iohannis Baptistae Matthei tertio, & Marci primo, & Iohannis primo, de calciamentis & de sandaliis possunt intelligi, quare ex illis verbis concludi non potest; quod Christus usus fuerit talibus calciamentis, quae communiter calciamenta vocantur. (Ex quibus verbis videtur, quod pro tempore vie praedicta tantum praedicta fuerunt eis interdicta.) Male & sophistice infert, quia non sequitur, pro via praedicta erant eis interdicta: ergo non erant eis pro alio tempore interdicta, quia ex affirmativa, negativa illa non sequitur: sicut nec ex affirmativa exponente potest exclusiva inferri. (Augustinus tamen, &c. falsum imponit Augustino, sicut ostensum est (in libro de concordia Evangelistarum) hoc ibi minime reperitur. (Illud) scilicet minime recipere sumptus. (Non fuit praeceptum, sicut probatur per exemplum de beato Paulo.) Non autem inuenitur, quod beatus Paulus portauerit vel possederit pecuniam, quo ad dominium seu proprietatem (quod illud praeceptum fuerit temporale, satis innuitur Lucae vigesimo secundo, vbi Dominus Apostolis dixit: quando misi vos sine sacculo & pera num quid defuit vobis?) Male arguit, quod illud praeceptum fuit temporale: quia Christus non dispensauit cum eis contra dictam praeceptum, nisi tempore necessitatis. Ex hoc autem non potest concludi, quod fuerit tempotale, quia tempore necessitatis multa licent multis: quae tamen simpliciter sunt eis prohibita. Patet exemplo, quod Christus dat de panibus propositionis: quia omnibus praeterquam sacerdotibus, erat simpliciter prohibitum comedere panes propositionis: & tamen tempore necessitatis extremae erat licitum comedere eos, sicut colligitur euidenter Matthei duodecimo, & Marci secundo, & Lucae sexto, (de illis certum est) de illis septuag. duob. non est certum, licet de aliis sit certum. (Multi ex discipulis) alii a 72. erant multa habentes, sicut Ioseph, & alii viri & mulieres, qui non erant de 72.
units.tr: (But shod with sandals.) From this it is clear that sandals can be called shoes, since no one is shod without shoes. So the words of the blessed John the Baptist in Matthew 3, Mark 1 and John 1 about shoes and sandals can be understood in this way, and nothing can be concluded from those words that Christ used such shoes as are commonly called shoes. (From these words it seems that those prohibitions were given only for the time of the aforesaid journey.) He inferes badly and sophistically: it does not follow that, because they were forbidden these things for the aforesaid journey, they were therefore not forbidden them for another time, since that negative does not follow from an affirmative, just as an exclusive proposition cannot be inferred from an affirmative exponent. (Augustine, however, etc. falsely imputes this to Augustine; as has been shown in the book on the harmony of the Evangelists, this is by no means found there.) (That is, that they were in no way to receive expenses.) (It was not a command, as is proved by the example of the blessed Paul.) Yet it is not found that the blessed Paul carried or possessed money as to ownership or property. (That this command was temporary is sufficiently indicated in Luke 22, where the Lord said to the Apostles: when I sent you without purse and bag, did you lack anything?) He argues badly that the command was temporary, since Christ did not dispense them from the said command except in a time of necessity. But from this it cannot be concluded that it was temporary, since in a time of necessity many things are permitted to many which are nevertheless simply forbidden to them. This is shown by the example of the bread of the Presence: all except the priests were simply forbidden to eat the bread of the Presence, and yet in a time of extreme necessity it was lawful to eat it, as is clearly gathered from Matthew 12, Mark 2 and Luke 6. (Concerning those it is certain; concerning those seventy-two it is not certain, though it is certain concerning others.) (Many of the disciples) other than the seventy-two had many possessions, like Joseph and other men and women who were not among the seventy-two.

units.la: CAP. CIII.
units.tr: CHAP. CIII.

units.la: Tamen consideremus tempus post reuersionem, tunc videtur quod eis habere licuerit praemissa, saltem in common, habuerunt enim Apostoli postquam reuersi fuerunt de praedicatione, panes & pisces, vt patet in miraculum & piscium, quae facta fuerunt, postquam de praedicatione ad illum redierunt, vt patet Marci sexto, vbi de Apostolis postquam a praedicatione redierant, dicitur sic: Et conuenientes Apostoli ad illum renunciauerunt illi omnia quae egerant & docuerant, scilicet in praedicatione. Ecce quod de praedicatione, ad quam missi fuerant, reuersi fuerant, & rationem Domino reddiderant de ea, in eodem capitulo sequitur miraculum quinque panum, & duorum piscium. Vbi Apostoli, cum Dominus dixisset eis: quod darent turbae manducare, dixerunt; euntes emamus ducentos panes: & dabimus illis manducare. Lucas vero nono dicitur sic: Et reuersi Apostoli narrauerunt illi quaecunque fecerant, & post sequitur in eodem capitulo miraculum praedictum quinque panum, vbi dicitur: quod cum Dominus Apostolis dixisset, vos date illis manducare: ille dixit; non sunt nobis plus quam quinque panes, & duo pisces, nisi forte nos eamus & emamus in omnem hanc turbam escas. Ex quibus patet, quod postquam reuersi sunt a praedicatione, Apostoli habuerunt & panes & pisces & pecuniam, de quatanta turbe, quanta erat, poterant emere cibos. Item quod postquam redierunt de praedicatione, habuerunt pecuniam, patet. Legitur enim Iohan. quart. quod Iesu sedente super fontem Iacob, discipuli eius abierunt in ciuitatem, vt cibos emerent. Sic patet, quod pecuniam habebant, cum emptio mediante pecunia fiat, Deuteron. primo capitulo, & tamen tum temporis Apostoli de praedicatione fuerant (vt videtur) reuersi, cum in capitulo praeallegato sic discipulis dixerit: Ego misi vos metere, quod non laborastis. Alii laborauerunt: & vos labores eorum introistis. Supposuit quoque evidenter scriptura Euangelica, ipsos post reuersionem predictam saculos, in quibus portabatur pecunia, & plures tunicas habuisse. Legitur enim Luca vigesimo secundo. Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum Apostoli dixisse: Qui habet sacculum, tollat: similiter & peram: qui non habet gladium, vendat tunicam suam, & emat gladium. Et sequitur, quod Apostoli dixerunt ei: Domine ecce duo gladii hic. Ex quo patet, quod duos gladios habebant. Petrus quoq; legitur Iohan. decim. octau. gladium habuisse. Vbi dicitur, quod Simon Petrus habens gladium eduxit eum, & percussit Pontificis seruum: cui Dominus dixit: Mitte gladium tuum in vaginam tuam.
units.tr: Yet let us consider the time after their return. At that point it seems that they could have had the things mentioned above, at least in common. For after the Apostles had returned from preaching, they had bread and fish, as is clear from the miracle of the loaves and fishes, which was performed after they had come back to him from preaching. Mark 6 shows this: "And the Apostles gathered together to him, and told him all that they had done and taught," namely in their preaching. Here we see that they had returned from the preaching to which they had been sent, and had given the Lord an account of it. In the same chapter there follows the miracle of the five loaves and two fishes. There, when the Lord had said to them that they should give the crowd something to eat, they said: "Let us go and buy two hundred loaves, and we will give them something to eat." Luke 9 says this: "And the Apostles, when they returned, told him all that they had done." Afterwards, in the same chapter, comes the aforesaid miracle of the five loaves, where it is said that when the Lord told the Apostles, "You give them something to eat," they replied: "We have no more than five loaves and two fishes, unless perhaps we go and buy food for all this crowd." From these passages it is clear that, after they had returned from preaching, the Apostles had bread, fish and money, so that from so great a crowd as there was they could buy food. Likewise, that after they had returned from preaching they had money is also plain. For we read in John 4 that while Jesus sat by Jacob's well, his disciples went away into the city to buy food. So it is clear that they had money, since buying is done by means of money (Deut. 1), and yet at that time the Apostles had (as it seems) returned from preaching, since in the chapter cited above he said to the disciples: "I sent you to reap, where you did not labour; others laboured, and you have entered into their labours." Moreover, the Gospel Scripture clearly implies that after the aforesaid return they had purses in which money was carried, and several tunics. For we read in Luke 22 that the Apostles said to our Lord Jesus Christ: "He who has a purse, let him take it, and likewise a bag; and he who has no sword, let him sell his tunic and buy a sword." And there follows, that the Apostles said to him: "Lord, behold, here are two swords." From this it is clear that they had two swords. Peter too is read in John 18 to have had a sword. There it is said that Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the servant of the High Priest, and the Lord said to him: "Put your sword into its sheath."

units.la: Postquam responsum est ad quæstionem, qua quæritur, an Apostoli aliquarum rerum habuerunt dominium, iuxta primum & secundum membrum distinctionis secundæ positæ supra capitulo nonagesimo sexto. Hic respondetur ad eandem, iuxta tertium membrum distinctionis eiusdem. Probatur enim hic, quod Apostolis, postquam fuerunt de prædicatione reuersi, licuit habere omnia, quæ eis pro tempore prædicationis præcedentis fuerant interdicta, quod ille vnica ratione tali probare videtur. Apostoli de facto postquam fuerunt de prædicatione reuersi habuerunt multa, quæ eis fuerant antea interdicta, ergo licuit eis habere omnia, quæ eis prius fuerant interdicta. Consequentia patet: quia Apostoli nulla habuerunt illicite, nec est ratio, quod licuerit eis habere plus illa, quam illa, ergo omnia licuit eis habere, quæ prius ipsis fuerant interdicta. Antecedens probat iste per multa exempla. Primo, quia postquam fuerunt de prædicatione reuersi, habuerunt panes, pisces & pecuniam ad emendos cibos pro magna turba hominum, secundo ibi: Item quod postquam, &c. specialiter probat, quod habuerunt pecuniam. Tertio ibi; supposit quod probat quod habuerunt sacculos pro pecunia deportanda & plures tunicas. Quarto ibi, sequitur quod Apostoli, ostendit quod habuerunt gladios.
units.tr: Having answered the question, whether the Apostles had ownership of certain things, according to the first and second members of the second distinction set out above in chapter 96, here the same question is answered according to the third member of that distinction. For it is proved here that, after the Apostles had returned from preaching, they were allowed to have all those things which had been forbidden them during the earlier time of preaching. This one argument seems to prove it: the Apostles in fact, after they had returned from preaching, had many things which had been forbidden them before; therefore they were allowed to have all the things which had previously been forbidden them. The consequence is plain, since the Apostles had nothing unlawfully, and there is no reason why it should have been lawful for them to have one thing rather than another; therefore they were allowed to have all the things which had previously been forbidden them. The antecedent he proves by many examples. First, because after they had returned from preaching they had bread, fish and money to buy food for a great crowd of people. Second, at the words "Likewise, that after..." he proves specifically that they had money. Third, at the words "it is supposed that" he proves that they had purses for carrying money, and several tunics. Fourth, at the words "it follows that the Apostles" he shows that they had swords.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt istum aperte errare, cum asserit, quod Apostoli post reuersionem à prædicatione habuerunt panes, pisces & pecuniam & tunicas & gladios, quo ad dominium & proprietatem, quod enim intelligat hic de modo habendi prædicta, quo ad dominium & proprietatem, patet: quia aliter ad propositam quæstionem de Apostolis iuxta tertium modum distinctionis suæ secundæ minime responderet: cum quæstio supradicta explicite quærat de modo habendi res temporales, quo ad dominium & proprietatem. De tali autem modo habendi res loquendo error est differentiæ: quod Apostoli habuerunt res quascunque postquam à prædicatione reuersi fuerunt, sicut multipliciter in capitulo precedenti, & in aliis capitulis quam pluribus probatum exstitit, & ideo isti circa istam pattem solummodo per literam discurrendo ad instantias respondere conantur, quas in suæ assertionis fulcimentum adducit.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he plainly errs when he asserts that the Apostles, after their return from preaching, had bread, fish, money, tunics and swords, as regards ownership and property. That he means here the manner of having these things, as regards ownership and property, is clear: otherwise he would not answer the question proposed about the Apostles according to the third manner of his second distinction, since the question stated above expressly asks about the manner of having temporal goods, as regards ownership and property. But speaking of this manner of having goods, the error is manifest: the Apostles had all sorts of things after they returned from preaching, as has been proved many times over in the preceding chapter and in many other chapters. And so these men, in dealing with this part only by the letter, try to answer the objections which he brings forward in support of his assertion.

units.la: (Si autem consideremus tempus post reuersionem: tunc videtur quod eis habere licuerit premissa saltem in communi.) Intelligendum est, quod intendit ipsis licuisse habere premissa, & quæcunque alia quo ad dominium & proprietatem, & non solum in communi, sed etiam in speciali: quia si non licuisset eis habere premissa & quæcunq; alia tam in speciali, quam etiam in communi, alia lex viuendi suisset ipsorum Apostolorum & quorundam aliorum discipulorum, quia quibusdam aliis discipulis licuit habere premissa & quæcunque alia tam in speciali quam etiam in communi. Ipse autem dicit, quod Apostoli non habuerunt aliam legem viuendi, quam quicunque alii discipuli: ergo &c. (habuerunt enim Apostoli postquam reuersi fuerunt de prædicatione panes & pisces) quo ad licitam potestatem vtendi & aliqualem dispensationem de concedentium voluntate. Et si quæratur, cuius fuerunt illi panes, quo ad dominium & proprietatem? potest dici, quod fuerunt mulierum, quæ, vt legitur Luca octauo, de facultatibus suis ministrabant eis, vel poterant esse aliorum sequentium Christum, vnde & Andreas, vt legitur Iohan. sext. vbi recitatur miraculum panum & piscium, dixit: Est puer vnus hic, qui habet quinque panes hordeaceos & duos pisces: & ita illi panes & pisces non erant Apostolorum quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Vnde dicunt quidam istorum impugnatorum, esse sciendum quod quædam res, quibus Christus & Apostoli vtebantur, pertinebant ad dominium & proprietatem offerentium, sicut ea quæ in cibo & potu consistunt, propter quod dicit Hieronymus quod Christus cibo vescebatur alieno.
units.tr: (If, however, we consider the time after their return, then it seems that they could have had the things mentioned above, at least in common.) It must be understood that he means that they were allowed to have the things mentioned above, and whatever else, as regards ownership and property, and not only in common but also in particular. For if it had not been lawful for them to have the things mentioned above, and whatever else, in particular as well as in common, then the Apostles and certain other disciples would have lived under a different rule, since some other disciples were allowed to have the things mentioned above and whatever else, both in particular and in common. He himself says that the Apostles did not have a different rule of living from any other disciples; therefore etc. (For the Apostles, after they had returned from preaching, had bread and fish) as regards the lawful power of using them, and some dispensation by the will of those who granted them. And if it is asked whose those loaves were, as regards ownership and property, it can be said that they belonged to women who, as we read in Luke 8, ministered to them from their substance, or they could have belonged to others who followed Christ. Hence Andrew too, as we read in John 6, where the miracle of the loaves and fishes is recited, said: "There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fishes." So those loaves and fishes were not the Apostles' as regards ownership and property. Hence some of these opponents say that it must be understood that certain things which Christ and the Apostles used belonged to the ownership of those who offered them, such as things consisting in food and drink; for which reason Jerome says that Christ ate food that belonged to another.

units.la: Sicut autem quædam in Veteri Testamento, quæ ad dominium specialiter pertinebant, sicut templum, arca, & quædam alia diuinis vsibus deputata, quæ non ad hominis, sed ad Dei dominium pertinebant, & quodammodo aliter quam aliæ res: quia aliæ res, quæ in nullius bonis erant, occupanti concedebantur, templum autem & quædam alia non concedebantur occupanti, quamuis in nullius hominis bonis essent, & ideo quodammodo specialiter ad Dei dominium pertinebant: sicut dicunt quidam de vestimentis Christi & Apostolorum. Alii dicunt quod vestimenta Christi & Apostolorum pertinebant ad dominium communitatis seu vniuersitatis fidelium (darent turba manducare) hic verbum dandi accipitur pro verbo ministrandi vel tradendi, non pro transferre dominium. (Euntes emamus ducentos panes.) Dicunt quod Apostoli tunc erant in casu necessitatis, quia erant in deserto, ideo pro vtilitate tantæ turbæ fuisset eis licitum emere panes ad reficiendum turbas: & talis emptio per ipsos poterat fieri: & absque hoc, quod portarent pecuniam: quia alius poterat portare eam, & absque hoc quod pecunia esset eorum quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, sicut certa docet experientia.
units.tr: But just as certain things in the Old Testament belonged specially to ownership, such as the temple, the ark, and certain other things set apart for divine uses, which belonged not to the ownership of man but of God, and in a way different from other things: for other things, which were the goods of no one, were granted to whoever took them, but the temple and certain other things were not granted to whoever took them, although they were the goods of no man, and so in a way they belonged specially to God's ownership. So some say of the garments of Christ and the Apostles. Others say that the garments of Christ and the Apostles belonged to the ownership of the community or the whole body of the faithful. (They should give the crowd something to eat) Here the word "give" is taken to mean "minister" or "hand over", not "transfer ownership". (Let us go and buy two hundred loaves.) They say that the Apostles were then in a case of necessity, because they were in the desert; therefore, for the benefit of so great a crowd, it would have been lawful for them to buy bread to refresh the people, and such a purchase could be made by them, even without their carrying money, since another could carry it, and without the money being theirs as regards ownership or property, as certain experience teaches.

units.la: Sed dicit ille forte, quare non ordinauerunt ipsi, quod alii irent ad emendum panes, ex quo non debebant habere pecuniam nec portare, nec quo ad dominium possidere. Ad hoc facile respondetur, quod ipsi Apostoli voluerunt ire & emere panes de pecunia mulierum ministrantium Christo de facultatibus suis, vel aliorum sequentium Christum, qui pati erant ad voluntatem Christi & aliorum Apostolorum pecuniam suam expendere. (Dabimus illi manducare) hic, sit prius, dare non accipitur pro transferre dominium, sed pro ministrare cibum.) Non sunt plus quam quinque panes & duo pisces) quo ad potestatem licitam dispensandi de habentium quo ad dominium voluntatem, (& emamus) de pecunia aliquorum sequentium Christum, qui libenter ad voluntatem nostram suam expendunt pecuniam) habuerunt panes & pisces, & pecuniam, de quatanta turba, &c.
units.tr: But perhaps someone will say: why did the Apostles themselves not arrange for others to go and buy bread, since they ought not to have money, nor carry it, nor possess it as their own? To this it is easily answered that the Apostles themselves wished to go and buy bread with the money of the women who ministered to Christ from their own resources, or of others who followed Christ, who were willing to spend their money at the will of Christ and of the other Apostles. (Give them to eat): here, at first sight, give is not taken to mean transferring ownership, but to mean supplying food. (We have here but five loaves and two fishes): with respect to the lawful power of dispensing what is held, with the consent of the owners as to ownership, (and let us buy) with the money of certain followers of Christ, who gladly spend their money at our will. (They had loaves and fishes and money, for so great a multitude), etc.

units.la: Verum est, quod habuerunt quo ad licitam potestatem vtendi panibus & piscibus: & etiam quo ad aliqualem potestatem disponendi etiam habuerunt pecuniam, quo ad potestatem recurrendi ad ipsam durante Domini voluntate pro suis & pauperum indigentiis releuandis: quemadmodum secundum modum loquendi aliquorum Fratres Minores dicuntur habere pecuniam, quae deposita est pro eorum necessitatibus subleuandis; cuius tamen pecuniae non habent dominium seu proprietatem. (Postquam redierunt de praedicatione, habuerunt pecuniam) modo praedicto: quia pro eorum & aliorum pauperum necessitatibus subleuandis erat pecunia aliqua deposita: quam tamen Apostoli non portabant, nec eius dominium habuerunt. (Abierunt in ciuitatem vt cibos emerent) hoc fuit eis licitam: quia tunc erant in casu necessitatis, cum essent inter Samaritanos, qui Iudaeos ad hospitium minime suscipiebant. Poterant autem emere cibos de pecunia aliorum deposita, pro eorum & pauperum necessitatibus, licet eiusdem pecuniae non haberent dominium: & quamuis etiam eandem pecuniam non portarent, cum saepe videamus, quod vnus facit contractum emptionis, & alius tradit pecuniam. (Pecuniam habebant) sicut Fratres Minores dicuntur nunc a nonnullis habere pecuniam, quae deposita est pro eorum indigentiis subleuandis, quae tamen est alterius vel aliorum quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, (cum emptio mediante pecunia fiat, non tamen semper pecunia est ementis quo ad dominium seu proprietatem.
units.tr: It is true that they had, with respect to a lawful power of using the loaves and fishes, and also, to some extent, a power of disposing of money, with respect to the power of drawing upon it, while the Lord willed, for relieving their own and the poor's needs; just as, in the manner of speaking of some Friars Minor, they are said to have money which has been deposited for relieving their needs, yet they do not have dominion or ownership of that money. (After they returned from preaching, they had money): in the aforesaid manner, because some money had been deposited for relieving their own and other poor people's needs; yet the Apostles did not carry it, nor did they hold its ownership. (They went away into the city to buy food): this was lawful for them, because they were then in a case of necessity, since they were among the Samaritans, who by no means received Jews into their homes. Moreover, they could buy food with money deposited by others for their own and the poor's needs, although they did not have ownership of that same money; and although they did not carry the same money, since we often see that one makes the contract of purchase and another hands over the money. (They had money): just as the Friars Minor are now said by some to have money, which has been deposited for relieving their needs, which however belongs to another or others as to ownership or property, (since a purchase is made by means of money, yet the money is not always the buyer's as to ownership or property.)

units.la: Nam saepe famulus emit res pro domino suo, ipso vel alio tradente pecuniam domini sui. (Sacculos in quibus portabatur pecunia) licet habuissent sacculos, in quibus portabatur pecunia, non tamen habuissent nec sacculos nec pecuniam, quo ad dominium seu proprietatem: nec tamen legitur saltem extra tempus necessitatis, quod habuerint sacculos tales (& plures tunicas) pro necessitate poterant plures tunicas habere. (Qui habet sacculum) Hic videtur Christus supponere, quod aliquis eorum habuit sacculum, quod de Iuda potest concedi, cum quo forte Christus dispensauit ad consulendum cupiditati eius. (Tollat similiter & petam) hoc fuit dispensatiue dictum pro tempore illo, teste Chrysostomo, qui ibidem ait: Relaxauit prioris legis rigorem ne grauis & intolerabilis fieret eis vita, & ita tunc Christus relaxauit prioris legis rigorem, ergo vsque ad illud tempus durauit lex praedicta: quod iste negat, (vendat tunicam suam & emat gladium.) Similiter intelligi debet ad literam, quod dispensatiue pro illo tempore dicebatur. (Ecce duo gladii hic) non dixerunt, habemus duos gladios quo ad dominium & proprietatem (duos gladios habebant) potest concedi de aliquo modo habendi; non de modo habendi quo ad dominium seu proprietatem. (Simon Petrus habens gladium) non quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, sed quo ad vsum pro tempore illo, (gladium tuum) quo ad vsum, non quo ad dominium.
units.tr: For often a servant buys things for his master, either the master himself or another handing over his master's money. (Purses in which money was carried): although they had purses in which money was carried, they had neither purses nor money as to ownership or property; nor is it read, at least outside a time of necessity, that they had such purses (and more tunics): for in necessity they could have more tunics. (He who has a purse): here Christ seems to suppose that one of them had a purse, which can be conceded of Judas, with whom Christ perhaps dealt so as to provide for his covetousness. (Likewise let him take it, and I will ask): this was said by way of dispensation for that time, as witnessed by Chrysostom, who says in the same place: He relaxed the rigour of the former law, lest life become heavy and intolerable for them; and so then Christ relaxed the rigour of the former law; therefore the aforesaid law lasted until that time, which he denies. (Let him sell his tunic and buy a sword): likewise it must be understood literally, that it was said by way of dispensation for that time. (Behold, here are two swords): they did not say, "We have two swords" as to ownership and property. (They had two swords): this can be conceded as to some manner of having; not as to the manner of having with respect to ownership or property. (Simon Peter, having a sword): not as to ownership or property, but as to use for that time, (your sword): as to use, not as to ownership.

units.la: Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod secundum istum modum respondendi nunquam posset probari, quod res esset alicuius quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, per hoc quod dicitur esse ipsius vel ipse habere eam, vel per quemcunque alium modum loquendi, nisi vocaliter nomen proprietatis vel dominii exprimatur: quod videtur absurdum.
units.tr: But perhaps someone will say that, according to this manner of answering, it could never be proved that a thing belongs to anyone as to ownership or property, from its being said to be his or his having it, or by any other manner of speaking, unless the name of property or ownership is expressed aloud; which seems absurd.

units.la: Ad hoc dicunt isti, quod ex locutionibus multiplicibus seu ambiguis nude sumptis nunquam potest concludi determinatus sensus: sed quando tales locutiones inueniuntur in scripturis, ex locis aliis scripturarum oportet sensum extrahere veritatis, & ideo quando inuenitur in scripturis diuinis, quod talis res est talis, vel quod talis habuit talem rem, vel aliqua huiusmodi locutio ambigua reperitur, ex aliis locis scripturae diuinae oportet elicere, sub quo sensu debet intelligi, sic est in proposito: quod quia ex diuersis auctoritatibus scripturarum colligitur, quod Apostoli postquam fuerunt ad Apostolatum assumpti nullius rei proprietatem & dominium habuerunt: ideo omnes locutiones, quibus asseritur Apostolos postea res aliquas habuisse, de alio modo habendi debent intelligi.
units.tr: To this they reply that from multiple or ambiguous expressions taken bare, a determinate sense can never be concluded; but when such expressions are found in the Scriptures, the sense of the truth must be drawn from other passages of Scripture; and therefore, when it is found in the divine Scriptures that such a thing is such, or that someone had such a thing, or some ambiguous expression of this kind occurs, it must be gathered from other passages of divine Scripture in what sense it is to be understood. So it is in the present case: since it is gathered from various authorities of Scripture that the Apostles, after they were taken up into the apostleship, held no ownership or dominion over any thing, therefore all the expressions by which it is asserted that the Apostles afterwards had certain things must be understood of another manner of having.

units.la: CAP. CIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER 104.

units.la: SI autem quaeratur de tempore post mortem Christi, videtur adhuc distinguendum inter tempus ante missionem Spiritus sancti & post missionem ipsius. Si quaeratur de tempore ante missionem Spiritus sancti, non legitur quod quo ad promissa circa eos aliquid fuerit immutatum, sed quod iuxta praeceptum Domini nostri dicentis Lucae vlt. Vos autem sedete in ciuitate quousque induamini virtute ex alto: expectauerunt in ciuitate aduentum Spiritus sancti.
units.tr: But if one asks about the time after the death of Christ, it still seems necessary to distinguish between the time before the sending of the Holy Spirit and the time after his sending. If one asks about the time before the sending of the Holy Spirit, it is not read that anything was changed with regard to the promises concerning them, but rather that, in accordance with the command of our Lord, who says in the last chapter of Luke: "But you, sit in the city until you are clothed with power from on high," they waited in the city for the coming of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Postquam ille impugnatus prosecutus est, secundam distinctionem positam supra capitulo vnagesimo sexto, quae comprehendebat primum membrum primae distinctionis: Hic prosequitur secunsecundum membrum eiusdem distinctionis primæ, ipsum primo distinguens, scilicet in tempus ante Spiritus sancti missionem, & in tempus post missionem Spiritus sancti. Secundo ibi; si quaeratur, prosequitur primum membrum illius distinctionis, dicens, quod pro illo tempore nihil fuit quantum ad temporalia circa Apostolos immutatum. Tertio in parte immediate sequenti ibi: Si autem quaeratur, prosequitur secundum membrum distinctionis hic positæ.{5}
units.tr: After he had finished attacking that point, he went on to the second distinction set down above in chapter 26, which contained the first member of the first distinction. Here he pursues the second member of that same first distinction, first dividing it, namely into the time before the sending of the Holy Spirit and the time after the sending of the Holy Spirit. Second, at si quaeratur, he pursues the first member of that distinction, saying that for that time nothing was changed as regards temporal things concerning the Apostles. Third, in the part immediately following, at Si autem quaeratur, he pursues the second member of the distinction set out here.{5}

units.la: Circa istam partem isti impugnatores nihil reputant improbandum, nisi inquantum innuit præmissa in aliis capitulis præcedentibus esse tenenda: & simul cum hoc asserit, quod nihil fuerit immutatum circa eos, quo ad temporalia habenda vel non habenda, quod sub uno intellectu non videtur omnino certum, si enim intelligat, quod eodem modo se per omnia habuerunt ad temporalia toto tempore ante missionem Spiritus sancti, quo se habuerunt tempore passionis Christi{10}: non videtur esse manifestum. Nam sicut tempus pacis post passionem rediit, ita cessare videtur dispensatio, quæ facta fuit tempore passionis, si autem intelligat, quod nihil fuit immutatum circa eos quo ad temporalia, quando eodem modo se haberent quo ad temporalia, sicut se habuerant tempore passionis vel tempore præcedenti, isti ipsum non reputant arguendum, nisi cointelligendo quod licuit eis temporalia, quo ad dominium & proprietatem habere.{15}
units.tr: In regard to this part, these opponents find nothing to object to, except insofar as it implies that the things set out in the preceding chapters are to be held. At the same time, it asserts that nothing was changed for them as regards having or not having temporal goods. This does not seem entirely certain under one interpretation. If he means that they were in every respect in the same condition regarding temporal goods throughout the whole time before the sending of the Holy Spirit as they were at the time of Christ's passion, that does not seem clear. For just as the time of peace returned after the passion, so the dispensation that was in force at the time of the passion seems to have ceased. But if he means that nothing was changed for them as regards temporal things, since they were in the same condition regarding temporal things as they had been at the time of the passion or in the period before it, these opponents do not think this needs to be disputed, except on the understanding that they were permitted to have temporal goods as regards ownership and property.{15}

units.la: (Non legitur quod quo ad præmissa circa eos aliquid fuerit immutatum) hoc potest habere duplicem intellectum, sicut dictum est,
units.tr: (It is not read that anything was changed in the promises made to them) This can have a double meaning, as has been said,

units.la: CAP. CV.
units.tr: CHAPTER CV.

units.la: SI autem quaeratur de tempore post missionem Spiritus sancti, videtur adhuc distinguendum inter illos, qui ex Iudaeis conversi fuerunt in primitiva ecclesia Hierosolymitana, & inter gentiles. Quo ad conversos ex Iudaeis videtur, quod Apostoli & discipuli Christi ex una parte, & illi qui postea ad prædicationem Petri & miracula fuerunt conversi, omnia quæ habebant sibi invicem communicauerunt: ita quod nullus ipsorum proprium sibi retinuerit, sed communia fuerunt effecta, & intelligo quod quo ad dominium illa fuerunt communicata, ut probatur Act. 2. & Actuum 4. ut superius est ostensum.
units.tr: If we ask about the time after the sending of the Holy Spirit, we still seem to need to distinguish between those who were converted from among the Jews in the primitive church at Jerusalem and the Gentiles. As for the converts from the Jews, it seems that the Apostles and disciples of Christ on the one hand, and those who were converted afterwards through Peter's preaching and the miracles, shared with one another all that they had, so that none of them kept anything as his own, but everything became common. I understand that, as to ownership, these things were shared, as is proved in Acts 2 and Acts 4, as was shown above.

units.la: Hic prosequitur secundum membrum prædictæ diuisionis, & diuiditur in duas partes: quia primo ostendit, quod Apostoli & quidam alii post missionem Spiritus sancti habebant omnia communia quo ad dominium. Secundo ostendit, quod gentiles post conversionem non habebant omnia communia, secunda ibi, quantum autem ad conversos. Prima diuiditur in duas: quia primo ponit suam assertionem: secundo pertractat assertionem contrariam appellantis in parte immediate sequenti: Et quia illa. Primo ergo distinguit inter Iudaeos conversos ex Iudaeis & inter gentiles, secundo ibi, Quo ad conversos, dicit quod omnia fuerunt communia, quo ad dominium Iudaeis conversis & Apostolis & aliis discipulis.{30}
units.tr: Here he takes up the second member of the aforesaid division, and it is divided into two parts. For first he shows that the Apostles and certain others, after the sending of the Holy Spirit, had all things in common as to ownership. Secondly, he shows that the Gentiles after their conversion did not have all things in common, the second part beginning at as to the converts. The first part is divided into two: for first he states his own assertion, and secondly he treats the opposing assertion of the objector in the part immediately following: And because that. First, then, he distinguishes between Jewish converts from among the Jews and the Gentiles; secondly, at As to the converts, he says that all things were common as to ownership for the Jewish converts, the Apostles and the other disciples.

units.la: Dicunt isti impugnatores, quod de ista materia tractatum est sup. c. 4. & 5. & 6. & 7. & 9. ideo hic amplius non insistunt: discurrunt tamen per literam.{35}
units.tr: These opponents say that this matter was treated above in chapters 4, 5, 6, 7 and 9, and therefore they do not dwell on it further here, but they run through the text.

units.la: (Apostoli & discipuli Christi ex parte una, & illi, qui postea ad prædicationem Petri, & miracula fuerunt conversi, omnia, quæ habebant sibi invicem communicauerunt) Hoc potest concedi, quantum ad aliquem modum communicandi, ut per omnia: scilicet secundum ordinationem superiorum indigentiis omnium succurreretur (Ita quod nullus ipsorum proprium sibi retinuerit) ista negativa est absolute concedenda, (& intelligo quod quo ad dominium illa fuerunt communicata) hoc dicunt isti omnino esse falsum de dominio pleno & libero (ut probatur Actuum secundo & quarto.) Istud per dictum istius supra capitulo octuagesimo octavo facile posset repelli, quia Actuum secundo & quarto nulla fit mentio, imo etiam de iure vtendi seu consumendi, vtendi, donandi, & ex ipsis rebus alia acquirendi, non fit mentio in capitulis supradictis, & ita per ista capitula Actuum Apostolorum non probatur dictum istius, nisi sophistice.{40}
units.tr: (The Apostles and disciples of Christ on the one hand, and those who were afterwards converted through Peter's preaching and the miracles, shared with one another all that they had.) This may be granted as to a certain manner of sharing, namely that, by the arrangement of the superiors, the needs of all were supplied. (So that none of them kept anything as his own.) This negative statement is to be granted absolutely. (And I understand that as to ownership these things were shared.) The opponents say this is wholly false as to full and free ownership. (As is proved in Acts 2 and Acts 4.) This could easily be refuted by what was said above in chapter 88, for Acts 2 and 4 make no mention of the right of use or consumption, of use, of giving away, or of acquiring other things from those goods; nor is any such mention made in the chapters cited. So the assertion of this man is not proved by these chapters of the Acts of the Apostles, except by sophistry.

units.la: CAP. CVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER 106.

units.la: ET quia ille hæreticus dicit, quod ista quæstio intelligitur de turba discipulorum, inter quos erant omnia communia, quæ habebant, non de Apostolis, qui nihil habebant in temporalibus nec in communi, nec in proprio: nisi tantum in rebus vsu consumptibilibus simplicem vsum facti. Dicimus quod hoc dicendo Apostolos à credentium numero euidenter excludit. Dicitur enim Actuum secundo, quod omnes, qui credebant, erant pariter & habebant communia omnia. Si ergo omnibus credentibus erant omnia communia, sequitur quod si Apostoli non erant communia, quod credentes non erant; quod est falsum, imo sicut ipsi inter credentes principaliores erant, sic, eis omnia communia principaliter existebant. Unde sicut principalioribus pecunia agrorum & domorum venditorum ante pedes Apostolorum ponebantur, ut legitur Actuum quarto. & hoc expresse probatur per epistolam Clementis recitatam pro parte duodecim. quæstion. prim. capitul. Dilectissimis, in qua beatus Clemens scribens condiscipulis suis Hierosolymis habitantibus cum beato Iacobo coepiscopo suo, sic dicit: Apostoli eorumque discipuli una nobiscum & vobiscum communem vitam duxerunt. Ut enim bene nostis, erat multitudinis eorum cor unum & anima una, nec quisquam eorum aut nostrum de his, quæ possidebat aliquid suum esse dicebat, sed omnia nobis erant communia. Vbi satis clare monstratur, quod Apostoli, & eorum discipuli illa quæ habebant, communicaue-runt{50}{55}{60} tunt Iudeis conuersis Hierosolymis: & econtra. Vnde Hieronymus etiam talem fuisse ecclesiam credentium primo in Christum, qualem nunc monachi etiam imitantur & cupiunt, vt nil cuiquam sit proprium: nullus inter eos dines, nullus pauper, patrimonium diuidatur: orationi vacetur & psalmis: doctrinae quoque & continentiae insistatur. Lucas manifeste refert, cum dicit, quotquot erant possessores agrorum aut domorum &c. Expresse quoque innuit & supponit, quod ante istam communionem habere poterant Apostoli & discipuli eorum aliqua in proprio seu communi.
units.tr: And because that heretic says that this question is to be understood of the crowd of disciples, among whom all their possessions were held in common, and not of the Apostles, who had nothing in temporal goods, either in common or as their own, except only the simple use in fact of consumable things: we reply that by saying this he plainly excludes the Apostles from the number of believers. For it is said in Acts 2 that all who believed were together and had all things in common. If therefore all things were common to all believers, it follows that if the Apostles did not have things in common, neither did the believers; which is false. Indeed, just as they were the principal men among the believers, so all things were principally common to them. Hence, just as the money from sold fields and houses was laid at the feet of the Apostles, as is read in Acts 4, principally for the chief men; and this is expressly proved by the letter of Clement quoted in Dist. 12, quaest. 1, cap. Dilectissimis, in which the blessed Clement, writing to his fellow disciples living in Jerusalem with the blessed James, their co-bishop, says: the Apostles and their disciples led a common life with us and with you. For, as you well know, the heart and soul of them all was one, and none of them, or of us, said that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to us. Here it is shown quite clearly that the Apostles and their disciples shared what they had with the Jewish converts at Jerusalem, and conversely. Hence Jerome also says that the church of believers in Christ was at first of such a kind as monks now imitate and desire: that nothing should belong to anyone, no one among them was rich, no one poor, the patrimony was divided, time was given to prayer and the psalms, and they devoted themselves to teaching and self-restraint. Luke also reports this plainly when he says, as many as were owners of fields or houses, etc. He also clearly implies and presupposes that before this community the Apostles and their disciples could have some things as private or common property.

units.la: Hic pertractat assertionem contrariam assertioni appellantis, dicentis secundum istum: quod illa non erant Apostolis communia. Et primo recitat eam. Secundo ipsam reprobare conatur ibi: Dicimus quod hoc dicendo. Reprobat autem primo ducendo ad hoc inconueniens, quod scilicet Apostoli essent a numero credentium excludendi. Secundo ibi: imo sicut ipsi, probat quod Apostolis erant principaliter omnia illa communia: quia ipsi erant inter omnes principaliores. Tertio ibi: Et hoc expresse, ostendit idem auctoritate beati Clementis. Quarto ibi: Unde Hieronymus, probat idem auctoritate beati Hieronymi, vltimo ibi: Expresse quoque, asserit, quod ante illam communionem Apostoli & discipuli eorum aliqua habuerunt in proprio vel in communi.
units.tr: Here he treats the assertion contrary to the assertion of the appellant, who, according to him, says that those things were not common to the Apostles. First he recites it. Second he tries to refute it, at We reply that by saying this. He refutes it first by drawing out the absurdity that the Apostles would have to be excluded from the number of believers. Second, at indeed just as, he proves that all those things were principally common to the Apostles, because they were the chief men among all. Third, at and this is expressly, he shows the same on the authority of the blessed Clement. Fourth, at hence Jerome, he proves the same on the authority of the blessed Jerome. Last, at also clearly, he asserts that before that community the Apostles and their disciples had some things as private or common property.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt hic primo: quod ille impugnatus appellanti falsum imponit. Secundo conantur ostendere, quod intentum suum sufficienter minime probat. Tertio manifestant, quod ad propositam quaestionem secundum intentionem quaerentium non respondet. Quod autem iste appellanti falsum imponat, ex verbis appellantis declarare nituntur. Ad cuius intentum dicunt esse sciendum, quod appellans non negat, imo concedit expresse, quod illa, de quibus Actuum 2. & 4. fit mentio, fuerunt communia Apostolis, sicut iste sibi imponit: sed dicit & asserit, quod illa non erant propria collegio Apostolorum, & ita neque in speciali, neque in communi in communitate scilicet speciali Apostoli habebant aliquid proprium: & illo modo non habuerunt dominium cuiuscunque rei pro tunc, neque in speciali, neque in communi.
units.tr: But these opponents say here, first, that the author under attack falsely imputes something to the appellant. Second, they try to show that he does not sufficiently prove his purpose. Third, they point out that he does not answer the question as the questioner intended it. That he falsely imputes something to the appellant they try to make clear from the appellant's own words. For this purpose they say that it must be understood that the appellant does not deny, indeed he expressly concedes, that those things mentioned in Acts 2 and 4 were common to the Apostles, as the author claims for himself. But he says and maintains that those things were not the property of the college of Apostles, and so the Apostles had nothing as their own, neither specially nor in common, that is, in a special community. In that sense they had no ownership of any thing at that time, neither specially nor in common.

units.la: Hoc est, nulla res erat propria alicui Apostolo neque etiam speciali collegio Apostolorum: cum quo stat, quod aliqua fuerant communia Apostolis & aliis: sed non erant propria Apostolorum, & quod ista fuerit intentio appellantis, ex verbis ipsius patenter habetur, quae sunt haec: Nec hic obuiare dignoscitur quod in Actibus Apostolorum dicitur, quod erant illa omnia communia: quia, sicut ibidem patet, loquitur de communitate generali & vniuersali credentium, & non de speciali communitate, sicut collegio Apostolorum &c. Residua verba, quibus praedicta declarat, quaere supra cap. 85. Ex his habetur aperte, quod iste appellans concedit, quod illa erant communia Apostolis & aliis. Sed tunc dicet iste, quod secundum hoc Apostoli habuissent dominium & proprietatem aliquarum rerum in communi: licet illud dominium commune non esset proprium collegio Apostolorum: & per consequens non habuerunt in rebus, quibus vtebantur, simplicem facti vsum, & eadem ratione Fratres Minores non haberent in rebus, quibus vtuntur, simplicem facti vsum. Alioqui esset eorum paupertas altior & perfectior Apostolica paupertate. Ad istud a diuersis diuersimode respondetur. Dicunt enim quidam: quod nec Apostoli, nec quicunque alii credentes habuerunt in illis bonis communibus dominium & proprietatem: quia nulli eorum etiam nomine communitatis licebat pro illis communibus in iudicio litigare, fuerunt tamen aliquo modo illius communitatis: quia deputata fuerunt ad sustentandum omnes de communitate illa: in quibus tamen illi nullum ius habebant, quemadmodum modo aliqua deputantur ad vsum Fratrum Minorum, in quibus tamen nullu ius habent, sed in hoc est differentia: quod illa, quae deputantur ad vsum Fratrum Minorum sunt Romanae ecclesiae, vel offerentium seu concedentium quo ad dominium seu proprietatem. Illa autem, quae deputata fuerunt ad sustentandos Apostolos, & alios fideles credentes, pertinebant specialiter ad dominium Dei, sicut & templum & quaedam alia in veteri testamento, & ideo nec pro derelictis habebantur, nec occupanti concedebantur: & secundum istos tam Apostoli quam alii credentes habuerunt in illis rebus simplicem facti vsum, erant tamen communia Apostolis & aliis: quia omnes habebant licitam potestate sustentandi se de bonis illis: sed ordinatio illorum erat, qui habebant illa bona diuidere. Alii dicunt, quod illa bona erant communia Apostolis & aliis quo ad aliquale dominium, quo aliquis nomine totius communitatis poterat habere potestatem pro eis in iudicio litigandi, & tunc Apostoli habebant simplicem vsum facti in huiusmodi rebus propter carentiam omnis iuris in eis, quod esset proprium cuicunque Apostolo vel toti collegio Apostolorum, non propter carentiam omnis iuris communis eorum collegio speciali etiam aliis: quemadmodum dicunt de Fratribus Minoribus, quod dicuntur habere in rebus, quibus vtuntur, simplicem facti vsum propter carentiam omnis iuris proprii sibi vel eorum collegio, non propter carentiam omnis iuris communis sibi & aliis fidelibus vniuersis: quia illi iuri communi toti vniuersitati fidelium non est licitum alicui fideli renuntiare, & illud ius commune dicunt omnes fideles habere in bonis ecclesiae, quae data sunt pro communi vtilitate omnium Christianorum, vt scilicet quibuscunque Christianis in casu per bona ecclesiae succurratur: dispensatio tamen bonorum illorum ad succurrendum indigentiis fidelium praelatis ecclesiae est commissa: quibus etiam datum est tale ius in eis, quod dispensationem praedictam & res ealdem possunt in iudicio defendere, ac etiam vendicare, & omne tale ius abdicant Fratres Minores, & non primum, secundum istos. Alii dicunt, quod illa bona communia, de quibus fit mentio Actor. 2. & 4. erant communia Apostolis quo ad licitam potestatem, secundum ordinationem illorum, ad quos distributio pertinebat de ipsis suas indigentias releuandi: sed quo ad aliquale dominium, quo poterant defendi in iudicio & vendicari, erant communia solummodo credentibus illis, qui abdicationem omnis dominii, sicut Apostoli, nequaquam voluerant: & ita secundum istos Apostoli nullum dominium, nec etiam aliquod ius, quo valerent in iudicio litigare, habuerunt in praedictis bonis: sed habebant in eis simplicem facti vsum per carentiam omnis iuris, quo valerent in iudicio litigare, sic etiam dicunt de Fratribus Minoribus, quod renunciauerunt omni iuri communi sibi & quibuscunque aliis, quo valeant in iudicio litigare nomine cuiuscunque communitatis.
units.tr: That is, no thing was the property of any Apostle, nor of the special college of Apostles, which is consistent with some things having been common to the Apostles and others, but not the property of the Apostles. That this was the appellant's intention is plainly seen from his own words, which are these: Nor is it seen to be contradicted by what is said in the Acts of the Apostles, that all those things were common, because, as is clear there, it speaks of the general and universal community of believers, and not of a special community, such as that of the college of Apostles, etc. For the remaining words, in which he explains the foregoing, see above, chap. 85. From these it is plainly clear that this appellant concedes that those things were common to the Apostles and others. But then the author will say that on this view the Apostles would have had ownership and property of some things in common, even though that common ownership was not the property of the college of Apostles; and consequently they did not have, in the things they used, a simple use in fact. By the same reasoning the Friars Minor would not have a simple use in fact of the things they use. Otherwise their poverty would be higher and more perfect than Apostolic poverty. To this different people reply in different ways. Some say that neither the Apostles nor any other believers had ownership and property in those common goods, because none of them, even in the name of the community, was allowed to litigate in court about those common goods; yet they were in some way part of that community, since they were assigned to sustain all members of that community, although they had no right in them. This is like how some things are assigned to the use of the Friars Minor, in which they nonetheless have no right. But the difference is this: the things assigned to the use of the Friars Minor belong to the Roman Church, or to those who offer or grant them as to ownership or property. Those things, however, which were assigned to sustain the Apostles and the other faithful believers belonged specially to the ownership of God, as did the temple and certain other things in the Old Testament; and so they were neither regarded as abandoned nor granted to whoever seized them. According to these people, both the Apostles and the other believers had only the simple use in fact of those things, yet they were common to the Apostles and others, because all had the lawful power of sustaining themselves from those goods, but their ordering belonged to those who had the task of distributing those goods. Others say that those common goods were common to the Apostles and others in a certain kind of ownership, by which someone in the name of the whole community could have power to litigate about them in court. And then the Apostles had only the simple use in fact of such things, because they lacked every right in them that would belong to any Apostle or to the whole college of Apostles. It was not because they lacked every common right of their college in particular and of others as well. They say the same of the Friars Minor: that they are said to have only the simple use in fact of the things they use, because they lack every right belonging to themselves or their college, not because they lack every common right to themselves and to all the faithful. For it is not lawful for any believer to renounce that common right of the whole body of the faithful, and they say all the faithful have this common right in the goods of the Church, which were given for the common benefit of all Christians, so that whatever Christians are in need may be helped from the goods of the Church. Yet the dispensing of those goods to relieve the needs of the faithful has been entrusted to the prelates of the Church, and they too have been given such a right in them that they can defend in court the said dispensation and the goods themselves, and even claim them. The Friars Minor renounce every such right, but according to these people the Apostles did not. Others say that those common goods mentioned in Acts 2 and 4 were common to the Apostles with respect to lawful power, according to the ordering of those to whom the distribution belonged, for relieving their needs from them; but as to a certain ownership, by which they could be defended in court and claimed, they were common only to those believers who had not wished, as the Apostles did, to renounce all ownership. And so according to these people the Apostles had no ownership, nor even any right by which they could litigate in court, in those goods; but they had a simple use in fact of them, because they lacked any right by which they could litigate in court. They say the same of the Friars Minor, that they have renounced every common right to themselves and to all others by which they could litigate in court in the name of any community.

units.la: Secundo dicunt isti impugnatores, quod iste impugnatus intentum suum sufficienter minime probat. Ad cuius intellectum dicunt esse sciendum, quod ipse intendit probare, quod Apostoli habuerunt verum dominium proprium sibi & aliis in bonis illis. Et quamuis hoc videatur prima facie appellanti minime obuiare, nisi intelligatur de dominio pleno & libero: tamen dicunt, quod rationes suae hoc non concludunt: & hoc de omnibus probant vnico modo sic. Rationes, quibus arguebatur a magis communi ad minus commune, sine distributione peccant per fallaciam consequentis. Aliqua autem esse communia aliquibus est magis commune quam esse communia quo ad dominium, cum igitur rationes suae solummodo probant, quod bona illa erant communia Apostolis & aliis: si ex conclusione probata velit inferre, quod erant communia quo ad dominium, committet fallaciam consequentis. Respondendo igitur ad omnes rationes concedunt, quod illa erant communia Apostolis & aliis: sed ex hoc non sequitur, quod erant communia quo ad dominium. Nam etsi conclusio esset vera, tamen in forma arguendi esset fallacia consequentis, specialius vero de eisdem rationibus patebit super literam.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents say that the man they are refuting does not sufficiently prove his thesis. To understand this, they say, we must note that he intends to prove that the Apostles had true and proper ownership of those goods, both for themselves and for others. Although this seems at first sight to be no objection to the appellant, unless it is understood as full and free ownership, they nonetheless say that his arguments do not establish this. They prove it in only one way, against all of them. Arguments that reason from what is more common to what is less common commit the fallacy of the consequent when they are not properly distinguished. Being common to some people is a more general thing than being common as regards ownership. Since his arguments only prove that those goods were common to the Apostles and to others, if he wants to infer from this proven conclusion that they were common as regards ownership, he commits the fallacy of the consequent. Replying, then, to all the arguments, they grant that those goods were common to the Apostles and to others, but it does not follow from this that they were common as regards ownership. For even if the conclusion were true, the form of the argument would still be a fallacy of the consequent. The point will become clearer about these same arguments when we come to the text itself.

units.la: Tertio isti manifestare nituntur, quod ille ad propositam quaestionem secundum intentionem quaerentium non respondet. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod non est intellectus quaestionis, an Apostoli per vnam horam vel per vnam diem post missionem Spiritus sancti habuerunt rerum dominium: sed an Apostoli toto tempore post missionem Spiritus sancti habuerunt temporalium rerum dominium & quale. Secundum istum autem illa communio, de qua fit mentio Actor. 2. & 3. non durauit per vnam diem. Nam non est probabile, quod tota ista communitas per totam vnam diem naturalem integram abstinuerit ab omni cibo & potu. Prima ergo die naturali, qua coepit dicta communio, aliqua comederunt & biberunt, ergo eadem die aliqua distributio communium extitit facta eis, sed secundum istum post distributionem factam quilibet fuit Dominus & proprietarius portionis sibi assignatae, ergo prima die cessauit illa communio secundum istum. Ipse autem non respondet ad propositam quaestionem, nisi pro tempore, quo omnia fuerunt communia, ergo non respondet ad propositam quaestionem, nisi pro vna hora, vel saltem nisi pro vna die integra naturali, & ita nec pro tempore praecedenti illam communionem sequenti missionem sancti Spiritus: nec pro toto tempore sequenti diem illam, in quo secundum istum fuit dicta communio, respondet ad propositam quaestionem. Verum quia licet hic non respondeat ad quaestionem propositam, pro toto tempore sequenti diem illam, in qua secundum eum fuit dicta communio: quia tamen ex dictis suis hic & alibi in multis locis praecedentibus intentio sua quantum ad quaestionem praedictam pro toto tempore sequenti diem illam, in quo facta fuit dicta communio, patenter apparet: ideo isti impugnatores ipsum aliqualiter prosequuntur dicentes, quod intendit asserere, quod Apostoli toto tempore sequenti diem illam, in qua secundum istum fuit facta dicta communio, habuerunt rerum temporalium proprietatem & dominium in speciali: ita quod quilibet eorum vere fuit proprietarius, & Dominus temporalium rerum. Istam autem opinionem isti impugnatores, quantum ad duo satagunt reprobare. Primo enim ostendunt, quod dicta communio non solum vna die, sed tempore multo durauit. Ex quo concludunt istum errare, cum prius dixit, quod quilibet post distributionem factam fuit proprietarius & Dominus portionis sibi assignatae. Secundo ostendunt, quod Apostoli toto tempore post missionem Spiritus sancti caruerunt omni proprietate & dominio temporalium rerum, saltem quod esset alicui Apostolo proprium vel etiam toti collegio Apostolorum, licet prius etiam caruerint tali dominio. Primum, scilicet quod illa communio, de qua Actuum 2. & 4. fit mentio, non durauerit vna hora, vel vna die tantum modo, declarare nituntur, licet, vt dicunt, ex his quae dicta sunt supra capitulo 9. pareat euidenter. Declarant autem sic: religiones monachorum ad imitationem communitatis illorum credentium, de quibus fit in Actibus mentio, sunt institutae, sed communio bonorum temporalium, quae est inter monachos, non durat vna die tantum modo, ergo nec illa communio durauit tantum modo vna die. Secundum, scilicet quod Apostoli toto tempore post missionem Spiritus sancti caurint dominio & proprietate omnium temporalium, dicunt ex supra dictis aperte patere, & tamen hic aliquae rationes eorum ad idem inferentur.
units.tr: Thirdly, these men try to show that he does not answer the question as posed, according to the intention of those who asked it. To make this clear, they say we must note that the question does not concern whether the Apostles had ownership of things for one hour or one day after the mission of the Holy Spirit, but whether the Apostles, throughout the whole time after the mission of the Holy Spirit, had ownership of temporal things, and of what kind. According to him, however, that community mentioned in Acts 2 and 3 did not last one day. For it is not probable that this whole community abstained from all food and drink for an entire natural day. On the first natural day on which that community began, some of them ate and drank. So on that same day some distribution of the common goods was made to them, and according to him, after the distribution, each man became the lord and owner of the portion assigned to him. Therefore, by his account, that community ended on the first day. But he does not answer the question as posed except for the time during which all things were common. Therefore he answers the question only for one hour, or at least only for one whole natural day, and so not for the time before that community which followed the mission of the Holy Spirit, nor for the whole time after that day on which, by his account, the community was established. Yet although he does not answer the question here for the whole time after that day on which, in his view, the community was established, nevertheless his intention regarding that question, for the whole time after the day on which the community was made, plainly appears from what he says here and in many earlier places.
