So these opponents follow him up to a point, saying that he intends to assert that the Apostles, throughout the whole time after the day on which, by his account, that community was made, had the particular possession and ownership of temporal things, so that each of them was truly an owner and lord of temporal things. These opponents labour to refute this opinion on two counts. First, they show that the community did not last one day only, but for a much longer time. From this they conclude that he is wrong, since he earlier said that each man, after the distribution, was owner and lord of the portion assigned to him. Second, they show that throughout the whole time after the mission of the Holy Spirit the Apostles lacked all ownership and possession of temporal things, at least anything that could be the property of one Apostle or even of the whole college of Apostles, although they had also lacked such ownership before. As for the first point, namely that the community mentioned in Acts 2 and 4 did not last one hour or one day only, they strive to make this clear, although, as they say, it is plain from what was said above in chapter 9. They explain it thus: the religious orders of monks were instituted in imitation of that community of believers mentioned in the Acts. But the common possession of temporal goods that exists among monks does not last only one day. Therefore that community did not last only one day either. As for the second point, namely that the Apostles throughout the whole time after the mission of the Holy Spirit lacked ownership and possession of all temporal things, they say this is plainly evident from what has been said above. Nevertheless, some of their arguments to the same effect are brought forward here.

units.la: Est autem prima ratio talis. Apostoli toto tempore postquam fuerunt a Christo sufficienter instructi, illud, quantum ad contemptum temporalium, seruauerunt, quod erat eis melius, & aliis vtilius, sed proprietatem omnium temporalium abdicare omni tempore fuit Apostolis melius, & proximis suis vtilius, ergo omni tempore postquam adhaeserunt toto corde doctrinae Christi, talem abdicationem proprietatis omnium seruauerunt. Maior est manifesta: quia aliter Apostoli fuissent de numero illorum, de quibus dicitur Matth. 7. Omnis qui audit verba mea haec, & non facit ea, similis erit viro stulto &c. Minor auctoritatibus sanctorum aperte probatur. Ait enim Ambrosius in libro de officiis: Officium omne aut medium aut perfectum est, & infra: Non homicidium facies: non adulterabis: haec media sunt officia, quibus aliquid deest, ideo sequitur: Si vis perfectus esse, vade & vende omnia quae habes & da pauperibus & sequere me. Hoc est igitur perfectum officium, quod Graeci καλοκἀγαθον vocant, quo corriguntur omnia quae alios poterant lapsus habere. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod vendere omnia & dare pauperibus, quod sine abdicatione proprietatis omnium fieri nequit: & sequi Christum, est officium, quo omnia corriguntur, & per consequens est melius, quod Augustinus in libro de bono coniugali, testatur expresse dicens: Bonum erat, quod faciebant, qui de substantia sua Christo, & eius discipulis ministrabant, sed melius, qui omnem substantiam dimiserunt, ut Christum Dominum expeditiores sequerentur. His concordat Bernardus super illud Matth. Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, qui ait: optime & non ad insipientiam tibi. Nam & mundus transit, & concupiscentia eius, & relinquere hac magis expedit, quam ab eis relinqui. Ex his aliisque quamplurimis habetur aperte, quod melius est proprietatem omnium abdicare, quam aliorum dominium retinere, ergo & Apostoli talem abdicationem usque ad finem vitae suae seruauerunt.
units.tr: The first argument is this. The Apostles, throughout the whole time after they had been sufficiently instructed by Christ, kept that which was better for them and more useful for others as regards contempt of temporal things. But to renounce ownership of all temporal things was always better for the Apostles and more useful to their neighbours. Therefore, at every time after they had cleaved with their whole heart to the teaching of Christ, they kept such a renunciation of all ownership. The major premise is manifest, for otherwise the Apostles would have been among those of whom it is said in Matthew 7: "Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them shall be like a foolish man," and so on. The minor premise is clearly proved by the authority of the saints. For Ambrose says in his book On the Duties: "Every duty is either intermediate or perfect." And further on: "You shall not commit murder; you shall not commit adultery. These are intermediate duties, which fall short of something. Therefore it follows: 'If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and follow me.' This, then, is the perfect duty, which the Greeks call the noble-and-good [καλοκἀγαθον], by which all the lapses that others might have had are corrected." From these words it is plain that to sell everything and give to the poor, which cannot be done without renouncing ownership of all things, and to follow Christ, is a duty by which all things are corrected, and consequently it is better. Augustine expressly testifies to this in his book On the Good of Marriage, saying: "It was good for those who ministered to Christ and his disciples from their own substance, but better for those who gave up all their substance so that they might follow the Lord Christ more freely." Bernard agrees with this on the words of Matthew, "Behold, we have left all things." He says: "Very good, and not to your folly. For the world passes away, and its lust too, and it is better to leave these things than to be left by them." From these and many other testimonies it is plainly established that it is better to renounce ownership of all things than to retain ownership of anything. Therefore the Apostles also kept such a renunciation until the end of their lives.

units.la: Secunda ratio est haec. Apostoli usque ad finem vitae suae Apostolicum fastigium nullatenus dimiserunt, sed omnium abdicare dominium & proprietatem est Apostolicum fastigium, ergo Apostoli talem abdicationem usque ad finem vitae praesentis minime dimiserunt. Maior est euidens, quia si Apostoli Apostolicum dimisissent fastigium, non fuissent Apostoli appellandi, nec profecissent, sed enormiter defecissent. Minor euidenter habetur per auctoritates Hieronymi ad Demetriadem & Ebidiam supra 9. c. allegatas.
units.tr: The second argument is this. The Apostles did not in any way give up the apostolic eminence until the end of their lives. But to renounce all ownership and possession of things is the apostolic eminence. Therefore the Apostles did not in any way give up such a renunciation until the end of this present life. The major premise is evident, for if the Apostles had given up the apostolic eminence, they would not be called Apostles, nor would they have made progress, but would have fallen away badly. The minor premise is clearly established by the testimonies of Jerome to Demetrias and to Ebidia, cited above in chapter 9.

units.la: Tertia ratio est haec. Apostoli, qui usque ad finem vitae suae debuerunt praedicare euangelicam veritatem, nullatenus debuerunt verbo vel facto innuere, quod causa lucri, non causa hominum praedicarent, sed si habuissent proprietatem auri vel argenti aut aliarum rerum temporalium, innuissent facto, quod causa lucri, non hominum praedicassent, teste Rabano, qui super illud Matth. Nolite possidere aurum &c. ait: Conuenienter haec praecepit euangelizatoribus veritatis, quibus ante dixerat: Gratis accepistis, gratis date. Si enim sic praedicant, ut pretium non accipiant, superflua est auri & argenti nummorum possessio. Nam si habuissent aurum vel argentum, viderentur non causa hominum, sed causa lucri praedicare, ergo Apostoli neque aurum neque argentum: & eadem ratione neque proprietatem quarumcunque rerum debuerunt habere usq; ad finem vitae suae.
units.tr: The third argument is this. The Apostles, who had to preach the gospel truth until the end of their lives, were in no way to suggest by word or deed that they preached for the sake of gain rather than for the sake of men. But if they had possessed gold or silver or other temporal things, they would have suggested by their conduct that they preached for the sake of gain and not for the sake of men. So Rabanus, on the words of Matthew, "Do not possess gold," etc., says: "He commanded this fittingly to the preachers of the truth, to whom he had said before: 'Freely you have received, freely give.' For if they preach so as to take no reward, the possession of gold and silver coins is superfluous. For if they had gold or silver, they would seem to preach not for the sake of men, but for the sake of gain." Therefore the Apostles had neither gold nor silver; and for the same reason they ought not to have had ownership of any things at all until the end of their lives.

units.la: Quarta ratio est haec. Apostoli usque ad finem vitae suae paupertatem euangelicam seruauerunt: alioquin mittentes manum ad aratrum retro aspexissent, sed paupertas euangelica abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum includit, ut supra c. 22. est ostensum, ergo talem abdicationem usq; in finem vitae suae Apostoli seruauerunt.
units.tr: The fourth reason is this. The Apostles kept evangelical poverty until the end of their lives, for otherwise, having put their hand to the plough, they would have looked back. But evangelical poverty includes the renunciation of ownership of all things, as was shown above in chapter 22. Therefore the Apostles kept such renunciation until the end of their lives.

units.la: Quinta ratio est haec, illi, qui usque ad finem vitae suae nulla superflua quaesierunt, usque ad finem vitae suae proprietatem rerum temporalium minime habuerunt: quia proprietas temporalium est inter superflua computanda, sicut ostensum est prius, sed Apostoli usque ad finem vitae suae nulla superflua quaesierunt, teste Beda, qui super illud Marci 6. praecepit eis, ne quid tollerent &c. Ait: ita Apostolis loquebatur, ut securi non possiderent neque portarent haec vitae necessaria, nec magna, nec minima, ideo posuit: non virgam: ostendens a fidelibus omnia deberi ministris suis nulla superflua quaerentibus. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod ministri Christi nulla quaerere debuerunt superflua, quod potissime de Apostolis habuit veritatem, ergo Apostoli usque ad finem vitae suae nulla superflua quaesierunt, ergo proprietatem temporalium usq; ad finem vitae suae minime habuerunt. Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod secundum hanc rationem nullus vnquam fuit perfectus minister Christi, qui habuit temporalium proprietatem. Ad hoc dicunt isti, quod habere proprietatem temporalium tantum modo amore Dei, vel pro utilitate proximorum non reddit aliquem imperfectum. Unde etiam reges aliqui, qui solummodo pro bono communi ad honorem Dei proprietatem regnorum & dominium tenuerunt, propter hoc nullatenus imperfecti fuerunt. Sed de Apostolis nulla causa apparet, quare debuerunt temporalium proprietatem habere: & multae rationes cogentes patent, quare expediens fuit eis & aliis omnium proprietatem relinquere, ergo ipsi minime perfectissimi ministri Christi fuissent, si proprietatem temporalium habuissent.
units.tr: The fifth reason is this. Those who never sought superfluities until the end of their lives never had ownership of temporal goods until the end of their lives, because ownership of temporal goods must be counted among superfluities, as was shown earlier. But the Apostles never sought superfluities until the end of their lives, as Bede testifies, who on Mark 6, "He commanded them that they should take nothing," says: "He spoke to the Apostles in such a way that they should not possess or carry these necessities of life, neither great nor small; therefore he said, not a staff, showing that the faithful owe everything to their ministers, provided these seek no superfluities." From these words it is plain that the ministers of Christ ought to seek no superfluities, and this was most especially true of the Apostles. Therefore the Apostles never sought superfluities until the end of their lives, and therefore they never had ownership of temporal goods until the end of their lives. But perhaps someone will say that by this reasoning no minister of Christ who held ownership of temporal goods was ever perfect. To this they reply that to hold ownership of temporal goods only for the love of God, or for the benefit of neighbours, does not make a man imperfect. Hence some kings, who held the ownership and lordship of their kingdoms only for the common good and the honour of God, were in no way made imperfect by this. But in the case of the Apostles no reason appears why they ought to have held ownership of temporal goods, and there are many compelling reasons why it was expedient for them, and for others, to relinquish the ownership of all things. Therefore they would not have been the most perfect ministers of Christ if they had held ownership of temporal goods.

units.la: Sexta ratio est haec. Apostoli usque ad finem vitae suae perfectionis consilium seruauerunt: quia nulla fuit ratio, quare debuerunt perfectionis consilium non seruare, sed omnia abdicare quo ad dominium & proprietatem & solis necessariis contentari, est perfectionis consilium, teste Bernardo, qui ait: habetur in euangelio & perfectionis consilium & remedium infirmitatis. Nolite thesaurizare vobis thesauros in terra: haec perfectio est: si quidem filius hominis, vbi caput reclinaret, non habebat: Petro & Iohanni nec aurum nec argentum erat: Paulus simplici victu vestituque contentus haec ipsa labore manuum acquirebat: sed non omnes capiunt verbum hoc, sicut nec consilium castitatis. Ex his verbis datur intelligi, quod consilium perfectionis est solum necessariis contentari, ergo Apostoli usque ad finem vitae suae, ex quo perfectionis consilium seruauerunt, solum necessariis contenti fuerunt: & per consequens usque ad finem vitae suae abdicationem proprietatis omnium seruauerunt.
units.tr: The sixth reason is this. The Apostles kept the counsel of perfection until the end of their lives, since there was no reason why they should not keep the counsel of perfection. But to renounce all things as to lordship and ownership, and to be content with the bare necessities, is the counsel of perfection, as Bernard testifies, who says: "The Gospel contains both the counsel of perfection and the remedy for weakness. 'Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth': this is perfection. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head; Peter and John had neither gold nor silver; Paul, content with simple food and clothing, earned these very things by the labour of his hands. But not all receive this word, just as not all receive the counsel of chastity." From these words it is understood that the counsel of perfection is to be content with necessities only. Therefore the Apostles, since they kept the counsel of perfection, were content with necessities only until the end of their lives, and consequently they kept the renunciation of ownership of all things until the end of their lives.

units.la: Septimo sic, illam perfectionem usq; ad finem vitae suae Apostoli seruauerunt, quam existentes in toto orbe peregrini tenuerunt, sed Apostolia in toto orbe peregrini praeceptum de non possiden-dis dis pecuniâ, calciamentis & huiusmodi, & eadem ratione consilium de abdicanda proprietate omnium tenuerunt, teste Hieronymo ad Hieremiam, qui ait: Apostoli toto orbe peregrini non ex in zona, non virgam in manu, non caligas habuere in pedibus; ergo Apostoli usque ad finem vitæ suæ abdicationem proprietatis omnium possederunt.
units.tr: Seventhly, thus: the Apostles kept until the end of their lives that perfection which they observed while wandering as strangers throughout the whole world. But the Apostles, while wandering throughout the whole world, observed the precept not to possess money, sandals, and things of that kind, and by the same reasoning they observed the counsel of renouncing ownership of all things, as Jerome testifies in his letter to Hedibia (or in his commentary on Jeremiah), who says: The Apostles, wandering throughout the whole world, had no money in their belts, no staff in their hand, no sandals on their feet. Therefore the Apostles possessed the renunciation of ownership of all things until the end of their lives.

units.la: Octauo sic, Qui sine ratione cogente abdicat omnium temporalium proprietatem propter Deum, non est perfectus. Hoc ex verbis Rabani super illud Euangelii: Si vis perfectus esse &c. colligitur euidenter, ait enim: in potestate nostra est, vtrum velimus esse perfecti: tamen quicunque perfectus esse voluerit, debet vendere quæ habet, & non ex parte vendere, sicut Ananias & Saphira, sed totum: & sic præparare sibi Christum in regno cælorum: nec hoc ad perfectionem sufficit, nisi Saluatorem sequatur. Ex his habetur aperte, quod qui vult esse perfectus, debet proprietatem omnium abdicare, quod debet intelligi, nisi habeat rationem mouentem, quare sibi aut aliis vel propter honorem Dei aut vtilitatem communem vel aliam rationem sufficientem non expedit proprietatem omnium abdicare: sicut in multis diuinitibus regibus & aliis tam in veteri quam in nouo testamento apparuit. Sed Apostoli fuerunt perfecti, & nulla ratio cogens mouit eos ad non abdicandum omnium proprietatem, ergo proprietatem omnium abdicarunt.
units.tr: Eighthly, thus: whoever renounces the ownership of all temporal goods for God's sake, without a compelling reason, is not perfect. This is clearly gathered from the words of Rabanus on the Gospel text, "If you wish to be perfect, etc.", for he says: "It lies in our power whether we wish to be perfect. Yet whoever wishes to be perfect ought to sell what he has, and not sell part of it, as Ananias and Sapphira did, but the whole; and thus he prepares for himself Christ in the kingdom of heaven. Nor is this sufficient for perfection unless he follows the Saviour." From this it is plainly held that whoever wishes to be perfect ought to renounce the ownership of all things. This must be understood to apply unless he has a motive, such that for himself or others, whether for the honour of God, the common benefit, or some other sufficient reason, it is not expedient to renounce the ownership of all things; as has appeared in many divinely appointed kings and others, both in the Old and in the New Testament. But the Apostles were perfect, and no compelling reason moved them not to renounce the ownership of all things. Therefore they renounced the ownership of all things.

units.la: Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod ratio cogens poterat eos mouere ad retinendum aliquam aliquarum rerum proprietatem scilicet propter eleemosynas faciendas, & bona temporalia pro bono communi vtiliter dispensanda.
units.tr: But perhaps someone will say that a compelling reason could have moved them to retain the ownership of some of their goods, namely for the sake of making alms and of dispensing temporal goods usefully for the common good.

units.la: Sed ratio hæc non concludit: quia circa orationem & prædicationem euangelii fuerunt vtilius occupati, propter quod etiam absque dominio & proprietate bona communia renuerunt dispensare, vt habetur Actor. 6. vbi conuocata multitudine discipulorum dixerunt Apostoli: Non est æquum derelinquere nos verbum Dei, & ministrare mensis, considerate ergo Fratres, viros ex vobis boni testimonii septem plenos Spiritu sancto & sapientia, quos constituamus super hoc opus, nos vero orationi & ministerio verbi insistentes erimus. Ex his verbis datur intelligi, quod Apostoli etiam circa communia dispensanda occupari nolebant, & ita nulla poterant ratione vrgenti moueri ad proprietatem temporalium retinendam.
units.tr: But this reason does not conclude, because they were more usefully occupied with prayer and the preaching of the Gospel. For this reason they also refused to dispense common goods without ownership and possession, as is found in Acts 6, where, the multitude of the disciples having been called together, the Apostles said: "It is not right that we should leave the word of God and serve tables. Therefore, brethren, look out among you seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business. But we will continue steadfastly in prayer and in the ministry of the word." From these words it is understood that the Apostles did not even wish to be occupied with the dispensing of common goods, and so they could not be moved by any pressing reason to retain ownership of temporal goods.

units.la: Nono sic: Apostoli statum tutissimum respectu temporalium elegerunt, sed status nec amantium nec habentium quo ad dominium temporalia tutissimus est, & tutior aliis statibus, teste Rabano super illud Euangelii: Si vis perfectus esse, qui ait: inter pecunias habere, & pecunias amare, nonnulla distantia est. Multi enim habentes non amant, multi non habentes amant. Item alii habent & amant: Alii nec habere nec amare se diuitias seculi gaudent, quorum tutior status est cum Apostolo dicentium: Nobis crucifixus est mundus, & nos mundo. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod nec habere nec amare diuitias: & eadem ratione nec habere quo ad proprietatem, nec amare quæcunque temporalia est status tutissimus, ergo illum statum Apostoli elegerunt: & ita nulla temporalia habuerunt, quod debet intelligi quantum ad dominium seu proprietatem.
units.tr: Ninthly, thus: the Apostles chose the safest state with respect to temporal goods. But the state of neither loving nor having, as regards ownership of temporal goods, is the safest and safer than other states, as Rabanus testifies on the Gospel text, "If you wish to be perfect," who says: "There is a considerable difference between having riches and loving riches. Many who have do not love, and many who do not have do love. Again, some both have and love; others neither have nor love, and rejoice in not having worldly riches, and their state is safer, with the Apostle saying: 'The world is crucified to me, and I to the world.'" From these words it is plain that neither to have nor to love riches, and by the same reasoning neither to have as to ownership nor to love any temporal things, is the safest state. Therefore the Apostles chose that state, and so they had no temporal goods, which must be understood with respect to lordship or ownership.

units.la: Decimo sic: Qui ad finem vitæ suæ minimi extiterunt, vsque ad finem vitæ suæ nihil penitus habuerunt quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, hoc ex Glossa super illud Matth. qui potum dederit vni ex minimis istis &c. euidenter colligitur, ait enim: minimi sunt, qui nihil penitus habent in hoc mundo: quod debet intelligi quod ad dominium seu proprietatem: quia quantum ad vsum facti vel consumptionem secundum modum istius loquendi omnes aliquid habent, sed Apostoli vsque ad finem vitæ suæ minimi extiterunt, ergo vsque ad finem vitæ suæ penitus nihil habuerunt quo ad dominium seu proprietatem.
units.tr: Tenthly, thus: those who were least until the end of their lives had nothing at all as regards lordship or ownership until the end of their lives. This is clearly gathered from the Gloss on the text of Matthew, "whoever gives a drink to one of these least," which says: "They are the least who have nothing at all in this world." This must be understood as regards lordship or ownership, because as regards use or consumption, all men have something according to the manner of speaking used here. But the Apostles were least until the end of their lives. Therefore until the end of their lives they had nothing at all as regards lordship or ownership.

units.la: Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod Glossa intelligit de istis, qui nihil penitus habent per inordinatum amorem, non de illis qui absque inordinato amore aliquid habent quo ad dominium seu proprietatem: sicut nec de illis qui aliquid habent quantum ad vsum, sed ad hæc faciliter per præcedentia respondetur. Nam verum est secundum istos, quod non repugnat formaliter minimo, sicut nec perfecto, habere aliquid quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, quia potest aliquis esse minimus & perfectus: licet ex causa vrgente propter Deum retineat temporalium proprietatem, sed si habet dominium temporalium absque causa vrgente propter Deum, non est inter perfectos & minimos computandus. Apostoli autem non habuerunt causam vrgentem, quare debuerunt temporalia quo ad dominium retinere, imo ex causa vrgente scilicet propter contemptum mundi perfectissime ostendendum, quod tunc erat necessarium, debuerunt omnium temporalium proprietatem abiicere: nec aliter ipsi minimi extitissent.
units.tr: But perhaps someone will say that the Gloss means those who have nothing at all through inordinate love, not those who have something without inordinate love as regards lordship or ownership, just as it does not mean those who have something as regards use. But this is easily answered from what has been said before. For it is true according to these men that it is not formally incompatible with being least, any more than with being perfect, to have something as regards lordship or ownership, since a man can be both least and perfect even though, for a pressing reason for God's sake, he retains ownership of temporal goods. But if he holds lordship over temporal goods without a pressing reason for God's sake, he is not to be counted among the perfect or the least. Now the Apostles had no pressing reason why they ought to retain temporal goods as regards lordship. Rather, for a pressing reason, namely to show most perfectly the contempt of the world, which was then necessary, they ought to have cast off the ownership of all temporal goods. Otherwise they would not have been the least.

units.la: Vndecimo sic: Apostoli vsque ad finem vitæ suæ occasiones peccatorum & pericula spiritualia, quantum licuit saluis honore Dei & vtilitate proximorum, studuerunt vitare, sed possessio quarumcunque rerum temporalium quo ad dominium & proprietatem, est peccandi occasio, spirituale periculum habens annexum, ergo possessionem temporalium quo ad dominium seu proprietatem quantum licuit saluis honore Dei & proximorum vtilitate, vitarunt. Non solum autem licuit, sed etiam expedit ad honorem Dei, & proximorum vtilitati fuit expediens omnium temporalium proprietatem relinquere, ergo Apostoli vsque ad finem vitæ suæ proprietatem omnium temporalium abiecerunt. Hic esset probandum, quod temporalia quo ad dominium possidere est peccandi occasio, spirituale periculum habens annexum: sed sufficienter probatum est supra capitul. 75. dicunt ergo isti propter rationes istas & alias multas, quod Apostoli à tempore assumptionis eorum ad Apostolatum vsque ad finem vitæ suæ proprietatem omnium temporalium abiecerunt tam in speciali quam etiam in communi: quia ad possidendum temporalia, vel in speciali vel in communi, appropriando scilicet aliqua temporalia eorum collegio moueri ex causa vrgente non poterant: quia de tali dominio seu proprietate, nec ipsis nec aliis spiritualis vtilitas accreuisset: sed potius decreuisset, quia & ipsi nequaquam mundi contemptum perfectissime ostendissent: & alii ad suspicandum, quod non perfecte mundum contemnerent, occasionem aliquam habuissent.
units.tr: Eleventh, thus: The Apostles, up to the end of their lives, strove to avoid occasions of sin and spiritual dangers, as far as was permitted consistently with the honour of God and the benefit of their neighbours. But possession of any temporal goods, as to ownership and property, is an occasion of sin with a spiritual danger attached. Therefore they avoided possession of temporal goods, as to ownership or property, as far as was permitted consistently with the honour of God and the benefit of their neighbours. Not only was it permitted, but it was also expedient for the honour of God, and for the benefit of their neighbours, to give up the property of all temporal goods. Therefore the Apostles, up to the end of their lives, renounced the property of all temporal goods. Here it would have to be proved that possessing temporal goods as to ownership is an occasion of sin with a spiritual danger attached, but this was sufficiently proved above, capitul. 75. They say, therefore, on these reasons and many others, that from the time of their call to the apostolate until the end of their lives the Apostles renounced the property of all temporal goods, both individually and in common. For to possess temporal goods, either individually or in common (namely by appropriating certain temporal goods to their college), they could not be moved by a pressing cause. From such ownership or property neither they nor others would have gained any spiritual advantage; rather it would have diminished, since they would by no means have displayed perfect contempt of the world, and others would have had some occasion to suspect that they did not despise the world perfectly.

units.la: (Et quia iste haereticus.) Dicunt isti, quod doctorem catholicum pro defensione fidei Christianæ se viriliter opponentem appellat haereticum in suæ animæ damnationem perpetuam. (Dicit quod illa communio intelligitur de turba discipulorum inter quos erant omnia communia, quæ habebant, non de Apostolis.) Hoc non dicit: imo dicit quod ista communio intelligitur de Apostolis. (Qui nihil habebant in temporalibus nec in proprio nec in communi.) Hoc habet vnum sensum verum secundum appellantem (scilicet quod nihil temporale erat proprium alicuius Apostoli, nec totius collegii specialis Apostolorum, quod etiam veritatem habuit secundum istum, quando illa bona erant communia, (nisi tantum in rebus vsu consumptibilibus simplicem vsum facti.) Hoc secundum appellantem est verum sine exclusione intelligendo simplicem vsum facti, per carentiam omnis iuris, quo valuissent Apostoli nomine proprio, vel etiam nomine collegii Apostolorum pro rebus temporalibus in iudicio litigare. Veruntamen in multis aliis rebus, quam in rebus vsu consumptibilibus, habuerunt simplicem facti vsum, sæpe enim domibus & aliis rebus non consumptibilibus vsu vtebantur.) Dicimus quod hoc dicendo.) Hic sicut prius, appellanti falsum imponit, quia non dicit, quod illa non erant communia Apostolis & aliis. (Apostolos à credentium numero euidenter excludit.) Quamuis hoc falsum sit secundum istos: tamen dicunt, quod si iste in Theologia fuisset instructus, & dictum Augustini dicentis & declarantis per plura exempla, quod sæpe in scripturis diuinis idem nomen quandoque accipitur generaliter, & quandoque particulariter seu specialiter, intellexisset: non haberet pro magno inconuenienti, quod hoc nomen credentes diceretur accipi aliquando particulariter seu specialiter pro aliis credentibus ab Apostolis: quemadmodum etiam secundum iura hoc nomen consuetudo, aliquando accipitur communiter pro iure scripto & non scripto: aliquando particulariter pro iure non scripto tantum. (Si Apostoli non erant communia.) Hoc non dixit appellans. (Sicut ipsi inter credentes principaliores erant: sic eis omnia communia principaliter existebant.) Hoc potest concedi quantum ad dignitatem habendi modo sibi conuenienti, quia magis digni erant illis communibus ad suas indigentias releuandas de illis, quam alii, quantum autem ad principaliorem habendi modum, quo ad dominium, non continet veritatem. (Sicut principalioribus.) Quo ad auctoritatem in spiritualibus & sanctitatem. (Pecunia, agrorum, & domorum venditorum ante pedes Apostolorum ponebantur.) Vt scilicet exprimerent quid de eis fieri vellent: quia alii parati erant Apostolorum parere in omnibus voluntati, & ideo ipsi Apostoli non tangebant pecuniam nec portabant: sicut ibi Glossa aperte insinuat: sed quomodo deberent distribui pecuniæ, indicabant. (Apostoli eorum, discipuli vna nobiscum & vobiscum communem vitam duxerunt.) Ex hoc patet, quod illa non erant communia per vnam horam vel vnam diem tantum modo, sed per multos dies: quia communem vitam ducere non est tantum communia diuidere, sed de communibus viuere, hoc est vitam suam de communibus sustentare. (Omnia nobis erant communia) quia per illa bona omnium debuerunt indigentiæ subleuari (vbi satis clare monstratur quod Apostoli & eorum discipuli illa quae habebant) quo ad vsum quantum ad Apostolos, vel quo ad dominium quantum ad quosdam alios discipulos & discipulas, (Communicauerunt Iudaeis conuersis Hierosolymis) vt per ipsa illorum indigentiis subueniretur si oportuisset (& econtra) hoc male dicitur intelligendo quod communicauerint omnia quae ante conuersionem habuerunt: quia immobilia sua non communicauerunt, sed vendiderunt, & pretium aliquo modo communicauerunt, hoc est ordinauerunt, vt per pretium indigentiis omnium occurreretur, prout esset decens & possibile (vnde Hieronymus &c.) Auctoritas Hieronymi tantum modo probat, quod monachi imitantur primitiuam ecclesiam: sed non probat, quod ad perfectionem Apostolicæ paupertatis attingat, & ideo non est ad propositum, quod iste intendit. Sicut enim superius cap. 17. ostensum est, multi imitantur paupertatem Christi & Apostolorum eius, qui tamen ad perfectionem eiusdem in summo gradu non attingunt: vt patet de his qui profitentur Regulam beati Augustini, & de monachis habentibus possessionum in communi proprietatem, qui in hoc vitam Christi & Apostolorum imitantur, q abdicauerunt rerum dominium in speciali, sed in hoc ab eius perfectione deficiunt, quod in communi proprietatem & dominium retinuerunt, quapropter ad perfectionem primorum credentium quantum ad altissimam paupertatem, non attigerunt. (An illam communionem habere poterant Apostoli &c.) verum est, quod habere poterant quo ad vsum, sed non quo ad dominium proprium alicui Apostolo vel collegio Apostolorum.
units.tr: (And because this heretic.) They say that he calls a Catholic teacher, who bravely opposes himself in defence of the Christian faith, a heretic, to the eternal damnation of his own soul. (He says that this communion is understood of the crowd of disciples, among whom all things they had were common, not of the Apostles.) He does not say this; rather he says that this communion is understood of the Apostles. (Who had nothing in temporal things, neither individually nor in common.) This has one true sense according to the appellant, namely that no temporal thing was the property of any Apostle, nor of the whole special college of Apostles, which was also true according to him when those goods were common (except only in things consumed by use, a simple use of fact). According to the appellant this is true without exclusion, understanding a simple use of fact, through the lack of any right by which the Apostles could have litigated over temporal things in their own name, or even in the name of the college of Apostles. Yet in many other things than consumable things they had the simple use of fact, for they often used houses and other non-consumable things. (We say that in saying this.) Here, as before, he imposes a falsehood on the appellant, because he does not say that those things were not common to the Apostles and others. (He clearly excludes the Apostles from the number of believers.) Although this is false according to them, they say that if he had been instructed in theology, and had understood the saying of Augustine, who states and shows by many examples that often in divine Scripture the same name is taken sometimes in a general sense and sometimes in a particular or special sense, he would not have regarded it as a great inconvenience that the name believers should be taken sometimes particularly or specially for other believers besides the Apostles. Just as also, according to the laws, the name custom is sometimes taken commonly for written and unwritten law, and sometimes particularly for unwritten law only. (If the Apostles were not common.) The appellant did not say this. (As they were the chief among the believers, so all things were principally common to them.) This can be conceded as to the dignity of having in a manner suited to them, because they were more worthy than others to use those common goods for relieving their needs; but as to the principal mode of having, namely as to ownership, it does not contain truth. (As to the principal ones.) As to authority in spiritual matters and holiness. (Money, and the proceeds of sold fields and houses, were placed at the feet of the Apostles.) That is, so that they might indicate what they wished to be done with them, because the others were ready to obey the Apostles' will in all things. Therefore the Apostles themselves did not touch the money nor carry it, as the Gloss there openly hints, but they indicated how the money was to be distributed. (The Apostles, their disciples, led a common life with us and with you.) From this it is clear that those things were common not for one hour or one day only, but for many days; for to lead a common life is not merely to divide common goods, but to live from common goods, that is, to sustain one's life from common goods. (All things were common to us.) Because the needs of all were to be relieved by those goods. (Where it is made clear enough that the Apostles and their disciples had those things) as to use, for the Apostles, or as to ownership, for certain other disciples, men and women, (communicated to the Jewish converts at Jerusalem) so that by these their needs might be met if it were necessary (and conversely). This is wrongly said, if it is understood that they shared all that they had before their conversion. For they did not share their immovable property, but sold it, and shared the price in some way, that is, arranged that the needs of all should be met by the price, as was fitting and possible. (Whence Jerome, etc.) The authority of Jerome only proves that monks imitate the primitive Church, but it does not prove that they attain to the perfection of Apostolic poverty, and therefore it is not to the point that this author intends. For, as was shown above in cap. 17., many imitate the poverty of Christ and His Apostles who nevertheless do not attain to its perfection in the highest degree, as is clear of those who profess the Rule of blessed Augustine, and of monks who hold possessions in common as property. In this they imitate the life of Christ and the Apostles, in that they have renounced ownership of goods individually, but in this they fall short of its perfection, in that they have retained property and ownership in common. Wherefore they have not attained to the perfection of the first believers as to the highest poverty. (Whether the Apostles could have that communion, etc.) It is true that they could have it as to use, but not as to proper ownership by any Apostle or college of Apostles.

units.la: CAP. CVII.
units.tr: CHAP. CVII.

units.la: Quantum autem ad conuersos ex gentibus, non videtur quod ipsi sibi inuicem & aliis credentibus communicauerint sua: imo videtur quod ipsa sibi retinuerint propria, sicut prius, vt probatur de Corinthiis, 1. ad Cor. vltimo, vbi dicitur sic: De collectis autem quæ fiunt in sanctos, sicut ordinaui in ecclesiis Galatiæ, ita & vos facite per vnam sabbati, vnusquisque vestrum apud se reponat recondens, quod ei bene placuerit. Item ad Philipp. 4. Apostolus Philippensibus sic dixit: Scitis autem & vos Philippenses, quod in principio euangelii, quando profectus sum à Macedonia in ratione dati & accepti nulla mihi communicauit ecclesia, nisi vni soli, quia & Thessalonicam, semel & bis in vsum misistis mihi, & sequiest, Repletus sum acceptis ab Epaphrodito, quæ misistis in odorem suauitatis. Item Actor. 11. legitur, quod cum Achabus Propheta in Antiochia in præsentia Barnabæ Apostoli & Sauli significasset per spiritum famem magnam suturam in vniuerso orbe terrarum, quæ facta est sub Claudio, discipuli, prout quisq; habebat, proposuerunt singuli ministerium mittere habitantibus in Iudæa fratribus, quod & fecerunt mittentes ad seniores per manus Barnabæ & Sauli. Et hoc est, quod Augustinus 3. de doctrina Christiana, dicit expresse, sic dicens: Tam capaces exiterunt Spiritus sancti, qui primo ex Iudæis crediderunt, ex quibus facta est prima ecclesia Hierosolymitana, vt & omnia sua venderent, eorumque pretium indigentibus distribuendum ante Apostolorum pedes ponerent, leque totos dedicarent Deo tanquam templum nouum in orationibus & fractione panis spiritualis & corporalis, quæ prius veteri templo seruiebant, quod nullas ecclesias gentium fecisse scriptum est: quia non tam prope erant, quæ simulacra manu facta deos habebant. Ex quo intelligimus, magnam vtilitatem fuisse Iudæos sub lege tanquam sub pædagogo custoditos, vt signa, quæ temporaliter eis carnaliter seruientibus erant impolita, ad vnius Dei cultus, qui fecit cœlum & terram, opinionem obseruandam religarent.
units.tr: As for the converts from the Gentiles, it does not appear that they shared their goods with one another and with the other believers. Rather, it appears that they kept their own property, as before. This is shown from the Corinthians, 1 Cor. last chapter, where it is said: "Now concerning the collections for the saints, as I have given order to the churches of Galatia, so do you also. On the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God has prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come." Likewise, to the Philippians, Phil. 4, the Apostle said: "Now you Philippians know also that in the beginning of the gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church communicated with me in the matter of giving and receiving but you only. For even in Thessalonica you sent once and again to my necessity. ... I am filled, having received from Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odour of sweetness." Also, Acts 11 records that when the prophet Agabus, in Antioch, in the presence of the Apostles Barnabas and Saul, signified by the Spirit that a great famine would come over the whole world, which happened under Claudius, the disciples, each according as he had, determined to send relief to the brethren who dwelt in Judaea, which they did, sending it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul. And this is what Augustine expressly says in book 3 of On Christian Doctrine, speaking thus: "The Spirit of God was so abundant in those Jews who first believed, out of whom the first Church of Jerusalem was made, that they sold all their possessions and laid the price at the feet of the Apostles to be distributed to the needy, and they dedicated themselves wholly to God as a new temple, in prayers and in the breaking of spiritual and bodily bread. Those who had formerly served the old temple did this, which is not written of any churches of the Gentiles, because they were not so near to it; they had images made by hand as gods." From this we understand that the Jews, kept under the law as under a schoolmaster, derived great benefit, so that the signs which were temporarily laid upon them, who served carnally, bound them to observe the worship of the one God who made heaven and earth.

units.la: Hic prosequitur secundum membrum secundæ distinctionis propositæ supra c. 103. ostendens, quod Gentiles non communicauerunt sibi inuicem omnia, quæ habebant, quod quatuor auctoritatibus probare conatur.
units.tr: Here he goes on to the second member of the second distinction proposed above in chapter 103, showing that the Gentiles did not share with one another all that they had. He tries to prove this by four authorities.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod hic nihil est penitus ad propositam quæstionem, nisi per hoc intendat probare, quod si gentes conuersæ proprium retinebant, etiam Apostoli conuersantes inter gentes proprium possidebant. Nam quæstio proposita non est de gentilibus, sed de Apostolis, an dominium rerum habuerint. Ostendere ergo, quod gentes non dimiserunt proprium, nihil est ad quæstionem, nisi velit ex hoc concludere, quod Apostoli, quando conuersabantur cum gentibus proprium habuerunt, sed illa probatio nulla est, quia sæpe homines diuersorum statuum insimul conuersantur, sicut laici & clerici, & nonnunquam etiam religiosi & seculares.
units.tr: But those who oppose this say that here there is nothing at all to the question proposed, unless he means by this to prove that, if the converted Gentiles kept their own property, then the Apostles, when they lived among the Gentiles, also possessed property of their own. For the question proposed is not about the Gentiles but about the Apostles, whether they had ownership of goods. So to show that the Gentiles did not give up their property has nothing to do with the question, unless he wants to conclude from it that the Apostles, when they dwelt among the Gentiles, had property of their own. But that proof is worthless, because people of different callings often live together, as laymen and clergy, and sometimes religious and secular too.

units.la: (Non videtur quod ipsi sibi inuicem & aliis credentibus communicauerunt sua.) Istud veritatem videtur habere de communitate quacunque gentilium in principio suæ conuersionis, postea tamen in Alexandria sub Marco nonnulli communem vitam duxerunt, (imo videtur quod ipsi retinuerunt sibi propria, sicut prius) verum est in principio conuersionis suæ, (sicut ordinau Galatiæ) non tanquam Dominus rerum ipsorum, sed sicut pater & doctor, cui sponte parebant (in vsum misistis mihi) non in dominium, quia Apostoli non quærebant nisi in vsum, non in dominium rerum, (acceptis) ad vtendū, non ad proprietatem habendam (per manus Barnabæ & Sauli) non quod ipsi portarent pecuniam, quamuis in tali necessitate licuisset, præsertim cum, vt videtur, non fuerint tunc Apostoli, sed dimiserunt per manus Barnabæ & Sauli, quia illi, qui portabant, erant in societate eorum, quibus non licuit aliquid facere de eleemosyna missa, nisi secundum dispositionem Barnabæ & Sauli, (vt omnia sua venderent.) Ex hoc patet secundum Augustinum, quod Iudæi illi conuersi vendiderunt possessiones suas, & nusquam inuenitur quod vendiderint nomine communitatis, quare non est dicendum, quod possessiones suas communitati dederunt, sed pretium ipsarum, (quod nullas ecclesias gentium fecisse scriptum est) nec in scripturis aliis reperitur, quod aliqua tota ecclesia gentium statim post conuersionem suam vel etiam citò post, hoc fecerit: tamen aliqui de ecclesia gentium hoc secerunt.
units.tr: ("It does not appear that they shared their goods with one another and with the other believers.") This seems true of any common life among the Gentiles at the beginning of their conversion. Afterwards, however, some under Mark in Alexandria did lead a common life. ("Rather, it appears that they kept their own property, as before.") This is true at the beginning of their conversion ("as I have given order to the churches of Galatia"), not as lords of their goods but as a father and teacher whom they obeyed willingly ("you have sent to my necessity"), not as ownership, because the Apostles sought only use and not ownership of goods ("having received") for using, not for holding property ("by the hands of Barnabas and Saul"). This was not because they themselves carried the money, although in such necessity it would have been lawful, especially since, as it seems, they were not then Apostles; rather they sent it by the hands of Barnabas and Saul, because those who carried it were in the company of those for whom it was not lawful to do anything with the alms sent except according to the arrangement of Barnabas and Saul. ("That they should sell all their possessions.") From this it is plain, according to Augustine, that those converted Jews sold their possessions, and nowhere is it found that they sold them in the name of a community. Therefore it should not be said that they gave their possessions to the community, but the price of them. ("Which is not written of any churches of the Gentiles.") Nor is it found in other Scriptures that any whole church of the Gentiles did this immediately after its conversion, or even soon after. Yet some individuals among the Gentile churches did this.

units.la: CAP. CVIII.
units.tr: CAP. CVIII.

units.la: Tertio videndum est vtrum pro rebus, quas habuerunt Apostoli, licet non legantur litigasse pro ipsis, eis licuerit litigare, & quod non licuerit, dicit hæreticus iste, ad quod probandum inducit Matth. 19. vbi Petrus pro se & aliis Apostolis Domino dixit: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia & secuti sumus te. Ex quo habetur secundum catholicos doctores, vt dicit, quod Apostoli reliquerunt ius agendi in iudicio, quod non stat cum tali persectione supererogationis, quæ implicat ad peccatum, sicut probat secundum eum Apostolus prima ad Corinth. 6. dicens: Iam quidem omnino delictum est in vobis: quia iudicia habetis inter vos, & ideo Christus, vt dicit, iniunxit perfectis, vt non litigent in iudicio Matth. 6. & Luc. 5. dicens, quod illa tantum intelligantur perfectis iniuncta, & similiter illud Apostoli prima Corinth. 6.
units.tr: Third, we must examine whether the Apostles, though they are not recorded as having gone to law over their property, were permitted to go to law, and whether this was not permitted, as this heretic says. To prove this he cites Matthew 19, where Peter said to the Lord on his own behalf and that of the other Apostles: "Behold, we have left all and followed you." From this, he says, the Catholic teachers conclude that the Apostles gave up the right to sue in court. That does not agree with such perfection of supererogation, which implies sin, as the Apostle proves according to him in 1 Corinthians 6, saying: "Now indeed there is altogether a fault among you, because you have lawsuits with one another." And therefore Christ, he says, enjoined on the perfect that they should not go to law in court (Matthew 6 and Luke 5), saying that only those precepts are understood to be enjoined on the perfect, and likewise that passage of the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 6.

units.la: Viso secundum istum, quod Apostoli, postquam fuerunt ad Apostolatum assumpti, habuerunt temporalium rerum dominium aliquando in speciali & aliquando in communi: Hic inquirit, an Apostolis licuit pro rebus temporalibus litigare. Et diuiditur in duas partes: quia primo improbat circa hanc quæstionem, assertionem appellantis. Secundo suam ponit assertionem. Secunda ibi: cum ergo quaeritur. Prima in duas: quia primo recitat assertionem appellantis, secundo ipsam impugnare conatur. Secunda in parte immediate sequenti ibi: In quibus iste hereticus mentitur. Primo ergo proponens quæstionem vtrum Apostolis licuit pro temporalibus litigare, dicit quod appellans tenet, quod non: fundans se in tribus auctoritatibus scripturæ diuinæ, sicut patet in litera.
units.tr: Having seen, according to him, that the Apostles, after they were called to the apostolate, at one time held dominion over temporal goods individually and at another time in common, he here asks whether it was lawful for the Apostles to go to law over temporal goods. The matter is divided into two parts: first he refutes the assertion of the appellant on this question; second he sets out his own assertion. The second begins at "therefore when it is asked." The first is in two parts: first he recites the assertion of the appellant, second he attempts to attack it. The second part begins immediately after, at "In which this heretic lies." So first, proposing the question whether the Apostles were permitted to litigate over temporal goods, he says that the appellant holds that they were not, relying on three authorities of divine Scripture, as is clear from the text.

units.la: (Ecce nos reliquimus omnia) Scilicet quæ non sunt necessaria ad vitæ sustentationem & officii nostri executionem. Huiusmodi autem est ius agendi in iudicio, ergo tale ius Apostoli reliquerunt. (quod non stat cum tali perfectione supererogationis) licet ius agendi in iudicio stet cum perfectione essentiali & primaria ac principali, scilicet cum caritate, quia (scilicet) potest quis stante caritate perfecta retinere vel ius agendi recipere in iudicio, quemadmodum sancti patres multi recipiendo dispensationem bonorum ecclesiae receperunt etiam ius agendi in iudicio solummodo propter Deum, & bonum commune retinuerunt. Tamen tale ius agendi in iudicio non stat cum perfectione secundaria, quae est abdicatio omnis proprietatis & iuris agendi, quemadmodum castitas coniugalis stat cum caritate perfecta, propter quod Augustinus non praefert caelibatum Iohannis Baptistae coniugio Abrahae: non stat tamen cum virginitate, (quae implicat ad peccatum) vellet dicere, quod implicat ad peccatum: quia non talis perfectio supererogationis, sed ius agendi implicat ad peccatum. (Iam quidem omnino delictum est in vobis: quia iudicia habetis.) Ista est secunda auctoritas, in qua fundat se appellans, de qua posterius disseretur. (Christus iniunxit perfectis ut non litigent in iudicio. Matth. 6. & Luca 6.) de hoc etiam post tractabitur, (dicens quod illa tantum intelligantur perfectis iniuncta) hoc non dicit sic nude appellans, ut postea apparebit. Unde dicunt isti, quod ille impugnatus saepe male & truncate ac peruerse dicta recitat appellantis.
units.tr: ("Behold, we have left all.") That is, things which are not necessary for the sustenance of life and the execution of our office. Such is the right to sue in court; therefore the Apostles left this right. (That this does not agree with such perfection of supererogation.) Although the right to sue in court agrees with essential, primary and principal perfection, namely charity, since (that is) a man may, while possessing perfect charity, retain or receive the right to sue in court, just as many holy Fathers, receiving the stewardship of the goods of the Church, also received the right to sue in court solely for the sake of God and the common good, and retained it. Yet such a right to sue in court does not agree with secondary perfection, which is the renunciation of all ownership and of the right to sue, just as conjugal chastity agrees with perfect charity, for which reason Augustine does not prefer the celibacy of John the Baptist to the marriage of Abraham; yet it does not agree with virginity, (which implies sin): he would say that it implies sin, because it is not such a perfection of supererogation, but the right to sue implies sin. (Now indeed there is altogether a fault among you, because you have lawsuits.) This is the second authority on which the appellant relies, which will be discussed later. (Christ enjoined on the perfect that they should not go to law in court. Matthew 6 and Luke 6.) This too will be treated afterwards, (saying that only those precepts are understood to be enjoined on the perfect): this the appellant does not say so baldly, as will appear later. Hence those men say that the one who is attacked often recites the words of the appellant badly, truncated and perversely.

units.la: CAP. CIX.
units.tr: CHAP. CIX.

units.la: IN quibus iste haereticus mentitur aperte: quia quod in Evangeliis praedictis dicitur, non potest de perfectis intelligi, prout ipse sumit perfectos. Illos enim solos perfectos asserit, qui a se temporalium omnium proprietatem abdicarunt & dominium sibi duntaxat retento simplici usu facti. Constat autem, quod illa verba ei, qui vult tecum in iudicio contendere & tunicam tuam tollere, dimitte ei & pallium, posita Matt. 5. & Luca 6. intelliguntur de his, qui in proprio temporalia obtinebant. Loquitur enim illi Dominus, qui tunicam habebat & pallium, cum dixit ei: qui voluerit tunicam tuam tollere, dimitte ei & pallium, sicque patet, quod & tunicam habebat & pallium is, cui loquebatur. Praeterea statim illi, cui praedicta iniunxerat, sic praecepit ibidem: Qui petit illa a te, da ei: & volenti mutuare a te ne avertere. Ex quibus etiam patet, quod habentibus temporalia est locutus, cum dixerit quod det ei qui a se petit: quod non posset facere, cum dare sit accipienti facere, nisi dominium quo ad temporalia obtineret: non etiam mutuare posset, nisi eius quod mutuaret esset Dominus, cum in mutuo a mutuante in eo, qui mutuum recipit, rei mutuatae sit dominium transferendum.
units.tr: In these matters this heretic plainly lies, because what is said in the Gospels cited above cannot be understood of the perfect as he takes the perfect. For he asserts that only those are perfect who have renounced the ownership of all temporal goods and retained for themselves merely the simple use of them. But it is clear that those words, to him who wants to go to law with you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well, set down in Matthew 5 and Luke 6, are to be understood of those who held temporal goods as their own. For the Lord spoke to a man who had a tunic and a cloak when he said, whoever wants to take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well; so it is plain that the man he was speaking to had both a tunic and a cloak. Moreover, straight after this, the same passage instructs the one to whom these things were addressed: Give to everyone who asks of you, and do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you. From this too it is plain that he was speaking to those who had temporal goods, since he said that one should give to the man who asks of him. This he could not do unless he held ownership of temporal goods, because giving means making something the recipient's; nor could he lend unless the thing lent were his own, since in a loan the ownership of the thing lent passes from the lender to the one who receives the loan.

units.la: Recitata assertione appellantis, hic nititur eam reprobare, ostendendo videlicet quod auctoritates, quas adducit pro se Matth. 5. & Luca 6. & de Apostolo 1. Corinth. 6. pro ipso non concludunt, & dividit in duas partes: quia primo ostendit, quod dictae auctoritates non faciunt ad propositum appellantis, secundo ipse exponit dictas auctoritates secundum mentem suam. Secunda ibi: & ideo dicendum quod praecepit illa. Prima in duas: quia primo conatur ostendere quod verba illa: Qui vult tecum in iudicio contendere &c. posita Matth. 5. & Luc. 6. appellans male intelligit. Secundo probat, quod male intelligit auctoritatem Apostoli prima Corinth. 6. Secunda ibi: Item illud Apostoli. Prima dividitur in quatuor: quia primo ostendit, quod verba praedicta non fuerunt dicta abdicantibus omnium proprietatem, sicut appellans intelligit, ut iste dicit. Secundo ostendit, quod non fuerunt dicta Apostolis. Tertio ostendit, quod Apostoli habuerunt ius agendi in iudicio. Quarto ostendit, quod verba illa omnibus dicta fuerunt. Secunda ibi: Item ipse intelligit. Tertia ibi: Item attendat. Quarta ibi: Et quod verba praedicta. In prima igitur parte ostendit, quod illa verba: qui vult tecum in iudicio contendere &c. dicta fuerunt tantum modo habentibus temporalia, quod primo ostendit ex ipsis verbis: quia loquitur illi, qui habebat tunicam & pallium. Secundo ibi: Praeterea statim, probat idem per verba, quae sequuntur, quae diriguntur danti & mutuanti, sed dans & mutuans habent rerum dominium, ergo praedicta verba solummodo dicta fuerunt dominium rerum habentibus.
units.tr: Having recited the assertion of the appellant, he here undertakes to refute it, namely by showing that the passages he adduces in support of himself, Matthew 5 and Luke 6, and the Apostle's words in 1 Corinthians 6, do not support his case. He divides the discussion into two parts: first he shows that the said passages do not serve the appellant's purpose; second, he himself expounds the said passages according to his own understanding. The second part begins at "and therefore it must be said that he commanded those things." The first part is divided into two: first he tries to show that the appellant misunderstands the words, who wants to go to law with you etc., set down in Matthew 5 and Luke 6; second, he proves that the appellant misunderstands the authority of the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 6. The second part begins at "likewise that saying of the Apostle." The first is divided into four: first he shows that the words cited were not spoken to those who renounce all ownership of property, as the appellant understands them, as this man says. Second, he shows that they were not spoken to the Apostles. Third, he shows that the Apostles had a right to sue in court. Fourth, he shows that those words were addressed to everyone. The second begins at "likewise he understands"; the third at "likewise let him consider"; the fourth at "and that the aforesaid words." In the first part, then, he shows that the words who wants to go to law with you etc. were spoken only to those who had temporal goods, which he shows first from the words themselves, because he speaks to the man who had a tunic and a cloak. Second, at "moreover straight after," he proves the same from the words that follow, which are addressed to the giver and the lender; but givers and lenders hold ownership of things; therefore the aforesaid words were spoken only to those who held ownership of things.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt ipsum tripliciter in praedictis deficere. Primo cum dicit, quod verba praedicta non fuerunt dicta perfectis, accipiendo perfectos pro illis, qui omnium temporalium abdicant proprietatem.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he fails in three respects in the foregoing. First, when he says that the aforesaid words were not spoken to the perfect, taking the perfect to be those who renounce all ownership of temporal goods.

units.la: Secundo dicunt, quod falsum imponit appellanti, cum asserit, appellantem illos solos vocare perfectos, qui omnium temporalium abdicant proprietatem, simplici usu facti sibi retento.
units.tr: Second, they say that he falsely imputes to the appellant that he calls perfect only those who renounce all ownership of temporal goods while keeping the simple use of them.

units.la: Tertio dicunt, quod argumenta, per quae conclusionem suam probare conatur, non concludunt.
units.tr: Third, they say that the arguments by which he tries to prove his conclusion do not prove it.

units.la: Ad evidentiam autem dicendorum est ad memoriam revocandum, quod secundum istos talia vocabula meum, tuum, suum, habere, ipsius, eius & consimilia in significatione convenientia multipliciter accipiuntur in scripturis, quia aliquando important dominium & proprietatem: aliquando important usum facti: aliquando ius vtendi: aliquando custodiam rei depositae vel commissae: aliquando consuetudinem habitandi vel alio modo vtendi: aliquando originem, & aliis modis, quos non est facile enumerare, accipi possunt. Ista per scripturas & modos loquendi vulgares possent patenter ostendi: etiam aliquo modo prius fuit ostensum.
units.tr: To make clear what is to be said, it must be recalled that, according to these men, such words as meum, tuum, suum, habere, ipsius, eius and similar terms of like meaning are used in many ways in Scripture: sometimes they signify ownership and property; sometimes they signify the mere use of a thing; sometimes the right of using it; sometimes the custody of a thing deposited or entrusted; sometimes the habit of dwelling or of using in some other way; sometimes origin; and they may be taken in other ways that are not easy to list. These points could be plainly shown from Scripture and from ordinary modes of speech, and in some measure this has been shown before.

units.la: Ex isto ostendunt, quod iste errat dicendo, quod verba praedicta: Qui vult tecum in iudicio contendere tendere &c. non fuerunt dicta abdicantibus omnia temporalia quo ad dominium, sed habentibus rerum dominium. Quia non magis debent nec possunt de iure retinere sibi res, quas habent quo ad vsum proprietatem omnium abdicantes contra voluntatem auferre volentium, quam habentes rerum dominium; cum nihil iuris vel minus iuris in huiusmodi rebus habere noscantur, sed omnium abdicantes dominium licite possunt habere tunicam & pallium ac multas res alias temporales: quarum tamen non habent dominium, ergo non magis possunt sibi res huiusmodi retinere contra voluntatem auferre volentium, quam illi qui huiusmodi rerum habent dominium. Si igitur secundum consilium Christi habentes talium rerum dominium, non debent eas contra voluntatem auferre volentium retinere, sed dimittere: Multo magis qui non habent, nisi solum vsum huiusmodi rerum non debent eas contra voluntatem auferre volentium retinere, sed secundum consilium vel praeceptum Christi dimittere.
units.tr: From this they argue that this man is wrong in saying that the aforesaid words, who wants to go to law with you etc., were not spoken to those who renounce all temporal goods as to ownership, but to those who hold ownership of things. For those who renounce all property, while retaining the use of goods, ought not, and by right cannot, keep those goods against the will of the one who wants to take them, any more than those who hold ownership of things; since they are known to have no right, or less right, in such goods. Those who renounce ownership may lawfully have a tunic, a cloak and many other temporal goods, of which, nonetheless, they do not hold ownership. Therefore they cannot keep such goods against the will of one who wants to take them any more than those who hold ownership of such goods. If, then, according to Christ's counsel, those who hold ownership of such things ought not to keep them against the will of one who wants to take them, but ought to let them go, much more those who have only the use of such goods ought not to keep them against the will of one who wants to take them, but according to Christ's counsel or command should let them go.

units.la: Item, si habentes res temporales quo ad vsum absque dominio non debent res suas dimittere, cum alius vult eas habere, quemadmodum debent illi, qui habent rerum temporalium proprietatem, ergo carentes proprietate debent res suas defendere, quando alii habentes proprietatem non debent res suas defendere: quod falsum est.
units.tr: Likewise: if those who have temporal goods as to use without ownership need not let their goods go when another wants to have them, as those who hold ownership of temporal goods need not, then those lacking ownership must defend their goods, while others holding ownership need not defend theirs. That is false.

units.la: Quia defendere res temporales contingit dupliciter, vel pro rebus in iudicio contendendo, vel per vim violentiam repellendo, sed carentes proprietate non debent res suas defendere in iudicio contendendo: cum absque omni iure agendi, & defendendi nullus valeat in iudicio litigare, ergo si carent omni iure in rebus, quo valeant in iudicio litigare, non debent res suas defendere in iudicio contendendo: nec debent res suas defendere per vim violentiam repellendo magis, quam alii habentes proprietatem rerum: cum eis non plus pugnare liceat, quam aliis proprietatem habentibus, ergo habentes tantum modo res, quo ad vsum, non debent magis res illas defendere, quam habentes rerum proprietatem.
units.tr: For defending temporal goods happens in two ways: either by contending for the goods in court, or by repelling force with force. But those lacking ownership need not defend their goods by contending in court, since no one can go to law without any right of suing and defending. Therefore, if they lack every right in the goods by which they could go to law in court, they need not defend their goods by contending in court. Nor need they defend their goods by repelling force with force any more than others who hold ownership of goods, since they are no more permitted to fight than others who hold ownership. Therefore those who hold goods only as to use ought not to defend those goods any more than those who hold ownership of goods.

units.la: Amplius, non minorem contemptum rerum temporalium debent ostendere & habere carentes rerum proprietate, quam habentes: sed habentes proprietatem rerum, & ipsas tamen volentibus auferre dimittentes, ostendunt se res temporales contemnere, ergo multo fortius haec debent facere non habentes proprietatem rerum, quibus vruntur sibi. Rursus, non magis debet vel tenetur quis exigere vel defendere illud, quod neque quam sibi debetur, vel minus debetur, quam alius illud, quod sibi debetur vel magis sibi debetur, sed res temporales non sunt debitae carentibus omni iure in eis, vel minus sunt debitae. Unde nullum habens ius in pallio, non potest petere pallium tanquam debitum, sed de gratia solum, res autem temporales sunt debitae illis, qui proprietatem habent in eis, ergo carentes proprietate & omni iure agendi in iudicio, non debent, neque magis exigere neque magis defendere res temporales, quam habentes proprietatem, ergo ita tenentur dimittere, sicut alii. Item, eisdem Christus dicit verba illa: qui vult tecum in iudicio contendere &c. quibus dicit, non resistere malo, sed Christus non dicit non resistere malo magis habentibus proprietatem temporalium, quam non habentibus, ergo nec illa verba, qui vult tecum in iudicio contendere &c. dixit plus habentibus proprietatem temporalium, quam non habentibus proprietatem.
units.tr: Furthermore, those lacking ownership of temporal goods ought to show and have no less contempt for them than those who have ownership. But those who hold ownership of goods, and yet let them go to those who want to take them, show that they despise temporal goods; therefore those who do not hold ownership of the goods they use ought much more to do this. Again, no one is bound to demand or defend what is not owed to him, or is owed to him less than to another, or what is owed to him more. But temporal goods are not owed to those who have no right in them, or are owed to them less. Hence someone with no right in a cloak cannot demand the cloak as a debt, but only as a gift; whereas temporal goods are owed to those who hold ownership of them. Therefore those lacking ownership and every right of suing in court ought not to demand or defend temporal goods any more than those who hold ownership; so they are bound to let them go just as others are. Likewise, Christ speaks those words, who wants to go to law with you etc., in the same passage in which he says do not resist evil; but Christ does not say do not resist evil more to those who hold ownership of temporal goods than to those who do not; therefore neither did he say the words who wants to go to law with you etc. more to those who hold ownership of temporal goods than to those who lack ownership.

units.la: Dicunt igitur isti quod Christus verba praedicta omnibus dirigebat, scilicet habentibus & non habentibus proprietatem, ut hic sit sensus: Qui vult tecum in iudicio contendere & tunicam tuam sive sit tua quantum ad vsum tantum, sive sit tua quantum ad proprietatem, tollere: dimitte ei & pallium, sive in pallio habeas vsum tantum, sive etiam habeas dominium & proprietatem, quando autem & quomodo haec sic sint implenda, in sequentibus declarabunt.
units.tr: Therefore these men say that Christ addressed the aforementioned words to all, that is, to those who have ownership and to those who do not, so that the sense is this: "If anyone wants to contend with you in judgment and take away your tunic," whether it is yours only as to use or yours as to ownership, "let him have your cloak also," whether you have only use of the cloak or also have lordship and ownership of it. When and how these things are to be fulfilled, they will explain in what follows.

units.la: Secundo dicunt isti, quod ille impugnatus appellanti falsum imponit, cum asserit eum illos solos vocare perfectos, qui omnium temporalium abdicant proprietatem, simplici vsu facti retento. Ad cuius evidentiam duo praemittunt: quorum primum est, quod aliud est esse perfectum, & aliud est esse in statu perfectionis. Multi enim sunt in statu perfectionis, qui tamen non sunt perfecti: sicut religiosi & praelati sunt in statu perfectionis, & tamen multi eorum non sunt perfecti: imo sunt scelerati & pessimi. Multi etiam non sunt in statu perfectionis, qui tamen non sunt perfecti perfectione essentiali & primaria, quae est caritas Dei, sicut multi reges & alii divites utentes coniugio, & proprietatem divitiarum habentes; fuerunt perfecti propter caritatem perfectam in eis, & tamen non fuerunt in statu perfectionis, secundum quod communiter de statu perfectionis moderni loquuntur. Secundum quod isti praemittunt est, quod sicut inter perfectos inveniuntur gradus: quia quidam sunt perfecti, quidam perfectiores, & quidam perfectissimi: ita inter status perfectionis reperiuntur gradus consimiles. Aliam vero distinctionem de perfectione essentiali & secundaria, ipsi supponunt tanquam alibi declaratam. Ex his ad propositum dicunt, quod appellans nequaquam dicit, quod illi soli sunt perfecti, qui omnium temporalium abdicant proprietatem, simplici vsu facti retento: nec etiam intendit quod illi soli sunt in statu perfectionis: sed intendit quod multi alii sunt perfecti perfectione essentiali, quae caritas est, & etiam multi alii sunt in statu perfectionis, sed non in statu perfectissimo, quantum ad euangelicam paupertatem: quamvis possint esse in statu perfectissimo quantum ad aliquas alias conditiones status perfectionis.
units.tr: Secondly, these men say that the one whom they attack imposes a falsehood on his opponent, since he asserts that only those are called perfect who renounce ownership of all temporal goods while keeping the simple use of things. To make this clear, they first set out two points. The first is that to be perfect is one thing, and to be in the state of perfection is another. For many are in the state of perfection who nonetheless are not perfect, just as religious and prelates are in the state of perfection, and yet many of them are not perfect; indeed, they are wicked and very bad. Many also are not in the state of perfection who nonetheless are not perfect in the essential and primary perfection, which is the love of God; just as many kings and other rich men who use marriage and hold ownership of riches were perfect because of the perfect love of God in them, and yet they were not in the state of perfection, according to the way that moderns commonly speak of the state of perfection. The second point they set out is that, just as there are degrees among the perfect (for some are perfect, some more perfect, and some most perfect), so similar degrees are found among the states of perfection. As for another distinction, between essential and secondary perfection, they take it as something explained elsewhere. From these points they argue to the matter at hand: the one who makes the assertion does not at all say that only those are perfect who renounce ownership of all temporal goods while keeping the simple use of them; nor does he intend that only those are in the state of perfection; rather, he means that many others are perfect in essential perfection, which is love, and that also many others are in the state of perfection, but not in the most perfect state with respect to evangelical poverty, although they may be in the most perfect state with respect to some other conditions of the state of perfection.

units.la: Tertio dicunt ipsum deficere: quia argumenta sua conclusionem suam quam intendit, non concludunt: quod perspicuo literam apparebit. (Quod in euangelijs prædictis dicitur non potest de perfectis intelligi,) Imo de illis potissime intelligitur: quia illi, qui omnia dimiserunt quo ad dominium & quo ad proprietatem, debent esse promti ad dimittendum vlum extra necessitatem extremam ex causa magis quam alii, (prout ipse sumit perfectos,) etiam sumendo perfectos strictissime pro illis, qui omnia dimiserant, retento simplici vsu facti, debent verba prædicta principaliter de eis intelligi, (illos enim solos perfectos asserit qui à se temporalium &c.) Dicunt isti, quod mentitur aperte: quia nusquam illos solos vocat perfectos, quamuis illos solos dicat esse in statu perfectissimæ paupertatis: sed multos dicit perfectos, qui non sunt in statu perfectissimæ paupertatis. (Intelliguntur de his qui in proprio talia obtinebant,) hoc est verum: sed non tantum de illis, sed etiam de aliis, & ideo ex hoc sequitur, quod non intelliguntur de perfectis tantum. (Loquitur enim Dominus illi qui tunicam habebat & pallium) verum est, siue haberet pallium & tunicam quo ad proprietatem, siue quo ad vsum: & ita loquebatur: & habentibus proprietatem tunicam & pallii, quamuis non omnibus præcipiendo, sed consulendo quibusdam & aliis præcipiendo: sicut post patebit, (tunicam tuam) siue quo ad proprietatem siue quo ad vsum (& tunicam habebat & pallium in cui loquebatur) vel habere poterat, & hoc quo ad proprietatem vel quo ad vsum: & ita plane patet, quod illud argumentum non concludit, quod Christus tantum modo loquebatur habentibus proprietatem: quia medium, in quo fundatur, est falsum, scilicet quod nullus habet tunicam & pallium, nisi habeat proprietatem. Fratres enim Minores secundum ipsorum Regulam possunt habere tunicas & libros & res alias multas: qui tamen nullius rei habent proprietatem, beatus etiam Paulus habuit vincula, sicut patet ad Philip. 1. & ad Colo. vltim. & 1. Thim. 1. quæ etiam dixit esse sua, quæ tamen non erant sua quo ad dominium, sed quo ad dominium erant gentilium, qui vinculis beatum Paulum ligauerant, & ideo dicunt, quod argumenta istius semper vel fere in tota ista materia per fallaciam æquiuocationis peccant aperte, si enim æquiuocationes nominum intellexisset, ex sola verecundia argumenta talia dimisisset. (Quipetitilla à te da ei) hoc est, dona vel concede, si cui licet, multi enim vtentes rebus alienis habent licentiam dandi & concedendi aliis res eadem, & in hoc casu non solum Dominus rei, sed etiam vtens re aliena: & habens talem licentiam debet concedere aut dare petenti, nisi ratio obstet, quare non expedit neque concedere neque dare, unde de isto amplius patebit inferius. (Et volenti mutuare à te ne auertere.) Sic habetur sub Bulla, cuius habui copiam pro opere isto, sed textus Bibliæ est: volenti mutuare à te ne auertaris, & illa est grammatica melior. Contingit autem mutuare absque rei mutuatæ dominio, sicut post patebit, ideo illa verba non tantum de habentibus proprietatem, sed etiam de aliis intelliguntur esse dicta. (Ex quibus etiam patet quod habentibus temporalia est locutus) sed non tantum illis, (cum dare sit accipientis facere.) De isto dictum est prius c. 9. vbi ostensum est, quod verbum dandi accipitur aliter, quam pro transferre rei dominium, sunt autem exempla ibi addita tam aperta, quod alia adducere ipsis videtur superfluum, dare igitur non est semper accipientis facere quo ad dominium, sed quo ad vsum, vel aliquo alio modo: sicut etiam non semper dando transfertur dominium, (habet eiusdem rei dominium.) Contingit dando transferre rei dominium dupliciter: scilicet auctoritate propria, vel auctoritate vel licentia alterius, quicquid sit de illo qui auctoritate propria dando transfert rei dominium, certum est de illo, qui auctoritate vel licentia alterius dando transfert rei dominium, quod non oportet quod habeat prius rei dominium, hoc auctoritatibus scripturæ diuinæ probatur aperte. Legitur enim Genes. 24. de seruo Abrahæ, quod prolatis vasis argenteis & aureis ac vestibus, quæ erant Domini sui, dedit eas Rebeccæ pro munere: & ita illa non erant serui quo ad dominium: & tamen dando transferebat dominium. De Moyse etiam dicitur Iosue 13. Dedit Moyses possessionem tribui filiorum Ruben. Illa tamen possessio non erat Moysi quo ad dominium, sed auctoritate Dei dedit. Aliæ auctoritates inueniuntur quamplurimæ, quibus patenter posset ostendi, quod aliquis nomine vel auctoritate seu de licentia alterius dando transfert rei dominium, cuius tamen non habet dominium seu proprietatem, & ita per hoc, quod aliquis dat rem accipienti, non potest ostendi, quod dans rei habuerit proprietatem.
