(Non etiam mutuare posset, nisi eius quod mutuaret esset Dominus,) hic etiam, vt dicunt, per æquiuocationem procedit, nam potest quis mutuare rem dupliciter, vel nomine proprio, vel nomine alterius seu de auctoritate aut de licentia alterius. Esto quod primus habeat dominium rei mutuatæ: secundus tamen non habet dominium rei mutuatæ. Sic enim seruus potest mutuare pecuniam Domini sui, quemadmodum potest facere eleemosynam de rebus Domini sui, & diuersis modis de rebus Domini sui disponere. Prædicta autem Domini verba, volentimutuare à te ne auertaris, non tantum diriguntur ad Dominos temporalium rerum, sed etiam ad omnes, qui aliquam dispensandi potestatem res temporales siue principalem sine secundariam seu commissariam noscuntur habere. Vult enim Dominus per verba prædicta vniversos, qui possunt, ad benefaciendum proximis inuitare, & ideo cum non solum Domini rerum, sed etiam nonnunquam dispensatores rerum, possint mutuare res temporales proximis opportunas, prædicta verba Saluatoris non solum ad Dominos, sed generaliter ad omnes, qui auctoritate, vel nomine quocunque possunt mutuare res temporales debent extendi: & ita falsum est, quod dicitur, quod nec mutuare posset nisi eius quod mutuaret esset Dominus. Est etiam falsum stricte capiendo vocabulum mutuandi scilicet pro transferre dominium rei mutuatæ: quia seruus potest transferre dominium rerum Domini sui, nomine Domini sui, & auctoritate eius: quarum tamen non habet dominium. De hac materia supra habetur capit. 30. vbi etiam iste impugnatus dicit hæc verba: Serum, qui iussu Domini sui pecuniam mutuat, non debet dici habere vsum seu abusum simplicem facti. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod seruus potest mutuare pecuniam Domini sui: & tamen non est Dominus pecuniæ mutuatæ. ( Cum in mutuo à mutuante in eum qui mutuum recipit rei mutuatæ fit dominium transferendum. ) Hoc etiam habet vnum sensum falsum: imo duos. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod mutuum in scripturis dupliciter accipitur. Vno enim modo accipitur pro illo, cuius dominium transfertur in recipientem. Alio modo accipitur pro præstito: siue transferatur in dominium recipientis, siue non transferatur in dominium eius. Primo modo accipiendo mutuum, non semper transfertur mutuum à mutuante, tanquam ab habente dominium: quia mutuans posset carere dominio rei mutuatæ, sicut patet in notabili præcedenti. Accipiendo etiam mutuum secundo modo, planum est, quod sic illud, quod hic dicitur, non continet veritatem. Item sicut quis potest commodare rem alteri absque translatione dominii, ita potest quis præstare rem alteri absque translatione dominii. Quod autem mutuum sic accipiatur, ex scriptura diuina patet aperte, sic enim accipitur 4. Regum 4. cum Helisæus cuidam mulieri dixit: vade & pete mutuo ab omnibus vicinis vasa vacua non pauca, quæ tamen vasa non debebant in eius transferri dominium, & ca. 6. sic legitur: Accidit autem, vt cum vnus materiam succidisset, caderet ferrum securis in aquam exclamauit ille, & ait: heu heu Domine mi, & hoc ipsum mutuo acceperam: vbi tamen rei mutuatæ non fuit translatum dominium in recipientem, sic ergo patet, quod non semper in mutuo transfertur dominium mutuatæ in eum qui recipit, licet accipiendo mutuum, vt in scientiis legalibus sæpe accipitur mutuo, rei mutuatæ dominium in eum qui recipit transferatur, sed scriptura diuina modis loquendi & vtendi vocabulis, scientiis legalibus nequaquam astringitur, sicut patet de commodato, quod secundum iura in rebus vsu consumptibilibus minime reperitur, nisi quando commodatur ad pompam, vt ditior quis appareat. In scriptura tamen diuina insinuatur aperte panes posse commodari ad vescendum. Vnde & Christus ait, sicut habetur Lucæ 11. Quis vestrum habebit amicum & ibit ad illum media nocte & dicet illi: amice commoda mihi tres panes, quoniam amicus meus venit de via ad me: & non habeo quod ponam ante illum. Ex quibus verbis aperte colligitur, quod panes commodari possunt ad vescendum, & ita scriptura sacra ad modos accipiendi vocabula scientiarum legalium artari non debet, licet igitur non inueniretur in aliqua scientia legali, quod non semper in mutuo rei mutuatæ transfertur dominium: in scriptura tamen diuina reperitur aperte, quod non semper in mutuo rei mutuatæ in eum qui recipit transfertur dominium, & sic accipitur mutuum in verbis Christi, cum dicit, volenti mutuari à te ne auertaris, cuius ratio est, quia, sicut dictum est prius, Saluator per verba prædicta discipulos suos ad benefaciendum proximis suis volebat inducere, contingit autem benefacere alicui mutuando rem sibi opportunam, non solum in eum transferendo dominium, sed etiam solummodo præstando eam sibi absque translatione dominii, quare mutuare communissime accipi debet, & non solum stricte pro transferre dominium. Ex prædictis patet, quod argumentum istud secundum non probat, quod verba prædicta: qui vult tecum in iudicio contendere &c. dicta fuerunt tantum proprietatem rerum habentibus: imo dicta fuerunt omnibus, vel qui nomine proprio vel qui nomine alieno res possunt dare vel præstare. Multi autem non habentes proprietatem rerum possunt nomine alieno, seu de licentia alterius res dare & præstare. Quia quandoque aliquas res possunt præstare, & per consequens mutuare large accepto vocabulo, quas tamen non possunt dare, multi etiam præstant res, quas nolunt dare, vt habeatur distinctio inter ista duo consilia Christi: qui petit à te da ei, & volenti mutuari à te ne auertaris, & talem distinctionem inter duo prædicta Glossa super præmissa insinuate videtur, cum dicit: duo genera præstandi complectitur: vel enim benevole damus vel reddituro commodamus, & Glossa super illud Lucæ 6. Et si mutuum dederis &c. Ait: duo sunt genera beneficii: vel cum benevole damus quod damus: vel cum reddituro commodamus. Qui enim petenti dat, benevole donat: qui autem mutuat, reddituro commodat: quia mutuum etiam large acceptum est reddendum. Ex prædictis autem Glossis etiam patet, quod mutuum in verbis Saluatoris pro commodato accipitur, quod autem commodatur, vt verbum commodandi in scriptura sacra accipitur, non semper in eius qui recipit transfertur dominium, quare nec mutuum, vt in euangelio accipitur, semper in eius qui recipit transfertur dominium.
units.tr: Thirdly, they say that he fails, because his arguments do not prove the conclusion he intends, as will be plain from the text itself. What is said in the aforementioned Gospels cannot be understood of the perfect, but on the contrary it is understood most of all of them. Those who have given up everything, both ownership and possession, ought to be readier than others to give up the use of things beyond extreme necessity, for that cause. [This is so] as he himself takes the perfect, even taking the perfect in the strictest sense as those who gave up everything while keeping the simple use of the thing. The aforesaid words ought chiefly to be understood of them, for he asserts that only those are perfect who renounce temporal goods from themselves, etc. These men say that he plainly lies, because he nowhere calls only those perfect, although he says that only they are in the state of the most perfect poverty. Rather, he calls many perfect who are not in the state of the most perfect poverty. They are understood of those who held such things as their own. This is true, but they are not understood of those only; they are understood of others too. Therefore it follows that they are not understood of the perfect alone. For the Lord spoke to the one who had a tunic and a cloak. This is true, whether he had the cloak and tunic as property or only in use, and so he spoke: and to those who have a tunic and cloak as property, though not commanding all of them but counselling some and commanding others, as will appear later. Your tunic, whether as property or in use, and he had a tunic and a cloak, in which he spoke, or could have had, and this either as property or in use. So it is plain that this argument does not prove that Christ spoke only to those who had property. For the middle term on which it rests is false, namely that no one has a tunic and cloak unless he has property. The Friars Minor, according to their own Rule, may have tunics, books and many other things, yet they have no property in any of them. The blessed Paul also had bonds, as appears in Philippians 1, Colossians last, and 1 Timothy 1, and he called them his own, though they were not his by ownership but belonged to the Gentiles who had bound the blessed Paul in chains. Therefore they say that the arguments of this man, always or almost always throughout this whole matter, plainly err by the fallacy of equivocation. For had he understood the equivocations of the terms, he would have dropped such arguments out of shame alone. Whoever asks of you, give to him: that is, give or grant if one is allowed to. For many who use other people's things have licence to give and grant the same things to others, and in this case not only the owner of the thing but also the one who uses another's thing. A person with such licence ought to grant or give to one who asks, unless some reason stands in the way why it is not expedient either to grant or to give. On this point more will be said below. And from him who would borrow, do not turn away. So it stands under the Bull, of which I had a copy for this work, but the Bible text reads: from him who would borrow, do not turn away, and that is the better grammar. Moreover, one may lend without ownership of the thing lent, as will appear later. Therefore those words were spoken not only of those who have property but also of others. From these things it is also plain that he spoke of those who have temporal goods, but not of those only, since to give is to make it the receiver's. This was said before, in chapter 9, where it was shown that the word to give is taken otherwise than for transferring ownership of a thing. The examples added there are so clear that to bring others would seem superfluous. Thus to give is not always, as to ownership, to make it the receiver's, but as to use, or in some other way. Likewise, by giving, ownership is not always transferred: he has the ownership of the same thing. By giving, ownership of a thing may be transferred in two ways: by one's own authority, or by the authority or licence of another. Whatever may be said of the one who by his own authority, in giving, transfers ownership of a thing, it is certain of the one who, by the authority or licence of another, in giving transfers ownership of a thing, that he need not first have ownership of the thing. This is proved plainly by the authorities of divine Scripture. For we read in Genesis 24 that the servant of Abraham brought out silver and gold vessels and garments, which were his master's, and gave them to Rebekah as a gift. So they were not the servant's as to ownership, and yet by giving he transferred ownership. It is also said of Moses in Joshua 13: Moses gave possession to the tribe of the sons of Reuben. Yet that possession was not Moses' as to ownership; he gave it by the authority of God. Very many other authorities could be found that plainly show that someone, in the name or by the authority or licence of another, in giving transfers ownership of a thing of which he has no ownership or property. So from the fact that someone gives a thing to the receiver, it cannot be shown that the giver had ownership of it. Nor could he lend, unless he were the owner of what he lends: here too, they say, the argument proceeds by equivocation. For a person may lend a thing in two ways: either in his own name, or in the name of another, or by the authority or licence of another. Suppose the first has ownership of the thing lent; the second nevertheless does not have ownership of the thing lent. Thus a servant may lend his master's money, just as he may give alms from his master's goods and dispose of his master's goods in various ways. The aforesaid words of the Lord, from him who would borrow, do not turn away, are addressed not only to the owners of temporal goods but also to all who are known to have some power of dispensing temporal goods, whether principal, secondary or entrusted. For the Lord by these words wishes all who are able to be invited to do good to their neighbours. Therefore, since not only the owners of things but sometimes also the stewards of things can lend temporal goods useful to neighbours, the aforesaid words of the Saviour must be extended not only to owners but generally to all who, by authority or in whatever name, can lend temporal goods. So it is false that he could not lend unless he were the owner of what he lends. It is also false, taking the word to lend strictly, namely for transferring ownership of the thing lent, because a servant can transfer ownership of his master's goods in his master's name and by his authority, though he has no ownership of them. This matter is treated above in chapter 30, where this man under attack also says these words: A servant who lends money at his master's command ought not to be said to have simple use or abuse of the thing. From these words it is plainly stated that a servant can lend his master's money, and yet he is not the owner of the money lent. Since in a loan ownership of the thing must pass from the lender to the one who receives the loan. This also has a false sense, indeed two. To make this clear, they say it must be known that loan is taken in Scripture in two ways. In one way it is taken for that whose ownership passes to the recipient. In another way it is taken for what is furnished, whether or not ownership passes to the recipient. Taking loan in the first way, the loan is not always transferred from the lender as from one who has ownership, because the lender may lack ownership of the thing lent, as appears in the preceding notable point. Taking loan in the second way, it is plain that what is said here does not hold. Likewise, just as one may lend a thing to another without transfer of ownership, so one may furnish a thing to another without transfer of ownership. That loan is so taken is plainly shown by divine Scripture. For it is so used in 4 Kings 4, when Elisha said to a certain woman: Go and borrow empty vessels from all your neighbours, not a few, which vessels were not to pass into her ownership. And in chapter 6 we read: But it happened that as one was felling timber, the iron of the axe fell into the water, and he cried out and said: Alas, alas, my lord, for I had borrowed it. Yet ownership of the borrowed thing was not transferred to the recipient. Thus it is plain that in a loan ownership of the lent thing does not always pass to the one who receives it. Although, taking loan as it is often taken in the legal sciences, ownership of the lent thing does pass to the recipient, divine Scripture is by no means bound to the modes of speaking and the vocabulary of the legal sciences. This is clear of commodatum (lending for use), which according to the laws is hardly found in things consumed by use, except when lent for display, so that someone may appear richer. Yet in divine Scripture it is plainly indicated that loaves can be lent for eating. Hence Christ also says, as we read in Luke 11: Which of you shall have a friend, and shall go to him at midnight and say to him: Friend, lend me three loaves, for my friend has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him. From these words it is plainly gathered that loaves can be lent for eating. So sacred Scripture ought not to be confined to the modes of taking the terms of the legal sciences. Therefore, even if it were not found in any legal science that ownership of the lent thing does not always pass in a loan, yet in divine Scripture it is plainly found that in a loan ownership of the thing lent does not always pass to the one who receives it. So loan is taken in the words of Christ, when he says: from him who would borrow, do not turn away. The reason is that, as was said before, the Saviour by these words wished to lead his disciples to do good to their neighbours. Now one does good to someone by lending him a thing useful to him, not only by transferring ownership to him but also by merely furnishing it to him without transfer of ownership. Hence to lend must be taken most commonly, and not only strictly for transferring ownership. From the foregoing it is plain that this second argument does not prove that the aforesaid words, whoever would contend with you in judgment, etc., were spoken only to those who have property in things. Indeed they were spoken to all who, either in their own name or in another's, can give or furnish things. Many who do not have property in things can, in another's name or by another's licence, give and furnish things. For sometimes they can furnish things, and consequently lend in the broad sense of the word, which yet they cannot give. Many also furnish things they are unwilling to give. So there is a distinction between these two counsels of Christ: Whoever asks of you, give to him, and from him who would borrow, do not turn away. The Gloss on the aforesaid passage seems to suggest such a distinction between the two, when it says: It embraces two kinds of furnishing: for either we give kindly, or we lend to be repaid. And the Gloss on Luke 6, And if you lend, etc., says: There are two kinds of benefit: either when we give kindly what we give, or when we lend to be repaid. For he who gives to one who asks, gives kindly; but he who lends, lends to be repaid, because a loan, even taken broadly, is to be repaid. From these Glosses it is also plain that loan in the words of the Saviour is taken for commodatum (lending for use). And what is lent for use, as the word to lend for use is taken in sacred Scripture, is not always transferred into the ownership of the one who receives it. Therefore neither is loan, as it is taken in the Gospel, always transferred into the ownership of the one who receives it.

units.la: CAP. CX.
units.tr: CHAPTER 110.

units.la: Item ipse intelligit, Apostolis datum prædictum mandatum fuisse, quod est falsum. Tempore enim illius sermonis in monte facti, in quo iniuncta fuerunt prædicta, nullus adhuc erat Apostolus, vt patet: quia sermo iste recitatur Matth 5. & Apostoli fuerunt facti post, vt patet Matth. 10. Vnde dici non potest, nisi mendaciter, quod illa præcepta contenta in illo sermone Domini in monte solis Apostolis facta fuerint, cum nondum Apostoli essent.
units.tr: Likewise he himself understands that the aforesaid command was given to the Apostles, which is false. For at the time of that sermon on the mount, in which the aforesaid things were enjoined, there was as yet no Apostle, as is clear: for this sermon is related in Matthew 5, and the Apostles were made afterwards, as is clear from Matthew 10. Hence it cannot be said, except falsely, that those precepts contained in that sermon of the Lord on the mount were given to the Apostles alone, since the Apostles did not yet exist.

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnatus intendit ostendere, quod verba sæpe dicta non fuerunt dicta Apostolis. Cuius ratio est: quia tunc non fuerunt Apostoli, sed facti fuerunt Apostoli post, Matth. decimo.
units.tr: On this point the one who is opposed here intends to show that the words often mentioned were not spoken to the Apostles. His reason is this: because there were then no Apostles, but the Apostles were made afterwards, in Matthew ten.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt ipsum hic patenter errare, cum asserit, quod tunc non erant Apostoli, quando illa præcepta de quibus Matt. 5. & Luc. 6. fit mentio, data fuerunt. Nā sicut ostensum est supra cap. centesimo, Christus, sicut patet Luc. 6. clare ordinauit eos Apostolos in monte: & postea sermonem fecit: & ita constat quod tunc erant Apostoli.
units.tr: But those who oppose him say that he here plainly errs, when he asserts that there were then no Apostles when those precepts of which Matthew 5 and Luke 6 make mention were given. For, as was shown above in chapter one hundred, Christ, as is clear from Luke 6, clearly appointed them Apostles on the mount, and afterwards he gave the sermon; and so it is evident that they were then Apostles.

units.la: (Ipse intelligit Apostolis datum praedictum fuisse mandatum.) Verum est secundum appellantem, quod datum fuit Apostolis sub praecepto, aliis autem datum fuit sub consilio. Et si dicas, quod sermoni in monte non interfuerunt, nisi soli Apostoli. Ad hoc dicunt isti, quod sive interfuerint soli Apostoli illi sermoni, sive non: dicta tamen verba omnibus dicta fuerunt quantum ad intentionem Christi, dicentis, quod voluit, quod Apostoli huiusmodi omnibus explicarent, & quando opportunitas adesset docerent. (Tempore enim illius sermonis in monte facti, in quo iniuncta fuerunt praedicta, nullus adhuc erat Apostolus.) Hoc falsum est, quia quamuis Matthaeus ibidem de ipsorum ordinatione non facit mentionem, ipsi tamen in monte facti fuerunt Apostoli ante sermonem, quod Lucas cap. 6. manifestat dicens: Exiit (scil. Christus) in montem orare: & cum dies factus esset, vocavit discipulos, & elegit 12. ex ipsis, quos & Apostolos nominavit. Postea autem descendit de monte & fecit sermonem, qui in eodem cap. recitatur, in quo dixit haec verba: ab eo qui aufert tibi vestimentum & tunicam, noli prohibere. (Quia sermo iste recitatur Matth. 5. & Apostoli fuerunt facti post ut patet Matth. 10.) Hic duplicirer deficit. Primo quia Matth. 10. de Apostolorum ordinatione nulla omnino fit mentio, sed Matthaeus 10. ibidem rememorat, quod Christus eis tribuit potestatem miracula faciendi, & eorum missionem ad praedicandum declarat. Secundo deficit: quia esto quod Matth. 10. tractaretur de ordinatione Apostolorum: ex hoc concludi non posset, quod antea Apostoli non fuerunt, quia saepe in euangelio prius factum posterius recitatur: & ita si ex hoc, quod Matthaeus ante sermonem illum in monte non facit mentionem de ordinatione Apostolorum, vult concludere, quod ante sermonem illum Apostoli non fuerunt, multo fortius ex hoc quod de ordinatione Apostolorum fit mentio. Lucae 6. & illa quae Matth. 10. de ordinatione Apostolorum narrari videntur, secundum istum, narrantur etiam Lucae 9. sequitur quod antequam facta fuerunt illa, quae narrantur secundum istum de ordinatione Apostolorum Matth. 10. Apostoli facti fuerunt, quod autem eadem, quae videntur narrari de ordinatione Apostolorum Matt. 10. narrantur etiam Luc. 9. patet aperte. Nam illa, quae secundum istum narrantur de ordinatione Matth. 10. comprehenduntur verbis Matthaei, cum dicit ibidem: Et convocatis duodecim discipulis dedit illis potestatem spirituum immundorum, ut eicerent eos, & curarent omnem languorem & omnem infirmitatem, quod enim ista verba secundum istum intelligantur de ordinatione Apostolorum, patet per verba supra posita, Luc. 10. ubi ait: cum eos Apostolos ordinavit, legitur Matt. 10. sic dixisse: Et convocatis duodecim discipulis suis dedit illis &c. Verba ergo ista Matt. 10. secundum istum intelliguntur de ordinatione Apostolorum, sed sententia illorum verborum ponitur Luc. 9. cum dicit Lucas: Convocatis autem duodecim Apostolis dedit illis virtutem & potestatem super daemonia, & ut languores curarent. Non plus ergo narratur de ordinatione Apostolorum Matth. 10. quam Luc. 9. Sed Apostoli fuerunt facti ante illa, quae narrantur Luc. 9. quia fuerunt facti Apostoli Lucae 6. ergo fuerunt facti ante illa, quae narrantur Matt. 10. & ita si ex ordine narrationis vult arguere ordinem rei gestae: sequitur evidenter, quod fuerunt Apostoli antequam contingerent illa, quae narrantur Matt. 10. Unde non potest dici, nisi mendaciter, quod illa praecepta contenta in illo sermone Domini in monte, solis Apostolis facta fuerint: sive Apostoli soli interfuerint dicto sermoni, sive non, illa contenta in dicto sermone non fuerunt facta solis Apostolis: quia pro omnibus dicit Christus verba illa, non tamen omnibus iniungendo, sed magis consulendo, (cum nondum Apostoli essent) hic assignat rationem dicti praecedentis, quod dictum praecedens licet esset verum, tamen ista ratio falsa est: quia tunc erant Apostoli, sicut ostensum est capitulo 100.
units.tr: (He himself understands that the aforesaid command was given to the Apostles.) It is true, according to the one who appeals, that it was given to the Apostles under command, but to others it was given under counsel. And if you say that only the Apostles were present at the sermon on the mount: to this these men reply that, whether or not only the Apostles were present at that sermon, the words were nonetheless spoken to all, as far as Christ's intention went, since he said that he wished the Apostles to explain such things to everyone and to teach them when the opportunity arose. (For at the time of that sermon on the mount, in which the aforesaid things were enjoined, there was as yet no Apostle.) This is false, because although Matthew there makes no mention of their appointment, they were nonetheless made Apostles on the mount before the sermon, as Luke chapter 6 makes plain, saying: He went out (namely Christ) into the mountain to pray; and when day had come, he called his disciples, and chose twelve of them, whom he also named Apostles. Afterwards, however, he came down from the mountain and gave the sermon, which is related in the same chapter, in which he said these words: From him who takes away your coat and tunic, do not withhold. (For this sermon is related in Matthew 5, and the Apostles were made afterwards, as is clear from Matthew 10.) Here there is a twofold failure. First, because Matthew 10 makes no mention at all of the appointment of the Apostles, but there Matthew recounts that Christ gave them power to work miracles, and declares their sending out to preach. Second, it fails: because even if Matthew 10 were dealing with the appointment of the Apostles, it could not be concluded from this that the Apostles did not exist earlier, since in the Gospel what happened first is often related afterwards; and so if from the fact that Matthew makes no mention of the appointment of the Apostles before that sermon on the mount he wishes to conclude that the Apostles did not exist before that sermon, much more strongly [it would follow] from the fact that mention is made of the appointment of the Apostles in Luke 6. And those things which in Matthew 10 seem to be related about the appointment of the Apostles are, according to him, also related in Luke 9; it follows that before those things were done which, according to him, are related about the appointment of the Apostles in Matthew 10, the Apostles had been made. That the same things which seem to be related about the appointment of the Apostles in Matthew 10 are also related in Luke 9 is plain. For those things which, according to him, are related about the appointment in Matthew 10 are contained in Matthew's words, where he says there: And calling together his twelve disciples he gave them power over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every sickness and every infirmity. That these words are understood by him to refer to the appointment of the Apostles is clear from the words quoted above, Luke 10, where he says: when he appointed those Apostles; it is read in Matthew 10 that he said thus: And calling together his twelve disciples he gave them, etc. These words of Matthew 10, then, are according to him understood to refer to the appointment of the Apostles, but the sense of those words is set down in Luke 9, where Luke says: And calling together the twelve Apostles he gave them power and authority over demons, and to heal diseases. Therefore nothing more is related of the appointment of the Apostles in Matthew 10 than in Luke 9. But the Apostles were made before those things which are related in Luke 9, since they were made Apostles in Luke 6; therefore they were made before those things which are related in Matthew 10. And so, if from the order of the narrative he wishes to argue the order of the events, it clearly follows that there were Apostles before those things occurred which are related in Matthew 10. Hence it cannot be said, except falsely, that those precepts contained in that sermon of the Lord on the mount were given to the Apostles alone: whether or not the Apostles alone were present at that sermon, those things contained in the sermon were not given to the Apostles alone; for Christ speaks those words to all, not enjoining them on all, but rather counselling them. (Since the Apostles did not yet exist) here he assigns the reason for the preceding statement; and although the preceding statement was true, this reason is false, because there were Apostles then, as was shown in chapter 100.

units.la: CAP. CXI.
units.tr: Chapter CXI.

units.la: Item attendat iste haereticus, quid Dominus praecepit Matth. 18. discipulis suis: si peccaverit, inquit, in te frater tuus, corripe eum inter te & ipsum solum, & sequitur: si autem non audierit, dic ecclesiae: si autem non audierit ecclesiam, sit tibi sicut ethnicus & publicanus. Voluit ergo Salvator noster, quod eius discipuli, inter quos erat Petrus, ut patet, quia statim sequitur ibi: Tunc accedens ad eum Petrus &c. conquererentur ecclesia de iniuriantibus sibi.
units.tr: Let this heretic also consider what the Lord commanded his disciples in Matt. 18: "If your brother sins against you," he says, "go and show him his fault between you and him alone," and it goes on: "But if he does not listen, tell it to the church. And if he refuses to listen even to the church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector." Our Saviour therefore wished that his disciples, among whom Peter was, as is clear from what immediately follows, "Then Peter came to him," should complain to the church about those who wronged them.

units.la: Hic ostendit, quod Apostoli habuerunt ius agendi in iudicio, cuius ratio est, quia, sicut habetur Matth. 18. Apostoli debuerunt conqueri de iniuriantibus sibi, & per consequens debebant conqueri de auferentibus temporalia ipsorum, sed qui potest conqueri de auferente temporalia sua, habet ius agendi in iudicio, ergo Apostoli habuerunt ius agendi in iudicio.
units.tr: Here he shows that the apostles had the right to act in court. The reason is this: as is stated in Matt. 18, the apostles were to complain about those who wronged them, and consequently they were to complain about those who took away their temporal goods. But whoever may complain about one who takes away his temporal goods has the right to act in court. Therefore the apostles had the right to act in court.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod istud argumentum non concludit, quod Apostoli poterant pro rebus temporalibus in iudicio litigare. Ad cuius evidentiam dicunt duo esse scienda. Primum est, quod aliquibus licet in iudicio litigare pro rebus temporalibus, & aliquibus non licet. Illis enim qui habent temporalia in speciali & in communi quo ad dominium, vel aliquod aliud ius positivum, non solum de gratia vel licentia aliorum, licet in iudicio litigare. Illis autem qui tale ius non habent, non licet in iudicio litigare. Secundo dicunt esse sciendum, quod potest quis fratrem suum fraternaliter corrigere, & propter bonum commune denuntiare ecclesiae extra iudicium, quamuis non possit rem petere in iudicio litigando.
units.tr: But these opponents say that this argument does not prove that the apostles could go to law over temporal goods. To make this clear, they say that two things must be known. The first is that some people are permitted to litigate over temporal goods and some are not. Those who hold temporal goods, specifically and in general, as to ownership or some other positive right, may go to law, and not merely by the grace or permission of others. Those who have no such right may not go to law. Second, they say it must be known that a man may correct his brother in a brotherly way, and for the common good report him to the church outside court, even though he may not sue to recover a thing by litigation.

units.la: Ex his dicunt, quod præceptum Domini (si peccauerit in te frater tuus &c.) extendebatur ad omnes, vt Fratrem suum peccantem corrigerent, non vt res aliquas temporales in iudicio repeterent: quia ex quo ius positiuum distinctum contra gratiam seu licentiam in rebus temporalibus non habebant, non poterant res repetere pro eis in iudicio litigando: poterant tamen, quando esset cognitum peccatum fratris, ecclesiæ nuntiare, si ex admonitione secreta correctus non fuisset (corripe eum inter te & ipsum solum.) Non vt res temporales recuperet, sed vt Fratrem tuum lucreris, (dic ecclesiæ) non temporalia repetendo, si omnia abdicasti, sed peccatum Fratris indicando, vt corrigatur, & alii à peccato consimili caueant. (Si autem non audierit ecclesiam, sit tibi sicut ethnicus & publicanus,) quicunque sit iste frater, siue subditus, siue prælatus, imo etiam si Papa in his, in quibus subest correctioni ecclesiæ, vt in causa hæresis, & in criminibus in quibus incorrigibilis videretur, non audit ecclesiam, pro ethnico & publicano debet haberi (conquererentur ecclesia de iniuriantibus sibi) verum est quod Apostoli debebant conqueri de iniuriantibus, quando conqueri expediebat, quando autem non expediebat conqueri: tunc conqueri non debebant: quia illud erat præceptum affirmatiuum. Ideo non obligabat pro semper, veruntamen conquerendo non habuerunt res temporales repetere, sed debuerunt procurare correctionem fratris & bonum commune cum debitis circumstantiis tantum. Ex hoc isti concludunt, quod cum dictum præceptum Christi ad omnes & singulos extendatur, sic quod papa, cum sit frater merito reputandus, si hæreticam prauitatem incurrat, & hæresim publice dogmatizet: licet cuilibet Christiano ipsum ecclesiæ de hæresi nuntiare.
units.tr: From these points they say that the command of the Lord ("If your brother sins against you," etc.) extended to all, so that they might correct a sinning brother, not so that they might recover any temporal goods through litigation. Since they did not have a positive right over temporal goods, distinct from grace or permission, they could not recover goods for themselves by going to law. Yet when a brother's sin had become known, they could report it to the church, if he had not been corrected by private admonition ("go and show him his fault between you and him alone"). Not to recover temporal goods, but "to win your brother"; (tell it to the church), not by demanding temporal goods, even if you have given up everything, but by pointing out the brother's sin, so that he may be corrected and others may guard against a similar sin. ("But if he does not listen to the church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector.") Whoever that brother is, whether subject or prelate, indeed even if the Pope, in those matters in which he is subject to the correction of the church, as in a case of heresy, or in crimes in which he seems incorrigible, does not listen to the church, he ought to be regarded as a Gentile and a tax collector. ("They should complain to the church about those who wronged them.") It is true that the apostles were to complain about wrongdoers when it was expedient to complain; when it was not expedient, they need not complain, since that was an affirmative command. Therefore it did not bind at all times. Yet by complaining they did not get to recover temporal goods; they were to seek the correction of the brother and the common good, and only with the due circumstances. From this they conclude that, since the said command of Christ extends to all and each, so that the Pope, who is rightly to be regarded as a brother, if he falls into heretical depravity and publicly teaches heresy, it is permitted to any Christian to report him to the church as a heretic.

units.la: CAP. CXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER CXII.

units.la: SEd quod verba prædicta Matth. 5. non solum perfectis, sed generaliter intelliguntur omnibus esse dicta, ex eo patet, quia illa verba sunt dicta in illo magno sermone Domini in monte, qui continetur Matth. 6. & 7. cap. in fine autem 7. cap. Dominus concludens sic dicit: Omnis ergo qui audit verba mea hæc, & facit ea, assimilabitur viro prudenti, qui ædificat domum suam supra petram &c. Et sequitur: Et omnis qui audit verba mea hæc & non facit ea, similis erit viro stulto, qui ædificauit domum suam supra arenam, cum ergo non dixerit, quod omnis qui audit verba mea: sed dixerit verba mea hæc: & facit ea assimilabitur viro sapienti, qui vero audit & non facit similis erit viro stulto: apparet quod non solum perfectis sunt dicta verba prædicta, imo & imperfectis, cum omnibus illa seruantibus promittatur regnum: & omnibus non seruantibus iam facit, quod Christus Apostolis Matth. vltim. dicit: Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes in nomine Patris & Filii & Spiritus sancti, docentes eos seruare omnia quæcunque mandaui vobis. Ex quibus etiam clare patet, quod mandata data discipulis, sicut illa data fuerunt, cum nondum essent Apostoli, vt patet ex prædictis, intelliguntur omnibus data, & hoc tenet Augustinus in libro de Sermone Domini in monte.
units.tr: But that the aforesaid words of Matthew 5 were spoken to all, and not only to the perfect, is clear from this: those words were spoken in that great sermon of the Lord on the mount, which is contained in Matthew chapters 6 and 7. At the end of chapter 7 the Lord concludes and says: "Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine and does them shall be likened to a wise man, who built his house upon a rock," and so on. And it follows: "And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them shall be like a foolish man, who built his house upon the sand." Since he did not say "everyone who hears my words," but "these words of mine," and said that whoever does them will be likened to a wise man, while whoever hears and does not do them will be like a foolish man, it is evident that the aforesaid words were spoken not only to the perfect but also to the imperfect. A promise of the kingdom is made to all who keep them, and the same holds for all who do not keep them. Christ says to the Apostles in the last chapter of Matthew: "Go therefore and teach all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you." From these words it also plainly appears that the commandments given to the disciples, as those were given (when they were not yet Apostles, as appears from what has been said), are understood to be given to all. Augustine holds this in his book on the Sermon on the Mount.

units.la: Hic iste impugnatus ostendit, quod prædicta verba de non contendendo, nec litigando in iudicio temporalia, omnibus dicta fuerunt, quod duabus auctoritatibus euangelicis probare conatur: & vltimo asserit Augustinum hoc expresse tenere.
units.tr: Here this man, who is being attacked, shows that the aforesaid words about not contending or going to law over temporal matters were spoken to all. He tries to prove this by two evangelical authorities, and finally he asserts that Augustine expressly holds this.

units.la: Isti impugnatores dicunt, quod licet hic contenta secundum bonum intellectum, non secundum intellectum istius, possint veritatem habere, sicut super literam apparebit: tamen aperte dicitis suis præcedentibus contradicunt. Nam sicut patet c. 107. ipse dicit, quod illud quod in euangelio prædictis dicitur, non potest de perfectis intelligi, hic autem dicit, quod non solum perfectis, sed generaliter omnibus dicta fuerunt, quæ est contradictio manifesta, cum perfecti inter omnes debeant comprobari.
units.tr: These opponents say that, although the things contained here may have truth when understood in a good sense (though not in his sense, as will appear from the letter below), nevertheless he openly contradicts his own earlier statements. For, as is clear from chapter 107, he says that what is said in the Gospel in these terms cannot be understood of the perfect; here, however, he says that the words were spoken not only to the perfect but generally to all. This is a plain contradiction, since the perfect must be counted among all.

units.la: (Non solum perfectis: sed generaliter omnibus intelliguntur esse dicta) Verum est, quod omnibus dicta fuerunt: sed diuersimode diuersis. Perfectis enim per votum abdicationis proprietatis omnium in speciali & in communi præceptorie dicta fuerunt, & tales fuerunt Apostoli. Aliis autem pro multis casibus dicta fuerunt sub consilio, quantum ad opus exterius. Fro aliquo autem casu secundum praeparationem animi tantum, vt inferius apparebit, (Quod continetur) magis dixisset grammatice, qui continetur. (Qui audit verba mea hæc & facit ea,) scilicet quæ facienda & prout facienda sunt iniuncta. Aliqua enim in dicto sermone dicta sunt informatorie siue instructorie: vt, Beati pauperes spiritu quoniam ipsorum est regnum cælorum &c. Aliqua commendatorie seu laudatorie: vt, vos estis sal terræ: vos estis lux mundi, aliqua præceptorie: sicut, diligite inimicos vestros. Attendite ne iustitiam vestram faciatis coram hominibus &c. Hypocrita, eiice primum trabem de oculo tuo &c. Attendite à falsis Prophetis &c. Et multa alia omnibus præceptorie dicta sunt, quædam vero dicuntur aliquibus consultorie, & aliquibus præceptorie: sicut, Qui vult tecum in iudicio contendere &c. Nolite thesaurizare vobis thesauros in terra. Nolite solliciti esse in crastinum. Qui ergo facit verba prædicta quantum ad ea, quæ præceptorie dicta sunt, assimilabitur viro sapienti, non enim voluit Christus, quod stricte loquendo omnia quæ dixerat facerent sibi obedientes. Inter eadem enim verba continetur, quod pater cœlestis solem suum facit oriri super bonos & malos, sed tamen facit solem oriri super bonos & malos, (assimilabitur viro prudenti) textus est, viro stulto, (qui edificat domum suam) sed textus est, qui edificauit (& non facit ea) scilicet quæ præceptis omnibus sunt iniuncta, (non solum perfectis sunt dicta verba prædicta imo & imperfectis) concedendum est, quod verba illa imperfectis consultorie dicta fuerunt (docentes eos seruare omnia) seruare est communius, quam facere : & ideo omnia, quæ Christus docuit, seruanda sunt : quia cum fide vera reuerenda & amore iugiter recitanda, quamuis non omnia sint facienda, sic loquitur Athanasius in Symbolo dicens : quam scilicet fidem nisi quisque integram inuiolatamque seruauerit, absque dubio in æternum peribit (Quicunque mandata vobis) quia omnia seruanda sunt per fidem vel operationem.) Ex quibus etiam clare patet, quod mandata data discipulis sicut illa fuerunt data cum nondum essent Apostoli, vt patet ex prædictis, intelliguntur omnibus data) ex dictis verbis Christi nude acceptis, Euntes docete, &c. non plus potest concludi, quod illa quæ continentur in sermone prædicto, omnibus data fuerunt, quam quod omnia quæ dixit Christus Apostolis Matthei decimo, & Lucæ vndecimo, quando misit eos ad prædicandum, omnibus dicta fuerunt, quia illa verba Euntes docete omnes gentes, &c. dixit Christus tam post prædictum sermonem; quam post præcepta, quæ dedit Apostolis, quando eos ad prædicandum destinauit.
units.tr: (Not only to the perfect, but are understood to be said generally to all.) It is true that they were said to all, but in different ways to different people. For to the perfect they were given as precepts, both specifically and in general, through the vow of renouncing all property; and such were the Apostles. But to others they were given as counsel for many cases, as far as outward action goes. For some cases, however, they were given only as a preparation of the mind, as will appear below. (Which is contained) would have been more grammatical as "who is contained." (He who hears these words of mine and does them) namely, those things which are to be done, and which are enjoined as to be done. For some things in that sermon are said by way of instruction: for example, "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven," and so on. Some are said by way of commendation or praise: for example, "You are the salt of the earth; you are the light of the world." Some are precepts: for example, "Love your enemies"; "Take heed that you do not do your righteousness before men," and so on; "Hypocrite, cast out first the beam from your own eye," and so on; "Beware of false prophets," and so on. Many other things are said as precepts to all, while some are given to some as counsel and to others as precepts: for example, "If anyone wants to sue you at law," and so on; "Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth"; "Do not be anxious about tomorrow." Therefore he who does the aforesaid words, as far as those things are concerned that are said as precepts, will be likened to a wise man. For Christ did not will that, strictly speaking, all the things he had said should be done by those obeying him. Among these same words it is stated that the heavenly Father makes his sun rise on the good and the evil; yet he does make the sun rise on the good and the evil. (Will be likened to a prudent man) is the text; (to a foolish man) is the text; (who builds his house) but the text reads "who built" (and does not do them), namely those things which are enjoined on all as precepts. (These words were spoken not only to the perfect, but also to the imperfect.) It must be granted that those words were spoken to the imperfect as counsel. (Teaching them to observe all things.) To observe is more general than to do; and therefore all that Christ taught is to be observed, because it is to be revered with true faith and continually recited with love, even though not all things are to be done. So Athanasius speaks in the Creed, saying: "which faith, unless each one keeps it whole and inviolate, he will without doubt perish forever." (Whatsoever I have commanded you.) For everything is to be observed either by faith or by practice. (From these words it also plainly appears that the commandments given to the disciples, as those were given when they were not yet Apostles, as appears from what has been said, are understood to be given to all.) From the said words of Christ, taken simply, "Go and teach," and so on, no more can be concluded that the things contained in the aforesaid sermon were given to all than that everything Christ said to the Apostles in Matthew 10 and Luke 11, when he sent them out to preach, was said to all. For Christ spoke the words "Go and teach all nations," and so on, both after the aforesaid sermon and after the instructions he gave the Apostles when he sent them out to preach.

units.la: Verba igitur scripturæ diuinæ sane intelligenda sunt, sicut à sanctis Patribus noscuntur exposita : & non ad omnem sensum, qui ex eis potest capi, trahenda, quod tamen iste tanquam Theologicæ facultatis ignarus, vtpote qui nunquam Theologiæ studium frequentauit, sola authoritate & potentia, absque literarum sacrarum peritia, fretus, facere in tota ista constitutione molitur, vt isti dicunt. (Et hoc tenet Augustinus in libro de sermone Domini in monte.) Augustinus tenet, quod omnibus dicta fuerunt : sed non omnibus præceptorie, quantum ad opus exterius.
units.tr: The words of divine Scripture are therefore to be understood soundly, as they are known to have been expounded by the holy Fathers, and not to be drawn to every sense that can be taken from them. Yet this man, as one ignorant of the faculty of theology, since he never attended the study of theology, relies on authority and power alone, without skill in the sacred letters, and in this whole constitution, as they say, he undertakes to do this. And Augustine holds this in his book on the Sermon on the Mount. Augustine holds that the things were said to all, but not to all as precepts, as far as outward action is concerned.

units.la: CAP. CXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER CXIII.

units.la: Item illud Apostoli prim. ad Corinthi. sext. Iam quidem delictum est in vobis, quod iudicia habetis inter vos. Quare non magis iniuriam accipitis ? quare non magis fraudem patimini ? sed vos iniuriam facitis & fraudatis, &c. non intelligitur dictum talibus personis, de quibus loquitur iste hereticus, scilicet qui à se dominium omnium temporalium abdicarunt, contenti solo simplici vsu facti. Loquebatur enim Apostolus Corinthiis conuersis ad fidem : qui quidem non renunciauerant bonis suis, nec ad inuicem communicauerant sibi, vt patet prim. ad Corinthi. vltim. in principio, vbi Apostolus hortatur eos, vt collectas inter se facerent deferendas Hierosolymis sanctis, sic dicens : de collectis quæ fiunt in sanctis, sicut ordinaui in ecclesiis Galatiæ, ita & vos facite per vnam sabbati. Vnusquisque autem vestrum apud se reponat recondens, quod ei placuerit. Hæc autem non facerent, si nihil haberent : & patet, sicut in articulo proximo latius continetur. Augustinus autem dicit, quod non legitur, quod conuersi ex gentibus communicauerint sua, quare patet, quod dictum Apostoli nihil pro ipso hæretico facit : quia non loquitur de perfectis, sicut ipse perfectos accipit, scilicet qui abdicauerunt omnium temporalium dominium solo simplici vsu facti contenti : sed loquitur omnibus Corinthiis ad fidem conuersis, qui dominium temporalium retinuerant sibi. Sane secundum hoc videtur, quod fidelibus non liceat litigare sine peccato : quod esset nimis durum.
units.tr: Likewise, there is that saying of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 6: "Now indeed there is a fault among you, because you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather suffer fraud? But you do wrong and defraud, etc." This is not understood as said to such persons as those of whom this heretic speaks, namely those who have renounced for themselves lordship over all temporal goods, content with the mere simple use of things. For the Apostle was speaking to the Corinthians who had been converted to the faith, and who indeed had not renounced their goods nor shared them with one another, as is clear in the last chapter of 1 Corinthians, at the beginning, where the Apostle exhorts them to make collections among themselves to be carried to the holy ones at Jerusalem, saying: "Concerning the collections that are made for the saints, as I ordered the churches of Galatia, so do you also. On the first day of the week let each of you put something aside, storing up whatever pleases him." They would not do this if they had nothing; and this is clear, as is set out more fully in the preceding article. Augustine says, moreover, that it is not read that the converts from the Gentiles shared their possessions. So it is clear that the Apostle's saying does nothing for this heretic, because it does not speak of the perfect as he understands the perfect, namely those who have renounced lordship over all temporal goods, content with the mere simple use of things; but it speaks to all the Corinthians converted to the faith, who had kept lordship over temporal goods for themselves. Indeed, according to this it seems that it is not lawful for the faithful to go to law without sin, which would be too harsh.

units.la: Postquam iste impugnatus conatus est ostendere, quod appellans male intelligit verba Christi, de non contendendo in iudicio : Hic probare molitur, quod male intelligit authoritatem Apostoli prim. Corinth. sext. de eadem materia ostendens, quod verba Apostoli non intelliguntur dicta iis, qui omnium temporalium abdicauerunt dominium, contenti solo simplici vsu facti, quod ostendit primo ostensiue sic, Apostolus loquebatur Corinthiis conuersis ad fidem, sed illi non renunciauerant bonis suis, ergo &c. Secundo ibi : Sane secundum hoc, probat idem ducendo ad inconueniens : quia si hoc esset, nulli fideli litigare liceret absque peccato.
units.tr: After this opponent had tried to show that the appellant misunderstands the words of Christ about not contending in judgment, here he undertakes to prove that he misunderstands the authority of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 6, on the same matter. He shows that the words of the Apostle are not understood as said to those who have renounced lordship over all temporal things, content with the mere simple use of things. He shows this first by a direct argument: the Apostle was speaking to the Corinthians converted to the faith, but they had not renounced their goods; therefore, etc. Second, at the words "Indeed, according to this," he proves the same by reducing the view to an absurdity: for if this were so, it would be lawful for no faithful person to go to law without sin.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod hic enormiter errat. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod auctor alicuius doctrinæ sæpe licet alicui vel aliquibus specialiter librum suum intitulet, non tamen vult alios doctrina sua carere : imo etiam intendit alios informare. Et ex illo dicunt, quod licet Apostolus specialiter scripserit Corinthiis ipsis : tamen solis loqui minime intendebat, & ideo non tantum ex intentione loquebatur Corinthiis, sed etiam verba prædicta locutus est perfectis, quos per doctrinam suam voluit informare, volens omnes perfectos & imperfectos Corinthios & alios, qui lecturi erant, & secundum doctrinam ipsius ad pacificam conuersationem absque contentione & litigio in iudicio instigare, præcipue tamen volebat perfectos & qui omnium abdicauerunt proprietatem inducere, ne in iudicio litigarent : quia magis vitiosum est in abdicatibus omnium proprietatem in iudicio litigare, quam in aliis, si ergo verba sua intelligi debent de Corinthiis, qui non renunciauerant bonis suis secundum istum : multo magis verba sua exhortatoria, non increpatoria, ad illos, qui bonis suis renunciauerant, debent intelligi esse dicta, si enim Corinthii, qui non renunciauerunt temporalibus suis, debuerunt magis iniuriam accipere, & magis fraudem pati, quam in iudicio litigare : multo magis hoc debebant illi, qui renunciauerunt omnibus bonis suis. Et per hoc patet, quod ratio sua prima non concludit, quia verba Apostoli intelliguntur dicta Corinthiis & aliis perfectis & imperfectis habentibus proprietatem & non habentibus. Secunda etiam ratio non concludit, quia, sicut post declarabitur, litigare in iudicio non semper est peccatum, nec appellans dicit quod semper est peccatum. (Iam quidem delictum est in vobis, quod iudicia habetis) Iudicia scilicet & litigia, quae exauaritia & cupiditate procedunt, talia enim iudicia nunquam sunt sine peccato illius, qui litigat ex auaritia vel cupiditate. Sunt vero verba ista Apostoli increpatoria, quae ad omnes sive habentes proprietatem sive carentes, qui huiusmodi quaerunt iudicia, extenduntur (quare non magis iniuriam accipitis? quare non magis fraudem patimini) ista verba sunt exhortatoria: quia per ista intendit omnes Corinthios & alios inducere, ut magis fraudem sustineant, quam ex auaritia iudicia quaerant, (sed vos iniuriam facitis & fraudatis) ista sunt verba increpatoria, quibus increpat non omnes Corinthios, quia nec omnes talia faciebant: sed increpat omnes in talibus vitiosos Corinthios & alios. (Non intelligitur dictum talibus personis, de quibus loquitur ipse) hic errat, quia & illis & aliis intelligitur esse dictum, quantum ad verba exhortatoria: quantum vero ad verba increpatoria, intelligitur esse dictum illis Corinthiis, qui vitiosi fuerunt, & etiam aliis omnibus, qui vitiosi fuerunt. (Loquebatur enim Apostolus Corinthiis conversis ad fidem) eis specialiter intitulando suam epistolam, ex intentione tamen aliis credentibus loquebatur, cupiens eos, sicut & Corinthios, per praedictam epistolam salubriter informare.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he errs greatly here. To make this plain, they say it must be known that the author of a teaching often addresses his book specially to one person or to some persons, yet does not wish others to lack his teaching; indeed he intends to inform others as well. From this they say that although the Apostle wrote specially to the Corinthians themselves, he did not intend to speak to them alone. So he spoke the aforesaid words not only with the Corinthians in view, but also to the perfect, whom he wished to instruct by his teaching. He wished all perfect and imperfect Corinthians, and others who were to read, to be urged by his teaching to a peaceful manner of life, without contention and litigation in court; but above all he wished to lead the perfect, who had renounced all ownership of property, not to go to law. For it is more sinful for those who have renounced all property to litigate in court than for others. If therefore his words must be understood as addressed to the Corinthians, who, according to him, had not renounced their goods, much more must his hortatory words (not his reproachful ones) be understood as addressed to those who had renounced their goods. For if the Corinthians, who had not renounced their temporal goods, ought rather to suffer wrong and be defrauded than litigate in court, much more ought those who had renounced all their goods to do so. And by this it is clear that his first argument does not conclude, because the Apostle's words are understood as spoken to the Corinthians and to other perfect and imperfect persons, both those having property and those not having it. His second argument also does not conclude, because, as will be declared afterwards, litigating in court is not always sinful, nor does the appellant say that it always is. ("Now indeed there is a fault among you, because you have lawsuits"): these are lawsuits and disputes that proceed from avarice and greed; for such lawsuits are never without sin on the part of the one who litigates out of avarice or greed. These words of the Apostle are reproachful, and extend to all, whether having property or lacking it, who seek such lawsuits. ("Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather suffer fraud?") These words are hortatory, because by them he intends to lead all the Corinthians and others to suffer fraud rather than seek lawsuits out of avarice. ("But you do wrong and defraud") These are words of reproach, by which he reproaches not all the Corinthians, since not all did such things, but reproaches all those, Corinthians and others, who were faulty in such matters. ("It is not understood as said to such persons as he himself speaks of") Here he errs, because it is understood to be said to both those and to others, as far as the hortatory words go; but as far as the reproachful words go, it is understood to be said to those Corinthians who were faulty, and to all others who were faulty. ("For the Apostle was writing to the Corinthians converted to the faith") He addresses his letter specially to them in its title, yet in intention he was speaking to other believers as well, desiring to instruct them healthfully by the said letter, just as the Corinthians.

units.la: Ad aliorum enim doctrinam ipse scripsit praedictam epistolam. Unde de ista epistola, sicut & de tota Scriptura sacra, possunt dicere universi fideles: quaecunque scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt. (Qui quidem non renunciaverunt bonis suis) potuit esse, quod aliqui renunciaverunt bonis suis, licet non omnes, (hortatur eos ut collectas inter se facerent, &c.) Istud non concludit efficaciter: quia poterat esse, quod aliqui renunciaverunt bonis suis, & illos poterat Apostolus exhortari ad faciendas collectas.
units.tr: For he wrote the aforesaid letter for the teaching of others. Whence, concerning this letter, as concerning all holy Scripture, all the faithful can say: "Whatever things were written, were written for our teaching." ("Who indeed had not renounced their goods") It could be that some had renounced their goods, though not all. ("He exhorts them to make collections among themselves, etc.") This does not conclude effectively, because it could be that some had renounced their goods, and the Apostle could exhort those same people to make collections.

units.la: (Augustinus quoque dicit, quod non legitur quod conversi ex gentibus communicaverint sua) Augustinus intelligit, quod non legitur, quod aliqua tota ecclesia in principio suae conversionis communicaverat omnia sua, sicut fecit prima ecclesia conversa ex Iudaeis (non loquitur de perfectis) imo loquitur de perfectis & de aliis (sicut ipse perfectos accipit scilicet qui abdicaverunt, &c.) ipse sic & aliter accipit perfectos, (loquitur omnibus Corinthiis ad fidem conversis) si intelligat, quod Apostolus omnia verba praescripta tam increpatoria, quam exhortatoria loquatur omnibus Corinthiis ad fidem conversis, non bene dicit, quia multi erant boni inter eos, qui talia increpanda minime faciebant: de verbis exhortatoriis poterit veritatem habere sub bono intellectu, (qui dominium temporalium retinuerant sibi) probare non poterit, quod omnes Corinthii retinuerunt sibi temporalium dominium (secundum hoc videtur quod fidelibus non liceat litigare sine peccato.) Hic non sequitur ex praedictis, quod Corinthii litigaverint cum peccato: & tamen de ista materia in sequentibus latius differetur.
units.tr: Augustine too says that it is not read that converts from the Gentiles shared their goods. Augustine means that it is not read that any whole church, at the beginning of its conversion, shared all its goods, as the first church converted from the Jews did. ("He does not speak of the perfect") Indeed he speaks both of the perfect and of others. ("As he takes the perfect, namely those who have renounced, etc.") He takes the perfect in this sense and in another. ("He speaks to all the Corinthians converted to the faith") If he understands that the Apostle addresses all the aforesaid words, both reproachful and hortatory, to all the Corinthians converted to the faith, he is not right, because many among them were good and did not do the things that needed rebuke. As for the hortatory words, he may have the truth under a good interpretation. ("Who had retained lordship of temporal goods for themselves") He cannot prove that all the Corinthians retained lordship of temporal goods for themselves. ("Indeed according to this it seems that it is not lawful for the faithful to go to law without sin.") It does not follow from what has been said that the Corinthians litigated with sin; yet this matter will be discussed more fully in what follows.

units.la: CAP. CXIV.
units.tr: Chapter 114.

units.la: ET ideo dicendum, quod praecepta illa Matthaei quinto data: si quis te percusserit in vna maxilla, praebe ei & alteram: &, Qui vult tecum in iudicio contendere & tunicam tuam tollere, dimitte ei & pallium: &, quicunque angariaverit te mille passus, vade cum eo & alia duo, secundum quod Augustinus dicit in libro de sermone Domini in monte, non sunt semper servanda in executione operis: Sed semper in praeparatione animi sunt habenda, ut scilicet simus parati hoc facere & sustinere, quando caritas hoc requiret, & resitatur 23. quaestion. 1. cap. paratus.
units.tr: And so it must be said that the precepts in Matthew 5, "If anyone strikes you on one cheek, turn to him the other also," "If anyone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well," and "Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two," are not always to be kept in the outward performance of the deed, as Augustine says in his book on the Lord's Sermon on the Mount. They must always be held in readiness of mind, so that we are prepared to do and endure these things whenever charity requires it. This is cited in Causa 23, quaestio 1, canon Paratus.

units.la: In parte praecedenti ostendit, quod dictae auctoritates non fecerunt ad propositum appellantis: Hic mentem suam circa auctoritates praetactas explicat manifeste, & dividit in tres partes, quia primo dicit, quomodo intelligit tres auctoritates sumptas ex Matthaeo quinto. Secundo exprimit, qualiter intelligit verba Apostoli. Tertio probare nititur ex scripturis, quod auctoritates sumptae ex Matthaeo quinto ita debent intelligi, sicut ipse exponit. Secunda in parte immediate sequenti, ibi: & propter hoc Apostolus. Tertia ibi: nec per sacram Scripturam, dicit ergo primo, quod praecepta illa Matthaei quinto non sunt semper servanda in executione operis: sed semper in praeparatione animi sunt habenda.
units.tr: In the preceding part he showed that these passages do not serve the appellant's purpose. Here he explains his view of the passages just named, and he divides this into three parts. First, he says how he understands the three passages taken from Matthew 5. Second, he sets out how he understands the words of the Apostle. Third, he tries to prove from Scripture that the passages from Matthew 5 must be understood as he explains them. The second part begins immediately below, at "and for this reason the Apostle." The third begins at "nor by holy Scripture." So he first says that those precepts of Matthew 5 are not always to be kept in the outward performance of the deed, but must always be held in readiness of mind.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod quia indistincte dicit illa praecepta, quorum unum est negativum & aliud affirmativum, non esse servanda in executione operis, sed in praeparatione animi semper habenda: non distinguens inter istos & illos, qui non debent semper praedicta praecepta in operis executione servare, errat aperte.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he errs plainly: he speaks indiscriminately of these precepts, one negative and the other affirmative, saying that they are not to be kept in the outward performance of the deed but must always be held in readiness of mind, and he does not distinguish between those who ought not always to keep those precepts in the performance of the deed and those who ought.

units.la: Ad evidentiam autem istius totius materiae dicunt aliqua esse notanda, quorum primum est, quod sicut habere divitiarum dominium in speciali non est malum secundum se: imo possunt haberi, acquiri & conservari absque peccato: ita repetere in iudicio divitias proprias non est secundum se peccatum, imo absque peccato etiam veniali repeti possunt non solum extra iudicium, sed etiam in iudicio.
units.tr: To make the whole matter clear, they say that certain points must be noted. The first is this: just as to hold ownership of riches in particular is not evil in itself, indeed riches can be held, acquired and kept without sin, so to reclaim one's own riches in a court of law is not in itself a sin. Indeed, they may be reclaimed without even venial sin, not only outside a court but also within one.

units.la: Quod vero habere divitiarum dominium non sit de se peccatum, patet aperte. Nam multi sancti absque peccato divitias possidebant. Abraham enim Isaac & Iacob, Moyses, Aaron, Samuel, David & alii sancti multi absque peccato diuites extiterunt, hinc est quod sancti Patres in Gangrensi concilio, ut habetur trigesim. distinctione. capitul. hac scripsimus, dixerunt: divites cum iustitia & operibus boni non abiicimus. Hic etiam dicit Glossa duodecim. quaestion. prim. Clericus: Non est peccatum habere diuitias, si adsint opera bona, potest igitur diuitiarum dominium proprium habere sine peccato, sic etiam possunt repeti in iudicio sine peccato: teste beato Augustino, qui, vt habetur decim. quart. quaestion. prim. capitul. quod debetur, ait: Quod debetur etsi benigne remittitur, non tamen inique repetitur. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod illud quod debetur, praesertim tanquam proprium, non inique repetitur, diuitiae ergo propriae absque iniquitate repeti possunt.
units.tr: That holding ownership of riches is not in itself a sin is plain. Many saints possessed riches without sin. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Samuel, David and many other saints were rich without sin. Hence the holy Fathers at the Council of Gangra, as is found in Distinctio 30, chapter Hac scripsimus, said: "We do not reject the rich who have justice and do good works." The Gloss on Causa 12, quaestio 1, canon Clericus also says: "It is not a sin to have riches, if good works are present." So a person can have proper ownership of riches without sin, and so too they can be reclaimed in a court without sin. This is the testimony of the blessed Augustine, who says, as is found in Causa 14, quaestio 1, chapter Quod debetur: "What is owed, even if it is kindly remitted, is nonetheless not unjustly demanded." From these words it is shown that what is owed, especially as one's own, is not unjustly demanded. Therefore one's own riches can be reclaimed without injustice.

units.la: Secundo notant isti, quod licet diuitiae absque peccato possint haberi: melius tamen est omnium diuitiarum dominium abdicare propter Deum, sicut supra capitulo quinto auctoritatibus Ambrosii & Augustini & Bernardi probatum existit, quibus etiam concordat Hieronymus ad Ebidiam dicens: vis esse perfecta & in primo stare fastigio dignitatis, fac quod fecerunt Apostoli, vende omnia quae habes, & da pauperibus, &c. & post: non vis esse perfecta, sed secundum gradum tenere non dimittendo omnia tua quae habes, da filiis, da propinquis: nemo te reprehendit, si inferiora sectaris, dum modo sciás illam tibi iure praelatam: quae elegerit prima. Ex quibus verbis euidenter colligitur, quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium diuitiarum proprietati earum praefertur, unde dicere, quod abdicare omnium proprietatem non est melius quam diuitias retinere: est error Vigilantii haeretici, de quo dicit Hieronymus: Quod autem asserit eos melius facere qui vtantur rebus, & paulatim fructus possessionum diuidunt, quam illos qui possessionibus venumdatis simul omnia largiuntur, non a me est, sed a Deo respondebitur: Si vis esse perfectus, vade vende omnia quae habes, & da pauperibus, & veni sequere me. sic ergo patet, quod licet habere diuitias non sit de se peccatum: melius tamen est omnium diuitiarum dominium abdicare, unde & ad perfectionem spectat omnium diuitiarum dominium abdicare, sicut supra est probatum.
units.tr: Second, these opponents note that although riches can be held without sin, it is nevertheless better to renounce ownership of all riches for God's sake. This was proved above in chapter 5 by the authorities of Ambrose, Augustine and Bernard, and Jerome agrees with them in his letter to Ebidia, saying: "If you want to be perfect and to stand at the first height of dignity, do what the Apostles did: sell all that you have and give to the poor," etc. And afterwards: "You do not want to be perfect, but to keep to the second degree, not giving away all that you have; give to your sons, give to your kin. No one blames you if you follow the lesser things, provided you know that the first place is rightly reserved for those who choose it." From these words it is plainly gathered that renouncing ownership of all temporal riches is preferred to owning them. Hence to say that renouncing ownership of everything is no better than keeping riches is the error of the heretic Vigilantius, of whom Jerome says: "As for his claim that those are better who use things and gradually distribute the fruits of their possessions, than those who sell their estates and give everything away at once, this is not from me, but God will answer it: If you want to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and come, follow me." So it is clear that although having riches is not in itself a sin, it is better to renounce ownership of all riches. Hence renouncing ownership of all riches belongs to perfection, as was proved above.

units.la: Tertio notant isti, quod sicut melius est omnium abdicare dominium, quam diuitiarum dominium retinere: ita melius est simpliciter nulla temporalia in iudicio repetere, quamuis repetere possit quis propria sine peccato, hoc notabile ex praecedenti colligitur euidenter.
units.tr: Third, these opponents note that just as it is better to renounce ownership of everything than to keep ownership of riches, so it is better simply to reclaim no temporal goods in a court, although a person may reclaim his own goods without sin. This point follows clearly from what was said before.

units.la: Quarto notant, quod sicut licet diuitiae possint haberi sine peccato, tamen raro & vix habentur sine peccato: sic licet repetere diuitias possit esse sine peccato, tamen repetere in iudicio diuitias vel quaecunque temporalia raro & vix inuenitur sine peccato, quod diuitiae raro vel vix habeantur sine peccato, innuit ipse Saluator dicens Matthaei decimo nono. Dines dissicile intrabit in regnum caelorum, & Lucae decimo octauo, ait: quam difficile qui habent pecunias intrabunt in regnum caelorum. Ex his datur intelligi, quod diuitiae vix habentur sine peccato: quia solum peccatum facit difficultatem intrandi in regnum caelorum.
units.tr: Fourth, they note that although riches may be held without sin, yet they are rarely, and scarcely ever, held without sin. So although reclaiming riches may be without sin, yet reclaiming riches or any temporal goods in a court is rarely, and scarcely ever, found without sin. That riches are rarely, or scarcely, held without sin is suggested by the Saviour himself, who says in Matthew 19, "A rich man will hardly enter the kingdom of heaven," and in Luke 18 he says, "How hard it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of heaven." From these words it is understood that riches are scarcely held without sin, because sin alone makes it hard to enter the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: Item Gregorius, vt habetur distinctione. vigesim. quint. capitul. quasi, loquens de peccato curae rei familiaris, ait: Peccatum cura rei familiaris, quae vix sine culpa agitur, vel ab ipsis qui culpam qualiter declinare debeant sciunt. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod possessio temporalium, quae sine cura rei familiaris esse non debet, vix sine culpa agitur: & ita temporalium dominium vix habetur sine peccato.
units.tr: Likewise Gregory, as is found in Distinctio 25, chapter Quasi, speaking of the sin of care for household affairs, says: "The care of household affairs, which can scarcely be carried on without fault, is a sin, or it is a sin for those who know how they ought to avoid fault." From these words it is plainly gathered that the possession of temporal goods, which cannot be without care for household affairs, can scarcely be carried on without fault. And so ownership of temporal goods is scarcely held without sin.

units.la: Quod etiam repetere in iudicio sua vix sine peccato fiat, probatur: quia non minus implicat ad peccatum in iudicio litigare, quod negociationis officium exercere, sed secundum Leonem Papam, vt habetur de poenitentia distinctione. quint. capitul. quaedam; difficile est inter ementis vendentisque commercium non interuenire peccatum, ergo non minus difficile est sine peccato in iudicio litigare, quam negotiationis officium exercere, & confirmatur haec ratio: quia sicut quasi naturale est in contrahentibus se inuicem decipere: ita quasi naturale est in litigantibus se inuicem velle decipere ad suum intentum habendum, sicut ergo negotiationis officium difficile est exercere sine peccato: ita difficile est in iudicio litigare sine peccato.
units.tr: That reclaiming one's own goods in a court is scarcely done without sin is proved as follows. Litigating in a court involves no less risk of sin than carrying on the business of trade. But according to Pope Leo, as is found in De poenitentia, Distinctio 5, chapter Quaedam: "It is hard for sin not to intervene in the dealings of buyer and seller." Therefore it is no less hard to litigate in a court without sin than to carry on a business of trade. This reasoning is confirmed: just as it is almost natural for those who deal with one another to deceive each other, so it is almost natural for litigants to wish to deceive one another in order to gain their aim. Therefore just as it is hard to carry on a trade without sin, so it is hard to litigate in a court without sin.

units.la: Quinto notant, quod in scripturis diuinis & sanctorum non solum dissuadentur illicita, sed etiam quaedam licita, quae implicant ad peccatum, sicut enim Christus perfectis, vtpote discipulis, dissuasit thesaurizare in terra Matthaei sexto, & tamen thesaurizare est licitum: sic etiam dissuasit cogitare de crastino, quod tamen non est illicitum reputandum, sic etiam habere diuitias, quia implicant ad peccatum, & plenae sunt periculis, dissuadetur, hinc etiam Gregorius in Moralibus ait: Solus iste in illicitis non cadit, qui se a licitis tamen restringit.
units.tr: Fifth, they note that the divine Scriptures and the saints do not only dissuade from unlawful things but also from certain lawful things which lead to sin. For Christ dissuaded the perfect, namely his disciples, from storing up treasure on earth (Matthew 6), and yet storing up treasure is lawful. So too he dissuaded them from being anxious about tomorrow, which is not to be reckoned unlawful. In the same way, having riches is dissuaded because they lead to sin and are full of dangers. Hence Gregory also says in the Moralia: "He alone does not fall into unlawful things who restrains himself even from lawful ones."

units.la: Sexto notant, quod licitum est Christianis, imo expediens, quamuis non toti communitati, se voto astringere ad non faciendum & non habendum illa, quae implicant ad peccatum, sine quibus contingit vitam praesentem transigere, & officia necessaria exercere. Nam fugere occasiones peccandi est laudabile: & per consequens se astringere per votum ad fugiendum occasiones peccandi, sine quibus vitam contingit sustentare, & officia necessaria exercere, est laudabile reputandum.
units.tr: Sixthly, they note that it is lawful for Christians, indeed expedient, even if not for the whole community, to bind themselves by a vow not to do or to have those things which entangle them in sin, and without which it is possible to pass the present life and carry out the necessary duties. For to flee the occasions of sinning is praiseworthy; and consequently, to bind oneself by vow to flee the occasions of sinning, without which it is possible to sustain life and carry out the necessary duties, is to be reckoned praiseworthy.

units.la: Quod beatus Hieronymus contra Vigilantium, qui statum secularem statui religionis conabatur praeferre, videtur asserere, quaerens enim in persona Vigilantii haeretici, ait: Cur pergis ad eremum? & respondet dicens: vt te non audiam, non videam, vt furore non moueat, vt tua bella non patiar, ne me capiat oculus meretricis, ne me forma pulcherrima ad illicites ducat amplexus. Respondebis hic: Noli fugere, sta in facie, aduersarium armatum obsiste, vt postquam vicerit, coronaris, f. iteor imbecillitatem meam: nolo spe pugnare victoria, ne perdam aliquando victoriam, si fugero gladium, deuitaui: si metero, aut vincendum mihi est aut cadendum. Quid necesse habeo certa dimittere, & etiam certare? nulla securitas est vicino serpente dormire: potest fieri vt me non mordeat, & tamen potest fieri vt aliquando me mordeat. Quod de libidine diximus, referamus ad auaritiam, & omnia vitia quae vitantur solitudine, & ideo vrbium frequentias declinamus, ne facere compellamur, quae nos non tam natura cogit facere quam voluptas. Ex his verbis datur intelligi, quod licet intrare religionem, quae sine voto non accipitur, ad fugiendum occasiones peccandi: & per consequens licet Christiano se voto astringere ad non faciendum, & non habendum illa, quae implicant ad peccatum, quod de illis debet intelligi, sine quibus contingit & humanam sustentare naturam, & officia necessaria exercere.
