units.tr: Blessed Jerome, against Vigilantius, who tried to set the secular state above the state of religion, seems to assert this, for in the person of the heretic Vigilantius he asks: Why do you hasten to the desert? and answers, saying: "So that I may not hear you, not see you, so that I am not moved to fury, so that I do not suffer your wars, so that the eye of a harlot does not take me, so that the most beautiful form does not lead me to unlawful embraces. Here you will reply: Do not flee, stand in the face of it, resist the armed adversary, so that after he has conquered you may be crowned; I confess my weakness: I am unwilling to fight with the hope of victory, lest I sometime lose the victory. If I flee the sword, I have avoided it; if I stand, either I must conquer or fall. Why do I need to give up what is certain and also to contend? There is no safety in sleeping beside a serpent: it may be that it does not bite me, and yet it may be that at some time it does bite me. What we have said of lust, let us refer to avarice, and to all the vices which are avoided by solitude; and therefore we avoid the crowds of cities, lest we be compelled to do those things which nature does not so much compel us to do as pleasure does." From these words it is understood that it is lawful to enter a religious order, which is not undertaken without a vow, in order to flee the occasions of sinning; and consequently it is lawful for a Christian to bind himself by vow not to do and not to have those things which entangle him in sin, which must be understood of those things without which it is possible to sustain human nature and carry out the necessary duties.

units.la: Sunt enim aliqua, quae implicant ad peccatum: sicut bibere, comedere & dormire, & alia huiusmodi, sine quibus vita non sustentatur humana, sine etiam acquisitione scientiae non potest praedicator euangelicus praedicationis officium exercere: & tamen scientia quodammodo implicat ad peccatum, quia scientia inflat, teste Apostolo.
units.tr: For there are some things which entangle in sin, such as drinking, eating and sleeping, and other things of this kind, without which human life is not sustained; and likewise, without the acquisition of knowledge the gospel preacher cannot carry out the office of preaching; and yet knowledge in some measure entangles in sin, because knowledge puffs up, as the Apostle witnesses.

units.la: Septimo notant, quod inter praecepta Christi, vel consilia posita in sermone Domini in monte, quaedam sunt negativa & quaedam affirmativa, negativa sunt: vt, non resistere malo: non contendere in iudicio: non repercutere: non thesaurizare in terra: non sollicitari superfluè de temporalibus: & huiusmodi, quaedam autem sunt affirmativa: vt, dimittere pallium: praebere alteram maxillam: & huiusmodi.
units.tr: Seventhly, they note that among the precepts of Christ, or the counsels laid down in the Lord's sermon on the mount, some are negative and some affirmative. The negative are: not to resist evil; not to contend in judgment; not to retaliate; not to lay up treasure on earth; not to be superfluously anxious about temporal things, and such like. Some are affirmative: to give up the cloak; to offer the other cheek, and such like.

units.la: Octauo notant: quod ad perfectionem spectat saepe velle vel desiderare aliquid fugere: & tamen in casu meritorium est illud suscipere vel etiam exercere: sicut perfectorum est velle, seu desiderare fugere praelationes & ecclesiasticas dignitates, & tamen in casu tales dignitates suscipere est meritorium & laudabile: sicut per Augustinum, & Gregorium, quorum auctoritates ponuntur octau. quaestion. prim. capitul. in scripturis: & capit. qui episcopatum, patet aperte. Praedicta ad propositum applicando dicunt isti, quod Christus illa quae necessaria sunt in praedictis praeceptis, suasit discipulis, in communi, in omni tempore, in operis executione seruare: quae tamen Apostolis imposuit sub praecepto, & ideo cum non contendere in iudicio, sicut necessarium Apostolis imposuit sub praecepto, & aliis saltem aliquibus suasit omni tempore dictum praeceptum, scilicet non contendere in iudicio, in operis executione seruare. Illa vero, affirmatiua sunt in dictis praeceptis, scilicet percutienti in vna maxilla praebere alteram, dimittere pallium absque violentia, cum angariante mille passus ire & alia duo, non imposuit Apostolis sub praecepto: nec suasit aliis omni tempore seruare in executione operis, sed secundum praeparationem animi.
units.tr: Eighthly, they note that it belongs to perfection often to wish or desire to flee something, and yet in a given case it is meritorious to undertake or even to exercise it; just as it belongs to the perfect to wish, or desire, to flee promotions and ecclesiastical dignities, and yet in a given case to accept such dignities is meritorious and praiseworthy, as is plainly shown by the authorities of Augustine and Gregory, which are set down in Dist. 8, qu. 1, cap. In scripturis, and cap. Qui episcopatum. Applying what has been said to the matter at hand, they say that Christ urged his disciples, in general and at all times, to observe in the execution of the work those things which are necessary in the aforesaid precepts; yet he laid upon the Apostles as a precept what is necessary; and so, since he laid upon the Apostles as a necessary precept not to contend in judgment, and urged at least some others to observe that precept at all times in the execution of the work, namely not to contend in judgment. But those affirmative things in the said precepts, namely to offer the other cheek to the one who strikes, to give up the cloak without violence, to go with the one who compels a thousand paces and two more others, he did not lay upon the Apostles as a precept, nor did he urge others to observe them at all times in the execution of the work, but according to the preparation of the mind.

units.la: Ratio autem differentiae est: quia velle omni tempore in executione operis pro temporalibus rebus non contendere in iudicio ad perfectionem spectat: & ideo sub voto cadere potest: & per consequens suaderi potest, dimittere autem cuique pallium absque omni violentia ad perfectionem non spectat: imo saepe ad malitiam vel stultitiam pertinere dignoscitur, gratis enim dimittere pallium rapienti ad malum finem fraternae dilectioni repugnat, qua quis a peccato, si potest, debet aliud revocare, & similiter est de aliis praeceptis affirmatiuis, & ideo quantum ad ista, seruanda est doctrina Augustini, qui, vt habetur in praeallegato capitulo, paratus, ait: Ista praecepta sunt magis ad praeparationem cordis quam ad opus, quod in aperto fit, vt teneatur in secreto animi patientia cum benevolentia, in manifesto autem id fiat, quod eis videtur prodesse, quibus bene vel- le debemus.
units.tr: The reason for the difference, however, is this: to wish at all times, in the execution of the work, not to contend in judgment over temporal things belongs to perfection, and therefore it can fall under a vow, and consequently can be urged; but to give up one's cloak to everyone without any violence does not belong to perfection; indeed it is often recognised as pertaining to wickedness or folly, for to give one's cloak gratis to a robber bent on an evil end is repugnant to brotherly love, by which one ought, if he can, to call another back from sin; and it is similar with the other affirmative precepts. Therefore, as regards these, the teaching of Augustine must be kept, who, as is found in the aforesaid chapter, Paratus, says: These precepts pertain more to the preparation of the heart than to the deed, which is done openly, so that it is held in the secret of the mind as patience with goodwill, but in the open let that be done which seems to profit those whom we ought to wish well.

units.la: Nec talia affirmatiua respectu cuiuslibet sub voto cadere debent. Non enim est licitum alicui vouere, quod omni volenti tunicam suam tollere, pallium libere dimittere eidem, quamuis sub voto cadere possit, nunquam velle pro tunica contendere in iudicio, similiter nullus debet vouere, quod quicunque angariauit eum mille passus, ibit cum eo alia duo: cum hoc possit vergere in detrimentum salutis, teste Sapiente, qui ait Ecclesiastici octau. cum audace non eas in via ne forte grauet mala sua in te. Talia autem semper ad praeparationem cordis non quantum ad opus exterius sunt seruanda. Non contendere autem in iudicio, licet in opere omni tempore seruare, & sub voto cadere potest: & ideo Christus hoc Apostolis imposuit sub praecepto quantum ad opus, & aliis nonnullis suasit, & quod Christus hoc imposuerit Apostolis, quantum ad executionem operis ostendunt isti.
units.tr: Nor ought such affirmative precepts to fall under a vow with respect to anyone whatsoever. For it is not lawful for anyone to vow that he will freely give his cloak to everyone who wishes to take his tunic, although it could fall under a vow; he must never vow to contend in judgment for his tunic; likewise no one ought to vow that he will go with whoever has compelled him a thousand paces two more, since this could tend to the detriment of salvation, as the Wise Man witnesses in Ecclesiasticus chapter eight: Do not go with a bold man on the way, lest perhaps he burden you with his evils. Such precepts, however, are always to be observed as regards the preparation of the heart, not as regards the outward deed. To not contend in judgment, however, can be observed in the deed at all times, and can fall under a vow; and therefore Christ laid this upon the Apostles as a precept as regards the deed, and urged it upon some others; and these men show that Christ laid this upon the Apostles as regards the execution of the deed.

units.la: Quibus imponitur proprietatem & ius positiuum in rebus temporalibus non habere, neque in speciali, neque in communi, quantum ad communitatem specialem eisdem imponitur, nec nomine proprio nec nomine suae communitatis specialis pro rebus temporalibus litigare: quia sine iure proprio vel communi non potest quis pro temporalibus in iudicio litigare, sed Christus imposuit Apostolis proprietatem & ius positiuum in temporalibus non habere, nec in speciali neque in communi, quantum ad communitatem specialem Apostolorum, ergo imposuit eis praedicto modo pro temporalibus in iudicio minime contendere.
units.tr: To those upon whom is laid not to have ownership and positive right in temporal things, neither in particular nor in common, as regards the particular community, is laid upon them, neither in their own name nor in the name of their particular community, to litigate for temporal things; for without a right of ownership or a common right one cannot litigate in court for temporal things; but Christ laid upon the Apostles not to have ownership and positive right in temporal things, neither in particular nor in common, as regards the particular community of the Apostles; therefore he laid upon them in the aforesaid manner not to contend at all in court for temporal things.

units.la: Secundo ostendunt, quod aliis hoc idem suasit. Primo sic: Christus suadens non contendere in iudicio, suasit illud quod est melius, sed nolle contendere in iudicio, est melius quam contendere, ergo hoc Christus quantum ad executionem operis, suasit.
units.tr: Secondly, they show that the same thing was urged on others. First, thus: Christ, urging not to contend in judgment, urged that which is better; but to be unwilling to contend in judgment is better than to contend; therefore Christ urged this, as regards the execution of the work.

units.la: Secundo sic: Christus per dictum praeceptum dissuasit illud opus, quod vix sine peccato potest exerceri, sed contendere in iudicio vix potest exerceri sine peccato, ergo Christus dissuasit, quantum ad operis executionem contendere in iudicio, & per consequens suasit non contendere.
units.tr: Secondly, thus: Christ by the said precept discouraged that work which can scarcely be exercised without sin; but to contend in judgment can scarcely be exercised without sin; therefore Christ discouraged contending in judgment as regards the execution of the work, and consequently urged not to contend.

units.la: Tertio sic: Per dictum praeceptum vel consilium dissuasit illud, quantum ad contentionem in iudicio quod implicat ad peccatum, licet non sit de se peccatum, sed actualiter quantum ad opus contendere in iudicio implicat ad peccatum, ergo Christus hoc dissuasit in praedicto consilio, & per consequens suasit non contendere in iudicio non solum quantum ad praeparationem cordis, sed etiam quantum ad opus.
units.tr: Thirdly, thus: By the said precept or counsel he discouraged that which, as regards contention in judgment, entangles in sin, although it is not in itself a sin; but actually, as regards the deed, to contend in judgment entangles in sin; therefore Christ discouraged this in the aforesaid counsel, and consequently urged not to contend in judgment not only as regards the preparation of the heart, but also as regards the deed.

units.la: (Prebe illi & alteram) Licet hoc semper sit servandum, quantum ad praeparationem cordis, & non sit semper servandum quantum ad opus exterius: imo aliquando hoc servare esset peccatum, & contra caritatem fraternam, puta si percutiens per correctionem fraternam posset corrigi de peccato commisso, & revocari a peccato committendo. Et ita licet in opere exteriori hoc servare sit quandoque illicitum: Tamen non repercutere semper est licitum. Et ideo licitum est nonnullis ad non repercutiendum se voto astringere: sed nulli est licitum, se voto astringere ad praebendam maxillam alteram percutienti, & ita inter negativum & affirmativum aperte differentia reperitur. (Vade cum eo alia duo) hoc etiam servare in opere exteriori potest esse illicitum ex multis causis, quas longum esset enarrare, & ideo hoc nequaquam sub voto cadere potest (qui vult tecum in iudicio contendere & tunicam tuam tollere, dimitte ei & pallium) hoc est, non contendas pro tunica & dimitte pallium: & ita in dictis verbis aliquid insinuatur negative, & aliquid affirmative.
units.tr: (Give him the other cheek also.) Although this must always be kept as regards the disposition of the heart, it is not always to be kept as regards the outward act. Indeed, sometimes keeping it would be sin and contrary to brotherly love: for example, if by brotherly correction the one who strikes could be corrected of a sin already committed and recalled from committing one. So although to keep this in outward action is sometimes unlawful, not to strike back is always lawful. Hence it is lawful for some to bind themselves by vow not to strike back; but it is lawful for no one to bind himself by vow to offer the other cheek to one who strikes him, and so a clear difference is found between the negative and the affirmative. (Go with him two miles.) To keep this also in outward action may be unlawful for many causes, which would take too long to set out; and therefore this can by no means fall under a vow. (If anyone wants to contend with you in judgment and take your coat, let him have your cloak also.) That is, do not contend for the coat, and let the cloak go. So in these words something is implied negatively and something affirmatively.

units.la: Negativum omni tempore servare multis est licitum, & ideo licite sub voto cadere potest: & ita potest suaderi pro omni tempore, quantum ad operis executionem, sed secundum nulli pro omni tempore & in omni casu potest esse licitum, sicut ostensum est prius, & ideo sub voto cadere nequaquam debet respectu cuiuscunque personae indifferenter, licet possit forte cadere sub voto in aliquo respectu illius, cui promitteret obedientiam per votum, (secundum quod Augustinus dicit) Augustinus intendit de affirmativis, non de negativis, sicut dictum est.
units.tr: To keep the negative at all times is lawful for many, and so it can lawfully fall under a vow; and thus it can be urged at all times as regards the carrying out of the deed. But the affirmative can at no time and in no case be lawful for anyone, as has been shown before; and therefore it must by no means fall under a vow in respect of any person whatever, although it may perhaps fall under a vow in some respect toward that person to whom one promised obedience by vow. (As Augustine says.) Augustine means the affirmatives, not the negatives, as has been said.

units.la: CAP. CXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER CXV.

units.la: ET propter hoc Apostolus non simpliciter dixit prima ad Corinth. sext. quare non iniuriam accipitis? sed dixit: Quare non magis iniuriam accipitis? & quod hoc eis simpliciter non interdixit, patet ex eo, quod in praecedenti capitulo prima Corinth. quint. amplius reprehenderat Corinthios, qui erant negligentes in iudicio faciendo, dicens eis: Nonne de his, qui intus sunt vos iudicatis? Item in praellegato capitulo prima Corinth. sext. Apostolus Corinthios reprehendebat, quia coram infidelibus litigabant & iudicium subibant, dicens: Audet (id est praesumit) aliquis vestrum habens negotium aduersus alterum iudicari, (id est iudicium subire) apud iniquos & non apud sanctos, id est fideles. Item ostendebat, quod hoc ad fideles pertinebat dicens: Et si in vobis (id est per vos) iudicabitur mundus (id est mundani) indigni estis qui de minimis (scilicet temporalibus) iudicetis: quasi dicat, non: quia qui maioribus, multo fortius minoribus est dignus, & sequitur: Secularia igitur iudicia, si habueritis, contemptibiles qui sunt in ecclesia illos constituite ad iudicium, hoc autem dicebat ipsis ironice, unde subdit: ad verecundiam vestram dico (subaudi, quia curritis ad iudicia infidelium.) Non est inter vos sapiens quisquam, qui possit iudicare inter fratrem & fratrem suum, sed frater cum fratre in iudicio contendit, & hoc apud infideles. Deinde reprehendit eos, quia iniuste & fraudulenter fratres suos ad iudicium trahebant, dicens: Iam quidem omnino delictum est in vobis, quia iudicia habetis inter vos, scilicet fraudulenta & iniuriosa, unde sequitur: sed vos iniuriam facitis & fraudatis & hoc fratribus. Et quod de fratribus, qui fraudulenter trahebant fratres ad iudicium, intellexerit Apostolus, patet, quia statim subiunxit: An nescitis, quia iniqui regnum Dei non possidebunt: eos agere inique supponens. Unde patet, quod Apostolus non interdixerit simpliciter Corinthiis conversis ad idem litigare: imo quod eis liceret ex multis, ut patet ex praedictis, ostendit, & ideo subiunxit: Omnia mihi licent. Glossa: Omnia mea licet repetere mihi.
units.tr: And for this reason the Apostle did not simply say, in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter six, "Why do you not rather suffer wrong?" but said: "Why do you not rather suffer wrong?" That he did not simply forbid them this is clear from the fact that in the preceding chapter, the fifth of the first Epistle to the Corinthians, he had already rebuked the Corinthians who were careless in judging, saying to them: "Do you not judge those who are within?" Likewise, in the chapter of the first Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter six, quoted above, the Apostle rebuked the Corinthians because they litigated before unbelievers and submitted to judgment, saying: "Does any one of you, having a matter against another, dare (that is, presume) to be judged (that is, to submit to judgment) before the unrighteous and not before the saints, that is, the faithful?" He also showed that this pertained to the faithful, saying: "And if the world shall be judged by you (that is, through you), are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters (namely temporal ones)?" As if he were saying: "Are you unworthy? For he who is worthy of greater matters is much more worthy of lesser ones." And it follows: "If then you have secular judgments, set those who are despised in the church to judge them." He said this ironically, whence he adds: "I say this to your shame" (understand: because you run to the judgments of unbelievers). "Is there not among you one wise man who is able to judge between brother and brother, but brother contends with brother in judgment, and that before unbelievers?" Then he rebukes them because they unjustly and fraudulently dragged their brothers to judgment, saying: "Now indeed there is altogether a fault among you, because you have lawsuits among yourselves," namely fraudulent and wrongful ones, whence it follows: "but you do wrong and defraud, and that your brothers." And that the Apostle understood this of brothers who fraudulently dragged brothers to judgment is clear, because he immediately added: "Do you not know that the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God?" assuming that they were acting unjustly. Hence it is evident that the Apostle did not simply forbid the converted Corinthians to litigate with one another; rather, as is clear from what has been said, he showed that they were permitted it in many cases, and therefore he added: "All things are lawful for me." Gloss: "I may reclaim all that is mine."

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnatus, qualiter intelligat verba Apostoli saepe dicta de iudicio, manifestat dicens, quod Apostolus non simpliciter interdixit Corinthiis iudicia seu contendere in iudicio: sed interdixit eis tantummodo iudicia fraudulenta & iniuriosa. Unde postea ostendit, quod eis non simpliciter interdixit iudicia, & hoc primo sic: qui reprehendit aliquos de non faciendo iudicium, non simpliciter interdicit eis iudicium, sed Apostolus reprehendit Corinthios de non faciendo iudicium, ergo, &c. Secundo sic: qui reprehendit aliquos, quod litigant coram infidelibus, ostendens, quod debent coram fidelibus litigare, non simpliciter interdicit eisdem litigare, sed Apostolus reprehendit Corinthios, qui coram infidelibus litigabant, ostendens quod deberent coram fidelibus litigare, & iudices constituere sapientes: ergo, &c. Secundo ibi: Deinde reprehendit, ostendit quod Apostolus simpliciter interdixit Corinthiis iudicia fraudulenta & iniuriosa per illud; miqui regnum Dei non possidebunt. Tertio ibi: Et ideo subiunxit, ostendit auctoritate Apostoli & Glossae quod licet repetere sua.
units.tr: In this part, this man, who is being attacked, explains how he understands the words of the Apostle, often quoted, about judgment, saying that the Apostle did not simply forbid the Corinthians judgments or contending in judgment, but forbade them only fraudulent and wrongful judgments. Whence he afterwards shows that judgments were not simply forbidden them, and he does this first thus: whoever rebukes some people for not holding judgment does not simply forbid them judgment; but the Apostle rebukes the Corinthians for not holding judgment; therefore, etc. Second, thus: whoever rebukes some people because they litigate before unbelievers, showing that they ought to litigate before the faithful, does not simply forbid them to litigate; but the Apostle rebukes the Corinthians, who litigated before unbelievers, showing that they ought to litigate before the faithful and appoint wise judges; therefore, etc. Second, there: Then he rebukes, he shows that the Apostle simply forbade the Corinthians fraudulent and wrongful judgments by that passage: the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God. Third, there: And therefore he added, he shows by the authority of the Apostle and of the Gloss that it is lawful to reclaim one's own things.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores dicunt eum errare, cum asserit, quod Apostolus solummodo interdixit Corinthiis iudicia, seu litigia fraudulenta & iniuriosa, & coram infidelibus: & quod alia iudicia minime reprehendit, nec alia dissuasit.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he is wrong when he asserts that the Apostle forbade the Corinthians only judgments or litigation that was fraudulent and wrongful, and before unbelievers; and that he by no means rebuked other judgments or dissuaded from them.

units.la: Ad cuius evidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod sicut diuitiarum possessio non solum reprehenditur, interdicitur, & dissuadetur, quando diuitiae acquiruntur iniuste: sed etiam quando amore nimio diliguntur, dissuadentur etiam diuitiae: quia ad inordinatum amorem implicant & peccata, sic in iudicio pro temporalibus litigare non solum reprehenditur & interdicitur, quando quis fraudulenter & iniuriose litigat in iudicio: sed etiam quando ex avaritia, vel alia mala radice procediturr, quamuis nihil in opere exteriori vel verbo secundum se illicitum committatur: licet opus exterius sit illo tempore malum, propter malitiam actus interioris, litigia vero licita non reprehenduntur, cum dissuadentur propter hoc, quia implicant ad peccata, & vix inueniuntur sine peccato. Ex hoc patet, quod erroneum est dicere, Apostolum non interdixisse simpliciter nisi iudicia fraudulenta & iniuriosa: quod probatur sic. Apostolus prim. ad Corinth. sexto. interdixit Corinthiis, & aliis omnia omnia litigia illicita & iniqua: propter quod dicit: An nescitis, quia iniqui regnum Dei non possidebunt, quasi diceret determinate omnia iniqua iudicia: quia iniqui regnum Dei non possidebunt, sed multa sunt iniqua iudicia seu litigia, siue contentiones iniquae & illicitae, praeter fraudulenta & iniuriosa, ergo non solum interdicit Apostolus simpliciter litigia fraudulenta & iniuriosa: sed etiam alia multa, quae sunt iniqua, siue ex iniqua intentione, siue ex alia iniquitate quacunque.
units.tr: To make this clear, they say it must be understood that just as the possession of riches is not only rebuked, forbidden and discouraged when riches are acquired unjustly, but riches are also discouraged when they are loved to excess, because they entangle a person in disordered love and in sins; so too, to litigate in court over temporal matters is not only rebuked and forbidden when someone litigates fraudulently and wrongfully, but also when it proceeds from avarice or another evil root, although nothing unlawful in itself is committed in the outward deed or word. The outward deed is then evil because of the wickedness of the inner act; but lawful lawsuits are not rebuked when they are discouraged for this reason, that they entangle one in sins and can scarcely be found without sin. From this it is clear that it is erroneous to say that the Apostle forbade only fraudulent and wrongful judgments. This is proved thus. In the first Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter six, the Apostle forbade the Corinthians and others all unlawful and unjust lawsuits, all of them; for which reason he says: "Do you not know that the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God?" as if he were determinately saying all unjust judgments; for the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God. But there are many unjust judgments or lawsuits, or unjust and unlawful contentions, besides fraudulent and wrongful ones; therefore the Apostle not only simply forbids fraudulent and wrongful lawsuits, but also many other things that are unjust, whether from an unjust intention or from any other injustice.

units.la: Secundo dicunt ipsum errare, cum insinuat quod Apostolus licita litigia minime dissuasit, sed magis eos voluit litigare.
units.tr: Secondly, they say he is wrong when he insinuates that the Apostle did not discourage lawful lawsuits at all, but rather wished them to litigate.

units.la: Quod enim hoc sit erroneum, probatur sic. Apostolus dissuasit omnia litigia, quae implicant ad peccatum, sed litigia etiam licita implicant ad peccatum, teste Chrysostomo super Matthaeum, qui ait: Omne iudicium, irritatio cordis est, & malarum cogitationum radix. Nam si videris, quod causa fraudibus & pecuniis expugnetur, & tu similiter causa tua adesse festinas, etsi ab initio hoc consilium non habuisti. Ex quibus euidenter habetur, quod litigium etiam in principio iustum & licitum irritatio cordis est & malarum cogitationum tadix: & per consequens implicat ad peccatum, ergo tale iudicium Apostolus dissuadet.
units.tr: That this is erroneous is proved thus. The Apostle discouraged all lawsuits that entangle one in sin; but even lawful lawsuits entangle one in sin, as Chrysostom testifies on Matthew, who says: "Every judgment is an irritation of the heart and a root of evil thoughts. For if you see that a cause is pursued by frauds and money, and you hasten likewise to press your own cause, even though you did not have this intention at the beginning." From these words it is plainly evident that a lawsuit which is at the beginning just and lawful is an irritation of the heart and a root of evil thoughts, and consequently entangles one in sin; therefore the Apostle discourages such a judgment.

units.la: Sed forte dices, quod secundum Chrysostomum, iudicium seu litigium tunc est irritatio cordis & malarum cogitationum radix, quando est ex alia parte fraudulentum.
units.tr: But perhaps you will say that, according to Chrysostom, a judgment or lawsuit is an irritation of the heart and a root of evil thoughts only when it is fraudulent on the other side.

units.la: Sed hoc non obstat: quia non solum tunc litigium est irritatio cordis & malarum cogitationum radix, quando est ex parte alia fraudulentum: sed etiam quando non est fraudulentum ex alia parte, saepe enim est irritatio cordis, si iudex non potest aut non vult statim ad litigantis voluntatem proferre sententiam. Frequenter etiam est irritatio cordis ex sollicitudine, quam circa productionem instrumentorum & testium, & circa alia quae iudiciarius ordo requirit, expedit adhibere, quare constat aperte, quod litigium etiam licitum non solum propter fraudulentiam aduersarii, sed etiam propter multa alia implicat ad peccatum.
units.tr: But this does not stand in the way; for a lawsuit is an irritation of the heart and a root of evil thoughts not only when it is fraudulent on the other side, but also when it is not fraudulent on the other side; for it is often an irritation of the heart if the judge cannot, or will not, at once pronounce sentence according to the will of the litigant. Frequently, too, it is an irritation of the heart through the anxiety that must be applied to the production of documents and witnesses, and to the other things that the course of judicial procedure requires. Hence it is plainly established that even a lawful lawsuit entangles one in sin, not only because of the opponent's fraud but also because of many other things.

units.la: Secundo sic: Apostolus dissuadet illa litigia, quae discordias & odia pariunt, sed litigia etiam non fraudulenta discordias & odia pariunt, teste beato Remigio, qui super epistolam prim. ad Corinth. sext. ait: Accusatio litem, lis discordiam, discordia odium generat, ergo Apostolus etiam alia litigia quam fraudulenta dissuadet.
units.tr: Secondly, thus: the Apostle dissuades those lawsuits which produce discords and hatreds; but even lawsuits that are not fraudulent produce discords and hatreds, as the blessed Remigius testifies, who, on the first Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter six, says: "Accusation begets strife, strife begets discord, discord begets hatred." Therefore the Apostle dissuades also lawsuits other than fraudulent ones.

units.la: Tertio sic: Apostolus dissuadet omnia litigia, quae dissuadentur a Christo, cum dicit Matthaei quinto, qui vult tecum in iudicio contendere & tunicam tuam tollere, dimitte ei & pallium, & Luc. sext. cum dicit: qui aufert quae tua sunt, ne repetas, sed Christus in verbis praedictis dissuasit non solum litigia fraudulenta, sed etiam alia, teste Remigio, qui ubi prius ait: ideo Apostolus dixit in veritate omnino delictum est in vobis, qui contra praeceptum Domini agitis, qui dixit, si quis aufert quae tua sunt ne repetas, & qui vobis pacem suam commendavit, quare non magis damnum sustinetis, ut praeceptum Domini custodiatis? Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod Dominus dissuasit litigare pro rebus ad litigantem pertinentibus, & per consequens dissuasit non solum litigia fraudulenta, sed etiam alia, ergo Apostolus etiam alia dissuasit.
units.tr: Thirdly, thus: the Apostle dissuades all lawsuits which Christ dissuades, since he says in Matthew, chapter five: "Whoever wishes to contend with you in judgment and take away your tunic, let him have your cloak also as well"; and in Luke, chapter six, when he says: "Whoever takes what is yours, do not ask it back." But Christ in the aforesaid words dissuaded not only fraudulent lawsuits but also others, as Remigius testifies, who, a little earlier, says: "Therefore the Apostle said, in truth there is altogether a fault among you, since you act against the command of the Lord, who said, if anyone takes what is yours, do not ask it back, and who commended to you his peace. Why do you not rather suffer loss, so that you may keep the command of the Lord?" From these words it is to be understood that the Lord dissuaded from litigating over things that belong to the litigant; and consequently he dissuaded not only fraudulent lawsuits but also others. Therefore the Apostle also dissuaded other lawsuits.

units.la: Quarto sic: Illi cui suadetur magis iniuriam suscipere, quam pro temporalibus litigare, dissuadetur litigium de se licitum, & non solum fraudulentum, sed Apostolus suadet magis iniuriam suscipere, quam pro temporalibus litigare, dicens: quare non magis iniuriam accipitis? quam scilicet pro temporalibus litigetis. Et quod haec sit intentio Apostoli, aperte Glossa testatur ibidem dicens: Non excusas quod hoc iuste agis: occurrit: Quare non magis iniuriam accipitis? Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod magis expedit iniuriam accipere, quam iustum litigium accipere, ergo Apostolus non solummodo litigia fraudulenta, sed etiam alia dissuadet.
units.tr: Fourthly, thus: a person who is urged to suffer wrong rather than go to law over temporal matters is dissuaded from a lawsuit that is lawful in itself, and not merely from a fraudulent one. The Apostle urges us to suffer wrong rather than go to law over temporal matters, saying: why do you not rather suffer wrong? That is, rather than go to law over temporal matters. That this is the Apostle's meaning the Gloss plainly bears witness in the same place, saying: You do not excuse yourself by saying that you act justly. The objection arises: Why do you not rather suffer wrong? From these words it is clear that it is more expedient to suffer wrong than to bring a just lawsuit. Therefore the Apostle dissuades not only fraudulent lawsuits but also others.

units.la: Quinto sic: Apostolus omnia illa litigia dissuadet, quae secundum veniam conceduntur infirmis, sed litigare in iudicio pro rebus temporalibus non solum fraudulenter, sed etiam absque fraudulentia concedit infirmis. ergo apostolus non solum litigia fraudulenta, sed etiam alia dissuadet. Maior est manifesta. Minor probatur auctoritate Augustini, qui ait Enchiridion c. 44. pertractans verba apostoli suprascripta: Nam & hic posset putari iudicium habere aduersus alterum non esse peccatum: sed tantummodo si extra ecclesiam vellet iudicari, nisi secutus adiungeret. Iam quidem omnino delictum est, quia iudicia habetis vobiscum & ne quis ita excusaret & diceret, se iustum habere negocium, sed iniquitatem pati, quam velit a se iudicii sententia removeri: continuo talib. cogitationib. vel excusationib. occurrit atque ait: Quare non magis iniuriam accipitis? quare non magis fraude patimini? ut ad illud redeatur, cp dominus ait: Si quis voluerit tunc tuam tollere & in iudicio tecum contendere, dimitte ei & pallium. & alio loco: Qui abstulerit, inquit, tua noli repetere, probabuit itaque suos de secularibus cum aliis habere iudicium. Ex qua doctrina apostolus dicit esse delictum: tamen cum sint in ecclesia talia iudicia finiri inter fratres fratribus iudicantibus extra ecclesiam terribiliter vetat. Manifestum est etiam quod hoc secundum veniam concedatur infirmis. Propter hoc atque huiusmodi peccata & alia licet his minora oportet ut devote crebroque oremus dominum atque dicamus, dimitte nobis debita nostra. Ex his evidenter apparet, quod contendere in iudicio etiam pro iusto negocio infirmis conceditur. Sexto sic: Apostolus dissuasit omnia litigia, quae vix inveniuntur vel nunquam inveniuntur sine peccato. sed litigia etiam quando pro iusto habentur negocio, vel vix vel nunquam sine peccato inveniuntur. Hoc ex verbis Augustini praedictis colligitur manifeste, cum dicit: posset putari iudicium habere aduersus alterum non esse peccatum. & cum dicit ex qua doctrina apostolus dicit esse delictum, scilicet litigare. & cum dicit, propter hac atque huiusmodi peccata, &c. quae verba, Augustini debent intelligi, quod vix aut nunquam invenitur litigium sine peccato. ergo apostolus omnia litigia fraudulenta & non fraudulenta dissuadet. Septimo arguunt sic: Apostolus dissuadet omnia illa litigia, quae non licent perfectis, sed nullum litigium in iudicio est licitum persectis, teste Glossa super apostoli verba ubi prius, quae ait: Ut autem praedicta verba apostoli, in quibus dicit: peccatum esse iudicium habere contra fratres, sane intelligantur, dicendum, quid in huiusmodi liceat perfectis & quid non: & quid infirmis & quid non. Perfectis igitur licet repetere sua simpliciter sine causa, sine lite, sine iudicio: sed non conuenit inde mouere causam ante iudicem. Infirmis vero licet repetere sua mouendo causam ante iudicem & iudicium habendo contra fratrem: sed non contentiose vel fraudulenter: nec apud infidelies iudices. ergo omne litigium apostolus dissuadet.
units.tr: Fifthly, thus: the Apostle dissuades from all those lawsuits which are granted to the weak by way of indulgence. But to go to law in court over temporal goods is granted to the weak not only when it is fraudulent but also when it is not. Therefore the Apostle dissuades not only fraudulent lawsuits but also others. The major premise is plain. The minor is proved by the authority of Augustine, who says in the Enchiridion, chapter 44, treating the Apostle's words quoted above: Here one might also suppose that it is no sin to have a lawsuit against another, but only if he wished to be judged outside the Church, were it not that the Apostle went on to add: "Now therefore there is altogether a fault among you, because you have lawsuits with one another." Lest anyone excuse himself and say that he has a just cause but suffers an injustice which he wishes to have removed from himself by the judgment of a court, the Apostle at once meets such thoughts and excuses and says: "Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather suffer fraud?" That we may return to what the Lord said: "If anyone wishes to take your coat and contend with you in judgment, let him have your cloak also," and in another place: "Whoever takes what is yours, do not ask it back." He therefore allowed his people to have lawsuits with others about secular matters. From this teaching the Apostle says that there is a fault; yet, since such lawsuits occur within the Church, he strictly forbids brothers to settle them before judges outside the Church. It is also plain that this is granted to the weak by way of indulgence. On account of this and similar sins, and others less than these, we must pray devoutly and often to the Lord and say: "Forgive us our debts." From these words it is evidently clear that even to contend in court over a just matter is granted to the weak. Sixthly, thus: the Apostle dissuades from all lawsuits which are scarcely or never found without sin. But lawsuits, even when held to concern a just matter, are scarcely or never found without sin. This is plainly gathered from the words of Augustine quoted above, when he says: one might suppose that it is no sin to have a lawsuit against another; and when he says: from this teaching the Apostle says there is a fault, namely in going to law; and when he says: on account of this and similar sins, etc. These words of Augustine ought to be understood to mean that a lawsuit is scarcely or never found without sin. Therefore the Apostle dissuades from all lawsuits, both fraudulent and not fraudulent. Seventhly, they argue thus: the Apostle dissuades from all those lawsuits which are not lawful for the perfect. But no lawsuit in court is lawful for the perfect, as the Gloss testifies on the Apostle's words cited above, which says: In order that the Apostle's words, in which he says that it is a sin to have a lawsuit against brothers, may be rightly understood, it must be said what is lawful for the perfect and what is not, and what is lawful for the weak and what is not. Therefore it is lawful for the perfect to demand back their own simply, without cause, without strife, without judgment; but it is not fitting to bring a cause before a judge. For the weak it is lawful to demand back their own by bringing a cause before a judge and holding a suit against a brother, but not contentiously or fraudulently, nor before unbelieving judges. Therefore the Apostle dissuades from every lawsuit.

units.la: Sed forte obiiciet aliquis contra praedicta tripliciter. Primo, quia apostolus nullum iustum dissuadet: quia omne iustum est bonum. nullum autem bonum est dissuasibile, sed magis suasibile. multa autem sunt litigia iusta. ergo non omnia litigia dissuadet apostolus. Item, apostolus non dissuadet illud, per quod conseruatur bonum commune, & quod quaeritur propter pacem. sed per litigia conseruatur bonum commune & quaeruntur propter pacem. unde & iudices dirimentes litigia pacem faciunt & conseruant: ergo, &c. Item apostolus non aliter dissuaderet litigium quam matrimonium: & sicut concedit matrimonium infirmis, ita & litigium. sed apostolus non dissuadet toti communitati fidelium matrimonium. ergo saltem non dissuadet toti communitati litigium.
units.tr: But perhaps someone will object to the foregoing in three ways. First, because the Apostle dissuades from nothing that is just, since everything just is good; and nothing good is to be dissuaded, but rather to be recommended. Yet many lawsuits are just. Therefore the Apostle does not dissuade from all lawsuits. Again, the Apostle does not dissuade from that by which the common good is preserved and which is sought for the sake of peace. But by lawsuits the common good is preserved and they are sought for the sake of peace; hence also judges who settle lawsuits make and preserve peace. Therefore, etc. Again, the Apostle would not dissuade lawsuits differently from marriage; and just as he grants marriage to the weak, so also lawsuits. But the Apostle does not dissuade marriage from the whole community of the faithful. Therefore at least he does not dissuade lawsuits from the whole community.

units.la: Ad primum istorum dicunt isti, quod multa quae iusta sunt, dissuadentur quantum ad opus exterius propter meliora habenda: sicut bona dissuadentur propter meliora. unde & matrimonium aliquo modo dissuadetur in quantum virginitas, quae est quid melius, suadetur: tamen iustum nec aliquod bonum est dissuadendum quantum ad praeparationem cordis, quod scilicet homo non esset paratus facere quodcunque bonum aut iustum, si hoc Deus praeciperet.
units.tr: To the first of these, they answer that many things which are just are dissuaded as to the outward act, on account of better things to be had, just as good things are dissuaded on account of better ones. Hence marriage too is in some way dissuaded, insofar as virginity, which is something better, is recommended. Yet what is just, and indeed any good, is not to be dissuaded as to the preparation of the heart, namely that a man should not be ready to do any good or just thing, if God commanded it.

units.la: Ad secundum dicunt, quod bene potest aliquid dissuaderi: per quod tamen in casu quasi per accidens conseruatur bonum commune & acquiritur. quemadmodum bella & arma bellica dissuadendar, & tamen quandoq; per ea conseruatur bonum commune & quaeruntur propter pacem, secundum Augustinum, ut habetur 23. q. 1. Noli aestimare. sed hoc est propter iniquitatem multorum qui aliter ad bonum & pacem revocari non possunt. sic est de litigiis, quod propter iniquitatem multorum quandoque quaeruntur, & nolle habere litigium debet esse voluntatis: sed habere quandoque necessitatis, quemadmodum dicit Augustinus ubi prius: Pacem habere voluntatis est bellum autem debet esse necessitatis. sic est ergo de litigiis, sicut est de bello, quod sicut melius esset omni bello carere quam bellum habere: & ideo bella dissuadentur, & pax suadetur: & tamen in casu aliquod bellum est iustum & meritorium: ita melius esset omni carere litigio quam habere, & tamen in casu meritorium potest esse alicui habere iustum litigium. & propter haec omnia litigia dissuadentur, nisi adsit necessitas.
units.tr: To the second, they say that something may well be dissuaded through which, however, in a case, as it were incidentally, the common good is preserved and gained. Thus wars and warlike arms are dissuaded, and yet sometimes through them the common good is preserved and sought for the sake of peace, according to Augustine, as found in C. 23, q. 1, Noli aestimare. But this is because of the wickedness of many who cannot otherwise be recalled to good and peace. So it is with lawsuits: they are sometimes sought because of the wickedness of many. Not wishing to have a lawsuit ought to be a matter of will, but having one sometimes is a matter of necessity, as Augustine says in the passage above: To have peace is a matter of will; war ought to be a matter of necessity. So it is with lawsuits as with war: just as it would be better to be free of all war than to wage war, and therefore wars are dissuaded and peace is recommended; yet in a case some war is just and meritorious. So it would be better to be free of all lawsuits than to have them, and yet in a case it may be meritorious for someone to have a just lawsuit. And for all these reasons, lawsuits are dissuaded unless necessity be present.

units.la: Ad tertiam dicunt, quod non est simile de matrimonio & litigio: quia matrimonium est absolute pro statu praesenti necessarium generi humano ad procreationem prolis ad cultum Dei: & ideo non debet toti communitati fidelium dissuaderi. sed litigium non est necessarium generi humano etiam pro statu praesenti, sicut nec bellum: & ideo toti communitati fidelium dissuadetur, quamuis in casu extremae necessitatis possit aliquibus suaderi, sicut & bellum.
units.tr: To the third, they say that marriage and lawsuits are not alike, because marriage is absolutely necessary for the human race in its present state, for the procreation of children and for the worship of God; and therefore it ought not to be dissuaded from the whole community of the faithful. But a lawsuit is not necessary for the human race even in its present state, nor is war; and therefore it is dissuaded from the whole community of the faithful, although in a case of extreme necessity it may be recommended to some, as war may be.

units.la: [Et propter hoc] scilicet quia praeceptum de non contendendo in iudicio non est seruandum in opere exteriori: sed in praeparatione cordis. [Apostolus non simpliciter dixit prima ad Corinth.
units.tr: [And for this reason], namely because the precept not to contend in court is not to be kept in the outward act, but in the preparation of the heart. [The Apostle did not simply say in the first letter to the Corinthians]

units.la: Kkkkk vinth. 6. quare non iniuriam accipitis: sed dixit, quare non magis iniuriam accipitis.] Dicunt itaque quod non propter rationem, quam iste assignat, non dixit vnum apostolus, sed aliud. Nam ideo non dixit: Quare non iniuriam accipitis: sed dixit, quare non magis iniuriam accipitis: quia noluit apostolus, quod proprietatem habentes semper in opere essent parati accipere iniuriam a quocunque. sed voluit quod magis & citius acciperent iniuriam, quam in iudicio pro temporalibus litigarent, nisi ratio cogens non desiderium rehabendi vel defendendi sua eos ad litigandum vrgeret. Sicut princeps non semper debet esse paratus accipere iniuriam ab inimico, quia hoc bono communi penitus obviaret: sed magis & citius debet accipere iniuriam, quam bellare, contra volentem inferre iniuriam, nisi iusta necessitate bellare cogatur. Nam & saepe nolle bellare in eo, cui bellare licet, esset peccatum. Unde Ambrosius, ut habetur 23. q. 3. ca. Fortitudo, ait: Fortitudo quae bello tuetur a barbaris patriam, vel domi defendit infirmos, vel a latronibus socios, plena iustitia est. [quod hoc eis non simpliciter interdixerit.] Hoc potest habere duplicem intellectum. Unus est, quod non simpliciter interdixit eis tanquam semper esset illicitum pro temporalibus litigare: & iste sensus verus est: sed secundum istum iste impugnatus verba illa nequaquam intellexit. Alius est, quod non interdixit eis, nisi tantum modo litigia fraudulenta & iniuriosa, & nulla alia. & iste sensus falsus est, ut dicunt isti. [Apostolus reprehenderat Corinthios, quia erant negligentes in iudicio faciendo.] Istud non facit pro eo: quia ibidem non reprehendit Corinthios, quia minime litigabant, sed quia delinquentem corrigere negligebant. & ideo apostolus numquam dissuasit Corinthiis constituere iudices ad vindictam malefactorum: sed dissuasit habere litigia coram iudicibus constitutis, quemadmodum in scripturis suadetur punire peccata malorum, & tamen peccata punienda scripturae efficaciter dissuadent. [Nonne de his qui intus sunt vos iudicatis.] Hic non loquitur iudicandis, sed iudicantibus, & saepe reprehenduntur iudicantes de negligentia iudicandi: & qui iudicantur reprehenduntur de hoc, quod eos iudicari oportet [Apostolos Corinthios reprehendit: quia coram infidelibus litigabant: & iudicium subibant.]
units.tr: 1 Cor. 6: "Why do you not suffer wrong?" but said, "Why do you not rather suffer wrong?" They say therefore that the Apostle did not say one thing for the reason this man assigns and another for a different one. For he did not say, "Why do you not suffer wrong?" but "Why do you not rather suffer wrong?" because the Apostle did not want those who have property always to be ready to suffer wrong from anyone at all, but wanted them to suffer wrong more readily and more quickly than to go to law over temporal goods, unless a compelling reason, not a desire to recover or defend their own, urged them to litigate. Just as a prince ought not always to be ready to suffer wrong from an enemy, because this would wholly oppose the common good, but ought rather and more quickly to suffer wrong than to make war against one who wishes to inflict it, unless he is compelled to make war by just necessity. For it would often be a sin not to wish to make war when it is lawful for one to do so. Hence Ambrose, as found in C. 23, q. 3, c. Fortitudo, says: "The fortitude which by war defends the homeland from barbarians, or at home defends the weak, or defends companions from robbers, is full of justice." [that he did not simply forbid them this.] This can have a twofold sense. One is that he did not simply forbid them, as though it were always unlawful to go to law over temporal matters; and this sense is true. But according to this sense, the opponent who attacked those words did not understand them at all. The other is that he forbade them only fraudulent and wrongful lawsuits and no others; and this sense, these men say, is false. [The Apostle rebuked the Corinthians, because they were negligent in holding judgment.] This does not help that view, because there he does not rebuke the Corinthians for litigating very little, but for neglecting to correct the wrongdoer. Hence the Apostle never dissuaded the Corinthians from appointing judges to punish evildoers; but he dissuaded them from having lawsuits before judges already appointed, just as Scripture urges the punishment of the sins of the wicked, and yet Scripture effectively dissuades sins that deserve punishment. [Do you not judge those who are within?] Here he is not speaking of those to be judged, but of those who judge; and judges are often rebuked for negligence in judging, while those who are judged are rebuked for the fact that they must be judged. [The Apostle rebukes the Corinthians because they litigated before unbelievers and submitted to their judgment.]

units.la: Dicunt quod verba Apostoli de ista materia sane intelligenda sunt: quia reprehensibiles erant, qui trahebant fideles ad iudicium coram infidelibus litigabant: quia causae fidelium inter se topiri poterant per fideles. Illi vero, qui iudicium subibant infidelium ab infidelibus coacti minime reprehensibiles videbantur: cum apostolus subditos monuerit, dicens etiam infidelibus obedire. Illi etiam qui infideles contrahebant ad iudicium infidelium, ex iusta & urgenti causa reprehensibiles non fuerunt. Nam & apostolus ad iudicium Caesaris appellavit. [Item ostendebat, quod hoc ad fideles pertinebat.] Scilicet litigantes pro temporalibus iudicare. Sed ex hoc non sequitur, quod litigare pro temporalibus sit minime dissuasum: sicut non sequitur, ad iudicem iustum pertinet homicidas, & alios scelerato debita poena punire: ergo homicidia, & alia scelera non sunt illicita. [Qui maioribus, multo fortius est minoribus dignus.] Esto quod haec sub aliquo sensu esset vera: tamen saepe competunt alicui maiora, cui minora non competunt, neque decent ipsum: non propter indignitatem ipsius, sed propter dignitatem ipsius & indignitatem, seu utilitatem minorum. Sicut decet regem portare purpuram, & non decet eum portare sordidas vestes. Decet etiam militem expugnare hostem: & non decet eum suspendere furem. Sic decent saepe perfectos maiora, quos non decent minora. Unde praedicare verbum Dei, consecrare episcopos, & dispensare ecclesiastica sacramenta & alia maiora decet summum pontificem: quem tamen non deceret in causa sanguinis, & rerum temporalium iudicare: & ideo non sequitur.
units.tr: They say that the words of the Apostle must be understood in this sense: those who dragged the faithful to court before unbelievers were blameworthy, since the cases of believers could have been settled among themselves by believers. Those who submitted to the judgment of unbelievers, when compelled by unbelievers, did not seem at all blameworthy, since the Apostle admonished subjects to obey even unbelievers. Those too who summoned others before the court of unbelievers were not blameworthy, if they had a just and pressing cause. For the Apostle himself also appealed to the judgment of Caesar. [He also showed that this pertained to believers.] Clearly, they were judging in suits about temporal matters. But it does not follow from this that going to law over temporal matters is in no way discouraged, just as it does not follow that, because it belongs to a just judge to punish murderers and other criminals with the penalty they deserve, therefore murders and other crimes are not unlawful. [He who is worthy of greater things is far more worthy of lesser things.] Even if this were true in some sense, greater things often suit someone to whom lesser things do not belong, nor become him. This is not because of his unworthiness but because of his dignity, and because of the unworthiness or usefulness of the lesser things. Thus it befits a king to wear purple, but it does not befit him to wear filthy clothes. It befits a soldier to storm an enemy, but it does not befit him to hang a thief. So greater things often befit the perfect, while lesser things do not. Hence it befits the highest bishop to preach the Word of God, to consecrate bishops, to administer the ecclesiastical sacraments and other greater duties, yet it would not befit him to judge in cases of blood and temporal property. Therefore the inference does not follow.

units.la: Aliquis debet in causa maiori iudicare, ergo debet iudicare in causa minori: quamvis quod non debeat iudicare in minori causa, non sit propter indignitatem, sed propter dignitatem ipsius.
units.tr: Someone ought to judge in a greater case; therefore he ought to judge in a lesser case. This does not follow, although his not being obliged to judge in a lesser case is not because of unworthiness but because of his dignity.

units.la: [Secularia iudicia si habuerint contemptibiles qui sunt in ecclesia illos constituite ad iudicium.] Si apostolus vocaret contemptibiles in ecclesia, homines insensatos, infames & criminosos: praedicta verba esse dicta ironice debent intelligi.
units.tr: [If you have secular courts, set up as judges those who are of no account in the Church.] If the Apostle were calling those of no account in the Church, senseless, infamous and criminal men, the words quoted above must be understood as spoken ironically.

units.la: Non enim poterit esse de mente apostoli, quod velit ut Corinthii homines contemptibiles propter ineptitudines aut peccata eorum constituerit sibi iudices, quamvis esset in ecclesia, hoc est inter Christianos qualitercunque numerandi. loquitur ergo sic ironice, hoc est contrarium innuendo, ut scilicet tales non eligant.
units.tr: For it cannot have been the Apostle's mind that he wished the Corinthians to set up as judges men of no account, on account of their incompetence or sins, even though they were in the Church, that is, were counted among Christians in whatever way. He therefore speaks ironically in this way, that is, by implying the contrary, namely that they should not choose such men.

units.la: Sed vt cando contemptibiles in ecclesia homines inferioris virtutis & graduum sunt summi & supremi in ecclesia: sic terio dicta praedicta verba debent intelligi in ecclesia, quae est congregatio fidelium, inueniri possunt inferiores bonitate bonitatis. & discretionis ad iudicandum de temporalibus & de secularibus, non debent supremi in ecclesia, circa negotia secularia occupari: sed ut habetur Actuum. 6. noluerunt derelinquere verbum Dei & ministrare mensis, sed orationi & ministerio verbi instare volebant, debent supremi in ecclesia praedicationi verbi, dispensationi sacramentorum ecclesiae & aliis spiritualibus bonis insistere, secularia iudicia secularibus relinquendo.
units.tr: But just as in the Church those of no account are men of lower virtue and rank, while the highest and greatest are in the Church, so the words quoted above must be understood in this way: in the Church, which is the congregation of the faithful, there can be found men inferior in goodness and in discretion for judging temporal and secular matters. The highest in the Church ought not to be occupied with secular business. Rather, as is said in Acts 6, they were unwilling to leave the Word of God and to serve tables, but wished to devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the Word. So the highest in the Church ought to devote themselves to the preaching of the Word, the administration of the sacraments of the Church and other spiritual goods, leaving secular judgments to secular men.

units.la: Et ista est sententia beati Gregorii, qui 19. libro Moralium pertractans praedicta verba apostoli ait: Spiritualia dona non caperent si terrena eos negocia deprimissent: longe ante praemisit dicens: contemptibiles qui sunt in ecclesia illos constituite ad iudicandum: ac si aperte diceret: qui minoris sunt meriti in ecclesia. clesia & nullis magnorum bonorum virtutibus pollent, ipsi de terrenis negociis iudicent. Item per quos magna nequeunt bona suppleantur minora: quos & contemptibiles nominat, & tamen sapientes vocat, cum dicit sic: Non est sapiens quisquam inter vos, qui possit iudicare inter fratrem suum. qua ex re quid colligitur nisi ut hi terrenas causas examinarent, qui exteriorum rerum sapientiam perceperunt, qui autem spiritualibus donis ditati sunt profecto terrenis non debent negociis implicari, ut dum non cogantur inferiora bona disponere, valeant bonis superioribus deservire. Ex his verbis datur intelligi, quod apostolus non vocat contemptibiles in ecclesia, viles, infames, & insensatos aut fatuos: sed vocat contemptibiles, sapientes, & in negociis secularibus peritos: qui & non viri spirituales, & supremi debent constitui iudices ad secularia litigia terminanda. Sed forte quis obiiciet dicens, quod sicut legitur in decretis distinctione 39. oportet episcopum secularium negociorum habere peritiam. quod B. Gregorius, ut habetur eadem distinctione capitulo Petrus. Videtur asserere manifeste. Frustra autem quaereretur in episcopis secularium negociorum peritia, nisi ad eos pertineret circa negocia secularia implicari. Ad hoc dicunt isti, quod non pertinet ad episcopos circa secularia implicari, nisi necessitate cogente, ut inquantum possint cauteant, ne circa secularia occupentur: necessitate tamen urgente possunt & debent in casu pro communi utilitate secularibus vacare negociis. Et ideo pro tali casu possibili oportet eos negociorum secularium habere solertiam, non quidem per longam experientiam, sed per quandam naturalem industriam, ut sint quodammodo natura prudentes. propter quod ait Carthaginense concilium, ut habetur distinctione 23: Qui episcopus ordinandus est, antea examinetur, si natura sit prudens, si docibilis, hoc est docilis. Talis enim prudentia cum sacrarum noticia litteratum episcopo sufficit ad hoc quod dicatur secularium negociorum habere industriam.[Ad iudicium.] Sic habetur sub Bulla, iuxta quam scripsi verba constitutionis istius.
units.tr: This is also the opinion of the blessed Gregory, who, treating the words of the Apostle in the nineteenth book of the Moralia, says: "Spiritual gifts would not be grasped if earthly business had weighed them down." Long before this he had said: "Set up as judges those who are of no account in the Church," as if he were plainly saying: "Let those who are of lesser merit in the Church, and are not strong in the virtues of great goods, judge earthly business. Likewise, let lesser goods be supplied by those through whom great goods cannot be supplied." He calls them of no account, yet he calls them wise, when he says: "There is not a wise man among you who could judge between his brother and his brother." What is gathered from this, except that those should examine earthly cases who have grasped the wisdom of external things, while those enriched with spiritual gifts ought certainly not to be entangled in earthly business, so that, not being compelled to arrange lower goods, they may be able to serve the higher goods? From these words it is shown that the Apostle does not call those of no account in the Church, base, infamous, senseless or foolish, but calls them of no account, yet wise and skilled in secular business. These are the ones, not spiritual men and not the highest, who ought to be appointed judges to settle secular suits. But perhaps someone will object, saying that, as is read in the Decretals, distinction 39, "A bishop ought to have skill in secular business," which the blessed Gregory, as is found in the same distinction, chapter "Peter," seems plainly to assert. But it would be pointless to seek skill in secular business in bishops, unless it pertained to them to be involved in secular affairs. To this they reply that it does not pertain to bishops to be involved in secular matters, except under compelling necessity, so that as far as they can, they take care not to be occupied with secular things. Nevertheless, when urgent necessity requires it, they can and ought, in such a case, for the common good, to devote themselves to secular business. And therefore, for such a possible case, they ought to have aptitude in secular business, not indeed through long experience, but through a certain natural industry, so that they are in some sense prudent by nature. For this reason the Council of Carthage says, as is found in distinction 23: "Whoever is to be ordained bishop should first be examined, whether he is naturally prudent, whether he is teachable," that is, docile. For such prudence, together with knowledge of the sacred writings, is enough for a learned bishop to be said to have aptitude in secular business. [For judgment.] So it is found under the Bull, from which I have written the words of this constitution.

units.la: tamen est, ad iudicandum. [Ad verecudiam vestram dico, subaudi: quia curritis ad iudicia infidelium.] Aliquando reprehendit eos, quia currebant ad iudicia infidelium, aliquando quia habebant iudicia fraudulenta, aliquando quia habebant iudicia alia illicita.
units.tr: Nevertheless, it is for judging. [I say this to your shame, understand: because you run to the courts of unbelievers.] At one time he rebukes them because they ran to the courts of unbelievers, at another because they had fraudulent courts, at another because they had other unlawful courts.

units.la: [Non est inter vos sapiens quisquam qui possit iudicare inter fratrem & fratrem suum.] Ex his verbis patet, quod apostolus volebat constitui iudices sapientes, qui possent volentibus litigare, sive fraudulenter, sive aliter iusticiam exhibere. Ex quo non potest concludi, quod non dissuasit pro temporalibus litigare: sicut nec ex hoc non dissuasit contendere, quia voluit constituit iudices sapientes, qui ita sopirent iudicia fraudulenta, sicut alia. [Sed frater cum fratre in iudicio contendit.] Hoc ut saepe malum est ex parte actoris: licet aliquando sit sine peccato ex parte rei, si ad odium, discordiam, & fraudem minime provocetur. [Et hoc apud infideles.] Hoc reprehensibile fuit in illo: quia alium ad iudicium infidelium protrahebat: & pro scandalo infidelium euitando debuit vel iniuriam sustinere, vel quaerere apud fideles iustitiam.] Deinde reprehendit eos qui iniuste & fraudulenter fratres suos, ad iudicium trahebant.] Quod de hoc apostolus specialiter Corinthios reprehenderit, ex textu non habetur: quamvis generaliter reprehendendo litigia iniqua, sua reprehensio sit ad fraudulenta & iniusta litigia extendenda, necipse hoc sufficienter probat, sicut post apparebit. [Iam quidem omnino delictum est in vobis quia iudicia habetis inter vos, scilicet fraudulenta & iniuriosa.] Haec Glossa ex textu apostoli trahi non potest. verba enim praedicta apostoli duplicem intellectum possunt habere. unus est iste: Iam omnino delictum est in vobis, hoc est aliqui inter vos delinquunt fraudem & iniuriam extra iudicium faciendo. quare aliqui coram iudice conqueruntur, & hoc solet frequenter accidere, quod multi in iudicio conqueruntur de delicto ante iudicium commisso in ipsos. Alius intellectus est iste: Iam quidem omnino delictum in vobis, trahentibus alios ad iudicium: quia iudicia habetis inter vos. hoc est quia citius amore temporalium trahitis alios ad iudicium, quam velitis amore proximi pro eius scandalo devitando, vel eius salute quaerenda, damnum temporalium sustinere. & ideo quaerit apostolus, quare non magis iniuriam accipitis? quare non magis fraudem patimini? quam ut iniuriantem ante iudicium. ad iudicium protrahatis: quasi dicat, ante debeteris pro salute proximi & perfectionis amore iniuriam accipere & fraudem pati, quam proximum delinquentem trahere ad iudicium. & ita in his verbis, quare non magis, &c. Apostolus non solum litigia illicita, sed etiam licita dissuadet: quando scilicet est licitum & expediens a licitis litigiis abstinere. Nam abstinere a litigiis illicitis necessitatis est. sed saepe a licitis cessare litigiis supererogationis & perfectionis est: sicut a coitu illicito abstinere, le necessitate salutis est a coitu vero licito abstinere non nunquam ad persectionem & supererogationem noscitur pertinere. quia igitur apostolus non tantum illa, quae sunt de necessitate salutis, sed etiam illa quae supererogationis voluit suadere: non tantum ab illicitis, sed etiam a quibusdam licitis abstinere suasit & ita per consequens quaedam licita litigia dissuasit. [unde sequitur: sed vos iniuriam facitis & fraudatis: & hoc fratribus.] hic dimittit verba media apostoli, illa scilicet, quare non magis iniuriam accipitis, &c. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod apostolus intendebat suadere Corinthiis, quod nonnunquam Corinthii perfectionis amore antea deberent iniuriam accipere & fraudem pati, quam in iudicio etiam absq; fraude & iniuria litigare] unde cum dicit apostolus sed vos iniuriam facitis, &c. Principaliter loquitur illis, qui extra iudicium fraudem & iniuriam faciebant, quamvis etiam ad illos intenderit loqui, qui fraudem & iniuriam in iudicio facere molirentur. [Et quod de talibus qui fraudulenter trahebant fratres ad iudicium intellexerunt apostolus] intellexit & de illis, siqui tales fuerunt, & etiam de aliis: imo aliqua verba intelle-
units.tr: [Is there not a wise man among you who could judge between brother and brother?] From these words it is clear that the Apostle wished to set up wise judges who could administer justice to those wishing to litigate, whether fraudulently or otherwise. From this it cannot be concluded that he did not discourage litigation over temporal matters, just as it cannot be concluded from this that he did not discourage contention, since he wished to set up wise judges who would settle fraudulent courts just as others. [But brother contends with brother in judgment.] This is often an evil on the part of the plaintiff, although it may sometimes be without sin on the part of the defendant, if he is not provoked to hatred, discord and fraud. [And this before unbelievers.] This was blameworthy in that man, because he was dragging another to the court of unbelievers; and to avoid scandal to unbelievers he ought either to have endured the wrong or to seek justice among believers.] Then he rebukes those who dragged their brothers to judgment unjustly and fraudulently.] That the Apostle rebuked the Corinthians specifically for this is not found in the text. Although, by rebuking unjust litigation in general, his rebuke extends to fraudulent and unjust litigation, and this alone sufficiently proves it, as will appear later. [Now indeed there is altogether a fault among you, because you have courts among you, namely fraudulent and injurious ones.] This gloss cannot be drawn from the Apostle's text. For the Apostle's words quoted above can have a twofold meaning. One is this: Now there is altogether a fault among you, that is, some among you commit fraud and injury outside the court. Hence some complain before a judge, and this commonly happens, that many in court complain of a wrong committed against them before the trial. The other meaning is this: Now indeed there is altogether a fault in you, in dragging others to court, because you have courts among you. That is, because you more readily, out of love of temporal things, drag others to court than, out of love of your neighbour, you are willing to suffer loss of temporal things in order to avoid his scandal or to seek his salvation. And so the Apostle asks: Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather suffer fraud? as if he were saying: rather than bring to court a neighbour who has wronged you before the trial, you ought, for your neighbour's salvation and for love of perfection, to accept wrong and suffer fraud. And so in these words, why not rather, etc., the Apostle dissuades not only unlawful litigation but also lawful litigation, namely when it is lawful and expedient to abstain from lawful litigation. For to abstain from unlawful litigation is a matter of necessity, but often to cease from lawful litigation belongs to supererogation and perfection, just as to abstain from unlawful intercourse is necessary for salvation, while to abstain from lawful intercourse is sometimes known to belong to perfection and supererogation. Therefore, since the Apostle wished to persuade them not only of those things which are necessary for salvation but also of those which are of supererogation, he persuaded them to abstain not only from unlawful things but also from certain lawful things, and so by consequence he dissuaded certain lawful litigation. [Hence it follows: but you do wrong and defraud, and this to your brothers.] Here he omits the intervening words of the Apostle, namely "why do you not rather suffer wrong," etc. From these words it is clear that the Apostle intended to persuade the Corinthians that sometimes, out of love of perfection, the Corinthians ought rather to suffer wrong and fraud than to litigate in court, even without fraud and injury. Hence when the Apostle says but you do wrong, etc., he speaks chiefly to those who were doing fraud and injury outside the court, although he also intended to speak to those who were contriving to do fraud and injury in the court. [And what the Apostle understood about those who fraudulently dragged their brothers to court] he understood also of those, if any such there were, and also of others. Indeed, some words he understood of those who lawfully drag others to court. [It is clear because he immediately added: or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God?] These words are against the opponent under attack, because by these words it is clear that the Apostle understood them of all who unjustly drag others to…

units.la: xit sit de licitè trahentibus alios ad iudicium. [Patet quia statim subiunxit, an nescitis quia iniqui regnum Dei non possidebunt.] Ista verba sunt contra istum impugnatum. quia per hæc verba patet, quod apostolus intellexit de omnibus iniquè trahentibus alios ad iudicium. multi autem præter fraudulentos trahunt alios iniquè ad iudicium, sicut qui ex odio, rancore, superbia, invidia, amore iniquo temporalium sine omni fraude trahunt alios ad iudicium, qui omnes iniqui sunt censendi, & regnum Dei minimè possidebunt [eos agere iniquè supponens] alios supponit agere iniquè, licet sine fraude agant: alios supponit à perfectione deficere, qui amore temporalium in iudicio litigabant.
units.tr: …it is lawful for those who draw others to judgment by lawful means. [It is clear because he immediately added, "Do you not know that the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God?"] These words are against the opponent under attack, because by these words it is plain that the apostle meant all who draw others to judgment unjustly. Many, however, besides the fraudulent, draw others to judgment unjustly, as those who from hatred, spite, pride, envy, or an unlawful love of temporal things draw others to judgment without any fraud. All of these are to be counted unrighteous, and they will by no means possess the kingdom of God. [Supposing that they act unjustly] he supposes others to act unjustly, although they act without fraud: he supposes others to fall short of perfection who went to law out of love of temporal things.

units.la: Et omnes apostolus instruit ad perfectionem exhortans, ut magis iniuriam accipiant & fraudem patiantur, quam pro temporalibus absque urgente necessitate vel evidenti utilitate speciali in iudicio litigare præsumant. [Unde patet quod apostolus non interdixerit simpliciter Corinthiis convertis ad fidem litigare] verum est, quod non interdixit tanquam malum nec semper omnibus litigare: dissuasit tamen omnibus irregulariter litigare, nisi urgente necessitate vel evidenti utilitate specialiter cogantur. omnia autem litigia illicita, fraudulenta & nociva, & alia qualitercunque illicita simpliciter interdixit. [imo quod eis liceret, &c.] licet quidem aliquando, & tamen nonnulla licita litigia dissuasit; sicut sancti plures multis matrimonium dissuaserunt, & tamen matrimonium illis licitum existebat.
units.tr: And the apostle instructs all of them, exhorting them to perfection, that they should rather accept injury and suffer fraud than presume to go to law over temporal things without urgent necessity or clear special advantage. [Hence it is clear that the apostle did not simply forbid the Corinthians who were converted to the faith to go to law] It is true that he did not forbid litigation as an evil thing, nor always for everyone; yet he dissuaded all from going to law irregularly, unless they were compelled by urgent necessity or clear special advantage. But all litigation that is unlawful, fraudulent, and harmful, and all other things unlawful in any way, he simply forbade. [Indeed that it would be lawful for them, etc.] It is true that sometimes it would be lawful, and yet he dissuaded some lawful litigation as well; just as the saints dissuaded many from marriage, and yet marriage was lawful for them.

units.la: [Omnia mihi licent. glossa: omnia mea licet repetere mihi.] Dicunt isti, quod apostolus loquebatur ibidem in persona illorum, qui proprium possident: & verum est de illis, quod licet eis sua repetere, sine fraude & dolo & absque omni mala intentione: tamen cum hoc stat, quod sæpe non repetere res proprias ad perfectionem & supererogationem pertineat. & ideo non repetere res proprias, quamvis sit aliquando licitum, imo aliquando expediens, sicut matrimonium aliquando est expediens, & similiter comedere carnes & bibere vinum: tamen apostolus Corinthiis volens eos ad perfectionem inducere, non repetere propria per iudicem conabatur.
units.tr: [All things are lawful for me. Gloss: all my things are lawful for me to reclaim.] These men say that the apostle was speaking there in the person of those who possess property. And it is true of them that it is lawful for them to reclaim their own things, without fraud or deceit and without any evil intention. Yet it is consistent with this that often not to reclaim one's own goods belongs to perfection and to works of supererogation. Therefore, not to reclaim one's own goods, although it is sometimes lawful, indeed sometimes expedient, just as marriage is sometimes expedient, and likewise eating meat and drinking wine, nevertheless the apostle, wishing to lead the Corinthians to perfection, was attempting to get them not to reclaim their property through a judge.

units.la: CAP XLVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER 46.

units.la: NEc per sacram scripturam patet, quod Christus seu apostoli secundum intellectum historicum semper strinuerunt prædicta præcepta. de Christo enim dominus noster legitur, Ioannis 14. quod cum unus ex ministris pontificis dedisset ei alapam, non sibi præbuit aliam, sed dixit ei: Si male locutus sum, testimonium perhibe de malo, si bene, cur me cædis? Item de beato Paulo legitur Actuum 22. quod cum tribunus cum iussisset flagellis cædi & torqueri, & constrinxisset eum loris, dixit astanti Centurioni Paulus: Si hominem Romanum & indemnatum licet vobis cædere: quo audito tortus non fuit. Item Actuum 23. Cum princeps sacerdotum & seniorum præcepisset os Pauli percutere, Paulus dixit ad eum. Percutiet te Deus, paries dealbate: & tu sedens iudicas me secundum legem, & contra legem iubes me percuti. Item eodem capitulo legitur, quod Paulus, cum audisset à filio sororis suæ, quod plures ex Iudæis deliberaverant se non manducaturos, neque bibituros, donec occiderent ipsum, misit ne nota eum suum ad Tribunum ad nuntiandum sibi prædicta. & sic cuasit, ut legitur. 13. q. 3. ca. Maximianus. Item cum Hierosolymis in manus Romanorum traditus fuisset: & Iudæis contradicentibus ipsum non expedirent, ad Cæsarem appellavit, ut legitur Actuum ultimo. Ex quibus satis liquet, quod non fuit intentio Salvatoris nostri probare hæreticos fideles se in iudicio defendere & res suas, nisi quando hoc bene fuerit suadere. quare patet quod prædictam hæreticus ut prævaricator legis divinæ allegaverat supradicta capitula, quæ non tangunt in aliquo nostras constitutiones prædictas.
units.tr: Nor does it appear from Holy Scripture that Christ or the apostles always kept the aforesaid precepts according to the historical sense. For we read of our Lord Christ, John 14, that when one of the servants of the high priest gave him a blow, he did not offer him another, but said to him: "If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil; if well, why do you strike me?" Likewise, we read of the blessed Paul, Acts 22, that when the tribune had ordered him to be scourged and tortured, and had bound him with thongs, Paul said to the centurion who stood by: "Is it lawful for you to scourge a Roman man who is uncondemned?"
