On hearing this, he was not tortured. Also, Acts 23: when the chief priest and the elders had ordered that Paul's mouth be struck, Paul said to him: "God shall strike you, you whitewashed wall! Do you sit to judge me according to the law, and yet against the law order me to be struck?" Also in the same chapter we read that Paul, when he had heard from his sister's son that more than forty of the Jews had bound themselves not to eat or drink until they had killed him, sent his nephew to the tribune to report these things to him; and so it came about, as we read, 13 q. 3, ca. Maximianus. Also, when he had been handed over into the hands of the Romans at Jerusalem, and the Jews opposed his being released, he appealed to Caesar, as we read in the last chapter of Acts. From these things it is quite plain that it was not the intention of our Saviour to prove that the faithful may not defend themselves in judgement and their goods; except when it would be well to advise this. Wherefore it is evident that the aforesaid heretic, as a transgressor of the divine law, had alleged the aforesaid chapters, which in no way touch our aforesaid constitutions.

units.la: Hic iste probare molitur, quod auctoritates suæ ex Matthæi quinto capitulo debent intelligi de præparatione cordis, & non de opere exteriori, & innuit ratione rationem. Christus & apostoli non semper servaverunt dicta præcepta in opere exteriori. ergo nec semper in opere sunt servanda.
units.tr: Here this man labours to prove that his authorities from Matthew 5 must be understood of the preparation of the heart, and not of outward action, and he argues by a reason: Christ and the apostles did not always keep the said precepts in outward action; therefore they are not always to be kept in action either.

units.la: Antecedens probat. Et primo, quod Christus non semper servavit, per unam auctoritatem. secundo quod beatus etiam Paulus non servavit, per quatuor auctoritates: quæ omnes patent in litera.
units.tr: He proves the antecedent. First, that Christ did not always keep them, by one authority; second, that the blessed Paul also did not keep them, by four authorities, all of which are plain in the text.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod istæ auctoritates probant tantum, quod præcepta quædam affirmativa data Matthæi quinto capitulo non semper obligant ad opus exterius: cum sim modi est, percutienti corporaliter alteram partem vel eandem percutiendam offerre, sed non probant, quod istud præceptum negativum.
units.tr: But these opponents say that these authorities prove only that certain affirmative precepts given in Matthew 5 do not always bind to outward action (for example, to offer the other cheek or the same one to be struck to a man who bodily strikes you), but they do not prove that this negative precept, not to contend in judgement, must be kept in action at all times.

units.la: Non contendere in iudicio pro rebus temporalibus: non sit omni tempore ab aliquibus quantum ad opus servandum, sicut nec probant, quod non repercutere corporaliter manu non sit ab aliquo omni tempore servandum. & ita istæ auctoritates pro illo impugnato nihil faciunt: quia appellans non intendit asserere, quod omni tempore percutienti sit pars eadem vel alia percutienda corporaliter offerenda: sed intendit, quod ad perfectionem spectat, nunquam velle corporaliter repercutere: & similiter ad perfectionem spectat nunquam velle pro temporalibus in iudicio litigare.
units.tr: Not to contend in judgement for temporal things is not, at every time and by some people, to be kept as regards outward action, just as they do not prove that not to strike back bodily with the hand must be kept by someone at every time. And so these authorities do nothing for that position which is being attacked; for the appellant does not intend to assert that at all times the same or another cheek must be offered bodily to the one who strikes; but he intends that it pertains to perfection never to wish to strike back bodily; and likewise it pertains to perfection never to wish to go to law in judgement for temporal things.

units.la: Quod vt melius intelligatur, Dicunt esse sciendum, quod aliquid est tolerabile, imo itio liberitorium & laudabile in vno, quod in alio est demeritorium & damnabile & ideo licet in aliquo tolerabile sit imo aliquando laudabile pro temporalibus litigare: tamen in volente nunquam velle pro temporalibus litigare est damnabile. & ideo Christus suadens dictam perfectionem concilii vouere nunquam velle pro temporalibus litigare, suadet, quod dictum suum consilium semper in opere exteriori seruetur. Et si dicas, quod Christus non loquitur ibi de aliquo voto. Respondent isti, quod quamuis vocaliter minime de voto loquatur, intentio tamen sua est perfectionem summam cuiuslibet veritatis in hac vita possibilem suadere. & ideo cum talia perfectiora sint cum voto quam sine voto: dictum consilium suum cum opere de voto debet intelligi: & ita suadere intendit & quod nullus pro temporalibus nisi necessitate vrgente, vel euidenti utilitate spirituali cogente contendat; & quod illi, qui volunt viam perfectionis assumere ad nunquam pro temporalibus contendendum voto se astringant. & ideo dicunt, quod dictum Christi consilium non est ab omnibus omni tempore & omni casu seruandum in opere. sed a vouentibus perfectionem praedictam & nullam dispensationem rerum ecclesiasticarum habentibus, non tantum quantum ad praeparationem cordis, sed etiam quantum ad opus, semper est seruandum.
units.tr: So that this may be better understood, they say that one must know that something is tolerable, indeed even lawful and praiseworthy, in one person, which in another is meritorious of blame and damnable. And so, although it is sometimes tolerable, indeed sometimes praiseworthy, to go to law for temporal things, yet for one who is willing never to wish to go to law for temporal things it is damnable. And so Christ, urging the said perfection of counsel, vowing never to wish to go to law for temporal things, urges that his counsel be always kept in outward action. And if you say that Christ does not speak there of any vow, they reply that although he does not speak of a vow in words, his intention nonetheless is to urge the highest perfection of every truth possible in this life. And so, since such more perfect things are with a vow rather than without one, his said counsel must be understood together with a vow; and thus he intends to urge that no one should contend for temporal things except under pressing necessity or compelling evident spiritual benefit; and that those who wish to take up the way of perfection should bind themselves by vow never to contend for temporal things. And so they say that the said counsel of Christ is not to be kept in action by everyone at all times and in every case, but by those who vow the aforesaid perfection and have no stewardship of ecclesiastical goods, it must always be kept, not only as regards the preparation of the heart but also as regards action.

units.la: [Nec per scripturam sacram patet quod Christus seu apostoli secundum sensum historicum semper seruauerint praecepta praedicta.] Verum est, quod non seruauerunt omnia praecepta praedicta nisi secundum praeparationem cordis: sed aliqua seruauerunt secundum opus semper, aliqua secundum praeparationem cordis. Christus enim nunquam repercussit, nec vnquam in iudicio pro temporalibus litigauit, similiter nec B. Paulus. Petrus vero percutiens reprehensus fuit a Christo, & post nunquam percussit. Constat igitur quod Christus & apostoli quaedam illorum praeceptorum semper seruauerunt: quaedam vero non semper. Vnde de Christo dicit B. Petrus canonica (lua 1. c. 2.) Cum maledicteretur non maledicebat: cum pateretur, non comminabatur. [Non fuit intentio Saluatoris nostri, prohibere fidales, se defendere in iudicio & res suas.] Multiplex est defensio personae. vna est per rationem, & illam Saluator noster nulli fideli prohibuit pro omni tempore, tamen exempla dedit aliquo tempore tacere. Nam vt refertur Matth. 26. Princeps sacerdotum dixit Iesu: Nihil respondes ad ea quae isti aduersum te testificantur: Iesus autem tacebat. Alia est defensio personae, quae est violentiae per vim repulsio. & taliter se defendere Saluator prohibuit alios fideles suos, s. apostolos suos & volentes vouere seu vouentes perfectionem huiusmodi. Non autem prohibuit omnes fideles se tali modo defendere. Defensio etiam rerum est multiplex: vna est, quae est violentiae per vim repulsio, & illam prohibuit Saluator quibusdam fidelibus, sed non omnibus. Alia est per litigium contentiosum in iudicio, & sic etiam prohibuit alios, & non omnes. multis tamen suadetur sic res suas nequaquam defendere, qui tamen a tali defensione nullatenus prohibentur. Alia est defensio per rationem extra iudicium per simplicem ammonitionem, ne res suae quantum ad dominium vel vsum auferantur iniuste & tali modo defendere res suas siue quantum ad dominium siue quantum ad vsum, Christus nullos fideles prohibuit, licet iniuxerit non defendere etiam tali modo quantum ad praeparationem cordis non quantum ad opus. [quare patet quod praedictus haereticus] dicunt isti, quod ista sunt verba contumeliosa omni veritate nudata, & per praecedentia asserunt aperte patere.
units.tr: [Nor does it appear from Holy Scripture that Christ or the apostles always kept the aforesaid precepts according to the historical sense.] It is true that they did not keep all the aforesaid precepts except according to the preparation of the heart; but some they kept always in action, and some according to the preparation of the heart. For Christ never struck back, nor ever went to law in judgement for temporal things; likewise neither did the blessed Paul. Peter, indeed, when he struck, was rebuked by Christ, and afterwards never struck. It is clear, therefore, that Christ and the apostles always kept some of those precepts, but not others always. Hence the blessed Peter says of Christ in his canonical epistle (1 Peter 2:23): "When he was reviled he did not revile; when he suffered, he did not threaten." [It was not the intention of our Saviour to forbid the faithful to defend themselves in judgement and their goods.] Defence of a person is manifold. One is by reason, and our Saviour forbade this to no faithful person at any time; yet he gave an example of keeping silent at some time. For, as is told in Matthew 26, the chief priest said to Jesus: "Do you answer nothing to those things which these men testify against you?" But Jesus was silent. Another is defence of a person by repelling violence by force; and our Saviour forbade this to his other faithful, namely his apostles, and to those wishing to vow or vowing such perfection. He did not, however, forbid all the faithful to defend themselves in this way. Defence of goods, too, is manifold: one is the repelling of violence by force, and this our Saviour forbade to certain faithful, but not to all. Another is by contentious litigation in judgement, and so he also forbade some, and not all. Yet to many it is urged not to defend their goods in this way at all, though they are in no way forbidden such defence. Another is defence by reason outside judgement, by simple admonition, lest their goods be taken away unjustly as regards ownership or use; and to defend their goods in such a way, whether as regards ownership or as regards use, Christ forbade no faithful at all, although he urged them not to defend themselves even in this way, as regards the preparation of the heart and not as regards action. [Wherefore it is plain that the aforesaid heretic] these men say that these are contumelious words stripped of all truth, and they assert that it is plainly evident from what precedes.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: Cum ergo quaeritur vtrum apostolis & discipulis ac eorum sequentibus pro rebus, quas habebant, licuerit & licet litigare. videtur dicendum quod illi qui propria non habebant pro rebus aliquibus tanquam propriis non licuit litigare. Illi autem, qui habebant communia, pro illis vt pro communibus animo ipsa bona communia defendendi vel repetendi sine fraude & alicuius iniuria licuit litigare: praesertim illis, qui curam habebant illius communitatis, vel alii eorum mandato: nisi forsan ex hoc graue scandalum sequi posset. quo casu esset iudicium differendum vel omittendum ne tam scandalum posset sequi.
units.tr: When it is asked whether it was and is lawful for the apostles, the disciples and their followers to go to law over the goods they had, it seems right to say that those who had no property of their own were not permitted to litigate over any goods as though they were their own. But those who had common goods could litigate over them as common goods, intending to defend or recover those goods without fraud and without injury to anyone. This was especially so for those who had charge of that community, or who acted by another's command, unless perhaps a grave scandal could follow from it. In that case the suit should be deferred or dropped, so that such scandal would not follow.

units.la: Post quam in parte praecedenti iste impugnatus improbauit assertionem appellantis circa quaestionem, qua quaeritur: an apostolis licuerit pro rebus temporalibus litigare? hoc ad eandem quaestionem proprium ponit sententiam. & quia ipse in hac parte istam quaestionem etiam ad discipulos & sequentes apostolorum extendit, ideo hic tria molitur ostendere. Primo enim proponens quaestionem determinat, quod apostolis licuit tam pro temporalibus propriis quam pro communibus litigare. Secundo ostendit, quod religiosis pluribus licet pro temporalibus litigare. Tertio probat, quod episcopis pro rebus ecclesiarum suarum liceat litigare: secundum facit in parte immediate sequenti, ibi: Et si diceretur, tertium ibi: Item quod praelatis. Primo igitur extendens quaestionem etiam ad alios quam ad apostolos, dicit quod cum quaeritur an apostolis & discipulis ac eorum sequacibus licuerit pro temporalibus litigare, videtur dicendum: quod illis qui propria non habebant, non licuerit tanquam pro propriis litigare: illis autem qui habebant communia licuerit tanquam pro communibus litigare. Per hanc assertionem vult asserere manifeste, quod apostolis pro rebus temporalibus tam tanquam pro propriis quam tanquam pro communibus licuerit litigare. qui aliquando apostoli habuerunt res proprias quantum ad dominium. quia secundum istum post distributionem bonorum communium, de qua fit mentio Act. 2. & 4. quilibet apostolus fuit proprietarius & dominus portionis sibi assignatae & ideo tunc potuit quilibet eorum pro rebus suis tanquam pro propriis litigare. Aliquando vero secundum ipsum non habuerunt nisi communia: sicut tempore, de quo dicitur Act. 4. & erant illis omnia communia. & tunc licuit eis pro rebus tanquam pro communibus litigare. & ita omni tempore postquam fuerunt facti apostoli ad apostolatum assumpti licuit eis pro rebus temporalibus litigare: sed aliquando sicut pro rebus propriis, & aliquando sicut pro rebus communibus.
units.tr: After the earlier part, in which this opponent rejected the appellant's assertion on the question whether the apostles were permitted to litigate over temporal goods, he now puts forward his own opinion on the same question. Since in this part he extends the question also to the disciples and successors of the apostles, he undertakes three things here. First, in proposing the question, he determines that the apostles were permitted to litigate over temporal goods, both their own and common ones. Second, he shows that many religious may litigate over temporal goods. Third, he proves that bishops may litigate over the goods of their churches. The second point is in the immediately following part, at "And if it were said," and the third at "Likewise, that prelates." So, first, extending the question to others besides the apostles, he says that when it is asked whether the apostles, disciples and their followers were permitted to litigate over temporal goods, it seems right to say this: those who had no property of their own were not permitted to litigate as over their own goods, but those who had common goods were permitted to litigate as over common goods. By this assertion he clearly means that the apostles were permitted to litigate over temporal goods both as their own and as common. For at some times the apostles had property of their own as far as ownership went. He holds that after the distribution of common goods mentioned in Acts 2 and 4, each apostle became the owner and proprietor of the portion assigned to him, and so each could then litigate over his goods as his own. At other times, however, according to him, they had only common goods. This was the time spoken of in Acts 4, when "all things were common to them," and then they were permitted to litigate over goods as common. And so at all times since they were taken up into the apostolate, the apostles were permitted to litigate over temporal goods: sometimes as over their own, and sometimes as over common goods.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores contra praedicta duo probare conantur. Primum est, quod apostolis non licuit pro rebus quibuscunque tanquam pro propriis litigare. Secundo, quod non licuit eis pro temporalibus tanquam pro communibus litigare. Primum probant primo sic. Apostoli postquam fuerunt ad apostolatum assumpti non habuerunt res proprias, sed qui non habet res proprias, non potest nec debet pro rebus tanquam pro propriis litigare etiam secundum istum. ergo apostolis non licuit pro temporalibus tanquam pro propriis litigare: maior in pluribus locis superius est probata: minorem iste concedit. Secundo sic. Apostolis postquam facti fuerunt praedicatores evangelicae paupertatis nullo modo licuit facere illud, quod auditores poterant auertere ab evangelica paupertate: quia ad evangelicam paupertatem doctrina & exemplo suos debuerant inducere auditores. Sed si litigassent pro temporalibus tanquam pro rebus propriis, exemplo suo auditores auertissent ab evangelica paupertate. Nam quodammodo naturale est auditoribus & inferioribus suos imitari magistros & praelatos. iuxta illud Sapientis Ecclesiastici 10. Secundum iudicem populi sicut & minister eius & qualis rector est civitatis, talis & inhabitantes in ea. ergo nullo modo licuit apostolis pro temporalibus tanquam pro propriis litigare. Quod autem apostoli, si litigassent pro temporalibus tanquam pro propriis exemplo auertissent alios ab evangelica paupertate, patet: quia ad evangelicam paupertatem pertinet abdicatio proprietatis omnium saltem in speciali, sicut superius probatum existit. Sed constat quod a tali abdicatione alios suo auertissent exemplo. ergo auertissent auditores ab evangelica paupertate.
units.tr: But these opponents try to prove two things against the points above. The first is that the apostles were not permitted to litigate over any goods as their own. The second is that they were not permitted to litigate over temporal goods as common. They prove the first in two ways. First: the apostles, once taken up into the apostolate, had no property of their own; but one who has no property of his own cannot and ought not to litigate over goods as his own, even by this author's own account. Therefore the apostles were not permitted to litigate over temporal goods as their own. The major premise has been proved in many places above, and this author concedes the minor. Second: once the apostles had become preachers of evangelical poverty, it was in no way lawful for them to do anything that could turn their hearers away from evangelical poverty, since by doctrine and example they ought to lead their hearers into it. But if they had litigated over temporal goods as their own, they would by their example have turned their hearers away from evangelical poverty. For hearers and inferiors naturally tend to imitate their masters and prelates, according to the saying of Ecclesiasticus 10: "As the judge of the people is, so are his ministers; and as the ruler of the city is, so are its inhabitants." Therefore it was in no way lawful for the apostles to litigate over temporal goods as their own. That the apostles, had they litigated over temporal goods as their own, would by their example have turned others away from evangelical poverty, is plain: renunciation of property, at least in particular cases, belongs to evangelical poverty, as has been proved above, and it is clear that by their example they would have turned others away from such renunciation. Therefore they would have turned their hearers away from evangelical poverty.

units.la: Sed forte dices, quod secundum hoc omnes episcopi habentes proprium & pro propriis gentes suos subditos ab evangelica paupertate auerterent. Dicunt isti concedendo conclusionem, quod exemplo quodammodo auertunt eos ab evangelica paupertate: sicut exemplo auertunt eos a religionis ingressu, licet hoc non intendant. & ideo in hoc non peccant: quia faciunt quod licet eis, licet supererogationis esset in eis si a talibus abstinerent. Apostoli autem non solum obligabantur ad ea quae necessitatis sunt: sed etiam ad ea quae supererogationis sunt, maxime quantum ad illa quae pertinent ab obedientiam, castitatem & paupertatem. & ideo ipsi peccassent, si exemplo suo auertissent ab evangelica paupertate.
units.tr: But perhaps you will say that by this reasoning all bishops who have property and litigate over it as their own would turn their subjects away from evangelical poverty. These men grant the conclusion, saying that in some measure they do turn them away by example, just as they turn them away from entering religious life by example, though they do not intend this. And therefore they do not sin in this, because they do what is lawful for them, and it would be a work of supererogation for them to abstain from such things. But the apostles were bound not only to what is necessary, but also to what is supererogatory, especially in those things that pertain to obedience, chastity and poverty. And therefore they would have sinned if by their example they had turned others away from evangelical poverty.

units.la: Tertio sic: non minus perfecte servabant apostoli praeceptum & doctrinam Salvatoris de non contendendo in iudicio, quam modo servant monachi alii religiosi. sed monachis & aliis religiosis non licet pro temporalibus tanquam pro rebus propriis in iudicio litigare, sicut per regulas eorundem & sacros canones liquido constat. ergo nec apostolis licuit pro temporalibus tanquam pro rebus propriis in iudicio litigare.
units.tr: Third, thus: the apostles kept the precept and teaching of the Saviour about not contending in judgement no less perfectly than monks and other religious now keep it. But it is not lawful for monks and other religious to litigate in court over temporal goods as their own, as is clear from their rules and the sacred canons. Therefore neither was it lawful for the apostles to litigate in court over temporal goods as their own.

units.la: Secundo ostendunt, quod etiam apostolis non licuit pro temporalibus communibus iudicio litigare. quod probant primo sic: Illis qui non debuerunt saecularibus negociis prohibitis implicari, etiam non licuit pro temporalibus communibus litigare: cum litigare pro temporalibus sit inter negocia saecularia prohibita computandum.
units.tr: Second, they show that the apostles were not permitted to litigate in court over common temporal goods either. They prove this first thus: those who ought not to be involved in forbidden secular business were not permitted to litigate over common temporal goods either, since litigating over temporal goods is to be counted among forbidden secular business.

units.la: Nam & Maguntinense concilium, ut habetur extra de clerici vel monachi saecularibus negociis se immisceant. c. 1. enumerans negocia saecularia inter alia ponit contentiones, lites, rixas & inplacitis saecularibus disputare. sed apostolis non licuit negociis saecularibus implicari. teste Apostolo, qui 2. ad Thym. 2. ait: Nemo militans Deo implicat se negotiis temporalibus. ergo apostolis non licuit pro temporalibus communibus litigare.
units.tr: For the council of Mainz also, as found in Extra, that clerics or monks should not mix themselves in secular business, c. 1, lists secular business among other things and includes contentions, lawsuits, quarrels, and to dispute in secular pleas. But the apostles were not permitted to be involved in secular business, as the Apostle bears witness when he says in 2 Tim. 2: No one who serves God entangles himself in temporal affairs. Therefore the apostles were not permitted to litigate over common temporal goods.

units.la: Secundo sic: Illis qui non habuerunt dominium commune temporalium, non licuit pro temporalibus communibus litigare. sed apostoli non habuerunt commune dominium temporalium. Hoc prius multipliciter est ostensum. ergo apostolis non licuit pro temporalibus communibus litigare.
units.tr: Second, thus: those who did not have common ownership of temporal goods were not permitted to litigate over common temporal goods. But the apostles did not have common ownership of temporal goods. This has been shown in several ways before. Therefore the apostles were not permitted to litigate over common temporal goods.

units.la: Tertio sic: Illud non licuit apostolis, quod secundum se implicat ad peccatum: & sine quo apostoli potuerunt vitam istam transire, & sua officia exercere. sed pro temporalibus communibus in iudicio litigare implicat ad peccatum: & sine tali litigio poterant vitam praesentem transigere & officia sua exercere. ergo non licuit apostolis pro communibus temporalibus in iudicio litigare.
units.tr: Third, thus: the apostles were not permitted to do what in itself leads to sin, and what they could do without while passing this life and carrying out their offices. But litigating in court over common temporal goods leads to sin, and without such litigation they could live the present life and carry out their offices. Therefore the apostles were not permitted to litigate in court over common temporal goods.

units.la: Quarto sic: Illud non licuit apostolis, quod apud infideles, quos apostoli laborabant convertere, suspicionem habuit cupiditatis: maxime si sine illo apostoli poterant communiter sustentari; & praedicationi ac spiritualibus bonis intendere, sed litigare pro communibus temporalibus apud infideles habuit suspicionem cupiditatis: quia nonnulli ita sunt cupidi bonorum communium, sicut proprium: vel saltem constat quod respectu communium temporalium potest esse cupiditas, praesertim quando non possunt in proprio possidere. Sine litigio autem poterant apostoli suam sustentare naturam, ac praedicationi, & aliis spiritualibus bonis convenienter insistere. ergo apostolis non licuit pro temporalibus communibus litigare.
units.tr: Fourth, thus: the apostles were not permitted to do what, among the unbelievers whom they laboured to convert, had the appearance of covetousness, especially if without it they could be supported in common and devote themselves to preaching and spiritual goods. But litigating over common temporal goods among unbelievers had the appearance of covetousness, since some are as covetous of common goods as of their own, or at least it is plain that with regard to common temporal goods covetousness can arise, especially when they cannot possess them as their own. But without litigation the apostles could sustain their nature and devote themselves fittingly to preaching and other spiritual goods. Therefore the apostles were not permitted to litigate over common temporal goods.

units.la: Sed
units.tr: But

units.la: Sed forte obiiciet aliquis: quod per primam rationem, & tertiam, ac quartam probaretur, quod prælatis ecclesiæ non liceret pro temporalibus communibus litigare, cum non debeant se negociis secularibus implicare, nec illa facere, quæ implicant ad peccatum, & debeant suspicionem cupiditatis auferre. Ad hoc dicunt isti, quod apostoli, qui erant primi fundatores ecclesiæ post Christum, ad maiorem supererogationis perfectionem obligati fuerunt quam prælati sequentes. & ideo multa non licuerunt apostolis, quæ tamen aliis prælatis modo licent. Ipsis enim non licuit portare pecuniam extra tempus necessitatis: quod tamen prælatis modo nullatenus interdictum existit, sicut non debuerunt portare calciamenta, quod tamen prælatis licet. Quinto sic argumunt isti: Paupertas Fratrum Minorum non est altior nec perfectior apostolica paupertate, cum ipsi paupertatem apostolicam imitentur. sed ex paupertatis altitudine, quam vouent Fratres Minores, ipsis non licet pro temporalibus etiam communibus in iudicio litigare: sicut ex rescriptis apostolicis, & decretalibus summorum pontificum patenter habetur. ergo multo fortius hoc non licebat apostolis. Dicunt igitur isti, quod apostolis, qui vitæ Christi, qui nunquam pro temporalibus litigavit, imitatores perfecti fuerunt, non licuit pro quibuscunque temporalibus litigare: quia litigare pro temporalibus, nec ipsis, nec suis auditoribus fuisset expediens: imo ad non litigandum pro quibuscunque temporalibus se voto astringere apostolis & aliis expediebat. per hoc enim ab impedimento prædicationis, orationis, & aliorum spiritualium se notabiliter abstrahebant: & se nullatenus pro temporalibus nec in speciali nec in communi veritatem evangelicam prædicare patentius ostendebant, seque perfecte confidere in divina providentia declarabant. Nec apparet aliqua ratio cogens, quare potestatem pro temporalibus litigandi non debuerunt relinquere, sicut omnia temporalia relinquebant.
units.tr: But perhaps someone will object that the first, third and fourth reasons would prove that the prelates of the Church may not go to law over common temporal goods, since they ought not to involve themselves in secular affairs, nor do the things that entangle them in sin, and they ought to remove any suspicion of greed. To this, those men reply that the apostles, who were the first founders of the Church after Christ, were bound to a greater perfection of supererogation than the prelates who followed them. So many things were not permitted to the apostles which are nevertheless now permitted to other prelates. For they were not permitted to carry money except in a time of necessity, yet this is in no way forbidden to prelates now; just as they were not to wear shoes, which prelates are allowed to do. Fifthly, these men argue thus: the poverty of the Friars Minor is not higher or more perfect than apostolic poverty, since they imitate apostolic poverty. But because of the height of the poverty which the Friars Minor vow, they are not permitted to go to law in court even over common temporal goods, as is plainly evident from apostolic rescripts and the decretals of the supreme pontiffs. Therefore this was much less permitted to the apostles. These men say, then, that the apostles, who were perfect imitators of the life of Christ, who never went to law over temporal things, were not permitted to litigate over any temporal goods whatever. To litigate over temporal things would have been expedient neither for themselves nor for their hearers. Indeed, it was expedient for the apostles and others to bind themselves by a vow not to litigate over any temporal goods whatever. For by this they notably withdrew themselves from the hindrance of preaching, prayer and other spiritual duties, and they showed more openly that they did not preach the gospel truth for temporal gain, either individually or in common, and they declared that they trusted perfectly in divine providence. Nor does any compelling reason appear why they should not have relinquished the power of litigating over temporal things, as they relinquished all temporal things.

units.la: Si enim dixeris, quod propter utilitatem fidelium, ut scil. temporalia fidelibus dispensanda, si auferrentur iniuste, recuperarent: vel si vendicarentur iniuste, retinerent, non debuerunt potestatem in iudicio litigandi relinquere: eadem facilitate tibi dicetur, quod debuerunt prædia, & possessiones, civitates & castra, aurum & argentum, ac alias divitias congregare, ut eas fidelibus utiliter dispensarent: & tamen pro utilitate spirituali omnium dimiserunt: & ita etiam pro bono spirituali omnium potestatem litigandi in iudicio pro quibuscunque temporalibus abiecerunt.
units.tr: For if you say that, for the benefit of the faithful, namely so that temporal goods might be dispensed to the faithful, and so that if they were unjustly taken away they might recover them, or if unjustly claimed they might keep them, the apostles ought not to have relinquished the power of litigating in court: with equal ease it can be said to you that they ought to have gathered estates and possessions, cities and castles, gold and silver, and other riches, so that they might usefully dispense them to the faithful. Yet they gave all of these up for the spiritual benefit of all. And so, for the spiritual good of all, they also cast away the power of litigating in court over any temporal things whatever.

units.la: [Cum ergo quæritur, utrum apostolis & discipulis & eorum sequacibus pro rebus quas habebant licuerit & licuit litigare.] Ista est nova quæstio, quæ antea non fuit proposita. Quia quæstio prior fuit tantum de apostolis: ista autem de apostolis & aliis. & ideo ad priorem, & ad istam non est eadem danda responsio. Nam ad priorem de apostolis tantum est respondendum simpliciter negative. Ad istam autem respondendum est partim negative, & partim affirmative: quia apostolis & quibusdam discipulis & sequacibus non licet nec licuit in iudicio litigare: quibusdam vero discipulis licuit non solum pro propriis & communibus, sed etiam pro villis & civitatibus, imo pro regnis sibi & aliis principibus licuit litigare: quia omnes Christianos nomine discipuli comprehendit. & ideo hic proponitur quæstio de omnibus Christianis. [Illi qui propria non habebant pro rebus aliquibus tanquam propriis non licuit litigare.] Hic non respondet directe ad quæstionem de apostolis: indirecte tamen respondet insinuans per argumentum a contrario sensu, quod apostolis, ex quo aliquando etiam post missionem spiritus sancti propria habuerunt, licuit pro propriis litigare. [Illis autem qui habebant communia pro illis ut pro communibus animo ipsa bona communia defendendi vel repetendi sine fraude, & alicuius iniuria licuit litigare.] Hic etiam innuit rationem ad quæstionem de apostolis, quod scil. illis pro communibus licuit litigare illo tempore, quo habuerunt temporalia communia. quod fuit quando Iudæi conversi ad prædicationem, Iudæi vendiderunt ea, quæ habebant, & posuerunt pretia ante pedes apostolorum [præsertim illis qui earum habent illum communitatis.] Ex hoc vult, quod ad apostolos pro illo tempore, quo habuerunt cum aliis omnia communia præcipue pertinebat pro communibus litigare [vel aliis eorum mandato] quia secundum eum per procuratores poterant litigare [nec forsan ex hoc grave scandalum sequi posset] tale posset esse scandalum, quod etiam non deberet quis pro propriis litigare.
units.tr: When therefore it is asked whether it was lawful, and whether it is lawful, for the apostles and disciples and their followers to litigate over the things they had. This is a new question, which was not raised before. For the earlier question concerned only the apostles, while this one concerns the apostles and others. Therefore the same answer cannot be given to the former and to this one. To the former, concerning the apostles alone, one must answer simply in the negative. To this one, however, one must answer partly negatively and partly affirmatively, for the apostles and certain disciples and followers were not, and are not, permitted to litigate in court. But to certain disciples it was lawful to litigate not only over their own and common goods, but also over villages and cities, indeed over kingdoms, for themselves and for other princes, since the name "disciple" comprehends all Christians. Therefore the question here is proposed concerning all Christians. Those who had no property of their own were not permitted to litigate over any things as if they were their own. Here he does not answer the question about the apostles directly, but he answers indirectly, suggesting by an argument from the opposite sense that the apostles, since at some time even after the mission of the Holy Spirit they had their own property, were permitted to litigate over their own goods. But to those who held common goods, it was lawful to litigate over those goods as common goods, with the intention of defending or recovering them without fraud and without injury to anyone. Here too he hints at the reason for the question about the apostles: namely, that they were permitted to litigate over common goods at the time when they held temporal goods in common. This was when the Jews who had been converted by the preaching sold what they possessed and laid the prices at the feet of the apostles. Especially to those who hold such goods in common. From this he wishes it to follow that, at the time when they had all things in common with the others, it pertained especially to the apostles to litigate over common goods or by the command of others among them, because, in his view, they could litigate through agents. Nor perhaps could great scandal follow from this, since such scandal could arise that one ought not to litigate even over one's own goods.

units.la: CAP. LXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 68.

units.la: Etsi dicteret, ut dicit iste hereticus, quod viris perfectis pro rebus religiosum fuerunt esse prohibitum litigare, omnes religiosi, qui renuntiaverunt propriis, & habent in communi, ut sunt illi qui vivunt secundum regulam beati Augustini ac sancti Benedicti, ac qui omnium aliorum sanctorum Patrum diversarum religionum fundatorum, qui habent in communi, in via damnationis existerunt bona communia in iudicio defendendo: qui tamen tenentur servare, tueri & defendere bona illa. quod ex eo patet, quod Augustinum ad Bonifacium dixit: Maximus episcopus Vogien. auxilium petiit ab imperatore Christiano contra hoc, non tam sui vindicandi causa quam tuenda ecclesiæ sanctitatis. quod si prætermisset, non eius fuisset laudanda patientia, sed negligentia merito culpanda.
units.tr: Even if, as this heretic says, it was forbidden to perfect men to go to law over the goods of religious orders, all religious who have renounced their own property and hold things in common, such as those who live under the rule of blessed Augustine and St Benedict, and those of all the other holy Fathers, founders of the various orders, who hold in common, would be in the way of damnation for defending common goods in court. Yet they are bound to keep, protect and defend those goods. This is clear from what he wrote to Boniface in Augustine: "Maximus, bishop of Vogien, sought the help of a Christian emperor against this, not so much to avenge himself as to protect the holiness of the Church. If he had neglected it, his patience would not have been praised, but his negligence would rightly have been blamed."

units.la: In ista parte probatur, quod pluribus religiosis licet pro temporalibus communibus litigare, imponens appellanti quod dicat non licere viris perfectis pro rebus religionum suarum litigare. quod probat primo ducendo ad inconveniens: quia si non liceret eis in iudicio litigare, omnes qui tenentur communia bona defendere, in statu damnationis existerent. Secundo ibi: quod ex eo patet, idem probare molitur auctoritate Augustini, quæ patet in litera. Sed isti impugnatores dicunt conclusionem, quam hic probat, esse veram: sed dicunt quod reprobat appellantem non ad intentionem ipsius: quia non intendit appellans asserere, quod omnibus viris quomodocunq; perfectis sit prohibitum pro temporalibus in iudicio litigare, sicut nec quibuscunq; perfectis fuit prohibitum matrimonio uti: imo sicut multi fuerunt perfecti, qui matrimonio usi fuerunt, ita multi fuerunt perfecti, qui pro temporalibus poterant litigare. sed intendit appellans, quod sicut qui sunt perfecti quadam perfectione supererogationis, quae est per votum virginitatis vel continentiae prohibentur uti matrimonio: ita qui sunt perfecti quadam perfectione supererogationis, quae est per votum abdicationis proprietatis omnium in speciali etiam & in communi, quales fuerunt apostoli, prohibentur pro temporalibus quibuscunque in iudicio litigare. & ita dicunt, quod iste contra appellantem cavillose procedit, sicut hactenus consuevit. [Quod viri perfecti pro rebus suarum religionum esset prohibitum litigare.] hoc non dicit appellans de omnibus religiosis, sed de his tantum qui proprietatem omnium in speciali & in communi abdicaverunt. [Omnes religiosi qui renuntiaverunt proprio &c.] hoc sequeretur, si appellans intellexisset de perfectis non ultima perfectione supererogationis; sed de illis minime intendebat, sed de aliis. [Maximus episcopus Vagien. &c.] licet conclusio prius habita sit vera: ista tamen auctoritas Augustini non facit pro ipsa, nisi dicas quod iste Maximus episcopus fuerit episcopus & religiosus.
units.tr: In this part it is proved that it is lawful for many religious to go to law over common temporal goods. The author charges the appellant with saying that it is not lawful for perfect men to litigate over the goods of their religious orders. He proves this first by reducing it to an absurdity: if they were not allowed to litigate in court, all who are bound to defend common goods would be in the state of damnation. Second, at "that is clear from", he tries to prove the same by the authority of Augustine, which is clear from the text. But these opponents say that the conclusion he proves here is true, but that he refutes the appellant without regard to the appellant's intention. For the appellant did not mean to assert that it is forbidden to every kind of perfect man to litigate over temporal matters in court, just as it was not forbidden to all perfect men to use marriage. Rather, just as many perfect men used marriage, so many perfect men could litigate over temporal matters. But the appellant meant that just as those who are perfect with the perfection of supererogation, which comes through a vow of virginity or continence, are forbidden to use marriage, so those who are perfect with the perfection of supererogation, which comes through a vow of renouncing all property, both individual and common, as the apostles did, are forbidden to litigate over any temporal matters in court. And so they say this man proceeds captiously against the appellant, as he has habitually done. [That perfect men were forbidden to litigate over the goods of their religious orders.] The appellant does not say this of all religious, but only of those who have renounced all property, both individual and common. [All religious who have renounced their own property, etc.] This would follow if the appellant had spoken of the perfect who lack the ultimate perfection of supererogation; but he did not mean those, only others. [Maximus, bishop of Vagien, etc.] Although the conclusion stated earlier is true, this authority of Augustine does not support it, unless you say that this Maximus was both a bishop and a religious.

units.la: CAP. LXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER 69.

units.la: Item quod praelatis, quorum status reputatur perfectior aliis, & qui locum tenent apostolorum pro rebus suarum ecclesiarum litigare liceat, patet. Nicolaus enim papa praecepit Archiepiscopo Treverensi & eiusdem ecclesiae filiis, ut spirituali simul & materiali gladio tam daemones occupatores possessionum & rerum ipsius ecclesiae insequerentur, eorumque fautores, quousque cum integritate possessiones & res alias ecclesiae occupatae fuerint revocatae. 16. q.1.c. Auctoritate. quod non fuisset, si hoc licitum non fuisset. ad quod facit extra de sententia excommunicationis ca. dilecto, libr. 6. de restitutione spoliatorum c. cum olim. Item in concilio Gangrensi statutum fuit, quod si quis oblata Deo dederit vel acceperit praeter episcopi consensum, qui ab eo institutus est, & qui dat & qui accipit anathema sit. & sequitur: Iniquum enim consensum, ut potius custodes cartarum, quam defensores rerum creditarum, ut praeceptum est, iudicentur, 16. q.1.c. In canonibus. Innocentius quoque tertium hoc, scil. quod renunciantibus propriis & habentibus in communi pro communibus liceat litigare, expresse determinasse videtur extra de iudiciis ca. Cum deputati.
units.tr: Likewise, that it is lawful for prelates, whose state is considered more perfect than others and who hold the place of the apostles, to litigate over the affairs of their churches, is clear. For Pope Nicholas commanded the archbishop of Trier and the sons of the same church that, with both the spiritual and the material sword, they should pursue the demons who occupy the possessions and goods of that church, and their supporters, until the possessions and other goods of the church that have been seized are recovered in full. 16 q.1 c. Auctoritate. This would not have been done if it were not lawful. To this pertains Extra, de sententia excommunicationis, c. Dilecto; Liber 6, de restitutione spoliatorum, c. Cum olim. Likewise, at the Council of Gangra it was decreed that if anyone gives or receives things offered to God without the consent of the bishop appointed by him, both the giver and the receiver are anathema. And it follows: "For it is an unfair consent that they should be judged keepers of documents rather than defenders of entrusted goods, as has been ordained." 16 q.1 c. In canonibus. Innocent III also seems to have expressly determined this, namely that for those who renounce their own property and hold in common, it is lawful to litigate over common goods. Extra, de iudiciis, c. Cum deputati.

units.la: Hic probat, quod episcopis etiam pro rebus ecclesiarum suarum liceat litigare: ad quod quinque auctoritates adducit. Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod praelatis ecclesiae non solum pro rebus ecclesiarum suarum, sed etiam pro rebus propriis, imo pro villis & civitatibus propriis est licitum litigare. & ideo quamvis nonnullae auctoritates adductae ad istam conclusionem non faciant, nec valet arguere: Praelati tenent locum apostolorum, & praelatis pro temporalibus litigare licet. ergo & apostolis licuit pro temporalibus litigare. Nam licet praelati quantum ad aliquid tenent locum apostolorum, (quantum ad iurisdictionem spiritualem & praedicationem evangelii & dispensationem sacramentorum: non tamen quantum ad omnia tenent locum apostolorum. imo nonnulla licent praelatis, quae apostolis non licebant. licuit enim episcopis habere uxores, quia quod episcopi non habeant uxores, non est ex statu episcopali, cum episcopi habeant uxores in ecclesia orientali, sed est ex ordinatione ecclesiae, & spontaneo episcoporum consensu in ecclesia occidentali. & ita quantum ad catholicatem episcopi non succedunt apostolis: nec etiam succedunt eisdem quantum ad abdicationem temporalium. & ideo tale argumentum: hoc licet episcopis, ergo licebat apostolis: sophisticum est censendum:
units.tr: Here he proves that it is lawful for bishops to litigate even over the goods of their churches, and for this he adduces five authorities. But these opponents say that church prelates may litigate not only over the goods of their churches but also over their own goods, indeed over their own villages and cities. So although some of the authorities adduced do not support this conclusion, the argument does not hold: prelates hold the place of the apostles, and it is lawful for prelates to litigate over temporal matters; therefore it was also lawful for the apostles to litigate over temporal matters. For although prelates in some respects hold the place of the apostles (in spiritual jurisdiction, the preaching of the gospel and the dispensing of the sacraments), they do not hold the apostles' place in all things. Indeed, some things are permitted to prelates which were not permitted to the apostles. It was lawful for bishops to have wives, because the fact that bishops do not have wives does not arise from the episcopal state, since bishops have wives in the eastern church; it arises from the ordinance of the Church and the voluntary consent of bishops in the western church. And so, in respect of catholicity, bishops do not succeed the apostles, nor do they succeed them in renouncing temporal goods. Therefore an argument such as "this is lawful for bishops, therefore it was lawful for the apostles" must be judged a sophism.

units.la: [Praelati quorum status reputatur perfectior aliis] quantum ad aliqua, non quantum ad omnia. [qui locum tenent apostolorum] quantum ad aliqua, non quantum ad omnia, eo quod multa licent episcopis, quae non licuerunt apostolis. Nam apostolis non erat licitum occupatores possessionum ecclesiarum insequi gladio materiali. [quod non fecisset, si hoc licitum non fuisset] melius dixisset & securius, quod universalis ecclesia minime approbasset, si licitum non fuisset. Papa enim potest illicita perpetrare. Nam multos Papas constat scelera immanissima commisisse, sicut haereses praedicasse, fuisse haereticis, diabolo fecisse homagium, catholicos impugnasse, homicidia perpetrasse, idolis immolasse, innasisse papatum, fornicationes, adulteria, rapinas, & alia flagitia peregisse.
units.tr: "Prelates whose state is considered more perfect than others" holds as to some things, not as to all. "Who hold the place of the apostles" holds as to some things, not as to all, since many things are permitted to bishops which were not permitted to the apostles. For it was not lawful for the apostles to pursue the occupiers of church possessions with the material sword. "Which he would not have done if it were not lawful": it would have been better and safer to say that the universal Church would not have approved it if it were not lawful. For the pope can commit unlawful acts. It is established that many popes committed most monstrous crimes: they preached heresies, were heretics, made homage to the devil, attacked Catholics, perpetrated murders, sacrificed to idols, intruded into the papacy, and committed fornications, adulteries, robberies and other shameful deeds.

units.la: [cum deputati] illud capitulum non loquitur de episcopis, sed de Templariis: & ita pro religiosis adducit debuit. sic est de quibusdam aliis capitulis, quae adducit.
units.tr: "Cum deputati": that chapter does not speak of bishops but of Templars, so he should have adduced it for religious. The same is true of some of the other chapters he adduces.

units.la: TERTIA PARS PRINCIPALIS OPERIS NONAGINTA DIERVM.
units.tr: THIRD PRINCIPAL PART OF THE NINETY DAYS' WORK.

units.la: CAP. CXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER 120.

units.la: ADhuc iste haereticus constitutionem quia quorundam repugnare nititur, dicens quod de clavibus ecclesiae male docere videtur, quia in dubium revocat sive negat, clavem scientiae ecclesiae catholicae esse clavem. Cum enim in dubium revocet, vtrum scientia clavis ecclesiae sit censenda: & super hoc opiniones contrarias & diversas recitet in partem istam, quod, cum a non sit clavis in ecclesia declinare videtur: cum dicat, quod Saluator noster in promissione clavium facta beato Petro hoc serviisse videtur expresse cum immediate post illam promissionem subiunxerit, quodcunque ligaveris super terram, erit ligatum & in coelis &c. nulla de scientia habita mentione. qui Iacta se ipsum a & sanctorum ecclesiae scientiam & doctrinam ecclesiae catholicae, ut dicit iste haereticus contradicuntur. Ad quod inducit quod legitur Luc. 11, vbi Saluator noster sic dixit: Ve vobis legis peritis, qui tulistis clavem scientiae: ipsi non introistis, & illos qui introibant prohibuistis. Ex quo patet, ut dicit, quod clavis scientiae est vna clavis ecclesiae a clave potentia separata.
units.tr: Furthermore, this heretic, who strives to oppose the constitution "Quia quorundam," says that the constitution teaches wrongly about the keys of the Church, because it calls into doubt, or denies, that the key of knowledge is a key of the Catholic Church. For when he calls into doubt whether knowledge is to be regarded as a key of the Church, and recites contrary and diverse opinions on this question in that part, he seems to deviate from the key of the Church. For he says that our Saviour, in the promise of the keys made to the blessed Peter, seems expressly to have served this purpose, since immediately after that promise he added: "Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven," etc., with no mention of knowledge. He says that those who cast away the knowledge of the saints and the teaching of the Church are contradicting the Catholic Church. To this he adduces what is read in Luke 11, where our Saviour spoke thus: "Woe to you lawyers, who have taken away the key of knowledge; you did not enter in yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering." From this, he says, it is evident that the key of knowledge is one key of the Church, separate from the key of power.

units.la: Ista est tertia pars principalis totius tractatus istius constitutionis, in qua postquam iste impugnatus respondit ad obiectiones appellantis contra constitutionem Ad tenditotem & contra constitutionem, Cum inter: Nunc respondet ad obiectiones eiusdem appellantis contra constitutionem, quia quorundam. & diuiditur in duas partes, secundum quod ad duas obiectiones contra duas assertiones eiusdem constitutionis, quia quorundam, nititur respondere. Secunda pars incipit ibi: Item impugnat adhuc. Prima diuiditur: quia primo recitat obiectionem appellantis. Secundo respondet eidem in parte immediate sequenti, ibi, Profecto dicit ergo primo, q appellans ipsum impugnare molitur, quia non ponit scientiam aliquo modo esse clavem ecclesiae, quod diuinae scripturae repugnat, cum Christus dicat Luc. 11. Ve vobis legisperitis qui tulistis clavem scientiae.
units.tr: This is the third principal part of the whole treatise of this constitution. In it, after the one attacked has answered the objections of the appellant against the constitution "Ad tenditotem" and against the constitution "Cum inter," he now answers the objections of the same appellant against the constitution "Quia quorundam." It is divided into two parts, according as he tries to answer two objections against the two assertions of the same constitution, "Quia quorundam." The second part begins at: "Item impugnat adhuc." The first is divided, because first he recites the objection of the appellant, and secondly he answers it in the part immediately following, at "Profecto dicit ergo." He says first, then, that the appellant labours to attack it because it does not hold that knowledge is in any way a key of the Church, which contradicts divine Scripture, since Christ says in Luke 11: "Woe to you lawyers, who have taken away the key of knowledge."

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod truncate recitat obiectionis appellantis: quia post dictam allegationem de Luc. 11. sumptam, appellans immediate subiunxit. Et Rabanus exponens illud Matth. Et tibi dabo claves regni coelorum, dicit sic: clavem autem regni coelorum ipsam discretionem & potestatem nominat potentiam quod liget vel soluat distinctionem, quia dignos vel indignos discernat, haec Rabanus. & in decretis 20. dicitur sic: In negotiis ad finiendis non solum necessaria est scientia, sed etiam potestas: Unde Christus dicturus Petro: quodcunque ligaueris &c. Primo sibi dedit claves regni coelorum, in altera dans ei scientiam discernendi inter lepram & leprosum, in altera dans sibi potestatem ligandi alios ab ecclesia vel recipiendi. haec ibi. Ex quibus clare patet, quod clavis scientiae est vna clavis distincta a clave potentiae. & contrarium dicere scripturae diuinae & ecclesiae catholicae obviat manifeste. & de hac materia in dicta appellatione prolixa clarius continetur. Ex his patet aperte, quod iste impugnatus aliquas obiectiones appellantis omittit, ad quas non respondet: quia dicunt, quod respondere non potest, quae autem sit intentio appellantis, in sequenti capitulo apparebit.
units.tr: But those who attack him say that he recites the objection of the appellant in a truncated form, because after the said citation from Luke 11, the appellant immediately added... And Rabanus, expounding that passage of Matthew, "And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven," says: "By the keys of the kingdom of heaven he names discretion and power, the power to bind or loose, the distinction by which he discerns the worthy from the unworthy," thus Rabanus. And in the Decretals, distinction 20, it is said: "In settling affairs not only knowledge is necessary, but also power. Hence Christ, about to say to Peter, 'Whatever you bind,' etc., first gave him the keys of the kingdom of heaven: in the one giving him the knowledge of discerning between leprosy and the leper, in the other giving him the power of binding others outside the Church or receiving them." Thus there. From these passages it is clearly evident that the key of knowledge is one key distinct from the key of power; and to say the contrary plainly contradicts divine Scripture and the Catholic Church. And this matter is set out more clearly and at length in the said appellation. From this it is openly plain that the one attacked omits some objections of the appellant, to which he does not reply, since they say he cannot reply to them; what the appellant's intention is will appear in the following chapter.

units.la: [Repugnare nititur ] Ita e ordinetur sub Bulla, artificiosius tamen dixisset, impugnare nititur. [In dubium revocat sive negat clavem scientia ecclesiae catholicae fore clavem ] non solum revocat hoc negat scientiam fore clavem distinctam realiter a clave potentiae: Sed etiam negat, quod est clavis distincta vel non distincta: & in hoc errat aperte. [Cum enim in dubium revocet vtrum scientia clavis ecclesiae sit censenda ] quia non solum revocat in dubium: An scientia sit clavis distincta realiter a clave potentiae: sed etiam an sit clavis. [nulla de scientia habita mentione ] vocaliter: sicut nec de clave potentiae mentio fit ibi vocalis, sed fit ibi mentio vocalis de actu ligandi & soluendi: de scientia autem & potentia sententialiter fit mentio, qua ad hoc q al qs rite ligat & soluat, oportet quod habeat & scientiam & potentiam. [Ex quo patet vt dicit quod clavis scientiae est vna clavis ecclesiae a clave potentiae separata. ] Hic male recitat appellantem, & sibi falsum imponit, quia nusquam dixit, quod clavis scientiae est vna clavis a clave potentiae separata, licet dicat, quod est a clave potentiae distincta. Nonne omne autem distinctum ab aliquo est separatum ab eodem. Anima enim distincta est a corpore, etiam existens in corpore: & ita anima tunc non est a corpore separata. Persona etiam filii distincta est a persona patris, secundum catholicam veritatem (licet iste impugnatus publice praedicauerit oppositum, sicut fertur) & tamen persona filii non est a patre separata, quia filius est in patre & pater in filio. Accidens etiam est distinctum a substantia in qua est: & tamen non est a substantia separatum. Sic dicunt illi, quod secundum appellantem clavis scientiae est aliquo modo distincta a clave potentiae vel secundum rem, vel secundum rationem, vel secundum nomen, quia aliud connotat effectum, vel quocunque alio modo: non tamen est a clave potentiae separata.
units.tr: [Repugnare nititur] Thus it is ordered under the Bull; yet he would have spoken more skilfully by saying "impugnare nititur" (strives to attack). [In dubium revocat sive negat clavem scientiae ecclesiae catholicae fore clavem] He not only calls it into doubt but denies that knowledge is a key really distinct from the key of power; but he also denies that it is a key, distinct or not distinct, and in this he plainly errs. [Cum enim in dubium revocet utrum scientia clavis ecclesiae sit censenda] For he not only calls into doubt whether knowledge is really distinct from the key of power, but also whether it is a key at all. [nulla de scientia habita mentione] Verbally: just as no verbal mention is made there of the key of power, but verbal mention is made of the act of binding and loosing; knowledge and power are mentioned in sense, since for anyone to bind and loose rightly, he must have both knowledge and power. [Ex quo patet, ut dicit, quod clavis scientiae est una clavis ecclesiae a clave potentiae separata.] Here he misquotes the appellant and imputes a falsehood to him, because he nowhere said that the key of knowledge is one key separated from the key of power, although he says it is distinct from the key of power. Now is not everything distinct from something also separate from it? For the soul is distinct from the body, even while existing in the body, and so the soul is then not separated from the body. The person of the Son is also distinct from the person of the Father, according to Catholic truth (although the one attacked has publicly preached the opposite, as is reported), and yet the person of the Son is not separated from the Father, because the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son. An accident too is distinct from the substance in which it is, and yet it is not separated from the substance. So they say that, according to the appellant, the key of knowledge is in some way distinct from the key of power, either in reality, or in reason, or in name, because it connotes a different effect, or in some other way; yet it is not separated from the key of power.

units.la: CAP. LXXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXI.

units.la: Profecto patet, quod rius malitia adeo istum haereticum excaecauit, quod ad veritatem aliquam nequit erigere intellectum. dicat nobis iste haereticus, quibus loquebatur Saluator in verbis praedictis. profecto negare non potest, quin loqueretur thariseis & scribis, quia hoc iste textus dicit expresse: quibus tamen claves ecclesiae traditae quoniam tempore nondum fuerunt. Vnde patet quod non intellexit loqui de clavibus ecclesiae dominium. dominus in verbis prædictis attendat adhuc iste hereticus verba Saluatoris nostri. Dixit enim, Vae vobis legisperitis qui tulistis clauem scientiæ. clauem dixit scientiæ, non dixit clauem regni cœlorum de quibus clauibus, cum de clauibus ecclesiæ loquimur, est intelligendum. Illas enim Petro à Christo promissas legimus, & non scientiæ clauem, vt patet Matth. 16. vbi dominus Petro sic dixit: Ego dico tibi, quod tu es Petrus: & super hanc petram ædificabo ecclesiam meam: & portæ inferi non prævalebunt aduersus eam: & tibi dabo claues regni cœlorum. De clauibus autem istis regni cœlorum Aug. primo de doctrina Christiana sic dicit: Has claues dedit ecclesiæ suæ vt quæ soluerent in terra soluta essent in cœlis: & quæ ligarent in terra ligata essent in cœlis. hoc etiam Saluator dixisse videtur expresse ibidem, sicut constitutio prædicta, quia quorundam, dixit quia immediate post verba illa tibi dabo claues regni cœlorum, subiunxit, quodcunque ligaueris super terram, erit ligatum & in cœlis: & quodcunque soluueris super terram erit solutum & in cœlis. Et si quaeratur, quae sit clauis scientiae, de qua dominus loquitur Luc. 11. Respondet Glossa, quod clauis scientiae diuinae est Christi humilitas, quam qui habet, habet apertum ostium ad intelligendum scripturam. hanc Pharisaei & legisperiti contempserunt, nec ipsi eam in lege & prophetis voluerunt intelligere, nec ab aliis intelligi permiserunt. Item clauis scientiae potest dici fides, secundum illud Esa. 7. Nisi credideritis non intelligetis. Hanc clauem scientiae, sc. Christi fidem, pharisaei & legisperiti suis prauis expositionibus, de lege & prophetarum dictis abstulerunt quantum in eis fuit, sicut & iste hereticus, vt patet, niititur auferre. Hanc clauem (sc. fidem:) habebat Petrus, antequam dominus sibi permitteret regni cœlorum claues, vt patet in prædicto capit. Matth. 16. Cum enim dominus apostolos interrogasset, quem dicebant homines esse filium hominis, & post modum diceret eis, vos autem quem me esse dicitis? Respondens Petrus dixit, tu es Christus filius Dei viui. Et sic patet, quod hanc clauem, sc. fidei, Petrus habebat ante promissionem prædictam. habebat etiam humilitatem: alius Deus pater hec non reuelasset ei, qui talia reuelare paruulis, i.e. humilibus consueuit, iuxta illud Matth. capit. 2. confiteor tibi pater, qui abscondisti haec a sapientibus & prudentibus, & reuelasti ea paruulis. & iuxta illud Psalmista: scientiam dat paruulis. & quod pater Petro reuelauit responsionem prædictam, hoc immediate subiunxit dominus noster, qui immediate post responsionem eiusdem Petri, eidem Petro sic dixit: Beatus es Symon Bariona: quia caro & sanguis non reuelauit tibi, sed pater meus qui in cœlis est.
units.tr: Plainly, the malice of this heretic has so blinded him that he cannot raise his intellect to any truth. Let this heretic tell us to whom the Saviour was speaking in the words quoted above. He surely cannot deny that he was speaking to the Pharisees and scribes, for this very text says so expressly; yet the keys of the Church had not yet been handed over to them at that time. Hence it is evident that he did not understand the Lord to be speaking of the keys of the Church. Let the heretic still consider the words of our Saviour. For he said, "Woe to you lawyers, who have taken away the key of knowledge." He said "the key of knowledge," not "the key of the kingdom of heaven," and it is of the latter keys that we must think when we speak of the keys of the Church. For it is those keys promised to Peter by Christ that we read of, and not the key of knowledge, as is evident from Matt. 16., where the Lord said to Peter: "I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven." Augustine, in the first book of On Christian Doctrine, says of these keys of the kingdom of heaven: "He gave these keys to his Church, so that what they loosed on earth would be loosed in heaven, and what they bound on earth would be bound in heaven." The Saviour also seems to have said this expressly in the same place, as the aforesaid statement shows; for immediately after those words, "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven," he added, "whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven." And if it is asked what the key of knowledge is, of which the Lord speaks in Luke 11., the Gloss answers that the key of divine knowledge is Christ's humility, and whoever has it has an open door to understand Scripture. The Pharisees and lawyers despised this; they did not want to understand it in the law and the prophets themselves, nor did they allow others to understand it. Likewise the key of knowledge can be called faith, according to that of Isaiah 7.: "Unless you believe, you will not understand." The Pharisees and lawyers, by their wicked interpretations of the sayings of the law and the prophets, took away this key of knowledge, namely Christ's faith, as far as they could, just as this heretic, as is evident, strives to take it away. Peter had this key (namely faith) before the Lord granted him the keys of the kingdom of heaven, as is evident in the aforesaid chapter, Matt. 16. For when the Lord asked the apostles whom men said the Son of Man was, and afterwards said to them, "But you, whom do you say that I am?", Peter answered, "You are Christ, the Son of the living God." And so it is evident that Peter had this key, namely of faith, before the aforesaid promise. He also had humility; otherwise the Father would not have revealed these things to him, since he is accustomed to reveal such things to little ones, that is, to the humble, according to that of Matthew (chapter 11): "I confess to you, Father, who have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones," and according to the Psalmist: "He gives knowledge to little ones." And what the Father revealed to Peter, namely the aforesaid answer, our Lord immediately added, for immediately after Peter's answer he said to him: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven."

units.la: In parte ista iste impugnatus ad præmissam obiectionem appellantis nititur respondere: dicens quod Christus in verbis præmissis non loquitur de clauibus ecclesiæ: & per consequens illa verba nihil faciunt pro appellante. quod autem ibi non loquatur de clauibus ecclesiæ, probat primo sic. Dominus loquitur ibi Pharisæis & scribis, sed illis nullo tempore datæ fuerunt claues ecclesiæ, ergo non loquitur ibi de claue ecclesiæ. Secundo ibi attendat adhuc, probat idem secundo sic: Dominus in verbis præmissis loquitur de clau scientiæ, non de clauibus regni cœlorum. sed claues ecclesiæ sunt claues regni cœlorum. ergo non loquitur de clauibus ecclesiæ. Quod claues ecclesiæ sint claues regni cœlorum, probat dupliciter. Primo, quia claues ecclesiæ sunt illæ, quas dominus promisit Petro & successoribus eius. sed Christus promisit Petro & successoribus eius claues regni cœlorum, sicut patet Matth. 16. ergo &c. Secundo probat idem auctoritate Augustini, primo de doctrina Christiana, ibi; & hoc etiam vt dixit. Tertio ibi, & si quaeratur, probat eandem quæstionem. Tertio sic: Clauis scientiæ, de qua loquitur dominus Luca 11. est Christi humilitas & fides Christi: quarum vtramque Pharisæi minime habuerunt. sed Petrus habuit vtramque, antequam dominus promitteret sibi claues regni cœlorum. ergo Petrus habuit clauem scientiæ antequam haberet claues regni cœlorum: & per consequens antequam haberet claues ecclesiæ. ergo clauis scientiæ non est clauis ecclesiæ: nec clauis regni cœlorum.
units.tr: In this part, the man who is attacked seeks to answer the objection made above by the appellant, saying that Christ in the words quoted does not speak of the keys of the Church, and that consequently those words do nothing in favour of the appellant. He proves first, as follows, that Christ is not speaking there of the keys of the Church: the Lord is speaking there to the Pharisees and scribes, but the keys of the Church were never given to them; therefore he is not speaking there of the key of the Church. Second, he proves the same thing by a second argument, which he calls "Let him consider further": the Lord in the words quoted is speaking of the key of knowledge, not of the keys of the kingdom of heaven; but the keys of the Church are the keys of the kingdom of heaven; therefore he is not speaking of the keys of the Church. That the keys of the Church are the keys of the kingdom of heaven he proves in two ways. First, because the keys of the Church are those which the Lord promised to Peter and his successors; but Christ promised to Peter and his successors the keys of the kingdom of heaven, as is evident from Matt. 16.; therefore, etc. Second, he proves the same by the authority of Augustine in the first book On Christian Doctrine, where he says: "and this as he said." Third, where he says "And if it is asked," he proves the same question. Third, he argues thus: the key of knowledge, of which the Lord speaks in Luke 11., is Christ's humility and Christ's faith; the Pharisees had neither of these at all. But Peter had both before the Lord promised him the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Therefore Peter had the key of knowledge before he had the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and consequently before he had the keys of the Church. Therefore the key of knowledge is not a key of the Church, nor a key of the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti, quod hic versute procedit, cernens enim se non posse conclusionem suam defendere, patentes obiectiones omittens, vnam, quae non est ita aperta, nititur impedire. Vnde isti contra ipsam duo faciunt. Primo enim conantur ostendere, quod erroneum est dicere, quod clauis scientiae nullomodo est clauis ecclesiae seu regni cœlorum. Secundo declarare conantur, quomodo membrum, quod impedire molitur, in suo robore perseuerat. Ad euidentiam primi dicunt esse sciendum, quod licet circa clauem scientiae an esset proprie clauis, videantur fuisse opiniones contrariae: tamen Doctores concordant in hoc, quod inter claues ecclesiae seu regni cœlorum est clauis scientiae aliquomodo ponenda, vel tanquam alia. Vnde Glossa dist. 20. super verbo claues, quaerit sic: qualiter dicitur scientia esse clauis, cum aliquis possit habere scientiam, qui non habet clauem: & e contra? sed dic quod licet scientia prius non fuisset clauis, antequam haberet ordinem: tamen post ordinem incipit esse clauis. Si tamen quaeras, quid proprie sit clauis sacerdotalis? dico ipsam potestatem sacerdotalem, per quam ligat & soluit. Ex his verbis videtur, quod secundum opinionem Glossatoris scientia non est proprie clauis: & tamen ipse idem ponit scientiam aliquomodo esse clauem: & constat quod loquitur de clauibus ecclesiae. ergo clauem scientiae reputat inter claues ecclesiae computandam: licet, vt videtur non reputet eam proprie clauem. Hoc viso probant isti, quod clauis scientiae est aliquomodo inter claues regni cœlorum, quae sunt claues ecclesiae, numeranda. quod probant tali ratione. Illa scientia, quae de non claue fit clauis in collatione sacerdotii, est aliquomodo clauis regni cœlorum; quia per collationem sacerdotii, non conferuntur aliae claues, quam claues regni cœlorum. sed scientia praecedens sacerdotium in collatione sacerdotii de non claue fit clauis. ergo scientia postquam facta est clauis, debet clauis regni cœlorum aliquomodo vocari. Maior est manifesta. minorem ponit Glossa praedicta; quam etiam asserit Magister sententiarum libr. 4. dist. 19. dicens: qui vero ante sacerdotium scientia discernendi praditi sunt, licet habeant discretionem, non tamen in eu clauis est: quia non valet ea claudere vel aperire. Ideoq; cum promovetur in sacerdotem, clavem discretionis recte dicetur accipere: quia & ante habita discretio augetur, ac fit in eo clavis, ut ea iam valeat uti ad claudendum vel aperiendum. Ex his aperte colligitur, quod nonnunquam discretio sive scientia in collatione sacerdotii de non clave fit clavis. ergo clavis regni coelorum debet aliquomodo vocari. Secundo sic arguunt: Illa clavis debet aliquomodo clavis regni coelorum censeri, qua habens claves regni coelorum utitur ad claudendum vel aperiendum. sed habens claves regni coelorum utitur clave scientiae seu discretionis ad claudendum vel aperiendum, teste Magistro Sententiarum in verbis superius recitatis, quod etiam asserere est discernere, soluere manifestat. dist. 18. qui loquens de clavibus regni coelorum ait: Usus vero harum clavium modo est discernere scil. ligandos & soluendos, ac deinde ligare & soluere. ergo clavis scientiae debet aliquomodo clavis regni coelorum haberi; quod Magister Sententiarum vbi prius tenet aperte, dicens: claves ista (scil. quas dominus tradidit Petro & successoribus eius) sunt non corporales, sed spirituales. sc. discernendi scientia & potentia iudicandi. vnde & idem concedit, quod alteram clavium non omnes habent sacerdotes sicut patet in eodem libr. dist. 19.
units.tr: But these men say that he proceeds craftily here: seeing that he cannot defend his conclusion, he omits the obvious objections and sets out to hinder one which is not so plain. Accordingly, these men do two things against it. First, they try to show that it is wrong to say that the key of knowledge is in no way a key of the Church or of the kingdom of heaven. Second, they try to explain how the point which he is labouring to hinder keeps its strength. To make the first clear, they say that we must know that although opinions have been opposed concerning the key of knowledge, whether it was properly a key, nevertheless the Teachers agree that the key of knowledge must be counted in some way among the keys of the Church or of the kingdom of heaven, either as another key or otherwise. Hence the Gloss on distinction 20, under the word "keys," asks thus: "In what sense is knowledge said to be a key, since someone may have knowledge without having the key? And conversely?" But it answers: although knowledge was not a key before one had the order, nevertheless after the order it begins to be a key. "If, however, you ask what is properly a priestly key? I say it is the priestly power itself, by which one binds and looses." From these words it seems that, according to the opinion of the Glossator, knowledge is not properly a key; and yet the same man holds that knowledge is in some way a key, and it is plain that he is speaking of the keys of the Church. Therefore he reckons the key of knowledge to be counted among the keys of the Church, although, as it seems, he does not reckon it properly a key. Having seen this, these men prove that the key of knowledge is in some way to be numbered among the keys of the kingdom of heaven, which are the keys of the Church. They prove it by this argument: that knowledge which becomes a key from not being a key in the conferring of the priesthood is in some way a key of the kingdom of heaven, because by the conferring of the priesthood no keys are conferred other than the keys of the kingdom of heaven. But knowledge, which precedes the priesthood, becomes a key from not being a key in the conferring of the priesthood. Therefore, after it has become a key, knowledge ought in some way to be called a key of the kingdom of heaven. The major premise is plain. The minor is asserted by the aforesaid Gloss, and also by the Master of the Sentences, book 4, distinction 19, who says: "Those who, before the priesthood, are endowed with the knowledge of discerning, although they have discretion, nevertheless the key is not in them, because they are not able to close or open with it. Therefore, when he is promoted to the priesthood, he will rightly be said to receive the key of discretion, because the discretion he had before is increased, and becomes a key in him, so that he may now be able to use it to close or open." From these words it is clearly gathered that sometimes discretion or knowledge becomes a key in the conferring of the priesthood, from not being a key. Therefore the key of the kingdom of heaven ought in some way to be so called. Second, they argue thus: that key ought to be reckoned in some way a key of the kingdom of heaven, with which one who has the keys of the kingdom of heaven uses to close or open. But one who has the keys of the kingdom of heaven uses the key of knowledge or discretion to close or open, as the Master of the Sentences testifies in the words recited above, which he also makes plain when he says that to discern is to loose. Distinction 18, where, speaking of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, he says: "The use of these keys now is to discern, namely who are to be bound and who loosed, and then to bind and loose." Therefore the key of knowledge ought in some way to be held a key of the kingdom of heaven; which the Master of the Sentences plainly holds in the place cited before, saying: "These keys (namely those which the Lord gave to Peter and his successors) are not bodily, but spiritual, namely the knowledge of discerning and the power of judging." Hence he also concedes that not all priests have the one of the two keys, as is plain in the same book, distinction 19.

units.la: Secundo isti impugnatores satagunt declarare, quod medium, quod iste nititur impedire, in suo robore perseverat. Ad cuius intentionem dicunt esse sciendum, quod in omni facultate pe arguitur per locum a minori, per illam regulam: Si illud quod minus inesse videtur insit & illud quod magis.
