Ex illo ad propositum dicunt, quod appellans non intendit per illam obiectionem asserere, quod illa clavis scientiae, de qua loquitur Christus Luca 11. sit clavis regni coelorum, vna scil. de illis, quas dominus dedit Petro: sed intendit arguere per locum a minori, quod si scientia, quam acceperunt Pharisaei & Scribae, ipsa veritate testante, potest vocari clavis: multo magis & scientia quae requiritur ad aperiendum vel claudendum regnum coelorum in sacerdotibus potest vocari clavis. & si potest in illis vocari clavis, cum sit ita ad vltimum vsum clavis regni coelorum ipsa potest appellari non solum modo clavis, sed etiam clavis regni coelorum, & etiam clavis ecclesiae. & ita stat argumentum, quod si dominus Luca 11. scientiam Scribarum & Pharisaeorum vocauit clavem, multo fortius scientia sacerdotum, quae est necessaria eis in soluendo & ligando, potest vocari clavis regni coelorum.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents take pains to show that the means which this man seeks to hinder still holds its force. To make their point they say that in every discipline one argues from a lesser case, by the rule: "If what seems less likely to belong does belong, then what is greater does too." Applying this to the matter at hand, they say the appellant did not mean by that objection to assert that the key of knowledge, of which Christ speaks in Luke 11, is one of the keys of the kingdom of heaven that the Lord gave to Peter. He meant to argue from the lesser case: if the knowledge which the Pharisees and scribes received can, as the truth itself testifies, be called a key, much more can the knowledge required of priests for opening or shutting the kingdom of heaven be called a key. And if it can be called a key in them, then, since it serves the final use of the key of the kingdom of heaven, it can be called not only a key but a key of the kingdom of heaven, and also a key of the Church. So the argument stands: if the Lord in Luke 11 called the knowledge of the scribes and Pharisees a key, much more can the knowledge of priests, which they need for loosing and binding, be called a key of the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: [Eius malicia &c.] Ista sunt verba contumeliosa, quae ad rem non pertinent. Nam per talia verba cuilibet etiam insipienti facile erit Doctore quemlibet solennem & egregium reprobare. [quibus tamen claves ecclesiae tradita quoui tempore non fuerunt.] hoc concedit appellans. Ex hoc tamen, quod Christus vocauit scientiam eorum clavem, concludi potest, quod scientia sacerdotum potest vocari clavis regni coelorum. [Patet quod non intendit loqui de clavibus ecclesiae dominus.] hoc concedit: ex hoc tamen, quod vocauit illam scientiae clavem, potest concludi propositum appellantis. [clave dixit scientia, non dixit clavem regni coelorum] conced= ex hoc tamen, quod dicit clave scientiae, concluditur aliud: quia ad argumentationem spectat concludere vnum ex alio. [Illas enim Petro a Christo promissas legimus & non scientia clavem.] Istius clausulae pars affirmatiua vera est, sed semper negatiua est falsa. Ad cuius intellectum dicunt esse sciendum, quod clavis scientiae dupliciter accipitur. vno modo pro scientia, quae est necessaria quilibet sacerdoti in soluendo & ligando. Aliter accipitur pro auctoritate sive potestate discernendi inter lepram & lepram. & vtramq; promisit implicite Christus Petro cum dixit: Tibi dabo claves regni coelorum. Promisit enim sibi claves scientiae. Primo modo, inquantum promisit quod etiam scientia, quam tunc habebat, fieret clavis, quae tunc non erat clavis. Secundam et sibi promisit: quia illam erat totaliter nouiter acceptuus a Christo, quando receptus erat potestatem ligandi & soluendi. Sed dicit iste impugnatus: quod claues, de quib. agitur, in collatione sacerdotalis ordinis conferuntur. Constat enim quod ordinato in sacerdotem scientia communiter non confertur. ergo scientia non est clavis. Ad hoc respondet Magister Sententiarum lib. 4. dist. 19. dicens, quod altera istarum clavium non semper conferetur in collatione Ordinis sacerdotalis. Vnde dicit sic: Alteram clauium i.e. scientiam discernendi, non omnes habent sacerdotes: unde dolendum est, atq; lugendum. Multi enim licet indiscreti, atq; scientia quae eminere debet sacerdos, exortes, sacerdotii gradum recipere praesumunt, vita & scientia eo indigni: qui nec ante sacerdotium, nec post, scientiam habent discernendi, qui ligandi sunt vel soluendi. ideoq; illam clauem in consecratione non recipiunt, quia semper scientia carent. Ex his habetur aperte, quod vnam clauem non semper in consecratione recipiunt sacerdotes: nec habent omnes, postquam fuerint consecrati. Potest tamen dici secundum istos, quod omnis sacerdos in consecratione sua recipit claues scil. potestatem discernendi, & etiam potestatem ligandi & soluendi. Sed tunc oporteret concedere, quod aliquomodo esset tres claues ponendae sc. scientia, quae non habent omnes sacerdotes, & aliae duae quas habent omnes. Et dicunt quidam, quod hoc non derogat scripturae diuinae: qua de numero clauium an sint tres vel duae, aut plures, nihil reperitur explicite in scriptura diuina. [De clavibus autem istis regni coelorum Augustinus primo de doctrina Christiana sic dicit. Has claves dedit ecclesia vt quae soluerent in terra soluta essent in coelis &c.] Ista auctoritas non concludit in aliquo, quod scientia non sit clavis. [Hoc etiam Saluator &c.] Verba Saluatoris non faciunt ad hoc, quod scientia non sit aliquomodo clavis.
units.tr: ["His malice etc."] These are abusive words that have nothing to do with the matter. By such words anyone, even a fool, could easily condemn any solemn and outstanding teacher. ["To whom, however, the keys of the Church were not handed over at any time."] The appellant concedes this. From it, however, the fact that Christ called their knowledge a key still allows us to conclude that the knowledge of priests can be called a key of the kingdom of heaven. ["It is plain that the Lord did not intend to speak of the keys of the Church."] This is conceded. Yet from the fact that he called it a key of knowledge, the appellant's proposition can be concluded. ["He said key of knowledge; he did not say key of the kingdom of heaven."] Conceded. Yet from the fact that he says key of knowledge, something else follows, since it belongs to argument to conclude one thing from another. ["For we read that the keys were promised to Peter by Christ, and not the key of knowledge."] The affirmative part of this clause is true, but the negative part is always false. To understand this, they say, it must be noted that the key of knowledge is taken in two ways. In one sense it means the knowledge every priest needs for loosing and binding. In another sense it means the authority or power of discerning between leprosy and leprosy. Christ promised both to Peter implicitly when he said: "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven." For he promised him the keys of knowledge. In the first sense, he promised that the knowledge Peter then had would become a key, though it was not yet a key. In the second sense he also promised it to him, since Peter was to receive it entirely new from Christ when he received the power of binding and loosing. But the opponent says: the keys in question are conferred in the ordination to the priestly order. It is certain, however, that knowledge is not commonly conferred on a man ordained priest. Therefore knowledge is not a key. To this the Master of the Sentences answers in book 4, distinction 19, saying that one of these keys is not always conferred in the ordination to the priesthood. He says: "One of the keys, namely the knowledge of discerning, not all priests have. This must be lamented and mourned. For many, though indiscreet and lacking the knowledge a priest ought to excel in, presume to receive the rank of priesthood, unworthy in life and in knowledge. Neither before nor after their priesthood do they have the knowledge of discerning who is to be bound or loosed. Therefore they do not receive that key in consecration, because they always lack knowledge." From this it is plainly held that priests do not always receive one of the keys in consecration, and not all have it after they have been consecrated. It can be said, however, according to these men, that every priest receives the keys in his consecration, namely the power of discerning and also the power of binding and loosing. But then one would have to concede that in some sense three keys must be posited: the knowledge, which not all priests have, and the other two, which all have. ["Some say that this does not detract from divine Scripture, since nothing is explicitly found in divine Scripture about the number of the keys, whether there are three or two or more."] [Augustine, in the first book of On Christian Doctrine, says this about the keys of the kingdom of heaven: "The Church has given these keys, so that what they loose on earth should be loosed in heaven," etc.] This authority does not in any way show that knowledge is not a key. ["The Saviour also etc."] The words of the Saviour do not bear on the claim that knowledge is in no sense a key.

units.la: [Et si quaeratur, quae sit clavis scientiae, de qua dominus loquitur Luc. 11. Respondet Glossa quod clavis scientiae diuinae est Christi humilitas.] Hoc concedi potest sub bono intellectu: tamen principaliter dominus Luc. 11. loquebatur de clave scientiae, quae est scientia legis diuinae quae acceperat legisperitus iuxta illud Saluatoris Matth. 23. super cathedram Moysi sederunt scribae & Pharisaei. omnia ergo quaecunque dixerit dixerit vobis, facies & servatis. & iuxta illud apostoli ad Rom. 2. Si autem tu Iudaeus cognominaris, & requiescis & in lege, gloriaris in Deo, & nosti voluntatem eius &c. Tamen humilitas Christi potest vocari clavis: quia secundum Salomonem, ubi humilitas ibi & sapientia. Omnis autem sapientia clavis, potest aliquomodo vocari. [Hanc scil. humilitatem Christi pharisai & legisperiti contemperunt.] Nec ipsam habuerunt: & tamen receperunt clavem scientiae, licet non ad utilitatem suam. [Item clavis scientiae potest dici fides.] Hoc concedi potest: cum hoc tamen stat, quod etiam scientia, quam acceperant legisperiti, potest vocari clavis scientiae. & illam vocavit Dominus clavem scientiae. [Abstulerunt quantum in eis fuit.] Hoc etiam concedi potest, cum quo tamen stat, quod clavem scientiae quae est notitia literalis legis divinae, habuerant. Ex praedictis autem infertur isti, quod licet Dominus Luc. 11. principaliter locutus fuerit de clave scientiae quae non est clavis regni caelorum: tamen secundum expositionem istius posset dici, quod ibi Dominus loquebatur de clave regni caelorum, quia cum Dominus dicit, vae vobis legisperitis: qui tulistis clavem scientiae &c. iste accipit ibi, tulistis pro contempsistis, vel abstulistis: ut iste sit sensus: qui tulistis i.e. qui contempsistis vel abstulistis quantum in vobis fuit clavem scientiae. secundum quam expositionem concedi debet, quod ipsi tulerunt clavem regni caelorum: quia clavem regni caelorum contempserunt & abstulerunt quantum in eis fuit. & ita secundum istum Dominus loquebatur de clave regni caelorum, quam abstulerant legisperiti quantum in eis fuit. [Haec clavem scil. fidem, habebat Petrus antequam Dominus sibi promitteret regni caelorum claves.] hoc concedi potest: tamen ista fides Petri, quae erat aliomodo clavis, non erat clavis regni caelorum: sed postea facta fuit clavis regni caelorum, sub fide includendo scientiam discernendi inter lepram & lepram. [Habebat etiam humilitatem.] Hoc etiam concedit: illa tamen humilitas non erat clavis regni caelorum. totum quod sequitur, concedunt isti, sed nihil facit contra appellantem.
units.tr: ["And if it is asked what the key of knowledge is, of which the Lord speaks in Luke 11? The Gloss answers that the key of divine knowledge is the humility of Christ."] This can be conceded in a good sense. Yet principally, in Luke 11, the Lord was speaking of the key of knowledge, which is the knowledge of the divine law that the lawyer had received, according to the Saviour's saying in Matthew 23: "The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat. Therefore all that they tell you, that observe and do." And according to the apostle to the Romans 2: "But if you are called a Jew, and rest in the law, and glory in God, and know his will," etc. Yet the humility of Christ can be called a key, because according to Solomon, where humility is, there wisdom is also. Every wisdom can in some way be called a key. ["This humility of Christ the Pharisees and lawyers despised."] They did not have it, and yet they received the key of knowledge, though not for their own benefit. ["Likewise the key of knowledge can be called faith."] This can be conceded, yet it still holds that the knowledge the lawyers had received can also be called the key of knowledge, and the Lord called it that. ["They took away, as far as lay in them."] This too can be conceded, though it still holds that they had the key of knowledge, which is the literal knowledge of the divine law. From what has been said, however, this man infers that although the Lord in Luke 11 principally spoke of the key of knowledge, which is not the key of the kingdom of heaven, yet on this exposition it could be said that there the Lord was speaking of the key of the kingdom of heaven. For when the Lord says, "Woe to you lawyers, who have taken away the key of knowledge," etc., this man takes "have taken away" to mean "have despised" or "have removed," so that the sense is: "you who have taken away, that is, who have despised or removed, as far as in you lay, the key of knowledge." On this exposition it must be conceded that they took away the key of the kingdom of heaven, since they despised and removed, as far as in them lay, the key of the kingdom of heaven. And so on his reading the Lord was speaking of the key of the kingdom of heaven, which the lawyers had removed as far as in them lay. ["This key, namely faith, Peter had before the Lord promised him the keys of the kingdom of heaven."] This can be conceded. Yet this faith of Peter, which was in some sense a key, was not a key of the kingdom of heaven. It was made a key of the kingdom of heaven afterwards, when the knowledge of discerning between leprosy and leprosy was included under faith. ["He also had humility."] This too they concede, yet that humility was not a key of the kingdom of heaven. Everything that follows they concede, but it does nothing against the appellant.

units.la: CAP. CXXII.
units.tr: Chapter 122.

units.la: Item impugnat adhuc iste haereticus constitutionem praedictam false imponens ei, quod dicit, quod summus pontifex in his quae ad fidem & mores pertinet, potest suorum praedecessorum definitiones & dicta revocare, & contrarium statuere, prout decreverit statuendum.
units.tr: Likewise, this heretic still attacks the aforesaid constitution, falsely imputing to it the claim that the supreme pontiff, in matters that pertain to faith and morals, can revoke the definitions and sayings of his predecessors and decree the contrary, as he judges fit to decree.

units.la: In parte ista pertractat secundam assertionem, quam impugnat appellans. Et primo recitat ipsam. secundo respondet in parte immediate sequenti.
units.tr: In this part he takes up the second assertion, which the appellant attacks. First he recites it; then, in the part immediately following, he replies to it.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti impugnatores, quod truncate verba recitat appellantis, quae sunt haec: Nemo error est: quia ipse in dicto statuto, quia quorundam, etiam dogmatizat, quod summus pontifex in his quae ad fidem & mores pertinent, potest suorum praedecessorum definitiones & dicta revocare, ac eis contrarium statuere, quod decernitur in eisdem. qui error expresse doctrinae sanctorum patrum, & sacrorum canonum, & fidei catholicae obviat & repugnat, sicut patet per ea quae legimus in decretis 25. q. 1. c. contra statuta patrum & q. 2. ca. sicut destruerent, & in pluribus aliis capitulis. Hoc poterit reperiri & 25 dist. sicut sancti, & extra de statu monachorum ca. cum ad monasterium in fine. Ex quo errore totius fidei & veritatis ecclesiae destructio sequeretur: quia sequeretur quod quilibet Romanus pontifex posset revocare & destruere omnia in fide & moribus a suis praedecessoribus definita: & sic tota auctoritas ecclesiae vacillaret & in fide & moribus foret instabilis & infirma. Unde dicta doctrina est haeretica indicanda: quia in articulum fidei, Et unam sanctam catholicam & apostolicam ecclesiam, vehementer impingit. Et si in decretali Exiit, in doctrina & vita Christi & apostolorum, & in approbatione Regulae & statum Fratrum Minorum, & in concilio Viennensi, quod dictam decretalem approbavit, concedecretur erratum, sequeretur quod tota ecclesia erraverit in fide male de vita Christi & apostolorum Christi diffinimdo & Fratrum Minorum statum (qui secundum opinionem haeretici praefati est illicitum & simulatum, ac fundatum in doctrina evangelicae veritatis contraria) approbando, & sanctum Franciscum & alios sanctos de Ordine Fratrum Minorum, qui in huiusmodi vita & doctrina professione finierunt dies suos, approbando tanquam sanctos & sanctorum catalogo solenniter ascribendo. Haec dicta appellantis. Cum autem dicit iste, quod appellans falso imponit sibi dictum errorem: dicunt isti, quod in sequenti capitulo determinatiue probabunt, quod veraciter eundem sibi errorem imponit.
units.tr: But these opponents say that he quotes the appellant's words in a truncated form. They are these: "This is an error, because he himself in the said statute, because of certain people, also dogmatizes that the supreme pontiff, in matters that pertain to faith and morals, can revoke the definitions and sayings of his predecessors and decree the contrary of what has been decreed in them. This error expressly opposes and contradicts the doctrine of the holy Fathers, the sacred canons and the Catholic faith, as is clear from what we read in the Decretum, 25 q. 1 c. Contra statuta patrum and 2 q. c. Sicut destruerent, and in many other chapters. This can also be found in 25 dist. Sicut sancti, and Extra, De statu monachorum, c. Cum ad monasterium, in fine. From this error would follow the destruction of all faith and truth in the Church, for it would follow that any Roman pontiff could revoke and destroy everything that his predecessors had defined in faith and morals; and so the whole authority of the Church would waver and be unstable and weak in faith and morals. Hence the said doctrine must be judged heretical, because it vehemently strikes against the article of faith, 'And one holy catholic and apostolic Church.' And if it were conceded that an error exists in the decretal Exiit, concerning the doctrine and life of Christ and the apostles, and in the approval of the Rule and the state of the Friars Minor, and in the Council of Vienne, which approved the said decretal, it would follow that the whole Church had erred in faith, defining wrongly concerning the life of Christ and the apostles of Christ, and approving the state of the Friars Minor (which, according to the opinion of the aforesaid heretic, is unlawful and feigned, and founded on a doctrine contrary to the truth of the Gospel), and approving as saints St Francis and the other saints of the Order of Friars Minor, who ended their days in such a life and profession of doctrine, and solemnly enrolling them in the catalogue of saints. These are the appellant's words." But when this man says that the appellant falsely imputes this error to him, these men say that in the following chapter they will prove conclusively that he truly imputes that very error to him.

units.la: CAP. CXXIII.
units.tr: Chapter 123.

units.la: Aperte iuxta mores suos mentitur iste haereticus supradictus. Constitutio enim illa hoc non dicit, nec de hoc facit aliquam mentionem, ut patere potest cuilibet intuenti: imo expresse negat, quod dicere Christum & apostolos non habuisse in his, quae habuerunt, nisi simplicem usum facti, nec ad fidem pertinet, nec ad mores ut in §. praeterea patet: in quo sic dicit: Praeterea dicunt nobis asserto-res huiusmodi, ubi legunt, quod ad fidem vel mores pertineat Christum & apostolos non habuisse in his quae habuerunt nisi simplicem usum facti. Profecto directe hoc ad fidem non pertinet, cum de hoc articulus non sit aliquis, nec sub quo valeat comprehendi, ut patet ex Symbolis, in quibus articuli fidei continentur. Nec etiam redactive quasi hoc sacra scriptura continet, quo negato tota sacra scriptura reddatur dubia: & per consequens articuli fidei, qui habentur per scripturam sacram praedicari, reddantur dubii & incerti. hoc enim in scriptura sacra non poterit, sed contrarium reperiri. Ex quibus concludit dicens: unde non possunt ex praedictis concludere, nisi false: quia contra ordinem per summos pontifices circa talia licet successoribus aliquid ordinare: quia Nicolaus tertius praefatus empresse in sua declaratione in scripsit, ut superius plenius continetur.
units.tr: Once again, this heretic mentions above lies openly, in keeping with his habits. That constitution does not say this, nor does it make any mention of it, as anyone who reads it can see. Indeed, it expressly denies that to say that Christ and the apostles had, in the things they possessed, only the simple use of the fact, pertains either to faith or to morals, as is clear in §. Praeterea, where he speaks thus: "Moreover, those who assert this, where they read that it pertains to faith or morals that Christ and the apostles, in the things they had, possessed only the simple use of the fact. Certainly this does not pertain directly to faith, since there is no article about it, nor is it included under any heading, as is clear from the Creeds, in which the articles of faith are contained. Nor does it pertain indirectly, as if Holy Scripture contained it; for if this were denied, all of Holy Scripture would be made doubtful, and consequently the articles of faith, which are held to be preached through Holy Scripture, would become doubtful and uncertain. Scripture cannot be shown to contain this, but rather the contrary." From these points he concludes, saying: "Therefore they cannot conclude anything from the aforesaid except falsely, because by the ordinance of the supreme pontiffs in such matters it is permitted to successors to ordain something; for Nicholas III, cited above, wrote expressly in his declaration, as is more fully contained above."

units.la: In parte ista ad dictam appellantis in praecedenti ca. nititur respondere dicens: quod falsum sibi imponit, quod per constitutionem, quia quorundam, probare conatur, quia in eadem continetur, quod Christum & apostolos non habuisse in his quae habuerunt, nisi simplicem facti usum, neque ad fidem pertinet, neque ad mores.
units.tr: In this part, he tries to answer the appellant's argument in the preceding chapter, saying that he falsely imputes to him that by the constitution, Quia quorundam, he tries to prove that it is contained in the same that Christ and the apostles had, in the things they had, only the simple use of the fact, and that this pertains neither to faith nor to morals.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores contra ipsum tria probare conantur. quorum primum est, quod ex serie verborum ipsius in constitutione, quia quorundam, euidenter haberi ipsum asserere, quod Romanus pontifex quantum ad ea quae ad fidem & mores pertinet, potest diffinitiones & dicta suorum praedecessorum revocare & contrarium diffinire: Secundo ostendunt, quod ipse de facto multa in determinationibus Romanae ecclesiae diffinita in suis constitutionibus revocauit, & contraria diffiniuit. Tertio specialiter moliuntur ostendere, quod asserere Christum & apostolos non habuisse in rebus, quibus usi fuerunt, nisi simplicem facti usum, ad fidem spectat vel mores. Primo ergo probant, quod ex serie verborum constitutionis quia quorundam aperte patet, quod ipse intendit asserere, quod Romanus pontifex potest in his quae ad fidem & mores pertinent, diffinitiones & dicta suorum praedecessorum revocare.
units.tr: But these opponents undertake to prove three things against him. The first is that from the sequence of his words in the constitution Quia quorundam it is plainly evident that he himself asserts that the Roman pontiff, as far as matters pertaining to faith and morals are concerned, can revoke the definitions and sayings of his predecessors and define the contrary. Second, they show that he has in fact revoked many things defined in the determinations of the Roman Church in his own constitutions, and has defined the contrary. Third, they specifically labour to show that to assert that Christ and the apostles had, in the things they used, only the simple use of the fact, pertains to faith or morals. First, then, they prove that from the sequence of the words of the constitution Quia quorundam it is plainly evident that he intends to assert that the Roman pontiff can revoke the definitions and sayings of his predecessors in matters pertaining to faith and morals.

units.la: Nam sicut patet ibidem, ipse quandam obiectionem aduersariorum suorum probare conantium, quod sibi non licuit illa quae de paupertate Christi & apostolorum per Nicolaum tertium fuerant diffinita, in dubium revocare vel contrarium affirmare, conatur dissoluere, asserendo, ponens assumptas, in illa obiectione esse falsas: & conclusionem, quam inferunt, esse falsam. Sed prima propositio, quam assumunt, & quam ipse dicit esse falsam, est illa. Illud quod per clavem scientiae in fide ac moribus semel diffinierunt Romani pontifices, adeo immutabile perseuerat, quod illud successori non licet revocare in dubium, nec contrarium affirmare. Haec est propositio prima aduersariorum: & ipse recitat in principio constitutionis Quia quorundam. Hanc autem propositionem ipse asserit esse falsam, dicens in haec verba: Quod autem in ratione praedicta praemittitur, videl. quod illa, quae per clavem scientiae in fide & moribus sunt a summis pontificibus diffinita, ab eorum successoribus revocari non licet in dubium, nec contrarium affirmare: licet secus sit, sicut dicunt, in his, quae per clavem potestatis per summos pontifices ordinantur, prorsus sit contrarium veritati, patet ex sequentibus evidenter. Ex his verbis patenter habetur, quod primam propositionem aduersariorum asserit esse falsam, & per consequens contrariam esse veram, s. quod illud, quod per clavem scientiae in fide ac moribus semel diffinierunt Romani pontifices, non adeo immutabile perseveret, quin illud successori liceat in dubium revocare, vel contrarium affirmare. & ideo appellans sibi falsum non imponit.
units.tr: For, as is clear in that same place, he tries to dissolve an objection of his adversaries, who were trying to prove that he was not permitted to call into doubt or affirm the contrary of what Nicholas III had defined about the poverty of Christ and the apostles. He argues that the premises they assume in that objection are false, and that the conclusion they draw is false. But the first proposition they assume, which he himself says is false, is this: "What the Roman pontiffs have once defined in faith and morals by the key of knowledge remains so immutable that a successor is not permitted to call it into doubt or affirm the contrary." This is the adversaries' first proposition, and he recites it at the beginning of the constitution Quia quorundam. But he asserts that this proposition is false, saying in these words: "What is premised in the aforesaid argument, namely that what the supreme pontiffs have defined in faith and morals by the key of knowledge may not be called into doubt or affirmed to the contrary by their successors, although it is otherwise, as they say, in matters ordained by the supreme pontiffs by the key of power, is entirely contrary to the truth, as is evident from what follows." From these words it is plainly held that he asserts the adversaries' first proposition to be false, and consequently that its contrary is true, namely that what the Roman pontiffs have once defined in faith and morals by the key of knowledge does not remain so immutable that it is not permitted to a successor to call it into doubt or affirm the contrary. Therefore the appellant does not falsely impute this to him.

units.la: Sed forte dicet aliquis habens maiorem quam iste in distinguendo inter propositiones peritiam, quod utraque praedictarum propositionum est falsa. Est autem prima falsa propter falsam implicationem, quia si implicatur per ipsam, quod Romani pontifices aliquid diffinierunt per clavem scientiae, quod non diffinierunt per clavem potentiae: quod constat esse falsum. & istam rationem, quare negat propositionem praedictam, videtur sequi in disputatione sua de clavibus. Sed ista cavillatio, ut dicunt isti, non facit pro isto. Nam verum est, quod per praedictam propositionem implicatur aliquid diffiniri per clavem scientiae. & hoc probabunt esse verum. Sed dicunt, quod per ipsam minime implicatur aliquid diffiniri a Romanis pontificibus per clavem scientiae, quod non diffinitur per clavem potentiae: cum in propositione praedicta nulla penitus mentio de clave fiat, licet in propositione, quam postea recitat, mentio de clave habeatur. Primum (s. quod per clavem scientiae aliquid diffiniatur in fide & moribus a Romanis pontificibus) isti probare conantur. Ad cuius evidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod, sicut de se patet, in praedicta propositione nequaquam asseritur, quod clavis scientiae de qua loquitur, sit clavis regni coelorum vel ecclesiae: sed absolute sine specificatione aliqua quantum ad clavem scientiae sic dicitur. Illud quod per clavem scientiae in fide ac moribus semel diffinierunt Romani pontifices, adeo immutabile perseverat, quod illud successori non licet revocare in dubium &c. ergo ad verificandam praedictam propositionem illud, quod per clavem scientiae in fide ac moribus semel diffinierunt Romani pontifices, adeo immutabile perseverat, sufficit ostendere, quod per aliquam clavem scientiae, siue debeat vocari clavis regni coelorum siue ecclesiae, siue non, aliquid potest in fide ac moribus a Romanis pontificibus diffiniri: & quod sic diffinitum rite non potest in dubium revocari, nec debet eius contrarium diffiniri.
units.tr: But perhaps someone more skilled than he in distinguishing propositions will say that both of the aforesaid propositions are false. The first is false because of a false implication: if it implies that the Roman pontiffs defined something by the key of knowledge which they did not define by the key of power, which is clearly false. And this reason, why he denies the said proposition, seems to follow in his disputation about the keys. But this quibble, as these men say, does not help him. For it is true that the aforesaid proposition implies that something is defined by the key of knowledge, and they will prove this to be true. But they say that it does not in the least imply that something is defined by the Roman pontiffs by the key of knowledge which is not also defined by the key of power, since no mention of a key is made at all in the proposition stated, although mention of a key is made in the proposition which he recites afterwards. They undertake to prove the first point, namely that something is defined in faith and morals by the Roman pontiffs by the key of knowledge. To make this evident, they say it must be understood that, as is clear in itself, the aforesaid proposition by no means asserts that the key of knowledge of which it speaks is the key of the kingdom of heaven or of the Church, but it is said absolutely, without any specification as to the key of knowledge. "What the Roman pontiffs have once defined in faith and morals by the key of knowledge remains so immutable that a successor is not permitted to call it into doubt", etc. Therefore, to verify the aforesaid proposition, "what the Roman pontiffs have once defined in faith and morals by the key of knowledge remains so immutable", it is enough to show that, by some key of knowledge, whether it ought to be called the key of the kingdom of heaven or of the Church or not, something can be defined in faith and morals by the Roman pontiffs; and that what has been so defined cannot rightly be called into doubt, nor ought its contrary to be defined.

units.la: Hoc igitur viso, probant quod aliquid in fide & moribus potest per clavem scientiae aliquid a Romanis pontificibus diffiniri. quod ostendit primo sic. Aliquid potest in fide Christi & moribus a Romanis pontificibus diffiniri: quia aliquid huiusmodi ab eis per sacram scripturam diffiniri potest. sed fides Christi secundum istam, sicut patet 6.12.1. est clavis scientiae. ergo aliquid potest a Romanis pontificib. in fide, ac moribus per clavem scientiae diffiniri. Item, antiqui patres veteris legis poterat aliquid per illud Lucae 11. ve vobis legisperitis qui tulistis clavem scientiae &c. ergo multo magis Romani pontifices per noticiam legis diuinae, quod est in eis clavis scientiae, si fuit clavis scientiae in scribis Iudaeorum, possunt aliquid in fide & moribus diffinire. Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod secundum ista quilibet habens noticiam legis diuinae posset per clavem scientiae aliquid in fide & moribus diffinire. quod constat esse falsum: cum ad solum concilium generale & Romanum pontificem pertineat diffinire dubia, quae circa fidem ac mores occurrunt. Ad istud dicunt, quod propter aequiuocationem huius verbi diffinire posset in aliquo sensu concedi, quod quilibet peritus in lege diuina posset aliquid diffinire per clavem scientiae: hoc est, constanter & irrevocabiliter asserere. non enim potest quilibet aliquid diffinire, sicut modo accipimus diffinire, quia licet habeat noticiam quae potest vocari clavis scientiae: sicut & fides vocatur clavis scientiae secundum istum: deficit ei tamen auctoritas & potestas iurisdictionis, quae ad talem diffinitionem requiritur. Sed tunc dicet aliquis, quod secundum hoc Romani pontifices diffiniunt aliquid in fide & moribus per clavem potentiae, & non solum per clavem scientiae. hoc concedunt isti, nec contrarium asseruit propositio saepe dicta: quia illa propositio non vult excludere clavem potentiae, quis de ista non faciat mentionem. & non sequitur, non exprimit clavem potestatis: ergo excludit ipsam. Sic ergo patet euidenter, quod praedicta propositio cum ista ratione per clavem scientiae continet veritatem, si ipsa sine tali adiectione debet concedi. & si negatur cum tali adiectione, debet negari sine ipsa. & ideo cum iste impugnatus negat illa propositionem: illud quod per clavem scientiae in fide, ac moribus semel diffinierunt Romani pontifices &c. Ipse etiam habet negare illa: illud quod in fide ac morib. semel diffinierit Romani pontifices, adeo immutabile perseverat, quod illud successori non licet revocare in dubium, nec contrarium affirmare. Ex quo sequitur, quod ipse debet concedere manifeste, quod diffinitum in fide ac morib. a Romanis pontificibus, potest successor eorum in dubium revocare, vel contrarium affirmare. Unde ad fidelium intelligentiam pleniorem isti dicunt advertendum: quod licet propositio praedicta cum ista adiectione per clavem scientiae contineat veritatem: pro eo quod noticia legis divinae, & et doctrina ecclesiae, sine qua nullus debet Romanus pontifex in fide ac morib. diffinire, imo in ea debet se fundare, potest vocari clavis scientiae, ex quo scientia scribarum & Pharisaeorum vocabatur clavis scientiae; & nihilominus potestas discernendi inter haereticum & catholicum, sine qua Rom. pontifex in fide & morib. nihil diffinit, potest aliquo modo vocari clavis scientiae: sive utraque vel altera debeat vocari clavis ecclesiae, seu regni coelorum, sive non: tamen ista adiectio per clavem scientiae quodammodo videtur superflua: & sine ipsa ita haberent intentum impugnatores istius impugnati, sicut cum ea. Et si illam adiectionem per clavem scientiae dimisissent, multae instantiae frivolae contra processum eorum exclusae fuissent, quia intentio eorum fuit asserere, quod illud, quod in fide & morib. semel diffinierunt, sive per clavem scientiae, sive per clavem potentiae, sive per auctoritatem papale, sive per quamcunque potestatem. Rom. pontifices, adeo immutabile perseverat, quod illud successori non licet revocare in dubium, nec contrarium affirmare: & ita sine illa additione (per clavem scientiae) habent intentum: quod quis videatur superflua, non tamen reddit propositionem falsam. quare cum iste impugnatus neget illam propositionem cum dicta additione: debet eam negare absolute sine illa additione: & per consequens absolute debet concedere quod Rom. pontifex potest illa quae sunt in fide ac morib. a Romanis pontificibus diffinita, revocare in dubium, vel contrarium affirmare. & hoc est quod sibi imponit appellans, quare non mentitur, sed asserit veritatem. Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod licet verba sua hoc praetendant, ipse tamen hoc non tenet: ergo ipsi non debet imponi. Ad hoc dicunt isti, quod appellans non habuit iudicare de mente istius, quae latebat in corde, sed tantum modo de processu doctrinae. & ideo doctrinam praedictam potuit ipsi imponere, si tamen postea mentem suam clare exprimeret, doctrinam, ut plata est, detestando praedicta & ipsam corripiendo, videtur quod non deberet eum propter hoc haereticum reputare: licet propter alia, quae pertinaciter sine omni pallio asserit, possit eum inter haereticos computare.
units.tr: Having seen this, they prove that the Roman pontiffs can define something in faith and morals through the key of knowledge. They show this first as follows. The Roman pontiffs can define something in the faith of Christ and in morals, because something of this kind can be defined by them from Holy Scripture. But the faith of Christ, according to this author, as is clear from 6.12.1, is the key of knowledge. Therefore the Roman pontiffs can define something in faith and morals through the key of knowledge. Likewise, the ancient teachers of the old law could define something by that passage of Luke 11, Woe to you lawyers, who have taken away the key of knowledge, etc. Therefore, much more the Roman pontiffs, through their knowledge of the divine law, which in them is the key of knowledge (if it was the key of knowledge in the scribes of the Jews), can define something in faith and morals. But perhaps someone will say that, on this reasoning, anyone who has knowledge of the divine law could define something in faith and morals through the key of knowledge. That is plainly false, since it belongs only to a general council and to the Roman pontiff to define doubtful questions that arise concerning faith and morals. To this they reply that, because of the ambiguity of the word define, it can be conceded in one sense that anyone skilled in the divine law could define something through the key of knowledge, that is, assert it firmly and irrevocably. For not just anyone can define something in the sense in which we now take define. Although he has the knowledge that can be called the key of knowledge (just as, according to this author, faith is called the key of knowledge), he lacks the authority and power of jurisdiction that such a definition requires. But then someone will say that, on this view, the Roman pontiffs define something in faith and morals through the key of power, and not only through the key of knowledge. Those men concede this, and the proposition so often mentioned does not assert the contrary, because that proposition does not wish to exclude the key of power, since it makes no mention of it. And it does not follow: it does not express the key of power, therefore it excludes it. So it is plain that the aforesaid proposition, together with this argument, contains the truth through the key of knowledge, if it ought to be conceded without such an addition. And if it is denied with such an addition, it ought to be denied without it. Therefore, since this man who is attacked denies that proposition, that which the Roman pontiffs have once defined through the key of knowledge in faith and morals, etc., he must also deny this: that which the Roman pontiff has once defined in faith and morals remains so unchangeable that it is not lawful for his successor to call it into doubt or to affirm the contrary. From this it follows that he ought plainly to concede that what the Roman pontiffs have defined in faith and morals can be called into doubt by their successor, or the contrary affirmed. Hence, for a fuller understanding by the faithful, these men say that it should be noted: although the aforesaid proposition, with this addition by the key of knowledge, contains the truth, because the knowledge of the divine law and the teaching of the Church, without which no Roman pontiff ought to define anything in faith and morals, but on which he ought rather to base himself, can be called the key of knowledge (since the knowledge of the scribes and Pharisees was called the key of knowledge), nevertheless the power of discerning between heretic and Catholic, without which the Roman pontiff defines nothing in faith and morals, can in some way also be called the key of knowledge, whether both or either ought to be called the key of the Church or of the kingdom of heaven, or not. Yet that addition by the key of knowledge seems somewhat superfluous, and without it the opponents of this man would have their aim just as with it. And if they had dropped that addition by the key of knowledge, many frivolous objections against their argument would have been excluded, since their intention was to assert that what the Roman pontiffs have once defined in faith and morals, whether by the key of knowledge, by the key of power, by papal authority, or by any power whatever, remains so unchangeable that it is not lawful for a successor to call it into doubt or to affirm the contrary. And so, without that addition (by the key of knowledge), they achieve their aim. The addition may seem superfluous, but it does not make the proposition false. Therefore, since this man who is attacked denies that proposition with the said addition, he ought to deny it absolutely, without the addition; and consequently he ought absolutely to concede that the Roman pontiff can call into doubt the things defined by Roman pontiffs in faith and morals, or affirm the contrary. This is what the appellant imputes to him, and he is not lying but asserting the truth. But perhaps someone will say that, although his words suggest this, he does not in fact hold it, and so it ought not to be imputed to him. To this these men reply that the appellant had no right to judge the mind of the man, which lay hidden in his heart, but only the course of his teaching. Therefore he was able to impute that teaching to him; yet if afterwards he had clearly expressed his mind, by renouncing and rebuking the aforesaid teaching, as has been said, it seems he ought not on that account to be counted a heretic, although for other things which he obstinately asserts without any cloak, he may be reckoned among the heretics.

units.la: Ulterius isti ad infringendum totum processum istius contra propositionem saepe factam, dicunt quod nihil facit contra dictam propositionem, quod clavis scientiae vel scientia non sit clavis ecclesiae vel regni coelorum: quia sive scientia sit clavis ecclesiae sive regni coelorum, sive non: saltem ipsa est aliquo modo clavis, ex quo fides est aliquomodo clavis secundum istum. & constat quod scientia legis divinae & doctrinae ecclesiae requiritur in summo pontifice ad hoc ut diffinat aliquid in fide & morib. ergo diffinit per clavem scientiae: & tamen diffinit etiam per clavem potentiae: sive illa clavis potentiae sit illa clavis, quae confertur in consecratione cuiuslibet sacerdotis, sive sit iurisdictio & potestas papalis. Et ex istis patent duo. Primum est, quod tota disputatio istius & recitatio opinionum de scientia, an sit clavis ecclesiae, nihil facit contra adversarios: quia ipsi de hoc se nullatenus intromiserunt, & ipsi habent intentum, si scientia nullo modo sit clavis ecclesiae, sicut si sit clavis ecclesiae, dummodo sit aliquomodo clavis. Secundum, quod colligitur ex predictis est, quod falsum imponit eis, cum dicit eos asserere, quod alia per clavem scientiae & alia per clavem potentiae statuuntur seu diffiniuntur; quia ipsi hoc non dicunt, sed intendunt quod ad debitam & rectam diffinitionem & constitutionem quorumcunque concurrit tam scientia, quae debet aliquomodo vocari clavis, quam potentia, quae etiam aliquomodo debet vocari clavis: non illa, quae circa fidem & mores diffiniuntur, tam per clavem scientiae quam per clavem potentiae immutabilia perseverant. Illa vero quae per clavem scientiae & per clavem potentiae a summis pontificibus circa agibilia de se indifferentia statuuntur, revocari possunt & contraria statui. Sed forte quaeret aliquis, ex quo ad diffinitionem eorum quae tangunt fidem & mores, & ad statuendum illa quae respiciunt agibilia de se indifferentia requiritur tam clavis scientiae quam clavis potentiae, quare dixerunt isti, quod illa quae per clavem scientiae in fide & morib. diffiniuntur, revocari non possunt &c. Licet secus sit in hoc, quod per clavem potestatis ordinatur et statuuntur: cum per talem modum loquendi innuatur, quod alia diffiniuntur per clavem scientiae, & alia statuuntur per clavem potentiae. Ad hoc dici potest, quod tali modo loquendi utuntur non ad insinuandum, quod alia per clavem scientiae non per clavem potentiae diffiniuntur in fide & moribus, & alia per clavem potentiae non per clavem scientiae circa agibilia de se indifferentia statuuntur: sed ad insinuandum, quod in diffinitione eorum, quae diffiniuntur circa fidem & mores quodammodo principalius se habet scientia & in constitutione eorum agibilium quae de se indifferentia sunt quodammodo principalius se habet potentia, quia in diffinitione eorum quae pertinet ad fidem & bonos mores, nihil diffinit potestas, nisi quod decreuit scientia: ita quod in illis potentia debet omnino regulari scientiam: quia si in minimo potentia aduersaretur scientiae, diffinitio esset nulla. quia si papa per quamcunque potentiam diffiniret aliquid contra illud, quod scientia dictat diffiniendum in fide, & in bonis moribus, diffinitio sua nulla penitus esset: immo liceret cuilibet Christiano hoc scienti ipsam detestari, consputere, & sicut haereticam reprobare. In agibilibus autem de se indifferentibus statuendis, potentia quodammodo supra scientiam principalitatem habet.
units.tr: Furthermore, to overthrow the whole argument of this man against the proposition so often mentioned, these men say that nothing tells against the said proposition, namely that the key of knowledge, or knowledge, is not the key of the Church or of the kingdom of heaven. For whether knowledge is the key of the Church or of the kingdom of heaven, or not, at least it is in some way a key, since faith is in some way a key according to this man. And it is agreed that the knowledge of the divine law and the teaching of the Church is required in the supreme pontiff so that he may define something in faith and morals. Therefore he defines through the key of knowledge; and yet he also defines through the key of power, whether that key of power is the key that is conferred at the consecration of any priest, or is jurisdiction and papal power. From these points two things are evident. The first is that this man's whole disputation, and his recital of opinions on whether knowledge is the key of the Church, does nothing against his opponents, because they have in no way meddled with this question, and they attain their aim whether knowledge is in no way the key of the Church, or is the key of the Church, provided it is in some way a key. The second thing that follows from what has been said is that he falsely imputes to them the claim that some things are defined by the key of knowledge and others are established by the key of power. For they do not say this. Rather they hold that for the due and right definition and establishment of any matter both knowledge, which must in some way be called a key, and power, which also must in some way be called a key, concur. Those things which are defined by the key of knowledge and by the key of power concerning faith and morals remain unchangeable; but those things which the supreme pontiffs establish through the key of knowledge and the key of power concerning matters of action that are in themselves indifferent can be revoked and their contrary established. But perhaps someone will ask: since both the key of knowledge and the key of power are required for defining what touches faith and morals, and for establishing what concerns matters of action that are in themselves indifferent, why do these men say that what is defined in faith and morals by the key of knowledge cannot be revoked, etc.? It is otherwise with what is ordained and established by the key of power, since by such a manner of speaking it is implied that some things are defined by the key of knowledge and others are established by the key of power. To this it may be replied that they do not use this manner of speaking to suggest that some things in faith and morals are defined by the key of knowledge and not by the key of power, while other things concerning matters of action indifferent in themselves are established by the key of power and not by the key of knowledge. Rather they use it to suggest that in the definition of matters defined concerning faith and morals knowledge holds a somewhat more principal place, and in the establishment of matters of action indifferent in themselves power holds a somewhat more principal place. For in the definition of what pertains to faith and good morals, power defines nothing except what knowledge has decided. So in those matters power must be wholly governed by knowledge, because if power opposed knowledge even in the smallest point, the definition would be null. For if the pope, by whatever power, were to define anything contrary to what knowledge dictates is to be defined in faith and good morals, his definition would be utterly null. Indeed, it would be lawful for any Christian who knows this to detest it, spit upon it, and reject it as heretical. But in establishing matters of action that are in themselves indifferent, power has, in a sense, a principality above knowledge.

units.la: Nisi papa in hoc statuendis a scientia quodammodo deviaret, & minus salubriter, & utiliter subditis ordinaret, obediendum esset eidem: sicut licet aliquem excommunicare contra scientiam & conscientiam iniuste, tamen timenda esset sententia. & ita in talibus quodammodo principalior est potentia quam scientia: quia in multis talibus est obediendum eidem, licet contra scientiam ad damnationem animæ suæ ipsa duxerit statuenda. & ad hæc innuenda volunt praedicto modo loquendi.
units.tr: Unless the pope, in ordaining such matters, departed somewhat from knowledge and ordained things less wholesomely and usefully for his subjects, he would have to be obeyed, just as one may excommunicate someone unjustly and against knowledge and conscience, yet the sentence must still be feared. So in such matters power is in some sense more principal than knowledge, since in many such cases obedience is owed to it, even when it has ordained things that are contrary to knowledge and to the damnation of one's soul. They wish to convey these things by the manner of speaking just mentioned.

units.la: Secundo isti impugnatores moliuntur ostendere, quod iste impugnatus quamplurima, quæ ad fidem pertinent & bonos mores, in determinationibus Romanæ ecclesiæ diffinita de facto revocavit, & contraria diffiniuit. quod probant primo sic: Nicolaus tertius in decretali, quæ incipit, Exiit qui seminat, diffiniuit in hæc verba: Porro cum regula ipsa expresse contineat, quod Fratres nihil sibi approprient, nec domum, nec locum, nec aliquam rem, sicq; declaratum per eundem prædecessorem Gregor. 9. & nonnullos alios hac seruari debere, tam in speciali quam etiam in communi, quam sic artam abdicationem, veneno sit obtrectationibus aliquorum infensata damnauit astutia, ne Fratrum eorundem perfectionis claritas talium imperitis sermonibus lacteretur. Disimus quod abdicatio proprietatis huiusmodi omnium rerum tam in speciali quam in communi, propter Deum meritoria est & sancta, quam & Christus viam perfectionis ostendens verbo docuit & exemplo firmauit: quamq; primi fundatores militantis ecclesiæ prout ab ipso fonte hauserunt, in volentes perfecte viuere per doctrinam ac vitam ipsorum alueos deriuarunt. Hæc verba Nicolai de bonis moribus, ac vita Christi & apostolorum eius: & per consequens de fide assertiue, & diffinitiue prolata. In quibus verbis una veritas spectans ad bonos mores: & quatuor pertinentes ad fidem, patenter habentur. Prima veritas spectans ad bonos mores est: quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium rerum tam in speciali quam etiam in communi est via perfectionis. Quia enim hanc veritatem diffinitiue hic asserat Nicolaus, liquide constat: tum quia dicit, quod Christus viam perfectionis ostendens talem abdicationem verbo docuit & exemplo firmauit: tum quia dicit apostolos in volentes perfecte viuere talem abdicationem per doctrinam & vitæ alueos diriuasse: tum quia asserit ipsam, artam, & meritoriam & sanctam. Via autem arta, meritoria & sancta est via perfectionis. tum quia loquens de abdicatione huiusmodi, & motiuum suæ diffinitionis assignans, dicit: Ne fratrum eorundem perfectionis claritas &c. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, q. abdicatio seu expropriatio huiusmodi ad perfectionis pertinet claritatem. Secunda veritas ad fidem pertinens est, q. Christus talem abdicationem docuit alios. Tertia est, quod ipse seruauit eandem, quia ipsam exemplo firmauit. Quarta est, quod apostoli talem abdicationem alios docuerunt. Quinta est, quod eam viuendo tenuerunt. Istas quinq; veritates iste impugnatus in suis constitutionibus reuocauit, & eis contraria diffiniuit. quod enim contrarium primæ veritati diffinierit patet aperte. Primo quia in constitutione Ad conditorem asserit manifeste, quod manente eadem sollicitudine in acquirendo, conseruando, & dispensando temporalia, post expropriationem seu abdicationem huiusmodi, quæ ante inerat, ipsa expropriatio ad perfectionem valet nihil conferre. cum ergo licite, imo meritorie posset manere eadem sollicitudo prædicta, imo maior post expropriationem huiusmodi, quæ ante inerat, sequitur q. ipsa expropriatio non est via perfectionis censenda secundum istum. Secundo patet idem, quia in eadem constitutione Ad conditorem diffinit, q. carentia proprietatis seu dominii, talis non reddit Fratres pauperiores. Ex quo sequitur, quod non reddit eos perfectiores: quia non redderet eos perfectiores, nisi quia redderet eos pauperiores. si autem non reddit eos perfectiores, non est via perfectionis. Tertio quia in eadem constitutione diffinit, quod in rebus usu consumptibilibus non potest visus fieri a proprietate seu dominio separari. Ex quo sequitur, quod sicut abdicatio omnis usus facti est illicita: ita abdicatio omnis proprietatis est illicita. sed abdicatio illicita non est via persectionis. ergo abdicatio omnis proprietatis huiusmodi non est via perfectionis. Quarto, quia abdicatio palliata, nuda & ænigmatica non est via perfectionis. sed abdicatio huiusmodi secundum istum est palliata, nuda & ænigmatica: quia si dominium Romanæ ecclesiæ est palliatum, nudum & ænigmaticum, sicut iste dicit, abdicatio Fratrum est palliata, nuda & ænigmatica: & per consequens non est via perfectionis.
units.tr: Secondly, these opponents undertake to show that this man has in fact revoked very many things pertaining to faith and good morals that were defined in the determinations of the Roman Church, and has defined the contrary. They prove this first as follows. Nicholas III, in the decretal that begins Exiit qui seminat, defined in these words: Moreover, since the rule itself expressly contains that the Friars should appropriate nothing to themselves, neither house, nor place, nor any thing; and since this has been declared by his predecessor Gregory IX, and that several others must be observed in this, both in particular and in common; and since such a strict renunciation has been condemned by the cunning of certain men hostile to it, poisoned by their detractions, lest the clear light of the perfection of these same Friars be darkened by the unskilled talk of such men: We declare that renunciation of ownership of all things of this kind, both in particular and in common, is meritorious and holy for God's sake, which Christ also taught by word, showing the way of perfection, and confirmed by example; and which the first founders of the militant Church, drawing it from its very source, handed down by teaching and by life to those who wished to live perfectly. These are Nicholas's words, spoken assertively and definitively about good morals, and about the life of Christ and his apostles, and consequently about faith. In these words one truth concerning good morals and four pertaining to faith are plainly to be found. The first truth concerning good morals is that renunciation of the ownership of all things, both in particular and in common, is the way of perfection. That Nicholas here asserts this truth definitively is clear, both because he says that Christ, showing the way of perfection, taught such renunciation by word and confirmed it by example; and because he says that the apostles handed down such renunciation by teaching and by the example of their lives to those who wished to live perfectly; and because he asserts that it is narrow, meritorious and holy. A narrow, meritorious and holy way is the way of perfection. Again, speaking of this renunciation and giving the motive for his definition, he says: lest the clear light of the perfection of these same Friars etc. From these words it is plainly gathered that this renunciation or dispossession pertains to the clarity of perfection. The second truth pertaining to faith is that Christ taught others such renunciation. The third is that he himself kept the same, since he confirmed it by example. The fourth is that the apostles taught others such renunciation. The fifth is that they kept it by living it. This man, in his constitutions, has revoked these five truths and defined the contrary. That he has defined the contrary of the first truth is plain. First, because in the constitution Ad conditorem he clearly asserts that, while the same care in acquiring, preserving and dispensing temporal goods remains, the dispossession or renunciation of this kind, which was there before, contributes nothing to perfection. Since therefore the same care could lawfully, indeed meritoriously, remain, indeed greater after such dispossession than before, it follows that, according to him, dispossession itself is not to be regarded as the way of perfection. Second, the same is plain, because in the same constitution Ad conditorem he defines that the lack of ownership or dominion does not make the Friars poorer. From this it follows that it does not make them more perfect, for it would make them more perfect only if it made them poorer. But if it does not make them more perfect, it is not the way of perfection. Third, because in the same constitution he defines that in things consumed by use, the use cannot be separated from ownership or dominion. From this it follows that, just as the renunciation of all actual use is unlawful, so the renunciation of all ownership is unlawful. But unlawful renunciation is not the way of perfection. Therefore renunciation of all such ownership is not the way of perfection. Fourth, because a renunciation that is veiled, bare and enigmatic is not the way of perfection. But such renunciation, according to him, is veiled, bare and enigmatic; for if the dominion of the Roman Church is veiled, bare and enigmatic, as he says, then the renunciation of the Friars is veiled, bare and enigmatic, and consequently is not the way of perfection.

units.la: Secundam etiam veritatem, s. quod Christus abdicationem huiusmodi docuit alios, reuocauit, & falsitatem contrariam diffiniuit, cum in constitutione præsenti, quia vir, recitans obiectionem appellantis & respondens eidem dicat in hæc verba: Ad hoc autem quod ipse dicit, quod ex hoc sequitur, quod Christus simulatam & fallacem doctrinam tribuit volentibus ad perfectionem attingere: quod omnia temporalia quo ad proprietatem & dominium relinquerent consulendo: dicimus falsum esse, quod hoc consuluerit apostolis vel discipulis suis ad minus, quod non haberent in communi. Ex hoc patet, quod secundum istum Christus non consuluit talem abdicationem apostolis nec discipulis: & per consequens nō docuit eam, quia si docuisset, maxime docuisset apostolos & discipulos, & per consequens eis consuluisset eandem. Nequaquam igitur secundum istum Christus viam perfectionis ostendens verbo docuit abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum in speciali & in communi: cuius contrarium Nicolaus tertius diffiniuit.
units.tr: He has also revoked the second truth, namely that Christ taught others such renunciation, and has defined the contrary falsehood, since in the present constitution, when the man recites the objection of the appellant and answers it, he says in these words: As for what he says, that it follows from this that Christ gave a feigned and deceptive teaching to those who wished to attain perfection, namely that they should leave all temporal things, as to ownership and dominion, by counsel: we say it is false that he counselled this to the apostles or to his disciples, at least that they should not have things in common. From this it is plain that, according to him, Christ did not counsel such renunciation to the apostles or to the disciples; and consequently he did not teach it, for if he had taught it, he would above all have taught the apostles and disciples, and consequently would have counselled them to it. By no means, therefore, according to him, did Christ, showing the way of perfection, teach by word the renunciation of ownership of all things, both in particular and in common; whereas Nicholas III defined the contrary.

units.la: Tertiam etiam veritatem catholicam, scil. quod Christus eandem abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum in speciali & in communi seruauit, quia exemplo firmauit secundum Nicolaum tertium, reuocauit & contrariam hæresim diffiniuit: tum quia, sicut patet supra, ca. 93. diffiniuit, q. Christus inquantum homo ab instanti suæ conceptionis ex Dei datione habuit regnum & universale dominium omnium rerum. tum quia, sicut patet supra c. 94. Christus postea diuersis modis ex collatione fidelium vel emptione diuersarum rerum temporalium acquisiuit dominium. tum quia, vt habetur
units.tr: He has also revoked the third Catholic truth, namely that Christ kept this same renunciation of ownership of all things, both in particular and in common, since he confirmed it by example according to Nicholas III, and has defined the contrary heresy. This is so, first, because, as is plain above in chapter 93, he defined that Christ, as man, from the moment of his conception, by the gift of God, had kingdom and universal dominion over all things. Second, because, as is plain above in chapter 94, Christ afterwards acquired dominion in various ways, by the gifts of the faithful or by buying various temporal things. Third, as is had in

units.la: berur betur c.95. Christus regno & dominio temporalium renunciare non potuit. Cum quia c.96. asserit manifeste, quod Christus non fuit pauper per carentiam dominii temporalis, tum quia in constitutione. Cum inter loquens de modo habendi res temporales quo ad dominium seu proprietatem, sicut probatum est supra c.85. dicit firmiter esse haereticum dicere Christum non habuisse in rebus ius utendi, vendendi & donandi, & ex ipsis alia acquirendi. Unde constat, quod in eade constitutione sententialiter diffinivit esse haereticum, quod Christus no habuit in quibuscunque reb' dominio. & ita Christus secundum eu abdicatione proprietatis omnium temporalium nequaquam assumpsit: cuius contrarium Nicol. tertius diffinivit.
units.tr: chapter 95, Christ could not renounce the kingdom and dominion of temporal things. Also, in chapter 96 he clearly asserts that Christ was not poor through lack of temporal dominion. Also, in the constitution Cum inter, speaking of the manner of having temporal goods as to dominion or ownership, as was proved above in chapter 85, he says it is firmly heretical to say that Christ had no right in things to use, sell and give them, and from them to acquire other things. Hence it is clear that in that same constitution he judicially defined it to be heretical that Christ had no dominion over any things whatever. And so, according to him, Christ by no means took upon himself the renunciation of ownership of all temporal things; whereas Nicholas III defined the contrary.

units.la: Quarta etiam veritatem catholicam. f. quod apostoli talem abdicationem a aliis docuerunt, revocat iste, & falsitate contrariam in suo antecedente determinat manifeste: quia ex quo secundum eum talem abdicationem nullatenus servaverunt, sicut itaque post patebit, & non docuerunt alios rem pauperta[ver]e, quam minime servaverunt: sequitur quod talem abdicationem minime docuerit.
units.tr: He also revokes the fourth Catholic truth, namely that the apostles taught others such renunciation, and clearly determines the contrary falsehood in his antecedent. For since, according to him, they by no means kept such renunciation, as will be shown below, and did not teach others to practise poverty, which they had in no way kept, it follows that he did not teach such renunciation at all.

units.la: Quintam etiam veritatem catholicam. (c. quod apostoli abdicatione huiusmodi servaverunt, revocat manifeste, & contrariam haeresim diffinitive determinat: quod patet, quia in constitutione (cum inter) determinat, quod habuerunt in rebus, quibus utebantur, ius utendi, vendendi, donandi, & ex ipsis alia acquirendi. & quod ibi loquatur de iure dominii, supra c.85. est probatum. & ita ibi sententialiter haeresim veritati praedictae contrariam diffinivit: quod etiam in ista constitutione, quia vir reprobus, non solum sententialiter, sed et vocaliter apte absque omni palliatione asserit, & diffinit, ex ultimata deliberatione determinans, aliosque compellens ad credendum, quod apostoli, postquam fuerunt ad apostolatum assumpti, non solum aliquando in communi, sed etiam saepe in speciali, vere habuerunt temporalium dominium & proprietatem, & quod habuerunt ac habere licite potuerunt praedia in Iudaea & inter gentes.
units.tr: The fifth Catholic truth, that the apostles observed such renunciation, he plainly revokes, and he definitively determines the contrary heresy. This is clear because in the constitution Cum inter he determines that they had in the goods they used the right to use, to sell, to give away, and to acquire other things from them. That this refers to the right of ownership has been proved above, chapter 85. So in that constitution he defined in a judgment the heresy contrary to the truth stated above. In this constitution too, since this man of reprobate mind asserts and defines not only in judgment but also aloud, and without any pretence, and determining from final deliberation, and compelling others to believe, that the apostles, after they were taken up into the apostolate, truly had ownership and property of temporal things, not only sometimes in common but often individually, and that they had and could lawfully have had estates in Judaea and among the Gentiles.

units.la: Unde quinque haereses praedictae veritati contrarias in constitutione ista, quia vir reprobus, dogmatizat. quarum prima est, quod apostoli post missionem spiritus S. habuerunt agros, domos, & praedia in communi quo ad dominium & proprietatem, dicens quod agri, & domus primorum conversorum in Iudea, post missionem spiritus S. fuerunt facti de dominio apostolorum in communi. Unde dicit in haec verba: Cum ergo prius dicat, quod inter credentes erant omnia communia: & post subiungat: quod agri vendebantur & domus: evidenter apparet quod illa communia antequam venderentur erant effecta. Item post asseruit manifeste, quod domorum & agrorum venditorum apostoli habuerunt dominium, licet sibi non retinuerunt idem dominium. haec supra c.4. & 5. patuerunt.
units.tr: Hence in this constitution, Quia vir reprobus, he teaches five heresies contrary to the said truth. The first is that after the mission of the Holy Spirit the apostles had fields, houses and estates in common as to ownership and property, saying that the fields and houses of the first converts in Judaea, after the mission of the Holy Spirit, became the common possession of the apostles. So he says in these words: "Since he first says that among the believers all things were common, and afterwards adds that fields and houses were sold, it clearly appears that those common things had been made such before they were sold." Likewise he afterwards asserted plainly that the apostles had ownership of the houses and fields that were sold, although they did not keep that ownership for themselves. These points were made clear above, chapters 4 and 5.

units.la: Secunda haeresis praedictae veritati contraria, quam iste dogmatizat, est quod apostoli non solum habuerunt praedia quo ad dominium, sed etiam sibi potuerunt praedia retinere in Iudea: unde sicut patet sup. c.3. dicit sic: Expradictis patet, quod apostolis licuit in Iudea si voluissent, retinere praedia: nec poto compulsi sunt, quod illa non retinuerunt, sed voluntate propria, quia se non contracturos mora inibi, sed transituros praevidebant ad gentes. Tertia haeresis saepe dictae veritati contraria est, quod apostoli in Iudaea prius missionem spiritus S. immobilia vendiderunt tanquam eorum habentes dominium in communi. nam, sicut patet sup. c.18. ipse loquens de apostolis air: verum est tamen quod in Iudaea non retinuerunt immobilia, sed ea potius vendiderunt. Quarta haeresis contraria veritati praefatae, quam ipse dogmatizat, est quod apostoli semper post missionem spiritus S. mobilia & immobilia, qualia habent monachi: & per consequens villas, civitates & castra, thesauros auri & argenti, ac alias res pretiosas habuerunt, seu licite habere potuerunt, quo ad dominium in communi. Quod non hoc teneat, patet, cum dicat expresse, sicut recitatum est, sup. c.18. constat autem quod monachi habent mobilia & immobilia quo ad proprietatem & dominium in communi, ut probatur. 18.q.2. c. in nullo. Quare videtur, quod etiam apostoli habuerunt seu habere potuerunt in communi, sed nonnulli monachi habet villas, civitates & castra, aurum & argentum, ac res alias pretiosas. ergo & apostoli secundum istum omnia talia habuerunt, seu habere licite potuerunt.
units.tr: The second heresy contrary to the said truth, which he teaches, is that the apostles not only had estates as to ownership but could also keep estates for themselves in Judaea. So, as is clear above, chapter 3, he says: "From what has been said it is evident that the apostles were free, if they wished, to keep estates in Judaea; nor were they compelled not to keep them, but did so by their own will, since they foresaw that they would not stay there but would pass on to the Gentiles." The third heresy, contrary to the truth often mentioned, is that the apostles in Judaea, before the mission of the Holy Spirit, sold immovable property as if they held ownership in common. For, as is clear above, chapter 18, he himself speaking of the apostles says: "It is true, however, that in Judaea they did not keep immovable property, but rather sold it." The fourth heresy contrary to the said truth, which he teaches, is that the apostles always after the mission of the Holy Spirit had movable and immovable goods, such as monks have, and consequently villages, cities and castles, treasures of gold and silver, and other precious things, or could lawfully have had them, in common as to ownership. That he does not hold this is clear, since he says expressly, as was quoted above, chapter 18. But it is established that monks have movable and immovable goods as to property and ownership in common, as is proved, 18 q. 2, c. In nullo. Therefore it seems that the apostles also had, or could have had, these in common; but some monks have villages, cities and castles, gold and silver, and other precious things. Therefore, according to him, the apostles too had all such things, or could lawfully have had them.

units.la: Quinta haeresis praefatae veritati contraria, quam iste dogmatizat, est quod beatus Petrus, & eadem ratione quilibet alius apostolus, vere fuit proprietarius: qua post missionem spiritus S. habens in speciali dominium & proprietatem rerum temporalium. sicut enim patet supra c.9. ipse dicit sic: Videtur etiam quod probabiliter posset dici quod proprietatis distributionem bonorum vsu consumptibilium, quae fiebat inter apostolos & credentes alios, ut dicitur Actuum 2. & 4. quilibet portionem sibi assignatam proprietarius & dominus dici posset. Et infra: Cum ergo dicat quod nullus eorum erat pro eo, quia vnicuique diuidebatur prout opus erat, supponit aperte, quod illud, quod vnicuique diuidebatur, usum cuiuslibet erat proprium. Et infra: Videtur quod quilibet fuerit dominus eius portionis quae sibi fuerat assignata. Et infra: Clare supponit angelus, quod caliga & vestimenta assignata Petro, propria quo ad dominium erant Petri. quare videtur quod pecunia, panis, vinum, & alia ad vsu consumptibilis sibi distributa pro vita sustentatione assignata similiter eius essent. Ex his constat aperte, quod secundum istum quilibet apostolus post missionem spiritus S. fuit proprietarius habens in speciali dominium temporalium rerum: & ita secundum istos. quintae haeresis contrariae quintae veritati praedictae a Nicolao tertio diffinitae in ista constitutione quia vir sententialiter & vocaliter aperte diffinit. Secundo idem f. contra nonnullas ad fidem vel bonos mores spectantia in determinationibus. Rom. ecclesiae diffinita iste impugnat, diffinit, sic ostendit Nicolaus tertius in decretali Exiit loquens de dominio rerum, quibus Fratres Minores utuntur, diffinit in haec verba: Retentio dominii namque talium rerum, cum concessione vsus factae pauperibus, non est infructuosa dominio, tunc meritoria ad aeterna & pietatem in pauperum oportuna, quia tanto sibi ei, eatur ueluti, quanto ipsum mutatur temporalia in aeterna. Quib. verbis nihil nouum statuitur vel ordinatur ad diuinum, sed quod fit sententia in rotatione dominii aliorum rerum, cum concessione vsus factae pauperibus declaratur, quia [illegible, ~20 letters] quod talis retentio dominii, est domino vtilis & fructuosa: quia meritoria ad aeterna & professioni pauperum oportuna. illa autem quae sunt vtilia & fructuosa, meritoria ad aeterna & professioni pauperum oportuna, ad bonos mores non est dubium pertinere. ergo Nicolaus in verbis predictis veritatem pertinentem ad bonos mores asserit & diffinit. sed iste impugnatus contra istam veritatem manifeste diffinit asserens & determinans, quod tale dominium est inutile reputandum, sicut patet in constitutione Ad conditorem, in qua asserit tale dominium esse verbale, nudum & aenigmaticum, & in ista constitutione, quia vsu, sicut patet supra rap. 11. affirmat aperte, quod dominium omni temporali commodo denudatum est inutile reputandum. ex quibus sequitur evidenter, quod retentio talis dominii, cum quacunque vsus concessione non est fructuosa domino nec meritoria ad aeterna, nec professioni pauperum oportuna, nec per eam commutantur temporalia pro aeternis: & ita contra praedictam determinationem Romanae ecclesiae aperte diffinit.
units.tr: The fifth heresy contrary to the said truth, which he teaches, is that blessed Peter, and by the same reasoning any other apostle, was truly a proprietor, having after the mission of the Holy Spirit ownership and property of temporal things individually. For, as is clear above, chapter 9, he says: "It seems that it could also be said with probability that the distribution of goods consumable by use, which was made among the apostles and the other believers, as is said in Acts 2 and 4, each could be called proprietor and owner of the portion assigned to him." And below: "Since therefore it says that none of them had anything of his own, but it was divided to each as he had need, it plainly implies that what was divided to each was the proper possession of each one's use." And below: "It seems that each was the owner of the portion that had been assigned to him." And below: "The angel clearly implies that the sandal and garments assigned to Peter were Peter's own as to ownership. Hence it seems that money, bread, wine and other things consumable by use, distributed to him and assigned for the support of life, were similarly his." From these things it is plainly established that, according to him, each apostle after the mission of the Holy Spirit was a proprietor, having ownership of temporal things individually. And so, according to them, this fifth heresy is contrary to the fifth truth stated above, defined by Nicholas III in this constitution, because this man plainly defines it in judgment and aloud. Secondly, the same man in his determinations attacks and sets aside, contrary to some definitions of the Roman Church concerning faith or good morals. How Nicholas III defined it in the decretal Exiit, speaking of the ownership of things which the Friars Minor use, he defines in these words: "The retention of ownership of such things, together with the grant of use made to the poor, is not unfruitful to the owner; it is then meritorious for eternal life and useful to the poverty of the poor, since it is changed into eternal things to the extent that the temporal things are changed." In these words nothing new is established or ordained concerning divine matters, but what is declared is a judgment about the retention of ownership of other things, together with the grant of use made to the poor, namely that such retention of ownership is useful and fruitful to the owner, since it is meritorious for eternal life and useful to the profession of poverty. Now things that are useful and fruitful, meritorious for eternal life and useful to the profession of poverty, undoubtedly pertain to good morals. Therefore Nicholas, in the words quoted, asserts and defines a truth pertaining to good morals. But this man, who is attacked, plainly defines against that truth, asserting and determining that such ownership must be reckoned useless, as is clear in the constitution Ad conditorem, in which he asserts that such ownership is merely verbal, bare and enigmatic; and in this constitution, Quia vir, as is clear above, chapter 11, he plainly affirms that ownership stripped of every temporal advantage is to be reckoned useless. From these things it clearly follows that the retention of such ownership, even with any grant of use, is neither fruitful to the owner, nor meritorious for eternal life, nor useful to the profession of poverty, nor are temporal things exchanged thereby for eternal ones; and so he plainly defines against the said determination of the Roman Church.

units.la: Tertio sic arguunt. Nicolaus aperte diffinit in haec verba: Condecens fuit ei profiteri, quod Christus pauperem in tali paupertate se elegit omnium abdicare dominium, & rerum sibi concessarum necessario vsu fore contentam.
