Ex quibus evidenter colligitur, quod Fratres Minores abdicando omnium rerum dominium, paupertatem Christi sectantur: & per consequens Christus talem paupertatem, quae est per abdicationem rerum omnium, seruauit. eius iam contrarium iste aperte diffinit dicens: Christum nunquam fuisse pauperem per carentiam domini, cuiuscunque rei temporalis.
units.tr: Thirdly they argue thus. Nicholas plainly defines in these words: "It was fitting for him to profess that Christ chose such poverty, to renounce all ownership and to be content with the necessary use of the things given to him." From these words it is clearly gathered that the Friars Minor, by renouncing ownership of all things, follow the poverty of Christ; and consequently that Christ kept such poverty, which consists in the renunciation of all things. This he plainly contradicts, saying: "Christ was never poor through lack of ownership of any temporal thing whatever."

units.la: Quarto sic arguunt. Nicolaus tertius loquens de abdicatione Fratrum Minorum diffinit in haec verba: patet itaque sane intelligentibus ex praedictis regulam quo ad abdicationem huiusmodi non solum obseruabilem, possibilem & licitam, sed meritoriam & perfectam esse, & eo magis meritoriam, quo per ipsam professores ipsum magis a temporalibus propter Deum, sicut praedicitur, elongantur. Ex quibus verbis clare patet, quod per talem abdicationem Fratres efficiuntur pauperes: quia qui magis a temporalibus elongantur, pauperes sunt censendi. Si enim magis elongantur affectu, sunt pauperes affectu: si vero magis elongantur effectu seu actu, sunt pauperes effectu seu actu. sed iste expresse diffinit contrarium, sicut patet in constitutione Ad conditorem, & supra 6. 77. dicens, quod abdicatio talis dominii, quale abdicant Fratres Minores, non efficit pauperem non habentem, & ita, vt dicunt, liquet aperte, quod illa, quae Nicolaus tertius de paupertate Christi & apostolorum eius, ac etiam de paupertate regulae beati Francisci diffinit, iste reuocat diffiniendo contraria. Unde dicitur, quod fere quicquid dixit Nicolaus tertius in praedictis, iste destruit & annullat, sicut discurrendo per singula dicta ipsius & istius posset aperte probari: sed causa breuitatis omittuntur. Quinto sic arguunt: Plures Romani pontifices diffinierunt, quod omnium rerum temporalium abdicato dominio tam in speciali quam in communi contingit licite vsum rerum habere. Hoc ex verbis Greg. 9. in declaratione sua super regulam beati Francisci euidenter habetur, ait enim: Dicimus itaque, quod nec in communi, nec in speciali debent proprietatem habere: sed rerum, & librorum, & bonorum mobilium, quae licet habere, Ordo vsum habeat, ergo omni abdicato dominio contingit licite vsum habere. Innocentius etiam quartus, & Alexander quartus in suis declarationibus dicunt in haec verba: Dicimus quod cum in ipsa regula continetur expresse, quod Fratres nihil sibi appropriant, nec domum, nec locum, nec aliquam rem, nec in communi, nec in speciali debent proprietatem habere: sed domorum ac locorum, & vtensilium, & librorum, & eorum mobilium quae licet habere, Ordo vsum habeat.
units.tr: Fourthly they argue thus. Nicholas III, speaking of the renunciation of the Friars Minor, defines in these words: "It is therefore clear to those who understand rightly from what has been said, that the rule concerning such renunciation is not only observable, possible and lawful, but also meritorious and perfect, and all the more meritorious the more the professors are thereby removed from temporal things for God's sake, as has been said." From these words it is clearly evident that by such renunciation the friars become poor, because those who are more removed from temporal things are to be counted poor. For if they are more removed in affection, they are poor in affection; if indeed they are more removed in fact or act, they are poor in fact or act. But he expressly defines the contrary, as is clear in the constitution Ad conditorem and above, chapter 77, saying that the renunciation of such ownership as the Friars Minor renounce does not make a man poor who does not have. And so, as they say, it is plainly evident that what Nicholas III defined concerning the poverty of Christ and his apostles, and also concerning the poverty of the rule of blessed Francis, this man revokes by defining the contrary. Hence it is said that almost everything Nicholas III said in these matters this man destroys and annuls, as could be plainly proved by going through his statements and Nicholas's one by one; but for the sake of brevity they are omitted. Fifthly they argue thus: Several Roman pontiffs have defined that, with ownership of all temporal things renounced, whether individually or in common, it is lawful to have the use of things. This is plainly found from the words of Gregory IX in his declaration on the rule of blessed Francis; for he says: "We say therefore that they ought to have property neither in common nor individually, but of things and books and movable goods, which the Order may lawfully have, the Order has use." Therefore, with all ownership renounced, it is lawful to have use. Innocent IV also, and Alexander IV, in their declarations say in these words: "We say that since it is expressly contained in the rule itself that the friars appropriate nothing to themselves, neither house, nor place, nor any thing, and ought to have property neither in common nor individually, but the Order has the use of houses, places, utensils, books and movable goods which it may lawfully have."

units.la: Item Clemens quintus in declaratione sua, quae incipit Exiui, ait: Proinde quum vir sanctus paupertatis primissa in regula monachorum exprimens dixit in eadem, quod Fratres nihil sibi appropriant, nec domum, nec locum, nec aliquam rem: sed tanquam peregrini & aduenae in paupertate & humilitate domino famulantes vadant prolemessima cassidemur: sicque declaratum per nonnullos praedecessores Romanos pontifices hanc expropriationem intelligi debere, tam in speciali quam in communi, propter quod etiam omnium rerum concessarum, abdicatarum, & donatarum Fratribus, quas & quarum vsum fecerunt, sc. Ordini vel ipsis Fratribus licet habere proprietatem & dominium in sa & Romanam ecclesiam receptam, dimisso ipsa Fratribus inter tantum modo vsu facti simplicis.
units.tr: Likewise Clement V, in his declaration that begins Exiui, says: "Therefore, when the holy man, setting forth the first principle of poverty in the rule of the monks, said in the same place that the Brothers appropriate nothing to themselves, neither house, nor place, nor any thing, but go about as pilgrims and strangers serving the Lord in poverty and humility [...], it has been declared by several of the earlier Roman pontiffs that this renunciation is to be understood both in the particular and in the common sense. For this reason also, all the goods granted, renounced and given to the Brothers, which they have used, may be held in ownership and dominion by the Order or by the Brothers themselves, and received by the Holy Roman Church, the Brothers retaining only the simple use of the fact."

units.la: Ex his aliisque quam pluribus diffinitionib. Romanorum pontificum patenter habetur, quod omnium rerum temporalium abdicato dominio, tam in speciali quam in communi contingit licite rerum vsum habere. Sed contra istam veritatem iste impugnatus multipliciter diffiniuit: expresse determinans, quod multarum rerum scilicet vsu consumptibilium non potest vsus facti, nec etiam actus consumendi a proprietate seu dominio separari, sicut patet in constitutione Ad conditorem, & in ista constitutione quia vsus ergo &c. Item sicut patet supra c. 58. ipse expresse diffinit, quod vsus non potest concedi absque iure vtendi, & ideo non potest quis in huiusmodi rebus habere simplicem facti vsum, quod determinationi Clementis praedicti obuiat manifeste. Item in multis locis diffinit aperte, quod non contingit habere vsum rerum: quod tamen praedictis diffinitionibus Romanorum pontificum patenter repugnat. Vnde pes praemissa in illo capitulo, & in toto opere illo per alias allegationes dicunt isti patere indubie, quod iste impugnatus plura quae pertinent ad fidem, & bonos mores a Romanis pontificibus diffinita de facto reuocauit, & contraria diffiniuit.
units.tr: From these and many other definitions of the Roman pontiffs it is plainly established that, with ownership of all temporal goods renounced, both in the particular and in the common sense, it is lawful to have the use of things. But against this truth the one under attack has defined in many ways, expressly determining that for things consumed by use, a simple use of fact cannot be separated from ownership or dominion, nor even the act of consuming, as is clear from the constitution Ad conditorem and from this constitution, quia vsus ergo, etc. Likewise, as is clear above in chapter 58, he expressly defines that use cannot be granted without the right of using, and therefore that no one can have a simple use of fact in such things, which plainly contradicts the determination of the aforesaid Clement. Likewise, in many places he openly defines that it is not possible to have the use of things, which nevertheless plainly conflicts with the aforesaid definitions of the Roman pontiffs. Hence, from the premises in that chapter and in the whole of that work, and from other citations, they say it is beyond doubt that the one under attack has, in fact, revoked many things pertaining to faith and good morals that were defined by the Roman pontiffs, and has defined the contrary.

units.la: [Aperte iuxta morem suum mentitur.] Dicunt quod appellans non mentitur, cum veritatem supra probatam pronunciet. [Constitutio enim ipsa hoc non dicit: nec de hoc aliquam facit mentionem.] Contrarium est ostensum in principio istius capituli. [imo expresse negat, quod dicere Christum & apostolos habuisse in hoc quae habuerunt nisi simplicem facti vsum, nec ad fidem pertinet, nec ad mores, vt in 9. praeterea patet.] Hic modo innuit iste, quod appellans imposuerit sibi, quod Romanus pontifex in his quae ad fidem & mores pertinent, potest suorum praedecessorum diffinitiones & dicta reuocare, & contrarium statuere, solummodo propter verba, quae dicit in constitutione, quia quaerendum in isto praeterea dicant nobis asserores huius &c. quod non est verum, imo principaliter imposuit sibi, quod hoc dixerit propter hoc, quod propositionem aduersariorum in principio capituli recitatam. s. illud quod per clauem scientiae in fide ac moribus semel diffinierunt Romani pontifices non adeo immutabile perseuerat, quod illud successori non licet reuocare in dubium, nec contrarium affirmare: ipse dixit contrariam esse veritati, quia si ista est contraria veritati, sua contradictoria est verba, haec. s. illud quod per clauem scientiae in fide ac moribus semel diffinierunt rationi pontifices, non adeo immutabile perseuerat, quin illud successori licet reuocare in dubium & contrarium affirmare: & ita negando unam, concedit aliam. Sed forte dicet aliquis, si illud quod per clauem scientiae in fide ac moribus semel diffinierunt Romani &c. ergo quicquid iste diffinit, non licet in dubium reuocare. Ad hoc dicunt isti quod quicquid iste diffinivit per clauem scientiae, dum erat summus pontifex, non licet in dubium reuocare; sed quicquid diffinivit contra diffinitiones Romanorum pontificum, non diffinivit per clauem scientiae, sed diffinivit per haereticam prauitatem, clauem scientiae, quae est noticia legis diuinae, reiecta. & ideo dicunt, quod quamuis ista adiectio in propositione aduersariorum per clauem scientiae videatur superflua: quia sine ea propositio bene intellecta continet veritatem. tamen non est simpliciter superflua, sed sane intellecta denotat quod quicquid diffinierunt Romani pontifices conformiter doctrinae ecclesiae, non debet in dubium reuocari, nec contrarium affirmari. Unde potest dici, quod isti aduersarii clauem scientiae vocant noticiam legis diuinae & doctrinae vniuersalis ecclesiae. [Vbi legunt quod ad fidem vel mores pertinet Christum & apostolos non habuisse in hoc quae habuerunt nisi simplicem vsum facti.] Hic notat isti duo, quorum primum est, quod aliquid pertinere ad fidem potest dupliciter intelligi. aliquid enim pertinet ad fidem sicut per fidem credendum: aliquid vero pertinet ad fidem, sicut per fidem negandum. sic enim eadem est scientia contrariorum, & oppositorum eadem est disciplina: ita ad fidem opposita pertinere noscuntur, quia sicut ad fidelem spectat per fidem credere catholicam veritatem, ita ad ipsum spectat negare haereticam prauitatem. Secundo notant, quod licet sub his verbis Christus & apostoli non habuerunt in his, quae habuerunt, nisi simplicem vsum facti, non legatur in scriptura diuina, tamen istam sententiam accipiunt a scriptura diuina ex doctrina ecclesiae, sicut superius in pluribus capitulis est ostensum, quae videtur superfluum replicare. [Profecto directe hoc ad fidem non pertinet, cum de hoc articulus non sit aliquis nec sub quo valeat comprehendi, vt patet ex symbolis in quibus articuli fidei continentur.] Hic impugnatores dicunt, quod veritas comprehenditur sub isto articulo fidei: Sanctam ecclesiam catholicam: quia sub illo articulo comprehenditur, quicquid per sanctam ecclesiam catholicam praedicatur, tenetur & docetur. Ecclesia autem catholica fundans se in scriptura diuina, tenet quod Christus & apostoli omne ius humanum, quo valebant in iudicio litigare, proprium alicui maiori eorum, vel etiam toti collegio speciali penitus reliquerunt, vsum rerum necessarium minime abdicando. Quod intelligunt isti, cum dicunt, quod non habuerunt nisi simplicem facti vsum [nec etiam reductiue quasi hoc sacra scriptura continet] dicit, quod hoc sacra scriptura continet, quamuis non sub verbis istis. Et si quaeratur, vbi continet hoc sacra scriptura? dicunt, quod licet hoc euidenter pateat ex multis capitulis istius operis, tamen breuissime recapitulando aliqua de capitulis dicunt, quod hoc sacra scriptura continet, vbi tradit Christum fecisse quae docuit, & vbi docuit apostolos reliquere omnia in temporalibus, quae non sunt necessaria: & vbi docuit adolescentem omnia vendere & dare pauperibus: quod docendo docuit relinquere omne ius in temporalibus quo quis valet in iudicio litigare: & vbi scriptura tradit apostolos omnia reliquisse, sicut Christus docuerat. Ex illis enim locis colligitur, quod Christus & apostoli omne ius, quo valerent in iudicio litigare in temporalibus reliquerunt. Ex aliis autem locis habetur aperte, quod temporalibus rebus vtebantur: ergo ex diuersis locis scripturae colligitur, quod non habuerunt in his, quae habuerunt, nisi simplicem facti vsum, hoc est vtebantur temporalibus absque omni iure, quo valebat nomine proprio vel nomine sui collegii speciali pro rebus eisdem in iudicio litigare [hoc enim in scriptura sacra non poterit: sed contrarium reperiri] hoc dicunt esse multiplicuter reprobatum [quin contra ordinata per summos pontifices circa talia liceat successoribus aliquid ordinare.] Dicunt isti, quod summi pontifices neque de paupertate Christi & apostolorum eius, neque de rebus quas habuerunt, neque de simplici vsu facti ipsorum aliquid vnquam ordinauerunt, sed veritatem de praedictis docuerunt, & ipsam esse tenendam diffinierunt & ideo non licuit isti nec ordinando nec diffiniendo nec docendo aliquid contrarium penitus attentare. Quia licet multa ordinata per summos pontifices, quae Fratres Minores seruare tenentur, possit Romanus pontifex mutare: de vita tamen Christi & apostolorum eius nihil potest penitus mutare, nec licet sibi aliter docere de vita eorum, quod sancti patres hactenus docuerunt. [quod Nicolaus tertius praefatus expresse in sua declaratione inserit, vt superius plenius continetur] nusquam legitur, quod Nicolaus tertius vnquam aliter docuerit vel diffinierit de vita Christi & apostolorum eius, quam praedecessores sui. effigie fecimus, seu appendi, ut sit iuxta nostrum desiderium ad communem deducta noticiam haereticorum doctrina praedicta pestifera sic suo praefocetur in ortu, quod nequaquam eiusdem virus nequiter ad inficiendum simplices viterius diffundatur. Datum Avinione. 16. Calend. Decembris, pontificatus nostri anno 9.
units.tr: [He lies openly, as is his custom.] They say that the appellant does not lie, since he asserts the truth proved above. [The constitution itself does not say this, nor does it make any mention of it.] The contrary has been shown at the beginning of this chapter, [indeed it expressly denies that to say Christ and the apostles had in these matters anything but the simple use of fact is related to faith or to morals, as is plain in the ninth chapter following.] Here he now hints that the appellant has imputed to him that the Roman pontiff, in matters that pertain to faith and morals, may revoke the definitions and sayings of his predecessors and establish the contrary, solely on account of the words he uses in the constitution, because it must be asked in this matter further, say the defenders of this man, etc. This is not true. Rather, he principally charged him with having said this because of the proposition of the opponents recited at the beginning of the chapter, namely that what the Roman pontiffs have once defined through the key of knowledge in faith and morals does not remain so unchangeable that it is not permitted to a successor to call it into doubt or to affirm the contrary. He said that this is contrary to the truth, because if this is contrary to the truth, its contradictory is these words: that what the Roman pontiffs have once defined through the key of knowledge in faith and morals does remain so unchangeable that it is not permitted to a successor to call it into doubt and affirm the contrary. Thus by denying the one, he concedes the other. But perhaps someone will say: if what the Romans have once defined through the key of knowledge in faith and morals, etc., then whatever this man defines may not be called into doubt. To this these men reply that whatever he defined through the key of knowledge while he was supreme pontiff may not be called into doubt; but whatever he defined against the definitions of the Roman pontiffs he did not define through the key of knowledge, but defined through heretical depravity, the key of knowledge, which is the knowledge of divine law, having been rejected. And so they say that although that addition in the opponents' proposition, "through the key of knowledge," seems superfluous, since without it the proposition, rightly understood, contains the truth, yet it is not simply superfluous; rightly understood, it signifies that whatever the Roman pontiffs have defined in conformity with the doctrine of the Church must not be called into doubt or the contrary affirmed. Hence it can be said that these opponents call the key of knowledge the knowledge of divine law and the doctrine of the universal Church. [Where they read that Christ and the apostles did not have in these matters which they had anything but the simple use of fact, as pertaining to faith or morals.] Here he notes two things. The first is that something may pertain to faith in two ways. For something pertains to faith as what is to be believed through faith; but something pertains to faith as what is to be denied through faith. Thus the knowledge of contraries is one and the same, and the discipline of opposites is one and the same; so opposites are known to pertain to faith, because just as it belongs to the faithful to believe the Catholic truth through faith, so it belongs to them to deny heretical depravity. Second, they note that although under these words, "Christ and the apostles did not have in these things which they had anything but the simple use of fact," is not read in divine Scripture, yet they derive this opinion from divine Scripture through the doctrine of the Church, as was shown above in several chapters, which seems superfluous to repeat. [Indeed, this does not directly pertain to faith, since there is no article about it, nor one under which it can be comprehended, as is clear from the creeds in which the articles of faith are contained.] Here the opponents say that the truth is comprehended under this article of faith: "the holy Catholic Church," because under that article is comprehended whatever is preached, held and taught through the holy Catholic Church. The Catholic Church, however, grounding itself on divine Scripture, holds that Christ and the apostles entirely left to some greater one of them, or even to the whole special college, every human right by which they were able to litigate in judgment, without at all renouncing the necessary use of things. What these men mean when they say that they had only the simple use of fact [nor indeed does holy Scripture contain this by implication] says that holy Scripture contains this, though not under these words. And if it is asked where holy Scripture contains this, they say that although this is plainly evident from many chapters of this work, yet, recapitulating very briefly, some of the chapters they cite say that holy Scripture contains this: where it relates that Christ did what he taught, and where he taught the apostles to leave all temporal things that are not necessary; and where he taught the young man to sell everything and give to the poor, which, by teaching, he taught them to leave every right in temporal matters by which one may litigate in judgment; and where Scripture relates that the apostles left everything, as Christ had taught. For from those passages it is gathered that Christ and the apostles left every right by which they could litigate in judgment concerning temporal things. From other passages, however, it is plainly held that they used temporal things. Therefore from diverse places of Scripture it is gathered that they had in those things which they had only the simple use of fact, that is, they used temporal things without any right by which they could litigate in judgment, in their own name or in the name of their special college, concerning those same things [for this cannot be found in holy Scripture, but the contrary is found]. This they say has been repeatedly rejected [nor is it permitted to successors to ordain anything about such matters contrary to what has been ordained by the supreme pontiffs.] These men say that the supreme pontiffs have never ordained anything either about the poverty of Christ and his apostles, or about the things they had, or about their simple use of fact, but have taught the truth about these matters, and have defined that it is to be held; and therefore it was not permitted to this man to attempt anything contrary, either by ordaining, defining or teaching. For although the Roman pontiff may change many ordinances made by the supreme pontiffs, which the Friars Minor are bound to observe, yet he can in no way change anything about the life of Christ and his apostles, nor is it permitted to him to teach about their life otherwise than the holy Fathers have taught hitherto. [which Nicholas III, mentioned above, expressly inserts in his declaration, as is more fully contained above] Nowhere is it read that Nicholas III ever taught or defined otherwise about the life of Christ and his apostles than his predecessors did. We have had it made, or appended, so that, brought to the common knowledge of the heretics, the aforesaid pestiferous doctrine may be so choked in its birth that the poison of the same may not be wickedly spread further to infect the simple. Given at Avignon, the 16th day before the Calends of December, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

units.la: Finito tractatu hic conclusio totius constitutionis subiungitur. In hac enim parte impugnatus ostendit, quare constitutionem fecerit ante dictam, ac qualiter ipsam duxerit promulgandam.
units.tr: Having finished the treatment, the conclusion of the whole constitution is added here. In this part the author who is being attacked shows why he issued the aforementioned constitution and how he chose to publish it.

units.la: Sed isti impugnatores cum in parte praecedenti, ut asserunt, sufficienter, probauerint, istam constitutionem esse haereticalem, hic per verba praemissa volunt aperte ostendere, quod conditor constitutionis eiusdem est pertinax & haereticus reputandus. Saepe enim doctrina alicuius est haeretica censenda, quamuis auctor eiusdem inter haereticos sit minime computandus. Ad cuius evidentiam dicunt esse sciendum: quod si quis errauerit circa veritatem catholicam, quam credere explicite non tenetur: si paratus est corrigi, non est haereticus reputandus. Sed si non est paratus corrigi, pertinax & haereticus est censendus. Unde August. ut habetur 24. q. 3. ca. dixit apostolus, ait: qui sententiam suam quamuis falsam ac perversam nulla pertinaciter animositate defendunt, praesertim quum non audacia sua praesumptionis peperierunt, sed a seductis atque in errorem lapsis parentibus acceperunt, quaerunt autem cauta sollicitudine veritatem, corrigi parati cum inuenerint, nequaquam sunt inter haereticos deputandi.
units.tr: But these opponents, having (as they claim) sufficiently proved in the preceding part that this constitution is heretical, now wish to show clearly by the words quoted above that its author must be regarded as obstinate and a heretic. For the teaching of a person is often to be judged heretical even though its author is by no means to be counted among the heretics. To make this clear, they say that the following must be known: if someone has erred concerning a Catholic truth, which he is not bound to believe explicitly, then, if he is ready to be corrected, he is not to be regarded as a heretic. But if he is not ready to be corrected, he is to be judged obstinate and a heretic. Hence Augustine, as it is found in 24 q. 3 c. (the chapter beginning with the words of the Apostle), says: "Those who defend their opinion, however false and perverse, with no obstinate animosity, especially since they did not bring it forth from their own presumptuous audacity but received it from parents who were led astray and had fallen into error, and who seek the truth with careful diligence, and are ready to be corrected when they have found it, are by no means to be counted among the heretics."

units.la: Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod qui parati sunt corrigi, non sunt haeretici deputandi. Sed si erant, & non quaerunt cauta sollicitudine veritatem, nec parati sunt corrigi, pro haereticis sunt habendi. Hinc Aug contra Manicheos, ut habetur eisdem causa & quaestione c. 1. qui in ecclesia, ait: qui in ecclesia Christi morbidum aliquid prauum, quid sapiunt, si correcti ut sanum rectumque, sapiunt resistunt contumaciter suaque pestifera ac mortifera dogmata emendare nolunt, sed defensarepter, fiunt haeretici sunt. Ex his verbis patet, quod habetur, quicunque aliquid contra scripturam, diuinam aut doctrinam vniuersalis ecclesiae tenuerit, nec paratus est emendare, est haereticus reputandus. Nam secundum beatum Augustinum qui morbidum aliquid prauumque sapiunt, nec emendare volunt, sunt haeretici reputandi. Sed omne falsum contrarium cuicunque contento & asserto in scriptura diuina, vel doctrina vniuersalis ecclesiae, est morbidum atque prauum. Ergo omnis sapiens tale falsum, si non est paratus se emendare, est inter haereticos numerandus. Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod secundum hoc non esset differentia inter tenentem aut sapientem haeresim iam damnatam, & inter sapientem haeresim non damnatam: quia aequaliter esset unus haereticus, sicut alius. Ad hoc dicunt nonnulli istorum, quod omnis haeresis est damnata vel explicite vel implicite. & ideo quantum ad hoc, quod aliquis in rei veritate sit haereticus, non refert an sapiat pertinaciter haeresim damnatam explicite, vel haeresim damnatam implicite: quia cuique haeresi damnatae explicite vel implicite pertinaciter adhaereat, vere apud Deum inter haereticos numeratur. Verumtamen quantum ad modum conuincendi aliquem esse haereticum in foro ecclesiae, & quantum ad formam procedendi contra haereticum est magna differentia attendenda inter sapientem seu tenentem haeresim damnatam explicite vel solum implicite: quia qui tenet haeresim damnatam explicite, si ostensa sibi damnatione ab vniversali ecclesia approbata se non statim correxerit, sed adhuc defensare praesumpserit, est haereticus reputandus. Qui vero tenet haeresim damnatam solum implicite, qualis est omnis falsitas doctrinae scripturae diuinae & ecclesiae vniuersalis qualitercunque repugnans, sed latenter tenetur talem haeresim reuocare, si sibi per scripturam sacram vel doctrinam vniuersalis ecclesiae ostensum fuerit euidenter, quod error suus scripturae sacrae aut doctrinae vniuersalis ecclesiae aduersatur. Iterum, contra tenentem haeresim damnatam explicite procedere potest quilibet episcopus catholicus, & etiam quilibet inquisitor haereticae prauitatis, si aliquid canonicum non obsistat. Contra tenentem autem haeresim damnatam implicite solum modo nullus episcopus inferior summo pontifice, nec aliquis inquisitor prauitatis haereticae iudicialiter potest procedere: quia non potest ipsum tanquam haereticum condemnare. Quod taliratione probatur. Qui non habet auctoritatem nec potestatem determinandi quaestionem motam de fide, non potest pro tali quaestione aliquem tanquam haereticum condemnare. Haec patens est: quia nullus debet tanquam haereticus condemnari, nisi pro haeresi manifesta. Sed nullus inferior summo pontifice potest quaestionem motam de fide terminare: teste Innocentio Papa, qui, ut habetur 24. q. 1. c. quotiens, ait: Quotiens fidei ratio ventilatur, arbitror omnes fratres & coepiscopos non nisi ad Petrum, id est, sui nominis & honoris auctoritatem referre debere. Vbi Glossa dicit, aliud est quaestionem de fide motam terminare, quod nulli praeterquam Romanae sedi permittitur, sicut hoc dicitur: aliud est ipsam sine diffinitione ventilare, quod patriarchae facere possunt. & infra Glossa obiiciens super verbo nisi ad Petrum, ait: Videtur contra extra de haereticis, ad abolendam. Nam ibi innuitur quod illi vitandi sunt tanquam haeretici, quos episcopi vitandos dixerunt. & respondens dicit sic: sed dicit quod illud intelligendum est, quando tale quid dicunt, quod certum est esse haeresim, hoc vero vbi dubium est. Ex his patet er habetur, quod nullus inferior Romano pontifice potest quaestionem motam de fide catholica determinare. quod Innocentius tertius vt habetur extra de baptismo & eius effectu, c. maiores, asserit manifeste dicens: Maiores ecclesiae causas praesertim articulos fidei continentes ad Petri sedem referendas intelligit, &c. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod quaestionem motam de fide, quia omnis quaestio mota de fide continget saltem illum articulum fidei: Sanctam ecclesiam catholicam: ad nullum inferiorem successorem B. Petri pertinet terminare. & ita contra tenentem haeresim damnatam, duntaxat implicite, nullus inferior vero Papa debet procedere.
units.tr: From these words it follows that those who are ready to be corrected are not to be counted as heretics. But if they were in error, and do not seek the truth with careful diligence, and are not ready to be corrected, they are to be held as heretics. Hence Augustine, against the Manichaeans, as found in the same cause and question, c. 1, says of those who are in the Church of Christ: "Those who hold some morbid and depraved opinion in the Church of Christ, if, when corrected, they stubbornly resist and refuse to amend their pestilent and deadly dogmas, but defend them obstinately, they become heretics." From these words it is clear, as it is held, that whoever holds anything contrary to divine Scripture or to the teaching of the universal Church, and is not ready to amend it, is to be regarded as a heretic. For according to the blessed Augustine, those who hold something morbid and depraved, and are unwilling to amend it, are to be regarded as heretics. But every falsehood contrary to anything contained and asserted in divine Scripture or in the teaching of the universal Church is morbid and depraved. Therefore everyone who holds such a falsehood, if he is not ready to amend himself, is to be numbered among the heretics. But perhaps someone will say that, on this view, there would be no difference between one who holds or favours a heresy already condemned and one who favours a heresy not yet condemned, since each would equally be a heretic. To this some of these men reply that every heresy has been condemned either explicitly or implicitly. Therefore, as far as the fact that someone is in truth a heretic goes, it makes no difference whether he obstinately favours a heresy condemned explicitly or one condemned implicitly, since whoever obstinately adheres to any heresy condemned explicitly or implicitly is truly counted among the heretics before God. Nevertheless, as regards the manner of convicting someone of being a heretic in the forum of the Church, and as regards the form of proceeding against a heretic, a great difference must be observed between one who holds a heresy condemned explicitly and one who holds one condemned only implicitly. For whoever holds a heresy condemned explicitly, if, once the condemnation approved by the universal Church has been shown to him, he does not at once correct himself but presumes to go on defending it, is to be regarded as a heretic. But whoever holds a heresy condemned only implicitly, such as every falsehood in any way opposed to the teaching of divine Scripture and of the universal Church, is secretly bound to retract such a heresy if it has been clearly shown to him, through holy Scripture or the teaching of the universal Church, that his error is contrary to Scripture or to the teaching of the universal Church. Again, against one who holds a heresy condemned explicitly, any Catholic bishop may proceed, and indeed any inquisitor of heretical depravity, provided no canonical impediment stands in the way. But against one who holds a heresy condemned only implicitly, no bishop inferior to the supreme pontiff, nor any inquisitor of heretical depravity, can proceed judicially, because he cannot condemn him as a heretic. This is proved by the following reasoning. He who does not have the authority or power to determine a question raised concerning the faith cannot condemn anyone as a heretic on account of such a question. This is clear, because no one ought to be condemned as a heretic except for manifest heresy. But no one inferior to the supreme pontiff can settle a question raised concerning the faith; this is attested by Pope Innocent, who, as found in 24 q. 1 c. Quotiens, says: "Whenever a question of faith is discussed, I judge that all brothers and fellow bishops ought to refer it only to Peter, that is, to the authority of his name and honour." Where the Gloss says: "It is one thing to settle a question raised concerning the faith, which is permitted to no one except the Roman see, as this text says; it is another to debate it without definitive decision, which patriarchs may do." And below, the Gloss, raising an objection on the words nisi ad Petrum, says: "It seems to contradict Extra, de haereticis, Ad abolendam, for there it is implied that those are to be avoided as heretics whom bishops have declared to be avoided." And in replying it says: "But that is to be understood as applying when they say something that is certainly heresy, whereas that is where there is doubt." From these things it is clear, as it is held, that no one inferior to the Roman pontiff can determine a question raised concerning the Catholic faith. Innocent III, as found in Extra, de baptismo et eius effectu, c. Maiores, asserts this plainly, saying: "He understands that the greater causes of the Church, especially those containing articles of faith, are to be referred to the see of Peter, etc." From these words it is clear that a question raised concerning the faith, since every such question concerns at least that article of faith, Holy Catholic Church, does not belong to any inferior successor of blessed Peter to settle. And so, against one who holds a heresy condemned only implicitly, no one inferior to the Pope ought to proceed.

units.la: Sed forte quaeret aliquis, quae sunt haereses damnatae solum implicite, & quae sunt haereses damnatae explicite. Ad istius quaestionis intelligentiam dicunt quidam impugnantium praedictorum esse notandum: quod approbatio veritatis est reprobatio contrariae falsitatis, & ideo aliqua veritate tanquam catholica approbata, eo ipso haeresis contraria intelligitur condemnata, propter quod quidam dicunt, quod ad hoc, quod aliqua haeresis debeat reputari damnata explicite vel implicite, non refert an ipsa damnetur, vel veritas catholica contraria approbetur. Item dicunt isti, quod damnatio falsitatis, & similiter approbatio veritatis, quaedam est specialis, quaedam est generalis, & quaedam est generalissima. Specialis approbatio & specialis damnatio est, quando de veritate catholica vel haeresi contraria expressa fit mentio. Sic damnata est haeresis Ariana, sic approbata est veritas de processione Spiritus sancti a Patre & Filio. Damnatio vel approbatio generalis est, quando aliqua veritas vel haeresis continetur explicite in aliquo toto speciali, de quo toto in approbatione vel damnatione expressa fit mentio. Sic approbatae sunt generaliter omnes veritates in scriptura divina contentae: & omnes haereses eis patenter omnibus advertentes sunt damnatae. Alia est approbatio & similiter damnatio generalissima, in qua, sc. de nullo toto speciali fit mentio; sed talis solummodo continetur sententia: Approbamus omnem catholicam veritatem, & damnamus omnem haereticam pravitatem. & talis est damnatio concilii generalis: extra de haereticis c. Excommunicamus: ubi sic dicitur: excommunicamus & anathematizamus omnem haeresim extollentem se &c. ubi de nulla scriptura speciali fit mentio. Per praedicta respondent isti ad propositam quaestionem dicentes: quod istae haereses debent reputari damnatae explicite, quae damnatae sunt damnatione speciali & generali: vel quae patenter omnibus intelligentibus sine subtili declaratione, veritatibus catholicis approbatis approbatione speciali vel generali contrariantur. Illae autem haereses, quae solummodo damnatae sunt damnatione generalissima vel solum latenter, ita quod tantum per subtilem considerationem sciri potest, quod contrariantur veritatibus catholicis approbatis approbatione speciali vel generali non explicite, sed solum implicite sunt damnatae. Ex his patet, quod omnis error, qui contradicit aperte scripturae divinae, vel determinationi ab universali ecclesia approbatae, est haeresis damnata explicite: & quam cito constaret aliquem tali errori pertinaciter adhaerere esset haereticus reputandus: ac contra talem posset Diocesanus tanquam contra haereticum manifestum procedere. Haereses autem, quae non contradicunt aperte nec scripturae divinae nec determinationi seu explicite doctrinae universalis ecclesiae, licet veraciter aduersetur, sed quae sic contrariantur, quod absque subtili & magis consideratione scire non possunt, sunt haereses tantum implicite condemnatae. & ideo quamvis quicunque tali haeresi pertinaciter adhaeserit, sit verus haereticus, liceatque omni scienti ipsum tali errori pertinaciter adhaerere, eundem haereticum reputare: nulli tamen inferiori summo pontifice licet ipsum quantumcunque fuerit pertinax, tanquam haereticum iudicialiter condemnare: quia causa huiusmodi ad nullum inferiorem Romano episcopo noscitur pertinere. Si tamen per universalem ecclesiam fuerit talis haeresis explicite condemnata, vel contradictoria veritas explicite approbata: ex tunc cuilibet episcopo licebit contra tali haeresi pertinaciter adhaerentem procedere iuxta canonicas sanctiones.
units.tr: But perhaps someone will ask which heresies are condemned only implicitly and which are condemned explicitly. To understand this question, some of the aforementioned opponents say that the following must be noted: the approval of a truth is the rejection of the contrary falsehood, and so, when some truth has been approved as Catholic, the contrary heresy is thereby understood to be condemned. For this reason some say that, for a heresy to be reckoned as condemned explicitly or implicitly, it makes no difference whether the heresy itself is condemned or the contrary Catholic truth is approved. These men also say that the condemnation of falsehood, and likewise the approval of truth, is of three kinds: special, general, and most general. A special approval and special condemnation occurs when a Catholic truth or its contrary heresy is expressly mentioned. Thus the Arian heresy was condemned, and thus the truth about the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son was approved. A general approval or condemnation occurs when some truth or heresy is contained explicitly within some whole of a special kind, and that whole is expressly mentioned in the approval or condemnation. Thus all the truths contained in divine Scripture have been approved in general, and all heresies clearly opposed to any of them have been condemned. The third kind, a most general approval and condemnation, is one in which no special whole is mentioned at all, but only a sentence such as this is contained: "We approve every Catholic truth and we condemn every heretical depravity." Such is the condemnation of a general council: Extra, de haereticis, c. Excommunicamus, where it is said: "We excommunicate and anathematize every heresy that exalts itself, etc.", where no particular Scripture is mentioned. In light of these things, these men answer the question proposed, saying: those heresies are to be reckoned as condemned explicitly which have been condemned by a special or general condemnation, or which clearly oppose Catholic truths approved by a special or general approval, so that anyone who understands can see it without subtle explanation. But those heresies which have been condemned only by a most general condemnation, or only secretly, so that it can be known only through subtle consideration that they oppose Catholic truths approved by a special or general approval, not explicitly but only implicitly, are condemned implicitly. Hence it is clear that every error which openly contradicts divine Scripture, or a determination approved by the universal Church, is an explicitly condemned heresy; and as soon as it is established that someone obstinately adheres to such an error, he is to be regarded as a heretic, and a diocesan may proceed against him as against a manifest heretic. But heresies which do not openly contradict either divine Scripture or a determination or explicit teaching of the universal Church, even though they truly oppose it, but which are so opposed that they cannot be recognized without subtle and fuller consideration, are heresies condemned only implicitly. Therefore, although whoever obstinately adheres to such a heresy is a true heretic, and although any person who knows of it may lawfully regard him as a heretic for obstinately adhering to such error, nevertheless no one inferior to the supreme pontiff may judicially condemn him as a heretic, however obstinate he may be, because a case of this kind is known not to belong to any bishop inferior to the Roman bishop. If, however, such a heresy has been explicitly condemned by the universal Church, or the contrary truth explicitly approved, then from that point on any bishop may proceed against one who obstinately adheres to that heresy, in accordance with the canonical sanctions.

units.la: His visis conantur isti impugnatores probare, quod iste impugnatus per verba propria in principio illius capituli recitata convincitur esse haereticus manifestus. Unde sic arguunt: qui gerens se pro Papa aliquam haeresim solenniter ex ultima deliberatione diffinit esse tenendam est pertinax: & per consequens haereticus reputandus. Sed iste impugnatus totam scripturam praecedentem multas haereses continentem solenniter ex ultima deliberatione diffiniuit esse tenendam; quia, sicut in principio istius capituli patet, totam scripturam praecedentem bulla sua munivit; & per consequens solenniter ex ultima deliberatione totam scripturam istam diffiniuit esse tenendam. Ergo est pertinax, & per consequens haereticus reputandus. Maior est manifesta tum quia talis non est paratus corrigi, tum quia talis in haeresi ultimate se firmavit: tum quia talis non quaerit cauta sollicitudine veritatem, sed de veritate informari renuit impudenter, tum quia secundum Isidorum in libro Etymologiarum pertinax dicitur aliquis qui est impudenter tenax. Constat autem quod qui haeresim solenniter sub bulla diffinit, est impudenter tenax. Ergo est pertinax, & per consequens haereticus reputandus. Tum quia qui nimis in aliqua erronea assertione persistit, aut perseverans, seu constans aut pertinax est censendus. Sed qui solenniter ex ultima deliberatione sub bulla aliquam haeresim diffiniuit esse tenendam, nimis in assertione erronea persistit. Ergo velest perseverans seu constans, aut pertinax reputandus. Sed non est perseverans nec constans, quia perseverantia est virtus, & similiter constantia. Ergo talis pertinax; & per consequens haereticus est censendus. Praeter hanc rationem, quae ex verbis istius impugnari assumitur, isti alias rationes ex factis & gestis ipsius acceptas adducunt ad probandum, quod sit inter haereticos computandus. Quarum prima est haec: qui minis, poenis, iuramentis & praeceptis cogit alios ad suas haereses pertinaciter defendendas, non solum haereticus, sed etiam haeresiarcha merito est censendus. Cum etiam secundum sacros canones, qui errori consentit, est similiter modo culpabilis reputandus, ut habetur. II. q. 3. c. qui consentit, & extra de haereticis qui alios. & 83. dist. error. Sed iste impugnatus omnes haereses in ista constitutione quia vir & in constitutionibus Ad conditorem; & Cum inter, &c. & quia quaerundam; cogit alios minis, poenis, iuramentis & praeceptis defendere. Unde non
units.tr: Having seen these points, these opponents try to prove that the man they attack is convicted, by his own words recited at the beginning of that chapter, of being a manifest heretic. They argue thus: whoever, claiming to act for the Pope, solemnly and after final deliberation defines some heresy to be held is obstinate, and consequently must be regarded as a heretic. But this man, after final deliberation, solemnly defined that the whole preceding writing, which contains many heresies, is to be held. For, as is plain at the beginning of this chapter, he fortified the whole preceding writing with his bull, and so solemnly and after final deliberation he defined that this whole writing is to be held. Therefore he is obstinate, and consequently must be regarded as a heretic. The major premise is evident, both because such a man is not ready to be corrected, and because he has confirmed himself finally in heresy, and because he does not seek the truth with careful diligence but shamelessly refuses to be informed about it, and because, according to Isidore in the Etymologies, someone is called obstinate who clings to his view shamelessly. Now it is clear that whoever solemnly defines a heresy under a bull is shamelessly tenacious. Therefore he is obstinate, and consequently must be regarded as a heretic. Again, whoever persists too much in some erroneous assertion is to be judged persevering, steadfast or obstinate. But whoever solemnly, after final deliberation and under a bull, defines some heresy to be held, persists too much in an erroneous assertion. Therefore he must be judged persevering, steadfast or obstinate. But he is neither persevering nor steadfast, since perseverance is a virtue, and likewise steadfastness. Therefore he is to be judged obstinate, and consequently a heretic. Besides this argument, which is taken from the man's own words, these opponents bring forward other arguments, drawn from his deeds and actions, to prove that he is to be counted among the heretics. The first of these is this: whoever compels others by threats, penalties, oaths and commands to defend their heresies obstinately is rightly to be judged not only a heretic but even a ringleader of heretics. For according to the sacred canons, whoever consents to error is likewise to be regarded as guilty, as is held in II, q. 3, c. Qui consentit, and in extra de haereticis, Qui alios, and in dist. 83, error. But this man compels others, by threats, penalties, oaths and commands, to defend all the heresies in that constitution, Quia vir, and in the constitutions Ad conditorem, and Cum inter, and Quia quaedam. Hence not

units.la: {y} Note: the text is printed in two columns; a page number and running head appear at top. Unde non solum haereticus, sed etiam haeresiarcha merito est censendus. maiorem isti probant in aliis allegationibus, multis rationibus, quas hic causa brevitatis omitto. minor quo ad aliquas eius partes ex constitutionibus suis colligitur evidenter: cum nonnullis poenam rebellionis & contumaciae affirmantibus contrarium illius, quod affirmat, imponat: nonnullosque mandet haereticorum poena puniri. Quantum autem ad istam partem de iuramentis, eadem minor ex gestis ipsius aperte probatur, cum compellat omnes magistrandos Patrius iurare, quod suas constitutiones tanquam catholicas in perpetuum observabunt.
units.tr: Hence he is rightly to be judged not only a heretic but even a ringleader of heretics. These opponents prove the major premise in their other allegations, by many arguments, which for brevity I omit here. The minor premise, as regards some of its parts, is evidently gathered from his constitutions, since he imposes the penalty of rebellion and contumacy on some who affirm the contrary of what he affirms, and orders some to be punished as heretics. As for that part concerning oaths, the same minor premise is plainly proved from his own deeds, since he compels all those about to take their degrees (magistrandi) to swear that they will observe his constitutions as Catholic for ever. Patrius.

units.la: Secunda ratio est haec. qui cogit aliquos veritatem catholicam abiurare, est veritatis catholicae pertinax impugnator: & per consequens inter haereticos computandus: quia si dubius in fide, infidelis est, ut habetur extra de haereticis. 1. multo fortius veritatis catholicae pertinax impugnator est haereticus reputandus: & per consequens qui cogit alios veritatem catholicam abiurare, est haereticus iudicandus. Sed iste impugnatus cogit Christianos veritatem catholicam abiurare, cum cogat multos veritatem declaratam per Nicolaum tertium de paupertate Christi abiurare. ergo debet inter haereticos computari.
units.tr: The second argument is this. Whoever compels some to abjure the Catholic truth is an obstinate opponent of the Catholic truth, and consequently is to be counted among the heretics, since, if one who doubts in the faith is an unbeliever, as is held in extra de haereticis, c. 1, much more is an obstinate opponent of the Catholic truth to be regarded as a heretic. And consequently whoever compels others to abjure the Catholic truth is to be judged a heretic. But this man compels Christians to abjure the Catholic truth, since he compels many to abjure the truth declared by Nicholas III concerning the poverty of Christ. Therefore he ought to be counted among the heretics.

units.la: Tertia ratio est haec. errans in fide si emendationi & correctioni illorum quorum interest subiicere se recusat, est haereticus reputandus. hoc patet: quia talis non est paratus corrigi. qui autem errat in fide, & non est paratus corrigi, est haereticus reputandus, sicut per doctrinam sanctorum & sacros canones posset aperte probari. Sed iste impugnatus errat in fide, sicut per totam istam constitutionem est ostensum, & recusat se subiicere correctioni & emendationi illorum, quorum interest. quia sicut per sacros canones isti impugnatores in libris suis multipliciter probant, ad concilium generale pertinet etiam Papam in his, quae fidei sunt, corrigere & emendare. Ipse autem non permittit generale concilium congregari: & ita se subiicere correctioni & emendationi illorum quorum interest, recusat. ergo haereticus est censendus.
units.tr: The third argument is this. Whoever in matters of faith refuses to submit himself to the correction and amendment of those whom it concerns is to be regarded as a heretic. This is clear, because such a man is not ready to be corrected. And whoever errs in faith and is not ready to be corrected is to be regarded as a heretic, as could be clearly proved from the teaching of the saints and the sacred canons. But this man errs in faith, as is shown by this whole constitution, and he refuses to submit himself to the correction and amendment of those whom it concerns. For, as these opponents prove in many ways in their books from the sacred canons, it belongs to a general council to correct and amend even the Pope in those things which pertain to faith. But he does not allow a general council to be convened, and so he refuses to submit himself to the correction and amendment of those whom it concerns. Therefore he is to be regarded as a heretic.

units.la: Quarta ratio est haec. qui scienter impugnat determinationem universalis ecclesiae vel doctrinam, est haereticus manifestus: nec talis per quamcunque ignorantiam vel simplicitatem potest excusari: quia talis est reputandus scienter haereticus, nec est a tali quaerendum, an paratus sit corrigi, sed quam cito constituit, quod scienter impugnat doctrinam universalis ecclesiae, sine alia examinatione vel quaestione est haereticus iudicandus: quia qui scienter impugnat regulam fidei, per quam debet errans in fide emendari & corrigi, non est examinandus, an paratus sit corrigi: ex quo negat regulam per quam deberet corrigi. Sed iste scienter impugnat doctrinam & determinationem universalis ecclesiae: non enim ignorat, quod determinaverit. Nicolaus tertius de paupertate Christi, quod scilicet exemplo firmavit abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum, sed ipsam saepe legit, quam tamen scienter impugnat sub bulla sua diffiniens, quod Christus in quantum homo mortalis numquam fuit pauper per carentiam temporalis domini: & per consequens nunquam firmavit exemplo abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum. ergo pertinax & haereticus sine ulteriori examinatione ab omnibus catholicis hoc scientibus est censendus.
units.tr: The fourth argument is this. Whoever knowingly attacks the determination or teaching of the universal Church is a manifest heretic, nor can such a man be excused by any ignorance or simplicity. For such a man is to be regarded as a knowing heretic, nor is it to be asked of him whether he is ready to be corrected. As soon as it is established that he knowingly attacks the teaching of the universal Church, he is to be judged a heretic without any further examination or inquiry, since whoever knowingly attacks the rule of faith, by which one who errs in faith ought to be amended and corrected, is not to be examined as to whether he is ready to be corrected, since he denies the rule by which he ought to be corrected. But this man knowingly attacks the teaching and determination of the universal Church, for he is not ignorant of what it has determined. Nicholas III determined concerning the poverty of Christ, namely that he confirmed by his example the renunciation of ownership of all things, and this he often read, yet he knowingly attacks it when, defining under his own bull, he says that Christ as mortal man never was poor through lack of temporal dominion; and consequently he never confirmed by example the renunciation of ownership of all things. Therefore he is to be regarded as obstinate and a heretic, without further examination, by all Catholics who know this.

units.la: Quinta ratio est. qui errat in fide, & de veritate ex certa scientia renuit informari, est haereticus reputandus: quia constat, quod talis non est paratus corrigi, nec cauta sollicitudine quaerit veritatem: & per consequens secundum beatum Augustinum, ut allegatum est supra, est inter haereticos computandus. Sed iste renuit ex certa scientia, imo ex malitia de veritate informari, cum veritatem volentes ostendere noluit audire. ergo est haereticus reputandus.
units.tr: The fifth argument is this. Whoever errs in faith, and from certain knowledge refuses to be informed about the truth, is to be regarded as a heretic, since it is plain that such a man is not ready to be corrected, nor does he seek the truth with careful diligence; and consequently, according to the blessed Augustine, as was alleged above, he is to be counted among the heretics. But this man refuses from certain knowledge, indeed from malice, to be informed about the truth, since when those who wished to show him the truth, he would not listen. Therefore he is to be regarded as a heretic.

units.la: Sexta ratio est haec. qui veritates catholicas per universalem ecclesiam etiam inter laicos & quoscunque simplices catholicos promulgatas negare, & haereses contrarias probare praesumit, est statim haereticus reputandus: quia de tali est praesumptio violenta, contra quam non est probatio in contrarium admittenda. qui enim non reputat doctrinam universalis ecclesiae veram & sanam, est haereticus manifestus. nec est quaerendum a tali, an sit paratus corrigi, cum neget regulam, scilicet doctrinam universalis ecclesiae, per quam corrigendus est errans. Sed iste impugnatus publice praedicat contra veritates per universalem ecclesiam, imo inter laicos & quoscunque simplices promulgatas. ergo est haereticus iudicandus. Maior est probata, minor etiam est manifesta.
units.tr: The sixth argument is this. Whoever presumes to deny the Catholic truths promulgated by the universal Church, even among laymen and any simple Catholics, and to prove contrary heresies, is at once to be regarded as a heretic, since there is a violent presumption against such a man, against which no proof to the contrary is to be admitted. For whoever does not regard the teaching of the universal Church as true and sound is a manifest heretic. Nor is such a man to be asked whether he is ready to be corrected, since he denies the rule, namely the teaching of the universal Church, by which one who errs is to be corrected. But this man publicly preaches against the truths promulgated by the universal Church, indeed among laymen and any simple people. Therefore he is to be judged a heretic. The major premise has been proved, and the minor is also manifest.

units.la: Nam omnibus notum est, quod apud omnes Christianos catholicos quantumcunque simplices exstitit probatum, quia animae reproborum sunt in inferno, & quod graviter cruciantur & quod daemones nunc puniuntur & graviter affliguntur: & quod beata virgo & apostoli, martyres, & alii sancti in caelo vident nunc Deum: & quod Christus erat pauper non habens dominium in quantum erat homo mortalis praediorum & thesaurorum & aliarum divitiarum pretiosarum: & tamen contra omnes istas veritates sic generaliter apud omnes catholicos promulgatas praedicat publice iste impugnatus. ergo est inter haereticos reputandus.
units.tr: For it is known to all that among all Catholic Christians, however simple, it has been established that the souls of the reprobate are in hell, and that they are grievously tormented, and that the devils are now punished and grievously afflicted, and that the blessed Virgin, the apostles, the martyrs and the other saints in heaven now see God, and that Christ, as man, was poor, not having dominion over estates, treasures and other precious riches as a mortal man. Yet this man publicly preaches against all these truths, which are so generally promulgated among all Catholics. Therefore he is to be counted among the heretics.

units.la: Septima ratio talis est: qui correctus legitime de errore se non corrigit nec emendat, est haereticus reputandus. Hoc per auctoritatem Augustini superius allegatam, quae ponitur 24. q. 3. c. qui in ecclesia, aperte probatur. Sed iste impugnatus est de multis haeresibus correptus legitime, & (e non corrigit, nec emendat. ergo est hæreticus reputandus. Ad euidentiam istius rationis isti conantur declarare, quæ correptio est legitima iudicanda: dicentes quod illa correptio est legitima censenda, quia euidenter erranti ostenditur, quod suus error regulæ fidei contradicit. nec refert à quo sibi hoc monstretur, siue à prælato, siue ab alio: cuius rationem assignant, quia fides nostra non innititur sapientiæ vel auctoritati hominis cuiuscunque mortalis. Si enim Papa & omnes cardinales ac omnes clerici mundi probarent contra minimam assertionem scripturæ diuinæ vel doctrinæ vniuersalis ecclesiæ, non esset eis quoquo modo credendum, sed regulæ fidei esset firmiter adhærendum. fides ergo nostra non innititur auctoritate cuiuscunque viuentis in hac vita mortali. Ex quo sequitur, quod non propter auctoritatem cuiuscunque, sed propter regulam fidei debet vnusquisque errorem suum corrigere. & ideo quicunque erranti euidenter ostenditur siue per librorum inspectionem, siue per propriam inuentionem, seu meditationem, siue per alterius prælati vel non prælati instructionem vel informationem, vel quocunque alio modo, quod error suus regulæ fidei, hoc est scripturæ diuinæ seu doctrinæ vniuersalis ecclesiæ aduersatur, statim absque mora corrigere se tenetur. quod si non fecerit, pertinax & hæreticus est censendus. Et hic apparet, quomodo concludit hæc ratio. nam constat, quod iste impugnatus per plures scripturas istius appellantis & aliorum legitime est correptus: quia in pluribus scripturis, quas vidit & legit, euidenter ostenditur, quod errores sui regulæ fidei contradicunt, & tamen se non correxit. ergo est hæreticus reputandus.
units.tr: The seventh argument runs as follows: whoever, once lawfully corrected, does not correct or amend his error is to be reckoned a heretic. This is clearly proved by the authority of Augustine cited above, which is found at 24. q. 3. c. qui in ecclesia. But this man under attack has been lawfully corrected of many heresies, and he does not correct or amend himself. Therefore he is to be reckoned a heretic. To make this argument plain, these men try to explain what kind of correction should be judged lawful. They say that a correction is to be regarded as lawful when it is shown to a man who is manifestly in error that his error contradicts the rule of faith. It does not matter by whom this is pointed out to him, whether by a prelate or by someone else. They give the reason: our faith does not rest on the wisdom or authority of any mortal man whatsoever. For if the Pope and all the cardinals and all the clergy of the world were to argue against the smallest assertion of divine Scripture or of the universal doctrine of the Church, they should not be believed in any way, but the rule of faith should be firmly adhered to. Our faith therefore does not rest on the authority of anyone living in this mortal life. It follows that everyone must correct his error not on account of anyone's authority, but on account of the rule of faith. Therefore, whenever someone is clearly shown that his error is opposed to the rule of faith, that is, to divine Scripture or the universal doctrine of the Church, whether this is shown by the reading of books, by his own discovery or meditation, or by the instruction or information of some prelate or non-prelate, or in any other way, he is bound to correct himself at once and without delay. If he does not do so, he is to be judged obstinate and a heretic. And here it appears how this argument reaches its conclusion. For it is established that this man under attack has been lawfully corrected through many writings of this appellant and of others, because in many writings which he has seen and read it is clearly shown that his errors contradict the rule of faith, and yet he has not corrected himself. Therefore he is to be reckoned a heretic.

units.la: Octaua ratio talis est. qui errat in fide, & in defensione suorum errorum persequitur & molestat illos, qui suorum errorum nituntur detegere prauitatem, est pertinax & hæreticus reputandus: quia talis errans non est paratus corrigi, ex quo declarationem veritatis & detectionem falsitatis satagit impedire. sed iste impugnatus crudeliter & acerbe persequitur omnes, qui suorum errorum nituntur detegere prauitatem. ergo hæreticus & nequaquam paratus corrigi est censendus. maior est euidens. minor etiam patet, quia appellantem & adhærentes sibi propter hoc, quod dicunt ipsum errare in fide, crudelissime persequi non desistit. Sed forte dicet aliquis, quod non erat licitum appellare ab ipso. Ad hoc dicunt, quod in aliis operibus multipliciter probant, quod appellans ab ipso licite appellauit: quia à gerente se pro Papa in causa hæresis est licitum appellare. Ad quod probandum multas rationes adducunt, quarum aliquæ tactæ sunt in principio huius operis: nec inuentus est aliquis, qui ad ipsas sciat motionem rationabilem inuenire. Propter dicta dicunt isti impugnatores aperte liquere, quod iste impugnatus est hæreticus manifestus. ex quo concluditur, quod est omni potestate, & auctoritate ac dignitate priuatus, ac etiam excommunicationis sententia innodatus, quia omnes hæretici nullo excepto per concilium generale, sicut patet extra de hæreticis, Excommunicamus, sunt damnati. quare cum Papa in causa hæresis generali concilio sit subiectus, constat quod iste, non obstante, quod fuerit ad Papatum assumptus, quamcito effectus fuit hæreticus, per canonem latæ sententiæ ipso facto fuit damnatus & priuatus. Ex quo sequitur, quod iste incidit in omnes sententias & pœnas per Romanos pontifices contra hæreticos indistincte prolatas. Etiam ex hoc inferunt isti, quod iste impugnatus ab omnibus scientibus eum esse hæreticum de necessitate salutis est vitandus. qui autem ignorant ipsum hæreticum: si laborant ignorantia crassa & supina, à peccato mortali grauissimo nullatenus excusantur: qui autem ignorant cum esse talem, & laborant ignorantia probabili vel inuincibili, per ignorantiam facti excusari videntur communicando & obediendo eidem. Vnde quantum ad hoc, quod vitetur vel non vitetur, simile est de ipso & muliere, si putaretur vir & ad Papatum assumeretur, quia illi, qui postea scirent eam esse mulierem, nullo modo deberent eam habere pro Papa, illi autem qui nescirent eam, & ignorantiam inuincibili laborant, ex quo habebatur pro Papa, habendo eam pro Papa per ignorantiam excusarentur: sic est de isto, quia non maiorem habet auctoritatem veram, quam habuit mulier illa, quæ sicut habetur in Chronicis, annis duobus, mensibus septem, diebus tribus venerabatur pro Papa ab vniuersali ecclesia. Et si dicat aliquis, quod hoc fiare non potest, quia ecclesia vniuersalis errare non potest. Ad hoc dicunt isti, quod quantum ad ea quæ fidei sunt, & bonorum morum, ecclesia vniuersalis errare non potest. sed quantum ad ea quæ facti sunt, ecclesia militans errare potest & decipi: & sic errauit fœminam venerando pro Papa. sic etiam errauit Anastasium secundum hæreticum antequam esset deprehensus habendo pro Papa. sic etiam sæpe errat, dum Papam virum scleratissimum, sanctum virum putat & bonum. nonne ecclesia errauit putans Syluestrum secundum, qui erat nigromanticus, & homagium fecerat diabolo, esse virum bonum. & de multis aliis pontificibus, ecclesia reputans eos sanctos viros, errauit. Vnde isti dicunt in Chronicis se legisse circa viginti septem vocatos Romanos episcopos, postquam ecclesia extitit temporalibus diuitiis dotata, qui sceleribus maximis publicis & notoriis, postquam fuerunt ad Papatum assumpti, vel in ipsa assumptione ad Papatum irretiti fuerunt, qui sc. crimen hæresis, idololatriæ, inrusionis, fautoriæ, prauitatis hæreticæ, blasphemiæ, fornicationis, & aliis multis enormibus criminibus inuoluti fuerunt. ecclesia ergo sæpe, quantum ad ea quæ facti sunt, errat. Secundo dicunt, quod simile est de isto impugnato quantum ad hoc, quod debeat vitari vel non vitari, & de aliquo non baptizato, si putatus baptizatus eligeretur in Papam: quia illi, qui scirent eum non baptizatum, nequaquam deberent eum habere pro Papa. Alios autem ignorantia excusaret. sic dicunt de isto, quod qui sciunt ipsum esse hæreticum, sibi non debet aliqualiter obedire. Alii autem qui ignorant, & non laborant ignorantia ignorantia crassa vel supina, licite sibi obediunt. Simile est etiam de isto & de non ordinato celebrante missam: quia qui sciunt eum non esse ordinatum audiendo missam eius peccant mortaliter, & adorando hostiam, quam elevat, committunt idololatriam. qui autem ignorant eum non esse ordinatum, per ignorantiam excusantur, si non est crassa & supina: sic debet esse de obedientibus isti, qui sciunt vel credunt esse talem, si obediunt, peccant mortaliter: si non reputat eum talem, & ignorantia non laborant crassa & supina, sibi obediunt, excusantur. Dicunt tamen isti, quod licet obedientes aliqui possint per ignorantiam excusari, non tamen possunt excusari per ignorantiam talem, qui appellantes contra ipsum & veritatem catholicam defensantes in favorem ipsius persequuntur vel molestant quoquo modo: quia scire tenetur omnes, quilibet Christianus potest se licite exponere pro defensione fidei Christianæ, multomagis quam pro defensione patriæ. & ideo quicunque dicit se appellare contra Papam pro defensione Christianæ fidei, antequam constiterit ipsum calumniose, vel alias inique procedere, non est ab aliquo molestandus, sed magis ab omnibus est vituperandus. Dicunt ergo isti impugnatores, quod iste impugnatus ab omnibus reputantibus eum hæreticum est vitandus, cum sit hæreticus manifestus, ut per rationes adductas superius evidenter est ostensum.
units.tr: The eighth argument runs as follows: whoever errs in the faith, and in defence of his errors persecutes and harasses those who seek to expose the wickedness of those errors, is to be reckoned obstinate and a heretic, because such a man in error is not ready to be corrected, since he labours to hinder the declaration of truth and the exposure of falsehood. But this man under attack cruelly and bitterly persecutes all who seek to expose the wickedness of his errors. Therefore he is to be reckoned a heretic who is by no means ready to be corrected. The major premise is evident. The minor also is plain, because he does not cease to persecute most cruelly the appellant and those who adhere to him, for the reason that they say he errs in the faith. But perhaps someone will say that it was not lawful to appeal from him. To this they reply that in other works they prove in many ways that the appellant appealed from him lawfully, because it is lawful to appeal from one who acts as Pope in a case of heresy. To prove this they bring forward many arguments, some of which were touched upon at the beginning of this work; and no one has been found who knows how to find a reasonable objection to them. On the basis of these things, these opponents say it is clear that this man under attack is a manifest heretic. From this it is concluded that he has been deprived of all power, authority and dignity, and has also been bound by the sentence of excommunication, because all heretics, none excepted, have been condemned by a general council, as is evident in the decretal Excommunicamus, extra de haereticis. Since the Pope in a case of heresis is subject to a general council, it is established that this man, notwithstanding that he was raised to the papacy, was condemned and deprived by the canon of automatic sentence (latae sententiae), by the very fact, as soon as he became a heretic. It follows from this that he has incurred all the sentences and penalties declared without distinction by the Roman pontiffs against heretics. These men also infer from this that this man under attack must be avoided, as a matter of necessity for salvation, by all who know him to be a heretic. As for those who do not know him to be a heretic: if they labour under gross and supine ignorance, they are in no way excused from the most grievous mortal sin; but those who do not know him to be such and labour under a probable or invincible ignorance seem to be excused, through ignorance of the fact, for communicating with him and obeying him. Hence, as regards whether he is to be avoided or not, the case of him and of a woman is alike: suppose a woman were thought to be a man and were raised to the papacy. Those who afterwards knew her to be a woman ought by no means to regard her as Pope; but those who did not know her and labour under invincible ignorance, since they regarded her as Pope, would be excused by their ignorance in regarding her as Pope. So it is with this man, since he has no greater true authority than that woman had, who, as is recorded in the Chronicles, was venerated as Pope by the universal Church for two years, seven months and three days. And if anyone says that this cannot happen, because the universal Church cannot err, these men reply that, as regards matters of faith and good morals, the universal Church cannot err, but as regards matters of fact the militant Church can err and be deceived; and so it erred in venerating a woman as Pope. So too it erred in regarding Anastasius II as a good Pope before he was discovered to be a heretic. So too it often errs when it thinks a most wicked man to be a holy and good man. Did not the Church err in thinking Sylvester II, who was a necromancer and had paid homage to the devil, to be a good man? And the Church, regarding many other pontiffs as holy men, has erred about them as well. Hence these men say that they have read in the Chronicles that about twenty-seven men called Roman bishops, since the Church was endowed with temporal riches, were involved in the greatest public and notorious crimes, either after they were raised to the papacy or were entangled in such crimes at the very moment of their elevation: namely the crimes of heresy, idolatry, intrusion, abetting heretics, heretical depravity, blasphemy, fornication, and many other enormous crimes. The Church therefore often errs as regards matters of fact. Secondly, they say that the case of this man under attack, as regards whether he ought to be avoided or not, is similar to that of an unbaptized person who, if he were thought to be baptized, were chosen as Pope: for those who knew him to be unbaptized should by no means regard him as Pope, while others would be excused by their ignorance. So they say of this man that those who know him to be a heretic ought in no way to obey him. Others, however, who are ignorant and do not labour under gross or supine ignorance, may lawfully obey him. The case of this man is also similar to that of a celebrant of Mass who has not been ordained: for those who know that he has not been ordained sin mortally by hearing his Mass, and by adoring the host which he elevates they commit idolatry; but those who do not know that he has not been ordained are excused by their ignorance, provided it is not gross and supine. So it must be with those who obey this man: those who know, or believe, him to be such, sin mortally if they obey him; those who do not regard him as such, and do not labour under gross and supine ignorance, are excused if they obey him. Yet these men say that, although some who obey him may be excused by ignorance, those cannot be excused by such ignorance who appeal against him, or who defend the Catholic truth against him, or who in any way persecute or harass them in his favour. For everyone is bound to know that any Christian may lawfully expose himself in defence of the Christian faith, much more than in defence of his country. Therefore whoever says that he appeals against the Pope in defence of the Christian faith, before it has been established that the Pope is proceeding calumniously or otherwise unjustly, is not to be harassed by anyone, but rather is to be reviled by all. These opponents therefore say that this man under attack is to be avoided by all who regard him as a heretic, since he is a manifest heretic, as has been clearly shown by the arguments adduced above.

units.la: Sed contra prædicta duæ obiectiones moventur. Prima est Fratris Giraldi Odonis, quæ talis est: Reges & Principes & prælati ac multitudo alia Christianorum habent eum pro vero & catholico Papa. ergo non est hæreticus reputandus. Secunda est quorundam aliorum dicentium, quod non est hæreticus, cum credat se catholicæ fidei minime obviare. Ad primam istarum obiectionum dicunt isti, quod prædictus Frater Giraldus tanquam hæreticus nititur hæreticum defensare, quia enim iste Giraldus sit hæreticus manifestus, per rationem secundam, qua ostenditur, quod iste impugnatus est hæreticus, & per tertiam, quintam & nonam monstratur aperte: tum quia iste Giraldus cogit alios ad constitutiones istius impugnati hæreticales pertinaciter defendendas: tum quia cogit alios veritatem catholicam abiurare: tum quia determinationem vniuersalis ecclesiæ scienter impugnat: tum quia defensores fidei catholicæ acerbissime & crudelissime persequitur & impugnat. Præterea itas rationes alias plures adducunt ad probandum, quod iste Giraldus hæreticus sit censendus, de quibus aliqua breviter hic tanguntur: quarum prima est hæc. Iste qui in favorem hæreticorum eorum veritates & scripturas catholicas prohibet probari & legi, est hæreticus vel saltem fautor istorum hæreticorum. Sed hoc facit iste Giraldus, cum in favorem istius impugnati prohibuerit prædicare animas sanctorum videre Deum in cœlo. & Parisius præcepit, quod determinatio domini Nicolai tertii minime legeretur. ergo, &c. Secunda ratio est hæc: qui impugnat veritatem agnitam est deterior hæretico nesciente. Sed iste impugnat veritatem agnitam de paupertate Christi & apostolorum: quia ipsam veritatem ipsemet tenere solebat: ergo, &c. Sed ad hoc forte dicet, quod adhuc tenet eam in corde, sicut cuidam Fratri per socium suum intimavit, ut fertur. Sed ista responsio ipsum nequaquam excusat, sed de mendacio in doctrina religionis & duplicitate ac falsitate accusat, sicut de se patet. Tertia ratio est hæc: qui in favorem hæreticorum novas hæreses nititur invenire & tenere, est hæreticus reputandus. Sed iste Giraldus in favorem istius impugnati novas hæreses fingit & tenet, de quibus aliquæ sunt præsentibus inserendæ. Quarum prima est: quod Papa intrans canonice non potest errare in fide, nec invenitur aliquis erravit. Secundus error, quæ tenet, est quod à Papa de iure appellari non potest. Tertius, quod Papa in causa fidei non habet superiorem in terris. Quartus, quod verus zelus fidei nunquam facit fugere pro causa fidei, nisi qui peregrinum cives non recipiunt, nec audire volunt, sed de sua civitate illum expellunt. Quintus est, quod paupertas B. Francisci & Regulæ suæ non est in paupertate Christi fundata. Sextus est, quod declarationes summorum pontificum super regulam B. Francisci sunt fermentum primæ puritatis regulæ corruptiuum. Septimus est, quod declarationes super regulam B. Francisci sunt hæreticales. Octavus est, quod regula B. Francisci intellecta, ut est pro summos pontifices declarata, est inobservabilis reputanda. Nonus est, quod Fratres Minorib. licet in communi propria possidere. Istos errores & alios sapientes hæresim manifestam iste Giraldus in favorem istius impugnati confingit & tenet. ergo hæreticus est censendus. hæreticus ergo, ut dicunt, p hæretico nititur allegare. Obiectio tamen sua non valet: tum quia sicut ostensum est ecclesia militans errare potest quantum ad ea quæ facti sunt: tum quia non tota multitudo Christianorum reputat eum catholicum. multi autem reges & principes, imo et nonnulli prælati pro forsitan pro ignorantiam excusari. De inultis autem rusticis & aliis simplicibus non est dubium, quia per ignorantiam excusentur.
