Quarum altera, scilicet pontificalis auctoritas, ad præsens diuino iudicio videtur expirasse de medio: vobis restat, & vestra per consequens interest, Imperator piissime, negotia fidei & pauperum causas indesinenter assumere & incessanter prosequi. Quapropter vestram magnificam clementiam & dominationem dignissimam instanter exoro, & humiliter supplico, quatenus infra scriptos breuiter errores Domini Iohannis, qui se Papam 22. appellat, videre placeat: & quam sint catholicæ fidei bonisq; moribus contrarii & noxii dignemini aduertere, & ad Ecclesiæ publicam notitiam, ne fideles valeant inficere, celeriter deducere.
units.tr: To the most serene and most Christian Prince, Louis, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans, father of the poor, champion of the Catholic faith and ever Augustus, and to the other princes, barons and nobles sitting with him in Parliament: Brother Michael, Minister General of the Order of Friars Minor, and a servant, though unworthy, together with the masters and other brothers who adhere to him in the truth, offers himself with all humility, devotion and submission. Since it is said in dist. 96: There are two things by which this world is principally governed: the sacred authority of the pontiffs and the royal power. Of these, the one, namely the pontifical authority, seems at present to have been removed from the middle by divine judgment. What remains is for you, most pious Emperor, and therefore it concerns you, to take up without ceasing and to pursue without end the affairs of the faith and the causes of the poor. Therefore I earnestly beg your magnificent clemency and most worthy lordship, and humbly petition that you be pleased to look at the errors of Lord John, who calls himself Pope XXII, set down briefly below; and that you would deign to notice how contrary and harmful they are to the Catholic faith and to good morals, and to bring them quickly to the public notice of the Church, so that the faithful may not be infected.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: PRimus itaq; error dicti Domini Iohannis in quodam suo libello appellationi per me interpositæ respondendo contentus & dogmatizatus est, quod Christus inquantum homo ab instanti suæ conceptionis habuit vniuersale dominium rerum temporalium, sicut verus rex & Dominus in temporalibus: & quod Christus non fuit dictus pauper & egenus propter carentiam dominii rerum temporalium, sed solum propter carentiam perceptionis fructuum & obuentionum regni, quia fructibus & obuentionibus non se iuuabat. Cuius verba eius in dicto libello contenta sunt hæc: Secundo quaeritur, vtrum Christus aliciuius rei temporalis dominium habuerit & quale? Quod autem dominium rerum temporalium habuerit, sacra scriptura tam Testamento Veteri quam novo in multis locis testatur. Multi quidem Prophetæ eum regem futurum populi Israelitici: & per consequens habere regni dominium prophetauerunt. Et infra: Premissa autem (scilicet regnum & vniuersale dominium) habuit Iesus inquantum Deus ab æterno, eo ipso quod Deus pater genuit eum: & inquantum homo ex tempore, scilicet ab instanti conceptionis suæ ex Dei dono. Et infra: Ad illud autem quod dicitur, quod scriptura sacra ipsum fuisse pauperem & egenum in pluribus locis testatur, est dicendum, quod non carentia dominii fecit eum pauperem & egenum, sed potius carentia perceptionis fructus & obuentionis rerum quarum Dominus erat. Nudum enim dominium separatum in perpetuum ab omni perceptione commodi rei habentem non facit diuitem, cum sit inutile reputandum. Unde habens tale dominium potest egenus & pauper merito reputari. Hæc sunt verba sua, quæ sunt hæretica: quia manifeste obuiant & repugnant catholicæ veritati. Quod patet primo per illud, quod ipse Christus Matth. 19. legitur dixisse cuidam adolescenti: Si vis perfectus esse, vade & vende omnia quæ habes & da pauperibus & veni & sequere me. Et sicut Lucas Euangelista refert, ille, cui Christus tale consilium dedit, fuit quidam princeps. Unde Lucas 18. refert dicens: Interrogauit eum quidam princeps &c. Ex quibus verbis Saluatoris liquet manifeste, quod ad perfectionem Euangelicam requiritur non solum temporalium fructuum & obuentionum, sed etiam temporalium dominiorum abdicatio & renuntiatio: Quia si vis, inquit, perfectus esse vende omnia quæ habes & da pauperibus. Venditio autem omnium, & ipsorum pauperibus libera elargitio, non minus de directo respicit seu includit temporalium dominiorum quam prouentuum translationem & abnegationem. Si ergo Christus inquantum homo non reliquit, sed sibi retinuit vniuersale dominium rerum temporalium, sicut verus rex & Dominus in temporalibus, vt dictus Iohannes asserit, sequitur necessario & euidenter, quod Christus secundum suum consilium perfectus non fuerit, nec de genere perfectorum, cum ad perfectionē Euangelicam secundum suum consilium temporalium dominiorū abdicatio seu renunciatio requiratur. Quod non tā erroneum, q; insanum censendum est: quia, vt ipse ait Luc. 6. c. Perfectus erit omnis si sit sicut magister eius. Ex quibus patet, quod Christus fuit veraciter pauper & egenus propter carentiam dominii rerum temporalium: & non solum propter carentiā perceptionis fructuum & obuentionum regni, cum in suo consilio præfato non minus temporalium dominiorum quam fructuum & obuentionum abdicatio & negatio includatur. Alioquin perfecte imitari volentes non debuissent iuxta Christi consilium & exemplum suarum rerum temporalium dominia, sed solum prouentus relinquere: q; est expresse contra Christi præfatum consilium. In quo cuidam principi quærenti ad perfectionem pertingere consuluit sui principatus dominium omne, & non solum prouentus relinquere & dimittere.
units.tr: The first error of the said Lord John, asserted and laid down in a certain little book of his, in answer to an appeal lodged by me, is that Christ, as man, from the very moment of his conception had universal lordship over temporal things, as a true king and lord in temporal affairs; and that Christ was not called poor and needy because he lacked lordship over temporal things, but only because he lacked the receipt of the fruits and revenues of the kingdom, since he did not benefit himself by the fruits and revenues. His words in the said book are these: Second, it is asked whether Christ had lordship over any temporal thing, and of what kind? That he had lordship over temporal things, sacred Scripture, both Old and New Testament, bears witness in many places. Indeed, many prophets foretold that he would be the future king of the Israelite people, and consequently that he would have lordship of the kingdom. And below: But the aforesaid things (namely, kingdom and universal lordship) Jesus had, as God, from eternity, by the very fact that God the Father begot him; and as man, from time, namely from the moment of his conception, by the gift of God. And below: As for what is said, that sacred Scripture bears witness in many places that he was poor and needy, it must be said that it was not the lack of lordship that made him poor and needy, but rather the lack of receiving the fruit and revenue of the things of which he was Lord. For bare lordship, cut off forever from every receipt of benefit from the thing, does not make a man rich, since it must be reckoned useless. Hence one who has such lordship can rightly be regarded as needy and poor. These are his words, which are heretical, because they plainly oppose and contradict Catholic truth. This is clear first from what Christ himself is read in Matthew 19 to have said to a certain young man: If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have and give to the poor, and come and follow me. And as the Evangelist Luke reports, the one to whom Christ gave this counsel was a certain ruler. Hence Luke 18 reports, saying: A certain ruler asked him, etc. From these words of the Saviour it is plainly evident that for evangelical perfection there is required not only the renunciation and surrender of the fruits and revenues of temporal things, but also of temporal lordships. For if you wish to be perfect, he says, sell all that you have and give to the poor. Now the selling of everything, and the free bestowal of it on the poor, bears directly upon and includes the transfer and renunciation of temporal lordships no less than of revenues. If therefore Christ, as man, did not relinquish but kept for himself universal lordship over temporal things, as a true king and lord in temporal affairs, as the said John asserts, it follows necessarily and evidently that Christ, according to his own counsel, was not perfect, nor of the number of the perfect, since for evangelical perfection, according to his counsel, the renunciation or surrender of temporal lordships is required. This is to be judged not so much erroneous as insane; for, as he himself says in Luke 6: Everyone who is perfect will be as his master. From these things it is plain that Christ was truly poor and needy because of his lack of lordship over temporal things, and not only because of his lack of the receipt of the fruits and revenues of the kingdom, since in the counsel mentioned the renunciation and refusal of temporal lordships is included no less than of fruits and revenues. Otherwise, those wishing to imitate perfectly, according to the counsel and example of Christ, ought to leave behind not the lordships of their temporal things, but only the revenues; which is expressly contrary to the aforesaid counsel of Christ. In that counsel he advised a certain prince who asked how to attain perfection to leave the whole lordship of his principality, and not merely to give up and dismiss the revenues.

units.la: Et præterea si retentio dominii vnius principatus particulariter non stat cum Euangelica persectione: quia ille, cui Christus tale consilium dedit, fuit secundum Lucam quidam princeps: multo magis retentio dominii vniuersalis regni vel Imperii non stat cum Euangelica perfectione: & non minus distrahit ab Euangelica perfectione dominium vniuersale, sicut regni vel Imperii, quam dominium particulare vnius principatus. Si ergo Christus non reliquit, sed sibi retinuit dominium vniuersale rerum temporalium, sicut verus rex & Dominus temporalium, sequitur, vt dictum est, q; ipse non fuerit perfectus, nec de genere perfectorum quod est blasphemum: Sequitur etiam, quod ipse non fuerit magnus in regno cœlorum: quia, vt ipse ait Matt. 5. c. Qui autem fecerit & docuerit, hic magnus vocabitur in regno cœlorum. Constat autem quod Christus docuit alios relinquere dominium suorum principatuum in eo quod dixit: Vende omnia quæ habes & da pauperibus. Si ergo ipse non reliquit, sed sibi retinuit dominium vniuersale principatus regni vel Imperii: sequitur q; ipse non fecerit quod docuit: & ita non fuisset magnus in regno cœlorum: quia qui fecerit, inquit, & docuerit hic magnus vocabitur in regno cœlorum. Ideo Actuum primo legitur: Cœpit Iesus facere & docere. Sequitur etiam, quod ipse Christus fuisset similis scribis & Pharisæis, qui dicebant & non faciebant. Quos Christus de hoc specialiter reprehendit: Dicunt enim & non faciunt, vt patet Matth. 22.
units.tr: And moreover, if retention of lordship over a single principality in particular is not consistent with evangelical perfection, because the one to whom Christ gave this counsel was, according to Luke, a certain ruler: much more is the retention of universal lordship over a kingdom or empire not consistent with evangelical perfection; and universal lordship over a kingdom or empire distracts from evangelical perfection no less than the particular lordship of a single principality. If therefore Christ did not relinquish but kept for himself universal lordship over temporal things, as a true king and lord of temporal things, it follows, as has been said, that he was not perfect, nor of the number of the perfect, which is blasphemous. It follows also that he was not great in the kingdom of heaven; for, as he himself says in Matthew 5: Whoever shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven. Now it is certain that Christ taught others to relinquish the lordship of their principalities, in that he said: Sell all that you have and give to the poor. If therefore he himself did not relinquish but kept for himself universal lordship over a principality, kingdom or empire, it follows that he did not do what he taught, and so would not have been great in the kingdom of heaven; for whoever shall do and teach, he says, shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven. Hence it is read in the first chapter of Acts: Jesus began to do and to teach. It also follows that Christ himself would have been like the scribes and Pharisees, who said and did not do. Christ reproved them specifically for this, For they say and do not do, as is plain from Matthew 22.

units.la: Item ille, qui ex perfectione virtutis reliquit proprium dominium domus: multo magis ex perfectione virtutis reliquit dominium vniuersale regni vel Imperii: quia non minus distrahit ab Euangelica perfectione dominium vniuersale regni, quam dominium particulare vnius domus. Sed Christus ex perfectione virtutis reliquit proprium dominium cuiuscunq; domus, secundum q; ipse dixit Matt. 8. & Luc. 9. c. Vulpes foueas habent & volucres cœli nidos: filius autem hominis non habet vbi caput suum reclinet. Vbi dicit Glossa: Quid me propter diuitias & lucra seculi vis sequi? cum ego ita sim pauper vt nec hospitium quidem habeam, nec meo vtar tecto. Et Beatus Iohannes Chrysostomus super Matthæum dicit sic: Aspice qualiter pauperta-tem, quam Dominus docuerat, per opera demonstrat. Non erat ei mensa, non candelabrum, non domus, nō q; quam talium. Hæc sanctus Ioannes Chrysost. Vnde sequitur, q; Christus ex perfectione virtutis reliquit dominium vniuersale regni vel Imperii temporalis. Itē sequeretur, q; Christus fuisset mentitus Pilato Ioh. 18. c. quando sibi dixit: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. Cum regnum seu vniuersale dominium rerum temporalium sit de hoc mundo, & de hoc mundo censendum sit. Quod etiam bene ostendit Christus per signum a posteriori seu ab effectu ibidem, scil. Iohan. 18. c. dicens: Si regnum meum esset ex hoc mundo, ministri mei vtiq; certarent vt non traderer Iudæis: nunc autem regnum meum non est hinc. Quod quidem medium Christi æque concludit regnum suum non fuisse de rebus temporalibus, sicut concludit ipsum non fuisse de hoc mundo. Quoniam si ideo regnum Christi non fuit de hoc mundo, quia ministri eius non decertauerunt pro ipso corporaliter: eadē ratione sequitur, quod regnum suum non fuit de rebus temporalibus, quia ministri ipsius non decertauerunt pro ipso temporaliter: quia virtute eiusdem medii tenet secunda consequentia, sicut prima consequentia, scil. virtute istius medii, q; tale fuit Christi regnū, quales sibi ministros elegit. Si ergo q; a Christus non elegit sibi ministros, q; pugnarent, p ipso corporaliter: ideo regnū suū non fuit de hoc mundo. Eadē ratione quia non elegit sibi ministros qui pugnarent pro ipso temporaliter: ideo regnū suū non fuit pro hac vita mortali de rebus temporalibus. Vnde beatus Augustinus pertractans verba Christi super Iohan. dicit sic: Audite Iudei & gentes: audi circumcisio: audi præputium: audite omnia regna terrena: non impedio dominationem vestram in hoc mundo: quia regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. Nolite metuere metu vanissimo, quo Herodes ille maior expauit, & tot infantes occidit: regum, inquit, meum non est de hoc mundo: quid vultu amplius? Venite ad regnum, quod non est de hoc mundo: venite credendo. Hæc Augustinus. Ex quibus patet, quod regnum Christi secundum Augustinum non fuit de rebus temporalibus: quia tunc impediisset dominationem aliorum dominorum temporalium in hoc mundo, qui sua dominia non recognouerunt a Christo secundum quod homo. Cum in eodem regno non possint esse plures Domini in solidum, quorum neuter alium impediat in suo dominio.
units.tr: Likewise, one who out of perfection of virtue relinquished the proper lordship of a house, much more out of perfection of virtue relinquished universal lordship over a kingdom or empire; because universal lordship of a kingdom distracts from evangelical perfection no less than the particular lordship of a single house. But Christ out of perfection of virtue relinquished the proper lordship of any house whatever, as he said in Matthew 8 and Luke 9: Foxes have holes and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head. Where the Gloss says: Why do you wish to follow me for the sake of riches and the gains of this world, since I am so poor that I have not even a lodging, nor a roof of my own to use? And Blessed John Chrysostom on Matthew speaks thus: Look how he shows by his works the poverty which the Lord had taught. He had no table, no lampstand, no house, nor anything of the kind. So says Saint John Chrysostom. Hence it follows that Christ, out of perfection of virtue, relinquished universal lordship over a temporal kingdom or empire. It would also follow that Christ lied to Pilate in John 18, when he said to him: My kingdom is not of this world. For a kingdom, or universal lordship over temporal things, is of this world and must be counted as of this world. Christ also shows this well by a sign from the effect, in the same place, namely John 18, saying: If my kingdom were of this world, my ministers would surely have fought that I should not be handed over to the Jews; but now my kingdom is not from here. This medium of Christ's concludes just as well that his kingdom was not of temporal things as it concludes that it was not of this world. For if Christ's kingdom was not of this world because his ministers did not fight for him bodily, by the same reasoning it follows that his kingdom was not of temporal things, because his ministers did not fight for him temporally: for by the force of the same medium the second consequence holds as the first, namely by the force of this medium, that Christ's kingdom was such as the ministers he chose for himself. If therefore Christ did not choose for himself ministers who would fight for him bodily, then his kingdom was not of this world. By the same reasoning, because he did not choose ministers who would fight for him temporally, his kingdom was not of temporal things during this mortal life. Hence Blessed Augustine, expounding the words of Christ on John, speaks thus: Hear, Jews and Gentiles: hear, circumcision: hear, uncircumcision: hear, all earthly kingdoms: I do not hinder your dominion in this world, because my kingdom is not of this world. Do not fear with that most vain fear with which that Herod the Great was terrified, and slew so many infants: my kingdom, he says, is not of this world: what more do you want? Come to the kingdom which is not of this world: come by believing. So Augustine. From these things it is plain that, according to Augustine, the kingdom of Christ was not of temporal things; for otherwise it would have hindered the dominion of other temporal lords in this world, who did not acknowledge their lordships from Christ according as he is man. For in the same kingdom there cannot be several lords holding the whole, none of whom hinders the other in his lordship.

units.la: Item, si Christus fuisset inquantum homo rex & Dominus in temporalibus: sequeretur q; ipse fallacem & mendacem doctrinam dedisset Iudæis Matt. 22. dicens: Reddite quæ sunt Cæsari Cæsari, & quæ sunt Dei Deo. Quia, vt dictum est, in eodem regno non possunt esse plures reges in solidum, quorum neuter subsit alteri: quia, vt habetur Matt. 6. Nemo potest duobus Dominis seruire. Constat autem, quod Cæsar non recognouit aliq; regnum temporale a Christo, secundum quod homo: sed potius sui ministri exegerunt tributum a Christo, vt patet Matth. 17. Nec Christus recognouit aliquod regnum a Cæsare: Calare: qa licet Christus iusserit Petro dare tributu ministris Caesaris: nō tamen hoc fecit recognitione alicuius regni, sed p vitatione scandali & humilitatis exemplo, vt patet ibidē, scil. Matt. 17. Ergo Christus nō fuit p hac vita mortali rex & Dominus in temporalibus: qa tunc in eodē regno fuissent plures reges in solidū, quorum neuter alteri subfuisset: vel falsacē & mendacē doctrinā docuisset mandando dari tributum Caesari. Vnde sanctus Leo Papa in sermone Epiphaniae dicit de Christo: Dominus mundi temporale regnum non quaerit, qui praestat eternum. Et Beatus Ambros. in Hymno Epiphaniae qui cantatur in Ecclesia, dicit: Non arripit mortalia, Qui regna dat coelestia.
units.tr: Likewise, if Christ as man had been a king and lord in temporal affairs, it would follow that he had taught the Jews a false and deceptive doctrine when he said in Matt. 22: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's. For, as has been said, in the same kingdom there cannot be several kings in full authority, none of whom is subject to another; as is written in Matt. 6: No one can serve two masters. It is certain, however, that Caesar did not acknowledge any temporal kingdom from Christ as man; rather, his ministers demanded tribute from Christ, as Matt. 17 shows. Nor did Christ acknowledge any kingdom from Caesar. Although Christ bade Peter pay tribute to the ministers of Caesar, he did not do so in recognition of any kingdom, but to avoid giving offence and as an example of humility, as the same passage, Matt. 17, shows. Therefore Christ was not a king and lord in temporal affairs during this mortal life; for then in the same kingdom there would have been several kings in full authority, none of whom was subject to another. Or else he would have taught a false and deceptive doctrine by commanding that tribute be paid to Caesar. Hence Pope Leo, in his sermon on the Epiphany, says of Christ: "The Lord of the world does not seek a temporal kingdom, he who bestows an eternal one." And Blessed Ambrose, in the hymn for the Epiphany that is sung in the Church, says: "He does not seize mortal kingdoms, who gives heavenly kingdoms."

units.la: Vnde ista fuit ad literam opinio haeretica Herodis & Iudaeorum, propter quam machinati sunt necem Christi: quia credebant, quod regnum Messiae futurum, de quo locuti sunt omnes Prophetae, esset regnum temporale & non spirituale. Qua opinione falsam & vanā Christus elidens ait: Regnū meū non est de hoc mundo: Id est regnū, de quo locuti sunt omnes Prophetae, non debet intelligi temporale & terrenū, sed spirituale & coeleste. Ideo Christus, qñ Iudaei voluerunt ipsum facere regē in temporalibus, fugit in montē, & noluit tale regnū recipere, vt patet Ioh. 6. Circa passione vero eius, qñ intellexerunt Christi regnū spirituale & coeleste, permisit se adorari, sicut regē, vt patet Ioh. 12. c. Quod bene Zachar-ias Propheta Zachariae 9. prophetauit dicens: Ecce rex tuus veniet tibi iustus & Saluator: & ipse pauper sedens super asinam & super pullū filium asinae. Et ita secundum Prophetam Christus fuit similiter rex & pauper temporaliter: qa suum regnum non debebat esse temporale, sed spirituale & coeleste. Cum enim paupertas simpliciter & absolute accepta dicat carentiā dominii rerum temporaliū, & non solū dicat carentiā perfectionis fructuum & obuentionū: Et cum Propheta dicat simpliciter & absolute, quod Christus foret pauper: sequitur q Christus fuerit pauper p carentiā dominii rerū temporaliū, & non solum per carentiā -ceptionis fructuum & obuentionū: & ita non fuit rex & Dominus in temporalib. Praedictus etiā error incidit aperte in haeresim damnata Vigilantii, q diuitias paupertati praeferebat: quia illud est simpliciter melius & perfectius, q Christus p seipso elegit. Nec obstat, q Mat. 21. legitur: Ite in castellū q contra vos est, & inuenietis asinā & pullum, soluite & adducite mihi: & si quis vobis aliquid dixerit, dicite q Dominus hō opus habet. Non obstat, quia Dominus ibi refertur ad Christi diuinitatem, & non ad eius humanitatem, vt Glossa dicit expresse. Quia vbicunq; in scriptura Dominus absolute absq; omni addito ponitur, Deus, qui est absolute Dominus, intelligitur, iuxta illud Apostoli primae ad Cor. 8. c. Nam etsi sunt Domini multi, nobis tamen vnus est Deus &c.
units.tr: Hence this was, in the literal sense, the heretical opinion of Herod and of the Jews, on account of which they plotted the death of Christ: they believed that the kingdom of the Messiah, of which all the Prophets spoke, would be a temporal and not a spiritual kingdom. Refuting this false and empty opinion, Christ said: "My kingdom is not of this world." That is, the kingdom of which all the Prophets spoke must not be understood as temporal and earthly, but as spiritual and heavenly. Therefore Christ, when the Jews wanted to make him king in temporal affairs, fled to the mountain and refused to accept such a kingdom, as John 6 shows. But near his passion, when they understood Christ's kingdom to be spiritual and heavenly, he allowed himself to be worshipped as a king, as John 12 shows. Zechariah the Prophet prophesied this well, saying in Zech. 9: "Behold, your king will come to you, just and a Saviour; and he is poor, sitting upon an ass and upon a colt, the foal of an ass." And so, according to the Prophet, Christ was in like manner a king and poor in temporal terms, since his kingdom ought not to be temporal but spiritual and heavenly. For poverty, taken simply and absolutely, means the lack of ownership of temporal goods, and not merely the lack of the enjoyment of fruits and revenues. Since the Prophet says simply and absolutely that Christ would be poor, it follows that Christ was poor through the lack of ownership of temporal goods, and not merely through the lack of the receipt of fruits and revenues; and so he was not a king and lord in temporal affairs. The aforesaid error also plainly falls into the heresy of Vigilantius, condemned for preferring riches to poverty; for that is simply better and more perfect which Christ himself chose. Nor is it an objection that Matt. 21 reads: "Go into the village over against you, and you will find an ass and a colt; loose them and bring them to me; and if anyone says anything to you, say that the Lord has need of them." This is no objection, because "Lord" there refers to Christ's divinity and not to his humanity, as the Gloss expressly says. For wherever in Scripture "Lord" is put absolutely, without any addition, God is understood, who is Lord absolutely, according to the saying of the Apostle in 1 Cor. 8: "For although there are many lords, yet for us there is one God," etc.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: SEcundus error Domini Iohannis in dicto libello contentus & dogmatizatus, est q Christus inquantū homo acquisuit sibi in speciali & habuit p successum temporis dominium proprium & immediatū vestimentorum, calciamentorum, alimentorum & loculoru. Qui quidem error obuiat doctrinae Euangelicae & apostolicae atq; ecclesiasticae. Obuiat, inq, doctrinae Euangelicae: quia, vt ipse Christus ait Luc. 14. c. Omnis ex vobis qui non renunciauerit omnibus quae possidet, non potest meus esse discipulus. Constat autem, q Christus fecit, quod docuit, ad perfectionem vitae: quia, vt legitur Actuum 1. c. coepit Iesus facere & docere. Aliter, vt prius dictū est, non fuisset magnus in regno coelorū: quia, vt ipse ait Mat. 5. c. Qui autē fecerit & docuerit, hic magnus vocabitur in regno coelorū. Ergo Christus renunciauit perfecte omnibus, quibus vsus est: aliter non fecisset & docuisset. Sed omnibus, quae possidentur, nō renunciatur perfecte, nisi renuncietur eis quo ad proprietatem & dominium: quia renunciare eis solū quo ad affectionē & curā superfluam, non est ipsis perfecte renunciare. Alioquin religiosi absq; p-rio viuere profitentes frustra & inutiliter renunciarēt in speciali proprietati & dominio omniū rerum temporalium: nisi renunciare eis quo ad proprietate & dominium esset perfectius & virtuosius, quā renunciare eis solum quo ad affectionem & curam superfluam. Et renunciatio Christi fuit forma & exemplar omnis renunciationis regularis: q omnis alia renunciatio canonica, & regularis habet ortū & originem ex Christi renunciatione. Ergo Christus renunciauit ad minus in speciali proprietatū & dominio omniū rerū temporaliū: & p consequens in nulla re temporali habuit in speciali proprietate & dominium proprium. Aliter omnibus rebus temporalibus perfecte non renunciasset: & per consequens alios perfecte renunciare non docuisset: cum nihil docuerit ad perfectionem pertinēs, quod ipse non fecerit. Et si non docuit alios perfecte renunciare omnibus temporalibus, sequitur quod sua doctrina perfecte & sufficiens non fuisset: cum perfecta & sufficiens doctrina doceat perfecte mundum contemnere & relinquere. Dicere autem & asserere, quod Christi doctrina fuerit imperfecta & insufficiens, est haereticum manifeste. Ita quod dicta verba Christi intelligantur de modo renunciandi omnibus temporalibus quo ad proprietatem & dominiū. Patet per illud, q beatus Basilius in sua Regula ab vniuersali ecclesia approbata petentibus Fratribus, vtrum venientes ad suam religionem deberent renunciare primo omnibus rebus? respondit in haec verba: Domino & Saluatore nostro dicente, Si quis venit ad me abneget semetipsum & tollat crucem suam, & sequatur me. Et iterum: qui non renunciauerit omnibus quae possidet non potest meus esse discipulus: qui ad hoc venit, vt Dominum sequatur, etiam semetipsum neget & tollat crucem suam. Haec sanctus Basilius in sua Regula. Et loquitur beatus Basilius de modo renunciandi quo ad dominium & proprietatem: quia loquitur de modo renunciandi quo venientes ad religionem renunciant in speciali proprietati omnium rerum. Ergo Christus renunciauit & docuit alios renunciare proprietati omnium rerum. Hinc etiam Beatus Gregorius super Euangelia in Homelia Vnius Martyris, dicit sic: Certe cum se sequentibus noua mandata proponeret, dixit: nisi quis renunciauerit omnibus quæ possidet, non potest meus esse discipulus. Ac si aperte dicat, qui per vitam veterem alienam concupiscitis, per nouam conseruationis studium etiam vestra largimini. Hæc Beatus Gregor. Papa & Doctor Ecclesiæ. Largitio autem sua, est renunciare eis quo ad proprietatem & dominium, & non solum quo ad affectionem & curam. Ergo secundum beatum Gregor. dicta verba Christi sunt intelligenda de modo renuntiandi quo ad proprietatem & dominium. Item, sanctus Hieronymus ad Heliodorum scribens dicit sic: Non tibi licet quicquam de tuis rebus habere: omnis, inquit Dominus, qui non renuntiauerit omnibus quæ possidet, non potest meus esse discipulus. Hæc sanctus Hieronymus, quibus nihil clarius ad ostendendum, quod dicta verba Christi intelliguntur de modo renuntiandi quo ad proprietatem & dominium. Secundo dictus error obuiat doctrinæ Apostolicæ: quia Actor. 4. cap. legitur de prima multitudine credentium sic: Multitudinis autem credentium erat cor vnum & anima vna: nec quisquam eorum quæ possidebat aliquid suum esse dicebat: sed erant illis omnia communia. Hæc ibi. Ex quibus patet, quod in illa multitudine credentium ab Apostolis & Spiritu sancto ordinata nullus retinuit sibi in speciali proprietatem alicuius rei: quod patet dupliciter. Primo quia nec quisquam eorum quæ possidebat aliquid suum esse dicebat. Quod autem est alicuius quo ad proprietatem & dominium, veraciter est & dicitur suum.
units.tr: The second error, contained and dogmatized in the said little book by Master John, is that Christ as man acquired for himself, in particular, and over time possessed, his own proper and immediate ownership of clothing, shoes, food and money. This error runs counter to the Gospel doctrine, to the apostolic doctrine and to the doctrine of the Church. It runs counter, I say, to the Gospel doctrine, because Christ himself says in Luke 14: "Whoever of you does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple." It is certain, however, that Christ did what he taught, to the perfection of life; for, as is read in Acts 1, "Jesus began to do and to teach." Otherwise, as was said before, he would not have been great in the kingdom of heaven; for, as he himself says in Matt. 5: "Whoever shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven." Therefore Christ renounced perfectly all the things he used; otherwise he would not have done and taught. But all the things that are possessed are not perfectly renounced unless they are renounced as to ownership and dominion; for to renounce them only as to affection and superfluous care is not to renounce them perfectly. Otherwise, religious who profess to live without property would renounce in vain and uselessly the particular ownership and dominion of all temporal goods, unless renouncing them as to ownership and dominion were more perfect and more virtuous than renouncing them only as to affection and superfluous care. And Christ's renunciation was the form and pattern of every regular renunciation, since every other canonical and regular renunciation has its origin and source in Christ's renunciation. Therefore Christ renounced, at least in particular, the ownership and dominion of all temporal goods, and consequently he had in no temporal thing a particular proper ownership and dominion. Otherwise he would not have renounced all temporal goods perfectly, and consequently he would not have taught others to renounce all temporal goods perfectly, since he taught nothing pertaining to perfection that he himself did not do. And if he did not teach others to renounce all temporal goods perfectly, it follows that his doctrine was not perfect and sufficient, since a perfect and sufficient doctrine teaches perfectly to despise and to leave the world. But to say and assert that the doctrine of Christ was imperfect and insufficient is manifestly heretical. Thus the said words of Christ are to be understood as concerning the manner of renouncing all temporal goods as to ownership and dominion. This is shown by what Blessed Basil, in his Rule approved by the universal Church, answered when the brethren asked whether those coming to his religious order ought first to renounce all things. He replied in these words: "Our Lord and Saviour says, 'If anyone comes to me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.' And again: 'Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple.' He who comes to follow the Lord, let him also deny himself and take up his cross." Thus Saint Basil in his Rule. And Blessed Basil speaks of the manner of renouncing as to dominion and ownership, because he speaks of the manner by which those coming to religion renounce the particular ownership of all things. Therefore Christ renounced, and taught others to renounce, the ownership of all things. Hence also Blessed Gregory, in his Homilies on the Gospels, in the homily on a single Martyr, says thus: "Certainly, when he set out new commandments to those who followed him, he said: 'Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple.' As if he were openly saying: you who through the old life covet what belongs to others, through the new life of the Lord's study, give away even your own." Thus Blessed Gregory, Pope and Doctor of the Church. But his giving away is renouncing as to ownership and dominion, and not only as to affection and care. Therefore, according to Blessed Gregory, the said words of Christ are to be understood of the manner of renouncing as to ownership and dominion. Likewise, Saint Jerome, writing to Heliodorus, says thus: It is not permitted to you to have anything of your own goods: "Everyone," says the Lord, "who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple." Thus Saint Jerome; nothing is clearer for showing that the said words of Christ are understood of the manner of renouncing as to ownership and dominion. Secondly, the said error runs counter to the apostolic doctrine, because Acts 4 reads thus of the first multitude of believers: Now the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul; nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them. Thus there. From these words it is plain that in that multitude of believers, ordered by the Apostles and the Holy Spirit, no one kept for himself any particular ownership of any thing; and this is shown in two ways. First, because no one of them said that anything he possessed was his own. What belongs to someone as to ownership and dominion truly is, and is called, his own.

units.la: Secundo quia vbi sunt omnia perfecte communia, ibi nihil est proprium: cum idem apud eosdem non possit simul esse proprium & commune. Et ita per se manifestum est, quod in illa multitudine nulli licuit habere in speciali proprietatem nec dominium proprii alicuius rei. Et si in illa multitudine à Christo deriuata & exemplata nullus habuit in speciali proprietatem aliquam: multo magis Christus, qui fuit forma & exemplar primarium & originale illius communitatis, non habuit in speciali proprietatem aliquam: cum perfectio corporis Ecclesiæ perfectionem capitis Christi nō excedat. Et præterea, sicut dicit Apostolus 1. Cor. 13. ca. Charitas non quærit quæ sua sunt. Constat autem quod charitas Christi fuit perfectior & maior charitate primorum credentium. Ergo Christus minus quæsiuit, quam illi de prima multitudine credentium. Si ergo in prima multitudine credentium nullus dicebat in speciali aliquid suum quod ad proprietatem & dominium, multo magis Christus nō dixit, nec habuit aliquid tanquam suum quod ad proprietatem & dominium. Et ideo vbicunque in scriptura legitur aliquid fuisse Christi, intelligendum est quo ad vsum vel ministerium, & non quo ad dominium. Item, sic scribitur in Psalmo: Ecce quam bonum & quam iucundum habitare Fratres in vnum. Quæ verba aperte beatus Clemens, qui fuit in societate primorum credentium, exponit de illis qui nihil habent proprii, sed omnia habent communia, vt patet ix. ca. q. 1. c. dilectissimis. Sed constat, quod Christus in sua vita tenuit maiorem vnitatem, concordiam, & communitatem, quam aliquis homo de mundo. Ergo ipse minus habuit in speciali aliquid proprium, quam aliquis homo de mundo: quia tanto sunt aliqui magis vnum inter se, quanto magis habent omnia communia, & nihil inter se proprium. Et ideo de primis credentibus qui nihil habebant proprii, sed erant eis omnia communia, scribitur erat eis cor vnum, & anima vna. Cum ergo Christo fuerit summe cor vnum, & anima vna cum Apostolis, & suis discipulis: sequitur quod inter eos nihil habuit proprium. Et oppositum asserere, sicut Dominus Iohannes asserit, est Christi charitatem & vnitatem extinguere atq; confundere.
units.tr: Secondly, where all things are perfectly common, nothing is proprietary, since the same thing cannot at once be both proprietary and common to the same people. It is therefore plain in itself that in that multitude no one was allowed to hold any particular property or ownership of anything. And if no one in that multitude, which was derived from and modelled on Christ, held any particular property, much more did Christ, who was the primary form, pattern and origin of that community, hold no particular property, since the perfection of the body of the Church does not exceed the perfection of its head, Christ. Moreover, as the Apostle says in 1 Cor. 13, Charity does not seek its own things. It is certain that Christ's charity was more perfect and greater than the charity of the first believers. Therefore Christ sought less than those of the first multitude of believers. If, then, in the first multitude of believers no one called anything in particular his own, in the sense of property and ownership, much more did Christ not call anything his own, nor have anything as his own, in the sense of property and ownership. Hence, wherever Scripture says that something belonged to Christ, it must be understood with respect to use or ministry, and not with respect to ownership. Likewise it is written in the Psalm: Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity. Blessed Clement, who lived in the fellowship of the first believers, plainly explains these words as referring to those who have nothing of their own but hold all things in common, as is clear in Dist. 9? (ix. ca. q. 1. c. dilectissimis). But it is certain that Christ in his life maintained greater unity, concord and community than any man in the world. Therefore he had less that was his own in particular than any man in the world, because people are the more one among themselves the more they hold everything in common and nothing as private to themselves. Hence of the first believers, who had nothing of their own but held all things in common, it is written: the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul. Since, then, Christ had supremely one heart and one soul with the Apostles and his disciples, it follows that he had nothing proper to himself among them. To assert the opposite, as Lord John asserts, is to extinguish and confound Christ's charity and unity.

units.la: Tertio dictus error obuiat determinationi sanctæ Ecclesiæ: quia, vt legitur & habetur in Regula sancti Basilii ab vniuersali Ecclesia approbata, quærentibus suis Fratribus, vtrum liceret ipsis habere aliquid proprium? respondit sanctus Basilius in hæc verba: Hoc contrarium est illi testimonio, quod in Actibus Apostolorum de illis qui credebant primitus, scriptum est. Ibi enim dicitur sic: Nemo ex bonis suis quicquam proprium esse dicebat: sed erant illis omnia communia. Si quis ergo aliquid proprium sibi dicit esse, sine dubio alienum se facit ab electis Dei & à charitate Domini, qui docuit verbo & opere compleuit, & animam suam posuit pro amicis suis. Si ergo ipse animam suam pro amicis suis dedit: & quomodo non vtiam quæ extra sunt propria dederit? Hæc sanctus Basilius in sua Regula ab vniuersali Ecclesia approbata. Ex quibus verbis Basilii, imo vniuersalis Ecclesiæ eius regulam approbantis, triplicitèr apparet, quod Christus non habuit inquantum homo, hac vita mortali aliquid proprium. Primo ex eo quod dicit, quod si quis aliquid proprium sibi dicit esse, alienum se facit ab electis Dei. Sed habens proprium ex hoc, quod proprium habet, non faceret se alienum ab electis Dei: si Christus, qui fuit caput electorum Dei, aliquid proprium habuisset, quia conformans se Christo in modo viuendi non se facit alienum à charitate Domini. Tertio ex eo quod dicit, quod Dominus hoc verbo docuit & opere compleuit: sed Dominus non docuisset hæc verbo, nec opere compleuisset, si ipse inquantum homo proprium aliquid habuisset. Ergo secundum determinationem sanctæ matris Ecclesiæ quæ errare non potest, Christus nullius rei temporalis proprietatem habuit. Item, extra de excess. prælat. c. Nimis pravum, habetur, quod Fratres Prædicatores Minores famulantur Christo pauperi in altissima paupertate. Sed Fratres Prædicatores & Minores nō sunt capaces secundum eorum regulam & professionem, aliquius proprietatis in speciali. Ergo multo magis Christus, cui prædicti Fratres famulantur in altissima paupertate, nō habuit in speciali proprietate aliculus rei: cū famulari Christo in altissima paupertate sit ipsum imitari & seq. & non præcedere. Item, in Regula beati Francisci ab vniversali Ecclesia approbata habetur in hæc verba: Regula & vita Fratrum Minorum hæc est, scil. Domini nostri Iesu Christi sanctæ Euangelii obseruare viuendo in obedientia sine proprio & castitate. Hæc sunt verba dictæ regulæ. Ex quibus verbis regulæ, imo vniuersalis Ecclesiæ regulam approbantis manifeste apparet, quod vita Euangelica Christi fuit absq; omni proprio viuere: quia regula, (inquit) & vita Minorum Fratrum hec est, scil. Domini nostri Iesu Christi sanctum Euangelium obseruare viuendo in obedientia sine proprio. Quod nequaq; verum esset, si Christus proprium aliquod habuisset. Item, Nicol.3. in decr. Exiit (Quae decretalis inserta in 6. lib. decre. & in Vienens. concilio approbata) dicit sic: Dicimus quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium rerum tam in speciali, li q etiā in cōmuni, pp̄ter Deum meritoria est & sancta, q; & Christus viam perfectionis ostendens verbo docuit & exemplo firmauit Haec Nicol.3. quae decretalis universali ecclesiae est recepta & approbata iam sunt quinque anni & amplius. Aut ergo universalis ecclesia erravit circa Christi paupertatem, quod est haereticum manifeste: aut ipse Dominus Iohannes errat circa ipsum negando Ecclesiae universalis determinationem, q; est haereticum evidenter. Ex quibus & quamplurimis aliis breuitatis causa omissis apparet manifeste, q; asserere Christum, sicut Dominus Iohannes asserit, habuisse in speciali proprietatem & dominium proprium vestimentorum, calciamentorum, alimentorum & loculorum, doctrinae Euangelicae & Apostolicae ac Ecclesiasticae contradicit & aduersatur expresse, propter quod est velut haereticum iudicandum: quia vt ait Augustinus de Trinitate li. 4. c. 6. Contra rationem nemo sobrius: contra scripturas nemo Christianus: contra Ecclesiam nemo pacificus senserit.
units.tr: Thirdly, the said error runs counter to the determination of the holy Church. For, as is read and found in the Rule of Saint Basil, which was approved by the universal Church, when his brethren asked him whether they might have anything of their own, Saint Basil answered in these words: This is contrary to that testimony which is written in the Acts of the Apostles concerning those who first believed. For there it is said thus: No one called anything of his goods his own, but they had all things in common. If, therefore, anyone says that something is his own, he undoubtedly makes himself a stranger to the elect of God and to the charity of the Lord, who taught by word and fulfilled by deed, and laid down his soul for his friends. If, then, he gave his soul for his friends, how will he not give the things that are outside himself, which are his? These are the words of Saint Basil in his Rule, approved by the universal Church. From these words of Basil, indeed of the universal Church which approved his rule, it appears in three ways that Christ, as a man, had no property during this mortal life. First, from the fact that Basil says, if anyone says that something is his own, he makes himself a stranger to the elect of God. But someone who had property would not, merely by having it, make himself a stranger to the elect of God, if Christ, who was the head of the elect of God, had had some property; for one who conforms himself to Christ in his manner of living does not make himself a stranger to the charity of the Lord. Thirdly, from the fact that he says the Lord taught this by word and fulfilled it by deed. But the Lord would not have taught this by word, nor fulfilled it by deed, if he himself, as a man, had had some property. Therefore, according to the determination of the holy mother Church, which cannot err, Christ had no ownership of any temporal thing. Likewise, in Extra, de excess. prælat., c. Nimis pravum, it is held that the Friars Preachers and Minor Friars serve Christ the poor in the utmost poverty. But the Friars Preachers and Minor Friars are not, according to their rule and profession, capable of any particular property. Therefore much more is it so with Christ, whom those friars serve in the utmost poverty, since to serve Christ in the utmost poverty is to imitate and follow him, not to go before him. Likewise, the Rule of Blessed Francis, approved by the universal Church, contains these words: The rule and life of the Minor Friars is this, namely, to observe the holy Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, living in obedience, without property and in chastity. These are the words of that rule. From these words of the rule, indeed of the universal Church which approved the rule, it clearly appears that the evangelical life of Christ was a life lived without any property, for the rule says: this is the rule and life of the Minor Friars, namely, to observe the holy Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, living in obedience without property. This would by no means be true if Christ had had any property. Likewise, Nicholas III, in the decretal Exiit (which decretal is inserted in the Sixth Book of Decretals and was approved at the Council of Vienne), says thus: We say that the renunciation of ownership of all things, both in particular and also in common, for God's sake, is meritorious and holy, and Christ, showing the way of perfection, taught it by word and confirmed it by example. Nicholas III said this; and the decretal has been received and approved by the universal Church for more than five years. Either, then, the universal Church has erred about Christ's poverty, which is manifestly heretical, or Lord John himself errs about him by denying the determination of the universal Church, which is evidently heretical. From these and very many other points, omitted for the sake of brevity, it clearly appears that to assert, as Lord John asserts, that Christ had in particular property and ownership of clothing, footwear, food and purses, expressly contradicts and opposes the doctrine of the Gospel, of the Apostles and of the Church, and on that account is to be judged as something like heresy; for, as Augustine says in On the Trinity, book 4, chapter 6: No sober man has ever held anything against reason, no Christian against Scripture, no peaceable man against the Church.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Tertius error Domini Iohannis in dicto libello contentus & dogmatizatus, est, q; Apostoli postquam fuerunt ad apostolatum assumpti, etiā post missionem Spiritus sancti habuerunt in speciali & sigillatim proprietatem & dominium proprium vestimentorum, alimentorum, caligarum & gladiorum ante passionem Christi. Qui quidem error contradicit & aduersatur aperte doctrinae Euangelicae & Apostolicae & Ecclesiasticae. Obuiat, inq; doctrinae Euangelicae: quia, vt habetur Mat.19. Petrus in persona omnium Apostolorum dixit: Domine: ecce nos reliquimus omnia, & secuti sumus te. Mar. vero 10. & Luc.17.c. habetur: Ecce nos dimisimus omnia & secuti sumus te. Quae quidem verba Petri intelligenda sunt de modo relinquendi & dimittendi omnia quo ad proprietatem & dominium. Quod patet dupliciter. Primo q; Petrus ibi, vt ex circumstantiis verborum patet, loquitur de modo omnia relinquendi perfecte & ultimate. Sed modus relinquendi omnia perfecte & ultimate est relinquere quo ad proprietatem, & non solum quo ad affectionem & curam superfluam. Alioquin frustra & inutiliter primi credentes reliquisent in speciali omnia quo ad proprietatem & dominium, nisi relinquere ipsa sic esset perfectius & virtuosius, q; relinquere ipsa solū quo ad affectionē & curam, q; sunt etronea. Quare relinquitur, quod predicta verba Petri intelliguntur de modo relinquendi & dimittendi omnia quo ad proprietatem & dominium: & p̄ consequens Apostoli in nulla re temporali habuerunt in speciali proprietate & dominium. Secundo patet hoc: q; non minus perfecte Apostoli omnia reliquerunt, q; ille iuuenis, cui Christus dixit: Vade & vende omnia q; habes & da pauperibus, reliquisset, si consilium seruasset. Patet, tum quia Petrus dixit predicta verba occasione iuuenis, qui Christi consilium in hoc seruare noluit: tum quia ille iuuenis non fuisset assumptus a Christo ad altiorem gradum perfectionis, quā Apostoli. Sed iuuenis debebat relinquere omnia q; habebat secundum Christi consilium quo ad proprietatem & dominium: quia vende, inquit, omnia quae habes & da pauperibus. Vendita autem & pauperibus data non remansissent amplius in dominio dantis. Ergo similiter Apostoli reliquerunt omnia quo ad proprietatem. Quae autem Apostoli semel ex perfectione virtutis reliquerunt: illa amplius stante Apostolica perfectione non resumpserunt, quia stante causa stat effectus. Ideo Luc. 9. ca. Nemo mittens manum suam ad aratrum & aspiciens retro aptus est regno Dei. Sed vt ostensum est, Apostoli reliquerunt omnia quo ad proprietatem & dominium ex perfectione virtutis. Ergo apostoli stante perfectione euangelica nunquam in aliqua re temporali proprietate vel dominium in speciali habuerunt. Unde Hier. scribes ad Heliodorum dicit sic: Non est tibi eadem causa q; caeteri: Dominū auscultā dicente: Si vis perfectus esse, vende omnia q; habes & da pauperibus & sequere me. Te autem perfectum esse pollicitus es: perfectum autem Christus nihil propter Christū habet: aut si propter Christū habet, perfectus non est. Haec sanctus Hieron. Ex qua auctoritate patet aperte, q; apostoli q; fuerunt assumpti ad statum perfectorum, reliquerunt omnia quo ad proprietatem & dominium. Quia perfectus, inquit, servus Christi nihil propter Christum habet, scil. quo ad proprietatem & dominium: q; quo ad vsum necessarium non est dubium aliquid fore habiturum. Item, sicut prius dictum est in secundo errore, Christus dicit Luc. 9. Omnis ex vobis q; non renunciauerit omnibus q; possidet, non potest meus esse discipulus. Sed apostoli fuerunt perfecti & supremi discipuli Christi. Ergo apostoli perfecte renunciauerunt omnibus temporalibus. Sed perfecte non renunciatur omnibus temporalibus, nisi renuncietur eis quo ad proprietatem & dominium: quia renunciare sic eis est perfectius, quam renunciare ipsis solum quo ad affectionem & curam, vt prius monstratum est. Ergo Apostoli non renunciauerunt proprietati & dominio omnium temporalium: & per consequens in nulla re temporali habuerunt in speciali proprietatem.
units.tr: The third error that Brother John contains and teaches in the said booklet is that the Apostles, after they were called to the apostolate, even after the sending of the Holy Spirit, held as individuals a special and particular ownership and personal dominion over clothing, food, shoes and swords, before Christ's passion. This error plainly contradicts and opposes the Gospel, Apostolic and ecclesiastical teaching. It conflicts first with the Gospel teaching, because, as is recorded in Matthew 19, Peter, speaking in the name of all the Apostles, said: "Lord, behold, we have left all and followed you." Mark 10 and Luke 17 have: "Behold, we have forsaken all and followed you." These words of Peter must be understood of the manner of leaving and giving up all things as regards ownership and dominion. This is clear in two ways. First, Peter there, as the circumstances of the words show, speaks of the manner of leaving all things perfectly and completely. But the manner of leaving all things perfectly and completely is to leave them as regards ownership, and not only as regards affection and superfluous care. Otherwise the first believers would have left everything in particular as regards ownership and dominion in vain and to no purpose, unless leaving them in this way were more perfect and virtuous than leaving them only as regards affection and care, which are erroneous. It follows, then, that the said words of Peter are understood of the manner of leaving and giving up all things as regards ownership and dominion; and consequently the Apostles held no temporal thing as their own particular property. Second, this is confirmed by the fact that the Apostles left everything no less perfectly than that young man to whom Christ said: "Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor," would have left, had he kept the counsel. This is shown both because Peter spoke those words on the occasion of the young man, who was unwilling to keep Christ's counsel in this matter, and because that young man would not have been called by Christ to a higher degree of perfection than the Apostles. But the young man ought to have left all that he had, according to Christ's counsel, as regards ownership and dominion, since he was told, "sell all that you have and give to the poor." Things sold and given to the poor would no longer remain in the dominion of the giver. Therefore the Apostles likewise left all things as regards ownership. Now, what the Apostles once left out of perfection of virtue, they did not take back again while that Apostolic perfection lasted, because while the cause remains, the effect remains. Hence Luke 9: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God." But, as has been shown, the Apostles left all things as regards ownership and dominion out of perfection of virtue. Therefore, while evangelical perfection lasted, the Apostles never held any temporal thing as their particular property or dominion. Hence Jerome, writing to Heliodorus, says this: "Your case is not the same as the others'. Listen to the Lord saying: 'If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and follow me.' But you promised to be perfect; yet the perfect man has nothing for Christ's sake, or if he has something for Christ's sake, he is not perfect." Thus holy Jerome. From this authority it is clear that the Apostles, who were called to the state of the perfect, left all things as regards ownership and dominion. For, he says, the perfect servant of Christ has nothing for Christ's sake, namely as regards ownership and dominion; for it is not doubtful that as regards necessary use he will have something. Likewise, as was said earlier under the second error, Christ says in Luke 9: "Whoever of you does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple." But the Apostles were the perfect and chief disciples of Christ. Therefore the Apostles renounced all temporal things perfectly. But all temporal things are not renounced perfectly unless they are renounced as regards ownership and dominion, since to renounce them in this way is more perfect than to renounce them only as regards affection and care, as was shown before. Therefore the Apostles did not renounce the ownership and dominion of all temporal things, and consequently they held no temporal thing as their particular property.

units.la: Secundo dictus error obuiat doctrinae apostolicae: quia, vt dictum est in secundo errore, in prima multitudine credentium nulli licuit in speciali habere proprietate nec dominium proprium alicuius rei. Ideo de ipsa scribitur Actuum 4.c. Nec quis q; eorum quae possidebat aliquid suum esse dicebat: sed erant illis omnia communia. Sed forma expropriationis Ecclesiae primitiuae ab apostolis ordinata & instituta non fuit altior nec perfectior ipsa expropriatione apostolorum. Tu quia expropriatio primitiuae Ecclesiae fuit instituta & ordinata ab apostolis iuxta, & non supra expropriationem apostolorum: tu q; status priorum credentium non fuit altior statu apostolorum. Si ergo in communitate primitiuae Ecclesiae nulli licuit in speciali habere proprietatem alicuius rei, vt prius dictum est, multo magis in communitate apostolorum, maxime post aduentum Spiritus sancti, nulli licuit in speciali habere proprietatem alicuius rei. Cuius oppositum Dominus Iohannes asserit: & per consequens doctrinae apostolicae contradicit.
units.tr: Second, the said error opposes the Apostolic teaching. For, as was said under the second error, in the first multitude of believers it was lawful for no one to have any particular property or personal ownership of anything. Hence it is written of that multitude in Acts 4: "Nor did anyone say that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them." But the form of expropriation of the primitive Church, ordained and instituted by the Apostles, was no higher or more perfect than the expropriation of the Apostles themselves. For the expropriation of the primitive Church was instituted and ordained by the Apostles in accordance with, and not above, the expropriation of the Apostles; and the state of the first believers was not higher than the state of the Apostles. If, then, in the community of the primitive Church it was lawful for no one to have particular property in anything, as was said before, much more in the community of the Apostles, especially after the coming of the Holy Spirit, was it lawful for no one to hold particular property in anything. Brother John asserts the opposite, and consequently contradicts Apostolic teaching.

units.la: Tertio dictus error contradicit doctrinae Ecclesiae, quoniam, vt habetur 19.q.1.c.6. Ex auctoritate, & est decredecretum beati Gregorii Papæ, Monachi tenent figuram Apostolorum. Sed monachis non licet habere in speciali proprietatem alicuius rei, vt habetur 12 q.1.c. Non dicatis, vbi sic dicitur: Non dicatis res aliquid habere proprium: sed sint vobis omnia communia. Et extra de statu monachorum & canonicorum regularium. c. Cum ad monasterium, in fine dicitur sic: Nec æstimet abbas quod super proprietate habenda possit cum aliquo monacho dispensare: quia abdicatio proprietatis, sicut etiam custodia castitatis, adeo est annexa regula monachali, quod contra eam nec summus pontifex posset licentiam indulgere. Hæc ibi. Ergo multo magis Apostoli, quorum figuram tenent monachi, non habuerunt in speciali proprietatem alicuius rei. Et oppositum dogmatizare est regulam monachorum, sicut erroneum, improbare: quod est hæreticum manifestum.
units.tr: Third, the said error contradicts the teaching of the Church, since, as is found in Decretum 19, q. 1, c. 6: "From the authority of the decree of blessed Pope Gregory: Monks hold the figure of the Apostles." But monks are not permitted to have any particular property, as is found in 12 q. 1 c.: "Do not say that anything is one's own, but let all things be common to you." And in the Extravagants, on the state of monks and regular canons, c. "Cum ad monasterium," at the end, it is said: "Let the abbot not think that he can dispense with any monk concerning the holding of property; for the renunciation of property, like the keeping of chastity, is so bound to the monastic rule that not even the supreme pontiff could grant license against it." Thus far there. Much more, then, the Apostles, whose figure the monks hold, did not have any particular property in anything. And to teach the opposite, and to condemn as erroneous the rule of the monks, is manifest heresy.

units.la: Item, sicut dictum est in secundo errore, beatus Basilius in sua Regula ab vniuersali Ecclesia approbata quærentibus Fratribus suis, si liceret ipsis habere aliquid proprium, respondit in hæc verba: Hoc contrarium est illi testimonio quod in Actibus Apostolorum de illis, qui primitus credebant, scriptum est. Ibi enim ita dicit: Nemo ex bonis suis quicquam proprium esse dicebat: sed erant illis communia omnia. Si quis ergo aliquid sibi proprium esse dicit, sine dubio alienum se facit ab electis Dei, & a charitate Domini, qui verbo docuit & opere complevit. Hoc sanctus Basilius in sua Regula ab vniuersali Ecclesia approbata.
units.tr: Likewise, as was said under the second error, blessed Basil, in his Rule approved by the universal Church, when his brethren asked whether it was lawful for them to have anything of their own, answered in these words: "This is contrary to that testimony which is written in the Acts of the Apostles about those who first believed. For there it is said: 'No one said that anything of his goods was his own, but all things were common to them.' If anyone therefore says that something is his own, he undoubtedly makes himself a stranger to the elect of God and to the charity of the Lord, who taught by word and fulfilled by deed." Thus holy Basil in his Rule, approved by the universal Church.

units.la: Sed habens proprium ex hoc, quod habet proprium, non se faceret alienum ab electis Dei, si Apostoli, qui fuerunt primi & præcipui electi Dei, aliquid proprium habuissent: quia conformans se in vita primis electis non se facit alienum ab electis Dei. Ergo secundum Regulam sancti Basilii ab vniuersali Ecclesia approbata Apostoli non habuerunt in speciali proprietatem alicuius rei.
units.tr: But one who has property by the very fact that he has property would not make himself a stranger to the elect of God, if the Apostles, who were the first and chief elect of God, had held any property; for one who conforms his life to the first elect does not make himself a stranger to the elect of God. Therefore, according to the Rule of holy Basil approved by the universal Church, the Apostles did not hold any particular property in anything.

units.la: Item, licut supra in secundo errore dictum est: in Regula sancti Francisci ab vniuersali Ecclesia approbata, sic habetur & continetur: Regula etiam vita Fratrum Minorum hæc est, scil. Domini nostri Iesu Christi sanctum Euangelium obseruare viuendo in obedientia sine proprio &c. Hæc verba dicte Regulæ. Sed Regula & vita Fratrum Minorum, quæ est sanctum Euangelium Domini nostri Iesu Christi obseruare, non esset viuere sine proprio, nisi vita Euangelica quo ad Christi consilia fuisset viuere sine proprio &c. Sine proprio autem viuere est absque omni proprietate viuere: quia negatio præpositionis præcedens terminum proprii negant ipsum vniuersaliter pro omni contento sub ipso. Ergo vita Euangelica quo ad consilia fuit viuere absque omni proprietate cuiuscunque rei: & per consequens Apostoli, qui fuerunt Christi professores Euangelii vixerunt absque omni proprietate rei temporalis.
units.tr: Likewise, as was said above in the second error: in the Rule of Saint Francis, approved by the universal Church, it is thus stated and contained: "The rule and life of the Friars Minor is this, namely, to observe the holy Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, living in obedience, without property, etc." These are the words of the said Rule. But the Rule and life of the Friars Minor, which is to observe the holy Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, would not be to live without property, unless the Evangelical life, as regards the counsels of Christ, were to live without property, etc. To live without property, however, is to live without any ownership whatever, because a negative preceding the word "property" denies it universally, for everything contained under it. Therefore the Evangelical life, as regards the counsels, was to live without any ownership of any thing whatever; and consequently the Apostles, who were the professors of Christ's Gospel, lived without ownership of any temporal thing.

units.la: Item, vt habetur 12.q.1.c. dilectissimis: Communis vsus omnium quæ sunt in hoc mundo omnibus hominibus esse debuit: sed per iniquitatem alius dixit hoc esse suum & alius illud. Et sic inter mortales facta est divisio. Et sicut non potest dividi aer nec splendor solis: ita nec reliqua quæ data sunt hominibus ad habendum dividi debere, sed habenda omnia esse communia. Istius consuetudinis more retento Apostoli eorumque discipuli vna nobiscum & vobiscum communem vitam duxerunt. Hæc verba ibi. Et est decretum beati Clementis, qui fuit in societate Apostolorum. Ex quibus verbis patet aperte & manifeste, quod sicut Apostoli non habuerunt in aere nec in splendore solis proprietatem nec dominium proprium: ita secundum beatum Clementem in nulla re temporali, quam vsi sunt, habuerunt in speciali proprietatem nec dominium proprium.
units.tr: Likewise, as is found in 12 q. 1, c. Dilectissimis: "The common use of all things that are in this world ought to belong to all men; but through iniquity one man said that this was his, and another that was his. And so division has come about among mortals. And just as neither the air nor the light of the sun can be divided, so neither should the remaining things that have been given to men for their possession be divided, but all things ought to be held in common. Retaining the custom of this way of life, the Apostles and their disciples led a common life, one with us and with you." These are the words there. And it is the decree of the blessed Clement, who was in the fellowship of the Apostles. From these words it is plain and manifest that, just as the Apostles had no ownership or proper dominion in the air or in the light of the sun, so, according to the blessed Clement, they had no special ownership or proper dominion in any temporal thing which they used.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus & consimilibus aliis breuitatis causa omissis patet manifeste, quod pertinaciter afferere & dogmatizare, sicut Dominus Iohannes asserit & dogmatizat, quod Apostoli habuerunt in speciali & sigillatim dominium proprium vestimentorum, alimentorum, caligarum & gladiorum, expresse contradicit & aduersatur doctrinæ Euangelicæ & doctrinæ Apostolicæ & Ecclesiasticæ sanctioni, propter quod est hæreticum iudicandum & censendum.
units.tr: From all these and other similar considerations, which for brevity's sake are omitted, it is manifestly clear that to assert stubbornly and to teach as dogma, as Lord John asserts and teaches, that the Apostles had in particular and individually proper dominion over garments, food, shoes and swords, expressly contradicts and opposes the Evangelical doctrine, the Apostolic doctrine, and the sanction of the Church, on account of which it is to be judged and held heretical.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Q Vartus error Domini Ioannis in dicto libello contentus & dogmatizatus, est quod Dominus Noster Iesus Christus non dedit aliam legem viuendi Apostolis quam discipulis: inter discipulos ibi specificans & specialiter numerans Ioseph ab Arimathia, qui fuit diues homo, in speciali secundum Matthæum Euangelistam: & Matthæ & Mariæ quæ secundum ipsum fuerunt dominæ castri: & Lazarum, Simonem Leprosum, & Dorcam, qui secundum ipsum etiam habuerunt in speciali dominium bonorum temporalium. Qui quidem error manifeste obuiat & repugnat tam doctrinæ Euangelicæ quam Ecclesiasticæ: quoniam si Dominus noster Iesus Christus non dedit aliam legem viuendi Apostolis & discipulis, vt dominus Iohannes dicit, & discipuli, quos ipse specialiter nominat & specificat & Apostolis in mundi contemptu æquiparat, habuerunt in speciali & sigillatim bonorum dominium temporalium: & aliqui ipsorum habuerunt in speciali secundum ipsum dominium castri: & aliquis eorum in speciali secundum ipsum etiam fuit diues homo: Sequitur necessario & euidenter, quod Apostoli potuerunt habere in speciali & sigillatim dominia castrorum & villarum, ac diuitiarum & bonorum temporalium quorumcunque: quod est manifeste hæreticum: quia vt habetur Matt. 19. c. Si vis perfectus esse vende omnia quæ habes: & da pauperibus & veni sequere me. Ex quibus manifeste patet, quod cum perfectione Apostolica non stat secundum Christi consilium retentio dominii castrorum, nec villarum, nec etiam diuitiarum quarumcunque: qa si vis, inquit, perfectus esse vade omnia quæ habes & da pauperibus. Venditio autem omnium & ipsorum pauperibus largitio de directo respicit dominii translationem & abnegationem. Quare si Apostoli potuerunt habere in speciali & sigillatim dominia castrorum & villarum, ac aliorum bonorum quorumcunque, sequitur manifeste quod ipsi non fuerunt perfecti, nec de genere perfectorum: imo sequitur, quod ipsi nunc fuerunt assumpti ad statum Euangelicæ perfectionis, cum Euangelica perfectio taliū dominiorum abnegatione includat: quod est omnino hæreticum. Quare dictus error manifeste sapit hæresim. Contra istum errorem in speciali est beatus Augustinus libro De bono coniugali, vbi dicit sic: Bonum erat quod faciebant, qui de sua substantia Christo ac Discipulis eius necessaria ministrabant: sed melius qui omnem suam substantiam dimiserunt vt expeexpeditiores eundem Dominum sequerentur. Hæc Augustinus. Ex quibus patet, q; Martha, & Maria, quæ Christo de sua substantia ministrabant, nō fuerunt in abdicatione temporalium pares Apostolis, qui omnem suam substantiā dimiserunt, vt Christū expeditiores sequerentur. Et ita falsum est & erroneū, quod Christus non dederit aliā legem viuendi Apostolis, q; dictis discipulis, quos Dominus Iohannes nominat, & Apostolis in modo viuendi æquiparat. Contra prædictum etiam errorē sunt directe omnia addueta contrā tertium errorē præcedentem: & plura alia breuitatis causa omissa.
units.tr: The fourth error of Master John, contained and taught in the said pamphlet, is that our Lord Jesus Christ gave the Apostles no other rule of living than he gave his disciples. There he names and specifically lists, as disciples, Joseph of Arimathea, who according to Matthew was a rich man; Matthew and Mary, who according to the same author were ladies of a castle; and Lazarus, Simon the Leper and Dorcas, who according to him also held ownership of temporal goods in particular. This error plainly opposes and conflicts with both the Gospel doctrine and the teaching of the Church. For if our Lord Jesus Christ gave the Apostles and disciples no other rule of living, as Master John says, and the disciples whom he names and specifies, and whom he equates with the Apostles in contempt of the world, held the ownership of temporal goods individually and severally, and some of them held the ownership of a castle, according to him, and one of them was a rich man, according to him too, then it necessarily and evidently follows that the Apostles could have held individually and severally the ownership of castles, villages, riches and temporal goods of every kind. That is plainly heretical. For it is written in Matthew 19: "If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me." From this it is plain that retaining the ownership of castles, villages or any riches is not consistent with Apostolic perfection according to Christ's counsel; for he says, "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor." Selling everything and giving it to the poor directly concerns the transfer and renunciation of ownership. So if the Apostles could have held individually and severally the ownership of castles, villages and other goods of every kind, it clearly follows that they were not perfect, nor of the class of the perfect. Indeed it follows that they were then taken up into the state of Gospel perfection, since Gospel perfection includes renunciation of such ownership; and that is wholly heretical. Therefore the said error plainly savours of heresy. Against this error in particular is Saint Augustine in his book On the Good of Marriage, where he says: "What they did was good, those who ministered necessities to Christ and his disciples out of their own substance; but better were those who gave up all their substance so as to follow the same Lord more unencumbered." Thus Augustine. From these words it is clear that Martha and Mary, who ministered to Christ out of their own substance, were not equal to the Apostles in renouncing temporal goods, for the Apostles gave up all their substance so as to follow Christ more unencumbered. So it is false and erroneous that Christ gave no other rule of living to the Apostles than to the said disciples whom Master John names and whom he equates with the Apostles in way of life. Everything adduced against the third error above, and many other points omitted for brevity, are also directly aimed against this error.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Quintus error domini Iohannis in dicto libello contentus & dogmatizatus, est q; Apostoli stante apostolica perfectione potuerūt licite recipere bona immobilia, vt agros & pdia quo ad dominiū in cōmuni. Et q; talia in Iudæa non receperunt, non fuit quod illa repugnarent apostolicæ perfectioni, sed qa præuidebant in spiritu se transituros ad gentes. Et fallaciter imponit Melchiadi Papæ. Qui error aperte obuiat veritati Euangelicæ & Ecclesiasticæ determinationi: Quoniam, vt sæpe dictum est, Christus cuidā adolescenti quærenti ad perfectionem pertingere respondit: Si vis perfectus esse vende omnia quæ habes: & da pauperibus: & veni sequere me: & habebis thesaurū in cœlo. Constat autē, quod simpliciter vedita non remanissent amplius in dominio vendentis in speciali nec in cōmuni: qa illa non debebat vendere cōmunitati Apostolorū, sed aliis hominibus. Ergo volens ad gradū Apostolicæ perfectionis ascendere, debebat secundū Christi consilii relinquere bona immobilia quo ad dominiū in speciali & in cōmuni. Et ita cum Apostolica perfectione non stat retentio dominii rerū immobilium in speciali nec in cōmuni. Causa ergo primaria & essentialis, quare Apostoli bona immobilia in cōmuni nō receperunt in Iudæa, nō fuit, qa præuidebant in spiritu se transituros ad gentes: sed quia dominiū talium nō poterat stare cū Apostolica perfectione secundū Christi consilii: qa si vis, inqt, perfectus esse. & non inqt, si vis transire ad gentes; vende omnia q; habes &c. Nec Melchiades Papa dixit, nec sensit, q; Apostoli p seipsis nō receperunt pdia in Iudæa, qa p̄sciebant se transituros ad gentes: sed dicit, q; Apostoli nō receperunt pdia in Iudæa p Ecclesia primitiua, q; regebat & gubernabat: qa præuidebant in spiritu Ecclesiā futurā in gentibus, sicut patet 12. q. 1. c. futurā. Licet etiā ratio & causa Melchiadis Papæ pro ipsa Ecclesia primitiua nō fuerit ratio literalis & principalis, sed accessoria & allegorica. Itē, q; bus ex perfectione virtutis nō licuit recipere in cōmuni bona mobilia quo ad dominiū: qa nō minus distrahit à perfectione virtutis bonorū immobiliū, q; dominiū bonorū mobiliū. Sed Apostolis, pter contemptū, & non pter futurū transitum ad gentes, fuit eis præceptū à Christo, Matt. 10. c. Ne possiderent aurū & argentū: quia licet pdia & agros Apostoli nō potuissent secū deferre ad gentes, dummodo eis licitū fuisset, Apostolis fuit interdictū ne possideret aurum & argentū & ne portaret calciamenta pter mundi contemptū & virtutis exemplū, & nō pter futurū transitū ad gētes: & hoc in speciali vel in cōmuni quātū ad cōmunitatē ipsorū speciale & pria. Et quomodocūq; talia, scil. aurū & argētū quo ad dominiū receperint, Christi Euangeliū venale fecissent, & cursum Euangelii impediuissent. Ergo multo magis Apostolis propter mundi contemptū & virtutis exemplū, & nō propter futurū transitū ad gentes, fuit inhibitū ne possideret bona immobilia quo ad dominium in cōmuni. Itē, nō minus distrahit à perfectione Euangelii retentio dominii bonorū immobiliū in cōmuni, q; solū renūciare suis q; sunt domi. Sed vt pater Lu. 9. ille q; renuit renuntiare suis, q; erāt domi, nō fuit aptus nec idoneus ad pdicatione Euangelii, sed ab ea à Christo fuit repulsus. Ergo multo magis retinēs sibi dominiū bonoꝝ immobiliū in cōmuni non est perfecte aptus nec perfecte dispositus ad pdicatione Euangelii. Ideo Christus, q nō erat transituras ad gētes, sed in Iudæa moriturus, pter Euangelii suū reliqt dominiū quoꝝcunq; bonorū immobiliū: qa nec domū nec pdiū aliq; legitur habuisse in speciali nec in cōmuni. Et eadē causa Apostoli se Christo cōformātes, talia in Iudæa nō receperunt, p seipsis in speciali nec in cōmuni: qa eadē causa abdicationis reporalium & nō alia fuit in Christo & in Apostolis ipsum sequētibus. Et ita talis doctrina erronea totū Euangeliū puertit & corrupit. Itē, dictus error obuiat directe & aperte ecclesiæ determinationi: qa, vt habetur in decretis Exiit. Domini Nicolai 3. (quæ decr. in corpore iuris suit clausa, & in sext. lib. decr. p Bonifacii 8 inserta, & p cōstitutionē q incipit Exiui de Paradyso, in Vienensi cōcilio facta approbata, ac p consequēs ab vniuersali ecclesia absq; cōtradictione aliquā recepta & approbata:) sic dicitur: Dicimus q abdicatio pprietatis omniū rerū tā in speciali quā in cōmuni, pter Dei meritoria est & sancta, quā Christus via perfectionis ostendēs verbo docuit & exemplo firmauit, quāq; primi fundatores militantis Ecclesiæ, put ab ipso fonte hauserant in volentes pfecte viuere p doctrinā ac vitā ipsorū alueos dirinarūt. Hæc Nicolaus prædictus in dicta decre. Ex qua decretali ab vniuersali Ecclesia recepta & approbata apparet manifeste, quod Apostoli stante apostolica perfectione non potuerunt retinere in speciali nec in cōmuni pprietatē bonorū immobilium: qa dicit, q Christus via pfectionis ostendēs, & Apostoli etiā volentes pfecte viuere: & ita secundū determinatione vniuersalis Ecclesiæ causa abdicationis proprietatis omniū rerum in speciali & in cōmuni in Christo & Apostolis fuit perfectionis exemplū, & nō transitus futurus ad gentes.
