Ex quibus & q pluribus aliis causa breuitatis omissis, apparet quod dictus error directe aduersatur & cōtradicit doctrinæ Euangelicæ vitæ Christi & Apostolorum, & vniuersalis ecclesiæ determinationi, propter q impingit in articulum fidei: Credo in vnā sanctā catholicā & Apostolicam Ecclesiam.
units.tr: The fifth error of Master John, contained and taught in the said pamphlet, is that the Apostles, while Apostolic perfection stood, could lawfully receive immovable goods, such as fields and estates, in common as to ownership. And that they did not receive such things in Judea was not because these were incompatible with Apostolic perfection, but because they foresaw in the Spirit that they would pass over to the Gentiles. He also falsely attributes this to Pope Melchiades. This error openly opposes the Gospel truth and the determination of the Church. For, as has often been said, Christ answered a certain young man who asked how to attain perfection: "If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me, and you shall have treasure in heaven." It is certain that, once sold, these things would not have remained in the ownership of the seller, either individually or in common, since he was not to sell them to the community of the Apostles but to other men. Therefore one who wishes to rise to the degree of Apostolic perfection must, according to Christ's counsel, leave behind immovable goods, both individually and in common. Thus retaining ownership of immovable things, either individually or in common, is not consistent with Apostolic perfection. The primary and essential reason, then, why the Apostles did not receive immovable goods in common in Judea was not that they foresaw in the Spirit that they would pass over to the Gentiles, but that ownership of such things could not stand together with Apostolic perfection according to Christ's counsel. For he says, "If you wish to be perfect," not "If you wish to pass over to the Gentiles": sell all that you have, and so on. Nor did Pope Melchiades say, or mean, that the Apostles themselves did not receive estates in Judea because they knew they would pass over to the Gentiles. He says rather that the Apostles did not receive estates in Judea through the primitive Church, which ruled and governed, because it foresaw in the Spirit the Church that would be in the Gentiles, as appears in 12 q. 1, c. "futurā". Although the reason and cause given by Pope Melchiades for the primitive Church itself was not literal and principal, but secondary and allegorical. Likewise, for the sake of perfection of virtue it was not lawful to receive movable goods in common as to ownership, for retaining ownership of movable goods distracts from the perfection of virtue no less than ownership of immovable goods does. But the Apostles were forbidden by Christ, not because of a future passage to the Gentiles but on account of contempt of the world, to possess gold and silver (Matthew 10): "Do not possess gold or silver." For although the Apostles could not have carried estates with them to the Gentiles, provided it had been lawful for them, they were forbidden to possess gold and silver, and to carry shoes, out of contempt for the world and as an example of virtue, and not because of a future passage to the Gentiles. This applies to ownership individually or in common, as far as their common life is concerned, in particular and first of all. And in whatever way they had received such things, namely gold and silver, as ownership, they would have made the Gospel of Christ a matter of sale and hindered the course of the Gospel. Therefore it was much more the case that the Apostles were forbidden, for the sake of contempt of the world and as an example of virtue, and not because of a future passage to the Gentiles, to possess immovable goods as ownership in common. Again, retaining ownership of immovable goods in common distracts from the perfection of the Gospel no less than merely renouncing those who are at home. But as appears in Luke 9, the man who refused to renounce those who were at home was not fit or suitable for preaching the Gospel, and Christ rejected him from it. Therefore one who retains for himself ownership of immovable goods in common is much less perfectly fit or perfectly disposed for preaching the Gospel. Hence Christ, who was not to pass over to the Gentiles but was to die in Judea, left behind for the sake of his Gospel the ownership of all immovable goods; for it is not read that he held any house or estate, either individually or in common. For the same reason the Apostles, conforming themselves to Christ, did not receive such things in Judea, either for themselves individually or in common, since the cause of renouncing temporal things was one and the same in Christ and in the Apostles who followed him, and no other. And so such erroneous doctrine overturns and corrupts the whole Gospel. Again, the said error directly and openly opposes the determination of the Church. For, as is found in the decretal of Pope Nicholas III, Exiit (which was closed into the body of canon law and inserted into the Sext by Boniface VIII, and was approved by the constitution beginning Exiui de Paradyso, made at the Council of Vienne, and consequently received and approved by the universal Church without any contradiction), it is said thus: "We declare that the renunciation of ownership of all things, both individually and in common, is meritorious and holy before God, which Christ taught by word and confirmed by example, showing it as the way of perfection; and which the first founders of the militant Church, drawing it from its very source, handed down by their teaching and life to those wishing to live perfectly." Thus Nicholas aforesaid in the said decretal. From this decretal, received and approved by the universal Church, it appears clearly that the Apostles, while Apostolic perfection stood, could not retain ownership of immovable goods either individually or in common. For it says that Christ showed it as the way of perfection, and that the Apostles too wished to live perfectly. And so, according to the determination of the universal Church, the cause of renouncing ownership of all things, individually and in common, in Christ and in the Apostles was an example of perfection, and not a future passage to the Gentiles. From these points, and from many others omitted for brevity, it appears that the said error directly opposes and contradicts the Gospel doctrine of the life of Christ and the Apostles and the determination of the universal Church; on account of which it strikes at an article of faith: "I believe in one holy, catholic and Apostolic Church."

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Sextus error Domini Iohannis in dicto libello contentus & dogmatizatus, est, quod Christus nunquam consuluit Apostolis nec suis Discipulis abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum ad minus in communi. Qui quidem error manifeste obuiat & repugnat determinationi vniuersalis Ecclesiæ & Euangelicæ doctrinæ. Determinationi, inquam, ecclesiæ vniuersalis repugnat: quia, vt dictum est in quinto errore præcedente, Dominus Nicolaus tertius diffinit & determinat in hæc verba: Dicimus q; abdicatio proprietatis omnium rerum tam in speciali q; in communi propter Deum meritoria est & sancta: quam & Christus viam perfectionis ostendens verbo docuit & exemplo firmauit &c. Ex qua decretali patet manifeste, q; Christus verbo & facto consuluit Apostolis ac aliis discipulis volentibus perfectionis sequi abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum in speciali ac etiam in communi; cuius oppositum Dominus Iohannes dogmatizat. Prædicta autem decretalis Domini Nicolai extitit ab vniuersali ecclesia recepta & approbata: quia illa determinatio seu diffinitio, quæ vbique terrarum apud cunctos Christi fideles per quinquaginta annos & amplius extitit publice & libere absque contradictione aliqua tam in clero quàm in populo prædicata & annunciata: & in scholis per omnia studia Vniuersitatum sub discretione præcepti sicut cetera Decretalis fideliter lecta & exposita: & in iudiciis & extra sicut sana & catholica reputata & iudicata: & in contrarium dogmatizantes & docentes cuiuscunq; status existerent sententia excommunicationis lata & religioni ab vniuersali ecclesia approbatæ ad comprobandum impositæ & seruata in corpore iuris canonici: & per constitutionem in generali concilio facta approbata, intelligitur ab vniuersali ecclesia recepta & approbata: qa si talis determinatio non foret determinatio vniuersalis ecclesiæ: tunc nunq; aliq; foret determinatio vniuersalis ecclesiæ, sed prædicta diffinitio Nicolaii tertii vbiq; terrarum apud cunctos fideles Christi per quinquaginta annos & amplius tam in clero q; in populo extitit publice & libere ac solenniter absq; contradictione aliqua prædicata, annunciata, & commendata in scholis: etiā per omnia studia Vniuersitatum sub discretione præcepti, sicut cetera decretales, lecta & fideliter exposita, & in contrarium dogmatizantes & docentes cuiuscunq; status, & conditionis existant, sententia excommunicationis lata, & religioni Fratrum Minorum ab vniuersali ecclesia approbatæ, sicut de substantia & fundamento suæ regulæ ad seruandum impositæ: ac etiā per quinquaginta annos & amplius à toto Ordine inuiolabiliter obseruata: & per Papā Bonifacium octauum 6. lib. decretalium sub titulo de verborum significatione inserta, & clausa p constitutione Dn. Clementis 5. q; incipit: Exiuis de Paradiso, in Vienensi Concilio edita approbatam: sicut omnia prædicta notoria vbiq; existunt. Quare dicta diffinitio intelligitur veraciter ab vniuersali ecclesia approbata. E. Dns Iohannes publice dogmatizās oppositū publicæ determinationi vniuersalis ecclesiæ se opponit: & per consequens in articulū fidei impingit: & non solū determinationi vniuersalis ecclesiæ se publice opponit, sed etiā, q; peius est, ipsam determinationē vniuersalis ecclesiæ sicut hæretica condenat, & iudicialiter sententiat, quia in sua constitutione, imo potius destitutione, Cū inter nullas, assertione dicentiū Christū & Apostolos non habuisse aliquid in speciali vel in communi, sicut hæretica declarat. Etin constitutione, Quia quorundā, omnes & singulos asserentes verbo vel scripto Christū & Apostolos non habuisse aliquid in speciali, vel in communi, condemnat, sicut hæreticos, & tanq; hæreticos esse censendos. Quare necessario sequitur, q; aut vniuersalis ecclesia vsq; pūc fuerit in errore & hæresi circa vitā Christi & Apostolorū, q; est hæreticū manifeste: Aut ipse Dn. Iohannes incidit in hæresim manifeste determinationem catholicam sanctæ matris ecclesiæ negando, & ipsam condemnando. Dictus etiam error obviat doctrinæ euangelicæ, quia, vt habetur Matt. 19. Marc. 10. & Luc. 18. Petrus in persona omnium Apostolorū dicit: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia (seu, dimisimus omnia) quæ verba Petri sunt intelligenda quo ad proprietatem & dominium, vt ostensum est in tertio errore: quia verba importantia vltimatā perfectionem Apostolorum non sunt minoris perfectionis, quam verba importantia vltimatam perfectionem primorū credentium: sicut status Apostolorū non fuit imperfectior statu primorū credentiū. Sed verba Act. 4. de credentibus dicta: Nec quisquis eorū &c. intelliguntur quo ad abdicationem proprietatis & dominii, sicut supra patuit. E. & hæc verba Petri, q; exprimunt vltimatā perfectionē Apostolorū quo ad mundi contemptū, qua nulla alia in scripturis quo ad mundi contemptū potior inuenitur, sunt intelligenda quo ad proprietatē & dominiū. Quod etiam per illud patet, q; August. dicit in libro de bono coniugali sic: Bonum fecerunt qui de sua substantia Christo, ac eius discipulis necessaria ministrabant. Sed melius, qui omnem suam substantiam dimiserunt, vt expeditiores eunde Dominū sequerentur. Hæc August. Prædicta etiā verba Petri sunt intelligenda in speciali & in communi. Quod patet primo, quia vbi nullus canon distinguit, nec nos distinguere debemus, quia aliter talis distinctio esset fictitia & vana. Sed nullus trium Euangelistarum prædicta verba Petri recitantium dicit plus in speciali quam in communi, sed quilibet eorum recitat dixisse Petrum simpliciter & absolute: Nos reliquimus omnia, seu dimisimus omnia. Nec ex aliquo alio passu Scripturæ habetur, q; debeant intelligi plus in speciali, q; in communi. Ergo in speciali, & in communi intelligenda sunt. Secundo quia verba communiter & indistincte prolata ex natura & forma verborum debent intelligi in communi & non in speciali solum. Sed Petrus dicit communiter & indistincte pro omnib' Apostolis: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia: nullam mentione faciendo plus de speciali q; de communi. E. in speciali & in communi intelligēda sunt. Tertio quia non minus perfecte Apostoli omnia reliquerunt, quā ille cui Christus dicit: vende omnia quæ habes &c. reliquisset, si Christi consilium seruasset. Sed ille si Christi consilium perfecte seruasset, debebat relinquere omniaquæ habebat in speciali & in communi: quia debebat omnia quæ habebat vendere & pauperibus dare. Vendita autem & pauperibus data non remansissent amplius in eius dominio in speciali nec in communi. Quare similiter Apostoli omnia vtroq; modo reliquerunt. Quarto quia verba importantia perfectionem Apostolorū non debent distrahi nec diminui, sed integre & plene, sicut sonant, exponi. Aliter enim esset detrahere & diminuere de perfectione Apostolorum, quod est impium & insanum. Sed prædicta verba Petri important quo ad mundi contemptum vltimatam perfectionem Apostolorum. Ergo non debent distrahi nec diminui, sed integre & plene, sicut sonant, exponi & intelligi. Sed dicere q; intelligantur in speciali & nō in communi, cū nullius euāgelistarū plā dicat in speciali q; in communi, est ipsa distrahere & diminuere, & à perfecto sensu trahere. Ergo in speciali & in communi intelligēda sunt: & hoc quo ad proprietatem & dominium, vt prius dictum est. E. Apostoli omnia reliquerunt in speciali & in communi quo ad dominium. Cuius oppositum Dominus Iohannes pertinaciter asserit, & ita determinationi vniuersalis ecclesiæ & doctrinæ euangelicæ contradicit.
units.tr: The sixth error contained and dogmatised by Dominus Iohannes in the said little book is that Christ never counselled his Apostles or his disciples to renounce the ownership of all things, at least in common. This error plainly opposes and contradicts the determination of the universal Church and the evangelical doctrine. It contradicts, I say, the determination of the universal Church: because, as was said in the fifth error above, Lord Nicholas III defines and determines in these words: We say that the renunciation of ownership of all things, both in particular and in common, for God's sake is meritorious and holy, which Christ also taught in words, showing the way of perfection, and confirmed by example, etc. From this decretal it is plainly evident that Christ, by word and by deed, counselled the Apostles and the other disciples who wished to follow perfection to renounce ownership of all things, both in particular and also in common; and the opposite of this Lord John dogmatises. Now the aforesaid decretal of Lord Nicholas has been received and approved by the universal Church. For that determination or definition, which for fifty years and more has existed everywhere in the world among all the faithful of Christ, publicly and freely, without any contradiction, has been preached, announced and commended, both among clergy and among people; it has been read and faithfully expounded in the schools, in all the studies of the universities, under the discretion of precept, like the other Decretals; sentence of excommunication has been pronounced against those who dogmatise and teach the contrary, of whatever status or condition they may be; it has been imposed, to be observed, on the religion of the Friars Minor, approved by the universal Church, as part of the substance and foundation of their rule; it has also been inviolably observed for fifty years and more by the whole Order; it was inserted by Pope Boniface VIII in the sixth book of the Decretals under the title on the meaning of words, and was enclosed by the constitution of Lord Clement V, which begins: Exiuis de Paradiso, issued at the Council of Vienne, and so approved; just as all the aforesaid things are notorious everywhere. Wherefore the said definition is rightly understood to be approved by the universal Church. Therefore Lord John, by publicly dogmatising the opposite of the public determination of the universal Church, sets himself against it, and consequently assails an article of faith; and not only does he publicly oppose the determination of the universal Church, but also, what is worse, he condemns that very determination of the universal Church as heretical and pronounces judgment upon it, for in his constitution, or rather deposition, Cum inter nullas, he declares heretical the assertion of those who say that Christ and the Apostles had nothing either in particular or in common. And in the constitution Quia quorundam he condemns all and each of those who assert by word or writing that Christ and the Apostles had nothing, either in particular or in common, and declares them to be considered heretics and as heretics. Wherefore it necessarily follows either that the universal Church has until now been in error and heresy concerning the life of Christ and the Apostles, which is manifestly heretical; or that Lord John himself has fallen into manifest heresy by denying and condemning the catholic determination of holy mother Church. This error also opposes evangelical doctrine, because, as is found in Matt. 19, Mark 10 and Luke 18, Peter in the person of all the Apostles says: Behold, we have left all things (or, we have forsaken all things). These words of Peter are to be understood with respect to ownership and dominion, as has been shown under the third error; for words expressing the ultimate perfection of the Apostles are not of lesser perfection than words expressing the ultimate perfection of the first believers, just as the state of the Apostles was not more imperfect than the state of the first believers. But the words of Acts 4 spoken of the believers: Neither did any one of them, etc., are understood with respect to renunciation of ownership and dominion, as was made plain above. Therefore these words of Peter, which express the ultimate perfection of the Apostles in contempt of the world, than which no other greater is found in the Scriptures in respect of contempt of the world, are to be understood with respect to ownership and dominion. This is also made clear by what Augustine says in his book On the Good of Marriage: They did well who ministered of their substance to Christ and his disciples as they needed. But better were those who gave up all their substance, so as to follow the same Lord more unencumbered. Thus Augustine. The aforesaid words of Peter are also to be understood both in particular and in common. This is clear, first, because where no canon makes a distinction, neither should we make one, since otherwise such a distinction would be feigned and vain. But none of the three Evangelists who record the aforesaid words of Peter says that he spoke more of particular things than of common things; rather each of them records that Peter said simply and absolutely: We have left all things, or we have forsaken all things. Nor does any other passage of Scripture show that they must be understood more of particular things than of common. Therefore they are to be understood both in particular and in common. Second, because words spoken in common and without distinction, by their nature and form, ought to be understood in common and not only in particular. But Peter speaks in common and without distinction on behalf of all the Apostles: Behold, we have left all things, making no mention of particular things more than of common. Therefore they are to be understood both in particular and in common. Third, because the Apostles left all things no less perfectly than he to whom Christ says: Sell all that you have, etc., would have left them, had he kept Christ's counsel. But if he had kept Christ's counsel perfectly, he would have had to leave all that he had, both in particular and in common, since he was to sell all that he had and give it to the poor. But things sold and given to the poor would no longer have remained in his dominion, either in particular or in common. Wherefore the Apostles likewise left all things in both ways. Fourth, because words expressing the perfection of the Apostles ought not to be pulled apart or diminished, but expounded whole and entire, as they sound. For otherwise it would be to detract from and diminish the perfection of the Apostles, which is impious and mad. But the aforesaid words of Peter express, with respect to contempt of the world, the ultimate perfection of the Apostles. Therefore they ought not to be pulled apart or diminished, but expounded and understood whole and entire, as they sound. But to say that they are to be understood of particular things and not of common, when none of the Evangelists says more of particular things than of common, is itself to pull apart and diminish, and to drag them away from the perfect sense. Therefore they are to be understood both in particular and in common; and this with respect to ownership and dominion, as was said before. Consequently the Apostles left all things, both in particular and in common, as regards dominion. The opposite of this Lord John stubbornly asserts, and thus contradicts the determination of the universal Church and the evangelical doctrine.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: SEptimus error Domini Iohannis est, quod Apostoli nunquam voluerunt omnia relinquere, nec vnquam votum relinquendi omnia emiserunt. Qui error aduersatur doctrinæ ecclesiasticæ & euangelicæ. Doctrinæ, inquam ecclesiasticæ aduersatur & contradicit: quia, vt habetur 16. q. 1. c. ex auctoritate, & est decretum beati Gregorii Papæ, Monachi tenent figuram Apostolorum. Sed Monachi vouent abdicationem proprietatis omnium, vt patet extr. de stat. mo. & cano. regularium c. Cum ad monasterium. Ergo multo magis Apostoli, quorum figuram tenent monachi, voluerunt abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum, cum figura non excedat veritatem. Item Alex. 4. in condemnatione libelli editi contra statum Fratrum Predicatorum & Minorum, determinat & diffinit, quod obseruantia dictorum Fratrum tenet formam euangelicæ perfectionis. Sed dicti Fratres vouent abdicationem proprietatis rerum. Ergo multo magis Apostoli, qui fuerunt primi & præcipui obseruatores euangelii, cuius perfectionis dictorum Fratrum obseruantia formam tenet, voluerunt sine proprio viuere. Item in regula sancti Francisci ab vniuersali ecclesia approbata habetur in hæc verba: regula & vita Fratrum Minorum, hoc est, Domini nostri Iesu Christi sanctum euangelium obseruare &c. Sed Minores, quorum vita & regula est sanctum euangelium obseruare, vouent abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum in speciali & in communi, vt patet per eorundem regulam & declarationes ab ecclesia Romana eis datas. Ergo multo magis Apostoli, qui fuerunt primi professores euangelii, voluerunt abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum in speciali & in communi. Item Nicolaus 3. in decr. Exiit, loquens de abdicatione per votum omnium rerum in speciali & in communi, dicit sic: Porro cum regula ipsa expresse contineat, quod Fratres nihil sibi appropriant, nec domum, nec locum, nec aliquam rem, sitque declaratum per eundem Greg. 9. predecessorem nostrum & nonnullos alios, hoc seruari debere tam in speciali quam in communi, quam sic artam abdicationem venenosis obtrectationibus, aliquorum insensata deprauauit astutia, ne Fratrum eorundem perfectionis claritas imperitis sermonibus lacesseretur: Dicimus q abdicatio proprietatis omnium rerum tam in speciali quam in communi propter Deum meritoria est & sancta, quam & Christus viam perfectionis ostendens verbo docuit & exemplo firmauit. &c. Hæc Nicolaus 3. Qui loquitur de abdicatione omnium rerum in speciali & in communi facta per votum, quod patet ex hoc, quod loquitur de abdicatione omnium rerum in speciali & in communi Fratrum Minorum. Abdicatio autem Fratrum Minorum votum includit. Et hanc abdicationem omnium rerum in speciali & in communi Fratrum Minorum, per votum factam dicit, quod Christus verbo docuit & exemplo firmauit; quod Apostoli eam per doctrinæ ac vitæ ipsorum alueos deriuarunt. Ergo secundum ipsum Apostoli vitā & doctrina deriuarunt in alios votum abdicandi proprietatem omnium rerum in speciali & in communi. Et dicta diffinitio ab vniuersali ecclesia extitit approbata & accepta, vt in errore præcedenti ostensum est. Ergo Dominus Iohannes dogmatizando, quod Apostoli non voluerunt relinquere omnia quo ad proprietatem & dominium determinationi vniuersalis ecclesiæ se opponit. Item ad hoc est expresse August. 17. lib. de ciuit. Dei cap. 4. dicens sic: Dixerant enim illi potentes: Ecce nos dimisimus omnia & secuti sumus te. Hoc votum potentissimi vouerant. Sed unde hoc eis, nisi ab illo, de quo hoc continue dictum est: damnas votum vouenti. Hoc August. Et quod Augustinus intelligat, quod Apostoli voluerunt relinquere omnia, & sequi Christum: patet ex hoc, quod prædicatum cadens simpliciter & absolute ac indistincte super aliquod copulatum, cadit ex natura sua super vtramque partem copulati: quia ad veritatem copulatiuam requiritur quod vtraq; pars sit vera. Sed istud prædicatum, hoc votum potentissimi voluerant, cadit simpliciter & absolute ac indistincte super illud copulatum: Ecce nos dimisimus omnia & secuti sumus te. Ergo votum cadit super vtramq; partem istius copulati: & per consequens Apostoli voluerunt dimittere omnia, & non solum sequi Christum. Item, ad hoc est beatus Greg. Papa super euangelia in homeliis Petri & Andreæ: vbi dicit, quod Apostoli non solum reliquerunt omnia temporalia, sed etiam renunciauerunt desiderijs & concupiscentiis habendi ipsa. Sed desiderijs & concupiscentijs habendi res temporales non renunciatur, nisi per votum licet posset imperfecte renunciari, absque voto: Ergo Apostoli renuntiauerunt per votum proprietati omnium temporalium, & oppositū astruere, sicut Dominus Iohannes astruit, est determinationi sanctæ matris ecclesiæ & sanctorum doctrinæ contradicere, & omnes religiones votum relinquendi omnia profitentes destruere: quia si Apostoli, qui fuerunt primi professores euangelii, & imitatores Christi, non voluerunt abdicationem proprietatis omnium temporalium, tunc religiosi quicunq; in vouendo abdicationem omnium rerum non sequerentur Christum nec Apostolos: quia in eo, quod Christus & Apostoli nunquam fecerunt, nullus dicitur eos sequi nec imitari: quod est omnem religionem habentem votum proprietatis annexum resoluere & dissoluere.
units.tr: The seventh error of Lord John is that the Apostles never wished to leave everything behind, and never made a vow to forsake everything. This error runs counter to ecclesiastical and evangelical teaching. It contradicts the teaching of the Church, I say, because, as is found in 16. q. 1. c. ex auctoritate, and is a decree of blessed Pope Gregory, "Monks hold the figure of the Apostles." But monks vow the renunciation of the ownership of all property, as appears in extr. de stat. mo. & cano. regularium c. Cum ad monasterium. Therefore much more the Apostles, whose figure the monks hold, desired the renunciation of ownership of all things, since a figure does not go beyond the truth. Likewise Alexander 4, in condemnatione libelli editi contra statum Fratrum Predicatorum & Minorum, determines and defines that the observance of the said Friars holds the form of evangelical perfection. But the said Friars vow the renunciation of the ownership of things. Therefore much more the Apostles, who were the first and chief observers of the gospel, whose perfection the observance of the said Friars holds in form, wished to live without property. Likewise, in the rule of Saint Francis, approved by the universal Church, it is found in these words: the rule and life of the Friars Minor is to observe the holy gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, etc. But the Minors, whose life and rule is to observe the holy gospel, vow the renunciation of the ownership of all things, in particular and in common, as appears from their rule and from the declarations given them by the Roman Church. Therefore much more the Apostles, who were the first professors of the gospel, desired the renunciation of the ownership of all things, in particular and in common. Likewise Nicholas 3, in the decretal Exiit, speaking of the renunciation by vow of all things, in particular and in common, says thus: Moreover, since the rule itself expressly contains that the Friars appropriate nothing to themselves, neither house, nor place, nor any thing, and since it has been declared by the same Gregory 9, our predecessor, and by several others, that this must be observed both in particular and in common; and since the crafty foolishness of some has corrupted such a strict renunciation with poisonous slander, lest the clear perfection of the same Friars be assailed by unskilled talk: we say that the renunciation of the ownership of all things, both in particular and in common, is meritorious and holy before God, which Christ also taught by word, showing the way of perfection, and confirmed by example. etc. Thus Nicholas 3. He speaks of the renunciation of all things, in particular and in common, made by vow; this is clear from the fact that he speaks of the renunciation of all things, in particular and in common, of the Friars Minor. But the renunciation of the Friars Minor includes a vow. And this renunciation of all things, in particular and in common, of the Friars Minor, made by vow, he says Christ taught by word and confirmed by example; the Apostles drew it into the channels of their doctrine and life. Therefore, according to him, the Apostles by their life and doctrine handed down to others the vow of renouncing the ownership of all things, in particular and in common. And this definition was approved and accepted by the universal Church, as was shown in the preceding error. Therefore Lord John, by teaching that the Apostles did not wish to leave everything behind as to ownership and dominion, sets himself against the determination of the universal Church. Likewise, Augustine expressly states this in book 17 of De civitate Dei, chapter 4, saying thus: For those powerful men had said: Behold, we have left everything and followed you. The most powerful men had vowed this vow. But whence did they have it, except from him of whom it is constantly said: you condemn the one who vows a vow. Thus Augustine. And that Augustine understood that the Apostles wished to leave everything and follow Christ is clear from this: a predicate that falls simply and absolutely, and without distinction, upon a conjunction, by its nature falls upon both parts of the conjunction, since for the truth of a conjunction both parts must be true. But this predicate, the most powerful had vowed this vow, falls simply, absolutely and without distinction upon that conjunction: Behold, we have left everything and followed you. Therefore the vow falls upon both parts of this conjunction, and consequently the Apostles wished to leave everything, and not merely to follow Christ. Likewise, blessed Pope Gregory, in his homilies on the gospels for Peter and Andrew, where he says that the Apostles not only left all temporal things, but also renounced the desires and lusts of having them. But renunciation of the desires and lusts of having temporal things is not made except by vow, although it could be made imperfectly without a vow. Therefore the Apostles renounced by vow the ownership of all temporal things, and to assert the opposite, as Lord John asserts, is to contradict the determination of our holy mother the Church and the doctrine of the saints, and to destroy all religious orders that profess the vow of leaving everything behind. For if the Apostles, who were the first professors of the gospel and imitators of Christ, did not wish the renunciation of the ownership of all temporal things, then no religious who vows the renunciation of all things would follow Christ or the Apostles, since no one is said to follow or imitate them in what Christ and the Apostles never did. This would dissolve and undo every religious order having the vow of ownership attached to it.

units.la: Secundo dictus error obuiat doctrinæ euangelicæ, quoniam constat quod oblatio euangelica non debet esse imperfectior legali, sicut nec euangelium lege. Sed oblatio antiquæ legis non erat perfecta, nec Deo perfecte grata, nisi fieret ex voto seu votum haberet adiunctum, iuxta illud q; Demandauit in Psalmo: Vouete & reddite &c. Ergo multo magis oblatio euangelica & Apostolica non fuit perfecta nec Deo perfecte accepta & grata, nisi fuisset facta ex voto seu votum habuisset annexum. nexum. Sed Apostoli tunc omnia temporalia Deo obtulerunt, quando ipsa p Deo & amore Christi reliquerunt. E. talis oblatio Apostolorum non fuisset perfecta nec Deo grata perfecte, nisi ex voto omnia reliquissent, seu voto omnia relinquendi emississent. Etiā preterea sicut Christus ait Matth. 16. Si quis vult post me abneget semetipsum. Sed voluntas non perfecte abnegatur, nisi per votum; quia voluntas non abnegatur perfecte, nisi abnegatur actu & potentia. Voluntas a. non abnegatur actu & potentia, nisi mediante voto. Ideo August. super illud Psalmi: votū vouit Deo Iacob; dicit, quo nihil gratius Deo offerri potest. Et ita secundū August. nihil est Deo gratius, q opus bonū ex voto procedens. Hinc est, q Anselmus in libro de similitudinibus dicit, q sicut offerens arborem cū fructibus plus offert, q offerens solum fructus retenta sibi arbore. Ita qui offert obedientia Deo ex voto, plus & gratius offert sibi, q ille qui offert obedientiam liberā absq; voto. Hinc est etiam, q Levit. 22. c. scribitur sic: Bouē & oue aure & cauda amputatū offerre potest, votū ex his solui non potest. Hoc ibi. Sed de boue & oue, aure & cauda amputatis nō posset magis oblatio fieri libera, quā votū plolui, nisi quia oblatio absq; voto nō est integra nec perfecta, sicut animal ampurata cauda & aure non est integrū & perfectū, sed diminutū & imperfectū. Cū ergo Apostoli integre & perfecte seipsos & sua abnegauerunt, sequitur q votum abnegandi omnia temporalia emiserunt. Aliter n. non integre nec perfecte omnia reliquissent, q est aperte impingere in Apostolicā perfectionem. Item licet ceremonialia & figuralia antiqui legis sint evacuata in nova lege: tamen moralia & naturalia non sunt evacuata, sed adimpleta, ut patet Matth. 5. Sed illud consilium datū in Psalmista: Vouete & reddite Domino, non fuit figurale nec iudiciale, sed mere morale, sicut iurāmentū. Ergo illud non est evacuatum in evangelio, sed adimpletū & perfectum. Constat a. q Christus apposuit Apostolis obseruantiā consiliorum evangelicorum, cum ipsi fuerint primi & præcipui obseruatores evangelii. Cum ergo votum sit consilium evangelicum, ut ostensum est: sequitur, quod Apostoli voluerunt abdicationem proprietatis rerum temporalium. Item abnegans a se propter Deum potestatem licitam resumendi temporalia quæ reliquit, votum emittere videtur. Cum votum non sit aliud, quam abnegatio potestatis licitæ propriæ voluntatis propter Deum factam. Sed iste, cui Christus dicit: Vende omnia quæ habes & da pauperibus & veni sequere me, debebat secundū Christi consilium abnegare potestatem resumendi temporalia, quæ videbatur relinquere: quia Venie, inquit, omnia & da pauperibus, amplius, scil. illa non resumpturus; & ita assumendus ad statum evangelicæ perfectionis debebat à se abnegare propter Deum potestatem resumendi talia, quæ videbatur relinquere. Constat autem, quod Apostoli fuerunt assumpti ad statum evangelicæ perfectionis. Ergo ipsi emiserunt votum abdicationis temporalium.
units.tr: Secondly, this error stands against evangelical teaching, since it is agreed that the evangelical offering ought not be more imperfect than the legal, just as the gospel is not less than the law. But the offering of the old law was not perfect, nor perfectly pleasing to God, unless it was made from a vow, or had a vow attached to it, according to what is commanded in the Psalm: Vow and render, etc. Therefore much more the evangelical and apostolic offering was not perfect, nor perfectly accepted and pleasing to God, unless it was made from a vow or had a vow attached to it. But the Apostles then offered all temporal things to God when they left them for God's sake and the love of Christ. Therefore the offering of the Apostles would not have been perfect, nor perfectly pleasing to God, unless they had left everything by vow, or had made a vow to leave everything behind. Moreover, as Christ says in Matthew 16: If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself. But the will is not perfectly denied except by vow, since the will is not perfectly denied unless it is denied in act and in power. But the will is not denied in act and in power except through a vow. Therefore Augustine, on that verse of the Psalm, Jacob vowed a vow to God, says that nothing more pleasing can be offered to God. And so, according to Augustine, nothing is more pleasing to God than a good work proceeding from a vow. Hence Anselm, in his book on similitudes, says that just as one who offers a tree with its fruits offers more than one who offers only the fruits while keeping the tree for himself, so one who offers obedience to God by vow offers more and more pleasing to God than one who offers free obedience without a vow. Hence too it is written in Leviticus 22: An ox or sheep with ear and tail cut off may be offered, but it cannot be used to fulfil a vow. Thus there. But an ox and a sheep with ear and tail cut off could not be offered more freely than a vow could be paid, unless because an offering without a vow is not whole or perfect, just as an animal with its tail and ear cut off is not whole and perfect, but diminished and imperfect. Since, then, the Apostles denied themselves and their possessions wholly and perfectly, it follows that they made a vow to renounce all temporal things. Otherwise they would not have left everything wholly and perfectly, which clearly contradicts apostolic perfection. Likewise, although the ceremonial and figurative things of the old law were abrogated in the new law, the moral and natural things were not abrogated but fulfilled, as appears from Matthew 5. But the counsel given in the Psalmist, Vow and render to the Lord, was neither figurative nor judicial, but purely moral, like an oath. Therefore it was not abrogated in the gospel, but fulfilled and perfected. It is agreed also that Christ laid upon the Apostles the observance of the evangelical counsels, since they were the first and chief observers of the gospel. Therefore, since a vow is an evangelical counsel, as has been shown, it follows that the Apostles wished the renunciation of the ownership of temporal things. Likewise, one who, for God's sake, renounces the lawful power of resuming temporal things which he has left seems to make a vow, since a vow is nothing other than the renunciation, made for God's sake, of the lawful power of one's own will. But he to whom Christ says: Sell all that you have and give to the poor and come, follow me, ought, according to Christ's counsel, to renounce the power of resuming temporal things which he seemed to give up, since sell, he says, all and give to the poor, that he should not take them back again; and so one who is to be taken up into the state of evangelical perfection ought, for God's sake, to renounce from himself the power of resuming such things as he seemed to leave. But it is clear that the Apostles were taken up into the state of evangelical perfection. Therefore they made a vow of renouncing temporal things.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: OCtauus error Dn. Iohannis in dicto libello contentus & dogmatizatus, est, q Apostolis licuit pro rebus temporalibus, sicut pro rebus suis propriis in iudicio contendere & litigare: licet eos contendisse & litigasse pro ipsis non legatur. Qui quidem error obuiat doctrinæ euangelicæ & Apostolicæ atq; ecclesiasticæ. Quoniam illis, quibus non licet habere aliquid proprium, non licet litigare & contendere pro rebus aliquibus sicut pro rebus propriis. Quia litigare pro rebus aliquibus, sicut pro rebus propriis, supponit ipsum litigante habere res proprias. Sed Apostolis non licuit habere in speciali nec in communi aliquid proprium: quia in speciali & in communi voluerunt abdicationem proprietatis omnium rerum, ut in sexto alio errore ostensum est. Ergo ipsis nec in speciali nec in communi licuit pro rebus temporalibus, sicut pro rebus propriis, in iudicio contendere & litigare. Item beatus Augustinus in Enchiridion 44. c. pertractans illa verba Apostoli: Iam enim delictum est in vobis q iudicia habetis &c. Dicit sic: Nam & hic posset putari iudicium habere aduersus alteram non esse peccatū, sed tantum modo si extra ecclesiam vellet iudicari nisi secutus adiungeret: Iam quidem omnino delictum est, quia iudicia habetis vobiscum. Et ne quis ita excusaret & diceret, se iustum habere negocium, sed iniquitatem pati, q velit à se iudicii sententia remoueri, continuo talibus cogitationibus, vel excusationibus occurrit atq; ait: Quare non magis iniquitatem patiamini? quare non potius fraudamini? Vt ad illud redeat, quod Dominus dicit: Si quis voluerit tunicam tuam tollere, & in iudicio tecum contendere, dimitte ei & pallium: & qui abstulerit, inquit, tua noli repetere. Prohibuit itaq; suos Dominus de secularibus cum alii habere iudicium. Et qua doctrina Apostolus dicit esse delictum, cum finit in ecclesia talia fieri inter fratres fratribus iudicantibus extra ecclesiam notabiliter vetat. Manifestum est etiam hoc, quid secundum veniam concedatur infirmis. Propter hec atq; huiusmodi peccata & alia hu maiora oportet vt quotidie crebro, oremus Dominum atq; dicamus: Dimitte nobis debita nostra &c. Hæc Augustinus. Ex quibus verbis Augustini manifeste patet, quod contendere in iudicio pro rebus aliquibus, sicut pro rebus propriis, conceditur secundum veniam infirmis & imperfectis. Cum ergo Apostoli fuerint in statu summæ perfectionis: sequitur quod eis non licuit contendere pro rebus temporalibus, sicut pro rebus propriis.
units.tr: The eighth error of Master John in the said little book, which he has held and taught as dogma, is that it was permitted to the Apostles to contend and go to law in judgment over temporal goods, just as over their own private property, although it is not read that they ever contended or went to law over such things. This error runs counter to the evangelical, apostolic and ecclesiastical doctrine. For those to whom it is not permitted to have anything of their own are not permitted to contend or litigate over any things as if they were their own property, since to litigate over things as one's own presupposes that the litigant has property of his own. But the Apostles were not permitted to have anything of their own, either individually or in common, since both individually and in common they willed the renunciation of the ownership of all things, as has been shown in the sixth error. Therefore they were not permitted, either individually or in common, to contend and litigate in judgment over temporal goods as if they were their own. Likewise, blessed Augustine in the Enchiridion, chapter 44, treating those words of the Apostle, "Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law with one another" (1 Cor. 6), says: "For here too one might think that it is not a sin to have a lawsuit against another, unless he were to add, if he wished to be judged outside the Church; but now indeed it is altogether a fault, because you have lawsuits among yourselves." And lest anyone excuse himself in this way and say that he has a just cause, but suffers wrong in that he wishes to be removed from the judgment of a sentence, immediately he meets such thoughts or excuses and says: "Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather be defrauded?" That is, to return to what the Lord says: "If anyone wishes to take away your coat and contend with you in judgment, let him have your cloak also; and whoever takes away your goods, do not ask them back." Therefore the Lord forbade his own people to have lawsuits about secular matters with others. And the Church, by that teaching by which the Apostle says it is a fault, that such things happen among brothers, brothers judging outside the Church, notably forbids. This is also plainly granted as a concession to the weak, by way of indulgence. On account of these and similar sins, and others greater still, we ought daily and often to pray to the Lord and say: "Forgive us our debts," etc. Thus Augustine. From these words of Augustine it is manifestly clear that to contend in judgment over some things, just as over one's own property, is granted by way of indulgence to the weak and imperfect. Since, therefore, the Apostles were in the state of highest perfection, it follows that it was not permitted to them to contend over temporal goods as if they were their own property.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: NOnus error Dn. Iohannis in dicto libello contentus, est, q votū religiosorū, absq; proprio viuere sitentiū, nō se extēdit ad illas res, quib' necessario eget vita humana, seu sine quib' humana vita trāsiri nō potest. Qui error directe & apte aduersatur & contradicit ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ & determinationi: quia
units.tr: The ninth error contained in the said little book is that the vow of religious who profess to live without property does not extend to those things which human life necessarily needs, or without which human life cannot be carried on. This error directly and plainly opposes and contradicts the discipline and determination of the Church, because:

units.la: {60} quia beatus Benedictus in sua regula ab vniuersali ecclesia approbata sic dicit: Nec quis præsumat aliquid dare aut accipere neque aliquid habere proprium, nullam omnino rem, neque codicem, neque tabulas, neque graphium, sed nihil omnino: quippe quibus nec corpora sua, nec voluntates licet habere in sua propria potestate, omniaque omnibus sint communia, vt scriptum est: nec quisquam aliquid suum esse dicat aut præsumat. Hæc sanctus Benedictus in sua Regula ab vniuersali ecclesia approbata. Ex quibus luce clarius patet, quod votum Fratrum sancti Benedicti se extendit vniuersaliter ad quascunque res, nulla excepta: quia dicit, & nullam omnino rem, & nihil omnino. Item beatus Augustin. in sua Regula ab vniuersali ecclesia approbata dicit sic: Sit vobis anima vna & cor vnum in Deo, & non dicatis aliquid proprium, sed sint vobis omnia communia, & distribuatur vnicuique vestrum a prepositio vestro victus & tegumentum. Sicut enim legistis in Actibus Apostolorum, quod erant illis omnia communia, & distribuebatur vnicuique prout opus erat. Hoc beatus Augustin. in sua Regula ab vniuersali ecclesia approbata. Ex quibus patet, quod votum Fratrum sancti Augustin. se extendit ad victum & regumentum, sine quibus humana vita transiri non potest. Item, vt supra patuit, beatus Basilius in sua Regula ab vniuersali ecclesia approbata quærentibus suis Fratribus, vtrum liceret ipsis habere aliquid proprium? respondit in hæc verba: Hoc contrarium est illi testimonio quod in Actibus Apostolorum de illis qui credebant primitus scriptum est. Ibi enim ita dicitur, quod nemo de bonis suis quicquam proprium esse dicebat, sed erant illis omnia communia. Si quis ergo proprium aliquid sibi dicit esse, sine dubio alienum se facit ab electis Dei, à caritate Dei, qui docuit verbo & opere compleuit. Hoc sanctus Basilius in sua Regula ab vniuersali ecclesia approbata. Ex quo patet, quod votum Fratrum sancti Basilii se extendit vniuersaliter & indifferenter ad quascunque res, nulla penitus excepta: quia dicit, nec quicquam proprium. Item Nicolaus 3. in decre. Exiit, dicit sic. Dicimus quod abdicatio proprietatis huiusmodi omnium rerum tam in speciali quam etiam in communi propter Deum meritoria est & sancta: quam & Christus viam perfectionis ostendens verbo docuit & exemplo firmauit &c. Hæc Dominus Nicolaus in dicta decretali: quæ decretalis, vt superius est ostensum, fuit ab vniuersali ecclesia recepta & approbata. Ex quo patet quod votum Fratrum Minorum, de quibus ibi ad literam loquitur, se extendit vniuersaliter ad omnes res in speciali. Cuius oppositum Dominus Iohannes dicit: qui dicit, quod votum religiosorum absque proprio viuere profitentium non se extendit ad illa, sine quibus vita humana transiri non potest, & ita aperte negat determinationem vniuersalis ecclesiæ, ac omnes religiones absque proprio viuere profitentes destruit & confundit, quod est hæreticum manifeste.
units.tr: {60} because blessed Benedict, in his Rule, which has been approved by the universal Church, speaks thus: Let no one presume to give or receive anything without the abbot's leave, or to have anything of his own: no thing at all, neither book, nor tablets, nor stylus, but absolutely nothing; since they may not have their bodies or wills in their own power. Let them expect all things from the father of the monastery, and let them have nothing which is not given or permitted by him. All things shall be common to all, as it is written; and let no one call anything his own or presume to do so. These are the words of St. Benedict in his Rule, approved by the universal Church. From them it is clearer than light that the vow of the brothers of St. Benedict extends universally to all things whatever, none excepted, because he says no thing at all, and absolutely nothing. Likewise blessed Augustine, in his Rule, which has been approved by the universal Church, speaks thus: Let your soul be one and your heart one in God, and call nothing your own, but let all things be common to you; and let food and clothing be distributed to each of you by your prior. For as you have read in the Acts of the Apostles, they had all things in common, and distribution was made to each as he had need. Blessed Augustine says this in his Rule, approved by the universal Church. From these words it is plain that the vow of the brothers of St. Augustine extends to food and clothing, without which human life cannot be carried on. Again, as was shown above, blessed Basil in his Rule, when his brothers asked whether it was lawful for them to have anything of their own? answered in these words: This is contrary to that testimony which is written in the Acts of the Apostles about those who first believed. For there it is said that no one called anything of his goods his own, but all things were common to them. If anyone therefore says that something is his own, he undoubtedly makes himself a stranger to the elect of God and to the love of God, who taught by word and fulfilled by deed. St. Basil says this in his Rule, approved by the universal Church. From this it is plain that the vow of the brothers of St. Basil extends universally and without distinction to all things whatever, none excepted at all, because he says nor anything of one's own. Likewise Nicholas III, in the decretal Exiit, speaks thus: We declare that the renunciation of property of this kind, of all things both individually and in common, for God's sake, is meritorious and holy; which Christ also taught by word, showing the way of perfection, and confirmed by example, etc. These are the words of Pope Nicholas in the said decretal, which decretal, as was shown above, was received and approved by the universal Church. From this it is plain that the vow of the Friars Minor, of whom he speaks there literally, extends universally to all things individually. Lord John says the opposite, when he says that the vow of religious who profess to live without property does not extend to those things without which human life cannot be carried on. In this way he plainly denies the determination of the universal Church, and destroys and confounds all religious orders that profess to live without property, which is manifestly heretical.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: DEcimus error Domini Iohannis in dicto libello contentus, est quod bona ecclesiæ primitiuæ, de qua scribitur Act. 4. c. Nec quisquam eorum quæ possidebat aliquid suum esse dicebat, sed erant illis omnia communia: non erant illis omnia communia quo ad dominium post distributionem bonorum factam inter credentes ipsos: sed solum ante distributionem. Post distributionem vero quilibet ipsorum efficiebatur in speciali proprietarius & Dominus portionis sibi assignatæ. Qui error manifeste repugnat intentioni sacræ scripturæ & ecclesiæ determinationi: quoniam illa, quæ primi credentes ex perfectione virtutis simpliciter reliquerunt, stante tali perfectione amplius illa non resumpserunt: quia stante causa stat effectus. Ideo Luc. 9. legitur: Nemo mittens manum ad aratrum & aspicens retro aptus est regno Dei. Sed primi credentes ex perfectione virtutis simpliciter reliquerunt in speciali proprietatem omnium quæ possidebant: vt patet, ex præmissis verbis Act. 4. cap. E. primi credentes, stante tali perfectione, dominium illorum amplius in speciali non resumpserunt. Sed post distributionem bonorum, quæ fiebant inter ipsos, non erant imperfectiores quam ante ipsam distributionem: alioquin illa distributio non fuisset fienda inter eos; quia distributio seu diuisio tollens perfectionem aliquorum, non est fienda inter illos, quorum perfectione tollit aut etiam diminuit: E. primi credentes post distributionem seu diuisionem bonorum facta inter ipsos non erat magis proprietarii & Domini in speciali portionis sibi assignatæ (quia illa diuisio siue distributio non fiebat quo ad dominium, sed solum quo ad vsum) quam ante: cuius oppositum Dominus Iohannes conatur astruere. Et ita manifeste detrahit perfectioni ecclesiæ primitiuæ & intentioni scripturæ sacræ, quia, vt habetur Matth. 10. c. Qui autem perseuerauerit vsque in finem, hic saluus erit. Non ergo renunciasse in speciali proprietati & dominio eorum, quæ primi credentes possidebant, magnum fuisset: sed in hoc perseuerando & continuando illud nunc resumpsisse fuisset gloriosum & laudabile. Item, sicut patet expresse ex verbis regularum sancti Benedicti, sancti Augustini & sancti Basilii in nono errore præcedenti adductis, forma abdicationis seu renunciationis Fratrum sancti Benedicti, sancti Augustini & sancti Basilii fundatur directe super formam abdicationis & renunciationis primorum credentium Act. 4. recitatam: & ad instar illius instituta & sumpta est. Si ergo bona primorum credentium non fuerint inter eos communia post distributionem, sed tantum ante, vt Dominus Iohannes astruit, sequitur necessario quod votum monachorum sancti Benedicti, sancti Augustini & sancti Basilii non intelligatur, nec sic perpetuo tempore, sed solum ad tempus, & quod omnes Fratres sancti Benedicti, sancti Augustini & sancti Basilii in omnibus portionibus eis assignatis sint in speciali proprietarii, sicut erant secundum Dominum Iohannem primi credentes, quorum vita & forma viuendi sunt præsti: quod est expresse omnium dictorum Fratrum votum & professionem ab vniuersali ecclesia approbatam destruere & confundere: quod est omnino hæreticum. Item, sicut habetur 12. q. 1. c. dilectissimi: Sicut non potest diuidi aer nec splendor solis: ita nec reliqua quæ data sunt hominibus ad habendum diuidi debet: sed habenda esse omnia communia ipsius consuetudinis more retento Apostoli, eorumque discipuli vna vobiscum et nobiscum communem vitam duxerunt. Vt enim bene nostis, multitudinis credentium erat cor vnum & anima vna: nec quisquam eorum aut nostrum de bona quæ possidebat aliquid suum esse dicebat: sed omnia illis & nobis erant communia. Hæc ibi. Et est decretum beati Clementis Papæ, qui, vt ipse hic testatur, fuit personaliter in illa sancta communitate ecclesiæ primitiuæ. Ex quibus patet expresse, quod sicut aer & splendor solis sunt omnibus hominibus in iure naturæ communia, nec diuiduntur quo ad dominiū & proprietatem: ita bona primorum credentium non fuerunt secundum beatū Clementem diuisa inter eos quo ad dominiū seu proprietatē plusquam aer vel splendor solis, sed solū quo ad vsum. Et ita Dn. Iohannes se aperte opponit ecclesiæ & scripturæ determinationi, ac sanctorum patrum catholicæ doctrinæ: quod hæreticum est manifeste.
units.tr: The tenth error contained in Lord John's said little book is that the goods of the primitive Church, of which it is written in Acts 4, Nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them, were not common to them with respect to ownership after the goods were distributed among the believers themselves, but only before the distribution. After the distribution, indeed, each of them became in particular the owner and lord of the portion assigned to him. This error plainly contradicts the intention of Holy Scripture and the determination of the Church, since those things which the first believers out of perfection of virtue simply left behind did not take them up again while that perfection remained, because where the cause remains, the effect remains. Therefore it is read in Luke 9: No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God. But the first believers, out of perfection of virtue, simply gave up individual ownership of all that they possessed, as is plain from the words of Acts 4 quoted above. So the first believers, while that perfection remained, did not take up their ownership again individually. But after the distribution of goods made among themselves, they were not more imperfect than before the distribution; otherwise that distribution should not have been made among them, because a distribution or division which removes or even diminishes the perfection of some ought not to be made among those whose perfection it removes or diminishes. Therefore the first believers, after the distribution or division of goods made among themselves, were no more owners and lords individually of the portion assigned to them than before (since that division or distribution did not concern ownership, but only use). Lord John tries to assert the opposite of this. Thus he plainly detracts from the perfection of the primitive Church and from the intention of Holy Scripture, since it is said in Matthew 10: But he who endures to the end, he shall be saved. It was therefore not a great thing to renounce individual ownership and dominion over what the first believers possessed; but to persevere and continue in this, and not to take it up again, was glorious and praiseworthy. Likewise, as is plain expressly from the words of the Rules of St. Benedict, St. Augustine and St. Basil quoted in the ninth error above, the form of renunciation of the brothers of St. Benedict, St. Augustine and St. Basil is founded directly upon the form of renunciation of the first believers in Acts 4, which is recited there, and was established and adopted after its pattern. If therefore the goods of the first believers were not common among them after the distribution, but only before it, as Lord John asserts, it follows necessarily that the vow of the monks of St. Benedict, St. Augustine and St. Basil is not to be understood as perpetual, but only for a time; and that all the brothers of St. Benedict, St. Augustine and St. Basil are individual owners of all the portions assigned to them, just as, according to Lord John, the first believers were. Yet their life and manner of living are set forth as a model. This plainly destroys and confounds the vow and profession of all these brothers, which the universal Church has approved, and is altogether heretical. Likewise, as is found in Causa 12, q. 1, c. Dilectissimi: Just as air and the light of the sun cannot be divided, so the other things which are given to men for their use ought not to be divided; but all things are to be held in common, the custom of the Apostles being retained, and their disciples lived a common life with you and with us. For as you well know, the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and none of them or of us said that anything of the goods he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them and to us. These are the words there; and it is a decree of blessed Pope Clement, who, as he himself testifies here, was personally in that holy community of the primitive Church. From these words it is plainly clear that, just as air and the light of the sun are common to all men by the law of nature and are not divided as regards lordship and ownership, so the goods of the first believers, according to blessed Clement, were not divided among them as regards lordship or ownership any more than air or the light of the sun, but only as regards use. Thus Lord John plainly sets himself against the determination of the Church and of Scripture, and against the Catholic teaching of the holy Fathers, which is manifestly heretical.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: VNdecimus error Dn. Iohannis in dicto libello contentus & dogmatizatus, est quod Dominus noster Iesus Christus non præcepit Apostolis simpliciter & absolute, ne possiderent aurū & argentum & pecuniā in zonis, & ne portarent calciamenta, sed solū inhibuit eis talia, pro tempore viæ quādo ibant ad prædicandum: post reditū vero à prædicatione poterant (vt dicit) libere talia possidere & habere ac etiā portare. Qui error seipsum convincit & euangelicæ & Apostolicæ ac ecclesiasticæ doctrinæ contradicit. Seipsum, inquā, convincit & destruit, quia Apostoli magis indigebant prædictis in via, quando ibāt ad prædicandum, quā domi existentes: quia magis communiter indiget viator calciamentis, propter itineris asperitatem, quā domi residens in loco plano. Similiter magis indiget viator pecunia apud extraneos & alienos, quā domi apud familiares & domesticos. Si ergo talia fuerunt interdicta Apostolis à Christo pro tempore viæ quando exibant ad prædicandum, multo magis intelliguntur fuisse eis interdicta post reditū à prædicatione & ante, quādo erant domi.
units.tr: The eleventh error that Master John holds and teaches in the said booklet is that our Lord Jesus Christ did not command the Apostles simply and absolutely not to possess gold, silver, or money in their purses, or to wear shoes, but forbade them such things only for the time of their journey, when they went out to preach. After they returned from preaching, he says, they could freely possess and have such things, and even carry them. This error refutes itself and contradicts the doctrine of the Gospel, the Apostles, and the Church. It refutes and destroys itself, I say, because the Apostles needed those things more while on the road, when they were going out to preach, than when they were at home. A traveller generally needs shoes more, because of the roughness of the road, than a man sitting at home on level ground. Likewise a traveller needs money more among strangers and foreigners than at home among friends and household. If, then, Christ forbade the Apostles such things for the time of their journey, when they went out to preach, much more must they have been forbidden to them after their return from preaching, and before, when they were at home.

units.la: Et hoc est quod dicit beatus Iohannes Chrys. super Matthæu sic inquiens: Sīc in aliena patria existentes & ad ignotos abeuntes nihil amplius oportet petere quotidiano cibo, quanto magis domi manentes. Hæc sanctus Ioh. Chrysost. Et ita secundū Iohan. Chrysost. & veritate, si talia fuerunt interdicta Apostolis pro tempore viæ, multo magis domi. Et ita dictus error seipsum convincit.
units.tr: This is what Blessed John Chrysostom says on Matthew, in these words: When we are in a foreign land and go among strangers, we ought to ask for nothing more than daily food; how much more when we remain at home. So says Saint John Chrysostom. Thus, according to John Chrysostom and the truth, if such things were forbidden to the Apostles for the time of the journey, much more were they forbidden at home. So the said error refutes itself.

units.la: Item si Apostolis non licuisset talia habere & portare, quādo ibāt ad prædicandū, & licuisset eis ipsa habere & portare post reditū à prædicatione, & ante nō: tunc fuisset visa quedā species deceptionis & fallaciæ seu hypocrisis & duplicitatis maiorē austeritatē prætendendo exterius in oculis aliorū, quā seruarent interius apud semetipsos. Quod de Christo & Apostolis dicere aut sentire est impiū & blasphemū.
units.tr: Likewise, if the Apostles were not allowed to have and carry such things when they went out to preach, but were allowed to have and carry them after their return from preaching, and not before, then there would appear a kind of deception, trickery, hypocrisy, and double-dealing: they would be feigning greater strictness outwardly in the eyes of others than they kept inwardly among themselves. To say or think this of Christ and the Apostles is impious and blasphemous.

units.la: Item vita sanctorum prædicatorum debet precedere & sequi ipsorum prædicationē. Ideo Matt. 5. c. de prædicatore veritatis legitur: Qui autem fecerit & docuerit, hic magnus vocabitur in regno cœlorum. Et de Christo primo veritatis prædicatore legitur Act. 1. Cœpit Iesus facere & docere.
units.tr: Likewise the life of holy preachers ought to go before and follow their preaching. Therefore in Matthew 5 it is read of the preacher of the truth: Whoever shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven. And of Christ, the first preacher of the truth, Acts 1 says: Jesus began to do and to teach.

units.la: Prius, ergo & post, vita prædicatorum sanctorum debet eorum doctrinæ concordare. Aliter n. leuis foret fama vitæ prædicatorum, quā nec prædicatione præcederet nec sequeretur, sed cum ipsa oriretur, & cum ipsa moreretur. Constat a. quod Christus interdixit prædicta Apostolis propter exempla vitæ, vt ipsorum vita doctrinæ concordaret, & rebus facta non verbis fidem darent, vt dicit Gregor. & Glossa ibi dicit expresse.
units.tr: Therefore, both before and after, the life of holy preachers ought to agree with their teaching. Otherwise the reputation of the preachers' life would be slight, since it would neither precede nor follow their preaching, but would arise together with it and die together with it. It is certain that Christ forbade these things to the Apostles on account of the example of their life, so that their life would agree with their teaching, and that they would win faith by deeds, not by words, as Gregory says, and the Gloss there states expressly.

units.la: Et Apostolis primis euangelium prædicatoribus, nec ante prædicationem, nec post reditū à prædicatione licuit communiter seu regulariter talia possidere & habere seu etiā portare, nisi in casu necessitatis extremæ ab omni lege exceptæ, quo eis via humana aliter subuenirī non potuisset. Quia extrema necessitas legibus non artatur. Propter quod legitur Ioh. 4. c. quod discipuli eius abierat in ciuitatē Samaritanorum, vt cibos emeret, non est contra prædicta quoniā si discipuli rūc portauerūt pecuniā, de hoc non posset esse magna quæstio, cū tunc fuerunt in casu necessitatis extremæ, quo eis aliter via humana subueniri non poterat, eo quod Samaritani inhospitales Iudæis erant, vt patet Ioh. 4. & Luc. 9. c.
units.tr: For the first Apostles, the preachers of the Gospel, it was not lawful, either before preaching or after their return from preaching, to possess or have such things, or even to carry them, as a common or regular practice, except in a case of extreme necessity, which is exempt from every law, where human means could not otherwise have helped them. For extreme necessity is not bound by laws. Hence it is read in John 4 that his disciples had gone into the city of the Samaritans to buy food. This is not against what has been said. If the disciples then carried money, there could be no great question about it, since they were then in a case of extreme necessity, in which human means could not otherwise help them, because the Samaritans were inhospitable to the Jews, as is clear from John 4 and Luke 9.

units.la: Eodē modo in deserto videntur fuisse in vtima necessitate, quæ legi communi non subiacet, vt patet Matth. 12. c. Itē Christus commisit Iudæ curā & custodiā loculorum, non solum pro tempore viæ, quando ibat ad prædicandum, sed etiam commisit sibi post reditum à prædicatione, vt patet expresse Ioh. 12. & 13. c. Sed Christus non commisisset Iudæ curam & custodiam loculorum post reditum à prædicatione, si Apostoli post reditum à prædicatione pecuniam communitatis portare potuissent.
units.tr: In the same way, in the desert they seem to have been in extreme need, which is not subject to the common law, as is clear from Matthew 12. Again, Christ entrusted the care and custody of the purse to Judas, not only for the time of the journey, when he went out to preach, but he also entrusted it to him after the return from preaching, as is clear expressly from John 12 and 13. But Christ would not have entrusted the care and custody of the purse to Judas after the return from preaching, if the Apostles could have carried the common money after their return from preaching.

units.la: Quia non est verisimile, nec probabile, quod Apostoli tantum abundauerunt in pecunia, quod eam per seipsos portare non potuerint. Quare relinquitur, quod Apostolis post reditum à prædicatione communiter portare pecuniam non licuerit, hoc est, quod dicit beatus Iohannes Chrysostomus, super illud Ioh. Quidam autem quia locutos habebat Iudas &c. sic inquiens: Et nimirum nullus discipulorum pecuniam effudit, sed per hoc, quod bursam habebat, occulte insinuat, quod quedam mulieres tum de suis facultatibus ministrabant. Hæc sanctus Iohannes Chrysostomus.
units.tr: For it is not likely or probable that the Apostles had such an abundance of money that they could not carry it themselves. Hence it follows that it was not lawful for the Apostles, after their return from preaching, to carry money as a common practice. This is what Blessed John Chrysostom says on that passage of John, Now Judas had the bag, etc., in these words: "Certainly none of the disciples poured out money, but by the fact that he had the bag he obscurely suggests that certain women then ministered to them from their own means." So says Saint John Chrysostom.

units.la: Item ad illud quod communiter licet alicui de communi lege, non indiget aliqua speciali dispensatione. Sed Christus imminente sua passione propter futuram persecutionem Iudæorum dispensauit ad tempus cum Apostolis, quod possent talia portare, sicut patet Luc. 22. c. vbi legitur dixisse eis: Quando misi vos sine sacculo & pera & calciamentis: Nunquid aliquid defuit vobis? At illi dixerunt, Nihil. Ait illis: Nunc autem qui habet sacculum tollat, similiter & peram: qui non habet, vendat tunicam suam & emat gladium. Vbi dicit Beda & Iohannes Chrysostomus, quod Christus dispensauit cum eis propter instantem persecutionem relaxauit cum eis prioris præcepti rigorem. Ergo antea ipsis de communi lege portare non licebat.
units.tr: Again, what is lawful for anyone in common law does not need any special dispensation. But Christ, with his passion impending because of the coming persecution of the Jews, dispensed with the Apostles for a time, so that they might carry such things, as is clear from Luke 22, where it is read that he said to them: When I sent you without purse, scrip, and shoes, did you lack anything? And they said, Nothing. He said to them: But now let him who has a purse take it, likewise a scrip; and let him who has none sell his tunic and buy a sword. Here Bede and John Chrysostom say that Christ dispensed with them because of the imminent persecution, and relaxed for them the rigour of the earlier command. Therefore before this it was not lawful for them to carry such things by common law.

units.la: Necesse intelligendum, quod tunc Christus dispensauit cum Apostolis, quod possent proprietatem seu dominium habere prædictorū, sed solū quod possent habere vsum eorum, quæ eis aliàs de communi lege non licebat, eo quod specialiter interdictū fuerat. Vnde Aug. super euangelium: Homo quidam descendebat ab Hierusalē, dicit sic: Chrisi medicamentum est, constringit vulnera, austeriora præcepta fouet laxiore. Item quando Petrus cum Iohanne illi claudo dicit: Argentum & aurum non est mihi: quod a. habeo hoc tibi do, tunc non ibant ad prædicandum, sed ad orandum, vt patet Act. 3. c. & tamen tunc talia non habebant. Item vt legitur Act. 4.
units.tr: It must be understood that Christ then dispensed with the Apostles so that they could have the ownership or dominion of those things, but only so that they could have the use of those things which otherwise by common law were not allowed them, because they had been specially forbidden. Hence Augustine on the Gospel: A certain man was going down from Jerusalem, he says thus: "The medicine of Christ binds up wounds; it soothes the harsher precepts with a gentler one." Likewise when Peter says to the lame man with John, Silver and gold I have not; but what I have, that I give you, then they were not going out to preach but to pray, as is clear from Acts 3, and yet at that time they had no such things. Likewise as is read in Acts 4.

units.la: Ioh. 4. & Luc. 9. c. Eodem modo in deserto videntur fuisse in vltima necessitate.
units.tr: John 4 and Luke 9. In the same way, in the desert they seem to have been in extreme need.

units.la: Act. 4. 6. Primi credentes pretia rerum venditarum ponebant ad pedes Apostolorum, & non ad manus eorum. Ex quo colligitur euidenter, quod Apostoli communiter pecuniam secundum Christi praeceptum non portabant. Unde Glossa ordinaria Act. 4. dicit sic: Destitutendum probat, q tangere denitat, & calcandum docet esse aurum, q subdit gressibus Apostolorum. Haec Glossa. Et ita ex textu & Glossa patet, quod Apostoli communiter pecuniam non portabant, nec etiam tangebant: cuius contrarium Dominus Iohannes pertinaciter asserit, & pertinaciter defendit, scripturam Apostolicā & euangelicā pervertendo & corrupendo: & ita dictus error seipsum convincit, & Christi euangelium puertit.
units.tr: Acts 4 and 6. The first believers laid the prices of the goods they had sold at the feet of the Apostles, and not into their hands. From this it is plainly gathered that the Apostles did not, according to Christ's precept, carry money as a common practice. Hence the Ordinary Gloss on Acts 4 says: "He proves that he should be cast off who refuses to touch it, and he teaches that gold is to be trampled, since it is placed under the feet of the Apostles." So the Gloss. Thus from the text and the Gloss it is clear that the Apostles did not commonly carry money, nor even touch it. Master John stubbornly asserts the opposite, and stubbornly defends it, perverting and corrupting Apostolic and evangelical Scripture; and so the said error refutes itself and overturns the Gospel of Christ.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Duodecimus error Domini Iohannis in dicto libello contentus, est q in rebus usu consumptibilibus nec usus iuris nec usus facti licitus potest a proprietate & dominio separari: eo quod per usum talium rerum, eadem proprietas & dominium consumatur, & salua earum substantia nulla potest uti vtilitas prouenire, nec sub usu earum saluetur proprietas nec dominium. Qui error quo ad conclusionem & quo ad medium manifeste aduersatur & contradicit doctrinae Apostolicae & doctrinae ecclesiasticae. Doctrinae, in q Apostolicae aduersatur & contradicit, quia, ut legitur Act. 4. cap. de prima multitudine credentium: Nec quisquam eorum quod possidebat aliquid suum esse dicebat: sed erant illi omnia communia. Quae verba, ut declarata sunt in 10. errore praecedenti, intelliguntur p toto tempore, quo durauit illa congregatio, siue ante diuisionem & distributionem bonorum, quae fiebat inter credentes illos, siue post. Et ita in illa communitate primorum credentium nullus habuit in speciali nec in communi dominium alicuius rei usu consumptibilis vel non consumptibilis, tum quia nec quisquam eorum quae possidebat aliquid suum id est, prius esse dicebat, ut verba de se sonant, & sanctus Benedictus, & sanctus Basilius, & sanctus Augustinus in suis Regulis ab vniuersali ecclesia approbatis, ut supra in 9. errore patuit, exponunt. Tum quia nisi sint omnia perfecte communia, sicut erant in illa multitudine vbi nihil est proprium, cum idem non possit simul proprium & commune esse: & tamen quilibet in illa multitudine habuit in speciali & sigillatim usum facti licitum rerum usu consumptibilium distinctum ab usu alterius: quia portio cibi vel potus, qua vtebatur de facto vnus, non vtebatur actu alius. Ideo Act. 4. scribitur, q diuidebantur omnia singulis prout opus erat. E. quilibet in illa multitudine habuit in speciali usum rerum usu consumptibilium separatum a proprietate & dominio earum. Similiter, vt ostensum est in nono errore praecedenti, Fratres Ordinis sancti Augustini, sancti Basilii & sancti Benedicti non debent habere in speciali proprietatem & dominium alicuius rei usu consumptibilis vel non consumptibilis, & tamen dicti Fratres habent in speciali usum rerum usu consumptibilium, quia habent in speciali usum vestium & usum alimentorum. E. dicti Fratres habent in speciali usum rerum usu consumptibilium separatum a proprietate & dominio: & ita per se manifestum est, q secundum doctrinam Apostolicam & doctrinam ecclesiasticam usus dictarum rerum est separabilis a proprietate & dominio speciali: & si usus earum est separabilis a proprietate & dominio speciali, eadem ratione sequitur, q de se & natura sua sit separabilis, a proprietate & dominio communi, quia stante eadem rerum natura genere & specie & dominio vniformiter consumptibili per usum, usus ipse est vniformiter separabilis vel inseparabilis a proprietate & dominio. Cum usus rerum non sit separabilis nec inseparabilis a proprietate & dominio, nisi propter naturalem conditionem & habitudinem ipsarum. Sed natura rerum usu consumptibilium est eadem genere & specie in communi & in speciali, quia idem panis & idem vinum genere & specie in communi & in speciali. Et p usum istarum rerum consumitur dominium commune, sicut dominium proprium. Et e conuerso dominium proprium, sicut dominium commune, & post usum rationabile ipsarum non plus remanet dominium commune, q proprium, nec proprium plus q commune. Similiter sub usu dictarum rerum non magis saluatur unum dominium q alterum, cum utrumque consumatur p usum. E. usus dictarum rerum vniformiter est separabilis a proprietate & dominio speciali, cum non sit magis ratio de uno dominio q de alio. Sed usus ipsarum est separabilis a proprietate & dominio secundum q ostensum est p doctrinam Apostolicam & ecclesiasticam de prima multitudine credentium, & de religiosis absq; omnium proprio viuere profitentib'. E. usus earum de se natura sua est separabilis a proprietate & dominio communi. Et oppositum pertinaciter asserere, sicut Dns. Iohannes asserit, est doctrinae Apostolicae & doctrinae ecclesiasticae se opponere & contradicere, ac omnes religiones sine proprio viuere profitentes destruere & confundere. Ite Dn. Greg. 9. in declaratione regulae beati Francisci, pronunciat in haec verba: Praeterea cu in ipsa regula continetur expresse, q Fratres nihil sibi appropriant nec domum nec locu nec aliq re ac ipsi processu temporis cotamari timeat ordinis paupertate, praesertim cu ita dixerint aliqui proprietatem mobilium pertinere ad totu ordine in communi, nobis fuit humiliter supplicatu ut in hoc dignaretur animarum prouidere periculu & totius ordinis puritati.
