Dicimus ipsaq; q nec in communi nec in speciali debent proprietate habere: sed vtensilium & librorum & eorum mobilium (q licet habere) ordo vsum habeat, & Fratres hu vt antur secundu q generales Ministri & provinciales dispensandu duxerint, & donorum dominio illu ad quos pertinet. Haec Dn. Greg. 9. qui fuit tempore beati Francisci, & ex speciali familiaritate quam habuit cum ipso sancto Francisco, debuit sup hoc nosse eius intentionem, ut in dicta declaratione ipse testatur expresse. Ex quibus verbis ipsius Dn. Greg. Papae patet aperte & manifeste, q Fratres ordinis sancti Francisci non debent secundum eorum statum habere aliqua proprietate alicuius rei mobilis nec immobilis in speciali nec in communi, & tamen dicti Fratres debent habere vsum rerum eis conuenientium, ut patet ex eadem regula & declaratione. E. dicti Fratres debent habere vsum rerum usu consumptibilium absq; proprietate & dominio in speciali & in communi, & ita usus eorum est separabilis a proprietate & dominio speciali & in communi. Ite Innoc. 4 & Alexand. 4. ut ipsemet dictus Iohannes recitat in constitutione seu potius destitutione, quia quorundam, in suis declarationib. sic dixerunt & distinguerunt: Dicim' insuper q cu in ipsa regula cotineatur expresse expressé quod fratres nihil sibi approprient nec domum nec locum nec aliquam rem q; nec in communi nec in speciali debent proprietatem habere: sed locorum & domorum ac utensilium & librorum & eorum mobilium quae licet habere, ordo vsum habeat & secundum quod generales ministri & provinciales ministri ordinandum duxerint hi vocantur, haec dicti Romani pontifices. Ex quorum verbis apparet aperte, quod dicti Fratres nullius rei de mundo mobilis debent proprietatem in speciali habere, nec in communi. Et cum dicti Fratres debent habere vsum rerum eis competentium: sequitur quod praedicti Fratres in speciali & in communi debent habere vsum absque proprietate & dominio, seu à proprietate & dominio separatum. Item Clemens 4. in quodam suo priuilegio dicit sic: Cum dilecti filii Fratres Minores ex professione sua voto adeo se voluntaria submiserint paupertati, vt nec diuisim nec communiter aliquid proprii valeant obtinere: sed omnia quae ipsis in eleemosynam erogantur, seu alias eorum contemplatione proueniunt, iuri & proprietati ecclesiae Romanae accrescere dignoscantur &c. Haec Clemens 4. Ex quibus patet, quod dicti Fratres non debent habere proprietatem alicuius rei de mundo in speciali nec in communi. Et cum dicti Fratres habent vsum rerum vsu consumptibilium: ergo ipsi habent vsum earum absque proprietate & dominio in speciali & in communi. Item Grego. 3. in quodam suo priuilegio dicit sic: Ordo Fratrum Minorum humilitati deditus paupertatis, & rem & nomen proprietatis abiecit: & quicquid ei obuenerit dignoscitur ipso facto in nostrum & ecclesiae Romanae dominium transire perhibetur, & tamen dictus Ordo habet vsum rerum vsu consumptibilium: ergo habet vsum talium rerum separatum à proprietate & dominio in speciali & in communi. Item Martinus 4. in quodam suo priuilegio, quod incipit Exultantes, dicit sic: Idem Fratres, qui pro nulla re temporali possint in iudicio experiri, vt exclusis quibuslibet sollicitudinibus & quietius diuino vacent obsequiis, & offerentium, donantium, concedentium aut in vltimata voluntate, in quantum Ordini praedicto vel Fratribus eiusdem Ordinis aliquid propter Deum, ne pia intentio fiat audetur, sitque nobis sollicitudini, quod praedictus ordo pro suis necessitatibus quotiens ingrueret necessitas, vel viitas suaderet, recurrere ad Romanam ecclesiam cogeretur, ad quam omnium rerum mobilium & immobilium, quibus Fratres vti possunt, ius, proprietas & dominium nullo medio spectat &c. Haec Dominus Martinus papa 4. quibus nihil clarius, quod dicti fratres in nulla re de mundo mobili vel immobili habent proprietatem nec dominium in speciali nec in communi: quia ius, proprietas & dominium omnium rerum, quibus vti possunt, immediate spectat ad Romanam ecclesiam: & per consequens in omnibus rebus, quibus vtuntur, habent vsum separatum à proprietate & dominio in speciali & in communi. Item Dominus Nicolaus 3. in decre. Exiit, quae decretalis, vt saepe dictum est, per papam Bonifacium 8. inserta est in 6. lib. decre. dicit sic: Dicimus quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium rerum tam in speciali quam in communi propter Deum meritoria est & sancta, quam & Christus viam perfectionis ostendens verbo docuit & exemplo firmauit. &c. haec Dominus Nicolaus 3. Sed si abdicatio proprietatis omnium rerum in speciali & in communi non esset meritoria nec sancta, nec possibilis: abdicatio autem vsus omnium rerum, & maxime vsus facti, non potest esse sancta nec meritoria: quia non est possibilis: sequeretur quod nulla abdicatio esset meritoria & sancta: cuius oppositum tenet dictus Dominus Nicolaus, ergo necesse est secundum eum, quod vsus omnium rerum est separabilis à proprietate & dominio speciali & communi. Item Clemens quintus in decretali Exiui de paradiso, in concilio Vien. edita, dixit sic: Proinde tu vir sanctus paupertatis promissae in regula beati Francisci exprimens dixit in eadem, Fratres nil sibi approprient nec domus nec locus nec aliquid &c. sicut Laurentius, praedecessores nostros Romanos pontifices hanc expropriationem intelligi debere tam in speciali quam etiam in communi, propter quod & rerum omnium concessarum, oblatarum & donatarum (quas & quarum vsum facti, scil. ius vel ipsis fratribus licet habere) proprietatem & dominium, in se & in Romana ecclesia receperunt, dimisso facti vsu in eis tantum modo vsu facti simplici. Haec Clemens 5. Et ita secundum praefatum Clementem Fratres vtuntur in omnibus rebus, quibus vtuntur, habent vsum facti separatum à dominio & proprietate speciali & communi. Ex quibus apparet aperte, quod secundum Dominum Gregorium 19. Innocentium 4. Alexandrum 4. Clementem 4. Gregorium 4. Martinum 4. Nicolaum 3. Bonifacium 8. & Clementem 5. & omnes alios intermedios praedictos sequentes vsque ad hunc novissimum, Fratres beati Francisci debent habere vsum rerum vsu consumptibilium separatum à proprietate & dominio speciali & communi: cuius oppositum Dominus Iohannes non veritus determinationes suorum praedecessorum ausus est pertinaciter asserere, & hostiliter defendere. Et ita omnis determinatio sacrosanctae matris ecclesiae se opponit & obiicit: quia determinatio tot Romanorum pontificum sibi invicem consentientium & nullam contradictionem in clero nec in populo patientem, & determinationem vniuersalis ecclesiae est habenda & tenenda. Et non solum dictus Dominus Iohannes determinationi sanctae matris ecclesiae se opponit & obiicit: sed etiam (quod peius est) ipsam determinationem sanctae matris ecclesiae quantum in se est, facit erroneam & schismaticam: quia in sua constitutione, imo potius destitutione, quia quorundam pronuntiat, quicunque scienter verbo vel scripto asseruerit aliquid contra determinata & diffinita in constitutione Ad conditorem, tanquam rebellis & contumax ecclesiae habeatur. In constitutione autem Ad conditorem determinat & diffinit expresse, quod vsus rerum vsu consumptibilium non potest proprietate & dominio separari. Et ita secundum ipsum, quicunque verbo vel scripto scienter asserit vsum talium posse à proprietate & dominio separari, tanquam rebellis & contumax ecclesiae est habendus. Scriptura autem Apostolica & sancta mater ecclesia euidenter asserit oppositum.
units.tr: The twelfth error of Lord John in the said little book is that in things consumable by use, neither a lawful use of right nor a lawful use of fact can be separated from ownership and dominion, because through the use of such things that same ownership and dominion is consumed, and no benefit can arise from them while their substance is preserved, nor is ownership or dominion preserved under their use. This error manifestly opposes and contradicts both the Apostolic doctrine and the doctrine of the Church, both in its conclusion and in its middle term. It opposes and contradicts the Apostolic doctrine, because we read in Acts 4 about the first multitude of believers: Nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own, but they had all things in common. These words, as they were explained in the tenth error above, are understood for the whole time that that congregation lasted, whether before the division and distribution of goods that was made among those believers or after it. And so, in that community of the first believers, no one had, either individually or in common, dominion over any thing consumable by use or not consumable by use. This is so, first, because nor did any of them say that what he possessed was his own, that is, previously, as the words sound about themselves, and as Saint Benedict, Saint Basil and Saint Augustine expound them in their Rules, which have been approved by the universal Church, as was shown above in the ninth error. Second, because unless they are altogether common, as they were in that multitude where nothing was private, a thing cannot be both private and common at once. Yet each person in that multitude had, individually and separately, a lawful use of fact of things consumable by use, distinct from the use of another, because the portion of food or drink that one used in fact was not actually used by another. Therefore Acts 4 says that all things were distributed to each one as he had need. Hence each person in that multitude had, individually, a use of things consumable by use separated from the ownership and dominion of them. Likewise, as was shown in the ninth error above, the Brothers of the Order of Saint Augustine, of Saint Basil and of Saint Benedict ought not to have, individually, ownership and dominion over any thing consumable by use or not consumable by use; and yet these Brothers have, individually, a use of things consumable by use, because they have, individually, a use of clothing and a use of food. Therefore these Brothers have, individually, a use of things consumable by use separated from ownership and dominion. And so it is plainly evident that, according to the apostolic doctrine and the doctrine of the Church, the use of those things is separable from individual ownership and dominion. And if its use is separable from individual ownership and dominion, then by the same reasoning it follows that it is by its own nature separable from common ownership and dominion as well, because, while the nature of the things remains the same in kind and species, and the dominion over them is uniformly consumed by use, the use itself is uniformly separable or inseparable from ownership. But the use of things is separable or inseparable from ownership only on account of their natural condition and character. Yet the nature of things consumable by use is the same in kind and species in common and in particular, since the same bread and the same wine are the same in kind and species, both in common and in particular. And by the use of these things common dominion is consumed, just as private dominion is. And conversely, private dominion is consumed just as common dominion is; and after a reasonable use of them, no more common dominion remains than private, nor more private than common. Likewise, under the use of those things, one dominion is not preserved any more than the other, since both are consumed by use. Therefore the use of those things is uniformly separable from individual ownership and dominion, since there is no greater reason for one dominion than for another. But their use is separable from individual ownership and dominion, as has been shown by the Apostolic and ecclesiastical doctrine concerning the first multitude of believers and concerning religious who profess to live without property of their own. Therefore their use is, by its own nature, separable from common ownership and dominion. And to assert stubbornly the opposite, as Lord John asserts it, is to oppose and contradict the Apostolic and ecclesiastical doctrine, and to destroy and confound all religious orders that profess to live without property of their own. Likewise Lord Gregory IX, in his declaration of the Rule of blessed Francis, pronounces in these words: Moreover, since it is expressly contained in the Rule itself that the Brothers appropriate to themselves nothing, neither house nor place nor any thing, and since, as time goes on, some fear that the poverty of the Order may be compromised, especially as some have said that ownership of movable goods belongs to the whole Order in common, we have been humbly asked to deign to provide, in this matter, for the danger to souls and for the purity of the whole Order. We say that they ought to have ownership neither in common nor in particular; but the Order may have the use of utensils, books and such movable goods as it is permitted to have, and the Brothers may use them as the Ministers General and Provincials shall have decided to dispense them, while the dominion of the gifts belongs to those to whom it pertains. Thus Lord Gregory IX, who was in the time of blessed Francis and, from the special familiarity he had with Saint Francis himself, ought to have known his intention in this matter, as he himself testifies expressly in that declaration. From these very words of Lord Pope Gregory it is clear and manifest that the Brothers of the Order of Saint Francis ought, according to their state, to have no ownership of any movable or immovable thing, either individually or in common; and yet these Brothers ought to have the use of the things suited to them, as is clear from the same Rule and declaration. Therefore the said Brothers ought to have the use of things consumable by use, without ownership and dominion, either individually or in common; and so their use is separable from individual and common ownership and dominion. Likewise Innocent IV and Alexander IV, as Lord John himself recites in his constitution, or rather destitution, because of certain persons, said and distinguished in their declarations as follows: We say moreover that, since it is expressly contained in the Rule itself that the brothers appropriate to themselves nothing, neither house nor place nor any thing, and that they ought to have ownership neither in common nor in particular; but the Order may have the use of places, houses, utensils and books and of such movable goods as it is permitted to have, and these are to be ordered as the Ministers General and Provincial Ministers have decided. These are the words of the said Roman pontiffs. From their words it appears clearly that the said Brothers ought to have ownership, individually or in common, of no movable thing in the world. And since the said Brothers ought to have the use of things suited to them, it follows that the aforesaid Brothers, individually and in common, ought to have a use without ownership and dominion, or a use separated from ownership and dominion. Likewise Clement IV, in a certain privilege of his, says this: Since the beloved sons, the Friars Minor, by their profession and by a vow have so voluntarily submitted themselves to poverty that they can obtain nothing of their own, either individually or in common, but all things that are bestowed on them as alms, or that otherwise come to them on their account, are acknowledged to accrue to the right and ownership of the Roman Church, and so on. Thus Clement IV. From these words it is clear that the said Brothers ought not to have ownership of any thing in the world, either individually or in common. And since the said Brothers have the use of things consumable by use, therefore they have the use of them without ownership and dominion, either individually or in common. Likewise Gregory X, in a certain privilege of his, says this: The Order of the Friars Minor, devoted to humility and poverty, has cast off both the thing and the name of ownership; and whatever comes to it is recognised to pass, by that very fact, into our dominion and that of the Roman Church. And yet this Order has the use of things consumable by use; therefore it has the use of such things separated from ownership and dominion, both individually and in common. Likewise Martin IV, in a certain privilege of his, which begins Exultantes, says this: The same Brothers, who may not sue in court for any temporal thing, so that, with every worry set aside, they may devote themselves more quietly to divine service; and so that the gifts, bequests and grants of those who offer, give or bestow anything, or who do so in their last will, for God's sake, to the aforesaid Order or to the Brothers of that Order, shall not be frustrated by a pious intention; and it is our concern that the aforesaid Order, whenever necessity presses or usefulness suggests, shall be compelled to have recourse to the Roman Church, to which the right, ownership and dominion of all movable and immovable things, which the Brothers may use, belong without any intermediary, and so on. These are the words of Lord Pope Martin IV, and nothing could be clearer: the said Brothers have no ownership or dominion, individually or in common, over any movable or immovable thing in the world, because the right, ownership and dominion of all the things they may use belong directly to the Roman Church. Consequently, in all the things they use, they have a use separated from ownership and dominion, both individually and in common. Likewise Lord Nicholas III, in the decretal Exiit, which, as has often been said, was inserted by Pope Boniface VIII into the sixth book of the Decretals, says this: We say that the renunciation of ownership of all things, both individually and in common, is meritorious and holy for God's sake, and Christ, showing the way of perfection, taught it in word and confirmed it by example, and so on. These are the words of Lord Nicholas III. But if the renunciation of ownership of all things, individually and in common, were neither meritorious nor holy nor possible, and the renunciation of the use of all things, and especially of use in fact, cannot be holy or meritorious because it is not possible, then it would follow that no renunciation would be meritorious and holy. Yet the said Lord Nicholas holds the opposite. Therefore, according to him, it is necessary that the use of all things is separable from individual and common ownership and dominion. Likewise Clement V, in the decretal Exiui de paradiso, published in the Council of Vienne, said this: Accordingly, you, holy man, expressing the promised poverty in the Rule of blessed Francis, said in that same Rule: "Let the Brothers appropriate to themselves nothing, neither house nor place nor anything," and so on. As Laurence, our predecessors the Roman pontiffs have declared that this expropriation must be understood both individually and in common; and for that reason they received into themselves and into the Roman Church the ownership and dominion of all the things granted, offered and given (of which the use in fact, that is, the right to have it, is permitted to the Brothers themselves), the use in fact being left to them only as a simple use in fact. Thus Clement V. And so, according to the said Clement, the Brothers, in all the things they use, have a use in fact separated from individual and common dominion and ownership. From these things it appears plainly that, according to Lord Gregory IX, Innocent IV, Alexander IV, Clement IV, Gregory X, Martin IV, Nicholas III, Boniface VIII, Clement V, and all the intermediate pontiffs named above who followed down to this most recent one, the Brothers of blessed Francis ought to have a use of things consumable by use, separated from individual and common ownership and dominion. The opposite of this Lord John, not fearing the determinations of his predecessors, has dared to assert stubbornly and to defend with hostility. And thus every determination of holy Mother Church he opposes and sets himself against; for the determination of so many Roman pontiffs, agreeing with one another and admitting no contradiction in clergy or people, is to be held and maintained as the determination of the universal Church. And not only does Lord John oppose and set himself against the determination of holy Mother Church, but also (what is worse) he makes the very determination of holy Mother Church, so far as lies in him, erroneous and schismatic. For in his constitution, or rather destitution, because of certain persons, he pronounces that whoever knowingly asserts, by word or in writing, anything contrary to what is determined and defined in the constitution Ad conditorem is to be regarded as a rebel and contumacious against the Church. But in the constitution Ad conditorem he determines and defines expressly that the use of things consumable by use cannot be separated from ownership and dominion. And so, according to him, whoever knowingly asserts by word or in writing that the use of such things can be separated from ownership and dominion is to be regarded as a rebel and contumacious against the Church. Yet Scripture and holy Mother Church, the Apostles, clearly assert the opposite.

units.la: Vnde patet ex praemissis, quod doctrinam Apostolicam & determinationem ecclesiasticam facit erroneam & schismaticam, & hoc pertinaciter: quia pertinaciter hoc asserit spaliter ex duobus vel ex tribus. Primo quia hoc asserit in tribus suis constitutionibus, vel destitutionibus sc. in constitutione Ad conditorem, in constitutione Quia quorundam, & in constitutione Quia vir reprobus. Quod autem in tribus constitutionibus contra tot appellationes in oppositum obiectas est determinatum, diffinitum & totiens iterum tialiter & iudicialiter replicatu & reiteratu intelligitur ptinaciter esse affirmatum & oppositum. Secundo, q appoint poenam rebellionis & contumaciae ecclesiae super hoc. Illud autem q sub poena rebellionis & contumaciae ecclesiae (quae est maxima poena post haeresim) statutu & diffinitum est, intelligitur ptinaciter assertu & creditum. Tertio q hoc statuendo & diffiniendo in nullo se vniversali ecclesiae, ad q contra ipsum saepe appellatu est, se submittit nec supponit: nec vniversali ecclesiae seu concilio generali, ad q & ad q appellatum & provocatum est contra ipsum, defert in aliquo: sed continue magis in sua pfidia obstinatur. Et ita manifestu est, q ipse pertinaciter facit determinationem ecclesiae catholicae erroneam & schismaticam: ac etiam fideles & catholicos ecclesiae p defensione veritatis catholicae & determinationis facit schismaticos, & finaliter haereticos: at p consequens ipse schismaticus & haereticus: qa in hoc altero pertinaciter iudicat, seipsum condemnat. Ead enim agit, quod iudicat, ad Rom. 2. ca. Et eodem iudicio, quo qs alteru ptinaciter iudicat, ipse hoc quoq; iudicandus est, Matt. 7. ca. Et ita ex multiplici capite Dominus Iohannes incidit in haeresim. Primo namq; incidit in haeresim, in quantu pertinaciter asserit, & ptinaciter defendit varios errores contra scripturae & ecclesiae determinatione. Secundo incidit in haeresim, in quantu diffinitionem scripturae & ecclesiae condemnat ptinaciter, sicut erroneam & schismatica. Tertio incidit in haeresim, in quantum determinationem scripturae & ecclesiae pertinaciter condemnat, sicut haereticam. Quarto incidit in haeresim, qa incidit in errorem Magistrorum solenniter per Romanos pontifices condemnatu. Quia, sicut ipsemet Dominus Iohannes asserit in sua constitutione, seu potius destitutione, quia quorundam, libellu & didta Magistrorum asserentiu pauptatem & vitam Fratru Praedicatorum & Minorum non esse euangelicam, nec apostolica, Romani pontifices condemnauerunt districtius p eorum literas inhibentes, ne quisq; praemissa, vel aliquod praemissorum auderet ptinaciter astruere, vel quomodolibet defensare, statutes, q contrariu praesumens tanq; contumax & rebellis ecclesiae haberetur. Ipse aut e Dominus Iohannes directe incidit in dicto errorem: qa ipse expresse asserit, q Apostoli potuerunt habere in communi bona immobilia sufficientia, & diuitias temporales, sicut habent monachi, quae Fratres Praedicatores & Minores secundum eorum regulam & statu habere nequaq; possunt. Et ita secundum ipsum paupertas Praedicatorum & Minorum non fuit pauptas euangelica Apostolorum: q quidem fuit error condemnatus dictorum Magistrorum. Et ita manifeste incidit in errorem Magistrorum damnatum sub poena rebellionis & contumaciae ecclesiae: licet non fuerit damnatus sub poena haeresis, sed hoc no excusat ipsum ab haeresi: qa error ptinaciter defensus sub quacunq; poena sit ab ecclesia damnatus, p haeresi est habendus. Quinto incidit in haeresim, qa errore & haeresim Vigilantii damnata ptinaciter defendit.
units.tr: Hence it is clear from what has been said that he makes the apostolic teaching and the ecclesiastical determination erroneous and schismatic, and he does so obstinately, since he obstinately asserts this in two or three ways. First, he asserts this in his three constitutions, or rather deposals: namely the constitution Ad conditorem, the constitution Quia quorundam, and the constitution Quia vir reprobus. That which has been determined, defined, and repeatedly restated and reiterated, verbally and judicially, in these three constitutions against so many appeals to the contrary, is understood to be obstinately affirmed and asserted in opposition. Second, he imposes the penalty of rebellion and contumacy against the Church on this matter. Whatever is established and defined under the penalty of rebellion and contumacy against the Church (which is the greatest penalty after heresy) is understood to be obstinately asserted and believed. Third, in making this statute and definition he submits and subjects himself to no universal Church, to which he has often been appealed against him, nor does he yield in any way to the universal Church or to a general council, to which appeal and provocation have been made against him. Instead he continually becomes more obstinate in his perfidy. And so it is manifest that he obstinately makes the determination of the Catholic Church erroneous and schismatic, and also makes the faithful and Catholics who defend Catholic truth and determination schismatics, and finally heretics. Consequently he himself is schismatic and heretic, because in obstinately judging the other he condemns himself. For he does the very things he judges (Rom. 2). And by the same judgment by which someone obstinately judges another, he himself is also to be judged (Matt. 7). Thus on many counts the Lord John has fallen into heresy. First, he has fallen into heresy inasmuch as he obstinately asserts and obstinately defends various errors against the determination of Scripture and the Church. Second, he has fallen into heresy inasmuch as he obstinately condemns the definition of Scripture and the Church as erroneous and schismatic. Third, he has fallen into heresy inasmuch as he obstinately condemns the determination of Scripture and the Church as heretical. Fourth, he has fallen into heresy because he has fallen into the error of the Masters solemnly condemned by the Roman pontiffs. For, as the Lord John himself asserts in his constitution, or rather deposal, Quia quorundam, the Roman pontiffs condemned more strictly, by their letters, the little book and the sayings of those Masters who asserted that the poverty and life of the Friars Preachers and Minors were neither evangelical nor apostolic. They forbade anyone to dare obstinately to assert or in any way defend the aforesaid propositions, or any of them, and decreed that whoever presumed to act contrary should be held as rebellious and contumacious against the Church. But the Lord John himself falls directly into the said error, because he expressly asserts that the apostles could have had in common immovable goods sufficient for themselves, and temporal riches, as monks have, which the Friars Preachers and Minors by their rule and state can by no means have. And so, according to him, the poverty of the Preachers and Minors was not the evangelical poverty of the apostles, which was indeed the error condemned by the said Masters. Thus he manifestly falls into the error of the Masters, condemned under the penalty of rebellion and contumacy against the Church, although he was not condemned under the penalty of heresy. This does not excuse him from heresy, because an error obstinately defended is to be held as heresy, under whatever penalty the Church has condemned it. Fifth, he has fallen into heresy because he obstinately defends the error and heresy of Vigilantius, already condemned.

units.la: Propter quae & plura alia erronea in dicto libello contenta, quae ad praesens causa breuitatis omittuntur: Ego secundu formam legis & canonicas sanctiones ab ipso, sicut ab haeretico, appellaui legitime ad sacrosancta matrem Romanam & vniuersale ecclesiam & generale concilium, q in fide & moribus praeest papae, sicut superior: eo q papa quicunq; errare potest in fide & moribus, sicut plures Romani pontifices exciderunt a fide. Vniuersalis aut ecclesia in fide & moribus errare non potest, cum sit articulus fidei, cui non potest subesse falsum: Credo in vnam sanctam catholicam & apostolicam &c. Concilio etiam generale rite & debite celebratu, cum repraesentet vniuersale ecclesiam, & vicem gerat vniversalis ecclesiae, quae errare non potest, ipsum quoq; similiter errare in fide & moribus minime potest. Quod aut e pro statu vitae mortalis non potest errare in fide vel moribus, superius est quocunq; potenti in praedictis errare. Et ad ipsum sicut ad superiore suum appellare licet & expedit. Et ad ipsu diffinitio & determinatio dubiorum in fide & moribus spectat ultimate de iure, quae de salute humana sentire non potest, propter q prima quaestio mota de fide scil. de circumcisione tenenda tempore Apostolorum, fuit decisa & determinata p concilium generale Apostolorum & Seniorum auctoritate totius ecclesiae, & non solu auctoritate Petri, nec sola auctoritate Apostolorum, quamuis essent pleni Spiritu sancto: sed auctoritate generalis concilii Apostolorum & Seniorum totius ecclesiae subsulta, & assensu vallata: sicut patet expresse Act. 15. ca. per totum. Super hoc omnes fuerunt in ea, & clamant vbique.
units.tr: For these reasons, and on account of many other errors contained in the said little book, which for the sake of brevity are now omitted, I, according to the form of law and the canonical sanctions, have lawfully appealed from him, as from a heretic, to the most holy Roman mother Church, to the universal Church, and to a general council. In matters of faith and morals the council is superior to the pope, as a superior is to one below. For any pope whatever can err in faith and morals, as several Roman pontiffs have fallen from the faith. But the universal Church cannot err in faith and morals, since this is an article of faith, to which falsehood cannot be subject: "I believe in one holy, catholic and apostolic Church," and so on. Likewise a general council rightly and duly celebrated, since it represents the universal Church and stands in its place, can by no means err in faith and morals. That the pope cannot err in faith or morals while in the state of mortal life has been refuted above, since any pope whatever can err in the aforesaid matters. It is lawful and expedient to appeal to the council as to one's superior. And to it, as the ultimate judge by right, belong the definition and determination of doubts in faith and morals, for it cannot err in judgment concerning human salvation. For this reason the first question about faith to be raised, namely whether circumcision was to be kept in the time of the apostles, was decided and determined by the general council of the Apostles and Elders, by the authority of the whole Church, and not by the authority of Peter alone, nor by the sole authority of the apostles, although they were full of the Holy Spirit. It was decided by the authority of a general council of the Apostles and Elders, supported by the whole Church and strengthened by its assent, as is clearly shown throughout Acts 15. "On this matter all were of one mind, and they cried out everywhere."

units.la: Item praedictus Dominus Iohannes anno praecedenti in quodam sermone publico, quem fecit coram omnibus audire volentibus de victoria Regis Castellae contra Sarracenos: qui sermo incipit, Iuste tulerunt spolia impiorum, dixit & asseruit, & pluries replicauit, & etiam probare conatus est, q Deus potentia sua absoluta non posset saluare hominem sine Sacramento baptismi: & q Deus non posset de potentia sua absoluta facere, q res alio modo euenirent, quam eueniant: q quidem est haereticum manifeste. Quoniam ex hoc sequitur, quod omnia, quae fiunt, de necessitate absoluta eueniant. Ex quo tollitur liberum arbitrium, meritum & demeritum perit humanu, gratia euacuatur, & Dei libera praedestinatio exsufflatur, & eius potentia annullatur, quia omnia sunt haeretica manifeste. Item hoc anno in Dominica de Aduentu, in quoda alio sermone publico coram omnibus audire volentibus: q sermo incipit, Gaudete in Domino semper, dixit & asseruit, q in Trinitate Filius non distinguitur a Patre, nec Spiritus sanctus distinguitur a Patre & Filio: q est haereticum manifeste: quia hoc est aperte confundere personas diuinas, sicut Sabellius haereticus confundebat, ideo manifeste incidit in haeresim Sabellii damnatam. Ex quibus & q pluribus aliis breuitatis causa omissis, ipse per sententiam generalis concilii latam extra de haer. c. excommunicamus, est excommunicatus & omni pontificali auctoritate priuatus & nudatus. Improbationes vero suorum erroru responsiones ad suas erroneas rationes plenius & diffusius continentur in Appellatione vltima per me facta, & in opusculis Magistrorum adversus ipsas editis.
units.tr: Likewise the aforesaid Lord John, in the previous year, in a certain public sermon which he gave before all who wished to hear, on the victory of the King of Castile against the Saracens (the sermon which begins "Iuste tulerunt spolia impiorum"), said and asserted, repeated many times, and even tried to prove, that God by his absolute power could not save a man without the sacrament of baptism, and that God could not by his absolute power bring it about that things happen otherwise than they do. This is manifestly heretical. For it follows from this that all things that happen come about by absolute necessity. From this free will is removed, human merit and demerit perish, grace is emptied, God's free predestination is blown away, and his power is annulled; all of which are manifestly heretical. Likewise this year, on the Sunday of Advent, in another public sermon given before all who wished to hear, which begins "Gaudete in Domino semper," he said and asserted that in the Trinity the Son is not distinguished from the Father, nor the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. This is manifestly heretical, because it openly confuses the divine persons, as the heretic Sabellius confused them, and so he manifestly falls into the heresy of Sabellius, which has been condemned. For these reasons, and many others omitted for brevity, he is excommunicated by the sentence of a general council, as in the decretal Excommunicamus, extra de haereticis, and is stripped and deprived of all pontifical authority. The refutations of his errors and the answers to his erroneous arguments are more fully and at greater length contained in the last appeal made by me, and in the little works of the Masters published against them.

units.la: Finis quorundam literarum sive Epistolarum Fratris Michaelis de Cesena olim Ministri Generalis Ordinis Divi & Seraphici Confessoris sancti Francisci. In quibus (sicut etiam in superiori Opere nonaginta dierum Guilhelmi de Ockam) plurima de gestis & factis dicti fratris Michaelis continentur: de quibus idem Guilhelmus de Ockam se locuturum in Dialogo suo spondera.
units.tr: The end of certain letters or epistles of Brother Michael of Cesena, formerly Minister General of the Order of the Divine and Seraphic Confessor Saint Francis. In these (as also in the earlier work, the Nonaginta dierum of William of Ockham) very many things concerning the deeds and actions of the said Brother Michael are contained, of which the same William of Ockham promised in his Dialogue that he would speak.

units.la: Iodoci Badii Ascensii ad Lectorem Epigramma.
units.tr: Epigram of Jodocus Badius Ascensius to the Reader.

units.la: Hac quoque Lectores, multo indagata labore Offerimus vestro dogmata iudicio. Scilicet auctori nihil hic subscribimus: at quae Scripserit, an bona sint, vestra erit inspicere. Verum impressori debetis multa Iohanni Trechsel, perspicua qui dedit arte premi. Multa quoque egregio certum est debere Iohanni Trittemio, cuius ducimur auspicio.
units.tr: Here too, reader, we offer to your judgment doctrines searched out with great labour. Of course we subscribe nothing here to the author: whether what he has written is sound, it will be for you to examine. But you owe much to the printer, John Trechsel, who has given them to be printed with clear art. It is certain too that you owe much to the distinguished John Trithemius, under whose auspices we are led.

units.la: ACTIO PETRI DE CVGNE- RIIS CONSILIARII REGII, ET PETRI BERTRANDI, CARDINALIS ROMANI, ET ARCHIEPISCOPI SENO- NENSIS EPISCOPIQUE HEDUENSIS, DE IVRISDICTIONE ECCLESIASTICA & Politica, coram PHILIPPO Rege Francia habita. Anno Domini M CCCXXIX.
units.tr: THE PLEADING OF PETER DE CUGNIÈRES, COUNSELLOR TO THE KING, AND OF PETER BERTRAND, CARDINAL OF ROME AND ARCHBISHOP OF SENS AND BISHOP OF AUTUN, CONCERNING ECCLESIASTICAL AND POLITICAL JURISDICTION, DELIVERED BEFORE PHILIP, KING OF FRANCE. IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1329.

units.la: Libellus iste conflatus est & compositus per Dominum Petrum Bertrandi utriusque Iuris Professorem, tunc Episcopum Eduensem, nunc vero Cardinalem: aduersus Dominum Petrum de Cugneriis super facto Praelatorum ecclesiae Gallicanae, Anno Domini Millesimo trecentesimo vicesimonono, die prima mensis Septembris. Dominus Philippus Dei gratia Francorum rex Christianissimus, filius quondam clarae memoriae Domini Caroli Comitis Valesii, mandavit Praelatos & Barones regni Franciae ad diem octabarum festi beati Andreae proximo subsequentis Parisius convenire per literas suas infra aram inclusas: quarum quidem literarum, Praelatis videlicet directarum, tenor sequitur & est talis.
units.tr: This little book was drawn up and composed by Lord Peter Bertrand, Professor of Both Laws, then Bishop of Autun and now a Cardinal, against Lord Peter de Cugnières, concerning the affair of the prelates of the Gallican Church, in the year of our Lord 1329, on the first day of September. Lord Philip, by the grace of God the most Christian King of the Franks, son of the late Charles, Count of Valois, of illustrious memory, ordered the prelates and barons of the kingdom of France to assemble at Paris on the octave of the feast of blessed Andrew next following, by his letters, which are included below. The text of those letters, addressed to the prelates, follows, and is as follows.

units.la: Philippus Dei gratia Francorum Rex dilecto & fideli nostro Episcopo Eduensi, Salutem & dilectionem. Quanto magis scientia divina, divinarumque scripturarum notitia, ac caeterarum virtutum magistrarum experientia vigent in vobis, tanto plenius nostris, quantum ac qualiter omnes & singuli clerici & laici Regni tanquam membra simul in uno corpore viventia sibi adinuicem tenentur compati, mutuumque praestare consilium & auxilium temporaliter & corporaliter, ad defensionem & custodiam unitatis, & optatae pacis mortalibus cunctis, & venienis, contraria suis quique contenti iuribus pro viribus propulsanda. Cum igitur ad nostram deductum fuerit notitiam, quod vos gentesque & officiales viri assensu per Ballivos & officiarios nostros, & per Barones aliquos regni nostri Franciae, vobis ac subditis vestris: dictique Ballivi & officiales nostri, ac Barones predicti assensu etiam per vos & officiales vestros, ac per curiam vestrarum satellites & cursores, nobis & ipsis, nostrisque & eorum subditis quamplura fuisse retroactis temporibus illata, & in praesenti adhuc inferri, bincinde gravamina insolitasque & indebitas novitates, propter quae illimitata unitatis connexio, quae inter vos & ipsos vigere debet, ut est dictum, sive quodammodo indissolubilitatis integritatem amisit. Quod si nobis, qui subditorum nostrorum, tam clericorum quam laicorum, concordiam & unitatem diligimus, non est mirum. Et idcirco volentes super his de salubri remedio, quantum cum Dei adiutorio possumus, providere: Requirimus vos nihilominus tenore praesentium mandantes, quatenus ad diem octabarum festi sancti Andreae proxime venturum Parisius personaliter interfitis aduisi super grauaminibus & nouitatibus, qua & quas per praedictos asseritis vobis fuisse illata & illatas. Nos autem praedictis Baillivis & officialibus nostris atque Baronibus damus per nostras alias literas in mandatis, vt della die Parisius similiter intersint personaliter, aduisi super grauaminibus & nouitatibus, quas sibi & subditis suis per vos & officiales vestros asserunt fuisse illatas, vt super his & singulis hinc inde illatis grauaminibus per nos & consilium nostrum de tam salubri posset remedio prouideri, quod inter vos & ipsos amoris vinculum incorruptibile & sincerae caritatis affectio indissolubilis futuris temporibus debeant observari. Datum Parisius, Prima die Septembris, Anno praedicto, die veneris 15. Decembris.
units.tr: Philip, by the grace of God King of the Franks, to our beloved and faithful Bishop of Autun, greeting and affection. The more the divine wisdom, the knowledge of the divine Scriptures, and the experience of the other virtues, as teachers, flourish in you, so much the more fully ought you to be bound to our people, in the way that all and each of the clergy and laity of the kingdom, as members living together in one body, are bound to have compassion on one another and to lend mutual counsel and aid, both temporal and bodily, for the defence and preservation of the unity and of the peace desired by all mortals, and to repel, as far as their strength allows, whatever is contrary to their rights. Since, therefore, it has been brought to our notice that you, your people and your officials, with the consent of our bailiffs and officials and of some barons of our kingdom of France, have inflicted many grievances and unusual and undue innovations, both in past times and now at present, upon them and upon their subjects, and that our said bailiffs and officials and the aforesaid barons, with the consent also of you and your officials and of the servants and messengers of your court, have inflicted the same upon us and upon our subjects, by which the boundless bond of unity which ought to exist between you and them, as has been said, has in some way lost its integrity of indissolubility. Now, if we love the harmony and unity of our subjects, both clerical and lay, this is no cause for wonder. And therefore, wishing to provide, as far as we can with God's help, a wholesome remedy for these matters, we require you, by the tenor of these present letters, commanding you nonetheless, that by the octave of the feast of St Andrew next coming you personally attend at Paris, to be heard concerning the grievances and innovations which you assert have been inflicted upon you by the aforesaid persons. We, moreover, by our other letters, command the aforesaid bailiffs, officials and barons likewise to attend at Paris in person on that day, to be heard concerning the grievances and innovations which they assert have been inflicted upon them and their subjects by you and your officials, so that concerning these grievances, inflicted on each side, a remedy so wholesome may be provided by us and our council, that the indissoluble bond of love and the sincere affection of charity between you and them may be preserved in future times. Given at Paris, on the first day of September, in the year aforesaid, on Friday, 15 December.

units.la: Die vero superius in dictis literis contenta praelati Parisius conuenerunt in palatio regali, & comparuerunt coram rege ibidem praelati adinuicem, videlicet Domini Bituricensis, Auxitanus, Turonensis, Rotomagensis, Senonensis archiepiscopi: Beluacensis, Cathalanensis, Laudunensis, Parisiensis, Nouiomensis, Carnotensis, Constantiensis, Andegauensis, Pictauensis, Meldensis, Cameracensis, Sancti Flori, Briocensis, Cabilionensis, & Eduensis Episcopi. Qua die, ipso Rege sedente & consiliariis suis, nec non aliquibus Baronibus ibidem assistentibus, & facta dignitati Regiae reuerentia per praelatos, nobilis & discretus vir Dominus Petrus de Cugneriis Miles & consiliarius dicti Domini nostri Regis, in praesentia omnium & in publico locutus est pro Rege, facto themate suo: Reddite quae sunt Caesaris Caesari: & quae sunt Dei Deo. Et prosecutus est iuxta illud thema materiam suam includendo ad duo. Primo quod regi debebatur reuerentia & subiectio. Secundo quod debebat esse spiritualium & temporalium diuisio: vt spiritualia ad praelatos, & temporalia ad Regem & Barones pertinerent. Et hoc probauit per multas rationes facti & iuris, prout in responsionibus factis infra sic per Senonensem Electum & Episcopum Eduensem plenius continetur. Et finaliter concluasit, quod praelati essent contenti spiritualibus, & in eis defenderet eos Rex. Quibus sermonibus completis dixit verba, quae sequuntur in Gallico: quod intentio regis erat reintegrare temporale. Deinde proposuit in Gallico articulos infra scriptos. Et postea tradidit in Gallico praelatis, licet sint translati in Latino, & proponendo eos, probat contenta in eisdem non pertinere ad praelatos, sed ad Dominos temporales: & quod iniuste procedebatur per praelatos super eis. Et nihilominus propositione facta, dixit idem Dominus Petrus, quod praelati super his deliberarent & consulerent Domino Regi tanquam eius fideles. Sunt autem hi articuli & responsiones super his factae, nec non grauamina regi tradita per praelatos. Quorum quidem articulorum in Gallico traditorum, in Latino tamen translatorum, tenor sequitur & est talis.
units.tr: On the day stated in the said letters, the prelates assembled at Paris in the royal palace, and there appeared before the King the prelates, one another: namely the archbishops of Bourges, Auch, Tours, Rouen and Sens; and the bishops of Beauvais, Catalonia, Laon, Paris, Noyon, Chartres, Constance, Angers, Poitiers, Meaux, Cambrai, Saint-Flour, Saint-Brieuc, Chalon and Autun. On that day, the King sitting with his counsellors, and with some barons also present, and with reverence paid to the royal dignity by the prelates, the noble and discreet man Lord Peter de Cugnières, knight and counsellor of our said Lord the King, spoke in public, in the presence of all, on behalf of the King, taking as his theme: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's. And following that theme, he developed his subject under two heads. First, that reverence and subjection were owed to the King. Second, that there ought to be a division between spiritual and temporal things, so that spiritual things pertained to the prelates and temporal things to the King and the barons. And he proved this by many reasons of fact and of law, as is more fully contained in the replies made below by the elect of Sens and the Bishop of Autun. And finally he concluded that the prelates should be content with spiritual things, and that the King would defend them in these. When these speeches were finished, he spoke the words which follow in French: that the King's intention was to recover the temporal. Then he set out the articles written below, in French, and afterwards handed them to the prelates in French, though they have been translated into Latin; and in setting them out he proves that the matters contained in them do not pertain to the prelates but to the temporal lords, and that the prelates had proceeded unjustly over them. Having made this proposal, the same Lord Peter also said that the prelates should deliberate on these matters and give counsel to the Lord King as his faithful subjects. These, then, are the articles and the replies made to them, as well as the grievances handed to the King by the prelates. The text of those articles, handed over in French but translated into Latin, follows, and is as follows.

units.la: HAEC SVNT GRAVAMINA ET VSVRPATIONES,
units.tr: These are the grievances and usurpations,

units.la: Quae & quas praelati & aliae personae ecclesiasticae Regni Franciae, veleorum officiales & iudices pro ipsis fecerunt & faciunt in praeiudicium iurisdictionis tem- poralis Domini Regis & Baronum, & aliorum subditorum suorum Dominorum temporalium.
units.tr: Which and what the prelates and other ecclesiastical persons of the Kingdom of France, or their officials and judges acting for them, have done and are doing to the prejudice of the temporal jurisdiction of the King, of the barons, and of the other subjects of their temporal lords.

units.la: 1. Primo de iure communi cognitio causarum, quae tangunt realitatem, siue sint in possessione siue in proprietate, pertinet ad iurisdictionem temporalem. Et officiales praelatorum impediendo iurisdictionem temporalem nituntur sibi attribuere cognitionem causarum realium specialiter sub possessione & super omnibus interdictis.
units.tr: 1. First, under the common law, the hearing of causes that concern land, whether they involve possession or ownership, belongs to the temporal jurisdiction. Yet the officials of the prelates, by obstructing the temporal jurisdiction, strive to claim for themselves the hearing of real actions, especially those concerning possession, and all matters under interdict.

units.la: 2. Item quando laicus turbatur vel impeditur in possessione tetrae suae per aliquem clericum, & propter hoc impetrat adiornamentum a iudice seculari in casu nouitatis vel alias: Officiales praelatorum impedientes iurisdictionem temporalem faciunt moneri ad instantiam clerici iudicem seculararem & partem, vt post adiornamentum cessent sub poena excommunicationis & certae pecuniae quantitatis.
units.tr: 2. Likewise, when a layman is disturbed or hindered in the possession of his land by some cleric, and for this reason seeks an adjournment from a secular judge in a case of new work or otherwise, the officials of the prelates who obstruct the temporal jurisdiction have the secular judge and the party summoned at the instance of the cleric, so that after the adjournment they cease, under penalty of excommunication and a certain sum of money.

units.la: 3. Item cum cognitio personarum laicarum pertineat ad iudicem seculararem, exceptis casibus spiritualibus, Officiales praelatorum faciunt eos citari coram se ad instantiam partis. Et si dictae personae laicae declinant iurisdictionem dictorum officialium, vel Domini, quibus subiiciuntur, requiruntur eas remitti coram eis tanquam coram Dominis vel iudicibus suis temporalibus, dicti officiales renuunt hoc facere, & compellunt per excommunicationem partes ad procedendum coram eis.
units.tr: 3. Likewise, since the hearing of lay persons belongs to the secular judge, except in spiritual cases, the officials of the prelates have such persons cited before themselves at the instance of a party. And if those lay persons decline the jurisdiction of the said officials, or the lords to whom they are subject request that they be sent back before those lords as their temporal lords or judges, the said officials refuse to do so and compel the parties by excommunication to proceed before them.

units.la: 4. Item officiales praelatorum faciunt saepe moneri personas laicas ad instantiam clericorum dicentium se esse impeditos in rebus hereditariis suis per laicos. Et si ipsi laici asseraunt realitatem, & ita sit in veritate, & super hoc petant remitti ad iudicem secularem, dicti officiales monent eos sub poena excommunicationis & sub magna poena pecuniaria, ne propter hoc vadant coram iudice seculari.
units.tr: 4. Likewise, the officials of the prelates often have lay persons summoned at the instance of clerics who say they are hindered by laymen in their hereditary property. And if the laymen assert the matter is real, and it is so in truth, and on this ground ask to be sent to the secular judge, the said officials warn them under penalty of excommunication and a heavy money penalty not to go before the secular judge on this account.

units.la: 5. Item officiales praelatorum nituntur habere cognitionem contractuum initorum in curia seculari per literas aut sine literis, & per monitiones & excommunicationis sententias nituntur excommunicationes facere talium contractuum super obligatis. 6. Item prælati faciunt consilia provincialia, & synodalia statuta, in quibus plura faciunt & ordinant in grandem præiudicium iurisdictionis temporalis, de qua non expectat eis quoquo modo cogi cogere vel se intromittere.
units.tr: 5. Likewise, the officials of the prelates strive to take cognizance of contracts entered into in the secular court, whether by documents or without them, and by warnings and sentences of excommunication they try to enforce excommunications against those bound by such contracts. 6. Likewise, the prelates hold provincial councils and synodal statutes, in which they enact and ordain many things to the great prejudice of the temporal jurisdiction, over which they have no right whatever to compel or interfere.

units.la: 7. Item prædicti officiales nituntur plures iuratos pro recipiendis obligationibus suis in contractibus, in illis iurisdictionibus atq; locis dominorum temporalium super venditionibus rerum hæreditariarum, & aliis: & sic nituntur impedire iurisdictionem temporalem, cum extra sedem suam obligationem recipere non debeant vel contractus.
units.tr: 7. Likewise, the said officials strive to appoint several sworn men to receive their obligations in contracts, in those jurisdictions and places of the temporal lords, concerning sales of hereditary property and other matters. And so they strive to impede the temporal jurisdiction, since they ought not to receive obligations or contracts outside their own seat.

units.la: 8. Item faciunt citari plures laicos ex officio suo super aliquibus, quæ sibi imponunt, maleficiis responsuros, de quibus impositis asserunt sibi cognitionem pertinere. Et quando citati huiusmodi venientes ad diem sibi, ut præmittitur, assignatam negabant maleficia opposita contra eos, dicti ossiciales ipsos detinent captos, nec volunt eos recedere, licet in casibus eis impositis pertineat recredetia, & licet captio & detentio ad eosdem officiales minime pertineat, sed ad iudices seculares.
units.tr: 8. Likewise, they have several laymen cited by their office, to answer for certain crimes which they impute to them, and they claim that cognizance of these charges belongs to them. And when those so cited, coming on the day assigned to them, as has been said, deny the offences charged against them, the said officials detain them as prisoners and will not let them go, although in the cases laid against them bail is allowed, and although arrest and detention do not belong to those officials at all, but to the secular judges.

units.la: 9. Item in casibus supradictis licet per inquestas & processus factos per officiales prædictos contra dictos laicos sic captos & detentos, iidem laici reperiantur puri & innocentes, & ab impposito sibi maleficio absoluantur: nihilominus dicti officiales nolunt eos expedire, donec pro scripturis processuum seu in quæsta prædictorum satisfactionem fecerint de magna pecuniæ quantitate: licet de iure in tali casu eis expensas restituere tenerentur.
units.tr: 9. Likewise, in the cases mentioned above, although by the inquests and processes made by the said officials against the laymen so seized and detained, those laymen are found pure and innocent and are acquitted of the crime imputed to them, nevertheless the said officials refuse to release them until, for the writings of the proceedings or the inquests, satisfaction has been made to them in a large sum of money, although by law in such a case they ought to restore the costs.

units.la: 10. Item memoria sit de loquendo super sententia excommunicationis, quæ datur per solam citationem, quoties quis deficit.
units.tr: 10. Likewise, mention should be made of speaking of the sentence of excommunication which is pronounced by citation alone, whenever anyone fails to appear.

units.la: 11. Item loquendo super obligationibus de nisi, per quas quis excommunicatur incontinenti, si non soluat certa die, licet nequeat soluere die illa.
units.tr: 11. Likewise, speaking of obligations with a clause de nisi, by which someone is at once excommunicated if he does not pay on a certain day, even when he cannot pay on that day.

units.la: 12. Item quandoq; aliqui, quiq; sint, excommunicantur virtute excommunicationis curiæ prælatorum: & tales excommunicati non satisfaciunt de summis contentis in excommunicatione: incontinenti reaggrauantur, & tunc iidem prælati vel eorum officiales faciunt moneri iudices seculares, q; sub pœna excommunicationis compellat per captionem bonorum tales sic excommunicatos ad faciendum se absolui, & ad debitum persoluendum. Et vbi iudices seculares non obediunt monitioni huiusmodi, ipsi excommunicantur, nec possunt absolui, nisi satisfaciant de debito, pro quo personæ prædictæ excommunicatæ existunt.
units.tr: 12. Likewise, sometimes certain persons, whoever they may be, are excommunicated by virtue of the excommunication of the prelates' court; and such excommunicated persons do not satisfy the sums contained in the excommunication, and are at once excommunicated again. Then the same prelates or their officials have the secular judges warned that, under penalty of excommunication, they must compel such excommunicated persons, by seizing their goods, to have themselves absolved and to pay the debt. And where the secular judges do not obey such a warning, they themselves are excommunicated, and cannot be absolved unless they satisfy the debt for which those excommunicated persons stand bound.

units.la: 13. Item si Balliui, Præpositi, vel Seruientes regii, aut alii subditi iudices seculares talibus monitionibus inclinauerint, nec aliqua bona penes excommunicatos prædictos inueniantur, oportet didtos officiarios regios ire cum expensis suis ad curiam prælatorum, & ibi iuramentum præstare, quod nulla bona inuenerunt penes excommunicatos: alioquin incontinenti denunciantur excommunicati, & per sententiam excommunicationis compelluntur ad satisfaciendum de debito pro ipsis excommunicatis.
units.tr: 13. Likewise, if bailiffs, provosts, or royal sergeants, or other secular judges under their authority, give way to such warnings, and no goods of the said excommunicated persons are found in their hands, the said royal officers must go at their own expense to the prelates' court and there swear that they found no goods belonging to the excommunicated persons. Otherwise the excommunicated are at once denounced, and by a sentence of excommunication are compelled to satisfy the debt on behalf of the excommunicated.

units.la: 14. Item si duo laici sint processu in curia alicuius Domini temporalis super actione reali vel personali, & contingat quod altera partium diffugiendo appellet ad curiam alicuius prælati coram ossiciali suo, post magnos processus factos & litem contestatam, Officiales dictarum curiarum nituntur retinere cognitionem talium causarum tam in reali quam personali, & virtute monitionum & sententiarum faciunt desistere Dominum temporalem à cognitione causæ post appellationem, quod nisi faciat, excommunicatur & trahitur ad emendam, ex quibus temporalis lædituri iurisdictio, & amittit retentum suum, quia nullus à curia prælatorum appellat ad curiam Regiam.
units.tr: 14. Likewise, if two laymen are in process in the court of some temporal lord concerning a real or personal action, and it happens that one of the parties, evading the matter, appeals to the court of some prelate before his official, after long proceedings have been held and the suit has been joined, the officials of those courts strive to keep cognizance of such causes, whether real or personal, and by warnings and sentences they make the temporal lord desist from hearing the case after the appeal; and unless he does so, he is excommunicated and dragged to a fine. From these things the temporal jurisdiction is harmed, and loses what it has retained, since no one appeals from the prelates' court to the royal court.

units.la: 15. Item si quis laicus in villa Regis facit arrestari debitorem suum laicum per iustitiam secularem, loci ii, ut arrestatus appellat illos, qui arrestant eum rei faciunt arrestari, officiales volunt habere cognitionem talem. Et si aliquid attentetur super appellatione, ipsi nituntur exigere emendam à iustitia, sicut ab illo cui factum est arrestum. Et si gentes regiæ compellunt eos ad resistendum, ipsi excommunicant eos.
units.tr: 15. Likewise, if a layman in a royal town has his lay debtor arrested by the secular justice, and the arrested person, or those who had him arrested, appeal to them, the officials want to have cognizance of this. And if anything is attempted against the appeal, they strive to exact a fine from the justice, as from the one by whom the arrest was made. And if the royal officers compel them to resist, they excommunicate them.

units.la: 16. Item dicti prælati habent magnam multitudinem officialium, quos vocant Præpositos clericorum, qui quidem officiales faciunt communiter citationes viua voce contra quasq; personas per dominiū regis & alibi sine commissione, licet in qualibet diœcesi esse non debebat, nisi sedes vna dumtaxat, vbi cognoscatur de causis. Et ex hoc accidit pluries, quod multæ personæ sine causa coram eis citantur, ad finem quod redimant se de magna pecuniæ quantitate: quod est in magnum præiudicium regis subditorumque suorum, & iurisdictionis temporalis eorundem.
units.tr: 16. Likewise, the said prelates have a great number of officials, whom they call provosts of the clergy, who commonly issue citations by word of mouth against whatever persons within the king's domain and elsewhere, without any commission, although in each diocese there ought to be only one seat where causes are heard. And from this it often happens that many persons are cited before them without cause, in order that they may buy themselves off for a large sum of money; this is to the great prejudice of the king, of his subjects, and of their temporal jurisdiction.

units.la: 17. Item dicti præpositi clericorum sigillant domos clericorum in villis regis & aliorum dominorum temporalium in præiudicium iurisdictionis Domini regis: & aliorum secularium licet in domibus & aliis tresfondis regis vel aliorum secularium dicti prælati exercere aliquam iurisdictionem non possint.
units.tr: 17. Likewise, the said provosts of the clergy seal the houses of clerics in the royal towns and those of other temporal lords, to the prejudice of the jurisdiction of the lord king; and of other laymen, although the said prelates cannot exercise any jurisdiction in the houses and other tenements of the king or of other laymen.

units.la: 18. Item dicti prælati vel eorum officiales sigillant bona mobilia clericorum coniugatorum & mercatorum, licet in talibus eorum cognitio pertineat ad iudicem vel curiam secularem.
units.tr: 18. Likewise, the said prelates or their officials seal the movable goods of married clerics and of merchants, although the cognizance of such matters belongs to the judge or secular court.

units.la: 19. Item compellunt personas laicas ad dandum iusiurandum clericis coram eis in curia ecclesiastica, maxime regis seruientes.
units.tr: 19. Likewise, they compel lay persons to take an oath before clerics in the ecclesiastical court, especially the king's servants.

units.la: 20. Item in iustitia & in dominio regis & subditorum faciunt gentes prælatorum inuentatoria de bonis laicorum decedentium.
units.tr: 20. Likewise, within the king's justice and lordship and that of his subjects, the prelates' men make inventories of the goods of laymen who have died.

units.la: 21. Item ipsi cognoscunt de actionibus hypotheticis, quæ sunt reales, vel saltem mixtæ.
units.tr: 21. Likewise, they take cognizance of hypothecary actions, which are real, or at least mixed.

units.la: 22. Item dicti prælati nituntur habere cognitionem personarum laicarū commorantiū in domibus Dei & leprosorum, villarum regiarum & subditorum suorum, vel extra villas: licet Domino regi vel eius subditis memoratis pertineat cognitio eorundem, & dant dicti prælati vel eorum officiales monitiones cum magnis poenis pecuniarum & sententias excommunicationis, quod nullus audeat illas personas in alia curia quam sua.
units.tr: 22. Likewise, the said prelates claim the right to take cognizance of lay persons who live in the houses of God and of lepers, in the king's towns and among their own subjects, or outside the towns, although the cognizance of these persons belongs to the lord king or to his aforesaid subjects. The said prelates or their officials issue monitions with heavy pecuniary penalties and sentences of excommunication, so that no one dares to bring these persons before any court other than their own.

units.la: 23. Item ad finem, quod dicta curia ecclesiastica augmentetur, dicti prælati faciunt magna multitudinem tonsuratarum pueris aetate minoribus, quorum aliqui sunt servorum filii, alii de illegitimo matrimonio procreati: ac hominibus coniugatis insufficientibus & illiteratis.
units.tr: 23. Likewise, in order that the said ecclesiastical court may be enlarged, the said prelates make a great number of tonsured clerks, some of them boys under age, some the sons of serfs, others born of unlawful marriage, and married men who are unfit and unlettered.

units.la: 24. Item faciunt contagiari & compelli per suos præpositos clericorum mulieres viduas, & nituntur habere eorum cognitionem: nec non pupillorum, & sibi applicare bona eorum, quando moriuntur, sicut de maioribus aetate, quando decedunt ab intestato, quorum quidem cognitio spectat ad regem: quia tales personae sunt cum bonis suis de gardia regis.
units.tr: 24. Likewise, through their provosts they cause the wives and widows of clerks to be summoned and compelled, and they claim cognizance of them; and likewise of orphans, and they seek to appropriate their goods when they die, as also those of adults who die intestate. Cognizance of these matters belongs to the king, because such persons, with their goods, are under the king's protection.

units.la: 25. Item faciunt per dictos praepositos clericorum & in dominio regis & alibi iuris ordine non serrato plures personas laicas, imponentes eis quod in aliquo casu commiserunt aliquid contra fidem, & detinent eos in carceribus, licet eorum captio & detentio spectare debeat ad regem, donec tales personae super illo casu impositio sint convictae.
units.tr: 25. Likewise, through the said provosts of the clergy, in the king's domain and elsewhere, they indict many lay persons without observing the due order of law, charging them with having committed something against the faith in some case. They keep them in prison, although their arrest and detention ought to belong to the king until such persons are convicted of that charge.

units.la: 26. Item exercent suas iurisdictiones currentes per villas regias & subditorum non debeant iurisdictionem tenere.
units.tr: 26. Likewise, they exercise their jurisdictions running through the king's towns and over subjects, though they ought not to hold jurisdiction there.

units.la: 27. Item quando isti prælati vel eorum officiales faciunt moneri praepositos ... & institiarios regis super aliquo faciendo per eos in suis monitionibus, magnam poenam applicantes prælatis, nisi fiat & completur, quod in monitionibus suis continent poenam excommunicationis apponunt, & hoc est inceptum de novo in praeiudicium ... ditorum suorum.
units.tr: 27. Likewise, when these prelates or their officials cause the provosts ... and the king's justices to be warned to do something in their monitions, they attach a heavy penalty payable to the prelates unless it is done and completed. In their monitions they add a penalty of excommunication, and this practice has lately begun to the prejudice of ... their subjects.

units.la: 28. Item quando prælati vel officiarii eorum prosequuntur aliquem laicum in curia sua exemptio & in casu huiusmodi deficiunt sibi testes: ipsi faciunt plures personas laicas ad ferendum testimonium in illa causa coram se citari: siue sit Burgensis regius & alterius cuiuscunque: & ipsis testibus noluntaliquid consignare pro expensis eorum. Et nisi veniant ad diem, ad quam citantur, excommunicantur.
units.tr: 28. Likewise, when prelates or their officials prosecute some lay person in their court, which is exempt, and in such a case lack witnesses, they cause many lay persons to be summoned before them to give testimony in that cause, whether they be citizens of the king's boroughs or of any other place. They are unwilling to set aside anything for the expenses of these witnesses, and unless the witnesses come on the day to which they are cited, they are excommunicated.

units.la: 29. Item si aliquis malefactor capiatur per aliquem iustitiarium regiu laisitus de furto suo: & ille, cui res est furata, veniat coram gentibus regiis, & probet rem huiusmodi furtivam suam esse: & ideo expediatur eidem per gentes regias, si ex post facto dicant praelati vel eorum officiarii malefactorem esse clericum, ipsi faciunt compelli per monitiones & citationes suas praedictas gentes regias ad restituendum eis rem furtivam praedictis: quod nisi fecerint, excommunicantur.
units.tr: 29. Likewise, if some wrongdoer is arrested by one of the king's justices for his theft, and the person from whom the goods were stolen comes before the king's officers and proves that the goods are his, and they are accordingly handed over to him by the king's officers, then, if afterwards the prelates or their officials say that the wrongdoer is a clerk, they compel the said king's officers, by their monitions and citations, to restore the stolen goods to those mentioned. If they do not do so, they are excommunicated.

units.la: 30. Item si contingat, quod gentes regiae capiant aliquem malefactorem pro crimine certo per eum commissio, & idem malefactor dicat se clericum esse, licet nec tonsuram nec habitum deferat clericales, officiales praelatorum faciunt in continenti detinentes & capientes compelli per monitiones & sententias ad restituendum sibi praedictum malefactorem tanquam clericum suum.
units.tr: 30. Likewise, if it happens that the king's officers arrest some wrongdoer for a certain crime committed by him, and the same wrongdoer says he is a clerk, although he wears neither tonsure nor clerical dress, the officials of the prelates immediately compel those who detain and arrest him, by monitions and sentences, to hand over the said wrongdoer to them as their clerk.

units.la: 31. Item si gentes regiae vel alii iustitiarii seculares ceperunt aliquem malefactorem latronem vel etiam homicidam, qui tonsuram deferat clericalem, eumque restituant praelatis, idem malefactor latis cito postmodum expeditur, licet recognoverit crimen, etiam licet aliqui laici, qui cum eo fuerunt socii in maleficiis, propter hoc iustitiari fuerint, eumque accusaverint de maleficio: & sic tales malefactores ad talia maleficia perpetranda facilius excitantur.
units.tr: 31. Likewise, if the king's officers or other secular justices have arrested some wrongdoer, a robber or even a murderer, who wears clerical tonsure, and hand him over to the prelates, the same wrongdoer is soon afterwards set free, even though he has confessed the crime. Even where some lay persons who were his accomplices in the wrongdoing have been punished for it, and have accused him of the crime, he is set free. Thus such wrongdoers are more easily roused to commit such crimes.

units.la: 32. Item si quis dicat se expoliatum fuisse, officialis sibi dabit incontinenti monitionem contra spoliatorem, & virtute monitionis huiusmodi monebitur per aliquem de praepositis clericorum, quod restituat sibi contenta in monitione, aut quod iuret, si spoliavit conquerentem de his, de quibus est conquestus, & si iurare renuerit coram praeposito, ipse praepositus incontinenti monitionem sigillat & excommunicat illum, qui noluit iurare: nec poterit postea absolvi, donec satisfecerit de contentis in monitione, de quibus conquerens se prius dixerat spoliatum.
units.tr: 32. Likewise, if someone says that he has been despoiled, the official will at once give him a monition against the despoiler, and by virtue of this monition the despoiler will be warned by one of the provosts of the clergy to restore to him the things contained in the monition, or else to swear, if he despoiled the complainant of those things of which he has complained. If he refuses to swear before the provost, the provost immediately seals the monition and excommunicates the man who refused to swear. Nor can he afterwards be absolved until he has made satisfaction for the things contained in the monition, of which the complainant had earlier said he was despoiled.

units.la: 33. Item si quis pro delicto suo detineatur in carcere alicuius iudicis secularis, licet captus fuerit in habitu laicali & sine tonsura, & qui gesserit se antea per totam vitam tanquam laicus, pro eo solum quod aduocabit se pro clerico, quia meliorem expedientiam habebit a praelato & officiariis, quam per seculares, & delictum remanebit impunitum, dicti officiarii faciunt moneri iudicem secularem, ut cito malefactorem restituat eis atque reddat: alioquin cessabitur eis incontinenti per totam villam, ubi sic captus tenebitur malefactor: & pro vitandis periculis, quae venire possunt occasione dicti cessus, oportet quod iudex reddat malefactorem in magnum praeiudicium iurisdictionis regis & temporalis, ad quem cognitio pertinet in casu reflorti.
units.tr: 33. Likewise, if someone is held in the prison of some secular judge for his offence, although he was arrested in lay dress and without tonsure, and although he has behaved as a layman all his life, merely because he claims to be a clerk, since he will obtain better treatment from the prelate and his officials than from the secular courts, and the crime will remain unpunished, the said officials cause the secular judge to be warned to restore and surrender the wrongdoer to them at once. Otherwise a cessation will at once be declared against them throughout the whole town where the wrongdoer is held in custody. And to avoid the dangers that may arise from that cessation, the judge must hand over the wrongdoer, to the great prejudice of the king's jurisdiction and of the temporal jurisdiction, to which cognizance belongs in a case of this kind.

units.la: 34. Item quando aliquis malefactor redditur iudicibus ecclesiae per iudices seculares tanquam clericus, amici ipsius malefactoris veniunt ad officiales praelatorum, & concordant cum eis: & sic dimittunt sine punitione ire: & sic peiora committunt quam ante, licet crimina essent notiora.
units.tr: 34. Likewise, when some wrongdoer is handed over to the judges of the Church by the secular judges as a clerk, his friends come to the officials of the prelates and come to terms with them. Thus they let him go without punishment, and so he commits worse crimes than before, even though his offences were more notorious.

units.la: 35. Item quam citius clerici coniugati, mercatores vel alii clerici cuiuscunque ministerii existant, trahuntur in causam coram iudice seculari pro aliquo delicto, ipsi clerici impetrant ab officialibus quaedam monitionem, & adducunt secum quendam presbyterum, per quem faciunt moneri iudicem secularem sub poena centum vel ducentarum marcharum argenti, & excommunicant ne curiam vel cognitionem de talibus teneant, & ne molestentur eos in corpore vel in bonis, & si Dominus iudex eos postea, cessaturi ibidem incontinenti a celebratione missarum, licet hoc pro facto suo suarum mercaturarum existat.
units.tr: 35. Likewise, as soon as married clerks, merchants or other clerks of any ministry are drawn into a case before a secular judge for some offence, these clerks obtain a monition from the officials and bring with them a certain presbyter, through whom they cause the secular judge to be warned under penalty of one hundred or two hundred marks of silver, and they excommunicate him so that he may not hold court or cognizance over such matters, and so that they may not be molested in body or goods. If the lord judge afterwards ... they are at once to cease celebrating masses there, even though the matter concerns their own business as merchants.

units.la: 36. Item dicti officiales conceduntur citationes sine numero contra personas laicas in casu assecurationis personaliter coram eis ad assecurandas personas taliter incognitas, & si cognitae sint, in citatiorecommendetur, quodillę, qui citatus est, monearur sub magna poena, ne illum, qui sic citari cum secerit ipsum, pendente citatione trahat ad iudicem secularem.
units.tr: 36. Likewise, the said officials are granted unlimited citations against lay persons in cases of surety, to be given personally before them, to secure persons unknown in such a way; and if they are known, in the citation it is to be commended that the person who is cited be warned under heavy penalty not to drag before a secular judge, while the citation is pending, the one who has so cited him.

units.la: 37. Item cum quis excommunicatus est in aliquo loco, dicti officiales dant citationes personalis super participibus, & faciunt citari totari totam patriam ad vnam vel duas leucas circunquaque, vel tales, qui nouerunt excommunicatum bene quadraginta, sexaginta, vel centum personæ purgaturæ se super participatione prædictorum. Ex quo sequitur, quod probi homines antiqui & senes redimunt se quilibet de duodecim denariis, vel de duobus solidis pro vitandis expensis & laboribus, & multæ vineæ & terræ dimittuntur incultæ, & plures boni homines loca propria dimiserunt.
units.tr: 37. Likewise, when someone is excommunicated in any place, the said officials issue personal citations concerning those who took part with him, and they cause the whole country within one or two leagues round about to be cited, or such persons as know the excommunicated man well: forty, sixty or a hundred persons, who are to purge themselves concerning participation in the said matters. From this it follows that worthy men, both old and aged, each redeem themselves for twelve pence or two shillings, to avoid expense and trouble; many vineyards and fields are left uncultivated, and many good men have abandoned their own places.

units.la: 38. Item dicti officiales imponunt pluribus personis famæ laudabilis & honestæ vitæ, quod sunt vsurarii, & oportet eos cum ipsis officiis concordare pro euitanda eorum infamia & labore.
units.tr: 38. Likewise, the said officials charge many persons of good repute and honest life with being usurers, and these persons must come to terms with the officials to avoid infamy and trouble.

units.la: 39. Item dicti officiales faciunt citari aliquem bonum hominem coniugatum, & imponunt ei quod adulteratus est cum aliqua. Et similiter mulierem aliquam coniugatam imponendo sibi, quod adulterata est, in perpetuam infamiam ipsorum coniugum, & cum hoc extorsionem pecuniarum recipiunt ab eisdem.
units.tr: 39. Likewise, the said officials cause some good married man to be cited and charge him with having committed adultery with a certain woman. Similarly, they charge a certain married woman with having committed adultery, to the lasting infamy of the spouses, and along with this they extort money from them.
