units.la: 40. Item memoria sit de magna multitudine procuratorum, qui comedunt totum mundum virtute citationum, recipiunt homines in gardia sua, & per villas tenent placita, & assisias suas, & auctoritate sua relaxant citationes propter pecunias, quas extorquent & recipiunt ob hoc ab eis citatis.
units.tr: 40. Likewise, let it be recorded how great a crowd of procurators there is, who devour the whole world by means of citations. They take men into their custody, hold pleas and assizes through the villages, and by their own authority cancel citations for money, which they extort and receive from those summoned on this account.

units.la: 41. Item alia grauamina, quæ Capitula, Abbates, Priores, Hospitalarii, & aliæ personæ ecclesiasticæ regni Franciæ faciunt contra propulū: talia sunt, quia faciunt citari plures burgenses regis & alios in pluribus & diuersis locis per priuilegia, videl. Baiocenses, Nannetenses, in Britannia, Lugduni, Masticoni, & alibi, specialiter Hospitalarii magis vtuntur istis communiter, quam alii, ex quib. multum damnificantur populus, & grauabitur multipliciter in futurum, nisi remedium apponatur.
units.tr: 41. Likewise, the other grievances which the chapters, abbots, priors, Hospitallers and other ecclesiastical persons of the kingdom of France inflict on the people are these: they have many of the king's burgesses and others cited in many different places under privileges, namely at Bayeux, Nantes, in Brittany, at Lyon, Mâcon and elsewhere. The Hospitallers in particular make more use of these than the others do. By these the people are greatly harmed, and they will be burdened in many ways in future unless a remedy is applied.

units.la: 42. Item iudices ecclesiastici in quocunque casu niituntur habere cognitionem iniuriarum, siue in verbis, siue in factis commissa sit iniuria: nec non vxorum clericorum, licet sint mercatrices, & eorum mariti similiter mercatores. Et si aliquando tales coniuges capiantur per iudices seculares, ossiciales faciunt cessum apponi in parochia illa, virtute Concilii Siluanectensis.
units.tr: 42. Likewise, ecclesiastical judges strive to take cognizance of injuries, whether the injury was committed in words or in deeds, and likewise of the wives of clerics, even when they are merchants, and of their husbands, who are likewise merchants. And if at any time such spouses are seized by secular judges, the officials cause an interdict to be placed on that parish, by virtue of the Council of Senlis.

units.la: 43. Item volunt habere cognitionem bonorum tam mobilium quam immobilium viduarum. Et si contingat, quod aliqua vidua mercatrix in villa regis per viā arresti laicam personam faciat conuenire coram iudice seculari, & iam sit processum, quod persona illa laica fuerit per sententiam iudicis secularis in peritis viduæ condemnata. Si veniat ad notitiam iudicis ecclesiastici, quod vidua illa in aliena curia suum conuenit debitorem, ipse iudex ecclesiasticus trahet ipsum ad emendam, & compellet eum emendare per monitiones & sententias, & hoc sæpe contingit.
units.tr: 43. Likewise, they wish to have cognizance of the goods, both movable and immovable, of widows. And if it happens that a widow who is a merchant in the king's town, by way of arrest, has a lay person brought before a secular judge, and proceedings have already gone so far that this lay person has been condemned by the sentence of the secular judge in favour of the widow, and it then comes to the notice of the ecclesiastical judge that the widow sued her debtor in another court, that ecclesiastical judge will drag him to amends and compel him to make amends by warnings and sentences. This often happens.

units.la: 44. Ita plures habitatores terræ dictorum prælatorum vocant se invicem ad curiam officialium ex quadam appellatione volagia, & nituntur officiales de talibus appellationibus cognoscere in præiudicium iurisdictionis temporalis domini regis.
units.tr: 44. Likewise, many inhabitants of the land of the said prelates summon one another to the court of the officials on a certain appeal called volagia, and the officials strive to take cognizance of such appeals, to the prejudice of the temporal jurisdiction of our lord the King.

units.la: 45. Item si quis in briga, vbi sanguinis effusio facta fuerit, capiatur per aliquam iustitiam secularem, puniendus, si laicus, vel restituendus iudicio ecclesiastico, si clericus existat. Si talis captus appellat ad curiam officialis, volūt dicti officiales de hoc cognitionē habere etiam de laico, sicut de clerico, & cum hoc niituntur exigere emendare à curia seculari, quæ prædictam fecit captionem, & si hæc permitterentur, nunquam malefactores punirentur, quia in continenti appellarent, & post appellationem statim fugerent.
units.tr: 45. Likewise, if anyone is taken in a brawl in which bloodshed occurred, by some secular justice, he is to be punished if he is a layman, or handed back to ecclesiastical judgement if he is a cleric. If such a prisoner appeals to the court of the official, these officials want to have cognizance of the matter even of a layman, as they do of a cleric, and at the same time they strive to demand amends from the secular court which made the arrest. And if these practices were permitted, malefactors would never be punished, because they would appeal at once and flee immediately after the appeal.

units.la: 46. Item si faciant citari plures ex officio, ipsi non admittuntur per procuratorem. Et si ad diem sibi assignatam accedunt, imponitur eis quod vsurarii, & nisi respondeant ad voluntatem promotorum detruduntur, licet sint puri laici, neque liberantur donec finantiam fecerint pro voluntate ossicialium, licet non sint vsurarii, & si qui sint vsurarii, officiales recipiunt ab eis emendas, & postea sicut prius permittuntur exercere vsuras, vt in eis solitas emendas exerceant.
units.tr: 46. Likewise, if they cause several men to be cited ex officio, they are not admitted through a procurator. And if they appear on the day assigned to them, they are charged with being usurers, and unless they answer as the promoters wish they are thrust into prison, even though they are mere laymen. Nor are they released until they have paid a fine at the officials' pleasure, even though they are not usurers. And if any are usurers, the officials take amends from them and afterwards, as before, they are permitted to practise usury, so that they may pay the customary amends for it.

units.la: 47. Item capi faciunt per suos seruientes, clericos in quocunque tresfunde, absque hoc, quod iustitiam loci faciant appellari, & si per aliquos in hoc impediantur, ipsi compellunt eos per sententiam excommunicationis ab impedimento desistere.
units.tr: 47. Likewise, they have their own servants seize clerics in any place whatever, without having the local justice called upon. And if anyone hinders them in this, they compel him by sentence of excommunication to desist from the hindrance.

units.la: 48. Item quotiens iudices temporales capiunt aliquem, qui postea requiritur & redditur tanquam clericus iudici ecclesiastico sine difficultate quacunque: nihilominus dicti officiales faciunt ipsos iudices excommunicaros à canone nunciari.
units.tr: 48. Likewise, whenever secular judges seize someone who is afterwards claimed and handed over, without any difficulty whatever, to the ecclesiastical judge as a cleric, nevertheless the said officials cause those judges to be publicly proclaimed excommunicate.

units.la: 49. Item faciunt prælati tonsuras hominibus 30. annorum & vltra, & etiam coniugatis aliquibus, quando veniunt ad eos metu intrusionis carceris & punitionis alicuius criminalis delicti, quod antea perpetrauit, & hoc pluries fuit factum.
units.tr: 49. Likewise, the prelates give tonsures to men of thirty years and over, and even to some who are married, when they come to them through fear of imprisonment and of punishment for some criminal offence which they committed earlier. This has happened several times.

units.la: 50. Item si contingat, quod aliquis homo regis vel alterius cuiuscunque excommunicatus existat, & velit satisfacere, & facere se absolui, genera prælatorum exigent ab eo emendam ad ipsorum arbitrium, vnde plures remanent in excommunicatione.
units.tr: 50. Likewise, if it happens that some man of the king, or of anyone else, is excommunicate and wishes to make satisfaction and have himself absolved, the prelates of various ranks demand from him a fine at their own discretion, so that many remain in excommunication.

units.la: 51. Item postquam propter debatum duarum personarum adinuicem contendentium super possessionem alicuius rei immobilis res contentiosa posita est in manu regis per aliquem seruientem regis, monent ipsum, ne perturbet alteram partium in possessione, & si fecerit, excommunicant eū.
units.tr: 51. Likewise, after a dispute between two persons contending with one another over the possession of some immovable property, the property in question has been placed in the king's hand by one of the king's sergeants. They warn him not to disturb either party in possession, and if he does so, they excommunicate him.

units.la: 52. Item dicti prælati decanique & capellani & aliæ gentes ecclesiasticæ tot & tantos labores dant officiariis regis ratione iurisdictionis regiæ, sicut prædictis, vlurpatæ, quod plures officiarii regii, expenderunt de suo pro iuribus regis obseruandis, & per vexationes & labores faciunt eis expendere quicquid habent.
units.tr: 52. Likewise, the said prelates, deans, chaplains and other ecclesiastical persons impose such great and numerous labours on the king's officers, by reason of royal jurisdiction usurped as stated above, that many royal officers have spent their own money in maintaining the rights of the king, and by vexations and labours they are made to spend whatever they have.

units.la: 53. Item si aliquis iusticiarius laicus pro certa & iusta causa ad requestam partis appellat man- num suam in rebus haereditariis clericorum iudices ecclesiae & eorum ministri faciunt monitiones in scripto contra dictum iusticiarium sub poena excommunicationis, & sub poena pecuniaria, ut manifestum leuet & amoueat: & iniungit eidem ut alteram partem de praedictis rebus gaudere permittat, alias ipsum denunciat excommunicatum, a qua sententia absolui non potest, nisi redimat se ad officialis arbitrium in praeiudicium resorti Domini nostri Regis.
units.tr: 53. Likewise, if any lay justice, for a certain and just cause at the request of a party, lays his hand on the hereditary property of clerics, the ecclesiastical judges and their ministers issue warnings in writing against that justice under penalty of excommunication and of a fine, that he remove and withdraw what he has seized, and they order him to allow the other party to enjoy the said property. Otherwise they denounce him as excommunicate, and he cannot be absolved from that sentence unless he redeems himself at the official's discretion, to the prejudice of the jurisdiction of our lord the King.

units.la: 54. Item iudices ecclesiastici quam citius audiunt, quod aliquis diues decessit, vel cogitant quod cito debet decedere, ipsi mittunt literas clausas capellano suo, quod nullatenus audeat inhumare ip- sum, licet fecerit testamentum, & ecclesiastica sacramenta receperit, & postmodum cum amici defuncti ad eos accedunt, ad eos sciturí, propter quae faciunt hoc, dicti officiales asserunt, quod dictus defunctus fuit usurarius, vel quod mandata ecclesiae non seruauit. Et tam diu faciunt corpus super terram teneri, quod oportet amicos redimere de magna quantitate pecuniae: & per talem modum magnas pecunias habuerunt.
units.tr: 54. Likewise, as soon as ecclesiastical judges hear that some rich man has died, or suspect that he is about to die shortly, they send sealed letters to their chaplain that he must on no account dare to bury the man, even though he has made a will and has received the ecclesiastical sacraments. Afterwards, when the friends of the dead man come to them to learn why they do this, the said officials assert that the deceased was a usurer, or that he did not observe the commands of the Church. And they keep the body above ground for so long that the friends must redeem it with a large sum of money. In this way they have obtained great sums.

units.la: 55. Item si in aliquo cimiterio fiat effusio sanguinis violenta, propter quam ponatur interdictum, ipsi praelati faciunt impositionem fieri decem librarum super omnibus parochianis pro salario suo reconciliationis cimiterii memorati, licet aliqui parochianorum a sua iurisdictione sint exempti, etiam licet illi tantum habeant vel plus de bonis illius, qui talem violentiam commisit.
units.tr: 55. Likewise, if violent bloodshed is committed in any cemetery, on account of which an interdict is placed upon it, the prelates themselves cause a levy of ten pounds to be imposed on all the parishioners, as their fee for reconciling the said cemetery. This is done although some of the parishioners are exempt from their jurisdiction, and even though those very people have as much or more of the goods of the man who committed the violence.

units.la: 56. Item aliqui capellani dicunt se habere priuilegia Apostolica, quorum virtute sibi constituunt iudices, quos volunt, & aliquotiens de suo proprio collegio. Et sic iudices in suis causis existunt, quod de iure non possunt. Vnde contingit, quod post magnos processus & expensis factis in aliqua magna inquesta saepius super realitate, quam alias, ad eorum notitiam per consiliarios vel procuratores suos peruenit, quod ipsi debent in causa succumbere, in continenti reuocant suos iudices memoratos, & sic sunt subditi regis damnificati, nec possunt ius habere ab ipsis.
units.tr: 56. Likewise, some chaplains say that they hold apostolic privileges, by virtue of which they appoint judges whom they choose, sometimes from their own college. Thus they are judges in their own causes, which by law they cannot be. Hence it happens that after great proceedings and expenses incurred in some large inquest, more often over a real matter than otherwise, when it comes to their notice through their counsellors or procurators that they must lose the case, they at once revoke the judges already mentioned. So the king's subjects are harmed, and they cannot obtain justice from them.

units.la: 57. Item si laicus vocat clericum in causa haereditaria coram iudice seculari, ipsi iudices ecclesiastici faciunt cessare processus sibi cognitionem attribuentes. Et cum hoc pro impetratione talium adiornatorum trahunt laicos ad emendam.
units.tr: 57. Likewise, if a layman summons a cleric in an hereditary matter before a secular judge, the ecclesiastical judges cause the proceedings to cease, assigning the cognizance to themselves. And at the same time, for obtaining such adjournments, they drag laymen to amends.

units.la: 58. Item cognitionem clericorum coniugatorum mercatorum, qui sunt manu operarii, quorum cognitio pertinet ad iudices seculares, specialiter super facto mercaturarum suarum, attribuere sibi niituntur ecclesiastici iudices.
units.tr: 58. Likewise, the ecclesiastical judges strive to assign to themselves the cognizance of married clerics who are merchants, or who work with their hands, whose cognizance belongs to secular judges, especially concerning the business of their trades.

units.la: 59. Item pluries posuerunt interdictum in pluribus villis, castris regis, & diuinum officium cessare fecerunt contra priuilegia, quae habuit dominus noster Rex a pluribus summis Pontificibus.
units.tr: 59. Likewise, on several occasions they have placed an interdict on several towns and castles of the king, and caused divine office to cease, contrary to the privileges which our lord the King has received from several supreme Pontiffs.

units.la: 60. Item pro custodia temporalitatis suae faciunt clericos suos Balliuos & seruientes suos & sic quando ipsi delinquunt, non possunt puniri, sicut decet, propter quod iustitia non seruatur.
units.tr: 60. Also, to guard their temporal property, they make their clerics, bailiffs and servants. So when these men offend, they cannot be punished as they ought to be, and justice is not upheld.

units.la: 61. Item iudices ecclesiastici habent procuratores, qui si teneant aliquem excommunicatum, siue iusta sit sententia, siue non, ipsi faciunt monitiones fieri, quod nullus operetur vel faciat negocium qualecunque ei, qui in tali statu consistit, propter quod terrae & vineae saepe remanent incultae in praeiudicium communitatis populi & regis.
units.tr: 61. Also, ecclesiastical judges have procurators who, if they hold anyone to be excommunicated, whether the sentence is just or not, have warnings issued that no one may carry on any business at all with a person in that state. As a result, lands and vineyards often lie uncultivated, to the prejudice of the community, the people and the king.

units.la: 62. Item promotores praedicti faciunt fieri citationes, per quas citari faciunt 20. 30. 40. personas, vel amplius, in citatione imponentes eis, quod participarunt cum talibus interdictis: & deno capiunt 10. & de altero 20. solidos, secundum quod possunt, unde communis populus est multum oppressus & granatus.
units.tr: 62. Also, the aforesaid promoters have citations issued by which they summon twenty, thirty, forty persons or more, charging them in the citation with having taken part with such interdicted persons. From one they take ten solidi, from another twenty, according to what each can pay, and so the common people is greatly oppressed and harassed.

units.la: 63. Item iudices ecclesiastici faciunt iurare omnes aduocatos curiarum suarum, quod nullus litigabit sine eorum licentia contra eos, propter quod ius pauperum multoties perit, & causae Regis retardantur: quia proprii pensionarii regis non sunt admissi ad ipsorum consilium accedere, nisi de ipsorum iudicum licentia speciali.
units.tr: 63. Also, the ecclesiastical judges make all the advocates of their courts swear that no one will bring a suit against them without their permission. As a result the right of the poor often perishes, and the king's causes are delayed, because the king's own paid advocates are not admitted to their counsel except by special licence of those same judges.

units.la: 64. Item volunt inuentaria facere de bonis illorum, qui ab intestato decedunt: voluntque bonorum tam mobilium quam immobilium possessionem habere, & ipsa per manus eorum distribui haeredibus, vel illis quibus volunt conferre.
units.tr: 64. Also, they wish to make inventories of the goods of those who die intestate. They want possession of both movable and immovable goods, and they want these to be distributed to heirs, or to those to whom they wish to give them, through their own hands.

units.la: 65. Item testamenta quoque volunt per manus suas executioni tradere: inuentaria facere bonorum defunctorum, eademque seruare & haeredibus distribuere, & habent officiales, qui super his exequendis duntaxat deputati existunt.
units.tr: 65. Also, they wish to carry wills into execution through their hands, to make inventories of the goods of the deceased, to keep them and distribute them to the heirs. They have officials who are appointed solely to carry these things out.

units.la: 66. Item quod aliquando testamentis coram tabellionibus factis nolunt adhibere fidem, nisi prius per ipsos officiales fuerint approbata.
units.tr: 66. Also, they sometimes refuse to give credence to wills made before notaries unless they have first been approved by these officials.

units.la: His auditis dixerunt praelati, quod super his volebant deliberare, & fuit assignata dies veneris sequens, qua die respondit pro praelatis dictus Dominus Electus Senonensis, & proposuit infra scripta apud Vicenas, ubi Rex tenuit dictam diem, dicens sic videlicet. Quia dominus Petrus de Cugneriis pridie proponens contra ecclesiam Gallicanam, cepit thema suum, quod scribitur Matthaei vigesimo tertio, Reddite quae sunt Caesari Caesari: & quae sunt Dei Deo. In quibus verbis dicebat notari duo. Primo praelatorum ad regis obedientiam, reuerentiam & subiectionem. Secundo iurisdictionis temporalis & spiritualis diuisionem. Et primum probabat per illud, quod scribitur 1. Pet. 2. Subiecti estote omni creaturae propter Deum, siue regi quasi praecellenti, siue ducibus tanquam ab eo missu in vindictam malo- rum, laudem vero bonorum. Secundum vero probabat per multa, quae Christus dixit Lucae 22. cum di- cerent terens Apostoli: ecce gladii duo: hic dixit Deus, sufficit: per duos gladios intelligens, duas iurisdictiones. Item pro eo quod Christus pro se & Petro voluit soluere tributum Matt. 10.7. ad dandum exemplum, quomodo ecclesiasticæ personæ tenebantur soluere & reddere potestati temporali temporalia. Et hoc confirmabatur per hoc, quod scribitur 11.q.1.c.si tributum: & c. magnū. Item quia bonum tur lege humana, cum dicitur: magna dona collata sunt, sacerdotium & imperium. Sacerdotium, vt diuinis imperium, vt humanis præesset, in corpore mystico ecclesiæ ... quomodo oportet ipsum & clericos ad ordines perduci in principio collationis prima. Ex quibus concludebat, quod cum istæ iurisdictiones sint distinctæ à Deo & vna sit reddita seu credita ecclesiæ, & aliis dominis temporalibus, quod nullomodo ecclesia debeat se intromittere de iurisdictione temporali, cum scriptum sit Prou. 22. Ne transgrediaris terminos antiquos, quos posuerunt patres tui. Et bene signanter dicit, antiquos, quia consuetudines, si quæ essent ad oppositum introductæ, non valerent: quinimo essent potius corruptelæ. Nec præscriptio potest habere locum: cum ius fisci sit imprescriptibile: nec rex etiam posset à se tale ius abdicare, sicut probat per multa capitula, quæ sunt 10. dist. Quare cum rex in sua coronatione iurasset iura regni non alienare: & alienata ad se revocare, si per ecclesiam aut per quemcunque alium erant vsurpata: tenebatur rex per iuramentum ad se illa renocare.
units.tr: When these complaints had been heard, the prelates said that they wished to deliberate on them, and the following Friday was fixed. On that day the Lord Elect of Sens replied on behalf of the prelates, and at Vincennes, where the king held that day, set out what is written below, saying as follows. Lord Pierre de Cugnières, speaking the day before against the Gallican Church, took as his theme the text in Matthew 23: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." In these words, he said, two things were to be noted. First, the obedience, reverence and subjection of prelates to the king. Second, the division of temporal and spiritual jurisdiction. He proved the first from 1 Peter 2: "Be subject to every creature for God's sake, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good." He proved the second from many things Christ said in Luke 22, when the apostles said, "Behold, two swords," and God said, "It is enough", understanding by the two swords two jurisdictions. Also, because Christ, for himself and Peter, wished to pay the tribute (Matt. 10.7), to give an example of how ecclesiastical persons were bound to pay temporal things to the temporal power and render them. This was confirmed by what is written in 11 q. 1 c. si tributum and c. magnum. Also, because it is set down by human law, when it is said: great gifts have been conferred, the priesthood and the empire. The priesthood, that it might preside over divine things, the empire, that it might preside over human things, in the mystical body of the Church ... how it is fitting that he himself and the clerics be brought to the orders at the first conferral. From these things he concluded that, since these jurisdictions are distinct from God, and one has been rendered or entrusted to the Church and the other to temporal lords, the Church must in no way meddle with temporal jurisdiction, since it is written in Proverbs 22: Do not pass over the ancient bounds which your fathers set. He says "ancient" very pointedly, because customs, if any had been introduced to the contrary, would have no force; rather they would be corruptions. Nor can prescription have any place, since the right of the fisc cannot be prescribed; nor could the king himself renounce such a right, as he proves from many chapters in dist. 10. Therefore, since the king swore at his coronation not to alienate the rights of the kingdom, and to recall to himself whatever had been alienated, if it had been usurped by the Church or by anyone else, the king was bound by his oath to recall them.

units.la: In speciali tradidit multos articulos: in quibus, vt dicebat, vsurpauerat ecclesia iurisdictionem temporalem. Vt ergo respondeam præmissis secundum concordantiam vocalem & realem, accipio quod Petrus protestatione præmissa, quicquid dicturus sum, volo dicere, non ad finem subiiendi quodcunque iudicii, sed solum ad hominis regis & aliorum assistentium conscientiam informandam. Thema tale: Deum timete, regem honorificate, 1. Pet. 2. In quibus verbis B. Petrus duo nobis ostendit, quo Deo debetur timor filialis & obedientia propter celsitudinem & imperium suæ maiestatis: Deum timete, secundo, quomodo debetur regi honor specialis & reverentia propter magnitudinem & fastigium suæ dignitatis; Regem honorificate. In Gallico: Premierement que nous debuons à Dieu doubtanze & tremour & amour pour sa grand' puissanze & haulte maieste, Deum timete. Secondement que nous debuons auroy reverenze & honeur pour sa grand' excellenze & haulte dignite, Regem honorificate. Et signanter præmittit Apostolus, quod primo debetur timor, secundo regi honor: quia Deo principaliter debetur timor, quia si contraria Deo iubeat rex vel alius, contempto rege, obediendum est Deo, Act. 5. Obediendum est Deo magis quam hominibus. Et 2. Macha. 7. Non obedio præcepto regis, sed præcepto legis. Et rationem huius reddit beatus Augustin. Et est in Glossa ad Roman. Et ponitur 11. quæst. 1. Qui resistit potestati superiori, voluntati & ordinationi Dei resistit. Sed quid si iubeat illud, quod non potes vel debes facere? hoc sane contemne minorem potestatem, timendo maiorem, ipsos humanarum rerum gradus addiscere. Sed aliquid iusti procurator, nunquam faciendum est, si contra proconsulem iubeat; si autem aliquid ipse proconsul iubeat & aliud imperator, & aliud Deus, contempto illo obtemperandum est Deo, maior enim potestas Deus est. Ille enim carcerem, iste gehennam minatur. Ille corpus occidere potest, iste corpus & animam mittere in gehennam ignis, merito igitur præmittitur, Deum timete, propter hoc dicitur Ecclesiastic. vlti. Deum time & mandata eius observa, hoc est omnis homo. Et videtur mihi, quod quis perceptitur Deum timere ex tribus: sci. ex grata munerum & donorum largitione, ex prouida seruitorum suorum honoratione, & ex integra rerum & bonorum redditione. In Gallico: Quant il sert deuotement, & loy donne largement: quant il le honoure saigement, & deuement: quant il luy rend le sien entierement, quia econtra qui ne le veult seruir, oy ne luy deigne obeir, oy veult le sien retenir, signum est quod non timet. Dico primo, &c. Et propter hoc Imperator Iustinianus dicit, quod licet pene nihil immensum sit bonum: tamen principem immensa dare ecclesiæ bonum est. Quid enim tenetur imperator, vt meliora det, cui plura dedit Deus habere, & multum donum esse, & facile dare, & maxime sanctissimis ecclesiis, in quibus optima mensura est dominicarum munerum immensitas. Et Gregorius Alberto patricio Gallorum, extra de donat. capitul. 1. dicit si hanc quodammodo nobilitas legem imponit, vt debere se quod spontè tribuit æstimet, & nisi in suis beneficiis creuerit, nihil se præstitisse putet, vnde Abel, qui de melioribus offerebat Domino, benedictus est à Deo, sicut patet Genes. 4. Vnde & reges quantum plurimum offerebant Deo: tantum fuerunt ab eo & spiritualiter & temporaliter benedicti, sicut patet de Iosue, Dauid & Salomone & aliis per totum librum Regum. Et ideo Numeri 18. scribitur: in donaria Dei separabitis optima, & primo Paralipom. vlt. im. dicebat Dauid: Latus obtuli vniuersa hæc: & populum tuum vidi cum ingenti donario offerre tibi donaria. Nec miraum, quia sicut ipse dicit ibidem: tua sunt Deus omnia, quæ de manu tua accepimus, dedimus tibi. Et ideo videtur mihi, quod quia inter cæteros reges, Franciæ reges plura dederunt Deo & ecclesiæ, & etiam Baronesregni: idcirco fuerunt super omnes felices, & quanta plura dederunt, tanto plura dedit eis Deus, sicut patuit de Clodoveo, Carolo, sancto Ludovico, & aliis. Quanto enim aliquis plura dat Deo, tanto Deus plura sibi dat. Cum ipse met promisit, date & dabitur vobis, Luc. 6. Vnde donum, quod princeps facit ecclesiæ, est donum, quod redditur cum maximo incremento, & tempore belli & tempore pacis. Tempore belli, quia victoria belli non aliunde quam à Deo sibi præstatur. Vnde 1. Machab. 4. c. Non in multitudine exercitus victoria belli, sed de cælo fortitudo est. & Exod. 17. dicitur, quia cum Moyses elevaret manum ad populum, vincebat Israel: sed si remittebat superabatur. Et 2. Machab. vlti. Iudas habiturus magnam victoriam de aduersis, vidit Amon & Ieremiam sacerdotes orantes pro populo & vniuersa ciuitate, &c.
units.tr: In particular he set out many articles in which, as he said, the Church had usurped temporal jurisdiction. So, to answer what has been said, according to verbal and real agreement, I accept, with the protest made beforehand, that whatever I am about to say I wish to say not to the end of submitting to any judgment, but only to inform the conscience of the king and of the others present. My theme is this: Fear God, honour the king, 1 Peter 2. In these words Blessed Peter shows us two things: to God is owed filial fear and obedience because of the height and power of his majesty: Fear God; and secondly, how special honour and reverence are owed to the king because of the greatness and eminence of his dignity: Honour the king. In French: First, that we owe to God awe, trembling and love for his great power and high majesty, Fear God. Second, that we owe reverence and honour for his great excellence and high dignity, Honour the king. The Apostle expressly puts first that fear is owed, and second that honour is owed to the king, because fear is owed to God principally. If the king or anyone else commands what is contrary to God, the king's command must be set aside and God obeyed: We must obey God rather than men, Acts 5; and I do not obey the king's command, but the command of the law, 2 Maccabees 7. Blessed Augustine gives the reason for this, and it is in the Gloss on Romans, and it is set down in 11 q. 1: Whoever resists the superior power resists the will and ordinance of God. But what if he commands what you cannot or ought not to do? Then, out of fear of the greater power, one must despise the lesser, and learn the degrees of human affairs. A procurator must never do anything at all if the proconsul commands it against the emperor's will. But if the proconsul commands one thing, the emperor another, and God another, then, scorning the former, one must obey God, for God is the greater power. The one threatens prison, the other gehenna; the one can kill the body, the other can cast body and soul into the fire of gehenna. Rightly, then, Fear God is put first; hence Ecclesiastes at the end: Fear God and keep his commandments, which is the whole duty of man. It seems to me that a man may be seen to fear God in three ways: by devoted service, by generous bestowal of gifts, and by full restitution of what is his. In French: how devoutly he serves, and how the law gives largely; how wisely and duly he honours him; how entirely he renders him what is his. On the contrary, he who will not serve him, nor deign to obey him, or wishes to keep what is his own, is a sign that he does not fear. I say first, etc. For this reason the Emperor Justinian says that although almost nothing is immense good, yet it is a good thing for a prince to give immense things to the Church. For what is the emperor bound to give of better things, to whom God has given more to have, and a great gift, and easy giving, and above all to the most holy churches, in which the greatest measure is the immensity of the Lord's gifts? And Gregory, writing to Albert, patrician of the Gauls (extra de donat. cap. 1), says: if nobility imposes this law in some way, that a man should consider that he owes what he gives freely, and unless he grows in his benefactions, he should think he has done nothing. Hence Abel, who offered of the best things to the Lord, was blessed by God, as appears in Genesis 4. Hence kings, as much as they offered to God, so much were they blessed by him both spiritually and temporally, as appears of Joshua, David, Solomon and others throughout the book of Kings. And so it is written in Numbers 18: You shall set apart the best as offerings to God, and at the end of 1 Chronicles David said: I have offered all these things willingly, and I have seen your people offer with great offerings to you. Nor is this surprising, since, as he says there, All things are yours, O God, which we have received from your hand, we have given to you. And so it seems to me that, because among other kings the kings of France have given more to God and the Church, and the barons of the kingdom also, therefore they were happier than all others; and the more they gave, the more God gave them, as appeared in Clovis, Charles, Saint Louis and others. For the more a man gives to God, the more God gives to him, since he himself promised: Give, and it will be given to you, Luke 6. Hence the gift which a prince makes to the Church is a gift returned with the greatest increase, both in time of war and in time of peace. In time of war, because victory in war is granted to us by God alone. Hence 1 Maccabees 4: Victory in war does not lie in the multitude of the army, but strength is from heaven. And Exodus 17 says that when Moses lifted up his hand, Israel prevailed over the people, but if he let it down, they were overcome. And at the end of 2 Maccabees, Judas, about to win a great victory over adversaries, saw Onias and Jeremiah, the priests, praying for the people and the whole city, etc.

units.la: Tempore etiā pacis, quia & vita regis & filiorū ac prosperitas, pax & obedientia porationē ecclesiæ conseruatur in regno, vnde Salomon quamdiu fuit intentus operi domus Dei, tādiu pacem habuit.
units.tr: Likewise in time of peace, since both the life of the king and of his sons and their prosperity are preserved in the kingdom by peace and by the people's obedience to the Church. Hence Solomon had peace for as long as he was occupied with the work of the house of God.

units.la: Unde Prouerb. 16. Complacuerunt Deo vias hominis: inimicos quoque eius conuertit ad pacem, unde 1. Esdr. 6. cap. dicitur de Sacerdotibus: Offerant oblationes Deo cœli, & orent pro vita Regis & filiorum eius. Bene ergo dicitur esse hoc donum fauorabile & irreuocabile, propter quod victoria tribuitur, vita concedi-tur, & pax & securitas conseruatur, seruire ergo sibi & dare liberaliter, est primum signum timoris & amoris, Ecclesiast. 2. Qui timetis Dominum, credite illi & non euacuabitur merces vestra.
units.tr: Hence Proverbs 16: "When a man's ways please the LORD, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him." And so 1 Esdras 6 says of the priests: "Let them offer oblations to the God of heaven, and pray for the life of the king and of his sons." Rightly, therefore, this is called a favourable and irrevocable gift, by which victory is granted, life is given, and peace and security are preserved. To serve him and give generously is therefore the first sign of fear and love. Ecclesiasticus 2: "You that fear the Lord, believe in him, and your reward shall not be taken away."

units.la: Dico secundo, &c. Scitis quod inter præcepta Domini, primum præceptum secundæ tabulæ est honorare patrem, quod præceptum sicut pulchre dicit Apostolus ad Heb. 11. est non solum de patre carnali, imo potius de patre spirituali: quia sicut spiritualia sunt potiora quibuscunque carnalibus seu temporalibus: ita tenetur tantum, vel plus filius spiritualis ad honorandum patrem spiritualem, sicut patrem carnalem. Patres autem spirituales prælati sunt, unde 4. Reg. 6. Israel Elisæum vocabat patrem dicens: nunquam pœnitebas pater mi. Et propter hoc Luc. decim. dicebat Saluator Apostolis, quorum successores sunt episcopi, Qui vos audit, me audit: & qui vos spernit, me spernit. Et primæ ad Thessalon. 4. Qui vos spernit, non homines spernit, sed Deum. Et ideo ille Iustinianus Imperator alibi dicit: sicut nos habemus magnam sollicitudinem circa Dei vera dogmata & sacerdotum honestatem, quam illis obtinentibus credemus, quia per maxima dona nobis dona dabuntur à Deo, & ea quæ sunt firma habebimus, & ea quæ nondum hactenus adeuenerunt acquiriemus. Et beatus Hieronymus in Registro scribens cuidam imperatori dixit sic, & habetur in decret. 11. quæst. 1. Sacerdotibus: non indignetur Imperator sacerdotibus super excellenti consideratione propter eum, cuius sunt seruii in eis dominetur, sic ut debitam reuerentiam impendat: quia illi aliquando in diuinis eloquiis Dii, aliquando Angeli nominantur. Exod. 22. Diis non detrahetis. Et Malach. 2. Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, angelus enim Domini exercituum est. Et subdit: quid mirum si nostra pietas illos dignetur honorare, quibus Deus in suo eloquio honorem tribuens, angelos & Deos appellat? Unde & ibidem refert de Constantino Imperatore, quod cum sibi oblatæ accusationes contra episcopos fuissent, libellos quidem accusationis recepit, & eosdem, quod accusati fuerant, episcopos conuocans in eorum conspectu libellos, quos acceperat, incendit dicens: Ite & inter vos causas disponite vestras: quia non dignum est, ut nos iudicemus Deos, quia scriptum est, Deus stetit in Synagoga Deorum: de medio autem eorum Deus diiudicat. Et subditur in eodem capitulo, quod pagani, qui Deos ligneos colebant & lapideos: tamen eorum sacerdotibus honorem maximum tribuebant. Quid igitur mirum, si Christianus imperator veri Dei sacerdotes honoret? quasi dicat, non est mirum, sed debitum. Et ratio est, quia sicut dominus Petrus pridie dicebat & bene, in hoc duæ sunt potestates, sacerdotium & regnum, spiritualis & temporalis: quia inter se differunt sicut Sol & Luna, sicut cœlum & terra, sicut aurum & plumbum. Et ideo si illi, qui præest potestati minori, est à subditis honor impendendus: multo fortius illi, qui præest in potestate maiori, est à quibuscunque sibi subditis honor debitus impendendus, sicut expresse dicit cap. solita, de maior. & obed. vbi expresse respondetur auctoritati, quam dominus Petrus allegabat pro se; videlicet subiecti estote omni potestati, propter Deum. & ibi loquitur de subiectione, quæ est propter virtutis meritum, non propter necessitatis debitum. Si enim loqueretur de subiectione, quæ est propter necessitatis debitum: sequeretur, quod quilibet episcopus deberet esse subiectus pauperiori venulæ, quæ sit Parisiis, cum textus dicat: Subditi estote omni creaturæ humanæ, dicta autem vetula est humana creatura. De dignitate episcopali dicit Ambrosius in Pastorali suo: sicut honor & sublimitas episcopalis nullis poteris adæquari comparabilibus: si regum fulgori compares, quasi plumbi metallum ad auri fulgorem compares: quippe cum videas regum colla, & principum subiunctis genibus sacerdotum, & deosculata eorum dextra orationibus extendem se credere communiri. Et quia reges Franciæ præ cæteris regibus istum honorem prælatis impenderunt: idcirco præ cæteris regibus prosperati fuerunt, quia Ecclesiast. 4. dicitur: Qui honorat patrem suum, iocundabitur in filiis. Et sequitur ibidem, qui honorat patrem suum, viuet vita longiore. Istud est ergo signum timoris Dei. Et ideo dicitur Ecclesiastic. quart. Qui timet Deum, honorat parentes.
units.tr: I say secondly, &c. You know that among the commandments of the Lord, the first commandment of the second table is "Honour thy father." As the Apostle rightly says in Hebrews 11, this commandment concerns not only the carnal father but still more the spiritual father, because spiritual things are better than any carnal or temporal things. So the spiritual son is bound to honour his spiritual father just as much as, or more than, his carnal father. Now spiritual fathers are prelates. Hence in 4 Kings 6 Israel called Elisha "father," saying, "Never wouldst thou repent, my father." For this reason the Saviour also said to the Apostles in Luke 10, whose successors are bishops, "He that heareth you heareth me, and he that despiseth you despiseth me." And in 1 Thessalonians 4: "He that despiseth you despiseth not men but God." Therefore the Emperor Justinian also says elsewhere: "As we take great care concerning the true doctrines of God and the honour of the priests, we believe that by their holding them the greatest gifts will be given to us by God, and we shall have what is firm, and acquire what has not yet come to us." And blessed Jerome, writing to a certain emperor in the Register, spoke thus, as it is found in Decretum 11, q. 1, Sacerdotibus: "Let the emperor not be indignant that priests are held in such high regard, since he whose servant he is rules over them, so that he may show them due reverence; for in the divine oracles they are sometimes called gods, and sometimes angels. Exodus 22: 'You shall not speak evil of the gods.' And Malachi 2: 'The lips of the priest keep knowledge, for he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.'" And he adds: "What wonder if our piety deigns to honour those whom God, bestowing honour in his own word, calls angels and gods?" Hence also in the same place he reports of the Emperor Constantine that when accusations against bishops were brought to him, he received the written charges, and summoning the bishops who had been accused, burned in their sight the documents he had received, saying: "Go and settle your causes among yourselves, for it is not fitting that we should judge gods, since it is written, 'God stands in the assembly of gods; in the midst of them he judges.'" And it is added in the same chapter that the pagans, who worshipped gods of wood and stone, nevertheless paid the greatest honour to their priests. What wonder, then, if a Christian emperor honours the priests of the true God? As if to say: it is not a wonder, but a debt. And the reason is this: as Lord Peter rightly said the day before, there are two powers in this matter, the priesthood and the kingdom, the spiritual and the temporal, because they differ from one another as the sun and the moon, as heaven and earth, as gold and lead. Therefore if honour is to be paid by subjects to one who presides over the lesser power, much more is due honour to be paid by any subjects whatever to one who presides over the greater power. This is expressly stated in chapter "Solita," de maioritate et obedientia, where the authority Lord Peter cited in his own favour, namely "Be subject to every power for God's sake," is expressly answered. There the subjection spoken of is that which is owed on account of the merit of virtue, not on account of the debt of necessity. For if it spoke of subjection owed by necessity, it would follow that every bishop must be subject to the poorest old woman in Paris, since the text says "Be subject to every human creature," and an old woman is a human creature. Concerning episcopal dignity, Ambrose says in his Pastoral: "As the honour and sublimity of the bishop can be compared with nothing; if you compare it with the splendour of kings, you compare lead with the brightness of gold. For you see the necks of kings and princes bowed, and their right hands kissed by priests, and they believe themselves strengthened by the priests' prayers." And because the kings of France have paid this honour to prelates more than other kings, they have for this reason prospered more than other kings, since Ecclesiasticus 3 says: "He that honours his father shall rejoice in his children," and it follows there, "He that honours his father shall live a longer life." This, therefore, is the sign of the fear of God. And so Ecclesiasticus 3 says: "He that fears God honours his parents."

units.la: Dico tertio, quod aliquis dicitur timere Deum ex integra rerum & bonorum redditione, qui enim non reddit alteri, quod suum est, sed conatur vsurpare, non timet Deum. Econtra autem qui reddit integraliter rem, dicitur diligere & timere, quia, sicut dicitur Eccles. 18. Qui timet Deum, faciet bona. Et Psalm. A iudiciis enim tuis timui. Feci iudicium & iustitiam. Sicut enim dicunt Iuristæ, & verum est, aliquid efficitur alicuius multis modis, aliquando ex successione, aliquando ex commutatione, aliquando ex præscriptione, aut alia acquisitione, iure aut consuetudine, & sic de aliis. Et quia dominus Petrus pridie per iurisdictionis distinctionem, scilicet temporalis & spiritualis, conabatur probare, quod habens iurisdictionem spiritualem non debebat habere temporalem: alioquin non esset distinctio, sed potius confusio iurisdictionum, idcirco volo probare oppositum, quod istæ iurisdictiones compatibiles sunt in eadem persona, & maxime in Ecclesiasticis, & hoc probo tam iure diuino & naturali, quâ iure canonico & ciuili consuetudinario & etiam priuilegiato: tamen prius præmitto, quod formæ accidentales quædam sunt sic distinctæ, quod non sunt contrariæ, sed disparesæ sive disparatæ, sicut albedo & dulcedo, & aliæ formæ. Et aliæ sunt formæ, quæ sunt sic distinctæ, quod sunt contrariæ, nec sunt compatibiles in eodem subiecto, unum enim contrarium expellit aliud, quia importat negationem alterius. Vnde contraria sunt, quæ à se inuicem maxime distant, & in eodem susceptibili vicissim insunt, non simul, sicut dicit Philosophus in prædicamentis. Sed illæ formæ, quæ sunt sic distinctæ, quod non sunt contrariæ, sci. disparatæ, sunt compatibiles in eodem subiecto, sicut quantitas & qualitas, quia distinguuntur genere generalissimo in eodem homine: sicut fortitudo & temperantia, quæ sunt species virtutis moralis, in eodem reperiuntur, sicut Logica & Grammatica, quæ sunt species in eodem intellectu. Non est ergo bonum argumentum: istæ formæ sunt distinctæ: ergo non sunt compatibiles in eodem subiecto, quia ergo iurisdictiones temporales & spirituales sic sunt tm distinctæ, quod non sunt contrariæ, sed bene compatibiles, q; patet, quia vnum contrariū nō ordinatur ad aliud, imo corrumpit ipsum. Iurisdictio autem spiritualis ordinatur ad temporalem, vel econtra, & melius: imo dependet ab ea, sicut claritas lunæ à claritate solis. Itē vna iurisdictio confortat & adiuuat aliā, p quod patet, quod non habent contrarietatē, & per consequens nō sequitur propter earum distinctionē, quin sint compatibiles in eadem persona, q; etiam patet de facto, quia in eadem persona Christi fuit vtraq; iurisdictio, nam Domini est terra & plenitudo eius or. ter. & 5. qui hab. in eo, patet etiā ex alio: quia si non essent compatibiles, sequeretur q; nulla psona ecclesiastica posset habere iurisdictionē temporalē, nec castrum, nec villam, nec aliquid aliud, q; est valde absurdū, vnde ex hoc sequitur, quod nulla persona ecclesiastica posset esse subdita regi: cum non possit sibi subesse ratione spiritualitatis, sed solum ratione temporalitatis, quod esset in magnā derogationem honoris regni, patet igitur, quod istæ iurisdictiones sunt compatibiles, non obstante earum distinctione ab inuicē. Et p hoc patet respōsio ad oia illa, per quæ dominus Petrus probat distinctionē istarū iurisdictionū.
units.tr: I say thirdly, that a man is said to fear God by the full restoration of things and goods. For he who does not give back to another what is his, but tries to seize it, does not fear God. On the other hand, he who restores a thing in full is said to love and fear God, because, as Ecclesiasticus 15 says, "He that fears God will do good," and Psalm 118: "I have feared thy judgments; I have done judgment and justice." For as the jurists say, and it is true, something becomes someone's in many ways: sometimes by succession, sometimes by exchange, sometimes by prescription or other acquisition, by right or by custom, and so on for the rest. And because Lord Peter had the day before tried to prove, by the distinction of jurisdiction, namely temporal and spiritual, that one who has spiritual jurisdiction ought not to have temporal jurisdiction, otherwise there would be no distinction but rather a confusion of jurisdictions, I therefore wish to prove the opposite: that these jurisdictions are compatible in the same person, and especially in ecclesiastics. I prove this by divine and natural law, by canon law, by civil and customary law, and also by privilege. Yet first I premise that some accidental forms are so distinct that they are not contrary but disparate, as whiteness and sweetness and other forms are. And other forms are so distinct that they are contrary and not compatible in the same subject, for one contrary expels the other, since it implies the negation of the other. Hence contraries are those that are at the greatest distance from one another and in the same susceptible subject take their place in turn, not together, as the Philosopher says in the Categories. But those forms that are so distinct that they are not contrary, that is, disparate, are compatible in the same subject, as quantity and quality are, since they are distinguished by the most general genus, and as in the same man there are found fortitude and temperance, which are species of moral virtue, and as logic and grammar, which are species, are found in the same intellect. It is therefore not a good argument: these forms are distinct, therefore they are not compatible in the same subject. So too, since temporal and spiritual jurisdictions are so distinct that they are not contrary but well compatible, this is clear, because one contrary is not ordered to the other, but rather destroys it. Spiritual jurisdiction, however, is ordered to temporal, or the reverse, and indeed better: it even depends on it, as the brightness of the moon depends on the brightness of the sun. Likewise one jurisdiction strengthens and assists the other, which shows that they have no contrariety, and consequently it does not follow from their distinction that they cannot be compatible in the same person. This is also clear from fact, since in the same person of Christ both jurisdictions were present: "The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell in it" (Psalm 23). It is clear also from another point: if they were not compatible, it would follow that no ecclesiastical person could hold temporal jurisdiction, neither a castle nor a village nor anything else, which is wholly absurd. Hence it would follow that no ecclesiastical person could be subject to the king, since he could not be subject to him by reason of his spirituality, but only by reason of his temporality, which would greatly derogate from the honour of the kingdom. It is therefore clear that these jurisdictions are compatible, notwithstanding their distinction from one another. And by this the answer is clear to all those arguments by which Lord Peter proves the distinction of these jurisdictions.

units.la: His præmissis procedo ad probādum, quod talis iurisdictio temporalis pōt cadere in personam ecclesiasticā habentem iurisdictionē spiritualem. Probatio, q; iurisdictio temporalis pōt cadere in personam ecclesiasticā. Primo de iure diuino, & primo ex Testam. Veteri. Ad cuius euidentiam est sciendum, quod Deus post creationem mūdi & hominis, quasi vsq; ad tempus Noe, mundum p seipsum regere voluit ministerio angelorum, vnde & ipse contra Cain sententiā protulit Gen. 4. c. Noe autem qui obtulit holocaustū Domino & ædificauit altare, sicut patet Gen 8. c. quod pertinebat ad solos sacerdotes, habuit regimen omnium, qui erant in Archa Noe etiā in temporalibus. Melchisedech etiā, qui fuit sacerdos Dei altissimi, fuit etiā rex Salem, sicut patet Gen. 14. & vtramq; iurisdictionem habuit, dicit n Magist. Historiar. Gen. 14. Omnes primogeniti à Noe vsq; ad Aaron fuisse sacerdotes, qui in conuiuiis & oblationibus populo benedicebant, qui tantum habebant im primogenitura: ex quo competebat eis regimen aliorū.
units.tr: Having laid down these premises, I proceed to prove that such temporal jurisdiction can fall upon an ecclesiastical person who holds spiritual jurisdiction. The proof is that temporal jurisdiction can fall upon an ecclesiastical person. First, by divine right, and first from the Old Testament. For the clarity of this, it must be known that God, after the creation of the world and of man, wished to govern the world himself, by the ministry of angels, as far as the time of Noah; whence he also pronounced sentence against Cain (Gen. 4). Noah, however, who offered a burnt offering to the Lord and built an altar (as is clear from Gen. 8), which belonged to priests alone, had the rule of all who were in Noah's ark, even in temporal matters. Melchizedek also, who was the priest of the most high God, was also king of Salem, as is clear from Gen. 14, and he had both jurisdictions, as the Master of the Histories says on Gen. 14: "All the firstborn from Noah down to Aaron were priests, who blessed the people at feasts and offerings, and who alone had the birthright; from this they had the right to rule the others."

units.la: Moyses etiam, de quo dicitur in Ps. Moyses & Aaron in sacerdotibus eius, qui etiā Aaron & filios eius consecrauit in sacerdotes, totum populum Israel quantum ad temporalia iudicauit etiam in causis hæreditariis & mere realibus, sicut patet Num. 27. c. & in multis aliis locis. Textus etiam hoc dicit expresse Deuteron. 18. c. vbi dicitur sic: Si difficile & ambiguum apud te iudicium esse prospexeris inter sanguinem & sanguinem, causam & causam, lepram & lepram: surge & ascende ad locum, quem elegerit Dominus Deus tuus, & venies ad sacerdotes Leuitici generis, & ad iudicem qui fuit illo tempore, quæ ab eis, qui indicabunt tibi iudicii veritatem: sequereque eorum sententiam, qui autem superbierit nolens obedire sacerdotis imperio & decreto iudicis, morietur homo ille. Ecce quam manifeste dicit, quod ad sacerdotem pertinebat iudicare nō solum inter lepram & lepram quantum ad cerimonialia & irregularitates legis, sc. inter sanguinem & sanguinē, quantum ad criminalia, & inter causam & causam quantum ad similia. Item hoc apparet de multis iudicibus in lib. Iudic. Samuel etiam, qui fuit propheta & sacerdos etiam, populum totum in temporalibus diutissime iudicauit: imo quando populus petiit regem, displicuit multum Domino, vnde dixit Samueli: non te abiecerunt sed me, ne regnem super eos, 1. Reg. 8. ca. imo ex tunc durantibus regibus in populo Dei, quamdiu reges vsi sunt consilio sacerdotum & Pontificum, bene fuit eis & regno, quando autem dimiserunt consilium sacerdotum & pontificum, regimen eorum factum est in dissipationem, & finaliter ducti sunt in captiuitatem, in qua captiuitate populus ex toto regebatur per sacerdotes & prophetas, sicut per Esdram & Neemiam. Nouissime vero opere Machabæorum regnum reductum est & regimen ad sacerdotes, & idem fuerunt Reges seu Duces populi, habentes regimen tā in spiritualibus quam temporalibus, sicut legitur 1. & 2. Mach. de Matthatia & filiis eius, videl. Iuda Machabæo, Ionata, Simone & Iohanne filio Simonis: qui in omnibus tam in spiritualibus, quam temporalibus præfuerunt populo Dei. Quinimo Ieremiæ, qui fuit de sacerdotibus, dictum est: Constitui te super gentes & regna, vt euellas, disperdas, destruas & dissipes, ædifices & plantes, Ieremiæ capitulo primo, quinimo etiam tempore Iudicum Eliachim & sacerdos in temporalibus iudicauit. Et tota lex vetus plena est istis.
units.tr: Moses too, of whom it is said in the Psalm, "Moses and Aaron among his priests," who also consecrated Aaron and his sons as priests, judged the whole people of Israel in temporal matters, even in causes of inheritance and purely real matters, as is clear from Num. 27 and in many other places. The text also says this expressly in Deut. 18, where it is said thus: "If you see that judgment is difficult and ambiguous among you, between blood and blood, cause and cause, leprosy and leprosy, arise and go up to the place which the Lord your God shall choose, and you shall come to the priests of the Levitical race, and to the judge who is in that time, and they shall tell you the truth of the judgment; and you shall follow their sentence; but whoever is proud and refuses to obey the command of the priest and the decree of the judge, that man shall die." See how plainly it says that it belonged to the priest to judge not only between leprosy and leprosy, as to ceremonial matters and irregularities of the law, but between blood and blood, as to criminal matters, and between cause and cause, as to similar matters. Likewise this appears from many judges in the book of Judges. Samuel too, who was both prophet and priest, judged the whole people in temporal matters for a very long time; indeed, when the people asked for a king, it displeased the Lord greatly, whence he said to Samuel: "They have not rejected you, but me, that I should not reign over them" (1 Sam. 8). Indeed, from that time, while kings reigned over the people of God, as long as the kings used the counsel of the priests and high priests, it went well for them and for the kingdom; but when they abandoned the counsel of the priests and high priests, their rule turned to ruin, and finally they were led into captivity; in that captivity the people was wholly governed by priests and prophets, as by Ezra and Nehemiah. Lastly, in the work of the Maccabees the kingdom and rule were restored to the priests, and the same men were kings or leaders of the people, having rule in spiritual as well as temporal matters, as we read in 1 and 2 Maccabees concerning Mattathias and his sons, namely Judas Maccabeus, Jonathan, Simon and John the son of Simon, who in all things, both spiritual and temporal, presided over the people of God. Moreover, of Jeremiah, who was of the priests, it was said: "I have appointed you over the nations and kingdoms, to pluck up, to destroy, to overthrow and to scatter, to build and to plant" (Jer. 1). Indeed, even in the time of the Judges, Eliakim, the priest, judged in temporal matters. And the whole Old Law is full of such things.

units.la: Secundo etiam probo hoc ex Nouo Test. Christus n. non solum secundā diuinam naturam, secundum q; omnia ex nihilo creauit: & per consequens erat Dominus oim, imo etiā secundum humanā habuit vtramq; potestatē. Ipse n. fuit sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedech, sicut dicitur in Ps. vt deducit Apost. ad Heb. qui habebat & in vestimento & in femore scriptum, Rex regum & Dominus dominantium, Apocal. 19. per vestimentum autem & femur intelligitur humanitas, quæ iungebatur diuinitati, sicut vestis vestito. Ipse etiam de seipso dicebat Matthæi vltimo. Data est mihi potestas omnis in cælo & in terra. Et ad Hebræos prim. dicitur, quem constituit heredem vniuersorum. Et in Psalm. & deducit Apostolus ad Hebr. 2. Minuisti eum pau. ab ang. g. & hom. cap. eum & constituisti eum super opera manuum tuarum. Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius o. & bo. insuper & pecora. In eo autem, quod omnia subiecit, nihil excludit nō subiectū ei, sicut dicit Apost. ibid. Ex quo patet, quod quantū ad naturam, in qua erat minor angelis, hoc est secundum humanam, omnia erant ei subdita; hoc etiam patet ad Philipp. 2. vbi dicit: humiliauit semetipsum, propter quod exaltauit illum, &c. Et sequitur: vt in nomine Iesu omne genu flectatur cælestium, terrestrium, & infernorum. Ecce patet, quod secundum naturam, secundum quam humiliatus est, exaltatus est: quia sibi flectitur omne genu. Hoc etiam dicit beatus Petrus Actor. 10. cap. quod ipse constitutus est à Deo iudex viuorum & mortuorum. Et loquitur de natura, quam Deus suscitauit tertia die, sicut patet ibidem, tota etiam sacra Scriptura hoc clamat. Beatus Petrus etiam hanc potestapotestatem habuit, quem Christus suum constituit vicarium, & instituit. Qui etiam Ananiam & Saphiram pro crimine furti & mendacii iudicaliter condemnauit. Paulus etiam conuiuium fornicatorem iudicauit 1. ad Corinth. 5. Quod autem Christus voluerit tale iudicium esse potius ecclesiam, videtur expresse dicere textus, Matth. 18. Si peccauerit in te frater tuus: vade & corripe eum inter te & ipsum solum, si te audierit, lucratus es fratrem tuum, si te non audierit adhibe tecum unum vel duos testes: vt in ore duorum vel trium testium stet omne verbum: quod si non audierit, dic ecclesiae, si autem ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi sicut ethnicus & publicanus. Amen dico vobis: quodcunque ligaueritis super terram, erit ligatum & in coelis: & quaecunque solueritis super terram, erunt soluta & in coelis. Ecce quam expresse yule, quod in omni re, in qua est peccatum vnius aduersus alterum, si ille qui delinquit monitus caritatiue non emendauerit, debet negocium ad iudicium ecclesiae referri, quod si ecclesiam non audierit, debet vitari sicut ethnicus & publicanus: hoc est, sicut ab ecclesia excommunicatus, ita vt non communionem nec participationem cum eo habeat. Et quod ista fuerit intentio Christi, videtur multum probari per hoc, quod quasi assignando rationem huius subiungit immediate: Amen dico vobis, &c. Vnde hic quicunque vniuersaliter distribuit, sicut hic omnia, vnde sicut Apostolus arguebat ad Heb. 2. & ponebatur supra in eo, quod si subiecit sibi omnia, et nihil dimisit non subiectum. Et ita possum arguere: si quaecunque, quae soluerit ecclesia, sint soluta: & quaecunque ligauerit, sint ligata; nihil est in quo ecclesia non possit soluere & ligare. Vel vt accipiatur Logice: nihil est ligatum per ecclesiam non ligatum in coelo, & tenet istud argumentum per quandam logicalem regulam, quod contraria per negationem postpositam aequipollent, omne autem & nihil, quicunque & nulla, sunt contraria: & sic nihil non, valet omne: & nulla non, valet quaecunque. Secundo probo hoc ex alio textu Luc. 22. quem dominus Petrus allegabat pro se, volo eum percutere de baculo suo, dicebat enim, & in hoc bene, quod per duos gladios intelligebantur duae potestates, videlicet temporalis & spiritualis, sed penes quos voluit esse istos duos gladios? certum est, quod penes Petrum & alios Apostolos. Petro autem successit dominus Papa. Apostolis autem succedunt alii episcopi, sicut discipuli, cuiati, vt apparet in Glossa Luc. 10. Ex quo ariguo sic, per duos gladios intelliguntur praedictae duae potestates, sed Christus voluit esse illos duos penes ecclesiam, ergo & vtramque potestatem. Sed dices, quod Christus reprehendit Petrum, quia percussit gladio temporali amputando auriculam dicens ei, Converte gladium tuum, &c. Sed hoc non valet, Christus enim non dixit Petro, quod expelleret a se talem gladium: sed reponeret in vaginam penes se, seruandum tamen in vagina: vt daret intelligi, quod talis potestas, etsi sit penes ecclesiam, tamen eius exercitium quantum ad causam sanguinis in noua lege vult esse in manu iudicis laicalis: sed forte secundum nutum & imperium sacerdotum. Tertio probo hoc ex intentione Pauli Apostoli 1. ad Corinth. 6. vbi dicit, quod habens negocium seculare etiam aduersus alterum debet iudicari apud sanctos. Vnde fecit tale argumentum: An nescitis quomodo scil. de hoc mundo iudicabunt, & si in vobis iudicabitur mundus, indigni estis vt de minimis iudicetis, quasi dicat, non nescitis quoniam angelos iudicabitis? quantum ergo magis seculària? Et sequitur: seculària igitur iudicia si habueritis, contemptibiles in ecclesia illos constituite ad iudicandum. Nec obstat quod subdit Apostolus ibidem, ad verecundiam vestram dico, quia illud refertur ad hoc, quod dicit contemptibiles constituite, vnde quasi ironice in hoc loquitur Apostolus, ac si diceret, quod citius deberet recurrere ad iudicium contemptibilium, qui sunt in ecclesia, quam ad iudicium aliorum qui sunt extra ecclesiam, ergo multo fortius deberet recurrere ad iudicium sapientum, qui sunt in ecclesia multi, vnde statim Apostolus, quam dixerat; ad verecundiam vestram dico, subiungit, si non est inter vos sapiens qui quam qui possit iudicare inter fratrem & fratrem suum, quasi dicat, imo est. Patet ergo ex istis & multis aliis, quae causa breuitatis omitto, quod vtraque potestas potest eadem in personam ecclesiasticam, & est persona ecclesiastica dictae iurisdictionis capax. Nec obstat si dicatur, quod Petrus & alii Apostoli, imo etiam Christus parum vsi sunt ista potestate temporali, in eis enim fuit alia ratio, quam nunc sit in nobis, sicut enim probatur 12. quaest. 1. cap. futuram, & in multis aliis c. Apostoli ab initio non recipiebant agros nec praedia, sed pretia eorum, quae tamen ecclesia valde rationabiliter recepit, etiam cum magno merito dantium & offerentium: sicut patet de Constantino & aliis. Et ratio diuersitatis tangitur in dicto cap. pro eo, quod Apostoli futuram ecclesiam in gentibus praeuidebant non apud Iudaeam remansuram, &c. consimiliter quia Christus & Apostoli ab initio totaliter erant nostrae saluti & conuersationi attenti, parum circa cuiuscunque iurisdictionis exercitium insistebant, attendentes illud primae ad Corinth. sext. Omnia mihi licent, sed non expedient omnia, & illud Ecclesiastic. 8. Omni negocio tempus est & opportunitas. Sed nunc per Dei gratiam totus populus Gallicanus colla Christiane fidei submisit, merito igitur ecclesia insistit circa delictorum punitionem, & iustorum iudiciorum redditionem. Erit enim opus iustitiae pax, Isa. 32. cap. In istis enim iudiciis hoc solum attenditur, vt vita hominum corrigatur, &c. patet ergo nostra conclusio aliqualiter de iure diuino fundata. Sed probo hoc de iure seu ratione naturali primo sic, Ille ad iudicandum videtur aptior & conuenientior, qui est Deo proximior: cum proprie Deus sit regula & director omnium iudiciorum, Proverb. 8. Per me reges regnant, & legum conditores iusta decernunt. Sed personae ecclesiasticae sunt Deo proximiores: cum sint electae in populum peculiarem Deo, de quibus dicitur prim. Pet. 2. capit. Vos estis genus electum, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus acquisitus, &c. ergo conueniens. quod ecclesia possit de talibus iudicare. Praeterea nullus dubitat, quin cognitio de peccato ad personas ecclesiasticas pertineat, cum ergo talia non perpetrentur sine peccato alterius partis, patet quod ecclesia cognoscere potest. Item, cuius est iudicare de fine, eius est iudicare de ordinatis ad finem, quia ratio eorum, quae [illegible, ~12 letters] ad finé, sumitur ex fine, cū igitur corpus ordinatur ad animā, & temporalia ad spiritualia tanq; ad finé, ecclesia quæ habet iudicare de spiritualibus, põt etiam merito de temporalib. iudicare. Et hoc satis deducitur ext. de iud. c. nonit. Et cõfirmatur, quia accessorium sequitur naturam principalis, & hoc satis apparet exemplo, cum igitur istæ duæ iurisdictiones cõparentur duob. luminaribus Solis & Lunæ: & tota claritas lunæ sit à sole & in sole formaliter & virtualiter, & nõ claritas solis à luna nec in luna, patet q; iurisdictio spiritualis, quæ cõparatur soli, habet in se formaliter vel virtualiter iurisdictionē temporalem, quæ cõparatur claritati lunæ; & nõ econtra, multæ aliæ rationes possunt adduci, sed omitto causa breuitatis. Tertio probatur de iure ciuili, dicit n. lex q; si iudex laicus fuerit suspectus: adiungatur ei episcopus ciuitatis: si autē fuerit negligens, totum iudicium ad episc. refertur, sicut probatur in corpore authentic. Ut diffe. iud. §. fi tamen coll. 9. Præterea Theodosius Imperat. talem legem condidit: Quicunq; litem habens siue petitor fuerit, siue ab initio litis vel decursu temporum curriculo, siue cum negocium peruenerit, siue cum inceperit perimi sententia, si iudicium elegerit sacrosanctæ sedis antistitis, illico sine aliqua dubitatione, etiam si alia pars refragatur, ad episcopum iudicium cum sermone litigantium dirigatur. Quam legem postea Carolus M. qui erat rex Franciæ, ita confirmauit: Volumus atq; precipimus ut omnes [illegible, ~8 letters] subiecti, tam Romani, quam Franci caeteriq; nobis subiecti vinculo legum videantur districti vel cõsuetudinario moribus, quibus inhæserint, perpetua legesanceant, id est, ut quicunq; litem habens, &c. ut supr. sicut recitatur [illegible, ~6 letters] & &c. Sed dices, quod ista lex est abrogata, ut videtur tangere Glossi. ibid. sed hoc non valet, quia licet ista lex nõ fuerit in corpore iuris redacta: tamen propter hoc nõ est abrogata, imo est priuilegium honorabile toti & omni ecclesiæ concessum, quod Imperator tollere non potest, ut notatur. Secundum Ego Ludouicus. Item hoc priuilegium cõfirmatum [illegible, ~10 letters] ext. de iudic. c. nonit, secundum Innocent. & Hostiensem etiam videtur esse confirmatum de sacro §. ec. l. priuilegia, licet nõ sit ibi expresse nominatum, sed generaliter, ut ibi patet. Ergo ciuili, est clarum, q; talis iurisdictio in personā ecclesiasticā cadit. Hoc etiā de iure canonico posset probari per infinita: quia 22. di. c. omnes Patriarchæ, 2. q. 5. c. si quis probatur, 11. q. 1. relatum, 25 di. acces ext. de iud. nouit, de fo. compe. licet & in multis aliis, imo intātum procedunt iura canonica, quod quicunq; talem iurisdictionē habentem de consuetudine niti[tur] impedire, sententiā excommunicationis ipso facto incurrit, sicut probatur in c. quoniam inter ext. de immu. ec. li. 6. Hoc etiā patet de cõsuetudine notoria & approbata, & tanto tempore obseruata, q; memoria in cõtrarium nõ existit, & temporib. Regum Christianorum & sanctorū. Talem aūt consuetudinem violare sacrilegium est 11. q. 1. 1. & c. fe. Cõsuetudo aūt secundum iura dat iurisdictionē, maxime psonæ capaci, imo cõsuetudo de cuius cõtrario memoria nõ est, habetur loco cõstituti iuris inter oēs psonas, & multo magis valet pro ecclesia ext. de præscr. c. episc. in sin. li. 6. Cum ergo ecclesia Gallicana cõsueuerit inter laicos cognoscere in actionib. psonalibus, & etiā in realib. alicuius ecclesiæ, patet q; cõsuetudo potuit sibi dare illā iurisdictionē, ideo &c. sed dicebat dominus Petrus, q; in hoc nõ poterat introduci cõsuetudo: quia in hoc nõ poteramus habere bonā fidem. Item, istud ius dicitur imprescriptibile: cū sit ius fisci. Sed ista non valent, ecclesia n. Gallicana magis vendicat sibi ius istud cõsuetudine, q; ex prescriptione: quia cõsuetudo videtur introduci magis ex voluntate & electione populi recurrentis ad iudicium ecclesiasticū potius, q; ad iudicium seculare & in fauorem eorum. Item, multum cõfirmatur ad hoc ista consuetudo, quia fuit in contradictorio iudicio obtenta, frequenter m. reclamantib. Baronibus, responsione prælatorum audita fuit per prædecessores vestros reges Franciæ cõsuetudo huiusmodi ecclesiæ firmata, & p ecclesiā pacifice obtenta, sed ad hoc põt hoc sibi vendicare ex præscriptione, &c. Ad præscriptionē a non requiruntur nisi tria, titulus, bona fides, & cõtinuitas temporis. Certum est aūt, q; ecclesia iustum titulum habuit, sicut priuilegium cõcessum à Theodosio Imp. & confirmatū à Carolo & mādatum inuiolabiliter obseruati. Item habuit titulū ex iure diuino, naturali & humano, sicut superius est expressum & allegatum, habuit etiam bonam fidem, nosc̄untur tot & tanti clari tituli suffragari, cõcurrit etiam continuitas tēporis & tanti, q; sufficiēt ad præscriptionē contra fiscum. Nõ n. fuit continuitas solum centū annorum, imo etiā sex centū & vltra. Nec est verum, q; istud ius sit imprescriptibile, maxime ab ecclesia, quæ quantū ad spiritualitatē non est subdita regi: imo nobilior sicut sol luna, aurū plumbo, & cælum terra. Certum est aūt, q; æqualis vel maior bene põt prescribere ius æqualis vel inferioris, sicut vnus rex ius alterius, quare patet, q; ecclesia hoc præscribere potuerit, etiā si esset ius fisci, q; tñ non est. Vltimo probat istud ex priuilegio cõcesso, & per Carolū regem M. Franciæ, ut dictum est prius, & p S. Ludouicum, & p Philippum auunculum vestrū, & p Ludouicum & Philippū cõsanguineos vestros Reges Franciæ, q; priuilegia habemus in promptu. Sed forte diceret, q; ista nõ possunt stare: sc. quod ista iurisdictio cõpetat ecclesiæ de iure, de cõsuetudine & de priuilegio: quia ista non stant simul. Si n. cõpetit ex vno: nõ videtur cõpetere ex alio. Sed ad hoc põt dupliciter responderi, primo quod priuilegium vel cõsuetudo põt esse dupliciter, quoddam nouī iuris editiuum; & istud non cõgruit cum aliis: aliud veteris iuris confirmatiuum seu declaratiuum; & istud bene potest cõcurrere. Et ista distinctio etiam locum posset habere in cõsuetudine. Et secundum hoc posset responderi, q; licet ecclesiæ cõpetat hæc iurisdictio de iure: cõpetit etiam de consuetudine & priuilegio, non noui iuris editiuis, sed antiqui declaratiuis & confirmatiuis, vel potest aliter responderi, quod habilitas & capacitas huius iurisdictionis competit de iure, sed actus & executio de consuetudine & priuilegio. Sed forte ad hoc dicetur: quare hoc sibi vendicat ecclesia Gallicana: cum aliæ ecclesiæ sibi in aliis regionibus hoc minimè vendicare noscant? Ad quod potest faciliter respondetur, si enim Reges Franciæ, quos Deus singularibus priuilegiis, gratiis, & honoribus præcæteris
units.tr: Secondly, I prove this from the New Testament. Christ is not only Lord according to his divine nature, by which he created all things out of nothing, and so is Lord of all, but he also possessed both powers according to his human nature. For he was a priest after the order of Melchizedek, as the Psalm says and as the Apostle draws out in Hebrews, and he had written on his garment and on his thigh, "King of kings and Lord of lords" (Rev. 19). By the garment and the thigh is understood the humanity, which was joined to the divinity as a garment is joined to the one who wears it. He himself also said of himself in the last chapter of Matthew: "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth." And in the first chapter of Hebrews it is said that he is "appointed heir of all things." And in the Psalm, which the Apostle draws out in Heb. 2: "You made him a little lower than the angels, and crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet, sheep and oxen, and the beasts too." In saying that "all things" were put under him, the Apostle excludes nothing that was not subjected to him, as he says in the same place. From this it is clear that, as to the nature in which he was lower than the angels, that is, the human nature, all things were subject to him. This is also clear from Phil. 2, where it says: "He humbled himself, therefore God exalted him," and so on. And it follows: "that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, on earth, and under the earth." Behold, it is plain that according to the nature in which he was humbled, he was exalted, since every knee bows to him. Blessed Peter also says this in Acts 10, that he "was appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead." And he speaks of the nature which God raised on the third day, as is plain from the same place; the whole of Holy Scripture also proclaims this. Blessed Peter likewise had this power, he whom Christ appointed and established as his vicar. He also condemned Ananias and Sapphira judicially for the crime of theft and lying. Paul too judged the fornicator at Corinth (1 Cor. 5). That Christ willed such judgment to belong rather to the Church, the text of Matthew 18 seems to state expressly: "If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. If he will not listen, take with you one or two witnesses, so that every word may be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses. If he refuses to listen, tell it to the Church; and if he refuses to listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector. Truly I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven." Behold how expressly it is laid down that in every matter in which one party has sinned against another, if the offender, admonished in love, does not amend, the case must be referred to the judgment of the Church; and if he does not listen to the Church, he must be avoided as a heathen and a tax collector, that is, as one excommunicated by the Church, so that one has no communion or fellowship with him. And that this was Christ's intention is strongly confirmed by the fact that, as if giving the reason, he immediately adds: "Truly I say to you," and so on. Hence whoever distributes universally, as here "all things," just as the Apostle argued in Heb. 2, and as was set out above, that he subjected all things to himself and left nothing unsubjected. And so I can argue: if whatever the Church loosens is loosed, and whatever it binds is bound, then there is nothing in which the Church cannot loose and bind. Or, if it is taken logically: nothing is bound by the Church which is not bound in heaven. This argument holds by a certain logical rule, that contraries with a negation placed after them are equivalent; but "all" and "nothing," "whatever" and "none" are contraries; and so "nothing not" is worth "all," and "none not" is worth "whatever." Secondly, I prove this from another text, Luke 22, which Peter alleged in support of himself when he said, "Lord, shall we strike with the sword?" and "Here are two swords." And indeed it is rightly said that by the two swords were meant the two powers, namely the temporal and the spiritual. But in whose hands did he will these two swords to be? It is certain that they were in the hands of Peter and the other Apostles. But the lord Pope succeeded Peter; and other bishops succeed the Apostles, as the disciples did, as appears in the Gloss on Luke 10. From this I argue thus: the two aforesaid powers are meant by the two swords; but Christ willed those two swords to be in the hands of the Church; therefore the Church has both powers. But you will say that Christ rebuked Peter because he struck with a temporal sword, cutting off an ear, saying to him: "Put your sword back in its place." But this does not follow: Christ did not tell Peter to throw such a sword away from himself, but to put it back in its sheath, to be kept in the sheath, so as to make it understood that such a power, although it is in the hands of the Church, nevertheless, as far as the cause of blood is concerned, under the new law, its exercise is to be in the hands of a lay judge, though perhaps at the nod and command of the priests. Thirdly, I prove this from the intention of the Apostle Paul in 1 Cor. 6, where he says that a man who has a secular matter against another ought to be judged before the saints. Hence he makes this argument: "Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more then matters of this life?" And it follows: "If then you have secular judgments, appoint as judges those who are of no account in the Church." Nor does what the Apostle adds in the same place, "I say this to your shame," stand in the way, for that refers to what he says, "appoint as judges those who are of no account." Hence the Apostle speaks here almost ironically, as if he were saying that one ought more readily to turn to the judgment of those of no account who are in the Church than to the judgment of others who are outside the Church; so much more then ought one to turn to the judgment of the wise, of whom there are many in the Church. Hence the Apostle immediately, after saying "I say this to your shame," adds: "Is there not among you one wise man who is able to judge between brother and brother?" as if to say, "Indeed, there is."
