It is plain then from these and many other arguments, which I omit for the sake of brevity, that both powers can apply to the same ecclesiastical person, and that an ecclesiastical person is capable of the said jurisdiction. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that Peter and the other Apostles, and even Christ, made little use of this temporal power, for in them there was a different reason from what there is now in us. For, as is proved in 12 quaest. 1, chapter "Futuram," and in many other chapters, the Apostles at the beginning did not receive fields or estates, but their price, which the Church nevertheless very reasonably received, and with great merit to the givers and offerers, as is clear in the case of Constantine and others. The reason for the difference is touched on in the said chapter: the Apostles foresaw that the future Church would be among the Gentiles and would not remain in Judea, and so on. Likewise, because Christ and the Apostles at the beginning were wholly intent on our salvation and conversion, they paid little attention to the exercise of any jurisdiction, bearing in mind that saying of the first Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 6: "All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient," and that saying of Ecclesiasticus 8: "For every matter there is a time and an opportunity." But now, by the grace of God, the whole Gallican people has submitted its neck to the yoke of the Christian faith. Therefore the Church rightly concerns itself with the punishment of crimes and the rendering of just judgments; for "the work of justice will be peace" (Isa. 32). In these judgments the only aim is that the life of men be corrected, and so on. It is plain, then, that our conclusion is in some measure founded on divine right. But I prove this first by natural right or reason, thus: that person seems more fit and more suitable to judge who is nearer to God, since God properly is the rule and director of all judgments (Prov. 8): "By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just." But ecclesiastical persons are nearer to God, since they are chosen as a peculiar people to God, of whom it is said in 1 Pet. 2: "You are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession," and so on. Therefore it is fitting that the Church should be able to judge such persons. Moreover, no one doubts that knowledge of sin belongs to ecclesiastical persons; since such things are not committed without sin on the part of the other party, it is plain that the Church can take cognizance of them. Likewise, whoever has the right to judge the end has the right to judge the things ordered to the end, because the reason for those things which are [illegible] to the end is taken from the end. Since, then, the body is ordered to the soul, and temporal things to spiritual things as to their end, the Church, which has the right to judge spiritual matters, can rightly also judge temporal matters. This is sufficiently drawn out in Extra, "De iudiciis," chapter "Nonit." And it is confirmed, because the accessory follows the nature of the principal; and this is sufficiently clear from the example: when these two jurisdictions are compared to the two lights of the sun and the moon, and the whole brightness of the moon comes from the sun and is in the sun formally and virtually, and the brightness of the sun does not come from the moon nor is in the moon, it is plain that the spiritual jurisdiction, which is compared to the sun, has in itself formally or virtually the temporal jurisdiction, which is compared to the light of the moon, and not the reverse. Many other reasons could be adduced, but I omit them for the sake of brevity. Thirdly, it is proved from civil law. For the law says that if a lay judge is suspected, a bishop of the city is to be joined with him; and if he is negligent, the whole judgment is referred to the bishop, as is proved in the Authentica, "Ut differentes iudices," §. "Fi tamen," Collatio 9. Moreover, the Emperor Theodosius enacted such a law: "Whoever has a suit, whether as plaintiff from the beginning of the case, or in the course of time, or when the matter has come to court, or when a sentence has begun to lapse, if he has chosen the judgment of the holy see's bishop, then at once, without any doubt, even if the other party objects, the judgment is to be sent to the bishop with the statement of the litigants." This law was afterwards so confirmed by Charlemagne, who was king of France: "We will and command that all [illegible] subject to us, both Romans and Franks and others subject to us, be bound by the bond of the laws or by the customs to which they have adhered, and that the law be perpetually established, that is, that whoever has a suit, and so on, as above, as is recited [illegible], and so on." But you will say that this law has been abrogated, as the Gloss on the same place seems to suggest. But this does not hold, for although this law was not incorporated into the body of the law, it is not on that account abrogated; indeed it is an honourable privilege granted to the whole Church and to every church, which an emperor cannot remove, as is noted in the Second, "Ego Ludovicus." Likewise, this privilege was confirmed [illegible] in Extra, "De iudiciis," chapter "Nonit"; according to Innocent and Hostiensis it also seems to have been confirmed in "De sacro," §. "Ec.," lex "Privilegia," although it is not there expressly named, but in general terms, as appears there. Therefore, under civil law it is clear that such jurisdiction falls to an ecclesiastical person. This could also be proved from canon law by countless texts: 22 dist., chapter "Omnes Patriarchae"; 2 quaest. 5, chapter "Si quis"; 11 quaest. 1, "Relatum"; 25 dist., "Accedens"; Extra, "De iudiciis," "Novit"; "De foro competenti"; and in many other places. Indeed canon law goes so far that whoever attempts, on the basis of custom, to hinder such a jurisdiction-holder incurs by that very fact the sentence of excommunication, as is proved in chapter "Quoniam inter," Extra, "De immunitate ecclesiarum," Liber 6. This is also plain from a custom that is notorious and approved and has been observed for so long that no memory exists to the contrary, and it was observed in the times of Christian kings and saints. But to violate such a custom is sacrilege (11 quaest. 1, chapters 1 and "Fe"). Now custom, according to the laws, gives jurisdiction, especially to a capable person; indeed a custom of which there is no memory to the contrary is held to have the force of an established law among all persons, and much more does it hold good for the Church (Extra, "De praescriptionibus," chapter "Episcopus," at the end, Liber 6). Since, then, the Gallican Church has customarily taken cognizance among laymen both in personal actions and in real actions of any church, it is plain that custom could give it that jurisdiction; therefore, and so on. But the lord Peter said that in this matter custom could not be introduced, because in this we could not have good faith. Again, this right is said to be imprescriptible, since it is a right of the treasury. But these arguments do not hold. For the Gallican Church claims this right more by custom than by prescription, since custom seems to be introduced rather by the will and choice of the people who have recourse to the ecclesiastical judgment rather than the secular, and in favour of those people. Again, this custom is greatly confirmed by the fact that it was obtained in a contested judgment, often with the Barons protesting; after the answer of the prelates had been heard, this custom of the Church was confirmed by your predecessors, the kings of France, and was peacefully obtained by the Church. But it can claim this for itself by prescription, and so on. For prescription only three things are required: title, good faith, and continuity of time. Now it is certain that the Church had a just title, as the privilege granted by the Emperor Theodosius, confirmed by Charles, and the command to be observed inviolably. Likewise it had a title from divine, natural and human right, as was set out and alleged above. It also had good faith; so many and such clear titles are known to support it. There is also continuity of time, and so great that it is sufficient for prescription against the treasury. For the continuity was not merely of a hundred years, but even of six hundred and more. Nor is it true that this right is imprescriptible, especially in the case of the Church, which in spiritual matters is not subject to the king; rather it is more noble, as the sun is to the moon, gold to lead, and heaven to earth. Now it is certain that an equal or greater can well prescribe the right of an equal or lesser, as one king prescribes the right of another; so it is plain that the Church could prescribe this, even if it were a right of the treasury, which however it is not. Lastly, he proves this from the privilege granted by Charlemagne, king of France, as was said before, and by St. Louis, and by Philip your uncle, and by Louis and Philip your kinsmen, kings of France, which privileges we have ready to hand. But perhaps someone would say that these cannot stand together: namely, that this jurisdiction belongs to the Church by right, by custom and by privilege, because these do not agree; if it belongs by one, it does not seem to belong by another. But to this it can be answered in two ways. First, that a privilege or custom can be of two kinds: one which is constitutive of a new right, and this does not agree with the others; another which confirms or declares an old right, and this can well coexist. And this distinction could also apply to custom. And according to this it could be answered that although this jurisdiction belongs to the Church by right, it also belongs by custom and privilege, not as constitutive of new right, but as declaratory and confirmatory of ancient right. Or it can be answered otherwise: that the aptitude and capacity for this jurisdiction belongs by right, but the act and exercise by custom and privilege. But perhaps it will be said to this: why does the Gallican Church claim this for itself, since other churches in other countries are known not to claim it at all? To which it can easily be answered: for if the kings of France, whom God has honoured above others with singular privileges, graces and honours, and has prospered, have granted many liberties to the churches among the rest, they did so for three reasons: namely, on account of their great faith toward God; also on account of their very great honour and reverence toward the Church; also on account of the justice they showed to the people subject to them…

units.la: [illegible, ~6 letters] ris regibus insigniuit & prosperati sunt, inter cæteros propter tria, sc. propter magnam fidem tionem ad Deum, item propter maximum honorem & reuerentiam ad ecclesiam, item propter iustitiam præstitibatam ad populū sibi subditū, ecclesiæ plures libertates concesserunt vel concessis viti libere pertinent, non est mirū, imo tanta fuit ad ecclesiam eorum deuotio, quod ecclesiæ tanto eis ppinquiores tanto pluribus libertatib. gaudent, nec ex hoc minus habuerunt, sed plus, sicut rei euidentia manifestat: imo hoc redundat in magnam nobilitatem regni & regis. Audiuit alias, quod quatuor vel quinq; sunt, quæ singulariter istud nobilitant benedictum regnum, primo fidei inuiolata sincer-itas: quia nunquam legitur quod reges Franciæ, ex quo susceperunt fidem, vllo vnq; tempore à fide aberrauerint, secundo sanguinis nobilitas: quia à Priamo rege Troianorum, & successiue à Carolo & aliis regibus tam inclitis descenderunt, tertio pacis & concordiæ vnitas, quæ potissime vigent in regno Franciæ, quarto prælatorum solennitas, quinto Baronum & aliorum subditorum ad obediendum voluntas. Si ergo prælati regni non haberent istud ius, sed tolleretur ab eis, iam perderet rex & regnum vnam de dictis nobilitatib. siue conditionibus, per q; multum nobilitatur, sc. prælatorum solennitate, tunc n. non essent solemniores, sed pauperiores & miseriores omnib. aliis, cum in hoc consistat magna pars emolumentorum suorum. Concludo ergo tanq; probatum de iure diuino, naturalique, canonico & ciuili, & consuetudine atq; priuilegio, quod ius cognoscendi de talibus temporalibus ecclesiæ cópetere potest, & cópetit ecclesiæ Gallicanæ. Ex quibus reduco thema domini Petri contra eum sic: suppono tamen primo tanquam clarum, quod ea quæ sunt oblata ecclesiæ & iam in dominium & proprietatem ecclesiæ conuersa Dei sunt imo & in tantū quod dedicata & sanctificata dicuntur, vt satis apparet p totum librum Leuitici. Et satis etiam apparet per hoc q; scribitur 1. Reg. 22. c. de panibus oblatis Deo, vnde dicitur ibi: nō habeo panes Laicis ad manducandū, sed tantum panem sanctū. Vnde de illis panibus non licebat laicis comedere, nisi in tempore necessitatis extremæ. Patet etiam istud clare Dan. 5. c. vbi legitur pro eo, quod cū Balthasar rex & optimates & vxor eius biberunt in vasis aureis & argenteis, quæ Nabuchodonosor aportauerat de templo, quod est in Hierusalem, apparuit manus scribentis in pariete, manet hec el phares, quod est dictum, sicut apparet ibidem, quod Deus numerat regnum suum & compleuerat quod appensus erat in statera & inuentus minus habens, & quod diuisum erat regnum suum & datum Medis & Persis. Vnde eadem nocte interfectus est, & successit Darius Medus in regno, vnde facta est tunc translatio monarchiæ Assyriorum in Medos, patet ergo, quod quæ sunt oblata ecclesiæ Dei sunt & adeo dedicata Deo, quod non licet laicis eis vti, quod etsi faciant, habent ducere vindictam diuinam, sicut habuit Balthasar. His ergo suppositis arguo ex themate domini Petri: Reddite quæ sunt Cæsaris Cæsari: & quæ sunt Dei, Deo. sed ista iurisdictio, quæ est, vt supra probaui, multipliciter in dominium & proprietatem ecclesiæ Gallicanæ conuersa, est iam Dei: ergo reddenda est sibi, vnde cuilibet violenti tollere deberet dicere, & quilibet prælatus bonus respondere, sicut respondit Ambrosius militibus Gothis missis ab imperatore. Respondit enim sic: Si quod meum est, petetis imperator, non denegarem, quamuis omnia mea pauperum sint, sed quia quæ Dei sunt postulat, in quibus imperator potestatem non habet, potius volo vt me in carcerem mittat, & vitam mihi auferat, quam sibi concedam. Vnde alludendo illi historiæ, quæ habetur 3. Regum 22. cap. de Naboth subiunxit: Naboth sanctum virum possessorem vineæ suæ scimus interpellatum petitione regia, vt vineam suam daret. Cumque respondisset: non ego possum patrum meorum tradere hereditatem, & sic regem contristatum esse. Et subdit: Si ille non tradidit vineam suam, nos trademus tibi ecclesiam Christi? Absit à me, vt tradam Christi hereditatem: non tradidit Naboth vineam, nec ego tradem eam quæ Christi est ecclesiam. Et subdit optimum verbum: templo Dei nihil possum decerpere nec tradere: cum istud custodiendum non tradendum acceperim. Deinde consulere me oportet imperatoris saluti: nec mihi expediret tradere nec illi accipere, sicut istud legitur 23. quæstio. vltim. cap. conuenient. Non est ergo Dei solum iurisdictio spiritualis, sicut supponebat dominus Petrus: sed etiam quæcunque iurisdictio, quæ ecclesiæ competit, siue de iure, siue de consuetudine, siue de priuilegio, intantum nobis non expedit eam tradere, nec regi pro certo recipere, sed dicebat dominus Petrus, quod Christus ad dandum exemplum soluerat tributum, hoc enim est falsum, vnde, sicut apparet Gene. 47. terra sacerdotum fuit libera & immunis ab omni tributo & seruitute præstanda, & si dominus Petrus bene inspexisset testimonium Matth. 17. Christus non soluit tributum ad præstandandum exemplum: imo prius probauit, quod non tenebatur soluere, concludendo, ergo liberi sunt filii, &c. sed soluit propter scandalum vitandum, vnde dicitur in textu: vt autem non scandalizemus eos, vadens mare, &c. sed forte dicetur, quod nos, &c. exemplo Christi ad euitandum scandalum debemus soluere, sed hoc non valet, quia duplex est scandalum, pusillorum sci. & Pharisæorum, propter scandalum pusillorum, quod est ex ignorantia, non ex malitia, sunt aliqua euitanda ad tempus, donec fuerint instructi, sicut dicit Apostolus ad Rom. 14. ca. sed propter scandalum Pharisæorum, qui peccant ex certa malitia, non est aliquid omittendum, sicut ipse Christus ait Matth. 16. dicentibus Apostolis sibi: scis quod Pharisæi audito hoc verbo scandalizati sunt? & quid respondit? Ecce finite illos, caci sunt & duces cæcorum, quia tempore Christi fuisset scandalum pusillorum, & nunc esset scandalum Pharisæorum, ideo tunc fuit soluendum propter scandalum vitandum, sed modo non. Patet ergo quod tertium signum timoris Dei est ex integra bonorum redditione, vnde de habente talem timorem, per quem reddit Deo quicquid suum est. Dicitur autem EcclesiasticI decim. cap. Semen hominum honorabitur, quod præterit mandata Domini, &c. Et sic patet primum, scilicet quomodo debetur Deo timor filialis & obedientia propter celsitudinem & imperium suæ maiestatis, quia Deus ut meto. Dico secundo, quod debetur regi honor specialis & reuerentia propter magnitudinem & fastigium dignitatis, quia sequitur in themate: regem honorate, & Ecc. 10. in medio fratrum rector illorum in honore. Et videtur mihi ad praesens, quod est duplex honor: unus verbalis, qui est adulatiuus & periculosus, de quo dicitur Matt. 7. Populus iste labiis me honorat, cor autem eorum longe est a me. Alius est honor realis, qui est debitus & virtuosus, & de isto, non de primo, dicitur regem honorate. Et videtur mihi, quod ille de facto & realiter & virtuose honorificat regem, qui vult eum seruare illa, per quae eius dominium diligitur, & eius potestas & excellentia non diminuitur, & eius fama custoditur ne perdatur, & eius conscientia non laeditur, in Gallico: Par quoy sa seigneurie est aymee, sa puissanze nest appetis see, sa renoumee est gardee, sa conscienze nest pas blecee. Et e contra ille non honorificat regem, qui suadet sibi opposita istis quatuor. Dico ergo primo, quod ille honorificat regem facto, qui suadet sibi illud, propter quod eius dominium diligitur, princeps enim debet studere potius diligi quam timeri. Thesaurus enim nobilior, quem possit habere princeps, est habere corda subditorum, sicut dicit Seneca de clementia ad Neron. Inexpugnabile munimentum amor ciuium: quid enim optabilius & pulchrius est quam viuere optantibus cunctis. Modo videtur mihi, quod nulla res facit tantum diligi principem, quantum seruare & augere libertates eis consuetas, & non inducere nouitates, ideo cuilibet regenti dicitur Prou. 22. quomodo dominus Petrus pro se allegabat: sed ego reduco contra eum: non transgrediaris terminos antiquos, quos posuerunt patres tui, nouitas enim parit discordiam, & ideo in rebus nouis constituendis cuidens debet esse vtilitas, vel vrgens necessitas. Et ideo si princeps vult libertates per suos praedecessores concessas tollere, eius dominium non diligitur, sicut patet de Roboam 3. Reg. 11. ca. Et apparet in Cronicis, ex hoc multa dominia & regna translata de gente in gentem, & de regno ad populum alterum, modo certum est, quod praedecessores vestri Carolus M. sanctus Ludouicus, Philippus pulcher, Ludouicus & Philippus filii eius, & plures alii istam ecclesiae libertatem confirmauerunt, & nos ibi de modo aliqua, ergo consulere vel requirere, quod vos tollatis aliquid ecclesiae, est consulere quod vos tollatis seu quod tollatur a vobis illud, propter quod dominium veritu diligitur. Et ideo nobis videtur consulere illud Matt. 2. c. Memento operum Patrum, qui fecerunt in generalibus suis, & accipietis gloriam magnam & nomen in aeternum. Nota hic, quomodo rex Philippus, auus S. Ludouici, fouebat & nutriebat in regno suo S. Thomam Cantuariensem Archiepisc. qui pro libertatibus ecclesiae defendendis fuerat de regno Angliae bannitus, quanto ergo magis decet vos defendere praelatos vestros in libertatibus suis per praedecessores vestros confirmatas, quia sicut dicit Gregor. & habetur 25. q. 2. c. si c. Si ea destruerem, quae praedecessores & antecessores mei statuerunt, non essem constructor, sed euersor esse iuste comprobarer, testante veritatis voce, quae ait: Omne regnum in se diuisum desolabitur: & omnis scientia & lex aduersum se diuisa destruetur, & alibi dicit idem: Nimis est asperum & praecipue bonis moribus inimicum, vt quempiam quacunque rationis excusatione, quae bene sunt ordinata, rescindere & exemplo donare cateros sua quandoque posse constituta dissoluere. Nota hic de castro dato sancto Remigio pro ecclesia Laudunensi per Clodoueum regem, quod postea Pipinus rex voluit habere facta recompensatione ecclesiae, cui dormienti apparuit beatus Remigius, & eum super hoc graviter increpauit dicens: Melior te mihi dedit, & tu vis auferre, & ideo eum percussit, qui in crastinum inuentus est totus denigratus. Et extunc reges Franciae non fuerunt ausi in illo castro iacere. Non honorificat ergo regem facto, qui consulit sibi, quod transgrediatur terminos antiquos, quos posuerunt patres sui: imo rex deberet eis dicere illud Iohan. octau. ego honorifico Patrem meum, seruando scilicet ecclesiae libertates, sicut ipsi fecerunt & concesserunt, vos autem inhonoratis me optatum sibi consulendo, quia scribitur Ecclesiastic. tert. Gloria hominis ex honore patris sui: & dedecus filii patris sine honore.
units.tr: ...ris kings, God has honoured them with singular privileges, favours and honours above all other kings. Among the other reasons, for three: their great faith and devotion to God; their very great honour and reverence towards the Church; and the justice they showed to the people subject to them. They have granted the Church many liberties, or what they granted has pertained to it freely. This is no wonder. Indeed, their devotion to the Church was so great that the Churches, the closer they stood to them, the more liberties they enjoyed, and they did not lose by this but gained more, as the evidence of the matter makes plain. Indeed, this redounds to the great nobility of the kingdom and the king. I have heard that there are four or five things which especially ennoble this blessed kingdom: first, the inviolate sincerity of the faith, since it is never read that the kings of France, from the time they received the faith, ever strayed from it at any time; second, the nobility of blood, since they descended from Priam, king of the Trojans, and afterwards from Charles and other most renowned kings; third, the unity of peace and concord, which flourish above all in the kingdom of France; fourth, the solemnity of the prelates; fifth, the willingness of the barons and other subjects to obey. If therefore the prelates of the kingdom did not have this right, but it were taken from them, the king and kingdom would already lose one of those nobilities or conditions by which they are much ennobled, namely the solemnity of the prelates. For then they would not be more solemn but poorer and more wretched than all others, since a great part of their emoluments consists in this. I conclude, then, as if proved by divine, natural, canon and civil law, and by custom and privilege, that the right of taking cognizance of such temporal matters of the Church can pertain to, and does pertain to, the Gallican Church. From these things I draw out the thesis of Lord Peter against him, as follows. I assume first, as clear, that those things which have been offered to the Church and have already been turned into the dominion and property of the Church are God's, indeed to such an extent that they are said to be dedicated and sanctified, as sufficiently appears throughout the whole book of Leviticus. It also sufficiently appears from what is written in 1 Kings 22, the chapter about the bread offered to God, whence it is said there: "I have no bread for laymen to eat, but only holy bread." Hence laymen were not permitted to eat of those loaves, except in a time of extreme necessity. This is also clearly shown in Daniel 5, where it is read that when Belshazzar the king, with his nobles and his wife, drank from the golden and silver vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had brought from the temple in Jerusalem, there appeared the hand of a writer on the wall, and the words written were "Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin", which means, as appears there, that God has numbered his kingdom and completed it; he was weighed in the balance and found wanting; and his kingdom was divided and given to the Medes and Persians. Therefore that same night he was slain, and Darius the Mede succeeded to the kingdom, and then the transfer of the monarchy of the Assyrians to the Medes took place. It is clear, then, that those things which have been offered to the Church of God are so dedicated to God that it is not lawful for laymen to use them; and if they do, they must expect divine vengeance, as Belshazzar did. On these premises I argue from the thesis of Lord Peter: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." But this jurisdiction, which, as I have proved above, has in many ways been turned into the dominion and property of the Gallican Church, is now God's; therefore it ought to be rendered to Him. Hence every violent person who wishes to take it away ought to be told so, and every good prelate ought to answer as Ambrose answered the Gothic soldiers sent by the emperor. For he replied thus: "If you, emperor, ask for what is mine, I would not deny it, although all my things belong to the poor. But since you demand what is God's, over which the emperor has no power, I would rather that he send me to prison and take away my life than that I should concede it to him." Alluding to that story which is found in 3 Kings 22 about Naboth, he added: "We know that Naboth, a holy man, the possessor of his vineyard, was petitioned by the king to give up his vineyard; and when he replied, 'I cannot give up the inheritance of my fathers,' the king was saddened." And he adds: "If he did not give up his vineyard, shall we give up to you the Church of Christ? Far be it from me that I should give up the inheritance of Christ. Naboth did not give up his vineyard, nor shall I give up the Church, which is Christ's." And he adds an excellent saying: "I can pluck nothing from the temple of God, nor give it up, since I have received it to be guarded, not handed over. Then it is my duty to consult the safety of the emperor; yet it would not be expedient for me to hand it over, nor for him to accept it," as this is read in Causa 23, question last, chapter "Conveniant." Therefore it is not only spiritual jurisdiction that is God's, as Lord Peter supposed; but any jurisdiction which pertains to the Church, whether by right, by custom or by privilege, it is in no way expedient for us to hand over, nor to receive it for certain for the king. But Lord Peter said that Christ paid the tribute to give an example. This is false. As appears in Genesis 47, the land of the priests was free and exempt from all tribute and service to be rendered. And if Lord Peter had rightly considered the testimony of Matthew 17, Christ did not pay the tribute to give an example; rather he first proved that he was not bound to pay it, concluding, "Therefore the sons are free," and so forth. But he paid it to avoid giving offence, whence it is said in the text: "But lest we should offend them, go to the sea," and so forth. But perhaps it will be said that we, following the example of Christ, ought to pay to avoid offence. This does not hold, because offence is twofold: that of the little ones, namely, and that of the Pharisees. Because of the offence of the little ones, which arises from ignorance and not from malice, some things are to be avoided for a time, until they are instructed, as the Apostle says in Romans 14. But because of the offence of the Pharisees, who sin from settled malice, nothing is to be omitted, as Christ himself says in Matthew 16, when the apostles said to him: "Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this word?" And what did he answer? "Let them alone; they are blind and leaders of the blind." For in the time of Christ it would have been an offence to the little ones, and now it would be an offence to the Pharisees; therefore then the tribute was to be paid to avoid offence, but now not. It is clear, then, that the third sign of the fear of God is the full restitution of goods, whence it is said of one who has such fear, by which he renders to God whatever is his. And it is said in Ecclesiasticus 10: "The seed of men shall be honoured" which transgresses the commandments of the Lord, and so forth. And so the first point is clear, namely how filial fear and obedience are due to God on account of the loftiness and sovereignty of his majesty, because God is as I said. I say secondly that special honour and reverence are due to the king on account of the greatness and eminence of his dignity, because it follows in the thesis: "Honour the king", and Ecclesiasticus 10: "The ruler is honoured among his brethren." And it seems to me for the present that there is a twofold honour: one verbal, which is flattering and dangerous, of which Matthew 7 says: "This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." The other is real honour, which is due and virtuous, and it is of this, not of the first, that it is said: "Honour the king." And it seems to me that he truly, actually and virtuously honours the king who wishes to preserve for him those things by which his dominion is loved, and his power and excellence are not diminished, and his reputation is guarded lest it be lost, and his conscience is not harmed; in French: "Par quoy sa seigneurie est aymee, sa puissanze nest appetis see, sa renoumee est gardee, sa conscienze nest pas blecee." And on the contrary, he does not honour the king who advises him to the opposite of these four things. I say therefore first that he honours the king in deed who advises him towards that by which his dominion is loved; for a prince ought to strive rather to be loved than feared. For the nobler treasure a prince can have is to possess the hearts of his subjects, as Seneca says in his De Clementia to Nero: "The love of citizens is an impregnable fortification; for what is more desirable and fairer than to live with everyone wishing it?" Now it seems to me that nothing makes a prince so loved as preserving and increasing the liberties customary for them, and not introducing novelties. Therefore to any ruler is said Proverbs 22, which Lord Peter alleged for himself; but I turn it back against him: "Do not transgress the ancient landmarks which your fathers have set." For novelty brings forth discord, and therefore in establishing new things there ought to be evident utility or pressing necessity. And so, if a prince wishes to take away liberties granted by his predecessors, his dominion is not loved, as is clear in the case of Rehoboam, 3 Kings 11. And it appears in the chronicles that from this many dominions and kingdoms have been transferred from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another people. Now it is certain that your predecessors, Charlemagne, Saint Louis, Philip the Fair, Louis and Philip his sons, and many others, confirmed this liberty of the Church, and we here have something of the kind; therefore to counsel or request that you take anything from the Church is to counsel that you take away, or that there be taken from you, that by which your dominion is truly loved. And so it seems to us to counsel that saying of Matthew 2: "Remember the works of the fathers, who did in their generations, and you will receive great glory and a name for ever." Note here how King Philip, grandfather of Saint Louis, cherished and nourished in his kingdom Saint Thomas of Canterbury, archbishop, who had been banished from the kingdom of England for defending the liberties of the Church. How much more, then, ought you to defend your prelates in their liberties confirmed by your predecessors, because, as Gregory says, and it is found in Causa 25, question 2, chapter "Si ea": "If I should destroy those things which my predecessors and forefathers established, I would not be a builder but would justly be proved an overthrower, the voice of truth testifying, which says: 'Every kingdom divided against itself shall be made desolate, and every science and law divided against itself shall be destroyed.'" And the same writer says elsewhere: "It is too harsh, and especially hostile to good morals, that anyone, under any pretext of reason, should rescind what has been well ordained, and by example give to others the power to dissolve what has at some time been established." Note here concerning the castle given to Saint Remigius for the Church of Laon by King Clovis, which afterwards King Pepin wished to have, a recompense having been made to the Church. To him, while he slept, Blessed Remigius appeared and sharply rebuked him on this, saying: "He gave you something better than me, and you wish to take it away." And so he struck him, and on the next day he was found completely blackened. From that time the kings of France did not dare to lie in that castle. He therefore does not honour the king in deed who advises him to transgress the ancient landmarks which his fathers set. Rather the king ought to say to them that saying of John 8: "I honour my Father," namely by preserving the liberties of the Church, as they themselves did and granted; but you dishonour me by counselling what is hateful to him, since it is written in Ecclesiasticus 3: "The glory of a man is from the honour of his father, and the shame of a son is a father without honour." <hi>...</hi>

units.la: Dico secundo, quod facto regem honorificat, qui suadet sibi illud, per quod sua potestas & excellentia non diminuitur, multum enim decet honorem suum augere potentia, & multum indecet eum diminuere, unde Imperatores consueuerunt se vocare Augustos, quasi rem publicam augentes. Dicere autem, quod vos aut praedecessores vestri non potuistis haec concedere ecclesiae, videtur esse valde in diminutionem vestrae potentiae & vestrae excellentiae, vos autem praecarissime Domine, qui ita pinguei us habetis in regno Franciae, quod non solum electione, sed iure hereditario possidetis & ad posteritatem transmittitis, quod non possitis istud concedere, videtur quamplurimum vestrae potentiae derogare, imo in tantum, quod si esset verum, quod absit, sequeretur praedecessores vestros in peccato continue fuisse, imo quod impium est dicere, B. Ludouicum, per quem tota Francia illustratur, non potuisse iuste canonizatum. Si enim, sicut proponens dicebat, iurauit non alienare, & alienata renocare, & istud esse inseparabile a corona, sequitur quod deierasset, & per consequens mortaliter peccasset, & ita canonizari non potuisset, quod est nepharium dicere. Et si dicatur, quod potuit poenitere cito, potest responderi, quod peccatum legitur, sed poenitentia non inuenitur, sicut de Salomone, quinimo si esset verum, quod dicit, sequeretur quod nihil possetis dare neq; Comitatum, neq; Castrum, neq; villam; & tamen pauci sunt, qui non libenter reciperent, non obstante iuramento fidelitatis, in quo vobis tenentur. Conseruet ergo & confirmet nobis vestra magnificentia Regalis, quod per tam inclitos progenitores vestros concessum est, aliquin honor vestrae excellentiae minor seruaretur, vt dicatis illud ad Rom. 11. munistrum meum honorificabo.
units.tr: I say, secondly, that a man honours the king when he advises him of that by which his power and excellence are not diminished. It befits his honour greatly to increase his authority, and it is very unbecoming to lessen it. This is why emperors used to call themselves Augusti, as though they were increasing the commonwealth. But to say that you or your predecessors could not grant these things to the Church seems to be a great diminution of your power and your excellence. Most dear Lord, you who hold the kingdom of France so richly that you possess it not only by election but by hereditary right, and pass it on to posterity, if it were true that you could not grant this, it would seem greatly to detract from your power. Indeed it would go so far that, if it were true (which God forbid), it would follow that your predecessors had continually been in sin. Worse, it would be impious to say that Saint Louis, through whom all France is made illustrious, could not have been justly canonized. For if, as the proponent said, he swore not to alienate and to revoke what had been alienated, and this were inseparable from the crown, it would follow that he had sworn falsely and so had sinned mortally, and thus could not have been canonized, which is an impious thing to say. And if it be said that he could have repented quickly, it may be answered that a sin is recorded but no repentance is found, as in the case of Solomon. Indeed, if what he says were true, it would follow that you could give nothing, neither a county, nor a castle, nor a village; and yet there are few who would not gladly receive these things, notwithstanding the oath of fidelity by which they are bound to you. Let your Royal Magnificence therefore preserve and confirm to us what was granted by so illustrious ancestors of yours. Otherwise the honour of your excellence would be kept less well, so that you may hear that word of Romans 11: munistrum meum honorificabo.

units.la: Dico tertio, quod ille honorificat regem facto, qui ei suadet illud, per quod sua fama custoditur, nec perditur. Inter cetera n. de quibus debet quilibet curare, est fama post conscientia, quia Prou. 22 scribitur: melius est nomen bonum, quam diuitiae multae. Super argentum n. & aurum gratia bona. Et B. Augustus dicit: duo sunt tibi necessaria, conscientia & fama, conscientia propter Deum, & fama propter proximum. Et ideo Ecc. scribitur: Curam habe de bono nomine, hoc enim magis permanebit tibi quam mille thesauri magni & preciosi. Istud autem nomen Dominus, qui vos vnxit oleo laetitiae prae cunctis Principibus vestris, vobis dedit in tam modico tempore, quod quasi miraculosum videtur. Et ideo summopere habetis curare, quod istud non permaneat, quia
units.tr: I say, thirdly, that he honours the king by deed who advises him in that which preserves his good name and does not let it perish. Among the other things about which everyone ought to take care, reputation comes after conscience, since it is written in Proverbs 22: A good name is better than great riches; loving favour is better than silver and gold. And Blessed Augustine says: Two things are necessary to you, conscience and reputation: conscience for God's sake, and reputation for the sake of your neighbour. And therefore it is written in Ecclesiasticus: Take care of a good name, for this will remain with you longer than a thousand great and precious treasures. Now the Lord, who anointed you with the oil of gladness above all your princes, has given you this name in so short a time that it seems almost miraculous. And therefore you must take the greatest care that it does not remain, because

units.la: Non minor est virtus quam quaerere parta tueri.
units.tr: To keep what has been won is no less a virtue than to win it.

units.la: vt non solum in vitam, sed etiam post mortem istud nomen permaneat gloriosum, ne aliquid fiat p vos, p qp in tanto nomine macula inveniatur, ac de vobis dicatur illud Prou. 10. Memoria iusti cum laudibus. Attendat ergo Regia Celsitudo, si temporib. vestris libertas ecclesiastica tollatur, qp absit, vel in aliquo diminuatur: si in vestro glorioso nomine aliqua macula se ingereret, cum multi essent, q hoc in Chronicis redigerent. Unde Christianissime Domine, si p huiusmodi, qui non sperabat aliam vitam, tn ppter famam, quae remanebat apud homines, adeo virtuose viuebant: quid nos Christiani, qui speramus vitam aeternam & memoriam perpetuam, facere debemus? Aduertat etiam dominatio vestra, si posset esse denigratio nominis, cum reges Franciae semper fuerunt Christianissimi Deo & ecclesiae, & semper dederunt exemplu aliis principibus dotandi & augendi ecclesias & libertates earum: si nunc (qp absit) qu ecclesia est in magna persecutione in aliquib. locis, vos daretis exemplum revocandi dona fata per praedecessores eorum ecclesiae. Eadem n. ratione posset aliquis imperator, si quis esset, revocare oia, quae data fuerunt ecclesiae per Constantinum Imp. & etiam alii reges data ecclesiae p eos in regnis suis. Absit aut, quod vos detis tale exemplum, qm pro certo plus vellem mortuus esse, q vobis cosuluissem, quod super re tam perniciosa praebuissetis exemplum: Ipsecialiter cum praedecessores vestri reges Franciae, qui volentes tollere libertates se pro ecclesia opposuerunt defensores, hoc tm est regum officium, dicit Hieronym. super Ieremiam, & habetur 23. q. 5. c. Regum, & quod dicit, habetur ibidem in c. princeps: Cognoscant principes saeculi Deo se debere esse reddituros rationem propter ecclesiam Christi, quam tuendam suscipiunt. Et nota hic aliqua exempla in Chronicis, quomodo hoc seruauerunt reges Franciae, exemplo ergo eorum & vos seruetis & augeatis. Tunc autem de vobis dici poterit illud Eccle. 37. Sapiens in populo hereditabit honorem. & Eccle. 3. Sicut qui thesaurizat, ita qui honorificat matrem suam. Dico quarto, quod ille honorificat regem facto, qui suadet sibi illud, propter quod conscientia sua non laeditur. Super omnia enim Christianus debet quilibet aduertere, ne faciat illud, per quod conscientia sua laedatur, quoniam anima plus est quam esca. Matth. 6. Et certe credo firmiter, qp pro toto mundo nolletis aliquid facere scienter, de quo conscientia vestra esset laesa, & merito, quanto n. Deus vos quasi miraculose ad regem vocauit, & vobis plures gratias fecit, tanto plus debetis & habetis cauere, ne eum offendatis, quia no dubitandum esset, quin contra vos acrius indignaret, sicut fecit contra Saul 1. Reg. 15. modo, Praecarissime, attendatis si vos in coronatione vestra iuraftis ista, & non plura, scil. quod episcopis & ecclesiis & eis commissis canonicum priuilegium & debitam legem & iustitiam seruaretis & defensione, & quantum posse tis exhiberetis. Item, qp vestro arbitrio omnis populus Christianus veram pacem Dei & ecclesiae suae omni tempore seruauerit. Item quod oes rapacitates & oes iniquitates omnib. gentib. interdicetis. Item qp in omnib. iudiciis equitate & misericordia praecipiendis. Ite qp de tota terra & iurisdictione vestra haereticos ab ecclesia denotatos p virib. bona fide exterminari studebitis. Ista iuraftis & no plura, salua reuerentia domini Petri, qui vos vnum aliud iurasse dicebat. Cum ergo sit priuilegiu ecclesiae canonicum & in corde canonis incorporatum 6. q. 1. quicunq; liteis habens: & sit etiam de consuetudine introducta, quae consuetudo est canonica, qp ecclesia possit cognoscere in multis casibus, contra quos sunt articuli positi, inter laicos, si istud no seruaretur ecclesiae, sic posset in aliquo vestra conscientia laedi. Ite si debetis pro posse facere, qp omnis populus Christianus veram pacem ecclesiae Dei omni tempore seruet: multo fortius habetis hoc procurare de Baronib. q semper fuerunt vnum & idem cum ecclesia, semper n. vbi fuit ecclesia in honore, ibi viguit Baronum & Militum strenuitas, & quoniam officium est ecclesiae defensare, sicut officium ecclesiae est p eis orare, & inde sacrificium p eis Deo offerre. Et ad hoc multum conatus est B. Ludouicus suo tempore, quia cum maiores Barones totius regni se confoederassent ad tollenda istam ecclesiae libertate, & ordinassent adhuc dare centesimam bonorum suorum, ipse nunc eis adhaesit, sed potius eos ab istis cooperiscuit. Et finaliter hanc libertate ecclesiae confirmauit. Nota hic, quod Innocentius Papa illo tunc contra illos Barones processit, &c. Et bene audeo dicere, qp si inter praelatos & Barones esset dissensio, dubitarem quin cito populus vellet dominium usurpare, sicut patuit de facto in multis locis. Et de facto quilibet nostrum potuit videre, quia cum aliqui incitassent populum contra curiam ecclesiasticam in aliqua parte Campaniae & Burgundiae intantum qp inimicus populus, quasi in qualibet villa fecerat regem, qui portantes citationes verberari faciebant; & Papam qui absoluebat, & sic statim idem populus contra dominos temporales insurrexit, & idem eis faciebat quousq; p potestatem regis multi fuerunt suspensi, & scandalum illud fuit sedatum, hoc fuit tempore Ludouici regis vltimi. Et vere Nobiles non deberent conqueri de his, quae habet ecclesia, qm enim pauci sunt, qui non habeant fratres aut propinquos, qui viuunt de bonis ecclesiae, qui diuiderent eis haereditatem, paulatim redigerent ad nihilu. Aduertant etiam Barones, quod pauci sunt, qui non sunt fideles ecclesiae. Ecclesia autem vna est, Canticor. 6. vna est columba mea, sic nec absque periculo transgressionis possent suadere, quod tales ecclesiae libertates tollerentur, vt ergo vestra conscientia immaculata remaneat, placeat vestrae Celsitudini priuilegium istud iustum & canonicum confirmare, attentata, si quae sint, per proclamationes vel alias revocare, & matrem vestram ecclesiam Gallicanam in suis Franchisiis, libertatibus & consuetudinibus conseruare, vt per vos in omnib. honorificetur Deus, cui est honor & gloria in secula seculorum, amen. 1. Petr. 4. & ipse vos honorificet. rificet, qui dicit primo Reg. 2. c. Quicunque honorificabit me, glorificabo eum in gloria, in qua est verus honor, qui nulli conceditur indigno: imo ad quem nullus admittitur, nisi dignus, sicut dicit B. August. quem honorem nobis & vobis concedat, qui est benedictus in secula seculorum amen. Et quia multi articuli proponebantur, quorum aliqui tota iurisdictionem eneruauerunt ecclesiasticam. Idcirco eos volumus defendere & tueri, cum praescriptum sit Eccl. 4. vsque ad mortem certa pro iustitia & Deus expugnabit pro te inimicos tuos. Aliqui alii sunt, qui cötinent solum abusum, quē nō credimus p gentes nostras fieri, & si fierent, nollemus aliqualiter tollerare easdem, & ideo propter honorem Dei principaliter, & propter exonerationē conscientiarū nostrarū, & propter regis reuerentiā populi profectū & pacem, oēs hic simul congregati disposuimus tale remedium apponere, quod abusus prædicti, si qui sint, cessabunt ad pacem populi & laudem Dei: cui est honor & gloria in secula seculorum, amen.
units.tr: I say, fourthly, that he honours the king in fact who persuades him of that by which his conscience is not harmed. For above all things every Christian ought to be careful not to do that by which his conscience is injured, since the soul is more than food (Matthew 6). And I firmly believe that you would not, for all the world, knowingly do anything by which your conscience would be harmed, and rightly so. For the more God has called you, as if miraculously, to be king, and the more favours He has shown you, the more you ought and must take care not to offend Him, since there is no doubt that He would be angrier with you, as He was with Saul (1 Kings 15). Now, most dear Lord, consider whether in your coronation you swore these things and no more: that you would keep the canonical privilege and due law and justice for the bishops, the churches, and those committed to them, and would defend them with all the power you have. Likewise, that by your decision the whole Christian people would always preserve the true peace of God and of His Church. Likewise, that you would forbid all rapacity and all iniquities among all peoples. Likewise, that in all judgments you would command equity and mercy. Likewise, that you would strive with all your strength, in good faith, to exterminate from the whole land and your jurisdiction the heretics condemned by the Church. These you swore, and no more, saving the reverence due to Lord Peter, who used to say that you had sworn some other thing. Since, then, the privilege of the Church is canonical and incorporated into the very heart of the canon (6 q. 1, quicunque litem habens), and since it is also a custom introduced, which custom is canonical, that the Church may take cognizance in many cases, against which articles have been drawn up, between laymen, if this were not maintained for the Church, then your conscience could be harmed in some respect. Likewise, if you ought to do what you can, so that the whole Christian people preserve the true peace of God's Church at all times, then much more strongly you ought to bring this about among the barons, who have always been one and the same with the Church. For wherever the Church has been honoured, there the valour of the barons and knights has flourished; and just as it is the office of the Church to defend them, so it is the office of the Church to pray for them, and therefore to offer sacrifice to God for them. Blessed Louis strove greatly for this in his own time, for when the greatest barons of the whole kingdom had banded together to abolish this liberty of the Church, and had resolved to give a hundredth of their goods, he did not join them but rather kept them away from such plans. And finally he confirmed this liberty of the Church. Note here that Pope Innocent then proceeded against those barons, etc. And I dare well to say that if there were dissension between the prelates and the barons, I would fear that the people would soon wish to usurp dominion, as has been plainly seen in fact in many places. And indeed each of us could see it, for when some stirred up the people against the ecclesiastical court in part of Champagne and Burgundy, to such an extent that the hostile people, as if in every town they had made a king, had those who carried citations beaten; and the Pope, who absolved, was likewise treated; and so at once the same people rose against the temporal lords, and did the same to them, until through the power of the king many were suspended, and that scandal was quelled. This happened in the time of King Louis the last. And truly, nobles ought not to complain about what the Church possesses. For since there are few who do not have brothers or relatives who live from Church goods, and who would divide the inheritance among them, these would gradually reduce it to nothing. Let the barons also consider that there are few who are not faithful to the Church, and the Church is one (Song of Songs 6: "one is my dove"). Thus they could not advise, without danger of transgression, that such liberties of the Church be taken away. So that your conscience may remain unstained, may it please your Highness to confirm this just and canonical privilege, to revoke by proclamations or otherwise any attempts, if there are any, and to preserve your mother the Gallican Church in its franchises, liberties and customs, so that God may be honoured in all things through you, to whom is honour and glory for ever and ever, amen (1 Peter 4). And may He honour you, who says in 1 Kings 2: "Whoever honours me, I will glorify him in glory, in which is true honour," which is granted to no unworthy person; indeed no one is admitted to it except the worthy, as blessed Augustine says. May He grant us and you that honour, who is blessed for ever and ever, amen. And since many articles were put forward, some of which would enervate the whole ecclesiastical jurisdiction, we therefore wish to defend and protect them, since it is written (Ecclesiasticus 4): "Even to death, fight for justice, and God will fight for you against your enemies." There are some others which contain only abuse, which we do not believe to be carried out by our people; and if they were, we would not wish in any way to tolerate them. And therefore, principally for the honour of God, and for the discharge of our consciences, and for the reverence of the king, the progress and peace of the people, all of us gathered here together have decided to apply such a remedy that the aforesaid abuses, if there are any, will cease, to the peace of the people and the praise of God, to whom is honour and glory for ever and ever, amen.

units.la: Altera autem die veneris immediate subsequenti, videl. die 29. Decemb. in palatio Regali Parisiis ad invicem convenerunt praelati: & rege ibidem more solito sedente, assistentibus sibi Consiliariis suis & Baronibus, reuerendus pater dominus Petrus Bertrandi divina providentia Eduensis episc. locutus est in publico coram Rege, facto pro themate suo: Ne indigneris Domine, si loquar, Gen. 18. ca. pro themate applicuit ad hoc, quod propter regis magnificentiam, consilii sui providentiam, & loquentis insufficientiam, cum magnum negocium esset, loqui formidabat. Sed de regia benignitate confisus audaciam assumebat. Et quia fuerat sibi a dominis praelatis iniunctum. Deinde fecit thema suum tale: Domine refugium factus es nobis in praesens. Et prosecutus est themaRegis magnificentiam commendando, vocationē suam ad regnum Franciae quasi mirabile declarando, tertio quod debet esse pugil ecclesiae ostendendo. Et ista probauit satis breuiter p auctoritates & rationes multas. Postmodum respondit ad ea, quae proposita fuerunt p dictū dominum Petrum de Cugneriis in modū infrascriptum, & ad informandū conscientiā domini regis, & ad praestandū consilium sup praedictis duntaxat, & non ad finē ordinandi iudicii seu responsionis faciendae, per q sententia, ordinatio vel statutū aut quiuis alius processus sequi possent, vel ius aliud psonae cuicunq; acquiri. Primo ad illud, q propositū est: Reddite quae sunt Caesarū Caesari, & quae sunt Dei Deo, Matt. 22. & Marc. 3. p quae verba proponebatur ad regē obedientia & subiectio, & spiritualiū & temporalium diuisio. Et primum membrum probatur per illud, q dicit 1 Pet. 2. c. Subiecti estote omni creaturae, rursus p verba, quae sunt in c. solita, ext. de ma. & obe. & per c. nouit, ext. de iud. & c. de sacerdotib. 10. q. 1. cū ibi notatis. Ad illud q dicitur de diuisione, probatur q temporalia debebant ptinere ad temporales, & spiritualia ad spirituales: tum quia Deus instituit duos gladios, unde dicit: Ecce duo gladii, Luc. 22. item Christus censum soluit, ut denotaret q temporalib. reddenda sunt temporalia, Matt. 17. & 12. & 11. q. 1. si tributū: & c. magnū. Praeter ea lege imperatoris cauetur ista diuisio, cū dicitur: magna n. a Deo collata sunt dona, sacerdotiū & imperium, sacerdotiū ut diuinus, imperium ut humanus praesset, in corpore autenticorū, Quō. opor. epi. in prin. colla. 1. & dicebatur, q isti erant termini, qui non debebant aliqualiter immutari, Prou. 23. c. & ff. de termino mo. le. 1. & vlt. Dicebatur etiā, quod talia iura regia rex non poterat a se abdicare, cum essent iuris sui regalis, & iurasset in coronatione sua iura regni non alienare, & alienata reuocare, & quod talia erant impraescriptibilia 10. di. c. quaest. & aliis pluribus c. eiusdē di. cum ibi no. Ad praedictam respondetur sic, q iurisdictio causarum ciuilium, de quib. agitur, ptinet ad ecclesiā de iure diuino & humano. Et de iure diuino probatur a tempore Adae vsq; ad Christū p ea, quae notantur p Innocent. c. licet, ext. de fo. compe. a tempore Christi citra, cōmissa fuit Petro & successoribus. 22. di. c. oēs Patriarchae, Matt. 16. & qualiter ecclesia in terris catholicorum principum istud ius obtinuerit & obtinet, probatur 2. q. 5. Si quis presbyter 11. q. 1. relatū 25. di. ecce. Et istud ius confirmauerunt imperatores in corpore autenticorū, ut ff. 3. 5. si causa col. 9. 23. q. vlt. c. hu & a quib. dicit etiam canon, & quod B. Petrus praecipiebat oēs principes terrae & caeteros homines episcopis obedire in c. oēs, ext. de ma. & obe. 16. di. duo sunt, quare concluditur, quod non est faciēda diuisio, ut haec ecclesiis auferantur, & si in tyrannorum regum terris status iste ecclesiae fuerit laesus vel etiā violatus, in regno trā Franciae benedicto vsq; ad haec tempora extitit obseruatus ext. de iudiciis c. nouit in parte decisa, &c. Praeterea leges Theodosii Imperat. & Caroli M. hanc iurisdictionem confirmarunt, ext. de iudiciis c. nonne all. 11. q. 1. quicunq; & c. fe. iurisdictio c. expresse cauetur, quod idem Carolus rex Franciae & imperator in Francia specialiter hoc ius cōstituit. Item de consuetudine a tanto tempore obtenta, quod in cōtrarium memoria hominum nō existit, horum iurisdictio pertinet ad ecclesiam Gallicanā omnium regum tempore Christianorum & sanctorū. Quis ergo videbit hanc consuetudinē violare sacrilegium est 11. q. 1. c. 1. & 2. Item non miretur regalis dignitas, si in regno Franciae nobiliore mundi haec praerogatiua ecclesiis debeatur, in hoc n. sua potentia & nobilitas decoratur, in corpore autenticorū: vt iudi. sine quoq, suffra. sin. in prin. collat. 2. Praeterea dominus rex in coronatione sua iurauit ad sancta Dei euangelia priuilegium canonicum seruare ecclesiae, omnes etiam Barones vel quasi sunt fideles ecclesiae, & iurauerunt fidelitatē, sub qua fidelitate tenentur p iuramentum iura ista seruare ecclesiae. Cum igitur omne iuramentum, q non tendit in interitum salutis aeternae, sit seruandum: istud, quod est in fauore ecclesiarum praestitum, multo fortius est seruandum: ext. de iureiur. c. si vero 22. q. 4. c. vlt. Itē B. Ludouicus, Philippus Aragonensis. Philippus pulcher, Ludouicus, Carolus M. & Philippus, priuilegia, consuetudines & libertates ecclesiae confirmauerunt, & dominus Philippus pulcher seruare, quare, &c. & omnes isti in suis coronationib. iurauerunt, ut supra. Quis ergo poterit isti domino regi absq; damnatione propria contrarium suadere, maxime in istis concessis, declaratis & confirmatis ecclesiae, cui donare immensitas est mensura, in autent. de non alien. at. permut. rec. ec. 5. si nimu coll. 2. Nec obstat, q dicitur, quod duo sunt gladii, &c. Et quod distinctum est sacerdotium ab imperio: quia verum est, quod sunt duo gladii, illud dictum ecclesiæ, & verum est, quod ius & potestas istorum duorum gladiorum est penes ecclesiam; licet executio gladii materialis sit penes temporales vel seculares, & hoc est quod dicitur Matt. 26. cum dixit Dominus: Converte gladium tuum in locum suum. Et q; dicitur, distinctum est sacerdotium & imperium, verum est ex parte finis, & quantum ad executionem sanguinis, & non ex parte principii seu subiecti, quia in eodem subiecto sunt & esse possunt, imo debent esse, ut superius est probatum. Ad illud quod dicitur, quod Christus soluit tributum: respondetur, quod non ideo, quod deberet soluere: quia certum est, quod filii regis non debebant, qualis ipse erat: sed propter scandalum hoc fecit, imo etiam nec clerici ad hoc tenerentur, Esdræ prim. & vlt. cap. Unde talia non sunt ad consequentiam trahenda, nec obstat de immutatione terminorum, quia dictum est, quod hæc allegatio sit pro ecclesia, cum ista ad ecclesiam pertineant, sicut dictum est. Nec obstat, quod Dominus rex non potest ista iura abdicare à se, maxime cum hoc iuraverit in coronatione sua, &c. Respondetur, quod imo potest totum abdicare, quia non abdicat à se, cum Deo & ecclesiæ dat, quia dictum est, Domini est terra. Tale enim dare nihil aliud est, nisi reddere Deo & ecclesiæ, quod suum est, quia sic sequeretur, quod donatio imperii ecclesiæ à Constantino non teneret, quod falsum est. Et hoc probatur 16. dist. cap. Constantinus, præterea imperator vel rex potest alienare res imperii. ff. de lege. l. apud Iulianum. §. vlt. nec per hoc læditur imperium vel regnum, eo quod res redit ad statum suum pristinum ff. de pactis l. unus §. pact. 35. di. ab exord. Præterea ista ratio proposita damnaret omnes reges Franciæ, qui fuerunt, & specialiter beat. Ludovicum, quia si vera essent (quod absit) omnes essent mortui peccato mortali & periuri, quod nephas est dicere. Nec obstat, quod dicitur, impræscriptibilia sunt talia: verum est ab alio quam ab ecclesia: vel aliter quam à subditis non possent præscribi, sed non à subditis sic, præterea ex quo potest alienari, potest præscribi, maxime de consensu regum, qui hoc confirmauerunt, & à tanto tempore, quod omne ius excludit & fiscale & ecclesiæ. Concluditur ergo, quod omnes prælati prædicta asserunt esse vera & tenenda, & supplicant domino regi pro salute animæ suæ & pace ecclesiæ seruanda, quod nihil immuter, sed prout prædecessores sui tenuerunt ecclesiam, ipse teneat & libertates ecclesiæ seruet. Et consideret quanta bona spiritualia habet quotidie ab ecclesia, & quod nunquam sibi defecit ecclesia Gallicana, cum opus fuit etiam in auxilio temporali: & ostendantur exempla & pericula, quæ facienti contrarium esse possunt. Et consideret qualiter dominus noster Papa, qui nunc est, diligit & dilexit regnum Franciæ & personam domini regis dicendo, quod nunquam fuit in sede B. Petri, qui regnum plus dilexerit eo. Et consideret, quod legitur Eccl. 6. c. vbi dicitur, in multitudine presbyterorum sta, & eis ex corde crede. Deinde præfatus dominus Eduensis episcopus, ad finem prædictum, videl. ad informandum conscientiam domini regis, & ad præstandum consilium super petitis, taxat, & non ad finem ordinandi iudicii seu responsionis faciendæ, per quam sententia, ordinatio vel statutum, aut quiuis alius processus sequi potuisset, vel ius aliquod personæ cuiq; acquiri, ad singulos articulos sic respondit, & diuisit articulos traditos in tres partes, quia quidam articuli tangebant iura ecclesiæ perpetua, & quæ pertinebant ad ecclesiam de iure & consuetudine, & de eis ecclesia iuste vtebatur, quos erant parati defendere, sicut B. Thomas Cantuariensis episcopus, cuius festum erat illa die, iura ecclesiæ defenderat. Secunda pars articulorum continebat abusus & errores, si veri essent, & illos nullomodo volebant defendere, imo prouidere ne talia fierent & corrigere, si quæ talia facta erant. Tertia pars continebat aliqua, quæ poterant esse iusta, & aliqua iniusta, quantum ad iusta, respondit vt de contentis in prima parte, quantum ad iniusta, vt de contentis in secunda. Omnes articuli contenti in prima parte, signati in margine per a. articuli contenti in secunda parte per b. articuli contenti in tertia per c. Deinde respondit singulariter ad singulos, prout sequitur. Et primo ad primum articulum qui loquitur de cognitione actionum realium personalium, mixtarum, & interdictorum, dicit dominus Episc. Eduensis, quod cum de iure sit probatum superius in generali responsione talium cognitionem illius ad ecclesiam pertinere de iure, & posse pertinere de consuetudine, maxime in actionibus personalibus de iure licet de abusu consuetudinario aliquando dicantur rebelles, quod in his ecclesia maxime illæ, quæ de consuetudine hoc habent nullam iniuriam regi vel dominis temporalibus faciebant. Et ad probandum istam responsionem, allegauit 63. d. c. Valentiniani 11. q. 1. quicunq; in autem, vt diffi. iudicii §. si tamen col. 9. ext. de iudi. c. nouit. 22. di. c. 1. 11. q. 1. relatum, 2. q. 1. Si quis presbyter. 1. di. consuetudo, induxit etiam ad hoc probandum priuilegia & libertates, confirmationes, & plures alias B. Ludovici & omnium aliorum regum prædecessorum istius. Ad secundum articulum, qui loquitur de clericis turbantibus possessiones laicorum, & de causa novitatis, dicit episcopus prædictus, quod vbi clericus impedimentum apponit vel violentiam, laicus est actor, & clericus est reus, & cum de iure & consuetudine actor teneatur sequi forum rei, non est irrationabile, maxime in ecclesiis, quæ de consuetudine hoc habent, si de talibus ecclesia cognitionem habeat. Alias enim sequeretur, quod iudices seculares pro voluntate sua haberent cognitionem clericorum pro eo, quod diceret hoc vel illud esse casum novitatis. Maxime quia in talibus impedimentis vel violentiis habent locum interdicta, quæ sunt personalia de iure, licet in re videantur concepta, ff. de inuest. l. 1. §. vlt. quæ sunt personalia de iure, quod superius est probatum. Et ad probandum prædicta allegat predictus episcopus extr. de fo. compe. si clericus 24. quæst. 3. Item quia. Et alia iura supradicta de consuetudine loquentia. Ad tertiu, qui loquitur de actionib. personalibus inter duos laicos vel inter clericu actore & laicū reū: dicit idē Episc. q; de iure & consuetudine notoriis cognitio talium actionū personalium pertinet ad ecclesiam, secundum quod superius est probatum, quare dicebat nulli super hoc iniuriam fieri, maxime me ratione peccati, quod committitur in retinendo illud, quod tenetur quis ad soluendum vel restituendum. Et ad hoc probandum induxit iura supra allegata, & de fo. compe. cum fit generale.
units.tr: On the next day, Friday, 29 December, the prelates met again in the royal palace at Paris. The king sat there in his usual manner, with his councillors and barons around him, and the reverend father Lord Pierre Bertrand, by divine providence bishop of Autun, spoke publicly before the king. For his text he took Ne indigneris Domine, si loquar (Gen. 18), and he applied it to the fact that, since the king's greatness, his counsel's wisdom and his own inadequacy made the matter so weighty, he was afraid to speak. Trusting in the king's kindness, however, he took courage, as the lord prelates had charged him to do. He then gave his second text: Domine refugium factus es nobis in praesens. He went on to praise the king's greatness, to declare his calling to the kingdom of France as something wonderful, and, third, to show that he ought to be the champion of the Church. He proved these points fairly briefly, by many authorities and arguments. Afterwards he replied to the points put forward by the said Lord Pierre de Cugnières, in the manner set out below. He did this only to inform the king's conscience and to give counsel on the matters aforesaid, and not with the purpose of issuing a judgment or a response, by which any sentence, ordinance or statute, or any other legal proceeding, could follow, or any right be acquired by any person. First, to what was proposed: Reddite quae sunt Caesaris Caesari, et quae sunt Dei Deo (Matt. 22; Mark 12), by which words obedience and subjection were urged upon the king, and a division of spiritual and temporal matters. The first member is proved by 1 Pet. 2, Subiecti estote omni creaturae; again by the words in the chapter solita, Ext. de maioritate et obedientia; and by the chapter nouit, Ext. de iudiciis, and the chapter de sacerdotibus, D. 10, q. 1, with the notes there. As to the division that was mentioned, it is proved that temporal matters ought to belong to temporal rulers and spiritual matters to spiritual rulers: first, because God instituted two swords, whence he says, Ecce duo gladii (Luke 22); also because Christ paid the tribute, to show that temporal things are to be rendered from temporal things (Matt. 17; and 12 and 11, q. 1, si tributum, and the chapter magnum). Moreover, this division is laid down by a law of the emperor, where it is said: magna enim a Deo collata sunt dona, sacerdotium et imperium; sacerdotium ut divinum, imperium ut humanum praesset (Authentica, Quomodo oportet episcopos, in the preface, collation 1). And it was said that these were the boundaries, which ought not to be altered in any way (Prov. 23; and D. de termino moto, l. 1 and last). It was also said that the king could not renounce such royal rights, since they belonged to his royal right, and he had sworn at his coronation not to alienate the rights of the kingdom, and to revoke what had been alienated; and that such rights could not be lost by prescription (D. 10, the chapter quaestio, and several others of the same distinction, with the notes there). To the aforesaid it is replied as follows: the jurisdiction over civil causes, of which the question is, belongs to the Church by divine and human right. By divine right it is proved, from the period from Adam to Christ, by what Innocent notes in the chapter licet, Ext. de foro competenti; and from the time of Christ onward it was committed to Peter and his successors (D. 22, the chapter omnes Patriarchae; Matt. 16). And how the Church in the lands of the Catholic princes has obtained and does obtain this right is proved by 2, q. 5, Si quis presbyter; 11, q. 1, relatum; and D. 25, ecce. The emperors confirmed this right in the Authentics, as in D. 3, 5, si causa, col. 9; and C. 23, q. last, c. hu, and from the sources from which the canon also speaks. And that St Peter ordered all princes of the earth and other men to obey the bishops is shown in the chapter omnes, Ext. de maioritate et obedientia, and in D. 16, duo sunt. From this it follows that the division ought not to be made so that these things are taken away from the churches; and if this state of the Church has been harmed or even violated in the lands of tyrannical kings, in the kingdom of France it has been observed, blessed, up to the present times (Ext. de iudiciis, c. nouit, in the part decided, etc.). Moreover, the laws of the emperor Theodosius and of Charlemagne confirmed this jurisdiction (Ext. de iudiciis, c. nonne; 11, q. 1, quicunque; and the chapter iurisdictio), and it is expressly laid down that the same Charles, king of France and emperor, established this right specially in France. Likewise, by a custom so long established that there is no memory of anything to the contrary, the jurisdiction over these matters belongs in the Gallican Church, in the time of all the Christian kings and saints. Whoever sees that this custom is violated, therefore, commits sacrilege (11, q. 1, c. 1 and 2). Again, let not the royal dignity marvel if, in the kingdom of France, the most noble in the world, this prerogative is owed to the churches; for in this its power and nobility are adorned (Authentic, ut iudices sine quoquam suffragio sint, in the beginning, collation 2). Moreover, at his coronation the lord king swore on the holy Gospels of God to keep the canonical privilege of the Church. All the barons, too, are, as it were, faithful to the Church, and they swore fidelity, under which fidelity they are bound by oath to keep these rights for the Church. Since, therefore, every oath that does not tend to the loss of eternal salvation must be kept, what has been sworn in favour of the churches must all the more be kept (Ext. de iureiurando, c. si vero; 22, q. 4, c. last). Likewise St Louis, Philip of Aragon, Philip the Fair, Louis, Charlemagne and Philip confirmed the privileges, customs and liberties of the Church, and Lord Philip the Fair ought to keep them, and so on; and all these men swore at their coronations, as above. Who, then, could persuade this lord king of the contrary without his own damnation, especially in these matters granted, declared and confirmed to the Church, to which immensity is the measure of giving (Authentic, de non alienandis aut permutandis rebus ecclesiae, 5; si nimium, collation 2)? Nor does it stand in the way that it is said there are two swords, etc., and that priesthood is distinct from empire. For it is true that there are two swords, and that this saying belongs to the Church; and it is true that the right and power over these two swords rests with the Church, although the execution of the material sword rests with temporal or secular rulers. This is what is meant in Matt. 26, where the Lord said: Converte gladium tuum in locum suum. And when it is said that priesthood and empire are distinct, this is true with regard to the end and the execution of blood-judgment, and not with regard to the origin or subject; for in one and the same subject they are and can be, indeed ought to be, as has been proved above. As to the objection that Christ paid the tribute: the reply is that he did not do so because he was obliged to pay, since it is certain that the sons of a king were not obliged to pay, being what he himself was; but he did it on account of scandal. Indeed, not even the clergy would be bound to this, as in 1 Esdras, first and last chapter. Therefore such things are not to be drawn into precedent. Nor does the point about the alteration of boundaries stand in the way, since it has been said that this argument is made on behalf of the Church, as these matters belong to the Church, as has been said. Nor does it stand in the way that the lord king cannot renounce these rights from himself, especially since he swore this at his coronation. It is replied that indeed he can give up the whole, since he does not renounce them from himself when he gives them to God and the Church, for it has been said: Domini est terra. For to give such a thing is nothing other than to render to God and the Church what is theirs; otherwise it would follow that the donation of the empire by Constantine to the Church would not hold, which is false. And this is proved in D. 16, c. Constantinus. Moreover, an emperor or king can alienate the goods of the empire (D. de legibus, l. apud Iulianum, §. last), and the empire or kingdom is not harmed by this, since the thing returns to its former state (D. de pactis, l. unus, §. pactum; 35, D. ab exordio). Furthermore, the argument put forward would condemn all the kings of France who have been, and especially the blessed Louis; for if these claims were true (which God forbid), all of them would have died in mortal sin and perjury, which it is impious to say. Nor does it stand in the way that it is said such rights cannot be lost by prescription: this is true as against another than the Church, or else they could not be lost by prescription against the subjects; but not against the subjects in this way. Moreover, since a thing can be alienated, it can be lost by prescription, especially with the consent of the kings, who confirmed this, and over so long a time that it excludes every right, both fiscal and ecclesiastical. It is concluded, therefore, that all the prelates assert the aforesaid things to be true and to be held, and they beg the lord king, for the salvation of his soul and for the keeping of peace in the Church, that nothing be changed, but that, just as his predecessors held the Church, he himself hold it and keep the liberties of the Church. And let him consider how many spiritual goods he receives daily from the Church, and that the Gallican Church has never failed him when there was need even for temporal aid. And let the examples and dangers that can befall one who acts to the contrary be set before him. And let him consider how our lord the Pope, who is now, loves and has loved the kingdom of France and the person of the lord king, saying that he who has ever been in the seat of St Peter has never loved the kingdom more. And let him consider what is read in Ecclesiasticus 6: in multitudine presbyterorum sta, et eis ex corde crede. Then the aforesaid lord bishop of Autun, for the aforesaid purpose, namely to inform the conscience of the lord king and to give counsel on the matters petitioned, and not with the purpose of issuing a judgment or a response by which any sentence, ordinance or statute, or any other legal proceeding, could follow, or any right be acquired by any person, answered each article in this way. He divided the articles handed over into three parts: some articles concerned the perpetual rights of the Church, and what belonged to the Church by right and custom, and of which the Church made lawful use; these the prelates were ready to defend, just as the blessed Thomas, bishop of Canterbury, whose feast fell on that day, had defended the rights of the Church. The second part of the articles contained abuses and errors, if they were true, and these they by no means wished to defend; indeed they wished to provide that such things should not happen, and to correct any such acts that had been done. The third part contained some matters that could be just and some unjust. As to the just ones, he replied as he had about the contents of the first part; as to the unjust ones, as about the contents of the second part. All the articles contained in the first part were marked in the margin with a; the articles contained in the second part with b; those in the third part with c. Then he replied individually to each one, as follows. First, to the first article, which concerns the cognizance of real, personal and mixed actions, and of interdicts, the lord bishop of Autun says that, since it has been proved by law above, in the general reply, that the cognizance of such matters belongs to the Church by right, and can belong to it by custom, especially in personal actions, and although by right they are sometimes called rebellious because of a customary abuse, nevertheless in these matters the Church, particularly those churches which have this by custom, did no injury to the king or the temporal lords. And to prove this reply he cited D. 63, c. Valentinianus; 11, q. 1, quicunque; the authentic ut differentiae iudiciorum, §. si tamen, col. 9; Ext. de iudiciis, c. nouit; 22, D. c. 1; 11, q. 1, relatum; 2, q. 1, Si quis presbyter; D. 1, consuetudo. He also adduced, to prove this, the privileges and liberties, the confirmations, and many other acts of the blessed Louis and of all the other kings his predecessors. To the second article, which concerns clerics disturbing the possessions of laymen, and the cause of new work (causa novitatis), the said bishop says that where a cleric puts an obstacle or violence in the way, the layman is the plaintiff and the cleric the defendant; and since by right and custom the plaintiff is bound to follow the forum of the defendant, it is not unreasonable, especially in churches which have this by custom, if the Church has cognizance of such matters. Otherwise it would follow that secular judges would have cognizance of clerics at their own pleasure, by saying that this or that is a case of new work. Especially since in such obstacles or violences interdicts have their place, which by right are personal, even though they seem to be conceived in a thing (D. de investituris, l. 1, §. last), which by right are personal, as has been proved above. And to prove these things the aforesaid bishop cites Ext. de foro competenti, c. si clericus; 24, q. 3, Item quia; and the other rights mentioned above speaking of custom. As to the third article, which concerns personal actions between two laymen, or between a cleric as plaintiff and a layman as defendant, the same bishop says that by right and by custom well known, the cognizance of such personal actions belongs to the Church, as has been proved above; wherefore he said that no injury is done to anyone in this, especially by reason of the sin that is committed in withholding what a man is bound to pay or restore. And to prove this he brought forward the rights cited above, and Ext. de foro competenti, since it is a general rule.

units.la: Ad quartum, qui loquitur de laicis iniuriam inferentibus in rebus hereditariis clericorum, dicit quod tam de iure communi, quam consuetudine, clericus potest quoscunque iniuriam sibi inferentes in hereditate sua coram iudice ecclesiastico conuenire, quia in hoc committitur sacrilegium, cuius ad ecclesiam duntaxat debet cognitio pertinere. Et ad hoc probandum induxit 24. q. 3. si quis de potentibus, & alia iura, quae superius tam de consuetudine, quam de iure fuerunt allegata.
units.tr: As to the fourth point, which concerns laymen who wrong clerics in respect of their inherited property: he says that, both by common law and by custom, a cleric may bring before an ecclesiastical judge whoever wrongs him in his inheritance, because sacrilege is committed in this, and cognizance of it ought to belong to the Church alone. To prove this he cited 24. q. 3. si quis de potentibus, and the other laws cited above, both on custom and on law.

units.la: Ad quintum, qui loquitur de contractibus initis coram iudice seculari, dicit quod cum talium contractuum petitiones sint personales de iure, maxime vbi est transgressio iuramenti, vel fides mentita, de quibus ecclesia solum habet cognoscere, nulla fit iniuria. Et licet ibi non esset iuramenti vel fidei transgressio, adhuc ratione personalitatis potest ad ecclesiam cognitio pertinere, & ad hanc responsionem probandam allegauit iura superius in articulis praecedentibus allegata.
