units.la: Et licet in aliquibus locis pro tollenda eorum malitia in talibus proclamationibus seu inhibitionibus verba, quæ sequuntur, apponant: videlicet quod laicus non trahat alium laicum coram ecclesia super casibus pertinentibus ad iudices seculares seu temporales, hoc est propter iura ecclesiæ vlurpanda: quia multa pertinent ad forum laicorum, quæ nihilominus pertinent ad ecclesiasticum. Et sicius & consuetudo tollerentur, per quæ in electione laici est, quod possit alios laicos in foro ecclesiæ conuenire. Item quia tales proclamationes seu inhibitiones factæ licet etiam essent benegenerales, dant occasionem omnimode iurisdictionem ecclesiasticam perturbandi, vnde reges Franciæ quondam semper prohibuerunt tales proclamationes seu inhibitiones fieri & factas pe‐nitus facicbant reuocari, & ad nihilum reduci.
units.tr: Although in some places, to curb their malice, such proclamations or prohibitions add the following words, namely that a layman may not summon another layman before the Church in cases belonging to secular or temporal judges, this is a usurpation of the Church's rights, because many matters belong to the lay courts which nevertheless belong to the ecclesiastical. In this way a statute and custom would be overturned by which it lies in a layman's choice to summon other laymen in the Church's court. Likewise, such proclamations or prohibitions, even if they were quite general, give occasion for disturbing ecclesiastical jurisdiction in every way. For this reason the former kings of France always forbade such proclamations or prohibitions to be issued, and they completely caused those that had been issued to be revoked and reduced to nothing.

units.la: Posthæc die veneris sequenti apud Vicenas venerunt prælati coram Domino Rege ad audi‐ endum responsionem suam, vbi Dominus Petrus de Cugneriis prædictus proposuit pro Domino Rege sic dicendo, Pax vobis, ego sum, nolite timere, & prosecutus est, qualiter prælati non essent turbati s de aliquibus, quæ essent dicta: quia intentio Domini Regis erat seruare iura ecclesiæ & prælato‐rum, quæ habebant tam de iure quam consuetudine bona & rationabili: & interseruit inter primam conclusionem & vltimam, & probare voluit quod causarum ciuilium non poterat ad ec‐ clesiam cognitio pertinere: quia talia erant temporalia, quæ debent pertinere ad temporales, & spi‐ ritualia ad spirituales. Et vltra rationes, quas alias proposuit, allegauit 86. d. cum ad verum allegauit et. iam, quod propter hoc clericis radebantur capita in signum, vt temporalia abiicerent. Et allegauit ad hoc 12. q. 2. duo sunt genera.
units.tr: Afterwards, on the following Friday, the prelates came to the Lord King at Vincennes to hear his reply. There the aforesaid Lord Pierre de Cugnières spoke on behalf of the Lord King, saying, Peace be unto you, it is I; be not afraid, and he went on to say that the prelates should not be disturbed by any of the things that had been said, because the intention of the Lord King was to preserve the rights of the Church and of the prelates, which they held by law and by good and reasonable custom. He interposed between the first conclusion and the last, and he wished to prove that cognizance of civil cases could not belong to the Church, because such matters were temporal, and ought to belong to temporal authorities, while spiritual matters belong to spiritual ones. Besides the other arguments he had put forward, he cited Dist. 86, Cum ad verum, and said that for this reason the heads of clerics were shaved as a sign that they should cast off temporal things. And to this he cited C. 12, q. 2, Duo sunt genera.

units.la: Item dicebat, quod de iure habebant prælati cognitionem in certis casibus in iure expressis. Vnde isti casus faciebant regulam contra eos. Ad hoc allegauit de regulis iuris c. i. ff. de lege. l. L. Titiæ victoris.
units.tr: Again he said that the prelates had by law a cognizance in certain cases expressed in law, and that these cases therefore made a rule against them. For this he cited De regulis iuris, c. 1; Digest., De legibus, l. Titiae Victoris.

units.la: Item dicebat, quod ratione peccati non poterat ad eos pertinere, quia decret. Novit, loquebatur de facto regis Franciæ, qui superiorem non habet, sed in aliis dicebat secus. Tum istis allegatis dixit & conclusit, quod Dominus Rex paratus erat audire informationem eorum, qui vellent eum super aliquibus consuetudinibus informare, & illas consuetudines, de quibus esset informatus, quæ essent bonæ & rationales, facere et obseruari. Qua responsione audita, cum non videretur sufficere prælatis, statim dictus Episcopus Eduensis respondit pro prælatis in modum, qui sequitur: Primo commendans bonam responsionem generalem, dixit sic: Laudabitur princeps populi in prudentia sermonis sui, Eccles. 9. c. Et circa hoc commendauit quantum ad bonam & generalem responsionem Domini Regis propositum & sermonem prolatum. Quantum vero ad illa, quæ Dominus Petrus dixit, quæ paricbant obscuritatem, & poterant dare materiam aliis Dominis temporalibus impedien‐ di iura & consuetudines ecclesiæ, & quia non erat clara responsio, vt videbatur prælatis: Dixit sic dictus Dominus Episcopus, Dixit mater ad filium: fili quid fecisti nobis sic? Et prosecutus est admiratiue loquendo & curialiter conquerendo de responsione facta, & postea respondit ad ea quæ dixerat Do‐ minus Petrus de Cugneriis. Primo ad c. cum ad verum, dixit quod superius est responsum de distin‐ ctione ista temporalium, quia possunt esse in eodem subiecto, vt superius probatum est. Nec obstat, quod dicebat idem Dominus Petrus, quod non possunt esse in eodem subiecto, quia ea quæ sunt diuersa & sunt sub eodem genere, vt homo & asinus, non possunt esse in eodem subiecto: sed si essent sub diuersis generibus, vt albedo dulcedo in lacte, bene possunt esse in eodem. Respondebatur, quod hoc dictum non erat verum, quia iustitia & temperantia sunt duæ diuersæ virtutes & sub eo‐ dem genere sunt, & tamen sunt in eodem subiecto. Præterea istæ species diuisæ, homo & asinus, non se compatiuntur in aliquo, sed aliæ de quibus agitur sic.
units.tr: Again he said that by reason of sin the matter could not pertain to them, because the decretal Novit spoke of the case of the King of France, who has no superior; but in other respects he said otherwise. With these citations laid out, he said and concluded that the Lord King was ready to hear the information of those who wished to inform him about any customs, and that he would make and observe those customs of which he was informed which were good and reasonable. When this reply had been heard, and since it did not seem sufficient to the prelates, the said Bishop of Autun at once answered on behalf of the prelates in the following manner. First, commending the good and general reply, he said: The prince of the people will be praised for the wisdom of his speech, Eccles. 9. And on this point he commended, as far as the good and general reply of the Lord King went, the proposal and the speech delivered. But as for those things which Lord Pierre had said, which produced obscurity and could give matter to other temporal lords for impeding the rights and customs of the Church, and because the reply did not seem clear to the prelates, the said Lord Bishop spoke thus: The mother said to the son: son, why have you done this to us? And he went on speaking in wonder and, in courtly fashion, complaining about the reply given, and afterwards he answered what Lord Pierre de Cugnières had said. First, as to c. Cum ad verum, he said that what was answered above concerning this distinction of temporal things holds, because they can be in the same subject, as was proved above. Nor does it stand in the way that the same Lord Pierre said that they cannot be in the same subject, because things that are different but fall under the same genus, such as man and ass, cannot be in the same subject; but if they were under different genera, such as whiteness and sweetness in milk, they can well be in the same. It was answered that this statement was not true, because justice and temperance are two different virtues and fall under the same genus, and yet they are in the same subject. Moreover, those divided species, man and ass, are not compatible with each other in any respect, but the other things under discussion are so.

units.la: Item ad illud, quod dicebatur de rasura capitis, quod ibi sunt corona & rasura: corona designat excellentiam & Dominium, & rasura significat quod non debent thesaurizare in temporali‐ bus, ibi cor applicando: sed temporalia debent sibi subiici, non ipsi temporalibus, vt in dicto c. duo sunt genera, innuitur & probatur.
units.tr: Again, as to what was said about the shaving of the head, that there are both the crown and the shaving there: the crown signifies excellence and dominion, and the shaving signifies that they ought not to store up treasure in temporal things, applying the heart there; but temporal things ought to be subject to them, not they to temporal things, as is hinted at and proved in the said c. Duo sunt genera.

units.la: Item ad illud, quod dicebatur de regula: respondebat dictus episcopus, quod regula est pro ecclesia, vt supra per iura probatum est.
units.tr: Again, as to what was said about the rule, the said bishop replied that the rule is for the Church, as was proved above by the laws.

units.la: Item consuetudo facit regulam pro ecclesia.
units.tr: Again, custom makes a rule for the Church.

units.la: Item iura semper excipiunt in quocunq; delicto consuetudinem; quare non obstat dictum suum.
units.tr: Again, the laws always except custom in whatever offence; therefore his statement does not stand in the way.

units.la: Item ad illud, quod dicebat de decretali nouit, respondebat dictus Episcopus, quod licet in di‐ cta decretali nouit, casus fuerit in persona regis: tamen ibi expresse dicitur in textu idem de quolibet Christiano. Et lex, licet loquitur ibi papa, idem tamen est in aliis episcopis in diœcesibus suis, 63. distinct. Valentinianus. Quare conclusit dictus episcopus, quod placeret Domino Regi magis claram & magis consolatiuam dare responsionem prælatis, ne ab ipsius præsentia recederent cô‐ tristati, & ne daretur laicis materia iura & consuetudines ecclesiæ impugnare: quia de ipsius Domini Regis bona conscientia nullatenus dubitabant. Et tunc fuit hoc responsum ex parte Domini regis, quod non erat intentionis suæ consuetudines ecclesiæ, de quibus sibi constaret, impugnare.
units.tr: Again, as to what he said about the decretal Novit, the said bishop replied that although in the said decretal Novit the case arose in the person of the king, yet it is expressly said there in the text that the same holds for every Christian. And although the law there speaks of the pope, it is the same for other bishops in their dioceses, Dist. 63, Valentinianus. Therefore the said bishop concluded that it would please the Lord King to give the prelates a clearer and more comforting reply, so that they should not depart from his presence downcast, and so that no matter should be given to laymen to attack the rights and customs of the Church, since they did not in any way doubt the good conscience of the Lord King himself. Then a reply was given on the King's behalf that it was not his intention to attack those customs of the Church of which he was certain.

units.la: Postmodum die Dominica sequenti iterato venerunt prælati ad Dominum Regem apud Vi‐ cenas: & proposuit Dominus Senonensis vltimam suppositionem factam per prælatos: & vltimam responsionem factam pro parte Domini Regis. Quod cum Dominus Bituricensis significasset prælatis, Dominum Regem dixisse, quod non timerent prælati, quia nihil suo tempore perderent, & q defenderet eos in suis iuribus & consuetudinibus: quia nolebat tempore suo exemplum dare alius ecclesiam impugnandi. Quæ verba asseruit ibidem se dixisse: de quibus verbis idem Dominus Seno‐ nensis nomine prælatorum regratiatus est Domino Regi. Secundo dixit idem Dominus Senonensis, quod quædam præconizationes factæ erant in præiudicium iurisdictionis ecclesiasticæ, quas suppli‐ cabant reuocari. Tunc Dominus Rex respondit ore proprio, quod non erant factæ de suo mandato, nec aliquid sciebat, nec eas ratas habebat. Tertio dixit, quod de aliquibus abusibus, de quibus temporales erant conquesti, taliter ordinauerant prælati, quod Dominus Rex & cæte‐ri, merito deberent contentari. Quarto supplicauit sibi, quod vellet eos consolari de benigna sua responsione clariori. Tunc respondit dictus Dominus Petrus pro Domino Rege, quod placebat regi, si prælati emendarent ea, quæ essent emendanda & corrigenda: & quod Dominus Rex expectaret vsque ad festum Natiuitatis Domini proximum venturum, infra quem terminum nihil innouaret. Et si infra dictum terminum prælati non emendassent emendanda, vel correxissent corrigenda: Dominus Rex apponeret tale remedium, quod esset gratum Deo & populo. Et sic prælati receperunt licentiam à Domino Rege & recesserunt.
units.tr: Afterwards, on the following Sunday, the prelates came again to the Lord King at Vincennes, and the Lord Bishop of Sens set out the last proposal made by the prelates and the last reply made on behalf of the Lord King. When the Lord Bishop of Bourges had reported to the prelates that the Lord King had said that the prelates should not fear, because they would lose nothing in his time, and that he would defend them in their rights and customs, since in his time he was unwilling to give an example of attacking the Church, the same Lord Bishop of Sens, on behalf of the prelates, thanked the Lord King for these words, which he asserted he had himself spoken there. Secondly, the same Lord Bishop of Sens said that certain proclamations had been issued to the prejudice of ecclesiastical jurisdiction, and they asked that these be revoked. Then the Lord King replied in his own words that they had not been issued by his command, and that he knew nothing of them, nor did he approve them. Thirdly, he said that the prelates had arranged matters concerning some of the abuses about which the laity had complained in such a way that the Lord King and the others ought rightly to be satisfied. Fourthly, he begged that the King would please console them with a clearer and kinder reply. Then the said Lord Pierre answered on behalf of the King that it pleased the King if the prelates would amend those things which were to be amended and corrected; and that the Lord King would wait until the coming feast of the Nativity of the Lord, within which term he would make no innovation. And if within the said term the prelates had not amended what needed amending or corrected what needed correcting, the Lord King would apply such a remedy as would be pleasing to God and to the people. And so the prelates received leave from the Lord King and withdrew.

units.la: [Sic re aliquandiu vtroque citroque agitata, cum Episcopi & Prælati se suo solito more reformarent, ita nempe, vt specie ac verbis iniuriarum quandam alleuiationem simularent, re autem ipsa eas potius angerent & aggrauarent quam diminuerent: demum Rex seneram quandam legem fert, qua talem Prælatorum audaciam & tyrannidem cohibet, seque ac suos in libertatem asserit.]
units.tr: Thus the matter was tossed back and forth for some time. While the bishops and prelates went through their usual reform, in such a way that they pretended by their words and appearance to lighten the abuses, but in fact rather stirred them up and made them worse than they diminished them, at last the King passed a rather severe law, by which he restrained the prelates' such audacity and tyranny, and asserted both himself and his people in their liberty.

units.la: Explicit quidem libellus de iuris dictione ecclesiastica, factus per Dominum Petrum Bertrandi, & in consilio convenientibus prælatis regni Francia verbotenus in Gallico per ipsum deputatum ex parte ipsorum prælatorum recitatus.
units.tr: The little book on ecclesiastical jurisdiction ends, made by Master Pierre Bertrand, and recited word for word in French, by the same man deputed on behalf of the prelates, to the prelates of the kingdom of France gathered in council.

units.la: MARSILII DE PADVA, PHILOSOPHI ET CONSILIARI CAESAREI, TRACTATVS DE IVRISDICTIONE IMPERATORIS IN CAVSIS MATRIMONIALIBVS, EDITVS NOMINE ET AVCTORITATE IMP. LV- DOVICI IV. BAVARIÆ DVCIS, &c. cum eiusdem Decretis super sententia separationis & dispensationis matrimo- niorum &c. FORMA DIVORTII MATRIMONIALIS INTER ILLVSTRES, VOCATOS CONIVGES, Iohannem videlicet filium Regis Bohemiæ, & Margaretam Ducissam Karinthiæ, celebrati per Dominum LV- DOVICVM QVARTVM Dei gratia Rom. Imp.
units.tr: MARSILIUS OF PADUA, PHILOSOPHER AND IMPERIAL COUNSELLOR, TREATISE ON THE JURISDICTION OF THE EMPEROR IN MATRIMONIAL CAUSES, PUBLISHED IN THE NAME AND WITH THE AUTHORITY OF LUDWIG IV, DUKE OF BAVARIA, etc., together with his decrees concerning the sentence of separation and the dispensation of marriages, etc. FORM OF MATRIMONIAL DIVORCE BETWEEN THE ILLUSTRIOUS, SO-CALLED SPOUSES, namely John, son of the King of Bohemia, and Margaret, Duchess of Carinthia, pronounced by Lord LUDWIG IV, by the grace of God Roman Emperor.

units.la: OS LVDOVICVS QVARTVS, Dei gratia Romanorum Imperator, Augustus, vniuersis Christi fidelibus, quorum interest, vel interesse poterit in futurum, manifestum esse volumus & facimus per præsentes: Quod in iudicio coram nobis per se seu per certos nuncios suos seu procuratores exposuit Illustris Margareta Ducissa Karinthiæ & Tyrolis comitissa: quod vir nobilis Iohannes Regis Bohemiæ filius iamdudum sibi matrimonio copulatus, & postmodum in etate debita constitutus, ac per tanta temporum spacia secum habitans, quanta sufficiunt ac sufficere debent, secundum statuta tam diuina quam humana legis, ad debitum carnalis copulæ per virum sive maritum suæ uxori reddendum, eadem Margaretha in etate sufficienti similiter constituta, & seipsam vt conueniens fuerat prabente & exhibente ad prefatam copulam carnalem explendam, non potuit dictus Iohannes neque valuit, sicuti neque valet, aut potest, nec vnquam posse creditur in futurum, eandem carnaliter cognoscere sibi coniugem Margaretam; quemadmodum multis & quasi omnibus possibilibus modis hoc tentans, eundem Iohannem impotentem & omnino inhabilem ad opus prefatum se dicit expertam: ac aduersus euneundem Iohannem, sibiq; prafatum defectum inexistere, coram nobis in iudicio se reddetan per experimenta sufficientia & testimonia qualiter ad hoc necessaria probaturam. Quare super hoc habito maturo & deliberato consilio suorum procerum & consiliariorum omnium, nostram clementiam atque iustitiam una cum prafatis implorauit & requisiuit instanter, ut eidem super hoc prouidere de conuenienti remedio dignaremur: & taliter etiam, quod per Ius siue sententiam nostram licite posset a supradicto Iohanne, iam vocato marito siue coniuge suo, de matrimonio separari, propter casum siue impedimentum predictum, & ab eodem Iohanne totaliter sic absolui, ut eidem de catero ad nullum matrimonii debitum teneretur, sed posset de se ipsa & suis omnibus ordinare, secundum quod sibi expedire videretur. Nos vero, cuius debitum est omnibus ac singulis reddere iustum, ex officio & auctoritate qua fungimur, prafatam Margaretham cum prafatis suis omnibus iustitiam instantissime requirentibus & supplicantibus, nobis dignum duximus exaudire; & nihilominus absque offensa iuris prafati Iohannis iam vocati coniugis sui, si ius aliquod in contrarium habuisset, ad expeditionem seu terminationem litis premissa inter vocatos coniuges prafatos processimus, in hac forma videlicet: quod vocatos coniuges prafatos citari fecimus atque vocauimus in iudicio coram nobis, assignantes eisdem secundum formam iuris debitum atque tutum locum, & temporis spacium, infra quod possent & deberent in iudicio coram comparere, ad agendum & defensandum, & cetera faciendum, qua necessaria forent pro inquirenda veritate super lite prafata. Verum & Margaretha iam dicta per se, seu per suos certos nuncios siue procuratores, sufficienter comparuit in iudicio coram nobis per omnes terminos sibi assignatos, & cum omnibus probationibus & testimoniis sufficientibus, ad conuincendum sape dictum Iohannem impotentem esse atque priuatum naturali potentia ipsam carnaliter cognoscendi, aut quamuis aliam mulierem, seipsam quoque virginem usque in tempus & diem data praesentis rescripti, per sufficientia testimonia demonstrauit. Supradictus vero Iohannes in prafatum iudicium coram nobis, impositi sibi defectus per prafatam Margaretham verisimiliter conscius, nec per se, nec per aliquem legitimum nuncium siue procuratorem comparuit tempore debito siue statuto, nec quicquam in contrarium impositi sibi defectus per Margaretham prafatam per se vel per alium allegauit: sed contumax ex natura se conuictum reddidit, atque confessum de his omnibus que sibi per predictam Margaretam fuerant tam imposita quam probata, sufficientia quidem ad matrimonii diuortium inter ipsam & prafatum Iohannem per sententiam consummandum. Nec poterit, nec vnquam cum veritate poterit sapedictus Iohannes, aut quiuis alter pro ipso, iudicem vel locum comparendi per nos sibi assignatum allegare suspectum. Nam hactenus retroactis temporibus tam Iohanni regi Bohemia patri suo, quam etiam Karolo de Bohemia fratri suo, pluries & locis pluribus nostra coactiue potestati subiectis, fidum ac tutum placitandi nobiscum assignauimus locum: in quo personaliter affuerunt, & cum omni tranquillitate manserunt, ac inde absque molestia qualibet secundum ipsorum beneplacitum recesserunt. Quod & antedicto Iohanni benigne offerri fecimus, & acceptare contemplit, ut supra iam diximus. Per auctoritatem ergo nobis rite debitam & concessam, & legi diuinae conformiter sicuti certum est, & asserunt sacrae scripturae siue leges diuinae, atque ciuiles sententia sufficientes, ac comprobati Doctores, ad diuortium siue separationem matrimonii faciendam inter vocatos coniuges Iohannem & Margaretam prafatos procedere volentes atque debentes, infrascriptam sententiam tulimus in hac verba: Nos Ludouicus quartus Dei gratia Romanorum Imperator, Augustus, pro tribunali iudice sedentes, in causa siue lite diuortii seu separationis matrimonii, qua vertebatur inter Illustres personas Iohannem Regis Bohemiae filium, requisitum parte ex vna, & Margaretham Ducissam Karinthia & Tyrolis Comitissam, ex altera parte, tanquam actricem, ac requirentem a dicta Iohanne iam vocato coniuge suo de matrimonio separari: Visis & intellectis tam per nos quam prafatos Doctores iuribus, rationibus, probationibus & testimoniis Margaretha prafata, nec non contumacia iam dicti Iohannis, dicimus, diffinimus & determinamus, prafatam Margaretham separari debere seu posse de matrimonio a supradicto Iohanne, e conuerso, cum eisdem vel ipsorum alteri id videbitur expedire. Ipsam quoque Margaretham hoc requirentem instanter, ut supra, separamus, absoluimus, & separatam esse iudicamus in matrimonio a iam dicto Iohanne per hanc nostram sententiam diffinitiuam. Similiq; modo supradictum Iohannem a prafata Margaretha in matrimonio per auctoritatem & per nostram sententiam diffinitiuam separantes: ita videlicet, quod de catero prafatum Iohannes supradicta Margaretam in nullo matrimonii debito teneatur, neque similiter prafata Margareta supradicto Iohanni: sed liberum sit vtrique de corpore proprio siue persona, & omnibus bonis propriis, iuribus ac rebus, tam mobilibus quam immobilibus facere vel disponere, & quodlibet ordinare pro sua propria libito voluntatis.
units.tr: LUDWIG IV, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans, Augustus, wish it to be known to all the faithful of Christ whom it concerns, or may concern in future, and we make it known by these presents: that in a court before us, the Illustrious Margaret, Duchess of Carinthia and Countess of Tyrol, has set forth, either in person or through her certain messengers or proctors, that the noble man John, son of the King of Bohemia, joined to her long ago in marriage and since grown to due age, and living with her over such spans of time as suffice and ought to suffice under the statutes of both divine and human law for the husband to render his wife the due of carnal union, while Margaret herself is likewise of sufficient age and has offered and presented herself, as was fitting, for the carnal union to be completed, the said John has not been able, nor is he able, nor is he believed ever to be able in future, to know his wife Margaret carnally. She says she has found this out by trying it in almost every possible way, and that the same John is impotent and wholly incapable of the said act. She says also that this defect is in him, and she offers to prove it before us in court by sufficient experiments and testimonies, as this requires. Therefore, after mature and deliberate counsel of all his nobles and counsellors, she has urgently implored and requested our clemency and justice, together with the aforesaid, that we would deign to provide her with a suitable remedy in this matter, and in such a way that, by law or by our sentence, she might lawfully be separated from the aforesaid John, now called her husband or spouse, on account of the said case or impediment, and be wholly absolved from him, so that she would no longer be bound to him by any marital debt, but might dispose of herself and all her possessions as seemed fitting to her. Now we, to whom it is a duty to render to each and all what is just, acting from the office and authority we hold, have thought it worthy to hear the aforesaid Margaret, who with all her supporters most insistently demands and begs for justice; and nonetheless, without prejudice to the right of the aforesaid John, now called her spouse, should he have had any right to the contrary, we have proceeded to the despatch and settlement of the aforesaid suit between the named spouses, in this form: that we caused the aforesaid spouses to be cited and summoned to court before us, assigning to them, according to the form of law, a due and safe place and a span of time within which they could and ought to appear in court, to act, defend, and do the other things that might be necessary for inquiring into the truth of the said suit. Indeed the said Margaret, in person or through her certain messengers or proctors, appeared sufficiently in court before us within all the terms assigned to her, and with all sufficient proofs and testimonies she demonstrated, through sufficient witnesses, both that the said John is often impotent and deprived of the natural power of knowing her carnally or any other woman, and that she herself remains a virgin up to the time and day of the present rescript. But the aforesaid John, being probably aware of the defects imposed upon him by the said Margaret, did not appear at the said court before us, either in person or through any lawful messenger or proctor, at the due or appointed time; nor did he allege anything to the contrary of the defect imposed on him by the said Margaret, either in person or through another. Rather, in his contumacy, he rendered himself convicted by his own nature, and confessed to all these things which were both imposed and proved against him by the aforesaid Margaret, sufficient indeed for the divorce of marriage between her and the said John to be completed by sentence. Nor can, nor ever with truth will the said John, or anyone else on his behalf, allege as suspect the judge or the place of appearance assigned to him by us. For hitherto, in past times, both to John, King of Bohemia, his father, and also to Charles of Bohemia, his brother, in many places subject to our coercive power, we have repeatedly assigned a safe and secure place for pleading with us, where they were present in person and remained in complete tranquillity, and from there they withdrew without any molestation, as they pleased. This we also caused to be kindly offered to the aforesaid John, who has scorned to accept it, as we have already said above. Therefore, by the authority duly and lawfully conferred upon us, and in conformity with divine law, as it is certain and as the sacred Scriptures or divine laws, and sufficient civil sentences and approved Doctors assert, wishing and being bound to proceed to the divorce or separation of marriage between the named spouses John and Margaret, we have pronounced the following sentence in these words: We, Ludwig IV, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans, Augustus, sitting as judge on the tribunal, in the cause or suit of divorce or separation of marriage, which was between the Illustrious persons John, son of the King of Bohemia, called on the one part, and Margaret, Duchess of Carinthia and Countess of Tyrol, on the other part, as plaintiff and demanding to be separated from the said John, now called her spouse, from the marriage: having seen and understood, both by us and by the aforesaid Doctors, the laws, reasons, proofs and testimonies offered by the aforesaid Margaret, as well as the contumacy of the said John, we say, decide and determine that the aforesaid Margaret ought to be, or may be, separated from the marriage with the aforesaid John, and conversely, as it shall seem fitting to them or to either of them. We also, urgently requiring this of the same Margaret, as above, separate, absolve, and judge her separated in marriage from the said John by this our definitive sentence. Likewise, separating the aforesaid John from the aforesaid Margaret in marriage by authority and by our definitive sentence, so that from now on the aforesaid John is bound to the aforesaid Margaret in no marital debt, nor likewise is the aforesaid Margaret bound to the aforesaid John; but it shall be free for each of them to dispose and arrange their own body or person, and all their own goods, rights and things, both movable and immovable, and to order whatever they like at their own pleasure.

units.la: FORMA DISPENSATIONIS SVPER AFFINITATE CONSANGVINITATIS INTER ILLVSTRES, LVDOVICVM MAR- CHIONEM Brandenburg. & Margaretam Ducissam Karinthiae: nec non legitimationis liberorum eorundem procreandorum, factae per Dn. LVDOVICVM QVARTVM, Dei gra- tia Rom. Imp.
units.tr: THE FORM OF DISPENSATION CONCERNING AFFINITY AND CONSANGUINITY BETWEEN THE ILLUSTRIOUS LUDWIG, MARGRAVE OF BRANDENBURG, AND MARGARET, DUCHESS OF CARINTHIA; AND ALSO CONCERNING THE LEGITIMATION OF THE CHILDREN TO BE BEGOTTEN BY THEM, MADE BY LORD LUDWIG IV, BY THE GRACE OF GOD ROMAN EMPEROR.

units.la: OS LVDOVICVS QVARTVS, Dei gratia Romanorum Imperator, Augustus, universis Christi fidelibus, quorum interest aut poterit interesse, notum esse volumus & facimus per seriem infra scriptam: Quod in nostra praesentia personaliter constituti Illustres Ludovicus Marchio Brandenburgensis, & Margarita Ducissa Karinthiae ac Tirolis Comitissa, post habitum ipsorum maturam ac deliberatum consilium animum atque actualem voluntatem habentes se invicem in matrimonio legitime copulandi: dubitante tamen praefato Ludovico & Margareta, ne gradu aliquo affinitatis sanguinis tale coniugium sive matrimonium humanarum legum aut Romanorum principum statuto, decreto, vel ordinatione alia, quomodolibet appellata, impedimentum aliquod paateretur: supplicarunt ac petierunt instanter, tale impedimentum consanguinitatis, si quod inter ipsos affuerit vel adesset, per dispensationem nostram relaxari, ac per nostram auctoritatem atque sententiam totaliter amoveri. Nos vero propter communem & evidentem Reipublica utilitatem manifeste visam sequi ad coniugii supradictum, praefatum impedimentum affinitatis sanguinis, si quod inter ipsos adesset, iudicamus esse tollendum, & simpliciter amovendum. Cum gradus affinitatis sanguinis, praesertim infra sorores & fratres, matrimonium non impediat divina seu Christiana legis statuto aliquo vel praecepto; quemadmodum certitudinaliter novimus tam per nos, quam per supradicta legis divinae idoneos ac probatos Doctores. Idque etiam asserente beato Augustino lib. 15. de civit. Dei, cap. 16. dum de talibus affinitatis sanguinis gradibus tractans inquit; Quod hoc videlicet matrimonium licitum fieri inter affines consanguineos, nec lex divina prohibuit, & nondum prohibuerat lex humana. Quibus siquidem verbis duas sententias expressit Augustinus: unam videlicet supradictam, Quod lege divina legitimum matrimonium fieri non est prohibitum inter personas sanguinis affinitate coniunctas. Secundam vero sententiam scire fecit, videlicet quod talis prohibitio matrimonii inter consanguineos fieri habeat auctoritate legislatoris humani, aut eius principantis, supremi principis Romanorum. Idem quoque concedere atque fateri convenit Romanum episcopum, Papam vocatum, cum suorum clericorum coetu, quos Cardinales appellant, veritate cogente. Nam prefatus Papa Romanus super impedimento affinitatis sanguinis per dispensationem tollendo a sanguinis affinitate coniunctis, inimicem matrimonium contrahentibus, ad suam auctoritatem asserit pertinere: as in talibus matrimoniis pluries dispensaverunt de facto praeteriti quidem Pontifices Romanorum. Quod si talis gradus affinitatis sanguinis matrimonium legitimum impediret legis divinae seu Christiana praeceptio, non posset aliquis hominum, quinimo neque angelus de coelo, dictum impedimentum per dispensationem aliquo modo amovere. Hoc Christo testante: Facilius est coelum & terram transfire, quam unum apicem a lege cadere. Rursusque idem Dominus dixit: Coelum & terra transibunt, verba autem mea permanebunt in aeternum. Ex quibus quidem manifeste apparet, ac fateri cogitur Romanus Episcopus, & per factum confirmatur ipsum, quod gradus affinitatis sanguinis non impediat matrimonium fieri legis divinae seu Christiana praecepto: & quod si gradus affinitatis sanguinis quanquam licitum matrimonium impediat fieri, hoc totum factum esset praecepto sive statuto legu humana: de cuius siquidem legis praeceptis sive statutis dispensare solummodo pertinet ad auctoritatem Imperatoris seu principis Romanorum. Nec obstat dicere, prefata matrimonia esse prohibita lege divina, eo quod mali moris sunt, & propterea etiam peccata mortalia fore prohibita, ac proinde obligantia contrahentes ad damnationem aeternam: & contrariam dispensationem in his ad ministrum solummodo ecclesiasticum, episcopum sive presbyterum pertinere. Hic enim sermo rhetoricus sive apparens Sophisticus est: falsum namque recipit: quoniam prefata matrimonia non sunt mali moris, praesertim in aliquo casu. Nam & ipsa tanquam in casu licita fieri concedit Romanus Episcopus. Nec etiam rursus mali moris sunt absolute loquendo: quoniam non sunt cum malitia connoluta confestim, veluti furtum & crimina reliqua: & propterea nec sunt lege divina prohibita, quemadmodum dixit beatus Augustinus. Non syllogizatur autem neque concluditur propterea, dispensationem de talibus ad Episcopum quenquam sive presbyterum pertinere: esto quod sint absolute prohibita lege divina, & sub poena damnationis aeternae. Quoniam de sic prohibitis nullus hominum, quinimo angelus de coelo dispensare posset, vel ordinare, sive concedere quod licite fierent, ut deductum est supra. Unde etiam iuxta praedicta de praeceptis sacra scriptura sive mandatis loquens Apostolus inquit: Et si angelus de coelo evangelizaret vobis aliud praeter id, id est, contra id, quod evangelizatum est a nobis, anathema sit. Nec propter aliud, nisi quod evangelizata erat per apostolum divina prohibita vel praecepta. Rursus quoniam prefata matrimonia non fuerunt mali moris, neque prohibita secundum veterem legem, quamvis aliquando peccata fiant sive fuerunt in antiqua lege, non quod sint absolute sive confestim cum malitia connoluta, neque mali moris, sed solummodo a lege prohibita fuerant: veluti carnes porcinas, & bestias non ruminantes comedere, quod ideo peccatum effectum est, quia prohibitum fuerat in lege Mosaica; non tamen propter malum aut mali moris ex se, quemadmodum furtum, homicidium, falsum testimonium, & huiusmodi reliqua, quae prohibita sunt legibus divinis & humanis, eo quod ex se mala sunt, & mali moris, confestim cum malitia connoluta. Ex his igitur omnibus iam praedictis manifeste apparet, cuilibet non corrupto ignorantia vel malitia, vel utraque, auctoritatem dispensandi atque tollendi a matrimonio impedimentum inter personas & a personis sanguinis affinitate coniunctis, ad Romanum principem pertinere. Propter quod Nos Ludovicus quartus Romanorum Imperator, Augustus prefatum affinitatis sanguinis impedimentum, si quod esset inter prefatos Ludovicum & Margaretam, quo minus possent aut prohiberentur per humana legis aut Romanorum principum statuta, sive decreta, vel alias ordinationes quomodolibet appellatas, in matrimonio copulari, tollimus, & per nostram auctoritatem in hac sententiam tenore praesentium totaliter annullamus. Concedentes eisdem ac cuilibet ipsorum, ut absque offensa cuiuslibet iuris humani, statuti vel ordinationis alterius quomodolibet nominata, licite se possint ac valeat in matrimonio copulare. Absoluentes etiam eosdem, ipsorumque legitimos filios, & filias, ac haeredes, nunc & in perpetuum a poena quaqumque reali, personali, & infamiae, & alia quavis quomodolibet nominata, si qua forent impositae contrahentibus matrimonium infra consanguinitatis gradus aliquos nominatos per quemquam Principem Romanum etiam, vel per leges, aut consuetudinem aliquam, collegium vel singularem personam, cuiuscumque auctoritatis vel dignitatis existantes. Quibus omnibus & singulis, & a quibus excipimus casum praedictum, de praefatis videlicet personis, Ludovicam & Margaretham iam dictos. Et in quantum huic nostro rescripto sive dispositioni, concessioni nostrae contradicunt totaliter aut in parte, per hoc ipsum praesens nostrum rescriptum derogamus & volumus derogari, eadem nihilominus semper in suo robore duraturo.
units.tr: We, Ludwig IV, by the grace of God Roman Emperor, Augustus, wish and make known through the following account to all the faithful of Christ whom it concerns or may concern: that the Illustrious Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg, and Margaret, Duchess of Carinthia and Countess of Tyrol, appeared personally in our presence. After mature and deliberate consideration, they have the intention and actual will to be lawfully joined together in marriage. Yet Ludwig and Margaret were in doubt lest some degree of affinity or blood relationship should place some impediment on such a union or marriage, under a statute, decree or other ordinance of human laws or of the Roman princes, however it may be named. They therefore earnestly begged and asked that any impediment of consanguinity that existed or might exist between them be relaxed by our dispensation and wholly removed by our authority and sentence. We, indeed, on account of the common and evident advantage of the Commonwealth, which is clearly seen to follow from the aforesaid marriage, judge that the aforesaid impediment of affinity or blood relationship, if any existed between them, is to be lifted and simply removed. For degrees of affinity by blood, especially among sisters and brothers, do not hinder marriage by any statute or precept of the divine or Christian law, as we know for certain both from ourselves and from the learned and approved teachers of the divine law mentioned above. This is also affirmed by the blessed Augustine, De Civitate Dei, book 15, chapter 16, where, treating of such degrees of blood affinity, he says: "That marriage between kindred by affinity is lawful, the divine law has not forbidden, and human law had not yet forbidden." By these words Augustine expressed two opinions. One is the one just mentioned, that marriage between persons joined by blood affinity is not forbidden as lawful under the divine law. The second opinion he made known, namely that such a prohibition of marriage between kindred must rest on the authority of a human lawgiver or of the one who rules him, the supreme prince of the Romans. It is also fitting that the Roman bishop, called the Pope, together with the company of his clerics whom they call Cardinals, should concede and confess this, compelled by the truth. For the said Roman Pope claims that it belongs to his authority to remove, by dispensation, the impediment of blood affinity for persons joined by blood affinity who contract marriage with one another; and the Roman Pontiffs of past times have in fact often dispensed in such marriages. But if the precept of the divine or Christian law forbade a lawful marriage on account of such a degree of blood affinity, no one among men, nor even an angel from heaven, could in any way remove that impediment by dispensation. Christ bears witness to this: "It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one jot of the law to fall." And again the same Lord said: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will remain forever." From these things it clearly appears, and the Roman Bishop is compelled to acknowledge, and it is confirmed by his practice, that degrees of blood affinity do not prevent marriage by a precept of the divine or Christian law. And if a degree of blood affinity does prevent a marriage that would otherwise be lawful, all of this would come about by a precept or statute of human law; and the power to dispense from the precepts or statutes of that law belongs solely to the authority of the Emperor or prince of the Romans. Nor is it an objection to say that the said marriages are forbidden by divine law because they are of evil custom, and therefore sins forbidden also under pain of eternal damnation, binding those who contract them to eternal condemnation; and that a contrary dispensation in these cases belongs only to the ecclesiastical minister, bishop or presbyter. For this is rhetorical talk, or a seeming sophistry: it takes a false premise, since the said marriages are not of evil custom, especially in some cases. For the Roman Bishop himself concedes that they may be lawfully made in certain cases. Nor are they again of evil custom absolutely speaking, since they are not at once bound up with wickedness, as theft and other crimes are; and therefore they are not forbidden by divine law, as the blessed Augustine said. Nor does it follow from this that the dispensation of such marriages belongs to any bishop or presbyter, even though they are absolutely forbidden by divine law under the penalty of eternal damnation. For no man, indeed not even an angel from heaven, could dispense with or ordain or grant that such things, forbidden in this way, might be done lawfully, as has been shown above. Hence also the Apostle, speaking of the precepts or commandments of Holy Scripture in accordance with what has been said, writes: "But even if an angel from heaven should preach to you anything other than what we have preached to you, let him be accursed" (Gal. 1:8). And this is for no other reason than that what the Apostle preached were divine prohibitions or precepts. Again, since the said marriages were neither of evil custom nor forbidden under the old law, although sometimes sins are committed, or were committed under the ancient law, not because they are absolutely or immediately bound up with wickedness, nor because they are of evil custom, but only because they were forbidden by law, as to eat pork and animals that do not chew the cud: this became a sin only because it had been forbidden in the Mosaic law. It was not however wrong or of evil custom in itself, as theft, homicide, false witness and the like are, which are forbidden by both divine and human laws because they are evil in themselves, of evil custom, and at once bound up with wickedness. From all these things already stated it clearly appears that for anyone not corrupted by ignorance or malice, or by both, the authority to dispense with and remove the impediment to marriage between persons and from persons joined by blood affinity belongs to the Roman prince. Wherefore we, Ludwig IV, Roman Emperor, Augustus, remove the aforesaid impediment of blood affinity, if any existed between the said Ludwig and Margaret, which would prevent them, or be forbidden them, from being joined in marriage by the statutes or decrees of human law or of the princes of the Romans, or other ordinances, however named; and by our authority, in this sentence, by the tenor of these present letters, we wholly annul it. We grant to them and to each of them that they may lawfully and validly join in marriage without offence to any human right, statute or ordinance of any other name whatever. We also absolve the same persons, and their legitimate sons and daughters and heirs, now and forever, from every penalty, real, personal, and of infamy, and every other penalty however named, if any had been imposed on those contracting marriage within any named degrees of kinship, by any Roman prince, or by any law or custom, corporate body or single person, of whatever authority or dignity they may be. We except from all these and each of them the aforesaid case, concerning the said persons Ludwig and Margaret. And insofar as anything in this our rescript, disposition or concession contradicts it, wholly or in part, we by this present rescript derogate from it and wish it to be derogated; yet these things shall always remain in their full force.

units.la: INCIPIT TRACTATUS CONSULTATIONIS PER MARSILIUM DE PADUA, super divortio matrimonii inter Illustres vocatos coniuges, Iohannem videlicet filium Regis Bohemiae, & Margaretham Ducissam Carinthiae, celebrato per Dominum Ludovicum quartum, Dei gratia Rom. Imp.
units.tr: BEGINNING OF THE TREATISE OF CONSULTATION BY MARSILIUS OF PADUA, concerning the divorce of marriage between the illustrious spouses called John, son of the King of Bohemia, and Margaret, Duchess of Carinthia, performed by Lord Ludwig IV, by the grace of God Roman Emperor.

units.la: A Dampliorem evidentiam tam dictorum, quam & dicendorum, ad redarguendum voces, & obstruendas fauces malignorum detractorum quorundam, nunc forte dicentium dicere volentium in futurum, nos in praesenti negotio sive iudicio processisse dolose tantum modo & non de iure: cum iudicium de matrimonii divortio faciendo spirituale sit, & proprie ad auctoritatem nostram minime pertineat, quemadmodum dicunt Episcopi quidam sive presbyteri suis seductoribus, minus vere: idque a paucis retro temporibus praedicaverunt, & per quasdam verborum fallacias hoc credere fecerunt plurimos simplices Christi fideles. Ad tollendum etiam scrupulum conscientiae ab huiusmodi fraude deceptorum, atque zizaniam de cordibus hominum per iam dictos veritatis praevaricatores, ac Romanorum principum persecutores infestos, & Imperialium iuium usurpatores manifestos: undique seminatas praefatorum Doctorum sententias sub breviloquio, quantum possunt, huic rescripto non inutiliter duximus inserendas.
units.tr: To make clearer both what has been said and what is still to be said, so as to refute the voices and stop the mouths of certain malicious detractors who now perhaps say, or will wish to say in future, that in the present affair or judgment we proceeded only by fraud and not by right, on the ground that the judgment of making a divorce of marriage is spiritual and does not properly belong to our authority (as some bishops or presbyters say to their followers, and less truly, and who have preached this in recent times and, through certain fallacies of words, have made many simple faithful of Christ believe it), and in order also to remove the scruple of conscience from those deceived by such fraud, and the tares sown everywhere in men's hearts by the aforesaid betrayers of the truth, hostile persecutors of the Roman princes and manifest usurpers of imperial rights, we have thought it not useless to insert in this rescript, in as brief a form as possible, the opinions of the aforesaid Doctors.

units.la: Dicunt ergo & scribunt seriosius in suis tractatibus iam dicti Doctores, quod Christi fideles regiuntur & viuunt sub duplici lege, divina videlicet & humana. Lex autem proprie sumpta praeceptiuum coactiuum est de faciendis aut omittendis humanis actibus, sub poena transgressoribus infligenda. Verum lex divina est coactiuum praeceptum a Deo factum immediate, absque humana deliberatione, propter finem in futuro seculo consequendum, & sub poena transgressoribus infligenda in eodem tantum modo, non praesenti. Sed lex humana voluntate seu deliberatione procedens, propter finem immediate in hoc seculo consequendum, & sub poena in eodem solum modo transgressoribus infligenda. Iuxta quae oportet attendere, quod secundum utramque iam dictarum legum sunt quaedam affirmatiue praecepta, de faciendis videlicet: quaedam vero negatiue, de omittendis scilicet non faciendis, vocata prohibita. Sunt & quaedam permissa fieri & non fieri, quae sub praecepto affirmatiue vel negatiue non cadunt, & in lege divina quaedam vocata consilia. Et iuxta dicta permissa generaliora praeceptis: quoniam omne praeceptum est permissum fieri, sed econtra non semper. Similiter quoque prohibitum fieri, permissum est non fieri: quamuis non in omnibus econtra. Simile quoque intelligendum secundum legem humanam in affirmatiuis praeceptis, permissis & prohibitis: quamuis differant sub poenis, quoniam secundum legem divinam praecepta & prohibita obligant transgressores ad poenam aeternam: secundum humanam vero ad poenam temporalem.
units.tr: The aforesaid Doctors, then, say and write more earnestly in their treatises that the faithful of Christ are governed and live under a twofold law, namely divine and human. Law, properly understood, is a precept, compelling the doing or omitting of human acts, with a penalty to be inflicted on transgressors. The divine law, however, is a compelling precept made by God immediately, without human deliberation, for the sake of an end to be attained in the future age, with a penalty to be inflicted on transgressors in that age only, and not in the present one. Human law, on the other hand, proceeds from will or deliberation, for the sake of an end to be attained immediately in this age, with a penalty to be inflicted on transgressors in this age only. In light of this we must observe that, under each of the two laws just mentioned, there are some affirmative precepts, that is, commands to do something, and some negative precepts, that is, commands to omit or not do something, called prohibitions. There are also some things permitted to be done or not done, which do not fall under an affirmative or negative precept, and in the divine law some things called counsels. And permissions are more general than precepts, since every precept is a permission to do, but not conversely. Likewise, what is prohibited is permitted not to be done, although not conversely in every case. The same is to be understood under human law concerning affirmative precepts, permissions and prohibitions, although they differ in their penalties: under divine law precepts and prohibitions bind transgressors to eternal punishment, but under human law to temporal punishment.

units.la: Est rursum aduertendum, quod secundum utramque iam dictarum legum, nomina praecepti & prohibiti duas intentiones sive significationes habere possunt, vnam videlicet, quod nomine praecepti sive prohibiti intelligatur actus praecipiendi sive praeceptio a praecipiente procedens, quasi actiue sumta. Reliquo vero modo, ut intelligatur per praedicta nomina non actus praecipiendi eius qui praecipit vel imperat, sed potius actus aut opus cui aliquid praecipitur seu imperatur, quasi passiue: quomodo dicitur ex usu, Seruum fecisse praeceptum Domini, cum id egit aut agere omisit, quod sibi per dominum suum praecipiebatur fieri vel omitti, verbi gratia, ut equum parare, vinum propinare, ac reliqua seruitia talia. Et isto modo significat sive sonat praeceptum sive prohibitum idem quod impetratum, non imperium sive actum praecipiendi sumtum actiue, quoniam hunc non fecit seruus, in quantum seruus, sed solum modo Dominus.
units.tr: It must further be noted that under each of the two laws just mentioned, the terms "precept" and "prohibition" can have two senses or meanings. One is that by the term "precept" or "prohibition" is understood the act of commanding, or the command proceeding from the one who commands, taken as active. The other is that by these terms is understood not the act of commanding of the one who orders or enjoins, but rather the act or work to which something is commanded or enjoined, taken as passive. In this way it is said in common usage that a servant has carried out his master's precept when he did or failed to do what his master had ordered to be done or omitted, for example to saddle a horse, to serve wine, and other such services. And in this way "precept" or "prohibition" signifies or means the same as what is commanded, not the command or act of commanding taken actively, since the servant did not give this command as a servant, but only the master did.

units.la: Amplius est etiam attendendum, quod praecepta tam affirmatiua quam negatiua, atque permissa vocata consilia, secundum legem divinam spiritualia sunt essentialiter atq; dicuntur. Primum quidem quoniam a Spiritu sancto immediate tradita & instituta sunt quemadmodum dicit B. Ambrosius super Apostolum post ad Cor. ca. 9. Spiritualia, inquit, sunt lex euangelica & verbum Dei. Et sunt etiam fortasse spiritualia, gratiae sive dona Spiritus sancti, quae fiunt & peruenient in animabus Christi fidelium a verbis Euangelicis supradictis. Secundo vero dicuntur etiam diuina praecepta spiritualia viuificando, quoniam ad viuificandum spiritum sive animam humanam data sunt. Sane & propter beatitudinem aeternam tradita & statuta fuerunt illa, quae dicuntur praecepta & prohibita legis diuinae actiue sumta. Alia vero spiritualia quaedam non sunt essentialiter, sed a quibusdam spiritualium vocabulum sumserunt, propterea quod ad praedicta spiritualia exercenda vel ministranda seruiunt, & sunt per homines ordinata; quemadmodum personae sive corpora sacerdotum. Sic etiam domus vocatur Ecclesia, secundum quandam Ecclesiae significationem. Sic quoque vestes, vasa, libri, & instrumenta quaequaedam alia ordinata per homines, propter cultum diuinum. Sic etiā ieiunia, eleemosynæ, acreliqui quidam actus & hominum opera de diuinis siue spiritualibus, & circa vel propter spiritualia, quibus inexistunt, veluti paramenta spiritualia dicta sunt. De quibus omnibus, quoniam nota, omittuntur exempla propter abbreuiationem sermonis. Proportionaliter quoque secundum legem humanam sunt præcepta, prohibita, & permissa actiue sumpta, & alia similiter impœtata, quæ omnia dicuntur temporalia; propterea quod ab homine tradita sunt, & immediate statuta. Et rursus propter vitam huius seculi temporalem vocatam, q tempore clanditur & finitur, talia statuta sunt & fuerunt.
units.tr: Further, it must also be noted that precepts, both affirmative and negative, and what are called permissions and counsels, under the divine law are spiritual essentially and are so called. First, indeed, because they were handed down and instituted immediately by the Holy Spirit, as Blessed Ambrose says on the Apostle after the letter to the Corinthians, chapter 9: "Spiritual," he says, "are the evangelical law and the Word of God." And perhaps there are also spiritual things, namely the graces or gifts of the Holy Spirit, which come to be and arrive in the souls of the faithful of Christ from the aforesaid Gospel words. Second, the divine precepts are also called spiritual because they quicken, since they were given to quicken the spirit or human soul. Indeed, those things which are called the precepts and prohibitions of the divine law, taken actively, were also handed down and established for the sake of eternal blessedness. Other things, however, are not spiritual essentially, but have taken the name of spiritual things from them, because they serve to exercise or minister the aforesaid spiritual things and have been arranged by men; such as the persons or bodies of priests. Thus also a house is called a church, according to a certain sense of the word church. So too garments, vessels, books and certain other instruments arranged by men for divine worship. So also fasts, almsgivings and certain other acts and works of men concerning divine or spiritual things, or around and on account of spiritual things in which they inhere, have been called spiritual ornaments. Since all these things are well known, examples of them are omitted for the sake of brevity. In a proportionate way, under human law there are also precepts, prohibitions and permissions taken actively, and other similarly commanded things, all of which are called temporal, because they were handed down by man and immediately established. And again, such statutes are and were made for the sake of this temporal life, as it is called, which is bounded and ended in time.

units.la: Insuper attendere conuenit, quod quamuis præcepta & prohibita & consilia secundum legem diuinam actiue sumpta, differant à præceptis secundum legem humanam; quoniam ab alio legislatore, & ad alium finem, & sub aliis pœnis, temporibus & modis eas transgressoribus, inferendi, statuta & ordinata sunt talia: tamen personæ cum suis actibus, imperatis, & operibus, quibus præcipitur siue imperatur per legem vtramque, in omnibus, quasi vel saltem in pluribus, eadem esse possunt & sunt. Verbi gratia, Furtum non fieri, vel homicidium & rapinam, vel fraudem, aut falsum testimonium, & similia reliqua, quæ præcipit tam diuina quā humana lex non esse fienda. Similiter quoque in cæteris præceptis, vt mutuum restituere, atque depositum. Rursus quod eadem esse possunt personæ, & earum consimiles actus, quibus & de quibus tam temporalia, quam circa spiritualia præcipit vtraque lex. Nam circa temporalia & de temporalibus tam per sacerdotes, episcopos, siue presbyteros, diaconos, & alios spirituales ministros, & similiter per non sacerdotes, vocatos seculares aut laicos, potest aliquid fieri vel omitti licitum aut illicitum, secundum præcepta vel contra tam diuinæ quam humanæ legis; & iuste corrigenda seu punienda tam in statu præsentis seculi, quam futuri, per pœnam videl. transgressores arcendo, qualia sunt crimina quæ quidem in exemplis adductæ sunt. Sic etiam de spiritualibus, & circa spiritualia quomodolibet appellata, potest licitum aliquid per prædictas personas & actus ipsarum, & illicitum similiter fieri vel omitti; veluti hæreses parere, siue actus illicitos docere, & bruta quædam baptisare, dæmonibus satisfacere, quemadmodum faciunt quidam scelerati sortilegi: alia quoque crimina committere, vt vasa, libros, vestes & reliqua choralia instrumenta cultui diuino deseruientia rapere vel furari, & reliqua similia hæc iuste in hoc seculo & suturo punienda per pœnam realem aut personalem, secundum legem vtramque diuinam videlicet & humanam, quamuis differenter & differentibus pœnis, ac iudice, loco, & tempore, quemadmodum dictum est, & infra seriosè dicitur.
units.tr: Furthermore, it is fitting to note that although precepts, prohibitions and counsels under the divine law, taken actively, differ from precepts under human law (since such things were established and ordained by another lawgiver, for another end, and with other penalties, times and methods of inflicting them on transgressors), nevertheless the persons with their acts, commands and works, to which something is commanded or enjoined by either law, can be and are the same in all cases, or at least in most. For example, that theft, murder, robbery, fraud, false witness, and the like, which both divine and human law forbid, should not be done. Likewise in the other precepts, such as to repay a loan and a deposit. Again, the persons and their like acts, to and concerning which both laws command, both in temporal matters and in matters concerning spiritual things, can be the same. For in temporal matters, and concerning temporal things, something may be done or omitted lawfully or unlawfully, according to or against the precepts of both divine and human law, both by priests, bishops or presbyters, deacons and other spiritual ministers, and likewise by non-priests called secular or lay people; and such things are to be justly corrected or punished both in the state of the present age and of the future, namely by penalty, excluding transgressors, as with the crimes that have been adduced as examples. So too concerning spiritual things, and things however called in relation to spiritual things, something lawful can be done or omitted by the aforesaid persons and their acts, and likewise something unlawful: for example, to beget heresies, or to teach unlawful acts, to baptise brute beasts, to satisfy demons, as certain wicked sorcerers do; or to commit other crimes, such as to seize or steal vessels, books, garments and the remaining choral instruments serving divine worship; and such things, and the like, are to be justly punished in this age and the next, by real or personal penalty, according to both divine and human law, although differently, and with different penalties, judges, places and times, as has been said and is discussed more fully below.

units.la: Est adhuc etiam aduertendum, quod si præcipit lex diuina fiendum vel omittendum aliquid, quod fieri vel omitti non præcipit lex humana, sed potius oppositum præcipiat vel permittat; debet seruari legis diuinæ præceptum, humana lege vel eius oppositō præcepto vel permisso contempto siue dimisso; quoniam præceptum legis diuinæ infallibilem continet veritatem, humanæ vero legis non sic. Rursum quoniam diuinum obligat transgressorem ad pœnam æternam: humanum vero ad temporalem siue finitam, & minus ab homine fugiendam.
units.tr: It must also be noted that if divine law commands something to be done or omitted, and human law does not command that but rather commands or permits the opposite, the precept of divine law must be observed and human law, or its contrary precept or permission, disregarded. This is because the precept of divine law contains infallible truth, but human law does not. Again, divine law binds the transgressor to eternal punishment, whereas human law binds him only to temporal or limited punishment, one that is less to be feared by man.

units.la: Est amplius attendendum, quod vtraq; iam dictarum legum habet proprium & diuersum immediatum legislatorem & iudicem, vt dictum est supra. Et rursus quoniam duplex est Iudex: vnus quidem doctor solummodo, & fortassis etiam de aliquibus operatur, sicut fidelis est, secundum qualibet disciplinam, quomodo etiam scripsit famosus ille philosophus Aristoteles nominatus: Quod vriusq; est bonus iudex eorum quæ nouit, & hoc bene iudicat: veluti medicus de sanis & ægris. Alius vero Iudex est Principans proprie vocatus, cui tradita auctoritas & data coactiua potestas transgressores legum per pœnas arcendi. Et est hic siquidem iudex secundum legem humanam, de quo dixit Apostolus: Quod non sine causa gladium portat, id est coactiuam & armatam potestatem habet: quoniam minister Dei est, vindex in iram ei qui malum agit: esto etiam quod humanarum legum doctor non existat. Secundum enim diuinam Iudex est coactiuus, de quo Apostolus dicit B. Iacobus in Canonica sua, vnus est legislator & iudex, qui potest perdere & liberare.
units.tr: It must further be noted that each of the two laws mentioned has its own and distinct immediate lawgiver and judge, as said above. Again, there are two kinds of judge. One is a teacher only, who perhaps also works in certain matters, as a faithful man does in any discipline. The famous philosopher Aristotle wrote that each is a good judge of the things he knows, and judges them well, as a physician judges the healthy and the sick. The other judge is properly called the ruler, to whom authority has been handed over and coercive power granted to keep transgressors of laws in check by punishments. This is the judge according to human law, of whom the Apostle said that he does not bear the sword in vain: he has coercive and armed power, since he is God's minister, an avenger for wrath against him who does evil, even though he may not be a teacher of human laws. For according to divine law the judge is coercive, of whom the blessed James says in his Epistle: there is one lawgiver and judge, who is able to destroy and to save.

units.la: His itaq; suppositis, tanquam veris & notis, dixerunt & scripserunt in suis tractatibus præfati Doctores, quod secundum legem diuinam legislator & iudex coactiuus secundum ipsam est Christus, sicut per beatum dictum est supra. Ipse enim tulit legem diuinam, seu Nouum Testam. per os tam Apostolorum quam aliorum sanctorum quorundam. Vnde Apost. An experimentum eius quæritis, qui loquitur in me Christus? & B. Petrus in sua Canonica dicit: Non ab humano spiritu allata est aliquando prophetia, sed Spiritu S. inspirati locuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Hic autem legislator statuit secundum hac legem transgressores iudicari, & per pœnas arceri in futuro seculo tantum modo, non in isto. Vnde scriptura: Cum venerit filius hominis in sede maiestatis suæ, sedebit & vos super sedes duodecim, &c. quod erit in futuro seculo, sicut manifeste sonat scriptura, & exponunt omnes expositores eiusdem. Sunt rursus iudices alii secundum legem diuinam, quos nihil prohibet esse plures in statu præsentis seculi, vocati Doctores, & secundum ipsam quorundam actuum siue operum ministri atq; factores, nullam coactiuam auctoritatem vel potestatem habentes à Christo seu lege diuina, arcendi quenquam in hoc seculo, ad aliquid agendum vel omittendum, per pœnam aliquam realem. Vnde Christus Marci vltimo tales iudices vocauit Doctores, dum ipsis in Apostolorum persona dixit: Euntes ergo, docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos, & per Malach. propheram: Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scripturam, & legem requirent ex ore eius. Et sunt hi iudices, episcopi, siue sacerdotes, vocati doctores. Carent autem præfati iudices, & carere debent auctoritate & potestate coactiua, per quamcunque pœnam arcendi, sicut dictum est pridem: quoniam tali auctoritate Christus in hoc seculo carere voluit in persona propria, in quantum homo
units.tr: With these things assumed as true and known, the aforesaid Doctors have said and written in their treatises that, according to divine law, the lawgiver and coercive judge is Christ himself, as the blessed one has said above. For he himself gave the divine law, or the New Testament, through the mouths of the Apostles and of certain other saints. Hence the Apostle says: "Do you seek proof of him who speaks in me, Christ?" And the blessed Peter says in his Epistle: "Prophecy never came by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit." This lawgiver has determined that transgressors of this law are to be judged and kept in check by punishments only in the future age, not in this one. Hence Scripture: "When the Son of man comes in the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones," etc., which will be in the future age, as Scripture plainly says and all its expositors explain. There are, again, other judges according to divine law, whom nothing prevents from being several in the state of the present age. They are called Teachers, and by that law they are ministers and doers of certain acts or works. They have no coercive authority or power from Christ or divine law to restrain anyone in this age from doing or omitting something by any real punishment. Hence Christ, at the end of Mark, called such judges Teachers when he said to them in the person of the Apostles: "Go therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them." And through the prophet Malachi: "The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth." These judges are bishops or priests, called teachers. The aforesaid judges lack, and ought to lack, authority and coercive power to restrain by any punishment, as said before, since Christ himself chose to lack such authority in this age in his own person, insofar as he was a man

units.la: {y} ... homo, cum dixit: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo: (ecce quantum ad auctoritatem) Si enim esset de hoc mundo, decertarent utiq; ministrim ei. (ecce quantum ad armatâ sine coactiuam potestatem.) Ecturssus idem petenti ab ipso diuisionem hæreditatis à fratre, respondit: Homo, quis me constituit iudicem aut diuisorem super vos, vel inter te & fratrem tuum? quasi diceret: Tale iudicium mihi non conuenit exercere. Sic etiam tali auctoritate aut coactiua potestate carere voluit Apostolos, & in ipsorum persona omnes episcopos siue presbyteros, successores ipsius, in quantum fuerat sacerdos humanus: quoniam in quantum Deus erat, nullus sibi hominum successit vel succedere potuit, dum ad ipsos inquit: Reges gentium dominantur eorum, vos autem non sic. Planum est, quod Apostolis interdicitur dominatu, sicut inquit Bernardus. Sic quoque sacram Scripturam intellexerunt & exposuerunt concorditer omnes sancti & approbati doctores, & idem secundum proprias sententias expresserunt. Quod etiam scies & de spiritualibus loquens, se non trahere potestatem quemquam arcendi, & multo minus de temporalibus, unde dicebat Corinthiis: Non dominamur fidei vestrae. Super quo verbo tam Ambrosius, quam Chrysostomus senserunt concorditer, & expresse dixerunt. Ambrosius quidem: non dominamur fidei vestrae, id est, non quia dominium aut coactionem patiatur fides vestra, qua voluntatis est non necessitatis. Chrysostomus autem: in ecclesia non coactum, sed adquiescentem oportet ad meliora conuerti. Quod admirabilis vir ille sciens, Apostolus videlicet, dicebat Corinthiis, Non dominamur fidei vestrae. subiungensque Chrysostomus ait: Non enim à legibus data est nobis, Episcopis siue presbyteris scil. talis potestas, ut auctoritate sententiae cohibeamus homines à delictis: neq; si data esset, haberemus vbi exercemus huiusmodi potestatem: cum Deus noster, Christus videlicet, non necessitate, id est violentia, aliquos homines traxerit à peccato; sed sua sese sponte subtrahentes remuneratus sit. In quibus etiam verbis supponit Chrysostomus, quod omnis coactiua potestas in hoc seculo datur à legibus siue principibus. Quod etiam dicit Hugo de S. Victore, De sacr. lib. 2. inquit enim sic: Quod licet ecclesia, id est ecclesiastica persona, Episcopi siue presbyteri, iurisdictiones coactiuas videlic. in personas seculares exerceant; hoc ipsum tamen quod exercent, à regia potestate se habere cognoscant. Non ergo à lege diuina, sed ab humana lege, conuenit cuiquam in hoc seculo auctoritas & coactiua potestas; præcipue Episcopo siue presbytero. Vnde Chrysostomus post verba prædicta subinfert: Homo vero si à fide vestra fuerit abductus, multum imminet sacerdoti patientia industria exhortationis; quod non potest errantem vi reducere, sed persuadere conabitur, vt ad fidem rectam reuertatur, à qua primitus cecidit. Idem quoque senserunt omnes sancti Doctores reliqui, atque expositores iuxta sacram Scripturam, quorum sententias hic omissas propter breuitatem copiose videre poterit, cui cura fuerit, in tractatibus nouis præfatorum doctorum.
units.tr: ... man, when he said: "My kingdom is not of this world" (see, as to authority); "For if it were of this world, my servants would surely fight" (see, as to armed or coercive power). Again, when someone asked him to divide an inheritance with his brother, he answered: "Man, who made me a judge or divider over you, or between you and your brother?" As if to say: such judgment is not fitting for me to exercise. So too he chose to lack such authority or coercive power, and in the persons of the Apostles, all bishops or elders, his successors, insofar as he was a human priest. For insofar as he was God, no man succeeded him or could succeed him, when he said to them: "The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, but you shall not be so." It is plain that domination is forbidden to the Apostles, as Bernard says. In the same way all holy and approved doctors understood and expounded Holy Scripture in agreement, and expressed the same in their own opinions. You will also know that, even when speaking of spiritual matters, he did not claim any power to restrain anyone, much less in temporal matters. Hence he said to the Corinthians: "Not that we have dominion over your faith." On this word both Ambrose and Chrysostom agreed and said so expressly. Ambrose: "We do not have dominion over your faith, that is, not because your faith suffers dominion or coercion; it belongs to the will, not to necessity." Chrysostom: "In the Church, one ought to be turned to better things not by compulsion but by consent. The admirable man, namely the Apostle, knowing this, said to the Corinthians: 'Not that we have dominion over your faith.'" Adding to this, Chrysostom says: "For such power has not been given to us, that is, to bishops or presbyters, by laws, so that by the authority of a sentence we might restrain men from sins. Nor, even if it had been given, would we have anywhere to exercise such power, since our God, Christ, has not drawn men from sin by necessity, that is, by violence, but has rewarded those who withdraw of their own accord." In these words Chrysostom also presupposes that all coercive power in this age is given by laws or princes. Hugh of St Victor also says this, in De sacramentis, book 2. For he says thus: "Although the Church, that is, ecclesiastical persons, bishops or presbyters, may exercise coercive jurisdiction, namely over secular persons, yet they know that what they exercise they have from royal power." Therefore authority and coercive power belong to anyone in this age not by divine law but by human law, especially to a bishop or presbyter. Hence, after the words quoted above, Chrysostom adds: "But if a man has been led away from your faith, much patience and skill in exhortation is required of the priest. He cannot bring back the erring by force, but will strive to persuade him to return to the right faith from which he first fell." All the other holy doctors and expositors of Holy Scripture have thought the same. Whoever cares to see their opinions, omitted here for brevity, may find them copiously in the new treatises of the aforesaid doctors.

units.la: Est etiam similiter secundum legem humanam legislator, vt ciuium vniuersitas, aut eius pars valentior, vel Romanus princeps supremus Imperator vocatus. Est & iudex coactiuus secundum legem eandem, vt vniuersitas iam dicta, vel Princeps; vel illi, cui vel quibus vniuersitas aut Princeps dederit coactiuam potestatem, per poenam realem aut personalem in seculo legis humanae transgressores coercendi. Nequaquam vero legislatores humani sunt Episcopi siue presbyteri, aut reliqui spirituales ministri, coniunctim vel diuisim, in quantum huiusmodi: sed fortassis in quantum pars aliquaciuitatis existunt: secundum quod per humanas rationes citatas & per sacram scripturam euidenter est monstratum, & per iam dictos Doctores nostros, & vt iam conuenienter deductum est supra. Sunt & alii iudices secundum legem humanam, vocati Iurisperiti siue Doctores, nullam coactiuam auctoritatem habentes, in quantum huiusmodi, arcendi quemquam in hoc seculo, per poenam aliquam realem aut personalem, ad agendum licitum aliquod, aut illicitum omittendum; sed solummodo ad docendum, & aliquid secundum legem operandum humanam, quemadmodum Episcopi siue presbyteri secundum legem diuinam. Propter quae manifestius intuendum, quod de humanis actibus & operibus circa diuina, & de diuinis, similiter quoque modo circa temporalia, & de temporalibus, potest dubitatio contingere duplex, & per consequens interrogatio siue quaestio fieri propter veritatem de dubitatis habendam. Vna quidem dubitatio est & quaestio, an videlicet actus illi & opera, de quibus quaeritur, sint fieri vel omitti praecepta vel prohibita, licita vel illicita, tam secundum legem diuinam quam humanam. Alia vero potest esse dubitatio, quaestio siue interrogatio ex praedictis, vtrum videlicet si per quemquam sint tales actus aut opera facta vel omissa, pertinent ad iudicium principantis? iudicis videlicet coactiui, cuius auctoritas est arcere per poenam realem aut personalem, transgressorem legis diuinae vel humanae, in praesenti seculo vel futuro.
units.tr: Likewise, according to human law, the lawgiver is the whole body of citizens, or its stronger part, or the supreme Roman prince, called Emperor. The coercive judge according to the same law is the aforesaid whole body, or the Prince, or those to whom the body or the Prince has given coercive power, to restrain transgressors of human law in this age by real or personal punishment. Bishops or presbyters, or other spiritual ministers, whether together or separately, insofar as they are such, are by no means human lawgivers; perhaps only insofar as they form part of some community. This has been clearly shown through the human reasons cited, through Holy Scripture, through the Doctors already named, and as has been fittingly deduced above. There are also other judges according to human law, called jurists or Doctors. Insofar as they are such, they have no coercive authority to restrain anyone in this age by any real or personal punishment, either to do something lawful or to omit something unlawful. They have authority only to teach, and to work something according to human law, just as bishops or presbyters do according to divine law. On account of this, it must be seen more clearly that, concerning human acts and works relating to divine matters, and concerning divine matters, and similarly concerning temporal matters and temporal things, a twofold doubt can arise, and consequently an inquiry or question may be made in order to obtain the truth about the doubtful matter. One doubt and question is whether those acts and works under inquiry are commanded or forbidden, to be done or omitted, lawful or unlawful, both according to divine and according to human law. The other doubt, question or inquiry, arising from what has been said, is whether, if such acts or works have been done or omitted by anyone, they belong to the judgment of the ruling, that is, coercive, judge, whose authority is to restrain by real or personal punishment a transgressor of divine or human law, in the present or the future age.

units.la: De priori quidem quaestione, dubitatione siue interrogatione, respondere ac iudicare seu per iudicium diffinire pertinet ad Doctores, seu ad iudices doctrinales, huiusmodi siquidem auctoritatem habentes; quales secundum legem diuinam sunt vel esse debent omnes Episcopi, siue presbyteri, quemadmodum ostensum est prius, & dixit Apostolus ad Timoth. Oportet Episcopum esse doctorem. Secundum humanam vero legem, pertinet haec auctoritas siue iudicium ad Iurisperitos siue humanae legis Doctores. Etenim eorum officium est, scire docere si oporteat, praedicare quae sint & qualia praecepta permissa vel prohibita secundum leges praedictas, licita etiam vel illicita fieri vel omitti in actibus humanis; & similiter de huiusmodi respondere, cum super his & de iis fuerint requisiti; omni tamen auctoritate & coactiua potestate carentes, quemquam cogendi per poenam in hoc seculo ad fugiendum vel faciendum aliquid, vt supra sufficienter induximus. Quemadmodum medici de sanitate corporis conseruanda vel omissa recuperanda docere habent & operari, secundum artis medicinae praecepta: nec tamen quemquam cogere possunt vitam seruare diaetam, aut declinare nociuam, per poenam aliquam realem aut personalem facientibus vel omittentibus inferendo. Sic quoque
units.tr: Answering and judging the first question, doubt, or inquiry, or settling it by judgment, belongs to the teachers, or doctrinal judges, who hold this authority. According to the divine law, all bishops or elders are, or ought to be, such judges, as was shown earlier, and the Apostle said to Timothy: A bishop must be a teacher. According to human law, this authority or judgment belongs to the jurists or teachers of human law.
