Their office is to know, to teach where it is needful, and to declare which precepts are commanded, permitted, or forbidden by those laws, and which acts of men may lawfully or unlawfully be done or omitted; and likewise to give answers on these matters when they are asked about them. Yet they have no authority or coercive power to compel anyone, by punishment in this life, to avoid or to do anything, as we have sufficiently shown above. Physicians likewise have the task of teaching and acting on the preservation or recovery of bodily health, according to the precepts of the medical art, yet they cannot compel anyone to keep his diet or to avoid a harmful one by inflicting any real or personal penalty on those who act or omit. So too

units.la: que qui medici sunt animarum, hominem in hoc mundo per poenam arcere possunt, sed ... [illegible, ~20 letters] ... Et propterea, quamvis licet condere seu facere ordinationes circa bonos mores & opera facienda, & malos & crimina fugienda: non tamen nunc huiusmodi ordinationes leges, sed potius documenta seu regulae. Neque ipsorum iudicium, quae tales regulas circa hominum actus debet appellari iurisdictio, siue forum: quia talia nomina proprie sumpta, iudicij coactiuo convenientia sunt, secundum primam & veram impositionem ipsorum. Potest autem praefatum iudicium, quoniam generale est, fieri ignoratis personis, de quibus, siue de quorum actibus, dubitatur & quaeritur.
units.tr: those who are physicians of souls can restrain a man in this world by punishment, but ... [illegible, ~20 letters] ... And therefore, although it is lawful to make or enact ordinances concerning good morals and the duties to be done, and concerning evils and crimes to be avoided, such ordinances are not now properly laws, but rather teachings or rules. Nor should their judgment, which lays down such rules for human acts, be called jurisdiction or a court, because such names, properly taken, belong to coercive judgment, according to their first and true imposition. The aforesaid judgment, since it is general, may be made without knowing the persons about whom, or about whose acts, doubt and question arise.

units.la: Secunda vero dubitatio, interrogatio & quaestio, potest contingere circa praedictos hominum actus & opera, Vtrum videlicet, si per quemquam sint tales actus aut opera facta vel omissa, pertinent ad iudicium principantis iudicis vel coactiui, cuius auctoritas est arcere per poenam realem aut personalem legum transgressores in praesenti seculo vel futuro; secundum legem diuinam vero est in futuro seculo tantummodo, non in isto. Talis iudex est Christus solus, & erunt fortasse secum duodecim Apostoli, de quibus legimus in Scriptura: Cum venerit filius hominis in sede maiestatis suae, sedebitis & vos, &c. Secundum vero legem humanam talis est princeps, auctoritate legislatorum humanorum, coactivam habens potestatem arcendi per poenam realem aut personalem transgressores legis humanae, in praesenti tantum seculo, non in illo. Verum ad suum iudicium coactivum exercendum non indiget iudex secundum legem diuinam inquirere veritatem per testimonium, neque testes arcere in iudicium pro veritate dicenda; quoniam omnia sunt nuda & aperta oculis eius, non indiget gladio seu armorum ministrorumque potentia coactiva, propter sententiam suam exequendam, poenam transgressoribus inferendo: quoniam ipse dixit & facta sunt. Sic non autem princeps coactivus humanus: quoniam ignorare potest, an quis delatus aut excusatus de illicito actu, illum admiserit, vel non. Ideoque tam litigantes, quam testes necesse habet in iudicium vocare, ipsosque recusantes per armatam potestatem ad hoc compellere; quoniam per ipsius simplex dictum fortasis non convenirent, rei praesertim, & qui poenam sibi debitam formidarent infligi.
units.tr: The second doubt, inquiry, and question can arise concerning the aforesaid acts and works of men, namely whether, if such acts or works have been done or omitted by anyone, they belong to the judgment of the governing or coercive judge, whose authority is to restrain by real or personal punishment the transgressors of the laws in this world or the next. According to the divine law, however, this is only in the next world, not in this one. Such a judge is Christ alone, and perhaps the twelve Apostles will be with him, of whom we read in Scripture: When the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit, etc. According to human law, however, such a judge is the prince, by the authority of human legislators, who has coercive power to restrain by real or personal punishment the transgressors of human law, in this present world only, not in the next. But to exercise his coercive judgment, a judge under divine law does not need to inquire into the truth by testimony, nor to summon witnesses to speak the truth; for all things are naked and open to his eyes, and he does not need the sword or the coercive power of arms and ministers to carry out his sentence by inflicting punishment on transgressors, since he spoke, and they were made. It is not so with a human coercive prince, for he can be ignorant whether someone accused or charged with an unlawful act has committed it or not. Therefore he must summon both litigants and witnesses to court, and compel those who refuse by armed power to do so; for by his simple word they perhaps would not come, especially the accused, who fear that the punishment due to them will be inflicted.

units.la: Ex his igitur iam dictis apparere potest responsio ad principale quaesitum, cuius videlicet iudicis sit auctoritas iudicandi de diuortio matrimonii, vel alterius vel utriusque coniugum facta requisitione. Quoniam si fuerit dubium vel quaestio, utrum propositum matrimonium ex aliqua causa illicitum aut prohibitum sit lege diuina, est auctoritas iudicandi de eo ac respondendi Episcoporum, siue presbyterorum, & legis diuinae doctorum ad huiusmodi statutorum, secundum legem honestam, ac consuetudinem regionis, in nullo repugnando coactiuae potestati legis diuinae. Ipsorum enim est scire praecepta, prohibita, & permissa, tam circa matrimonium, quam circa reliquos actus humanos & opera, de quibus & secundum quem modum licite habet fieri vel omitti, secundum legem praedictam. Vt si dubium sit & quaeratur ab ipsis, an impotentia vnius coniugum ad debitum carnale reddendum suo compari coniugi, sit causa sufficiens ad diuortium matrimonii licite faciendum inter ipsos, secundum legem diuinam; iudicare habent & respondere de hoc supradicti sacrae Scripturae ministri atque doctores. Quoniam (vt saepe diximus) hoc officium est ipsorum: quinimo non facientes hoc, punirentur per iudicem coactiuum secundum legem diuinam, quamuis in futuro seculo, non in isto. Unde Apostolus: Vae mihi si non evangelizavero, quod mihi incumbit. Sed si dubium fuerit & quaeratur, an talis defectus, propter quem potest & debet licite fieri diuortium, inexistat alteri coniugum, & alter suo compari siue coniugi inexistere asserat; & propterea coniunx non patiens petat velitque ab impotente siue defectum patiente coniuge de matrimonio separari: est auctoritas siue coactiuum iudicium de hoc Christi siue Dei, secundum legem diuinam, ad arcendum per poenam coniugem non iustum in futuro tantum seculo, non in isto: vtpote si alium coniugem iuste agentem liberum non permittat, sed violentiam inferens in persona vel rebus ipsum detineat, impediat vel coarctet. Neque super hoc eget hic Iudex informari per testes, ad sciendum vtrum talis defectus alteri coniugum inexistat, propter quem de matrimonio debeat separari: quoniam nihil occultum est oculis eius, quemadmodum dictum est prius.
units.tr: From what has now been said, the answer to the principal question can therefore be seen: to which judge belongs the authority to judge about the divorce of a marriage, when either one or both spouses have made the request. For if there is doubt or question whether the proposed marriage is unlawful or forbidden by divine law for some cause, the authority to judge and answer about it belongs to the bishops or elders and the teachers of divine law, who must give their decision according to honest law and the custom of the region, in no way contrary to the coercive power of divine law. For it is their task to know the precepts, prohibitions, and permissions, both concerning marriage and concerning the other human acts and works: which may be done or omitted lawfully, and in what manner, according to that law. For example, if it is doubtful and they are asked whether the inability of one spouse to render the marital debt to the other is a sufficient cause for lawfully making a divorce between them under divine law, the aforesaid ministers and teachers of Holy Scripture must judge and answer on this. For (as we have often said) this is their office; indeed, if they did not do it, they would be punished by the coercive judge under divine law, though in the next world, not in this one. Hence the Apostle: Woe is me if I do not preach the gospel, which is laid upon me. But if it is doubtful and asked whether such a defect, on account of which a divorce can and ought to be lawfully made, exists in one of the spouses, and the other spouse asserts that it does; and therefore the spouse who is not willing to suffer it seeks, and wishes, to be separated from the marriage from the impotent or defective spouse: the authority or coercive judgment in this matter belongs to Christ or God, under divine law, to restrain by punishment in the next world only, not in this one, the spouse who is unjust; for example, if he does not allow the other spouse, acting justly, to go free, but detains, hinders, or constrains that spouse by violence against person or property. Nor does this judge need to be informed by witnesses on this matter, in order to know whether such a defect exists in one of the spouses, on account of which they ought to be separated from the marriage; for nothing is hidden from his eyes, as was said before.

units.la: Secundum vero legem humanam, pertinet hoc iudicium diuortii coactiuum, per poenam in hoc seculo transgressoribus inferendam, ad principantem auctoritatem legislatoris humani. Nam quamuis ad legislatorem humanum, vel ipsius iudicem coactiuum, non pertineat statuere aut condere spiritualia siue diuina praecepta, prohibita, vel permissa, siue consilia: tamen de actibus hominum & circa ipsa, quantum circa temporalia, licite vel illicite factis vel omissis, tam per sacerdotes seu per spirituales ministros, quam per laicos siue seculares personas (cum spirituales non sint essentialiter) iudicare coactiuo iudicio, & arcere per poenam in hoc seculo committentes illicita, ad praefatum pertinet legislatorem humanum & iudicem. Vnde Apostolus ad Romanos decimo tertio generaliter neminem excipiendo, malefactores seu legis humanae non repugnantis legi diuinae transgressores, presbyterum siue non presbyterum, inquit: Omnis anima subdita sit potestatibus sublimioribus, Regibus videlicet, Ducibus, & Tribunis, secundum sanctorum expositionem ibidem.
units.tr: Under human law, however, this coercive judgment of divorce, to be inflicted as punishment on transgressors in this life, belongs to the ruling authority of the human legislator. For although it does not belong to the human legislator, or to his coercive judge, to establish or enact spiritual or divine precepts, prohibitions, permissions, or counsels, yet concerning men's acts, and about those things as far as they concern temporal matters, whether done or omitted lawfully or unlawfully, it belongs to the aforesaid human legislator and judge to judge by coercive judgment, and to restrain by punishment in this life those who commit unlawful acts, whether through priests or spiritual ministers, or through laymen or secular persons (since they are not spiritual in essence). Hence the Apostle, in Romans chapter thirteen, excepting no one in general, whether elder or not, speaks of malefactors, or transgressors of human law not opposed to divine law, saying: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers, namely kings, dukes, and tribunes, according to the holy expositors on that passage.

units.la: Et scribit: Qui enim potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit: & qui ipsis resistunt, damnationem sibi adquirunt, aeternam videl. Et inquit rursus: Minister enim Dei est, vindex in iram, ei qui malum agit, supple, quicunque sit ille. Non enim sine causa gladium portat, id est, habet armatam & coactiuam potestatem. Quod de nullo spirituali ministro dixit Apostolus, sed oppositum magis, dum inquit: Arma militiae nostrae non sunt carnalia. Et rursus ad Timotheum: Nemo militans Deo implicat se saecularibus negociis, id est, litigiosus sis ciuilibus. His etiam attestatur beatus Petrus in sua Canonica, dum ad omnes indifferenter, neminem excipiens, inquit; Subditi estote omni humanæ creaturæ propter Dominum, in principatu videl. constitutæ, & Regi tanquam præexcellenti, & Ducibus tanquam ab eo missis, ad vindictam malefactorum, laudem vero bonorum: quia est voluntas Dei.
units.tr: And he writes: For whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God, and those who resist shall acquire damnation for themselves, that is, eternal damnation. And again he says: For he is the minister of God, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil, understood, whoever he may be. For he does not bear the sword in vain, that is, he has armed and coercive power. The Apostle did not say this of any spiritual minister, but rather the opposite, when he says: The weapons of our warfare are not carnal. And again to Timothy: No one who serves as a soldier of God entangles himself in worldly business, that is, you should not be litigious in civil matters. Blessed Peter also bears witness to this in his Canonical Epistle, when he speaks to all indifferently, excepting no one: Be subject to every human creature for the Lord's sake, whether to the king as the preeminent one, or to governors as sent by him, for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of those who do well: for so is the will of God.

units.la: Hoc igitur modo de matrimonio & reliquis spiritualibus, secundum quod ipsa, vel hominum actus de ipsis, & circa ipsa, in aliquibus conditionibus referuntur ad statuta legis humanæ facta de ipsis; statuta, in quantum non repugnantia legi diuinæ, sed potius sibi consona & decentia, statuere legislatorem; & iudicare coactivum iudicem secularem competens est, quinimo necessitas requirit. Igitur quantum circa matrimonium contrahendum aut iam contractum, interueniunt plurima, quæ per actus hominum possunt licite vel illicite fieri vel omitti: quæ siquidem regulari oportet per legislatorem humanum, aut eius auctoritate iudicem coactivum, transgressores arcendo per pœnam. Cuius siquidem rei casum sumendo ponatur, quod alter coniugum post latam sententiam de fiendo diuortio matrimonii inter ipsos, ab altero coniuge discedere noluerit; sed secum ipsum per violentiam detinere, aut ipsum etiam personaliter, aut res siue ipsius bona contrectare, quemadmodum durante matrimonio seu ante factum per sententiam diuortium contrectabat; puniendus atque cogendus esset per pœnam realem aut personalem, in hoc seculo, & à iudice coactivo: tanquam iudicatum siue sententiam non obseruans. Quædam enim viro licebant supra & contra sibi coniugem mulierem, in persona & rebus ipsius exercere ante factum diuortium inter ipsos, quæ sibi post diuortium non licent: veluti iam dictam sibi coniugem matrimonio separatam arguere, increpare, ac verbis contumeliosis afficere, carnale debitum ab ipsa exigere, aut eandem quomodolibet aliter corporaliter tractare, impudice tangendo, aut flagellando, aut de bonis suis dotalibus, & aliis præter ius consensum disponere volendo; & similibus reliquis. Ex quibus multa & periculosa scandala post diuortium, si fierent, prouenirent. Propter quæ omnia tollenda seu prohibenda, & propter communem & euidentem utilitatem, imo necessitatem, competit ac debet, debet & potest legislator humanus de talibus fiendis vel omittendis statuere, iudicare atque compellere videlicet contendentes in iudicium conuenire, testes similiter pro veritate dicenda vocare, & transgressores ad comparendum arcere per pœnam, reliquum quoque, sententiam diffinitiuam super diuortio matrimoniali fiendo, vel non, proferre. Conformiter tamen in hoc legi diuinæ, ipsius videlicet præceptis ac prohibitis nihil per suam sententiam præcipiendo repugnans. Amplius vtrumque contendentium siue litigantium in iudicio post latam sententiam, ad iudicatum per ipsum tenendum & obseruandum compellere, per pœnam in hoc seculo transgressori sententiæ inferendam. Non enim de prædictis corrigendis seu regulandis per pœnam in hoc seculo transgressoribus inferendam, diuina lex aliquid ordinauit aut statuit: neque coactiuus iudex secundum ipsam contra quemquam in hoc seculo transgressorem, per se; neque per aliquem successorem, siue Episcopum, siue presbyterum, aut spiritualem ministrum, coniunctim vel diuisim, mandauit aut voluit coactiuum iudicium exerceri. Nec ex his potest proprie inferri, quod humanæ legi subiaceat lex diuina, vel legislator ipsius; sed vt potius è contrario. Nam legislator humanus præcipit fiendum, quod statutum est per diuinum legislatorem, aut legem diuinam. Neque similiter per ipsius iudicem coactiuum, Christum videlicet, sed potius è contrario. Veruntamen iuste præcipit, quod præcipere potest legislator diuinus, & ipsius auctoritate iudex siue principans coactiuus legis humanæ, in istis prædictis & reliquis secularibus, nihil illicitum agere circa spiritualia seu de ipsis, nec circa ipsa temporalia vel de ipsis: ac mandat ministris licita ac sibi debita officia de talibus, ac circa talia exercere; ipsosque rationabiliter in hoc seculo per pœnam arcere personalem atque realem, si transgressi fuerint humanæ legis præcepta, legis diuinæ præceptis non repugnantia. Nam ex officio sibi commisso secundum legis diuinæ ac humanæ præcepta tenent Episcopos seu presbyteros ad docendum, prædicandum, & spiritualia Christi fidelibus ministrandum, vt baptismum, & reliqua similia fidelibus exhibendum. Propter hoc enim ipsis ministrantur carnalia siue corporalia per Christi fideles, unde Christus: Dignus est enim operarius cibo suo. & Apostolus prim. Corinth. 9. Si nos vobis spiritualia seminamus, non est magnum, si vestra carnalia, id est temporalia metamus. Propter quod tanquam operarii suscipientes, aut qui suscepcrunt mercedem, obligati sunt & tenentur, ac arceri possunt per pœnam in hoc seculo, ac per coactiuum humanum iudicem, ad docenda spiritualia, & modo debito & tempore ministranda.
units.tr: Thus, then, concerning marriage and the other spiritual matters, insofar as marriage itself, or the acts of men concerning it and about it, are in some respects referred to human laws made about them, it belongs to the lawgiver to enact such statutes, provided they do not conflict with divine law but rather agree with and befit it; and it belongs to a coercive secular judge, indeed necessity requires it, to pass judgment. For there arise, in connection with contracting or already contracted marriage, very many matters which can be done or left undone lawfully or unlawfully by the acts of men. These ought indeed to be regulated by the human lawgiver, or by a coercive judge acting on his authority, restraining transgressors by punishment. To take an example of this: suppose that after sentence has been given concerning the divorce to be made between a married couple, one spouse refuses to depart from the other, but holds the other by force, and handles either the person itself or the goods of the other, as he used to do while the marriage lasted or before the divorce was made by sentence. He ought to be punished and compelled, by a real or personal penalty in this world, by a coercive judge, as one who does not observe the judgment or sentence. For some things were permitted to a husband, above and against his wife, to exercise upon her person and goods before the divorce between them was made, which are no longer permitted to him after the divorce: such as to accuse his wife, now separated from him in marriage, to upbraid her, to assail her with abusive words, to demand the conjugal debt from her, or to treat her bodily in any other way, by touching her immodestly, by beating her, or by wishing to dispose of her dowry goods and other property against right and consent; and the like. From these, if they were done, many dangerous scandals would arise after the divorce. For removing or prohibiting all these things, and for the common and evident utility, indeed necessity, it belongs to and is the duty and power of the human lawgiver to enact, to judge and to compel concerning such acts to be done or omitted: namely, to summon the contending parties into court, likewise to call witnesses to tell the truth, to restrain transgressors from appearing by punishment, and finally to pronounce the definitive sentence concerning whether the matrimonial divorce is to be made or not. Yet in this he conforms to divine law, decreeing nothing by his sentence that conflicts with its precepts and prohibitions. Furthermore, after sentence has been pronounced, he may compel each of the contending or litigating parties in the court to hold and observe the judgment, inflicting punishment in this world upon the transgressor of the sentence. For divine law has ordained or enacted nothing about correcting or regulating the aforesaid matters by punishment inflicted in this world upon transgressors; nor has it ordered or willed that a coercive judgment be exercised against any transgressor in this world, either by itself, or through any successor, whether bishop or presbyter or spiritual minister, jointly or severally. Nor can it properly be inferred from these things that divine law, or its lawgiver, is subject to human law; rather the reverse. For the human lawgiver commands to be done what has been established by the divine lawgiver or divine law; nor likewise by its coercive judge, namely Christ, but rather the reverse. Yet the human lawgiver, and the coercive judge or ruler acting on his authority, justly commands, in these aforesaid matters and the other secular ones, that nothing unlawful be done concerning spiritual things or about them, nor concerning temporal things or about them; and he orders ministers to perform the lawful and due duties concerning such things and in such matters, and rightly restrains them in this world by personal and real punishment if they have transgressed the precepts of human law that do not conflict with the precepts of divine law. For by the office committed to them, according to the precepts of divine and human law, bishops or presbyters are bound to teach, to preach, and to minister spiritual things to the faithful of Christ, such as baptism and the other like things to be given to the faithful. For this reason carnal or bodily things are ministered to them by the faithful of Christ; whence Christ says: "For the workman is worthy of his food." And the Apostle, 1 Cor. 9: "If we have sown spiritual things among you, it is no great thing if we reap your carnal things, that is, temporal things." Therefore, as workmen receiving, or who have received, wages, they are obliged and bound, and can be restrained in this world by punishment, and by the coercive human judge, to teach spiritual things and to minister them in the due manner and at the due time.

units.la: Ex prædictis igitur euidenter apparet, iudicium coactiuum siue sententiam proferre, ac exequi per coactiuam potestatem, super diuortio matrimoniali fieri requisito, ad Romani principis siue nostram auctoritatem, vel eorum quibus per nos concessa fuerit talis auctoritas siue potestas, solummodo pertinere. Propter quod ad diuortium matrimonii consummandum inter Iohannem & Margaretam prædictos:
units.tr: From the foregoing it therefore plainly appears that to pronounce a coercive judgment or sentence, and to execute it by coercive power, concerning the requested matrimonial divorce, belongs only to the authority of the Roman prince, or of us, or of those to whom such authority or power has been granted by us. Wherefore, for the consummation of the divorce of marriage between the aforesaid John and Margaret:

units.la: Nos Ludouicus Quartus Dei gratia Romanorum Imperator Augustus, pro tribunali iudice sedentes, in causa siue lite diuortii seu separationis matrimonii, quæ vertebatur inter illustres personas, Iohannem Regis Bohemiæ filium, requisitum parte ex vna, & Margaretham Ducissam Karinthiæ & Tyrolis Comitissam, ex altera parte, tanquam actricem, ac requirentem à dicto Iohanne iam vocato coniuge suo de matrimonio separari; visis & intellectis tam per nos quam prafatos Doctores iuribus, rationibus, probationibus & testimoniis Margaretha prædictæ, nec non contumacia iam dicti Iohannis, dicimus, diffinimus & determinamus; prædictam Margaretham separari debere seu posse de matrimonio à sepedicto Iohanne, éque conuerso, cum eisdem vel ipsorum alteri id videbitur expedire. Ipsam quoque Margaretham hoc requirentem instanter, vt supra, separamus, absolvimus, vt separatam esse iudicas. ludicamus in matrimonio iam dicto Iohanne per hanc nostram sententiam diffinitiuam. Simili quoque modo supradictum Iohannem à prefata Margaretha in matrimonio per auctoritatem & hanc nostram sententiam diffinitiuam separantes: ita videlicet, quod de cetero prefatus Iohannes supradicta Margaretha in nullo matrimonii debito tenetur: neque similiter prefata Margaretha supradicto Iohanni. Sed liberum sit utrique de corpore proprio siue persona, & omnibus bonis propriis, iuribus ac rebus tam mobilibus quam immobilibus facere vel disponere, & quod libet ordinare pro sua propria libito voluntatis.
units.tr: We, Ludwig IV, by the grace of God Emperor Augustus of the Romans, sitting as judge on the tribunal, in the cause or suit of divorce or separation of marriage which was being contested between the illustrious persons, John, son of the King of Bohemia, the petitioned party on the one side, and Margaret, Duchess of Carinthia and Countess of Tyrol, on the other side, as plaintiff and as one demanding to be separated in marriage from the said John, now summoned as her spouse; having seen and understood, both by us and by the aforesaid Doctors, the rights, arguments, proofs and testimonies of the aforesaid Margaret, as well as the contumacy of the said John, we say, define and determine that the aforesaid Margaret ought to be, or may be, separated in marriage from the aforesaid John, and conversely, as it shall seem expedient to them or to either of them. We also, urgently requested by her, as above, separate and absolve the said Margaret, and we judge her to be separated. We judge in the aforesaid marriage with John by this our definitive sentence. Likewise, by the authority and this our definitive sentence, we separate the aforesaid John from the aforesaid Margaret in marriage; so that henceforth the aforesaid John is bound to the aforesaid Margaret in no conjugal debt, nor likewise the aforesaid Margaret to the aforesaid John. But let it be free to each to make or dispose of their own body or person, and all their own goods, rights and things, both movable and immovable, and to order whatever they like at their own pleasure.

units.la: INCIPIT TRACTATVS CONSVLTATIONIS PER FRATREM GVILHELMVM OCCAM editus, super dispensatione in gradu consanguinitatis siue affinitatis inter personas Illustres, Ludouicum videlicet Marchionem Brandeburgensem, & Margaritham Ducissam Karinthiae, matrimonialiter copulari volentes; necnon legitimationis liberorum eorundem procreandorum, facta per Dominum LVDOVICVM IV. Dei gratia Rom. Imp.
units.tr: A TREATISE OF CONSULTATION, PUBLISHED BY BROTHER WILLIAM OCCAM, concerning dispensation in the degree of consanguinity or affinity between illustrious persons, namely Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg, and Margaret, Duchess of Carinthia, wishing to be joined in marriage; and likewise concerning the legitimation of children to be procreated by them, made by Lord LUDWIG IV, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans.

units.la: Hunc Tractatum habes supra in primo Tomo huius Collectionis Monarchica, sol. 21. & sequent.
units.tr: You have this treatise above, in the first volume of this Monarchic Collection, p. 21 and following.

units.la: RICHARDI ARCHI- EPISCOPI ARMACHANI DEFENSIO CVRATORVM, CONTRA EOS QVI se dicunt Priuilegiatos; & vicissim Defensio Priuilegiatorum, seu Mendicantium.
units.tr: Richard, Archbishop of Armagh: The Defence of the Parish Priests, against those who call themselves privileged; and conversely, the Defence of the Privileged, or Mendicants.

units.la: Per M. ROGERIVM CHONNOE. Iodocus Badius Ascensius Marco Alexandro Beneuentano, viro doctissimo & apprime religioso, salutem dicit.
units.tr: By M. Rogerius Chonnoe. Jodocus Badius Ascensius greets Marcus Alexander Beneventanus, a most learned man and especially religious.

units.la: Ceeiterum, Marce suauissime, quiddam manusculi, quod à Trechsel tuo hilari fronte suscipias velim. Cuius quidem imprimendi hanc accepimus occasionem. Siquidem cum post Summam de Ecclesia domini Ioannis de Turrecremata, Trechsel tuus opusculum Octo quaestionum M. Guilhelmi de Ockam super potestate Apostolica & Imperiali tuo nomine dicatum impressisset, mirabantur nonnulli, in quorum manus deuenerat, atqui tam dissona & aduersa (vt aiebant) fronte pugnantia, ab vna eademque officina sua prodire sineret. Ad quod ille ad manum habens quod respondeat: Philosophicum (inquis) atque adeo vetus est deuerbium: Opposita iuxta se posita magis elucescere, quocirca vt diuersis auditis opinionibus veritas patescat, diuersa & fere contraria opera pretium duximus imprimere. Non enim nostrum est auctorum scripta censere aut diiudicare: sed ea fideliter per impressionem multiplicata, ad studiosorum iudicia referre. Tum illorum manus vir sane doctus & religiosus, Simon Bergeri: recte, inquit, instituisti; atque vt pergas habeo duo opuscula mere inimica, atq; inter se repugnantia, quae coimpressa velim: quorum alterum Defensorium Curatorum contra eos qui se priuilegiatos dicunt: alterum Defensorium religionis Mendicantium & priuilegiatorum inscribitur, quorum prius quidem editum a domino Richardo Armachano nuper impressum est: posterius autem a religioso viro Rogerio Chonnoe Ordinis Fratrum Minorum compositum nondum impressum, imprimis tamen dignissimum est. Perlectis autem utrisque comperit iam saepe dictus M. Ioannes Trechsel in posteriori opusculo multa cum Opere 90. dierum M. Guilhelmi de Ockam quadrantia contineri, quapropter utile visum est, vt in eadem chartarum forma coimprimeret, vt cum illo aut cum alio eiusdem quantitatis opere colligari posset. Admonuitq; vt hac paternitati tuae, Marce praestantissime, nota faceret, precarerque vti gratanter tantillum muneris accipere digneris. Qua in re seclusa morositate eisdem fere, quibus ab illo accepi hec consecutus sum. Vale philosophiae praesidium. Ex Lugduno ad idus Octobrias, Anno MCCCC. XCVI.
units.tr: Furthermore, most sweet Marcus, I would like you to take with a cheerful countenance a little handbook that your Trechsel has printed. We were given the opportunity to print it as follows. When, after the Summa on the Church of Lord John of Torquemada, your Trechsel had published the little work of William of Ockham's Eight Questions on Apostolic and Imperial Power, dedicated in your name, some people into whose hands it came were surprised that he would let out from one and the same workshop things so discordant and so opposed, as they said, in their front. To this he had a ready reply: "There is a philosophical and indeed old saying," he said, "that opposites placed side by side shine out more clearly. Therefore, so that the truth may become evident once diverse opinions have been heard, we have thought it worthwhile to print works that are diverse and almost contrary. For it is not our business to judge or assess the writings of authors, but to pass on faithfully, by multiplying them in print, to the judgement of scholars." Then Simon Bergeri, a man truly learned and religious, one of those present, said: "You have done right, and so that you may go on, I have two little works that are purely hostile and mutually contradictory, which I would like printed together. One is entitled The Defence of the Parish Priests against those who call themselves privileged; the other is entitled The Defence of the Religion of the Mendicants and of the Privileged. The former, by the lord Richard of Armagh, has been recently printed; the latter, composed by the religious man Rogerius Chonnoe of the Order of Friars Minor, has not yet been printed, yet it is above all most worthy of printing." Having read both, the aforesaid M. John Trechsel found that the later little work contains many points that match the Work of Ninety Days of William of Ockham, quire for quire; therefore it seemed useful to him to print it in the same page format, so that it could be bound together with that work or with another work of the same size. He also advised that this be made known to your fatherhood, most excellent Marcus, and he asked that you would deign to accept graciously this small gift. In this matter, setting aside any fussiness, I have obtained almost the same things that I received from him. Farewell, bulwark of philosophy. From Lyon, on the Ides of October, in the year 1496.

units.la: IN NOMINE PATRIS, ET FILII ET SPIRITUS SANCTI, Amen. INCIPIT PROPOSITIO RICHARDI AR- CHIEPISCOPI ARMACHANI PRIMATIS HYBERNIÆ, FACTA IN consistorio coram domino Papa & dominis Cardinalibus ac Præla- tis, ad vtilitatem cleri & populi Christiani, super materia mendici- tatis ac priuilegiorum contra Fratres de ordinibus Mendicantium quibuscunque, apud Auinionem octaua die mensis Nouem- bris, anno Domini millesimo tricentesimo quin- quagesimo septimo. Cuius quidem pro- positionis thema fuit hoc.
units.tr: IN THE NAME OF THE FATHER, AND OF THE SON, AND OF THE HOLY SPIRIT, Amen. BEGINS THE PROPOSITION OF RICHARD, ARCHBISHOP OF ARMAGH, PRIMATE OF IRELAND, DELIVERED IN CONSISTORY BEFORE THE LORD POPE AND THE LORD CARDINALS AND PRELATES, FOR THE BENEFIT OF THE CLERGY AND THE CHRISTIAN PEOPLE, CONCERNING THE MATTER OF BEGGING AND OF PRIVILEGES AGAINST THE FRIARS OF WHATEVER MENDICANT ORDERS, AT AVIGNON, ON THE EIGHTH DAY OF THE MONTH OF NOVEMBER, IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1357. The theme of this proposition was this.

units.la: Nolite iudicare secundum faciem: sed iustum iudicium iudicate Iohann. 8. Pater Sanctissime, in principio mei sermonis protestor, quod non intendo aliquid asserere aut temere affirmare, quod fidei obuiet Christianæ aut doctrinæ Catholicæ, quod etiam non est intentionis meæ destructionem seu cassationem Ordinum Mendicantium approbatorum ab ecclesia, aut à summis Pontificibus confirmatum expetere, aut etiam suadere. Sed potius suadebo ipsos ordines debere reduci ad puritatem suæ institutionis primariæ: semper sanctitatis vestræ correctioni obedire paratus. Et vt ad materiam meam statim descendam: ecce, Pater sanctissime, accedens Londonijs pro mea ecclesia Armachanæ quibusdam negociis, Doctores aliquos satis doctos super mendicitate & mendicatione Christi Saluatoris nostri ex aduerso reperi disceptantes. Et sæpius inuitatus, vt populo prædicarem, septem aut octo sermones ibi protuli in vulgari, & sub protestatione præscripta in publico nouem conclusiones expressi, propter quas & quæ tunc dixi Fratres ad istam sanctam sedem, licet friuole, appellarunt.
units.tr: Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment, John 8. Most Holy Father, at the beginning of my address I protest that I do not intend to assert or rashly affirm anything that is contrary to the Christian faith or to Catholic doctrine. Nor is it my intention to seek, or even to urge, the destruction or abolition of the mendicant orders that have been approved by the Church and confirmed by the supreme Pontiffs. I would rather urge that these orders be brought back to the purity of their original institution, and I am ready always to obey the correction of Your Holiness. And to come straight to my subject: Most Holy Father, when I was in London on certain business for my church of Armagh, I found some fairly learned doctors disputing on the other side about the poverty and begging of Christ our Saviour. Often invited to preach to the people, I delivered seven or eight sermons there in the vernacular, and under the protest described above I set out in public nine conclusions, on account of which, and on account of what I then said, the friars appealed to this holy see, though frivolously.

units.la: Prima conclusio hæc erat: quod Dominus Iesus Christus in sua conuersatione humana semper pauper erat, non quia propter se paupertatem dilexit aut voluit.
units.tr: The first conclusion was this: that the Lord Jesus Christ, in his human conversation, was always poor, not because he loved or willed poverty for its own sake.

units.la: Secunda fuit, quod Dominus noster Iesus Christus nunquam spontanee mendicauit.
units.tr: The second was that our Lord Jesus Christ never begged of his own accord.

units.la: Tertia erat, quod Christus nunquam docuit spontanee mendicare.
units.tr: The third was that Christ never taught that one should beg of one's own accord.

units.la: Quarta conclusio erat, siue quartus articulus, quod Dominus noster Iesus Christus docuit non debere hominem spontanee mendicare.
units.tr: The fourth conclusion, or fourth article, was that our Lord Jesus Christ taught that a man ought not to beg of his own accord.

units.la: Quinta conclusio erat siue quintus articulus, quod nullus potest prudenter & sancte spontaneam mendicitatem super se assumere perpetuo obseruandam.
units.tr: The fifth conclusion, or fifth article, was that no one can prudently and holily take upon himself voluntary begging to be observed in perpetuity.

units.la: Sexta conclusio quod non est de regula Fratrum Minorum mendicitatem spontaneam obseruare.
units.tr: The sixth conclusion was that it is not part of the rule of the Friars Minor to observe voluntary begging.

units.la: Septima conclusio erat de materia illa, quod Bulla domini Alexandri Papæ quarti, quæ Magistrorum libellum condemnat, nullam præmissarum conclusionum impugnat.
units.tr: The seventh conclusion concerned that matter: that the bull of Pope Alexander IV, which condemns the little book of the Masters, does not impugn any of the aforesaid conclusions.

units.la: Octaua conclusio & prima de priuilegiorum materia erat ista: quod pro confessione Parochianorum alicuius ecclesiæ facienda cum exclusione loci alterius eligibilior est parochialis ecclesia, quam Fratrum oratorium siue ipsorum ecclesia.
units.tr: The eighth conclusion, and the first on the matter of privileges, was this: that for the confession of the parishioners of any church, with the exclusion of any other place, the parish church is a more suitable choice than the friars' oratory or their church.

units.la: Nona conclusio erat & secunda in ista materia, quod ad confessionem parochianorum cuiusuis ecclesiæ vni personæ singulariter faciendam, eligibilior est persona ordinaria seu ordinarii quam Fratrum persona.
units.tr: The ninth conclusion, and the second on this matter, was that for the confession of the parishioners of any church to be made to one particular person, an ordinary person or the ordinary is a more suitable choice than a friar.

units.la: Has conclusiones, Pater sanctissime, in publicis meis sermonibus, Scripturis sacris & rationibus tanquam probabiles suasi, vt potui, & in præsenti Deo duce suadebo. Et etiam declarabo aliqua graviora, quæ ibi tunc non dixi, sicut Fratribus ipsis ibi promisi, adiiciam: in præsenti sanctitati vestræ humiliter supplicans & deuote, quod in conclusionibus prætactis & rationibus, quas ad eas suadendas adduxi & adducam: & Fratrum rationibus ex aduerso iustum iudicium adhibeatur, vt si Fratrum rationes fuerint fortiores, sim ego punitus, si vero econtra, ipsi Fratres pro scandalis, detractionibus & conuiciis publice & occulte mihi per eos illatis, super qua materia malo tolerare quam agere, legitime puniantur. Obseruato quo ad omnia quod primo assumpsi: Nolite iudicare secundum faciem: sed iustum iudicium iudicate.
units.tr: These conclusions, Most Holy Father, I urged in my public sermons as probable, by holy Scripture and by reasons, as best I could; and I shall now urge them again, God being my guide. I shall also declare some weightier points which I did not then state, and add them, as I promised the friars themselves there. At present I humbly and devoutly beg Your Holiness that in the aforesaid conclusions and the reasons which I have adduced and shall adduce in support of them, and in the reasons of the friars on the other side, righteous judgment be applied; so that if the friars' reasons prove the stronger, I may be punished, but if the contrary, the friars themselves be lawfully punished for the scandals, detractions and reproaches inflicted on me by them, both publicly and in secret, a matter in which I would rather suffer evil than do it. Let this be observed in all things, as I first laid down: Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.

units.la: Sed quia secundum legem Dei & naturæ commune negocium priuato præferri debet: à priuilegiorum materia, quæ totum clerum & totum populum Christianum concernit, volo incipere. Et dico, vt mihi videtur, quod si quæratur quis locus est eligibilior pro confessione à Parochianis ecclesiæ singulariter facienda: videtur mihi quod sua parochialis ecclesia est locus eligibilior oratorio Fratrum siue ipsorum ecclesia, quia est pro conscientia Parochiani confessi huiusmodi locus securior & plura vitans incommoda, quam Fratrum oratorium. Quod Parochialis ecclesia sit locus securior, vt singulariter scilicet cum exclusione cuiuscunque loci alterius ibi fiat confessio, & etiam vt sepultura fiat inibi, quam Fratrum ecclesia, patet. Quia est locus à Deo & lege eius praeceptus. Dicitur enim Deuteronomii cap. 12. Haec sunt praecepta & iudicia, quae facere debetis. Et cito post: Ad locum quem elegerit Dominus Deus vester de cunctis tribubus vestris, vt ponat sumum nomen ibi & habitet in eo, venietis & offeretis in illo loco holocausta & victimas vestras, decimas & primitias manuum vestrarum, & vota atq; donaria primogenita boum & ovium. Et postea sequitur ibidem prohibitio hoc modo: Caue ne offeras holocausta tua in omni loco, quem videris; sed in loco quem elegit Dominus in una tribuum tuarum offeres hostias & facies quaecunq; praecipio tibi. Haec ibi. Vbi constat, quod non tantum est praeceptum, vt in loco electo à Deo (quem ecclesiam Parochialem iuxta verba praedicta debemus intelligere; siue accipere, in quo debemus accipere cuncta, quae praecepit Dominus ex sacramentis) facere debet quisque; de quibus est confessio facienda. Sicut patet Leuit. 4. cap. vbi dicitur, quod quicunq; per ignorantiam peccauerit, offeret sacerdoti; & ipse orabit pro eo, & dimittetur ei. Sed ecce etiam, quod alia loca quaecunque sunt à lege prohibita. Certum autem videtur, quod locus Fratrum non est à Deo per legem suam ad haec facienda electus; sed tantum à summis pontificibus est concessus, sed iuxta verba praemissa est de lege prohibitus. Cum ergo locus praeceptus sit certior loco de lege diuina prohibito, ac solummodo permissio aut concesso: sequi videtur, quod Parochialis ecclesia est locus certior siue securior ad confessionem Parochianorum suorum pandendam, quam oratorium Fratrum siue eorum ecclesia. Item Parochianus non haesitat nec suspicari habet (intelligo de cursu communi) quod sua Parochialis ecclesia suppositia sit interdicto ecclesiastico. Hoc autem verisimiliter poterit suspicari de Fratrum ecclesia. Vnde videtur quod ecclesia sua est locus sibi securior. Suadetur minor per decretalem illam, de sepulturis, in sexto, animarum periculis. vbi sub certo modo poena interdicti tam ecclesiae quam cimiterii infligitur quibuscunque religiosis, qui inducunt aliquos ad vouendum iuramento seu fide interposita vel aliàs promittendum, vt apud eorum ecclesias eligant sepulturam vel iam electam vltterius non immutent. Et communiter affirmatur, quod Fratres ita inducunt homines. Vnde constat, quod Parochianus verisimiliter poterit suspicari, quod loca eorum sunt suppositia interdicto ecclesiastico. Istud aliter confirmatur: quoniam videtur, quod nullus Parochianus sciens vt scire tenetur, quod sua Parochialis ecclesia est locus à Deo ad sacramenta exercenda electus atq; praeceptus, & locus Fratrum à lege prohibitus; ibi nisi informatus aut suasus à Fratribus eligeret sepeliri. Quoniam satis firmum videtur, quod nullus Parochianus ad hoc faciendum est à seculari aliquo taliter informatus, aut ita inductus; vel vt verius dicam seductus. Ex his videtur posse concludi, sicut fieri potest in materia morali, quod Parochialis ecclesia est pro confessione pandenda Parochianis suis locus securior loco Fratrum. Dixi, & dico secundo, quod Parochialis ecclesia Parochianis ipsius est pro confessione pandenda & etiam sepultura habenda locus utilior loco Fratrum. Primo quia est locus à Deo electus; ac per hoc à Deo amplius acceptatus quam Fratrum ecclesia; quae à Deo non est expresse electa: sicut nec à sua ecclesia, sed solum ad procurationem Fratrum concessa. Vnde videtur vtilior, ex quo est acceptior Deo. Item in parochiali ecclesia Parochianus, vt debet, rite confessus duplicis obedientiae meritum sibi acquirit; scilicet meritum obedientiae qua paret mandato Dei de confessione pandenda, & meritum obedientiae qua obedit praecepto diuino de loco ad hoc à Deo electo seruando. Hoc secundo merito obedientiae caret (vt videtur) quisquis apud Fratres quoscunq; confessus, cum nulla lex Parochiano praecipiat aut etiam illi suadeat, vt apud Fratres confiteatur, aut habeat sepulturam. Ergo Parochialis ecclesia est Parochianis pro istis exercendis locus utilior loco Fratrum. Item in Parochiali ecclesia sunt vbique aut quasi vbiq; aut esse debent de iure diuino & suae ecclesiae plures in decuplo communiter oratores, quam in ecclesiis Fratrum sint Fratres. Vnde debet quisque Parochianus verisimiliter aestimare, qui ibi per orationes plurium poterit amplius adiuuari, quam in Fratrum ecclesiis. Dixi & dico tertio, quod confessio facta in Parochiali ecclesia modo praedicto vitat plura incommoda, quam confessio facta in Fratrum ecclesia. Et similiter ibi habita sepultura. Quoniam ex quo ibi sunt vtilitas ampliot & maior securitas: econtra si omitteretur & fieret confessio singulariter, vt supra expressi, in Fratrum ecclesia, tolleretur securitas, ac etiam tollerentur vtilitates praemissae. Et haec sunt (nemo dubitat) grauia multum incommoda siue dispendia.
units.tr: But since, according to the law of God and of nature, the common cause ought to be preferred to the private, I wish to begin with the matter of privileges, which concerns the whole clergy and the whole Christian people. And I say, as it seems to me, that if it is asked which place is the more suitable for a parishioner to make his confession to one particular person, it seems to me that his parish church is a more suitable place than the friars' oratory or their church. For such a place is safer for the parishioner's conscience and avoids more inconveniences than the friars' oratory. That the parish church is the safer place, both for confession made there singly, with the exclusion of any other place, and for burial to be made there, rather than the friars' church, is plain. For it is a place commanded by God and by his law. For it is said in Deuteronomy, chapter 12: These are the precepts and judgments which you must observe. And soon after: To the place which the Lord your God shall choose out of all your tribes, to put his name there and dwell in it, you shall come and offer in that place your burnt offerings and victims, your tithes and the firstfruits of your hands, and your vows and gifts, and the firstborn of your oxen and sheep. And afterwards the same book gives the prohibition in this way: Take heed that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see; but in the place which the Lord shall choose in one of your tribes you shall offer your victims, and do all things that I command you. Thus far there. From which it is clear that there is not only a command that each man must do in the place chosen by God (which, according to the words above, we ought to understand as the parish church, or to take it so, in which we ought to receive all that the Lord has commanded concerning the sacraments, among which is the confession to be made), as is plain from Leviticus, chapter 4, where it is said that whoever sins through ignorance shall offer to the priest; and he shall pray for him, and it shall be forgiven him. But see also that every other place is forbidden by the law. Now it seems certain that the friars' place has not been chosen by God through his law for these acts, but has only been granted by the supreme pontiffs; and according to the words quoted, it is forbidden by the law. Since, therefore, a place commanded is more certain than a place forbidden by divine law, and a place merely permitted or conceded, it seems to follow that the parish church is a more certain or safer place for parishioners to unfold their confession than the friars' oratory or their church. Likewise, a parishioner has no hesitation and no reason to suspect (I speak of the ordinary course) that his parish church is subject to an ecclesiastical interdict. But he may probably suspect this of the friars' church. Hence it seems that his own church is the safer place for him. The minor premise is supported by that decretal, de sepulturis, in the Sixth Book, on the perils of souls, where a penalty of interdict, both of the church and of the cemetery, is inflicted in a certain form on any religious who induce persons, by oath or by pledge of faith or otherwise by promise, to choose burial at their churches, or not to change a burial already chosen. And it is commonly affirmed that the friars do thus induce men. Hence it is clear that a parishioner may probably suspect that their places are subject to ecclesiastical interdict. This is confirmed in another way: for it seems that no parishioner, knowing what he is bound to know, that his parish church is the place chosen and commanded by God for the exercise of the sacraments, and that the friars' place is forbidden by the law, would choose to be buried there unless he had been informed or persuaded by the friars. For it seems sufficiently firm that no parishioner is so informed, or so induced (or, to speak more truly, so seduced), by any secular person to do this. From these points it seems that one may conclude, as can be done in moral matters, that the parish church is for parishioners the safer place for unfolding their confession than the friars' place. I have said, and I say secondly, that the parish church is for the parishioners of that church the more useful place, both for making their confession and for having burial, than the friars' place. First, because it is a place chosen by God, and therefore more acceptable to God than the friars' church, which has not been expressly chosen by God, nor by its own church, but only conceded for the convenience of the friars. Hence it seems more useful, since it is more acceptable to God. Likewise, a parishioner who, as he ought, has duly confessed in the parish church acquires for himself a twofold merit of obedience: namely the merit of obedience by which he obeys God's command to unfold his confession, and the merit of obedience by which he obeys the divine precept to keep the place chosen by God for this. A man who confesses to any friars lacks this second merit of obedience (as it seems), since no law commands the parishioner, or even urges him, to confess to the friars or to have his burial with them. Therefore the parish church is a more useful place for parishioners for these acts than the friars' place. Likewise, in the parish church there are everywhere, or almost everywhere, or ought to be by divine right, and generally in its church, more than ten times as many people praying as there are friars in the friars' churches. Hence every parishioner may reasonably judge that he can be helped there by the prayers of many more than in the friars' churches. I have said, and I say thirdly, that confession made in the parish church in the aforesaid manner avoids more inconveniences than confession made in the friars' church, and likewise burial there. For since there is greater usefulness and greater security there, on the contrary, if confession were omitted and made singly, as I stated above, in the friars' church, both the security would be lost and the aforesaid advantages would be lost too. And these (no one doubts it) are very grave inconveniences or losses.

units.la: Dixi & dico secundo principaliter, si quaeratur, quae persona est eligibilior pro confessione Parochiani sui singulariter faciénda, scilicet an persona Fratris vel ordinarii sui persona? quod ordinarii persona eligibilior est censenda Fratrum personis, quia securior & vtilior. Et quia confessio sibi facta singulariter vitat plura incommoda & dispendia. Dico primo, quod ordinarii est persona securior: quia est (vt in articulo praecedenti suasi) persona à Deo praecepta & à sua ecclesia de lege communi. Et fratris persona de lege prohibita. Vnde consequitur, quod ordinarii persona est securior. Item persona ordinarii est Parochianis suis personis Fratrum amplius obligata. Vnde rationabiliter potest de ea confidere, quod sollicitior erit ad prouidendum eis, quam Frater, qui est sibi persona extranea. Sicut persona medici corporalis est aegroto magis carnaliter secura, quae est aegroto magis obligata. Item quia Parochianus de lege siue de cursu communi non haesitat nec haesitare habet de ordinarii sui persona, quod eius potestas absoluendi suos subditos sit ligata. De Fratrum vero personis habet verisimiliter suspicari, quod propter excommunicationes varias est in eas potestas testas ligata. Nec est dubium, quin securius sit homini confessionē pandere liberam potestatem habenti, quam habenti potestatem ligatam. Ergo persona ordinarii est certior siue securior. Probatur minor praetacta. Primo per ca. religiosi in Clementinū de decimis: vbi dicitur, quod ecclesias non habentes, qui novalium aut aliàs decimas ecclesiis debitas ad eos ex aliquo apropriare sibi praesumpserint, aut exquisitis fraudibus siue coloribus usurpare tentauerint &c. sententiam ex-communicationis incurrunt. Nec videtur ambiguum: Quod de iure diuino legatorum & liberè donatorum decimae sunt soluendae: & hoc ecclesiis & earum gratis. Quod etiam Innocentius dicit & Ostiensis affirmat. Unde sequitur, quod quicunque Fratres, qui de legatis eis & de eis donatis decimas ab ecclesiis subtrahunt, & eas sibi appropriant, sententiam excommunicationis incurrunt: cum de illis nunquam decimas soluant, vt communiter affirmatur. Secundo probatur minor praedicta per cap. Religiosi, de priuilegiis, in Clementinis: vbi omnes religiosi sunt excommunicati de facto, quia à sententiis latis per statuta prouincialia seu synodalia quoscunque absoluunt. A quibus sententiis, vt communiter affirmatur, ab ecclesiae praelatis & poenitentiariis eorundem saepe, imo communiter ligatos Fratres confessiones audientes absoluunt. Ego enim in mea dioecesi Armachana, vt puto, habeo duo milia subditorum, qui singulis annis per sententias excommunicationis latas contra homicidas voluntarios, fures publicos, incendiarios & istis consimiles sunt excommunicationis sententiis inuoluti: de quibus vix veniunt ad me seu poenitentiarios meos quadraginta in anno: & recipiunt sacramenta omnes tales, vt caeteri, & absoluuntur vel absoluti dicuntur, nec per alios quam per Fratres. Non dubium, cum nulli alii ipsos absoluunt, absoluti creduntur. Unde Parochianus potest verisimiliter suspicari, quod illi confessores sunt tali sententiae inuoluti: ita quod potestas sacerdotalis est in eis ligata. Et ita minus tutum est eis talibus confiteri, ex quo sine peccato mortali non possunt eos absoluere. Etsi illud credant ipsi confessi, consentiunt Fratrum peccatis, si absolutionem accipiant. Ait enim Apostolus ad Rom. primo cap. Qui talia agunt, digni sunt morte. Non solum autem qui talia faciunt, sed qui consentiunt facientibus. Et secundo Paralipomenon 19. cap. dicitur, quod Iehu Propheta dixit ad Iosaphat regem Iuda: Impio praebes auxilium, & his qui oderunt Dominum amici-tia iungeris. Et idcirco iram quidem Domini merebaris. Unde consequitur, quod securior est persona ordinarii, scilicet Curati, quam Fratrum personae. Idem etiam suadetur per cap. cupientes, de poenis in Clementinis, vbi triplex est lata excommunicationis sententia.
units.tr: I have said, and I say again, as a second main point: if it is asked which person is the more suitable to hear the individual confession of his parishioner, namely the friar or the parishioner's own ordinary, then the ordinary's person is to be judged the more suitable than the friars', because he is the safer and the more useful. The individual confession made to him also avoids many inconveniences and losses. I say first that the ordinary is the safer person, because (as I argued in the preceding article) he is a person commanded by God and by his Church under the common law, whereas the friar is a person prohibited by law. It follows that the ordinary is the safer person. Likewise, the ordinary is more bound to his parishioners than the friars are, since the friar is a stranger to them. So the parishioner can reasonably trust that the ordinary will be more careful to provide for them than a friar would be. The physician of the body is the more trustworthy to the sick man in bodily matters precisely because he is more bound to him. Again, the parishioner, by the ordinary course of law, does not doubt, and has no reason to doubt, that his ordinary's power to absolve his subjects is unimpeded. But concerning the friars he may reasonably suspect that, because of various excommunications, their power to absolve is tied up. Nor is there any doubt that it is safer to lay open one's confession to a man who has full power than to one who has restricted power. Therefore the ordinary's person is the more certain, or safer. The minor premise just stated is proved, first, by the chapter Religiosi in the Clementines, On Tithes, where it is said that those who do not have churches, and who presume to appropriate to themselves the tithes of new land or other tithes due to churches, or who attempt to usurp them by devised frauds or pretexts, etc., incur the sentence of excommunication. Nor does it seem doubtful that by divine law the tithes of bequests and freely given gifts are to be paid, and this to the churches and their ministers. Innocent also says so, and Ostiensis affirms it. Hence it follows that any friars who withdraw from the churches the tithes on bequests and gifts made to them, and appropriate them to themselves, incur the sentence of excommunication, since, as is commonly affirmed, they never pay tithes on such things. Secondly, the same minor premise is proved by the chapter Religiosi, On Privileges, in the Clementines, where all religious are excommunicated by the fact itself, because they absolve from sentences pronounced under provincial or synodal statutes, whoever they may be. As is commonly affirmed, the friars who hear confessions often absolve, or rather commonly absolve, those bound by these sentences, with the prelates of the churches and their penitentiaries. For I have in my diocese of Armagh, as I think, two thousand subjects who every year are caught up in sentences of excommunication pronounced against voluntary murderers, public thieves, arsonists and the like. Of these scarcely forty in a year come to me or to my penitentiaries, yet all such persons receive the sacraments like the rest and are or are said to be absolved, and this by no one but the friars. Since no others absolve them, they are believed to be absolved, no doubt. Hence the parishioner may reasonably suspect that those confessors are themselves caught up in such a sentence, so that their priestly power is tied. And so it is less safe to confess to such men, since without mortal sin they cannot absolve them. And even if the penitents themselves believe this, they consent to the sins of the friars if they receive absolution. For the Apostle says in Romans, chapter 1: Those who do such things are worthy of death; not only those who do them, but those who consent to those who do them. And in 2 Chronicles, chapter 19, it is said that the prophet Jehu said to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah: Do you help the wicked, and join yourself in friendship with those who hate the Lord? Therefore you deserved the wrath of the Lord. Hence it follows that the person of the ordinary, that is of the parish priest, is safer than the persons of the friars. The same is also urged by the chapter Cupientes, On Penalties, in the Clementines, where a threefold sentence of excommunication is pronounced.

units.la: Prima est lata in omnes religiosos, qui aliquos vt audientes à solutione decimarum ecclesiis debitarum retrahunt in sermonibus suis vel alibi proferre praesumunt: quod faciunt, vt fertur, communiter confessores de Fratribus. Affirmant enim in publico, quod nec de eleemosynis panis & vini, cerevisiae aut aliarum rerum huiusmodi modicarum teneantur donantes in decimando lucra mercationis ipsorum addecimare. Ego vero contrario affirmaui, quod de paruis, sicut de magnis donariis, tenentur inter lucra sua mentionem facere: quia alias possent mercatores quicunque totum lucrum totius anni per talia parua dona ita distrahere, quod de maximo lucro suo nihil debent penitus decimare, totum per modica distribuendo pauperibus, & illusio fieret iuri communi. Sunt ergo Fratres tales maioris excommunicationis sententiis inuoluti. Item per eandem decretalem, Cupientes, sunt omnes Fratres ab officio praedicationis suspensi, & consequenter excommunicati: qui infra certum terminum conscientiam eis confessis de decimis soluendis non faciunt, vbi vt verisimiliter aestimatur, omnes confessores deputati de fratribus, vel quasi omnes sunt ista sententia canonis inuoluti: quia, vt fertur communiter, & per eos qui eis confitentur, potest probari quod aliqui de hoc penitus nihil dicunt confessis eis, quicquid loquuntur, proferunt nuda verba non pro materia sed pro forma videlicet: quod non est conscientiam facere, sed magis illudere. Unde ad consensum constituentis canonem conscientiam facerent ipsos eis confessos de rebus quibuslibet decimandis de modo & de tempore informarent. Et quia non faciunt, non video, quin incidant in istam excommunicationis sententiam. Item per idem cap. Cupientes, omnes religiosi sunt excommunicati, qui aliquos ad vouendum iuramento vel fide media seu ad aliis promittendum inducunt, vt sepulturam apud eorum ecclesias eligant, vel iam electam vlterius non immutent. Quod tamen facere fratres affirmat clericorum & laicorum communis opinio. Et ad haec videtur ratio satis probabilis iam adducta ad confirmationem secundae rationis primae conclusionis articuli praecedentis. Item quod persona ordinarii sit Parochiano suo securior, aliter suadetur: scil. quia de eius persona rationabiliter Parochianus poterit iudicare, quod quo ad hoc scilicet per poenitentiam congruam & vtilem sibi imponendam pro suis peccatis est iudex sibi minus suspectus seu aequior. Quoniam quaestum subsidii temporalis per confessionis suae auditionem in suo ordinario non habet supponere aut aliqualiter suspicari: cum necessaria vitae de lege Dei & suae ecclesiae ordinarii ministerio sint annexa. De personis vero Fratrum econtra. Quoniam, vt in appellatione, quam contra me fecerunt in Anglia, continetur, ex sua fundatione ad mendicitatem & pauperartatem artissimam asserunt se constrictos, non obstante in eis facultate audiendi confessiones omnium sibi confiteri volentium. Unde quaestum releuationis mendicitatis in eis causam auditionis confessionis hominis extranei probabiliter Parochianus poterit suspicari, & rationabiliter in animo suo ita arguet, cur iste mendicus hic meam confessionem audiendo & à necessariis in victu sibi acquirendis desisteret, nisi de metale suffragium expectaret? Unde cum egestas ad peccatum, cuius mediatione indigentiae succurratur, impellat, iuxta illud Salomonis Proverbiorum 30. capit. Mendicitatem & diuitias non dederis mihi: sed tribue tantum victui meo necessaria: ne forte satiatus illiciar ad negandum te, & dicam, quis est Dominus & egestate compulsus furer, & periurem nomen Dei mei. Consequitur, quod pro omni genere peccatorum eleemosynā applicando, qua poterit eius mendicitas releuari, velit mihi imponere; & ita non ero spiritualiter bene sanatus. Saluator enim suis discipulis quaerentibus: Quare non potuimus eiicere daemonium illud ? respondit: Hoc autem genus daemoniorum non eiicitur nisi per orationem & ieiunium. Matth. 17. c. Ex quo dicto colligitur, quod sicut cuicunq; morbo corporali diuerso diuersa congruit medicina: sic spirituali morbo cuilibet est prouidenda propria medicina, qualem iste medicus circa sua intentus, vt suspicor, mihi nullatenus ministrabit. Confirmatur haec ratio: quoniam satis apparet in facto, quod isti Fratres vbique per orbem post priuilegium de confessionibus audiendis obtentum monasteria pulcherrima & regalia palatia construxerunt. Cuius rei euidentia siue causa praecipua illa est confessiones audiendi facultas: quoniam antequam illam facultatem haberent, nullatenus talia construere potuerunt. Item nunquam auditur, quod Fratres ad refectionem defectuum parochialis ecclesiae aut stratae communis seu ad pontium reformandos defectus tales eleemosynas largiendas confessis imponunt: nec Minores, vt eas Praedicatoribus, aut Praedicatores seu quicunq; de aliis Mendicantium ordinibus Minoribus largiantur: sed imponunt cunctā sibi & suo ordini applicantes. Vnde verisimiliter poterit iudicari, quod quaestus proprius est in causa, quare talis mendicus pro persona extranea est ita sollicitus, quod tempus mendicationis negligit illi extraneo totus intentus. Item feci ad hoc & facio semper in praesenti quintam rationem, cuius conclusionem nolebam asserere. Dixi tamen in publico, & in praesenti dico, quod rationem illam nesciebam dissoluere. Conclusio illius rationis est ista: quia quisq; parochianus confessus Fratribus, Curatis suis ordinariis neglectis iuxta potestatem, quam habent, post confessionem huiusmodi remanet in peccato mortali: & a nullo peccato mortali absoluitur.
units.tr: The first is pronounced against all religious who, in their sermons or elsewhere, presume to draw any of their hearers away from paying tithes owed to churches. As is said, confessors from among the friars commonly do this. For they openly declare that those who give alms of bread, wine, beer, or other such small things are not bound to add to their tithe the profits of their trade from such gifts. I, on the contrary, have maintained that they are bound to mention these small gifts among their profits, just as they must for large ones; otherwise merchants could distribute the whole profit of the year through such small gifts to the poor, so that they would owe no tithe at all on their greatest profit, and the common law would be mocked. Therefore the friars are caught up in the sentences of greater excommunication. Again, by the same decretal, Cupientes, all friars are suspended from the office of preaching, and consequently excommunicated, who within a certain time do not make their confessors to pay the tithes due. There, as is reasonably judged, all the confessors appointed from among the friars, or almost all, are caught up in the sentence of this canon. For, as is commonly said, and as can be proved by those who confess to them, some of them say nothing at all about this to those confessing, whatever they may say; they utter bare words, not for the substance but only for the form. This is not to make conscience but rather to mock it. So, to meet the intention of the author of the canon, they would have to inform those confessing to them about the tithing of all kinds of things, as to measure and time. And since they do not do so, I see no reason why they should not fall under this sentence of excommunication. Again, by the same chapter, Cupientes, all religious are excommunicated who induce anyone, by oath or by a pledge of faith, or by any other promise, to choose burial in their churches, or to change a burial place already chosen. That friars do this is affirmed by the common opinion of clergy and laity alike. And to this the reason already adduced, quite probable, seems to apply, to confirm the second reason of the first conclusion of the preceding article. Again, that the ordinary's person is safer for his parishioner is argued in another way, namely: the parishioner can reasonably judge that the ordinary, as to this, that is in imposing a fitting and useful penance for his sins, is a judge less suspect to him and fairer. For he does not have to suspect or in any way fear that the ordinary is seeking gain of temporal support through the hearing of his confession, since the necessities of life are bound by the law of God and of his Church to the ministry of the ordinary. Concerning the friars' persons, on the other hand, the opposite holds. For, as is contained in the appeal which they made against me in England, they assert that by their foundation they are bound to mendicancy and the most extreme poverty, notwithstanding their faculty to hear the confessions of all who wish to confess to them. Hence the parishioner may reasonably suspect that, because they seek profit for relieving their mendicancy, the reason for hearing a stranger's confession is gain; and he will reason in his own mind, not unreasonably: why would this beggar, by hearing my confession, abstain from acquiring what is necessary for his livelihood, unless he expected some reward of a material kind? Hence, since poverty drives men to sin, by which indigence is relieved, according to that saying of Solomon in Proverbs 30: Give me neither poverty nor riches; give me only the necessities of my food, lest perhaps, being full, I be tempted to deny you and say, Who is the Lord? or, being compelled by want, I steal and perjure the name of my God. It follows that he will wish to impose on me, for every kind of sin, an alms-giving by which his mendicancy may be relieved; and so I shall not be spiritually well healed. For the Saviour, when his disciples asked, Why could we not cast out that demon? answered: This kind of demon is not cast out except by prayer and fasting, Matthew 17. From that saying it is gathered that just as a different bodily disease calls for a different medicine, so for any spiritual disease its own proper remedy must be provided, which this physician, who is busy with his own affairs, as I suspect, will by no means supply to me. This reasoning is confirmed, for it appears plainly in fact that these friars everywhere in the world, after obtaining the privilege of hearing confessions, have built most beautiful monasteries and royal palaces. The chief evidence or cause of this is the faculty of hearing confessions, for before they had that faculty they could never have built such things. Again, it is never heard that friars, for the repair of defects in a parish church, or of a common road, or for the repair of bridges, impose such alms-giving on their penitents; nor do the Minorites give these to the Preachers, nor the Preachers to the Minorites, or to any of the other mendicant orders; but they impose everything applicable to themselves and their own order. Hence it may probably be judged that private gain is at stake, which is why such a beggar is so anxious about a stranger's person that, intent wholly on the stranger, he neglects the time of begging. Again, I have made, and still do make, in the present, a fifth reason, the conclusion of which I was unwilling to assert. Yet I have said in public, and say now, that I did not know how to dissolve that reason. The conclusion of that reason is this: because every parishioner who has confessed to the friars, having neglected his ordinary parish priest, according to the power they have, remains after such a confession in mortal sin, and is absolved from no mortal sin.

units.la: Ad hanc conclusionem aliqualiter suadendam, nitebar vnum principium suadere, quod etiam principium propter constitutionem Iohanninam Vae electionis volebam astruere: quoniam ibi damnantur de dictis Magistri Ioannis de Poliaco tres subsequentes articuli. Primus est, quod confessi Fratribus habentibus licentiam generalem audiendi confessiones tenentur eadem peccata, quae confessi fuerunt, iterum confiteri proprio sacerdoti. Secundus articulus est, quod stante statuto, Omnis utriusq; sexus edito in concilio generali Romanus pontifex non potest facere, quod Parochiani non teneantur confiteri omnia sua peccata semel in anno suo proprio sacerdoti, quem dicit Parochialem curatum, imo nec Deus posset hoc facere, quia (vt dicebat) hoc implicat contradictionem. Tertius articulus est, quod Papa non potest dare generalem potestatem audiendi confessiones, quin teneantur eadem peccata iterum confiteri suo proprio sacerdoti, quem dicit (vt praemittitur) Parochialem Curatum. Et erat principium ad hoc probandum, quod simul possunt stare: & nullatenus repugnat, quod quisq; Parochianus Fratribus sit confessus, & quod idem Parochianus teneatur sub praecepto ecclesiae omnia sua peccata semel in anno suo sacerdoti proprio siue ordinario confiteri.
units.tr: To support this conclusion somewhat, I was trying to establish one principle, which I also wanted to assert on the basis of the Johannine constitution Vae electionis, since in that document three of the following articles from the teaching of Master John of Poilly are condemned. The first is that those who have confessed to Friars who hold a general licence to hear confessions are bound to confess the same sins again to their own priest. The second article is that, while the statute Omnis utriusque sexus, issued by a general council, stands, the Roman pontiff cannot make it so that parishioners are not bound to confess all their sins once a year to their own priest, whom he calls the parish curate. Indeed, God himself could not do this, because (as he used to say) it implies a contradiction. The third article is that the Pope cannot grant a general power to hear confessions without the penitents being bound to confess the same sins again to their own priest, whom he calls (as has been said) the parish curate. My principle for proving this was that both can stand together, and that it is in no way inconsistent for a parishioner to have confessed to the Friars and for the same parishioner, under the precept of the Church, to be bound to confess all his sins once a year to his own priest or ordinary.

units.la: Primo istud suasi: quia non amplius repugnare videretur confiteri Fratribus, & nihilominus obligare siue teneri semel in anno omnia sua peccata mortalia suo ordinario siue suo sacerdoti proprio confiteri, intelligendo de confessione quantum ad id quod est iterabile in eadem, quum sibi repugnant semel aut saepius apud Fratres offerre & teneri siue obligari, vt semel aut bis siue ter teneatur in sua ecclesia parochiali in anno offerre: cum vnus actus sit iterabilis meritorie, sicut alter. Ista vero duo vltima in nullo sibi repugnant. Igitur nec duo prima mutuo se impugnant. Item nullus ambigit, quin quaecunq; duae propositiones affirmatiue super simili actu iterabili a diuersis personis aut ab eadem persona pro diuersis locis ac diuersis temporibus prolatae valeant simul stare, sicut q iste Parochianus audiet vnam missam vel plures apud Parochialem ecclesiam, saltem semel in mense, & maxime si vterq; actus sit meritorius & Deo acceptus, qualis actus non dubium extat consessio. Omnes autem Doctores in illo concordant, quod actus confessionis est iterabilis meritorie, quantum ad expressionem peccatorum & poenitentiam. Et nos omnes saepe sic agimus Deo, vt credimus, sic praestantes obsequium. Nec mirum est, quoniam actus tales iterabiles meritorie possunt cadere sub praecepto, vt supra expressi in principio articuli praecedentis. Possunt igitur confessio facienda Fratri & confessio eorundem peccatorum ordinario facienda cadere sub praecepto. Igitur multo fortius potest vna confessio sub praecepto venire, altera libera remanente. Item Dn. Martinus Papa quartus, qui Fratribus Minoribus facultatem audiendi confessiones concessit, in ipsius priuilegii fine sic dicit: Volumus autem quod hi qui Fratribus confitebuntur eisdem suis Parochialibus presbyteris confiteri saltem semel in anno, prout generale concilium statuit, nihilominus teneantur: quodque idem Fratres eos ad hoc diligenter & efficaciter secundum datam eis a Domino gratiam exhortentur. Nulli ergo &c. Haec ibi. Vnde iste Dominus Papa mandat aperte, quod non obstante confessione facta Fratri, confitens teneatur iuxta concilii generalis statutum eadem peccata suo presbytero Parochiali confiteri. Sed huic decreto videtur haec constitutio Iohannina Vae electionis iuxta sensum, quem Fratres de ea concipiunt obuiare, & populum eo modo informant in publico seipsos (vt videtur) & illos damnando, si praemissum mandatum Domini Martini sit firmum, sicut firmum videtur esse iuxta rationes praemissas. Ideo, pater sanctissime, ne tantum dispendium continuetur in populo Christiano, amore Crucifixi illa constitutio cum celeritate possibili declaretur. Mihi enim videtur, quod ita potest intelligi, & sic intelligo: quod nullus confessus Fratribus tenetur propter defectum potestatis absoluendi in Fratribus eadem peccata confiteri suo proprio sacerdoti. Cuius contrarium Magister Iohannes de Poliaco intellexisse videtur. Item videtur valde mirabile, qua fronte Fratres audentastruere, quod simul stare non possunt, vt quis sit confessus Fratribus de suis criminibus, & eadem teneatur suo ordinario siue suo sacerdoti proprio confiteri: cū econtra in sua regula (vt communiter affirmatur) habeant, quod quicunque in ordine ipsorum professus seu habitum ipsorum assumeat in sua professione aut in suo ingressu, non obstante quacunque confessione priori facta, teneatur vni ipsorum omnia sua crimina confiteri. Cur ei abnegant de nobis posse seruari, quod de seipsis obseruatur. Videtur mirabile. Item Dominus Benedictus vndecimus in constitutione sua revocatoria constitutionis Bonifacii Super cathedram, quae incipit: Si bene recordor, ad perpetuum fratribus mandat, quod ipsi hortentur eis confessos, quod eadem sua peccata confiteantur suo proprio sacerdoti. Ipse ergo sensit, vt videtur, quod vna confessio obligationem ad alteram omnino non tollat. Quoniam si in simul stare possunt, potest alterum praecipi, altero libero remanente, vt mihi videtur, iuxta adducta superius. Item sanctus Augustinus in De vera & falsa poenitentia, capitulo nono, & sanctus Thomas & Bonaventura, & alii Doctores & Glossatores catholici saepe affirmant, quod expedit eadem peccata saepius confiteri. Cur igitur illud sub peccato venire non possit propter meritum in populo non video cumulandum. Nam sicut posset sancte praecipi a praelato, quod quilibet Parochianus audiret singulis diebus dominicis duas missas.
