Hoc igitur principio probabiliter suasio, nimis dura videtur posse inferri conclusio, scilicet quod quisque Parochianus confessus Fratri, ordinariis suis curatis omissis, per totum annum neglectis, (pretiis siue contemptis: est contemptor siue transgressor mandati ecclesiae contenti in illa decretali, Omnis utriusque sexus: & per consequens redit a fratre cum peccato mortali: Et cum Deus non remittat peccatum mortale vnum, nisi mortalia cuncta relaxet: infertur ulterius, quod taliter a fratre confessus reuertitur cum omnibus peccatis mortalibus, cum quibus oneratus accessit ad fratrem. Et quid isto intolerabilius aut damnosius possit in ecclesia Christi accidere? Vere Pater Sanctissime, istam rationem nescio soluere, nec scio in praesenti dissoluere. Vnde rogaui Londoniis ipsos Fratres in publico, vt me informarent verbo vel scripto, qualiter possem praemissam rationem dissoluere. Sed illud huc vsque non valui obtinere ab eis. Igitur mihi videtur, quod ex praemissis possum inferre, quod persona curati ordinarii est Parochiano secuftor pro confessione pandenda singulariter scilicet vni personae quam fratris persona. Super quo, Pater Sanctissime, Nolite iudicare secundum faciem: sed rectum iudicium iudicate.
units.tr: First I argued this: it would seem no more inconsistent to confess to the Friars and nevertheless to be obliged, or bound, to confess all one's mortal sins once a year to one's ordinary or own priest, understanding this of confession as far as it is something that can be repeated. For it is no more inconsistent to offer one's confession once or several times to the Friars and to be bound to offer it once, twice or three times a year in one's own parish church, since one act is meritoriously repeatable, just as the other is. Those last two points are in no way inconsistent with each other, so neither are the first two mutually opposed. Again, no one doubts that any two affirmative propositions about a similar repeatable act, uttered by different persons, or by the same person for different places and different times, can stand together. For example, this parishioner may hear one Mass or several at the parish church, at least once a month, and especially if both acts are meritorious and acceptable to God, which confession certainly is. Moreover, all the Doctors agree that the act of confession is meritoriously repeatable as far as the declaring of sins and penance go. We all often act in this way, as we believe, offering obedience to God. Nor is it surprising, since such meritoriously repeatable acts can fall under a precept, as I set out above at the beginning of the previous article. Therefore confessing to a Friar and confessing the same sins to one's ordinary can both fall under a precept. Much more strongly, then, one confession can come under a precept while the other remains free. Again, Lord Pope Martin IV, who granted the Friars Minor the faculty of hearing confessions, says at the end of that privilege: We wish, however, that those who confess to the Friars nevertheless be bound to confess the same sins to their own parish priests at least once a year, as the general council has decreed; and that the same Friars diligently and effectively exhort them to this, according to the grace given them by the Lord. Therefore let no one &c. So far there. Hence this Lord Pope plainly commands that, notwithstanding a confession made to a Friar, the penitent is bound, according to the statute of the general council, to confess the same sins to his parish priest. But the constitution Vae electionis, according to the sense which the Friars take from it and which they openly impress on the people, seems to stand against this decree, and (it seems) it condemns both themselves and those people, if the aforesaid mandate of Lord Martin is firm, as it seems firm according to the reasons given above. Therefore, most holy Father, lest so great a loss continue for the Christian people, for the love of the Crucified let that constitution be declared as quickly as possible. For it seems to me that it can be understood in this way, and so I understand it: that no one who has confessed to the Friars is bound, on account of a lack of power to absolve, to confess the same sins to his own priest. Master John of Poilly seems to have understood the opposite. Again, it seems very strange with what effrontery the Friars dare to assert that a man cannot both confess his crimes to the Friars and be bound to confess the same things to his ordinary or own priest. On the contrary, in their rule (as is commonly affirmed) they have it that whoever is professed in their order, or takes up their habit at his profession or entry, must confess all his crimes to one of them, notwithstanding any earlier confession. Why do they deny that we can keep what they themselves observe? It seems strange. Again, Lord Benedict XI, in his constitution revoking the constitution of Boniface Super cathedram, which begins Si bene recordor, commands the Friars in perpetuity that they should exhort their penitents to confess the same sins to their own priest. He therefore thought, as it seems, that one confession does not altogether remove the obligation to another. For if both can stand together, one can be commanded while the other remains free, as it seems to me, according to what was adduced above. Again, St Augustine in De vera et falsa poenitentia, chapter nine, and St Thomas and Bonaventure, and other catholic Doctors and Glossators, often affirm that it is profitable to confess the same sins more often. Why, then, I do not see that this cannot come under a sin on account of merit, which is not to be heaped up among the people. For just as a prelate could rightly command that every parishioner hear two Masses on each Sunday... Having argued this principle with some probability, a conclusion seems to follow that is too harsh: namely, that any parishioner who has confessed to a Friar, having neglected his ordinary curates and let them go unheeded for the whole year (or despised them), is a contemner or transgressor of the church's command contained in that decretal Omnis utriusque sexus; and consequently he comes from the Friar with mortal sin. And since God does not remit one mortal sin unless he remits all mortal sins, it further follows that whoever has so confessed to a Friar returns with all the mortal sins with which he came burdened to the Friar. And what could happen in the Church of Christ that is more intolerable or more harmful than this? Truly, most holy Father, I do not know how to answer this argument, nor do I know how to resolve it at present. Therefore at London I asked the Friars themselves publicly to inform me, by word or in writing, how I might resolve the aforesaid argument. But so far I have not been able to obtain this from them. It seems to me, then, that from what has been said I can infer that the person of the ordinary curate is more suitable for the parishioner to disclose his confession to, singly, that is, to one person, rather than the person of a Friar. On this matter, most holy Father, Judge not according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment.

units.la: Dico secundo & dixi, quod persona ordinarii est Parochiano suo vtilior pro sua confessione pandenda, quam fratris persona; quia est persona a lege Dei & suae ecclesiae ordinata atque de mandato Dei ad illud ministerium explendum exhibita. Frater vero ex sola concessione siue licentia summi pontificis ad id obtinet facultatem. Nec videtur ambiguum, quin quisque obseruando siue sequendo praeceptum vtilius sibi agit, quam praecepto neglecto sequendo siue obseruando licentiam: cum sequendo solam licentiam nullus ob hoc praemium mereatur: & quisque obseruando praeceptum mereatur. Vnde consequitur, quod vtilius confiteri potest quisque Parochianus (de cursu communi intelligo) ordinario suo quam cuique Fratri. Non tamen nego, quin raro in casu contrarium possit contingere: sicut cum ordinarius ex aliqua causa certa redditur suo Parochiano suspectus. Item hoc sequi videtur, sicut in priori articulo: quia suo ordinario confitendo habet duplicis obedientiae meritum, scil. obedientiae quo ad legem confessionis, & etiam quo ad legem personae. Et confitendo fratri caret horum meritorum praemio. Secundo cum non sit Parochianis praeceptum siue consultum, quod Fratribus sint confessi. Vnde confiteri ordinario videtur sibi vtilius. Item persona ordinarii est amplius suo Parochiano obligata, quam fratris persona & amore sancto, vt quisque de cursu communi debet supponere amplius, vt tenetur ex cura suo Parochiano magis afsecta. Vnde videtur, quod sollicitior erit ad vtilem medicinam spiritualem sibi adhibendam, quam Frater, cum sit sibi extraneus. Igitur ex illo capite videtur confessio vtilior. Item quia iuxta conclusionem immediate praemissam persona ordinarii est ad hoc persona securior: vnde consequitur, quod est vtilior. Item Innocentius in cap. illo, Ut si animarum, vnam causam ad istam conclusionem assignat, scilicet quia facilior ad curatum, quam ad extraneum habetur accessus, Concludens quod vtilius pandenda est illi Parochiani confessio. Et haec causa specialiter habet locum in causa infirmitatis de nocte, quando non poterit haberi accessus ad Fratrem, nec Fratri ad infirmum: cum tamen de nocte patet accessus ad Curatum. Ita quod tunc non obstante consessione antea facta fratri Parochianum oportebit ordinario confiteri, vbi illi confesso multum esset expediens, quod ordinarius suam vitam priorem agnoscerer: quoniam sic posset sibi poenitentiam magis aptam imponere, cum sit notum, quod quanto quisque saepius remissionem acceperit de peccatis, & quanto peccata ante remissa graviora existunt, tanto redditur gravius sequens delictum. Qualiter ergo eo casu poterit ordinarius Parochiano aptam & congruam poenitentiam ignorans sua propria peccata imponere, aut saltem tam congruam, sicuti sicut eius priorem vitam agnosceret? Omnino igitur, vt cerno, vtilius esset confessio propter casus huiusmodi ordinario confiteri Fratri. Item Innocentius secundam causam adduxit, scilicet quod in confessione ordinario facta est erubescentia amplior, quam cum confessio est Fratri facta: quoniam quisque amplius erubescit pandere sua peccata illi, quem quotidie cernit praesentem, quam vni extraneo, quem fortasis non videt nisi semel in anno. Item multum est vtile vxoratis, vt vnus suam & suae vxoris confessione audiat indiuise: quia sic eorum confessor tanquam medicus singulorum duorum membrorum vni corporis vtilius potest languidis in spiritu, sicut infirmis corporaliter prouidere, quam duo medici: quorum vnus vnum membrum duntaxat, & secundus medicus aliud membrum solummodo curare laborat. Vir vero & mulier vnum sunt corpus. Itaq; ait Saluator: Iam non sunt duo, sed vna caro, Matth. 19. cap. Satis ex istis videtur, quod persona ordinarii est persona vtilior pro sui patochiani confessione illi pandenda, quam fratris persona. Super quo, pater sanctissime, Nolite iudicare secundum faciem: sed iustum iudicium iudicate.
units.tr: Second, I say and have said that the person of the ordinary is more useful to his parishioner for disclosing his confession than the person of a Friar. For he is a person ordained by the law of God and of his Church, and presented by the command of God to fulfil that ministry. The Friar, on the other hand, obtains that faculty from the sole concession or licence of the supreme pontiff. Nor does it seem doubtful that anyone who observes or follows a precept does himself more good than one who neglects the precept and follows or observes a mere licence. For by following only a licence no one merits a reward for this, but by observing a precept one does merit. Hence it follows that any parishioner (I mean in the ordinary course) can confess more profitably to his ordinary than to any Friar. I do not deny, however, that in rare cases the opposite may happen, for example when the ordinary is for some certain cause suspect to his parishioner. Again, this seems to follow, as in the previous article: for by confessing to his ordinary he has the merit of a double obedience, namely obedience to the law of confession and also obedience to the law concerning the person. But by confessing to a Friar he lacks the reward of these merits. Secondly, since there is no precept or counsel for parishioners to confess to Friars, confessing to the ordinary seems to be more profitable for him. Again, the person of the ordinary is more bound to his parishioner than the person of a Friar, and by holy love, as anyone in the ordinary course ought to assume, he is more bound, in that he is more attached to his parishioner through the cure of souls. Hence it seems that he will be more careful in applying to him a useful spiritual medicine than a Friar, since the Friar is a stranger to him. So from this point of view confession seems more profitable. Again, because by the conclusion immediately premised the person of the ordinary is the safer person for this purpose, it follows that he is more profitable. Again, Innocent, in that chapter Ut si animarum, assigns one reason for this conclusion, namely that access to the curate is easier than to a stranger, and concludes that the parishioner's confession ought to be disclosed more profitably to that curate. This reason applies especially in a case of sickness by night, when access to the Friar cannot be had, nor the Friar's access to the sick man, whereas by night access to the curate is open. So in that case, notwithstanding a confession previously made to a Friar, the parishioner will have to confess to his ordinary, where it would be very useful for that penitent that the ordinary recognise his earlier life. For thus he could impose on him a penance more fitting, since it is well known that the more often a person has received remission of sins, and the more grave the sins previously remitted, the more serious his subsequent offence becomes. How, then, in that case can the ordinary impose on the parishioner a fitting and proper penance if he does not know his own sins, or at least a penance as proper as he would impose if he knew his earlier life? Altogether, then, as I see it, it would be more profitable for such cases to confess to the ordinary rather than to the Friar. Again, Innocent adduced a second cause, namely that in confession made to the ordinary there is greater shame than when the confession is made to a Friar: for a person blushes more to disclose his sins to one whom he sees every day present, than to a stranger whom perhaps he sees only once a year. Again, it is very useful for married people that one man hear the confession of himself and his wife together, indivisibly: for thus their confessor, like a physician of the two members of one body, can more profitably provide for those sick in spirit, just as physicians provide for the bodily sick, than two physicians, of whom one labours to cure only one member and the second physician labours to cure only the other member. But husband and wife are one body. So the Saviour says: So they are no longer two, but one flesh, Matth. 19. From these things it seems sufficiently clear that the person of the ordinary is a more useful person for his parishioner to disclose his confession to than the person of a Friar. On this matter, most holy Father, Judge not according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment.

units.la: Dico tertio, vt tunc dixi, quod confessio facta ordinario singulariter, vt praescripti, vitat plura incommoda siue dispendia, quam facta fratris persona. Vbi incepi dilatare materiam suadendo quod Priuilegia ea quae in capitulo Dudum, expressiuntur, Fratribus esse concessa, & etiam alia multiplicia afferunt & inducunt dispendia: & per consequens obseruantia iuris communis in illorum priuilegiorum materia multa vitat incommoda. Dico ergo, quod priuilegiorum horum obseruantia non solum abusus eorum a fratribus, afferunt multa incommoda confessis, curatis, clero, populo Christiano & fratribus. Dico primo, quod horum priuilegiorum abusus a fratribus plurima incommoda afferunt confessis eisdem: quoniam auferunt securitatem praetactam in prima conclusione huius articuli. Item vtilitates praescriptas in secunda conclusione huius articuli: quarum oblatio infert confessis fratribus contraria eis incommoda, quae debent quasi intolerabilia iudicari. Item iuxta verba Domini Innocentii quarti, vbi supra, alia plurima dispendia inde proueniunt. Dixit enim hoc modo: Attendentes quod ex vsurpatione huiusmodi non tantum contemptum & indeuotionem populi producunt contra proprios sacerdotes: verum erubescentia, quae est maxima pars poenitentiae, tollitur: cum quis non proprio sacerdoti, quem habet continuum & praesentem, sed alieno & aliquando transeunti, ad quem difficilis & aliquando impossibilis est recursus, sua trimina confitetur. Ecce incommoda confessis tria, scil. contemptus proprii sacerdotis: & indeuotio & sublatio erubescentia, q maximam poenitentiae partem affirmat: quae ex confessione facta fratribus proueniunt & sequuntur immediate. Quoniam damnabilis etiam est oblationum detentio & periculosa detractio decimarum. Quae non (vt quidam mendaciter asserunt (velut ceremonialia transeunt: sed ei a quo omnia recepimus in signum domini reseruari parochialibus ecclesiis indixerunt. Haec ibi. Vbi duo alia damna adiungit: scilicet detentionem oblationum, quae solent a confitentibus saepe solui eis, qui eorum confessionem auscultant, & Fratres eas sibi appropriant, cum parochialibus ecclesiis debeantur; & est in Fratribus damnabile, vt affirmat. Quae etiam duo sunt curatis damnosa: quia ea, quae pro victu eis de lege Dei & suae ecclesiae prouidentur, per fratres ratione huius priuilegii subtrahuntur. Dicitur enim Num. 18. cap. Omnia quae sanctificantur a filiis Israel, tibi tradidi & filiis tuis pro officio sacerdotali legitima sempiterna. Et ibidem: Omnis oblatio & sacrificium & quicquid pro peccato atq; delicto redditur mihi aut accedit in sancta sanctorum, tuum erit & filiorum tuorum. Item per vsum horum priuilegiorum a fratribus proueniit ipsis curatis vnum aliud mirabile dispendium: scilicet quod vultus suorum peccorum, quorum curam ab episcopo suo recipiunt, non agnoscunt. Quod in curam gerente carnalem de animalibus quibuscunq; esset damnosum. Item est valde damnosum curatis a suis Parochianis contemni: & tamen contemptus eorum, vt supra Innocentius affirmat, procedit in populis ex hoc, quod Parochiani ipsorum Fratribus confitentur. Item est grauius damnum curatis, quod occasione abusus priuilegiorum fratribus concessorum quo ad tres quartas omnium funeralium & etiam omnium aliter prouenientium fratribus ex legatione siue donatione distincte siue indistincte: ad vsus quoscunq; in capitulo, Dudum, concessas; & quo ad quartam concessam curatis & ibi taxatam. Quam quartam de multis legatis donatis atque oblatis fratres non soluunt curatis, sed infinitis cautelis adhibitis, vt curati asserunt, ipsi fratres sibi appropriant diuersis quaestiis coloribus, quod inter eos & fratres quasi vbique in populis Christianis sunt lites, contentiones & iurgia infinita: ita quod in locis quamplurimis a verbis peruenitur ad verbera, & in mentibus caritas procul abiicitur. Quae etiam incommoda curatis ex alterius priuilegii abusu proueniunt: scilicet quod cum fratres habent conseruatorias duas, nolunt curatos aut alios habentes quaestiones cum ipsis coram propinquiore suo conseruatore facere ad iudicium euocari: sed citari eos faciunt coram magis ab eis remoto, vt propter vexationis timorem, vt dicitur, compellant eos a causarum suarum prosecutione desistere; quod in mea prouincia saepius actum extitit, vt aliqui in ista curia praesentes affirmant: & est super hoc fama communis. Haec & alia multa incommoda ex vsu, vel verius ex abusu priuilegiorum fratribus concessorum proueniunt in Curatis.
units.tr: I say thirdly, as I said then, that confession made singly to the ordinary, as prescribed, avoids many inconveniences and losses that confession made to a friar brings. Here I began to expand on the matter, arguing that the privileges expressed in the chapter Dudum were granted to the friars, and that they also bring about and cause many other kinds of loss. Consequently, observance of the common law in the matter of those privileges avoids many inconveniences. I say, therefore, that the observance of these privileges causes many inconveniences, not only through the friars' abuse of them, for the penitents, the parish priests, the clergy, the Christian people and the friars themselves. First, I say that the abuse of these privileges by the friars brings many inconveniences to the penitents themselves, since it takes away the security mentioned in the first conclusion of this article, and the advantages stated in the second conclusion of this article. The offering of these brings the friars' penitents contrary harms, which ought to be judged almost intolerable. Also, according to the words of Lord Innocent IV, cited above, many other losses arise from this. For he spoke in this way: Considering that from such usurpation not only do contempt and lack of devotion arise among the people against their own priests, but also the sense of shame, which is the greatest part of repentance, is removed, when someone confesses his sins not to his own priest, whom he has continually and present, but to another, sometimes a passing stranger, to whom recourse is difficult and sometimes impossible. Behold, there are three harms to penitents: namely, contempt for one's own priest, lack of devotion, and the removal of the sense of shame, which he affirms to be the greatest part of repentance, and which arise and follow immediately from confession made to friars. For the withholding of offerings is also damnable, and the dishonest taking of tithes is dangerous. These are not, as some falsely assert, passed over as merely ceremonial; rather, God, from whom we have received all things, has ordered that they be reserved for the parish churches as a sign of his lordship. Thus far he. There he adds two other losses: namely, the withholding of the offerings, which penitents often pay to those who hear their confession, and which the friars appropriate to themselves, though they are owed to the parish churches; and this, he affirms, is damnable in the friars. These two things are also harmful to the parish priests, because what is provided for their sustenance by the law of God and of his Church is withdrawn by the friars on account of this privilege. For it is said in Num. 18: All that is sanctified by the children of Israel I have given to you and to your sons as a perpetual right for the priestly office. And in the same place: Every offering and sacrifice, and whatever is paid for sin and trespass, which is brought to me or enters the holy of holies, shall be yours and your sons'. Also, through the use of these privileges by the friars, the parish priests themselves suffer another remarkable loss: they do not recognise the faces of their flocks, whose care they have received from their bishop. This would be harmful in a carnal shepherd of any animals. Likewise, it is very harmful for the parish priests to be despised by their own parishioners, and yet, as Innocent says above, such contempt arises among the people from the fact that the parishioners confess to the friars. It is also a greater loss to the parish priests that, on account of the abuse of the privileges granted to the friars, three quarters of all funeral dues, and indeed everything else coming to them by bequest or gift, whether specified or unspecified, for whatever uses, are granted to the friars in the chapter, Dudum, while only a quarter is granted to the parish priests, and is taxed there. The friars do not pay this quarter of the many legacies, gifts and offerings to the parish priests; rather, by means of countless cautious devices, as the parish priests assert, the friars appropriate it to themselves under various pretexts. Hence there are, almost everywhere among the Christian peoples, endless disputes, quarrels and wrangles between them and the friars, so that in very many places they come from words to blows, and charity is cast far from their minds. Also, these inconveniences for the parish priests arise from the abuse of another privilege: namely, that since the friars have two conservators, they do not want the parish priests, or others who have disputes with them, to be summoned to judgment before their nearer conservator, but make them cited before one more distant from them, so that, through fear of harassment, as it is said, they force them to abandon the prosecution of their cases. This has often happened in my own province, as some present in this court affirm, and there is common report of it. These and many other inconveniences arise for the parish priests from the use, or rather the abuse, of the privileges granted to the friars.

units.la: Item ex abusu priuilegiorum fratribus concessorum incommoda multa in clero proueniunt. Primo quod occasione priuilegii super confessionibus audiendis iuuenes quasi omnes in studiis generalibus & in domibus parentum suorum, in quibus quasi vbique fratres propter facultatem audiendi confessiones tanquam familiares existunt, fratribus confitentur: qui iuuenes fratrum fraudibus; & eorum munusculis datis allecti: quia homines proue�tae aetatis circumuenire non possunt, eorum ordines ingrediuntur, nec postmodum permittuntur, vt fama laborat, quod exeundi ab ordine habeant libertatem, sed cum eis detinentur inuiti; donec profiteantur in ordine: imo nec permittunt (vt dicitur) quod cum patre aut matre loquantur; nisi sub fratrum custodia & timore. Super quo, isto die in exitu mei hospitii vnus probus homo de Anglia, qui ob remedium obtinendum ad curiam istam accessit, mihi exposuit, quod statim post Pascha proxime iam elapsum Fratres apud Studium Oxoniense eo modo sibi suum filium non habentem annos tredecim subtraxerunt: cum quo illuc adueniens non poterat, nisi sub fratrum custodia existente habere colloquium: cum scriptura sacra præcipiat: qui furatus fuerit hominem & vendiderit eum, capitis reus morte moriatur, Exodi vigesimo primo cap. Hanc igitur pœnam si non subeant aut aliam pœnam legitimam, non mihi videtur iustum. Si enim secundum legem pro furto bouis aut ouis debet quis puniri: multo potius pro graviori furto, & proximo læso magis nociuo amplius deberet quisque puniri. Quale est furtum huiusmodi puerorum ante annos discretionis à custodia suorum parentum. Nec poterunt affirmare, quod quia pueri sic surreptí ad Deo obsequendum devotius adducunt. Ideo furari eos & circumuenire licet fraudibus, mendaciis & fictis promissis: quoniam hoc est contra decretum Apostoli affirmare. Dicit enim: Ecce non sicut blasphemamur, & sicut aiunt quidam nos dicere: faciamus mala ut veniant bona. Quorum damnatio iusta est: ad Romanos 3. capitulo. Vtinam viderent in contrarium hoc dicentes libros beati Augustini, De mendacio & contra mendacium, in quibus aperte declarat, quod non est faciendum mendacium pro aliquo malo vitando: nec pro commodo acquirendo. Etiam nec pro hominis liberatione aut vita saluanda. Et pariter videtur de aliis generibus peccatorum. Et exprimit vnam inter alias pulcherrimam rationem: Si, inquit, liceret ex tali causa proferre mendacium, tota ecclesia doctrina periret. Quoniam tunc prædicans fidem in publico ex tali causa posset mentiri. Cum ergo in docendo fidem, sicut & cætera, auditores in cordibus suis non ita possent arguere? Iste secundum suam doctrinam potest dicere licite in multiplici casu mendacium, nescio nec scire nunc possum an talis casus iam infiet sibi: igitur fidem in docendo non debeo adhibere. Vnde concludit, quod ad officium iusti hominis nunquam pertinet vllatenus proferre mendacium. Item hoc est nouæ legis præceptum, sicut patet Marci decimo cap. vbi quærenti à Domino: Quid faciam, vt vitam æternam percipiam: taliter respondetur: Præcepta nosti. Ne adultereris: ne occidas: ne furteris: nec falsum testimonium dixeris: nec fraudem feceris. Honora patrem & matrem, &c.
units.tr: Also, many inconveniences for the clergy arise from the abuse of the privileges granted to the friars. First, because of the privilege concerning the hearing of confessions, almost all young men in the general schools, and in their parents' homes, where the friars, on account of their faculty to hear confessions, are almost everywhere present as familiars, confess to the friars. These young men, enticed by the friars' frauds and the small gifts given them, since they cannot deceive men of more advanced age, enter their orders. Afterwards, as rumour has it, they are not permitted to leave the order freely, but are kept there against their will until they profess in the order. Indeed, they do not even allow them (as it is said) to speak with their father or mother except under the friars' watch and fear. On this matter, on the day I was leaving my lodging, a certain upright man from England, who had come to this court to obtain a remedy, explained to me that, immediately after last Easter, the friars at the University of Oxford had taken away his son, who is not yet thirteen years old, from him. When he went there, he could not speak with him except under the custody of the friars. Yet Holy Scripture commands: He who steals a man and sells him shall be put to death, Exod. 21. If they do not undergo this penalty, or some other lawful penalty, it does not seem just to me. For if, according to the law, a man ought to be punished for stealing an ox or a sheep, then much more, for a greater theft and a more harmful injury to a neighbour, should each man be punished more severely. Such is the theft of boys below the age of discretion from the custody of their parents. Nor can they claim that, because boys so snatched away are led to serve God more devotedly, it is therefore lawful to steal them and to deceive them by frauds, lies and false promises; for to affirm this is contrary to the decree of the Apostle. For he says: And why not do evil that good may come? As we are slanderously reported, and as some affirm that we say, their condemnation is just, Rom. 3. Would that those who say this had read the books of Blessed Augustine, On Lying and Against Lying, in which he plainly declares that a lie must not be told to avoid any evil, nor to acquire any advantage, nor even to free a man or save his life; and he holds the same view regarding other kinds of sin. He sets out one reason, among others, most excellent: If, he says, it were lawful to tell a lie for such a cause, the whole doctrine of the Church would perish. For then one preaching the faith in public could, for such a cause, lie. Therefore, when teaching the faith, as in other things, how could the hearers not argue in their hearts? He, according to his doctrine, can say lawfully in many cases that he has told a lie; I do not know, nor can I now know, whether such a case will befall him; therefore I ought not to rely on him in teaching the faith. Hence he concludes that it never pertains to the office of a righteous man in any way to tell a lie. Likewise, this is a precept of the New Law, as is clear from Mark 10, where, when someone asked the Lord: What shall I do to inherit eternal life?, he was answered thus: You know the commandments: You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not defraud, honour your father and mother, etc.

units.la: Non autem licet homini propter causam aliquam à seipso inuentam præceptum soluere, vt videtur. Tum quia propter hoc Saul electus erat à regno suo, quia contra præceptionem diuinam de demolienda tota Amalechitarum substantia animalia pinguiora pro offerendo Deo sacrificio reseruabat, vbi à Samuele Propheta est sibi responsum: Melior est obedientia quam victima. Et auscultare magis quam offerre adipem arietum. Quoniam quasi peccatum ariolandi est repugnare & quasi scelus idololatriæ non acquiescere, prim. Regum 15. cap. Item quia Oza extendit manum ad arcam Dei, & tenuit eam, quoniam recalcitrauerunt boues & declinauerunt eam: iratus indignatione Dominus contra eum, percussit eum super temeritate sua, & mortuus est, 2. Regum 6. cap. Item Propheta Domini, qui de Iuda missus est in Bethel, quia contra præceptum Domini, ne comederet aut biberet in illo loco, ibi comedit & bibit, & tamen seductus & inuitatus ab alio Propheta loci illius, qui auditoab eo diuino præcepto dicit se esse Prophetam sibi similem, à Leone est in redeundo occisus, sicut scribitur 3. Reg. 13. cap. Hæc & istis similia satis affirmant esse delictum mortale in Fratribus puerosita furari à suis parentibus: imo non solum videntur peccare mortaliter propter furtum, sed etiam propter circumuentionem & fraudem, cum Dominus ipse in auctoritate prætacta ita affirmet esse præceptum: Ne fraudem feceris: sicut affirmat esse præceptum, ne occidas: aut etiam, ne fureris. Item pariter affirmat ibi falsum testimonium esse prohibitum & vitari præceptum, quod tamen (vt videtur) fratres exercent in pueris, cum eos suis circumuentionibus ita alliciunt. Vnde Paulus Apostolus præcepit: ne quis supergrediatur neq; circumueniat in negotio fratrem suum: quoniam vindex est Dominus de his omnibus, primæ ad Thessalon. 4. cap. Ex istis consequitur graue damnum in populo, quia à multis frustrabitur id, quod amplius diliguntin hoc mundo. Item consequitur graue damnum in clero in hoc, quod iam in studiis regni Angliæ propter talem subtractionem a suis parentibus puerorum laici vbique retrahunt suos filios, ne mittant eos ad studium, quia potius eligunt eos facere cultores agrorum eos habendo, quam sic in studiis eos taliter amittere. Et sic fit, quod vbi in studio Oxoniensi adhuc meo tempore erant triginta millia studentium, non reperiuntur sex millia hic diebus. Et maior huius minutionis causa siue occasio præmissa puerorum circumuentio æstimatur. Et quid est isto damno grauius toti clero? non video. Item aliud damnum tam graue, quod tenditad consummationem seu euacuationem doctrinæ in secularibus cuiuslibet facultatis est, quod isti ordines mendicantium propter infinita lucra, quæ mediantibus prædictis priuilegiis de sepulturis, & confessionibus, & aliis quæ acquirunt, tantum multiplicati sunt in conuentibus & personis conuentuum, quod non reperitur in studiis communibus de facultate artium sacræ theologiæ & iuris canonici, vt fertur à pluribus, de facultate medicinæ aut de facultate iuris ciuilis, nisi raro, aliquis vtilis multum liber venalis, sed omnes emuntur à fratribus, ita vt in singulis conuentibus sit vna grandis ac nobilis libraria, vt singuli fratres habentes statum in studiis, quales sunt modo innumeri, nobilem habent librariam.
units.tr: It is not lawful, however, for a man to set aside a precept on some ground he has devised for himself, as it seems. First, because for this reason Saul was rejected from his kingdom: contrary to the divine command to destroy utterly all the substance of the Amalekites, he kept back the fatter animals to offer as sacrifice to God. The prophet Samuel answered him: Obedience is better than sacrifice, and to listen is better than to offer the fat of rams. For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and not to yield is like the crime of idolatry, 1 Kings 15. Likewise, Uzzah stretched out his hand to the ark of God and held it, because the oxen had stumbled and tilted it. The Lord, angered with indignation against him, struck him for his rashness, and he died, 2 Kings 6. Again, the prophet of the Lord who was sent from Judah to Bethel, though the Lord had forbidden him to eat or drink in that place, ate and drank there. Yet he was deceived and invited by another prophet of that place, who, having heard the divine command from him, said that he himself was a prophet like him. On his way back he was slain by a lion, as is written in 3 Kings 13. These and similar examples sufficiently show that it is a mortal sin for the Friars to deceive boys so as to steal them from their parents. Indeed, they seem to sin mortally not only through theft but also through deceit and fraud, since the Lord himself, in the authority cited above, affirms it as a precept: You shall not commit fraud, just as he affirms the precept, You shall not kill, or also, You shall not steal. Likewise he there affirms that false witness is forbidden and to be avoided, which the friars (as it seems) practise on boys when they entice them by their deceits. Hence the Apostle Paul commanded: that no one should go beyond or defraud his brother in business, because the Lord is an avenger of all these things, 1 Thessalonians 4. From these things a grave loss follows for the people, since they are cheated of what they most value in this world. A grave loss also follows for the clergy in this respect: already in the schools of the kingdom of England, because of such enticement of boys away from their parents, laymen everywhere withdraw their sons, so that they do not send them to study, preferring to make them tillers of the fields rather than lose them in this way to the schools. And so it happens that where in the University of Oxford, even in my time, there were thirty thousand students, not six thousand are found there now. And the chief cause or occasion of this decline is thought to be the deceit of boys mentioned above. And what loss is graver than this to the whole clergy? I do not see one. Another loss, as grave, which tends to the destruction or emptying of learning in the secular faculties of every kind, is this: these orders of mendicants, on account of their endless gains, which they acquire through the aforesaid privileges concerning burials, confessions and other matters, have so multiplied in their convents and in the members of the convents that, as is commonly reported, there is not to be found in the common schools of the faculty of arts, of sacred theology and of canon law, or of the faculty of medicine or of civil law, any useful and fairly priced book for sale, except rarely; but all are bought up by the friars, so that in each convent there is a large and splendid library, and each friar who holds a position in the schools, of whom there are now countless numbers, has a splendid library.

units.la: Vnde etiam de meis subiectis Rectoribus tres aut quatuor misi ad studium, & dictum est mihi, quod quia nec Bibliam eis vtilem nec libros alios Theologiæ venales eis congruos ibi poterant reperire, ad suam patriam sunt reuersi, aut vnus eorum saltem rediit iam. Si ista non sit in clero grandis iactura, nulla poterit in ipso esse, cum ad exitum talem, vt videtur, intendat quod clericus in ecclesia nullus remaneat propter fratres: & sic peribit fides ecclesiæ, nisi quatenus residebit in Fratribus. Et ita, vt multis videtur, potius expediret quod prælati eis crederent, vt totam, ad quod ambulare videntur, habérent Ecclesiam, quam quod eam demoliantur hoc modo. Unde non solum admiror, sed stupeo quali audacia tot homines supra omnes mortales in sapientia se publice extollentes contra Physicam rationem & contra sacræ scripturæ doctrinam taliter se sine modo multiplicant. Dixit enim Arist. secundo libro De anima, quod omnium natura constantium determinata est ratio magnitudinis & augmenti. Unde consequitur, quod legem naturæ non servant, sed eam abiiciunt, q in magnitudine & augmento terminum sibi non statuunt. Item, cum scriptura nos instruat Sapien. 11. ca. quod Deus omnia in mensura, numero & pondere disposuit: cum talis multiplicatio super mendicitate seu mendicatione, ut Fratres asserunt, sit fundata, quæ nec personarum numerum certū potest statuere, quibus prouideat: imo nec uni personæ de cætero poterit prouidere, nec pondus, scil. ut locum fixum Mendicantes obtineant, possit præfigere. Cum vero mendici per singulos dies aut quasi suum locum egestate urgente compellātur exire, nec mensuram personis possint statuere, scil. ut in singulis diuinis officiis sint in numero certæ personæ, cum pari modo egestate compulsi ministeriis relictis medicare sæpissime oportebit, consequitur quod modum omnipotētis sapientiæ disponendi isti de mendicantium Ordinibus se hoc modo multiplicant per hoc clerum & populum importune velut effrontes vbilibet onerantes. Iam enim istis in temporibus non poterit magnus aut mediocris in clero & populo vix cibus sumi, nisi tales non vocati affuerint mendicantes, non more pauperum petentes ad portas vel ostia humiliter Eleemosynam, ut Franciscus in testamento præcepit & docuit mendicando: sed curias siue domos sine verecundia penetrantes, & inibi hospitantes nullatenus inuitati edunt & bibunt, quæ apud eos reperiunt. Secum nihilominus aut grana aut similia, aut panes aut carnes seu caseos etiam si in domo nō fuerint nisi duo, secum extorquendo reportant, nec quisquam eis poterit denegare, nisi verecundiam naturalem abiiciat. Et est mirum, quod Domini Gregorii Papæ sententiam non formidant, qui in quodam priuilegio publicato prælatis Ecclesiæ ita scribit: Quia vero vitia sape sub specie virtutum occulte subintrant: & Angelus Sathanæ in angelum lucis se pterumq; simulate transformat, præsentium vobis mandamus auctoritate, quatenus si quos Prædicatorum Fratrum Ordine se dicentes in vestris partibus prædicauerint ad quæstum pecuniæ se conuertendo, per quod religionem eorum, qui paupertatem professi sunt, contigerit infamare: vos tanquam falsarios capiatis & condemnetis eosdem. Tanta est iam in ipsis subtilitas huius artis. Unde pauperes Vicarii & Rectores & omnes de populo, quasi vbiq; istis temporibus conqueruntur. Mirabilis iste modus viuendi apparet in istis, qui se affirmant debere ex sua professione Euangelium obseruaturos contra Christi sententiam Discipulos ad Euangelizandum mittentis: Nolite transire de domo in domum. Lucæ decim. cap. & contra aliam scripturam dicentem: Vita nequam hospitari de domo in domum, Eccles. trigesim. non. ita de curia in curiam, de domo in domum discurrere, vt eorum claustrum eis sit carcer. An non est istud damnum graue in clero & populo? veraciter hoc multis appareret & omnia occasionaliter ex vsu priuilegiorum, imo abusu prouenient, quoniam ipsa priuilegia prædicationis & auditionis confessionum tam extense exercere prætendunt, quod quisq; eos verecundatus repellere.
units.tr: Hence, too, I sent three or four of my subject rectors to study, and I was told that, since they could find neither a Bible useful to them nor other theological books for sale suited to them, they returned to their own country, or at least one of them has already returned. If this is not a great loss to the clergy, none can be; for it seems to aim at such an outcome, that no clergyman remains in the Church because of the friars, and so the faith of the Church will perish, except insofar as it remains among the friars. And so, as many think, it would rather be expedient that the prelates should entrust to them the whole Church, towards which they seem to be heading, than that they should demolish it in this way. Hence I not only wonder but am astonished at the audacity of so many men who publicly exalt themselves above all mortals in wisdom, yet, against natural reason and against the teaching of Holy Scripture, multiply themselves in this unrestrained way. For Aristotle said in the second book On the Soul that for all things that persist in nature a measure of size and growth is determined. It follows that they do not keep the law of nature but cast it aside, since they set no limit to themselves in size and growth. Again, since Scripture teaches us, Wisdom 11, that God has ordered all things in measure, number and weight, and since such multiplication is founded, as the friars assert, upon mendicancy or begging, which can fix neither a certain number of persons to be provided for, nor even provide for any one person in the future, nor fix the weight, that is, a fixed place where the mendicants may hold their residence: and since, when beggars are compelled by pressing want to leave their place day by day, and cannot set a measure for persons, namely so that there be a certain number of persons at each divine office, and since in like manner, compelled by want, they will very often have to leave their ministries and seek remedy, it follows that they multiply in this way, contrary to the manner of the omnipotent wisdom of God's ordering, by thus burdening the clergy and the people importunately, like shameless men, wherever they go. Indeed, in these times no great or middling person in the clergy or among the people can scarcely take a meal without these uninvited mendicants being present, not begging humbly at the gates or doors in the manner of the poor for alms, as Francis commanded and taught in his Testament, but penetrating courts or houses without shame, and, uninvited, staying there, they eat and drink whatever they find. Moreover, they carry off with them grain or the like, or bread or meat or cheese, even if there are only two people in the house, extorting it, and no one can refuse them unless he has cast off his natural shame. And it is remarkable that they do not fear the sentence of Pope Gregory, who in a certain privilege published to the prelates of the Church writes thus: Since indeed vices often secretly creep in under the appearance of virtues, and the angel of Satan often disguises himself as an angel of light, we command you by the present authority that, if any who call themselves of the Order of Preaching Friars should preach in your parts, turning themselves to the gain of money, so that the religion of those who have professed poverty is brought into disrepute, you should seize and condemn them as forgers. So great is now the cunning of this art among them. Hence poor vicars, rectors, and all the people complain almost everywhere in these times. This strange manner of living appears in those who affirm that by their profession they ought to observe the Gospel, against the sentence of Christ, who sent his disciples to preach the Gospel: Do not go from house to house, Luke 10; and against another Scripture saying: A wicked life runs from house to house, Ecclesiasticus 30. To run thus from court to court and from house to house, so that their cloister is a prison to them: is this not a grave loss to the clergy and the people? Truly this would appear to many, and all these things arise incidentally from the use, indeed the abuse, of the privileges, since they claim to exercise the privileges of preaching and of hearing confessions so widely that no one could repel them without shame.

units.la: Item, ista priuilegia & alia infra tangenda afferunt ipsis Fratribus multa incommoda: quia videtur, quod inficiunt eos multis generibus peccatorum. Peccatum enim est se immergere peccato inobedientiæ, peccato auaritiæ, & peccato superbiæ. Videtur enim tam procuratio quam observantia horum priuilegiorum omnium contentorum in capitulo Dudum, de sepulturis, in Clementinis, & etiam aliorum præmissorum peccatis Fratres inficere. Procuratio eorum videtur eos inficere quo ad curatos in peccato iniuriæ: quia facta est contra ius siue diuinum mandatum, quo dicitur: Non concupisces domum proximi tui. Non desiderabis uxorem eius: non ancillam: non bovem, non asinum: nec omnia quæ illius sunt, Exod. vigesim. cap. Constat autem quod hęc iura procurata à Fratribus fuerant tempore procurationis contra iura curatorum. Igitur contra diuinum mandatum tunc fuerat ea concupiscere. Procuratio vero concupiscentiam habebat annexam & pœnitentiam (alias pœnuriam) in quocunq;. Item, cum non licebat tunc concupiscere bouem aut asinum curatorum iuxta diuinum præceptum: multo magis licuit concupiscere ea quæ curatis erant vtiliora, scil. iura præmissa. Item, illa procuratio fiebat contra præceptum de dilectione proximi: Diliges proximum tuum sicut te ipsum: quoniam quisq; seipsum sic diligit, quod nollet alterum indebite concupiscere bona sua. Constat autem quod illa iura curatorum tunc non debebantur Fratribus. Igitur erant ab eis indebite procurata. Et sic contra mandatum Dei præmissum. Item, pariter suadetur per illud: Omnia quæcunq; vultis vt faciant vobis, vos facite illis. Hæc est enim Lex & Prophetæ. Vbi constat, quod per ly facere tam agere quam omittere debemus accipere, scil. vt omittamus aliis facere ea quæ nollemus: vel quæ nolle deberemus nobis fieri. Et quis Fratrum vellet aut secundum eos velle deberet, quod ab eis Monachi aut Canonici Regulares, aut Fratres alterius Ordinis tollerent ab eis priuilegia, quæ iam habent? non puto quod aliquis. Igitur nec ipsi talia iniuriosa curatis illi facere debuerunt. Item priuilegiorum procuratio peccato inobedientiæ Fratres inficit: quoniam ipsa priuilegia Regulas siue professiones impugnant.
units.tr: Moreover, these privileges, and others to be touched on below, bring many disadvantages to the Friars themselves, for they seem to infect them with many kinds of sin. For it is a sin to plunge oneself into the sin of disobedience, the sin of avarice, and the sin of pride. Both the procuring and the observance of all these privileges contained in the chapter Dudum, de sepulturis, in the Clementines, and of the other aforementioned privileges seem to infect the Friars with sin. Their procuring seems to infect them with the sin of injustice towards the parish priests, because it was done against the right or divine command which says: "You shall not covet your neighbour's house. You shall not desire his wife, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor anything that is his," Exod. 20. It is certain that these rights, procured by the Friars, were at the time of the procuring contrary to the rights of the parish priests. Therefore, at that time, to covet them was against the divine command. The procuring indeed had covetousness annexed to it, and penance (alias penury) in whatever respect. Also, since it was not then lawful, according to the divine precept, to covet the ox or ass of the parish priests, much more was it unlawful to covet those things which were more useful to the parish priests, namely the aforesaid rights. Also, that procuring was done against the precept concerning love of neighbour: "You shall love your neighbour as yourself," since whoever loves himself in such a way would not wish another to covet his goods unjustly. It is certain that those rights of the parish priests were then not owed to the Friars. Therefore they were procured by them unjustly, and so against the aforesaid command of God. Likewise it is urged by that saying: "Whatever you wish that men should do to you, do so to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets." Here it is clear that by the word "do" we must understand both acting and omitting, namely that we should refrain from doing to others what we would not want done, or what we ought not to wish done to us. And which of the Friars would wish, or by their own reasoning ought to wish, that Monks or Regular Canons, or Friars of another Order, should take from them the privileges they already have? I think none would. Therefore neither ought they to have done such injurious things to those parish priests. Also, the procuring of these privileges infects the Friars with the sin of disobedience, since these very privileges attack their Rules or professions.

units.la: Primo quidem: quia in approbatione sua lupponunt & suggerunt, quod illi quatuor Ordines ab Ecclesia sunt instituti atque fundati super mendicitate atque arctissima paupertate. Videtur autem quod habere ius prædicandi fidelibus non potest stare cum huiusmodi fundamento, si huic priuilegio siue iuri sit annexa potestas exigendi necessaria vitæ ab his, quibus dicti Fratres Euangelium annunciant: sicut erat in Christi Discipulis, quando ad illud miniministerium exercendum eos direxit, iuxta illud Luc. 10. c. iam prætactum: In quamcunque domum intraveritis &c. Dignus est enim operarius mercede sua. Mendici vero recte taxes, ut videtur, dici non possunt. Qualiter enim dici possit vere mendicus (non dico mendicans) habens ius liberum vitæ necessaria exigendi, non video. Unde nec Inquisitores prauitatis hæreticæ qui dicuntur abuti sæpissime potestate eis concessa, vexantes sæpe diversas personas literatas & laicas volentes remedium quærere de iniuriis illatis per eosdem Inquisitores aut Ordinis sui Fratres, ita ut timore verecundiæ seu notationis super causa hæresis & falsis iniusti iudicii, quale dicuntur sæpius exercere, pecuniæ summas graves ab eis extorquent. Nec quivis pœnitentiarius aut lector habens de certo siue ex pacto necessaria vitæ suæ, videtur dici vere mendicus.
units.tr: First indeed, because in their approval they assume and suggest that those four Orders were instituted and founded by the Church upon begging and most strict poverty. Now it seems that a right to preach to the faithful cannot stand with such a foundation, if annexed to this privilege or right is the power of exacting from those to whom the said Friars announce the Gospel what is necessary for life; as was the case with Christ's disciples when he sent them out to exercise that ministry, according to the passage of Luke 10 already cited: "Into whatever house you enter, etc. For the labourer is worthy of his wages." But, as it seems, they cannot rightly be called beggars. For I do not see how one can truly be called a beggar (I do not say begging) who has a free right to exact what is necessary for life. Hence neither do the Inquisitors of heretical depravity, who are said very often to abuse the power granted to them, harassing often various learned and lay persons who wish to seek a remedy for injuries inflicted by the same Inquisitors or by Friars of their Order, so that, through fear of shame or of a stain upon their name in a matter of heresy, and through false and unjust judgments, which they are said to exercise quite often, they extort heavy sums of money from them. Nor does any penitentiary or lecturer, who has the necessities of his life from a fixed source or by agreement, seem truly to be called a beggar.

units.la: Et sic ista ministeria procurando & etiam exercendo suam professionem dissoluunt. Et ita videtur quam procurando quam volendo tale priuilegium ipsi procurantes suam regulam de mendicitate, non dico de mendicatione, quæ actum solum signat, volebant abiicere: & sic eam in cordibus suis abiecerunt, sicut in simili ait Saluator: Qui viderit mulierem ad concupiscendum eam iam mœchatus est in corde suo, Matth. 5. cap. Si vero Fratres astruxerunt (& vere, ut mihi videtur, sicut inferius suadebo) quod huic ministerio siue officio prædicandi in ipsis non est annexa facultas exigendi vitæ necessaria ab his, quibus Euangelium Christi annunciant: quoniam non sunt vocati Fratres aut missi ad tale ministerium exercendum: sed nudam habent literam (alias licentiam) qua hæc præcepit eis, aut eos exhortatur, ut ministerium illud exerceant: ex alio capite idem consequitur, scilicet ex priuilegiis sepulturæ & facultatis recipiendi oblata Deo; & ex priuilegio audiendi confessiones omnium sibi confiteri volentium: quoniam de lege Dei confessi non apparebunt vacui in conspectu Dei; scilicet ingredientes Ecclesiam Dei pro sacramentis habendis, sicut patet Exodi vigesimo tert. cap. inobedientiæ peccatum incurrunt: quia contra doctrinam Apostoli ad Romanos decim. cap. illud exercent; cum dicat: Quomodo prædicabunt nisi mittantur? sicut scriptum est, Quam speciosi pedes evangelizantium pacem, evangelizantium bona. Et ad Hebræos quinto: Nemo sumat sibi honorem, sed qui vocatur à Deo sicut Aaron. Et contra Christi doctrinam: Nolite vocari Rabbi, nec vocemini magistri. Unus enim est magister vester Christus. Matth. 23. Sunt ergo obedientes, qui in professione sua Euangelium Christi seruare promittunt: & tamen contra legem suam in Euangelio traditam priuilegium tale procurant.
units.tr: And so, by procuring and also by exercising these ministries, they dissolve their profession. Thus it seems that by procuring, and by willing such a privilege, those who procure it were wishing to cast off their rule of mendicity (I do not say of mendicancy, which signifies only the act), and so they cast it out of their hearts, as the Saviour says in a similar case: "Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery in his heart," Matt. 5. But if the Friars have asserted (and truly, as it seems to me, as I shall argue below) that the faculty of exacting what is necessary for life from those to whom they announce the Gospel of Christ is not annexed in them to this ministry or office of preaching, since the Friars have not been called or sent to exercise such a ministry, but have only the bare letter (alias licence) which commands or urges them to exercise that ministry, then from another head the same follows: namely, from the privileges of burial and of the faculty of receiving things offered to God, and from the privilege of hearing the confessions of all who wish to confess to them. For by the law of God they will not appear empty before the face of God, Exod. 23; that is, those entering the Church of God to receive the sacraments incur the sin of disobedience, because they exercise that function against the teaching of the Apostle in Romans 10, who says: "How shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is written, How beautiful are the feet of those who preach peace, who preach good things." And in Hebrews 5: "No one takes this honour for himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was." And contrary to the doctrine of Christ: "Do not be called Rabbi, nor be called teachers, for one is your teacher, Christ." Matt. 23. They are therefore disobedient, since in their profession they promise to keep the Gospel of Christ, and yet they procure such a privilege contrary to the law of their own profession, which is handed down in the Gospel.

units.la: Item, de Fratribus Minoribus hoc specialius videtur posse inferri: quoniam nemo ambigit, quin facilioris & laxioris observantiæ ac minoris meriti sit in eis cum istis priuilegiis super facultate prædicandi, confessiones audiendi, sepulturas habendi, & tres quartas omnium proventuum sibi appropriandi, malle vitam transfigere, quam vivere sine illis, sine quibus à Beato Francisco fuerunt instituti.
units.tr: Likewise, this can be inferred more specifically concerning the Friars Minor: for no one doubts that among them, with these privileges concerning the faculty of preaching, hearing confessions, having burials, and appropriating to themselves three quarters of all revenues, it is a matter of a less demanding and laxer observance and of lesser merit to prefer to pass their lives thus, rather than to live without those things without which they were instituted by Blessed Francis.

units.la: Igitur illa priuilegia procurando retro respexerunt, postquam miserunt manus ad aratrum contra præceptum & regulam sancti Francisci. Dicitur enim in eius regula isto modo cap. secundo: Finito vero anno probationis recipiantur ad obedientiam promittentes, istam vitam & regulam semper observare & nullo modo licebit eis de ista religione exire iuxta mandatum Domini Papæ: quia secundum sanctum Euangelium: Nemo mittens manum suam ad aratrum & respiciens retro aptus est regno Dei. Hæc ibi. Qui igitur talia priuilegia procurarunt: quia retro non dubium respexerunt, peccatum inobedientiæ contraxerunt.
units.tr: Therefore, by procuring those privileges, they looked back after they had put their hands to the plough, against the precept and rule of Saint Francis. For it is said in his rule, in the second chapter, in this way: "When the year of probation is finished, let them be received to obedience, promising always to observe this life and rule, and in no way shall it be lawful for them to leave this religion, according to the command of the Lord Pope: because according to the holy Gospel, 'No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.'" Thus far there. Those, therefore, who procured such privileges, because they undoubtedly looked back, contracted the sin of disobedience.

units.la: Item, cum dicatur in principio eiusdem secundi capituli: Si qui voluerint hanc vitam accipere, & venerint ad Fratres nostros, mittant eos ad suos ministros provinciales; quibus solummodo & non aliis recipiendi Fratres licentia concedatur. Ministri vero diligenter eos examinent de fide catholica & de Ecclesiasticis sacramentis: Et si hæc omnia credant, & velint ea fideliter confiteri & vsq; in finem fideliter observare &c. Finito vero anno probationis &c. Fratres vero econtrario priuilegium procurarunt, quod tam inferiores in ordine, quam provinciales ministri possunt homines ad ordinem suum recipere; imo ipsi Fratres indifferenter hoc faciunt. Et cum sic priuilegium procurando volebant regulam suam in illa parte dissoluere seu laxare: consequitur, quod peccatum inobedientiæ commiserunt, aut si sine priuilegio ista agunt, non minus contra suam professionem inobedienter hoc agunt.
units.tr: Also, since it is said at the beginning of the same second chapter: "If any wish to take up this life and come to our Friars, let them send them to their provincial ministers, to whom alone, and not to others, permission to receive Friars is granted. The ministers shall carefully examine them concerning the Catholic faith and the ecclesiastical sacraments. And if they believe all these things, and wish to confess them faithfully and to observe them faithfully to the end, etc. When the year of probation is finished, etc." But the Friars, on the contrary, procured a privilege by which both the lower ranks of the order and the provincial ministers may receive men into their order; indeed the Friars themselves do this indiscriminately. And since by procuring the privilege in this way they wished to dissolve or relax their rule in that part, it follows that they committed the sin of disobedience; or, if they act without the privilege, they act no less disobediently against their profession.

units.la: Item, hoc eidem consequitur propter illam clausulam regulæ: Ministri vero diligenter eos examinent &c. Contra quam clausulam directe agunt quotidie, cum quasi nullus ad eos accedat, nisi inuenis circumuentus, qui nec scit quot aut qualia sunt Ecclesiæ sacramenta, nec scit fidem ab hæresibus separare, & nihilominus vix reperitur Fratrum locus notabilis, quin sit ibi puerorum infra decennium continentus vnus autem saltem dimidius. Quis potest ambigere, quin istud in Fratribus inobedientiæ sit peccatum? proueniens in ipsis ex priuilegiis prætactis, quibus ita ditantur & taliter honorantur, quod pueri ad eorum vota facilliter inclinantur, & præcipue quia audiunt confessiones in domibus suis, & in domibus patentium puerorum. Igitur huiusmodi procuratio priuilegiorum istorum & abusus eorum peccato inobedientiæ inficit ipsos Fratres.
units.tr: Likewise, the same follows from that clause of the rule: Ministers, however, shall diligently examine them, etc. They act directly against this clause every day, since almost nobody comes to them except a youth who has been taken in, who neither knows how many or what kinds of sacraments the Church has, nor knows how to separate the faith from heresies. Yet there is hardly any notable place of the Friars where there is not some boy under ten years old, or at least one half-grown. Who can doubt that this is a sin of disobedience in the Friars? It arises in them from the aforementioned privileges, by which they are so enriched and so honoured that boys are easily inclined to their wishes, especially because they hear confessions in their own houses and in the houses of the boys' parents. Therefore the procurement of these privileges and their abuse infect the Friars themselves with the sin of disobedience.

units.la: Item, cum in Regula sancti Francisci dicatur, & in capitulo, Exiit de verborum significationibus libro 6. etiam declaratur à Fratribus obseruandum, quod Fratres non prædicent in Episcopatu absque licentia Episcopi, cum ab illo fuerit illis contradictum. Et sanctus Franciscus in testamento suo sic dicit: Et si haberem tantam sapientiam, quantam habuit Salomon; & inuenirem pauperculos sacerdotes huius seculi in parochiis, vbi morantur, nolo prædicare vltra voluntatem ipsorum, & ipsos omnes alios volo timere, amare, & honorare, sicut meos Dominos &c. & Domini mei sunt &c. Hæc ibi. Qualem vero reuerentiam Fratres sacerdotibus pauperculis exhibent, ostendi non potest nec poterit, cum sit nulla, sed irreuerentia vbilibet loco sui reperiri poterit subrogata. Ipsi econtra priuilegium in Capitulo Dudum, contentum procurarunt sibi concedi, & sic procurando in voluntate sua peccatum inobedientiæ habuerunt: quia legem illam eis prius impositam tollere voluerunt. Dicit enim Beatus Augustinus super illo versiculo Psalmi 118. Legem pone mihi Domine, hoc modo; Qui timore poenæ non amore iustitiæ opera legis facit, profecto inuitus facit. Quod autem inuitus facit, si fieri posset, vellet utique non iuberi: ac per hoc legis, quam vellet non esse, non est amicus, sed potius inimicus: nec mundatur opere, qui immundus est voluntate. Hæc Augustinus. Constat autem, quod Fratres procurantes, vt non obtenta licentia Episcopi in sua diocesi possint prædicare, & confessiones audire, volebant regulam contrariam omnino non esse. Et sic extunc eam non amore iustitiæ, sed solum timore poenæ seruauerunt: & volebat eis illam iussam non esse, & ita non illius legis prioris amici, sed inimici tunc erant, & secundum Augustinum immundi voluntate.
units.tr: Likewise, since the Rule of Saint Francis says, and in the chapter Exiit, On the meanings of words, book 6, it is also declared by the Friars that they must observe that the Friars shall not preach in a bishopric without the bishop's permission, once it has been forbidden them by him. And Saint Francis says in his testament: And if I had as much wisdom as Solomon had, and found poor priests of this world in the parishes where they dwell, I would not preach against their will; and I wish to fear, love and honour them all, as my lords, etc., and they are my lords, etc. So far he. But what reverence the Friars show to the poor priests cannot be shown, nor ever will be, since it is nonexistent; rather, irreverence may be found everywhere in its place. On the contrary, they have procured for themselves the privilege contained in the chapter Dudum, and in procuring it according to their own will they have incurred the sin of disobedience, because they wished to remove that law previously imposed on them. For Blessed Augustine, on that verse of Psalm 118, Set me a law, O Lord, says this: He who does the works of the law through fear of punishment, and not through love of righteousness, certainly does them unwillingly. But what he does unwillingly, if it could be done, he would surely wish not to be commanded; and so he is not a friend of the law which he would wish not to exist, but rather an enemy; nor is he cleansed by works who is unclean in his will. So Augustine. It is clear, then, that the Friars who procured that, so that without obtaining the bishop's licence they might preach and hear confessions in his diocese, wished the contrary rule not to exist at all. And so from then on they kept it not through love of righteousness but only through fear of punishment; and they wished it not to be commanded, and so they were then not friends but enemies of that former law, and, according to Augustine, unclean in will.

units.la: Item, isti procuratores priuilegia, quæ suam regulam seu professionem impugnant, non possunt (vt videtur) fideliter eo casu proferre illam clausulam orationis dominicæ: Fiat voluntas tua sicut in cælo & in terra, Matth. sext. cap. cum tamen ad id ex professione Euangelii teneantur. Sic enim sanctus Franciscus suam Regulam inchoat: Regula & vita Fratrum Minorum haec est: scilicet Domini nostri Iesu Christi sanctum Euangelium obseruare, cum nulli sit dubium quin voluntas Dei, scil. eius præceptum siue consilium sit, quod Fratres suam Regulam ab eis professam in finem obseruent, cum hoc etiam præcipiat in Regula secundo cap. & isti procurantes in corde suo econtra procurant, vt obseruantia relaxetur. Vnde consequitur, quod procurantes peccato inobedientiæ quo ad Deum & quo ad suam regulam sunt infecti.
units.tr: Likewise, those procurers of privileges which oppose their rule or profession cannot (so it seems) faithfully pronounce in that case the clause of the Lord's Prayer: Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven, Matt. ch. 6, although they are bound to it by their profession of the Gospel. For Saint Francis begins his Rule thus: The rule and life of the Friars Minor is this: namely, to observe the holy Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. Since there is no doubt that the will of God, that is, his precept or counsel, is that the Friars observe to the end the rule they have professed, and since he also commands this in the second chapter of the Rule, those who procure the contrary in their heart procure that the observance be relaxed. Hence it follows that those who procure it are infected with the sin of disobedience both towards God and towards their rule.

units.la: Item, ex alio capite videtur hoc: quoniam nec confessiones audire, nec prædicationis officium exercere poterunt isti Fratres, sicut nec alii nisi ad sacros ordines promoti, ad quos cum peccato inobedientiæ (vt videtur) promouentur, cum sit lex communis Ecclesiæ quod nullus promoueatur ad ordinem sacrum, nisi habeat titulum sufficientem ad vestitum habendum & victum, qualem titulum, quia Fratres non habent, cum sint (vt dicunt) vere mendici: contra hanc legem vt videtur, omnes & singuli promouentur: & sic non tantum inobedientiæ, sed etiam ambitionis causa sublimem statum procurando sibi concedi, peccatum incurrunt.
units.tr: Likewise, it seems so from another point: these Friars will be able neither to hear confessions nor to exercise the office of preaching, any more than others unless they are promoted to holy orders; and (so it seems) they are promoted to these with the sin of disobedience, since it is the common law of the Church that no one be promoted to holy orders unless he has a sufficient title for having clothing and food. Since the Friars do not have such a title, being (as they say) truly beggars, it seems that all and each are promoted contrary to this law. And so they incur the sin not only of disobedience but also of ambition, by procuring for themselves a grant of this exalted status.

units.la: Item, cum Regula sancti Francisci præcipiat eodem capitulo de prædicationibus quod nullus Fratrum populo penitus audeat prædicare, nisi a Generali Ministro huius Fraternitatis fuerit examinatus & approbatus, & ab eo prædicationis officium sibi concessum. Et contra est priuilegium procuratum, vt scil. ministri prouinciales possint id facere. Fratres hoc procurantes iterum contra suam regulam procurabant: peccatum per consequens inobedientiæ committendo. Item, sanctus Franciscus in testamento suo sic præcepit: Præcipio firmiter obedientiam Fratribus vniuersis quod vbicunque sint, non audeant petere aliquam literam in curia Romana per se vel per interpositam personam, neque pro Ecclesia neque pro aliquo loco neque sub specie prædicationis neque pro defensione suorum corporum. Hæc tibi. Et Fratres econtra per seipsos ista priuilegia & etiam per literas procurabant: quoniam in ipsis priuilegiis continetur, vestris precibus inclinati &c. Et sic videtur, quod illa procuratio ipsos procurantes inobedientiæ peccato infecit. Sed forsitan Fratres hic dicerent, quod Dominus Papa Gregorius nonus, sicut dicitur in decr. Domini Nicolai tertii, Exiit qui seminat, declarauit Fratres non teneri ad mandatum Francisci in illo testamento contentum. Et respondetur eidem Fratribus, quod Dominus Nicolaus non asseruit, quod Gregor. nonus taliter declarauerit: sed dicit, sicut asseritur. Vnde videtur, quod Fratres super hoc nullam declaratoriam literam habuerunt: quoniam verisimile est, si quam literam habuissent, quod illam exhibuissent coram Domino Nicolao. Et tunc, vt videtur, non dixisset vt asseritur, sed vt in eis literis vidimus contineri.
units.tr: Likewise, since the Rule of Saint Francis in the same chapter, concerning sermons, commands that none of the Friars dare to preach at all to the people unless he has been examined and approved by the General Minister of this Brotherhood, and has been granted the office of preaching by him. And the privilege procured is contrary to this, namely that the provincial ministers may do it. The Friars who procured it were again procuring against their own rule, thereby committing the sin of disobedience. Likewise, Saint Francis in his testament commanded thus: I firmly command obedience to all the Friars that, wherever they may be, they not dare to ask for any letter from the Roman curia, either themselves or through an intermediary, neither for a church, nor for any place, nor under the guise of preaching, nor for the defence of their bodies. So he. And the Friars, on the contrary, procured these privileges for themselves, and also by letters; for in the privileges themselves it is contained: inclined by your prayers, etc. And so it seems that this procurement infected the procurers with the sin of disobedience. But perhaps the Friars here would say that Pope Gregory IX, as is said in the decretal of Pope Nicholas III, Exiit qui seminat, declared that the Friars were not bound by the command contained in that testament of Francis. And it is answered to these Friars that Pope Nicholas did not assert that Gregory IX had declared it in this way, but says as it is asserted. Hence it seems that the Friars had no declaratory letter on this matter; for it is likely that, if they had had any such letter, they would have produced it before Pope Nicholas. And then, it seems, he would not have said as it is asserted, but as we have seen contained in those letters.

units.la: Item esto, quod Dominus Gregorius taliter declarauerit, non aliud intendebat, quam id rationes concludunt. Dicit enim Dominus Nicolaus in prædicta decretali, Exiit, isto modo loquens de ipso Domino Gregorio nono, Qui, sicut asseritur, attendens periculum animarum & difficultates quas propter hoc possent incurrere dubietatem de ipsorum cordibus amouens dicit Fratres ipsos ad ipsius mandati obseruantiam non teneri, quod sine consensu Fratrum & maxime ministrorum, quos vniuersos tangebat, obligare nequiuit: nec successorem suum quomodolibet obligauit, cum non habeat in parem par imperium. Nos autem circa præsentem articulum nihil duximus innouandum. Hæc ibi: vbi quia Dominus Gregorius dicit, videtur quod Dominus Gregorius, si quid fecit, non aliud in hoc egit, quam decretum aut declarationem, quod Fratres ad illud mandatum sancti Francisci non fuerant obligati intelligendo quatenus erat mandatum ipsius: quoniam nil amplius probatur per rationes ipsius, scil. quia non fuerant euocati ad hoc omnes, quorum interfuit: & quod par in parem non habet Imperium. Cum qua declaratione videtur stare, quod Fratres illud testamentum nihilominus seruare tenebantur & in præsenti tenentur, si auctoritate diuina per Franciscum illud traditum erat eis: quoniam ad mandatum Dei non oportuit vocare ministros, nec successor Francisci Deo mandanti par fuit: sic quod rationes illæ non obstant, quin de mandato Dei & auctoritate eius intimatis Fratribus per Franciscum, Fratres tunc tenebantur & in præsenti tenentur illud testamentum seruare.
units.tr: Likewise, granted that Pope Gregory declared it thus, he intended nothing other than what the reasons conclude. For Pope Nicholas says in the aforementioned decretal, Exiit, speaking in this way of Pope Gregory IX himself: Who, as it is asserted, attending to the peril of souls and the difficulties which they might incur on account of this, removing doubt from their hearts, says that the Friars are not bound to the observance of that command, which he could not bind without the consent of the Friars, and especially of the ministers, whom it concerned universally; nor did he bind his successor in any way, since he does not have power over an equal. We, however, have thought nothing in the present article should be altered. So far there; where, because Pope Gregory says it, it seems that Pope Gregory, if he did anything, did in this only what a decree or declaration would do, namely that the Friars were not bound to that command of Saint Francis insofar as it was his command; for nothing more is proved by his reasons, namely that not all whose interest was concerned had been summoned to it, and that an equal has no power over an equal. With this declaration it seems consistent that the Friars were nevertheless bound, and are still bound at present, to keep that testament, if it was handed down to them by Francis by divine authority; for it was not necessary to summon the ministers to a command of God, nor was Francis's successor an equal to God commanding. So those reasons do not stand in the way: by a command of God and by the authority of Him made known to the Friars through Francis, the Friars were then bound, and are at present bound, to keep that testament.

units.la: Quod autem sic fuerit, ex eode testamento in fine videtur, vbi sic dicitur: Et nō dicant Fratres: Hæc enim est alia regula, quæ est recordatio, admonitio & exhortatio & meum testamentum, quod ego Frater Franciscus parvulus facio vobis Fratribus meis benedictis, propter hoc ut regulam, quam Dominus promisimus melius catholice observemus & generales ministri & omnes alii ministri & custodes per obedientiam teneantur in istis verbis non addere vel minuere, & semper hoc scriptum habeant secum iuxta regulam & in omnibus capitulis quae faciunt quando legunt regulam, legant & ista verba & omnibus fratribus meis clericis & laicis praecipio per obedientiam, ut non mittant Glossas in regulam, nec in istis verbis dicendo ita volunt intelligi: sed sicut mihi dedit Dominus pure & simpliciter dicere & scribere regulam istam, & verba ista simpliciter & sine Glossa intelligatis, & cum sancta intentione observetis usque in finem. Hæcibi. Ex quibus videtur, quod Fratres possunt unum eligere de duobus, aut institutorem Ordinis sui Franciscum mendacium affirmasse: & ita esse damnatum, vel verum est quod dicit, quod sci icet suum testamentum non est alia regula, sed recordatio prius datae: & ita sicut tenentur priorem regulam, sic & hoc testamentum tenentur servare. Item, cum Franciscus affirmet, quod propter hoc ipse testamentum hoc fecit Fratribus suis benedictis, ut regulam quam Deo promiserunt melius catholice observarent. Aut illud fecit mendacio, & iterum dicent illum damnatum: aut testamentum suum servando suam regulam magis catholice observarent, & per consequens sine observantia testamenti illius minus catholice suam regulam observarent, & ita fuerunt in procurando declarationem contrariam respicientes retro, & in via regni Dei retrogradi & inepti: & sic obedientiae peccato infecti. Item, cum ipse per obedientiam Fratribus suis praeceperit, quod non adderent nec immutarent, & quod istud testamentum secum haberent, & cetera quae sequuntur: aut impie in negocio tanti periculi praecepit, & astruere debent hoc peccato ipsum esse damnatum: aut quod iuste & sancte ita praecepit, & habent ostendere, cur alleviando tantae sanctitatis pondus non respexerint retro sic se regno Dei faciendo ineptos.
