Item, cum in his verbis Franciscus affirmet, quod Dominus dedit sibi simpliciter & pure hanc regulam, & haec verba dicere & scribere: aut propter tantum mendacium in exitu huius vitae dicent eum damnatum, aut quod vere Dominus dixit sibi; quia & ita diceret Fratribus suis: & sic ipse divinum mandatum in hoc Fratribus suis dixit: & per consequens non obstante quod illud testamentum ratione mandati sancti Francisci non teneantur Fratres servare, nihilominus quia est mandatum Dei eis per sanctum Franciscum suum institutorem expressum, istud servare tenentur. Eligant Fratres, quod voluerint ex duobus: & puto quod eligent affirmare, quod sancte sine tantorum mendaciorum peccatis decessit. Et sequitur quod Fratres procurando literas Apostolicas contra mandatum Dei & suae regulae se peccato inobedientiae infecerunt.
units.tr: That this is so appears from the same testament at its end, where it says: And let the Brothers not say: For this is another rule, which is a reminder, admonition and exhortation, and my testament, which I, Brother Francis the little one, make for you, my blessed Brothers, so that we may observe more Catholically the rule which the Lord has promised us, and so that the general ministers and all the other ministers and custodians are bound by obedience not to add or subtract anything from these words, and always keep this writing with them along with the rule, and whenever they read the rule in the chapters, they should also read these words. I command all my Brothers, clerics and laymen, by obedience, not to put glosses on the rule or on these words, saying that they are to be understood in a certain way. Rather, just as the Lord has given me to say and write the rule and these words purely and simply, so you should understand them simply and without gloss, and observe them with holy intention to the end. So far the text. From these words it appears that the Brothers must choose one of two options: either the founder of their Order, Francis, told a lie and is therefore damned, or what he says is true, namely that his testament is not another rule but a reminder of the earlier one, and so, just as they are bound to keep the earlier rule, they are bound to keep this testament too. Again, since Francis states that for this reason he made this testament for his blessed Brothers, so that they might observe more Catholically the rule they had promised God, either he did it by a lie, and again they will say he is damned, or by keeping his testament they would observe his rule more Catholically, and consequently without observing that testament they would observe their rule less Catholically. So in seeking a contrary declaration they were looking backwards, and on the way to the kingdom of God they are backward and unfit, and so stained with the sin of disobedience. Again, since he commanded his Brothers by obedience that they should not add or change anything, and that they should keep this testament with them, and the rest that follows, either he commanded impiously in a matter of such great peril, and they must argue that he was damned for this sin, or he commanded justly and holily, and they must show why, by lightening the weight of such great holiness, they did not look back and thus made themselves unfit for the kingdom of God. Again, since in these words Francis affirms that the Lord gave him this rule and these words to say and write simply and purely, either they will say he was damned at the end of his life for so great a lie, or the Lord truly spoke to him, and so he also said this to his Brothers, and thus he spoke a divine command to them in this matter. Consequently, although the Brothers are not bound to keep that testament by virtue of the command of Saint Francis, nevertheless, because it is a command of God expressed to them through Saint Francis their founder, they are bound to keep it. Let the Brothers choose whichever of the two they wish; I think they will choose to affirm that he died holily, without the sin of so many lies. It follows that by seeking Apostolic letters against the command of God and of their own rule, the Brothers have stained themselves with the sin of disobedience.

units.la: Loquor contra Fratres Minores diffusius super isto: quia ipsi Londoniis incoarunt negotium, occasionem aliis Ordinibus ministrantes. Et quia ipsi prae ceteris de perfectione Euangelica disputantes eam spontaneae mendicitati ascribunt in tantum, quod vnus de ipso Ordine praedicando in Festo omnium Sanctorum, ut mihi fuerat reportatum, descriptis quatuor gradibus paupertatis, quartum perfectionis maioris, imo summae perfectionis Euangelicae affirmabat: scilicet nihil in mundo habere proprium aut commune, sed mendicare cum Christo. Quod dictum statum vestrum, sicut & omnium nostrum, qui sumus inferiores, pater sanctissime scandalizat. Et ob hoc (sicut super aliis supra tactis) Nolite iudicare secundum faciem: sed rectum iudicium iudicate. Videtur enim valde mirabile: imo verius loquendo verisimile non videtur, quod per mille annos & fere ducentos nullus ordo erat in Christi Ecclesia militante, quam Iohannes Apostolus appellat Hierusalem circa principium Apocalypsis 21. cap. Et ego Iohannes vidi civitatem sanctam Hierusalem novam de caelo descendentem a Deo paratam, sicut sponsam ornatam viro suo, qui perfectionem Euangelicam obseruauit. Sed quod Franciscus ad hoc primo ordinem adinuenit. Si enim Ecclesia militans in verbis Iohannis (si pro quia) Hierusalem appellatur, cum affirmet eam de caelo descendere, satis constat quod tempore illo Ecclesia militans, quia de coelesti triumphante descendens sui institutoris Christi perfectionem habebat tanquam sponsa a Christo sponso suo ornata, & non erat ita deformis, ut apice summae perfectionis careret tunc & tot annis sequentibus. Quis tolerabiliter possit audire, quod Franciscus in fide nouitius melius atque vilius viam humanae perfectionis instituit, quam Deus omnipotens, omnibonus, omnisapiens fecerat in hominis institutione primaria, quem tamen Deus instituit, quod eo formato statim posuit in Paradyso, ut operaretur & custodiret illum initio sacrae scripturae tradente, vbi operationem corporalem sufficientiam ac possessionem rerum immobilium & earum pro visu custodiam mendicitati, ut mihi videtur docuit praeferendas, quem tamen in Paradyso posuit ut operaretur & custodiret illum. Et alia scriptura concordat: quia homo nascitur ad laborem, ut avis ad volandum, Iob quinto. Et ut illum Paradysum sed tanquam suum custodiret, in quo bonorum mobilium & immobilium affluentiam obtineret, scilicet de isto infra loquar diffusius. Videtur igitur ex praemissis, quod Fratres procurando ista priuilegia seipsos peccato inobedientiae infecerunt.
units.tr: I speak more fully against the Lesser Brothers on this point, because they began the business in London, giving an occasion to other Orders. And since they, above all others, when disputing about evangelical perfection, ascribe it so much to voluntary mendicancy, that one of that Order, preaching on the feast of All Saints, as was reported to me, having described four degrees of poverty, affirmed the fourth to be of greater perfection, indeed of the highest evangelical perfection, namely to have nothing in the world as one's own or in common, but to beg with Christ. Holy Father, this saying scandalises your state, and that of all of us who are inferior. And for this reason (as with other matters touched on above) "Judge not according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment." For it seems very remarkable, or rather, to speak more truly, it does not seem probable, that for a thousand years and nearly two hundred more there was no Order in the militant Church of Christ, which the Apostle John calls Jerusalem near the beginning of the Apocalypse, chapter 21: "And I John saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband," who observed evangelical perfection. But Francis first devised this Order for the purpose. For if the militant Church is called Jerusalem in the words of John (if "for" is meant), since he says that it comes down from heaven, it is quite clear that at that time the militant Church, descending from the heavenly triumphant Church, possessed the perfection of its founder Christ as a bride adorned by Christ her bridegroom, and was not so deformed as to lack the summit of supreme perfection then and for all the years that followed. Who could tolerably hear that Francis, a novice in the faith, established a better and more excellent way of human perfection than God almighty, all-good and all-wise, made in the first institution of man, whom God nevertheless established, placing him at once in Paradise after he was formed, to work and keep it, as the beginning of Holy Scripture relates, where, as it seems to me, he taught that bodily labour, sufficiency, and possession of immovable goods, with careful keeping of them, are to be preferred to mendicancy; yet he placed him in Paradise to work and keep it. And another Scripture agrees: "Man is born to labour, as the bird to fly," Job 5. And to keep that Paradise, but as his own, in which he might obtain an abundance of movable and immovable goods, I shall speak more fully about this below. It seems therefore from what has been said that the Brothers, by seeking these privileges, have stained themselves with the sin of disobedience.

units.la: Item, in procurando ista priuilegia Fratres videntur peccatum avaritiae incurrisse. Primo quia non procuraverunt sibi priuilegia alia super aliis articulis sacerdotalis officii, scilicet ut possent pueros baptizare, ut possent in subsidium curatorum in die Paschae parochianis sacramentum Eucharistiae ministrare, aut extremae unctionis eis sacramentum conferre, vbi esset tantum meritum pietatis, quantum in istis aut amplius. Sed super his solum priuilegia huiusmodi, omissis caeteris, procurabant, quibus directe vel indirecte commoda temporalia annectuntur, mirabiliores fiores cunctis mercatoribus & etiam artificibus in hoc effecti artifices quo ad lucrum adiuncta sua professione, quam fingunt super sua mendicitate seruanda. Non enim puto, quod erat à mundi origine via fallacior siue callidior ad opes facile conquirendas, quam per praemissa priuilegia mendicitati factae obligatione vere seu ficte adiuncta.
units.tr: Again, in seeking these privileges the Brothers seem to have incurred the sin of avarice. First, because they did not seek other privileges concerning the other parts of the priestly office, namely that they might baptise children, that they might minister the sacrament of the Eucharist to parishioners at Easter in aid of the parish priests, or confer on them the sacrament of extreme unction, where there would be as much merit of piety as in these or more. But they sought privileges of this kind only, leaving aside the rest, to which temporal advantages are attached directly or indirectly, and in this they have become more wonderful merchants than all merchants, and even craftsmen, in their trade, adding to their profession, which they feign to keep in their mendicancy, the craft of gain. For I do not think there has been from the origin of the world a more deceptive or cunning way of easily acquiring wealth than through the aforesaid privileges, joined truly or falsely to the obligation of mendicancy.

units.la: Item, cum constet non obstante quod Fratres haberent potestatem liberam recipiendi ad sepulturam in locis ipsorum: nihilominus remanere poterat in suo robore ius commune, scilicet quod omnes oblationes & omnia funeralia deberentur Ecclesiis & ipsorum curatis. Quod igitur vnum cum altero à Fratribus fuerat procuratum, patenter videtur innuere, quod illius procurationis auaritia causa erat. Est enim Regula Aristotelis primo posteriorum: Ad cognoscendum alicuius passionis seu effectus subiectum seu causam praecipuam, vt prouide inquiratur, quae est causa, quae immediate posita ponitur ipse effectus: & quae peremptae perimitur. Quae Regula satis affirmat, quod commodum temporale fuit in procuratione horum priuilegiorum causa praecipua, cum sine illa procuratio haec non fiebat: & ea sola fuerant procurata, quae ista commoda obtinebant. Cuius rei satis patens est signum, quod non more Thobiae ad sepeliendum rapiunt corpora pauperum defunctorum, sed instar vulturis vltra mare ad quingenta miliaria sua alimenta odorando sentientes ea quaerunt, sicut dicit Auerrois Commentator secundo de anima, sicut recolo, capitulo de odore. Hoc enim signum satis affirmat, quod Fratres istud sepulturae cum aliis apexis oblationibus priuilegium propter alimentum praecipue, non propter misericordiae exercendae meritum procurarunt.
units.tr: Again, since it is agreed that, although the Brothers had the free power of receiving burial in their own places, the common law could nevertheless remain in its force, namely that all offerings and all funeral fees are owed to the churches and their parish priests, the fact that the Brothers sought the one along with the other clearly seems to imply that avarice was the cause of that procuring. For there is the rule of Aristotle in the first book of the Posterior Analytics: To know the principal subject or cause of some affection or effect, one must inquire carefully what it is whose positing immediately posits the effect itself, and whose removal removes it. This rule sufficiently affirms that temporal advantage was the principal cause in seeking these privileges, since without it the seeking was not done, and only those things were sought which obtained these advantages. A plain sign of this is that they do not, in the manner of Tobias, snatch the bodies of poor dead people to bury them, but, like vultures, smelling their food from five hundred miles across the sea, they seek them out, as the Commentator Averroes says in the second book of On the Soul, as I recall, in the chapter on smell. For this sign sufficiently shows that the Brothers sought this privilege of burial, along with the other offerings, chiefly for the sake of food, not for the merit of exercising mercy.

units.la: Item, de priuilegio audiendi confessiones omnium indistincte, aliud probabiliter, vt videtur, suspicari non poterit: cum quisque sanctus praeter ipsos audire confessiones horrescat: quoniam nimium est cuique peccata sua agnoscere etsi aliena non discat. Vnde nec monachi albi aut nigri, nec regulares canonici officium tale desiderant aut alii viri sancti: nec dubium, si ex devotione sancta talis procuratio praecederet, quod in aliquibus aliis viiis devotis non in solis Fratribus aliquotiens appareret.
units.tr: Likewise, concerning the privilege of hearing the confessions of everyone without distinction, one probably cannot suspect any other motive, as it seems. Every holy man shudders at hearing confessions other than his own, since it is too much for anyone to recognise his own sins, even if he learns nothing of others'. Hence neither the white nor the black monks, nor the regular canons, nor other holy men desire such an office. And there is no doubt that if such a pursuit had arisen from holy devotion, it would sometimes appear in other devout men, and not only in the Friars.

units.la: Vnde probabiliter potest inferri, quod auaritia tanquam causa praecipua in tali procuratione mentem procurantis infecit. Item, ad hoc, quod Regula sancti Francisci praecipiat isto modo: Praecipio firmiter Fratribus vniuersis ne habeant suspecta consortia vel consilia mulierum, neque ingrediantur monasteria monacharum praeter illos, quibus à Sede Apostolica concessa fuerit licentia speciales. Et ne fiant compatres virorum aut mulierum, ne hac occasione inter Fratres vel de Fratribus scandalum oriatur: & Fratres econtrario procurarunt, videlicet vt audire possint consilia secretissima mulierum reginarum & aliarum omnium indistincte, etiam capite inclinato ad caput multum irreuerenter non insequentes vestigia sancti Iob, qui dicit trigesimo primo cap. Pepigi foedus cum oculis meis ne cogitarem quidem de virgine: ita vt per tale consortium iam cum pulcherrimis dominabus philosophentur in cameris. Vnde per orbem scandala, quae nolo exprimere, de Fratribus sunt exorta patenter, vt multis videtur, per abusum huius priuilegii. Imo per abusum suae Regulae a priuilegio occasione sumpta inobedientiae peccato seipsos inficiunt.
units.tr: Hence it can probably be inferred that avarice, as the chief cause, has infected the mind of those who pursue such a function. Further, the Rule of St Francis commands as follows: I firmly command all the Friars not to have suspicious associations or counsels with women, nor to enter the monasteries of nuns, except those to whom special licence has been granted by the Apostolic See. Nor are they to become godfathers to men or women, lest from this occasion a scandal arise among the Friars or concerning the Friars. But the Friars, on the contrary, have contrived to hear the most secret counsels of women, of queens and of all others without distinction, even with the head bowed very irreverently close to the head. They do not follow the footsteps of holy Job, who says in chapter 31: I made a covenant with my eyes that I would not even think of a virgin. So through such intercourse they now philosophise with the most beautiful ladies in their chambers. Hence scandals, which I do not wish to spell out, have openly arisen throughout the world concerning the Friars, as it seems to many, through the abuse of this privilege. Indeed, by abusing their own Rule, and taking occasion from the privilege, they infect themselves with the sin of disobedience.

units.la: Item, quod horum priuilegiorum procuratio peccato superbiae mentes procurantium infecit, multipliciter suadetur. Primo quia in decretali, Exiit, Clementinis de verborum significatione affirmat, quod sanctus Franciscus suos Fratres in paupertate summa & humilitate fundare volebat. Et constat, quod procurare honoris Ecclesiastici statum sublimem, humilitatem impugnat & ambitionis peccatum habet annexum. Ergo &c. Probatur minor assumpta per auctoritates iam tactas, & per illud Saluatoris filio Zebedaei responsum: Nescitis quid petatis, ipsis per matrem suam petentibus quod vnus eorum sederet ad dexteram eius in regno suo & alius ad sinistram. Super quo dicit Chrysostomus: O error salutaris, qui totius mundi soluit errorem. Si enim Apostoli non errassent, vnde nos cognoscere poteramus, quia non omne quod videtur bonum desiderare bonum est? Nunc autem scimus quia aliud est opus bonum, aliud primatus honoris. Et scito post: Nam desiderium primatus ex iactantia nascitur cordis. Qui autem est humilis corde, nunquam desiderat superior apparere. Et infra: Secularem quidem primatum desiderare & si ratio non est vel causa est, quia si iustum non est, vtile est. Primatum autem Ecclesiasticum concupiscere neque ratio est neque causa. Quia neque iustum est neque vtile. Haec ibi. Et multa addit similia, quibus nititur suadere, quod nunquam sine ambitione desideratur primatus in Ecclesia.
units.tr: That the procuring of these privileges has infected the minds of those who procure them with the sin of pride is urged in many ways. First, because in the decretal Exiit, in the Clementines, concerning the meaning of words, it is affirmed that St Francis wished his Friars to be founded in the utmost poverty and humility. And it is plain that to seek a lofty status of ecclesiastical honour opposes humility and carries with it the sin of ambition. Therefore etc. The minor premise is proved by the authorities already cited, and by the reply of the Saviour to the son of Zebedee, when through their mother they asked that one of them should sit at his right hand in his kingdom and the other at his left: You do not know what you are asking. On this Chrysostom says: O salutary error, which dissolves the error of the whole world! For if the Apostles had not erred, how could we have known that not everything that seems good is good to desire? But now we know that one thing is a good work, another the primacy of honour. And a little later: For the desire for primacy is born of the boasting of the heart. But he who is humble in heart never desires to appear superior. And below: To desire the secular primacy, even if it is not reasonable or has a cause, since if it is not just, it is useful. But to covet the ecclesiastical primacy is neither reasonable nor has a cause, since it is neither just nor useful. So far he says there. And he adds many similar things, by which he strives to persuade that the primacy in the Church is never desired without ambition.

units.la: Constat autem quod habere statum praedicandi & confessiones audiendi, est in Ecclesia status honoris siue primatus. Inficit se ergo peccato superbiae, qui illum procurat. Item, confirmatur hoc aliter. Cum enim Apostolus dicat: Quomodo praedicabunt nisi mittantur sicut scriptum est: Quam speciosi pedes Evangelizantium pacem, & Evangelizantium bona, ad Roman. decim. cap. necipsi sunt missi a Deo ad illud officium per aliquod praeceptum, quod ego vidi hucusque. Sed videtur qui ex praesumptione propria ad officium illud ascendunt. Caueant ne aliunde quam per Christum ostium ascendentes, vt latrones ab eo iudicentur & fures, iuxta dictum ipsius Iohannis decim. c. Amen, amen dico vobis qui non intrat per ostium in ovile ovium, sed aliunde ascendit, ille fur est & latro. Et consequenter affirmat: Ego sum ostium. Et sic videntur esse de eis Prophetis aut eis similes, de quibus dicitur Hieremiae 22. Non mittebam Prophetas & ipsi currebant: non loquebar ad eos, & ipsi prophetabant. Vnde citto adiungitur: Ecce ego ad Prophetas, dicit Dominus, qui furantur verba mea vnusquisque à proximo suo. Si enim non sunt missi à Christo, ipsi furantur verba curatorum & superiorum suorum, quibus ... lum de iure communi in officium prædicandi dicitur conuenire.
units.tr: It is plain, however, that to have the status of preaching and of hearing confessions is, in the Church, a status of honour or primacy. Therefore whoever seeks it infects himself with the sin of pride. Again, this is confirmed in another way. For since the Apostle says: How shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: How beautiful are the feet of those who preach peace, and who bring good tidings (Rom. 10), I have not hitherto seen any command by which they were sent by God to that office. But those who ascend to that office by their own presumption seem to be of this kind. Let them take care lest, ascending by any other way than through Christ the door, they be judged by him as thieves and robbers, according to the saying of John himself in chapter 10: Truly, truly I say to you, he who does not enter by the door into the sheepfold of the sheep, but climbs up another way, that man is a thief and a robber. And consequently he affirms: I am the door. Thus those prophets or men like them seem to be the ones of whom it is said in Jeremiah 22: I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied. Hence soon after is added: Behold, I am against the prophets, says the Lord, who steal my words, each from his neighbour. For if they have not been sent by Christ, they steal the words of the curates and of their superiors, to which ... by the common law it is said to belong to the office of preaching.

units.la: Item, quod obseruantia priuilegiorum istorum inficiat obseruantes, etiam modo prænissò suadetur. Quoniam nec præcipitur Fratribus nec ad eorum professionem seu regulam pertinet prædicationi officium exercere. Unde licitum non videtur eis prædicare in publico aut confessiones audire. Cum ergo officium tale volunt admittere, videtur peccare mortaliter.
units.tr: Likewise, that the observance of these privileges infects those who observe them is urged even in the manner stated above. For the office of preaching is neither commanded to the Friars nor pertains to their profession or Rule. Hence it does not seem lawful for them to preach in public or to hear confessions. Therefore, since they wish to admit such an office, they seem to sin mortally.

units.la: Primo quia noscunt aut scire deberent, quod priuilegia ista erant procurata mediantibus peccatis mortalibus supra tactis, & pro usu iplorum. Cum ergo illis vtuntur, gratificant procurationem iniquam: sicut quis manducans de rapina aut furto obtento pro usu ipsius gratificaret manducando ipsam rapinam aut furtum; & possidens beneficium ad eius commodum simoniace procurarum, communicaret cum procurante in simoniæ peccato: & illud gratum haberet & esset sub illo decreto Apostoli ad Romanos primo cap. Qui talia agunt, digni sunt morte: non solum eam et cc. vt supra posui. Nec excusari per concessionem siue licentiam Domini Papæ potuerunt (vt videtur) quoniam Dominus Papa in sua concessione obstantiam illam non posuit, nec eum eam ponere decuisset, scilicet, Concedimus ista Fratribus non obstante conscientia eorum peruersa: sed solas substantias iurium humanorum videtur intendere relaxare: sicut si homicidae, simoniaco, aut habenti corporalem defectum latentem, qui eum redderet inhabilem, concederet facultatem plura beneficia curata retinendi: non propter hoc potest inferri, quod licite siue iuste illa poterit retinere, sed iuste secundum quid, scil. quantum ad hoc quod non impugnaret illius legis obstantiam. Et sicsi beneficia retineret, non obstante dispensatione peccaret mortaliter. Sic etiam mihi videtur in nostro proposito: scil. quod licet quo ad ius illud, quo talia ministeria solum debentur caratis per Dominum summum Pontificem cum Fratribus dispensetur, non propter hoc potest inferri, quod Fratres iuste poterunt simpliciter priuilegiis illis uti, sed iuste secundum quid, scil. quo ad hanc legem eis prius obstantem. Cum quo stare videtur, quod sine peccatis mortalibus illis priuilegiis uti non possunt, quoniam (vt videtur) per gratificationem illam continue ab eis retentam semanent in peccato mortali, ac si ipsi tunc aut procurarent aut procurantibus assentirent. Et si dixerint ipsi Fratres, quod Fratres possunt & poterunt poenitere de isto peccato: & sic non potest concludi, quod iam aliqui non remaneant in peccato. Econtra dicetur, quod sicut in furto non poterit quis veraciter poenitere, nisi prius facta restitutione sublati, sic nec in nostro proposito. Sed dicerent, quod in præsenti saltem habent iuste quantum ad curatos hæc iura & emolumenta inde sequentia: quia per summum pontificem, qui sufficientem potestatem habet & habuit ad eadem concedenda, & ita ea restituere non tenentur. Ibi econtra dicetur, quod non obstante titulo acquisito per Dominum summum pontificem restituere inditecte, licet non directe, arctari videntur: quoniam Dominus Papa illam culpam gratificationis prætactam in concedendo priuilegium non relaxat, immo nec potuit relaxare Fratribus ipsis non vere poenitentibus aut contritis. Et quamdiu illud peccatum manet in Fratribus, non possunt (vt videtur) veraciter poenitere, nisi iuxta subtractam restituant ribus quantum in eis est, restituant.
units.tr: First, because they know, or ought to know, that these privileges were procured through the mortal sins mentioned above, and for their own use. Therefore, when they use them, they ratify the wicked procuring, just as someone who eats of plunder or of stolen goods obtained for his use would ratify the robbery or theft by eating it; and one who possessed a benefice simoniacally procured for his advantage would share in the procurer's sin of simony, and would hold it in favour and be under that decree of the Apostle in Romans 1: Those who do such things are worthy of death; not only do they do them, but they also approve those who practise them, as I have set out above. Nor, as it seems, can they excuse themselves by the concession or licence of the Lord Pope, since the Lord Pope did not place that obstacle in his concession, nor ought he to have placed it, namely: We grant these things to the Friars notwithstanding their perverse conscience. Rather, he seems to intend to relax only the substance of human rights. Just as if he granted a murderer, or a simoniac, or one who has a hidden bodily defect that would render him unfit, the faculty of retaining several curacies, it could not on this account be inferred that he could lawfully or justly retain them, but justly in a certain respect, namely in that he would not oppose the obstacle of that law. And if he retained the benefices notwithstanding the dispensation, he would sin mortally. So it seems to me also in our present matter: that although, as regards that right by which such ministries are owed solely to the curates, the Friars are dispensed by the Lord Supreme Pontiff, it cannot on that account be inferred that the Friars may simply use those privileges justly, but only justly in a certain respect, namely as regards that law which previously stood in their way. With this it seems to agree that they cannot use those privileges without mortal sins, since (as it seems) by that ratification, which they continually retain, they remain in mortal sin, as if they were then either procuring or assenting to those who procure. And if the Friars themselves should say that the Friars can and may repent of this sin, and so it cannot be concluded that some of them now remain in sin, the answer is that just as one cannot truly repent of theft unless restitution of what was taken is first made, so too in our present matter. But they would say that at present, at least as regards the curates, they hold these rights and the emoluments following from them justly, because they have them from the Supreme Pontiff, who has, and has had, sufficient power to grant them, and so they are not bound to restore them. To this the reply will be that, notwithstanding the title acquired through the Lord Supreme Pontiff, they seem bound to restore indirectly, though not directly; since the Lord Pope does not relax that aforementioned fault of ratification in granting the privilege, and indeed could not relax it even for Friars who are not truly repentant or contrite. And as long as that sin remains in the Friars, they cannot (as it seems) truly repent, unless they make restitution, so far as lies in them, of the withdrawn rights.

units.la: Unde videtur quod Fratres quamdiu non restituunt illa iura, quamuis etiam propter concessionem Domini Papæ factam Fratribus non debeantur de lege humana curatis, Fratres non possunt veraciter poenitere. Quis enim vere poeniteat de alicuius rei acquisitione iniqua, & nihilominus de eius retentione lætatur? nemo, vt videtur probabiliter iudicandum. Fratres igitur poenitentes & ipsa priuilegia obseruantes, sunt peccatis prætactis mortalibus inuoluti siue infecti.
units.tr: Hence it seems that, as long as the Friars do not restore those rights, they cannot truly repent, even though, by the concession of the Lord Pope made to the Friars, those rights are not owed under human law to those who are cared for. For who truly repents of an unjust acquisition of something, and yet rejoices in keeping it? No one, as it seems we must probably judge. Therefore the Friars, both repenting and observing those same privileges, are caught up in or infected by the aforementioned mortal sins.

units.la: Item, de ista licentia in casu consimili tractat Beatus Bernhardus diffuse in secunda Epistola ad Adam Monachum. Et est casus, quod ille monachus post professionem suam in monasterio factam quo ad perpetuam morum ibidem, sicut habent de more, vt dicitur, ad aliud monasterium cum suo abbate accessit, vbi moratus est de licentia sui abbatis: & eius mandato petita etiam super hoc summi pontificis licentia & obtenta. Quem Bernhardus aperte redarguens nititur ratione multiplici affirmare, quod nec sine peccato etiam de iussu sui abbatis debebat hoc facere, nec de licentia summi pontificis, cuius licentiam petere non debebat. Ad suadendum primum supponit v. num principium, quod etiam Aristoteles tertio Ethicorum describit, & ponit scil. quod sunt aliqua simpliciter bona, quæ fieri mala non possunt: & aliqua mala, quæ fieri simpliciter bona non possunt. Et inter ista extrema sunt duo media, quæ bene fieri possunt & male. Exempla primi sunt secundum eum charitas, fides, & spes. Exempla secundi, furtum, homicidium, incestus, & istis similia. Exempla tertii gradus sunt, obedientia, ieiunium & istis similia, quæ etiam bene & male possunt fieri iuxta conditiones annexas. In quibus solum, vt sibi videtur, obedientia locum habet. Hoc posito inquiritur in quo gradu sit hoc factum, in quo paruit influi sui abbatis, & affirmat quod fuit in secundo, scil. in gradu malorum simpliciter, ex hoc, vt sibi videtur, vere concludens, quod non potuit bene fieri & ob hoc in hoc facto iussioni sui abbatis parere non debuit, sed plane resistere, quia in tali opere de se malo, scil. in solutione promissi sui abbatis debebat obstere. Item, ponit pro Regula, quod duobus præcipientibus contraria potius maiori est parendum.
units.tr: Likewise, Blessed Bernard treats this question at length in a similar case in the second Epistle to Adam the Monk. The case is this: after his profession in a monastery, made for perpetual residence there, that monk, as they say is customary, went with his abbot to another monastery, where he stayed with his abbot's permission. He also sought and obtained the licence of the supreme pontiff on this matter. Bernard openly rebukes him and labours to show by many arguments that he ought not to have done this, not even at his abbot's command, nor with the licence of the supreme pontiff, whose licence he ought not to have sought. To support the first point, he lays down a principle that Aristotle also describes in the third book of the Ethics: there are some things that are simply good and cannot become evil, and some that are simply evil and cannot become good. Between these extremes lie two middle kinds, which can be done either well or badly. Examples of the first kind are, in his view, charity, faith and hope; examples of the second are theft, murder, incest and the like; examples of the third degree are obedience, fasting and similar things, which can be done well or badly according to the conditions attached. In these alone, as it seems to him, obedience has its place. Given this, he inquires to which degree the act belongs, in which the monk obeyed his abbot's command, and he affirms that it belongs to the second, that is, to things simply evil. From this, as it seems to him, he rightly concludes that it could not be done well, and that for this reason the monk ought not to have obeyed his abbot's command in this act, but plainly to resist it, since in such a work, evil in itself, namely the breaking of his promise to his abbot, he ought to have stood in the way. He also lays down as a rule that when two persons command contrary things, the greater authority is to be obeyed.

units.la: Cum igitur Deus præcipiat vota seruare, & obedientiam sibi debere obseruari, stabbas sunt Deo inferior præceperit illud dissoluere, debebat Deo potius obedire, mandato sui abbatis con[illegible, ~6 letters] Bernhardus allegat illud Saluatoris Matth. decim. octau. cap. Qui scandalizauerit unum de pusillis istis, qui in me credunt, expedit ei ut suspendatur mola asinaria in collo eius, & demergatur in profundum maris. Vae mundo ab scandalis, necesse est enim ut veniant scandala. Verumtamen vae homini illi, per quem scandalum venit. Atque adiungit, quod ille Adam monachus suum monasterium deserendo non solum scandalizauit unum Christi pusillum, sed multos. Ex hoc apparet, ut sibi videtur, concludens quod ipse & illud Salvatoris incurrit suo abbati parendo in casu praemisso. Vtinam igitur Fratres exterruerint, quia per istorum privilegiorum abusum ab eis non solum scandalizantur pauci & pusilli, sed multi & magni, & per totam Christi Ecclesiam, & ex illo coram Deo sancte concludetur, quid merentur, & multa alia ibi adduxit. Item, quantum ad licentiam summi pontificis dicit aperte, quod affert mali compendium: quia non excusat factum sequentis de se malum: & eius petitio fuit mala. Quia, ut dicit, velle habere ad malum licentiam, semper est malum.
units.tr: Therefore, since God commands that vows be kept and that obedience be rendered to himself, if the abbot (who is inferior to God) commanded the dissolving of that vow, the monk ought to have obeyed God rather than his abbot's command. Bernard also cites the Saviour's words in Matth. 18: But whoever shall cause one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck and he were drowned in the depth of the sea. Woe to the world because of stumbling-blocks! For it must needs be that stumbling-blocks come; but woe to that man through whom the stumbling-block comes. And he adds that that monk Adam, by deserting his monastery, gave offence not only to one little one of Christ but to many. From this, as it seems to him, it appears, and he concludes, that both he and the words of the Saviour fall upon him, by obeying his abbot in the case supposed. Would then that the Friars might be frightened by this, since through the abuse of these privileges not only a few and little ones but many and great are offended, and throughout the whole Church of Christ; and from this it will be rightly concluded before God what they deserve. He brings forward many other things there as well. Again, as to the licence of the supreme pontiff, he says plainly that it brings a gain of evil, because it does not excuse an act that is evil in itself, and the seeking of it was evil. For, as he says, to wish to have a licence for evil is always evil.

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters] ad Dominum Papam concedentem licentiam, ipse sic dicit: Quis esse malum ... sensum praebere malo? quod tamen fecisset summam pontificem, aliquam crediderim, nisi circumuentam mendacio, aut importunitate victum. Haec est sancti Bernhardi sententia. Videant aut ipsi Fratres, an non ita sit circa istam licentiam impetratam per eos, sicut circa Adae monachi licentiam procuratam, & cum sancto Bernhardo concludant, quod peccatum procurationis licentiae cum inobedientia & solutione suae Regulae subsecuta affert eis mali compendium, sicut ipse Bernhardus affirmat in simili. Item, ex quo quisque Frater cum praedicationis officium aut audiendae confessionis exercet, possit id respuere, sine peccato consequitur (ut videtur) quod ipse illud officium tunc contra suam professionem gratis assumit. Et ita sicut in procuratione privilegiorum patuit superius est suasum, quod procurantes peccauerunt mortaliter contra divina praecepta ibi expressa, sic iste peccat mortaliter contra eadem divina mandata libere utendo licentia impie procurata: & incurritur peccatis iniuriae, inobedientiae, avaritiae, atque superbiae, ut videtur, cum ex eisdem causis iniquis ipse utatur licentia procurata, ex quibus aliud procurauit, scilicet propter ditationem & honorem. Vtinam adulterium huius visus licentiae causa tertia non existat, licet super hoc in clero & in populo sit communis fama.
units.tr: ... to the Lord Pope granting the licence, he speaks thus: Who would give a meaning to evil? Yet I should believe that the supreme pontiff would not have done so, unless he had been deceived by a lie or overcome by importunity. This is the opinion of Saint Bernard. Let the Friars themselves see whether it is not the same with the licence obtained by them as with the licence procured for the monk Adam, and let them conclude with Saint Bernard that the sin of procuring a licence, followed by disobedience and the breaking of their Rule, brings them a gain of evil, just as Bernard himself affirms in a similar case. Again, since every Friar who exercises the office of preaching or of hearing confession could refuse it without sin, it follows (as it seems) that he then takes up that office freely, contrary to his profession. And so, just as it was shown above in the procuring of the privileges that those who procured them sinned mortally against the divine precepts expressed there, so this man sins mortally against the same divine commandments when he freely uses the licence impiously procured. He also incurs, as it seems, the sins of injustice, disobedience, avarice and pride, since he uses the licence procured for the same wicked reasons for which he procured the other, namely for the sake of wealth and honour. Would that adultery were not a third cause of this seeking of a licence, although on this point there is common report among the clergy and the people.

units.la: De ista privilegiorum materia & eorum abusu & contrarietate ad professionem Fratrum, & quo ad duas conclusiones per me suasas superius ista mihi sufficiant in praesenti. Alia plura, si oportebit, adiiciam: & non ambigo quin si vellem illud facere, alii non omitterent. Super his omnibus per me modo petitis atque expressis, pater sanctissime, Nolite iudicare secundum faciem: sed iustum iudicium iudicate: per vestram sanctitatem, aut per aliquos meos dominos Cardinales, suspenso usu privilegiorum, praetactam per me materiam contingentium in quacunque sui parte lite pendente & praedicta constitutio declaratur, si id fuerit visum iustum.
units.tr: These matters concerning the privileges, their abuse and their contrariety to the profession of the Friars, and the two conclusions I have argued above, shall suffice for me at present. I shall add more if it is necessary, and I have no doubt that others would not omit to do so, if I wished to. On all these matters, now sought and set out by me, most holy Father, Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment. May it please your Holiness, or some of my lords the Cardinals, to suspend the use of the privileges while the case is pending, and to declare, if it seems just, the aforesaid constitution concerning the matter I have touched upon, in whatever part of it is in dispute.

units.la: Prima conclusio erat, quod Dominus Iesus Christus in conuersatione sua humana semper pauper erat, non quia propter se paupertatem dilexit aut voluit, verum quia quo ad paupertatem, quam Dominus noster sustinuit, mihi aduersantes & ego non fuimus contrarii: sed quo ad modificationem adiectam, non quia propter se paupertatem dilexit aut voluit, illam particulam suadebo. Primo ... esse pauperem est esse miserum siue in miseria esse. Nemo vero propter se diligit miseriam. Ergo nullus propter se diligit paupertatem.
units.tr: The first conclusion was that our Lord Jesus Christ in his human life was always poor, not because he loved or willed poverty for its own sake, but because, as regards the poverty which our Lord endured, my opponents and I are not at odds. But as to the added qualification, not because he loved or willed poverty for its own sake, I shall argue for that clause. First: to be poor is to be wretched, or to be in misery. But no one loves misery for its own sake. Therefore no one loves poverty for its own sake.

units.la: Item secundum doctrinam Aristotelis in primo Ethicorum: Nihil est propter se diligibile, nisi quod sublato omni commodo subsequente gratitudo caperetur. Paupertas vero, etsi propter eius tolerantiam facit ut homines mereantur: tamen si nihil commodi propter tolerantiam sequeretur, nec a Deo nec ab homine nec a Diabolo caperetur. Igitur paupertas a Christo propter se nunquam est dilecta.
units.tr: Likewise, according to the teaching of Aristotle in the first book of the Ethics: Nothing is lovable for its own sake unless, with every advantage that follows removed, it would still be desired. But poverty, although by enduring it men may merit something, yet if no advantage followed from enduring it, it would not be sought by God, by man, or by the Devil. Therefore poverty was never loved for its own sake by Christ.

units.la: Item, nullus effectus peccati est propter se diligibilis: sicut nec ipsum peccatum est diligibile, etiam si corrupto animo paupertas diligatur. Paupertas vero est effectus peccati. Ergo &c. Probatur minor: quoniam si primi parentes nostri innocentiam tenuissent, nunquam de nostra progenie pauper aliquis extitisset. Item, nulla privatio boni est per se diligibilis, cum omnis habitus bonus sit propter se diligibilis: & iuxta Regulam Philosophi tertio Topicorum: Si propositum de proposito & oppositum de opposito. Item, quod si habitus est bonus, privatio est mala. Et si privatio est bona, habitus eius est malus. Ditatio vero, quae est habitus bona est & Deo amabilis, cum ipse summe sit dives. Ergo paupertas, quae ditationem priuat, est mala. Non est ergo propter se diligenda paupertas. Et videtur nimis puerile ad istud probandum insistere: cum nemo, ut puto, nisi propter defectum in Physica aut Logica, diceret oppositum.
units.tr: Likewise, no effect of sin is lovable for its own sake, just as sin itself is not lovable, even if poverty is loved by a corrupt mind. But poverty is an effect of sin. Therefore, etc. The minor is proved: if our first parents had kept their innocence, no one of our progeny would ever have been poor. Likewise, no privation of good is lovable in itself, since every good habit is lovable for its own sake; and according to the rule of the Philosopher in the third book of the Topics: If the proposition holds of one thing, the opposite holds of the opposite. Likewise, if a habit is good, its privation is bad, and if a privation is good, its habit is bad. But wealth, which is a good habit, is good and lovable to God, since he himself is supremely rich. Therefore poverty, which deprives of wealth, is bad. Poverty is therefore not to be loved for its own sake. And it seems too childish to insist on proving this, since no one, I think, would say the opposite unless from some defect in Physics or Logic.

units.la: Secunda conclusio erat, quod Dominus noster Iesus Christus nunquam spontanee mendicauit: quam sic primo suasi. Si ipse spontanee mendicasset, contra diuinum mandatum egisset: Non concupisces domum proximi tui. Non desiderabis uxorem eius: non seruum: non ancillam: non bovem: non asinum, nec omnia quae illius sunt, Exod. vigesim. cap. quoniam qui spontanee mendicat, perit: & per consequens concupiscit rem proximi sui. Igitur qui spontanee mendicat, facit contra diuinum praeceptum. Quod de Christo nemo auderet asserere.
units.tr: The second conclusion was that our Lord Jesus Christ never begged of his own accord. I first argued it thus. If he had begged of his own accord, he would have acted against the divine command: You shall not covet your neighbour's house. You shall not desire his wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor anything that is his, Exod. 20, since whoever begs of his own accord perishes, and consequently covets his neighbour's goods. Therefore whoever begs of his own accord acts against the divine precept. No one would dare to assert this of Christ.

units.la: Item, si Christus spontanee mendicasset, aliud mandatum diuinum soluisset, scilicet: Omnino egenus & mendicus non erit inter vos, Deuteron. decim. quint. cap. quoniam, scilicet non servaret. maret legem regiam praecipientem, quod in ciuitate non sit quisquam inermis, qui permitteret aliquos esse inermes, cum posset eis de armis succurrere. Sed ille qui cum posset remanere armatus, arma sua sponte in flumine demergeret, esset inermis & sineret alios esse inermes. Ergo peccaret. Sic ille sacerdos in Ecclesiae legem delinqueret, qua sacerdotibus est praeceptum, vt offerant dona & sacrificia pro peccatis, qui ad hoc sponte se redderet impotentem siue inhabilem. Sed nemo, vt aestimo, auderet de Saluatore asserere, quod fecerit contra diuinum mandatum. Nunquam ergo ispontaneè mendicauit gratis se faciens mendicum. Nec fingere quis potest, quod praemissum praeceptum est ceremoniale, cum sit vere morale, & artius in lege noua, quam in lege antiqua expressum, cum Saluator praecipiat Lucae vndecim. cap. Quod superest date Eleemosynam, & ecce omnia munda sunt vobis, vbi quicquid est vltra sufficientiam praecipitur dari, vt nullus mendicus sine egens in plebe remaneat, & non seruanti comminatur poenam aeternam, Matth. vigesimo quint. cap. isto modo: Esurivi, & non dedistis mihi manducare &c. Ite maledicti in ignem aeternum qui paratus est Diabolo & angelis eius. Vnde clarescit quod arctius Christicolae obligantur a Domino ad non permittendum inter eos mendicos, quam homines sub lege antiqua.
units.tr: Likewise, if Christ had begged of his own accord, he would have broken another divine command, namely: There shall be no poor man or beggar among you, Deut. 15, since he would not have kept the royal law that commands that there be no one unarmed in the city. He would have permitted some to be unarmed, when he could have helped them with arms. But one who could have remained armed, and who of his own accord threw his weapons into the river, would be unarmed and would allow others to be unarmed as well. Therefore he would sin. Likewise that priest would transgress the law of the Church, by which priests are commanded to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, if he of his own accord made himself unable or unfit for this. But no one, I judge, would dare to assert of the Saviour that he acted against the divine command. Christ therefore never begged of his own accord, making himself a beggar for no reason. Nor can anyone pretend that the precept mentioned is ceremonial, since it is truly moral, and it is expressed more strictly in the new law than in the old. For the Saviour commands in Luke 11: Give alms of what remains, and behold, all things are clean for you, where whatever is beyond sufficiency is commanded to be given, so that no beggar or needy person remains among the people. He threatens eternal punishment to the one who does not keep this, in Matth. 25: I was hungry, and you gave me no food, etc. Depart into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels. Hence it is clear that Christians are bound by the Lord more strictly not to allow beggars among them than men were under the old law.

units.la: Item, Christus imperatoriae legi erat subiectus: quoniam & soluit tributa Caesari, sicut legitur Matth. decim. septim. cap. vbi sic dicitur: Et cum venisset Capharnaum, accesserunt qui didrachma accipiebant ad Petrum & dixerunt ei, Magister vester non soluit didragma? Et cum introisset domum, vocauit eum Iesus dicens: Quid tibi videtur Simon? Reges terrae a quibus accipiunt tributum vel censum, a filiis suis, an ab alienis? Et ille dixit, ab alienis. Dixit ille Iesus: Ergo liberi sunt filii. Vt autem non scandalizemus eos: vade ad mare & mitte hamum: & eum piscem, qui primus ascenderit, tolle. Et aperto ore eius inuenies staterem, illum sumens da eis pro me & te. Haec ibi. Et decreuit tributum illi esse soluendum, cum quaerentibus ab eo, an licet censum dare Caesari, & obtulerunt ei denarium cuius superscriptio Caesaris erat, ait illis: Reddite ergo quae sunt Caesaris Caesari: & quae sunt Dei Deo, Matth. vigesim. secund. cap. Nec suisset conueniens, vt videtur, quod ipse tanquam legem communem decreuisset esse seruandam, quam subire nolebat. Voluit igitur tali legi esse subiectus, sicut erat subiectus Ioseph fabro: quanto magis (vt videtur) voluit esse subiectus legi imperatoriae, quae fuerat naturalis, quae praecipiebat vt mendicantes validi non remanerent in ciuitatibus. Et quanto magis nec mendicantes spontanee in ciuitatibus debuerant remanere.
units.tr: Likewise, Christ was subject to the imperial law, since he also paid tribute to Caesar, as we read in Matth. 17, where it is said: And when he had come to Capernaum, those who received the didrachma came to Peter and said to him, Does not your Master pay the didrachma? And when he had entered the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying: What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth take tribute or customs, from their sons or from strangers? And he said, From strangers. Jesus said to him: Then the sons are free. But so that we may not offend them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up. And when you open its mouth you will find a stater; take that and give it to them for me and you. So far there. He also decided that tribute was to be paid, when people asked him whether it was lawful to give the census to Caesar, and they showed him a denarius with Caesar's inscription on it. He said to them: Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's, Matth. 22. Nor, it seems, would it have been fitting for him to decree as a common law something to be kept, which he himself was unwilling to undergo. He therefore willed to be subject to such a law, just as he was subject to Joseph the carpenter. How much more, it seems, did he will to be subject to the imperial law, which was natural, and which commanded that able-bodied beggars should not remain in the cities. And all the more should beggars not have remained in cities of their own accord.

units.la: Item, si Christus spontanee mendicasset, legem de dilectione proximi mendicando soluisset. Quoniam qui vere diligit proximum suum, sicut seipsum, non vexat eum indebite: sicut nec velle debet seipsum a proximo vexari indebite. Petere vero a proximo quod suum est non egendo: est ipsum vexare indebite. Christus ergo nunquam sic egit. Item, cum Scriptura dicat: Proximo suo pauper odiosus erit, Prouerb. 14. cap. quanto magis mendicus proximo redditur odiosus. Si ergo Christus spontanee mendicasset, se reddidisset proximis suis odiosum: quod non videtur, nisi alia rationabilis causa subesset.
units.tr: Likewise, if Christ had begged of his own accord, he would have broken the law of love for one's neighbour by begging. For whoever truly loves his neighbour as himself does not burden him unduly, just as he ought not to wish himself to be burdened unduly by his neighbour. But to ask of a neighbour what is his own, when one is not in need, is to burden him unduly. Christ therefore never acted in this way. Again, since Scripture says: The poor man is hated even by his neighbour, Prov. 14, how much more is the beggar made hateful to his neighbours. If therefore Christ had begged of his own accord, he would have made himself hateful to his neighbours. This does not appear, unless some reasonable cause lay behind it.

units.la: Item, si Christus spontanee mendicasset, suo Euangelio offendiculum posuisset, quod ipse miraculis confirmauit. Quoniam audientes eius doctrinam & videntes eius miracula rationabiliter (vt videtur) potuissent illa potius dicere esse illusiones & magica, quam vera miracula, cum sit verisimile, quod quilibet sibi potius ac prius succurrere debet quam alteri. Quomodo ergo pasceret ille quatuor aut quinque millia hominum faciendo miraculum, qui sibi non poterat procurare victum, sicut alias illudebant ei in cruce pendenti ita dicentes: Alios saluos fecit, seipsum non potest saluum facere: si rex Israel est descendat de cruce nunc & credemus ei, Matth. vigesim. septim. cap. Item, si Christus spontanee mendicasset, legem suam propriam, quam dicit esse legem & Prophetas, soluisset: Omnia quaecunque vultis vt faciant vobis homines, vos facite illis. Haec enim est lex & Prophetae, Matth. septim. cap. Quoniam nec ipse velle aliis debebat, vt ipsi sine indigentia inquietarentur ab eo: quod tamen facit, quicunque spontanee, scilicet non egendo, mendicat.
units.tr: Likewise, if Christ had begged of his own accord, he would have placed a stumbling block before his Gospel, which he confirmed by miracles. For those who heard his teaching and saw his miracles could reasonably (it seems) have said that they were illusions and magic rather than true miracles, since it is likely that everyone ought to help himself first and before others. How then could he feed four or five thousand people by a miracle, when he could not procure food for himself? Likewise, as they mocked him while he hung on the cross, saying: He saved others, he cannot save himself. If he is the King of Israel, let him come down from the cross now, and we will believe him, Matth. 27. Likewise, if Christ had begged of his own accord, he would have broken his own law, which he said was the law and the Prophets: Whatever you wish that men should do to you, do so to them. For this is the law and the Prophets, Matth. 7. For he ought not to wish others to trouble him, when he was not in need, which nevertheless whoever begs of his own accord (that is, while not in need) does.

units.la: Item, Paulus Apostolus 1. ad Timoth. 6. cap. condemnat eos, qui quaestum aestimant pietatem. Quicquid vero Paulus condemnat, Christus per Paulum condemnat: quia Euangelium suum accepit per reuelationem ipsius, vt ipse Paulus affirmat ad Galatas primo cap. Igitur si Christus spontanee mendicauit, cum spontanee mendicare, sit quaestum expetere vel verius procurare: Christus excercuit per seipsum, quod condemnauit per Paulum, & erat sibi contrarius (quod nephas est dicere.) Ergo Christus nunquam spontanee mendicauit. Item, si Christus spontanee mendicauit: Christus facto fecit mendacium: quoniam quis ita facto contra mentem agendo, sicut verbo mentitur. Qui vero non egendo, sed spontanee postulando Eleemosynam affirmaret verbo se esse egenum siue mendicum mentiretur in verbo. Igitur qui ita petit Eleemosynam non egendo, facto mentitur, quod nemo dicit de Christo. Item, si Christus spontanee mendicauit, vere fuit hypocrita apparens mendicus, non vere existens. Christus vero nunquam fuit vere mendicus: quoniam nullus est vere mendicus, quamuis mendicet: sed fictus, qui sibi potest sufficere. Qui vero mendicat spontanee, est sibi sufficiens: alias scilicet non spontanee, sed impellente indigentia mendicaret. Christus ergo ex quo non erat hypocrita, nunquam facte aut spontanee mendicauit. Item, si Christus spontanee mendicauit, cur Petrus Apostolus matrem sancti Clementis Discipuli sui, quam ad laborandum manibus aestimabat fuisse robustam, quia eam inter mendicantes reperit, acriter increpauit, sicut fecisse legitur in vita sancti Clementis. Ex uno in hoc secuta est Christum. Qui igitur Christum dicunt spontanee mendicasse, habent ostendere: quod, ut videtur, non possunt. Nunquam ergo Christus spontanee mendicavit. Item, si Christus spontanee mendicavit, Clemens Petri successor multum erravit, qui mendicitatem in cunctis conversis ad fidem pro viribus excludere laboravit. Ex hoc specialiter ab Ecclesia commendatus: cum mendicitas ipsorum perfectionem secundum istam Philosophiam auxisset. Item, si Christus spontanee mendicavit, cur Clemens Iacobo Hierosolymitano Episcopo in Epistola sibi directa, ut ponitur in decretis 12. q. 1. c. dilectissimis, doctrinis & exemplis Apostolorum obedire praecepit, si mendicare ad perfectionem vitae pertineat. Et inter Apostolos & Discipulos, ut & ibi praemittitur, nullus erat egens: & sic dicentes habent ostendere. Item, si Christus summus sacerdos existens spontanee mendicavit, Ecclesia sancta scienter erravit: cum statuit nullum debere sine sufficienti titulo ad sacros Ordines promoveri, cum caput Ecclesiae suo exemplo docuerit mendicandum. Item, si Christus spontanee mendicavit, scandalum intulit Ordini clericali: cum iuxta canonicas sanctiones Episcopus aut clericus mendicans inferat Ordini clericali opprobrium.
units.tr: Likewise, the Apostle Paul, in 1 Tim. 6, condemns those who think gain is godliness. Whatever Paul condemns, Christ condemns through Paul, because he received his Gospel by revelation from him, as Paul himself affirms ad Galatas primo cap. Therefore, if Christ begged of his own accord, since to beg of one's own accord is to seek, or rather to pursue, gain, Christ would have done by himself what he condemned through Paul, and would have been contrary to himself (which it is impious to say). Therefore Christ never begged of his own accord. Likewise, if Christ begged of his own accord, Christ would have lied by his deed, since one who acts against his mind by deed lies just as one lies in word. But whoever, not being in need, but asking alms of his own accord, would affirm in words that he is needy or a beggar, would lie in words. Therefore whoever thus asks alms without need lies by his deed, which no one says of Christ. Likewise, if Christ begged of his own accord, he was truly a hypocrite, appearing to be a beggar without really being one. But Christ was never truly a beggar, since no one is truly a beggar, though he begs, unless he is feigned and can support himself. Whoever begs of his own accord is able to support himself; otherwise he would beg not of his own accord, but under the compulsion of need. Therefore, since Christ was not a hypocrite, he never begged deceitfully or of his own accord. Likewise, if Christ begged of his own accord, why did the Apostle Peter sharply rebuke the mother of St Clement, his disciple, whom he judged to be strong enough to labour with her hands, because he found her among the beggars? It is read to have happened thus in vita sancti Clementis. Clement followed Christ in this one thing. Those who say that Christ begged of his own accord must therefore show it, which, as it seems, they cannot do. Christ therefore never begged of his own accord. Likewise, if Christ begged of his own accord, Clement, the successor of Peter, erred greatly, who laboured with all his strength to exclude beggary among all who were converted to the faith. He was specially commended for this by the Church, although their beggary would, according to that philosophy, have increased their perfection. Likewise, if Christ begged of his own accord, why did Clement, in an Epistle sent to him, command James, Bishop of Jerusalem, to obey the doctrines and examples of the Apostles (as is set down in the Decretum, 12 q. 1, c. dilectissimis), if begging pertained to the perfection of life? And, as is also said there, among the Apostles and disciples there was no one in need. So those who say this must show it. Likewise, if Christ, being the High Priest, begged of his own accord, the holy Church erred knowingly, when it decreed that no one should be promoted to holy orders without a sufficient title, since the head of the Church, by his example, had taught that one may beg. Likewise, if Christ begged of his own accord, he brought scandal upon the clerical order, since according to the canonical sanctions a bishop or cleric who begs brings disgrace upon the clerical order.

units.la: Item, si Christus spontanee mendicasset, reddidisset seipsum de peccato suspectum: quoniam sibi verecundiam intulisset: cum non aliunde praecipue dicatur spontanea mendicatio meritum mendicanti acquirere, nisi quia est actus humilis atque difficilis propter annexam erubescentiam naturalem. Erubescentia vero sive verecundia non cadit in hominem studiosum, sicut affirmat Aristoteles quarto Ethicorum, in fine. Non ergo erat in Christo: & per consequens nec spontanee mendicavit. Item, si Christus spontanee mendicavit, mendicare spontanee ad perfectionem vitae pertinuit. Inepte igitur dedit Christus Dominus legem antiquam statuens, ut sacerdotes, in quibus debebat esse summa vitae perfectio, possessiones haberent & decimas, si eis fuisset persectius mendicare. Item, si sic, totus mundus sub lege naturae erasset, statuens sacerdotibus proinde de publicis horreis circa cibaria: sicut legitur in fine Genesis, si eis fuisset amplioris meriti mendicare. Item, si Christus spontanee mendicavit: tunc mendicitas ad perfectionem Evangelii pertinet, & Ecclesia Dei erravit, scienter dationem Ecclesiarum admittens: & sic perfectionem suorum praelatorum imminuens, quod dicere mihi nephas videtur: licet nescio quae somnia ferant in contrarium.
units.tr: Likewise, if Christ had begged voluntarily, he would have made himself open to suspicion of sin, since he would have brought shame upon himself. Voluntary begging is usually said to win merit for the beggar for no other reason than that it is a humble and difficult act, because of the natural shame attached to it. Shame, however, does not fall upon a virtuous man, as Aristotle affirms in the fourth book of the Ethics, at the end. Therefore it was not in Christ, and consequently he did not beg voluntarily. Likewise, if Christ begged voluntarily, then voluntary begging belongs to the perfection of life. It was therefore foolish of Christ the Lord, in giving the old law, to ordain that priests, in whom the highest perfection of life ought to be, should have possessions and tithes, if begging had been the more perfect course for them. Likewise, if so, the whole world would have erred under the law of nature in appointing food for priests from the public granaries, as is read at the end of Genesis, if begging had been of greater merit for them. Likewise, if Christ begged voluntarily, then begging belongs to the perfection of the Gospel, and the Church of God erred knowingly in admitting the endowment of churches, and so diminished the perfection of its prelates. To say this seems to me wicked, although I know not what dreams they bring forward to the contrary.

units.la: Item, si mendicatio sive mendicitas ad perfectionem vitae pertineret Christianae, ut a Fratribus Mendicantibus affirmatur; cur nec Christus nec Spiritus sanctus in scripturis sacris super hoc alicubi nos instruxit: videtur nimis mirabile, nec verisimiliter credi potest. Et puto quod erit mirabilius: quia a principio sacrae Scripturae usque in finem, unum ad hoc verbum notabile non potest inveniri, quia ad alium sensum sit dictum. Item, cum Christus Discipulis suis promiserat: Cum autem venerit ille Spiritus veritatis, docebit vos omnem veritatem, Iohannis decim. sext. capitulo: aut Spiritus sanctus sui officii erat oblitus, quando venit ad Apostolos in Die Pentecostes non docens hanc veritatem mendicitatis Apostolos; cum de hoc penitus in eorum actibus nihil appareat: aut ipsi posteris invidentes veritatem eis doctam a Spiritu sancto tradere noluerunt. Quorum neutrum, prorsus homo affirmabit. Non ergo pertinuit spontanea mendicatio sive mendicitas ad tradendam per Apostolos veritatem.
units.tr: Likewise, if begging or mendicancy belonged to the perfection of the Christian life, as the Mendicant Friars affirm, then why have neither Christ nor the Holy Spirit instructed us anywhere in the sacred Scriptures on this matter? That seems exceedingly strange, and cannot plausibly be believed. And I think it will be stranger still, since from the beginning of Holy Scripture to its end, not a single notable word on this point can be found that is said in any other sense. Likewise, when Christ had promised his disciples: But when the Spirit of truth is come, he will guide you into all truth, John 16, either the Holy Spirit forgot his office when he came to the Apostles on the day of Pentecost and did not teach them this truth of begging, although nothing of it appears anywhere in their acts; or else they, begrudging posterity, were unwilling to hand down to them the truth taught them by the Holy Spirit. No man will affirm either of these. Therefore voluntary begging, or mendicancy, did not belong to the handing down of truth through the Apostles.

units.la: Item, quid dicent ipsi de Melchisedech, qui erat sacerdos Dei altissimi & rex Salem, quem supra Abraham Paulus extollit, ad Hebraeos septimo cap. qualiter sine mendicatione spontanea tantus erat, cum non ipse, secundum cuius Ordinem Christus erat sacerdos; non ut Christus spontanee mendicavit ordinem suum tradens: habent contrarium affirmantes ostendere. Item, cum Propheta dicat Prophetice: Non vidi iustum derelictum, nec semen eius quaerens panem: quomodo mendicitas Christo ascribitur contra Sermonem Propheticum, qui erat iustissimus? Item, si Christus spontanee mendicavit, cur mittens Discipulos ad Evangelium praedicandum, non id eis praecepit, sed directe contrarium, scilicet ut de mercede laboris sui manducarent & biberent, ita dicens: In quamcunque domum intraveritis, in eadem domo manete edentes & bibentes quae apud illos sunt. Dignus est enim operarius mercede sua, Lucae decim. capitulo. Item, si Christus spontanee mendicavit, nunquam laborem ad victum acquirendum mendicationi praeposuisset: quoniam si e contra fecisset, scilicet si laborem aliquoties praetulisset, nullus exeius operibus didicisset nunc quid eligibilius esset, videlicet victum sine mendicatione manuum labore perquirere; an labore postposito mendicare. Quod autem Christus victum laborando sibi acquisivit probabile est, quod a vulgo non solum vocarus filius fabri, sed faber: quoniam ex hac appellatione vulgari videtur, quod pro victu suo cum Ioseph patre putativo opus fabrile exercuit. Pro ista conclusione ad nunc ista sufficiant, donec adversantes fortiora adducendo ista impugnent.
units.tr: Likewise, what will they say about Melchizedek, who was the priest of the Most High God and king of Salem, whom Paul exalts above Abraham, Hebrews, chapter seven? How was he so great without voluntary begging, when Christ, after whose order he was priest, did not beg voluntarily, handing down his order? Let those who affirm the contrary show it. Likewise, since the Prophet says prophetically: I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread, how is begging ascribed to Christ, contrary to the prophetic saying, when he was most righteous? Likewise, if Christ begged voluntarily, why, when he sent his disciples to preach the Gospel, did he not command this to them, but directly the opposite, namely that they should eat and drink of the wages of their labour, saying: And into whatsoever house ye enter, there abide, eating and drinking such things as they give: for the labourer is worthy of his reward, Luke 10. Likewise, if Christ begged voluntarily, he would never have put begging before labour for acquiring food. For if on the contrary he had at any time preferred labour, no one from his works would have learned which was more to be chosen now: to seek food by the labour of one's hands without begging, or to beg with labour set aside. But that Christ acquired his food by labour is probable, since he was called by the common people not only the son of a carpenter but a carpenter himself. For from this common appellation it seems that he worked at carpentry with his putative father Joseph for his food. Let these things suffice for the present in support of this conclusion, until our opponents bring forward stronger arguments to attack them.

units.la: Tertia conclusio huius materiae fuit: quod Christus nunquam docuit spontanee mendicare. Haec taliter suadetur. Christus coepit facere & docere, Actuum primo capitulo. Si igitur mendicare spontanee docuisset, cum iuxta praecedentem conclusionem nunquam spontanee mendicavit, fuisset sibi contrarius in opere & sermone, scilicet docens & non faciens, quod non verisimile videtur. Item, si Christus nunquam spontanee mendicavit, & alios docuit mendicare, reddidisset se de sua doctrina suspectum, sicut patet in argumento sexto conclusionis prioris. Item, potuisset offendiculum Evangelio suis Apostolis, sicut deducitur in sexto argumento ibidem. Item, sic dicendo legem imperatoriam iustam soluere docuisset, sicut ibi in tertio art. tactum est. Item, si docuisset spontanee mendicandum contra leges superius allegatas & rationes quasi omnes ad precedentem conclusionem adductas fecisset. Quae ita istam, sicut & illam conclusionem affirmant. Item, si docuisset spontanee mendicandum, tunc Petrus particeps huius doctrinae nimis imprudenter egisset in allegando causas meritorias praemii sibi reddendi illam tam sublimem, secundum istos causam merendi tacens, cum dicit, sicut legitur Matth. decimo non. capitulo: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia & secuti sumus te, non addens, & mendicauimus spontanee propter te: quod quia non fecit, consequi satis videtur, quod illa conditio ad statum perfectionis non pertinet.
units.tr: The third conclusion of this matter was that Christ never taught voluntary begging. It is argued thus. Christ began to do and to teach, Acts, chapter one. If, then, he had taught voluntary begging, while according to the preceding conclusion he never begged voluntarily, he would have been contrary to himself in deed and word, teaching and not doing, which does not seem likely. Likewise, if Christ never begged voluntarily but taught others to beg, he would have made himself open to suspicion regarding his own teaching, as is evident in the sixth argument of the former conclusion. Likewise, he could have become a stumbling block to the Gospel for his Apostles, as is drawn out in the sixth argument there. Likewise, by teaching this he would have taught that the imperial law might be broken justly, as was touched on there in the third article. Likewise, if he had taught voluntary begging, he would have acted against the laws cited above and against almost all the reasons adduced for the preceding conclusion. These things affirm this conclusion just as they affirm that one. Likewise, if he had taught voluntary begging, then Peter, a sharer in this doctrine, would have acted most imprudently in citing the meritorious causes of the reward to be given him, so sublime, while according to them keeping silent about the cause of merit. For he says, as is read in Matthew 19: Behold, we have forsaken all, and followed thee, without adding, and we have begged voluntarily for thy sake. Since he did not add this, it seems sufficiently to follow that this condition does not belong to the state of perfection.

units.la: Quarta conclusio fuit, quod Dominus noster Iesus Christus docuit non debere hominem spontanee mendicare, sicut scribitur Lucae 14. capitulo: Cum facis conuiuium, voca pauperes & debiles, claudos & caecos, & beatus eris. Quia non habent, unde possunt retribuere tibi. Igitur non debent vocari ad Eleemosynae conuiuium pauperes robusti: quia possunt retribuere saltem suo labore: sicut nec diuites debiles, claudi aut caeci debent ad tale conuiuium vocari, quia habent unde retribuere possunt. Non cerno cur surdos, monachos & mutos non nominat inter vocandos: quia nec ipsi, si sint debiles & claudi vel caeci, possunt mendicando transire de loco in locum, quod facere nequeunt debiles, claudi & caeci: sed Domini Fratres istam expositionem ponunt inter errores. Item, Paulus Apostolus tanquam decretum affirmat: Qui non vult operari, non manducet, loquens de hominibus, qui aliunde victum de certo non habent, secunda ad Thessalonicenses tertio capitulo. Et sequitur poena, quam praecepit non parenti suis dictis infligi: quod si quis non obedierit verbo nostro per Epistolam, hunc notate, & ne commisceamini cum illo, ut confundatur. Nec dubium, quoniam non praeciperet tam grauem poenam negligenti laborare, nisi quia valde graue tali casu delictum committit. Dicit enim ibidem de seipso hoc modo: Ipsi enim scitis, quemadmodum oporteat imitari nos: quoniam non inquieti fuimus inter vos. Nec gratis panem manducauimus ab aliquo: sed in labore & fatigatione nocte & die operantes, ne quem vestrum grauaremus, non quasi non habuerimus potestatem: sed ut nosmetipsos formam daremus vobis ad imitandum nos. Nam & cum esse mus apud vos, hac denunciauimus vobis: ut qui non vult operari, non manducet. Vbi satis apparet, quod a fortiori volebat arguere: scilicet ex quo ipse, qui potestatem habuit sumendi carnalia ab his, quibus tanquam verus Apostolus seminabat spiritualia, ne quenquam grauaret, potius nocte & die in fatigatione erat atque labore pro victu: tanto magis alii potestatem huiusmodi non habentes laborare deberent & non inquirendo alios mendicare. Et vtinam hi homines, qui labori otium mendicationis praeponunt, attenderent librum Beati Augustini De opere monachorum, vbi hanc conclusionem pertractans per totum librum vsque prope finem conatur ostendere, quod labor debet otio contemplationis praeferri; cuius in praesenti rationes omitto, sed alias eis vtar.
units.tr: The fourth conclusion was that our Lord Jesus Christ taught that a man ought not to beg voluntarily, as is written in Luke 14: When thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind: and thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee. Therefore strong poor people ought not to be invited to the banquet of alms, since they can repay at least by their labour; just as rich men, or the crippled, lame or blind, ought not to be invited to such a banquet, since they have the means to repay. I do not see why he does not name the deaf, the monks and the dumb among those to be invited, since they too, if they are crippled, lame or blind, cannot go from place to place by begging, which the crippled, lame and blind cannot do; but the Brethren of the Mendicant Orders put that interpretation among the errors. Likewise, the Apostle Paul affirms as a decree: If any would not work, neither should he eat, speaking of men who have no certain means of livelihood otherwise, 2 Thessalonians, chapter three. And the penalty follows, which he commanded to be inflicted on anyone who did not obey his words: And if any man obey not our word by this epistle, note that man, and have no company with him, that he may be ashamed. There is no doubt that he would not prescribe so grave a penalty for one who neglected to work, unless such a case involved a very grave offence. For he says there of himself in this way: For yourselves know how ye ought to follow us: for we behaved not ourselves disorderly among you; neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you: not because we have not power, but to make ourselves an ensample unto you to follow us. For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat. Here it appears plainly that he wished to argue a fortiori: since he himself, who had the right to take carnal things from those to whom as a true Apostle he sowed spiritual things, yet so as not to burden anyone, rather laboured and toiled night and day for his food, all the more should others who do not have such a right work, and not seek to be fed by begging from others. And would that those men who put the idleness of begging before labour would attend to the book of Blessed Augustine On the Work of Monks, where, treating this same conclusion, he strives through nearly the whole book, almost to the end, to show that labour ought to be preferred to the leisure of contemplation. I omit his arguments for the present, but I shall use them against them on another occasion.

units.la: Item, ex quo sacra scriptura pigrum hominem reprehendit Proverbiorum sext. hoc modo: Vsque quo piger dormiis? Quando consurges e somno tuo &c. paululum manus conseres, vt quiescas, veniet tibi quasi viator (alias turbo) egestas tua & mendicitas (alias pauperies) quasi vir armatus. Eiusdem vigesim. cap. Propter frigus piger arare noluit: mendicabit ergo in aestate, & non dabitur ei. Et eiusdem vltim. cap. commendat mulierem fortem, cuius digiti apprehendere fusum. Constat igitur, quod per haec dissuadetur mendicationis ocium labore neglecto.
units.tr: Also, since Holy Scripture rebukes the idle man, Proverbs 6 says: "How long will you sleep, O sluggard? When will you rise out of your sleep? ... a little folding of the hands to rest, and your poverty will come upon you like a traveller (others: a whirlwind), and your want (others: penury) like an armed man." In the twentieth chapter of the same book: "The sluggard would not plough because of the cold; he shall therefore beg in harvest, and nothing shall be given him." And in the last chapter of the same book he commends the strong woman whose fingers grasp the spindle. It is clear, then, that these passages dissuade idleness in begging, when labour is neglected.

units.la: Item, sanctus Franciscus in suo Testamento dicit sic: Et ego manibus meis laborabam, & volo vos laborare.
