Et omnes alii Fratres firmiter volo quod laborent & viuant de labore suo, quod pertinet ad honestatem: & qui nesciunt, discant non propter cupiditatem recipiendi mercedem laboris, sed propter exemplum boni operis & ad repellendum ociositatem. Et quando non datur nobis precium laboris, recurramus ad mensam Domini petendo Eleemosynas ostiatim. Haec ibi. Et in Regula, sua dicit sic: Fratres illi, quibus gratiam Dominus dedit laborandi, laborent fideliter & devote. Vnde est valde mirandum, qua fronte Fratres audeant aut spontaneam mendicationem exercere, aut mendicationem laboriscontrario suo instituitori praeferre: & eo amplius est mirandum, quod homo ad laborem nascitur, vt dicitur Iob quinto cap. & mendicare est contra legem institutionis nostrae primariae: in qua seruata nullus fuisset vnquam mendicus siue mendicans.
units.tr: Also, St Francis says in his Testament: "And I laboured with my own hands, and I wish you to labour. And I firmly wish all the other Brothers to labour and to live by their labour, which pertains to honesty; and those who do not know how, let them learn, not from desire for receiving the wage of labour, but for the example of good work and to drive away idleness. And when the price of labour is not given us, let us return to the table of the Lord, begging alms from door to door." So far there. And in his Rule he says: "Those brothers to whom the Lord has given grace to labour, let them labour faithfully and devoutly." Hence it is very much to be wondered at with what brazenness the Friars dare either to practise voluntary begging, or to prefer begging to labour, contrary to their founder. It is even more to be wondered at that man is born to labour, as is said in Job 5, and that to beg is against the primary law of our institution, in which, had it been kept, no one would ever have been a beggar or a mendicant.

units.la: Item, Christus in hoc non mendicare spontanee docuisse videtur, quod ipse in sua persona vtiam potius miraculo voluit, quam mendicare: scilicet cum misit Petrum ad mare, vt staterem in ore piscis reciperet inuentum, & exactoribus didragmatis pro se & pro Petro Petrus exsoluceret: cum tamen eo casu tam honoratus in populo staterem mendicando facile impetrasset.
units.tr: Also, Christ seems to have taught in this matter not to beg voluntarily, in that in his own person he chose to use a miracle rather than to beg. Namely, when he sent Peter to the sea, so that he would take the stater found in the mouth of a fish and pay it to the collectors of the didrachma for himself and for Peter. Yet on that occasion, being so honoured among the people, he could easily have obtained the stater by begging.

units.la: Item, alia facta eius idem videntur ostendere, quoniam potius visus fuisse videtur illa legem Diuina: Dignus est operarius mercede sua, Lucae decimo capitulo, ac Matthaei decimo. Dignus est operarius cibo suo. Sicut Discipulis suis indixit, quando asinum, cui insedit, sibi iussit adduci. Et quando aperte Zacheo praecepit: Zachee festinans descende: quia hodie in domo tua oportet me manere: Vbi tanquam ad hoc potestatem habens apertissime imperauit: Festinans descende. Sic quando erat in templo, & circumspectis omnibus, cum iam vespera esset facta, exiuit in Bethaniam cum duodecim, sicut legitur Marci vndecim: potius illo iure vti voluit, quam ab aliquibus mendicare. Prius enim in Bethania Euangelium nunciabat. Aut si potestate hac vsus non fuerat, sed declinauit ad amicos, tunc saltem maluit amicos onerare, quam ab aliquo mendicare. Item, hoc aperte praecepisse videtur suis discipulis eos mittens: Nolite transfire de domo in domum, Luc. 10. capitulo. Quod tamen de cursu communi oportet facere mendicantes (scriptura nihilominus alia affirmante) Vita nequam hospitari de domo in domum, Ecclesiast. vigesim. non. capitulo. Sacra scriptura alibi talem mendicitatem pariter reprobante hoc modo: Pes fatui facilis in domo proximi, Ecclesiast. vigesim. prim. cap. & Ecclesiast. quadragesim. cap. Fili mi tempore vitae tuae ne indigueris. Melius est enim mori quam indigere. Vir respiciens in mensam alienam, non est vita eius in cogitatione vitus. Alit enim animam suam cibis alienis. Vir autem disciplinatus & eruditus custodiet se. In ore imprudentis conculcabitur inopia, & in ventre eius ardebit ignis. Haec ibi. Item iuveni, ut esset perfectus, ita consuluit, ut venderet omnia sua & daret pauperibus & sequeretur eum. Eius vero sequelam in modo viuendi non dubium debemus accipere.
units.tr: Also, his other deeds seem to show the same, since he seems rather to have regarded that divine law: "The labourer is worthy of his hire," Luke 10, and "The labourer is worthy of his food," Matthew 10. He laid this down for his disciples when he ordered the ass on which he sat to be brought to him. And when he openly bade Zacchaeus: "Zacchaeus, make haste and come down, for today I must stay in your house." Here, as one having authority in this matter, he most plainly commanded: "Make haste and come down." Likewise, when he was in the temple and had looked round at everything, and when evening had already come, he went out to Bethany with the twelve, as is read in Mark 11. He preferred to use that right rather than to beg from anyone. For first in Bethany he was proclaiming the Gospel. Or if he had not used this power, but turned aside to friends, then at least he preferred to burden friends rather than beg from anyone. Likewise, he seems to have plainly commanded his disciples when he sent them out: "Do not go from house to house," Luke 10. Yet mendicants must do this in the ordinary course, although Scripture affirms the contrary: "A wicked life goes from house to house as a guest," Ecclesiasticus, chapter 29. Scripture elsewhere likewise reprobates such begging: "The foot of a fool is easy in his neighbour's house," Ecclesiasticus, chapter 21; and Ecclesiasticus, chapter 40: "My son, do not lack in the time of your life. For it is better to die than to be in want. The man who looks to another's table, his life is not to be counted as life, for he feeds his soul on other men's food. But the disciplined and instructed man will guard himself. In the mouth of the imprudent poverty will be trampled, and in his belly a fire will burn." So far there. Likewise, he counselled the young man, in order that he might be perfect, to sell all his goods, give them to the poor, and follow him. But we ought not to doubt that his following consisted in his manner of living.

units.la: Cum igitur secunda conclusio confirmauit, quod Christus nunquam spontanee mendicauit; consequitur quod sine spontanea mendicatione docuit iuvenem debere ipsum sequendo esse persectum. Et sic saltem perfectum docuit non debere spontanee mendicare. Ex his probabiliter poterit inferri, quod Dominus noster Iesus Christus docuit hominem non debere spontanee mendicare.
units.tr: Since, then, the second conclusion has confirmed that Christ never begged voluntarily, it follows that by following him without voluntary begging the young man was taught that he must be perfect. And so at least he taught that the perfect ought not to beg voluntarily. From these things it may probably be inferred that our Lord Jesus Christ taught that a man ought not to beg voluntarily.

units.la: Quinta conclusio huius materiae mendicitatis erat; quod nullus potest prudenter & sancte spontaneam mendicitatem super se assumere perpetuo observandam. Ista sequitur plane ex aliis suprasuasis: quoniam ex quo talis mendicitas vel mendicatio est dissuasa a Christo Apostolis & Discipulis, & ab Ecclesia sacris scripturis etiam reprobata; consequitur, quod non potest prudenter & sancte assumi, quamvis secundum aemulationem Dei possit assumi: sicut Marcus imprudenter, etsi zelo bono, pollicem sibi praecidit. Item, sic mendicitatem assumens se in tentationem inducit contra doctrinam Orationis Dominicae, Matth. 6. capitulo: Et ne nos inducas in tentationem. Qua enim conscientia potest quis petere a Deo, ne Deus inducat eum, id est permittat induci, in tentationem, qui se spontanee in tentationem inducit. Quae enim est maior tentationis occasio, quam mendicitatem assumere? cum Salomon aperte dicat & pronunciet: Mendicitatem & divitias ne dederis mihi: sed victui tantum tribue necessaria, ne forte satiatus alliciar ad negandum te & dicam, quis est Dominus? Et egestate compulsus furer & periurem nomen Dei mei, Proverbiorum trigesim. cap. Vbi patenter ostendit, quod mendicus ad furtum & periurium nominis Dei sui facile impulsu egestatis vrgetur. Unde Ecclesiastici vigesim. septim. capitulo dicitur: Propter inopiam multi deliquerunt. Constat ergo, quod qui mendicitatem super se sponte assumit, occasionem grauem & facilem tentationem assumit. Item, sic mendicitatem assumens ad officium sacerdotale, imo ad omnes Ordines sacros, ut videtur, se reddit inhabilem, cum sine titulo sufficienti de victu & vestitu secundum Ecclesiae leges satis talis habere non possit. Quod non videtur prouide esse factum, sed potius imprudenter.
units.tr: The fifth conclusion of this matter of begging was that no one can prudently and holily take upon himself voluntary begging to be observed perpetually. This follows plainly from the other arguments above. Since such begging or mendicancy has been dissuaded by Christ to the Apostles and disciples, and has also been reprobated by the Church from the sacred Scriptures, it follows that it cannot be prudently and holily undertaken, although it may be undertaken out of zeal for God, as Mark imprudently, though with good zeal, cut off his own thumb. Likewise, by taking up begging one leads oneself into temptation, contrary to the teaching of the Lord's Prayer, Matthew 6: "And lead us not into temptation." For with what conscience can someone ask God not to lead him, that is, not to permit him to be led, into temptation, when he himself voluntarily leads himself into temptation? For what greater occasion of temptation is there than to take up begging? Solomon plainly says and declares: "Give me neither beggary nor riches; give me only the necessities of life, lest perhaps, being satiated, I be drawn to deny you and say, Who is the Lord? Or, being compelled by want, I steal and perjure the name of my God," Proverbs 30. There he clearly shows that the beggar is easily driven by the pressure of want to theft and to perjury of the name of his God. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus 27: "On account of poverty many have sinned." It is plain, then, that he who takes up begging voluntarily takes upon himself a grave occasion and an easy temptation. Likewise, one who takes up begging in order to hold the priestly office, indeed any of the sacred Orders, makes himself, as it seems, unfit, since without a sufficient title of food and clothing, according to the laws of the Church, he cannot in fact have such a title. This does not seem to have been done prudently, but rather imprudently.

units.la: Item, talem mendicitatem assumens se arctare videtur ad Dei leges praedictas in conclusione secunda de Christi mendicitate soluenda, scilicet Non concupisces domum proximi tui &c. Et, omnis egens & mendicus non erit inter vos. Et, omnia quaecunque vultis &c. Et fere rationes omnes conclusionum trium praecedentium hanc, ut illas affirmant. Unde non video in sermonibus, de quibus in propositionis istius principio mentionem iam feci, qualiter ista opinio de observantia mendicitatis spontaneae fuerat introducta, nisi ignorando scripturam, aut fingendo eam esse Christi vitae conformem, ut per ipsam quaestus amplior haberetur.
units.tr: Likewise, one who takes up such begging seems to bind himself to the divine laws mentioned in the second conclusion, which must be answered concerning Christ's begging: namely, "You shall not covet your neighbour's house," etc.; "there shall be no beggar or mendicant among you"; and "all things whatsoever you would that men should do to you," etc. Almost all the arguments of the three preceding conclusions affirm this one, just as they affirm those. Hence I do not see, from the sermons of which I have already made mention at the beginning of this proposition, how this opinion about observing voluntary begging had been introduced, except by ignoring Scripture, or by pretending that it conforms to the life of Christ, so that a greater gain might be had from it.

units.la: Unde sexta conclusio materiae huius erat, quod non est Regula Fratrum Minorum mendicitatem spontaneam observare. Haec occulta fide poterit suaderi per hoc, quod in Regula & in Testamento sanctus Franciscus suis Fratribus indistincte mendicationi praefert laborem. Item, rationes conclusionum precedentium istam probant, ut illas principio hoc adiecto, quod Regula ipsa est sancta, quod principaliter asseritur & probatur capitulo, Exiit, supradicto.
units.tr: Hence the sixth conclusion of this matter was that the Rule of the Friars Minor does not require voluntary begging to be observed. This can be persuaded by a hidden faith, through the fact that in the Rule and in the Testament St Francis indistinctly prefers labour to begging for his brothers. Likewise, the arguments of the preceding conclusions prove this one, with this added at the start: that the Rule itself is holy, which is principally asserted and proved in the chapter "Exiit", cited above.

units.la: Septima conclusio huius materiae erat, quod bulla Domini Alexandri quarti, quae libellum Magistrorum condemnat, nullum praemissarum conclusionum impugnat. Haec taliter suadetur, quod Dominus Iohannes vigesim. secund. in constitutione sua, Quia quorundam, dicit expresse, quod Dominus Nicolaus tertius illam Bullam, & omnes literas praedicti Alexandri quarti, quantum ad omnes articulos, quos sua declaratio retinet, reuocauit.
units.tr: The seventh conclusion of this matter was that the bull of Lord Alexander IV, which condemns the little book of the Masters, does not impugn any of the aforesaid conclusions. This is persuaded thus: Lord John XXII, in his constitution "Quia quorundam", expressly says that Lord Nicholas III revoked that Bull and all the letters of the aforesaid Alexander IV, as far as all the articles are concerned which his declaration retains.

units.la: Constat autem, quod paupertatem Fratrum Minorum, quam arctam esse debeat, Nicolaus tertius declarauit, quam Fratres mendicitatem intelligunt.
units.tr: It is clear, moreover, that Nicholas III declared how strict the poverty of the Friars Minor ought to be, which the friars understand as mendicancy.

units.la: Item constat, quod Dominus Nicolaus tertius de Fratrum labore declarat, & etiam de praedicatione non facienda in Episcopatu alicuius Episcopi, cum ab eodem eis fuerit contradictum. Ergo quo ad istos articulos Bulla Domini Alexandri est a Nicolao quassata. Nec in ipsa Bulla recordor aliud quicquam esse, quod aliquam praemissarum conclusionum infirmet.
units.tr: Likewise, it is clear that Lord Nicholas III makes a declaration concerning the labour of the friars, and also concerning the non-performance of preaching within the diocese of any bishop, since it was contradicted by him to them. Therefore, as regards these articles, the Bull of Lord Alexander has been shaken by Nicholas. Nor do I recall anything else in that Bull that weakens any of the aforementioned conclusions.

units.la: Dicerem multa plura obiiciendo contra mea propria dicta & respondendo: & praemissa, quae dixi, amplius solidarem: sed sanctitatem vestram & dominorum meorum reuerentiam satis vexaui.
units.tr: I could say a great deal more, raising objections against my own statements and answering them, and could strengthen further what I have said above; but I have sufficiently tried the patience of your holiness and of my lords.

units.la: Unde concludo & humiliter ac devote deposco, quod super his, sicut supra materiam primam per me tactam iuxta petitionem quam feci: Nolite iudicare secundum faciem: sed iustum iudicium iudicate.
units.tr: Hence I conclude and humbly and devoutly ask that, concerning these matters, just as concerning the first matter touched on by me above, in accordance with the petition I have made: Judge not according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment.

units.la: DIXI.
units.tr: I HAVE SPOKEN.

units.la: Finis Defensionis Curatorum contra eos, qui se privilegiatos dicunt: habita a Domino Richardo Armachano coram summo pontifice Innocentio sexto & Dominis Cardinalibus, Anno Domini M. CCC. LVII. die vero 14. mensis Novembris: Pontificatus dicti Innocentii sexti Anno quinto, loco quo supra dictum est.
units.tr: The end of the Defence of the Parish Priests against those who call themselves privileged: delivered by Lord Richard of Armagh before the supreme pontiff Innocent VI and the Lord Cardinals, in the year of the Lord 1357, on the 14th day of the month of November, in the fifth year of the pontificate of the said Innocent VI, in the place mentioned above.

units.la: SEQVITVR DEFENSIO RELIGIONIS MENDICANTIVM CONTRA EA, QVAE IN PRAECEDENTI ET IN ALIIS DOMINI RICHARDI ARMA- CHANI Archiepiscopi operibus contra eam obiiciuntur: edita a religioso viro, Magistro Rogerio Chonoe Ordinis Minorum.
units.tr: THE DEFENCE OF THE RELIGION OF THE MENDICANT FRIARS AGAINST THE OBJECTIONS RAISED AGAINST IT IN THE PRECEDING WORK AND IN THE OTHER WORKS OF LORD RICHARD ARMACHANUS, ARCHBISHOP: PUBLISHED BY A RELIGIOUS MAN, MASTER ROGER CHONOE OF THE ORDER OF FRIARS MINOR.

units.la: Cuius haec est Praefatio.
units.tr: Of this work, this is the Preface.

units.la: Confessio & pulchritudo in conspectu eius: sanctimonia & magnificentia in sanctificatione eius, Psal. 95. Beatus Bernhardus Epistola 113. & est ad Sophiam virginem, volens ostendere quod confessionem sequatur decor pulchritudinis dicit: Reuera ubi confessio, ibi pulchritudo, ibi decor. Si peccata sunt, confessione lauantur. Si bona opera, confessione commendantur. Cum peccata tua confiteris, sacrificium est Deo spiritus contribulatus. Cum Dei confiteris beneficia, immolas Deo sacrificium laudis. Bonum anima ornamentum confessio: qua & peccatorem purgat, & iustum reddit purgatiorem. Absque confessione iustus iudicatur ingratus: & peccator mortuus reputatur. A mortuo quippe tanquam qui non sit (alias nihil sit) perit confessio. Confessio igitur peccatoris est vita, iusti gloria, & necessaria est peccatori: & nihilominus iustum decet. Haec ille. Hanc proinde confessionem, quae, ut dictum est, ipsos peccatores per lacrymas poenitudinis & moeroris, purgat a maculis turpitudinis & foetoris: ornat floribus pulchritudinis & decoris: vulgat titulus sanctitudinis & honoris, iuxta illud Psalmistae praeallegati: Confessio & pulchritudo &c. Multa sunt, quae confessionem impediunt, secundum Hugo. De claustro animae lib. quarto, cap. 10. Multifariam hostes Iudeos invaduni. Demetrium (inquit) Nichanorem ducem Elephantorum misit in Iudaam, ut Iudam caperet. 1. Macchabaeorum 7. Quid enim per Demetrium, qui vos modo persequens interpretatur, nisi Diabolum possumus accipere? Quid per Nichanorem bugrnam stantem, nisi nostram elationem? Nichanor, inquit, Elephantorum turmis praeponitur, quotiens incorrigibilium mentibus superbia dominatur. Crura siquidem Elephantorum iuncturis carent. Unde superbi assimulantur, qui a proposito suo flecti nequaquam possunt. Mittitur itaq; Nichanor a Demetrio, id est spiritus elationis a Diabolo, in Iudaea, ut destruat confessionis terram, ut Iudam capiat, id est eos qui peccata sua confitentur, curiositate teneat & perversa consuetudine liget: & eos qui confitentes consolantur, impediat, & otiosa cogitatione perturbet. Haec ille. Sane quandoquidem venerabilis patris & Domini sacraq; Theologiae Doctoris famosi, Domini Richardi Armachani Archiepiscopi quendam tractatum contra Fratres quatuor Ordinum Mendicantium super constitutione extravagante felicis recordationis Iohannis Papae 22. Vas electionis, liberas confessiones libere impugnantem, reuerendissimis patribus & Dominis meis, Dominis Cardinalibus praesentatum, nuper recepi. Ad quem dignatus est me rogare quidam venerabilis pater ac magister, qui me potuit obligare mandato, quod eiusdem Domini dictis & calumniis pro viribus obuiarem. Verum quia in tam arduo negotio quantum imperantis vrgebat auctoritas, tantum terrebat subtilitas aduersantis, ad perplexorum omnium consuetum refugium dulcis Iesu matrem & virginem tota mentis fiducia me conuerti, implorans & obsecrans quatenus mihi inter sacrae paginae Professores Ordinis Fratrum Minorum minimo, & pene nullo spiritus sapientiae flatum per modicum impetraret dignaretur a filio: quo reuocari possint errantes, & confortari Deum imitantes & dubii: at pertinaciter reluctantes & obuii vel in motico mitigari. Sic tandem eorum, quae tam experientia, quam poetica, vel sacrae scripturae doctrina didiceram, reminiscens: sciebam quod tyrica de veneno venenatorum confecta, mortiferum nonnunquam pellit venenum: quodq; repercussiones hastae Peliadae suorum vulnerum praestabant medelam: quod etiam humiliter Dauid Goliam suo gladio peremit: & Holofernem truncauit proprio pugione Iudith vidua delicata: quibus non modicum animatus totum me dedi vtiusla complerem. Quod si alicubi sensus hebes, aut calamus praeceps oberraverit (quod absit) a semita veritatis, sanctae matris Ecclesiae, vestrorum dominorum meorum Cardinalium correctioni me submitto per omnia, nullum probam & eruditum quemuis aduersarium renuens correptorem. [illegible, ~20 letters] suo tractatu principaliter quatuor intendit Dominus iste. Primum est, quod primo prædicitur in capitulo, Dudum cum de sepulturis libro septimo, hoc est, in clementina, nec aliquod priuilegium ei simili tollit aut impugnat statutum concilii generalis, Omnis utriusque sexus.
units.tr: Confession and beauty are in his sight; holiness and majesty are in his sanctuary, Ps. 95. Blessed Bernard, Epistle 113, written to the virgin Sophia, wishing to show that beauty and grace follow confession, says: Truly, where there is confession, there is beauty and grace. If there are sins, they are washed away by confession. If there are good works, they are commended by confession. When you confess your sins, it is a sacrifice to God, a contrite spirit. When you confess God's benefits, you offer to God the sacrifice of praise. Confession is the good ornament of the soul: it both cleanses the sinner and makes the righteous man purer. Without confession the just man is judged ungrateful, and the sinner is reckoned dead. For confession perishes with the dead, as with one who does not exist (otherwise it would be nothing). Confession, therefore, is the life of the sinner and the glory of the just; it is necessary for the sinner, and it is fitting for the righteous as well. So far he. This confession, then, which, as has been said, cleanses the sinners themselves from the stains of filth and stench through the tears of penitence and sorrow, adorns them with the flowers of beauty and grace, and spreads abroad the title of holiness and honour, according to that saying of the Psalmist cited above: Confession and beauty, etc. Many things hinder confession, according to Hugh, On the Cloister of the Soul, book 4, chapter 10: Enemies attack the Jews in many ways. He (it says) sent Demetrius Nicanor, the commander of the elephants, into Judea, to take Judas (1 Maccabees 7). For what can we understand by Demetrius, who now persecutes you, except the Devil? What by the standing Nicanor, except our own pride? Nicanor, it says, is placed over the squadrons of elephants whenever pride rules the minds of the incorrigible. For the legs of elephants lack joints; hence the proud are compared to those who can by no means be bent from their purpose. Nicanor is therefore sent by Demetrius, that is, the spirit of pride by the Devil, into Judea, to destroy the land of confession, to take Judas, that is, to hold those who confess their sins in curiosity, to bind them with a perverse custom, to hinder those who comfort them in their confession, and to disturb them with idle thoughts. So far he. Since I have lately received a certain treatise of the venerable father and lord, the holy theologian and famous Doctor, Lord Richard, Archbishop of Armagh, against the four orders of Mendicant Friars, concerning the extravagant constitution of Pope John XXII of happy memory, Vas electionis, which freely attacks free confessions, and which was presented to my most reverend fathers and lords, the lord Cardinals. A certain venerable father and master, who could bind me by command, asked me to oppose the statements and calumnies of this lord as far as I could. But since the authority of the one commanding urged me on in so arduous a matter as much as the subtlety of the opponent frightened me, I turned, with my whole trust of mind, to the sweet Jesus' mother and virgin, the usual refuge of all who are perplexed, beseeching and entreating that she would deign to obtain from her son for me, the least of the professors of sacred Scripture in the Order of Friars Minor, and almost no one, a small breath of the spirit of wisdom, by which those who are erring might be recalled, those who imitate God might be strengthened, and those who are doubtful but obstinately resist and oppose might be softened even a little. Thus at last, recalling what I had learned both from experience and from poetry and from the teaching of Sacred Scripture, I knew that a Tyrian remedy made from the venom of venomous creatures sometimes drives out deadly poison; that the blows of the spear of Peleus provided a cure for the wounds they made; that David humbly slew Goliath with his own sword; and that Judith, a delicate widow, beheaded Holofernes with his own dagger. Encouraged by these examples, not a little, I gave myself wholly to the task of completing what I had undertaken. But if anywhere a dull mind or a hasty pen should wander (which God forbid) from the path of truth, I submit myself in all things to the correction of holy mother Church and of my most reverend lords the Cardinals, refusing no upright and learned opponent as my corrector. [illegible, about 20 letters] In his treatise this lord chiefly aims at four things. The first is that which is first stated in the chapter Dudum cum de sepulturis, book 7, that is, in the Clementines, and that no privilege of this kind is removed or attacked by the statute of the general council Omnis utriusque sexus.

units.la: Secundum est, quod Parochiani confessi & absoluti a Fratribus habentibus generalem licentiam audiendi confessiones, & confessos absoluendi, tenentur semel in anno iuxta statutum concilii generalis, Omnis utriusque sexus, eadem peccata, quæ, ut prædicitur, confessi sunt, iterum confiteri suo proprio sacerdoti. Hoc tenere generaliter & uniuersaliter esse verum, vbi Fratres non habeant aliam auctoritatem vel licentiam, quam prædictam licentiam.
units.tr: The second is that parishioners who have been confessed and absolved by Friars having a general licence to hear confessions and absolve the confessed are bound once a year, according to the statute of the general council Omnis utriusque sexus, to confess again those same sins which, as has been said, they have confessed, to their own priest. He holds that this is true generally and universally wherever the Friars have no other authority or licence than that aforementioned licence.

units.la: Tertium est, quod prædicta conclusio non potest damnari tanquam erronea. Ex quo est conclusio vera, nisi ad illum intentum, scilicet quod Parochiani de voluntate proprii sacerdotis confessi Fratribus habentibus licentiam, tenentur iterum eadem peccata confiteri, vel quod tenentur eadem peccata confiteri ex defectu sacramenti pœnitentiæ, vel potestatis in fratre, quod dicere erit erroneum. Similiter quod prædictæ conclusionis oppositum non possit diffinire tanquam catholicum, cum sit & contingens & falsum, nisi cum modificationibus immediate prædictis.
units.tr: The third is that the aforesaid conclusion cannot be condemned as erroneous. Hence the conclusion is true, unless it is taken to mean that parishioners, by the will of their own priest, who have confessed to Friars holding a licence, are bound to confess those same sins again; or that they are bound to confess those same sins because of a defect in the sacrament of penance, or in the power of the friar, which would be erroneous to say. Likewise, the opposite of the aforesaid conclusion cannot be defined as Catholic, since it is both contingent and false, except with the qualifications stated immediately above.

units.la: Quartum est, quod intellectus, quem Fratres habent de isto capitulo, Vas electionis, est erroneus: & ideo suadet & petit instanter ipsum declarari: & ponit declarationes prædictas suo iudicio apparentes.
units.tr: The fourth is that the interpretation which the Friars give of this chapter, Vas electionis, is erroneous; and therefore he urges and earnestly asks that it be declared, and he sets out the declarations mentioned above, which seem right to his judgement.

units.la: Circa quæ mihi videtur hoc ordine procedendum. Primo enim circa hoc statutum Omnis utriusque sexus, distinguuntur quædam multiplicia. Secundo circa idem supponentur quædam necessaria. Tertio quædam correlaria inferentur. Quarto destruuntur quæ ex eodem pullulant erronea. Quinto idem statuto reducetur capitulum, Vas electionis, & fratrum priuilegia. Sexto huius patris documenta reproba & temeraria ostendentur. Septimo dissoluentur quæ apparent vel apparere possunt his contraria. Octauo exponentur ea, quæ eiusdem libellus iudicialiter continet de hac materia, & sic tandem quædam iustitiæ supplicationes & precamina Cardinalium dominationibus præponentur.
units.tr: In these matters, it seems to me, the order of procedure should be as follows. First, concerning this statute Omnis utriusque sexus, certain things with many aspects are distinguished. Second, certain necessary matters are assumed concerning the same. Third, certain corollaries are drawn. Fourth, the errors that spring from the same are refuted. Fifth, the chapter Vas electionis and the privileges of the friars are brought back to the same statute. Sixth, the reproachable and rash teachings of this man are shown. Seventh, the things which appear, or may appear, to be contrary to these are resolved. Eighth, those things which his little book judicially contains on this subject are set out, and so at last certain petitions and prayers for justice are laid before the lordships of the Cardinals.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Ponit varias distinctiones terminorum multiplicium, ad statutum Omnis utriusque sexus deservientes.
units.tr: He sets out various distinctions among the many senses of the terms, which serve the statute Omnis utriusque sexus.

units.la: Radicem itaque & principium processus ponam in distinctione multiplici, ne in æquiuoco præcedatur.
units.tr: I will therefore lay down the root and principle of the whole argument in a manifold distinction, so that nothing is taken in an ambiguous sense.

units.la: I. Dico igitur inprimis, quod potestas ligandi & soluendi in foro pœnitentiæ duplex est: quia quædam est potestas, quæ contertur ex vi ordinis sacerdotalis vel ordinationis in sacerdotem. Et hæc potestas in omnibus sacerdotibus est æqualis, sicut patet in canone distinct. 16. in nova testamento. Secunda quæstione 7. puto & 24. quæstione primo loquitur Dominus. Et hæc vocatur potestas officii vel ordinis sacerdotalis, quæ secundum Linco. in lib. de obligationibus & præceptis, perpetua & inamissibilis est, sicut character ordinis sacerdotalis: & est causa remota ab actu & exercitio: quod magis proprie dicitur potentia quam potestas.
units.tr: I. I say first, then, that the power of binding and loosing in the forum of penance is twofold. For there is one power, which is conferred by the very power of the sacerdotal order or by ordination to the priesthood. This power is equal in all priests, as appears in the canon of the distinction 16, "In the New Testament," in Secunda quaestione 7, and I think in Quaestio 24, first part, where the Lord speaks. This is called the power of the office or of the sacerdotal order. According to Linco., in his book De obligationibus et praeceptis, it is perpetual and cannot be lost, like the character of the sacerdotal order. It is a remote cause of the act and its exercise, and it is more properly called a potency than a power.

units.la: Alia est potestas executionis & hæc duplex est; Quædam n. est executionis simplicis, sine qua habens potestatem primam neminem ligat vel absoluit: & hæc aliquando cum ordine non accipitur, ut puta cum quis ordinatur ab episcopo, qui renunciauit officio; extra eodem, requisiuit: vel cum aliquis ordinatur ab episcopo sine licentia sui episcopi, vel cum quis ordinatur ab hæretico excommunicato vel degradato, seu suspenso: quorum omnium vnica est ratio, videlicet quod episcopi ordinantes in casibus prædictis non habent huiusmodi potestatem executionis. Et ideo illam ad aliquos non transmittunt, quia quod non habebat quis, alteri dare non potuit, sicut patet 1. quæstione 1. qui perfectionem. Et capitulo, verum est, & 1. quæstione 7. Dyabertum. Et idem contingeret, si essent similia impedimenta talia. Nam occurrit aliquando, quod etiam habita perpetuo vel ad tempus suspenditur a iudice vel a iure. Quas varietates causa breuitatis pertranseo, tanquam modo proposito impertinentes. Alia est potestas iurisdictionis, quæ requirit relationem super plebem aliquam vel personam, tanquam super materiam, in qua tam prima quam secunda debeat exerceri. Vnde sicut faber vel artifex quicunque non potest operari nisi habeat materiam, in qua operetur: sic nec sacerdos potest quenquam absoluere vel ligare, nisi sibi ministretur materia supradicta. Quam materiam solus Papa mediate vel immediate tribuit sacerdotibus vel auferit, sicut suæ placuerit voluntati, tanquam ille, in quo solo huiusmodi plenitudo potestatis, extra de vsu palliii. Ad honorem.
units.tr: The other is the power of execution, and this is twofold. For there is one of simple execution, without which a person who has the first power binds or absolves no one. This is sometimes not taken together with the order: for example, when someone is ordained by a bishop who has resigned his office, extra (as in the same place) requisivit; or when someone is ordained by a bishop without the permission of his own bishop; or when someone is ordained by a heretic who is excommunicated, deposed, or suspended. The single reason for all these cases is that the bishops who ordain in the aforesaid cases do not have this power of execution. Therefore they do not pass it on to anyone, because a person cannot give to another what he did not have, as appears in 1. quaestio 1, "qui perfectionem," and in the chapter "verum est," and in 1. quaestio 7, "Dyabertum." The same would happen if there were similar impediments of this kind. For it sometimes occurs that a person who has been given the power, even for life or for a time, is suspended by a judge or by law. I pass over these varieties for the sake of brevity, as irrelevant to the matter proposed. The other is the power of jurisdiction, which requires a relation to some people or person as the matter over which both the first and the second power ought to be exercised. Hence, just as a smith or any craftsman cannot work unless he has the material in which to work, so neither can a priest absolve or bind anyone unless the aforesaid matter is supplied to him. The Pope alone, mediately or immediately, grants this matter to priests or takes it away, as he pleases, as the one in whom alone this fullness of power resides, extra, "De usu pallii," "Ad honorem."

units.la: Veruntamen est hic aduertendum, quia nullus homo est materia, in qua exercetur ista potestas, nisi ratione criminis vel reatus criminis, quo teneretur astrictus. De peccato enim, quod quisquam nunquam commisit, nec cuius reatui nunquam fuerat astrictus, non dubium quod non absoluitur nec potest absolui. Et idcirco peccatum est per se materia, in qua hæc potestas debeat exerceri: & peccator per accidens materia eiusdem.
units.tr: Yet it must be noted here that no man is the matter in which this power is exercised, except by reason of a crime or the guilt of a crime by which he is bound. For concerning a sin which someone has never committed, and to whose guilt he was never bound, there is no doubt that he is not absolved and cannot be absolved. Therefore sin is in itself the matter in which this power ought to be exercised, and the sinner is the matter of it only by accident.

units.la: Rursum potestas iurisdictionis quaedam est ordinaria, quae scilicet alicui in officio, beneficio vel dignitate constituto competit ipso iure. Et haec potestas est ordinaria. Taliter enim curator in isto foro est iudex ordinarius; & potest alteri vices suas committere, extra de officio iudicis ordinarii, cap. eis (alias his) quibus ex officio.
units.tr: Again, the power of jurisdiction is in some cases ordinary, that is, it belongs by law itself to someone appointed to an office, benefice, or dignity. This power is ordinary. For in this forum a curator is an ordinary judge, and he may commit his powers to another, extra, De officio iudicis ordinarii, cap. "eis" (alias "his") "quibus ex officio."

units.la: Alia est extraordinaria seu commissa. Et haec duplex: quia quaedam est commissa. Et haec & limitata solum ad arbitrium committentis, & per se nullo iure suffulta, sed per accidens, quia forte iura declarant talium potestatem. Et haec est simpliciter commissa. Et haec est potestas alieni sacerdotis super alterius Parochianum obtenta licentia proprii sacerdotis; extra de poenitent. & remiss. Omnis utriusq;. Alia est potestas media, quae servata forma in iure statuta arbitrio committentis ampliari potest, non restringi. Et haec est potestas Fratrum Mendicantium absoluendi & ligandi, extra de sepulturis. Dudum, libro septimo.
units.tr: Another is extraordinary or committed power. And this is twofold: for there is one that is committed, which is limited solely to the will of the one who commits it and rests on no law in itself, but only by accident, since perhaps the laws declare the power of such persons. This is simply committed. This is the power of another priest over the parishioner of someone else, obtained with the permission of one's own priest, extra, De poenitentiis et remissionibus, "Omnis utriusque". The other is a middle power, which, when the form prescribed in law is observed, can be enlarged at the discretion of the one who commits it, but not restricted. This is the power of the Mendicant Friars to absolve and bind, extra, De sepulturis, "Dudum," book seven.

units.la: Amplius, confessio peccatorum in foro poenitentiae duplex est. Quaedam enim est extraiudicialis, quae scilicet propter impedimentum concurrens ex parte confitentis vel confessionem audientis seu ipsius confessionis sententiam virtute clavium ecclesiae absolutoriam non attingit. Et haec non est sacramentalis. Et de ista loquitur beatus Augustinus De vera & falsa poenitentia, & ponitur quarto Sententiarum distinctione 18. & in canone de poen. distinctione 1. Quem poenitet. Vbi dicitur, quod si deest sacerdos, confiteatur proximo, qui quamvis potestatem soluendi non habet, tamen dignus est venia ex desiderio sacerdotis. Et de ista loquitur capitulum extra de poen. & re. quod quidam. Vbi dicitur, quod quidam ad confessionem de criminibus veniunt, se tamen asserunt abstinere non posse: quorum tamen confessionem sacerdos debet recipere, & consilium de criminibus exhibere. Quia licet non sit vera eorum poenitentia, admittenda est tamen eorum confessio & crebris & salutaribus monitis est poenitentia inducenda. Ecce quod confessio est admittenda, & poenitentia non est vera nec sacramentalis, quia talem Deus non absoluit, vt dicit beatus Augustinus libro De poenitentia & ponitur De poenitentia dist. tertia, sunt plures. Et per consequens non sunt absoluendi, sicut patet ii. quaestione 3. tunc vera. Quare confessio huiusmodi sacramentalis non est. Alia est confessio iudicialis, quae scilicet omni remoto impedimento attingit sententiam absolutionis praedictam, sicut & quantum exigit debitum sacramenti poenitentiae distincta, contra contritionem & satisfactionem actu vel affectu ad salutem peccatoris postquam peccaverit necessario requisita ad absolutionem & susceptionem satisfactionis debitae ordinata. Sicut enim contritio est dolor voluntarie assumptus pro peccatis cum proposito confitendi & satisfaciendi: sicut patet in canon. distinct: i. per totum sic sacramentalis confessio est peccatorum nuda expressio cum proposito absolutionem & satisfactionem suscipiendi. & ideo poenitens confitens debet ista petere in confessione, sicut illa ad quae confessio ordinatur. Unde peccator semper debet confessionem acquirere quousque fuerit absolutus: dum tamen poterit habere copiam idonei sacerdotis. Et de ista confessione loquitur statutum concilii generalis Omnis utriusq;, cum dicit quod si quis vult confiteri alieno sacerdoti, petat & obtineat licentiam proprii sacerdotis: alioquin alienus illum absoluere non potest nec ligare. Ex qua littera satis constat, quod haec licentia frustra peteretur, si confessio esset valida sine absolutione; vel si confessio sacramentalis non includeret in se absolutionem actualem, si potest haberi. Similiter non dubium quod quantumcumque & cuicunque quis confiteatur, nisi receperit absolutionis beneficium semper ad confessionem faciendam non minus remaneat obligatus: si tamen poterit ad hoc sacerdotem idoneum reperire. Similiter constat, quod ad audiendam nudam confessionem peccatorum, exclusa absolutione & susceptione satisfactionis, non requiruntur claves ecclesiae: nec plus proprius sacerdos quam alienus: nec sacerdos plusquam laicus: nec alicuius licentia, vt fiat cuicunque. Quia haec ab omnibus possunt ceteris paribus exerceri. Sacerdotes etiam curati quandoque audiunt expressionem peccatorum non sacramentaliter. Igitur ad sacramentalem confessionem aliqua alia requiruntur. Patet igitur haec distinctio cum suis partibus lucide declarata.
units.tr: Furthermore, the confession of sins in the forum of penance is twofold. For there is one which is extrajudicial, that is, which, because of an impediment arising on the part of the penitent or of the one hearing the confession, does not reach the sentence of absolution by virtue of the keys of the Church, nor the sentence of the confession itself. This is not sacramental. Blessed Augustine speaks of this in De vera et falsa poenitentia, and it is cited in the Fourth Book of Sentences, distinction 18, and in the canon De poenitentia, distinction 1, "Quem poenitet." There it is said: that if a priest is lacking, let him confess to a neighbour, who, although he does not have the power of loosing, is nonetheless worthy of pardon through the priest's desire. And the chapter extra, De poenitentiis et remissionibus, "quod quidam" speaks of this. There it is said: that certain people come to confession of their crimes, yet they assert that they cannot abstain from them; their confession, however, the priest ought to receive, and to offer counsel about their crimes. For although their penitence is not true, their confession is nonetheless to be admitted, and penitence is to be induced by frequent and wholesome admonitions. Behold, the confession is to be admitted, and the penitence is neither true nor sacramental, because God does not absolve such a penitent, as blessed Augustine says in the book De poenitentia, and it is set down in De poenitentia, distinction 3, "sunt plures." And consequently such persons are not to be absolved, as appears in II. quaestio 3, "tunc vera." Wherefore a confession of this kind is not sacramental. The other is judicial confession, which, when every impediment is removed, reaches the aforesaid sentence of absolution, just as the due requirements of the sacrament of penance, distinct from contrition and from satisfaction in deed or in intention for the salvation of the sinner after he has sinned, demand as necessary for absolution and for the reception of the satisfaction due. For just as contrition is sorrow undertaken voluntarily for sins, with the purpose of confessing and making satisfaction, as appears in the canon of distinction 1, "per totum," so sacramental confession is the bare expression of sins with the purpose of receiving absolution and satisfaction. Therefore the penitent who confesses ought to ask for these things in confession, as those to which confession is ordained. Hence the sinner must always seek confession until he has been absolved, provided that he is able to have access to a suitable priest. And the statute of the General Council, Omnis utriusque, speaks of this confession, when it says: that if anyone wishes to confess to a priest not his own, he is to seek and obtain the permission of his own priest; otherwise the other cannot absolve or bind him. From this letter it is clear enough that this permission would be sought in vain, if confession were valid without absolution, or if sacramental confession did not include in itself actual absolution, where that can be had. Likewise there is no doubt that, however much and to whomever someone confesses, unless he has received the benefit of absolution he remains bound no less to make confession, provided he can find a suitable priest for this. Likewise it is established that for hearing the bare confession of sins, with absolution and the receiving of satisfaction excluded, the keys of the Church are not required, nor is the proper priest more fit than another, nor a priest more than a layman, nor is anyone's permission needed for it to be done by anyone. For these things can, other things being equal, be done by all. Parish priests also sometimes hear the expression of sins non-sacramentally. Therefore other things are required for a sacramental confession. This distinction, then, with its parts, is clearly set out.

units.la: Amplius licentia generalis audiendi confessiones duplex est. Quaedam enim est generalissima, quae non est aliud quam commissio executionis simplicis, quam is, cui committitur, recipit, quando ordinatur in sacerdotem, vel postea a suo praelato recipit illam, quam ex aliquo impedimento prius non habuit: sicut praedictum est in secunda distinctione: aut quam praehabuit, sed amisit. Et idcirco haec est generalissima: quia non est ad aliquem populum, nec ad aliqua crimina limitata. Alia est generalis, quae scil. est commissio iurisdictionis super plebem aliquam indistincte: sicut super materiam, in qua sua potestas exerceatur. Et est differentia magna inter illam licentiam generalissimam, & hanc generalem: quia virtute solius licentiae generalissimae nullus poterit quenquam absoluere vel ligare propter defectum materiae. Virtute autem secundae quilibet, qui habet eam poterit materiam sibi subiectam, prout sibi subiicitur, soluere vel ligare. Similiter haec declaratio secunda includit primam, non econuerso.
units.tr: Moreover, the general licence to hear confessions is of two kinds. One is most general, which is nothing other than the commission to carry out the simple function, which the person to whom it is committed receives when he is ordained a priest, or which he later receives from his superior if he did not have it before because of some impediment, as was said in the second distinction, or which he once had but lost. This is the most general, because it is not directed to any particular people or to any limited sins. The other is the general licence, which is the commission of jurisdiction over some people without distinction, as over the matter in which his power is to be exercised. There is a great difference between that most general licence and this general one. By virtue of the most general licence alone, no one can absolve or bind anyone, because the matter is lacking. By virtue of the second, anyone who has it can loose or bind the matter subject to him, insofar as it is subject to him. Likewise, this second declaration includes the first, not the reverse.

units.la: Rursum absolutio in foro poenitentiae duplex est, scilicet quaedam, quam solus Deus impendit, & sacerdos a Deo factam ostendit. Et haec absolutio est a reatu vel macula culpae mortalis & debito poenae vel mortis aeternae: sicut patet quarto Sententiarum, distinctione 18. Alia est, quam sacerdos realiter & vere impendit, & non solum impensam ostendit: de qua absolutione qualis sit & quid soluit, in sequente capitulo ostendetur. Ex quibus omnibus patet, quod statuta, de quibus nobis sermo est, loquuntur de potestate absoluendi, quae est potestas iurisdictionis relatae ad materiam, in qua debeat exerceri, secundum quod huiusmodi materia subiicitur sacerdoti, & quod non loquuntur de alia potestate aliqua, nisi prout aliae in hac potestate includuntur. Patet etiam, quod non loquun-turtur de confessione, quæ est sola nuda expressio peccatorum, non includens absolutionem & susceptionem satisfactionis, sed solum de sacramentali confessione, quæ includit prædicta. Et quod licentia generalis audiendi confessiones, de qua loquitur constitutio Vas electionis, non est illa licentia, virtute cuius nullus potest quemquam sibi confessum soluere vel ligare: sed de licentia generali, virtute cuius absolutionis beneficium potest impendi, sicut prædictum est.
units.tr: Again, absolution in the court of penance is of two kinds. One is that which God alone bestows, and which the priest shows to have been done by God. This absolution is from the guilt or stain of mortal sin and from the debt of punishment or eternal death, as is clear in Fourth Book of the Sentences, distinction 18. The other is that which the priest really and truly bestows, and does not merely show to have been bestowed. What kind of absolution this is, and what it loosens, will be shown in the following chapter. From all of these things it is clear that the statutes we are discussing speak of the power of absolving, which is a power of jurisdiction related to the matter in which it ought to be exercised, insofar as such matter is subject to the priest, and that they do not speak of any other power, except insofar as other powers are included in this one. It is also clear that they do not speak of confession, which is merely the bare expression of sins without including absolution and the reception of satisfaction, but only of sacramental confession, which includes the aforesaid things. And the general licence to hear confessions, of which the constitution Vas electionis speaks, is not that licence by virtue of which no one can loose or bind anyone confessing to him, but the general licence by virtue of which the benefit of absolution can be bestowed, as was said above.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Ponis sex necessaria, & præsupponenda ad eiusdem statuti declarationem conducibilia.
units.tr: It sets out six premises necessary and to be presupposed for explaining the said statute.

units.la: OMissis igitur aliis distinctionibus causa breuitatis, supponuntur quædam necessaria huic proposito pertinentia, & cuilibet litterato euidenter vera.
units.tr: Setting aside, therefore, other distinctions for the sake of brevity, certain premises pertinent to this proposition are presupposed, and are plainly true to anyone who is literate.

units.la: I. Dico igitur quod in ecclesiastica Hierarchia semper est, aut debet esse, sub CHRISTO vnus summus princeps, in quo ecclesiæ plane secundum se totam residet auctoritas iurisdictio seu potestas, à qua in inferiores præsidentes quoscunque mediate vel immediate omnis ecclesiastica iurisdictio, quam obtinent, sine sui detrimento iuxta summi pontificis arbitrium derivatur. Hæc patent in canone 19. distinctione, ista Dominus, & distinctione 21. in nouo testamento, & extra de usu pallii, ad honorem. Et est tam per se nota, quod eius impugnator esset igne vel gladio puniendus.
units.tr: I. I say, then, that in the ecclesiastical hierarchy there always is, or ought to be, under Christ, one supreme prince, in whom the whole authority, jurisdiction or power of the Church resides in its own right; and from him all ecclesiastical jurisdiction that the presiding officers below him hold, whether mediately or immediately, is derived, to be exercised according to the judgment of the supreme pontiff without any loss to himself. These things are evident in canon 19, distinction "Ista Dominus", and distinction 21, in the New Testament, and Extra, On the use of the pallium, Ad honorem. And it is so self-evident that whoever opposed it would deserve to be punished with fire or sword.

units.la: II. Amplius quilibet habens ordinariam iurisdictionem administrandi subditis necessaria ad salutem, obligatur per se vel per alium eisdem talia ministrare: sicut & prout subditorum necessitas hæc requirit. Alioquin enim cum non sit maior ratio de uno quam de alio habente huiusmodi iurisdictionem: quilibet habens huiusmodi iurisdictionem posset licite nec per se nec per alium talia ministrare. Nec ad talia ministrandum alium vel alios subrogare, vel incorrigibilem remouere, seu eidem alium vel alios substituere vel coassignare: sed posset licite salutem negligere subditorum: quod est contra illud Ezech. 3. capitulo: sanguinem eius de manu tua requiram. vbi loquitur de prælato, qui salutem negligit subditorum, secundum Gregor. super Ezechielem tertia Homil. Unde consequitur, quod omnes huiusmodi iurisdictionem habentes ad eandem exercendam, seu subditis pro loco & tempore administranda, sunt communiter obligati. Cuius figura præcessit Numeri 11. quando Dominus dixit Moysi: Auferam de spiritu tuo & tradam eis vt sustentent tecum onus populi & non tu solus grauareris. Ex quo sequitur, quod Dominus Moysi obligationem non sustulit, sed eius minuens laborem ampliauit nihilominus dignitatem. Sequitur etiam, quod inferiores superiorum in talibus tenent vicem. Alioquin inferiores, cum superioribus onus populi nullatenus sustentarent: vel isti, vel illi soli grauarentur.
units.tr: II. Further, anyone who has ordinary jurisdiction to administer to subjects what is necessary for salvation is bound, either in person or through another, to provide these things to them, as the necessity of the subjects requires. For otherwise, since there is no greater reason regarding one holding such jurisdiction than another, anyone holding such jurisdiction could lawfully provide such things neither in person nor through another. Nor could he substitute another or others to minister such things, or remove an incorrigible person, or appoint another or others to him as substitutes or co-assignees; rather he could lawfully neglect the salvation of his subjects. This is contrary to that of Ezekiel 3: his blood I will require at your hand, where he speaks of the prelate who neglects the salvation of his subjects, according to Gregory on Ezekiel, Homily 3. Hence it follows that all who hold such jurisdiction are commonly obliged to exercise it, or to administer it to subjects in place and time. Its figure preceded in Numbers 11, when the Lord said to Moses: I will take of the spirit that is upon you and will put it upon them, that they may bear the burden of the people with you, and you alone not be burdened. From this it follows that the Lord did not remove Moses' obligation, but, while lessening his labour, nonetheless enlarged his dignity. It also follows that inferiors take the place of superiors in such matters. Otherwise, inferiors would in no way bear the burden of the people with the superiors, and either those or these alone would be burdened.

units.la: III. Amplius, quicunque in aliquo foro ligat alium vel absoluit: ille vel est suus iudex, vel sui iudicis vicem tenens. Quod si neutrum est, nihil facit circa eum, quem soluere nititur aut ligare. Extra de consuetudine, ad nostram: &, de iudiciis: &, si clerici. Et de pœnitentiis & remissionibus, quod autem.
units.tr: III. Further, whoever binds or absolves another in any forum is either that person's own judge, or holds the place of his judge. If he is neither, he does nothing with regard to the one whom he tries to absolve or bind. Extra, On custom, Ad nostram; and On judgments, and If clerics; and On penances and remissions, Quod autem.

units.la: IV. Rursum ad propositum speciali[us] descendendo, pono vnam suppositionem tripartitam: videlicet quod prima pars statuti omnis utriusque, quæ est quod omnis utriusque sexus postquam ad annos discretionis peruenerit, saltem semel in anno omnia peccata sua confiteantur suo proprio sacerdoti, & iniungam sibi pœnitentiam studeat proprijs viribus adimplere: & sic ad minus in pascha suscipiat reue-renter Eucharistia sacramentum. Hæc pars obtinet vim præcepti: quia materia est necessaria & salubris, quod sine statuto quilibet confiteri teneretur ex lege, quæ obtinet vim præcepti: & per statutum solum limitatur tempus, infra quod quilibet debet confiteri. Supponitur etiam, quod secunda pars, scilicet qui voluerit ex iusta causa alieno confiteri sacerdoti, petat & obtineat licentiam proprii sacerdotis, sit dispensatoria super prima parte, quæ alias obtinet vim præcepti: etiam istud concedit aduersarius in sui tractatus articulo vertio, iuxta finem, & in articulo quinto, in responsione secunda ad caput. Vas electionis, per totum. Supponitur etiam, quod finis secundæ partis, scilicet quod sine licentia proprii sacerdotis non potest sibi confessum soluere vel ligare, sit diffinitoria, quod licentia proprii sacerdotis sit sufficiens & requisita ad hoc, quod alienus possit alterius Parochianum soluere vel ligare. Hæc quantum ad omnes sui partes, patet ex intentione seu forma prædicti statuti concilii generalis.
units.tr: IV. Moreover, descending more specifically to the proposition, I posit a threefold supposition: namely, that the first part of the statute Omnis utriusque, which is that every one of either sex, after reaching the years of discretion, should at least once a year confess all their sins to their own priest, and take care to perform the penance enjoined on them with their own strength; and so at least at Easter reverently receive the sacrament of the Eucharist, has the force of a command. For the matter is necessary and salutary, and apart from the statute anyone would be bound by law to confess, which has the force of a command; and the statute alone limits the time within which each must confess. It is also supposed that the second part, namely that whoever for a just cause wishes to confess to another priest should seek and obtain the licence of his own priest, is a dispensation from the first part, which otherwise has the force of a command; the adversary himself concedes this in his treatise, article three, near the end, and in article five, in the second answer to the chapter Vas electionis, throughout. It is also supposed that the end of the second part, namely that without the licence of his own priest he cannot absolve or bind a confessor, is definitive, so that the licence of his own priest is sufficient and required for another to be able to absolve or bind another's parishioner. As to all its parts, this is evident from the intention or form of the said statute of the general council.

units.la: V. Amplius, iste terminus proprius in statuto nec Papam nec episcopos excludit, quo minus sint proprii sacerdotes ad mentem statuti: imo eisdem æquivalenter vere includit. Patet per Iohannem Andreæ in nouella eodem titulo, super verbo nullatenus audiatur. Qui dicit, quod Papa, episcopus proprius: legatus in provincia, archipresbyter sedis, presbyter Parochialis, sunt proprii sacerdotes. Huius etiam oppositum est nimis erroneum, ut patebit.
units.tr: V. Further, this proper term in the statute excludes neither the Pope nor the bishops from being "own priests" in the sense of the statute; indeed it truly includes them equivalently. This is shown by John Andreae in the Novella on the same title, on the words nullatenus audiatur, who says that the Pope, the proper bishop, the legate in a province, the archpriest of the see, and the parish priest are all "own priests". The opposite of this is also exceedingly erroneous, as will become clear.

units.la: Iterum, obligatio confitendi duplex est. Una scilicet quae consurgit ex hoc, quod quis suo peccato actuali vel ex reatu culpae inde contracto factus est debitor sacramenti poenitentiae: & per consequens sacramentalis confessionis. Alia quae consurgit ex praecepto ecclesiae in praefato statuto concilii generalis, omnis utriusque, vel aliis statutis factis de confessionibus peccatorum quarum obligationum secunda nihil addit super priorem, nisi limitationem temporis infra quod, & determinationem personae vel personarum, cui vel quibus est confessio facienda. Secunda tamen primam naturaliter praesupponit: quia constat, quod si nullus peccasset, nec reatum peccati contraxisset, nunquam ex statuto ecclesiae esset debitor confessionis faciendae.
units.tr: Again, the obligation to confess is twofold. One is that which arises from the fact that someone, by his actual sin or by the guilt contracted thereby, has become a debtor to the sacrament of penance, and consequently to sacramental confession. The other arises from the precept of the Church in the aforesaid statute of the general council, Omnis utriusque, or other statutes made concerning confession of sins; of these obligations the second adds nothing to the first except the limitation of time within which, and the determination of the person or persons to whom confession is to be made. Yet the second naturally presupposes the first, because it is clear that if no one had sinned, nor had contracted the guilt of sin, he would never by a statute of the Church be a debtor to make confession.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Infert sex Corollaria, seu propositiones ex dictis.
units.tr: He draws six corollaries, or propositions, from what has been said.

units.la: Generali igitur notitia terminorum per distinctiones & suppositiones praemissa: Superest, ut ex praedictis aliqua corollaria inferantur.
units.tr: Now that the terms have been explained generally through the distinctions and suppositions set out above, some corollaries remain to be drawn from what has been said.

units.la: I. Ex praedictis igitur sequi videtur, quod quamvis in statuto concilii generalis caveatur sub praecepto, quod quilibet Parochianus confiteatur proprio sacerdoti: tamen quod quilibet confiteatur proprio sacerdoti in persona sua, nullatenus est praeceptum. Quod sic probatur. Secunda pars statuti praefati est dispensatoria super prima parte eiusdem domini, sicut patet ex secunda parte quartae suppositionis. Igitur impleni secundam partem, ad primam vlterius non tenetur, & per consequens non tenetur confiteri personaliter proprio sacerdoti. Igitur per statutum nullatenus est praeceptum. Amplius confessus sacerdoti secundum formam statuti non tenetur ex vi statuti amplius pro illo anno personaliter confiteri proprio sacerdoti. Igitur confessus alteri sacerdoti functo vice proprii sacerdotis, non tenetur illo anno amplius confiteri personaliter proprio sacerdoti: quia nisi alienus sacerdos functus vice proprii sacerdotis audiendo Parochianum, eum aequaliter deobligaret ab omni confessione, sicut si proprius sacerdos audivisset eundem, non esset in hac parte functus vice proprii sacerdotis. Amplius, proprius sacerdos non tenetur artare Parochianum confessum alieno sacerdoti de sua licentia per censuras statuti ad sibi personaliter confitendum. Sed si Parochianus alteri confessus de licentia proprii sacerdotis teneretur non minus personaliter confiteri proprio sacerdoti, proprius sacerdos teneretur eum ad hoc compellere per censuras eiusdem statuti: sicut patet ex secunda suppositione: quia Dominus sanguinem subditi de manu praelatorum requiret, si sint negligentes in necessariis ad salutem. Quare sequitur, quod sic confessus non tenetur proprio sacerdoti personaliter confiteri. Amplius a tempore statuti editi & vina proprii sacerdotes consueuerunt audire sibi subiectos per sacerdotes functos vice sua, quos ecclesia, quae non errat in necessariis ad salutem, reputavit praedicto statuto satisfacere modo praedicto absque facta confessione personaliter proprio sacerdoti. Igitur de praecepto non est, quod confessio fiat personaliter proprio sacerdoti, sed sufficit quod fiat alieno de licentia proprii sacerdotis. Ex qua conclusione sequitur, quod praeceptum statuti super confessione Parochianorum semel in anno faciendae est disiunctiuum: scilicet quod fiat proprio sacerdoti vel alteri de licentia proprii sacerdotis. Sed hic diceret Dominus Armachanus archiepiscopus, quod est distinguendum de licentia proprii sacerdotis: quia, sicut statutum praefatum, Omnis utriusque, habet duas partes: quarum prima praecipit confessionem semel in anno fieri proprio sacerdoti, & alteram quae concedit quod Parochianus poterit alieno confiteri de licentia proprii sacerdotis: quia alias non posset ab alieno solvi vel ligari: sic potest duplex esse licentia. Una super secunda parte statuti tantum, scilicet dispensando solum, quod alienus potest soluere vel ligare subditum alienum sibi confessum, & illa licentia proprii sacerdotis non obstante subditus de hac sola licentia confessus non minus tenetur confiteri proprio sacerdoti. Alia licentia potest concedi, scilicet quod alienus sacerdos audiret & absolueret subditum alienum vice proprii sacerdotis, qui hanc licentiam praeconcessit, & sic dispensaretur super utraque parte statuti, & sic confessus non tenetur pro tunc proprio sacerdoti.
units.tr: I. From what has been said it seems to follow that, although the decree of the General Council lays down under precept that every parishioner should confess to his own priest, it is by no means a precept that each person must confess to his own priest in person. This is proved as follows. The second part of the aforesaid decree is a dispensing clause on the first part of the same decree, as is clear from the second part of the fourth supposition. Therefore, whoever fulfils the second part is no longer bound by the first, and consequently is not bound to confess in person to his own priest. Therefore the decree does not in any way make this a precept. Furthermore, one who has confessed to a priest according to the form of the decree is not bound by virtue of the decree to confess again in person to his own priest in that year. Therefore one who has confessed to another priest acting in place of his own priest is not bound to confess in person to his own priest again that year. For if another priest, hearing a parishioner, acting in place of his own priest, did not release him equally from all obligation of confession, as if his own priest had heard him, then that other priest would not in this respect be acting in place of his own priest. Furthermore, a parish priest is not bound to compel a parishioner, who has confessed to another priest with his permission, to confess in person to himself by the censures of the decree. But if a parishioner who had confessed to another with the licence of his own priest were still bound to confess in person to his own priest, then his own priest would be bound to compel him to do so by the censures of the same decree, as is clear from the second supposition, since the Lord will require the blood of the subject at the hands of prelates if they are negligent in what is necessary for salvation. Hence it follows that one who has confessed in this way is not bound to confess in person to his own priest. Furthermore, since the decree was issued, and up to the present, own priests have customarily heard those subject to them through priests acting in their place, and the Church, which does not err in what is necessary to salvation, has judged that the aforesaid decree is satisfied in the way described, without a confession being made in person to his own priest. Therefore it is not a matter of precept that confession be made in person to one's own priest; it is enough that it be made to another with the licence of one's own priest. From this conclusion it follows that the precept of the decree concerning the confession of parishioners once a year is disjunctive, namely that it be made either to one's own priest or to another with his licence. But here the Lord Archbishop of Armagh would say that a distinction must be drawn concerning the licence of one's own priest. For, as the aforesaid decree, Omnis utriusque, has two parts, the first of which commands that confession be made once a year to one's own priest, and the second of which grants that a parishioner may confess to another with the licence of his own priest (since otherwise he could not be loosed or bound by another), so the licence may be of two kinds. One is given with regard to the second part of the decree only, namely a dispensation only that another priest may loose or bind a subject of another who has confessed to him; and with this licence alone, notwithstanding the licence of his own priest, the subject who has confessed is no less bound to confess to his own priest. Another licence may be granted, namely that another priest may hear and absolve a subject of another in place of his own priest, who has granted this licence beforehand; and thus he is dispensed from both parts of the decree, and the one who has confessed is then not bound to his own priest.

units.la: Contra hanc responsionem autem probando hanc conclusionem pro secunda parte, scilicet quod quilibet sacerdos alienus audiens confessionem Parochiani alieni de quacunque licentia, virtute cuius licentiae potest illius subditum soluere vel ligare: fungitur in hac parte vice illius, qui sibi hanc licentiam praeconcessit: probatur sic ex tertia suppositione. Quilibet qui in quocunque foro alium potest soluere vel ligare, est suus iudex, aut in hoc sui iudicis vicem tenens ex tertia suppositione & sui probatione. Igitur alienus audiens confessionem Parochiani alieni de licentia proprii sacerdotis tantum super hoc articulo statuti, scilicet quod possit suum subditum soluere vel ligare in foro conscientiae est iudex illius Parochiani sibi confessi, vel est sui iudicis vicem tenens. Sed constat, quod si sit suus iudex, tunc non est sibi alienus, sed est proprius eius sacerdos cuius oppositum datum est. Si sui iudicis vicem tenens: tunc cum virtute licentiae praeconcessae nullius vicem teneat, nisi illius, qui hanc licentiam praeconcessisset: sequitur quod talis tenet vicem proprii sacerdotis, & sic nec prima licentia differet a secunda: nec confessus de prima licentia tenetur netur protunc confiteri personaliter, proprio sacerdoti. Et idem argumentum potest fieri de quacunque licentia, virtute cuius potest quis alienum soluere subditum vel ligare. Amplius quilibet alienus audiens alterius Parochianum de licentia proprii sacerdotis, de qua licentia loquitur statutum, sic audiendo tenet vicem proprii sacerdotis, sibiq; confessus non tenetur protunc confiteri personaliter proprio sacerdoti.
units.tr: Against this reply, however, I prove this conclusion for the second part, namely that every other priest who hears the confession of another's parishioner, under whatever licence by virtue of which he may loose or bind that subject, acts in this respect in place of the one who granted him this licence. It is proved thus from the third supposition. Whoever can loose or bind another in any forum is his judge, or in this respect holds the place of his judge, by the third supposition and its proof. Therefore another priest who hears the confession of another's parishioner by the licence of his own priest, only as to this article of the decree, namely that he may loose or bind his subject in the forum of conscience, is the judge of that parishioner who has confessed to him, or holds the place of his judge. But it is clear that if he is his judge, then he is not another priest to him, but is his own priest, which has been denied. If he holds the place of his judge, then, since by virtue of the licence previously granted he holds the place of no one but the one who granted that licence, it follows that such a man holds the place of the own priest, and so the first licence does not differ from the second, and one who has confessed under the first licence is then not bound to confess in person to his own priest. And the same argument can be made concerning any licence by virtue of which someone may loose or bind another's subject. Furthermore, any other priest who hears another's parishioner by the licence of his own priest, of which licence the decree speaks, in so hearing holds the place of the own priest, and one who has confessed to him is then not bound to confess in person to his own priest.

units.la: Constat autem quod statutum praecise loquitur de licentia, quae sufficit, & requiritur ad hoc quod alienus sacerdos possit alterius Parochianum soluere vel ligare: sicut patet ex fine secundae partus eiusdem statuti, quae est diffinitio eiusdem veritatis.
units.tr: It is certain, however, that the decree speaks precisely of the licence which is sufficient and required for another priest to be able to loose or bind another's parishioner, as is clear from the end of the second part of the same decree, which is the definition of this very truth.

units.la: Constat etiam quod huiusmodi est licentia primo modo accepta in distinctione supradicta. Quare sequitur, quod quilibet alienus audiens alterius Parochianum de licentia praedicta vel de quacunq; licentia, cuius virtute possit alterius Parochianum soluere vel ligare, tenet in hoc vicem proprii sacerdotis. Amplius, communis animae conceptio est, quod nullus concedit, nisi illud quod & quatenus est de iure vel de foro suo. Igitur proprius sacerdos non concedit alieno licentiam illam, quod possit nude subditum suum soluere vel ligare, nisi quatenus talis subditus est de iure & de foro proprii sacerdotis. Constat autem, quod nullus concedit illud, quod est iuris sui simpliciter nisi vel cedendo iuri suo, vel ius dominii in alterum transferendo, vel ius suum alteri communicando, aut vicem suam alteri committendo. Istorum autem quatuor modorum duo primi non habent hic locum. Si igitur detur tertium, scilicet quod proprius sacerdos committat alieno ius suum, sequitur quod vtens illo iure, quod sibi sic communicatur, vtitur illo auctoritate alterius & non sua: & per consequens vtitur illo iure vice alterius: & perinde est ac si proprius sacerdos hoc faceret in persona sua.
units.tr: It is also certain that such a licence is of the first kind taken in the distinction above. Hence it follows that any other priest who hears another's parishioner by the aforesaid licence, or by any licence by virtue of which he may loose or bind another's parishioner, holds in this respect the place of the own priest. Furthermore, it is the common conception of the mind that no one grants anything except that which is, and insofar as it is, within his own right or jurisdiction. Therefore the own priest does not grant to another that licence by which he may simply loose or bind his subject, except insofar as such a subject is within the right and jurisdiction of the own priest. But it is certain that no one grants what is simply his own right except either by yielding his right, or by transferring the right of lordship to another, or by sharing his right with another, or by committing his place to another. Of these four modes, the first two have no place here. If therefore the third is granted, namely that the own priest commits his right to another, it follows that the one who uses that right which is so shared with him uses it by the authority of another and not his own, and consequently uses it in place of another; and it is just as if the own priest were doing this in his own person.

units.la: Cum enim quis praecipit aliquid vel concedit auctoritate Papae, idem est ac si Papa praeciperet vel concederet. Et caeteris paribus ad illud praeceptum & illud privilegium est aequalis transgressio seu contemptus: & per consequens sequitur, quod nec iste tertius modus differt a quarto: nec prima pars suae distinctionis discrepat a secunda. Amplius, statutum tantum loquitur de licentia audiendi confessiones, quam proprius sacerdos potest concedere ex hoc, quod est proprius sacerdos. Sed potestas concedendi licentiam, de qua loquitur statutum, debet esse communis & in potestate proprii sacerdotis. Sed solam licentiam audiendi confessiones & confessos absoluendi vice sua potest proprius sacerdos concedere, in quantum talis, quia illam licentiam potest concedere quilibet proprius sacerdos ex hoc, quod est curatus ordinarius, & ex hoc est curatus ordinarius, quod est proprius sacerdos. Et si nullam aliam potest concedere, nisi istam, non minus esset proprius sacerdos, sicut notum est. Quare sequitur, quod statutum solum loquitur de licentia audiendi confessiones vice proprii sacerdotis.
units.tr: For when someone commands or grants something by the authority of the Pope, it is the same as if the Pope himself commanded or granted it. And, other things being equal, the transgression or contempt of that command and that privilege is the same. Consequently it follows that this third mode does not differ from the fourth, nor does the first part of his distinction differ from the second. Furthermore, the decree speaks only of the licence to hear confessions, which the own priest can grant by the fact that he is the own priest. But the power to grant the licence of which the decree speaks must be common to all and within the power of the own priest. But the own priest can grant only the licence to hear confessions and absolve penitents in his place, insofar as he is such, because any own priest can grant that licence by the fact that he is the ordinary parish priest, and he is the ordinary parish priest by the fact that he is the own priest. And if he could grant no other licence than this, he would be no less the own priest, as is well known. Hence it follows that the decree speaks only of the licence to hear confessions in place of the own priest.

units.la: Superius autem probatum est, quod statutum loquitur de licentia, quae sufficit ad hoc, quod alterius Parochianum sibi confessum alienus possit soluere & ligare, & sine qua non potest hoc facere. Igitur licentia audiendi confessiones vice proprii sacerdotis est illa licentia, sine qua alienus non potest alterius subditum soluere vel ligare, & quae sufficit ad praedicta. Illa igitur licentia, quae primo modo dicta audiendi confessiones & confessos absoluendi, quam iste Dominus concessit, aut est licentia absoluendi vice proprii sacerdotis, aut non. Si non, igitur non sufficit ad hoc, quod habens eam possit alterius subditum soluere vel ligare. Et sequitur, quod illa super neutra parte statuti dispensat, cuius oppositum dicit Dominus iste. Si autem est licentia absoluendi vice proprii sacerdotis, sequitur quod illa, est eadem cum licentia posita etiam secunda parte distinctionis, & dispensat super utraque parte statuti: cuius etiam oppositum ponit Dominus iste. Ex quo cum praecedentibus sequitur, quod omnis licentia, virtute cuius alienus sacerdos possit alterius subditum soluere vel ligare, est licentia absoluendi eundem, virtute illius, qui illam licentiam sic concessit: & quod de illo posita est nulla, nec distinguentem liberat, sed inuoluit: & quod confessus alieno de licentia quacunque proprii sacerdotis, virtute cuius ipse potest ipsum soluere & ligare, non tenetur ex statuti confiteri personaliter proprio sacerdoti: & quod praeceptum statuti est, vt praedicitur, disiunctiuum, scilicet quod fiat proprio sacerdoti personaliter, vel alieno de licentia proprii sacerdotis.
