units.tr: Above it has been proved that the statute speaks of the licence which is sufficient for an outsider to absolve and bind a parishioner of another who has confessed to him, and without which he cannot do this. Therefore the licence to hear confessions in place of one's own priest is that licence, without which an outsider cannot absolve or bind another's subject, and which suffices for the aforesaid. That licence, then, which was mentioned first, to hear confessions and absolve the confessed, which this Lord granted, is either a licence to absolve in place of one's own priest or it is not. If it is not, then it is not sufficient for the one who holds it to absolve or bind another's subject. It follows that it dispenses from neither part of the statute, whereas this Lord asserts the opposite. But if it is a licence to absolve in place of one's own priest, it follows that it is the same as the licence posited also in the second part of the distinction, and that it dispenses from both parts of the statute, which this Lord also asserts to be the opposite. From this, together with what precedes, it follows that every licence by virtue of which an outside priest can absolve or bind another's subject is a licence to absolve that same person, by virtue of the one who granted it. A licence granted for that person is nothing and does not free the one making the distinction, but entangles him. And a person who confesses to an outside priest under any licence of his own priest, by virtue of which the latter can absolve and bind him, is not bound by the statute to confess personally to his own priest. The precept of the statute is, as has been said, disjunctive: that confession be made either to one's own priest personally, or to an outsider by licence of one's own priest.

units.la: Superest ostendere, quod fuit suppositum in quarta distinctione primi capituli: scilicet quod sacerdos virtute clauium non solum poenitentem absolutum ostendit, sed eidem vere absolutionis beneficium impendit: & ea confessio sacramentalis, & statutum concilii generalis praecipit, illam, veram absolutionem coexigit & includit. Et primo probatur primum sic. Christus promittens Petro claves regni caelorum, Matthaei 16. dicens: Tibi dabo claves regni caelorum, subiunxit: quodcunque ligaveris super terram erit ligatum & in caelis. Et quodcunque solueris super terram, erit solutum & in caelis.
units.tr: It remains to show what was assumed in the fourth distinction of the first chapter, namely that a priest, by virtue of the keys, does not merely show the penitent to be absolved but truly bestows on him the benefit of absolution. Sacramental confession, which the statute of the general council commands, requires and includes that true absolution, insofar as the key demands it. First, the first point is proved as follows. Christ, promising Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven, Matthew 16, said: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and added: whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.

units.la: Si igitur sacerdos non aliter soluteret, nisi quia poenitentem diuinitus absolutum ostenderet: sequitur quod quemcunque Petrus vel suus vicarius aut sacerdos, cuius auctoritate virtute clavium absolueret, id est absolutum ostenderet, coram Deo solutus esset. Quod est contra canones, qui dicunt, quod sacerdotes frequenter soluunt indignos: & contra canonem II. quaestione 5. sunt. tunc vera, vbi dicit, quod tunc vera est absolutio sacerdotis, cum interest sequitur arbitrium iudicis. Gloss. id est Dei. Vel, quod Petrus ostenderit diuinitus absolutum, nec forte in peccatum esset propter obstinatiam absoluendus, & tunc falsum esset euangelium dicens: Quodcunque absolutum erit coram Deo. Amplius, lux potior est quam umbra; & veritas quam figura. Sed notum est, quod resuscitatio Lazari, Iohannis 11. fuit figura iustificationis peccatoris per poenitentiae sacramentum, sicut patet per beatum Ambrosium, & ponitur in canone de poenitentia distinctione 1, quamuis igitur, & per beatum Augustinum De vera & falsa poenitentia, & ponitur ibidem cap. quem poeniset: in qua figura Christus Lazarum non solum ad vitam deduxit ad motum vel sensum, eduxit ad lucem: sed etiam realiter adhuc vinculis alligatum assignauit discipulis absoluendum, dicente euangelio: Et prodiit ligatus manus & pedes. Et sequitur: soluite eum & dimittite abire. Cuius figurae veritas est, quod Christus non solum peccatorem viuificat gratiae infusione, & culpae ac poenae aeternae remissione mot ificat, vel significat cordis contritione, vocis oris confessione: sed adhuc ligatum assignat sacerdotibus disligandum vera absolutione. Discipuli enim non solum eum absolutum ostenderant, sed nondum totaliter absoluti, realiter absoluerunt. Quare sic debet esse in peccatoris iustificatione, ut sibi mutuo correspondeant veritas & figura. Item, quemcunq; sacerdos ostendit diuinitus esse absolutum ab aliquo mortali: ostendit esse ab omnibus absolutum. Deus enim nullum absoluit ab vno, quem non absoluit ab omnibus, secundum beatum Augustinum libro De vera & falsa poenitentia, vt ponitur in canone, distinctione 3. de poenitent. Sunt plures. Quare sacerdos nullum ostendit esse absolutum diuinitus ab vno, quem non ostendit ab omnibus esse absolutum. Constat autem, quod non omnem, quem sacerdos absoluit ab vno, absoluit ab omnibus, quia frequenter remittit poenitentem superioribus absoluendum. Quare sequitur, quod praeter hoc, quod ostendit poenitentem a Deo esse absolutum, ipse realiter absoluit. Et confirmatur istud. Non enim dixerat Christus Apostolis, quorum ostenderitis peccata remissa, remittentur eis: sed quorum remiseritis peccata, Iohannis 20. Amplius si sacerdos virtute clauium nullum specialem effectum operaretur circa poenitentem, quo ostendat a Deo absolutum: sed solum nude ostendit absolutum esse: videtur quod frustra dentur claues sacerdotibus ad hunc effectum. Tum quia, sicut ostendetur, ostium clausum vel apertum non potest esse effectus primus clauis materialis: sic nec ostendere poenitentem solutum esse vel ligatum, potest esse primus effectus clauis spiritualis. Tum etiam quia ille effectus potest aeque esse sine claue, sicut cum clave: & per consequens virtute clauis non ostendetur esse solutus: & tunc aeque solueret laicus, sicut sacerdos, id est, absolutum ostenderet, vel neuter: imo tamen videtur, quod cum poenitens prius & efficacius ostendit se esse solutum, quam sacerdos, eo quod sacerdos nullum ostendit esse absolutum, nisi quem ex signis poenitentiae credit esse poenitentem; & ex hoc a Deo esse absolutum, sequitur quod ipse poenitens debeat dici habere clauem, & vti clave potius, quam sacerdos, si clauis esset vtilis & necessaria ad hunc effectum. Tum tertio: quia videtur repugnantia manifesta, quod sacerdos virtute clauium ostendit peccatorem esse a Deo absolutum, & tamen per nullum effectum vel signum, quod procedit ab eo virtute clauium. Quare sequitur, quod sacerdos virtute clauium operetur aliquem effectum primum & immediatum circa poenitentem, quo secundario ostendat eum esse absolutum a Deo, cum prius naturaliter res sit, quam operetur vel ostendat aliud. Et constat, quod cum ille effectus sit immediatus effectus illius sub ratione; qua est clauis: oportet quod ille effectus sit claudere vel aperire. Et cum habet naturaliter ostendere poenitentem esse absolutum: oportet ex conformitate signi ad signatum, quod ille effectus sit absoluere. Quare sequitur, quod sacerdos prius secundum naturam absoluit poenitentem, & postea eadem absolutione monstrat eum a Deo esse absolutum. Et ex isto argumento patet, quod confessio sacramentalis, quae absque dubio requirit effectum & operationem clauium, inquantum clauis hanc absolutionem coexigit & includit, saltem ex parte sacerdotis confessionem audientis & ex parte poenitentis ad hoc, quod sua confessio sit legitima & valida ad salutem, maxime vbi habetur copia idonei sacerdotis, quod erat probandum. Et si quaeratur, a quo absoluit sacerdos poenitentem, ex quo peccata sunt deleta in contritione quo ad reatum culpae mortalis & poenae aeternae? Respondetur, quod sacerdos absoluit poenitentem a peccato & reatu eiusdem peccati mortalis, a quo Deus prius eum absoluerat: nec potest eum in isto foro absoluere, nisi esset prius tempore vel natura absolutus a Deo. Et ideo est aduertendum, quod sicut nihil prohibet vnius & eiusdem homicidii reatum esse deletum quod ad regem, cuius seruus fuit occisus: & tamen remanere quo ad vicinum, cuius pater filius vel frater fuit idem occisus. Unde & reges quando remittunt tale homicidium, semper addunt in carta remissionis sic: salua semper iustitia partis. In quo casu & si pars offensa isti reo poenitenti & petenti remissionem teneretur statim remittere, & eum dimittere liberum & immunem: si ipse non peteret remissionem ab eodem, cum posset, iuste esset reus mortis, non directe propter reatum homicidii a rege vel per regem remissi: sed propter hoc, quod de vel pro tali reatu non satisfecit parti, cui tunc remansit, & nunc ex suo defectu permanet reus, cum nihil prohibet eiusdem peccati eundem reatum esse deletum quo ad Deum & remanere quo ad ecclesiam: quia non deletur simpliciter, sed salua iustitia ecclesiae. Quod si non satisfaciat confitendo, poenitendo & remissionem seu veniam expetendo, si haberet copiam sacerdotis, qui potest illam satisfactionem recipere, reus est mortis, non directe propter peccatum iam dimissum, sed indirecte quod de & pro tali peccato quo apud ecclesiam continue mansit remanet reus in casu praedicto de peccatis, non sicut debuit, satisfecit. Et hoc est quod dicit beatus Ambrosius, & ponitur in canon. de poen. distinct. 1. quantumlibet. Vbi dicit sic canon: Quantumlibet igitur foetor mortui sit, abluetur omnis, ubi sacrum redoleverit unguentum: surgit defunctus & dissolui iubentur eius vincula, quod adhuc in peccato est quo ad ecclesiam quamvis sit in gratia. Patet per hoc, quod immediate sequitur sic: Tollitur velamen de facie eius, quod veritatem gratiae quam acceperat obumbrabat. Potest etiam dici, quod peccatum delectum in contritione remanet quoad alium effectum. Sicut enim non solum originale in sanctis Patribus deletum fuit quoad reatum culpae & poenae aeternae per sacrificium & circumcisionem: sed etiam multa actualia per poenitentiam & confessionem, sicut patet de sancto Dauid 2. Reg. 12. & aliis, de quibus non dubium, quin decesserunt in gratia: & tamen in eis remanserunt peccata quoad hunc effectum, quod clauserunt eis ianuam, quae sine passione Christi non aperitur, sicut dicit Magister Sententiarum, quae passio nondum fuerat facta. Sic potest dici, quod quantumcunque dimittatur peccatum, & conferatur gratia in contritione: tamen semper remanet peccatum quoad hunc effectum, quod claudit nobis ianuam tam ecclesiae militantis quo ad meritum & susceptionem sacramenti eucharistiae: quam ecclesiae triumphantis quo ad praemium & degustationem gloriae quousque eadem ianua aperiatur per applicationem passionis Christi, quam applicat peccatori solus sacerdos ministerialiter, quando absolvit eum ab hoc reatu, si tamen (ut saepe dictum) habeatur copia idonei sacerdotis. Sic igitur praemissa conclusio patet quoad singulas eius partes.
units.tr: If, therefore, the priest did not loose otherwise than by showing the penitent to be absolved by God, it would follow that whomever Peter, or his vicar or priest, absolved by authority and virtue of the keys, that is, showed to be absolved, would be loosed before God. This is contrary to the canons, which say that priests often absolve the unworthy. It is also contrary to the canon in question 5 of cause 2, where it is true that the absolution of the priest is then valid when it follows the judgment of the judge, with the gloss: that is, of God. Or else, if Peter showed him to be divinely absolved, the man might perhaps still have to be refused absolution on account of obstinacy, and then the gospel saying, "Whatever is loosed will be loosed before God," would be false. Moreover, light is better than shadow, and truth than figure. But it is well known that the raising of Lazarus, John 11, was a figure of the justification of a sinner through the sacrament of penance, as is clear from blessed Ambrose and as is set down in the canon on penance, distinction 1; and also from blessed Augustine, On True and False Penitence, and as is set down in the chapter there. In this figure Christ not only brought Lazarus back to life, by motion or sense, and led him out into the light, but also really handed him over to the disciples, still bound, to be loosed, the gospel saying: "He came out bound hand and foot," and continuing: "Loose him and let him go." The truth of this figure is that Christ not only quickens the sinner by the infusion of grace, and mortifies him or signifies it by contrition of heart and confession of the mouth, remitting guilt and eternal punishment; he also hands the sinner over, still bound, to the priests to be unbound by true absolution. For the disciples not only showed Lazarus to be absolved, but, while he was not yet fully freed, they actually absolved him. Therefore it must be so in the justification of a sinner, that truth and figure correspond to each other. Likewise, whomever the priest shows to be divinely absolved from some mortal sin, he shows to be absolved from all. For God absolves no one from one sin whom he does not absolve from all, according to blessed Augustine in his book On True and False Penitence, as set down in the canon, distinction 3, on penance. Therefore the priest shows no one to be divinely absolved from one sin whom he does not show to be absolved from all. But it is certain that not everyone whom the priest absolves from one sin he absolves from all, since he often sends the penitent to superiors to be absolved. Therefore it follows that, besides showing the penitent to be absolved by God, the priest really absolves him. This is also confirmed: Christ did not say to the Apostles, "Whose sins you shall show to be forgiven, they shall be forgiven them," but "Whose sins you remit, they are remitted," John 20. Moreover, if the priest, by virtue of the keys, worked no special effect on the penitent by which he shows him to be absolved by God, but merely showed that he was absolved, it would seem that the keys are given to priests in vain for this purpose. For, as will be shown, an open or shut door cannot be the first effect of a material key; so neither can showing that a penitent is loosed or bound be the first effect of a spiritual key. Also, that effect could equally come without the key as with it, and consequently by virtue of the key he would not be shown to be loosed; then a layman would loose just as well as a priest, that is, show him absolved, or neither would. Indeed, the penitent seems to show himself loosed earlier and more effectively than the priest does, since the priest shows no one to be absolved except one whom, from signs of penitence, he believes to be penitent and therefore absolved by God. It would follow that the penitent himself ought to be said to have the key and to use it, rather than the priest, if the key were useful and necessary for this effect. Thirdly, it seems a manifest contradiction that the priest, by virtue of the keys, shows the sinner to be absolved by God, and yet does so by no effect or sign that proceeds from him by virtue of the keys. Therefore it follows that the priest, by virtue of the keys, works some first and immediate effect on the penitent, by which he secondarily shows him to be absolved by God, since by nature the thing is prior to what it works or shows. And it is clear that, since that effect is the immediate effect of the key, it must be either to shut or to open. And since it naturally has the function of showing the penitent to be absolved, it must be, by the correspondence of sign to signified, that the effect is to absolve. Therefore it follows that the priest by nature absolves the penitent first, and afterwards, by that same absolution, shows him to be absolved by God. From this argument it is clear that sacramental confession, which without doubt requires the effect and operation of the keys, insofar as the key requires and includes this absolution, is necessary at least on the part of the priest who hears the confession and on the part of the penitent, if his confession is to be lawful and valid for salvation, especially where a suitable priest is available. This was to be proved. And if it is asked from what the priest absolves the penitent, since sins are already blotted out in contrition as to the guilt of mortal sin and eternal punishment: the answer is that the priest absolves the penitent from the sin and guilt of that same mortal sin from which God had earlier absolved him. Nor can he absolve him in this forum unless he was first absolved by God, either in time or in nature. Therefore it must be noted that, just as nothing prevents the guilt of one and the same homicide from being blotted out as regards the king, whose servant was killed, while it remains as regards the neighbour, whose father, son or brother was the one killed, so also kings, when they remit such a homicide, always add in the charter of remission: "saving always the right of the party." In this case, even if the injured party were bound to remit at once to the penitent guilty man who asked for remission, and to let him go free and immune, yet if he himself did not seek remission from that party when he could, he would justly be guilty of death. This would not be directly on account of the guilt of homicide remitted by or through the king, but because he did not make satisfaction to the party for such guilt, which remained with that party; and now, through his own default, he remains guilty. For nothing prevents the same guilt of the same sin from being blotted out as regards God and remaining as regards the Church, since it is not blotted out simply, but with the right of the Church saved. But if he does not make satisfaction by confessing, repenting and seeking remission or pardon, and if he has access to a priest who can receive that satisfaction, he is guilty of death. This is not directly on account of the sin already forgiven, but indirectly, because he remains guilty of such sin, which continually remained before the Church, in the aforesaid case, since he did not make satisfaction as he ought. This is what blessed Ambrose means, and it is set down in the canon on penance, distinction 1, where the canon says: "However great the stench of the dead, everything is washed away where the holy ointment has given its fragrance; the dead man rises, and his bonds are ordered to be loosed," which he is still in sin as regards the Church, although he is in grace. This is clear from what immediately follows: "The veil is taken from his face, which had obscured the truth of the grace he had received." It can also be said that sin blotted out in contrition remains as regards another effect. For just as original sin in the holy Fathers was not only blotted out as to the guilt and eternal punishment through sacrifice and circumcision, but also many actual sins were blotted out through penance and confession, as is clear of holy David, 2 Samuel 12, and others, of whom there is no doubt that they died in grace, and yet sins remained in them as regards this effect, that they "shut the door to them, which is not opened without the passion of Christ," as the Master of the Sentences says, and that passion had not yet been undergone. So it can be said that however much sin is forgiven and grace conferred in contrition, sin nevertheless always remains as regards this effect: that it shuts against us the door both of the militant Church, as to merit and the reception of the sacrament of the Eucharist, and of the triumphant Church, as to reward and the tasting of glory, until that same door is opened by the application of the passion of Christ. The priest alone applies this to the sinner ministerially when he absolves him from this guilt, if indeed (as often said) a suitable priest is available. So the conclusion set out above is clear in each of its parts.

units.la: Ultimum quod in hoc articulo deducetur, est quod quantum ad materiam confessionis per istud capitulum, Omnis utriusque, nihil novi iuris vel antiqui proprio vel alieno sacerdoti deperditur vel acquiritur, plus quam ante: solo hoc excepto, quod tempus confessionis nouiter limitatur. Probatur sic: sola hac dictione semel in anno posita vel remota, ponitur vel remouetur tota differentia, quae est inter confessionem, quam homines tenebantur facere ante editam constitutionem seu tenerentur facere constitutione deleta, & quam tenebantur seu tenentur facere constitutione remanente, & similiter interea quae licuissent vel non licuissent & quae modo licent vel non licent: & eodem modo expedienti &c. Et haec dictio semel in anno nihil addit praeter dictam temporis limitationem. Igitur nihil novi iuris acquiritur, vel antiqui deperditur ad erutro praedictorum, sola limitatione temporis excepta, quod erat probandum. Assumptum quantum ad singulas sui partes satis patet: & ideo non insisto.
units.tr: The last thing to be deduced in this article is that, as regards the matter of confession under this chapter, Omnis utriusque, no new right, whether of the proper priest or of another, is either lost or acquired beyond what there was before, the only exception being that the time of confession is newly limited. This is proved thus: by placing or removing this single expression semel in anno (once a year), the whole difference is placed or removed between the confession which men were bound to make before the constitution was issued, or would be bound to make if the constitution were abolished, and the confession which they were bound to make, or are bound to make, while the constitution remains; and likewise between what was or was not permitted in the meantime and what is or is not permitted now, and in the same way what is expedient. Moreover, this expression semel in anno adds nothing beyond the said limitation of time. Therefore no new right is acquired, nor any old right lost, in respect of any of the aforesaid things, apart from the limitation of time; which was to be proved. The assumption is sufficiently clear as to each of its parts, and so I do not dwell on it.

units.la: Ex istis nempe sequuntur aliae duae quasi correlariae. Prima est & quinta in ordine totali: quod quicunque confessus proprio sacerdoti suo personaliter, seu cuicunque, alteri de licentia proprii sacerdotis, virtute cuius licentiae ipse poterit sibi confessum soluere & ligare: ac ab eodem vere solutus quantum ad ea quae sic confessus est satisfaciet concilio generali omnis utriusque: nec remanet ad eorundem confessionem ex vi statuti ulterius obligatus. Et quilibet qui peccauerit & non fuerit sic confessus, ad sic confitendum ex vi statuti remanet obligatus. Haec sequitur directe ex prima & ex secunda conclusionibus & probationibus eorundem.
units.tr: From these there follow two other, as it were, corollaries. The first, which is the fifth in the whole order, is this: whoever has confessed personally to his own priest, or to anyone else with the licence of his own priest, by virtue of which licence that priest may absolve and bind the one confessing, and has been truly absolved by him as regards those things which he has thus confessed, satisfies the general council omnis utriusque, and does not remain further bound by the statute to confess those same things. And whoever has sinned and has not thus confessed remains bound by virtue of the statute to confess in this way. This follows directly from the first and second conclusions and their proofs.

units.la: Secundum correlarium, & est sexta conclusio in ordine, est quod praeceptum statuti praedicti quantum ad confessionem omnium peccatorum debet intelligi quoad peccata, aliis legitime, ut praedicitur, non confessa, vel quae creduntur firmiter aut probabiliter dubitantur legitime non confessa. Hoc patet: quia quoad illa peccata, quae aliis, ut praedicitur, sunt legitime confessa, satisfactum est statuto: sicut patet ex conclusione immediate praecedente: & per consequens praeceptum statuti ad illa minime se extendit. Et quod ad alia se extendit, patet ex secunda parte conclusionis praecedentis &c.
units.tr: The second corollary, which is the sixth conclusion in the order, is that the precept of the aforesaid statute, as regards the confession of all sins, must be understood of those sins which, as has been said, have not been legitimately confessed to others, or which are firmly believed or probably doubted not to have been legitimately confessed. This is clear: for as to those sins which, as has been said, have been legitimately confessed to others, the statute has been satisfied, as is evident from the conclusion immediately preceding; and consequently the precept of the statute does not extend to them at all. And that it does extend to the others is evident from the second part of the preceding conclusion, etc.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Destruit & reprobat, quae ex dictis aduersarii pullulant erronea.
units.tr: It destroys and refutes the errors that spring up from the assertions of the opponent.

units.la: EXpeditis igitur his, quae circa capitulum Omnis utriusque videntur esse distinguenda: quia multiplicia supponenda tanquam necessaria, & inferenda velut correlaria. Sequitur consequenter videre, quae ex eodem statuto pullulabant erronea: ut ipsorum euulsis radicibus, eorundem nec repullulent frondes, nec flores, aut fructus in perpetuum renascantur. Occasione igitur secundae partis statuti huius: scilicet quod alienus non obtenta licentia proprii sacerdotis non poterat eius subditum soluere vel ligare: Fuerunt aliqui, qui tenuerunt & asseruerunt, quod Fratres habentes privilegium & licentiam generalem audiendi confessiones sibi conficeri volentium, non poterant virtute huius licentiae sibi confessos soluere & ligare sine licentia Parochialium. Et haec fuit opinio Guilhelmi de Sancto amore & suorum sequacium: sicut patet in bullis Alexandri quarti, Cum olim, & Non sine multa, & Romanus pontifex, & in eisdem est damnata. Ista tamen opinio habuit motiva diversa. Quidam enim existimabant in Fratribus esse duplicem defectum ad potestatem absoluendi: scilicet defectum executionis, & iurisdictionis defectum: & isti quantum ad defectum iurisdictionis Fratrum in extrinsecos suo ordini non errabant. Quantum autem ad defectum executionis, fuerunt motisic. Quod religiosi mendicantes non habent proprium episcopum: & ideo necessario ordinantur ab episcopo non suo. Quare sequitur quod episcopi executionem in praedictos Fratres non transmittunt, sicut in secunda distinctione secundi capituli fuit declaratum: & ideo credebant, q; licentia generalis Fratribus concessa fuit illa licentia generalissima quam descripsi 1. cap. dist. 5. Quae solum est licentia seu potestas executionis immediatae praedictae, q; scil. episcopus non possit conferre alienis sine licentia suorum episcoporum. Et ideo hac solum posita licentia, & non alia, quae est iurisdictionis: non dubium quod Fratres non poterant solvere vel ligare Parochianos sine licentia proprii sacerdotis. Et haec fuit opinio Bernhardi Glossatoris in cap. praedicto omnis, super verbo alieno. Et ideo allegant ibidem: q; si de duabus servitutibus una tolleretur, remanet altera, extra de usu pallii, ex tuarum, cum suis concordantiis. Hoc est, quod quamuis tollatur impedimentum, quod decurrit ex defectu consecutionis: non tamen propter hoc tollitur impedimentum occurrens ex parte iurisdictionis. Haec a. opinio quamuis habeat magnum colorem, quantum ad religiosos, qui sive ordinantur antequam ingrediantur ordinem, sive post, semper remanent ab executione audiendi confessiones suspensi, quousque per suos praelatos eisdem talis executio concedatur, cuiusmodi sunt Fratres Minores: quia apud illos, qui non sunt per leges sui ordinis sic suspensi (si aliqui tales sunt) nihil vel modicum haberent de colore, nihilominus deficit in duobus: quia nullum ius, quod loquitur de ordinato ab episcopo non suo suspendit ordinatum ab executione praedicta, ubi episcopus ratificat ordinationem subditi sui, vel suo nomine gestum esset cum licentia debita petita & obtenta. Quae conditiones non deficiunt in Fratribus, sicut constat cuilibet, eo quod de sola licentia praelatorum suorum possunt a quocunque episcopo catholico ordinari, quam licentiam eis dedit episcopus Romanus, qui solus est episcopus eorundem. Et ideo omnes sic ordinati habent ex ipsa ordinatione sua potestatem executionis, nisi obstent leges ordinis sui, sicut de Fratribus Minoribus dictum est. Hanc igitur executionem non fuit necessarium petere a Papa: quia habuerunt vel habere poterant semper a suo praelato.
units.tr: Having therefore dealt with the points that seem to need distinguishing in the chapter Omnis utriusque, since many things must be assumed as necessary and drawn as corollaries, it follows next to see what errors sprang from the same statute. Once their roots are pulled up, neither their leaves nor their flowers nor their fruit may grow back again. Occasioned, then, by the second part of this statute, namely that an outsider, without obtaining the licence of the proper priest, could not absolve or bind that priest's subject, some people held and asserted that friars who had a general privilege and licence to hear the confessions of those who wished to confess to them could not, by virtue of this licence, absolve or bind those confessing to them without the licence of the parish priests. This was the opinion of William of Saint-Amour and his followers, as is clear from the bulls of Alexander IV, Cum olim, and Non sine multa, and it was condemned in them by the Roman pontiff. This opinion, however, had various grounds. Some thought that friars had a twofold defect in the power to absolve: a defect of execution and a defect of jurisdiction. These men were not wrong about the defect of jurisdiction over outsiders to their order. But as to the defect of execution, they were moved by the following reasoning. Mendicant religious have no proper bishop, and so they must necessarily be ordained by a bishop who is not their own. It follows that the bishops do not transmit the power of execution to these friars, as was declared in the second distinction of the second chapter. They therefore believed that the general licence granted to the friars was that most general licence which I described in 1. cap. dist. 5. This is only a licence or power of the immediate execution just mentioned, namely that a bishop could not confer it on outsiders without the licence of their own bishops. Therefore, with only this licence granted and not the other, which concerns jurisdiction, there was no doubt that the friars could not absolve or bind parishioners without the licence of the proper priest. This was the opinion of Bernard the Glossator on the said chapter Omnis, under the word alieno. And so he argues there that if one of two servitudes is removed, the other remains, citing extra de usu pallii, ex tuarum, with their concordances. That is to say, although the impediment arising from a defect in the execution is removed, the impediment arising from the side of jurisdiction is not thereby removed. Yet although this opinion has a great show of plausibility as regards religious who are ordained either before or after they enter the order, and who always remain suspended from the execution of hearing confessions until their superiors grant them such execution, as is the case with the Friars Minor (for among those who are not so suspended by the laws of their order, if any such there are, it would have little or no plausibility), it nevertheless fails in two respects. First, no law that speaks of a man ordained by a bishop who is not his own suspends the man so ordained from that execution, where the bishop ratifies the ordination of his subject, or where the act was done in his name with the due licence sought and obtained. These conditions are not lacking in the friars, as is plain to anyone, since by the licence of their superiors alone they can be ordained by any Catholic bishog, a licence which the Roman bishop, who alone is the bishop of them all, has given them. Therefore all who are so ordained have from that very ordination the power of execution, unless the laws of their order stand in the way, as has been said of the Friars Minor. It was not necessary, therefore, to seek this execution from the Pope, since they had, or could always have had, it from their own superior.

units.la: Secundo deficit in hoc, quod credebant quod licentia generalis praedicta non praebuit fratribus iurisdictionem vel materiam, in qua exercerent huiusmodi potestatem. Et potest iste error contingere in hoc, quod non viderant Fratrum privilegia quo ad singula iam praedicta. Unde fratrum privilegia concedebant eis, quod possunt audire confessiones & absolvere poenitentes, & eisdem iniungere poenitentiam salutarem, quae (non dubium) fieri non possunt sine potestate iurisdictionis, & sine materia, in qua haec potestas exerceatur. Et similiter non attendebant, quod nisi Papa per huiusmodi privilegium hanc potestatem iurisdictionis Fratribus concessisset ultra privilegia priora, scilicet quod possunt a quocunq; episcopo catholico ordinari: & sic beneficium pontificis esset nullum. Hoc idcirco tam late expositi: quia haec motiva in aliquorum cordibus radicantur. Patet tamen cuilibet sapienti, quod haec motiva nulla stabili fulciuntur ratione.
units.tr: Secondly, it fails in this, that they believed the said general licence gave the friars no jurisdiction or matter over which they might exercise such power. This error may have arisen because they had not seen the privileges of the friars with respect to each of the points just mentioned. For the friars' privileges granted them that they may hear confessions, absolve penitents, and impose a salutary penance on them, which (there is no doubt) cannot be done without the power of jurisdiction and without a matter over which this power may be exercised. Likewise they did not notice that, unless the Pope had granted the friars this power of jurisdiction by such a privilege, over and above the earlier privileges (namely that they could be ordained by any Catholic bishop), the favour of the pontiff would be empty. I have set this out at such length because these arguments take root in the hearts of some. Yet it is plain to any sensible person that these arguments rest on no firm reason.

units.la: Alii autem, qui fuerunt huius opinionis, existimabant, sicut adhuc ab omnibus aestimatur, scilicet quod soli parochiales sacerdotes sunt proprii sacerdotes, de quibus loquitur statutum. Et ex hoc concludebant, quod sine istorum licentia nullus subditus eorum a Fratribus absolvi poterit vel ligari. Et ideo licentia generalis Papae fuit insufficiens Fratribus ad hoc, quod solverent vel ligarent. Istud autem motivum in suo fundamento, scilicet quod soli Parochiales presbyteri vel curati sunt Parochianorum proprii sacerdotes, ad mentem statuti fuit fundamentum Magistri Iohannis de Poliaco. Quantum ad errores suos, sicut expresse patet in capitul. Vaselectionis 2. & 3. cap. eiusdem. Et est hodie opinio Domini Reuerendi, contra quem agitur in praesenti. Sicut patet in multis locis sui tractatus praedicti, & specialiter in quarto & quinto articulo eiusdem, quae periculosa est nimis & multorum radix errorum, sicut probabitur in continenti. Ad quod arguitur sic: quia primo sequitur, quod Parochiani committentes tam gravia, quod non possunt absolvi nisi a Papa vel episcopis vel poenitentiariis eorundem non tenentur ex vi statuti eius confiteri Papae peccata illa vel episcopis, supposito illo quod habeant copiam eorundem: quia nullus Parochianus ex vi huius statuti praedicti tenetur confiteri, nisi proprio sacerdoti, scilicet Parochiali presbytero seu curato. Sed ex hypostasi, Papa & episcopi non sunt huiusmodi. Igitur nullus Parochianus ex vi statuti tenetur eisdem confiteri. Quod autem istud sit erroneum, patet: quia quilibet Parochianus tenetur in paschate recipere eucharistiae sacramentum, saltem si non obstet consilium Parochialis presbyteri vel curati. Igitur si non tenetur confiteri, licet sibi sine confessione & absolutione gravissimorum criminum, habita tamen copia illorum, qui possunt eum absolvere, recipere eucharistiae sacramentum: quod non dubitatur esse erroneum ab aliquo sanae mentis. Amplius ponitur, quod aliquis parochianus sit irretitus peccatis Deo, Papae & episcopis reseruatis. & nullius aliis mortalibus. Et sequitur quod Parochianus irretitus gravissimis criminibus tenetur ex vi statuti confiteri Parochiali presbytero: qui non potest eum absolvere & non tenetur ex vi statuti ea confiteri alicui, qui potest eum absolvere a peccatis. Istud patet: quoniam quilibet Parochianus tenetur semel in anno omnia peccata sua confiteri suo Parochiali presbytero vel curato: & nulli alteri tenetur aliquis Parochianus ex vi statuti confiteri. Igitur &c. Amplius, retento casu priori sequitur, quod Parochianus confessus Papæ vel episcopo suo, & absolutus ab eisdem tenetur eadem peccata, quæ confessus est vel suo Parochiali presbytero vel curato iterum confiteri; & hoc ex vi statuti: & per consequens cum Papa non potest aliquem plus privilegiare, quam ipsemet sit privilegiatus: sequitur quod stante statuto illo non potest facere, quod Parochiani non teneantur confiteri omnia peccata sua semel in anno suo presbytero Parochiali vel curato. Et iste est error suus in forma sua damnatus in cap. vas electionis. Rursus sequitur, quod Papa & Episcopi non possunt, stante statuto, dare alienis potestatem absoluendi quoscunque Parochianos sibi confessos: non obtenta licentia proprii sacerdotis, id est, Parochialis presbyteri vel curati: quia secundum diffinitionem concilii generalis nullus habet potestatem absoluendi vel ligandi sibi confessum sine licentia Parochialis presbyteri seu curati. Igitur si Papa vel episcopi darent alienis potestatem, vt prædicitur, absoluendi, ipsi destruerent diffinitionem concilii generalis. Quare sequitur, quod non possunt stante statuto dare talem potestatem sacerdotibus alienis. Et iste error fuit in æquivalenti damnatus per Alexandrum quartum. Amplius sequitur, quod Papa & episcopi non possunt stante statuto prædicto quenquam soluere vel ligare sibi confessum sine licentia Parochialis presbyteri vel curati: quia ex hoc, quod non possunt hanc potestatem dare alienis sacerdotibus, sequitur quod non habent eam ordinate, extra de offic. iudi. ordi. eiu quibus, aliis bis quibus. Nec habent eam per commissionem, non est dubium, nisi forsan de commissione proprii sacerdotis. Igitur non habent huiusmodi potestatem: similiter Papa & episcopi, ex quo non sunt proprii sacerdotes: non dubium, quod ad mentem statuti quicunque non sunt proprii sacerdotes episcopi, si sint sacerdotes, sunt alieni. Quare Papa & episcopi secundum mentem statuti sunt sacerdotes alieni, & per consequens secundum statutum non possunt soluere vel ligare sine licentia proprii sacerdotis: & hoc contra euangelium Matth. 16. & 18. c. & Ioh. 20. quorum remiseritis peccata &c. Amplius sequitur, quod Papæ & episcoporum iurisdictio minuitur vel restringitur per substitutionem Parochialis presbyteri seu curati, quod non permittit prima suppositio cap. 2. & specialiter cum etiam concilium generale non possit Papæ legem præfigere, extra de electione & electi potestate, significasti. Et sequitur etiam, quod per huiusmodi substitutionem potest eius potestas tantum minui, quod aliquando simpliciter esset nulla, quod est piarum aurium merito offensiuum. Amplius ex eodem sequitur, nullus est; nec potest esse proprius sacerdos, nec aliquis qui potest absoluere pœnitentes. Probatur, quia Papa & episcopi non habent potestatem absoluendi Parochianos sine licentia proprii sacerdotis. Ergo non possunt huiusmodi potestatem dare cuicunque i. quaest. i. t. qui perfectionem & c. ventum est & i. quaest. 7. Dayberrum. Igitur si nullo modo essent Parochiales presbyteri vel curati, sed omnes essent mortui, sicut fuerunt in multis locis tempore pestilentiae, Papa & episcopi non possent sibi hanc potestatem accipere, nec eam alienis conferre: nec per consequens Parochiales presbyteros instituere. Et constat, quod æque modicum Papa & episcopi poterant instituere proprios sacerdotes, quando primo instituebant eos, sicut modo. Quare sequitur, quod tunc nulli erant facti proprii sacerdotes, nec adhuc sunt: & per consequens nullus potest absoluere pœnitentes. Et quod rogo potest esse magis horrendum & crudele menti Christianæ? Hæc igitur & multa plura, quæ causa brevitatis transeo, sequuntur hoc dato, quod statutum concilii generalis sub nomine proprii sacerdotis Papam & episcopos non includat, sed excludat tantum Parochiales presbyteros seu curatos includendo.
units.tr: Others who held this opinion thought, as it is still held by everyone, that only parish priests are the proper priests of whom the statute speaks. From this they concluded that none of their subjects could be absolved or bound by the Friars without the consent of these priests. For this reason, they said, the Pope's general licence was insufficient for the Friars to absolve or bind. This argument, namely that only parish priests or curates are the proper priests of their parishioners, was the foundation of Master John of Pouilly's view, in keeping with the meaning of the statute. As to his errors, they are plainly set out in capitul. Vaselectionis 2. & 3. cap. eiusdem. This is also the present opinion of the Reverend Lord against whom the case is now brought, as is plain in many places of his aforesaid treatise, and especially in quarto & quinto articulo eiusdem. That opinion is very dangerous and the root of many errors, as will be shown directly. Against it the argument runs as follows. First, it follows that parishioners who commit such grave sins that they cannot be absolved except by the Pope, the bishops or their penitentiaries are not bound by virtue of the statute to confess those sins to the Pope or the bishops, even supposing they have access to them. For no parishioner is bound by virtue of this statute to confess except to his proper priest, that is, to his parish priest or curate. But by hypothesis the Pope and the bishops are not such priests. Therefore no parishioner is bound by the statute to confess to them. That this is erroneous is plain, because every parishioner is bound to receive the sacrament of the Eucharist at Easter, at least unless the counsel of his parish priest or curate prevents it. So if he is not bound to confess, then he may receive the sacrament of the Eucharist without confession and absolution of the gravest crimes, provided he has access to those who can absolve him. No one of sound mind doubts that this is erroneous. Furthermore, suppose a parishioner is entangled in sins reserved to God, the Pope and the bishops, and in no others that are mortal. It follows that a parishioner entangled in the gravest crimes is bound by virtue of the statute to confess them to his parish priest, who cannot absolve him, and is not bound by the statute to confess them to anyone who can absolve him from sins. This is plain, since every parishioner is bound to confess all his sins once a year to his parish priest or curate, and no parishioner is bound by the statute to confess to anyone else. Therefore &c. Again, keeping the former case, it follows that a parishioner who has confessed to the Pope or to his own bishop, and has been absolved by them, is still bound by the statute to confess the same sins again to his parish priest or curate. Consequently, since the Pope cannot grant anyone more privilege than he himself enjoys, it follows that, while that statute stands, he cannot bring it about that parishioners are not bound to confess all their sins once a year to their parish priest or curate. This is the error that was condemned in form in cap. vas electionis. Further, it follows that, while the statute stands, the Pope and the bishops cannot give to alien priests the power to absolve any parishioners who have confessed to them, unless the licence of the proper priest, that is, of the parish priest or curate, has been obtained. For according to the definition of a general council, no one has the power to absolve or bind one who has confessed to him without the licence of the parish priest or curate. Therefore, if the Pope or the bishops were to give alien priests the power to absolve, as has been said, they would destroy the definition of the general council. Hence it follows that, while the statute stands, they cannot give such power to alien priests. This error was also condemned in an equivalent form by Alexander IV. Furthermore, it follows that the Pope and the bishops, while the aforesaid statute stands, cannot absolve or bind anyone who has confessed to them without the licence of the parish priest or curate. For since they cannot give this power to alien priests, it follows that they do not possess it lawfully, extra de offic. iudi. ordi. eiu quibus, and in the other place, bis quibus. Nor do they have it by commission, undoubtedly, unless perhaps by the commission of the proper priest. Therefore they do not have this power. Likewise the Pope and the bishops, since they are not proper priests, are, according to the meaning of the statute, alien priests, if they are priests at all; there is no doubt of this. Hence the Pope and the bishops, according to the meaning of the statute, are alien priests, and consequently, according to the statute, cannot absolve or bind without the licence of the proper priest. And this is contrary to the Gospel, Matth. 16. and 18. and John 20., whose sins you remit &c. Furthermore, it follows that the jurisdiction of the Pope and of the bishops is diminished or restricted by the substitution of the parish priest or curate, which the first supposition, cap. 2., does not allow; and especially since a general council cannot prescribe a law to the Pope, extra de electione & electi potestate, significasti. It also follows that by such a substitution his power could be so reduced that at times it would be simply nothing, which is rightly offensive to pious ears. Further, from the same premises it follows that there is, and can be, no proper priest who is able to absolve penitents. This is proved because the Pope and the bishops do not have the power to absolve parishioners without the licence of the proper priest. Therefore they cannot give this power to anyone, i. quaest. i. t. qui perfectionem & c. ventum est and i. quaest. 7. Dayberrum. Therefore, if there were no parish priests or curates at all, but all were dead, as they were in many places at the time of the plague, the Pope and the bishops could not take this power to themselves, nor confer it on others, nor consequently institute parish priests. And it is certain that the Pope and the bishops were then no more able to institute proper priests when they first instituted them than they are now. Hence it follows that no one was then made a proper priest, nor are they yet; and consequently no one can absolve penitents. And what, I ask, can be more horrible and cruel to a Christian mind? These and many more consequences, which for the sake of brevity I pass over, follow from this premise: that the statute of the general council, under the name of proper priest, does not include the Pope and the bishops, but excludes only the parish priests or curates by including them.

units.la: Tertii fuerunt, qui tenuerunt eundem errorem, scil. quod Fratres habentes licentiam generalem audiendi confessiones &c. non poterant sibi confessos soluere vel ligare sine licentia proprii sacerdotis ex hoc motiuo: quod quamuis Fratres huiusmodi possunt Parochianorum audire confessiones & eosdem absoluere, quantum est ex parte potestatis fratribus collatæ: ipsi tamen Parochiani non possunt eisdem confiteri sine licentia proprii sacerdotis. Et ideo fratres non possunt eos absoluere, obstante impedimento ex parte confitentium: quamuis nullum sit impedimentum ex parte potestatis fratrum. Et huius opinionis est iste Dominus Reuerendus in 5. cap. sui tractatus in secunda responsione ad cap. vas electionis, seu in secunda expositione seu Gloss. cap. supradicti. Videin propositione, quam coram vestra reuerentia fecit, dixit, quod confessi sic fratribus sine licentia proprii sacerdotis: & omnino per totum annum proprio sacerdote a nullo peccato mortali absoluuntur: sed redeunt onerati omnibus peccatis, cum quibus accesserant ad eosdem. Sed contra istud arguitur sic: quia sicut fuit dictum in principio, potestas ligandi & soluendi sibi confessos, quam habent fratres ex generali licentia audiendi confessiones eis, confessa, non est solum potestas ordinis & executionis nudae: sed potestas iurisdictionis, per quam tribuitur materia, in qua potestas ordinis executionis exerceatur. Ergo concessio huiusmodi potestatis est concessio materiæ. Cum igitur per se materia audiendi confessiones & absoluendi sit peccatum seu peccator sub ratione, qua peccatum suum confitetur: sequitur quod concedens huiusmodi potestatem concedit, quod Parochiani possint eis confiteri. Amplius, Parochialis curatus per licentiam, quam concedit Parochiano, quod possit Fratribus confiteri, nullam potestatem concedit fratribus per se, sed solum per accidens: quia suum subditum concedit suæ potestati: sicut ille, qui concedit fabro ferrum, nullam potestatem per se tribuit fabro; quamuis faber non poterit operari sine ferro. Igitur Parochialis presbyter prius concedit suum subditum alienæ potestati, vel prius concedit, quod possit alieno confiteri quam proprio concedit fratri seu alieno illam potestatem accidentalem: quia prius est illud, quod est per se, quam illud quod est per accidens. Sed constat, quod omnem per se potestatem, quam habet frater antequam recipiat licentiam Parochialis curati, habet frater antequam præsentetur episcopo vel antequam licentia generalis audiendi confessiones conferatur eidem. Et antequam illam recipiat licentiam generalem, sibi solum deficit hæc potestas accidentalis seu per accidens. Igitur Papa vel episcopus conferens fratri huiusmodi licentiam generalem, prius confert sibi materiam, scilicet quod Parochianus possit Fratri confiteri, quam concedat fratri illam potestatem accidentalem, scilicet quod possit eum audire & absoluere. Amplius, summi pontifices in priuilegiis suis, in quibus concedebant fratribus licentiam audiendi confessiones, & confessos absoluendi, præceperunt curatis & quibuscunque aliis, quod eosdem in executione commissionis talis officii nullus molestaret, sed hortabantur eos, quod suos Parochianos ad faciendum fratribus confessionem inducerent & monerent: & per consequens sequitur, quod concesserunt Parochianis licentiam eisdem fratribus confitendi: puta si fratres virtute huius generalis licentiæ sibi concessæ possunt Parochianos audire & absoluere in confessione, cum ipsi Parochiani non possunt virtute talis licentiæ eisdem confiteri: sequitur à fortiori, quod quamuis alieni possent audire confessiones non suorum Parochianorum virtute licentiæ Parochialis presbyteri seu curati eisdem alienis concessæ, Parochiani tamen non possunt virtute eiusdem licentiæ confiteri eisdem: & sic sequitur, quod obstante isto impedimento confessi sacerdotibus alienis de licentia Parochialis presbyteri redeunt suis peccatis onerati à nullo penitus absoluti. Amplius, constat quod nullus potest concedere cuicunq; fratri potestatem absoluendi & audiendi subditum vel Parochianum non suum, sed tantum concedit hanc licentiam super subditum suum. Igitur talem licentiam concedendo super subditum suum concedit subdito correlatiuam potestatem. Alioquin æque concederet vel concedere posset hanc potestatem super subditum alienum, sicut super proprium. Concedit igitur subdito licentiam, quod possit fratribus confiteri. Igitur quemcunque fratres possunt in confessione audire & absoluere, ipse quantum est ex parte sui, potest sibi econtra si voluerit confiteri. Quod si habens hanc licentiam indiget licentia Parochialis presbyteri vel curati, sequuntur omnes errores superius prædicti.
units.tr: Third were those who held the same error, namely that friars who have a general licence to hear confessions etc. could not absolve or bind those who confessed to them without the licence of their own priest, for this reason: although such friars can hear the confessions of parishioners and absolve them, so far as the power granted to the friars is concerned, the parishioners themselves cannot confess to them without the licence of their own priest. And therefore the friars cannot absolve them, because of an obstacle on the part of the penitents, although there is no obstacle on the part of the friars' power. Of this opinion is that Reverend Lord in the fifth chapter of his treatise, in the second answer to the chapter "vas electionis", or in the second exposition or gloss of the chapter cited above. In the proposition which he made before your reverence, he said that those who confess to the friars without the licence of their own priest are absolved of no mortal sin by anyone for the whole year, but return burdened with all the sins with which they had come to them. But against this it is argued thus: because, as was said at the beginning, the power of binding and loosing those who confess to them, which friars have by the general licence to hear confessions, is not merely a power of order and bare execution, but a power of jurisdiction, through which the matter is granted in which the power of order is exercised. Therefore the grant of such a power is a grant of the matter. Since, then, the matter of hearing confessions and absolving is in itself a sin, or the sinner under the aspect in which he confesses his sin, it follows that whoever grants such a power grants that the parishioners may confess to them. Furthermore, a parish priest, by the licence which he grants to a parishioner that he may confess to friars, grants no power to the friars in themselves, but only by accident: because he grants his subject to his own power, just as one who gives iron to a smith grants no power in itself to the smith, although the smith cannot work without iron. Therefore the parish priest first grants his subject to another's power, or first grants that he may confess to another's keeping, before he grants to his own friar, or to another, that accidental power. For that which is per se comes before that which is per accidens. But it is plain that every power per se which a friar has before he receives the licence of the parish priest, he has before he is presented to the bishop, or before the general licence to hear confessions is conferred upon him. And before he receives that general licence, only this accidental power is lacking to him. Therefore the Pope or bishop who confers such a general licence on a friar first confers on him the matter, namely that the parishioner may confess to the friar, before he grants him that accidental power, namely that he may hear and absolve him. Furthermore, the supreme pontiffs, in their privileges in which they granted friars the licence to hear confessions and absolve those who confessed, commanded the parish priests and all others that no one should molest them in the execution of the commission of such an office, but encouraged them to lead and admonish their own parishioners to make confession to the friars. And consequently it follows that they granted to the parishioners the licence to confess to those same friars. For if friars, by virtue of this general licence granted to them, can hear and absolve parishioners in confession, when the parishioners themselves cannot by virtue of such a licence confess to them, it follows a fortiori that, although strangers could hear the confessions of others' parishioners by virtue of the licence of the parish priest or curate granted to those strangers, the parishioners nevertheless cannot by virtue of that same licence confess to them. And so it follows that, because of this obstacle, those who confess to priests not their own, with the licence of the parish priest, return burdened with their sins, not absolved at all by anyone. Furthermore, it is plain that no one can grant to any friar the power to absolve and hear a subject or parishioner who is not his own; he grants this licence only over his own subject. Therefore, by granting such a licence over his own subject, he grants a correlative power to the subject. Otherwise he would grant, or could grant, this power over another's subject just as over his own. He therefore grants the subject licence to confess to friars. Therefore whomever the friars can hear and absolve in confession, he himself, so far as it lies in his own part, can, if he wishes, confess to them in return. But if one who has this licence needs the licence of the parish priest or curate, all the errors mentioned above follow.

units.la: Ad argumenta huius Domini, quibus probat hoc motiuum, respondetur per ordinem. Arguit enim sic. Ponatur quod vnum capitulum habeat statutum, quod vacante ecclesia eligat vnum de capitulo, & quod nullum eligat extrinsecum capitulo sine licentia Decani: concedit Dominus Papa monachis fratribus vel religiosis priuilegium, quod possunt eligi à quibuscunque volentibus eos eligere. In quo casu constat, quod capitulum non potest fratrem seu monachum eligere sine licentia Decani, obstante statuto prædicto: & tamen constat, quod frater seu monachus eligi potest. Igitur consimiliter erit ex parte alia.
units.tr: To the arguments of this Lord, by which he proves this reason, an answer is given in order. For he argues thus. Suppose that one chapter has a statute that, when the church is vacant, it shall elect one of its own members, and that it shall elect no one from outside the chapter without the licence of the dean; and suppose the Lord Pope grants to friars or religious men the privilege that they may be elected by anyone who wishes to elect them. In this case it is plain that the chapter cannot elect a friar or monk without the licence of the dean, the statute above standing in the way; and yet it is plain that a friar or monk can be elected. Therefore, similarly, it will be the case on the other side.

units.la: Ad illud dico, quod exemplum exemplato non correspondet: sed discordat in multis. Primo: quia sicut statuit quod quilibet debet confiteri proprio sacerdoti vel alicui de sui licentia: ita dicitur in exemplo statuti, quod capitulum debet eligere Decanum vel alium de licentia sua. Et credo quod raro vel nunquam huius licentiam obtineret. Secundo non cauetur in casu, vtrum statutum sit factum auctoritate capituli vel Papæ. Constat autem de statuto, super quo agitur, quod fuit factum auctoritate concilii generalis. Et secundum hoc esset varie respondendum. Tum quia Papa potest ignorare statutum capituli priuati: & de illo forsan esset mentio facienda in priuilegio: alioquin non valeret priuilegium contra statutum. Argumentum extra de rescriptis. constitutio. Sed non ita potest ignorare statutum ecclesiæ, cum habeat in scrinio sui pectoris omnes leges. Tum etiam, quia sicut statutum esset statutum ecclesiæ & singulare pro vno capitulo, videtur quod huiusmodi generale priuilegium non deroget statuto speciali, & quamuis ita esset, quod tamen generaliter non est verum, cum nihil arguit in proposito, vbi tam statutum quam priuilegium est generale. Et per consequens potest derogare statuto extra de rescriptis. Sicut Romana. Tertio argumentum deficit in hoc, quod in casu non cauetur, quod Fratres possunt eligi & sortiri effectum electionis virtute electionis factæ: sicut in alia parte cauetur, quod possit in effectum omnem, qui adiungitur cum audientia consessionum. Quarto deficit in hoc, quod istud priuilegium, de quo fit mentio in argumento, non datur per decanum, qui decanus potuit dare licentiam, mediante qua & monachus posset eligi & statutum seruari: sicut in alia parte priuilegium datur per Papam: qui, vt probatum est, est proprius sacerdos & tanquam talis potest dare licentiam, virtute cuius & statutum seruetur & fratres confessiones audiant & absoluant. Istis vero defectibus & similibus restauratis dico, quod sicut frater potest eligi, ita quilibet de capitulo potest eundem eligere statuto non obstante. Huiusmodi vero exempla quamuis prima facie appareant, tamen de existentia nihil habent.
units.tr: To this I say that the example does not correspond to the thing exemplified, but differs in many respects. First, because just as the statute lays down that everyone must confess to his own priest or to someone with his licence, so in the example of the statute it is said that the chapter must elect a dean or another with its licence. And I believe that it would rarely or never obtain such a licence. Second, the argument does not take into account, in the case, whether the statute was made by the authority of the chapter or of the Pope. But it is plain of the statute under discussion that it was made by the authority of a general council; and according to this it would have to be answered in various ways. For the Pope can be ignorant of the statute of a private chapter, and perhaps mention of it ought to be made in the privilege; otherwise the privilege would not be valid against the statute (argument: extra, de rescriptis, constitutio). But he cannot be so ignorant of a statute of the Church, since he has all the laws in the coffer of his breast. Third, also, because, even if the statute were a statute of the Church and particular to one chapter, it seems that such a general privilege does not derogate from a special statute; and even if this were so, it is not true in general, since nothing follows for the present point where both the statute and the privilege are general; and consequently it can derogate from the statute (extra, de rescriptis, Sicut Romana). Fourth, the argument fails in this, that the privilege mentioned in the argument is not granted by the dean, who could have given the licence by which both the monk might be elected and the statute kept; whereas in the other case the privilege is granted by the Pope, who, as has been proved, is the proper priest and, as such, can give the licence by virtue of which both the statute is kept and the friars hear and absolve confessions. But when these defects and similar ones have been remedied, I say that just as a friar can be elected, so anyone of the chapter can elect him, the statute notwithstanding. Such examples, although they appear at first sight, have nothing in fact to support them.

units.la: Item arguit sic: non obstante priuilegio fratribus concesso, quod possunt liberè audire confessiones omnium sibi confiteri volentium. Moniales non possunt Fratribus confiteri sine licentia suorum superiorum, nec Prædicatores monachi moribus, nec econuerso sine licentia suorum superiorum speciali. Respondeo, quod verum est quod dicit in isto argumento. Et causa est, quia in iure seu priuilegio fratribus concesso, bene cauetur, quod fratres non habeant licentiam in casibus & personis episcopis reseruatis: cuiusmodi sunt moniales, quæ non sunt Parochianæ. Aut si sint, sunt episcopis quo ad omnem iurisdictionem huiusmodi reseruatæ: nec sunt subiectæ Parochialibus presbyteris vel curatis. Et hæc est causa, quare pro audiendis earum confessionibus episcoporum haberi tenetur licentia specialis. Sed quod Fratribus Prædicatoribus non licet audire Minores, vel econtra causa est, quia episcopi, qui committunt fratribus licentiam generalem confessiones audiendi, non possunt Minoribus committere super prædicatoribus vel econtra, eo quod neutri sunt sui subditi in hac parte, quamvis in multis aliis sunt subditi. Et idem dico de monachis & similibus. Et ideo ad istos hæc licentia nullatenus se extendit. Et idem dico de licentia Domini Papæ audiendi Parochianos dicecesis alienæ, quam Dominus Papa in hoc casu ad licentiam episcopi modificat & restringit.
units.tr: Likewise he argues thus: notwithstanding the privilege granted to the friars, that they may freely hear the confessions of all who wish to confess to them, nuns may not confess to the Friars without leave of their superiors, nor may Preaching monks (Dominicans) confess to Minorites, nor conversely, without a special licence from their own superiors. I reply that what he says in this argument is true. And the reason is that in the law or privilege granted to the friars, care is clearly taken that the friars do not have licence in cases and persons reserved to the bishops: of which kind are nuns who are not parishioners. Or if they are, they are reserved to the bishops in respect of all jurisdiction of this kind, and they are not subject to parish priests or curates. And this is the reason why a special licence of the bishops must be held for hearing their confessions. But that Friars Preachers may not hear Minorites, or the reverse, is because the bishops, who commit to the friars a general licence to hear confessions, cannot commit to Minorites authority over Preachers, or the reverse, since neither is subject to the other in this matter, although in many other respects they are subject. And I say the same of monks and the like. Therefore this licence does not in any way extend to them. And I say the same of the licence of the Lord Pope to hear parishioners of another diocese, which the Lord Pope in this case modifies and restricts by the licence of the bishop.

units.la: Iterum arguit sic: ratio naturalis affirmat, quod libertas patiendi in patiente non arguit libertatem agendi in agente. Respondeo, quod si loquamur de libertate a culpa, sicut videtur argumentum procedere, sic concedo quod istum pati absque culpa non arguit alium efficere hanc passionem sine culpa, nec etiam cum culpa. Et ideo potest esse sine culpa & cum culpa secundum varietatem materiæ subiectæ. Et ideo argumentum de se est neutrum seu negandum. In proposito tamen dico, quod pensatis circumstantiis materiæ, de qua agitur, libertas patiendi in patiente præsupponit libertatem agentis in agente, ut supra probatum est. Ex prædictis igitur patet, quod salua semper reverentia Domini mei hæc prædicta, quæ tenet, non sunt sana, nec aliqua evidentia notabili sunt fulcita.
units.tr: Again he argues thus: natural reason affirms that the freedom of the patient to suffer does not imply freedom of the agent to act. I reply that if we speak of freedom from fault, as the argument seems to proceed, so I grant that one who suffers without fault does not imply that another brings about this suffering without fault, nor even with fault. And so it can be without fault and with fault according to the variety of the matter concerned. And so the argument in itself is neither true nor to be denied. In the present case, however, I say that, weighing the circumstances of the matter under discussion, the freedom of the patient to suffer presupposes the freedom of the agent to act, as has been proved above. From what has been said it therefore appears that, with all due reverence for my Lord, the aforesaid propositions which he maintains are not sound, nor are they supported by any notable evidence.

units.la: Rursum occasione primæ partis eiusdem statuti fuerunt & sunt aliqui solennes, qui tenent & tenuerunt, quod confessi fratribus habentibus licentiam generalem audiendi confessiones & confessos absoluendi ac iniungendi pœnitentiam salutarem, huiusmodi confessione non obstante tenentur eadem peccata, quæ fuerunt confessi, iterum confiteri proprio sacerdoti. Huius opinionis fuit Magister Iohannes de Poliaco: & fuit in parte motus ex hoc, quod sibi videbatur, quod huiusmodi licentia generalis non tollat statutum concilii generalis. Credebat enim quod si confessi fratribus non tenebantur, ut prædicitur, iterum confiteri, statutum per huiusmodi licentiam tolleretur: ideo posuit, quod stante statuto nec Papa nec Deus potest facere, quod Parochianus semel in anno non teneatur confiteri omnia peccata sua Parochiali presbytero seu curato. A qua opinione quantum ad conclusionem & motivum prædictum in nullo discrepat Armachanus archiepiscopus, ut patebit.
units.tr: Again, on the occasion of the first part of the same statute, there were and are some eminent men who hold and have held that persons who have confessed to friars having a general licence to hear confessions and to absolve the confessed and to impose a salutary penance, are, notwithstanding such confession, bound to confess again to their own priest the same sins which they confessed. Master John of Polliaco was of this opinion, and he was moved in part by this, that it seemed to him that such a general licence does not remove the statute of the general council. For he believed that if those who had confessed to friars were not bound, as has been said, to confess again, the statute would be undone by such a licence; therefore he held that, while the statute stands, neither the Pope nor God can bring it about that a parishioner is not bound to confess all his sins once a year to his parish priest or curate. The Archbishop of Armagh does not differ at all from this opinion, as to the conclusion and the aforesaid reason, as will become clear.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Reducens eidem statuto, Omnis utriusque sexus; cap. Dudum. Et cap. Vas electionis.
units.tr: Referring to the same statute, "Every one of either sex"; the chapter Dudum; and the chapter Vas electionis.

units.la: RESTAT igitur modo eidem statuto reducere capitulum Dudum; & capitulum Vas electionis; ac fratrum priuilegia, quæ in hac materia ad cap. Dudum hodie sunt reducta. Ideo ostendetur, quod capitulum Dudum prædicto statuto non obuiat nec repugnat. Verumtamen quia in hoc videor cum adversario concordare: ideo ne laboremus in æquivoco, sciendum; quod ex statuto concilii generalis consurgit duplex obligatio seu debitum confitendi. Vna est generalis perpetua & mansiua: alia est specialis seu particularis transiens & fluxiua. Prima est, qua quilibet siue cōfiteatur siue nō, semper ex vi statuti ad confessionem faciendam semel in anno remanet obligatus. Cum quo stat, quod hic peccator pro hoc anno de his peccatis, quæ fecit, non tenetur confiteri, quia forte confessus est legitime de eisdem. Secunda est, qua quis in speciali de istis peccatis in particulari demonstratis, & quod hoc singulari tempore vel anno tenetur confiteri, quæ obligatio est transiens & fluxiua, quia hac particulari obligatione soluta non remanet amplius eadem obligatione obligatus; quamuis prima obligatione semper remaneat obligatus. Alioquin n. nisi soluto particulari determinato remaneret in genere obligatus, sequeretur quod semel confessus secundum formam statuti quantumcunq; postea peccaret, non teneretur ex vi statuti iterum confiteri. Horum exemplum manifestum est de reddditu annuo, quo quis tenetur; transeo quia notū est. Aliud exemplū potest esse; q hæc propositio vniversalis omnis homo est animal secundum Philosophum est perpetuæ veritatis; quia est necessaria, cuius quilibet singularis est contingens, cuius veritas transit cū sua entitate. Ad propositum dico, q cap. Dudum non obuiat nec repugnat statuto concilii generalis Omnis utriusq; sexus, nec quo ad obligationē primam, nec quo ad secundam. Dico tamen, quod frequenter tollit eius obligationem secundam, tū non tollit primam. Et si arguitur, quod hoc capitulum tollit statutū quo ad obligationē secundam: ideo saltem in hoc sibi obuiat seu repugnat. Constat q argumentū non valet: quia quicunq; confitetur personaliter suo proprio sacerdoti, ipse tollit statutum quo ad obligationē secundā: & tamen talis nec in hoc nec in aliquo alio obuiat statuto nec eius obligationi, sed ipsam statutum perficit, & eius obligationem secundam soluit & implet. Sed ad hunc intellectū dico, q capitulū Dudum prædicto statuto nec obuiat neq; repugnat. Quæ est forma & modus vnus, q quē statutū pficitur & impletur. Dominus vero Armachanus aliter intelligit, scil. q per illud capitulū non est modus hec forma quo illud statutum impletur: & ideo reputat, q si confessus fratri eadem peccata iterum confiteretur, tunc capitulum Dudum, & fratrum priuilegia tollunt statutum prædictum quo ad vtrumq; debitū supradictum. Quod non est verum: & ideo arguitur ad propositum breuiter sic. Nulla licentia proprii sacerdotis suo Parochiano concessa, quod alienus sacerdos potest eundem audire in confessione & absoluere vice sua obuiat vel repugnat statuto concilii generalis. Alioquin statutum sibiipsi repugnaret: & iam aduersarius concedit hanc maiorem. Sed omnis licentia audiendi confessiones & confessos absoluendi per capitulum Dudum, fratribus concessa est huiusmodi licentia. Igitur nec talis licentia nec capitulum Dudum, quod huiusmodi licentiam concedit, eidem statuto obuiat nec repugnat. pugnat. Minor probatur: quia q; huiusmodi licentia sit licetia proprii sacerdotis, patet per improbationem secundi erroris capituli immediate praecedentis. Et quod est concessa Parochianis, q; possint fratribus confiteri; patet per improbationem tertii erroris eiusdem capituli. Et quod fratres virtute illius licentiae absoluunt vice proprii sacerdotis, patet ex prima conclusione tertii capituli. Cum igitur nihil impugnans hoc vel istorum aliquid in praedicto capitulo contineatur, sequitur quod capitulum Dudum, praefato statuto non obuiat nec repugnat.
units.tr: It remains, then, to refer to the same statute the chapter Dudum, the chapter Vas electionis, and the privileges of the friars which in this matter have today been referred to the chapter Dudum. I will therefore show that the chapter Dudum neither opposes nor conflicts with the aforesaid statute. Yet because in this I seem to agree with my opponent, so that we do not labour under an ambiguity, it must be understood that from the statute of the general council arise two obligations, or debts, of confessing. The first is general, perpetual and abiding; the second is special or particular, passing and fleeting. The first is that by which everyone, whether he confesses or not, remains always bound by virtue of the statute to make confession once a year. With this it is consistent that this sinner, for this year, is not bound to confess the sins he has committed, because perhaps he has lawfully confessed them already. The second is that by which someone is bound, in particular, concerning these sins specifically pointed out, to confess them at this particular time or year. This obligation is passing and fleeting, because once this particular obligation is discharged he is no longer bound by that same obligation, although he always remains bound by the first. Otherwise, if after the particular determined obligation had been discharged he remained bound in general, it would follow that someone who had confessed according to the form of the statute, however often he sinned afterwards, would not be bound by virtue of the statute to confess again. A clear example of this is an annual rent, which someone is bound to pay; I pass over it since it is well known. Another example may be this: the universal proposition "every man is an animal" is, according to the Philosopher, of perpetual truth, because it is necessary, whereas each singular instance of it is contingent, and its truth passes away together with its existence. To the point: I say that the chapter Dudum neither opposes nor conflicts with the statute of the general council, "Every one of either sex," either as to the first obligation or as to the second. I do grant, however, that it frequently removes the second obligation, but it does not remove the first. And if it is argued that this chapter removes the statute as to the second obligation, and so at least in this respect opposes or conflicts with it, that argument is plainly invalid: for whoever confesses personally to his own priest removes the statute as to the second obligation, and yet such a person neither in this nor in any other respect opposes the statute or its obligation, but rather fulfils the statute, and discharges and completes its second obligation. But in this sense I say that the chapter Dudum neither opposes nor conflicts with the aforesaid statute; rather it is one form and mode by which the statute is fulfilled and completed. The lord Archbishop of Armagh, however, understands it otherwise, namely that by that chapter this form is not a mode by which that statute is fulfilled; and therefore he holds that if someone who has confessed to a friar confesses the same sins again, then the chapter Dudum and the privileges of the friars remove the aforesaid statute as to both of the obligations mentioned above. This is not true; and therefore the argument to the point is briefly this. No licence granted by one's own priest to his parishioner, that another priest may hear him in confession and absolve him in his place, opposes or conflicts with the statute of the general council. Otherwise the statute would conflict with itself; and my opponent already concedes this major premise. But every licence to hear confessions and absolve the confessed, granted to the friars by the chapter Dudum, is a licence of this kind. Therefore neither such a licence nor the chapter Dudum, which grants such a licence, opposes or conflicts with the same statute. The minor is proved as follows: that this licence is the licence of one's own priest is evident from the refutation of the second error of the immediately preceding chapter; and that it is granted to parishioners, so that they may confess to the friars, is evident from the refutation of the third error of the same chapter; and that the friars, by virtue of that licence, absolve in place of the proper priest is evident from the first conclusion of the third chapter. Since, then, nothing opposing this or any of these points is contained in the aforesaid chapter, it follows that the chapter Dudum does not oppose or conflict with the aforesaid statute.

units.la: Amplius, capitulum Dudum, in concilio generali Lugdunensi fuit eodem sacro instante & approbante concilio innouatum, sicut patet ex eiusdem decretalis principio, in quo haec licentia audiendi confessiones & confessos absoluendi, quam fratres modo habent, secundum formam in eodem expressam fuit prouide ordinata. Igitur tota ecclesia in illam licentiam pro se ac singulis personis, quarum interest, consensit vere vel interpretatiue, tacite vel expresse. Et per consequens Parochiales presbyteri seu curati consenserunt, vel saltem ecclesia per procuratores sufficientes eosdem repraesentans vere consensit & concessit licentiam supradictam, quam nec ipsi nec eorum successores sine consensu Domini Papae vnquam poterant postea nec adhuc poterunt reuocare. Igitur haec licentia est non solum per Papam, archiepiscopos & episcopos concessa: sed etiam per Parochiales presbyteros & curatos; & ob hoc fratres praesentantur & per eos admittuntur nomine eorundem. Quare sequitur, quod haec licentia non aliter statuto concilii generalis obuiat vel repugnat, quam si fratres essent praesentati & admissi a presbyteris Parochialibus seu curatis.
units.tr: Furthermore, the chapter Dudum was renewed at the general council of Lyons, with the same holy council present and approving, as is clear from the opening of that same decretal, in which this licence to hear confessions and absolve the confessed, which the friars now have, was providently ordained in the form there expressed. Therefore the whole Church consented, truly or by interpretation, tacitly or expressly, to that licence on its own behalf and on behalf of each of the persons concerned.
