And consequently the parish priests or curates consented, or at least the Church, representing them through sufficient proxies, truly consented and granted the aforesaid licence, which neither they nor their successors could ever afterwards revoke, nor can they now, without the consent of the lord Pope. Therefore this licence has been granted not only by the Pope, archbishops and bishops, but also by the parish priests and curates; and for this reason the friars are presented and admitted by them in their name. Hence it follows that this licence opposes or conflicts with the statute of the general council in no other way than if the friars had been presented and admitted by the parish priests or curates.

units.la: Amplius, statutum concilii generalis solum obligat Parochianos disiunctiue: scilicet ad confitendum semel in anno, proprio sacerdoti vel alteri de licentia proprii sacerdotis. Igitur hanc obligationem plene persoluens, p aliquo tempore, p eodem tempore statuto non obuiat vel repugnat. Sed confessus fratri iuxta formam capituli Dudum, superius memorati plene persoluit obligationem statuti: quia, sicut dictum est, confessus est habenti licentia cuiusuis proprii sacerdotis. E. talis statuto non obuiat. Praeterea statutum concilii generalis solum obligat Parochianos ad confessionem, quae coexigit beneficium vere absolutionis & susceptionem satisfactionis: sicut patuit in tertia conclusione tertii capituli supradicti. Sed constat quod capitulum Dudum concedit fratribus licentia conferendi vbiq; absolutionem & imponendi debitam satisfactionem. Igitur confessus fratri iuxta cap. Dudum, alteri statuto non obuiat vel repugnat. Et per consequens cap. Dudum, eidem statuto non repugnat.
units.tr: Furthermore, the statute of the general council obliges parishioners only disjunctively: namely, to confess once a year either to their own priest or to another with the licence of their own priest. Therefore someone who fully discharges this obligation, at whatever time, does not at that same time oppose or conflict with the statute. But a parishioner who has confessed to a friar according to the form of the chapter Dudum mentioned above has fully discharged the obligation of the statute, because, as has been said, he has confessed to one who has the licence of any proper priest. Therefore such a person does not oppose the statute. Moreover, the statute of the general council obliges parishioners only to a confession which carries with it the benefit of true absolution and the receiving of satisfaction, as was shown in the third conclusion of the third chapter above. But it is clear that the chapter Dudum grants the friars licence to confer absolution everywhere and to impose due satisfaction. Therefore a parishioner who has confessed to a friar according to the chapter Dudum does not oppose or conflict with the same statute. And consequently the chapter Dudum does not conflict with the same statute.

units.la: Amplius, circumscripta omni obligatione, qua quis obligatur per dictum statutum Parochianus confessus fratri iuxta formam capituli Dudum, satisfaceret obligationi, per quam ex suo peccato actuali factus est debitor sacramenti poenitentiae in hac parte, scil. quantum ad confessionem, sed constat, q; p praefatu statutu non plus debet, vel obligatur in hac parte q; si remoto vel circumscripto statuto esset tantum debitor sacramenti poenitentiae post solam limitationem temporis, infra quod tenetur confiteri. Igitur confessus fratri iuxta formam capituli Dudum, & seruata temporis limitatione in statuto concilii generalis satisfecit tam debito sacramenti poenitentiae quam debito statuti concilii generalis: cui per consequens praefatum capit. Dudum, nec obuiat nec repugnat. Praeterea secunda pars est dispensatoria super praecepto primae partis. Igitur nullus implens secundam partem statuti praefato statuto obuiat vel repugnat. Sed constat quod confessi fratribus implent secundam partem statuti omnis utriusque, sicut supra probatum fuit. Igitur tales eidem statuto non obuiant nec repugnant. Ex opposito itaq; praedictae conclusionis sequuntur multa erronea & blasphemosa, sicut postea deducetur. Patet tamen euidenter ex praedictis, quod cap. Dudum, seu fratrum priuilegia statuto Omnis utriusq; sexus, nullo modo obuiant nec repugnant: sed eam perficiunt & adimplent, & concordant optime cum eodem. Quapropter ex praedictis sequitur, quod confessi fratribus praedictis non plus tenentur peccata iterum confiteri, quam si illa fuissent confessi proprio sacerdoti, sicut post plenius deducetur. Et hoc est quod in cap. Vae electionis diffinitur: cuius oppositum ibidem velut erroneum reprobatur. Veruntamen quia iste Dominus Reuerendus dicit, quod intellectus fratrum de ista constitutione est erroneus & non sanus: ideo consequenter ostendam, q; intellectus fratrū de ista constitutione est catholicus & salubris, vt ex hoc pateat, q; ista constitutio a praedictis capitulis non discordat. Intellectus igitur fratrum de hac constitutione Vae electionis non est, quod scil. confessi fratribus habentibus licentiam generalem audiendi confessiones & confessos absoluendi &c. nullo casu tenentur eadem peccata iterum confiteri, sicut eis imponit iste Dominus sine causa. Sed confessi fratribus habentibus licentia generale non magis tenentur eadem peccata iterum confiteri, q; si alias ipsa confessi fuerint proprio sacerdoti; hoc est, in nullo casu tenentur iterum ea confiteri, quin in eodem casu vel consimili tenerentur eadem iterum confiteri, quamuis ea prius fuissent confessi proprio sacerdoti. Et q; iste intellectus sit sanus & catholicus, patet sic: quia negatiua supradicta in forma, qua praescribitur, est diffinita catholica atq; vera. Igitur illa pro catholica est tenenda.
units.tr: Furthermore, setting aside every obligation by which someone is bound by the said statute, a parishioner who has confessed to a friar according to the form of the chapter Dudum would satisfy the obligation by which, through his actual sin, he has become a debtor of the sacrament of penance in this respect, namely as regards confession. But it is clear that by the aforesaid statute he owes or is bound in this respect no more than he would be if, with the statute removed or set aside, he were a debtor of the sacrament of penance only subject to the limit of time within which he is bound to confess. Therefore a parishioner who has confessed to a friar according to the form of the chapter Dudum, and has kept the time limit set in the statute of the general council, has satisfied both the debt of the sacrament of penance and the debt of the statute of the general council; and consequently the aforesaid chapter Dudum neither opposes nor conflicts with it. Furthermore, the second part is dispensatory with respect to the precept of the first part. Therefore no one who fulfils the second part of the statute opposes or conflicts with the aforesaid statute. But it is clear that those who confess to the friars fulfil the second part of the statute "Every one of either sex," as was proved above. Therefore such persons neither oppose nor conflict with that statute. From the opposite of the aforesaid conclusion, then, many erroneous and blasphemous consequences follow, as will be shown later. It is nevertheless evident from what has been said that the chapter Dudum, or the privileges of the friars, in no way oppose or conflict with the statute "Every one of either sex," but fulfil and complete it, and agree very well with it. Wherefore it follows from the foregoing that those who have confessed to the aforesaid friars are not bound to confess the same sins again any more than if they had confessed them to their own priest, as will be set out more fully later. And this is what is defined in the chapter Vae electionis, whose opposite is there rejected as erroneous. Yet because this reverend lord says that the friars' understanding of this constitution is erroneous and unsound, I shall therefore go on to show that the friars' understanding of this constitution is catholic and wholesome, so that it may be plain that this constitution does not disagree with the aforesaid chapters. The friars' understanding of this constitution of Vae electionis is therefore not that those who have confessed to friars having a general licence to hear confessions and absolve the confessed, etc., are in no case bound to confess the same sins again, as this lord imposes on them without cause. Rather, those who have confessed to friars having a general licence are no more bound to confess the same sins again than if they had confessed them to their own priest; that is, they are in no case bound to confess them again unless in the same or a similar case they would be bound to confess the same sins again even though they had first confessed them to their own priest. And that this understanding is sound and catholic is shown thus: the aforesaid negative proposition, in the form in which it is laid down, is a catholic and true definition. Therefore it is to be held as catholic.

units.la: Amplius, prius sacerdos non magis tenetur audire confessiones eorundem peccatorum sui parochiani, qui prius confessus fuit fratri habenti licentiam generalem &c. q; si ideo Parochianus fuisset eadem alias confessus proprio sacerdoti. Igitur Parochianus confessus fratri huiusmodi magis tenetur eadem peccata iterum confiteri, quam si illa confessus fuisset proprio sacerdoti. Argumentum & assumptum patet ex secunda suppositione secundi capituli praecedentis.
units.tr: Further, a parish priest is no more bound to hear the confessions of his parishioner who has previously confessed the same sins to a friar holding a general licence, etc., than if that parishioner had confessed those sins to his own priest. Therefore a parishioner who has confessed to such a friar is more bound to confess those same sins again than if he had confessed them to his own priest. The argument and the minor premise are clear from the second supposition of the second chapter above.

units.la: Amplius, confessus huiusmodi fratri est confessus eidem vice proprii sacerdotis. Igitur confessus non magis tenetur eadem peccata iterum confiteri, quam si fuisset illa confessus proprio sacerdoti. Assumptum patet ex tertia suppositione secundi capituli & secunda conclusione tertii capituli & ex improbatione secundi erroris capituli immediate praecedentis.
units.tr: Further, one who has confessed to such a friar has confessed to him in place of his own priest. Therefore he is no more bound to confess the same sins again than if he had confessed them to his own priest. The minor premise is clear from the third supposition of the second chapter, from the second conclusion of the third chapter, and from the refutation of the second error in the chapter immediately preceding.

units.la: Amplius, confessus huiusmodi Fratri satisfecit statuto concilii Generalis omnibus vtrinsq; Igitur confessus eidem non magis tenetur eadem peccata iterum confiteri, quam si illa fuisset confessus proprio sacerdoti. Assumptum patet ex quarta suppositione secundi capituli & prima conclusione tertii & ex correlario huius conclusionis cum praecedente coclusione huius capituli cum suis rationibus.
units.tr: Further, one who has confessed to such a friar has satisfied the statute of the General Council Omnis, for all parties. Therefore one who has confessed to him is no more bound to confess the same sins again than if he had confessed them to his own priest. The minor premise is clear from the fourth supposition of the second chapter, from the first conclusion of the third chapter, and from the corollary of this conclusion, together with the preceding conclusion of this chapter and its arguments.

units.la: Item, confessus huiusmodi Fratri & absolutus ab eodem satisfecit debito sacramenti poenitentiae & debito praecepti Ecclesiae. Igitur huiusmodi Fratri confessus & absolutus ab eodem non magis tenetur iterum confiteri, quam si ab eodem fuisset confessus proprio sacerdoti. Assumptum patet ex sexta suppositione secundi capituli & ex quinta conclusione tertii capituli & eiusdem probationibus.
units.tr: Likewise, one who has confessed to such a friar and been absolved by him has satisfied the obligation of the sacrament of penance and the obligation of the Church's precept. Therefore one who has confessed to such a friar and been absolved by him is no more bound to confess again than if he had confessed to his own priest and been absolved by him. The minor premise is clear from the sixth supposition of the second chapter, from the fifth conclusion of the third chapter, and from the proofs of the same.

units.la: Amplius, confessus huiusmodi Fratri & absolutus ab eodem est sibi sacramentaliter & iudicialiter in foro poenitentiae confessus. Igitur huiusmodi Fratri sic confessus non magis debet vel tenetur eadem peccata iterum confiteri, quam si illa fuisset sacramentaliter confessus proprio sacerdoti. Assumptum patet ex ratione distinctionis quartae primi capituli cum suis probationibus & ex tertia conclusione tertii capituli cum suis probationibus vniuersis. Item, omnia argumenta immediate facta in hoc capitulo istam veritatem probant, lucide & deductiue, & in sequenti capitulo probabitur satis clare.
units.tr: Further, one who has confessed to such a friar and been absolved by him has confessed to him sacramentally and judicially, in the forum of penance. Therefore one who has so confessed to such a friar ought not, and is not bound, to confess the same sins again any more than if he had confessed them sacramentally to his own priest. The minor premise is clear from the reasoning of the fourth distinction of the first chapter with its proofs, and from the third conclusion of the third chapter with all its proofs. Likewise, all the arguments set out immediately in this chapter prove this truth clearly and by deduction, and the following chapter will prove it quite plainly.

units.la: Quantum ad affirmationem supradictam, scil. quod confessi Fratribus habentibus licentiam generalem audiendi confessiones &c. tenentur eadem peccata praeconfessa iterum confiteri, patet quod illa sit erronea & damnata in praedicta constitutione. Nam illud quod negatur in propositione negativa diffinita, debet secundum idem & ad idem & similiter & in eodem tempore affirmari in propositione affirmativa damnata vel saltem quaelibet propositio affirmativa tali negativae sic repugnans necessario secundum idem & ad idem &c. est damnata. Igitur illa affirmativa supradicta aut illa quae ponitur in praedicta constitutione ad intellectum istius necessario est damnata. Et confirmatur istud ex hoc quod dicitur in constitutione in fine, quod Papa damnat illos errores Ioannis de Poliaco. Ibidem enim Dominus Papa dicit sic: Omnes praedictos articulos & quemlibet illorum tanquam erroneos ac a sacra doctrina devios auctoritate Apostolica damnamus & reprobamus de fratrum concilio praedictorum, doctrinam contrariam ipsis veram esse & catholicam asserentes cum illi qui praedictis Fratribus confitentur non magis tenentur &c. intendit exprimere in suo opposito intellectum, ad quem vult aliam a forma damnari. Patet igitur quod intellectus Fratrum de ista constitutione catholicus est & sanctus, & quod hoc capitulum ab aliis praedictis capitulis non discordat, cum illud sit factum ad concordiam eorundem.
units.tr: As to the above assertion, namely that those who have confessed to Friars holding a general licence to hear confessions, etc., are bound to confess again the sins previously confessed, it is plain that this assertion is erroneous and condemned in the aforesaid constitution. For what is denied in a definite negative proposition must, according to the same respect, to the same thing, in the same manner and at the same time, be affirmed in a condemned affirmative proposition; or at least any affirmative proposition so repugnant to that negative, in the same respect and to the same thing, etc., is necessarily condemned. Therefore the above affirmative, or the one put forward in the aforesaid constitution as its sense, is necessarily condemned. This is confirmed by what the constitution says at the end, that the Pope condemns the errors of John of Poliacum. For there the Lord Pope says thus: We condemn and reprove all the aforesaid articles and each of them, as erroneous and deviating from sacred doctrine, by Apostolic authority, with the advice of the aforesaid Friars, asserting the doctrine contrary to them to be true and Catholic, since those who confess to the aforesaid Friars are no more bound, etc. He intends to express in its opposite the sense which he wishes to be condemned in another form. It is therefore plain that the Friars' understanding of this constitution is Catholic and sound, and that this chapter does not disagree with the other chapters mentioned, since it was written to bring them into agreement.

units.la: Verum contra ista arguit iste Dominus Reuerendus multipliciter. Primo sic: haec negativa, nulli confessi Fratribus habentibus licentiam generalem tenentur eadem peccata confiteri suo proprio sacerdoti, ex quo est falsa & contingens, non possit diffiniri tanquam catholica & fidei concernens, quae fidei catholicae est necessaria in omni suo articulo. Et ideo si ista esset diffinita diffinitio super illam facta non teneret. Similiter affirmativa isti contraria non potuit damnari tanquam erronea, cum sit vera & contingens, & si damnaretur, illa damnatio non teneret. Ad hoc adducit argumentum Domini Papae Iohannis 22. re. Quia vir reprobus. Item, confessus Fratri potest obligari legitime ad iterum confitendum. Igitur non est contra fidem credere, quod confessus Fratri teneatur iterum confiteri. Assumptum patet de his qui voluerunt iterum confiteri, & quibus praeceptum est vel iniunctum in poenitentia iterum eadem peccata confiteri, vel qui habent conscientiam quod tenentur iterum confiteri & in casibus aliis multis. Item, demonstratur aliquibus in casibus proximi argumenti argumentur sic. Isti tenentur confiteri omnia peccata sua totius anni suo proprio sacerdoti, & isti sunt confessi Fratribus habentibus generalem licentiam &c. Igitur confessi Fratribus habentibus generale licentiam tenentur eadem iterum peccata confiteri proprio sacerdoti suo. Haec conclusio secundum fratres est haeretica, & maior est catholica non repugnans. Igitur minor quae est fratrum, est haeretica. Item, ponatur quod poenitentiarius aliquis Romanae curiae iniungat alicui confesso, quod omnia peccata sua totius anni confiteatur suo parochiali Presbytero: qui parochianus rediens confiteatur Fratri omnia tali peccata, & quaero nunquid tenetur ad poenitentiam sibi iniunctam a Papa vel no? Si non, igitur evacuatur auctoritas Papae per liberum factum Fratrum: quod affirmare videtur haereticum. Similiter habeat talis conscientiam, quam non potest deponere, quod teneatur poenitentiam iniunctam implere. Tunc enim dicere, quod non teneatur talem conscientiam sequi, etiam videtur erroneum. Relinquitur igitur, quod tenetur poenitentiam iniunctam implere, ne eo ipso fiat haereticus.
units.tr: But this Reverend Lord argues against these points in many ways. First thus: this negative proposition, that none of those who have confessed to Friars holding a general licence are bound to confess the same sins to their own priest, since it is false and contingent, cannot be defined as Catholic and pertaining to faith, whereas whatever is necessary to the Catholic faith is necessary in every one of its articles. And therefore, if this were defined, the definition made on it would not hold. Likewise the affirmative contrary to it could not be condemned as erroneous, since it is true and contingent, and if it were condemned, that condemnation would not hold. To this he adduces the argument of Pope John XXII, Re: Quia vir reprobus. Again, one who has confessed to a Friar can be lawfully obliged to confess again. Therefore it is not contrary to the faith to believe that one who has confessed to a Friar is bound to confess again. The minor premise is clear from those who wished to confess again, and to whom it has been commanded, or imposed as a penance, to confess the same sins again, or who have a conscience that they are bound to confess again, and from many other cases. Again, it is shown in some cases of the preceding argument, which argues thus: those who are bound to confess all their sins of the whole year to their own priest are those who have confessed to Friars holding a general licence, etc. Therefore those who have confessed to Friars holding a general licence are bound to confess the same sins again to their own priest. This conclusion, according to the Friars, is heretical, and the major premise is Catholic and not repugnant. Therefore the minor premise, which belongs to the Friars, is heretical. Again, suppose that some penitentiary of the Roman Curia enjoins on someone who has confessed that he should confess all his sins of the whole year to his parish priest; and that this parishioner, returning, confesses such sins to a Friar. I ask whether he is bound to the penance enjoined on him by the Pope or not? If not, then the Pope's authority is nullified by the free act of the Friars, which seems to be heretical to affirm. Likewise, suppose such a man has a conscience which he cannot put aside, that he is bound to fulfil the penance enjoined. Then to say that he is not bound to follow such a conscience also seems erroneous. It remains, therefore, that he is bound to fulfil the penance enjoined, lest by that very fact he become a heretic.

units.la: Item, si praedicta propositio affirmativa sit haeretica. Aut igitur surgit ista haeresis ex hoc, quod confessio eorundem peccatorum non est iterabilis. Aut quia non esset debita & obligata. Aut quia non potest esse debita, quod fiat suo proprio sacerdoti. Tertium poni non potest, & ponentes primum & secundum damnant Dominum Papam Innocentium quartum, Dominum Papam Martinum quintum, Dominum Benedictum undecimum, Clementem octavum, Dominum Innocentium sextum iam praesentem, qui statuerunt vel praeceperunt diffinitiuam illa in sua forma. Et sic Hostiensem & Ioannem Monachum, Cardinalem Bernhardum, Glossatores & Doctores eximios, Alexandrum de Halis, Henricum de Gandavo, Fratrem Raymundum, Fratrem Bonaventuram, imo sanctam Ecclesiam catholicam, quae praecepit in certis casibus fieri iterationem confessionis eorundem peccatorum. Item, quod intellectus Fratrum de hac constitutione vas electionis sit erroneus, patet: quia Fratres ordinum mendicantium asserunt denunciationes in praedicta constitutione contentas esse veras & catholicas, & assertiones illis contrarias esse reprobas & erroneas, forma verborum servata, nihil addito nihilq; subtracto: sicut patet in quadam petitione Fratrum data Dominis Cardinalibus per procuratorem, & multos nostros Ordinum prædicatorum. Cum igitur articulus constitutionis sensus varios habeat: quorum vnus est verus, & alter est falsus: & suus sensus sit verus, & sensus Fratrum falsus: sequitur quod Fratres errant, & non ipse. Item, Fratres multo magis debent concedere se ex fide tenere cunctas denunciationes Christi in sancto Euangelio contentas, seruata forma, nihil addito nihilq; subtracto, quam denunciationes in prædicta constitutione contentas. Et per consequens habent concedere se ex fide tenere nullo addito, nulloque subtracto, illud Salvatoris, mea doctrina non est mea. Et illud: Ego non ascendam ad diem festum hunc. Et illud: Non mea, sed tua voluntas fiat: quæ nisi aliquid addatur in sensu, veritatem non habent. Ad ista argumenta potest breuiter responderi, scilicet quod quamuis videantur concludere, quod confessus Fratri teneatur iterum confiteri proprio sacerdoti: quia tamen non probant, quod teneantur confiteri ex vi statuti concilii Generalis Omnis, non probant quod intendunt. Nam iste Dominus intendit affirmare, confessi Fratribus teneantur eadem peccata iterum confiteri proprio sacerdoti: quia sunt ad hoc obligati ex statuto: & per consequens secundum eum ex vi statuti tenentur iterum confiteri. Sed argumenta hoc non concludunt: quia positis casibus, ex quibus iste Dominus arguit æqualiter tenentur vel non tenentur iterum confiteri statuto remoto & destructo: sicut eodem posito & firmato. Aliter etiam ad illa & similia potest dici, quod Fratres non negant, quod confessi non solum Fratribus, sed Papæ & Episcopis & parochialibus Presbyteris seu curatis teneantur eadem peccata iterum confiteri in multis casibus, qui possunt poni: sed negant quod confessi Fratribus plus teneantur eadem peccata iterum confiteri, vel in aliis casibus quam in illis in quibus vel eorum similibus tenentur iterum confiteri, etiam si ea fuissent confessi proprio sacerdoti. Constat autem quod in casibus argumentorum præmissorum & eorum similibus si parochiani fuissent confessi proprio sacerdoti cuicunque, ipsi æque tenerentur iterum confiteri, sicut in casibus præmissis. Quare argumenta contra constitutionis intentionem & Fratrum intellectum penitus non concludunt.
units.tr: Again, if the aforesaid affirmative proposition is heretical, then this heresy arises either because the confession of the same sins is not repeatable, or because it would not be owed and obligatory, or because it cannot be owed that it be made to one's own priest. The third cannot be maintained, and those who maintain the first and second condemn Pope Innocent IV, Pope Martin V, Pope Benedict XI, Clement VIII, and Pope Innocent VI, who is now living, who ordained or commanded the definition in its form. And so they condemn Hostiensis and John the Monk, Cardinal Bernard, the glossators and eminent doctors, Alexander of Hales, Henry of Ghent, Friar Raymond, Friar Bonaventure, indeed the holy Catholic Church, which in certain cases has commanded that the confession of the same sins be repeated. Again, that the Friars' understanding of this constitution is erroneous, the chosen vessel, is plain: because the Friars of the mendicant orders assert that the declarations contained in the aforesaid constitution are true and Catholic, and that the assertions contrary to them are reprobate and erroneous, the form of words being kept, nothing added and nothing taken away; as is plain from a certain petition of the Friars given to the Lord Cardinals through a procurator, and from many of ours of the Orders of Preachers. Since therefore the article of the constitution has various senses, of which one is true and another false, and its sense is true while the Friars' sense is false, it follows that the Friars err, and not it. Again, the Friars ought much more to concede that they hold by faith all the declarations of Christ contained in the holy Gospel, the form being kept, nothing added and nothing taken away, than the declarations contained in the aforesaid constitution. And consequently they must concede that they hold by faith, with nothing added and nothing taken away, that saying of the Saviour, My doctrine is not mine (John 7.16). And that: I go not up unto this feast (John 7.8). And that: Not my will, but thine, be done (Luke 22.42). Unless something is added to their sense, these have no truth. To these arguments a brief reply can be made: although they seem to conclude that one who has confessed to a Friar is bound to confess again to his own priest, yet because they do not prove that they are bound to confess by virtue of the statute of the General Council Omnis, they do not prove what they intend. For this Lord intends to affirm that those who have confessed to Friars are bound to confess the same sins again to their own priest, because they are obliged to do so by the statute; and consequently, in his view, by virtue of the statute they are bound to confess again. But the arguments do not conclude this, because, with the cases posited, from which this Lord argues, they are equally bound or not bound to confess again whether the statute is removed and destroyed or whether it is posited and confirmed. Otherwise also, to those and similar arguments it can be said that the Friars do not deny that those who have confessed not only to Friars but to the Pope, the bishops and the parish priests or curates are bound to confess the same sins again in many cases that can be posited; but they deny that those who have confessed to Friars are bound to confess the same sins again more, or in other cases, than in those in which they, or cases like them, are bound to confess again, even if they had confessed to their own priest. Now it is agreed that in the cases of the foregoing arguments, and similar ones, if the parishioners had confessed to their own priest, whoever he was, they would be bound to confess again just as in the cases stated. Wherefore the arguments do not at all conclude against the intention of the constitution and the Friars' understanding.

units.la: Sed hic videat fugere argumenta, respondeo ad singula. Et primo ad primum: cum dicitur quod hæc negatiua: Nulli confessi Fratribus habentibus generalem licentiam audiendi confessiones tenentur eadem peccata quæ confessi sunt iterum confiteri proprio sacerdoti; non potuit diffiniri tanquam catholica & fidem concernens id quod est contingens, vt patet. Dico quod hæc propositio, quam assumit, non est diffinita in constitutione Vas electionis, sed ista, nulli confessi Fratribus habentibus generalem licentiam magis tenentur eadem peccata eis confessa iterum confiteri, quam si fuissent ea confessa proprio sacerdoti: quæ propositio non est contingens & falsa. Quare argumentum non prohibet istam non posse diffiniri: sicut de facto diffinita est. Sed iste Dominus, salua sua reuerentia, accipit propositiones laterales & impertinentes, vt magis appareat & decipiat quam concludat. Sed frustra iacitur rete ante oculos pennatorum, Prouerb. prim. Et consimiliter dico, quod affirmatiua damnata ad sensum isti negatiuæ oppositum in affirmatiua; in illo sensu non est contingens & vera: sed in casibus, quos ponit iste Dominus, est falsa. Quare nihil prohibet ipsam damnari. Et quando dicit, quod fides catholica est necessaria in omni suo articulo, si intelligatur de necessario, prout distinguit contra contingens & impossibile, vt videtur fieri in proposito: quia aliquin argumentum æque esset contra eum, sicut contra Fratres: tunc non dubium, quin illud assumptum sit hæreticum. Generale enim iudicium viuorum & mortuorum: & generalis resurrectio mortuorum, necesse sic necessaria necessitate absoluta. Similiter incarnatio, passio, resurrectio, quas sancti patres antiqui testamenti credebant esse futuras, non fuerunt necessariæ, sed contingentes. Nec est ad propositum quod adducit pro se de Domino Iohanne & suo libello, Quoniam vir reprobus: quia ille loquitur de diffinitione facta super propositione impossibili. Iste autem Dominus loquitur de diffinitione facta super propositione contingente, vt dicit. Quare argumentum non valet pro suo proposito concludendo. Ad secundum, cum arguitur: Confessus Fratri potest legitime obligari ad iterum confitendum eadem peccata proprio sacerdoti: igitur non est contra fidem credere, quod confessi Fratribus teneantur iterum confiteri. Dico quod accipiendo semper propositionem in sensu prædicto, scilicet quod confessus Fratri &c. plus potest legitime obligari: vel potest obligari in casibus, in quibus vel eorum similibus confessus proprio sacerdoti, non potest ad hoc legitime obligari. Assumptum est falsum, sicut supradictum est. Et similiter argumentum non valet: quia conclusio non plus sequitur ex præmissis, quam si diceretur sic. Virgo non obligata castitati potest legitime obligari perpetuæ castitati. Igitur non est contra fidem credere, quod virgo non obligata castitati tenetur ad perpetuam castitatem: quia antecedens est verum, & consequens falsum, dicente Apostolo: quod si virgo nupserit non peccauit, i. ad Corinth. 6. Similiter aliud exemplum dicendum est. Non enim sequitur, potest esse quod sacerdos dicens verba consecrationis cum intentione debita consecrandi, non consecrat. Ergo non est contra fidem credere, quod huiusmodi sacerdos non consecrat: quia dubium, quod antecedens sit verum saltem de potentia Dei, quæ non est obligata sacramentis: & per consequens est falsum. Similiter aliud exemplum est. Non enim sequitur, mulier obligata viro potest esse soluta legitime a viri potestate: ergo non est contra fidem credere, quod mulier obligata viro sit soluta a viri potestate: quia antecedens est verum, & consequens contra Apostolum vbi supra. Nec argumentum prædictum potest tenere, nisi per hoc medium non est contra fidem aliquid credere, quod potest esse verum, quod, sicut notum est, satis est erroneum. Ad tertium argumentum dico, quod conclusio in sensu, in quo damnatur, non sequitur ex præmissis. Ideo nihil ad propositum. Ad quartum cum ponitur, quod poenitentiarius curiae Romanae iniungat alicui sibi confesso, quod omnia peccata sua confiteatur proprio sacerdoti: & quod talis rediens confiteatur ea Fratri: & quaeritur, nunquid talis teneatur iterum ea confiteri suo proprio sacerdoti. Respondeo: ponatur quod idem poenitentiarius iniungat alteri confesso, quod confiteatur alicui certo Fratri: & quod ille rediens confiteatur suo proprio sacerdoti. Quaeritur igitur, nunquid talis teneatur eadem confessa sacerdoti proprio, iterum illi Fratri confiteri. In quibus casibus dico, quod uterq; iterum confiteri tenetur: & non plus nec minus quam alius caeteris omnibus paribus. Et hoc ex non sequitur, quod confessus Fratri plus vel magis teneatur iterum confiteri, quam si in altero casu confessus fuisset proprio sacerdoti. Quare argumentum non procedit contra intellectum constitutionis vel Fratrum. Ad quintum dico, quod haeresis illa nec sunt ex prima causa, nec secunda, nec tertia. Et ideo argumentum procedit ab insufficienti diuisione. Sed ex hoc surgit, quod confessio eorundem peccatorum facta Fratri, non magis est iterabilis, quam confessio facta sacerdoti, caeteris paribus: nec iteratio eorundem peccatorum Fratri confessorum plus potest venire sub praecepto, quam potest iteratio confessionis peccatorum sacerdoti proprio confessorum: nec plus potest venire sub praecepto, quod fiat proprio sacerdoti, quam quod fiat Fratri. Verum tamen qualiter eorum confessio est iterabilis & qualiter non, quomodo etiam potest venire sub praecepto & quomodo non, postea dicetur. Et cum additur de Dominis summis Pontificibus, Cardinalibus, & Doctoribus: dico, quod nullus eorum unquam posuit praescripta, nec aliqua, ex quibus surgit error praedictus. Quare Fratres nec illos condemnant, neque eos damnatos reputant: sed velut suis temporibus fuerunt solennissimi, in omnibus venerantur. Ad sextum dico, quod petitio Fratrum, de qua in argumento fit mentio, est rationabilis catholica, & omnes denunciationes in praedicta constitutione sunt verae forma verborum seruata, nihil addito, nihilque subtracto: & quod assertiones illis contrariae quae accipiunt contrarium, hoc est oppositae, sunt reprobae & erroneae forma verborum seruata, nihil addito nihilque subtracto. Et cum infertur: igitur primus articulus est erroneus eadem forma verborum &c. Negatur assumptum: quia secundum istum Dominum primus articulus nullo addito nulloque subtracto non est oppositus alicui denunciationi eiusdem constitutionis. Modo solum Fratres loquebantur de assertionibus oppositis denunciationibus seu diffinitionibus eiusdem constitutionis. Quare non sequitur conclusio, quam intendit. Verum quia ille articulus est damnatus, sicut ibi iacet scriptus sub forma verborum eadem nullo addito nulloque subtracto. Ideo dico aliter: scilicet quod ille articulus seruata forma verborum, nullo addito &c. est reprobus & erroneus. Et ideo quando dicitur in illo argumento, quod ille articulus habet sensus varios, quorum unus est verus & alter falsus. Dico, nihil prohibet eundem articulum esse damnatum seruata tali forma verborum: & etiam eundem expressum sub uno intellectu esse damnatum & expressum sub alio catholicum. Quis enim dubitat hanc esse haeresim pessimam: filius in diuinis non est genitus de patre vel de substantia patris, & tamen ad hunc intellectum filius non est genitus de patre vel de substantia patris per decisionem, sed per communicationem substantiae, hoc est ita catholicum quod eius oppositum sit haereticum. Et ideo si arguatur, sicut arguit Dominus iste, sic: Ista propositio seruata forma verborum nullo addito nulloque subtracto est falsa vel damnata: igitur qualitercunque mutata forma verborum ipsa non est damnata. Argumentum nihil valet, sicut patet in exemplo supradicto. Et ideo quando Fratres in petitione posuerunt ista verba, satis sciebant illam logicam non valere. Ad ultimum de denunciationibus Euangelii, dico quod seruata forma verborum &c. sub qua Ecclesia nobis tradidit illas, illae sunt concedendae & catholicae. Et quando dicitur, veritatem non habent, nisi aliquid addatur in sensu: Non dubium, quin priusquam aliquid adderetur in sensu illis propositionibus eas esse vel fuisse veras: sed tantum propositionum veritatem declarat illud quod additur. Unde dico, quod illa verba sub forma, sub qua sunt tradita Ecclesiae, vera sunt, & oppositum dicere est erroneum. Non nego tamen, quod illa verba aliquo addito non solum in sensu, sed etiam ad formam verborum vera essent. Sed nunquid propositio haeretica fit concedenda catholica propter verum sensum, quem potest habere: vel propositio catholica eadem forma seruata sit censenda haeretica propter sensum falsum quem potest habere: iudicet vestra reuerentia: quia tunc circa fidem peribunt omnes Ecclesiae sanctiones: & licebit cuicunque dicere quod libebit. In proposito tamen nostro iste Dominus, salua sua reuerentia non solum asserit damnata in forma, qua damnantur, sed etiam in sensu in quo damnantur, & negat diffinita non solum in forma sua, sed in sensu quo sunt ab Ecclesia diffinita, sicut in sequenti capitulo plus patebit.
units.tr: But here let him see that the arguments are fleeing; I will answer each one. And first, to the first: when it is said that this negative proposition, "No one confessed to the Friars who have a general licence to hear confessions is bound to confess again to his own priest the same sins which he has confessed," could not be defined as Catholic and concerning faith, because it concerns what is contingent, as is evident: I say that this proposition, which he assumes, is not what is defined in the constitution Vas electionis; rather, the proposition defined is this: "Those confessed to Friars who have a general licence are more bound to confess again the same sins confessed to them, than if they had confessed those sins to their own priest." That proposition is not contingent and is false. Therefore the argument does not prevent that proposition from being defined, just as it has in fact been defined. But this Lord, with all due respect, takes side propositions that are irrelevant, so that they may appear and deceive rather than conclude. But "in vain is the net spread before the eyes of the winged creatures" (Prov. 1). And similarly I say that the condemned affirmative, in the sense opposed to the negative, is not contingent and true in that sense; but in the cases which this Lord sets out, it is false. Therefore nothing prevents its being condemned. And when he says that the Catholic faith is necessary in every one of its articles, if it is understood of what is necessary, as distinguished from what is contingent and impossible, which seems to be done in the present case (since otherwise the argument would apply equally to him as to the Friars), then there is no doubt that the assumption is heretical. For the general judgement of the living and the dead, and the general resurrection of the dead, are necessary with an absolute necessity. Likewise the incarnation, passion and resurrection, which the holy fathers of the Old Testament believed were to come, were not necessary but contingent. Nor is what he adduces in support of himself, from Lord John and his little book, "Since a reprobate man," to the point: for that refers to a definition made concerning an impossible proposition. But this Lord speaks of a definition made concerning a contingent proposition, as he says. Therefore the argument does not hold, concluding for his purpose. To the second, when it is argued: "One who has confessed to a Friar can lawfully be obliged to confess again the same sins to his own priest; therefore it is not contrary to the faith to believe that those confessed to Friars are bound to confess again": I say that, always taking the proposition in the aforesaid sense, namely that one confessed to a Friar etc. can be lawfully obliged more, or can be obliged in cases in which one confessed to his own priest cannot be lawfully obliged to this, the assumption is false, as has been said above. And similarly the argument does not hold, because the conclusion does not follow from the premises any more than if it were put thus: "A virgin not bound to chastity can lawfully be bound to perpetual chastity; therefore it is not contrary to the faith to believe that a virgin not bound to chastity is bound to perpetual chastity": since the antecedent is true and the consequent false, the Apostle saying that "if a virgin marry, she has not sinned" (1 Cor. 7). A similar example must be given. For it does not follow: "It can be that a priest, saying the words of consecration with the proper intention of consecrating, does not consecrate; therefore it is not contrary to the faith to believe that such a priest does not consecrate": because it is doubtful that the antecedent is true, at least by the power of God, which is not bound to the sacraments; and consequently it is false. Likewise another example: it does not follow that "a woman bound to her husband can be lawfully freed from her husband's power; therefore it is not contrary to the faith to believe that a woman bound to her husband is freed from her husband's power": since the antecedent is true and the consequent contrary to the Apostle, as above. Nor can the aforesaid argument hold, unless through this middle term: that it is not contrary to the faith to believe something which can be true, which, as is well known, is quite erroneous. To the third argument I say that the conclusion, in the sense in which it is condemned, does not follow from the premises; therefore it is nothing to the point. To the fourth, when it is put that a penitentiary of the Roman Curia enjoins on someone confessing to him that he confess all his sins to his own priest, and that such a person, returning, confesses them to a Friar; and it is asked whether such a person is bound to confess them again to his own priest: I answer: let it be supposed that the same penitentiary enjoins on another person confessing to him that he confess to a certain Friar, and that this person, returning, confesses to his own priest. The question then is whether such a person is bound to confess the same things again to that Friar, having confessed them to his own priest. In these cases I say that each is bound to confess again, and no more nor less than the others, all other things being equal. And from this it does not follow that one confessed to a Friar is more or rather bound to confess again than if in the other case he had confessed to his own priest. Therefore the argument does not proceed against the meaning of the constitution or of the Friars. To the fifth I say that those heresies do not arise from the first cause, nor the second, nor the third. And therefore the argument proceeds from an insufficient division. But from this it follows that the confession of the same sins made to a Friar is no more repeatable than confession made to a priest, all other things being equal; nor can the repetition of the same sins confessed to a Friar come under a precept any more than the repetition of the confession of sins confessed to one's own priest; nor can it come under a precept that it be done to one's own priest any more than that it be done to a Friar. Yet how their confession is repeatable and how not, and how it can come under a precept and how not, will be said afterwards. And when it is added concerning the Lord supreme Pontiffs, Cardinals, and Doctors: I say that none of them ever laid down the prescribed things, nor any of those from which the aforesaid error arises. Therefore the Friars neither condemn them nor regard them as condemned; but as they were most solemn in their own times, they are venerated in all things. To the sixth I say that the petition of the Friars, which is mentioned in the argument, is reasonable and Catholic, and all the declarations in the aforesaid constitution are true, the form of words being preserved, nothing added and nothing taken away; and that the assertions contrary to them, which take the opposite, that is, which are opposed, are reprobate and erroneous, the form of words being preserved, nothing added and nothing taken away. And when it is inferred: "therefore the first article is erroneous in the same form of words etc.": the assumption is denied, because according to this Lord the first article, with nothing added and nothing taken away, is not opposed to any declaration of the same constitution. Now the Friars spoke only of assertions opposed to the declarations or definitions of that same constitution. Therefore the conclusion he intends does not follow. But since that article was condemned, as it stands written there under the same form of words, with nothing added and nothing taken away, I say otherwise: namely that that article, the form of words being preserved, nothing added etc., is reprobate and erroneous. And therefore when it is said in that argument that the article has various senses, of which one is true and another false, I say: nothing prevents the same article from being condemned with such a form of words preserved, and also the same article, expressed under one meaning, being condemned, and expressed under another, being Catholic. For who doubts that this is a most wicked heresy: "The Son in the divine nature is not begotten of the Father or of the Father's substance"; and yet in this sense the Son is not begotten of the Father or of the Father's substance by division, but by communication of substance; so that it is Catholic in such a way that its opposite is heretical. And therefore if one argues, as this Lord argues, thus: "This proposition, with the form of words preserved, nothing added and nothing taken away, is false or condemned; therefore, however the form of words be changed, it is not condemned": the argument is worth nothing, as is evident from the example above. And therefore when the Friars in their petition put these words, they knew well that that logic does not hold. To the last point, concerning the declarations of the Gospel, I say that with the form of words preserved etc., under which the Church has handed them down to us, those are to be granted and are Catholic. And when it is said that they have no truth unless something is added in sense: there is no doubt that before anything was added in sense, those propositions were or had been true; but what is added only declares the truth of the propositions. Hence I say that those words, under the form in which they have been handed down to the Church, are true, and to say the opposite is erroneous. I do not deny, however, that those words, with something added, would be true not only in sense but also in form of words. But is a heretical proposition to be granted as Catholic because of the true sense which it may have; or a Catholic proposition, with the same form preserved, to be deemed heretical because of the false sense which it may have? Let your reverence judge; for then all the sanctions of the Church concerning the faith would perish, and it would be lawful for anyone to say whatever he pleased. In our present case, however, this Lord, with all due respect, not only asserts that things are condemned in the form in which they are condemned, but also in the sense in which they are condemned; and he denies that things are defined not only in their form but in the sense in which they have been defined by the Church, as will be made clearer in the following chapter.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Ostendit documenta Armachani esse reproba & erronea.
units.tr: He shows that the documents of Armachanus are reprobate and erroneous.

units.la: Istis denique vacuatis calumniis & contrarietatibus plus apparentibus quam existentibus declaratis, restat declarare, quod huiusmodi documenta in hac materia sunt temeraria, reproba & suspecta. Docuit namque & tenuit publice, & docet, tenet & asserit de praesenti, & super hoc libellos edidit, tenuit & publicauit, quod confessi Fratribus habentibus generalem licentiam audiendi confessiones & confessos absoluendi, tenentur eadem peccata, quae confessi fuerunt eidem, iterum confiteri suo proprio sacerdoti: & hoc tenet & docet generaliter esse verum, nisi Fratres habeant aliam potestatem, quam illam generalem licentiam, & quamuis nullam sit impedimentum ex parte Fratris, vel confessi, nisi quod idem omittat confiteri semel in anno suo proprio sacerdoti. Et quod istud sit temerarium, reprobum & suspectum, arguitur sic. Iste articulus est in sua forma & sub isto sensu damnatus & prohibitus, ne teneatur tanquam à catholicis mentibus respuendus. Igitur est articulus iste temerarius, reprobus & suspectus. Argumentum seu consequentia eius patet ex hoc, quod solum temeraria, reproba & suspecta sunt à Sede Apostolica damnata & prohibita ne teneantur. Et assumptum patet ex constitutione Vas electionis, vbi prohibitio ponitur sub forma prædicta.
units.tr: Having thus disposed of these calumnies and contradictions, which appear more than they really exist, it remains to show that these documents on this matter are rash, reprobate and suspect. This lord has taught and held publicly, and still teaches, holds and asserts, and has put out, held and published pamphlets on this point, that those who have confessed to Friars who have a general licence to hear confessions and absolve penitents must repeat those same sins in confession to their own priest. He holds and teaches that this is generally true, unless the Friars have some power other than that general licence; and although there is no impediment on the part of the Friar or the penitent, except that the penitent omits to confess once a year to his own priest. That this is rash, reprobate and suspect is argued as follows. This article, in its form and in this sense, has been condemned and prohibited, so that it may not be held as something Catholic minds should reject. Therefore this article is rash, reprobate and suspect. The inference is clear, because only what is rash, reprobate and suspect is condemned and prohibited by the Apostolic See so that it may not be held. The minor premise is clear from the constitution Vas electionis, where the prohibition is laid down in the aforesaid form.

units.la: Amplius, ex isto articulo sequuntur alii articuli damnati. Igitur iste articulus est temerarius & suspectus: Assumptum patet; quia ex isto articulo sequitur, quod parochiani confessi Fratribus tenentur eadem peccata iterum confiteri parochiali curato. Sed constat quod haec obligatio sic iterum confitendi non consurgit ex necessitate sacramenti poenitentiae secundum eundem Dominum istum, & secundum Dominum Iohannem Monachum, quem allegat super hoc. Igitur nullo alio casu posito surgit ex necessitate praecepti illius statuti, omnis utriusque &c. Et hoc concedit Dominus iste, & per consequens statuto sic stante vel sic obligante, nec Romanus Pontifex, nec Deus potest facere, quod parochiani confessi Fratribus modo praedicto non teneantur eadem iterum confiteri suo parochiali Presbytero vel curato, nisi possent facere, quod statuto stante vel sic obligante non staret nec sic obligaret: quod est impossibile. Quare sequitur à fortiori, quod nec Romanus Pontifex nec Deus possunt facere, quod stante statuto praedicto parochiani non teneantur semel in anno omnia peccata sua confiteri suo parochiali Presbytero vel curato. Et iste est tertius articulus in capitulo Vas electionis, reprobatus & damnatus.
units.tr: Furthermore, other condemned articles follow from this article. Therefore this article is rash and suspect. The minor premise is clear, because from this article it follows that parishioners who have confessed to Friars must repeat the same sins in confession to their parish priest. But it is evident that this obligation to confess again does not arise from the necessity of the sacrament of penance, according to this same lord, and according to Lord John the Monk, whom he cites on this point. Therefore, with no other case supposed, it arises from the necessity of the precept of that statute, omnis utriusque etc. This lord concedes this, and consequently, while the statute stands and binds in this way, neither the Roman Pontiff nor God can make it so that parishioners who have confessed to Friars in the aforesaid manner are not bound to repeat the same sins to their parish priest or curate, unless they could bring it about that the statute, while standing or binding in this way, neither stood nor bound; which is impossible. Hence it follows a fortiori that neither the Roman Pontiff nor God can make it so that, while the aforesaid statute stands, parishioners are not bound to confess all their sins once a year to their parish priest or curate. And this is the third article in the chapter Vas electionis, rejected and condemned.

units.la: Amplius, ex eodem articulo sequitur tertius articulus damnatus in praedicta constitutione: ergo ille articulus est erroneus & suspectus. Assumptum probatur sic. Romanus pontifex voluit dare aliquibus scilicet Fratribus generalem potestatem audiendi confessiones, sic quod eisdem confessi non tenerentur eadem peccata iterum confiteri parochiali Presbytero vel curato: & fecit ad hoc quantum potuit, sicut patet ex cap. Dudum, & ex constitutione Vas electionis. Non enim potuit Papa ad hoc plus facere, quam dare potestatem generalem, & declarare illam esse efficaciae supradictae: Sed Papa secundum istum Dominum, talem potestatem non dedit: quia non obstante potestate, quam dedit secundum istum, adhuc confessi tenentur eadem, ut praedicitur, confiteri. Igitur talem dare non potuit. Et haec est prima pars articuli tertii in illa constitutione damnati: Ex qua statim sequitur secunda pars sic: Cuicunque sacerdoti potest Deus dare potestatem generalem audiendi confessiones, & confessos absoluendi: & talis efficaciae, quod confessus non teneatur eadem peccata iterum confiteri: eidem potest Romanus Pontifex dare similem potestatem & similis efficaciae ex plenitudine potestatis sibi datae. Cum igitur Romanus Pontifex non potest dare generalem potestatem talis efficaciae: sequitur quod nec Romanus Pontifex nec Deus potest dare Generalem potestatem audiendi confessiones, quin confessus habenti illam potestatem teneatur eadem peccata iterum confiteri parochiali Presbytero vel curato. Et iste est tertius articulus in forma sua: sequitur quod iste Dominus habet concedere omnes errores Magistri Iohannis de Poliaco damnatos in constitutione Vas electionis.
units.tr: Furthermore, from the same article there follows the third article condemned in the aforesaid constitution; therefore that article is erroneous and suspect. The minor premise is proved as follows. The Roman Pontiff wished to give some, namely Friars, a general power to hear confessions, such that those who confessed to them would not be bound to repeat those same sins to their parish priest or curate; and he did as much as he could toward this, as is clear from the chapter Dudum and from the constitution Vas electionis. For the Pope could do no more toward this than to grant a general power and declare that it had the aforesaid efficacy. But according to this lord the Pope did not grant such a power, since, despite the power he granted according to this lord, penitents are still bound to confess the same things, as has been said. Therefore he could not grant such a power. This is the first part of the third article condemned in that constitution. From this there immediately follows the second part, as follows: to any priest to whom God can give a general power to hear confessions and absolve penitents, of such efficacy that the penitent is not bound to repeat the same sins in confession, to that priest the Roman Pontiff can likewise give a similar power of similar efficacy, from the fullness of the power given to him. Since, then, the Roman Pontiff cannot give a general power of such efficacy, it follows that neither the Roman Pontiff nor God can give a general power to hear confessions without the penitent to the one holding that power being bound to repeat the same sins to his parish priest or curate. And this is the third article in its form; it follows that this lord must concede all the errors of Master John de Polliaco condemned in the constitution Vas electionis.

units.la: Amplius, non dubium, quin Deus potest, & etiam Papa potest, dare generalem potestatem audiendi confessiones volendo, statuendo & exprimendo, quod ista tantum sufficiant confesso habenti talem potestatem ad omnem effectum, & similiter tantae efficaciae sicut si fuisset data eidem confessori super eodem confesso, & super eodem crimine in speciali. Igitur si Papa non potest: imo nec Deus dare potest generalem potestatem audiendi confessiones, quae sufficiat confessis habentibus talem potestatem, quod non teneantur eadem peccata iterum confiteri suo parochiali curato, sicut habet iste Dominus concedere, ut patet ex argumento immediate praecedenti deducto contra eundem. Sequitur quod Papa non potest: imo nec Deus dare potest cuicunque potestatem speciale pro quotunque quae sufficiant confesso habenti illam potestatem pro eodem, quod non teneantur eadem peccata iterum confiteri suo proprio parochiali curato: & per consequens sequitur, quod confessi poenitentiariis Domini Papae & Episcoporum vel aliis quibuscunque, quibus Papa vel Episcopi committunt in speciali potestatem audiendi confessiones tenentur eadem peccata iterum confiteri suo parochiali curato. Praeterea ex isto sequitur, quod Papa & Episcopi non habent ordinariam potestatem audiendi confessiones suorum subditorum, quae sufficiat confessis, quod non teneantur eadem peccata iterum confiteri suo parochiali curato. Quia si haberent huiusmodi ordinariam potestatem, possent alii committere vicem suam. Rursum cum ex statuto omnis utriusque sexus quilibet parochialis curatus possit dare potestatem audiendi confessiones, quae sufficiat confesso habenti illam potestatem, quod non teneatur eadem peccata confiteri parochiali curato: sequitur quod parochialis curatus potest dare potestatem alicui, quam nec Papa potest dare eidem: & per consequens sequitur, quod parochialis curatus habet potestatem plioris potestatis quam Papa vel Deus.
units.tr: Furthermore, there is no doubt that God can, and the Pope too can, by willing, ordaining and expressly stating, give a general power to hear confessions, declaring that these alone suffice for the penitent who has such a power, for every effect, and with the same efficacy as if that power had been given to the same confessor specifically, over the same penitent and the same crime. Therefore, if the Pope cannot, nay, neither can God give a general power to hear confessions which suffices for penitents who have such a power so that they are not bound to repeat the same sins to their own parish curate, as this lord is obliged to concede, as is clear from the argument immediately preceding, directed against him, it follows that the Pope cannot, nay, neither can God, give anyone a special power, for however long, which suffices for the penitent who has that power for the same matter, so that they are not bound to repeat the same sins to their own parish curate. And consequently it follows that penitents of the penitentiaries of the Lord Pope and of the Bishops, or of any others to whom the Pope or the Bishops specially commit the power to hear confessions, are bound to repeat the same sins to their parish curate. Moreover, from this it follows that the Pope and the Bishops do not have the ordinary power to hear the confessions of their subjects which suffices so that penitents are not bound to repeat the same sins to their parish curate. For if they had such an ordinary power, they could commit their office to others. Again, since by the statute omnis utriusque sexus any parish curate can give a power to hear confessions which suffices for the penitent who has that power, so that he is not bound to confess the same sins to the parish curate, it follows that the parish curate can give a power to someone which neither the Pope can give to that person; and consequently it follows that the parish curate has a power greater than that of the Pope or of God.

units.la: Amplius sequitur, quod parochialis curatus non habeat potestatem a Papa, cum nec Papa nec Deus habeat hanc potestatem, non possunt eam dare parochiali curato, i, q. 1. de perfectionem. & c. ventum est. & ibidem. q. 7. Dabertum.
units.tr: Furthermore it follows that the parish curate does not have his power from the Pope; since neither the Pope nor God has this power, they cannot give it to the parish curate. i, q. 1. de perfectionem. & c. ventum est. & ibidem. q. 7. Dabertum.

units.la: Amplius sequitur ex eisdem, quod Papa non potest, imo nec Deus facere non potest, quod nullus teneatur suo parochiali confiteri. Sequitur enim, Deus non potest facere q; nullus confessus habeat. habentigeneralem potestatem &c. non teneatur eadem peccata iterum confiteri suo parochiali curato. Igitur a fortiori Deus non potest facere, quod non confessus tali non teneatur suo parochiali curato confiteri. Igitur cum obligatio de faciendá confessione parochiali curato teneatur ex præcepto divino vel ex præcepto Papæ, sequitur quod Deus non potest dispensare super præcepto suo, nec super præcepto Papæ: & multo minus potest Papa super præcepto suo dispensare. Quæ omnia sunt erronea & absurda.
units.tr: Furthermore it follows from the same premises that the Pope cannot, nay, God cannot fail to bring it about that no one is bound to confess to his parish priest. For it follows: God cannot bring it about that no penitent has a general power etc. and is not bound to repeat the same sins to his parish curate. Therefore, a fortiori, God cannot bring it about that one who has not confessed to such a person is not bound to confess to his parish curate. Therefore, since the obligation to make confession to the parish curate arises from either a divine precept or a precept of the Pope, it follows that God cannot dispense from his own precept, nor from the precept of the Pope; and much less can the Pope dispense from his own precept. All of which are erroneous and absurd.

units.la: Amplius redeo ad primum articulum istorum, & arguo sic. Confessus Fratri satisfecit secundæ parti statuti, quæ est dispensatoria super prima parte eiusdem: & tamen secundum istum Dominum sic confessus remanet obligatus sicut prius. Igitur dispensatio huiusmodi non tollit vim præcepti huius statuti: & cum eadem sit ratio cuiuslibet statuti, & huius statuti in hac parte: sequitur quod nullius legis dispensatio tollit præceptum, super quo dispensat: quod est erroneum. Item, ex isto sequitur alius error impius & crudelis: videl. quod ex quo qualis est comparatio dispensationis legis ad præceptum legis: talis est comparatio dispensationis legislatoris ad præceptum suum & legem suam: cum lex non habeat vigorem, nisi a legis conditore, & cum omne legis præceptum seu dispensatio sit legislatoris præceptum seu dispensatio: sequitur quod nullus legislator potest super præcepto suo generali particulariter dispensare, quin is, cum dispensat, manet obligatus sicut prius.
units.tr: Furthermore, I return to the first of these articles and argue thus. A penitent who has confessed to a Friar has satisfied the second part of the statute, which is dispensatory with respect to the first part of the same; and yet, according to this lord, such a penitent remains bound just as before. Therefore a dispensation of this kind does not remove the force of the precept of this statute; and since the reason is the same for any statute, and for this statute in this respect, it follows that the dispensation of no law removes the precept on which it dispenses; which is erroneous. Likewise, from this there follows another impious and cruel error, namely that since the relation of a dispensation of law to a precept of law is what it is, so is the relation of the lawgiver's dispensation to his own precept and law, since a law has no force except from its author, and since every precept or dispensation of the law is the precept or dispensation of the lawgiver; it follows that no lawgiver can dispense particularly from his own general precept without remaining bound just as before when he dispenses.

units.la: Amplius ostenditur idem de præceptis & dispensationibus divinis. Si enim (si pro quia) qualis comparatio hominum prælatorum ad præcepta sua & dispensationes suas: talis comparatio Dei ad præcepta sua & dispensationes suas: & per consequens non plus potest Deus super præcepto suo dispensare, quam homo super suo, quod non est tantum erroneum, sed blasphemum.
units.tr: Further, the same is shown concerning the precepts and dispensations of God. For if the comparison of prelates of men to their precepts and their dispensations is such, then the comparison of God to his precepts and his dispensations is such too. Consequently God can dispense from his precept no more than a man can from his own, which is not merely erroneous but blasphemous.

units.la: Amplius sequitur, quod nec Deus nec homo quacunque fultus auctoritate, dato semel aliquo præcepto, potest quemcunque postea ad contrarium obligare: quia cum minus sit facere, quod aliquid liceat fieri, quam quod illud fieri teneatur, qui non potest dispensare super actu quocunque, quod licite fiat, non potest facere quod ille actus fieri teneatur, & per consequens ipse Deus non potuit facere, quod Iudæi circumcidi non teneantur: nec quod liceat eisdem dimittere ritum suum: imo sequitur quod in Deo esset tantum potestas ligandi & non solvendi. Et multo plus hoc sequitur de Papa, quod est contra Euangelium, Matth. decim. sext. & decim. octau. & Iohan. vigesim. Item, sequitur quod dispensatio Dei, quæ à sanctis vocatur revelatio, non tollit vim præcepti, & per consequens Abraham peccavit ingrediendo ad ancillam Sarai, Genes. decim. octau. contra legem matrimonii, & quod æque peccavit Iacob habendo duas uxores. Genes. vigesim. non. Sicut Lamech, Genes. quart. quia uterque æque venit contra decretum primi parentis: et erunt duo in carne una, Genes. secund. Et idem sequitur de dolo Iacob, Genes. trigesim. de spoliatione Ægypti, Exod. duodecim. de multiplicatione uxorum Dauid secund. Reg. & prim. Paralip. tertiu capitulu, contra legem Deuteronom. decim. septim. & de libello repudii, Deuteronom. vigesim. quart. & de multis aliis in scriptura.
units.tr: Further, it follows that neither God nor man, however supported by authority, can, once some precept has been given, bind anyone afterwards to the contrary. For since it is less to allow that something may be done than to require that it be done, whoever cannot dispense from any act, so that it may lawfully be done, cannot make that act required. Consequently God himself could not have made it so that the Jews were not bound to be circumcised, nor so that they were allowed to give up their rite. Indeed it would follow that God would have only the power of binding and not of loosing. And much more does this follow for the Pope, which is contrary to the Gospel, Matth. 16. & 18. & Iohan. 20. Likewise it follows that the dispensation of God, which the saints call revelatio, does not take away the force of a precept; and consequently Abraham sinned in going in to Sarah's maidservant, Gen. 18., against the law of marriage; and Jacob equally sinned in having two wives, Gen. 29.; and so did Lamech, Gen. 4., since each equally went against the decree of the first parents: and they shall be two in one flesh, Gen. 2. The same follows concerning Jacob's deceit, Gen. 30.; concerning the plundering of Egypt, Exod. 12.; concerning the multiplying of David's wives, 2 Sam. and 1 Chron. chap. 3., against the law of Deut. 17.; and concerning the bill of divorce, Deut. 24.; and concerning many other things in Scripture.

units.la: Amplius sequitur, quod dispensationes Papæ communes super illegitimitate & irregularitate & de consanguinitate seu affinitate ad contrahendum, super altari portatili ad celebrandum, de votis ieiuniorum, peregrinationum & similium non tollunt vim præcepti, & per consequens tam dispensantes quam utentes dispensationibus prædictis graviter peccarent. Præterea omnis dispensatio est quædam concessio, quæ facit aliquid esse licitum, quod alias non liceret. Sed constat quod omne illicitum est tale per aliquod quod obtinet vim præcepti. Igitur omnis dispensatio facit esse licitum, quod stante præcepto esset illicitum. Si igitur dispensatio non tollit præceptum: sequitur quod unum & idem per dispensationem est licitum, & per præceptum: quod non tollitur est illicitum sicut prius, quod non solum est erroneum, sed sibimet contrarium & repugnans.
units.tr: Further, it follows that the common dispensations of the Pope concerning illegitimacy, irregularity, and kinship or affinity for contracting marriage, concerning a portable altar for celebrating mass, and concerning vows of fasts, pilgrimages and the like, do not take away the force of the precept; and consequently both those who grant these dispensations and those who use them would sin gravely. Moreover, every dispensation is a certain concession which makes something lawful that otherwise would not be lawful. But it is clear that everything unlawful is such because of something that has the force of a precept. Therefore every dispensation makes lawful what, with the precept standing, would be unlawful. If, then, a dispensation does not take away the precept, it follows that one and the same thing is both lawful by dispensation and, by the precept which is not taken away, unlawful as before. This is not only erroneous but self-contradictory and inconsistent.

units.la: Amplius sequitur, quod dispensatio super lege illa, qua tenetur quod nullus sacerdos alienum parochianum in confessione audiat vel absolvat, non tollit vim præcepti illius legis, & sic sequitur, quod dispensatio proprii sacerdotis facta sacerdoti alieno super grege suo, nihil operatur nec tollit vim præcepti legis eiusdem: & per consequens nullus parochianus potest confiteri sacerdoti alieno de licentia quacunque proprii sacerdotis. Nec potest iste Dominus iuvari per hoc, quod in suo tractatu dicit: quod Magister Iohannes de Poliaco posuit suos articulos propter defectum potestatis absoluendi in Fratre habente generalem licentiam &c. quia Magister Iohannes præfatus tenuit, quod huiusmodi licentia generalis non tribuit Fratri sufficientem potestatem absolvendi confessum, sicut patet ex tertio articulo eiusdem: & ideo ille erravit. Sed iste Dominus non posuit articulum propter defectum absolutionis, sed propter necessitatem antiqui præcepti illius capituli omnis utriusque sexus. Et quia secundum eum, voluntarium non tollit necessarium, & sic nullum tenet, ut dicit, errorem. Hæc cavillatio non iuvat. Tum quia in capitulo definitur, quod confessi Fratribus &c. non magis tenentur iterum confiteri, quam si fuissent confessi proprio sacerdoti, nec tenerentur propter defectum absolutionis seu potestatis absoluendi: nec propter necessitatem præceptionis illius iterum confiteri. Igitur confessi Fratribus &c. non tenentur propter necessitatem præceptionis iterum confiteri. Tum secundo quia ista modificatio est condemnata in secundo articulo damnato in cap. supradicto. Nam sequitur: Isti (demonstratis his, qui confessi sunt Fratribus) propter necessitatem præcepti illius capituli, Omnis utriusque sexus, tenentur iterum confiteri. Igitur nec Papa nec Deus potest facere, quod eodem præcepto stante non teneamur ipsi confateri, & e contra. Igitur concedens alteram seu errans in altera habet concedere vtramque vel errat in vtraque, et militer sequitur, quod damnato vno damnatur vterque: & iste est secundus error vel secundum erroneum quod affirmat. Tum tertio: quia ipse imponit Magistro Ioanni praefato falsum: quia sicut patet ex c. 3. eiusdem, ipse non posuit in Fratribus simpliciter defectum potestatis absoluendi à peccatis: sed cum modificatione, scil. defectum potestatis absoluendi de obligantis confessum abiteranda confessione proprio sacerdoti, & eundem defectum ponit iste Dominus. Quare sequitur quod errant aequaliter: vel neuter errat. Tum quarto quia haec responsio nimis impingit in Papam & Ecclesiam Sacrosanctam, scil. quod Ecclesia dedit Magistro Ioanni antedicto plenam audientiam: & per consequens non ignorauit istam modificationem vel motiuum erroneum seu causam sui erroris praedictam: nihilominus tamen damnauit articulum, qui secundum istum Dominum est catholicus atq; verus nullum errorem continens, & subticuit motiuum erroneum, vel causam sui erroris praedictam; cum tamen sciebat, quod sicut ex falsis vera & ex impossibilibus necessaria: sic ex erroneis seu haereticis catholica consequuntur. Tum quia, sicut dictum est, huiusmodi responsio aperit viam defensionis omnium errorum: quia non est aliquis error, qui non potest per huiusmodi modificationem confictam defendi. Quare sequitur, quod haec responsio errorem potius auget quam excusat: nec respondentem liberat, sed inuoluit. Tum sexto: quia hoc, quod frequenter allegat, scil. quod voluntarium non tollit necessarium, implicat multos errores, sicut superius est ostensum. Nec valet motiuum istius Domini, quod ponit pro responsione supradicta, scil. quod ex ipso eodem articulo Vas electionis, cum ibidem dicitur: Felicis recordationis Alexandri 4. & Clementis quinti Romanorum pontificum praedecessorum nostrorum vestigia imitando: apparet vt dicit, quod ille damnauerunt ante illa eadem, quae ibidem Dominus Iohannes Papa damnauit: quia solum damnauerunt istum errorem in materia praefata: scilicet quod Fratres habentes &c. non possent confessiones audire vel absolutionis beneficium impendere praelatorum inferiorum vel parochialium sacerdotum assensu vel licentia minime requisita. Ex quo videtur, quod Dominus Iohannes voluerit hoc damnari tantum, & quod non intendebat excludere confessiones fratribus a confessione iterandα proprio sacerdoti. Haec ille. Hoc inquam motiuum non valet: quia (cum omni tamen reuerentia) assumit falsum. Et huic cap. Vas electionis contrarium, quod Alexander & Clemens damnauerunt ea, quae Iohannes damnauit, vel quod Iohannes damnauit: & tunc in eodem cap. ea quae ipsi damnauerunt suo tempore, sicut patet expresse de tenoribus articulorum damnatorum ab eisdem. Et quod dicitur in cap. Vas electionis, praedecessorum nostrorum vestigia imitando, non refertur ad articulos damnatos, sed ad praeceptum vel prohibitionem quae sequitur verba praemissa immediate, scilicet ne quisquam dictos articulos per eum damnatos, vel contenta in eis seu in aliquo praedictorum, vtpote a catholicis mentibus respuendos decetero defendere audeat vel tenere: quia ab Dicto Domini summi pontifices similes fecerunt prohibitiones super damnatis articulis per eosdem. Huic tamen prohibitioni, quo ad vtramq; eius partem, non est veritus contraire.
units.tr: Further, it follows that a dispensation from that law by which it is required that no priest hear or absolve in confession someone else's parishioner does not take away the force of that law's precept. And so it follows that a dispensation granted by one's own priest to another priest over his flock accomplishes nothing and does not remove the force of the same law; and consequently no parishioner can make confession to another priest by any licence of his own priest. Nor can this gentleman be helped by what he says in his treatise: that Master John of Poliaco set down his articles because of a lack of power to absolve in a friar who had a general licence, and so on. For the aforesaid Master John held that such a general licence does not give a friar sufficient power to absolve a penitent, as is clear from the third article of the same; and so he was in error. But this gentleman has set down no article because of a lack of absolution, but because of the necessity of the old precept of that chapter, all of either sex. And since, in his view, the voluntary does not remove the necessary, and so holds no error, as he says, this quibble does not help him. First, because the chapter defines that those who have confessed to friars, and so on, are no more bound to confess again than if they had confessed to their own priest; nor are they bound because of a lack of absolution or of power to absolve, nor because of the necessity of that precept to confess again. Therefore those who have confessed to friars, and so on, are not bound to confess again because of the necessity of that precept. Second, because this modification was condemned in the second article condemned in the chapter mentioned above. For it runs: These persons (those who have confessed to friars being pointed out) are bound to confess again because of the necessity of that precept of the chapter, All of either sex. Therefore neither the Pope nor God can bring it about that, while the same precept stands, we are not bound to confess again to them, and conversely. Therefore whoever grants the one, or errs in the one, must grant both or err in both; and likewise it follows that when one is condemned both are condemned. This is his second error, or the second error that he affirms. Third, because he falsely imputes to the aforesaid Master John something he did not say. For as is clear from chapter 3 of the same, he did not set down simply a lack of power to absolve from sins in the friars, but with the modification, namely, a lack of power to absolve one who is obliged to abandon confession to his own priest; and this same lack is what this gentleman sets down. Hence it follows that both err equally, or neither errs. Fourth, because this answer too strongly reflects on the Pope and the most holy Church: namely, that the Church gave the aforesaid Master John full hearing, and consequently was not ignorant of this modification or of the erroneous motive or the cause of his error as stated; nevertheless it condemned the article which, according to this gentleman, is catholic and true, containing no error, and it passed over the erroneous motive or the cause of its error as stated; although it knew that, just as true things come from false and necessary things from impossible, so catholic things come from erroneous or heretical ones. Fifth, because, as has been said, an answer of this kind opens the way to defending all errors, since there is no error which cannot be defended by such a made-up modification. Hence it follows that this answer increases the error rather than excuses it; it does not free the one answering but entangles him. Sixth, because what he frequently alleges, namely that the voluntary does not remove the necessary, involves many errors, as was shown above.
