Nor does the argument of this gentleman, which he puts forward for the answer mentioned above, hold good: namely, that from that same article Vas electionis, where it is said: Imitating the footsteps of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Alexander IV and Clement V of happy memory, it appears, as he says, that they condemned before those same things that Lord John, the Pope, condemned there: because they only condemned that error in the matter aforesaid, namely that friars having, and so on, could not hear confessions or bestow the benefit of absolution without the consent or licence of inferior prelates or parish priests, which was not required at all. From this it seems that Lord John wished only this to be condemned, and that he did not intend to exclude from confession, to be repeated to their own priest, those who had confessed to friars. Thus he. I say, this argument does not hold, because (with all due reverence) it assumes what is false. And the contrary is found in that chapter Vas electionis: that Alexander and Clement condemned the things that John condemned, or that John condemned them; and then, in the same chapter, the things they themselves condemned in their own time, as is expressly clear from the wording of the articles condemned by them. And what is said in chapter Vas electionis, imitating the footsteps of our predecessors, does not refer to the condemned articles but to the precept or prohibition that immediately follows the words quoted: that no one should dare henceforth to defend or hold the said articles condemned by him, or the matters contained in them or in any of them, as things to be rejected by catholic minds; for the supreme pontiffs, following the example of the Lord, made similar prohibitions regarding the articles condemned by them. Yet he has not feared to contravene this prohibition, in both of its parts.

units.la: Secunda responsio, seu expositio praefatae constitutionis extravagantis, scilicet Vas electionis, quam ponit vt euadat, non potest eum defendere ab errore. Dicit enim, quod omnes articuli damnati & similiter articulus ibidem approbatus possunt intelligi cum adiectione secundae partis capi. Omnis vtriusque, videlicet, si quis alieno sacerdoti &c. Unde dicit, quod erroneum est dicere, quod confessi Fratribus habentibus licentiam generalem audiendi confessiones, scilicet cum beneplacito proprii sacerdotis, tenentur eadem peccata, quae confessi fuerant, iterum proprio sacerdoti confiteri. Et sic est verum atque catholicum, quod illi qui praedictis Fratribus confitentur, scilicet forma illa seruata, non magis tenentur eadem peccata iterum confiteri, quam si alias illa confessi fuissent proprio sacerdoti iuxta dictum concilii Generalis. Istum intellectum constitutionis praedicta probat sic: quod ex quo secundus articulus Magistri Iohannis de Poliaco fuit damnatus: sequitur quod eius oppositum est approbatum, scilicet quod Romanus Pontifex statuto stante Omnis vtriusque: potest facere, quod parochiani non teneantur semel in anno omnia peccata sua confiteri proprio sacerdoti, scilicet parochiali curato. Istud autem verificari non potest, nisi fiet statutum concilii generalis. Statutum autem concilii generalis stare non potest, nisi fiet illa particula: scilicet quod si quis ex iusta causa velit alieno sacerdoti confiteri, petat & obtineat licentiam sui proprii sacerdotis. Stante autem illa particula, nullus confessus Fratribus est exemptus a generali statuto quo ad primam partem ipsius, nisi illa secunda clausula obseruata. Igitur obseruantia illius clausulae est necessaria cuilibet confesso Fratribus, vt sit exemptus a prima particula eiusdem. Et per consequens cum illa modificatione debet intelligi ista diffinitio. Haec Dominus iste.
units.tr: The second answer, or explanation, of the aforesaid extravagant constitution, namely Vas electionis, which he offers in order to escape, cannot defend him from error. For he says that all the condemned articles, and likewise the article approved there, can be understood with the addition of the second part of the chapter: Omnis utriusque, namely, "If anyone to a foreign priest," etc. Hence he says that it is erroneous to say that those who have confessed to Friars holding a general licence to hear confessions, namely with the consent of their own priest, are bound to confess again to their own priest the same sins which they had confessed. And so it is true and Catholic that those who confess to the aforesaid Friars, that form being observed, are no more bound to confess the same sins again than if they had confessed them elsewhere to their own priest, according to the decree of the General Council. This Lord proves this interpretation of the constitution as follows: since the second article of Master John of Poliaco was condemned, its opposite must have been approved, namely that the Roman Pontiff, with the statute standing, can bring it about that parishioners are not bound to confess all their sins once a year to their own priest, namely the parish priest. But this cannot be true unless the statute of the General Council is made to hold. And the statute of the General Council cannot stand unless that clause holds good: namely, that if anyone for a just cause wishes to confess to another priest, he must seek and obtain the licence of his own priest. With that clause standing, however, no one who has confessed to the Friars is exempt from the first part of the general statute unless the second clause is observed. Therefore observance of that clause is necessary for every person who has confessed to the Friars, if he is to be exempt from the first part of it. And consequently this definition must be understood with that qualification. So says this Lord.

units.la: Primo igitur respondetur ad motiuum: & consequenter probabitur intentum. Et ne praecedatur annullatorie, suppono: quod ad hoc, quod statutum concilii generalis obseruetur, sufficit quod parochianus habeat licentiam proprii sacerdotis ad hoc quod confiteatur alieno: siue illam petierit siue non: quia a tempore dicti statuti fuit statutum, quod etiam parochiales curati dabant parochianis licentiam non petitam, quando curati volebant sibi adhibere coadiutores in hac parte: & absit quod dicatur parochianos in casu fuisse transgressos hoc statutum. Et ratio hoc declarat. Nam cum sit praecise propter habere vel obtinere: posito quod parochianus habeat licentiam, superfluit petere eam. Quo supposito respondeo ad argumentum, quod positum articuli secundi est approbatum, scilicet quod Romanus Pontifex stante statuto potest facere, quod parochiani non teneantur confiteri parochiali curato: & tunc ... quod illud sit approbatum, non potest esse verum, nisi stet secunda particula statuti, scilicet quod habeatur licentia proprii sacerdotis. Dico quod si sub nomine proprii sacerdotis includatur Papa & legati in suis prouinciis, & patriarchæ, archiepiscopi & episcopi & parochiales curati, illa propositio est vera. Si autem per proprium sacerdotem intelligitur parochialis curatus tantum; tunc propositio est falsa, (scilicet quod oppositum articuli sic, vt prædicitur, approbatum non potest esse verum, nisi parochianus ad confitendum alteri obtineat licentiam parochialis curati. quod valet tantum ac si diceretur, quod Romanus pontifex, stante statuto prædicto, potest facere quod parochiani non teneantur semel in anno confiteri parochiali curato. sed non potest hoc facere, nisi parochianus obtineat licentiam parochialis curati ad confitendum alteri. Hoc autem propter errores in quarto capitulo deducios ex ipso non potest esse verum. Illa etiam propositio sic restringendo proprium sacerdotem ad parochialem curatum nullo modo sequitur ex assumptis. Et conformiter dico ad conclusionem, quæ infertur, scilicet quod obseruantia secundæ clausulæ, scilicet quod habeatur proprii sacerdotis licentia, non tamen parochialis curati, est necessaria cuilibet confesso fratri ad hoc, quod sit exemptus à confessione facienda proprio sacerdoti. iam enim quilibet fratri confessus & absolutus habet licentiam proprii sacerdotis, sicut superius frequenter probatum est. & ideo non oportet ponere illam adiectionem ad licentiam proprii sacerdotis, quia illa etiam licentia intelligitur in licentia generali, quam habent fratres, sicut dictum est. Ista etiam responsio seu expositio quæstionis supradictæ non potest istum Dominum defendere ab errore: quia cum Dominus iste dicit, quod articuli damnati & reprobati possunt intelligi cum adiectione secundæ particulæ statuti, scilicet quod habeatur licentia proprii sacerdotis, aut hoc intelligit de licentia parochialis curati tantum, sicut videtur intelligere, aut de licentia Papæ vel episcoporum, sicut supradictum est. non secundo modo, quia hoc esset superfluum, cum in articulis dicatur, quod confessi fratribus habentibus generalem licentiam, quam nullus dubitat esse licentiam Papæ vel episcoporum seu parochiali curatis tenentur iterum confiteri. nec per hoc euaderet errorem: quia iam ponit, quod confessi fratribus habentibus generalem licentiam proprii sacerdotis illo modo loquendo de proprio sacerdote tenentur eadem peccata cóiteri proprio sacerdoti: & per consequens ponit illud, quod ipsemet in responsione dicit esse erroneum & damnatum. Si vero intelligat proprium sacerdotem parochialem curatum tm: tunc quamuis sit verum, s. quod erroneum sit dicere, quod confessis fratribus habentibus licentiam generalem audiendi confessiones obtenta licentia parochialis curati tenentur eadem peccata iterum confiteri: tn quia hmoi licentia parochialis curati sit requisita: sic quod licentia non obtenta tenentur iterum confiteri; sicut error Ioan. de Poliaco, qui solum loquebatur de habentibus licentiam generalem tm, nulla habita licentia speciali sacerdotis curati, sicut patet ex 2. articulo eiusdem erroris damnati, & articuli approbati in constitutione, supponunt licentiam generalem tantum: & per consequens constitutio damnat articulos & approbat de confessis fratribus habentibus licentia generale tm nulla habita licentia speciali parochialis curati. Præterea sic restringendo proprium sacerdotem adiecta clausula secunda statuti Omnis utriusque sexus &c. cum, vt dicit, in illa continetur, quod non obtenta licentia proprii sacerdotis, sacerdos alienus non potest alterius parochianum soluere vel ligare: sequitur, quod stante illa parte statuti nullus alienus sacerdos potest alterius parochianum de quacunq; licentia alia soluere vel ligare: & per consequens non solum sequuntur oes errores in 4. c. prædicti: sed sequitur quod fratres habentes generalem licentiam audiendi confessiones non habent potestatem soluendi sibi confessos. & sequitur, quod iste Dns habet ponere in fratrib. defectum potestatis absoluendi: & per consequens approbat illum errorem, quem ipse iponit magistro Ioh. de Poliaco. Amplius ex ratione sequitur, quod Romanus pontifex stante statuto non potest facere, quod confessi fratribus habentibus generalem licentiam audiendi confessiones non habita licentia parochialis curati non teneantur eadem peccata fratribus confessa iterum confiteri parochiali curato: imo nec Deus potest hoc facere: & quod stante statuto nec Papa nec Deus possunt dare fratribus potestatem absoluendi parochianos non obtenta licentia parochialis curati; imo quod non possunt dare alicui, qui non est parochialis curatus, potestatem absoluendi sine licentia parochialis curati: & per consequens ipsemet non habet potestatem absoluendi parochianos sine licentia parochialis curati: & sic de ceteris blasphemiis in 4. ca. prædeductis. Patet igitur, quod hæc responsio respondentem non liberat ab errore: & quod iste Dominus, salua sua reuerentia, tenet errores damnatos in forma vel in sensu, in quo sunt damnati: & qui si non essent damnati, essent damnabiles propter errores, qui sequuntur ex eisdem; quos omnes iste Dominus habet concedere consequenter.
units.tr: First, then, I reply to the argument, and afterwards the intended point will be proved. And so that it is not rejected outright, I suppose the following: for the General Council's statute to be observed, it is enough that the parishioner has the licence of his own priest to confess to another, whether he has sought it or not. For since the time of that statute it has been the custom that even parish priests gave parishioners a licence not asked for, whenever the priests wished to have assistants in this matter; and far be it that it should be said that the parishioners in such a case broke this statute. And the reason declares this: since the licence is required only in order to have or obtain something, once it is granted that the parishioner has a licence, there is no need to seek it. On this supposition I reply to the argument that the posited article of the second, namely that the Roman Pontiff, with the statute standing, can make it so that parishioners are not bound to confess to the parish priest, is approved; and then ... that this be approved cannot be true unless the second part of the statute stands, namely that a licence of their own priest is had. I say that if under the name of their own priest the Pope and legates in their provinces, and patriarchs, archbishops and bishops, and parish priests are included, that proposition is true. But if by their own priest only the parish priest is meant, then the proposition is false (namely that the opposite of the article, thus approved as stated, cannot be true unless the parishioner obtains from the parish priest a licence to confess to another). This amounts to saying that the Roman Pontiff, with the aforesaid statute standing, can make it so that parishioners are not bound to confess once a year to the parish priest; but he cannot do this unless the parishioner obtains from the parish priest a licence to confess to another. Yet this cannot be true, on account of the errors deduced in the fourth chapter from it. Nor does that proposition, so restricting "their own priest" to the parish priest, follow in any way from the premises. And I likewise say, regarding the conclusion drawn, namely that observance of the second clause, that is, that a licence of their own priest, but not of the parish priest, is had, is necessary for every confessed Friar so that he is exempt from confessing to his own priest: for indeed every Friar who has confessed and been absolved already has the licence of his own priest, as has often been proved above. And so there is no need to add the phrase to the licence of their own priest, since that licence too is understood within the general licence which the Friars have, as has been said. This answer or explanation of the above question also cannot defend this Lord from error. For when this Lord says that the condemned and reprobated articles can be understood with the addition of the second part of the statute, namely that a licence of their own priest is had, he either means this of the licence of the parish priest only, as he seems to mean, or of the licence of the Pope or bishops, as has been said above. Not the second way, since that would be superfluous, when the articles say that those who have confessed to Friars holding a general licence, which no one doubts is the licence of the Pope or bishops, are bound to confess again to the parish priest. Nor would he escape the error by this, since he now posits that those who have confessed to Friars holding a general licence of their own priest, speaking in that way of their own priest, are bound to confess the same sins again to their own priest; and consequently he posits that very thing which he himself in his answer says is erroneous and condemned. But if he means only the parish priest as their own priest, then although it is true that it is erroneous to say that those who have confessed to Friars holding a general licence to hear confessions are bound to confess the same sins again once the licence of the parish priest has been obtained, yet, since such a licence of the parish priest is required, so that without it they are bound to confess again, this is like the error of John of Poliaco, who spoke only of those holding a general licence alone, with no special licence of the parish priest had, as is clear from the second article of that condemned error. The articles approved in the constitution presuppose only a general licence, and consequently the constitution condemns and approves articles about confessed Friars holding only a general licence, with no special licence of the parish priest had. Moreover, by thus restricting "their own priest," with the second clause of the statute Omnis utriusque sexus added, since, as he says, it contains that without the licence of their own priest, another priest cannot absolve or bind another's parishioner, it follows that with that part of the statute standing, no foreign priest can absolve or bind another's parishioner on any other licence whatever. And consequently not only do all the errors in the aforesaid fourth chapter follow, but it also follows that Friars holding a general licence to hear confessions do not have the power to absolve those who have confessed to them. And it follows that this Lord must place in the Friars a lack of the power of absolving, and consequently he approves the very error which he himself imputes to Master John of Poliaco. Furthermore, it follows from the argument that the Roman Pontiff, with the statute standing, cannot make it so that those who have confessed to Friars holding a general licence to hear confessions, without a licence of the parish priest having been obtained, are not bound to confess the same sins again to the parish priest; indeed, not even God can do this; and that, with the statute standing, neither the Pope nor God can give the Friars power to absolve parishioners without a licence of the parish priest having been obtained; indeed that they cannot give to anyone who is not a parish priest the power to absolve without a licence of the parish priest; and consequently he himself does not have the power to absolve parishioners without a licence of the parish priest. And so with the other blasphemies deduced in the fourth chapter. It is clear, then, that this answer does not free the respondent from error, and that this Lord, with all due respect, holds the errors condemned either in their form or in the sense in which they are condemned; and which, even if they were not condemned, would be damnable on account of the errors that follow from them, all of which this Lord must consequently be willing to concede.

units.la: CAP. VII. In quo dissoluuntur quæ apparent vel apparere possunt prædictis contraria.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. In which the things that appear, or can appear, to contradict the above are resolved.

units.la: VErum quia prædictus archiepiscopus Armachan in tractatu suo articulo 2. per magnum processum nititur prædictos errores defendere probando, quod nec præfatum capitulum dudum, nec aliquod priuilegium illi consimile tollit aut impugnat statutum antiquum Omnis utriusque sexus quoad confessiones parochianorum semel in anno faciendas proprio sacerdoti; volo deinceps suis rationibus respondere. Ista tn conclusio, quam intendit probare, potest habere duplicem intellectum, secundum quod ex statuto omnis utriusque consurgit duplex obligatio vel duplex debitum confitendi, sicut patuit in prin. 2. capituli, vnum s. generale & perpetuum & manuum; aliud spale seu particulare transiens & fluxiuum. Sic in ppsito contra supradicta pot intelligi sic. s. quod c. dudum nec aliquod priuilegium sibi simile tollit aut impugnat statuta omnis utriusque, quoad debitum primum confitendi. & sic conceditur conclusio, quam proponit, vel quoad obligationem secundam cundam seu debitum cõfitendi, sic loquendo. c. dudū. & Fratrum priuilegia tollunt statutū, sed nō impugnant. ipsa n. tollunt statutum quoad obligationem secundam: quia soluunt debitum eiusdem obligationis sic, quod confessus non remanet ex vi statuti eodem debito amplius obligatus. Et ex eadem ratione patet quod Fratrum priuilegia statutum non impugnant, sicut ex eodem s. c. per totum patuit euidenter. Secundum igitur primum intellectum posset concedi conclusio sua supradicta & omnes rationes quas inducit: quia tñ aliquæ suæ rationes videntur aliter procedere, per singulas est breuiter transcurrendum. ¶ Arguit igitur primo sic: ista duo capitula continent duas affirmatiuas super eodem actu iterabili, s. super confessione eorundem peccatorum iterabili, s. quod aliquis sit confessus fratri omnia peccata sua, & quod teneatur semel in anno confiteri suo proprio sacerdoti, quæ non magis se impugnant, quam duæ affirmatiuæ similes in alia materia, s. quod aliquis audiat missam apud fratres vel offerat ibidem, & quod teneatur semel in anno audire missam in sua parochiali ecclesia, & ibid. semel vel ter offerre sicut præcipitur Exo. 23. sed constat quod istæ duæ ultimæ non repugnant, quare nec primæ. & quia iste Dns (vt dicit) hoc argumentum nescit soluere: ideo aliquos excitat ad soluendum ipsum, vel ad concedendum articulum quem concludit. Huic igitur argumento suppposito sicut in hoc & in ceteris argumentis quod fiat sermo de confessione facta fratri de licentia seu confessione capituli dudū, & confessio facienda proprio sacerdoti seu eius vicem tenenti ex vi statuti omnis utriusq; & quod pro eodem toto anno & pro eisdem peccatis fratri confessus: quia alioquin non esset ad propositum. Respondetur primo reducendo argumentum contra se ipsum, sic. non plus repugnant istæ duæ affirmatiuæ super eodem actu iterabili: sc. super confessione eorundem peccatorum, quam. sc. aliquis facit Papæ vel episcopo proprio, & quod teneatur eadem peccata suo parochiali curato confiteri iterum: quam duæ affirmatiuæ similes de offerendo eisdem aut audiendo missas eorundem, sed non dubium, quod non repugnant, quod aliquis audiat missam Papæ vel episcopi. & quod fecerit eisdem oblationem, & quod teneatur nihilominus audire missam parochialis curati & sibi offerre. igitur primæ duæ affirmatiuæ non repugnant. ecce idem argumentum & eadem vel consimilis conclusio, quæ infertur: quia non dubium, quod illæ propositiones formaliter non repugnant: & concessa illa conclusione, non plus sequitur quod confessi fratribus quam confessi Papæ vel episcopis teneantur parochiali curato iterum confiteri. & ideo argumentum nullius est ponderis vel valoris. Et si arguitur, quod sequitur, quod saltem capitulum dudum, non tollit statutum generalis concilii omnis utriusq; sexus. Respondeo, quod quamuis conclusio sit vera ad sensum immediate quasi antedictum: illa tamen non sequitur ex assumpto, cuius exemplum est. Posito quod Petrus habeat ex præcepto omni anno ieiunare semel in pane & aqua: non est dubium, quod istæ duæ affirmatiuæ non repugnant: sc. quod Petrus modo ieiunauerit: & quod teneatur alius infra annum consimiliter ieiunare. & tamen non sequitur: igitur ieiunium Petri non tollit obligationem præcepti pro illa vice. Si tñ dicatur, quo hoc non soluit: quia repugnantia est quod Petrus ieiunauerit: & quod teneatur isto anno ex vi præcepti eiusdem dati iterum ieiunare. Solutio: dico quod consimiliter est aperte istic. repugnantia est. n. quod aliquis sit confessus fratri habenti generalem licentiam, &c. & quod teneatur ex vi statuti omnis utriusq; iterum confiteri, eque n. implent Petrus confitendo fratri prædicto statutū, sicut fecit præceptū ieiunii vna vice ieiunare, do ceteris paribus, vtrobiq; Aliter respondetur negando assumptum, cum dicitur, quod illa duo capitula continent illas duas affirmatiuas, &c. quod sc. aliquis sic confessus fratri. & quod teneatur semel in anno cõfiteri proprio sacerdoti suo. non enim continet illas affirmatiuas, sed istas: quod licet aliquis fratri confiteri; & quod teneatur semel in anno confiteri proprio sacerdoti suo vel alteri de licentia proprii sacerdotis: sicut patet in prima conclusione tertii ca. præcedentis. Ex quibus non plus sequitur, quod confessus fratri teneatur eadem peccata iterum confiteri proprio sacerdoti: quam quod confessus alieno de licentia parochialis curati tenetur iterum eadem confiteri suo parochiali presbytero vel curato. & totum est, quod vltimum non sequitur: igitur nec primum. Similiter nec ex hoc sequitur, quod ca. dudū, non tollit statutum concilii generalis omnis utriusque: imo potius sequitur oppositum, scilicet quod tollit ipsum quo ad eius obligationem particularem, sicut supradictum est. s. modo quo implens præceptum tollit obligationem præcepti pro illa vice. Tertio aliter respondetur negando illud assumptum propter aliam falsitatem, quam continet, scilicet quod non plus repugnant istæ duæ affirmatiuæ, scilicet quod aliquis sit confessus fratri, & quod teneatur eadem peccata confiteri suo proprio sacerdoti, quam duæ, affirmatiuæ similes de missis apud fratres & parochialem ecclesiam audiendis, vel de oblationibus ibidem faciendis: quia loquendo de confessione sacramentali, vtrobique primæ affirmatiuæ repugnant secundum legem præsentem. Secundæ vero non repugnant. hoc patet sic: quia necessitas confitendi ex statuto ecclesiæ præsupponit necessitatem sacramenti pœnitentiæ, sicut patet ex vltima suppositione secundi capituli. igitur sequitur, iste tenetur ex statuto ecclesiæ hæc peccata confiteri: ergo sacramentum pœnitentiæ est sibi necessarium pro his peccatis, & esset necessarium ecclesiæ statuto cessante. quicquid igitur repugnat conclusioni, repugnat assumpto. sed constat etiam per aduersarios, quod repugnantia est, quod aliquis fratri sit confessus loquendo de confessione prædicto, & quod sacramentum pœnitentiæ sit sibi necessarium pro peccatis confessis eodem statuto remoto. quare sequitur, q repugnantia est. q aliquis sit confessus, & q ex statuto ecclesiæ teneatur eadē peccata iterū confiteri, & maxime cum sic confessus ipleuit præceptum statuti, sicut est in proposito. quare sequitur, q assumptū ex ea parte sit sallsum, & ad exempla q. ponuntur, rñ q
units.tr: But because the aforesaid archbishop of Armagh, in his treatise, article 2, labours through a long argument to defend the aforesaid errors by proving that neither the aforementioned chapter dudum nor any similar privilege removes or impugns the ancient statute Omnis utriusque sexus, as regards the confession of parishioners to be made once a year to their own priest, I wish now to answer his reasons. The conclusion he intends to prove can have a twofold meaning, since from the statute omnis utriusque arises a twofold obligation, or twofold debt of confessing, as was shown in the first part of the second chapter: one general, perpetual and standing; the other special or particular, passing and transient. In the present matter, against the above, the conclusion can thus be understood: that chapter dudum and no similar privilege removes or impugns the statute omnis utriusque as regards the first debt of confessing; and so the conclusion he proposes is granted. Or it can be understood as regards the second obligation, or debt of confessing, speaking thus: chapter dudum and the privileges of the friars do remove the statute, but do not impugn it. For they remove it as regards the second obligation, because they discharge the debt of that obligation in such a way that the one who has confessed is no longer bound by force of the statute to that debt. And for the same reason it is plain that the privileges of the friars do not impugn the statute, as was made clear throughout the same chapter. According to the first sense, then, his conclusion stated above and all the reasons he brings could be granted. But since some of his reasons seem to proceed differently, each must be briefly run through. He argues first thus: these two chapters contain two affirmations about the same repeatable act, namely the repeated confession of the same sins: that someone has confessed all his sins to a friar, and that he is bound to confess once a year to his own priest. These do not conflict any more than two similar affirmations in another matter, namely that someone hears mass at the friars' church or makes an offering there, and that he is bound to hear mass once a year in his own parish church and to make an offering there once or three times, as is commanded in Exo. 23. But it is clear that these last two do not conflict, so neither do the first. And since this lord (as he says) does not know how to solve this argument, he urges some to solve it, or to grant the article he concludes. To this argument, then, let it be supposed, as in this and his other arguments, that the discussion concerns confession made to a friar by licence or under the privilege of chapter dudum, and confession to be made to one's own priest, or to one holding his place, by force of the statute omnis utriusque; and that the person has confessed to a friar for the whole year and for the same sins. Otherwise the argument would not be to the point. The reply is, first, to turn the argument back against itself. These two affirmations about the same repeatable act, namely confession of the same sins, conflict no more than this: that someone makes confession to the Pope or to his own bishop, and that he is bound to confess the same sins again to his parish curate. Likewise, two similar affirmations about offering or hearing the same masses do not conflict. Yet there is no doubt that these do not conflict: that someone hears the mass of the Pope or of a bishop and makes an offering to them, and nevertheless is bound to hear the mass of the parish curate and make an offering to him. Therefore the first two affirmations do not conflict. Here is the same argument, and the same or a similar conclusion is inferred. For there is no doubt that those propositions do not formally conflict; and granting that conclusion, it does not follow any more that those confessed to friars are bound to confess again to the parish curate than that those confessed to the Pope or to bishops are so bound. So the argument is of no weight or value. And if it is objected that at least it follows that chapter dudum does not remove the statute of the general council Omnis utriusque sexus, I answer that although the conclusion is true in the sense just stated, it does not follow from the assumption, of which here is an example. Suppose Peter is bound by precept to fast once a year on bread and water. There is no doubt that these two affirmations do not conflict: that Peter has now fasted, and that another is bound likewise to fast within the year. Yet it does not follow that Peter's fast removes the obligation of the precept for that occasion. If it is said that this answer does not hold, because it is contradictory that Peter has fasted and yet is bound this year, by force of the same precept, to fast again, the reply is that here too there is plainly a contradiction. For it is contradictory that someone has confessed to a friar holding a general licence, etc., and that he is bound by force of the statute omnis utriusque to confess again. Peter, by fasting once, fulfils the precept of fasting, and by confessing to the aforesaid friar he fulfils the statute, other things being equal on both sides. Otherwise it is answered by denying the assumption, when it is said that those two chapters contain those two affirmations, namely that someone has so confessed to a friar and is bound once a year to confess to his own priest. For they do not contain those affirmations, but these: that one may confess to a friar; and that he is bound once a year to confess to his own priest, or to another with his own priest's licence; as is evident in the first conclusion of the third chapter above. From these it does not follow any more that one confessed to a friar is bound to confess the same sins again to his own priest, than that one confessed to another with the licence of the parish curate is bound to confess the same sins again to his parish priest or curate. And since the last does not follow, neither does the first. Likewise, it does not follow from this that chapter dudum does not remove the statute of the general council omnis utriusque. Rather the opposite follows: that it removes it as regards its particular obligation, as was said above, in the way that one who fulfils a precept removes the obligation of the precept for that occasion. Thirdly, it is answered otherwise, by denying that assumption on account of another falsehood it contains: namely that these two affirmations, that someone has been confessed to a friar and that he is bound to confess the same sins again to his own priest, conflict no more than two similar affirmations about hearing mass at the friars' church and at the parish church, or about making offerings there. For, speaking of sacramental confession, the first affirmations conflict on both sides under the present law, but the second do not. This is shown thus: the necessity of confessing by the statute of the Church presupposes the necessity of the sacrament of penance, as is evident from the last supposition of the second chapter. Therefore, if this person is bound by the statute of the Church to confess these sins, the sacrament of penance is necessary for him for these sins, and would be necessary even if the statute of the Church ceased. Whatever therefore contradicts the conclusion contradicts the assumption. But it is also agreed by the opponents that it is contradictory for someone to have confessed to a friar, speaking of confession of the aforesaid kind, and for the sacrament of penance to be still necessary for him for the sins confessed, with that statute removed. Hence it follows that it is contradictory that someone has confessed, and that by the statute of the Church he is bound to confess the same sins again, especially since, having so confessed, he has fulfilled the precept of the statute, as is the case here. Hence it follows that the assumption is false on that side, and as to the examples which are put forward, I reply that

units.la: Contains marginal line numbers 5 to 50 in the right margin, not reproduced as text. exempla in multis deficiunt, quæ non sunt hic reperta: quia ad hoc, quod exempla essent conformia exemplato, oporteret, quod nullus posset audire missam, nec offerre apud fratres, nisi de licentia proprii sacerdotis, & quod celebrare missas vel recipere oblationes esset actus iurisdictionis, qui non posset à non suo iudice exerceri, & quod parochiani essent obligati audiendi missam proprii sacerdotis vel alterius de licentia eiusdem. & igitur consimiliter sibi offerendum, q etiā eiusdem plebis essent multi proprii sacerdotes, qui possent missas celebrare & oblationes recipere: & ad hæc facienda aliis licentiam impertiri, & quod tandem fratres haberent à Papa & episcopis ac parochialib. curatis vel ab aliquo eorundem licentiam ad prædicta, & multa similia ad conformitatem faciendam essent requisita, quæ in toto vel in maiori parte deficiunt in exemplis positis, quibus positis esset similis repugnantia vtrobique. Quarto aliter respondetur, quod scilicet assumptum est falsum secundum aliquos pro eo quod supponit, quod confessio sacramentalis eorum peccatorum sit iterabilis non ex eo, quod absolutio vera, quam exigit & includit, secundum quod est sacramentalis, vel quam requirit ad hoc quod sit sacramentalis, sicut patuit ex tertia conclusione tertii capituli, iterabilis non est: & pro eo etiam, quod debitum vel necessitas sacramenti pœnitentiæ, quæ consurgit ex peccato actuali commisso, vel ex reatu culpæ inde contracto iterabilis non est pro eodem peccato: nisi dicatur, quod idem peccatum vel reatus eiusdem potest redire, quod communiter non tenetur: non sequitur, quod assumptum in ea parte secundum istos est falsum. & quicquid sit de illis, hoc verum est, quod consessio prædicta non potest aliter iterari quam absolutio, quam coexigit & requirit, & quod debitum vel necessitas sacramenti pœnitentiæ quam præsupponit poterunt iterari: de quo peccato dicetur postea.
units.tr: Examples fail in many respects, and these are not found here. For the examples to conform to the model, it would be necessary that no one could hear mass or offer at the brethren's altar except by licence of his own priest; that celebrating masses or receiving offerings were an act of jurisdiction, which could not be exercised by one who is not his own judge; and that parishioners were bound to hear mass from their own priest, or from another with his licence. Likewise, for the conformity, it would have to be granted that there were many proper priests of the same parish who could celebrate masses and receive offerings and grant permission to others to do so; and that the friars had licence from the Pope, the bishops, and the parish curates, or from one of them, for these things. Many similar conditions would also be required for the conformity, and these are wholly or for the most part lacking in the examples given. Were they supplied, there would be a like contradiction on both sides. Fourthly, it is answered in another way, that the assumption is false according to some, because it supposes that sacramental confession of those sins can be repeated. The true absolution which it demands and includes, insofar as it is sacramental, or which it requires in order to be sacramental, as became clear from the third conclusion of the third chapter, cannot be repeated. Nor can the debt or necessity of the sacrament of penance, which arises from an actual sin committed or from the guilt of fault contracted thereby, be repeated for the same sin, unless it is said that the same sin or its guilt can return, which is commonly not held. It does not follow, according to these men, that the assumption in that part is false. And whatever be the case with them, this is true: the aforesaid confession cannot be repeated apart from the absolution which it co-requires and demands, whereas the debt or necessity of the sacrament of penance which it presupposes can be repeated. About that sin it will be said later.

units.la: Et tunc ad auctoritates beati Augustini de vera & falsa pœnitentia, & aliorum Doctorum, qui dicunt, quod confessio non solum est iterabilis, sed quod de eisdem peccatis meritorie iteratur. Respondetur quod Aug. & alii Doctores non dicunt hoc de confessione sacramentali, quæ est tertia pars sacramenti pœnitentiæ distincta contra contritionem & satisfactionem: sed de confessione, quæ est pars satisfactionis, prout includit erubescentiam, quæ est pœna satisfactoria, sicut est ieiunium ac cilicium & similia. quod evidenter patet ex auctoritate beati Augustini inducta, cum dicit, quod dignus est misericordia, qui sp rituali labore petit gratiam non enim loquitur de misericordia, qua remittitur reatus culpæ quia ille remittitur in prima confessione; nec de gratia infusa in contritione: sed de gratia & remissione pœnæ temporalis remanentis post confessionem, pœnitentiam & contritionem. Similiter in eadem auctoritate vocat hanc confessionem spiritualem laborem, id est, pœnam. laborat, inquit, mens patiendo erubescentiam concludit; & quoniam verecundia magna est pœna, qui erubescit pro Christo de peccatis, dignus est misericordia; & per consequens loquitur de confessione quæ est pœna satisfactoria. quod etiam patet, cum subinfert: quanto ergo pluribus confitetur sub spe veniæ turpitudinem criminis: tanto facilius consequitur gratiam remissionis. Ex quo patet, quod non loquitur de gratia seu venia, quæ fuit facta in confessione prima & contritione seu absolutione; sed de illa, quæ fit per quamcunque pœnam satisfactoriam, sicut est verecundia prædicta; & ieiunium & cilicium & eleemosyna, & similia. Vel potest dici, quod B. Augustinus loquitur de crimine publico, patet in eodem libro modicum post; Si peccatum, inquit occultum est, sufficit referre in notitiam sacerdotis: non dicit sacerdotum. & sequitur: intus suscitavit puellam, quam intus inuenit, id est, in occulto. secus autem de illis, quos inuenit extra; ut patet ibidem. Ex quibus patet, quod illud argumentum, quod credebatur insolubile, non deficit nisi in duobus, scilicet, in materia, quia sumit multa falsa; & in forma, quia conclusio non sequitur ex assumptis, & miror quod tantus clericus non viderit hæc prædicta.
units.tr: And as for the authorities of blessed Augustine on true and false penance, and of other teachers, who say that confession is not only repeatable but is also repeated meritoriously for the same sins: the answer is that Augustine and the other teachers do not say this of sacramental confession, which is the third part of the sacrament of penance, distinct from contrition and satisfaction; they speak of the confession which is a part of satisfaction, insofar as it includes shame, which is a satisfactory penalty, as are fasting, sackcloth and the like. This is evident from the passage of blessed Augustine cited, where he says that he is worthy of mercy who seeks grace by spiritual labour. He is not speaking of the mercy by which the guilt of fault is remitted, for that is remitted at the first confession, nor of the grace infused in contrition, but of the grace and remission of the temporal punishment remaining after confession, penance and contrition. Likewise, in the same passage he calls this spiritual confession a labour, that is, a penalty: the mind labours, he says, by suffering shame, and he concludes: since shame is a great penalty, whoever blushes for Christ over his sins is worthy of mercy; and consequently he speaks of the confession which is a satisfactory penalty. This is also clear when he adds: therefore the more one confesses the shame of his crime, in hope of pardon, the more easily one obtains the grace of forgiveness. From this it is plain that he is not speaking of the grace or pardon which was granted in the first confession, contrition or absolution, but of that which is obtained through any satisfactory penalty, such as the aforesaid shame, fasting, sackcloth, almsgiving and the like. Or it may be said that blessed Augustine is speaking of public crime; this appears in the same book a little later: If the sin is hidden, he says, it is enough to report it to the knowledge of the priest. He does not say of the priests. And he goes on: he raised up within the girl, whom he found within, that is, in secret; otherwise with those whom he found outside, as is evident in the same place. From these things it is clear that the argument which was thought insoluble fails in only two respects: in its matter, because it assumes many false things, and in its form, because the conclusion does not follow from the assumptions. I wonder that so learned a clergyman did not see these things.

units.la: Secundo arguit sic: Dominus Martinus Papa quartus in fine privilegii fratribus concessi adiecit sic: Volumus autem, quod hi qui fratribus confitebuntur eisdem suis parochialibus presbyteris confiteri semel in anno prout generale concilium statuit nihilominus tenantur, &c. Unde sequitur, quod huius domini voluntas sic expressa tenuit vim præcepti. igitur confessi pro tunc tenebātur eadem peccata, quæ confessi fuerant, iterum confiteri. Ad istud respondeo concedendo, quod dominus Papa illa verba adiecit in fine privilegii, ex quibus verbis nec in forma sua nec ad intellectum domini Papæ sequitur, quod ipse voluit confessos fratribus eadem peccata parochialibus presbyteris iterum confiteri: nec sequitur quod ipsi tenebantur itetum confiteri. Tum quia dominus Papa non dixit volumus quod hi qui fratribus confitebuntur eisdem semel eodem anno & de eisdem peccatis, quæ confessi fuerant, tenean-tur suis parochialib. presbyteris iterum confiteri. Tum etiam quia adiecit, prout generale concilium statuit, & constat quod concilium generale nunquam statuit confessionem factam fratribus vel alienis de licentia proprii sacerdotis vel aliunde legitime factā quo ad eisdem peccata seu crimina iteranda. Alioquin sequeretur, quod confessi alienis de quacunque licentia proprii sacerdotis & confessi Papæ vel episcopis seu pœnitentiariis eorundem tenerentur eadem peccata iterum confiteri. Tum quia illud statutum non obligat ad confitendum peccata plene dimissa; quia tunc quilibet teneretur semel in anno confiteri omnia, quæ fecit à iuventute, quod est falsum. igitur ex quo Papæ verba præmissa limitarad statutum, sequitur quod non intendebat, quod confessi fratribus tenerentur iterum eadem peccata confiteri. quare non sequitur conclusio, quam deducit. Et si dicatur, quod secundum hanc responsionem nihil operatur illa adiectio domini Papæ prædicta: respondetur, quod non sequitur, quia obiectio temouet errorem, qui potest contingere, & qui forte contingebat illis verbis priuilegiis aliis non adiectis. Nam saltem simplices scientes, quod ante huiusmodi priuilegia tenebantur semel in anno soli proprio sacerdoti, vel alieno de licentia proprii sacerdotis, & audientes quod parochiani poterant ex statuto ecclesiae licite confiteri fratribus habentibus generalem licentiam Papae vel episcoporum, inferiorum licentia minime requisita, poterant credere quod statutum praedictum esset similiter sublatum, sicut credit Dominus iste in casu praesenti, nisi confessi fratribus teneantur eadem iterum confiteri. quem errorem iste dominus voluit remouere, ostendens quod statutum semper obligat in genere, quamuis non in specie quoad peccata fratribus confessa ita voluit remouere errorem in parte, quod scilicet confessi fratribus teneantur confiteri proprio sacerdoti: prout generale concilium statuit, & tamen non tenentur confiteri peccata legitime praeconfessa. & sicremanet statutum quoad obligationem eius primam supradictam, non quo ad secundam. Aliter respondetur, quia dato hoc falso: scilicet quod tunc confessi habentibus licentiam generalem audiendi confessiones tenebantur confessa peccata eisdem iterum confiteri: tamen non ex hoc sequitur, quod modo consimiliter teneantur. & hoc ideo: quia alia est licentia generalis, quam nunc fratres, & alia quam tunc habuerunt. Nam licentia audiendi confessiones, quam nunc habent fratres, est generalis quo ad omnes fratres praesentatos & admissos: & ad omnes earundem dioecesium pro quibus praesentantur eis confiteri volentium & quo ad omnes vitos ecclesiasticos quorum poterat vel poterit interesse, qui sacro instante & approbante concilio hanc licentiam concesserunt & consenserunt ad eandem: & per consequens haec licentia non solum est Papae, sed episcoporum seu etiam parochialium sacerdotum curatorum: nisi dicatur, quod parochiales curati vel non sunt ab ecclesia, vel non consenserunt vere vel interpretatine hoc quod concesit & ordinauit concilium generale. Illa vero licentia, quam tunc habebant, quamuis esset generalis quo ad personas fratrum & etiam aliorum eis confiteri volentium: tamen non fuit ita generalis quoad personas huiusmodi licentiam concedentes. & per consequens fiat simul, quod confessi fratrib. habentib. generalem licentiam tenebantur eadem peccata iterum confiteri: vel saltem quod hoc asserere non fuerit nec sit erroneum: & quod confessi fratribus hanc licentiam generalem modernam non tenentur eadem peccata iterum confiteri: sed quod sit erroneum & haereticum asserere pertinaciter, quod teneantur eadem peccata iterum confiteri: & maxime ex quo huiusmodi assertio isto modo est damnata, quae illo modo non fuit damnata: & tamen in rei veritate aeque falsa fuit illa assertio, sicut ista, sicut dicebatur in responsione praecedenti. & sic patet, quomodo dominus Martinus & sui sequaces non fuerunt contrarii in hac parte.
units.tr: Secondly, he argues thus: Lord Martin the Fourth, Pope, added at the end of the privilege granted to the friars these words: We will, moreover, that those who confess to the friars shall nevertheless be bound to confess to their own parish elders once a year, as the general council has decreed, etc. Hence it follows that the will of this lord, so expressed, held the force of a precept; therefore those who had then confessed were bound to confess again to their parish priests the same sins which they had confessed. To this I answer, granting that the lord Pope added those words at the end of the privilege; but from those words, neither in their form nor according to the Pope's intention, does it follow that he wished those who had confessed to the friars to confess again to their parish elders the same sins, nor that they were bound to confess again. First, because the lord Pope did not say: we will that those who confess to the friars, once in the same year and of the same sins which they had confessed, be bound to confess again to their parish elders. Second, because he added as the general council has decreed, and it is certain that the general council never decreed that a confession made to the friars, or to others with the licence of one's own priest, or otherwise lawfully made, must be repeated as to the same sins or crimes. Otherwise it would follow that those who had confessed to others with any licence of their own priest, and those who had confessed to the Pope, the bishops, or their penitentiaries, would be bound to confess again the same sins. Third, because that statute does not oblige one to confess sins fully forgiven; for then everyone would be bound once a year to confess everything he had done from youth, which is false. Therefore, since the Pope's words above limit the statute, it follows that he did not intend that those who had confessed to the friars be bound to confess the same sins again; so the conclusion which he deduces does not follow. And if it is said that on this answer that addition of the lord Pope accomplishes nothing, the answer is that it does not follow, because the objection removes an error which could arise, and which perhaps did arise, when those words were absent from the other privileges. For at least simple people, knowing that before such privileges they were bound once a year to confess only to their own priest, or to another with the licence of their own priest, and hearing that parishioners could lawfully confess to friars having the Pope's or bishops' general licence, without requiring the licence of inferiors, could believe that the aforesaid statute had likewise been abolished, as this lord believes in the present case, unless those who had confessed to the friars were bound to confess the same things again. This error the lord wished to remove, showing that the statute always binds in general, though not in particular as to sins confessed to the friars. He wished to remove the error in part, namely that those who confessed to the friars must confess to their own priest, as the general council decreed, and yet they are not bound to confess sins already lawfully confessed. Thus the statute remains in force as to its first obligation stated above, not as to the second. Otherwise it is answered: even granting this false claim, namely that those who then had a general licence to hear confessions were bound to confess again the sins already confessed to them, it still does not follow that those now are bound in the same way. This is because the general licence which the friars now have is other than the one they then had. For the licence to hear confessions which the friars now have is general as to all friars presented and admitted, and as to all those of the dioceses for whom they are presented, who wish to confess to them, and as to all ecclesiastical persons over whom it could or can extend; it was granted and consented to by those who, with the council sitting and approving, gave and consented to this licence. Consequently this licence belongs not only to the Pope but also to the bishops and to the parish curates, unless it is said that the parish curates either are not of the Church, or have not truly or by interpretation consented to what the general council granted and ordained. But the licence which they then had, although it was general as to the persons of the friars and of others who wished to confess to them, was not so general as to the persons granting such licence. Consequently it follows at once that those who had confessed to friars holding a general licence were bound to confess the same sins again, or at least that to assert this was not and is not erroneous; and that those who have confessed to the friars under the present general licence are not bound to confess the same sins again; but it is erroneous and heretical to assert stubbornly that they must confess those sins again. This is especially so since such an assertion has now been condemned in this form, which was not condemned in that form; yet in the truth of the matter that assertion was equally false as this one, as was said in the preceding answer. And so it is evident how lord Martin and his followers were not at odds with one another on this point.

units.la: Et per hoc respondetur ad argumenta alia cum arguitur sic, quod dominus Clemens diffiniret oppositum decreti aut statuti domini Martini, cum de hoc nullam facit mentionem, verisimile non videtur. Item de hac auctoritate dominorum summorum pontificum quisque poterit merito fluctuare occasione praestita per eosdem, si quod unus statuit, alter erroneum diffinuit.
units.tr: And this answers the other arguments, when it is argued thus: that Lord Clement would have defined the opposite of the decree or statute of Lord Martin. Since he makes no mention of this, it does not seem likely. Likewise, on the authority of these supreme pontiffs, anyone may reasonably waver, given the occasion offered by them, if one of them ruled one thing and another defined the opposite as erroneous.

units.la: Ad quod respondetur iuxta rationem primam secundi articuli: quod Clemens non diffinivit contrarium statuti domini Martini: quia Martinus non statuit eadem peccata in confessione iteranda; & dato quod fecisset, non fuisset ad propositum: eo quod diffinitio unius & statutum alterius non fuerunt super eodem alia & alia existente generali licentia vtrobique. Et consimiliter dico ex eisdem rationibus: nihil quod unus statuit alter oppositum diffinuit, sicut patet ex praemissis.
units.tr: To this it is answered, in line with the first reason of the second article, that Clement did not define the contrary of Lord Martin's statute, because Martin did not lay down that the same sins must be repeated in confession. And even if he had, it would not have been to the point, since the definition of one and the statute of another, concerning the same matter, were not in conflict, as each had a general license on both sides. I say the same for the same reasons: nothing that one ruled has been defined by another as its opposite, as is clear from what has been said above.

units.la: Item arguitur sic: constitutio synodalis domini episcopi Auinionen. edita per dominum Iohannem quodam episcopum ibidem, & confirmata per dominum Clementem sextum iam praesentem, fuit & est, quod si aliquis a quatuordecim annis & supra, confiteri contempsit saltem semel in anno suo proprio sacerdoti, aut alteri de eius licentia: si vnquam fuerit ei vsque ad satisfactionem condignam ingressus ecclesiam. Si autem mortuus fuerit ei ecclesiastica interdicatur sepultura. ex quibus videtur sequi, quod secundum illos dominos illae duae affirmatiuae simul stabunt. Respondetur, quod constitutio synodalis fuit & est bona & sancta, & nihil aliud statuens, quam quod in statuto conciliigen-ralis continetur. & ideo confessi fratribus implent praeceptum constitutionis & statuti, & euadunt consimiliter poenam vtriusque.
units.tr: Again it is argued thus: the synodal constitution of the lord bishop of Avignon, issued by Lord John, a bishop there, and confirmed by Lord Clement VI, now present, was and is that if anyone from the age of fourteen and upward has neglected to confess at least once a year to his own priest, or to another with his license, then, if he ever enters the church before making condign satisfaction, [let him be punished]. If he dies, ecclesiastical burial is to be denied him. From this it seems to follow that, according to those lords, these two affirmatives will stand together. It is answered that the synodal constitution was and is good and holy, and decrees nothing other than what is contained in the statute of the general council. Therefore those who confess to the friars fulfil the precept of the constitution and the statute, and likewise escape the penalty of both.

units.la: Item arguit per dominum Innocentium quartum, qui fecit quandam constitutionem seu rescriptum, quod incipit: Et sicanimarum, vbi sic scribit Fratribus: Vniuersitati vestrae per apostolica scripta mandamus, vt parochianos alienos diebus dominicis & festiuis non recipiatis decetero in vestris ecclesiis seu oratoriis ad diuina: nec ipsos sine suis sacerdotis licentia ad poenitentiam ullatenus admittatis: tamen si quis alienos sacerdoti iusta de causa voluerit confiteri peccata sua iuxta statutum concilii generalis licentiam primum postulare ac obtinere debeat proprii sacerdotis: vel saltem sibi primo confiteri & accipere beneficium absolutionis ab eodem. Aliter namque ab ipso absolui non poterit nec ligari, & e contra, si quis vero huius nostrae prohibitionis transgressor contra praemissa vel aliquid praemissorum venire praesumpserit, praeter inobedientiam volumus gradus sui periculo subiacebit, &c.
units.tr: Again he argues from Lord Innocent IV, who issued a certain constitution or rescript, beginning "Et sicut animarum," in which he writes thus to the Friars: "We command your university by apostolic writing that from now on you do not receive other men's parishioners into your churches or oratories for divine services on Sundays and feast days, nor in any way admit them to penance without the license of their own priest. Yet if anyone, for a just cause, wishes to confess his sins to another priest, in accordance with the statute of the general council, he ought first to ask for and obtain license from his own priest, or at least first confess to him and receive the benefit of absolution from him. For otherwise he cannot be absolved or bound by that priest. On the other hand, if anyone presumes to transgress this our prohibition, or to act against any part of what has been said, we want him to be liable to the penalty of his rank, besides his disobedience," etc.

units.la: Ad illud respondetur: & dico, quod haec omnia per successorem eius Alexandrum quartum fuerunt plenarie revocata, tanquam talia quae per occupationem vel festinantiam, congruae deliberationis limam praeteribant, sicut patet in bulla eiusdem. Nec insolitum itum est nec iouum, quod etiam salua reuerentia debita & devota sic poterit errare: quia cum ibidem dicatur, quod si quis alieno sacerdoti iusta de causa volucrit confiteri iuxta statutum concilii generalis, licentiam obtinere debeat proprii sacerdotis: vel saltem sibi primo confiteri, & absolutionis beneficium recipere ab eodem. hoc secundum videtur destrui ratione. cum enim parochianus habeat unam causam, te subtrahendi a suo sacerdote parochiali, quomodo potest sibi confiteri, sinon potest suam licentiam ut confiteatur alteri, obtinere? quare sequitur, quod hoc ... in summa propositum nihil facit, & dato quod rescriptum in suo robore permanserit, dicitur ... cui in responsione secunda ad rescriptum domini Martini fuit responsum.
units.tr: To this it is answered, and I say, that all these things were fully revoked by his successor Alexander IV, as things passed through haste or occupation, without the careful file of mature deliberation, as is clear from his bull. Nor is it unusual or unjust, with due and devout reverence, that such a thing could err in this way. For since it is there said that if anyone for a just cause wishes to confess to another priest, in accordance with the statute of the general council, he ought to obtain license from his own priest, or at least first confess to him and receive the benefit of absolution from him, this second part seems to be destroyed by reason. For when a parishioner has one reason to withdraw from his parish priest, how can he confess to him, if he cannot obtain license to confess to another? Hence it follows that this proposition in sum has no bearing, and even granting that the rescript remained in force, it is said... to which an answer was given in the second response to the rescript of Lord Martin.

units.la: Item arguit sic. Fratres habent de more, ut dicitur, quod quilibet apud eos professus tenetur prius vice alicui ipsorum omnia peccata sua mortalia confiteri. Mirandum est igitur, cur non sentiant ecclesiam etiam de aliis, sicut de se ipsis, cur non fatentur se haereticos aut erraticos, sed alios economo. Ad quod respondeo, quod si dominus reputet hoc argumentum esse aeque bonum: iste dominus habet de more, ut dicitur, sentire & docere aliquos de peccatorum confessione aliter quam sacrosancta Romana ecclesia praedicat & observat. Est igitur mirabile, cur non incidit in capitulum extra de haereticis, cum argumentum illud non sit melius quam sit istud: ideo unico responsione respondeat ad utrumque. Verum tamen (quod ego sciam) fratres nunquam habuerunt de more hoc, quod dicit. Habent tamen de more, quod consulunt eisdem, quod confiteantur pure, & maxime si incurrerint aliquas poenas & sententias iuris, a quibus fratres possunt absolvere omnes volentes suo consortio aggregari.
units.tr: Again he argues thus. It is customary among the friars, as is said, that whoever is professed among them must first confess all his mortal sins to one of them. It is therefore to be wondered at why they do not think the Church should do the same, as they do for themselves; why they do not confess that they are heretics or wanderers, but call others so. To this I answer that if the lord considers this argument to be equally good, then this lord, as is said, customarily thinks and teaches some things about the confession of sins differently from what the most holy Roman Church preaches and observes. It is therefore strange why he has not fallen under the chapter Extra de haereticis, since that argument is no better than this one. So let him answer both with one response. Yet (so far as I know) the friars have never had the custom he describes. They do, however, have the custom of advising those who wish to be received into their fellowship to confess sincerely, especially if they have incurred any penalties or sentences of law, from which the friars can absolve all who wish to join their company.

units.la: Item arguit sic. Monachi alibi habent eandem constitutionem, sc. quod quilibet confessus alicui monacho ipsius conventus & de licentia sui abbatis, nihilominus tenetur semel in anno confiteri suo abbati. Cur igitur similia non sunt in fratribus & curatis, fratres habent ostendere, & hoc monachos condemnare. Hinc respondetur, quod quamvis iste dominus per istud argumentum velit monachos contra pauperes fratres concitare, tamen non erit per Dei gratiam quod intendit. Et ideo dico, quod monachi habent hanc constitutionem de hac materia, quod monachi & conversi, qui saltem semel in anno abbati proprio, cuius copia habuerunt, fideliter & integre negligerent confiteri, vincula excommunicationis incurrerunt, nisi sint innotuerint iretitos, in qua nulla fit mentio de his, qui ex licentia abbatis sunt confessi alicui monacho: & ideo male allegat constitutionem monachorum contra fratres. Et ideo si monachus esset confessus alicui monacho de licentia sui abbatis, non teneretur de iure ex vi huius statuti illa peccata, de quibus est legitime absolutus, suo abbati iterum confiteri.
units.tr: Again he argues thus. Monks elsewhere have the same constitution, namely that anyone who has confessed to a monk of the same convent, with the license of his abbot, is nonetheless bound to confess once a year to his own abbot. Why then are there not similar rules for the friars and parish priests? The friars must show this, and in doing so condemn the monks. To this it is answered that although this lord, by this argument, wants to stir up the monks against the poor friars, by God's grace it will not turn out as he intends. And so I say that the monks have this constitution on this matter: that monks and converts who, at least once a year, faithfully and completely neglect to confess to their own abbot, of whom they have had the opportunity, incur the bonds of excommunication, unless they have been declared to be bound by it. No mention is made there of those who have confessed to a monk with the abbot's license. Therefore he wrongly cites the constitution of the monks against the friars. And so, if a monk had confessed to another monk with his abbot's license, he would not be bound by law, by virtue of this statute, to confess again to his abbot those sins from which he has been lawfully absolved.

units.la: Dato etiam, quod monachi praedictum statutum sic interpretentur & observent: scilicet quod monachus confessus de licentia sui abbatis teneatur eadem peccata, quae confessus est monacho, & de quibus virtute praefatae licentiae est plene absolutus ab eodem suo abbate, iterum confiteri. quamvis in hoc orbitent a communi iure sicut notum est. nullus enim confessus alicui de licentia parochialis curati tenetur idem peccatum, quod confessus est tali, & de quo virtute praefatae licentiae est plene absolutus, parochiali curato iterum confiteri: tamen ex hoc non sequitur, quod consimiliter fieri debeat vel possit in alia parte. Et causa est, quia cum duplex est confessio, sicut supradictum est, sc. sacramentalis, quae est tertia pars sacramenti poenitentiae, quae receptionem absolutionis & effectum coexigit & includit; & alia quae non est sacramentalis, nec includens praedicta, quarum prima de iure communi venit sub obligatione, quia ex vi sacramenti poenitentiae est necessaria ad salutem peccatoris postquam mortaliter peccavit. Secunda autem quamvis sit licita, meritoria atque sancta: quia tamen est difficilis & contra inclinationem omnium hominum generaliter, & non est sic necessaria ad salutem; ideo non potest alicui sine suo consensu venire regulariter sub praecepto. Cum igitur monachi & alii regulares propter votum obedientiae non habent confessum nec voluntatem, nisi voluntatem suorum praelatorum, saltem in his in quibus sunt eis subiecti: & ideo quicquid volunt praelati, illud debet dici referendo ad voluntatem suae professionis vere esse & est de consensu subditorum. & ideo si praelati monachorum sic constitutionem illam interpretentur & observent, hoc faciunt de consensu vere vel interpretatione subditorum. & ideo ipsi remanent obligati: tamen sic non est in alia parte. Seculares enim & alii parochiani habent propriam suam voluntatem, & ideo sine suo consensu non possunt sic regulariter obligari. Quare ex statuto sic interpretato monachorum non potest inferri similis interpretatio, nec quod possit fieri universalis constitutio ex parte secularium aliorum. & sic argumentum non concludit.
units.tr: Granted, even, that the monks interpret and observe the aforesaid statute in this way: namely, that a monk who has confessed with his abbot's license must confess again to the same abbot the sins he has confessed to a monk and of which he has been fully absolved by virtue of that license. Even so, they stray from common law, as is well known. For no one who has confessed, with the license of a parish priest, to another person is bound to confess again to his parish priest the same sin he confessed to that person and of which he has been fully absolved by virtue of that license. Yet it does not follow from this that the same should be done or could be done in the other case. The reason is that confession is twofold, as said above: sacramental confession, which is the third part of the sacrament of penance, and which requires and includes the reception of absolution and its effect; and confession which is not sacramental and does not include those things. The first, by common law, falls under obligation, because by virtue of the sacrament of penance it is necessary for the salvation of a sinner who has sinned mortally. The second, although it is lawful, meritorious and holy, is difficult and generally contrary to the inclination of all men, and is not so necessary for salvation. Therefore it cannot ordinarily be brought under precept for anyone without his consent. Since monks and other regulars, by reason of the vow of obedience, have no will of their own but the will of their superiors, at least in those matters in which they are subject to them, whatever the superiors wish must be said, with reference to the will of their profession, to truly be and to be the consent of the subjects. Therefore, if the superiors of the monks interpret and observe that constitution in this way, they do so with the true consent or interpretation of the subjects, and so they remain bound. But it is not so in the other case. Secular men and other parishioners have their own will, and so cannot be regularly bound in this way without their consent. Hence from the statute of the monks, so interpreted, no similar interpretation can be inferred, nor that a universal constitution could be made on the part of other secular men. And so the argument does not conclude.

units.la: Item arguitur sic: est regula scripta, in corde cuiuslibet, quod legis praeceptum obligatorium per factum voluntarium a quoquam obligato dissolui non potest. cum igitur confessio facienda semper sacerdoti sic obligatoria, & confessio facienda fratri sit voluntaria, per hanc secundam ... legis praeceptum. Ad istud dico, quod si primum assumptum sic intelligatur, quod factum voluntarium sic dissolvit praeceptum simpliciter, quin etiam quod tunc ... praecepto (quia si aliter intelligitur, non potest sequi conclusio ex assumptione. Secundum assumptum non est verum nec sanum: sed merito est suspectum. Quia ex isto ... nulla potest ... sed tene-atur
units.tr: Likewise it is argued thus: there is a rule written in everyone's heart that a binding precept of the law cannot be dissolved by a voluntary act of anyone who is bound by it. Since, therefore, confession that must always be made to a priest is binding in this way, and confession made to a brother is voluntary, [it follows] by this second ... of the law's precept. To this I reply that if the first assumption is understood to mean that a voluntary act simply dissolves the precept, indeed that then ... the precept (for if it is understood otherwise, the conclusion cannot follow from the assumption). The second assumption is neither true nor sound, but is rightly suspect. Because from this ... nothing can ... but he is held

units.la: {i} ... alicui monacho de licentia ... atur implere præceptum: cum sic vti, sit factum voluntarium; & per consequens nullus potest dispensare super aliquo præcepto: & sequuntur multa inconvenientia & suspecta, quæ supra in isto capitulo sunt deducta. Sequitur etiam quod præceptum disiunctivum non posset implseri: quia per nullam partem disiunctionis: cum quodlibet sit pure voluntaria per se sumptum, nec per utramque copulatiue, quia non est dubium, quod non tenetur ex præcepto facere utramque. & per consequens facere utramque est pure voluntarium, & non deobligat eum a præcepto: quare sequitur, quod iste non potest implere præceptum: quod est satis absurdum. Secundum etiam assumptum est falsum: scilicet quod confessio facienda proprio sacerdoti est obligatoria: & maxime si intelligatur, quod fiat personaliter proprio sacerdoti; quia sufficit quod fiat de eius licentia alieno.
units.tr: ... to some monk by licence ... he is bound to fulfil the precept: for to use it in this way is a voluntary act, and consequently no one can dispense from any precept. And many inconveniences and suspect consequences follow, which have been drawn out above in this chapter. It also follows that a disjunctive precept could not be fulfilled, since by neither part of the disjunction, because each taken by itself is purely voluntary, nor by both together conjunctively, since there is no doubt that he is not bound by precept to do both. And consequently doing both is purely voluntary and does not release him from the precept. Hence it follows that this man cannot fulfil the precept, which is quite absurd. The second assumption is also false, namely that confession to be made to one's own priest is binding, and especially if it is understood that it must be made in person to one's own priest, since it is sufficient that it be made to another with his licence.

units.la: Item arguit sic: si stante fratrum privilegio daretur nouiter præceptum omnis utriusque, confessus fratri teneretur semel in anno sacerdoti proprio confiteri. Sed præceptum ita arctat modo, sicut si nouiter fieret in præsenti: quia est eiusdem auctoritatis & formæ. Igitur confessi fratribus tenentur iterum confiteri. Huic respondeo, quod primum assumptum est falsum; quia, sicut frequenter dictum est, statutum non obligat nunc: nec tunc obligaret aliquem ad confitendum determinate & personaliter proprio sacerdoti. Secundum etiam assumptum, scilicet quod præceptum modo ita arctat confessum fratri, sicut si nouiter fieret in præsenti, si intelligatur generaliter, sicut apparet quod intelligat Dominus iste, quod nulla diversitas proveniat ex ordine, ubi est eadem auctoritas & forma præcepti: si, inquam, sic intelligatur, est negandum tanquam erroneum & suspectum. quod patet sic. constat enim, quod decretum primi parentis de inseparabili vnione coniugum expressum per illa verba, relinquet homo patrem & matrem, &c. Gen. 2. fuit factum auctoritate Dei, sicut patet Matth. 19. & Mar. 10. capitulis. postea vero Deus dedit Hebræis privilegium de libello repudii, Deutero. 9. Et iterum idem Deus revocavit suum præceptum, & protoplasti decretum eadem auctoritate & forma qua prius. Si igitur præcedens privilegium ita arctat privilegiatos, sicut sequens præceptum; sequitur quod filii Israel modo post revocatum præceptum dando libellum repudii & aliis mulieribus nubendo non committunt adulterium: quod est contra euangelium vbi sup. vel quod filii Israel tempore legis consimiliter faciendo peccabant & tenebantur præcepto obligati, sicut modo. & commiserunt adulterium ex privilegio; & quod transgrediendo præceptum simul peccabant mortaliter, & fuerunt excusati a peccato per concessum privilegium; quod est nimis erroneum & suspectum.
units.tr: Likewise he argues thus: if, while the privilege of the friars stands, a new precept of confessing to each and every priest were given, one who had confessed to a friar would be bound to confess once a year to his own priest. But the precept now binds in the same way as if it were newly made at present, because it is of the same authority and form. Therefore those who have confessed to friars are bound to confess again. To this I reply that the first assumption is false, because, as has often been said, a statute does not bind now, nor would it then bind anyone to confess specifically and personally to his own priest. The second assumption also, namely that the precept now binds one who has confessed to a friar in the same way as if it were newly made at present, if it is understood generally, as this author evidently means, that no difference arises from the order, where there is the same authority and form of precept: if, I say, it is understood thus, it must be denied as erroneous and suspect. This is clear as follows. It is certain that the decree of the first parent concerning the inseparable union of spouses, expressed in these words, leave his father and mother, etc. (Gen. 2.), was made by the authority of God, as appears in Matth. 19 and Mar. 10. Afterwards, however, God gave the Hebrews the privilege of a bill of divorce (Deut. 9). And again the same God revoked his precept and the decree of the first-formed man by the same authority and form as before. If, therefore, the earlier privilege binds the privileged in the same way as the later precept, it follows either that the sons of Israel, after the precept had been revoked, by giving a bill of divorce and marrying other women, do not commit adultery, which is contrary to the Gospel loc. cit., or that the sons of Israel in the time of the law, doing the same thing, sinned and were bound by the precept as now, and yet they committed adultery by privilege, and that by transgressing the precept they at the same time sinned mortally, and were excused from sin by the privilege granted. This is far too erroneous and suspect.

units.la: Item arguit de illo, qui fecit votum, quod quacunque confessione facta vel facienda enicunque non obstante confiteretur semel in anno suo proprio sacerdoti, ex quo talis teneretur votum implere; & cum præceptum ita arcte obligat, sicut votum; pari ratione quilibet tenetur modo præceptum implere. Ad quod dico, quod si aliquis simile votum fecisset de confitendo fratri, æque sequeretur quod talis teneretur eadem peccata, quæ confessus fuit proprio sacerdoti, tali fratri iterum confiteri, & non dubium quod neutrum sequitur ex vi statuti: & ideo argumentum non est ad propositum. Quando tamen inferatur, quod pari ratione modo tenetur quilibet ex præcepto, negatur consequentia. Tum quia nullum est præceptum, quod obligat aliquem ad confitendum determinate & personaliter proprio sacerdoti. Tum etiam quia, sicut dictum est in solutione secundi argumenti, non potest passim præcipi, quod homo confessus uni postea confiteatur alteri, sicut potest voueri. quare argumentum non concludit. Et conformiter negatur ad argumentum sequens, cum dicitur, quod confessus fratri posset accipere a fratre loco pœnitentiæ, quod confiteatur eadem postea proprio sacerdoti. videlicet primo, quod illa confessio non fieret ex vi statuti. secundo quod confessio non posset passim imponi. tertio quod ita potest fieri econuerso. quarto quod ex isto argumento & similibus patet quod hæc secunda confessio si fieret, non esset sacramentalis, de qua loquitur statutum, sed esset pœnitentia satisfactoria & latis factionis. quare sequitur, quod huiusmodi confessio est impertinens materiæ quam proponit.
units.tr: Likewise he argues about the man who made a vow that, whatever confession has been or will be made to anyone, he would nevertheless confess once a year to his own priest, since such a man is bound to fulfil the vow; and since the precept binds just as tightly as a vow, by the same reasoning anyone is now bound to fulfil the precept. To this I say that if someone had made a similar vow about confessing to a friar, it would equally follow that such a man was bound to confess again to such a friar the same sins that he had confessed to his own priest; and there is no doubt that neither follows from the force of the statute, and therefore the argument does not bear on the point. Yet when it is inferred that by the same reasoning anyone is now bound by precept, the consequence is denied. Partly because there is no precept that binds anyone to confess specifically and personally to his own priest; partly also because, as was said in the answer to the second argument, it cannot be prescribed generally that a man who has confessed to one should afterwards confess to another, as a vow can be made. Therefore the argument does not conclude. And likewise we deny the following argument, when it is said that one who has confessed to a friar could take from the friar, as repentance, that he should afterwards confess the same things to his own priest. Namely: first, that such a confession would not be made by force of the statute; second, that the confession could not be imposed generally; third, that it can be done the other way round; fourth, that from this argument and similar ones it is clear that this second confession, if it were made, would not be the sacramental confession of which the statute speaks, but would be satisfactory repentance and a work of satisfaction. Hence it follows that a confession of this kind is irrelevant to the matter he proposes.
