units.la: Item simile argumentum est de homine habente conscientiam, quod tenetur proprio sacerdoti iterum confiteri, videlicet quod talis peccaret mortaliter faciendo contra conscientiam suam, nisi iterum confiteatur. ad quod dico, quod si haberet similem conscientiam de confitendo fratribus, pari ratione sequeretur idem, scilicet quod peccaret mortaliter, nisi confiteretur fratri. & similiter si haberet conscientiam, quod eorundem peccatorum confessio nunquam esset iteranda, si eam iteraret, peccaret mortaliter. & per consequens nunquam teneretur confiteri de eisdem. cuius oppositum dicit dominus iste. & ideo quamuis quilibet peccaret, qui ageret contra conscientiam, tamen periculosum esset dicere, quod quilibet teneretur conformiter agere conscientiæ suæ.
units.tr: Likewise a similar argument concerns a man who has a conscience that he must confess again to his own priest, namely that such a man would sin mortally by acting against his conscience unless he confesses again. To this I say that if he had a similar conscience about confessing to friars, by the same reasoning the same would follow, namely that he would sin mortally unless he confessed to a friar. And likewise if he had a conscience that confession of the same sins was never to be repeated, then if he repeated it he would sin mortally, and consequently he would never be bound to confess the same things. But this author says the opposite. And therefore, although anyone who acted against his conscience would sin, it would nevertheless be dangerous to say that anyone was bound to act in accordance with his own conscience.

units.la: Item arguit sic: ponatur, quod aliquis fuerit fratri plene confessus, & quod privilegium confessionis fuerit consequenter suspensum quo ad fratres, & quod iste veniens ad eucharistiam sumendam sit prioris confessionis oblitus, vel quod in eodem casu loco suspensionis credat omnes fratres esse excommunicatos; aut Papa præciperet, quod nullus fratri confiteretur; vel in casu suspensionis aut excommunicationis prætacta confessus fratri negligeret pœnitentiam sibi a fratre iniunctam; seu quod in casu oblivionis seu negligentiæ prædicto confessus fratri non potest etiam aliquem liquem alium confessorem reperire, vel nullum reputaret idoneum, nisi proprium sacerdotem in quibus casibus sequeretur, quod sic confessus fratri teneretur eadem peccata iterum confiteri suo proprio sacerdoti. Ad ista & omnia similia dico, quod in casibus similibus cum econuerso sequeretur, quod confessi proprio sacerdoti tenerentur fratribus eadem iterum confiteri: & tamen neutrum sequitur ex vi statuti, quare suum propositum non concludit. Similiter ex istis casibus & similibus positis, econuerso sequitur, quod confessi fratribus non magis tenentur iterum confiteri eadem peccata proprio sacerdoti, quam si alias eadem fuissent confessi proprio sacerdoti: cuius oppositum deberet concludi.
units.tr: Likewise he argues thus: suppose that someone has fully confessed to a friar, and that the privilege of confession has consequently been suspended as regards the friars, and that this man, coming to receive the Eucharist, has forgotten his earlier confession; or that in the same case, instead of the suspension, he believes all the friars to be excommunicated; or the Pope were to order that no one confess to a friar; or in the case of the aforesaid suspension or excommunication, one who has confessed to a friar neglects the repentance imposed on him by the friar; or that in the case of the forgetfulness or negligence mentioned, one who has confessed to a friar cannot find any other confessor at all, or regards no one as suitable except his own priest. In these cases it would follow that one who has thus confessed to a friar is bound to confess the same sins again to his own priest. To these and all similar cases I say that in similar cases the converse would follow, namely that those who have confessed to their own priest would be bound to confess the same things again to friars; and yet neither follows from the force of the statute, so his proposition is not concluded by it. Likewise, from these and similar cases posited, the converse follows: that those who have confessed to friars are no more bound to confess the same sins again to their own priest than if they had confessed the same things to their own priest in the first place. The opposite ought to have been concluded.

units.la: Item arguit sic, videtur regula generalis, quod Dominus papa nullum statutum antiquum, & praecipue concilii generalis, tollit in toto vel in parte per constitutionem posteriorem priori manifeste non contrariam in intentione vel in verbis, nisi de hoc expressam faceret mentionem. Igitur cum Dominus Clemens in cap. dudum, nullam fecerit mentionem de sublatione concilii generalis omnis utriusque, nec etiam Dominus Iohannes in constitutione Vas electionis, quando videtur illud statutum potius approbasse. Igitur non intendebant illi statuto derogare. Ad q respondeo concedendo conclusionem deductam: quia confessi fratribus habentibus licentiam iuxta formam cap. dudum, sufficienter impleverunt: & plene praeceptum capituli & statuti concilii generalis. & sic illa capitula non derogant statuto, sed erogant: unde potest multiplicius adimpleri.
units.tr: Likewise he argues thus: there seems to be a general rule that the lord Pope does not remove any old statute, and especially that of a general council, wholly or in part, by a later constitution which is not manifestly contrary to it in intention or in words, unless he makes express mention of this. Therefore, since Lord Clement, in cap. dudum, made no mention of the removal of the general council's omnis utriusque, nor did Lord John in the constitution Vas electionis, when he seems rather to have approved that statute, it follows that they did not intend to derogate from that statute. To this I reply by granting the conclusion drawn: for friars who had licence according to the form of cap. dudum have sufficiently fulfilled and fully satisfied the precept of the chapter and of the statute of the general council. Thus those chapters do not derogate from the statute but rather extend it, whence it can be fulfilled in more ways.

units.la: Item arguit sic, non videtur quod aliquis summus pontifex tantum vellet detrahere de merito subditorum, sicut modo fit per intellectum praedictum constitutionis dudum, aut statuti omnis utriusque, satis enim firmiter, ut videtur, in propositione facta coram domino nostro papa & coetu dominorum cardinalium fuit suasum, quod confessio facta proprio sacerdoti fuit securior, utilior & vitans plura incommoda in confessis, in curatis & clero & populo & in ipsis fratribus: quae incommoda proveniunt ex constitutione parochianorum confessionibus fratribus rarum factis quibus cognitis non dubium, quin Dominus papa cum omni celeritate possibili suam constitutionem declararet aut tolleret: alias enim seipsum de mala conscientia damnaret.
units.tr: Likewise he argues thus: it does not seem that any Supreme Pontiff would wish to diminish the merit of his subjects so much as is now done by the aforesaid interpretation of the constitution dudum, or of the statute omnis utriusque. For in the proposal made before our lord the Pope and the college of the lord cardinals, it was argued quite forcefully, as it seems, that confession made to one's own priest is safer, more useful, and avoids many inconveniences for the confessors, for the parish priests, the clergy and the people, and for the brothers themselves. These inconveniences arise from the constitution that parishioners' confessions made to the brothers are rare. Once these were known, there is no doubt that our lord the Pope would declare or revoke his constitution with all possible speed; otherwise he would condemn himself of a bad conscience.

units.la: Ad istud dico, quod nec confessio facta solis fratribus, nec etiam confessio facta solis sacerdotibus personaliter aliquid regulariter detrahit de merito subditorum. potest enim esse & frequenter contingit, quod nunc melius sit confiteri illis, nunc melius confiteri istis, iuxta varias personarum circumstantias.
units.tr: To this I say that neither confession made to the brothers alone, nor confession made to priests alone and personally, takes away anything from the merit of the subjects as a general rule. For it can be, and frequently happens, that at one time it is better to confess to these, at another time to those, according to the varying circumstances of persons.

units.la: Et ad probationem cum allegat se in propositione sua firmiter probasse, quod confessio parochiali facta curato sit securior & utilior & plura vitans incommoda &c. Dico quod in eadem propositione ille Dominus assumpsit ad hoc probandum multa erronea & absurda, ex quibus sequuntur haereses, schismata & rebelliones contra sacrosanctam ecclesiam, inter quae in hac materia assumpsit, quod praeceptum dominicum est, quod cuncta, quae lex praecipit de sacramentis, inter quae computanda est confessio, debent fieri in ecclesia parochiali, ad quae exercenda omnia alia loca sunt a Deo, & de lege eius prohibita.
units.tr: As for his claim that in his proposal he had firmly proved that confession made to the parish priest is safer and more useful and avoids many inconveniences, etc., I say that in that same proposal the lord in question assumed, in order to prove this, many erroneous and absurd things, from which heresies, schisms and rebellions against the holy Church follow. Among these, in this matter, he assumed that it is the Lord's command that all things which the law prescribes concerning the sacraments, among which confession must be counted, must be done in the parish church; and that all other places are, by God's law, forbidden for performing all these things.

units.la: Item quod parochialis ecclesia est locus a Deo praeceptus, quod ibi fiant confessiones & omnis alius locus est prohibitus, & quod praeceptum est quod persona ordinarii audiat confessiones, & quod persona fratris est ab ecclesia & a lege communi prohibita.
units.tr: Likewise, he asserts that the parish church is a place commanded by God for confessions to be made there, and that every other place is forbidden; that it is commanded that the ordinary's person hear confessions; and that the person of a brother is forbidden by the Church and by common law.

units.la: Item quod procuratio, acceptatio & confessio privilegium exemptionis, sepultu-ræ, auditionis confessionum, & consimilium sunt contra divina mandata, & contra legem naturae & alia multa etiam alias materias concernentia asserit ad probandum erronea, quae deduxit ab erroribus supradictis. ex quibus recogitent domini mei, quod Dominus papa & tota ecclesia sacrosancta admisit, concessit & ordinavit, ac etiam ipse praebuit, quod sacramenta exerceantur in locis prohibitis a Deo & a lege sua, & quod quicunque privilegiati faciant contra mandata Dei & ipsa iura naturae, & quod papa non possit necalquis alius legislator sine peccato super aliquo iure dispensare positivo. quae omnia & multo plura sequuntur ex praedictis.
units.tr: Likewise, he asserts, in order to prove erroneous points which he drew from the errors above, that the procuration, acceptance and confession, the privilege of exemption, burial, the hearing of confessions, and similar things, are contrary to the divine commands and to the law of nature, and he touches on many other related matters too. From these things let my lords consider that our lord the Pope and the whole holy Church have admitted, granted and ordained, and indeed he himself has allowed, that sacraments be administered in places forbidden by God and by his law, and that whoever enjoys privileges acts against the commands of God and the very laws of nature, and that the Pope, or any other lawgiver, cannot dispense from any positive law without sin. All these things, and far more, follow from what has been said.

units.la: Mirot tamen qualiter vocat privilegium exemptionis, quo quis eximitur ab eo, cui tenetur in possibilibus obedire, & subiicitur alteri, cui tenetur obedire in omnibus, quae non sunt contra Deum.
units.tr: Yet I wonder how he calls it a privilege of exemption, by which someone is freed from the one to whom he is bound to obey in what is possible, and is made subject to another, to whom he is bound to obey in all things that are not against God.

units.la: Si enim aliquis esset exemptus, ne offerret denarium, & esset astutus offerre florenum, videtur potius esse privilegium subiectionis quam exemptionis. Et non dubium, quin si Dominus papa sciret, & domini cardinales scirent, quae & qualia ex dictis suis sequuntur, non permitterent ea sub silentio pertransire, cum sint positi in ecclesia non ad occultandos errores, sed ad eosdem radicitus extirpandos.
units.tr: For if someone were exempted from offering a penny, and were then crafty enough to offer a gold florin, it seems rather to be a privilege of subjection than of exemption. And there is no doubt that if our lord the Pope knew, and the lord cardinals knew, what and what sort of things follow from his statements, they would not allow them to pass over in silence, since they have been placed in the Church not to conceal errors but to root them out completely.

units.la: Item inducit pro parte sua dominum Iohannem Monachum Cardinalem: qui in Glossa sua super capitulum Bonifacianum Super cathedram tunc extravagans tenet, quod confessi fratribus tenentur parochiali presbytero iterum confiteri: & inducit aliquas rationes eiusdem. Ad q dico, quamvis Dominus Ioan. in hoc tenuerit contra rei veritatem, non tenuit contra sedis apostolicae auctoritatem: quia nondum fuit opinio damnata, quæ nunc est: & similiter non tenuit hoc, quod tenetur ille, quia non fuit tunc eadem simpliciter licentia audiendi quæ nunc est: eo quod tunc capitulum Bonefacianum Super cathedram non fuit sacro instante & approbante concilio roboratū & auctorizatum: cuius auctoritate factum est, quod licentia fratrum, quam modo habent, est licentia papæ, episcoporum & parochialium curatorum præsuppositā forma statuti: tunc autem non fuit sic. & ideo, sicut dictum est, stant simul, quod necessitas iterandi confessionem factas fratri virtute illius licentiæ non sit damnata. Ad argumenta igitur respondetur. ad primum prædicti domini Iohannis, cum arguit primo, quod illud speciale & aliud generale non se impugnant, sed compatiuntur se & tale speciale, generale non tollit, dictum est supra, quia primum argumentum huiusmodi fundetur in assumpto huius argumenti & concedo quod unum non tollit aliud, nisi sicut implens præceptum tollit eius obligationem pro illa vice, pro qua impleuit præceptum.
units.tr: Likewise he cites on his side Lord John the Monk, the Cardinal, who in his gloss on Boniface's chapter Super cathedram, then an extravagant decretal, holds that those who have confessed to the brothers are bound to confess again to the parish priest; and he adduces some reasons for this. To this I say: although Lord John held this against the truth of the matter, he did not hold it against the authority of the Apostolic See, because the opinion which is now condemned had not yet been condemned. Likewise, he did not hold what that man holds, because at that time there was not the same unqualified licence for hearing confessions that there is now, since the chapter of Boniface Super cathedram had not then been strengthened and authorised with the holy council present and approving. By its authority it came about that the licence which the brothers now have is a licence of the Pope, of the bishops and of the parish curates, presupposing the form of the statute; but at that time it was not so. And therefore, as has been said, both stand together: the necessity of repeating a confession made to a brother by virtue of that licence has not been condemned. So, to the arguments: to the first argument of the said Lord John, where he argues first that the special and the other general do not oppose each other, but agree with each other, and that the general does not remove the special, it has been said above that this first argument of this kind rests on the assumption of this argument; and I concede that one does not remove the other, except that, as one who fulfils a command removes its obligation for that occasion for which he has fulfilled the command.

units.la: Ad secundum cum dicitur, quod si confessus fratri non haberet quandoq; tenerti ad curatum, posset eius potestas in additione confessionum prorsus exhauriri: & cum dicit, privilegium non tenet, quod regit in alterius enormem lesionem. Respondeo, quod idem esset argumentū, si aliquis confiteretur archipresbytero vel pœnitentiario papæ vel episcopi, vel si homines abstinerent à peccatis: in quibus casibus potestatem curati exhauriri non vergit in eius enormem: imo nec in aliquam eius lœsionem. & idem dico, quod de quocunque casu, in quo saluti confessi debite prouidetur: nisi forsan aliquid temporale pro confessione exigatur, sicut videtur quidam Glossator dicere, q ideo sit præiudicium curato, quia in aliquibus locis confessi debent portare quilibet unum denarium vel ouum unum, quod si debet exigi à confessis, iudicet vestra dominatio, quæ nouit quod quamuis hoc esset licitum, quod non credo: tamen esset secundum Apostolum ab omni specie mala abstinendum.
units.tr: To the second argument, where it is said that if a person confessed to a brother were not sometimes bound to the curate, the curate's power in the addition of confessions could be entirely exhausted; and where he says, a privilege does not hold which rules to the enormous injury of another. I answer that the same argument would hold if someone confessed to an archpriest, or to the Pope's or a bishop's penitentiary, or if men abstained from sins: in such cases the curate's power is not tending to be exhausted to his enormous loss, indeed not to any loss of his at all. And I say the same of any case in which due provision is made for the salvation of the one confessing, unless perhaps something temporal is demanded for the confession, as a certain Glossator seems to say, that it is therefore prejudicial to the curate, because in some places those confessing must each bring a penny or an egg. If this is to be required from those confessing, let your lordship judge, who knows that although this would be lawful (which I do not believe), nevertheless, according to the Apostle, one should abstain from every kind of evil.

units.la: Ad tertium cum dicit: quod si curati non interfit propter subditum, interest tamen curati propter agnoscere vultum pecoris sui, cui dicitur Eccl. 32. ca. curam illorum habe; Respondeo quod aut interest sui propter se: & illud est propter periculum suum vitandū: & tunc falsum est assumptū: quia cum cura prælati circa subditum sit cura circa salutem: subditi non interesset sui propter se. Et similiter cum curatus non potest habere aliam nec ampliorē in hac parte noticiam, quam subditus vult sibi dare, nullum contingit periculum curato, si subditus non dat sibi noticiam. Aut interest sui propter se, id est propter emolumentum temporale: & tunc notum est quod curatus sit mercenarius & non pastor. Similiter æque posset curatus agnoscere vultum pecoris sui per fratre, sicut per unum alienum sacerdotem: alium si odium non esset in causa. Et vere mitor: quia hæc auctoritas totiens introducitur, & ad hoc propositum, & maxime per theologos: cum secundum Lynconiensem in libro de obligatis & præceptis. Hæc auctoritas, agnosce vultum pecoris tui, teneat vim præcepti: & non dubium notitia, quæ habetur virtute sacramentalis confessionis, non est in potestate cuiuscunque curati, sed solum subditi: & per consequens cum nullus obligatur iuste ad aliquid, quod non est suæ potestatis, sequitur quod hæc notitia non potest intelligi de notitia sacramentalis confessionis: sed intelligitur secundum eum de notitia iudicialis inquisitionis.
units.tr: To the third argument, where he says that if it is not the curate's concern on account of the subject, it is nevertheless the curate's concern to know the face of his flock, to whom it is said in Eccl. 32, in the chapter "Take care of them": I answer that it is either of concern to him for his own sake, and that is to avoid his own danger; and then the assumption is false, because since the prelate's care for the subject is care for salvation, it would not be of concern to the subject for his own sake. Likewise, since the curate cannot have any other or fuller knowledge in this respect than the subject wishes to give him, no danger comes to the curate if the subject does not give him that knowledge. Or it is of concern to him for his own sake, that is, for temporal gain; and then it is well known that such a curate is a hireling and not a shepherd. Likewise, the curate could equally well come to know the face of his flock through a brother as through some other outside priest, if hatred were not the cause. And truly, this authority is so often introduced, and for this purpose, especially by theologians, since according to Lincolniensis in his book On obligations and precepts, this authority, "Know the face of your flock", holds the force of a command. And there is no doubt that the knowledge which is had by virtue of sacramental confession is not in the power of any curate whatsoever, but only of the subject; and consequently, since no one is justly bound to anything that is not in his power, it follows that this knowledge cannot be understood as knowledge from sacramental confession, but according to him it is understood as knowledge from judicial inquiry.

units.la: Ad quartum cum dicitur, qualiter dabit curatus subdito eucharistiæ sacramentū, cum non nouit eum esse dispositū: & maxime vbi sunt nota crimina alia, quæ non potest reuelare. Ad istud respondeo & quæro eandem quæstionem ab eo de vno confesso alieno de licentia sua vel de confesso suo superiori. & quæro qualiter ipse curatus dabit eucharistiam subdito sibi confesso quem nouit indispositum: quia vel est confessus nota crimina, vel non vult ea recognoscere, vel si recognoscat non vult abstinere in casu capituli. exitā de pœnitentiis & remissionibus quod quidem. Vel non pœnitentem, sed solum fingit se pœnitere: nunquid repellet eum publice? nonne eum tunc reuelauerit indirecte. ideo pro istis & similibus dico, quod in isto foro æque nouit eum dispositum se ipso confitente, quod confessus est sicut si esset sibi confessus: & eque tenetur sibi credere.
units.tr: To the fourth point, where it is said: how will the curate give the sacrament of the Eucharist to a parishioner whom he does not know to be disposed, especially where there are other notorious crimes which he cannot disclose? To this I answer, and I ask the same question of him concerning one who has confessed to another priest with his permission, or who has confessed to his own superior. I ask how the curate himself will give the Eucharist to a parishioner who has confessed to him and whom he knows to be unprepared, because either he has confessed notorious sins, or he does not wish to acknowledge them, or, if he acknowledges them, he does not wish to abstain in the case of the chapter Exitā de poenitentiis et remissionibus, which indeed... Or he is not penitent but only pretends to be; will he repel him publicly? Will he not then have disclosed him indirectly? Therefore, for these and similar cases I say that in this forum he knows the man to be disposed just as he is by his own confession, because the man has confessed to him as if he had confessed to him, and he is equally bound to believe him.

units.la: Ad quintum cum dicitur, quod hoc indultum operari potest multos effectus, cum hoc quod stet dictum concilii generalis. igitur stabit indultum cum concilio generali.
units.tr: To the fifth point, where it is said that this indult can produce many effects, namely that the decree of the general council stands. Therefore the indult will stand together with the general council.

units.la: Et similiter ad sextum, cum dicitur, papa propter indultum non aufert potestatem curati. Dico quod hæc & similia currunt per imaginationes, quod priuilegium tollit statutum vel potestatem curati. quod non aliter est verum, quam quod confessus eidem curato vel suo superiori aut alieno de eius licentia tollit eius potestatem: quod si multi aduertissent, nec fecissent hæc argumenta, nec opinionem erroneam tenuissent.
units.tr: Likewise to the sixth point, where it is said that the Pope, by reason of the indult, does not take away the power of the curate. I say that these and similar arguments run on imaginings, namely that a privilege takes away the statute or the power of the curate. This is true in no other way than that a confession made to that same curate, or to his superior, or to another with his permission, takes away his power. If many had noticed this, they would neither have made these arguments nor held this erroneous opinion.

units.la: Ad septimum cum dicitur, quod voluntarium non tollit necessarium. idem est supra. Istud assumptum est valde erroneum & suspectum.
units.tr: To the seventh point, where it is said that the voluntary does not take away the necessary: the same answer as above applies. This assumption is very erroneous and suspect.

units.la: Ad illa quæ concludit per magistrum Alexandrum & dominiū Bonaventuram, patet quod ipsi sunt ad propositum fratrum. distinguunt enim inter illos, quibus est auctoritas seu potestas concessa simpliciter aut in casu. Et in primo casu, scil. quando est auctoritas eis concessa simpliciter, est dicendum de eis, sicut de superiori ordinario, scil. quod non tenentur parochiali curato seu presbytero confiteri. Si autem auctoritas est commissa in casu: sicut est de illis, qui obtentu alicuius priuilegii, vt pote prædicatoribus, qui habent potestatem audiendi illos, qui veniunt ad eorum sermones, si aliqui forsan fuerint tunc compuncti. in quo casu dicunt isti, quod tenentur semel in anno confiteri proprio sacerdoti, si ab ipsis requirantur, ne aliter sint contempti: non tamen dicunt, quod tenentur peccata præconfessa iterum confiteri, sed alia illis non confessa. Talis autem fuit licentia fratribus concessa in principio ordinum: virtute cuius fratres non poterant audire, nisi illos, qui ex sermonibus suis vel fratrum suorum tunc compuncti volebant statim confiteri. & ista licentia non fuit licentia generalis, nec simpliciter concessa: sed specialis & in casu. & ideo quamvis confessi fratribus habentibus hanc licentiam specialem: & in casu tenerentur eadem peccata praeconfessa iterum confiteri, quod non concedo: cum non sequitur, quod confessi fratribus habentibus generalem licentiam tenerentur peccata praeconfessa iterum confiteri. & quod haec sit intentio istorum Doctorum, patet ex secunda obiectione, quam inducit de dictis eorundem: ubi dicunt, quod nullus debet propria auctoritate confiteri alii quam proprio sacerdoti. Unde cum tunc dicunt sic: Unde si quis velit alteri confiteri, hoc faciat auctoritate proprii sacerdotis aut sui superioris: aut praeconfiteatur proprio, & postea alieno. ubi satis expresse volunt, quod obtenta licentia parochialis curati vel sui superioris non plus tenentur eadem peccata parochiali curato iterum confiteri, quam si ea fuissent confessi proprio: sicut patet ex contextu divisionis, quem ponunt. quare sequitur, quod isti in sententia praemissa non loquebantur de his, qui habent licentiam generalem papae vel episcoporum aut parochialis curati: sed potius senserunt oppositum de his, qui talem licentiam habuerunt.
units.tr: As to those things which he concludes through Master Alexander and Lord Bonaventure, it is clear that they are on the side of the brothers. For they distinguish between those to whom authority or power is granted simply, and those to whom it is granted in a particular case. In the first case, namely when authority is granted to them simply, it must be said of them as of an ordinary superior, namely that they are not bound to confess to the parish curate or priest. But if the authority is committed in a particular case, as is the case with those who, by virtue of some privilege, as for example the preaching friars, who have the power of hearing those who come to their sermons, if perhaps any of them have then been pricked in conscience, in that case they say that such persons are bound to confess once a year to their own priest, if he requires it, lest otherwise they be despised; yet they do not say that they are bound to confess again the sins already confessed, but the other sins not yet confessed. Such was the licence granted to the brothers at the beginning of the orders, by virtue of which the brothers could hear only those who, moved by their sermons or the sermons of their brothers, then wished to confess immediately. And this licence was not a general licence, nor granted simply, but special and in a particular case. Therefore, although those confessing to brothers holding this special licence, and in that case, would be bound to confess again the same sins already confessed, I do not grant it, since it does not follow that those confessing to brothers holding a general licence are bound to confess again the sins already confessed. And that this is the intention of these Doctors is clear from the second objection, which he brings from their words, where they say that no one ought to confess on his own authority to anyone other than his own priest. Hence when they then say: Therefore if anyone wishes to confess to another, let him do so by the authority of his own priest or of his superior, or let him first confess to his own and afterwards to another. There they very plainly want it that, once the permission of the parish curate or of his superior has been obtained, they are no more bound to confess those same sins again to the parish curate than if they had confessed them to their own priest; as is clear from the context of the division which they set out. Wherefore it follows that those men, in the opinion stated above, were not speaking of those who have a general licence from the Pope or the bishops or the parish curate, but rather they thought the opposite of those who had such a licence.

units.la: Ad obiecta, quae includit per Henricum de Gandavo septimo quodlibet. quaest. 22. quod vere poenitens confessus ac rite absolutus ab eo, qui potest, non tenetur regulariter peccata iam confessa iterum confiteri, nec eidem sacerdoti nec alieno: potest tamen in casu teneri, videlicet in casibus, qui notantur in canone. de poenitentia. di. 1. his auctoritatibus, super verbo denuo. Et ad hoc allegat fratrem Raymundum. Respondeo, quod haec obiectio non est contra fratres: sicut patet quantum ad primam partem responsionis suae satis plane: sed quantum ad hoc quod addit, scilicet quod rite absolutus potest teneri & tenetur in casibus, qui in decreto allegato in glos. numerantur.
units.tr: To the objections which he includes through Henry of Ghent, Quodlibet 7, question 22: that a penitent who has truly confessed and been rightly absolved by one who has power, is not ordinarily bound to confess again the sins already confessed, neither to the same priest nor to another; yet he may be bound in certain cases, namely in the cases noted in the canon De poenitentia, distinctio 1, his auctoritatibus, under the word denuo. And to this he cites Brother Raymund. I answer that this objection is not against the brothers, as is clear quite plainly as far as the first part of his answer is concerned; but as to what he adds, namely that one who has been rightly absolved can be bound, and is bound, in the cases which are enumerated in the decree cited in the gloss.

units.la: Dico, sicut supradictum est, quod eo modo, quo in illis casibus aliqui confessi fratribus tenentur iterum confiteri sicut quicunque fuissent confessi tenerentur iterum confiteri: sed hoc non esse virtute statuti omnis utriusque, nec contra intellectum capituli vas electionis. quia in illis casibus confessi fratribus non magis tenentur eadem peccata iterum confiteri, quam si fuissent eadem alias confessi proprio sacerdoti.
units.tr: I say, as has been said above, that in those cases some who have confessed to the brothers are bound to confess again in the same way as anyone who had confessed would be bound to confess again; but that this is not by virtue of the statute Omnis utriusque, nor against the sense of the chapter Vas electionis. For in those cases those who confessed to the brothers are no more bound to confess the same sins again than if they had confessed the same sins elsewhere to their own priest.

units.la: Potest etiam aliter responderi: scilicet quod loquendo de confessione sacramentali, quae est tertia pars sacramenti poenitentiae & veram absolutionem coexigit & requirit: & per consequens praesupponit confitentem adhuc reatu culpae esse obstrictum: in nullo casu tenetur aliquis sic confessus eadem peccata, quae sic confessus est, iterum confiteri ex hoc, quia reatu culpae poenae soluto iterum solvi non potest: quia eiusdem peccati reatu iterum constringi non potest: & per consequens non potest iterum vere absolvi. quare sequitur quod cum eorundem peccatorum confessio iteratur, altera confessio quantum ad effectum sacramenti praedictum, scilicet verae absolutionis a peccato vel peccatis non est plus sacramentalis, quam si fieret laico seculari.
units.tr: It can also be answered otherwise: namely that, speaking of sacramental confession, which is the third part of the sacrament of penance and requires and demands true absolution, and therefore presupposes that the penitent is still bound by the guilt of sin, no one so confessing is in any case bound to confess again the same sins which he has so confessed, on this ground, that once the guilt and the penalty are loosed he cannot be loosed again, because he cannot be bound again by the guilt of the same sin; and consequently he cannot be truly absolved again. Hence it follows that when the confession of the same sins is repeated, the second confession, as far as the effect of the sacrament is concerned, namely true absolution from sin or sins, is no more sacramental than if it were made to a secular layman.

units.la: Unde in casibus praeallegatis: quorum primus est, cum quis confitetur sacerdoti imperito. Secundus cum quis confitetur sacerdoti, qui propter enormitatem criminis remittit cum superioribus absolvendum. Tertius, cum quis confessus & absolutus negligit seu contemnit facere poenitentiam sibi iniunctam & acceptam. Quartus cum quis confitetur, sed aliqua subticet, quae confiteri debebat: in quorum tribus primo, secundo, quarto iteratur confessio: quia confessus non est absolutus, immo ex necessitate sacramenti confessus tenetur sacramentaliter confiteri, quia facta confessio non fuit sacramentalis. In tertio vero casu quamvis prima confessio fuit sacramentalis quo ad peccata tunc confessa: debet tamen sacramentaliter confiteri de peccato nouiter commisso, scilicet de negligentia vel contemptu poenitentiae, quam amisit, quae fuit iniuncta pro peccatis praeconfessis, quo casu non confitetur sacramentaliter de peccatis praeconfessis, quamvis illa exprimat sigillatim. loquitur igitur Magister Henricus de confessione in genere, prout est expressio peccatorum & communis ad confessionem sacramentalem & non sacramentalem: de qua solum loquuntur capitula supradicta: & sic Magister Henricus nihil dicit contra fratres.
units.tr: Hence in the cases cited before, of which the first is when someone confesses to an unskilled priest; the second, when someone confesses to a priest who, on account of the enormity of the crime, has to refer the absolution to his superiors; the third, when someone who has confessed and been absolved neglects or despises performing the penance enjoined on him and accepted; the fourth, when someone confesses but keeps silent about some things which he ought to confess: in the first, second and fourth of these three the confession is repeated, because the one confessing has not been absolved, and indeed by the necessity of the sacrament the one confessing is bound to confess sacramentally, because the confession made was not sacramental. In the third case, although the first confession was sacramental as to the sins then confessed, he must nevertheless confess sacramentally about the sin newly committed, namely the negligence or contempt of the penance which he has lost, which was enjoined for the sins already confessed; in which case he does not confess sacramentally about the sins already confessed, although he states them one by one. Master Henry therefore speaks of confession in general, as it is the expression of sins and is common to sacramental and non-sacramental confession; and of this only the chapters mentioned above speak. And so Master Henry says nothing against the brothers.

units.la: Ad secundum obiectum quod dicitur, quod in Quodlibeti quaest. 1. dicit idem Henricus, quod non est erroneum dicere, quod confessus & rite absolutus ab eo, qui potest etiam si non nisi de gratia & privilegio tenetur peccata illi confessa iterum confiteri de iure communi virtute illius statuti omnis utriusque. dicens, quod si iste Dominus intelligat, quod non sit erroneum contra rei veritatem, est sibi contrarius, qui in praecedenti responsione tenuit oppositum. ex istis casibus per Raymund. & Gloss. decreti allegati expressis, de quibus non est dubium quod non obligant virtute statuti praedicti, sed aeque obligaretur quis in illis casibus iterum confiteri ad modum dictum, si nunquam fuisset editum hoc statutum. Si vero intelligat, quod non est erroneum contra auctoritatem & determinationem ecclesiae, certe pro tunc verum dixit: quia pro tunc non fuit facta constitutio Vas electionis. modo autem secus est. Si autem simpliciter intelligat, quod non est erroneum contra rei veritatem, negandus est simpliciter Henricus in huiusmodi claudicans & vacillans.
units.tr: To the second objection, which is put forward, namely that in Quodlibet 1, question the same Henry says that it is not erroneous to say that one who has been confessed to and rightly absolved by one who has power, even if only by grace and privilege, is bound to confess again those sins to him by the common law, by virtue of that statute Omnis utriusque, saying that if this Lord means that it is not erroneous against the truth of the matter, he contradicts himself, since in the preceding answer he held the opposite. From those cases expressly cited by Raymund and the Gloss of the cited decree, about which there is no doubt that they do not bind by virtue of the aforesaid statute, but a man would be equally bound in those cases to confess again in the manner stated, even if this statute had never been issued. If, indeed, he means that it is not erroneous against the authority and determination of the Church, then certainly at that time he said what was true, because at that time the constitution Vas electionis had not been made; but now it is otherwise. If, however, he means simply that it is not erroneous against the truth of the matter, Henry must simply be denied, as one who in such matters limps and wavers.

units.la: Ad illa quæ inducit de domino Hostiensi. Respondeo, ad dictum domini Iohannis Monachi sufficienter est responsum.
units.tr: As to those things which he brings forward concerning the lord Hostiensis: I answer that the saying of the lord John the Monk has been sufficiently answered.

units.la: Ad illud etiam Innocentii quarti superius in responsione sexti articuli plenarie est responsum.
units.tr: As to that also of Innocent IV, it has been fully answered above, in the reply to the sixth article.

units.la: Ad hoc quod allegat de Benedicto 11. qui præcipit fratribus, qui hortentur cōfessos iterum confiteri. Dico quod idem Benedictus in eadem constitutione inter cunctas, dicit plane, quod confessi fratribus non tenentur eadem peccata iterum confiteri. & ideo præcipit, quod fratres hortentur eos: non tamen præcipit, quod eis hæc imponant. quare in hac parte Benedictus est contra istum dominum, non pro ipso. Sic igitur responsum est ad omnia argumenta facta in contrarium, quæ quidem in contrarium facta inueni.
units.tr: As to what he alleges about Benedict XI, who enjoins on the friars that they should exhort those who have confessed to confess again: I say that the same Benedict, in the same constitution Inter cunctas, plainly states that those who have confessed to the friars are not bound to confess the same sins again. And so he enjoins that the friars should exhort them, but he does not enjoin that they impose this upon them. Therefore in this matter Benedict is against this lord, not for him. Thus I have answered all the arguments made to the contrary, which I have found made to the contrary.

units.la: CAP. Octauum & vltimum, in quo exponuntur ea quæ libellus domini Armachani iudicialiter datus continet de hac materia.
units.tr: CHAPTER 8, the last, in which those things are set out which the libel of the lord Archbishop of Armagh, given in judgement, contains on this matter.

units.la: SVperest nunc ostendere, quid libellus domini Armachani iudicialiter datus continet de hac materia. cuius libelli mens & intellectus in suo tractatu, de quo nunc agitur, exprimitur magis plene. Est igitur sciendum, quod in enarratione præfati libelli positis quibusdam, quæ contingunt materiam confessionis, dicit quod parochiani omiserunt & omittunt semel in anno secundum statutum concilii generalis omnis utriusque, propriis sacerdotibus confiteri: & recurrunt ad fratres dictis confessionibus & absolutionibus faciendis: & consequenter parum ante conclusionem eiusdem libelli dicit sic: Cum igitur dictas constitutiones, concessiones, priuilegia & alia indulta responsa eiusdem statuti in professioni eorum (scil. fratrum) super quibus, ut asserunt, fundantur, sunt repugnantia & aduersa ex causis præmissis & aliis diuersis, sana non poterunt retinere conscientia, nec eisdem gaudere & uti fratres prædicti. Petit igitur &c. In qua conclusione petit declarari, pronunciari & decerni vsum & omne exercitium, concessionem & constitutionem priuilegiorum prædictorum ipsis Ordinibus & Fratrib. eorundem insuper & confessionibus audiendis, sepulturis recipiendis, & prædicationibus faciendis interdicendos fore & interdici ac perpetuo inhiberi, ne acta huiusmodi præsumant: ipsi quoque non licuisse nec licere prædicta facere vel fecisse. Postea in eadem conclusione quærit extravagantem Vas electionis, declarari & moderari: & vlterius iuxta præmissum libellum ad concordandum cum constitutionibus omnis utriusque reduci. hæc ibi. Et cum ista particula conclusionis immediate ante præmissa incipit tractatum, contra quem agitur de præscriptis, in quo ponit declarationes erro- neas & suspectas ac sensui eiusdem constitutionis contrarias: sicut patet ex quinto & sexto capitulis supradictis, quas instanter petit iudicio vestro confirmari. Si igitur vltima conclusionis particula: scil. quod petitur illa constitutio Vas electionis declarari &c. quæ constitutio, sicut ex ipsius tenore patet, loquitur de fratribus habentibus generalem licentiam audiendi confessiones & con- fessos absoluendi, ex nulla particula narrationis eiusdem libelli potest descendere, nisi ex prima parte narrationis suprascripta, scil. quod parochiani omiserunt & omittunt semel in anno confiteri &c. nec etiam potest ex illa descendere, nisi illa particula ad fratres, quibus præfata constitutio loquitur, solum extendat, liquet quod præfata particula ad fratres habentes licentiam generalem supradictam iuxta intentionem libelli & dantis eum debet extendi. asserit ergo præfata particula, quod parochiani recurrunt ad fratres habentes licentiam generalem audiendi confessiones, vt confiteantur eisdem: & quod illo recursu non obstante tenentur ex vi statuti generalis concilii semel in anno confiteri suo proprio sacerdoti: & quod omittunt eisdem confiteri vt tenentur. ex qua assertione sequitur, quod primus articulus in constitutione Vas electionis damnatus est. Nam demonstratis peccatis alicuius parochiani, quæ fecit infra annum, & q̄ confessus est fratri, & quæ omisit semel in anno confiteri proprio sacerdoti. & arguitur sic: Quicunque tenetur hæc peccata ex vi sta- tuti semel in anno confiteri proprio sacerdoti, & omittit sic, vt prædicitur, confiteri, est transgressor statuti: & ad confitendum de istis peccatis remanet obligatus; iste parochianus illa peccata, q̄ confessus est, tenetur ex vi statuti fratri habenti licentiam generalem præconfessa suo sacerdoti confiteri. igitur iste parochianus illa peccata, quæ confessus est fratri tali, tenetur ex vi statuti con- fiteri proprio sacerdoti. hæc conclusio: igitur iste parochianus illa peccata, quia confessus est fratri tali, tene- tur ex vi statuti iterum confiteri proprio sacerdoti, est primus articulus magistri Iohannis de Poliaco, in constitutione Vas electionis damnatus. & maior est necessaria: igitur minor est erronea & damnata quia tamen minor est particula libelli dati contra fratres ex eadem etiam narrationis particula sequuntur alii duo articuli eiusdem magistri Iohannis, & cum erronea destructione sortiæ oppositionis quarti articuli supradicti, & in 6. articulo prædeducta.
units.tr: It remains now to show what the libel of the lord Archbishop of Armagh, given in judgement, contains on this matter. The mind and meaning of that libel is expressed more fully in his treatise, of which we are now speaking. It must therefore be known that, in the narration of the aforesaid libel, after certain matters touching the matter of confession have been laid down, he says that parishioners have omitted, and still omit, to confess once a year to their own priests, according to the statute of the general council, Omnis utriusque, and instead have recourse to the friars for the hearing of confessions and the giving of absolution. And consequently, shortly before the conclusion of the same libel, he says thus: Since therefore the said constitutions, concessions, privileges and other indults and responses of the same statute, on which, as they assert, the friars rest their profession, are repugnant and adverse, for the causes premised and for other diverse causes, the aforesaid friars cannot retain them with a sound conscience, nor enjoy and use them. He therefore asks, etc. In which conclusion he asks that it be declared, pronounced and decreed that the use and every exercise, grant and constitution of the aforesaid privileges are to be forbidden to the same Orders and friars, and moreover that the hearing of confessions, the receiving of burials and the preaching of sermons are to be forbidden and perpetually prohibited, lest they presume to do such acts; and that they have not been, and are not, permitted to do or to have done the aforesaid things. Afterwards, in the same conclusion, he seeks that the extravagant Vas electionis be declared and moderated, and further, according to the aforesaid libel, be brought back into agreement with the constitutions Omnis utriusque. Thus far there. And since this particle of the conclusion immediately before the foregoing begins the treatise against which the proceedings are directed, in which he lays down erroneous and suspect declarations contrary to the sense of the same constitution, as is clear from the fifth and sixth chapters above, which he urgently asks to be confirmed by your judgement: if, therefore, the last particle of the conclusion, namely that it be asked that that constitution Vas electionis be declared, etc., which constitution, as is clear from its own tenor, speaks of friars holding a general licence to hear confessions and absolve the confessed, can follow from no particle of the narration of that libel except the first part of the narration above written, namely that parishioners have omitted and still omit to confess once a year, etc.; and if it cannot follow from that either, unless that particle extends only to the friars to whom the aforesaid constitution speaks, it is clear that the aforesaid particle must, according to the intention of the libel and of its author, be extended to friars holding the general licence mentioned above. The aforesaid particle therefore asserts that parishioners have recourse to friars holding a general licence to hear confessions, in order to confess to them; and that, notwithstanding that recourse, they are bound by virtue of the statute of the general council to confess once a year to their own priest; and that they omit to confess to them as they are bound. From this assertion it follows that the first article in the constitution Vas electionis is condemned. For, the sins of some parishioner being demonstrated, which he committed within the year, and which he confessed to a friar, and which he omitted to confess once a year to his own priest, the argument runs thus: Whoever is bound by virtue of the statute to confess these sins once a year to his own priest, and omits, as has been said, to confess them, is a transgressor of the statute, and remains bound to confess these sins; this parishioner is bound by virtue of the statute to confess to his own priest those sins which he has confessed to the friar. Therefore this parishioner is bound by virtue of the statute to confess to his own priest those sins which he has confessed to such a friar. This conclusion: therefore this parishioner, because he has confessed to such a friar, is bound by virtue of the statute to confess again to his own priest, is the first article of Master John of Pouilly, condemned in the constitution Vas electionis. And the major premise is necessary; therefore the minor is erroneous and condemned. Yet because the minor is a particle of the libel given against the friars, from the same particle of the narration there follow also the other two articles of the same Master John, and, together with the erroneous destruction of the opposing force of the fourth article above, and in the sixth article previously deduced.

units.la: Amplius, ex alia parte narrationis suprascriptæ, scil. cum vero dictas, quas petit pronunciari, decerni & declarari vsum & omne exercitium &c. patet de intentione & mente libelli eiusdem damnati est quod constitutiones seu concessiones & priuilegia indulta fratribus super prædicationibus, confessionibus & sepulturis sunt statui & professioni fratrum repugnantia & aduersa, & quod fratres non possunt illa sana retinere conscientia; nec vti vel gaudere prædictis, seu illa observare aut licite exercere; ex quibus sequuntur errores infrascripti: primo scil. quod qualitercunque & ad quemcunque sensum fratres obseruent huiusmodi priuilegia; & vtantur eisdem, ipsi necessario abutuntur eisdem: quia si statui & professioni fratrum repugnant, sequitur quod vti eisdem sit abuti: & in hoc fundat se principaliter ad probandum, quod fratres privilegiis abuntur.
units.tr: Furthermore, from the other part of the aforesaid narration, namely, Since the said things, which he asks to be pronounced, decreed and declared, the use and every exercise, etc., it is plain from the intention and mind of the same condemned libel that the constitutions or concessions and privileges granted to the friars regarding preaching, confessions and burials are repugnant and adverse to the statute and profession of the friars, and that the friars cannot retain them with a sound conscience, nor use or enjoy the aforesaid things, nor observe or lawfully exercise them. From these there follow the errors below. First, namely, that however and in whatever sense the friars observe such privileges and use them, they necessarily abuse them; for if they are repugnant to the statute and profession of the friars, it follows that to use them is to abuse them. And on this he mainly rests in proving that the friars abuse their privileges.

units.la: Secundo sequitur, quod secundum istum dominum papa non potest licite ubique per mundum mittere fratres ad praedicandum & ad audiendum confessiones, secundum suae beneplacitu voluntatis, nec archiepiscopi & episcopi in suis dioecesibus, & fratres missi ab eisdem non possunt licite praedicare & confessiones audire, nec absoluere poenitentes: cuius oppositum quo ad singula fuit determinatum per Alexandrum quartum: & ista dicentes fuerunt coacti ea revocare tanquam erronea & suspecta, sicut patet ex bulla eiusdem quae incipit cum olim.
units.tr: Secondly, it follows that, according to this lord, the pope cannot lawfully send friars everywhere through the world to preach and to hear confessions at his pleasure, nor can archbishops and bishops do so in their dioceses; and friars sent by them cannot lawfully preach, hear confessions, or absolve penitents. The contrary of each of these points was determined by Alexander IV, and those who said these things were compelled to revoke them as erroneous and suspect, as is clear from his bull which begins Cum olim.

units.la: Tertio sequitur, quod sunt status ab ecclesia approbati, quorum professoribus ex sua institutione & regula competit praedicare: quibus secundum istum ex sua professione repugnat praedicare: & per consequens secundum istum huiusmodi status includunt in se repugnantia; nec obligant suos professores: & iterum cum sint approbati eorum professori, non repugnat praedicare: & sic non solum sequitur error, sed contradictio manifesta. Quod autem huiusmodi status sunt ab ecclesia approbati, quibus ex institutione & regula competit praedicare, patet de ordine Fratrum praedicatorum, qui ex institutione eorum ad praedicandum sortitur hoc nomen; & de ordine Fratrum Minorum, quibus ex nono capitulo Regulae suae competit praedicare: & hoc ibidem testatur Dominus papa Gregorius nonus in bulla sua, Quoniam abundaunt iniquitas; dicens quod ad officium praedicandi sunt ex professione ordinis sui deputati.
units.tr: Thirdly, it follows that there are orders approved by the Church, to whose professors, by their institution and rule, it belongs to preach; and it is repugnant to them, according to this lord, to preach by their profession; and consequently, according to him, such orders include within themselves repugnancies, and do not bind their professors; and again, since they are approved, it is not repugnant to their professors to preach; and so not only does error follow, but manifest contradiction. That orders of this kind are approved by the Church, to which by institution and rule it belongs to preach, is plain of the Order of Preaching Friars, who from their institution receive this name for the sake of preaching; and of the Order of Friars Minor, to whom by chapter nine of their Rule it belongs to preach. And this Lord Pope Gregory IX bears witness to in his bull Quoniam abundaverit iniquitas, saying that they are deputed to the office of preaching by the profession of their order.

units.la: Quarto sequitur secundum istum dominum, quod ecclesia tales constitutiones ordinando & privilegia concedendo dedit eisdem fratribus auctoritatem & consensum ad faciendum contra suam professionem: & per consequens ad peccandum, & ad peccata defendendum, & ad pertinaciter persistendum in eisdem: & per consequens erraunt in moribus vel scientia: & sequitur quod vel non est eius determinatoribus adhaerendum propter errorem in scientia: vel quod scienter facta est nouerca filiis, quibus debuit esse mater.
units.tr: Fourthly, it follows from this lord's view that the Church, by ordaining such constitutions and granting such privileges, gave these friars authority and consent to act against their profession, and consequently to sin, to defend their sins, and to persist obstinately in them. Consequently they err either in conduct or in knowledge. It follows either that we must not adhere to its determinations because of error in knowledge, or that the Church has knowingly become a stepmother to the children to whom it ought to have been a mother.

units.la: Quinto sequitur, quod secundum istum dominum nec Romanus pontifex, nec ecclesia potest dispensare cum fratribus, quod eisdem liceat praedicare vel confessiones audire: quia Romanus pontifex sacro instante & approbante concilio noluit dispensare cum eisdem, & fecit ad hoc quod potuit. & cum secundum istum praedicta non licent eisdem, ergo nec Romanus pontifex nec ecclesia potuit in eisdem dispensare.
units.tr: Fifthly, it follows that, on this lord's view, neither the Roman pontiff nor the Church can dispense the friars so that they may preach or hear confessions. The Roman pontiff, with the sacred council urging and approving, was unwilling to dispense them, and did what he could to prevent it. Since, on this lord's view, the aforesaid activities are not lawful for them, neither the Roman pontiff nor the Church could have dispensed them.

units.la: Sexto sequitur, quod plene subiectis Romano pontifici & ex sua professione & ecclesiae sacrosanctae non licet super praedicationibus faciendis ecclesiae Romanae vel summo pontifici obedire: quia nulli licet obedire super aliquo actu exercendo, super quo non licet dispensari, quod licite fieret ab eodem.
units.tr: Sixthly, it follows that, on this view, those who are fully subject to the Roman pontiff, both by their profession and to the most holy Church, may not lawfully obey the Roman Church or the supreme pontiff in regard to preaching. For no one may lawfully obey a command to perform an act from which the pontiff himself could not lawfully dispense.

units.la: Septimo, posito quod praedicare statui & professioni fratrum repugnaret, sicut dicit Dominus iste, quod cum papa non possit super articulo tam fructuoso & utili toti mundo dispensare: scilicet quod fratres possint licite praedicare & audire confessiones fidelium, cum sint secundum istum ad oppositum obligati. sequitur, quod pari ratione papa non potest super quocunque obligato, ut fiat huiusmodi oppositum, dispensare. igitur secundum istum sequitur, quod fundatores ordinum praedicatorum, scilicet sancti Dominicus & Franciscus, qui sunt ab ecclesia canonizati, damnabiliter erraverunt, & quod damnabiliter vixerunt & obierunt: quia per totam vitam suam temporibus oportunis praedicaverunt, & suis subiectis praeceperunt praedicare: & super hoc licentiam a summis pontificibus impetraverunt; & sic non est alicui canonizationi fidei per ecclesiam credendum, quia de quacunque potest continuliter dubitari. Quod autem ipse de hoc dubitet, apparet ex hoc, quod ille Dominus in nullo scripto vel dicto suo vocat eos Sanctos, forte non reputans eos tanto titulo dignos. Et specialiter, quia vocat sanctum Franciscum in fide novitium, vel ad fidem noviter conversum: de quo cum fuerit quadraginta annorum quando obiit, & fuit parvulus in fide parentum baptizatus, nunquam legitur quod postea fuerit infidelis. Nec scio unde procedit erga istum Sanctum tanta indevotio: cum Fratres Ordinis sui fuerint istum dominum in favoribus & promotionibus eis possibilibus prosecuti. Cum igitur secundum istum dominum praedicare & confessiones audire repugnet statui & professioni Mendicantium: qui tamen ex sua professione non sint vita alios clericos & sacerdotes, nisi ad quaedam consilia obligati; quae Christus & sui apostoli docuerunt & opere servaverunt: sequitur, quod praedicare & consessiones audire vitae Christi & apostolorum aequaliter repugnabat: & per consequens cum ipsi per totum mundum praedicaverint, quia in omnem terram exivit sonus eorum: sequitur quod ipsi illicite fecerunt, vixerunt & obierunt: quod est haereticum etiam cogitare.
units.tr: Seventhly, grant that preaching were contrary to the status and profession of the friars, as this lord says. Since, he says, the pope cannot dispense on an article so fruitful and useful to the whole world, namely that the friars may lawfully preach and hear the confessions of the faithful, although on his view they are bound to the contrary, it follows that by the same reasoning the pope cannot dispense anyone bound to the contrary so that such an opposite course may be taken. So, on this lord's view, it follows that the founders of the preaching orders, namely St Dominic and St Francis, who have been canonized by the Church, erred damnably, and lived and died damnably. For throughout their whole lives they preached at fitting times and ordered their subjects to preach, and they obtained licence for this from the supreme pontiffs. Thus no canonization is to be believed by the Church in matters of faith, since anything whatever can be continually doubted. That he himself doubts this appears from the fact that this lord, in no writing or speech of his, calls them Saints, perhaps not thinking them worthy of so great a title. And especially because he calls St Francis a novice in the faith, or one newly converted to the faith, although when he died at the age of forty, and had been baptized as a child in the faith of his parents, it is never read that he afterwards became an unbeliever. Nor do I know whence comes such great disrespect towards this saint, since the friars of his order have served this lord with every favour and promotion available to them. Therefore, since on this lord's view preaching and hearing confessions are contrary to the status and profession of the mendicants, who by their profession are not bound, beyond certain counsels which Christ and his apostles taught and practised, to a life different from other clergy and priests, it follows that preaching and hearing confessions were equally contrary to the life of Christ and the apostles. Consequently, since they have preached throughout the whole world, for their sound has gone out into all the earth, it follows that they acted unlawfully, lived unlawfully, and died unlawfully. This is heretical even to think.

units.la: Item cum sepulturas fidelium, tam ratione funeris quam ratione etiam funeralium, quae obveniunt fieri apud ecclesias quacunque, sit pure positivum de solo iure humano statutum, si recipere huiusmodi sepulturas sit tam repugnans statui & professioni fratrum, quod super hoc ecclesia non poterit dispensare, tunc sequitur quod non omne ius ecclesiasticum pure positivum sit in potestate Romani pontificis & ecclesiae sacrosanctae. Sublato enim omni iure ecclesiastico pure positivo ad sepulturas pertinente, non dubium quod fratres possunt saltem de licentia papæ recipere sepulturas ratione funeris: & possunt recipere funeralia nomine pure eleemosynæ: quia tunc funeralia essent in spontanea dispensatione dantium vel legantium. Si igitur papa in concilio generali non potest tollere iura positiva quæcunq; vel super ea dispensare, sequitur quod non tota ecclesiastica iurisdictio seu auctoritas residet in Romano pontifice & ecclesia sacrosancta.
units.tr: Likewise, since the burial of the faithful, both as regards the funeral and as regards the funeral rites which are customarily performed at any church, is purely positive law established by human right alone, if receiving such burials is so contrary to the status and profession of the friars that the Church cannot dispense them in this matter, then it follows that not all purely positive ecclesiastical law lies in the power of the Roman pontiff and the most holy Church. For if all purely positive ecclesiastical law relating to burials were abolished, there is no doubt that the friars could at least by the pope's licence receive burials as regards the funeral, and could receive funeral offerings as pure alms, since the funeral offerings would then depend on the free dispensation of those who give or bequeath them. If therefore the pope in a general council cannot remove, or dispense from, any positive right whatever, it follows that the whole ecclesiastical jurisdiction or authority does not reside in the Roman pontiff and the most holy Church.

units.la: Præterea autem istos & alios errores & repugnantias multiformes, iste Dominus impingit in dominos summos pontifices, videlicet Innocentium tertium & Honorium tertium successorem eius. Dicit enim in fine tractatus sui, de quo nunc agitur, quod ipse reppulit sanctos Dominicum & Franciscum, petentes suos Ordines confirmari: cum tamen hoc non sit verisimile neq; verum: quia non apparet verisimile, quod ille, qui prædictos Ordines approbavit, renuit eos confirmare.
units.tr: Moreover, this lord charges these and other manifold errors and contradictions against the lord supreme pontiffs, namely Innocent III and his successor Honorius III. For at the end of the treatise now under discussion he says that Innocent repulsed the holy Dominic and Francis when they asked that their orders be confirmed, although this is neither likely nor true, for it is not likely that he who approved the aforesaid orders refused to confirm them.

units.la: Quod autem iste Ordines istos approbavit, testatur Honorius successor eius in bulla confirmationis Regulæ Fratrum Minorum sic dicens: Ea propter dilecti filii vestri precib. inclinati ordinem vestrum regulam à bonæ memoriæ Innocentii papa prædecessore nostro approbatam, auctoritate vobis apostolica confirmamus &c. & non dubium, quin de ordine Fratrum Prædicatorum simile habeatur, nec est verum, quod dicit Dominus iste in proposito: quia expresse dicit chronica Martini, quod Dominus Innocentius Ordines istos confirmare disposuit, sed non potuit morte prævenus. Et quod addit iste Dominus dicens, quod Innoc. tertius in concilio generali novas religiones institui inerdixit: & ex hoc impingit in dominum Honorium tertium dicens, quod ipse confirmavit prædictos contra decretum concilii generalis, vehementer admiror, quod iste Dominus aut non videret aut non recordatur, quod concilia generalia non possunt ecclesiæ legem præfigere, cum eius auctoritate robur accipiant: & in eorum statutis Romana patenter excipiatur auctoritas, extra de el. & ele. pa. significasti. quapropter Dominus Innoc. in concilio generali novas religiones institui interdixit: successorum suorum tamen & ecclesiæ Romanæ auctoritatem excepit: & per consequens Dominus Honorius prædictos Ordines confirmando contra decretum concilii generalis nihil fecit. Amplius cum statutum concilii Lateranen. præsidente Domino Innocentio tertio supradicto pontificatus sui anno 17. celebrari prohibuerit novas religiones per modum in cap. ne nimia. extra de relig. domi. cum expressum de præfatis ordinibus ante præfatum concilium institutum & ab eodem Domino Innoc. approbatum, sicut dictum est, nullam mentionem faciendo tacite vel expresse, per quod prædictum capitulum ne nimis trahi potest ad eosdem, plane videtur quod prædictum statutum ad supradictos Ordines minime se extendat: & per consequens Dominus Honorius contra decretum concilii generalis nihil penitus attentavit.
units.tr: That Innocent did approve these orders is attested by his successor Honorius in the bull confirming the Rule of the Friars Minor, which says: Therefore, moved by the prayers of your beloved sons, we confirm by apostolic authority the rule of your order, approved by our predecessor of good memory, Pope Innocent, and so on. There is no doubt that a similar statement is found concerning the Order of Friars Preachers, and what this lord says on the point is not true. For the Chronicle of Martin expressly says that Lord Innocent intended to confirm these orders but was prevented by death. As for what this lord adds, saying that Innocent III forbade in general council the founding of new religious orders, and that by this he charges Lord Honorius III with confirming the aforesaid orders against the decree of a general council, I am greatly surprised that this lord either did not see or does not remember that general councils cannot prescribe law for the Church, since they receive their force from its authority; and in their statutes the authority of Rome is plainly excepted: Extra, de elect. et elect. pot., significasti. Therefore Lord Innocent, in general council, forbade the institution of new religious orders, but excepted the authority of his successors and of the Roman Church. Consequently Lord Honorius, in confirming the aforesaid orders, did nothing against the decree of a general council. Furthermore, since the statute of the Lateran council, held under the presidency of the aforesaid Lord Innocent III in the seventeenth year of his pontificate, forbade the founding of new religious orders by the method laid down in cap. Ne nimia, extra de relig. dom., and since that statute makes no express or tacit mention of the aforesaid orders, which had been founded and approved by Lord Innocent before that council, as has been said, so that the said chapter Ne nimis cannot be drawn to apply to them, it is plainly clear that the said statute does not in the least extend to the aforesaid orders. Consequently Lord Honorius attempted nothing whatever against the decree of a general council.

units.la: Prætermissis igitur articulis erroneis & aliis in quarto & sexto capi. supradictis nimis periculosis, vestræ discretionis libra pensatis, quorum aliqui sunt pensati contra omnipotentiam Dei, propter quod incidit in capitulum excommunicamus itaq, extra de hæreticis. & aliqui contra veritatem scripturæ tam legalis quam evangelicæ. Aliqui contra potestatem Romani pontificis & episcoporum suorum, qui fuerunt alias condemnati: propter quod ipse damnatorum errorum commentator existens privilegii damnationis sententia tenetur astrictus. 24. q. 1 maiores. Et quia in hæresim alias damnatam lapsus est, in eius damnatione seipsum inuolvit, ibidem Achatius. cum etiam sint de confessione peccatorum, de qua iste Dominus aliter sentit & tenet, quæ sancta Romana ecclesia prædicat & observat: quare incidit in capitulum ad abolendam. extra de hæreticis. Quia postremo cum iste tractatus suus supradictus & libellus iudicialiter datus contra Fratres continet similia libello Guilhelmi per dominum Alexandrum quartum excommunicationis vinculo innodati, sicut patet ex bulla eiusdem, quæ incipit, Ex alio: Vestris dominationibus instanter & humillime supplicamus, quatinus prædictis erroribus penitus renuntiatis, non obstantibus obiectionibus suis frivolis & obiectionibus peruersis, aut contra mentem statutorum in dictis eiusdem ausus temerarios vestri iudicii examine dignemini refrenare, & innocentes, quos vexat iniuste, ab eius vexatione citius absolvere, ipsumq; propter libellum & tractatus prefatos ac omnes eandem libellum dantes & defensantes seu eidem in hac parte adhærentes ab omni iudiciorum modo legitime repellatis præcludendo sibi & aliis aditum similia perpetrandi. DIXI.
units.tr: Therefore, setting aside the erroneous articles and the other very dangerous matters in the fourth and sixth chapters above, which have been weighed in the balance of your discretion, some of which are blasphemies against the omnipotence of God, on account of which he falls under the chapter Excommunicamus, itaque, extra de haereticis; and some against the truth of Scripture, both of the law and of the Gospel; and some against the power of the Roman pontiff and of his bishops, who were condemned on other occasions, for which reason he, being a commentator on condemned errors, is bound by the sentence of the privilege of condemnation (24, q. 1, Maiores). And since he has fallen into a heresy already condemned elsewhere, he entangles himself in its condemnation (ibidem, Achatius). Moreover, since they concern the confession of sins, on which this lord thinks and holds otherwise than the holy Roman Church teaches and observes, he falls under the chapter Ad abolendam, extra de haereticis. Finally, since this treatise of his, and the libel given judicially against the friars, contains things similar to the libel of William, who was bound by the bond of excommunication by Lord Alexander IV, as appears from the bull of that pope which begins Ex alio: We earnestly and most humbly beseech your lordships that, these errors having been wholly renounced, you deign, notwithstanding his frivolous objections and perverse objections, or the rash attempts he has made against the spirit of the statutes, to restrain him by the examination of your judgment, and that you quickly absolve from his vexation the innocent whom he unjustly harasses; and that you legitimately repel him, on account of the aforesaid libel and treatises, and all who give or defend the same libel, or who adhere to it in this matter, from every mode of judicial process, cutting off from him and from others the way to commit similar acts. I have spoken.

units.la: Explicite sunt Defensiones Rogerii Chonnoe pro Mendicantibus contra Armachanum. Ex quibus evidenter liquet, quod Archiepiscopus Armachanus & Primas Regni Hiberniæ, plenitudinem potestatis Papalis in Ecclesia Catholica ipsius est oppugnare, quam iste Magister Chonnoe pro suo fundamento posuit.
units.tr: The Defences of Roger Chonnoe on behalf of the Mendicants against the Armagh man are set out explicitly. From them it is clearly evident that the Archbishop of Armagh and Primate of the Kingdom of Ireland is attacking the fullness of papal power in the Catholic Church, which this Master Chonnoe took as his foundation.

units.la: FRANCISCI PETRARCHAE CANONICI CATHEDRALIS ECCLESIAE SENENSIS, PHILOSOPHI EMI- NENTISSIMI, & POETAE LAUREATI, EPISTOLAE DE IVRIBVS IMPERII ROMANI, ET INIVRIIS PAPAE ROMANI EIVSQVE ASSECLARVM.
units.tr: Letters of Francis Petrarch, Canon of the Cathedral Church of Siena, Most Eminent Philosopher and Laureate Poet, On the Rights of the Roman Empire and the Wrongs of the Roman Pope and His Adherents.

units.la: De invidia, avaritia, luxuria, ecclesia Romana Procerum vitiis.
units.tr: On envy, avarice and luxury: the vices of the great men of the Roman Church.

units.la: FRAN. PETRARCHA Hannibali Tusculanensi salutem. Infelicem invidiam, dixit Maro: nec immerito. Quid enim infelicius, quam suis malis, alienisque simul bonis affligi. Non ineleganter quidem in Mutium nescio quem apprime invidum atque maliolum lusisse legitur Publius quidam. Cum enim tristiorem solito vidisset: Aut Mutio (inquit) nescio quid incommodi accessit, aut nescio cui aliquid boni. Protulus ita est.
units.tr: Francis Petrarch to Hannibal of Tusculum, greetings. "Hateful envy," said Maro, and not without reason. For what is more wretched than to be tormented by one's own evils and at the same time by another's good fortune? Publius, I read, once made a rather witty joke about a certain Mutius, a very envious and spiteful fellow. When Publius saw him looking gloomier than usual, he said: "Either some misfortune has befallen Mutius, or some good has befallen someone else." That is exactly how it is.

units.la: Invidus alterius bonum suis ad scribit incommodis, & ut ait Flaccus, Invidus alterius rebus macrescit opimis.
units.tr: The envious man grieves at another's good fortune as if it were his own misfortune, and, as Horace says, "The envious man wastes away at another's rich possessions."

units.la: Magna miseria, non aliter saturitate alterius quam fama propria torqueri, atque alio pinguescente, non secus ac se esuriente macrescere. Sed haud temere definierim, an non invidia tantum, sed vitiis omnibus infoelicior avaritia sit. Invidia namoesta est saepe, sed otiosa est; avaritia tristis, & occupata; superbia, dum se aliquid magnum putat, falsa licet opinione de se stratur. Avaritia semper se famelicam, & egenam sentit, neque fallitur. Verissimum enim est poeticum illud: Semper avarus eget.
units.tr: It is a great misery to be tormented not by another's abundance but by one's own lack, and to waste away while another grows fat, as if one were starving. Yet I would not rashly decide whether avarice is not the most wretched of all vices, not merely envy. Envy is often sad but idle; avarice is gloomy and busy. Pride, while it thinks itself something great, is deceived by a false opinion of itself. Avarice always feels itself hungry and needy, and is not deceived. The poet's saying is most true: "The avaricious man is always in need."

units.la: Nam si avarus est, cupit, quod ipsum vitii nomen indicat. Sane quod ait Seneca: Non qui parum habet, sed qui plus cupit pauper est. Et hoc inde concluditur, non paucitas rerum inopem facit, cum pauci natura contenta sit, cui qui rite satisfecerit, dives est, & nihil ei deest, sed cupiditas expleta, quod indicat sibi tum deesse, quantum cupit: cupit autem omnia, & optando supervacua fecit necessaria. Ita egestatem minimam, cuique potest facile succurri poterat, irremediabilem atque insanabilem fecit. Rursus enim & illud est verum, quod Philosophis placet: Avaro tam quod habet deest, quam quod non habet.
units.tr: For if a man is avaricious, he desires, as the very name of the vice indicates. Seneca rightly says: "It is not he who has little, but he who desires more, who is poor." And from this it follows that it is not the scarcity of things that makes a man needy. A few things suffice for nature, and whoever has duly satisfied nature is rich, and nothing is lacking to him; but desire, once satisfied, shows that he lacks as much as he desires. Yet he desires everything, and by wishing for superfluous things he makes them necessary. So he has made a small want, which could easily have been relieved, irremediable and incurable. Again, that saying of the philosophers is also true: "What the avaricious man has is as much lacking to him as what he does not have."

units.la: Nisi mihi quidem magis videtur, avaro deesse quod habet, quam quod non habet. Ex illo nihil praeter sollicitudinem perpetuam, & veros motus, ex hoc nonnunquam breve falsum gaudium capit, dum sibi arridet, & optatum bonum, spe fallente, percupit. Ita nonnunquam satiatur fera quadam (ut aiunt) & inhumana dulcedine: avaritia vero nunquam. Nam ut successibus inardescit, & Satyricum illud verum est: Crescit amor nummi, quantum ipsa pecunia crescit.
units.tr: Indeed, it seems to me rather that the avaricious man lacks what he has more than what he does not have. From the former he gains nothing but constant anxiety and real torments; from the latter he sometimes gains a brief, false joy, while hope smiles on him and he longs for a good he has not yet got, though hope deceives him. Thus he is sometimes satisfied, by a certain wild and inhuman sweetness, as they say; but avarice never is. For as it is inflamed by success, that satirist's line is true: "The love of money grows as money itself grows."

units.la: Et minus hunc optat, qui non habet. Cuius rei causam una (nam plures excogitari queunt) in epistola quadam ponit Annaeus Seneca: Nemine (inquit) pecunia divitem fecit, imo contra nulli non maiore sui cupidinem incussit. Et sequitur: Quaeris, quae sit rei huius causa? Plus incipit habere posse, qui plus habet. Venio ad reliquas pestes, & eius quidem, quae accidiam nostri vocant, eadem ratio est, quae invidiae fuit. Gula autem ac libido saepe suis fruuntur deliciis, quibus exultant, & gaudia fugitiva capiunt; avaritia nulla requiritur, nisi curis amarissimis. Dum enim quaerendis inhiat, & illa non habet, & quaesita non videt, nisi ad supplicium, hinc trepida, inde sollicita. Quae cum ita sint, iure avaritia sororum omnium pestilentissima dici potest, quae radicem malorum omnium vocat Apostolus. Nec sum nescius, te mirari quid hodie tecum hac (ut aiunt) importuna Philosophia praeter solitum vti velim. Ego autem monte magis, quam mortales fere oes, & prope tuum genus alloquor, inter quos maxime & solium posuisse, & vexillum fixisse victrix mihi videtur & imperiosa cupiditas. Quod eo indignantius miror, quo minor vobis cupidinum causa est. Cui in hos auri cumulos acervatis? Legitima quidem vobis negata posteritas, vos parcus & exiguus cultus decet, reliqua pauperum Christi sunt, quos fraudare praedari, non timebis, domino illorum spectante desuper & minitante vindictam, & nescitis cui vestrum crimen vitae sit futurum, quod vobis interim laboriosum, pestiferumque & funestum est.
