Multi se propter filios excusant, & vitio animi velut pietas obtenditur. Sic leaena, sic tygris, sit enixa ferocior, & animalia mansueta, novae prolis amor exasperat. Vobis excusatio nulla, velut en vitii nullum est, ante totius orbis oculos nudi estis, digitoque monstramini, populorum omnium cum exprobratione mordaci: Ecce virtutis (inquiunt) praecones, qui cum de vita aeterna, neque animi libertate multa magnifice loquantur, sine causa tamen & temporalibus addicti, auaritiæ serui sunt. Re enim vera & si de omnib. dicat, non ne de vobis tatum sensisse videtur Deuid, vbi ait: vniuersa vanitas omnis homo viuens, verumtamen in imagine pertransit homo, sed & frustra conturbatur. Et vt rabiem potificialis auaritiæ tot post seculis futuram notaret expressius, ait (inquit) & ignorat cui congregabit ea. Hæc vtique vobis ante alios, auari pontifices, dicta sunt: Parentes quidem thesaurizantes filiis & legimus & vidimus, quamuis sepe fortuna paternis votis obstante, quod aliis partum erat ad alios devolvatur; parentum tamen intentio nota est. Vestra intentio quænam, quæso? Quid agitis? cui thesaurizatis? nisi diabolo & angelis eius, qui sollicite vos observant, numerant dies, & hereditatem vestram quidissime præstolantur, gratissima trophæa vestris inscripta nominibus, in limine tartari de manibus spoliatorum pauperum erepturi? Sed admirans percontabere, cur hodie potius ista quam alias: an vel hactenus vos non avaros, vel avaritiam vitiū non fuisse, vel me hunc primum oculos aperuisse crediderim qui prius ista non videram? Respondebo admirationi tuæ: Et sciebam vos avaros: & avaritiam vitium esse, nemo vsquam est qui nesciat, & in vtrumque non nunc primum oculos aperio, sed cum forte nudiusterius venissem ad te, altaria tua, imo vero altaria Domini virtutum, argento atque auro, & gemmis onusta conspexi, atque insanis fulgoribus perculsus obstupui, & dixi mecum: Ecce nova avaritiæ arma, novum pereundi genus.
units.tr: And he who does not have money desires it less. Seneca, in a certain letter, gives one cause for this (there could be several): "Money," he says, "has never made anyone rich; on the contrary, it has inspired in everyone a greater craving for itself." And he goes on: "Do you ask what the reason for this is? He who has more begins to be able to have more." I come to the other plagues. The reasoning about the one we call sloth is the same as that about envy. Gluttony and lust often enjoy their pleasures, in which they exult, and take fleeting joys; avarice requires nothing but the most bitter cares. For while it gapes after things to be sought, it does not have what it lacks, and what it has sought it does not see except for its own torment: on one side anxious, on the other worried. Since this is so, avarice can rightly be called the most pestilential of all the sisters of vice, which the Apostle calls the root of all evils. Nor am I unaware that you wonder why I want to speak with you today in this (as they say) troublesome philosophy, beyond my usual manner. But I address you more than almost all mortals, and especially your class, among whom I think a victorious and domineering desire has set up its throne and planted its banner. I marvel at this all the more indignantly because your causes for desire are so small. Why do you heap up these mounds of gold? Lawful posterity has been denied you; a sparing and modest way of life suits you. The rest belongs to the poor of Christ, whom you will not hesitate to defraud and plunder, while their Lord looks down upon you, threatening vengeance; and you do not know for whom your sin will be, which for you is meanwhile toilsome, pestilential and deadly. Many excuse themselves on account of their sons, and piety is held out as a cover for a vice of the mind. So the lioness and the tigress become fiercer after giving birth, and the love of a new offspring makes even gentle animals savage. You have no excuse: there is no such thing as a vice that is not open. You stand naked before the eyes of the whole world, and are pointed at by the fingers of all peoples, with biting reproach: "Look at the heralds of virtue, who, though they speak grandly of eternal life and of freedom of the spirit, nonetheless, without cause, are devoted to temporal things and are slaves to avarice." Indeed, even if he speaks of all men, does not David seem to have meant you alone, when he says: "Surely every man walks in a vain show, and he is disquieted in vain"? And so that he might more clearly point out the rage of papal avarice, which would come many centuries later, he adds: "and he does not know who will gather them." These words were certainly spoken to you before others, avaricious pontiffs. We have read and seen that parents store up treasure for their sons, although often fortune, opposing the parents' wishes, passes what was gained for some to others; yet the parents' intention is known. What, I ask, is your intention? What are you doing? For whom are you storing up treasure? Surely for the devil and his angels, who watch you closely, count the days, and eagerly await your inheritance, ready to snatch from the hands of the despoiled poor the most welcome trophies inscribed with your names, at the threshold of hell. But you will wonder, marvelling, why I say these things now rather than before: whether I believe that until now you were not avaricious, or that avarice was not a vice, or that I am the first to have opened my eyes, who had not seen these things before. I will answer your wonder. I knew that you were avaricious and that avarice is a vice; there is no one anywhere who does not know this. And I have not just now opened my eyes to either point. But when I came to you the other day by chance, I saw your altars, or rather the altars of the Lord of hosts, loaded with silver, gold and jewels, and I was struck with wonder by their wild glitter, and I said to myself: "Behold, new weapons of avarice, a new way of perishing."

units.la: Avaritia nobis nostra non sufficit, nisi aurum quoq; CHRISTVM facimus, & diuos ipsumque vocamus in partem, prædamque louem (vt Virgilius ait.) Vos quidem diuitias male partas iustificasse videamini, si prædæ rapinarumque vestrarum pauperem CHRISTVM cogitis esse participem, & auro obsideris inuitum. Non hic placandi numinis modus. An non legistis apud Senecam, Deos tunc propitios fuisse, cum fictiles fuerunt? Atqui Deos nunquam propitios fuisse, nec esse potuisse certum est. Quomodo enim propitius aliis esse potest, qui miserrimus est sibi? Placet igitur non hæc Senecæ sententia, sed verba, quæ feliciori materiæ licet inserere. Profecto CHRISTVS tempest propitius humano generi, sed tunc præsentior fuit, cum fictilis fuit. Nunc aureus atque gemmatus irascitur, & preces nostras iustissima indignatione non audit. Non aurum odit illa, sed cupidos, quibus optandi, quærendique nullus est finis. Primi hominum, quod erat, aperte profitebatur, quærebant diuitias, vt abundarent: vos quæritis, vt ornetis CHRISTVM: pium opus, si spoliis illa miserorum, & non potius virtutibus ac devotione fidelium, vellet ornari, & si non fictioni iuncta cupiditas, odiosior Deo esset. Animadverti olim tale aliquid in principibus dominisque terrarum, qui omni studio libros quærunt, petunt, rapiunt, mercantur, non literarum amore quas ignorant, sed auaritia inducti, nec animi, sed thalami quærentes ornatum: nec scientiam, sed nomen: neq; librorum sententias, sed pretia egitantes. Verum his colorata excusatio, licet falsa, non deerit. dicent enim, sobolem se ac posteros cogitare, & verbo quidem nondum natis, aut quod vitæ genus eligant prorsus incertis, veræ autem auaritiæ propriæ atq; ignorantiæ bibliotheca congeritur. Vobis congerendarum opum quis est color? Vt CHRISTI templa farciatis auro. Sed quid Persio dicitis exclamanti? O curua in terris anima & cælestium inanes Quid iuuat hos templu vestros immittere mores.
units.tr: Our avarice is not enough for us unless we also make Christ a partner of our gold, and call the gods into our share, and the booty, as Virgil says, to Jove. You seem to justify your ill-gotten riches, if you make the poor Christ a sharer in your plunder and robberies, and besiege him with gold against his will. There is no limit to such appeasing of the deity. Have you not read in Seneca that "the gods were then favourable when they were made of clay"? Yet it is certain that the gods were never favourable, nor could they be; for how can one who is most wretched to himself be favourable to others? So I approve not this saying of Seneca's but the words which may be applied to a more fortunate subject. Surely Christ was once favourable to the human race, but he was then more present when he was of clay. Now, gold-plated and bejewelled, he is angry, and in his most just indignation he does not hear our prayers. It is not gold that he hates, but the greedy, for whom there is no end to wishing and seeking. The first men openly professed what they were doing: they sought riches in order to abound. You seek to adorn Christ. It would be a pious work, if he wished to be adorned with the spoils of the wretched, rather than with the virtues and devotion of the faithful; and if desire joined to a pretence were not more hateful to God. I once noticed something of this kind among princes and lords of the earth, who with all their zeal seek, demand, seize and buy books, not out of love of the letters they do not know, but led by avarice; seeking the ornament of their chambers, not knowledge but a name; chasing not the meaning of books but their prices. Yet a coloured excuse, though false, will not be lacking to them. They will say that they are thinking of their offspring and descendants; and while in word the children are not yet born, or what kind of life they will choose is quite uncertain, a library is meanwhile piled up out of true avarice and ignorance of their own. And what pretext have you for piling up wealth? That you may stuff the temples of Christ with gold. But what will you say to Persius, who cries out: "O souls bent low on earth and empty of heavenly things, what good does it do to bring such manners into these temples of yours?"

units.la: Neue hoc aliis dictum crederetis, audite, vt statim vestro nomine vos appellat: Dicite Pontifices in sancto quid facit aurum?
units.tr: Lest you think this was said to others, listen: he addresses you by name at once: Tell me, Pontiffs, what does gold do in the sanctuary?

units.la: Respondete pontifices, vobis enim loquitur: Respondete tot senes vni iuueni, tot Theologi vni poetæ, tot Christiani vni pagano. Quid dicitis? In sancto quid aurum? Si respondere negligitis poetæ, an non saltem respondebitis Prophetæ, qui non aurum, sed alia quædam à vobis ornamenta templorum exigit? Apud Malachiam legitis: Filius honorabit patrem, & seruus dominum suum timebit. Si ergo pater ego sum, vbi est honor meus? Et si Dominus ego sum, vbi est timor meus? dicit Dominus exercituum. Et vt noscatis quia vobis dicit, sequitur: Ad vos, ô sacerdotes qui despicitis nomen meum. Nisi forte quisquā est qui putat, vlla vnquam ætate dignius hoc quæsitum quam nunc quæritur. Video quidem, vt dixi, vulgus auaritia ardere, & fareor, nihil excusat. Nulla est enim excusatio peccati, sed natorū charitas, multiplex quo nec iustitas, & vulgaris ignorantia crimen leuant. Vos vero pontifices, dicite, oro; Quid sibi vult hęc rabies habēdi inter diuitias tā certas, in tanta rerū diuinarū humanarumq; notitia, in vita solitaria, & cælibe & decrastino cogitare prohibita? Illud mihi forte notissimū ingeretis: Aurum habet ecclesia. Bene, si habet, pessime, si habetur: placere possunt diuitiæ virorū, viri diuitiarum penitus nō placent, qui cum somno suo dormiunt, in manib. suis nihil inueniunt. Verear igitur illa responsio, q; p contactioni pprie Persius ipse subiecit. Cū n. secundo quisset: In sancto quid facit aurum? intulit: Nempe hoc, quod Veneri donata a virgine pupa.
units.tr: Answer, Pontiffs, for he is speaking to you. So many old men must answer one young man, so many theologians one poet, so many Christians one pagan. What do you say? What does gold do in the sanctuary? If you neglect to answer the poet, will you not at least answer the prophet, who demands from you not gold but other ornaments for the temples? In Malachi you read: A son honours his father, and a servant fears his master. If then I am a father, where is my honour? And if I am a Lord, where is my fear? says the Lord of hosts. And so that you may know he is speaking to you, it follows: To you, O priests, who despise my name. Unless perhaps someone thinks that this question has ever been asked more fittingly in any age than it is now. I see, as I said, that the common people burn with avarice, and I confess that this excuses nothing. For there is no excuse for sin; but the love of children, which takes many forms, does not lighten the guilt, nor does ordinary ignorance. But you, Pontiffs, tell me, I beg you: what does this mad desire to have riches mean, amid such certain riches, amid such knowledge of divine and human things, in a solitary and celibate life, where thinking about tomorrow is forbidden? You will perhaps throw at me the most familiar answer: the Church has gold. Good, if it has it; very bad, if it is held as a possession. Riches may please men, but men of riches do not at all please, who sleep with their sleep and find nothing in their hands. I would therefore fear that answer which Persius himself appended to the same contact with the question. For when he had said, What does gold do in the sanctuary? he added: Certainly this: the doll that a maiden gives to Venus.

units.la: Facessat, oro, iam rande aurum templis inutile, & in alia templa Dei, hoc est, in vnos homines erogatium conferatur. Sit Christi charitas, q̃ seculi pompa est, nec temp sub obtentu deuotionis idololatriæ seruiatur. Nescitis quod auaritia est idolorum seruitus. Nulla tot idolis, quot auri pondera, hahere, sed nolcit: diues esse potuit, dum inter homines agebat, pauperta te maluit. Fictilibus vtuscit. Nolite, pontifices, excutationes friuolas auciupari, auaritiæ, & vestris alimenta furoribus aggregare. Christus vestro auro... nonib. delectatur, puri ac nudi cordis est, appetens piorum ... honestas ... voluntatum. Quis inter hæc auro locus? Nolite miseri curare, quam superbe sacrificia, quam splendide, sed quam pie, quam humiliter, quam caste, quam sobrie sacrificate, de duptis vinculis liberatis. liberatori suo Rex propheta sacrificat, hostiam [?]c. laudu: Sacrificate sacrificium iustitiae, & sperate non in auro, sed in Domino. Audite psalmistam surdi, diebus ac noctibus clamantem: sacrificium Deo spiritus contribulatus. Quid hic opus est auro? Spiritu opus est, eoq; non nisi contribulato; opus est corde, sed contrito & humiliato. Hoc est sacrificium Deo gratu, atq; homini sine terrarum effossione parabile. Submisso & immaculato opus est animo. Cotra nec iertio nec rudi auro opus est. Nescio quid amplius dicam, & vereor verba iactare, sed si post prophetam, ipsum quoque Persium poetam audire, non piget, videte, quid ibidem paganus homo pontificibus suis dicat.
units.tr: Let gold, I beg you, now at last depart from the temples where it is useless, and let it be contributed to other temples of God, that is, distributed to human beings. Let there be Christ's charity, which is the pomp of the world, and let no idolatry be served under the pretext of devotion. Do you not know that avarice is the slavery of idols? Christ had no idols, as many as there are pounds of gold; he could have been rich while he lived among men, but he preferred to be poor. He used earthenware. Pontiffs, do not catch at frivolous excuses, nor add nourishment to avarice and your own frenzies. Christ does not delight in your gold; he is of a pure and naked heart, seeking the honest wills of the pious. What place does gold have among these things? Wretched men, do not care how proudly, how splendidly, you sacrifice, but how piously, how humbly, how chastely, how soberly you sacrifice, freed from the bonds of sin. The king and prophet sacrifices to his liberator, a victim [...] praise: Offer the sacrifice of righteousness, and trust not in gold but in the Lord. Hear the psalmist, who cries out to the deaf day and night: The sacrifice to God is a broken spirit. What need is there of gold here? What is needed is a spirit, and that a broken one; what is needed is a heart, but a contrite and humbled one. This is a sacrifice pleasing to God, and one that can be prepared by man without digging up the earth. A humble and unstained mind is needed. Neither gold, whether refined or rough, is needed. I do not know what more to say, and I fear to throw out words; but if, after the prophet, it is not beneath us to hear the poet Persius too, see what the pagan man says to his pontiffs on the same subject.

units.la: Quin damus id superis, de magna quid dare lance,Non possit magni Messalae hippa profligo.
units.tr: Why do we not give to the gods what the great dish of the spendthrift could not give, the prodigal grandson of great Messalla?

units.la: Et ne dubium foret, quid esset quod superis offerendum, quod genere atq; opibus superbi caeci diuitum filii non possent, subsecutus expressit.
units.tr: And lest there be any doubt what it was that had to be offered to the gods, which the blind sons of the rich, proud of their birth and wealth, could not give, he followed on and expressed it.

units.la: Compositum ius, fasq; animi sanctosq; recessusMentu, & incoctum generoso pectus honesto.
units.tr: A mind composed in right and justice, the holy recesses of the soul, and a breast steeped in noble honesty.

units.la: Praeclarum verbum, dignumque de Christo dictum esset. Tu vale, & quam fidelibus convitiis autem praebe.
units.tr: A splendid word, and one worthy to have been said of Christ. Farewell; and as for the faithful, offer them not reproaches but...

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Ad CAROLI QVARTI IMP. Literas dilationis excusatorias responsio; & excusationum infirmatio.
units.tr: Reply to the letter of Emperor Charles IV excusing the delay, and refutation of the excuses.

units.la: CAESAREOS apices triennio fere, postq; a te discesseram, ad me peruenisse miraberis: sic est tamen. Non iam soli tuisq; religionibus, sed nunciis quoq; & epistolis tuis, Caesar, iter immeabiles alpes sunt. Ego quidem, ut vehementer id doleo sic, fateor, gaudeo, & mihi clam gratulor, id tacito meno fieri. Clamaui equidem, sed frustra, nec duab. epistolis auditus sum, quatu etsi stylus aurib. forte tuis incomptior; profecto & sententia verax, & pura scribentis fides est, q; Romanorbis totus attestabitur. Agendq; rei opportunissimu tempus erat; clamo num etiam, q; tibi frustra ne an efficaciter faciam, tu videris: Mihi frustra non erit, quicquid fideliter egero. Etsi aliis namq; non proderit, mihi certe profuerit, satisfecisse officio, implesse q; debeo. Equidem ego ingens, & quo nullum inter homines maius possum, affectus mei pmium tuli testimonii maiestatis tuae, q; fidem meam laudibus multis accumulat: Consiliu v. non amplectitur. Malo mihi fidem sine prudentia constare, q; sine fide prudentiam. Dum tibi mea fides & devotio pbetur, non magnopere solertiae titulu aucupabor, cosiliumq; meu aequo animo fera vel respui vel differri: q; n etia gaudebo, & haud merito gloriabor, te no modo me, sed oes mortales, ut Impii dignitate, sic cosilii viuacitate pcellere. Suasi quidem, & psuasisse credidera, celeritate tuis conatibus oportuna. Ita n. mihi: tibi v. aliter videtur: tu frenum terris, tu clauu pelago regis: tuo stabitur iudicio, ego fideliter locutus dicar. Satis est mihi prudentia inter professores prudentiae requiratur. Si tn interpretari dictum meu non prohibeor, ita ego tibi celeritatem suasi, ut segnitiem excuterem, non ut in aliud extremorum te impellerem. Sciebam n. q; praecipitatio cum in rebus omnibus turpis sit, tum in summi imperii administratione turpissima est. Suasi ergo celeritatem non pcipitem, sed matura. Maturate fugam, inquit Maro. Quem locum Macrobius exponens; & contraria, inquit, videtur fuga maturati. Et post pauca: Maturate, inquit, q; neq; citius neq; serius, sed medium quidda & temperatum est. Quam sententia Caesar Augustus sequebatur, ut ad rem gerendam simul adhiberetur & industria celeritas, & tarditas diligentia: Ex quibus duobus contrariis fit maturitas. Multa ibi similia. Sed redeo ad rem. Si ergo tibi, Caesar, hoc consilium non placet, placeat fides ut facit. Mea a. quid dicturu putas? Nempe mihi consilium aliud nullum est: Sed optabo, ut quicquid elegeris, secundet omnipotens Deus, & moram tua mundo vtilem, tibi gloriam velit, & ait psalmista, tribuat tibi secundu cor tuum & omne consilium tuum confirmet. Verum quia nondum functus officio sum, nisi omne, q; mens parturit, & lingua pepererit, sic iam, Caesar, epistolae tuae respondebo, ut intelligas me de sententia non tam rationib. literarum tuarum, quam tui nominis maiestate depositum. Quis n. sani capitis contra Caesarem sentire audeat, & praesertim in rebus Imp.? Si de poetica, aut si omnino de literis sermo esset, vterer forte libertate Lucii Poetae, quem Iulio Caesari in poetarum consilium venienti no assurgere solitu accepimus, non contemptu principis, sed professionis propriae fiducia: Nunc cum de imperio agitur, quis tibi non assurgat? quis non cedat, nisi amens oblitusq; rerum omniu? Loquor itaq; non ut te refellam, sed ut exerceam, non ut aduerser, sed ut me tibi penitus aperiam, nudemq; quicquid animus latebris suis regit. Primu quide tarditati meae clypeum prendis mutatione temporu, q; multiplicibus verbis exaggeras, ut aliqui magis distantis ingeniu, qua Imperatoris animum mutari cogar ac laudare. Quid n. quaeso est, quod aliquando non fuerit; imo v. quid pat maiorum nostrorum laboribus periculisq;, perpetimur, dum Brennus Italiam, dum Pirrhus, dum Hannibal vastabat? quae nam comparatio rerum est? ut v. nobis omne mortiferum vulnus sit, non rerum natura, sed mollities nostra facit. Quod ridebant proaui nos lugemus, & ad omnem difficultatis occursum cohorrescimus ac torpemus: Cum nulla interim in coquirendis excusationib. nulla aetas & nulla gens promptior. Olim, inquis, Romana Respublica diu cis fuit. Quis, oro te, diu ite illa fecit, nisi civium suorum virtus ac modestiae studiu, & iustitiae cultus, & rei bellicae disciplina? Quid a. maius censes inter tot gentes indomitas, inter tot populos, phibentes eu exisse in sylvis dumosis, & in collibus imperuiis inaudi u illis temporibus & inuisum nomen, ad haec statibus fundamentis, & reuerentia nominis toto orbe diffusa sanctae collapsam restituere? Hic mihi mutationes quis obiiciat, no audi, vel si audia, ridebo.
units.tr: You will be surprised that the imperial letter reached me almost three years after I had left you, but so it is. Not only the Alps, but your religions, Caesar, and your messengers and letters are now impassable. I grieve greatly at this, yet I confess I am also glad and secretly congratulate myself that it has happened by such a quiet arrangement. I did cry out, but in vain, and I was not heard in two letters. Although my style may be somewhat unpolished for your ears, my opinion is truthful and the writer's faith is sincere, as the whole Roman world will attest. The time was most suitable for acting, and I cried out. Whether I did so in vain or to good effect is for you to judge. Whatever I have faithfully done will not be in vain for me. Even if it does not benefit others, it will at least benefit me to have satisfied my duty and fulfilled what I owe. Indeed, I have received, as the greatest reward my devotion could have among men, the testimony of your majesty, which heaps many praises upon my loyalty, though it does not embrace my counsel. I prefer my faithfulness to stand without prudence rather than prudence without faithfulness. As long as my faith and devotion are proved to you, I will not greatly seek the title of cleverness, and I will bear calmly that my advice is either rejected or postponed. Indeed, I will rejoice, and I will not without reason boast, that you have excelled not only me but all mortals in the dignity of your piety and the vigour of your counsel. I did advise, and I believed I had persuaded you, that speed was fitting for your undertakings. That is what I think; you think otherwise. You rule the lands with a bridle and the sea with a rudder; your judgement will prevail, and I shall be said to have spoken faithfully. It is enough for me that prudence is sought among the professors of prudence. But if I am not forbidden to interpret my own words, I urged you to speed so as to shake off sluggishness, not to drive you into the opposite extreme. For I knew that haste is shameful in all affairs, and most shameful in the administration of the highest power. So I urged speed, but not headlong speed; I urged timely speed. Hasten your flight, says Maro. Macrobius, explaining this passage, says that flight and haste seem to be opposites. And a little later: Hasten, he says, which is neither too quick nor too slow, but something in between and moderate. Caesar Augustus followed this maxim, so that in carrying out affairs both activity and speed, and both slowness and diligence, were brought together; from these two opposites comes timeliness. There are many similar things there. But I return to the matter. If this counsel of mine does not please you, Caesar, let my faithfulness please you, as it does. What, then, do you think I will say of my own? Surely I have no other counsel. But I shall pray that Almighty God prosper whatever you choose, and grant you glory and a delay useful to the world; and the psalmist says, may he grant you according to your heart and confirm all your counsel. But since I have not yet discharged my duty, I shall answer your letter now, Caesar, so that you may understand that I have set aside its opinion not so much by the reasons of your letter as by the majesty of your name. For who of sound mind would dare to disagree with Caesar, especially in imperial matters? If the discussion concerned poetry, or literature in general, I might perhaps use the freedom of the poet Lucius, who, as we are told, was accustomed not to rise when Julius Caesar came into the council of poets, not from contempt for the prince but from confidence in his own profession. But now that the matter concerns empire, who would not rise for you? Who would not give way, unless he were mad and had forgotten everything? I speak, then, not to refute you but to exercise myself, not to oppose you but to open myself fully to you, and to lay bare whatever my mind hides in its recesses. First, you take up the shield against my slowness by pointing to the change of times, which you magnify with many words, so that I might be compelled to admire and praise a mind more distant from the old than that of the Emperor. For what, I ask, is there that has not happened before? Or rather, what hardships and dangers of our ancestors do we not endure, while Brennus laid waste Italy, while Pyrrhus and Hannibal did so? What comparison of circumstances is this? Every deadly wound is made for us not by the nature of things but by our own softness. What our forefathers laughed at, we lament; at every encounter with difficulty we shudder and grow numb, while in the meantime no age and no nation is more ready to seek excuses. The Roman Republic, you say, once flourished for a long time. Who, I ask you, made it flourish for so long, if not the virtue of its citizens, their devotion to modesty, their cultivation of justice, and the discipline of warfare? And what do you think greater, among so many untamed nations, among so many peoples, who, in those times, when the hated name had not yet gone out into the thorny forests and the impassable hills, could restore the sacred fallen state, founded on these foundations, and the reverence for the name spread throughout the whole world? If anyone should throw in my face the changes of time, I shall not listen; or if I do listen, I shall laugh.

units.la: Credere
units.tr: To believe

units.la: Crede enim mihi Cæsar, mundus idem est qui fuit, idem sol, eadem elementa: virtus sola decrevit ciuitatum nempe manuq; congestarum molium aliæ creauerūt, decreuere aliæ, quædam fundinus corruerunt, nostris quædam surrexere temporibus. Vetus est vicissitudo rerum humanarum, qd hinc elicis? Iterum quæso, crede mihi, si Roma illa, unde titulum trahis; & si Cæsar ille, cuius nomen atq;(vt speráre solebamus) animum habes, hodie viuerent, multo citius quam tu mad arcem rerum atque Imperii fastigium peruenirent.
units.tr: For believe me, Caesar, the world is the same as it was, the same sun, the same elements. Only virtue has decreed the fortunes of states. Some were created by the hands and labours of men, others were decreed; some collapsed in ancient times, others arose in our own. The change of human affairs is old. What do you deduce from this? Again I ask, believe me: if that Rome from which you draw your title, and that Caesar whose name you bear, and whose spirit (as we were wont to hope) you have, were alive today, they would reach the summit of affairs and of empire far more quickly than you do.

units.la: Tunc enim repugnantiæ multum fuit graue nostris periculum, ingens labor: nunc plana & facilis via est: sed viator deest, luxus & inertia late regnant. Ignauia orbem terrarum possidet armato Cæsari mox cessura, imo vel pro te partes actura. Notum etenim tuum nomen, pauci s bonis & amatoribus virtutis atq; imperii adiutum, aduersus inermem luxum, inermemque superbiam facile bellum omne conficeret. Vis non modo probem, sed ostendam tibi ista esse vt dico? ecce, nudius tertius caput extulit, quidam est plebe humili non Romanus Rex, non Consul, non patricius, & vix bene cognitus Romanus civis, nullis titulis suorū, nullis maiorum magnibus, deniq; nullis id tempus virtutib. suis clarus, qui vindicem se Romanæ libertatis asseruerat. Obscuri hominis clara pfessio, illico, vt scis, Tuscia cupide manus dedit, imperia excepit. Iam sensim omnis Italia sequebatur, iam Europa, iam totus orbis in motu erat. Quid multis est opus? non legimus ista, sed vidimus. Iam redisse iustitia & pax & harum comites alma fides, tranquilla securitas, ad postremū aurei seculi vestigia videbantur: Ille tamen in ipso rerū flore patuit alteri: nolo sibi culpam dare, nec alteri: non condemno hominem, imo absoluo, non sum iudex, quid opiner scio, & sumpserat ille titulum Tribuni, quod inter Romuleas dignitates humillimum nomen fuit. Si tantum ergo tribunitium potuit, quid Cæsareum nomen posset? At si differs, si hæres, & q; tibi sub oculis posui fugà temporis non attendis, actum est, ruit Imperium, perit libertas. Noli, oro te Cæsar, hæc cum stomacho legere, quæ forsan gustui minus dulcia sunt, quā velles. Nescio quid bilem concitecam remedia nisi amara non penetrat. Ego tibi verum dicere non metuo, quoniā amare te verum noui, odisse blandicias prudenter, optime, magnifice: aconita regnum sunt, irrisio potētum, mors principum, arma fidelium. Sed enim nescimus, quanta belua sit imperium. Hic enim alter excusationum tarum color fuit. Quod dictum miror cur Augusto tribueris, cum Tiberii sit, nisi forte vel rerum cura præsentium memoriam vetustatis obnubilat, vel communicato vt cabulo, quemlibet imperatorem vt Cæsarem, sic Augustū vocas. Fecisti forsan id sciens, vt ab ii signi authore dicto, quo vti decreueras, auctoritas quæreretur, non ignarus inter Augustum & Tiberium quid intersit. Ille principum sapientissimus atque optimus fuit; hic obscoenus ac ferox, & vt de se proprie dixit, quietum lutum à sanguine maceratum: Hoc tamen idem dicto quo tempore sit visus nostri, vel si quid obliuionis inter tot maiores curas obreperit, apud Tranquillum leges. Eo quidem tempore hoc dixit, quo exempto iam rebus humanis Augusto successor longe impar impudentissime arreptum rebus ipsi imperium, verbis tamen ambiguis fallacisque & varia dissimulatione renuebat, falsum modū, ita nomen quærens, usque adeo vt rergiuersanti quidam in faciem elegantissime cauillatus illuderet, cateros homines, quod promittant sero implere: illum vero quod impleat, serius pollicerī. Sed esto, sit dictum boni principis, sit non ficto animo prolatum, ipse sit autor Augustus, quid ad rem? Nescius, inquit, quanta belua sit Imperium. Imo scimus eximie; belua potentissima est, quia frenum docta manus excipiat belua ingens, eo tractabilis quid nitractetur indomita? Aude, age, frenum manu arripe, soliumque tibi debitum conscende, si metuis, sessorem inueniet. Iulius Cæsar, cuius, vt modo dicebam, hæreditarium nomen habes, equum apud se ortum & alterius impatientem ascendit, & in delicijs habuit, tu solium non alterius sessoris impatiens, sed à tot retro principibus insessum, & tuæ sessionis auidissimum solus fugis? Verum enim vero cuncta priusstentanda, quam ferrum. Hæc inter excusationes tuas vltima est, vbi nescio an illud gloriosi militis apud Terentium esse oblitus: omnia prius experiri, o filio, quam armis sapientem decet. Nihil enim aliud ad patrocinium tarentiae huius affaris, nisi quid & medicos docuisse ais, & Cæsares didicisse: bene quidem multum disparia coaequasti. Nam & Cæsares ægro orbi mederi solitos accepimus, nunc & ipsi cum reliquis ægrotant. & mundus æger medico caret, & mors vniuersalis in foribus est. Dic autem mihi, Cæsar, quid ex omnibus interatum est verba, preces, nunc blanditiæ, apparatus. Quid restat, nisi vt hostib. imperii (i. e. Papæ & Reg. Siciliæ) supplex ad genua prouoluaris: Si id audituc, fœdum & indignum est, serum superest, vltima Veterno sorum vicerum medicina. Nam quid amplus expectas? Padus vt ad fontem redeat: Ibit ille qua solitus est, & cum amne fluent anni, quodque non nunc nouiter ex me audis, iuuentam senectus excipiet, senectutem mors, nihil prorsus hinc auferes, nisi quod bene seu quod male gesseris: nihil hic dimittes tuum præter nominis memoriam & exangue corpusculum. Illud quoque non iam tuum, sed terræ parentis ac vermium, non magis Caturibus quam plebeis parcentium, imo quidem auidius corpora nobiliora rodentium. Quid de aliis fiet, quæ videntur tua? Certe opes & imperium linquas alteri necesse est, & ignoras cui. Hæc humana conditio est, cui nec Cæsar nec pontifex Romanus, denique nec regum nec omnino hominum vllus eximitur. Nunc igitur nunc cura, quod semper nō poteris, quā ita scil. esse velis, quæ propria & irreuocabiliter tua sunt, animam & famam. Inter temeritatem & inertiam nescio quid eligam: sæne temeritas felicior fuit: non delector extremis medium quæro: sed heu vereor (quod pace sit dictum tua omnium quæ, qui in perio vili prosunt, quique gerendarum rerum officia suscepepunt) ne penitus verum sit, quod in ore semper habeo: singulæ.
units.tr: For then there was great danger and immense labour for our side in resisting, but now the way is smooth and easy. The trouble is that there is no traveller: luxury and idleness reign far and wide. Ignorance holds the world, a world that will soon fall to an armed Caesar, or rather will act on your behalf. Your name is well known, and with the help of a few good men and lovers of virtue and of empire, you could easily win every war against an unarmed luxury and an unarmed pride. Do you want me not merely to prove these things, but to show you that they are as I say? Look: the day before yesterday a man rose up from the humble plebs, not a Roman king, not a consul, not a patrician, scarcely a well-known Roman citizen, with no titles of his own, no greatness of ancestors, and in short no distinction of his own in that age, who declared himself the champion of Roman liberty. The bold profession of this obscure man was at once welcomed, as you know, by Tuscany eagerly, and it took up command. Soon all Italy followed, then Europe, and then the whole world was in motion. Why say more? We are not reading these things; we have seen them. Justice and peace already seemed to have returned, with their companions kindly faith and quiet security, and at last the traces of the golden age seemed to appear. Yet he was cut down in the very flower of the affair, and it was open to another. I do not want to blame him, nor anyone else. I do not condemn the man; rather I acquit him. I am no judge. I know what I think, and he had taken the title of Tribune, which among the Roman offices was the humblest name. If the tribunate could accomplish so much, what could the name of Caesar do? But if you delay, if you hesitate, and you do not heed, as I have set before your eyes, the flight of time, it is over: the empire falls, liberty perishes. Caesar, I beg you, do not read these things with resentment. They may be less sweet to your taste than you would like. I do not know what bile they may stir, since only bitter remedies penetrate. I do not fear to tell you the truth, because I know that you love the truth and wisely hate flatteries, best and most magnificent of men. Aconites are kingdoms, the mockery of the powerful, the death of princes, the arms of the faithful. But indeed we do not know how great a beast empire is. This was the other colour of your excuses. I wonder why you attributed this saying to Augustus, when it belongs to Tiberius, unless perhaps the care of present affairs has clouded your memory of the past, or, as is common, you call any emperor Caesar and so Augustus. Perhaps you did this knowingly, so that authority might be sought from the author of the saying you had decided to use, aware of the difference between Augustus and Tiberius. The former was the wisest and best of princes; the latter was foul and fierce, and, as he said of himself, a quiet lump of mud soaked in blood. Yet if you wish to know at what time he said this, or if anything of it has crept into your memory amid so many greater cares, you will find it in Suetonius. He said it at the time when, Augustus having departed from human affairs, his far less worthy successor, most shamelessly, had seized the empire for himself, yet with ambiguous and deceitful words and varied dissimulation he refused, seeking a false way of taking the name, to such an extent that someone, mocking a man who kept dodging, witheringly and elegantly jeered that other men are slow to fulfil what they promise, but he was slow to promise what he would fulfil. But grant it: let it be the saying of a good prince, uttered with an honest mind; let Augustus be its author. What does that matter? "I do not know," he says, "how great a beast the empire is." Indeed we know this very well: it is a most powerful beast. It is a huge beast, yet so tractable that a skilled hand receives the bridle. What is it not possible to manage if it is untamed? Dare, go on, seize the bridle in your hand and mount the throne that is owed to you. If you are afraid, it will find a rider. Julius Caesar, whose hereditary name you bear, as I was just saying, mounted a horse born in his own house, impatient of any other rider, and he kept it among his delights. Will you alone flee the throne, which is impatient of no other occupant, but has been occupied by so many princes in the past, and which is most eager for your seat? But indeed, all things must be tried before the sword. This is the last of your excuses, and I do not know whether you have forgotten that saying of the glorious soldier in Terence: "It befits a wise man to try everything before arms, my son." For there is nothing else to support this hesitation of yours, except what you say physicians have taught and Caesars have learned. Indeed you have joined together things that are very different. For we have heard that Caesars were accustomed to heal the sick world, but now they themselves are sick with the rest. The world is sick and lacks a physician, and universal death is at the door. But tell me, Caesar, what has been done with all of these: words, prayers, and now flatteries and display? What remains, except that you should prostrate yourself as a suppliant at the knees of the enemies of the empire (that is, the Pope and the King of Sicily)? If you still hear this, it is shameful and unworthy, and there is little left: the last remedy for the old sores of the empire. For what more do you expect? For the Po to return to its source? It will go where it is accustomed to go, and as the years flow with the stream, and as I say to you now not for the first time: old age will follow youth, and death will follow old age. You will take nothing from here except what you have done well or badly. You will leave nothing here except the memory of your name and a bloodless little body. Not even that will be yours any longer, but the property of the earth, the mother and of the worms, which spare no more the mighty than the common people, and indeed gnaw nobler bodies all the more greedily. What will become of the other things that seem to be yours? Surely you must leave your wealth and empire to another, and you do not know to whom. This is the human condition, from which neither Caesar nor the Roman pontiff, nor indeed any king or any man at all, is exempt. Now therefore, now take care of what you cannot always do, namely to be the sort of person you wish to be, and of what is truly and irrevocably your own: your soul and your reputation. I do not know which to choose between rashness and idleness. Rashness has often been the more fortunate. I do not take pleasure in extremes; I seek the middle course. But alas, I fear (may it be said with your peace, of all those who serve in public office and have taken on the duties of managing affairs) that what I always have on my lips may be entirely true: that each single vice has its own single excuse, but idleness alone has all of them.

units.la: singulæ singula vitia singulas excusationes habere, inertiam solam omnes. Si diu deliberasset Africanus, Italia deferebatur à suis & Afrorum erat. Si diu deliberasset Nasica, libertas Romana Gracchi conatibus & audaciæ succumbebat. Si Claudius Nero (non dicam superuacua multa & longa, sed unum quod necessarium videbatur & breue erat) senatusconsultum expectasset, coniunctus fratri Hasdrubal Romanum proculcabat nomen. Quid inter minores hæreo? ipse, quem sepe nomino, Iulius Cæsar si procrastinator fuisset, nunq; in tam paruo tempore hanc tantâ, quæ vix omnium studio sustinetur, fundasset erexissetque rerum molem, cui imperii nomen est. Tu si cuncta deliberas & singulis immoraris, prædicam tibi, & si forte non animo tuo gratu, ac certe fidei meæ debitum, falsus utinam sim aruspex, nullus erit rerum finis, alii ex aliis erumpent laquei: nunq; te Italia, nunquam tu Italiâ videbis, extra quam ubi Imperii caput quæras nescio, proinde quod scribis: te non ambitione tractum ad imperium aspirasse, sed difficultatis haud nescium diuina iussioni paruisse, credo. Nam & prudentiam & modestiam tuam novi; sed vide ne hoc tibi primum calcar & maximum esse debuerit, quo diuini certus auxilii properares. Tu quidem patrii regni finibus contentus, Imperatorii oneris & honoris sarcinam ultro aliis linquebas. Hanc infallibilis ipse rerum sator, rector & cognitor multis cupientibus ereptam humeris tuis imposuit, paruisti. Non acceptare Imperium forte magnum fuerit: de hoc tamen docti viderint: Certe sine scelere poterat non recipi; receptum negligi sine scelere non potest. Deus enim tibi (sicut ipse non dissimulas) Deus inquam, non tuus labor aut ambitio imperii auctor est. Times eo duce proficisci, quo iubente & Abraham unicum filium mactare, & Moyses pastor incomitatus faciem superbi & obstinati regis adire non timuit. Scio multa te vellicant, quibus compositis alia atq; alia emergerent. Credisne tu, Cæsar, in imperio sine curis vitam agere, quam pastor in tugurio non agit? Nam illa qualia sunt, quibus inniteris? nonne quot publicæ mundi clades, tot priuatim famæ tuæ vulnera; quotque hinc excusationes efficere vbiuis, tot in te conficis argumenta? Cuius enim pudorem, nisi regis, prægrauant Regni mala? Diruta est, inquis, Imperii libertas. Tu pater Imperii dirutam restaurabis. Sumpta Latinis seruitus, tu illam tuorum cæruicib. excutes. Ad auaritiæ Lupanar prostituta iustitia, tu illam ad sua sacra penetralia revocabis: pax è mentibus lapsa mortalium, tu illam in sua sede restitues. Ad hoc n. natus, huic officio destinatus es, vt Reip. deformitates aboleas, & pristinâ faciem mundo reddas. Tunc verus mihi Cæsar verusq; videberis Imperator, cum officiû tuum impleueris, sine quo nedum Princeps, sed ne priuatus quispiâ iure laudabitur. Addis a. (stupeo auditu) nesciam tunc secessionis Italiâ. Quando, obsecro, id fuit? Ego n. in Annalib. vix aut vllum tale tepus inuenerim, aut inueniri posse crediderim: Sileo illa vetustiora, ipsius vrbis originem & primos muros fraterna cæde madentes, & impio scelere quæsita diademeta: Quotiens parta iam libertate plebs indignans secessit à patribus? testes sunt mons sacer, Ianiculum, Auentinus. Pyrrhus in Italiâ traiecit, opem nempe laturus rebellantibus Tarentinis. Eodem tempore & Brutii defecerant & Lucani aliæque gentes Italicæ, quas omnes bello contundi & nolentes in fidem redigi oportuit. Secutus est Annibal, defecit Capua magnis Romanorum obstricta beneficiis, & vt proprie dicam, populi Romani libertá, sed infidelis & ingrata. Imo v. quis ea tempestate non defecit? Relege historias. Decem octo Coloniæ, p omnê Italiâ in fide manserunt, quarum subsidio, vt Liui summi historici verbis vtar, tunc imperiû populi Rom. stetit, iunq; gratia in senatu & apud populû acta. Quid totiens Hernicos rebellantes, quid perpetuos hostes Volsos Æduosq; commemorem? Quot cum Latinis bella ppè ciuilia (vnum n. corpus imperii videbatur) quot vrbes euersæ, atq; inprimis ipsa Rom. imperii parens Alba? q; vt fieret, quid nisi defectionû metus ac memoria horrabatur? Quotiens cû Sabinis ancipiti acie decertatû, cum Vmbris, cû Samnitibus, cum Etruscis, cû Liguribus ac Boiis & Gallis Insubribus, vbi Mediolanû Ticinûmq; vrbes sunt? Sed quid Longius feror? Tibur ac Tusculû, & Præneste, triaque suburbia vrbis Romæ, bellorû casus ac materiâ præbuere, cû non suis tm virib. insultarent, sed externis hostibus auxiliû ac receptacula pbuissent. Ad hæc Veii vix decennio diruti, exustę Sidenæ sanctitatis admirarione, Phalerii subacti, vi capta Neapolis, coeptumq; Brundusiû, & Conoli, & Fregellæ, & Sora, & Algidum, & Corniculû, ac Sutricû, & Bonillæ, & Venilæ, & Fesulæ, vnde patriæ meæ fundamenta fluxerût. piget fateor, maximis parua connectere. Sed vt iâ præualidæ robustæque ciuitati nihil arduû sit tenere ac vix dû pubescenti Reip. nullus aculeus parû erat. Adde Syracusanâ obsidionê longâ atq; difficilê clarissimeq; vrbis interitû, q Duces quoq; hostiû ad comiserationê lachrymasq; cõpelleret. Adde Firmium atq; Esculum, & Picenû omne pdomitum, Vescinosq; & Marsos & Pelignos; interq; tot externos tumultus intestinas domi seditiones, & Senatus insolentiâ, & tribunitiam rabiem, & turbulentissimos Agrariæ legis motus, vt reliquos fileâ, quos enumerare nõ sufficio. Adde postquâ res ad vnius imperiû rediit. coniurationes innumeras & totiens, licet frustra petitum insidiis Augustum caput, vt omittam qui veneno vel gladio petierê. Adde famem Perusinam, & obsidionem Mutinensem, & defectionê Coloniæ Cremonensiû, q vna fuerat inter paucas fidelissima, quarum paulo ante memineram. Longum nimio historiæ iter atripui, sed subsistam. Omnis enim ætas secessionib. Italicis ac defection bus plena est, vt forti animo & veterum memori nihil possit insoliti terroris occurrere, vtque nimis proprie dictum & ex ipso naturæ gremio sumtus videatur, quod Virgilius ait:
units.tr: Each of the vices has its own excuses; idleness alone has them all. If Africanus had deliberated for long, Italy would have been surrendered by his own people to the Africans. If Nasica had deliberated for long, Roman liberty would have yielded to the efforts and audacity of Gracchus. If Claudius Nero had waited for a decree of the senate (I will not mention the many superfluous and lengthy matters, but only the one that seemed necessary and was brief), he would have joined his brother Hasdrubal and trampled the Roman name underfoot. Why do I linger among lesser examples? Julius Caesar himself, whom I mention so often, if he had been a procrastinator, would never in so short a time have founded and raised up that great structure of affairs, which can scarcely be sustained even by the zeal of all, and which bears the name of empire. If you weigh everything and dwell on each detail, I predict to you (and may I be a false soothsayer, if it is not your own wish, and certainly what I owe to my loyalty), there will be no end to affairs; snares will break out one after another, and you will never see Italy, and Italy will never see you, unless you seek the seat of empire somewhere else, I do not know where. Therefore, as you write, that you aspired to empire not drawn by ambition, but, not unaware of the difficulty, you obeyed a divine command, I believe it. For I know both your prudence and your modesty; but take care that this should have been for you the first and greatest spur, by which you hastened to the certain help of God. You, indeed, content with the borders of your ancestral kingdom, were willing to leave the burden and honour of the imperial office to others. This the infallible sower, ruler and knower of things himself, snatched from many who desired it and placed on your shoulders; you obeyed. Perhaps it would be a great thing not to accept the empire; but learned men may consider that. Surely it could not be refused without wrongdoing; and once accepted, it cannot be neglected without wrongdoing. For God, not your labour or ambition, is the author of this (as you yourself do not conceal), God, I say, not your labour or ambition, is the author of it. You fear to set out under a leader by whose command Abraham also was ready to slay his only son, and Moses, a shepherd without companions, did not fear to approach the face of the proud and obstinate king. I know that many things trouble you, and that, if they were set in order, other and different things would emerge. Do you believe, Caesar, that in empire you live without cares, when the shepherd in his hut does not live so? For what are those things on which you rely? Are not the calamities of the public world so many wounds to your reputation in private; and do you not, as many excuses as you make from them everywhere, equally build as many arguments against yourself? For whose shame, unless the king's, do the evils of the realm weigh down? The liberty of the empire, you say, has been overthrown. You, the father of the empire, will restore what has been overthrown. Servitude has been taken up by the Latins; you will shake it off from their necks. Justice, prostituted to the brothel of avarice, you will recall to her own sacred shrine; peace, fallen from the minds of mortals, you will restore to her own seat. For you were born for this, destined for this office, that you should abolish the deformities of the commonwealth and restore its former face to the world. Then you will appear to me a true Caesar and a true emperor, when you have fulfilled your duty, without which no one, not to say a prince, but not even a private citizen, will be rightly praised. You add (I am astonished to hear it) that you would then not know of a secession from Italy. When, I ask, was that? For in the Annals I could scarcely find, or believe that one could find, any such time. I pass over those more ancient things: the origin of the city itself and its first walls, wet with fraternal slaughter, and the diadems sought by impious crime. How often, once liberty had been won, did the indignant plebs secede from the patricians? Witnesses are the Sacred Mountain, the Janiculum, the Aventine. Pyrrhus crossed into Italy, of course to bring aid to the rebellious Tarentines. At the same time the Bruttii had revolted, and the Lucanians and other Italian peoples, all of whom had to be crushed in war and brought back into allegiance against their will. Hannibal followed, and Capua, bound by great benefits from the Romans, revolted, and, to speak properly, against the liberty of the Roman people, but faithless and ungrateful. Indeed, who in that age did not revolt? Read the histories. Eighteen colonies, throughout all Italy, remained loyal; by whose aid, to use the words of Livy, the great historian, the empire of the Roman people then stood, and favour was secured in the senate and among the people. Why should I recall how often the Hernici rebelled, or the Volsci and Aedui, perpetual enemies? How many wars with the Latins, almost civil (for they seemed one body of the empire), how many cities were overthrown, and especially Alba, the very parent of the Roman empire? And to bring this about, what was it that made the fear and memory of revolts horrible? How often was the fight doubtful against the Sabines, the Umbrians, the Samnites, the Etruscans, the Ligurians, and the Boii and Gauls, the Insubres, where the cities of Milan and Ticinum are? But why am I carried further afield? Tibur and Tusculum and Praeneste, and the three suburbs of the city of Rome, provided the chances and matter of wars, since they did not attack with their own forces alone, but had given aid and refuge to foreign enemies. Besides these, Veii, scarcely destroyed after ten years; Sidicina, burned for admiration of its sanctity; Faleri, subdued; Naples, taken by force; and Brundisium, begun and then abandoned, and Cono­lium, Fregellae, Sora, Algidum, Corniculum, Sutrium, Bonella, Venilia, and Fesulae, from which the foundations of my fatherland flowed. I am sorry to confess, I connect small things with great. But although it is nothing arduous for a very strong and robust state to hold together, and to a commonwealth scarcely grown up, no sting was small. Add the long and difficult siege of Syracuse and the most famous destruction of that city, which would move even the enemy leaders to pity and tears. Add Firmum and Asculum, and all Picenum subdued, and the Vescini, the Marsi and the Paeligni; and among so many external tumults, the internal seditions at home, the arrogance of the senate, the tribunician frenzy, and the most turbulent movements of the agrarian law; and I pass over the rest, which I am not able to enumerate. Add, after affairs came back to the rule of one man, the countless conspiracies, and the head of Augustus so often sought by ambush, though I omit those who sought it with poison or sword. Add the famine at Perusia, the siege of Mutina, and the revolt of the colony of Cremona, which alone had been most faithful among the few I mentioned a little before. I have taken too long a road through history, but I will stop. For every age is full of Italian secessions and revolts, so that for a brave spirit, mindful of the ancients, nothing of unusual terror can occur, and what Virgil says seems said too aptly and drawn from the very bosom of nature:

units.la: Grauidam imperiû bellisque frementem, Italiam
units.tr: Italy, pregnant with empire and roaring with wars

units.la: Talis n. ab initio fuit, talis est hodie, talis ad extremû erit. Illa v. q valida? paupertas remoratur. Quid haber paupertas cômune cû Cæsare? aut quo modo pauper est, qualias dicat? animus pauperê facit, & diuitem pauper sum: & Iulius ante Imperium pauper fuit, post imperium non diues: Nemo enim liberalius victoria vsus est, vt ait Annæus Seneca, nihil sibi retinuit præter dispensandi potestatem. Postremo, pauper sum: multos in bellum impulit paupertas, multis animos dedit, præsertim si aduersarius diues sit. Diuitias nempe viris fortibus bellum facit. At monet paucitas meorum Comites, bellum parat, terret fama vulgaris. Quorundam minimarum rerum aliquando magnum est nomen, & sæpe fama terribilior quam conspectus. Opinio rem non mutat, q tui nequeunt oculi, tuorum vident, non quia vegetiores, sed quia propinquiores. Multa de longinquo cernentib. metuêda, propinquatibus apparuere ridicula. Ecce q tibi multa, Cæsar, p tribus epistolis scripsi, si forsitan ter vocatus exaudias, & vt quem non potes aliter, in his literis animum meum cernas. Mallem posse tibi armatis legionibus obuiam ire imperata facturus: quod vnum datur, animo atq; exhortationibus occurro, neq; iam satis scio, quid vltra loquar, neq; si hoc non sufficit, quid ex me sufficere possit intelligo. In te magnanime Cæsar, in te, inquâ, esse debet ignis ille, quem speramus nobis & algenti iustitiæ succursurum. Sed is forsan extinctus est. Nequicquam flamus in cinerem. Improbi viri verbum est, sed hac in parte vetidici virtutem verba non addere. Excitare illam potest adhortatio, non dare. Itaq; nihil amplius dicam, nisi id, in quo totius negotii vis est, omnia consilio Cæsar degert, sed nihil inertia. Et est, vbi non multum consultasse consilium sit. Vale 9. Cal. Decemb.
units.tr: Such has it been from the beginning, such it is today, and such it will be to the end. But what is strong in that? Poverty holds it back. What does poverty have in common with Caesar? Or how is he poor, or what sort of poverty does he mean? The mind makes a man poor or rich: I am poor. Julius was poor before he held power and was not rich after it, for no one has used victory more generously, as Annaeus Seneca says; he kept nothing for himself but the power to distribute. Finally, I am poor: poverty has driven many into war and given courage to many, especially when the opponent is rich. It is indeed the rich whom poverty makes war upon, and brave men have the riches. But he warns that my companions are few, and he prepares for war, and common rumour frightens him. The names of some very small things are sometimes great, and rumour is often more terrifying than the sight of the thing. Opinion does not change the reality. What your eyes cannot see, your men's eyes do see, not because they are sharper but because they are nearer. Many things that are feared when seen from afar appear ridiculous when we come close. Look, Caesar, I have written you many things in three letters, in case you may hear me after being called a third time, and so that, since you cannot see me in any other way, you may see my mind in these letters. I would rather be able to meet you with armed legions and carry out your orders; since that is the one thing granted to me, I meet you with my spirit and my exhortations, and I no longer know what more to say, nor do I understand what I could add if this is not enough. In you, great-hearted Caesar, in you, I say, that fire must be, which we hope will come to our aid in our chilled justice. But perhaps it has been extinguished. We blow in vain upon the ashes. It is the word of a dishonest man, but in this matter it is not the part of a truthful man to add words that are not true. Exhortation can kindle that fire, but it cannot give it. So I will say nothing more except this, on which the whole force of the business rests: Caesar, manage everything by counsel, but not by inertia. And there are times when having taken too much counsel is itself no counsel at all. Farewell, the ninth day before the Kalends of December.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Increpatio ad Imperatorem, quod Italiam Imperio debitam Papæ & aliis iniustis incubatoribus relinquat, nec ad eam venirent.
units.tr: A rebuke to the Emperor, because he abandons Italy, which is owed to the Empire, to the Pope and other unjust usurpers, and does not come to it.

units.la: FR. PETRARCHA CAROLO IV. ROMAN. IMP. S. Italos fines & claustra nostri orbis intranti nuper animo tibi obuius & literis fui; nec multo post à te vocatus, & corpore abeuntem animo quoq; sequor & literis. Hoc intelligi potest, quod tunc læta literæ lætusq; animus fuit, nunc mœsta sunt omnia. Ergo tu, Cæsar, quod auus tuus innumeriq; alii tanto sanguine quæsierunt tantisque laboribus, sine labore adeptus & sanguine complanatam apertamque Italiam, patens limen vrbis Romæ, sceptrum facile, imperturbatum ac pacificum Imperium, incruenta diademata, vel tantorum ingratus munerum, vel rerum non idoneus æstimator & hæc linquis? &, ô naturam mutare magnus labor, ad barbarica rursum regna reuolueris? Non audeo clare tibi dicere, q mens resque exigunt, ne te verbo contristem, qui me & mundum facto contristas tuo, non quod ob inuidiuas ac satyras (merito panegyricum debeatur) aut aliam ob causam loqui vetet; nisi q hoc tuo tam præcipiti digressu fugaque, verum vti fatear, simillimo te neminem arbitror tristitem, quo magis magisque me attonitum habet, hoc consilium, cui an fortuna vnquam fautura sit nescio: certe ratio & virtus & boni omnes totumque, si loqui posset, Imperium aduersantur, mali omnes plaudunt, ac rebelles. Itamen, quando ita fixum animo est: sed hoc quoque memoriæ vt affigas velim, & valedicentis memoriale munusculum tecum feras, à nullo vnquam principum tantam spem, tam floridam, tam maturam, tamque honestam sponte desertam. Neque v. minor animus Romanum Principem decebat quam Macedonum Regem, qui mox finibus patriæ egressus non se Macedoniæ dominum, sed terrarum omnium dici iussit, cum nō esset. Tu Imperii Dominus Romani nil nisi Boëmiam suspicas. Quando hoc, quæso, fecisset auus tuus aut genitor, qui etsi non Imperator ipse esset, sola paterni Imperii memoria tot vrbium ius quæsiuit, sed non est hæreditarium bonum virtus, quamuis ego nec tibi imperandi scientiam deesse crediderim, nec bellandi. Fons actionum omnium voluntas est. O si in ipsis Alpium iugis tibi nunc paterq; siant obuii: quid dicturos putas? crede illos audias vel absentes. Profecisti exinde, ingens Cæsar, hoc tuo tot per annos dilato in Italiam aduentu, & festinato abitu refers demum istud ferreum, illud aureum diadema, simul ac sterile nomen imperii. Imperator Romanorum vocitabaris, Boëmiæ rex solius, qui vtinam vnquam esses, vt vel sic altius coacta virtus assurgeret, famesque domestica neglectum aniti patrimonii cultum suaderet. Sed iam breui impetu defessus calamus requiescat & vere, vt augurror, fatigatis auribus der quietem. Salutem mihi Læpius meus tuis verbis attulit, quæ mihi iaculum anceps & lethale vulnus fuit, simulque Cæsareum effigiem peruetusti operis, quæ si vel ipsa loqui posset, vel tu illam contemplari, ab hoc te prorsus inglorio, ne dicam infami, itinere retraxisset. Vale Cæsar, & quid linquis, & quid petis, cogita.
units.tr: FRANCIS PETRARCH TO CHARLES IV, ROMAN EMPEROR. Greetings. Lately, as you entered the Italian borders and the gateway of our world, I met you in spirit and in letters. Not long after, summoned by you, I follow you in spirit as you depart, and in letters too. From this one can see that the letter and the spirit were then glad, and that now everything is sorrowful. So you, Caesar, who obtained by great bloodshed and great labour what your grandfather and countless others obtained, Italy levelled and laid open without labour or bloodshed, the gate of the city of Rome standing open, the sceptre won easily, an empire undisturbed and peaceful, crowns won without bloodshed: are you so ungrateful for such great gifts, or so poor a judge of affairs, that you leave all this? And, O, that it is a great labour to change one's nature, have you turned back again to barbarian kingdoms? I do not dare to tell you plainly what my mind and the facts demand, lest I grieve you with words, you who grieve me and the world by your deed. Not that I forbid speaking because of invective and satire (which would rightly be due to panegyric), or for any other reason. Only, to confess the truth, I think that no one is more like you in this headlong departure and flight. What astonishes me more and more is this plan, and whether fortune will ever favour it I do not know. Certainly reason, virtue, all good men, and the whole Empire, if it could speak, are opposed to it; all the wicked and the rebels applaud. Yet since this is fixed in your mind, I would still like you to fix this also in your memory, and to carry with you as a parting keepsake this thought: that no prince has ever freely abandoned such great hope, so bright, so ripe, and so honourable. Nor should the Roman prince have a smaller spirit than the King of the Macedonians, who, having just left the borders of his homeland, ordered himself to be called not lord of Macedonia but of all lands, though he was not. You, lord of the Roman Empire, look only to Bohemia. When, I ask, did your grandfather or your father do this? Your father, though he was not himself emperor, sought by the memory of the imperial rule alone the right over so many cities. But virtue is not an inherited good, although I would not believe that you lack the knowledge of ruling or of waging war. The source of all actions is the will. O, if your father and grandfather now met you on the very ridges of the Alps, what do you think they would say? Believe that you hear them even though they are absent. You have accomplished, great Caesar, this coming into Italy, delayed for so many years, and by your hasty departure you finally bring back that iron crown and that golden diadem, together with the empty name of empire. You were called Emperor of the Romans, king of Bohemia alone; would that you had been only that, so that compelled virtue might rise higher, and domestic hunger might urge you to cultivate the neglected patrimony you strive for. But now let my pen, weary after this brief assault, rest, and, as I augur, give rest to your truly wearied ears. My Laelius brought me greetings in your words, which were to me a double-edged javelin and a deadly wound; and at the same time the image of Caesar in a very ancient work, which, if it could speak itself, or if you could gaze upon it, would have drawn you back from this wholly inglorious, not to say infamous, journey. Farewell, Caesar, and consider what you leave and what you seek.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Increpatio ad Imperatorem, quod se tam humiliter Papa Romano prosternat.
units.tr: A rebuke to the Emperor, because he prostrates himself so humbly before the Roman Pope.

units.la: FR. PETRARCHA NERIO SVOS. Nondum superiori epist. signum impresseram, dum ecce alia superueniens coegit, vt posito annulo, depositū calamum rursus arripere, & quamuis tua hæc superiore sit longior, responso tñ breuiori contenta erit. Nā nec cui nostri querelam iterare est necesse, q & tacitus loquor, & ipsa res clamat, nec quicquam prohibet, q in illa dixerā, ad hāc transferri. Neq; n. aut minor est hodie dolor meus, q heri & nudius tertius fuit, neq; min' efficax epistolæ tuæ hodiernæ solatiū, quam hesternę. Accedit quod neq; de his, quæ nouissime scripsisti, ausim aperte pronunciare, q sentio, neq; tu ideo minus quid sentiam, quidve pnunciem intelligis. Sæpe silentium ad exprimendos animi conceptus, quovis sermone potentius fuit, nec minus silentio Niobe, quam latratu Hecuba, dolore animo insignitum designabat: itaque cum illa in saxum, hæc in canem versa fingatur, non minus mutum illius simulachrum, quam huius querula rabies, suam miseriam loquebatur. Illud non siluerim, agnoscere me Cæsarum fatum, quod & in occasu solis, & sub austro, denique ubi libet felicius fuerit, quam sub arcto, ita ibi gelida omnia, nullus ardor nobilis, nullus vitalis calor Imperii. Redde nobis fortuna, si Romuleos Cæsares, Parcæ vetant; at saltem ab Hispania Theodosios, Seueros ab Africa, ex Arabia Philippos, è Syria Alexandros. Heu quid nunc diceret architector ille magnus, successorem suum, cum sacerdote humili(i.e. Papa) de humilitate certare, dum meminisset superbissimum olim Galliarum Regem, dum simplex, ut ait Florus historicus, in castra venisset, phaleras & sua arma ante Cæsaris genua prosternere, ac dixisse: Habe hæc, virum fortem, vir fortissime, vicisti. Multa se offerunt id genus: Nam & loquentia materia & multiloqua indignatio est: sed frenabo impetum, ut qui hæc ipsa, non nisi interrogante ac dictante profuderim. Sane de Cæsaris Legatique congressu, quod prouidentissime vaticinaris, amplector & probo, & pene rem ipsam videor videre: non quod omnia ista me moveant, contra quæ multa sæpe disserui, sed ex præteritis ventura coniicio. Itaque non tangor, quod Legati semper in Cæsarem calcitrarit, quam quod calcitrare animos novi, & scio quod omnis potestas est consortis impatiens (cuius rei nisi antiqua sufficerent, vereor ne recens nobis exemplum casus attulerit, neve iam pontifex Romanus, Principem Romanum Romæ esse vetuerit, quod & fama loquitur, & fuga Cæsaris indicio est, qui non cupidius Italiam petiit, quam reliquit, ut mihi quidem super vacuo pelli videatur, qui tam libens fugit, quem tenere si velis sine magno nequeas labore: ut enim nunc intelligo, non huc aliam ob causam venit; nisi ut Diadema Cæsareum tua in sede susciperet, tantum ad hucreverentiæ, nō amplius, superest: ac successor Petri, Cæsaris successore securior, ista non curat, suumque ipse Diadema non pluris apud Tyberim quam apud Rhodanum facit. is ne diademate contentum & imperii titulo Roma digredi non solum patitur, sed iubet? & quem Imperatorem dici sinit, imperare a nullo sit securus modo, huic, o partes hominum mirae, penetrale diadematis templum aperit, arcem sedemque Imperii urbem claudit! Hæc hactenus. Lælium meum, imo tuum, imo nostrum, familiarissimum Cæsari factum gaudeo, non miror, nihil. a. est virtute rapacius, nihilque tenacius: rapit, vincitque animos hominum, vinctosque semel in perpetuum vinctos tenet. Nulla mihi dubitatio vnquam fuit, qui non solum ab illo humanissimo principum, sed ab alio quolibet licet asperioris ingenii, cui tamen virtus in pretio fit, posset ille vir amorem promereri, non modo notitia meruisset. Quis enim tam agrestis est, ut Lælium non amet, & sapientiæ laude conspicuum, & in amicitiis faustum nomen, quod si sola virtutis fama efficit, ut quem nunquam vidimus, senem illum Lælium amemus, quid huius nostri virtus, ac præsentia posse debent? Itaque minus miror, quod de Legato sedis Apostolicæ idem scribis, cum quo familiaritas Lælii vetus est; illud potius miror, quod prioribus literis prætermissum his inserui, quid ita illum ad coronandum Cæsarem diu ante digressum iste præuenerit, nisi quia (ut arbitror & ut solet) illum fortuna segnem, huc sollicitum virtus facit; Vnum non mirari cum eodem nequeo: ambo pergerent, Modanoque dimisso Tyberim peterent; unde reverentior adhuc Romanus Princeps, diadema supremum poscit, quod Petri successor Cæsaris successorem securior non curat. Qui fieri potuit, ut Cardinalis rutilo vertice, & purpureo fulgidus amictu, tantoque spectabilis comitatu, nostri huius lyncea lumina fugerit, aut cum hic Pilas, ille vix dum ianuam peruenisset, ita ut illi obuiam iste redierit. Auguror sane alterum terra, mari alterum venisse. De hoc equidem & reliquo statu vestro, tuis ac suis literis certior fieri velim. Ad singula respondisse videor. Nam ad epistolæ tuæ finem de familiaribus, cuius stylo alio & eorsum loquar ut soleo. Gratias autem tibi, quod quas ipse iam obliuioni tradideram, adeo ut ne locutum tibi de his aliquid me putarem, tam memoriter teneres, ut facile pateat, rerum te mearum curiosiorem esse, quam me ipsum. Mirum & pene incredibile, nisi charitatis tuæ miraculo incuriositas mea longe lateque nota detraheret. Vale feliciter nostri memor.
units.tr: FR. PETRARCH TO NERIO AND HIS FRIENDS. I had not yet pressed my seal on my previous letter when another arrived, and forced me to set aside my ring and take up my pen again. Your letter is longer than the previous one, but my reply will be shorter. There is no need to repeat my complaint to you, for I speak it silently and the matter itself cries it out. Nor is anything that I said there prevented from applying to this present case. My grief today is no less than it was yesterday or the day before, and your consolation in today's letter is no less effective than yesterday's. Besides, I would not dare to state plainly what I think about the things you wrote most recently, yet you understand what I think and what I am about to say all the same. Often silence has expressed the feelings of the mind more forcefully than any speech. Niobe in her silence, and Hecuba in her barking, each marked a grief stamped upon the mind. So, although the one is said to have been turned into stone and the other into a dog, the mute image of the first spoke her misery no less than the complaining rage of the second. One thing I will not keep silent about: I recognize the fate of the Caesars. Whether in the west or under the south wind, or wherever you like, it has been more fortunate than under the north, where everything is cold, there is no noble fire, and no vital warmth of the Empire. Give us back, Fortune, the Caesars of Romulus, if the Fates forbid it; but at least give us Theodosius from Spain, the Severi from Africa, Philip from Arabia, and Alexander from Syria. Alas, what would that great builder say now, if he saw his successor contending about humility with a humble priest (that is, the Pope)? He remembered that the once most proud King of the Gauls, when he came into the camp as a simple man, as the historian Florus says, laid his trappings and arms down before Caesar's knees and said: "Take these, brave man, most brave man; you have conquered." Many things of this kind present themselves. The subject is talkative, and my indignation is many-worded. But I will check my onrush, since I have poured out these very things only at your questioning and prompting. Certainly, concerning the meeting of Caesar and the Legate, which you prophesy so shrewdly, I accept and approve, and I almost seem to see the thing itself. This is not because all those things move me, against which I have often argued at length, but because I conjecture the future from the past. So I am not troubled that the Legates have always kicked against Caesar, as much as that I know they kick against spirits, and I know that all power is impatient of a partner. If the ancient examples did not suffice for this, I fear that a recent case may have brought us an example, and that the Roman Pontiff has now forbidden the Roman Prince to be at Rome. Rumour says so, and Caesar's flight is the sign of it. He did not seek Italy more eagerly than he left it, so that to me he seems to have been placed on empty ground, since he flees so willingly from what, if you wished to keep him, you could hardly hold without great labour. For, as I now understand, he came here for no other reason than to receive the Caesarean diadem in your see. Nothing more remains of that reverence than this. And the successor of Peter, more secure than Caesar's successor, does not care about these things, and values his own diadem no more on the Tiber than on the Rhone. Does he suffer the one who is content with a diadem and the title of Empire to depart from Rome, and even order it? And he who allows him to be called Emperor, and is himself secure from any command, opens to him, O strange ways of men, the inner temple of the diadem, and shuts the citadel and seat of the Empire, the city! So much for that. I rejoice that my Laelius, or rather yours, or rather ours, has become most intimate with Caesar. I am not surprised, for nothing is more grasping than virtue, and nothing more tenacious. It seizes and conquers the minds of men, and once conquered, it holds them bound for ever. I have never had any doubt that this man could earn love, not only from that most humane of princes, but from any other, however rough his nature, in whom virtue is held in esteem. He would have earned it, not merely by acquaintance. For who is so rustic as not to love Laelius, who is conspicuous for the praise of wisdom and whose name is blessed in friendships? If the mere fame of virtue makes us love that old Laelius whom we never saw, what ought the virtue and presence of this man of ours to accomplish? So I am less surprised that you write the same about the Legate of the Apostolic See, with whom Laelius has long been on familiar terms. What I rather marvel at is this: in my earlier letter I left something out and have inserted it here. Why did he go ahead so long before to crown Caesar, having set out earlier? Unless, as I suppose and as usually happens, fortune makes him slow and virtue makes this man anxious. One thing I cannot help but wonder at along with him: both of them were to proceed, and having dismissed Modena, make for the Tiber. From there the Roman Prince, still more reverent, demands the supreme diadem, which the successor of Peter, more secure, does not care about in the successor of Caesar. How could it happen that the Cardinal, bright with his ruddy crown and glittering in his purple cloak, and conspicuous with so great a retinue, escaped the lynx-eyes of this man of ours? Or when this one had scarcely reached Pilas, and that one had hardly reached the gate, how did it happen that the one returned to meet the other? I surely guess that one came by land and the other by sea. I would like to be informed about this, and about the rest of your state, by your letters and by theirs. I seem to have answered each point. As for the end of your letter about our friends, I will speak in another style and in another direction, as I usually do. I thank you, however, for remembering so exactly the things that I had already consigned to oblivion, so that I thought I had said nothing to you about them. It is clear that you are more curious about my affairs than I am myself. It is strange, and almost incredible, were it not that my own carelessness, well known far and wide, detracts from the wonder of your affection. Farewell, and remember me fondly.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Exhortatio ultima ad Imperatorem, de recuperanda Italia ab iniustis usurpatoribus.
units.tr: Final exhortation to the Emperor, on recovering Italy from the unjust usurpers.

units.la: FRAN. PETRARCHA CAROL. IV. ROM. IMP. S. Fessus præteriti, nec futuri fidens, Cæsar, calamum tuum in exhortationibus pene attritum recusantemque reposueram. Alit inter difficultates, refouetque animum spes successus, qua sublata quis est amens adeo, ut non infruetuoso labori requiem anteponat? Vt ad stylum redeam, sacer amor cogit, sive miles hic tuus huius nominis, sive ille sacer animi calor, qui mihi a parentibus relictus atque erga tuam semper, ex quo mihi primum notus es, erga vere Romani Imperii maiestatem ab infantia nutritus in praecordiis meis viuit, & indicis crescit, sine quod est verius, vterque. Nam neque meus amor tot iam clamoribus totque conatibus perditis vltro ad laborem inutilem rediisset, neque hic miles quamuis & amicus fecundus & sapiens me monuisset, nisi intus in anima vivas adhuc fauillas priscæ fidei, quas admoto magnæ spei fomite leui folle suauissimæ orationis attenderet, innuisset. nisset multis & magnis indiciis generosas animi tui curas, vereque Cæsareo libenter felicitatis & gloriæ tuæ crudelis auribus insusurans, quibus de prædiffidentiæ gelu nouæ spei feruore dissolueret. Eia igitur, Cæsar, duce Deo, quod tibi commisit imperium, surge, & dilatum sed magnum honestissimum, dum possis, felciter. Gloriosus finis lentum principium excusabit. Omnes te alto contient, quod nondum messis Hesperia plene maturuisset, in quam vtiliter falx Cæsaris nostra famesmorte ...
units.tr: FRANCISCUS PETRARCHA, TO CHARLES IV, ROMAN EMPEROR, GREETING. Weary of the past and not trusting in the future, Caesar, I had put my pen away, nearly worn out and unwilling, after so many exhortations. Hope of success nourishes the spirit amid difficulties and revives it, and without that hope who would be so mad as to prefer rest to fruitless labour? To return to my pen: sacred love compels me, whether it is this soldier of yours who bears that name or that sacred warmth of spirit which was left to me by my parents, which has lived in my heart since childhood, nourished by my love for the majesty of the truly Roman Empire, and which grows with signs of it, or, what is truer, both.
