For my love would not have returned unbidden to such useless labour after so many cries and so many failed attempts, nor would this soldier, though a friend and a wise man, have admonished me, unless he had signalled that there are still living embers of the old faith within your soul, which he might fan with the light bellows of the sweetest speech, applying the tinder of great hope. By many great signs he had whispered in your ear the noble cares of your mind, and, truly and gladly eager for your felicity and glory, he sought to dissolve with the warmth of new hope the frost of your former distrust. Come then, Caesar, with God as your guide, rise up to the empire entrusted to you, and while you can, happily undertake the postponed but great and most honourable task. A glorious end will excuse a slow beginning. All things urge you on, since the Hesperian harvest has not yet fully ripened, into which our Caesar's sickle may usefully ... [the remainder of the sentence is lost in the redaction].

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: De Maiestate Imperii Romani per homines Papales læsa vindicanda & dignitate Imperii in libertatem asserenda.
units.tr: On the majesty of the Roman Empire, injured by the men of the Pope, and on vindicating the dignity of the Empire into liberty.

units.la: FRAN. PETRARCHA PRINCIPI ROMANO S. Quid hinc humanitatis aut clementiæ, seu quid omnino iustitiæ sperare possis, excellentiæ tuæ nuntius expertus testabitur. nouum genus sævitiæ, puerum incomitatum, incautum, innocentem, hostiliter aggredi, virgulam, quam si quid sani esset, & vereri & temere debuerat, capsulam quoque gratissimis ac suauissimis literis refertam, in caput immeritum, donec vtrumque frangeretur, allidere, ipsas quoq; literas, quæ marmoreos animos mollire potuissent, disceptas effundere. En hospitalitas, en charitas, ad Durentiam captus, tortus, flagellatus, & ciuitatis ingressu prohibitus, nuntius tuus, minas cum verberibus, ac vulneribus referens, ad pedes tuos, vertice cruentato rediit. O vere Durentia, vt vulgus appellat, duritiæ gentium, siue vt quidem scriptores vocant, Ruentia, à ruendo diceris, præceps fluuius, damnosusque, cuius accolæ nihil vndis & alueo mitiores, & ipsi tanto impetu in quodlibet scelus ruunt. O impudenter elati! O irruentes & indeuoti amnes! O non tua sorbens & tumide in Dominum surgens Sorgal. O Rhodanus rodens omnia, sic Tyberim recognoscitis, sic Romanam dominam honoratis? O Auinio, cuius vinea (si quid consectoribus fidei est) botros amarissimos, & cruentam profert vindemiam, sic dominam Romanam colis, sic tui, sic illius, sic propriæ seruitutis, sic summi imperii memores! Væ tibi infœlix, si illa coeperit expergisci; imo vero si caput extulerit, & dormienti sibi illatas iniurias ac damna prospexerit. Exper-
units.tr: Francis Petrarch to the Roman Prince, greetings. What humanity or mercy, or indeed any justice, you may hope for from this quarter, your excellency's messenger will bear witness from his own experience. It is a new kind of cruelty: to attack a boy who was unaccompanied, unguarded and innocent, as an enemy would. They struck him with a rod, which, if they had any sense, they ought to have feared and respected, and they also struck a small case full of the most welcome and pleasant letters against his undeserving head, until both were broken; then they tore open the letters themselves, which could have softened hearts of marble. See the hospitality, see the charity! At the Durance your messenger was seized, tortured, flogged, and barred from entering the town. He returned to your feet with a bloodied head, bringing threats together with blows and wounds. O Durance, which the common people call hard, as the peoples' hardness, or as the writers call you, Ruentia, from ruere, to rush headlong: you are a headlong and destructive river, whose inhabitants are no gentler than your waves and bed, and who themselves rush into every crime with such violence. O shamelessly proud! O raging and undutiful streams! O Sorgue, who do not drink in your own waters and rise up in swelling pride against your Lord! O Rhône, who gnaw everything! Is this how you acknowledge the Tiber, is this how you honour the Roman mistress? O Avignon, whose vine (if the pursuers of the faith have any claim) yields most bitter clusters and a bloody vintage: is this how you worship the Roman mistress? Is this how you remember yourself, her, your own slavery, and the supreme empire? Woe to you, unhappy one, if she begins to wake, indeed if she lifts her head and looks upon the injuries and losses done to her while she slept. You shall learn by experience—

units.la: Expectate enim iam nunc est, crede mihi, non dormit, sed silet, & somnia praeteriti temporis sub silentio repetit, & quid surgens actura sit cogitat. Expectato paululum, & videbis magnalia in orbe terrarum, fierique mirabere, quae ante factum impossibilia iudicasti. An quid las, an ubi sis, an cui subsis ignoras? An provinciae nomen nescis, unde descendat? Quis nam furor hic? Quaenam ista dementia? sic modico sereno tempestatum omnium surrepsit oblivio? Siccine provinciarum dominam veneratis? Sopi[?] tu mortuam credidisti, ac velut morte dominae liberrari reddita, adhuc servam te puta. Nisi libertatem ipsam Hagitus approbares, esse aliquid posse, aliquid videri cupis, nos aliquandiu te voti compotem deliberando feci[?]us, tempus est, ut nobis admonentibus respicias. Multorum nempe potentia, non improprie viribus, sed in aliena debilitate fundata est. Verum haec adversario conualescente cohibet oportet.
units.tr: For believe me, she is now waiting; she is not asleep but silent, and she recalls in silence the dreams of past time, and considers what she will do when she rises. Wait a little, and you will see great things in the world, and you will marvel at deeds which you judged impossible before they happened. Or do you not know where you are, or to whom you are subject? Do you not know the name of your province, or whence it comes? What madness is this? What insanity is this? Has forgetfulness of all past storms crept in with such a brief calm? Is this how you honour the mistress of provinces? You thought she was dead, and, as if liberated by the death of your mistress, you still reckon yourself a slave. Unless you approve of liberty itself as a vanity, and wish to be and seem something, we have for a while made you, by deliberation, a man who has his wish; it is time that, at our admonition, you look back. The power of many, indeed, is founded not so much on their own strength as on the weakness of others. But this must be restrained while the adversary is recovering.

units.la: Tu ergo quid fueris intelliges, cum quid adhuc sit Roma, cognoveris, cuius modo nuncius sic timidus putans non esse qui vindicet in caelo Deus, est qui vindicet in terris animus Dei quem tu vires, quas ne suspicari quidem potes. Ha[?] miseria, sed experiere illico ut spero, tuae nobis vim nostram iniuriae reddidere. Cum primum dolere coepimus, magno tractu, et ad sanitatem et robur accessimus. Tu vires nostras misereare, vir illustris; erige surgentem patriam, et gentibus quid nunc etiam Roma possit ostende. De reliqua etiam Italia, cui dubium est, quin, quantum potuit, possit, nec vires, nec opes, nec animos defore, sed consensum. Qui si unus adfuerit, illud dentibus nomini Italico, tenore praesentis epistolae, propinquam stragem, perniciemque denuncio. Tu (inquam) quem tantae rei ducem fata constituunt, perge quae coepisti; nihil formidaveris, nebeculae istae sole radiante dissilient: vulpecularum astutiae Leonis imperium non ferent. Ingressus es gloriose: i fortiter, constanter ad reliqua, ostende superbiae quantum humilitate sit inferior, avaritiae quantum largitate pauperior, fallaciae quam stulta sit adiecta prudentiae, voluptati, quam turpis admota temperantiae atque decori. Agnoscat tandem fucus hypocrisis, quam nihil sit, ubi vera virtus affulserit. Eia age, rumpe moras, & ranam tumore tidiculo, molem solidi bovis imitantem protere, frange, conculca. Non loquor ut incitem, nec impulsore, nec lenitore indiges, & calcar, & frenum in potestate habes, sed dolorem animi tacitus ferre non potui. Dolor loquendo auctus querelam fudit, & vicissim sermo indignationi aliientum praebuit, & indignatio sermoni. Quis enim tranquillus haec videat, violatum ius gentium, spreta humanitatis iura, melius inter barbaros hostes fuisset nuncius tuus, quam inter eos, quos & rebaris Latinos & benevolos mereberis. Evoluant historias, si modo quicquam praeter, quibus inhiant, divitias spectare queant; inquirant, & mihi respondeant, quae barbaries legatos violavit unquam? Nisi perraro, nulla praesertim causa intervenient? Tentavit hoc quondam, in legatis nostris fallax, & infida Carthaginensium plebs; sed prohibita vis est magistratuum interventu. Hanc vim, quaeso, quis prohibuit; Quis facta punivit? Durior sum, imo vero quis arguit, vel reprehendet? Quanto tutius nuncius tuus esset in Parthiam, truncatis Crassis & legionibus nostris fusis? Quanto intactior esset in Germaniam, caesis Teutonis & Mario triumphante, quam huc venit, te Romanam Ecclesiam filialiter veneranti? Certe ne victoris insolentia, nec victi hostis dolor tantum praesumpsisset, quantum fidae amicitiae praesumptio invidia, facilius puer, tuus nemorosum Pelion, & algentes Tauri colles hyemे medii, quam Organis planitiem, autumnali tempore transiuisset, liberius Gangem & Tyberim, quam Differentiam transnatasset. Haec levandi animi gratia dixisse volui. Te v. vir magnifice, nec iniuria, nec iniuriae illatores, nec vilia prorsus fallae magnitudinis simulachra permoveant, non est vera magnitudo, nec verum robur posse nocere: id enim minimis atque infirmissimis animantibus datum est. Magnitudo vera est posse prodesse. Veriora velle potuerunt nocere nocentissimi hominum innocenti puero, & boni nuncii vicem hanc referre, quid hic magni est? imo v. quid nisi nihilominus? Si enim peccatum omne nihil est, eo magis est nihil, quo peccatum maius? ita peccati magnitudo, nihil est. Hic modo magnitudine viri fortes & suis atribus vires sunt, potuerunt quod scorpius, quod aranea potuisset, nocuerunt uni ex tuis, & quod est in hac humanitate conspectus, nocere voluerunt, nec tibi ut tibi, sed ut libertatis ac iustitiae defensor. Te enim non nisi propter illas odio habent; illas a propter se, ut quas iniusto, quo superbiunt imperio contrarias norunt. Tu si ad magnitudinem animi tui redis, horum tumidum, & inane propositum, simul oderis & contemnes: aeria quidem ista & aucta, sed parva sunt. De maioribus agitur. Haec cum universitate transibunt, & servi tui ultio latebit, sub Reipub. vindicta. Vale & perfice quod coepisti.
units.tr: You will therefore understand what you have been, once you have learned what Rome still is, whose messenger you now see so timid, thinking that there is no one who will avenge, that God is not in heaven, but there is a spirit of God on earth who will avenge, a spirit whose powers you cannot even suspect. Alas, this is a misery; but you will soon experience, I hope, that our strength has been returned to us by your injury. When we first began to grieve, we came back to health and vigour in a great stride. Have pity on our strength, illustrious man; raise up your country as it rises, and show the nations what Rome can still do. As for the rest of Italy, there is no doubt that it will lack neither strength, nor resources, nor spirit, but only unanimity, to the extent that it can do anything. If even one city joins in, I announce by this letter a near ruin and destruction to the Italian name. You (I say) whom the fates have appointed leader of so great a matter, go on with what you have begun. Fear nothing: those little clouds will scatter when the sun shines. They will not bear the rule of the foxes' cunning over the lion. You have entered gloriously; go on boldly and steadily to the rest. Show how far pride is inferior to humility, how much poorer avarice is than generosity, how foolish is the appearance of wisdom added to deceit, how base is pleasure brought near to temperance and decency. Let the mask of hypocrisy at last recognise how worthless it is when true virtue shines forth. Come, come, break the delays, trample underfoot and crush the frog that swells in ridiculous pride, imitating the bulk of a solid ox. I do not speak to incite you; you need neither a pusher nor a moderator, you hold both spur and bridle in your power. But I could not bear silently the grief of my spirit. Grief, increased by speaking, poured out a complaint, and in turn speech gave an outlet to indignation, and indignation to speech. For who could view these things calmly: the law of nations violated, the rights of humanity scorned? Your messenger would have fared better among barbarian enemies than among those whom you deserve to regard as Latins and well-wishers. Let them unroll the histories, if they can look at anything but the riches for which they gasp; let them search, and answer me: what barbarism has ever violated envoys, except very rarely, and especially when there was no cause? The treacherous and faithless populace of Carthage once attempted this against our envoys, but force was prevented by the intervention of the magistrates. Who, I ask, prevented this force? Who punished the deeds? Am I too harsh? Indeed, who would accuse or reprove me? How much safer would your messenger be in Parthia, after the Crassi were cut down and our legions routed? How much more untouched would he be in Germany, after the Teutons were slaughtered and Marius triumphed, than he is here, coming to you who revere the Roman Church as a son? Certainly the insolence of a victor, or the grief of a defeated enemy, would not have presumed so much as the presumption of envy has presumed against faithful friendship. Your boy would more easily have crossed wooded Pelion and the icy hills of Taurus in midwinter than the plain of the Organ in autumn; he would have swum the Ganges and the Tiber more freely than the Durance. I wished to say these things to relieve my spirit. As for you, magnificent man: neither injury nor those who inflict injury, nor the worthless images of false greatness, should move you. It is not true greatness, nor true strength, to be able to harm; that power is given to the smallest and weakest creatures. True greatness is the power to do good. The most guilty of men could wish to harm an innocent boy, and to repay a good messenger in this way: what great thing is this? Or rather, what is it but nothing all the same? For if every sin is nothing, is it not all the more nothing the greater the sin? So the greatness of sin is nothing. Here, only by greatness do brave men and their own virtues have strength; they could do what a scorpion or a spider could do; they harmed one of yours, and what is most visible in this kind of humanity, they wished to harm, not you as you, but as the defender of liberty and justice. For they hate you only on account of those things; they hate those things for their own sake, since they know them to be opposed to the unjust empire by which they take pride. If you return to the greatness of your spirit, you will both hate and despise their swollen and empty purpose: those things are airy and inflated, but small. We are concerned with greater matters. These things will pass away together with the whole world, and the vengeance on your servant will lie hidden under the vengeance of the Commonwealth. Farewell, and bring to completion what you have begun.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Romam Italiæ coniungere an vtile.
units.tr: Whether it is useful to join Rome to Italy.

units.la: FRAN. PETRARCHA PRINCIPI ROMANO S. Leve est quod nunc animum premit, egerendum tamen, ne neglectum stomacho obsit, plus enim quam pro quantitate bilem excitet, & patuum licet, ingentis nauseæ materiam fert. Olet nempe virus abditum profundi vetustique odii. ita mihi visum est, ita tibi visum iri certus sum, & si latius innotescat totius Pop. Rom. atq; omnium Italorum animis, incussurum iustissimæ indignationis aculeos, spero, excussurumque grauedinem corporis, quo nunc priscæ generosæ indolis vigor repet, cui vi vel sponte totus olim orbis cesssit, nunc (pudor) vltimi hominum insultant, non inutile opus Reip. si successerit vt opto; breuis scintilla, magnum mouit incendium, verbum vnum multarum & magnarum rerum fuit indicium. Sed iam res ipsa tractanda est, nec tam magis exaggeranda sermonibus, quam indignatione legentium. Nuper equidem inter quosdam, ex his qui sibi videntur sapientes, aliis forte non ita, dubitatum & in quæstionis formam propositum fuit: Expediret ne terrarum orbi, vrbem Romam & Italiam esse vnanimes atque pacificas. Et quamuis rerum illa dubitatio, satis puerilis & inepta sit, tamen disputandi studio vtrunque poterat excusari, nisi multis argumentis vtro citroque iactatis, is qui omnium sapientissimus habebatur, cum plausu & fauore omnium nullatenus expedire, venenata diffinitione firmasset. Quod tu, quæso, vir eloquentissime, cum primum vt soles, in publico perorabis, populo Romano meis verbis indica, vt intelligat, quæ sunt horum procerum, de nostra salute, per quas, etsi nihil nocent, animos tamen suos ventosa loquacitate detegunt, dum quod de nobis cupiunt, tam vehementer cupiunt, vt dissimulare non possint, & votum iniquissimum ac hostile propositum suum in rationis locum tranferre contendunt cæcitate turpissima. Sed ipsi quidem in erroribus suis morientur. Nos in manibus Dei sumus, fortunam non quam ipsi volunt, sed quam ille nobis præparauerit habituri. Non tamen his deliramentis interfui, contristassem fortasse aliquos. neque enim aut honestum, aut mihi possibile, in tam impia loquacitate silentium fuisset. Cæterum vt res ad me perlata est, indignatus graviter & tunc inter nostros contrarium diffinixi, & nunc, & apud te libertatis nostræ principem quantuluncunque auctoritate diffinio. Teque ante alios & Romanum populum atque vniuersam Italiam, vt quod ego verbis assero, rebus approberis, per omnes cœlicolas supplex oro, & vt in statu prospero diu viuas, & Remp. fortiter liberatam, fœlicicer regas, opto.
units.tr: Francis Petrarch to the Roman Prince, greetings. What now weighs on my mind is slight, yet it must be got rid of, lest, left neglected in my stomach, it do harm; for it would stir up more bile than its size warrants, and though small, it carries the stuff of a huge nausea. Indeed a poison of deep and ancient hatred gives off its smell. I thought so, and I am certain it will seem so to you as well. I hope that if it becomes more widely known to the minds of the whole Roman people and of all Italians, it will drive in the sharp sting of most righteous indignation, and shake off the heaviness of the body by which the vigour of your old, noble nature now sinks back; to that vigour the whole world once yielded, either by force or willingly, while now (shame!) the vilest of men insult it. This would be no useless work for the commonwealth if it succeeds, as I hope. A small spark has kindled a great fire; one word has been a sign of many great matters. But now the matter itself must be treated, and it should be exaggerated less by talk than by the indignation of the readers. Lately, indeed, among some who seem wise to themselves, though perhaps not to others, it was doubted and put forward as a question whether it would be advantageous for the world that the city of Rome and Italy should be one in harmony and at peace. And although that doubt is quite childish and foolish, it could still be excused by the eagerness of debate, had not one who was held to be the wisest of all, after many arguments had been tossed back and forth, with applause and approval from everyone, settled by a poisonous definition that it was in no way advantageous. This, I beg you, most eloquent man, when you first make your speech in public, as is your custom, declare to the Roman people in my words, so that they may understand what these leading men are like concerning our welfare. Though they do no harm, through their empty chatter they reveal their minds, while they desire so eagerly what they wish for us that they cannot conceal it, and with the greatest blindness they try to put their most unjust and hostile purpose in place of reason. But they themselves will die in their errors. We are in the hands of God; we shall have the fortune not which they wish for us, but which He has prepared for us. Yet I was not present at these follies, lest I might have grieved some people; for it would have been neither honourable nor possible for me to keep silence in such impious chatter. However, as soon as the matter was reported to me, I was seriously indignant, and I then gave the contrary judgment among our own people, and now I pronounce it, for what little authority it has, before you, the prince of our liberty. And I earnestly beg all the heavenly inhabitants that you, before all others and before the Roman people and all Italy, may confirm by deeds what I assert in words; and I pray that you may live long in a prosperous state and rule the commonwealth, now bravely freed, happily.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: An Romanum Imperium adhuc Roma sit.
units.tr: Whether the Roman Empire is still at Rome.

units.la: FRAN. PETRARCHA Populo Romano S. Apud te quidem Inuictissime, dominorumque terrarum populeque meus, apud te clam paucis, res magna tractanda est. aduertite animos, quæso, obtestorque vos, viri clarissimi, vestra res agitur. Magna (inquam) nec solum magna, sed maxima, & cui in terris nulla par esse potest, neue forsitan sciendi auidos, expectatione conficiam, aut rem suapte natura permaximam, nitar verbis augere, præfationibus omisis, ad ipsam rem venio. Tribunus olim vester, nunc captiuus alienus, o triste spectaculum, ceu fur nocturnus aut patriæ proditor, ex vinculis causam dicit, & quæ nulli vnquam sacrilego prærepta est, apud iudices orbis terrarum, & iustitiæ magistros iustæ sibi defensionis facultas eripitur. Est ille forte non indignus hæc perpeti, qui in suo ingenio, suisque, vt ita dixerim, manibus plantatam, & iam radicatam, florentemque Remp. in ipso gloriosissimi successus flore destituit: At minime digna est Roma, cuius olim ciues lege inuiolabiles, & supplicio exempti, nunc non modo sine sceleris infamia, sed multa quoque cum laude virtutis, passim sæuo quorumlibet arbitrio violentur. Ne enim causam ignoretis, viri illustres, qua olim caput & Rector, nunc ciuis dicam, an exul vester opprimitur, rem nescio, an nobis incognitam, sed certe mirabilem, & indignā audietis. Non ille quidem neglectæ, sed defensæ libertatis arguitur: nec desecerti, sed occupati Capitolii reus est. Illud sibi summum, & crucibus expiandum scelus, obiicitur, quod affirmare præsumpserit, Romanum Imperium nunc etiam Romæ, & penes P. R. esse. O impia secula! O truculentam inuidiam! O maleuolentiam inauditam! Tu v. nunc infallibilis & incorrupte rerum arbiter Christe quid agis? Vbi sunt oculi tui, quibus humanarum miseriarum nebulas serenare solitus es? Cur illos auertis? Cur non ancipiti fulmine causam dirimis sceleratam? Et si non meremur, aspice in nos, & miserere nostri, respice inimicos nostros, nec minus tuos, quoniam multiplicati sunt, & odio in quo oderunt nos, nec minus te. Discerne, quæsumus inter partes, omni ex parte dissimiles. Denique de vultu tuo iudicium nostrum prodeat, oculi tui videant æquitatem. Certe si iugo Romano quod omnium iustissimum atque suauissimum fuit, aliqua gens, imo v. gens omnis, vt cernimus, voluit colla subducere, nihil est quod indignemur aut miremur. Est enim animis mortalium, libertatis insitus appetitus, sæpe enim inconsultus ac præceps, & sæpe dum parere melioribus pudor vetat, qui bene subesse nt, male præsident: sic omnia miscentur. tur, atque turbantur, vnde nonnunquam in loco digni imperii seruitutem indignam, & in loco iusti seruitii iniustum imperium videmus. Quod nisi ita esset, meliori loco essent res humanæ, & adhuc incolumi capite, mundus integrior. Id si mihi non creditur experientiæ credatur, quando vnquam tanta pax, tanta tranquillitas, tanta iustitia, tanta virtutis honor, tanta bonis præmia, tanta malis supplicia, tam bene consultum rebus, quam postquam vnum caput orbis habuit, caputque ipsum Roma fuit? Quo potissimum tempore, amator pacis atque iustitiæ nasci Deus ex virgine, terrasque visitare dignatus est. Singula quidem singulis corporibus data sunt capita & orbis vniuersus, cui à poeta magni corporis nomen ascribitur vno temporali capite, debet esse contentus. Monstruosum est enim omne animal biceps; quanto magis horrendum, & immane prodigium est, animal mille capitum diuersorum, lese que mordentium, inuicemque pugnantium? Quod si capita plura sint, vnum tamen, quod cuncta compescat, atque omnibus præsit, esse debere non ambiguitur, vt totius corporis pax inconcussa permaneat. Certe ex experimentis innumeris, & doctissimorum hominum auctoritate deprehensum est, & in cœlo, & in terra, optima semper fuit vnitas Principatus. Id sane supremum caput, velle se Deus omnipotens, non aliud esse, quam Romam, multiplicibus declarauit indiciis, quam belli, pacisque gloria quam mirabilem sine exemplo virtutis, tanta præeminentia dignam fecit: quæ quamuis ita sint, adhuc tamen si humani more animi, malo suo cotidie gaudentis, aliqua gens, vt dixi, damnosam & ambiguam libertatem, quam tuum & salutare publice matris imperium mallet amplecti, positque insolentiæ, vel inscitiæ venia deberi: illud vero, quis inoffensis auribus accipiat, inter homines doctos quæri, An Romanum imperium Romæ sit? Ergo apud Parthos, Persasque & Medos, Parthorum, Persarumque & Medorum regna consistent; Romanum imperium vagum erit? Quis hanc indignitatem stomachus ferat? Quis non potius euomat, penitusque reiiciat? Si imperium Romanum Romæ non est, vbi quæso est? Nempe si alibi est, iam Romanorum imperium non est, sed eorum, penes quos illud volubilis fortuna deposuit. Etsi enim sæpe Romani Imperatores, pro necessitate Reipub. in orientis, aut occidentis extremo, sæpe sub Borea, vel austro cum exercitibus agerent: Romanum tamen interim imperium Romæ erat, & de Romanis Imperatoribus, quo vel præmio, vel supplicio digni essent, Roma censebat. De Capitolio petebatur quis honorandus, quis plectendus, quis vrbem priuatus, quis ouans, quis triumphans introiret, si inquirant post iul. Cæsaris seu tyrannidem; seu dicere malumus Monarchiam, Romanos principes; quanquam iam Deorum concilio ascripti, adhuc tamen à S. P. Q. R. gerendarum rerum licentiam postulasse compertum est, & data, vel denegata licentia, egisse quem destinauerant, vel cessasse, Imperatores igitur vagi esse possunt, stabile fixumque semper imperium est, nec de temporali statu, sed de perpetuitate imperii dixisse credendus est Maro, vbi ait;
units.tr: Francis Petrarch to the Roman People, greetings. To you alone, most invincible people, lords of the lands and my own people, I must speak privately and briefly about a great matter. Pay attention, I beg you, and I call on you, most distinguished men: your own cause is at stake. It is great, I say, not only great but the greatest, and nothing on earth can match it. Lest I keep eager listeners waiting, or try to magnify by words a matter already very great in its own nature, I will leave aside the prefaces and come straight to the point. Your former tribune, now a foreign captive, a sad spectacle, pleads his case from his chains like a nocturnal thief or a traitor to his country. He is denied before the judges of the world, and the masters of justice, the right to a just defence, which was never snatched from any criminal. Perhaps he does not undeservedly suffer these things, he who abandoned the commonwealth, planted and already rooted by his own talent and, as I may say, by his own hands, flourishing at the very height of its glorious success. But Rome is by no means deserving of this, Rome whose citizens were once inviolable by law and exempt from punishment, and who now are violated on every side at the savage will of anyone, not only without the stain of crime but even with much praise for their virtue. For, distinguished men, so that you may not be ignorant of the cause for which he who was once your head and ruler, now your citizen, is oppressed, or rather your exile, you will hear a matter which I do not know is unknown to you, but which is certainly astonishing and unworthy. He is accused not of neglecting liberty but of defending it; he is guilty not of deserting the Capitol but of seizing it. The charge laid against him is the greatest crime, one to be expiated by crosses: that he presumed to affirm that the Roman Empire is still at Rome, and in the hands of the Roman People. O impious ages! O savage hatred! O unheard-of malice! And you, Christ, the infallible and incorruptible judge of affairs, what are you doing now? Where are your eyes, with which you were wont to clear away the mists of human misery? Why do you turn them away? Why do you not cut through this wicked cause with a two-edged thunderbolt? And if we do not deserve it, look upon us and have mercy on us; regard our enemies, who are no less yours, since they have multiplied and hate us, and hate you no less. Distinguish, we pray, between the parties, which are utterly unlike in every respect. Finally, let our judgment come forth from your countenance, and let your eyes behold equity. Certainly, if some nation, indeed every nation, as we see, has wished to shake off the Roman yoke, which was the most just and the most sweet of all, there is nothing for us to be indignant or surprised about. For there is in the minds of mortals an innate desire for liberty, often thoughtless and headlong, and often, while shame forbids obeying the better, those who ought to be well ruled rule badly; so all things are mixed up and thrown into confusion, whence sometimes we see in a place worthy of rule an unworthy servitude, and in a place of just servitude an unjust rule. If it were not so, human affairs would be in a better state, and with the head still safe, the world would be sounder. If this is not believed to me, let it be believed to experience: when was there ever such peace, such tranquillity, such justice, such honour for virtue, such rewards for good men, such punishments for bad, such good order in affairs, as after the world had one head, and that head was Rome itself? Especially at that time, when God deigned to be born of a virgin and to visit the lands, the lover of peace and justice. Indeed, separate bodies are each given a single head, and the whole world, to which the poet ascribes the name of a great body, ought to be content with one temporal head. For every animal with two heads is a monstrosity; how much more horrible and monstrous a prodigy is an animal with a thousand diverse heads, biting one another and fighting among themselves? And if there are several heads, it is beyond doubt that there ought to be one that restrains all and presides over all, so that the peace of the whole body may remain unshaken. Surely, by countless experiences and the authority of the most learned men, it has been established that in heaven and on earth the unity of the principate has always been best. Almighty God himself has declared by many signs that this supreme head, which he willed to be none other than Rome, he made worthy of such pre-eminence, with a glory of war and peace wonderful and without example in virtue. Yet, although these things are so, still, if some nation, as I said, through the human habit of a mind that rejoices daily in its own harm, preferred to embrace a ruinous and uncertain liberty rather than the rule of its own mother, which is both sovereign and salutary for the public, pardon should be granted for its insolence or its ignorance. But that this should be asked among learned men, and be heard by ears that take no offence, namely whether the Roman Empire is at Rome, is something no one would accept: Therefore the kingdoms of the Parthians, Persians and Medes will remain in Parthia, Persia and Media, while the Roman Empire will be a wanderer? Who could bear this indignity with patience? Who would not rather vomit it up and reject it utterly? If the Roman Empire is not at Rome, where, I ask, is it? Clearly, if it is elsewhere, then it is no longer the empire of the Romans, but of those into whose hands fickle fortune has laid it down. For although the Roman emperors often campaigned with their armies at the far end of the East or the West, often under the North or the South wind, as the needs of the commonwealth required, yet the Roman Empire was at Rome all the while, and it was Rome that judged the Roman emperors, deciding by what reward or punishment each was worthy. From the Capitol it was asked who should be honoured, who punished, who should enter the city as a private man, who in an ovation, who in a triumph. If they examine what came after the tyranny of Julius Caesar, or, if we prefer to say, the monarchy, the Roman princes, though now numbered in the council of the gods, were found to have still requested from the Senate and People of Rome the licence to conduct affairs, and, the licence being granted or refused, they acted as they had intended or ceased. Emperors therefore can be wanderers, but the empire is always stable and fixed; and it must be believed that Virgil spoke not of a temporal state but of the perpetuity of the empire, where he says:

units.la: Dum domus Aeneæ Capitoli immobile saxum accolet, imperiumque pater Romanus habebit.
units.tr: While the house of Aeneas shall dwell on the immovable rock of the Capitol, and the Roman father shall hold the empire.

units.la: Neque enim hæc dicens, centum aut mille annorum, sed immortalem illis duobus gloriam spondebat. Neue quisquam verba hæc blanditias vocet; quæ profecto, nec lingua mea, nec vestris auribus dignæ sunt, digressione opus est. Scio ego, de hac re Virgilium quodam loco ab Augustino reprehensum, non iniuste, sed ibidem mox iustissime excusatum, cum Poeta loquentem de vobis iouem facere, sic ait:
units.tr: For in saying this he was promising them not a hundred or a thousand years, but immortal glory. Nor let anyone call these words flattery; they are certainly worthy neither of my tongue nor of your ears, but a digression is needed. I know that Virgil in a certain place was rebuked by Augustine, not unjustly, but soon after most justly excused, because in speaking of you the poet makes Jupiter say:

units.la: Romulus excipiet gentem & Mauortia condet Mama, Romanosque suo de nomine dicet. & origini perpetuitatem adiicens, inquit: His ego nec metas rerum nec tempora pono. Imperium sine fine dedi.
units.tr: Romulus shall receive the nation and found the Mavortian walls, and shall call the Romans by his own name. And adding eternity to their origin, he says: I set no bounds to their affairs nor limits of time. I have given empire without end.

units.la: Hoc non immerito quidem notat Augustinus. Quomodo enim imperium sine fine dabit, qui nihil vnquam dedit aut dare potuit, nisi quod homo sceleratus, & mortalis potest, falsa diuinitatis opinione, non ornatus sed oneratus, & oppressus? præterea autem hæc, quisquis imperium Romanum dedit (quod non dedisse certum est, nisi omnipotentem Deum, cuius in cœlo & in terra imperium vnum est, vnde imperia cuncta descendunt) vbi tamen hoc imperium sit quærit Augustinus: in terra, an in cœlo? Et vtique (inquit) in terra est, & si esset in cælo, cœlum & terra transient, quæ ipse fecit Deus, quanto citius, quæ condidit Romulus? Hæc Augustinus in Virgilium. Et certe perspicuum est regna omnia, quicquid vsquam clarum, aut magnificum oculis nostris apparet, & si ante non ruerunt, tunc saltem ruitura esse dum cœlum & terra mouebuntur: Illa concutiente qui creauit, quique nouum cœlum nouamque terram faciet, non mentiturus vt Iupiter, cum ipse sit veritas. Eius est illud regnum, Principio carens & fine carituram, de quo scriptum est: Et regni eius non erit finis, quod licet forte Virgilius ignoraret, cui Deus ingenium excellens, eloquiumque præstiterat, verum hæcà sapientibus abscondita & paruulis reuelanda negauerat; illud certe non ignorabat, peritura esse omnia regna, quæ initium habuissent. Ingenti igitur cautela visus est, siquidem vbi immortalitatem Romano pollicebatur in alterio, non ipse loquebatur ex persona propria, sed totem loquentem induebat, ut mendacis Dei mendax oraculum esset & falsa promissio. Ipse a. ad gratiam P. R. alieno mendacio utebatur, at alibi, quando ex persona sua loqui voluit, veritatem ipsam idem Poeta non tacuit.
units.tr: Augustine rightly notes this. For how will he give empire without end, who never gave anything, or could give anything, except what a wicked and mortal man can give, adorned not with true divinity but burdened and oppressed by a false opinion of it? Moreover, whoever gave the Roman Empire (which it is certain was given by none but almighty God, whose empire in heaven and on earth is one, from whom all empires descend), Augustine asks where this empire is: in earth or in heaven? And surely, he says, it is on earth; and if it were in heaven, heaven and earth, which God himself made, would pass away, how much more quickly would those things pass away which Romulus founded? Augustine says this against Virgil. And certainly it is plain that all kingdoms, whatever appears bright or magnificent to our eyes, if they have not yet fallen, will at least fall when heaven and earth are shaken, He who made them shaking them, and who will make a new heaven and a new earth, not lying like Jupiter, since he is truth itself. His is that kingdom, without beginning and destined to be without end, of which it is written: And of his kingdom there shall be no end. Although perhaps Virgil did not know this, to whom God had given an excellent genius and eloquence, but had refused to reveal these things, hidden from the wise and revealed to little ones, yet he certainly did not fail to know that all kingdoms which had a beginning were doomed to perish. He seems therefore to have used great caution: when he promised immortality to the Roman people in one place, he did not speak in his own person, but put on the character of another speaking, so that the lying oracle would be that of a lying god and a false promise. He used another's falsehood for the favour of the Roman People; but elsewhere, when the same poet wished to speak in his own person, he did not keep silent about the truth itself.

units.la: At enim res Romanæ perituræque regna.
units.tr: But surely Roman affairs and kingdoms destined to perish.

units.la: Quis non clare videat, inter imperium sine fine, perituraque regna, quid interest? sed hic Virgilius, ibi Iupiter loquebatur, hic somnoingeniosus, ibi falsus Deus. aliis quidem verbis, (sed hac plane sententia Virgilium accusat & excusat Augustinus, secundum quam intelligo quæ dixi, & quæ dicam. Certe Romanus erat ille qui scripsit: Omnia orta occidunt, & aucta senescunt. Senescent ergo hæc omnia, si durent, & si cuiusque rei finis est senectus sua, utique omnia senescent, nisi iam forte senuerint, quando & quæ itant, cuncta occident, & occasum si non prævenerit, saltem cohibitabitur senectus. Ita nulla est exceptio, seu durent, seu non durent, orta omnia, aut serius, aut citius tandem occident, & senescent. Volvet motu continuo totam suam instabilis fortuna, & de gente in gentem volubilia regna versabit. Faciet illa cum volet reges ex servis, servos ex regibus, & in urbem Romam, & in orbem Romanum, suam inelucrabilem potentiam exercebit. Quam præcipue in vos, viri optimi, multis forte miserantibus, nullo penitus succurrente, diu miserabilibus modis exercuit & exercet. Scio, doleoque, & plus quam credi possit indignor, quid amplius faciam non habeo. Nec me angit, quod fortuna iure suo utitur, ut in reliquis, sic in vobis, atque ut se rerum humanarum plane dominam probet, ipsum rerum caput attingere non veretur. Scio violentiam, instabiles mores novi, quorundam v. indomitarum gentium inanem iactantiam ægre fero, quarum nunc Romano trita ingo colla lasciunt, ita pudor & felix fabula iam (ut cætera multa & gravia sileam) in quæstionem venit: An Romanum Imperium Romæ sit. Etenim uero ubi nunc horrida sylva est, poterunt regia tecta consurgere, atque ubi nunc atria sunt, auro rutilante fulgentia poterunt cupidi greges patri, & penetralibus regum, vagus pastor insistere. Non detracto fortunæ Imperium, poterit illa funditus, ut urbes alias, sic reginam urbium pari nisu, ruina maiore prosternere, quod heu magna ex parte iam fecit. Illud profecto nunquam potuit efficere, ut Romanum Imperium alibi sit quam Romæ, simul enim ut alibi esse coeperit, desinet esse Romanum. Hæc le mirabilis civis vester affirmasse & affirmate non negat; & hoc est illud graue crimen, unde in discrimen capitis adducitur, addit autem se multorum consilio sapientum dixisse: nec puto mentitur, & defensionis copiam, advocatumque sibi dari flagitat. Negatur, & nisi divina misericordia, vesterque favor occurreret, actum est, innocens, indefensusque damnabitur. Hominum pars magna comparetur, nemo fere est, qui non misereatur præter eos, quibus proprium erat misereri, & parcere erroribus, non inuidere virtutibus. Iurisconsulti iis signes hic etiam non desunt, qui iure civili asserant, hanc ipsam sententiam probati clarissima ratione. Nec desunt qui ex historiis se multa & valida probaturos dicant ad eiusdem sententiæ firmitatem, modo liberam vocem liceat emittere. Nunc tamen nemo est, qui mutare audeat, præter quam in angulis, in tenebris, in timore. Ego ipse qui vobis hæc scribo, & forte pro veritate non recusem mori, si mea mors collatura aliquid Reip. videatur, nunc taceo, neque his ipsis ad vos scriptis meum nomen adiicio, stylum ipsum sufficere arbitratus; hoc adiecto, civem Romanum esse, qui loquitur. quod si tuto in loco, apud æquum iudicem, & non ad tribunal hostium res agatur, spero veritatem animum illustrante, & linguam, seu calamum dirigente Deo posse aliquid dicere, quo luce clarius appareat, Imperium Romanum, quanquam fortunæ iniuria attritum, oppressumque, diu & quanquam varie ab Hispanis, Afris, Gallis, Theutonis occupatum, adhuc tamen quantumcunque est, Romæ esse non alibi, idemque mansurum, certi nihil prorsus ex tanta urbe, præter nudum saxum Capitolii superesset. quin etiam tunc, quando nondum externis manibus agebamur, tantumque Romani Cæsares imperitabant, non penes eos, sed penes Capitolii arcem, ac populum Romanum, omne iuris imperii fuisse, si verum est, quod malæ fidei possessor vilo tempore non præscribat. In hoc a. veritum statu, dum dies trahitur, quid forte desuper datum est, ut quod modo nec sperare quidem auderetis, tanta res in lucem veniat. Unum quod ad vestram, & Romani nominis dignitatem spectare visum est, dissimulare non potui, cogente me ad calamum fide illa, qua vos urbemque vestram, inter omnes singulari quodam amore ac veneratione complector. Clarissimam igitur vestra hortor, atque obsecro, ne cive vestrum in extremis positum deseratis, sed vestrum esse monstretis, solennibus eum nunciis respicentes. etsi n. vobis imperii titulum mitantur eripere, nondum tamen eo vestantæ sunt eucti, ut negare audeant, eos in vestros cives iuris habere. Certe si quid homo iste peccavit, nec dubitari potest de commissis Romæ peccatis, vestrum est iudicium, nisi vobis fundatoribus legum atque cultoribus & qui iura gentibus tradidistis, eripitur iuis commune. Vbi enim iustius delicta castiges, quam vbi commissa sunt? Vbi scilicet & locus ipse memoriam criminis renovauis, scelratis pars nō parua supplicii & scelerū spectatores, pene spectaculū, aut solebitur, aut terreat. Quod si forte tribunus vester, quoniam multi, quin potius boni omnes ita sentiunt, non supplicio, sed præmio dignus est, vbinam melius quod meretur accipiet, quam vbi fecit propter quod talia meretur? Nusquam dignius præmium, viri fortis exoluitur quam vbi fortiter gesserit, ut qui actum viderint, ad imitandum præmio accedantur. Fidenter itaque reposcite ciuem vestrum: nihil nouum, nihil iniustum poscitis, potiusq; delinquitis, si tacetis. Quod si communis iure patriæ vbi nunc. [illegible, ~3 letters]captus est, puniendus asseritur, quanto verius communis patria Roma est, vbi ille natus educatusque est, vbi quicquid idem, vnde accusatur, admisit, qui contra nihil hic vel laude, vel vituperio dignum fecit, si vero contra morem maiorum, cum fortuna ceciderunt animi, adeoque degeneratum est, vt iustitiam poscere temeritas videatur, his, quorum patribus nihil difficile olim visum est, at saltem quod ab omni, quae legibus viuat, barbarie posci potest: poscite, vt ciui vestro audientia publica, & defensionis legitimae non negetur copia, neue qui in luce fecit omnia, imo qui quantum per hominem fieri poterat, lucem mundo reddidit, in tenebris condemnetur. Ostendite vos denique causam ac fortunam non negligere ciuis vestri, resistite iniuriae, prohibete nephas, protegite innocentem reum, vel nocentem iudicate, aut saltem, ne pro cuiusque libidine iudicetur occurrite. Ferte quam potestis & quam debetis opem Tribuno, vel si id nomen euanuit, ciui vestro multa de Republica bene merito; aut illud inprimis, quod quaestionem magnam atque vtilem mundo, multis sopitam, ac sepultam seculis, suscitauit, quae vna ad reformationem status publici, atque ad aurei seculi initium, via est: succurrite illi viro, neque contempseritis salutem eius, qui pro vestra salute, sese mille periculis, ac sempiternae obiecit inuidiae, illius propositum atque animum cogitate, & memineritis, quo in statu res vestrae fuerant, & quam repente vnius viri consilio atque opere, quantum in spem non Roma tantum, sed Italia omnis erecta est, quantum subito nomen Italicum, quo renouata ac deterso Romana gloria, quantus hostium metus ac dolor, quantum gaudium amicorum, quanta populorum expectatio, quam immutatus rerum tenor, quam facies orbis alia, quam diuersus habitus animorum, quam nihil sibi simile, & ex omnibus quae sub coelo sunt, tam mira & tam repentina mutatio rerum fuit. Septem enim mensium non amplius spatio, frena Reipublicae tenuit, vt vix ab origine mundi maius aliquid attentatum rear, & si successisset vt coeperat, diuinum potius quam humanum opus esse videretur. Et profecto, quicquid ab homine bene agitur, diuinum opus est. Huic ergo, quem vestrae gloriae, non ambitioni propriae desudasse notum est, fauor haud dubius debetur, de euentu fortuna culpanda est, si quis autem torpor feruenti principio interuenit, humanae varietati atque imbecillitati veniam date, & dum licet vindicate ciuem vestrum ab iniuria, qui Graecos a Macedonum, Siculos a Carthaginensium, Campanos a Samnitium, Tuscos a Gallorum iniuriis, non sine graui vestro periculo vindicastis. Extenuatae sunt fateor opes vestrae; at nunquam plus animorum patribus vestris fuit, quam dum Romana paupertas, diues virtutum viguit.
units.tr: Who does not plainly see what difference there is between "an empire without end" and "kingdoms destined to perish"? Here it is Virgil who speaks; there it is Jupiter, the dreamy poet's god, a false god. The words are different, though the sense is clearly the one by which Augustine accuses and excuses Virgil, and by which I understand what I have said and what I am about to say. Certainly the Roman who wrote, "All things that rise fall, and things that grow are made old," was right. So all these things will grow old, if they last at all. Since old age is the end of everything, all things will surely grow old, unless perhaps they have already grown old. Whatever rises, all of it falls, and if old age does not forestall its fall, at least old age will hold it back. So there is no exception: whether they last or not, all things that have risen will fall, sooner or later, and grow old. Unstable fortune, by its ceaseless motion, turns the whole world, and it moves kingdoms from nation to nation like a rolling wheel. It makes kings out of slaves and slaves out of kings whenever it pleases, and it exercises its unavoidable power over the city of Rome and the Roman world. Above all, good men, it has exercised this power against you, and it still does, for a long time now, in miserable ways, while many pity you and no one at all comes to your aid. I know this and I grieve, and I am indignant beyond what anyone could believe; I have no further remedy. Nor does it trouble me that fortune uses its right, not only over the rest, but over you too; and that, to show itself plainly the mistress of human affairs, it does not shrink from striking at the very head of those affairs. I know the violence; I know the unstable habits of men. It grieves me to see the vain boasting of certain untamed peoples, whose necks, now freed from the worn yoke of Rome, have been loosed. So shame and a happy fable (to pass over many other grave matters) have come into question: whether the Roman Empire is still at Rome. For indeed, where there is now a wild forest, royal houses may rise; and where there are now halls gleaming with gilded splendour, greedy herds may graze, and a wandering shepherd may stand in the chambers of kings. Without taking anything from fortune's empire, it may overthrow Rome, the queen of cities, with equal effort and with greater ruin than it has used against other cities, as it has already largely done, alas. It could never bring it about that the Roman Empire should be anywhere but at Rome, for as soon as it began to be elsewhere, it would cease to be Roman. Your remarkable fellow citizen has asserted this, and he does not deny that he asserted it. This is the grave charge by which he is brought into danger of his life. He adds that he said it on the advice of many wise men, and I do not think he lies. He demands the chance to defend himself and an advocate to be assigned to him. He is refused, and unless the divine mercy and your favour intervene, the matter is done: he, innocent and undefended, will be condemned. Let a great part of mankind be compared with him, and hardly anyone will fail to pity him, except those whose nature it is to pity, to pardon errors and not to envy virtues. Here too there are not lacking jurists who, on the authority of civil law, maintain this very opinion, proved by the clearest reasoning. Nor are there lacking those who say they will prove from histories many strong points in support of the same opinion, if only they are allowed to speak freely. Yet now there is no one who dares to change his view, except in corners, in darkness, in fear. I myself, who write these things to you, and who perhaps would not refuse to die for the truth, if my death seemed likely to bring any benefit to the commonwealth, now keep silent, and I do not add my name even to these very writings to you, thinking the pen alone sufficient, and adding only this: that he who speaks is a Roman citizen. But if the matter were pursued in a safe place, before a fair judge, and not before the tribunal of enemies, I hope that God, who lights up the mind with truth and directs the tongue or the pen, might be able to say something by which it would appear clearer than light that the Roman Empire, though worn down and oppressed by the injury of fortune, and though long and variously occupied by Spaniards, Africans, Gauls and Teutons, is still, however much of it there is, at Rome and nowhere else, and will remain so; and that nothing at all certain would be left of so great a city except the bare rock of the Capitol. Indeed, even at the time when we were not yet under foreign hands, when the Roman emperors ruled, the whole right of empire was not in their hands but in the citadel of the Capitol and the Roman people, if it is true that a possessor in bad faith never prescribes by any lapse of time. In this uncertain state of affairs, while the days drag on, perhaps something will be given from above, so that a matter which you did not dare even to hope for just now may come to light. I could not pass over one thing that seemed to concern your dignity and the dignity of the Roman name, since that loyalty, by which I embrace you and your city with a singular love and reverence beyond all others, compels me to my pen. I therefore urge and beseech you most illustrious men not to abandon your citizen, who is in extremity, but to show that he is yours, looking upon him with public messages. For even if they are trying to snatch from you the title of empire, they have not yet grown so bold as to deny that they have rights over your citizens. Certainly, if this man has sinned in anything, and there can be no doubt about the sins committed at Rome, the judgment is yours. Unless it is taken away from you, the founders of laws, the guardians of law, you who have handed down rights to the nations, what is common to all is seized from you. For where could you more justly punish crimes than where they were committed? There, surely, the very place would renew the memory of the crime, and a great part of the punishment would be the spectators of the wicked deeds, and the spectacle itself would either warn or terrify. But if perhaps your tribune, since many, or rather all good men, think he deserves not punishment but reward, where could he receive what he deserves better than where he did the deeds for which he deserves such things? Nowhere is a reward of a brave man paid more worthily than where he acted bravely, so that those who saw the deed might be spurred to imitate it by the reward. Demand your citizen with confidence: you demand nothing new and nothing unjust, and you would rather be at fault if you were silent. But if it is asserted that he should be punished under the common law of the fatherland, where [illegible] he has been captured, then how much more truly is Rome the common fatherland, where he was born and brought up, where whatever he is accused of was committed, and where he did nothing here worthy of praise or blame! And if, against the custom of our forefathers, when fortune has fallen, the spirit has also fallen, and so far degenerated that it seems rash to demand justice, then at least demand, from men whose fathers once found nothing difficult, what can be demanded from every people that lives under laws and is not barbarous: demand that a public hearing be granted to your citizen, and that the opportunity of a lawful defence not be denied him, and that he who brought all things to light, indeed who, as far as a man could, restored light to the world, not be condemned in darkness. Finally, show that you do not neglect the cause and fortune of your citizen. Resist the injury, forbid the wrong, protect the innocent accused, or judge him guilty, or at least take care that no one is judged according to his own whim. Give the tribune, as much as you can and as much as you ought, your help; or, if that name has faded, give it to your citizen, who has deserved so well of the commonwealth; or above all to that great and useful question which he has raised for the world, a question buried and sunk in sleep for many centuries, and which is the one road to the reform of the public state and to the beginning of a golden age. Help that man, and do not despise the safety of him who has exposed himself to a thousand dangers and to everlasting hatred for your safety. Consider his purpose and his spirit, and remember what state your affairs were in, and how suddenly, by the counsel and work of one man, not Rome alone but all Italy was raised to hope; how suddenly the Italian name was renewed and the glory of Rome was restored and cleansed; how great was the fear and grief of enemies, how great the joy of friends, how great the expectation of peoples, how changed the course of affairs, how different the face of the world, how different the disposition of minds; how nothing like it, and of all things under heaven, so wonderful and so sudden a change of affairs has happened. For he held the reins of the commonwealth for no more than seven months, so that I think nothing greater has been attempted since the origin of the world; and had it succeeded as it began, it would seem a divine work rather than a human one. And indeed, whatever is done well by a man is a divine work. Therefore a favour not doubtful is owed to this man, who is known to have toiled for your glory and not for his own ambition. If the outcome was unfortunate, fortune is to blame; but if some sluggishness crept in after a fervent beginning, pardon it as human variability and weakness; and while it is allowed, defend your citizen from injury, as you once defended the Greeks from the wrongs of the Macedonians, the Sicilians from those of the Carthaginians, the Campanians from those of the Samnites, and the Tuscans from those of the Gauls, not without grave danger to yourselves. I admit that your resources have been diminished; but never was there more spirit in your fathers than when Roman poverty, rich in virtues, flourished.

units.la: Imminuta vestra potentia est, non ignoro, sed mihi credite, si qua pristini sanguinis gutta superest, non parua vobis est maiestas, neque mediocris auctoritas. Audete aliquid, adiuro vos per memoriam rerum Romanarum, per maiorum cineres ac gloriam, per nomen imperii, per misericordiam Iesu Christi, qui diligi proximum & succurri iubet afflictis. Audete, oro, aliquid, praesertim cuius & honesta petitio, & inhonestum & turpe, silentium est, etsi non propter illius salutem, at propter vestrum decus. Audete aliquid, si vultis esse aliquid, nil minus Romanum est, quam timor, praedico autem vobis, quoniam si timetis, si vos ipsos contemnetis, multi vos quoque contemnent, metuet nullus: sin spem nolle coeperitis, longe lateque metuemini; quod cum saepe olim, tum nuper apparuit, illo Rempublicam gubernante, de quo loquor. Aperite tantum vnanimiter ora vestra, sentiat mundus vnam esse vocem P. Rom. nemo vsquam illam irridebit. Reposcite modo captiuum hunc, vel iustitiam poscite; alterum non negabitur. Et qui patua quondam legatione, Regem Aegyptium, sub obsidione Syriaca liberastis, nunc ciuem vestrum, ab indignis carceribus liberate, & valete.
units.tr: Your power has been diminished, I am not unaware of it, but believe me, if any drop of the former blood remains, your majesty is not small and your authority is not mean. Dare something, I beseech you by the memory of Roman affairs, by the ashes and glory of your ancestors, by the name of the empire, by the mercy of Jesus Christ, who bids us love our neighbour and help the afflicted. Dare something, I pray, especially since silence is shameful and disgraceful when the request is honourable, and that silence concerns not so much his safety as your own honour. Dare something, if you wish to be something; nothing is less Roman than fear. I tell you this: if you fear, if you despise yourselves, many will despise you too, and no one will fear you. But if you begin to refuse hope, you will be feared far and wide, as has often appeared before, and recently too, under that man of whom I speak, who governed the Republic. Only open your mouths together, and let the world perceive that the Roman people speak with one voice; no one anywhere will mock it. Only demand back this captive, or demand justice; the other thing will not be refused. And you who once, by a small embassy, freed the king of Egypt from the Syrian siege, now free your citizen from unworthy prisons, and farewell.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: De statu occidua Babylonis, quae est Roma.
units.tr: On the state of the western Babylon, which is Rome.

units.la: FRANCISC. PETRARCHA Amico suo. Si quid animus meus fert, de huius occiduae Babyloniae statu, cuius fato seu verius peccato meo, inuitus totiens ciuis fio, velim stylo committere, vereor, pater, ne & dolorem meum lamentis exaggerem, & sanctissimas curas tuas, occupationesque pulcherrimas, intempestiuis & inutilibus querimoniis interpellem. In summa scito, non modo hunc, sed ne Ciceronianum quidem calamum rebus parem. Quicquid de Assyria, vel Aegyptia Babylone, quicquid de quatuor Labyrinthis, quicquid denique de Auerni limine, deque Tartareis syluis, sulphureisque paludibus legisti, huic tartaro admotum, fabulosa est. Hic turrificus simulatque terrificus Nemroth, hic pharetrata Semiramis, hic inexorabilis Minos, hic Rhadamantus, hic Cerberus vniuersa consumens, hic tauro suppositra Pasiphae, mixtumque genus (quod Matt) prolesque biformis Minotaurus inest, Veneris monimenta nefandae, hic postremo quicquid confusum, quicquid atrum, quicquid horribile vsquam est, aut fingitur aspicias, o semper virtutibus tuis foelix, nunc etiam absentia foeliciortua. Putasne ciuitatem hanc esse quam vidisti? Longe alia est, longeque dissimilis, fuit illa etenim omnium pessima, eaque tempestate foedissima: haec vero non iam ciuitas, sed laruarum, & lemurum domus est, & vt breuiter dicam, scelerum ac dedecorum omnium sententia, atque ille viuentium infernus, tanto ante Dauidico ore notatus, quam fundatus, aut cognitus. Ah quotiens redit ad memoriam illa tua penitus paterna vox & salutaris admonitio, dum digressum paranti diceres; Quo abis? quid moliris? quae te tui immemorem rem trahit ambitio? nescis quid petis? quid relin quis? an sciens ad indignum te laborem vadis? vide, quæso, acriter quid agas? quo properes? si bene mihi notus es, pœnitebit te professionis tuæ, curiæ laqueos expertus totiens, an ignoras, in quos vbi semel incideris, absolui non poteris cum voles. Hæc & his similia te suadente, quid responderem aliud non erat, nisi me charitate victum amicorum notas ad miserias reuerti dicebam, hæc nec mentiebar, necdum me charitatis illius pœnitet; sed an libertatem meam, amicorum commodis habuisse pœniteat incertus sum. Certe nunc tibi male crediti, & sero probati consilii tui magnas gratias habeo, cui hactenus non impune fuit non parere: sed parebo melius, si vnquam hinc emersero, quod Christo dextram porrigente non despero, & in quod summis iam nisibus accingor. Hæc tibi, pater, ne ante scriberem pudor inhibuit, turpe enim & indecorum viro est; velle quod max nolit.
units.tr: Francis Petrarch to his friend. If my mind were able to bring forth anything on the state of this western Babylon, by whose fate, or more truly by my own sin, I am so often and so unwillingly made a citizen, I would gladly commit it to writing; but I fear, father, that I would both magnify my grief with lamentations and interrupt your most sacred cares and most excellent occupations with untimely and useless complaints. In short, know that not only this pen but not even a Ciceronian pen would be equal to the subject. Whatever you have read about Assyrian or Egyptian Babylon, about the four labyrinths, about the threshold of Avernus, and the Tartarean woods and sulphurous marshes, compared with this Tartarus is fabulous. Here you see Nimrod, the builder of towers and the terror of the world; here Semiramis with her quiver; here the inexorable Minos, here Rhadamanthus, here Cerberus devouring everything; here Pasiphae, who was placed under the bull, and the mixed breed, and the two-formed offspring, the Minotaur, monument of unspeakable lust; finally, here is whatever is confused, whatever is dark, whatever is horrible anywhere, either existing or imagined. O you who are always happy in your virtues, now even happier in your absence! Do you suppose that this city is the one you saw? It is far different and far unlike it; for that city was indeed the worst of all, and at that time the most foul; but this is no longer a city, but a house of ghosts and spectres, and, to put it briefly, the verdict of all wickedness and disgrace, and that hell of the living which was marked long ago by the mouth of David, before it was founded or known. Ah, how often does that voice of yours, so truly fatherly and that wholesome admonition come back to my memory, when you said to me as I was preparing to leave: Where are you going? What are you planning? What ambition, forgetful of yourself, drags you away? Do you not know what you seek? What you leave behind? Or do you go knowingly to unworthy toil? Consider, I beg you, how seriously you act; where are you hurrying? If I know you well, you will repent of your profession, having so often experienced the snares of the court; or do you not know into what snares, once you have fallen into them, you will not be able to get free when you wish? When you urged these things and things like them, I had no other answer than to say that I was returning to wretched affairs, overcome by love for my friends; I was not lying in this, and I do not regret that love; but whether I regret having held my liberty subordinate to the advantages of my friends, I am uncertain. Certainly now I am very grateful to you for your counsel, which I have trusted too late and proved too late, and for which it has so far not been without penalty to have disobeyed; but I shall obey better, if ever I emerge from here, which I do not despair of, with Christ stretching out his right hand, and for which I am now girding myself with the greatest efforts. These things, father, shame prevented me from writing before, for it is base and unbecoming for a man to wish what he ought not to wish.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: De tertia Babylone, & quinto Labyrintho, idest, Avinione in Gallia, vbi sedes Papalis.
units.tr: On the third Babylon and the fifth Labyrinth, that is, Avignon in Gaul, where the Papal seat is.

units.la: FRANCISC. PETRARCHA Amico S. Subscriptiones epistolarum mearum miraris, nec immerito; non nisi geminam enim Babylonem cum legeris, alteram apud Assyrios olim, vbi clarum Semiramis nomen habet, alteram apud Ægyptios nostra ætate florentem, quæ Cambysem habet auctorem, cuius nunc Babylonis inauditum tibi nomen ingeritur tecum voluis, nō quod nescias, quondam ex nostris Romam, quasi alteram Babylonem propter proportionem imperiorum, & climatum latitudinis, quam quia me almam, sanctam & reginam vrbem vocitare sulitum tenes, huius nouissimæ Babylonis, tibi nunc etiam stupor manet. Define iam mirari: & sua Babylon huic terrarum tractui est, vbi enim quæso dignius, quam in occidentali plaga ciuitas confusionis existeret? A quibus quidem condita incertum, sed à quibus habitata notissimum; certe ab his, à quibus iure optimo nomen hoc possidet. Et si vis, hic mihi crede, Nemroth potens in terra, & robustus venator, contra Dominum, ac superbis curribus cœlum petens, hic pharetrata Semiramis, hic Orientali quoque vesanior Cambyses & ipse Regum primo ceruicibus actus, postremo defectus epidis, & pastus cæde suorum, ab insonti principio, redactus ad miserrimam egestatem. Non ergo te ad poetas, neque enim Pierium opus est; non te ad Historicos mittam; consule catholicos tractatores, sed præcipue Augustinum super eo Psalmo qui sic incipit, Vt epistolarum ad te mearum aliquæ quæ desunt, inuenies, quid sibi Babylonicum nomen velit, quod cum legeris, dices non minus Rhodano, quam Euphrati debitum, quam Nilo, neque vero miraberis, si in mentem redit, Ambrosium in eo libro, quo indignum Valentiniani iunioris interitum deflet, hoc vsum esse cognomine, dum de Rhodano loqueretur, atque vt hac admiratione succisa, à radice aliam conuellam, de quinque Labyrinthis potes etiam mirari. Cum apud cæteros Scriptores, non nisi de quatuor mentionem inueneris, vt puto, in quibus cum famam habeant Ægyptius, Lemnius, Creticus & in Italia Clusius, Labyrinthum Rhodani tacuerút, omnium inextricabilissimum ac pessimū: siue quia nondum erat, siue quia nondum noscebatur. Huius apud me mentio crebra est, quam iuste autem, qui noscere cupit, huc properet: non hic carcer horrendus, non tenebrosæ domus error, non fatalis vrna humani generis fata permiscens: denique non imperiosus Minos, non Minotaurus vorax, non damnatæ Veneris monimenta defuerint: sed remedia, sed amor, sed charitas, sed promissorum fides, sed amica consilia, sed fila perplexum itertacita ope signantia, sed Ariadna, sed Dædalus, vna salutis spes in auro est, auro placatur rex ferus, auro immane monstrum vincitur, auro salutare lorum rexitur, auro durum limen ostenditur, auro vectes, & saxa franguntur, auro tristis ianitor mollitur, aurum cœlum panditur, quid multa? auro Christus venditur.
units.tr: FRANCIS PETRARCH to his friend S. You wonder at the subscriptions of my letters, and not without reason. When you read of two Babylons, one long ago among the Assyrians, where the famous name of Semiramis lives on, and the other flourishing in our own age among the Egyptians, which has Cambyses as its founder, you find this newest Babylon, whose name you have never heard, thrust upon you. You say this with me, not because you do not know that our Rome was once called another Babylon, on account of the similarity of empires and the breadth of its climates, but because you remember that I am accustomed to call the city almighty, holy and queen, and so you still marvel at this latest Babylon. Stop wondering now. This region of the earth has its own Babylon. For where, I ask you, would a city of confusion more fittingly stand than in the western quarter? Who founded it is uncertain, but who inhabits it is very well known: certainly those who hold this name by the best right. And if you wish, believe me here: Nimrod, mighty on the earth and a strong hunter against the Lord, who sought heaven with proud chariots, is here; here is the quiver-bearing Semiramis; here is Cambyses, more mad than the Oriental one, and he himself, the first of kings, driven by his own necks, at last worn out by dropsy and fed on the slaughter of his own people, reduced from an innocent beginning to most wretched want. So I will not send you to the poets, for there is no need of the Pierian work; I will not send you to the historians. Consult the Catholic writers, but above all Augustine on that Psalm which begins, As for those of my letters to you which are lacking. There you will find what the name Babylon means. When you have read it, you will say that it is owed no less to the Rhone than to the Euphrates or the Nile. Nor will you be surprised if it comes to mind that Ambrose, in that book in which he laments the unworthy death of the younger Valentinian, used this same name when he spoke of the Rhone. And so that, once this wonder is cut away, I may pull up another from the root, you may also marvel at the five Labyrinths. Among the other writers you will find mention of only four, as I think: the Egyptian, the Lemnian, the Cretan, and in Italy the Clusian. They have passed over the Labyrinth of the Rhone, the most inextricable and worst of all, either because it did not yet exist or because it was not yet known. I mention it often. Whoever wishes to know it should hasten here with good reason. Here there is no dreadful prison, no error of a dark house, no urn of fate mixing the destinies of the human race. In short, there lack neither an imperious Minos, nor a voracious Minotaur, nor the monuments of a damned Venus. But there are also remedies, love, charity, the faith of promises, friendly counsels, threads that untangle the maze by a secret help, Ariadne, Daedalus. The one hope of safety lies in gold. A fierce king is appeased by gold, a monstrous beast is overcome by gold, the saving thong is loosened by gold, the hard threshold is shown by gold, bars and rocks are broken by gold, the grim doorkeeper is softened by gold, heaven is opened by gold. What more? By gold Christ is sold.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Ecclesia Catholica oppressionem per Papam luget.
units.tr: The Catholic Church laments the oppression by the Pope.

units.la: FRANCISC. PETRARCHA Amico S. Vt vides, eunt res, imo vero non eunt, sed retinebuntur: nihil est præsidii in virtute: iustitia periit, libertas abiit, æquitas victa est, libido regnat, sæuit auaritia, feruet inuidia, omne genus hominum suos patitur tyrannos. Ad laudes ore & animo canendas Deo geniti, totam vitam in contentionibus & æmulationibus agimus, insignis illa Iesu Christi aula; illa olim arx diuini cultus eximia, nunc tandem peccatis nostris id agentibus cœlesti auxilio destituta, immanium spelunca latronum facta est, ex vno quidem fonte descendit origo mali, accedunt fontes alii minores, ex quibus ingens omnimodæ miseriæ flumen exfluat? Quod necesse est propediê pereamus, supremisq; malorum obruamur fluctib. ac nisi humanæ perfidiæ diuina pietas occurrit, triste naufragium patiatur ecclesia. Quam vero diuersi mores, quam aduersa ædificantiū, & euertentiū mens? prouideat domui suæ Deus omnipotes, ego n. nihil habeo, quod tam multis contra nitentibus præstare possim, præter cōmiserationem matri debitam, & mihi placitam, vt vides fugam, quam oculos meos tam mosto liberem spectaculo. Video quidem eminus, sed prohibere non valeo; cominus videre renuo, artificium hoc obscoenum & infame, quo ecclesiasticus ille Dionysius, nostras vexat ac spoliat Syracusas. Video qua arte virum mentita Semiramis, frontem tegit, ingenioque oculos perstringit astantium, & incestis polluta complexibus, viros calcat. Video quibus artibus, noster hic Pericles se tuetur, vt quae reddi nequit, non cogatur reddere rationem, & hic suum habet Alcibiadem, & nemo velocius iniquis consiliis acquiescit. Turbat igitur omnia, miscetque de industria, quam putas ob causam, nisi vt circulatorum more, vel perplexo loco, vel confuso vulnere licentius fallat, & fraus propria sub umbraculo turbatae Reipublicae delitescat? Et ille quidem pro qualitate propositi, artibus vtitur non novis. Nam & in fruticoso gaudet auceps, piscator in turbido, fur in tenebris: nobis autem pro inertia nostra, quid possim optare miserius, quam vt nostri similes semper simus, coram adultero vigili nare stertentes ad calicem. Nescio fateor, an illius impudentia, an patientia nostra sit turpior.
units.tr: FRANCIS PETRARCH, To a friend S. As you see, things are going badly. Indeed, they are not so much going as being held back. There is no help in virtue: justice has perished, liberty has departed, fairness has been defeated, lust reigns, greed rages, envy seethes, and every class of men suffers its own tyrants. Born to sing God's praises with voice and heart, we spend our whole lives in quarrels and rivalries. That famous court of Jesus Christ, once the outstanding citadel of divine worship, has now been abandoned by heavenly help because of our sins, and has become a den of savage robbers. From one source indeed the origin of evil descends, and other smaller springs join it, from which a vast river of every kind of misery flows out. We must soon perish and be overwhelmed by the final waves of troubles, and unless divine mercy meets human treachery, the Church will suffer a sad shipwreck. Yet how different are the morals, and how hostile the minds of those who build and those who tear down! May almighty God provide for his own house. For I have nothing that I can offer against so many who strive against it, except the pity owed to a mother, and the flight, which pleases me, as you see, because I would gladly free my eyes from so foul a spectacle. I see indeed from afar, but I cannot prevent it. I refuse to look at close hand at this obscene and infamous trickery by which that ecclesiastical Dionysius harasses and plunders our Syracuse. I see by what art the lying Semiramis hides her brow and dazzles the wits of onlookers, and, polluted by incestuous embraces, tramples on men. I see by what arts our Pericles protects himself, so that he who cannot give an account is not forced to give one; he has his own Alcibiades, and no one yields more quickly to wicked counsels. He therefore confuses everything and mixes things up on purpose. Why do you think, unless it is that, like charlatans, he may deceive more freely in a confusing place or with a muddled wound, and his own fraud may lie hidden under the shade of a disturbed commonwealth? And he, according to the nature of his purpose, uses arts that are not new. For the fowler delights in bushy places, the fisherman in muddy water, the thief in the dark. But as for us, given our sloth, what could I wish for more wretched than that we should always be just as we are, snoring over the cup in front of a watchful adulterer? I confess I do not know whether his shamelessness or our patience is the more disgraceful.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: De Gallia Pontificia sedis residentia vitanda.
units.tr: On Avoiding Residence in Papal Gaul.

units.la: FRANCISCVS PETRARCHA Amico S. Diu distuli expectans & materiam, & nuncium: vtrumque simul affuit, quamuis vt es tu semper honestorum actuum praelargus, ego etsi ingenii inops scripturae vtique non auarus, horum alterum deesse non posse. Adest ecce nuncius, vltra quam optaui idoneus, nihil tibi devotius, nil mihi familiarius; adest scribendi materia, peregrinationis tuae rumor longe difficilis & inamoenae, qui mihi iam pridem calamum suggerebat, nisi quia incertus eram, vbinam terrarum esses inueniendus, neque enim aut ipse mihi persuadebam, longas te moras apud inferos exacturum sponte tua; aut omnino suspicari poteram, te illuc aliter quam coactum cuiuspiam magnae necessitatis imperio perrexisse. Itaque tuum tacitus excusabam iter, quod illa iussisset, quae adamantinum saepe Regum Pontificumque ceruicibus iugum imponit. Nunc quia incolumem te reuersum gaudeo, familiaritate illa, quam mihi peperit tua dignatio, fidesque mea, libet ex te quaerere, quid viro optimo cum pessimis locis, quid tibi cum Babylone? Fortissimos Romanorum legimus vitare solitos Campaniae Baias, apricum licet & salubrem locum, vbi vt exiguum honestatis, sic saltem voluptatis & laetitiae multum erat, adeo rebus omnibus neglectis, vni studio virtutis intenti erant. Si hoc ita est, quis non Rhodanum vitet? quis oro, non sugiat Babylonem, & vitiorum simul omnium, & laboris ac totius miseriae moestam domum? De quo quidem aliquid nosse debes, visa loquor, non audita, fato meo pessimo, in eas terras puer euectus, cui vsque ad hanc aetatem, indignari equidem, sed fortunae compedibus, nescio quibus victo, magnae illic partes aetatis in gemitibus abierunt. Noui expertus, vt nulla ibi pietas, nulla caritas, nulla fides, nulla Dei reverentia, nullus timor, nulli sancti, nulli iusti, nulli aequi, nihil pensi, nihil denique vel humani. Amor, pudor, decor, candor inde exulant. De veritate quidem sileo, nam quis vsquam vero locus, vbi omnia mendaciis plena sunt, aer, terra, domus, turres, vici, atria, plateae, porticus, vestibula, aulae, thalami, tectorum laquearia, murorum rimulae, diuersoria aedium, penetralia templorum, iudicum subsellia, Pontificum sedes, ad postremum ora hominum, nutus, gestus, voces, frontes, animi? Quid ais? An mentior, an vero de mendaciis verum loquor? si illic fuisti, & nullo tuo maiore negotio distractus, & in nephariam illam scelerum coenam, acumen ingenii, atque oculos intendisti, alium iudicem non optabo, quam scilicet omnia ibi virtute, veroque sint vacua, plena criminibus, plena fallaciis, plena fucis, plena blanditiis, plena pessimis artibus, ambitionis, auaritiae, superbiae, liuoris. Vidisti ficte & inaniter fieri omnia, non tantum hominibus sed Deo; notasti subdolos risus, corda flebilia, serena supercilia, nubilas mentes, molles manus, actus asperrimos, angelicas voces, daemoniacas intentiones, suaues cantus, ferrea pectora, & verba praedulcia pulmone amaro, & sicco ore cadentia, summisque labiis vix expressa, in quibus plane Dauidicum illud impletur: Molliti enim sunt sermones eorum super oleum, & ipsi sunt iacula. Neque vero impunitum modo apud eos, sed gloriosum etiam est, mentiri, ceu maioris sit ingenii qui fefellit, maioris status, quem increpare audeat nemo. Nolo hunc articulum scrupulosius exequi, ne forsan vrgente materia, stylus eat quo non expedit. Res est insuper mundo nota, neque probationis omnino, neque sermonis egens. Vnum & breve, & ad reliqua perdiscenda satis efficax miseram, cui ego ipse qui loquor interfui.
