Duo simul e conscriptis Patribus, in quibus orbis terrae, & ostium domus Dei, velut in cardine voluitur, a palatio Pontificis Maximi densa stipati famulorum acie, descendebant, turba ingens expectantium, quibus ante omnes illa infoelix & Deo odiosa ciuitas plena est, de more surdu illud, & praedurum limen obsederant, qui ducibus suis visis, in quibus spem habebant, circumstrepere coeperunt, & pro se quisque anxie percontari, quae fortuna, quisve suarum rerum apud Pontificem status esset. Tunc vnus patrum, nihil motus in re subita, vt qui iam pridem talibus assueuisset, nihil adhuc verecundia tactus aut misericordia miserorum, inter spes vanissimas animam, vitam, fortunasque suas, & tempus omne perdentium, insignis mendaciorum opifex, multa mentiri orsus & fingere, quid cuique spei reliquum, quid ad huius aut illius postulata pontifex respondisset, singula constanti impudentia, & in nullo haesitans prosecutus est. Quibus auditis creduli omnes, & hic quidem, vt sit laetior, ille subtristis in diversum abeunt. Alter autem patrum & naturae nobilioris, & verecundioris animi, & qui nisi ex illo esset ordine, vir bonus esse potuisset in collegam tocans; Nihil mi te (inquit) pudet his simplicibus viiis illudere, & pro arbitrio fingere responsa Pontificis; quem ut scis non modo hodie, sed multis iam diebus proximis videre nequimus? Ad hoc ille reverendus pater & egregius veterator, ut erat fronte meretricia & attrita subridens. Imo vero te (inquit) pudeat, tam ingenio tardum fore, ut curiae artes addiscere, ratio iam tempore nequeas. Quo dicto in stuporem ego: caeteri autem in risum resoluti omnes, & responsum nebulonis illius multis laudibus efferentes, virum argutissimum praedicarunt, qui iam prompte mentiri didicisset ac fallere, verum ego nimis latae materiae campum, nec epistolae, sed libri opus ingressus sum, itaque frenam iam contraham. Ad te vero pater optime, stylum vertens, oro, obsecro, obtestor, adiuro te per temetipsum, si tibi charus es, si solitam animae curam geris, ne quando tibi postea in cor veniat illuc ire, unde nemo unquam exemplo melior factus, pessimi autem innumerabiles redierunt. Adde quod nemo inde unquam non moestus exiuit, nisi eo forte laetus, quod euaserat, & infaustum limen fusco calle repererat. Ad summa quoniam tua omnia cupide semper in optimam ac felicissimam partem traho, profectionem hanc tuam necessariam, breuem, unicam, non modo nihil nociturum tibi, sed plurimum profuturam spero. Quid enim aliud, ut seria fabulosis aspergam, quid sibi vult Achilles Homericus, dum ut impenetrabilis ferro fiat, fertur ad inferos, & tartareis undis abluitur, nisi ut vitiorum fluctibus tantis exercitatus, contrarii sui odio, solida tua virtus induruerit roburque contraxerit, contraque omnem humanarum, cuspidem passionum, iam prorsus inuiolabilis facta sit? placet, laudo, approbo, modo ne redeas. Senecae verbum est: Non tantum corpori, sed etiam moribus salubrem locum eligere debemus, illeque autem unde te dehortor & corpori pestilens & animo, nec omnino te dignus est, non convenient mores. Sit igitur inter vos diuortium tempiterna, eant illuc, qui artes illas discere cupiunt, quarum ibi sunt innumeri professores, tu domi mane, inque tuo proposito, & tua sede constiste, quam tibi clarissimam virtus dedit, cum clariorem etiam mereare. Sin, ut est, animus honesti motus appetens, quoniam quod eruditissimis quibusdam placitum viris scio, unum hoc nobis caelestis originis argumentum est, ut motu perpetuo delectemur, loco te si movere volueris, ad nos veni, vide Romam, vide Mediolanum, vide Venetias, vide Florentiam, vide Patauium tuum, vide Bononiam, vbi honestis in studiis egisti adolescentiam, & integritatem patriam Italicis artibus adornasti: postremo quidlibet vide, Indos quoque, modo ne videas Babylonem, neque descendas in internum viuens.
units.tr: Francis Petrarch to a friend, greetings. I have put off writing for a long time, waiting for both a subject and a messenger. Both have now arrived together. You, as always, are most generous in honourable deeds, and I, though poor in talent, am certainly not stingy with my pen, so I know that neither of these can be lacking. Here is the messenger, more suitable than I could have wished, nothing more devoted to you and nothing more familiar to me. And here is the subject for writing: the report of your journey, which was far from easy and far from pleasant. It has long been urging me to take up my pen, except that I was unsure where on earth you were to be found. I could not persuade myself that you would willingly spend a long time among the dead, nor could I suspect at all that you had gone there under any compulsion other than the command of some great necessity. So I silently excused your journey, since it was ordered by that power which often lays its adamantine yoke on the necks of kings and popes. Now, since I rejoice that you have returned safe, I want to ask you, out of that intimacy which your kindness and my own loyalty have created, what business a good man has with the worst places, and what business you have with Babylon. We read that the bravest Romans used to avoid Baiae in Campania, a sunny and healthy spot, where there was, if little honour, at least a great deal of pleasure and gaiety, though they were so intent on virtue alone that they neglected everything else. If that is so, who would not avoid the Rhône? Who, I beg you, would not flee Babylon, the sad home of all vices, of toil and of every misery? You ought to know something of it, since I speak of what I have seen, not what I have heard. By my very bad luck I was carried there as a boy, and through the whole of my life until now I have been indignant, yet, conquered by I know not what shackles of fortune, a great part of my life has passed there in groaning. I know from experience that there is no piety there, no charity, no faith, no reverence for God, no fear, no saints, no just or fair men, nothing weighed, nothing in the end even human. Love, shame, decency and honesty are exiled from there. I say nothing of the truth, for where is truth anywhere when everything is full of lies: the air, the land, the houses, the towers, the streets, the courtyards, the squares, the porticoes, the vestibules, the halls, the bedchambers, the panelled ceilings, the cracks in the walls, the inns of the houses, the innermost parts of the temples, the benches of the judges, the seats of the popes, and finally the mouths of men, their nods, gestures, voices, faces and minds? What do you say? Am I lying, or do I speak the truth about lies? If you were there, and, distracted by no greater business of your own, turned your keen wit and your eyes upon that wicked banquet of crimes, I would wish for no other judge. You would find that everything there is empty of virtue and truth, and full of crimes, full of deceits, full of masks, full of flatteries, full of the worst arts of ambition, greed, pride and envy. You saw that everything is done falsely and vainly, not only before men but before God. You noted the deceitful laughter, the tearful hearts, the serene brows, the clouded minds, the soft hands, the harshest deeds, the angelic voices, the devilish intentions, the sweet songs, the iron breasts, and words most sweet yet uttered from a bitter lung, from a dry mouth, and barely pronounced by lowered lips. In these the words of David are plainly fulfilled: "Their words were softer than oil, yet they are drawn swords." Nor is lying among them merely unpunished, but even glorious, as if it marked greater talent in the one who deceives, and a greater rank, and no one dares to rebuke him. I do not want to pursue this point too closely, lest, once my material carries me on, my pen should go where it is not wise to go. Besides, the matter is well known to the world and needs neither proof nor argument. I will mention one thing only, brief and sufficiently effective for learning the rest: a wretched scene at which I myself, who am speaking, was present. Two of the enrolled Fathers, on whom the whole world and the door of God's house turn as on a hinge, were coming down from the palace of the Supreme Pontiff, surrounded by a dense line of attendants, and a huge crowd of those waiting, with whom that unhappy city, hateful to God, is always full, had besieged the usual deaf and very hard threshold. When they saw the leaders on whom they had placed their hopes, they began to clamour around them, and each anxiously asked what his fortune was, or what the state of his affairs was with the Pontiff. Then one of the Fathers, unmoved by the sudden situation, as one long accustomed to such things, touched by no shame and no pity for the wretched, and, among those losing their souls, their lives, their fortunes and all their time to most vain hopes, a notable manufacturer of lies, began to invent and fabricate many things. What hope remained for each one, what the Pontiff had answered to this man's or that man's requests, he recounted item by item with steady impudence, hesitating over nothing. All the credulous people, having heard this, went off in different directions, one somewhat happier, another rather sad. But the other Father, of nobler nature and a more modest spirit, one who, had he not belonged to that order, could have been a good man, called his colleague aside and said: "Are you not ashamed to mock these simple folk with such lies, and to make up at will the Pontiff's answers, when, as you know, we cannot see him not only today but for many days past?" To this that reverend father and distinguished old trickster replied, smiling with a brazen and worn face: "Rather you should be ashamed, that you are so slow of wit that, though you have been here so long, you still cannot learn the arts of the court." At this remark I was stunned, but all the others burst into laughter, and, praising that rascal's answer with many compliments, they proclaimed him a most shrewd man, who had already learned to lie and deceive readily. But I have entered on a field of matter too broad for a letter, and it is the work of a book, so I will now draw in my reins. To you, excellent father, I turn my pen and beg, entreat, implore and adjure you by yourself: if you hold yourself dear, if you take your customary care of your soul, never let it come into your heart later to go there, from which no one has ever returned better, while countless wicked men have come back. Add that no one has ever left there without sadness, unless perhaps glad because he had escaped and had found the unlucky threshold by a dark path. Since I always eagerly interpret all your affairs in the best and happiest light, I hope this journey of yours, necessary, brief and only once, will not only do you no harm but will benefit you greatly. For what else, to sprinkle serious things with fables, does Homer's Achilles mean when, to be made impenetrable to iron, he is said to have gone to the underworld and been bathed in the waters of Tartarus, except that, tested by such great waves of vices, your solid virtue, hardened by hatred of its opposite, has grown firm and gained strength, and has become altogether invulnerable against every spear of human passions? I approve, I praise, I commend it, provided you do not come back. It is Seneca's saying: We ought to choose a place healthy not only for the body but also for the character. That place from which I advise you to keep away is harmful to the body and to the mind, and it is not fitting for you at all, nor will your character agree with it. Let there therefore be an everlasting divorce between you and it. Let those go there who wish to learn those arts, of which there are countless teachers there. You, stay at home, abide by your purpose and keep to your seat, which virtue has given you as most illustrious, since you deserve to become even more illustrious. But if, as is the case, your spirit, seeking honourable motion, which, as I know from certain very learned men, is the one sign of our heavenly origin, that we delight in perpetual motion, should wish to move from its place, then come to us. See Rome, see Milan, see Venice, see Florence, see your Padua, see Bologna, where you spent your youth in honourable studies and adorned your native integrity with Italian arts. In short, see whatever you like, even the Indians, provided you do not see Babylon, nor go down alive into the underworld.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Calamitatem Vrbis Romae deplorat, quam Imperator Iupiter Papa in seruitutem reliquit.
units.tr: He laments the calamity of the city of Rome, which the Emperor Jupiter, the Pope, has left in servitude.

units.la: FRANCISC. PETRARCHA Amico S. Quocunque te conuerteris, idem es, & pariter me delectas, uniformi enim amoris tui dulcedine, sed multiplici & varia verborum tuorum consolatione reficior, siue ab oriente, siue occidente, & desertis montibus: Quoniam licet Deus iudex sit, & hunc humiliet, hunc exaltet, tamen te mihi semper humilem, semper altum, semper amabilem, & ab omni parte suauiter spirantem dulce curarum mearum refrigerium seruat. Epistolae quidem illi veris simis, grauissimisque sententiis exundanti, vbi diuinae facundiae tuae fons, et terra arida ac squalenti, & omnis boni vacua, terra (ut prophetae egregii verbo vtar) deserta, inuia, & inaquosa, oculos meos atque aures, animumque compleuit, iucunditate mirabili, neque perennibus ingenii scatebris, mutati loci nocuisse malignitas quiuit; quid prius tibi respondeam, non habeo, quam ut miserari me sortem tuam, quae in terra florentissima ortum te, & ab incunabulis enutritum, nunc repente patriis finibus auulsum ad extrema terrarum, & hominum inopina rerum mutatione transfulerit.
units.tr: FRANCIS PETRARCH to a friend, greeting. Wherever you turn, you are the same, and you delight me equally. For I am refreshed by the uniform sweetness of your love, and by the varied and manifold comfort of your words, whether they come from the east, from the west, or from the deserted mountains. For although God is the judge, who humbles this man and exalts that one, yet your constancy keeps for me, always humble, always high, always lovable, and breathing sweetness on every side, a sweet refreshment for my cares. Your letter, overflowing with the most true and weighty sayings, where is the fountain of your divine eloquence, and where the earth was dry and squalid and empty of all good, a desert, pathless and waterless (to use the words of the outstanding prophet), filled my eyes, my ears and my mind with a wonderful delight. Neither the malice of a changed place nor the ever-flowing springs of your talent could harm it. I do not know what to answer first, except to pity your lot, which, after you were born and reared from the cradle in a most flourishing land, has suddenly torn you from your native borders and carried you to the ends of the earth, through an unexpected change of fortune.

units.la: Sit illud gratulari, quod iudicium tuum vel opinionibus vel persuasionibus falsis inuolui, abducique e vero non est passa: tali enim ingenio, humani nihil incognitum esse debet. Poteras fortassis errare, poteras suspicari, poteras credere his, quibus (ut dici solet) praeter pretium in pretio nihil est; nunc vero neque veritas opinionibus cedet, neque cuiquam potius, quam oculis ipse tuis, & experientiae fidem dabis. Ecce iam oculis vides, iam manibus palpas, qualis est Babylon illa nouissima feruens, aestuans, obscoena, terribilis, quam nec Cambysis opus Babylon Niliaca, nec illa vetustior regia Semiramidis Babylon aequet Assyria, Nilum & Euphratem Rhodanus vincit: nempe qui tartarea flumina Cocytum vincit, & Acherontem, quicquid vspiam perfidiae & doli, quicquid inclementiae, superbiaeque, quicquid impudicitiae, effrenataeque libidinis audiuisti, aut legisti, quicquid denique impietatis & morum pessimorum spatium habet, aut habuit orbis terrae, totum istic cumulatim videas, aceruatimque reperias. Nam de auaritia, deque ambitione superuacuum est loqui, quarum alterum ibi regni sui solium posuisse, unde orbem totum populetur, ac spoliet, alteram vero alibi nusquam habitare compertum est, de quibus omnibus ad te dudum non Epistolam, sed librum scribere meditabar, ne in rebus, scilicet a prima mihi aetate notissimis, amicum falli sinerem, etsi enim nolim, mihi tunc mirabiliter & miserabiliter inuiscato, eisdem tu fuisses in locis, vbi velut in coeno, imo quidem, velut in igne aurum, amicitiam primum tuam longe auro chariorem reperi: tunc tamen & inexpertior rerum aetas, & iudicii minor vis & morae tuae breuitas vero obstabant, insuper & exilio, in peius infinita mutatio facta erat. Redisti ergo & aetate iam, & iudicio pleniore & mora non ad sufficientiam modo, vel satietatem, sed nisi fallor ad fastidium prolixa, vt qui optima rerum probe noueras in pessimis non errares, quique virtutem semper amauerat. aquaueras, ad vehementius amandum, quod efficacissimum est vitiorum odio animum excitares. Et si Christum colis, quod semper religiosissime fecisti, conspecta hostium eius impietas, manum pietati, & fidei tuae calcar adiiceret: vides enim populum, non modo Christi aduersarium, sed quod est gravius sub Christi vexillo rebellantem Christo, militantem Sathanae, & Christi sanguinetumidum, atque lasciuientem: Labia nostra a nobis sunt, quis noster Dominus est? Populum duricordem & impium, superbum, famelicum, sitientem, hianti rostro, acutis dentibus, procaris vnguibus, pedibus lubricis, pectore saxeo, corde chalybeo, plumbea voluntate, voce melliflua, populum cui non modo proprie convenire dixeris Euangelicum atque prophecam: Populus hic me labiis honorat, cor autem eorum longe est a me. Sed illud etiam laude laetitiae, qui Dominum suum prodens, & exosculans aiebat: Ave Rabbi, & Iudaeorum qui induitum purpura, coronatum spinis, percutientes & conspuentes illusione amarissima flexis poplitibus adorabant & salutabant, Ave Rex Iudaeorum, quem neque ut regem diuinis, aut humanis honoribus, sed ut reum mortis ac blasphemum, contumeliis dignum, atque supplicis in humano iudicio destinarunt. Quid enim, quid oro, aliud assidue geritur, hos inter Christi hostes, & nostri temporis Pharisaeos? Nonne etenim Christum ipsum, cuius nomen die ac nocte altissimis laudibus attollunt, quem purpura atque auro vestiunt, quem gemmis onerant, quem salutant & adorant cernui, eundem in terra emunt, vendunt, nundinantur, eundem quasi velatis oculis non visurum, & impiarum opum vepribus coronant, & imparissimi oris spuris inquinant, & vipereis sibilis infectantur, & venenatorum actuum cuspide feriunt, & quantum in eis est illusum, nudum, inopem, flagellarum iterum atque iterum in Calvariam trahunt, ac nefandis assensibus, cruci rursus affigunt. Et o pudor, o dolor, o indignitas, talium hodie, ut dicitur, Roma est patientibus, quorum erat obstare, tanto illam factu sibi vendicant, ut quam suam volunt, aspicere degignentur, & pro qua olim orbe toto tantus fluxit cruor, tot clari duces, tot exercitus cecidere, eam nunc nescio, quot indigesti & infames rustici nutu, regunt & captam, velut ab hostibus, nullam iam contradictore dilacerant: O mi consulte princeps ac prodige, nesciebas quantis laboribus constaret imperium, quod tam facile dispergebas: solent in studiis adolescentes a patribus quaesita prodigere, nempe ignari, unde vel qualiter parta sint, siquidem indigentiae ac laborum recordatio, magnum prodigialitati ac lasciviae frenum ponit. At tu senex, quid agebas, ubi eras? si videri munificum delectabat, de proprio largireris, tuum donasses: imperii haereditatem, quam curator acceperas, successoribus integram reliquisses. Nescio quidem an potueris, sed fecisti, ut ad has tunc humiles, nunc superbas manus, heu longe, aliis manibus fundari status administratio peruenit. De quo non illepide iocans quidam ait:
units.tr: Yet this at least is cause for rejoicing: your judgment has not been allowed to be wrapped up in opinions or false persuasions, nor led away from the truth. For with such a mind nothing human ought to be unknown to you. You might perhaps have been mistaken, might have suspected, might have believed those men for whom, as the saying goes, nothing is worth anything except what it costs. But now neither truth will yield to opinions, nor will you give your trust to anyone rather than to your own eyes and experience. Behold, now you see with your eyes and touch with your hands what kind of Babylon that latest one is: seething, boiling, obscene, terrible, to which neither the Babylon of Cambyses on the Nile, nor that older royal Babylon of Semiramis in Assyria, is equal. The Rhone surpasses the Nile and the Euphrates; indeed it surpasses Cocytus and Acheron, the rivers of hell. Whatever treachery and deceit, whatever cruelty and pride, whatever impurity and unbridled lust you have heard of or read of, whatever of impiety and of the worst morals the extent of the world has or has had, you may see it all there in heaps, and find it piled up. For it is superfluous to speak of avarice and ambition, of which the one has set up its throne there, from which it plunders and despoils the whole world, while the other is known never to dwell anywhere else. On all these matters I had long been planning to write to you not a letter but a book, so that I would not allow my friend to be deceived about things that have been most familiar to me since my earliest youth. For even if I did not wish it, I was then wonderfully and miserably caught in the same places where you were, as if in mud, or rather, as gold is refined in fire; there I first found your friendship, far dearer than gold. Yet at that time both my age, still inexperienced in affairs, and my power of judgment, which was less, and the brevity of your stay stood in the way. Besides, in addition to the exile, there had been an endless change for the worse. So you have returned now with a riper age and a fuller judgment, and with a stay that was not merely long enough, or more than enough, but, unless I am mistaken, long enough to bring on disgust. Since you had thoroughly known the best things, you would not go wrong among the worst, and since you had always loved virtue, you would have been stirred to love it more vehemently, which is the most effective way to rouse the mind to a hatred of vices. And if you worship Christ, as you have always done most devoutly, the sight of his enemies' impiety should add a spur to your piety and faith. For you see a people that is not only the adversary of Christ, but, what is worse, rebelling against Christ under Christ's own banner, fighting for Satan, drunk with the blood of Christ and wantonly reveling: Our lips are our own; who is lord over us? A people hard of heart, impious, proud, hungry, thirsty, with gaping beak, sharp teeth, hooked claws, slippery feet, a breast of stone, a heart of steel, a leaden will, and a honeyed voice. Of this people you could fittingly say not only what the Gospel and the prophet say: This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. But you could also add that other saying, of one who, betraying his Lord and kissing him, cried out with joy: Hail, Rabbi! and of the Jews who, having clothed him in purple and crowned him with thorns, struck and spat on him, and in bitter mockery bent their knees and greeted him: Hail, King of the Jews! They did not appoint him to divine or human honours as a king, but condemned him as one deserving death and a blasphemer, worthy of insults, and a suppliant in human judgment. For what, I ask you, else is continually going on among these enemies of Christ, these Pharisees of our time? Do they not sell and buy, and trade in Christ himself, whose name they praise day and night with the highest praises, whom they clothe in purple and gold, whom they load with jewels, whom they greet and worship on bended knee? Do they not, as if his eyes were veiled and he would never see, crown him with the thorns of their impious wealth, defile him with the spittle of their most unclean mouths, assail him with viperous hisses, strike him with the point of their poisonous deeds, and, as far as they can, drag him again and again, mocked, naked and destitute, with scourges to Calvary, and nail him once more to the cross with their wicked consent? And, oh shame, oh grief, oh indignity, such are those who today, as it is said, hold Rome, those who ought to have stood against her, and so unjustly claim her for themselves that they disdain to look upon her as their own. For her sake formerly such great bloodshed flowed through the whole world, so many famous leaders and so many armies fell; now I know not how many base and infamous peasants rule her at a nod, and tear her, seized as if from enemies, with no one left to contradict them. O my prudent prince and prodigal, you did not know at what labour the empire was won, since you scattered it so easily! Young men at their studies are accustomed to squander what their fathers have acquired, plainly unaware of where or how it was gained, since the remembrance of hardship and toil sets a great brake on prodigality and wantonness. But you, old man, what were you doing, where were you? If you delighted in being thought generous, you should have given away what was your own, and left the inheritance of the empire, which you had received as a guardian, whole to your successors. I do not know whether you could have, but you did, so that the administration of the state has passed, to these hands that were then humble and are now proud, to be founded, alas, far off, by other hands. Some man, joking not unpleasantly about this, said:

units.la: Roma tibi fuerant servi, Domini Dominorum,
units.tr: Rome once were your slaves, lords of lords,

units.la: Seruorum servi, nunc tibi sunt Domini.
units.tr: Slaves of slaves, now they are your lords.

units.la: Hanc Historiam, quæ nescio, an ab aliis scripta sit, iam curiose retexui, vt si tibi nota est, & mihi cognitam scias: si ignota autem, ex me discas, neu gnarus veterum, præsentium sis ignarus, his vero nunc ducibus agimur, quibus præda sumus atque odio, & simulato contemptui, & timori vero. Et si quis etiam nunc ex nostris metu & verecundia magis, quam iudicio, assumptus in eo numero est, quasi lucidus riuus, torrenti mixtus turbido, natiuum depositum colorem, inque plurium naturam, & externos mores abiit. Etiam prorsus nihil est reliqui, nisi Christum precari, hicque eripiam tradat aliis, quorum non & pœniteat simul, & pudeat humanum genus. Hi enim tales sunt, quales dico, fallor, imo vero quales dicere nequeo, sic ad extrema dedecorum atque nequitiæ, quæ vtcunque olim fuerat, prolapsa res est, ex quo sancta & potens tunc Romana, nunc Auinionensis ecclesia tangit vertice sydera & digito cœlum voluit, & Iudas si triginta illos suos argenteos pretium sanguinis attulerit, admittetur, & pauper a limine Christus arcebitur, quod ita esse Christianus nemo est qui nesciat, nemo qui non doleat, nemo qui vindicet. Ita dum alius alium expectat, malorumque impunitas, quantum vides crevit, & quod a principio medicabile malum fuerat, iam tempore putruit. Cœperat enim; fateor, ante etiam ætatem nostram, vt ab auis accepimus, fœdum hoc vicus inflari, sed quod molestum diceres, intemperans morbum auxit exiguum. Itaque iam hæc possis ad interitum spectat, totaque saniies in nostrum tempus erupit flebile, nisi vnum tantis in malis solatii genui esset. Dicam vero tibi nunc, quod interdum dixi ei, qui solus e cunctis superfuit, illo grege pessimo, melioribus pascuis dignus erat, ingenti cum assensu eius, licet ipse dicto, non tam morum respectu, quam statu atque originis tangeretur: si quidem enim, quoniam mortalium res oportet esse mortales, duo hæc mundi luminaria extingui, duosque gladios retundi, decreti necessitas cogebat, quamuis vtrumque, præcipueque alterum, occasui exemptum, promissis cœlestibus, sperare mus, nec desperandum sit, omnia hæc cum funditus ruerint, surrectura altius, si tamen hæc tam graui rerum eminentium ruina, nostro seculo impendebat. Gaudeo, Hercule, quod cum in manib. nostris lux, & vigor suus hic manserit, in alienis hæc tanta mutatio facta est, tantæque culpa partem habet illa horrida & immitis: partem hæc mollis & enerwata barbaries. Quibus ille auditis, libertate mea nihil offensus: Graviter, inquit, & libere, & aliorum fortasse auribus importune, meis certe fidentissime, & vt te decuit verissime locutus es. Neu me forsan veri insciun, aut diversæ sententiæ arbitreris, duos Clementes nostros plus attriuisse ecclesiam paucis annis, quam septem Gregorii vestri, multis seculis restaurare possent: Nec ego dubito, nec dubitare aliquem existimo. Ille quidem hæc suspirans, nos autem zelo domus tuæ Christe Iesu iam satis eucti sumus, nec vllus sub sole aliorum rerum trames, stylo potuerat occurrere, itaque redeundum est. Ad hunc ergo populum, Amice, sanctis tuis, ut tibi quietem inuidentibus an doctrinam ingerentibus venisti, peregrinatione dica exilio, vtili magis quam iucunda, quo effectu est, vt & tibi legedi, & mihi conceptu scribendi negotiu abstuleris. Iam profecto nec mihi, nec alteri doctus, quid sit, Babylon Rhodani, qualiterue sit exulibus Sion inter flumina Babylonis, de quib, adeo magnifice tua mecum nup egit epistola, vt illius setine abdita dita funditus scrutatus omnes eius Labyrinthi latebras penitus inspexisse videare, multo tædio, multisque reor angoribus, huius veri notitiam comparasti. Illud tibi pergratum, mihi inuidiosum affuit tamen, quod inter tantas vitiorum tenebras, quatuor magnis illis quidem viris, velut totidem lucidissimis te sideribus usum scribis, quos nescio, an annorum crimen (ipsos enim optimos, integerrimosque; hominum noui) an quæ fallacissima vitæ spes, an quæ fortunæ violentia, tristisque necessitas, ibi detineat, quare permitte, quæso, vt quod in animo est, vel inamœno sermone explicem, quasi, inquam, in cloaca solis radios & loci simul obscœnitatem omnem suolumine nudantes, & circumfusis sordibus inaccessos.
units.tr: I have now carefully unravelled this story, which I do not know whether others have written; I do so that, if it is known to you, you may know that I too am acquainted with it, and if it is unknown to you, you may learn it from me, lest, being acquainted with the ancients, you be ignorant of the present; for now we are led by those leaders by whom we are made prey, objects of hatred, of pretended contempt and of real fear. And if anyone from our own ranks, taken into their number now more from fear and shame than from judgment, has been like a clear stream mixed with a muddy torrent, he has lost his native colour and passed into the nature of the many and into foreign manners. Indeed nothing remains for us except to pray to Christ, who may rescue us from them and hand us over to others, at whom the human race would both grieve and blush. For they are such as I describe them, or rather I am at fault in saying so, since I cannot say what they are. The state of things has so fallen to the utmost of disgrace and wickedness, whatever it was once, since the holy and then powerful Roman Church, now the Avignonese, has touched the stars with its head and rolled the heavens with its finger. And if Judas should bring back his thirty silver pieces, the price of blood, he will be admitted, and Christ, poor, will be shut out from the threshold. That this is so no Christian is ignorant, no one fails to grieve, no one avenges it. Thus, while one waits for another, the impunity of evils has grown, as you see, and what at the beginning was a curable evil has by now rotted with time. For it had begun, I admit, even before our age, as we have heard from our grandfathers, to swell into this foul sore; but, what you might call troublesome, a little intemperance increased the disease. So now you could look upon this as tending to destruction, and all the foulness has burst out into our weeping age, were it not that in such great evils we have one consolation. I will now tell you what I sometimes said to him who alone of all has survived from that most wicked flock, and who deserved better pastures. He agreed greatly, although he was himself touched not so much by regard for their morals as by their condition and origin. For if, since mortal things must be mortal, the necessity of fate required that these two luminaries of the world be extinguished and these two swords be blunted, though we hope, and must not despair, that both, especially the one, will be rescued from the setting and, with heavenly promises, will rise higher again once all these things have been overthrown to the ground, yet if such a grievous ruin of the eminent things was hanging over our century... I rejoice, by Hercules, that while the light and vigour of this have remained in our hands, this great change has been made in the hands of others; and that horrid and savage barbarism has a share in so great a guilt, and this soft and enervated barbarism another part. When he had heard these things, he, not offended in the least by my frankness, said: "You have spoken gravely and freely, and perhaps inopportunely in the ears of others, but certainly most confidently to me, and as was fitting for you, most truly. Lest you think me perhaps ignorant of the truth, or of a different opinion, I say that our two Clements have worn out the Church in a few years more than your seven Gregories could restore in many centuries. I do not doubt it, nor do I think anyone else does." He, sighing these things, and we already well stirred up by zeal for your house, O Christ Jesus, and no other path under the sun could have come before my pen, so I must return. So, my friend, did you come to this people, whether to offer your holy ones, who envy you your quiet, or to press doctrine upon them? I call your sojourn an exile, more useful than pleasant; by its effect you have taken from me the task of reading and from you the business of writing. Indeed, neither I nor anyone else learned, not even the learned, what Babylon on the Rhône is, or in what state the exiles of Sion are among the rivers of Babylon, about which your letter lately treated with such magnificence with me, so that you seem to have searched out thoroughly the hidden depths of that sewer and to have looked into every lurking place of its labyrinth; you have acquired knowledge of this truth, I think, with much weariness and many anxieties. It was very pleasing to you, though to me not without envy, that among such great darkness of vices you write that you were supported by four great men, as by so many most bright stars. I do not know whether the wickedness of the age (for I know them to be the best and most upright of men), or some most deceptive hope of life, or the violence of fortune and sad necessity, holds them there. Therefore, I beg you, permit me to set out what is in my mind, even in an unpleasing style, as if, I say, rays of the sun in a sewer, uncovering at once all the filth of the place, and inaccessible because of the dirt that surrounds them.

units.la: XIIII.
units.tr: XIIII.

units.la: Babylonem Gallicam describit in sede Papali Auinionensi.
units.tr: He describes Gallic Babylon, the papal seat at Avignon.

units.la: FRANC. PETRARCHA Amico S. Et quid adhuc hæres? ac non hæres, sed teneris, & obluctans raperis, hoc potius reor, malo vim, quam socordiam opinari, non est tuum torpor, ardens ingenium, mens ignea, generosus impetus. Sed quid hæc, si fortius impedimentum est, quam virtus? magna etiam vis habet oppositam vim maiorem: necessitati omnia succumbunt. Illa te Babylon traxit, illa te detinet: durum sed ferendum, loci natura est. Omne bonum ibi perditur, sed primum omnium libertas, mox ex ordine quies, gaudium, spes, fides, charitas, animæ iacturæ ingentes. Sed in regno auaritiæ, nihil damno ascribitur, modo pecunia salua sit. Futuræ ibi vitæ spes inanis quædam fabula, & quæ de inferis narrantur fabulosa omnia, & resurrectio carnis, & mundi finis, & Christus ad iudicium venturus, inter nænias habentur. Veritas ibi dementia est, abstinentia vero rusticitas, & pudicitia probrum ingens, denique peccandi licentia magnanimitas, & libertas eximia, & quo pollutior, eo clarior vita, quo plus scelerum, eo plus gloriæ, bonum nomen, cœno vilius, atque vltima mercium fama est. Habes quantum in tam paucis licuit illius sacræ vrbis expressum, quem non magis in his terris hodie, quam in illorum frontibus hominum, quotidie perlegis, quorum vitam nullus stylus, nullum æquet ingenium. Cæterum prima omnium vt dixi, ibi libertatis iactura est, quisquis limen illud introit, confestim suus esse desiit, iam nec quiescere nec abire permittitur, sed rotatur, & inefficaci labore consumendus atteritur. Paucos inde diuina clementia eripi à lege, vt Hierusalem diligant, atque oderint Babylonem. Hæc mihi dete spes reliqua est, alioquin tuis de rebus actum crederem, tam tenaci, profundoque hinc te demertum & infixum video: interim non voluntati, aut iudicio: necessitati imputo & fortunæ, quod tam diu ibi sis, & moras quas vehementer odi, libenter excuso, quod si qua fortassis in profectione culpa fuit, in mora ipsa, vtique iam non culpa, sed supplicium, & purgatio culpæ est. Sed quoniam multi, multa sæpe in carcere didicerunt, quid te vetat, in vinculis discere aliquid, quo perpetuo sis doctior? Quidam nullo modo, melius quam contrario discunt, ideoque qui Mathematicas artes docent, si quando parum veri capax mens discipuli visa erit, solent falsa proponere, quæ dum refugit animus, ad veriora confugiat. Tu quoque solitus & religioni semper, & honestati operam dare, quarum altera ad illius aspectum erigit optantem animam, de quo ait Psalmista, Quærite faciem eius semper. Alterius ea facies est, quæ si oculis cerneretur, vt ait Plato, miris animum amoribus inflammaret, neque tamen ideo minus amanda est, quo animo cernitur, si quid tibi nunc etiam ad vtriusque notitiæ summâ deesse putas, omne studium in aduersa reflectito, arrige aures, fige oculos, intende animum. Vis pulchritudinem Dei noscere? cerne quanta est hostium eius obscœnitas.
units.tr: FRANCIS PETRARCH to his friend, greetings. And why do you still hesitate? Or rather, you do not hesitate, but you are dragged along, struggling against it. I would rather think it is force than sloth. Your mind is not sluggish: it is a burning intellect, a fiery spirit, a noble impulse. But what use are these, if the obstacle is stronger than virtue? Force can meet with a greater opposing force, and everything gives way to necessity. Babylon has drawn you there, and Babylon holds you. The nature of the place is harsh, but it must be endured. Every good thing is lost there, and above all liberty; then order, rest, joy, hope, faith and charity. The losses to the soul are enormous. But in the kingdom of avarice nothing is counted as loss, so long as the money is safe. There the hope of a future life is an empty tale, and everything that is told about the underworld is fable: the resurrection of the flesh, the end of the world, and Christ's coming to judgement are all counted as nonsense. There truth is madness, abstinence is boorishness, and chastity a great disgrace. Finally, the licence to sin is greatness of spirit, and liberty of the highest kind. The more defiled a life is, the more distinguished it is; the more crimes, the more glory. A good name is cheaper than mud, and the last of all merchandise is reputation. You have now what I could set out in so few words of that sacred city, which you read every day not so much in this world as on the faces of those men, whose way of life no pen and no talent could equal. But, as I said, the first loss there is liberty. Whoever enters that threshold at once ceases to be his own master; he is not allowed to rest or to leave, but is spun round and worn down by labour that achieves nothing. Few, I think, does divine mercy snatch from that law, so that they love Jerusalem and hate Babylon. This is the one hope left to me; otherwise I would believe your affairs were finished, for I see you sunk and fixed so deeply and so tenaciously in that place. Meanwhile I blame not your will or your judgement but necessity and fortune for your staying there so long. I readily excuse the delays, which I hate intensely. If there was some fault in setting out, the delay itself is now no longer a fault but a punishment and a purging of the fault. But since many have often learned much in prison, why should anything stop you from learning something in your chains, something that will make you wiser for ever? Some learn best not by direct means but by their opposite. For this reason those who teach the mathematical arts, when a pupil's mind seems hardly capable of the truth, are accustomed to propose falsehoods, so that the mind, shrinking from these, may take refuge in what is truer. You too have always been accustomed to devote yourself to both religion and honour. The one lifts the longing soul to the sight of him of whom the Psalmist says: "Seek his face always." The other has a face which, if it were seen with the eyes, as Plato says, would inflame the soul with wonderful loves; yet it is no less to be loved for being seen only by the mind. If you think something is still lacking to you for the full knowledge of both, turn all your zeal to the opposite. Prick up your ears, fix your eyes, bend your mind. Would you know the beauty of God? Behold how great is the foulness of his enemies.

units.la: Non sunt autem longe quærendi, Babylone habitant, omnis vicus his vermibus scatet. Vis formam ac decus honestatis agnoscere? contemplare quanta est fœditas vitiorum, quorum omnium exemplar in oculis est tibi. Quocunque respexeris, videbis cuius odio simul Dei & virtutis amantior fieri queas. Tu autem gaude, contrario saltem magistra virtutum: gaude (inquam) & ad aliquid vtilis, inuenta gloriare, bonorum hostis & malorum hospes, atque asylum pessima rerum Babylon, feris Rhodani ripis imposita famosa dicam an infamis meretrix fornicata cum regibus terræ. Illa equidem ipsa es, quam in spiritu sacer vidit Euangelista. Illa eadem, inquam, es non alia, sedens super aquas multas, siue ad littora tribus cincta fluminibus, siue rerum atque diuitiarum turba mortalium, quibus lasciuiens, ac securâ insidens, opum immemor æternarum, siue vt idem qui vidit expositum, populi & gentes, & lingua, aquæ sunt super quas meretrix sedet. Recognosce habitum: Mulier circumdata purpura, & coccino, & inaurata auro, & lapide pretioso, & margaritis, habens poculum aureum in manu sua, plenum abominatione, & immunditia fornicationis eius. Noscisne teipsam Babylon? Nisi illud forsan errorem facit, quod in illius fronte scriptum erat, Babylon magna, tu vero Babylon parua es. Parua vtiq; murorum ambitu, sed vitiis & ambitu animorum, & infinita cupidine, cumuloq; malorum omnium, non magna modo, sed maxima, sed immensa es. Et certe quod sequitur, tibi vni conuenit, non alii, Babylon mater fornicationum, & abominationum terræ. Mater impia, partuum pessimorum quando quod vsquam terrarum abominabile, quicquid fornicatorium ex te prodit, & cum semper parias, semp tumens, & talium plenus ac grauidus uterus tuus est. Si nunc quoq; dissimulas, audi reliqua. Et vidi (inquit) mulierem ebriam ostende, aut omnino si potes, te hanc ebriam nega. Vera enim Euangelistæ & Apostoli visio sit oportet, qui si te in Spiritu videns miratus est, admiratione magna, quanta nos admiratione perfundemur, mur, qui aperte oculis te videmus? Ex omnibus quidem fornicationibus tuis, de quibus liberunt omnes gentes, & reges terræ, & ex omnibus abominationibus quid expectes, nisi quod sequitur ide ait: Cecidit, cecidit Babylon magna, & facta est habitatio Dæmoniorum. Nota sunt quæ sequuntur. Vere iam talis facta es, quanto enim homo perditus, & desperatæ nequitiæ demone melior? Vere habitatio: imo regnum dæmonum facta es, quæ suis artibus humana licet effigie, in terrenam. Tacero
units.tr: Nor do we need to look far, for they live in Babylon; every street swarms with these worms. Would you recognise the form and beauty of honour? Consider how great is the ugliness of vices, whose whole pattern is before your eyes. Wherever you look, you will see what you can hate, and by hating it become more devoted both to God and to virtue. But you, rejoice, at least, as a teacher of virtues by contraries. Rejoice, I say, and boast that you have found something useful: you, enemy of the good and host of the wicked, and refuge of the worst of things, Babylon, placed on the wild banks of the Rhône. Shall I call you a notorious or an infamous harlot who has committed fornication with the kings of the earth? Indeed you are the very one whom the holy evangelist saw in the Spirit: the same, I say, and no other, sitting upon many waters, whether on the shores girded by three rivers, or the multitude of mortals of worldly things and riches, among whom she wantons and sits secure, forgetful of eternal riches; or, as the same seer explained it, "the peoples and nations and tongues are the waters upon which the harlot sits." Recognise her dress: "The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and decked with gold and precious stone and pearls, having a golden cup in her hand, full of abominations and the filthiness of her fornication." Do you not know yourself, Babylon? Unless perhaps the error lies in what was written on her forehead: "Babylon the great." But you, Babylon, are small. Small indeed in the circuit of your walls, but in your vices and in the circuit of minds, in your endless greed and heap of every evil, you are not only great but very great, and immense. And surely what follows applies to you alone and to no other: "Babylon, the mother of fornications and abominations of the earth." Impious mother of the worst offspring! Whatever abominable thing there is anywhere on earth, whatever harlotry comes forth from you; your womb is always bearing, always swelling, always full and heavy with such things. If you still dissemble, hear the rest. "And I saw a woman drunk," he says. Show us that she is not drunk, or else, if you can at all, deny that you are that drunken woman. For the vision of the evangelist and apostle must be true; if he, seeing you in the Spirit, was astonished, with what great astonishment shall we be overwhelmed, we who see you plainly with our eyes? Of all your fornications, with which all nations and the kings of the earth have been defiled, and of all your abominations, what else should you expect but what follows: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, and has become the habitation of demons." What follows is well known. Truly you have become such a thing, for what man, lost and in despair of wickedness, is better than a demon? Truly you have become a habitation, nay, a kingdom of demons, who by your arts, though with human appearance, are earthly.

units.la: Amice, cum eodem Apostolo, audi vocem aliam de cœlo dicentem: Exite de illa populus meus, & ne participes sitis delictorum eius, & de plagis eius non accipiatis, quoniam pervenerunt peccata eius usque ad cœlum, & recordatus est Dominus iniquitatum eius, quantum glorificavit se, & in deliciis fuit, tantum date illi tormentum, & luctum: quia in corde suo dicit: Sedeo regina, vidua non sum, & luctum non videbo, ideo in una die, venient plagæ eius, mors, & luctus, & fames, & igni comburetur, quia fortis est Deus, qui iudicabit illam. Hæc & quæ Apostolicus ille locus habet, audi omnia, audi & fuge, si qua via est, nec innocentiam tuam ruinæ nocentium, & Babyloniæ premant iniquitates, quarum non modus, non numerus, non mensura, non existimatio demum est. Taceo hæreditatem Simonis, & illam hæresis speciem non ultimam, Spiritus sancti dona mercantium. Taceo mali illius auaritiam matrem, quæ idolorum servitus, ab Apostolo dicta est. Taceo utriusque pestis artifices, & concursantes pontificum thalamis prostituere. Taceo crudelitatem humanitatis immemorem, & sui ipsius oblitam insolentiam, atque illos vanissimos tribus tensos vires. Taceo denique illa prodigia, quæ insensibilis, vereque orbus terrarum orbis, tandiu quasi Ætnam Enceladus, aut Typheus Inarime pati potest, quorum omnium mors sicut, & severa narratio est. Ad ridicula simul atque odiosa festino. Quis enim, oro, non irascatur & rideat illos senes pueros, coma candida, togis amplissimis adeoque lasciviis animis, ut nihil illud videatur, quam quod ait Maro:
units.tr: Friend, hear with the same Apostle another voice from heaven saying: "Come out of her, my people, lest you be partakers in her sins, and lest you receive of her plagues; for her sins have reached unto heaven, and the Lord has remembered her iniquities. As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much torment and mourning give her; for she says in her heart, 'I sit a queen, I am no widow, and I shall see no mourning.' Therefore in one day shall her plagues come: death, and mourning, and famine; and she shall be burned with fire, for strong is the Lord God who shall judge her." These things, and all that the apostolic passage contains, hear them all; hear them and flee, if there is any way, lest the ruin of the guilty and the iniquities of Babylon, whose measure, number, extent and, finally, whose estimate there is none, crush your innocence. I say nothing of the inheritance of Simon, and of that not least form of heresy, the traffic in the gifts of the Holy Spirit. I say nothing of that evil mother, avarice, which the Apostle calls "the slavery of idols." I say nothing of the artificers of both plagues, who run about and prostitute themselves in the bedchambers of the pontiffs. I say nothing of the cruelty that forgets humanity, and of the insolence that has forgotten itself, and of those most vain men stretching their strength over the tribes. Finally, I say nothing of those monstrous things which the insensible and truly orphaned world can bear for so long, as Enceladus bears Etna or Typhoeus bears Inarime; all of them are as dreadful as they are grave to narrate. I hasten to things at once ridiculous and hateful. For who, I ask, would not be angry and laugh at those old men who are boys, with white hair, in the most ample togas, and with minds so wanton that it seems nothing other than what Maro says:

units.la: Frigidus in venerem senior?
units.tr: Is an old man cold toward love?

units.la: tam calidi, tamque præcipites in venerem senes sunt, tanta eos ætatis & status, & virium cœpit oblivio, sic in libidines inardescunt, sic in omne ruunt dedecus, quasi omnis eorum gloria, non in cruce Christi sit, sed in commessationibus, & ebrietatibus, & quæ has sequuntur in cubilibus, impudicitiis: sic fugientem manu retrahunt iuventam, atque hoc unum senectutis ultimæ lucrum putant, ea facere, quæ iuvenes non auderent. Hos animos, & hos nervos triuit, hinc Bacchus indomitus, hinc orientalium vis Bactharum. O Ligustici & Campani palmites, o dulces arundines, & Indicæ nigrantes arbustulæ, ad honestas delitias, & vilitates hominum creatæ, in quos visus, & quantam animarum perniciem, clademque vertimini? Spectat hæc Satan ridens, atque in paritripudio delectatus, interque decrepitos ac puellas arbiter sedens, stupet plus illos agere, quam se hortari, ac ne quis rebus torpor obrepat, ipse interim, & senilès lumbos stimulis incitat, & cæcum peregrinis solibus ignem ciet, unde fœda passim oriuntur incendia, mitto stupra, raptus, incestus, adulteria, qui iam pontificalis lasciviæ ludi sunt. Mitto raptarum viros, ne mutire audeant, non tantum auitis latribus, sed finibus patriis exturbatos, quæque contumeliarum grauissima est, & violatas coniuges, & externo semine grauidas rursus accipere, & post partum reddere, ad alternam satietatem abutentium coactos. Quæ omnia non unus ego, sed vulgus novit, etsi taceat, quamuis ne idipsum taceat, iam maior est indignatio, quam metus, & minacem libidinem vicit dolor. Hæc, inquam, uniuersa prætereo: Malo quidem hodie, ad risum quam ad iracundiam provocare, ita enim quæ vlcisci nequit, in se flectitur, & in Dominum suum sævit. Fuit ergo senicculus quidam, ex eo numero unus, cunctis annalibus implendis idoneus, hircina libido homini inerat, vel si quid libidinosius, atque olentius hirco est, hic seu mures metuens, seu lemures, dormire solus non audebat, nil apud eum tristius, nil miserius cœlibatu, novas cotidie nuptias celebrabat, & creber vagis amplexibus sponsus erat, cum & os illi vacuum, & ætas plena esset, septuagesimum pridem annum excesserat, septimo vix iam dente superstite. Erat illi pullarum auceps unus ex multis, Domini sui libidine nihilo segnior, eius retia & laquei, omnes vicos, omnium, & præsertim pauperum domos obsederant, huc pecunias, huc redimicula, huc anulos, huc postremo blanditias, huc cœnæ reliquias, huc omne genus escarum, & quæcunque flexura muliebres animos, conuchebat, ipse interim suspensus animo canebat. Nam & revera cantor erat, sed qui vocem ab altaribus ad choreas, & lupanaria transtulisset. Noram hominem vulgi digito monstrarum, qui his artibus, multas prædas, in os lupi senis, inferre solitus diceretur. Mille locus hic ridiculosas historias capit, unum accipe. Multis ille polliticis, misellam virgunculam, an meretriculam illexerat, ut Domino eius, utique & excelsi gradus, & magnarum opum, sed nec formæ, nec ætatis amabilis, obsequi in animum induceret. Quid multis agam? Acquiescit, & velut Psyche illa Lucii Apulei, felicibus nuptiis honestanda, ignoti viri thalamum subit. Recomperta, impatiens moræ, senex aduolat, & vlnis arreptam, pendulis labiis exosculans, atque inermi ore commorsitans, consummare novas nuptias anhelabat: repentino malo percita, & olente senio, & vultu lucido deterrita, exclamat, ad magnum se quendam, & insignem prælatum, non ad deformem, & decrepitum sacerdotem adeniisse, non posse sibi fraudem fieri. Vis si fiat, manibus quoad possit, deinde gemitibus atque vlulatibus occursuram, neque dum reliquiæ spiritus vllæ essent, passuram se à tam turpi sene violari. Hæc vociferans vbertim flebat: ille autem, & manu scabra, & ore hispido, spumantique tenerum os præcludens, fletibus & querimoniis conabatur obstare atque incondito murmure, & ineptissimis blanditiis (erat enim præter cætera blæsus adeo, ut à nemine posset intelligi) ægram animi solari. Sed cum nihil proficeret senex egregius, in secretarium se proripit, arreptoque, quo conscripti patres, à reliquis discernuntur, rubenti pileo, & insigne suum, albo caluoque vertici imponens, Cardinalis sum, inquit, Cardinalis sum, ne timeas filia. Sic amasiolam adhuc flentem, & praesenti specie, & futura spe magnifice consolatus, in geniale cubiculum deduxit, pronuba non Iunone, sed Ctesiphone, ac Megaera. Adhunc modum Cupidinis veteranus, Baccho lacer, & Veneri, non armatus, sed togatus, & pileatus de suis amoribus triumphavit. Plaude: fabula acta est. Nosses hominem, iucundissime sonniffes. Et huius & reliquorum mille sunt talia, quorum quaedam non ludicra, sed pudenda, alia vero inania, & horrenda sunt. I nunc, mirare, ducibus his, & propitium populo suo Christum, & Rempub. prosperari.
units.tr: Such old men are so hot and so headlong toward lust. They forget entirely their age, their station and their strength. They blaze up with lusts and rush into every kind of disgrace, as if all their glory lay not in the cross of Christ but in drinking parties, and drunkenness, and the wantonness that follows them in bedchambers. So they pull back youth that is slipping away from their grasp, and they count it the one remaining gain of extreme old age to do things that young men would not dare. These are the spirits and sinews they wear down. From here comes unbridled Bacchus, from here the strength of the Bactrian Orientals. O Ligurian and Campanian vines, O sweet reeds, and black little Indian shrubs, created for honest pleasures and for human vileness: into what sights, what great destruction of souls, and what ruin are you turned? Satan watches this laughing and delighted in the triple dance, and sitting as judge among the decrepit men and the girls, he marvels that they do more than he could urge them to do. Lest any sluggishness creep over their affairs, he himself meanwhile spurs on their senile loins and kindles a blind fire with foreign suns, from which foul conflagrations arise everywhere. I say nothing of debaucheries, abductions, incest and adulteries, which are now the games of papal lewdness. I say nothing of the husbands of the abducted women, who dare not utter a murmur, driven out not only from their ancestral hearths but from their native lands. And I say nothing of the most grievous insult of all: wives who have been violated, pregnant by a foreign seed, taken back again and returned after childbirth, forced to submit to the alternating satiety of their abusers. All these things are known not to me alone but to the common people, even if they keep silent. Yet even if they do not keep silent on this very point, indignation is now greater than fear, and grief has overcome a threatening lust. These things, I say, I pass over altogether. Today I would rather provoke laughter than anger, for anger that cannot take vengeance turns back upon itself and rages against its own master. There was therefore a certain little old man, one of that number, fit to fill all the annals alone. He had a goatish lust, or if anything is more lustful and more smelly than a goat. Fearing mice or ghosts, he dared not sleep alone; nothing seemed to him more dreadful, nothing more wretched, than celibacy. Every day he celebrated new marriages and was a frequent bridegroom in promiscuous embraces, although his mouth was toothless and his age was full, for he had long passed his seventieth year, with only one tooth left. There was for him a certain fowler of young women, one of many, no less eager in his master's lust. His nets and snares besieged every street and every house, especially those of the poor. Here he gathered money, here hair ribbons, here rings, here finally flattery, here the leftovers of dinners, here every kind of bait that might bend women's minds, while he himself, suspended in mind, sang. For he was indeed a singer, but one who had carried his voice from the altars to the dances and the brothels. I knew the man, pointed at by the finger of the common people, who was said to be accustomed by these arts to bring many prey into the mouth of the old wolf. This place could hold a thousand ridiculous stories; take one. He had enticed, with many flatteries, a poor little maiden, or rather a little harlot, so that she would bring herself to submit to his master, who had high rank and great wealth, but was neither handsome nor lovable in face or age. What more shall I say? She consents, and like that Psyche of Lucius Apuleius, to be honoured with a happy marriage, she goes into the bedchamber of an unknown man. The old man, discovered and impatient of delay, flies up, seizes her in his arms, kisses her with hanging lips, and biting at her with a toothless mouth, he panted to consummate the new marriage. She, startled by the sudden evil, and repelled by the stinking old age and the shining face, cries out that she had come to some great and distinguished prelate, not to a deformed and decrepit priest, and that no deceit could be practised on her. If force were applied, she would resist with her hands as far as she could, and then with groans and howls, and as long as any remnant of breath was left, she would not suffer herself to be violated by so shameful an old man. Shouting these things, she wept copiously. But he, with a scabby hand and a bristly mouth, foaming, sought to block her tender mouth, and with tears and complaints he tried to resist and to soothe the sick woman's mind with a jumbled murmur and most inept flatteries (for besides his other faults he was so lisping that no one could understand him). But when the outstanding old man achieved nothing, he rushed into the robing room, seized the red hat by which the conscript fathers are distinguished from the rest, and placing his badge on his white and bald crown, said: "I am a Cardinal, I am a Cardinal; do not fear, daughter." Thus he magnificently consoled his little love, still weeping, with the present appearance and the future hope, and led her into the nuptial chamber, with Juno not as bridesmaid, but Ctesiphon and Megaera. In this manner the veteran of Cupid, mangled by Bacchus, and not armed but robed and hatted, triumphed over his loves. Applaud: the play is over. You would have known the man, most pleasant sniffer. Of this man and the others there are a thousand such stories, some of which are not laughable but shameful, and others empty and horrible. Go now, and wonder that with such leaders Christ is favourable to his people and the commonwealth prospers.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Egresso de Babylone Romana gratulatur, & ut in posterum ab ea caveat, hortatur. Item de Pontifice Romano in ordinem per Imperatorem redigendo.
units.tr: He congratulates a man who has escaped from Babylon of Rome, and urges him to beware of it in future. Also concerning the Roman Pontiff, who is to be brought back into order by the Emperor.

units.la: FRANC. PETRARCHA Amico S. Euasisti, erupisti, enatasti, evolasti, bene est: timebam, sateor tibi, timebam animae tuae, ne post descensum ad inferos, non cum vellet emergere sciebas, & iterni descensum facilem, & apertum Labyrinthi limen laboriosum, atque operosum exitum. Dicebam mecum, O si meus Alcides, o si Theseus meus ab inferis redeat? O ne mali pondus illum opprimat, neque pedes ad virtutem, volucres, adamantinae scelerum catenae vinciant, detineatque. Inter haec vota, hosque inter metus emersisti, Deo gratias, qui ex inferno in se sperantes animas educit, exoptatus, evocatus, expectatus adveniis. His igitur primum terris redditus, quae te illi Herebo crediderant, non Phoebo, ut Daedalus, sed Christo alarum remigium consecrabis, & caveb is, ne unquam amplius Gnosum speces. Non est saepius retentanda fortuna, periculum sine periculo non fit, id cum semel evaseris, declina, ne quando corruas unde non surgas, nulla unquam te mala cupiditas tangat, ut illos principes tenebrarum rursus adeas. Quos cum suis opibus, suisque flagitiis dii, deaeque omnes, imo vero deorum Deus, vivos ac mortuos male perdat, quae caelestis agni sanguine laginati, calcitrant ac rebellant, eo me mirum, meus ille nunc evocat, quo te praesente, persuaderi mihi non potuit ut venirem, ille mihi hortator est fidus quidem, sed improvidus, ut Babylone viuere eligam ac mori. Cur autem siue ad quid, ut videam bonos mergi, malos erigi, reptare aquilas, volare asinos, vulpes in curribus, coruos in turribus, columbas insterquilinio, liberos lupos, agnos in vinculis, Christum denique exulem, Antichristum Dominum, Beelzebub iudicem. Haec ad spectacula revocor, non audiam, male mihi cum illis, male illis mecum convenit. O crudelis & impia secta hominum, nil nisi seipsos amantium, idque ipsum peruerse prorsus ac nephariē. Quis releuabit oppressum orbem? Quis vindicabit afflictam urbem? Quis euersos mores reformabit? Quis colliget sparsas oues? Quis pastores erroneos arguet? Quis reducet aut retrahet in sedem suam? nullus ne licentiae ac scelerum modus erit, an frustra per Propheram Spiritus sanctus intonuit? Haec fecisti & tacui, existimasti iniquē, quod ero tui similis. Arguam te & statuam contra faciem tuam. Intelligite qui obliviscimini Deum ne quando rapiat, & non sit qui eripiat. Intelligite (inquam) nobis loquitur, Dei hostes intelligite. Surdis loquitur, sopitique nunquam intelligent, nisi horrendo tonitru, seu quoniam tonuisse non sufficit, trisulco fulmine experrecti. Ad te mihi nunc sermo est, Inuictissime Regum nostri temporis, quem non nomino, quando & nomen obstat inscriptioni, & abunde te nominat ipsa rerum ac gloriae magnitudo, nam quid opus est verbis, ubi res loquitur. Haud immerito tantis te victoriis ornatum credere phas est, qui praeter principalis tuae causae iustitiam, vulpes illas veternosas, foedis, & non suis e caveis, Christique sponsam coeno, ac vinculis eruere potens es. Et facies spero iure, tibi perpetuam foelicitatem, & votivum coepti exitum quisque fidelium optaverit. Pastorem illum, & senio, & sopore, & mero gravidum, nunquam sponte latebris, & amatis fornicibus egressurum, solus manu prehensum, & verbis increpitum, ac verberibus castigatum, in antiquum penetrale restitues. Id si forte tibi caelitus non datur, quanquam nec dignatus pluribus, neque hoc munere dignior quisquam sit, venient alii, quorum quo foedior manus, eo pulchrior vindicta. Denique qualia multa undique crebrescunt, vel praedonum iusta acie, vel salubri peste, clementique caeli inclementia, ad postremum plaga aliqua evidenti, quoniam minis ad prodigiis cor Pharaonis obduratum, superbumque non tangitur, sponte Christus superveniet laboranti. O quid scripsi? O quid mihi venit in animum, quo prodiit lingua? quo progressus est calamus? possem cum Iob & ego fortassis dicere: Unum locutus sum quod utinam non dixissem, dixi tamen, & iam non dixisse non possum, delere autem etsi adhuc liceat, non libet, tantus est veri amor, tantumque mali odium, ut periculi omnis interim obliviscar: In uno consilium senis illius sequar, quia cum infinita se nunc offerant, & perexigua dicendorum pars exacta sit, frenabo impetum & si cum eodem Iob, manum meam ponam super os meum, & his ultra non addam.
units.tr: FRANCIS PETRARCH to his friend. You have escaped, broken out, swum out, flown out: good, it is well. I confess to you, I was afraid for your soul, lest after going down to the underworld, when you did not want to, you would not know how to come up again. The descent into hell is easy and its gate is open, but the way out of the labyrinth is hard and laborious. I said to myself: O, if only my Hercules, if only my Theseus, were to return from the dead! O, may the weight of evil not crush him, nor the adamantine chains of sin bind and hold back his feet from virtue and his wings. In the midst of these prayers and these fears you have emerged. Thanks be to God, who leads out of hell the souls that hope in him; longed for, called, awaited, you have arrived. Now restored to this earth, which Erebus had entrusted to you and not Phoebus, you will not, like Daedalus, consecrate the oarage of your wings to Apollo, but to Christ, and you will take care never again to look upon Gnossus. Fortune must not be tested too often; danger is not met without danger. Now that you have escaped once, turn aside, lest you fall somewhere you cannot rise again. Let no evil desire ever touch you, so that you go back to those princes of darkness. Let all the gods and goddesses, or rather the God of gods, destroy them, living and dead, with their wealth and their vices, those who, washed in the blood of the heavenly Lamb, kick and rebel. Yet that same man who now calls me, to whom I could not be persuaded to come while you were present, is a faithful but short-sighted counsellor, urging me to choose to live and die in Babylon. Why, and to what end? So that I may see the good drowned and the wicked raised up, eagles creeping, asses flying, foxes in chariots, ravens in towers, doves in a dunghill, wolves free, lambs in chains, and finally Christ an exile, Antichrist lord, and Beelzebub judge. I am being called back to these spectacles; I will not listen. Ill does he agree with me, and ill do I agree with him. O cruel and impious sect of men, loving nothing but themselves, and that too in a utterly perverse and abominable way! Who will relieve the oppressed world? Who will avenge the afflicted city? Who will reform the corrupted morals? Who will gather the scattered sheep? Who will reprove the wandering shepherds? Who will lead them back or draw them back to their seat? Will there be no limit to licence and crime? Or has the Holy Spirit thundered through the prophet in vain? You have done these things and I have been silent; you have unjustly supposed that I would be like you. I will reprove you and set them before your face. Understand this, you who forget God, lest he tear you away and there be no one to deliver you. Understand, I say: he speaks to us, understand, enemies of God. He speaks to the deaf, and the drowsy will never understand unless they are roused by a terrible thunderclap, or, since thunder is not enough, by a three-forked lightning bolt. Now my words are addressed to you, most unconquered of the kings of our time, whom I do not name, since the name would be an obstacle to the inscription, and the very greatness of your deeds and glory names you abundantly. For what need is there of words where the deeds speak? It is right to believe that you, adorned with such victories, are rightly one who, besides the justice of your principal cause, are able to snatch those old and foul foxes from their own cages, and the Spouse of Christ from mire and chains. I hope that by right you will have everlasting happiness, and that every faithful person will wish for a successful end to what you have begun. That shepherd, heavy with old age, sleep and wine, who will never of his own accord come out of his hiding places and beloved vaults, you will alone take by the hand, rebuke with words, chastise with blows, and restore to his ancient sanctuary. If perhaps this is not granted you from heaven, though he is not worthy of more, and no one is more worthy of this task, others will come, and the fouler their hand, the more beautiful the vengeance. In short, many such things are everywhere increasing, either by the just battle line of robbers, or by a healthful plague, or by the harshness of a gentle sky, and finally by some evident blow; since the heart of Pharaoh, hardened and proud, is not moved by threats or prodigies, Christ will come of his own accord to the one who labours. O what have I written? What has come into my mind? Where has my tongue run? Whither has my pen advanced? Perhaps I, like Job, could say: I have spoken once, which I wish I had not said; yet I have said it, and now I cannot unsay it. Yet, though it is still allowed to erase it, I do not wish to, so great is my love of truth and so great my hatred of evil, that for the moment I forget all danger. In one thing I will follow the counsel of that old man: since infinite matters now present themselves and only a very small part of what must be said has been finished, I will restrain my impetus, and, with the same Job, I will lay my hand upon my mouth, and will add nothing more to these things.

units.la: MAGISTRI IORDA- NI, MONACHI AVGVSTI- NIANI ARGENTINENSIS CHRONICA: QVALITER ROMANVM IMPERIVM TRANSLATVM FVIT IN GER- MANOS.
units.tr: THE CHRONICLE OF MASTER JORDANUS, AUGUSTINIAN MONK OF STRASBOURG: HOW THE ROMAN EMPIRE WAS TRANSFERRED TO THE GERMANS.

units.la: Anno Domini 1400.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1400.

units.la: Et primo, quare Romanum Imperium sit honorandum.
units.tr: First, why the Roman Empire is to be honoured.

units.la: {a}MULTIFARIE multisque modis Dominus vniuersorum, in diebus suae carnis, dignatus est honorare Romanum imperium, dando in semetipso exemplum Dominus & magister, Romanum imperium fore ab omnibus honorandum. Honorauit quidem Dominus Caesarem siue Romanum regem, mundum ingredientem, in mundo progredientem, & mundum egredientem: verbi gratia, mundum istum secundum carnem. Et ingrediens in duobus honorauit Romanum imperium. Primo in hoc, quod tempus sui aduentus per ipsum Caesarem totum orbum pacauit, vt per ipsius Domini praesentiam pax esset in vniuersa terra, ad significandum quod ipse esset pax nostra, & per eum, vt dicit Apostolus ad Colossenses: reconcilianda erant omnia quae sunt in coelo & in terra. Vnde Psalmista, posuit prodigia & iudicia futura reconciliationu super terram, auferens bella usque ad fines terrae, & alibi. Secundo, ingressu suo approbauit & honorauit Romanum imperium: mox vt natus est, censui Caesaris se subdendo. Vnde Augustinus in gloss. super Euangelium Lucae sic dicit: Humilitas Christi commendatur, quia non solum incarnari voluit, sed etiam nasci illo tempore, in quo natus & mox censui subderetur. Natus est enim in diebus professionis: quando singuli ibant in suas ciuitates unde oriundi erant, ut profiterentur tribum suam, censum & regem. Sic ergo Dominus mundum ingrediens dupliciter honorauit Romanum imperium, siue Caesarem, & vniuersum mundum ministerio pacando, & censui Caesaris se subiiciendo.
units.tr: In many ways and by many means the Lord of all things, in the days of his flesh, deigned to honour the Roman Empire, giving in himself an example, as Lord and Master, that the Roman Empire is to be honoured by all. The Lord honoured Caesar, or the Roman king, in entering the world, in progressing through the world, and in leaving the world, that is, this world according to the flesh. In entering, he honoured the Roman Empire in two ways. First, in that at the time of his coming he brought the whole world to peace through Caesar, so that by the presence of the Lord himself there might be peace throughout the whole earth, signifying that he himself is our peace, and that through him, as the Apostle says to the Colossians, all things which are in heaven and in earth were to be reconciled. Hence the Psalmist: He has set forth wonders and judgments of future reconciliations upon the earth, taking away wars to the ends of the earth, and elsewhere. Second, by his entrance he approved and honoured the Roman Empire, by submitting himself to Caesar's census as soon as he was born. Hence Augustine in his gloss on the Gospel of Luke says: The humility of Christ is commended, because he wished not only to be made flesh but also to be born at that time, in which he was born and immediately made subject to the census. For he was born in the days of the registration, when each went to the cities from which they were sprung, to declare their tribe, census and king. So the Lord, entering the world, honoured the Roman Empire, or Caesar, in two ways: by bringing peace to the whole world through his ministry, and by subjecting himself to Caesar's census.

units.la: Item, Dominus in diebus suae carnis progrediens in hoc mundo, Romanum imperium dupliciter honorauit. Primo, quia non solum dedit ei tributum, sed etiam praecepit pro se dari & beato Petro, vt legitur Marci 12. cap. Secundo, quia non solum tributum ei dedit, sed etiam praecepit ei dari, Matth. 22. cap. Reddite Caesari quae sunt Caesaris, &c. Augustinus super hoc dicit, Censum & tributum.
units.tr: Likewise the Lord, progressing in this world in the days of his flesh, honoured the Roman Empire in two ways. First, because he not only gave it tribute but also commanded that it be paid for himself and for the blessed Peter, as is read in Mark chapter 12. Second, because he not only gave it tribute but also commanded that it be given to it, Matthew 22: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, etc. Augustine on this says: census and tribute.

units.la: Item Dominus egrediens mundum, bis honorauit Caesarem siue Romanum imperium. Primum, dum dicentib. Apostolis, Ecce duo gladii hic, Dominus respondit, Satis est. Ecce duo gladii, qui duas potestates significant, hic in praesenti seculo satis sunt. Et quid est dicere, Satis est, nisi, sufficit & nihil deest? Protestatus ergo Dominus est sua ipsius voce, potestatem sacerdotalem & imperialem, quae tunc maxime vigebat, mundo sufficere: & ei quoad regnum, tam in spiritualibus quam in temporalibus hic deesse. Vnde Gelasius papa distin. 96. duo dicit: Duo sunt quibus hic mundus principaliter regitur, Pontificalis authoritas, & Regalis potestas. Hae sunt principales potestates, per quas Deus discernit & distribuit vitam humano generi, vt genus humanum per iuris regulas ad vitandum mala, & faciendum bona salubriter informetur. Secundo, Dominus morte instante honorauit Romanum imperium. Dum enim Pilatus iactaret se de potestate quam haberet in Christum, & diceret ei, Nescis, quia habeo potestatem crucifigere te, & dimittere te? vt dicit Ioannes, respondit: Non haberes vllam potestatem in me, nisi datum esset tibi desuper. Et secundum gloss. duobus modis exponitur: vno modo sic: Desuper, id est, a Deo, quia non est potestas nisi a Deo, vel desuper, id est, a Caesare, qui Pilatum praefecerat in praesidem. Vnde super his verbis, Si hunc dimittis, non es amicus Caesaris, dicit gloss. Iudaei terrent Pilatum in Caesare, quem non potest, vt authorem sua potestatis, contemnere. Deus enim fuit author potestatis Caesaris. Secundum hunc posteriorem intellectum, Deus in verbis istis multum commendat Romanum imperium. Ostendit enim, potestatem Caesaris aliis potestatibus mundanis praeeminere, & ipsas sub Caesaris contineri. Quid est enim potestatem desuper dari, nisi dari ab eo cuius supereminet potestas in alias potestates mundanas, tanquam inferiores, & minores sub se continet & concludit? Item non solum Dominus honorauit & honorat Romanum imperium in hoc, quod Romano imperio stante & durante, non veniet homo peccati, filius perditionis, vt legitur in epistola secunda ad Thessal. cap. 2. vbi dicit Apostolus: Qui tenet, teneat, donec de medio fiat, & tunc revelabitur ille iniquus, quem Dominus interficiet spiritu oris sui. Super verbis istis Apostoli, dicit Gloss. quod Apostolus in his verbis, Qui tenet, teneat, &c. Romanum imperium designat, quo destructo veniet Antichristus. Deinde Romanum Imperatorem, qui Romanum imperium sive mundum tenet, de Rege ad regem successive significare, donec de medio auferatur. De medio enim auferri, est de communi conspectu hominum auferri. Augustinus in secundo libro de civitate Dei, super his verbis Apostoli sic dicit: Illud quod dicit Apostolus, Tantum ut qui modo tenet, teneat donec de medio fiat: non absurde de Romano imperio creditur dictum, tanquam dictum sit: Qui modo imperat, donec de medio fiat, id est, de medio tollatur, & tunc revelabitur ille iniquus, quo significari Antichristum nemo ambigit. Magnus honor est Romano imperio, quod Dominus in hoc prae caeteris ipsum priuilegiare dignatus est, quod non veniet Antichristus, Christi & membrorum eius adversarius, nisi prius Romanum imperium penitus sit ablatum. Ablato autem Romano Imperio erit tribulatio tanta & talis, qualis & quanta, ut legitur in Matthaeo, non fuit ab initio mundi usque nunc. In diebus illis tantum abundabit iniquitas & infidelitas, ut in errorem ducantur, si fieri potest, & electi. Et huius tribulationis gravissimae & maximae tempora priora videntur tempora pacis fuisse. Unde Psalmista: Oritur in diebus eius iustitia & abundantia pacis, donec auferatur luna: id est, Romanum imperium, quod per lunam designatur. Unde Apostolus Timotheo scribit: Hoc autem scito, quod in diebus novissimis instabunt tempora periculosa: & ideo instabunt, quia prius non fuerunt ita periculosa.
units.tr: Likewise the Lord, leaving the world, honoured Caesar, or the Roman Empire, twice. The first time, when the Apostles said, Behold, here are two swords, the Lord answered, It is enough. Behold, two swords, which signify the two powers, are enough here in the present age. And what is it to say, It is enough, except that it suffices and nothing is lacking? The Lord therefore declared by his own voice that the priestly and imperial power, which was then especially flourishing, suffices for the world, and that for him, as far as his kingdom is concerned, both in spiritual and temporal things, nothing is lacking here. Hence Pope Gelasius, distinction 96, says: There are two things by which this world is principally governed: the pontifical authority and the royal power. These are the principal powers through which God distinguishes and distributes life to the human race, so that the human race may be wholesomely instructed by the rules of law to avoid evils and do good. Second, with his death at hand, the Lord honoured the Roman Empire.
