units.la: INsuper, vt ego vtar propositione singulari, cum verecundius audeo sic sentire, quod ad regnum vniuersalis Ecclesiae nil competentius expediat, quam vt sanctissimus pater Romanorum Pontifex, qui pro tempore fuerit, diligentiam adhibeat, vt Gallicum studium Parisiense suo tempore floreat & fructificet ad confutandum haereticorum versutias & errores, & vt Germanorum imperium in suo dilatetur robore ad supprimendas gentes & omnes barbaras nationes, & vt sacerdotium Romanorum in suo robore consistat & firmetur ad congregandos filios ecclesiae, ad amorem & obedientiam per gratias competentes, & iustitiam expeditam. Hic non est attendenda Clericorum studentium indiscreta dissolutio, cum adolescentiores & delicatiores de cunctis mundi partibus in vnum locum congregati, singuli secum mores suos ferant.
units.tr: Moreover, that I may make a single proposition, since I dare to think this with rather more modesty: nothing is more fitting for the rule of the universal Church than that the most holy father, the Roman Pontiff for the time being, should take care that the French study at Paris flourish and bear fruit in its time, for refuting the cunning and errors of heretics; that the empire of the Germans be extended in its strength for suppressing the peoples and all barbarous nations; and that the priesthood of Rome stand firm and be strengthened in its vigour, for gathering the sons of the Church to love and obedience through fitting graces and righteous judgment. Here the undisciplined dissolute behaviour of students is not to be considered, since the younger and more delicate men gathered into one place from every part of the world each bring their own manners with them.

units.la: Nec est attendenda Praesulum Germanorum secularis conuersatio, ipsi enim sacerdotium repraesentant Samuelis; qui licet esset Sacerdos, tamen Iudicis officium exercebat ipse, & Regem elegit in Israel, & electum consecrauit. Praesules Germaniae non sunt illius Vicarii, qui relicto sindone nudus aufugit, sicut Episcopi Italici: sed eius Vicarii, qui dixit: Domine, paratus sum tecum in vinculum et in mortem ire. ta & in morte tecum ire: & in tempore tribulationis eduxit gladium, & amputauit seruo Pontificis auriculam dextram; non amputauit ei pedem, sed auriculam, vt ostenderet quod ei caput libentissime amputasset. Ergo licet ipsi alii ad vocem ancillae Christum negent, tamen frequenter surgunt fortiores. Nihil enim inordinatum in operibus Creatoris. Et sicut tempus pacis & belli, sic & sunt homines ad pacem & bellum deputati. Confidentius loquor; si Romani Principes cum suis fidelibus Romano Imperatori, tanquam Aduocato Ecclesiae, fideliter assisterent, sicut in temporibus praeteritis consueuerunt, tunc absque dubio omnis potestas contraria esset parua: non solum Graecia, sed etiam Chaldaei contremiscerent cum Ægypto. Aues viso flore cantant & laetantur, sed ad aquilae intuitum silent & fugiunt: sic omnes barbarae nationes aliorum Regum insignia despiciunt, sed Germanorum & Romanorum aquilas timent naturaliter & abhorrent. Insuper non est aduertenda Romanorum ciuium, & sibi quasi innata discordia, licet ipsi propter amorem dominandi & habendi sint discordes: tamen per Dei gratiam in fide Catholica tenacissime sunt concordes. Fateor me in praecedentibus ab aliorum scriptis in quibusdam deuiasse: sed sicut ipsi in suis originalibus credunt veritatem vsurpasse; sic ego nullam puto admisisse falsitatem, petens tamen humiliter veniam de erratis.
units.tr: Nor is the worldly way of life of the German prelates to be taken into account, for they represent the priesthood of Samuel; who, although he was a priest, nevertheless himself exercised the office of judge, and chose a king in Israel and consecrated the one chosen. The prelates of Germany are not vicars of him who, having left his linen cloth behind, fled away naked, like the Italian bishops; they are vicars of him who said: "Lord, I am ready to go with thee into prison and into death" [Luke 22.33]. And in the time of tribulation he drew the sword and cut off the right ear of the servant of the Pontiff; he did not cut off his foot, but his ear, to show that he would most gladly have cut off his head. Therefore, although others deny Christ at the voice of a maidservant, nevertheless the stronger ones frequently rise up. For there is nothing disordered in the works of the Creator. And as there is a time for peace and a time for war, so men are appointed to peace and to war. I speak with more confidence: if the Roman princes, with their faithful followers, were to assist the Roman Emperor faithfully, as the Advocate of the Church, as they have been accustomed to do in past times, then without doubt every opposing power would be small: not only Greece, but even the Chaldeans would tremble with Egypt. Birds sing and rejoice when they see a flower, but at the sight of the eagle they fall silent and flee: so all barbarous nations despise the insignia of other kings, but they naturally fear and shrink from the eagles of the Germans and the Romans. Moreover, the discord of the Roman citizens, which is as it were innate to them, is not to be noticed; although they are discordant through love of domination and possession, nevertheless by the grace of God they are most firmly united in the Catholic faith. I confess that in what has gone before I have departed in some matters from the writings of others: but just as they believe that in their originals they have followed the truth, so I think I have admitted no falsehood, yet humbly beg pardon for my errors.

units.la: EXPLICIT CHRONICA MAGISTRI IORDANIS, ORDINIS Fratrum sancti Augustini de Heremo in Conuentu Argentinensi.
units.tr: HERE ENDS THE CHRONICLE OF MASTER JORDAN, OF THE ORDER OF THE FRIARS OF ST AUGUSTINE OF THE HERMITAGE, IN THE CONVENT AT STRASBOURG.

units.la: THEODORICI à NIEM EPISCOPI VERDENSIS ET CAMERACENSIS, PROTONOTARII S. Roman. Ecclesiae
units.tr: THEODORIC OF NIEM, BISHOP OF VERDEN AND OF CAMBRAI, PROTONOTARY OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

units.la: EXCERPTA EX LIB. III. DE SCHI- SMATE VNIVERSALI, DE POTESTATE PONTIFICIS ATQVE IMPERATORIS; & an Imperator in temporalibus subsit Pontifici. CAP. VII.
units.tr: EXCERPTS FROM BOOK III OF ON THE UNIVERSAL SCHISM, ON THE POWER OF THE POPE AND OF THE EMPEROR, AND WHETHER THE EMPEROR IS SUBJECT TO THE POPE IN TEMPORAL MATTERS. CHAPTER VII.

units.la: DEO rationabiliter fieri posset per Regem vel Imperatorem Romanum & illos Ecclesiasticos praelatos, nec non populum Christianum, prout ciuiliter intelligentibus est notum, & praecipue interest Imperatoris aut Regis Romani, quod Catholicus, vnicus & mundus Papa sedeat in sede Petri, cum Rex & Imperator sit filius spiritualis Ecclesiae, ac Rex Regum & Dominus Dominantium, cuius potestas a Deo est: &, vt dicit Apostolus, qui ei resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit, & sibi damnationem acquirit, quia in facinorosos aduertit: non enim sine causa gladium portat, Dei enim minister est. Quod autem imperium principaliter & immediate pendet a Deo, sicut Ecclesia seu ecclesiastica potestas, patet per rationes euidentes, & sic etiam firmatur & habetur in Decreto, vbi legitur, & scribit Papa Imperatori in hunc modum: Ecclesia mea, cui Deus noster sacerdotium meum vobis res humanas regentibus deputauit, &c. & hocidem in plerisque aliis locis patet in iure. Ex quo infertur, quod fatue & adulatorie loquuntur illi, qui dicunt, quod Papa seu Ecclesia duos habet gladios, scilicet spiritualem & temporalem, cum in Euangelio Petro sit dictum; Conuerte gladium tuum in vaginam: & ibidem addita ratione, videlicet, Omnis enim qui gladio ferit, &c. etenim si vterque gladius apud Papam existeret, superuacue vel ficte Imperator vel Rex Romanus illud nomen haberet.
units.tr: It could reasonably be brought about by God through the King or Emperor of the Romans and those ecclesiastical prelates, and also the Christian people, as is known to those who understand matters of this world. It is especially in the interest of the Emperor or the King of the Romans that the Catholic, sole and undefiled Pope sit in the seat of Peter, since the King and Emperor is a spiritual son of the Church, and the King of kings and Lord of lords, whose power is from God. As the Apostle says, whoever resists him resists the ordinance of God and brings condemnation upon himself, because he punishes wrongdoers: for he does not bear the sword in vain, since he is God's minister. That the empire depends principally and immediately on God, just as the Church or ecclesiastical power does, is clear from evident reasons. It is also confirmed and found in the Decretum, where it is read that the Pope wrote to the Emperor in this manner: "My Church, which our God has entrusted to me as priest, to you who govern human affairs..." and the same thing appears in many other places in the law. From this it follows that those speak foolishly and flatteringly who say that the Pope or the Church has two swords, namely a spiritual and a temporal one, since in the Gospel it is said to Peter: "Put your sword back into its sheath," and the reason is added there: "For all who take the sword will perish by the sword," and so on. For if both swords were in the Pope's hands, the Emperor or Roman King would have that name in vain or as a mere pretence.

units.la: Sed isti adulatores seu assentatores per talia scripta & dicta inducunt maximum errorem in tota Christianitate, & suscitant quodammodo perpetuam aemulationem seu discordiam inter Papam & Imperatorem.
units.tr: But these flatterers and sycophants, through such writings and speeches, lead the whole of Christendom into a very great error, and in a way stir up a perpetual rivalry or discord between the Pope and the Emperor.

units.la: Conculcatur enim per hoc Imperialis authoritas, & eius potestas sub dubio collocatur in totius reipublicae detrimentum, vt videmus. Patet etiam ex decreto, quod cum schisma viget in Romana sede, quod propter authoritatis excellentiam & in temporalibus potentiam Imperator, vel Rex Romanus praelatos Ecclesiasticos potest conuocare, vt illud omnino tollatur: quod credo intelligi debere de illis, qui re & nomine Imperatores vel Reges existunt Romani: non autem de illis, qui desides, seu solo nomine Imperatores aut Reges Romani sunt, sicut fuerunt Reges & Imperatores Romani, quos nostro tempore habuimus & habemus. Illi enim non merentur Imperatores vel Reges Romani nominari, qui sunt pusillanimes & effoeminati. Exempli gratia, de hoc in Decretis legimus in haec verba: Hinc est, cum authoritas Theodorici Regis ex diversis provinciis ad urbem Romanam sacerdotes venire praecepisset, ut sanctam Concilium iudicaret de his, quae venerabili Papa Symmacho praesuli Apostolicae sedis ab adversariis ipsius dicebantur impingi, Liguria & Etruria Episcopi seu Venetiarum suggesserunt ipsum, qui dicebatur impeditus, debere synodum convocare, scientes quia eius sedi primum Apostoli Petri meritum, deinde secuta iussione Domini Concilium venerandorum authoritas singularem in Ecclesiis potestatem tradidit, nec antedicta sedi Antistitem minorum subiacuisse iudicio. Ad hanc serenissimum Rex inspirante Deo respondit, synodalis esse arbitrium in tanto negocio sequenda perscribere, nec aliquid ad se praeter reverentiam de Ecclesiastico negocio pertinere, committens etiam potestati Pontificum, ut sive propositum vellent audire negotium, sive nollent, quod magis putarent utile deliberare, dum modo pro venerandi providione Concilii pax in civitate Romana daretur. Episcopi vero in synodo residentes congregata authoritate eiusdem dixerunt, Symmachus Papa Apostolicae sedis praesul ab huiusmodi oppositionibus impetitus, quantum ad homines respicit, sit immunis & liber, cuius causam totam Dei iudicio reservavimus. De clericis vero memorati Papa, qui ab Episcopo suo ante tempus contra regulas discesserunt, & schisma fecerunt, hoc fieri decrevimus, ut hi satisfacientes Episcopo suo misericordiam consequantur, & beneficiis ecclesiasticis fegaudeant restituti. Laurentius Episcopus Mediolanensis ecclesiae huic statuto nostro, in quo totam causam Dei iudicio commisimus, subscripsit, Petrus Episcopus Ravennatius sub eisdem verbis subscripsit, & post eum LXXV. &c. Cum autem ita sit, miserandum est, quare dominus Rupertus modernus Rex Romanus tam frequenter dictum Errorium (Gregorium) in eius manifesta pertinacia, schismate ac haeresi contra eiusdem Errorii promissa, vota & iuramenta sponte praestita & totiens repetita fovet & defendat, quod utique tendit in maiorem scissuram Ecclesiae. Et quid ad ipsum Regem aliud spectasset in hac parte, nisi quod iuxta formam dicti Canonis immediate praecedentis ad instar dicti Regis Theodorici praefatis Errorio & Petro de Papatu contendentibus seueriter scripsisset atque mandasset, quod unionem facerent in Ecclesia, ad hoc quod pax fieret, nedum in urbe, sed in tota Christianitate, maxime cum ad illud etiam irrequisito dicto Rege Ruperto sponte & libere obligassent, iurassent & vouissent, illudque sibi solenniter intimassent, nec non, ut ad hoc suffragaretur, eundem pariter requisissent.
units.tr: For by this the imperial authority is trampled underfoot and its power is put in doubt, to the great harm of the whole commonwealth, as we see. It is also clear from the decree that when a schism is raging in the Roman see, the Emperor or Roman King, because of the excellence of his authority and his power in temporal matters, can summon the ecclesiastical prelates so that the schism may be entirely removed. I believe this must be understood of those who are truly and in name Emperors or Kings of the Romans, and not of those who are idle, or who are Emperors or Kings of the Romans in name only, as were the Kings and Emperors of Rome whom we have had in our own time. For those who are fainthearted and effeminate do not deserve to be called Emperors or Kings of the Romans. For example, we read about this in the Decretals in these words: Hence it was that, when the authority of King Theodoric had ordered bishops to come from various provinces to the city of Rome, so that the holy council might judge the matters which were being charged against the venerable Pope Symmachus, the bishop of the Apostolic See, by his adversaries, the bishops of Liguria and Etruria, and of Venice, suggested that he who was said to be hindered should convene the synod, knowing that to his see belongs first the merit of the Apostle Peter, and then, by the order of the Lord which followed, the authority of the venerable council has given him singular power in the Churches, and that the occupant of the aforesaid see was not subject to the judgment of his inferiors. To this the most serene King, inspired by God, replied that it was for the synod to decide in so great a matter what should be written, and that nothing beyond reverence pertained to him in an ecclesiastical matter; he also committed it to the power of the Pontiffs, so that whether they wished to hear the matter or not, they might deliberate on what they thought more useful, provided that peace was secured in the city of Rome through the providence of the venerable council. The bishops sitting in the synod, by the authority of the same King, then said: "Pope Symmachus, the Prelate of the Apostolic See, who was assailed by such objections, is, so far as men are concerned, free and immune; his whole cause we have reserved to the judgment of God. As for the clergy of the said Pope, who departed from the rules before time, without their bishop, and made a schism, we have decreed this: that they, making satisfaction to their bishop, may obtain mercy and, restored, may rejoice in ecclesiastical benefices." Laurence, Bishop of the Church of Milan, subscribed to this our decree, in which we have committed the whole cause to the judgment of God; Peter, Bishop of Ravenna, subscribed in the same words, and after him seventy-five others, etc. Since this is so, it is a matter for pity that Lord Rupert, the present King of the Romans, so often cherishes and defends the said Gregory, in his manifest obstinacy, schism and heresy, against the promises, vows and oaths which Gregory freely made of his own accord and repeated so often; and this surely tends to a greater rending of the Church. And what else would have concerned the King himself in this part, except that, in the manner of the said King Theodoric, he should have written and commanded strictly, in accordance with the form of the canon immediately preceding, that the said Gregory and Peter de Luna, contending for the papacy, should make union in the Church, so that peace might be made not only in the city but throughout Christendom, especially since they had also, without any request from the said King Rupert, freely and willingly bound themselves, sworn and vowed to this, and had solemnly notified him of it, and likewise had asked him to support this?

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Gesta atque triumphi Dieterichi de Bern, alias de Verona.
units.tr: The deeds and triumph of Dietrich of Bern, otherwise called of Verona.

units.la: Nimirum igitur si generale Concilium tunc congregatum detulit reuerenter dicto Theodorico Regi magnifico, qui tunc Occidentale Imperium strenue gubernabat, & qui revera Rex fuit re & nomine, quia non verbis, sed factis gloriabatur: huic enim Romani, Aprutini, Siculi, Calabri, Tusci, Etrusci, Ligures, Veneti, Illyrici, Istri, Foroiulienses, Sueui, Getarum, & Pannoniarum incolae, atque Galli usque ad Hispaniam, & multae aliae generationes hominum cum summa reverentia obediebant: hic etiam propter eius liberalitatem, strenuitatem, magnificentiam, nec non in arte bellandi peritiam, & crebras eius cum rebellibus imperio victorias, Pater Regum, & Princeps principum appellatus est suo tempore: qui descendens a vero Imperatore Constantinopolitano meruit eius effigiem sive statuam Imperiali edicto attante in foro publico eiusdem civitatis collocari.
units.tr: Surely, then, if the general council assembled at that time paid due reverence to the magnificent King Theodoric, who then governed the Western Empire with vigour, and who truly was king in deed and in name, since he prided himself not on words but on deeds, then it is not surprising: for to him the inhabitants of Rome, Apulia, Sicily, Calabria, Tuscany, Etruria, Liguria, Venetia, Illyria, Istria, Friuli, Swabia, the lands of the Goths and Pannonia, and the Gauls as far as Spain, and many other nations of men, rendered obedience with the greatest reverence. He too, on account of his generosity, vigour, magnificence, his skill in the art of war, and his frequent victories over rebels against his rule, was called in his own time Father of Kings and Prince of princes. Descended from the true Emperor of Constantinople, he deserved to have his effigy or statue set up in the public square of that city by imperial edict.

units.la: Hic etiam de Graecia veniens per Illyricum & Pannoniam ac demum per Theutoniam appropinquans Veronae, ibi cum potentissimo Rege Odoacre Principe Ruthenorum, qui tunc Romam & totam Italiam tyrannice occupabat, sibi occurrente conflixit, quem bello campestri devictum, & vix equi subsidio ad Papiam fugientem persequebatur continue, & ibi denuo bello commisso victor iterum extitit, nec non ipsum Odoacrem ad Rauennam usque fugauit, in qua per gyrum diutine illum obsidendo tandem vivum sibi transmissum gladio interemit, sicque dominium totius Italiae, postquam illud idem Odoacer per duodecim annos detinuit, sortitus est, Papa tunc dissimulante, & quod apud eum ipsi duo tunc essent gladii, ut aestimo, non dicente, neque illud coram se in publico praedicari permittente.
units.tr: Coming from Greece through Illyricum and Pannonia, and at last approaching Verona through Germany, he there met in battle the very powerful King Odoacer, prince of the Ruthenians, who was then tyrannically occupying Rome and all Italy. He defeated him in a pitched battle and pursued him relentlessly as he fled, barely with the help of his horse, to Pavia. There he joined battle again and was again the victor, and he drove Odoacer as far as Ravenna. There he besieged him for a long time and at last, when Odoacer was sent to him alive, killed him with the sword. Thus he obtained dominion over all Italy, after Odoacer himself had held it for twelve years. The Pope was then silent about this, and, as I think, did not say that the two swords were then with him, nor did he permit this to be proclaimed publicly in his presence.

units.la: Hic etiam Rex Theodoricus excellentissimos & nobiles viros Cassiodorum & Sydonium literarum scientia eruditissimos Cancellarios habuit, qui eum laudibus eximiis extulerunt, ut historiae per eos descriptae demonstrant. Hunc etiam Regem Theodoricum Alemani dilexisse videntur, quem adhuc Theodoricum de Berna Germaniae vulgus appellat, nec non quasdam de illo cantilenas in vulgari Theutonico ad ipsius Regis laudem dictaverunt, quae adhuc plerumque per rusticos & mechanicos decantantur.
units.tr: Here King Theodoric had as his chancellors the most excellent and noble men Cassiodorus and Sidonius, most learned in literature, who extolled him with outstanding praises, as the histories written by them show. The Germans also seem to have loved this King Theodoric, whom the German common people still call Theodoric of Bern. They also composed certain songs about him in the vernacular German in praise of the King, which even now are for the most part sung by peasants and artisans.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: An Papa delinquens debeat & possit ab Imperatore corripi: & de gestis circa eam rem, atque laude Ottonis Primi, Romanorum Imperatoris.
units.tr: Whether a Pope who offends ought to be and can be rebuked by the Emperor; and concerning the deeds done in this matter, and the praise of Otto the First, Emperor of the Romans.

units.la: SEd certe nostri moderni Reges & Imperatores longe in talibus ab eodem Theodorico Rege distare videntur, qui maiori cura priuatum patrimonium suum, quam iura eiusdem Imperii cosertare conantur. Quod autem imperialis potestas sit praecipue super malum & incorrigibilem Pontificem Romanum, per quem scandalizatur Ecclesia, ex gestis Imperatorum seu Regum Romanorum satis constat. Nam Ioannes Papa duodecimus fuit vnicus & indubitatus Papa, qui ante papatum vocabatur Octauianus, de nobili & potenti genere procreatus, qui postquam assumptus erat ad Papatum, venationibus ferarum sylvestrium quandoq; interfuit, necnon libidinose ac lubrice viuens cum suspectis mulieribus fortes posuit, ac etiam aliquos ex suis Cardinalibus eum propterea arguentes male tractauit & multauit. Quod audiens Otto Primus magnus Augustus de hoc ex corde doluit: ex Germania propterea Romam veniens, eidem Papae, cur illic venerat, expostuit. Quod audiens Papa valde timuit, promittens Imperatori, quod eius vitam subito emendare vellet. Imperator autem credens eum ita facturum, ad Papiam e Roma recessit, vbi hyemando remansit, vt scrutaretur interim, si forsan praefati Papae dictis facta responderent: sed quia difficile est consuetarelinquere, Papa ipse nec Deum nec Imperatorem habens prae oculis, mala malis accumulauit. Quod sentiens Augustus irato animo ad vrbem rediit, vt diiudicaret de ipso Papa: qui hoc audiens, vtpote sibi ipsi male conscius, se inde fugae subsidio e vestigio absentauit ad Campaniam declinando. Sed impiger Imperator Concilium cleri Romani contra eundem Papam in ipsa vrbe conuocauit, in quo dicto Papae communi voto eius Concilii depositio vir laudabilis famae & sanctae conuersationis alter Leo huius nominis Octauus extitit surrogatus. Ipse autem Octauianus ne ad manus Imperatoris deueniret, abdita loca perquirens in ipsa Campania misere diem clausit extremum. Profecto tunc temporis Papa non habuit tot temporalia, sicut Romana Ecclesia nunc videtur habere, quia ipse magnus Augustus & de ipso descendentes, Secundus & Tertius eiusdem nominis Augusti, ipsam Romanam & alias ecclesias in Italia & Germania secularibus dominiis ditarunt, & ita manifeste apparet in libris, quae super donationibus Ecclesiae factis per Imperatores & Reges Romanos confecti sunt, & in Thesauraria seu camera Apostolica conseruantur. Praeterea tunc erat adeo excellens Augustus, quod nemo contra eius voluntatem aliquem Papam, praesertim malignum, abiectum vel schismaticum ausus fuisset publice confouere: alias certe idem Octauianus, vt existimo, reperisset aliquem potentem, qui ipsum in sua malitia & tyrannide confouisset, nec ciuitatem Auinionensem cum eius mirando palatio tenuit Romana Ecclesia, sed potius magno Ottoni obsequebatur.
units.tr: But certainly our present kings and emperors seem far different in such matters from that same King Theoderic, who with greater care try to protect their private patrimony than the rights of the same Empire. That imperial power is especially over a wicked and incorrigible Roman Pontiff, through whom the Church is scandalised, is quite clear from the deeds of the Emperors or Kings of the Romans. For John the Twelfth was the one and undoubted Pope, who before his papacy was called Octavian, born of a noble and powerful family; after he had been raised to the papacy, he sometimes took part in the hunting of wild beasts, and living lustfully and wantonly with suspect women he begot children, and he also treated badly and fined some of his own Cardinals who rebuked him for this. Hearing this, Otto the First, the great Augustus, grieved for it from his heart; coming from Germany to Rome for this reason, he called the same Pope to account for why he had come there. Hearing this, the Pope was greatly afraid and promised the Emperor that he would at once amend his life. The Emperor, believing he would do so, withdrew from Rome to Pavia, where he remained over the winter, to see meanwhile whether the deeds of the said Pope would perhaps match his words; but because it is difficult to give up a habit, the Pope himself, having neither God nor the Emperor before his eyes, piled evil upon evil. Perceiving this, the Augustus returned to the city in an angry mind, to pass judgment on the Pope himself; the Pope, hearing this and being conscious of his own guilt, at once absented himself by flight, withdrawing to Campania. But the vigorous Emperor called together a council of the Roman clergy against the same Pope in the city itself; in that council, by the common vote of the council, the said Pope was deposed, and in his place Leo the Eighth of that name, a man of praiseworthy reputation and holy life, was substituted. Octavian himself, so as not to fall into the Emperor's hands, searching out hidden places in Campania, wretchedly ended his last day. Certainly at that time the Pope did not have so many temporal possessions as the Roman Church now seems to have, because the great Augustus himself and his descendants, the Second and Third Augustus of the same name, enriched the Roman and other churches in Italy and Germany with secular dominions; and so it plainly appears from the books that were drawn up concerning the donations made to the Church by the Emperors and Kings of the Romans, and are kept in the Treasury or Apostolic Chamber. Moreover, the Augustus was then so eminent that no one would have dared openly to favour any Pope, especially a wicked one, cast down or schismatic, against his will; otherwise, I think, Octavian himself would have found some powerful man who would have supported him in his malice and tyranny, nor would the Roman Church have held the city of Avignon with its wondrous palace, but rather would have obeyed the great Otto.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: An expediat Reipub. Christianae Pontificem Romanum rerum temporalium dominiis auctum fuisse, & adhuc ipsa mordicus tenere.
units.tr: Whether it is expedient for the Christian commonwealth that the Roman Pontiff should have been enriched with dominions over temporal things, and that the Church should still hold on to them tooth and nail.

units.la: QVid igitur inducit aliud haec Pompa tantorum temporalium dominiorum, de quibus nunc gloriatur Ecclesia Romana, quam negligentiam in spiritualibus, & erectionem tyrannorum in iisdem dominiis, & diuisiones seu schisma in eadem Ecclesia, & alia mala plurima, satis est notum. Hic etiam Otto magnus duo schismata succesiue orta in Romana Ecclesia, dum ageret in Gallia & Alemania, cum ingenti exercitu ad vrbem Romanam rediens manu potenti sustulit: & vnum in Capitolio tunc fortissimo, & alium in Castro nouo sancti Angeli, quod tunc carcer Theodorici vocabatur, loco firmissimo, contendentes tunc de Papatu prima facie cum machinis & aliis rebus bellicis expugnando coepit, & multorum nobilium ac potentorum Romanorum eos fouentium palatia in vrbe destruxit, & multos eorum ingulauit, seu gladio interemit, sicque ipsas Ecclesias ad vnionem Deo ordinante, perduxit. Et post longa tempora orto alio schismate in ipsa Ecclesia, iterum rediit ad vrbem ipsam, & causa cognita vtriusque contendentis, & clero per Concilium subito conuocato, & vno declarato Papa, alterum scilicet Benedictum Secundum in Saxoniam in exilium deportauit.
units.tr: What, then, does this display of such great temporal dominions, of which the Roman Church now boasts, bring about other than negligence in spiritual matters, the raising up of tyrants within those dominions, divisions or schism in the same Church, and very many other evils? It is sufficiently well known. Here too Otto the Great, while he was engaged in Gaul and Germany, returned to the city of Rome with a mighty army and by strong hand put an end to two schisms that had arisen one after another in the Roman Church: one in the Capitol, then a very strong fortress, and the other in the new Castle of Saint Angelo, which was then called the prison of Theodoric, a most secure place. Since the rival claimants were at first contending for the papacy, he began to storm them with siege engines and other weapons of war, destroyed in the city the palaces of many noble and powerful Romans who supported them, and slew many of them with the sword; and so, with God ordaining it, he brought the churches themselves back to unity. And after a long time, when another schism had arisen in the Church itself, he returned to the city; and, having examined the cause of both contenders, and with the clergy suddenly summoned by a council, and one pope having been declared, he deported the other, namely Benedict the Second, into exile in Saxony.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: Quod ad Imperatorem maxime pertineat schismata tollere: Author in Pontifices criminosos inuehitur: & an iuxta Canonum Decreta tales Pontifices à nemine possint, aut debeant iudicari.
units.tr: That it belongs chiefly to the Emperor to remove schisms. The author inveighs against criminal Popes, and asks whether, according to the decrees of the canons, such Popes can or ought to be judged by no one.

units.la: ECce quantus & qualis fuit iste Augustus, qui tot laboribus & expensis pro reformatione vnionis in ipsa Ecclesia vltro se submittit, & foelicior operatus est: nam mali inquietem alijs præparantes cogendi sunt ad pacem & ad bonum. Regiæ potestatis interest præcipue, vt per eam mali coerçeantur à malo, & boni quiete inter malos viuant, vt sacri canones docent, sed non intelligitur de alia potestate, quam Imperiali, quæ omnes potestates temporales excellit. Et omnes quasi Reges mundi & tot præsati Ecclesiastici & communitates egregiarum ciuitatum ad extirpandum Ichisma nouissimum ab ipsa Ecclesia hactenus efficaciter proficere non potuerunt, nec possunt, & quis tunc disputasset, cum eodem magno Augusto Ottone de ipsius iudicio super contendentes super Papatu seu peruerso vnico Papa, scilicet quod nisi à Deo possint iudicari? Vtinam talis Imperator surgeret temporibus nostris, quia nunc cessaret scripturarum multiplicitates in hoc labyrintho, quæ adeo creuerunt propter multitudinem scribentium in hoc passu, quod vix eos centum camelì portarent.
units.tr: Behold how great and what kind of man this Augustus was, who at so many labours and expenses for the restoration of unity in the Church voluntarily submitted himself, and was the more fortunate in his work, for the wicked who prepare restlessness for others must be compelled to peace and to what is good. It is above all the interest of royal power that through it the wicked are restrained from evil and the good live quietly among the wicked, as the sacred canons teach. But this is not to be understood of any power other than the Imperial, which surpasses all temporal powers. All the kings of the world, and the aforesaid ecclesiastics and communities of distinguished cities, have not been able, and cannot, to bring about the extirpation of this latest schism from the Church effectively so far. And who would have disputed then with the same great Emperor Otto about his judgment over those contending for the papacy, or over the one perverse Pope, namely that they could be judged only by God? Would that such an Emperor might arise in our times, for then the multiplicity of writings in this labyrinth would cease, which have grown so much through the number of writers on this point that a hundred camels could scarcely carry them.

units.la: Clarum est enim, quod omnium Christianorum maxime interest, quod Papa, à quo omnes normam viuendi capiunt, esse debet mundus, non simoniacus, sanguinolentus, adulter, vel lubricus aleator, ebriosus, venator, seu Venereus, vel aliter publicus balatrator. Quis enim sciens Papam esse talem posset sine remorsu conscientiæ aut adulationis vitio illius pedes vel manus osculari, aut illum patrem sanctum cordialiter nominare? Igitur idem Augustus sic faciendo non peccauit vel excessit, quin imo, vt Dei minister, optime fecit, qui fuit adeo gloriosus & constantis animi, Deificus mundusque Imperator, vt eius magnificentia & memoria digna gesta testantur, sicut vnquam fuit Romanus aliquis Patritius, Rex vel Augustus: nec tenetur forte, communi vtilitate suadente, Imperator vel Rex Romanorum, fidelitatis iuramentum præstitum tali peruerso Papæ, vel alteri Ecclesiastico Prælato, notorio peccatori, vel incorrigibili, obseruare, quia ibi VIRTVS deficit potestatis, vbi succedit abusus: & IVRAMENTVM iniquitatis vinculum esse non debet: alias enim sequeretur, quod artante illo iuramento tales peruersos & malos nemo impedire, atque, vt ad viam redirent, admonere posset, quod iuri communi & rectæ rationi repugnat, & cederet in reipublicæ detrimentum: quia non turbando peruersos, cum possis, est ipsos in eorum malitiis confouere, & ERROR, cui non resistitur, approbari videtur. Cum oporteat esse Episcopum sine crimine, quasi dispensatorem Dei, sed multo magis Papam, qui omnibus præest. Nec credo illud obstare, quod Canonistæ dicunt, quod Papa, nisi à fide sit deuius, deiici non possit, & quod nemo iudicat primam sedem, quodque nullus potest auferre authoritatem vel potestatem, quam conferre non potest.
units.tr: It is clear indeed that it matters most of all to Christians that the Pope, from whom all take the rule of living, should be pure: not simoniacal, not bloodthirsty, not an adulterer, nor a lewd gambler, a drunkard, a hunter, a lover of Venus, or otherwise a notorious brawler. For who, knowing the Pope to be such, could kiss his feet or hands, or heartily call him Holy Father, without a pang of conscience or the vice of flattery? Therefore the same Augustus did not sin or go beyond bounds in so acting; rather, as a minister of God, he acted very well, being so glorious and steadfast of spirit, a divinely favoured and upright Emperor, as his magnificence and memorable deeds attest, as never was any Roman patrician, king or Augustus. Nor is the Emperor or King of the Romans perhaps bound, as common utility suggests, to keep the oath of fidelity given to such a perverse Pope or other ecclesiastical prelate, a notorious or incorrigible sinner, because there the strength of power fails where abuse succeeds, and an oath of iniquity ought not to be a bond. Otherwise it would follow that, with that oath binding them, no one could hinder such perverse and wicked men, or admonish them to return to the right way. This is contrary to common law and right reason, and would turn to the detriment of the commonwealth: for by not disturbing the perverse when you could, you foster them in their malice, and ERROR, which is not resisted, seems to be approved. A bishop must be without crime, as God's steward, but much more so the Pope, who presides over all. Nor do I think that what the canonists say stands in the way, namely that the Pope cannot be deposed unless he has departed from the faith, that no one judges the first see, and that no one can take away an authority or power which he cannot confer.

units.la: Ex his & similibus volunt inferre, quod nemo nisi solus Deus, Papam potest, seu licet iudicare, quia Papatus omnes dignitates excellit, quia Papa est Dei vicarius, & ipse omnes iudicat. Quæ licet ita teneantur, tamen in putatiuo & contendente de Papatu in schismate variantur nec subsistunt, nec etiam intelliguntur rationabiliter in vno & indubitato Papa, malefico & Ecclesiam scandalizante, quia ille reuera dici non potest Christi vicarius, quia Christi opera & mandata non sequitur, nec obseruat, in detrimentum maximum Christianorum: & sic non Papa sed bestia magis propriè appellatur, qui enim à ratione deuiat, non homo sed animal irrationabile iure censetur. Et talis existens Papa videtur etiam esse tyrannus potius, quam Dei minister, & ideo propter eius demerita fit omnibus despectior, &, vt indignus à tanto regimine sanctissimo remouetur: quia malus sacerdos non dicitur sacerdos, & malus Episcopus non est Episcopus. Hoc probare videtur authoritas Euangelii, vbi dicitur Petro conditionaliter; Si diligis me, pasce oues meas: ex quo infertur, quod qui non diligit Deum, scilicet si est simoniacus, adulter, vel alias publicus peccator incorrigibilis, non meretur esse, nec est verus pastor ouium, sed mercenarius siue lupus, quia boni & veri pastoris officium non exercet, & ideo potest & debet per alios iudicari.
units.tr: From these and similar points they wish to infer that no one but God alone can or may judge the Pope, because the papacy surpasses all dignities, since the Pope is God's vicar and judges everyone. Although these things are held in this way, nevertheless in the case of a putative Pope contending for the papacy in schism they vary and do not hold, nor are they reasonably understood of one undoubted Pope who is a wrongdoer and scandalises the Church. For he cannot truly be called Christ's vicar, since he does not follow or observe Christ's works and commands, to the very great detriment of Christians; and so he is properly called not Pope but rather a beast, for whoever deviates from reason is judged by law not a man but an irrational animal. Such a Pope seems rather to be a tyrant than a minister of God, and therefore on account of his demerits he is more despised by all and, as unworthy, is removed from so holy a government, for a bad priest is not called a priest, and a bad bishop is not a bishop. This seems to be proved by the authority of the Gospel, where it is said to Peter conditionally: If you love me, feed my sheep. From this it is inferred that whoever does not love God, namely if he is simoniacal, an adulterer, or otherwise a notorious incorrigible sinner, does not deserve to be, and is not, a true shepherd of the sheep, but a hireling or a wolf, because he does not exercise the office of a good and true shepherd, and therefore can and ought to be judged by others.

units.la: IOANNIS EPISCOPI, LEODIENSIS, S. ROMAN. ECCLE- SIAE CARDINALIS, S. ROM. IMPERII Principis, Ducis Bauariae & Bullionae, Comitis Hollandiae, &c.
units.tr: JOHN, BISHOP OF LIÈGE, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, PRINCE OF THE HOLY ROMAN EMPIRE, DUKE OF BAVARIA AND BULLION, COUNT OF HOLLAND, ETC.

units.la: EPISTOLA, QVATENVS PAPAE SIT OBEDIENDVM,
units.tr: A LETTER: TO WHAT EXTENT THE POPE IS TO BE OBEYED

units.la: Scripta ad Theodoricum à Niem, Protonotarium Romanæ Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Written to Dietrich of Niem, Protonotary of the Roman Church.

units.la: VENERABILIS amice charissime, scripta vidimus per latorem præsentium oblata, quibus per singula respondere non permittit temporis angustia, & etiam lator ipse causam latius referre poterit: vnum non intendemus omittere, quod ab obedientia & iustitia hactenus obseruatis nunquam recedere certum est, iuramentis & obligationibus efficacissimis est firmatum, & sic apparet mendacissime illa, quæ scribitis, fuisse diuulgata. Vnum solum est studium vsque ad mortem inclusiue persequendum, votis, promissis & iuratis, atque per mundum vniuersum iam publice diuulgatis, & vnioni Ecclesiæ velle insistere, & sic authoritatum rationum ve multiplicata congeries locum habebit, suosque intellectus locis & temporibus coartatos. Ita tamen est, vera & sana doctrina, quæ in nullo aduersatur eisdem, quod Deo magis obediendum est, habetur.
units.tr: Most venerable and dearest friend, we have seen the writings brought to us by the bearer of these present letters. The shortness of time does not allow us to answer them point by point, and the bearer himself will be able to explain the matter more fully. We do not intend to omit one thing: it is certain that we have never departed from the obedience and justice observed until now, and it has been confirmed by the most binding oaths and obligations; thus it is clear that those things you write were spread abroad with the greatest lying. There is one sole aim to be pursued even unto death: to hold to our vows, promises and oaths, which have already been published openly throughout the whole world, and to press on toward the unity of the Church. Thus the heaped-up mass of authorities and reasons will have its place, and their meanings, confined by places and times, will be applied accordingly. Yet this is the true and sound doctrine, which contradicts none of these, that God is to be obeyed rather than men.

units.la: Si enim illa Papa mandet, vel ad ea cogere vellet, quæ animas in præcipitium ducunt, & animæ perditionem includunt, sibi non fore obediendum iure diuino & humano notissimum est, secundum Doctores sanctum Augustinum, Ambrosium, Bedam, & alios, imo non obediendo & propter hoc eius seueritates sustinendo & censuras meretur homo. Ista pro nunc sufficiant, tacemus de modis hactenus obseruatis in faciendo & non faciendo, & lapsu temporis tanti, in quo quid & quantum actum sit in causa Dei, & sub quibus coloribus & quantum fundatis, ex quibus quanta affectio fuit tollendi schismatis, & si illa ad fautoriam magis pertineant, non intendimus nos dilatare. Postea tamen de hoc videri poterit plenius, & quid mundus, quoad hoc, reputet aut teneat, vnusquisque poterit perpendere. Vnum est, quod nihil aliud agitur, quam mundo & Christianitate languentibus, & conscientiæ atque famæ prouidere cum omni sinceritate & charitate, prout cunctis hoc fiet manifestum. Aliud, præmissis non obstantibus, cum festinantia duximus adiungendum, quod quicunque sunt illi, quibus talentum à Domino quale & quantum cuique creditum est, maxime qui statu ecclesiastico gloriantur, suntque illuminati scientia, & se vnionis zelatores esse profitentur, se ad currum deberent adiungere, & etiam cooperatores existere, & illi maxime quibus innotescit, quanta fuerunt hactenus adhibita molimina non ad vnionem veniendi iuxta promissa & iurata, sed potius impediendi, & ea pro posse improbandi. Scripta Pisis altera die Ascensionis.
units.tr: For if the Pope were to command, or wished to compel, things which lead souls into the abyss and involve the destruction of the soul, it is most well known by divine and human law that he is not to be obeyed; so teach the Doctors, Saint Augustine, Ambrose, Bede and others. Indeed, a man deserves, by not obeying in this matter, to endure his severities and censures. Let these things suffice for now. We keep silent about the methods observed until now in doing and not doing, and about the lapse of so much time, in which what and how much has been done in the cause of God, and under what colours and on what grounds; we do not intend to enlarge on whether these things pertain more to favouritism, nor on what the world thinks or holds about these matters, since everyone can weigh that for himself later and more fully. This one thing is certain: nothing else is being done than to provide, with all sincerity and charity, for the conscience and reputation of the world, which is languishing and for Christendom, as will become clear to all. We have thought it necessary to add quickly another thing, notwithstanding what has been said: whoever they are to whom a talent has been entrusted by the Lord, of whatever quality and quantity, especially those who boast of their ecclesiastical status, who are enlightened by knowledge and profess themselves zealots for unity, ought to join themselves to the chariot and even become fellow-workers; and especially those who know how great the endeavours have been until now, not aimed at coming to unity according to promises and oaths, but rather at hindering it, and at condemning these, as far as they are able. Written at Pisa, the day after the Ascension.

units.la: THEODORICI à NIEM EPISCOPI VERDENSIS ET CAMERACENSIS
units.tr: Theodoric of Niem, Bishop of Verden and Cambrai

units.la: EXHORTATIO AD DOMINVM RVPERTVM REGEM ROMANORVM, vt surgat à diuturno somno, quodque vt extirpetur schisma Pontificum ab Ecclesia, & iura Imperii reformentur, intendat.
units.tr: An Exhortation to the Lord Rupert, King of the Romans, that he should rise from his long sleep and take care that the schism of the Popes is removed from the Church and the rights of the Empire are reformed.

units.la: SERENISSIMO Principi, Domino RVPERTO Regi Romanorum, animum virilem, & pro republica, vt propriis, semper dispositum & paratum. Dominatur excelsus in regno hominum, & cuicunque voluerit, dabit illud. Ecce postquam de Mense Augusti proxime praeterito Dominus Gregorius Papa duodecimus, disposuit cum eis curia ab urbe recedere, prout postea fecit, Dominum Cardinalem de Transtyberim iuniorem aetate caeteris omnibus Dominis Cardinalibus, in spiritualibus, & Paulum de Vrsinis Capitaneum gentium armigerarum tunc & diu ante Ecclesiae generalem, in temporalibus, rectores eiusdem Vrbis, pro seinterim, quod absens esset ab eadem vrbe, deputauit: qui postquam ipse Dominus Papa recessisset ab inde, infra paucos dies inceperunt circa moenia dictae vrbis, & extra vias insolita fossata facere, nec non vrbicolas ad laborandum in illis diebus pluribus aggregauerunt, unde multorum vineae destructae aut deminutae fuerunt.
units.tr: To the most serene Prince, the Lord Rupert, King of the Romans, a manly spirit, always disposed and prepared for the commonwealth as for his own affairs. The Most High rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he wills. Behold, after the month of August just past, when Pope Gregory XII decided with his court to leave the city, as he later did, he appointed the Lord Cardinal of Trastevere, the youngest in age of all the other Lord Cardinals, as ruler of the city in spiritual matters, and Paolo Orsini, captain of the men-at-arms, then and for long before, of the general Church, as ruler in temporal matters, to govern in the meantime while Pope Gregory was absent from the city. Within a few days after the Pope himself had left, they began to dig unusual ditches around the walls of the said city and outside the roads, and they gathered many of the city dwellers to labour on them over several days, so that the vineyards of many people were destroyed or diminished.

units.la: Postquam haec autem, vt populus vidit diligentiam pro eius securitate fieri, annuit pro vberioribus impensis stipendiariis faciendis, quod gabellae prius satis onerosae in urbe ipsa duplicari deberent, prout factum fuit mora cessante: ac successiue pro tractu aliquarum Septimanarum Rectores ad hoc vt multiplicaretur eorundem stipediariorum numerus, imposuerunt horribilem multaclero vrbis praefatae, ascendentem ad triginta millia florenorum aureorum, quam poenaliter etiam percaptionem & detentionem in carceribus multarum personarum Ecclesiasticarum, secularium & regularium, ac etiam distractionem multorum sacrorum valorum & pretiosorum, rotalium, Ecclesiarum & monasteriorum finaliter reportarunt: multos etiam priuatos cives, & incolas habitatores dictae vrbis exactionarunt, quemlibet iuxta eius statum, exinde varias & magnas pecuniarum summas quomodolibet reportando. Interim vero creuit fames in eadem vrbe, potissime nuper in Quadragesima, ita vt difficulter panis aut granum venalia reperirentur in ipsa, quamuis maxima in eadem vrbe grani abundantia existeret: sed habentes illud auaritia obcaecati semper, vt carius fieret, praestolantes, veteri more ipsorum, neque dare neque vendere competenti pretio illud indigentibus voluerunt: unde maledictio venit merito super eos, iuxta id Salomonis, Qui abscondit frumenta in tempore famis, maledicitur in populis: benedictio autem super caput vendentium, Prouerb. vadecim.
units.tr: After this, when the people saw that such diligence was being taken for their safety, they agreed to pay higher wages to the mercenaries, so that the taxes in the city, already quite burdensome, had to be doubled, which was done at once. Then, for some weeks, in order to increase the number of those mercenaries, the rulers imposed a terrible levy on the clergy of the aforesaid city, amounting to thirty thousand gold florins. They finally extracted it by penalties, including the seizure and imprisonment of many ecclesiastical persons, both secular and regular, and the sale of many sacred and precious goods of votive vessels, churches and monasteries. They also levied money from many private citizens and inhabitants of the said city, each according to his rank, thereby extracting various large sums by whatever means. Meanwhile hunger grew in the same city, especially lately in Lent, so that bread or grain was hard to find for sale, although there was the greatest abundance of grain in the city. But those who had it, always blinded by greed and waiting for it to become dearer, as is their old custom, were unwilling either to give it to the needy or to sell it at a fair price. Hence a curse has justly come upon them, according to the saying of Solomon: "He who withholds grain in time of famine is cursed among the peoples, but blessing is upon the head of those who sell." Prov. 11.

units.la: Committebantur etiam impune multa scelera, inter & prope ipsam vrbem: nam accedentes ad illam peregrini, & alii crebro spoliabantur rebus eorum, & male tractantur per stipendiarios & latrones, & inprimis in septimana sancta centum peregrini, vel circa, innocenter & crudeliter pro eo, quod spoliantibus ipsos resistere in Romanorum districtu conabantur, per aliquos Satellites dicti Pauli interempti fuerunt.
units.tr: Many crimes were also committed with impunity, both within and near the city itself. For pilgrims and others coming to it were often robbed of their goods and roughly treated by mercenaries and brigands. Especially in Holy Week, about a hundred pilgrims, or so, were innocently and cruelly killed by some of the attendants of the said Paolo, because they tried to resist those who were plundering them in the district of the Romans.

units.la: Haec & innumera alia flagitia intus & extra ipsam vrbem quotidie perpetrabantur impune: quorum clamorem tandem, vt aestimo, diuina iustitia pie respiciens, & tacentibus & dissimulantibus ipsis, ad quos talium correctio pertinebat, salutare volens remedium adhibere, suscitauit Spiritum Domini Ladislai Regis Siciliae contra Romanos, qui nuper in eadem septimana sancta Romae cum Galeis per mare, & gentibus armorum per terram cum valido exercitu appropinquauit, tamen in qua forma & qualiter id fieri debuit, factumque extitit: iam sunt sex septimanae, vel circa, praeteritae. Apud nos in Romana curia publice dicebatur, quod Rex prima die expugnauit Ostiam, quae est praesidium portus Romani circa mare, quam quidam nobiles Romani, mihi noti, mediocris status, tunc pro quadam pecuniae summa titulo pignoris tenuerunt, vbi hostes modicam resistentiam receperunt. Capta igitur ciuitate Ostiensi nunc modica, terra, olim autem magna & opulenta ciuitate, vt veteres & horribiles visu eius ruinae testantur, vi per Regem & eius exercitum ante dictos, inter quos etiam fuerunt Columnenses Barones, & nonnulli alii ciues Romani, ipsi vlterius versus eandem vrbem iter egerunt. Sed qualitercunque Rex burgum sancti Petri, scilicet ciuitatem Leoninam absque effusione sanguinis subito subintrauit: quia
units.tr: These and countless other outrages were committed daily, with impunity, inside and outside the city. Divine justice, as I judge, mercifully regarded their outcry at last. Since those to whom the correction of such things belonged were silent and dissembling, God wished to apply a healthful remedy, and he roused the Spirit of the Lord against the Romans in the person of Ladislaus, King of Sicily. Lately, in that same Holy Week, he approached Rome with galleys by sea and an armed force with a strong army by land. In what manner and how it ought to have been done, and was done, six weeks or so have now passed. In our Roman court it was publicly said that on the first day the King stormed Ostia, which is the guard of the Roman port by the sea, and which certain Roman nobles, known to me and of middling rank, then held as a pledge for a sum of money. There the enemy met only slight resistance. Ostia, now a small town but once a great and rich city, as its old and dreadful ruins testify, was taken by force by the King and his aforesaid army, among whom were also the Colonna barons and some other Roman citizens. They then marched further toward the same city. But however it was done, the King suddenly entered the borough of St Peter, namely the Leonine city, without bloodshed, because

units.la: Non opus est gladiu, vbi vox submissa triumphat.
units.tr: There is no need of the sword where a gentle voice triumphs.

units.la: Dictus vero Cardinalis, qui prope Basilicam Apostoli in palatio populi morabatur, hoc sentiens, ilico fugam cœpit extra vrbem antedictam, & nisi per aliquas gentes armigeras dicti Pauli tunc benè associatus extitisset, ad manus eorundem Columnensium sibi per iter insidientium vbique peruenisset: qui tamen hodie, vel cras hic erit. Dictus autem Paulus factus est capitaneus generalis exercitus huiusmodi Regis eiusdem, promisitque ipse Rex præfatus, quod omnia castra & terras per eum quomodolibet ablata illis de domo Vrsinensi restituet incunctanter eisdem, nec non ipse habebit singulariter sibi recommissos, ac prosequetur honoribus & gratiis multis ac magnis. Die vero imminenter sequenti, postquam Rex ipse taliter vrbem habuit, granum minus valuit vno floreno, quam ibidem per tempus aliquod inantea vendebatur: fecit enim Rex ipse in signum tantæ, tamen absque bello, victoriæ aliquos Milites, inter quos erat Ludouicus nepos domini Innocentii Papæ Septimi, qui quidem Ludouicus domino Innocentio nunc viuente, vndecim regentes tunc in vrbe mactauit, necnon Sutrios de Paterno, qui sunt magni capitanei in eodem exercitu Regis memorati.
units.tr: The said Cardinal, who was staying near the Basilica of the Apostle in the people's palace, perceived this and at once began to flee beyond the aforesaid city. Unless he had been well escorted by some of the men-at-arms of the said Paolo, he would have fallen into the hands of the Colonna men, who lay in wait for him along the way. He, however, will be here today or tomorrow. The said Paolo has been made general captain of the army of this same King, and the King promised that he would restore without delay to those of the Orsini house all the castles and lands taken from them in any way, and that he himself would treat with many great honours and favours the men entrusted to him in particular. On the following day, as soon as the King had thus taken the city, grain sold for less than one florin, whereas it had been selling there for some time before. The King, as a sign of such a great victory, though won without war, made some knights, among whom was Ludovico, nephew of Lord Innocent VII. This Ludovico, while Lord Innocent is now alive, slaughtered eleven regents then in the city, and also Sutrio of Paterno, who are great captains in the aforesaid army of the King.

units.la: Et quod sic negocia hucusque in vrbe ac circa eam processerint, vt hic communis fama laborat, nimis multa & certa indicia manifestant, & adhuc sunt hic Ambasiatores dicti Regis, qui raro, vel nunquam nobis, postquam de Roma ipsa nouissime recessimus, defecerunt, imo semper nos consecuti fuerunt. Butigallus autem gubernator dominii ciuitatis Iannensis pro Rege Francorum, nuper misit vndecim galeas armatas in subsidium Romanorum contra galeas & naues Regis præfati: sed tarde venere Bubulci: quia percipientes in via, quam in mari tunc fecerunt, iam Regem præfatum Romam pacto subintrasse, moræ sublato dispendio ad propria sine bello reuersi fuerunt. Et citius illuciuissent, nisi maris tempestas per dies aliquos tunc impediuisset eosdem: quia sic forte dispositum erat deluper. Sed quæ & qualia inde sequentur, futurus declarabit euentus, & iam proinde terribilia pullulare incipiunt, quæ toti Christianitati sunt maxima dispendia verisimiliter producetura.
units.tr: That affairs have so far proceeded in the city and around it, as common report here laments, is made plain by very many and certain signs. The ambassadors of the said King are still here; since we last left Rome they have rarely or never failed us, indeed they have always followed us. Buttigallo, governor of the lordship of the city of Genoa for the King of France, lately sent eleven armed galleys to aid the Romans against the galleys and ships of the aforesaid King. But the herdsmen came late. For, perceiving on the voyage they then made by sea that the aforesaid King had already entered Rome by agreement, they returned home without battle, having lost time and money. They would have arrived sooner had storms at sea not hindered them for some days, for perhaps so it was ordained from above. But what and what sort of things will follow, the future outcome will declare, and already terrible things begin to sprout, which will probably bring the greatest losses to all of Christendom.

units.la: Quid autem nunc profuit dicta fossata fecisse? quid denique expediens erat sic spoliari Ecclesias & templa Dei, sacris vasis & Rotalibus, Deo & eius sanctis ac devotis Christicolis consecratis, ac denudare irreuerenter multorum ipsorum sanctorum venerandas reliquias, tunc auro, & argento, & gemmis pretiosis, etiam ipsorum Christianorum bonis & laboribus devote in eisdem Ecclesiis ac monasteriis reconditas, nec non ipsas reliquias viliter reicere, aurumque & argentum huiusmodi exinde tractatum in vsualem monetam redigere seu conflare, ac tempore oportuno nihil resistetiæ seu virilitatis ostendere, saltem tunc fictis ac veris hostibus eorundem? sic etiam, vt hic fertur, idem contigit in Verona Vicentia & Padua, necnon Pisa ciuitatibus egregiis & splendidis Romani Imperii, quæ nunc væcordia & desidia illorum, qui eas merito protexisse atque conseruasse debuissent, passim ad manus mercatorum etiam taliter deuenerunt. Et quid mirum, quod talibus non dicam, diuinorum & humanorum iurium transgressoribus & sacrilegis maleaccidat, qui Deum & sanctos eius, a quibus præsidium, præsertim vrgente necessitate, postulare deberent, omni timore postposito ipsius Dei, hominumque verecundia, necnon in pessimum exitium aliorum insipienter ofundunt? Puto, quod tales non aduertunt, qualiter Heliodorus, qui templum Dei in Hierusalem eius thesauris spoliare nitebatur, iusto Dei iudicio, a duobus illis iuuenibus flagellis creberrime cædebatur: vnde fusa oratione summi Pontificis ad Deum pro eius salvatione, & sic dono Dei & flagellatoribus liberatus, ipse Heliodorus gratias Pontifici, & recepto exercitu repedat ad Regem. Cum autem Rex interrogaret eum, quis aptus esset adhuc semel Hierusalem mitti: respondens ait; Si quem habes hostem, aut regni insidiatorem, mitte illum & flagellatum eum recipies: si tamen euaserit, eo quod in loco isto sit veri Dei quædam virtus, vt legitur secundo Machabæorum tertio. Præterea non legerunt istud, puta Danielis prophetæ, vt dicit Balthasari Regi Chaldæorum; Tu quoque non humiliasti cor tuum, sed adversus dominatorem cœli eleuatus es, & vasa domus eius allata sunt coram te: & tu & optimates tui, & vxores concubinaque tuæ vinum bibistis in eis. Porro Deum, qui habet flatum tuum in manu, sua, & omnes vias tuas, & eius nomen non glorificasti. Idcirco diuisum est regnum tuum, & datum est Medis & Persis, Danielis quinto. Hic tamen Balthasar Rex non recepit illa, sed pater eius, de templo: nec ea conflauit in monetam, sed tantum ad vanam gloriam illa vice vtebatur eisdem: veruntamen pro illo in persona mortem, & regni sui perpetuam destructionem etiam diuinitus reportauit.
units.tr: But what good has it now done to have made those ditches? What was the advantage in despoiling the churches and temples of God in this way, stripping of their sacred vessels and votive objects, consecrated to God, his saints and devout Christians, and irreverently stripping the venerable relics of many of those saints, and casting the relics aside cheaply, while the gold, silver and precious stones, which had been devoutly stored in those churches and monasteries by the goods and labours of Christians themselves, were melted down and turned into common coin? And in the appropriate time they showed no resistance or manliness, at least not against the false and true enemies of these things. As is also said here, the same happened in the splendid cities of the Roman Empire, Verona, Vicenza and Padua, and Pisa, which, through the folly and sloth of those who ought rightly to have protected and preserved them, have passed into the hands of merchants everywhere. And what wonder is it that evil befalls such people, I will not say transgressors of divine and human law and sacrilegious men, who, having cast aside all fear of God himself and all human shame, foolishly pour themselves out for the worst destruction of others, when they should ask for help from God and his saints, especially in pressing need? I think such men do not notice how Heliodorus, who tried to despoil the temple of God in Jerusalem of its treasures, was by the just judgment of God most severely beaten with rods by two young men. Then, after the prayer of the high priest to God for his salvation, Heliodorus was freed by the gift of God and his scourgers, and gave thanks to the priest, and, having recovered his army, returned to the King. When the King asked him whom he thought fit to be sent once more to Jerusalem, he answered: If you have some enemy or plotter against your kingdom, send him there, and you will receive him back flogged, if indeed he escapes; for in that place there is a certain power of the true God. So we read in 2 Maccabees 3. Moreover, have they not read that passage of the prophet Daniel, which he spoke to Belshazzar, King of the Chaldeans: You also have not humbled your heart, but you have exalted yourself against the Lord of heaven, and the vessels of his house have been brought before you; and you and your nobles, your wives and concubines, have drunk wine from them. But you have not glorified the God who holds your breath and all your ways in his hand. Therefore your kingdom has been divided and given to the Medes and Persians. Daniel 5. Yet King Belshazzar did not receive those vessels from the temple; it was his father who did. Nor did he melt them down into coin; he used them only for vain glory on that occasion. Still, for this, he was divinely punished with death in person and with the perpetual destruction of his kingdom.

units.la: Nunquid etiam legitur in historiis Romanis, quod rex Vandalorum paganus, Roma per ipsum vi capta, tempore beati Hieronymi sub pœna capitis prohibuit suis omnibus, ne aliquam persona Ecclesiasticam vtriusque sexus, lecularem vel regularem offenderent, aut sanctorum reliquias seu iocalia, durante quadam die integra, reciperent, vel auferrent? Et vt dictum suum inuiolabiliter remaneret, in eius propria persona per totam vrbem tunc captam semper ipsum, vsque ad dictam Basilicam sancti Petri presbyteros & clerum die illa processionaliter cum eorum reliquiis & iocalibus illic fugientem associauit, nil eis penitus auferendo, aut auferri per suos permittendo. Ex quibus (proh dolor) elicitur, quod quia pro magna parte nunc Christianicirca hæc & alia, quæ fidei nostræ religionem respiciunt, sunt nimis tepidi: imo ad offendendum Deum & sanctos huiusmodi feruidi & procaces, quod mundus diuersimode iam affligitur, nunc inauditis per prius frigoribus ac schismatibus in Ecclesia & Imperio Romanorum, necnon crebris guerris, famaeque ac mortalitate grauatur, vt verificatur id Salomonis: Verti me ad alia, & vidi calumnias, quae sub sole geruntur, & lachrymas innocentium, & neminem consolatorum, nec posse resistere eorum violentia cunctorum auxilio destitutos. Laudaui magis mortuos, quam viuentes, & felicciorem vtrisque iudicaui, qui necdum natus est, nec vidit mala, quae sub sole fiunt. Surgite ergo vos pigri & desides Principes, qui turbis praesidetis, ac tot malis resistite aliquando, quia data est a Domino potestas vobis, & virtus ab altissimo, quoniam interrogabit opera vestra, & cogitationes scrutabitur: quoniam cum essetis ministri regni illius, non recte iudicastis, neque custodistis legem iustitiae, nec vigilanter vobis commissa ministeria peregistis, neque secundum voluntatem Dei ambulastis. Cito apparebit vobis, quoniam iudicium durissimum his, qui praesunt, fiet: exiguo enim concedetur misericordia, potentes autem potenter tormenta patientur. O Rex gentium & desideratus eorum veni, propera, accingere gladio tuo super femur tuum potentissime: renoca memoriae hominum magnifica facta quorundam tuorum praedecessorum etiam nationis Alemaniae, qui rempublicam feliciter & strenue gubernarunt. Praeterea in secundo anno assumptionis tuae ad regni fastigium, si bene recolis, Ruperte Rex, Marchiones Misnenses amici tui, & pene omnes nobiles & Barones regni Bohemiae, propter inordinatum regimen Regis VVenceslai, respicientes, quod ipse tuos progressus vbique nitebatur modis omnibus impedire, contra ipsum Regem in simul concordarunt, quod eum tibi subiicerent manu forti, dummodo eis in hoc potenter absisteres, vt sic vnicus gloriosus existeres, ac insignia Imperialia per eundem VVenceslaum Regem tunc & hodie praeter omnem iustitiam occupata, prout tuam deceret gloriam, recuperares ab ipso. Et quamuis libens tantam oblationem tunc assumeres, ipsisque tuis, quod vel in propria persona, seu per vnum de tuis filiis cum mille lanceis strenue auxiliari velles, dummodo ipsi tantum negotium inciperent, fideliter & constanter promisisses, tamen, postquam illi promissa eorum obseruauerant, & dictum Regem VVenceslaum in Praga Boemiae vnica Metropoli valida obsidione per vnum mensem & vltra constringerent, credentes, quod eis vtique magnifice subuenires pro reipublicae vtilitate, non venisti illuc, necalium loco tui misisti ad eos, qui tantum negocium in se sub tua spe, fideque, licet fatue, suscederunt. Vnde postea tantus exercitus idoneo capitaneo carens, aliquibus receptis promissionibus ab ipso Rege VVenceslao, sed eis per ipsum minime seruatis, ab obsidione huiusmodi, desperato tanto negatio remanente, recesserunt, tuque propterea saltem insigniis huiusmodi & obedientia dicti Regis VVenceslai caruisti, & cares hodie: multique eorum, qui tunc in eadem obsidione proptere a rebus & corporibus eorum destructi sunt. Sed tanta desidia & negligentia, quae redundat in totius Christianitatis & reipublicae maximum detrimentum, indirecte in alia vocabula, scilicet in pietatem & misericordiam tibi a rudibus conuertuntur: sicque Rex piger & negligens, pius & misericors appellatur ab illis: de quo tamen tibi, vt aestimo, non est cura, quia extra Heidelbergam non est vita. Venisti etiam ante tempus congruum & contra consilium tuorum Principum ad Italiam, in qua tunc aduersarium potentissimum reperisti, te potius auaritia, quam virtutis gloria stimulante. Sed abinde paulo post lares proprios repetisti, tamen nihil vtilitatis in ipsa Italia disponendo, sed post hoc infra paucos menses mortuo dicto aduersario, & non apparenti tibi aliquo valido aduersario in eadem Italia, illam extunc imperialiter visitare, ac in eadem iura reformare dicti Imperii non curasti. Credis forte, quod haec & alia tua facta in tui gloriam non scribantur: imo iam de illis membranae plurimae, nisi me fallit opinio, denigrantur. Scio, vt leges tuae dicunt, quod Romanus Princeps dicitur communis omnibus post Deum, & quod per eius maiestatem iuratur, quae secundum Deum generi humano est diligenda & colenda.
units.tr: Is it not also recorded in the Roman histories that the pagan king of the Vandals, when Rome had been taken by force in the time of blessed Jerome, forbade all his men on pain of death to harm any ecclesiastical person of either sex, lay or regular, or to take or carry off the relics of the saints or sacred vessels for one whole day? And so that his command might remain inviolable, he himself, in his own person, accompanied the priests and clergy through the whole captured city, always, as far as the said Basilica of St Peter, where they fled in procession that day with their relics and sacred vessels. He took nothing from them at all, and permitted none of his men to take anything. From this (alas) it follows that, since for the most part Christians are now too lukewarm about these matters and others that concern the religion of our faith, yet fervent and insolent in offending God and the saints in such ways, the world is now afflicted in various ways. Now it is burdened by unheard-of coldness and schisms in the Church and the Empire of the Romans, and also by frequent wars, famine and mortality, just as that saying of Solomon is borne out: I turned to other things, and I saw the oppressions that are done under the sun, and the tears of the innocent, with no one to comfort them, and no power to resist their violence, since they lacked the help of all. I praised the dead more than the living, and I judged him happier than both, who has not yet been born and has not seen the evils that are done under the sun. Rise up then, you lazy and idle princes who preside over the tumults, and at last resist so many evils, for power has been given you by the Lord, and strength by the Most High, who will question your works and search out your thoughts; because, though you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly, nor keep the law of justice, nor faithfully carry out the duties committed to you, nor walked according to the will of God. Swiftly and terribly will it appear to you, for a most severe judgment will fall on those who rule; mercy is granted to the lowly, but the mighty will suffer mighty torments. O King of the nations, and their desire, come, hasten, gird your sword upon your thigh, most mighty one! Call back to the memory of men the splendid deeds of some of your predecessors, even of the German nation, who governed the commonwealth happily and vigorously. Moreover, in the second year after you assumed the height of the kingdom, if you remember well, King Rupert: your friends the Margraves of Meissen, and almost all the nobles and barons of the kingdom of Bohemia, on account of the disorderly rule of King Wenceslas, seeing that he was striving in every way to hinder your advances, agreed together against that same King that they would subject him to you by a strong hand, provided only that you would vigorously stand by them in this, so that you alone would become glorious and recover from him the imperial insignia, which King Wenceslas had then, and still has today, seized contrary to all justice, as would befit your glory. And although you gladly accepted so great an offer at the time, and faithfully and steadfastly promised them that you would help vigorously, either in your own person or through one of your sons with a thousand lances, provided only that they began this enterprise, yet after they had kept their promises and had pressed the said King Wenceslas in the Bohemian capital of Prague with a strong siege for a month and more, believing that you would surely come to their aid magnificently for the benefit of the commonwealth, you did not come there, nor did you send anyone in your place. Those who took this great enterprise upon themselves, on the strength of your hope and faith, did so foolishly. Hence afterwards so great an army, lacking a fit captain, having received some promises from King Wenceslas himself, which he in no way kept, withdrew from such a siege, the great undertaking left in despair. You therefore, at least, lost the insignia of this kind and the obedience of the said King Wenceslas, and you lack them today; and many of those who were then destroyed in that same siege, in their property and their bodies, were destroyed on your account. But such sloth and negligence, which redounds to the greatest harm of all Christendom and the commonwealth, is turned by the uneducated into other names for you, namely piety and mercy: and so a lazy and negligent King is called by them pious and merciful. Of this, I think, you have no care, since outside Heidelberg there is no life. You also came to Italy before a fitting time and against the advice of your princes, where you then found a most powerful adversary, spurred on more by greed than by the glory of virtue. But shortly after you went back to your own hearth, doing nothing useful in Italy itself; and after the said adversary died within a few months, and no strong adversary appeared to you in the same Italy, you did not care to visit it thereafter as an emperor, nor to reform the rights of the said Empire there. Perhaps you believe that these and your other deeds are not being written down to your glory; indeed, unless my opinion deceives me, many parchments are already blackening them. I know, as your laws say, that the Roman Prince is called common to all after God, and that by his majesty oaths are sworn, which, after God, is to be loved and revered by the human race.

units.la: Nam Imperator cum Augusti nomen accepit, tanquam praesenti & temporali Deo fidelis est praestanda devotio, impendendusque peruigil famulatus, qui Deo regnat authore: sed subaudi, quando magis publico, quam priuato bono princeps intendit. Igitur exurge Domine, & visita viridarium tuum, & oves pascuae tuae, quia nihil pigrius est amante. Tolle moras, semper enim nocuit differre paratis. Vsque quo piger dormis? quando consurges a somno tuo? Deus erit adiutor, si veneris, nec timeas quenquam, quia qui timet hominem, cito corruet: qui sperat in Domino, subleuabitur, quia Rex qui in veritate pauperes iudicat, thronus eius firmabitur in aeternum. Tuaque tem apud Rhenum iam diu cubando, de subditis tuis in Italia, & alibi in remotis partibus, infinitis oppressis calamitatibus, modicum vel nil cogitas, dicendo, quid ad nos, de his quae foris sunt? quod volui, apprehendi: transite ad me omnes qui concupiscitis me; dulcis amor patriae, haec requies mea in seculum seculi: hic habitabo, quoniam elegi eam. Absit hoc a te, absit omnino, quod effeminato conuenit Sardanapalo, non autem Regi magnanimo & diligenti. Sed parce vera dicenti: Quid frustra scriptis & dictis te fore Caesarem Augustum gloriaris? nempe sub typo negligentiae, ac torpore circa imperium commissis per tuum praedecessorem immeritum ad culmen imperii deuenisti, asserens tunc te velle facere mirabilia, & quod schisma in Ecclesia per triginta annos iam induratum tolleretur, omnino fideliter & constanter laborare, & omissa, necnon neglecta etiam desidia ac pigritia per dictum praedecessorem recuperare pro posse: qui tamen pro decisione praedicti schismatis nihil hactenus efficaciter fecisse videris, ac etiam nihil extunc de iuribus Imperii recuperasti, imo pene totum residuum, te dissimulante, quomodolibet perdidisti, ita quod prius bruchus non comedit, te regnante eruca consumpsit. O peruigil custos Imperii, o prope & quasi Caesar Augustus. O bellator & triumphator eximius. Quid cogitas sic agendo? credis forsan verbo defendere ac inquirere cuncta, ignorans quia scriptum est: Non verbis, sed factis prosperare debe
units.tr: For when an Emperor has taken the name of Augustus, the devotion owed is to be rendered to him as to a present and temporal god, and a vigilant service is to be given, which reigns under God as its author; but understand, when the prince attends more to the public good than to his private advantage. Therefore arise, O Lord, and visit your vineyard, and the sheep of your pasture, for nothing is more sluggish than a lover. Remove delays, for delay has always harmed those who are ready. How long will you sleep, lazy one? When will you rise from your sleep? God will be your helper if you come, and do not fear anyone, for he who fears man will quickly fall; he who hopes in the Lord will be lifted up, for a king who judges the poor in truth, his throne will be established forever. Yet you, lying idle for so long by the Rhine, think little or nothing of your subjects in Italy and elsewhere in distant parts, who are oppressed by countless calamities, saying: what is it to us, what lies outside? What I wanted, I have grasped; come to me, all you who desire me. Sweet love of the fatherland, this is my rest for ever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have chosen it. Far be this from you, far altogether, for it suits an effeminate Sardanapalus, not a magnanimous and diligent King. But forgive one who speaks the truth: why do you boast in vain, in words and deeds, that you are Caesar Augustus? Indeed, under the pretext of negligence and torpor in governing the Empire entrusted to you by your unworthy predecessor, you came to the height of empire, declaring that you then wished to do wonders, and that you would labour faithfully and steadfastly, by all means, to remove the schism that had by then hardened in the Church for thirty years, and to recover, as far as possible, what had been omitted and neglected through the sloth and laziness of that predecessor. Yet you seem to have done nothing effective so far towards settling that schism, nor have you recovered anything of the rights of the Empire since then; indeed, while you have pretended not to notice, you have lost almost all that remained in whatever way. So that what the locust did not eat before, the caterpillar consumed in your reign. O vigilant guardian of the Empire, O almost and nearly Caesar Augustus! O outstanding warrior and triumphant one! What do you intend by acting thus? Perhaps you think to defend and investigate everything by words, ignoring that it is written: We ought to prosper not by words, but by deeds.

units.la: mm, mus, & nomina debent esse consona rebus. Vtaris igitur eodem nomine Romani Principis verbo tantum, prout fecisti hactenus. Sed ipse Ladislaus Rex nunc Tertius in ordine Regum Romanorum insimul concurrentium, seu tales se appellantium, non scriptis sed factis se gloriatur. Tu dormis, & ille vigilat: quem, vt fertur, ipsi Romani iam Imperatorem Romanum appellant. Cuius autem culpa, nisi negligentia tua? si fas est loqui verum. O quot effudit ille Ladislaus Rex millia florenorum, ante quam Romam totaliter attingere posset? Quae, qualisque hic & vbique locorum insamia, ex tanta tua desidia & vaecordia tibi orta est, qui olim credebaris esse liberator magnificus fidelium imperii, etiam in partibus istis?
