units.la: Unde dicimus, quantum nobis hic satis est, quod universalitas est in operatione & abstractione, quam facit intellectus ex rerum singularium exteriori cognitione, videndo qualiter ipsae res adinvicem conveniunt vel differunt essentialiter vel accidentaliter: ut quod quilibet homo convenit essentialiter in hoc cum altero, quod est animal rationale: quod intellectus attendens abstrahit innata sibi virtute similitudinem hanc: quae non est extra, nisi singulariter in singulis hominibus: & denudet eam à loco, à tempore, & ab omni generalium accidentium confusione: & ita remanet universalis & absolutus conceptus hominis in anima: qui nihilominus originatur ex rebus ad extra singularibus. Sic de ecclesiastica potestate sentire possumus, dum in se formaliter & absolute consideratur. Omnes enim sacerdotes conveniunt in sacerdotio omnes episcopi in episcopatu: & ita de reliquis. Quaeret forte aliquis, quo pacto ecclesia Romana dicatur eadem isto modo, cum ab initio fuerit Petrus in Antiochia? Responsio facilis est, fiat abstractio talis à connotatione loci: & dicamus quod ecclesia Romana est illa dioecesis, provincia vel sedes, quae peculiariter habet regi per autoritatem papalem, & eam complectitur, sic veritatem habet vulgata vox, ubi Papa ibi Roma. Nec in dubium verti debet, quin isto modo Romana sedes & ecclesia sit caput, mater & magistra caeterarum: quia suprema Petri potestatem includit.
units.tr: So we say, as is enough for our purpose here, that universality lies in the operation and abstraction which the intellect performs from its external knowledge of singular things, by seeing how those things agree or differ with one another, essentially or accidentally. Thus every man agrees essentially with every other in this, that he is a rational animal. The intellect, attending to this, abstracts by its innate power that likeness, which exists outside only singly in individual men, and strips it of place, time and all the confusion of general accidents. So the universal and absolute concept of man remains in the soul, which nevertheless originates from singular things outside. We may think in the same way of ecclesiastical power, when it is considered formally and absolutely in itself. For all priests agree in priesthood, and all bishops in episcopacy, and so with the rest. Perhaps someone will ask how the Roman church can be called the same in this way, since Peter was at Antioch from the beginning. The answer is easy: let such an abstraction be made from the connotation of place, and let us say that the Roman church is that diocese, province or see which is peculiarly governed by papal authority and embraces it. So the common saying holds true: "Where the Pope is, there is Rome." Nor should it be doubted that in this sense the Roman see and church is the head, mother and teacher of the others, because it includes the supreme power of Peter.

units.la: CONSIDERATIO VIII.
units.tr: CONSIDERATION VIII.

units.la: POtestas ecclesiastica considerata respectiue & quodammodo materialiter, prout applicatur ad hoc vel illud suppositum, potest dici variabilis & auferibilis in casibus multis. Hoc perspicuum est quotidie dum fiunt immutationes, nunc per novam consecrationem, nunc per novam electionem vel institutionem ministrorum. Ita consequenter dicere possumus de potestate papali, quod mutabilis est & auferibilis per mortem naturalem, sicut constat: vel per civilem, videlicet per depositionem (saltem quo ad plenitudinem suae iurisdictionis, quae depositio qualiter & ex quibus causis fieri possit, latius in aliis opusculis apertum est.
units.tr: Ecclesiastical power, considered relatively and in a sense materially, as applied to this or that subject, may be called variable and removable in many cases. This is plain every day, when changes are made, now by new consecration, now by new election or institution of ministers. So we may consistently say of papal power that it is changeable and removable: by natural death, as is clear, or by civil death, namely by deposition (at least as regards the fullness of its jurisdiction). How such deposition can be made, and from what causes, has been set out more fully in other little works.

units.la: Unde sicut papa renunciare potest papatui, & dare libellum repudii ecclesiae etiam sine culpa ipsius sponsae, licet hoc facere non debeat sine causa. Si ecclesia potest hunc vicarium sponsi sui dimittere, & ei libellum repudii dare etiam sine culpa sua, licet non sine causa. Exemplificauimus aliis in sex casibus: in quibus verus papa deponi potest ex culpa sua, etiam vbi non esset realiter haereticus ad intra, quamuis ad extra talis iudicaretur. Exemplificauimus in aliis sex casibus, quibus deponi potest papa sine culpa sua, licet non sine causa, etiam praeter liberam eius cessionem. Tractatulus intitulari potest de auferibilitate papae ab ecclesia, & incipit: Venient autem dies, cum auferetur ab eis sponsus: propterea brevitatis amor hic ista non repetit.
units.tr: Hence, just as the pope can renounce the papacy and give a bill of divorce to the Church, even without fault on the part of the bride, though he ought not to do so without cause, so the Church can dismiss this vicar of her bridegroom and give him a bill of divorce, even without her own fault, though not without cause. We have given examples elsewhere, in six cases, in which a true pope can be deposed for his own fault, even where he would not really be a heretic inwardly, though outwardly he would be judged one. We have also given, in six other cases, in which the pope can be deposed without his own fault, though not without cause, even apart from his free resignation. A little treatise could be entitled On the Removability of the Pope from the Church, and it begins: "The days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them." For love of brevity I do not repeat these matters here.

units.la: Verum potestatem hanc ecclesiasticam, quae respicit institutionem ministrorum ecclesiae à summo usque deorsum confundit magna caligine cupiditas ambitiosa: quaerens quae sua sunt, & quae crescentibus beneficiorum dotationibus impudenter excrevit: ita ut vix discerni modo possit, quid ex primaria institutione Christi vel inuaribiali iure divino renendum sit in huiusmodi ministrorum ordinatione. Mira siquidem quo ad usum talis potestatis varietas incessit, quae ex Chronicis summorum pontificum, & ex tenore generalium conciliorum et decretorum se ostendit. Nec est opusculi praesentis per haec omnia discurrere. Sed dicamus hic aliter esse discernendum in ecclesiastica politia, dum est ordinata complete sub quadam explicatione perfecta & numerosa membrorum suorum in ministris per status, gradus & officia. Aliter dū ab initio firmata est ecclesia in magna tam ecclesiasticorum quam fidelium paucitate, velut in quodam seminario vel germine seu botro. Potuit enim tunc rationabiliter supremus ille pontifex Petrus habere faciliter praesentiam concilii generalis, sicut in electione Matthiae & cessatione legalium. Potuit & instituere ministros per diversas provincias & loca de mandato suo, sicut ad eum facilis patebat accessus. Nec vigebat auariria: quia primi primo petebantur ad mortem. Quae omnia cessant in hac tam copiosa fidelium multitudine post totiura, tot leges, tot decreta & decretales summorum pontificum & generalium conciliorum editas ad regendam feliciter ecclesiam.
units.tr: But this ecclesiastical power, which concerns the institution of the ministers of the Church from the top down, is confounded by a great darkness of ambitious greed, which seeks its own interests and has shamelessly grown with the increasing endowment of benefices. So it can now scarcely be discerned what in the appointment of such ministers must be retained from Christ's primary institution or from unchangeable divine right. A remarkable variety has indeed arisen in the use of this power, as appears from the Chronicles of the supreme pontiffs and from the tenor of general councils and decrees. Nor is it the purpose of the present little work to run through all of these. But let us say here that the Church must be judged differently in its polity when it is fully ordered, with its members explicitly and numerously arranged in ministers by estates, grades and offices, and differently when the Church was established at the beginning, when there were few clergy and few faithful, as in a seedbed, or germ, or bud. For then that supreme pontiff Peter could reasonably have easily had the presence of a general council, as in the election of Matthias and the abolition of the legal rites. He could also institute ministers through various provinces and places by his own command, since access to him was easy. Nor did avarice flourish, since the first men were sought out for death. All these things cease in this so numerous multitude of the faithful, after so many laws, so many decrees, and decretals of the supreme pontiffs and general councils have been issued to govern the Church happily.

units.la: Suppetit hoc loco conuenientissime consilium Ietro datum Moysi Exod. 18. quod sic habet: Stulto labore consumeris tu & populus tuus qui tecum est, vltra vires tuas est negotium: solus illud sustinere non poteris. Sed audi verba mea & consilia mea, & erit Dominus tecum. Esto tu populo in hiis quae ad Deum pertinent vt referas quae dicuntur ad eum, ostendasque populo ceremonias & ritum colendi, viamque per quam ingredi debeant & opus quod facere debeant: provide autem de omni plebe viros potentes & timentes Deum in quibus sit veritas: & qui oderint avaritiam, & constitue ex eis tribunos & centuriones, quinquagenarios & decanos qui iudicent populum in omni tempore. Quicquid autem maius fuerit, referant ad te, & ipsi facilius a tantum modo iudicent. Leuius quoque tibi sit partito in alios onere: si haec feceris, impolebis imperium Dei: & praecepta eius poteris sustinere: & omnis hic populus reuertetur cum pace ad loca sua. Quibus auditis Moyses fecit omnia quae ille fugesserat.
units.tr: Here the counsel given by Jethro to Moses, Exod. 18., fits most appropriately, and it reads thus: "You will wear yourself out with foolish labour, you and the people who are with you; the business is beyond your strength, and you alone will not be able to bear it. But listen to my words and my counsels, and the Lord will be with you. Be for the people in those things which pertain to God, that you may bring before him the matters that arise, and show the people the ceremonies and the rite of worship, and the way in which they ought to walk and the work they ought to do. But provide from all the people men who are able and who fear God, men of truth, who hate avarice, and appoint from them tribunes and centurions, leaders of fifties and of tens, who shall judge the people at all times. But whatever is greater, let them refer to you, and let them judge the lesser matters themselves. The burden will be lighter for you when it is shared with others. If you do this, you will fulfil the command of God, and you will be able to endure it, and all this people will return in peace to their places." When Moses had heard these things, he did all that Jethro had said.

units.la: Edocemur ex hac scriptura calamo Dei scripta de multis. Specialiter, quod si Moyses loquens Deo familiariter sicut amicus ad amicum, obedienter audiuit consilium gentilis hominis in regimine totius synagogae: quanto magis debet hoc summus pontifex ad dictamen totius ecclesiae vel generalis concilii suo nomine?
units.tr: We are taught from this Scripture, written by the finger of God, about many things. Specifically: if Moses, who spoke with God familiarly as a friend with a friend, obediently listened to the counsel of a Gentile man in governing the whole synagogue, how much more ought the supreme pontiff to do this, in his own name, at the dictation of the whole Church or of a general council?

units.la: Rursus si iudicia minora reprobantur in Moyse, videamus in summo pontifice & curia sua quid de tot prophanissimis & indignissimis causarum & litigiorum continuis & anxiis occupationibus? quid de beneficiorum quorumcunque etiam minorum collationibus & signationibus manu papae? quid de annatarum exactionibus? quid de innumeris similibus dicendum iudicabitur, relicta omni cura, sollicitudine vel studio de omni eo, quod spirituale est, quod diuinum est, quod denique fidem concernit & religionem Christianam?
units.tr: Again, if lesser judgments were rejected in Moses, let us see what shall be said of the supreme pontiff and his curia, concerned with so many profane and most unworthy, continual and anxious occupations of lawsuits and disputes; what of the conferring and signing by the Pope's hand of any benefices, even minor ones; what of the exactions of annates; what of countless similar matters, all care, concern and study for everything that is spiritual, everything that is divine, and, in short, everything that concerns the faith and the Christian religion having been set aside?

units.la: Concludimus tandem ex dato Moysi consilio & praecepto legis Deuter. 18. & ex institutione Christi Matth. 18. quod nulla fuit hactenus nec erit in posterum perniciosior pestis in ecclesia, quam omissio generalium conciliorum & provincialium, vel in re ipsa vel auctoritate. Auctoritas itaque nulla erit, si solus summus pontifex omnia velit inferiorum ecclesiasticorum vsurpare institutiones, iura, status, gradus & officia. Meminerit itaque summus pontifex datam sibi a Deo potestatem supremam in ecclesia ad aedificationem eius, prout Sapiens iudicabit. Iudicat autem sapiens de potestatis vsu variabiliter inuariabilis existens, sicut est generale concilium: & hoc pro temporum, locorum, reliquarumque circumstantiarum diuersa qualitate. Teneat ergo suum iudicium & manear ecclesiastica politia optimo regimine: quale fuit sub Moyse gubernata: quoniam mixta fuit ex triplici politia. Regali in Moyse: Aristocratica in 72. senioribus: & in timiocratica, dum de populo & singulis tribubus sub Moyse rectores sumebantur.
units.tr: We conclude at last, from the counsel given to Moses and the precept of the law in Deut. 18, and from the institution of Christ in Matt. 18, that there has been hitherto, and will be in future, no more pernicious plague in the Church than the omission of general and provincial councils, either in fact or in authority. There will therefore be no authority if the supreme pontiff alone wishes to usurp all the institutions, rights, positions, grades and offices of the inferior churchmen. Let the supreme pontiff therefore remember that the supreme power in the Church was given him by God for its edification, as the wise man shall judge. Now the wise man judges concerning the use of power, which, while varying, is invariable, as a general council is; and this according to the diverse quality of times, places and the other circumstances. Let him therefore keep his judgment, and let the ecclesiastical polity remain under the best government, such as it was governed under Moses; for it was mixed from a threefold polity: a royal one in Moses, an aristocratic one in the seventy-two elders, and a timocratic one, since rulers were taken from the people and from the individual tribes under Moses.

units.la: Sed opponunt plurimi nolentes ad ordinatos remitti ministrorum ecclesiasticorum institutiones, neque per electionem, neque per collationem. Expertum est, inquiunt, quod turbarent omnia, venderent, dissiparent, partim cupiditate carnali, partim seculari potestate tracti: de literarum quoque studiis actum esset. Verum in promptu est responsio: corrigeret summus pontifex abusus huiusmodi, & auctoritatis securitate suprema vigilanter adhibita poneret alpera in vias planas: deponeret potentes intrusos de sede: & exaltaret humiles sine prece vel munere. Hoc est enim architectoris officium. Dum vero peccat in his summus pontifex: quis ministrorum corrigere vel praesumet vel poterit? Dices quod hoc poterit generale concilium. Vide quia nec crebro nec facile habetur. Vix enim statuit libenter aliquis sibi correctionis iudicium. Denique si propter abusus ordinariorum in ministrorum institutione putent aliqui sublatum esse ab eisdem hoc exercitium: similem in papa rationem, quod ab eo debeat vsus tolli nunc inueniri dicitur ab aliis maxime dum recipit annatas, quoniam ex hac copula quamdiu perseuerauerit, otietur inuitabiliter leprosa pestis simoniae, inficiens sua contagione nedum caput, sed pene singula ecclesiae membra. Superest vt apponatur, sicut apponi quaeritur in reformatione prouisio.
units.tr: But many object, unwilling that the institution of ecclesiastical ministers be referred to the ordinaries, neither by election nor by collation. It has been found, they say, that they would throw everything into confusion, sell, and squander, partly drawn by carnal greed, partly by secular power; and the study of letters would also be undone. But the answer is at hand: let the supreme pontiff correct abuses of this kind, and, by vigilantly applying the security of his supreme authority, let him make the rough places plain; let him depose the powerful intruders from their seats and exalt the humble without prayer or bribe. For this is the office of the architect. But when the supreme pontiff sins in these matters, who among the ministers will presume, or be able, to correct him? You will say that a general council could do this. See that it is neither frequently nor easily convened. For hardly anyone willingly submits himself to the judgment of correction. Finally, if some think that, on account of the abuses of the ordinaries in the institution of ministers, this function has been taken away from them, the same reasoning applies to the Pope: that his use ought to be removed from him. It is said now to be discovered by others, especially while he receives annates, since as long as this union persists, the leprous plague of simony will inevitably linger, infecting by its contagion not only the head but almost every member of the Church. It remains that a provision be applied, as it is sought to be applied in the reformation.

units.la: CONSIDERATIO IX.
units.tr: CONSIDERATIO IX.

units.la: POtestas ecclesiastica si consideretur quo ad vsum vel exercitium, illa mutabilis est & multipliciter variabilis.
units.tr: Ecclesiastical power, if it is considered as to its use or exercise, is changeable and varies in many ways.

units.la: Haec consideratio cum duabus praecedentibus soluit protinus quaestionem hanc: Si potestas ecclesiastica sit immediate a Deo vel mediate ab hominibus? Nam considerando ecclesiasticam potestatem primo modo, concedendum est absq; vlla dubitatione, quod illa fuit & est immediate a Deo homine Christo, sic quod a nullo altero fuit instituta. Nec congregatio totius vniuersitatis hominum, seclusso Christo, docuisset sibi potestatem huiusmodi instituere: quemadmodum potuit vel posset instituere sibi potestatem imperialem super omnes regalem, potestatem Ducatuum, Comitatuum & Baroniarum: & ita de reliquis potestatibus pure secularibus. Non autem potuisset sibi instituere sacerdotium nec papatum, sicut habet ecclesia. Nec similiter destituere, sicut nec mutare legem Christi: quod mutatio sequitur de necessitate prout arguit Apostolus, quod translato sacerdotio est vt legis translatio fiat.
units.tr: This consideration, together with the two preceding ones, immediately resolves the question whether ecclesiastical power is from God immediately or mediately from men. For if we consider ecclesiastical power in the first way, it must be conceded without any doubt that it was and is immediately from God, the man Christ, so that it was instituted by no other. Nor could the assembly of the whole universe of men, Christ being set aside, have resolved to institute such a power for itself, just as it could have instituted for itself, or could now institute, imperial power over all kings, the power of dukedoms, counties and baronies, and likewise the other purely secular powers. But it could not have instituted for itself the priesthood or the papacy, as the Church has them. Nor could it similarly abolish them, any more than it could change the law of Christ; for a change of law follows of necessity, as the Apostle argues, that when the priesthood is changed, a change of law must also take place.

units.la: Si vero potestas Ecclesiastica consideretur secundo modo, tunc in principio nascentis Ecclesiae collata est immediate à Deo tam Petro quam Apostolis & Discipulis, quibus immediate Christus contulit sacerdotium super corpus suum verum & super mysticum. Unde & Apostolus dicit se recepisse Euangelium non per hominem: & similiter mysterium & ministrationem corporis Christi: Ego enim accepi à Domino quod & tradidi vobis &c.
units.tr: If, however, ecclesiastical power is considered in the second way, then at the beginning of the nascent Church it was conferred immediately by God upon Peter as well as upon the Apostles and Disciples, to whom Christ immediately gave the priesthood over his true body and over his mystical body. Hence the Apostle also says that he received the Gospel not through man, and likewise the mystery and ministry of the body of Christ: "For I received of the Lord that which I also delivered to you," etc.

units.la: Et ita consequenter probabile est, quod sicut Christus immediate contulit hanc potestatem primitus suis Apostolis & Discipulis, applicando scil. eam istis & non aliis: sic & immediate concessit usum, actum vel exercitium: quia dans formam, dat consequentia ad formam.
units.tr: And so it is consequently probable that just as Christ immediately conferred this power first upon his Apostles and Disciples, namely by applying it to them and not to others, so he also immediately granted its use, act or exercise; for he who gives the form also gives the consequences of the form.

units.la: Dicimus tandem his non obstantibus, vel ita te habentibus, quod successores Petri & aliorum Apostolorum de communi lege seclusò miraculo vel nova revelatione, fuerunt & sunt instituti mediate per homines, vt per consecrationem vel electionem vel aliam institutionem. Vsum similiter vel exercitium receperunt atque recipiunt mediate per humanum ministerium vel concessionem.
units.tr: We say finally, notwithstanding these points, or with these matters thus standing, that the successors of Peter and of the other Apostles were and are instituted, under the common law and apart from a miracle or new revelation, mediately through men, namely through consecration, election or some other institution. Likewise they receive and do receive the use or exercise mediately through human ministry or concession.

units.la: Et forte quo ad vsum vel exercitium potestatis Ecclesiasticæ sic evenit ipsis etiam Apostolis & Discipulis, quod post immediatam concessionem vtriusque, scil. potestatis & vsus factam à Christo postmodum crescente numero fidelium fuit ad tollendum schisma: & ad exemplar dandum posteris limitatio facta talis potestatis quo ad vsum: & hoc per Petrum summum pontificem de consensu totius Ecclesiæ primitiuæ vel generalis concilij: vt non quilibet posset in quemlibet vti potestate sua, attenta Christi ordinatione primaria, qua voluit Ecclesiam suam regi principaliter sub vno & ab vno monarcha: sicut est vna fides, vnum baptisma, & vna Ecclesia, vnitate capitis tam primatij quam vicarij: quoniam iste est optimus principatus, præsertim in spiritualibus ad conseruationem vnitatis fidei, ad quam obligantur omnes. Non sic autem est de legibus ciuilibus, quod debeant esse similes & eadem apud omnes nationes, propter varietatem morum & conditionum in diuersis prouinciis. Quoniam insuper gladius Ecclesiæ spiritualis est, videlicet excommunicatio, quæ potest extendere se quantùmlibet in longinquas nationes. Aliter est de gladio materiali. Proptereaque oportuit, nec forsitan expediuit, quod in temporali potestate esset vna perseuerans monarchia per orbem vniuersum: sicut de spirituali potestate præ ceteris institutum fuisse iure diuino primitus in persona Petri Iohan. vltim. Pasce oues meas, prout sancti Doctores & Ecclesia tenendum tradiderunt.
units.tr: And perhaps as regards the use or exercise of ecclesiastical power it happened even to the Apostles and Disciples themselves that, after the immediate concession of both, namely of the power and of its use, made by Christ, the number of the faithful later increasing, a limitation of such power as to its use was made, in order to remove schism and to give an example to posterity; and this was done by Peter, the supreme pontiff, with the consent of the whole primitive Church or of a general council, so that not just anyone might use his power over just anyone, given the primary ordering of Christ, by which he willed his Church to be ruled principally under one and by one monarch, just as there is one faith, one baptism and one Church, by the unity of a head, both primary and vicarious. For this is the best principality, especially in spiritual matters, for the preservation of the unity of faith, to which all are bound. It is not so, however, with civil laws, which ought not to be alike and the same among all nations, on account of the variety of customs and conditions in different provinces. Moreover, the sword of the Church is spiritual, namely excommunication, which can extend itself as far as one likes into distant nations. It is otherwise with the material sword. Therefore it was necessary, and perhaps not expedient, that in temporal power there should be one lasting monarchy throughout the whole world; whereas over spiritual power, above all others, it was instituted by divine law, first in the person of Peter (John, last chapter): "Feed my sheep," as the holy Doctors and the Church have handed down that it must be held.

units.la: Sumamus exemplum materiale, conforme, vt tradit Dionys. spirituali, quod inuenitur in sole: qui fons luminis est, non illuminatus ab alio corpore, sed illuminans. Deinde sunt aliqua, quæ ab eo illuminantur, & consequenter illuminant: nonnulla verò quæ illuminantur, sed illuminandi virtute carent, quoniam in ipsis lux occumbit.
units.tr: Let us take a material example, one that corresponds, as Dionysius hands down, to the spiritual, which is found in the sun: it is the fount of light, not illumined by another body, but illuminating. Then there are some things which are illumined by it and consequently illumine in turn; but some things are illumined yet lack the power of illuminating, because light perishes in them.

units.la: Exemplum aliud est in angelica triplici hierarchia: vnde licet quo ad naturam, gratiam & gloriam sit quilibet angelus immediate formatus à Deo: nihilominus quo ad exercitium actuum hierarchicorum, qui sunt purgare, illuminare & perficere: tres primi ordines hierarchizant, non hierarchizantur ab aliis. Tres medii hierarchizantur & hierarchizant. Tres infimi hierarchizantur, & non alios angelos hierarchizant. Papalis auctoritas suo modo cum cardinalibus imitatur triplicem primam. Alteram verò mediam imitatur Patriarchalis, Archiepiscopalis, Episcopalis & Sacerdotalis auctoritas in habentibus subiectos sibi. Quod dicitur propter curatos, vel etiam propter solos titulares Episcopos carentes plebe. Vltimi sunt instar tertiæ hierarchiæ, qui hierarchizantur in Ecclesia: sed non alior auctoritatiue hierarchizant, quemadmodum sunt populi & simplices religiosi secundum Dionysl.
units.tr: Another example is in the angelic threefold hierarchy. Although, as to nature, grace and glory, each angel is immediately formed by God, nevertheless, as to the exercise of the hierarchical acts, which are to purify, to illuminate and to perfect, the three first orders hierarchize, and are not hierarchized by others. The three middle orders are both hierarchized and hierarchize. The three lowest are hierarchized and do not hierarchize other angels. The papal authority, with the cardinals in its own way, imitates the first triad. The middle triad is imitated by the patriarchal, archiepiscopal, episcopal and priestly authority over those who have subjects under them. This is said on account of parish priests, or also on account of titular bishops alone who lack a flock. The last are like the third hierarchy, which are hierarchized in the Church but do not by authority hierarchize others, as are the common people and simple religious, according to Dionysius.

units.la: CONSIDERATIO X.
units.tr: CONSIDERATIO X.

units.la: Potestas Ecclesiastica in sua plenitudine est formaliter & subiectiue in solo Romano Pontifice.
units.tr: Ecclesiastical power in its fullness is formally and subjectively in the Roman Pontiff alone.

units.la: Supponitur itaque primo, quod licet aliquis possit eligi in Papam non sacerdos: sicut eligitur aliquis in Episcopum. Ipse nihilominus appellari non potest aut debet summus Pontifex, nisi fuerit in sacerdotem & Episcopum consecratus. Et quamuis ex electione posset aliquid iurisdictionis habere, non tamen habet ante consecrationem in Episcopum plenitudinem Ecclesiasticæ potestatis tam ordinis quam iurisdictionis vtriusque, quod perspicuum est ex terminis.
units.tr: First, then, it is assumed that although someone who is not a priest may be elected Pope, just as someone may be elected bishop, he cannot nevertheless be called, or ought to be called, supreme Pontiff unless he has been consecrated a priest and bishop. And although he could have some jurisdiction from his election, he does not, before consecration as bishop, possess the fullness of ecclesiastical power, both of order and of jurisdiction, as is clear from the terms themselves.

units.la: Hinc autem consurgit æquiuocatio non modica propter Dominos Iuristas, qui loquentes de plenitudine potestatis Papalis solùm loqui videntur, de potestate iurisdictionis, ex qua locutione videtur hæc absurditas sequi, quod pure laicus, imo & fœmina posset esse Papa, & habere plenitudinem Ecclesiasticæ potestatis.
units.tr: Hence arises no small equivocation on account of the lawyers, who, when they speak of the fullness of papal power, seem to speak only of power of jurisdiction. From this way of speaking there seems to follow the absurdity that a purely lay person, or even a woman, could be Pope and have the fullness of ecclesiastical power.

units.la: Supponitur insuper ex iam dictis, quod ex institutione Christi nullus in Ecclesia debet dare vel suscipere gradus hierarchicos, qui sunt purgare, illuminare & perficere: si non interueniat vere vel interpretatiue auctoritas supremi hierarchæ vel monarchæ in Ecclesia sancta Dei, quatenus in ea vitetur confusio, & optimo regimine gubernetur ad exemplar Ecclesiæ triumphantis: propter quod dicit Iohan. in Apocalypsi se vidisse nouam ciuitatem Hierusalem descendisse de cœlo. Et Moysi dictum est: Vide vt omnia facias iuxta exemplar quod tibi ostensum est in monte.
units.tr: It is further assumed from what has been said that by the institution of Christ no one in the Church ought to confer or receive hierarchical degrees, which are to purify, enlighten and perfect, unless the authority of the supreme hierarch or monarch in the holy Church of God intervenes, truly or by interpretation, so that confusion is avoided in it and it is governed in the best order after the pattern of the Church triumphant. For this reason John says in the Apocalypse: I saw the new city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven. And it was said to Moses: See that you make all things according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain.

units.la: Supponitur rursus illud Philosophi, quod actiones sunt suppositorum.
units.tr: Again, the saying of the Philosopher is assumed: that actions belong to supposits.

units.la: Tandem ex his praecedentibus possumus describendo dicere, quod plenitudo potestatis Ecclesiasticae est potestas ordinis & iurisdictionis, quae a Christo collata est supernaturaliter Petro, licut vicario suo & monarchae primo pro se & suis successoribus legitimis vsq; in finem seculi ad aedificationem Ecclesiae militantis, pro consecutione felicitatis aeternae.
units.tr: Finally, from these preceding points we can, by way of description, say that the fullness of ecclesiastical power is the power of order and jurisdiction, conferred supernaturally by Christ on Peter as his vicar and first monarch, for himself and his legitimate successors until the end of the age, for the building up of the militant Church and the attaining of eternal happiness.

units.la: Dicitur in hac descriptione supernaturaliter, ad differentiam potestatum vel iurisdictionum, quae successoribus Petri potuerunt convenire secundum leges humanas civiles & politicas, vel damen iuris naturalis: quod vult, vt supremus in aliqua politia gaudeat multis honoribus & privilegiis super alios vel ex speciali dotatione seu donatione principum & aliorum secularium: vel tandem ex ipsius ecclesiae seu conciliorum generalium favorabili concessione: sicut communitas perfecta suo capiti naturaliter dare potest. Cuius concessionis vna fuit ratio non mala, quatenus honoretur in interpretandis iuribus & emergentibus quotidie dubiis circa regimen ecclesiasticum: quia facilior est recursus ad Papam cum curia sua, quam ad ipsum generale concilium. Quae causa mouit ab initio reges instituere: & eis potestatem leges condendi & interpretandi tribuere.
units.tr: In this description the word supernaturally is used to distinguish it from the powers or jurisdictions which could belong to the successors of Peter under human civil and political laws, or at least under natural law. These include that the supreme man in some polity enjoys many honours and privileges above others, whether from a special endowment or gift of princes and other secular persons, or finally from the favourable concession of the Church itself or of general councils, as a perfect community can naturally grant to its head. One reason for such a concession, and not a bad one, was that the Pope be honoured in interpreting the laws and in the doubts arising daily concerning ecclesiastical government, since recourse to the Pope with his curia is easier than recourse to a general council itself. This consideration moved kings from the beginning to establish laws and to grant them the power of enacting and interpreting laws.

units.la: Hanc autem distinctionem non attendentes aliqui putauerunt omnia, quae nunc summis pontificibus conueniunt, competere ex primaria Christi institutione, & immutabili iure diuino: quod falsum est: quoniam staret aliquem esse verum Papam & perfectum, qui careret actualiter multis talibus priuilegiis & honoribus, in quibus non consistit plenitudo Ecclesiasticae potestatis: qualem in Petro fuisse descripsimus: & quam nullus hominum praeter Christum, imo nec Ecclesia tota conferre potuit, ita nec auferre, sicut in consideratione nona notatum est.
units.tr: Some, however, not attending to this distinction, have thought that all the things which now belong to the supreme pontiffs belong to them from Christ's primary institution and by an immutable divine right. This is false, since it would follow that someone could be a true and perfect Pope while actually lacking many such privileges and honours, in which the fullness of ecclesiastical power does not consist, such as we have described in Peter; and which no man except Christ, indeed not even the whole Church, could confer, nor likewise take away, as was noted in the ninth consideration.

units.la: Contendunt nunc aliqui pollentes literis, quod post institutas per generalia concilia regulas super electionibus faciendis, & beneficiis per ordinarios conferendis iuxta fundatorum intentionem: quemadmodum obseruatur de iure patronatus apud laicos, nequaquam licitum fuit Papae tales cassare regulas: praesertim ita generaliter & passim per reservationes & alias, sicut visum est a centum annis vel vltra. Non licuit praeterea facere tot & tales non obstantias eorum, quae constituta sunt in generalibus conciliis, quot & qualibus non obstantiis vti solet passim in bullis suis: adeo quidem vt Alexander quintus indultus sit in praetensis quibusdam bullis ponere non obstantiam huius salutherrimi ac celebriter obseruati statuti: Omnia vtriusque sexus.
units.tr: Now some men skilled in letters contend that, after rules had been established by general councils for making elections and for conferring benefices through ordinaries according to the intention of the founders, just as is observed concerning the right of patronage among laymen, it was by no means lawful for the Pope to annul such rules, especially in so general and widespread a way, through reservations and other means, as has been seen for a hundred years or more. Moreover, it was not lawful to make so many and such non obstante clauses against what has been established in general councils, of the kind and number commonly used everywhere in his bulls; so much so that Alexander V was accustomed to insert, in certain so-called bulls, a non obstante against this most salutary and widely observed statute: Omnia utriusque sexus.

units.la: Atvero respondent alii non ad originem Ecclesiasticae potestatis positam a iure diuino tantundem considerantes, quantum respiciunt decretales cum glossis, allegationibus, concordantiis sine numero doctorum vnius ad alterum, vt omnium gregi mos est. Respondent, inquam, per vnicum verbum, quod semper intellexit concilium generale auctoritatem summi pontificis exceptam esse in omni constitutione sua qualicunq;. Nimirum quia posuerunt isti Papalem auctoritatem supra concilium, aut saltem non imparem. Est autem certum apud eos, quod par in parem, & minor in superiorem, non habet imperium.
units.tr: Others, however, respond without considering the origin of ecclesiastical power as established by divine law, but looking only at the decretals with their glosses, allegations, and countless concordances of one teacher with another, as is the custom of the whole flock. They respond, I say, with one word, which the general council has always understood: that the authority of the supreme pontiff is excepted in every constitution of its own, of whatever kind. This is because these men have placed papal authority above the council, or at least not unequal to it. It is, however, certain among them that an equal has no command over an equal, nor a lesser over a greater.

units.la: Benedictus autem Deus, qui per hoc sacrosanctum Constantiense concilium illustratum diuinae legis lumine dante ad hoc ipsum vexatione praesentis schismatis intellectum, liberauit Ecclesiam suam ab hoc pestifera perniciosissimaque doctrina: quia semper manente perseuerasset semper schisma nutritum ab ea. Declaratum nempe decretumque est, quod & sine Papa generale concilium conuocari: & a concilio Papa iudicari certis casibus potest. Quod insuper habet auctoritatem generale concilium praescribere leges seu regulas, secundum quas plenitudo potestatis Papalis non quidem in se, quae semper eadem est, sed in usu suo moderanda: regulandaque est.
units.tr: Blessed be God, who, through this most holy Council of Constance, illuminated by the light of divine law, and, through the trouble of the present schism, granted understanding for this very purpose, freed his Church from this pestilent and most pernicious doctrine; for had it remained, the schism would always have been fed by it. It was declared and decreed that a general council can be convoked even without the Pope, and that the Pope can be judged by a council in certain cases. Moreover, a general council has authority to prescribe laws or rules according to which the fullness of papal power is to be moderated and regulated, not indeed in itself, which is always the same, but in its use.

units.la: Neque putandum est insuper concilia generalia sic excepisse Papalem auctoritatem in constitutionibus suis, vt eidem permitteretur effrenis libertas, ea destruendi leuissime, quae tanta gravitate & digesta sapientum maturitate condita sunt. Intelligitur ergo Papalis auctoritatis exceptio facta, prout occurrens necessitas vel euidens vtilitas postulabat: vbi protunc recursus ad generale concilium non patebat. Alioquin non erat ibi vti plenitudine Papalis potestatis, sed abuti plenissime.
units.tr: Nor must it be thought that general councils so excepted papal authority in their constitutions as to grant it an unbridled freedom to destroy lightly those things which were established with such gravity and arranged with the maturity of the wise. The exception made for papal authority is therefore understood as applying as pressing necessity or evident usefulness required; where, at that time, recourse to a general council was not open. Otherwise it would not be using the fullness of papal power there, but most fully abusing it.

units.la: Vtrum vero validum fuerit & ratum, quicquid ex abusu tali processit, diffinire sub vna generalitate non audeo. Scio quod multa fiunt iniqua, multa inexpediter, multa in deformationem Ecclesiae, quae tamen facta tenent. Caeterum videtur apponenda per hoc sacrosanctum generale concilium talis declaratio, per quam appareat, quo pacto auctoritas Papalis & quicunque cognoscatur excepta, in constitutionibus vel iam factis, vel de nouo condendis: quoniam, vt aiunt, non est ad praeterita lex. Omnium deniq; male gestorum praeteritis temporibus cessatio vel annullatio, neq; facilis, neq; forte iuridica, & inexperiendis plane expediretur.
units.tr: Whether whatever proceeded from such abuse is valid and ratified, I do not dare to define under one general rule. I know that many things are done unjustly, many inexpediently, and many to the deformation of the Church, which nevertheless stand once done. Moreover, it seems that such a declaration should be added by this holy general council, by which it may appear in what way papal authority, and whoever is known to be excepted, is to be treated in constitutions either already made or to be newly enacted; since, as they say, law does not apply to past things. Indeed, the cessation or annulment of all the wrongs done in past times is neither easy nor perhaps lawful, and would be plainly inexpedient for the future.

units.la: Attendantur regulae, quae sequuntur facientes ad elucidationem praecedentium de legum vel constitutionum interpretatione.
units.tr: Let the following rules be noted, as they pertain to clarifying what has gone before concerning the interpretation of laws or constitutions.

units.la: Prima: leges humanae dantur secundum illa, quae vt in pluribus accidunt. Quoniam omnes casus particulares enumerare & remedium specialis legis apponere, neque possibile est humano legislatori, cum sint in infinitum variabiles: sed nec expedit propter confusionem fastidiosissimam, imo & perplexam: quæ ex illa multiplicitate consurgeret. Erit autem lex secundum Isidor. honesta, iusta, possibilis servari, & secundum consuetudinem patriæ, loco temporis conveniens, necessaria, utilis, manifestaq;, ne aliquid per obscuritatem in captione contineat, nullo primario commodo, sed pro communi civium utilitate conscripta.
units.tr: First: human laws are given according to what happens in most cases. For it is neither possible for a human legislator to enumerate all particular cases and apply a special remedy to each, since they are infinitely variable, nor is it expedient, on account of the most tedious and even perplexing confusion that would arise from such multiplicity. A law, however, according to Isidore, will be honest, just, possible to keep, suited to the custom of the country and to time and place, necessary, useful, and clear, lest through obscurity it contain anything that could entrap; it is written for no primary advantage, but for the common utility of the citizens.

units.la: Altera regula: Leges humanæ quæ feruntur generaliter, possunt & debent exceptionem recipere, dum deficit ratio legis: quando videlicet legislator si adesset, vel alius prudens interrogatus, exciperet generali constitutione casum particularem: qui taliter aut taliter occurreret. Hæc autem exceptio multipliciter nominatur: quandoque ἐπιείκεια, sicut ab Aristot. quandoq; iuris interpretatio, sicut a legistis: quandoque dispensatio, sicut a canonistis: quandoque bona fides, sicut a politicis, dicentibus bonam fidem esse, vbi non simulatur vnum & aliud agitur: quandoque dicitur æquitas, sicut ait Propheta Domino: Omnia mandata tua æquitas: hoc est secundum æquitatem implenda.
units.tr: Second rule: human laws which are enacted in general terms can and ought to admit an exception when the reason of the law fails; that is, when the legislator, if he were present, or another wise man if asked, would except from the general constitution a particular case which would occur in such and such a way. This exception is named in many ways: sometimes epieikeia [ἐπιείκεια], as by Aristotle; sometimes interpretation of the law, as by the jurists; sometimes dispensation, as by the canonists; sometimes good faith, as by the political writers, who say that good faith is where nothing is pretended and something else is done; sometimes it is called equity, as the Prophet says to the Lord: All your commandments are equity: that is, to be fulfilled according to equity.

units.la: Tertia regula: Triplex invenitur iuris interpretatio vel exceptio. Quædam est iudicialis potestatis spectans ad legislatorem & iudices: quemadmodum dici solet: Cuius est condere, eius est interpretari. Quædam est Doctoralis auctoritas, spectans ad illos quibus data est auctoritate summi pontificis licentia interpretandi Scholastice iura, vel qui super his interpretandi scientia pollent, arte vel experientia, iuxta illud: Cuilibet experto in sua scientia credendum est. Et iterum: Vnusquisque bene iudicat de quibus novit. Quædam interpretatio est inevitabilis necessitatis, potens cadere circa quemlibet, dum certitudinaliter videt imminens periculum suum, nisi vim vi repulerit, & egerit contra generalia verba legis: quo casu est sine culpa apud Deum, quamuis dolere debeat quod incidit in hanc necessitatem. Et si docere potest legitimis testimoniis apud iudicem humanum absolutus erit: aliter non: quoniam apud illud idem est de illis quæ non sunt & quæ non apparent.
units.tr: Third rule: there are three kinds of interpretation or exception of law. One belongs to judicial power and pertains to the lawgiver and the judges, as the saying goes: whoever has the power to make a law has the power to interpret it. Another is doctoral authority, which pertains to those to whom the supreme pontiff has granted licence to interpret the laws scholastically, or who excel in such interpretation by skill or experience, according to the saying: one must trust whoever is expert in his own field. And again: everyone judges well in matters he knows. A third is an interpretation of unavoidable necessity, which can befall anyone when he clearly sees that danger is imminent unless he repels force with force, and so acts against the general words of the law. In that case he is without guilt before God, although he ought to grieve that he has fallen into such necessity. If he can prove this by lawful testimony before a human judge, he will be acquitted; otherwise not, since before that judge what is not and what does not appear are the same.

units.la: Quarta regula: Iuris interpretatio seu dispensatio vel exceptio, quæ est iudicialis potestatis: hoc operatur quod agens contra verba legis non punitur apud homines in exteriori foro, sed apud Deum in foro conscientiæ peccabit vterque, scil. dispensans & cum quo dispensatur, si talis non fuerit qui dispensat qualem descripsit Christus, fidelis & prudens. Fidelis ne commodum proprium, favorem vel honorem quæsiuerit derelicto diuino vel communi bono. Prudens, vt cum circumspiciatur vndique ratio legis & legislatoris intentio. Est enim dispensatio, commensuratio seu distributio boni communis: quale est lex ad singulos secundum legis intentionem, prout circumstantiarum varietas occurrerit: quæ dispensatio si non fideliter & prudenter fiat, eam appellat Bernhardus dissipationem: intellige quo ad Deum & conscientiam, si hoc constiterit, aut constare debuerit. Tenet vero frequenter apud homines secundum exteriora iudicantes, hæc dispensatio, si non contineat errorem apertum. Aut nisi fuerit superiori lege prohibita: quod dicitur propter statuta fieri possibilia circa Papalis vsum potestatis per generale concilium.
units.tr: Fourth rule: interpretation, dispensation or exception of law, which belongs to judicial power, has this effect: one who acts against the words of the law is not punished by men in the external forum, but both parties sin before God in the forum of conscience, namely the one who dispenses and the one with whom dispensation is made, if the dispenser is not such as Christ described, faithful and prudent. He is faithful if he does not seek his own advantage, favour or honour, abandoning the divine or common good. He is prudent if he considers on all sides the reason of the law and the intention of the lawgiver. For dispensation is the proportioning or distribution of the common good, such as the law is to individuals according to the intention of the law, as the variety of circumstances arises. If this dispensation is not carried out faithfully and prudently, Bernard calls it a squandering. Understand this with regard to God and conscience, if this is or ought to have been evident. Yet this dispensation often holds among men who judge by external appearances, provided it does not contain manifest error, or unless it has been forbidden by a higher law. This is said because of the statutes that make it possible for the general council to act against the use of papal power.

units.la: Quinta regula: Iuris interpretatio vel exceptio quæ est Doctoralis auctoritatis, releuat plurimum non obedientes nudo legis verbo, tam quo ad iudicia forensia, sicut est ab expensis relatio, quam in foro conscientiæ & diuino iudicio, præsertim dum sunt Doctores famati plures & experti in arte sua; & in morum honestate probati. Alioquin sæpe mentitur iniquitas sibi, dum corrupta est prece vel pretio. Excæcant enim munera etiam oculos prudentium. Et si creditur Aristoteli experientiæ verba loquenti Malitia facit errare, nedum circa conclusiones elongatas a primis principiis, sed in ipsissimet principiorum moralium ianuis: quemadmodum reputabatur olim latrocinium apud Alemanos licitum, teste Iulio de Bello Gallico: Ac peccatum innaturale & sordidum apud Romanos, secundum Apostolum ad eosdem. Et ita de pluribus hominibus datis in reprobum sensum, pro varietate damnationis vitiorum.
units.tr: Fifth rule: interpretation or exception of law which belongs to doctoral authority greatly benefits those who do not obey the bare words of the law, both in forensic judgments, such as the remission of expenses, and in the forum of conscience and divine judgment, especially when there are several teachers who are well reputed and experienced in their art and proven in the honesty of their morals. Otherwise iniquity often lies to itself, when it has been corrupted by prayer or price, for gifts blind even the eyes of the wise. And if we believe Aristotle speaking from experience, wickedness causes error, not only in conclusions far removed from first principles, but even at the very gates of the moral principles themselves. Thus robbery was once regarded as lawful among the Germans, as Julius testifies in On the Gallic War; and an unnatural and filthy sin was so regarded among the Romans, according to the Apostle to the same. And so it is with many men given over to a reprobate mind, according to the variety of their vices' condemnation.

units.la: Sexta regula: Iuris interpretatio, exceptio vel dispensatio similiter exigit, dum sit altero prædictorum modorum iudicialiter vel doctrinaliter, quod habeatur duplex intuitus: vnus ad bonum diuinum & publicum: alter ad particulare commodum illius pro quo sit iuris interpretatio vel dispensatio. Euenit itaq; sepius, quod dum passim laxatur rigor legis ex quadam, vt fingitur, compassione & misericordia condescensione ad aliquos particulares positos sub lege, deperit ex altera parte stabilitas & rigor disciplinæ: qui rigor est præcipue in omni lege seruandus. Docuerunt hoc Romani, qui proprios etiam filios occiderunt, qui in seipsos rigorem legum suarum exercuerunt, quatenus disciplina militaris & obedientia legalis inuiolata maneret. Docent hoc Fratres Carthusienses, qui super esu carnium, vel nunquam vel rarissime dispensationem recipiunt. Ac proinde disciplina regularis viget apud eos, quæ quantum sit collapsa apud religiones quasdam alias passim dispensationibus vtentes videre stupor & dolor est. Super qua re iam Bernhardi pro tempore suo querela nascebatur. Quid modo dicendum putabimus de tam facili, vt appellant, dispensatione per Papam & prælatos, super iuramentis licitis? super votis rationabilibus? super immensa beneficiorum pluralitate? super generali conciliorum non obstantia? super priuilegiorum & exemptionum commune ius priuantium concessione? Quis omnia dinumeraret, per quæ nunc vigor Ecclesiasticæ, imo & Euangelicæ disciplinæ totus terè languit, emarcuit, euanuit? Prouideat super omnibus sacro sanctum hoc Constantiense concilium.
units.tr: Sixth rule: interpretation, exception or dispensation of law likewise requires, when it is carried out judicially or doctrinally in one of the aforesaid ways, that a double regard be had: one to the divine and public good, the other to the particular advantage of the person for whom the interpretation or dispensation is made. It therefore often happens that, while the rigour of the law is everywhere relaxed out of some supposed compassion and mercy, and out of condescension to particular persons placed under the law, stability and the rigour of discipline are lost on the other side; yet this rigour is above all to be observed in every law. The Romans taught this, who even put their own sons to death, and who exercised the rigour of their laws upon themselves, so that military discipline and legal obedience might remain unbroken. The Carthusian brothers teach this, who either never or very rarely receive dispensation concerning the eating of meat. Accordingly regular discipline flourishes among them, and it is a cause of astonishment and grief to see how far it has collapsed among certain other orders which everywhere use dispensations. Bernard already complained of this matter in his own time. What shall we now think should be said of such easy dispensation, as they call it, by the Pope and prelates, concerning lawful oaths? concerning reasonable vows? concerning the immense plurality of benefices? concerning the general non-obstante of councils? concerning the grant of privileges and exemptions that deprive the common law of its force? Who could enumerate everything by which the vigour of ecclesiastical, indeed even of evangelical, discipline now almost wholly languishes, withers and vanishes? Let this most holy Council of Constance provide for all these things.

units.la: Ioan. 3. Fundatur in hac radice stabilitas legum, quod consuetudo est optima legum positionarum interpres: ita si neque iuri diuino neque naturali fuerit contraria. Fundatur & illud Aristotelis politizantis: Non esse dandum praemium inuenientibus nouas leges, quamuis in se meliores existerent: quoniam mutatio legum frequens causat instabilitatem: neque permittit eas in consuetudinis fixa radice roborari. Hoc animaduertant, qui ad omnem motum capitis, ad omne quod bonum agi fantasiatum fuerit, condere satagunt nouas leges, poenas poenis adiicere quasi super omni re quae bona est, si fieret bonum sit & expediens legem poenalem addere. Non enim respublica regitur per simile.
units.tr: John 3. The stability of laws is grounded in this root: custom is the best interpreter of positive laws, provided it is not contrary to divine or natural law. This also is grounded in the words of Aristotle, speaking of politics: new laws should not be rewarded for their inventors, even if they were better in themselves, since frequent change of laws causes instability, and does not allow them to be strengthened by the firm root of custom. Let those take note who, at every stirring of the head and at everything imagined to be done well, strive to make new laws and to add penalties to penalties, as if in every matter that is good it were good and expedient to add a penal law. For the commonwealth is not governed by such means.

units.la: Fundatur in eadem radice rationabilitas abolitionis vel abrogationis quarundam legum positiuarum per oppositos mores subditorum, qui versi sunt in naturam.
units.tr: The reasonableness of abolishing or repealing certain positive laws through contrary customs of subjects, who have turned into a second nature, is grounded in the same root.

units.la: Fundatur & rationabilitas permissionis quorundam malorum, non vt approbentur, sed ne punita ruant in deterius.
units.tr: The reasonableness of permitting certain evils is also grounded here, not so that they may be approved, but lest punished things collapse into something worse.

units.la: Fundatur & ius praescriptionis punientis, ne fiant incerta dominia, neglectores rerum propriarum, ac iuste transferentes etiam apud Deum, & conscientiam tale dominium in bona fidei possessorem & praescriptorem legitimum.
units.tr: The right of prescription, which punishes those who neglect their own property, is also grounded here, lest ownership become uncertain; and so that such ownership, justly transferred even before God and conscience, passes to the possessor in good faith and to the lawful prescriber.

units.la: CONSIDERATIO XI.
units.tr: CONSIDERATIO XI.

units.la: POtestas Ecclesiastica in sua plenitudine est in Ecclesia sicut in fine: & sicut in regulante applicationem & visum huiusmodi plenitudinis Ecclesiasticae potestatis per seipsam, vel per generale concilium ipsam sufficienter & legitime repraesentans. Constat vtiq; datam fuisse Petro plenitudinem Ecclesiasticae potestatis a Christo ad aedificationem Ecclesiae suae, sicut conformiter ad Apostolum ponit descriptio.
units.tr: Ecclesiastical power in its fullness resides in the Church, as in its end, and as in the one who regulates the application and the exercise of this fullness of ecclesiastical power, either by itself or through a general council that sufficiently and lawfully represents it. It is certain that the fullness of ecclesiastical power was given to Peter by Christ for the building up of his Church, as the description, conformably to the Apostle, sets forth.

units.la: Propterea loquitur Augustin. cum aliis quibusdam, quod claues Ecclesiae datae sunt non vni, sed vnitati: & quod datae sunt Ecclesiae. Et hoc conuenienter potest intelligi modis, quos explicat consideratio: quoniam claues datae sunt propter Ecclesiam & vnitatem eius tanquam propter finem.
units.tr: Therefore Augustine, along with certain others, says that the keys of the Church were given not to one person but to unity, and that they were given to the Church. This can be understood fittingly in the ways that the consideration explains, since the keys were given on account of the Church and its unity, as for an end.

units.la: Potest etiam dici in Ecclesia vel in concilio haec plenitudo Ecclesiasticae potestatis nedum in se finaliter, sed aliis duobus modis: vicem quo ad applicationem ad hanc vel illam personam. Et quo ad visum regulandum, si fortassis in abusum verti quaereretur. Constat his tribus modis plenitudinem Ecclesiasticae potestatis esse in ecclesia, & in generali concilio tanquam in gerente vices eius. Et quidem de duplici modo primo & secundo non est difficultas. Similiter nec de tertio, si consideremus descriptionem plenitudinis ecclesiasticae potestatis; vbi ponitur quod data est ad aedificationem ecclesiae. Cum igitur summus pontifex habens eam subiectiue, sit peccabilis & possit hanc potestatem in destructionem velle conuertere. Similiter sacrum collegium, quod ei datum est, & coassistit quasi communitas Aristocratica, non est in gratia vel fide confirmatum; superest, vt aliqua sit relicta inobliquabilis & indeuiabilis regula ab optimo legislatore Christo, secundum quam possit abusus huiusmodi potestatis reprimi, dirigi atq; moderari. Haec autem est vel ecclesia vel generale concilium. Vnde cum medium virtutis aliter non habeatur, nisi prout sapiens iudicabit: finalis resolutio ad hanc sapientiam fiet ad ecclesiam; vbi est sapientia indeuiabilis: vel ad generale concilium.
units.tr: This fullness of ecclesiastical power can be said to be in the Church, or in a council, not only finally in itself, but in two other ways: vicariously, as to its application to this or that person, and as to the regulating of its exercise, should it perhaps be asked whether it might be turned to abuse. It is established that the fullness of ecclesiastical power is in the Church in these three ways, and in a general council as acting in its place. As to the first two ways there is no difficulty, nor as to the third, if we consider the description of the fullness of ecclesiastical power, where it is stated that it was given for the building up of the Church. Since, then, the supreme pontiff, who holds it subjectively, is liable to sin and might wish to turn this power to destruction, and since the sacred college, which was given to him and assists him as a kind of aristocratic commonwealth, is not confirmed in grace or faith, it follows that some unchanging and unerring rule must have been left by Christ, the best of lawgivers, by which abuse of this power may be restrained, directed and moderated. This rule is either the Church or a general council. Hence, since the mean of virtue cannot otherwise be had than as the wise person judges, the final resolution is referred to this wisdom, which is found in the Church, where unerring wisdom is, or to a general council.

units.la: Hinc fundantur ea multa, quae per hoc sacrum concilium & constituta & practicata sunt. Vt quod Papa iudicari potest & deponi per concilium. Quia eidem in regulatione suae potestatis quo ad visum subiicitur: & sibi potest dici: Cur ita facis? & ita de pluribus quae recollecta sunt in illo sermone: Prosperum iter faciet nobis Deus.
units.tr: From this are founded the many things that have been both decreed and practised through this sacred council: for example, that the Pope can be judged and deposed by a council, because he is subject to it as to the exercise of his power in its regulation, and it can be said to him: Why do you act thus? and so on about many things gathered in that sermon: May God make our journey prosperous.

units.la: Possumus ad hanc considerationem addere, quod plenitudo ecclesiasticae potestatis si consideretur in sua latitudine, ipsa non est in solo Papa, nisi quodam modo fontaliter potestative & originaliter suo modo. Haec enim latitudo potestatis completitur in se alias potestates ecclesiasticas collectiue a summo vsq; ad deorsum. Et est in eis plenitudo ecclesiasticae potestatis Papalis tanquam pars integralis in suo toto: & ita non est maior vel superior ad totam ecclesiam, sicut nec pars maior toto. Si vero consideretur haec plenitudo in sua supremitate, tunc absq; vlla dubitatione plenitudo ecclesiasticae potestatis Papalis superior & maior est ad reliquas: sed iam illud, quod reliquum est, nullo pacto potest constituere generale concilium: iuxta illud quod dictum est prius, quod generale concilium in sua ratione formali includit de necessitate Papalem auctoritatem, siue Papa sit, siue non sit: quia si Papa est & vult facere debitum suum de conuocando concilium: certe debet authorizari per ipsum. Si vero pertinaciter renuit in destructionem ecclesiae, iam tunc agendum est acsi non esset: & remanet in ecclesia potestas seipsam congregandi & sibi prouidendi ac ordinandi de potestate papali, secundo & tertio modis quo ad applicationem & ad visum: sicut de capitulo & decano, vel de vniuersitate & rectore suo modo diceretur.
units.tr: We may add to this consideration that the fullness of ecclesiastical power, if it is considered in its breadth, is not in the Pope alone, except in some manner fontally, potentially and originally in his own way. For this breadth of power is fulfilled in itself by other ecclesiastical powers collectively, from the highest down to the lowest, and in them the fullness of papal ecclesiastical power exists as an integral part within its whole. Thus it is not greater or superior to the whole Church, just as a greater part is not greater than the whole. But if this fullness is considered in its supremacy, then beyond any doubt the fullness of papal ecclesiastical power is superior and greater than the rest. Yet what remains cannot by any means constitute a general council, according to what was said before: that a general council in its formal nature necessarily includes papal authority, whether the Pope exists or not. For if the Pope exists and wishes to perform his duty of convoking the council, he certainly ought to be authorized by it. But if he obstinately refuses, to the destruction of the Church, then it must be acted as though he were not there, and there remains in the Church the power to assemble itself and to provide for itself and to ordain concerning papal power, in the second and third ways, as to application and exercise, just as might be said of a chapter and its dean, or of a university and its rector, in their own fashion.

units.la: Sed occurrit difficultas principalis, quid mortuo Papa, vel electo possit ipsum concilium.
units.tr: But the principal difficulty arises: what can the council itself do when the Pope has died, or has been elected?

units.la: Potest itaq; primo constituere sibi Papa vno modo solito per electionem dominorum Cardinalium vel alio modo per compromissum vel per vim Spiritus sancti, si probabiliter ita speraretur posse fieri quod omnes concordarent in vnum. Vel forte per expectationem diuini miraculi, sicut fuit in electione Matthiæ. Et de hac prima potestate concilii non est difficultas, quin sibi possit facere capax unum.
units.tr: First, then, while the Pope is still living, it can appoint for itself a Pope, in one of the usual ways, by the election of the lords Cardinals, or in another way, by compromise, or by the power of the Holy Spirit, if it could probably be hoped that all would agree on one. Or perhaps by waiting for a divine miracle, as happened in the election of Matthias. Concerning this first power of the council there is no difficulty, that it can make one capable for itself.

units.la: Alia multa sunt, quæ Papa mortuo vel ejecto potest exercere concilium per seipsum vel per organum aliquod vice omnium: quemadmodum sæpe practicatum est in hoc concilio de diversis sententiis & decretis respicientibus exercitium iurisdictionis coercitiuæ: sicut in vocatione & depositione Papæ, sicut in excommunicatione & interdicto, relaxatione & absolutione factum est in causa Tridentina & Argentina: in quibus omnibus introducitur sancta Synodus loquens, decernens, diffiniens. Sic invenitur in primis conciliis tempore Apostolorum & aliorum, quod concilium loquebatur, & non Papa, etiam dum viuebat. Unde dixerunt Apostoli & Seniores Act. 15. scribentes ad ea illius concilii: Visum est Spiritui sancto & nobis. Et similiter notatur Act. 6. de convocatione Ecclesiæ per 12. Apostolos: & in conciliis generalibus tales inveniuntur modi loquendi: Placuit sancto concilio: vel concilium diffinit: vel statuit sanctum concilium, vel sacri authoritatis concilii, vel Synodalis ordinatio vigeat: & ita in similibus.
units.tr: There are many other matters which the council, after the Pope's death or deposition, can exercise, either itself or through some organ acting in the place of all: as has often been practised in this council concerning various decrees and decisions bearing on the exercise of coercive jurisdiction, as in the summoning and deposition of a Pope, as in excommunication and interdict, release and absolution, as was done in the case of Trent and Argentina. In all these cases the holy Synod is introduced speaking, decreeing, defining. So it is found in the first councils, in the time of the Apostles and afterwards, that the council spoke, and not the Pope, even while he was living. Hence the Apostles and the Elders said, writing to the churches of that council: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us (Acts 15). Similarly it is noted in Acts 6 concerning the convocation of the Church by the twelve Apostles. And in general councils such forms of speech are found: It pleased the holy council; or the council defines; or the holy council decrees; or the authority of the sacred council, or the synodal ordinance holds; and so in similar cases.

units.la: Deniq; tertio sunt talia quæ non possunt exerceri, nisi per suppositum determinatum iuxta iam allegatum, quod actiones sunt suppositorum.
units.tr: Finally, there are third matters which cannot be exercised except through a determinate subject, according to what has already been alleged, that actions belong to subjects.

units.la: Circa quæ distinguendum est, quia vel illa sunt talia, quæ nullus potest exercere, nisi sit Papa: nec per commissionem, nec aliter. Vel sunt talia, quæ committi possunt per aliquem vel aliquos, per quos hoc exerceri non posset, sed alius capax est. Exemplum de curato non sacerdote, qui potest committere simplici sacerdoti non habenti plebem aliquam, quod in cura sua celebret missam & consecret, quod audiat confessiones & absolvat, quod ministret Eucharistiam: & ita de reliquis spectantibus ad sacerdotium. Poterit igitur similiter concilium committere sacerdotibus, ut agant talia, quæ nec concilium per se nec illi sacerdotes sine commissione vel licentia concilii possent exequi, saltem licite.
units.tr: Concerning these a distinction must be made, because either they are such that no one can exercise them unless he is the Pope, neither by commission nor otherwise; or they are such that they can be committed to some person or persons through whom this could not be exercised, but another is capable of it. An example is a parish curate who is not a priest, who can commit to a simple priest, one who has no parish of his own, that he celebrate Mass and consecrate in his cure, that he hear confessions and absolve, that he administer the Eucharist, and so with the rest that pertain to the priesthood. Therefore the council can likewise commit to priests that they perform such things as neither the council itself nor those priests could carry out without a commission or licence from the council, at least lawfully.

units.la: Quocirca restat cognoscendum de illa conditionali, si sit aliqua potestas in Papa, quæ possit in aliquid, in quod nulla altera potestas Ecclesiastica potest attingere neque de facto neque de iure. Et videtur prima facie, quod non: iuxta communiorem Doctorum sententiam, qui dicunt potestatem ordinis esse æqualem in omnibus sacerdotibus, comprehendendo more Apostoli Episcopatum sub sacerdotio. Non enim videtur, quod sit aliquis actus ordinis, in quem possit Papalis auctoritas, quin illum possit de facto potestas Episcopalis. Cæterum de potestate iurisdictionis quocunq; fiat sermo, videtur quod concilium possit illam concedere in defectu Papæ, ut in subiiciendo A Episcopo tales populos quales voluerit pro sacramentorum licita & rata ministratione. Et ita practicavit hoc concilium circa Samaritas, legatos eis dando, qui licite possent omnia, quæ sunt ordinis & spiritualis iurisdictionis. Proinde quid de largitione indulgentiarum tenendum sit, lectori interim considerandum relinquo, si soluis Papæ concessione mediate vel immediate tradi possint. Putant aliqui, quod potestas hæc respicit claves in foro pœnitentiæ. Propterea conuenit in eodem foro cuilibet sacerdoti, maxime Episcopo, si non fuerit hæc potestas a superiore quoad usum limitata: aut conuenit illi qui habet curam communitatis Ecclesiæ secundum Thomam: Concilium vero talem curam habet.
units.tr: Hence it remains to consider that conditional: whether there is any power in the Pope which can reach something that no other ecclesiastical power can attain, either in fact or by right. And at first sight it seems not: according to the more common opinion of the Doctors, who say that the power of order is equal in all priests, including, in the manner of the Apostle, the episcopate under the priesthood. For it does not seem that there is any act of order to which papal authority could extend that the episcopal power could not in fact also attain. Moreover, whatever is said of the power of jurisdiction, it seems that the council could grant it in the absence of a Pope, as in subjecting peoples of whatever kind it wishes to a bishop, for the lawful and valid administration of the sacraments. So this council acted concerning the Samaritans, sending legates to them who could lawfully do all things that belong to order and spiritual jurisdiction. Accordingly, what is to be held about the granting of indulgences I leave for the reader to consider meanwhile, whether they can be handed on, mediately or immediately, by the concession of the Pope alone. Some think that this power concerns the keys in the forum of penance. Therefore it is suitable in that forum for any priest, especially a bishop, unless this power has been limited by a superior as to its use; or it belongs to him who has the care of the community of the Church, according to Thomas. But the council has such a care.

units.la: Porro iuxta hunc dicendi modum potest occurrere scandalum trahens ad hoc inconveniens, quod Ecclesia posset bene regi usque in finem seculi sine Papa: ut si generale concilium daret licentiam omnibus Episcopis sacerdotibus cuilibet supra plebem suam absque ulla iurisdictionis limitatione vel restrictione: quia sic Episcopus posset constituere sacerdotes, imo & Episcopus licite & rate & ut clavibus, & ita de reliquis omnibus Hierarchicis actibus.
units.tr: Moreover, on this way of speaking there may arise a scandal leading to this absurdity: that the Church could be well governed until the end of the age without a Pope. For example, if a general council were to give every bishop and every priest, each over his own people, a licence without any limitation or restriction of jurisdiction, then a bishop could lawfully and rightly appoint priests, and indeed a bishop could exercise the keys, and the same with all the other hierarchical acts.

units.la: Respondemus, quod etsi ad tempus aliquod generale concilium possit aliquid tale facere: quoniam habere Papam est præceptum affirmativum obligans ad semper, sed non pro semper: sicut apparuit dum vacuit sedes per duos aut tres annos, sicut & nunc vacat. Nihilominus generale concilium neque debeeret neque posset talem defectum capitis usque in finem seculi tolerare stante lege: potest tamen supplere, dum necessitas urget vel suadet evidens utilitas: & hoc vel per unum Episcopum quasi vicarium, vel per plures simul, aut successive. Et hoc modo dicitur esse plenitudo potestatis Ecclesiasticæ in Ecclesia supplettiue.
units.tr: We reply that although a general council might do something of this kind for a time, since having a Pope is an affirmative precept binding always, but not for always, as became clear when the see was vacant for two or three years and is now vacant again. Nevertheless, a general council ought not, and cannot, tolerate such a lack of a head until the end of the age while the law stands. It can, however, supply the want when necessity presses or evident advantage urges, and it can do so either through one bishop as a kind of vicar, or through several together or in succession. In this way the fullness of ecclesiastical power is said to exist in the Church by way of supply.

units.la: Cognoscimus ex his quod falsæ sunt & iniuriosæ concilio generali tales assertiones, quæ negant ab eo vel Ecclesia executionem potestatis supremæ iurisdictionis. Negant insuper decernendi vel diffiniendi potestatem dum Papa est, reponentes in eo solo hanc auctoritatem diffiniendi: cum ex multis conciliis & certa ratione constet oppositum. Unde & Apostoli miserunt in Samariam Petrum & Iohannem tanquam subditos Ecclesiæ. Et Iacobus protulit diffinitionem sacri concilii super cessatione legalium, de quo Actorum decimo quinto notatum est: quando tamen Petrus præsidebat & residebat in Ecclesia legitime, cum esset in gratia confirmatus die Pentecostes.
units.tr: From these things we recognise that those assertions are false and injurious to a general council which deny that the execution of supreme jurisdiction belongs to it or to the Church. They also deny the power of decreeing and defining while the Pope is alive, claiming that this authority of defining resides in him alone; yet the contrary is established by many councils and by sound reason. Hence the apostles also sent Peter and John into Samaria as subjects of the Church. And James put forward the decision of the sacred council on the cessation of the legal observances, which is noted in Acts chapter fifteen, when nevertheless Peter was presiding and residing lawfully in the Church, having been confirmed in grace on the day of Pentecost.

units.la: Possumus tandem canones apparenter discordes super laude plenitudinis potestatis Papalis rationabiliter ad concordiam revocare, si distinctionem trimembrem acceptionis Ecclesiasticæ potestatis acute viderimus. Hanc enim potestatem formaliter & in se consideratam primo modo iudicare potest, neque Augustus, neque populus, neque totus clerus: imo nec vniversalis Ecclesia. Secus in alio duplici modo. Unde sicut ex consideratione potestatis huius stupendæ & miraculosæ, Imperatores etiam & reges procumbunt ad oscula pedum Papæ. Et inde consurgit aliquam quando ex humana fragilitate arrogans superbia in persona Papae referentis ad se quod impendit potestati. Non aliter existimandum est de prioribus sanctis propter tribus extollentibus Papam miris modis. Et inde suborta est in quibusdam summis pontificibus arrogantia maior debito: quod est usurpare id, quod iure non poterat. Hinc cuidam gloriant, quod pedibus suis conculcaret imperatoris caput, retudit hanc arrogantiam acriter satis imperator hoc mordaci verbo: Non tibi, inquit, sed Petro.
units.tr: Finally, we can reasonably bring the canons, which seem to disagree about the praise of the fullness of papal power, back to agreement, if we have carefully seen the threefold distinction in the way ecclesiastical power is understood. For this power, considered formally and in itself, neither the Augustus, nor the people, nor the whole clergy, nor indeed the universal Church can judge in the first way. It is otherwise in the two other ways. Hence, from consideration of this stupendous and miraculous power, emperors and kings too fall prostrate to kiss the Pope's feet. And from this there arises, when through human frailty, an arrogant pride refers to the person of the Pope what is owed to the power. The same must be thought of the earlier holy men, because of the three who exalt the Pope in marvellous ways. And from this there has arisen in some supreme pontiffs an arrogance greater than is due, which is to usurp what they could not by right. Hence one of them boasted that he would tread the emperor's head under his feet; the emperor rebuffed this arrogance sharply enough with a biting word: Not to you, he said, but to Peter.

units.la: Hinc fit praeterea, quod absque mendacio vel adulatione Papa nequissimus potest appellari sanctissimus: potest adorari cultu dulie usque ad oscula pedum: et ita de reliquis honoribus.
units.tr: Hence it follows further that, without lying or flattery, the most wicked Pope can be called most holy, can be worshipped with the cult of dulia even to kissing his feet, and so with the rest of the honours.
