units.la: Sic Ecclesia, quae maculam non habet neque rugam, quae instar Mariae virgo est & Mater, introducitur quandoque; tanquam peccatrix & sordida, non quidem pro se & ibi se, sed pro peccatis filiorum: sicut anima sana fert & regit corpus aegrotum.
units.tr: Thus the Church, which has no spot or wrinkle, which is like the Virgin and Mother Mary, is sometimes presented as sinful and filthy, not indeed for herself and in herself, but on account of the sins of her children, just as a healthy soul bears and rules a sick body.

units.la: CONSIDERATIO XII.
units.tr: CONSIDERATION XII.

units.la: POtestas Ecclesiastica Papalis non ita habet dominia & iura terreni simul & coelestis imperii, quod possit ad libitum suum de bonis clericorum, & multo minus laicorum disponere: quamvis concedi debeat, quod habet in eis dominium quoddam directivum, regulativum & ordinativum.
units.tr: The Papal ecclesiastical power does not hold the dominions and rights of the earthly and the heavenly empire together in such a way that it may dispose at its pleasure of the goods of the clergy, and much less of the laity; although it must be conceded that it has over them a certain directive, regulative and ordering dominion.

units.la: Declaratione huius considerationis, quam discretio moderatrix atque mediatrix ponit inter errores oppositos: dum facere meditatur, occurrere visa est protinus in ipso meditationis meae secreto duplex improba pestis. Nomen unius detractio liuida. Nomen alterius adulatio subdola. Prima potestatem Ecclesiasticam deprimens subiiciebat temporali. Altera sustollebat in immensum, velut ad similitudinem altissimi: confundens iura cuiuslibet alterius potestatis. Tolle tolle, clamat detractio, temporalitatem omnem, ius vel dominium ab Ecclesiasticis. Quare? quia sic instituit Christus, cuius ista vox est: Nisi quis renunciaverit omnibus quae possidet, non potest meus esse discipulus. Sic improbat Iulianus apostata Christianis, rapiens eorum facultates. Addit detractio, quod Ecclesiastici nequaquam capaces sunt iurisdictionis temporalis, etiam si principes alii conferre voluerint. Inducit Apostolum: quia militans Deo implicat se negotiis secularibus. Addit detractio, nihil habere Ecclesiasticos neque decimas neque oblationes, quanto minus alias dotationes vel possessiones, nisi ex pura Eleemosyna donantium. Et quod ab Ecclesiasticis peccantibus saltem habitualiter possent per secularem potestatem optimo iure tolli: quia data est potestas haec securalis in vindictam malefactorum, neque sine causa gladium portat. Addit quarto innitens Apostoli verbis: Habentes alimenta & quibus tegamur, his contenti simus: quia quicquid habent Ecclesiastici ultra simplicem victum & vestitum, totum illud est pauperum: cuius retentio nedum furtum vel rapina simplex est, sed sacrilegium: prout detorquet ad hanc sententiam tam Hieronymi verba, quam Bernhard. Vult tandem detractio Ecclesiasticos omnes ad illam Apostolorum & Discipulorum primam paupertatem sine equis, sine thesauris, sine calciamentis, sine possessionibus de necessitate salutis redigere, execrans in Ecclesiasticis pompam omnem vel sertientium, vel ciborum, vel equorum, vel indumentorum.
units.tr: In explaining this consideration, which moderating and mediating discretion sets between the opposing errors, while I was meditating on writing it, there immediately seemed to present itself, in the very secret of my meditation, a double wicked plague. One is the livid detraction; the other is the sly flattery. The first, depressing ecclesiastical power, made it subject to the temporal. The other lifted it immensely, as if to the likeness of the Most High, confusing the rights of every other power. "Take away, take away," cries detraction, "all temporality, right or dominion, from the ecclesiastics. Why? Because Christ so ordained, and this is his voice: Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple." So the apostate Julian reproved the Christians, seizing their property. Detraction adds that ecclesiastics are in no way capable of temporal jurisdiction, even if princes wish to confer it on them. It brings forward the Apostle: No one who serves God gets entangled in secular business. Detraction adds that the ecclesiastics have neither tithes nor offerings, much less other endowments or possessions, except from the pure alms of donors; and that from ecclesiastics who sin, at least habitually, these could rightly be taken away by secular power, because this secular power was given for the punishment of evildoers, and it does not bear the sword in vain. In the fourth place, it adds, relying on the words of the Apostle: Having food and clothing, let us be content with these. Therefore whatever the ecclesiastics have beyond simple food and clothing is entirely the poor's; to retain it is not merely theft or simple robbery but sacrilege, as the words of both Jerome and Bernard are twisted to this opinion. Detraction finally wants all ecclesiastics reduced to that first poverty of the apostles and disciples, without horses, without treasures, without shoes, without possessions, as a matter of necessity for salvation, and it execrates in the ecclesiastics every show, whether of garments, of foods, of horses, or of clothing.

units.la: Consurgit ex adverso blandiens & subdola adulatio, & ad aures Ecclesiasticorum, praecipue summi pontificis insusurrans: O quanta est, quanta sublimitas Ecclesiasticae potestatis tuae! O sacer clere, quam nihil est saecularis auctoritas tuae comparata! Quoniam sicut Christo collata est omnis potestas in coelo & in terra, sic eam Christus omnem Petro suisque successoribus dereliquit. Unde & nec Constantinus quicquam Syluestro Papa contulit, quod non esset prius suum, sed reddidit iniuste detentum. Porro sicut non est potestas nisi a Deo, sic nec aliqua temporalis vel Ecclesiastica, Imperialis vel regalis nisi a Papa: in cuius femore scripsit Christus: Rex regum, Dominus dominantium. De cuius potestate disputare instar sacrilegii est: cui neque quisquam dicere potest: Cur ita facis? Sic etiam temporalia omnia si Ecclesiastica bona atque dominia mutanerit, diripuerit, distraxerit. Mentior si non inveniuntur haec scripta ab illis etiam qui sapientes sunt in oculis suis: Si praeterea non inveniuntur fuisse per aliquos summos pontifices haec credita.
units.tr: On the opposite side rises flattering and sly adulation, whispering into the ears of the ecclesiastics, especially of the supreme pontiff: "O how great, how sublime is your ecclesiastical power! O holy cleric, how nothing is secular authority compared with yours! For just as all power in heaven and on earth was given to Christ, so Christ left all of it to Peter and his successors. Hence not even Constantine conferred on Pope Sylvester anything that was not already his own; he returned what had been unjustly held. Moreover, just as there is no power except from God, so no temporal or ecclesiastical, imperial or royal power exists except from the Pope, on whose thigh Christ wrote: King of kings, Lord of lords. To dispute about his power is like sacrilege; no one can say to him: Why do you do so? So too, if he should change, plunder or sell all the temporal goods, including the ecclesiastical goods and dominions, I would be lying if these writings were not found from those who are wise in their own eyes, and if it were not found that these things have been believed by some supreme pontiffs."

units.la: Notum est illud Satyrici: Nihil est quod credere de se Non possit, cum laudatur Dis aequa potestas.
units.tr: Well known is that saying of the satirist: "There is nothing a man cannot believe about himself, when power equal to the gods is praised."

units.la: Et illud Comici de adulatore: Hic profecto ex stultitia insanos facit.
units.tr: And that saying of the comic poet about the flatterer: Truly, this man makes the mad out of fools.

units.la: Sentiens autem adulatio quandoque nimis se cognoscit studet quasi modestiori sermone deprestius uti ut credibilior appareat. Concedit saeculari potestati possessiones & iurisdictiones proprias, quas tollere nequit pro libitu Papa. Recognoscit Constantinum vel alios Principes aliquid Ecclesiae nouiter contulisse. Nihilominus tradit, quod summus pontifex supremus est monarcha: nedum in spiritualibus, sed temporalibus, habens potestatem hanc immediate a Christo. [?]ed alii reges omnes & principes suam recipiunt dominationem ab eo, & solum mediate a Deo. Alioquin ut monstruosus esset hic mundus, si haberet tot capita, quae non sub unico regerentur: Rediretque Manichaei deliramentum ponentis duo principia, Unum bonorum & spiritualium: aliud malorum & temporalium. Unde & sicut corpus est propter animam & ab anima viuit & regitur, sic potestas saecularis propter spiritualem, a qua recipit suum esse legitimum. Quam auctoritatem spiritualem qui negant vel impugnant, sint intus, sint foris ecclesiam possunt gladio vel spirituali excommunicationis sicut catholici: vel debellationis, sicut infideles feriri, & eorum dominia vel bona in alios transferri.
units.tr: Flattery, however, when it perceives that it has gone too far, sometimes strives to use a more moderate speech, as if it were humbler, so that it may appear more credible. It concedes to secular power its own possessions and jurisdictions, which the Pope cannot take away at his pleasure. It acknowledges that Constantine or other princes have newly conferred something on the Church. Nevertheless, it teaches that the supreme pontiff is the supreme monarch, not only in spiritual but also in temporal matters, having this power immediately from Christ. But all other kings and princes receive their dominion from him, and only mediately from God. Otherwise this world would be monstrous, if it had so many heads that were not governed under a single one; and the raving of the Manichaean would return, who posited two principles, one of good and spiritual things, the other of evil and temporal things. Hence, just as the body exists for the sake of the soul and lives and is governed by the soul, so secular power exists for the sake of the spiritual, from which it receives its lawful being. Those who deny or attack this spiritual authority, whether they are inside or outside the Church, can be struck by the sword of spiritual excommunication, as by Catholics, or by war, as infidels are struck, and their dominions or goods transferred to others.

units.la: Hanc aestimationem habuisse visus est Bonifacius octavus in quadam decretali. Et in hac fundari putatur ab aliquibus Dominorum Prutenorum aduersus infideles debellatio, suorumque bonorum & dominiorum conquisitio. Putatur ab aliis depositio vnius regis Franciae per Papam Zachariam hic esse fundata, tanquam Papa sit, qui transferre possit reges & regna.
units.tr: Bonifacius VIII appears to have held this view in a certain decretal. On this foundation some think the Lords of Prussia rest their war against the infidels and their claim to the goods and dominions of others. Others think that the deposition of a king of France by Pope Zachary is founded here, as though the Pope were the one who could transfer kings and kingdoms.

units.la: Rursus animadvertens adulatio, durum esse multis hunc sermonem: & ideo minus credibilem, studet loqui restrictius, concedens quod sicut ante Petrum fuerunt apud infideles vera dominia: quemadmodum irrefragabilis auctoritas sacrae scripturae & euangelicae narrationis testis est: Sic non oportet nunc post Petrum, ut omnis potestas Imperialis, regalis vel altera secularis sit immediate robur habens a summo pontifice: sicut rex Francorum Christianissimus superiorem hoc modo non habet, nec recognoscit in terris. Idcirco transfert verbum suum adulatio loqui de dignitatibus, officiis & bonis ecclesiasticorum, quae omnia sic subiicit summo pontifici, ut quicquid circa ea placuerit disponere mutando, transferendo, appropriando, hoc possit, hoc teneat, & ratum sit: licet hoc sine causa, licet cum peccato suo peregerit, quamuis peccatum circa hoc vult adulatio longe a Papa sic facere, ut eum simoniam posse neget committere: quoniam sua sunt omnia ecclesiastica bona. Concedit insuper, quod super ius est potens ab altero ius suum tollere: & quod nec ab eo appellari neque etiam iudicialiter euocari, nec obedientiam ab eo subtrahi, praesertim extra casum haeresis sit aliquatenus possibile. Hic solus symbolum fidei condere: hic solus causas eiusdem fidei & maiores caeteras tractare potest, solus ut iam tactum est, diffinitiones, regulas, leges & canones condit. Alioquin quicquid per alios diffinitur, decernitur, conditur, statuitur, irritum est & inane. Nec aliquid ex eis quae statuerit potest, nisi per ipsum quomodolibet cassari vel infringi. Fallor si non ante celebrationem huius Sacrosanctae Constant. synodi sic occapauerat mentes plurimorum, literalium magis quam literatorum ista traditio: ut oppositorum dogmatizator fuisset de haeretica pravitate vel notatus vel damnatus. Huius rei signum accipe: quia post declarationem ex theologiae principiis luce clariorem, & quod vrgentius est post determinationem & praticationem eiusdem sanctae synodi, inveniuntur qui talia palam asserere non paueant, tam radicatum, & ut cancer serpens tam medullitus imbibitum fuit hoc prisce adulationis virus lethiferum.
units.tr: Again, flattery, noticing that this doctrine is harsh for many and therefore less credible, tries to speak more narrowly. It concedes that just as before Peter there were true dominions among the infidels, as the unshakeable authority of Holy Scripture and the Gospel narrative bears witness, so now, after Peter, it is not necessary that every imperial, royal or other secular power should have its strength immediately from the supreme pontiff; for the most Christian king of France has no superior in this way and acknowledges none on earth. Therefore flattery turns its word to speak of the dignities, offices and goods of churchmen, all of which it subjects to the supreme pontiff in such a way that whatever he pleases to arrange concerning them, by changing, transferring or appropriating, he may do, he may hold, and it shall be ratified: even if he does this without cause, even if he does it with sin on his part. Although flattery wishes to remove sin from the Pope so far in this matter that it denies he can commit simony, since all ecclesiastical goods are his own. It further concedes that one who is powerful above the law may take away another's right, and that it is scarcely possible, at least outside the case of heresy, for him to be appealed from, or even summoned judicially, or for obedience to be withdrawn from him. He alone can frame the creed of the faith; he alone can handle the causes of that faith and the greater matters, and, as has already been touched upon, he alone makes definitions, rules, laws and canons. Otherwise whatever is defined, decreed, enacted or established by others is void and empty. Nor can anything he has decreed be annulled or infringed in any way except by himself. I am mistaken if this tradition, more of the literate than of the learned, had not so taken hold of the minds of very many before the celebration of this Most Holy Council of Constance, that whoever taught the opposite would have been marked or condemned for heretical perversity. Take this as a sign of the matter: after the declaration, clearer than the light from the principles of theology, and, what is more pressing, after the determination and practice of this same Holy Synod, there are those who do not hesitate to assert such things openly, so deeply rooted, and so thoroughly soaked into the marrow, like a creeping cancer, is this deadly poison of ancient flattery.

units.la: Tandem miserante Deo moderatrix discretio, collustrata lumine legis euangelicae, mediam ac regiam viam veniens inter devios errores extremos, detractionis & adulationis ponit dictam hanc considerationem duodecimam tam prioribus tanquam signum aliquod ostensivum itineris recti: ne forte offendant ad lapidem erroris pedem suae inquisitionis scrutatores veritatis. Unde dicimus ecclesiasticos & capaces esse bonorum temporalium, & multa eis ex debito, non ex eleemosyna pura competere: & non debere eos coercere vel spoliari per saecularem potestatem, nisi vocata sit in sui iuris subsidium, quod dicitur propter haereticos & rebelles. Possunt ipsi denique cum divitiis aliter quam Apostoli viuere, conuersari vel incedere pro temporum, locorum & aliarum circumstantiarum varia qualitate, prout sapiens iudicabit. Nec ita sunt Hieronymi, vel Bernhardi verba generaliter ad omnes ecclesiasticos tanquam proprium habeant nihil, de[?]torquenda Monachis autem, quibus loquebantur, alia lex est.
units.tr: At last, by the mercy of God, moderating discretion, illumined by the light of the evangelical law, coming upon the middle and royal way between the wandering extremes of error, of detraction and of flattery, sets forth this twelfth consideration, as a kind of pointer to the right road for the earlier ones, lest the seekers of truth stumble in their inquiry against the stone of error. Hence we say that churchmen are capable of temporal goods, and that many things are due to them by right, not by pure alms; and that they ought not to be coerced or despoiled by secular power, unless it has been called in as an aid to their own right, which is said to be on account of heretics and rebels. Finally, they may live and conduct themselves with riches otherwise than the Apostles did, according to the varying character of times, places and other circumstances, as the wise man shall judge. Nor are the words of Jerome or Bernard spoken generally to all churchmen as though they all have nothing of their own; but the law is different for the monks to whom they were speaking.

units.la: Vitamus ex adverso stultas & falsas adulationis insanias attribuentes summo pontifici plenitudinis potestatem, qualem descripsimus: quae tanta est, quantam sapientissimus legislator CHRISTVS praeuidit sufficere ad aedificationem continuam ecclesiae dilectissimae sponsae suae, quam propria morte firmauit & dotauit: Cui potestati detrahere esset impietas sacrilegaque indignissimaque. Sed glorificent Deum, qui potestatem talem dedit hominibus misericordissima pietate sua: quae potestas quanto sublimior est, pulchrior & dignior, tanto ne veritatur in abusum vilem, turpem & indignum prouidere debet summus pontifex: & eam, ut sapiens iudicabit regulare. Quid autem sapientius in terris generali concilio, quod & Spiritu sancto regitur: & cuius agi frenis summa libertas est? Praeclare dixit Aristoteles: Non esse seruitutem obedire legibus.
units.tr: On the other side, we avoid the foolish and false frenzies of flattery which attribute to the supreme pontiff a plenitude of power of the kind we have described: a power so great as Christ, the most wise lawgiver, foresaw to be sufficient for the continual building up of the Church, his most beloved spouse, whom he confirmed and endowed by his own death. To detract from this power would be impiety, sacrilege and most unworthy. But let them glorify God, who has given such power to men by his most merciful goodness; and the more sublime, fairer and worthier this power is, the more the supreme pontiff ought to take care that it is not turned to vile, shameful and unworthy abuse, and that he rule it as the wise man shall judge. Yet what is wiser on earth than a general council, which is also governed by the Holy Spirit, and whose bridles to be driven are the greatest freedom? Aristotle said well: that it is not slavery to obey the laws.

units.la: Addamus summum pontificem cum collegio suo ita praesidere bonis ecclesiasticis, ut de eis statuam habere sufficientem & decentem oporteat. Sed non ita, ut caput grauidum membra reliqua obruat mole sua: neque velit vsurpare contra naturam singularis membri omnia officia membrorum, quibus singulis, ut ait Apostolus, proprium datum est officium. Nam si omnia oculus vel caput, vbi pes? vbi manus? Concernit hoc collationem beneficiorum multiplicitatem exemptionum odiosissimam plenam erroris & confusionis in ecclesiastica hierarchia: & ita de reliquis. Reseruationem praeterea tot casuum, tot excommunicationum in foro conscientiae, euocationem tam facilem omnium causarum ab ordinariis: sint causae illae prophanae, sint lucrae fidei: quales fidei causas omnes ab ordinariis singulis, praesertim in doctrinis notorie scandalizantibus, diuceses suas, & vbi vigent studia literarum, velle prohibere, quid aliud est quam ianuam grandem erro-ribus aperire?
units.tr: Let us add that the supreme pontiff, together with his college, should so preside over ecclesiastical goods that it is fitting for him to have a sufficient and decent provision concerning them. But not in such a way that the pregnant head overwhelms the other members with its mass, nor that he wishes to usurp, contrary to the nature of a single member, all the offices of the members, to each of which, as the Apostle says, a proper office has been given. For if the eye were all, or the head, where would the foot be? Where the hand? This concerns the multiplying of the conferral of benefices, the most odious multiplication of exemptions, full of error and confusion in the ecclesiastical hierarchy; and so with the rest. Moreover, the reservation of so many cases, so many excommunications in the forum of conscience, and so easy a summoning of all causes away from the ordinaries, whether those causes be profane or touch the faith: what else is it than to open a great gate to errors, when one wishes to forbid the ordinaries, each in their own dioceses, and where the study of letters flourishes, to deal with all such causes of faith, especially in doctrines that are notoriously scandalous?

units.la: Postremo suis se terminis ita potestas ecclesiastica coerceat, vt meminerit potestatem secularem etiam apud infideles sua habere propria iura, suas dignitates, suas leges, sua iudicia: de quibus occupare se ecclesiastica potestas non praesumat vel vsurpet, nisi dum redundat abusus potestatis secularis in impugnationem fidei & blasphemiam creatoris & in manifestam ecclesiasticae potestatis iniuriam. Tunc enim attendere conuenit vltimam huius considerationis duodecimae particulam, quod in his ecclesiastica potestas habet dominium quoddam regitiuum, directiuum, regulatiuum & ordinatiuum.
units.tr: Finally, let ecclesiastical power so restrain itself within its own limits that it remembers that secular power, even among the infidels, has its own rights, its own dignities, its own laws and its own judgments; with these ecclesiastical power should not presume to concern itself or usurp, except when the abuse of secular power overflows into an attack on the faith and a blasphemy of the Creator, and into a manifest injury to ecclesiastical power. For then it is fitting to attend to the last part of this twelfth consideration, that in such matters ecclesiastical power has a certain dominion which is ruling, directive, regulative and ordaining.

units.la: Concludunt hoc & nihil fere aliud rationes & allegationes omnes induci solitae, quod plenitudo potestatis Papalis superior est & ad omnem aliam ecclesiasticam & temporalem. Quamuis sub hoc respectu potestas vniuersalis ecclesiae vel generalis concilii legitime congregati dici possit maior in amplitudine vel extensione, maior in infallibili directione, maior in morum reformatione in capite & in membris, maior in coercitiua potestate, maior in saluarum fidei difficilium vltimata decisione, maior denique quia copiosior. Completitur enim saltem virtualiter omnem potestatem & omne politicum regimen, Papale, imperiale, regale, aristocraticum & timocraticum: prout alias deductum est ex descriptione concilii generalis, quae talis est:
units.tr: All the reasons and allegations customarily brought forward conclude this, and almost nothing else: that the plenitude of papal power is superior and above every other ecclesiastical and temporal power. Although in this respect the power of the universal Church or of a lawfully assembled general council may be called greater in breadth or extent, greater in infallible direction, greater in the reform of morals in head and members, greater in coercive power, greater in the final decision of difficult matters of saving faith, and, in short, greater because more abundant. For it completes, at least virtually, every power and every political government, papal, imperial, royal, aristocratic and timocratic, as was elsewhere deduced from the description of a general council, which is as follows:

units.la: Concilium generale est congregatio legitima auctoritate facta ad aliquem locum ex omni statu hierarchico totius ecclesiae catholicae: nulla fideli persona, quae auditri requirat, excluIa, ad salubriter tractandum & ordinandum ea, quae debitum regimen eiusdem ecclesiae in fide & moribus respiciunt.
units.tr: A general council is a lawful congregation, made by lawful authority, at some place, from every hierarchical rank of the whole Catholic Church, no faithful person who asks to be heard being excluded, for the salutary treatment and ordering of those matters which concern the due government of the same Church in faith and morals.

units.la: Dicamus hic aliqua circa diffinitionem hanc concilii generalis. Et primo, quod congregatio legitima auctoritate facta dicitur regulariter a Papa, sicut sonant decreta & decretales innumerae. Excipiuntur tamen tres casus, vbi congregatio concilii generalis fit legitime sine Papa. Vnus dum desiit esse per mortem naturalem vel ciuilem seu canonicam, quae est depositio. Vel si cadat in perpetuam maniam. Aut si ad eum captiuatum non pateat accessus. Alius dum sufficienter requisitus de conuocando concilium renuit contumaciter in perniciem ecclesiae, praesertim si tangat ipsum. Tertio si concilium postquam est a Papa legitime congregatum, statuat certum tempus & locum pro celebrando generali concilio: sicut infra triennium, vel de decennio in decennium, etiam vbi Papa renueret. Nec refert in primo & secundo casu, per quos euocetur concilium: dummodo congregatur, quemadmodum fuit Pisis. Nihilominus expedit decernere pro futuro modum conuocationis: sicut in reformatione salubriter est auisatum, vtinam & synodaliter iam esset diffinitum.
units.tr: Let us say here a few things concerning this definition of a general council. And first, that a "lawful congregation made by lawful authority" is ordinarily said to be by the Pope, as countless decrees and decretals declare. Yet three cases are excepted, where a congregation of a general council is lawfully made without the Pope. One is when he has ceased to be, through natural or civil or canonical death, which is deposition; or if he falls into perpetual madness; or if access to him, when he is held captive, is not open. Another is when, though sufficiently requested to convoke a council, he stubbornly refuses, to the ruin of the Church, especially if the matter touches himself. Third, if the council, after it has been lawfully assembled by the Pope, decrees a certain time and place for celebrating a general council, such as within three years, or from decade to decade, even where the Pope would refuse. Nor does it matter in the first and second cases by whom the council is summoned, provided it is assembled, as happened at Pisa. Nevertheless it is expedient to decree for the future the manner of convocation, as has been wisely advised in the reformation, and would that it had already been defined by the synod.

units.la: Dicamus secundo iuxta probabilem valde sententiam, quod de statu hierarchico ecclesiae non sunt proprie, nisi duo status: Praelatorum maiorum videlicet, qui succedunt Apostolis & sunt episcopi, archiepiscopi, & ita sutsum: Et minorum, qui successores sunt septuaginta duorum discipulorum. Et dicuntur praelati secundi ordinis dignitatis vel honoris, quales sunt curati, quibus ex statu & ordinatio iure conueniunt tres actus hierarchici primarie, essentialiter & immediate a Christo: qui sunt purgare per correctionem, illuminare per doctrinam & praedicationem, perficere per sacramentorum ministrationem. Fundatur haec sententia Matth. 16. vbi postquam Christus dixerat, dic ecclesiae: subiunxit de quibus loquebatur dum ait: Quodcunque solueritis super terram &c. Constat autem quod nedum Apostolis, sed & discipulis loquebatur: iuxta Glossas Doctorum in hoc loco: & Matth. 10. & Luc. 10. vbi fit sermo de missione septuaginta duorum discipulorum: & Matth. 16 vbi Christus Petro dixit pro omnibus: Quodcunque ligaueris. E iterum: Super hanc petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam: & porta inferi non praeualebunt aduersus eam.
units.tr: We say, secondly, following a very probable opinion, that in the hierarchical state of the Church there are properly only two states: that of the greater prelates, namely those who succeed the Apostles and are bishops, archbishops, and so on upwards; and that of the lesser, who are successors of the seventy-two disciples. Prelates of the second order of dignity or honour are called such, as parish priests are, to whom by their status and ordinary right belong three primary, essential and immediate hierarchical acts from Christ: these are to purge by correction, to enlighten by teaching and preaching, and to perfect by the administration of the sacraments. This opinion is grounded in Matthew 16, where, after Christ had said, "Tell it to the Church," he added, speaking of those things, "Whatsoever you shall loose on earth," etc. It is certain, however, that he spoke not only to the Apostles but also to the disciples, according to the glosses of the teachers on this passage; and also Matthew 10 and Luke 10, where there is talk of the sending out of the seventy-two disciples; and Matthew 16, where Christ said to Peter, speaking for all: "Whatsoever you shall bind." And again: "Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it."

units.la: Concordant August. Hieron. Isidor. Beda, Magister vbi prius, & expresse multum Damasus Papa: Non amplius, inquit, quam duos ordines inter discipulos Domini esse cognoscimus, id est, duodecim apostolorum & 72. discipulorum. Vnde iste processerit ignoramus: & quod ratione caret, extirpare necesse est: loquitur contra episcopos.
units.tr: Augustine, Jerome, Isidore, Bede, the Master in the place cited above, and very expressly Pope Damasus agree. "We know," he says, "that there are no more than two orders among the disciples of the Lord, that is, of the twelve apostles and the seventy-two disciples. Whence this other order arose we do not know; and what lacks reason must be uprooted." He is speaking against bishops.

units.la: Dicamus tertio naturam generalis concilii talem esse, vt nullus fidelis, qui audire voluerit, debeat excludi ab audientia, quatenus vel doceatur vel doceat: sicut legitur in principio concilii.
units.tr: We say, thirdly, that the nature of a general council is such that no faithful person who wishes to hear should be excluded from the hearing, insofar as he is either taught or teaches, as is read at the beginning of the council.

units.la: Distingui tamen solet de habentibus vocem in concilio. Quidam habent consultiuam, alii diffinitiuam. Primi sunt, quibus inest notitia talium, quae tractantur etiam usque ad mechanicas artes. Vtiliter quaeratur de modo reparationis ecclesiarum materialium, esse poterit in latomis vox consultiua. Sic in aurifabris & fabris. Sic dum fit quaestio de philosophicis & moralibus disciplinis, vt sunt praecepta decalogi, possunt seculares eruditi in philosophia, legibus & moribus, dare consilium, & aliquando salubrius quam nonnulli praelatorum vel curatorum vel etiam theologorum, vsque adeo quod in generalibus conciliis contra Arrium tempore Athanasii fuerit interrogatus gentilis philosophus de materia nedum pure morali, sed quae tangebat beatae trinitatis eandem essentiam.
units.tr: It is customary, however, to distinguish those who have a voice in a council. Some have a consultative voice, others a decisive one. The first are those who possess knowledge of the matters treated, even of the mechanical arts. When the question is how material churches may usefully be repaired, masons may have a consultative voice; likewise goldsmiths and smiths. Likewise, when the question concerns philosophical and moral disciplines, such as the precepts of the Decalogue, learned laymen in philosophy, law and morals can give counsel, and sometimes more wholesomely than some prelates, parish priests, or even theologians; so much so that in the general councils against Arius, in the time of Athanasius, a pagan philosopher was asked about a matter not purely moral, but touching the very same essence of the blessed Trinity.

units.la: Caeterum de voce diffinitiua quales eam habeant, non est dubium de episcopis & superioribus praelatis: sicut iuxta praedicta practicatum saepius inuenitur in prioribus conciliis. Sed neque videtur ambiguitas esse de minoribus praelatis, qui sunt curati & hierarchae: neque de illis, qui ad hunc duplicem prælatorum ordinem reducuntur: quibus non ex privilegio solo, sed ex statu & ordinario iure competit animarum cura: quemadmodum sunt multi abbates, Decani, præpositi, cum similibus.
units.tr: Moreover, concerning who have a decisive voice, there is no doubt for bishops and higher prelates, as, according to what has been said, is frequently found in the earlier councils. Nor does there seem to be any ambiguity about the lesser prelates, who are parish priests and hierarchs, nor about those who are reduced to this twofold order of prelates, to whom the cure of souls belongs not by privilege alone but by status and ordinary right; such as many abbots, deans, provosts, and the like.

units.la: Facit ad hoc determinatio sacræ facultatis theologiæ Parisiensis nuper edita contra temeritatem extollentium priuilegiatos super curatos in prædicationibus & confessionibus: vbi sic dicitur in duobus primis articulis.
units.tr: To this bears the determination of the sacred faculty of theology of Paris, recently published against the rashness of those who exalt privileged persons above parish priests in preaching and confessions; where it is stated thus in the first two articles.

units.la: Domini curati sunt in ecclesia minores prælati & hierarchæ ex primaria institutione Christi: quibus competit ex statu im prædicandi, ius confessiones audiendi, ius sacramenta ecclesiastica secundum ex gentium sui status & parochianorum ministrandi, ius sepulturas dandi, ius insuper decimas & alia iura Parochialia recipiendi.
units.tr: The parish priests are in the Church the lesser prelates and hierarchs by the primary institution of Christ; to them belongs by their status the right of preaching, the right of hearing confessions, the right of administering the ecclesiastical sacraments according to the needs of their status and parishioners, the right of giving burial, and moreover the right of receiving tithes and other parochial rights.

units.la: Secundus articulus, quod ius prædicandi & confessandi competit prælatis & curatis principaliter & essentialiter, & Mendicantibus de per accidens ex privilegio: quoniam sunt introducti vel admissi ex concessione & beneplacito Dominorum prælatorum.
units.tr: The second article: the right of preaching and confessing belongs to prelates and parish priests principally and essentially, and to the Mendicants only by accident, by privilege; since they have been introduced or admitted by the grant and pleasure of the lord prelates.

units.la: Dicamus postremo quod licet ea, quæ statim dicta sunt, consonare videantur iuri diuino & observationi priorum conciliorum atque rationi: Nihilominus concilium potest certis de causis & ad tempus constituere voces diffinitivas in pluribus vel paucioribus, & in aliis quam dicti sint satis similiter ad illa quæ facta sunt & fieri possunt vario modo circa institutionem prælatorum ecclesiasticorum maiorum & minorum, quæ quandoque fiebant a toto populo & clero: quandoque a clero solum: quandoq; a solis canonicis ecclesiæ cathedralis: & nouissime crebrius per solum Papam, sicut plurimorum est iudicium.
units.tr: Lastly, we say that although the things just said seem to agree with divine law, with the observance of the earlier councils, and with reason, nevertheless a council may, for certain causes and for a time, establish decisive voices in more or fewer persons, and in others than those named, in a manner similar enough to those things which have been done and can be done in various ways concerning the institution of greater and lesser ecclesiastical prelates; which at times were made by the whole people and clergy, at times by the clergy alone, at times by the canons of the cathedral church alone, and most recently more often by the Pope alone, as is the judgment of most.

units.la: CONSIDERATIO XIII.
units.tr: CONSIDERATION XIII.

units.la: Potestas ecclesiastica, sicut & alia quælibet, originatur a prima iustitia, secundum quam iura omnia leges, iurisdictiones atque dominia pulchra ordinis varietate fundantur.
units.tr: Ecclesiastical power, like any other power, arises from primary justice, by which all rights, laws, jurisdictions and dominions are founded in a fine variety of order.

units.la: Describitur itaque iustitia, quod est perpetua & constans voluntas, ius suum vnicuique tribuens. Hæc autem descriptio competit principaliter iustitiæ diuinæ in ordine ad suas creaturas. Deus nempe solus est, qui voluntate perpetua & constanti dat vnicuique rei quod suum est: suum inquam, non ex debito rigoris, sed ex liberalissima & dignissima donatione creatoris. Sic in qualibet re tantumdem est de iure, quantum de entitate. Habet enim res quælibet ius seu titulum id habendi, quod habet ex dictamine rectissimo primæ iustitiæ.
units.tr: Justice is thus described: it is a perpetual and constant will giving each person his own right. This description applies chiefly to divine justice in relation to its creatures. God alone gives each thing what is its own by a perpetual and constant will: its own, I say, not from a debt of strict justice but from the most liberal and worthy gift of the Creator. Thus in any thing there is as much of right as there is of being. For every thing has a right or title to have what it has, according to the most upright dictate of primary justice.

units.la: Ius vero sic describitur: Ius est potestas seu facultas propinqua conueniens alicui secundum dictamen prima iustitia.
units.tr: Right is described thus: Right is a power or faculty, proximate, belonging to someone according to the dictate of primary justice.

units.la: Porro dictamen hoc lex dicitur, quia lex est regula conformitatem habens ad dictamen rectæ rationis. Dictamen vero rectæ rationis primæ, & iustitia conueniunt in Deo synonyme. Proinde dictum est in descriptione iuris, quod est facultas propinqua &c. propter illa quæ in potentia obedientiali conuenire possunt cuilibet creaturæ, quod posse dicere possumus vel obediential vel logicale, secundum quale non dicitur proprie res habere ius vel legem, sicut non dicimus quod damnati ius habeant ad beatitudinem æternam. Nec quod stella ius suum seu facultatem habeat in tanta luce, quanta refulget in sole: licet in potentia obedientiali creaturæ vel absolute Dei possint hæc omnia fieri.
units.tr: This dictate is called law, because law is a rule conforming to the dictate of right reason. In God, the dictate of primary right reason and justice are synonymous. Therefore, in the description of right, it was said to be a "proximate faculty" and so on, on account of those things which can belong to any creature by obediential potency, which we may call obediential or logical potency. According to this potency, things are not properly said to have a right or law, just as we do not say that the damned have a right to eternal blessedness, nor that a star has a right or faculty to shine with the light that blazes in the sun. Yet by the obediential potency of creatures, or absolutely by the power of God, all these things could be made to happen.

units.la: Consequenter ab hac amplissima iuris & legis acceptione, sicut vtitur scriptura dum ait: Hæ sunt leges cœli & terra &c. & alibi pluries: & apud Boetium: Legemiq; pati sidera cogis: fit descensus restrictior ad ea, quæ creatu iam rationalem respiciunt, vt rationalis est.
units.tr: Consequently, from this most broad sense of right and law, as Scripture uses it when it says These are the laws of heaven and earth, etc., and elsewhere often, and as Boethius has it, You compel the stars to obey law, there is a narrower descent to those things which concern the rational creature insofar as it is rational.

units.la: Fit subinde distinctio de iustitia: quia quædam est essentialis & primaria, qualis prædescripta est. Altera est participata seu derivata & attributiue dicta, quæ sic describitur: Iustitia est habitus vel tanquam habitus conformis diuinæ iustitiæ, eiusque imitatiuus per participationem, quo habitu inclinatur habens eam facere ius vel reddere. Ita quod ius est velut actus, vel visus, vel effectus, vt titulus talis iustitiæ.
units.tr: Then a distinction is made concerning justice. One justice is essential and primary, as just described. Another is participated or derived, and is called so by attribution. It is described thus: Justice is a habit, or as a habit, conformed to divine justice and imitating it through participation, by which habit the one who has it is inclined to do or render what is right. So right is, as it were, the act, or the view, or the effect, which is the title of such justice.

units.la: Rursus de iustitia sic accepta participatiue dicimus, quod quædam est iustitia originalis, quædam regni cœlestis: vt ibi: Primum quærite regnum Dei & iustitiam eius. Et hæc duplex est, quædam gloriæ, quædam gratiæ.
units.tr: Again, taking justice in this participated sense, we say that some justice is original, and some is of the heavenly kingdom, as there: Seek first the kingdom of God and his justice. And this is twofold: some is of glory, some of grace.

units.la: Altera iterum est iustitia legalis, alia ciuilis. Iustitia vero ciuilis alia distributiua: alia commutatiua. Et ita de reliquis acceptionibus iustitiæ specialibus.
units.tr: Again, one justice is legal, another civil. Civil justice is again of two kinds: distributive and commutative. And so with the other special senses of justice.

units.la: Iustitia legalis est omnis virtus, sicut charitas est tota lex Christi.
units.tr: Legal justice is every virtue, just as charity is the whole law of Christ.

units.la: Porro iustitiæ distributiuæ contrariantur promotiones indignæ, & intrusiones in officiis reipublicæ & beneficiis ecclesiæ. Commutatiuæ autem contrariantur contractus illiciti, vsura & fraus in temporalibus, simonia & gezia in spiritualibus, de quibus non est hic dicendum per singula.
units.tr: Distributive justice is opposed by unworthy promotions and intrusions into offices of the commonwealth and benefices of the Church. Commutative justice is opposed by illicit contracts: in temporal matters, by usury and fraud; in spiritual matters, by simony and gezia. These need not be discussed here one by one.

units.la: Dicamus præterea tot esse legum varietates, quot modis iura variantur secundum dictamen participatæ iustitiæ. Propterea sunt quædam leges proprie diuinæ, quædam proprie naturales: quædam positiuæ vel humanæ. Quarum aliquæ sunt canonicæ vel ecclesiasticæ: aliæ sunt ciuiles seu politicæ. Et quamuis paucæ reperiantur leges, quin mixtæ sunt ex participatione diuersarum: nihilominus denominatur lex à prædominanti seu à principaliori, quod in ea reperitur. Quibus præsuppositis dicamus vlterius descriptiones huiusmodi legum.
units.tr: Let us further say that there are as many varieties of law as there are ways in which rights vary according to the dictate of participated justice. Therefore some laws are properly divine, some properly natural, and some positive or human. Of these, some are canonical or ecclesiastical, others civil or political. And although few laws are found that are not mixed, being participations of various kinds, nevertheless a law is named from what predominates in it, or from its principal element. With these things presupposed, let us go on to describe such laws.

units.la: Et quoniam lex dicitur à ligando, id est, obligando: vel à legendo, id est; dictando quid agendum sit, conformiter ad hanc obligationem seu dictamen rectæ rationis describemus principaliter leges obligatorias: quia de consultoriis & permissiuis, & si quæ sint aliæ, facilis habebitur ex his cognitio.
units.tr: Since law is named from binding, that is, from obliging, or from reading, that is, from prescribing what is to be done, we will describe chiefly obligatory laws, in accordance with this obligation or dictate of right reason. From these, knowledge of consultative and permissive laws, and of any others, will be easily gained.

units.la: Lex diuina obligatoria est signum verum reuelatum creaturæ rationali notificatiuum rectæ rationis diuinæ volentis teneri seu ligari illam creaturam ad aliquid agendum vel non agendum pro consecutione felicitatis æternæ. Dicitur hic & infra: Signum notificatiuum: quoniam proprie nulla lex obligat liberum arbitrium, si notificata non fuerit. Hoc autem signum triplex est: quoddam mentale, quoddam vocale, quoddam scriptum: sicut est lex scripta prolata indita, literalis, vocalis, mentalis. De mentali scribitur in Psalmo: Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui Domine. Et ad Roman. 2. pulchre per totum. Et iterum in Psal. Legem tuam in medio cordis mei.
units.tr: Divine obligatory law is a true sign, revealed, notifying to the rational creature the right reason of God, who wills that creature to be bound or obligated to do or not do something for the attainment of eternal happiness. It is said here, and below, notifying sign, because no law properly binds the free will unless it has been notified. This sign is threefold: one mental, one vocal, one written; as there is a written law, promulgated, innate, literal, vocal and mental. Of the mental law it is written in the Psalm: The light of your countenance, Lord, is signed upon us. See also Romans 2, beautifully throughout. And again in the Psalm: Your law is in the midst of my heart.

units.la: Lex naturalis obligatoria describitur, quod est signum naturaliter habitum, notificatiuum rectæ rationis diuinæ, volentis creaturam rationalem humanam teneri seu ligari ad aliquid agendum pro consecutione finis sui naturalis, qui est felicitas humana, siue monastica, siue œconomica, siue politica. Dicitur autem signum pure naturaliter habitum illud quod inditum est cuilibet homini, non impedito in vsu debito rationis. Impeditur autem per corpus, per errores, per vitia multa.
units.tr: Obligatory natural law is described as a sign naturally possessed, notifying the right reason of God, who wills the human rational creature to be bound or obligated to do something for the attainment of its natural end, which is human happiness, whether monastic, economic or political. A sign is said to be purely naturally possessed when it is implanted in every man and is not hindered in the due use of reason. It is hindered, however, by the body, by errors, and by many vices.

units.la: Notificatur ex hac duplici descriptione differentia & conuenientia diuinæ legis ad naturalem principaliter ex modo acquisitionis & ex parte finis. Lex enim diuina de ratione sua habet primo, vt acquiratur per reuelationem. Deinde quod ordine de proximo & per se ad felicitatem æternam. Lex vero naturalis etsi possit sic acquiri & ordinari, sicut patet in datione præceptorum decalogi, in vtraq; lege veteri & noua: hoc tamen non habet de ratione sua, vt sui naturalis est, sed transit diuinam.
units.tr: From this twofold description, the difference and agreement between divine law and natural law become clear, chiefly in terms of the manner of acquisition and in terms of the end. For divine law, by its nature, first has this feature: that it is acquired through revelation. Second, that it is ordered directly and per se to eternal happiness. Natural law, though it can also be acquired and ordered in this way, as is evident in the giving of the precepts of the Decalogue in both the old and the new law, does not have this by its nature as natural; it passes over into the divine.

units.la: Lex canonica describitur, quod est signum habitum per humanam traditionem notificatiuum rectæ rationis diuinæ, volentis creaturam rationalem humanam teneri seu ligari ad aliquid agendum vel non agendum principaliter pro consecutione felicitatis æternæ. Per hanc vltimam clausulam conuenit lex canonica cum diuina, & differt à naturali. Et per primam ab vtraque sub sua ratione, quæ est vt habeatur eius cognitio & robur per humanam traditionem magis quam per puram reuelationem vel naturalem euidentiam.
units.tr: Canonical law is described as a sign possessed through human tradition, notifying the right reason of God, who wills the human rational creature to be bound or obligated to do or not do something, chiefly for the attainment of eternal happiness. By this last clause canonical law agrees with divine law and differs from natural law. By the first clause it differs from both, under its own aspect, which is that its knowledge and its force are obtained through human tradition rather than through pure revelation or natural evidence.

units.la: Lex ciuilis describitur, quod est signum habitum per humanam traditionem positiuam volentem quod homo teneatur seu ligetur aliquid agere vel non agere pro consecutione finis sui naturalis: quæ est humana felicitas vel monastica vel œconomica vel politica. Patet descriptio ex prioribus.
units.tr: Civil law is described as a sign possessed through positive human tradition, willing that a man be bound or obligated to do or not do something for the attainment of his natural end, which is human happiness, whether monastic, economic or political. The description is clear from what has been said before.

units.la: Vnde diligenter attendendum est, quod sicut in speculabilibus sunt primo principia naturaliter nota. Sunt secundo conclusiones euidenter ab illis principiis demonstratæ. Sunt consequenter tertio conclusiones tantummodo prohibiliter deductæ ex prædictis veritatibus, circa quas est solum opinio. Tandem quarto sunt aliæ propositiones sic elongatæ à primis veritatibus, quod non apparet, quod ex illis sequantur vel repugnent: vt si astra sint paria vel imparia. Proportionabiliter suo modo dicendum est de veritatibus moralibus sub hac distinctione quadruplici. Et iuxta duplicem primum gradum accipitur ius pure diuinum, si veritates sint certitudinaliter reuelatæ, vel ex reuelatis manifeste reductæ. Sed si cognoscantur per euidentiam naturalem accipitur ius proprie naturale. Circa tertium gradum & quartum proportionabiliter sumitur ius canonicum & ciuile: addita legislatoris auctoritate, quæ facit vt propositio moralis aliunde solum probabilis vel impertinens legibus proprie diuinis vel naturalibus robur habeat & vim obligationis ad alterum finem vel superiorem naturalem: & sic est lex canonica: vel naturalem, & sic lex ciuilis vel politica nominatur. Rememorandum est tamen id, quod iam dictum repetitur: paucissimas inueniri leges, quæ non se mutuo participent: sed ratio distinguit eas & secernit.
units.tr: Hence it must be carefully noted that, as in speculative matters there are, first, principles naturally known; second, conclusions evidently demonstrated from those principles; third, conclusions only probably deduced from the aforesaid truths, about which there is only opinion; and fourth, other propositions so remote from the first truths that it does not appear whether they follow from them or conflict with them, as whether the stars are even or odd in number. Proportionately, in its own way, the same must be said of moral truths under this fourfold distinction. According to the first two grades, purely divine right is taken if the truths are certainly revealed, or are manifestly drawn from revealed truths. But if they are known by natural evidence, properly natural right is taken. For the third and fourth grades, canonical and civil law are taken in proportion: with the added authority of the lawgiver, which gives a moral proposition, otherwise only probable or not pertinent to properly divine or natural laws, strength and binding force toward another end or a higher natural end. In this way it is canonical law; or, if it is natural, it is called civil or political law. It must be remembered, however, what has already been said and is repeated here: very few laws are found that do not share in one another, but reason distinguishes and separates them.

units.la: Transeamus consequenter post sermonem de iustitia, de iure, de lege: loqui de iurisdictione, de dominio & de politia. Iurisdictio describitur vel interpretatur, quod est iuris ditio, id est, potestas seu facultas exercendi ius. Vel dicitur iurisdictio quasi iuris dictio, id est, pronunciatio seu promulgatio iuris.
units.tr: Let us next move on, after our discussion of justice, right and law, to speak of jurisdiction, dominion and polity. Jurisdiction is described or interpreted as the power of right, that is, the power or faculty of exercising right. Or it is called jurisdiction, as if it were the pronouncing of right, that is, the proclamation or promulgation of right.

units.la: Quæ iurisdictio quadruplex est iuxta quadruplicem legem: diuina scilicet naturalis, canonica, ciuilis. Itaque iurisdictio diuina est potestas exequendi ius, quod competit alicui secundum legem propriam diuinam, & hoc in alterum vel tanquam in alterum. Non enim proprie dicitur habere quis iurisdictionem in semetipsum, nisi forte consideretur tanquam alter sit, vt vellent aliqui dæ pœnitentia dicere.
units.tr: There are four kinds of jurisdiction, corresponding to the fourfold law: divine, natural, canonical and civil. Divine jurisdiction is therefore the power to carry out the right that belongs to someone under the proper divine law, and this is exercised over another or toward another. For one is not properly said to have jurisdiction over oneself, unless perhaps one considers oneself as if one were another, as some wish to say about penance.

units.la: Proportionabilis est descriptio triplex triplicis alterius iurisdictionis secundum triplicem legem.
units.tr: The threefold description of the other jurisdiction, according to the threefold law, is proportionate.

units.la: Diuiditur autem quandoq; iurisdictio in coercitiuam: quæ scil. fertur in inuitum: & in directiuam seu regulatiuam & ordinatiuam, qualis fuisset etiam in statu innocentiæ: & qualis est sapientis ad insipientiores, & perfectioris ad imperfectiorem, vt in angelis etiam posuit Dionysius. Subjungamus de dominio, quod ita describi potest: Dominium est potestas propinqua ad, amendi res alias: vel ut alias in sui facultatem vel usum licitum secundum iura vel leges rationabiliter institutas.
units.tr: Jurisdiction is sometimes divided into coercive, that is, exercised against the unwilling, and directive, or regulative and ordinative. The latter would have existed even in the state of innocence, and it belongs to the wise over the less wise, and to the more perfect over the less perfect, as Dionysius also placed among the angels. Let us add something about dominion, which may be described thus: dominion is a proximate power to acquire other things, or to bring them under one's control and lawful use, according to rights or laws rationally instituted.

units.la: Inuenitur autem hoc modo dominium sextuplex: Beatificum, originale, gratificum, euangelicum, canonicum, politicum. Beatificum est dominium secundum leges gloriae. Originale dominium est secundum leges originalis iustitiae. Gratificum est dominium secundum leges gratiae gratificantis. Euangelicum est dominium secundum legem proprie euangelicam. Et ita de reliquis duobus suo modo. Primum fundatur in titulo gloriae: secundum in titulo originalis iustitiae: & ita de reliquis suo modo.
units.tr: Dominion is found in six kinds: beatific, original, gratifying, evangelical, canonical and political. Beatific dominion is according to the laws of glory. Original dominion is according to the laws of original justice. Gratifying dominion is according to the laws of gratifying grace. Evangelical dominion is according to the law proper to the gospel. And the other two are similar in their own way. The first is founded on the title of glory, the second on the title of original justice, and so on for the rest in their own way.

units.la: Possumus autem contractius loqui de triplici dominio: quorum unum fundatur in titulo charitatis gratificantis. Alterum in titulo alicuius gratiae supernaturalis solum gratis datae, non gratificantis. Tertium in titulo doni alicuius pure naturalis, sicut est electio vel naturalis successio ad aliquem principatum.
units.tr: We may speak more narrowly of a threefold dominion. One is founded on the title of gratifying charity. Another on the title of some supernatural grace that is given only freely, not gratifying. The third on the title of some purely natural gift, such as election, or natural succession to some principate.

units.la: Describitur autem dominium, quod appellatur a multis euangelicum, per appropriationem, quod est dominium immediate a Deo institutum compatiens secum ex aequo quotlibet Dominos & in abdicabile seruata charitate se extendens ad omnia. De hoc dicit Apostolus, quod nostra sunt omnia: quia diligentibus Deum omnia cooperantur in bonum: quoniam in titulum charitatis adiiciuntur omnia abunde ad fruendum vel vtendum, quae in coelis sunt & in terra, in mari & in omnibus abyssis.
units.tr: Dominion, which many call evangelical, is described by appropriation: it is dominion instituted immediately by God, which equally admits any number of masters alongside one another, cannot be renounced while charity is kept, and extends itself to all things. Of this the Apostle says that all things are ours, because all things work together for good for those who love God. For under the title of charity all things are added abundantly for enjoyment or use, whether they are in heaven or on earth, in the sea or in all the depths.

units.la: Describeretur conformiter dominium originalis iustitiae, quod est donum Dei, quod creatura rationalis ius habet immediate a Deo assumere alias res inferiores in sui vsum & conuersationem pluribus competens ex aequo: & inabdicabile seruata originali iustitia, seu integritate naturali. Hoc modo habuit Adam dominium super volucres coeli & pisces maris.
units.tr: In a similar way one would describe the dominion of original justice, which is a gift of God: the rational creature has the right to take other inferior things immediately from God for its own use and dealing, and this belongs equally to many, and it cannot be renounced while original justice, or natural integrity, is preserved. In this way Adam had dominion over the birds of the air and the fish of the sea.

units.la: Describeretur proportionabiliter dominium libertatis creatae, quod est facultas propinqua resultans ex liberalissima condescensione Dei donantis ad agendum vel non agendum cum anima rationali in productione suorum actuum eliciturum vel in eorum suspensione ad finem consequendae beatitudinis ordinata.
units.tr: In proportion one would describe the dominion of created liberty, which is a proximate faculty arising from the most bountiful condescension of God who gives it, to act or not to act together with the rational soul, in the production of its acts, which it will elicit, or in their suspension, ordered toward the end of attaining blessedness.

units.la: Porro quod sit dominium aliud fundatum in gratia supernaturali solum gratis data potest apparere consideranti naturam gratiae talis: sicut debet Apostolus, Quod spiritus Prophetarum subiecti sunt eis: & fides informis facit miracula.
units.tr: That there is another dominion, founded on supernatural grace given only freely, can appear to one who considers the nature of such grace: as the Apostle says, "the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets" (1 Cor. 14), and "unformed faith works miracles."

units.la: Contractius tamen locuti sumus in prima consideratione, dum potestatem ecclesiasticam descripsimus, quae dominium ecclesiasticum dici potest.
units.tr: We spoke more narrowly in the first consideration, when we described ecclesiastical power, which may be called ecclesiastical dominion.

units.la: Praeterea ciuile dominium seu politicum est dominium peccati occasione introductum, non competens pluribus ex aequo retinibile & abdicabile, seruata vel non seruata charitate fundatum in legibus ciuilibus & politicis, secundum quas potest abdicari vendendo, donando, negligendo, permutando. Unde & apud ecclesiasticos inuenitur tale dominium suo modo. Nec fundatur in charitate, nec in fide: quoniam apud infideles & iniustos peccatores iuste manet tale dominium.
units.tr: Moreover, civil or political dominion is a dominion introduced on account of sin. It does not belong equally to many, and it can be retained or renounced whether charity is kept or not. It is founded on civil and political laws, by which it may be renounced through selling, giving, neglecting or exchanging. Hence such dominion is also found among churchmen in its own way. It is founded neither on charity nor on faith, since such dominion rightly remains with unbelievers and unrighteous sinners.

units.la: Postremo tandem habito sermone de iustitia, de iure, de lege, de iurisdictione, de dominio, loquamur aliquid de politia describentes eam, quod est communitas ordinata ad finem aliquem perfectum. Est autem ordinatio vel ordo, parium dispariumque rerum sua vnicuiq; tribuens dispositio. Conuenit igitur prorsus ordo cum iustitia, quae dat vnicuiq; quod suum est. Propterea diuine fuit enunciatum per Prophetam, quod opus iustitiae est pax. Cur ita? Plane quia nihil aliud est pax, quam ordinis tranquillitas. Hanc vero tranquillitatem ordinis facit iustitia, ius suum vnicuiq; tribuens. Qua in re dictum est: iustitia & pax osculatae sunt.
units.tr: Finally, having spoken of justice, right, law, jurisdiction and dominion, let us say something about polity, describing it as a community ordered to some perfect end. Now ordering, or order, is a disposition that assigns to each thing, whether equal or unequal, what is its own. Order therefore agrees entirely with justice, which gives each person what is his own. Hence it was divinely declared through the prophet that the work of justice is peace. Why is this? Plainly because peace is nothing other than the tranquility of order, and justice, rendering to each his right, produces this tranquility of order. On this matter it has been said: righteousness and peace have kissed each other.

units.la: Politiarum vero alia est coelitus, de qua nihil ad praesens. Alia est humana duplex viatorum: Vna est quae vulgato & appropriato nomine dicitur ecclesiastica. Altera secularis. Secularis autem diuiditur ab Aristotele politiz in tres. Quarum primam vocat regnum. Secundam dicit aristocraticam. Tertiam nominat vocabulo generali appropriate politiam, quam dicere possumus timocratiam.
units.tr: Of polities, one is heavenly, about which nothing need be said at present. The other is human, and for us as wayfarers it is twofold: one is what is commonly and properly called ecclesiastical; the other is secular. Aristotle divides secular polity into three kinds. The first he calls kingdom. The second he calls aristocracy. The third he names, in the general sense, polity in the proper sense, which we may call timocracy.

units.la: Describitur regnum, quod est politia sub vno bono. Vel expressius, quod est congregatio communitatis perfectae sub vno secundum leges suas bonas pro republica. Dicitur autem vnus ille bonus vel rex, vel Imperator seu monarcha, qui non proprium principaliter, sed commune bonum intendit in suo principatu. Describitur aristocratia, quod est politia sub paucis bonis; vel expressius quod est congregatio communitatis perfectae sub paucis bonum reipublicae per leges suas principaliter intendentibus, vt senatus.
units.tr: Kingdom is described as a polity under one good man; or, more expressly, it is a gathering of a perfect community under one man, who rules according to his good laws for the commonwealth. That one good man is called king, or emperor, or monarch, who in his rule intends chiefly not his own good but the common good. Aristocracy is described as a polity under a few good men; or, more expressly, it is a gathering of a perfect community under a few, who by their laws chiefly intend the good of the commonwealth, such as a senate.

units.la: Describitur politia appropriato nomine seu timocratia, quod est politia sub plurimis bonis. Vel expressius, quod est congregatio communitatis perfectae sub plurimis vtilitatem reipublicae per leges suas principaliter intendentibus. Dicitur perfecta communitas ad differentiam oeconomicae conuersationis, qui sibi perfecte non sufficit. Dicitur secundum leges suas: quoniam in hoc attenditur principatus dominantis, si secundum leges suas inueniatur vltro regere politiam, aliena lege non artatus.
units.tr: Polity in the proper sense, or timocracy, is described as a polity under many good men; or, more expressly, it is a gathering of a perfect community under many, who by their laws chiefly intend the usefulness of the commonwealth. It is called a perfect community in contrast to the household, which is not perfectly self-sufficient. It is said to be according to its own laws, since what is considered here is the rule of the governing power, namely whether it is found to govern the polity of its own accord according to its own laws, and is not bound by another's law.

units.la: Omnis idcirco politia ecclesiastica siue dominetur vnus, siue pauci, siue plures boni, dicitur propriae diuina: quia secundum leges supernaturales debet quaebet regulationem accipere. Et ita perspicuum est, quod tres istae politiae vniuntur in ecclesia aliter, quam in ciuili politia, propter diuinae legis vnitatem.
units.tr: Therefore every ecclesiastical polity, whether ruled by one, by a few, or by many good men, is rightly called divine, because it ought to receive its regulation according to supernatural laws. And so it is clear that these three forms of polity unite in the Church differently than in civil polity, on account of the unity of the divine law.

units.la: Perspicuum est consequenter quaestionem hanc sapere blasphemiam & haeresim Pelagianam; in ecclesiastico regimine theologia praeponi debeat alteri scientiae naturali vel humanae. Non enim sumitur hic ecclesia pro templo materiali: quod aedificare melius sciret latomus, quam theologus aut iurista. Nec de ecclesia tantum modo debet fieri sermo pro solis prouentibus & redditibus & iurisdictionibus ecclesiasticis ad temporalitatem & vitam hanc civilem respicientibus: quoniam esset hoc pure gentiliter sapere. Ita tamen animales etiam de ecclesia plerumque concipiunt, pro ut operibus & verbis insinuant extollentes usque in coelum: si quis episcopus aut abbas laboraverit, ut stent moenia & praedia cum suis iurisdictionibus & permittat ruere subditos per errorum deuia in fide catholica & bonis moribus. Sic autem posset saecularis unus expertus oeconomicus iudicari frequenter utilior in ecclesiastico regimine, quam theologus aut iurista.
units.tr: It follows that this question smacks of blasphemy and the Pelagian heresy: whether in ecclesiastical governance theology ought to be preferred to other natural or human sciences. For church is not taken here as a material temple, which a mason would know better how to build than a theologian or a lawyer. Nor should discussion of the Church be confined to the revenues, incomes and ecclesiastical jurisdictions that concern temporal and civil life, for that would be to think in a purely worldly way. Yet natural men commonly conceive of the Church in this way, as their deeds and words reveal, extolling to heaven any bishop or abbot who has labored to keep the walls and estates with their jurisdictions intact, while allowing the subjects to wander into the errors of the Catholic faith and good morals. In this way an experienced secular manager could often be judged more useful in ecclesiastical governance than a theologian or a lawyer.

units.la: Considerari igitur debet ecclesia prout instituta est a Christo supra firmam petram fidei ad finem supernaturalem secundum legem euangelicam & sacrae scripturae diuinitus reuelatae: secundum quam debet regulari iudicium de fide & moribus subditorum: quoniam rectum est iudex sui & obliqui.
units.tr: The Church, therefore, must be considered as it was instituted by Christ upon the firm rock of faith, aiming at its supernatural end, according to the evangelical law and the Holy Scripture divinely revealed. By this standard the judgment concerning the faith and morals of its members ought to be regulated, since the straight is the judge both of itself and of the crooked.

units.la: Pro qua fide conseruanda si deberent in curia romana constitui auditores causarum fidei in theologia peritissimi nec corrupti moribus: quas causas omnes dicunt aliqui ad sedem Apostolicam referendas esse: licet hoc nimis generaliter intelligant, attendatur si hoc aeque rationabiliter fieret, sicut auditores causarum prophanarum sunt ordinarie & collegialiter instituti.
units.tr: If, in order to preserve this faith, hearers of cases of faith, most skilled in theology and not corrupt in morals, were to be appointed in the Roman curia (and some say that all such cases ought to be referred to the Apostolic See, though they understand this too generally), let it be considered whether this could be done as reasonably as the hearers of secular cases are ordinarily and collegially appointed.

units.la: Possumus conformiter ad praedictam Philosophi politiam tripliciter distinctam in naturaliregimine politiam ecclesiasticam diuidere: quod alia est Papalis, alia collegialis, alia synodalis seu concilii generalis. Papalis imitatur regalem. Collegialis Dominorum cardinalium imitatur aristocratiam. Synodalis generalis imitatur politiam seu timocratiam. Vel potius est perfecta politia quae resultat ex omnibus.
units.tr: Following the aforementioned division of the Philosopher into three kinds of polity under natural government, we may divide the ecclesiastical polity in the same threefold way: one form is papal, another collegial, and another synodal, that is, of a general council. The papal form imitates the kingly; the collegial, that of the lord cardinals, imitates aristocracy; the general synodal form imitates polity, or timocracy. Or rather, the perfect polity is that which results from all of them together.

units.la: Sunt ex aduerso politiae si taliter appellari merentur, quae non libero & tanquam paterali regimine ducuntur, sicut praecedentes, sed despotico & seruili iugo trahuntur: vel ex proprio demerito permittente Deo, qui regnare facit hypocritam, dicente Iob, propter peccata populi. Vel aliunde iusto eiusdem Dei iudicio. Vocat autem eas Aristot. primam; tyrannidem: alteram, oligarchiam, tertiam, democratiam. In tyrannide praesidet vnus proprium tantum modo bonum inquirens, volens subditus impotentes, indoctos & diuisos ab inuicem esse. In oligarchia praesident pauci similis conditionis super alios: In democratia praesidet sibipsi multitudo nequam, vbi quaerit vnusquisque quae sua sunt, non quae communia.
units.tr: On the other side are the polities, if they deserve to be so called, which are not led by a free and, as it were, paternal government, as the former are, but are dragged under a despotic and servile yoke. This happens either through their own demerit, God permitting it, who makes a hypocrite to reign, as Job says, because of the sins of the people; or else from some other cause, by the just judgment of the same God. Aristotle calls these, first, tyranny; second, oligarchy; third, democracy. In tyranny one man presides, seeking only his own good, and wanting his subjects to be powerless, untaught, and divided from one another. In oligarchy a few of the same condition preside over the rest. In democracy the wicked multitude presides over itself, where each one seeks what is his own, not what is common.

units.la: Cognoscet ex his studiosus lector, si possit in ecclesiastica politia tale aliquid tripliciter & proportionabiliter inuenire.
units.tr: The diligent reader will recognise from these points whether anything of this kind can be found in the ecclesiastical polity, in each of the three forms and in proportion to them.

units.la: Deniq; de politiis mixtis nihil expressimus, quoniam fere nulla est, quae mixtionem excludat, scilicet a praedominanti talis vel talis nominatur. Haec vero latius explicata sunt in tractatu quodam De vita spirituali, & in sermone illo: Dedit ei patet omnia in manus.
units.tr: Finally, we have said nothing about mixed polities, since there is almost none that excludes a mixture, so that it is named after whichever element predominates. These matters have been explained more fully in a certain treatise, On the Spiritual Life, and in that sermon on The Father hath given all things into his hand.

units.la: Epilogus praemissorum.
units.tr: Epilogue to the foregoing.

units.la: EPilogando dicimus, quod a prima iustitia deriuatur ius, generaliter in omnem creaturam, speciali-ter in creaturam rationalem, & hoc secundum multiplices leges: Secundum proprie diuinam, secundum proprie naturalem, secundum canonicam, secundum ciuilem. Fundatur inde participata iustitia imitatrix diuinae.
units.tr: In summing up we say that right derives from primary justice, generally into every creature and specially into the rational creature, and this according to several laws: according to the properly divine law, according to the properly natural law, according to the canon law, and according to the civil law. From this is founded participated justice, which imitates divine justice.

units.la: Dehinc iurisdictio quadruplex secundum quadruplicem legem: proprie diuinam, proprie naturalem, canonicam & ciuilem.
units.tr: Hence jurisdiction is fourfold, according to the fourfold law: properly divine, properly natural, canonical and civil.

units.la: Et de qualibet harum duplíciter haberi sermo potest. Quoniam alia est coercina in inuitum: Alia doctrinalis directiua vel arbitraria seu spontanea dici potest. Porro secundum leges & iurisdictiones fundantur dominia. Vnum gloriae: alterum iustitiae originalis: aliud gratiae gratificantis, aliud euangelicum secundum leges proprie diuinas, aliud euangelicum secundum leges canonicas: aliud politicum vel ciuile secundum leges ciuiliter datas. Amplius vero fundantur secundum praedicta diuersae politiae. Vna regalis seu libera: altera seruilis & despotica. Et vtraq; diuiditur in ecclesiasticam & secularem. Secularis libera & bona diuiditur in regnum, in aristocratiam, & timocratiam. Seruilis & mala in tyrannidem, in oligarchiam & democratiam. Ecclesiastica bona diuiditur proportionabiliter in Papatum, in cardinalatum & synodum. Mala vero re ipsa magis huic aduersio triplici modo cognoscitur, quam nomine.
units.tr: Each of these can be spoken of in two ways, since one kind is coercive, against the will of the unwilling, while the other may be called doctrinal, directive, arbitrary or voluntary. Moreover, according to the laws and jurisdictions, dominions are founded: one of glory, another of original justice, another of gratifying grace, another evangelical according to the properly divine laws, another evangelical according to the canon laws, and another political or civil according to laws given by civil authority. Furthermore, according to the aforesaid, diverse polities are founded: one royal or free, the other servile and despotic. Each of these is divided into ecclesiastical and secular. The good secular polity, which is free, is divided into kingdom, aristocracy and timocracy; the servile and bad into tyranny, oligarchy and democracy. The good ecclesiastical polity is divided in a corresponding way into papacy, cardinalate and synod. The bad ones, however, are known in fact rather than by name, and are opposed to these in a threefold way.

units.la: Tandem sub ecclesiastica politia continetur appropriato nomine potestas ecclesiastica, quae primo diuiditur; quoniam vna est ordinis: altera iurisdictionis. Potestas ordinis duplex. Vna super corpus Christi verum in consecratione: altera super corpus Christi mysticum in sacramentorum ministratione. Potestas iurisdictionis duplex. Vna in foro exteriori: altera in interiori. Potestas in exteriori duplex. Vna coercionis seu correctionis secundum legem proprie diuinam, quae est excommunicatio, altera secundum leges positiuas, canonicas seu ciuiles, quae iurisdictioni seculari similis est. Rursus potestas iurisdictionis in foro interiori duplex est. Vna clauium scientia & potestas testatis in absolutione seu remissione culparum. Altera in poenae commutatione per largitionem indulgentiarum.
units.tr: Finally, under ecclesiastical polity is contained, by its proper name, ecclesiastical power, which is first divided, since one part belongs to order and the other to jurisdiction. Power of order is twofold: one over the true body of Christ in consecration, the other over the mystical body of Christ in the administration of the sacraments. Power of jurisdiction is also twofold: one in the external forum, the other in the internal. Power in the external forum is twofold: one of coercion or correction according to the properly divine law, which is excommunication; the other according to positive, canonical or civil laws, which is similar to secular jurisdiction. Again, power of jurisdiction in the internal forum is twofold: one is the knowledge of the keys and the power of declaring absolution or remission of faults; the other is the commutation of penalty through the granting of indulgences.

units.la: Postremo tripliciter habet considerari potestas ecclesiastica. Uno modo in se formaliter vel absolute, alio modo, ut in hoc vel illo supposito materialiter seu subiectiue: tertio modo visualiter vel exercitatiue. Visus vero quadruplex est, licitus & ratus, licitus & non ratus; illicitus & ratus, illicitus & irritus. Ratus vero dupliciter; vel de iure, vel de facto.
units.tr: Lastly, ecclesiastical power has to be considered in three ways: in one way formally or absolutely, in itself; in another way materially or subjectively, as it is in this or that subject; and in a third way visually, or as it is exercised. The exercise is fourfold: lawful and ratified; lawful and not ratified; unlawful and ratified; unlawful and void. Ratification is twofold: either by right or in fact.

units.la: Finit tractatulus magis ad inquisitionem veritatis, quam ad determinationem editus & pronunciatus Constantiae tempore generalis concilii pro parte Cancellarii Parrhisiensis, Anno a natiuitate Domini M.CCCCXVII. die 6. Februarii.
units.tr: Here ends the little treatise, which was published and pronounced at Constance, during the time of the general council, on behalf of the Chancellor of Paris, more for the inquiry into truth than as a determination, in the year of the Lord's nativity 1417, on 6 February.

units.la: CONCORDIA QVOD PLE- NITVDO POTESTATIS ECCLESIASTICAE SIT IN SVMMO PONTIFICE ET IN ECCLESIA, QVAMVIS NON omnino simpliciter: & hoc sub triplici conclusione. Cuius declaratio patet ex tractatu, cuius titulus est De potestate ecclesiastica, de origine iuris & legum.
