Postremo quo ad hoc videnda sunt scripta continentia rationes contra Benedictum: & videantur similiter responsiones atque ponderentur. Et forte videbimus quicquid sit in re quod non poterit sufficienter de haeresi aut schismate conuinci: quod tamen exigitur. Est enim difficilimum conuincere aliquem pertinacem & incorrigibilem fuisse ante iudicium. Nam etsi aliquis millesies repetierit & protestatus fuerit ante sententiam, quod defendit errorem suum, nec revocabit: tamen admittitur ad veniam in puncto sententiæ proferendæ, si se monstret poenitere & velle telle stare iudicio (superioris sui, quamuis ipse Ockam videatur oppositum in Dialogo suo suasisse. Contra quod est vsus & lex ecclesiae.
units.tr: Thirdly, the argument is made on the side of the means of treating it. Let us suppose, then, what is not likely, that all of this obedience, by unanimous assent, wish to meet in council to treat this matter, though not the only one, yet especially and principally. It is clear that Benedict and his followers will be heard in their own defence. Therefore it must be seen first of all whether the things now opposed against him, or to be opposed, are of such a kind that they ought to carry conviction for all, even for those who obey and favour him. For if they are not of such a kind, and not so evident, we who defend the continuation of the withdrawal will not only propose them in vain but to our own confusion, and we will put ourselves in danger of a stirred-up schism and of shameful condemnation. Add to this that favour and love greatly hinder the judgments of men, even just men, though they do not believe or see this. Since, therefore, the greater part of the council will be of those who condemn the withdrawal, or at least the continuation of the withdrawal, nothing remains but that we be condemned. Nor is it any good to say that the Lord will not allow the council to err, since in matters of fact or positive law, and briefly in all matters except those purely of faith, the Church can err and be deceived, provided charity is kept. This is plain when it compels someone to live in what is not his own. Those propositions, however, "The withdrawal was rightly done" or "wrongly done," are not propositions purely of faith; they presuppose other matters which are purely of fact. Again, to the same point: if Benedict is accused of certain things, who doubts that he will accuse his brothers and other adversaries of many things, perhaps of greater, more plausible, and better grounded things, both in matters of faith and in matters of schism? For example, he will accuse the Cardinals of rebellion against him, conspiracy, and the crime of deceitful machinations, or of other crimes such as simony and the like. Likewise he has certain writings of some men in which there are manifest heresies, while they believe they are attacking him: such as that only the cardinals are the successors of the Apostles; that the whole Church could not create a Pope except through the mediation of the Cardinals, nor ever could; that a thing expressly forbidden by God, if sworn to, must be kept out of reverence for the oath; that Jephthah deserved well for killing his own daughter; that God can be bound. Likewise, of others: that there can be several supreme pontiffs; that decrees and decretals have done the Church more harm than good; that the keys were given to unity, not to one person; that every one who obeys, or procures obedience to, Benedict, while the terms stand in which the supreme one is a schismatic, is consequently obstinate; that it is an error in faith and morals, while there is a probable and notorious doubt, to say of some contending for the papacy that one should be obeyed rather than the other. For since the present schism is in just such a probable and notorious doubt, if such a doubt ever was or will be, all who have obeyed until now, or obey, one party or the other, err in faith and morals. Likewise, that in the same doubt every contender is bound to yield his right, if he has one, and similar things. Likewise, that one may appeal from the Pope, and that an appeal has been lawfully made in this matter, though the opposite was recently determined, it is said, by the whole council of Cardinals. Likewise, perhaps many will be accused of many crimes, both in faith and in morals, which ought to be punished by death, and by the laws and decrees the perpetrators of such deserve to be disinherited together with their posterity; and so it is easy to see that a dreadful split would result. Yet it seems more likely that the matters mentioned must be treated in this way. For if Benedict accuses himself and his supporters to death, is it not credible, considering his character, that he will likewise accuse others to death if he can? Especially if he has supporters of those whom he wishes to accuse as hateful enemies. Indeed, perhaps he will accuse the prelates of the kingdom of many sentences of excommunication, and by name, because, as he will say, they consented against the laws and against ecclesiastical liberty, granting subsidies to temporal lords without cause of manifest necessity, and so on. The prelates, on the other hand, will want to defend themselves. They will also want to give benefices at will, as now, and perhaps Benedict and his cardinals will not want this. Likewise, perhaps he will turn everything back against his predecessor Clement and his supporters, who will be cited against him, at least as regards those things which concern the various ways of plotting to impede unity. I do not say justly, but not even unjustly; may God spare everyone. Finally, in this regard the writings containing arguments against Benedict must be examined, and likewise the replies, and they must be weighed. And perhaps we shall see that, whatever the truth of the matter, he cannot be sufficiently convicted of heresy or schism, which nevertheless is required. For it is most difficult to prove that someone was obstinate and incorrigible before judgment. For even if someone has a thousand times repeated, and protested before sentence, that he defends his error and will not revoke it, yet he is admitted to pardon at the moment the sentence is pronounced, if he shows that he repents and is willing to abide by the judgment of his superior, although Ockham seems to have argued the opposite in his Dialogue. Against this stands the custom and law of the Church.

units.la: Quarto sic arguitur ex fine concilii in obediendo. Videamus itaque secundum veram & iustam aestimationem: Si quilibet de concilio tenebit maiorem partem bene sententiasse quantumcunque sit in sui opprobrium vel damnum vel infamiam. Nam cum concilium etiam totum posset errare, vt dictum est in his quae tractanda hic proponuntur: nonne poterit leviter dicere condemnatus in hoc concilio: certe concilium erravit, concilium male sententiavit. Fuit hic inimicitia vel odium vel ignorantia facti vel alicuius similis. Consideremus obsecro, si pars, quae subtraxit nec vult obedire, condemnaretur male egisse aut saltem debere obedire, an pareret huic sententiae, scio quod facile est dicere, ita: obedirentur, scio quod etiam ita obedire possent. Sed an hoc deberet secundum mortalem aestimationem & coniecturam credi ex his, quae vt in pluribus accidunt humanitus, viderint qui sic vident, ego non video. Si vero nihil sententietur, irrisorium & vanum erit concilium. Si aliquid sententietur, quod non teneatur, erit perniciosum & scandalosissimum pro omnibus conciliis in posterum celebrandis, & erit schismatum innumerabilium & irreparabilium causatiuum: non solum inter istam obedientiam in partibus suis, imo & inter istam obedientiam & alteram: quoniam remanebimus in irrisione & in infamia apud eos perpetua, in fabulam quoq; & derisum. Et forte non poterit esse concordia in modo restituendi: quia alii volent ex toto, alii ex parte. Isti volent in spiritualibus, alii in temporalibus. Aut ergo volumus nos qui subtraximus restituere obedientiam: & ita melius est quod nosipsos liberefaciamus quam coacti iudicio. Aut nolumus: & ita exponimus nos periculis praetactis, si petamus concilium.
units.tr: Fourthly, the argument runs as follows from the purpose of the council regarding obedience. Let us consider it according to a true and just estimation: if each member of the council holds that the majority has judged well, however much it may be to his disgrace, loss or infamy. For since the council, as has been said in the matters proposed for treatment here, can also err as a whole, will not the one condemned in this council easily say: "Certainly the council has erred, the council has judged badly. There was enmity, or hatred, or ignorance of the facts, or something of the kind here." Let us consider, I beg you, whether the party which has withdrawn and refuses to obey should be condemned as having acted badly, or at least ought to obey, and whether it would submit to this sentence. I know it is easy to say yes, they ought to obey; I know they could also obey in this way. But whether they ought to believe this on the basis of mortal estimation and conjecture, drawn from those things which for the most part happen among men, those who see such things may see; I do not see it. If, on the other hand, nothing is decreed, the council will be laughable and vain. If something is decreed which is not binding, it will be harmful and most scandalous for all councils to be held hereafter, and it will be the cause of countless and irreparable schisms: not only between that obedience in its own parts and the other, but also between that obedience and the other; since we shall remain in perpetual ridicule and infamy before them, a story and a laughingstock. And perhaps there will be no agreement on the manner of restoring unity: some will want it wholly, others in part; these will want it in spiritual matters, others in temporal ones. Therefore either we who have withdrawn are willing to restore obedience, and so it is better that we free ourselves than be compelled by judgment; or we are unwilling, and so we expose ourselves to the aforementioned dangers if we seek a council.

units.la: Sed dicet aliquis, istud concilium peti debere: non quod fieri debeat aut speretur: sed quod interim absque scandalo tempus protrahatur: quo currente morietur Benedictus: & liberabit nos Dominus & eligendi libertatem dabit. Posset hic allegari illud vulgatum pueris notissimum:
units.tr: But someone will say that this council ought to be sought, not because it ought to take place or is hoped for, but so that in the meantime time may be protracted without scandal; while it runs, Benedict will die, and the Lord will deliver us and give us freedom of choice. Here that well-known saying, familiar to boys, could be cited:

units.la: In mortem alterius noli sperare salutem.
units.tr: In the death of another, do not hope for salvation.

units.la: Quis scit enim quantum viuet, quando morietur? Et interim in quo statu sumus: imo in quos status currimus, nemo non videt. Porro & si cras moreretur Benedictus, attendamus incredibilia pericula. Primo diceretur ab inobedientibus sibi, quod mors eius fuisset proditorie accelerata: & ita suspecti de hoc persequerentur. Item obedientes nunc sibi obedientiam negarent ab illo, qui noliter esset electus. Tum quia iudicarent Cardinales a misisse ius electionis: tum quia verisimiliter alium eligerent per aliquos Cardinales, qui non subtraxerunt. Aut forte ad aliam obedientiam se diverterent. Imo rebus se habentibus inter nos, vt se habent, caecus est qui non aspicit periculum dissensionis civilis in regno Franciae, qualis non fuit a diebus suae institutionis. Et sane eo periculosior esset diuisio, quo magis intranea, & quo magis inter capita regni, & quo sub specie religionis fieret. Nam tunc expectandum esset illud, quod dicit Scriptura: Amicus qui vult recedere ab amico, occasiones quaerit. Et illud decreti: Schisma disponit ad haeresim: quia recedens ab ecclesia, errores fingit, vt recte discessisse videatur. Et hoc iam periculum habemus in ianuis, nisi celeriter & cautissime prouiderimus. Addito quod nulla sit implacabilior & irremediabilior diuisio, quam illa quae fit sub religionis praetextu. Intantum quod in hoc casu putet frater se obsequium praestare Deo pro equendo fratrem. Addito praeterea quod magna pars ne dicam maior non sponte consensit in subtractionem. Vel nunc dum videt, quae secuta sunt voluntaria & pronissima est obedire & reuerti: nec obstat forte ad reuertendum nisi timor, quo sublato & data audacia, ipsi etiam cum periculo corporis & rerum suarum suam ostenderent voluntatem. Quid si descenderimus ad particularia, quae scienter omittimus: arbitramur indubie, quod rei huius ingens & horrendus pateret aspectus, & stuporem vehementem sola cogitatione causaret. Vae vae regno huic a scandalis: vae pesti schismatice, si diuisionem in regno adducat, sicut iam positum in Imperio. Sed vae supra modum, si nobis haereticis parturiatur, ipsum schisma irremediabiliter radicetur: & radicatum iugiter alatur, crescat, dilatetur atque roboretur.
units.tr: For who knows how long he will live, or when he will die? And meanwhile, in what state we are, or rather into what states we are running, everyone sees. Moreover, even if Benedict were to die tomorrow, let us consider the incredible dangers. First, those who are disobedient would say that his death had been hastened by treachery, and so those suspected of this would be persecuted. Likewise, those who now obey him would deny obedience to the one who would be elected unwillingly, because they would judge that the Cardinals had lost the right of election; and because they would probably elect another through some Cardinals who had not withdrawn. Or perhaps they would turn aside to another obedience. Indeed, with things as they stand among us, he is blind who does not see the danger of civil dissension in the kingdom of France, such as has not existed since the days of its founding. And truly the division would be the more dangerous, the more it were internal, the more it were among the heads of the kingdom, and the more it were done under the appearance of religion. For then that would have to be expected which Scripture says: "A friend who wishes to withdraw from a friend seeks occasions." And that saying of the decree: "Schism disposes to heresy," because one who withdraws from the Church invents errors so that his withdrawal may appear justified. And we already have this danger at our doors, unless we provide quickly and most cautiously. Added to this, there is no division more implacable and more irremediable than that which is made under the pretext of religion; so much so that in such a case a brother thinks he is rendering service to God by persecuting a brother. Added besides, a large part, not to say the greater part, did not consent to the withdrawal willingly. Now, seeing what has followed, they are willing and most ready to obey and return; and perhaps only fear stands in the way of their returning, and once that is removed and courage given, they would themselves, even at risk to body and goods, show their will. What if we descend to particulars, which we knowingly omit? We think without doubt that the aspect of this huge and horrible matter would open up, and would cause great stupor by thought alone. Woe, woe to this kingdom because of scandals; woe to the schismatic plague, if it brings division into the kingdom, as has already happened in the Empire. But woe beyond measure, if it should be born among us heretics, and the schism itself be irremediably rooted; and once rooted, be continually nourished, grow, spread and be strengthened.

units.la: Ex his omnibus hinc inde tactis & insolutis perspicuum est, in quali labyrintho vix egresisibi positi sumus: & vinculis vix extricabilibus irretiti, quasi videlicet Posuerimus in retibus pedes: & in maculis eorum ambulemus, iuxta verba Iob.
units.tr: From all these things, touched on here and there and left unresolved, it is clear into what labyrinth we have been placed, scarcely able to get out, and caught in bonds scarcely to be untied; as if, indeed, "they have set their feet in nets, and walk upon their meshes," according to the words of Job.

units.la: Cum igitur angustiae nobis sint undiq; : & cum ignoramus quid agere debeamus, ego in insipientia mea hoc solum video residui & concilii cum Iosaphat rege 2. Paral. 20. vt oculos nostros ad Deum dirigamus: si forte aueriat iram suam a nobis. Si forte non auferat consilium a prudentibus & senioribus: sicut videtur hactenus abstulisse: Quamuis hoc fieri in tanta peccatorum abominabilium colluvione, & in tam obstinata & incorrecta flagitiorum nephandorum multiplicatione vix expecto & vix spero: nisi quod miserocordiae Dei non est numerus: & solus est medicus, qui desperatos morbos ad sanitatem adducit: ne glorietur ante eum stulta praesumptio omnis carnis, quasi homo pacem effecerit.
units.tr: Since, therefore, straits surround us on every side, and since we do not know what we ought to do, I in my foolishness see this only as the remaining counsel, together with King Jehoshaphat, 2 Chronicles 20: that we direct our eyes to God, if perhaps He may turn away His wrath from us; if perhaps He may not take counsel away from the prudent and the elders, as He seems hitherto to have taken it away. Yet, amid such a foul heap of abominable sins and in such obstinate and uncorrected multiplication of wicked crimes, I scarcely expect and scarcely hope for this; except that the mercies of God are without number, and He alone is the physician who brings desperate diseases to health, so that no foolish presumption of all flesh may glory before Him, as if man had made peace.

units.la: Si quid autem vel in dubio dicere necesse sit, pro remedio praesenti dicam sub correctione. Videretur itaque ante omnia tractandum hoc negocium inter Dominos omnes de sanguine Regio, communi consensu & absque malevola, aut acerba contentione, cum quibusdam pertis non nimis hinc vel inde affectatis. Et qui non tantum timerent de statu suo in posterum, nec tantum affectarent nouam status exaltationem, quod mentiri velle præsumerentur inordinato timore, odio vel fa-uore cuiuscunque. Quibus in unum congregatis & ambulare volentibus in domo Domini cum consensu: sperandum est in illo, qui est Deus pacis & dilectionis, cuius locus in pace factus est, & qui est in medio eorum qui se congregant in nomine suo, quod ipse expediens aliquid in materia ministrabit. Alioquin si seorsum per contentiones & partialitates & simultates & comminationes negotium hoc de pace restaurandā tractetur: non nisi diuisionem crudeliores & multipliciores generabuntur: & erit immedicabile vulnus. Et tandem quod Dei pietas auertat, super capita nostra, dum contendemus & rixabimur: imo dum nos plus quam hostiliter ad mortem persequemur, irruent quaquaueisum hostes alieni insidiatores regni huius ad prædandum & vastandum paratissimi: & nos iam non vt hostes suos, sed vt schismaticos & hæreticos & Saracenos liberius persequendos intuadent, vt in fabulis aquila fecisse fingitur, de rana & mure certantibus. Sit vtinam vanus iste timor, quem timeo: nec tamen timere desinam, priusquam aliquod remediandi genus aliud, quam quæri video, aspicere meruero.
units.tr: If, however, something must be said even in doubt, I will say it for the present remedy, subject to correction. It seems that before all else this matter should be treated among all the lords of royal blood, by common consent and without malicious or bitter contention, with certain persons not too strongly inclined to either side; and who would not fear too much for their own state in the future, nor desire too much a new exaltation of their own status, so that they would not be presumed to wish to lie out of inordinate fear, hatred or favour toward anyone. When these have been gathered together, and are willing to walk in the house of the Lord with one accord, we must hope in Him who is the God of peace and love, whose place has been made in peace, and who is in the midst of those who gather in His name, that He will supply something useful in the matter. Otherwise, if this business of restoring peace is handled apart, through contentions, partialities, enmities and threats, it will only generate more cruel and more numerous divisions, and the wound will be incurable. And at last, may the piety of God avert it, while we contend and wrangle, indeed while we persecute one another more than hostilely unto death, foreign enemies, plotters against this kingdom, most ready for plunder and devastation, will rush in from every quarter; and they will attack us, no longer as their enemies, but as schismatics, heretics and Saracens to be more freely persecuted, as in the fable the eagle is said to have done, when the frog and the mouse were fighting. Would that this fear which I fear were vain; yet I shall not cease to fear before I am granted to see some other kind of remedy than the one I see being sought.

units.la: QVÆDAM PER PRÆFA- TVM DOMINVM IOHANNEM GERSON EDITA TEMPORE SHISMATIS ECCLESIÆ.
units.tr: Certain matters set forth by the aforesaid Master Johannes Gerson during the time of the schism of the Church.

units.la: Aturus occasionem sapientibus, vt sapientiores fiant: propono eorum examinationi propositiones negatiuas: quæ sequuntur super materia communis concilii huius obedientiæ. Ex quibus patebit citius, si sit expediens aut non, concilium huiusmodi celebrari: & si sic, quæ cautela debeat observari.
units.tr: Intending to give the wise an occasion to become wiser, I put before their examination the following negative propositions concerning the question of a general council of this obedience. From these it will become clearer whether such a council ought to be held or not, and if so, what caution should be observed.

units.la: Non expedit fieri concilium generale huius obedientiæ ad tractandum & sententiandum de criminibus Domini Benedicti sibi per quosdam impositis: vtputa de periurio & schismate & hæresi, aut de suspitione vehementi super istis.
units.tr: It is not expedient to hold a general council of this obedience to treat of and pass sentence on the crimes which certain men have imputed to Lord Benedict, namely perjury, schism and heresy, or on strong suspicion of these.

units.la: Primo, quia obedientia ista in se & in partibus suis diuisa est circa iudicium de actis per Papam, aliis dicentibus: quia bonus est & sufficienter obtulit, præsertim nouissime: aliis contrarium asserentibus. Tra[?]reigitur talia coram multitudine tam multipliciter diuisa, esset potius induratio & noua multiplicatio diuisionum, quam illarum sedatio: attento quod ita requireret Dominus Benedictus fieri super dictis hæreticis illorum qui sibi subtraxerunt.
units.tr: First, because this obedience is itself divided, both as a whole and in its parts, over the judgment on the acts of the Pope: some say that he is good and has sufficiently made offers, especially most recently; others assert the contrary. Therefore, to deal with such matters before a gathering so variously divided would be rather a hardening and a fresh multiplication of divisions than their calming, especially since Lord Benedict would require that this be done concerning those heretics who withdrew from him.

units.la: Secundo, quia concilium huiusmodi ad hunc finem, aut fieret secundum formam præscriptam iure, aut noua inuentione. Si primo modo constat, quod Benedictus deberet præsse etiam sub noua submissione: & tamen rebus stantibus vt stant, non videtur quis locus esset aptus sibi ad securitatem, cum detinetur inclusus. Nec videtur quod permanentes in subtractione suae vocationi obedirent: & ita nihil ageretur. Si autem fieret concilium per nouos modos præter formam iuris: non videtur modus verisimilis ante celebrationem concilii, quomodo prælati & principes in vnum concordarent: vno volente vnum modum, altero alium, & esset tractatus in tractando hoc dispendiosissimus & sumptuosissimus sine magno fructu.
units.tr: Second, because a council of this kind, to achieve this end, would either be held according to the form prescribed by law, or by some new device. If by the first method, it is clear that Benedict would have to be present even under a new submission; yet, with things standing as they now stand, no place seems suitable for his safety, since he is kept shut in. Nor does it seem that those who persist in their withdrawal would obey his summons, and so nothing would be accomplished. But if the council were held by new methods apart from the form of law, there seems to be no plausible way, before the council is convened, for the prelates and princes to agree on one plan: one wanting one method, another wanting a different one, and the negotiation over this would be enormously costly and burdensome without great profit.

units.la: Tertio, quia in determinatione huius materiæ necesse esset multa concurrere & allegare, tangentia fidem & mores: sed tales materias non expedit in hoc concilio ventilare ad determinandum, prout statim dictum est.
units.tr: Third, because in settling this matter it would be necessary to bring together and allege many things touching faith and morals; but, as has just been said, it is not expedient to debate such matters in this council for the purpose of determining them.

units.la: Quarto quia nunc omnia possunt fieri ad vnitatem vniuersalem ecclesiæ, erga alias procurandam, quemadmodum si tota hæc materia esset in concilio isto terminata, siue Papa remaneat, siue non, attento quod offert omnia quæ nouiter electus quicunque posset offerre: imo apud talem aut pro tali nouiter electo fieri possent nouæ colligationes & confirmationes peiores prioribus: & fieret verisimiliter noua diuisio, aut iam facta continuaretur in hac obedientia.
units.tr: Fourth, because now everything can be done to secure universal unity of the Church with the others, just as if this whole matter were settled in this council, whether the Pope remains or not, since he offers everything which any newly elected man could offer. Indeed, with such a man, or for such a newly elected man, new alliances and confirmations worse than the earlier ones could be made; and there would likely be a new division, or the division already made would be continued in this obedience.

units.la: Non expedit fieri concilium ad tractandum determinatiue materias fidei. Ratio ad hoc: quia esset dare occasionem scandali & periculi magni in fide nostra, si aliud determinaret illa pars siue altera, in materia quæ omnes tangit, & quæ ab omnibus debet approbari: quemadmodum patuit de Latinis & Græcis. Facile tamen esset & verisimile, quod determinationem in hac parte factam non approbaret altera pars: præsertim si in aliquo tangi videretur status eorum in materia hac schismatis, sicut tamen tangeret etiam apud istam partem. Et forte ita apud aliam dicuntur multæ assertiones de fide, in quibus esset aduersissima sententia inter diuersas obedientias: imo & inter multos eiusdem obedientiæ. Vt super materia appellationis à Papa. Et super eo quod renuens cedere aut cessionem facere, est schismaticus. Et quod nō adhærens subtractioni est suspectus de schismate, vel ecclesiæ aduersus, vel in latitudine schismaticorum: & ita de similibus multis. Constat quod de prima istarum propositionum est controuersia in regno Franciæ apud Theologos & Decretistas, & inter multos-
units.tr: It is not expedient to hold a council for determining matters of faith by decree. The reason is much the same as for the preceding proposition: it would give occasion for scandal and great danger to our faith if one side or the other determined a matter which touches everyone and must be approved by all, as was made plain in the case of the Latins and the Greeks. It would, however, be easy and likely that the determination made on one side would not be approved by the other, especially if their own status in this matter of the schism seemed to be touched, as it would indeed be touched on that side too. And perhaps on many articles of faith, the opinions of the different obediences would be most opposed, indeed even among many within the same obedience. For example: concerning the matter of appeal from the Pope; concerning the claim that whoever refuses to yield or to make a cession is a schismatic; that whoever does not adhere to the withdrawal is suspect of schism, or is an opponent of the Church, or belongs to the broad class of schismatics; and many similar matters. It is certain that there is controversy over the first of these propositions in the kingdom of France, among theologians and Decretists, and among many

units.la: tos de concilio regis & de parlamento, & alios de vniuersitate, & inter se mutuo. Et de aliis duabus assertionibus similiter & amplius, quoniam altera obedientia nunquam tales concederet, imo reputaret erroneas. Propter quod perspicuum est non esse tutum talia determinare per modum autoritatis concilii generalis. Sed nec deberent tales assertiones leuiter in particularibus poni, quia reputatur hoc ab aliis ad iniuriam suam, vt dicere quod error sit in fide, si asseratur quod stante dubio probabili de Papatu apud duos contendentes alteri sit adhærendum quia non esse possibile maius dubium probabile, quam sit in casu præsentis schismatis, & tamen vtique obedientia dixit obediendum suo. Et ita de similibus, vt quod non sit alia via humanitus inueniendis ad sedandum schisma, quam via cessionis, cum iam videatur reddita per se inefficax, nisi concurrat saltem concilium generale, quod excludere non bene saperet, & quia certe circumstantiis negotiorum variatis possunt viæ & remedia ad vnitatem habendam vario modo reperiri: sicut & necessarium esse experientia præsens notum facit.
units.tr: others: about the council of the king and of the parlement, and others about the university, and among themselves mutually. The same holds, and more so, for the other two assertions, since the other obedience would never grant such things and would indeed regard them as erroneous. For this reason it is plain that it is not safe to determine such things by the authority of a general council. Nor ought such assertions to be lightly put forward in particular settings, since others take this as an injury to themselves, as when one says that it is an error against the faith to assert that, while there is a probable doubt about the papacy between two contenders, one should adhere to the other, since there cannot be a greater probable doubt than in the case of the present schism; and yet that obedience has said that its own must be obeyed. And so with similar claims: that there is no other human way of ending the schism than the way of cession, since this already seems to have been rendered ineffective in itself unless at least a general council concurs, which would not sound well to exclude; and because, when the circumstances of affairs change, ways and remedies for achieving unity can certainly be found in various ways, as present experience makes clear is also necessary.

units.la: Non expedit fieri concilium huiusmodi ad tractandum reformationem ecclesiæ in moribus per modum determinationis. Ratio ad hoc est quo ad multa eadem, sicut ad præcedentem propositionem: addito quod reformatio ecclesiæ vniuersalis fieri non potest in moribus sine abolitione multorum statutorum super excommunicationibus & cæteris traditionibus nimis multiplicatis, quæ nec obseruantur nec obseruari possunt rationabiliter vbique propter varietatem morum & temporum. Et tamen tales remotiones statutorum & canonum antiquorum, aut addition noorum fieri nequeunt rationabiliter pro tota ecclesia sine consensu communi: alias possent durare diu sitas nimia in moribus & iudiciis, quo ad ea, quæ Papa & concilia statuerunt. Si vero decerneretur, quod multa bona possunt ibi auisari & discuti, sed non determinari: pauca esset ibi vtilitas in comparatione tanti facti. Nam pauci viri literati & probi faciliter, & forte congruentius ista considerant, extraherent & ordinarent. Nolo tamen dicere quin in multis partibus possit ecclesia per suas partes reformari, imo hoc necesse esset. Sed ad hoc agendum sufficerent concilia prouincialia, & ad quædam satis essent concilia diœcesana & synodalia: prout super hac re iam aliqua scripta sunt & auisata, si quis vellet ad opus manum mittere & ad fortia. Sed heu desolatione desolata est omnis terra, quia nemo est qui recogitet corde, & quærunt omnes quæ sua sunt.
units.tr: It is not expedient to hold a council of this kind to deal with the reform of the Church in morals by way of determination. The reason is, as to many points, the same as for the preceding proposition, with the addition that the reform of the universal Church in morals cannot be carried out without abolishing many statutes concerning excommunications and other traditions, which have been multiplied too much, and which are neither observed nor can reasonably be observed everywhere, because of the variety of customs and times. Yet such removal of old statutes and canons, or the addition of new ones, cannot reasonably be done for the whole Church without common consent; otherwise there could long remain excessive diversity in morals and judgments regarding what the Pope and councils have decreed. If, on the other hand, it were decreed that many good things might be suggested and discussed there but not determined, there would be little benefit in comparison with so great an undertaking. For a few learned and upright men could more easily, and perhaps more suitably, consider these things, extract them, and set them in order. I do not, however, wish to say that the Church cannot be reformed in many parts through its own regions; indeed this would be necessary. But for this task provincial councils would suffice, and for certain matters diocesan and synodal councils would be enough, as some writings have already been produced and suggestions made on this very question, if anyone were willing to put his hand to the work and to the strong measures. But alas, "all the land is made desolate with desolation, because there is no man that layeth it to heart, and all seek their own things."

units.la: Non expedit pro restituendo obedientiam Papæ in spiritualibus fieri concilium huiusmodi generale. Primo, quia videtur implicatio (sicut tactum est) quod maneat subtractio huiusmodi à Papa, & quod fiat concilium. Secundo, quia facilius ista restitutio & reductio tractari poterit in solo regno Franciæ: si verum sit, quod omnes alii iam restituerunt obedientiam, aut in ea permanserunt, si verum sit etiam quod subtractio non est facta Papæ etiam in regno, nisi sub conditione explicita, vt quidam dicunt: aut saltem implicita, & quæ de iure & æquitate debet intelligi. Hæc conditio est, quousque Papa fecerit debitum suum, & concesserit ea quæ sibi petebantur; & propter quorum negationem fiebat subtractio. Nam cessante causa cessare debet effectus. Addito hoc quod subtractio nullo modo potuit fieri iuste, nisi ad finem vnionis tanquam medium ad hoc necessarium. Alioquin tantum malum & insolitum nullo modo posset a culpa defendi. Si ergo nunc videatur, quod subtractio non prodest ad vnionem, vel non est necessaria propter condescensionem Papæ ad ea quæ petebantur, cessare ipsa debet; quia si rebus stantibus vt stant erga Papæ promptitudinem decedendo, non potest de novo fieri subtractio, sicut concedere habent aduersarii, vt videtur, non potest aut debet eisdem rebus stantibus eadem subtractio continuari. Tertio, quia restitutio huius obedientiæ quo ad spiritualia fieri commodius & breuius potest per assensum cardinalium & reconciliationem mutuam indulgendo præterita, ratificando quæ ratificanda essent ad cautelam futurorum & emendationem securiorem præteritorum & conscientiarum serenationem, & ad abolendam omnem infamiæ aut rebellionis notam, & quatenus in viam pacis communi animo & eodem pede procederet hæc obedientia concordius; quoniam faciendo restitutionem debitis modis, nec subtrahentes, nec ille à quo factu est subtractio, remanerent notati de talibus, quod difficilius esset euadere, si per concilium aliquod fieret determinatiua decisio.
units.tr: It is not expedient for a general council of this kind to be held in order to restore obedience to the Pope in spiritual matters. First, because it seems a contradiction (as has been touched on) that this withdrawal from the Pope should continue and yet a council be held. Second, because this restoration and return could be more easily dealt with in the kingdom of France alone, if it is true that all others have already restored obedience or remained in it; and if it is also true that the withdrawal was not made from the Pope even in the kingdom except under an explicit condition, as some say, or at least an implicit one, which ought to be understood in law and equity. This condition is that it was to last until the Pope did his duty and granted what was asked of him, and for the refusal of which the withdrawal was made. For when the cause ceases, the effect ought to cease as well. Add to this that the withdrawal could in no way have been made justly, except for the purpose of union, as a necessary means to that end. Otherwise so great and unusual an evil could in no way be defended from fault. If therefore it now appears that the withdrawal does not help toward union, or is not necessary because the Pope has yielded to what was asked, it ought itself to cease; for if, with things standing as they now stand, with the Pope's readiness to withdraw, a new withdrawal cannot be made, then, as our opponents seem to concede, the same withdrawal cannot and ought not to be continued under the same circumstances. Third, because the restoration of this obedience in spiritual matters can be achieved more conveniently and quickly by the agreement of the cardinals and by mutual reconciliation, by pardoning what is past, by ratifying what ought to be ratified for the security of the future and a safer amendment of the past and the peace of consciences, and for wiping away every mark of infamy or rebellion; and insofar as this obedience would proceed on the path of peace with a common mind and on the same footing more harmoniously. For if restoration were made by the proper means, neither those who withdrew nor the one from whom the withdrawal was made would remain marked by such things, which would be harder to escape if a definitive decision were made by some council.

units.la: Non expedit concilium tale celebrari pro restituendo obedientiam Papæ in administrationibus beneficiorum & aliorum huiusmodi, quia licet annexa sint spiritualibus, tamen possunt temporalia nominari. Primo, quia rationes aliquæ priores de non expediendo reformationem ecclesiæ vniuersalem in moribus tractare faciunt pro hac parte. Tamen aduertendum est, quod & siconcederetur Papam habere dominium diuino dominium vniuersale spiritualium & temporalium, respectu omnium: tamen constat quod pro diuersitate temporum & locorum & statuum, nec Papa nec ecclesia habuerunt aut habere debent in talibus dispensationibus aut administrationibus beneficiorum temporalium iurisdictionum simile exercitium aut executionem aut vsum. Itaq; notum est, quod ecclesia tempore Christi & Apostolorum nullum habuit exercitium aut executionem iuridicam & ciuiliter circa huiusmodi temporalia: imo Christus plus videtur facto & verbo tale exercitium iurisdictionis ciuilis prohibuisse quam permisisse: licet non dicam, quod prohibuerit aut opposition consuluerit, nisi pro loco & tempore. Quia enim ecclesia tunc multiplicanda erat per discursum Apostolorum & fidelium: ideo talis iurisdictio temporalis & possessiones fuissent eis ad impedimentum, & tales sunt ad hoc congruentiæ multæ. Sed pro tempore Syluestri & Constantini Magni placuit Domino ad dilatationem ecclesiae inspirare, tum Constantino quod tales possessiones daret, tum ecclesiae quod reciperet: & durauit huiusmodi dotatio ecclesiae vsque ad tempora nostra per successiones sanctissimorum patrum Gregorii & Ambrosii & aliorum, quos non est credibile in retentione talium errasse contra Christi iussionem. Sed longe aliter in primitiua dotatione distribuebantur bona talia, quam postmodum tempore praelatorum, qui caeperunt paulatim refrigescere a sanctitate priorum: tandem abusi sunt taliter collationibus beneficiorum & huiusmodi administratione, quod Papae paulatim & successiue ad se multa reuocauerunt, vsque adeo quod finaliter datis occasionibus & acceptis, quas non est hic opus recitare, quasi tota collatio & iurisdictio talis penes Papam & eius curiam remanebant. Ita vt vix esset praelatus, qui posset minimum beneficium conferre. Concurrebant ad hoc exactiones multiplices pro statu Papae & cardinalium: & si fraudes & abusus & simoniae committerentur, relinquo iudicandum expertis.
units.tr: A council of this kind should not be called to restore obedience to the Pope in the administration of benefices and similar matters, because although these are attached to spiritual things, they can still be called temporal. First, some of the earlier reasons against reforming the universal Church in matters of morals make for this view. Yet it must be noted that even if it were granted that the Pope has universal dominion over spiritual and temporal things, given to him by divine right, over all persons, it is nonetheless clear that, because of differences of times, places and conditions, neither the Pope nor the Church has had or ought to have the same exercise, execution or use of such temporal jurisdiction in dispensing or administering temporal benefices. It is well known that in the time of Christ and the Apostles the Church had no judicial or civil exercise or execution of this kind concerning temporal goods. Indeed, by word and deed Christ seems to have forbidden such an exercise of civil jurisdiction more than he permitted it. I do not say that he forbade it or opposed it absolutely, but only with respect to place and time. For since the Church was then to be multiplied through the travels of the Apostles and the faithful, such temporal jurisdiction and possessions would have been a hindrance to them, and there are many reasons for thinking so. But in the time of Sylvester and Constantine the Great, it pleased the Lord to inspire Constantine to give such possessions and the Church to receive them, in order to extend the Church. This endowment of the Church has lasted until our own times through the succession of the most holy fathers Gregory, Ambrose and others, who we cannot believe erred in keeping such things against Christ's command. But the original endowment distributed these goods very differently from later times, when prelates began gradually to grow cold from the holiness of their predecessors. In the end they so abused the conferring of benefices and their administration that the Popes gradually and successively drew many of these powers to themselves, until finally, through occasions given and accepted (which need not be recounted here), the whole conferring and jurisdiction of this kind came to rest in the hands of the Pope and his court. As a result there was scarcely a prelate who could confer even the smallest benefice. Manifold exactions added to this, for the upkeep of the Pope and the cardinals; and as for whether frauds, abuses and simony were committed, I leave that to be judged by those who have experience of it.

units.la: Haec idcirco dixi, quoniam forte aliquibus videretur, quod sit expediens ecclesiae vniuersali redire omnia ad pristinum statum ecclesiae seu illius qui fuit tempore apostolorum quantum fieri congrue posset: abiectis talibus iurisdictionibus pro magna parte, quae reddiderunt ecclesiam totam brutalem & carnalem, & nihil fere sapientem de his, quae Dei sunt erga salutem animarum, non ex se quidem, sed abutentium vitio. Vel redeundum esset ad statum ecclesiae tempore Sylvestri & Gregorii, quando quilibet praelatus dimittebatur in sua iurisdictione & sollicitudinis parte: & Papa tenebat quae sua erant absque tot reseruationibus, tot & continuis magnisque exactionibus pro sustinendo statum curiae & capitis nimis forte crescentem suum caeterosque membrorum status.
units.tr: I have said this because perhaps some would think it expedient for the universal Church to return everything to its former state, to the condition of the Church in the time of the Apostles as far as this can fittingly be done, casting off to a great extent those jurisdictions which have made the whole Church brutish and carnal and almost unwise in those matters which concern God and the salvation of souls. This is not the fault of the Church in itself, but of those who abused it. Or else it would be necessary to return to the state of the Church in the time of Sylvester and Gregory, when each prelate was left in his own jurisdiction and share of care, and the Pope kept what belonged to him without so many reservations, and so many continual and heavy exactions to sustain the state of the court and the head, which has perhaps grown far too large, and the other states of the members.

units.la: Ad sciendum igitur istud cum multis appendiciis de prouisione clericorum sufficientium &c. & ad prouidendum: expediens est fieri determinationem vniuersalem ecclesiae. Nam vniuersalem ecclesiae statum tangit. Sed dictum est prius, quod reformatio talis fieri non debet in consilio solius obedientiae istius.
units.tr: Therefore, to know this, together with the many related matters concerning the provision of sufficient clergy, and in order to provide for them, it is expedient that a universal determination be made by the Church. For it touches the universal state of the Church. But it has been said before that such a reform ought not to be made by the council of this obedience alone.

units.la: Si vero quis obiiciat, quod istud sic stare non potest cum eis quae dicta sunt de restitutione obedientiae quod ad spiritualia: quoniam esset ita bene periculum inobedientiae culpabilis in vno sicut in alio. Respondetur quod latissima est differentia in spiritualibus & temporalibus quo ad hoc, & vtinam fuisset bene semper intellecta a prioribus & modernis: forte quod adhuc starent Graeci cum Latinis. Patet enim ex priori deductione, quod Papa potest remanere Papa vniuersaliter in perfectione magna, imo maiori quam erat Sylvester, & tamen nullum habebit exercitium actuale circa temporalia ecclesiae vniuersalis per dioeceses, quantumcunque habeat dominium vel plenitudinem potestatis in habitu: quae potestas ex causis certis potest cohiberi & arceri, imo debet, ne exeat in actum, sed dimittat singula singulis ministrare. Nonne Christus fuit Papa perfectissimus? nonne similiter Petrus? ipsi tamen omne exercitium abdicauerunt a se in talibus, quanquam Christus cum summa facilitate illud obtinere potuisset. Nihil ergo de perfectione status summi pontificis diminuitur, si pro causa rationali remouetur ad tempus aut suspenditur sibi tam anxia sollicitudo, tot curarum immortalium & periculosissimarum in anima & corpore pro huiusmodi exercitio circa temporalia distribuenda aut conferenda: augetur potius sua perfectio, & gratulari profecto deberet in Domino.
units.tr: But if someone objects that this cannot stand together with what has been said about restoring obedience in spiritual matters, since the danger of culpable disobedience would be just as great in one case as in the other, the answer is that the difference between spiritual and temporal matters in this respect is very wide. Would that it had always been well understood by those before us and by those of our own time; perhaps the Greeks would still be standing with the Latins. For it is clear from the earlier argument that the Pope can remain Pope universally, in great perfection, indeed in greater perfection than Sylvester was, and yet he will have no actual exercise concerning the temporal affairs of the universal Church through the dioceses, however much dominion or fullness of power he may have in habit. This power can be restrained and kept back for certain causes, and indeed ought to be, so that it does not pass into act, but so that each person ministers to each in his own sphere. Was not Christ the most perfect Pope? And likewise Peter? Yet they both renounced all exercise of such things, although Christ could have obtained it with the greatest ease. Therefore nothing is taken away from the perfection of the state of the supreme pontiff if, for a rational cause, such a troubling care is removed or suspended for a time: the care of so many immortal and most dangerous concerns for soul and body in distributing or conferring temporal goods. Rather his perfection is increased, and he ought truly to rejoice in the Lord.

units.la: Videtur vlterius pro hoc multis, quod non expedit vnum solum caput praesse in tali exercitio administrationis temporalium, sicut expedit, imo sicut necesse est vnum solum praesse in spiritualibus respectu omnium. Cuius ratio est: quia ea quae fidei sunt, debent eadem esse apud omnes: & haec identitas & vnitas vix aut nunquam perpetuari potest, nisi recursus esset finalis ad vnum caput. Sed de traditionibus humanis pro regimine temporalium ecclesiae, totaliter oppositum inuenitur: quoniam secundum varietatem temporum, locorum & gentium & respectuum variandae sunt decretales & ordinationes super collationibus & regimine talium temporalium.
units.tr: Many also argue further for this view, that it is not expedient for one single head to preside over such an exercise of temporal administration, as it is expedient, indeed as it is necessary, for one single head to preside over spiritual matters with respect to all. The reason is this: the things that belong to faith must be the same among all, and this identity and unity can hardly or never be perpetuated unless there is a final appeal to one head. But with regard to human traditions governing the temporal affairs of the Church, the opposite is found entirely, since decretals and ordinances concerning the conferring and governing of such temporal goods must vary according to the variety of times, places, peoples and circumstances.

units.la: Ex his omnibus quae latius possunt deduci probabiliter, vellent aliqui dicere non esse expediens fieri concilium decisiuum super restitutione vniuersali temporalis administrationis Papae: sed super hoc debet concilium vniuersale celebrari. Nec oportet illos esse vel dici schismaticos, qui occasione data & accidente talem in temporalibus fecerunt aut faciunt subtractionem: quia etiam stante vnitate ecclesiae talis subtractio contingebat vel in toto vel in parte fieri fortassis debuisset, & hoc si absque graviori scissura in spiritualibus hoc potuisset contingere, & ita sapientissima lucet in hac parte Dei prouidentia, quae ex malo schismatis, alia bona sciet elicere. Et si petatur de quo viueret Papa interim & cardinales. Respondetur quod si faciant debitum suum laborando & diligenter inquirendo finem schismatis: praesumendum est quod cito inuenirent, & tunc prouidebit eis concilium generale qualiter erit expediens honestum pro statu tantorum dominorum. Similiter de modo prouisionis sufficientium clericorum tunc tractandum esset pro futuro.
units.tr: From all these things, which can be drawn out at greater length with some probability, some would wish to say that it is not expedient for a council to be held that would decide the universal restoration of the Pope's temporal administration; rather a universal council should be held on this matter. Nor is it necessary for those who, when the occasion arose and an accident occurred, have made or are making such a withdrawal in temporal matters to be called or regarded as schismatics. For even while the unity of the Church remained, such a withdrawal might perhaps have had to be made in whole or in part, and this would have been possible without a more serious split in spiritual matters. Thus the most wise providence of God shines forth in this respect, since out of the evil of schism it knows how to bring forth other goods. And if it is asked on what the Pope and the cardinals are to live in the meantime, the answer is that if they do their duty by working diligently and seeking an end to the schism, it must be presumed that they will soon find one; and then the general council will provide for them in whatever way is fitting and honourable for the state of such great lords. Likewise, the manner of providing sufficient clergy would then have to be dealt with for the future.

units.la: Non expedit concilium praefatum fieri tanquam viarum vnionis tantummodo repertiuum. Ratio est: quoniam materia huiusmodi iam totaliter aperta est & discussa quo ad possibilitatem viarum & rationabilitatem vel irrationabilitatem earum: & non restat nisi conuenire istam obedientiam cum altera in aliqua viarum. Hoc autem fieri potest, si vnquam debeat fieri absque tali concilio huius obedientiae, quoniam non videtur quod alia conclusio ibidem concluderetur, quam quod summarentur aduersarii de aliqua via assumenda. Si enim vna particularis via limitaretur, incideremus in inconueniens, quale patimur.
units.tr: The aforesaid council should not be called merely as a means of finding ways of union. The reason is that the matter of this kind has already been fully opened up and discussed, as to the possibility of the ways, and their reasonableness or unreasonableness; and nothing remains except to bring this obedience into agreement with the other in some one of the ways. This could be done, if it ever ought to be done without such a council of this obedience, since it does not seem that any other conclusion would be reached there than that the opponents should be summoned to adopt some way. For if one particular way were limited to, we would fall into the very inconvenience we now suffer.

units.la: Ex his omnibus non determinatiue positis, sed tantummodo examinatiue: videtur sequi quod nullo modo expedit nunc concilium istius obedientiae fieri: nisi forte solum ad habendum liberam in consulendo deliberationem: & plenam concordiam capitis & membrorum ad inuicem, super modo & forma viuendi hanc obedientiam secum & cum alia: & hanc vnionem concorditer prosequendi.
units.tr: From all these things, put forward not as determinations but only as examinations, it seems to follow that in no way is it now expedient for a council of this obedience to be held, except perhaps solely to have free and deliberative counsel, and full agreement of head and members among themselves, concerning the manner and form of living in this obedience with itself and with the other, and of pursuing this union with one accord.

units.la: Ad quod amplius declarandum possent adduci particulares circumstantiae super diuersis assectionibus & intentionibus diuersorum: & super periculo maximo nouarum d. sensionum subordinandarum: & vix vnquam sopiendarum in spiritualibus & temporalibus. Nisi prius ante omnia limitarentur ea, quae tractanda essent in concilio super quibus fieret. Nisi praeterea fieret talis prouisio super praemissis non determinandis quae tangunt fidem, & vniuersalem ecclesiam, quod convocatio concilii nulli super ipsa disceptare aut saltem determinare praesumerent. Denique constat aliquos affectare totalem penitus dece sionem Benedicti, & alii penitus hoc nolunt: sed totis viribus obnitterentur: nec est ratio patens ad sui destitutionem statim sic inuenienda, vt dicunt.
units.tr: To make this clearer, one could cite particular circumstances concerning the differing inclinations and intentions of various men, and the very great danger of new dissensions, which would have to be settled and could hardly ever be quieted, in spiritual and temporal affairs. This would hold unless, first of all, the matters to be treated at the council were limited and the subjects on which it was to act were fixed in advance. It would also hold unless provision were made that the aforesaid matters, which touch the faith and the universal Church, are not to be determined, so that once the council is convened, no one would presume to dispute them or at least to settle them. Finally, it is clear that some desire the total and complete deposition of Benedict, while others entirely refuse it and would resist with all their strength. Nor is there any clear reason, as they say, for finding a way to remove him at once.

units.la: Restat igitur communi & concordi Concilio vel deliberatione tantummodo quaerere cum aliisviam aliquam, in qua nobiscum conueniant pro vniendo ecclesiam, siue via illa sit conuentio, siue compromissio: habens vim concilii generalis in modificatione sua: siue concilium generale formaliter, siue cessio, siue omnes viae in vnum, si debeat perfectus haberi finis, prout multi Doctores opinantur. Nam & cessio (vt dicunt) fieri nequit, quae vnionem det veram in ecclesia sine concilio generali: & per consequens neque absque conuentione: & praesertim renuente cedere altero contendentium: quoniam per concilium taliter artabitur quilibet, aut artari poterit quod requiretur eorum consensus. Nam si dissenserit obedire con cilio erunt palam schismatici: & si schismatici, erunt deponendi. Quibus depositis procedendum erit ad nouam electionem libere fiendam, sicut eis a vita separatis aut libere cedentibus. An vero ista sola causa vltimo tacta sit sufficiens causa ad hoc, quod expediat aut de necessitate celebrandum sit huiusmodi concilium commune istius obedientiae attenta difficultate in conuocando & expensis & periculis continuandis indicent illi ad quos spectat & in conuenientibus maioribus prudenter occurrant.
units.tr: What remains, then, is to seek, by the common and harmonious counsel or deliberation of all, some other way by which they may agree with us to unite the Church, whether that way is an agreement or a compromise, having the force of a general council in its modification; whether it is a general council formally convened, or a cession, or all the ways brought into one, if a perfect end is to be attained, as many Doctors think. For a cession (as they say) cannot be made that would give a true union in the Church without a general council, and consequently not without an agreement, especially when one of the contending parties refuses to cede. For by the council each party will be so bound, or can be so bound, that their consent will be required. If one dissents from obeying the council, he will plainly be a schismatic; and if a schismatic, he must be deposed. Once they are deposed, it will be necessary to proceed to a new election, freely made, just as it would be if they had withdrawn from life or freely ceded. Whether this sole cause, touched on last, is a sufficient reason why such a common council of this obedience should be held, or must of necessity be held, let those judge to whom it belongs, weighing the difficulty of convoking it, the expenses and the dangers to be endured, and let them prudently meet the greater inconveniences.

units.la: Vt veritatis flamma ex discussionis ventilatione clarior emergat, proponemus, & soluemus obiectiones contra viam mediam: quae prout expedit tacta est. In primis dicent aliqui contra secundum expediens, quod absque discussione eorum quae hactenus facta sunt, non potest syncere & proconscientiarum serenatione illud fieri quod proponitur. Nam si Bened. & s ex vna parte cum suis adhaerentibus: aut alii ex altera fiunt culpabiles de schismate aut haeresi vel de rebellione, aut alio tali vitio: qualiter tales absque recognitione propriae culpae & postulatione veniae indulgentiam apud Deum & homines merebuntur? non remittitur poena, nisi confiteatur culpa.
units.tr: So that the flame of truth may shine out more clearly from the airing of the discussion, we shall set out and answer the objections against the middle way, which has been touched on as far as is expedient. First, some will object against the second expedient that, without discussion of what has been done so far, what is proposed cannot be carried out sincerely or with the tranquillity of consciences. For if Benedict and his adherents on one side, or others on the other, have become guilty of schism or heresy or rebellion, or some other such vice, how will such men merit indulgence before God and men without acknowledging their own fault and asking pardon? Punishment is not remitted unless the fault is confessed.

units.la: Sed respondemus, quod haec obiectio friuola est & sophistica: atque fieri posset in omni materia dubia, sicut fieret ad impediendum viam cessionis liberae absque discussione iustitiae. Dicimus igitur secundum catholicam veritatem, quod in dubiis potest fieri confessio sub conditione: & ex tali confessione veniam absolutam peccator consequetur. Addimus ad haec quod omnia & fere omnia dici possunt dubia in foro exteriori, quae nondum sunt iudicialiter diffinita. Proptrea nulluserit scrupulus obediendo Domino Benedicto, etiam vbi fuisset haereticus aut schismaticus, si respiscet: vel si hoc non constaret per diffinitiuam sententiam ecclesiae. Similiter de subditis rebellantibus si quis fuissent dicerentur: Quis nesciat multa apud antiquos patres, & nunc quotidie tolerari: vt de simoniis & aliis: quae si iudicialiter essent ventilata & conuicta, tolerari non possent? Superaddimus quod tota res praesens magnis dubiorum inuolucris contecta est & vtriusque colorata. Sed necsunt aliqua, quae proprie & nude tangant oppositia fidei: quin magis in factis diuersis & diuersimode receptis, quam in iure consistunt. Nulli idcirco possunt aut vix possunt de schismate & haeresi pertinaces conuinci in hac parte. Denique dicimus, quod regula magistralis Theologiae non debetnos scrupulis inquietare, vt fiat discussio illa scilicet regula: quod si illud sit dubium an liceat, an non liceat illud fieri: si fiat, certum est illud esse peccatum: quoniam per praedicta non habebitur rationabiliter dubium de eis quae fuerint concordata: & praesupponetur quilibet aut non erraßse, aut de erratis poenitere: & ita in suo honoris gradu, iure aut saltem misericordia remanere.
units.tr: But we answer that this objection is frivolous and sophistical, and it could be raised in every doubtful matter, just as it would be raised to block the way of free cession without a discussion of justice. We say, therefore, according to Catholic truth, that in doubtful matters confession can be made under a condition, and from such a confession the sinner will obtain full pardon. We add that almost all things can be called doubtful in the outward forum which have not yet been judicially defined. Therefore no scruple should arise in obeying Lord Benedict, even if he had been a heretic or schismatic, provided he repents, or if this has not been established by a definitive sentence of the Church. Similarly, if subjects were said to have rebelled: who does not know that many things were tolerated among the ancients and are tolerated daily even now, such as simony and others, which, if they were judicially aired and proved, could not be tolerated? We add that the whole present affair is covered with great wrappings of doubt and coloured on both sides. Nor are there any matters which touch the opposites of faith properly and nakedly; rather they consist more in diverse facts received in diverse ways than in law. Therefore none, or scarcely any, can be convicted of obstinate schism and heresy in this respect. Finally, we say that the magisterial rule of theology ought not to trouble us with scruples so that this discussion of the rule itself should take place. For if it is doubtful whether it is permitted or not permitted to do this, and it is done, it is certain that it is a sin. For by the aforesaid, there will be no reasonable doubt about those things that have been agreed; and it will be presupposed that each either has not erred, or repents of his errors, and so remains in his rank of honour, by right or at least by mercy.

units.la: Caeterum ab aliis secunda fieret obiectio contra secundum expediens. Crimina, inquisunt, non ita generaliter remanere debent impunita: alioquin incentiuum tribuerent delinquendi. Sed necsalua conscientia forsan poterit Dominus Benedictus ea ratificare, aut non infringere quae facta sunt: nisi praesertim veniam & nouam confirmationem singuli pro se petant: aut nisi de nouo habilitentur & ordinentur. Sed respondemus, quod frequenter praecipue in delictis tangentibuscommunitatem aut homines grandis status, consultius tolerantur errores communes, quam vindicari seuero rigore quaererentur. Nunquid non tolerat ecclesia meretrices? Nonne haec est expressa prudentissimi Augusti sententia in scriptis suis multis, cuius dicta sient nec aliorum hic non inseriimus: quia a clericis satis cognoscuntur: quia insuper magis rationem, quare talia dicta sunt quam vbi dicta sunt nunc & alius offerre conamur. Non deessent rationes & exempla nisi breuitatis amor obstaret: & si non experientia doctrice pateret veritas. Praeterea quod additur de conscientia Domini Benedicti satis dissoluitur per hoc idem dictum: quod etiam vbi fuissent mala perpetrata, illamini Benedicti satis dissoluitur per hoc idem dictum; quod etiam vbi fuissent mala perpetrata, illa potest salua conscientia pro bono & vtilitate tanti negotii complendi tolerando dissimulare. Sicut regulariter verum est quod prælatus non solum potest, imo debet aliqua agere vel omittere propter generalem inclinationem subditorum: vbi etiam quandoque mala esset, quæ alias agere vel omittere in graue delictum sibi verteretur. Iuxta quod inferunt aliqui, quod etiam vbi via cessionis minus bona fuisset: tamen attentis deliberationibus omnium subditorum super postulatione huius viæ: Dominus Benedictus illam acceptare tenebatur, sicut nunc acceptauit, quantumcunque alias ad eam acceptandam non fuisset artatus vel artandus. Sed hoc omittamus: Volumus enim nihil discuti de factis hactenus vel inde. Rursus ea quæ facta sunt in promotionibus & similibus, durante subtractione, autorizata sunt per ordinarios locorum, ad quos de iure communi spectabant talia. Cur ergo non poterit Dominus Benedictus præsumere illos, qui à se aut prædecessoribus suis fuerant ad hæc electi & promoti, immemores non fuisse suæ salutis? quare nequibit absq; scrupulo tolerare, ne dicamus approbare quæ facta sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, a second objection would be raised by others against the second expedient. Crimes, they ask, ought not to remain so generally unpunished; otherwise they would give an incentive to offend. But perhaps Lord Benedict cannot, with a clear conscience, ratify or leave unbroken what has been done, unless each man asks pardon and fresh confirmation for himself, or unless they are newly qualified and ordained. We answer that often, especially in offences touching the community or men of high standing, common errors are more wisely tolerated than sought to be punished with severe rigour. Does not the Church tolerate prostitutes? Is this not the express judgement of the most prudent Augustine in his many writings? We do not insert his sayings here, since they are sufficiently known to the clergy; and moreover we try to give the reason why such things were said, more than where they were said, now and elsewhere. There would be no lack of reasons and examples, were it not for love of brevity, and were the truth not plain from teaching by experience. Moreover, what is added about the conscience of Lord Benedict is sufficiently resolved by this same saying: that even where evil things have been committed, that matter can, with conscience intact, be tolerated and passed over for the good and advantage of completing so great a business. Just as it is generally true that a prelate not only can but ought to do or omit certain things on account of the general inclination of his subjects, even where something might sometimes be evil, which otherwise, if done or omitted, would be turned into a grave offence against him. Hence some infer that even if the way of cession had been less good, yet, having regard to the deliberations of all the subjects on the request for this way, Lord Benedict was bound to accept it, as he has now accepted it, however little he was otherwise constrained, or was to be constrained, to accept it. But let us leave this aside: for we wish nothing to be discussed about the facts so far, or arising from them. Again, the things done in promotions and similar matters during the withdrawal of obedience were authorised by the ordinaries of the places, to whom such matters belonged by common law. Why, then, could Lord Benedict not presume that those who had been chosen and promoted to these offices by him or his predecessors were not unmindful of their salvation? Why could he not tolerate, without scruple, let alone approve, what has been done?

units.la: Denique quod subiungitur de venia sigillatim postulanda magis ad verecundiam multorum turbationem quam ad tranquillitatem & pacem, satis esse debebit postulatio veniæ generalis, & modis honestis executa. Facit pro prædictis quod omnia sacramenta, nisi forte pœnitentia, vim suam habent, vt collatio ordinum baptismus & similia, quantumcunque fuerint à peccatoribus distributa: stante tamen debita intentione faciendi, quæ ecclesia facere intendit: & præcipue vbi non ex affectata ignorantia iuris, sed ex facti insidia peccatum exortum est: propterea non erunt reordinandi iam ordinati.
units.tr: Finally, as for what is added about asking pardon individually, which would cause more shame and disturbance to many than tranquillity and peace, a request for general pardon, carried out by honourable means, should be sufficient. In support of what has been said above, all sacraments, except perhaps repentance, retain their force, such as the conferring of orders, baptism and the like, however much they have been administered by sinners, provided the due intention of doing what the Church intends is present; and especially where the sin has arisen not from affected ignorance of the law but from the snare of a fact. Therefore those already ordained will not need to be ordained again.

units.la: Deinde tertio obiiciunt alii contra idem secundum & tertium expediens: & dicent quod implicatio est in terminis, vt Domino Benedicto fiat obedientia tanquam summo pontifici: & nihilominus coartetur eius potestas ad certa & per certos modos, & quod sibi coadiutores socientur.
units.tr: Thirdly, others object against the same second and third proposals and say that it is a contradiction in terms that obedience should be rendered to Lord Benedict as supreme pontiff, and yet that his power should be restricted to certain matters and by certain methods, and that co-adjutors should be joined to him.

units.la: Sed respondemus primo iuxta positionem illorum, qui subtractionem ꝯ licite fieri potuisset confirmant, sicut reuera aut in isto aut in multis casibus potest euenire. Dicimus itaq; quod Papalis dignitas non pro extollentia aut fauore personæ, sed pro ecclesiæ vtilitate à Christo statuta est. Quamobrem secundum exigentiam vtilitatis ecclesiæ tanquam finis debet hæc dignitas agibilia sua moderari, præsertim in eis, quæ non sunt expressa in iure diuino. Hoc enim dicere esset de iure naturali cuiuslibet politiæ, quod violari non potest aut mutari. Si ergo contingit, quod prædicta fieri sit expediens pro ecclesia, attentis circumstantiis negotiorum, aut videlicet propter culpam Domini Benedicti seu aliquas eius conditiones minus ciuiles & vtiles ecclesiæ, etiam vbi non essent culpabiles, aut propter generalem affectionem & deliberationem omnium subditorum, etiam vbi errarent & minus bene iudicarent, dicimus non solum ista licere fieri, imo posse consurgere obligationem ad agendum. Neque in hoc derogatur autoritati Papali; neque plenitudini potestatis suæ collatæ sibi à Christo, sed impletur. Nam posse mala & inexpedientia ecclesiæ fatere, quis diceret esse posse? quis crederet hoc à Christo collatum extitisse? Porro de istis temporalibus administrationibus ecclesiarum possessionum, iurium, beneficiorum; & similium Christus per seipsum immediate nullatenus se intromisit: nec ordinare curauit: sciens & volens talia esse variabilia secundum exigentiam temporum, personarum & locorum, ad commanem ecclesiæ vtilitatem: non ad vniusaut paucorum singularem pompam, aut inutilem vanitatem siue voluntatem. Ratio postulat, nec negamus, vt Domino Papæ & suis Cardinalibus fiat sufficiens prouisio de bonis ecclesiasticis, sicut olim summo sacerdoti inferiores suas decimas offerebant. Sed hæc prouisio non ne poterat adimpleri absque hoc, quod necesse sit ex toto ius ordinariorum cassari vel suspendi? Profecto sic.
units.tr: But we answer first, in accordance with the position of those who maintain that the withdrawal could be lawfully made, as indeed in this or in many cases it may happen. We say therefore that the Papal dignity was established by Christ not for the exaltation or favour of a person, but for the good of the Church. Wherefore, according to the requirement of the Church's advantage as its end, this dignity ought to moderate its actions, especially in those matters which are not expressed in divine law. For to say otherwise would be to claim, under the natural law of any polity, something that cannot be violated or changed. If therefore it happens that the aforesaid measures are expedient for the Church, given the circumstances of the affairs, either on account of the fault of Lord Benedict or some of his conditions less civil and useful to the Church, even where these were not blameworthy, or on account of the general inclination and deliberation of all the subjects, even where they err and judge less well, we say that these things not only may lawfully be done, but that an obligation to act may even arise. Nor in this is the authority of the Pope diminished, nor the fullness of his power conferred on him by Christ, but rather it is fulfilled. For who would say that it could be that the Church should suffer evils and inexpedient things? Who would believe that this was conferred by Christ? Moreover, Christ himself immediately never intervened in these temporal administrations of the Church's possessions, rights, benefices and the like, nor did he care to ordain them; knowing and willing that such things are variable according to the requirement of times, persons and places, for the common good of the Church, and not for the singular pomp of one or a few, or for useless vanity or will. Reason demands, and we do not deny, that sufficient provision be made for Lord Pope and his Cardinals from ecclesiastical goods, just as in former times the lesser men offered their tithes to the high priest. But could this provision not be carried out without it being necessary entirely to annul or suspend the right of the ordinaries? Assuredly so.

units.la: Postremo dicent alii, quod hæc via, quæ dicitur media, compleri non potest absque concilio huius obedientiæ generali: & ita cadit in illud, quod videtur velle fugere. Hic respondemus, quod si concilium generale non quæreretur fieri nisi sub modificationibus tactis in hac via media, non videtur inconueniens aut periculum celebrare huiusmodi concilium. Cessarent enim omnia quæ contra ipsius vtilitatem audiuimus allegari. Nihilominus illud concilium nequaquam iudicamus necessarium pro complemento celeriori & faciliori huius viæ: & absque impetisis innumeris & tractu temporis, quia nunc interim prius quam ista concordata sint: dubia quædam orientur super conuocatione concilii, & quibusdam similibus, quæ hic cessant. Dubitabit forte alius, quod Dominus Benedictus audita ista viam illam aut impediet, aut non concordabit. Propterea forte tutius est, vt ante omnia secrete quantum fieri poterit habeatur consensus maior omnium istius obedientiæ, aut saltem principalium, vt communi consensu totius suæ obedientiæ fiat oblatio talis, cui vniuersali consensui si renuat assentire, quis non videbit tunc eius modum procedendi penitus improbabilem esse? quis non iudicabit ab eo iure recedendum fore? Non enim poterit aliqua tergiuersatione fautoria schismatis & subuersionis ecclesiæ denegari.
units.tr: Lastly, others will say that this way, which is called the middle way, cannot be completed without a general council of this obedience, and so it falls into the very thing which it seems to wish to avoid. Here we answer that if a general council were not to be sought except under the modifications touched upon in this middle way, it does not seem inconvenient or dangerous to hold such a council. For all the objections we have heard alleged against its usefulness would cease. Nevertheless we do not judge that council to be by any means necessary for a quicker and easier completion of this way, and without countless expenses and the lapse of time; because meanwhile, before these agreements are concluded, certain doubts will arise concerning the convocation of the council and similar matters, which here cease. Perhaps someone will doubt that Lord Benedict, on hearing these proposals, will either obstruct that way or will not agree to it. Therefore it is perhaps safer that, above all, as far as possible, a greater consent of all this obedience, or at least of its principal members, be obtained in secret, so that such an offering be made by the common consent of the whole obedience. If he refuses to assent to this universal consent, who will not then see that his mode of proceeding is wholly unacceptable? Who will not judge that the law must be departed from? For no evasion can deny that he is a promoter of schism and of the subversion of the Church.

units.la: Quod si quis ad extremum dubitauerit similiter de principibus aliis, quod non approbabunt viam hanc mediam: fatemur hoc non vsquequaq; certum esse: nisi prout in moralibus lumenda est certitudo ex his, quæ vt in pluribus secundum verisimiles & probabiles coniecturas eueniunt. Si in omnibus prædicta via nihil petit difficile aut onerosum vel inhonestum: quæritur propter quid principes & prælati debeant improbare: maxime pro tanto bono reunitionis obedientiæ huius totalis obtinendo. Quid enim graue erit, quod omnia indulgeantur præterita, & non discutiantur: quod Dominus Benedictus habeat bonos consiliarios, non suspectos cuicunq; parti: secundum quorum iudicium agat, quod acturus est: quod ipse à vindicando propriας aut alienas iniurias immunis sit, & Deo committat: aut certe vniuersali bono Ecclesiæ & pacis illas donet. Idem dicimus de subditis quibuscunq; erga dominum Benedictum. Profecto nihil istorum difficile est: nisi forte apud illos, apud quos humilitas & charitas & ecclesiastica vnitas fuerint onerosæ, scil. qui turbationibus gaudent, & quærunt quæ sua sunt, non quæ Iesu Christi. Aut qui suis sententiis cerusicosa animositate nimis credunt. Aut si difficilia esse ista quisquam contenderit: animaduertat ille obsecro, si plures sint in aliis viis difficultates & ambages: aut viam aliquam omni difficultate carentem asserat in medium, nos lætis animis complectemur. Quod si hoc vel facere non vult, vel quod magis credimus, non potest: tunc cum aliquid agere necesse sit, pergat nobiscum in hanc sententiam & attendat, quid plus habeat damni pro ecclesia: vel sic stare, imo quotidie magnis lapsibus corruere & dominum Benedictum incarceratum esse, & Cardinales suis honoribus spoliatos, & principes ad contentionem periculosam dispositos videre: aut quod ita præparemus nos per hanc reunitionem primam & totalem huius obedientiæ: quod cum alia celeriter & utiliter tractare valeamus: & qualiter (si quis quæsiuerit) iam in parte responsum est, & à prudentioribus erit diligentius inquirendum & inueniendum facilius.
