Hæc ego loquor, Liberius, quo mihi conscius sum, non ex quæstu, non ambitu, non ad laudem propriam meæ professionis, sed pro assertione veritatis & utilitate publica hæc dicere. Quia ad veritatem curia ista Theologiam hactenus minus debito promouit, ne dicam spreuit: quæ tamen omnem sibi, qua polleret, gloriam acquisiuit. Per quid? Per prædicationem humilem generatricem deuotionis in cordibus fidelium, maxime principum. Nam si desit religiosa deuotio, honoratio ecclesiarum qualis erit? Prouideat gratia summi Pontificis, vt nunc cæpit.
units.tr: Since the grace of God appears in the circumcision of the humble child Jesus, every prince and prelate, even if he is said to be released from the laws, ought to submit to the law which he himself has enacted, both as an example to his subjects and to show reverence to God. Thus the grace of God appears in him, and impiety or worldly desires do not seem to rule. Here one could cite examples from the Gentiles, who observed even the harshest laws laid upon themselves, of which Valerius makes mention. But the example of Christ, the supreme lawgiver and the supreme Pontiff, is enough. He did not wish to dissolve his own law but to fulfil it in himself, so that his action might be an instruction to princes and prelates in this matter. Here, nonetheless, a note must be made against those who cling so stubbornly to dead human laws that they either entirely ignore or despise the living law, founded on the eternal law and on equity: the law is perfected and fulfilled when it is ordered either to a better end or by more wholesome means, and that end is charity, according to the Apostle. Otherwise Christ would not have fulfilled the old law, which he would have dissolved. This teaching bears not a little on the present schism, whose sedition human laws already enacted would not suffice to discover, unless the higher divine law, living and architectonic, is consulted. Because perhaps this has not been done sufficiently up to the present, what the Lord says in Isaiah has come to pass: Their fear of me is taught by the commandment of men and by doctrines. Therefore, behold, I will add to make the people wonder with a great and astonishing miracle. For the wisdom of its wise men shall perish, and the understanding of its prudent men shall be hidden. From this passage Jesus took up the reproach against the Pharisees that they made the commandment of God void because of their traditions. Would that those who forsake the gospel law and the divine law together with its teachers, and devote themselves wholly to human inventions, would hear these things with their own ears, so that they can neither lift their eyes to that higher law, from ignorance, nor will to, from iniquity, nor do so, from sluggish idleness. Yet where human laws do not suffice (as has been found to be the case in the present schism), it is necessary that recourse be had to the root and interpretation of the divine law, and that constitution be formed according to it. What evil, what danger, what confusion has the contempt of the holy Scripture brought, which is surely sufficient for the governance of the Church (otherwise Christ would have been an imperfect lawgiver)? Let experience be asked. Let the clergy be considered, to whom wisdom, which is from above, peaceable and pure, ought to have been betrothed: has it not itself committed fornication with that adulterous little harlot, earthly, sensual and devilish wisdom? Moreover, has not the state of the Church become wholly, as it were, brutish and monstrous, where heaven is below, that is, what is spiritual, and earth is above, the spirit serving and the flesh ruling, the principal becoming accessory and the accessory principal? To such a degree that some do not hesitate to rave that the Church is regenerated better by human inventions than by the divine evangelical law, as if the soul were less than the body and spiritual fruit less than carnal. By my faith this assertion is blasphemy, not merely false. For the evangelical doctrine, through its professors, has extended the Church up to heaven, whereas the sons of Hagar, seeking the wisdom which is of the earth, have thrust it down into the mire. And that it has not fallen altogether is by the grace of God and our Saviour. I say these things, Liberius, as I am conscious, not from gain, not from ambition, not for my own praise of my profession, but for the assertion of truth and public benefit. For this court has hitherto promoted theology to the truth less than was due, not to say that it has despised it, though theology has won for itself all the glory it possesses. By what means? By humble preaching, which begets devotion in the hearts of the faithful, especially of princes. For if religious devotion is lacking, what will the honour of the churches be? Let the grace of the supreme Pontiff provide, as it has now begun.

units.la: CONSIDERATIO II.
units.tr: CONSIDERATIO II.

units.la: Apparens gratia in humilitate pueri Iesu circumcisi, docet prælatum quemlibet, vt iuxta consilium sapientis positum à Tullio: quanto maior est, humiliet se in omnibus. & ab omni se superbiæ intemperantiæque signo circumcidat. Tanto enim esse humilior & ad seruiendum promptior quisque debet ex munere, ait Gregor. quanto se obligationem esse conspicit in reddenda ratione. Nam ab eo cui plus committitur, plus exigitur. Ita vt saluberrimum sit Christi documentum metaphysicali ratione fundatum: Qui voluerit esse maior inter vos, erit omnium minor & minister: quia secundum magnitudinem dominationis est subiectionis grandior obligatio, quamobrem summus Pontifex non ficta verborum humilitate, sed veritatis attentione profunda nominatur Seruus seruorum. Et certe ita seruus, vt secundum præparationem cordis, etsi non semper secundum exhibitionem operis ipse vitam suam, quanto magis statum suum exponere pro cuiuslibet subditi sui salute, nedum pro toto grege teneatur. Hoc ita sentire catholicum est stabilitum in hoc veritatis verbo: Bonus pastor animam suam ponit pro ouibus suis. Et ita corde creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem vel scripto confessio fit ad salutem. Alioquin non iniustus fit Lucifer, qui initia præesse voluit (secundum doctores) vt subiectionis vicissitudinem subditis non referret: cum ex opposito ipse plus aliorum commodis obsequi velle debuerat. Ex hac iterum consideratione culpanda redditur pompa superba, pompa male sobria prælatorum quorundam in fastu mundano quærentium nihilominus excusationes in peccatis, & dicentium quod hæc pompa honorat ecclesiam. Honorat vero, imo vere onerat & destruit factis & exemplis. Neque enim in ornatu splendido, neq; in lauto conuiuio, neq; enim in discholorum & comatulorum clientium numero: sed in spiritu mundo & consideratione sancta honor ecclesiasticus illustratur. Quia si quis prælatorum in pompis istis puerili & vana exultatione delectetur, si ad honores caducos gloriabundus exhilaresc at, si de se factat idolum & statuam Nabuchodonosor gaudens laudari, gaudens coli, & non potius exhorreat instar Christi, qui summos inter honores fleuit: si non memor sit iubentis: in vestitu ne glorieris vnquam, & in die honoris tui ne extollaris. Videat obsecro, videat talis, ne tandem seipsum tanta propriæ & alienæ adulationis ludificatione decipiat: quod iuxta verbum comici: Exstultus (hoc est, ex vane gloriosos) insanus fiat. Qualiter insanus? Certe læsus in iudicio rationis, sicut lædiatur philocaptus. Omnis quippe passio profundata & radicata circa aliquod concupiscibile, sit illud honor, sit opulentia, sit ambitio, sit voluptas: reddit hominem dæmoniaco similem, secundum dictum Origenis in experientia fundatum. Mentior si non tempore meo talis apparuit, & verborum copia & iurium scientia & abstinentia famatus, corpore vegeto & forti, quem vsque ad hoc insanum reddidit ambitio cæca, contemptrix alieni omnis consilii laudibusque suis credula, vt putauerit post illusiones plurimas esse verus Papa concorditer electus. Et cum ita desiperet, nihilominus affirmabat se per multos annos nihil tentationis à vana gloria sensisse. Cum præterea moneretur, vt sapientiorum crederet consilio: non, inquit, quia factum meum tale tantumque est, vt alius a me nemo illud intelligat. Sed quid mirandum est in homine fragili dementiam hanc surrepsisse cum sapientissimus olim angelorum Lucifer, quia seipsum non in luce veritatis, sed umbra propriæ vanitatis intuebatur, esse voluerit non solum similis altissimo, sed extollitur super omne quod dicitur Deus, ex insania & fantastica præconceptæ dominationis libidine. Vult quoque ritibus & sacrificiis coli per similitudinem ad Deum, sicut sacrilegæ artes magicæ palam tradunt.
units.tr: The grace that appeared in the humility of the boy Jesus, when he was circumcised, teaches every prelate, as the saying of the sage quoted by Tully puts it, that the greater he is, the more he should humble himself in all things. He should also circumcise himself from every sign of pride and intemperance. For, as Gregory says, each person ought to be the more humble and the readier to serve in proportion to the office he holds, when he sees that he is under obligation to render an account. For from the one to whom more has been entrusted, more will be required. Thus the most wholesome teaching of Christ, grounded in a metaphysical reason, holds: Whoever wishes to be greater among you shall be the least of all and the minister. For the greater the power of rule, the greater the obligation of submission. That is why the supreme Pontiff is called the Servant of servants, not from a feigned humility of words but from a deep attention to the truth. And truly he is a servant in such a way that, in the readiness of his heart, if not always in the actual performance of the work, he must be prepared to lay down his own life, and even more his station, for the salvation of any one of his subjects, not to mention the whole flock. That this is the Catholic way of thinking is settled in the saying of truth: The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep. And so, with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth or in writing confession is made unto salvation. Otherwise Lucifer, who (according to the doctors) wished to rule first, would not be unjust in failing to return the reciprocal submission to his subjects, when on the contrary he ought to have wished to serve the advantages of others more. From this same consideration the proud pomp, and the ill-sober pomp of certain prelates, who seek excuses for their sins in worldly display and say that such pomp honours the Church, must be condemned. It does not honour it; indeed it truly burdens and destroys it by deeds and examples. For ecclesiastical honour is not made illustrious by splendid attire, nor by a lavish banquet, nor by a crowd of pages and curled attendants, but by a worldly spirit and holy consideration. For if any of the prelates takes delight in such pomps with childish and empty exultation, if he rejoices with vainglory in fleeting honours, if he makes an idol of himself and, like Nebuchadnezzar, delights to be praised and worshipped, and does not rather shrink from it after the example of Christ, who wept amid the highest honours; if he is not mindful of the command: Never glory in your clothing, and do not exalt yourself in the day of your honour. Let such a man see to it, I beg, let him see, lest at last he deceive himself by so great a mockery of his own and others' flattery, so that, as the comic poet says, he becomes insane out of his mind (that is, out of vainglory). In what way insane? Certainly impaired in the judgment of reason, as the lovesick man is impaired. For every passion deeply rooted and fixed upon some object of desire, whether it be honour, wealth, ambition or pleasure, makes a man like one possessed by a demon, according to the saying of Origen, founded on experience. I would be lying if I did not say that in my own time such a man appeared, famed for his abundance of words, his knowledge of law and his abstinence, with a vigorous and robust body, whom blind ambition, scornful of every counsel of others and credulous of his own praises, drove to such madness that, after many illusions, he thought himself the true Pope, lawfully elected. And while he was so out of his wits, he nevertheless affirmed that for many years he had felt no temptation from vainglory. When he was further advised to trust the counsel of wiser men, he said: "No, because my deed is of such a kind and such weight that no one else but me can understand it." But why should it be wondered at that this madness crept into a frail man, when Lucifer, once the most wise of the angels, because he looked upon himself not in the light of truth but in the shadow of his own vanity, wished to be not only like the Most High, but exalted above everything that is called God, out of insanity and the fantastic lust of pre-conceived dominion? He also wishes to be worshipped with rites and sacrifices as if he were God, just as the sacrilegious arts of magic openly teach.

units.la: Præterea saluberrimum est, vt prælatus libenter audiat & frequenter quæ humilia sunt & culpabilia de seipso: quia nemo est qui non peccet, dicatque cum propheta: Increpabit me iustus, &c. Nimis enim habet multos, qui vel adulatione vel dignitatis honoratione sibi loquuntur magnifica: apponentes fomentum morbo superbiæ: quem vix vllum medicamen vel theriaca propriæ reprehensionis & fragilitatis sufficit expellere, & dare locum gratiæ Dei saluatoris nostri.
units.tr: Moreover, it is most salutary for a prelate to listen gladly, and often, to what is humbling and blameworthy about himself. For there is no one who does not sin, and who does not say with the prophet: The righteous man shall reprove me, etc. For there are far too many who speak great things to him, whether by flattery or by honouring his dignity, thereby applying fuel to the disease of pride, which hardly any remedy or theriac of self-reproach and acknowledgement of frailty is enough to expel, so as to give place to the grace of God our Saviour.

units.la: CONSIDERATIO III.
units.tr: CONSIDERATIO III.

units.la: APparens gratia Dei Saluatoris nostri in subiectione ad legem propriam circumcisionis documento est prælatis, vt iuste viuentes non imponant onera grauia statutorum & legum humeris subditorum: digito autem suo nolint illa mouere, quemadmodum improperat Christus Pharisæis. Hæc consideratio redit ad primam, innitentem illi sententiæ exemplo Christi firmatæ Patere legem quam ipse tuleris. Et esset profecto grandis in hoc loco querelarum materia contra tot & tam leues excommunicationum & irregularitatum fulminationes: contra tot onera statutorum prouincialium & synodalium: ad lucrum quale vel animæ vel bursæ nouit Deus. Contra tot reseruatores casuum in foro confessionis præsertim occultorum, quæ confessionem supra quam dici potest, impediunt. Loquor expertus & doctus ab expertis. Sed de his alias. Christus legislator nonne legem euangelicam dilatare potuerat? Potuerat equidem: sed humanæ fragilitati gratiose condescendens necessaria nos docuit ad salutem: ea pro nihilo quasi deputans, quæ mortalem hanc vitam iamiam in momento perituram vel regere vel sustentare viderentur: sciens quod nisi lex viua euangelica & æterna dominetur, leges scriptæ non solum superuacuæ, sed crebro perniciosæ reddantur. Vult ergo prælatus ecclesiam subditam feliciter dirigi. Vult arbitror bonos ille viros, timentes Deum æquitate & meritis conspicuos regimini præficiat: non oneribus legum & statutorum subditos premat. Nam super hunc cardinem volui debet Ecclesiæ reformatio: quoniam si columnæ putres, si inualidæ sunt sustentare debentes ecclesiam; partes reliquæ quali virtute subsistent, innitentes parieti inclinato maceriæ depulsæ? Multiplicentur quantumlibet humanæ traditiones: Si cupiditas carnalis & fastus non humilitas regnet in prælatis: audiamus quid sequitur incommodi. Etenim potestas conferendi beneficia & similia aut relinquetur talibus. Et quis dubitauerit, quis non viderit quantum subuertent, peruertent & euertent omnia promotionibus indignorum. Si ablatio fiat abeis retinente sibi omnium collationem summo Pontifice, nunquid non supra vires erit hoc negocium? nunquid non cum Moyse stulto labore consumetur? Nonne monstruosum erit videre caput vsurpans membrorum omnia inferiorum officia: & quasi sit gladius delphicus ad omnia se aptans? Sed & curia sua, curia Romana, quæ ad similitudinem Hierarchiæ Angelicæ ordinanda erat & replenda viris charitate feruidis & contemplatione suspensis, vt Seraphin; viris sapientia diuina splendidis, vt Cherubin; viris æquitate firmissimis, vt Throni: nonne mutabitur in curiam peccantium? & qui nutriri debebant in croceis, amplexabuntur stercora. Ita enim arbitratus est omnia temporalia æquus arbiter Apostolus. Fient quoque multi procuratores & conrotarii beneficiorum (nolo de simonia quicquam dicere.) Fient insuper non tam promotores quam inuolutores causarum friuolarum atque prophanarum dimissa omni spiritualis cura. Quid dico dimissa? Vtinam hoc esset, licet sit nequissimum, irridebitur, abominabitur, persequetur, & ad imitationem curiæ diabolicæ maior ille frequenter erit qui astutior, qui perfidior, qui importunior, deterior, cupidior, misefrior. Auertat hoc nefas gratia Dei & Saluatoris nostri.
units.tr: The grace of God our Saviour, appearing in his subjection to the law of circumcision, is an example to prelates that, living righteously, they should not lay heavy burdens of statutes and laws on the shoulders of their subjects, while they themselves are unwilling to move them with a finger, as Christ reproaches the Pharisees. This consideration goes back to the first, resting on that saying confirmed by the example of Christ: Abide by the law which you yourself have enacted. There would indeed be great matter for complaint in this place against so many and such trivial fulminations of excommunications and irregularities; against so many burdens of provincial and synodal statutes, for gain of a kind that God alone knows, whether for the soul or for the purse; against so many reservers of cases in the forum of confession, especially of hidden sins, which hinder confession beyond what can be said. I speak from experience and from learned men who have experience. But of these things at another time. Did not Christ the lawgiver have the power to extend the evangelical law? He certainly had the power; but, graciously condescending to human frailty, he taught us only what was necessary for salvation, regarding as nothing those things which seemed to govern or sustain this mortal life, which in a moment will soon perish, knowing that unless the living and eternal evangelical law rules, written laws will become not only superfluous but often harmful. The prelate therefore wishes the subject Church to be happily directed. I suppose he wishes to set over it good men who fear God, who are conspicuous for fairness and merits, and not to oppress the subjects with the burdens of laws and statutes. For the reformation of the Church ought to be turned upon this hinge. For if the pillars that ought to sustain the Church are rotten and weak, with what strength will the remaining parts stand, leaning on a wall that is leaning and pushed out of line? However much human traditions are multiplied, if fleshly desire and arrogance, and not humility, reign in the prelates, let us hear what harm follows. For the power of conferring benefices and the like will either be left to such men, and who would doubt, who would not see, how much they will undermine, pervert and overturn everything by the promotion of the unworthy? If the power is taken from them and the supreme Pontiff retains for himself the conferral of all of them, will not this business be beyond his strength? Will it not be consumed with the labour of a foolish Moses? Would it not be monstrous to see a head usurping the duties of all the inferior members, and, like the Delphic rule, adapting itself to everything? But also his court, the Roman court, which ought to be arranged in the likeness of the angelic hierarchy and filled with men burning with charity and absorbed in contemplation, like the Seraphim; with men shining with divine wisdom, like the Cherubim; with men most firm in equity, like the Thrones; will it not be changed into a court of sinners? And those who ought to be nourished on saffron will embrace dung. For the fair judge, the Apostle, reckoned all temporal things in this way. There will also become many procurators and agents of benefices (I say nothing here about simony). Moreover, there will become not so much promoters as entanglers of frivolous and profane lawsuits, all spiritual care having been dismissed. Why do I say dismissed? Would that this were all! Though it is most wicked, he who is more cunning, more treacherous, more importunate, worse, more covetous and more wretched will be laughed at, abhorred, persecuted, and, in imitation of the diabolical court, will often be the one who is held in highest esteem. May the grace of God and of our Saviour avert this wickedness.

units.la: CONSIDERATIO IV.
units.tr: CONSIDERATION IV.

units.la: APparens gratia Dei & Saluatoris nostri Iesu exigit, vt prælatus non potentiam subditis, sed gratiam ostendat: vt ipse præterea dolores & gemitus offerat Deo pro eis se circumcidens, pieque viuens: nedum aliis prædicauerit (officio enim prælationis adiuncta est obligatio prædicationis) ipse reprobus inueniatur. Quid ni prælatus gratiosum se, non rigorosum præbeat: cum ipse circumdatus sit infirmitate, egens gratia Dei, nesciens introitum & exitum suum: ignoransan turbationes in subditis ex culpis propriis tanquam occultis, vel ab alienis, vel simul ab vtrisque suscitentur: ita vt necesse habeat obsecrare cum propheta: Ab occultis meis munda me Domine: & ab alienis parce seruo tuo. Nam sicut pro delicto populi pastor, ita pro pastoris errore populus plectitur. Hoc vidit Iob, qui dicit de Deo, quod regnare facit hypocritam propter peccata populi. Qualis autem perniciosior pestis pro populo alia est, quam hypocrisis in suo vel principe vel prælato. Sed ita digni sunt aliqui non nisi per reprobos regi: & alii non nisi reprobis præfici demerentur. Quidni igitur ipse pastor semper pauidus inueniatur: non se iustificans, nec iustificari cupiens: extimescens ne dederit causam scandalo, dicens cum Dauid: Ego sum qui peccaui: & cum Iona: Si propter me turbatio facta est, mittite me in mare. Quo verbo magnum illum Gregorium Nazianzenum vsum fuisse: & ob hoc vrbi Constantinopolitanæ, cui perutilis erat, cessisse, Ecclesiastica meminit historia. Recogitet prælatus etiam denotionis sibi conscius: præsertim dum innumerabiles viri in oppositam ad se pergunt sententiam. Recogitet quid dicat Apostolus: Nihil mihi conscius sum: sed non in hoc iustificatus sum. Quis ad hoc verbum non expauescat? Sed & angelus Sathanæ transfigurat se in angelum lucis: insidiatur in abscondito: spargit vbilibet laqueos, quos obumbrat specie virtutum. Ita vt horrendum valde sit quod dicit sapiens: Est via quae videtur homini iusta: nouissima autem eius ad mortem ducunt. Sic prælatus nonnunquam dum esse gloriatur plenus gratia Dei: repletus est insensibiliter astutia diaboli. Quam multa quotidie (exempli gratia) credit aliquis facere ex magnanimitate, quæ fiunt ex arrogantia præsumptione, quam multa ex indulgentia humilique pietate, qu[illegible, ~6 letters] vel certe (quod mirandum est) ex vana ostentatione & gloriatione [illegible, ~8 letters] vt patientiæ & misericordiæ laudem cum magnis viris meruisse credatur. Sic furor incautus & æmulatio maledicta, quia pertinax. Zelus quoque non secundum scientiam, durus, cerui oculus, inexorabilis, imperterritus, nemini cedens, nullum scandalum reformidans, sed dicens: si damnati volunt, qua ratione saluare possum vel teneor inuitos? Talis inquam furor mentitur se zelum boni publici & communis libertatis. Sic implicatio friuola, & stultus laboriosa minimis tanta se diligentia simulans: sic perplexa scrupulositas semper vacillans, nihil expediens, bonæ sibi conscientiæ nomen usurpat, quæ est ex radice superbiæ nolentis se peritorum iudicio conformare. Sic ambitus honoris palliat se, quod non proficere, sed pro dignitatis honore & aliorum ædificatione perquiritur. Sic ambitio retentione dignitatum, in perniciem ecclesiæ subtili malo fingit se velle multis proficere, nec ecclesiam exponere discrimini peruersorum. Et hoc plane est dæmonium meridianum, quod facit quandoque esse martyrem diaboli, dum esse gloriatur quis in persequentibus martyr Dei. Monet insuper dicere hominem, quia dives sum, & nullius egeo. Et nescit quia pauper est & miserabilis & cæcus & nudus. Sed quid innumerabilia diaboli machinamenta dinumerare contendimus, quibus mentitur & blanditur iniquitas sibi, quasi plena sit gratia Dei? Dicimus potius, quis euasurus est illa? Respondeat: non ego, sed propheta, per oraculum quale factum est Antonio: Humiliatus sum & liberauit me: humiliatus intellectu, humiliatus affectu. Interrogata nimirum gratia Dei, quæ essent signa eius, quibus apparet in homine? Respondit: Primum & præcipuum signum meum est humilitas: hæc sedes mea, hæc requies. Deus itaque humilibus dat gratiam. Cognosce igitur humilitatem, & tu meam habitationem ignorare non poteris. Interrogata vero humilitas de signis suis, multa numerans: & tandem ad duo perstrinxit, quæ sunt humile sapere, & humile velle, adiungens de homine, quem inhabitauerit, quod eum reddit tractabilem quasi perfusum oleo lætitiæ, suasibilem, bonis consentientem, minus semper proprio quam alieno fidentem consilio, abiectus est & vilis in oculis suis, non seictans, non iustificans, non magna promittens, non sollicite se excusans. Ex aduerso cognita sunt superbæ elationis signa, si se colit, si amat, si complacet in se sibi, si sapiens est in oculis suis: alienum vel non requirens, vel odiens, vel non implens consilium: pro sancto iam se habet & pro tali qui dignus sit revelationibus atque miraculis regi. Et quoniam obstupuit in malis, neque se neque morbum suum nouit: se humiliorem, se sanctiorem omnibus iudicat: solos qui loquuntur placentia retinet sibi, alios odit, tandemque abiicit quocunque quæsito colore, & si ad horam dissimulectamare se veritatem. Si scandalizantur alii, non vritur, sed irascitur eius, tanquam solus immunis sit a delicto: tanquam scandalo causam nullam præbuerit, immanet in opinionibus propriis, quas deserere, neque aliorum monitis, neque concilio, neque experientia malorum & sequentium persuaderi potest. Ægrescit potius & excandescit aduersus monita salubria. Væ væ ecclesiæ & religioni cuiquam a peste tali.
units.tr: The appearing of the grace of God and of our Saviour Jesus requires that a prelate show not power to his subjects but grace, and that he also offer groans and tears to God on their behalf, circumcising himself and living piously. For the duty of preaching is joined to the office of prelate, and he must not himself be found reprobate after preaching to others. Why should a prelate not show himself gracious rather than harsh, since he is himself beset by weakness, in need of the grace of God, not knowing his own coming in and going out, and ignorant whether disturbances among his subjects arise from his own hidden faults, or from others' faults, or from both together? So he must pray with the prophet: Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord, and spare your servant from the faults of others. For as the people are punished for the sin of the minister, so the people suffer for the minister's error. Job saw this when he said of God that he makes the hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people. Indeed, what more pernicious plague can there be for a people than hypocrisy in its prince or its prelate? Yet some people deserve to be ruled only by reprobates, and others deserve to be set over reprobates only. Why then should the minister not always be found anxious, neither justifying himself nor wishing to be justified, fearing lest he give occasion for scandal, saying with David: I am the one who has sinned, and with Jonah: If it is on account of me that this tumult has arisen, throw me into the sea. It is recorded in ecclesiastical history that the great Gregory Nazianzen used this word, and on account of it yielded to the city of Constantinople, to which he was very useful. Let the prelate also reflect, even if he is conscious of his own good intention, especially when countless men set themselves against him. Let him reflect on what the Apostle says: I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not thereby justified. Who does not tremble at this word? Satan's angel also transforms himself into an angel of light; he lies in wait in secret, and everywhere spreads snares which he overshadows with the appearance of virtues. So dreadful is what the wise man says: There is a way which seems right to a man, but its end leads to death. Thus the prelate, who sometimes boasts that he is full of the grace of God, is imperceptibly filled with the cunning of the devil. How many things, for example, does someone daily believe he does out of magnanimity which are done out of arrogant presumption; how many out of indulgence and a humble piety, which are, or certainly (what is to be wondered at) are done out of empty show and boasting, so that he believes he has earned the praise of patience and mercy along with great men. So too an incautious rage and a cursed emulation, because they are stubborn. Zeal also, not according to knowledge, harsh, with the eye of a stag, inexorable, undaunted, yielding to no one, fearing no scandal, but saying: "If the damned want it, by what reason can I save them, or am I bound to save them against their will?" Such rage, I say, falsely claims the name of zeal for the public good and common liberty. So too a trifling entanglement, and a foolish labour which pretends such great diligence in very small matters; so too a perplexed scrupulosity, always wavering, accomplishing nothing, usurps the name of a good conscience, though it springs from the root of pride, which is unwilling to conform itself to the judgment of the experienced. So too ambition cloaks itself, seeking not to profit but for the honour of rank and the edification of others. So too ambition, in retaining its dignities to the ruin of the Church, under a subtle evil pretends that it wishes to profit many, and does not expose the Church to the danger of the perverse. And this is clearly the noonday demon, which sometimes makes a man a martyr of the devil, while he boasts that among his persecutors he is a martyr of God. Moreover, it warns a man to say: "I am rich, and I lack nothing." And he does not know that he is wretched and pitiable and blind and naked. But why do we strive to enumerate the countless machinations of the devil, by which iniquity lies to and flatters itself, as if it were full of the grace of God? Rather let us ask: who is going to escape these? Let him answer: not I, but the prophet, through an oracle such as came to Antony: I was brought low, and he saved me: brought low in understanding, brought low in affection. When the grace of God was asked what its signs were, by which it appears in a man, it answered: My first and chief sign is humility: this is my seat, this my rest. God therefore gives grace to the humble. Know, then, humility, and you will not be able to be ignorant of my dwelling. When humility was asked about its signs, it enumerated many, and at last it reduced them to two, which are to think humbly and to will humbly, adding about the man in whom it dwells that it makes him tractable, as if anointed with the oil of joy, persuadable, agreeing with good things, always trusting less in his own counsel than in another's; he is cast down and mean in his own eyes, not boasting, not justifying himself, not promising great things, not anxiously excusing himself. On the other hand, the signs of proud elation are known: if a man admires himself, if he loves himself, if he is pleased with himself, if he is wise in his own eyes; he either does not seek or hates or does not follow another's counsel; he already holds himself to be holy and worthy of being ruled by revelations and miracles. And since he has grown numb to his own evils, he knows neither himself nor his sickness; he judges himself humbler and holier than all; he keeps for himself alone those who speak pleasing things, hates the others, and at last casts them off under whatever pretext, and if for an hour he dissembles, he loves the truth. If others are scandalized, he is not burned by it but is angered, as if he alone were free from fault, as if he had given no cause for scandal; he persists in his own opinions, which he cannot be persuaded to abandon, neither by the admonitions of others, nor by counsel, nor by the experience of evils and of those who follow him. He rather grows sick and is inflamed against wholesome admonitions. Woe, woe to the Church and to any religion from such a plague.

units.la: Vix enim satis deprehendi potest, quia tegitur quina pelle, sed per doctissimos scientes probare spiritus, si ex Deo sunt, ex fructibus cognoscitur, & maxime dum ad inhonorationis cuiuslibet vel paruam æstimationem quasi furit, vt Philocaptus amaræ suæ læsionem exhorresit. Nihilominus cum per tales deprehensa fuerit, vix est inuenire remedium, quia nec expelli facile potest, nec retenta corrigi, nisi per miraculosam operationem gratiæ Dei Saluatoris nostri.
units.tr: For indeed it can scarcely be detected, since it is covered by a fivefold skin; but by the most learned, who know how to test the spirits whether they are of God, it is known from its fruits, and especially when it rages at the slightest lessening of any dishonour, as Philocaptus shuddered at the bitter wound to his own pride. Nevertheless, when such a fault has been detected in such men, it is hardly possible to find a remedy, because it cannot easily be expelled, nor corrected if it is kept, except by the miraculous operation of the grace of God our Saviour.

units.la: Talem cursum habuerit sermo noster per primum signum, quo apparuit gratia Dei & Saluatoris nostri, in eius humilitate subiiciente se legi circumcisionis, & de ipsius imitatione debita per prælatos & clerum, vt patiatur prælatus legem, quam tulerit: vtque quanto maior est, humiliet se in omnibus, vtque non imponat onera grauia cerviciibus subditorum, vtque gratiosum se, non rigorosum ostendat, & ita abnegata impietate & secularibus desideriis, & sobrie & iuste & pie viuamus in hoc seculo.
units.tr: Our discourse has run this course through the first sign by which the grace of God and our Saviour appeared, in his humility in submitting himself to the law of circumcision; and it has run through the due imitation of this by prelates and clergy: that the prelate should bear the law which he has imposed; that the greater he is, the more he should humble himself in all things; that he should not lay heavy burdens on the necks of his subjects; that he should show himself gracious, not harsh; and so, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we may live soberly, justly and piously in this present age.

units.la: Reliquum est, vt per secundum signum diuinæ gratiæ, quod esse diximus benignitatem seu charitatem plenius signatam in nominis impositione, sermonis nostri cursus consummationem accipiat. Vocatum est nomen eius Iesus, inquit Euangelista. O nomen totiens vocatum & desideratum, nomen tamdiu cum suspiriis expectatum: sed hodie primitus impositum, cum vocatum est nomen eius Iesus. Dudum enim longe a peccatoribus salus, id est Iesus, & prope erat vltionum Dominus. Hoc Dauid cognoscens postulabat nomen non potentiæ & damnationis, sed gratiæ & benignitatis. Dic, inquit, anima mea, salus tua ego sum. Iesus tuus ego sum. Nam quid est Iesus, nisi salus? Nonne sic tibi loqui videtur Dauid Deo, satis dixisti, ego Dominus, ego omnipotens, ego iustus & terribilis. Abscondantur obsecro hæc nomina potestatis, & exhibeatur nomen gratiæ & benignitatis. Et dico ego Iesus. Hoc est nomen nouum, quod os Domini nominauit, quod vocatum est ab Angelo priusquam in vtero conciperetur, nomen ab Apostolis prædicatum, sicut dicunt Actus Apostolorum, quod omni die non cessabant in templo & circa domos euangelizantes Iesum. Hinc magnus ille prædicator, qui loquebatur sapientiam inter perfectos, nihil iudicabat se scire, nisi Iesum Christum, & hunc crucifixum. Iesum præterea totiens viuens & morientem [illegible, ~10 letters] eius Ignatius.
units.tr: It remains that, through the second sign of divine grace, which we have said is goodness or charity, more fully marked in the giving of the name, our discourse should reach its completion. His name was called Jesus, says the Evangelist. O name so often called and desired, name so long awaited with sighs, but today first given, when his name was called Jesus. For long ago salvation, that is Jesus, was far from sinners, and the Lord of vengeance was near. David, knowing this, asked for the name not of power and condemnation but of grace and goodness: Say, he says, to my soul, I am your salvation. I am your Jesus. For what is Jesus but salvation? Does David not seem to speak to God thus: "You have said enough: I am the Lord, I am the almighty, I am just and terrible." I beg that these names of power be hidden, and that the name of grace and goodness be shown. And I say: I am Jesus. This is the new name, which the mouth of the Lord named, which was called by the Angel before he was conceived in the womb, the name preached by the Apostles, as the Acts of the Apostles say, who did not cease every day in the temple and in the houses, evangelizing Jesus. Hence that great preacher, who spoke wisdom among the perfect, judged that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. Moreover, Ignatius, living and dying with Jesus [illegible] of him.

units.la: Nonne præterea a creaturis omnibus adoratum, quia in nomine Iesu omne genu flectatur cœlestium, terrestrium & infernorum: quod perspicue fecit miraculorum operatio. Nomen deinde ab omnibus inuocandum: quia omnibus [illegible, ~6 letters] nam omnis qui inuocauerit nomen Domini [illegible, ~4 letters] mini, hic salus erit. Et nomen aliud nomen sub coelo (affirmat Petrus) datum hominibus, in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri. Et iterum: Nec est in aliquo alio salus. Si poenites, & baptizetur unusquisque vestrum in nomine Iesu Christi, in remissionem peccatorum vestrorum, &c. Appella ad Deum gratiarum, dicens: ut peccatorum nomen suum Iesus, scribi tibi Iesus: quoniam scribit nobis filiolis suis Ioannes: quia remittuntur tibi peccata propter nomen eius. Nam quis legitur in evangelio invocasse nomen Iesu, & exauditum non fuisse? Si damnata morte peccatorum manet morbus concupiscentiae audi: quia in nomine Iesu serpentes malarum suggestionum tollunt. Et si mortiferum quid delectationis bibitur, non nocebit. Si feroces insultus inimicorum omnium timueris, attende quia in nomine Iesu daemonia eiiciuntur, & ferae mansuescunt: ut gloriabitur Agatha: & turris fortissima praedicatur a sapiente nomen Domini. Si tentatione vel afflictione fatigatus depri-mis, imitare Apostolos qui ibant gaudentes a conspectu concilii: quoniam digni habiti sunt pro nomine Iesu contumeliam pati. Et Apostolus paratum se offert, non solum litigari, sed & mori in Hierusalem pro nomine Iesu. Apparet igitur gratia Dei in hoc nomine Iesu: quod non est in remedium contra malum culpae: in refrigerium contra malum concupiscentiae: in praesidium contra malum pugnae: & in solatium contra malum poenae. Amplius, quia necesse est nobis viatoribus inquirentibus coelestem Hierusalem viam agnoscere: animadvertamus, quia deducit nos Dominus super mitas iustitiae propter nomen suum. Porro quia ignobilis est, nobilitari desideras: dat Dominus potestatem filios Dei fieri his, qui credunt in nomine eius. Magna plane nobilitas: quia si filii Dei, & haeredes: haeredes quidem Dei, coheredes autem Christi: & ex consequenti eius fratres. Quod agnoscens angelus, adorari a Ioanne noluit, Vide ait, ne feceris: conservum enim tuus sum & fratrum tuorum habentium testimonium Iesu. Egenuses, & multa te petere necesse est: offertur tibi Iesus pro titulo petitionis in curia Dei patris: sicut observuat ecclesia instituta ab eo qui dixit: Quicquid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Quo nomine qui insigniti fuerint, salvabuntur: iuxta figuram Ezechielis de signo thau, quo signati salvati sunt. Denique nemo virtutem, nemo sanitatem huius nominis novit, nisi qui accipit per experientiam, & gustat quid illud est: Oleum effusum nomen tuum. Qualiter accepe-rat qui dicebat: Domine nomen tuum & memoriale tuum in desiderio animae. Et alter: In te gloriticabuntur omnes, qui diligunt nomen tuum. Rursus alius: Ego autem in Domino gaudebo: & exultabo in Deo Iesu meo: quasi di. Gaudeant alii in anxia diviciarum & sarcinarum inutilium accumulatione: alii in effrenatione sordida voluptatum: alii in aliis noxiis atque praeduris: ego autem exultabo in Deo Iesu meo: quoniam potissimum apparuit gratia Dei in eo.
units.tr: Is he not also adored by every creature, since at the name of Jesus every knee bows, of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth? The working of miracles makes this plain. Then the name is to be invoked by all, since "whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved" (Joel 2:32; Acts 2:21). And, as Peter affirms, there is "no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4:12). And again: "Neither is there salvation in any other." "Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of your sins," and so on. Appeal to the God of grace, saying: let Jesus be the name of sinners, let Jesus be written for you, since John writes to us, his little children, that our sins are forgiven for his name's sake (1 John 2:12). For where is it read in the gospel that someone called on the name of Jesus and was not heard? If the disease of concupiscence remains after the death of sin, listen: in the name of Jesus the serpents of evil suggestions are taken up. And if something deadly of pleasure is drunk, it will not harm you (Mark 16:18). If you fear the fierce assaults of all enemies, note that in the name of Jesus demons are cast out and wild beasts grow tame, as Agatha boasts; and the wise man proclaims the name of the Lord a most strong tower (Prov. 18:10). If you are worn down by temptation or affliction and sink in spirit, imitate the Apostles, who went out rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer shame for the name of Jesus (Acts 5:41). And the Apostle offers himself ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of Jesus (Acts 21:13). So the grace of God appears in this name of Jesus: it is a remedy against the evil of guilt, a refreshment against the evil of concupiscence, a defence against the evil of strife, and a solace against the evil of punishment. Further, since we are travellers seeking the heavenly Jerusalem, we must know the way; let us note that the Lord leads us along the paths of righteousness for his name's sake (Ps. 23:3). Moreover, since you are ignoble and long to be ennobled, the Lord gives power to become sons of God to those who believe in his name (John 1:12). Great indeed is this nobility: if sons, then heirs; heirs indeed of God, and joint-heirs with Christ, and consequently his brothers (Rom. 8:17). The angel, recognising this, would not be adored by John: "See," he said, "do not do it; for I am your fellow-servant and of your brethren who hold the testimony of Jesus" (Rev. 19:10). You are needy and must ask for many things: Jesus is offered to you as the title of your petition in the court of God the Father, as the Church, instituted by him who said, "Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you" (John 16:23), observes. Those who are marked with this name will be saved, according to Ezekiel's figure of the sign tau, by which the marked were saved (Ezek. 9:4). Finally, no one knows the power and health of this name except the one who receives it by experience and tastes what it is: "Your name is oil poured out" (Song 1:3). So had he received it who said, "Lord, your name and your memorial are the desire of my soul" (Isa. 26:8). And another: "In you shall all who love your name be glorified" (Ps. 5:11 ff.). Again another: "But I will rejoice in the Lord, and exult in God my Jesus." Let others rejoice in the anxious heaping up of riches and useless burdens, others in the filthy unbridling of pleasures, others in other harmful and hard things; but I will exult in God my Jesus, since the grace of God has appeared most of all in him.

units.la: Sed ecce denuo sermonem interrumpere conatur studiositas importuna. Et quaerit quomodo verum habet, quod omnis qui invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit: cum alibi scriptum sit: Non omnis qui dicit mihi Domine Domine intrabit in regnum coelorum. Responsio: requiritur tertium Domine, quod est operis, sicut primum est cordis, secundum est oris. Dic, cur Apostolus tantus vir petens in nomine Iesu carnis stimulum tolli, exauditus non potuit? Responsio: non petiit ad salutem. Associari quippe debet oratio quatuor comitibus, ut exaudibilis semper fiat: quod pie, id est ad salutem: quod perseveranter sine peccati interruptione: quod iuste, hoc est in gratia & pro se. Et ita quisquis in ipso etiam mortis articulo petitha punini in curia gratiae, liberabitur a poena futura: ubi est curia iustitiae: & volabit liber in coelum, sicut deducit Dominus Antisiodorensis, mediante merito Christi & poena habita in praesenti. Verbum quidem, quod dicit Apostolus, quia nemo potest dicere Dominus Iesus nisi in Spiritu sancto: cum pessimi nedum illud nominare, sed in virtute eius miracula facere memorentur: quemadmodum viderunt Apostoli quendam in nomine Iesu daemonia eiicientem: sicut & illi reprobi, qui dicent in iudicio Domino: Nonne in nomine tuo prophetavimus: & in nomine tuo virtutes multas fecimus? &c. quibus dicetur: Nescio vos. Responsio, quod nemo potest dicere Dominus Iesus, nisi in Spiritu sancto illustrante intellectum, sicut nec aliquam veritatem, vel ipso simul movente affectum & illustrante intellectum ut in bonis. Quod autem mali faciunt miracula, hoc est per potestatem publicae iustitiae in attestationem veritatis. Propterea non sufficiunt ostendere aliquem sanctum, nisi comes fuerit humilitas & sanctitas. Haec vero gratia miraculorum ideo datur quandoque reprobis ad ipsorum condemnationem, ne iusti pro magno deputent, sive habeant vel non habeant hanc gratiam. Nolite, inquit Christus, gloriari quod Spiritus vobis subiiciuntur, &c. Quod si sigillum & signum proprium divinae potestatis, quod est miraculum adhiberi quaeratur in testimonium falsitatis: Deus hoc nunquam permittit, quin reclamaverit vel reclamet, quemadmodum praedixit, ne credamus signis Antichristi. Et hoc est ad probationem electorum.
units.tr: But look, once more an importunate curiosity tries to interrupt my discourse, and asks how it can be true that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved, when it is written elsewhere: "Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter the kingdom of heaven" (Matt. 7:21). Answer: a third "Lord" is required, that of works, just as the first is of the heart and the second of the mouth. Tell me, why could the Apostle, so great a man, not be heard when he asked in the name of Jesus that the sting of the flesh be taken away? Answer: he did not ask for salvation. Prayer ought indeed to be accompanied by four companions if it is always to be heard: it must be pious, that is, directed to salvation; it must be persevering, without interruption by sin; it must be just, that is, made in grace and for oneself. And so whoever, even at the very point of death, asks to be punished in the court of grace will be freed from future punishment, where the court of justice is, and will fly free into heaven, as the Lord of Auxerre teaches, through the merit of Christ and the punishment undergone in the present life. As for the word the Apostle uses, that no one can say "the Lord Jesus" except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12:3): wicked men are recorded not only to have named him but also to have worked miracles in his power, as the Apostles saw a certain man casting out demons in the name of Jesus (Mark 9:38); and so the reprobate who will say to the Lord at judgement, "Have we not prophesied in your name, and in your name done many mighty works?" (Matt. 7:22), will be told, "I never knew you." Answer: no one can say "the Lord Jesus" except in the Holy Spirit, who enlightens the understanding, just as no truth can be grasped unless the same Spirit at once moves the affection and illumines the understanding, as in the good. As for the miracles wrought by the wicked, they are done by the power of public justice, for the attestation of truth. Therefore it is not enough to show that someone is holy unless humility and holiness go with it. This gift of miracles is sometimes given even to the reprobate for their own condemnation, so that the just may not reckon it great, whether or not they have this grace. "Do not rejoice," says Christ, "that the spirits are subject to you" (Luke 10:20). But if the seal and proper sign of divine power, which is the miracle, is sought to be used as testimony for falsehood, God never permits this without protesting, or without protesting still, just as he foretold that we should not believe the signs of Antichrist. And this is for the proof of the elect.

units.la: Properabat rursus quaerere studiositas: Cur non modo fit baptismus ut olim in nomine Iesu? & cur non ad invocationem eius dantur genera linguarum & operationes miraculorum & similia? Dum haec inter loquendum superirruit zelus feruidus, filius charitatis: abscede hinc (ait) o studiositas speculatrix: non est tempus disputandi, sed plorandi, nam si propterea Deus appellatus est Iesus: si in hoc apparuit gratia ipsius ut salvemur: unde tot nobis mala, tot incommoda: qui in ipsum credimus, ipsum invocamus? Ecce imminuti sumus ex ira Dei effusa super nos plus quam gentes, quae nomen Domini non noverunt neque invocaverunt. Et ut alia praeteream, ecce quam exerando schismate ecclesiam sponsam suam concuti sinit, deiici, proteri, rumpi, lacerari. Et ubi sunt miserieordiae tuae antiquae Domine? ubi est illa quam Apostolus tuus scribit apparuisse gratia? ubi est nomen sanctum tuum atque gloriosum, quod invocatum est super nos? Cur derelinquis nos Domine Deus noster? Ubi abundantia illa pacis, quam oriturum asseruit propheta in diebus bus tuis: & quam angeli cecinerunt, dicentes: Gloria in excelsis Deo: & in terra pax hominibus bonæ voluntatis. Sed væ tibi mala voluntas, voluntas ingrata: tu istam à nobis Dei gratiam abscondis, tu divinum illud carmen obturbas dissonis moribus tuis, tu surripis gloriam Deo partem suam. Quidni pace spolieris parte tua? Tu igitur bene viuere docenda esse, non acute disputare, neque fortassis tempus docendi, sed faciendi: quoniam mala radicata, quia in mores abierunt, non verborum fomentis, sed factorum securibus atque ferramentis extirpare necesse est. Sed assir potius tempus miserendi Domine Iesu: tempus miserendi eius, quia venit tempus, succurrat gratia tua. Appareat illa miseris, quia adiutorium in opportunitatibus, in tribulatione. Impera ventis & cessabit quassatio, & aura leuerior & spectator. Recorderis gratiæ tuæ antiquæ Domine, recorderis infantiæ suscepto propter nos, sed & circumcisionis tuæ & nominationis saluiferæ memor esto. Benedic principio anni benignitatis tuæ, quod principium tu corona misericordiæ & miserationibus: quoniam illud tibi dedicamus, non fabuloso Iano bifronti: scientes quoniam beatus est vir, cuius est nomen Domini spes eius, & non respexit in vanitates & insanias falsas. Tu summus es Pontifex noster: des in nouitate ortus tui & coronationis tuæ gratiarum vbertatem, & indulgentiarum plenitudinem elargire. Signare dignetur gratia tua nostras expectationes ad prædendas cœlestis illius & cathedralis ecclesiæ tuæ magnæ Hierusalem ecclesiæ triumphantis ad quam tendimus: quam tota devotione cupimus, expectantes beatam spem. Non confundas nos ab expectatione, quia væ patientibus repulsam, si vel in signatione, vel in bullis, vel processu, vel possessione defecerint. Sit hodierna sanguinis tui effusio expectationum nostrarum valida signatio, sit æternum salutare, ut vbi iniquitas abundauit, superabundet & gratia.
units.tr: Curiosity hastened again to ask: why does baptism not now take place in the name of Jesus as once it did? And why, at the invocation of his name, are there no gifts of tongues, no workings of miracles and the like? While these questions were being raised, a fervent zeal, a son of love, broke in: "Away with you, speculative curiosity! This is no time for disputing but for weeping. For if God has been called Jesus for this reason, and if his grace has appeared in this so that we may be saved, whence come so many evils and so many troubles upon us who believe in him and call upon him? Behold, we are diminished by the wrath of God poured out upon us more than the nations, who have not known or called upon the name of the Lord. And to pass over other things: behold how, with schism raging, he allows his bride the Church to be shaken, cast down, trampled, torn and mangled. And where, Lord, are your ancient mercies? Where is that grace which your Apostle writes has appeared? Where is your holy and glorious name, which has been called upon us? Why do you forsake us, Lord our God? Where is that abundance of peace which the prophet declared would arise in your days, and which the angels sang: 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will'? But woe to you, ill will, ungrateful will! You hide this grace of God from us; you disturb that divine song with your discordant ways; you steal from God the glory that is his part. Why should you not be stripped of your share of peace?" So you must learn to live well, not to dispute sharply; and perhaps this is a time not for teaching but for doing, since evils rooted deep, which have passed into manners, must be cut out not with the fomentations of words but with the axes and iron tools of deeds. But rather, Lord Jesus, now is the time for mercy, the time of his mercy; since the time has come, let your grace come to our help. Let it appear to the wretched, as a help in opportunities, in tribulation. Command the winds, and the shaking and the breeze will cease, and the watcher will be calmer. Remember, Lord, your ancient grace; remember your infancy undertaken for our sake, and your circumcision, and be mindful of your saving naming. Bless, at the beginning of the year, the beginning of your kindness, you who are the crown of mercy and of compassions; for we dedicate it to you, not to the fabled two-faced Janus, knowing that "blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not turned to vanities and lying follies" (Ps. 40:4). You are our high priest. Grant, at the newness of your rising and of your crowning, an abundance of graces and an outpouring of indulgences. May your grace deign to seal our expectations for that heavenly and cathedral church of yours, the great Jerusalem, the church triumphant towards which we strive, which we desire with all devotion, waiting for the blessed hope. Do not confound us in our expectation, for woe to those who suffer repulse, whether in the sealing, the bulls, the process, or the possession, if these should fail. Let today's effusion of your blood be a strong seal of our expectations, and let it be an eternal salvation, so that where sin has abounded, grace may abound all the more.

units.la: Talis erat in meditatione mea zeli plangor querulus, commouens, orans & obtestans, ut sublata mala voluntate de medio nostri (illa enim sola pacem cogit in exilium, illa schisma parit, fouet & nutrit) nos coadiutores gratiæ Dei sumus, quæ piis conatibus non deerit. Cui studiositas, & cur ait non inquirit clerus cum prælatis suis, qualibus viis occurrere conuenit tantis & tot incommodis. Seu per congregationem factam in nomine Iesu, qui aderit in medio. Seu per sedulæ disputationis officium tendentis non ad contentionem, sed veritatis inquisitionem. Seu per inuestigationem criminum regnantium in Christianitate vt euelli cognita possent. Et esset clerus exemplo Iesu populi saluator, non lupus dissipator. Expedit ne me studiositatem in talibus occupari? Cui zelus: Expedit quidem & iam multa à tuis sectatoribus conscripta sunt, vt omnia rite præparentur, quæ agenda fuerint in concilio: alioquin verendum est, ne schismati radicationem afferret exemplo Græcorum, & ne scissuras (quod auertat Dei gratia) multiplicaret ampliores: qualia nunc omnia dicere reclamat, vt vides, breuitatis amor & subdola blandaque adulatio contradicit. Nihilominus, obsecratione facta per gratiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi, & per me zelum domus Dei, vt tempus modicum detur veritati & eius inquisitioni, propulso omni mordacitatis desiderio, quod longissimum frequenter vanitati datur & fabulationi. Dic tu studiositas radices aliquas ex iure diuino sub generalibus principiis vtiles ad sedandum pestiferum schisma, quoniam illud primum & principalius occurrit in ecclesia reformandum. Tunc studiositas visa est quædam aperire sub consideratione quadruplici, quæ qualia sunt, vestrum erit iudicium.
units.tr: Such was the plaintive lament of my zeal in meditation, stirring, praying and beseeching that, the ill will being removed from our midst (for it alone drives peace into exile; it gives birth to schism, fosters and nourishes it), we may be co-workers with the grace of God, which will not be lacking to pious endeavours. To this Studiositas replied: and why does the clergy, with its prelates, not inquire what ways it is fitting to meet such and so many evils? Whether by an assembly gathered in the name of Jesus, who will be present in the midst; or by the duty of a diligent disputation aiming not at contention but at the inquiry into truth; or by the investigation of the crimes reigning in Christendom, so that, once known, they might be uprooted. And the clergy, following the example of Jesus, would be a saviour of the people, not a wolf who scatters them. Is it useful for me, Studiositas, to occupy myself with such matters? Zelus replied: It certainly is useful, and already many things have been written by your followers so that everything that must be done at the council may be duly prepared; otherwise it is to be feared lest it bring schism deep roots after the example of the Greeks, and multiply still greater divisions (which the grace of God forbid). As you see, the love of brevity and a deceitful, flattering adulation forbid me to say all these things now. Nevertheless, I beseech you through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and through me, zeal for the house of God, that a short time be given to the truth and its inquiry, setting aside all desire for biting words, which is very often given to vanity and idle talk at great length. Tell me, Studiositas, some roots from divine law, under general principles, useful for quelling the deadly schism, since that is the first and principal thing that presents itself for reform in the Church. Then Studiositas seemed to open up certain points under a fourfold consideration; what kind they are, the judgment will be yours.

units.la: QVATVOR CONSIDERATIONES DE PACE, PRÆDICATÆ TARASCONE.
units.tr: FOUR CONSIDERATIONS ON PEACE, PREACHED AT TARASCON.

units.la: CONSIDERATIO I.
units.tr: CONSIDERATION I.

units.la: Finis politiæ ecclesiasticæ & cuiuslibet legis eam regulantis est pax salutifera. Hoc satis expressit diuinus noster Philosophus Paulus, qui finem legis & præcepti nunc dilectionem esse dixit, nunc Iesum, intelligens in dilectione pacem, in Iesu salutem, ut sit finis pax salutaris. Neque opus est anxia deductione alia, cum natura nos doceat ens quodlibet non minus suam vnitatem & pacem appetere quam entitatem, secundum deductionem diuini Dionysii, Augustini & Boetii: ita ut pax sit bonum, quod omnia appetunt, adeo quod particularis ordo naturæ plerumque immutatur in rebus, ut vnitas conseruetur.
units.tr: The end of ecclesiastical polity, and of every law that regulates it, is salutary peace. Our divine philosopher Paul has expressed this well enough. He called the end of the law and of the precept now love, now Jesus, understanding love as peace and Jesus as salvation, so that the end is saving peace. No lengthy further argument is needed, since nature teaches us that every being seeks its unity and peace no less than its existence, following the reasoning of the divine Dionysius, Augustine and Boethius. Peace is therefore the good that all things seek, so much so that the ordinary course of nature in particular things is often altered so that unity may be preserved.

units.la: Manifestat hoc ascensus grauis sursum, & leuis deorsum. Si in corpore vero, cur non in mystico potest vicissitudo talis quæri, ut pro pace retinenda fiat deorsum quod sursum est ut pax permaneat? Cum igitur secundum exigentiam finis cætera debeant moderari, & finis est, qui imponit necessitatem rebus: necessitas vero legem non habet, perspicuum est, quod nulla lex habeat aliquid firmitatis, si paci faciendæ vel conseruandæ inuenitur contraria, sed debet interpretari ut seruiat paci, vel penitus aboleri, alioquin iuxta dictum Comici: summum ius summa est malitia: conformiter ad iusfionem sapientis: Noli esse iustus nimis. Sic Athenienses fecerunt ad tempus leges Lycurgi non esse, ut semper essent, & Nasica Scipio: Dum consul, inquit, iuris ordinem sequitur, id agit ut cum omnibus legibus Romanum corruat imperium. Nullo pacto igitur seruatur lex, non obseruato legis fine, qui est pax. Sicut in simili Christianam doctrinam scribens Augustinus deducit pro regula memoranmoranda: quod nullum textum sacrae scripturae in sua expositione retinet sensum Spiritus sancti, nisi ille charitatem aedificet. Et quoniam huius schismatis tam extranea videtur esse pestis, ut tale nunquam visum fuerit minus habens provisionis humanae remedium: docente hoc sua indies radicatione, expedit ad eius expulsionem instituto novorum canonum: cum ea quae de novo emergunt, novo egeant auxilio: vel iam conditorum necessaria est moderatio. Sed qualis & per quid moderatio? Sane per regulam infallibilem & inobliquabilem legis divinae: cuius sectatoribus & amicis pax multa est, si prophetae creditur: & non est illis scandalum. Ex quibus elicitur conclusio saluberrima: quod nulla via proficiens ad sedationem schismatis repudianda est, quantumcunque iura vel leges humanae videantur opponi: ut de electione summi pontificis, quod est sic & sic celebranda, & similes, dummodo divinum mandatum vel iuris maneat inviolatum. Quod scire ad illam spectat scientiam, per quam legum conditores iusta decernunt, legem aeternam imitantes. Haec est lex evangelica: quae si contemnatur ab aliquibus, illi sunt inepti pacis ecclesiasticae tractatores: quemadmodum inutiles sunt homines ita adhaerentes nudis textibus, ut Ἀπειθεῖαν, hoc est aequitatem ignorent, quales Aristo nominavit immansuos in opinionibus propriis. Ex his denique quis non videat quam impium est praesertim apud eos qui se ecclesiasticos dici volunt, si peritos in evangelica lege vel non consultare vel abiicere, vel maiori sacrilegio habere probro cognoscantur, hinc praesumptuosae assertiones, hinc perplexitates inexplicabiles, hinc obstinatae defensiones adinuentionum humanarum in perniciem ecclesiae & pacis salutiferae finis sui surgunt: ut quod non licet disputare de potentia papae: quod non potest sibi dici, cur ita facis? cum tamen sit peccabilis, quod non potest in aliquo casu ecclesia sine eo convocari vel aggregari: quod hic est fidei articulus, Benedictus est papa (exempli gratia,) quod non potest in aliquo casu ad concilium papa vocari: Quod absque eo non stat salus, cum tamen salus ecclesiae in solum Deum ordinetur absolute & essentialiter: & in hominem Christum de ordinata lege: sed accidentaliter ordinatur in papam mortalem, alioquin dum vacat sedes per mortem papae, vel naturalem vel civilem: ut puta si sit haereticus depositus, quis hominum salvus esset? Alii papam praedicant impeccabilem, alii omnipotentem, alii sine ulla exceptione credunt extra salutis statum quemlibet suae parti non obedientem. Quod quanta temeritate dicatur, ipsi viderint assertores.
units.tr: The rising of heavy things upward and of light things downward shows this. If in the natural body such a change can be found, why should it not also be sought in the mystical body, so that for the sake of keeping peace what is above is brought down, and peace may remain? Since, then, all other things ought to be governed according to the demands of the end, and it is the end that imposes necessity on things, while necessity has no law, it is plain that no law has any firmness if it is found to be opposed to making or preserving peace. Rather it must be interpreted so as to serve peace, or else be abolished altogether; otherwise, as the comic poet says, the highest law is the highest injustice, and in agreement with the saying of the wise man: Be not overly just. So the Athenians, for a time, made the laws of Lycurgus as if they did not exist, so that they might not always exist; and Scipio Nasica said: While consul, he follows the order of law, and he brings it about that the Roman empire falls together with all its laws. In no way, then, is a law kept if the end of the law, which is peace, is not observed. Likewise, Augustine, writing on Christian doctrine, lays down as a rule to be remembered that no passage of Holy Scripture, in its exposition, retains the sense of the Holy Spirit unless it builds up charity. And since this pest of schism seems so foreign, and such a thing has never been seen before, and since human provision has less remedy for it, while its daily rooting teaches this, it is expedient for its expulsion to institute new canons, since things that newly arise need a new help; or else the moderation of already established canons is needed. But what kind of moderation, and by what means? Surely by the infallible and unbending rule of the divine law, whose followers and friends have much peace, if the prophet is to be believed, and for whom there is no stumbling block. From this a most salutary conclusion is drawn: that no way that is useful for calming the schism should be rejected, however much human rights or laws may seem to stand in the way, as with the election of the supreme pontiff, which is to be celebrated in this way or that, and similar matters, provided that the divine command or right remains inviolate. To know this belongs to that science by which the makers of laws decree what is just, imitating the eternal law. This is the gospel law. If some despise it, they are unskilled handlers of ecclesiastical peace, just as men who cling so tightly to bare texts that they are ignorant of [ἐπιείκειαν], that is, equity, are useless; Aristo called such men monstrous in their own opinions. Finally, who does not see how impious it is, especially among those who wish to be called ecclesiastical, if they are known either not to consult those skilled in the gospel law, or to reject them, or to hold them in greater disgrace as a sacrilege? From this arise presumptuous assertions, from this inexplicable perplexities, from this stubborn defences of human inventions, to the ruin of the Church and of the salutary end of peace. Thus: it is not permitted to dispute about the power of the pope; no one may ask him, "Why do you act thus?", although he is capable of sin; that in no case can the Church be convoked or gathered without him; that this is an article of faith, "Blessed is the pope" (for example); that in no case can a pope be summoned to a council; that salvation does not stand without him, although the salvation of the Church is ordered absolutely and essentially to God alone, and to the man Christ by an ordained law, but is ordered only incidentally to a mortal pope. Otherwise, while the see is vacant through the pope's death, natural or civil (as for instance if he has been deposed as a heretic), who among men would be saved? Some proclaim the pope sinless, others all-powerful, and others, without any exception, believe that anyone who does not obey his party is outside the state of salvation. The assertors themselves will see how great a rashness it is to say such things.

units.la: CONSIDERATIO II.
units.tr: CONSIDERATIO II.

units.la: Quaelibet in ecclesiastica hierarchia potestas in pacem salutiferam ordinatur. Haec infertur ex primo. Cum igitur non sit data potestas in destructionem, sed aedificationem, teste Apostolo: Si quis abusui potestatis, hoc est tyrannidi resistit, ille non resistit Dei ordinationi: sed obedit qui iubet malum tollere de medio sui & partem scandalizantem abiicere: sicut & licet cuicunque ergo quemcunque vim illatam vi repellere cum appositione moderatae cautelae. Haec consideratio facili deductione traducit quorundam scripta super obedientiae laudibus & inobedientiae poenis ad oppositum illius quod persuadere conantur. Nam si obediendum est hominibus, quanto magis Deo?
units.tr: Every power in the ecclesiastical hierarchy is ordained for a saving peace. This follows from the first point. Since power is given not for destruction but for edification, as the Apostle witnesses, whoever resists an abuse of power, that is, tyranny, does not resist God's ordinance. Rather, he obeys who commands that evil be removed from the midst and the offending part cast away, just as anyone may repel force with force, provided moderate caution is applied. This consideration, by an easy deduction, turns the writings of certain men, which praise obedience and threaten the penalties of disobedience, against the very thing they try to persuade us of. For if we must obey men, how much more must we obey God?

units.la: Elucet praeterea, quod si salutifera pax rollatur, ex eo quod in Ioanne (exempli gratia) potestas ecclesiastica quaedam remanet, qua repudiata pax redireт: abiicere potestatem in hoc casu est eadem bene uti: retentio autem verteretur in abusum. Addito quod nulla potestas inveniatur hic in via, quae non subiiciatur legi divinae & naturali: & quae non sit peccabilis & auferibilis vel abdicabilis aut pro tempore ab executione suspensibilis. Fundatur in hac consideratione dictum illud memorabile & vere dignum a summo pontifice, quod his auribus pluries accepi ab ore Domini nostri, hoc sine adulationis spiritu refero: Paratus sum, inquit, etiam usque ad mortem vel immolationem proprii corporis, si itaque exigat, ecclesiasticam unionem procurare: quanto amplius usque ad proprii status abdicationem. Nam quando daret vitam, qui non deiceret vestem aut vitam, coronam seu mitram? Vellent aliqui rursus obiicere contra epistolam Anglicanam, quod via cessionis in effectu reddi possitptacabilis casu propositio: inuitis etiam contendentibus de papatu: quanquam si habeat hic allegationem rationabilem coactio, ipsi viderint: velint itaque, nemo cogit. At vero quicquid de hoc sit, constat viam cessionis esse possibilem: imo in casu necessariam: ad cuius laudem spectat quod scribit Dionysius (non ille Ariopagita) ad Donatum, recitatiue in Ecclesiastica historia: Dionysius Donato fratri salutem. Si invitus ut ais in hoc venisti, offendis in eo si dimiseris volens: oportuerat quidem etiam pati omnia pro eo ne sciinderetur ecclesia Dei: & erat non inferior gloria sustinere martyrium pro eo ne scinderetur ecclesia quam est illa, ne idolis immoletur: imo secundum meam sententiam maius hoc puto martyrium esse quam illud: quia ibi unusquisque pro sua tantum anima: in hoc vero pro omni ecclesia martyrium sustinet. Haec ille. Denique plura sequerentur de quibus non est dicendum per singula.
units.tr: It is also clear that if saving peace is to be brought about, and if in John (for example) some ecclesiastical power remains by which peace could return once that power is renounced, then giving up the power in this case is the same as using it well, whereas keeping it would turn into abuse. Add to this that no power is found here on earth which is not subject to divine and natural law, and which is not capable of sin, of being taken away or resigned, or for a time suspended from exercise. On this consideration rests that memorable saying, truly worthy of the highest pontiff, which I have heard more than once from the lips of our Lord, and I report it without any spirit of flattery: "I am ready," he said, "even to death, or to the sacrifice of my own body, if it so demands, to procure ecclesiastical unity; how much more, then, to the abdication of my own status." For when he would give up his life, who would not cast off his robe, his life, or his crown or mitre? Some would again object against the English letter that the way of resignation could in fact be made impossible in this case, the proposal being opposed even by those who contend for the papacy. Yet if coercion has here some reasonable justification, let them see to it; let them therefore wish it, and no one compels. But whatever the case, it is established that the way of resignation is possible, indeed necessary in this case. To its praise belongs what Dionysius (not the Areopagite) writes to Donatus, quoted in the Ecclesiastical History: "Dionysius to his brother Donatus, greetings. If you came into this unwillingly, as you say, you give offence if you depart willingly. Indeed it was right to suffer all things for his sake, lest the Church of God be torn apart; and the glory of enduring martyrdom to prevent the Church from being torn is no less than that of not sacrificing to idols. Indeed, in my judgement, this is a greater martyrdom than that one: for there each one suffers for his own soul alone, but here one suffers martyrdom for the whole Church." So he. Finally, much more would follow, which need not be discussed point by point.

units.la: CONSIDERATIO III.
units.tr: CONSIDERATIO III.

units.la: Quilibet rationis capax obligatur secundum vocationem suam, pacem ecclesiae salutiferam procurare. Ille orando, hic disputando, hic praedicando, hic exhortando, hic agendo, vel quolibet modo alio. Sumerentur argumenta pro hac consideratione ex radice filiationis ad ecclesiam: & ex radice dilectionis & iustitiae ad proximum: ex radice pietatis seu religionis ad Deum Nulla siquidem in praesenti schismate potest serpere deterior labes, quam inertia quaerendi pacem. siue illa proueniat ex ambitione, vel adulatione, vel timore, aut alia occupatione non admittente curam hanc salubriorem:
units.tr: Anyone capable of reason is bound, according to his calling, to procure a saving peace for the Church: one by praying, another by disputing, another by preaching, another by exhorting, another by acting, or in some other way. Arguments for this consideration may be drawn from the root of filial duty to the Church, from the root of love and justice towards our neighbour, and from the root of piety or religion towards God. For indeed, in the present schism no worse plague can creep in than the sloth of not seeking peace, whether that sloth arises from ambition, flattery, or fear, or from some other preoccupation that does not allow this more wholesome care:

units.la: Pectora nostra duas non admittentia curas,
units.tr: Our breasts, which do not admit two cares,

units.la: ait Satyricus. Audiamus a sapiente quid pigricies stulta operatur in agro vel vinea ecclesiae? Per agrum, inquit, viri pigri transiui, & per vineam viri stulti: & ecce totum repleuerant urtica: & operuerant faciem eius spina: & materia lapidum destructa erat.
units.tr: says the satirist. Let us hear from the wise man what foolish laziness does in the field or the vineyard of the Church. "I passed by the field of the slothful man, and by the vineyard of the foolish man; and behold, it was all grown over with nettles, and thorns had covered its face, and the stone wall was broken down." I went by the field of the slothful, and by the vineyard of the man void of understanding; and lo, it was all grown over with thorns, nettles had covered its face, and the stone wall was broken down. (Prov. 24.)

units.la: Quod si pestiferum est & maledictioni proximum negligere opus hoc diuinum, quam criminosum est, quam nephatium laborantibus non applaudere, sed irasci?
units.tr: If it is pestilent, and close to a curse, to neglect this divine work, how criminal it is not to applaud those who labour for it, but to be angry with them!

units.la: Propterea stat aliquem adhaerentem iustae parti plus esse de schismate culpabilem, quam alterum qui adhaeret parti falsae: vt si primus aliqua passione vitiosa tractus obsistat quo minus fiat pax, ne audire paratus sit ecclesiam. Alius quaerit cum omni sollicitudine vias pacis, promptum habens animum obediendi ecclesiae iudicio seu veritati dum sibi clarescceret. Ea namque quae dissensionem afferunt in praesenti schismate sunt talia quae in facto maxime consistunt: in quibus errare sine periculo salutis potest non solum iste vel ille: sed etiam in talibus ecclesia fallere dicitur & falli, sicut dum multo tempore foeminam pro papa coluit.
units.tr: Therefore it is established that one who adheres to the just party is more guilty of schism than another who adheres to the false party, if the first, drawn by some vicious passion, stands in the way so that peace is not made, and is unwilling to hear the Church; whereas the other seeks the ways of peace with all care, having a mind ready to obey the judgement of the Church, or the truth, as soon as it becomes clear to him. For the matters that cause dissension in the present schism are of a kind that consists chiefly in fact, in which not only this or that man may err without danger to salvation, but the Church too is said to deceive and to be deceived, as when for a long time it honoured a woman as pope.

units.la: Porro manifestari potest ex radice hac quales excusantur a vitio schismatis. Et quod stat scire, quod schisma est in ecclesia: & tamen nescire quis in ea sit schismaticus. Ex hoc consequenter aperitur, quales sunt anathematizandi & vitandi, & quales non. Nam velle omnes indifferenter partis falsae extra ecclesiam & salutem trudere: quale sit iam tetigimus.
units.tr: Furthermore, it can be shown from this root who are excused from the fault of schism: namely, that it is one thing to know that there is a schism in the Church, and yet not to know who in it is the schismatic. From this it follows, in turn, who are to be anathematized and avoided, and who are not. For to wish indiscriminately to thrust all of the false party outside the Church and salvation is something we have already touched upon, and what sort of thing it is.

units.la: His ex rebus perspicuum fit deinceps, quanta laude, quibus praeconiorum titulis, commendanda redditur partis nostrae diligentia: praesertim in inclitissimo Franciae regno: & quantum a schismatis obstinatione procul exstat: vbi quaesita est hactenus pax salutifera tanto labore, tot expensis, tot legationibus, assiduisque consiliis. Necesse est quod aliquis opponat quasdam vel zizanias vel paleas malarum actionum in quibusdam ortas inter hanc virtuosae operationis segetem: vel quod non satis efficaciter diligentia respondit ad votum. Ascribatur hoc humanae fragilitati. Raro enim nascitur granum virtutis sine palea aliqua defectuositatis. Nihilominus habet profecto plus veracis laudis zelus ille diligens, quam aliorum negligens torpor: quoniam schisma si dimittitur absque agitatione, proferet radices malas altius & ineuulsibiles, & productas roborabit.
