units.tr: From these considerations it becomes clear, in consequence, with what praise, and with what titles of commendation, the diligence of our party is rendered worthy of commendation, especially in the most famous kingdom of France; and how far it stands from the obstinacy of schism, where a saving peace has so far been sought with such labour, so many expenses, so many embassies and unceasing counsels. It must be that someone objects that some tares or chaff of bad actions have sprung up among this crop of virtuous work, or that the diligence has not responded to the desire with sufficient efficacy. Let this be ascribed to human frailty. For rarely is the grain of virtue born without some chaff of defect. Nevertheless that diligent zeal certainly has more of true praise than the negligent torpor of others, since if schism is allowed to continue without stirring, it will send its evil roots deeper and more firmly, and, once grown, will strengthen them.

units.la: Nam mala per longas conualuere moras.
units.tr: For evils grow strong through long delays.

units.la: Docet nos schisma Graecorum, quod iam non curatur, nemo non desperat. Quo in loco grandis offertur ad loquendum materia super laudibus Parisiensis Vniuersitatis praeclarissimae studiorum super zelo feruido ipsius: quae non cessauit hactenus eniti pedibus, vt dicitur, & manibus: aliter quam desides aliqui & inutiles, qui facere nihil volunt vel nesciunt, obstrepunt tamen facientibus, solis cotumeliis fortes & armati. Sed silentium imperat, tum benignitas, tum modestia, ne in eius laude videamur propriam quaerere. Ecce autem quis est qui non dicat, qui non clamet: pax, pax: fiat pax, pacem volo, pacem super omnia concupisco. At vero nonne irridetur Deus? quoniam simile est pacem non velle: & illam vel inutiliter & desidiose velle, vel impossibiliter velle: hoc est mediis ad eam impossibilibus contendere: vt si quaeratur vnio aliqualiter, qualiter haberi non valet, neque via debellationis, neque via rationis seu reductionis, neque via anathematizationis seu separationis, neque via condescensionis, aut similiter. Cum itaque pastor teneatur non minus reuocare oues, quas iudicat errantes, quam seruare non errantes: nonne debet vt fiat vnum ouile modum possibilem & verisimilem hoc agendi vel prosequi, etiam cum dimissione gregis proprii & obedientis, si per hoc seruatur & vnitur grex vterque? Nec est hoc deserere gregem more mercenarii & fugere, sed saluare: & vt vere sic dicamus fugiendo manere. Sed haec cessio dicit aliquis fieret perniciosum posteris exemplum? fatemur id posse contingere: nam quibus rebus non contingit abuti? attamen pro incerto malorum euentu, non esset iam certum & optandum praesentis pacis bonum repudiandum vel negandum.
units.tr: The schism of the Greeks, which is now neglected, teaches us that no one fails to despair. Here a great opportunity arises to speak of the praises of the most famous University of Paris and of its fervent zeal, which has not ceased to strive, as the saying goes, with feet and hands. Some idlers and useless people, who want or know how to do nothing, carp at those who act, bold and armed only with insults, unlike them. But silence is commanded, both by kindness and by modesty, lest in praising it we seem to seek our own glory. Yet who does not say, who does not cry out: peace, peace; let there be peace; I want peace, I desire peace above all things? But is God not mocked? For it is much the same not to wish for peace at all as to wish for it uselessly and idly, or to wish for it impossibly, that is, to strive after it by means that cannot lead to it. If union is sought in some way that cannot be achieved, whether by the way of war, or by the way of reasoning or reconciliation, or by the way of anathema or separation, or by the way of condescension, or the like, it is futile. Since, then, a minister is bound no less to call back the sheep he judges to be straying than to keep those who have not strayed, ought he not to seek one fold by a possible and probable method of acting or proceeding, even with the loss of his own obedient flock, if by this both flocks are saved and united? Nor is this to abandon the flock like a hireling and flee, but to save it; and, to speak truly, by fleeing to remain. But someone will say that this concession would set a harmful example for posterity. We admit that this may happen, for what things cannot be abused? Yet, because the outcome of evils is uncertain, the certain and desirable good of present peace ought not therefore to be rejected or denied.

units.la: CONSIDERATIO IV.
units.tr: Consideration IV.

units.la: Tantum est pacis salutiferae bonum, vt pro eius adeptione neque mundanus honos, neque status, neque gradus, neque propria vtilitas debeant aliquem deterrere, & nihil prorsus nisi peccatum contra legem Dei aeternam. Haec consideratio posita est contra illos qui dicunt: Obseruetur honor partis nostrae: habeamus victoriam: confusionem euitemus. Ecce qualia sustinuit opprobria summus pontifex Christus, vt faceret vtraque vnum: reconcilians in suo sanguine ea, quae in coelo sunt & in terra: factus opprobrium hominum & abiectio plebis, & non dicens: seruetur honor meus. Sufficiebat ei testimonium bonum conscientiae apud Deum. Igitur vt pax habeatur, nulla plane via repudianda est, quae potest absque peccato deduci: & quanto breuius, tanto salubrius: quanto insuper patentius, tanto acceptius apud omnes: quoniam res tangit omnes, & veritas lucem amat. Quocirca viae per Dominum nostrum oblatae (proferam hoc sine adulationis oleo, quo non indiget, & salua pace omnium) quia nunquam mihi viae sunt iuri diuino palam contraire, nunquam viae sunt similiter penitus reprobandae: nisi forte struatur calumnia ex iuramento suo, & ex totius obeobedientiæ suæ consensu, iudicio & requestis aliorum tendentibus. Propterea rursus non improbabile videtur attentis circumstantiis offerentibus se in præsenti schismate: si pars iusta possit à iuris sui prosecutione desistere, ut ad iniustam ius suum transferret & fieret iusta: seu per novam electionem intrusi: seu per aliam viam in iure scripto non habitam: dummodo ius diuinum vtrobique inviolatum maneret, & hæc via propter timorem inhonorationis mundanæ non esset penitus abhorrenda. Nam quicquid à maleuolis interpretibus diceretur, desuper resideret inspector cordium Deus, & iudex veritas & charitas abunde remunerans. Nonne laudata, nonne victrix effecta est mater illa vera infantis apud Salomonem: quæ filium maluit integrum abiicere, illoque carere, quam diuisus in suam cederet portionem? Denique in laude Q. Fabii Maximi præclarissimam dixit Ennius: quod
units.tr: So great is the good of saving peace that for its attainment no worldly honour, status, rank, or private advantage should deter anyone, and nothing at all except sin against the eternal law of God. This consideration is set against those who say: "Let the honour of our party be preserved, let us have the victory, let us avoid confusion." Behold what reproaches Christ, the supreme high priest, endured, so that he might make both one, reconciling in his own blood the things in heaven and the things on earth; he was made the reproach of men and the outcast of the people, and did not say, "Let my honour be preserved." It was enough for him to have the good testimony of a conscience before God. Therefore, if peace is to be had, no way that can be followed without sin should be rejected; and the shorter the way, the more wholesome it is, and the more open it is, the more acceptable it is to all, since the matter touches everyone and truth loves the light. Accordingly, the ways offered through our Lord (I will say this without the oil of flattery, which it does not need, and with the peace of all preserved) are never to be openly opposed to divine law, and are likewise never to be wholly condemned, unless perhaps a calumny is built upon his oath, upon the consent of his whole obedience, and upon the judgements and requests of others that tend in that direction. Therefore, again, it does not seem unreasonable, given the circumstances that present themselves in the present schism, that if the just party could desist from pursuing its right, so that its right would pass to the unjust party and that party would become just, whether by a new election of an intruder or by some other way not found in the written law, provided that divine law remained inviolate on both sides, and provided that this way is not wholly to be shunned out of fear of worldly dishonour, then it should be considered. For whatever malicious interpreters might say, God, the inspector of hearts, sits above, and truth and charity, the judges, will reward abundantly. Was not that true mother in Solomon praised and made victorious, who preferred to give up her son whole and to be without him, rather than that he be divided and fall to her share? Finally, in praise of Quintus Fabius Maximus, Ennius said most admirably:

units.la: Non ponebat rumores ante salutem.
units.tr: He did not put rumours before safety.

units.la: Nonne sanctius est vltro dare gratiæ, dari charitati fraternæ, & pacî honorem suum caducum: imo vitam propriam cum merito, quam sine laude & pace mox naturalis necessitas vtrumque diripiat? Concedatur ergo libenter gratiæ id quod velit, nolit obtinens; protinus relinquetur naturæ. Amplius non videtur improbabile, quin expediat in casu ecclesiam ad tempus summo pastore carere: vt interim per tractum vel aliter adeptio pacis celerior haberetur. Quod si canones oppositum sanxerunt, lex diuina non dissonat. Nam ex dicto potest absque papa mortali stare salus. Quod si timetur infamatio partis illius vel illius, iam responsum posuimus. Consequenter deducimus, quod propter timorem succumbendi aut inhonorationis humanæ, quæ vtique vitiosa non sunt, concilium generale vniuersalis ecclesiæ non videtur repudiandum: sed pium est credere, quod in tractatione præsentis materiæ non erraret. Audiamus rationem: constat itaque quod in materiis fidei terminandis error non cadit in generali concilio. Rationem dant Doctores ex speciali assistentia Spiritus sancti & Christi regentis ecclesiam: nec permittentis errare in his, ad quæ humana inuestigatio peruenire non potest. Secus in his, quæ vel facti sunt, vel humana ratione terminari possunt. Nunc autem schisma præsens quanquam in his quæ facti sunt plurimum hæreat, eius nihilominus terminatio tam perplexa cernitur, tamque difficilis, vt supra hominum vires, ingenia, inuentiones & consilia videatur. Vbi vero deest humanum, potest & debet absque temeritate diuinum auxilium etiam miraculosum expectari. Ita enim de sortibus mittendis in casu determinat Augustinus dum sequentibus tyrannis inquiritur quis de multis prælatis pro gregis salute remanebit, qui recedent? Nonne igitur absque periculo causa illa committi Deo & vniuersali concilio posset absque formidine, quam maior pars vinceret, si esset iniustior: & maxime in perniciem ecclesiæ, quod addo: quoniam in casu communis error faceret ius: præsertim error facti vel ex facto ortum habens. Auxilium tale miraculosum nonne in bello corporali Iudas Machabæus, nonne Moyses, nonne fidelium alii taliter expectauerunt, quando persequebatur vnus mille, & duo fugabant decem millia? quanto securiori fide pro hoc schismate finiendo potest in opitulationis diuinæ assistentia speciali per tractatum vniuersalis concilii spes haberi. Et quis obsecro tantæ præsumptionis inueniri poterit, vt determinatis per tot viros celeberrimos, propriam opinionem vel præferret, vel eorum dictamen non imitaretur? Pium quoque sentire est, vt non nisi viam mediam, viam pacificam, & vtrobique honorabilem sententiam teneat concilium. Nec tamen ignoro multas circa hæc & alia suboriri difficultatum nebulas. Sed eas omnes lux diuinæ legis suis radiis facilitet eiiceret: si non vltra ceruicosa contradicendi libido obstiterit. Si oculos rationis neque segnities inquirendi claauserit, neque ruditas obtuderit, neq; eos lippitudo carnalitatis, neque curarum puluis, neque fumus præsumptionis suffoderit, neque postremo malitia cæcauerit: quo minus apparere possit gratia Dei saluatoris nostri. Ita studiositas per zelum stimulata pergebat in longius. Cuius ego sermonem interrumpens & finiens exclamaui: Appareat tandem aliquando gratia tua, vt post illustrationem synceram & agenda videamus: & ad ea quæ vidimus implenda conualescamus. Res quippe in obscuro nimis demersa est, nam & nobis caliginet, puluereseque difficultatum ambulando sponte suscitamus. Deest insuper apud multos gratia humani concilii: quæ simul apparere & cooperare debuerat gratiæ Dei. Obfuscat eam præterea vel abscondit amor proprius quærens quæ sua sunt: & incircumciso corde ambulans post desideria carnalia atque seculària: neque sobrie, neque iuste, neque pie viuens in hoc seculo: quasi non expectaret beatam illam spem, quæ sola desideranda est, sola velut encenium diuinæ gratiæ iugiter postulanda. Prouideat meliora vicinioraque saluti gratia eadem Dei & Saluatoris nostri: hic nos iustificans, glorificans in futuro.
units.tr: Is it not holier to give freely to grace, to give to fraternal charity, and to give one's own fleeting honour to peace; indeed, one's own life along with merit, which natural necessity will soon snatch away from both, without praise and without peace? Let us therefore willingly concede to grace whatever it wishes, obtaining what it wills whether one wishes it or not; it will be left to nature at once. Further, it does not seem unreasonable that in such a case it might be expedient for the Church to be without a supreme pastor for a time, so that meanwhile the attainment of peace might be achieved more quickly, whether by an agreed arrangement or otherwise. But if the canons have decreed the opposite, divine law does not disagree; for according to the saying, salvation can stand without a pope. As for the fear that the reputation of this or that party might be damaged, we have already given an answer. Consequently we deduce that, because of fear of defeat or of human dishonour, which are certainly not vicious, a general council of the universal Church does not seem to be rejected; rather, it is pious to believe that in handling the present matter it would not err. Let us hear the reason: it is established that in determining matters of faith, error does not fall into a general council. The Doctors give as the reason the special assistance of the Holy Spirit and of Christ governing the Church, who does not permit it to err in those things to which human inquiry cannot attain. It is otherwise in matters that are merely of fact, or that can be settled by human reason. Now, although the present schism clings very much to matters of fact, its settlement nevertheless appears so perplexed and so difficult that it seems to lie beyond human strength, abilities, inventions and counsels. But where the human fails, divine help, even miraculous help, can and should be awaited without rashness. For so Augustine determines concerning the casting of lots in a case where, with tyrants following, it is asked which of many prelates will remain for the salvation of the flock and which will withdraw. Could not that cause then be entrusted to God and to a universal council without danger, and without the fear that the greater part would prevail even if it were the more unjust, and especially to the ruin of the Church, which I add: since in such a case a common error would make right, especially an error of fact or one arising from a fact? Did not Judas Maccabaeus, Moses, and other faithful men look for such miraculous help in corporal war, when one pursued a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight? With how much surer faith may hope be had, for ending this schism, through the special assistance of divine help by means of the deliberation of a universal council. And who, I ask, could be found of such presumption that he would either prefer his own opinion to what has been determined by so many most celebrated men, or would not imitate their judgement? It is also pious to think that the council should hold to no other course than the middle way, the peaceful way, and a judgement honourable to both sides. Nor do I ignore that many clouds of difficulties arise concerning these and other matters. But the light of divine law would dispel all of them with its rays, if the stubborn lust for contradiction did not stand in the way. If neither sluggishness in inquiring has closed the eyes of reason, nor dullness has dulled them, nor the blear of fleshliness, nor the dust of cares, nor the smoke of presumption has blinded them, and finally malice has not made them blind, so that the grace of God our Saviour cannot appear. Thus zeal, spurring on the eagerness of the discussion, went further. Interrupting and ending his speech, I cried out: "Let your grace at last appear, so that after sincere enlightenment we may see what is to be done, and gain strength to fulfil what we have seen. For the matter has been plunged too deeply into obscurity: it casts a mist over us, and as we walk we stir up the dust of difficulties of our own accord. Moreover, among many the grace of a human council is lacking, which ought to have appeared and co-operated together with the grace of God. Furthermore, self-love seeking its own things obscures or hides it, and so does a man who walks with an uncircumcised heart after carnal and worldly desires, living neither soberly, nor justly, nor piously in this world, as though he did not await that blessed hope, which alone is to be desired, which alone is to be constantly sought as the reward of divine grace. May that same grace of God and our Saviour provide better things, and things nearer to salvation: here justifying us, and in the future glorifying us."

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: EPISTOLA EIVSDEM AD DO- MINVM AVRELIANENSEM DE s- ermone præcedente.
units.tr: The same author's letter to the Lord of Orléans, concerning the preceding sermon.

units.la: SErenissimo Principi & militi regis poli Domino Aurelianensi suus Ioannes Cancellarius ecclesiæ Parisiensis indignus, obsequium humile, pacisque præsentis cum æterna donum fœliciter adipisci. Multa hactenus scripsi, strenuissime Domine. Plurima dixi, quæ ad ecclesiasticam pacem vtilia videbantur: prosequens pacem exultantem latratu quo potui: ego de genere catulus, offerens insuper pro virili portione ad opus tabernaculi Dei cum hominibus, ea quæ de manu sua videbar suscepisse. Nec ignoro posse ea à tot capitibus in varias facile traduci sententias, & forsan aduersas: quæ tamen omnia si cum distinctione temporum, circumstantiarum quoque sese offerentium multiplicitate pensari digna fuerint: arbitror ea inuenturis nexu concordi veritatis inter se iuncta esse: vtpote quæ circa idem centrum eundemque cardinem pii desiderii volebantur. Viam itaque cessionis bene practicatam ego breuissimam & optimam censui: iudicans ad eius receptionem secundum præparationem animi ambos contendentes de papatu iure diuino constrictos. Nec erat quod allegarent coactionem. Vellent itaque, cogebat nemo. Porro in conclusione subtractionis non affui: quam tamen conclusam impugnare pertinaci animositate non præsumpsi. Sed postquam Dominus noster Benedictus viam cessionis, & alia quæ petebant accommoda pro pace & reformatione ecclesiæ dictus est acceptasse: opponit se paruitas mea cum odiis & discriminibus non modicis, vt ipse neque papatum de facto irreuersibilem amisisse: neque hæreticus aut schismaticus iudicando esse causaretur. Placuit quoque restitutio: quam & prædicaui coram celeberrimo cœtu Apostolicorum. Per hanc itaque ab ea natura secum vnita, portum pacis generalis attingere facilius sperabatur. Denique non tam missus quam coactus Legatus, ad Dominum nostrum super hac materia pro parte Vniuersitatis præclarissimæ studiorum, cui ego filius negare potui nihil, proposui primo Massiliæ, de hinc Tarasconæ sermonem hunc, quem decorus præsentiæ vestræ nobilissimæ fulgor illustrauit. Hunc sermonem, sicut & præsentem propositionem, postulare dignata est celsitudo vestra ab ex guitate mea, qualis autem ego sum, vt vel hoc vel aliud quippiam denegare præsumpletrim? Accipite itaque sermonem qualiscunque ille est: vbi aliqua, sed pauca ex dictatis in margine posita sunt: quæ breuitas præceps eripuit ne proferrem. Bene valeat præclara dominatio vestra ad communem pacem & propriam salutem consequendam. Scriptum Tarasconæ Anno Domini, 1403. in vigilia Epiphaniæ.
units.tr: To the most serene Prince and soldier of the King of Heaven, the Lord of Orléans, his John, Chancellor of the Church of Paris, though unworthy, offers humble obedience and prays that he may happily obtain the gift of peace in the present life together with peace that is eternal. Most vigorous Lord, I have written much hitherto and said very much that seemed useful for the peace of the Church. In pursuing that peace, I have barked as loudly as I could, being a puppy by birth, and I have also offered, for my own part, to the work of God's tabernacle among men, those things which I seemed to have received from his hand. I am not unaware that these things can easily be turned by many minds into various opinions, and perhaps opposing ones. Yet if all of them are weighed with due regard to the differences of times and to the variety of circumstances that present themselves, I believe they will be found to be joined together by a harmonious bond of truth, since they all aimed at the same centre and the same hinge of a devout desire. Accordingly, I judged the way of resignation, well trodden, to be the shortest and best, reckoning that both contending parties, who were bound by the papacy by divine right, would accept it if their minds were prepared. Nor had they any reason to plead compulsion: let them will it, for no one was forcing them. Moreover, I was not present at the conclusion of the withdrawal, yet I did not presume to oppose what had been concluded with stubborn hostility. But after our Lord Benedict was said to have accepted the way of resignation and the other measures they sought, suitable for peace and the reform of the Church, my littleness has stood in opposition, with no small hatreds and dangers, so that he could neither be charged with having in fact lost the papacy irreversibly, nor with being judged a heretic or schismatic. The restitution also pleased me, and I preached it before a most distinguished assembly of the Apostolic men. By this, joined to that nature, it was hoped that we might more easily reach the harbour of general peace. Finally, I was sent, or rather compelled, as legate to our Lord on this matter on behalf of the most distinguished University of Studies, to which I, a son, could refuse nothing. First at Marseille, and afterwards at Tarascon, I set forth this sermon, which the noble splendour of your presence adorned. Your Highness has deigned to request this sermon, as also the present proposal, from my insignificance; and what sort of man am I, that I should presume to deny this or anything else? Accept, then, the sermon in whatever form it is, in which some few notes placed in the margin from the dictated text are included, which the haste of the speaking tore from me so that I could not publish them. May your illustrious lordship fare well, in order to obtain the common peace and your own salvation. Written at Tarascon in the year of the Lord 1403, on the vigil of the Epiphany.

units.la: EPISTOLA DOMINO CA- MERACENSI EXISTENTI IN CVRIA.
units.tr: EPISTLE TO THE LORD OF CAMBRAI, BEING IN THE COURT.

units.la: DEcreueram, Reuerende pater & præceptor singularis, accuratius si vacasset per dictata quædam scribere, conquesturus de sinistra vel interpretatione vel relatione dictorum: imo plurium non dictorum in sermone Circumcisionis habito Tarasconæ coram Domino nostro, tempore legationis meæ pro parte almæ Vniuersitatis Parisiensis matris meæ. Experior itaque veram esse Comici sententiam: nihil esse quin male narrando possit deteriorari. Hanc ego esse vnam ex maximis difficultatibus æstimo: quæ reddunt officium prædicationis onerosissimum: quas difficultates atque discrimina Gregor. & Chrysostom. quilibet in suo pastorali: & Augustin. 4. de doct. Christiana copiosissime narrauerunt. Fit enim plerumque (loquor centies expertus) vt potentes in sermone aliquo non solum depravent bene dicta, sed ea quæ nullo modo dicta sunt, constanter affirment pro prolatis. Stultorum quidem infinitus est numerus. Est tamen sapientis assertio: Stultus non capit verba prudentiæ, nisi ea dixeris quæ versantur in corde suo. Verum quoque est dictum Apulei: multos esse qui solis auribus corporis philosophantur: intellectum vero vel nullum habent: vel illum variant pro varietate passionum & affectionum: quemadmodum in sonitu campanarum sumimus argumentum. Dicunt enim (vt vulgari more loquar) quod volumus. Porro mihi conscius sum, nihil protulisse tunc quod non esset sacræ fidei, monitisque salubribus accommodam, & examinata veritate stabilitum. Nihilominus quot, bone Iesu, super eodem sermone mihi relata sunt, quæ nedum non dixeram, sed nec cogitaueram. Quot peruerse capta & peruersius impugnata audacter asserere quosdam postmodum potentes: viderint ipsi quo studio vel contradicendi vel vane complacendi, seu zelo vel ignorantia moti, quæsisse veritates per me positas impugnare, & per rationes palam erroneas: sed nolo sequi relationes solas hominum in tanto negotio defendendæ veritatis: ne pugnemus, vt dicitur, in tenebris. Habuisset igitur dictorum meorum formam propriam & limitamitationem, adeo vt transpositio saepe vel omissio vnius vocabuli sententiam variasset. Habuissent, in quam, formam ipsam: habuissem viceversa solide quae dixissent: nunquam refugissem pro veritatis defensione congredi, sed quid agerem? nihil obiectum est quod sciverim dum essem praesens: potenseque verbotenus respondere: sed longo postmodum intervallo me absente & surdo, vocibus eorum plurima variaque in oppositum dicta praedicataque, ego solis rumoribus accepi: quibus cur non magno conatu respondere parauerim, iam expressi. Nouissime autem hesterno vespere scripsit vnus ex amicis fidelissimis le audisse ab Astero, qui similiter audierat ab aliis gravibus (vt dicebat) viris: me dixisse inter caetera: quod homine in articulo mortis existente, quilibet sacerdos habet aequalem potestatem cum papa in indulgentiis dandis a poena & culpa. Hanc vero assertionem certissimus sum nec sensisse nec dixisse: quanquam si de potestate ordinis in casu necessitatis fieret locutio: scitum est satis, quid Doctores sententiant. Denique quid dixerim, unde error talis potuerit in aliquibus parum forsan aduertentibus ad verborum formam elici. Pono diffusiori sermone in chartula colligata in praesentibus. Tu praeceptor sapientissime, coram tuis oculis totus palam sum tibi intus & in cute notus. Digneris accipere baculum defensionis meae in hoc articulo: quo apprehenso voces oppositas (si ita dignum visum fuerit) valeas compescere. Postremo totum ipsum sermonem, quem hactenus reconditum absque multiplicatione in alias manus habui mittere (si ita censueris) paratus sum intentione talis finis. Det Dominus ipse bene valere iugiter in Domino ad consecutionem beatae spei, & ad visionem celerius remeandam in regionem ecclesiae sanctae Dei.
units.tr: I had decided, Reverend Father and singular teacher, to write out in more detail, if I had had the leisure, some dictated notes, complaining of the wrong interpretation and reporting of what was said, or rather of the many things that were not said, in the sermon on the Circumcision that I preached at Tarascon before our Lord, during my embassy on behalf of the gracious University of Paris, my mother. I find, then, that the saying of the comic poet is true: nothing can be so good that it cannot be made worse by bad telling. I judge this to be one of the greatest difficulties that make the office of preaching most burdensome, and Gregory and Chrysostom in their works on the pastoral office, and Augustine in Book 4 of On Christian Doctrine, have described these difficulties and perils very fully. For it very often happens (I speak from a hundred experiences) that powerful men not only distort what was well said, but firmly assert as spoken things that were never said at all. Of fools there is indeed an endless number. Yet the saying of the wise man is true: A fool does not grasp the words of prudence, unless you speak those things that lie in his own heart. And the saying of Apuleius is also true: there are many who philosophise only with the ears of the body, and have no understanding at all, or they vary their understanding according to the variety of their passions and affections, as we take a comparison from the sound of bells. For they say (to speak in the common way) what they wish. Moreover, I am conscious to myself that I then put forward nothing that was not consonant with sacred faith and with wholesome admonitions, and that had not been established by examined truth. Nevertheless, good Jesus, how many things have been reported to me about that same sermon, which I not only had not said but had not even thought! How many things, taken perversely and attacked more perversely, have some powerful men since then boldly asserted! Let them themselves see with what zeal, moved either by a wish to contradict or by a vain desire to please, or by ignorance, they have sought to attack the truths I laid down, and to do so by reasoning that is plainly erroneous. But I do not wish to follow the reports of men alone in so great a matter as the defence of truth, lest we fight, as they say, in the dark. My own words would therefore have had their proper form and limit, so that a transposition or the omission of a single word would often have altered the meaning. They would have had that form itself, and conversely I would have had what they said solidly; I would never have shrunk from engaging in the defence of truth. But what was I to do? Nothing was put to me that I knew of while I was present, and I was able to answer on the spot. But after a long interval, while I was absent and deaf, I learned from mere rumours the many and various things said and proclaimed in opposition by their voices; why I did not prepare to answer them with great effort, I have already explained. Most recently, however, last evening, one of my most faithful friends wrote that he had heard from Asterus, who had likewise heard from other grave men (as he said), that I had said, among other things, that when a man is in the article of death, any priest has equal power with the pope to grant indulgences from penalty and from guilt. I am most certain that I neither thought nor said this assertion; although if the discussion had been about the power of orders in a case of necessity, it is well enough known what the Doctors hold. Finally, I have set out in a more extended discussion, in the little paper attached to the present letter, what I did say, and whence such an error could be drawn, in the wording, by some who perhaps paid little attention. You, most wise teacher, see me before your eyes; I am known to you inside and out. Please accept the staff of my defence in this matter, by which, once you have taken hold of it, you may be able to check the opposing voices (if it seems fit to you). Lastly, I am ready, if you so advise, to send the whole of that sermon, which I have so far kept hidden, to other hands without making copies, for the sake of such an end. May the Lord himself grant that you always fare well in the Lord, to the attaining of the blessed hope, and to a speedier return to the realm of the holy Church of God.

units.la: SERMO FACTVS CORAM ALEXANDRO PAPA PER MAGISTRVM IOANNEM DE GERSON, CANCELLARIVM PARISIENSEM, IN die Ascensionis Domini.
units.tr: SERMON DELIVERED BEFORE POPE ALEXANDER BY MASTER JOHN GERSON, CHANCELLOR OF PARIS, ON THE DAY OF THE LORD'S ASCENSION.

units.la: ADIVVA REX COELESTIS, ET TV REGINA genetrix Virgo pauperem & inopem de regno Israelitico locuturum.
units.tr: Help me, heavenly King, and you, Queen and Mother, Virgin, that I, poor and needy, may speak about the kingdom of Israel.

units.la: Domine si in tempore hoc restitues regnum Israel? Originaliter Actor. 1. cap. & recitatiue in epistola praesentis festiuitatis.
units.tr: Lord, wilt thou at this time restore the kingdom to Israel? Literally in Acts 1, and recited in the epistle for this feast.

units.la: Non sum nescius, beatissime Pater, vosque Cardinales orbis terrarum, & caeteri Domini sapientia clara fulgentes, me subire sermonis onus prorsus impar exiguis viribus. Idcirco pulsabo ianuas deuote regis coelestis, vt imperfectum meum suppleat: humili det gratiam: linguam infantis faciat disertam. Et quo facilius exaudiar, oretur pariter eius pia genitrix, illique salutatio praesentetur angelica: Aue gratia plena &c.
units.tr: I am not unaware, most blessed Father, and you, Cardinals of the world, and the other men shining bright with wisdom, that I take on a burden of speech far beyond my meagre strength. So I will knock at the doors of the devout heavenly King, that he may supply what is lacking in me, give grace to the humble, and make the tongue of an infant eloquent. And so that I may be heard more readily, let his loving mother be asked to pray with me, and let the angelic greeting be offered to her: Hail, full of grace, etc.

units.la: Domine si in tempore hoc &c. Quaesierunt hoc Apostoli ab ascendente Domino: eisdem quidem verbis, sed sensu vario: qua varietate brevitatis studio praeterita: quoniam duplex est regnum Israel, hoc est videntium Deum, alterum coeleste triumphantis ecclesiae, cuius cives Deum vident per speciem; alterum terrestre militantis, cuius cives Deum intuentur per fidem. Dicam primum quomodo coelestis: deinde terreni ruinas ascensio Dominica hodie restituerit. Hanc mihi partitionem non meus sensus, sed diuinus contulit Apostolus. A quo scriptum memini Deum patrem proposuisse in dispensatione plenitudinis temporum instaurare omnia in Christo, quae in coelis & in terra sunt. Ecce me docet Apostolus tuus vas electionis tuae Domine Iesu: quae tibi respondere licuerit quaerentibus discipulis, Domine si in tempore hoc &c. Nam si per te essent instauranda, quae sunt in coelis, vti affirmare illum perspicio, quid tibi leuius quam hanc illis veritatem respondere propterea scandere coelos, vt ciuitatem diminutam, & magna parte sua per scelus orbatam turpe reintegrantes. Ipsa malorum omnium prima parens superbia, Luciferum illum, qui mane oriebatur, cum tertia stellarum parte traxit ad tenebrosum occasum. Et quis crederet non inde regni supernicaritatem obumbratam? Tollite ex hoc coelo visibili Luciferum, & cum eo tertiam partem stellarum: cui dubium est noctes obscuriores futuras? Quis nesciat imperfectam remansisse sanctorum angelorum societatem suo numero diminuto? Quis in dubium vocabit corpus ciuitatis istius praestantissimorum membrorum auulsione laesionem, & integritatem pulcherrimam amisisse? Nullus opinor. Ergo claudicabit sanctorum gloria, nec Dei ciuitas de sui integritate laetabitur. Si natura tanto tempore vacuum insectetur, & sic exhorrescat: quo pacto supernas sedes vacuas oculis aequis aspiciet sanctorum gloria? Denique gaudent angeli ad poenitentiam peccatorum. Quod si gaudium ingerant oculis lachrymae meae, quid delitiae meae? Et si delitiae meae gaudium sit angelorum: quomodo magis fuisset eorum qui ceciderunt permansio? At illud ciuitati coelesti deest. Fuisset igitur aliqua sanctorum iucunditas stantibus angelis, quae ruentibus sublata est. Ergo, inquies, confirmati spiritus caeterorum ruinam moesti deplorauerunt: & qua parte beatorum ciuitatem luctus ingrederctur: non dico fleuisse, non moestos, non tristes extitisse: viderunt culpam peccantium: non inde laetari sunt propter charitatem, neque contristati propter confirmationem. Viderunt deinde poenam, & laetati sunt iusti videndo vindictam: atque ad deiectionem impiorum affuerunt conditori. Etenim Michael & angeli eius praeliati sunt cum dracone: & putas victoria potitos non inde sumpsisse gaudium? Sed aliud est aliquam deesse laetitiam imperfectae ciuitati, aliud tristitiam admittere. Nonne vides delectationes ipsas intellectu purissimas & contrarietate carentes, cum adsunt, laetificare: cum absunt, non contristare. Accessit ad mali cumulum, quod ea superbia, quae conceperat in coelis dolorem, in Paradiso terrestri peperit iniquitatem: quando per invidiam indignata carnem eo viliorem ascendere, unde praestantior spiritus corruerat: homini condito ad replendas sedes in coelos vacuefactas, in serpente dirum virus aspersit. Sic enim invidia mors intrauit in orbem terrarum: quamuis initium extiterit omnis peccati superbia. Ita ex omni parte optatae restitutioni supernae ciuitatis malignus obuiabat. Attamen spes eum fefellit: restituta est, imo & amplificata dignitate. Cecidit Lucifer per superbiam: ascendit alius Lucifer per humilitatem. Inuectae tenebrae per occasum primi, purgatae fuerunt per ortum secundi. Ille minuit sanctorum numerum: iste restauravit & amplificauit diminutum. Ille regni violauit integritatem, iste violatam reparauit. Ille in coelo sedes vacuefecit, iste nouis laudatoribus vacuefactas adimpleuit. Ille multos ex angelis exemplo malo traxit in praeceps: iste plurimos homines iustificatos tanquam centesimam ouem prius errantem propriis humeris reportauit in coelos. Iste ex omni parte Sathan deluditur: nec enim in coelos reascendere potuit, unde tanquam fulgur ceciderat, hoc est, furoris impetu fuerat praecipitatus: & ascensum, quem homini, atque restitutionem quam inuidit ciuitati, nullatenus impedire praevaluit. Verum gladio suo manu potentioris erepto iugulatur: & dum intentione corrupta ab ingressu gloriae nouos ciues prohibere, gloriosumque Dei regnum integritate pulcherrima fraudare satagit: tam ciuibus fabricat coronas, quam nouum dignitate regnum honestat. Lucifer inde cecidit, sol ascendit. Vanitas a coelis eiecta est, veritas in coelo reucta est. Amiserat illa ciuitas creatum angelum, ac recepit creatorem hominem. Unde & hic verum est illud Apostoli: Nonne sicut delicium, ita & donum. Vis etiam audire nouum genus gaudii: quod nisi homo peccasset, ciuitas illa non sensisset? Non vereor ne nimis audacter loqui videar, cum sequar Bernardum autorem: qui non putat Deum nostrum totam habituram gloriae suae laudem, donec veniant qui in conspectu angelorum psallant sibi: Laetati sumus pro diebus quibus nos humiliasti: annis quibus vidimus mala. Hoc genus laetitiae coeli nescierunt, nisi per ecclesiae filios: hoc nemo unquam laetatur, qui non laetatur. Opportune post tristitiam gaudium subit, post laborem quies, post naufragium portus: placet cunctis securitas, sed ei magis qui timuit. Iucunda omnibus lux: sed euadenti de potestate tenebrarum iucundior. Transisse de morte ad vitam vitae gratiam duplat: deest laudi si desunt qui dicant: Transiuimus per ignem & aquam & eduxisti nos in refrigerium.
units.tr: Lord, wilt thou at this time, etc. The Apostles asked this of the Lord as he ascended, in these same words but with a different sense. I have passed over that difference for the sake of brevity. For the kingdom of Israel is twofold: the one heavenly, of the Church triumphant, whose citizens see God face to face; the other earthly, of the Church militant, whose citizens behold God through faith. I shall first say how the heavenly kingdom has been restored, and then how the ruins of the earthly one have been restored today by the Lord's ascension. This division was suggested to me not by my own judgment but by the divine Apostle. I remember that he wrote that God the Father purposed, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, both those in heaven and those on earth. So your Apostle, the chosen vessel of you, Lord Jesus, teaches me what answer you might give to the disciples' question: Lord, wilt thou at this time, etc. For if the things in heaven were to be restored through you, as I clearly see him affirm, what could be easier for you than to answer them with this truth: that you were ascending into heaven precisely in order to repair the diminished city, which had been robbed of a great part of its own members by sin? Pride, the first parent of all evils, drew that Lucifer, who rose in the morning, together with a third part of the stars, down to a dark fall. And who would not believe that the heavenly kingdom was thereby overshadowed? Take Lucifer and the third part of the stars out of this visible heaven: who doubts that the nights will be darker? Who does not know that the society of the holy angels remained incomplete, its number diminished? Who will doubt that the body of that city lost its beautiful wholeness when its most excellent members were torn away? No one, I think. Therefore the glory of the saints would limp, and the city of God would not rejoice in its own completeness. If nature abhors and shudders at a long-empty void, how will the glory of the saints look with untroubled eyes upon the heavenly seats left empty? Finally, the angels rejoice at the repentance of sinners. But if my tears can bring joy to their eyes, what then of my delights? And if my delights are the joy of the angels, how much more would the perseverance of those who fell have been? Yet that is what the heavenly city lacks. There would therefore have been some joy for the saints while the angels stood, and that joy was taken away when they fell. Therefore, you will say, the spirits who were confirmed mourned sorrowfully over the ruin of the others, and in what respect would grief enter the city of the blessed? I do not say that they wept, or were downcast, or were sad. They saw the sin of the sinners; they did not rejoice in that, nor were they saddened by their own confirmation, for it was out of love. They saw the punishment, and the righteous rejoiced in seeing the vengeance, and they stood by the Creator in the casting down of the wicked. For Michael and his angels fought against the dragon, and do you suppose that, having won the victory, they took no joy from it? But it is one thing for an imperfect city to lack some joy, and another for it to admit sorrow. Do you not see that those pleasures, which are purest in understanding and free from contrariety, gladden when they are present, but do not sadden when they are absent? And to crown the evil, that pride which had conceived grief in heaven brought forth iniquity in the earthly Paradise: through envy, it was indignant that the flesh, which was baser, should rise to where the nobler spirit had fallen, and so it poured deadly poison into the serpent, to lure man, created to fill the seats emptied in heaven. For thus death entered the world through envy, although pride was the beginning of every sin. So from every side the malign spirit stood in the way of the longed-for restoration of the heavenly city. Yet his hope deceived him: the city has been restored, and indeed increased in dignity. Lucifer fell through pride; another Lucifer rose through humility. The darkness brought in by the fall of the first was cleansed by the rising of the second. The one diminished the number of the saints; the other restored and enlarged what was diminished. The one violated the integrity of the kingdom; the other repaired what was violated. The one emptied the seats in heaven; the other filled the emptied seats with new praisers. The one drew many angels headlong by his evil example; the other brought back, on his own shoulders, the many justified men who had first wandered like the hundredth sheep into heaven. In every respect Satan is mocked by this one: he could not climb back into heaven, from which he had fallen like lightning, that is, been hurled down by the rush of divine wrath; and he has been unable at all to hinder the ascent he begrudged man, or the restoration he envied the city. Rather, he is slain by his own sword, taken from his hand by one stronger; and while with corrupted intent he strives to bar new citizens from entering glory and to defraud God's glorious kingdom of its beautiful wholeness, he makes crowns for the citizens just as he honours the new kingdom with dignity. Lucifer fell thence; the sun ascended. Vanity was cast out of heaven; truth was brought back into heaven. That city had lost a created angel, and received a created man as its Creator. Hence also that saying of the Apostle is true here: Is it not as the delight, so also the gift? Would you also hear a new kind of joy, which that city would not have felt had man not sinned? I do not fear that I seem to speak too boldly, since I follow Bernard as my authority, who does not think that our God will have the whole praise of his glory until those come who sing to him in the sight of the angels: We have rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us, and for the years in which we saw evils. The heaven did not know this kind of joy except through the sons of the Church; no one rejoices in this who does not rejoice. Joy comes fittingly after sorrow, rest after labour, harbour after shipwreck: security pleases all, but most those who have feared. Light is pleasant to all, but more pleasant to one who has escaped the power of darkness. To pass from death to life doubles the grace of life; it lacks praise if there are none who say: We went through fire and water, and you brought us out into a place of refreshment.

units.la: Hodie felix illa ciuitas nouis exultat gaudiis: ad hunc diem coelestes ruinae perdurauerunt. Ante hunc diem nemo ascendit in coelos: cum de Christo scripserit propheta, quod ascendit pandens ante eos iter. An vero ipso ascendente coascenderint qui cum resurgente resurrexisse leguntur? animas omni labe purgatas credo: sed de corporibus haud quicquam temere diffinire vellim.
units.tr: Today that happy city exults in new joys: until this day the heavenly ruins endured. Before this day no one ascended into heaven, although the prophet wrote of Christ that he ascended, opening the way before them. But were those who are read to have risen with the Risen One also ascending with him? I believe their souls were cleansed of every stain, but I would not rashly determine anything about their bodies.

units.la: Ergo laeti fuerunt, angeli Christo concepto, laeti nascente, laeti praedicante, laeti hominem redimente, laeti resurgente, sed laetiores ascendente. Quid ita? quia multa docentur mysteria Christo praesente, quae prius absente nescierunt. Nec id mirum videatur, cum scripsit Apostolus: Innotescere principibus & potestatibus in coelestibus per ecclesiam multiformem sapientiam Dei. Porro quod prius solasipe tenuerant: ruinas suas resartiendas hodie re laetiore comprehendunt.
units.tr: Therefore the angels rejoiced: they rejoiced when Christ was conceived, rejoiced at his birth, rejoiced when he preached, rejoiced when he redeemed man, rejoiced at his resurrection, but rejoiced most of all at his ascension. Why so? Because many mysteries are taught while Christ is present, which they did not know while he was absent. Nor should this seem strange, since the Apostle wrote: That the manifold wisdom of God should be made known through the Church to the principalities and powers in heavenly places. Moreover, what they had previously held in their own hands alone, they now today grasp with greater joy: that their ruins are to be repaired.

units.la: Quis mihi det, o Domine Iesu, o gloriosissime restitutor regni coelestis? quis mihi det ut possim concipere quanta intuleris hodie coelis festa gaudiorum: quanta iucunditate beatorum spirituum agmina ad nouam solennitatem inuitaueris: quanta tibi laetitia calcatori torcularis cum rubris vestimentis coelos introgrediendi tota superna curia certatim obuiam venerit, aduenisse gratulata est: quantis laudibus triumphatorem prosecuta est: quam iocundis obsequiis in sedem excelsiorem collocare studuerit. Si plus gaudeat super unius peccatoris poenitentia, quam super nonaginta nouem iustis, qui ea non egent: quantum de te gauisa est Deo homine mortis victore: tot poenitentes in ipsam domum paternam non reducente, sed reportante: qui ipse es summum eius gaudium, summus amor, summa suauitas. In te enim tota desiderat conspicere: te suipsius oculis ex propinquo contuendum praesentabas. Quam incredibili voluptate sensus omnium intimos tua vox illa permulsit. Congratulamini mihi, o amici & vicini: quia inueni ouem, quae perierat: inueni drachmam perditam, mortuus filius reuixit. Celebremus alacriter, o Christianitatis rectores inclyti, celebremus tantam festiuitatem, repraesentemus in terris angelorum laetitiam, quae pro nostra illis salute partim ingesta est. Nobis congratulemur, quorum est hodie relaxata, imo & captiuata captiuitas, ascendens enim Christus in altum captiuā duxit captiuitatem. Gaudium ingens: hodie chirographū nostræ damnationis deletum est. Quidni? illa natura hodie in cœlum it, cui dictū ante fuerat: terra es & in terram ibis. Et vt thematis sententia concludatur: à Domino in tempore hoc restitutum est cœleste regnum Israel. Hæc pro priori parte nostri sermonis satis sint. Domine si in tempore hoc &c.
units.tr: Who will give me, O Lord Jesus, O most glorious restorer of the heavenly kingdom? Who will give me the ability to conceive how great a feast of joys you have brought to the heavens today; with what gladness you have summoned the companies of blessed spirits to a new solemnity; with what joy, when you, the treader of the winepress in red garments, entered the heavens, the whole heavenly court eagerly came to meet you and rejoiced at your arrival; with what praises they accompanied the victor; with what delightful services they strove to set you in the highest seat. If there is more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous who need no repentance, how greatly has God rejoiced in you, God-man, victor over death, who did not lead so many penitents back to the Father's house, but carried them back to it: you who are his supreme joy, supreme love, supreme sweetness. For in you the whole of him desires to be seen; you presented yourself to be beheld closely by his own eyes. With what incredible pleasure your voice soothed the innermost senses of all! Rejoice with me, O friends and neighbours, for I have found the sheep that was lost; I have found the lost drachma; the dead son has come back to life. Let us celebrate eagerly, O famous rulers of Christendom, let us celebrate so great a feast; let us present on earth the joy of the angels, which in part was spent for our salvation. Let us rejoice for ourselves, whose captivity has today been released, nay, the captivity itself has been taken captive, for Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive. Great joy: today the handwriting of our condemnation has been blotted out. Why not? Today that nature goes up into heaven to which it was said: You are earth, and into earth you shall go. And to bring the sentence of the theme to a close: at this time the heavenly kingdom of Israel has been restored by the Lord. Let these things suffice for the first part of my sermon. Lord, wilt thou at this time, etc.

units.la: Tractetur iam hæc interrogatio de regno peregrinationis ecclesiæ: qþ ab Abel iusto ducens originem, etsi postea sæpe laborauerit: tamen nunquam vniuersum intercidit. Sæpe expugnauerunt me à iuuentute mea: & non potuerunt mihi. Floruit aliquando sub Patriarchis, ducibus, iudicibus, regibus, sacerdotibus: verum Apostolorum tempore nationibus subiectū mire defloruerat. Responde tu quærentibus, Domine Iesu: tibi ego sicuti certe nunc opibus, nunc vocibus respondisti: & si minus fortassis ad effectū quærentiū, tamen ad veritatem. Audistis quoniam misi vos vt eatis & fructū afferatis eripiendo ciues Israeliticos è manibus regis Babylonis. Auditis qm præcipio vobis vt euntes in mundū vniuersum prædicetis euangelium omni creaturæ: vt sitis mihi testes in Hierusalē & in Iudæa & Samaria & vlq; ad extremū terræ. Cur hoc, nisi vt quaquauersum hoste depulso regnū Israeliticū vestro ministerio dilatetur. Huius rei gratia dedi quosdā vestrum Apostolos, quosdā Prophetas, quosdā Euangelistas: alios autē pastores & doctores ad consummationem sanctorū in opus ministerii, in ædificationē regni Israel. Propterea alteri vestrū alterā manifestationem Spiritus partim dedi: partim dabo ad vtilitatē reparationis regni desolati: & ne nudos hostiū telis exponerē: succinxi lumbos vestros in veritate: indui vos loricā iustitiæ: dedi pedū calceos in præparatione euangelii pacis: contuli scutū fidei, galeā salutis & gladiū Spiritus, qþ est verbū Dei.
units.tr: Let us now treat this question concerning the kingdom of the church in its pilgrimage. The church, tracing its origin from the righteous Abel, though it has often laboured since, has never been utterly destroyed. They have often fought against me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me. It flourished at times under the patriarchs, leaders, judges, kings and priests, but in the time of the Apostles, though subjected to the nations, it had wonderfully flourished. Lord Jesus, answer those who ask you, as you have indeed answered them, now by deeds and now by voices, and if perhaps not to the effect the askers desired, yet to the truth. You have heard that I sent you to go and bear fruit, rescuing the citizens of Israel from the hands of the king of Babylon. You hear that I command you, going into the whole world, to preach the gospel to every creature, that you may be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in Judea, in Samaria, and to the uttermost part of the earth. Why this, except that, the enemy having been driven off everywhere, the kingdom of Israel should be enlarged by your ministry? For this purpose I gave some of you as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the kingdom of Israel. Therefore I have given to one of you one manifestation of the Spirit and will give another to another, for the benefit of restoring the desolate kingdom. And lest I expose you naked to the weapons of the enemy, I have girded your loins in truth, clothed you with the breastplate of righteousness, put shoes on your feet in preparation for the gospel of peace, and bestowed the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

units.la: Quia vero imbecillibus, quales adhuc estis, hæc arma potius forent oneri q̄ vsui: Edico vobis ab Hierosolymis ne discedatis, quo adusq; recepitis virtutē Spiritus sancti supuenientis in vos, qua non arma tantū sine molestia ferre: verūetiam cunctos impetus hostiles elidere: imo & exercitus fundere atq; fugare possitis. Nam quo dāna cœlestia restituentur, nisi ex his ciuibus regni terrestris quidā sursum ascenderint. Hæc illis charus præceptor, cuius vocibus diligēter paruerunt. Vnde post Spiritus sancti susceptione ˌpfecti prædicauerunt verbū Domino cooperante & sermone confirmante sequentibus signis. Vbiq; circūtulerunt sagittas potētis acutas cū carnibus desolatoriis: vbiq; vicerunt regna: effugarunt aciē gladii: fortes fuerunt in bello: castra verterunt exterorū. Ita breui creuit ecclesia: inclyta facta est & posita est in superbia seculorū: dominata est à mari vsq; ad mare: & à flumine vsq; ad terminos orbis terrarū. Adorauerunt eum omnes reges: omnes gentes seruierunt ei. Sed quid ad hæc ascensio, multū per omne modū. Quippe q̄diu Dominus in terræ discipulis conuersatus est, humi repsit eorū dilectio: dulciter siq̄dem eū amauerunt: & præ eius dilectione spreuerunt alia. Ecce inquiunt reliquimus omnia & secuti sumus te. Verū nescio quo præsentia vitæ carnis spiritualis amoris puritatē non admittebat. Inde sæpe tanq̄ carnales obiurgantur. Inde Petrus impatienter audiens verbū de morte magistri, sathanas vocatur. Inde cuncti molestę tulerunt, qþ de ascensuri magistri discessu audierunt. Inde plus illis sapiebat verbū caro, q̄ verbū sapientia, iustitia, virtus, pietas. Inde scriptū est illud: Nisi ego abiero, paracletus non veniet. Et illud aliud: Nondū erat Spiritus datus: quia nondū fuerat Iesus glorificatus. Sed post magistri discessionē, aptiores subinde fuerunt sanctū suscipere Spiritū: à quo roborati atq; firmati discerent amare valide, prædicare veritatē intrepide, frigida corda succēdere, discerent plus invenire saporis in verbo Deo, q̄ in verbo homine. Experirentur altiorē amoris gradum iā eis ostensum à Christo dicente, Spiritus est qui viuificat: caro non prodest quicquam. Ad hunc gradū Paulus ascendisse videbatur, dū dicebat, Et si cognouimus Christū secundum carne, sed iam non nouimus. Fortassis & Prophetā cū diceret, Spiritus ante faciē nostrā Christus Dominus. Huius igitur spiritualis amoribus viribus ac robore regnū Israeliticū restituerunt. Sed heu & plus quā millies heu, quam grandis nobis materia lachrymarū obiicitur. Circumferamus oculos quorsumcunq; libuerit, nusquam pax, nulla tranquillitas, nusquā secura quies, vbi calamitas, afflictio, perturbatio. O me miserū: quō regnum vbiq; diffusum per bellatores inclytos, coartauit in angustum ac restrinxit rex impius Babylonis, quō maiorē antiqui regni portionem abstulit Christo, & eam ipsam, quæ secundū sibi nomē retinuit, innumeris tempestatibus iactata afflixit. Nam quota sunt humani generis portio Machometici, ac ab octigentis ferme annis suauē Christi iugū ceruicibus excusserunt? Quota Indi feruntur Christianæ crucis insignibus exornati, sed ecclesiæ Romanæ primatū ignorare? Quota Græci, at illos mala tempestas à sede Petri disiectos, non modo schismatis, sed nonnullius etiā hæresis macula fœdauit. Latinitas ipsa purior ac immaculatior sedem habet Petri, cuius fide ne deficeret specialiter oratu it ille, q in omnibus exauditus est pro sua reuerentia. Ipsa tamen tā multis q̄ diuturnis q̄ violentis schismatibus, tū antea sepe, tum nostra tēpestate miserabiliter concussa languit.
units.tr: But since these weapons would rather be a burden than a use to you, who are still feeble, I charge you not to depart from Jerusalem until you have received the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, by which you will be able not only to bear the arms without trouble, but also to repel every hostile assault, and even to rout and put to flight armies. For how shall the heavenly kingdoms be restored unless some of these citizens of the earthly kingdom ascend on high? So their dear teacher spoke, and they diligently obeyed his voice. Hence, after receiving the Holy Spirit, they went forth and preached the word, the Lord working with them and confirming the word with the signs that followed. Everywhere they carried sharp arrows of the mighty with the coals of desolation; everywhere they conquered kingdoms, put armies to flight with the sword, were strong in war, and turned the camps of foreigners. So in a short time the church grew; she became renowned and was placed in the pride of the ages: she ruled from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. All kings worshipped him; all nations served him. But what has the Ascension to do with these things? Indeed, as long as the Lord lived among the disciples on earth, their affection crept along the ground; they loved him sweetly, and because of their love for him they despised other things. Behold, they say, we have left all and followed you. Yet, I know not how, the presence of his bodily life did not admit the purity of spiritual love. Hence they were often rebuked as carnal. Hence Peter, hearing impatiently the word about the death of the Master, was called Satan. Hence all of them were grieved when they heard of the departure of the Master who was about to ascend. Hence the word of the flesh had more savour for them than the word of wisdom, righteousness, virtue and godliness. Hence that saying is written: If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come. And that other: The Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified. But after the Master's departure, they were from then on better fitted to receive the Holy Spirit, by whom strengthened and confirmed they might learn to love vigorously, to preach the truth fearlessly, to kindle cold hearts, and to find more savour in the word of God than in the word of man. They would experience a higher degree of love, already shown to them by Christ saying, It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. Paul seemed to have ascended to this degree when he said, And even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer. Perhaps also the Prophet, when he said, The Spirit before our face, the Lord Christ. By the loves, powers and strength of this spiritual love, therefore, they restored the kingdom of Israel. But alas, and more than a thousand times alas, what a great matter for tears is set before us! Let us look round wherever we will: nowhere peace, nowhere tranquillity, nowhere secure rest, but everywhere calamity, affliction and disturbance. Oh, wretched me! How the impious king of Babylon has confined and narrowed the kingdom, once spread everywhere through renowned warriors; how he has taken the greater part of the ancient kingdom from Christ, and has afflicted with countless storms even that part which still keeps the name of Christ. For what a portion of the human race is Mohammedan, and for nearly eight hundred years has shaken off the sweet yoke of Christ from its neck! How many Indians are said to be adorned with the badges of the Christian cross, yet are ignorant of the primacy of the Roman church! How many Greeks, whom an evil storm has torn from the seat of Peter, are stained not only with schism but also with some heresy! The Latin church itself, purer and more unspotted, has the seat of Peter, for whose faith, that it might not fail, he specially prayed, and he was heard in all things because of his reverence. Yet it too, by so many and such long and violent schisms, both formerly often and in our own time, is miserably shaken and languishes.

units.la: Vnde nup tantarū calamitatum impatiens ecclesia, multis suspiriis ac gemitibus clamauit ad Dominū, Domine si tempore hoc restitues regnū Israel. Aliqua ex parte audita est. Excitatus est tanq̄ dormiens Dominus, tanq̄ potens crapulatus à vino. Et pcussit inimicos suos in posteriora, opprobriū sempiternū dedit illis. Asportauit duplicē Sobnam, tanq̄ gallum gallinaciū, & fidelē Eliachim substituit. Nā cuius est ista tua substitutio P.B. nisi Christi? Vñ conuocatio cociliii tā mira? Vnde prius discordantiū cōsensio, vndetor psulū ac sapientū concursus tā celer? nō causa certe dissensionis sed pacis. Nō vocauit papa, fuit conuenticulū. O ridenda ac irrationalis nimiū ratio. Neq; vero ad quatuor illa cōcilia, q in Actibus Apostolicis describuntur, Petrus vocasse memoratur. Neq; Synodus Nicena iussu Syluestri, sed Constantini conuenisse legitur. Ad quintū vniuersale patrū concilii contra Theodorū Nestorii discipulū, nemine conuocante sese certatim patres exhortati sunt. Fuere ergo conuenticula? Caue dixeris. Colūtur ab Aug. tanq̄ euangelia. Quid si schisma dubios reddit Christianos, quē duorum pro papa colant? Quid si (qþ perrarum est) summus pontifex labatur in hæresim, vt legimus Liberiū Arrianæ prauitati subscripsisse, Marcellinum idolis sacrificasse? Quid si in tolerandis oneribus Christianitatē grauaret? An aduersus tantos morbos vllā relinqs medelā? Relinquo inquies. Credo sane. Nam impfectam nimium ecclesiastica politia astrueres, nec à Deo cuius pfecta sunt opa salubriter institutam, qþ credere nefas est, si qs in eam morbus possit incurrere, contra quē nulla posset adhiberi medicina, sed tamen nulla memoratis casibus relinquitur, si non aliquando sine papæ vocatione conuenire possit ecclesia. Libenter hic diutius insisterem, sed breuitate prohibeor. Quoniam ergo te certum ac indubitatum pontificem nobis exhibuit Deus, vt reliqua mala per te tollat: & regnum Israel nimis instrictum iterum amplietur, ad te iam conuertitur & clamitat ecclesia querens: Domine si in tempore hoc &c. Non ab longis, inquit, retro diebus quisquam me summus pontifex in tantam spem erexit recuperandæ meæ dignitatis antiquæ, sicuti tu, quem video contraire dispositiis illis, qui me dimiserunt. Facob secro vt non frustra sperauerim. Considera etiam atq; etiam, quod cum mihi donatus es, tuus esse certe destiti, nec sit te vocem Dominum, tu me propter ea famulam arbitreris. Sic Sara obediebat Abrahæ Dominum illum vocans. Non ego certe tua, sed tu meus: omnia siquidem mea sunt: siue Paulus, siue Apollo, siue Cephas. Tu te etiam filiorum meorum seruū vocas, si non es cur te vocas? Si vere es, negato Domini, & vide quantum mihi debes. Si quispiam te filiorum meorum rationabiliter vti velit, non potes te sibi negare vel furari, qui suus es, quin per te vel alium suæ necessitati succurras, quamuis nil ambitioni, nihil auaritiæ vel malitiæ debeas, si tantum singulis, quantum vniuersis, tantū mihi, quare suspirabunda atq; plorabunda peto, vt mala mea respicias, vt regnum Israel hoc tempore restituas. Iustum petit, pater beatissime: eam exaudi, vniuersum studium tuū ad regni sui restitutionem conferas de vetusta illa Saracenorum ruina, quis ô si resarciretur. Vix ausim aliquid dicere, licet non existimentur Christiani populi rectores hoc absoluti præcepto, quod hodie tuis auribus intonuit: Euntes in mundum vniuersum, prædicate euangelium omni creaturæ: aliisque similibus, quamdiu fuerit aliqua gens sine Christo, nec se putassent patres eorum Apostoli, nec illi quatuor principales doctores ecclesiæ, post quorum tempora tanta pestis exorta est. Verum ab hac disputatione breuitatis amor auocat, ac prope rapit ad alia. De Indis quid dicā? Habent Christum, an pure qs doceat? Quis te vetat ad eos mittere, qui referent omnia? Facile in eis fidei sinceritas corrumpitur, cum ecclesiæ Romanæ non cohæreant, à qua fidei certitudo petenda est.
units.tr: Hence the church, now impatient of such great calamities, has cried out to the Lord with many sighs and groans: Lord, if at this time you will restore the kingdom of Israel. In some measure she has been heard. The Lord has been roused as one sleeping, as a mighty man heavy with wine. And he has struck his enemies on the hinder parts, and given them everlasting shame. He has removed the double Shebna, like a cock of the henhouse, and set up the faithful Eliakim. For whose is this substitution of yours, Most Blessed Father, except Christ's? Whence so wonderful a calling of a council? Whence the agreement of those formerly at odds, and whence so swift a gathering of bishops and wise men? Surely not the cause of dissension but of peace. The pope did not call it; it was a conventicle. Oh, laughable and exceedingly unreasonable argument! Nor is it recorded that Peter summoned those four councils which are described in the Acts of the Apostles. Nor is it read that the Nicene Synod assembled at the command of Sylvester, but of Constantine. For the fifth universal council of the Fathers against Theodore, the disciple of Nestorius, the Fathers were stirred up to come eagerly, with no one summoning them. Were they then conventicles? Beware of saying so. Augustine reveres them as the gospels. What if the schism makes Christians doubtful, when they honour two for the pope? What if (which is very rare) the supreme pontiff should slip into heresy, as we read that Liberius subscribed to Arian perversity and Marcellinus sacrificed to idols? What if he burdened Christians beyond what they could bear? Would you leave any remedy against such great diseases? You will say, I leave it. I quite believe it. For you would assert that the ecclesiastical polity is too imperfect, and not wholesomely established by God, whose works are perfect, which it is wrong to believe; if any disease could fall upon it against which no medicine could be applied. Yet no remedy is left in the cases mentioned, unless the church can sometimes assemble without the calling of the pope. I would gladly dwell on this longer, but brevity forbids me. Therefore, since God has shown us you as the certain and undoubted pontiff, so that you may remove the remaining evils through yourself, and the kingdom of Israel, too much narrowed, may be enlarged again, the church now turns to you and cries out, asking: Lord, if at this time, etc. "Not from long days past," she says, "has any supreme pontiff raised me to such hope of recovering my ancient dignity as you do, whom I see acting contrary to those who dismissed me. I beg you that I may not have hoped in vain. Consider again and again that, since I have been given to you, I have certainly ceased to be yours, and let it not be that you think me your servant because of this, calling me Lord. Sara obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. I am certainly not yours, but you are mine; for all things are mine, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas. Do you also call yourself the servant of my sons? If you are not, why do you call yourself so? If you truly are, deny that you are the Lord's, and see how much you owe me. If anyone reasonably wishes to use your services for my sons, you cannot deny yourself to them or steal yourself away, since you are their own, but must help their need through yourself or another, although you owe nothing to ambition, nothing to avarice or malice; if you give as much to each as to all, then give as much to me. Therefore, sighing and weeping, I ask that you look upon my troubles, and that at this time you restore the kingdom of Israel. She asks what is just, most blessed Father; hear her. Direct all your zeal to restoring her kingdom from that ancient ruin of the Saracens, which would be repaired, oh, if only it were. I scarcely dare say anything, although the rulers of Christian peoples are not thought bound by that absolute precept which today has thundered in your ears: Going into the whole world, preach the gospel to every creature; and by other similar sayings, as long as there is any nation without Christ. Nor would their fathers, the Apostles, nor those four principal teachers of the church, after whose times so great a plague arose, have thought otherwise. But love of brevity calls me away from this disputation, and almost hurries me to other things. What shall I say of the Indians? Do they have Christ, or does anyone teach them purely? Who forbids you to send to them those who will report everything? In them the sincerity of the faith is easily corrupted, since they do not cohere with the Roman church, from which the certainty of faith must be sought."

units.la: Impiger extremos currit mercator ad Indos, Per mare pauperiem fugiens, per tela, per ignes.
units.tr: The eager merchant runs to the farthest Indians, fleeing poverty across the sea, through weapons, through fires.

units.la: & ex te nullus eo currer spelucri faciendæ tantæ gentis: memento tamen illi te esse debitorem. Iam vero de Græcis loquerer, quibus multa Latini debemus. Verum hunc locū eo negligentius transeo, quod te erga Græcorum reuocatione omnes adhibituum operas intelligo, festina pater festina, ne fugiat hora, ne labatur occasio desup oblata, cui non est facile similis reditura. Ad rem feliciter tractandam tempus omnium primum est. Itidem dicendū puto de ea parte Latinorū, quæ nondum tuam claram iustitiam insequitur, sed duobus hominibus humano iudicio diutinoq; condemnatis adhuc inhærēt, quoniā & tua vigilantia, & obedientium principum sedulitate, & tuæ veritatis pspicuitate, spes est cito Deo bene iuuante reditura. Labore tantum opus est. Igitur his tanta breuitate decursis, pergit iterum ecclesia quærere de ea parte, quæ tuā iustitiam agnoscit: Domine si in tempore hoc &c. Tecū forte cogitas, cur hoc quaerat? nam cū hæc pars sit schismate liberata, quam in ea ruinæ reparandæ relinquuntur? Gaudet sane schisma esse hinc depulsum: sed nō radicitus credit auulsum. Hærent terræ radices, ex quibus pullulauerat malū germen. Veretur ne, si non succindantur, denuo repullulet, quare cupit vt fodiat altius labor tuus, non futura sine metu, nisi viderit cunctas malorū germinū stirpes penitus auulsas. Sed q sunt aliæ radices? Absit si hoc à mea tenuitate, prsus absit vt tuā summā sapientiā velim instruere: scio ab infantia paululū distare volentē docere Mineruam. Sed effundo coram te cordis mei affectum, imo profero voces ecclesiæ sanctorū, & sine suspitione docendi oro vt eas exaudias. Quis enim nesciat nos in orationibus effundere coram Deo corda nostra, nec eum velle docere? Malo tñ dicat ipsamet ecclesia voces sanctorū suorū, dicat quas velit stirpes excindi, & quas plantari. En loquitur, non iam in me, sed in eam intendite. Væ misere mihi, væ infelici, ex quo dignitatis culmine manibus iniquorū detracta sum, quo mutatus est color optimus, obfuscatus faciei nitor. Cœlestis pulchritudo terrenis sordibus inquinata, exangue corpus effectū, miserandū, incultū, hispidum, vestimentis fragrantibus spoliatū. Ecce rex & conditor meus, me regni sanctorū cœlestis expressam imaginem esse decreuerat, vt quantū fas esset, terrenarū rerum oblita cœlo ppinquarem, & regnū illud supernum oculis mortaliū præsentarem. Sic n. sub Moyse nomine dictum fuerat: Vide omnia facias secundū exemplar tibi monstratū in monte. Sic retulit postea discipulus quē dilexit, se vidisse ciuitatē sanctā Hierusalem descendentem de cœlo habentē claritatem. Duplici vero similitudine illam imitabar. Primum quidē, qa sicut in cœlesti regno Cherubin Seraphin & cæteri quiq; vsq; ad angelos ordinantur sub vno capite Deo, ita in meo corpore sub summo pontifice primates vel Patriarchæ, archiepiscopi & episcopi, archipresbyteri, presbyteri & abbates & reliqui. Est alia principalior, & cuius gratia hæc institutā fuit, vt quantum patitur corpus corruptibile, q cœlestes habent pfecte, habeant terrestres ex parte. Illi vident per speciem, videant isti per sapientiam, & fidem. Illi Deum tenent præsentē per comprehensionē, teneant absentē isti pspem. Illi Deo fruūtur plena charitate, fruantur isti quāta possunt in corpore prægrauante. Deū colant & adorent quō beati, casti sint quō beati, sapiant q sursum sunt, non quæ sup terram quō beati, & sic possem discurrere p cæteras virtutes, recte sane sic ordinauit sapientis artifex. Nā si ppria ratio mea quæritur, & mei collatio ad cœleste ciuitatem facienda est. Ego sum via & motus in illā, illa finis ac terminus. Ego pegrinatio raptim transiens, illa patria semp manens. Ego militantium iuge certamen, illa lætus victorum triumphus. Ego vallis miseriæ, illa mons lætitiæ. Ego mare tempestuosum, illa portus tranquillus. Ego exilium, illa natale solū. Itaq; quemadmodū motus ex suo termino ad quem vadit, sic ego ex illa ppriam traho ratione. Quantū ad illam accessero, tm veritatis acqto. Si tendere desidero, amisso nomine pp Potestates autem terrenas quis ordinatas ambigat? Non est potestas nisi a Deo: quae autem a Deo sunt ordinatae sunt. Verum ordinis mei pulchritudo longe praestantior, expressior atq; vicinior. Huius curam quam ac pene unicam, custodibus, quos mihi reliquit in terris, meus conditor mandavit. Exemplum, inquiens, dedi vobis: ut quemadmodum ego feci, ita & vos faciatis. Si similitudines pulcherrimas coelestis ordinis in terris posui, vos illas servate: vestrum est officium, ut cæteros purgetis, illuminetis, perficiatis, quatenus coelestem portent imaginem. Idcirco vos purgavi, illuminavi, perfeci: quia nec sordulentum mundificat, nec tenebrosum illuminat, nec diminuta perficiunt.
units.tr: And from you no one will run there to make gain from so great a people. Yet remember that you are in debt to them. Indeed, I would speak of the Greeks, to whom the Latins owe much. But I pass over this point the more quickly because I understand that all your efforts are directed to recalling the Greeks. Hurry, father, hurry, lest the hour flee and the opportunity offered from above slip away, for it will not easily return in a similar form. For handling the matter successfully, time is above all things needed. Likewise, I think I should speak of that part of the Latins which does not yet follow your clear justice but still clings to the two men condemned by human judgment and for a long time. For both your vigilance, and the diligence of the obedient princes, and the clarity of your truth, there is hope that, with God helping well, they will soon return. Only labour is needed. So, having run through these matters with such brevity, the Church again asks about that part which acknowledges your justice: Lord, if at this time etc. Perhaps you wonder to yourself why she asks this? For since this part has been freed from the schism, what ruins are left to be repaired in it? She rejoices indeed that the schism has been driven out from here, but she does not believe it has been torn up by the roots. The roots of the earth still cling, from which the evil shoot had sprouted. She fears that, unless they are cut away, it will sprout again, and so she wishes that your labour dig deeper, nor will the future be free of fear unless she sees all the stocks of these evil shoots utterly torn out. But what are the other roots? Far be it from my slight ability, far be it that I should wish to instruct your supreme wisdom; I know that one who wishes to teach Minerva is a little distant from the childhood of learning. But I pour out before you the feeling of my heart, indeed I bring forward the voices of the saints of the Church, and I pray that you hear them without suspicion of teaching. For who does not know that we pour out our hearts before God in prayers, and that he does not wish to be taught? Yet I prefer that the Church herself speak the voices of her saints, and say which stocks she wishes to be cut out and which to be planted. Behold, she speaks, not now in me, but attend to her: Woe is me, wretched, woe to me unhappy, since from the height of my dignity I have been dragged down by the hands of the wicked, since my excellent colour has changed, the brightness of my face been dimmed. Heavenly beauty is stained with earthly filth; I have become a bloodless body, pitiable, uncared for, rough, stripped of my fragrant garments. Behold, my king and creator had decreed that I should be the express image of the heavenly kingdom of the saints, so that, as far as is right, forgetful of earthly things, I might draw near to heaven and set before mortal eyes that supernal kingdom. For thus it was said under the name of Moses: See that you make all things according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain. Thus afterwards the disciple whom he loved related that he saw the holy city Jerusalem coming down from heaven, having its brightness. Indeed, I imitated that pattern in a double likeness. First, because just as in the heavenly kingdom the Cherubim, Seraphim, and all the others down to the angels are ordered under one head, God, so in my body, under the supreme pontiff, are the primates or patriarchs, archbishops and bishops, archpresbyters, presbyters, abbots, and the rest. There is another, more principal likeness, and for its sake this order was instituted: that, as far as a corruptible body allows, what the heavenly beings have perfectly, the earthly ones should have in part. Those see by sight; these should see by wisdom and faith. Those hold God present by comprehension; these should hold him absent by hope. Those enjoy God with full charity; these should enjoy him as far as they can in a burdensome body. Let them honour and worship God as the blessed do, let them be chaste as the blessed are, let them savour the things that are above and not those on the earth, as the blessed do. And I could run through the other virtues in the same way; wisely, indeed, did the wise craftsman so arrange it. For if my own proper nature is sought, and my comparison with the heavenly city is to be made: I am the way and the movement toward it, it is the end and the limit.
