I am a pilgrimage passing swiftly, it is a homeland always remaining. I am the constant struggle of those fighting, it is the joyful triumph of the victors. I am the valley of misery, it is the mountain of joy. I am the stormy sea, it is the calm harbour. I am exile, it is the native soil. Therefore, just as motion takes its nature from the term toward which it goes, so I draw my own nature from that city. As much as I come near to it, so much do I gain of truth. If I desire to strive towards it, I lose the name of ... Who would doubt that earthly powers are ordained? There is no power except from God, and those that are from God are ordained. But the beauty of my order is far more outstanding, more expressed, and closer. My Creator entrusted the care of this, which is almost the only care, to the guardians whom he left me on earth. He said: I have given you an example, that as I have done, so you also should do. If I have placed the most beautiful likenesses of the heavenly order on earth, keep them: it is your duty to cleanse, enlighten, and perfect the others, so that they may bear the heavenly image. For this reason I have cleansed you, enlightened you, perfected you: because nothing unclean is made clean, nothing dark is enlightened, and nothing imperfect is perfected.

units.la: Et vos quales custodes meae sponsae substitueritis, etiam atque etiam caute consideretis, quamdiu recte his mandatis est obeditum, Spiritus valuit: caro iacuit: eximia per totum orbem terrarum diffusa sunt. Pax ubique portabatur: ubique recipiebatur: ferrea corda linguis igneis & verbis ignitis liquescebant. Sed heu quid de calamitate praesentium temporum querar misera? quibus pro coelesti ordine perturbor confusione: & ex similitudine coelesti quae mihi vita est, ad inferni similitudinem, ubi nullus ordo, sed sempiternus horror inhabitat: quae mihi mors est manibus impii pertrahor? Denique ex distinctissima membrorum decentia in chaos Anaxagoreum, nisi manus conditoris retentaret, prope dilaberer. Siccine mi rex te sequor? Siccine coelos peto? Siccine matris coelestis veneratur imago? Vix iam ordo meus, quem instituisti, legitur in libris, quanto minus in moribus? Cernere est archiepiscopos, primates suos, vel ignorare vel contemnere, adversus illos, aut consuetudinis diuturnae praescriptionem aut exceptionem allegare. Et nonne haec eadem ab inferioribus suis archiepiscopi patiuntur? Cernere est professos paupertatem: ita ut nec in privato nec in communi sibi quicquam reservaverint: quo liberius in terris charitatis ardore Seraphin, scientiae plenitudine Cherubin imitarentur: aut ad praelaturas nisibus summis aspirare: aut si hoc non audeant, ad beneficiorum minorum, quod est inusitatius commendas currere: non veritos nec cum uxore Loth retrospicientes, in salis effigiem redigantur: neque satis memores Ananiae & Saphyrae. Mirum est non alios aeque festinare ditari his quorum professio vetat dignitati.
units.tr: And you, consider again and again with great caution what kind of guardians you appoint for my bride. As long as these commands were obeyed, the Spirit prevailed, the flesh lay low, and outstanding things spread throughout the whole world. Peace was carried everywhere and received everywhere; hard hearts were melted by tongues of fire and burning words. But alas, wretched me, what shall I complain of the calamity of the present times? Now I am disturbed by a confusion contrary to the heavenly order, and from a likeness of heaven, which is my life, I am dragged by the hands of the impious toward the likeness of hell, where there is no order but everlasting horror, which is my death. Finally, from the most distinct comeliness of my members I am almost falling into an Anaxagorean chaos, did not the hand of my Creator hold me back. Is it so, my king, that I follow you? Is it so that I seek the heavens? Is it so that the image of the heavenly mother is worshipped? My order, which you instituted, is scarcely read any longer in books, much less in morals. One sees archbishops either ignoring or despising their primates, and pleading against them either the prescription of long custom or an exception. And do not the archbishops suffer the same from their own inferiors? One sees those who profess poverty so that they have kept nothing for themselves, either privately or in common, reserved for themselves; so that, the more freely on earth, they might imitate the Seraphim in the ardour of charity and the Cherubim in the fullness of knowledge: yet they strive with the greatest effort for prelacies, or, if they do not dare that, they run, which is more unusual, to commendams of lesser benefices, not fearing nor looking back like Lot's wife, so that they are turned into a pillar of salt, nor remembering Ananias and Sapphira well enough. It is a wonder that others do not hurry just as eagerly to be enriched by those things which their profession forbids to dignity.

units.la: Cur enim assidue pulsant aures Apostolicas, quatenus nova privilegia valeant extorquere. Si hoc ut publice proficiant, magis quam marsupia repleant, splendide viuant: paupertatem quam voluerunt exuant: ipsi viderint: quanquam multa me experientia magistra docuerit: nolim tamen iudicare. Videas alios novem ordinibus non contentos: non enim novenis beneficiis saturantur: tamdiu novos hiatus pandere quamdiu viuant: coniungere domum ad domum, agrum agro copulare: quasi in medio terrae soli habitarent: ipsum verum vae propheticum pro fabula contemnere. Videas fere omnes summis importunitatibus in leges irruere: dum nunc petunt gratiam obtinendorum simul incompatibilium: nunc in absentia posse fructus colligere: nunc ante omnes magnas dignitates assequi: nunc ad sacros ordines non compelli: & mille alia rectis legibus vetita. Vbi non est intolerandum magnos praelatos commissos sibi greges lupis exponere: & quotidie ad denariorum regiorum supputationes sedere: non veritos praeceptum Apostolicum transgredi t Nemo militans Deo implicat se negotiis saecularibus, eo sensu quo per sacrosanctum concilium olim expositum fuit.
units.tr: For why do they constantly beat upon the apostolic ears, so that they may be able to extort new privileges? If this were for the public good, so that they might prosper more than fill their purses, live splendidly, and cast off the poverty they once chose, let them see to it themselves; although much experience, as my teacher, has taught me, yet I would not wish to judge. You may see others not content with nine orders, for they are not satisfied with nine benefices, gaping wide for new ones as long as they live, joining house to house and field to field, as though they were dwelling in the middle of the earth alone, despising the true prophetic woe as a fable. You may see almost all rushing into the laws with the greatest importunity, now seeking the grace of obtaining incompatible things together, now collecting fruits in absence, now attaining all the great dignities before others, now not being compelled to sacred orders, and a thousand other things forbidden by right laws. Where it is not to be tolerated that great prelates expose the flocks committed to them to wolves, and sit daily at the reckonings of royal pennies, not fearing to transgress the apostolic precept: No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs, in the sense in which it was once expounded by the sacred council.

units.la: Quid de illis loquar, qui de more patriae pro mitris vtuntur galeis: pro veste linea vestiuntur ferrea: arma ferunt, bella gerunt, fundunt sanguinem: praesules negant, duces exhibent: Spiritum nesciunt, carnem fovent, quasi arma militiae nostrae essent carnalia & non potentia Deo ad destruendum omnem altitudinem extollentem se adversus scientiam Dei. Quod si ad haec arma necessitas vigentior detruserit (uti nonnunquam accidere fateor) non est magis speranda victoria ex pugna Iosuae, quam oratione Moysi. Porro illud quam absurdum in hierarchiis institutis nullos actus hierarchicos exhibere: nop purgare, non illuminare, non perficere. Atque utinam exemplo suo malo non inficerent, in errores traherent, ac imperficerent pauperem plebeculam paratam in alterutrum sequi, aut bona exempla virtutum, aut prava vitiorum. Quid turpius quam videre doctos aut bene moratos, aut extra ordines iacere, aut in imis collocatos: ignaros autem & improbos altissimum gradum tenere: videre alios esurire, alios ebrios esse? Quod si ad institutionem sacerdotum atque prouisionem venire delectet, doleo seminaria seri litium, vbi lites sequi prope nefas est. Vix aliquod beneficium infra praelaturas confertur, quin ipsum, vni summus pontifex, alteri vero legatus aliquis, item ordinarius alteri conferat. Quid est hoc aliud quam litium materiam exhibere? Nec illud minus absonum quam magis favoribus humanis, aut gratia, aut metu, aut cupiditate, aut consanguinitate, aut affinitate, aut aliquo impetu animi quam iudicio aut delectu prouisiones istae fiunt. Nec ad ea dona spectatur, quae Spiritus sanctus membris meis variis varia distribuit ad regimen ordinatum, atque per se sufficiens mei corporis. Unde fit ut auris ad videndum, ad audiendum oculus nonnunquam applicetur: similisque caeterorum membrorum confusio fiat, qua nulla maior pernicies. Ex quibus haec radicibus pullulasse crediderim? profecto ex foedis inquinamentis clericorum.
units.tr: What shall I say of those who, following the custom of their country, wear helmets in place of mitres, and in place of linen vestments are clothed in iron? They carry weapons, wage wars, and shed blood. They deny the bishops' office and play the commanders. They know nothing of the Spirit and cherish the flesh, as if the weapons of our warfare were carnal and not "mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds, casting down every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God." But if a more pressing necessity thrusts them into these arms (as I admit happens at times), victory is no more to be hoped for from the fighting of Joshua than from the prayer of Moses. Again, how absurd it is that in the institutions of the hierarchy they exercise no hierarchical acts: they do not purify, do not enlighten, do not perfect. Would that they did not also infect others by their bad example, and draw into error and corrupt the poor common people, who are ready to follow one another either into good examples of virtue or into the evil of vice! What is more shameful than to see the learned and the well-behaved lying outside the ranks or placed at the bottom, while the ignorant and the wicked hold the highest rank; to see some starving and others drunk? If it pleases them to come to the training and provision of priests, I grieve that seminaries are sown with lawsuits, where to pursue lawsuits is almost a crime. Scarcely any benefice below the prelacies is conferred without the supreme pontiff conferring it on one man, some legate on another, and the ordinary on yet another. What is this but to supply the matter of lawsuits? Nor is it less absurd that these provisions are made more by human favour, whether through partiality, fear, greed, kinship, marriage connections, or some impulse of the mind, than by judgement or choice. Nor is regard had to those gifts which the Holy Spirit distributes variously among my members for their ordered rule and for the sufficiency of my body as a whole. Hence it happens that the ear is sometimes applied to seeing and the eye to hearing, and a similar confusion of the other members follows, and nothing is more destructive than this. From what roots, I ask, do I believe these evils have sprung? Surely from the foul defilements of the clergy.

units.la: Unde periere virtutes, ex quibus secunda similitudo mea ad coelestem hierarchiam intemerata saluabatur: sublatus est simul omnis decor ordinis, in quo prima fundabatur. Priores illi, sub quibus magna felicitate floruit sapientia coelesti, fideque feruebant. Isti posteriores carnali prudentia corrumpuntur. Illi inflammabantur amore Dei: isti flagrant amore mundi. Illi firmabantur in vero bono spe fößda: isti spe mendacii falsis bonis inhærescunt. Quo fit vt quemadmodum illi per sapientiam Spiritus cæterasque claras virtutes meum regnum fundauerunt, ornauerunt, ampliauerunt: sic isti per carnis prudentiam cæteraque fœda vitia idem diruant, maculent, restringant. Nam cum caro concupiscat aduersus Spiritum: cui dubium est leges carnis spiritualem politiam potius subruere quam saluare, deterrere quam emendare, minuere quam augere? Recte dicit Ethnicus: Impëtium facile hiis artibus retineri, quibus initio partum est.
units.tr: Hence the virtues have perished by which my second likeness to the heavenly hierarchy was kept unspoiled; at the same time all the grace of the order on which the first was founded has been removed. Those former men, under whom heavenly wisdom flourished with great happiness, were burning with faith. These later men are corrupted by carnal prudence. Those were inflamed with the love of God; these blaze with the love of the world. Those were established in the true good, fixed in hope; these cling to false goods through the hope of a lie. So it is that, just as those men, by the wisdom of the Spirit and their other bright virtues, founded, adorned and enlarged my kingdom, so these men, by carnal prudence and their other foul vices, pull it down, stain it, and narrow it. For since the flesh lusts against the Spirit, who doubts that the laws of the flesh rather overthrow the spiritual polity than save it, deter rather than correct it, diminish rather than increase it? A heathen writer rightly says: Empire is easily kept by the same arts by which it was first gained.

units.la: Unde quia meis propugnatoribus artes illæ desuNt, quibus mihi dignitatem ac opes antecessores eorum pepererunt, vndiq; in meam dignitatem ac diuitias fit impetus. Et sicut ex illis tanquam pacis radicibus pax latissime exorta est: sic ex istis tanquam discordiarum stirpibus omnia schismata & creata sunt & nutrita. O indignum facinus, ô sceleratissimam proditionem: milites mei & iidem filii quos ad honores maximos opesque sublimaui, protectis armis sponsi mei, loricaiustitiæ, scuto fidei, galea salutis & gladio Spiritus ad hostem capitalem transfugerunt: pactoque turpissimæ pacis fœdere armaturam illius induerunt: loricam iniustitiæ, scutum prudentiæ carnalis, galeam amoris mundani, gladium carnis, quod est verbum mendax diaboli. Unde pugnant contra me & in materna viscera vires conuertunt. Quos aduocem defensores, quos quæram adiutores, quos mihi propugnatores sperem; non a filiis derelicta tantum, sed hostiliter impugnata? Olim, olim sæuiente tyrannorum rabie, me tutata est constantia martyrum: inualescente hæreticorum fraudulenta calliditate me protexit sapientia doctorum: modo quid agam cum amici mei & proximi aduersum me appropinquauerunt & steterunt? An non ergo sunt prudentes congerendis opibus, instruendis dapibus, cumulandis honoribus, pompis fouendis, & negligentes regendis plebibus, alendis pauperibus, diligendis humilibus & superfluitatibus coercendis? An non potius de beneficiis disceptant per leges Iustiniani, quam populum erudiant & doceant legem Christi? doceant dico, imo discant. Nam quem è sacerdotum numero mihi dabis non ignarum legis Christi? An non augmentis plus inhiant facultatum quam lucris animarum? Quis autem hæc à carnis prudentia prosicisci negauerit? Iam vero multas mihi mouerunt lachrymas carnalis amoris argumenta clarissima: cum alium ambitione corruptum per scelus dignitates rapere conari cernerem: ingratum abire, earum vi potentia, per eam vim adhibere, aurum polliceri, minis terrere, allicere blanditiis: fas nefasq; confundere, non reuocatum neque metu legum neque exemplorum Dathan & Abyron, Simonis magi, regis Ozeæ. Lugebam quoque cernens alios auaritia rapaci oues ípoliare exactionibus: exactiones cumulare, accusationes struere, ferere lites: falsis criminibus innocentes impetere, congerere pecunias, terrenis tantum modo negotiis intendere: quibus salubriter consultum putarent, si mallent Aristotelem audire, quam Apostoli præterire mandatum. Ille patribus familias opulentis consilium dat, vt administrandarum facultatum atque familiæ negotium procuratoribus imponant: ipsi vero simul viuant aut philosophentur. Sed modicum miror apud istos Aristotelem contemni: apud quos nihil valet Apostolorum exemplum salubre: qui ne verbum Dei relinquere cogerentur, septem Diaconos pro ministerium mensarum instituerunt. Nec sine lachrymis inspicere poteram alium concubinatu pollui: cui tamen vt puritatem euangelicam æmuletur connubium est interdictum: luxuriam non clam, sed in propatulo habere, fœdis factis fœda verba coniungere: dapibus implere ventrem: inebriari vino doctum: & ad calicem vigilanti stertere naso: & mille malis aliis prope conspectis, fluebant mihi lachrymæ: nec fluere desinent, nisi malas istas radices peiorum germinum matres succisas agnouero.
units.tr: Therefore, since those arts are lacking among my defenders, by which their predecessors won me my dignity and wealth, attacks are made on my dignity and riches from every side. And just as from those roots, as it were, of peace, peace has spread most widely, so from these, as it were, stocks of discord, all schisms have both been born and been nourished. O unworthy deed, O most wicked treachery! My soldiers, who are also my sons, whom I have raised to the greatest honours and riches, have deserted to the chief enemy, having had their armour protected by my Spouse: the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit. And by a shameful treaty of peace they have put on the armour of that enemy: the breastplate of unrighteousness, the shield of carnal prudence, the helmet of worldly love, the sword of the flesh, which is the lying word of the devil. From this they fight against me and turn their strength into their mother's bowels. Whom shall I call as defenders, whom shall I seek as helpers, whom shall I hope for as champions, when I am not only abandoned by my sons but also attacked as enemies? Formerly, while the fury of tyrants raged, the constancy of the martyrs defended me; when the deceitful cunning of heretics grew strong, the wisdom of the teachers protected me. Now what am I to do, when my friends and neighbours have approached and taken their stand against me? Are they not then wise in gathering wealth, in providing feasts, in piling up honours, in fostering pomp, and negligent in ruling the people, feeding the poor, loving the humble, and restraining excess? Do they not rather dispute about benefices by the laws of Justinian than instruct and teach the people the law of Christ? I say teach; nay rather, learn. For which of the priests will you give me who is not ignorant of the law of Christ? Do they not long for increases of property more than for gains of souls? Yet who would deny that these things proceed from carnal prudence? Indeed, the clearest proofs of carnal love have often drawn tears from me: when I saw another, corrupted by ambition, trying wickedly to seize dignities; when I saw him go away ungrateful, using the power of his office to force his way, promising gold, terrifying with threats, enticing with flatteries, confusing right and wrong, and not called back either by fear of the laws or by the examples of Dathan and Abiram, of Simon the magician, or of King Hoshea. I also mourned when I saw others, with rapacious greed, plundering the sheep by exactions: piling up exactions, building up accusations, stirring up lawsuits, attacking the innocent with false charges, heaping up money, and devoting themselves only to earthly business. They would think it wholesome for them if they preferred to hear Aristotle rather than to disregard the command of the Apostle. Aristotle advises wealthy heads of families to hand over the business of managing their property and household to stewards, while they themselves live at ease or philosophize. But I wonder a little that Aristotle is despised by these men, among whom the wholesome example of the Apostles counts for nothing: who, so that they should not be forced to leave the word of God, appointed seven deacons for the ministry of tables. Nor could I look on without tears when another was polluted by concubinage, to whom, nevertheless, marriage is forbidden so that he may imitate evangelical purity; when he kept luxury not in secret but in the open, joining foul words to foul deeds, filling his belly with feasts, made drunk with wine, and snoring at the chalice with a wakeful nose; and with almost a thousand other evils in view, tears flowed for me. Nor will they cease to flow until I recognize these evil roots, the mothers of worse offspring, as cut away.

units.la: Nam quid postremo de spe mendaci proferam? Quid sacerdotes sperare dicam: vtrum sempiternam gloriam? Hæc profecto eorum postrema cura est. Sed quid? Sperant beneficia consequi, sperant emolumenta terrena: sub noua lege veterascunt: cum nouis præmiis æternisque relictis ad legis Moysis vetustatem resoluuntur: & ex schola credo Stoicorum, non certe Christianorum honores istos caducos beneficiorum virtutis præmia ducunt. Quod facturos non existimo, nisi ita oculos ad opes honoresque conuerterent, vt onera non aduerterent: nisi honorum dulcedinem & non onerum amaritudinem inspicerent.
units.tr: For what, finally, shall I say of their lying hope? What shall I say that priests hope for: eternal glory? Surely that is their last concern. But what? They hope to obtain benefices, they hope for earthly gains; under the new law they grow old, and, leaving behind the new rewards and eternal ones, they relapse into the antiquity of the law of Moses; and, following, I believe, the school of the Stoics rather than of the Christians, they count these fleeting honours as the rewards of virtue. I do not think they would do this unless they turned their eyes so towards wealth and honours that they did not notice the burdens, unless they looked on the sweetness of the honours and not the bitterness of the burdens.

units.la: An tibi videtur nauclerus summis tempestatibus vsque ad finem dierum meorum mariinandus recte præmium putare terrenum commodum, quod tantis periculis coniunctum videri? Non putabit, inquies, nisi tempestatis immemor. Caeterum quis viator pro laborum premio eam pecuniam sumpserit, quam nisi per medios latrones prædonesque manu semper portauerit possidere non liceat? Nullus inquies nisi salutis oblitus. Ergo si in beneficiis statum lubricum sempiterneque poenę nimis facile periculum inesse certum sit, quis intelligens non ea magis suscipere metuat timore periculorum quam quaerat spe commodorum? Quocirca soleo mirari quid hi sibi voluerunt, qui primum gratias expectatiuas applantauerunt? sed vt video iam dudum vera rerum vocabula amissa sunt.
units.tr: Does it seem to you that a sailor who must sail through the greatest storms until the end of my days rightly regards as his reward an earthly advantage which seems joined with such great dangers? "He will not think so," you will say, "unless he forgets the storm." But what traveller would take as the reward of his labours that money which he could not keep at all unless he always carried it in his hand through the midst of robbers and plunderers? "No one," you will say, "unless he has forgotten his salvation." Therefore, if it is certain that in benefices there is a slippery state and a danger of eternal punishment that is too easily incurred, who that understands would not fear to undertake them from fear of dangers rather than seek them in hope of advantages? Wherefore I am accustomed to wonder what those men meant who first wore out the expectative graces; but, as I see, the true names of things have long since been lost.

units.la: Habes itaque vel maximas afflictionis meæ causas: quia dum omnes quæ sua sunt quærunt non quæ Iesu Christi: & quod sibi vtile est, non quod multis: dum suaui carnis pastui tantum carnalesque intendunt, currunt ad honores: onera reiiciunt: quærunt iucunda, molesta fugiunt, quod in alieno statu dulce viderint ad se rapere, quod in proprio amarum cognouerunt in alios proiicere moliuntur. Inde discordiæ, lites, schismata, rixæ, timultates, & totius ordinis mei turpissima confusio. Quæro, Domine, si ab his pestibus hoc tempore liberabis ac restitues regnum Israel? Et precor vt restituas. Quod factum subinde spero. Quippe spiritualibus literis eruditissimos sacerdotes Dei legem ignorare non feres, vti sine damnationis periculis ignorare nequeunt. Quod multis auctoritatibus sacræ scripturæ confirmatum: sed breuitati studendum est.
units.tr: So you have the chief causes of my affliction. While everyone seeks his own things, not the things of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21), and what is useful to himself rather than what is useful to many (1 Cor. 10:33), while they pursue only the sweet feeding of the flesh and carnal things, they rush after honours, they shirk burdens, they seek pleasant things and flee unpleasant ones. What they have seen to be sweet in another's state they strive to snatch for themselves, and what they have found bitter in their own they labour to throw onto others. Hence discords, lawsuits, schisms, quarrels, tumults, and the most shameful confusion of my whole order. Lord, I ask whether you will free us from these plagues at this time and restore the kingdom to Israel (Acts 1:6). I pray that you will restore it, and I hope it will be done in due course. For you will not allow the most learned priests of God, who are instructed in spiritual letters, to be ignorant of the law, since they cannot be ignorant of it without danger of damnation. This is confirmed by many authorities of Holy Scripture, but I must be brief.

units.la: Denique cum à puero te cœlestis religio susceptum adeo spiritualiter viuere docuerit: vt id tibi in naturam conuersum sit: aduocabis spirituales viros ad beneficia, ab his carnales arcebis. Excludes quos spes improba ad importunè petendum impulerit: sed inuitos intrare coges quos parui pendere terrena comparatione cœlestium agnoueris. Exinde confusionem præsentis temporis reduces ad distinctionem ordinis. Coges quenque suum tenere locum, suo gradu contentari: officium exercere ordinis suscepti: limites non excedere: non perturbare terminos positos à patribus. Iubebis quemlibet esse contentum mensura statuum decente. Et quoniam prauæ cupiditati terminum imponit nemo: tu omnibus præfigere conaberis. Præcipies seminare spiritualia, qui metunt carnalia. Et contra leges recte latas quantalibet importunitate petentium fatigeris, nunquam dispensabis nisi aut necessitas vrgeat, aut communis prouocet vtilitas. Alioquin fuerit potius crudelis dissipatio quam iusta dispensatio. Cauebis dispensationem ipsam lege communiorem facere, ne turpe sit, si regulam sua vincat exceptio. Si hæc feceris ad quæ te suscepti officii debitum astringit: tum schismatum auulsis radicibus pax ipsa Christiana sibi terrarum orbem denuo vendicabit. Et in hoc positum est vnicum pacis stabile fundamentum: sine quo si quis ædificare voluerit, nihilo plus agit, quam si det operam vt grauia tecta parietibus arundineis superimponat. Morum corruptio fuit prima causa mali: quorum morum correctio erat prima causa boni. Verum hic labor, hic opus est, ne hoc facere possis, nisi te propinqui tui ac domestici iuuerint. Proinde Gregoriano exemplo persuasus aduocabis tibi tantorum laborum socios clericorum ac religiosorum quosque prudentissimos ac optimos. Ornabis domum tuam sanctis, prudentibus, modestis, integris, incorruptis. Quam enim domum decet sanctitudo, si non tuam Domine? Certe parum profutura est tua vnius iustitia, si ea vicerit dissimilis aliorum affectio. Veteris subinde membris tuis, regisque summi secutus exemplum, quemadmodum ab illo discurrunt assidue Spiritus angelici ad hominum ministeria: sic diriges per orbem terrarum pacis nuncios. Vide tamen qualibus membris vtaris: sunt quædam paralytica, quæ si volueris in dextrum mouere, prauè potius ferentur in sinistrum. Proinde magna cura tibi subeunda est, vt ad hoc ministerium idonea diligas. Posthabebis rerum minorum curas, vt huic maximæ maior ac efficacior inseruias. Vide quæso si careas oneribus: vide si quis alius tanta sollicitudine fatigetur, quanta tu. Vere hoc dixerim, summus honor, summum onus. Sed ne te onus terreat, si bene ministraueris, summi oneris summum præmium. Vide denique si non tibi incumbat cum eximio rege psallere: durum quidem, sed vigilantis viri canticum: Si dedero somnum oculis meis, & palpebris meis dormitationem, & requiem temporibus meis, donec inueniam locum Domino. Sed quem locum? Pacem nempe. In pace factus est locus eius. Sed quæ nam est hæc pax? tranquilla bonorum concordia. Non enim est pax impiis, dicit Dominus. Tolle igitur vitia: reduc virtutes. Redde mihi formam, redde vitam, redde etiam cum Domino gratum locum inuenire cum hoc tempore regnum Israel restitueris. Hæc ecclesia tecum. Cuius vocibus nihil aliud adiicio, nisi precationem humilem: vt det Deus dies vitæ ac robur virtutis, vt sub tuo pontificio pulchræ pacis dilatationem amplissimam videre possimus, Amen.
units.tr: Finally, since the heavenly religion, from your boyhood, has taught you to live so spiritually that this has become second nature to you, you will summon spiritual men to benefices and keep carnal men away from them. You will exclude those whom wicked hope has driven to seek importunately, but you will compel those unwilling to enter whom you recognise as caring little for earthly things in comparison with heavenly. Then you will lead the present confusion back to the distinction of orders. You will compel each to keep his own place, to be content with his own rank, to perform the duties of the order he has taken up, not to exceed his limits, and not to disturb the boundaries set by the Fathers. You will order everyone to be content with a measure of status that befits him. And since no one sets a limit to wicked desire, you will try to set one for all. You will command those who reap carnal things to sow spiritual things. And though you be worn down by whatever importunity of petitioners, you will never dispense against laws rightly enacted, unless necessity presses or common advantage calls for it. Otherwise dissipation would rather be cruel than dispensation just. You will take care not to make the dispensation itself more common than the law, lest it be shameful if the exception should overcome the rule. If you do these things, to which the obligation of the office you have undertaken binds you, then, with the roots of the schisms torn away, Christian peace itself will reclaim the whole orb of the earth for itself. In this lies the one stable foundation of peace; whoever wishes to build without it accomplishes no more than if he laboured to place heavy roofs upon walls of reeds. The corruption of morals was the first cause of evil; the correction of morals was the first cause of good. But this is the labour, this is the work, and you cannot do it unless your relatives and household help you. Therefore, persuaded by the example of Gregory, you will summon to yourself as companions in such great labours the most prudent and best of the clergy and religious. You will adorn your house with holy, prudent, modest, upright, and incorrupt men. For what holiness befits a house, if not yours, Lord? Surely your righteousness alone will avail little if the dissimilar affection of others prevails. Then, following the example of the supreme King, from whom the angelic spirits run constantly to the ministry of men, you will send messengers of peace throughout the world. Yet see what members you use: some are paralysed, and if you wish to move them to the right, they are carried rather wrongly to the left. Therefore great care must be taken by you to choose those suitable for this ministry. You will set aside the cares of lesser things, that you may serve this greatest task with greater and more effective diligence. Please see whether you are free of burdens; see whether anyone else is worn down by such anxiety as you are. I may truly say this: it is the highest honour and the highest burden. But lest the burden frighten you, know that if you minister well, the highest burden has the highest reward. Finally, see whether it does not befall you to sing with that excellent king: it is hard indeed, but it is the song of a watchful man: If I give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord (Ps. 132:4-5). But what place? Peace, of course. His place is made in peace. But what is this peace? The quiet concord of good men. For there is no peace to the wicked, says the Lord (Isa. 48:22). Therefore take away vices; restore virtues. Give me back the form, give me back life; give back also, when you have restored the kingdom of Israel at this time, a place pleasing to the Lord to be found. This is the Church speaking to you. To her voices I add nothing except a humble prayer: that God may grant days of life and strength of virtue, so that under your pontificate we may see the most ample extension of beautiful peace, Amen.

units.la: SERMO EIVSDEM HABITVS MASSILIÆ CORAM PAPA BENEDICTO, ANNO M. CCCCIII. NONA Nouembris.
units.tr: A sermon by the same man, delivered at Marseille before Pope Benedict in the year 1403, on the ninth of November.

units.la: Benedic hæreditati tuæ sanctissime pater Benedicte: benedic obsecramus, vt secundum nomen tuum sit & laus & operatio tua: det benedictionem Benedictus: quoniam absque benedictione præuia eloquium nostrum prorsus esset inualidum, eloquium, inquam, quod ego seruus tuus pro parte & nomine hereditatis tuæ peculiaris, quæ est Vniuersitas Parisiensis præclarissima, absque dubitatione & primogenita studiorum habiturus sum cum istis legatis suis præclarissimis & probatissimis certe viris sanctitati tuæ fidelissimis: quibus assotiatus sum immeritus, & dux verbi factus: & hoc te propitio, pater beatissime, te benedicente, te benigno. Alioquin nisi tu Dominus dederis benignitatem: terra nostra, quæ est hæreditas tua, quo pacto dabit fructum suum. Nisi benedictionem dederit legislator: subditi quibus passibus ibunt de virtute in virtutem? Denique nisi tu Dominus iusseris benedicere: quo ausu auderet paruitas mea coram summa tuæ beatitudinis celsitudine in conspectu huius celebris conuentus indignum os aperire. Igitur Benedicte pater sancte, benedic tu mihi: benedic & hereditati tuæ. Hanc ego benedictionis gratiam reportare sperans à beneuolentissimo & serenissimo S. T. spiritu: aperio rursus fidenter os meum: vtens compellatione singulari: non quidem pro indignitate (procul nefas tale) sed pro singulari dignitate: sicut tua singularis est dignitas: ne quis indigne ferat morem istum loquendi ad Deum: & priscam sanctorum patrum & oratorum consuetudinem: & obsecrans dico prophetica imprecatione: Benedic hereditati tuæ.
units.tr: Bless your inheritance, most holy Father Benedict; bless it, we beg you, so that both praise and work may be yours according to your name. May Benedictus give the blessing, since without a prior blessing our speech would be altogether weak. I mean the speech which I, your servant, am about to deliver, without doubt, on behalf of and in the name of your own peculiar inheritance, the most distinguished University of Paris, the firstborn of the studies, together with these your legates, most distinguished and approved men, certainly most faithful to your holiness. I, though unworthy, have been joined with them and made the spokesman of the word, and this with your favour, most blessed Father, with your blessing and your kindness. Otherwise, unless you, the Lord, give kindness, how will our land, which is your inheritance, yield its fruit? Unless the lawgiver gives the blessing, with what steps will the subjects go from virtue to virtue? Finally, unless you, the Lord, command a blessing, with what daring would my littleness presume to open an unworthy mouth before the supreme height of your blessedness, in the sight of this crowded assembly? Therefore, holy Father Benedict, bless me, and bless your inheritance too. Hoping to obtain this grace of blessing from the most benevolent and most serene Holy Spirit, I again confidently open my mouth, using this singular form of address. I use it not from unworthiness (far be such a thought) but from your singular dignity, just as your dignity is singular, so that no one may take it amiss that I speak thus to God, following the ancient custom of the holy Fathers and orators. Pleading, I say, with a prophetic prayer: Bless your inheritance.

units.la: Hæreditas hæc tua, cuius benedictionem expetimus, duplex inuenitur: vniuersalis & partialis: iuxta quod orationem nostram in duos secernimus articulos: sicut ad duo principaliter missi sumus. Primum & hoc præcipuum est quærere pacem super Israel: hoc est super ecclesiam, quæ est vniuersalis hereditas tua. Hereditas mea Israel, ait ille, cuius vicarius es in terris: & à quo tu pastor illi, tu colonus & agricola supremus prælatus es. Propterea sane cum beato Martino, cuius instat celebritas, felicem hanc virtutum suarum consummationem existimare debes, si pacem ecclesiæ integram reliqueris. Alter proinde nostræ legationis articulus est: benedictionem gratiarum postulare pro altera hereditate tua quodammodo peculiari: & quæ est ecclesiasticæ hereditatis pars quædam florentissima & præclarissima & electa: pace aliarum dixerim. De qua gloriari potes prophetica exultatione: etenim hereditas mea præclara est mihi. Hæc est humilis & devota S. T. filia Parisiensis Vniuersitas: quæcum Iacob non dimittit te, nisi benedixeris ei, consurgente aurora benignitatis tuæ. Eget nimirum utraque hereditas ista benedictione tua: vt aperiente te manum tuam, manum tuæ benedictionis omnia impleantur bonitate: & Domini sit salus, & super populum tuum benedictio tua. Inuasit itaque hereditatem ecclesiæ aper de sylua & singularis ferus depastus est eam. Oues quoque & cæteros armentorum greges, hoc est populos simplices & omnis conditionis homines miserando more & execranda penitus diuisione dispersserunt, & hereditatem tuam vexauerunt. Quam ego olim cladem iuuenis pastorio carmine deplorans Ethæus inquam: Heu gregis impacata lues nimis: heu graue iurk Exitium experta: heu pecoris sors altera semper: Aut perit externo insultu, suffert vel acerbos Hærentesque cuti morbos vicinaue damna, Qualia mysteria nunc patitur pecus: omnia postquam Fato versa malo tempus tulit & fuit error, Rixaque pastorum, sub quem me & innocuus grex Ductorem trepidat: fugiunt pars altera Tybrim, Pars Rhodanum, nullo incerto pars altera sistit.
units.tr: This inheritance of yours, whose blessing we seek, is found to be twofold: universal and partial. Accordingly we divide our address into two parts, since we have been sent principally for two purposes. The first, and this the chief, is to seek peace upon Israel, that is, upon the Church, which is your universal inheritance. My inheritance, Israel, says He whose vicar you are on earth, and of whom you are the shepherd, the supreme farmer and husbandman. Therefore, indeed, together with blessed Martin, whose feast is at hand, you ought to regard this as a happy completion of his virtues, if you leave the peace of the Church whole. The second part of our embassy, then, is to ask a blessing of grace for your other inheritance, which is in a certain way peculiar to you, and which is a most flourishing, most distinguished and chosen part of the ecclesiastical inheritance, I would say, without disparaging the others. Of it you may boast with prophetic exultation: for my inheritance is goodly to me. This is the humble and devoted daughter of Your Holiness, the University of Paris, who, like Jacob, will not let you go unless you bless her, as the dawn of your kindness rises. Both inheritances certainly need your blessing, so that, as you open your hand, all things may be filled with the goodness of the hand of your blessing, and that the salvation may be of the Lord and your blessing may be upon your people. Thus a boar out of the wood has invaded the inheritance of the Church, and a wild beast has fed upon it. They have also scattered the sheep and the other flocks of the herds, that is, the simple peoples and men of every condition, with a pitiable manner and a wholly detestable division, and have harassed your inheritance. I, lamenting this ruin once as a young man in pastoral song, Ethaeus I say: Alas, the unappeased plague of the flock! Alas, the heavy ruin it has suffered! Alas, the flock's fate is always another: either it perishes by a foreign assault, or it suffers bitter diseases clinging to its skin and neighbouring losses. Such are the calamities the flock now endures, after time, with every thing turned by evil fate and error, and the quarrel of the shepherds, under which I, and my harmless flock, fearful, have a leader: one part flees to the Tiber, another part to the Rhône, another part stands still in no uncertain place.

units.la: Tuum vero est, pater beatissime, talibus hereditatis tuæ calamitatibus obuiare, suæ desolationi opem ferre: suum quoque maledictionis schismaticæ opprobrium in benedictionem pacis decoram & fœcundam immutare. Oues in hac hereditate tua dispersæ sunt, tu eas collige: confractæ sunt, tu alliga: lauciæ sunt, tu sana: errantes sunt, tu reuoca: perditæ sunt, tu eas quæsitas inuentas propriis humeris & beatis, benignus imponens gregi suo consocia. Quod si aliquae fortassis miserabili vicissitudine mutatae sunt in lupos & beluas feroces & saevas, vt de sociis Vlyssis per Circen poetica & moralis est narratio, tu eas non enecare, non perdere volueris. Bonis quidem & discholis debitores, sapientibus & insipientibus. Sed potenti virtute benedictionis tuae in misericordia & mansuetudine, tales rursus in ouium simplicitatem transformare stude. Si versa est pars haereditatis tuae in amaritudinem & salsuginem: ob pestiferum schisma in similitudinem horrendi deserti & vastae solitudinis, sicubi pro vuis labruscae, pro frugibus
units.tr: It is yours, most blessed Father, to meet such calamities of your inheritance, to bring help to its desolation, and also to turn the disgrace of a schismatic curse into a seemly and fruitful blessing of peace. The sheep in this your inheritance are scattered; gather them. They are broken; bind them up. They are wounded; heal them. They are wandering; call them back. They are lost; seek them out, find them, and, kindly, place them on your own shoulders, blessed, joining them to your flock. If perhaps some have been changed by a pitiable turn of fortune into wolves and fierce and savage beasts, as in the poetic and moral narrative of Ulysses' companions among Circe's people, you should not wish to destroy them or to lose them. You owe a debt to the good and to the sluggish, to the wise and to the foolish. But by the powerful virtue of your blessing, in mercy and gentleness, strive to transform such again into the simplicity of sheep. If a part of your inheritance has been turned into bitterness and brackishness, through the pestilent schism, into the likeness of a horrible desert and a vast solitude, where, instead of grapes, wild vine appears, and instead of crops,

units.la: Infelix lolium & steriles dominantur avenae: vt Poeta loquitur, & vt Scriptura ait: sicubi terra maledicta spinas & tribulos germinat. Flabit Domine spiritus tuus bonus & suavis, & fluent aquae gratiarum, pinguescent speciosa deserti, & tuae benedictionis irroratione renouabitur facies terrae, facies vniuersalis haereditatis tuae. Nam & matrem humoris Philosophi lunam vocant.
units.tr: Unhappy darnel and barren oats hold sway, as the Poet says, and as Scripture says: where a cursed earth brings forth thorns and thistles. Lord, let your good and sweet Spirit blow, and the waters of grace will flow; the fair places of the wilderness will grow fat, and by the sprinkling of your blessing the face of the earth will be renewed, the face of your universal inheritance. For the philosophers also call the moon the mother of moisture.

units.la: At dices: magna sunt ista nimis & supra virtutem hominis posita. Magna sunt, nec inficior, pater beatissime, imo maxima: sed virtus Dei, cui inniti te conuenit, immensa est. Omnia possum (inquit Apostolus) in eo qui me confortat, Christus. Sed maledictus qui confidit in homine, & ponit carnem brachium suum. Magna sunt, propterea magno egent studio, curia, sollicitudine, vigiliis & labore. Nam vbi intenderis ingenium, valet: ait Iulius Caesar apud Sallustium. Magna sunt, propterea deserenda sunt exigua, & dispertienda linquendaque minoribus. In hoc opus vnum praecellentissimum figendi sunt considerationis oculi, mittenda est manus ad fortia, tempus quoque res omnium praetiosissima, in aliis non nisi parcissima raritate dispensandum, alioquin tale aliquid fieret, quasi quis piscaretur hamo aureo, iuxta verbum vnius e Caesaribus: aut quasi vile aliquid quaereretur in tenebris cum cereo centum aureorum. Alioquin praeterea rediret illa inculpatio Hietro ad Moysen: Stulto labore consumeris. Sic Petrus Clementem, sic Bernardus Eugenium, imo sic Apostolus discipulum suum charissimum monuerunt: Nemo militans, &c. Secularia iudicia, &c. Et in Actibus Apostolorum: Non est aequum, &c. Notiora sunt haec quam vt allegationibus indigeant. Magna denique sunt ista pacis vniuersalis opera: quamobrem ea tecum a multis quaerere conuenit. Nam vulgato proverbio, quod a pluribus quaeritur, citius inuenitur: & vbi duo vel tres congregati sunt in nomine meo, &c. inquit Christus &c. Et quis est, o Deus aequissime, quis est ex Christianis ecclesiae filiis, qui non inniti debeat pro sua portione & vocatione tantis opitulari miseriis? Quis tam luctuosae desolationi? quis labefactioni tantae haereditatis tuae non condolebit, & condolens quis pro viribus non obuiabit? Sed neq; hoc prohibere quisquam nisi mentis inops voluerit, vt in communi periculo commune sit auxilium. Quod si parum prospere successit hactenus labor plurimorum: non ideo desperandum, non succensendum eis, non spernenda prorsus operae:
units.tr: But you will say: these things are too great and placed beyond the power of man. They are great, I do not deny it, most blessed Father; indeed they are very great. But the power of God, on which it is fitting that you lean, is immeasurable. I can do all things (says the Apostle) in him who strengthens me, Christ. But cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm. These things are great, and therefore need great zeal, care, solicitude, vigils and labour. For, where you have directed your talent, it prevails, says Julius Caesar, as reported by Sallust. These things are great, and therefore small matters must be abandoned, and left to the lesser men to deal with. In this one most excellent work the eyes of consideration must be fixed, the hand must be sent to brave deeds; and time too, the most precious of all things, must be spent with the utmost scarcity on other matters, lest something of this kind should happen, as if someone were fishing with a golden hook, to use the words of one of the Caesars, or as if something worthless were sought in the dark with a candle of a hundred gold pieces. Otherwise that reproach would return, which was addressed to Jethro by Moses: You will wear yourself out with foolish labour. Thus Peter admonished Clement, thus Bernard admonished Eugenius, indeed thus the Apostle admonished his most beloved disciple: No one who serves as a soldier, etc. Worldly judgments, etc. And in the Acts of the Apostles: It is not fitting, etc. These things are better known than to need citations. Finally, these works of universal peace are great, and therefore it is fitting to seek them with you from many. For by the common proverb, what is sought by many is found more quickly, and where two or three are gathered together in my name, etc., says Christ, etc. And who is there, O most just God, who is there among the Christian sons of the Church who ought not to strive, according to his portion and calling, to bring help to such great miseries? Who will not grieve at such a sorrowful desolation, at the overthrow of so great an inheritance of yours? And who, grieving, will not, as far as his strength allows, oppose it? Nor would anyone wish to forbid this, unless he were lacking in mind, so that in a common danger there may be common help. But if the labour of many has so far met with little success, we must not on that account despair, nor be angry with them, nor utterly scorn the work:

units.la: Non est in medico semper, releuetur vt aeger.
units.tr: There is not always a physician at hand, so that the sick may be relieved.

units.la: Nec semper feriet quodcunque minabitur arcus.
units.tr: Nor will the bow always strike whatever it threatens.

units.la: Neque enim qui plantat, neque qui rigat est aliquid: sed qui incrementum dat Christus. Et non mentiebatur qui dixit: Timida sunt & incerta prouidentia nostra. Si post primum naufragium nauta nauem, & post prima vulnera miles aciem, & post vnam sterilitatem rusticus agrum desereret, ascriberetur hoc no cautelae, sed ignauiae, & qui sic consuleret, ageret insulse. Beniamitae iussu Domini bis descenderunt in praelium, bis victi sunt: vt primum purgati, humiliati & eruditi, victoriam tertio praelio sortirentur. Super omnia post opitulationem diuinam si pacem vniuersalem quaerimus, non inefficaciter perquiramus: quaeratur necesse est concors vnio huius obedientiae tecum, P.B. & secum: hoc est in capite & membris: praesertim in praeclarissimo, potentissimo, Christianissimo Franciae regno: cuius laudes quia per se celebres sunt, non enumero. Pax male per schisma & contentiones quaeritur. Nam vbi divisio perseuerat, audiatur quod omne regnum intra se diuisum desolabitur & quia
units.tr: For neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase. And he did not lie who said: Our providence is timid and uncertain. If a sailor, after his first shipwreck, abandoned his ship, or a soldier after his first wounds abandoned the battle line, or a farmer after one bad harvest abandoned his field, this would be ascribed not to caution but to cowardice, and whoever counselled so would be acting foolishly. By the command of the Lord the Benjamites twice went down to battle and twice were defeated, so that, having first been cleansed, humbled and instructed, they gained the victory in the third battle. Above all, after the help of God, if we seek universal peace, let us not seek it without effect: a harmonious union of this obedience with you, Holy Father, and with it, that is, in head and members, must surely be sought, especially in the most famous, most powerful and most Christian kingdom of France, whose praises I do not enumerate because they are famous in themselves. Peace is sought in vain through schism and quarrels. For where division persists, let us hear that every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and because

units.la: Conueniet nulli qui secum dissidet ipse.
units.tr: He who is at odds with himself will agree with no one.

units.la: Absint igitur procul omnes animositates odiosae. Non fiat aspectus retrorsum in quibus periculis & procellis nauis ecclesiae hactenus iactata sit: sed docti ab Apostolo extendentes nos & velum in anteriora, portum pacis optatum concordi laboris annisu petamus. Docent nos historiae gentilium, praesertim Romanorum consulum, qui licet aliunde dissiderent hostiliter mox in amicitiam conueniebant, dum reipublicae pax & vtilitas quaereretur. Hoc T. Liuius, hoc Valerius exemplis docent: & vetere Graecorum instituto charistia (seu communis gratia fiebat pro communi vtilitate, non prorsus dissimiliter ab anno iubilaeo Iudaeorum. Quod si filii Israel animo pacifico ibant ad praelium, filii ecclesiae quibus animis debent quaerere pacis bonum? Si Herodes & Pilatus facti sunt amici ad persequendum Christum, qualis debet esse pax ad eundem adorandum? His exemplis cum certa ratione permota humilis & devota S. T. filia, quam primum vniuit se in se, reuocans omnes perditos a suo consortio vel gremio quomodolibet alienatos, & ad honores pristinos restituens, monens insuper & maternaliter iubens vt iniuriarum praeteritarum nemo memor sit amplius, sed honori matris & vtilitati pacis omnia condonentur. Recedant vetera, noua sint omnia, quatenus liberioribus animis eo pax vniuersalis quaeratur, quo nulla particularis obstiterit discordia. Concordia (inquit Sallustius) parvae res crescunt, discordia maximae dilabuntur. Quidque concordiam Fratrum Praedicatorum antea fere desperatam operata est, commemorans & literis suis inserens zelum gradem, quem pro eadem concordiam dudum Parrisiis ostenderas, studens in hoc & sperans filia tua, tuae sanctitati non mediocriter complacere.
units.tr: Let all hateful animosities therefore be far away. Let us not look back at the dangers and storms through which the ship of the Church has hitherto been tossed; rather, taught by the Apostle, stretching ourselves and our sail forward, let us seek the desired harbour of peace with united effort of labour. The histories of the gentiles teach us, especially those of the Roman consuls, who, though they were hostile to one another for other reasons, soon came together in friendship whenever the peace and advantage of the commonwealth was sought. T. Livy and Valerius teach this by examples. And by the ancient custom of the Greeks, the charistia, or common grace, was held for the common advantage, not altogether unlike the Jubilee year of the Jews. If the sons of Israel went to battle with peaceful minds, with what dispositions ought the sons of the Church to seek the good of peace? If Herod and Pilate became friends for the purpose of persecuting Christ, what sort of peace ought there to be for worshipping him? Moved by these examples and by sound reason, your humble and devoted daughter, the Holy T., has at once united herself with herself, recalling to her company and bosom all the lost who have in any way been estranged from it, and restoring them to their former honours; she further admonishes and, as a mother, commands that no one be mindful any longer of past injuries, but that everything be pardoned for the honour of the mother and the advantage of peace. Let the old things pass away, let all things be new, so that universal peace may be sought with freer minds, the more so since no particular discord stands in the way. Concord, says Sallust, makes small things grow, discord makes the greatest things fall apart. And the concord of the Preaching Friars, which had been almost despaired of before, was brought about by her, she recalling and inserting into her letters the zeal you had long ago shown in Paris for the same concord, your daughter striving for this and hoping that she would not a little please Your Holiness.

units.la: Habes igitur, pater beatissime, filiam pacificam, & euangelicæ beatitudinis participem, dignam insuper quæ ad pacem vniuersalis hæreditatis tuæ quærendam admittatur, vt dicat exlententia: Facta sum coram eo quasi pacem reperiens. Scit ipsa quoniam tale est pacis bonum, vt multa propter eam tolerare, multa indulgere, dissimulare plurima: quæ vel corrigi, vel ad regulam duci nequeunt, oportet. Hoc sancti Patres scriptis suis, hoc exemplis docuerunt. Habentur in promptu dicta eorum in decretis & alibi copiose. Sed eorum dicta nunc allegare quotando coram scientibus legem loquor, & vbi res in se perspicua est, superfluum ne dicamus curiosum iudicamus, & à sanctorum Patrum vestigiis alienum, quia & ostentationem redolet, & cicatricosam fluidamque reddit orationem.
units.tr: You have therefore, most blessed Father, a peaceable daughter, a sharer in the blessedness of the gospel, worthy moreover to be admitted to seek the universal peace of your inheritance, so that the saying may apply: I have become in his eyes as one who finds peace. She knows that the good of peace is such that for its sake many things must be endured, many things indulged, and very many things overlooked, which cannot be corrected or brought under the rule. The holy Fathers taught this in their writings and by their examples. Their sayings are at hand in the decrees and elsewhere in abundance. But I judge it superfluous, not to say over-curious, to cite their sayings now, when I speak the law before those who know it, and where the matter is clear in itself; and it is foreign to the footsteps of the holy Fathers, since it smells of ostentation and makes the speech scarred and flowing.

units.la: Oritur ex præmissis consequenter intellectus dicti illius saluberrimi & verissimi si sane capiatur, quod communis error facit ius: hoc est, quod prælatus dominante opinione, etiam erronea in subditis, multa vel agere vel omittere tenetur, qualia si faceret aut dissimularet opinione huiusmodi non extante, ipse graui delicto teneretur obnoxius. Quæ doctrina præsenti negocio accommodatissima est, si iam eam dilatare liceret, sed oratio nostra certis coartanda est limitibus, & ad alia deproperat.
units.tr: From what has been said there follows an understanding of that most wholesome and most true saying, if it is rightly taken, that a common error makes law: that is, that a prelate, while a prevailing opinion, even an erroneous one, holds among his subjects, is bound both to do and to omit many things, which, if he did or overlooked them when no such opinion existed, he would himself be held liable for a grave offence. This doctrine is most suited to the present business, if it were now permitted to expand upon it; but our discourse must be confined within certain limits, and it hastens on to other matters.

units.la: Attamen prætergredi vllo modo neque possum nec debeo, dum ad concordem huius obedientiæ vanitatem exhortor: suadens iniuriarum quarumlibet obliuisci, quin summam tuæ mansuetudinis & mititatis laudem admirer, quæ exemplum mansuetudinum Dauid insecuta, caput ad maledictionem inclinauit, vt à Domino benedictionem pro maledictione reportaret, & benedictione hæreditatem possideret. Et cum Iuda Machabæo esset memoria tua in æternum in benedictione. Ecce Sathan accepta à Deo licentia (alioquin quid ipse potuisset) percussit te plagis multis tribulationum & angustiarum, iustissime quidem in ordine ad prouidentissimam Dei dispositionem: quoniam iustus est in omnibus viis suis, & sanctus in omnibus operibus suis. Per cuius prouidentiam fit, vt diligentibus Deum omnia cooperentur in bonum. Et qui secundum merita plebium disponit vitam rectorum, vt ait Gregorius, qui etiam proprio filio non pepercit, quin eum saturaret opprobriis. Demum nihilominus has commotiones peruersissimo intentionis fine mihi suscitasse videtur, ad quid? Nimirum vt essent pedibus tuis in laqueum & offensiones & scandalum. Quo pacto sic? Vt animus tuus generosus in indignatione & de indignatione in impatientiam, & de hoc in odium & diffidentiam & suspiciones anxias & trepidas quæ multos supplantarut laberetur, & in vindicandi libidinem excandescerent, & vt tandem abiecta mansuetudine dimisso omni consilio ad postremum omni studio prosecutionis ecclesiasticæ pacis: spiritus tuus natura mitis & suauis ad solam vindictæ carnificinam sub zeli iusti specie raperetur, lacerarentque oues proprias, protereret, abiceret, dissiparet: & propter suspiciones infidas & turbidas, res omnes timide gelideque ministraret: quali arte venatores aprosin propriam irritant necem, & lepusculos per vanam pennæ volitantis formidinem in verum tradunt periculum & laqueum. At benedictus Dominus & benedictus tu: quoniam laqueus iste desiderii vindictæ contritus est. Tua quippe mansuetudo non solum non lædata est à S. T. his fraudibus: sed mira quadam effulgentia magis & magis emicuit, vsque ad quendam intuentium stuporem, vsque ad pias lachrymas audientium, vt ad exemplum memoriale & vere Christianum apud omnes generationes posterorum. Quæ exempla omnia si referre voluero, nitar incassum, prius tempus & lingua deficient. Vnum tamen ex innumeris (quod fidelissima relatione didici) commemoretur exemplum: quod dum Parrisiis in sermone publico restitutionis pro parte regis feria secunda post Pentecostes coram populosissima & celeberrima vtriusque status frequentia retulissem illud suis suspiriis altis & subditis tacentes approbarunt, & non pauci ad pias vsque lachrymas (nec mirandum) compuncti sunt. Postquam sæuientibus vndique intumescentibusque procellis circa nauem ecclesiæ tu mysticus Ionas proiectus es in mare: hoc est in amaritudinem tribulationis, non deseruit te Deus, sed mirabiliter in ventre sacri palatii velut in ventre ceti conseruatum eduxit ad litus libertatis, & facta est tranquillitas maior. Tota quippe obedientia ista à tumultu siluit, eo tunc venit ad verendam tuæ celsitudinis pœnitentiam homo quidam non infimæ fortunæ, qui vltro confessus est te Patrem & Dominum suum, imo nostrum omnium, te Christum Domini nedum impie tangere, sed crudeli inauditoque parricidio interficere semel & iterum voluisse. Experunt opinor qui aderant, qua fronte vir tanti sacrilegii, vir tam nefarii facinoris conscius nō solum hoc facere, sed vel comparere præsumpsisset. Multi coeperunt toruos in eum oculos flectere, dentib. fremere, vix manus continere, nisi quod tuam expectabant sententiam, & qualem expectabant nisi vt diceres: Tollatur impius, exturbetur sacrilegus, ligatis manibus & pedibus trahatur ad carcerem, vt tradatur in mortem. At vero tu nihil horum dixisti pater clementissime: sed misericordiæ & mansuetudinis sinum aperiens, & clementiæ virgam extendens, præoccupasti confitentem reum, priusquam verba orationis complesset, serenissimo quoque vultu & verbis suauibus plenam præconcepti huius flagitii veniam indulsisti, vincens in bono malum: & cuius esses spiritus, cuius insuper vicarius, facto certissimo palam docens. Hoc egisse nonne satis erat ad misericordiam? Addita est assecuratio, trepidare vetans iureiurando firmata. Nam fit cui multum dimittitur, multum ingratum si de dimissione hæsitauerit. Dixit namque spiritus tuus bonus & suauis: Hoc faciat mihi Dominus & hoc addat, si vllas vnquam aduersum te odii vel vindictæ reliquias apud me seruauero: imo si quam pœnam in te posterius exercere voluero, illa in caput meum prior cadat. Nec indulgentiam tantummodo ego præsto, si deinceps bene te habueris, sed & tibi tuisq; similibus omnibus benevolentiam polliceor amplioræ. O dignissidignissimam summo Pontifice vocem. O responsum diuino viro conuenientissimum, O factum misericordiæ singularis: quod patrem & pastorem euangelicum repræsentat. Qui post persecutiones Paulum, post trinam negationem Petrum, & post portionem hereditatis luxuriose consumptam, iuniorem filium plus amauit. O diuinum factum, quod vtinam omnes populi, omnes quaquauersum nationes audirent: tum pro exemplo & imitatione, tum pro arguendo mendacii eos qui te rigidum & austerum, aut iræ memorem criminari moliuntur. Hæc est plane victoria Christiana, iniurias & iras non iniuriis & ira, sed misericordia & mansuetudine vincere, & imitari eum, qui etiam in cruce positus dixit: Pater ignosce illis, &c. Sic beatissimus Martinus, cum vrgeretur vt Briccium sibi contumeliosum abiiceret: Si, inquit, Christus Iudam: Martinus cur non Briccium tolerabit? Sileant nunc historiæ gentilium: quæ suorum quondam principum mansuetudinem amplissimis verbis extulerunt, vt Seneca Neronem in duobus voluminibus, Cicero Iulium Cæsarem in orationibus, Suetonius, Octauianum Augustum in historiis, & alii alios: comparantes eos vel asylo Romuli, vel ciuitatibus refugii, vel templo misericordiæ, quale describit Statius Thebaidos. Siquidem incomparabilis est istorum laus ad tuam gloriam, sicut vmbra ad serenam lucem, fumus obscurus ad purum ignem: palea volatilis ad solidum granum, imo sicut vitium ad virtutem.
units.tr: Yet I can and ought in no way pass over, while I exhort to the harmonious vanity of this obedience, urging that one forget whatever injuries, that I admire the highest praise of your gentleness and meekness, which, following the example of David's mildness, bowed its head to cursing, so that it might receive a blessing from the Lord in place of a curse, and possess the inheritance by blessing. And, as with Judas Maccabeus, your memory is in blessing for ever. Behold, Satan, having received permission from God (otherwise what could he have done himself), has struck you with many plagues of tribulations and distresses, most justly indeed in relation to the most provident disposition of God, since he is just in all his ways and holy in all his works. By his providence it comes about that all things work together for good for those who love God. And he who, as Gregory says, disposes the lives of rulers according to the merits of the peoples, who did not spare even his own Son but filled him with reproaches. Finally, he seems nevertheless to have stirred up these commotions for me with a most perverse purpose: to what end? Surely that they might be a snare, offences and a stumbling block at your feet. In what way so? That your generous spirit might slip, through indignation, from indignation into impatience, from this into hatred and distrust and anxious and trembling suspicions, which have overthrown many; that it might flare up into a lust for vengeance; and that at last, mildness cast aside and every plan dismissed, with every zeal for pursuing the ecclesiastical peace abandoned, your spirit, naturally gentle and sweet, might be dragged under the appearance of just zeal to the mere butchery of revenge, and might tear, trample, cast down and scatter its own sheep, and, because of faithless and turbid suspicions, administer all matters timidly and coldly. By such an art hunters provoke the boar to its own death, and by the vain fear of a flying feather they deliver hares into real danger and a snare. But blessed be the Lord, and blessed be you, since that snare of the desire for vengeance has been crushed. Your mildness, indeed, was not only not harmed by these deceits of the Holy T., but shone forth more and more with a wondrous radiance, even to the astonishment of onlookers, even to the pious tears of hearers, so as to be a memorable and truly Christian example among all the generations of posterity. If I should wish to recount all these examples, I would strive in vain; time and tongue would fail first. Yet let one example out of countless others be recorded, which I learned from a most trustworthy report: when, at Paris, in a public sermon on the restoration on behalf of the king, on the Monday after Pentecost, I had recounted it before the most crowded and most famous assembly of both estates, they approved it with deep sighs and, silent, with their subjects, and not a few were pricked to pious tears (nor is this to be wondered at). After the storms raging and swelling on every side around the ship of the Church, you were cast, like the mystical Jonah, into the sea, that is, into the bitterness of tribulation; God did not forsake you, but, preserving you wondrously in the belly of the sacred palace as in the belly of the whale, brought you forth to the shore of liberty, and a greater calm ensued. Indeed, that whole obedience fell silent from its tumult. Then there came to your venerable penitence a certain man of no humble fortune, who freely confessed that you are his Father and Lord, indeed of us all, and that you, the Christ of the Lord, not only had impiously touched him, but had twice wished to kill him with a cruel and unheard-of parricide. Those who were present, I believe, experienced with what brazenness a man guilty of such sacrilege, a man conscious of so wicked a crime, had presumed not only to do this but even to appear. Many began to turn fierce eyes upon him, to gnash their teeth, and could scarcely restrain their hands, except that they were awaiting your sentence, and what sentence did they await, but that you should say: Let the impious man be removed, let the sacrilegious man be thrust out, let him be dragged with hands and feet bound to prison, to be handed over to death? But you, most merciful Father, said none of these things; rather, opening the bosom of mercy and mildness and extending the rod of clemency, you anticipated the confessing offender before he had finished the words of his speech, and with a most serene countenance and gentle words you granted full pardon for this crime long premeditated, conquering evil with good; and by a most certain deed you plainly showed whose spirit you were, and, moreover, whose vicar. Was it not enough for mercy to have done this? An assurance was added, confirmed by an oath, forbidding him to tremble. For when much is forgiven, it is most ungrateful if one hesitates about the forgiveness. Indeed your good and sweet spirit said: May the Lord do so to me, and more also, if I have ever kept any remnants of hatred or vengeance against you in my heart; indeed, if I should wish to inflict any punishment on you afterwards, may that fall first upon my own head. Nor do I offer only pardon, if you conduct yourself well from now on, but I also promise goodwill to you and all your like, in ever greater measure. O most worthy voice of the supreme Pontiff! O response most fitting to a divine man! O deed of singular mercy, which represents a father and an evangelical shepherd! Who, after persecutions, loved Paul; after Peter's threefold denial, loved him; and after the portion of the inheritance wastefully consumed, loved the younger son more. O divine deed, which would that all peoples and all nations everywhere might hear: both for example and imitation, and for refuting those who strive to accuse you as harsh and austere, or as mindful of anger. This is plainly Christian victory: to conquer injuries and wrath not with injuries and wrath, but with mercy and mildness, and to imitate him who, even placed on the cross, said: Father, forgive them, etc. So the most blessed Martin, when he was urged to cast away Briccius, who had insulted him: If, he said, Christ bore Judas, why will Martin not bear Briccius? Let now the histories of the gentiles be silent, which once extolled with the most ample words the gentleness of their princes: as Seneca praised Nero in two volumes, Cicero praised Julius Caesar in his orations, Suetonius praised Octavian Augustus in his histories, and others others, comparing them to the asylum of Romulus, or to cities of refuge, or to the temple of mercy, such as Statius describes in the Thebaid. For indeed the praise of these men is incomparable beside your glory, as shadow is beside clear light, dark smoke beside pure fire, flying chaff beside solid grain, or rather as vice beside virtue.

units.la: Ipsa enim talium mansuetudo non pro diuino honore & authoritate, quam spernebant, & tu colis vnicam, sed inanem iactantiam, quam tu calcas, anhelabat. Collaudabunt alii cruentas bellorum victorias: & ambitiosos ex his triumphos mirabuntur. Plus apud me valet assertio sapientis: quod melior est sapiens viro forti: & qui dominatur animo suo, expugnatore vrbium. Quam sententiam aliis verbis Lyricus explicat: Latius regnes fragilem domando spiritum, quam si Lydiam remotis Gadibus iungas, & vterque Pænus serviat uni.
units.tr: For the mildness of such men was not aimed at divine honour and authority, which they despised, and which you alone cultivate, but at empty show, which you trample underfoot. Others will praise the bloody victories of wars and marvel at the triumphs that ambition wins from them. More weight with me is the saying of the wise man: a wise man is better than a strong man, and one who rules his own spirit is better than one who captures cities. The Lyric poet explains this same thought in other words: You would rule more widely by taming a restless spirit than if you joined Lydia to distant Gades and both Carthaginians served one man.

units.la: Quamobrem agnoscæ, Pater beatissime, cum quanta conscientiæ securitate, cum quali serenitate cordis fas habet dicere religiosissima devotio tua, dum crebro vel orat vel missam celebrat: Pater dimitte mihi debita mea, sicut & ego dimitto debitoribus meis. Et rursus cum Propheta: Domine Deus meus fecisti istud, si est iniquitas in manibus meis, &c. Ita pater beatissime imitaris Christum, qui cum maledice retur, non maledicebat, qui tentatus est per omnia vt misericors fieret: quem videmus propter passionem gloria & honore coronatum. Tantummodo non eripiat tibi blanda prosperitas misericordiam illam illam patientiam pene diuinam, quam sæviens aduersitas & seruauit & reddidit clariorem. Da veniam, si scrupulosior sim in hac parte. Nam fit aliquando suadente pacis inimico, nunc per se, nunc per adulatores, qui sunt arma sua & sagittæ, vt homo qui calamitate pressus, æquanimiter omnia nedum tolerauerat, sed indulserat: postmodum succedentibus prosperis repetit omnia a debitoribus suis cum rigore & fœnore, vt appareat indulgentiam priorem non ex virtute, sed vindicandi impossibilitate natam, nec dimisisse ex corde, sed in tempus more simiarum distulisse. Non cadat in hanc exprobrationem vera & perfecta dilectionis tuæ mansuetudo, neque fallat eam simulacrum fictum iustitiæ, quasi non melius sit vicisse mala per indulgentiam quam sæueritate, quasi rursus non sit præclarissima iustitia indulsisse simplicibus, & subditis pepercisse. Sic misericordiam & gratiam inuenias in conspectu tremendi iudicii Dei, qui sub bullis patentibus promisit misericordiam misericordibus, qui semel dimissa non repetit, qui iussit non esse memorem iniuriæ ciuium suorum. Sic in oratione tua confitens Domino exaudiaris, & non audias horrendum illud improperium Domini irascentis: Serue nequam nonne omne debitum dimisi tibi, &c. Sic præterea cum Dauid consequaris sedem regni in misericordia & mititate possideas terram, & delectaris in multitudine pacis super eam.
units.tr: Therefore, most blessed Father, recognise with what security of conscience and what serenity of heart your most religious devotion may rightly say, when you often pray or celebrate mass: Father, forgive me my debts, as I also forgive my debtors. And again with the Prophet: O Lord my God, if there is iniquity in my hands, you have done this, etc. Thus, most blessed Father, you imitate Christ, who, when he was reviled, did not revile, who was tested in all things so that he might become merciful, and whom we see crowned with glory and honour because of his passion. Only let not smooth prosperity snatch from you that mercy and that almost divine patience which raging adversity both preserved and made more illustrious. Pardon me if I am over-scrupulous on this point. For it sometimes happens, at the urging of an enemy of peace, now directly and now through flatterers, who are his weapons and arrows, that a man who, pressed by calamity, bore everything calmly and not only tolerated but forgave, afterwards, when prosperity follows, demands everything back from his debtors with harshness and interest. It then appears that his earlier indulgence was born not of virtue but of inability to take revenge, and that he did not forgive from the heart but only put off the matter for a time, like apes. Let the true and perfect mildness of your love not fall under this reproach, nor let a feigned image of justice deceive it, as if it were not better to overcome evils by indulgence than by severity, and as if it were not most excellent justice to have pardoned the simple and spared subjects. So may you find mercy and grace in the sight of the dreadful judgment of God, who in open charters promised mercy to the merciful, who does not demand again what has once been released, and who commanded that we not remember the injuries of our fellow citizens. So, confessing to the Lord in your prayer, you may be heard, and not hear that dreadful reproach of the angry Lord: Wicked servant, did I not forgive you all that debt? etc. So also, with David, you may attain the throne of the kingdom, and in mercy and meekness possess the land, and delight in the abundance of peace upon it.

units.la: Tandem propter mititatem doceat te Dominus vias suas, vt absque offendiculis ad impatientiæ lapidem dirigat pedes tuos in viam pacis, quam a te pacem petimus pater beatissime, dicentes: Benedic hereditati tuæ. Non quasi humana virtus quælibet hanc pacem præbere non insufficiens sit & infirma; nisi maior agat Deus, vt apud Virgilium est, præsertim in tam desperato & radicato schismate, quod est quasi cancer ægrescens medendo, & ingressibilis Dedali labyrinthus, & caput hydræ fabulosæ sua rescissione fœcundus, ita vt perisse videatur consilium a sapientibus, & dicere conueniat cum Iosaphat rege: Cum ignoramus quid agere debemus, hoc solum habemus residui, vt oculos nostros ad te dirigamus. Scimus nihilominus te post Deum, cui vicarius es, decere. Scimus ad te Hierarcham supremum spectare benedictionem huiusmodi hereditatis ecclesiasticæ, vt fiat pax in diebus nostris, & tu maxime inter montes suscipias pacem populo. Quod si perficis, benedictus eris in omnes generationes, & memoriam æternam his qui post te futuri sunt relinquis. Sin autem nō perfeceris, inchoaueris tamen & elaboraueris bona & antiqua fide, diligenti studio, pia & humili voluntate, per te si tuos (tui quippe sunt omnes) non perdetur merces tua, non laus, non gloria: res ipsa condemnabit mendacii eos, qui vel ignorantia vel liuore criminantur summam T.S. dignitatem, tuam vigilantiam, tuam charitatem. Facis hoc sedulo. Ita enim te facere & me sentire æquum est.
units.tr: Finally, may the Lord, because of your meekness, teach you his ways, so that he may direct your feet without stumbling, away from the stone of impatience and into the way of peace. This is the peace we ask of you, most blessed Father, saying: Bless your inheritance. Not as if any human virtue, however great, were sufficient and not weak in bestowing this peace, unless God acts more greatly, as in Virgil; and especially in so desperate and deep-rooted a schism, which is like a cancer that grows worse under treatment, an inextricable labyrinth of Daedalus, and a hydra's head made more fruitful by its cutting. So it seems that the counsel of the wise has perished, and it is fitting to say with King Jehoshaphat: When we do not know what we ought to do, we have this one thing left, that we turn our eyes to you. Nevertheless we know that you, after God, whose vicar you are, ought to do so. We know that the blessing of such an ecclesiastical inheritance looks to you as supreme Hierarch, that there may be peace in our days, and that you, above all, among the mountains may receive peace for the people. If you accomplish this, you will be blessed in all generations, and you will leave an eternal memory to those who come after you. But if you do not accomplish it, yet you will have begun and laboured with good and ancient faith, diligent zeal, and a pious and humble will; then your reward, your praise and your glory will not perish through you, if your people (for all are yours) are not lost through you. The thing itself will condemn as liars those who, out of ignorance or envy, accuse the supreme dignity of Your Holiness (T.S.), your vigilance and your charity. You do this diligently; for it is right that I think and feel that you do so.

units.la: Sed quo amplius stimuleris ad agendum: ascende frequenter sublimem mentis tuæ lucem, leuando te super te: vbi despectis elursum terris, versus iugiter & acriter ante mentis oculos in lumine fidei, in sublimitate spei, in latitudine charitatis, cum illo qui ait: Cogitaui dies antiquos, &c.
