For the connection of such a civil polity comes principally through laws and the gifts of nature, and it establishes its unity in these. The Church, however, as an ordered polity, has this unity, and beyond it has another, supernatural and divine, which has been mentioned. And so it follows consequently that the ecclesiastical polity is governed by more laws than any other polity.

units.la: Quarta: Congregatio ecclesiastica non habet vel habuit ex se potestatem ordinandi & consumendi per gradus varios atque Hierarchicos dignitatum & administrationum, quales in ipsa reperimus a summo praesulatu vsque ad infimum administrationis gradum, quicunque sit ille. Patet, quia supernaturalis est haec institutio, consurgens ex solo beneplacito liberalissimi conditoris. Nec (vt opinor) voluisset vnquam oppositum sentire praefatus magister Henricus de Hassia, dum ponit quod ecclesia posset sibi instituere summum Pontificem, si non fuisset immediate constitutus a Christo. Addit enim quod hoc potuisset ecclesia a Spiritu sancto edocta & authorizata, quod est probabiliter sentiendum.
units.tr: The fourth: the ecclesiastical congregation does not have, or has not had, of itself the power of ordaining and constituting, through various and hierarchical grades, the dignities and administrations which we find in it, from the highest prelacy down to the lowest grade of administration, whatever that may be. This is evident, because this institution is supernatural, arising from the good pleasure of the most generous founder alone. Nor (as I think) would the aforementioned master Henry of Hesse ever have held the opposite, when he states that the Church could have instituted for itself a supreme Pontiff, had he not been constituted immediately by Christ. For he adds that the Church could have done this, taught and authorised by the Holy Spirit, which is probably to be held.

units.la: Quinta: Congregatio corporis mystici ad vnum caput Christum semper habebit per omnem iunctutam gradus dignitatum & officiorum & administrationum, de quibus dictum est: patet ex illo verbo, donec occurramus omnes, &c. Propterea dicitur ecclesia desponsata Christo in sempiternum Osee 1. Dicitur praeterea habere semper in se semen ad sui propagationem & conseruationem vsque ad consummationem seculi.
units.tr: The fifth: the congregation of the mystical body under Christ as its one head will always have, through every joint, the grades of dignities, offices and administrations of which we have spoken. This is clear from that word, until we all come, and so on. Therefore the Church is said to be betrothed to Christ for ever, Hosea 1. It is further said always to have within itself the seed for its propagation and preservation until the end of the age.

units.la: Sexta: Congregatio ecclesiastica ad vnum caput Christum lege stante, non remanebit in sola muliere, imo nec in solis laicis, sed erunt vsque ad consummationem seculi episcopi & sacerdotes aliqui fideles.
units.tr: The sixth: the ecclesiastical congregation under Christ as its one head, while the law stands, will not remain in women alone, nor even in laymen alone, but there will be bishops and some faithful priests until the end of the age.

units.la: Septima: Congregatio ecclesiastica dici potest habere duplices partes integrantes eam, quaedam sunt fluentes, quaedam permanentes, & vt ita loquamur, essentiales. Primae sunt ipsae per-sonae sonæ mortales constitutæ in graduum varietate. Aliæ sunt ipsimet gradus dignitatum & administrationum. Exemplum in Papa & Papatu, in episcopo & episcopatu, & similibus: Papa fluit, Papatus stabilis est.
units.tr: The seventh: the ecclesiastical congregation may be said to have a twofold set of parts integral to it: some are flowing, and some are permanent and, so to speak, essential. The first are the persons themselves, mortal, constituted in the variety of grades. The others are the grades of dignities and administrations themselves. An example is the Pope and the Papacy, the bishop and the episcopate, and similar things: the Pope flows, the Papacy is stable.

units.la: Octaua: Congregatio ecclesiastica constituitur in suis partibus fluentibus & quodammodo materialibus, ministerio hominum secundum legem primitus indiram & insitam ipsi corpori ecclesiastico: & prout ipsum habet in se semen viuum & efficax seipsum multipicandi atque conseruandi in successione specificatam ad partes fluentes, & in successione eadem materiali, quam ad essentiales. Patet veritas ex illo verbo Apostoli: Nemo sibi assumat honorem, &c æterna. Et de prædicatoribus dicit: Quomodo prædicabunt nisi mittantur, &c. Et hæc veritas similiter posset inflectiad depositiones & degradationes & resecationes partium scandalizantium: sed pronunc omittatur.
units.tr: The eighth: the ecclesiastical congregation is constituted in its flowing and in some way material parts by the ministry of men, according to a law first impressed and implanted in the ecclesiastical body itself; and insofar as it has within itself a living and effective seed for multiplying and preserving itself, it is specified in succession both for the flowing parts and in the same material succession which it has for the essential ones. The truth is clear from that word of the Apostle, No one takes this honour to himself, and so on, eternal. And concerning preachers he says: How shall they preach unless they are sent?, and so on. And this truth could similarly be applied to depositions, degradations and the cutting off of scandalous parts; but for now let it be passed over.

units.la: Nona: Congregatio ecclesiastica habet claues ordinis & iurisdictionis alio & alio modo in se & in suis partibus fluentibus. Vt exempli gratia: claues datæ sunt Petro authoritatiue & exercitatiue, sed toti ecclesiæ vniuersaliter & susceptiue. Vel datæ sunt ecclesiæ vt in actu primo: & Petro vt in actu secundo.
units.tr: The ninth: the ecclesiastical congregation has the keys of order and jurisdiction in one way in itself, and in another way in its flowing parts. For example: the keys were given to Peter authoritatively and executively, but to the whole Church universally and receptively. Or they were given to the Church as in the first act, and to Peter as in the second act.

units.la: Decima: Congregatio ecclesiastica sic instituta est, vt castrorum acies ordinata, vel vt corpus integerrime perfectum: sic quod non est in potestate Papæ, vel alterius cuiuscunque deordinationem vel multitudinem in suis partibus essentialiter inducere. Vnde nec Papa posset inducere, quod nulli essent episcopi, nec curati, nec cardinales, pro quanto sunt successores Apostolorum in ecclesia sancta Dei. Sunt enim gradus omnes seminati à Christo in ecclesia primitiua, quanquam paruula: in qua nondum erant sic explicati gradus ecclesiasticæ Hierarchiæ, vt nunc inspicimus: quemadmodum spica totos numeros suos habet in grano, & nux arbor in nuce virtualiter continetur. Has vocant Philosophi incantationes formarum in materia.
units.tr: The tenth: the ecclesiastical congregation has been so instituted that it is like an ordered battle-line of camps, or like a body most perfectly whole; so that it is not within the power of the Pope, or of anyone else, to bring about in its parts essentially any disorder or multiplicity. Hence not even the Pope could bring it about that there should be no bishops, no parish priests, and no cardinals, insofar as they are successors of the Apostles in the holy Church of God. For all the grades were sown by Christ in the primitive Church, though in a small way; in it the grades of the ecclesiastical hierarchy were not yet so unfolded as we now see them, just as an ear of grain has all its numbers in the grain, and a nut-tree is virtually contained in the nut. The philosophers call these the incantations of forms in matter.

units.la: Vndecima: Congregatio ecclesiastica licet non possit instituere Papatum vel destituere, nihilominus potest per se vel per concilium eam repræsentans statuere alium modum eligendi Papam, quam modo fit, vt alias visum est. Potest insuper remouere Papam etiam rite electum & alium constituere, si ita sibi visum fuerit expedire ad ædificationem ecclesiæ, vt in casu grauis scandali vel in dubio aliter interminabili quam per cessionem vel deiectionem Papæ, aut alio tali casu. Ipse enim pastor instituitur pro vtilitate gregis, & dum præsidentia sua cedit in graue detrimentum, mercenarius reputandus est, imo latro, imo lupus rapax: si quæritin præsidentia tam damnosa remanere. Et hic fundatur possibilitas practicandi viam cessionis saltem quo ad effectum suum contradicentibus, contendentibus & inuitis. Hic fundatur præterea, quomodo in casu veritatis istius congregatio vrgens Papam, ad cessionem deiiciens eum, si pertinaci libidine dominandi motus renuat, non est iudicanda, quod eum persequatur: sed ei potius & Deo & ecclesiæ toti multipliciter oblequatur.
units.tr: The eleventh: the ecclesiastical congregation, although it cannot institute or depose the Papacy, can nevertheless, either by itself or through a council representing it, establish another mode of electing a Pope than the one now in use, as has been said elsewhere. Moreover, it can remove even a Pope who has been duly elected, and appoint another, if it has seemed to it expedient for the edification of the Church, as in a case of grave scandal or in a doubt otherwise endless, than by the cession or deposition of the Pope, or in some other such case. For the pastor is appointed for the good of the flock, and when his presidency turns to grave loss, he is to be regarded as a hireling, indeed a thief, indeed a ravening wolf, if he seeks to remain in a presidency so harmful. And here is founded the possibility of pursuing the way of cession, at least as far as its effect goes, even against those who contradict, contend and are unwilling. Here is further founded how, in the case of this truth, a congregation pressing the Pope, casting him down to cession, if he refuses out of stubborn lust for domination, is not to be judged to be persecuting him; rather, it is serving him, and God, and the whole Church, in many ways.

units.la: Duodecima: Congregatio ecclesiæ licite & meritorie potest in casu fieri sine Papa vel authoritate sua. Itaque cum possit dupliciter fieri congregatio: vno modo concordatiue vel assentiue seu charitatiue, alio modo authoritatiue. Constat de primo congregandi modo, quod sine Papa possibilis est: imo fuit sæpissime practicatus tam apud Apostolos, quam apud Imperatores sanctos & catholicos, qui sæpe conuenerunt in vnum, priusquam essent euocati vel authorizati à Papa. Patet de quatuor primis conciliis memoratis in Actibus Apostolorum. De primo nondum erat adhuc Petrus factus Papa, quin simul erant congregati ad examinationem testimoniorum de resurrectione. Vnde & quælibet congregatio libera non subiecta tyrannidi habet hanc facultatem seipsam congregandi. Patet in confraternitatibus, & aliis multis conuentionibus charitatiuis. Secundus modus conuocationis habet maiorem quæstionem: nihilominus oportet eum concedere possibilem: alioquin periclitaretur respublica ecclesiæ, si necesse esset authoritatem Papæ prius interuenire. Exempli gratia. Immineat casus periclitationis ecclesiæ, sit in temporalibus, sit in spiritualibus, & quod tunc nullus esset Papa, nec posset prius institui quam esset prouidendum ecclesiæ per assensum communem. Item in casu quo Papa perdidisset vsum rationis perpetuæ. Item in casu quo Papa deprauatus esset in intellectu per hæresim, & in effectu per enormes & scandalosos mores, & ad destructionem ecclesiæ patenter laboraret.
units.tr: The twelfth: a congregation of the Church can lawfully and meritoriously be held in a case without the Pope or his authority. For a congregation can be held in two ways: in one way by agreement, or by assent, or by charity, and in another way by authority. It is established that the first way of gathering is possible without the Pope; indeed it was very often practised, both among the Apostles and among holy and Catholic emperors, who often assembled together before they were summoned or authorised by the Pope. This is clear from the first four councils mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles. At the first, Peter had not yet been made Pope, yet they were all gathered together to examine the testimonies about the resurrection. Hence any free congregation, not subject to tyranny, has this power of gathering itself. This is clear in confraternities and many other charitable assemblies. The second mode of convocation raises a greater question; nevertheless it must be conceded as possible, otherwise the commonwealth of the Church would be in peril, if it were necessary for the authority of the Pope to intervene first. For example: let there be an imminent case of peril to the Church, whether in temporal or in spiritual matters, and let there then be no Pope, nor could one be instituted before the Church had been provided for by common consent. Likewise, in the case where the Pope had lost the use of reason permanently. Likewise, in the case where the Pope had been corrupted in understanding by heresy, and in practice by enormous and scandalous morals, and was openly labouring to the destruction of the Church.

units.la: Item in casu quo requisitus sufficienter & monitus dare nollet authoritatem concilio: vt forte est in præsenti casu, quia signum est quod non vult audire ecclesiam, si non vult eam congregare.
units.tr: Likewise, in the case where, when sufficiently asked and warned, he is unwilling to give authority to the council, as perhaps is the case now, since it is a sign that he does not wish to hear the Church if he will not call it together.

units.la: Item vbi probabiliter dubitatur, quod fideles nunquam ei præstabunt obedientiam qualemcunque, aut non satis vtiliter atq; concorditer. In talibus & similibus casibus congregatio ecclesiastica sumit authoritatem & virtutem seipsam vniendi ex diuino semine per vniuersum corpus suum diffuso, vt dictum est, Et ad hoc est textus legis Deuter. 17. & notat Christus Matth. 18. resoluens tandem omnia ad ecclesiæ iudicium: Si inquit ecclesiam non audierit.
units.tr: Likewise, where it is probably doubted that the faithful will ever render him any obedience at all, or not one that is sufficiently useful and harmonious. In such and similar cases the ecclesiastical congregation takes to itself the authority and power of uniting itself, drawn from the divine seed diffused through its whole body, as has been said. To this point belongs the text of the law in Deuteronomy 17, and Christ notes it in Matthew 18, finally resolving all things to the judgment of the Church: "If he," he says, "will not hear the Church."

units.la: Obmutescat igitur animalis siue literalis & carnalis homo, & spirituali magis credat deducenti & probanti per priora, quod expedit quo ad primam considerationem, & decet quo ad secundam, & licet quo ad hanc quartam, quod congregentur filii Israel & Iuda pariter. Ad quid nimirum vt ponant sibimet caput vnum, non ad disceptandum & discutiendum & arguendum & litigandum, sicut phantasiari videbatur animalis homo. Hoc enim fortasis inducere posset indecentiam & multam tribulationis materiam. Cæterum quo ad allegationem quæ fiebat ab animali homine: quod necesse & expediens erat esse schisma, sicut olim Dominus voluit dissensionem esse inter filios Israel & filios Iuda. Solutio facilis est, quoniam non sunt facienda per homines mala, ut eueniant bona. Neque enim scient ex malis bona elicere, sicut Dominus ex nostris peccatis & scandalis potenter elicit bona, tanquam attingens a fine peccatorum usque ad finem comprehensorum fortiter, & disponens omnia suauiter faciendo, ut omnia cooperentur in bonum his qui secundum propositum vocati sunt sancti. Denique non potest lege stante politia ecclesiastica, quae est monarchica, in aliam transformari, sicut est in alia politia.
units.tr: Let therefore the animal or literal and carnal man be silenced, and let him believe rather the spiritual man who leads and proves by what has gone before: what is expedient as to the first consideration, what is fitting as to the second, and what is lawful as to this fourth, that the sons of Israel and Judah should be gathered together. Surely this is so that they may set for themselves one head, not for disputing, discussing, arguing and quarrelling, as the animal man seemed to imagine. For this might perhaps bring about indecency and much matter of tribulation. As for the allegation made by the animal man, that it was necessary and expedient that there be a schism, just as the Lord once willed there to be dissension between the sons of Israel and the sons of Judah: the answer is easy, since evils are not to be done by men so that good things may come of them. For they will not know how to draw good out of evils, whereas the Lord mightily draws good out of our sins and scandals, reaching from the end of sins to the end of the saved with strength, and disposing all things sweetly, so that all things work together for good for those who are called according to purpose, who are saints. Finally, while the law stands, the ecclesiastical polity, which is monarchical, cannot be transformed into another, as is the case with other polities.

units.la: Tandem multis praetermissis, neque enim locus neque tempus, non stilus neque ingenium, non memoria patiuntur omnia dicere quae dicenda essent: fiat ad opuscula & tractatus super his consectos recursus liberior. Concludamus ergo ex quatuor causis per totidem considerationes tactis potius quam deductis, quod expedit, decet & licet quod congregentur filii Israel & Iuda pariter. Congratulatur amatrix bonorum omnium Parisiensis Vniuersitas, mater mea, ut dicere coepimus, congratulatur vestrae devotioni, vestro zelo feruenti, vestrae religiosissimae ad matrem ecclesiam pietati: vestrae tandem laudabilissimae legationi, o reuerendissimi & spectabiles viri patres & fratres, det auxilium Deus in progressu egressum felicissimum & votiuum. Denique offert seipsam totam & iu membris singulis eadem vniuersitas ad omnia communi consensu & deliberatione aquisanda, tractanda, communicanda, concludenda, prosequenda cum omni humilitate & fauore, nihil quaerendo quod suum esse videatur, sed quod omnium, ut habeatur unum & certum caput secundarium in ecclesia sancta Dei, postpositis contentionibus omnibus & discussionibus odiosis, quae ad hanc rem non satis attinent, sed magis ad diuisionem, & practicando viam compendiosissimam & sanctissimam cessionis amborum contendentium, ut iurauerunt solenniter & vouerunt. Neque praeterea sit contentio, quis in hoc negocio prosequendo videatur esse maior vel potior vel doctior. Scit eadem vniuersitas, quod stabimus omnes ante tribunal Dei, illic videbitur, quo quisque animo, quo zelo, qua intentione pacem veram suae sponsae quaesierit. Sit igitur haec gloria nostra testimonium conscientiae nostrae, sit gloria Deo. Nam denuntians angelus pacem hominibus promisit: Gloria in excelsis Deo.
units.tr: Finally, with many things passed over, since neither place nor time, neither style nor talent, nor memory allows everything that ought to be said to be said, let recourse to the little works and treatises devoted to these matters be made more freely. Let us therefore conclude, from four causes touched upon rather than developed through as many considerations, that it is expedient, fitting and lawful that the sons of Israel and Judah be gathered together. The Parisian University, lover of all good things, my mother, as we have begun to say, congratulates your devotion, your fervent zeal, your most religious piety towards mother Church, and finally your most praiseworthy embassy, O most reverend and distinguished men, fathers and brothers. May God grant help in the progress, and a most happy and desired outcome. Finally, the same University offers itself wholly, and each of its members, to seek, treat, communicate, conclude and pursue all things by common consent and deliberation, with all humility and goodwill, seeking nothing that seems to be its own, but what belongs to all, so that there may be one certain secondary head in the holy Church of God, all contentions and odious discussions being set aside, which do not sufficiently pertain to this matter but rather tend to division, and by practising the shortest and most holy way of the ceding of both contending parties, as they solemnly swore and vowed. Let there be no further contention as to who in prosecuting this business seems to be greater, more powerful or more learned. The same University knows that we shall all stand before the judgment seat of God, where it will be seen with what mind, what zeal, and what intention each sought the true peace of his spouse. Let this, then, be our glory: the testimony of our conscience, and let the glory be to God. For the angel announcing peace promised peace to men: "Glory to God in the highest."

units.la: Denique si filii Israel, prout Scriptura loquitur, ibant animo pacifico ad praelium: quali animo & quam pacifico eundum erit ad hoc pacis concilium, sine aemulatione, sine contentione, sicut decet congregationem sanctorum, sine irascendo in via, quemadmodum monuit Ioseph fratres.
units.tr: Finally, if the sons of Israel, as Scripture speaks, "went to battle with a peaceful mind," with what mind and how peaceful ought one to go to this council of peace, without rivalry, without contention, as befits the congregation of saints, without anger on the road, as Joseph admonished his brothers.

units.la: Praeterea nullus detur locus diabolo, qui in seditionibus habitat. Fiat in pace locus Deo, qui dirigat pedes nostros in viam pacis, & doceat viam prudentiae ipse qui est via, veritas & vita, & Deus benedictus in saecula. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, let no place be given to the devil, who dwells in sedition. Let there be room in peace for God, who may direct our feet into the way of peace, and teach the way of prudence himself, who is the way, the truth and the life, and God blessed for ever. Amen.

units.la: TRILOGVS IN MATERIA SCHISMATIS EIVS- DEM CANCELLARII.
units.tr: A Trilogue on the Schism of the Same Chancellor

units.la: Aepenumero sublimem rationis speculam (nec mentior) solus ascendi, quatenus super omnes vitiosarum passionum nebulas, positus eo quoque omnia supergressus quantum fas habui, quae aspectui vero obstare crederentur, ego liberiores mentis oculos hac illacq; versarem super hoc mare magnum & spatiosum humanae fluxibilitatis, praesertim ad videnda quae pro sedatione procellarum suarum elationum contra nauem ecclesiae hactenus agitantur. Honesto memorans conspicio naucleros ecclesiasticae nauis huius strictis quasi gladiis verborum acutorum decertare mutuo, faces insuper ardentes contumeliarum & exprobrationum scriptis insertarum iactare. Omnes se vicissim impetere, ita demum confligere, ita colludi, quod omissis hostibus exteris & spretis salutaribus studiis id unum satagere credi possunt, ut quilibet quemlibet extra nauem ecclesiae deiiciat & deturbet, seorsum vos acclamant isti horrifico boatu, seorsum vos in malam horam vestram procul abscedite, quoniam schismatici estis, viperarum genimina estis: Infelix cuculi proles estis, vos denique omni multatione & anathemate debito parricidis & patriae proditoribus digni estis. Aliorum ex aduerso etsi mitior sit res, tamen acerba est, imo vos, inquiunt discedite a nobis, ut schismatis nutritores & fautores, ut criminis participes cum schismatico, cum periuro, cum haeretico, cum ecclesiae subuersore certissimo. Inter has belligerantium voces, inter literas maledicas hincinde volitantes timor & tremor venerunt super me, & contexerunt me tenebrae, mala sunt & valde mala, quae video, sed nesciens interim quorsum res euadat deteriora praesagio, vae vae si haeresis caput extulerint. Iam tamen quaestiones fidei iactantur inter eos, multa quoque pro solidis veris hactenus habita proponuntur, ut dubia, & quis nouit si corruptus passione praesenti animus errabit (ut solet) a vero, seu determinando quae falsa sunt, aut quae non expediunt, seu repudiando ea, quae ab aliis vere determinata cognoscentur. Caeterum a nonnullis pugnatur velut in tenebris, ita ut amicos non secernuntab hostibus, ita quid feriendum, quid ve impugnandum sit, non vident, oculos petere habent, & feriunt tales palpantes velut caeci & ambulantes in circuitu. Exemplo quoque eorum, qui domum Loth circumuallabant, ipsi tanquam acrisia percussi, viam neque egrediendi neque ingrediendi inueniunt. Ipsi rursus machinas magnas grauissimarum infamiarum congerunt ex iurium allegatione generali. Sed infirmo vel deficiente veritatis fundamento in eis quae facti sunt, nutabunde redduntur hae machinae, imo corruunt, & in eis aedificantes & egestae eosdem propria mole sternunt, talis est de gigantibus poetica fabula, hodie praeterea velut olim in ipso Babylonicae turris aedificatione fit in ecclesia confusio linguarum, ut se non intelligant hi, qui vel aedificant vel aedificare se dicunt turrim eius. Quid acturus sum miser haec aspiciens? quid moliar haec aduertens? obsistere neque fas neque vires habeo nec moueri impossibile. Sic lugebam moestus, sic angustiabar anxius, vae & vae crebris plangoribus ingeminans, dum ex secreto mentis triclinio duae comites germanae cum fratre uterino astitisse mihi visae sunt, familiariter satis notae, nomen fratris zelus, cuius habitatio in camerula irascibilis, nomen vnius sororis benevolentia, cuius locus est in concupiscibili. Altera vocatur discretio residens in rationali, hae sibi mutuo datae erant in adiutorium, tanquam vno germanitatis nexu circumplectentes secum fratre, quoniam zelus absque benevolentia nimium rigidus est, grauis & austerus. Benevolentia absque zelo mollis & languida, zelus demum & benevolentia sunt absque discretione ad seductionem errorumque valde prona. Porro absque eis discretio quid possit, quid prodest? Haec ttina societas die noctuque pluries altercata est intra secreta domus meae cubicula, meum quoque frequenter rupit silentium, zelus praecipue cuius aliquando vehemens adeo improbusque fit impetus, ut nunc verbis, nunc scriptis erumpere gestiret extrinsecus, non hoc, non illud discrimen aduertens neutri parti satis parcens, dummodo, pax, pax fiat, acclamaret. At vero benevolentiae tractus quasi contrarius, & si suauior, non multo minus validus erat ad ignoscendum omnibus, & de eis fauorabili intentione iudicandum. Quibus sic decertantibus discretio se mediatricemque praebebat. Operosum magis vero impossibile mihi esset hoc certamen describere, nihilominus aliqua stylo mandare curaui, tum ad obliuia vitae sollicitae, etenim
units.tr: I have often climbed alone, and I do not lie, to a lofty vantage point of reason, placed above the mists of all faulty passions, and having gone beyond everything as far as I was permitted, so that I could direct my freer eyes here and there over that great and wide sea of human instability. I wanted especially to see what has so far been done to calm the storms of its pride against the ship of the Church. Speaking honestly, I see the pilots of this ecclesiastical ship fighting one another with drawn swords of sharp words, and hurling burning torches of insults and reproaches written into their pamphlets. All of them attack one another in turn, and so they clash and collude, so that, leaving aside outside enemies and neglecting wholesome pursuits, they seem to strive for this one thing alone: that each may throw down and drive out of the ship of the Church whoever he can. Each of them shouts from his side with a terrible roar: "Away from here, in an evil hour, you schismatics! You are the brood of vipers, the offspring of the cuckoo! Unhappy children, you deserve every punishment and the anathema due to parricides and traitors of the fatherland." From the other side, though the matter is milder, it is still bitter: "Indeed, you depart from us, they say, as fosterers and supporters of schism, as sharers in the crime of the schismatic, the perjurer, the heretic, the certain subverter of the Church." Amid these voices of combatants, and abusive letters flying back and forth on every side, fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me. Evil, very evil, are the things I see, yet not knowing where the matter will end, I foresee something worse: alas, alas, if heresy should raise its head! Already questions of faith are being thrown about among them, and many things hitherto held as solid truths are now put forward as doubtful. And who knows whether a mind corrupted by present passion will stray from the truth, as it usually does, either in determining what is false or inexpedient, or in rejecting what others have rightly determined? Moreover, some fight as if in darkness, so that they do not distinguish friends from enemies, and do not see what must be struck or what must be attacked. They have eyes to strike with, yet they strike such men groping like the blind and walking in circles. Like those who besieged the house of Lot, they too, struck as with blindness, find neither a way to go out nor a way to come in. Again, they heap up great engines of most grievous infamies from a general allegation of rights. But these engines, lacking a firm foundation of truth in the facts, totter and indeed collapse; crushing those who build upon them, they are cast down by their own weight. Such is the poetic fable of the giants. Today, moreover, just as once at the building of the tower of Babylon, there is confusion of tongues in the Church, so that those who either build the tower or claim to be building it do not understand one another. What shall I, wretched man, do, seeing these things? What shall I attempt, noticing them? I have neither the right nor the strength to resist, and to move them is impossible. Thus I mourned in sadness, thus I was anxiously distressed, repeating "alas, alas" with frequent laments, when from the secret room of my mind there seemed to stand beside me two sisters, sisters-german, together with a uterine brother, familiar enough: the brother's name is Zeal, whose dwelling is in the irascible little chamber; the name of one sister is Benevolence, whose place is in the concupiscible part; the other is called Discretion, residing in the rational part. These had been given to one another as helpers, embracing the brother with a single bond of kinship, since zeal without benevolence is too harsh, heavy and austere, while benevolence without zeal is soft and languid; and zeal and benevolence alike, without discretion, are very prone to seduction and error. Moreover, without them, what can discretion do, and what does it profit? This triple company argued day and night, many times, within the secret chambers of my house, and often broke my silence. Zeal especially, whose impulse was sometimes so vehement and reckless that it longed to burst out in words or in writings, paying no heed to this or that distinction, sparing neither party enough, and crying out only that peace, peace be made. But the pull of Benevolence, somewhat opposite though sweeter, was not much less strong in pardoning everyone and in judging them with a favourable intention. While these two contended thus, Discretion presented herself as mediator. It would be a laborious, and indeed an impossible, task for me to describe this contest; nevertheless I took care to commit some of it to writing, partly to forget a life full of anxious cares, and indeed

units.la: Dulce loqui miseris veteresq; euoluere quaestus,
units.tr: It is sweet to speak of our troubles and to unroll the sorrows of the past,

units.la: tum praeterea ad exercitium qualecunque otioli studii, hoc mihi si dabitur, satis erit, & si nemini exaliis sim allaturus quippiam commodi, attamen si quos iuuat adesse nisi paulisper secedant a me, & zelum beneuolentiamque & discretionem non me loqui putent, zelum in primis.
units.tr: and partly for whatever exercise of idle study it may be. If I am allowed this, it will be enough for me. And even if I shall bring no benefit to anyone else, still, if anyone is glad to be present, let them not think that I am speaking, unless they step aside for a little while from me, and that I am speaking of zeal, goodwill and discretion. Zeal first.

units.la: Zelus. Quid superest consilii, o sorores, quousque non pudebit inertiae, vsque quo tandem mens placida contenta quiete est? Quale quantumque sit concordiae bonum, qua parvae res crescunt, sicut discordia maximae dilabuntur? dum etiam atque etiam etiam recogito, quibus non auxietatibus vrgeor, quibus non mordeor doloribus, quando per quatuor lustra & amplius propriam ego matrem intueor. Et o qualem matrem Christe? illam tuam sponsam vnicam ecclesiam intueor (dico) non in vna sui parte, non vno laetali vulnere sauciatam, quin insuper eam ipsam non barbarica tantum debacchatione laedi conspicio, sed per suos introrsum in visceribus suis eo acerbius, quo delicatior locus est video (heu) his oculis per schismatica beluam infinitorum capitum, illam piam matrem deiici, lacerari, & per omnes artus truculenta rabie ac plus quam beluina feritate discerpi, ferre nequeo credite, & si ferreus esset animus, si naturales affectus etiam in bestiis, si passiones vitiosae in reprobis tanta audent, quanta recensere stupor sit: non minas, non ictus, non verbera, non fustes, non ignes, non ipsa demum mortis immania, imminentis horrenda discrimina pauent, dum sequantur, qua sua voluptas quemque trahit, vel sua passio rapit, horum exempla tum in animalibus respectu foetuum, tum in hominibus philocaptis, in auaris, in vane gloriosis, in iracundis, & caeteris huiusmodi quotidiana cernuntur. Si hoc inquam ita in furore vel vitio? quid audere debet pietatis? quid posse virtutis affectio? quam tanto vehementiorem ad bonum esse conuenit, quanto diuiniorem, & ex consequenti fortiorem illam esse constat, propterea nemo dinumerauerit, quin verus matris ecclesiae zelator neque incedat, quam sibi monstrauerit vel ratio vel conscientia vel auctoritas vel inspiratio, vel tandem ipsa necessitas ad liberationem suae matris ab hac mortifera peste & a voracibus bestiae huius schismaticae faucibus, quod si prodesse fors acerba vetuerit, tum pulcherrimum erit pro matre, pro pace, pro libertate tali occumbere morti, sed neque hoc magnum nobis, quibus pro praemio spes fida regnandi promittitur, quando gentes, quae spem non habent sponte nec scire deuouisse, celebres collaudent historiae, tum Romanorum de duobus Decils & Curtio, tum exterorum de Codro. Ipsos lubinde martyres nostros, quia singuli singulas animas suas pro fide ecclesiae tradentes saluauerunt, nos in mortali deuotionis titulo templis extollimus. Quid de labore illo quo non vna anima, non paucae, sed totum ecclesiae corpus praesens & futurum sua salute potietur?
units.tr: Zeal. What counsel remains, O sisters? How long will you feel no shame at your idleness? How long will a calm mind be content with rest? How great is the good of harmony, by which small things grow, while discord brings down the greatest? As I think again and again, what anxieties press upon me, what sorrows bite me, since for more than twenty years I have looked upon my own mother. And, O Christ, what a mother! I see your one bride, the Church, not wounded in just one part, not struck by a single deadly blow. Worse still, I see her harmed not only by barbarous frenzy, but by the wounds within her own bowels, which are the more painful the more tender the place is. Alas, with these eyes I see that dutiful mother cast down and torn by the schismatic beast of countless heads, and mangled in every limb with savage rage and a fury more than bestial. Believe me, I cannot bear it. If my spirit were iron, and if natural affections, even in beasts, and sinful passions, even in the reprobate, dare such things as are shameful to recount, if they do not fear threats, blows, beatings, clubs, fires, or even the monstrous horrors of death itself impending, as long as they follow wherever their pleasure draws them or their passion carries them, then we see such examples every day: in animals concerning their young, in men who are captivated by others, in the greedy, the vainglorious, the angry, and others of that kind. If this is so, I say, in fury or vice, what ought piety to dare? What power ought the affection of virtue to have? It is fitting that it should be as much more vehement toward the good as it is more divine, and it is plain that it must consequently be stronger. Therefore no one will count it, unless a true zealot of his mother the Church goes forth, whenever reason, conscience, authority, inspiration, or finally necessity itself shows him the way to free his mother from this deadly plague and from the voracious jaws of this schismatic beast. But if perhaps bitter fate forbids him to help, then it will be a most glorious thing to die for the mother, for peace, for such liberty. Yet this is not a great thing for us, for whom a sure hope of reigning is promised as a reward, when famous histories praise with high commendation peoples who have devoted themselves, without hope and without knowledge, such as the Romans with the two Decii and Curtius, and foreigners with Codrus. Indeed, we raise our own martyrs to the honour of the altars, because each, by giving up his own soul for the faith of the Church, has saved it, and we proclaim them with the mortal title of devotion. What of that labour by which not one soul, nor a few, but the whole body of the Church, present and future, obtains its salvation?

units.la: Discretio. Tace frater obsecro & feruentiorem iusto spiritum comprime. Caueto tu sciens & videns ne nos & te in apera pericula mittas. Egisti hoc pluries, dum succensus quispiam feruido spiritum tuo se medium se veluti contentiones se daturum inter pugnantes vtrinque conflictus oppoluit, ita Christum comedit zelus domus Dei dum mortuus est, vt faceret vtraque vnum. Sic apud Poetam,
units.tr: Discretio. Be quiet, brother, I beg you, and restrain a spirit more heated than is right. Be careful, knowing and seeing it, that you do not send us and yourself into open danger. You have done this before, when someone fired by a hot spirit placed himself as a mediator among those fighting on both sides, as if to offer himself to the contention. So the zeal of God's house consumed Christ when he died, so that he might make the two into one. Thus in the Poet:

units.la: Senior ille Galesus,
units.tr: That old man Galesus,

units.la: Occubuit, dum medium paci se offert iustissimus vnus
units.tr: Fell, while the most just man alone offered himself as a mediator for peace.

units.la: Quafuit &c.
units.tr: Qua fuit &c.

units.la: Et pius Æneas dextram tendebat inermem, pacem exclamans dum iaculo femur transfixus est: hac tu recogitatione deterreri poteras, vt sapientis vsus consilio non miscères te rixæ alienæ: neve te & nos omnes morsibus sæuis odiorū & infamiæ lacerandos obiectares, lacerandos dixerim, aut ab altera partiū seu (vt frequens est) ab vtraq; vulgati dicti meminéris: natans inter duas aquas in vtraq; submergitur. Iam experientia ppria hoc te docere etsi cætera deessent, debuerat. Nonne tutius erat consilium propheticum Amos: vir prudens in illo tempore tacebit: quia dies mali sunt? Nonne præterea salubrius id, quod Ezechielis visio habet: lugere & gemere super cunctis abominationibus quæ fiunt: aut cum Hieremia sedere tristem, aut cum regio propheta optare pennas sicut columbæ, volare & requiescere & in solitudine saluum fieri à pusillanimitate; dum est contradictio in ciuitate, vbi sine passione tumultibus se audiant, semet intelligant, se coram videant: fallit me expectatio mea, si non protinus abiectis armis ambulabunt in domo Domini cum consensu, aut ostenso signo ad sagittam: hoc est sine debito, ipsum sine diuinatione improuida medium veritatis attingent: aut si pugnandum fuerit argumentationibus, ipsi exemplo Israelitarum ibunt omnes animo pacifico ad prælium.
units.tr: And the pious Aeneas stretched out his unarmed hand, crying for peace, when he was pierced in the thigh by a javelin. You could have been deterred by this thought, so that, following the counsel of the wise, you would not mix yourself into another's quarrel, nor expose yourself and all of us to be torn by the savage bites of hatred and infamy. I say torn, and you should remember the common saying, whether from one side or, as is often the case, from both: "swimming between two waters, one is submerged in both." Your own experience ought to have taught you this already, even if nothing else had. Was not the prophetic counsel of Amos safer: the prudent man will keep silent in that time, because the days are evil? Was not what the vision of Ezekiel holds also more wholesome: to mourn and groan over all the abominations that are done; or to sit sorrowful with Jeremiah, or, with the royal prophet, to wish for wings like a dove, to fly away and rest, and to be saved from faintheartedness in the wilderness, while there is contradiction in the city, where men may hear the tumults without passion, understand themselves, and see themselves before their own eyes? My expectation deceives me if, once their weapons are laid down, they do not walk in the house of the Lord in agreement, or, with a sign shown at the arrow, that is, without debt and without rash divination, they reach the middle of the truth themselves; or, if they must fight with arguments, they will all go into battle with peaceful minds, following the example of the Israelites.

units.la: Zelus. Quid me aspicitis ô sorores: grandia videor polliceri: sed grandiora fides potest: amor auder, doloris materni necessitas inuitat.
units.tr: Zeal. Why do you look at me, sisters? I seem to promise great things, but faith can do greater; love dares, and the necessity of a mother's grief urges me on.

units.la: Beneuolentia. Magnas prorsus repromittis frater, sed maior in exoluendo difficultas reponitur, tot sapientes hucusque nequeunt id facere quod attentas solus & iustus, ita ne tot animorum varietates, tot votorum mille species adunabis? quando idem homo plerumque secum diffidet: & in eadem domo rixæ regnant incompescibiles? Quid ages, præsertim vbi animo deliberato placet error, placet diuisio: pax sola voce, non corde conquiritur: vbi denique tanta quanta esse potest finium varietas inuenitur?
units.tr: Goodwill. You promise great things indeed, brother, but a greater difficulty lies in fulfilling them. So many wise people have hitherto been unable to do what you, alone and just, attempt. How will you bring together so many differences of minds and a thousand kinds of wishes? Since the same man is often at odds with himself, and quarrels rule unchecked in one and the same house! What will you do, especially where, after deliberate judgment, error pleases and division pleases; where peace is sought only with the voice and not with the heart; and where, in the end, there is as great a variety of opinions as can possibly be found?

units.la: Zelus. Noli tandem obsecro ô germana Beneuolentia, noli molestum silentium tam pertinaciter indicere, permitte me confabulari in amaritudine animæ meæ: sine illud quod me premit cuomere: dolor inclusus vrit acrius. Ego saltem literulis infodiam quæ sentio, nullum ibi discrimen formidatur.
units.tr: Zeal. Do not, I beg you, sweet Goodwill, do not impose so stubbornly this troublesome silence. Allow me to speak out in the bitterness of my soul; let me pour out what presses on me, for enclosed grief burns more fiercely. At least I will bury what I feel in little letters; there is no danger to be feared there.

units.la: Discretio. Age ergo frater si detinere non possumus, permittimus interim scribere te omnia, quæ in animum venerint: tantummodo ab iniuriosa temeritate, ab irreuerentia qualibet abstineto. Caue deseras negermanas tuas Beneuolentiam & Discretionem, quatenus beneuolus sit & discretus sermo tuus, ne accusans alios plus debito: sed aurea mediocritate semper in te ornatus effulgeat & placeat mordaci odiosa dicacitate eiecta.
units.tr: Discretion. Then, brother, since we cannot hold you back, meanwhile we allow you to write everything that comes into your mind. Only abstain from injurious rashness and from every kind of irreverence. Take care not to abandon your sisters Goodwill and Discretion, so that your speech may be kindly and discreet, not accusing others more than is right, but that it may always shine, adorned with the golden mean, with biting and hateful sharpness cast aside and pleasing to all.

units.la: Zelus. Faciam quod hortaris, soror Discretio. Nam & tu Beneuolentia significas te huius esse sententiæ: vis enim omnia interpretari beneuole, sed in nomen tuum: non tamen ita beneuole quod lædatur veritas, sed vt charitas nutriatur, & veniat dies qua exultantes canere fas sit canticum; Misericordia seu beneuolentia & veritas obuiauerunt sibi: iustitia & pax osculatæ sunt.
units.tr: Zeal. I will do as you urge, sister Discretion. For you too, Goodwill, show that you hold this opinion; you wish everything to be interpreted kindly, but not so kindly that the truth is harmed, rather so that charity may be nourished, and the day may come when it is right to sing the hymn with rejoicing: Mercy or goodwill and truth have met each other; righteousness and peace have kissed.

units.la: Beneuolentia. Assentio frater, nil aliud sane magis expostulo, sed ipsum agere supernus arbiter Deus concesserit. Comitabimur ergo te, tu id quod suggesserimus, tuis verbis exprimito, at vero super omnia vide ne sis zelus talis, qualem Apostolus nominauit, non secundum scientiam, quem præterea dixit zelum contentionis, quia videlicet nec discretionem nec beneuolentiam germanas tuas audiebat zelus talis.
units.tr: Goodwill. I agree, brother; I ask for nothing else more earnestly, but may God, the heavenly judge, grant that it be done. We will therefore accompany you. Whatever we have suggested, you must express in your own words. Above all, take care that you are not such a zeal as the Apostle named, not according to knowledge, and which he also called zeal of contention, because clearly such a zeal would listen neither to its sisters Discretion nor Goodwill.

units.la: Zelus. Fiet vtrique ne dubites, & quicquid in vtramque partem dicendum videbitur, illud deliberato, sed breui libramine rationis explicabo. Nunc alloquens omnes in commune, nunc ad particulariora me deflectens, quod si post finito verbo deprehenderitis me præuaricatorem pacti huius, vestra erit correctio, & meum vltro parcere corrigentibus. Multa tamen (id aduertite) locuturus sum nominatim sub modo triplicis epistolæ, qualis loqui vel posse vel debere personas introductas non me licentia oratoria coniecturate.
units.tr: Zeal. It will be done as you both wish, do not doubt it. Whatever seems to be said on either side, I will explain it deliberately, but in a brief balance of reason. Now addressing you all in common, now turning to more particular matters: if, when I have finished speaking, you find me to have transgressed this agreement, the correction will be yours, and I will gladly forgive those who correct me. Yet I am going to speak by name on many matters (take note of this) under the form of a threefold letter, and the freedom of oratory does not allow me to guess what the introduced persons could or should say.

units.la: Et inprimis omnes in commune conueniam. Si sententiæ diueriæ sint inter vos, vt humana fert fragilitas, quoniam incertæ ac timidæ sunt prouidentiæ nostræ, præsertim vbi variatur narratio in eis quæ facta sunt. Nunquid præterea contentiones odiosæ regnabunt inter vos? nunqd exemplo mulierculărum res iniuriis peragetur? Nonne salubrius est & Christiano dignius vinci à bono, quam malo vincere? imo hoc pessimum est, illud optandum. Credite mihi, pax male per schismata quæritur, non vtiliter iniuria iniuriis, sic nec calliditas calliditate, nec morbus morbo repellitur aut sanatur. Si præterea contentiones & rixæ sint inter vos, nonne carnales estis? ego quidem dico quod vnusquisque vestrum dicit, Ego sum Benedicti, ego subtractionis, ego neutrius, & quod venire solet inter oues, dum cœca nocte prædator lupus irruerit fugiunt, pars hæc fauces lupi nescia incurrit, hæc in oppositum parietem impingit, hæc nullo certo vagatur attonita. Non aliter spiritu quodam vertiginis agitatur cœtus ecclesiæ, pars palpat velut in tenebris, ignorans quæ petat, pars ambulat in circuitu, pars sistit expectans lucem veritatis certam de tenebris splendescere. Pars neque scit neque nouit quicquam agere, nihilominus ipsa & agentes vtrinque ridens diiudicat. Alios rapiunt & transuersos agunt passiones variæ, pessimæ consiliatrices, ira, odium, inuidia, cupiditas, ambitio, timor & similes, adeo vt pro personis persequendis syncerus amor pacis, & serenissima veritatis amicitia deserantur aut impugnentur, quo facinore, quale aliud execrabilius cogitari possit, nequaquam inuenio. Per tales si non obuiatum exiterit, exponetur fides discrimini, si suis literis fidentes, si eas instrumenmentum suarum passionum efficere molientes determinauerint aut asseruerint leuius debito, in hanc vel illam partem ea quae melius intractata manerent, vt si diceretur papam non esse caput vniuersale ecclesiae iure diuino, papam non expedire esse vnicum pro ecclesia, papae passim in facie resistendum esse, passim & ab eo appellandum, vel ex aduerso si quis assereret quod in nullo casu papae dicere liceret, cur ita facis, & similia.
units.tr: And first I will address you all in common. If opinions differ among you, as human frailty brings, since our foresight is uncertain and timid, especially where the account varies about the things that were done, will hateful contentions then reign among you? Will affairs be carried on by injuries, after the example of silly women? Is it not more wholesome, and more worthy of a Christian, to be conquered by a good man than to conquer by a bad one? Indeed, the latter is the worst, and the former is to be desired. Believe me, peace is sought badly through schisms; injury is not usefully repelled by injuries, nor is cunning by cunning, nor is disease cured or healed by disease. Moreover, if there are contentions and quarrels among you, are you not carnal? I indeed say what each of you says: "I am of Benedict," "I am of the withdrawal," "I am of neither." And what usually happens among sheep, when a predator wolf attacks in the blind of night: they flee, one part runs into the jaws of the wolf without knowing it, another dashes against the wall opposite, another wanders about dazed with no certain course. In the same way the assembly of the Church is driven by a kind of spiritual vertigo: one part gropes as in darkness, not knowing what to seek; one part walks in a circle; one part stands still, waiting for the light of certain truth to shine out of the darkness. One part neither knows nor understands how to do anything, yet it judges both itself and those acting on either side with mockery. Various passions, the worst counsellors, carry others off and drive them across: anger, hatred, envy, greed, ambition, fear and the like, so that sincere love of peace and the most serene friendship of truth are abandoned or assailed, for the sake of pursuing persons. What more execrable crime than this, or any other that could be thought more execrable, I cannot find at all. If such people are not met and checked, faith will be exposed to danger, if, trusting their own letters, or striving to make them the instrument of their passions, they settle upon or assert, more lightly than is right, things that would have remained better untreated, in one direction or the other: for example, that the Pope is not the universal head of the Church by divine right; that it is not expedient for the Church to have a single Pope; that the Pope must be resisted to his face everywhere and appealed from everywhere; or, on the other side, if someone asserted that in no case may one say to the Pope, "why do you do this?" and similar things.

units.la: Quosdam praeterea videre est, qui tanta animositate suis aut ceptis aut consultis inhaerent, vt nullis ad oppositum rationibus, nulla incommodorum experientia flecti possint. Malunt omnia secum ruere, omnia frangi vel turbari, quam pedem retrorsum retrahere a via semel inuia, & ob hoc iam non via, quoniam progressui obstare reperiuntur, vel spinarum, hoc est vitiorum saepes horrida, vel fossatorum, hoc est cordium profunditas incognita, vel latrunculorum malignitas, vel comitum mutua impugnatio, vel viarum distractus humiles, quos ceruicosa turgidaq; praesumptio nequit praetergredi, quia nequit humiliari. Irascuntur denique; tales odio immortali contra omnes, quos viderint vel audierint, non dicam aduersari sibi, sed non plenis vocibus & totis assentire sententiis. Alios ad omnem ventum instar arundinis videmus mutabiles, qui pro buccella panis iustitiam desererent. Alios tandem inuenimus (& vtinam multos) qui parati sunt obedire veritati cognitae, seq; praeterea q sequi licebit vel expediet. Multa quidem licent quae non expediunt, hi nullos odiunt, nullos persequuntur, quos absq; malignitatis admixtione cum puro & simplici oculo veritatem quaerere cognouerint, etiam si non datum fuerit inuenire. Reminiscuntur quod Paulus & Barnabas absque peccato dissenserunt, ita vt discederent ab inuicem, nullo tamen odio seipsos prosecuti sunt, nullis maledictis & iniuriis se inuicem consectari leguntur. Qua in re videntur regisse non satis benevole nec discrete (ne loquamur acerbius) illi qui sub nomine Venerabilis Vniuersitatis Tholosanae quondam nuper epistolam grandem Serenissimo Francorum Regi transmiserunt plenam maledictis pungentem iniurias, corruptam opprobriis, in illos omnes qui non secum sentiunt, qui subtrahendo non secum in obedientia (vt dicunt) debita perseuerant. Verum sepositis interim propriis ad seipsos affectionibus & odiis ad alios (obnubilant enim ista veri iudicium) animaduertant quid ex opposito subtrahentes possunt rescribere, nominatim illi de alma Vniuersitate Parisiensi, qui profundiori nota quaeruntur inuri.
units.tr: Moreover, there are some to be seen who cling to their undertakings or their counsels with such obstinacy that they can be moved by no arguments to the contrary and no experience of inconvenience. They prefer that everything collapse, that everything be broken or disturbed, rather than draw back a foot from a way once entered upon, a way that is now no longer a way, since it is found to block progress: either a horrid hedge of thorns, that is, of vices; or a pit, that is, the unknown depth of hearts; or the malice of brigands; or the mutual assault of companions; or the lowly divisions of the roads, which a stiff-necked and swollen presumption cannot cross, because it cannot be humbled. Finally, such men grow angry, with an immortal hatred against all whom they have seen or heard, I will not say opposing them, but not assenting to their views with full voices and whole opinions. Others we see changeable like reeds in every wind, who would give up justice for a morsel of bread. Finally, we find others (and would that there were many) who are ready to obey the truth once known, and besides, to follow whatever it will be permitted or expedient to follow. Many things are indeed permitted that are not expedient. These men hate no one and persecute no one whom they have recognised seeking the truth with a pure and simple eye, free from any admixture of malice, even if it has not been given them to find it. They remember that Paul and Barnabas disagreed without sin, so that they departed from each other, yet they pursued neither themselves with hatred, nor are they read to have hunted each other down with curses and injuries. In this matter those seem to have acted not sufficiently kindly or discreetly (not to speak more harshly) who, under the name of the Venerable University of Toulouse, not long ago sent a great letter to the most Serene King of France, full of curses, stinging with injuries, defiled with reproaches, against all who do not think with them, who, by withdrawing, persevere (as they say) outside the due obedience. But setting aside for the moment their own affections toward themselves and their hatreds toward others, for these cloud the judgment of truth, let them consider what those who withdraw could write back in reply, especially those of the nourishing University of Paris, who are sought to be branded with a deeper mark.

units.la: Exemplar literarum responsiuarum ex persona Vniuersitatis Parisiensis ad epistolam Tholo- sanam.
units.tr: Copy of the letter of reply, written in the name of the University of Paris, to the letter from Toulouse.

units.la: Postulata in primis, Rex Christianissime, maiestatis tuae licentia, conuertit se humilitas tua respondere Tholosanis quibusdam per epistolam tali sobrietate, qualem te audire & nos loqui decet, textam non qualiter maledicti improbi, qui execrandis execrationibus infamare regnum dignitatem cum generali concilio suo conati sunt, rupto derepente diutino silentio. Loquimur ergo sic ad eos Rex Serenissime, te audiente, te iudice. Ea fratres super quibus accusamur a vobis, si talia erant, charitatiua illa epistola vestra nisi canina potius mordet) charitatiua illa epistola vestra nisi canina potius mordax esse debuit...
units.tr: First of all, most Christian King, with your Majesty's permission, may your humility be pleased to answer certain people of Toulouse in a letter of such moderation as becomes you to hear and us to speak. It is not written in the manner of wicked slanderers, who have tried to defame the kingdom and its dignity with execrable curses together with their so-called general council, breaking a long silence all at once. We therefore speak to them thus, most serene King, with you listening and you as judge. Brothers, as for the matters on which you accuse us: if they were such, your letter ought to have been charitable, unless it bites more like a dog and is savage.

units.la: Nam tua res agitur, paries cum proximus ardet.
units.tr: For your own affair is being discussed when the neighbouring wall is on fire.

units.la: Poterat vnicuique vestrum si obmutire praesumpsisset, simile contigisse, nondum vero ita desipitis, fratres, vt haec dicatis, & si ita loquimur, alioquin quo animo certare vos pollicemini vsq; ad mortem pro iustitia, qui nondum vsq; ad sanguinem restitistis? si vos plus triennio pauor pueriles exterruisset, trepidantes timore vbi non erat timor. Nam qualis timori locus seruabitur, vbi tam promptos defensores & propulsores iniuriae episcopus ille mox inuenit Dominos Ducetes, sicut testamini.
units.tr: Any one of you could have suffered the same, had he presumed to keep silent. Yet you are not so foolish, brothers, as to say these things. And if we speak in this way, otherwise, with what spirit do you promise to contend even unto death for justice, you who have not yet resisted even unto blood? If for more than three years fear has frightened you like children, trembling where there was no fear. For what room for fear will be left, where that bishop soon found such ready defenders and repellers of injury, the Lords Dukes, as you yourselves testify?

units.la: Quid si cerebrosus, si capitosus, si praesumptuose loquax aut minax erat ille vester episcopus? non est nostrum diffinire, sed neq; est vsque quam incredibile, cum si talis erat, dum in turbam alacrium ingeniorum vinacium iuuenum incautum impegit, quod exagitatus ab eis secundum meritum suum, & exibilatus extitit. Sed ad silentium vestrum regredimur. Respondere postulamus, vbi tunc erat dolor ille ingens, qui (sicut ex historiis trahitis) mutos etiam ex natura loqui cogit, dum recentior erat iniuria? dum plaga noua curationi proximior? dolor iste vester, quo nunc aestuare vos iactatis, quorsum abierat? aut vnde nunc subitus emergit? deniq; dolor iste dum ab initio erat quasi multum nouum absq; spiraculo, nonne in strepitus vastos fortius erumpere? nonne clamores horridiores extorquere debuerat? At vero scandalum vobis erat formidini. Quale scandalum, passiuum an actiuum, datum scilicet an acceptum? & rumorem qualemcunque paueritis damnat Greg. qui tradit non esse deserendam propter scandalum veritatem vitae, doctrinae & iustitiae, qualem hic asseritis. Sed exitum subtractionis aut (sicut sermo vester loquitur) partum infelicem praestolabamini, quid ita quaesumus? nunquid ab euentu negotiorum, metiri iam actorum bonitatem congruum vel necessarium iudicatis? videte ne fallamini. Quanta sunt optimo initiata principio, quanta in quibus nihil virtuosa & moralis prudentia defuit, quae tamen successu prospero vel intento caruerunt, ad quod potest violate traduci illud: Careat successibus opto Quisquis ab euentu facta notanda putat. Nostrum est plantare, nostrum est rigare secundum prudentiam à Deo nobis insitam, hæc vero nihil sunt omnia, sed qui incrementi consummationem dat, Christus est. Narrat Iudicum lib. filios Israel pugnantes Domini monitu bis magna strage corruisse, quis tamen dixerit eos de aggressu pugnæ propter hoc inculpandos? At forte prolixus sermo epistolæ vestræ talem temporis tractum ut elaboraretur exigebat, utque coaceruaretur interim grandis congeries maledicorum in nos verborum, ut interim grandiloquam tragœdiam contumeliarum, ut sales aspersos, satyrica improbaque reprobationis expueret in nos fraterna illa vestra dilectio. Sed profecto si fuisset iniquitas nostra, ut talia audire meruisset (quod libera voce refellimus) certe tamen vestra amicitia ex similitudine quadam studiorum nobis obnoxia, vestraque prudentia & gravitas qualis decet studiosos, digna apparebat, qua pulchrior & non illoto obscœnoq; sermone uteretur, dignum erat illud speculum, quale vos esse gloriamini, quod radiis purioribus rutilaret: digna denique vinea vestra, quæ non in his maledictorum labruscas degeneraret. Poeticum est inuolucrum, musas agrestes ideo in picas conuersas esse, & quosdam agrestes in ranas, & alios in simias, Aragnen in araneam, Nioben in silicem, & alios in alia, quia linguis abusi sunt, eas in maledicta laxantes. Præclare demum ab Aristo. dictum est: Honorem esse in honorante, ita proculdubio illiberalis & contumeliosa vituperatio sordidat exprobrantem. Nam qualis unusquisque est, talia dicit, sicut qui de terra est de terra loquitur. Sed vituperare nos, sicut tamen epistola facies ostendit, vestra nullatenus erat intentio, qualem ergo nimium laudare obedientiam & inobedientia scelus detestari, causam præterea defendere papæ & ecclesiæ, denique à devio nos infauste subtractionis auertere? Est ne igitur vestra, fratres, prudentia tam oblita sui, ut arroget sibi docendi nos officium in præsertim notissima, quod obedientia bona est, inobedientia mala grauiterque plectenda, quis hoc ignorare præsumi potest? Maxime apud nos, quorum studium antiquius solenniusque tam numero quam merito & autoritate semper extitisse nec ipsi negaretis. Nam & inimici nostri sunt iudices, quod tantum cæteris supereminet vniuersitas nostra, quantum inter virgulta cupressi.
units.tr: What if that bishop of yours was hot-headed, headstrong, presumptuously talkative or threatening? It is not for us to define, but neither is it at all incredible that, if he was such, when he ran into a crowd of lively, wine-flushed, incautious young men, he was harassed by them according to his deserts and hissed off. But let us return to your silence. We ask you to answer: where was that great grief which (as you draw from histories) compels even the naturally dumb to speak, while the injury was still fresh and the new wound nearer to healing? That grief of yours, over which you boast that you now seethe, where had it gone? Or whence does it now suddenly emerge? Finally, if that grief, at the beginning, was like something very new and without breath, should it not have burst forth into vast uproar? Should it not have wrung out more horrible clamours? But indeed, scandal was a terror to you. What scandal is this, passive or active, that is, given or received? And you feared some rumour, of whatever kind. Gregory condemns this, who teaches that the truth of life, doctrine and justice, such as you assert here, is not to be abandoned on account of scandal. But you were waiting for the outcome of the withdrawal, or (as your letter puts it) its unhappy offspring. Why so, we ask? Do you judge that the goodness of deeds should now be measured by the outcome of affairs? Take care lest you be deceived. How many things were begun with the best principle, in which virtuous and moral prudence was not lacking, and yet lacked a prosperous or intended success? To these that verse may be wrongly applied: "Let him lack success, I pray, whoever thinks deeds are to be condemned from their outcome." It is ours to plant, ours to water, according to the prudence implanted in us by God; but all these things are nothing, and it is he who gives the increase, Christ. The book of Judges tells how the sons of Israel, fighting at the Lord's command, twice fell with great slaughter; yet who would say they were to be blamed for having gone into battle because of this? But perhaps the long discourse of your letter required such a stretch of time, so that meanwhile a great heap of slanderous words against us might be piled up, and that your fraternal love might spew out, meanwhile, a grandiloquent tragedy of insults, sprinkled with wit, satirical and wicked reproach against us. But certainly, if our fault had been such that we deserved to hear such things (which we refute with a free voice), yet your friendship, bound to us by a certain likeness of studies, and your prudence and gravity, such as befits scholars, seemed worthy that a more elegant speech, not foul and unclean, should be used. That was the worthy mirror you boast you are, which ought to shine with purer rays; finally a vineyard worthy of you, which should not degenerate into these wild grapes of slander. It is a poetic fable that the country muses were turned into magpies, and certain rustics into frogs, others into apes, Arachne into a spider, Niobe into stone, and others into other things, because they abused their tongues, loosing them into slander. Aristotle rightly said: honour lies in the one who honours. So undoubtedly illiberal and abusive reproach defiles the one who utters it. For whatever each one is, such things he says; as one who is of the earth speaks of the earth. But to revile us was by no means your intention, as the face of your letter shows. Why, then, do you so much praise obedience and detest the crime of disobedience, and moreover defend the cause of the pope and the Church, and finally try to turn us away from our devious and unhappy withdrawal? Is your prudence, brothers, so forgetful of itself that it claims for itself the office of teaching us in what is most well known: that obedience is good, and disobedience is bad and to be punished severely? Who could presume to be ignorant of this? Especially among us, whose study has always been older and more solemn, both in number and in merit and authority, as you yourselves would not deny. For even our enemies are judges that our university stands out above the rest as much as the cypress stands above the brambles.

units.la: Amplius vero pro inobedientia (si ita necesse fuerit) nos edocenda erat, ne dispendiosissimus sermo trahendus per autoritates emendicatas, ingestaque sine ordine per pueriles periodos assidue similes, & plus æquo sonora, per fastidiosam nugacis repetitionis eiusdem finistreitatem, denique irascendo, dentibus frendendo & tabescendo nos, quasi beluina feritate mox concul-candi lacerandi deuorandique videremur. Poteratis, fratres, poteratis ali-ter vestram iactare eloquentiam, aliter vestrum officium, vel docendi vel monendi vel corrigendi ventilare. Nimis elapsum esse à memoria vestra monstratis illud Ciceronis documentum, cui scriptura sape concordat: sit monitio sine contumelia vel exprobratione. Nam & Michael disputans cum diabolo de corpore Moysi.
units.tr: Moreover, if we were to be taught about disobedience (should it be necessary), the discourse should not be dragged out at such expense, through borrowed authorities and heaped up without order in childish periods, constantly similar, more sonorous than fitting, through the tedious tautology of a trifling repetition. Nor should it be drawn out by raging, gnashing our teeth and wasting away at us, as if we seemed about to be trampled, torn and devoured with beastly ferocity. You could, brothers, you could have displayed your eloquence otherwise, and debated your office otherwise, whether of teaching, admonishing or correcting. You show that you have forgotten that precept of Cicero, with which Scripture often agrees: admonition should be without insult or reproach. For even Michael, disputing with the devil about the body of Moses...

units.la: Rursus, fratres, elocutionis vestræ accuratio vel deserenda erat penitus, vel accuratius incorruptiusque seruanda. Quod dictandi vitium non magnopere culparemus, si non vitiosissimo & prorsus intolerabili genere consutationis uteretur, illa elegans eloquentia vestra, quæ enim vitiosior confutatio seu argumentatio adduci poterat, quam quæ ad vtrunque flecti potest? Quem defectum si per totum hunc terminum oculis videre nequiuit vestra solertia, tot literis erudita, quo ausu nos in obscurioribus commonere præsumpserit, consideret. Hoc itaque quod dicimus, monstrabimus digito: tantummodo oculos aperire non pudeat. Si obedientia laudanda est, ut totiens inculcatis, quasi non ita sentiremus, si hæc sit gladius vester acutissimus, quo nos iugulare, imo cruentis vulneribus confodere sat agitis, attendite quam facili retorsione gladium vestrum in iugulum vestrum conuertimus: obedire siquidem oportet Deo magis quam hominibus: non hoc inficiabimini. Oportebat ergo ut Deo iubentirecedere à consortio vel hæretici vel schismatici, vel in talibus vehementer notorie diffamati, aut in nocumentum ecclesiæ præsidenti, vos ipsos præstaretis obedientes: quod quia non fecistis, sas habemus ex consequenti more vestro concludere, quod inobedientia hæc vestra plecti debet pœna tali, imo maiori quam nostra factu ut fieri dicitis eius vicrio, nam contemnenda est hæc potestas, ut altera superior honoretur.
units.tr: Again, brothers, the care you took in your style ought either to have been abandoned altogether or kept more accurately and purely. We would not greatly blame this fault of composition if it did not employ a most vicious and utterly intolerable kind of refutation. That elegant eloquence of yours: what more vicious refutation or argument could be brought forward than one that can be bent to either side? If your skill, so learned in letters, could not see this defect with its own eyes throughout this whole stretch, let it consider with what daring it presumed to admonish us in obscure matters. So let us point with a finger at what we say; only do not be ashamed to open your eyes. If obedience is to be praised, as you so often urge, as if we did not think so, and if this is your sharpest sword, with which you are busy cutting our throats, or rather stabbing us with bloody wounds, mark how easily we turn your sword against your own throat. We must obey God rather than men; this you will not deny. Therefore it was necessary, as God commands, to withdraw from the fellowship of either heretics or schismatics, or of those notoriously and vehemently defamed in such matters, or of those who preside to the harm of the Church. You yourselves should have shown obedience in this. Since you did not, we have a right, by consequence, to conclude in your own manner that this disobedience of yours ought to be punished with such a penalty, indeed a greater one than ours, which, as you say, was done in its victory. For this power is to be despised, so that the higher one may be honoured.

units.la: Scimus his auditis quid agitis, quid obstrepitis & quid rugatis faciebus stomachantes acclamatis? Nescente nullum fouemus in hac parte schismaticum, nullum hereticum, nullum depopulatorem ecclesiæ, nullum de his vehementer & notorie diffamatum. Ita excusatis vos fratres, nos econtra proponimus, accusamus, suademus, purgantes nos similiter per negationem eorum, quæ nobis imponitis, erat idcirco radix hæc difficultatis & controuersiæ ad quam euillendam totis eloquentiæ illius vestræ Tulliana nerui incumbere debuerat charitas vestra, quatenus probare videlicet Dominum Benedictum non esse schismaticum, non hæreticum, non aduersantem ecclesiasticæ vnitati, aut non de his merito vehementer infamatum, aut esse talem, qui non conuertit obedientiam suam honorem in instrumentum destructionis ecclesiæ, hoc est, quod in contentione versari, quod vnicum confutari conueniebat, non de obedientiæ præconiis & inobedientiæ suppliciis, imo de partialibus maledictis membranam occupare. Et istud tamen cur modo & non antea citius effecerit vestra fraternitas, nondum perspicua ratio inuenta est, nisi forte uti voluerimus suspitionibus maleuolis in vos, qualiter abutimini in nos. Diceret enim forsan suspitiosus aliquis, quod liuida æmulatio vestra ob præclarissimam studii nostri famam, aut aliunde male parta, nunc tandem nacta opportunitate egesta est, quasi sit aperiatur sepulchrum patens intus spurcidum & olidum. Suspicabitur alius non inuidiam, non odium, non rancorem: sed vel adulationem vel ambitionem sua promotionis auidam, rupisse hos vestrum silentium, dum spes arrisit nouarum prouisionum habendarum, si noua restitutio fieret, præsertim vobis petentibus & altercantibus, & vsque ad periculum capitis decertare pollicentibus, longe vero sint à nobis interpretationes huiusmodi maleuolæ & incertæ, fratres charissimi. Nunquam id agere nos contingat, quod in nos fierirationabiliter inculpamus. Ista quidem est rixatio vel fœminea vel canina, seu puerilis dentibus & vnguibus inuriarum causam ducere, ista pugna Goliad à contumeliosa contemptu certamen inire. Esto tamen fuerit in nobis (ut aut nostrum nonnullis intentionis corruptio, quoniam quis potest gloriari se mundum habere cor, cum non sit homo super terram iustus, qui non peccet. Nihilominus quale super hac corrupta adducitis efficax argumentum, ut tam certo, tam absoluto, tam in generali vos feriatis iudicio, quasi vocis illius immemores intonantis: nolite iudicare, & non iudicabimini. Esto sint inter nos aliqui ambitiosi ad beneficia, aliqui leues ad iudicia, aliqui odiosi ad Dominum Benedictum: unde tamen constat subtractionem per tales emersisse?
units.tr: Do we know what you are doing when you hear these things, what you mutter, and what you shout, fuming with wrinkled brows? We foster no schismatic in this part, no heretic, no destroyer of the Church, no one notoriously and vehemently defamed in these matters. So you excuse yourselves, brothers; on the other hand, we propose, accuse, persuade, and clear ourselves likewise by denying what you impute to us. This was therefore the root of the difficulty and controversy, and to uproot it your charity ought to have applied all the nerves of that Tullian eloquence of yours: namely, to prove that Lord Benedict is not a schismatic, not a heretic, not opposed to ecclesiastical unity, nor deservedly and vehemently defamed in these matters, nor such a one as turns his obedience and honour into an instrument for destroying the Church. That is what should have been contended and what alone needed refuting, not filling the parchment with praises of obedience and punishments of disobedience, but with partisan slanders. And why your brotherhood has done this now and not sooner, no clear reason has yet been found, unless perhaps we wish to use malicious suspicions against you, as you abuse them against us. For some suspicious person might say that your livid rivalry, provoked by the very famous reputation of our study, or else ill-gotten, has now at last found its opportunity and come forth, as if a gaping sepulchre were opened, foul and stinking within. Another will suspect not envy, not hatred, not rancour, but flattery or ambition, greedy for its own promotion, which broke your silence, since hope smiled on you of obtaining new provisions if a new restoration came about, especially as you petition, quarrel and promise to contend even to the peril of your life. But far be such malicious and uncertain interpretations from us, dearest brothers. May it never happen that we do what we reasonably blame in others. Indeed, to draw a cause of injury with teeth and nails is a wrangling either womanish, doglike or childish; to enter into a contest of contumelious contempt like Goliath's is a fight of that kind. Yet suppose there was in us (as in some of ours there is corruption of intention, since who can boast that he has a clean heart, when there is no just man upon earth who does not sin)... Nevertheless, what effective argument do you draw from this corrupt matter, that you strike so surely, so absolutely, and so universally in judgment, as if forgetful of that voice thundering: Judge not, and you shall not be judged. Suppose there are among us some ambitious for benefices, some light in judgments, some hostile to Lord Benedict: yet from what evidence does it appear that the withdrawal arose through such persons?

units.la: Omittamus nos respondere quomodo talia fingere habet vestra discretio de rege nostro & vestro, de Dominis Ducibus consanguineis suis, de Baronibus regni: praeterea de consilio regis, de prelatis & toto clero Francia? postremo de toto regno Hispania? Exclamabitis hic primo, iam exclamastis quod per nos seducti sunt, excaecati sunt, alienati sunt, mirum vero si vos soli & absentes & pauci apertos habetis oculos in eorum regimine, si vobis solis sua illuminatio, suaque directio debeatur. Attendite ne intolerabiliter nimis arrogetis. Scitis & creditis firmiter, quod Rex & Domini de suo sanguine generoso non adhaerent subtractioni pertinaciter, hoc est vestrum verbum: certe neque nos pertinaciter adhaeremus. Adhaeremus tamen sicut & ipsi, donec interim nobis paratis corrigi si erramus, clarius aliquid commodiusque pro ecclesia dilucescat. Aut igitur eos omnes pari nobis concrimine parique reatu conuoluite, quia subtraxerunt, sicut non vultis, quia non audetis, aut nos sicut ipsos habetote excusatos, quoniam pertinaces esse non volumus: quod tamen omnino facere refugitis: sed dicetis si non estis pertinaces, cur a damnata subtractionis continuatione non cessatis? Interrogetis similiter cur ab eadem rex non abscedit, quod si perurgetu quarentes rationem, nostra est communis responsio, quoniam nostram interim conscientiam sequimur.
units.tr: Let us not stop to answer how your discretion has invented such things about our king and yours, about the lords dukes, his kinsmen, the barons of the realm, the king's council, the prelates and the whole clergy of France, and finally about the whole kingdom of Spain. You will cry out here first, and you have already cried out, that they have been seduced by us, blinded, and alienated. Yet it would be remarkable if you alone, absent and few as you are, had open eyes in their government, and if their enlightenment and direction were owed to you alone. Take care not to be intolerably arrogant. You know, and firmly believe, that the King and the lords of his noble blood do not cling to the withdrawal obstinately; that is your word. Certainly we too do not cling to it obstinately. We cling to it as they do, until something clearer and more advantageous shines forth for the Church, and meanwhile we are ready to be corrected if we are in error. Either therefore charge them all with the same crime and the same guilt as us, since they withdrew, which you do not wish to do because you do not dare, or hold us excused just as you hold them, since we do not wish to be obstinate.
