Yet this you utterly shrink from doing. But you will say: if you are not obstinate, why do you not cease from continuing the condemned withdrawal? Likewise you will ask why the king does not depart from it. If you press this question urgently, our common answer is that meanwhile we follow our own conscience.

units.la: Nam quantum licet dubitare de Domino Benedicto, an perdiderit ius in papatu: aut quod obedientia adipsum est ecclesia pestifera, tantundem fas est ab eius obedientia secedere. Neque enim negabitis, quoniam pro culpa haeresis aut schismatis papa fieret inferior quolibet Christiano. Iura sunt ad hoc planissima. Neque praeterea latet vos potestatem papalem datam esse in aedificationem ecclesiae, non destructionem. Quo abusu in destructionem ecclesiae notorio existente, nonne exemplo Pauli resistere in facie gerenti se pro papa, liceret? nonne sibi dici posset, cur ita facis? Athanasius summus olim pontifex & aliorum nonnulli super hoc sunt in exemplum. Et o Deus arbiter aequissime, & quo pacto mirantur istud quidam hominum quasi non intelligibilis sit hac absurditas? cum in rebus longe minoribus id licere fieri, magno assensu concederent? Si enim palatium suum, si ciuitatem suam papa facibus accensis pro sua libidine quaereret concremare, si paganos armatos, si agrorum depopulatores moliretur apud Christianos intromittere, etiam vbi nihil fidei praedicaretur aduersum, si virgines ingenuas, aut matronas honorabiles violare satageret: quis tam indulgentissimus vnquam aut blandus adulator ad papam fuit, quin negaret his auSibus obuiandum esse, qui papam ipsum, si verba non sufficerent, diceret non debere factis arceri? Iure naturali conceditur vim vi repellere, ideoque conceditur vt persona singulari fas esset papam aut regem vel ligare vel carceri mancipare si eis iniuste persequentibus hanc personam, si sibi non aliunde pateret propria mortis aut impudica violationis effugium, si hoc in damnis corporalibus tam liquidum est, quid de spiritualibus incommodis longe grauioribus relinquitur aestimandum? Iungamus hanc rationem ad rem quaagitur.
units.tr: For, to the extent that one may doubt whether Lord Benedict has lost his right to the papacy, or whether obedience to him is harmful to the Church, to that same extent it is lawful to secede from his obedience. For you will not deny that, on account of the crime of heresy or schism, a pope would become inferior to any Christian. The laws on this point are most plain. Nor is it hidden from you that papal power was given for the building up of the Church, not its destruction. When such an abuse is notoriously leading to the destruction of the Church, would it not be lawful to resist to his face, as Paul did, one who claims to act for the pope? Could one not say to him: why do you act thus? Athanasius, once the chief pontiff, and some others, are an example in this matter. O God, the most righteous judge, and in what way do some men marvel at this, as if this absurdity were unintelligible, when they would readily grant that it is permitted in matters far less serious? For if the pope were to seek to burn his palace or his city with lighted torches at his pleasure; if he were to undertake to bring armed pagans or plunderers of the fields among Christians, even where nothing hostile to the faith was being preached; if he were to strive to violate freeborn virgins or honourable matrons: who ever was so indulgent or so fawning a flatterer of the pope that he would deny that such attacks must be opposed, and that one who, if words did not suffice, said he must not be checked by deeds? By natural law it is granted to repel force by force. Therefore it is granted that a private person may lawfully bind the pope or the king, or hand him over to prison, if they unjustly pursued this person, and if no other escape from his own death or shameful violation lay open to him. If this is so clear in bodily harms, what must be judged concerning spiritual injuries, far more grievous? Let us join this reasoning to the matter in question.

units.la: Si subtracti habuerunt probabiles vehementesque coniecturas, aut certas rationes ex his quae facti sunt, quod Dominus Benedictus aduersabatur ecclesiasticae vnitati: nunquid non bono fine & intentione poterat hac fieri subtractio? quaeretis quo pacto sic? quippe vt non assumeret obedientiam sibi factam in velamen aliquod nequitiae aut protelationis schismatica prauitatis. Ex quibus mille mediis, aut continuando honores suos sine procuratione vnionis, aut promouendo sibi fauentes in hac libidine dominandi, aut nunc aperte, nunc occulte, non fauentes sibi persequendo.
units.tr: If those who withdrew had probable and strong conjectures, or certain reasons drawn from what has been done, that Lord Benedict was opposing the unity of the Church, could the withdrawal not have been made with a good end and intention? You will ask how so? Namely, so that he would not take the obedience paid to him as a cover for some wickedness or for delaying the perversity of schism. From these, a thousand means: either by continuing his honours without any care for achieving unity, or by promoting those who favour him in this lust for domination, or by persecuting, now openly, now secretly, those who do not favour him.

units.la: Videtis clare, si quid videtis, quod nullis hoc loco, vt imur sophismatibus, imo ne sophismatum paralogismi vos decipiant (sicut fefellisse videntur) nos ipsam ad nudam difficultatem reuelamus, cum proprium sit sophistarum se celare & positiones suas vel inuoluere vel transferre. Nullas praeterea legum interpretationes subdolas aut fictas adducimus, solis innitimur regulis iuris diuini & naturalis, quas pro vobis assumitis, quasque immutabili veritate subsistere, nequaquam ignoratis. Ha sunt regulae quibus summus ecclesiae prelatus propter ecclesiae vtilitatem stabilitus est. Quod papa si apostatat a fide resistendum est in facie, & si non recte ambulet ad veritatem euangelii, quod vim vi licet repellere, quod Deo magis est obediendum quam hominibus, quod bonum publicum praeferendum est bono particulari, quod ad publicum ordinatum est. Istis inquam innitimur non vt falso criminamini talibus, quod facienda sunt mala vt bona eueniant: quod persequendus est papa verus, vt schismaticis salus detur. Nondum ita vestri similes sumus, vt ita desipiamus. Quid ergo multos turpiter plane inuoluunt sophismata, dum nimis fugiuntur, quia enim videre nequeunt qualem papa verus aut pro tali habitu desinere possit esse papa, aut habendus est pro tali, ipsi non capiunt qua ratione subtractio possit (imo & debeat in casu) iustissima reputari, hoc est inquiunt inobedientem esse, hoc est persecutorem capitis existere, cum tamen nulla successio a capite dici debeat inobedientia, neque persecutio, nisi legi diuinae fuerit contraria. Est autem diuina lex iubens recedere a tabernaculis impiorum, iubens fratrem post quam audire noluerit ecclesiam, habendum esse sicut ethnicum & publicanum, iubens praeterea oculum aut membrum aliud eruendum esse, ne totum corpus sua contagione depraret, qua diuina iussio qualiter ad rem quae tractatur adaptari debeat, insinuatum est. Scimus tamen quid adhuc respondetis, negatis in hoc negotio causas tales in facto. Hoc vero est quod in disceptatione nostra versatur, hoc probare quod negamus, aut improbare quod aestimamus, debuerat charitatis vestra prudentia, aut non notissima ingerere, non nos mille conuiciis insectari, non nos priusquam intelligeretis arguere. Et quoniam idipsum non peroratis & res longiori disputatione eget, quam vt sub epistola breuitate possit coartari, quia denique iam pluries tam scripturis quam viuis vocibus rationabilitatem nostra subtractionis, si non potius libellus diffamatorius appellari meruit, nec latet nos qua multa alia posuistis, quae si rigidum examen intrarent, illa de errore in fide, de crimine in bonis moribus, de inobedientia laesae maiestatis regiae, & aliis pluribus damnanda paterent, quae omnia ostendere sicut & principale causam nostrae iustificare paratos nos offerimus, quantum & quemadmodum tu, rex sapientissime, iusseris, qui hactenus nos indiuiduos coadiutores tuos assumere dignatus es, neq; enim diuersum a te quicquam agere fas putat discretio nostra. Et si improbe vocari ad certamen impar minus numero & virtute sufferre molestum sit. Potuerant ista sufficere, si no vicissitudine referre vellemus, reddentes p malo bonu, & benedictione monitoria pro exprobatione maledica cu illo q cu glorifica-dis. dū ait, maledicimur & benedicimus, itaque petimus rationem, fratres, quo fructu, quave utilitate complacuerit seiungi à communi regis & regni concilio. Periret quippe omnis politicus ordo, si ea quae communi sunt assensu conclusa quilibet pro suo motu capitis vel inculpare, vel ad novam censuram revocare contenderet. Vbi enim fuit vnquam tam aperta, tam concors sententia, quae non aduersis calumniantium linguis carpi posset? aliis amore, aliis ignorantia, aliis sola contrariandi proteruia aut pruritu novas res moliendi vexatis, sed neque concilii generalibus praestitus est olim assensus vnanimis taliter, vt non ex aliqua parte contradictores inuenirentur. Æquum est idcirco legibusque & consuetudine sancitum, vt in ore maioris partis stet omne communitatis iudicium. Alioquin si cuilibet assidue fas esset obniti, nihilo plus ageretur, quam si inter nauclerios eiusdem navis odiosum continuaretur iurgium, illis velum tendere, istis laxare, aliis dextrorsum, aliis sinistrorsum ex adverso conari implicabili animositate tractantibus, deliberatione enim maioris partis exceptata, nonne consultius est ei vos opem ferre, vel nequaquam pertinaciter aduersari, & ita portum qualemlibet attingere, quam sub dubia spe meliores portus confundere interim omnia seditione certissima, multa proinde tolerari debent iam facta, quorum inceptis contradicere dignum erat: Esto vobis appareant, vel forte sint saniora consilia, nihilominus apud communitatem, cuius est pars parua, ambulantem in opposita sententia, quid prodest tractus vester pertinax aliorsum, imo quid aliud operatur quam contentiones, scandala, animositates & disturbia ad rem omnem quae agitur, saluberior finienda? Negotium aliud grande priusquam certa conclusione firmetur, opus habet consultatione, in qua sit animus in consulendo liber, porro acceptata conclusione, tunc est tempus faciendi, non diiudicandi.
units.tr: You see clearly, if you see anything, that we here use no deceitful sophisms, nor do we seek to escape by them, nor are we deceived by the paralogisms of sophisms, as you seem to have been. We lay bare the matter to its bare difficulty, since it is the mark of sophists to hide themselves and either to entangle or to shift their positions. Nor do we bring forward any crafty or fabricated interpretations of the laws. We rely only on the rules of divine and natural law, which you yourselves assume on your side and which, as you well know, stand on immutable truth. These are the rules by which the chief prelate of the Church was established for the Church's benefit: that if the pope apostatises from the faith he must be resisted to his face; that if he does not walk uprightly towards the truth of the gospel he must be resisted; that force may be repelled by force; that God must be obeyed rather than men; that the public good is to be preferred to a particular good, since the particular good is ordered to the public. It is on these, I say, that we rely, not so that you may falsely accuse us of such things as that evil must be done that good may come, or that the true pope must be persecuted so that salvation may be given to the schismatics. We are not yet so like you that we would talk such nonsense. Why then do sophisms so shamefully entangle many of you, while you flee so much? For since you cannot see in what way a true pope could cease to be pope by such a condition, or be held to be such, you do not grasp by what reasoning the withdrawal can be considered most just (indeed, in this case, ought to be so). That is, you say that it is disobedience, that it is persecution of the head; yet no disobedience or persecution ought to be said to follow from the head, unless it is contrary to divine law. Now divine law commands us to withdraw from the tents of the wicked; it commands that a brother who refuses to hear the Church be held as a heathen and a tax collector; it commands moreover that an eye or another member be plucked out, lest the whole body be corrupted by its contagion. How this divine command ought to be applied to the matter under discussion has been explained. Yet we know what you still reply: you deny that such causes exist in fact in this business. But the point at issue in our dispute is this: to prove what we deny, or to disprove what we judge, your charitable prudence ought to have brought forward either things not most well known, or not to have assailed us with a thousand insults, nor to have accused us before you understood us. And since you do not argue this very point, and the matter needs a longer disputation than can be confined within the brevity of a letter; since, finally, many times already our reasoning for the withdrawal, if it has not rightly been called a defamatory pamphlet, has deserved to be called so, both in writings and in spoken words; and since we are not unaware of the many other things you have advanced, which, if they entered a rigorous examination, would appear to deserve condemnation: those concerning error in the faith, crime against good morals, disobedience to the royal majesty, and many others. All of these we offer ourselves ready to show, as well as our principal cause, to justify it, as far as and in the manner you, most wise king, have ordered, you who have hitherto deigned to take us as your individual helpers. For our discretion thinks it right to do nothing differing from you. And although it would be troublesome to suffer being summoned unfairly to a contest, unequal in number and strength, these things might have sufficed, if we wished to requite in return, rendering good for evil, and a blessing of admonition for a cursing reproach, along with him who, when he was glorified, said: "We are cursed, and we bless." Therefore, brothers, we ask for the reason, and with what fruit or what advantage it has pleased you to be separated from the common council of the king and the realm. For every political order would perish if whoever wished, by his own impulse, to find fault with or to call back to a new examination those things that have been concluded by common consent. For where was there ever a judgment so open, so harmonious, that it could not be picked apart by the hostile tongues of slanderers, some vexed by love, others by ignorance, others by mere contrariness or the itch of stirring up new things? Yet even general councils have never been given unanimous assent in such a way that opponents were not found on some side. It is therefore just, and sanctioned by law and custom, that the judgment of the whole community rests in the mouth of the greater part. Otherwise, if it were always lawful for anyone to resist, nothing more would be done than if among the sailors of one ship a hateful quarrel went on, some trying to spread the sail, others to slacken it, some striving to steer to starboard, others to port, all acting with inextricable hostility. For when the deliberation of the greater part has been accepted, is it not more advisable either to bring help to it, or at least not to oppose it obstinately, and so to reach some harbour, however poor, than to throw everything into confusion, in a doubtful hope of better harbours, meanwhile with the most certain sedition? Therefore many things already done must be tolerated, though it would have been right to oppose their beginnings. Even if other and perhaps sounder counsels appear to you, nevertheless, what good does your obstinate pulling in the opposite direction do, before a community of which you are a small part? Indeed, what does it accomplish but contentions, scandals, animosities and disturbances, rather than bringing the whole matter at hand to a more wholesome end? Any other great business, before it is settled by a firm conclusion, needs deliberation, in which the mind is free in advising. But once the conclusion has been accepted, then is the time for acting, not for judging.

units.la: Quod si opposuerit u praeceptum Domini, vt non peccet aliquis sequendo multitudinem, hoc de criminibus, quae bene fieri nequeunt, intelligi necesse est, non enim talia vnquam licere facies quantuslibet numerus peccantium, & stultorum, quorum infinitus est numerus. At vero secus est in eis quae fieri bene possunt, in quibus conscientiam propriam ad aliorum formare iudicium quandoque licitum, quandoque debitum est, qualiter esse dicimus in proposito, vbi ea quae in facto sunt, non quae fidem immediate respiciunt, ventilantur. Obiicietis fortasse, quod non syncerIS animis, non mediis vsquequaque iuridicis, non per personas omni vitio carentes conclusio substractionis exceptaest, quasi non ita possit fingi in omni negotio publico, quasi praeterea per solos bonos beneplacitum suum operatur Deus, operatur & per malos, quales etiam inter vos aliqui sunt, & si confirmatos vos pharisaice iactetis pra ceteris hominibus, & exceptos ab illa regula, si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus. Quot principes infideles, quot tyrannos iniquos legimus & vidimus, à quibus aequissimas leges & edicta quis nesciat emanasse? qua in re perspicuum esse debet, quod negotii qualitatem magis attendere conueniet, si iusto fine, si pia intentione fieri potuerit, quam suspicionibus duci ex agentium hac vel illa voluntate.
units.tr: If someone objects to the command of the Lord, that one does not sin by following the multitude, this must be understood of crimes which cannot be done rightly; for no number of sinners, however great, and of fools, whose number is endless, ever makes such things lawful. But it is otherwise with things which can be done rightly, in which it is sometimes lawful and sometimes a duty to form one's own conscience in accordance with the judgment of others; as we say is the case in the present matter, where the question concerns things that have been done, not those which touch faith immediately. You will perhaps object that the conclusion of the withdrawal was reached without sincere minds, without fully just means, and not through persons free of every fault, as if such a thing could not be imagined in every public business; as if God works his good pleasure only through good men, and works also through bad men, of whom there are some among you too; and if you boast in the Pharisaic manner that you are confirmed above other men and exempt from that rule, "if we say that we have no sin". How many unbelieving princes, how many wicked tyrants have we read and seen, from whom, as everyone knows, most equitable laws and edicts have proceeded? In this matter it ought to be plain that one should rather attend to the character of the business, if it can be done with a just end and a pious intention, than be led by suspicions drawn from this or that will of those who act.

units.la: Praeterea fratres, cessent contumelia, abeant sinistra de nobis suspiciones, quales habere de vobis nec vultis nec volumus. Credite fratres nos bene conscii nobis sumus de processu hoc ad pacem ecclesiae: qui vtinam tam prosperum successum caperet, quam pie semper optamus, optare autem hoc magis nostrum est, quam illud exhibere.
units.tr: Moreover, brethren, let reproaches cease, let those sinister suspicions about us depart, such as neither you wish to have of us nor we of you. Believe us, brethren, we are well aware of ourselves concerning this process for the peace of the Church; would that it might meet with as prosperous a success as we always piously desire. Yet to desire this is more our part than to bring it about.

units.la: Tandem quia res (vt arbitramini) discussionem exigit ampliorem (non enim propter aliud nos ad certamen provocare deberetis) obsecramus te, rex serenissime, sicut iam obsecrauimus, pro concilio totius obedientia istius celebrando, in quo conueniant seniores, videre de factis & de iure (quod ex factis exoritur) examinatissimam veritatem, quam semper ampleciti paratos nos offerimus in nomine eius, qui est veritas, in quo bene valere & sobria modestia sapere omnes optamus fratres nostros in eodem Domino charissimos.
units.tr: Finally, since the matter (as you think) demands a fuller discussion (for you ought not to challenge us to contest for any other reason), we beseech you, most serene king, as we have already besought you, to call a council of the whole obedience, in which the elders may meet, to see the most carefully examined truth concerning the facts and the law (which arises out of the facts), which we always stand ready to embrace and to offer in the name of him who is the truth, in whom we all wish our brethren, most dear in the same Lord, to fare well and to be wise with sober moderation.

units.la: Talia in aliorum personam transfigurata sint (o sorores) pro recusione eorum, qui nimia acritate sententiam propriam defendere, & alienam carpere reperti sunt. Et quoniam ita tibi placitum est, o soror Beneuolentia (hoc enim nutu tuo significas) conuertatur oratio nostra ad eos, qui acta omnium, praesertim superiorum, tota severitate recensent atque diiudicant, nullum eis refugium ad correctionem, nullum locum ad veniam vel excusationem relinquentes, cum pfecto male nimis essent res humanae, si semel peccantibus clauderetur misericordiae sinus, q si misericordia cocedi tur hominibus, illa obsecro quibus rationabiliter iudicio praestabitur, q hominibus occupatis, q hominibus ad regimen reipublicae constitutis, liquide ad eos ex omni parte fallendos inuigilat assidue subditorum quorundam malignitas, nunc mendaciorum fuco, nunc blanditiis adulationum, nunc accusationum confictionibus, nunc ingestione suspitionum, vt vel sic rapiant, spolient & detrahant, vel vt amorem simulent, tanquam solliciti de salute Domini sui, si multos accusauerint, si mendacibus novitatibus aures prurientes principum fricauerint, si accensos odiis, si stimulatos ira animos eorum magis inflammare vrgereque studuerint. Quam ob rem non abs re videtur dixisse Seneca consulendum esse bonae menti suadere, quam inquit bonam mentem nemo occupatus inuenit, & alibi tradit hac ratione esse vel difficile vel impossibile, vt idem sit princeps & vir bonus. Ipsi profecto superiores non tam super homines, quam homines super eorum capita positi sunt, & non tam inuidia quam misericordia digni habendi, tanquam miserabiliores caeteris hominibus, & velut positi ad sagittas causa deceptoriae iaculationis, quorum multorum stultitiam adulatio in insaniam vertit, aliorum iracundiam in furorem, aliorum beneuolentiam indulgentemque naturam trahit ad prodigalitatem crudelissimam. Rapiunt enim à pauperibus, quod apud ditiores effundant. Parcunt denique delinquentibus languida quadam specie benignitatis illecti: sed redit haec misericordia fatua, innocentum perniciem truculentam. Quantus erat ille rex & propheta Dauid, quam sagax, quam peruigil? ipse cum ad vnius serui mendolam vocem seductus est, vt haereditatem, cuius pater Dauid optime meruerat, ad eundem seruum traduceret, postmodum quod etiam monitus non restituit, sed diuidendam imperauit. Quorsum haec omnia? nimirum vt commonefacerem tolerandos esse pia comcompassione defectus superiorum magisque diiudicatione secuta persequendos. Neque mihi quisquam opposuerit illud sapientis: exiguo conceditur misericordia. Potentes autem tormenta potenter patientur. Ipsi vero principes in hoc exigui sunt, eoque amplius si ex ignorantia forte sua ipsi sibi grandes, sibi fortes & beati videantur. Rursus si plura in hominibus vitia correctionis impositia tolerat: referuans ea divinae censurae iudicii, idem fieri de principatuum delictis necessitas magis expostulat. Ut non protinus pro quolibet errato spernatur eorum principatus: cum Apostolus Dominis etiam dischollis, & Christus Pharisaeis hypocritis obedire praeceperit: & ... diffinit principem non debere repercuti. Vidit hoc Tragicus ille, qui monuit Athenienses ... introducerent in civitatem: introductum vero eum cum omni mansuetudine & lenitate tractarent: quae similitudo satis est accommoda rei, quam agimus. Quod si de quolibet principante haec vera sunt, ipsi Domino omnium: & eo servo omnium, quo Domino omnium, Papam loquor: quis non hoc commune misericordiae debitum impendendum arbitretur? Esto Dominus Benedictus erraverit in non offerendo celeriter viam cessionis; attendatur in eo potuisse cadere deceptiones, quales numeramus provenientes ex ... Attendatur humani cordis fragilitas ad honores quaerendos avida, & pertinax ad retinendos, attendatur quantas vires habeant suspiciones ingestas malevolis: necesse facile illos pro libito diffluere. Attendatur insuper poenitentia ipsius offensis iam pridem id quod ab initio quaerebatur. Denique si erratum est ab eo, nunquid sibi ... poenitentiae quae cuilibet inferiori aperta est, occludetur? Nunquid poenalis carcer, nunquid ... dolores alii in corpore, in bonis & in fama iam plus quadringenti ... diluere sufficiunt hoc erratum? Videriint si qui sint monstrantes oppositum verbo vel opere: ne plus hostili odio personae, quam unitatis publicae zelo se prodant inflammatos. Itaque placet hoc loco inserere quandam Epistolam quasi nomine suo ad Regem Franciae destinatam, quae sic contexta est.
units.tr: Let such things be turned into the person of others (O sisters), on account of the refusal of those who are found to defend their own opinion with excessive sharpness and to carp at another's. And since it has pleased you so, O sister Benevolence (for this is what you signify by your nod), let our discourse be turned to those who scrutinize and judge the acts of all, especially of superiors, with the utmost severity, leaving them no refuge for correction and no place for pardon or excuse; for human affairs would indeed be in very bad case if the bosom of mercy were once closed to sinners. And if mercy is granted to men, I beg you, let it be granted rightly to those judged, and especially to men occupied and set over the government of the commonwealth. The malice of certain subjects watches constantly to deceive them on every side: now with the paint of lies, now with the flatteries of flattery, now with the fabrications of accusations, now by the throwing in of suspicions, so that they may either seize, despoil and defame, or feign affection, as if anxious for the safety of their lord; if they have accused many, if they have rubbed the itching ears of princes with lying novelties, if they have striven to inflame still more the minds kindled with hatred or goaded with anger. For this reason it seems not without cause that Seneca said one ought to counsel a good mind by persuasion, which, he says, no busy man finds a good mind; and elsewhere he teaches that by this reasoning it is either difficult or impossible for the same man to be a prince and a good man. Truly the superiors themselves are placed not so much above men as men are placed above their heads, and are to be considered worthy not so much of envy as of pity, as more wretched than other men, and as if set up as targets for a deceptive shot; in many of them flattery turns folly into madness, in others it turns anger into fury, and in others it draws a kindly and indulgent nature into the most cruel prodigality. For they seize from the poor what they may squander among the rich. Finally, they spare offenders, drawn on by a languid semblance of kindness; but this foolish mercy returns as a savage ruin to the innocent. How great was that king and prophet David, how shrewd, how watchful? Yet he himself, when he was seduced by the lying voice of one servant, transferred to the same servant the inheritance for which his father David had deserved so well; afterwards, even when warned, he did not restore it, but commanded it to be divided. Why all this? Surely to remind us that the failings of superiors are to be tolerated with pious compassion, and pursued rather with judgment following. Nor let anyone set against me the saying of the wise man: "Mercy is granted to the little one; but the mighty shall suffer mighty torments." Princes themselves are little in this matter, and all the more so if, through their ignorance, they seem to themselves great, strong and blessed. Again, if men bear more vices than are imposed by correction, leaving them to the judgment of divine censure, the same necessity more urgently demands that the same be done for the offences of princedoms. So that their principate is not at once despised for any error, since the Apostle commanded obedience even to harsh masters, and Christ to hypocritical Pharisees; and ... defines that a prince ought not to be struck back. That tragic poet saw this, who admonished the Athenians ... to introduce into the city; and having been introduced, they should treat him with all gentleness and mildness. That comparison is apt enough for the matter we are treating. But if these things are true of any ruler, of the Lord of all himself, and of that servant of all, who is the Lord of all, I mean the Pope: who would not think that this common debt of mercy ought to be paid? Granted that Lord Benedict may have erred in not quickly offering the way of withdrawal; let it be considered that he could have fallen into deceptions of the kind we count arising from ... Let the frailty of the human heart be considered, greedy in seeking honours and tenacious in keeping them; let it be considered how great power the suspicions poured in by malevolent men have, so that they easily flow away at will. Let it be considered further that repentance, the very thing which was sought from the beginning, is already present in the offended. Finally, if he has erred, will the repentance which is open to any inferior be closed to him? Will a penal prison, will ... other pains in body, in goods and in reputation, now more than four hundred ... suffice to wash away this error? Let those see to it, if there are any who show the contrary by word or deed, lest they betray themselves inflamed more by hostile hatred of a person than by zeal for public unity. Therefore it pleases us to insert at this point a certain Letter, addressed to the King of France as if in his own name, which is composed thus.

units.la: Benedictus Episcopus servus servorum Dei charissimo filio in Christo Carolo Francorum Regi Christianissimo salutem, Apostolicamque benedictionem & misericordiae spiritum assumere. Si demolitio Hierusalem terrestris bimi perstrinxit ad lachrymas cor Prophetae Hieremiae & Salvatoris Iesu: Si praeterea corporalis separatio sponsi a sponsa fidelis tanta est molestia: si denique ipsa etiam natura suo docet instinctu turturem assiduos gemitus edere, dum compari viduatam se senserit: nullus mirabitur si in desolatione mirabili spiritualis Hierusalem, & in acerbissima separatione, quam in ea sensit animus, conqueror & ploro. Quid igitur dabit capiti meo aquam & oculis meis fontem lachrymarum, ad deflendum sugitter luctuosissimam Sacrosanctae Ecclesiae labefactionem diminutionemque? Quis me consolabitur? quis medebitur? Consilium quale mihi perveniet? ita planctus lugubris; dolor & angustia tanguntur omnes in communi filios Ecclesiae. Sed longe saevius atque profundius dilaceret infelix cor meum inaudita miseria, hoc exterminium. Ista perditio nimirum data mihi illa est in sponsam singularem, quae omnium mater est universalis: his nihilominus ... tam nefando ... hismate eam, quae mater est pacis & unitatis, tam excranda & atroci persecutione eam sedari; quae fons est pietatis, tandem vili deiectione & ignominiosa servitute eam ipsam proteri, quae libertatem & honores largitur aeternos. O piae mater omnium, o mea singularis sponsa quousque durabit pessimus iste languor tuus? quamnam debachabitur furor impius in viscera tua, satiusque nimisque tuis in membris perseverat hoc horrenda divisio. Et heu quale tibi ministrabo consilium? tuis quo pacto medebor incommodis? Cruentum hoc vulnus tuum in me descendit ut vides: quoniam hinc vastatrices curae, hinc sollicitudines perigiles, intus timores anxii, foris pugnae, in tribulatione violentia, & diuturno indignoque tractare, qui mihi de propria comparatus est domo, & de speciosa olim nunc domesticorum manu obruto palatio. Quid referam probra? quid diffamationes iniquas? quid sinistrae interpretationes dictorum factorumque meorum? quid illae mei & meorum inenarrabiles afflictiones? Attamen non est haec malorum summa: vtinam in caput meum refluerent omnes erumnae tuae? O fidelis sponsa usque ad duram mortis perpessionem sine detrimento animae. Et tu benedicta libertate foveres in gremio pacis omnes filios tuos & oves pascua tua. Et o pater maxime & optime; o salutifer Christe, ut quid natus sum videre mala gentis meae? ut quid datus sum custos, sponsus & pastor, si non aliam opem, aliud solamen, & aliud ferri dabatur auxilium? porro si sancti patres, quibus infausta tempestate succedo, gemebant olim sub verendo pondere curae pastoralis: sicuti Gregorius & aliorum plurimi, etiam dum Ecclesia suo honore & prosperitate floreret: quid nunc dicturus sum in sua & mea tam incomparabili calamitate & in tanta malorum mole? Hinc vel maxime perspicuum esse debet me in tali statu afflictionis morarum & perniciose retinendo non esse contumacem. Aliquin profecto miserabilior & stolidior sum omnibus hominibus, qui miseriam certam cum certa damnatione quaererem, sed auertat hanc insaniam a servo suo misericors Deus. Caeterum nonne varus & laboriosus antea legationibus attritus sum, si forte resarciretur truculenta haec ruptura, & si discussis tenebris serena veritas oriretur. Sed nunc elevans me dignitas gravius allisit, & coangustavit undique. Itaque gravis fortinsecus cernitur corporalis afflictio. Subter vero introrsus plaga saevit acrior, dum pia retractatione considero, quemadmodum omnes conatus mei, omnis zelus pius, omne ferens desiderium ad pacem adipiscendam cassati sunt. Et o mores, o tempora; etce quod supra modum auget infelicitatis tumulum, a nonnullis etiam de peruersa intentione notor & inculpor. Quid dicam ad haec? plane & constanter negabo. Potuit aliqua fortasis suspicere ignorantia, quae tam vitiosa est humana fragilitati, & in hoc me meaque omnia prorsus iustificare nequaquam audebo. Illud namque Apostolicum verbum quem hominum non exterreat? nihil mihi conscius sum: sed non in hoc iustificatus sum. Cuius dicti quae alia est ratio: nisi quod in multis offendimus, & quoniam non est homo super terram qui viuat & non peccet, & quod incerta sunt prouidentia nostra & iustitia omnes sordidae tanquam pannus menstruatae: denique quales sumus in oculis divinae maiestatis, novit nullus. E- si iustus fuero (inquit Iob) hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea: verum si maligna fraude, si cupida ambi-tione. Putaui quicquam agere quod Ecclesiastice vnioni vel obstaret vel eam retardaret: sit in animam iudex Deus, quoniam potius talia ab initio vsque in praesens obtuli, quae salubria & sufficientia pro vnitatu prosecu-tione fideliter aestimabam & adhuc existimo, si non obfuisset pater ille mendacii, qui omnia in malum & turbationum euertisset. Nosse potes hac omnia, fili Serenissime & Christianissime, coram quo fiducialiter haec querelam effudi, nec habeo necesse regias aures adimplere longa narratione talium oblationum per me factarum, tam de via concordiae utriusque obedientia per consilium a fratribus meis Cardinalibus primitus datum, quam de via compromissi, & nouissime de via cessionis. Cui via, imo & martyrio, sicuti palam testatus sum, iugiter adhaesi secundum praeparationem animi. Nec ab hac vnquam promptitudine discessurus sum, si & dum veram parere vnionem cessio videbitur, testes sunt apud te harum oblationum patentes litera mea: nisi dolose aliarum silentio contecta sint. Arbitror autem nunc elucescere, si leuior fuisset & opportunior pro incundo tractatu vnionis, prima conuentionis oblatio, quam subito incursu talem arripere viam, quam in has truderet angustias, & cui nullum vnquam praebuerunt assensum aduersarii, absque quibus generalem fieri vnionem quis expectet? Nolo tamen, inclyte fili, ex his dictis vel dicendis tuam inculpare devotionem ad pacem Ecclesiae: quae vinam devotio nulla vnquam mendaci informatione super meis & aliorum gestis quaesita fuisset illudi & terripi. Sed admirari non sufficio quo pacto ego, qui sic egerim, sic tracter, infamer, includar, & nondum pro liberatione ab indignis carceribus tuum meruerim auxilium. Nonne tui antecessores proprium habuerunt succurrere non solum vexationibus Ecclesiae: non solum summis pontificibus in sua sede reponendis, sed omnibus communiter iniuste passis: quasi nobilis Francia domus templum tale esset misericordiae, quale apud Athenas fuisse memoratur, vbi cunctis afflictis erat praesto subsidium. Nunc enim, fili carissime, verae regum Franciae progenies & haeres exemplorum insignium, vides coram oculis tuae serenitatis illum: quem pro iusto Papa coluisti & colu illum: quem vt patrem summum in terris & animae tuae pastorem sanctum frequentibus titulis extulisti: Illum praeterea, quem tu cum regnotu succesisse confiteris per electionem legitimam Christo & Petro, illum quoque, quem viuentem prudentissimus pater tuus viuens coluit vt talem, illum denique, qui etiamsi caduci numerentur honores, nobilis est prosapia, illum denique qui Deo propicio vitam hucusque duxit innocuam, sine qualis infamiae nota deformis: quia quid intus agatur, iudex erit cordium inspector Deus: tu, inquam, talis vides me talem (de me enim loquor, & me laudasse coegit necessitas) vides modo sic inclusum, sic contumeliose tractatum tanquam essem vnus ex seruis abiectissimis, sine honore, sine dignitate, sine statu, sine genere, & vitae celebritate. Nihilominus autem dissimulas, fili, aut contemnis prabere succursum: neque me expediri iubes, qui vnico mandato tuo ab his me incommodis potes liberare. Quanquam compertum habeo non te iubente itafieri, neque persuaderi sane potest, vt credam generosum animum tuum erga meas arumnas tanta duritie stringi: quoniam mollesceret ad compassionem, si profunda & religiosa consideratio oculos ad tanta rei indignitatem conuerteret. Quid de te loquor? quoniam ipsos etiam barbaros, & paganos pietas naturalis tangeret, si viderent personam nuper talis auctoritatis, gradus & honoris & nobilitatis repente deiici & concludi intra parietes domesticos & hostiliter oppugnari. Existimo quod & in regno tuo maxima pars mea calamitati compatitur, sicut & dolorem aliorum regnorum experior. Proinde si ex consiliariis tuis aliqui (vtinam boni sint omnes & fidi) seducere vellent regium animum, ne mihi meoque statui miserentur: videant saltem tales & ponderent tuam & regni tui famam: quoniam dedecus filii est pater sine honore, & in subditorum infamiam redundat praesidentis opprobrium, quale est insuper illud, quod ab aduersariis & aemulis quotidiana insultatione iactatur. Vellem silerent, & ego digitum ponerem ori meo: sed vox altior & populosior est, quam vt regi possit, & qualis vox? quod a Gallicis tenetur obsessus dire & hostiliter Papaftus: vox quod Domino suo supremo aduersi sunt; nec alterum sequuntur & suum persequuntur, vox quod pro habito mutant Papas, nunc instituunt, mox destituunt: vox quod facto ipso etsi non verbo fatentur se reos in schismate, & partem corroborant quam impugnant, tales & plures circumuolant rumores & improperia, & quam apparenter id fiat, viderint illi qui talium sunt occasio. Atvero fortasis obiicient aliqui, me in causa esse omnium quae lugemus. Nam cur inquiunt dignitatem tuam per fas aut nefas retines? cur non ad ea quae petuntur condescendis? Possem huic obiectioni planis & validissimis obniti responsionibus ad iustitiam meam (nisi quod propositum hic habeo alterum) & quoniam aduertis, quam lubricus & instabilis esset omnis dominii status, si repente ad vocem cuiuslibet cedendum esset iuri suo, iure vel iniuria sine discretione, sine fructu, sine manifesta necessitate: sed non hic insistendum detrexi. Hoc vnum postulo & exhortor in Domino, pro communi bono totius Ecclesiae quatenus depulsis ira, odio & vindicta & quae retro sunt obliuiscentes, extendamus nos in anteriora ad vnionem promerendam, tu praecipue inter caeteros, qui singularis protectores & cultor Ecclesiae, vt sollicite consulas. Quid prodest, imo quantum paci obest, quod includor carcere ego, qui tam libero & parato sum animo ad omnia pro eadem pace, vbi nihilominus pars aduersa perstat in errore suo: neque verbo significans, neque facto velle se cognoscere veritatem iustitiae nostrae, neque offert aut recipit viam aliquam, per quam intrusus suam habeat sedem deserere, quam occupat vel saltem pari pede pax quaeratur. Scis tamen quot & quantis legationibus pulsatisunt, ex quibus ita esse non ignoras, si non fictitiis relationum commentis elusues. Nunc quali ipse prosequimur partem vniversalem, si particularis, simultiplex & origis sit inter nos diuisio? Qua fiducia resistimus falsitati, si veritatem nostram inutiliter confundimus? prodesse quid expectamus in non obediendo ei, qui canonice non dubitatur electus & esse tanquam corpus lacerum membris a capite diuulsis, quando ternimus aliospertinaci animositate in sua vnitate non vere vna coniunctos. Nec ifia dico sit veritas tanta sollicitudine ad liberationem corporalem (quam etsi tamen opto, quis mirabitur?) quantum pro affectu boni & honoris totius & dignitatis pontificalis sanctae Sedis Apostolicae, tui praeterea & re-gni tui & totius obedientiae adherentis veritati. Quamobrem concludendo precor & obsecror, fili carissime in Christo, quatenus hanc querimoniam filiali devotione & Christiano altoque animo suspicions iubeas caveas circa me cessare custodiam, quae prorsus indigna est: & si non forte de meritis propriis erga Deum: Ecclesiastica tamen dignitati illi proinde qui pater nominatur, & talis regis, qui demum Christianus est Christus Domini. In quem Christianos, imo filios proprios abuti senitia tyrannorum quantum qualeq; piaculum sit animadvertis. Audent quidam sacrilega impietate (sicut accepi) impurum & procax os laxare, ad notandum me pro haeretico aut schismatico: qui utinam tam tenaces essent fidei aut religionis, quam longe sum ab hac blasphemia. Errare ut cum Augustino fatear potero: sed haereticus non ero: neq; est alia indignius a me vel impatientius ferenda iniuria. Ideo obnitens talibus cum vnosanctorum patrum libere pronuntio, mentiuntur. Terrusus invoco, fili, ut feras mihi fi afflicto velociter auxilium: quemadmodum in tali necessitate (qualis nec tibi unquam nec sanguini contingat tuo) nequaquam dissimulare: sed totis conatuum viribus obviare satagerem. Pone quaeso ante providentiae tuae oculos, qualis futura esset Ecclesiae facies, & quam foeda negotiorum turbatio, perplexitas & insolutio scaturirent, si nunc migrarem a carne, non habito prius alio rerum stabilimento, vel ordinis serenitate: sicut haberi potest dum vivo, si non vel nequiter vel prauiter abiicior.
units.tr: Benedict, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son in Christ, Charles, Most Christian King of the French: greeting, and the Apostolic blessing, and the spirit of mercy. If the desolation of earthly Jerusalem moved the heart of the prophet Jeremiah and of the Saviour Jesus to tears, and if the bodily separation of a faithful bride from her bridegroom is so great a grief, and if nature itself teaches the turtledove to utter constant moans when it feels itself widowed of its mate, then no one will wonder that I complain and weep over the wonderful desolation of spiritual Jerusalem and the most bitter separation that my soul feels in her. What then will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that I may mourn without ceasing the most sorrowful overthrow and diminishing of Holy Church? Who will console me? Who will heal me? What counsel will come to me? Such is the mournful lament, and grief and distress touch all the children of the Church in common. But my unhappy heart is torn far more cruelly and deeply by this unheard-of misery, this destruction. Surely this ruin has been brought upon me, through that unique bride who is the universal mother of all. Yet with such wicked ... with such ... she who is the mother of peace and unity is to be quieted by so accursed and savage a persecution; she who is the fountain of piety is at last to be trampled down by vile humiliation and shameful servitude, she who bestows liberty and eternal honours. O loving mother of all, O my unique bride, how long will this wicked languor of yours last? With what raging fury will impious madness rage against your vitals, and how long will this dreadful division persist in your members? Alas, what counsel shall I give you, and how shall I heal your troubles? This bloody wound of yours has come down upon me, as you see, for from here come devastating cares, from here perilous anxieties, within are anxious fears, without are battles, in tribulation violence, and for a long time an unworthy treatment of me, who was provided from my own house, and of the palace once famous, now overwhelmed by the hand of my own household. Why should I recount the reproaches? Why the unjust defamations? Why the sinister interpretations of my words and deeds? Why the unspeakable afflictions of myself and mine? Yet this is not the sum of evils. Would that all your miseries might flow back upon my head! O faithful bride, who endure even hard death without harm to the soul! And you, blessed in liberty, would cherish in the bosom of peace all your sons and your flock of pasture. And O greatest and best Father, O saving Christ, why was I born to see the evils of my people? Why was I appointed guardian, bridegroom and shepherd, if no other help, no other solace, and no other aid were to be brought? Moreover, if the holy fathers, whom I succeed in this unhappy tempest, groaned of old under the awesome weight of pastoral care, as Gregory and very many others did, even when the Church flourished in her honour and prosperity, what shall I now say in my own and her so incomparable calamity, and under so great a mass of evils? From this above all it ought to be plain that in such a state of affliction I am not obstinate in the pernicious retention of delay. Otherwise I would truly be more wretched and more foolish than all men, seeking certain misery with certain condemnation; but may merciful God keep this madness from his servant. Moreover, have I not formerly been worn out with labour and toil in embassies, if perhaps this savage rupture might be repaired, and if, the darkness being dispelled, the serene truth might arise? But now my dignity, lifting me up, has dashed me down more heavily and hemmed me in on every side. Thus a grave bodily affliction is seen from without; but beneath, within, a sharper wound rages, while I consider in pious reflection how all my efforts, all my pious zeal, and every longing bearing toward the attaining of peace have been frustrated. O manners, O times! And what increases beyond measure the mound of my unhappiness is that by some I am also branded and blamed for a perverse intention. What shall I say to this? I will deny it plainly and steadfastly. Perhaps some ignorance may have crept in, which is so frequent a fault of human frailty, and I shall by no means dare to justify myself entirely in this. For who is not terrified by that word of the Apostle? I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not thereby justified. What other reason is there for that saying, except that we all offend in many things, and since there is no man upon earth who lives and does not sin, and our foresight and justice are uncertain, and all are filthy like a menstrual cloth; in short, what we are in the eyes of the divine majesty, no one knows. "If I shall be just," says Job, "my soul will not know this itself; but if it is by evil fraud, by covetous ambition..." I thought I was doing nothing that would either hinder or delay the unity of the Church. God is judge of my soul, for I have always offered such things from the beginning until now as I faithfully judged, and still judge, to be wholesome and sufficient for pursuing unity; if that father of lies, who would turn everything into evil and disorder, had not stood in the way. You, most serene and most Christian son, can know all these things, before whom I have confidently poured out this complaint; nor do I need to fill your royal ears with a long account of such offers made by me, both on the way of concord by mutual obedience, first given by counsel of my brother cardinals, and on the way of compromise, and most recently on the way of resignation. To this way, indeed even to martyrdom, as I have openly declared, I have constantly clung, according to my readiness of mind. Nor shall I ever depart from this eagerness, if and when resignation shall seem to bring forth true union; my open letters are witnesses before you of these offers, unless they have been craftily concealed by the silence of others. But I think it now becomes clear that the first offer of agreement, which rushed suddenly into such a way, the way that thrust us into these straits and to which the adversaries never gave any assent, would have been lighter and more suitable for the pleasant conduct of union, if it were lacking. Without them, who would expect a general union to come about? Yet, illustrious son, I do not wish to blame your devotion to the peace of the Church from these things said or to be said; would that no devotion had ever been deceived and terrified by a lying report concerning my acts and those of others. But I cannot wonder enough how I, who have acted thus, am thus treated, defamed, shut up, and yet have not, for my release from unworthy prisons, deserved your aid. Did not your predecessors have it as their own duty to help not only in the vexations of the Church, not only in restoring the supreme pontiffs to their see, but all who suffer unjustly in common? As if noble France were a house of mercy such as is recorded to have existed at Athens, where help stood ready for all the afflicted. For now, dearest son, true offspring and heir of the kings of France of distinguished example, you see before the eyes of your serenity him whom you honoured as a just pope, and whom you extolled with frequent titles as the supreme father on earth and holy shepherd of your soul; him again whom you confess to have succeeded with your kingdom by lawful election to Christ and to Peter; him also whom your most prudent father, while living, honoured as such; and finally him who, though fleeting honours are counted, is of noble lineage; finally him who, by God's favour, has led an innocent life until now, without the stain of any disgraceful infamy, since what goes on within is known to God, the inspector of hearts. You, I say, see me such (for I am speaking of myself, and necessity has compelled me to praise myself), you see me now thus shut up, thus contemptuously treated, as if I were one of the most abject slaves, without honour, without dignity, without rank, without family, and without the renown of my life. Nevertheless, son, you either dissimulate or disdain to give aid, and you do not order that I be released, though with a single command you could free me from these troubles. Yet I know for certain that it is not by your command that this is done, nor can one persuade me, truly, to believe that your generous spirit is held in such hardness toward my hardships; for it would soften to compassion if a deep and religious consideration turned your eyes to the great unworthiness of the matter. Why do I speak of you? Natural piety would move even barbarians and pagans, if they saw a person lately of such authority, rank, honour and nobility suddenly cast down and shut up within domestic walls and assailed like an enemy. I think that in your kingdom too the greater part sympathises with my calamity, just as I perceive the grief of other kingdoms. Therefore, if some of your counsellors (would that all were good and faithful) wish to lead the royal mind astray, so that they have no pity on me and my condition, let them at least see and weigh your reputation and that of your kingdom; for a father without honour is a disgrace to a son, and the reproach of a ruler redounds to the infamy of his subjects, as does also that which is daily thrown out in mockery by adversaries and rivals. I would wish they were silent, and I would lay my finger on my mouth; but the voice is too loud and too public to be kept from the king, and what voice is it? That the Papists, beset by the French, are cruelly and hostilely...; the voice that they are opposed to their own supreme lord, and do not follow one another but persecute their own; the voice that they change the popes they have, now appointing, soon deposing; the voice that by the very deed, if not by word, they confess themselves guilty in the schism, and strengthen the very party they attack. Such and many more rumours and reproaches fly about, and how openly this is done, let those who are the occasion of such things consider. But perhaps some will object that I am the cause of all that we lament. For why, they say, do you hold your dignity by right or wrong? Why do you not yield to what is asked? I could resist this objection with plain and very strong answers, drawn from my own justice (except that I have another purpose here); and since you perceive how slippery and unstable every state of lordship would be, if one had at once to give up his right at the voice of anyone, whether with right or wrong, without discernment, without profit, without manifest necessity; but I have decided not to dwell on this point. This one thing I ask and exhort you in the Lord: for the common good of the whole Church, that, putting aside anger, hatred, revenge, and forgetting the things that are behind, we stretch ourselves forward to deserve union; and you especially among the others, as the singular protector and cultivator of the Church, should take care to consult it. What good is it, nay, how much does it hinder peace, that I, who am so free and ready in mind for all things for that same peace, am shut up in prison, while the opposing party nevertheless persists in its error, neither signifying by word nor by deed any wish to know the truth of our justice, nor offering or accepting any way by which, the intruder having been removed, it may leave the seat it occupies, or at least peace may be sought on equal terms? Yet you know how many embassies have been sent, as you know well enough if you are not deceived by the fictitious inventions of reports. Now how should we pursue the universal party, if the particular division between us is so manifold and of such origin? With what confidence do we resist falsehood, if we uselessly confound our own truth? What do we expect to gain by not obeying him who is not doubtfully elected by canonical right, and to be like a body torn with its limbs wrenched from the head, when we see others, by obstinate animosity, not truly joined together in their unity? Nor do I say this in order that the truth may be sought with such anxiety for my bodily liberation (though I wish it, and who would wonder?), as for the zeal of the good and honour of the whole and of the pontifical dignity of the holy Apostolic See, and besides for you and your kingdom and the truth of the whole obedience adhering to it. Wherefore, concluding, I beg and entreat you, dearest son in Christ, that you receive this complaint with filial devotion and a Christian and lofty spirit, and order that the custody, which is wholly unworthy, be ceased from my case, and that, if not on account of my own merits toward God, yet on account of the ecclesiastical dignity of him who is called father, and of such a king, who is at last Christian, the Lord's anointed. You observe with what great wickedness the tyrants' cruelty abuses Christians, indeed its own sons. Some, with sacrilegious impiety (as I have heard), dare to loosen their impure and insolent mouths to brand me as a heretic or schismatic; would that they were as tenacious of faith or religion as I am far from this blasphemy. I can confess with Augustine that I may err, but I shall not be a heretic; nor is there any injury more unworthy or less endurable for me to bear. Therefore, resisting such men, I freely declare with the holy fathers: they lie. Wherefore, son, I beseech you to bring me quick help in my affliction, as in such a necessity (such as may never befall you or your blood) I should by no means dissemble, but strive to oppose it with all the strength of my endeavours. Set before the eyes of your providence, I beg, what kind of face the Church would have, and what foul disorder, perplexity and unsettlement would spring up in affairs, if I were now to depart from the flesh, without first having some other settlement of matters or orderly serenity, such as can be had while I live, unless I am cast off wickedly or perversely. [Finally, if thus far some have proceeded more reasonably, as human ignorance or weakness allows, let them not be ashamed to be late in acknowledging and overcoming the truth; let them not lie in their fall, but rise from it and think it over. For in no other way can simple purity of conscience be more effectively shown in the process, and that...]

units.la: Postremo si hucusque, ut humana est ignorantia vel infirmitas, quidam rationabilius processerint: non pudeat vel sero vincirationc, & superamiveritate, nec in casu iaceant, sed inde resurgendo cogitent. Neque enim poterit aliter efficacius ostendi simplex conscientia puritas in processu, & quod non praeceps ira, non tumens ambitio, non caecus odii rancor, vel edax vindicta furor, sed pacis amor unicus dominabitur tractantibus ipsum hoc tanta sobrietatis & reverentia negocium.
units.tr: Finally, if until now some have proceeded more reasonably, as human ignorance or weakness allows, let them not be ashamed to be overcome late by reason and truth, nor let them lie in their fall, but rise from it and consider. For in no other way can a simple purity of conscience be shown more effectively in the process, and it will be clear that it is not headlong anger, swelling ambition, blind rancour of hatred, or the consuming fury of revenge that rules those who handle this matter, but the sole love of peace, which governs a business of such sobriety and reverence.

units.la: Et utpater misericordiarum & Deus totius consolationis & pacis: qui promisisti misericordiam misericordibus: qui dimittere praecipis, si nobis dimitti volumus, da clementer veniam delictis propriis & alienis, sis mihi propitius ut hic una vindicta contentus sim, quod errata corigas, suppleas defectus, & deinceps omnium pedes in viam salutiferae pacis dirige: denique cor regis, quod in manu tua est, ad hoc inclina & inclinatum corrobora: cui des gloriam & honorem nunc & imperpetuum.
units.tr: And so, Father of mercies and God of all consolation and peace, who promised mercy to the merciful, who command us to forgive if we wish to be forgiven: graciously grant pardon for our own offences and those of others. Be merciful to me, so that I may be content with this one vengeance, that you correct the errors, supply what is lacking, and direct the feet of all into the way of saving peace. Finally, incline the heart of the king, which is in your hand, to this, and once inclined, strengthen it. To you be glory and honour now and for ever.

units.la: His ita se habentibus & allegatis sentio quid postulatis, o sorores charissimae. Postulatis itaque, ne tegam silentii velo vnam ex Epistolis, quales mihi videri possunt ab inclytissimo Franciae Rege pridem, velut post redditum ab ambasiata facta summo pontifici, subtractione nondum facta. Parebo libens, vos assistite.
units.tr: With these things thus stated and alleged, I understand what you ask, most dear sisters. You ask, therefore, that I not conceal under the veil of silence one of the letters which, as they seem to me, came some time ago from the most renowned King of France, as though after his return from the embassy to the supreme pontiff, before the withdrawal was made. I will gladly comply. Do you stand by me.

units.la: Patere (obsecro sancte Pater) perpaucis alloqui pastoralem celsitudinis tuae praesidentiam, patere rogare ea, quae ad pacem sunt Hierusalem: quatenus benigne facias in bona voluntate tua Sion, ut aedificentur muri Hierusalem. Nihil hic exprobrando dicturus sum: sed te obsecraturus sum, ut patrem: tum hortando, tum commonefaciendo cum instructione filii mei, ut ea ante oculos tuos statuantur, quorum attentionem actualem, obliterare potuerunt: seu cura varia turbantes rationis oculum suo pulvere: seu blanda quorundam adsentatio communis magnatibus malum, nihil ad veritatem, omnia ad gratiam dicentium. Aut proinde natu alis quidam amor sub quo sui cognitio nonnunquam impeditur, aut denique subdola machinamenta eorum, qui sub ovina pelle vulpem tegunt. Quae enim ex sublimioribus personis se ab hoc pestibus securam satis esse iactaverit? Vide Pater sancte: & si videas non pigeat profundius iterum atque iterum circumspicere, quale quantumve est pacis bonum, quod omnes in communi appetunt conclamitantes, pax pax: adeo sine pacis pulchritudine omnia sunt deformia, anxia, molestaque. Omnia quoque pacem suam quandam non minus quam vitam desiderant, abhorrentes divisionem, quanto magis ignoscere, imo vero dignam pro meritis laudem rependere te convenit, pater sancta, omnibus & singulis, quos pacem appetere, quaerere persequique cognoveris, quos audieris persequentes ex adverso: exitiale schisma praesens quacunque sum via: praesertim quam compendiosiorem eu vel ratio vel necessitas cognata rationis ostendunt. Talem de te spem tui motus, tua vita a puero bene instituta mundo praebuerunt: hanc insuper expectationem, tua gesta responsaque in negocio praesentis schismatis apud omnes genuerunt, ut tu praecipuus indicatus fis, cui pastoralis baculus pro conterendo nequissimum maligni schismatis caput donaretur: quem praeterea Papalis sedes suscipere et ornando sessione tua, si praesideres in ea. Nihilominus ultronea cessio, si ita res exigeret, locum liberum ad pastoris unici collationem apparet. Videbantur haec sufficere tali omni expectationi: attamen ipsam valuit iniurandum, quo controversia omnis finem capit. Sed, o dolor plusquam dolor, o sancti sanctaeque omnes, unde malum istud irrupit, quod confunderet nos ab expectatione nostra? Heu quantum mortalia pectora caeca nobis habent: quam terribiliter nulles excipiens enunciavit propheticus sermo: Pravum cor hominis & impenetrabile, quis cognoscet illud? Da veniam, pater sancte, fideli mea interrogationi, si animus nostris hanc in veritate ipsam tui, ipsius ingenueras: si cor in ore & fronte gerebas, quid causa quidve fascinationis irrepsit, quod nos vel falleret vel confunderet ab expectatione, a bilia inquam expectatione, qua pollicebatur nobis te agente reversuram pacem Ecclesiae, rediturum seculum aureum in terris? In cuius praeterea assumptione ad Papatum nova lux oriri visa est: in hoc quoque diluculo matutino sidus quoddam benevolum sereno nobis fulgore micare putabamus. At heu expectavimus pacem, & ecce turbatio: in deterius quippe versa confusaque sunt omnia. Meruit hoc, inquies subditorum improbitas volens meipsum patrem eorum ad illud compellere, quod ultroneus agere debueram. Primum (pater sancte) non violentia, sed oratio plurima praemissa est. Petis a quo? a me filio tuo, cuius tota Ecclesia regni mei: per tales, quales nosti, tales quibus alii supplicant, & quorum fide ac prudentia gubernamur: Frater Germanus & duo patrui. Quod si suspitiosum forsan erat orare illud ducum quasi foret species violentia iubendi, facilis plane patebat exitus, praeoccupasses eorum preces, offerens absque ulla procrastinatione illam quam petebatur. Iuramenti impletionem ostendisses praeparationem animi ad cedendum, si & dum cessio tua pacem illatura esset Ecclesiae. Itaque via cessionis nonne ab omnibus quantumcunque tibi vel tuae aestimationi favendibus esse sanctissima & compendio pendiosissima indicata est? quanquam non esse te cogendum ad ipsam fuerit quorundam sententia, sed te voluntrium, tesponte offerentem eam, quae communi assensu probatur, viam quis vero coegisset? Si quid vsquam fuerit coactio, ex renisu tuo venit. Affirmant viri sapientes & literati, qui mecum sunt, te pro salute gregis astrictum esse secundum praeparationem animi non solum ad cessionem, sed ad martyrium. Et hoc modo non est relinquere gregem, sed saluare. Quid quod vltra communem legis diuinae oblivionem iuramentum solenne superadditum te ligauit? Dices forte te nec iuramento nec officio constrictum, ut confestim Papatui renunciet: praesertim non expectato fructu pacis. Profecto pater sancte, neque hoc quaerebatur, quod si de me meorumque sinceritate quaedam malevola suspitiones alienae ab hac veritate gratis assumptae sunt: audi quoniam multos supplantauit suspitio illorum, qualibus utique suspitionibus praebere leuem auditum nihil magno viro indignum, nihil pro suo & sua republica statu incommodius reperitur: hoc quippe agit suspitio talis apud rempublicam, quod zelotypia apud domesticam. Zelotypia autem quales non domos inquietat & turbat, eas aliquando funditus euertens. Esto fuerint qui stillarent auribus tuis, quod aliqui magis ad personam tuam delectionem, quam Ecclesiae reformationem anhelabant: quod Papatum ambiebant alii: quod pars una Papam aptabat ad cognationem & patriam: quod pars altera pro ambitione aut vindicta, aut alia causa reprobis incedebat in via pacis. Examinandum sane erat non quid tales dicerent: non quid garrirent incerto auctore susurri: sed quid veritas a Domino dirigenda postulabat. Neque enim staret omnis politia, si pro adulantium aut male suspicantium confessione, & non pro agendorum veritate regeretur. Et meminerit, pater, si fefellit te talis malevolorum suspitio, dum te protestationem publicare suasit, quam postmodum libens retractasti.
units.tr: Permit me, I beg you, holy Father, to address your lofty pastoral presidency in a few words; permit me to ask for those things which concern the peace of Jerusalem, so that in your good will you may graciously do good to Zion, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built. I shall say nothing here by way of reproach, but I shall plead with you as a father, both by exhorting and by reminding you, with the instruction of a son, that those things may be set before your eyes whose present attention may have been blotted out, either because various cares have clouded the eye of reason with their dust, or because the flattering assent of certain men, who give evil to the great and say nothing true but everything to win favour, has done so, or else some natural love, under which self-knowledge is sometimes hindered, or finally the crafty machinations of those who hide a fox under a sheep's skin. For who among persons of high rank has boasted that he is safe enough from these plagues? Look, holy Father, and if you see, do not be reluctant to look deeper again and again, at how great and of what kind is the good of peace, which all cry out for together, saying, "Peace, peace", so entirely without the beauty of peace are all things deformed, anxious and troubled. All things also desire their own peace no less than life, shrinking from division. How much more ought you, holy Father, to pardon all and each, and to render them the praise their deserts merit, when you know that they seek, pursue and strive for peace, and when you hear that they are pursuing from the opposite side the deadly schism that now proceeds by whatever way, especially by the shorter route that reason and kindred necessity point out. Your own disposition, and your life, well brought up from boyhood, have given the world such hope of you; and your deeds and answers in the matter of the present schism have created this same expectation among all, so that you were marked out as the chief man to whom the pastoral staff would be given to crush the most wicked head of the malignant schism; which, moreover, the Papal see would receive and adorn with your session, if you were to preside in it. Nevertheless, a voluntary resignation, if the matter required it, would seem to leave a free place for the conferring of the one shepherd. These things seemed enough for every such expectation; yet an oath, by which every controversy comes to an end, was able to prevail over it. But, O grief beyond grief, O all you saints, whence did that evil break in which confounded us in our expectation? Alas, how blind mortal hearts are to us, and how terribly the prophetic word has declared this, receiving no exceptions: "The heart of man is crooked and unsearchable; who shall know it?" Pardon, holy Father, my faithful question, if your mind was in truth so ingenuous towards us: if you bore your heart on your lips and brow, what cause or what spell crept in that either deceived us or confounded us in our expectation, a vain expectation, I say, by which it was promised us that peace would return to the Church through your action, and the golden age would come back to earth? Moreover, in your elevation to the Papacy a new light seemed to rise, and in this morning dawn we thought a certain benevolent star was shining on us with a clear radiance. But alas, we hoped for peace, and behold, turmoil: for all things have turned for the worse and been thrown into confusion. "The wickedness of your subjects deserved this," you will say, "since they wished to force me, their father, to do what I ought to have done of my own accord." Firstly, holy Father, it was not violence but much entreaty that was sent before. Entreaty from whom? From me, your son, whose whole Church is my kingdom; through such men as you know, men whom others also entreat, and by whose faith and prudence we are governed: my brother Germanus and two uncles. But if it was perhaps suspicious to beg those leaders, as though there were the appearance of violent command, an easy way out was plainly open: you could have anticipated their prayers, offering without any delay what was being sought. You would have shown, by fulfilling your oath, a readiness of mind to resign, if and when your resignation would bring peace to the Church. Therefore, was not the way of resignation pointed out by all, however much they favoured you or your reputation, as most holy and most expedient? Although it was the opinion of some that you were not to be compelled to it, but that you, offering of your own accord the way approved by common consent, would be a willing agent; yet who would have compelled you? If there has been any compulsion anywhere, it came from your own resistance. Wise and learned men who are with me affirm that you are bound, for the salvation of the flock, to a readiness of mind not only for resignation but even for martyrdom. And in this way it is not abandoning the flock, but saving it. What of the fact that, beyond the general forgetting of the divine law, a solemn oath added to it has bound you? You may perhaps say that you are constrained neither by oath nor by duty to renounce the Papacy at once, especially since no fruit of peace is to be expected. Truly, holy Father, this was not what was being asked. And if certain malicious suspicions, far from the truth, have been gratuitously taken up about me and my people's sincerity, hear how many suspicions of those men have supplanted you: for to give a light hearing to such suspicions is by no means unworthy of a great man, and nothing is found more harmful to his own state and that of his commonwealth. For such suspicion works in the commonwealth as jealousy works in the household. And jealousy, of what kind it is, does not disturb and trouble households only, but sometimes overthrows them utterly. Granted that there were some who whispered in your ears that some were longing more for your personal affection than for the reform of the Church; that others were courting the Papacy; that one party was adapting the Pope to its own kin and country; that another party, for ambition or revenge or some other cause, walked in the way of peace with bad intent. Certainly it needed to be examined, not what such men said, not what whispers with an uncertain author chattered, but what the truth, to be directed by the Lord, required. For no policy would stand if it were governed by the confession of flatterers or of those who suspect wrongly, and not by the truth of what is to be done. And remember, Father, whether that suspicion of ill-wishers deceived you, when it persuaded you to publish a protest, which you afterwards willingly retracted.

units.la: Protestationis autem haec erat sententia: quod visis modo procedendi, qui ergo te & tuos tenebantur (notabas violentiam) tu omne inde secutarum & per concessurum inualidum reputabas & inane: quasi videlicet te pertinacem facere contenderet, aut blanda adulatio, aut subdola inimicorum confessio, nisi sagaci retractione prouidisses. Quin etiam si quaesisset aliquorum (ut tibi videtur) vel arrogantia vel impietas cogere te ad illud, quod sponte agere volueras: nonne satius erat te vincere in bono malum, quam a malo vinci? sapientiam enim non vincit malitia. Pessima certe victoria, vincere voluit aliquis homines, si ab ira, ab odio, ab impatientia & vindicta zelo superatur: & adeo superatur aliquando, ut omissis omnibus, quae alioquin agenda fore cognosceret, ipse se in apertam peccata & in magna mortis huius & aeternae discrimina tradit: dum frendens dentibus ait: Ergo ne inuitus compellar ad hoc vel ad illud? ergo ne malis fratribus meis haec & illa sum acturus? Itane ego Domino obtemperabo subditus, tanquam eorum vilis seruus? quis contemptum hunc, quis mea huius dignitatis vituperium ferre posset? mori satius est quam talia perpeti: fractis prorsus animi & abiecti esset talibus assentire. Haec voces, Pater sancte, siu non esse modestiae Christianae: neque de schola illa prodire, ad quam inuitans Christus, Dicite, inquit, a me: qui mitis sum & humilis corde: qui cum maledicerentur non maledicebat, cum pateretur comminabatur. Quid si quis ex aemulo tuae dignitatis cognitus magnitudinem cordis tui: aut suspicans forte partialitatem ad suspicationes superseris rumusculos tales pro exagitatione turbida suscitanda, per quem omnia tibi suspecta fierent: ac proinde certum discrimen intrares: sic aprum vani catulorum latratus a tuto cubili remouent & offerunt eneciandum: sic qui timet pruinam, irruet super eam nix: sic postremo trepidantes auicula in veros laqueos cadunt ob inanem motarum plumarum formidinem. Aruero suspitionibus pro reiectio ne ab eis dum reprobamus capi videamur: audire te videor & dicere: quod viam aequissimam obtulisti, viam conuentionis in quam totus etiam coetus cardinalium primitus condescendit. Viam praeterea quam appellas iustitiae: viam primam Pater sancte nondum quenquam repudiasse cognoui: nisi quod per se insufficiens apparebat: propter quod vlterior oblatio viae cessionis quaerebatur. Ad quid ita? nimirum ut tantus apparatus conuentionis nequaquam sine congruo fraudaretur: qui finis ex omnium, quos consulimus & aliorum pene omnium iudicio non aliter commode quam per vtrumque contendentium cessionem haberi sperabatur. Sufficiebat autem (ut tibi visum est) oblatio tua generalis, ne eadem facta in particulari cornua darentur aduersus patritanquam diffidere de iure tuo, qui tam leuiter suspiciens: sed non fallitur, non irridetur inspector cordium Deus: sapiens (ut quidam ait,) vitam suam non popularis rumore, sed conscientia veritatis metitur. Quid si quidam imperiti, aut superbi, aut maleoli tuam hanc humilitatem sanctissimam, tuam charitatem Christi imitatricem, tuum zelum feruentissimum in oblatione spontanea via cessionis sinistra detorsissent, ut formidas, alii super numerum plures, graviores insuper, tum fide, tam amicitia tua, tum pietate catholica te hac agente collaudassent, vtentes Salomonis iudicio: quod veram habuisses maternam charitatem, qui infantem Christum vivum in Ecclesiastica sede sua alteri cedere maluisses quam dimidi. Caeterum vero non parum vigebat te praestitum iuramentum: nisi gloriosi corruptis aliquis illud foedare voluerit, aut dicere quod quia in deteriorem exitam vergebat, non erat observandum: absit pater, ut nos omnes tuae obedientiae filii indicaverimus vnanimiter: ut qui discors sit nescio, quod via cessionis caeteris eminebat, eratque sancta & Deo accepta, si ipsa sub iura& shy;mento promissa requiret salubriter vel offerri vel exequi. Quid verisimilius est decipi vel vnum vel vniuersos? quid probabilius falli paucorum conscientias vel omnium? Addo quod si erraret vniuersitas obedientia tua in hac sententia: nihilominus pastoralis pietas astringebat te potius condescendere nobis pie erroribus, quam omnia tam certa turbationi exponere: quippe ad huius intellectum vere enuntiatum est, quod communis error facit ius. Non enim praesumere debueras omnes ad tuam sententiam citius attrahendos fore, quam ad aliorum iudicium te vnicum vel admodum paucos tecum posse conuerti. Nam hoc vltimum liberum tibi erat non alterum, obstantibus tot capitibus, quod tamen conuenisse in vnam via cessionis oblationem, nonne miraculum est & pene diuinum? Opponet demum aliquis Pater sancte, nunc quam inutilis & cassa fuerit hac via cessionis, quae nihil hactenus pro pace valuit operari. Hoc argumento viam conuentionis aut illam quae sine nomine iustitiae lucet inculpare, quam nihil adhuc profecisse cognoscimus. Seo non accepta sunt responsabilis in via, ideoque non tentata. Ita certe nec viam cessionis acceptasti, cuius interest eandem primitus offerre. Eandem dico, totiens anti Papatum per te, pater, ventilatam, laudatam & fere pro vnica commendatam. quod si praesumitur pro via conuentionis aut altera si fuissent acceptata quod dedissent pacem Ecclesiae: multo amplius hoc existimare conuenit de acceptione libera via concessionis. Quod si post oblationem tuam charitatiuam alterapars conuenaciter renuisset peragere, ipsa de se suaq; salute vidisset, tu liberatus nobiscum, tu gloriosus, tu ab omnibus reputatus Benedictus euasisses. Verum ignosce, Paterssanctè, si nimis vrget celsitudinem tuam multiloquium zeli. Talia ego non ad damnandum, sed hortandum pronuncio: quatenus quispacem Beneuolentiae prosequuntur, non inculpes sinistris interpretationibus, quasi depravato animo erga te vel dignitatem tuam moueatur: quatenus praeterea condescendente te capite nostro ad humilem membrorum, velut item instar Christi ambulantibus omnes vno animo, vno passu, vna via, donec oscurrat nobis pax vera in eo, qui fecit vtraq; vnum, Domino nostro Iesu Christo, qui est Deus benedictus in secula.
units.tr: The sense of the protest was this: since you saw the manner of proceeding by which you and yours were pressed (you pointed out the violence), you judged everything that followed from it, and everything conceded under it, to be invalid and empty. As if, forsooth, flattering adulation or the sly confession of enemies were trying to make you obstinate, unless you had provided against it by a shrewd retraction. Indeed, even if (as it seems to you) the arrogance or impiety of some people sought to force you into what you had wished to do of your own accord, was it not better for you to overcome evil with good than to be overcome by evil? For wickedness does not overcome wisdom.
