Surely it is a most wretched victory when a man wishes to conquer others but is himself overcome by anger, hatred, impatience and the zeal of revenge; and he is sometimes so overcome that, setting aside all the things he ought otherwise to know must be done, he delivers himself into open sin and into the great dangers of this death and of eternal death, gnashing his teeth and saying: "Shall I then be compelled against my will to this or that? Shall I then do this and that for my wicked brethren? Am I to obey the Lord as a subject, as their base servant? Who could bear this contempt, this disparagement of my dignity? It is better to die than to suffer such things; to assent to them would be to break and abase the spirit altogether." These words, Holy Father, I say, are not of Christian modesty, nor do they come from that school to which Christ invites us: "Learn of me," he says, "for I am meek and lowly in heart; when they reviled him he did not revile again, when he suffered he did not threaten." What if someone, seeing your greatness of heart, a rival of your dignity, or suspecting partiality, were to stir up such little rumours to fan a turbulent agitation, by which everything would look suspicious to you, and you would thus enter upon a certain danger? So do vain barkings of puppies drive the boar from his safe lair and offer him to be slain; so the one who fears the frost is struck down by the snow falling upon it; so, finally, timid little birds fall into true snares through the vain dread of fluttering feathers. Lest we seem to be caught by suspicions while we reject them, I seem to hear you say: "You have offered the most equitable way, the way of agreement, to which the whole college of cardinals first agreed. Moreover, the way you call that of justice: I have not yet known anyone, Holy Father, to reject the first way, except that it appeared insufficient in itself, and therefore a further offer of the way of cession was sought." Why so? Clearly so that so great a preparation for agreement should not be wholly wasted without a fitting outcome. This end, by the judgment of all whom we consulted and of almost everyone else, was hoped to be attainable only through the cession of both contending parties. Your general offer, however (as it seemed to you), was sufficient, lest, if the same were made in particular, horns should be given against the father, as if he distrusted his own right. But he who looks so lightly into suspicions is not deceived, and God, the inspector of hearts, is not mocked. A wise man (as someone says) measures his life not by popular rumour but by the consciousness of truth. What if some unskilled, proud or ill-disposed persons had twisted your most holy humility, your charity imitating Christ, and your most fervent zeal, in the spontaneous offer of the way of cession, into a sinister sense, as you fear; and if others, more in number and weightier besides, had praised you for acting thus, both for your faith and friendship and for Catholic piety, using the judgment of Solomon: that you had shown true maternal charity, preferring to yield the living infant Christ in your ecclesiastical see to another rather than see him cut in half. Moreover, the oath you had sworn was of no small force, unless some glorious one wished to defile it, or to say that because it tended to a worse outcome it need not be kept. Far be it, Father, that we, all the sons of your obedience, should be unanimously of that opinion. I do not know what discord there might be; the way of cession stood out above the rest, and it was holy and acceptable to God, if it were healthfully offered or carried out as the oath promised. Which is more likely, that one or all of us are deceived? Which is more probable, that the consciences of a few or of all have been misled? I add that even if your obedience's whole body erred in this opinion, pastoral piety nevertheless bound you rather to yield to us kindly in our errors than to expose everything, so certain, to disturbance. For to understand this rightly it has been truly said that common error makes law. You ought not to have presumed that all would be drawn to your opinion more quickly than you alone, or very few with you, could be turned to the judgment of others. For this last was open to you, not the other, given so many heads; yet that the offer of the way of cession should have agreed in one, is it not a miracle and almost divine? Finally, someone will object, Holy Father, how useless and empty this way of cession has been, which has so far achieved nothing for peace. By this argument they blame the way of agreement, or that which shines without the name of justice, which we know has so far accomplished nothing. But these have not been accepted as a responsible way, and therefore have not been tried. Indeed, you yourself did not accept the way of cession, whose very interest it was to offer it first. The same way, I say, which you, Father, have so often aired, praised, and almost commended as the only one, before the Papacy. If it is presumed that, had the way of agreement or the other been accepted, it would have given peace to the Church, it is much more fitting to judge this of the free acceptance of the way of cession. But if, after your charitable offer, the other party had obstinately refused to carry it through, that party would have borne the consequences for itself and its own salvation, and you would have come off freed with us, glorious, and blessed in the judgment of all. But forgive me, Holy Father, if the abundance of zeal presses too hard upon your Highness. I say these things not to condemn but to exhort: that those who pursue peace in a spirit of goodwill you should not blame by sinister interpretations, as if they were moved by a depraved mind towards you or your dignity; and that, as you condescend, as head, to the humble members, so also we, walking in the manner of Christ, all with one mind, one step, one way, may until true peace meet us in him who made both one, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God blessed for ever.

units.la: Quid superest agere, ô sorores: dum pars inuenit vtraque causas, tum excusationis propriae, tum accusationis alienae? qua ratione potest hoc fieri, etiam si tu Beneuolentia tanto nisu conateris, vt pars excusanda censeretur: sed neq; in tam contrariis iudiciis videri possunt accidi. Et ô sanctissima mater Ecclesia, cui sententiae interim cessura es? quam amplexaberis, quam probabis? Christiana respublica inter has contentiones animosas & incertas quid aget? interea quo se vertet, quali poterit regimine gloriari? Dudum contendentibus Pompeio & Iulio Caesare ciuilibus armis Romana respublica neutrum partem probas remanserat in medio desolata cum Catone, qui nulli similiter parti fauens erat. Nam enim dicit Seneca: Vtrum verosimile sit in schismate nostro tanto deteriori, quanto animae mors, quam corporis plus horroris habet non determino. Vtinam veniat Dominus, qui illuminet abscondita tenebrarum, & posita in lucem compleat in opere: parum quidem videre est, si non datur operari. Hoc quidem solum relictum videtur: vt quia cum ignoramus quid agere debeamus humano consilio, confugiamus ad diuinum: nisi vobis aliud, ô sorores, videatur.
units.tr: What remains to do, O sisters, since each side finds reasons, both for excusing its own and for accusing the other? In what way can this be done, even if you, Goodwill, strive with such effort that the party to be excused may be judged so; but in such contrary judgments they cannot seem to agree. And O most holy mother Church, to which opinion will you yield in the meantime? Which will you embrace, which approve? What will the Christian commonwealth do amid these spirited and uncertain contentions? Meanwhile, to what will it turn, and by what government will it be able to glory? Long ago, while Pompey and Julius Caesar contended with civil arms, the Roman commonwealth, favouring neither part, had remained desolate in the middle, along with Cato, who likewise favoured no party. For Seneca says: "Whether it is probable in our schism, so much the worse as the death of the soul has more horror than that of the body, I do not determine." Would that the Lord might come, who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and bring the things set in light to completion in the work; it is indeed hard to see anything if it is not granted to work. This alone seems to be left: that since we do not know what we ought to do by human counsel, we should flee to the divine, unless, O sisters, another course seems good to you.

units.la: Beneuolentia. Mihi Beneuolentiae idem prorsus est iudicium, Frater: vt nullus accusatus maleuole, sicut obseruare (nisi me fallit amor tui) studuisti, conuertamus nos ad Dominum, quatenus ad nos conuertatur, ambulans super aquas praesentis fluctuationis, ventisq; imperans & mari, & sicat eo iubente tranquillitas: quid tacita recogitas soror nostra Discretio? dic & tu quid censes agendum?
units.tr: Benevolence. My judgment, brother, is entirely the same: that, provided no one is maliciously accused (as you have tried to observe, unless my love for you deceives me), we should turn ourselves to the Lord, so that he may turn to us, walking upon the waters of the present turmoil, commanding the winds and the sea, and at his command there may be calm. But what are you silently pondering, our sister Discretion? Tell us too what you think should be done.

units.la: Discretio. Ego vero hoc idem nihilo minus, ne tentari videatur Deus, conari decet nos ad laborem, si forte piis attentationibus aspirat Deus vires.
units.tr: Discretion. I think the same thing, nevertheless. Lest God seem to be tempted, we ought to strive toward the work, if perhaps God breathes strength into our pious endeavours.

units.la: Zelus. Verissime suades per meam fidem, ô soror Discretio, saluberrime & diuine? vis igitur vt ea praelia, quae penes nos seruamus, recondita super hoc negocio proferamus in medium, tum de medio pacis inueniendo, tum de concilio sic vel non celebrando, tum de Papae accusatione & excusatione cum reliquis? illorum enim inspectio dare posset occasionem sapientibus profundiora cogitandi.
units.tr: Zeal. You advise most truly, sister Discretion, and most wholesomely and divinely, I swear by my faith! Do you therefore wish that those battles which we keep hidden among ourselves concerning this matter be brought out into the open: both the search for a middle way to peace, and whether or not to convene a council in this way, and the accusation and excuse of the Pope, along with the rest? For an examination of those things could give the wise occasion to think more deeply.

units.la: Discretio. Video te, Frater, ad ingenium redis, totus flamma es: nequis non velle foras erumpere: scio quae tu loqueris, illa quodam impetu magis proiecta sunt, quam digeste ordinata, sine stilo, sine limitatione. Attamen si ita fert animus tuus, nec compescì potest: tu in alia nobiscum concione ea propone, nos secedere ad alia tempus vocat & verba tua (vt aspicis) iam popularis concio, iam scholasticus coetus, iam curia regalis expectat. Tuam rem ergo age & bene habe.
units.tr: Discretion. I see you, brother, returning to your natural temper; you are all flame, and cannot help wanting to burst forth. I know what you are saying: those things were thrown out with a certain impetus rather than digested and ordered, without style, without limit. Still, if your spirit so bears you and cannot be restrained, put them forward in another assembly with us. Time calls us to withdraw to other matters, and, as you see, a popular assembly already awaits your words, a scholastic gathering already, a royal court already. So go about your business, and farewell.

units.la: Zelus. Polliciti memor obedientia vltro, & tu bene habeas soror, nec vllo vnquam in negotio me desere, tuo quoque spiritu ô germana Beneuolentia procul omnis a nobis & caeteris maligna persecueritas extur-betur &c.
units.tr: Zeal. Mindful of my promise, I obey gladly. And you, sister, farewell, and never desert me in any business. By your spirit too, dear Benevolence, may all malicious perversity of others be driven far from us, etc.

units.la: EPISTOLA CHRISTIANIS- SIMI REGIS FRANCIAE, IVSTIFICATIVA SVB- TRACTIONVM FACTARVM A PETRO DE LVNA: NON obstante obedientia suo praedecessori & sibi quandoq; praestita.
units.tr: LETTER OF CHARLES, KING OF FRANCE, JUSTIFYING THE WITHDRAWALS MADE BY PETER DE LUNA, NOTWITHSTANDING THE OBEDIENCE ONCE RENDERED BY HIM TO HIS PREDECESSOR AND TO HIMSELF

units.la: Arolus Dei gratia Francorum rex, vniuersis Christi fidelibus salutem in Domino, & ad eam quam summopere desideramus Ecclesiasticam vnionem vnanimiter aspirare. Pax Ecclesiastica, quae sub vnico & certo Christi vicario coniungere debet vniuersa membra populi Christiani secundum ipsius Christi & Apostoli sui documentum, dum olim post mortem felicis recordationis Gregorii Papae vndecimi conturbari cepisset: dumque schisma perniciosum, monstrum horrendum ingens in eadem Ecclesia suboriri cerneretur ex causis toto orbe notissimis: Christianissimus tunc ac praeclarissimae memoriae progenitor noster Carolus Quintus suasus multis vehementibusque rationibus deliberauit adhaerere, & obedientiam praestare illi, quem collegium Cardinalium iureiurando asseruit in vita & in morte: atque publicauit se canonice in summum pontificem & verum Christi vicarium sponte & concorditer elegisse. Arbitrabatur namque verisimiliter idem progenitor noster & erat totus feruens in zelo domus Dei, & ex sua fide pia alios diiudicans: quod caeteri principes ac praelati eum vniuerso clero & populo protinus obedirent consimiliter: dum electione huiusmodi per collegium praefatum Cardinalium sufficienter eis innotescceret rite fuisse celebratam. Sed aliter euenisse dudum iam deploramus. Neque enim potuerunt vsque hodie dicti Cardinales hoc ipsum. Nos idcirco cernentes experientia, temporeque docentibus, quod haec obedientia praestita inualida erat ad tollendum funditus schisma pestiferum, quod in exilium grauissimum pacem desideratissimam & optimam detruserat, deliberamus eandem pacem ad proprium cubile suum, quod est Ecclesia, velut ad suam regionem per alias vias totis conatuum viribus reducere. Hinc concilia crebra, hinc legationes laboriosissimae ac sumptuosissimae per omnes pene Christianitatis regiones frequentatae: tandem aspirante Deo via cessionis utrique contendentium pro reuersione pacis turpiter exulantis inuenta est compendiosior absq; vlla dubitatione expedientior iudicata. Hanc proinde via cum omni solennitate praesentari fecimus successori illius, cui progenitor noster (sicut diximus) obedientia praestiterat. Quo obedientia ideo maxime postmodum ab eodem successore pro tempore subtraximus: quia nō satis aperte per viae cessionis compendium videbatur velle pacem reducere, postpositis disceptationum interminabilium anfractibus & ingressibilibus aliarum viarum labyrinthis. At vbi visus est nobis ad salubrior ra se conuertisse consilia, rursus absque omni mutabilitatis culpabilis nota obediuimus eidem sita tamen animo nostro gerentes, si & quamdiu haec obedientia nostra non obstaret Ecclesiasticae vnioni: quemadmodum in concilio vltimo Ecclesiae regni nostri meminimus satis datum intelligi. Neque enim voluimus vnquam scienter (neque fas esse credimus) obedientiam praestare cuiquam mortalium in pacis vniuersalis praeiudicium, in schismatis fomitem, in discordiae instrumentum. Et o salutifer Christe princeps pacis, quamdiu iam quaesiuimus pacem & non venit? Expectauimus tempus medelae: tempus scilicet iuratae conuentionis vtriusque contendentium pro cessione celebranda, & ecce turbatio. Animaduertite haec, Domini principes Christiani, quibus est dolori talis, tantaqs matris dissipatio. Attendite insuper vobis & vniuerso populo Christiano vos sacri pontifices, in quo posuit vos Spiritus sanctus Episcopos regere Ecclesiam Dei, quam acquisuit sanguine suo. Attendite quaesumus, nolite dissimulanter agere: vbi depopulatur grege Christi miseris modis, tempestas haec saeuissima horrendaqs vorago. Exurgat in vnum populus vniuersus tollere de medio sui deformissimum hoc portentum, vnde fit in opprobrium hostibus incredulis propriisque animabus damnationis aeternae discrimen apertum decidat vel inuitus vnus aut alter: imo vtrique contendentium ab occupata Sede Petri potius, quam vnitas eorum contentione depereat. Nam dum neutri populus obediet, neuter amplius deprimatu vel frustra contendet. Neque audieturultra vox illa crudelissimae foeminae: nec mihi nec tibi, sed diuidatur: sed illa piae matris: date illi infantem viuum. Nos vero qui nihil ita post animae salutem desideramus, quam videre serenissimam pacis faciem nostris effulgere temporibus, iudicamus ex praemissorum & similium consideratione nullum ad praesens patere validius in tam desperato malo remedium, quam quod neuter contendentium aut sibi forte successorum praesterur deinceps obedientia a populo Christiano: deficiente siquidem fomento tantus ignis iste infernalis in se tandem deficiens dante Deo collabetur.
units.tr: Charles, by the grace of God king of the French, to all the faithful of Christ, greeting in the Lord, and to aspire unanimously to that ecclesiastical unity which we greatly desire. The ecclesiastical peace, which under the one and certain vicar of Christ ought to join together all the members of the Christian people, according to the teaching of Christ himself and of his Apostle, began to be disturbed once, after the death of Pope Gregory XI of happy memory, when a pernicious schism, a huge and horrible monster, was seen to arise in the same Church from causes well known throughout the world. At that time our most Christian and most renowned predecessor, Charles V, persuaded by many weighty arguments, resolved to adhere to and render obedience to him whom the college of cardinals, under oath, had declared to be pope in life and in death, and he published that he had freely and harmoniously chosen him canonically as supreme pontiff and true vicar of Christ. For our predecessor, who was altogether burning with zeal for the house of God and judged others by his own pious faith, reasonably supposed that the other princes and prelates, together with the whole clergy and people, would at once obey in like manner, once the election, duly carried out by the said college of cardinals, became sufficiently known to them. But we now deplore that matters turned out otherwise. For the said cardinals have not been able, even to this day, to bring about this very thing. We, therefore, seeing by experience and by the lessons of time that this obedience rendered was powerless to root out the baneful schism, which had thrust the most desired and best peace into the gravest exile, have resolved to bring that peace back by other ways, with all the strength of our efforts, to its own home, which is the Church, as to its proper country. Hence frequent councils, and hence very laborious and very costly embassies have been sent to almost all the regions of Christendom. At last, with God aiding, the way of resignation by both contending parties, for the return of peace which had shamefully gone into exile, was found, and was judged without any doubt to be the shorter and more expedient. Accordingly, we caused this way to be presented with all solemnity to the successor of him to whom our predecessor (as we have said) had rendered obedience. We withdrew our obedience from the same successor for the time being chiefly because it did not seem to be plainly willing to restore peace by the shortcut of resignation, but preferred the windings of endless disputations and the entangled labyrinths of other ways, which are hard to enter. But when it seemed to us that he had turned to more wholesome counsels, we again rendered obedience to him, without any blameworthy mark of inconstancy, yet keeping in our mind this reservation: if and as long as this our obedience should not stand in the way of ecclesiastical unity, as we recall it was sufficiently made clear in the last council of our kingdom. For we have never wished knowingly (nor do we believe it is lawful) to render obedience to any mortal to the prejudice of universal peace, as a fuel of schism, or as an instrument of discord. And O Christ, Saviour, Prince of peace, how long have we sought peace, and it has not come! We have waited for a time of healing, namely the time for the sworn agreement of both contending parties to carry out the resignation, and behold, turmoil. Consider these things, lords and Christian princes, you to whom such a tearing apart of so great a mother is a grief. Furthermore, take heed to yourselves, and to the whole Christian people, you sacred pontiffs, to whom the Holy Spirit has entrusted to rule the Church of God, which he won with his own blood. Take heed, we beg you, do not act with pretended unconcern, when this most savage tempest and horrible abyss lays waste the flock of Christ in wretched ways. Let the whole people rise up together to remove from its midst this most deformed monstrosity, by which there comes disgrace to unbelieving enemies, and the open peril of eternal damnation to souls. Let one or another fall, even against his will; indeed, let both contending parties perish from the seat of Peter which they have seized, rather than the unity of the Church perish through their contention. For while the people obey neither, neither will any longer hold the upper hand or contend in vain. Nor will that cruel woman's cry be heard again: "Neither mine nor yours, but let it be divided," but rather that of the true mother: give her the living child. We, indeed, who desire nothing so much after the salvation of the soul as to see the most serene face of peace shine forth in our times, judge, from consideration of the above and similar matters, that at present there is no more effective remedy in so desperate an evil than this: that obedience be rendered by the Christian people to neither of the contending parties nor to any of their successors. For when this fuel is lacking, that infernal fire, so great, will at last die down of itself and collapse, with God's permission.

units.la: Quapropter praecedentibus & habitis super hoc vicibus repetitis, magnis & maturis deliberationum consiliis cum sapientibus peritis & devotis hominibus Deum & eorum salutem gerentibus præ oculis. Nos ut ecclesia regni nostri ac Delphinatus Viennensis pro nobis & subditis nostris eorundem Regni & Delphinatus decrevimus talem amplecti neutralitatem in festo Ascensionis proxime venturo: nisi interea nobis ultro pax advenerit, processuri nihilominus ulterius assidua, sollicitudine cum aliis principibus & catholicis omnibus, donec cuiusdam schismate pax plantetur. Quod si mirabuntur forsan aliqui ex aliter affectatis, unde nobis ista licent: attendant potius quod hanc nobis legem facit ipsa, quae legem nescit, dura necessitas: imo & filialis pietas, quae per medios etiam ignes & gladios matrem talem ita collaborantem eripere conaretur. Ecce morbus inveteratus & putridus, qui ex fomentis leuioribus in deteriora quotidie velut cancer serpit: si ergo ferramentum cauterizans adhibeatur, nullus recte culpaverit. Demum cum pro hac neutralitate in unum tractanda principes ac magnates utriusque obedientiae commoda celeritate congregari non possent, nullus suo quæsumus contemptui deputetur partis nostrae, quam probabilissima ratione præibatus progenitor noster & nos hactenus fuimus insecuti, in hac neutralitate condemnatum vel depressum: cum nunc non de iure huius vel illius, sed descendendo iuri vero vel prætenso pro unione consequenda res agatur. Quamobrem vos omnes & similes hortamur in Christo, & per eam quam de immaculata sponsæ suæ ecclesiæ laceratione fœda compassionem geritis, obtestamur: arripite nobiscum validum hoc & efficax, sicut expectamus in Dei virtute, pestis huius exterminium, ut denegatio hæc obedientiæ utrique contendentium afferat nobis tandem perpetuam unanimemq; obedientiam sub uno & certo Christi vicario: quatenus seruiamus Deo in pulchritudine pacis & requie opulenta. In quorum omnium fidem & testimonium præsentes literas nostri sigilli fecimus munimine roborari. Datum Parrhysius die XII. Ianuarii. Anno Domini M. CCCCVII. & regni nostri XXVIII.
units.tr: Therefore, after previous and repeated deliberations on this matter, and after mature and lengthy counsels with wise, experienced and devout men who had God and their salvation before their eyes, we have decided, for ourselves and our subjects of our kingdom and of the Dauphiné of Vienne, that the church of our kingdom and of the Dauphiné should embrace such a neutrality from the coming feast of the Ascension, unless in the meantime peace comes to us of its own accord; and we shall nonetheless proceed further, with constant care, together with the other princes and all Catholics, until peace is established for the schism. If perhaps some of those who think otherwise should wonder whence we have this right, let them rather consider that the hard necessity which knows no law makes this law for us; indeed, filial piety too, which would try to snatch such a mother, labouring thus, even through fires and swords. Behold, an old and rotten disease, which creeps day by day from lighter fomentations into worse, like a cancer: if therefore a cauterizing iron is applied, no one will rightly blame it. Finally, since the princes and magnates of both obediences could not be gathered quickly to deal with this neutrality together, let no one, we beg, consider that our party, which our most approved predecessor and we have hitherto followed by most probable reasoning, is to be condemned or lowered to contempt in this neutrality, since the matter now concerns not the right of this or that party, but the yielding of right, whether true or claimed, in order to secure unity. Therefore we exhort all of you and others like you in Christ, and we beseech you by that compassion you feel for the foul laceration of the spotless bride of Christ, his Church: take up with us this strong and effective, as we expect in the power of God, means of destroying this plague, so that this refusal of obedience to both contending parties may at last bring us perpetual and united obedience under one and certain vicar of Christ, so that we may serve God in the beauty of peace and abundant rest. In witness and faith of all these things we have caused these present letters to be strengthened by the protection of our seal. Given at Paris, on the 12th day of January, in the year of the Lord 1407, and the 28th year of our reign.

units.la: DISCEPTATIO MENDICI- TATIS ET PROPRIETATIS, SIVE DE VTILI DO- MINIO BONORVM ECCLESIASTICORVM, PER EVNDEM IOHANNEM DE GERSON: sumpta ex Sermone facto Constantiæ in Concilio generali, in festo S. Antonii.
units.tr: DISPUTATION ON MENDICANCY AND PROPERTY, OR ON THE USEFUL DOMINION OF ECCLESIASTICAL GOODS, BY THE SAME JOHN DE GERSON: taken from the sermon preached at Constance in the General Council, on the feast of St Anthony.

units.la: CONSIDERATIO II.
units.tr: CONSIDERATION II.

units.la: IN nuptiis crescentis Ecclesiæ dum vinum sacræ scripturæ seu theologicum propinabatur discumbentibus principibus & aliis ab architriclinis, qui fuerunt Doctores Theologici: tunc ecclesia dotata fuit ampla temporalitate: sic formidandum est ex contemptu Vini huius ne tollantur aut notabiliter minuantur dotes huiusmodi temporales ab eadem ecclesia.
units.tr: When the Church was wedded in its infancy, and the wine of Holy Scripture, or theology, was poured out for the princes and others reclining at table, served by the head waiters who were the theological doctors, the Church was then endowed with ample temporal possessions. So we must fear that, through contempt for this wine, such temporal endowments may be taken away from the same Church or notably diminished.

units.la: EXPOSITIO.
units.tr: EXPOSITION.

units.la: FERVOR itaque devotionis, qui principes & alios dotantes ecclesiam movit, unde quaeso genitus fuit, si non ex præconcepto calore vini spiritualis sacrae scripturae vehentis ad æterna mentes suas terrenorum amore calcato? Nunc autem si viderint pincernas vini huius prælatos & doctores labi funditus in inferiora terræ, neque vllam de spiritualibus sollicitudinem gerere, quid ni repetant quæ dederunt causa cessante conferendi, quod a nova saltem donatione tepescant? Ecce iam vidimus plurimos in sacris etiam literis eruditos, qui vitiis prælatorum irretiti, zelantes domum Dei non secundum scientiam nequaquam timuerunt suggerere principibus & populis vsque ad permissionem mortis, quod fas erat eis tollere temporalia clericorum habitualiter delinquentium. Rursus quod bona eorum nō erant nisi pure eleemosynæ. Quod insuper non erant tradita nisi sub conditione bene viuendi & vtendi: quo deficiente peribat titulus iuris, neque quicquam reliquum clerico tali supererat. Adde quod non defuerunt neque desunt seculares cupidis auribus & assensu talia recipientes. Nihil autem facilius quam persuadere volentibus spolia clericorum, dum vel auaritia, vel odium, vel invidia, vel zelus indiscretus trahit eos. Opponunt alii prælatis & clericis paupertatem ecclesiæ primitiuæ in Apostolis & discipulis: autenticant cælo missam vocem, dum à Constantino dotata est ecclesia, magis diuino iuxta prophetiam Danielis de regno Christi, quam humano constitutio; Hodie venenum effusum est in ecclesiam DEI. Quae omnia, quid aliud quam spoliandum esse loquuntur ecclesiam? Verum quid antiqua? quid sola lectione cognita commemoramus? Praedicatum est solenniter apertissimis verbis, quod mendicitas erat solum vel praecipuum medium predicationis verbi Dei: quia spinae divitiarum suffocant Verbum. Et paulo ante dum quaereret ipse praedicans, qui sunt praedicantes? Respondit, prosecto soli mendicantes, quoniam pauperes, inquit euangelizantur. Taceo quod dixerat ante quidam ex Mendicantibus praelatis: nos pro nobis principes habebimus aduersos praelatos; superaddit alius: ac etiam mulieres: subintulit alter minaci vultu: Nos tale seminabimus semen in vno die quod eradicare per annum nescietis neq; poteritis: Haec & similia si nihili pendunt a platis secularibus sibi defensores suos seculares Theologos vinum sacrae sapientiae ministrantes in puritate vel abiiciunt vel negligunt vel opprimunt: quid consequentius est, quam ut principes dicant & statuant apud semetipsos: si mendicitas solum vel praecipuum medium est ad predicationem verbi Dei: cum nihil magis incumbat ecclesiae praelatis, quam huiusmodi praedicatio, propter quam Apostoli dixerunt: Non est nos aequum relinquere verbum Dei & ministrare mensis. Et Paulus ait: Non misit me Dominus baptizare sed praedicare: quid eligibilius est nobis quam ut praelatos reducamus ad mendicitatem sublatis tot divitiis & donationibus in quibus otiosi gloriantur atque superbiunt supra regum & principum potestatem. Nihilominus haec & similia cum praedicantur dotationis ecclesiae subuersiua, fit applausus: significatur vt excurrat sermo: dum vero pro fauore debito probatorum, pro libertatibus eorum, pro fidei q tueri professi sunt vsque ad morte defensione praedicatio fit, mox oscitant, inquietantur, submurmurant, exibilant, tumultuantur, finem figent. Attendat pastoralis sollicitudo, ne per impunitatem talium crescat in ecclesiastica hierarchia deordinatio, horror atq; confusio. Unde si medicitas post Apostolos & sanctos doctores nouiter subintroducta ministraret hodie sola vinum praedicationis per Apostolos in ecclesiae nuptiis. In multis itaq; nunc male est fateor ecclesiae, sed in multis deteriora venirent: quemadmodum sumi poterit ex dicendis in altera consideratione patens argumentum. Ecce vero dum talia meditatio cordis mei secum reuoluerat, conspicere visa est hinc mendicitatem Religiosorum: hinc proprietatem praelatorum, quarum vtraque praedicabat laudes suas, alterius altera statui praeferre contendens. Praeoccupauit Mendicitas: Et quis dubitauerit, inquit, me praeferenda esse proprietati vel appropriationi temporalium, quae volens esse perfecta abiii iuxta consilium Christi, & vendidi omnia quae habui & dedi pauperibus: vt nuda, sequerer expedite nudum Christum. Praecello quidem in multis, sed quinq; praerogatiuas enumerasse sufficerit. Mens nonne mihi liberior est ad contemplationem? quoniam egena sum, non potens epulari quotidie laute & splendide. Propterea neq; cibo, neque vino gravior in crapula & ebrietate, iacco somno vnioq; sepulta. Sum insuper aptior ad praedicationem, quam doceo nedum verbis studiosissime compositis in allegationibus, in rythmis, in ratiocinationibus, miscendo seculares autores, poetas & rhetores. Sed exemplo proprio, quod efficacissimae doctrinae genus est, praedico, contemnendas esse seculi diuitias, pompas honores, atque delicias, sequens Christum, qui prius coepit facere, post docere. Quid tertio? quod elongatior sum ab adulatione, quia non temporale lucrum, non fauorem diuitum, non applausum populorum, sed spiritualem duntaxat animarum salutem exquiro, quid enim mihi est super terram? Quid praeterea quarto? quod a formidine resistentium verbo Dei liberata sum, dum ab eis maior efficior non ambio, sed refugio, quaerens in nuptiis ecclesiae locum nouissimum: nolens primos recubitus in coenis, nec salutationes in foro, nec vocari ab hominibus rabbi: neque primas cathedras in synagogis, saeuiat mundus vniuersus aduersum me, ad quam me poterit sortem vilioriem deiicere, quam mendica quaeram panem meum? Constat denique me liberatam esse ab omni sollicitudine, Cur enim de crastino cogitarem, quae habens alimenta vndecunque quaesita & quibus tegar, etiam vilissimis resarcitisq; saccis contenta dego: considerans aues coeli, quae neq; laborant, neque nent, neque congregant in horrea, & pater caelestis pascit eas.
units.tr: Whence, I ask, came the fervour of devotion that moved princes and others to endow the Church, if not from the warmth of the spiritual wine of Holy Scripture, which lifts minds to eternal things and tramples underfoot love of earthly things? But now, if they see the cupbearers of this wine, the prelates and doctors, sinking utterly into the lower things of the earth and taking no care for spiritual matters, why should they not take back what they gave, now that the cause for giving has ceased? Or at least why should they not cool in making new gifts? Indeed we have already seen many men learned even in sacred letters, who, ensnared by the vices of the prelates, zealous for the house of God but not according to knowledge, did not fear to urge princes and peoples, even to the point of death, that it was lawful to take away the temporal goods of clerics who were habitual offenders. Again, they argued that the goods of the clergy were nothing but pure alms; that they had been given only on condition that they be well lived and well used; and that when this condition failed, the title of right perished, and nothing remained to such a cleric. Add that there were not lacking, nor are there now lacking, secular men who receive such things with greedy ears and assent. Nothing is easier than to persuade those who are moved by greed, hatred, envy, or indiscreet zeal to plunder the clergy. Some oppose to the prelates and clergy the poverty of the primitive Church among the Apostles and disciples. They claim the heavenly voice, which said that the Church was endowed by Constantine, was more divine, according to the prophecy of Daniel about the kingdom of Christ, than human ordinance: Today poison has been poured out into the Church of God. All these things say nothing else than that the Church must be despoiled. But why speak of antiquity? Why recall only what is known from reading? It has been preached solemnly, in the plainest words, that mendicancy was the sole or chief means of preaching the Word of God, because the thorns of riches choke the Word. And a little before, when the preacher himself asked, "Who are the preachers?", he answered, "Surely only the mendicants, since the poor, it is said, are evangelised." I say nothing of what some mendicant prelates had said before: "We shall have princes as our adversaries against the prelates"; another added, "and even women"; another went on with a threatening look: "We shall sow such seed in one day that you will not be able to root it out in a year, nor will you be able to." If these men care nothing for the secular prelates, and if the secular theologians who serve the wine of sacred wisdom in its purity are rejected, neglected, or oppressed, what follows more logically than that the princes should say and decide among themselves: if mendicancy is the sole or chief means of preaching the Word of God, and nothing lies more upon the prelates of the Church than such preaching, for which the Apostles said, "It is not right that we should leave the word of God and serve tables," and Paul said, "The Lord did not send me to baptise but to preach," what is more desirable for us than to reduce the prelates to mendicancy, taking away so many riches and gifts in which the idle glory and become proud above the power of kings and princes? Nevertheless, when these and similar things are preached as subversive of the Church's endowment, there is applause; it is signified that the speech should run on. But when preaching is made in due favour of the approved, in defence of their liberties, and of the faith which they professed to defend even to death, at once they yawn, grow restless, mutter, hiss, make a tumult, and set an end to it. Let pastoral care take heed lest, through the impunity of such men, disorder, horror and confusion grow in the ecclesiastical hierarchy. Therefore, if mendicancy, newly introduced after the Apostles and holy teachers, served today as the sole wine of preaching, as it was through the Apostles at the wedding of the Church... In many respects, I confess, the Church is now in a bad way; but in many respects worse things would come about, as may be gathered from the clear argument set out in the next consideration. Now, while my heart was turning these thoughts over within itself, there seemed to appear on one side the mendicancy of the religious, and on the other the property of the prelates; each was proclaiming its own praises, each striving to be preferred to the other's state. Mendicancy spoke first: "Who would doubt that I am to be preferred to property or the appropriation of temporal goods? I, wishing to be perfect, have gone away, according to the counsel of Christ, and sold all that I had and given to the poor, so that, naked, I might follow the naked Christ without encumbrance. I excel indeed in many respects, but it will suffice to enumerate five advantages. Is not my mind freer for contemplation, because I am needy and not able to feast daily lavishly and splendidly? Therefore I am weighed down neither by food nor by wine into gluttony and drunkenness, nor do I sink into sleep, buried in these. I am moreover better suited to preaching, which I teach not only with words most carefully arranged in allegations, rhythms and reasonings, mixing in secular authors, poets and rhetoricians, but with my own example, which is the most effective kind of teaching: I preach that the riches, pomps, honours and delights of the age are to be despised, following Christ, who began to do before he taught. What is the third? That I am further removed from flattery, because I seek not temporal gain, not the favour of the rich, not the applause of the peoples, but only the spiritual salvation of souls; for what have I upon earth? What is the fourth? That I am freed from the fear of those who resist the Word of God; for I do not seek to become greater among them but flee, seeking in the wedding of the Church the lowest place, unwilling to take the first couches at feasts, or greetings in the market-place, or to be called rabbi by men, or the first seats in the synagogues. Let the whole world rage against me; to what lowlier lot can it cast me down than that I, a beggar, should seek my bread? Finally, it is clear that I am free from all anxiety. For why should I think about tomorrow, I who, having food from wherever it is got, and clothing, live content even with the cheapest and patched sacks, considering the birds of heaven, which neither labour, nor spin, nor gather into barns, and the heavenly Father feeds them.

units.la: Proprietas ex aduerso contendebat; primo iuxta sententiam Aristotelis arguentis politiam Socratis & Platonis, quod erat expedientior apud homines praesupposito peccato secus in statu gloriae; secus in originalis statu iustitiae, fuissent omnia communia, vbi nullus proprium dixisset, hoc meum est: hoc est vero tuum: quoniam vnicuique fuissent omnia subiecta pedibus eius. Omittatur de singulis hominibus, fiat de praelatis ecclesiae tantum sermo: quibus ego proprietas multum offero fructum spiritus, praesertim quintuplicem in edificationem subditorum. Habent ex me primo subsidia temporalium, vnde misericordiam exerceant apud subditos, egentes, aegros & debiles, pupillos, viduas, neque sub specie pietatis & quaestus spolia quaerunt ouium, neq; lac emungunt vsque ad sanguinem, quod vt exercere posset sanctus Thomas Cantuariensis studuit vsque ad mortem pro seruatione redditum ecclesiasticorum decertare. Habent ex me praelati secundo decentem & honestum statum fulgentem & reprehendum coram populis, qui sicut animales neq; satis capiunt coelestia, neq; virtutes interiores plene consiliantur, propterea aliter egenos & pannosos homines, praecipue si opportune & importune quaestuati fuerint, ratiunt in opprobrium vel contemptum, maxime dum assunt eis operationes heroicae & miraculosae, quemadmodum fuit in sanctis Apostolis & plurimis successorum, alioquin si quis ornatum exteriorem splendidum culpat in praelatis, tollat ex consequenti praeciosissimos & clarissimos quoslibet ritus ecclesiae, quae incedit sicut regina in tunicis, casulis, cappis & caeteris vestimentis deauratis circumdata varietate. Adde tertio quod tyrannis incutio formidinem ego proprietate; dum attribuit me paratam & potentem & talem esse, quae sufficiam eis resistere. In subditos praeterea discholos & insolentes ties ego disciplinatas punitiones potens exerceo, ne sua contra proborum vitam tam quietam praevaleat effrenis iniquitas, & ut regentis conservetur auctoritas. Postremo sollicitudinem anxiam, & quandoque fraudium sectatricem ego proprietas à praelatis & domesticis suis excludo: distribuens unicuique prout opus est: ne vel cogitare supra modum de crastino compellat eos egestas: cui parum esse fidei dicit Satyricus & lex. Haec est ecclesiae primitiva institutio: haec aurea mediocritas, quam Salomon optando descripsit: Divitias, inquit, & paupertatem ne dederis mihi: sed tantum victum meo tribus necessaria: pusilli animi est (dicit Seneca) non posse pati divitias & indicere sibi eodem animi vel argenti: refrenetur cupiditas, & sufficit.
units.tr: Property argued on the other side. First, according to the opinion of Aristotle, who argued for the polity of Socrates and Plato, it would have been more expedient among men, presupposing sin; otherwise, in the state of glory, and in the state of original justice, all things would have been common, where no one would have said "this is mine" and "this is yours," since all things would have been subject to each one's feet. Let us leave aside single men; let the discussion concern only the prelates of the Church. To them I, property, bring much fruit of the Spirit, especially a fivefold benefit for the edification of their subjects. First, they have from me the resources of temporal goods, by which they may exercise mercy among their subjects, the needy, the sick and the weak, orphans and widows; they do not seek the spoils of the sheep under the guise of piety and gain, nor milk them to the point of blood. Saint Thomas of Canterbury strove to contend, even to death, for the preservation of the revenues of the Church, which he could thus exercise. Second, from me the prelates have a becoming and honourable state, conspicuous and reputable before the peoples, who, being like animals, neither grasp heavenly things sufficiently nor are fully instructed in interior virtues. Therefore, if poor and ragged men, especially if they beg importunately and inopportunely, are despised and held in contempt, especially when heroic and miraculous works are not present to them, as was the case in the holy Apostles and in very many of their successors, then whoever blames the splendid external adornment of the prelates would consequently also take away the most precious and famous rites of the Church, which goes forth like a queen clothed in tunics, chasubles, copes and other vestments of varied gold. Add thirdly that I, property, instil fear into tyrants, since I am said to be ready and powerful enough to resist them. Moreover, I am able to exercise disciplined punishments upon unruly and insolent subjects, lest their unbridled wickedness prevail against the quiet life of the upright, and that the authority of the ruler be preserved. Lastly, I, property, exclude from the prelates and their household the anxious care, and sometimes the pursuit of frauds: distributing to each as need requires, lest want compel them to think beyond measure about tomorrow, which, as the satirist and the law say, shows little faith. This is the primitive institution of the Church; this is the golden mean which Solomon described when he prayed: Give me neither riches nor poverty, but only the food necessary for my sustenance; it is the mark of a small mind (says Seneca) not to be able to bear riches, and to be unable to set limits to one's own mind or silver: let desire be restrained, and it is enough.

units.la: Parabat ad haec Mendicitas contentiosa voce responsionem adiicere: proponens se talem esse, cui mediocritas amica est: quoniam nihil habens ipsa iure proprietario, possidet omnia charitatis & sufficientiae titulo: quaerit enim primum regnum Dei & iustitiam eius: omnia idcirco opponuntur ei. Nihil insuper se timere defendit, nimirum quia nihil perdere habet, inculcans illud Satyrici:
units.tr: Mendicancy, meanwhile, prepared to add a reply in a contentious voice. It presented itself as one to whom moderation is a friend: since it holds nothing by proprietary right, it possesses everything under the title of charity and sufficiency, for it seeks first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and so all things are added to it. It further declared that it fears nothing, since it has nothing to lose, and pressed that line of the satirist:

units.la: Cantabit vacuus coram latrone viator.
units.tr: The empty-handed traveller will sing before the robber.

units.la: concludit proprietatem esse tumidam, elatam, pomposam, iactricem sui, desidiosam, caecam, insciam & hebetem: quae quia tangit picem divitiarum, inquinatur ab ea: & spinarum aculeis cruentata suffocatur, neque pascit: quae mercenaria est, oves proprias pabulo doctrinae, sed emungit usque ad sanguinem, & excoriat usque ad interiora ossium & discrimen vitae.
units.tr: It concludes that property is swollen, puffed up, showy, boastful of itself, idle, blind, unskilled and dull. Because it touches the pitch of riches, it is defiled by it; and bloodied by the prickles of thorns, it is choked and does not feed. It is a hireling, which does not feed its own sheep on the pasture of doctrine but milks them until they bleed and flays them down to the inner marrow of their bones and to the peril of their lives.

units.la: Caeterum has impatienter ferens medicitatis contumelias ipsa proprietas dici non potest, qualia quantaq; reddere verba parabat: Vocans eam inprimis apostatam à lege qualibet naturae, scripturae & gratiae: nec deerat allegationum multiplicatio, seductricem insuper arguebat eam, fallacem gyrovagam, quae penetrat sub obtentu nedum prolixae orationis (prout loquitur Apostolus) sed confessionis, domos, captivas ducens mulierculas oneratas peccatis: quae rursus nomen humile paupertatis facit instrumentum sibi & medium sub velamine privilegiorum ad omnes divitias, delitias, pompas, cum summo ocio sine labore plus caeteris hominibus assequendas. Pergebat ultro proprietas inducere testas autenticos pro se Vitas patrum, Augustinum de opere monachorum, librum de sancto amore, Propositiones Domini Armacani, cum similibus multis. Quae demum sectas habens inter se pro diversitate habitum & doctrinarum coniungitur ad impugnationem caeterorum seculariarum & regularium praelatorum & doctorum.
units.tr: Property itself, bearing these insults of mendicancy impatiently, cannot easily be described, so many and such were the words it prepared to return. First it called mendicancy an apostate from every law of nature, Scripture and grace. Nor was there a lack of multiplied allegations. Moreover, it accused mendicancy of being a seductress and a deceitful vagabond, who creeps into houses under the pretext not only of long prayers (as the Apostle puts it) but of confession, leading captive silly women laden with sins. Again, mendicancy makes the humble name of poverty into a tool for itself and a means, under the veil of privileges, to gain with great ease and without labour all riches, delights and pomps, more than other men. Property went on to bring forward as authentic witnesses in its favour the Lives of the Fathers, Augustine's On the Work of Monks, the book On Holy Love, the Propositions of the Lord of Armagh, and many similar works. At last, property, which has sects among itself according to the variety of habits and doctrines, joins forces to attack the other secular and regular prelates and teachers.

units.la: Tum exhorrui, fateor, in ipsa meditatione mea, quando talem suboriri contentiosam hostilitatem proprietatis & mendicitatis animadverti: qui prius in audiendis laudibus utriusque sedulus delectabar. Exclamo protinus: abite precor hinc: neque iurgiis istis me fatigaveritis. Itaque
units.tr: I confess that I shuddered then, in my very meditation, when I noticed such a contentious hostility arising between property and mendicancy, I who had before been glad to hear eager praises of both. I cried out at once: "Go away from here, I beg you, and do not weary me with these quarrels." And so:

units.la: Non nostrum inter vos tantas componere lites.
units.tr: It is not for us to settle such great disputes among you.

units.la: Ite potius ad experientiam: haec siquidem mentiri nescit, de quibus novit: novit autem omnia & mentientes non patitur, non redarguit, haec ideo testis idonea, haec iudex incorruptissima: quae querelam hanc suscepit, suggerat & in sinu & sacrosancto generali concilio. Quid sentiendum insuper allegatis utrinque quid demum faciendum? Etenim si mendicitas probare voluerit testimonii operum dilucidis, quod ad illa per eam proposita sit efficax mediatrix ipsa prorsus suspicienda foventaque iudicabitur. Similiter & proprietas laudabitur & in praelatis si tales in eis, quales proponit, effectus operetur. Verum praeclarum dictum est a quodam, Respublica vel ecclesiastica non regitur perf, sed nec solo dictamine speculativae vel imaginariae rationis gubernatur: executio requiritur in practicatione operis, quantum res humanae prolocis, temporibus & personis patiuntur. Denique est invenire statum, imo nec hominum unicum, nisi rarissime, in quo granis virtutum mixtae sunt plures numero palae defectuum: Nam & cum tritico crescunt zizania, qualia tolerare conuenit: vel sic eradicare, ne simul cuellatur & triticum. Similiter vinū devotionis secū fertacinos & seces quorundam defectuum humanae corruptionis. Enitatur statum quilibet esse talis qualem vult se aestimari: atq; respectu finis suae constitutionis caetera conetur moderari. Sit mendicitas, ut praetendit, ad contemplationem liberior: sit ad praedicationem utilem aptior: sit ab adulatione longior: sit a formidine & ambitione remotior, sit ab omnium temporalium sollicitudine quietior. Proprietas vero, sicut gloriatur hospitalitatem exerceat: decentem & venerandum absque fastu superfluo statum teneat, formidinem tyrannis incutiat, subditos insolentes coerceat: sollicitudinem noxiam & anxiam procul a se suisq; familiaribus abiiciat. Meminerit tandem utraque iuxta Comici sententiam: quoniam haec omnia in mendicitate & proprietate talia sunt, qualis est animus utentis, hoc cernere est in vino bono sapientiae salutaris. Cuius odor, sapor & visus sit aliis in aegritudinem & mortem, aliis autem proficit ad sanitatem & vitam perpetuam.
units.tr: Rather, go to experience. For experience cannot lie about what it knows, and it knows everything and does not suffer liars, nor fails to refute them. Therefore it is a fit witness and the most incorruptible judge. Let it take up this complaint and report it both in the bosom of the Church and in the holy general council. What ought we to think of the allegations made on both sides, and what, finally, ought to be done? For if mendicancy wishes to prove by clear evidence of its works that it is an effective mediator for the things it proposes, it will be judged worthy of respect and support. Likewise property will be praised, and among prelates too, if it produces in them the effects it promises. It has been well said by someone that a commonwealth or the Church is not ruled by speculative or imaginary reason alone; execution is required in the practice of the work, as far as human affairs, places, times and persons allow. In short, one can find no state, nor almost any man, except very rarely, in which the grains of virtue are not mixed with many chaff-like defects. For tares grow along with the wheat, and such must be tolerated, or else uprooted in such a way that the wheat is not pulled up with them. Likewise the wine of devotion carries with it the dregs and lees of certain defects of human corruption. Let each state strive to be such as it wishes to be esteemed, and let it endeavour to moderate the rest with respect to the end of its founding. Let mendicancy, as it claims, be freer for contemplation, more apt for useful preaching, further from flattery, more remote from fear and ambition, and quieter from the anxiety of all temporal things. Let property, as it boasts, practise hospitality, keep a decent and venerable state without superfluous pride, strike fear into tyrants, and restrain insolent subjects; let it cast off from itself and from its household harmful and anxious care. Finally, let each remember the saying of the comic poet: in mendicancy and in property, all these things are such as the mind of the one using them is; this is to be seen in the good wine of saving wisdom, whose smell, taste and sight bring sickness and death to some, but profit to others for health and eternal life.

units.la: SERMO FACTUS IN LOCO SESSIONIS CONCILII GENERALIS CONSTANTIENSIS, POST NOVUM RECESSUM PAPÆ IOANNIS XXIII. eodem Concilio Anno Domini M. CCCCXV. vigi- lia Dominicæ Ramispalmarum.
units.tr: SERMON DELIVERED IN THE SESSION HALL OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL OF CONSTANCE, AFTER THE NEW WITHDRAWAL OF POPE JOHN XXIII, in the same Council, in the year of our Lord 1415, on the vigil of Palm Sunday.

units.la: Ambulate dum lucem habetis, ut non tenebræ vos comprehendant. Iubet hoc Christus, patres orthodoxi: patres non in tabulis æreis, ut olim apud Romanos, sed in libro vitæ conscripti. Iubet inquam Christus originaliter Ioan. 12. & recitatiue in euangelio Sabbati præsentis. Vos obedientes audite, ambulate non passibus corporis, sed gressibus mentis: ambulate de virtute in virtutem dum lucem habetis. Et qualem lucem? Respondeat lux vera, cuius hoc est verbum: Qui sequitur me, non ambulat in tenebris: sed habebit lumen vitæ.
units.tr: Walk while you have the light, so that darkness may not overtake you. Christ commands this, orthodox fathers: fathers written not on bronze tablets, as once among the Romans, but in the book of life. Christ commands it, I say, originally in Ioan. 12. and in recitation in the Gospel of this present Sabbath. You, obeying, listen: walk not with the steps of the body but with the strides of the mind; walk from virtue to virtue while you have the light. And what light? Let the true light answer, whose word this is: He who follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.

units.la: Adsis inuocatus Domine Iesu præclarissime, sol iustitiæ: disiice terræ nebulas & pondera mollis, atque tuo splendore mica. Absque te enim præcipiti mersa profundo mens hebet, & propria luce relicta tendit in externas ire tenebras. Hoc ne fiat, tu mediatrix, tu aduocata & exoratrix nostra supplicGiter adeunda es Virgo gloriosissima, quæ tui nominis interpretatione tam illuminata quam illuminatrix diceris. Et quo lumine? prorsus lumine gratiæ, quo sic illuminata es, ut dicaris in Apocal. mulier amicta sole. Hoc tu nobis lumen ut infundas de plenitudine tua supplíter imploramus, salutantes & dicentes: Aue &c.
units.tr: Be present, invoked, most bright Lord Jesus, sun of righteousness: scatter the clouds of the earth and the weight of softness, and shine with your splendour. For without you the mind, sunk in a headlong depth, grows dull, and, leaving its own light, tends to go out into outer darkness. That this may not happen, you, most glorious Virgin, must be approached as our mediatrix, advocate and intercessor, who by the interpretation of your name are called as much enlightened as enlightening. And what light? Truly the light of grace, by which you were so illumined that in the Apocalypse you are called "a woman clothed with the sun." That you pour this light upon us from your fullness we humbly implore, greeting you and saying: Hail, etc.

units.la: Ambulate dum lucem habetis, ut non tenebra vos comprehendant. Lux ista est, iam dixi & repeto, lux ista est, patres celeberrimi, Deus, qui glorificatur in Consilio sanctorum, dicente Psalmus: Magnus & terribilis super omnes qui in circumitu eius sunt. Cuius hanc tenemus infallibilem promissionem Matth. 18. Vbi duo vel tres congregati fuerint in nomine meo, ibi in medio eorum sum. Sicut vidit Psalmo, dum cecinit: In consilio iustorum & in congregatione magna opera Domini. Et magna plane: imo ingentia iam vidimus in hoc consilio iustorum Dei opera, spontaneam & vix speratam cessionis viam. Porro cum propter semetipsum, & ut glorificetur, fecerit omnia Deus, quo pacto credendus est praeclariori celebritate gloriari quam in consilio iustorum, quæ vera laus est in ecclesia sanctorum? Tales vos esse conuenit orthodoxi & Deo amabiles patres ac Domini: ut consilium sitis sanctorum & iustorum, quos posuit Deus in mundo quasi vera totidem luminaria. Vos, inquit, estis lux mundi. Siquidem in hoc constituti estis alios purgare, illuminare atque perficere, nunc maxime, cum factus conuentus iste Sacrolanctus, dum adunatus est coetus, dum congregata est ecclesia, ut de Machabeis scribitur, quatenus orarent & peterent misericordiam a Deo, & ut opitulante eo decerneretur quid facto opus esset. Exultat animus profecto, leuans in circumitu oculos, & videns omnes istos, qui congregati sunt tibi, hoc est ad vtilitatem tuam, o populle Christiane: congaudet admirans Spiritus meus, & in hac erumpit ecclesiastici cantus vocem, Cives Apostolorum & domestici Dei aduenerunt hodie portantes facem illuminantes patriam, dare pacem gentibus & liberare populum Domini. Qualiter liberare? exhortando clamandoque: Ambulate dum lucem habetis, ut non tenebra vos comprehendant. Cuius deliciae sunt esse cum filiis hominum, ipsæ tenebræ demum horridæ tot vitiorum per ecclesiasticum corpus, vasto quodam turbine miserabiliter exundantium. Ambulate igitur dum lucem habetis, ut non hæ vos tenebræ comprehendant. Lucem itaq; habetis, patres luminosissimi, Christum, qui vere est in loco isto, vel Emanuel, qui interpretatur nobiscum Deus, cuius est hæc certissima promissio: Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus vsq; ad consummationem seculi. Deus iste est, qui glorificatur in concilio sanctorum, magnus & terribilis super omnes qui in circumitu eius sunt. Et bene in circumitu tuo, Domine, res omnes esse dicuntur, quoniam tu velut sphæra intelligibilis, cuius centrum vbique est, circumferentia nusquam: tu vbique es extra non exclusus, supra non elatus, infra non prostratus, ideo magnus valde, terribilis, gloriosus & superaltatus in secula.
units.tr: Walk while you have the light, so that darkness may not overtake you. This light, as I have already said and repeat, is that light, most famous fathers: God, who is glorified in the council of the saints, as the Psalm says: great and terrible above all who are round about him. We hold his infallible promise on this, Matth. 18: Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them. As the Psalmist saw when he sang: In the council of the righteous and in the great assembly, the works of the Lord. And great indeed: nay, we have already seen immense works of God in this council of the righteous, a voluntary and scarcely hoped-for path of yielding. Moreover, since God made all things for himself and that he may be glorified, in what way is he to be believed to glory in a more distinguished assembly than in the council of the righteous, which is true praise in the Church of the saints? It is fitting that you, orthodox and God-beloved fathers and lords, be such: a council of saints and righteous men, whom God has placed in the world as so many true lights. You, he says, are the light of the world. For indeed you are established to purge, enlighten and perfect others, now especially, when this most sacred assembly has been convened, when the gathering has come together, when the Church has been brought together, as is written of the Maccabees, that they might pray and seek mercy from God, and that, with his help, it might be decided what needed to be done. Surely the mind exults, lifting its eyes round about and seeing all those who have gathered to you, that is, for your benefit, O Christian people; my spirit rejoices in wonder, and in it breaks out the voice of the church's song: The citizens of the Apostles and the household of God have come today, carrying torches, lighting the fatherland, to give peace to the nations and to free the people of the Lord. How to free them? By exhorting and crying out: Walk while you have the light, so that darkness may not overtake you. Whose delight is to be with the sons of men: those very darknesses, the dreadful darkness of so many vices, pouring out miserably through the body of the Church in a vast whirlwind. Walk, then, while you have the light, so that these darknesses may not overtake you. You have the light, most luminous fathers: Christ, who is truly in this place, or Emmanuel, which is interpreted "God with us," whose most certain promise is this: Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age. He is that God who is glorified in the council of the saints, great and terrible above all who are round about him. And rightly are all things said to be "round about you, Lord," since you are like an intelligible sphere whose centre is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere: you are everywhere, not excluded from without, not raised above, not cast down below; therefore you are exceedingly great, terrible, glorious and exalted for ever and ever.

units.la: Ecce patres orthodoxi, quod ad hoc ipsum, ut glorificetur Deus, & illustretur ecclesia nunc celeberrima Parisiensis Vniuersitas, cultrix & amatrix eorum omnium, quæ Christianæ religionis pietatem quæ sanam doctrinam respiciunt, ipla ad exemplar Christianissimi Regis Francorum patris sui dignantissimi legationem mittit, quærens primo ea, quæ pacis sunt: denique secundo quæ fidei sunt, deniq; tertio quæ virtutis & ecclesiasticæ sunt libertatis: quoniam ad hæc tria principaliter synodus hæc sacra tedit. Iussit hesterno vesperi per Ambasiatores & Nuncios suos hic præsentes, quatenus hoc matutino tempore essem habituros orationem nomine suo pro veritatis elucidatione circa ea, quæ per hoc sacrum concilium agenda videntur occurrere. Nullus opinor mirabitur si ad hanc iussionem ego fragilitatis meæ conscius & temporis artatione pressus expaui. Nihilominus in Deo, cuius gloriificatio quæritur nisus, & de studio præterito super hanc veritatis inquisitione memor, regis pterea & ecclesiæ regni sui voluntate per instructiones cognita: Iussioni denique matris inclitissimæ, cuius legem dimittere nequeo, monitus a sapiente: ego tanquam obedientiæ filius parere desiderans, conatus sum aggredi cum humili dicendorum omnium ad hoc sanctorum concilium submissione, ut iure suo dirigat omnia vel acceptet vel corrigat.
units.tr: Behold, orthodox fathers, for this very purpose, that God may be glorified and the Church illumined, the now most famous University of Paris, cultivator and lover of all those things which concern the piety of the Christian religion and sound doctrine, after the example of its most worthy father, the most Christian King of the French, sends an embassy, seeking first those things which pertain to peace, secondly those which pertain to faith, and finally those which pertain to virtue and ecclesiastical liberty, since this holy synod is chiefly concerned with these three. Yesterday evening it ordered, through its ambassadors and envoys present here, that at this morning hour I should deliver an address in its name for the clarifying of truth concerning those matters which seem likely to arise for treatment by this holy council. I think no one will wonder that, on receiving this command, I, conscious of my own frailty and pressed by the shortness of time, was alarmed. Nevertheless, trusting in God, whose glory is sought, and mindful of my earlier zeal for this inquiry into truth, and having learned the will of the king and of the Church of his realm through their instructions; finally, admonished by the command of the most illustrious mother, whose law I cannot set aside, and advised by the wise, I, desiring to obey as a dutiful son, have undertaken to proceed with a humble submission of all that I am to say to this holy council, so that it may by its right direct, accept or correct all things.

units.la: Et in primis quatenus habeatur ordo dicendorum lucidus & breuis, quia vel est quod texitur ordine longum, conuertamus interim dilato themate oculos nostræ considerationis ad hoc quod dictum est, Deum esse qui glorificatur in concilio sanctorum, qui magnus est & terribilis super omnes qui in circuitu eius sunt. Desigamus in hoc Psalmistæ verbo mentis intuitum, ne per multa vagemur: fallor si non ibi videbimus huius sacrosanctæ synodi causam quadruplicem: efficientem, scil. formalem, finalem & materialem &c. Vult aliquis cognoscere causam efficientem: plane illa est: Deus magnus & terribilis: cuius institutu, miseratione, afflatu & attractu, collecta est nunc ecclesia: sicut eleuatus spiritu præcecinit Psalmus: Deus esse qui dispersiones Israelis congregabit, qui congregat electos suos à quatuor ventis, à solis ortu & occasu, ab aquilone & mari: tantummodo qui coepit orandus est, vt ipse perficiat. Leua in circuitu tuo, ô sacer cœtus, oculos tuos & vide: omnes isti congregati sunt, venerunt tibi. Quidni contingat tibi quod idem propheta loquitur Esaias: Tunc videbis & affluES & mirabitur ac dilatabitur cor tuum: & si dilatetur: numquid non implebit illud spiritus sui Deus: Porro causa formalis est hæc ipsa collectio seu connexio concilii sanctorum, vel Spiritu sancto formante & exemplante, qui est nexus & vinculum compaginans in vnum diuersa membra sanctorum: sic agnoscit ecclesia petens pro seipsa, vt Spiritu sancto congregata, hostili nullatenus incursione turbetur. Quæritur aliquis præterea finalem huius sacri conuentus causam: sane illa est, vt glorificetur Deus magnus & terribilis: iuxta vocem Apostoli dicentis: Omnia in gloriam Dei facite. Hæc itaque recta, hæc efficax semita ad omnium quæ voluerimus adeptionem: si primo quæsierimus gloriam suam: docet hoc intelligi dum ait: Primum quærite regnum Dei & iustitiam eius: & hæc omnia adiicientur vobis.
units.tr: First, so that the order of what is to be said may be clear and brief (for what is woven at great length is long in its order), let us for now set aside the theme and turn the eyes of our consideration to what has been said: that God is he who is glorified in the council of the saints, who is great and terrible above all who are round about him. Let us fix the gaze of the mind on this word of the Psalmist, lest we wander through many things. I am mistaken if we shall not see there the fourfold cause of this most sacred synod: efficient, formal, final and material, etc. If anyone wishes to know the efficient cause, it is plainly this: God great and terrible, by whose institution, mercy, inspiration and drawing the Church is now gathered; as the Psalm sang beforehand, lifted up in spirit: God who gathers the dispersions of Israel, who gathers his elect from the four winds, from the rising and the setting of the sun, from the north and the sea. He alone is to be prayed to, that he may bring it to completion. Lift up your eyes round about you, O sacred assembly, and see: all these have gathered, they have come to you. Why should there not befall you what the same prophet Isaiah says: Then you shall see and flow together, and your heart shall wonder and be enlarged; and if it be enlarged, will not God fill it with his Spirit? The formal cause is this very gathering or connection of the council of saints, with the Holy Spirit forming and exemplifying it, who is the bond and chain joining the diverse members of the saints into one; thus the Church, praying for itself, acknowledges that, being gathered by the Holy Spirit, it may by no hostile incursion be disturbed. Someone may further ask the final cause of this holy assembly: surely it is that God, great and terrible, may be glorified, according to the voice of the Apostle saying: Do all things to the glory of God. This, then, is the straight and effective path to the attainment of all that we may wish, if first we seek his glory; the text teaches us to understand this when it says: Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you.

units.la: Omnes postremo, qui in circuitu Dei sunt, accipiuntur veluti pro causa materiali, & de se informi. Nam sicut hominibus per schismata peccantibus consequens est vniuerso, sub Deo quodammodo deformati: quoniam homo finis est omnium, dicentibus Platone & Aristotele: necesse est autem secundum exigentiam finis omnia moderari: sic ex aduerso veniunt omnia per hoc sanctorum concilium Domino efficiente, formante & finiente reformanda. Ita enim de pretioso sanguine Christi canit ecclesia: Terra, pontus, astra mundus, quo lauantur flumine.
units.tr: Finally, all who are round about God are taken as it were for the material cause, and as formless in themselves. For just as men who sin through schisms bring a consequent deformity on the whole universe under God, since man is the end of all things, as Plato and Aristotle say: it is necessary, moreover, that all things be regulated according to the requirement of the end, so on the contrary all things are to be reformed through this holy council, with the Lord working, forming and finishing them. For thus the Church sings of the precious blood of Christ: "Earth, sea, stars, world, in whose stream they are washed."

units.la: Quocirca videre fas est deinceps, quo titulo relucet in causa efficiente, ac residet inscrutabilis auctoritas, quæ causa est Deus magnus & terribilis: ex quo omnia in mensura. Relucet in causa formali exemplaris vnitas, vt sint omnes vnum, sicut estis nunc in concilio sanctorum, & hoc in Deo per quem omnia in numero. Relucet in causa finali spiritualis utilitas: quia vt glorificetur Deus, in quo omnia in pondere. Demum concluditur in causa materiali generalis vniendorum reformandorumq; vniuersitas: omnium scilicet quæ incircuitu Dei sunt, quatenus omnia reformentur in numero, pondere & mensura, concedente Deo. Ex quo omnia, hinc modus, vnitas & mensura. Per quem omnia: hinc species, veritas & numerus. In quo omnia: hinc ordo, bonitas & pondus: quo pondere refluunt omnia in causam, quæ dedit esse.
units.tr: Therefore it is right to see next under what title there shines forth, in the efficient cause, the inscrutable authority that resides there. That cause is the great and terrible God, from whom all things come in measure. In the formal cause there shines forth the exemplary unity, that all may be one, just as you now are in the council of the saints; and this is in God, through whom all things come in number. In the final cause there shines forth spiritual usefulness, because God is glorified, in whom all things are in weight. Lastly, in the material cause there is concluded the general totality of those to be united and reformed, namely all who are round about God, so that all things may be reformed in number, weight and measure, God granting. From whom all things: hence mode, unity and measure. Through whom all things: hence species, truth and number. In whom all things: hence order, goodness and weight, by which weight all things flow back into the cause that gave them being.

units.la: Cæterum prima triplicitas appropriatur Patri, secunda Filio, tertia Spiritui S. bene habet, iacta sunt fundamenta soliditate quadrangula, superædificare possumus tetras Pythagoricum, hoc est quadruplicem constructionem parietem vel structuram, & dicere, p prima constructione: Deus magnus & terribilis si glorificatur in hoc concilio sanctorum, q eide sufficiente pbet & infallibilem auctoritatem, vt causa efficiens, quo ad primum fundamentum. Rursus, p secunda constructione: Deus magnus & terribilis trahit & attrahit omnes in communi Christianos ad vnius veri capitis vnitatem: tanquam causa formans & exemplans, quo ad secundum fundamentum primum in reformatione. Ampliùs pro tertia constructione: Deus magnus & terribilis sic glorificari vult in hoc concilio sanctorum, q omnia principe fiant ad honorem & conseruationem suæ legis ac fidei, sine qua ei placere nemo potest: quo ad tertium fundamentum, secundum in reformatione. Demum p quarta conclusione: Deus magnus & terribilis paratus est rebus omnibus, maxime hominibus concedere per hoc concilium sanctorum quædam reformationem pulchritudinis, glorificationem ordinem & decorem cum prouisionibus idoneis aduersus eos, qui non in redundine morum, sed in circuitu pergunt vitiorum: & hoc p quarta constructione super vltimum fundamentum, quod est tertium in reformatione.
units.tr: Moreover, the first triad is appropriated to the Father, the second to the Son, the third to the Holy Spirit. The foundations have been well laid with quadrangular solidity, and we can build upon them the Pythagorean tetractys, that is, a fourfold construction of wall or structure, and say: by the first construction, the great and terrible God, if he is glorified in this council of saints, proves himself a sufficient and infallible authority, as efficient cause, with respect to the first foundation. Again, by the second construction: the great and terrible God draws and attracts all Christians together to the unity of the one true head, as forming and exemplary cause, with respect to the second foundation, the first in reformation. Further, for the third construction: the great and terrible God wishes to be glorified in this council of saints in this way, that all things be done, first of all, for the honour and preservation of his law and faith, without which no one can please him; this is with respect to the third foundation, the second in reformation. Lastly, by the fourth conclusion: the great and terrible God is ready to grant to all things, and above all to men, through this council of saints, a certain reformation of beauty, glorification, order and decorum, with fitting provisions against those who persist not in the amendment of their morals but in a round of vices. This is by the fourth construction upon the last foundation, which is the third in reformation.

units.la: Poterat hic ordo teneri sub his terminis, sed alia progredi via suaserunt verba thematis, quia in metaphora lucis fundata sunt. Reuertamur igitur & ponam lucè diuini precepti, quia præceptum Domini lucidum illuminans oculos. Lucernam in super diem legis, sicut Petrus loquitur, vt iubente Deo posita super candelabrum, luceat omnibus qui in domo sunt, quæ domus est ecclesia, vel hoc sacrum concilium vice sua. Diffundat & spargat consequenter lux ipsa veritas euangelicas 12. considerationes quasi totidem effulgentissimos radios veritatum particularium splendidos & coruscantes.
units.tr: This order might have been kept under these headings, but the words of the theme persuaded us to take another way, because they are founded in the metaphor of light. Let us therefore return and set forth the light of the divine precept, because "the commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes." It is a lamp shining, as Peter speaks, which God commanding places upon the lampstand so that it shines on all who are in the house. That house is the Church, or this holy council in its place. Consequently let the light of truth itself, the gospel, diffuse and scatter its twelve considerations, like so many most brilliant and sparkling rays of particular truths.

units.la: Ponamus in primis, imo iam positam digito sicut aiunt, demonstremus lucem Apostolici symboli quo dicitur: Credo in Spiritum S. & viuificantem. Quid viuificantem? Certam vnam sanctam catholicam & Apostolicam ecclesiam: vnam, propter colligationem & ad vnum caput primarium Christum & vicarium summum pontificem, sanctam, propter sanctorum communionem & remissionem peccatorum, vt infra subditur: catholicam, hoc est Vniuersalem, quoniam ab eius obligatione nullus viator immunis est: Apostolicam, quoniam in Apostolorum & Prophetarum, per quos Spiritus S. loquutus est, doctrinis fundata est, & similium filiorum successione duratura. Certus sum, quod nullus, qui vel haberi vel dici vult Christianus, caligare se dicit ad hanc lucem.
units.tr: Let us first set out, or rather, as they say, already set out on the finger, the light of the Apostles' Creed, in which it is said: I believe in the Holy Spirit, the giver of life. What giver of life? One certain holy, catholic and Apostolic Church. One, on account of its binding together to the one primary head, Christ, and to the supreme pontiff, his vicar. Holy, on account of the communion of saints and the forgiveness of sins, as is added below. Catholic, that is universal, since no wayfarer is exempt from its obligation. Apostolic, since it is founded on the teachings of the Apostles and Prophets, through whom the Holy Spirit spoke, and will endure by the succession of like sons. I am certain that no one who wishes to be had or called a Christian says that he is in darkness as to this light.

units.la: Superaddamus lucem alteram Apostolici verbi conformem huic luci: Solliciti seruare vnitatem spiritus in vinculo pacis, vnum corpus & vnus spiritus, sicut vocati estis in vna spe vocationis vestrae, vnus Dominus, vna fides, vnum baptisma, vnus Deus & pater omnium, qui super omnes, per omnia & in omnibus nobis. Sequitur: & ipse dedit quosdam quidem Apostolos, quosdam autem Prophetas: alios vero euangelistas, alios autem pastores & doctores ad consummationem sanctorum in opus ministerii, in aedificationem corporis Christi, donec occurramus omnes in vnitate fidei cognitionis filii Dei, in virum perfectum, in mensuram aetatis plenitudinis Christi. Sequitur: veritatem autem facientes in charitate crescamus in illo per omnia qui est caput Christus, ex quo totum corpus compactum & connexum per omnem iuncturam subministrationis secundum operationem in mensuram vniuscuiusque membri augmentum corporis facit in aedificationem sui in charitate.
