I have indeed learned this from important people as the reason for it: sometimes two, sometimes three or four persons were elected in the same church, and from this hatreds and serious lawsuits have sometimes arisen, with great inconvenience and loss to the churches. Such a reservation was therefore expedient for the Roman Pontiff, to meet such cases.

units.la: PAVL. Cur ergo cessante causa huiusmodi, non reseruatio cessat, saltem quoad electores eorum, qui concorditer & sancte sunt electi? quoniam etiam & in his practicatur, res vtrique graviter est suspecta. Ergo quomodo talibus, quae non communiter accidunt, imo raro, expediebat ponere talia remedia, per quae tam grauibus erroribus via patet, quos inde multipliciter experimur. Nulli dubium, quin haec reseruatio siue regula detestanda, pluribus & grauibus erroribus viam aperuit, inserius declarandis. Nec hoc est ambigendum, quod nisi haec fuissent, nunquam talia emanassent. Dato enim, sed non concesso, quod tales electiones in discordia communiter euenirent, nonne etiam hoc casu iura sufficienter & salubriter prouiderunt? Et si bene perpenditur, dicta reseruatio non adimit simpliciter electionem capitularis, sed sub conditione, quia in reseruatione dicitur: In quan-tum tum ea uti voluerimus, & sic tacite admittit, ut capitula pastorem sibi eligant. Sed electionis approbatio a Papæ dependet voluntate: qui quantumcunque electi in concordia illuc venerunt, fatigati gravibus laboribus & expensis, intentionibus frustrantur, sic decepti.
units.tr: PAUL. Why then, when the cause of this kind ceases, does the reservation not cease, at least as regards those electors who have been elected harmoniously and rightly? For this too is practised, and the thing is gravely suspect on both counts. How then was it expedient to set up such remedies for cases that do not commonly occur, indeed rarely, by which a way has been opened to very grave errors, which we experience in many ways? There is no doubt that this reservation, or rule, which ought to be condemned, has opened the way to many and grave errors, to be set out below. Nor is there any doubt that, had these not existed, such things would never have arisen. For granted, but not conceded, that such elections commonly came to discord, would not the laws, even in this case, have made sufficient and wholesome provision? And if it is rightly weighed, the said reservation does not simply take away the chapter's election, but makes it conditional, since the reservation says: as far as we choose to use it; and so it tacitly admits that the chapters choose a shepherd for themselves. But the approval of the election depends on the will of the Pope; however much the electors came together there in agreement, wearied by heavy labours and expenses, they are frustrated in their intentions, thus deceived.

units.la: CAP. V. In quo dimisi errores Romana curia circa promissiones & executiones beneficiorum, indulgentiarum, &c. detegguntur.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. In which the errors of the Roman curia concerning promises and executions of benefices, indulgences, etc., are disclosed.

units.la: PET. Quid ergo valent iura, multis vigiliis, magnaque maturitate & sollicitudine sanctorum Patrum inventa, præsertim de electionibus, cum tamen Papa pro suo libito contra electionem quantumcunq; canonicam, de ecclesiis disponit, & monasteriis? imo inutiliter membranas occupant. Doctores vero, ac seculares ea legentes, inani labore se consumunt.
units.tr: PET. What, then, is the value of laws found through many vigils, great deliberation and the care of the holy Fathers, especially concerning elections, when nevertheless the Pope disposes of churches and monasteries at his pleasure, against any election, however canonical? Indeed, they fill the parchments to no purpose. And teachers and laymen who read them wear themselves out in empty labour.

units.la: PAVL. Sic sic Papa faceret, ut asseris, erroneum sine dubio censeretur. Nec error suus huiusmodi excusationem haberet: quia nequaquam immutare posset, quæ instinctu Spiritus sancti pro utilitate totius vniuersalis Ecclesiæ multis temporibus, pro vigili sollicitudine sanctorum Patrum, conciliorumque generalium sunt digesta, nisi subesset causa valde rationabilis & euidens, aliquando contrarium faciendi.
units.tr: PAUL. If the Pope acted in the way you assert, he would without doubt be judged to be in error. Nor would his error have any such excuse: for he could by no means alter what has been laid down, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, for the benefit of the whole universal Church over many ages, through the watchful care of the holy Fathers and the general councils, unless there were some very reasonable and evident cause for doing the contrary.

units.la: PET. Nunquid sub nomine Rationabilis causæ, includitur pecunia?
units.tr: PET. Is money included under the name of "reasonable cause"?

units.la: PAVL. Absit hoc Petre, & valde absit à Christi vicario, quod tanta dementia insaniret, abiecta perfectionis Apostolicæ disciplina, cuius cathedram decet, non vendere, sed regere, & fideliter dispensare.
units.tr: PAUL. Far from it, Peter, and far indeed from the vicar of Christ, that he should rave with such madness as to cast aside the discipline of apostolic perfection, whose chair befits not selling but ruling and faithfully dispensing.

units.la: PET. Miror, Paule, nimium, si hoc tu ignoras, quod fere nedum totus mundus scit, sed ruinam maximam & corruptionem ex hoc patitur, & est passus, & scandalizatus per ea, quæ fiebant in Romana curia continue, & nunc fiunt. Tenamque certifico, sic etiam per inspirationem Dei notorium esset, de aliquo facta electio, & persona quantumlibet vilis, docta atque sancta, nisi dederit pecunias, vel de soluendo prius pacta fuerit, quasi superuacua pro sua confirmatione, aut alias pro quocunque ecclesiastico beneficio laborabit.
units.tr: PET. I marvel greatly, Paul, if you do not know what almost the whole world knows, and what suffers the greatest ruin and corruption from it, and has been scandalised by the things that were, and are now, continually done in the Roman curia. I assure you that, even by the inspiration of God it would be plain, that if some election has been made, and a person however lowly, learned and holy, has not given money, or has not first agreed to pay, he will labour in vain for his confirmation as superfluous, or else for any ecclesiastical benefice whatever.

units.la: PAVL. Ignorare non possum, Petre: sed doleo plus quam stupeo, quod tam grauissima plaga, Deo permittente, propter peccata nostra, fœuit in populum Christianum, multo dolore quassantur præcordia. Heu quoties tot & tantos errores in ecclesia conspicio Christiana?
units.tr: PAUL. I cannot be ignorant of it, Peter; but I grieve more than I am astonished that such a most grievous plague, by God's permission, for our sins, rages against the Christian people; my heart is shaken with great sorrow. Alas, how often do I see so many and so great errors in the Christian Church?

units.la: PET. Nonne totum hoc sua venalitate tota curia Romana propagauit, cum sic exorbitantes promouentur episcopi inutiles, idiotæ, scandalosi, ambitiosi, subditis violenti, aliisq; beneficiis ecclesiasticis, tam curatis quam non curatis, sine differentia discretionis personarum, & inaniter præficiuntur, lenones, coci, stabularii equorum, & pueri. Tot ibi fiunt pactiones, tot quotidie intercedunt solutiones, quot sine omni timore & verecundia tractatores seu mediatores simoniæ, quasi forum constituentes publicum. Iam pro signatura Papæ super tali beneficio, vel gratia, debes tantum: iam pro dispensatione super talib. incopatibilibus, un.: pro tali indulto, tantum: pro absolutione à tali excommunicatione, vel irregularitate, tantum: pro talibus indulgentiis, tantum, &c. publice paciscountur & fortisant. Et ille plus diligitur, qui astutiori sollicitudine, & maiori astutia plures simplices decipit, & plures denarios scit venari. Tot & tantæ fiunt etiam exorbitantes gratiæ: sed reuera multo verius dicerentur mercantiæ, quæ nunc fiunt, & appellantur de die obitus, nunc dies obitus cum declaratione, nunc perpetuum silentium, nunc clausula ante ferri, vel antelationis: nunc de proprio motu Papæ, nunc de clausula ceterorum quæ tollit iura quæsitum. Nunc fiunt anticipationes datarum, nunc data Cardinalium concedunter nunc data Papæ, iam reuocantur, iam immutantur, iam ad certum tempus duraturæ limitantur, iam renouantur, iam prælati de una ecclesia ad aliam transferuntur, iam beneficiis suis propter pecuniam spoliantur. In omnibus his tota devotio consistit, ut denarii acquiratur.
units.tr: PET. Has not the whole Roman curia spread all this by its venality, when such unsuitable, ignorant, scandalous, ambitious bishops, violent towards their subjects, are promoted beyond measure, and to other ecclesiastical benefices, both with cure and without cure, without any distinction of persons, and are set over them to no purpose: pimps, cooks, grooms of horses and boys? So many agreements are made there, so many payments pass every day, as the brokers or go-betweens of simony carry on without any fear or shame, as if setting up a public marketplace. Now, for the Pope's signature upon such a benefit or favour, you must pay so much; now, for dispensation from such incompatibles, so much; for such an indult, so much; for absolution from such excommunication or irregularity, so much; for such indulgences, so much, etc. They openly bargain and haggle over these things. And he is the more esteemed who, with more cunning care and greater craft, deceives more simple people and knows how to hunt down more pennies. So many and such great exorbitant favours are also made; but in truth they would be called far more truly trade, which is now carried on and called "of the day of death", now "day of death with declaration", now "perpetual silence", now "clause before ferri" or "of precedence"; now "of the Pope's own motion", now "of the clause of the others which takes away acquired rights". Now "anticipations of dates" are made, now "dates of the Cardinals" are granted, now "dates of the Pope"; now they are revoked, now they are changed, now they are limited to last for a certain time, now they are renewed, now prelates are transferred from one church to another, now they are stripped of their benefices for money. In all these things the whole devotion consists, that money may be acquired.

units.la: PAVL. Res multum miranda, sed magis est formidanda, quod facta Romanæ curiæ, & hæc tam perniciosa exemplo deliria, ludo scacorum assimilantur. Quis nam tam simplex esse poterit, qui non intelligat, ex auaritiæ radice procedere? quis tam iustus, qui in bonum tam exorbitantia facta interpretari valeat? Quis tam sanctus, ut non expauescat, vel non scandalizetur? imo toti clero ambitionis datur materia, via gravibus & plurimis litibus aperitur, quam omnia iura fugere conabantur. Et non dubium, quin homicidia ex hoc etiam consequantur.
units.tr: PAUL. A thing truly to be marvelled at, but still more to be feared, that the deeds of the Roman curia, and these follies so pernicious as an example, are likened to a game of chess. Who could be so simple as not to understand that they spring from the root of avarice? Who is so just as to be able to interpret such exorbitant deeds for good? Who is so holy as not to be alarmed, or not to be scandalised? Indeed, material for ambition is given to the whole clergy, and a way is opened to grave and very many lawsuits, which all laws have tried to avoid. And there is no doubt that murders also follow from this.

units.la: PET. Imo certum est. Nam vix contigit vacare beneficium ecclesiasticum, vbi duo, tres, quatuor, vel sex, ad impetrandum non concurrant, & sæpius ipsi, vel amici eorum, hac occasione se armis inuadunt bellicis, & mutuo se occidunt. Currunt quoque ribaldi ad curiam, sicut ad forum publicum, & vbi duo vel tres conueniunt, pro prima vel secunda salutatione se suscipiunt. Quantum iam valet data Papæ, quantum Cardinalium, quantum proprius motus Papæ, quantum tales indulgentiæ, &c. Quomodo ergo errores esse non debeant, vbi Christus, vera lux, non illuminat, sed cæcitas auaritiæ corda venalitate obfuscat? Quid enim propinquius totius ecclesiæ destructioni?
units.tr: PET. Indeed it is certain. For scarcely does it happen that an ecclesiastical benefice falls vacant without two, three, four or six men competing for it, and often they themselves, or their friends, on this occasion attack one another with weapons of war and kill each other. Ruffians also run to the curia as to a public marketplace, and wherever two or three meet, they greet each other with the first or second salutation. How much now is a Papal date worth, how much a Cardinal's, how much the Pope's own motion, how much such indulgences, etc.? How then can there not be errors, where Christ, the true light, does not illuminate, but the blindness of avarice darkens hearts with venality? For what is nearer to the destruction of the whole Church?

units.la: PAVL. Plane non regitur sic ecclesia, sed destruitur, vt ait Bernard. scribens super Cantica, sermone 78. Non est hoc custodire, sed perdere: non est defendere, sed exponere: non est instituere, sed prostituere: non est pascere gregem Dominicum, sed mactare, & devorare, dicente cente Domino de illis: Qui devorant plebem meam, sicut escam panis. Nec rectores, sed destructores dici debeant, tam promouentes, quam promoti.
units.tr: PAUL. Surely the Church is not governed in this way, but destroyed, as Bernard says, writing on the Canticles, sermon 78. This is not to keep watch, but to lose; not to defend, but to expose; not to instruct, but to prostitute; not to feed the Lord's flock, but to slaughter and devour it, the Lord saying of such men: "Who devour my people as they eat bread." Those who promote, and those who are promoted, should be called not rulers but destroyers.

units.la: PET. Ex his, vt apparet mihi, resultat vnius membri veritas supra capitulo tertio distinctionis iam praemissae, quod omnes sic promoti ad titulos, sicut eos iniuste acquisierunt, sic semper cum salutis periculo detinent sic quaesitos. Sed redeundo ad propositum, iam declara, qui sunt qui iuste quaerunt titulos, & quaesitos iuste tenent.
units.tr: PET. From this, as it seems to me, there follows the truth of one member stated above in the third chapter of the distinction already premised: that all who are thus promoted to titles, as they have unjustly acquired them, so always, with danger to their salvation, hold them when so acquired. But returning to our purpose, now declare who they are who justly seek titles, and justly hold what they have acquired.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Quo dantur quatuor regulae, quibus cognoscitur, quando provisio tituli est simoniaca, aut canonica: & declaratur, quomodo in provisione simoniaca non datur titulus.
units.tr: Four rules are given by which it is known when the provision to a title is simoniacal or canonical, and it is shown how no title is given in a simoniacal provision.

units.la: PAVL. In hac materia te breuiter per quatuor regulas expediam, tota memoria perpetuo retinendas. Quarum prima sit ista: Iuste intitulari quaerit, qui intentione principalissima honorem Dei, aut salutem proximi, finem constituit, & demum per media debita, & canonica, de quibus supra dictum est, scilicet canonicam electionem, legitimam patroni praesentationem, aut sufficientem personae examinationem, & interuenientibus aliis requisitis, de quibus supra, obtinere quaerit. Non enim sufficit bonum finem intendere, nisi per modos & vias licitas & honestas fiat, hoc enim necessario requiritur ad quemlibet actum ordinatum: & dico tam in suscipiente, quam in conferente. Secunda regula est ista, quod quantumcunque recipiens beneficium, honesto fine motus intitulari queat, ad beneficium ecclesiasticum, per media debita & canonica. Si tamen eo ignorante, vel sciente, conferenti per aliquem offertur pecunia, & conferens non habito respectu principaliter ad electionem canonicam, praesentationem aut valorem personae, sed ad pecuniam, aut fauorem humanum, aut preces carnales, aut obsequium, &c. & propter hoc confert beneficium ecclesiasticum, alias non facturus, nullum ius per hoc in dicto beneficio ecclesiastico est recipienti acquisitum. Quod hoc sit verum, praeter id quod inferius latius apparebit, videre poteris ex eo: quia quam cito ad notitiam possidentis devenerit talis collatio, tenetur dimittere beneficium, vt in cap. ex insinuat. de simo. & ipsum sine noua collatione non poterit obtinere: vt ibidem. Tertia regula, quantumcunque promouendus ad aliquem titulum ecclesiasticum, siue beneficium, finem intendat bonum, vt puta praedicare, ruinam ecclesiae reformare, & multa bona facere: si tamen in acquirendo non incedit per media debita iuris, vt supra, sed per pactiones, solutiones, preces carnales, obsequium, promotiones, principum adulationes, &c. & conferens, vt sic etiam sibi confert, scilicet propter pecunias principaliter, & preces, &c. vt supra: & partim propter Deum, seu virtutes personae coniunctim, nec iste confert titulum, nec ille ex tali collatione aliquod ius acquirat. Quarta regula: Licet promouendus impetrando beneficium ecclesiasticum, intendat finem principaliter in honestum, vt puta honorem temporalem, seu mundanum, aut propter delicatam vitam deducendam, aut propter consanguineos promouendos, si tamen est alias canonice electus, aut idoneus iusto examine repertus, & per talia media canonica intitulari quaerit, & conferens, vt sic motus, sibi conferat, quamuis ipse recipiens propter depravatam intentionem peccat mortaliter, tituli tamen facta collatio tenet. Et idem est dicendum, si recipiens, quantum in eo fuit, prouisionem per simoniam obtinere conabatur, & voluit: conferens tamen non intuitu pecuniae, sed intuitu virtutum personae contulit, &c. Et per has conclusiones, seu regulas, si eas debita masticatione consideraueris, de infinitis casibus in hac materia es expeditus. Nam aliquando quis quaerit beneficium canonice, & etiam quaesitum iuste tenetur: vt dicitur prima regula. Aliquando iuste quaerit, sed quaesitum iniuste tenet: vt dicit secunda regula. Quandoque vero iniuste quaerit, & quaesitum tamen iuste tenet: vt dicit quarta regula. Interdum autem iuste quaerit, & quaesitum cum peccato mortali, & salutis suae detrimento tenet, vt dicit tertia regula.
units.tr: PAUL. In this matter I will briefly settle the question by four rules, to be kept in memory at all times. The first is this: he seeks to be rightly entitled who, with the chief intention, sets as his end the honour of God or the salvation of his neighbour, and who in the end seeks to obtain it by the due and canonical means spoken of above, namely canonical election, the lawful presentation of the patron, or a sufficient examination of the person, and with the other requirements mentioned above. For it is not enough to intend a good end, unless it is pursued by lawful and honourable ways and means; this is required necessarily for any ordained act, and I say this of the one receiving as much as of the one conferring. The second rule is this: however much a man who is moved by an honest end may seek to be entitled to an ecclesiastical benefice, by the due and canonical means, if, however, money is offered to the conferring person through someone, whether the recipient knows of it or not, and the conferrer, without having regard chiefly to canonical election, presentation or the worth of the person, but to the money, or human favour, or carnal entreaties, or service, and on account of this confers the ecclesiastical benefice, which he would otherwise not have done, no right in that benefice is acquired by the recipient through this. That this is true, apart from what will appear more fully below, you may see from this: because as soon as such a conferment comes to the knowledge of the possessor, he is bound to give up the benefice, as in the chapter Ex insinuat, de simonia, and he cannot obtain it again without a new conferment, as in the same place. The third rule: however much a man who is to be promoted to some ecclesiastical title or benefice may intend a good end, for instance to preach, to reform the ruin of the church and to do many good things, if however in acquiring it he does not proceed by the due means of law, as above, but by bargains, payments, carnal entreaties, service, promotions, flattery of princes, and so on, and the conferrer likewise confers on him, namely chiefly on account of money and entreaties, as above, and partly on account of God or the virtues of the person taken together, then neither does this one confer a title, nor does that one acquire any right from such a conferment. The fourth rule: although the one to be promoted, in seeking an ecclesiastical benefice, intends chiefly an end that is in itself honest, for instance temporal or worldly honour, or to maintain a delicate life, or to advance his relatives, yet if he is otherwise canonically elected or found fit by a proper examination, and seeks to be entitled by such canonical means, and the conferrer, moved in this way, confers it on him, then although the recipient himself sins mortally on account of his depraved intention, the title and the conferment made still hold. The same must be said if the recipient, as far as lay in him, tried and wished to obtain the provision by simony, but the conferrer conferred it not in view of money but in view of the virtues of the person, and so on. And by these conclusions, or rules, if you consider them with due chewing, you will be freed from infinite cases in this matter. For sometimes a man seeks a benefice canonically and also rightly holds what he has sought, as the first rule says. Sometimes he seeks rightly but holds what he has sought wrongly, as the second rule says. But sometimes he seeks wrongly yet holds what he has sought rightly, as the fourth rule says. At other times he seeks rightly, yet holds what he has sought with mortal sin and to the loss of his salvation, as the third rule says.

units.la: PET. Valde horribilis & supra modum terribilis haec tua videtur sententia, & si bene aduerto, non solum promotos his temporibus in Romana curia, sed quasi totius mundi clerum videntur haec regulae condemnare. Quod quia non verisimile est, quod tanta multitudo beneficiatorum pereat, vt sunt multi valentes Theologi, ac vtriusque Iuris professores, aliqui viri literatissimi, tam promouentes quam promoti, non tibi tanquam in singulari opinione laboranti consentio, & maxime, quia & secunda & tertia regulis videris nimium delirare.
units.tr: PET. This your opinion seems exceedingly dreadful and beyond measure terrible, and if I understand it rightly, these rules seem to condemn not only those promoted in these times in the Roman court, but almost the whole clergy of the world. Since it is not likely that so great a multitude of beneficed men should perish, among them many learned theologians and professors of both laws, and some most learned men, both those who promote and those who are promoted, I do not agree with you as one labouring under a singular opinion, and especially because you seem to me to rave too much in both the second and the third rules.

units.la: PAVL. Profecto Petre, si quis sollicitae considerationis animo, quod dictum est amplectitur, non tam terribilis apparebit haec sententia, quam vera: nec singularem me in ea reputo, quam notoria dicta Saluatoris, & ratio approbauit, necnon etiam Ecclesiae institituta: nec multitudo errantium, ac error multitudinis, eius poterit veritatem aliquatenus immutare, & potius consequendus est Christus, qui est vera via, & veritas, quam tumultus errantium, quantumcunque peritorum. Audi canonem: Quia non minus ardebunt, qui cum multis ardebunt 2.q.1. multi.
units.tr: PAUL. Truly, Peter, if anyone embraces what has been said with a mind of careful consideration, this sentence will appear not so much terrible as true; nor do I count myself singular in it, since the well-known sayings of the Saviour and reason have approved it, and also the institutions of the Church; nor can the multitude of those who err, or the error of the multitude, change its truth in any way; and rather we must follow Christ, who is the true way and the truth, than the tumult of the erring, however skilled they may be. Hear the canon: Because they will not burn less who burn with many, 2 q. 1, Multi.

units.la: PET. Rationabiliter utique haec dixisti: sed ostende quaeso, hoc ex dictis Scripturarum, aut nominibus, vt si forte verum inueniam quod asseris, periculum damnationis euitabo.
units.tr: PET. You have indeed spoken reasonably; but please show me this from the sayings of Scripture or from its names, so that if by chance I find that what you assert is true, I may avoid the danger of damnation.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: In quo declaratur veritas secunda & tertia regularum multipliciter.
units.tr: In which the truth of the second and third rules is declared in many ways.

units.la: PAVL. Considerare oportet primo, Petre, Saluatoris dictum in Euangelio Iohan. 10. vbi dicitur: Amen amen dico vobis, qui non intrat per ostium in ouile ouium, sed ascendit aliunde, ille fur est, & latro. Qui autem intrat per ostium, pastor est ouium, huic ostiarius aperit, & oues vocem eius audiunt. Quid autem sit ostium, quid ouile, & quæ oues, nobis dubitantibus cum Apostolis, exponit ibidem dicens: Amen amen dico vobis, quia ego sum ostium ouium: per me si quis introierit, saluabitur. Conclude tuá contrario sensu: Si non per me introierit, damnabitur. His diligenter pensatis, considerandum est, quod sicut ostium materiale est medium intrantem ouile, & aperientem: ita secundum rationem doctorum, & intellectum verum, & per multa iura approbarum, Christus, qui est verum ostium (vt dicit textus Euangelicus) debet esse medium inter intrantem ouile, id est titulum ecclesiasticum, & inter aperientem, id est, conferentem. Hoc est dicere, quod Christus debet esse causa collationis in conferente, & etiam receptionis in suscipiente, quod vterque facit propter Christum. Vnde, si conferens non confert pure & principaliter propter Christum, sed propter aliam causam temporalem, ostium sine dubio non est apertum. Ex quo sequitur, quod iste non intrat: & per consequens, non acquirit. Præterea conferens propter aliam causam, quam propter Christum principaliter, vt puta propter pecunias, propter consanguinitatem, obsequium, preces carnales, fauorem patriæ, vel linguagii, timorem humanum (qui non cadit in constantem virum) vel fauorem: vt adulationes mendacii, lenocinii, vel cuiuscunque peccati, non solum sibi conferendo titulum, sed dando causam aliunde ascendendi, facit ipsum furem & latronem: & per consequens, suæ damnationis participem. Patet hoc ex eo, quia ascendens aliunde, est fur & latro, vt dicit Christus. Et ad idem est prima quaestion. prim. ordinationes. Ergo ex tali collatione non habet aliquod ius in beneficio, & per consequens, non aliquem titulum. Ex quo titulus non est aliud, quam ius spirituale in aliquo beneficio, vt supra definitum est. Consequentia tamen videtur esse nota ex eo, quia si talis haberet ius, sine titulum in beneficio, faceret fructus suos, & contrectaret rem suam, non alienam: & per consequens, non esset fur, cuius contrarium est veritas Euangelica. Confirmatur hoc argumentum optime per cap. gratia. prim. quaestion. prim. Idem est dicendum, si conferet partim propter pecuniam, vel aliam causam temporalem, & partim propter Christum: ita scilicet, quod nec collaturus esset propter pecunias tantum, nec solum propter Christum, sed propter vtrumque simul: sine dubio talis per ostium non intrat, & per consequens, non habet titulum. Quomodo autem ratione naturali hoc probetur, patebit inferius, cum tractabitur de plenitudine potestatis Papæ. Præterea, iure canonico talis nunquam potest agere veram poenitentiam pro peccatis, quandiu non dimittit titulum, seu beneficium taliter acquisitum: vt l.q.1.si quis dator. & l.q.1.ordinat. &c. si quis neque sanctus, & ibi expressa per B. Gregorium & cap. siquidem. & 1. qu. 7. requirentis. Item ad idem est cap. nisi cum pridem. de renun. quia necessario sunt talia dimittenda, quæ etiam post peractam poenitentiam impediunt executionem ordinis, aut beneficii retentionem: vt ibi, & in c. inquisitionis, de accus. Et dicit Glossa eiusdem c. nisi cum pridem, super verbo illius: quod simoniacus, & intrusus, non habent titulum, sed sint fures & latrones. concor. in hoc casu Io. Teu. Vin. & Io. Fau. & Io. An. ib. Item nec etiam saluari talis poterit, nisi pro viribus omnia restituat sic percepta ecclesiæ, in cuius ignominiam talia sunt perpetrata, vt 17. q. 4. si quis, matr. 27. q.1. si quis rapuerit. Et de sim. 6. de hoc cum sim. Quod vtique non procederet, si illi fuisset aliquod ius quæsitum.
units.tr: PAUL. First, Peter, we must consider the saying of the Saviour in the Gospel of John, chapter 10, where it is said: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, he that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber. But he that entereth in by the door is the shepherd of the sheep; to him the porter openeth, and the sheep hear his voice." What the door is, what the sheepfold is, and who the sheep are, he explains there when we, together with the Apostles, are in doubt, saying: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, I am the door of the sheep; by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved." Conclude from this by the contrary sense: if he does not enter by me, he shall be condemned. Having weighed these things carefully, we must consider that just as a material door is the means by which one who enters the sheepfold also opens it, so, according to the reasoning of the teachers and the true understanding, and as is approved by many laws, Christ, who is the true door (as the Gospel text says), ought to be the means between the one entering the sheepfold, that is, the ecclesiastical title, and the one opening it, that is, the one conferring it. That is to say, Christ ought to be the cause of the conferring in the one who confers, and also of the receiving in the one who receives, since each does what he does on account of Christ. Hence, if the one conferring does not confer purely and chiefly on account of Christ, but on account of some other temporal cause, the door is without doubt not opened. From this it follows that such a one does not enter, and consequently does not acquire. Moreover, a conferrer who acts on account of some other cause than chiefly Christ, as for instance on account of money, kinship, obsequiousness, carnal entreaties, favour of country or of language, human fear (which does not befall a steadfast man), or favour, such as the flatteries of lying, of procuring, or of any sin whatever, not only by conferring the title on himself but by giving the cause for climbing up some other way, makes him a thief and a robber, and consequently a sharer in his own damnation. This is evident from the fact that one who climbs up some other way "is a thief and a robber," as Christ says. And to the same effect is the first question of the first part, "Ordinationes." Therefore he has no right in the benefice from such a conferring, and consequently no title. Whence a title is nothing other than a spiritual right in some benefice, as has been defined above. The consequence, however, seems to be plain, because if such a one had a right, or a title, in the benefice, he would take its fruits and handle his own property, not another's, and consequently would not be a thief, whereas the contrary is the Gospel truth. This argument is excellently confirmed by the chapter "Gratia," first question, first part. The same must be said if he confers partly on account of money or some other temporal cause, and partly on account of Christ: in such a way that he would not have conferred on account of money alone, nor solely on account of Christ, but on account of both together; without doubt such a one does not enter by the door, and consequently has no title. How this is proved by natural reason will become clear below, when we treat of the plenitude of the power of the Pope. Moreover, by canon law such a one can never perform true repentance for sins, so long as he does not give up the title, or benefice, so acquired; see Causa 1, "Si quis dator," and Causa 1, "Ordinat., etc., Si quis neque sanctus," and what is expressed there by St. Gregory; and the chapter "Siquidem," and Causa 1, question 7, "Requirentis." Likewise to the same effect is the chapter "Nisi cum pridem," on renunciation, because those things must necessarily be given up which, even after repentance has been completed, hinder the exercise of an order or the retention of a benefice; see there, and in the chapter "Inquisitionis," on accusation. And the Gloss of the same chapter "Nisi cum pridem," on the word "illius," says that the simoniac and the intruder have no title, but are thieves and robbers; agreeing in this case are John Teutonicus, Vincentius, John of Faenza and John Andreae, in the same place. Likewise, such a one cannot be saved either, unless he restores, so far as he can, everything so received to the Church, to whose dishonour such things were perpetrated; see Causa 17, question 4, "Si quis"; Causa 27, question 1, "Si quis rapuerit"; and De simonia, chapter 6, "De hoc cum simonia." Which would certainly not hold if he had some right acquired in it.

units.la: PET. Non sequitur, quod vltimo intulisti, nam suspenso ab officio, & etiam excommunicato, excommunicatione durante, subtrahuntur proventus beneficii, vt in c. pastoralis; & perceptos tenetur restituere, & tamen nihilominus retinet titulum beneficii illius.
units.tr: PET. What you have just concluded does not follow, for a man suspended from office, and even excommunicated while the excommunication lasts, loses the revenues of the benefice, as in the chapter "Pastoralis"; and he is bound to restore those he has received, and yet he nevertheless retains the title of that benefice.

units.la: PAVL. Ignorantia iuris te decipit. Nam excommunicatus, aut suspensus ab officio, non perdit fructus ipso facto, & ideo ratione tituli, quem habet, durante excommunicatione, fructus perceptos non restituit, nisi per sententiam iudicis subtrahantur, quod innuit Inno. in dicto cap. pastoralis. Translatio autem tituli in ipso collationis initio vitiatur modo supra dicto, propter quod tenetur omnia restituere. Quæ n. malo inchoantur principio, nunquam peraguntur bono fine l.q.1. principatus.
units.tr: PAUL. You are deceived by ignorance of the law. For an excommunicate man, or one suspended from office, does not lose the fruits by the very fact, and therefore, by reason of the title which he holds while the excommunication lasts, he does not restore the fruits received, unless they are withdrawn by the sentence of a judge; this Innocent indicates in the said chapter "Pastoralis." But the transfer of the title at the very beginning of the conferring is vitiated in the manner stated above, on account of which he is bound to restore everything. For what is begun from a bad beginning is never carried through to a good end; see Causa 1, "Principatus."

units.la: PET. O Paule, cum exultatione animi iam tua dicta recipio, taliter declarata. Iam vere conspicio, quam plurimos quotidie grauiter delirare, verumtamen dic etiam specialius circa alias regulas, vt ipsarum veritas clarius patefiat.
units.tr: PET. O Paul, with joy of spirit I now receive your words, so clearly declared. Now I truly see how very many people go grievously astray every day. Yet tell me also more particularly about the other rules, so that the truth of them may be made clearer.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: In quo declaratur veritas quarta regula: & datur ratio, quare non transfertur titulus, si datur simoniace, & tamen si solum recipitur, simoniace tenet.
units.tr: In which the truth of the fourth rule is declared, and the reason is given why a title is not transferred if it is given simoniacally, yet if it is only received, it holds as simoniacal.

units.la: PAVL. Aliqualiter procedendo retrograde, prius quartam regulam in ordine tibi taliter declarabo. Quilibet enim titulus beneficialis institutus est effective & finaliter, propter aliquod officium, vel ministerium ecclesiasticum, vt honor debitus referatur creatori, & ad hoc sunt fructus beneficiorum à fidelibus assignati, vt supra circa diffinitionem tituli sufficienter audiuisti. Si ergo aliquis peruerso isto ordine suum honorem, vel commodum temporale, &c. finem principaliter constituit, id quod debetur Deo, sibi vsurpando, quantum in eo est, Deo subtrahit: & per consequens, in aspectu eius qui suam intentionem peruersam clarissime intuetur, est fur iudicatus. Praterea talis illud temporale plus eligit, & per consequens plus diligit, quod sibi principalius finem constituit. Ex quo sequitur, quod ipse sua intentione à recti charitate recedit, cum illud quod est per se bonum & diligibile, dimittit: & bonum transitorium, quod est bonum per accidens, eligit: quod non nisi in ordine ad Deum debet diligi, & per consequens, verae dilectioni contrarium faciens, peccat mortaliter, quia repugnat verae charitati. Nō nego tamen, quin propter temporale commodum assequendum, non tamen principaliter, licitum est beneficium ecclesiasticum postulare, seu pro vt est quoddam adminiculum ad salutem, vel in quantum proprie fini non derogat: propter quem illud beneficium est institutum. Et licet hoc in actu sue intentionis non habeat tunc, quando promoneri quaerit, vel desiderat: sufficit enim, quod hoc habeat in habitu & virtute, sci. quod potius vellet eligere, carere tali beneficio, quam aliter facere, quam secundum quod finis exigit, propter quem est tale beneficium finaliter & principaliter institutum.
units.tr: PAUL. Proceeding somewhat in reverse order, I will first explain the fourth rule to you in its place. Every benefice title is instituted effectively and finally for the sake of some ecclesiastical office or ministry, so that the honour due is referred to the Creator. To this end the fruits of the benefices are assigned by the faithful, as you have sufficiently heard above in the definition of a title. If, then, anyone, in this perverse order, makes his own honour or temporal advantage, and so on, his chief end, usurping to himself what is owed to God, he withdraws it from God as far as he can, and consequently, in the sight of him who clearly perceives his perverse intention, he is judged a thief. Moreover, such a person chooses and therefore loves more that temporal thing which he makes his principal end. From this it follows that by his intention he departs from the charity of what is right, since he sets aside what is good and worthy of love in itself and chooses the transitory good, which is good only by accident, and which ought to be loved only in relation to God. Thus, doing what is contrary to true love, he sins mortally, because it is opposed to true charity. I do not deny, however, that for the sake of obtaining a temporal advantage, though not as the principal aim, it is lawful to ask for an ecclesiastical benefice, either as an aid to salvation or insofar as it does not detract from the proper end for which that benefice was instituted. Although he does not have this in the actual exercise of his intention at the time when he seeks or desires to be promoted, it is enough that he has it in disposition and in virtue, namely, that he would rather choose to go without such a benefice than act otherwise than the end requires, the end for which such a benefice is finally and principally instituted.

units.la: PET. Vsque nunc vnam partem quartae regulae sufficienter ostendisti, placeat etiam modicum dicere de secunda. Quae enim potest esse ratio, quod mala conferentis intentio totum debet inficere titulum, vt dicebatur supra in secunda & tertia regulis? Puta, cum confert principaliter propter pecuniam, vel aliam rem temporalem: & tum mala recipientis voluntas hoc non potest vitiare, vt dicit secunda pars quartae regulae, cui dicto videtur expresse contradicere cap. vlt. de si. vbi Gloss. & doct. sentiunt, quod mentalis simonia non est simonia.
units.tr: PETER. Up to now you have sufficiently shown one part of the fourth rule. Please also say a little about the second. What can be the reason why the evil intention of the conferrer must taint the whole title, as was said above in the second and third rules? Suppose he confers principally for money or some other temporal thing, and then the evil will of the recipient cannot vitiate it, as the second part of the fourth rule says. That statement seems to contradict expressly cap. vlt. de si., where the Gloss and the doctors hold that mental simony is not simony.

units.la: PAVL. Haec est huius ratio. Nam titulus beneficialis, sive ius, dependet ab actu conferentis, & non a recipiente, qui quo ad hoc habet se pure passiue. Si ergo fundamentum actus conferendi est infectum, id quod inde sequitur nullum est in effectu, fundamentum autem conferendi est sic, quo ad hoc: quia potentia conferendi est ligata lege diuina. Nam intentio Christi in Euangelio est, quod verum ostium aperitur, & quod non rumpatur foramen vt supra, alioqui si secus fieret, factum non valeret. Si ergo ea quae contra fiunt, debent pro infectis haberi, vt dicit regula iuris, lib. 6. si hoc est verum de iure humano, fortius vtique de diuino. Et de hoc inferius latius apparebit. Quotiescunque ergo aliquod temporale, vel aliquod peccatum in recipiente existens, est causa collationis, vt adulatio, mendacium, lenocinium, aut aliud genus peccati, quo est data occasio, conferentem praecise mouens, vt tale beneficium conferat, non alias collaturus, quia causa huiusmodi non est sufficiens mouendi, virtutem clauium ad actum conferendi, si tamen ea conferens nihilominus mouetur, titulum non confert expedite: qui non confertur, nisi virtute clauium: sed solum quaedam vmbra apparet in opere, sed nulla veritas in effectu. Absit enim, quod Christianus dicat talem in peccando intrare per ostium Christi, qui est via veritas & vita: cum omne peccatum sit tortuositas, falsitas & mors. Sic conferens mouetur in conferendo virtutibus personae, quia tunc Christus est ostium, titulus collatus tenet, quamuis recipiens, intendens illum simoniace consequi, peccet: tamen postquam poenituerit, & licite beneficium recipiet, & alia exercebit. Quod asseris, mentalem simoniam non esse simoniam, dictum videtur derisorium, cum simonia vocalis nunquam esset simonia, nisi quia subordinatur mentali simoniae. Non enim intentio verbis, sed verba intentioni deseruiunt: de verbor. sig. in his. & c. intelligentia. Bene fateor, quod est peccatum criminale, id est publice punibile per ecclesiam. Nec obstat c. vlt. de simo. quod loquitur, ad resignationem acquisitorum simoniace non teneri, quae nullo pacto, sed affectu animi praecedente vtraque acquiruntur, quod intelligitur, quando conserens, quamuis spem de aliquo recipiendo habuit, tamen nihilominus fuisset collaturus, vel quando de mala intentione poenituerit, antequam contulit: vel quia non concluserat animo, quamuis recipere proponebat, vel loquitur in foro iudicii contentiosi.
units.tr: PAUL. This is the reason. The benefice title, or right, depends on the act of the conferrer and not on the recipient, who in this respect stands purely passive. If, then, the foundation of the act of conferring is tainted, what follows from it is null in effect. But the foundation of conferring is of this kind in this respect, because the power of conferring is bound by divine law. For the intention of Christ in the Gospel is that the true door is opened and that the hole is not broken through, as above. Otherwise, if it were done contrary to this, the deed would not be valid. If, then, those things which are done contrary to law ought to be held as invalid, as regula iuris, lib. 6. says, then, if this is true of human law, it is surely much more so of divine law. This will appear more fully below. Whenever, therefore, some temporal thing or some sin existing in the recipient is the cause of the conferring, such as flattery, lying, procuring, or another kind of sin, which gives the occasion, moving the conferrer alone to confer such a benefice, which he would not otherwise confer, because a cause of this kind is not a sufficient motive, then the power of the keys is not brought to the act of conferring, and if the conferrer is nevertheless moved in this way, he does not confer the title effectively. The title is not conferred except by the power of the keys; only a certain shadow appears in the outward act, but there is no truth in the effect. Far be it that a Christian should say that such a person enters in sinning by the door of Christ, who is the way, the truth and the life, since every sin is crookedness, falsehood and death. So when the conferrer is moved in conferring by the virtues of the person, because then Christ is the door, the conferred title holds, although the recipient, intending to obtain it simoniacally, sins. Yet after he has repented, he will receive the benefice lawfully and exercise it. What you assert, that mental simony is not simony, seems a derisive statement, since vocal simony would never be simony unless it were subordinate to mental simony. For words do not serve the intention; rather the intention is served by the words, de verbor. sig. in his. & c. intelligentia. I indeed grant that it is a criminal sin, that is, one publicly punishable by the Church. Nor does c. vlt. de simo., which says that those who acquired things simoniacally are not bound to resign them, stand in the way. Those things are acquired not by any agreement but by a prior disposition of the mind in both cases. This is understood when the conferrer, although he had hope of receiving something, would nevertheless have conferred it anyway, or when he repented of his evil intention before he conferred, or because he had not concluded in his mind, although he proposed to receive something, or it speaks in the court of contentious judgment.

units.la: PET. Efficax est certe ratio, mihi tamen ex ea oritur hoc dubium. Nam liquet ex determinatione sanctorum doctorum, ac etiam ecclesiae, quod quantumcunque propter pecuniam, vel aliam rem illicitam, quis conferat sacros ordines, vel corpus Christi conficiat, vel baptizet, &c. dummodo intendat finem, quem intendit ecclesia, collatio taliter facta tenet, & recipiens recepit characterem, propter quod sacramenta etiam toliter collata non debent iterari.
units.tr: PETER. The reason is certainly strong, yet from it there arises this doubt for me. For it is clear from the determination of the holy doctors, and also of the Church, that however much someone may confer holy orders for money or some other unlawful thing, or consecrates the body of Christ, or baptizes, and so on, provided he intends the end which the Church intends, the conferral done in this way holds, and the recipient receives the character. For this reason sacraments conferred in this way too ought not to be repeated.

units.la: PAVL. Potentia, ô Petre, ad efficiendum talia, non sic limitatur, quae est indelebilis character, impressus animae, quando adhibita forma statuta verborum, cum materia necessario requisita, & intentione faciendi, sequitur effectus sacramenti. Illa autem quae sunt iurisdictionalis exercitii, & in quibus character non imprimitur, nec certum de necessitate requiunt ordinem, facilius impediuntur. Vnde nec ab haereticis excommunicatis suspensis exercentur, & tamen ab eis collata sacramenta, vel confecta, non carent effectu 32. di. ad hoc, quamvis executionem non conferant, quae etiam solicarent.
units.tr: PAUL. O Peter, the power for effecting such things is not limited in this way. The indelible character is impressed on the soul when, with the prescribed form of words, the requisite matter, and the intention of doing it, the effect of the sacrament follows. But those things which belong to the exercise of jurisdiction, in which no character is impressed and which do not of necessity require a fixed order, are more easily impeded. Hence they are not exercised by heretics, excommunicated or suspended persons. Yet the sacraments conferred or consecrated by them do not lack effect, 32. di. ad hoc, although they do not confer the executive power, which would also be given to them.

units.la: PET. De quarta regula, & secunda, per omnia iam contentor, in quibus clare conspicio, paucissimos habere iustos titulos, & heu, infinitam multitudinem beneficiatorum, graui damnationis praecipitio laborate. Progredere, si placet, vlterius, ad tertiam regulam, quae videtur multum dura, & quoniam non solum clerus, sed & populus per ipsam videtur magnis periculis inuolutus, igitur hoc loco edisseras, Vtrum episcopi, & superiores eis Abbates, & omnes alii quicunque beneficiati, sic promotioad titulos ecclesiasticos, vt dicit tertia regula, aliquo modo saluari poterunt, absque hoc quod renuncient suis titulis taliter acquisitis: & vtrum illa quae faciunt, ratione huiusmodi tituli de iure subsistant.
units.tr: PETER. I am now fully content with the fourth and second rules, in which I clearly see that very few have just titles, and alas, an infinite multitude of beneficed men are labouring under the precipice of grievous damnation. Proceed further, if you please, to the third rule, which seems very harsh. Since not only the clergy but also the people seem to be caught up in great dangers through it, therefore explain here whether bishops, and their superiors the abbots, and all other beneficed persons whatsoever, who are promoted to ecclesiastical titles in the way the third rule states, can in any way be saved without renouncing their titles so acquired, and whether those things which they do by reason of such a title subsist in law.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: In quo declarantur duo. Primum, quomodo salvari non poterit, qui beneficium per simoniam obtinuit, nisi illud dimittat. Secundum, de suspensione simoniaci in beneficio, & irregularitate.
units.tr: In which two things are set out. First, how one who has obtained a benefice through simony cannot be saved unless he gives it up. Second, on the suspension of the simoniac in the benefice, and on irregularity.

units.la: PAVL. Ni scripturae & scriptae doctorum me decipiant, veritas utrique hoc cogit dicere, quod tales, nisi renuncient, laborant quotidie in statu propriae damnationis, nec aliquod aliud est remedium. Aliter enim, vt supra dictum est, non poterunt agere poenitentiam pro peccato sic commisso duodecim. distinction. nervis, & caetera. Ad hoc autem scriptura & iura canonica, vt euitetur sermonis prolixitas, non expedit allegare: quoniam concors in hoc omnium est sententia, & iura sunt valde plana, & inferius plus patebit. Dicunt enim doct. Raym. Vlric. Ioan. in Summis suis, & alii: quod si aliquis scit, vel credit, sibi collatum beneficium principaliter propter obsequia, sive preces carnales a se vel ab alio interpositas, debet resignare: quia huiusmodi preces, seu obsequia, succedunt loco precii. Aliqui tamen volebant hoc esse verum, si ille non fuerit dignus, vt refert Gloss. in cap. tuam in Domino. de aeta. & qua. Secus dicunt, si dignus: quia tunc solum poenitebit de intentione corrupta. Sed salua reuerentia, error est, quia tituli translatio non dependet a dignitate vel indignitate seu poenitentia recipientis. Si enim recipiens esset quantumcunque dignus, & conferens non dignitate personae attenderet, sed preces, aut promotiones principum, vel aliua huiusmodi, nullus esset titulus, vt dictum est supra. Sicut enim teneretur resignare, si adeptus fuisset per pecuniam, quantumcunque fuisset dignus, sic etiam eadem ratione, si per preces, obsequia, vel aliquod aliud temporale, quia ista succedunt loco precii. Hoc efficaciter probant verba beati Gregorii, in canon. si quis neque. 1. qu. 1.
units.tr: PAUL. If the Scriptures and the writings of the teachers do not deceive me, the truth compels us both to say that such people, unless they resign, are daily in a state of their own damnation, and there is no other remedy. For otherwise, as said above, they cannot do penance for a sin so committed Dist. 12, Nervis, and so on. To avoid prolixity, it is not necessary to cite the Scripture and the canon law on this point, since all agree in this opinion, the laws are very plain, and more will be made clear below. For the teachers Raymond, Ulrich, and John say in their Summae, and others too, that if anyone knows or believes that a benefice was conferred on him chiefly because of services or carnal entreaties, made by himself or by another, he ought to resign it, since such entreaties or services take the place of a price. Some, however, held that this is true only if the recipient was not worthy, as the Gloss reports on cap. Tuam in Domino, de aetate et qualitate. They say otherwise if he was worthy, since then he would repent only of a corrupt intention. But with all due respect, this is an error, because the transfer of the title does not depend on the worthiness or unworthiness, or the repentance, of the recipient. For if the recipient were as worthy as one could be, and the one conferring the benefice did not look to the person's merit but to entreaties or the promotions of princes or something of that sort, there would be no valid title, as has been said above. For just as he would be bound to resign if he had obtained it for money, however worthy he was, so by the same reasoning, if he obtained it through entreaties, services, or some other temporal thing, because these take the place of a price. The words of blessed Gregory in canon Si quis neque, 1 qu. 1, prove this effectively.

units.la: PET. Concedo tibi, vbi ista succedunt loco precii: vt quia dominus, qui tenetur alicui pro suo seruitio sibi exhibito, dat ecclesiasticum beneficium pro satisfactione, &c. aut cum praelatus, dat consanguineo suo beneficium eo animo, vt domus sua vel parentela per hoc magnificetur, & per hoc ipse fiat potentior, qui illam gloriam sive potentiam sibi comparat per huiusmodi spiritualia, redditur his casibus simoniacus. Sed quando episcopus suo nepotulo donat praeposituram, sive custodiam ecclesiasticam, &c. non habito respectu an per hoc ipse magnificetur, vel sua progenies, sed quia est consanguineus, qui si non fuisset sibi ita propinquus, ei tale beneficium non dedisset, videtur quod illa sanguinis propinquitas loco precii succedat.
units.tr: PET. I grant you this where such things take the place of a price: for example, when a lord, who is under obligation to someone for service rendered to him, gives him an ecclesiastical benefice in payment, and so on; or when a prelate gives a benefice to his kinsman with the intention that his house or family may be enlarged by it, and he himself may become more powerful, since he procures for himself that glory or power by such spiritual things; in these cases he becomes a simoniac. But when a bishop gives his little nephew a provostship or an ecclesiastical guardianship, and so on, without regard to whether he himself or his family thereby gains honour, but because the boy is a kinsman, and if he were not so closely related he would not have given him such a benefice, it seems that this closeness of blood takes the place of a price.

units.la: PAVL. Quoniam apud conferentem dicta consanguinitas non ordinatur in aliud, veluti in alio casu praemisisti, & ob hoc quamquam conferens hoc casu non dicetur simoniacus, quia nihil intendit per hoc accipere pro spirituali beneficio, tamen quia pure propter propinquitatem dat, alias non facturus, nullum transfert in eum titulum, vt superius est expressum.
units.tr: PAUL. Since the kinship mentioned is not directed towards anything else on the part of the one conferring the benefice, as you suggested in another case, then although the one conferring it in this case will not be called a simoniac, because he intends to receive nothing for the spiritual benefice through it, nevertheless, since he gives purely on account of kinship, and would not otherwise have given, he does not transfer a title to him, as was stated above.

units.la: PET. Perge nunc ad secundam quaestionem.
units.tr: PET. Now go on to the second question.

units.la: PAVL. Quo iure, aut qua ratione putas, vt valeant facta, per non habentem titulum, cum tam iure diuino, quam canonico, nullam administrandi, vtendi, vel dispensandi recepit potestatem ? Dicimus enim communiter in iure canonico, quod omnis simoniacus ratione defectus tituli iusti, siue sit simoniacus in ordine, siue in beneficio, est suspensus ab officio, ipso iure prim. quaestion. prim. reperiuntur. de accusat. inquisitionibus. Veruntamen de simoniaco in beneficio, doctores quoad hoc videntur differentes. Nam Innocent. & sequaces dicunt, simoniacum in beneficio curato, vel dignitate, occultum esse, quoad se suspensum, non quo ad alios. Secus de notorio. Goffr. vero, & Hosti. in suis Summis, titul. de Simonia, quod siue sit occultus, siue notorius, sit suspensus, quo ad alios, per cap. dudum. secund. de electio. Vbi dicitur, quod talis decipit animas subditorum: simoniacus tamen occultus in simplici beneficio est suspensus, quoad se tantum. Si vero est notorius, tunc etiam est suspensus, quoad alios, vt in ca. quaesitum. de temp. ordi. Idem videtur sapere Glo. in c. per tuas. 2. de sime.
units.tr: PAUL. By what right, or on what reasoning, do you think that acts done by a man without a title can be valid, since he has received no power to administer, to use, or to dispense, either by divine law or by canon law? For we commonly say in canon law that every simoniac, by reason of the lack of a lawful title, whether he is a simoniac in orders or in a benefice, is suspended from office by the law itself prima quaestio prima, Reperiuntur; de accusationibus, Inquisitionibus. However, the teachers seem to differ about the simoniac in a benefice. For Innocent and his followers say that a simoniac in a cure of souls or a dignity is suspended as far as himself is concerned, if the matter is hidden, but not as regards others; it is otherwise if the matter is notorious. Goffredus, and Hostiensis in their Summae, title De simonia, hold that whether he is hidden or notorious he is suspended as regards others too, by cap. Dudum, secunda, de electione, where it is said that such a man deceives the souls of his subjects. But a hidden simoniac in a simple benefice is suspended only as regards himself. If he is notorious, then he is also suspended as regards others, as in cap. Quaesitum, de tempore ordinationis. The Gloss on c. Per tuas, 2, de simonia seems to share this view.

units.la: PET. Haec materia solida eget expeditione, quoniam quotidie practicabilis necessaria est, opinionibus hinc inde vacillantibus, nec vsque modo sufficienter per aliquem expedita. Ad occurrendum igitur multis animarum periculis, in ea parte extende.
units.tr: PET. This solid matter needs clearing up, since it is daily needed in practice, and opinions waver on both sides, and no one has yet sufficiently settled it. Therefore, to meet the many dangers to souls, please extend your treatment to this part.

units.la: PAVL. Ad habendam ergo veritatem in hac materia, sic distingue. Aut loquimur de simoniaco in ordine, aut in beneficio. Si primum, quoniam ordo duo respicit, scili. Deum, vel ea quae immediate Dei sunt, sicut diuinum officium, vigesim. prim. distinction. clericos. vigesim. quint. distincti, perlectis. Secundo respicit hominem, scilicet in quantum sibi confertur. Primo casu, sive sit notorius, sive occultus, est suspensus tantum, quoad se, directe: quoad alios, indirecte. Quia alii possunt audire diuina simoniaci manifesti, quousque toleratur: per ea quae leguntur & no. in capit. vestra. & in capitulo vltimo. de coha. cler. & mul. Prohibemur enim solum audire diuina ab eo, vt verecundia
units.tr: PAUL. So, to get at the truth in this matter, make the following distinction. Either we are speaking of a simoniac in orders, or in a benefice. If the first, since orders relate to two things, namely God, or those things which belong immediately to God, such as the divine office Dist. 21, Clericos; Dist. 25, Distincti, Perlectis, and secondly they relate to the man, insofar as they are conferred on him. In the first case, whether he is notorious or hidden, he is suspended only as far as he himself is concerned, directly; as far as others are concerned, indirectly. For others may hear the divine services of a manifest simoniac, so long as he is tolerated, as is read and noted in cap. Vestra, and in the last chapter, de cohabitatione clericorum et mulierum. For we are forbidden only to hear divine services from him, so that he may be corrected from sin by a feeling of shame

units.la: Oooooo cundia tactus, à peccato corrigatur trigesim. distinction. ad hac, ad finem. Si autem ordo respicit hominem, aut recipitur à simoniaco simoniace, aut non simoniaco: si primum recipiens non habet executionem ordinis sic suscepti, prim. quaestion. prim. de simoniac. tanta, &c. penultim. imo perdit executionem aliorum, non simoniace receptorum. Si recipit à simoniaco, non tamen simoniace, recipiens ordinis duntaxat recepti non habet executionem, cum nihil dat quod non habet prim. quaestion. septi. Diabertum. Et ideo, siue sit simoniacus in ordine, siue in beneficio, non dat executionem, & per consequens, ordinati ab episcopis simoniacis in dignitate episcopali, non dico solum in ordine episcopali, sed qui ad regimen ecclesiae per simoniam sunt ingressi, nullam ab eis recipiunt executionem prim. quaestion. tert. ea qua, quia fur censetur, de electione. dudum. secund. Idem notat per Doctores in cap. per tuas. 2. de simoniac. Si vero recipitur à non simoniaco, sed simoniace, recipiens caret executione, omnino sicut si recepisset à simoniaco, vt supra; & conferens simoniace suspensus est triennio à collatione, quoad se tantum, si est occultum. de simoniac. cap. penultimo. Si autem loquimur de simoniaco in beneficio, in titulo ecclesiastico, de quo ad propositum aut consideratio est quoad Deum, siue diuinum officium, & sic quantumcunque notorius, dum tamen toleratur, est suspensus, quoad se directe, quoad alios indirecte, vt supra eadem ratione. Excipiuntur in iure canonico baptismus, & corpus Christi, quae conferuntur tempore necessitatis simoniaci, trigesim. secund. distinctio. ad hoc. Si autem quae ad alios sit consideratio, hoc dupliciter: aut loquimur in spiritualibus actibus, vt sunt excommunicare, absoluere, conferre beneficia, &c. aut loquimur in temporalibus, vt est emere, donare, alienare, & similia facere in temporalibus. Si primo modo, quia rite & efficaciter non possunt exerceri talia spiritualia, nec in virtute Dei specialiter, siue Spiritus sancti, vt prim. qua. prim. sic populus, cum multis seq. Talis autem simoniacus in beneficio, cum non habeat iustum titulum, per consequens caret virtute tali spirituali, quae datur homini in iusto titulo. Ex quo talis, quoad ista spiritualia executionem non habet, dicitur non solum suspensus, quo ad se, sed etiam quoad alios: & hoc, siue sit occultus, siue manifestus, siue toleratus per ecclesiam, siue non. Non enim talis tolerantia dat sibi ius coercendi talia, siue coloratus titulus, vel opinio hominum communis, quae non exercentur, nisi vt dictum est: quia Deus opiniones hominum non curat, cum omnia eius sunt clara: prim. quaestion. prim. Spiritus sanctus. trigesim. secund. distinctio. erubescent. trigesim. quart. quaest. tert. Deus. Et opinio Hosti. & Goffr. procedit, de qua supra. Si vero loquimur de simoniaco in beneficio, quoad temporalia, vel etiam quoad actus mere ciuiles, vt iudicare, procurare, &c. tunc dico, quod ille coloratus titulus, & communis opinio adiuuans, validat omnia, quae fiunt; quandiu talis toleratur ab ecclesia, quamuis immiscens se peccet, De electione. nihil est, & no. de resti. spo. in litteris. Et sic est solum suspensus, quoad se, ad talia exercenda: sed non, quoad alios. Et sic procedit opinio Inno. Ioan. An. & aliorum sequentium. Et hoc operatur publica utilitas, quod ea quae per talem putatiuum iudicem, vel praelatum fiunt, valent. Quemadmodum dicimus de excommunicato occulto, per ea quae no. in cap. exceptionem. de excep. &c. ad probandum. de sent. & re. iudic. Constat autem quod si suspensus ab officio exerceat ea quae sunt ratione officii, & officio accidunt: sicut sunt excommunicare, absoluere, beneficia conferre, vel ordinum executionem, &c. nulla sunt ipso iure, de consuet. cum dilectus, & ibi per Ioan. An. plene. de excess. praelat. cap. ultim. & in capi. cum inter. de sent. & re. iudi. libr. 6. propter quod determinant Doctores communiter, quod nullo modo debent recipi ordines a talibus, quia executionem ordinis dare non possunt, 1. qu. 1. reperiuntur. & in c. tanta. de simon. imo potius excommunicationem sustinere debet, de hoc in Gloss. Or. & etiam per Inno. in c. per tuas. 2. de simo. Et probatur etiam in c. inquisit. de sent. exco. Insuper est communis regula in iure canonico, quod suspensione durante, ingerens se diuinis & ministrans in suis ordinibus, sicut prius, efficitur irregularis. ii. q. 3. si quis episcopus. secundum Inno. & in c. nisi cum pridem. de re. nunc. de sent. & re iudi. cum aterni. & de sent. exco. c. 1. & c. is qui lib. 6. per Io. An.
units.tr: being moved by shame, be corrected from sin Dist. 30, Ad haec, at the end. If, however, orders relate to the man, then they are received either from a simoniac in a simoniacal way, or from a non-simoniac. If the first, the recipient has no power to exercise the order so received prima quaestio prima, De simoniacis, Tanta, etc., penultimate; indeed he loses the power to exercise other orders received without simony. If he receives from a simoniac, but not simoniacally, the recipient has no power to exercise only the order received, since one gives nothing that one does not have prima quaestio septima, Diabertum. Therefore, whether he is a simoniac in orders or in a benefice, he confers no power, and consequently those ordained by simoniacal bishops in episcopal dignity (I do not mean only in episcopal orders, but also those who have entered the government of the Church by simony) receive from them no power at all, prima quaestio tertia, Ea quae, since such a man is considered a thief, de electione, Dudum, secunda. The teachers note the same in cap. Per tuas, 2, de simonia. If, however, he is received from a non-simoniac but simoniacally, the recipient lacks the power, altogether as if he had received it from a simoniac, as above; and a man who confers simoniacally is suspended for three years from conferring, as far as himself alone is concerned, if the matter is hidden, de simonia, cap. penultimo. If, however, we are speaking of a simoniac in a benefice, in an ecclesiastical title, whose concern in the matter at hand is towards God, that is, the divine office, then however notorious he is, so long as he is tolerated, he is suspended directly as far as himself is concerned, and indirectly as far as others are concerned, for the same reason as above. In canon law, baptism and the body of Christ are excepted, since they are conferred by simoniacs in a time of necessity, Dist. 32, Ad hoc. If, however, what concerns others is in question, this is twofold: either we speak of spiritual acts, such as excommunicating, absolving, conferring benefices, and so on, or we speak of temporal matters, such as buying, giving, alienating, and similar acts in temporal affairs. In the first way, since such spiritual acts cannot be validly and effectively exercised, nor exercised in the special power of God, or of the Holy Spirit, as in prima quaestio prima, Sic populus, with many following, such a simoniac in a benefice, since he does not have a lawful title, consequently lacks that spiritual power which is given to a man in a lawful title. Hence such a man has no power in these spiritual matters, and he is said to be suspended not only as far as himself is concerned, but also as far as others are concerned; and this holds whether he is hidden or manifest, whether tolerated by the Church or not. For such toleration does not give him a right to exercise such things, nor does a coloured title or the common opinion of men, since these are not exercised except as has been said, because God does not regard the opinions of men, since all things are clear to him: prima quaestio prima, Spiritus sanctus; Dist. 32, Erubescant; quaestio 34, tertia, Deus. And the opinion of Hostiensis and Goffredus, mentioned above, holds here. But if we are speaking of a simoniac in a benefice as regards temporal matters, or even as regards purely civil acts, such as judging, managing, and so on, then I say that that coloured title and the common opinion supporting it validate everything that is done, so long as such a man is tolerated by the Church, although by meddling he sins, De electione, Nihil est, and note de restitutione spoliatorum, In litteris. And so he is suspended only as far as himself is concerned, from exercising such things, but not as far as others are concerned. And so the opinion of Innocent, John Andreae, and the others who follow them holds. And public utility brings it about that what is done by such a putative judge or prelate is valid, just as we say of a hidden excommunicate, according to what is noted in cap. Exceptionem, de exceptionibus, etc.; ad probandum, de sententia et re iudicata. It is certain, however, that if a suspended man exercises those things which pertain to office by reason of his office and accompany the office, such as excommunicating, absolving, conferring benefices, or the exercise of orders, and so on, they are void by the law itself, de consuetudine, Cum dilectus, and there John Andreae fully discusses it; de excessibus praelatorum, cap. ultimo; and in cap. Cum inter, de sententia et re iudicata, libro sexto. Hence the teachers commonly determine that orders must in no way be received from such men, since they cannot give the power of orders, prima quaestio prima, Reperiuntur, and in c. Tanta, de simonia. Indeed, rather, such a man ought to bear excommunication; on this see the Gloss, and also Innocent on c. Per tuas, 2, de simonia. It is also proved in c. Inquisitioni, de sententia et re iudicata. Moreover, it is a common rule in canon law that a man who, while suspended, meddles with divine services and ministers in his orders as before, becomes irregular, causa 2, quaestio 3, Si quis episcopus, according to Innocent, and in c. Nisi cum pridem, de renunciatione; de sententia et re iudicata, Cum aeterni; and de sententia et re iudicata, cap. 1, and cap. Is qui, libro sexto, as John Andreae explains.

units.la: PET. Praedictis videntur expresse noua iura obuiare, quibus dicitur, quod quotiescunque sententia, &c. fertur à iure vel ab homine, episcopi non intelliguntur suspensi, nisi specialiter exprimantur: vt in c. si compromissorias. § porro. de elect. & in capitul. quia periculosum. de sentent. ex lib. 6.
units.tr: PET. The foregoing seem clearly to be opposed by the new laws, which say that whenever a sentence is pronounced by law or by a man, bishops are not understood to be suspended unless this is expressly stated, as in c. si compromissorias. § porro. de elect. & in capitul. quia periculosum. de sentent. ex lib. 6.

units.la: PAVL. Iura praemissa locum sibi vendicant in suspensionibus latis per modum sententiae, cum verbo Suspendimus, &c. ab alicuius virtutis exercitio, vel actu: qua suspensione sublata, vel relaxata, nulli repugnat exercere talem actum, qualiter non est in simoniaco: ex eo, quia quantumcunque tolleretur per praelatum suspensio, & ageretur poenitentia quantacunque, perseuerante illo in beneficio per simoniam acquisito, semper impeditur executio, per c. nisi cum pridem. §. in tua. de renunc. & in c. inquisit. de accu. cum similibus. Praeterea c. quia periculosum, &c. praesupponit executionem Pontificalis officii in episcopis, à qua non debent suspendi, nisi exprimatur in fauorem Pontificalis officii, & etiā subditorum. Illi autem qui quaerunt titulos episcopales per simoniam, frequenter non sunt episcopi, sed inferiores praelati, vel canonici: igitur iura non obstant. Episcopus enim iam consecratus, eo ipso quod per simoniam aliquam sedem episcopalem, vel archiepiscopalem, seu patriarchalem, &c. nanciscitur, posito quod non esset suspensus per aliquam sententiam canonis, vel hominis, nihilominus ipsa notorietate facto capitali infamis: & per consequens, irregularis episcopus non est pro quolibet capitali crimine deponendus de iure communi: vt in c. si quis episcopus. 50. Et licet quodlibet tale infamat, vt patet sext. quaestion. prim. infames. &c. omnis. tert. quaestion. quart. §. porro maxime tamen crimen simoniae non solum in ordine, sed etiam commissum in adipiscenda Pontificali dignitate, &c. quia ista tria parificantur, crimen haeresis, laesae maiestatis, & simonia, dec. quint. quaestion. 3. sane. sane. quilibet enim infamis est irregularis: vt no. Guilhelm in Spec. tit. de leg. §. iuxta vir infamis. & Ioann. An. post eum. idem Ioan. Teu. &c. Et hoc sufficit, siue sit infamia facti, de accu. episcopus. secund. quaest. tert. §. hinc colligitur octauage. prim. distinct. tantu Daniel. Nam talia crimina, ex quibus oritur huiusmodi infamia, seu irregularitas, etiam post peractam poenitentiam, etiam in occultis impediunt ordinis executionem: vt dicunt praedicti Doct. Unde consueuerunt aliqui notare, in cap. ex tenore, & in capitul. vltim. de temp. ordin. aliquas in hac materia regulas. Prima, quod crimen enorme, quantumcunque occultum, etiam post peractam poenitentiam, impedit ordinis executionem, & fortius impedit promouendum, nisi cum tali prius dispensetur, multomagis, si est publicum. Secunda regula: Mortaliter peccans, si est occultus, post peractam poenitentiam, licet administratur, & exequatur, & ad superiora ascendit: quia deleto peccato, deletur sequela peccati. Tertia regula, quod publice mortaliter peccans, hoc non potest propter scandalum subortum, propter quod eget dispensatione superioris: & tamdiu irregularis est, quamdiu cum eo non est dispensatum. Quarta regula est, quod omne peccatum mortale, quantumcunque occultum & leue, ante poenitentiam facit hominem irregularem, quae irregularitas cum sua radice tollitur per poenitentiam. Haec secundum Io. de Lig. Idem no. 50. dist. in summa.
units.tr: PAVL. The laws cited above apply to suspensions pronounced by way of sentence, with the words Suspendimus, etc., from the exercise of some power or act. When such suspension is lifted or relaxed, nothing prevents a man from performing that act. This is not so for a simoniac, because however far the prelate removes the suspension, and however great the penance performed, while he remains in a benefice acquired by simony, the execution of his office is always hindered, by c. nisi cum pridem. §. in tua. de renunc. & in c. inquisit. de accu. and similar passages. Moreover, c. quia periculosum, etc., presupposes the exercise of the pontifical office in bishops, from which they ought not to be suspended unless this is expressed in favour of the pontifical office and also of their subjects. Now those who seek episcopal titles by simony are frequently not bishops but inferior prelates or canons; therefore the laws do not stand in the way. For a bishop already consecrated, by the very fact that he obtains by simony any episcopal, archiepiscopal or patriarchal see, etc., is infamous, even if he was not suspended by any sentence of canon or man, by the very notoriety of a capital crime. Consequently a bishop who is infamous is not, by common law, to be deposed for any capital crime, as in c. si quis episcopus. 50. And although any such crime makes a man infamous, as is clear from sext. quaestion. prim. infames, &c., omnis, tert. quaestion. quart. §. porro, yet the crime of simony especially, whether committed in holy orders or in obtaining pontifical dignity, etc., makes him so, because these three are equated: the crime of heresy, of treason, and of simony, dec. quint. quaestion. 3. sane. For anyone who is infamous is irregular, as noted by Guilhelm in Spec. tit. de leg. §. iuxta vir infamis, and by Ioann. An. after him; the same Ioan. Teu., etc. And this suffices, whether the infamy is of fact, de accu. episcopus, secund. quaest. tert. §. hinc colligitur, octauage. prim. distinct. tantu, Daniel. For such crimes, from which infamy or irregularity of this kind arises, prevent the execution of orders even after penance has been done, and even when they are secret, as the aforementioned Doctors say. Hence some have been accustomed to note, on cap. ex tenore and on the last chapter de temp. ordin., certain rules on this matter. The first is that a heinous crime, however secret, even after penance has been done, prevents the execution of orders, and prevents promotion all the more unless one is first dispensed from it, much more so if it is public. The second rule: one who sins mortally in secret, after penance has been done, may be ordained and exercise his office and ascend to higher orders, because when the sin is blotted out, its consequence is blotted out too. The third rule: one who sins mortally in public cannot do so, on account of the scandal arising, and therefore needs dispensation from the superior, and he remains irregular as long as he has not been dispensed. The fourth rule is that every mortal sin, however secret and slight, makes a man irregular before penance, and this irregularity, together with its root, is removed by penance. These are the rules according to Io. de Lig. The same is noted on dist. 50 in the Summa.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: In quo declaratur, quomodo officiales, vel vicarii episcoporum, vel aliorum intrantium per si- moniam, & familiares, sunt participes simoniae, & omnes alii, qui participant in his quae spectant ad titulum per simoniam acquisitum, sunt in statu damnationis, vt canonici, &c.
units.tr: In which it is explained how the officials or vicars of bishops, or of others who enter by simony, and their household servants, share in the simony, and how all others who take part in matters pertaining to a title acquired through simony are in a state of damnation, such as canons, etc.

units.la: PET. Si comes est mihi ratio, clare inspicio, excommunicationes, institutiones, beneficiorum collationes, absolutiones, &c. in spiritualibus per simoniacos factas, non valere, veluti per suspensos, & stupore magno totus intra me commoueor, tantam caecitatem eorum, episcopatus, abbatias, aut alia beneficia ecclesiastica ambientium, quod tanto studio properant, pro certo non aliud quaerunt, quam se laqueis suspendere aeternae damnationis. Sed quomodo tenendum sit etiam de vicariis, aut officialibus simoniacorum huiusmodi, an excusari valeant, quaeso pro salute plurimorum iam edicas.
units.tr: PETER. If reason is on my side, I clearly see that excommunications, institutions, collations of benefices, absolutions, etc. in spiritual matters made by simoniacs are invalid, just as those made by suspended men are. I am moved within myself with great amazement at the blindness of those who court episcopacies, abbeys, or other ecclesiastical benefices, and who hasten so eagerly toward them, when what they really seek is nothing other than to hang themselves in the snares of eternal damnation. But I beg you, for the salvation of very many, now to declare how we should hold also concerning the vicars or officials of such simoniacs, and whether they can be excused.
