units.la: PAVL. Scriptum est: Nihil dat, quod non habet: & nullus plus iuris in alium transferre potest, quam ipse habeat, vt dicit regula iuris lib. 6. Cum ergo simoniaci nullum ius obtineant in beneficiis per simoniam acquisitis, prout satis superius est ostensum: quomodo executionem transferre possunt in aliquem, a qua & ipsi sunt suspensi? Renera non video, nisi quod ipsorum officiales & vicarii iniustae executioni se immiscent, nec eos a statu damnationis valeo excusare, quandiu persistunt in officiis. Nam tales scientes fore simoniacos, ac verisimiliter praesumentes, eis in crimine simoniae participant.
units.tr: PAUL. It is written: "No one gives what he does not have," and no one can transfer more right to another than he himself has, as the rule of law in Book 6 says. Since therefore simoniacs obtain no right in benefices acquired through simony, as has been sufficiently shown above, how can they transfer the execution of them to anyone, when they themselves are suspended from it? Indeed I see no way, except that their officials and vicars take part in an unjust execution, and I cannot excuse them from the state of damnation as long as they remain in office. For such men, knowing that they are simoniacs, or at least presuming it, share in the crime of simony.

units.la: PET. Ex dictis, vt apparet, hoc inconueniens videtur inferri, quod non simoniacorum huiusmodi officiales, verum tota ipsorum familia, quinimo prelati & canonici illius ecclesiae, qui talem reciperent pro episcopo, praelato aut canonico, & sibi sua communicant consilia & auxilia, ex eodem capite in statu damnationis videntur laborare. Et quod grauius, fateri contra oportet, quod tota illa dioecesis, a qua sui status recipit sustentamenta, simili periculo subiacet: quoniam horum quilibet obediens, participare videtur in crimine simoniae.
units.tr: PETER. From what you have said, it seems to follow, as is evident, that not only the officials of such simoniacs but their whole household, indeed the prelates and canons of that church who receive such a man as bishop, prelate or canon, and who share their counsel and help with him, appear from the same principle to be labouring in a state of damnation. And, what is more serious, I must admit against my will that the whole diocese, from which those men receive their means of support, is subject to a similar danger, since each of them who obeys him seems to share in the crime of simony.

units.la: PAVL. Omnes quippe, Petre, condemnare non audeo: nec etiam omnes valeo excusare. Sed vt breui sermone perstringam, quid in hoc habeat veritas, hanc distinctionem diligenti animo ponderabis. Aut notorium est, puta per confessionem, aut per sententiam iudicis, aut per euidentiam facti, talem esse simoniacum: aut non est notorium. Si primo modo, aut loquimur de familiaribus, aut de aliis. Si primum, dico, si tales familiares eius suum impendunt seruitium in his quae spectant ad huiusmodi titulum per simoniam acquisitum, siue in spiritualibus, induendo eum pontificalibus, portando crucem, aut curuaturam ante eum, & quaecunque in ecclesia vel extra disponendo vel ministrando, vt archiepiscopo vel episcopo, in temporalibus vt procurando bona mensae episcopalis, aut aliud quodcunque officium, vel seruitium in sua curia exercendo: omnes tales peccant mortaliter, quia participant in crimine simoniae criminoso. Secus est, si procurarent sua bona patrimonialia sibi, vel in alio honesto seruitio deseruirent, quod non esset ratione simoniaci tituli. Si autem loquimur de aliis extra suam familiam, hoc dicunt, aut tales sunt personae, quarum requiritur consilium, aut auxilium actiue seu cooperatiue ad aliquid faciendum, quod incumbit ratione huiusmodi beneficii seu tituli, sicut sunt praelati, & canonici ecclesiae, & alii quorum interdum requiratur consensus, interdum consilium, interdum auxilium reale, & tales omnes quotiescunq; dederint consilium vt consilium, aut talem pro episcopo, praelato, aut canonico receperint, siue etiam ab eis illa susceperint quae ratione huiusmodi tituli conferuntur, vt plebanias, & alia iura, beneficia ecclesiastica, aut auctoritatem audiendi confessiones, aut licentiam praedicandi, & similia, sine dubio participes sunt simoniae. Si autem sunt personae inferioris status, secus est: quia non actiue, sed potius passiue se habent ad huiusmodi simoniacum sustinendum, quorum resistentia nullum effectum faceret. Hoc verum est, si non recipiant ab eo beneficia, & similia, quia iam hoc facto in vitium eius consentirent. Excipio tamen articulum necessinecessitatis, in quo licet baptismum & corpus Christi à talibus recipere: vt in capitul. ad hoc vero trigesim. secund. distinction. §. porro. Ratio pro praedictis est haec. Quandocunque aliquid prohibetur, prohibentur omnia quae sequuntur ex illo. de consti. nam concupiscentia.
units.tr: PAUL. Indeed, Peter, I dare not condemn all of them, nor can I excuse all of them. But to set out briefly what the truth holds in this matter, you will weigh the following distinction with a careful mind. Either such a man is notoriously a simoniac, for example by confession, by the sentence of a judge, or by the evident fact; or he is not notorious. If the first, then we speak either of household servants or of others. If of the household, I say that if such servants render their service in those matters which pertain to a title acquired through simony, whether in spiritual things (by dressing him in pontifical vestments, carrying the cross, or bowing before him, and by arranging or administering whatever in the church or outside it, as for an archbishop or bishop), or in temporal things (by managing the goods of the episcopal table, or by exercising any other office or service in his court), all such men sin mortally, because they share in the grave crime of simony. It is otherwise if they manage their own patrimonial goods or serve in some other honest employment, which would not be on account of the simoniacal title. If, however, we speak of others outside his household, these are either persons whose counsel or active or cooperative help is required for doing something which belongs to this benefice or title, such as prelates and canons of the church and others whose consent, counsel or real help is sometimes required; and all such persons, whenever they have given counsel as counsel, or have received such a man as bishop, prelate or canon, or have even accepted from him those things which are conferred by reason of this title, such as parishes and other rights, ecclesiastical benefices, or the authority to hear confessions, or permission to preach and the like, are without doubt sharers in the simony. If, however, they are persons of inferior rank, it is otherwise, because they do not stand in an active but rather a passive relation to sustaining such a simoniac, and their resistance would have no effect. This holds true if they do not receive benefices or the like from him, for by that very act they would consent to his fault. I except, however, the article of necessity, in which it is lawful to receive baptism and the body of Christ from such men, as in the chapter "ad hoc vero," 32nd distinction, §. "porro." The reason for what has been said is this: whenever something is forbidden, all that follows from it is forbidden. de consti. nam concupiscentia.

units.la: Cum ergo prohibita est emptio & venditio beneficii ecclesiastici iure divino, vt inferius apparebit, prohibita est consequenter illius empti executio, & per consequens, non potest dare bont fidia, nec dispensare sacramenta. Si ergo aliquis spontanee recipit à tali aliquid illorum, iam consentit in id quod est illi prohibitum: & per consequens, est particeps peccati ipsius. Si vero crimen ipsius non est notorium, sed solum manifestum, siue famosum, ante pene occultum, inter quae, quoad hoc non facio differentiam: quae consistit, quando est publica fama, quod talis sit simoniacus, non tamen est euidens factum, sed nec notorium omnibus, aut maiori parti, sed solum paucis, vel etiam si non est fama: Et tunc aut loquimur de ipsis paucis scientibus, aut de illis non scientibus, sed solum credentibus. Si primum, aut illi scientes possunt hoc iudiciali iter conuincere legitime, aut non. Si primum, & hoc tunc potius debuerunt facere circa confirmationem, vel prouisionem, si fuerunt praesentes, per cap. constitutus. de appellat. cum similibus. Si non fuerunt praesentes, tunc circa ipsius receptionem debuerunt excipere, & ipsius possessionis apprehensionem elidere, per cap. accedens. de accusat. Sed cum ista facere neglexerunt, in suum & ecclesiae dispendium: verum, quia
units.tr: Since therefore the buying and selling of an ecclesiastical benefice is forbidden by divine law, as will appear below, the execution of the one who bought it is consequently forbidden too, and so he cannot give good faith [i.e. valid guarantee] or dispense the sacraments. If therefore anyone willingly receives any of these things from such a man, he already consents to what is forbidden to him, and consequently he is a partaker in his sin. If, however, the crime is not notorious but only manifest or infamous (I make no difference between these in this respect), which consists in this, that there is public report that such a man is a simoniac, but there is no evident fact, nor is it notorious to all or to the greater part, but only to a few, or even if there is no report at all; then we speak either of those few who know, or of those who do not know but only believe. If the first, either those who know can legitimately prove it in a judicial way, or they cannot. If they can, they ought rather to have done this at the confirmation or provision, if they were present, according to cap. constitutus. de appellat. and similar passages. If they were not present, then at the reception they ought to have objected, and to have blocked his taking possession, according to cap. accedens. de accusat. But since they neglected to do these things, to their own loss and to the loss of the church: indeed, because

units.la: Turpius eiicitur quam non suscipitur hospes.
units.tr: It is more disgraceful to be cast out than to be not received as a guest.

units.la: nihilominus non debent dormire in hoc, sed pro amotione sui laborare.
units.tr: Nevertheless they must not sleep on this, but must labour to remove him themselves.

units.la: PET. Graviter per hanc distinctionem me inuoluis. Qua fronte pro amotione huius personae apud eum laborandum videtur, qui hoc modo illum voluit promouere? Dic ergo in hoc consultius, aut etiam quid executoribus, vel etiam, subexecutoribus exorbitantium literarum, scientibus, aut etiam canonicis, vel capellanis esset consulendum, vt damnationis euaderent labyrinthum, quibus scribitur vt tali prouideant, vel talem recipiant in praelatum, &c.
units.tr: PET. You entangle me badly with this distinction. How can it be right to labour for the removal of this person from the one who promoted him in this way? So tell me, more fully, what should be advised to the executors and sub-executors of the exorbitant letters, who know the facts, or to the canons or chaplains, so that they may escape the labyrinth of damnation, to whom it is written that they should provide for such a man, or receive such a man as prelate, etc.

units.la: PAVL. Aestimo, quod ex praemissis posses edoceri. Nam cum simonia est lege diuina prohibita, prohibentur omnia per quae possit ad ipsius effectum peruenire: vt sunt, receptio & prouisio per regulam iuris, cum quid. De re. iur. libro sexto. unde ex quo principale, scilicet prouisio nulla est, vt supra, nec accessorium, scilicet receptio, aut recepti processuum fulminatio, non est, per regulam accessorium, libro sexto. Et talis processuum fulminatio non est diuina ecclesiae volenti formidanda, scilicet in priuato propter scandalum euitandum, dummodo constet de ipsius simoniaca prouisione. In quo casu quilibet praedictorum potius deberet excommunicationis sententiam sustinere, quam vtique coelestis curia non approbat, si non essent ad obuiandum alia remedia, quam sic prouidendo vel recipiendo talibus Papae obedire, probatur de rest. spo. literas. de sent. exco. inquisit. & ibidem etiam per Innoc. &c.
units.tr: PAUL. I think you could be taught this from what has been said. For since simony is forbidden by divine law, everything by which its effect could be reached is forbidden too, such as reception and provision, by the rule of law cum quid. De re. iur. libro sexto. Hence, since the principal thing, namely the provision, is null, as above, and the accessory, namely the reception or the thundering of the processes of the one received, is not valid, by the rule accessorium, libro sexto. Such a thundering of processes is not something the divine Church, wishing it, should fear, namely in private, to avoid scandal, provided it is established concerning the simoniacal provision itself. In that case each of the aforesaid persons ought rather to bear the sentence of excommunication, which the heavenly court in any case does not approve, if there were no other remedies to avoid it than by providing or receiving in this way and obeying such Papal commands. This is proved by de rest. spo. literas. de sent. exco. inquisit. and there also by Innocent, etc.

units.la: PET. Et si quispiam, vel alicuius viduatae ecclesiae capellanum postulanti se recipi; obiiceret vitium simoniae, & per consequens ex hoc contractam irregularitatem & infamiam, & ob hoc causa huiusmodi ad curiam deueniret, nonne Papa de suae potestatis plenitudine in eo haec omnia posset extinguere, & totaliter abolere? quo facto, obtineret etiam intentum.
units.tr: PET. And if someone, or the chaplain of some vacant church, objecting the vice of simony to one who asks to be received, and on this account bringing the matter to the curia, would not the Pope, from the fullness of his power, be able to extinguish all these things in him and abolish them entirely? Once this is done, he would also obtain his aim.

units.la: PAVL. Hunc casum, Petre, in facto intellexi viros aliquius ecclesiae formidasse. Sed ignorantia iuris tibi, Petre, in hoc dubium, sicut & illis incussit hunc timorem. Clare namque in hoc iura videntur contradicere, sollicite intuenti, cum talis nullo modo veram posset agere poenitentiam in beneficio sic obtento, vt supra est ostensum. Et post quantamcunque poenitentiam, non solum impeditur beneficii retentio, sed & ordinis executio, de accusation. inquisitionis. Imo si diceretur, quod talis purgatio simoniace non procedit eodem fonte, seu causa, qua prouisio cessit: sed Papa rationabiliter ad dispensandum mouebatur, & ad purgandum priora. Respondeo, quod iuris praesumptio est in contrarium, & de iure, quae contrariam sibi non recipit probationem: quoniam nec probari hoc posset. Simile de spon. Isqui.
units.tr: PAUL. Petrus, I have understood this case, as it stands in fact, to be what the men of a certain church feared. But ignorance of the law, Petrus, has raised this doubt in you, just as it struck this fear into them. For clearly the laws seem to contradict each other in this matter, to one who looks at it carefully, since such a man can in no way truly perform repentance while holding the benefice so obtained, as has been shown above. And after whatever penance, not only is the retention of the benefice prevented, but also the exercise of the order, de accusation. inquisitionis. Indeed, even if it were said that such a purgation of simony does not proceed from the same source or cause from which the provision came, but that the Pope was reasonably moved to dispense and to purge the earlier things, I answer that there is a presumption of law to the contrary, and one of law, which does not admit contrary proof, since this could not be proved in any case. Similar is de spon. Isqui.

units.la: PET. Nonne minus malum esset, Papae in talibus obedire, quam excommunicationem, inhabilitationem, praeuaricationem beneficiorum, &c. fortasse ab eodem sustinere?
units.tr: PET. Would it not be the lesser evil to obey the Pope in such matters, rather than to suffer from him, perhaps, excommunication, disqualification, deprivation of benefices, etc.?

units.la: PAVL. Probabiliter & scholastice dici posset, quod nec excommunicatio Papae, &c. teneret in hoc casu. Et quamuis ex iusta causa lata de iure teneat, si tamen intolerabilem errorem contineat, aut falsitatem causae manifestam, non teneret per ea quae leguntur & notantur in c. per tuas. & in c. satis. de sent. exco. & c. ti. venerabilibus pe. lib. 6.
units.tr: PAUL. It could be said probably and in the manner of the schoolmen that neither the excommunication of the Pope, etc., would hold in this case. And although a sentence pronounced for a just cause holds by law, yet if it contains an intolerable error, or a manifest falsity of cause, it would not hold, according to what is read and noted in c. per tuas. & in c. satis. de sent. exco. & c. ti. venerabilibus pe. lib. 6.

units.la: PET. Redeundo ad propositum tuae distinctionis, dic de illis qui sciunt aliquem esse simoniacum, sed conuincere non valent liquide, quid iuris sit.
units.tr: PET. Returning to the point of your distinction, tell me about those who know someone to be a simoniac, but cannot clearly convict him, and what the law is for them.

units.la: PAVL. De ipsis loqui possumus dupliciter, secundum quod tales ipsis simoniacis contingit dupliciter participare, aut enim participant eis in talibus ad titulum per simoniam acquisitum spectantibus, in quibus de necessitate iuris compelluntur, &c. aut loquimur de participatione in voluntariis nobis.
units.tr: PAUL. We can speak of them in two ways, according to the two ways in which such people may come to share in the simoniacs' acts: either they share in those matters pertaining to the title acquired through simony, in which they are compelled by necessity of law, etc., or we speak of participation in things that are voluntary for us.

units.la: Exemplum primi, vt sibi consulere in capitulo requirenti auxilium praebere, & iniunctum mandatum ab eo recipere, & executioni mandare, vel etiam secum cantare, &c. & tunc, aut ista fieri madat in priuato, & tunc enodatur sine ratio vel alio bono modo, quia qui scit cum habere non ingressu canonicu, plus certiorari non debet. Si aut hoc fit coram aliis, & non occurrit aptus modus excusandi se, aut forte ab illo non recipitur: obediendum est sibi, quadiu toleratur ab ecclesia n.q. in eorum 15.qu.vlt. c.pl. vel q fecit augo. auctoritate iuris, non peccat, 24.q. 4. qui peccat. Illa autem iuris necessitas non excusat eos qui scientes, factum legitime conuincere valentes, non resistunt, quia sevoluntarie tali necessitati submiserunt. Si autem loquimur de his quae nobis sunt voluntaria, vtputa tali simoniaco seruire, vt tali promoto, aut ab eo beneficia seu prebendas aut decimas recipere, aut aliqua huiusmodi, nullo modo licet, quia videremur sic illius turpitudinem facto approbare, vt supra. Idem dicas de illi per omnia, quia licet non habent certam scientiam, habent tamen probabilem credendi causam ex verisimilibus coniecturis, seu suspitionem vehementem. Hoc probatur per c. inquisitioni, de sent. excom. cum si. Causa probabilis credendi colligitur ex qualitate personae promotae, dispositione curiae, & publica fama, &c. Et haec pro primo tractatu sufficiant, Domino adiuuante.
units.tr: An example of the first: to advise him in chapter, to give help to one who asks, to receive a mandate imposed by him and carry it out, or even to sing with him, etc. In that case, if this is ordered to be done in private, it is dealt with without argument or some other good means, because one who knows him to have entered not canonically ought not to be more fully informed. But if this is done before others, and no suitable way of excusing oneself occurs, or perhaps he is not received by him, one must obey him as long as the Church tolerates it n.q. in eorum 15.qu.vlt. c.pl. or, one who acts under the authority of law does not sin, 24.q. 4. qui peccat. That necessity of law, however, does not excuse those who, knowing the fact and able to convict it lawfully, do not resist, because they voluntarily submitted to such necessity. But if we speak of those things that are voluntary for us, for instance to serve such a simoniac so that he may be promoted, or to receive from him benefices or prebends or tithes, or anything of this kind, it is in no way permitted, because we would seem thereby to approve his baseness by our deed, as above. Say the same of one in all respects, because although they do not have certain knowledge, they nevertheless have a probable cause for believing from likely conjectures, or a strong suspicion. This is proved by c. inquisitioni, de sent. excom. with the sign. A probable cause for believing is gathered from the quality of the person promoted, the disposition of the curia, and public report, etc. And let these things suffice for the first treatise, the Lord helping.

units.la: SECVNDA PARS.
units.tr: The Second Part.

units.la: Ars secunda huius tractatus, in qua multipliciter destruuntur scripta & dicta, erroneae & minus catholicae Sorbonae, cum praesertim in iure canonico, quae videntur dare causam seu occasionem multis erroribus in Dei ecclesia, & praesertim circa simoniam. Et continet quinque capitula. In primo capitulo arguitur, quod Papa possit recipere pecuniam pro beneficiis ecclesiasticis, & plura iura ad hoc, & dicta doctorum adducuntur quae dicta damnantur, & ad iura respondetur. In secundo capitulo, auctoritatibus sacrae Scripturae reprobatur praedictorum doctorum sententia: & probatur, quod Papa non potest recipere pecuniam in aliquo casu pro beneficiis, & quod hoc etiam quoad Papam, est realis simonia. In tertio capitulo probatur id, quod immediate supra ex iure canonico auctoritate generalis concilii ponitur. In quarto capitulo conuincitur idem, quod immediate supra rationibus multipliciter, dato quod nulla esset lex scripta. In quinto capitulo destruitur communis distinctio de simoniacis quia prohibitis, & de prohibitis, quia simoniacis, ex iure canonico. Secundo declaratur, quod nulla sunt simoniaca secundum suam naturam, ad intentionem illorum. Item quod nulla sunt simoniaca, quia prohibita, sed sunt ideo lege diuina & etiam canonica prohibita, quia peccata simoniaca.
units.tr: The second article of this treatise, in which in many ways the writings and sayings of the Sorbonne, erroneous and less than Catholic, are destroyed, especially in canon law, which seem to give cause or occasion to many errors in the Church of God, and especially concerning simony. It contains five chapters. In the first chapter it is argued that the Pope can receive money for ecclesiastical benefices; several laws are adduced for this, and the sayings of the teachers that are cited are condemned, and the laws are answered. In the second chapter, by the authority of holy Scripture, the opinion of the aforesaid teachers is refuted, and it is proved that the Pope cannot receive money in any case for benefices, and that this, even as regards the Pope, is real simony. In the third chapter, what was set down immediately above from canon law is proved by the authority of a general council. In the fourth chapter the same point as immediately above is demonstrated in many ways by reasons, even supposing there were no written law. In the fifth chapter the common distinction concerning simoniacal things because forbidden, and forbidden things because simoniacal, is destroyed from canon law. Secondly, it is declared that nothing is simoniacal according to its own nature, as far as those intentions go. Likewise, that nothing is simoniacal merely because it is forbidden, but is therefore forbidden by divine law and also by canon law because it is a simoniacal sin.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CAP. I.

units.la: In quo arguitur, quod Papa possit recipere pecuniam pro beneficiis ecclesiasticis: & plura iura & dicta doctorum ad hoc adducuntur, quae dicta damnantur, & iuribus respondetur.
units.tr: In which it is argued that the Pope may receive money for ecclesiastical benefices. Several laws and sayings of the teachers are adduced for this; the sayings are condemned and the laws are answered.

units.la: PET. Non me quaeso relinquas in ambiguo. Nam scripturae, rationes, & iura superius adducta, meam inuincibilem mentem ligant. Econtra video tot & tantos scribentes in iure canonico, & si iniustas, simoniae vitium in Romana curia excusare. Si tibi contra tantam doctorum multitudinem adhaesero, eos videbor arguere de errore, quod non licet secundum honestatem. Si contrarium fecero, praemisso non potero suffragari.
units.tr: PET. I beg you, do not leave me in doubt. The Scriptures, the reasons and the laws cited above bind my unconquered mind. On the other hand, I see so many and such great writers in canon law who, if I am not mistaken, excuse the vice of simony in the Roman court. If I cling to so great a multitude of teachers, I shall seem to accuse them of error, which propriety does not allow. If I take the opposite view, I shall not be able to support it on the premises stated.

units.la: PAVL. Conferantur quaestiones contrariae adinuicem, scripturaeque canonicae debite ponderentur: & quid in hoc veritas habeat, vtique elucescet, vel forte videbitur, si fumus diuersi tantummodo, non aduersi.
units.tr: PAUL. Let the opposing questions be set side by side, and let the canonical Scriptures be weighed carefully. Then what truth holds in this will surely shine forth, or perhaps it will appear that the smoke is only of different kinds, not opposed to one another.

units.la: PET. En primum & maximum fidei meae argumentum. Nam Bernhard. in Glossa or. de offic. dele. in cap. experte, in gloss. 2. ponit hanc communissimam distinctionem simoniae, dicens, quod quaedam sunt simoniaca, quia prohibita, scilicet constitutione ecclesiae. Quaedam prohibita, quia simoniaca de sui natura, quae scilicet Novo & Veteri Testamento prohibita sunt: vt, emere vel vendere sacramenta. Hanc distinctionem repetit de pact. cum pridem. in glossa super v. illuc pactionis. de iureiur. & si Christus. in gloss. quedam, & in aliis. de simon. Ad idem est Gloss. or. in cap. Saluator. prim. quaestion. tert. super 5. iudicem. Hanc distinctionem recipiunt communiter doctores, scribentes in iure canonico. Et summistae, Ray. VVilh. Ioann. in Summa de casibus, super vltim. Bart. Pisanus, Hosti. &c. Simoniaca, quia prohibita dicuntur, quae solum sunt spiritualia ex constitutione ecclesiae, quae a natura non fuerunt spiritualia, quia non fuerunt sicut tituli beneficiorum ecclesiasticorum, & dicuntur, talia iure positiuo inducta: quia tempore Apostolorum non fuerunt decanatus, archidiaconatus, & caetera. Sic similiter dicunt, ea vendere vel emere est simonia: eo quia constitutione ecclesiae, emptio vel venditio talium est prohibita: Et ideo dicuntur simoniaca, quia prohibita, & ideo dicit Bernhard. in cap. cum pridem, praeallegato, quod excusat auctoritas Papae, qui habet in talibus dispensare.
units.tr: PET. Here is my first and greatest argument. Bernhard, in the Gloss on the decretal Experte, on the office of the delegate, gloss 2, lays down this most common distinction of simony. He says that some things are simoniacal because they are prohibited, namely by the constitution of the Church. Others are prohibited because they are simoniacal by their own nature, being forbidden by both the New and the Old Testament, such as buying or selling the sacraments. He repeats this distinction in the gloss on the decretal Pactum cum pridem, on the word illuc pactionis, on the oath; in the gloss quaedam on Si Christus; and in others, de simonia. The Gloss on the decretal Salvator says the same thing, in the first question, third, on the fifth judge. Writers on canon law commonly accept this distinction, and so do the summists: Raymond, William, John in the Summa de casibus, on the last..., Bartholomew of Pisa, Hostiensis and others. Those things are called simoniacal because prohibited which are spiritual only by the constitution of the Church and were not spiritual by nature. They are not like the titles of ecclesiastical benefices, and such things are said to be introduced by positive law, since in the time of the Apostles there were no deaneries, archdeaconries and the rest. Similarly, they say that buying or selling such things is simony, because the constitution of the Church forbids the buying or selling of them. Therefore they are called simoniacal because prohibited. Bernhard says so in the chapter Cum pridem, cited above, and he adds that the authority of the Pope excuses the act, since the Pope has power to dispense in such matters.

units.la: PAVL. O Petre, quantam animarum multitudinem cateruatim transmisit, & transmittit ad infernum, haec superstitialis & damnanda distinctio, quae multis est occasio, & viam aperit ad ruinam damnationis aeternae: solus nouit, qui nihil ignorat. Quantum autem erroris aut veritatis habeat, inserius apparebit.
units.tr: PAUL. O Peter, how many multitudes of souls this superstitious and damnable distinction has driven headlong into hell, and still drives! It is an occasion for many and opens the way to the ruin of eternal damnation. Only he knows this who is ignorant of nothing. How much error or truth it contains will appear below.

units.la: PET. Et qua temeritatis audacia asseris, omnes homines a veritate deuiasse: cum iura plura videantur fouere praemissam distinctionem, etiam ipsius fautoribus suffragari? Quis enim dubitat, titulos ecclesiasticos iure positiuo inductos? Nam solus Papa facit dignitates, instituit praelatos latos, &c. vigef. secund. distinction. omnis. & in cap. perlectis. vigesim. quint. distinction. Sed Papa recipit pecuniam pro talibus, & voluntas Papæ habetur pro iure: Institut. de iur. naturali. §. sed quod principi. vndecim. quæstion. tert. cuncta per mundum, & capit. per principalem. Vnde sola voluntate tacita vel expressa tollitur, vt in Cle. quoniam. immuni. ecclesiastic. de concess. præben. Vnde propoluerunt, de cog. spi. capitulo primo, libro sexto. item, Si doctor vel magister in vrbe Romana doceat, recipiendo pro doctrina immunitatem habeat, siue percipiat salarium, siue non, vt ff. de excusation. tu. in l. graca si dugs. §. amplius. & ideo dixit Goff. & alii, quod simonia non habet locum in curia Romana, sicut nec lex Iulia de ambitu, ff. ad l. Iuliam de ambitu. l. vna.
units.tr: PET. With what rash boldness do you assert that all men have strayed from the truth, when many laws seem to favour the aforesaid distinction and even to support its champions? For who doubts that ecclesiastical titles are introduced by positive law? The Pope alone makes dignities and appoints prelates, as in the twenty-second distinction, Omnis, and in the chapter Perlectis, twenty-fifth distinction. Yet the Pope receives money for such things, and the will of the Pope is held as law: Institutes on natural law, sed quod principi; the eleventh question, third, cuncta per mundum; and the chapter Per principalem. Hence a thing is removed by the sole will of the Pope, tacit or express, as in the Clementine Quoniam immunes ecclesiasticae on the grant of prebends; hence Propositum est, on knowledge of the spirit, first chapter, book six. Likewise, if a teacher or master teaches in the city of Rome, he has immunity for his teaching, whether he takes a salary or not, as in the Digest, de excusationibus tutorum, the law Graeca, si quis, §amplius. And therefore Goffredus and others said that simony has no place in the Roman court, just as the Julian law on bribery does not apply there, Digest, ad legem Iuliam de ambitu, law una.

units.la: PAVL. Concordat namque in hoc famosus canonista Hosti. in c.1. ne prala. vi. su. sub annuo censu, &c. Notando dicebat, quod in simoniacis, quia prohibitis, auctoritas & scientia Papæ excusat vitium, per Gloss. 2. c. ex parte. de ossi. dele. cum concor. Idem repetit in Summa e. tit. ne prala. vi. su. §. in summa, dicens, quod l. Iulia. ff. de ambitu, quæ punit eum qui se eligi facit ad aliquam dignitatem, seu administrationem, & in ciuitate Romana non vendicat sibi locum: quia princeps ibi eligit magistratum, qui solutus est lege. Ideo Io. An. post Goff. & Hosti. notauit in c. 1. de sim. & communiter alii dicunt ibidem, quod Papa potest vendere titulum ecclesiasticum, & omnes quotquot sunt in hoc grauissimo errore concurrentes, habent refugium ad dictum capit. ex parte prim. de off. dele. & ad dictam l. de ambitu. & ibi suas hauriunt probationes tales quales. Sed salua tot & tantorum reuerentia, vuas acerbas comederunt, secundum sententiam beati Hieronymi super Esaiam, Scripturas sacras aliter intelligentes quam veritas habet, & 37. distinction. vino inebriantur. Quantis autem malis, & haereticis delramentis paraverunt ingressum hæc incauta scripta, & erronea, cotidie experimur tam in capitibus, quam in membris: cum tamen leges ciuiles adducta pro contrario, & quæcunque similes, loquantur de dignitatibus & officiis secularibus. Sicut enim multum inter se differunt spirituales res, & temporales: sic etiam inter se potestates, dignitates, & officia actiura spiritualia & seculania: vt in cap. solita. dema. & obedient. Et ergo ab vno eorum ad aliud, non oportet semper valere argumentum. Nam sicut res temporales, in quantum visui nostro deseruiunt, sunt in potestate nostra, & ideo vendi & emi possunt, sic similiter iura & officia & dignitates ordinatae ad gubernationem, seu dispensationem, quandocunque talium naturæ non repugnat quod vendantur, sed soli constitutioni principis. Sed contrarium est: Spiritualia quæ in nullius dominio sunt, nisi solius Dei, sicut sunt virtutes spirituales, quarum naturæ repugnat venditio, prim. quæstion. prim. gratiay cum nullum precium est, quo æstimari possunt, sic etiam iura, officia, dignitates, quæ disponunt, vel inquantum verantur obiective circa talia, sunt eiusdem naturæ, vel sunt ipsæmet virtutes spirituales, imo quilibet titulus ecclesiasticus est quædam spiritualis potestas, seu virtus, ad exercendum aliquos actus spirituales.
units.tr: PAUL. The famous canonist Hostiensis agrees with this in the chapter Ne prelati vices suas, sub annuo censu, and so on. Commenting there, he said that in simoniacal matters, which are prohibited, the authority and knowledge of the Pope excuse the vice, citing the Gloss 2 on the chapter Ex parte, de officio delegati, with the concordance. He repeats this in his Summa under the same title, Ne prelati vices suas, §in summa, saying that the Julian law, Digest de ambitu, which punishes one who has himself put forward for election to any dignity or office, does not claim its place in the city of Rome, because the prince there elects the magistrate, who is released from the law. Therefore John Andreae, following Goffredus and Hostiensis, noted on chapter 1, de simonia, and others commonly say in the same place that the Pope can sell an ecclesiastical title. All who are caught up in this most grave error take refuge in the said chapter Ex parte, first, de officio delegati, and in the said law de ambitu, and draw from them their proofs, such as they are. But with all due reverence to so many and such great men, they have eaten sour grapes, according to the saying of blessed Jerome on Isaiah, who understood the holy Scriptures otherwise than the truth has them, and (Dist. 37) they have been made drunk with wine. We daily experience, both in the head and in the members, what great evils and heretical dregs these incautious and erroneous writings have prepared a way for, although the civil laws cited for the contrary, and all like them, speak of secular dignities and offices. For just as spiritual and temporal things differ greatly from one another, so too the powers, dignities and offices that act in spiritual and in secular matters differ among themselves, as in the chapter Solita, de maioritate et obedientia. Therefore it does not always hold that an argument drawn from one applies to the other. For just as temporal things, in so far as they serve our sight, are in our power and so can be bought and sold, so likewise rights, offices and dignities ordained for government or dispensation may be sold, whenever the nature of such things does not oppose their sale, and they depend only on the constitution of the prince. But the contrary holds: spiritual things, which are in no one's dominion but God's alone, such as spiritual virtues, whose nature is opposed to sale (first question, first, gratia), since no price can be set by which they might be valued. So too rights, offices and dignities which dispose of such things, or which are concerned with such things as their object, are of the same nature, or are themselves spiritual virtues. Indeed, every ecclesiastical title is a certain spiritual power or virtue for exercising some spiritual acts.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: In quo auctoritatibus sacræ Theologiæ vel Scripturæ reprobatur prædictorum doctorum sententia, & probatur, quod Papa non potest pecuniam recipere pro beneficiis, & etiam quod quoad Papam est realis simonia.
units.tr: In which, by the authorities of sacred theology or Scripture, the opinion of the aforesaid teachers is refuted, and it is proved that the Pope cannot receive money for benefices, and also that, as regards the Pope, it is real simony.

units.la: PETRVS. Contentor vtique de his, quæ dixisti. Verum si de mentibus simplicium conaris hunc errorem euellere, necesse habes prius curiensibus Romanæ curiæ sufficienter reprobare, & penitus destruere huius propositionis sententiam, in assensu quorundam eorum, aliorum vero in effectu firmiter radicatam, sc. dicentium, quod in simoniacis, quia prohibitis, Papa potest facere, vel etiam dispensare, quod venditio & emptio non sit peccatum.
units.tr: PETER. I am certainly content with what you have said. But if you are trying to root this error out of the minds of simple people, you must first thoroughly refute the Roman curialists and completely destroy the opinion of this proposition, which is firmly rooted in the assent of some of them and in the practice of others, namely those who say that, since simony is forbidden, the Pope can make it, or even dispense, so that buying and selling is not a sin.

units.la: PAVL. Quamuis falsitas dictæ propositionis firmata videatur multis scripturarum auctoritatibus, sanctorum doctorum expositionibus, & canonum institutis: tamen quia scripturæ, & cætera, non expresse Papam nominant, forsan creditur ab errantibus, ipsum etiam sacris legibus non ligari. Igitur dicta falsitas principaliter declaratur penes tria, quæ Papæ habent restringere potestatem, scilicet, lex diuina, ius naturale, quod est lex omni creaturæ rationali indita, & auctoritas totius Ecclesiæ militantis, sanctis Conciliis generalibus, præsertim quatuor principalibus dedicatis scilicet Niceno, Constantinopolitano, Ephesino, & Chalcedonensi, decim. quint. distinction. Canones, &c. sicut. & sequent. Quo ad legem diuinam, patens scriptura est Matthæi decimo, vbi Saluator instruens Apostolos, docuit omnes Apostolici officii successores, dicens: Euntes autem prædicate dicentes, quod appropinquauit regnum cœlorum: infirmos curate, mortuos suscitate, leprosos mundate: Nolite possidere aurum, neque argentum & pecuniam. Et non est dubium, quin secundum expositores, hoc dixerit non solum de expressis in Euangelio, scilicet curatione infirmorum, suscitatione mortuorum, & cætera, sed omnia etiam alia dona sua gratuita, & effectus ipsorum, siue ministerium, eadem ratione includere voluit, sicut quodlibet exercitium potestatis ecclesiasticæ, vel ipsammet potestatem.
units.tr: PAUL. Although the falsity of that proposition seems confirmed by many authorities of Scripture, by the expositions of holy teachers, and by the institutions of the canons, nevertheless, because the Scriptures and the other sources do not expressly name the Pope, perhaps it is believed by those who err that he is not bound even by the sacred laws. Therefore the falsity in question is principally shown by reference to three things which limit the Pope's power: namely, the divine law; the natural law, which is the law implanted in every rational creature; and the authority of the whole militant Church, especially of the holy general Councils dedicated to the four principal ones, namely Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon (Distinction 15, canons, etc., "sicut" and following). As for the divine law, the plain Scripture is Matthew 10, where the Saviour, instructing the Apostles, taught all the successors of the apostolic office, saying: "Going, preach, saying that the kingdom of heaven has drawn near; heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers. Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money." And there is no doubt, according to the expositors, that he said this not only of the things expressed in the Gospel, namely the healing of the sick, the raising of the dead, and the rest, but that by the same reasoning he meant to include all his other gratuitous gifts and their effects, or ministry, just as any exercise of ecclesiastical power, or power itself.

units.la: Quis enim dubitabit, potestatem conferendi beneficia ecclesiastica, & ipsius potestatis actum, vel officium, esse donum a Deo gratis acceptum, dicente Domino: Quodcunque ligaueris super terram, & cætera. & per consequens, gratis donandum, vel dandum? Præterea ad idem, alibi legimus Christum dixisse, Ichan. decim. Qui non intrat per ostium in ouile ouium, sed ascendit aliunde, ille fur est. Iuxta de hoc supra satis dictum est, capitulo septimo, quod hic repetere. Praeterea etiam alibi scribitur, Matthaei vigesimo primo, Marci decimo, Lucae decimo nono. Et cum Iesus venisset Hierosolymam, intrauit in templum Dei, & eiiciebat omnes ementes & vendentes in templo, mensasque numulariorum & cathedras vendentium columbas euertit, & dixit eis: Domus mea domus orationis vocabitur omnibus gentibus, vos autem fecistis eam speluncam latronum. Quo facto Saluator in materiali templo, secundum omnes doctores: verum fortius in spirituali, quod est sibi plus acceptus (quia materiale est propter spirituale, & eadem causa prohibitionis est, quoad templum spirituale, quae ad materiale scilicet) quia domus mea domus orationis, & cetera. Et sicut dicit canon. prim. quaestion. tert. ex multis, exponens haec verba Euangelica dicens, Nolite facere domum Patris mei domum negotiationis: Illud quoque in eodem facto sollicite considera, quod per totum textum sancti Euangelii nunquam legitur, Dominum tanta seueritate, tam distributa censura peccantes corripuisse, cum non solum eloquio increpans, verum etiam facto flagello de funiculis verberans omnes eliminauit de templo: aperte demonstrans, quod tales negociatores non sicut ceteri sunt corripiendi peccatores, sed a templo, id est, a sancta ecclesia longius sunt proiiciendi. Et vltra subiungit: Nam sicut per columbarum venditores illi denotantur, qui sacramenta manus impositione vendere conantur, sic per numularios ecclesiasticii beneficii venditores designantur, qui domum Dei, teste Euangelio speluncam latronum efficiunt, haecibi. Sic etiam beatus Augustinus intelligitur, cuius verba canon. prim. quaestion. tert. Saluator, sibi in auctoritatem adducit.
units.tr: For who will doubt that the power of conferring ecclesiastical benefices, and the act or office of that power itself, is a gift received from God freely, the Lord saying: "Whatever you bind on earth," and so on? And consequently it must be given freely, or be given. Moreover, to the same effect, we read elsewhere that Christ said in John 10: "He who does not enter by the door into the sheepfold of the sheep, but climbs in some other way, is a thief." On this, enough has been said above, in chapter seven, which need not be repeated here. Furthermore, it is also written elsewhere, in Matthew 21, Mark 11 and Luke 19: "And when Jesus had come to Jerusalem, he entered the temple of God, and drove out all who bought and sold in the temple, and overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold doves, and said to them: My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations, but you have made it a den of robbers." By this act the Saviour, according to all the teachers, acted in the material temple; but more strongly in the spiritual one, which is more acceptable to him (because the material exists for the sake of the spiritual, and the same reason for prohibition applies to the spiritual temple as to the material), since "my house is a house of prayer," and so on. And as the canon in Causa 1, question 3, "Ex multis," says, expounding these Gospel words: "Do not make the house of my Father a house of trade." Consider also in the same deed carefully this, that throughout the whole text of the holy Gospel we never read that the Lord rebuked sinners with such severity and such a measured censure, since he not only rebuked them in words but, striking them with a whip made of cords, drove everyone out of the temple, plainly showing that such traders are not to be corrected like other sinners, but cast far away from the temple, that is, from the holy Church. And further it adds: "For just as those who try to sell the sacraments by the laying on of hands are signified by the sellers of doves, so those who sell ecclesiastical benefices are designated by the money-changers, who, as the Gospel witnesses, make the house of God a den of robbers," thus far. So also the blessed Augustine is understood, whose words the canon in Causa 1, question 3, "Salvator," adduces as authority.

units.la: Vbi subiungitur: Pensandum vero est, quapoena multentur, qui iam Deo & ecclesiae sua oblata vendunt, & emunt, si cum flagellis a templo Dei eiecti sunt, qui Deo offerenda vendebant vel emebant. Si Deo offerendorum venditoribus & acceptoribus dictum est, Vos fecistis domum Patris mei domum negotiationis, & speluncam latronum: quid dicetur de ecclesiae iam oblatorum venditoribus, vel emptoribus? Qui ergo audacia excusatores simoniacae haeresis putant se verum dicere, Papam nedum dispensare posse, sed etiam tollere, ut simoniaca quia prohibita, & pro episcopatibus, vel quibuscunque beneficiis ecclesiasticis pecuniam recipere, non video: nisi forte pertinacitatis caecitate, vel caecitatis pertinacia astruant, Christum non potuisse Papae legem ponere: vel quod Papa possit pro suo libito euangelium immutare: vel forsitan sanctos doctores minus benefecisse, dictum Euangelicum exponentes, & ecclesiam Romanam huiusmodi intellectum approbantem, non solum in praedictis canonibus, sed in multis capitulis aliis delirasse.
units.tr: Then it is added: "But we must consider what punishment is due to those who sell and buy things already offered to God and to the Church, if those who sold or bought what was to be offered to God were cast out of the temple of God with whips." If it was said to the sellers and buyers of things to be offered to God, "You have made the house of my Father a house of trade and a den of robbers," what will be said to the sellers or buyers of things already offered to the Church? Those, then, who in their audacity, as defenders of the heresy of simony, think they speak the truth, namely that the Pope can not only dispense but even remove what is simoniacal because it is forbidden, and that he may receive money for bishoprics or any ecclesiastical benefices whatever, I cannot see; unless perhaps by the blindness of obstinacy, or the obstinacy of blindness, they assert that Christ could not lay down a law for the Pope; or that the Pope may change the Gospel at his pleasure; or perhaps that the holy teachers have done ill in expounding the Gospel saying, and that the Roman Church, approving this interpretation, has raved not only in the aforesaid canons but in many other chapters.

units.la: Praeterea nonne etiam in Veteri Testamento legimus, Balaam prophetam huius criminis damnatione reprobatum, quando ad Balach regem Moabitarum proficiscenti, angelus Domini euaginato gladio aduersus eum in via apparuit? Numer. vigesim. secund. Praeterea nonne legimus, Iezi filium Elizaei percussum lepra, eo quod pro effectu doni Dei gratuiti, scilicet sanitate impensa per Elizaeum ipsi Naaman, accepit argentum & vestes? de quo quart. Regum quint. capitulo. Ex quo in veteri lege sic punitum sit hoc genus peccati, quanto magis puniendum est hoc tempore Euangelii, cum sint iam talia dona gratuita magis nota, quam tunc erant?
units.tr: Moreover, do we not also read in the Old Testament that the prophet Balaam was condemned and rebuked for this crime, when, as he set out to Balak king of the Moabites, the angel of the Lord appeared to him on the way with a drawn sword? Numbers 22. Furthermore, do we not read that Gehazi, son of Elisha, was struck with leprosy because, for the effect of God's free gift, namely the health conferred through Elisha upon Naaman himself, he accepted silver and garments? Of this, 2 Kings chapter 5. If this kind of sin was so punished under the old law, how much more ought it to be punished in this age of the Gospel, since such gratuitous gifts are now better known than they were then?

units.la: Praeterea etiam aliud non omittam, nec videatur tibi, quoad hoc genus peccati, aliter de effectu sacramenti ecclesiae, & aliter de titulo beneficiali sentiendum: vtputa tanquam circa secundum, & non primum, valeat dispensari. Allegatur factum Simonis magi, quod nobis in hac materia quotidie adducitur pro exemplo: vt videatur, pro quo beatus Petrus Apostolus tanta maledictione Simoni mago expostulavit. Legitur enim Actuum octau. capitulo: Cum autem vidisset Simon, quia per impositionem manus Apostolorum daretur Spiritus sanctus, obtulit eis pecuniam, dicens: Date mihi hanc potestatem, vt cuicunque impoSuero manus, accipiat Spiritum sanctum. Ex quo constat, quod Simon gratiam non emere voluit gratificantem seu iustificantem, quae datur virtute sacramenti: sed potestatem sacerdotalem, seu episcopalem, quam quilibet successor Apostolorum habet, seu praelatus Ecclesiae, etiam si sit in peccato mortali: & non solum potestatem ordinis sacerdotalis emere voluit, sed etiam iurisdictionis, quae datur in isto titulo, Cuicunque manus imposuero. Et Simon magus non emit hanc potestatem, sed eam emere voluit, & pro ipsa habenda pecuniam obtulit. Quid Apostolus respondit? Pecunia tua tecum sit in perditionem, quoniam existimas donum Dei pecunia possideri. In felle enim amaritudinis & obligationis iniquitatis video te esse.
units.tr: Furthermore, I will not omit another point, nor should it seem to you that, as regards this kind of sin, the effect of the sacrament of the Church is to be judged differently from a benefice title; as if one could dispense with the second but not the first. The deed of Simon the magician is alleged, which is brought forward to us daily in this matter as an example, so that it may be seen for what reason the blessed Apostle Peter rebuked Simon the magician with such a curse. For we read in Acts chapter 8: "When Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the Apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying: Give me also this power, that on whomever I lay my hands, he may receive the Holy Spirit." From this it is clear that Simon did not wish to buy the grace that justifies and sanctifies, which is given by the virtue of the sacrament, but the sacerdotal or episcopal power, which every successor of the Apostles or prelate of the Church has, even if he is in mortal sin; and he wished to buy not only the power of the priestly order but also the jurisdiction, which is given in that title, "on whomever I lay my hands." And Simon the magician did not buy this power, but wished to buy it, and offered money in order to have it. What did the Apostle answer? "May your money perish with you, because you think the gift of God can be possessed with money. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity."

units.la: PET. De his contentus quilibet esse debet intelligens. Verum imperitus canonista, nec sibi probatum reputat, nisi etiam authoritas Canonis adducatur. Quid etiam igitur est sentiendum ex vigore generalium Conciliorum, de quibus praemisisti, in medium iam proponas.
units.tr: PETER. Anyone who understands should be content with these things. But an unskilled canonist does not regard a point as proved unless the authority of a canon is also adduced. What, then, must be thought from the force of the general Councils, of which you spoke before, do you now put forward for consideration?

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: In quo probatur idem quod supra, ex iure Canonico, auctoritate generalis Concilii.
units.tr: In which it is proved, from canon law and by the authority of a general council, the same point as above.

units.la: PAVLVS. Quantum autem ad statuta generalis Concilii, de quibus, & eorum auctoritate, habetur decim. quint. distinctione. Canones, & per totum: haec est quasi omnium doctorum concors sententia, quod Papa non potest tollere, vel dispensare contra ea, quae generalibus quatuor maxime principalibus Conciliis sunt diffinita. Vnde dicit ille foelicissimus Papa Gregor. in c. sicut 100. dist. Sicut sancti Euangelii quatuor libros, sic quatuor Concilia hac suscipere & venerari me fateor, & ipsa tota devotione complectar, ac integerrima approbatione custodio. Quia in his velut in quadrato lapide constructura sancta fidei consurgit, & cuiuslibet vita ac communis actionis norma consistit. Cum itaque dare vel permittere pecuniam pro fructibus primi anni, ut conferatur episcopatus, vel quicunque alter titulus magni vel parui beneficii, vel etiam pro signatura supplicationis, sit in Chalcedonensi & generali Concilio prohibitum, vno de quatuor principalibus Conciliis, quae prohibitio canonizata est, & habetur 1. q. 1. Si quis episcopus: vt ibi habetur in superscriptione ex concilio Chalcedonensi: & probat hoc idem Canon 1. q. 3. Saluator, nisi alioquin. & c. ex multis, & c. peruenit, qui canones ad probandam illicitam pactionem seu mercationem in beneficiis quibuscunque ecclesiasticis, & aliis spiritualibus, referunt se ad dictum Concilium dicti c. si quis. Et ibi in c. ex multis, dicitur, quod haec sententia invenitur in secundo capitulo Chalcedonensis concilii. Et nisi hoc scelus esset fidei canonicae contrarium, non tata execrationis seueritate fuisset a sanctis patribus proscriptum & damnatum, quod etiam haeresis nuncupatur 1. q. 1. Petrus & c. cum omnes, & c. eos qui. In quo dicitur, Tolerabilior est Macedonii & sequacium impia haeresis, qui asserunt Spiritum sanctum creaturam, & seruum Patris & Filii. Isti autem venditores & emptores spiritualium efficiunt Spiritum sanctum seruum suum, quod sic probat: Sicut enim vendens, vendit id quod possidet: sic & emens, emit, volens esse Dominus eius quod emit, &c. Et consequenter ibi probatur, quomodo tales sunt blasphematores Christi, cum illis Iudaeis, dicentibus, In Beelzebub principe daemoniorum eiicit daemonia: Matt. 12. & traditores cum Iuda, qui Christum tradidit: Matth. 26. Quod nisi etiam esset contra statum vniuersalis Ecclesiae, quid putas quod tanta sollicitudine sanctorum patrum fuissent tot solennia Concilia, totque Canones prohibitionis super hoc prodiissent, & sanctorum doctorum (quod ad hoc) tanta copia scripturarum, nec non tot decretales epistolae ad diuersas partes mundi emanassent, vt liquet haec omnia intuenti, si Papa contrarium posset facere pro suo libito voluntatis?
units.tr: PAULUS. As for the decrees of a general council, concerning which and their authority there is a whole title in Decretum, distinction fifteen, Canones, and throughout: this is almost the unanimous opinion of all the teachers, that the Pope cannot remove or dispense against those things which have been defined by the four chief general councils. Hence that most blessed Pope Gregory says in c. Sicut, dist. 100: Just as I acknowledge the four books of the holy Gospel, so I confess that I receive and venerate these four councils, and I embrace them with my whole devotion, and I keep them with the most unimpaired approval. For upon these, as upon a square stone, the holy structure of faith rises, and the rule of every life and common action stands. Since, therefore, to give or permit money for the first year's fruits, so that a bishopric or any other title of a great or small benefice be conferred, or even for the signing of a supplication, is forbidden at the Council of Chalcedon, one of the four principal councils, which prohibition has been made canonical and is found in 1. q. 1. Si quis episcopus, as it is there stated in the heading, from the council of Chalcedon; and the same canon proves this in 1. q. 3. Salvator, nisi alioquin. & c. ex multis, & c. pervenit, which canons, to prove the unlawful bargaining or trafficking in any ecclesiastical benefices and other spiritual things, refer back to the said Council in the said c. si quis. And there, in c. ex multis, it is said that this sentence is found in the second chapter of the Council of Chalcedon. And unless this crime were contrary to the canonical faith, it would not have been proscribed and condemned by the holy Fathers with such severity of execration, that it is even called heresy: 1. q. 1. Petrus & c. cum omnes, & c. eos qui. In which it is said: The impious heresy of Macedonius and his followers, who assert that the Holy Spirit is a creature and a servant of the Father and the Son, is more tolerable. But these sellers and buyers of spiritual things make the Holy Spirit their servant, which they prove thus: For just as the seller sells what he possesses, so the buyer, wishing to be the lord of what he buys, buys, etc. And consequently it is shown there how such people are blasphemers of Christ, along with those Jews who said, He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons, Matt. 12, and traitors with Judas, who betrayed Christ, Matth. 26. Now if this were not also against the state of the universal Church, what do you think: would the Fathers have issued so many solemn councils and so many canons of prohibition on this matter with such great care, and would so great a store of writings by the holy teachers on this point, and so many decretal letters sent out to the various parts of the world, as is clear to anyone who considers all this, if the Pope could do the contrary at his own pleasure?

units.la: PET. Ex quo quaeso capite glossator Bernhard. & quamplures alii, hanc scribendi sumpsere audaciam? & vt iam conspicio, non sine grauii animarum periculo apparent contra diuinae legis eulogia, Papae laxantes potestatem, & legibus ciuilibus conantes humana ratione determinare contrarium Euangelicae veritati. Vt igitur magis ac magis huius erroris falsitas appareat, ad roborandum praedicta rationibus iam ostende.
units.tr: PET. From what source, I ask, did the glossator Bernhard and very many others take up this boldness of writing? And, as I now see, they appear, not without grave danger to souls, to be loosening the Popes' power against the blessings of the divine law, and by human reason they try to determine what is contrary to the truth of the Gospel. So that the falsity of this error may appear more and more, now prove the aforesaid points with arguments.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAP. IV.

units.la: In quo conuincitur idem rationibus, quod in duobus precedentibus capitulis multiplicatur.
units.tr: In which the same point is proved by reasons, as the two preceding chapters have multiplied it.

units.la: PAVLVS. Quantum ad tertium, scilicet ius naturale, intrando hanc materiam profundius, gratia maioris contemptus, & opprobrii tanti sceleris, cesset gratia argumenti, cuiuslibet legis scriptae prohibitio, adhuc ipsum viuens ratio abhorrebit. Vbi pro clariori intelligentia aduertendum est, quod circa personam Papae, vel potius circa gerenda per ipsum, considerari expedit, vnde sibi haec tanta potestas, quam habet, & propter quid est? Et apud Christianum non est dubium, eam causatiue & principaliter non esse ex homine, sed solum dispositiue, in quantum electionem canonicam, tanquam dispositionem praeuiam, sequitur spiritualis potestas, efficiente Christo. Iuxta illud Matthaei 16. Quodcunque ligaueris super terram, &c. Et haec potestas sunt illae claues, quas Christus Petro promiserat, inquiens: Tibi dabo claues regni coelorum, &c. Quare autem haec autoritas siue potestas Apostolica dicebatur Claues in plurali, dictum est supra, prima parte, capitulo quarto. Hanc potestatem, seu clauem, Magister Sententiarum in 4. dist. 18. sic describit: Clauis est potestas ligandi & soluendi, qua ecclesiasticus iudex dignos recipere, & indignos excludere debet de regno Dei. Aliter etiam praeconsiderandum est, quid est Papae datum: secundo, quis dedit: tertio, cui datum est: quarto, propter quid datum est. Ex his consideratione debita masticatis, clare iuris propositi veritas lucebit. Quia non est rem perfectius cognoscere, quam per suas causas: quia sicut se habet res ad esse, ita se habet ad cognosci. Pro primo igitur notando constat, in Papa, etiam a iure potestatis magnitudinem esse nullo humano ingenio acquisibilem: alioquin potius huiusmodi potestatis virtus fuisset in Philosophis, quam in papa. Nec etiam habetur per assuefactionem, quemadmodum virtutes morales & virtus scientiarum acquiruntur: quia plures contingeret, maxime deuotos monachos & studentes, habere hanc virtutem. Nec inest a natura specifica, quia sic omnis homo eam haberet. Nec ex complexione corporum accidit, quemadmodum accidentia corporalia sequuntur complexiones: quia multi essent eiusdem potestatis. Et breuiter, iura etiam de electione papae superuacue laborarent. Nec etiam est ab hominibus principaliter, scilicet ex electione: quia electio nihil dat, quod non habet, nec etiam posset tali potestate aliquem effectum spiritualem efficere, sicut absoluere, cum ad hoc humana virtus non sufficit, & nihil agit vltra propriam virtutem, vt dicunt Philosophi. Igitur necesse est dicere, talem potestatem esse donum Dei: & quia sine aliqua commutatione, vel pretio, pugnat pretii aestimatio, dicitur gratuitum: non tamen gratificans, siue gratia, quod est idem. Si enim, inquit Apostolus, gratia ex meritis est, iam non est gratia: sed quia non datur gratis, sed propter merita:
units.tr: PAUL. As to the third point, namely natural law: if we enter this matter more deeply, then even if the occasion for so great a contempt and disgrace of so great a crime were removed, and there were no prohibition in any written law, reason itself, still living within us, would shrink from it. To understand this more clearly, we must note that concerning the person of the Pope, or rather concerning what is done through him, it is useful to consider whence he has this great power that he holds, and on account of what it is given. Among Christians there is no doubt that it does not come from man as its efficient and principal cause, but only as a disposing cause, in so far as spiritual power follows the canonical election as a prior disposition, with Christ as the agent. This accords with Matthew 16: Whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth, etc. And this power is those keys which Christ promised to Peter, saying: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, etc. Why this apostolic authority or power is called keys in the plural has been said above, in the first part, chapter four. The Master of the Sentences, in 4 dist. 18., describes this power, or key, thus: The key is the power of binding and loosing, by which the ecclesiastical judge ought to admit the worthy and exclude the unworthy from the kingdom of God. We must also consider beforehand, in another way, what has been given to the Pope: second, who gave it; third, to whom it was given; fourth, for what purpose it was given. When these have been duly weighed, the truth of the matter in question will shine out clearly. For nothing is known more perfectly than through its causes, since a thing is related to being just as it is related to being known. Taking the first point, then, it is evident that in the Pope the greatness of this power, even as to its right, cannot be acquired by any human talent; otherwise this power would rather have been found in the philosophers than in the Pope. Nor is it had by habituation, as moral virtues and the virtue of the sciences are acquired, for then it would happen that many, especially devout monks and scholars, would have this power. Nor does it inhere from specific nature, for then every man would have it. Nor does it arise from the constitution of bodies, as bodily accidents follow from constitutions, for then many would be of the same power. And, in short, the laws concerning the election of the Pope would labour in vain. Nor is it principally from men, namely from election, since election gives nothing that it does not have, and could not produce any spiritual effect by such a power, such as absolving, since human strength is not sufficient for this, and nothing acts beyond its own power, as the philosophers say. It is therefore necessary to say that such power is a gift of God; and because it is given without any exchange or price, since the estimation of a price is opposed to it, it is called gratuitous; yet not gratifying, or grace, which is the same thing. For if, says the Apostle, it is of grace, it is no more of works: but because it is not given freely, but on account of merits,

units.la: & & quia per naturam acquiri non potest, dicitur supernaturale. Et quia ad perfectionem spiritus humani siue animæ seruit per se, & principaliter, dicitur & est spirituale.
units.tr: and because it cannot be acquired by nature, it is called supernatural. And because it serves, through itself and principally, the perfection of the human spirit or soul, it is called and is spiritual.

units.la: Causa autem materialis, siue subiectum capax, etiam requiritur: vt sicut humana potestas, quo ad esse sui, ex quatuor generibus causarum constituitur, sic etiam habet cognosci. Et ergo referendo singula singulis, potest sic notificari, & describi: Potestas Apostolica est donum Dei, gratuitum per se, non gratificans humana natura, supernaturaliter infusum per se & principaliter ad perfectionem humanæ animæ, vel animarum destinatum. Hoc donum, & alia dona gratuita, & eorum exercitia, siue actus pariter & effectus, iussit Saluator gratis dare: Matthæi decimo, Gratis accepistis, gratis date.
units.tr: A material cause, or capable subject, is also required; so that, just as human power, as to its being, is constituted from the four kinds of causes, so it may also be known in the same way. Therefore, by referring each to each, it can be made known and described thus: Apostolic power is a gift of God, gratuitous in itself, not gratifying human nature, supernaturally infused, through itself and principally destined for the perfection of the human soul, or of souls. This gift, and other gratuitous gifts, and their exercise, or acts and effects alike, the Saviour commanded to be given freely: Matthew 10: Freely you have received, freely give.

units.la: Præterea adhuc prænotandum est, quod sicut Deus est causa productiua omnium citra se, sic etiam causa finalis omnium. Et ita omnia sunt & agunt propter ipsum, & desiderantur propter ipsum: solus ipse est sui ipsius gratia, & ens liberrimum, vt habet videri per Philosophum primo Metaphysica, & in multis locis philosophiæ: Insuper, sicut omnia agunt propter illum finem, sic etiam appetunt ulterius & ulterius perfici, & se sibi assimilare & appropinquare, inquantum vnumquodque secundum suam naturam potest. Imperfectius autem se appetere horret quælibet creatura. Hinc est, quod aliquis dicitur plus vel minus perfici, de quanto plus vel minus assimilatur vel appropinquat in ordine perfectionalis lineæ, ipsi Deo, vltimo fini. Et habet alibi videri: hæc incidenter dico, propter finem descriptionis Apostolicæ potestatis. Sic etiam est in genere accidentium. Accidentia quæ plus faciunt assimilari, vel appropinquare vltimo fini, perfectius subiectum perficiunt, & sunt perfectiora. Vnde accidentia spiritualia, vt sunt virtutes morales, scientiæ & dona supernaturalia, sunt longe perfectiora accidentib. corporalibus: vt nigredine, albedine, &c. spiritualibus adhuc differentibus. Nam aliqua eorum plus faciunt fini assimilari, quam alia: vt potestas Apostolica, vel ecclesiastica, quæ solum datur militantibus sub lege Euangelica, quæ est super omnem legem. Verum, quoniam hæc potestas conuenit bonis & malis prælatis, non ita perfecte assimilat Deo summo bono, sicut gratia gratum faciens, siue charitas, quæ est omnium accidentium perfectissima, & finis, vt dicit Apostol. 1. Cori. 13. Maior autem horum est charitas. Hæc enim non solum Deo assimilat, sed vnit & incorporat sibi, vt legitur 1. Iohan. 4. Qui manet in charitate, in me manet, & ego in eo. Et hæc quamuis sit vltimum in genere perfectionis accidentium, tamen in omni operatione ordinata & meritoria debet esse primum: quia finis est primum in intentione, & vltimum in executione, vt in ædificatione castri, cuius finis est secura ab insultibus inimicorum habitatio: cuius habitationis amore non solum ædificatio, sed omnia quæ ad ædificationem iuuant & administrant, amore finis principaliter intenti, diliguntur. Ad propositum, potestas ecclesiastica quamuis spiritualiter per se perficiat, est tamen conferenda & retinenda amore finis, propter quem est à Domino destinata: quia est ministerialis virtus ad ipsam charitatem seminandam, & conseruandam in corpore Christi mystico. Ad propositum principale redeundo, certum est, hanc Apostolicæ potestatis gratiam esse donum Dei gratuitu, seu gratis datum, & gratis dandum: quia hæc est eius natura, vt dictum est. Cum ergo aliquid proipsa, vel ipsius actu recipitur, &c. natura ipsius gratiæ, quatum in emente vel vendente est, tollitur: quia venditio excludit gratitudinem, vt dicunt etiam leges ciuiles. ff. de contrahen. empt. l. 2. §. sine precio. l. c. empti fides, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, it must further be noted beforehand that, just as God is the productive cause of all things other than himself, so too he is the final cause of all. Thus all things exist and act on account of him, and are desired on account of him; he alone is for his own sake, and is the most free being, as may be seen from the Philosopher in Metaphysics book one, and in many places of philosophy. Furthermore, just as all things act for that end, so also they strive to be perfected further and further, and to make themselves like him and draw near to him, insofar as each can according to its nature. Every creature, however, shrinks from desiring itself in a more imperfect way. Hence it is that one is said to be more or less perfected, according as one is more or less made like, or draws nearer, in the order of the line of perfection, to God himself, the ultimate end. And this may be seen elsewhere; I say it here incidentally, for the purpose of describing apostolic power. It is so also in the genus of accidents. Accidents which make a subject more like, or nearer, to the ultimate end perfect that subject more, and are more perfect. Hence spiritual accidents, such as moral virtues, sciences and supernatural gifts, are far more perfect than bodily accidents, such as blackness, whiteness, etc., though spiritual accidents also differ among themselves. For some of them make us more like the end than others do, as apostolic or ecclesiastical power does, which is given only to those fighting under the Gospel law, which is above every law. But since this power belongs to good and bad prelates alike, it does not make a man as perfectly like God, the highest good, as sanctifying grace or charity does; charity is the most perfect of all accidents and the end, as the Apostle says, 1 Cor. 13: But the greatest of these is charity. For this makes us not only like God, but unites and incorporates us with him, as we read in 1 John 4: He who abides in charity abides in me, and I in him. And although this is the last in the order of the perfection of accidents, nevertheless in every ordered and meritorious action it ought to be first; for the end is first in intention and last in execution, as in the building of a castle, whose end is a dwelling safe from the assaults of enemies; for love of this dwelling not only the building but all the things that help and serve the building are loved, out of love for the end principally intended. To the point: ecclesiastical power, although it perfects spiritually in itself, is nevertheless to be conferred and retained out of love for the end for which it was appointed by the Lord; for it is a ministerial power for sowing and preserving charity itself in the mystical body of Christ. Returning to the principal point, it is certain that this grace of apostolic power is a gratuitous gift of God, or given freely, and to be given freely, since this is its nature, as has been said. Therefore, when something is received on account of it, or on account of its act, etc., the nature of the grace itself is removed, so far as it lies in the buyer or seller; for sale excludes gratuitousness, as the civil laws also say. Digest, de contrahenda emptione, law 2, §. sine pretio; law: empti fides, etc.

units.la: Secundo arguitur. In vendente huiusmodi dona Dei, duo est considerare, quæ concurrunt in tali commutatione, Vnum, quod est: suum quodque est sibi & cuilibet homini naturale, scilicet benevolentiam exhibere alteri. Hoc lex naturæ rationalis dictat. Aliud vero, quod non est suum, sed Dei specialiter: scilicet tale donum, quod est sibi commissum ministrare gratis, vt supra. Cum ergo recipiens, vel petens pecuniam pro actu, siue exercitio dictæ suæ potestatis, aut recipit pro primo quod est suum, pro benevolentia: aut pro secundo, sci. actu potestatis: aut pro vtroque, & quocunque modo, sic est contra ordinem naturæ facere.
units.tr: Secondly, it is argued thus. In one who sells such gifts of God, two things are to be considered, which come together in such an exchange. One is what belongs to him, and is natural to himself and to every man: namely, to show goodwill to another. This the law of rational nature dictates. The other, which is not his own but specially God's, is the gift that has been committed to him to minister freely, as above. Therefore, when one who receives or asks money for the act, or exercise, of his said power receives it either for the first, which is his own, namely goodwill; or for the second, namely the act of power; or for both; and in whatever way, it is then against the order of nature to act so.

units.la: Si enim recipit pro alieno, peccat multipliciter. Primo, contra naturam doni: item contra fidelitatem ministerii sibi commissi: item nobilem rem pro vili commutat, item rem in alium finem ordinat, scilicet pecuniam, quam illa res fuit destinata. Si vero vendit benevolentiam, quam naturaliter gratis exhibere debet, ipsius benevolentiæ contra se prouocat authorem, vt iusto iudicio, huiusmodi ingrato nulla benevolentia fiat. Et quia legem naturæ peruertit, vendendo id quod ex ordinatione summæ sapientiæ gratis exhibere debet, derogat ipsi sapientiæ diuinæ: quia alium suis donis nititur dare ordinem, vendendo illa, quæ naturalis ordo vendi prohibet: ac si sic non esset bene ordinatum, & per consequens, per authorem ordinis rerum iustissime puniendus.
units.tr: For if he receives money for something that is not his own, he sins in several ways. First, he acts against the nature of the gift. He also breaks faith with the ministry entrusted to him. He exchanges a noble thing for a base one, and he directs a thing to another end, namely money, when that thing was destined for something else. If he sells goodwill, which he ought to offer freely by nature, he provokes the very Author of that goodwill against himself, so that by his just judgment no goodwill is shown to such an ungrateful man. And because he subverts the law of nature by selling what he ought to give freely by the ordinance of supreme wisdom, he detracts from divine wisdom itself. He tries to give his gifts a different order by selling what the natural order forbids to be sold, as if things were not well ordered as they are, and so he deserves to be punished most justly by the Author of the order of things.

units.la: Præterea sumendo rationem à causa efficienti principali, arguitur sic: Cum enim ipse author omnium diuitiarum nullo indigeat, quia omnia sunt sua, omnia habet, cum sit summe diues: non indiget suorum donorum tali commutatione, vel venditione, pro alio bono quocunque, nec etiā voluit ea dare, nisi gratis: quia hoc suæ repugnat liberalitati, cum sit summe liberalis, nec voluit ea seruari apud eos quibus dantur, quia hoc repugnaret diuinæ summæ magnificentiæ, & dicut Philosophi: Bonum quanto plus commune, tanto plus diuinum. Et quia naturaliter omnis artifex diligit opus suum, maxime tamen creator hominis, quæ fecit Dominus ad imaginem suam, repugnare videretur eius pietati & naturali iustitiæ, vni se velle communicare, & non alteri: nec decet honorem suum & magnificentiam minui, sed augeri. Et etiam ex quo contractus venditionis propter indigentiam hominum inuentus est, mercator spiritualium donorum facit summe diuitem dominū egere, & tali lucro indigere. digere, & per consequens maculat gloriam suam. In eo autem quod isto modo disponit, detrahit ipsius sapientiæ, quæ alio modo disposuit. In eo autem, quod non vult sua dona dare gratis, detrahit ipsius summæ libertati. Et quia apud se seruat tale donum, & aliis non communicat, detrahit suæ magnificentiæ, & minuit summam honorem & gloriam, occultat pietatem patris ad filios adoptionis, negat fructum salutiferæ redemptionis, pactum infringit diuinæ promissionis, dilectione creaturæ subtrahit sui conditoris, propter quæ omnia maiestatis diuinæ summus honor & gloria se exinanire voluit, & usque ad effusionem sanguinis & mortem turpissimam sibi filius Dei non pepercit. Præterea attende etiam, cui datur hæc potestas spiritualis, quæ ex præmissis est donum Dei gratuitum, & quod ministrari debet aliis, & gratis, sine aliqua commutatione. Quid aliud concluditur, quam quod is cui datur, non Dominus, sed minister est dictæ potestatis ac dispensator, siue executor, vel etiam instrumentum per quod illa potestas siue doni virtus spiritualitatis habet exercere operationem? hoc Saluator notabiliter expressit Matth. 10. Scitis quia hi qui videntur principari gentibus, dominantur eis, & principes ipsorum potestatem habent eorum, non ita autem est in vobis: sed quicunque voluerit fieri maior, erit vt minister: & quicunque in vobis voluerit fieri primus, erit omnium seruus. Nam & filius hominis non venit vt ministraretur ei, sed vt ministraret, & daret animam suam redemptionem pro multis. Idem Lucas 22. Simile est autem, sicut in aliis virtutibus organicis, ponatur enim, quod potentia visiua debeat exse actum videndi producere: sed organo oculi vtitur pro instrumento, instrumentum autem ex se non potest.
units.tr: Moreover, reasoning from the principal efficient cause, the argument runs thus. The Author of all riches needs nothing, since all things are his and he has all things, being supremely rich. He has no need of such an exchange or sale of his gifts for any other good whatever. Nor did he wish to give them except freely, because this would be contrary to his liberality, since he is supremely liberal. Nor did he wish them to be kept by those to whom they are given, because this would be contrary to God's supreme magnificence, and as the philosophers say: The more common a good is, the more divine it is.
