And since every craftsman naturally loves his own work, and the Lord above all loves the creature of man, whom he made in his own image, it would seem contrary to his goodness and natural justice to wish to share himself with one person and not with another. Nor does it befit his honour and magnificence to be diminished rather than increased. Furthermore, since the contract of sale was invented on account of human need, a merchant of spiritual gifts makes the supremely rich Lord appear to be in need and to require such gain, and so he stains his glory. By disposing things in this way he detracts from his wisdom, which disposed them otherwise. By not wishing to give his gifts freely, he detracts from his supreme liberality. And because he keeps such a gift for himself and does not share it with others, he detracts from his magnificence and diminishes his supreme honour and glory. He obscures the Father's love toward the children of adoption, denies the fruit of saving redemption, breaks the covenant of divine promise, and by a love of the creature withdraws himself from his Creator. For all these reasons the Son of God did not spare himself, but, though the highest honour and glory of the divine majesty chose to empty itself, he endured the shedding of blood and the most shameful death. Furthermore, consider also to whom this spiritual power is given, which, from what has been said, is a free gift of God, and which ought to be administered to others, and freely, without any exchange. What else follows, than that the one to whom it is given is not the Lord but the minister and steward of that power, or its executor, or even the instrument through which that power or virtue of the spiritual gift exercises its operation? The Saviour expressed this remarkably in Matth. 10: You know that those who seem to rule over the nations lord it over them, and their princes have power over them; but it is not so among you. Whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your minister; and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be the slave of all. For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. Likewise Luke 22. It is like the other organic powers: suppose that the power of sight is to produce the act of seeing; it uses the eye as an instrument, but the instrument cannot act of itself.

units.la: Ex quibus colligitur, quod talis nihil habet ibi dominii, vt scilicet, quod possit aliter pro voluntate sua facere, quam nudum ministerium exhibere, per nudum verbum. Non excludo cognitionem causæ, &c. sed solum voluntatem sine causa simpliciter in conferendo, non in cui dando. Cum ergo confirmare electionem, providere de episcopatu, abbatia, prioratu, canonicatu, plebania, aut de quocunque beneficio ecclesiastico, est sine dubio actus potestatis Apostolicæ, seu operatio propria doni Dei gratuiti, vt dictum est (pone enim pro possibili, quod illa virtus, seu potestas tollatur ab eo) amplius quicquid faceret, vt Papa, non valebit, vt notum est.
units.tr: From these things it is concluded that such a person has no lordship there, so that he could act otherwise at his will than by offering a bare ministry, through a bare word. I do not exclude consideration of the cause, etc., but only an arbitrary will in conferring without cause, not in giving something. Therefore, since to confirm an election, to provide for a bishopric, abbey, priory, canonry, parish, or any ecclesiastical benefice, is without doubt an act of apostolic power, or the proper operation of the free gift of God, as has been said (for suppose, as a possibility, that this virtue or power were taken away from him), then whatever he did as Pope would have no validity, as is well known.

units.la: Similiter super pluralitate beneficiorum dispensare, vel quomodolibet aliter absoluere, &c. quotiescunque Papa vel alius recipit pecuniam, pretium, obsequium, vel fauorem, &c. pro actu huiusmodi conferendi, dispensandi, absoluendi, alias non facturus hoc: non videtur iam, nec est nudus minister, siue executor dictæ potestatis Apostolicæ: sed pro libito suo sic faciens, vsurpat in eo sibi dominium: & per consequens, iniuriam facit vero Domino.
units.tr: Likewise, to dispense concerning the holding of several benefices, or to absolve in any other way, etc.: whenever the Pope or anyone else receives money, price, service, or favour, etc., for the act of conferring, dispensing, or absolving of this kind, which he would not otherwise have done, he does not seem, and is not, a bare minister or executor of that apostolic power. Acting at his own pleasure in this way, he usurps lordship for himself, and consequently does wrong to the true Lord.

units.la: PET. Fac me clarius hoc intelligere, quod immediate nunc dixisti. Non enim videtur pecunia recipi pro potestate Apostolica: quia illa non potest transferri in alium de Papa, nisi ipse deponeretur, nec pro actu, siue exercitio potestatis eius: quia illud est cito transiens, non permanens. Datur ergo pecunia pro beneficio reali, scilicet episcopatu, præpositura, &c. quod nec est potestas papæ spiritualis, nec actus eius.
units.tr: PET. Make me understand more clearly what you have just said. For it does not seem that money is received for apostolic power, since that cannot be transferred to another unless the Pope himself were deposed; nor for an act or exercise of his power, since that is passing quickly and not lasting. So the money is given for a real benefice, namely a bishopric, a provostship, etc., which is neither the Pope's spiritual power nor his act.

units.la: PAVL. Respondeo ad hæc, primo philosophice, quod talis separatio non potest esse in causis sibi inuicem essentialiter subordinatis: quoniam vendito uno, venditur reliquum. Quemadmodum posita tali potestate, cum tali actu dandi tanquam causa efficiente, necessario ponitur causa finalis, seu obiectum formale, mouens virtutem ad actum, scilicet id quod datur, & e contrario. Vel aliter, & grossius, sic respondetur: Certum est quod papa non habet aliquod dominium, quod possit ordinare, vel quomodocunque disponere in beneficiis, vel in rebus ecclesiasticis, nisi tali iure, scilicet spirituali potestate, vt dixi, nullam penitus habet dispositionem in eis, sicut nec alia priuata persona. Ergo dans alicui beneficium ecclesiasticum, dat seu transfert in eum, id quod suum est, in tali beneficio: & quia suum nihil est, nisi potestas spiritualis, qua sibi illud beneficium subiicitur, & non aliter, ergo talem potestatem spiritualem sibi dat: & quia intuitu pecuniarum, igitur, &c. Nullus enim bonus emptor emeret aliquam rem, nisi ius illius rei, quo venditor eam possideret, transferretur in eum. Et allegamus quotidie, quod nemo plus iuris in alium transferre poterit, quam ipse habeat, de reg. iur. 1. regula lib. 6. Præterea talis venditor tituli beneficii ecclesiastici, vendit non suum, sed alienum, ad quod ipse solum est minister, seu instrumentum. Igitur pretium quod inde recipiet, non erit suum, sed eius cuius res venditur, scilicet Dei. Et quia in eius vilitatem non convertitur, qui cum sit honestissimum & sufficientissimum bonum, vtiq; illo non indiget, quod solum propter nos creauit: ergo si in priuata commoda conuertitur, res contrectatur aliena inuito Domino.
units.tr: PAUL. I answer these points first philosophically: such a separation cannot exist in causes that are essentially subordinated to one another, since when one is sold, the rest is sold too. Just as, when such a power is posited together with such an act of giving as efficient cause, the final cause, or formal object, moving the power to the act, namely what is given, is necessarily posited, and conversely. Or, more crudely, the answer may be put thus. It is certain that the Pope has no dominion which he can order or in any way dispose of in benefices or in ecclesiastical things, except by such a right, namely spiritual power. As I said, he has no disposition over them at all, just as no other private person has. Therefore, in giving an ecclesiastical benefice to someone, he gives or transfers to that person what is his in such a benefice; and since what is his is nothing but the spiritual power by which that benefice is subjected to him, and not otherwise, he therefore gives him that spiritual power; and since he does so in view of money, therefore, etc. For no good buyer would buy anything unless the right to that thing, by which the seller possessed it, were transferred to him. And we daily cite that no one can transfer more right to another than he himself has, de reg. iur. 1. regula lib. 6. Moreover, such a seller of the title of an ecclesiastical benefice sells not what is his, but what belongs to another, of which he is only the minister or instrument. Therefore the price he receives from it will not be his, but that of the owner of the thing sold, namely God's. And since it is not turned to the advantage of him who, being the most honourable and self-sufficient good, has no need of that which he created solely for our sake, then if it is turned to private profit, the thing is handled as another's against the Lord's will.

units.la: Consueuerunt pro hoc respondere in curia, huiusmodi sanctorum canonum Glossatores: quod talis pecunia conuertitur pro bono communi, & reipublicæ necessario, scilicet primo fuit pro ædificatione castri sancti Angeli, Capitolii Romani, pro egestate armorum: in finem, vt bona temporalia ecclesiæ, ciuitates, castra, villæ, &c. per tyrannos occupata, ad possessionem ecclesiæ reducantur, possessa teneantur, & inimicis Ecclesiæ fortius resistatur, quod si non esset, ecclesia Romana in bonis, interdum etiam in personis, periculum pateretur.
units.tr: To this the glossators of these sacred canons are accustomed to reply at the Curia: that such money is turned to the common good and to the necessary needs of the commonwealth. Namely, first, it was for the building of the castle of St Angelo, of the Roman Capitol, and for the lack of arms; and finally, so that the temporal goods of the Church, cities, castles, villages, etc., occupied by tyrants, might be restored to the possession of the Church, held once possessed, and that resistance might be made more strongly against the enemies of the Church. For if this were not so, the Roman Church would suffer danger in its goods and sometimes even in its persons.

units.la: PAVL. Profecto hæc simoniaca obiectio excusare non videtur, sed potius paciscentium turpitudine allegare. Putas ne vt imare filiū in conspectu patris: & qua ratione creditur ordine peruerso obsequium præstandum Deo, cœlestibus terrena, & spiritualibus temporalia hoc modo præponendo? Præterea & idcirco quartum & principaliter, a fine propter quem, rationem sumendo arguitur sic: Quotiescunque aliquid sic eligitur, appetitur, donatur propter aliud, illud aliud, propter quod fit, magis eligitur, appetitur, diligitur, &c. per regulam consequentem Physicam: Propter quod. quod enim vnumquodque tale est, & ipsum magis tale. Quis enim dubitabit, terminum viæ, ad quam attenditur, esse appetibiliorem, quam ipsam viam? cum via nec esset, nec desideratur, nisi propter terminum attingendum, ad quem illa via ducit, seu dirigit? Sed certe episcopatus, abbatias, prioratus, præposituras, canonicatus, & quæcunque alia beneficia quæ sunt per se primo fundata pro laude & gloria Dei, & spirituali profectu Christi fidelium, vt supra patet, dans seu concedens talia, seu personas de vno loco ad alium transferens, &c. propter pecuniam habendam, siue talis pecunia ordinatur in finem, vt reuelentur, ditentur & sublimentur propinqui, parentelæ suæ, in finem & effectum, vt bona temporalia etiam ecclesiastica defensentur, &c. vt dicit tua precedens obiectio, vt etiam facti veritas iam longo tempore declarauit prædicta. Conclude ergo ex præmissis necessario, quod pecunia plus eligitur, appetitur, & diligitur: & per consequens, parentela, vel bona temporalia, etiam ecclesiastica, quâ honor, laus & gloria Dei, & profectus spiritualis proximi & Christi. Nihil ergo velles iterum dicere, quod talia beneficia non sunt per se & principaliter pro honore Dei, &c. quia tunc, quamuis consequentia esset bona, tamen minoris assumptum esset falsum. Cui obiectioni respondent sufficienter canones, quo ad primum minoris illius dictum, t.q.3. Saluator. & c. ex multis. & c. res ecclesiæ, & alii plures, talia dona esse Dei: ideo, quia à Deo fidelibus & à fidelibus Deo donantur. Ecce finis principalis: quemadmodum à Deo gratis accipiuntur, ideo gratis dari debent, hoc in cap. Saluator.
units.tr: PAUL. Certainly this simoniacal objection does not seem to excuse the matter but rather to charge the parties to the bargain with baseness. Do you think a son can be made to appear in his father's sight in this way? And by what reasoning is it believed that service is owed to God in a perverse order, putting earthly things before heavenly and temporal before spiritual? Moreover, the argument is made fourth and chiefly from the end, reasoning thus: whenever something is so chosen, sought or given for the sake of something else, that other thing for whose sake it is done is chosen, sought and loved more, and so on, by the consequent rule of natural philosophy, "for the sake of which": for whatever a thing is, that very thing is more so. For who will doubt that the goal of a road, toward which one aims, is more desirable than the road itself, since the road would neither exist nor be desired except for the sake of reaching the end to which it leads and directs? But certainly bishoprics, abbeys, priories, provostships, canonries and whatever other benefices are founded first and per se for the praise and glory of God and the spiritual progress of Christ's faithful, as appears above, are given or granted, or persons are transferred from one place to another, for the sake of having money; or such money is directed to the end that relatives and kin may be enriched, raised and exalted, to the end and effect that temporal goods, even ecclesiastical ones, may be defended, as your preceding objection says and as the fact itself has long declared. Conclude therefore of necessity from the premises that money is chosen, sought and loved more, and consequently kin or temporal goods, even ecclesiastical ones, more than the honour, praise and glory of God and the spiritual profit of the neighbour and of Christ. You would therefore not wish to say further that such benefices are not per se and chiefly for the honour of God, and so on, because then, although the consequence would be sound, the minor premise would be false. To this objection the canons sufficiently reply, as to the first part of that minor premise, in t.q.3 "Saluator", "ex multis", "res ecclesiae", and many others, that such gifts belong to God, because they are given by God to the faithful and by the faithful to God. Here is the principal end: as they are received from God freely, so they ought to be given freely; see cap. "Saluator".

units.la: Et etiam vbi quæso legimus, Christum tanta sollicitudine iniunxisse Petro curam tantam de causis, & bonis temporalibus? quanta maturitate etiam vsque ad trinam interrogationem & responsionem fuit illud dictum, Pasce oues meas? Aut quomodo potestate ligandi & soluendi sibi tradita, voluisset Christus Petro ditare consanguineos suos, qui dixit: Veni separare hominem aduersus patrem suum, & filiam aduersus matrem suam, & nurum aduersus socrum suam, & inimici hominis erunt domestici eius item: Qui amat patrem suum, aut matrem suam plus quam me, non est me dignus. Qui non accipit crucem suam, & sequitur me, non est me dignus: Matthæi decimo & alibi legitur, cuilibet menti cultæ valde notabile: Qui non odit patrem & matrem propter me, non potest esse meus discipulus Si ergo non discipulus, quomodo summus Apostolus erit? Non ergo videtur negandum fuisse antecedens, & per consequens, nostri argumenti illatum consequens concedendum est, & fatendum.
units.tr: And where, I ask, do we read that Christ enjoined on Peter such a great concern for causes and temporal goods? With what seriousness was that saying, "Feed my sheep," spoken, even through a threefold question and answer? Or how, having given him the power of binding and loosing, would Christ have wished Peter to enrich his kinsmen, who said: "I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man's foes shall be those of his own household"; and again: "He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. He who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me" (Matthew 10), and elsewhere, which is very noteworthy to any cultivated mind: "He who does not hate father and mother for my sake cannot be my disciple." If then he is not a disciple, how will he be the chief Apostle? It therefore does not seem that the antecedent should be denied, and consequently the conclusion drawn from our argument must be conceded and confessed.

units.la: PAET. Ligat me fortiter argumentum hoc, veruntamen ex eo resultat dubium. Videtur inferri posse, quod non liceat aliqua temporalia vendere, vel commutare. Ratio, quia finis primo & principaliter omnium est Deus, & omnia agunt propter ipsum, vt dictum est: non licebit ergo ea in alium finem ordinare: & per consequens, rem temporalem, vt equum, villam, &c. non licebit pro pecuniis, nec econuerso pecunias pro ipsis dare. Alioquin sequi videtur, quod villa seu pecunia plus diligitur quam Deus, qui est finis illorum. Imo videtur ex præmissis, quod bona temporalia beneficiorum non possent vendi, quia talia pure propter Deum tanquam finem principalem, & per se primo sunt deputata.
units.tr: PET. This argument binds me strongly, but a doubt arises from it. It seems to follow that it is not lawful to sell or exchange any temporal goods. The reason is that the end of all things, first and chiefly, is God, and all things act for his sake, as has been said; it will therefore not be lawful to order them to another end, and consequently it will not be lawful to give a temporal thing, such as a horse or a farm, for money, nor, conversely, money for such things. Otherwise it seems to follow that the farm or the money is loved more than God, who is their end. Indeed, it seems from the premises that the temporal goods of benefices could not be sold, because such goods are assigned purely for God as the principal and first end.

units.la: PAVL. Res temporales sicut dupliciter se habent, ita dupliciter considerantur: primo, inquantum sunt naturales, & naturalium operum productiuæ: vel etiam inquantum sunt essentiales causæ & effectus inter se. Et hoc modo considerando, res temporales non sunt in potestate nostra, quin placeant vel displiceant nobis, exercent enim suas operationes, vt secundo Ethicorum circa principium: & vt sic sumptæ, neque commutari per nos eorum natura potest, nec etiam vendi vel emi possunt. Alio modo considerantur, prout inter se sunt causæ & effectus per accidens, prout vna aliam perficit accidentaliter.
units.tr: PAUL. Temporal things are related in two ways, and so they are considered in two ways. First, insofar as they are natural and productive of natural works; or also insofar as they are essential causes and effects of one another. Considered in this way, temporal things are not in our power, so as to please or displease us, for they exercise their own operations, as in the second book of the Ethics at the beginning; and so considered, their nature cannot be altered by us, nor can they be sold or bought. They are considered in another way, insofar as they are causes and effects of one another accidentally, insofar as one perfects the other accidentally.

units.la: Vna enim quæque res secundum naturam suæ speciei est sic perfecta, quod non plus perficitur, accidentaliter tamen plus & plus perficere potest. Vnde equus est causa per accidens perfectionis hominis, quia perficit hominem accidentaliter, homo enim ex se indispositus est ad mouendum se in breui tempore per longum spacium, sed quando equo vtitur, defectus humanus seu imperfectio suppletur. Sic suo modo vestimento, castro, &c. Et hoc modo considerare in quantum defectus humani supplementa & utilia sunt, in potestate nostra est eis uti vel non, & per consequens, commutari pro alio vtili. Omnia enim ista ad vsum humanum sunt creata, dicente Propheta: Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius. Sic etiam bona temporalia beneficiorum, quamuis sunt data Deo prima animi destinatione, non tamen per se & immediate sunt destinata seu ordinata, quantum est ex parte materiæ, donatæ in eum vsum.
units.tr: For each thing, according to the nature of its kind, is so perfect that it is not made more perfect in itself, yet it can accidentally be made more and more perfect. Hence a horse is an accidental cause of human perfection, because it perfects a man accidentally: a man is of himself unfit to move himself over a long distance in a short time, but when he uses a horse the human defect or imperfection is supplied. So too with a garment, a castle, and so on. And considered in this way, insofar as they are supplements of human deficiency and useful, it is in our power to use them or not, and consequently to exchange them for something else useful. For all these things are created for human use, as the Prophet says: "You have put all things under his feet." Likewise the temporal goods of benefices, although they are given to God by the primary intention of the mind, are not however destined or ordered per se and immediately, so far as the matter given to that use is concerned.

units.la: Quod patet, quia prout sunt naturalia, non sunt in potestate nostra, & per consequens, sic darinon potuerunt. Ergo prout vtilia homini, sic ordinari in Deum res per se non possunt, quia Deus non vtitur, nec potest vti eis, quia hoc est perfectionis accidentalis, & imperfectionis vtentis, vt dictum est: quia sunt remota à Deo, ergo oportet dici per accidens, scilicet in quantum actu, siue ministeriali vsu, aut vsuali ministerio suo disponunt aliquem ad finem ab ipso donante destinatum: & habent se ad spiritualem perfectionem, sicut candelabrum sustentans candelam se habet ad lumen: & sic potest fieri eorum commutatio pro alio sustentante, vel vtili.
units.tr: This is clear, because insofar as they are natural they are not in our power, and consequently they could not have been given in that way. Therefore insofar as they are useful to man, things cannot be ordered toward God per se, because God does not use them, nor can he use them, since this belongs to accidental perfection and to the imperfection of the one who uses, as has been said; they are remote from God. Hence it must be said that they are so per accidens, namely insofar as, by actual or ministerial use, or by their serviceable ministry, they dispose someone to the end destined by the giver. They stand toward spiritual perfection as a candlestick holding a candle stands toward the light; and so they may be exchanged for another supporting or useful thing.

units.la: PET. Potest adhuc contra prædicta fortiter obiici, sicut aliqui dicunt, putantes bene se vtique respondere, quod Papa non recipit pecuniam pro beneficiis, sed pro fructibus pro se reseruatis.
units.tr: PET. Still, it can be strongly objected to what has been said, as some do, who think they answer well enough: that the Pope does not receive money for benefices but for fruits reserved to himself.

units.la: PAVL. Si hoc est verum, fateri oportet, quod omnis cui Papa confert beneficium, non habeat titulum beneficii, nec debet episcopus dici talis ecclesiæ præpositus, vel canonicus, &c. nec debent exercere ea, quæ sunt officii illius beneficii, & quia quilibet talis, gerit se nomine, re & facto, pro tali beneficiato, cuius beneficii fructus hoc modo, scilicet emptionis, percipit. Ergo quilibet talis, & taliter beneficium de manibus Papæ recipiens, est fur & latro. Insuper Papales literæ super talibus provisionibus confectæ, patentissime declarant contrarium, vbi providendo personæ institutuntur, 5 & institutiuan dantur. Institutionem autem est, ius canonicum in ecclesia, vel ecclesiastico beneficio conferre: vt in eo frequentius, deinde. Qualiscunque autem huiusmodi literarum sit veritas, quibus scribitur: Quia vitæ & morum honestas, & literarum scientia, aliaque laudabilia virtutum merita nos inducunt, vt tibi ad gratiam reddamur liberales, &c. totus de hoc mundus est repletus. Et mirabile esset, quod Papa daret pro 50. flor. fructuum annuum censum, qui aliquando 400. florenis etiam ad tempora vitæ darent. Nullus modus esset melior iuris mercatoribus, lucrandi bona temporalia, quam iste quem curia Romana adinuenit. Et quia non venditur, non quidem propter incapacitatem personæ, quia laicus bene potest vti boni ecclesiasticis, quia eis locari possunt fructus decimarum, vt in caput. secund. de loca. & conduct. Ergo necesse est dicere, quod non solum fructus beneficiorum, qui sunt accessorii ad titulum, venduntur, sed illud mere spirituale & principale, scilicet titulus seu potestas excrendi tale ministerium in ecclesia, propter quod sunt tales fructus deputati. Hoc clare expressit canon, Si quis obiecerit. 1. qu. 3. Vbi dicitur: Quisquis horum alterum vendit, sine quo nec alterum possent neutrum invenditum derelinquit.
units.tr: PAUL. If this is true, one must admit that everyone to whom the Pope confers a benefice does not have the title of the benefice, nor should the bishop be called provost of such a church, or canon, and so on; nor should they exercise the duties of that benefice; and since each such person acts in name, in fact and in deed as beneficed in that office, and receives the fruits of the benefice in this way, namely by purchase, every such person, and everyone who receives a benefice in this way from the Pope's hands, is a thief and a robber. Moreover, the papal letters drawn up concerning such provisions declare the contrary most plainly, where, by providing the person, they are instituted and given institution. Now institution is the canonical right of conferring a church or an ecclesiastical benefice, as is more often the case later on. Whatever the truth of such letters, in which it is written: "Because the honesty of life and morals, the knowledge of letters, and other praiseworthy merits of virtue move us to make you generous to us in grace," and so on, the whole world is full of this. And it would be remarkable if the Pope gave for fifty florins a yearly rent of fruits which sometimes would bring four hundred florins even for life. No method would be better for merchants of law for gaining temporal goods than this one which the Roman curia has devised. And it is not sold because of any incapacity of the person, for a layman may well use ecclesiastical goods, since the fruits of tithes can be let to him, as in cap. secundum "de locato et conducto." Therefore it must be said that not only the fruits of benefices, which are accessory to the title, are sold, but that the purely spiritual and principal thing, namely the title or power of exercising that ministry in the church, for which such fruits are assigned, is also sold. The canon "Si quis obiecerit" (1 q.3) clearly expresses this, where it is said: "Whoever sells one of these two, without which neither could be possessed, leaves neither unsold."

units.la: PET. Si debite te intelligo, videntur hæc repugnare prius dictis, vbi dicitur, quod fructus beneficiorum possunt vendi, &c.
units.tr: PET. If I understand you rightly, these points seem to contradict what you said earlier, where you stated that the revenues of benefices can be sold, and so on.

units.la: PAVL. Si bene ponderantur prædicta, patet sic iam solutio. Vel etiam potest, quod prout talis res est spiritualis, seu ad talem finem, puta honorem Dei destinata, nullo modo vendi. Secus, prout est visualis, & ad humanam indigentiam: quia sic solum per accidens ordinatur in Deum, sed primo modo per se. Vel si placet aliter, & physice: quia quilibet actus humanus est ad instar operationis in rebus naturalibus, in quibus est dare quatuor genera causarum, ad esse, seu ad substantiam rei concurrentium, quæ sunt: efficiens, finis, materia, forma. Sic etiam est in actibus humanis, vt in proposito.
units.tr: PAUL. If the points above are weighed carefully, the solution is already plain. Or it may be said that a thing, insofar as it is spiritual, or destined to such an end, namely the honour of God, can in no way be sold. It is otherwise insofar as it is a visible thing, serving human need, for in that respect it is ordered to God only accidentally, whereas in the first respect it is ordered to Him essentially. Or, if you prefer, one may speak in physical terms: every human act is like an operation in natural things, in which four kinds of cause concur to the being, or substance, of a thing: the efficient, the final, the material, and the formal. The same holds for human acts, as in the present case.

units.la: Ille qui donat talia bona ecclesiæ, est efficiens. Deus, propter quem, vel tale officium ecclesiasticum, propter quod dat, est finis: a quo est denominatio rei. Actus donandi, est forma, quæ dat tale esse rei. Res quæ donatur, est materia. Ex his resultat res, scilicet donum Dei, composita ex materia, scilicet eius quod datur, & forma, scilicet actus donandi, tanquam suis principiis intrinsecis, & sic substantialibus. Et dicitur, quod talis res donata ad honorem Dei, prout materia, actus donandi, constituens cum ipsa substantialiter, siue essentialiter, donum Dei, & sic certe per se & principaliter ordinatur, & etiam immediate ad honorem Dei, & sic nullo modo potest vendi: quia nulla est res mundi, quæ illi fini præeligi debeat, nec sic possunt ab invicem separari materia & forma: quia statim desineret esse donum Dei, siue res spiritualis. Sic loquitur capit. proxime allegatum.
units.tr: The one who gives such goods to the Church is the efficient cause. God, on whose account he gives, or the ecclesiastical office for which he gives, is the final cause, from which the thing receives its name. The act of giving is the form, which gives the thing this kind of being. The thing given is the matter. From these there results a thing, namely a gift of God, composed of matter, that is, the thing that is given, and form, that is, the act of giving, as its intrinsic and so substantial principles. It is said, then, that such a thing given for the honour of God, as matter, together with the act of giving, which constitutes with it substantially, or essentially, a gift of God, is certainly ordered to that end per se and principally, and also immediately to the honour of God; and in this respect it can in no way be sold. For no worldly thing ought to be preferred to that end, nor can matter and form be separated from each other in this way, since the thing would at once cease to be a gift of God, or a spiritual thing. This is what the chapter cited just above means.

units.la: Sic etiam loquuntur iura superius allegata, scilicet cap. Saluator. & cap. ex multis. prim. quæstion. tert. quæ dicunt, quod sicut res a Deo fidelibus, ita res a fidelibus Deo datæ, dicuntur dona Dei. Alio modo dicta res donata potest considerari, quamuis respectu illius actus donantis habet se per modum materiæ: tamen respectu hominis, vel alterius rei, potest se habere per modum actus, seu formæ, scilicet in quantum humanæ vel alterius rei perfectibilis accidentaliter, & sic est in potestate nostra, ea perfici, vel vti, vel non, & per consequens, emere vel vendere.
units.tr: The laws cited above speak in the same way, namely cap. Saluator and cap. ex multis, 1 qu. 3, which say that just as things are given by God to the faithful, so things given by the faithful to God are called gifts of God. But the given thing may also be considered in another way: although with respect to the act of the giver it stands as matter, nevertheless with respect to a man, or to another thing, it can stand as act or form, namely insofar as it is accidentally perfectible by a human being or by another thing. In this respect it is in our power to perfect it, or to use it, or not, and consequently to buy or to sell it.

units.la: PET. Opinio quippe de contrario in me iam sufficientissime est extructa, per hæc tua dicta: quæ grato animo recipio, & errores in hac materia, quibus olim cum aliis errantibus ipse adhæseram, penitus sunt remoti.
units.tr: PET. Indeed, the opinion I held to the contrary has now been very thoroughly overturned by these words of yours. I gratefully accept them, and the errors on this subject, to which I once clung together with other mistaken men, have been entirely removed.

units.la: Reuertere nunc ad illius communis distinctionis sententiam, de simoniacis quia prohibitis, & prohibitis quia simoniacis: breviter pertractando, quæ prædictis erroribus videntur ministrasse occasionis fundamentum & fomentum.
units.tr: Now return to the view of that common distinction: that things are forbidden because they are simoniacal, and simoniacal because they are forbidden. Let us briefly examine what appear to have furnished the foundation and the fuel for these errors.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: In quo primo destruitur prædicta distinctio, de simoniacis quia prohibitis, ex iure canonico. Secundo declaratur, quod nulla sunt simoniaca secundum sui naturam, ad intentionem illorum. Item quod nulla sunt simoniaca quia prohibita.
units.tr: In which the aforesaid distinction, that things are simoniacal because they are forbidden, is first overthrown by canon law. Second, it is shown that nothing is simoniacal by its own nature, as far as their meaning goes. Likewise, that nothing is simoniacal merely because it is forbidden.

units.la: PAVL. Mirari sufficienter renera non valeo, de tot & tam famosis doctoribus, scribentibus in iure canonico, quos communiter in præmissa distinctione concordes reperio, hunc gravissimum & periculosissimum errorem non vidisse: & prædicta nedum non esse fundata aliquo textu iuris canonici, vel etiam aliqua ratione fulcita: imo non solum contra Euangelium, &c. sed contra solidos textus eiusdem Canonicæ facultatis videntur apparenter laborare, videlicet contra scripta solenniter canonizata sanctorum doctorum, scilicet Gregorii, Augustini, &cæter. diuina ne legis scripturas tractantium, ut aliqualiter tactum est c. Saluator, & alia supra, ut habentur verba Beati Augustini Euangelium exponentis, quo prohibetur omnis talis venditio. Quæ prædicti minus caute scribentes asseruerunt simoniaca, quia prohibita constitutione Ecclesiæ. Præterea, nonnè habentur vana, ad textum Beati Gregorii, Euangelium tractantis in canone, Sunt nonnulli, 1. quæst. 1. vbi ad declarandum modos simoniæ, adducit ad probandum dictum prophetiæ, iustum virum describentis, Isaiæ 33. cap. Beatus qui excutit manus suas ab omni munere: & ibi ipsam sic exponit: Tunc ab omni munere manus excutit, quando in diuinis rebus non solum nullam pecuniam, sed nec etiam humanam gratiam requirit. Et nisi etiam hoc intelligeretur de beneficiis, quæ etiam non minus sunt diuina, ut supra. Male etiam Papam, hanc auctoritatem exponendo, ad suum propositum allegaret, in cap. etsi quæstiones. de simon. præterea cap. in Ecclesiæ corpore. eo. tit. quod emanauit ex Concilio Lateranensi, expresse legitur: Quicunque acceperit pecuniam pro Episcopis, abbatibus, prioribus, seu quibuscunque personis Ecclesiasticis, ponendis in sede, seu introducendis in Ecclesiam, siue pro ingressu religionis, pro sepulturis, pro benedictionibus nubentium, &c. In primo dicit canon ille: Qui dederit vel receperit, vel consenserit, partem se cum Simone non dubitet habiturum. In alia dicit: Sciat se cum Iezi portionem habiturum. Idem 1. quæst. 3. Si quis, & multis aliis. Quod nisi talia emere vel vendere fuisset damnatum lege naturali, vel diuina, in personis Iezi, vel Simonis magi: quomodo hoc posset esse verum, quod ibi dicitur, nisi vendere, vel emere beneficia Ecclesiæ esset peccatum eiusdem speciei, scilicet simoniæ, vel Iesiæ, cum peccatis illorum? quod scilicet sic est: Si vnum similium sic indiuiduorum est lege diuina, seu naturali prohibitum, omnia similia sunt prohibita: quia idem est de similibus omnibus iudicium, vt in c. inter caeteras. de re. permut. in cap. inter corporalia. de translat. prælat. Si autem non sunt eiusdem speciei, quomodo constitutio Papæ vel concilii posset efficere, quod is qui non peccauit eodem peccato, vel eadem specie peccati cum Iezi, vel Simone, debeat magis cum eis portionem habere, quam cum homicidis, &c. aut cum eis similem damnationem incurrere, cum tamen non similiter cum eis peccauit? Cum dissimilium causarum dissimiles debeant esse effectus.
units.tr: PAUL. I honestly cannot marvel enough that so many famous teachers who have written on canon law, whom I find in agreement in the distinction above, have failed to see this most grave and dangerous error. Not only is the aforesaid view not founded on any text of canon law or supported by any reasoning, but it also seems to work openly against the Gospel, etc., and against the solid texts of this same canonical faculty. It runs against the writings of the holy teachers, solemnly accepted as canonical, namely Gregory, Augustine, etc., and the others who treated the Scriptures of the divine law, as was touched on in some measure in c. Saluator and elsewhere above, where the words of Blessed Augustine expounding the Gospel are found, in which every such sale is forbidden. Those who wrote too carelessly, as mentioned above, have declared these things simoniacal because they are forbidden by a constitution of the Church. Moreover, are not the following idle? In the canon Sunt nonnulli, 1. quæst. 1., Blessed Gregory, expounding the Gospel, in order to explain the kinds of simony, cites in proof the saying of the prophet describing the just man, Isaiah 33: "Blessed is he who shakes his hands free from every bribe." And there he explains it thus: Then a man shakes his hands free from every bribe when he seeks in divine matters not only no money, but not even human favour. Unless this also were understood of benefices, which are no less divine, as above. The Pope also wrongly applies this authority to his own purpose, in expounding it, in cap. etsi quæstiones. de simon. Further, in cap. in Ecclesiæ corpore. eo. tit., which issued from the Lateran Council, it is expressly read: Whoever shall have received money for bishops, abbots, priors, or any ecclesiastical persons, to be placed in a see or introduced into the Church, or for entry into a religious order, for burials, or for the blessings of those marrying, etc. In the first place that canon says: Whoever has given or received, or has consented, let him not doubt that he will have a share with Simon. In another place it says: Let him know that he will have a portion with Gehazi. Likewise 1. quæst. 3. Si quis, and many others. But unless buying or selling such things had been condemned by natural or divine law, in the persons of Gehazi or Simon the magician, how could what is said there be true, namely, that buying or selling benefices of the Church is a sin of the same species, that is, simony, or of Gehazi's sin, along with their sins? The reasoning is this: if one such individual act is forbidden by divine or natural law, all like acts are forbidden, since the same judgment holds for all like cases, as in c. inter caeteras. de re. permut. and in cap. inter corporalia. de translat. prælat. But if they are not of the same species, how could a constitution of the Pope or of a council bring it about that one who has not sinned with the same sin, or the same species of sin, as Gehazi or Simon, should rather have a share with them than with murderers, etc., or incur a like condemnation with them, when he has not sinned in a like manner with them? For dissimilar causes ought to have dissimilar effects.

units.la: Præterea ad idem: Quomodo posset credi hoc esse verum, quod factum, quod secundum naturam siue speciem non est peccatum simoniæ, idem propter constitutionem Papæ fiat simonia? quis eadem ratione, quod dese non est adulterium, vel homicidium, &c. posset esse potestate tale: quod est vtiq; erroneum dicere. Nomen quidem posset habere simonia ex constitutione Papæ, quia etiam posset vocari alba vacca, sicut quidam vocabant colorantes, vt in cap. in tantum. de simon: Sed si causæ essendi simoniæ ad factum con concurrunt; non potest Papa naturam rei aliter quam est appellare, vt in Can.plerique 14.quæst.3. aut vnum peccatum de sua specie in aliam transferre. Præterea legitur etiam in prædictis capitulis, non satis, & in cap. cum in Ecclesia, quod nec sub obtentu cuiusquam consuetudinis, reatum suum quis tueatur & adiicit: Quia diuturnitas temporis non minuit peccata, sed auget. In alio dicit, quod tanto graviora sunt peccata, quanto diutius infelicem detinent animam alligatam. Et in cap. in tantum. & in cap. sicut de simon. Et sequitur, quod consuetudo in talibus non excusat. Ex quibus, si bene perpenditur, constat hæc esse diuino vel naturali iure prohibita: cui consuetudo contraria quantumcunque diuturna derogare non potest, sicut iure positiuo potest. Vt in cap. vltim. de consuetud. sicut aliis pluribus non solum est derogatum, sed plura sunt abrogata 4. dist. 3. §. leges, & cap. statuimus. de treu. & pa. & cap. 1. Et manifeste textus loquitur in cap. ex diligenti. de simon. quod talis simonia in beneficio, de qua ibi casus, diuinis ac humanis legibus dignoscitur contraire. Bernh. & sequaces exposuerunt diuinis, id est canonicis. Non tamen est verum, sed stat proprie, pro vt lex diuina distinguitur contra canonicam: quia si Papa voluisset dicere canonicis, sicut communiter vtitur in aliis capitulis isto termino, ita leuiter dixisset canonicis, sicut diuinis, arg. decre. ad audientiam. de decim. & multis aliis rationibus in iuribus conuinci posset, hanc distinctionem, quoad illam partem, de simoniacis quia prohibitis, non posse subsistere: quæ propter breuitatem omittuntur, contra illos qui dicunt, titulos Ecclesiasticos non esse spiritualia de sui natura, ex constitutione Ecclesiæ sic vocata, quia ad similitudinem spiritualium.
units.tr: Moreover, to the same point: how could it be believed true that a deed which by its nature or kind is not a sin of simony becomes simony by the Pope's constitution? By the same reasoning, something that is not adultery or homicide, etc., could by power become such, which is certainly erroneous to say. Indeed, the name "simony" could be given by a papal constitution, just as some colourers were called "white cows", as in vt in cap. in tantum. de simon. But if the causes of being simony concur in the deed, the Pope cannot call the nature of a thing otherwise than it is, as in Can.plerique 14.quæst.3., or transfer one sin out of its own kind into another. Moreover, it is also read in the aforesaid chapters, non satis, and in cap. cum in Ecclesia, that no one may defend his guilt under the pretext of any custom whatever: Quia diuturnitas temporis non minuit peccata, sed auget ("Because length of time does not diminish sins, but increases them"). In another it says that tanto graviora sunt peccata, quanto diutius infelicem detinent animam alligatam ("sins are the heavier, the longer they hold the unhappy soul bound"). And in cap. in tantum. and in cap. sicut de simon., and it follows that custom excuses nothing in such matters. From these texts, if they are weighed carefully, it is established that these things are forbidden by divine or natural law, to which a contrary custom, however long-standing, cannot derogate, as it can derogate from positive law. As in cap. vltim. de consuetud.; just as many others have not only been derogated from, but several have been abrogated: 4. dist. 3. §. leges, & cap. statuimus. de treu. & pa. & cap. 1. And the text speaks plainly in cap. ex diligenti. de simon., that such simony in a benefice, of which the case there treats, diuinis ac humanis legibus dignoscitur contraire ("is recognized to be contrary to divine and human laws"). Bernard and his followers explained diuinis, id est canonicis ("divine, that is, canonical"). But this is not true; it stands properly, since divine law is distinguished against canonical law. For if the Pope had wished to say "canonical", as he commonly uses this term in other chapters, he would easily have said "canonical" just as he said "divine", cf. decre. ad audientiam. de decim. And by many other reasons drawn from the laws, it could be shown that this distinction, as far as that part concerning simoniacs because they are forbidden, cannot stand. These are omitted for brevity, against those who say that ecclesiastical titles are not spiritual by their own nature, but are called spiritual by a constitution of the Church, because they are like spiritual things.

units.la: PET. Non aliquid quæso relinquatur ambigui, sed etiam quoad aliam partem distinctionis iam descende. A nonnullis etiam dicitur ex scribentibus, beneficia non esse spiritualia de sui natura, sed ex constitutione Ecclesiæ sic vocata: quia ad similitudinem spiritualium sunt redacta. PAVL. Vt penitus euacuetur, videndum est primo, quæ sint illa vere spiritualia, quæ de sui natura talia. Si dicitur, sicut ab illis dicitur, quod sacramenta Ecclesiæ: & illud non est verum, quod essent de sui natura spiritualia, vt patet ex definitione sacramentorum: quæ est, Sacramentum est sacra rei signum: vel aliter, Est inuisibilis gratiæ visibilis forma, secundum Beatum Augustinum, & Magistrum sententiarum in quarto, dist. 1. Hæc autem visibilis forma, cum sit ens corporeum, non potest esse essentialiter, vel secundum sui naturam spirituale, sed solum per accidens. Præterea sacramenta non sunt spiritualia, nisi per sacramenta: sed quod sunt sacramenta, non est hoc secundum naturam eorum, sed ex institutione legis, vt notum est. Præterea solum accidentia spiritualia, sicut sunt virtutes, dona & scientiæ, sunt essentialiter, & secundum sui naturam spiritualia, vt notum est: & in his non committitur simonia, quæ est diuina lege prohibita. Quia nec etiam deliberatio, seu electio voluntatis emendi vel vendendi, cadit super talia.
units.tr: PETER. I beg that nothing ambiguous be left behind, but go down now also to the other part of the distinction. Some of the writers also say that benefices are not spiritual by their own nature, but are called so by the constitution of the Church, because they have been brought into the likeness of spiritual things. PAUL. To empty this completely, one must first see which things are truly spiritual by their own nature. If it is said, as they say, that the sacraments of the Church are such, that is not true, that they are spiritual by their own nature, as is plain from the definition of sacraments, which is: Sacramentum est sacra rei signum ("A sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing"); or otherwise: Est inuisibilis gratiæ visibilis forma ("It is the visible form of invisible grace"), according to Blessed Augustine and the Master of the Sentences in quarto, dist. 1. But this visible form, since it is a corporeal being, cannot be spiritual essentially or by its own nature, but only accidentally. Moreover, sacraments are not spiritual except through the sacraments; but that they are sacraments is not so by their nature, but from the institution of the law, as is known. Moreover, only spiritual accidents, such as virtues, gifts and knowledges, are essentially and by their own nature spiritual, as is known; and in these simony, which is forbidden by divine law, is not committed. Neither does the deliberation or choice of the will to buy or sell fall upon such things.

units.la: Quia si quis vellet talia emere, nec etiam posset quis vendere: quia voluntas non est impossibilium, vt patet tertio Ethicorum. Ergo necesse est dicere, quod simonia committatur in his quæ sunt per accidens spiritualia: scilicet quæ de se sunt corporalia, vt sacramenta, & eis annexa, vt vasa, vestimenta, &c. Similiter virtutes corporales, ministerium siue actus membrorum corporalium circa talia, vere & essentialiter sunt spiritualia: vt cantare, legere, conferre, absoluere: vel eis annexa, vt decimæ, &c. Et hæc omnia non quidem secundum sui naturam sunt spiritualia, sed per accidens: quia ad aliquod spirituale verum consequendum, fouendum, vel augendum, lege diuina vel canonica (non curo, quia hoc non diuersificat speciem spiritualium) ordinata, vel quia diuersificant species ad spiritus seu animæ perfectionem accidentalem. Quia hoc importat iste terminus prædicamenti qualitatis spirituale, qui formaliter connotat spiritualitatem, secundum quam anima perficitur. Et hæc ratio etiam omnibus spiritualibus conuenit, non solum sacramentis. Præterea consueuit à prædictis dici, quod venditio sacramentorum de sui natura est simoniaca, ideo quia lege diuina prohibita, & non peccatum, quia prohibita. Ex quo infertur, quod oportet dicere, quod ante prohibitionem legis diuinæ non fuerunt peccata, & per consequens, non simoniaca. Ex quo sequitur, quod Simon magus non peccauit isto peccato. Quia antequam Petrus maledixit ei, non fuit hoc peccatum prohibitum: nisi tunc prohibitio eius fuit facta, quando maledixit sibi, dicens: Pecunia tua sit tecum in perditionem. Et sequitur etiam, quod Petrus iniuste sibi maledixit, ex quo non peccauit, & per consequens, Simon non commisit tunc peccatum simoniæ, ex quo adhuc lege non fuit prohibitum. PAVL. Rationabiliter potest dici, quod in Veteri Testamento fuit prohibitum in persona Iezi. PAVL. Dicam de Iezi similiter, sicut de Simone: similiter etiam de Balaam Propheta, qui fuit ab angelo correptus pro eodem peccato, quia precium prophetiæ suæ acceperat, & tamen nullam legem receperat de prohibitione peccati istius. PET. Per sacramenta datur gratia: etiam sic ratione gratiæ est peccatum, ea vendere. Non sic est de beneficiis. PAVL. Tunc sequitur, quod quia sacramenta nouæ legis solum conferunt gratiam, & noua lege instituta est, quod etiam tunc primo incœpit peccatum simoniæ. Ex quo sequitur, quod Iezi, qui præcessit nouam legem, non peccasset hoc peccato, cuius contrarium Scripturæ prætendunt. Præterea arguitur, quod omnia spiritualia in quantum talia, sunt eiusdem speciei. Res dicuntur eiusdem speciei dupliciter, aut de se, & secundum naturam propriam, aut secundum aliquod accidens: hoc est dicere in Logica, aut per se, aut per accidens. Sacramenta alia non sunt spiritualia per se, quia per se esse seu dici præsupponit de omni, & semper, vt patet primo Posteriorum. Planum autem est, quod sacramenta non semper fuerunt talia, quia ante institutionem legis. Non ergo solum per accidens sunt eiusdem speciei: quia in eo quod conueniunt in aliqua qualitate eis communi, sunt similia inter se: vt homo albus, equus albus, in eo quod conueniunt in albedine, secundum quam sunt similes, dicuntur eiusdem speciei, non simpliciter, sed per accidens, secundum id accidens in quo communicant. Vel logicaliter, illa dicuntur eiusdem speciei per accidens, quæ significantur vniuoce per aliquem terminum communem accidentalem, vel de eis prædicabilem: vt per illum terminum albus, qui est de tertia specie prædicamenti Qualitatis. Sic in proposito: Omnia illa quæ non sunt per se, siue secundum eorum naturam spiritualia, sed per accidens, vt loca, ædificia, vestimenta, vasa, actus & operationes corporales: seu officia quæ exercentur organis corporalibus, vt legere, consecrare, pronunciare in Episcopum, supplicationes signare, sacramenta conferre, &c. quamuis inter se differunt specie sicut equus & asinus, tamen in eo conueniunt, & sunt similia secundum illam denominationem accidentalem: quia omnia dicuntur spiritualia propter officium quod habent ex institutione ad esse, & simpliciter spiritualia per accidens sunt eiusdem speciei. Et quia ille terminus Spirituale, prædicatur de his vniuoce, habes quod omnia sunt similia. PET. Videtur quod spirituale non vniuoce, sed æquiuoce, vel amphibologice dicatur de sacramentis, & aliis sacramentalibus. Nam sacramenta per prius & potiori ratione debent dici spiritualia, ex eo quod propinquius se habent ad gratiam, siue mere spirituale, scil. quod significant ex institutione, & efficiunt gratiam. Alia autem quæcunq; sacramentalia non significant, nec efficiunt. PAVL. Nec sacramenta, inquantum signa sunt gratiæ, dicuntur spiritualia: quia sic omne habens rationem signi, vt circulus ante tabernam, &c. esset spirituale. Nec etiam inquantum efficiunt quod figurant: quia sic quodlibet habens rationem causæ efficientis, esset spirituale, & sic de aliis considerationibus. Ergo necesse est dicere, quod sunt spiritualia, quia ad aliquem effectum spiritualem ordinantur. Vel ex aliquo spirituali principali, siue sit causa, instrumentum vel actus, siue per se, siue per accidens. Præterea dicit Philosophus secundo de Anima, quod actus distinguuntur per obiecta, & potentiæ per sensus, causæ vel virtutes per actus: quæcunque virtutes vel actus circa idem obiectum versantur, formaliter sunt eiusdem speciei. Sed omnium spiritualium rerum constat esse obiectum formale, scilicet esse spirituale. Ergo omnia spiritualia loca, cœmiteria, ædificia, vt Ecclesia, capella, vestimenta, casulæ, vasa, & calices, actus seu officia ministrorum Ecclesiasticorum circa talia, vt archidiaconorum, custodum, canonicorum, &c. prout concurrunt ad eundem finem, & ad idem obiectum consistunt, sunt eiusdem naturæ, vel rationis. Et per consequens, ex opposito venditio vel emptio eorum sunt peccata eiusdem speciei, per regulam Topicam: Sicut oppositum in opposito, sic propositum in proposito. Ex quibus inferri poterit, quod recipere vel dare pecuniam pro aliquo sepeliendo in cœmiterio, vel Ecclesia, non est minus simonia, quam vendere sacramenta. Et tamen per vnum quis plus peccat quam per aliud, propter circumstantias aggrauantes, vt patet infra. Item, dare vel recipere pecuniam pro beneficio Ecclesiastico, quantumcunque simplici, non est minus simonia, quam vendere vel emere corpus Christi. Item, ita non differunt secundum speciem peccati, dare indulgentias propter habendam pecuniam, & vendere quæcunque sacramenta, vel spiritum prophetiæ. Præterea nec ista minus differunt specie, recipere vel dare pecuniam pro officio audiendi confessiones, vel pro licentia conferendi vel recipiendi sacrum ordinem, quam vendere verum Deum pro triginta argenteis, sicut Iudas simoniacus & traditor fecit. Præterea nec etiam aliud est peccatum, dare beneficium Ecclesiasticum alicui propter consanguinitatem, vt inde parentela sua magnificetur, &c. vel preces carnales, seu amicitiam, vel obsequium, quæ vendere pro pecuniis. Infertur, quod nulla sunt simonica ideo, quia constitutione Ecclesiæ prohibita. Item, nulla sunt simoniaca, quia lege diuina prohibita sunt: quia ante legem diuinam erant simoniaca ex natura rei. Ex præmissis etiam colligitur, quod nulla sunt simoniaca ideo quia constitutione Ecclesiæ prohibita: imo econuerso propter hoc sunt prohibita tam diuina lege quam constitutionibus Ecclesiæ, quia peccata simoniaca. Sequitur insuper, quod nulla sunt simoniaca ideo, quia diuina lege prohibita, patet: quia antequam expressa prohibitio illius peccati fuit, siue Ecclesiæ promulgatio, sicut in maledictione Simonis magi, &c. prius vtiq; hoc peccatum commiserat. Quia alias oporteret inferri, quod prius fuisset punitus, quam peccasset: quod est inconueniens. Sequitur ergo, illud peccatum, ex quo prohibitionem legis præcessit, non esse simoniacum quia prohibitum. Nec ista dicitur prohibitio legis, sed potius pœnæ pro tali peccato manifestatio. Patet ergo, quod omne peccatum simoniæ est prohibitum, quia de sui natura peccatum, etiamsi nulla lex esset præter naturalem rationem. Et est ideo simoniacum, quia emptio, siue voluntas emendi quælibet spiritualia, est actus eiusdem speciei cum peccato Simonis magi. Et ad hunc sensum, quælibet emptio talium est prohibita, quia simoniaca. Venditio autem talium etiam dicitur simoniaca, capiendo generaliter: & ita vsus obtinuit. Proprie autem dicitur Iezia, à Iezi: vel Balaamia, à Balaam: qui fuerunt venditores doni Dei gratuiti. P E T. Iezi non vendidit aliquid spirituale, quia recepit argentum & vestimenta a illo, quem pater suus Elizeus curauit à lepra corporali. Recipere autem pro sanitate corporali, quæ est accidens corporis, differt specie ab actu recipiendi pro re spirituali: ex quo actus distinguuntur per obiecta, vt dixisti. Et per consequens, venditores spiritualium non conuenienter dicuntur Iezitæ, sicut emptores dicuntur simoniaci. P A V L. Dupliciter aliquid dicitur spirituale. Vno modo, in quantum effectiue seu obiectiue terminatur ad aliquod spirituale, vt dictum est. Alio modo, habendo respectum ad suum principium, à quo procedit: puta quod competit alicui ex quodam spirituali dono, vel officio. Et sic actus sanandi corpus miraculose, quemadmodum fecit Elizeus, fuit effectus spiritualis doni Dei gratuiti.
units.tr: PAUL. For if someone wished to buy such things, one could not even sell them, since the will is not directed at impossible things, as is clear in the third book of the Ethics. Therefore we must say that simony is committed in those things that are spiritual only by accident: namely, things that are corporeal in themselves, such as sacraments and things attached to them, like vessels, vestments, and so on. Likewise, bodily powers, or the ministry and actions of the bodily members in relation to such things, such as singing, reading, conferring, and absolving, are truly and essentially spiritual, or else attached to them, like tithes. None of these is spiritual by its own nature, but only by accident, because they are ordained by divine or canonical law (I do not care which, since this does not alter the species of spiritual things) to attain, foster, or increase some true spiritual end, or because they contribute to the accidental perfection of the spirit or soul. This is what the predicament of quality means by the term "spiritual," which formally connotes the spirituality by which the soul is perfected. And this reason applies to all spiritual things, not only to sacraments. Furthermore, it is commonly said by those mentioned above that the sale of sacraments is simoniacal by its very nature, because it is forbidden by divine law, and not a sin merely because it is forbidden. From this it follows that we must say that before the prohibition of divine law there were no sins, and consequently no simony. From this it follows that Simon Magus did not commit this sin: for before Peter cursed him, this sin had not been forbidden, unless its prohibition was made at the time he was cursed, when Peter said, "Let your money perish with you." It follows too that Peter cursed him unjustly, since Simon had not sinned, and consequently Simon did not then commit the sin of simony, since it had not yet been forbidden by law. PET. It can reasonably be said that in the Old Testament it was forbidden in the person of Gehazi. PAUL. I will say of Gehazi what I said of Simon; likewise of Balaam the prophet, who was rebuked by an angel for the same sin, because he had accepted payment for his prophecy, and yet had received no law forbidding that sin. PET. Grace is given through the sacraments; therefore, because of grace, it is a sin to sell them. This is not the case with benefices. PAUL. Then it follows that since the sacraments of the new law only confer grace, and the new law was instituted, the sin of simony began then for the first time. From this it follows that Gehazi, who preceded the new law, did not commit this sin, although the Scriptures maintain the contrary. Furthermore, it is argued that all spiritual things, as such, are of the same species. Things are said to be of the same species in two ways: either in themselves and according to their own nature, or according to some accident; that is, in the language of logic, either per se or per accidens. Sacraments are not spiritual per se, because what is said per se must hold of everything and always, as is clear from the first book of the Posterior Analytics. Now it is plain that sacraments were not always such, since they existed before the institution of the law. Therefore they are not of the same species only by accident, because things that agree in some quality common to them are alike among themselves: as a white man and a white horse, insofar as they agree in whiteness, by which they are alike, are said to be of the same species, not absolutely, but accidentally, according to the accident in which they share. Or, logically, those things are said to be of the same species accidentally which are signified univocally by some common accidental term, or term predicable of them: as by the term "white," which belongs to the third species of the predicament of Quality. So in the present case: all those things which are not spiritual per se, or according to their nature, but only accidentally, such as places, buildings, vestments, vessels, bodily acts and operations, or offices exercised by bodily organs, such as reading, consecrating, pronouncing a man bishop, signing supplications, conferring sacraments, and so on, although they differ in species as a horse differs from an ass, nevertheless agree in this, and are alike according to that accidental designation: for all are called spiritual because of the office they have by institution, and things that are spiritual only by accident are of the same species in the strict sense. And since the term "spiritual" is predicated of them univocally, you have that all are alike. PET. It seems that "spiritual" is said of sacraments and other sacramentals not univocally but equivocally, or ambiguously. For sacraments ought to be called spiritual first and in the stronger sense, because they stand nearer to grace, or to what is purely spiritual, namely, because they signify by institution and effect grace. But all other sacramentals neither signify nor effect. PAUL. Nor are sacraments called spiritual insofar as they are signs of grace, for then everything having the character of a sign, such as a circle before a tavern, would be spiritual. Nor insofar as they effect what they figure, for then whatever has the character of an efficient cause would be spiritual, and so on with other considerations. Therefore we must say that they are spiritual because they are ordained to some spiritual effect, or because of some principal spiritual thing, whether it be cause, instrument, or act, whether per se or per accidens. Furthermore, the Philosopher says in the second book of On the Soul that acts are distinguished by their objects, powers by their operations, and causes or virtues by their acts: whatever powers or acts are concerned with the same object are formally of the same species. But it is evident that the formal object of all spiritual things is to be spiritual. Therefore all spiritual things, places, cemeteries, buildings such as a church or chapel, vestments, chasubles, vessels and chalices, and the acts or offices of ecclesiastical ministers in relation to them, such as those of archdeacons, sacristans, canons, and so on, insofar as they concur toward the same end and rest upon the same object, are of the same nature or kind. Consequently, by the opposite reasoning, buying or selling them are sins of the same species, by the rule of the Topics: as the opposite is to the opposite, so the proposition is to the proposition. From these points it may be inferred that to receive or give money for burying someone in a cemetery or church is no less simony than selling sacraments. And yet one person may sin more than another through the same act, because of aggravating circumstances, as will appear below. Likewise, to give or receive money for an ecclesiastical benefice, however simple, is no less simony than to sell or buy the body of Christ. Likewise, giving indulgences in order to obtain money does not differ in species from selling any sacraments, or the spirit of prophecy. Furthermore, receiving or giving money for the office of hearing confessions, or for licence to confer or receive holy orders, differs no less in species than selling the true God for thirty pieces of silver, as Judas, the simoniac and traitor, did. Moreover, it is no different sin to give an ecclesiastical benefice to someone on account of kinship, so that his family may be magnified, and so on, or for carnal entreaties, friendship, or favour, than to sell it for money. It follows that nothing is simoniacal merely because it is forbidden by church constitution. Likewise, nothing is simoniacal merely because it is forbidden by divine law, since before the divine law they were simoniacal by the nature of the thing. From what has been said it is also gathered that nothing is simoniacal merely because it is forbidden by church constitution; rather, on the contrary, for this reason they are forbidden both by divine law and by the constitutions of the Church, because they are simoniacal sins. It further follows that nothing is simoniacal merely because it is forbidden by divine law; this is clear, because before the express prohibition of that sin, or the promulgation by the Church, as in the cursing of Simon Magus, that sin had already been committed. Otherwise it would have to follow that he was punished before he sinned, which is absurd. It follows, then, that the sin which preceded the prohibition of the law is not simoniacal because it is forbidden. Nor is this called a prohibition of the law, but rather a declaration of the punishment for such a sin. It is plain, therefore, that every sin of simony is forbidden because it is a sin by its very nature, even if there were no law except natural reason. And it is simoniacal because buying, or the will to buy, any spiritual things is an act of the same species as the sin of Simon Magus. And in this sense, every purchase of such things is forbidden because it is simoniacal. Selling such things is also called simoniacal, taking the term generally, and this usage has prevailed. But properly it is called "Gehazism" from Gehazi, or "Balaamism" from Balaam, who were sellers of the free gift of God. PET. Gehazi did not sell anything spiritual, since he received silver and garments from the man whom his master Elisha had healed of bodily leprosy. But to receive payment for bodily health, which is an accident of the body, differs in species from the act of receiving payment for a spiritual thing, since acts are distinguished by their objects, as you said. Consequently, sellers of spiritual things are not fittingly called Gehazites, as buyers are called simoniacs. PAUL. Something is called spiritual in two ways. In one way, insofar as it is effectively or objectively directed to some spiritual thing, as has been said. In another way, by having regard to its principle from which it proceeds, namely, that it belongs to someone by some spiritual gift or office. And so the act of healing a body miraculously, as Elisha did, was an effect of the spiritual gift of God's free grace.

units.la: P E T. Grauissimæ mihi videntur dictæ conclusiones, imo errori sunt vicinæ. Nam non est sceleratius delictum, quod est gravius vindicatum. 24. q. 1. auferimus. Et in quo maior fuerit culpa, maior exercetur vindicta. 3o. di. quia in tua. Sed graviori pœna punitur venditor vel emptor sacramentorum, quam beneficiorum, vel aliorum inferiorum spiritualium, de accu. super his, & c. inquisitionis de simo. tantam. 1. q. 3. peruenit. Si ergo quoad pœnam sunt diuersa, ergo erunt diuersa quo ad culpam: quia iuxta qualitatem delicti debet esse plagarum modus, & per consequens, diuersa erunt peccata quoad speciem. P A V L. Quod peccatum aliud est culpabilius, vel magis puniatur quam aliud, provenit non solum ex natura actus, sed quandoq; propter circumstantias aggrauantes, quæ sunt in duplici differentia. Quædam transmutant in aliam speciem peccati. Exemplum: Si furtum fit in sacro loco, vel de re sacra, iam non dicitur simpliciter furtum, sed propter illas circumstantias actus dicitur sacrilegium. Sic vendere vel emere rem sacram, iam venditio est simonia: vbi si non esset res sacra, non esset simonia. Et tales circumstantiæ sunt de necessitate confessionis sacramentalis, de pœni. dist. 5. considéret: vbi clare habetur de eis. Aliæ autem sunt circumstantiæ aggrauantes peccatum, sed non transmutantes in aliam speciem: scil. dignitas personæ, vel res circa quam peccatum committitur. De quibus dantur metra: Aggrauat ordo, locus, peccata, scientia, tempus, Status, conditio, numerus, mora, copia, causa.
units.tr: PETER. The conclusions seem to me very grave, indeed close to error. For no crime is more wicked than one that is punished more severely. 24. q. 1. auferimus. And the greater the fault, the greater the punishment inflicted. 30. di. quia in tua. But the seller or buyer of sacraments is punished more severely than the seller or buyer of benefices or other lesser spiritual things: de accu. super his, &c.; inquisitionis de simo. tantam; 1. q. 3. peruenit. If, then, they differ as to punishment, they must also differ as to guilt, because the measure of the blows must match the nature of the offence, and consequently the sins will differ in kind. PAUL. That one sin is more culpable, or punished more heavily, than another arises not only from the nature of the act but sometimes from aggravating circumstances, which are of two kinds. Some change the act into a different kind of sin. For example, if theft is committed in a holy place or of a holy thing, it is no longer called simple theft but sacrilege, because of those circumstances. So to sell or buy a holy thing is already simony, whereas if the thing were not holy it would not be simony. Such circumstances are necessarily part of sacramental confession: de pœni. dist. 5. considéret, where they are clearly set out. Other circumstances aggravate the sin without changing it into another kind, namely the dignity of the person or the matter about which the sin is committed. Verses are given about these: "Rank, place, sins, knowledge, time, status, condition, number, delay, abundance, cause, aggravate."

units.la: Et licet æque omnia dicuntur spiritualia, tamen quia vnum propinquius perficit spiritualiter, vt sacramenta; per quæ immediate confertur gratia, quam alia remotiora: igitur plus peccat vendendo sacramenta, quam alias res spirituales: quia illud, quod propinquius fini, & magis diligibile, minus diligit: & per consequens, à charitate plus distat. Et sic etiam quanto sacramentum est excellentius, vt corpus Christi, plus peccat illud vendendo, quam alia sacramenta. Magis autem, vel minus, non diuersificat speciem. P E T. Quid respondebitur communiter dicentibus, quod tituli sunt inducti, & inuenti iure positiuo? vt in principio huius secundæ partis allegaui superius. P A V L. Plane dicendum est, hoc non est verum. Inducti enim fuerunt in Veteri Testamento, Numer. 18. vbi Dominus commisit spirituale ministerium Aaroni sacerdoti, & Leuiticæ tribui, dicens: Tu autem, & filii tui ministrabitis in tabernaculo testimonii, excubabuntque Leuitæ ad præcepta tua & ad cuncta opera tabernaculi. Tu autem & filii tui custodite sacerdotium vestrum, & omnia quæ ad cultum altaris pertinent. Et quia propter officium datur beneficium, paucis interpositis subdit: Ego dedi tibi custodiam primitiarum mearum: omnia quæ sacrificantur à filiis Israel, tradidi tibi & filiis tuis, pro officio sacerdotali legitima sempiterna. Ibidem Deut. 14. & in aliis locis, Ecce quomodo ius sacerdotii in tabernaculo committebatur Leuitis, & alia ad cultum diuinum exercendi: quod idem est in specie cum iure tituli, quo nunc exercentur spiritualia in Ecclesia. Quamuis in accidentalibus, seu accessoriis, vt in ceremonialibus, &c. sit differentia, sicut & nunc omnes tituli Ecclesiastici sunt eiusdem speciei, sed solum diuersificantur penes accessoria. A quibus accessoriis frequenter recipiunt denominationem. Nam praepositura, cantoria, archidiaconatus, custodia, & sic de aliis, circa idem obiectum principaliter versantur, & ad eundem finem, scilicet diuinum officium peragendum in Ecclesia, accessorie habent exercere aliqua vltra alios circa diuinum officium, sicut res Ecclesiae custodire, in choro praecinere, &c. quamuis illa nomina titulorum non fuerunt tempore Apostolorum, vel ante in Veteri Testamento: fuerunt tamen similia diuersis cermoniis, vel officiis correspondentia. Et haec sufficiant pro secundo tractatu, Domino annuente.
units.tr: And although all of these are said to be spiritual, nevertheless, since one thing perfects spiritually more closely, as the sacraments do, through which grace is conferred immediately, while other things are more remote, it follows that a person sins more by selling sacraments than by selling other spiritual things. For what is nearer to the end and more to be loved, one loves less, and consequently stands further from charity. And so too, the more excellent the sacrament, such as the body of Christ, the more one sins in selling it than in selling other sacraments. Yet greater or lesser does not diversify the kind. PET. What will be answered by those who commonly say that titles were introduced and devised by positive law, as I alleged above at the beginning of this second part? PAUL. It must plainly be said that this is not true. For they were introduced in the Old Testament, Numbers 18, where the Lord committed the spiritual ministry to Aaron the priest and the tribe of Levi, saying: But thou and thy sons shall minister in the tabernacle of the testimony, and the Levites shall watch at thy commandments and at all the works of the tabernacle. But thou and thy sons keep your priesthood, and all things that pertain to the altar. And because a benefice is given on account of the office, after a few intervening words he adds: I have given thee the keeping of my firstfruits: all the things that are sacrificed by the children of Israel I have given to thee and to thy sons, by a perpetual statute for the priestly office. Likewise Deut. 14, and in other places. See how the right of the priesthood in the tabernacle was committed to the Levites, and the right to perform other parts of the divine worship, which is the same in kind as the right of title by which spiritual things are now exercised in the Church. Although there is a difference in accidentals or accessories, as in ceremonial matters, just as all ecclesiastical titles now are of the same kind but are distinguished only by their accessories. From these accessories they often take their names. For the provostship, the precentorship, the archdeaconry, the wardenship and the like are concerned principally with the same object and for the same end, namely the performance of divine worship in the Church, and they have accessorily to exercise certain functions beyond others in connection with divine worship, such as keeping the church's property or leading the chant in the choir. Although those names of titles did not exist in the time of the Apostles or earlier in the Old Testament, there were nonetheless similar things corresponding to various ceremonies or offices. Let these suffice for the second treatise, the Lord willing.

units.la: TERTIA PARS.
units.tr: THE THIRD PART.

units.la: HVius Tractatus Pars Tertia ex veris fundamentis declarat Romanam curiam esse erroneam, & in statu damnationis laborantem, cum omnibus qui exorbitantes gratias a iure communi, & beneficia Ecclesiastica suntadepti. Et declaratur plenitudo potestatis Papae, & habet quatuor capitula.
units.tr: This third part of this Treatise, on sound foundations, declares that the Roman curia is in error and lies in a state of damnation, together with all those who have obtained extraordinary graces contrary to the common law and ecclesiastical benefices. It also sets out the fullness of the Pope's power, and it has four chapters.

units.la: In primo capitulo ostenditur, de omnibus officialibus dictae curiae, & aliis Curtisanis, qui impendunt aliquod seruitium pro gratia simoniace obtinenda, siue circa supplicationes, literas, siue lites, ipsos esse simoniae participes. In secundo capitulo declaratur, quomodo Cardinales non possunt excusari a participatione simoniae: & quantum ipsorum negligentia & taciturnitas est culpabilis, & nociua. In tertio capitulo, obiicitur propter latitudinem potestatis Papae. Et condemnatur multiplicatio gratiarum, cum illis qui sunt consecuti beneficia per exorbitantes gratias. In quarto obiicitur propter plenitudinem potestatis Papae, distinctio, per quam cognoscitur, circa quae & quomodo consistit dicta plenitudo potestatis Papae: & quae sunt dispensabilia, & quae indispensabilia, declaratur.
units.tr: In the first chapter it is shown that all the officials of the said curia, and the other courtiers who render any service in order to obtain a grace by simony, whether in connection with supplications, letters or lawsuits, are themselves sharers in the simony. In the second chapter it is explained how the cardinals cannot be excused from sharing in simony, and how far their negligence and silence are blameworthy and harmful. In the third chapter, an objection is raised on account of the breadth of the Pope's power, and the multiplication of graces is condemned, together with those who have obtained benefices through extraordinary graces. In the fourth, an objection is raised on account of the fullness of the Pope's power, and the distinction by which we recognise what the said fullness of the Pope's power concerns and how it consists is set out, and which things are dispensable and which indispensable is declared.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAP. I.

units.la: In quo ostenditur, vt supra in summa capitulorum.
units.tr: In which it is shown, as above in the summary of the chapters.

units.la: PET. Iam clare videtur, quod executoribus simoniae est sublata executio: & fundamentum, quo videbantur innixi, radicitus extirpatum. Vt mihi videtur, haeresis est, asserere quod Papa licite possit pro spirituali titulo recipere pecuniam: & multo magis, hoc facere in effectu. Propter quod videtur mihi, Paule, quod tota Romana curia est in via damnationis, per ea quae superius demonstrasti. Omnis enim curtisanus ipso facto sui officii videtur particeps Simoniae: etsi dicam, non tamen forte incurrit, fautor haereticae prauitatis. PAVL. Si huius rei quaeris euidentiam, hoc attende. Sicut enim actu meritorio, de quanto aliquis magis vel propinquius iuuat ad consummationem illius, de tanto (caeteris paribus) magis meretur: quia in omnibus bene ordinatis, de quanto aliquid fini propinquius, de tanto in primo ordine perfectionis laudabilius: vt patet 1. Ethicorum. Dico, caeteris paribus, quia vidua duo minuta offerens, plus aliis magis offerentibus meruit. Luc. 21. Sic est e conuerso in actu turpitudinis, & demeritorio, per cuiuscunque factum, officium, siue ministerium magis promouetur actus simoniacus, quo fini ad ipsius effectum propinquius peruenitur, caeteris paribus sine dubio magis peccat. Sic dicimus de homicidio, per ea quae leguntur in cap. sicut dignum. de homi. vbi habetur casus de Beato Thoma Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo. Ratio huius habet se per oppositum, ad rationem precedentem. Quia in persecutione actus vel effectus simoniaci, in ordine actuum concurrentium, ipsum actum vel effectum praecedentium, de quanto actus effectui propinquior, de tanto inordinatior, quia magis distat a vero ordine, in ipsum exercendo peius eligit, quia sine electione & voluntate ipsum non exercet. Ex quo sequitur, quod minus diligit, & per consequens, plus distat a vera & ordinata dilectione seu charitate, & ita plus peccat. PET. Fiat Curtisanus in factis Romanae curiae, exempli gratia, vt huius conclusionis experiamur plenius veritatem, & per hoc tam ipsius quam eorum conuersio salubrius consolatur. PAVL.
