Si enim in gratiis, siue indulgentiis obtinendis aliqui sunt, qui ad obtinendum iuuant, vt supplicationes scribentes, & scriptas deferentes ad eos qui vlterius promouent, & porrigunt ad signandum. Aliqui vero sunt, vel aliquis, qui prouidet, quem exprimere non oportet, ad maiorem notitiam declarandam. Tertii sunt, qui in prouisione simoniaca, facta ad effectualem ipsius consummationem habendam, sua seruitia impendunt: vt puta datarius, qui datam apponit. Secundo, defertur ad registrum supplicationum. Tertio, ibi registratur. Quarto, registratae portantur ad cancellariam. Quinto, per vicecancellarium distribuuntur abbreuiatoribus. Sexto, per ipsos conficiuntur minutae, & soluitur quod taxatur. Septimo, ad ingrossandum scriptoribus distribuuntur. Octauo, taxantur. Scriptae vero, taxatae, & solutae, in cancellaria iudicantur, & interdum cancellantur. Nono, ad bullandum portantur: tandem registrantur, & iuramenta in camera fiunt pro annatis, & etiam solutiones pro pacatis. Et hi omnes secundum ordinem, & quicunque alii, sicut sunt sollicitatores, seu procuratores literarum huiusmodi, vel scriptores processuum, & generaliter quicunque aliquid seruitii impendunt, vt tales literae effectum habeant, peccant mortaliter: quia omnes participes sunt simoniae.
units.tr: PETER: It is now clearly evident that the executors of simony have had their execution taken away, and the foundation on which they seemed to rest has been torn up by the roots. It seems to me heretical to assert that the Pope may lawfully receive money for a spiritual title, and much more so to do this in effect. For this reason, Paul, it seems to me that the whole Roman curia is on the road to damnation, according to what you have demonstrated above. For every courtier, by the very fact of his office, seems to be a partaker in simony; and although I may say so, he perhaps does not fall into the guilt of heretical depravity. PAUL: If you seek clear evidence of this, consider the following. Just as in a meritorious act, the more closely and directly someone helps towards its completion, the more (other things being equal) he merits; because in all well-ordered things, the closer a thing is to its end, the more praiseworthy it is in the first order of perfection, as is clear from the first book of the Ethics. I say "other things being equal," because the widow who offered two small coins merited more than the others who offered more (Luke 21). It is the same in the converse case, in an act of wickedness and demerit: through whatever deed, office or ministry an act of simony is advanced, by which the end of its effect is reached more closely, other things being equal, without doubt he sins more. We say the same of homicide, according to what is read in the chapter "Sicut dignum," On Homicide, where there is the case of the Blessed Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. The reason for this stands in opposition to the preceding reason. For in the pursuit of a simoniacal act or effect, among the acts concurring in order, the closer an act is to the effect itself, the more disordered it is, since it departs further from the true order; in carrying it out, he chooses the worse, for he does not carry it out without choice and will. From this it follows that he loves less, and consequently is further from true and ordered love or charity, and so sins more. PETER: Let us take a courtier in the business of the Roman curia, for example, so that we may experience the truth of this conclusion more fully, and through this their conversion may be more wholesomely consoled. PAUL: If, in obtaining favours or indulgences, there are some who help to obtain them, such as those who write supplications and carry the written ones to those who advance them further and hand them up for signature; and some who provide (whom it is not fitting to name), in order to declare the greater knowledge; and third are those who, in a simoniacal provision, devote their services to bringing it to its effective completion, as for example the datary, who affixes the date: (1) it is then referred to the register of supplications; (2) it is registered there; (3) the registered documents are carried to the chancery; (4) they are distributed by the vice-chancellor to the abbreviators; (5) the drafts are made by them, and the taxed sum is paid; (6) they are distributed to the scribes to be engrossed; (7) they are taxed. Written, taxed and paid documents are judged in the chancery, and sometimes cancelled. (8) They are carried to be sealed with the bulla; finally they are registered, and oaths are taken in the camera for the annates, and also payments are made for the pacts. All of these, in order, and whoever else, such as the solicitors or agents of such letters, or the writers of the proceedings, and generally whoever renders any service so that such letters may have effect, sin mortally, because all are partakers in simony.

units.la: PET. Mira res igitur est, quod extractis literis non solum cum peccato vnius, sed multorum primo, tunc ad lites perveniitur: cuius contrarium raro accidit, in quibus odia excitantur, & homines se consumunt gravibus laboribus & expensis, & quod hoc in cor praesidentium non ascendit. PAVL. In his quae ad lites huiusmodi, aut potius ad consummationem effectus simoniaci concurrunt litigantibus auxilia, similiter aliam lineam, quam praememoratam poteris facere per hunc modu. Nam scribitur commissio, in qua auditori committitur, ut citet, & iustitiam faciat. Secundo, manus apponitur, ut appareat de mandato Domini Papae. Tertio, auditori praesentatur: qua humiliter recepta, notario assignatur, citatio decernitur, demum citationis fit executio. Postea ad actus iudiciales observandos, sollicitatorum, procuratorum, & notariorum concurrit diligentia, & communia patrocinia advocatorum. Demum auditoris fertur sententia: quae cum executioni demandatur, tunc per festissime simonia consummatur. Haec dearticulate dico, ideo quod nullus Cuiusquam se credere debeat excusatum. Et dixi notanter, quod per cuiuscunque factum propinquius, vel magis peruenitur ad effectum peccati, ceteris paribus, ille plus peccat ex ordine supra dicto. Nam stat bene, primum, vel secundum, in prosecutione facti magis peccare, ut patet, quam ultimum, ex aliis circumstantiis peccatum aggravantibus puta, qui scribens supplicationem, vel datam, &c. est Episcopus, vel Doctor, vel religiosus, vel plura exercens officia: & sic de aliis circumstantiis, de quibus plene in Can. consideret. de poen. dist. 5. de quibus dantur metra:
units.tr: PETER: It is a strange thing, then, that once the letters have been obtained, litigation follows not only with the sin of one person but first of many; whereas the opposite rarely happens, in which hatreds are stirred up and men consume themselves with heavy labours and expenses, and this does not come into the hearts of those who preside. PAUL: In these matters, which contribute to such litigation, or rather to the completion of the simoniacal effect, the litigants receive help, and you may draw a similar line to the one mentioned before, in this way. For a commission is written, by which the auditor is charged to summon and do justice. Second, a hand is placed upon it, so that it appears to be by the mandate of the lord Pope. Third, it is presented to the auditor; once humbly received, it is assigned to a notary, a citation is decreed, and at last the citation is executed. Afterwards, to observe the judicial acts, the diligence of solicitors, procurators and notaries concurs, and the common patronage of advocates. At last the sentence of the auditor is pronounced; and when this is committed to execution, then simony is most fully consummated. I say these things point by point, so that no one may believe himself excused. And I have said deliberately that, through whatever deed the effect of sin is reached more closely or more directly, other things being equal, that person sins more, according to the order stated above. For it is well established that the first or second person in the carrying out of a deed sins more, as is evident, than the last, when other circumstances aggravate the sin: for example, he who writes the supplication, or the date, is a bishop, a teacher, a religious, or one who holds several offices; and so with other circumstances, of which more fully in the Canon "consideret," On Penance, distinction 5, of which verses are given:

units.la: Quis, quid, vbi, per quod, quotiens, cur, quomodo, quando, Quilibet obseruet animae medicamina dando.
units.tr: Who, what, where, by what means, how often, why, in what manner, when: let everyone observe these remedies for the soul in giving them.

units.la: PET. Contingit, Paule, saepius, quod una persona plura exercet officia, sicut vnus abbreviator scribit supplicationem minutam & grossam, & in causa sollicitat. Sic etiam procurator quamuis vnu exercet officium, tamen plures causas fouet, & procurat. Similiter aduocatus, & auditor. Praeterea, etsi est vnica causa, & non plures, tamen in ea interpollatim plures actus exercentur. Dic quid tibi videtur hic? an istorum quilibet pro officiis, omnibus actibus & causis simul sumptis, vnum tantum peccatum mortale incurrat, vel pro quolibet illorum singulariter aliud & aliud sit peccatum? PAVL. Attende in hoc dictum Philosophi 5. Physicorum, vbi innuit, quod quilibet actus mensuratur penes terminum a quo, & terminum ad quem. Si igitur terminus a quo, est vnus numero, & terminus principalis ad quem, est diuersus numero: actus oportet esse diuersos, & econuerso. Vnde si duo concurrent ad eundem effectum in numero, puta ad occidendum hominem vnum, quamuis idem sit numero effectus amborum, tamen duo sunt actus, & per consequens, peccata e conuerso, licet eadem persona in numero, tamen quia pluribus causis distinctorum numero effectuum ministrat, tot vere peccata committit, quot erunt supplicationes, literae, aut causae, quibus ministrat ad distinctos fines inducendos ordinate. Et ideo non sufficit confitenti dicere, Ego fui notarius, vel procurator, &c. in talibus causis, vel factis, &c. sed necesse habet, si recordari poterit, numerum dicere: Tot supplicationes, minutas, literas scripsi, in prouisionibus per simonam obtentis: vel in tot causis, tale officium, a principio vsque ad finem ipsarum exercui, &c. Hinc est, si vna persona exercet diuersa ossicia, vel in vno officio multos actus, tunc si haec omnia concurrunt ad eundem effectum inducendum, omnia illa intermedia erunt vnus totalis actus: & per consequens, vnum peccatum. Hoc tamen verum, quod de quanto plura exercet officia, vel in eodem officio plures actus, tanto peccatum illius plus aggravatur. Sufficit tamen ad mortale vnus actus. PET. Inter illos, plures arguit mortale: an primus, scil. ad dicendum contra commissionem, vel secundus ad libellandum assignatus, & sic de aliis, & quodcunq; eorum assignatur, eadem ratione erit quilibet eorum peccatum. Et sic necesse habes dicere, quod quilibet actus prohibiti seu illiciti negotii partialis, est mortale: vel ex aduerso oportebit asserere, quod nullus eorum sit peccatum. Praeterea in actibus illicitis corporeis, in quibus naturaliter cadit successiua interruptio, pro quolibet debito est vnum: vt in l. foramen. ff. de seruitut. praedio. PAVL. Cum enim peccatum potenter & radicaliter existat in anima, quod est auersio voluntatis a bono incommutabili ad bonum commutabile, communiter in actu exteriori, siue corporeo, tanquam ab ipsa voluntate imperato: ideo quam cito voluntas consentit tali negotio prohibito peragendo, iam etiamsi nullus actus consequeretur, peccatum est nihilominus in voluntate perpetratum: sed non nisi peracto negotio, actibus corporeis dicitur consummatum. Vnde stante eodem consensu voluntatis, sine interruptione a principio negotii vsq; ad finem, quamuis naturaliter illi actus partiales integrantes negotium interrumpunt, tamen quia eis non correspondet iterario voluntatis, saltem habitualis, non possunt dici plura peccata, sed vnum. Quia idem est terminus a quo, scil. eadem voluntas, & terminus ad quem, etiam idem omnium mediorum. Secus esset, etiam si in prosecutione, vel ante, mutaretur voluntas ad contrarium, & postmodum voluntatem resumeret in prosequendo, & tunc, quotiescunq; mutatam voluntatem resumeret, totiens peccaret. Nec illa intermedia essent vnus actus, quamuis ad eundem effectum tenderent, sed diuersi, propter diuersum terminum a quo scil. mutatione voluntatis, vel etiam si finis per se daretur cuilibet actui specialis.
units.tr: PET. Paul, it often happens that one person exercises several offices. For example, one abbreviator writes a supplication in both the minute and the engrossed form, and also solicits in the case. Likewise a procurator, although he exercises one office, nevertheless fosters and conducts several cases. The same holds for an advocate and an auditor. Moreover, even when there is only one case and not several, several acts are performed in it at intervals. Tell me what you think here. Does each of these people, for all his offices and acts and cases taken together, incur only one mortal sin, or is each sin separate and different for each one taken singly? PAUL. Consider in this matter the saying of the Philosopher in the fifth book of the Physics, where he hints that every act is measured by its terminus from which and its terminus to which. If, then, the terminus from which is one in number, and the principal terminus to which is different in number, the acts must be different, and conversely. Hence, if two agents combine toward the same effect in number, for example to kill one man, then although the effect of both is numerically the same, there are still two acts, and consequently two sins; and conversely, although the same person in number, yet because he ministers to several effects distinct in number, he commits as many true sins as there are supplications, letters, or cases by which he ministers to distinct ends brought about in order. And therefore it is not enough for the penitent to say, "I was a notary or procurator," etc., in such cases or deeds, etc.; he is bound, if he can remember, to state the number: "I wrote so many supplications, drafts and letters, in provisions obtained through simony," or "in so many cases I exercised such an office from the beginning to the end of them," etc. Hence, if one person exercises diverse offices, or many acts in one office, and if all these combine to bring about the same effect, then all those intermediate acts will be one total act and consequently one sin. This is true, however, in that the more offices a person exercises, or the more acts he performs in the same office, the more his sin is aggravated. Yet a single act is enough for a mortal sin. PET. Among those several acts you argue that one is mortal: is it the first, namely the one aimed at drawing up the commission, or the second, the one assigned to drafting the libel, and so on? And by the same reasoning, whichever of them is assigned will be a sin in itself. So you must say either that every act of a forbidden or illicit partial business is mortal, or else you will have to assert that none of them is a sin. Moreover, in illicit bodily acts, in which successive interruption naturally occurs, there is one act for each debt, as in the law foramen, ff. de servitutibus praediorum. PAUL. For since sin exists potentially and radically in the soul, being the aversion of the will from the unchangeable good to a changeable good, and commonly shows itself in an external or bodily act as commanded by the will itself, therefore as soon as the will consents to carrying out such a forbidden business, the sin is nonetheless already committed in the will, even if no act follows; but it is said to be consummated in bodily acts only when the business is completed. Hence, while the same consent of the will continues without interruption from the beginning of the business to its end, although those partial acts that make up the business naturally interrupt one another, they cannot be called several sins but one, because they do not correspond to any renewed act of the will, at least not a habitual one. For the terminus from which, namely the same will, is one, and the terminus to which, the same end of all the means, is also one. It would be otherwise if, in the course of the business, or before it, the will were changed to the contrary, and afterwards it resumed the will in carrying on; then, as often as he resumed the changed will, he would sin that many times. Nor would those intermediate acts be one act, although they tended to the same effect, but distinct acts, on account of the distinct terminus from which, namely the change of will, or even if a specific end were assigned to each act by itself.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: In quo declaratur, quomodo Cardinales non possunt excusari à participatione simoniæ: & quantum eorum negligentia & taciturnitas est culpabilis, & nociua.
units.tr: In which it is shown how the Cardinals cannot be excused from participation in simony, and how far their negligence and silence are culpable and harmful.

units.la: PET. Modo non est mentio facta de Dominis Cardinalibus, officia non habentibus. Ideo nunc expedit, vt etiam à tanto sopore lamentabilis negligentiæ congruis persuasionibus excitentur.
units.tr: PET. Hitherto no mention has been made of the lord Cardinals who hold no office. Therefore it is now expedient that they too be roused, by fitting persuasions, from so great a slumber of lamentable negligence.

units.la: PAVL. Si animaduertitur mente sollicita, quanto mysteria à cardinibus, vel quatuor cardinalibus virtutibus, quibus pollere debent (scil. prudentia, temperantia, fortitudine & iustitia) Cardinales sunt nuncupati, & ad construendam conseruandamq; sacro Christi sanguine fundatâ Ecclesiam, superna prouidentia instituti (magnum quippe & arduissimum est eorum officium) profecto destrui non debèrent exemplis auaritiæ: non obdormire tantam ruinam in ipsa Ecclesia Dei, & prostitutionem sceleratissimam, nec non diuisionem hæreticam Christi sponsæ admixtere. Nam certo certior sum, quod præter hæc quod cum Simone mago colligunt, non solum prædictorum omnium in curia Romana peccatorum sunt participes, verum omnium malorum quæ fiunt vbiq; in Dei Ecclesia: de quanto ea aut reformare, aut prædictis prouisionibus exorbitantibus, & inutilibus (quæ sunt infinitorum malorum radix & fomentum) contradicere cum effectu negligunt: aut consentiunt in errores impiorum, negligentiam, desidiam detestabilem, vel consensum, noscuntur sine dubio redundare.
units.tr: PAUL. If one considers with an attentive mind how great are the mysteries of the Cardinals, who are named after the hinges (cardines), or the four cardinal virtues, which they ought to excel in (namely prudence, temperance, fortitude and justice), and how they were appointed by heavenly providence to build up and preserve the Church founded on the holy blood of Christ (for their office is great and very arduous indeed), surely it ought not to be destroyed by the examples of avarice. They should not sleep through such a great ruin in the Church of God itself, such most wicked prostitution, and also the heretical division of Christ's bride. For I am most certain that, besides these things which they gather together with Simon Magus, they are not only partakers in all the aforesaid sins committed in the Roman court, but also in all the evils that happen everywhere in the Church of God. For they either neglect to reform these things, or to contradict with effect the aforesaid exorbitant and useless provisions (which are the root and fuel of infinite evils), or they are known without doubt to redound to them by consenting to the errors of the impious, by detestable negligence, sloth, or consent.

units.la: PET. Iniuriose, & recte non videris dicere, quod Cardinales cum Simone colligunt: cum tamen sine solutione pecuniæ à Papa obtinent, quod intendunt. PAVL. Ignosce mihi, Petre, hunc errorem, quo me fateor oberrasse. Non enim debui dicere cum Simone, sed cum Iezi habent partem, cum sine ipsorum consilio de Episcopatibus &c. non fiunt huiusmodi prouisiones: qui non solum assensu & consilio, sed etiam ad ipsas cooperantur per effectum, cum mutua seruitia, &c. à tali recipiunt, turpiter contrahentes.
units.tr: PET. You do not seem to speak justly and rightly in saying that the Cardinals join with Simon, since they obtain what they intend from the Pope without paying money. PAUL. Forgive me, Peter, this error, by which I confess I have gone astray. For I ought not to have said "with Simon," but that they have a share with Gehazi: since such provisions to bishoprics etc. are not made without their counsel, and they cooperate in them not only by assent and counsel but also in effect, receiving mutual services from such men, and so shamefully entering into contracts.

units.la: PET. O felicissima Apostolorum tempora, primitiuæ ecclesiæ: dum etsi vnus érat malus inter duodecim: nunc autem inter duodecies duodecim nullus, aut vix vnus bonus. O quanto periculo fluctuat Petri navicula? prædicatio Pauli contemnitur, & doctrina Saluatoris non curatur: & quod in Curia Romana ecclesiæ, quæ est omnium ecclesiarum caput à planta pedis vsque ad verticem capitis non est sanitas.
units.tr: PET. O most happy times of the Apostles, of the primitive Church, when even if one was wicked among the twelve, now among twelve times twelve there is none, or hardly one good! O in what peril Peter's little boat is tossed! The preaching of Paul is despised, the doctrine of the Saviour is not cared for; and in the Roman Curia, which is the head of all the churches of the Church, from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: Chapter III.

units.la: In tertia parte huius Tractatus cap. tert. continuatur, pro latitudine potestatis Papæ, & soluitur, & declaratur plenitudo potestatis ipsius: condemnatur multitudo gratiarum, cum illis qui sunt consecuti beneficia per exorbitantes gratias.
units.tr: In the third part of this treatise, chapter 3 continues: it sets out the breadth of the Pope's power, and resolves and explains his fullness of power. It condemns the multitude of graces, together with those who have obtained benefices through extravagant graces.

units.la: PET. Adhuc restat ibi discutiendum in hac materia, quoniam Gloss. ordinariæ sonant, quod conditor canonis, vel legis, potest mihi dare rem alienam, & tutus ero, vt dicit Gloss. 2. in c. vigilanti. de præscript. per l. Lucius ff. de c. vict. & Cod. de quadrien. præscript. bene à Zenone, & per totum. Gloss. vero in c. per principale, 9. q. 3. idem dicit. Et plus superaddituir, quod Papa potest alicui beneficium recipere, remittit 19. distinctione in memoriam extra, de offic. dele. dilectus de concess. præben. quia diuersitatem. Et potest episcopum deponere, sed non omnes: quia sic vniuersalem ecclesiam turbaret. Horum occasionem præmissorum, & etiam Gloss. in c. à nobis de deci. quidam notauerunt, quod Papa posset vnum episcopum deponere sine causa, sed non omnes, ne videretur statum ecclesiæ vniversalis immutare, quod non potest. Nonnulli etiam famosissimi canonistæ videntur asserere, quod Papa posset etiam contra ius naturale dispensare. Gloss. Ord. dict. c. à nobis, Innocent. in cap. cum ad monasterium de sta. mo. & sequaces dicentes, quod Papa in voto continentiæ posset dispensare. Item etiam contra iuramentum 15. q. 3. auctoritatem item, quoniam etiam Gloss. innuit, quod posset contra diuinam legem dispensare: vt in c. propositum de concess. præben. in eo quod dispensare posse videtur contra Apostolum, vt promoueantur ad sacros ordines bigami. 33. dist. lector. Hæc allegata, maxime videntur Papæ laxasse potestatem. Necesse igitur habes de mentibus simplicium & errantium excutere, quicquid erroris in animis non bene intelligentibus est seminatum occasione præmissorum.
units.tr: PET. There is still something to be examined in this matter, since the ordinary Glosses say that the author of a canon or law can give me another's property, and I will be safe, as the Gloss says at 2 on c. Vigilanti, de praescriptionibus, by the law Lucius, ff. de captivis, and in Cod. de quadriennii praescriptione, rightly under Zeno, and throughout. The Gloss on c. Per principale, 9 q. 3, says the same. And it adds further that the Pope can receive someone to a benefice, and he remits it, in distinction 19, in memoria, extra de officio delegati, dilectus, de concessione praebendae, because of the difference. He can also depose a bishop, but not all of them, because that would disturb the universal Church. Some have noted, on the basis of these premises and also the Gloss on c. A nobis, de decimis, that the Pope could depose one bishop without cause, but not all, lest he seem to alter the state of the universal Church, which he cannot do. Some very famous canonists also seem to assert that the Pope could dispense even against natural law: the ordinary Gloss on the said c. A nobis, Innocent on c. Cum ad monasterium, de statu monachorum, and their followers, who say that the Pope could dispense from a vow of continence. Likewise even against an oath, 15 q. 3, Auctoritatem. Again, the Gloss also hints that he could dispense against divine law, as in c. Propositum, de concessione praebendae, in that he seems able to dispense against the Apostle, so that bigamists may be promoted to sacred orders, 33 dist., Lector. These citations especially seem to have relaxed the power of the Pope. It is necessary, therefore, that you shake out of the minds of the simple and the erring whatever error has been sown in the minds of those who do not understand these matters well, on the occasion of the aforesaid.

units.la: PAVL. Non est quippe necesse dicere aliquid, si non exuberasset tanta cupiditas, ambitio, & omnium malorum radix avaritia, quæ corticibus iurium contenta, & errore, ad medullam non sit pertingere veritatis. Sed vt etiam in his cæcitati cupidorum & ambientium penitus occasio subtrahatur, vt vtar verbis Apostoli: hic primo quæritur inter dispensatores, vt fidelis quis inueniatur. Et quis est iste fidelis dispensator & prudens, quem constituit Dominus super familiam suam? quem recommendat Saluator Lucas 12. quem vtique prudentem & fidelem esse oportet. Infidelis autem est, qui dimisso communi bono, ampleditur priuatum. Imprudens vero est, qui sine discretione & sine causa dispensat, quia huic dicetur: Serve nequam, redde rationem villicationis tuæ: Iam non poteris vltra villicare, Lucæ 16. circa principium. Seruus enim qui non facit voluntatem Domini, plagis vapulabit multis. Cum autem secundum Gloss. Or. 1. q. 1. requiritur, in verb. pro tempore dispensatio est communis iuris relaxatio, facta cum causæ agnitione, ab eo qui ius habet dispensandi: necesse diuersa pensare habet, qui dispensare vult, cum à iure communi non est facile intuitu alicuius recedendum 31. dist. iuramentum & contrarium facere non est populo consulere, sed nocere nec præstare regnum, sed augere discrimen, vt ibidem. Eo minus adhuc Saluator dispensatorem assumpsit: supra etiam Apostolus, scilicet prout dispensatio est quædam commensuratio ad singula: prout dicit beatus Thomas in secunda parte secunde, 97. art. vlt. & Io. An. post eum in nouella cap. de multa de præben. Inde gubernator familiæ dicitur dispensator, qui dispensat & distribuit singulis, laborem, & etiam pretium. Ad hoc autem, vt dispensatio vtroque modo valeat & teneat, necessario requiritur vnum de duobus aut dispensandi necessitas, aut publica vtilitas. Iura sunt ad hoc multa, dicto c. requiritur, cum multis sequi. & 78. distinct. si cognita concor. &c. de alia. Dicunt iura, vt prærogatiua meritorum, &c. ad ista requirantur. Necessitas enim & vtilitas inducunt dispensationem, vt in c. exposuisti de præben. Cum ergo hæc dispositio sit fundata lege diuina, quia hoc ad fidelem & prudentem dispensatorem pertinet, vt supra: & etiam ratione, quoniam hoc dictat legalis iustitia, cuius est, necessitati & vtilitati publicæ consulere, quæ non est sine prudentia, quæ hæc considerat, vt patet 6. Ethicorum. Ex quibus sequitur, quod Romanus pontifex pro libito contrarium facere non potest. Nam dicit Bernhard. 3. de Consideratione cap. 23. quod si faceret, non dispensare esset, sed dissipare. Et hoc est quod volunt doctores communiter, & Gloss. Or. Quod si Papa dispensat cum aliquo, siue in pluritate incompatibilium beneficiorum, siue in voto &c. & causa rationabilis non subest, talis non est tutus quoad Deum, vt in cap. non est, de voto & voto redempt. & in c. dudum de elect. secundum Hosti. & alios. Dico, si certum est, q rationabilis causa non subsit dispensandi. Certum n. est, q talis dispensatio, vel potius ficta prouisio, nullius est momenti. Declaratur, quod omnes qui obtinuerunt beneficia per exorbitantes gratias, & praeiudiciales aliis, dato quod non dederunt pro eis pecunias, nisi dimittant beneficia taliter acquisita, certi sunt de sua damnatione. Ex quo sequitur, quod omnes qui per exorbitantes gratias, & praeiudiciales aliis sunt adepti aliquod beneficium, sicut sunt dies obitus, perpetua silentia, proprii motus, clausulae antelationis, & similes, cum quibuscunq; clausulis derogatoriis iuris alterius, dato quod non dederint pro eis pecunias, sed solum posito quod aliis praeiudicatum est sine causa & necessitate, per eas in iure sine in beneficio iam quaesito, siue ad rem inquirendo, nisi dimittant beneficia taliter acquisita, & egerint poenitentiam, certi sunt de damnatione. Patet etiam hoc ex eo. Nam clarum est, quod habens beneficium ecclesiasticum sine institutione canonica, possideri non potest, ut dicit l. regula de reg. iur. lib. 6. Et quia etiam constat, quod per huiusmodi gratias quae a iure communi exorbitant, non est ingressus canonicus, imo contra canones, contra ius diuinum & naturale, ex quo fit cum iniuria aliorum: igitur quilibet talis est malae fidei possessor, quae vllo tempore non praescribit. Ex his vlterius sequitur, quod gratiarum mutatio & multiplicatio, est realis deceptio, & damnatio animarum. Obiectio. Praeterea, quod Papa sine rationabili causa & euidenti non potest immutare, vel eius contrarium facere, quod per praedecessores suos rationabiliter statutum est, ut probatum est supra prima parte huius Tractatus cap. 3. Praeterea, ratione pro praedictis sic arguitur: Quandocunq; Papa facit aliquid contra legem diuinam vel naturalem, dispensando super incompatibilibus, innocentes deponendo, vel transferendo praelatos, & sic de aliis quae habent fieri virtute clauium Ecclesiae, quotiescunque non subesset necessitas, aut communis utilitas, ex tali dispensatione nullus exequitur effectus, sed solum quaedam umbra apparet in opere, sed nulla veritas subsequitur in effectu. Quod sic probatur. Nam quilibet actus seu operatio producitur ab aliqua virtute, seu potentia, quam in agibilibus potestatem seu legem appellamus: hoc utique notum est ad sensum & intellectum. Sed nullus actus, in quantum contrarius iuri diuino, militans, producitur ab aliqua potentia: Ergo nullus, in quantum talis, in re est aliquis actus: & per consequens, nullus est effectus. Consequentia de se nota est, quia regulariter penes secundum modum secundae figurae. Minorem sic declaro: Omnis potentia, qua Papa potest aliquid facere, aut est virtute legis diuinae, aut naturalis sibi. Hoc est dicere: aut facit ut vicarius Christi, & sic non facit virtute sua, sed Christi: aut non facit ut homo, vel animal, &c. non potest dici, quod virtute legis diuinae possit dispensare, &c. sine causa: quia cum causa secunda non agit nisi in virtute prioris, sic oporteret concedere, quod Christus dedisset sibi hanc potestatem contra se & suam legem faciendi, qui tamen ipsum voluit esse fidelem, & ob hoc prudentem, ut supra. Et sequitur, quod lex Dei esset sibi contraria, & infinita inconuenientia sequerentur. Habetur ergo pro constanti, quod vigore legis Christi non est potentia. Non etiam potest ut homo: quia sic non oporteret currere pro beneficiis ad Papam, vel alios, si naturalis virtus humana sufficeret ad ea dispensanda. Praeterea non est dubium, quamlibet virtutem humanam esse subordinatam Dei potentiae, in genere causae efficientis. Cum igitur causa inferior non potest influere aliquam actionem vel virtutem causa superiori sic, et e contrario: igitur, &c.
units.tr: PAUL. There is indeed no need to say anything, were it not that such great greed, ambition, and avarice, the root of all evils, has overflowed, which, content with the bark of rights and with error, does not reach the marrow of truth. But so that the blindness of the greedy and ambitious may be utterly deprived of occasion, to use the words of the Apostle: "Here it is required first of stewards that someone be found faithful." And who is this faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord has set over his household, whom the Saviour commends in Luke 12, and who certainly ought to be both prudent and faithful? He is unfaithful who, neglecting the common good, pursues his private advantage. He is imprudent who dispenses without discernment and without cause, for to him it will be said: "Wicked servant, render an account of your stewardship; now you can no longer be steward," Luke 16, near the beginning. For the servant who does not do the will of his Lord will be beaten with many stripes. Since, however, according to the Gloss, Ordinary, 1 q. 1, on the words "pro tempore", dispensation is a relaxation of common law, made with knowledge of the cause, by one who has the right to dispense, he who wishes to dispense must weigh many things, since one should not easily depart from common law for the sake of any one person, 31 dist., Iuramentum; and to act contrary is not to consult the people but to harm them, nor to secure the kingdom but to increase its peril, as there. All the more, therefore, the Saviour did not take on a dispenser: the Apostle above also, namely in so far as dispensation is a certain proportioning to individuals, as blessed Thomas says in the second part of the second part, question 97, last article, and John Andreae after him, in the novella on c. De multa, de praebendis. Hence the governor of a household is called a dispenser, who dispenses and distributes to each his labour and also his pay. For a dispensation to be valid and binding in either way, one of two things is necessarily required: either the necessity of dispensing or public utility. There are many laws for this, cited in c. Requiritur, with many following, and in distinction 78, Si cognita concordia, etc., de alia. The laws say, as the prerogative of merits, etc., that these must be required. For necessity and utility bring about dispensation, as in c. Exposuisti, de praebendis. Since, therefore, this arrangement is founded on divine law, because it pertains to a faithful and prudent steward, as above, and also on reason, because legal justice dictates this, whose office it is to provide for public necessity and utility, which is not without prudence, which considers these things, as is clear from the sixth book of the Ethics, it follows that the Roman pontiff cannot do the contrary at his pleasure. For Bernard says in the third book On Consideration, chapter 23, that if he did, it would not be dispensing but squandering. And this is what the doctors commonly hold, and the Gloss, Ordinary: if the Pope dispenses with someone, whether in plurality of incompatible benefices or in a vow, etc., and no reasonable cause underlies it, such a man is not safe before God, as in c. Non est, de voto, and in the vow of redemption, and in c. Dudum, de electione, according to Hostiensis and others. I say, if it is certain that no reasonable cause underlies the dispensation. For it is certain that such a dispensation, or rather feigned provision, is of no weight. It is declared that all who have obtained benefices through extravagant graces, and prejudicial to others, even if they did not give money for them, are certain of their condemnation unless they give up benefices so acquired and do penance. From this it follows that all who have obtained some benefice through extravagant graces and prejudicial to others, such as the days of death, perpetual silences, proper motus, clauses of antelation, and similar things, with whatever derogatory clauses against another's right, even if they did not give money for them, but only on the assumption that others have been prejudiced without cause and necessity, through these in law or in a benefice already sought, whether by the right of inquiry, unless they give up benefices so acquired and do penance, are certain of damnation. This is also clear from the following. For it is plain that one who holds an ecclesiastical benefice without canonical institution cannot be possessed of it, as the rule, de regulis iuris, book 6, says. And since it is also established that through such graces, which depart from common law, there is no canonical entry, but rather against the canons, against divine and natural law, from which arises injury to others, therefore anyone of this kind is a possessor in bad faith, which prescription never validates at any time. From these things it further follows that the alteration and multiplication of graces is a real deception and the damnation of souls. Objection. Moreover, the Pope cannot, without a reasonable and evident cause, change or do the contrary of what has been reasonably established by his predecessors, as has been proved above in the first part of this treatise, chapter 3. Furthermore, on the basis of reason, the aforesaid is argued thus: Whenever the Pope does anything against divine or natural law, by dispensing with incompatibles, deposing innocent men, or transferring prelates, and so on with other things that are to be done by virtue of the keys of the Church, whenever there is no necessity or common utility, no effect follows from such a dispensation, but only a certain shadow appears in the work, and no truth follows in the effect. This is proved thus. For every act or operation is produced by some virtue or power, which in matters of action we call authority or law; this is surely known to sense and intellect. But no act, insofar as it is contrary to divine law and in conflict with it, is produced by any power. Therefore no such act, insofar as it is such, is anything real, and consequently it has no effect. The consequence is self-evident, since it generally follows the second mode of the second figure. I explain the minor premise thus: every power by which the Pope can do anything is either by virtue of divine law or natural to him. That is to say: either he acts as Christ's vicar, and so he does not act by his own virtue but by Christ's, or he does not act as a man or an animal, etc. It cannot be said that by virtue of divine law he could dispense without cause, etc., since a secondary cause acts only by virtue of the prior; thus we would have to concede that Christ gave him this power of acting against Himself and His law, though He willed him to be faithful and therefore prudent, as above. And it would follow that the law of God would be contrary to itself, and countless absurdities would follow. It is therefore held as certain that there is no power by virtue of the law of Christ. Nor can he act as a man, for then there would be no need to run to the Pope or others for benefices, if human natural power were sufficient to dispense them. Moreover, there is no doubt that every human virtue is subordinate to the power of God, in the genus of efficient cause. Since, therefore, an inferior cause cannot bring about any action or virtue in a superior cause, and vice versa, therefore, etc.

units.la: PET. Haec ratio cogit inuincibiliter ad assensum. Sed sensus exterior mihi contrarium experimentum. Nam videmus ad experientiam, quod quantumcunque Papa excedit limites legis diuinae in prouidendo, &c. spiritualia dispensando, siue pro illo recipit pecuniam, siue alio modo: tamen nihilominus, quam cito ore pronunciat aliquem in episcopum alicuius ecclesiae, statim habetur pro tali prouiso, & communiter recipit possessionem, & ea exercet quae talis habet exercere. Similiter cum supplicationi apponit calamum, signando per Fiat, &c. mox illi beneficium est assectum, ita quod talis suo tempore illud consequitur in effectu, cuius tamen contrarium tua ratio nititur demonstrare: & ideo apparet, quod sit plus fantastica & sophistica, quam realis.
units.tr: PET. This argument compels assent with invincible force. But my outward senses give me the opposite experience. We see in practice that however far the Pope exceeds the limits of divine law in providing and dispensing spiritual things, whether he takes money for it or in some other way, still, as soon as he pronounces by word of mouth that someone is bishop of some church, that person is at once regarded as duly provided, usually takes possession, and exercises the functions that such a bishop has to exercise. Likewise, when he puts his pen to a supplication and marks it with Fiat, the benefice is at once granted to the petitioner, so that in due time he obtains it in fact. Yet your argument labours to prove the contrary. And so it appears to be more fanciful and sophistical than real.

units.la: PAVL. Rusticanam profecto aestimationem videris habere. Nam cum rurali hebetudini praedicitur de ineffabili bonitate coelestis patriae, & si dicitur quod ibi non comedemus nec bibemus, non cadit in mentem rusticam quod ibi est omnis plenitudo. Non mirum, quod umbram in opere sensu perceptibilem sequeris cum erratibus, & non facti veritatem, quae nisi ratione intueri poterit efficaci. Quia enim potentia vel virtus Dei, qua Papa dispensat spiritualia, est mere spiritualis, non corporalis (quemadmodum est potentia ad proferendum verba, vel ad scribendum) similiter ipsius actus & effectus proprius est mere spiritualis, nullo sensu perceptibilis, vtitur tamen ad exercendum proprium effectum pro instrumento, natura humana, & ipsius membris corporalibus. Si igitur debeat tibi aliquid praedictorum spiritualium ad sensum innotescere, oportet non aliter quam per signa corporalia iudicare, quae illorum sunt vestigia, siue signa: sicut actus pronunciandi, siue supplicationem signandi, quoad conferentem, aut possessionem corporalium, sine quibus talia spiritualia non sunt apprehendenda, quoad recipientem. Quando ergo Papa facit quod est contrarium scripturae vel rationi actus illius potentiae diuinae, virtute cuius hoc deberet, conquiescat: & per consequens, sua pronunciatio vel scriptura, quae deberet esse signum actus illius spiritualis, nulla in re habet correspondentiam ex parte signati, sed solum apparet significare, & nihil significat in effectu. Nec etiam stat ibi pro se: quia actus proferendi vel signandi supplicationem ex sui natura, non potest talem effectum causare, ut notum est: sicut nec tu in alio homine priuato, & per consequens, nec stat ibi naturaliter pro se, nec significatiue pro alio, sed solum est quaedam umbra in opere, sed nulla veritas sequitur in effectu, ut dicit tex. c. quando de consue. Et sic errantes, possessioitem apprehendentes disponunt de rebus, in veritate nullum ius habentibus. Et ex istis patet intellectus allegatorum, quae erroribus fauere videbantur. Nam si sic glossatores voluissent intelligere, quod Papa posset recipere beneficium vni, sine causa rationabili, & dare alteri cum iniuria, vellent beneficia esse perpetua 55. distinct. precepta 70. distinct. sanctorum. Et no. de sepul. presby. veniens, cum omni audacia dicerem, quod se non intellexerunt, nec hoc potest concludi ex dicto c. per principalem, nec ex aliquo alio. Ex quo patet, quod pueriliter dicitur, quod Papa potest vnum episcopum deponere sine causa, sed non omnes. Nec est illud recitatione dignum, quod hic dictum est, Papam licentiam habere pueriliter & sine prudentia agendi, quem prudentem esse oportet, vt dicit Apostolus. Et etiam est contra textum c. intra corporalia. de translat. vbi dicitur, quod non humana, sed diuina potestate coniungi spirituale dissoluitur, cum per translationem, depositionem vel cessionem auctoritate Romani pontificis, quem constat esse vicarium Iesu Christi, episcopus ab ecclesia remouetur. Sed intelligendum est, quod quacunque causa dispensare non potest solus, sine generali ecclesiae concilio: vbi ex dispensatione sua discolorareretur status vniuersalis Ecclesiae, secus, vbi hoc non timetur. Et sic intelligendae sunt Gloss. Or. & alia scripta doctorum.
units.tr: PAUL. You certainly seem to have a rustic estimate of things. When the inexpressible goodness of the heavenly fatherland is described to a rustic dullness, and it is said that there we shall neither eat nor drink, the rustic mind does not grasp that there is all fullness. It is no wonder that you follow a shadow that can be perceived in the outward work, with its errors, and not the truth of the matter, which can be seen only by effective reason. For the power or virtue of God, by which the Pope dispenses spiritual things, is purely spiritual and not bodily (as is the power to utter words or to write). Likewise its act and proper effect is purely spiritual and perceptible by no sense. Yet to carry out its proper effect it uses, as instruments, human nature and its bodily members. If, then, any of those spiritual things is to become known to you by the senses, you must judge in no other way than by bodily signs, which are their traces or signs. Such are the act of pronouncing, or of marking a supplication, on the side of the one who confers, and the possession of bodily goods, without which such spiritual things cannot be apprehended on the side of the one who receives them. When therefore the Pope does what is contrary to Scripture or to reason, the act of that divine power by virtue of which he ought to act must be at rest. Consequently his pronouncement or writing, which ought to be the sign of that spiritual act, has no correspondence in any respect with the thing signified. It only seems to signify, and signifies nothing in effect. Nor does it stand for itself, since the act of pronouncing or of marking a supplication cannot by its own nature cause such an effect, as is well known. Nor does it stand there naturally for itself or significantly for another, any more than you would in another private person. It is only a certain shadow in the work, and no truth follows in effect, as the text says in c. quando de consue. And so those who are in error, grasping possession, dispose of things to which in truth they have no right. From these points the meaning of the passages cited, which seemed to favour the errors, is also clear. For if the glossators had wished them to be understood in this way, that the Pope could grant a benefice to one man without reasonable cause and give it to another to his wrong, they would make benefices perpetual; see 55. dist. Praecepta and 70. dist. Sanctorum. And note on de sepul. presby. veniens. I would say with all boldness that they did not understand themselves, and this cannot be concluded from the said chapter per principalem, nor from any other. From this it is evident that it is said childishly that the Pope can depose one bishop without cause, but not all. Nor is it worth repeating what is said here, that the Pope has a licence to act childishly and without prudence, whereas he ought to be prudent, as the Apostle says. It is also contrary to the text in c. intra corporalia. de translat., where it is said that what is spiritually joined is dissolved not by human but by divine power, since a bishop is removed from the church by translation, deposition or resignation by the authority of the Roman bishop, who is plainly the vicar of Jesus Christ. But it must be understood that he cannot dispense alone, by whatever cause, without a general council of the Church, where by his dispensation the state of the universal Church would be disturbed. Where this is not feared, it is otherwise. And so the Gloss. Or. and other writings of the teachers are to be understood.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAP. IV.

units.la: In capitulo quarto huius Tractatus, obiicitur pro plenitudine potestatis Papae: & ponitur distinctio, per quam cognoscitur, circa quae & quomodo consistat dicta plenitudo: & quae sunt dispensabilia, & quae indispensabilia, declaratur.
units.tr: In the fourth chapter of this treatise, arguments are raised for the fullness of the Pope's power. A distinction is laid down by which we may learn where and how that fullness consists, and it is explained which matters are dispensable and which are indispensable.

units.la: PET. Peregrina iuri apparent quae dixisti, cum princeps non teneatur sua lege: Cod. de leg. digna. Nam licet conditori constitutionis ex certa scientia contra suam constitutionem dispensare, sine causae cognitione: alias non de confir. vel inuti. ad nostram. Item Gloss. in c. gratiose de rescript. lib. 6. Nota, quod solus Papa sub conditione & ad tempus, sicut vult, potest beneficia concedere, seu conferre allegat. 7. q. 1. pastoralis de si. presb. veniens. In his quae vult, est apud ipsum pro ratione voluntas, Institut. de iure naturali §. sed & quod principi.
units.tr: PET. What you have said seems foreign to the law, since a prince is not bound by his own law (Cod. de leg. digna). For although the author of a constitution may, from certain knowledge, dispense from his own constitution without a hearing of the case, otherwise it would not be valid or confirmed (de confir. vel inuti. ad nostram). Likewise, the Gloss on c. gratiose de rescript. lib. 6 notes that the Pope alone may grant or confer benefices conditionally and for a time, as he wishes (cited at 7 q. 1, pastoralis, de si. presb., veniens). In those matters which he wills, the will of the ruler is the reason itself (Institutes, de iure naturali, §. sed & quod principi).

units.la: PAVL. Glossam pro illo allegato intellige, quod Papa potest conferre ad tempus sicut vult: id est, sicut debet velle, si necessitas suaderet. Et etiam hoc intendunt iura, per Gloss. allegata. Vt de hoc scire vales labyrintho, expedit te notare, quod inter ea quae sunt pro humana vita dirigenda statuta, quaedam sunt, quorum sola voluntas constituentis est causa, quia scilicet sic principi placuit & haec dicuntur iura propria mere positiua, vt quod sententia non teneat nisi per sedentem lata, vel quod sacri ordines celebrentur per interstitia quatuor temporum, & talibus apud principem est pro ratione voluntas: & in talibus iura loquuntur allegata superius, & similia. Alia autem sunt, quorum causa non est sola voluntas, sed dictamen rationis cognitum: lex diuina. Et ista tunc habent se per modum praemissorum, ad ius canonicum. Impossibile ergo, tollere veritatem consequentis, nisi etiam tollatur veritas antecedentis. Quia consequentia concluditur in antecedente, & necessario sequitur ex antecedente, vt patet primo & secundo Priorum. Si igitur debet tolli ius canonicum per huiusmodi causas inductum, necesse est vt per easdem causas in contrarium agens dissoluatur, scilicet si suadet ratio, aut lex diuina: per regulam, omnes res de iure.
units.tr: PAUL. Understand the Gloss on that citation to mean that the Pope may confer for a time as he wishes, that is, as he ought to wish if necessity should so require. The laws cited, with their Gloss, have this same intent. So that you may find your way out of this labyrinth, you should note that among the statutes laid down for directing human life, some depend solely on the will of the one who makes them, because it so pleased the prince. These are called purely positive laws, such as that a sentence is not binding unless pronounced by the judge who sits, or that sacred orders are conferred in the intervals of the four seasons. In such matters the will of the prince is the reason, and the laws cited above, and similar ones, speak of such matters. Other laws, however, have as their cause not the mere will but a reason recognised by judgement: the divine law. These laws stand to the canon law in the relation of premises to conclusion. It is therefore impossible to remove the truth of the consequent without also removing the truth of the antecedent, since the consequence is contained in the antecedent and follows necessarily from it, as is clear from the first and second Prior Analytics. If, then, canon law introduced for such causes ought to be abolished, it is necessary that it be dissolved by the same causes acting in the opposite direction, namely, if reason or the divine law so persuades. This follows the rule: all things are by law.

units.la: PET. Videtur per hoc in Papa negari plenitudo potestatis, quae est supra ius commune. Cum etiam Petrus in administratione maior fuerit Paulo Apostolo, 40. distinct. in illis. Et ideo videtur nonnullis doctoribus, non esse iuris, si contra Apostolum Paulum Papa valeat dispensare.
units.tr: PET. By this it seems that fullness of power is denied to the Pope, a power which stands above the common law. Also, Peter was greater than the Apostle Paul in administration (40 dist., in illis). And so it seems to some teachers that it is not lawful for the Pope to dispense against the Apostle Paul.

units.la: PAVL. Absit, quempiam dicere, quod aliquid huiusmodi valeat sine causa. Cum enim in veteri & nouo Testamentis non contineatur nisi veritas doctrinae, fidei, & moris, contra naturae & gratiae: qua ratione Papa pro libito posset dispensare? cum Christus non venerit legem soluere, aut Prophetas, sed adimplere: Matth. 5. Fateor, quod in bigamia posset dispensare, & contra ius naturale, secundum intentum prius dictum, scilicet ipsum exemplum in casu, quem ponit Innocentius & communiter Doctores in cap. cum ad monasterium de statu monachorum, sed si tota Christianitas, vel aliqua eius pars, vel prouincia esset in periculo, nisi monachus fieret rex, & regnum in suum recipiat, suis heredibus relinquendum, quia habebat forte ante monachatum filios: & quia forte non est qui sciat regnum regere: quo casu, quilibet debet se totum inholocaustum Deo offerre, vt sibi seruiat in eo in quo ei plus placet. Sed prae omnibus placet creaturam spiritualem rationabiliter & temporaliter conseruari, pro qua & ipse animam posuit: & hoc casu dispensare potest, vt proprium habeat. Similiter super continentia, quia dicunt illi de regno: Quia si debent dare regnum, volunt quod recipiat talem reginam in uxorem, alias dabunt eam infideli. Et hoc casu non debet etiam tantum diligi contemplatio huiusmodi monachi, contra maius bonum: & eius continentia non debet credi, quod Deus non velit prouisionem sui vicarii Christianitati hoc modo pudere. Aliter n.q. p charitate instituto, militarer contra charitatem: vt dicit Hugo, Io. Teu. & beat' Thom. in scripto super quarto Sent. etiam, & dominus Hugo cardinalis. Unde pro magna guerra sopienda, aut pro cultu Dei ampliando, si essent pauci fideles, vt fuit tempore Abrahae, aut pro vitanda strage animarum, posset dispensare, vt etiam moniales contraherent. Et ita etiam concedit Magister sententiarum. Quamuis beatus Thom. in secunda secunda, ll. q. ar 16. scripsit, quod in voto religionis solenni non potest fieri dispensatio, quia illi castitas essentialiter est annexa. Secus dicit in voto solennizato per susceptionem sacri ordinis: quia illi continentia non est annexa essentialiter, sed ex statuto ecclesiae. Hic tamen attende diligenter, quod si non subesset causa, aut forte esset minus urgens quam vt praedicatur, aut si insufficiens, & Papa nihilominus dispensaret cum moniali aut monacho, sic contrahendo matrimonio, non esset matrimonium, sed adulterium. Richardus vero de Media villa, quarto Sententiarum dist. 38. q. 1. ar. dicit: Quod dispensatio potest accipi dupliciter. Vno modo, pro iuris laxatione, vt dictum est. Alio modo, pro iuris declaratione. Et hoc respectu dicimus Papam dispensare super iure naturali vel diuino, declarando vel interpretando. Primo modo dicit nullum votum esse dispensabile, quia volens obligatur Deo, cuius voti expletio est sub praecepto, iuxta illud prophetae: Vouete, & votum reddite Domino. Primum, scilicet Vouete, est consilium: secundum, scilicet Reddite votum Domino, est praecepti, de vot. & vot. redempt. magna.
units.tr: PAUL. Far be it that anyone should say that anything of this kind is valid without cause. For since the Old and New Testaments contain nothing but the truth of doctrine, faith and morals, how could the Pope dispense at his pleasure against the law of nature and of grace? Christ came not to destroy the law or the Prophets, but to fulfil them (Matt. 5). I grant that he could dispense in bigamy, and against natural law, according to the purpose stated earlier, namely the example in the case which Innocent and the Doctors commonly put in c. cum ad monasterium, de statu monachorum. But if the whole of Christendom, or some part or province of it, were in danger unless a monk became king and received the kingdom, to be left to his heirs, because perhaps he had sons before entering the monastery, and because perhaps there is no one who knows how to rule the kingdom, then in such a case anyone ought to offer himself wholly to God as a burnt offering, to serve him in whatever pleases him most. But above all it pleases God that the spiritual creature be reasonably and temporally preserved, for whom he himself laid down his life; and in this case he may dispense so that the monk may have his own. Similarly with regard to continence, because those of the kingdom say: if they are to give the kingdom, they want him to take such a queen as wife, otherwise they will give her to an unbeliever. And in this case the contemplation of such a monk ought not to be valued so highly as to outweigh the greater good, nor should it be believed that God does not wish the provision of his vicar for Christendom to be hindered in this way. Otherwise, a vow made in charity, if it acts against charity, is a fight against charity, as Hugh, John of Teu. and blessed Thomas say in their writings on the fourth book of the Sentences, and Lord Hugh the cardinal too. Hence, to quell a great war, or to extend the worship of God if there were few faithful, as there were in the time of Abraham, or to avoid the slaughter of souls, he could dispense so that even nuns might marry. The Master of the Sentences also grants this. Although blessed Thomas, in the second part of the second part, question 88, article 16, wrote that in a solemn vow of religion no dispensation can be given, because chastity is essentially attached to it, it is otherwise in a vow solemnised by the reception of holy orders, because continence is not essentially attached to that, but comes from the statute of the Church. Here, however, note carefully that if no cause lay behind it, or if it were less pressing than alleged, or insufficient, and the Pope nonetheless dispensed a nun or monk so that they might contract marriage, it would not be a marriage but adultery. Richard of Middleton, in the fourth book of the Sentences, distinction 38, question 1, article ..., says: dispensation may be understood in two ways. In one way, as a relaxation of the law, as has been said. In another way, as a declaration of the law. And in this respect we say that the Pope dispenses in matters of natural or divine law, by declaring or interpreting. In the first sense he says that no vow is dispensable, because one who vows is bound to God, whose fulfilment of the vow is under precept, according to the word of the prophet: Vow, and pay your vow to the Lord. The first, namely Vow, is counsel; the second, namely Pay your vow to the Lord, is a precept (de vot. & vot. redempt., magna).

units.la: Sed secundo dicit quaedam vota dispensabilia, quaedam non. Illa namq; dispensabilia non sunt, quae dignam compensationem habere non possunt: vt votum Christianae religionis, quod emittitur in baptismo. Hoc seruare enim, est ad salutem necessarium. Alia vero fiunt super erogatione, id est ad maius bonum agendum: & talia sunt dispensabilia. Quia potest inveniri causa rationabilis, scil. profectus maioris boni, vel vitatio mali. Et hoc modo proprietas, vel continentia in monacho, non est simpliciter bona: quia maius bonum invenitur. Secus de dilectione Dei. PET. Grata mente optatae institutionis hoc Speculum in tuis dictis recipio, quo se spirituales, maxime moderni temporis, valeant intueri. Quamobrem Tractatulus hic Aureum Speculum non immerito poterit appellari: qui etiam succedit pro Chronica posteris, ad cautelam, quo ad gesta in ecclesia his temporibus, Papa Bonifacio 9. natione Neapolitanensi, annis tunc fere 15. Romanae ecclesiae iam praesidente, & schismate in ecclesia tunc iam ab annis 18. perdurante. PAVL. Reformet vnigenitus Dei filius suam Ecclesiam, secundum eius gloriam, genitricisq; suae gloriosissimae, ac totius coelestis curiae: Amen. Audax manus ad calamum, supra vires scribens arripuit negotium: Anno currente nativitatis eiusdem Domini millesimo quadringentesimo quarto. Et eodem Domino tunc dirigente sic compleuerit, consulens toto desiderio ad obviandum malis vniuersis, pro Ecclesiae Concilio generali &c.
units.tr: But secondly he says that some vows are dispensable and some are not. Those are not dispensable which cannot have a worthy compensation, such as the vow of the Christian religion which is made in baptism; for to keep this is necessary to salvation. But other vows are made as works of supererogation, that is, to perform a greater good, and such vows are dispensable, because a reasonable cause can be found, namely the advancement of a greater good or the avoiding of an evil. In this way, property or continence in a monk is not simply good, because a greater good is to be found. It is otherwise with the love of God. PET. With a grateful mind I receive this Mirror of the desired institution in your words, by which spiritual people, especially of our present time, may be able to look at themselves. For this reason this little treatise may not undeservedly be called the Golden Mirror, which also serves as a chronicle for posterity, as a warning, concerning the deeds in the Church in these times, when Pope Boniface 9, a native of Naples, was already presiding over the Roman Church for almost fifteen years, and the schism had by then lasted in the Church for eighteen years. PAUL. May the only-begotten Son of God reform his Church according to his glory, and that of his most glorious Mother and of the whole heavenly court. Amen. A bold hand took up the pen and began a task beyond its strength, in the current year of the birth of the same Lord, one thousand four hundred and four. And with the same Lord directing, it has been completed thus, with the whole desire of one who considers how to meet all evils, for a general Council of the Church, etc.

units.la: Explicit Dialogus Petri & Pauli, de insolentiis & erroribus Romanae Curiae, 1467. Caeterum in Processu Ioannis Hussae sepe fit huius Aurei Speculi mentio.
units.tr: Here ends the Dialogue of Peter and Paul, concerning the insolences and errors of the Roman Curia, 1467. Moreover, in the Process of John Hus, mention is often made of this Golden Mirror.

units.la: AENEAE SILVII PICCOLHO- MINEI SENENSIS EPISCOPI TERGESTINI, ET SENENSIS: POSTEA PII PAPAE II. COGNOMENTO TRACTATVS: DE ORTV ET AVTHORITATE IMPERII ROMANI, AD SERENISSIMVM ET INVICTISSIMUM PRINCIPEM, FRIDERICVM ROMANORUM REGEM.
units.tr: Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, Sienese, Bishop of Trieste, and Sienese by origin, afterwards Pope Pius II: a treatise on the origin and authority of the Roman Empire, addressed to the most serene and invincible prince Frederick, King of the Romans.

units.la: FRIDERICO ROM. IMP. AVGVSTO, Aeneas Syluius Piccolomineus S.
units.tr: To Frederick, Roman Emperor, August: Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini sends greetings.

units.la: Ompellit me, Diue Friderice, Caesar Auguste, Imperator pientissime, nonnullorum insania (seu pertinacia est atque rebellio) tibi vt aliqua scribam, cum de Origine progressuque sacri Imperii, tum de potestate authoritateque sua. Nam cum dictum meis auribus perstrepant imperitorum, ne dicam maledicorum hominum voces, qui populos quosdam ac principes, sic liberos Francos, dicunt, vt nullo penitus iure Romano Imperio sint obnoxii, et vero subiectum legibus: nihil ex priuilegiis cuiuis datis te posse detrahere, & a tuis sententiis atque mandatis appellare fas esse contendant: statui breuiter, non quod mihi videtur, sed quod maximi autores, tam legum interpretes, quam sancti doctores, de Caesarea sentiant potestate, in medium afferre: tuaq; magnitudini non ad notitiam (quid enim est quod Principis pectus ignoret?) sed ad recentiorem quandam memoriam renocare: ut confundantur, qui non veritati suos affectus, sed veritatem affectibus coaptare nituntur. Accipe igitur pauca ex multis, ac brevissima ex amplissimis: lege quod scribo, bonq; consule. Tenamq; res ista concernit, ad me nihil spectat praeter laborem & invidiam: quam ex aemulorum Imperii, tuorumq; hostium indignatione consecuturum me scio. Sed magis ego veritatem veneror, quam illos timeo.
units.tr: Compelled by the folly (or rather the obstinacy and rebellion) of certain men, divine Frederick, Caesar Augustus, most devout Emperor, I must write something for you concerning both the origin and progress of the holy Empire and its power and authority. For while the voices of the ignorant, not to say the malicious, ring in my ears, saying that certain peoples and princes, free Franks for instance, are in no way bound to the Roman Empire by any law, but are subject only to their own laws; that nothing can be withdrawn from any privilege once granted; and that it is lawful to appeal from your judgements and commands, I have resolved to set out briefly, not what seems right to me, but what the greatest authorities think about imperial power, both the interpreters of the law and the holy teachers. My aim is to recall it to your greatness, not as news (for what is there that a prince's mind does not know?), but to refresh your memory; so that those are confounded who strive to fit the truth to their passions rather than their passions to the truth. Accept then a few things out of many, and very brief things out of very large ones; read what I write and judge it kindly. This matter, indeed, concerns me, and nothing is to my advantage except toil and ill will, which I know I shall incur from the indignation of the rivals of the Empire and of your enemies. But I revere the truth more than I fear them.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CAP. I.

units.la: Quo nam modo, & qua nam causa civilis vita caeperit.
units.tr: By what manner, and for what cause, civil life began.

units.la: ROMANA Regia potestas, quam sacrum Romanum Imperium appellamus, ab ipsa humanae naturae ratione, quae optima viendi dux est, cuiq; omnes parere oportet originem ducit. Exactis namque ex Paradiso deliciarum primis parentibus, cum in agris homines atque in sylvis bestiarum modo vagarentur, victuque sibi ferino vitam propagarent: animadvertit homo (nam rationis participem illum Deus creavit) hominem homini ad bene viuendum maxime conducere, societatemq; fore plurimum necessariam. Sic ergo qui segregati prius vitam in sylvis, more ferarum ducebant, sive docente natura, sive Deo volente, totius naturae Magistro, insimul convenere, societates instituerunt, domos aedificaverunt, oppida muris cinxerunt, artes invenerunt. Et cum alter alterius commodis inserviret, placebat mirum in modum singulis vita civilis: dulcisque nimium videbatur & propinquorum & amicorum consuetudo, cuius fuerant prius expertes.
units.tr: The royal power of the Roman Empire, which we call the Holy Roman Empire, takes its origin from the very reason of human nature, which is the best guide to living and to which all men ought to submit. For when the first parents had been driven out of the Paradise of delights, and men wandered in the fields and the woods like wild beasts, sustaining their life on savage food, man (for God created him a sharer in reason) perceived that it was greatly to men's advantage that man should live with man, and that society would be most necessary. Thus those who had previously lived apart in the woods, after the manner of wild beasts, whether taught by nature or willed by God, the Master of all nature, came together, formed societies, built houses, girded towns with walls, and invented the arts. And since each served the advantage of the other, civil life pleased each of them remarkably, and the company of relatives and friends seemed exceedingly sweet, having been unknown to them before.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: Unde & qua ratione Regia potestas caeperit.
units.tr: Whence and by what reasoning royal power began.

units.la: VErum sicut ab homine multa parantur homini commoda: sic nulla est pestis, quae homini ab homine non nascatur. Coeperunt itaque homines violare societatem, fidem frangere, pacem turbare, iniuriari conciuibus, vicinorumq; tum opibus tum matrimoniis insidiari, rapere aliena, fas omne abrumpere. Nec enim pacis aemula, mater litium, suique prodiga cupiditas passa est, diu manere ius sanctae societatis illaesum. Cum ergo premeretur ab initio multitudo ab his qui viribus erant editiores, ad unum aliquem confugere placuit, virtute praestantem, qui & iniurias prohiberet inferri tenuioribus: & aequitate constituta, summos cum infimis pari iure teneret: idque nondum una in gente, sed in pluribus factum est. Atque hi sunt qui postea Regis nomen obtinuerunt, quorum constituendorum causam publica dedit utilitas, iusti prope mater & aequi. Nec sane aliam ob causam rege fuerat opus, nec tantae dignitatis fastigium cuiquam committere oportebat, ut caeteris omnibus praeferretur, honoraretur ab omnibus, ac praeciperet omnibus, nisi ut esset qui publica tueretur, & iustitiam ministraret.
units.tr: Indeed, just as many goods are procured by man for man, so there is no plague that does not arise from man for man. Men therefore began to violate fellowship, to break faith, to disturb peace, to wrong their fellow citizens, and to lay snares for their neighbours' wealth and marriages, to seize what belonged to others and to break off all right. For greed, the rival of peace, the mother of quarrels and prodigal of itself, did not allow the right of holy fellowship to remain unharmed for long. Therefore, when at the beginning the multitude was oppressed by those who were stronger in strength, it was agreed to take refuge in some one man, outstanding in virtue, who would both prevent wrongs being inflicted on the weaker and, with justice established, hold the highest and the lowest under the same law; and this was done not yet in one nation but in several. These are the men who afterwards obtained the name of king, and the cause of their appointment was public advantage, almost the mother of what is just and fair. Indeed, there was no other reason for a king to be needed, nor ought the summit of so great a dignity to be entrusted to anyone, so that he should be preferred before all others, be honoured by all, and command all, unless it were that there should be someone to protect the public good and administer justice.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Quid potissimum deceat Reges.
units.tr: What chiefly befits kings.

units.la: ESt enim Iustitia quiddam civile, societatis humanae vincula custodiens, dum vel malefactorum punit iniquitatem, vel bonis viris praemia tribuit. Est igitur Regum proprium (sicut Hieronymus inquit) facere iudicium atq; iustitiam, liberare de manu calumniantium vi oppressos, ac peregrino, pupillo & viduae, qui facilius a potentibus opprimuntur, auxilium impertiri. Quocirca niti omni studio Reges debent, ut id muneris expleant, ad quod se nosci ut esse vocatos, ne iustitiam negligant, sed & pauperi simul & diviti suum ius tribuant: sic enim pacem suis subditis, & sibi tutum tranquillumque regnum parabunt. Sicut namque Scriptura testatur: Quando rex iustus sederit super sedem, non aduersabitur sibi quisquam malignum. Principio igitur gentium nationumq; (veluti dictum est) summa potestas penes reges erat: quos ad fastigium huius maiestatis non ambitio popularis, sed spectata inter bonos moderatio provehebat. Populus nullis legibus tenebatur, arbitria Principum pro legibus erant: his fines regni tueri magis, quam proferre mos erat, atque inter suam cuique patriam regna finiebantur.
units.tr: Justice is indeed something civil, guarding the bonds of human society, while it either punishes the wickedness of wrongdoers or grants rewards to good men. It is therefore the proper task of kings (as Jerome says) to render judgment and justice, to free from the hand of calumniators those oppressed by force, and to bring help to the stranger, the orphan and the widow, who are more easily oppressed by the powerful. Wherefore kings ought to strive with all zeal to fulfil that office to which they are known to have been called, not neglecting justice, but giving their due right both to the poor and to the rich: for in this way they will secure peace for their subjects and a safe and tranquil kingdom for themselves. For, as Scripture bears witness: When a righteous king sits upon the throne, no one who is evil shall stand against him. At the beginning, therefore, among the peoples and nations (as has been said), supreme power rested with kings, whom to the height of this majesty not popular ambition but moderation observed among good men advanced. The people were bound by no laws; the decisions of princes stood in place of laws. It was their custom to defend the boundaries of their realm rather than to extend them, and kingdoms were bounded within each man's own homeland.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: Quare Monarchia, Regiaq; Romana potestas instituta fuerit.
units.tr: Why the Monarchy and the Roman imperial power were instituted.

units.la: VErum cum plurimos Reges orbis haberet, coepit (vt fit) pluralitas principum discordiam parere. Namque cum modo de finibus, modo de iurisdictione contenderent, nec esset qui lites dirimeret, nisi gladius, cum nemo minorem se altero reputaret, strepentibus bellis, nec ciuitas cum ciuitate, nec prouincia cum prouincia conuenire poterat, dulceq; illud ac suauissimum humanæ societatis commercium prohibebatur. Sed affuit præsto benigna humanæ naturæ prouidentia, quæ suopte ingenio ad optima tendit, nec vult quæ sunt, quaeq; futura sunt, male disposita. Hac igitur operante, ad vnum principatum, quē Græci Monarchiam, nostri vero Imperiū vocitant, reduci singula placuit. Namque vt priuatorum hominum exorbitantes impetus iusta Regum moderatione compesci natura disposuit: sic & ipsorum regum per vnum principem immensas frenare cupiditates instituit. Nec enim aliter pax vniuersalis haberi poterat. Hinc illud Assyriorum Imperium exortum est, quod Ninus Semiramis coniunx, super omnes populos Orientes extendit: quod nonnunquam per Medos & aliquando per Persas constat administratum. Hinc Græcorum principatus, Alexandri Magni virtute atque fortuna, ex Europa in Asiam atque Lybiam ampliatus, ad obedientiam sui mundum redegit. Hinc Carthaginense dominium per Africam Europamque late patens, ad Scipionis vsque victoriam perduravit. Sed cum hæc imperia nunquam sibi totum orbem subiecissent, ac propterea pacem vniuersalem parere non potuerint, placuit siue natura humani generis altrici, siue ipsius naturæ domino rectorique Deo Romanum Imperium excitare.
units.tr: But since the world had very many kings, the plurality of rulers (as usually happens) began to breed discord. For while they contended now over boundaries, now over jurisdiction, and there was no one to settle the disputes except the sword, and since no one thought himself inferior to another, wars rang out, and neither city could meet with city nor province with province, and that sweet and most pleasant intercourse of human society was forbidden. But the kindly providence of human nature was at hand, which by its own disposition tends toward what is best, and does not wish what is, or what is to come, to be ill arranged. Under its guidance, therefore, it was agreed that all things should be brought back to one sovereignty, which the Greeks call Monarchia and we call Imperium. For just as nature has ordained that the excessive impulses of private men be restrained by the just moderation of kings, so too it has established that the boundless desires of the kings themselves be curbed by one prince. Indeed, universal peace could not otherwise be maintained. Hence arose that Assyrian empire, which Ninus and his wife Semiramis extended over all the peoples of the East; it is known to have been administered at times by the Medes and at times by the Persians. Hence the Greek sovereignty, enlarged from Europe into Asia and Libya by the courage and fortune of Alexander the Great, brought the world to obedience to itself. Hence the Carthaginian dominion, extending widely through Africa and Europe, lasted until the victory of Scipio. But since these empires never subjected the whole world to themselves, and therefore could not produce universal peace, it pleased either the nurturing nature of the human race, or God, the lord and ruler of nature itself, to raise up the Roman Empire.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: Quibus olim magistratibus vrbs Romana regi cœperit. Et unde maiestas Imperialis fuerit instituta.
units.tr: By what magistrates the city of Rome first began to be governed, and whence the Imperial majesty was instituted.

units.la: ROma vero ab initio per Reges gubernata est, septemq; Regibus paruit, quos constat omnem habuisse potestatem. Quibus exactis, Consules constituti sunt: penes quos summum ius vti esset, lege rogatum est. Sed hi quamuis possent ciues coercere, atque in vincula publica deducere, in caput tamen ciuis Romani animaduertere non valebant: nec prouocatio erat ab his prohibita. Quo in regimine permulti tumultus fuere, sæpeq; plebe cum patribus discordante, variata est gubernatio ciuitatis. Nam & aliquando per Decemviros, & aliquando per Tribunos, sæpius tamen per Consules regimen actum est. Populo deinde aucto, cum crebra orirentur bella, & acriora quædam à finitimis inferrentur, vrgente necessitate, placuit maioris potestatis constitui magistratum: prodieruntq; Dictatores, à quibus nec prouocandi ius fuit, & quibus etiam capitis animaduersio data est: sed temporaria fuit istorum potestas. Paulatim namque natura ad id quod optimum erat, iter parabat. Ad extremum autem, cum neque populus, neque Senatus, nec alii magistratus, satis probe prouincias vrbemque regerent, necesse fuit Reipublicæ per vnum consulii constitutoque Principe, datum ei ius est, vt ratum esset quicquid ab eo constitueretur. Cui rei principium Iulium Cæsarem præstitisse, non est ambiguum. Per eum namq; regimina reipublicæ ad Imperatores perpetuo sunt translata.
units.tr: Rome, to be sure, was from the beginning governed by kings, and obeyed seven kings, who are agreed to have had complete power. When these were driven out, Consuls were appointed, in whose hands the supreme right was to rest, as was enacted by law. But although these could restrain citizens and lead them into public chains, they could not punish a Roman citizen with death, nor was appeal from them forbidden. Under this form of government there were very many disturbances, and often, with the plebs at odds with the patricians, the government of the state was changed. For at times the government was carried on by the Decemvirs, at times by the Tribunes, but more often by the Consuls.
