Then, as the people grew and frequent wars arose, and some fiercer attacks were made by neighbouring peoples, necessity pressing, it was decided that a magistrate of greater power should be set up; and so Dictators appeared, from whom there was no right of appeal, and to whom the power of capital punishment was also given; but their power was temporary. For nature was gradually preparing the way towards what was best. At last, since neither the people, nor the Senate, nor the other magistrates governed the provinces and the city well enough, it became necessary for the commonwealth to be ruled by one man; and with a Prince appointed, he was given the right that whatever he decreed should be binding. That Julius Caesar was the first to set this in motion is not in doubt. For through him the governments of the commonwealth were permanently transferred to the Emperors.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Imperatoriam maiestatem diuinitus à Christo Iesu adprobatam esse.
units.tr: That the imperial majesty has been approved by Christ Jesus from heaven.

units.la: IMperatorum potestas non solum vi naturæ introducta est ad publicam vtilitatem, sed etiam per Dominum & Saluatorem nostrum Christum Iesum, Dei filium (in cuius manu sunt omnia regna mundi) & verbo comprobata reperitur, & facto: qui & nasci voluit cum vniuersus describeretur orbis, & Augusti Cæsaris censum tulit. Nec hoc contentus, dari etiam pro se ac Petro tributum iussit. Interrogatus quoque, An Cæsari dare censum liceret? viso numismate, Reddite, inquit, quæ sunt Cæsaris Cæsari, & quæ sunt Dei Deo. Hinc beatus Ambrosius, Sitributum, inquit, petiū Imperator, non negamus, agri ecclesiæ soluant. Et insuper magnum quidem est, & speciale documentum, quo Christiani vni sublimioribus potestatibus docentur esse subiecti, ne quis constitutionem terreni regis putet esset soluendam. Si enim censum filius Dei soluit, quis tantus es, qui non putas esse soluendum? Adsunt & alia Christi oracula, quibus Imperii potestas extollitur. Namque dum ait Pilato; Non haberes aduersum me potestatem vllam, nisi tibi datum esset desuper: quid aliud ostendere voluit, quam Romani principis, cuius vicem Pilatus gerebat, ex Deo potestatem prodire? Quod si desuper ad Cæsarem referamus, qui erat potestatis Pilati author, tantundem habemus. Nam illam Christus approbat, ac secundum carnem se illi submittit. Inde Iustinianus Cæsar Imperium sibi à cœlesti maiestate traditum asserit.
units.tr: The power of the emperors was not only introduced by the force of nature for the public advantage, but is also found to be approved both by word and by deed by our Lord and Saviour Christ Jesus, the Son of God (in whose hand are all the kingdoms of the world). He chose to be born when the whole world was being registered, and he paid the census of Augustus Caesar. Not content with this, he also ordered tribute to be paid for himself and for Peter. Asked also whether it was lawful to give the census to Caesar, he looked at the coin and said: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." Hence blessed Ambrose said: "If the Emperor demands tribute, we do not deny it; the fields of the Church pay it." Indeed, it is a great and special proof by which Christians are taught to be subject to the higher powers, so that no one should think that the ordinance of an earthly king need not be paid. For if the Son of God paid the census, who are you, that you think it need not be paid? There are also other sayings of Christ by which the power of the empire is exalted. For when he says to Pilate, "You would have no power at all against me, unless it had been given you from above," what else did he wish to show than that the power of the Roman prince, whose place Pilate held, came forth from God? And if we refer "from above" to Caesar, who was the author of Pilate's power, we have just as much. For Christ approves that power, and submits himself to it according to the flesh. Hence the Emperor Justinian asserts that the empire was handed down to him from the heavenly majesty.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Ecclesiasticam potestatem à Christo pariter esse constitutam.
units.tr: That ecclesiastical power was likewise instituted by Christ.

units.la: HInc etiam illa Christi verba trahuntur, cum dicenti discipulo, Ecce gladii duo hic: Sufficit, inquit. Quo dicto spiritualia summo Pontifici, & temporalia Cæsari, uti doctores interpretantur, subiecit: Ac si diceret: Duæ potestates sunto, spiritualis & temporalis. Nam satis sunt ad vniuersalis ecclesiæ gubernationem. Hinc sacri canones ad firmamentum cœli, id est, vniuersalis Ecclesiæ, fecisse Deum in principio duo magna luminaria dicunt: id est, duas potestates instituisse, quæ sunt Pontificalis authoritas, & Regalis potestas: & altera diebus, id est, spiritualib, altera vero noctibus, id est temporalibus esse. Duo sunt n. (Gelasius inquit) quibus principaliter hic mundus regitur: authoritas sacra pontificum, & Regalis potestas. Quod si quis percontetur, cum tantopere laudetur vnitas, cur duab' his potestatib' vna duntaxat persona non sit præfecta? cum & apud gentiles nonnunquam sacerdotis officium obiuerit Imperator: & in veteri Testamento legamus, Melchisedech regem ac sacerdotem fuisse, Nicolaum Papam audire debemus. Sic enim ait: Cum ad verum ventum est, vltro sibi nec Imperator iura pontificatus arripuit, nec pontifex nomen Imperatorium vsurpauit: quoniam mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus, pro actibus propriis & dignitatibus distinctis, officia potestatis vtriusq; discreuit, propria volens medicinali humilitate sursum efferri, non humana superbia rursus in inferna demergi vt & Christiani Imperatores pro aterna vita pontificibus indigerent, & pontifices pro cursu temporalium tantummodo rerum Imperialibus legibus vterentur. Quamuis spiritualis actio à carnalibus distaret incursibus, & Deo militans minime secularibus negociis implicaret, ac vicissim non ille rebus diuinis præsidere videretur, qui esset secularibus negociis implicatus. In patrimonio tamen beati Petri (sicuti Canones asserunt) libere potest Apostolica sedes, nedum summi Pontificis authoritatem exercere, sed etiam summi Principis exequi potestatem.
units.tr: From this also come those words of Christ, when the disciple said, Behold, here are two swords. It is enough, he said. By these words, as the teachers interpret them, the spiritual things were subjected to the supreme Pontiff and the temporal things to Caesar: as if he had said, "Let there be two powers, spiritual and temporal; for they are enough for the government of the universal Church." Hence the sacred canons say that God, for the firmament of heaven, that is, of the universal Church, made in the beginning two great lights: that is, He instituted two powers, which are the pontifical authority and the regal power, and that the one is for the days, that is, the spiritual, and the other for the nights, that is, the temporal. For there are two (says Gelasius) by which this world is chiefly ruled: the sacred authority of the pontiffs and the regal power. But if someone should ask, since unity is so greatly praised, why these two powers are not entrusted to one and the same person, seeing that even among the Gentiles the emperor sometimes performed the office of priest, and we read in the Old Testament that Melchizedek was both king and priest, we ought to hear Pope Nicholas. For he says: When the true one came, neither did the emperor of his own accord seize the rights of the pontificate, nor did the pontiff usurp the imperial title; because the Mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, distinguishing the offices of each power by their own actions and distinct dignities, willed that what was proper to each should be raised up by a humility that heals, and not thrust down again into the depths by human pride; so that Christian emperors would need pontiffs for eternal life, and pontiffs would use imperial laws only for the course of temporal affairs. Although spiritual action was far removed from carnal assaults, and the soldier of God was not entangled in secular business, and conversely he did not seem to preside over divine things who was entangled in secular business. Yet in the patrimony of blessed Peter (as the canons assert) the Apostolic See may freely exercise not only the authority of the supreme Pontiff but also the power of the supreme Prince.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XVIII.

units.la: Antichristum non venturum, donec Imperium Romanum steterit.
units.tr: That Antichrist will not come as long as the Roman Empire stands.

units.la: HAbet quoque Romanum Imperium (vt quidam autumant) aliud priuilegium: nec enim ea stante venturum existimant Antichristum. Sic enim doctoris gentium Pauli verba illa interpretantur: Qui tenet, teneat, donec de medio fiat: & tunc revelabitur ille filius iniquitatis, quem Dominus spiritu oris sui interficiet. Quam sententiam etiam diuum Augustinum liquet esse secutum. Hæc igitur summa Romani principis authoritas, quam communis vtilitas desiderauit, natura inuenit, Deus dedit, Filius confirmauit, consensus hominum approbauit, de stirpe duarum rerum, sicut Iustinianus ait, proueniens, vimq; suam exinde muniens: felix Romanorum genus omnibus anteponi nationibus, omnibusque populis dominari fecit. Nec gens vlla fuit orbe toto, quæ collum non inclinarit Imperio, nisi cui Romanus populus fœdum putauit imperare. Et quamuis aliquando summa potestas penes populum fuit: constituto tamen (vt diximus) principe, lege antiqua, quæ Regia nuncupatur, populus ei, & in eum omne suum Imperium ac potestatem contulit. Nec enim vel populare regimen, quod Politicum, vel optimorum ciuium, quod Aristocraticum appellatur, tam iustum tamq; pacificum esse potest, quam Monarchicum, quod in Romano principe recognoscimus. Quod aliquando per Italos, aliquando per Hispanos, interdum per Afros, Dalmatasque constat administratum. Peruenit etiam ad Græcos diuq; apud Constantinopolim tantæ gloriæ dignitatis permansit. Et quamuis aliquando duo simul fuerint Augusti, vt Diocletianus & Maximianus, nonnunquam etiam plures, id tamen vsurpatione magis quam iure contigit. In apibus enim, inquit beatus Gregorius, princeps vnus est; grues vnum sequuntur, Imperator vnus. Obuenit autem hæc dignitas, nunc senatus electione, nunc militari fauore, nunc principis ordinatione.
units.tr: The Roman Empire also has, as some maintain, another privilege: they think Antichrist will not come while it stands. For this is how they interpret the words of Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles: He who now letteth, let him let, until he be taken out of the way; and then shall that Wicked be revealed, whom the Lord shall consume with the spirit of his mouth. It is clear that blessed Augustine also followed this opinion. This supreme authority of the Roman prince, which the common good desired, nature discovered, God gave, the Son confirmed and the consent of men approved, springing from the stock of two things, as Justinian says, and strengthening its power from that source, made the happy Roman race rank above all nations and rule over all peoples. There was no nation in the whole world that did not bow its neck to the Empire, except those whom the Roman people thought it shameful to rule. And although at times the supreme power lay with the people, nevertheless, once a prince had been established (as we have said) by the ancient law called Regia, the people conferred all their empire and power on him and into him. For neither popular government, which is called Political, nor the government of the best citizens, which is called Aristocratic, can be as just and as peaceful as the Monarchical, which we recognise in the Roman prince. This has been administered at one time by Italians, at another by Spaniards, sometimes by Africans and Dalmatians. It also reached the Greeks and for a long time remained at Constantinople in such glory and dignity. And although at times two Augusti were together, such as Diocletian and Maximian, and sometimes even more, this came about by usurpation rather than by right. Among bees, says blessed Gregory, there is one prince; cranes follow one leader, one emperor. This dignity comes to a man now by election of the senate, now by the favour of the army, now by appointment of the prince.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: Quare Romanum Imperium fuerit à Græcis ad Germanos translatum.
units.tr: Why the Roman Empire was transferred from the Greeks to the Germans.

units.la: DEnum vero negligentibus Romam Græcis, eamq; nunc Barbarorum, nunc aliorum direptionibus relinquentibus, populus iste Romanus, qui suo sanguine tantum parabat Imperium, qui suis virtutibus monarchiam fundauerat orbi, venientem in auxilium eius Carolum Magnum Francorum regem natione, Germanum, qui urbem sacraque loca ab omni hostium incursione defendit, primo Patricium post Augustum, concurrente summi Pontificis consensu salutauit Cæsarem. Generali itaq; modo in Germanos Romanum Imperium constat esse translatum, quod per varias manus deductum, ad te denique, Diue Cæsar Friderice, per legitimam electionem deriuatum est, tibiq; suprema in temporalibus est ex alto commissa potestas, vt bella fœliciter peragas, pacem decores, & reipublicæ statum sustentes. Ad quas res omnes populi, omnes rationes, omnesq; reges & principes tuo debent Imperio libentibus animis se submittere.
units.tr: Since the Greeks neglected Rome, and left it now to the plunderings of barbarians, now to those of others, the Roman people, who had acquired the empire with their own blood and had founded a monarchy for the world by their virtues, received Charles the Magnus, king of the Franks and a German by nation, who came to their aid and defended the city and the holy places from every incursion of the enemy. They first hailed him Patrician after Augustus, and then, with the consent of the supreme Pontiff, saluted him as Caesar. It is therefore established that in general the Roman Empire was transferred to the Germans, and, having been carried through various hands, it has at last come by lawful election to you, divine Caesar Frederick; and the supreme power in temporal affairs has been committed to you from on high, so that you may successfully carry on wars, adorn peace, and sustain the state of the commonwealth. To all these matters all peoples, all nations, and all kings and princes ought willingly to submit themselves to your empire.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: Omnes & populos & potentatus iure sub Romano Imperatore esse in temporalibus & secularibus, vti Pontifice Max. in spiritualibus.
units.tr: That all peoples and powers are rightly subject to the Roman Emperor in temporal and secular matters, just as the Supreme Pontiff is in spiritual matters.

units.la: NAmque sicut in spiritualibus Romano Pontifici singuli Patriarchæ, Primatesq; cæterique Pontifices & Prælati subiecti sunt, quamuis & hoc aliquando Græci negarint, & adhuc perfidi Hussitarum genus inficietur: sic & Romano principi temporales quoslibet liquet esse subiectos. Enim cum Canonum authoritas Imperatorem in temporalibus eos præcellere dicat, qui ab eo accipiunt temporalia: quis non videt & populos & principes omnes ab Imperatore (qui mundi Dominus est) recipere temporalia, sibiq; idcirco debere obedientiam? Iure enim humano (vt Augustinus inquit) dicitur, Hæc villa mea est, hic seruus meus est, hæc domus mea est: iura autem humana, iura Imperatorum sunt. Exinde, sicut ab initio retulimus, cum ratio ipsa naturalis ostendat, vnum esse principem oportere, qui lites dirimat, iustitiam administret, populos in pace custodiat, ac temporalibus præsit omnibus: manifestum est, huius muneris dignitatem Romano regi competere, quem diu constat in possessione eius fuisse. Nempe quamuis aliqui parere Romano negent Imperio, nemo tamen post Augusti Octauiani monarchiam, tantam vesaniam induit, vt sub alio quam sub Romani Regis titulo, mundi Dominum orbisq; principem sese ausus fuerit appellare.
units.tr: For just as in spiritual matters all the Patriarchs, Primates and other Pontiffs and Prelates are subject to the Roman Pontiff, although the Greeks sometimes denied this and the treacherous race of the Hussites still denies it, so it is clear that all temporal rulers are subject to the Roman prince. For since the authority of the Canons says that the Emperor excels in temporal matters those who receive their temporal goods from him, who does not see that all peoples and princes receive their temporal goods from the Emperor (who is the Lord of the world), and therefore ought to render him obedience? For by human law (as Augustine says) it is said, This villa is mine, this slave is mine, this house is mine: but human laws are the laws of Emperors. Hence, as we set out at the beginning, since natural reason itself shows that there must be one prince who settles disputes, administers justice, keeps peoples in peace, and presides over all temporal affairs, it is evident that the dignity of this office belongs to the Roman king, who has been, as is well known, long in possession of it. Indeed, although some deny that they owe obedience to the Roman Empire, yet no one since the monarchy of Augustus Octavian has been so mad as to dare to call himself the Lord of the world and prince of the globe under any title other than King of the Romans.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: Errare eos, qui se ita asserunt exemptos, vt nihil Imperio debeant.
units.tr: That those who claim to be so exempt that they owe the Empire nothing are mistaken.

units.la: CÆterum, vt horum sententiam expendamus, qui se tanta fretos asserunt libertate, vt omnino Imperio teneantur, quadamque se potiri dicunt exemptione: (quamuis istorum proteruitati potius armis, quam legibus obuiandum foret, vt quo iure se putant exemptos, eodem se scirent esse subiectos) libet tamen aliquid in hac re scribere. Cuncti profecto qui se esse sub iugo negant Imperii, aut id priuilegio se asserunt assecutos, aut virtute aliqua. Priuilegium autem ex beneficentia Imperii suscepisse, aut aliunde: hoc secundo casu non est opus confirmatione. Cum enim Romanum Imperium adeo super omnes mortales in temporalibus sit erectum, manifesti iuris est, neminem esse, qui ei possit inferre præiudicium. Cassa nanque sunt omnia, atq; irrita, quæ abeo fiunt, qui potestatem non habet: nec ratum est quicquam, quod per iniuriam agitur. Quod fiab Imperio talis manauerit exemptio, dicimus eam & hoc casu nullius esse momenti. Nam etsi maxima sit atque amplissima Romani principis authoritas: eo tamen priuatur Augustus, vt sui similem non possit efficere. Quod certe faceret, si regem aliquem in omnibus liberum a se redderet, & exemptum. Posset nanque successu temporis tot eximere, vt nedum sibi parem, sed etiam maiorem se inueniret. Quod esse absurdum, neminem fugit. Idcirco nanque princeps Romanus Augusti nomen accepit, vt non minuere, sed augere Imperii potestatem deberet. Nec propterea minor est eius authoritas, quia similem sibi non potest creare: sicut nec Deus desinit esse omnipotens, quamuis in Deitate non possit nisi vnicus fore.
units.tr: But, to weigh the opinion of those who assert that they rely on so great a liberty that they are wholly bound to the Empire, and yet say that they hold some exemption (although their insolence ought rather to be met with arms than with laws, since they would know that they are subject by the very right by which they think themselves exempt), it is nevertheless worth writing something on this matter. Certainly all who deny that they are under the yoke of the Empire either claim to have obtained this by privilege, or by some virtue of their own. As for a privilege received from the kindness of the Empire, or from elsewhere: in the second case no confirmation is needed. For since the Roman Empire is so set over all mortals in temporal matters, it is a plain point of law that there is no one who could inflict an injury upon it. For all things done by one who lacks power are void and null, and nothing is valid that is carried out by wrong. As for whether such an exemption arose from the Empire itself, we say that in this case too it is of no weight at all. For although the authority of the Roman prince is very great and very wide, yet Augustus is so limited that he cannot make anyone like himself. He certainly could do so if he rendered some king entirely free and exempt from himself. For over time he could exempt so many that they would find someone not only equal to him but even greater. That this is absurd, no one fails to see. For the Roman prince received the name Augustus precisely so that he should augment, not diminish, the power of the Empire. Nor is his authority any less because he cannot create one like himself, just as God does not cease to be omnipotent, although in the Godhead there can be only one.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: Monarchiam vel solam pacis vniuersalis esse causam, quam & illa conseruet.
units.tr: That monarchy alone is the cause of universal peace, and that it also preserves that peace.

units.la: PRæterea cum (sicut supra retulimus) ex iure naturæ fundatum constet Imperium, atque ad pacem tenendam, iustitiamque distribuendam Monarchia sit necessaria, certum est, talia priuilegia non valere, quæ multitudinem summarum afferunt potestatum. Nascuntur enim ex hoc discordiæ, frequentes fiunt rapinæ, multimodæ committuntur neces absque numero: cum, pace turbata, hinc atque inde bella grassentur, existente nemine qui maior omnibus iuris ordine litibus possit imponere modum. Quod si vno sub capite viueremus, si vnam omnes sequeremur obedientiam, si vnum duntaxat in temporalibus supremum Principem recognosceremus, floreret vbique terrarum pax optima, dulcique omnes concordia frueremur. Cuius rei signum est manifestum, quod ab initio nascentis mundi vsq; in hoc ævi, nunquam pacem fuisse legimus vniversalem, nisi cum in vnum Cæsarem Augustum, in modum cœlestis regni, totus orbis oculos dirigebat. Quod licet ob reuerentiam Christi redemptoris nostri tunc contigerit, qui nostram humanamque formam induit: sufficere tamen debet, diuinum illum mundi fabricatorem, viam hanc ostendisse pacis habendæ, cum orbis sub vno principe regeretur. Liquet igitur, priuilegia, quæ monarchico regimini obuiant, ex quacunque veniant potestate, non habere vigorem, eaq; non solum per successorem, sed ab ipso quoque qui concessit, esse cassanda: nec enim tolerare Principem decet, quæ ad subuersionem tendunt Imperii.
units.tr: Moreover, since (as we have said above) the empire is founded on the law of nature, and since a monarchy is necessary for keeping the peace and distributing justice, it is certain that privileges which create a multitude of sovereign powers are not valid. For from this arise discords, robberies become frequent, and killings are committed without number, since, with peace disturbed, wars rage on every side, and there is no one greater than all who, by the order of law, could impose an end on disputes. But if we lived under one head, if we all followed one obedience, if we acknowledged one supreme prince in temporal matters, the best peace would flourish everywhere on earth, and we would all enjoy sweet concord. A clear sign of this is that, from the beginning of the newborn world down to this age, we read of universal peace only when the whole world turned its eyes to one Caesar Augustus, after the manner of the heavenly kingdom. Although this came about at that time out of reverence for Christ our redeemer, who took on our nature and human form, it ought nonetheless to be enough that the divine maker of the world showed this way of having peace, namely when the world was ruled under one prince. It is clear, therefore, that privileges which stand in the way of monarchical government, from whatever power they come, have no force, and that they must be annulled not only by the successor but also by the very one who granted them; for it is not fitting that a prince tolerate things that tend to the overthrow of the empire.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: Errare quoq; eos, qui se suis virtutibus exemptionem ab Imperio meruisse ferunt.
units.tr: That those also err who claim that they earned exemption from the Empire by their own virtues.

units.la: SEd aiunt aliqui, propriis se virtutibus id priuilegii meruisse, quamuis Imperii non interuenit authoritas. Dicunt n. se suis armis, suoq; sanguine prouincias vendicasse, quæ vel a barbaris, vel ab hostibus Christiani nominis occupabantur, nec Romanū recognoscebant Imperium. Quod quam ridiridiculum sit, iniustum, absonum, ex superioribus licentiuri. Insuper quoque, si dignum hoc est, nec illud erit indignum, si quod aliquis iniuste rapuit, alius vi recipiat sibique teneat, nec vero Domino reddat: Quod nemo dixerit esse iustum. Constat enim omnes prouincias (vt ante diximus) sub Imperio quondam fuisse, cuius directum dominium apud Romanum principem assidue mansit. Itaque licet barbari superuenerint, viq; illas inuaserint, si tamen postea recuperantur, non vindicatori dandæ, tanquam exempto, quamuis laudandus præminandusq; sit, sed Imperio sunt restituendæ. Nullius enim tanta laus est tantaque virtus, vt eius causa destitui debeat imperium. Semper namque maior est vtilitas publica, quam priuata: nec committendum (vt iam probauimus) quod propter cuiusquam merita, potestas aliqua erigatur Imperio similis: qualis in exemptis esset, qui nullum superiorem admitterent. Quare res Monarchiæ dignitatis neruos elidit, schisma sub Imperio facit, & omnem humanæ societatis concordiam dirimit.
units.tr: But some say that they earned that privilege by their own virtues, even though the authority of the Empire did not intervene. They claim that with their own arms and their own blood they won back provinces that were occupied either by barbarians or by enemies of the Christian name and no longer acknowledged the Roman Empire. How ridiculous, unjust and absurd this is may be gathered from what was said above. Moreover, if this were worthy, it would not be unworthy for whatever one man has unjustly seized, another to take by force and keep for himself, and not return to its lord, which no one would call just. For it is agreed that all provinces (as we said before) were once under the Empire, and its direct dominion always remained with the Roman prince. Therefore, although barbarians came in and seized them by force, if they are afterwards recovered, they must be restored to the Empire, not handed over to the one who reclaimed them as if he were exempt, however much he may deserve praise and preeminence. For no one's glory or virtue is so great that the Empire ought to be deprived on his account. The public advantage is always greater than the private, and it must not be allowed (as we have already proved) that on account of anyone's merits some power similar to the Empire should be raised up, such as would exist among the exempt, who acknowledge no superior. Such a thing shatters the sinews of the dignity of monarchy, creates a schism within the Empire, and dissolves all concord of human society.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CAP. XIV.

units.la: Quid veniat appellatione Sub Imperio esse.
units.tr: What is meant by being under the Empire.

units.la: NOn tamen propterea Regum & aliorum principum magnam esse potestatem inficiamur, sed esse eos sub Imperio dicimus: eorumq; correptionem, quando tyranni efficiuntur, ad Romanum principem pertinere, causas regum asserimus Cæsari remittendas, teneriq; omnes pro salute communi Imperatori parere, venire ad bellum vocatos, conferre impensas, mittere auxilia, præbere transitum, elargiri commeatum, nihilq; fugere quod Cæsarea maiestas iniunxerit. Vt quam ipsi à suis subditis obedientiam exigunt, eandem suo Domino præstent Imperatori.
units.tr: Yet we do not on that account deny that kings and other princes have great power; we say that they are under the Empire. We maintain that the correction of kings, when they become tyrants, belongs to the Roman prince, and that the causes of kings are to be referred to Caesar. All are bound, for the common safety, to obey the Emperor: to be summoned to war, to contribute expenses, to send auxiliary troops, to grant passage, to supply provisions, and to shun nothing that Caesarean majesty has enjoined. Let them render to their Lord the Emperor the same obedience which they themselves demand from their own subjects.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CAP. XV.

units.la: Quibus de causis ab Imperatore priuilegia data reuocari possint.
units.tr: On what grounds privileges granted by the Emperor may be revoked.

units.la: VErum quoniam de Priuilegiis mentio incidit, dicemus aperte, quid in re hac priscæ doctores sapientiæ tradiderint. Est equidem Romani Principis, ciuitatibus, principibus, regibus, tum propter merita, tum propter vrgentes causas, priuilegia elargiri, sed ea talia esse conuenit, quæ vires Imperatoriæ potestatis nequaquam extinguant: eaq; potest Imperator tam à seipso, quam à suis antecessoribus concessa declarare, interpretari: ac cum causa fuerit, abrogare, vel illis derogare. Auferuntur namque priuilegia, cum ex falsis narrationibus obtenta sunt: impetratis namque carere debet mendax precator. Reuocantur, cum male vtuntur, qui illa sunt assecuti. Priuilegium meretur amittere, qui concessa sibi abutitur potestate. Cassantur, cum male merere incipiunt, qui eadem bene merendo obtinuerunt. Irritantur, si damnosa Reipublicæ reperientur: quæ cum data fuerunt, erant vtilia, vel si bonis moribus contrariantur: aut si magnam Imperio iacturam seruata faciunt, quæ subiata grandem præberent vtilitatem. Quoniam sicut maius bonum minori præponitur, ita communis vtilitas speciali præfertur vtilitati. Nec iane priuilegia vlla conferre, vel tolerare Cæsarem conuenit, quæ vel delicta inducant, vel communem auferant commoditatem. Ideo namque imperialem fortunam rebus humanis Deus præposuit, vt possit omnia quæ nouiter contingunt, & emendare, & componere, & modis & rebus competentibus tradere. Absq; tamen rationabili causa necauferenda sunt priuilegia, nec derogandum est eis. Omnis namq; potestas quæ à Deo data est, vt inquit Apostolus, in ædificationem tradita est, non destructionem. Quæcunq; igitur priuilegia iuste concessa sunt, manentq; iuste, sine detrimento Reipublicæ seruanda sunt. Decet n. priuilegium principis esse mansurum. At cum priuilegium quod olim vtiliter concessum est, damnosum efficitur: satius est euellere malam arborem, quam nutrire. Si enim iuxta Euangelicam veritatem, arbor quæ fructum non adfert, excindi debet, in ignemque mitti: quanto magis excindenda est, quæ Reipublicæ officit arbor?
units.tr: But since the matter of privileges has come up, we shall state plainly what the ancient teachers of wisdom have handed down on this subject. It is indeed the right of the Roman Prince to grant privileges to cities, princes and kings, both on account of merits and on account of pressing causes; but such privileges ought to be of a kind that in no way destroy the powers of imperial authority. The Emperor may declare and interpret privileges granted both by himself and by his predecessors, and, when there is cause, may abrogate them or derogate from them. Privileges are taken away when they were obtained on the basis of false accounts, for a lying petitioner ought to lose what he has obtained by request. They are revoked when those who have obtained them make bad use of them; one who abuses the power conceded to him deserves to lose the privilege. They are cancelled when those who obtained them by good service begin to serve badly. They are annulled if they are found to be harmful to the commonwealth: those which were useful when they were granted, or which are contrary to good morals, or which, if they are kept, cause great loss to the Empire, while their removal would bring great advantage. For just as the greater good is preferred to the lesser, so the common advantage is preferred to a particular advantage. Nor indeed is it fitting for the Emperor to confer or tolerate any privileges which either induce wrongdoing or take away the common good. For this reason God placed imperial fortune over human affairs, so that it might be able both to correct and to settle all things that newly arise, and to hand them over by fitting means and methods. Yet privileges are not to be taken away without a reasonable cause, nor is anything to be detracted from them. For every power that is given by God, as the Apostle says, is given for edification, not destruction. Therefore whatever privileges have been justly granted, and remain just, are to be preserved without detriment to the commonwealth. For a prince's privilege ought to endure. But when a privilege that was once granted for a useful purpose becomes harmful, it is better to uproot the bad tree than to nourish it. For if, according to the Gospel truth, a tree that does not bear fruit must be cut down and cast into the fire, how much more must that tree be cut down which harms the commonwealth?

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CAP. XVI.

units.la: Imperatorem non obligari ad rationem reddendam suorum factorum, sed de iis bene præsumendum esse.
units.tr: That the Emperor is not bound to give an account of his acts, but that good ground is to be presumed for them.

units.la: VErum, cum in omnibus quæ geruntur à Principe, causa præsumatur & ratio facti, si quando vel abrogare priuilegia, vel ipsis derogare Principem contingat iniuste: quamuis liceat eum per viam supplicationis informare, humiliterq; petere restitutionem, non tamen reclamare licet, vituperare vel impugnare, si perseuerat, cum nemo sit, qui de suis factis temporalibus possit cognoscere. Tolerandum est patienter, quod princeps facit, quamuis iniquè, expectandaque est successoris emenda, vel supremi correctio iudicis, qui violentias atque iniurias non finit esse perpetuas. Cogitandum insuper est, quod Princeps agit, Dei fieri permissione. Quia cor Regis (vt inquit Scriptura) in manu Dei est, & vbi voluerit, inclinabit illud. Deus autem sæpe propter peccata subditorum deprauari permittit vitam rectorum. Ex quo fit, vt occulto Dei iudicio apud Deum iusta nonnunquam reperiantur, quæ nobis videntur iniusta.
units.tr: Yet since, in all that is done by a prince, a cause and a reason for the act are to be presumed, if ever the prince should abrogate privileges or act to their detriment unjustly, then although it is lawful to inform him by way of supplication and humbly to seek restitution, it is nonetheless not lawful to cry out against him, revile him or attack him if he persists, since no one can know the reasons behind his temporal acts. What the prince does, though unjustly, must be borne patiently; one must await the amendment of his successor or the correction of the supreme Judge, who does not allow violence and injustice to last forever. Moreover, it must be considered that what the prince does takes place by the permission of God. For the heart of the king (as Scripture says) is in the hand of God, and he will incline it wherever he wills. God, however, often permits the lives of rulers to be corrupted on account of the sins of subjects. Hence it comes about that, by the hidden judgment of God, things that seem unjust to us are sometimes found to be just before God.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CAP. XVII.

units.la: Cæsarem etiam malis vel bonis, auferre posse bona temporalia.
units.tr: That the Emperor may take temporal goods from both the bad and the good.

units.la: Dicendum est etiam aliud, quod aliquibus fortasse durum videbitur, & absurdum: sed non detaceri, quod verum est, dictuque utile. Quid obstas penna? quid molesta es? cur non reddis tramentum? exprime Cæsaris priuilegium: nullum timeas, dum vera scribis. Nempe liberum Imperatori, non solum homini nequam, sed etiam viro bono, ac de republica bene merito, propter agrum, proprias domos, propriasque possessiones auferre, si Reipublicæ necessitas id expostulat. Hinc videmus prædia rustica, quæ bellis imminentibus damnosa sunt ciuitati, cum ædificiis incendi, agros effodi, vineas amputari, frumenta ex priuatis horreis, pecuniasque ex arcis ad publicum vsum deduci, quamuis hoc singularibus hominibus videatur esse damnosum: minus tamen malum est priuatos viros luere, quam Rempublicam perfundari.
units.tr: There is another thing to be said, which will perhaps seem harsh and absurd to some; yet it must not be passed over, since it is true and useful to say. Why do you hinder my pen? Why do you trouble me? Why do you not hand over the ink? Produce the Emperor's privilege: fear nothing, so long as you write what is true. Indeed it is lawful for the Emperor to take away fields, private houses and private possessions, not only from a wicked man but also from a good man who has deserved well of the commonwealth, if the necessity of the state demands it. Hence we see that country estates, which when wars are impending are harmful to the state, are burned along with their buildings, fields are dug up, vineyards are cut down, grain is taken from private granaries, and money from strongboxes is brought into public use. Although this may seem harmful to individual men, it is a lesser evil for private men to suffer loss than for the commonwealth to be destroyed.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XVIII.

units.la: Rempublicam ab omnibus esse priuatæ rei utilitatis, prasponendam.
units.tr: The commonwealth must be preferred to every private advantage of each citizen.

units.la: Nam nec opes priuatæ stare possunt, nisi salua Republica. His tamen hominibus qui propter Rempublicam singularia perferunt detrimenta, ex publico compensandum est: atque ita curandum, vt incommoditas belli non ad vnum vel paucos, sed ad omnes æqualiter peruenisse videatur. Quod si Reipub. status id non patitur, tolerabilius vnum est pati, quam [illegible, ~4 letters] pro salute sua omnia dabit quæcunque habet, quanto magis id Reipub. causa facere? cum non tan-um nobis nati simus, sed etiam Reipub. cui non minus quam nobis ipsis debemus parare diuitias. Nautæ, cum tempestas emersit, quæcunque sunt in navi bona, pro salute personarum deiciunt. Quod si hominem aliquem mari Nagii præstare causam putant, & hunc etiam marinis committunt fluctibus: sicut de Iona legimus in sacris, & apud gentiles de Orione scribunt. Expedit nanque vnum hominem mori pro populo, ne tota gens pereat: quam rem bonus civis æquo animo pro Reipub. tolerabit. Apud Romanos Curtius libenti pronoque animo pro salute reliquorum ciuium in hiatu terræ sese præcipitauit. Apud Græcos, Iphigeniam pro felici omnium navigatione, iubente patre, sacrificatam, Historici tradunt. Sicut enim membra quædam amputantur, si ipsa languere, & tanquam spiritu carere coeperint, ne reliquis nocEant ceteris partibus: sic & aliqui homines pro Republica pati debent, quamuis nihil mali videantur promeruisse, si cum ipsis Respublica perirt, quæ sine ipsis salua esset. Turpis enim est omnis pars, quæ suo toti non conuenit, & semper minus malum tolerandum est, vt euitetur maius: nec graue videri debet, si pro salute corporis pedem vel manum, vt sunt in Repub. ciues, dicimus resecandam, cum princeps qui caput est mysticî Reipub. corporis, cum salus communis expostulat, vitam ponere teneatur: sicut Athenien-sem Codrum, & apud Lacedæmonios Leonidam tradunt fecisse, qui pro salute suorum ciuium vltroneas obierunt mortes. Imitandus est enim Christus Iesus, qui non solum pastoribus vt animas pro suis ouibus ponerent, imperauit, sed ipse quoque cum esset caput Ecclesiæ, princeps & rector, vt nobis mortem demeret voluntariam mortem subiuit. Nunc quemadmodum circa leges habere se Princi-pem oporteat, breuiter absoluendum est.
units.tr: For private wealth cannot stand unless the commonwealth is safe. Yet those men who suffer private losses for the sake of the commonwealth must be compensated from public funds, and care must be taken that the burden of war falls not on one or a few but appears to have come equally upon all. But if the condition of the commonwealth does not allow this, it is more tolerable for one man to suffer than for the whole commonwealth to perish; for everyone who wishes to be safe gives up whatever he has, and how much more should he do so for the sake of the commonwealth, since we are born not for ourselves alone but also owe no less to the commonwealth than to ourselves, and must provide it with its riches. When a storm breaks out, sailors throw overboard whatever goods are on the ship to save their own lives. If men think that one man must be given to the sea to appease it, they also hand him over to the waves, as we read of Jonah in the sacred books, and as the Gentiles write of Orion. For it is expedient that one man die for the people, so that the whole nation may not perish, and a good citizen will bear this with an equal mind for the commonwealth. Among the Romans, Curtius gladly and willingly threw himself into the chasm of the earth for the safety of the rest of the citizens. Among the Greeks, the historians relate that Iphigenia was sacrificed at her father's command for the safe voyage of all. For just as certain limbs are cut off when they have begun to languish and, as it were, lose their life, lest they harm the other parts, so also some men ought to suffer for the commonwealth, even though they seem to have deserved no evil, if the commonwealth would perish with them when it would have been safe without them. For every part that does not agree with its whole is corrupt, and a lesser evil must always be endured so that a greater may be avoided. Nor should it seem grievous if, for the safety of the body, we say that a foot or a hand, as citizens are in the commonwealth, must be cut away; since the prince, who is the head of the mystical body of the commonwealth, is bound to lay down his life when the common good demands it. Thus they relate that Codrus of Athens, and among the Lacedaemonians Leonidas, did, who of their own accord died for the safety of their citizens. For Christ Jesus is to be imitated, who not only commanded the ministers to lay down their lives for their sheep, but who himself, being the head, prince and ruler of the Church, underwent a voluntary death to take away ours. Now it must be briefly explained how the prince ought to conduct himself with regard to the laws.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CAP. XIX.

units.la: Imperatoris adeo, Cæsaris esse, condere, soluere, interpretari, leges.
units.tr: That it belongs to the Emperor, to Caesar alone, to make, repeal and interpret laws.

units.la: Leges sacratissimas, quæ constringunt hominum vitas, vniuersique mundi ceruicibus imponuntur, solius Imperatoris est condere, cui quicquid placuerit, legis habet vigorem. Quodcunq; n. Imperator per epistolam & subscriptionem statuit, vel cognoscens decreuit, vel de plano interlocutus est, vel dicto præcepit, legem esse constat. In legibus autem conditis, si quid visum fuerit ambiguum ad imperiale culmen, per iudices referri debet, vt ex authoritate Augusta manifestetur, cui solum concessum est leges condere & interpretari. Nec quisquam sanæ mentis negabit leges posse ab eo dissolui, à quo sunt conditæ: cumque Imperator sit, qui vim legibus authoritatemq; impar-tit, constat & ipsum legibus derogare posse, illasque abrogare, cum causa fuerit rationabilis. Etenim si Decemuiris data facultas est, decem tabulas legum ex Græcia missas interpretari atque corrigere, si Prætoribus permissum est, ius nouum condere, vetusque reprehendere, quis non hanc facultatem in Cæsare recognoscat? in quem totam (sicut ante relatum est) Romani populi potestatem constat esse translatam.
units.tr: The most sacred laws, which bind the lives of men and are laid upon the necks of the whole world, belong to the Emperor alone to make, and whatever pleases him has the force of law. For whatever the Emperor has laid down by letter and signature, or decided upon examination, or settled after hearing the parties informally, or ordained by spoken command, is established as law. Moreover, in laws already enacted, if anything seems ambiguous to the imperial summit, it ought to be referred through judges, so that it may be made clear by the Augustan authority, to whom alone it has been granted to make and interpret laws. Nor will anyone of sound mind deny that laws can be dissolved by him by whom they were made; and since it is the Emperor who bestows force and authority on laws, it is clear that he too can derogate from laws and abrogate them, whenever there is a reasonable cause. For if the Decemvirs were given the power to interpret and correct the ten tables of law sent from Greece, and if the Praetors were permitted to frame new law and reprove old, who would not acknowledge this power in Caesar? Over him, as was said before, the whole power of the Roman people is well established to have been transferred.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: Imperatores non esse Legibus subiectos, oportere tamen illos iuxta leges iudicare.
units.tr: That emperors are not subject to the laws, yet ought nonetheless to judge according to the laws.

units.la: Verum cum nihil tam studiosum in omnibus rebus inueniatur, quam legum authoritas, quæ & diuinas & humanas res bene disponit, & omnem iniquitatem expellit: dignum est Principem secundum eundum leges & viuere & iudicare. Est enim lex inuentio quædam & donum Dei, oculus ex multis oculis, & intellectus sine affectu. Nec facile dissolui debet, quod à pluribus accurate digestum est, cum magna lucubratione introductum. Hinc dicere consueuit Imperator: Digna vox est maiestate regnantis, legibus alligatum se Principem profiteri. Quod quamuis pulchrum est dicere, non tamen asserendum est, Imperatorem legibus esse subiectum, cum sit solutus. Est enim aliud quiddam, cui plus q; legibus obnoxius est Imperator. Hoc ipsum æquitas est, quæ non semper inuenitur scripta. Æquitas enim est, quod præter legem scriptam iustum est. Quod si aliud lex iubet, aliud æquitas suadet, conuenit Imperatorem iuris rigorem æquitatis frœno temperare, cui soli inter æquitatem iusq; interpositam interpretationem licet, & incumbit inspicere. Præsertim cum nulla iuris sanctio, quantumcunque digesto perpensa consilio ad varietates humanæ naturæ; & machinationes eius inopinabiles, sufficiat.
units.tr: But since nothing is found to be so zealously sought in all matters as the authority of the laws, which order both divine and human affairs well and expel all injustice, it is fitting that the prince both live and judge according to the same laws. For law is a certain invention and gift of God, an eye out of many eyes, and intellect without passion. Nor should that be easily dissolved which has been carefully arranged by many and introduced with great labour. Hence the emperor is accustomed to say: It is a worthy utterance of ruling majesty for the prince to profess himself bound by the laws. Although this is fine to say, it must not be asserted that the emperor is subject to the laws, since he is loosed from them. For there is something else to which the emperor is bound even more than to the laws. This is equity itself, which is not always found in writing. For equity is what is just beyond the written law. But if the law commands one thing and equity suggests another, it is fitting that the emperor temper the rigour of the law with the bridle of equity, since he alone is permitted, and it falls to him, to interpose interpretation between equity and justice and to look into it. Especially since no legal sanction, however carefully weighed in deliberation, is sufficient for the varieties of human nature and its unforeseen machinations.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: Leges humanas quandoque mutari, abrogariq; posse.
units.tr: That human laws may sometimes be changed and abrogated.

units.la: Cum q; humani iuris conditio semper in infinitum decurrat, nihilque sit in ea quod stare perpetuo possit (multas enim formas eadem natura nouas deproperat, & secundum tempora statuta variantur humana) manifestum est æui cursu, quæ leges olim iustæ fuerunt, iniustas reddi, fieriq; nunc inutiles, nunc duras, nunc iniquas. Ad quas moderandas opus est principe, qui legum Dominus est. Nam si quid in eis latum fortassis obscurius fuerit, Imperatorem conuenit declarare, duritiamque legum suæ humanitati contrariam & incongruam emendare. Quod enim dicitur, legem quamuis duram esse seruandam, inferiores iudices, non Cæsarem respicit. In quo est vis illa moderandarum legum, quam ἐπιεικείαν vocant, quæ tam annexa est summo principi, ut nullis possit humanis euelli decretis. Sed hac suprema potestate sine magna & urgenti causa uti principem minime conuenit. Imitandus est enim ille Theopompus Aristotelicus, qui, ut principatum suum efficeret diutur niorem, raro hanc potestatem exercebat. Quamuis enim lex Imperii, solennibus iuris Imperatorem soluerit: tamen nihil tam proprium est Imperii, quam legibus viuere. Nec mutandæ sunt leges sine causa, nec nouæ instituendæ absque euidenti utilitate, & licet in omni Principis actione legitimam subesse causam, reputare nos decet, qui ab eius placito non possumus resilire, cauendum tamen Imperatori est, ne sine ratione libidines potius suas, quam iustas leges sequatur, fiatque Deo maximo reus apud quem potentes potenter tormenta patiuntur, qui iuris æquitatisque tramitem reliquerunt.
units.tr: Since the condition of human law always runs on into infinity, and there is nothing in it that can stand forever (for nature herself keeps producing new forms, and human statutes vary with the times), it is clear that with the passing of time laws that were once just become unjust, and some become useless, some harsh, and some iniquitous. To moderate these, a prince is needed, who is the lord of the laws. For if anything in them has perhaps been expressed too obscurely, it befits the emperor to declare it, and to amend the harshness of the laws, which is contrary and out of keeping with his humanity. For the saying that a law, however harsh, must be observed, looks to inferior judges, not to the emperor. In this lies that power of moderating laws which they call epieikeia [ἐπιείκεια], which is so bound up with the supreme prince that it cannot be torn away by any human decree. But it is by no means fitting for the prince to use this supreme power without a great and urgent cause. For he should imitate that Theopompus of Aristotle's account, who, in order to make his rule more lasting, exercised this power rarely. For although the law of the Empire has released the emperor from the usual forms of law, nothing is so proper to empire as to live under laws. Laws should not be changed without cause, nor new ones instituted without evident usefulness; and although we ought to consider that every action of the prince has some lawful cause underlying it, since we cannot resist his pleasure, the emperor must nonetheless take care not to follow his own lusts rather than just laws without reason, lest he become guilty before almighty God, before whom the powerful suffer powerful torments when they have abandoned the path of law and equity.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CAP. XXII.

units.la: Ab Imperatoris sententia nec posse, nec debere prouocari.
units.tr: That one may neither rightly nor ought to appeal from the sentence of the Emperor.

units.la: Nunc vltimo loco de appellationibus transigamus: eosque confutemus, qui à sententia summi Principis asserunt appellandum. Etenim si à præfectis prætorio prouocatio non recipitur, qui subsunt Cæsari: multo minus recipienda est, si Cæsar ipse sententiam tulit, qui nullum habet in temporali causa superiorem. Hinc litigatores causas iubentur suas, quæ coram tribunali ventilantur Augusto, plene instruere, ne lis incognito negotio dirimatur, adempta copia conquirendi. Exinde cum in præfectis prætorio idcirco non admittatur prouocatio, quia credit princeps, eos qui ob singularem industriam, explorata eorum fide & grauitate, ad huius officii magnitudinem adhibentur, non aliter iudicaturos esse q; ipse iudicaturus fuisset, quis non intuetur aperte, rationem istam multo magis in Cæsare nullam prouocationem admittere? quis insuper prouocari à præfectis prætorio prohibuit, nisi Cæsar? q; si Cæsar sic iudicem ex suis aliquem extollit, ut ab eo appellari nequeat: quis tam hebes est, ut à Cæsare reputet appellandum? Notum insuper est, non licere à legibus appellare. Lex enim (ut dictum est) quanquam dura, ferenda est. At cum sententia Principis, partibus omnibus constitutis lata, non solum illi causæ pro qua introducta est, sed omnibus similibus lex sit: quis eo temeritatis excedit, ut à sententia, quæ vim legis habet, appelleț cum Romani non solum à legibus, sed ab his quoque appellare prohibuerint, qui iussu populi decem tabulas intueri legum, reformareque tenebantur? Sed appellant quidam rursus ad Cæsarem adiunctis principibus, quasi maior sit Imperator cum illis, quam sine illis. Quod si verum esset, iterum etiam ab Imperatore ac Electoribus ad ipsos adiunctis aliis Principibus, appellare liceret, & usque in infinitum processus fieret, cum homines in propriis factis affectione magis quam veritate ducantur, ac ut plurimum iustam se putent habere causam, minusq; iuste contra se iudicata approbant. Sed vana atque inania sunt istorum fundamenta. Tanta est enim in Cæsare potestas, sine Principibus, quanta cum ipsis. Amat enim vnitatem suprema potestas, suaq; sponte ex multitudine fugit ad vnum.
units.tr: Now, lastly, let us deal with appeals, and refute those who assert that one may appeal from the sentence of the highest Prince. For if no appeal is admitted from the praetorian prefects, who are subject to Caesar, much less is it to be admitted if Caesar himself has pronounced the sentence, since he has no superior in a temporal cause. Hence litigants are ordered to set out their cases fully when they are argued before the tribunal of the Augustus, so that a suit is not decided with the matter unknown, the opportunity of inquiring having been taken away. Then, since an appeal is not admitted from the praetorian prefects for this reason, that the prince believes those whom he raises to the greatness of this office on account of their outstanding diligence, and with their fidelity and gravity proven, will judge in no other way than he himself would have judged, who does not plainly see that this reasoning applies much more strongly to Caesar, so that no appeal is admissible from him? Moreover, who forbade appeal from the praetorian prefects, except Caesar? And if Caesar raises any of his own men to be judge in such a way that no appeal can be made from him, who is so dull as to think one may appeal from Caesar? It is well known besides that one may not appeal from the laws. For the law (as has been said) must be borne, however harsh it is. But since the sentence of a Prince, pronounced with all parties present, is a law not only for that cause for which it was brought in but for all similar cases, who would be so reckless as to appeal from a sentence that has the force of law? The Romans forbade appeal not only from laws but also from those men who, by command of the people, were bound to examine and reform the laws of the Ten Tables. But some again appeal to Caesar with the princes added, as if the Emperor were greater with them than without them. But if this were true, one could again appeal from the Emperor and the Electors to those same men with other princes added, and the process would go on to infinity, since men are led by affection in their own deeds rather than by truth, and for the most part think they have a just cause, and approve of judgments given against them less justly. But the foundations of these men are empty and vain. For the power in Caesar is as great without the princes as with them. Supreme power loves unity, and of its own accord flees from the many to the one.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: Imperatorem bifariam offendi ab eo, qui ab eius appellat sententia.
units.tr: An emperor is offended in two ways by one who appeals from his sentence.

units.la: CVmque in Cæsare summa potestas sit, summaque authoritatis plenitudo, nihil est quod adhuc Cæsaris principibus authoritatis tradat: quoniam neque summo adiici quicquam potest, neque plenum potest effici plenius. At qui provocat, quasi superiorem appellat, qui latæ contra se iniquam sententiam corripiat. Qua in re, duplici temeritate Maiestatem lædit Imperialem. Nam & superiorem nititur assignare ei, qui omnibus principibus est superior: & iniquitatem illi ascribit, quem semper æquum iustumq; reputare debemus. Quapropter qui talia tentant, non solum prohibendi sunt, sed etiam debitis pœnis atq; animaduersionibus coercendi. Cum iuxta canonicas sanctiones quædam sint culpæ, in quibus culpa est relaxare vindictam. Etenim quamuis à summo solio nonnunquam procedat iniquitas, iniustumque iudicium prodeat: non tamen idcirco locus est appellationi, cum nemo sit iudex, qui temporalia Cæsaris facta valeat examinare. Vtilius insuper est Reipublicæ ad extinguendas lites, paucis iniuste oppressis appellationis beneficium denegari: q; multis calumniantibus, postq; iuste dominati fuerint, querelarum ianuas aperire. Cum rarissimi sint, q se iuste reputent condemnatos: semperq; minus malum tolerandum sit, ut euitetur maius. Nempe vbi semper licitum est appellare, ibi quoq; lites sine fine reperiuntur: ibi sunt inimicitiæ, ibi contentiones, ibi noua die rim scandala. Quod si ciuitates aliquæ à suis præsidibus appellari non sinunt, quis tu es, qui velis à supremo Cæsaris tribunali appellare? maiorisq; authoritatis virum ciuem in dignitate constitutum, quam Imperatorem reputare? An non, supra omnes mortales unum caput est, à quo nulli appellare licet; & ad quem ab omni appellatione recurrere communis in temporalibus observare? Romani pontificis sententiam nullus est in iis vocare. Romani principis voluntatem nemo potest impugnare. Satius enim est iniustam sententiam istam ferre, vel illum, quam per querelas id agi, ut imperio superior detur. Si enim ab Imperatore vis appellare, ab eo quoq; provocare desideras condemnatus, quem post Cæsarem appellasti, nec tuis iniquitatis appellationibus modus. Quod si altioris iudicio vis quiescere: quin potius arbitrio ... quem super omnes mundi homines in temporalibus Deus constituit? Sit caput inter principes, sit qui temporalia terminet: auferatur materia litigandi homines se principi esse subiectos, Imperatoremque mundi Dominum, tanquam Dei vice in temporalibus gerentem venerentur. Sicut quæ Deus iubet implenda sunt, nihilque contra replicandum est, sic temporalia Cæsaris mandata sine repugnatione suscipiant. Curent autem ipsi Cæsares, ne quenquam iniuste opprimant, causamque præbeant hominibus ad Deum clamandi, cuius est terra & plenitudo eius, qui nec obliuiscitur clamorem pauperum, & propter iniustitiam de gente in gentem transfert imperium. Nihil est enim quod illi maximo Deo, rectori orbis, cœlique fundatori grauius sit, quam iustitiæ neglectus, indignaque pauperum oppressio: Sicut enim Psalmista canit: Non in finem obliuio erit pauperis. Patientia pauperum non peribit in finem.
units.tr: Since supreme power and the fullness of authority reside in the emperor, there is nothing further that he could hand over to the emperor's princes, for nothing can be added to the supreme, and what is already full cannot be made fuller. Yet whoever appeals does so as if he were appealing to a superior, when he seizes upon a sentence passed against him as unjust. In this he offends the imperial majesty in two ways. First, he tries to assign a superior to the one who is superior to all princes. Second, he ascribes injustice to the one whom we must always regard as fair and just. Therefore those who attempt such things must not only be forbidden but also restrained by due punishments and penalties, since by the canonical sanctions there are certain faults in which it is a fault to relax vengeance. For although injustice sometimes issues from the supreme throne and an unjust judgment comes forth, there is nonetheless no room for appeal, since there is no judge who could examine the temporal acts of the emperor. Moreover, it is more useful to the commonwealth, for putting an end to lawsuits, to deny the benefit of appeal to a few who have been unjustly oppressed than to open the gates of complaint to many who, once they have ruled justly, are calumniated. Those who think they have been justly condemned are very rare, and a lesser evil must always be endured so that a greater one may be avoided. Indeed, where it is always lawful to appeal, there lawsuits also have no end: there are enmities, there are quarrels, there new scandals arise every day. But if some states do not allow appeals from their own governors, who are you that you would wish to appeal from the supreme tribunal of the emperor? Or do you think a citizen of greater authority, placed in a dignity, is to be regarded above the emperor? Is there not, above all mortals, one head from whom no one may appeal, and to whom, in temporal matters, all are commonly bound to have recourse from every appeal? No one has the right to summon the sentence of the Roman pontiff; no one can oppose the will of the Roman prince. It is better to bear that unjust sentence, whether it comes from him or from that other, than to bring it about through complaints that someone be set above the empire. For if you wish to appeal from the emperor, you will also wish to appeal from him by whom you were condemned after you appealed to the emperor, and there will be no limit to your appeals of injustice. But if you wish to rest in the judgment of a higher one, why not rather in the judgment of ... the one whom God has set over all men of the world in temporal matters? Let there be a head among the princes, let there be one who ends temporal disputes, and let the matter of litigation be removed: let men acknowledge that they are subject to the prince, and let them venerate the emperor as lord of the world, bearing the office in temporal matters in the place of God. Just as what God commands must be fulfilled and nothing is to be objected against it, so let them receive the temporal commands of the emperor without resistance. But let the emperors themselves take care that they do not unjustly oppress anyone, and let them give men cause to cry out to God, whose is the earth and its fullness, who does not forget the cry of the poor, and who on account of injustice transfers dominion from nation to nation. For there is nothing more grievous to that greatest God, the ruler of the world and founder of heaven, than neglect of justice and the unworthy oppression of the poor. As the Psalmist sings: "The poor man's forgetfulness shall not be forever; the patience of the poor shall not perish unto the end." (Psalm 9[9].18)

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: Summatim neminem rebus in omnibus temporalibus esse Imperatore superiorem, post Deum Opt. Max.
units.tr: In brief: that no one in all temporal matters is superior to the Emperor, after God Most Good and Great.

units.la: HÆc tibi, Diue Cæsar Friderice, de tua sufficiat suprema potestate, breuiter & succincte scripsisse: ex quibus percipere potes, quanta sit tui solii, quamque admirabilis authoritas, cum nemo tibi in temporalibus præsit, & tu omnes præcellas, cum nemo sit qui tuum in temporalibus refugere possit imperium, & tuum sit omnibus imperare, cum nemo ex tuo iudicio sit exemptus, & tu omnes temporales valeas iudicare, cum nemo à te provocare queat, & ab omnibus ad te liceat appellare temporalibus, cum priuilegia legesque possis interpretari atque corrigere: cum ad tuendam Imperii Maiestatem, Reique publicæ statum seruandum, omnes populi, nationes principes, reges, tuis debeant obedire mandatis. Quæ cum ita sint, cauere tamen debes, ne sine ratione aliquid agas, ne vel ad tuam voluptatem potius quam ad subditorum vtilitatem regas Imperium, atq; sic ex rege fias tyrannus, cum quo nulla nobis societas, nullumque debet esse commercium, sed potius summa distractio. Quod vt euites, tanto magis eniti debes, quanto propter pacem populis datam iustitiam bene administratam, Remque publicam rite directam, te auctorem facti in sublime prouectum, gratiori semper tranquillitate Deus custodit. Vale feliciter, ex Vienna Cal. Martii: M.CCCCXLV, Regni tui anno sexto.
units.tr: Let this suffice for me to have written to you, divine Caesar Frederick, concerning your supreme power, briefly and concisely. From these things you can perceive how great your throne is and how admirable your authority: since no one is set over you in temporal matters, and you surpass all; since no one can escape your temporal rule, and it is yours to command all; since no one is exempt from your judgment, and you are able to judge all temporal persons; since no one may challenge you, and it is lawful for all to appeal to you in temporal matters; since you can interpret and correct privileges and laws. Since all peoples, nations, princes and kings ought to obey your commands in order to protect the majesty of the Empire and preserve the state of the commonwealth. Since this is so, you must nevertheless take care not to do anything without reason, nor to rule the Empire for your own pleasure rather than for the benefit of your subjects, lest you turn from king into tyrant, with whom we can have no fellowship or dealings, but rather the utmost separation. That you may avoid this, you ought to strive all the more, since God, who has raised you on high as the author of the peace given to the peoples, of justice well administered and of the commonwealth rightly directed, will always keep you under a more favourable tranquillity. Farewell happily. From Vienna, the Kalends of March, 1445, the sixth year of your reign.

units.la: FR. IACOBI DE PARADY- SO CARTHVSIENSIS, DOCTORIS ERDFORDENSI- S
units.tr: Brother Jacob de Paradiso, Carthusian, Doctor of Erfurt

units.la: COLLECTVM DE SEPTEM STATIBVS ECCLESIAE IN APOCALYPSI mystice descriptis: & de authoritate Ecclesiae: & de eius reformatione: sumptum ex eius QVODLIBETO STATVVM HVMANORVM.
units.tr: A collection on the seven states of the Church mystically described in the Apocalypse, and on the authority and reformation of the Church, taken from his QUODLIBET OF HUMAN STATES.

units.la: LICET praeter ea quae dicenda sunt, speculariter, conformiter, de sanctis revelationibus Iohannis, in Apocalypsi ostensis, à praemissis non alienis quaedam referre. Ipse enim Iohannes post visionem specialiter septem Ecclesiis, & earum Angelis, id est, Episcopis exhibitam, sanctum stylum suum vertit ad generalem Ecclesiae vniuersalis statum describendum, à temporibus Apostolorum, vsque ad secundum Christi aduentum, in sexto & septimo capitulis, quem statum nomine septem Sigillorum signauit. Quae septem sigilla, agnus, id est, Christus occisus aperuit. Et apertio sigillorum non est aliud, nisi statuum Ecclesiae manifestatio, vsq; in finem seculi.
units.tr: Although I must, besides what is to be said, report certain things in a speculative and fitting way about the holy revelations of John shown in the Apocalypse, drawn from the foregoing and not unrelated matters. For John himself, after the vision specially shown to the seven churches and their angels (that is, their bishops), turned his holy pen to describe the general state of the universal Church from the times of the Apostles until the second coming of Christ, in the sixth and seventh chapters. He marked this state by the name of the seven seals, which the Lamb, that is Christ slain, opened. And the opening of the seals is nothing other than the manifestation of the states of the Church until the end of the world.

units.la: Aperto primo sigillo, visus est à Iohanne equus albus, id est status Ecclesiae tempore Apostolorum purissimus, propter Baptismi gratiam per eos praedicatam: & vitae sanctimoniam, quae illo tempore viguit in numero fidelium, vt Actorum Apostolicorum testatur Historia: Erant, inquit, illis omnia communia. In quo statu, Simon Magus cum omnibus suis successoribus erat eiectus, & damnatus: qui proh dolor, hodie in vniuerso pene orbe, sua semina venenata in medio tritici superseminauit, & (vt vereor ego) sinenda crescere vsque ad messem, cum paterfamilias dicturus sit: Colligite Zizania, & alligate ea in fasciculos, ad comburendum ea.
units.tr: When the first seal was opened, John saw a white horse, that is the state of the Church in the time of the Apostles, most pure because of the grace of baptism preached by them, and because of the holiness of life which flourished at that time among the number of the faithful, as the history of the Acts of the Apostles testifies: "They had all things common." In this state Simon Magus, with all his successors, was cast out and condemned. Alas, today they have sown their poisonous seeds almost throughout the whole world among the wheat, and (as I fear) they are allowed to grow until the harvest, when the householder will say: "Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them."

units.la: In apertione secundi sigilli, vidit Iohannes equum russum, in quo signatur secundus status Ecclesiae, qui est status sanctorum martyrum tempore tyrannorum, scilicet principum & imperatorum gentilium, à tempore Neronis vsque ad tempus Constantini, à sancto Syluestro baptizati. In quo statu multa millia sanctorum stolas suas in sanguine agni, scilicet Christi, rubricauerunt, Christi passionem imitati. Nam vt litera ibidem dicit, sumpta est pax de terra, & datus est sessori equi illius gladius magnus.
units.tr: At the opening of the second seal, John saw a red horse, in which the second state of the Church is marked, namely the state of the holy martyrs under tyrants, that is, under pagan princes and emperors, from the time of Nero until the time of Constantine, who was baptized by holy Sylvester. In this state many thousands of saints reddened their robes in the blood of the Lamb, that is Christ, imitating the passion of Christ. For, as the text there says, peace was taken from the earth, and a great sword was given to the rider of that horse.

units.la: In apertione tertii sigilli, id est, in tertio statu Ecclesiae, vidit Iohannes equum nigrum, qui est scelus haereticorum, Ecclesiam persequentium, niger in vitiis, in quo nulla claritas lucet veritatis, nec albedo aequitatis. Et qui sedebat super equum nigrum, scilicet Diabolus, regens hunc equum, habebat stateram in manu sua, scilicet peruersam scripturae expositionem, flectens eam faciliter ad quemcunque partem desiderat, sicut haeretici facere consueuerunt. Et hoc tempus erat tempus Arrii, & aliorum, vt in Ecclesiasticorum narratur historia: in quo concurrebant Sancti Doctores prius dicti, iustam libram, id est, rectam expositionem manibus suis gestantes: quod ita esse, praeterita secula non ignorant.
units.tr: At the opening of the third seal, that is in the third state of the Church, John saw a black horse, which is the wickedness of heretics persecuting the Church, black in vices, in which no brightness of truth shines, nor whiteness of fairness. And he who sat upon the black horse, namely the Devil, ruling this horse, held a balance in his hand, that is, a perverse exposition of Scripture, bending it easily to whatever side he desires, as heretics are wont to do. And this time was the time of Arius and others, as is related in the Ecclesiastical histories, in which the holy teachers mentioned earlier came together, carrying in their hands a just balance, that is, a right exposition. That this is so, past ages do not fail to know.

units.la: In apertione quarti sigilli, visus est equus pallidus: id est, in quarto gradu viguerunt hypocritae, falsa religione palliati. Et qui sedebat super illud, nomen illi mors: id est, aeterna damnatio illis debetur. Unde & infernus sequebatur eum, vt dicit litera. Et data est sessori illius equi, potestas super quatuor partes terrae: id est, à Deo permissa, interficere gladio iniquitatis & dolositatis: fame, id est, carentia verbi Dei: morte, id est, doctrina mortifera (coacervabunt enim sibi homines illius temporis magistros prurientes auribus, loquentes eis placentia) & bestiis terrae: id est, vnient se principibus, ad se fortificandos in viis suis, & hoc super quatuor partes terrae: id est, in omnibus mundi finibus abundabit scelus hypocritarum. In quo statu, vt arbitrari possum, hodie laboramus. In omni enim genere hominum, ficte sanctitatis viros & foeminas videmus, quorum aut Deus venter est, aut famam aucupant laudis humanae, & prae aliis honorari & venerari volunt, praecellere caeteros in mundi sapientia, in doctrinae praestantia, in operum externorum excellentia: cum tamen plures vacui cernantur, in verae virtutis, scilicet humilitatis, refulgentia: quod, quam verum sit, à consideranti studia hominum, ad quos fines tendant, palpari potest, sub colore enim honestatis, militat omnis pene actio humanae conuersationis, etiam in his qui animabus lucrandis deserdeseruiunt. Ideo enim pallidi coloris equus describitur, quasi speciem præferens mortificatæ carnis, ad ostendendum hominis exterioris sanctitatem: nec tamen plane spem habens albedinis, aut puritatis.
units.tr: At the opening of the fourth seal, a pale horse was seen, that is, in the fourth stage hypocrites flourished, cloaked in false religion. And he who sat upon it, whose name was Death, that is, eternal damnation is owed to them. Hence also Hell followed him, as the text says. And power over a fourth part of the earth was given to the rider of that horse: that is, permitted by God, to kill with the sword of iniquity and deceit, with famine, that is, the lack of the Word of God, with death, that is, deadly doctrine (for men of that time will heap up for themselves teachers having itching ears, who speak pleasing things), and with the beasts of the earth, that is, they will join themselves to princes, to strengthen themselves in their ways. And this will abound over a fourth part of the earth: that is, the wickedness of hypocrites will abound in every corner of the world. In this state, as I may judge, we labour today. For in every rank of men we see men and women of feigned holiness, whose god is their belly, or who hunt after the fame of human praise, and wish to be honoured and revered before others, to excel the rest in worldly wisdom, in the eminence of teaching, in the excellence of outward works; yet many are seen to be empty, lacking the shining of true virtue, which is humility. How true this is can be felt by anyone who considers the pursuits of men and the ends to which they tend: for almost every action of human conduct fights under the colour of honesty, even among those who serve in winning souls. Therefore a horse of pale colour is described, as if presenting the appearance of a mortified flesh, to show the outward holiness of the man; yet it has no clear hope of whiteness or purity.

units.la: In apertione quinti sigilli, vidit Iohannes sub altari Dei animas occisorum propter verbum Dei, & propter testimonium quod habebant, vindictam petentes de iis qui habitant in terra. Et dictum est illis, ut quiescerent adhuc modicum tempus, donec compleatur numerus fratrum eorum, qui interficiendi sunt, sicut & illi. Qui status quintus, credendus est partim competere animabus sanctis, iam exutis corporibus: partim etiam sanctis adhuc in hac vita degentibus, etiam tempore pacis Ecclesiæ: qui licet materiali gladio non trucidantur, tamen seipsos mortificatione desideriorum carnalium quotidie mactant, quasi videntes se vbiq; hypocritis & fictis hominibus sive religiosis sive secularibus circumseptos, tædio affecti, longitudine temporum, & acerbitate hypocritarum vbiq; prævalentium, orant dissolvi, & esse cum Christo. Et vere molestiorem statum, quoad quotidianam internam & externam pugnam tam diuturnam, in hoc tempore pacis intelligere & sentire possunt: hi se in innocentii vitæ conservare volunt, qua illi priores sancti: qui licet acerbiori, quoad pœnarum genus, celeriori tamen, quantum ad tempus, suam vitam finierunt.
units.tr: At the opening of the fifth seal, John saw under the altar of God the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held, crying with a loud voice, how long. And it was said to them that they should rest yet for a little season, until their fellow servants also and their brethren, that should be killed as they were, should be fulfilled. This fifth state is to be believed to belong partly to holy souls now stripped of their bodies, and partly also to saints still living in this life, even in the time of peace of the Church. These, although they are not slaughtered by the material sword, nevertheless put themselves to death every day by mortifying carnal desires, as if seeing themselves surrounded everywhere by hypocrites and feigned men, whether religious or secular, and weary, because of the length of the times and the bitterness of hypocrites prevailing everywhere, they pray to be dissolved and to be with Christ. And they can truly understand and feel this more troublesome state, as regards the daily inward and outward struggle so long-lasting, in this time of peace; they wish to preserve themselves in an innocent life, as those earlier saints did. Although those earlier saints, as regards the kind of punishments, ended their lives with greater bitterness, yet in respect of time they ended them more quickly.

units.la: Isti igitur duo status immediate præcedentes, videntur concurrere in unum tempus, scilicet modernum: licet non in unum quoad actiones in tempore uno agendas. Non latuit hoc genus hypocritarum sanctum Paulum, 2. Corinth. 3. inter cæteras pestes nouissimorum temporum, vbi ait: Habentes quidem speciem pietatis, virtutem autem eius abnegantes, & aliis etiam locis similibus.
units.tr: These two states immediately preceding, therefore, seem to meet in one time, namely the present one, although not in one time as regards the actions to be performed. This kind of hypocrite did not escape the notice of holy Paul, in 2 Corinthians 3, among the other plagues of the last times, where he says: having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof, and also in other similar places.

units.la: In apertione sexti sigilli, quod nihil aliud est quam manifestatio sexti status in Ecclesia, vidit Beatus Iohannes magnum terræmotum fieri, & solem denigrari, sicut cilicinum saccum, & lunam sanguineam, & stellas cadere super terram, & cœlum recedere sicut librum inuolutum, &c. vide Apocalyps. 6. circa finem. In quo designatur tempus Antichristi, qui impugnaturus est Ecclesiam. In quo tempore fiet magna commotio secularium contra Ecclesiam. Et Sol, id est, Christus alios illuminans, vilissimus reputabitur à reprobis, sicut saccus cilicinus vilescit, & opinio Christi pro nihilo reputabitur, dominantibus reprobis, & deficientibus electis: quia nullum signum Deitatis ostendet, adiuuando suos. Imo Christus dicetur peccator & seductor & dignus pœnitentia, quia saccus cilicius est habitus pœnitentium. Et tunc Luna, id est, congregatio fidelium, fiet sicut sanguis: quia sanguis multorum effundetur, aut vilis reputabitur, & contemnetur, sicut sanguis conculcabitur. Et stellæ cadent in terram: id est multi prælati & doctores adhærebunt Antichristo, & suis terrenis promissionibus, ad instar ficorum, qui non firmiter adhærent tamis arborum.
