Et Cœlum (secundum literam) recedet sicut liber inuolutus: id est, sancti, qui pluuiam verbi Dei spargere consueuerant, & iustitiam Dei annunciare aliis debebant, occultabunt doctrinam præ nimietate persecutionum Antichristi: sicut liber inuolutus, continens in se & contegens veritatis scripta, à notitia hominum: quia celabunt sapientiam suam, annunciare non audentes, & fugient à conspectu hominum. Et montes, id est, alti in virtutibus: & insulæ, id est sancti, tribulationum fluctibus turbati, de locis suis mouebuntur, id est, separabuntur à cæteris peruersis. Et Reges, principes, tribuni, fortes, & diuites, serui & liber, abscondent se in speluncis & petris montium: & dicent montibus & petris, Cadite super nos, & abscondite nos, à facie sedentis super thronum, & ab ira agni: id est, maiores de Ecclesia, seculares & spirituales, petent suffragia Angelorum, & aliorum sanctorum, ut protegantur eorum orationibus, ne & ipsi deficiant in illis persecutionibus Antichristi, sicut & reprobi, & ne similes aliis efficiantur, negantes Christum, ut euadant iram agni, id est, damnationem æternam, ne & ipsi acerbitate pœnarum vincantur, sicuti cæteri. Et quis poterit stare, scil. in tantis tormentis, seu etiam voluptatibus non vinci? Quasi diceret: Nisi adiutus precibus sanctorum, nemo potest firmiter stare in confessione veritatis.
units.tr: At the opening of the sixth seal, which is nothing other than the manifestation of the sixth state in the Church, the blessed John saw a great earthquake take place, and the sun become black like sackcloth of hair, and the moon become like blood, and the stars fall to the earth, and the heaven depart like a rolled-up book, etc. See Apocalypse 6, near the end. In this is designated the time of Antichrist, who is going to attack the Church. In that time there will be a great commotion of secular men against the Church. And the Sun, that is Christ, who gives light to others, will be reckoned most worthless by the reprobate, just as sackcloth of hair becomes worthless, and the opinion of Christ will be counted as nothing, the reprobate ruling and the elect failing, because he will show no sign of his divinity in helping his own. Indeed Christ will be called a sinner and a seducer and worthy of repentance, because sackcloth of hair is the garb of penitents. And then the Moon, that is the congregation of the faithful, will become like blood: because the blood of many will be poured out, or will be considered worthless and despised, and trampled like blood. And the stars will fall to the earth: that is, many prelates and teachers will cling to Antichrist and to his earthly promises, like figs that do not cling firmly to the branches of trees. And the heaven (according to the letter) will depart like a rolled-up book: that is, the saints, who were accustomed to scatter the rain of the Word of God and ought to proclaim the justice of God to others, will hide their teaching because of the excess of the persecutions of Antichrist, like a rolled-up book, containing and covering the writings of truth from the knowledge of men; for they will conceal their wisdom, not daring to announce it, and will flee from the sight of men. And the mountains, that is, the lofty in virtues, and the islands, that is the saints, troubled by the waves of tribulations, will be moved from their places, that is, they will be separated from the other perverse. And the kings, princes, tribunes, the strong, and the rich, the servants and the free, will hide themselves in the caves and rocks of the mountains; and they will say to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb: that is, the greater men of the Church, secular and spiritual, will seek the intercession of angels and other saints, that they may be protected by their prayers, lest they too fail in those persecutions of Antichrist, like the reprobate, and lest they become like others, denying Christ, so that they may escape the wrath of the Lamb, that is eternal damnation, lest they too be overcome by the bitterness of punishments, as the rest are. And who shall be able to stand, namely, not to be overcome in such great torments, or even in pleasures? As if he said: unless helped by the prayers of the saints, no one can stand firmly in the confession of the truth.

units.la: Deinde in capitulo septimo, post acerbitatem persecutionum, vult consolationem fidelium, de prohibitione persecutorum innuere, & de auditorio Angelico, ne persecutiones tantum, quantum velint inardescant: & ne noceant terræ, mari, neque arboribus: id est, habitantibus in hac vita: quoad usque sancti angeli, custodes fidelium, signent servos Dei in frontibus eorum: id est, prædestinatos distinguant à non prædestinatis.
units.tr: Next, in the seventh chapter, after the bitterness of the persecutions, he wishes to offer comfort to the faithful by hinting at the restraint placed on the persecutors and at the angelic hearing, so that the persecutions do not blaze up as much as they wish, and do not harm the earth, the sea, or the trees; that is, the inhabitants of this life, until the holy angels, the guardians of the faithful, seal the servants of God on their foreheads: that is, they separate the predestined from the non-predestined.

units.la: Et Iohannes audiuit numerum prædestinatorum, 144000. signati. Et vidit turbam magnam, quam nemo dinumerare poterat, ex omnibus gentibus tribubus, & linguis: vt ex tribubus filiorum Israel & gentibus fiat vnum ouile, & vnus eorum pastor. Ecce quam magna fidelium consolatio, post prænunciationem persecutionis Antichristi.
units.tr: And John heard the number of the predestined who were sealed, 144,000. And he saw a great multitude, which no one could number, out of all nations, tribes, and tongues, so that from the tribes of the sons of Israel and from the Gentiles there might be made one fold and one shepherd. Behold how great a consolation for the faithful after the announcement of the persecution of Antichrist.

units.la: Deinde circa finem septimi capitis, ponit Iohannes septimum & vltimum statum Ecclesiæ, cessante persecutione Antichristi, & eo occiso, in visione apertionis septimi sigilli, eius qualitatem exprimit dicens: Factum est silentium in cælo, quasi media hora: id est, Pax reddetur Ecclesiæ, vt libera fiat sanctis prædicatio, ad confortandum fideles, & ad pœnitentiam agendam illorum qui deuiauerunt. Hoc fiet paruo tempore, secundum Bedam, Hieronymum & Danielem, per 45. dies.
units.tr: Then, near the end of the seventh chapter, John sets out the seventh and last state of the Church, when the persecution of Antichrist has ceased and he has been slain. In the vision of the opening of the seventh seal he expresses its quality, saying: There was silence in heaven, about the space of half an hour: that is, peace will be given to the Church, so that preaching may be free for the saints, to strengthen the faithful and to bring repentance to those who have gone astray. This will happen in a short time, according to Bede, Jerome and Daniel, for 45 days.

units.la: Quanto autem tempore mundus post hoc stabit, puto neminem scire, de communi lege. Ideo Danielis 12. quod ipse dixit Angelo: Domine mi, quid autem post hoc? Et ait ei Angelus: Vade Daniel, quia clausi sunt signatique sermones usque ad tempus præfinitum. Posuit tamen Angelus, quamdiu duduratura esset persequutio Antichristi, scilicet dies 1290. quidies complent numerum annorum, scilicet tres anni cum dimidio, quibus Antichristus regnabit. Quo mortuo, dabuntur electis 52. dies pro poenitentia, qui additi ad primos, facient dies mille trecentos triginta quinque. Quos etiam Angelus in eodem capite circa finem enumerat dicens; Beatus qui expectat: id est, perseuerare potest, prae acerbitate persecutionis: & peruenit, scilicet poenitendo, addies 1337. Et credo secundum intellectus mihi paruitatem, & temporum ac hominum nostri temporis qualitatem, quod hodie currunt ea quae dicta sunt in quarta & quinta visione, quae durabunt usque ad aduentum Antichristi, licet etiam habitudines aliorum trium statuum possunt in parte aliqua nostris temporibus intervenire: scilicet equus albus partialis russus, scilicet persecutiones tyrannorum: ut niger, id est, haereticorum prauitas, in quibusdam saltem partibus. Vt ante nos fuit persecutio Bohemorum, quo ad articulos fidei, & Ecclesiae contrarios: unde sequebatur magna sanguinis effusio, tam in clero quam in vulgo: tamen prae omnibus temporibus vniuersaliores erant, & maiores. Sicq; noster status mixtus est cum aliis: licet multitudo & magnitudo hypocrisis spiritualem sibi vendicat nominationem. Et ut verum fatear, non habeo aliquas apparentias in sacris literis in infallibilibus rationibus, quod status nostri temporis generaliter reformari debeat aut possit, dietim impoenitentis hominum crescentibus, sicut & in processu rerum naturalium & elementa & elementata viribus suis decrescunt. Imo verisimiliter opinabile mihi est, statum praesentem continuandum, imo peiorandum usq; ad sextum statu, scil. Antichristi: cuius experientia docere agnoscimus, hos magis contra niti reformationi generali Ecclesiae, quos magis deceret conatu toto ad reformationem tendere, cupiditate & primatu honorum eos ad hoc impellente. Etsi quandoq; conatus Deum timentium, ad reformandum opera dare intendat, tamen in hoc mundo celebriores & potentes viros, plus Ecclesiasticos q; seculares, videmus se fortiter opponere, adhesionem sibi attrahentes principum & potentum secularium, quorum multitudo aut potentia scintillam inchoatam extinguit. Vnde & Deus iusto suo iudicio vilescere facit statum religiosorum, & Ecclesiasticarum personarum. Inde & bella ac lites in plurib. mundi partibus inualescunt, impugnanturq; viri spirituales tam a secularibus quam a spiritualibus: quod & Iohanni in dicta Apocalypsi reuelatum est, c. 13. in quo de impugnatione Ecclesiae, sub figura duarum bestiarum, duplex genus persequutorum Ecclesiae depingitur. Vna ascendit de mare, id est, de tempestuosa huius seculi procella: scilicet principes seculares, atq; laici, Ecclesiam bonorum impugnantes. Alia ascendit de terra, id est, quae deberet stabilis & immobilis persistere: per quam (secundum Glossam) intelligitur malitia clericorum, & cupiditas praelatorum Ecclesiam impugnantium. Quod quam late, & clare pateat, nemo, qui sensum habet ignorat. Nam post reditum filiorum Israel de captiuitate Babylonica, ex filiis Israel primitus exierunt iniqui, ad Reges gentium, qui conturbabant populum suum, ut Machabaorum in principio testatur historia. Et licet Ecclesiae Dei sufficienter prouisum sit in doctrinis, quoad modum conuersandi, tam quoad Ecclesiasticam dignitatem, quam quoad religiosorum monasticam conuersationem, per canonum aciurium determinationem, nec non per sacram Theologicam Facultatem: tamen parua, seu nulla certa istorum fit executio. Legitur quidem in cathedris: sed cum venitur ad praxim, tunc canitur canticum illud; Modicum ibi, modicum ibi. Et processu temporis, & frequentia multitudinis sic opposita, iurium robur accipiunt: ut si quis oppositum dicere aut facere velit, velut insanus aestimetur, sicq; Dei iustitia fit humana aestimatione iniustitia, & defenditur vitiositas multitudinis, & laudatur peccator in desideriis animae suae: sicut olim fecisse Sodomitas, scriptura in Genesi testatur.
units.tr: As for how long the world will stand after this, I think no one knows, by the common law. Therefore, in Daniel 12, when he said to the angel: My lord, what will be after this? the angel said to him: Go, Daniel, for the words are shut up and sealed until the appointed time. Yet the angel did indicate how long the persecution of Antichrist would last, namely 1290 days, which make up the number of years, that is three and a half years, during which Antichrist will reign. When he is dead, 52 days will be given to the elect for repentance, which, added to the first, make 1335 days. The angel also enumerates these at the end of the same chapter, saying: Blessed is he who waits: that is, he can persevere in spite of the bitterness of the persecution; and comes, namely by repenting, to the 1337 days. And, according to my small understanding and the condition of the times and of the men of our time, I believe that what is said in the fourth and fifth visions is happening today, and will last until the coming of Antichrist; although the circumstances of the other three states may also in some part arise in our times: namely, the white horse, partly red, that is, the persecutions of tyrants; and the black, that is, the wickedness of heretics, at least in certain parts. Just as before us there was the persecution of the Bohemians, concerning the articles of faith and contrary to the Church, from which great bloodshed followed, both among the clergy and among the common people; yet it was more widespread and greater than all previous times. And so our state is mixed with others, although the multitude and magnitude of hypocrisy claims for itself the name of spirituality. And to tell the truth, I have no indications in Holy Scripture, in infallible reasons, that the state of our time ought or can be reformed in general, since men daily grow more unrepentant, just as in the course of natural things both the elements and the things made of them decline in their powers. Indeed, it seems to me probable that the present state will continue, or rather grow worse, even until the sixth state, namely that of Antichrist. Experience teaches us that those who oppose a general reformation of the Church most are those who ought most of all to strive with their whole effort toward reformation, being driven to this by their desire for and pursuit of honours. And although sometimes the efforts of those who fear God are directed toward reforming works, yet in this world we see the more celebrated and powerful men, more ecclesiastical than secular, opposing them strongly, drawing to themselves the support of secular princes and the powerful, whose multitude or power extinguishes the spark that has been kindled. Hence also God, by his just judgment, makes the state of religious and ecclesiastical persons become contemptible. Thence wars and quarrels grow strong in many parts of the world, and spiritual men are attacked both by secular and by spiritual men; this was also revealed to John in the said Apocalypse, chapter 13, where, under the figure of two beasts, a twofold kind of persecutors of the Church is depicted. One rises out of the sea, that is, out of the stormy tempest of this age: namely secular princes and laymen, attacking the Church of the good. The other rises out of the earth, that is, what ought to remain steady and immovable; by it (according to the Gloss) is understood the wickedness of the clergy and the greed of the prelates who attack the Church. How widely and clearly this extends, no one who has understanding is ignorant. For after the return of the sons of Israel from the Babylonian captivity, wicked men first arose from the sons of Israel and went to the kings of the nations, who troubled their own people, as the history at the beginning of the Maccabees attests. And although the Church of God has been sufficiently provided for in doctrines, as to the manner of living, both as to ecclesiastical dignity and as to the monastic conduct of the religious, by the determination of the canons of the councils, and also by the sacred Theological Faculty; yet there is little or no sure execution of these things. They are indeed read in the chairs; but when it comes to practice, then that song is sung: A little here, a little there. And with the passage of time, and through the frequency of the multitude thus opposed, these customs gain the strength of rights; so that if anyone wishes to say or do the contrary, he is esteemed as a madman; and thus God's justice becomes injustice by human estimation, the vice of the multitude is defended, and the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, just as Scripture in Genesis witnesses that the Sodomites once did.

units.la: Hoc latissime hodie patet in Simoniaca prauitate. Arbitror enim homines in statu Ecclesiae praesentis tandem ante aduentum Antichristi, ad infimum gradum virtutum, imo ad profundum vitiorum peruenturos, ut de meritis eorum exigentibus digni erunt, filium perditionis ductorem iniquitatis ipsorum suscipere, ut sicut in Apocal. dicitur, Qui in sordibus sint, sordescant adhuc. Et ut dicit Christus Matth. 24. de temporibus nouissimis: Quoniam abundabit iniquitas, refrigescet charitas multorum: ut sic Deus in poenam ponat eis offendiculum, & tradat illos in desideria cordis eorum: Ad Rom. 1. ut procedant de vitio in vitium, ducente eos filio iniquitatis. Continuabitur enim iniquitas hominum vitiosorum, cum auctore omnium malorum. Ideo in profundum malorum, ut puto, tunc homines sunt futuri.
units.tr: This is today most widely evident in simoniacal depravity. For I judge that men in the present state of the Church, before the coming of Antichrist, will at last reach the lowest grade of virtues, indeed the depth of vices, so that, as their merits require, they will be worthy to receive the son of perdition as their leader of iniquity; as it says in the Apocalypse, Let him who is filthy be filthy still. And as Christ says in Matthew 24 about the last times: Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold; so that God, as a punishment, places a stumbling block before them, and gives them up to the desires of their hearts, Romans 1, so that they proceed from vice to vice, the son of iniquity leading them. For the iniquity of vicious men will continue, together with the author of all evils. Therefore, as I think, men will then be going to the depth of evils.

units.la: Non tamen inficior, quin semper iusti perseueraturi sunt, nec defecturi filii salutis, usque ad consummationem mundi: secundum Christi promissum, Matthaei ultimo, Ecce ego vobiscum sum, &c. licet secundum magis & minus: tum autem, ut ego puto, in minimum numerum, secundum dictum Christi: Veniens filius hominis, putas inueniet fidem in terra? Non quidem, ut non inueniat, sed in paucis inueniet. Aestimo enim, ante aduentum filii perditionis, in praelatis Ecclesiarum oppositum reperiri, praelatis primitiue Ecclesiae, scilicet Apostolorum: ut sit in illis cupiditas, ambitio, superfluitas, voluptas, negligentia, proprius amor, & alienatio timoris Domini: quorum opposita clarissime patuerunt in patribus primitiuae Ecclesiae. In clericis vero & Deo sacratis populis, immunditia, amor lucri temporalis, defectus praedicationis, corporis cura, vestium mollities, dissolutio morum, & conformitas vitae secularis: ut tunc fiat sacerdos sicut populus, secundum vocem Prophetae. In religiosis vero tunc erit inobedientia superiorum, proprietatum vsurpatio, vitae dissolutio, transgressio statutorum a patribus sanctis editorum, & votorum ipsorum transgressio: solus habitus, & tonsurae ostensio, & nihil aliud nisi imago quaedam depicta religionis: quod etiam hodie clare speculantibus in multis locis religionis reperitur, obstinato animo publice defendefendentium suas iniquitates, scilicet etiam contra substantialia religionum militantes. Simplices enim, puritas, & pauperras voluntaria, exulabunt tunc à religiosis: quorum etiam multi reperiuntur hodie praecursores. Quis sapiens, & intelliget haec! Erit tunc status secularium, tam principum quam subditorum, pene in omnibus confusus, studentes iustitiae, rapaces, violenti, incompassiui, quae sua sint quaerentes, innocentibus non parcentes, dolosi, fraudulenti, honorum secularium cupidi, auari, omni timore Dei destituti. Laici vero criminosi, luxuriosi, mendaces, periuri, praelatis inobedientes, diuitiarum amatores, voluptatum sectatores, vilificantes omnia quae ad Dei cultum pertinent, & Dei cultores contemnentes. Haec & multa alia etiam innumerabilia tunc reperientur, tam in praeambulatoribus Antichristi, quam & in Antichristo: vt conformia fiant praecedentia sequentibus, & finis status precedentis, quo ad malitiam, fiat par malitiae status sequentis. Quemadmodum in alterationibus naturalibus fieri, docet Naturalis Philosophia, vt gradus vltimus formae accidentalis corrumpendae, fiat pene similis primo gradui formae generandae, videl. de immutatione aeris in ignem: id est, de generatione & corruptione.
units.tr: Yet I do not deny that the righteous will always persevere, and the sons of salvation will not fail, until the consummation of the world, according to Christ's promise in the last chapter of Matthew: Behold, I am with you, etc., although in greater or lesser measure; then, as I think, they will be reduced to the smallest number, according to the saying of Christ: When the Son of man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth? Not that he will find none, but he will find it in few. For I judge that before the coming of the son of perdition, the opposite will be found among the prelates of the Churches, compared with the prelates of the primitive Church, namely the Apostles: that there will be in them covetousness, ambition, excess, pleasure, negligence, self-love, and estrangement from the fear of the Lord; the opposites of which were most clearly seen in the Fathers of the primitive Church. Among the clergy and the peoples consecrated to God, there will be uncleanness, love of temporal gain, lack of preaching, care for the body, softness of clothing, dissolute morals, and conformity to secular life; so that then the priest will be just like the people, according to the voice of the Prophet. Among the religious there will then be disobedience to superiors, usurpation of property, dissolute living, transgression of the statutes issued by the holy fathers, and transgression of their own vows; only the habit and the display of the tonsure, and nothing else but a certain painted image of religion; which is also found today, clearly, by those who look closely, in many places in religion, with minds obstinately defending their iniquities in public, even fighting against the essentials of the religious orders. For simplicity, purity, and voluntary poverty will then be driven out from the religious; and many forerunners of this are found today. Who is wise and will understand these things? Then the state of secular people, both princes and subjects, will be confused in almost every respect: men who pursue justice, but are rapacious, violent, without compassion, seeking their own things, sparing no innocent, deceitful, fraudulent, desirous of secular honours, greedy, and destitute of all fear of God. The laity, moreover, will be criminal, luxurious, lying, perjured, disobedient to prelates, lovers of riches, pursuers of pleasures, despising all that pertains to the worship of God, and scorning the worshippers of God. These things and many others, indeed countless, will then be found, both among the forerunners of Antichrist and in Antichrist himself; so that the things that come before are made to conform to those that follow, and the end of the preceding state, as to wickedness, becomes equal in wickedness to the state that follows. Just as Natural Philosophy teaches happens in natural changes, that the last degree of an accidental form being corrupted becomes nearly similar to the first degree of the form being generated, namely in the change of air into fire: that is, in generation and corruption.

units.la: Reformationem autem generalem Ecclesiae, extreme necessaria fore nostris temporibus, mores corrupti totius orbis praenunciant: cum reuera pene omnis caro corrupit viam suam. Sed quomodo eam fore possibilem in effectu fieri, nondum est positum ad praxim. Licet aliquoties per Concilia generalia sit attentatum. Et licet quaedam decreta in hunc finem predierunt ab iisdem conciliis, tamen tanta resistentia altae dignitatis personarum tam spiritualium quam secularium facta est, vt vidimus, & totum negotium lugemus infectum: & cum tempus pariendi aduenisset, vires non habuit parturiens. Tanta denique crudelitate debacchati sunt, vt non tantum prolem sanctam, scil. reformationem necare contendant: sed & matrem, scil. authoritatem conciliorum, & eorum conuocationem occidant, pro vt res in prospectu declarat. Per quorum tamen concilium authoritatem, maior esset spes ad viam reformationis obtinendam. Haec vero via reformationis, si esset possibilis, aut immediate fieret à Deo, per inspirationem, aut ab hominibus (neq; enim videtur alia via danda) quis dubitat de potentia Dei, si velit corda pontificum & principum secularium illuminare, vt quilibet se reformet? Sunt autem corda hominum in manu Dei, vt quocunque voluerit, vertat ea, secundum scripturae veritatem. Sed hactenus sine medio agere Deus non consueuit, ne superuacue videatur Scripturae sacrae & intellectuum illuminatio etiam humanitus concessa. In his, sicut & in aliis, per media agere consuevit, secundum Dionys. Est tamen alia via emendandi vitia humana, scilicet à Deo per peccatorum punitione & castigationem inflectionem, quam scriptura sacra testatur in libro Iudicum, cuius etiam meminit Dauid sanctus dicens: Cum occideret eos, quaerebant eum & reuertebatur, in diluculo veniebant ad eum. Quanq; non semper haec via poenarum profuit peruersis, dicente Ieremi. Percussisti eos, nec doluerunt, attriuisti eos vt acciperent disciplinam, &c. eiusdem 5 cap. Quod forte etiam modernis temporibus videtur in multis habere locum. Et in alio loco Ieremi dicit Deus: Interfeci & perdidi populum meum, & tamen à viis suis non sunt reuersi, ciusdem 15. c. Has poenas possemus imaginari; graues pestilentias, haereticorum violentias, infidelium inuasiones in ecclesiam, captiuitates Christianorum per gentilium nationes, famis, & huiusmodi, quas in Prophetis legimus comminatas: videl. in captiuitate Babylonica, filiorum Israel, post eorum peccata. Si vero per homines erit spes reformandi, haec maxime residet apud praesidentes, rā ecclesiasticos praelatos quam principes terrae, qui non solum verbis persuasiuis, sed & comminationib. poenarum, vim haberet coactiuam, ad reformandum primo se voluntarie, deinde alios sibi subiectos. Legimus in sacris literis, reformationem ecclesiae quoad vnā progeniem, factam per reges sanctos, scil. Dauid, Ezechiā, & Iosiam, qui abidolorum cultura filios Israel copescebant, & ad Domini legē conseruandam homines reuocabant. Etiam tempore Constantini Imperatoris, tempore Beati Syluestri Papae, legimus Ecclesiam ab errore hereticae prauitatis conseruata, & errores multos extinctos. Et tempore concilii Nicæni, similiter antiquorum conciliorum conuocatorum, multae haereses inualuerunt, rabie persecutionis prohibente, ne fideles conuocari possent ad errorum extirpationem. Hic simili modo verendum, ne si nostris temporibus longo tempore differretur conciliorum conuocatio, impediretur ecclesiae reformatio. Nisi enim in primitiua Ecclesia sanctorum Apostolorum & seniorum fuisset factum Hierosolymis concilium, de obseruatione legalium, error damnabilis inualuisset apud fideles, prout testantur Acta Apostol. 15. c. Cum igitur teneamus, per potentes & praesidentes, tam spirituales quam seculares, possibile sore Ecclesiae reformationem, tam in capite quam in membris: aut ergo per vnum hominem, aut per multos. Non per vnū, quantumcunq; praefulgeat morum venustate, aut scientia, aut alia dignitate, etiam forte si miraculis clarescerent (nam legimus plures tales fuisse, quorum tamen temporibus Ecclesia non fuit reformata, etiam ichismatibus continuatis) neq; etiam, vt puto, per solum summum Pontificem. Nam de facto tot sunt editi canones decretales & constitutiones per eosdem, & tamen in cassum membranas occupant, nulla sequente reformatione. Item, quia palpabiliter cernitur, ipsam eius curiam maxima indigere reformatione, sicut omnia clamauerunt vltimo celebrata generalia Concilia. Quam suam curiam, si non potest aut non velit reformare, quā sub aliis suis contegit: quomodo credendum est, quod tam late diffusam reformare possit Ecclesiā? Etiam per constitutiones, per quas creditur reformari Ecclesia, debet moribus vtentiū approbari, & debent edi cum consensu eorū qui debent eis vti: alias non erunt acceptabiles, nec forte dignae acceptari, quia caput sine membris nihil nouì edere potest, de quo prioribus non est mentio facta. Item, quia diceretur eidem: Prius medicinam vulneribus tuis dispone, tanquam capiti: quo sanato, & membris facilius edes medicinam. Quare medice cura teipsum. Quin prius eiicies trabem de oculo tuo, deinde festucam de oculo fratris tui: alias in praeposterò ordine nihil proficiet. Sale enim infatuato, nihil cōditur. Ideo iusto Dei iudicio minus sunt acceptabilia sua decreta, nisi seipsum & suos reformauerit. Et hanc profecto potissima reor causam deformationis Ecclesiæ, quia cernitur in capite vulnus, q; necesse habeat ante curari. Nā dicit vnus de eis: Cūm vita reprehenditur, testatur vt eius praedicatio contemnatur. Et Paulus dicit: In omnibus praebe teipsum exemplū bonorum operum. Et talia innumerabilia, in libro de Cura pastorali beati Gregorii continentur. Vnde mihi vix credibile videtur, posse Ecclesiā generalē reformari, nisi curia Romana fuerit ante reformata. Quod tamen quā difficile sit, cursus temporū præsentium manifestat: cum nulla gens aut natio fidelium tanta resistentiam faciat reformationi vllius Ecclesiæ, sicut natio Italica, & alii applaudentes, spe promotionis aut lucri, aut temporalis cōmodi, aut timore amissionis dignitatū ligati. Cōtremiscunt enim solo auditu congregationis generalis concilii, cū sciant per experientiā, q; Concilia generalia palpate nesciunt, sed corrigere & emendare, sine personarū acceptione: cū ibi cōgregentur de omnibus mundi partibus, qui vitiis non parcunt, nec amore nec timore seducti. Et facilius inuenitur veritas, passionibus humanis seclusis. Imo nec veritati patere potest aditus, oculis rationis & passiones obnubilatis: psidentesque ex parte Papæ cōciliis, q; a vident contra dominū suū, & contra se negotium consiliorū disponi: quid aliud agere existimandi sunt, q; vt tota authoritate, decretis conciliorū obicē ponant, aut per dissolutionē conciliorū, aut per discordiarū seminationem: sicq; opus totū redditur infectum, ac per hoc iter in antiq; syluam, scil. erroris & tenebrarū. Quod quā verum sit, nullus ignorat, nisi inexpertus temporū preteritorū. Clare enim probat hoc tragœdia, nostris temporibus in Basiliensi concilio practicata; q; hi norunt, qui ē oculis subiecerunt. Et ex hoc ortū est vulnus, nescio qñ curabile, contra authoritatē conciliorū generalium, vt ab excedentibus Papa aut suis sidentibus, à loco concilii, vel differentia exorta inter partes eiusdē, cēt tamen concilium dissolutū: resideatq; in personam Papæ, de plenitudine potestatis, authoritas dissoluendi aut transferendi generalia concilia, put Eugenius olim Papa de An. Dom. 1437 decisse cōprobatur. Hocq; venenū effusum est p eum in Ecclesiam, per aduersarios conciliorū, inde lebiliter obseruandū, & literis autem in gestis conciliorū annotandum: ad q; refugiū habebunt, vt fulcimentū sui erroris, vt subterfugere valeant correctionē & reformationē: ita vt etiam modernis temporibus frontosē aliarū scientiarū viri dogmatisare audeant, In quolibet Papa residere plenitudinem potestatis, non solū super quolibet membro singulari Ecclesiæ, sed & super tota Ecclesia conciliariter cōgregata, ad libitū ipsam disponendi, decretandi, dissoluendi, transferendi, corrigendi, authorisandi: vt nullus ei audeat dicere, Cur ita facis? Et sic totaliter niuntur suffocare authoritatē conciliorū, contra decretationem ab omnib. acceptā, in Constantiensi, Basiliensi, generalibus conciliis, publice promulgatā, & contra pragmaticā sanctionē super hoc editā atq; factam. Talesq; sic dogmatizantes, & eis consentientes, arbitrantur se obsequiū præstare Romanis pontificib. Sed non aduertunt, quantū salutī aduersantur eorundē. Nā salubernimā misericordiā & medicinā eiusdem proiicindunt, scil. fraternā correctionē: & capiti Ecclesiæ morbido non patiuntur adhibere medelā: quod quantæ sit crudelitatis, nemo sanus ignorat, vt August. testatur in Regula sua. Si enim singulis membris medicina est parata, cur capiti denegatur? cū hoc magis indigeat sanatione, q; alia: quia eo ægrotante, omnia membra ægrotare videtur.
units.tr: A general reformation of the Church is bound to be extremely necessary in our times, as the corrupt morals of the whole world foretell, since indeed almost all flesh has corrupted its way. But how it can be carried out in practice has not yet been settled, although it has been attempted at times through general councils. Some decrees were indeed issued to this end by those same councils, yet such great resistance was offered by persons of high dignity, both spiritual and secular, that, as we have seen, the whole undertaking has been brought to nothing, and we mourn it: when the time of birth had come, the mother had no strength to bring forth. Finally, they have raged with such cruelty that they strive not only to kill the holy offspring, namely reformation, but also to slay the mother, namely the authority of the councils and their convocation, as the outcome of events makes clear. Yet it is through the authority of those councils that there would be greater hope of obtaining the way of reformation. Now this way of reformation, if it were possible, would either come about immediately from God, by inspiration, or from men (for no other way seems to be available). Who doubts God's power, if he were willing to enlighten the hearts of popes and secular princes so that each of them reformed himself? "The hearts of men are in the hand of God; he turns them wherever he wills," according to the truth of Scripture. But hitherto God has not been accustomed to act without means, lest the illumination of the sacred Scripture and of the understanding, which has also been granted by human means, should seem to be in vain. In these matters, as in others, he is accustomed to act through means, according to Dionysius. There is, however, another way of correcting human vices, namely by God through the punishment and chastisement of sins, which holy Scripture bears witness to in the Book of Judges, and of which holy David also speaks, saying: When he slew them, they sought him, and they returned and came early to him. Yet this way of punishments has not always profited the perverse, as Jeremiah says: You have struck them, and they did not grieve; you have worn them down, that they might receive correction, etc., in the fifth chapter of the same book. This perhaps seems to apply in many cases even in modern times. And in another place of Jeremiah God says: I have slain and destroyed my people, and yet they have not turned from their ways, in the fifteenth chapter of the same book. We could imagine such punishments: grievous pestilences, the violence of heretics, the invasions of unbelievers into the Church, the captivity of Christians among the heathen nations, famine, and the like, which we read were threatened in the Prophets, namely the Babylonian captivity of the sons of Israel after their sins. But if there is hope of reforming through men, it lies chiefly with those who preside, both ecclesiastical prelates and the princes of the earth, who would have a coercive power, not only through persuasive words but also through threats of punishment, to reform first themselves willingly, and then those subject to them. We read in the sacred writings that the Church was reformed, for a time, by holy kings, namely David, Hezekiah and Josiah, who restrained the sons of Israel from the worship of idols and called men back to the keeping of the Lord's law. Also in the time of the Emperor Constantine, and in the time of Blessed Pope Silvester, we read that the Church was preserved from the error of heretical perversity and that many errors were extinguished. And in the time of the Council of Nicaea, and likewise of the other ancient councils that were convened, many heresies gained strength, since the rage of persecution prevented the faithful from being gathered to root out errors. Here, in a similar way, we must fear that if the convocation of councils were delayed for a long time in our own days, the reformation of the Church would be hindered. For unless a council had been held at Jerusalem in the primitive Church, by the holy Apostles and elders, concerning the observance of the legal rites, a damnable error would have gained strength among the faithful, as the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 15, bears witness. Since therefore we hold that the reformation of the Church, both in head and in members, can be brought about through powerful men who preside, both spiritual and secular, the question is whether it would be by one man or by many. Not by one man, however much he may shine with the grace of his morals, or with learning, or with some other dignity, even perhaps if he were distinguished by miracles (for we read that there were many such men, in whose times the Church was nevertheless not reformed, even though schisms continued); nor, as I think, by the Pope alone. For in fact so many decretal canons and constitutions have been issued by popes, and yet they fill parchment to no purpose, with no reformation following. Likewise, because it is plainly seen that the Roman curia itself stands in the greatest need of reformation, as all the general councils lately held have cried out. If the Pope cannot or will not reform his own curia, but shelters it under other names, how is it to be believed that he could reform a Church so widely spread? Moreover, the constitutions by which the Church is thought to be reformed ought to be approved by those who use the morals, and they ought to be issued with the consent of those who are to use them; otherwise they will not be acceptable, nor perhaps worthy of acceptance, because the head without the members can produce nothing new, about which nothing was said before. Again, it would be said to him: "First arrange the medicine for your own wounds, as for the head; once it is healed, you will more easily issue medicine for the members." Hence: Physician, heal yourself. First cast out the beam from your own eye, and then the mote from your brother's eye; otherwise he will achieve nothing in such a perverse order. For if the salt has lost its savour, nothing is seasoned. Therefore, by the just judgment of God, his decrees are less acceptable, unless he has first reformed himself and his own. And this, I think, is indeed the chief cause of the deformation of the Church: a wound is seen in the head, which must first be healed. For one of them says: "When life is found fault with, the preaching of him who lives so is despised." And Paul says: "In all things show yourself a pattern of good works." And countless such things are contained in the book on the Pastoral Care of Blessed Gregory. Hence it seems to me scarcely credible that the universal Church can be reformed unless the Roman curia has first been reformed. How difficult this is, the course of present times makes plain: since no people or nation of the faithful offers such resistance to the reformation of any Church as the Italian nation, and others who applaud them, bound by hope of promotion or gain, or by temporal advantage, or by fear of losing their dignities. For they tremble at the mere hearing of a general council being called, since they know from experience that general councils do not spare them, but correct and amend without regard to persons, when men from all parts of the world gather there, who spare no vices, swayed neither by love nor by fear. And truth is more easily found when human passions are set aside. Indeed, no entry can even be open to truth when the eyes of reason are clouded by passions; and the prelates on the Pope's side, seeing that plans are being laid against their lord and against themselves in the councils, what else are they thought to be doing but placing a barrier, with all their authority, against the decrees of the councils, either by dissolving the councils or by sowing discord; and so the whole work is rendered void, and the road leads back into the ancient forest, that is, of error and darkness. How true this is, no one is unaware, except one who has no experience of past times. For the tragedy staged in our own times at the Council of Basel clearly proves it; those who were present at it know, and they have seen it with their own eyes. And from this has arisen a wound, I know not when curable, against the authority of the general councils: when, through a dispute arising between the parties of the council, either because the Pope or those who sit with him have departed from the place of the council, the council has been dissolved, and the authority to dissolve or transfer general councils is claimed to reside in the person of the Pope, by the fullness of power, as Pope Eugenius was once shown to have decided in the year of our Lord 1437. And this poison has been poured into the Church by him, by the adversaries of the councils, to be observed thereafter, and to be noted in writing in the acts of the councils, so that they may have recourse to it as a prop for their error, that they may be able to escape correction and reformation. Hence even in modern times men shameless in other branches of learning dare to teach that in any Pope there resides the fullness of power, not only over any single member of the Church but also over the whole Church gathered in council, to dispose, decree, dissolve, transfer, correct and authorize it at will, so that no one may dare to say to him: "Why do you do so?" And so they strive utterly to suffocate the authority of the councils, against the decree accepted by all and publicly promulgated at the general councils of Constance and Basel, and against the Pragmatic Sanction issued and enacted on this matter. And those who so teach, and those who agree with them, think they render service to the Roman pontiffs. But they do not notice how greatly they work against their salvation. For they cast away the most wholesome mercy and remedy of the same, namely fraternal correction, and they do not allow medicine to be applied to the diseased head of the Church. How great a cruelty this is, no sane man is unaware, as Augustine bears witness in his Rule. For if medicine is prepared for each of the members, why is it denied to the head? Since it stands in greater need of healing than the others, because when it is sick, all the members seem to be sick.

units.la: Nisi forte quis insaniens ad hunc errorē prumperet, q; diceret Papā impeccabile, & indeuiabilem, quasi iā extra terminū viatorū volentes eū collocare. Non recensent, Petrū primū Papā fuisse reprehensum à Paulo, vno singulari, & sibi inferiore: ad Gal. 2. Et Ecclesiastica historia, & Speculū historiale, & certa ac indubitata experientia manifestat, eū & in fide & morib. similē esse posse cæteris peccatoribus, ex vertibilitate liberi arbitrii nondū cōfirmati. Auferre igitur à Papa correctionē, imo potestatē deponendi, est maximę impietatis: & ipsum statuere in plena audacia peccādi, & p cōsequens furioso dare gladiū, vt seipsum sine resistentia interimat. Mittunt igitur Papā in foueā dānationis, & cū eo dānantur, q eū subesse Ecclesiæ vniuersalis correctioni cōtradicunt. Quo igitur pacto talis vniuersalē Ecclesia solus reformare valeat, q & ipse infirmitati subiectus est, indigēs per se reformari? Vt pono, q sit aliq; talis. Et quomodo filius Ecclesiæ cēseri potest, q matri suę obedire contēnit, & quē Ecclesia corrigere p suis excessib. nō potest? Et si nō filius Ecclesiæ, quomodo erit hæres ;remissionū Ecclesiæ p Christū factæ? prsus enim se ab hæreditate paterna alienū pnunciat, q se filiū ecclesiæ negat. Ponere igitur le supra totā Ecclesiā, aut supra generalia cōcilia legitime cōgregata, vniuersalē Ecclesiam repsentantē, nō est aliud, q tota ipē reformationis Ecclesiæ auferre, & vni homini peccabili se cōmittere, q & se & Ecclesiā p deuia erroris ducere potest. Inde infertur hoc inconueniēs, q Christus Ecclesiæ suæ, post suā ascensionē, insufficienter puidit, cōmittens eā vni, q eā in damnationē inducere potest: pro qua & eius salute ipse de cœlo descēdens, pprium sanguinē fudit, & animā suā ponere dignatus est in morte. Et qs regū tēporaliū peregre pficiscens, in omnē euentū absolute & sine correctione cōmittet populū suū vni ad gubernādū, sine omni cōditione, & sine omni cōtradictione singulorū, ne aliter facere auderet, q ille sceptrum esset, siue bene siue male? & nō potius populus in vnū cōgregatus, incarceraret aut deponeret illū puer, regnū gubernante? Sic de sponsa, cōmissa per sponsum peregrinātē vni militi, qui eā stuprare vellet, deberet ne ei ex commissione generali sponsi obedire? Quis hoc nisi insanus diceret? sic simili modo, in Papa & Ecclesia. Et quid mirum, si vniuersalis Ecclesia congregata argueret Papā, ac etiā puniret, si incorrigibilis esset? cū etiā asina Prophetam legitur arguisse, voce hominis loquēs, Nū. 22. Et Apost. dicit, sibi & sui similib. datā potestatē in ædificationē, & nō in destructionē, 2. Cor. 10. Et quis auderet asserere, quod correctio fraterna, in Euangelio expressa, non haberet locum in Papa, cū & ipse frater sit censendus? Et si ecclesia scandalizaret p publica crimina, aut ad malū filios ecclesiæ traheret, aut p eius desidia aut negligētiā oues sibi cōmissæ in scipitiū ruēent, q nullā deberet aut posset habere correctionē, q eum monerent semel, bis aut ter: & postea co indutate, possent procedere ad depositionem eius, alio utiliori substituto: aliud dicere, persuasum mihi videtur esse impiu &iniquu. Et nisi in futuro concilio celeri remedio prouideatur huic veneno recenter introducto, de authoritate conciliorum supra Papam, cuius contrarium dogmatizant alii, & maxime de curia Papae, & eiusdem assentatores: clarum est, quanta inconvenientia inde sequantur. Primo, quod datur Papae audacia impune peccandi, & disponendi omnia negotia Ecclesiae ad libitum suum. Secundo, quod datur lubiectis in toto orbe occasio vilipendendi, imo contemnendi omnes constitutiones, ordinationes & mandata Papae. Videntes enim Rom. pontifices non curare decreta sacrorum canonum, pro libito dispensare ea, & contravenire eisdem, quod aliud, quod iusto Dei iudicio punituntur, subditi, ne & ipsi tenentur in obedientia constitutionum Papalium, & murmurent, dicentes: Tu prius patere legem, quam tulisti? Minimus enim in regno coelorum vocabitur is, qui solverit unum de his mandatis minimis, & docuerit: vox est Salvatoris. Sicq; derisioni patet apud mentes secularium Sedes Apostolica, vt in praesentiarum est videre: nec cessat Ecclesiasticae spirituales iudices latae hodie curantur. Cum enim pastor per abrupta graditur, necesse est vt in praecipitium grex sequatur. Tertio sequitur, quod si in antea fieret convocatio concilii generalis, totius Germaniae principes & praelati, Doctores ac Magistri se subducerent a Concilio. Ex quo enim tota dispositio Ecclesiae, in mente vnius peccabilis hominis residere debet (vt olim Papa Eugenius decreuit irritare decreta conciliorum, transferens de plenitudine potestatis concilii ad Ferrariam) superuacua esse videtur multorum congregatio, vbi vnus solus contra aliorum vota debet & potest authorisare: maxime cum causam exigeret, quod negocium Papam tangeret. Mox enim excitaretur discordia, & recederent praesidentes, & fieret dissolutio concilii. Et quomodo in concilio Constantiensi, non obstante Papae recessu, & suorum, decretum fuit, integrum mansisse concilium: cuius tum oppositum fuit practicatum in concilio Basiliensi: & quis inantea frequentaret Concilia? Reuera Ieremias si adesse posset, iteraret suos Threnos, dicens: Via conciliorum luget, eo quod non sunt qui veniunt ad solemnitatem. Exinde ludibrio ducerentur concilia: maxime quia videmus, quod omnia quae tantis laboribus, impendiis, in retroactis Conciliis elaborata sunt, penitus irritantur, & tanquam pulveres ventis obnoxii conculcantur. Fontale vero principium omnium illorum malorum, secundum Apostolum, & cupiditas, quae sibi vendicat locum pene in omnibus clericis: quoniam secundum Ieremiam, a maximo vsque ad minimum omnes auaritiae student. Ad quam satiandam, non reperiunt Ecclesiastici viri commodiorem opportunitatem, quam in adipiscendis dignitatibus & beneficiis Ecclesiasticis. Et hic sentiunt conferri per Papam, qui sibi per haec attrahere consueuit pene totam Ecclesiasticorum virorum cohortem. Ideo adhaerentiam copiosam sibi parit per horum prouisionem. Sed quia generalia concilia, per sua decreta saluberrima prouidere voluerunt, vt secundum sacrorum canones veteres, ab inspiratione Spiritus sancti emanatos, beneficia Ecclesiastica & iudicia debito ordine procedere possint, de Annatis non soluendis, de electionibus secundum Canones faciendis, & de reseruatis gratiis extirpandis, de beneficiis per locorum ordinarios conferendis, de causis in prouinciis iudicandis secundum concilium Nicaenum, & aliis multis: quibus auditis cupiditatum seruì totis viribus se opposuerunt, & decreta & concilia detestati sunt, confugerunt que ad Sedem Apostolicam, quae libenter fauit eisdem, eodem morbo laborans: quae sub occasione abundantiae, (qua necesse haberet summus Pontifex, ne egeret pro sua curia sustentanda) omnia irritauit, relabens in antiquum morem, a canonibus improbatum: quasi non esset alter modus prouidendi curiae & Sedi Apostolicae, quam iste improbatus. Sicq; abusus iste reuixit, & beneficia venduntur & potentes magis timentes sacculos, & minus idonei beneficia pinguiora reportant, aliis dignioribus repudiatis: sicut etiam synodus Basiliensis per organum Iuliani Cardinalis sancti Angeli, legatis Domini Eugenii Papae dedit pro responsis, Anno Domini 1435. in responso quod incipit, Decret.
units.tr: Unless perhaps someone, gone mad, should break out into this error, to say that the Pope is impeccable and inerrant, as if they wished to place him already beyond the limits of those who journey on earth. Do they not recall that Peter, the first Pope, was rebuked by Paul, a single man and one inferior to him (Gal. 2)? Church history, the Speculum historiale, and certain and indubitable experience show that he, too, in faith and morals, can be like other sinners, given the mutability of a free will not yet confirmed. To take from the Pope correction, indeed the power of deposing him, is therefore the greatest impiety. It sets him in full license to sin, and consequently hands a madman a sword with which to kill himself without resistance. They therefore cast the Pope into the pit of damnation, and along with him are damned those who deny that he is subject to the correction of the universal Church. How, then, can such a universal Church be reformed by one who is himself subject to weakness and needs to be reformed in his own right? Suppose there were such a one. And how can he be counted a son of the Church who refuses to obey his mother, and whom the Church cannot correct for his excesses? And if he is not a son of the Church, how will he be an heir of the forgiveness of sins which Christ obtained for the Church? For he who denies that he is a son of the Church clearly declares himself a stranger to his father's inheritance. To set himself above the whole Church, or above the general councils lawfully gathered, which represent the universal Church, is nothing other than to remove altogether the reformation of the Church and to commit it to one fallible man, who can lead both himself and the Church along the byways of error. From this follows the absurdity that Christ, after his ascension, made insufficient provision for his Church, by entrusting her to one man who can bring her to damnation, for whose sake and salvation he himself descended from heaven, shed his own blood, and deigned to lay down his life in death. And what king, setting out on a journey abroad, would commit his people absolutely, and without any correction, in every eventuality, to one man to govern, without any condition and without any objection from individuals, lest that man should dare to do otherwise than that he were the sceptre, whether for good or ill? Would not the people, gathered together, rather imprison or depose such a ruler, if he governed the kingdom badly? So too with a bride, committed by her absent bridegroom to one soldier who wished to ravish her: would she be bound to obey him by the bridegroom's general commission? Who would say this except a madman? In the same way, it is so with the Pope and the Church. And what wonder is it if the universal Church, gathered together, should reprove the Pope and even punish him, if he were incorrigible? For we read that even the she-ass reproved the prophet, speaking with a human voice (Num. 22). And the Apostle says that the power given to him and to others like him is for building up and not for destruction (2 Cor. 10). And who would dare to assert that fraternal correction, expressed in the Gospel, has no place in the Pope, since he too must be counted a brother? And if the Church were to scandalize people by public crimes, or lead the sons of the Church into evil, or if, through his idleness or negligence, the sheep committed to him were to rush into ruin, so that he ought not, and could not, have any correction, which would admonish him once, twice, or three times, and afterwards, if he remained obstinate, proceed to his deposition, with another more useful man put in his place: to say otherwise seems to me to be persuaded of impiety and iniquity. And unless at a future council a swift remedy is provided against this poison recently introduced, namely the doctrine concerning the authority of councils above the Pope, the contrary of which others teach, and above all the curia of the Pope and his flatterers, it is clear what great absurdities follow from it. First, the Pope is given the audacity to sin with impunity and to dispose all the affairs of the Church at his own pleasure. Second, subjects throughout the world are given occasion to despise, indeed to scorn, all the constitutions, ordinances, and mandates of the Pope. For seeing that the Roman pontiffs do not care for the decrees of the sacred canons, dispense with them at will, and act against them, the subjects, who by the just judgment of God are punished for this, may think themselves no longer bound to obey papal constitutions, and murmur, saying: "Do you first keep the law which you have passed?" For he who breaks one of the least of these commandments, and teaches others to do so, will be called least in the kingdom of heaven: so says the Saviour. And thus the Apostolic See is exposed to ridicule in the minds of the secular people, as can be seen at present; nor does the ecclesiastical judgment, spiritual judges, cease to be neglected today. For when the shepherd walks by precipitous ways, the flock must necessarily follow him into the abyss. Third, it follows that if a general council were to be convened in future, the princes and prelates, doctors and masters of all Germany would withdraw from the council. For since the whole disposition of the Church must reside in the mind of one fallible man (as Pope Eugenius once decreed, to annul the decrees of councils, transferring the council to Ferrara by the fullness of papal power), the gathering of many seems superfluous, where one alone must and can give authority against the votes of the others, especially when the matter concerns the Pope. Soon discord would be stirred up, the presidents would withdraw, and the council would be dissolved. And how, at the Council of Constance, although the Pope and his followers withdrew, was it decreed that the council remained whole? The opposite was put into practice at the Council of Basel. Who would henceforth attend councils? Indeed, if Jeremiah could be present, he would repeat his lamentations, saying: "The ways of the councils mourn, because none come to the solemn assembly." Then the councils would be made a mockery, above all because we see that everything that was worked out with such labour and expense in the councils of former times is utterly annulled and trampled underfoot like dust exposed to the winds. But the fountain-head of all these evils, according to the Apostle, is covetousness, which claims for itself a place in almost all clerics; for, according to Jeremiah, "from the greatest even to the least, all are given to covetousness." To satisfy this, ecclesiastical men find no more convenient opportunity than in obtaining ecclesiastical dignities and benefices. And here they perceive that they are conferred by the Pope, who is accustomed by these means to draw to himself almost the whole band of ecclesiastical men. Thus by providing these benefices he creates a large body of adherents to himself. But since the general councils, by their most salutary decrees, wished to make provision so that ecclesiastical benefices and judgments might proceed in due order according to the ancient sacred canons, issuing from the inspiration of the Holy Spirit (concerning the non-payment of annates, concerning elections to be made according to the canons, concerning the extirpation of reserved graces, concerning benefices to be conferred by the local ordinaries, concerning causes to be judged in the provinces according to the Council of Nicaea, and many others), these men, when they heard of them, opposed them with all their might, as slaves of their desires, detested both the decrees and the councils, and took refuge in the Apostolic See, which gladly favoured them, labouring under the same disease. This See, on the pretext of abundance (which the supreme Pontiff needed, lest he lack means to sustain his curia), annulled everything and, slipping back into the old custom, condemned by the canons, acted as if there were no other way of providing for the curia and the Apostolic See than this condemned one. Thus this abuse revived, and benefices are sold; the powerful, more fearful of their purses, and the less fit, carry off the richer benefices, while more worthy men are rejected. So too the Synod of Basel gave, through the agency of Julian, Cardinal of Sant'Angelo, to the legates of Lord Pope Eugenius, as its responses in the year of the Lord 1435, in the response which begins, Decret.

units.la: Et vt lucidius de authoritate speculari valeamus, apprehendamus viam resolutoriam contra personam Papae. Prima resolutio, ostendit nobis naturam eius absolute, in qua par est omnibus rebus naturalibus ex materia & forma compositis, nil ei amplius tribuens, quam alteri elemento, & elementato, scil. simplici atq; mixto, scil. lapidi & ligno.
units.tr: And that we may see more clearly into the authority [of the Pope], let us take up a resolving path against the person of the Pope. The first resolution shows us his nature in the abstract, in which he is like all natural things composed of matter and form, attributing to him nothing more than to other elements and elemented things, namely the simple and the mixed, that is, stone and wood.

units.la: Secunda resolutio, ostendit ipsum animal sensitiuum, an potentia sensitiua decoratum, in qua passiones fundantur, scil. ira, timor, amor, cupiditas, gaudium, spes, dolor, vt declarat Philosophus 7. Physicorum. Et quantum ad hanc resolutionem, circumscripta ratione, est ipse & alii homines, non aliud quam bestia & animal.
units.tr: The second resolution shows him as a sensitive animal, or as one endowed with the sensitive power, in which the passions are founded: anger, fear, love, desire, joy, hope, sorrow, as the Philosopher declares in the seventh book of the Physics. As far as this resolution goes, with reason set aside, he and other men are nothing other than beast and animal.

units.la: Tertia resolutio eius, ostendit hominem rationis capacem, qui legibus diuinis & humanis est informabiliter ad imaginem Dei conditus, a bono malum discernens. Et quo ad hoc similiter nihil habet Papa vltra alium hominem simplicem.
units.tr: His third resolution shows him as a man capable of reason, who, under divine and human laws, is made in the image of God in a way that cannot be unformed, distinguishing evil from good. In this respect too, the Pope has nothing beyond any other plain man.

units.la: Quarta resolutio contra Papatum, quae competit ei ex electione canonica per illos facta, quibus de iure competit potestas eligendi, per quam traditur simul authoritas & ministerium super membra Ecclesiae a Deo principaliter, licet ministerialiter ab electoribus, & instrumentaliter, secundum quod Apostoli vndecim Matthiam elegerunt, dicentes: Ostende quem elegeris, &c. quasi dicerent: Quem tu diuinitus elegeris, illum ostende tu nobis per hanc sortem. Igitur Deus est principalis elector & collator authoritatis Apostolicae, homines vero solum iudicatione: cum non potest aliud signum diuinae electionis haberi, quam praenuntia, scilicet spiritus inuocatione, pluralitas vocum, & consensus plurimorum. Et sic haec resolutio praesentat nobis Christi vicarium a Deo electum. Et inde surgit authoritas Papae, vt habeat potestatem dispensandi ministeria & dona Dei, secundum Paulum 1. Corinth. 2. Sic nos existimet homo, vt ministros Christi, & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. Fluit igitur & emanat haec potestas a Deo, secundum quod Regulae diuinitus traditae docent dispensandum. Aliter enim vicarius fidelis, non debet negocia principalia committentis disponere, quam reuera scit ipsum principalem velle: alias non esset fidelis dispensator, sed crudelis dissipator: cum conformes debeant esse actus principales actorum, & instrumenti quod ab actore dirigitur. Qui vicarius si Regulam principalem constituentis egreditur, & transgreditur, iam resilit ab illa parte resolutionis, & labitur ad inferiores partes, scilic. hominis, aut bestiae. Vnde, vt sic, non est eius vicarius. Dicit enim Paulus 2. Corin. 2. Si quid donaui propter vos in persona Christi, glorior at si Christus donasset, conformans se in donatione sua Christo, scilicet vice & authoritate Christi: quasi ipsius & Christi esset eadem donatio & dispensatio. Si igitur exit Papa has regulas Christi, iam induit personam hominis, aut bestiae. Inde est, quod si contraria Christo iubet, in peccatis dico mortalibus, hic non agit vt Papa, sed vt bestia, ratione non participans. Igitur non est inobediens censendus, qui ei in talibus non obtemperat: saltem dico directe contrariis Christo. In caeteris indifferentibus sibi iudicii relinquitur, vt fideliter prudenterque dispenset, vt iusta ratione aestimet, Christum scilicet velle, si ipse per se adesset. Ideoque Paulus hanc resolutionem non ignorans, dicit ad Roman. 13. Non est potestas nisi a Deo: Qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit. Ponit, inquā, in abstracto potestas, non in concreto potens: quia potens potest esse non a Deo, quia officium potestatis semper iustum est, quia ordinatū secundum regulas Dei rationabiliter institutum, licet potens ea abutitur. Ideo Deus dicit per Oseam: Ipsi regnauerunt, & non ex me, &c. Et Iohannis decimo nono dicit Christus Pilato: Non haberes in me potestatem vllam, nisi tibi data esset desuper. Potestas igitur iusta erat, sed ille ea abutebatur, iniuste Christum condemnando. Vnde subdit Paulus: Qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit. Non dicit, qui potenti in concreto resistit, abutenti sua potestate, Deo resistit: imo talis sic resistens contrario Deo praecipienti, non Deo resistit, sed ei se conformat. Non igitur tanta potestas in omnem euentum data crededa est Papae, quod omnia ad libitum suum disponere habet, postposito respectu ad Deum constituentem. Non enim sunt dona propria, sed Dei, ad cuius honorem & vtilitatem debemus omnia mensurare. Non enim putandus est Deus, quod in homine indistincto suum arbitrium strictum posuerit, quia nec de alio homine puro arbitrandum est. In cuius exemplum inspiciamus primum Papam, qui cum in verae fidei confessione Christum Dei filium pronunciasset, dictum est ei a Christo: Beatus es Simon bar Iona. Cum vero a vera Dei regula, quoad Christi passionem impediendam (quanquam pie illud visus fuisset sensisse) ei dixisset; Absit a te Domine, non erit tibi hoc, respondit Iesus Petro: Vade post me Sathana, scandalum mihi es, quia non sapis ea quae Dei sunt, sed ea quae hominum: Matthaei decimo sexto. Ecce qualis mutatio facta est in eodem homine, non persona mutata, sed habitu mutato, de beatitudine in Sathanam? Et si simile contingeret in persona Papae, cur non simile sibi attribueret in appellatione, cum ipse successor sit Petri? Non inde potestas culpatur, sed vitium personae, in reprobum sensum mutatae. Cur ergo quis audeat dicere, Papam non posse corrigi, aut deponi per ecclesiam, conciliariter congregatam: cum tunc non censetur agere vt Papa, sed vt vitiosus, degenerans de dignitate Papali, si incorrigibilis existit, & scandalizat ecclesiam? sicut Petro dictum est, Scandalum mihi es: cum dixit Christus Matthaei decimo octau. Qui scandalizauerit vnum ex pusillis istis, qui in me credunt, expedit ei vt suspendatur mola asinaria in collo eius, & demergatur in profundum maris. Et vae homini illi, per quem scandalum venit. Si vnum ex pusillis scandalizans, talem poenam meretur: quid de illo qui totam ecclesiam scandalizat? Et quis erit executor poenae, nisi ille, vel illa, de quo dixit Christus: Dic ecclesiae, tanquam superiori te. Quia Petro Papae hoc dixit tanquam inferiori ecclesiae, quem vtique non ad inferiorem misit, sed ad iudicem superiorem, secundum diuini & humaniiuris dispositionem. Neque vero, quia ministeriale caput super singula membra est constitutus, ideo nobilior & dignior dicendus est tota ecclesia vniuersali, quia & papa est censendus inter membra ecclesiae, cuius principale & essentiale caput est Christus: secundum illud ad Eph. 4. Veritatem facientes in charitate, crescamus in illo per omnia qui est caput nostrum Christus, ex quo totum corpus connexum & compactum, &c. sumus enim omnes Christiani, tam papa quam alii, corpusque Christi, & membra eius. Vnde oportet & ipsum papam subiectum esse legibus Christi, & totius corporis Christi, quod est ecclesia: ad Ephes. 4. Nec mirum: quia etiamsi angelorum eminentia aliud doceret, quam ecclesia sancta Catholica decertasset, secundum sancti Spiritus inspirationem, quam residere in vniuersali ecclesia non est dubium, anathema essent censendi: ad Gal. prim. Quanto magis, si homo mortalis, & vertibilis de malo in bonum, & e contrario, passionibus & erroribus diuersis subiectus, aliter docereret, anathema esset dicendus? Sed Papa, cui nunquam legimus tantam assistentiam indeficibilem diuinam pollicitam esse, sicut toti ecclesiae, Christo dicente: Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsque ad consummationem mundi, Matthaei vltimo, neque Petro tanta adfuit assistentia incommutabilis, quum & ante passionem Christi, & post eiusdem passionem legitur cecidisse a veritate. Scimus etiam, Christo teste, ipsum esse vitem, omnesque alios palmites: inter quos & Petrus papa erat connumeratus, de quibus palmitibus dicit: Omnem palmitem in me non ferentem fructum, agricola tollet, & in ignem mittet, & ardebit. Et per quem potius tollendus est palmes, nisi per ecclesiam vniuersalem, cum & Papa sit palmes in vite? Iob. 15. Haec omnia quae praemissa sunt, in istum finem militant, vt sciamus per vnum hominem defectibilem ecclesiam reformari non posse. Et quod ecclesiae vniuersali conciliariter congregatae, papam esse inferiorem non dubitemus. Et quod authoritas ecclesiae integre seruanda est super omnem, quacunque præfulgeat, dignitatem, etiamsi papali, in his quæ ad fidem & ad schismatis extirpationem, & ad generalem Ecclesiæ reformationem pertinent, in capite & in membris.
units.tr: The fourth resolution, against the Papacy, belongs to him by canonical election made by those who by right have the power of electing, through which authority and ministry over the members of the Church are conveyed at once: principally by God, though ministerially by the electors and instrumentally, in the way that the eleven Apostles chose Matthias, saying: Show us whom you have chosen, etc., as if they said: Whom you have chosen by divine decision, show him to us by this lot. Therefore God is the principal elector and bestower of apostolic authority, while men are only its judges; for no other sign of divine election can be had than the things that go before it, namely the invocation of the Spirit, the plurality of voices, and the consent of many. And so this resolution presents us with Christ's vicar chosen by God. From this arises the authority of the Pope, that he may have the power of dispensing the ministries and gifts of God, according to Paul, 1 Corinthians 2: Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God. This power therefore flows and proceeds from God, in the way that the rules divinely delivered teach it is to be dispensed. For a faithful vicar ought not to dispose the principal affairs of the one who commits them except as he truly knows the principal himself wishes; otherwise he would not be a faithful steward but a cruel squanderer, since the actions of the principal and of the instrument directed by the agent ought to agree. If such a vicar goes out from and transgresses the principal rule of the one who appointed him, he already slips away from that part of the resolution and falls to the lower parts, namely of man or beast. Hence, insofar as he does so, he is not his vicar. For Paul says, 2 Corinthians 2: If I have forgiven anything for your sakes, in the person of Christ, I forgive it, conforming his giving to Christ, that is, acting in the place and authority of Christ, as if the giving and dispensing were the same for him and for Christ. If therefore the Pope departs from these rules of Christ, he now puts on the person of a man or a beast. Hence, if he commands things contrary to Christ, I mean in mortal sins, he is not acting as Pope but as a beast, not partaking of reason. Therefore he is not to be deemed disobedient who does not obey him in such things, at least where he directly commands what is contrary to Christ. In other matters that are indifferent, judgment is left to him so that he may dispense faithfully and prudently, weighing by just reason what Christ would wish, were he himself present. And so Paul, not ignorant of this resolution, says in Romans 13: There is no power but of God: whoever resists power resists the ordinance of God. He speaks, I say, of power in the abstract, not of the one who holds it in the concrete; for the one who holds power may be not of God, while the office of power is always just, being ordained according to the rules of God and reasonably instituted, even though the holder of it abuses it. Thus God says through Hosea: They have reigned, but not by me, etc. And Christ says to Pilate, John 19: You would have no power at all against me, unless it had been given you from above. The power, then, was just, but he abused it, unjustly condemning Christ. Hence Paul adds: Whoever resists power resists the ordinance of God. He does not say that whoever resists the one who holds power in the concrete, abusing his power, resists God; rather, one who so resists a God who commands the contrary does not resist God but conforms himself to him. Therefore such great power is not to be believed to have been given to the Pope for every outcome, so that he may arrange all things at his pleasure, with regard to God who appointed him set aside. For these are not his own gifts but God's, by whose honour and profit we ought to measure everything. For God is not to be thought to have placed his strict judgment in an undistinguished man, since neither is it to be judged so of any other plain man. Let us look at the first Pope as an example: when in confessing the true faith he had declared Christ to be the Son of God, Christ said to him: Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona. But when, on the matter of preventing Christ's passion, he had said, departing from the true rule of God (although he seemed to have felt this piously): Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you, Jesus answered Peter: Get behind me, Satan; you are a scandal to me, for you do not savour the things of God, but the things of men, Matthew 16. See what a change took place in the same man: not a change of person, but a change of disposition, from blessedness to Satan. And if something similar happened in the person of the Pope, why should it not be likewise ascribed to him in his title, since he is the successor of Peter? The power is not blamed for this, but the fault of the person, changed into a reprobate mind. Why then would anyone dare to say that the Pope cannot be corrected or deposed by the Church, lawfully assembled in council, since when he is incorrigible and gives scandal to the Church he is not held to act as Pope, but as a vicious man degenerating from the Papal dignity? Just as Peter was told: You are a scandal to me, when Christ said in Matthew 18: Whoever shall scandalize one of these little ones who believe in me, it is better for him that a millstone be hanged about his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea. Woe to that man through whom the scandal comes. If one who scandalizes one of the little ones deserves such a penalty, what of him who scandalizes the whole Church? And who will be the executor of the penalty, if not he or she of whom Christ said: Tell the Church, as to one above you? For he said this to Peter the Pope as to one inferior to the Church, whom indeed he did not send to an inferior but to a superior judge, according to the arrangement of divine and human law. Nor, because he is appointed as ministerial head over the individual members, is the whole universal Church therefore to be called nobler and worthier; for the Pope too is to be counted among the members of the Church, whose principal and essential head is Christ, according to that saying in Ephesians 4: Speaking the truth in love, let us grow up in all things into him who is our head, Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and knit together, etc. For we are all Christians, the Pope as well as the others, and the body of Christ and its members. Hence the Pope himself must be subject to the laws of Christ and of the whole body of Christ, which is the Church: Ephesians 4. Nor is this surprising: for even if the eminence of angels taught otherwise than the holy Catholic Church had determined, according to the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, which without doubt resides in the universal Church, they would be deemed anathema: Galatians 1. How much more, then, if a mortal man, changeable from evil to good and the reverse, subject to various passions and errors, taught otherwise, would he have to be called anathema? But the Pope, to whom we never read that such indefectible divine assistance was promised as to the whole Church, Christ saying: Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the world, Matthew last, nor was such unchangeable assistance granted to Peter, since he is read to have fallen from the truth both before Christ's passion and after it. We also know, on Christ's testimony, that he is the vine and all the others are branches, among whom Peter the Pope was also counted; of these branches it is said: Every branch in me that bears no fruit, the vinedresser will take away and cast into the fire, and it will burn. And by whom is a branch rather to be removed, if not by the universal Church, since the Pope too is a branch on the vine? John 15. All that has been set out above serves this end: that we may know that the Church cannot be reformed through one defectible man; and that we should not doubt that the universal Church lawfully assembled in council is superior to the Pope; and that the authority of the Church must be kept whole over every dignity, however it shines, even the papal, in those matters that pertain to the faith, to the extirpation of schism, and to the general reformation of the Church, in head and in members.

units.la: Secundo, Concilium punire potest & debet quemlibet etiam papam, qui contumaciter statutis & præceptis eius obedire contempserit, ad alia etiam iuris remedia, si opus fuerit, recurrendo. Ex præmissis infertur: si vniuersalis Ecclesia, tam in capite quā in membris debet reformari, oportet hoc fieri per totam Ecclesiam conciliariter congregatam, à capite incipiendo. Neque enim spiritus mendax credendus est fuisse in ore omnium illorum celeberrimorum virorum, in Constantiensi Synodo congregatorum, qui hoc sanxerunt per decretum frequens, licet quidam ex Italica natione, de collateralibus papæ, molestè illud tulerunt: postea tamen omnes consenserunt de superioritate Concilii generalis super papam, licet inimicus homo iterum superseminaret zizaniam.
units.tr: Second, a council can and should punish any pope whatever who stubbornly refuses to obey its statutes and commands, having recourse also to other legal remedies if need be. From what has been said it follows that if the universal Church must be reformed both in its head and in its members, this must be done by the whole Church gathered in council, beginning from the head. For we must not think that the lying spirit was in the mouths of all those most famous men gathered at the Council of Constance, who enacted this by the frequent decree. Some of the Italian nation, the pope's collateral officials, took it badly, yet afterwards all agreed on the superiority of a general council over the pope, although the enemy man sowed tares once more.

units.la: Quid ergo ? putamus ne ecclesiam posse recipere reformationem generalem ? Et quidem ad hunc statum deuenire, vt omnia vitia tollantur ab ecclesia ? Ego iudico impossibile humano modo: quia nunquam ab exordio mundi fuit hoc possibile, ab Abel, à quo coepit, vsque ad nostra tempora. Semper enim Sathan mixtus erat cum filiis Dei, & lagena euangelica trahit pisces bonos cum malis, & virgines fatuæ mixtæ sunt cum prudentibus, & zizania crescit cum tritico vsque ad messem. Conandum quidem est, vt singula eradicentur: sed omnia simul est impossibile extirpare. Sicut dicimus de peccatis venialibus, quorum nullum dandum est, quin sit deuitabile: sed non omnia simul. Sed est alia reformatio, de qua quæritur, vt scil. ea quæ sint decoloratiua statuum & personarum tam sæcularium quam spiritualium, ad rectam formam perducantur: vt reformatio pacis inter regna & principes, extirpatio hæresum & schismatum, simoniaceæ prauitatis à curia Romana, & ab omnibus ecclesiæ prælatis, & concubinariorum repressionis, visitatio effectualis & vtilis clericorum, provincialia & synodalia Concilia: idoneorum prælatorum, clericorum, & parochialium ecclesiarum rectorum institutio, & ad ordinum promotiones: & legitima admissio eorum qui vita, scientia & ætate sunt apti. Quid quod ad sacrorum ritum pertinet legitima executio, & quantum ad diuini cultus honorem in ecclesiis spectat, solers circumspectio? In religionibus amputatio dissolutionum, excessuum, euagationumque restrictio, tam in clericis quam in religiosis honestas habituum & tonsurarum, obseruantiarum regularium custodiæ, disciplinæque monasticæ in omnibus peruigil obseruantia: adulteriorum & cuiuslibet impudicitiæ compressio, ecclesiarum frequentatio, diuini verbi sedula tam propositio quam auditio, sabbathorum sanctificatio.
