Et vt cum seueritate debita coerceantur diuinatores, incantatores, arioli, aruspices, somnia obseruantes, carminibus illicitis insistentes, & benedictionibus superstitiosis ac nigromanticis artibus operam impendentes: altaria aut ecclesias in conuenticulis locorum, sub spe miraculorum aut sacrorum erigentes, propter turpem quæstum: abusiones communitatum, ciuitatum, prouinciarum, villarumque, à fide & bonis moribus alienas cohibere, & omnes prauas consuetudines, & magis corruptelas sanæ doctrinæ repugnantes, in Ecclesiis Cathedralibus, collegiatis, & conuentibus, quorumcunque monasteriorum ac ecclesiarum prohibere.
units.tr: What then? Do we suppose the Church can receive a general reformation, and that it can come to such a state that all vices are removed from the Church? I judge this impossible by human means, because it has never been possible from the beginning of the world, from Abel, where it began, down to our own times. For Satan was always mixed with the sons of God, the gospel net draws in good fish with bad, the foolish virgins were mixed with the wise, and the tares grow with the wheat until the harvest. Each thing indeed must be done away with, but it is impossible to root out everything at once, just as we say of venial sins: none of them is to be allowed, yet not all can be avoided at once. But there is another reformation of which we are asking, namely that those things which disfigure the states and persons, both secular and spiritual, be brought back to right form: the reformation of peace between kingdoms and princes; the extirpation of heresies and schisms; the removal of simoniacal corruption from the Roman curia and from all the prelates of the Church; the suppression of concubinage; effective and useful visitation of the clergy; provincial and synodal councils; the institution of suitable prelates, clergy and parish rectors, and the promotion to orders and the lawful admission of those who are fit by life, learning and age. What of the lawful performance of the sacred rites, and of the careful attention that the honour of divine worship in the churches requires? In religious orders: the cutting off of dissolute living and excesses, and the restraint of wandering about; in both clergy and religious, the decency of dress and tonsures; the keeping of the rules of the orders; and in all things a watchful observance of monastic discipline; the suppression of adultery and of every kind of impurity; the frequenting of churches; the diligent preaching as well as hearing of the divine Word; the sanctification of the sabbaths. And that diviners, enchanters, soothsayers, augurs, those who observe dreams, those who devote themselves to unlawful charms and to superstitious blessings and nigromantic arts, and those who set up altars or churches in the meeting-places of the locality under hope of miracles or of sacred rites for shameful gain, be restrained with due severity; that the abuses of communities, cities, provinces and villages, alien to faith and good morals, be checked; and that all depraved customs, and corruptions rather, which oppose sound doctrine be forbidden in cathedral and collegiate churches and in the convents of whatever monasteries and churches.

units.la: Et quis omnia enarrare ac enumerare sufficiat, quibus ecclesia modernis temporibus cernitur deformata? Putamusne hæc omnia aliquando posse reformari? Persuaderi mihi videor, quod nec ætas nostra, nec futura hæc patietur: cum non habeam rationes probantes, quomodo illud fieri possit. Primo, propter inueteratam & inolitam consuetudinem, quæ difficile curatur: secundo, propter potentium, tam in scripturis quam in altis dignitatibus resistentiam: tertio, propter auaritiæ morbum, qui vbique inualuit, maximeque in altis sedibus, qui nullo modo patientur sibi auferri honoris, fastus, diuitiarum & voluptatis amplitudinem. Et qui amplius insistere deberent reformationibus, pompis amplius delectantur, fingentes ipsis colores sub specie defensionis Ecclesiasticæ. Et ideo eos oporteat abundare, ne status eorum vilescat: & vt habeant armatam militiam, qua compescere valeant, violantes bonorum ecclesiasticorum detentores. Et ideo oportet, vt dicunt, eos fulcitos esse pluralitatibus beneficiorum atque dignitatum, sed timedum est, ne lateat anguis in herba: fingentes excusationes in peccatis, magis vt quæ sua sunt quærentes, quam Dei. Nam veram puto sententiam B. Hieronymi super Ionam, scil. quod Rex Niniue nouissime audiuit sermonem Ionæ: quia difficile potentes, nobiles, diuites, & multo his difficilius homines eloquentes credunt Deo, & aures accommodant verbo Dei, excæcatur enim mens eorum. Concordat huic sententiæ Apostolica doctrina 1. Corin. 1. Non multi potentes, non multi nobiles, non multi sapientes secundum carnem, sed quæ stulta sunt mundi, elegit Deus, vt confundat sapientes. Æstimo igitur mundum dictum decrescere in prauis moribus, salua diuina dispositione, cuius consilium nemo nouit, vsque ad profundum delictorum, quousque veniat filius perditionis, qui cooperabitur delictis seculi, & fortificabit omnes operantes iniquitatem, vt fiat supra modum peccator obnoxius peccatorum. Posset quidem fieri vniuersalis reformatio Ecclesiæ per prædicta, sicut & iamdudum factum est: quæ si ad executionem ponerentur, nulla alia reformatione indigeremus. Sed sicut de decretis sanctorum patrum veterum factum est, sic fiet & de nouis, nulla super his facta executione. Neque diffiteor partiales fieri posse locorum reformationes, sicut & iam per gratiam Dei in multis monasteriis fiunt: sic & prælati, quorum Deus corda tangeret, possent se & suos à malis cohibere: cum Deus nouit qui sunt sui, & quos præsciuit & prædestinat conformes fieri imaginis filii sui, à voraginibus peccatorum, in quibus multitudo præambulat, potest præseruare.
units.tr: And who would be able to recount and enumerate all the ways in which the Church is seen to be deformed in these modern times? Do we think all these things can ever be reformed? I seem to be persuaded that neither our age nor the future will allow it, since I have no reasons showing how it could be done. First, because of the long-standing and deep-rooted custom, which is hard to cure. Second, because of the resistance of the powerful, both in the Scriptures and in high dignities. Third, because of the disease of avarice, which has gained strength everywhere, and most of all in high seats, who will in no way suffer the abundance of honour, pomp, riches and pleasure to be taken from them. And those who ought to press more for reforms take more delight in display, inventing colours for it under the appearance of defending the Church. And so, they say, it is necessary for them to abound, lest their status become cheap, and that they may have an armed soldiery by which they can hold down those who violate the holders of ecclesiastical goods. And so, they say, it is necessary for them to be propped up by pluralities of benefices and dignities; but we must fear lest a snake lie hidden in the grass, as they make excuses for their sins, seeking more what is their own than what is God's. For I hold the true opinion of blessed Jerome on Jonah, namely that the king of Nineveh was the last to hear the preaching of Jonah: because the powerful, the nobles and the rich find it hard to believe God, and men who are eloquent find it much harder, and they do not lend their ears to the word of God, for their mind is blinded. The apostolic teaching of 1 Corinthians 1 agrees with this opinion: "Not many powerful, not many noble, not many wise according to the flesh; but God has chosen the foolish things of the world, that he might confound the wise." I judge therefore that the world, with God's disposition, whose counsel no one knows, remaining safe, will go on declining in wicked morals, down to the depth of crimes, until the son of perdition comes, who will work together with the crimes of the age and strengthen all who work iniquity, so that the sinner becomes beyond measure liable to sins. Indeed a universal reformation of the Church could be brought about by the aforesaid means, as has already been done long ago; if these were put into execution, we would need no other reformation. But just as has happened with the decrees of the holy ancient fathers, so it will happen with new ones, no execution having been carried out on these. Nor do I deny that partial reformations of places can be made, as indeed by the grace of God is already happening in many monasteries; and prelates, whose hearts God might touch, could restrain themselves and their people from evils, since God knows who are his own, and can preserve from the whirlpools of sins, in which the multitude goes ahead, those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.

units.la: Recensentes veteres historias, ex serie sanctarum scripturarum scimus, quando iniquitas hominum minum inualescebat, Deus eis posuit modum, aut totum mundum perimendo, paucis exceptis, propter speciem conseruandam, vt in diluuio: aut in posteris nationibus, propter iuramentum Noæ factum, ne amplius diluuium faceret, particulares generationes delendo, vt in Pharaone submerso cum omnibus suis. Peruersam multitudinem filiorum Israel contra Deum & Moysen rebellantium in deserto, per 40. annos delendo de tanta multitudine, sc. 603550. solum duo homines intrauerint in terram promissionis, vt Num.14. Deinde cum iterum tempore Ieroboam multiplicati fuissent, & idolis seruissent per 200. annos, Deus tradidit decem tribus in captiuitatem Medorum & Persarum, vsque ad præsens. Generationem autem Iudæ & Beniamin tradidit in captiuitatem regis Babylonis per 70. annos. Post reditum vero de captiuitate, per Esdram, & Ihesum filium Iosedech sacerdotem, & Nehemiam, qui ædificarunt templum, & emendati sunt, vsque ad tempora Machabæorum, & vsque ad Christum. Nec leguntur idola coluisse, saltem vt plures: donec Christum occiderent & vsque ad tempora Titi & Vespasiani Romanorum principum, qui eos in excidio Hierusalem miserabiliter trucidarunt, ac aliquos vendiderunt. Sicque semper pœna secuta est culpā. Quid ergo pro nostris culpis passuri sumus, quæ vtique, vt timendum est, modo impar est præteritorum culpis? Et licet idola manufacta non colantur à Christianis, tamen idola mentalia fabricata frequentius coluntur, sc. auaritia, quæ est idolorum seruitus: ventris voluptas, quæ est idolum ventris; (quorum inquit Paulus, Deus venter est:) idolum superbiæ, Beelzebub, & Baal, & cætera. Quorum cultura quanto occultius, tanto amplius frequentatur. Gaudet quidem nostris temporibus, sci. nunc de anno Domini 1449. Ecclesia de vnico & indubitato pastore, sc. Nicolao Papa V. sed luget de conculcatione decretorum in transactis conciliis editorum, & videt quomodo contraria decretis practicantur. Suadendum tamen totis conatib. videtur, quod illud decretum frequens de conciliis generalib. continuandis non aboleatur: per quod vulnus, de superioritate Papæ supra Ecclesiam per Eugenium olim Papam inflictum, sanari potest. Licet enim plures contradicent, tamen per gratiam Dei pene totus orbis viros insignes in se continet, qui ab authoritate Ecclesiæ, per futuram atque nostram generationem non recedent, atque in ea vitam etiam finire gaudent, propter efficaces rationes id concludentes. Quibus nulla ratio humana defecuta, à passionib. resistere potest: præsertim cum Deus suam indefectibilem assistetiam nulli singulari personæ mortali legatur pollicitus esse, sicut toti Ecclesiæ, Ecce ego vobiscum, &c. Nec etiam primo summo Pontifici, qui & ante missionem Spiritus sancti, & post legitur errasse, licet Christus ei dixit: Ego pro te rogaui Petre, vt non deficeret fides tua. Hoc tamen in persona ecclesiæ sibi dixit. Qui cupit hanc veritatem de authoritate Ecclesiæ clare intueri, abstergat crassam nubem passionum & cupiditatum de ecclesiis suis, & mox clarius luce meridiana mutabit affectum, & pronunciabit ita esse. Nam & doctrina Philosophi in Politicis, idem sentire videtur, quod pluralitas sapientum certius iudicabit, & in toto orbe per regna, communitates, ciuitates, atque omnes prouincias, concilium plurimarum prouinciarum esse validius, quam vnius: sicut & Apostoli spiritu pleni, notabilia ecclesiæ negocia, in quod decernebat non Petrus solus, vt Act.6.12.17. & per totum quasi textum. Notabiliora vero negocia ac vtiliora, in ecclesia inuenire non possumus, quam hæresum extirpationem, schismatum eradicationem, & ecclesiæ generalem reformationem, tam in capite quam in membris: in quibus tribus præfertur authoritas Ecclesiæ, personæ Romani Pontificis.
units.tr: Reviewing the old histories, we know from the sequence of the holy Scriptures that when the iniquity of men grew, God set a limit for them, either by destroying the whole world, except a few, to preserve the kind, as in the Flood; or, in later nations, because of the oath made to Noah that he would no longer bring a flood, by destroying particular generations, as with Pharaoh drowned with all his people. He destroyed the perverse multitude of the sons of Israel who rebelled against God and Moses in the desert over forty years, so that of so great a multitude only two men entered the land of promise: Num.14. Then, when they had again multiplied in the time of Jeroboam and had served idols for 200 years, God handed over the ten tribes into captivity to the Medes and Persians, down to the present. He handed over the generation of Judah and Benjamin into captivity to the king of Babylon for 70 years. After their return from captivity, through Ezra, Jesus the son of Jozadak the priest, and Nehemiah, they built the temple and were reformed, down to the times of the Maccabees and down to Christ. Nor do we read that they worshipped idols, at least not many, until they killed Christ, and down to the times of Titus and Vespasian, Roman emperors, who slaughtered them wretchedly at the destruction of Jerusalem and sold some of them. And so punishment always followed guilt. What then are we going to suffer for our sins, which, as is to be feared, are surely now not less than the sins of the past? And although the Christians do not worship idols made by hands, nevertheless mental idols are worshipped more frequently: (of whom Paul says, God is their belly:) avarice, which is the slavery of idols; the pleasure of the belly, which is the idol of the belly; the idol of pride, Beelzebub, and Baal, and the rest. The worship of these is more frequent the more hidden it is. The Church rejoices indeed in our times, namely now in the year of the Lord 1449, in the one and undoubted shepherd, that is Pope Nicholas V; but she mourns the trampling underfoot of the decrees issued in the councils of the past, and sees how things contrary to the decrees are practised. Yet it seems to be urged with every effort that the frequent decree concerning the continuing of general councils should not be abolished, by which the wound of the superiority of the pope over the Church, inflicted once by Pope Eugenius, can be healed. For although many will contradict, nevertheless by the grace of God almost the whole world contains distinguished men who will not withdraw from the authority of the Church through this and future generations, and who rejoice to end their lives in it, on account of the effective reasons that conclude this. No human reason failing these men, they can resist passions; especially since God is not read to have promised his indefectible presence to any single mortal person, but to the whole Church: Behold, I am with you, etc. Nor indeed to the first supreme pontiff, who is read to have erred both before and after the sending of the Holy Spirit, although Christ said to him: I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail. Yet he said this to him in the person of the Church. Whoever desires to see clearly this truth about the authority of the Church, let him wipe away the thick cloud of passions and desires from his eyes, and soon he will change his feeling more clearly than the light of midday and will pronounce that it is so. For also the doctrine of the Philosopher in the Politics seems to hold the same view, which the plurality of the wise will judge more surely, and that throughout the world, among kingdoms, communities, cities and all provinces, the council of many provinces is stronger than that of one; just as the Apostles, full of the Spirit, decided notable matters of the Church, in which it was not Peter alone who decided, as in Acts 6.12.17. and through nearly the whole text. Yet we cannot find in the Church any more notable and more useful matters than the extirpation of heresies, the eradication of schisms and the general reformation of the Church, both in its head and in its members; and in these three the authority of the Church is preferred to the person of the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Quicquid igitur in saluo præsentis tractatuli dixi de habitudine status ecclesiæ vsque in finem seculi, lector meus benevolus suscipiat æstimatiue dictum. Cum enim prophetiæ spiritus hodie abest doctoribus, nunc authoritas & infallibilis ratio occurrebat, quibus contraria possem probare, relinquens in his ecclesiæ suæ statum Deo ad disponendum, secundum ordinem suæ excellētis sapientiæ. Omnia enim scimus agi propter electos, quibus omnia cooperantur in bonum, siue bona siue mala, siue prospera siue aduersa, vt filii prædestinationis exerceantur, purgentur, & probentur: filii vero perditionis affligantur & puniantur, sicut aurum & palea in eodem igne, scil. æqualiter pœnam sentiant: sed aurum purgatur, & palea consumitur. Manet enim dissimilitudo passarum in similitudine passionum, vt dicit August. 1.lib.de Ciuitate. Unde, non qualia quisque patiatur, sed qualis patitur, aduertendum est. Quecunque vero de authoritate vniuersalis ecclesiæ per generalia concilia repræsentante dicta leguntur, nouit tanquam indubitata hucusque me posuisse. Nec fateor me facile recedere à decretis, nisi per informationem efficaciorem vniuersalis ecclesiæ, aut sanius me sentientis, cuius iudicio me semper pariturum submitto, nihil pertinaciter in his propter paruitatem defendendo, sed me ecclesiæ iudicio submittendo.
units.tr: Whatever I have said in this little treatise about the condition of the Church until the end of the age, let my kind reader take as said tentatively. For since the spirit of prophecy is not present in the teachers today, I had only authority and infallible reason to go by, by which I could prove the contrary; so in these matters I leave the state of the Church to God to dispose, according to the order of his surpassing wisdom. For we know that all things are done for the sake of the elect, for whom all things work together for good, whether good or evil, prosperous or adverse, so that the sons of predestination may be exercised, purified and tested; but the sons of perdition are afflicted and punished, like gold and chaff in the same fire: they feel the punishment equally, but the gold is purified and the chaff is consumed. For, as Augustine says in the first book of the City of God, there remains a difference between those who suffer alike in the likeness of their sufferings. Hence it must be noted not what each man suffers, but what kind of man he is who suffers. As for whatever is read about the authority of the universal Church, represented by general councils, let the reader know that I have hitherto laid it down as indubitable. Nor do I confess that I readily depart from the decrees, unless by a more effective instruction of the universal Church, or by someone who judges more soundly, to whose judgment I submit that I shall always obey; I defend nothing obstinately in these matters on account of my littleness, but I submit myself to the judgment of the Church.

units.la: SIGISMVNDI ARCHIDVCIS AVSTRIÆ, &c. APPELLATIO A BVLLA EXCOMMVNICATIONIS PII PAPÆ II. ad Concilium generale & liberum.
units.tr: SIGISMUND, ARCHDUKE OF AUSTRIA, etc. APPEAL FROM THE BULL OF EXCOMMUNICATION OF POPE PIUS II, to a General and Free Council.

units.la: NARRATIO PAPAE PII DE GESTIS Sigismundi Austriæ Ducis contra Dominum Cardinalem de Cusa.
units.tr: NARRATIVE OF POPE PIUS CONCERNING THE DEEDS OF SIGISMUND, DUKE OF AUSTRIA, AGAINST LORD CARDINAL OF CUSA.

units.la: IVS Episcopus servus servorum Dei universis Christi fidelibus ad quos hæ literæ peruenerint, salutem & Apostolicam benedictionem. Iustissima quamuis iudicia & honestissima sint quæuis Apostolicæ sedis decreta, & opera eius mortalis arguere nemo potest, quia tamen multi reperiuntur iniquæ mentis homines, qui erecto supercilio tollere os in cœlum non verentur, & gradiente lingua eorum super terram in Christi vicarium iactantes opprobria, factæ eius damnare sæpenumero audent, & nitidam veritatis faciem, confusis mendaciorum tenebris obnubilare conantur, operæ pretium esse censemus, quæ per hos dies adversus Sigismundum ex Principibus Austriæ, sua contumacia & iniquitate requirente, per nos & factum collegium nostrum, statuta, ordinata & iudicata sunt, ad noritiam vestram his scriptis perducere, ne fama velox præcurrens, falsa pro veris persuadere, & suo more, aut addens gestis, aut adimens fallere possit. Rem igitur, sicut gesta est, ante oculos vestræ mentis ponemus, vos benevolas aures adhibete, & boni consulentes, matris vestræ & omnium fidelium nostræ sacrosanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ, primæque sedis, digna & solita reuerentia, decretum sententiamq; suscipite. Ecclesia Brixinensis quæ olim Sabiensis, & aliquando Brixinensis est appellata, in Alpibus sita est, quæ Germaniam ab Italia seiungunt, admodum insignis. Siquidem Romanorum Pontificum priuilegiis quamplurimis honestata, & Imperatorum largitate donata, non solum prædia sed arces & oppida munitissima possidet, & ipsius Brixinensis urbis ciuile dominium habet, diœcesis eius ad Enum fluuium protenditur, qui Danubio in Bauaria apud Patauiam miscetur, & in Athesim respicit, qui Tridentum Veronamque præterfluens insignes urbes in Adriatico exoneratur pelagus. Episcopus eius inter principes Imperii collocatur, & ab Imperatore absq; medio in feudum recipit principatum ac regalia. In ecclesiasticis negotiis ecclesiæ Salzburgensis suffraganeus est, & metropolitico iure illi subiectus. Aduocatus eius in temporalib. causis, si quid aduersi patiatur, Comes Tyrolis ab Imperatoribus constitutus est, qui tueatur ecclesiam, non qui impugnet: ob eam rem non parum utilitatis quotannis accipiens. Nam feuda opulenta & amplissima, ab ipsa Brixinensi ecclesia noscitur obtinere. Principium autem aduocationis in Comite Alberto fuit, qui primo per Conradum ipsius Ecclesiæ Pontificem, non sine pluribus conditionibus assumptus, & de ipsa aduocatia, quæ feudum est ecclesiæ, inuestitus, ab Imperatore confirmationem obtinuit. Vacante autem hac ecclesia, sedente Nicolao V. prædecessore nostro, Nicolaus ipse de fratrum consilio, dilectum filium nostrum Nicolaum titulí S. Petri ad vincula Presbyterum Cardinalem, in episcopum & pastorem præfecit. Qui etsi diu contradicente & reluctante Sigismundo, possessionem tamen pacificam & quietam ecclesiæ suæ deniq; consecutus est, & uiliter plebi per plures annos prædicando, monendo, hortando, & pontificale officium exercendo præfuit. Sed cum sedente Calixto III. qui noster fuit immediatus prædecessor, Cardinalis, ipse atque episcopus Brixinensis, more boni patrisfamilias & diligentis atque attenti prælati, pia loca reformans, & iura ecclesiæ suæ exacte perquirens, inuenisset Sigismundum emendationi monasterii in Sonnenberg ex eo aduersum, quod nihil sine eius assensu fiendum præsumeret, ac eum Tyrolensem Comitem pleraque magni momenti feuda, ab ecclesia sua obtinere, quæ minime ut moris est recognouisset, hortaretur que spirituale iurisdictionem ne pertubaret, & nouam reciperet inuestituram, iusque iurandum præstaret, mox dissensiones ortæ sunt, & ipsius Sigismundi grande odium aduersus Cardinalē excitatur. Propter quæ cum statuisset Cardinalis, ut fidelis archimandrita, suas oues diligentius respicere, & à noxiis itineribus retrahere, cunctosq; malos mores eradicare, & plantare bonos, eliminare vitia & seminare virtutes; surrexissentq; propterea maligni quidam homines, tam clerici quam laici, quib. amara erant præcepta iustitiæ, & aduersus salutifera Cardinalis reformationē cōtumaciæ & rebellionis cornua erigeret, cepit Sigismundus malignantiū patrocinium. Et quis esset ipse quoq; ex ouibus, Cardinali tanquam Episcopo Brixinensi commissis, in pastorem tamen & patrem ac magistrum animæ suæ, sese extollere non expauit, sed omni studio atque conatu adorsus est, ne salutifera morum reformatio, aut in clero aut in populo Brixinensi locum haberet, adeoque bonis actibus ipsius Cardinalis obicem sœ præbuit, vt Monialium quoque, quarum supra meminimus, dissolute & turpissime viuentium, ne recludi reformarique possent, protectionem & tutelam aduersus Cardinalem acceperit, adeoque ab honestate procul abiit, vt Cardinalem ipsum, neque in sua dioecesi, neque in ciuitate tutum esse, aut pontificale munus exercere posse permitteret, introductis & persuasis sectariis, qui vitæ eius insidiarentur. Quod cum Calixtus antea dictus accepisset, mox literas monitorias aduersus Sigismundum decreuit, præcipiens ei, ne Cardinalem in Ecclesia sua, in qua Pontificio fungeretur, ab executione sui officii quoquo pacto deterreret, eumve suum munus exercentem impediret. Si secus ageret, anathema esset, pœnas læsæ maiestatis incurreret, & omni territorio suo sacrum interdictum ipso facto intelligeret. Obaudiuit Sigismundus Pontificis maximi vocem atque contempsit, & interposita quadam appellatione, malo deceptus consilio à Romano throno (quod nulli permissum est) contra ius fasque prouocauit, & in rebellione perseuerans, nouis dictum contumeliis Cardinalem affecit. Creuere supra modum Sigismundi odia aduersus Cardinalem, nec poterat ei quicquam pacifice loqui. Ob quas res cum tuto sibi esse in ecclesia sua non posse Cardinalis animaduerteret, ad nos confugit. Per idem tempus iam propemodum accincti eramus recedere, Mantuanum conuentum petituri, quem pro tuitione fidei aduersus Turcos indixeramus. Eum igitur ab ecclesia sua, quem admodum profugum cæpimus benigne, & pro tempore consolati, Legatum de latere, qui vicem nostram in vrbe Romana & circumiacenti regione impleret, consulentibus fratribus & cohortantibus reliquimus; Ipsi Mantuam pro communi salute, cum Romana curia petimus. Vbi cum aliquibus mensibus commorati essemus, & Sigismundum ad nos venientem intellexissemus, vt componere inter eos concordiam, & tam atroces inimicitias amputare possemus, Cardinalem accersimus, quo veniente, & Sigismundo præsente, pluribus diebus modo per Cardinales & alias interpositas etiam illustrium personas principum, modo per nos ipsos reconciliare alterum alteri conati sumus, atque huic pacis negocio, summo nisu operam dedimus; nihil profecimus, incassum abiere studia nostra, irriti omnes labores fuerunt; quamuis Cardinalis iudicio nostro se submittens, & arbitros non suspectos accepturum, iudicens, viam iuris nunquam recusaueritaut refugerit. Abiit ex Mantua Sigismundus in patriam infecta pace, minarum plenus & iræ, & cum paulo post, nos quoque translato conuentu, donum repetere statuissemus Cardinalis ex permisso nostro ad Dioecesim suam se transtulit, asserentibus amicis adhuc pacem inueniri posse, nec Brixinam petiit: nihil enim tutum ibi esse sciebat, sed in arcem quandam sui episcopatus munitissimam se recepit. Vbi cum aliquandiu consedisset, hortantibus nonnullis non paruæ auctoritatis viris, qui se partibus ambabus amicos ostendebant, & nihil periculi, nihil insidiarum timendum esse dicentibus, ad Brunecam se contulit, quod & ipsius ecclesiæ Brixinensis non parui momenti oppidum, literis maxime fretus, quibus idem Sigismundus suo signo obsignatis, bona fide promittit, ecclesiam Brixinensem & Cardinalem quoad vixerit se protecturum, ad quem locum misit mox Sigismundus vnum ex consilio suo Nobilem virum, inter aulicos suum primarium, qui Cardinalem in suam traheret voluntatem, sed is multa cum Cardinale prolocutus, cum nihil posset ei iniustum suadere, quia iura ecclesiæ suæ nollet proiicere, concordia tamen in omnibus reperta est, vnico excepto articulo, qui regalia concernebat, & cum in eo aliter conuenire non posset, de suspensione temporali actum est. In qua cum orator biennales, Cardinalis vero metuens moram tam diuturnam ecclesiæ suæ periculosam esse, semestres tantum treugas offerret, tandemque interueniente capitulo etiam biennales admissurus esset; pendente adhuc tractatu, & oratore non à Brunegka digresso, Sigismundus non tam concordiam, vt opere conprobauit, quam confusionem Cardinalis, & furoris sui cursum quærens, turgidus & animum tumens non iracundiam cohibere, non se vllo pacto vincere potuit; cessit audaciæ, succumbit temeritati, rancori atque odio paruit, iussit accersiri milites, exercitum congregari, belli machinam apparari, quibus expeditis, misso caduceatore, qui bellum Cardinali indiceret, quamuis esset maior & sacra hebdomada, & tempus pœnitentiæ datum, copias eduxit, & iter faciës ipsa die paschæ, ante Brunegkam armatas militum acies collocauit, machinas admouit, insultum fecit, oppidum cepit. Non moratus arcem quoque summa vi oppugnare aggressus est, in qua cum familia Cardinalis sese receperat. Pugnatum est aliquandiu non parua contentione, sed cum persuasum esset Cardinali, arcem diu defendi non posse, & perundum omnibus esse, nisi se dederint, interuenientibus mediatoribus, certis conditionibus conclusa est pax; in quibus erat comminatum, quod vel arx vel Cardinalis in potestatem Sigismundi venirent: Et nihilominus cum iussisset pacem & securitatem publicari, claues arcis extorquens, & munitionem ac Cardinalem artissima custodia seruari iussit, sicque per aliquot dies cum summo probro & ignominia, & omni contumeliarum genere, Cardinalis in potestate Sigismundi retentus est, nec libertatem obtinere potuit, nisi remissis iniuriis, castro quodam ecclesiæ tradito, magno auri pondere soluto, restituto creditorum chirographo, compluribus aliis extortis conditionibus, præter eas, quibus pax antea fuerat publicata, omnibus denique ecclesiæ iuribus & priuilegiis ereptis. Neque his contentus, sed iniquitatem iniquitati congeminans, cum sacerdotes ob piaculum commissum iuri parentes, à sacris abstinerent, non veritus est, necem Cardinali denunciare, nisi ad prophanationem sacrorum illos compelleret. Temerarius atque infelix, qui talia gerens, nihilominus eius ecclesiæ protectotectorem se iactat, cuius est euersor inuentus, quæ singula cum nobis ex ordine renuciata essent, mirum in modum horrximus, congelatum est illico pectus & in stuporem sumus conuersi, nec satis detestari aut abominari facinus tam horribile poteramus, in sacerdotem, in pastorem, in episcopum suum, in Cardinalem ecclesiæ Romanæ, in fratrem nostrum, in excellens Apostolicæ sedis membrum violenta manus Sigismundi temeritas, non exhorruit, & quo tempore anni patrata sunt, nempe in die Paschæ, in die illa maxima & sanctissima, in die qua victor mortis, & inferorum triumphator, Dominus resurrexit, in die qua Christiani singuli, redemptori gratias agunt, & expurgato veteri fermento sacratissimo Christi corpori & sanguini communicant, in qua dies nemo tam scelera-tus est, tam impius, tam immanis, si modo Christianus est, qui non sacerdotibus sese subiiciat, eosque summis prosequatur honoribus. Sed qua die suarum rectoribus animarum cæteri præcipue studient, ea die sacerdotem suum Sigismundus inuasit, cœpit, in carcerem coniecit, inhoneste tauit, spreuit, turpiter habuit. Fuimus diu anxii & admodum dubii his cognitis, nec satis tenebamus, quid esset agendum, quamuis non dubius rumor, sed certissimus nuncius perpetrati scelus ad nos peruenisset.
units.tr: Pius, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of Christ to whom these letters come, greeting and apostolic blessing. Although the most just judgments and the most honourable decrees of the Apostolic See, and its works, no one can rightly find fault with, yet there are many men of wicked mind who, with lofty brows, do not hesitate to raise their mouths to heaven, and whose tongues walk upon the earth, heaping reproaches upon Christ's vicar, and who often dare to condemn his acts and try to darken the bright face of truth with the confused shadows of lies. We think it worth while to make known to you in writing what has been determined, ordained and judged during these days by us and our college against Sigismund of the house of Austria, since his obstinacy and iniquity demanded it. We do this so that swift rumour, running ahead, may not persuade you of falsehoods as truths, or, in its usual way, deceive you by adding to or taking away from the facts. We will therefore set the matter before the eyes of your mind as it was done. Lend us your kind attention, and, judging it fairly, receive the decree and sentence with the honour and customary reverence due to your mother, our holy Roman Church, and to all the faithful, and to the first See. The church of Brixen, once called Sabiona and at one time Brixen, lies in the Alps, which separate Germany from Italy, and is very distinguished. Honoured with very many privileges of the Roman Pontiffs and endowed with the generosity of the Emperors, it possesses not only estates but strong fortresses and towns, and holds civil lordship over the city of Brixen itself. Its diocese extends to the river Enns, which mingles with the Danube at Passau in Bavaria, and it looks towards the Adige, which, flowing past Trent and Verona, discharges into the Adriatic sea, famous cities. Its bishop is ranked among the princes of the Empire, and he receives from the Emperor, without any intermediary, the principality and the regalia as a fief. In ecclesiastical affairs he is suffragan to the church of Salzburg and subject to it by metropolitan right. Its advocate in temporal causes, should it suffer any adversity, is the Count of Tyrol, appointed by the Emperors to defend the church, not to attack it; and for this he receives no small yearly profit. For he is known to hold rich and very large fiefs from the church of Brixen itself. The beginning of this advocacy lay with Count Albert, who was first taken on by Conrad, then Bishop of this church, not without several conditions, and who, invested with the advocacy itself, which is a fief of the church, obtained confirmation from the Emperor. When this church fell vacant, during the pontificate of Nicholas V, our predecessor, Nicholas himself, with the advice of the brethren, set over it as bishop and pastor our beloved son Nicholas, Cardinal Priest of St Peter ad Vincula. Although Sigismund long opposed and resisted him, he at last obtained peaceful and quiet possession of his church, and for several years presided over the people there, preaching, admonishing, exhorting and exercising the pontifical office. But when Cardinal Calixtus III, who was our immediate predecessor, held the see, the cardinal, being bishop of Brixen himself, acted like a good householder and a diligent and attentive prelate. He reformed the pious houses and carefully inquired into the rights of his church. He found that Sigismund, in opposition to the reform of the monastery at Sonnenberg, presumed to do nothing without his assent, and that, as Count of Tyrol, he held many fiefs of great importance from his church, which he had not, as is customary, acknowledged. The cardinal urged him not to disturb the spiritual jurisdiction, to receive new investiture and to take the oath of fealty. Straightway quarrels arose and a great hatred of Sigismund himself was stirred up against the cardinal. Because of these things, the cardinal, as a faithful archimandrite, resolved to look more carefully after his sheep, to draw them back from harmful paths, to root out all evil customs and plant good ones, to remove vices and sow virtues. Certain wicked men, both clergy and laity, to whom the precepts of justice were bitter, rose up for this reason, and raised the horns of stubbornness and rebellion against the salutary reformation of the cardinal. Sigismund took up the protection of these evildoers. And he, who was himself one of the sheep committed to the cardinal as bishop of Brixen, did not shrink from setting himself up as shepherd, father and master of his soul. He applied himself with all zeal and effort so that the salutary reform of manners should find no place either among the clergy or among the people of Brixen. He so placed an obstacle in the way of the cardinal's good works that, in order to prevent the nuns, of whom we have spoken above, who lived dissolutely and most shamefully, from being shut up and reformed, he took them under his protection and guardianship against the cardinal. He departed so far from honour that he allowed the cardinal to be safe neither in his diocese nor in the city, nor able to exercise the pontifical office, having brought in and persuaded sectarians to lie in wait for his life. When Calixtus, already mentioned, learned of this, he straightway decreed letters of admonition against Sigismund, ordering him not to deter the cardinal in any way from carrying out his office in his church, in which he exercised the pontifical office, nor to hinder him from performing his duty. If he acted otherwise, he would be under anathema, incur the penalties of treason, and understand that the sacred interdict had come into effect by the act itself over all his territory. Sigismund disobeyed the voice of the chief Pontiff and despised it. Interposing a certain appeal, deceived by bad counsel, he appealed from the Roman throne (which is permitted to no one) against right and law. Persisting in rebellion, he further loaded the cardinal with fresh insults. Sigismund's hatred of the cardinal grew beyond measure, nor could anyone speak peaceably to him. For these reasons the cardinal, perceiving that he could not be safe in his church, fled to us. About the same time we were almost ready to leave for the congress at Mantua, which we had summoned for the defence of the faith against the Turks. So we kindly received the cardinal, who had come to us as a fugitive from his church, and, after consoling him for the time being, at the urging of our brethren, left him as legate a latere to fulfil our office in the city of Rome and the surrounding region. We ourselves set out for Mantua, with the Roman curia, for the common safety. When we had stayed there for some months and learned that Sigismund was coming to us, in order that we might bring about concord between them and cut off such fierce enmities, we summoned the cardinal. When he arrived, with Sigismund present, for several days we tried to reconcile one to the other, sometimes through cardinals and other interposed persons, even illustrious princes, sometimes through ourselves, and we applied our highest effort to this business of peace. We accomplished nothing; our efforts came to nothing, and all our labours were in vain, although the cardinal, submitting himself to our judgment and judging that he would accept impartial arbiters, never refused or shrank from the way of law. Sigismund left Mantua for his country with peace unaccomplished, full of threats and anger. Soon afterwards, when we too had transferred the assembly and resolved to return home, the cardinal, with our permission, went to his diocese, his friends asserting that peace could still be found. He did not make for Brixen, for he knew that nothing was safe there, but withdrew into a certain very strongly fortified castle of his bishopric. When he had remained there for some time, at the urging of certain men of no little authority, who showed themselves friends to both parties and said that there was no danger and no plot to fear, he betook himself to Bruneck, an town of no small importance belonging to the church of Brixen itself. He relied chiefly on a letter, sealed with his own seal, by which Sigismund pledged in good faith that he would protect the church of Brixen and the cardinal as long as he lived. Sigismund at once sent to that place one of his counsellors, a noble man, the chief of his courtiers, to draw the cardinal to his own will. But this man, after much discussion with the cardinal, since he could not persuade him to anything unjust, because the cardinal would not give up the rights of his church, nevertheless found agreement on all points except one article, which concerned the regalia. As they could not agree on that, the matter was referred to a temporary suspension. In this, the envoy offered two years, while the cardinal, fearing that so long a delay would be dangerous to his church, offered only six months' truce, and was at last to admit even two years, once the chapter had intervened. While the negotiation was still pending, and the envoy had not left Bruneck, Sigismund, seeking not so much concord, as he afterwards proved by his deeds, as confusion for the cardinal and the course of his own fury, swollen and puffed up in spirit, could not restrain his anger or conquer himself in any way. He yielded to audacity, succumbed to rashness, and obeyed rancour and hatred. He ordered soldiers to be summoned, an army to be assembled and the machinery of war to be prepared. When these were ready, he sent a herald to declare war on the cardinal. Although it was Holy Week, and a time of penance, he led out his forces, and on the very day of Easter, on the march, he drew up armed lines of soldiers before Bruneck, brought up siege engines, made an assault and took the town. Without delay he set about attacking the castle also with the greatest force, into which the cardinal's household had retreated. They fought for some time with no small struggle. But when it was made clear to the cardinal that he could not hold the castle long, and that all would perish unless they surrendered, a peace was concluded through intermediaries on certain conditions. In these it was threatened that either the castle or the cardinal would come into Sigismund's power. Nevertheless, when he had ordered peace and security to be proclaimed, he extorted the keys of the castle, and ordered the fortress and the cardinal to be kept under the closest guard. Thus for some days the cardinal was held in Sigismund's power with the greatest disgrace and shame and every kind of insult. He could not obtain his liberty except by remitting injuries, by handing over a certain castle of the church, by paying a large weight of gold, by restoring the creditors' bond, and by several other conditions extorted from him, beyond those by which peace had previously been proclaimed; and finally all the rights and privileges of the church were taken away. Not content with these things, but adding iniquity to iniquity, when the priests, obeying the law because of the crime committed, abstained from the sacred offices, he did not hesitate to threaten the cardinal with death unless he compelled them to profane the sacred rites. Reckless and unhappy man! Though doing such things, he nevertheless boasts that he is protector of that church whose overthrower he has been found to be. When these things were reported to us one by one in order, we shuddered wonderfully; our breast was straightway frozen and we were turned to stupor. Nor could we sufficiently detest or abominate so horrible a deed. Against a priest, a pastor, his own bishop, a cardinal of the Roman Church, our brother, an excellent member of the Apostolic See, the violent hand of Sigismund's rashness did not shrink back. And at what time of the year these things were done! It was on Easter Day, on that greatest and most holy day, on which the Lord rose as victor over death and triumpher over the underworld, on which each Christian gives thanks to the Redeemer and, the old leaven being purged out, communicates in the most sacred body and blood of Christ. On this day no one is so wicked, so impious, so savage, if he is indeed a Christian, that he does not submit himself to priests and show them the highest honour. But on the very day on which the other men are most eager to serve the rulers of their souls, Sigismund attacked his priest, seized him, threw him into prison, dishonoured him, spurned him and treated him shamefully. We were long anxious and greatly doubtful when we learned these things, nor did we clearly know what was to be done, although the news that this crime had been committed reached us not as a doubtful rumour but as a most certain report.

units.la: Nam huius atrocissimi sceleris notorium factum, ad exigendum ultionem pœnamque inuitabat. Inde vetus benevolentia, qua quondam Sigismundo coniuncti fuimus, ad clementiam & misericordiam prouocabat. Nos enim cum in minoribus ageremus, apud Fridericum Romanum Imperatorem tunc dominum, nunc filium charissimum, diu conuersati fuimus, ac consiliariatus munere honestati, multisque gratiis & fauoribus cumulati, plurimos annos in eius curia atque familia mansimus, nec vnquam indignatum aut nubilosum erga nos ipsius Imperatoris vultum inuenimus, semper læta, semper blanda nobis eius facies fuit, semper benigna & affecta mens, & nostri honoris percupida. Sigismundus cum primo Imperatorem adiuimus, puer bonæ admodum indolis erat, & sub tutela patruelis sui degens, modestis imbutus moribus, amorem in se omnino alliciebat. Alloquebatur nos sæpe blando sermone, quærebat nostras epistolas & legebat, ut qui tam bene viuendi cupidus & literarum cultor & nostri amans videbatur, dimissus extra tutelam, & in adolescentia sua, ad regendam patris prouinciam profectus, sæpe ad nos literas dedit, & nostras accepit, sæpe sua negotia apud Imperatorem iuuimus, cum eo nonnunquam domi suæ fuimus, neque sine honore & singulari gratia ab eo recessimus. Et cum gesta eius in Cardinalem, nondum cognita nobis essent, ad conuentum vsque Mantuanum, continuata est, vt antea, semper caritas nostra; ad quem Sigismundus ipse, splendidum & magnificum duxit comitatum, ut qui gratias nobis referre statuerat, pro pace Suitensium, bellicosarum & fortissimarum gentium, quos sibi missis legatis, apud Constantiam reconciliauimus. Vertebantur hæc omnia in mente nostra, & tanquam recenter gesta essent, ante cordis oculos volebantur.
units.tr: For the notoriety of this most atrocious crime urged us to exact vengeance and punishment. Yet our old goodwill toward Sigismund, by which we were once bound to him, called us to clemency and mercy. For when we were still young men, we spent a long time with Frederick, then Roman Emperor and now our dearest son, and having been honoured with the office of counsellor and laden with many favours and kindnesses, we remained for many years in his court and household. Never did we find the Emperor's countenance angry or clouded toward us; his face was always cheerful and kind toward us, his mind always benevolent and eager for our honour. When we first approached the Emperor, Sigismund was a boy of very good disposition, and living under the guardianship of his cousin, imbued with modest manners, he entirely won affection for himself. He often addressed us in a friendly way, sought out and read our letters, since he seemed so keen to live well, so devoted to letters and so fond of us. When he was released from guardianship and, in his youth, set out to govern his father's province, he often wrote to us and received our letters in return; we often helped his affairs with the Emperor, we were sometimes at his home, and we never left him without honour and special favour. And when his deeds against the Cardinal were not yet known to us, our affection continued as before, down to the Congress of Mantua, to which Sigismund himself led a splendid and magnificent retinue, since he had resolved to thank us for the peace with the Swiss, that warlike and most valiant people, whom we had reconciled at Constance by sending envoys. All these things turned over in our mind, and as if they had just happened, they passed before the eyes of our heart.

units.la: Suadebant imperatoris iusfinita erga nos beneficia, vt patrueli & sanguini suo ignosceremus, exposcebat ipsius Sigismundi, qua nos longo tempore complexus est, ingens benevolentia, vt hanc sibi culpam condonaremus. Vrgebant inclitæ domus Austriæ, quæ hunc Sigismundum genuit, ingentia in nos, & diu continuata merita, vt sublimi & alto sanguini veniam largiremur. Instare & Albertus videbatur, alter Sigismundi patruelis, & ipse Dux Austriæ atque Imperatoris germanus, & cum eo pariter illustris memoriæ Ladislai Vngariæ, & Bohemiæ regis, paulo ante vita defuncti, proximi eius consanguinei petere vehementer ac rogare per veterem amicitiam (ambo enim alii quando nos dilexerunt, & verbis & factis ornarunt) ne sua ex familia vindictam exigeremus, occurrebant infinitæ regum & magnorum principum facies, qui Australi domui coniuncti sanguine hanc nobis prosapiam summus precibus commendaturi offerebant.
units.tr: The Emperor's boundless benefits toward us urged us to pardon our kinsman and blood relation; the great goodwill of Sigismund himself, which had embraced us for a long time, begged us to forgive him this fault. The illustrious house of Austria, which gave birth to this Sigismund, pressed us with its great and long-continued services to us, that we should grant pardon to so high and noble a blood. Albert also seemed to insist, another cousin of Sigismund and himself Duke of Austria and brother of the Emperor, and together with him the close kinsmen of King Ladislaus of Hungary and Bohemia, who died shortly before, of illustrious memory, who earnestly begged and asked us, by our old friendship (for both of them, at other times, had loved us and honoured us in word and deed), not to exact vengeance on their family. Countless faces of kings and great princes came before us, who, joined to the Austrian house by blood, offered to commend this lineage to us with the most urgent prayers.

units.la: Sed cum hæc iam pene victi consentientes, animo voluimus; & ad veniam tractiam iam misericordiæ iustitiam cedere mandaturi fuimus, excitata in aduersum conscientia nostra, & miris calefacta modis: Quid tu (inquit) Pie Pontifex agis? An ignoras quem tenes locum, quam geris personam? Non tu modo ille Æneas es, qui Siluio quondam genitus patre, Frederico Imperatori seruiuisti.
units.tr: But when we had almost been overcome by these things and were inclined in spirit to agree, and were about to yield justice to the pity of pardon, our conscience was stirred against it and heated in wonderful ways: "What are you doing, Pius Pontiff?" it said. "Do you not know what place you hold, what role you bear? You are not merely that Aeneas who, born of Silvius long ago, served the Emperor Frederick."

units.la: Mutata est conditio tua, mutata persona, nosce teipsum, Tu Pius es Romanæ Præsul ecclesiæ, Christi vicarium & Petri successorem geris, te caput ecclesiæ militantis, te ducem, te magistrum, te Doctorem, te iudicem Christiani populi constituit Dominus, & claues tibi regni cælorum tradidit. Nihil quaerere fieri iudex, inquit sapiens, nisi valeas virtute irrumpere iniquitatem, ne forte extimescas faciem potentis, & poenas scandalum in agilitate tua. Super gentes & regna moderator cœli, & mundi Dominus te Christus ordinauit, vt destruas & euellas, ædifices & plantes. Et quid agis? quid dubitas malas euellere plantas? Nemo iuste iudicat, qui vel odio vel gratia vel metu flectitur. An ignoras, Sigismundus quam scelestum, quam atrox, quam tetrum ac horrendum admisit facinus? In Episcopum, in Cardinalem, in teipsum, si tui corporis Cardinales, vt iura volunt, parres habentur, iniurius & improbus fuit? Non Presbyteratui, non Episcopatui, non Cardinalatui, non Papatui, non Christo pepercit, cuius sacratissimum diem, pugna iniqua, & Cardinalis captiuitate fœdauit.
units.tr: Your condition has changed, your person has changed; know yourself. You are Pius, the Prelate of the Roman Church; you bear the place of Christ's vicar and the successor of Peter; the Lord has appointed you the head of the militant Church, its leader, its master, its teacher, the judge of the Christian people, and has delivered to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. "Seek nothing," says the wise man, "to be made a judge unless you are able by virtue to break down iniquity, lest perhaps you fear the face of the powerful and your ease bring a stumbling block to punishment." Over the nations and kingdoms Christ, the governor of heaven and Lord of the world, has ordained you, that you may destroy and pluck up, build and plant. And what are you doing? Why do you hesitate to pluck up the bad plants? No one judges justly who is swayed by hatred, favour or fear. Do you not know what a wicked, atrocious, foul and dreadful crime Sigismund has committed? Was he not unjust and wicked toward a bishop, toward a cardinal, toward yourself, if, as the laws say, the cardinals are regarded as the parts of your body? He spared neither the priesthood, nor the episcopate, nor the cardinalate, nor the papacy, nor Christ, whose most sacred day he defiled by an unjust battle and the capture of a cardinal.

units.la: Et quis clericorum posthæc tutus habebitur? si episcopi, si Cardinales armis atque insidiis capiuntur? & qui deinceps vindictam timebit, si violatores tantarum dignitatum impune abeant? Adam de omni clero deque omni religione fuerit, si qui tecum vnum sunt, absque vltionis periculo violantur. Summa sacerdotalis dignitas, B. Petri auctoritas, Iesu Christi maiestas, palam in hoc scelere læsa est; & tu tanti piaculi vindictam assumere dubitas, putasque Imperatorem vel alium quemuis principem ægre laturum, si iudicium feceris.
units.tr: And who among the clergy will be considered safe after this? If bishops and cardinals are seized by arms and ambush, and who will fear vengeance in future if the violators of such great dignities go unpunished? If whoever is one with you is violated without danger of vengeance, what will become of all the clergy and all religion? The supreme sacerdotal dignity, the authority of Blessed Peter, the majesty of Jesus Christ, has openly been injured in this crime; and you hesitate to take up vengeance for so great a sacrilege, and you think that the Emperor or any other prince will bear it with difficulty if you pass judgment.

units.la: Abßt à te hic metus, nihil est cur hæc nomina timeas. Iustus est Imperator, & honesti tenax, iustus Albertus, iusti & cæteri principes, qui non consanguineos solum sed ipsos quoque filios ex se genitos legum vinculis coerceri, plectique si peccauerunt non indigne ferent, magna vis iustitiæ est, quæ vel damnatum, iure se passum esse fateri cogit. Nihil imperatori magis cordi est, quam iustitia, communis & sanctissima virtus. Scit sua mansuetudo, quia iustitia pacem quærit, gentem elevat, solium & regnum confirmat, lætitiam gignit, & amatores suos beatos & immortales efficit, vtilius Imperatori videbitur, infructuosum palmitem amputari, quam in perniciem bonæ vitis retineri. Nec propterea domus Austriæ gloria interibit, quia vnus aut alter ex principibus eius damnatur, quæ Rudolphos, Albertos, Fridericos, Leopoldos, Ernestos, VVilhelmos & alios quam plures illustres animas peperit, non Austriæ solum ac Sueuiæ, sed Hungariæ, Bohemiæ, & ipsius Romani Imperii Gubernatores. Æacidarum quippe decus, Orestis infamia non extinxit, nec splendorem Iuliæ gentis Neronis turpitudo deleuit, nec Francorum lucem Hilderici obfuscauit ignauia, nec senatus Apostolici puritatem atque nitorem impurus ac fœtidus Iudas commulare potuit, illustrium familiarum non texisse, sed non habuisse maleficium vera est & solida laus. Rara prosapia est, quæ non aliquando monstra pepererit. In omni gente & in omni domo Catilinam inuenies & Cethegum.
units.tr: Put this fear away from you; there is nothing for which you should fear these names. The Emperor is just and tenacious of what is honourable; Albert is just, and the other princes are just, who will not unworthily bear it if not only their kinsmen but also their own sons, begotten of themselves, are restrained by the bonds of law and punished if they have sinned. Great is the power of justice, which compels even a condemned man to confess that he has rightly suffered. Nothing is dearer to the Emperor than justice, the common and most holy virtue. His gentleness knows that justice seeks peace, raises up a people, confirms a throne and a kingdom, begets joy, and makes its lovers blessed and immortal; it will seem more useful to the Emperor to cut off an unfruitful branch than to keep it to the ruin of the good vine. Nor on that account will the glory of the house of Austria perish, because one or another of its princes is condemned; it has brought forth Rudolphs, Alberts, Fredericks, Leopolds, Ernests, Wilhelms and many other illustrious souls, who have been governors not only of Austria and Swabia but of Hungary, Bohemia and the Roman Empire itself. Indeed the glory of the Aeacids was not extinguished by the infamy of Orestes, nor did the baseness of Nero blot out the splendour of the Julian family, nor did the cowardice of Hilderic dim the light of the Franks, nor could the impure and foul Judas tarnish the purity and brightness of the Apostolic senate. It is a true and solid praise of illustrious families not to have concealed wickedness but not to have had it. Rare is the lineage that has never at some time given birth to monsters. In every nation and in every house you will find a Catiline and a Cethegus.

units.la: CITATVR SIGISMVNDVS DVX AD RE- SPONDENDVM DE FIDE.
units.tr: Sigismund the Duke is summoned to answer concerning the faith.

units.la: PIvs Episcopus, seruus seruorum Dei, vniuersis & singulis Christi fidelibus salutem & Apostolicam benedictionem: Contra Sathanæ, aduersarii Christi domini & Saluatoris nostri, indeficientes insidias, quas in sua membra tendere non desistit, vt Christianorum improuidas animas maculet, nos qui licet immeriti pastorale tenemus officium, vigili oportet sollicitudine speculari.
units.tr: Pius, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all and each of the faithful in Christ, greeting and apostolic blessing. Against the unceasing snares of Satan, the adversary of Christ our Lord and Saviour, which he never stops laying for his members in order to stain the unwary souls of Christians, we who, though unworthy, hold the pastoral office must watch over them with vigilant care.

units.la: Nam ex quo Sathanæ ipsius membrum principale, impius Sigismundus ex Austriæ principibus, qui aliquando nobiscum Christi & ecclesiæ membrum fuerat, in sacratissima Paschalis festi celebritate, in sathanicam se à catholicorum coetu abscissus præcipitauit ingluuiem, & ab Apostolica ecclesia transfuga effectus, sub diaboli cœpit vexillo militare, anathema proh dolor incurrit, & demum infamias cumulando, & sese apostatare superbiendo facto quoque se vnitatis ecclesiæ fidem, auctoritatisque eius rationem per censurarum contemptum non habere palam demonstrauit, & demum vt eum in malorum omnium profundum peruenisse omnibus certum foret, eadem iactat temeritate, nec sacrosanctos canones, nec Apostolicæ præcepta iustissima nec iudicia ex canonicis sanctionibus facta solennissime, eum in vllo posse contingere, quamquam ipse Dei nefarius derisor & ecclesiæ contemptor, de Christiano adhuc non erubescat nomine gloriari, ob quas res tametsi propter facti notorietatem, vnusquisque ipsum rectissime hæreticum iudicarit, vt tamen ex suo ore iudicium etiam prodeat, habentes priores nostros processus, in quibus anathematis, criminis læsæ maiestatis, & fautoriæ hæresis declaratus est, poenas incurrisse, in his literis pro inuiolatis & expressis, quo constare valeat, non solum ex operum improbitate scelestorum, sed sua etiam propria confessione, an sit hæreticus vel non, nouum denuo processum inchoauimus aduersus dictum Sigismundum; tanquam de damnatissima hæresi, quæ est omnium hæresum hæresis, non solum suspectum notorie sed sensibiliter maculatum, tanquam sanctæ fidei non recipientem articulum, quem per hæc symboli Apostolici verba, fidelium exprimit vnusquisque: Credo in vnam sanctam catholicam & Apostolicam ecclesiam. Nam cum ipsius ecclesiæ Romanus Pontifex caput sit, canonesque & censuræ sic sint ecclesiæ, quod quisque in ecclesia positus est, & credens capiti, canonibus & eius censuris teneatur obedire.
units.tr: For since Sigismund, the impious prince of Austria, who was once a member of Christ and the Church along with us, but who, on the most sacred feast of Easter, cut himself off from the assembly of Catholics and threw himself into Satan's sink of filth, and who, having become a deserter from the apostolic Church, began to serve under the standard of the devil, has incurred anathema, alas; and since, piling up infamies and boasting of his apostasy, he has openly shown by deed that he holds no regard for the faith of the unity of the Church or for her authority, through contempt for her censures; and finally, so that it might be certain to all that he has sunk into the depths of every evil, he persists with the same recklessness, declaring that neither the most sacred canons, nor the most just precepts of the Apostolic See, nor the judgments solemnly given under canonical sanctions can apply to him in any way. Although he, the wicked mocker of God and despiser of the Church, is still not ashamed to boast of the Christian name, for these reasons, although on account of the notoriety of the deed every man has rightly judged him a heretic, nevertheless, so that the judgment may also come forth from his own mouth, we have, holding our earlier proceedings, in which he was declared to have incurred the penalties of anathema, of the crime of high treason, and of favouring heresy, to be inviolate and in force for these letters, so that it may be established whether he is a heretic or not, not only from the wickedness of his works but also from his own confession, begun a new process again against the said Sigismund. He is suspected notoriously of the most damnable heresy, which is the heresy of all heresies, and is sensibly tainted by it, as one who does not receive an article of holy faith, which every faithful man expresses in these words of the Apostles' Creed: "I believe in one holy catholic and apostolic Church." For the Roman Pontiff is the head of that Church, and the canons and censures of the Church are such that whoever is placed in the Church, and believes in the head, is bound to obey its canons and censures.

units.la: Dictus quidem Sigismundus non solum illis non obedit, sed prædicat insuper, quod minime obedire teneatur, atque in suam proteruam sententiam, tam subditos quam quoscunque potest, accedere compellit, & hæc vbique sunt notoria, nec hodieque cessat per se & suos hanc suam perfidiam diuulgare, quæ cum ad vehementissimam suspicionem plus quam satis sint aperta, idcirco ipsum Sigismundum notorie de hæresi suspectum per præsentes auctoritate Apostolica peremptorie citamus & requirimus, vt sexagesima die ab hac die datæ, quæ & affixionis huius, ad valuas ecclesiæ principis Apostolorum de Vrbe, & vt sequitur successive computanda, personaliter coram nobis compareat, & de fide catholica, præsertim in prætacto articulo vnitatis ecclesiæ, & quæ ad ipsum ex sanctorum doctorum doctrina sequuntur respondeat, & verbo & facto se purget de suspicione, sub confessi & conuicti criminis hæresis poena, alioquin nos contra ipsum, tanquam confessum & conuictum Dei omnipotentis nomine ad diffinitiuam sententiam, iustitia mediante procedimus.
units.tr: The said Sigismund not only does not obey these, but moreover proclaims that he is under no obligation to obey, and he compels both his subjects and whomever he can to adopt his shameless opinion. These things are notorious everywhere, and even today he does not cease to spread this perfidy of his by himself and his followers. Since these facts are more than enough to make him openly suspected of heresy with the strongest suspicion, we therefore, by these present letters and by apostolic authority, peremptorily cite and require the said Sigismund, notoriously suspected of heresy, that on the sixtieth day counting from the date of these letters, which is to be reckoned from the day of their posting at the doors of the church of the Prince of the Apostles in the City, and so on in succession, he appear in person before us, and answer concerning the Catholic faith, especially concerning the aforesaid article of the unity of the Church, and what follows from it according to the teaching of the holy doctors, and that he purge himself of the suspicion by word and deed, under the penalty for the crime of heresy confessed and proved. Otherwise we shall proceed against him, as one who has confessed and been convicted, in the name of Almighty God, to a final sentence, with justice as our guide.

units.la: Similiter etiam Georgium pro Tridentinense Episcopo se gerentem, ob notoriam eius adhæsionem, quam facto quotidie Sigismundo ostendit, cum quo & idem sentire videtur censuras contemnencontemnendo, & ideo de fide catholica vehementer suspectum, necnon Gregorium de Heimburg, Laurentium Glömenovv erroneos Doctores, Parcifalum de Annenberg, Iacobum Traff, Bathalarum de VVelschberg & Oualdum VVolckensteiner, aliosque omnes ipsius Sigismundi consiliarios & domesticos, atque etiam oppidanos & incolas oppidorum de Meran, Curiensum, Halis, Infpruck & Steizingen Brixinensis diœcesis, omnesque etiam ipsius Sigismundi subditos Curiensis Tridentinensis & Brixinensis diœcesis, ciuesque Brixinenses, & illius ecclesiæ subditos, qui interdictum ecclesiasticum, & ecclesiasticas vilipendunt censuras, ac VVolffgangum Nidlinger, Stephanum Steinhorn assertos canonicos Brixinenses; Georgium in Stams, Ingeminum in VViltina, Iohannem in Monte sancti Georgii Abbates; Casparem Præpositum Nouæcellensem, & Barbaram assertam Abbatissam in Sonnenburg, monasteriorum dictæ Brixinensis diœcesis, atque etiam vniuersos & singulos canonicos ipsius ecclesiæ Brixinensis, plebanos quoque siue vicarios ecclesiarum Parochialium ciuitatum & diœcesEon prædictarum, ac cunctos Presbyteros etiam Religiosos exemptos & non exemptos, qui temere prophanando, Apostolicum interdictum non obseruare, & sic per sedem Apostolicam & nos prohibitis diuinis intromittere non verentur, quorum omnium ac singulorum nomina & cognomina ac si de verbo ad verbum exprimerentur, præsentibus haberi volumus pro sufficienter expressis, quos omnes censurarum & Apostolicorum mandatorum contemptores, de hæresi vehementer non immerito suspectos reputamus, vt die & sub poena prædictis compareant personaliter coram nobis, de ipsa fide catholica, & præsertim articulo prædicto legitime responsuri, & se modo prædicto purgaturi.
units.tr: Likewise also Georgius, who calls himself Bishop of Trent, on account of his notorious adherence, which he shows daily by his deeds to Sigismund, with whom he also seems to think alike, despising the censures, and for that reason is vehemently suspected of the Catholic faith; likewise Gregorius de Heimburg, Laurentius Glömenovv, erroneous teachers; Parcifal of Annenberg, Jacob Traff, Bathalarum of Welschberg, and Oswald Wolkenstein, and all the other counsellors and household servants of this same Sigismund; likewise also the townsmen and inhabitants of the towns of Meran, Chur, Hall, Innsbruck and Steinach in the diocese of Brixen; all the subjects of this same Sigismund in the dioceses of Chur, Trent and Brixen, the citizens of Brixen and the subjects of that church, who make light of the ecclesiastical interdict and ecclesiastical censures; and Wolfgang Nidlinger and Stephen Steinhorn, self-styled canons of Brixen; Georg in Stams, Ingemin in Wilten, and John in Monte San Giorgio, abbots; Caspar, self-styled provost of Neustift, and Barbara, self-styled abbess of Sonnenburg, of the monasteries of the said diocese of Brixen; and also all and each of the canons of the church of Brixen, likewise the parish priests or vicars of the parish churches of the cities and dioceses aforesaid, and all the priests, both religious exempt and non-exempt, who, rashly profaning things, do not observe the Apostolic interdict and do not fear to intrude into divine offices forbidden by the Apostolic See and by us. The names and surnames of all and each of these we wish to be held in these present letters as sufficiently expressed, as if they were set down word for word. All of them, as despisers of the censures and Apostolic mandates, we judge to be vehemently and not undeservedly suspected of heresy, and they are cited to appear in person before us on the day and under the penalty mentioned above, to answer lawfully concerning the Catholic faith itself, and especially concerning the aforesaid article, and to purge themselves in the manner stated.

units.la: Cum certificatione modoque & forma præmissis citamus etiam per præsentes. Volumus autem & dicta auctoritate tenore præsentium decernimus, quod hæc nostræ literæ, sicut præmittitur, affixæ & executæ, prædictos omnes & singulos sic arceant & astringant, ac si eis omnibus & singulis in specie & in genere ac præsentialiter lectæ & insinuatæ fuissent, cum non sit verisimile apud eos remanere incognitum, quod tam patenter omnibus extitit publicatum. Datum Romæ apud sanctum Petrum Anno Incarnationis Dominicæ Millesimo quadringentesimo sexagesimo, 10. Calen. Februarii, Pontificatus nostri Anno tertio.
units.tr: We cite them also by these presents, with the warning, manner and form stated above. We wish, and by the said authority and the tenor of these presents we decree, that these our letters, once posted and executed as has been said, shall restrain and bind all and each of the aforesaid persons just as if they had been read and intimated to each of them, individually and collectively, in person; since it is not likely that a matter so openly made public to all could remain unknown to them. Given at Rome, at Saint Peter's, in the year of the Lord's Incarnation 1460, the 10th day before the Calends of February, in the third year of our pontificate.

units.la: DE CITATIONE PRAESCRIPTA APPELL- AT Sigismundus.
units.tr: On the Prescribed Citation of the Appellant, Sigismund

units.la: CVm in grauatorum atque læsorum, necnon lædi, & opprimi timentium subsidium, appellationis remedium sit adiuuentum: Quare nos Sigismundus Dei gratia Austriæ, Styriæ, Carinthiæ, Carniolæ Dux, Comesque Tyrolis, &c. Vniuersis iustitiæ cultoribus, fautoribus innocentiæ, cæterisque quos virtus humanitatis ad compassionem oppressorum adhortatur, notum esse cupimus, quod Romanus Pontifex nondum satiatus iniuriis suis, quibus nos ac subditos nostros affecit, audientiam nobis denegando, defensiones auferendo, legatum nostrum minis ac terrore carceris disterrendo, & sacra violando (siquidem legati iure publico inter sacra referuntur) ecclesiasticæ censuræ poenas in nos pro libito plus quam medicendo quam edicendo, noua nunc in nos nostrosque molimina parat.
units.tr: Since the remedy of appeal is a help for the burdened and wronged, and for those who fear being harmed and oppressed, we, Sigismund, by the grace of God Duke of Austria, Styria, Carinthia and Carniola, and Count of Tyrol, etc., wish it to be known to all lovers of justice, friends of innocence, and all others whom the virtue of humanity moves to compassion for the oppressed: the Roman Pontiff, not yet satisfied with the injuries he has done to us and our subjects, by denying us a hearing, taking away our defences, terrifying our envoy with threats and the terror of prison, and violating sacred things (for envoys are reckoned among sacred things by public law), is now preparing new schemes against us and ours, imposing at his pleasure the penalties of ecclesiastical censure upon us, more to harm than to heal, and more by proclamation than by correction.

units.la: Quippe relatum est nobis, qualiter Romanus Pontifex, nos omnesque subditos nostros fingat, de hæresi sibi suspectos, quod nemo vnquam de nobis neque de subditis nostris principatus nostri Tyrolis suspicatus est. Suspitio autem non fingi, sed indiciis non quidem æmulorum aut suspectorum, sed fide dignorum & honestorum virorum apparere debet, antequâ prælatus odorem bonæ famæ commaculet, aut sinceritatem fidei Christianæ & subditorum simplicitatem perturbet. Sed dicit Papa, nos esse contemptores censurarum atque de hæresi suspectos. Nos vero iam dudum respondimus, nulla censura nos ligaros, quos Papa contemnere audire. Auditus est Adam prævaricator, Cain fratricida, Sodomitæ visitati sunt post clamorem qui ab eis in cœlum ascenderat, dicente Domino; descendam & videbo an clamorem qui ad me peruenit opere compleuerunt. Nobis audientia negata & defensio ablata est: hanc negamus esse censuram, quam Papa pro libito & contra legem naturæ aduersum nos effluit. Hanc primum iustificet, antequam nos arguat de contemptu censurarum. Ipse vero Pontifex, nos omnesque subditos nostros nuper apud Robertum velut in albo prætoris edicto affixo ad vrbem Romanam dicitur euocasse, quatenus super articulis fidei personaliter respondeamus. Operfunctoriam citationem absque discretione sexus, ætatis, valetudinis, infantiæ, pubertatis, sanæ mentis, vel amentiæ! O confusam plusquam centum millium personarum euocationem, & vnde ememus panes vt manducent? Quis baiulabit infantulos & lactantes? quis gestabit valetudinarios? quis cæcos ducet? quis prægnantibus & parturientibus obstetricabit? at omnes illos sine delectu personaliter euocauit. Oportet autem superioris præcepta possibilia, iusta & honesta, factuque facilia esse. Quis vero domum seruabit? quis arces tutabitur? quis patriam defendet? si nos cum subditis nostris emigrabimus. Hoc ergo Papale mandatum, quid aliud in se habet, nisi quod præcipere videtur, quatenus relictis sedibus nostris, cum coniugibus & liberis nostris exulemus? quod nulla vnquam barbara potestas postulauit, nullus tam crudelis post victoriam à vitiis expetiuit, hoc ipse pater spiritualis à nobis requirit, qui virtutibus nostris inuidet, quod in salvatore nostro Iesu gloriamur, dum de nobis loquens dicit: De Christiano adhuc non erubescit nomine gloriari, propter quod vnusquisque ipsum rectissime hereticum iudicabit. Et infra subdit: suis literæ prioribus lesa
units.tr: For it has been reported to us that the Roman Pontiff pretends that we and all our subjects are suspected of heresy, though no one has ever suspected us or the subjects of our principality of Tyrol. Yet suspicion must not be invented but must appear from evidence given not by rivals or the suspect themselves but by trustworthy and honourable men, before a prelate stains the good name of anyone or disturbs the sincerity of the Christian faith and the simplicity of his subjects. But the Pope says that we are despisers of censures and suspected of heresy. We have already answered that we are bound by no censure that the Pope may think fit to hear us despise. Adam the transgressor was heard; Cain the murderer was heard; the Sodomites were visited after the cry that had risen to heaven from them, the Lord saying: I will go down and see whether they have completed the outcry that has come up to me. We have been denied a hearing and our defence has been taken away. We deny that this is a censure, and what the Pope pours out against us at his pleasure and against the law of nature. Let him first justify this before he accuses us of contempt of censures. Moreover, the Pontiff himself is said to have summoned us, all of us and our subjects, to the city of Rome, having posted the citation at Robert's, as on a praetor's edict fixed to a notice board, so that we should answer in person on the articles of faith. What a summons to the dead! Without regard to sex, age, health, infancy, youth, sound mind or madness! O confused summons of more than a hundred thousand persons! And where shall we buy bread for them to eat? Who will carry the infants and the nursing mothers? Who will carry the sick? Who will lead the blind? Who will assist the pregnant and those in labour? Yet he has summoned all of them without distinction, in person. But the precepts of a superior must be possible, just, honest and easy to perform. Who, then, will keep the house? Who will guard the fortresses? Who will defend the country, if we and our subjects emigrate? What else, then, does this papal mandate contain, than what it seems to command: that we should leave our homes and go into exile with our wives and children? What no barbarous power has ever demanded, what no cruel conqueror has ever sought from the vanquished, this spiritual father demands from us, who begrudges our virtues, because we glory in our Saviour Jesus, while he speaks of us and says: He is not yet ashamed to glory in the name of Christian, on account of which everyone will rightly judge him a heretic. And further down he adds: that he has incurred the penalties of treason and of favouring heresy, by his earlier letters.

units.la: { } Fine of the printed page; catchword "lesa" set at the right below the last line. læsæ maiestatis & fautoria hæresis pœnas incurrisse declaratum esse. Hæc sunt ex quibus hæresis suspicionem Papa de nobis sibi fingit. Quorum alterum (semet vtique iustificat, eo quod quisque Christianus, in Christo rite gloriatur, cuius nomen gestat, & nomen eius in se sanctificari deprecatur. Alterum vero à suspecto Pontifice contra indefensum emanauit.
units.tr: { } End of the printed page; the catchword "lesa" is set at the right below the last line. that he has incurred the penalties of treason and of favouring heresy, has been declared. These are the grounds on which the Pope fabricates for himself a suspicion of heresy against us. The first of them justifies itself, since every Christian rightly glories in Christ, whose name he bears, and prays that his name be sanctified in him. The second, however, has issued from a suspect Pontiff against a man who was not heard in his defence.

units.la: Non possumus autem hoc loco praeterire, quin illorum ineptiam perstringamus. Inquit Papa, se Mantuæ fataisse, ne quis ad futurum concilium appellet, quod nusquam est, contrafacientes anathematisarit læsæ maiestatis hæresisque crimine multarit, ac reos esse decreuerit, Sigismundus ex Austriæ Ducibus, duobus postea mensibus elapsis, quod est tempus nouis constitutionibus præfinitum, contrauenit, ergo est læsæ maiestatis hæresisque reus. Nos autem edocti sumus, quod magna Synodus Constantiensis decreuit, vniuersale concilium à Christo immediate potestatem habere super Papam, in his quæ fidei, reformationis & pacis esse dignoscuntur, quæ etiam sacra Basiliensis Synodus innouauit, & Eugenius ac Nicolaus Romani Pontifices recognouerunt. Vnde ergo Papa Pius auctoritatem vsurpauit, vt superiori suo, scilicet vniuersali Concilio, manum clauderet, cui & ipse tenetur obedire? nec quisquam miretur, si ad concilium, quod nondum est congregatum, appellatur, quoniam auctoritas ecclesiæ, quæ immortalis est, firma persistit, & quæ nunc existit in ecclesia toto orbe dispersa, tunc erit in illa ipsa legitime congregata. Quod vero nescitur, quando congregabitur, hoc ipsum non est impedimento, quo minus illuc appelletur. Hoc enim scitur, quod ex decretis magnæ Synodi Constantiensis de decennio in decennium perpetuis temporibus concilia habent celebrari, & nunc tempus interpellat obligationis, dies cessit, sed cuius culpa impeditur, vel differtur executio, illi imputetur in pœnam, nam qui vetat iudicium fieri, is vtique de sua iustitia diffidere convincitur.
units.tr: We cannot pass over here without exposing their silliness. The Pope says that he has decreed at Mantua, lest anyone appeal to the future council, that those acting contrary to this be cursed and punished with the crime of treason and heresy, and be declared guilty.
