This third mode of appeal I offer, and I submit myself to such a judgment. In sum, I submit to papal cognition on this condition: that the cause of suspicion be removed from the midst. And this fourth order removes every mark of evasion which Cusan impudence could cast upon me, under whose guidance all these things are directed. If the Pope scorns all of these, what remains but to appeal to the universal Church, just as we often find appeals made from the Senate to the Roman people? Let the Pope not object to me that the Church is not assembled, since this is hindered and disturbed by his own factions. For me there is no delay, no fault anywhere, since it stands not through me but through him that it does not happen. For if someone summoned to court forcibly escapes, he removes contumacy from the summoned party, but transfers all fault and crime onto himself. The Pope has put fear upon me; he has himself declared justice against himself. He who by his insults has made himself suspect to me, who has declined to bind himself to the judgment of a wise man, refuses to test the suspicion, and does not deign to delegate a judge free of suspicion, and who denies that a universal council should be convened: if he attempts anything against me, I appeal against him, step by step and alternately, as I have set out; and I demand testimony of that fact, and I protest before neighbours of a just fear. If he desists, I will pursue, if need be, and if opportunity is granted, as the reason of public law requires, the right of adding being preserved, along with all remedies introduced by custom and law.

units.la: Ista appellatio est interposita per Doctorem Gregorium Heimburg, de mense Ianuarii anno M.CCCCLXI.
units.tr: This appeal was lodged by Doctor Gregor Heimburg, in the month of January, in the year 1461.

units.la: REPLICA THEODORI LÆLII EPISCOPI FELTRENSIS, PRO Pio Papa II. & sede Romana, ad su- perius Scriptum Gregorii Heimburg.
units.tr: REPLICA OF THEODORICUS LAELIUS, BISHOP OF FELTRE, ON BEHALF OF POPE PIUS II AND THE ROMAN SEE, IN REPLY TO THE WRITING OF GREGORY HEIMBURG ABOVE.

units.la: BLATRANTEM te, Gregori, aduersus Christum Domini ore sacrilego, & impiis vocibus obstrepentem, Pius Pontifex Maximus iure contempsit: non quod garrulitati tuæ atque blasphemiæ disertissimus virorum respondere non posset, sed quia æterni Pastoris, cuius vices gerit, qui cum malediceretur non maledicebat, cum pateretur, non comminabatur, imitandum humilitatis exemplum putauit. Meminerat quippe & Christum Dominum à Pharisæis, quorum tu perfidiam imitaris, crebris conuiciis lacessitum, & nunc voracem, nunc vini potatorem, nunc Samariten & Dæmoniacum appellatum: & patientiæ ipsius documenta suscipiens, illud dominicum arcano volebat in pectore; Non est seruus maior Domino suo, nec discipulus eo qui misit illum. Quoniam si patremfamilias Beelzebub vocauerunt, quanto magis domesticos eius. Sic ille non quod tu merebaris, sed quid se deceret, attendit. Verum & plurimi & magno atque excellenti ingenio viri tuis blasphemiis respondere potuissent, si vel ad illos maledicta illa sacrilega peruenissent, vel ineptissimum, atque perditissimum hominem coinquinationis & maculæ voluptatibus fluentem, & tanquam bestiam inter luxum semper epulasque sudantem, dignum responso putauissent: quorum pleriq; insaniam incidentem, atq; iuxta Sapientis eloquium in ore stulti esse baculum contumeliæ agnoscentes, illud ex Sapiente pferebunt: Noli respondere stulto secundum stultitiam suam, ne forte similis fias ei.
units.tr: Gregory, it was right that the Supreme Pontiff Pius should despise you for barking against Christ the Lord with a sacrilegious mouth and drowning him out with impious voices. Not that the most eloquent of men could not answer your chatter and blasphemy, but because he thought it fitting to imitate the example of humility set by the eternal Shepherd, whose place he holds: when he was reviled, he did not revile back; when he suffered, he did not threaten. He remembered that Christ the Lord, whose perfidy you imitate, was assailed by the Pharisees with frequent insults, called now a glutton, now a wine-drinker, now a Samaritan and a demoniac; and taking to heart the lessons of that patience, he kept in his heart the saying of the Lord: "A servant is not greater than his master, nor an apostle greater than the one who sent him. If they have called the head of the household Beelzebub, how much more will they call his household." So he considered not what you deserved, but what was becoming to himself. Indeed, many men of great and outstanding talent could have answered your blasphemies, had those sacrilegious slanders reached them, or had they thought that a man so foolish and utterly lost, given over to the pleasures of defilement and stain, sweating like a beast amid constant luxury and feasting, was worth a reply. Many of them, recognising that his madness is an attack, and that according to the word of the Wise Man a rod of insult is in the mouth of a fool, would quote that same Wise Man: "Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you too become like him."

units.la: Ineptum sane existimabant congredi recum, cum nec docere indocibilem, nec reducere pertinacem, nec cohibere furentem posse considerent. Ac talia cogitantes errantem perfidum hactenus silentio contempsere. Sed cum patientia illorum abutens contra lenitatem odio & aduersus Pontificis mansuetudinem furore & insania bacchari coepisses, & blasphemiarum tuarum exempla per Italiam Germaniamque dispergere, me vnum ex pusillis Curiæ & Apostolicæ sedis ministris domus DEI zelus accendit, vt diutius me continere non possem, quin volantia iam pene toto orbe iacula falsitatis, clypeo veritatis exciperem. Verebar enim, ne si nullus tuis calumniis responderet, iam patientia diffidentiæ inciperet imputari, vt vel saltem iniustæ damnationis tuæ Apostolica sedes videretur crimen agnoscere. Licet enim apud ipsius sedis Pontificem iusti iudicii conscientia sola sufficeret: non incongruum tamen visum est, & reliquis, si qui forte quasi de iniusto anathemate tuo viderentur offensi, cogrue satisfacere. Sic quodam Gelasius ac Nicolaus sanctissimi dissertissimique Pontifices, alter de Achatii, alter de Phocii Pseudoepiscoporum damnatione, Anastasio Michaelique Principibus & Orientalibus populis tomos scribentes satisfecerunt. In quo genere illud aureum Pii Pontificis flumen eloquentiæ omnes facile superasset, nisi illum vel indignitas tua, vel criminis euidentia, vel forsan remledicendi apud quosdam suspicio retraxissent. Mouit nos pterea & Catholicæ fidei ratio, cōtra quæ multa in ipsis tuis blasphemiis hæretice impieq; plata legisse, & scandalo & periculo verebar amplius esse silentium, ac proinde populare quasi apud Christianos tuendæ fidei ōmnium arbitrabar. Nam etsi cætera crimina silentio præteriri queant, hoc tamen in fide si fiat, & scandalum & periculum generat. Licet apud te cassò labore desudem, apud cæteros tamen, quos tuis blasphemiis forsan concitasti, atque impia & maledicta seminando tui erroris comites effecisti, spe-ramus Deo propitio aliquid profuturos. Nam qui per errorem moti sunt tuo mendacio fallente, facilius veritatem admittent ratione cogente. Respondebimus ergo licet incompositis verbis, veniam à legentibus rudioris styli facile præsumentes: quoniam contra impias blasphemias iustitiæ ac fidei patrocinium suscepturi non nitori sermonis, sed veritati studemus. Ante tamen quàm tuis maledictis respondeam, abs te postulare libet, Doctorum eximiè & Iurisconsultorum disertissime, qui tibi utriusque iuris scientiam vendicas, & (ut tuis verbis utar) qui te quicquid ratio & industria præcipuum habet, & quidquid tradunt utriusque iuris instituta, percepisse gloriaris; hoc ne in legibus aut Canonibus, aut in moralibus disciplinis didicisti, ut contra Pontificem summum, Ecclesiæ caput & Principem, & miseræ animæ tuæ Episcopum atque Pastorem, vel quomodolibet læsus incheres? Hominum perditissime, quis unquam hæreticorum, qui à Romana damnati sunt sede, in illius antistitem talia maledicta congessit? Lege Nestorium, Macedonium, Eutychen, Cœlestinum atque Pelagium, Macarium atque Dioscorum, & cæteras hæreticorum pestes: quis unquam tam turpiter ora laxavit? Qui licet damnationem suam graviter tulerint, tamen à talibus blasphemiis temperarunt. Unus inventus est Dioscorus, qui pro eo solo, quod Anathema dicere in sanctum & venerabilem Leonem ausus est, in Chalcedonensi Synodo sine vlla fuit restitutione damnatus. Cuius præsumtionem ob hoc potissimum sancti Patres detestati sunt, quia ponens os in cœlum, & lingua eius transeunte super terram, inferior maiorem iniuriis lacessere ausus est. Et hoc noscens Concilii fuisse statutum, adhuc Conciliorum audes mentionem facere, nec reererris illorum pro minori culpa censuram. Miserrimè hominum, non te terruit Euangelica illa tuba, quod qui scandalizaverit unum expusillu illa minimis, qui in me credunt, expedit ei, ut suspendatur mola asinaria in collo eius, & demergatur in profundum. Quod si scandalizanti unumquemque pusillum in Christum credentem talem vindictam comminatur; qua ultione plectendus eris, qui totum corpus scandalizas Ecclesiæ, qui Ecclesiarum omnium patrem & pastorem, hæreticum, garrulum, insanum, & quicquid turpitudinis tuæ immunditiæque fœtor ingerit, in illum causaris? Nec mirum quidem, quoniam non potest nisi spurce loqui, qui consueuit spurca committere. Ex abundantia enim cordis os loquitur, & malus homo de malo cordis thesauro non potest nisi mala proferre. An verò quanti sacrilegii sit Principi populi maledicere, ex lege discere non potuisti? quæ maledictio æterna morte condemnat. Cuius verba non modo in Romani, sed omnium Episcoporum inunctione solemni, inter ipsa sacra terribiliter intonantur, pronunciante Episcopo & conformantibus cæteris: Qui maledixerit tibi, sit ille maledictus, & qui benedixit, ipse benedictionibus repleatur. Quod si de probis non de reprobis Principibus ac Sacerdotibus dictum esse contendis, audias Paulum Apostolum, qui cum iussu Principis Sacerdotum iniustè cæsus illi diuinam vltionem precaretur, atque astantes dicerent, summum Sacerdotem Dei maledicis? mox territus lege diuina se purgans, ait: Nescieban, fratres, quia Princeps esset Sacerdotum. Scriptum est enim, Principem populi tui non maledices. An forte iustè homini iniquo, sacrilego, & contra legem agenti se maledixisse contendit, & non potius errari veniam petiit, & nefas Principi Sacerdotum maledicere legis auctoritate professus est? Sed quid ego Paulum memoro? Ipse Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS, summus Sacerdos, Rex & Iudex, usque ad passionis suæ diem non solum bonis & piis, sed etiam indignis & reprobis detulit Sacerdotibus: quamuis illi nec timorem DEI, nec agnitionem CHRISTI seruassent. Vt enim alia omittamus, ipse subditus passioni cum alapam accepisset, & ei diceretur, sic respondes Pontifici? nihil contumeliose in personam locutus est, quem sciebat esse sacrilegum, sed magis innocentiam suam tutatus est, dicens: Si male locutus sum, testimonium perhibe de malo: si autem bene, cur me cedis? Quod idem beato Cypriano teste & Canone attestante factum est, ut humilitatis & patientiæ ipsius haberemus exemplum. Docuit enim Sacerdotes veros plenius honorandos, dum ipse circa falsos talis extiterit. At verò Gregorius contra legem se asserens iniustè comunione deiectum, non solum in verba contumeliæ iniuriæque prorupit, sed famosum libellum totam scandalizantem Ecclesiam blasphemans euomuit: nec illi satis est deliquisse, nisi de malitia gloriabundus exemplaria congreget, & publicè legenda dispergat. Leges ciuiles, quarum se Professorem vaniloquus temerator gloriatur, eum qui libellum famosum in iniuriam alicuius ediderit, vel ab alio editum non caluerit, capitali sententia damnant. Et tamen audet leges appellare, qui tàm sacrilege committit in legem. Prævaricator legis legem attende, quoniam non in vnumquemque priuatum, sed Dei vicarium atque legatum, gregis dominici directorem, Ecclesiarum omnium Patrem, sed & miseræ animæ tuæ & cunctorum fidelium Episcopum atque Pastorem parricidali furore baccharis, lingua interficis, maledictis discerpis, blasphemiis laceras, & quantum ad regnum tuum attinet, tanquam truculentus homicida transfodis ac iugulas. Homicidam reclamavi: cùm ex Canone tria homicidiorum genera, & pœnam eorum parilem cognoscis: inter quæ detractores linguis proximos confodientes constat esse deterrima, Impudentissime hominum, non te diuina terruerunt exempla, cùm legas Mariam sororem Aaron, quæ prima post transitum maris rubri in tympano hymnum can-tare tare meruerit, eo quod murmurasset in Moysen, lepra fuisse percussam. Ecce tu non solum murmurasti, sed publicè blasphemasti, cerre nō Moysen (qui & ipse inter Sacerdotes inscribitur, Psalmista testante atque dicente: Moyses & Aaron in Sacerdotibus eius) sed Moysē non merito, sed auctoritate maiorem. Oziam audisti pro eo, quod Sacerdotes contemnens sacrorum praesumtor extiterit, simili plaga percussum esse. Bethleemiticos pueros ob derisionem Prophetæ morte damnatos. Ecce autem plusquam Moyses aut aliquis Prophetarum, quem tu impie blasphemas, nisi forte mentitus sit Bernhardus Doctor illustris, qui Eugenium Papam ad considerationem suæ auctoritatis adducens, atque ostendens, qualem in Dei Ecclesia Romanus Pontifex personam gerat: Attende, inquit, quis sis, & quam videlicet pro tempore in Ecclesia Dei personam geras. Sacerdos magnus es, summus Pontifex, Princeps Episcoporum, tu heres Apostolorum, tu primatus Abel, gubernatione Noah, patriarchatu Abraham, ordine Melchisedech, dignitate Aaron, auctoritate Moyses, iudicatu Samuel, potestate Petrus, unctione Christus. Tu es cui claves traditæ, cui oves creditæ sunt. Hunc ergo perfidissime blasphemare non veritus es: saltem illud considerasses arcanum, quod in Epistola Clementis habetur, quæ aliàs Petri dicitur in ordinatione Clementis, cuius plurima in Decretis & Conciliorum gestis propter auctoritatem habentur excerpta: ubi clauiger regni cœlestis Clementem sibi ordinans successorem, postquam illius Ecclesiastici Principatus ministerium multis verbis extulerat, cunctos fideles quanta reverentia illum observare, quo timore reverei, quo affectu complecti debeerent, admonuit. Vbi inter reliqua: Vos, inquit, fratres & conservi mei, huic, qui præsidet vobis, in omnibus obedire oportet, atque summo studio uniti, ut omni erga eum vinculo amoris innexi, plenissime erga eum inhæreatis affectu. Rursus si inimicus fuerit Clemens iste alicui, pro actibus suis, nolite vos expectare, ut ipse vobis dicat: Illi nolite amici esse, sed prudenter observare debetis, & voluntati eius absque commonitione obsecundare. Et paulò post in tui sindes maledictionem terribilem comminatur, quæ tuæ iniquitatis merito iam interiora tua intrauit, ut subter te scateat: Scimus, inquit, quod si quis hunc contristauerit, Christum, qui ei cathedram, non recipit: & eum qui Christum non suscepit, non suscipietur in regnum cœlorum. Et verum terribilius insonat: Quicunque contristauerit Doctorem veritatis, peccat in Christum, & patrem omnium exacerbat Deum, propter quod & vindicabitur. Hæc tu inde excerpta in Canonibus legere debuisses.
units.tr: It seemed to them foolish indeed to engage a madman, since they considered that one cannot teach the unteachable, bring back the obstinate, or restrain the raging. Thinking thus, they had until now despised the wandering and treacherous man with silence. But when you took advantage of their patience, began to rage against their gentleness with hatred and against the Pontiff's mildness with fury and madness, and to scatter examples of your blasphemies through Italy and Germany, the zeal of God's house kindled me, one of the lesser ministers of the Curia and the Apostolic See, so that I could no longer hold back from catching, with the shield of truth, the darts of falsehood now flying almost through the whole world. For I feared that if no one answered your calumnies, the Apostolic See would soon be charged with diffidence in its patience, so that it might seem to acknowledge the crime of your unjust condemnation, at least by silence. For although the consciousness of a just judgment would suffice for the Pontiff of that See himself, it still seemed not unfitting to make suitable satisfaction also to the rest, should any perhaps be offended as if by your unjust anathema. Thus the most holy and eloquent Pontiffs Gelasius and Nicholas, the one concerning the condemnation of the pseudo-bishop Acacius, the other concerning that of the pseudo-bishop Photius, satisfied the emperors Anastasius and Michael and the Eastern peoples by writing tomes. In this kind of writing that golden river of eloquence of Pius the Pontiff would easily have surpassed everyone, had not your unworthiness, the evidence of your crime, or perhaps the suspicion of your re-cursing among some held him back. Moreover, the cause of the Catholic faith moved us, since I had read in your blasphemies many things impiously and heretically set forth against it; and I feared that silence would now be a greater scandal and danger, and therefore I judged that the defence of the faith was a common matter for all Christians. For although other crimes may be passed over in silence, if this happens in matters of faith it breeds both scandal and danger. Although I labour in vain with you, yet among the others whom you perhaps stirred up with your blasphemies, and whom by sowing impious and abusive words you made companions of your error, we hope, with God's favour, to accomplish something. For those who have been moved into error by your deceiving lie will more readily admit the truth when reason compels them. We shall therefore reply, though in unpolished words, easily presuming pardon from readers of a rougher style; for in undertaking the defence of justice and faith against impious blasphemies we aim at the truth, not at polish of speech. Before I answer your abuse, however, I wish to ask of you, most distinguished of Doctors and most skilled of Jurists, who claim for yourself the knowledge of both laws and who boast (to use your own words) that you have grasped whatever reason and diligence hold most excellent, and whatever the institutes of both laws hand down: did you learn from the laws, the Canons, or the moral disciplines that you may rage in any way against the supreme Pontiff, the head and Prince of the Church, and the bishop and pastor of your wretched soul? Most abandoned of men, who of the heretics condemned by the Roman See ever heaped such abuse upon its prelate? Read Nestorius, Macedonius, Eutyches, Celestius and Pelagius, Macarius and Dioscorus, and the other plagues of heretics: who ever opened his mouth so shamefully? Although they bore their condemnation grievously, they nevertheless refrained from such blasphemies. Only one is found, Dioscorus, who, for the sole reason that he dared to pronounce an anathema against the holy and venerable Leo, was condemned at the Council of Chalcedon without any hope of restoration. The holy Fathers detested his presumption chiefly for this reason: that, setting his mouth against heaven, and his tongue passing over the earth, an inferior dared to assail a greater with insults. And knowing that the Council had decreed this, you still dare to mention the Councils, and you do not fear their censure for a lesser fault. Wretched of men, did not that Gospel trumpet terrify you: whoever shall offend one of these little ones who believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck and he were drowned in the depth of the sea. If the one who offends each little one who believes in Christ is threatened with such vengeance, by what punishment will you be struck, who offend the whole body of the Church, who accuse of heresy, garrulity, madness, and whatever filth the stench of your baseness and uncleanness pours forth, the father and pastor of all the Churches? Nor is it surprising, since he who has been accustomed to do filthy things cannot speak otherwise than filthily. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart can bring forth nothing but evil. But did you not learn from the law how great a sacrilege it is to curse the Prince of the people? That curse condemns to eternal death. Its words are thundered terribly not only at the solemn anointing of the Roman but of all bishops, amid the sacred rites themselves, the bishop pronouncing and the others responding: Let him who curses you be cursed, and let him who blesses you be filled with blessings. But if you contend that this was said of good princes and priests, not of wicked ones, hear the Apostle Paul, who, when he was unjustly struck at the command of the High Priest and called down divine vengeance upon him, and those standing by said, Do you revile God's High Priest? at once, terrified and purging himself by the divine law, said: I did not know, brethren, that he was the High Priest. For it is written, You shall not speak evil of the ruler of your people. Or does he perhaps claim that he cursed a wicked, sacrilegious man who was acting against the law, and did he not rather ask pardon for his error, and confess by the authority of the law that it is wrong to curse the High Priest? But why do I mention Paul? Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, the supreme Priest, King and Judge, up to the day of his passion bore with the priests not only the good and pious but also the unworthy and reprobate, although they had kept neither the fear of God nor the knowledge of Christ. For to pass over other things: when he, subjected to the passion, had received a blow and was asked, Do you answer the High Priest so? he spoke nothing insulting against the person whom he knew to be sacrilegious, but rather defended his innocence, saying: If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil; but if well, why do you strike me? The same was done, as the blessed Cyprian bears witness and the Canon attests, so that we might have the example of his humility and patience. For he taught that true priests are to be honoured more fully, while he himself behaved thus towards false ones. But Gregory, asserting that he was unjustly cast out of communion against the law, not only broke out into words of insult and injury, but vomited forth a defamatory libel blaspheming the whole scandalized Church; nor is it enough for him to have sinned, unless he also gathers copies out of malice, boasting of it, and scatters them to be read publicly. The civil laws, whose professor this babbling violator boasts himself to be, condemn with capital sentence the one who publishes a defamatory libel to the injury of anyone, or who does not take care to suppress one published by another. And yet he dares to appeal to the laws who sins so sacrilegiously against the law. Prevaricator of the law, attend to the law: for you rage not against some private person, but against the vicar and legate of God, the director of the Lord's flock, the Father of all the Churches, and the bishop and pastor of your wretched soul and of all the faithful; with parricidal fury you rage, you slay with your tongue, you tear apart with abuse, you lacerate with blasphemies, and, as far as your kingdom reaches, like a savage murderer you stab and cut the throat. I cry out, "Murderer!" since from the Canon you know the three kinds of homicide and their like punishment; among these it is established that slanderers who stab their neighbours with the tongue are the most wicked. Most shameless of men, did not divine examples terrify you, since you read that Miriam, sister of Aaron, who first after the crossing of the Red Sea deserved to sing a hymn with the timbrel, was struck with leprosy because she had murmured against Moses? Behold, you not only murmured, but publicly blasphemed, not Moses only (who is also inscribed among the priests, the Psalmist bearing witness and saying: Moses and Aaron among his priests), but Moses who is greater not by merit but by authority. You heard that Uzziah, because he despised the priests and presumed upon the sacred things, was struck with a similar plague. The boys of Bethlehem were condemned to death for mocking the Prophet. But behold, one greater than Moses or any of the Prophets, whom you impiously blaspheme, unless perhaps the illustrious Doctor Bernard lied, who, leading Pope Eugenius to consider his authority and showing what sort of person the Roman Pontiff bears in God's Church: Consider, he says, who you are, and what person you bear for the time in God's Church. You are the great priest, the supreme Pontiff, the Prince of bishops, you are the heir of the Apostles, you the primacy of Abel, the governance of Noah, the patriarchate of Abraham, the order of Melchizedek, the dignity of Aaron, the authority of Moses, the judgment of Samuel, the power of Peter, the anointing of Christ. You are the one to whom the keys have been given, to whom the sheep have been entrusted. This one, then, most treacherous man, you were not ashamed to blaspheme: at least you should have considered that secret which is found in the Epistle of Clement, which is otherwise said to be Peter's, in the ordination of Clement, many passages from which are excerpted in the Decretals and in the acts of Councils on account of its authority. There the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, ordaining Clement as his successor, after he had extolled in many words the ministry of that ecclesiastical principate, admonished all the faithful with what reverence they ought to observe him, with what fear they ought to revere him, with what affection they ought to embrace him. Among other things: You, brethren and my fellow servants, must obey in all things him who presides over you, and, united with the greatest zeal, bound to him by every tie of love, you must cling to him with most full affection. Again: if this Clement should be an enemy to anyone on account of his acts, do not wait for him to tell you, "Do not be friends with him," but you ought to observe prudently and obey his will without need of admonition. And a little after he threatens with terrible curse the one who grieves him, which, by the merit of your iniquity, has already entered your inner parts so that it may seethe beneath you: We know, he says, that whoever grieves him rejects Christ, who gave him the chair; and he who has not received Christ shall not be received into the kingdom of heaven. And more terribly still it sounds: Whoever grieves the teacher of truth sins against Christ and provokes God, the Father of all, to anger, wherefore he shall also be avenged. These things you ought to have read, excerpted from the Canons.

units.la: Verùm non vno tantùm blasphemiæ sacrilegio contentus, ne aliquid intentatum relinqueres, etiā in alterum Monarcham maledicta depromis, Cæsarem vaecordiæ ignauiaeq; condemnas, vt vtramq; potestatem, quibus principaliter hic mundus regitur, blasphemares, Senatum quoq; Ecclesiæ, videlicet Cardinalium cœtum, tanquam consilii expertem & temerarium, tu totius orbis censor notas & arguis: in vnum, contra quem commissum nefarium sacrilegium defendis, plus cæteris debacchans, & virum sanctissimum, vita & religione, doctrina & integritate incomparabilem, Cardinalem S. Petri ad vincula, infamia conaris aspergere. Et cùm nihil comperias, quo innocentiam vitæ etiam inimicis percognitam obfuscare queas, tu omnium factiosissimus & procacissimus ipsum modo factionis, modo procacitatis accusas. O linguam maledicam & radicitus præcidendam? Nonne licet cum Propheta clamare: Disperdat Dominus labia dolosa, & linguam magniloquam. Nempe ex illis es, qui dixerunt, Linguam nostram magnificabimus, labia nostra à nobis sunt. Quibus noster Dominus vere inquit: Tu ex illis es inflatus sensu carnis, nullum in terris agnoscens caput, qui ordinatas à Deo potestates blasphemare te putas impune.
units.tr: But not content with the one sacrilege of blasphemy, and lest you leave anything untried, you also pour out curses against the other Monarch. You condemn the Emperor as mad and cowardly, so that you blaspheme both powers by which this world is chiefly ruled. You, the censor of the whole world, also mark and accuse the senate of the Church, that is, the college of Cardinals, as lacking counsel and rash. Raging more than all the rest against the one whom you defend against the sacrilege committed, you try to stain with infamy that most holy man, incomparable in life and piety, learning and integrity, the Cardinal of St Peter ad Vincula. And since you discover nothing with which you could obscure the innocence of his life, which is known even to his enemies, you, the most factious and insolent of all men, accuse him now of faction, now of insolence. O slanderous tongue, to be cut out by the roots! Is it not permitted to cry out with the Prophet: May the Lord destroy deceitful lips and the boastful tongue. Indeed you are one of those who said: With our tongue we will prevail; our lips are our own. To such as these our Lord truly says: you are one of those puffed up with the mind of the flesh, acknowledging no head on earth, who think you can blaspheme the powers ordained by God with impunity.

units.la: Cæterum ne putes, me execrationibus blasphemiarum tuarum detrectare pugnam, & manum non audere conferre, vel tuos inextricabiles nodos non posse dissoluere, ecce iam ad singula festinat oratio. Postquam noster Demosthenes altius quædam de vi consilii experte ac moderata exorsus, caua verba in modum vesicarum tumentia buccis ebuccinauit inflatis, primum accusationis caput intendit, questus se contra diuinam & humanam legem non vocatum damnatum. Quod indignum facinus esse proclamans exempla producit primi parentis & Cain, quorum alter propter prævaricationem, alter propter homicidium non nisi vocati damni fuere. Subdens ipsum Deum, cui aperta sunt omnia, ut nos à præcipitante sententiæ temeritate compesceret, Sodomos prius perdere noluisse, quàm eorum scelera manifeste cognoscerat. Sicque trifaria exemplorum compage, quasi phalange quadam aciem struit. Verùm nos inualidam struem vno possemus arietis ictu concutere, & paria referendo exemplorum syluam obiicere. Sed ut ex multis pauca proferamus, Moysen legimus comperto populi scelere, quod palam contra Deum commissum erat, nulla accusatione vel cognitione præuia vindicasse, & immane idololatriæ crimen plurima populi strage expiasse. Phinees accepimus vltionem non præmissa sententia, cùm agentes contra legem & edictum ante prolatum propria manu transfoderet. Nouimus, Heliam Sacerdotes Balaam priùs ad supplicium quàm ad iudicium produxisse. Eundem scimus, Ochoziæ Regis nuntios igne de cœlo impetrato cremasse. Par zelus in scripturis Eleazari commendatur. Et vt ad recentiora veniamus, constat, Petrum Apostolorum principem mox prolato mendacio Ananiam & Saphiram morte mulctasse. Paulum verò Coapostolum eius Cliniam magum resistentem Spiritui sancto subita cœcitate damnasse. Et vt efficacius aliquid proferamus, Apostolus absens corpore, spiritu præsens, Corinthium excommunicauit, tradens in interitum carnis, vt saluus fieret spiritus, nullus adhibitus stepitus fori, nullus iudiciarius ordo, nulla tela iudicii. Nunquid Prophetæ Domini, nunquid Apostoli perperam aliquid egerunt?
units.tr: Moreover, lest you think I shrink from the battle of your blasphemous curses, and do not dare to join hand to hand, or that I cannot untie your inextricable knots, behold, my speech now hastens to each point. After our Demosthenes had begun somewhat loftily about the power of counsel, which is unacquainted with and moderate in itself, he puffed out hollow words, swelling like bladders with breath blown into his cheeks. He pressed forward the first head of his accusation, complaining that he had been condemned without being summoned, contrary to divine and human law. Proclaiming this an unworthy deed, he produces the examples of the first parent and of Cain, of whom the one was condemned for transgression and the other for murder, and neither without being summoned. He adds that God himself, to whom all things are open, in order to restrain us from the rash haste of judgment, was unwilling to destroy the Sodomites before he had clearly known their crimes. And so, with a threefold connection of examples, he arrays his line as if in a phalanx. But we could shatter this feeble array with a single blow of the ram, and by returning like for like, set against it a forest of examples. To bring forward a few out of many: we read that Moses, when the people's crime, which had been committed openly against God, came to light, avenged it without any prior accusation or examination, and expiated the monstrous crime of idolatry by a great slaughter of the people. We are told that Phinehas executed vengeance without any previous sentence, when he ran through with his own hand those who acted against the law and the edict already published. We know that Elijah led the priests of Baal to punishment before judgment. The same Elijah, we know, burned with fire called down from heaven the messengers of King Ahaziah. A like zeal is commended in the Scriptures of Eleazar. And to come to more recent times: it is established that Peter, the prince of the Apostles, straightway after the lie was told, punished Ananias and Sapphira with death. Paul, his fellow Apostle, condemned Elymas the magician, who resisted the Holy Spirit, to sudden blindness. And to bring forward something more effective: the Apostle, absent in body but present in spirit, excommunicated the Corinthian, delivering him over to destruction of the flesh so that the spirit might be saved; no noise of the forum was used, no judicial order, no weapons of legal process. Did the prophets of the Lord, or the Apostles, ever act wrongly?

units.la: Nunquid præcónes legis legem transgressi sunt, vel nuntii potuerunt his, quæ à Spiritu S. edocti erant, aduersa docere? Sunt ergo iudicia Domini vera, iustificata in semetipsa: quoniam ea-q vlta & vindicata præscripsimus, ita & clara & aperta erant, vt ad tenorem cæterorū & ædificationem nascentis Ecclesiæ plectenda magis quàm discutienda viderentur: Hoc est quod Canones sæpe proclamant, Quod nota & manifesta inquisitione non indigent. Talibus sanctionibus referti sunt Codices: & tu id simulas ignorare. Satis ad excómunicationem tuam Ambrosi. in Epist. Pauli sufficiebat auctoritas, dicentis: Licet iudicū nō sit fine accusatione damnare, quia Dominus Iudam cum fur esset non eiecit: Apostolus tamen cognito Cerinthi opere, cum docetu fraternitatis eiecit. Omnes enim sciebant crimen tum, publicè nouercam loco vxoris habebat: in qua re nec opus erat testibus, nec aliqua tergiuersatione tegi poterat crimen. Vides quantum inter occultum, quale Iudæ fuit, & manifestum quale Cerinthi, crimen interfit. An verò inficiari poteris crimen tuum non fuisse notorium? qui palam criminosum & sacrilegum Sigismundum in crimen confouebas, qui in elusionem Ecclesiasticæ districtionis damnatam appellationem emiseras, qui eam ipsam per vrbes, oppida, plateas & vicos palam iactitabas. Nec verò calumnieris, id non permanentis facti fuisse notorium. Non enim distat euidentia facti ab eo, qui in publico opere, & quidem participatione continua criminis suum etiam reatum publicè confitetur, & (quod deterius est) Daemonum imitando duritiem iure factum esse contendit, quod publicis sanctionibus nouerit esse damnatum. Verùm vt intelligas te omnino non sapere, & vix prima legum & Canonum rudimenta gustasse, intellige q vel omnino nescis, vel te scire dissimulas. Inter modernos veteresque iuris interpretes fuit sæpe tractatum, an in re notoria, de qua Canones loquuntur, sit præmittenda citatio? In quo quidem inter notorium & manifestum iuris, & notorium facti distinxerunt: Omnes tamen in eam sententiam conueniunt, vt si tale sit factum & tam manifestum, vt nulla ad eius probationem indagine opus esse videatur, nec possit aliqua tergiuersatione celari contra quod nec vlla competere possit defensio, quia id criminosum agat, quod iam constat esse damnatum, nullam exigi citationem. Pro quo expressi Canones allegantur, quos tu nisi inuitus fateri volueris, ipse coperies. Rursus & id conuenit inter eos, quod vbi apud iudicem & in iudicis conspectu delinquitur, potest is quidem id mox damnare, ac plectere delinquentem minimè citatum. At in te quis negare potest vtrumque concurrere, qui non solum factum damnatum veritæ appellationis palam admiseras, verùm in iudicem & iudicis præsentiam plus quàm notorie deliqueras: qui in Pontificis curia funestas schedulas appellationum in basilicarum foribus platearumque porticibus appendi curaueras?
units.tr: Did the heralds of the law transgress the law? Or could messengers taught by the Holy Spirit teach anything contrary to what they had been taught? Therefore the judgments of the Lord are true and justified in themselves; for the punishments and vengeances we have cited were so clear and open that they seemed to be inflicted for the terror of others and the edification of the newborn Church rather than to be examined. This is what the Canons often proclaim: that matters which need no careful inquiry, being notorious and manifest... The codices are full of such sanctions, and you pretend to be ignorant of them. For your excommunication, the authority of Ambrose on the Epistle of Paul was enough, when he says: Although judgment cannot condemn without accusation, since the Lord did not cast out Judas although he was a thief, yet the Apostle, when he recognised the work of Cerinthus, cast him out for the sake of the teaching of brotherhood. For all knew that crime: he publicly had his stepmother in place of a wife. In this matter there was no need of witnesses, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion. You see how much difference there is between a hidden crime, such as Judas's was, and a manifest one, such as that of Cerinthus. Can you indeed deny that your crime was not notorious? You who openly favoured the criminal and sacrilegious Sigismund, who had uttered an appeal condemned in mockery of ecclesiastical restraint, and who openly boasted of that same appeal through cities, towns, squares and villages. Nor can you falsely claim that it was not notorious because the deed did not persist. For there is no difference between the evidence of a deed and that of a man who, in public work, and indeed in continuous participation in the crime, publicly confesses his own guilt, and (what is worse) in imitation of the hardness of demons contends that the deed was lawful, because he knew it had been condemned by public sanctions. But so that you may understand that you are wholly without wisdom, and have scarcely tasted the first rudiments of law and the Canons, understand that you either know nothing at all or pretend not to know. Among modern and ancient interpreters of law it has often been debated whether, in a notorious matter of which the Canons speak, a citation must be sent beforehand. Here they distinguished between the notoriety of law and manifest matters, and the notoriety of fact. Yet all agree on this view: if the fact is of such a kind and so manifest that no search for its proof seems needed, and it cannot be concealed by any evasion, and no defence can be made against it, because he is acting criminally in a way already established as condemned, then no citation is required. For this, express Canons are cited, which you will discover for yourself, unless you are unwilling to admit them. Again, they agree on this too: where an offence is committed before a judge and in his sight, he may condemn at once and punish the offender without summoning him. But who can deny that both cases apply to you? You not only openly admitted the deed of a forbidden appeal, but you also offended notoriously against the judge and in his very presence. You had baleful schedules of appeal hung on the doors of the basilicas and on the porticoes of the squares at the Pontiff's court.

units.la: Verùm ne tibi inter opinionum varietatem contentionis relinquatur occasio, aliud tuæ garrulitati responsum opponamus, quod te scio torvo oculo & elato supercilio audituros. Disce miser, inter principalem & priuatam multum distare iudicandi potestatem. Formam iudiciorum cæteris esse præfixam, ad temeraria coërcenda iudicia. Principem verò legibus solutum formæ non subiici: atque proinde quicquid censeatur in aliis, tamen liberè atque intrepidè confitendum, processum atque sententiam Pontificis summi in notoriis absque citatione valere, præsertim vbi notorietas ipsa resurgit ex his, quæ acta sunt coram eo. Hæc non nostra, sed probatissimorum Iurisconsultorum verba sunt, quorum in scholis & iudiciis gratissima fuit auctoritas atque sententia. Attende simile aliquid in iure scripto, reperies testamentum, quod exactam scrupulosamque solemnitatem exigit, ex Principis præsentia sine vlla obseruatione vires assumere, propter principalem præsentiam cuncta supplentem, quæ formæ à lege introductæ non subditur. Ex hac quidem auctoritate Gelasius Papa Sillanos in ius non vocatos, ob notorium proprii antistitis parricidium damnauit. Innocentius III. electionem Philippi ad imperium, Henrici persecutoris Ecclesiæ stirpe progeniti, licet non citati, ob notorium defectum iure dicit improbatam. Innocentius IV. Clericos, qui Friderico fatali Ecclesiæ hosti adhæserant. Clemens IV. auctores cædis Siluani Episcopi, & idem eos, qui Conradino paruerunt, anathematis mucrone & temporalium mulctatione damnauit: sicut nos vel ex Canonibus, vel ex Pontificum gestis agnouimus, quæ si quis curiosius perscrutetur, exempla plura reperiet. Scio te inclamaturum, & more, quo soles cuncta censere, dicturum, ad adulationem Pontificum ista praescripta. Verùm quis loquacitati tuæ plura tribuet, quàm probatissimis Iurisconsultis?
units.tr: But lest an occasion for contention be left to you amid the variety of opinions, let us set against your chatter another answer, which I know you will hear with a grim eye and a haughty brow. Learn, wretch, that there is a great difference between the judicial power of a prince and that of a private person. The form of judgments is prescribed for others, to restrain rash judgments. But the prince, freed from the laws, is not subject to form. Therefore, whatever may be thought in other cases, it must be freely and fearlessly confessed that the process and sentence of the supreme Pontiff in notorious matters, without citation, are valid, especially where the notoriety itself arises from what has been done before him. These are not our words but those of the most approved jurists, whose authority and opinion have been most welcome in the schools and the courts. Notice something similar in written law: you will find that a will, which demands exact and scrupulous solemnity, gains its force in the presence of the Prince without any observance of form, because the Prince's presence supplies everything and is not subject to the form introduced by law. By this authority Pope Gelasius condemned the Sillani, who had not been summoned to court, for the notorious parricide of their own bishop. Innocent III declared the election of Philip to the empire, a scion of the stock of Henry, the persecutor of the Church, invalid by law for a notorious defect, although he had not been summoned. Innocent IV condemned the clerics who had adhered to Frederick, the deadly enemy of the Church. Clement IV condemned the authors of the murder of Bishop Silvanus, and likewise those who had obeyed Conradin, with the sword of anathema and the penalty of temporal losses. We know this from the Canons or from the deeds of the Pontiffs, and if anyone examines these more closely, he will find more examples. I know you will cry out, and, in your usual way of judging everything, say: these things were written to flatter the Pontiffs. But who will attribute more weight to your chatter than to the most approved jurists?

units.la: At nunc missa omnia priora faciamus. Tu qui tibi vtriusque juris vendicas principatum, tuam aliquando inscitiam (ne dicam ruditatem) agnosce, atque intellige, te aristas tantùm in studiis messuisse. Nonne intelligis permagni referre, an de crimine contra quempiam inquiratur, vt damnetur, vel tantùm declaretur, aliquem suo facto damnatum in poenam à iure aut statuto promulgatam incidisse. Non enim aliquid noui facit, qui declarat, non damnat, non pronuntiat, sed aliquem in poenam iam legis constitutione irrogatam incidisse denuntiat. In quo casu constat, non exigi citationem, cùm non sententiam ferre, sed magis sententiam à iure latam judex exequi videatur. Quod vsque adeo tenuere Doctores, vt censuerint excommunicatum siue monitioni subditum eo casu, quo à iure vel statuto excommunicatus apparet, non incurrere poenam à Canonibus inflictam. Hoc iuris interpretes constanter affirmant: quos si forte non legeris, tuam ignorantiā fateare; si verò legisti, dolum atq; perfidiam confiteri necesse est, qui generalibus vulgatisq; etiam apud pueros diuini testimonii exemplis odiū & inuidiam Romano Pontifici concitare voluisti. Iam igitur obtrectator absolue te ab hoc nexu, si potes.
units.tr: Now let us set all the earlier matters aside. You, who claim the leadership of both laws, should at last acknowledge your ignorance (not to say your crudeness) and understand that in your studies you have only gathered ears of grain. Do you not see how much it matters whether an inquiry is made into a crime against someone in order to condemn him, or whether it is merely declared that someone has, by his own deed, already fallen into the penalty promulgated by law or statute? For one who declares does nothing new. He does not condemn or pronounce sentence, but announces that someone has already incurred a penalty imposed by the enactment of the law itself. In such a case it is clear that no citation is required, since the judge does not seem to pronounce a sentence but rather to carry out a sentence already passed by law. The Doctors held this so firmly that they judged that an excommunicated person, or one subject to a warning, in the case where he is evidently excommunicated by law or statute, does not incur the penalty inflicted by the Canons. The interpreters of law affirm this consistently. If you have perhaps not read them, you must confess your ignorance; if you have read them, you must admit that you acted with deceit and treachery, since you wished to stir up hatred and odium against the Roman Pontiff with examples of divine testimony that are general and commonly known even among boys. Now then, slanderer, free yourself from this bond, if you can.

units.la: Pridem facta generali constitutione sancitum, & quidem æquissimè, vt infra subiungetur: Ne quis in illusionem ecclesiastica censura ad futurum Concilium, sub pœna anathematis & læsæ Maiestatis appellaret. Appellasti, & quidem notorie, & appellationem etiam palam non tam insinuare quam inculcare curasti. Declarat te Pontifex pro eo, quod damnatum iam facinus admisisti, in spirituales ac temporales pœnas à lege inflictas incidisse. Quid habes, quod conqueraris? quid quod detestaris, quid quod inclames diuina & humana iura violata? te non citatum, ob illa quæ non fecisti publicè confiteris, sed tumentibus buccis in cœtu Principum te fecisse gloriaris. Satis superque, satis te blasphemiæ & procacitatis arguimus, & obiectam diuini iuris violati calumniam confutauimus utriusque Testamenti exemplis. Ostendimus facinorosos homines pro manifestis criminibus sine vllo iudiciario ordine potuisse damnari: & probauimus, delictum tuum omnibus fuisse notorium, in conspectu summi iudicis & contemptum Apostolicæ Maiestatis admissum: ab eo prolatum esse iudicium, qui supra ius constitutus iuris ordini & formæ non subditur. Postremò, non ab homine neque per hominem, sed ex lege & per legem, merito tuæ iniquitatis te fuisse damnatum. Superest, vt reliquas inuectiuarum tuarum partes percurrentes, non solùm procacem te atque maledicum, sed etiam hæreticum & infidelem, ex ipsis tuis sermonibus conuincamus.
units.tr: Some time ago a general constitution was enacted, and most justly so, as will be added below: "That no one, in mockery of ecclesiastical censure, may appeal to a future Council under penalty of anathema and of injured majesty." You appealed, and indeed notoriously, and you took care to proclaim the appeal openly, not so much to hint at it as to hammer it home. The Pontiff declares that, because you have committed a crime already condemned, you have incurred the spiritual and temporal penalties inflicted by law. What is there for you to complain about? Why do you protest, why do you cry out that divine and human laws have been violated? You confess publicly that you were not cited for those things you did not do in public, but with puffed-up cheeks you boast that you did them in the assembly of princes. We have more than enough shown you to be blasphemous and insolent, and we have refuted the charge of violating divine law with examples from both Testaments. We have shown that wicked men could be condemned for manifest crimes without any judicial order; and we have proved that your offence was notorious to all, committed in the sight of the supreme Judge and in contempt of apostolic majesty; that judgment was pronounced by one who, set above law, is not subject to the order and form of law; and finally, that you were rightly condemned, for the sake of your iniquity, not by a man nor through a man, but from law and through law. It remains, running through the rest of your invective, to convict you from your own words not only as insolent and abusive, but also as a heretic and an unbeliever.

units.la: Prosequamur igitur reliqua, & ne nos carpendi studio aliquid confingere suspicetur, ipsa prout locutus es, verba proponamus. Quam tenuem, inquit, etiam exorsus, quam debilem texit rationem, quasi videte. Saluator, inquit, noster Petrum Apostolorum Principem ad gubernationem Ecclesiæ substituit, &c. Quis ignorat omnibus Apostolis à Iesu esse præceptum, vt eam orbem prædicaturi fidem, baptismum & salutem? Quis nescit pastum omnibus esse permissum, ligatum in cœlis quod ipsi ligarent in terris, & soluturos, quod soluerent. Sed quod Cephas singulariter dictum est, Tibi dabo claues cœlorum, hoc ait Hieronymus factum, vt subiiciatur tollereture occasio. Et Ambrosius in suo Pastorali dicit: Quod nedum Petro trina rogatione interrogato, an amaret, ac trina responsione subsequente, amare se teste ipso interrogatore Iesu, traditas sibi esse claues, sed omnibus ipsis contraditas, Apostolosque post ascensionem Domini conuenisse, ac Petrum sibi Principem constituisse, & Antiochiæ in cathedra collocasse referuntur. Nihil tamen de potestate vniuersis Apostolis à Saluatore data, ipsorum omnium vniuersali missione diminuerunt. Ergo & hodie exorat Ecclesia Catholica, sese per Apostolos ipsos continua protectione custodiri, quos Saluator ipse vicarios tanti operis constituit præsides Pastores. Horum legitimos successores constat esse vniuersalia Concilia, Christianæ fidei fundamenta, quæ Pontificum actiones pro tempore saluberrimis doctrinis instruxerunt, errores emendarunt. De quibus summus ille Pontifex Gregorius scribit: Quisquis illa destruere tentaret, seipsum destruit. Sed quorsum hæc? Eo certè pertingunt, vt conuellatur illa superstitio, in qua Pius Papa factionibus Cardinalis Cusani astruit, Concilium supra Papam non esse, dum dicit, (vt eius verbis vtar) ad futurum Concilium appellari non posse, quod supra Christi vicarium esse nequit. Videte ergo quam vim consilii exsortem Papa inferre tentauit.
units.tr: Let us therefore proceed to the rest, and lest he suspect us of inventing something out of a zeal to carp, let us set out his very words as you spoke them. How thin, he says, and how feeble is the reasoning he weaves even at the outset, as you see. Our Saviour, he says, appointed Peter, the prince of the Apostles, to govern the Church, etc. Who does not know that it was commanded by Jesus to all the Apostles that they should preach the faith, baptism and salvation to the world? Who does not know that it was permitted to all of them to bind on earth what they would bind in heaven, and to loose what they would loose? But that Cephas was singled out with the words, I will give you the keys of the heavens, this, says Jerome, was done so that the occasion of schism might be removed. And Ambrose in his Pastoral says: It is related that the keys were handed over not only to Peter, who was asked three times whether he loved, and answered three times, Jesus the questioner himself being witness that he loved; they were also handed over to all of them, and the Apostles, after the Lord's ascension, came together and appointed Peter as their prince, and placed him in the chair at Antioch. Yet they diminished nothing of the power given by the Saviour to all the Apostles by their universal mission. Therefore the Catholic Church also prays today that it may be guarded by continual protection through the Apostles themselves, whom the Saviour himself appointed as vicars and presiding ministers of so great a work. It is agreed that the legitimate successors of these are the universal Councils, the foundations of the Christian faith, which from time to time, by the most salutary teachings, have instructed the actions of the Pontiffs and corrected errors. Of these that great Pontiff Gregory writes: Whoever should attempt to destroy them destroys himself. But to what end are these things said? Surely they tend to overthrow that superstition by which Pius the Pope, following the factions of Cardinal Cusanus, asserts that a Council is not above the Pope, since he says (to use his words) that one cannot appeal to a future Council, because it cannot be above Christ's vicar. See then with what force the Pope tried to attack a counsel that he had no part in.

units.la: Nam si omnes Apostoli sunt missi à Domino Iesu, dicente illis, Ite in orbem, quodcunque ligaueritis &c. quos constat postea conciliariter congregatos, ac ipsum Cephan in mensem Domini misisse, quis dubitat Concilia sacra vicem Christi gerere, quæ cœtui Apostolico successisse comprobantur, siquidem orbi maior est vrbe. Hæc sunt illius portenta verborum. Miror profectò, cùm apud Aurelium Augustinum legerim, nullam falsam esse quæ non aliqua vera permisceat, Gregorium in tantam prolapsum esse vaesaniam, vt breui verborum serie pene quasi plura expresserit vitia, quàm verba: sicut quisque facile percipere potest. In ipso namque sermonis huius exordio pariter Apostolis Ecclesiam fuisse commissam, ex missionis, Baptismi ac prædicationis communione coniectat, ipsosque in traditione clauium parem potestatem accepisse profitetur. Tum verò ob hoc vni singulariter claues esse permissas, vt schismatis tollatur occasio, Apostolum Petrum apostolica & humana institutione Cathedram & prælationem accepisse. Et ne dubium relinqueretur ex præmissis, primatum Petri negasse, etiam veterum hæreticorum ab arcanis vsque depromptum de missione Petri argumentum inducit, innuens maiorem misso esse mittentem. Inde transuolans ad alia, vt quem singulis æquauerat Apostolis, in vnum collectis ostenderet fuisse minorem, vniuersalia Concilia (vt ineptis suis vtar) Apostolorum dicit legitimos successores. Quorum auctoritatem extollens tria plane infert ridicula: Concilia Christianæ fidei fundamenta, Pontificum actiones instruxisse, & errata correxisse, eadem vicem Christi gerere, & ab illo potestatem accipere, ac propterea Petro illiusque successoribus superiora esse contendit.
units.tr: For if all the Apostles were sent by the Lord Jesus, who said to them, Go into the world, whatsoever you bind, etc., and it is certain that they were afterwards gathered in council, and that Peter himself was sent into the world by the Lord, who doubts that sacred Councils bear the place of Christ, since they are shown to have succeeded the Apostolic assembly, the world being greater than the city? These are his monstrous words. I am truly amazed, since I have read in Augustine that no falsehood is made without mixing in some truth, that Gregory has fallen into such madness that in a short series of words he has expressed almost more faults than words, as anyone can easily perceive. For at the very beginning of this speech he conjectures, from the common mission, baptism and preaching, that the Church was entrusted equally to the Apostles, and he professes that they received equal power in the handing over of the keys. Then, on the ground that the keys were given to one alone so that the occasion of schism might be removed, he claims that the Apostle Peter received the chair and the preeminence by apostolic and human institution. And lest any doubt be left from what has been said, he brings in the argument from Peter's mission, drawn even from the secrets of the ancient heretics, hinting that the one who is sent is less than the one who sends. Passing from there to other matters, so that he might show that Peter, whom he had made equal to the other Apostles, was less when they were gathered together, he says that universal Councils are the legitimate successors of the Apostles (to use his absurd words). Extolling their authority, he draws three plainly ridiculous conclusions: that the Councils are the foundations of the Christian faith and have instructed the actions of the Pontiffs and corrected errors; that they bear the place of Christ and receive power from him; and therefore he contends that they are above Peter and his successors.

units.la: Sequamur ordinem propositionum suarum, veniam (vt opinamur) impetraturi, si paulò altius principia repetentes sermonem longius protendamus. Necesse est enim, vt vana procacitas, quæ sibi non legum tantùm & Canonum, sed omnium diuinarum atque humanarum rerum arrogat sapientiam, non diuinis solum atque humanis testimoniis, sed ex ipsis quoque naturæ principiis reuincatur, vt iuxta Apostolum se euanuisse in cogitationibus suis & obseruatum insipiens cor eius agnoscat, qui cùm dixerit se sapientem, stultum se factum intelligat. Credere te Gregori arbitramur, Ecclesiam Christi, quæ in hoc mundo peregrinatur ex fide viuens, aliquo ordine esse distinctam, vtpote ab eo constitutam, cuius perfecta sunt opera, quinque hanc legem naturæ indidit, vt infima summis, summa infimis per media copulentur, qui ordinem cœlis ac terris dedit. Nam cùm dicat Apostolus, Quæ à Deo sunt, esse ordinata, aut Ecclesiam ex Deo non esse, aut ab illo ordinatam esse oportere, præsertim cùm illam Spiritus sanctus vocet in Canticis, Castrorum aciem ordinatam, & superiori Hierarchiæ dicatur exemplata diuinitus, in qua (vt scribit Gregorius) coelestium militiarum exempla nos instruunt. Quia dum sunt Angeli & Archangeli, liquet non esse æquales, sed ordine & potestate discretos. Nec enim vniversitas posset alia ratione subsistere, nisi huiusmodi magnus eam talis, qua totum corpus sanum sit, & quæque organa suis fungantur officiis, differentiæ ordo seruaret. Porro si ordinem non disserteris, magis ex naturæ principiis, quibus tamen per omnia non in uno solo, quod præoptas, non solum ex diuina institutione, sed ex ipsis quoque naturæ principiis, cuiusuis politiæ recto regimine vnum caput, vnius ecclesiastici corporis, vnum Principem sanctæ ciuitatis, vnum monarcham ecclesiasticæ hierarchiæ, vnum Pastorem dominici gregis atque ouilis in terris fateare necesse est. Nam cum omnis ordo sit multorum in gradibus differentium, & idipsum sit secundum prælationem & subiectionem, ad vnum tantum deueniri necesse est, in quo finis statusque constistat, vt cuitetur infinitas: quem supremum in Ecclesia Principem atque Rectorem esse constat, in quo & ex quo totius Ecclesiæ potestas & status. Vbi enim vnitas, ibi perfectio: reliqui numeri perfectionem non habent, sed diuisiones ab vnitate recedentes. Porro vt Aurel. Augustinus ait, Multa præponitur vnum. Non enim a multis vnum, sed multa ab vno. Cærerum nemo tam iniquus existimator esse poteit, vt regimen Ecclesiæ minus ordinatum esse credat, quam naturæ: cum gratia supergrediatur superetque naturam. Quod si in his, quæ a natura sunt, omne regimen naturale ad vnum dirigitur principale, quod regit, vt in corpore multa membra varietate compacta vnius capitis sumunt influxum, & de fonte vno riui plurimi defluunt, & multi arboris rami ad vnum stipitem reducuntur, & multi stipites yna radice figuntur, & inferioris corporis motus vno primo mobili mouetur & regitur, quis non credat, Ecclesiam diuersis gradibus in vnum Christi corpus vnitam, vno in terris capite gubernari? Præsertim cum dicat Propheta: Congregabuntur filii Iuda & filii Israel pariter, vt ponant sibi caput vnum. Probat autem ratio finis, qui pax est, & vnitas subditorum, quæ quidem nisi ab vno & per vnum constistere non posset. Ad hoc enim diuina prouidentia gradus & ordines constituit esse distinctos, vt ex reuerentia inferioris ad caput vera concordia fieret, & ex diuersitate contextio, & recte officiorum gereretur administratio singulorum. Quod etiam Philosophorum Princeps in Metaphysicis recognouit, dicens: Entia nolle male disponi. Pluralitatem principatuum malam. Necessario igitur vnum Principem esse fatendum. Natura enim principiorum amat singularitatem, vt beatus Augustinus ait: Ita vt ipsius singularis principatus bonum etiam quibusdam ingerat animantibus, vt in apibus vnus principetur. Et sicut beatus quoque Hieronymus ait, grues vnam sequuntur ordine literario. Hoc nobis repræsentat ad Moysen de figura coelestis hierarchiæ diuina præceptio dicens: Omnia fac secundum exemplar tibi in monte monstratum. Et visio Ioannis in Apocalypsi reuelata, qui ciuitatem sanctam Ierusalem nouam descendentem de coelo se vidisse perhibuit: quam figuram clarus ille Doctor, Claræuallis Abbas eximius Bernardus exponit, dicens: Non vilis putanda est forma terrestris Hierusalem, quæ formam habet a coelo, vt sicut ibi Seraphin & Cherubin & cæteri ordines sub vno capite Deo, ita & hic Patriarchæ, Archiepiscopi, & reliqui sub vno summo Pontifice. Hoc denique ratio vnitatis insinuat, vt vnius corporis vnum caput necessario prædicetur. Nam si secundum Apostolum vnum corpus multi sumus, & vnam esse Ecclesiam Spiritus S. in Canticis, consequens est, quod beatus ac facundissimus Martyr Cyprianus ait, cuius verba tam de parilitate Apostolorum hæresin transfodiunt atque confundunt: Inquit Dominus ad Petrum: Ego dico tibi quia tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam. Super vnum ædificat Ecclesiam. Et quamuis omnibus Apostolis post resurrectionem parem potestatem tribuat, dicens: Sicut me misit pater, & ego mitto vos, accipite Spiritum sanctum. Tamen vt vnitatem manifestaret, vnitatis eiusdem originem ab vno incipientem sua auctoritate disposuit. Et post pauca: Exordium ab vnitate profisci, vt Ecclesia Christi vna monstretur, quoniam vnam Ecclesiam Spiritus S. in Cantico Canticorum experssona Christi designat, & dicit: Vna est columba mea, perfecta mea, vna est matris suæ filia, electa genitrici. Hoc denique Christi institutio nobis insinuat, qui velut pastor bonus oues errantes collecturus aduenerat, & vnitatem nobis ostendens de diuina auctoritate venientem, ait: Ego & Pater secundum diuinitatem vnum sumus. Ad quam vnitatem redigens Ecclesiam suam, dicit: Erit vnum ouile & vnus pastor. Qui cum in tantum dilexisset Ecclesiam, vt propter nimiam charitatem sanguinem suum profuderit, nusquam putandus est illi in necessariis defuisse. Cum & de Synagoga per Isaiam ipse prædixerit: Quid vltra facere debui vinea mea, & non feci? Defuisset utique, si ascensurus ad Patrem, & corporalem præsentiam suis fidelibus subtracturus aliquem non substituisset, qui vice sua vniuersali Ecclesiæ præsideret, & cum illa visibiliter versaretur, ac vniuersa Rectoris impleret officia. Ne ergo vllo munere illi deesset, ipsius curam Apostolorum Principi Petro commisit, qui suæ fidei stabilitate cæteros in Christiana religione firmaret. Propter quod illum ante passionem admonuit, dicens: Et tu aliquando conuersus confirma fratres tuos. Et post passionem gregem sibi commendans: Pasce, inquit, oues meas. Quæ verba exponens Bernhardus præclarus Doctor Ecclesiæ, in opere insigni, quod ad Eugenium Papam de consideratione conscripsit: Sunt, inquit, quidem & alii cæli ianitores, & gregum pastores: sed tu tanto gloriosius, quanto & differentius præ cæteris nomen hæreditasti. Habent illi sibi assignatos greges, singuli singulos, tibi vniversi assignantur. Nec modo ouiam, sed & Pastorum tu vnus omnium pastor. Vnde probem quæris? Si me amas, Petre, pasce oues meas. Quas? Illius vel illius populi, ciuitatis, aut regionis, aut certi regni? Oues meas, inquit. Cui non planum est, non designasse aliquas, sed designasse omnes. Nihil excipitur, vbi distinguitur nihil. Et forte præsuniti & cateri discipuli erant, cùm committens vni vnitatem omnibus communicaret in vno grege & vno pastore, secundùm illud: Vna est columba mea, formosa mea, perfecta mea. Vbi vnitas, ibi perfectio. Et post pauca: Inde est, quod alii singuli singulas sortiti sunt plebes, scientes Sacramentum. Denique Iacobus, qui videbatur columna Ecclesia, vna contentus est Hierosolyma, Petro vniuersitatem credens. Pulchrè verò ibi positus est suscitare semen fratris defuncti, vbi occisus est ille: nam dictus est frater Domini. Petro cedente, Domini frater, quis se alter ingerat Petri prærogatiuam? Ergo (iuxta Canones tuos) alii in partem sollicitudinis, tu in plenitudinem vocatus es potestatis. Aliorum potestas certa artatur limitibus, tua extenditur & in ipsos, qui super alios potestatem acceperunt.
units.tr: Let us follow the order of your propositions, hoping (as we think) to be pardoned if, by going back to somewhat deeper principles, we extend our discussion a little. For vain boldness, which claims for itself the wisdom not only of laws and canons but of all divine and human things, must be refuted not only by divine and human testimonies but also from the principles of nature itself. So, as the Apostle says, it may recognise that it has become vain in its thinking, that its foolish heart has been darkened, and that one who called himself wise has become a fool. We believe, Gregory, that you hold that the Church of Christ, which journeys in this world living by faith, is distinguished by some order, since it was established by him whose works are perfect, who implanted in nature this law, that the lowest be joined to the highest and the highest to the lowest through intermediates, he who gave order to heaven and earth. For since the Apostle says that the things which are from God are ordered, either the Church is not from God, or it must be ordered by him. This is especially so since the Holy Spirit calls it in the Canticles "an army set in array," and it is said to have been divinely modelled on the higher hierarchy, in which (as Gregory writes) the examples of the heavenly armies instruct us. For since there are angels and archangels, it is clear that they are not equal, but distinguished by order and power. Indeed the universe could not subsist in any other way unless a great order of difference, by which the whole body is sound and each organ performs its office, preserved it. Moreover, if you will not dispute the order, you must acknowledge, from the principles of nature (which nevertheless do not in all things favour a plurality in place of the single head you prefer), and not only from divine institution, that in the right government of every polity there is one head, one prince of the holy city, one monarch of the ecclesiastical hierarchy, one shepherd of the Lord's flock and fold on earth, and of one ecclesiastical body one head. For since every order consists of many things differing in grades, and this same order consists in pre-eminence and subjection, it must come down to one alone, in whom the end and the standing of the whole rests, so that infinity is avoided. It is clear that this one is the supreme Prince and Ruler in the Church, in whom and from whom is the power and the standing of the whole Church. For where there is unity, there is perfection; the other numbers do not have perfection, but divisions receding from unity. Moreover, as Augustine says, "The one is put before the many. For the one does not come from the many, but the many from the one." Again, no one can be so unfair a judge as to believe that the government of the Church is less ordered than that of nature, since grace surpasses and exceeds nature. But if in those things which are of nature every natural government is directed to one principal ruler, so that in the body many members, held together in variety, receive influence from one head; and many streams flow from one spring; and many branches of a tree are traced back to one trunk; and many trunks are fixed in one root; and the motion of the lower body is moved and governed by one first mover; who would not believe that the Church, united in diverse grades into one body of Christ, is governed on earth by one head? Especially since the Prophet says: "The sons of Judah and the sons of Israel shall be gathered together, that they may set for themselves one head." Moreover, the reason of the end, which is peace and the unity of the subjects, proves this, which indeed could not stand unless it were from one and through one. For to this end divine providence has established distinct grades and orders, so that true concord might arise from the reverence of the lower toward the head, and a close-knit fabric from their diversity, and the administration of each one's duties be rightly carried out. The Prince of the Philosophers also recognised this in the Metaphysics, saying: "Beings do not wish to be badly ordered. A plurality of principalities is bad." It must therefore be confessed that there is one Prince. "For the nature of first principles loves singularity," as blessed Augustine says, so that the good of this single principate is also conferred on some living creatures, as among bees one rules. And, as blessed Jerome also says, cranes follow one in a literal order. The divine precept to Moses about the figure of the heavenly hierarchy sets this before us, saying: "Make all things according to the pattern shown you on the mountain." And the vision revealed to John in the Apocalypse, who related that he saw the holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down from heaven. This figure the illustrious doctor, the outstanding abbot of Clairvaux, Bernard, expounds, saying: "The earthly Jerusalem is not to be thought of as cheap, since it has its form from heaven; so that just as there the Seraphim and Cherubim and the other orders are under one head, God, so here the Patriarchs, Archbishops and the rest are under one supreme Pontiff." Finally, the reason of unity suggests this, that one head must necessarily be assigned to one body. For if, according to the Apostle, we are many but one body, and the Holy Spirit in the Canticles declares the Church to be one, it follows what the blessed and most eloquent martyr Cyprian says, whose words pierce and confound the heresy of the equality of the Apostles: "The Lord says to Peter: 'I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.' He builds the Church upon one." And although he grants equal power to all the Apostles after the resurrection, saying: "As the Father has sent me, so I send you; receive the Holy Spirit," yet, in order to show unity, he arranged by his own authority the origin of that same unity as beginning from one. And a little later: "To set out from unity" so that the Church of Christ may be shown to be one. For the Holy Spirit in the Song of Songs, speaking in the person of Christ, designates the Church as one, and says: "One is my dove, my perfect one; she is one of her mother, chosen for the one who bore her." Finally, the institution of Christ suggests this to us. He, as a good shepherd who had come to gather the wandering sheep, and showing us the unity that comes from divine authority, says: "I and the Father are one according to the divinity." Bringing his Church back to this unity, he says: "There shall be one fold and one shepherd." He who loved the Church so much that he poured out his blood out of excessive charity is surely never to be thought to have been wanting in necessary things. Since he himself also foretold about the Synagogue through Isaiah: "What more ought I to have done for my vineyard, and did not?" He would certainly have been wanting if, about to ascend to the Father and to withdraw his bodily presence from his faithful, he had not appointed someone to preside in his place over the universal Church, and to be visibly present with it and fulfil all the duties of a ruler. So that he might be wanting in no office, he committed his care to Peter, the Prince of the Apostles, who would strengthen the others in the Christian religion by the steadfastness of his faith. On account of this he warned him before the passion, saying: "And you, when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers." And after the passion, commending the flock to him: "Feed," he says, "my sheep." Expounding these words, Bernard, the renowned Doctor of the Church, in his notable work which he wrote to Pope Eugenius On Consideration says: "Indeed there are other gatekeepers of heaven and shepherds of flocks, but you have inherited a name so much more glorious, and so much more distinct than the rest. They have flocks assigned to them, each one his own; to you all are assigned together. And not only the sheep, but also the shepherds, you alone are the shepherd of all. Do you ask whence I prove this? 'If you love me, Peter, feed my sheep.' Which ones? Those of this or that people, city, or region, or of a certain kingdom? 'My sheep,' he says. Is it not plain that he did not designate some, but designated all? Nothing is excepted where nothing is distinguished." And perhaps the other disciples were also presumed, when, committing unity to one, he shared it with all in one flock and one shepherd, according to that saying: "One is my dove, my beautiful one, my perfect one. Where there is unity, there is perfection." And a little later: "Hence it is that the others each received their own peoples, knowing the sacrament." Finally, James, who seemed to be a pillar of the Church, was content with one Jerusalem, trusting the universality to Peter. Moreover, he was rightly placed there to raise up seed for his dead brother, where that one was killed; for he was called the brother of the Lord. With Peter yielding, who else would thrust himself in as the brother of the Lord to claim Peter's prerogative? Therefore (according to your canons) the others were called into a share of the care, but you into the fullness of power. The power of the others is confined within certain limits; yours is extended even over those who have received power over others.

units.la: Audis igitur, quæ Doctor eximius loquitur, ex quo discere potuisti, Petri potestatem à cæteris Apostolis & vniuersitate & prælatione discretam: cùm illi singulis, iste vniuersis plebibus & ipsis quoq; Apostolis, (quos ex ouibus Christi, & Petro commendatas fuisse nemo ambigit) prælatus extiterit. Scio te frontem contracturum, & (sicut assoles) nos Horatiano sale decisurum atque dicturum: Troianum gemino bellum ordiri ab ouo.
units.tr: You hear, then, what that eminent Doctor says, from which you could learn that Peter's power was distinct from that of the other Apostles both in its universality and in its preeminence, since he was set over the individual peoples, while Peter alone was set over all the peoples and over the Apostles themselves, who, as no one doubts, were entrusted to Peter from the sheep of Christ. I know you will frown and, as you are wont, will cut us down with Horatian wit and say that we are starting the Trojan War from the egg, as it were, with twins.

units.la: Sed tua nos coëgit impudentia, qui corusc ante Euangelio, & totiens in consortibus tuis damnatis hæreticis, singularem Petri in vniuersalem Ecclesiam potestatem diffitentibus, tu eandem palàm ingerere & refutare curasti. Audi igitur vel inuitus, quos prædictus Doctor ex Euangelio typos annectit, quos recensendos existimo, quo magis confutetur tua insania. Accipe (inquam) illud, quo nihilominus idipsum confirmatur. Discipuli navigabant, & Dominus apparebat in litore, quod quàm iucundius erat in corpore redivivo. Sciens Petrus quia Dominus est, in mare se misit, & sic venit ad ipsum, alii navigio pervenientibus. Quid istud? Nempe signum singulorum Pontificatus Petri, per quod non nauim vnam, vt cateri quisque suum, sed seculum ipsum suscepit gubernandum. Mare enim seculum, & naues Ecclesiæ. Inde est, ip altera vice instar Domini gradientis super aquas, vnicus se Christi vicarius designauit, qui non vni populo, sed cunctis præesse debet. Siquidem aqua multa populi multi. Ita cum quisq; caterorum habeat sitam, tibi vna commissa est grandissima nauis, facta ex omnibus ipsa vniuersalis Ecclesia toto orbe diffusa.
units.tr: But your impudence has forced us, you who, though you are a glittering light of the Gospel and have so often, among your condemned heretic associates, denied Peter's unique power over the universal Church, have taken pains to thrust that same power openly upon us and then to refute it. Hear then, even against your will, the types that the aforesaid Doctor draws from the Gospel. I think they should be reviewed, so that your madness may be refuted all the more. Take (I say) that passage, by which that same point is nonetheless confirmed. The disciples were sailing, and the Lord appeared on the shore, a sight all the more joyful because he was in his risen body. Peter, knowing that it was the Lord, threw himself into the sea and came to him, while the others arrived by boat. What is this? Surely it is a sign of Peter's individual pontificate, by which he received not one ship, as each of the others did, but the whole world to govern. For the sea is the world, and the ships are the Church. Hence, once again, as the Lord walking upon the waters, the sole vicar of Christ has marked himself out, who ought to preside not over one people but over all. For the many waters are many peoples. So, while each of the others has a ship assigned to him, to you has been committed one very great ship, made up of all, the universal Church spread through the whole world.

units.la: Cùm igitur superiorum omnium ratio deducta concludat singularem Petri in vniversalem Ecclesiam potestatem, quæ & in naturis ostenditur, in cœlo exemplificatur, in operibus typicè demonstratur, & in toto corpore mystico obseruatur, & in lege diuina ac Euangelio commendatur: Tu tamen, virorum acutissime, ausus es quibusdam verborum strophis illam parilem cæteris Apostolis iudicare, atque ex humana magis quàm diuina institutione, vel ab Apostolis sine imminutione propriæ potestatis, vel consensu Ecclesiæ in remedium schismatis, attributam asserere: illud in tui erroris argumentum adducens, quod cæteri quoque Apostoli claues (vt tuis vtar verbis) contradite fuerint. Ad quod licet per superiora monstrauerim, ita reliquis traditas claues, vt tamen Petro præ omnibus, & pro omnibus ante tradiderit, ita à se petra Petri nomen indicens, & in illo huius muneris Sacramentum imponens, vt non nisi per Petrum velut à capite in eos sit deriuata potestas, eaque non vniuersaliter, sed certis coartata limitibus; trium tamen sanctorum Patrum super ea re visum est tibi explicare sententias, vt eorum mentes ædificent, quos forte verborum tuorum virus infecit. Possemus quidem infinita congerere: sed cui pauca non sufficiunt, nec multa proficiunt.
