Primus igitur excitetur beatus Martyr Anacletus, vicinus Apostolorum, atque ipsius Petri successor: qui tuæ respondens insaniæ, in decretali Epistola ita præfatur: Sacrosancta Romana Ecclesia & Apostolica, non ab Apostolis, sed ab ipso Saluatore primatum obtinuit, sicut beato Apostolo dixit: Tu es Petrus. Et post aliqua: Inter beatos Apostolos quædam fuit discretio potestatis, & licet omnes essent Apostoli, Petro tamen concessum est à Domino, & ipsi inter se voluerunt idipsum, vt reliquis omnibus præesset Apostolis, & Cephas, id est, caput & principium teneret Apostolatus. Exsurgat & Canonis lator, veritatis præco, Leo Papa in Canone dicens: Ita Dominus noster Iesus Christus humani generis Saluator instituit, vt veritas, quæ antea legis & Prophetarum præconio continebatur, per Apostolicam eubam in salutem vniuersitatis exiret, sicut scriptum est: In omnem terram exiuit sonus eorum, & in fines terræ verba eorum. Sed huius muneris Sacramentum ita Dominus ad omnium Apostolorum officium pertinere voluit, vt in beatissimo Petro Apostolorum omnium summum principatum collocaret, vt ab ipso quasi quodam capite dona sua velut in corpus omne diffunderet, vt exsortem se ministerii intelligeret esse diuini, qui ausus fuisset à Petri soliditate recedere. Hunc enim in consortium indiuiduæ vnitatis assumptum, quod erat ipse, Dominus voluit nominari, dicendo: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, vt æterni templi ædificatio mirabili munere gratia Dei in Petri soliditate existeret, hanc Ecclesiam sua etiam corroborans firmitate, vt illam nec humana temeritas posset appetere, nec porta inferi contra illam prævalerent. Et continuo, quasi Gregorium hæreticum & blasphemum spiritu prævidens, adiecit: Verum hanc petram ipsius sacratissimam firmitatem Deo (vt diximus) adificante constructam, nimis impia vult præsumptione violare, qui quis eius potestatem tentat infringere, id quod accepit à veteribus non sequendo. Clangat nunc tuba Euangelii; tuba (inquam) sacerdotalis, qua clangente sicut olim muri Hiericho, ita Nestoriana atque Eutychiana propugnacula corruerunt. Magnus ille Leo, quem Chalcedonensis Synodus columnam fidei, Oecumenicum atque Apostolicum acclamauit, cuius auctoritati Canon tantum attribuit, vt si quis eius dicta vsque ad totam scrutari voluerit, & non in omnibus reuerenter recepetit, anathema sit: is ergo in sermone de ordinatione sua, de primatu Petri sic loquitur: Vtile ac dignum est, ad beatissimi Apostoli Petri gloriam contemplandam aciem mentis attollere, qui ab ipso omnium chrismatum fonte tam copiosis est irrigationibus inundatus, vt cum multa solum acceperit, nihil in quequam sine illius participatione transferit. Et iterum in eadem: De toto mundo vnus Petrus eligitur, qui & vniuersarum gentium vocationi, & omnibus Apostolis, cunctisque Ecclesiæ partibus præponatur: vt quamuis in populi populo Dei multi Sacerdotes sint, multiq; Pastores, omnes tamen regat Petrus, quos principes ipsius. Magnum & mirabile huic vno consortium potestatis suae tribuit diuina dignatio, ...
units.tr: Since, then, the reasoning of all the foregoing arguments concludes that Peter had a unique power over the universal Church, a power that is shown in nature, illustrated in heaven, demonstrated typologically in the works of God, observed in the whole mystical body, and commended in the divine law and in the Gospel, you nevertheless, most acute of men, have ventured with certain flourishes of words to judge that his power was equal to that of the other Apostles, and to assert that it was granted to him by human rather than divine institution, either by the Apostles without diminution of their own power, or by the consent of the Church as a remedy for schism. In proof of your error you adduce the point that the other Apostles also received the keys (to use your own words) in a contested manner. To this, although I have shown above that the keys were handed on to the others as well, yet they were handed on to Peter before all, and for all, so that he named himself Peter from the rock, and placed in him the sacrament of this office, so that power is derived to them only through Peter, as from the head, and that not universally, but restricted within fixed limits. Nevertheless you thought it right to explain the opinions of three holy Fathers on this matter, so that they may build up those whom perhaps the poison of your words has infected. We could indeed heap up countless testimonies, but to those for whom a few do not suffice, many do not help. Let us first call up the blessed martyr Anacletus, close to the Apostles and the successor of Peter himself. Answering your madness, he begins thus in his decretal letter: "The most holy Roman and Apostolic Church holds its primacy not from the Apostles, but from the Saviour himself, as he said to the blessed Apostle: You are Peter." And after some words: "Among the blessed Apostles there was a certain distinction of power, and although all were Apostles, yet it was granted by the Lord to Peter, and they themselves willed the same among themselves, that he should preside over all the other Apostles, and that Cephas, that is, the head and beginning, should hold the Apostolate." Let the author of the canon also speak up, the herald of truth, Pope Leo, saying in the canon: "Thus our Lord Jesus Christ, the Saviour of the human race, ordained that the truth, which before was contained in the proclamation of the Law and the Prophets, should go forth for the salvation of all through the Apostolic trumpet, as it is written: Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. But the Lord willed that the sacrament of this office should pertain to the duty of all the Apostles, yet placed the highest headship of all the Apostles in the most blessed Peter, so that, as from a certain head, he might pour out his gifts upon the whole body, so that anyone who dared to depart from Peter's firmness would understand that he was excluded from the divine ministry. For he, taken into the fellowship of indivisible unity, was named by the Lord what he himself was, saying: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; so that the building of the eternal temple might come about through the wonderful gift of God's grace in the firmness of Peter, strengthening this Church also by his own steadfastness, so that human rashness could not assail it, nor the gates of hell prevail against it." And at once, as if foreseeing the heretic and blasphemer Gregory in spirit, he added: "But this rock, built with its most sacred firmness by God (as we have said), he presumes with impious daring to violate, whoever tries to break his power, not following what he has received from the ancients." Now let the trumpet of the Gospel sound; the priestly trumpet (I say), at whose sound, as once the walls of Jericho, so the bulwarks of Nestorius and Eutyches fell. That great Leo, whom the Council of Chalcedon acclaimed as the pillar of the faith, the ecumenical and apostolic one, to whose authority the Canon ascribes so much that whoever wishes to scrutinise his sayings down to the last detail and does not receive them all with reverence, let him be anathema: this Leo, then, in his sermon on his own ordination, speaks thus about the primacy of Peter: "It is useful and fitting, for the glory of the most blessed Apostle Peter, to raise the eye of the mind to contemplate him, who was so abundantly flooded with the streams of all gifts from that very fountain, that although he received much, he transmitted nothing to anyone without sharing it with him." And again in the same sermon: "From the whole world one Peter is chosen, who is set over both the calling of all nations and all the Apostles and all parts of the Church; so that, although there are many priests and many pastors among the people of God, yet Peter governs them all, along with those who are his principal ones. The divine condescension has bestowed upon this one man a great and wonderful fellowship of his power..."

units.la: ca: Ego dico tibi, quia tu es Petrus, hoc est, sicut tibi Pater meus manifestauit diuinitatem meam, tibi notam facio excellentiam tuam, quia tu es Petrus, id est, cum ego sim immobilis petra, ego qui facio utraque unum, ego fundamentum praeter quod nemo potest aliud ponere: tum tu quoque mea virtute solidatus, vt qua mihi potestate sunt propria, sint tibi participatione communia. Et dabo tibi claues regni caelorum, & quaecunque ligaueris &c. Transiuit quidem & in alios Apostolos ius potestatis istius, & ad omnes Ecclesiae Principes decreti huius constitutio commigrauit: sed non frustra vni commendatur, quod omnibus intimatur. Petro ideo singulariter hoc creditur, quia cunctis Ecclesiae Rectoribus Petri forma proponitur. Quid ergo hoc testimonio firmius, quid hac assertione stabilius esse potest? Et post haec tanta testimonia non erubescit insaniens, paritatem in Apostolis potestatis atque iurisdictionis asserere, & in augmentum sui erroris etiam impia veterum haereticorum argumenta non veretur congerere. Sic enim in superioribus dixit: Apostolos conciliariter congregatos, & ipsum Cephan in messem Domini transmisisse, quasi superioritatem ex missionis authoritate pronuntians. Hoc idem pronuntians argumentabatur impius Arrius, adstruens in diuinis personis inaequalitatem subesse, pro eo quod Filius & Spiritus sanctus mitti dicuntur. Ignorabat quippe, quod tu quoque ignoras, aut ignorare te simulas, triplicem missionis modum, vel secundum authoritatis imperium, prout Dominus seruum emittit, vel secundum originem, prout florem arbor producit (ex quo sensu missio licet sublimius atque ineffabilius dicitur in diuinis) vel secundum consilium, prout Consiliarii Regem mittere dicuntur ad bellum, cum tamen eundem ipse sit Dominus. Adiicere nos possumus missionem secundum amorem. His duobus extremis modis Samariam ab Apostolis missus est Petrus, consilio quidem illorum atque suasu, & amore eorum, ad quos mittebatur impulsus, cum inter Apostolos maiori auctoritate atque miraculorum gratia coruscaret. Haec quidem dicimus de vestrantes sermones tuos: neque enim aliam Petri in messem Domini legimus missionem. Nam forte Romam Petrum ex Antiochia a reliquis Apostolis asseris transmissum fuisse, quam te continuo mendacii falsitatisque conuincat Eusebius Caesariensis historiae Ecclesiasticae scriptor illustris, Marcellus Papa ac Martyr insignis, & magnus ille Leo vir authoritatis incomparabilis, qui diuina reuelatione & Dei institutu ad oppugnandum Simonem Magum testantur esse profectum. Sic namque secundo Ecclesiasticae historiae libro testatur: Ipsis Claudii temporibus diuinam clementiam probatissimum omnium Apostolorum, & maximum fidei magnificentia meritoque virtutis Principem, Petrum ad vrbem Romam velut aduersum humani generis perniciem communem deduxisse. Marcellus quoque beatissimus, scribens vniuersis Episcopis per Antiochiae constitutis prouinciam, in haec verba consentit: Rogamus vos dilectissimi, vt non aliud doceatis quam quod a beato Petro & a reliquis Apostolis accepistis. Ipse enim est caput totius Ecclesiae, cuius sedes apud vos fuit, quae postea iubente Domino Romam translata est. Leo quoque ad Petrum dirigens epistolam ita testatur: Iam Antiochenam Ecclesiam (vbi primum Christiani nominis dignitas exorta) fundaueras, iam Pontum, Galatiam, Cappadociam, Asiam atque Bithyniam legibus Euangelicae praedicationis impleueras. Nec aut dubius de prouentu operum, aut de sperio tua ignarus ad crucis Christi Romanis arcibus inferebas. Quodque diuinis praeparationibus anteibant & honor potestatis & gloria passionis, merito dixit, diuina praeordinatione id ante fuisse statutum, in quantum per Isaiam antea fuerat prophetatum, vrbem Romam orbis caput iugo Christi per Apostolorum Petri & Pauli praedicationem subigendam. Sic enim prophetauerat: Ciuitatem sublimem humiliabit & conculcabit eam pes pauperum, scilicet Christi, & egenorum, id est, Apostolorum Petri & Pauli, vt sacri expositores Doctores. Cui sententiae adstipulatur & beatus Ambrosius Doctor, diuinitus institutum fuisse confirmans, vt in vrbe Romana, qua caput obtinet Nationum, vno die & sub vno persecutore Apostolorum Principes paterentur, & vbi erat caput superstitionis, illic caput quiesceret Sanctitatis: & vbi gentilium principes habitabant, illic Ecclesiae principes morarentur.
units.tr: ca: I tell you that you are Peter, that is, just as my Father has revealed my divinity to you, so I make your excellence known to you, that you are Peter, that is, since I am the immovable rock, I who make both one, the foundation beside which no one can lay another; so you too, strengthened by my power, so that what belongs to me by my own power may be shared with you by participation. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind, etc. Indeed the right of this power passed also to the other Apostles, and the constitution of this decree migrated to all the leaders of the Church; but it is not without reason that what is announced to all is committed to one. It is believed that this was granted to Peter singularly, because Peter's form is set before all the rulers of the Church. What, then, can be firmer than this testimony, what more stable than this assertion? And after such great testimonies, this madman is not ashamed to assert equality of power and jurisdiction among the Apostles, and, to add to his error, he does not hesitate to heap up even the impious arguments of the old heretics. For he said above: that the Apostles, gathered in council, and Cephas himself, sent into the harvest of the Lord, thereby pronouncing superiority from the authority of the mission. Arius, the impious one, argued the very same thing when he pronounced it, maintaining that there is inequality among the divine persons, because the Son and the Holy Spirit are said to be sent. For he did not know, as you also do not know, or pretend not to know, that there is a threefold mode of sending: either according to the command of authority, as a master sends a servant; or according to origin, as a tree produces its flower (in which sense the sending is spoken of in divine things more loftily and ineffably); or according to counsel, as counsellors are said to send a king to war, although he is the same Lord. We may add the sending according to love. In these two last modes Peter was sent by the Apostles to Samaria, through their counsel and persuasion, and moved by their love towards those to whom he was sent, since he shone among the Apostles with greater authority and the grace of miracles. These things we say concerning your empty words; for we read of no other sending of Peter into the harvest of the Lord. For you assert that Peter was sent from Antioch to Rome by the rest of the Apostles; but this is refuted at once as a lie and a falsehood by Eusebius of Caesarea, the illustrious writer of Ecclesiastical History, by Marcellus the Pope and famous martyr, and by that great Leo, a man of incomparable authority, who bear witness that he set out to oppose Simon Magus by divine revelation and by the institution of God. For in the second book of his Ecclesiastical History he bears witness thus: In the very times of Claudius, the divine clemency led Peter, the most approved of all the Apostles and the greatest prince of the faith through the magnificence and merit of his virtue, to the city of Rome, as if against the common destruction of the human race. The most blessed Marcellus also, writing to all the bishops established throughout the province of Antioch, agrees in these words: We beg you, most beloved, that you teach nothing other than what you have received from the blessed Peter and the rest of the Apostles. For he is the head of the whole Church, whose see was among you, and which afterwards, at the Lord's command, was transferred to Rome. Leo too, addressing a letter to Peter, bears witness thus: You had already founded the Church of Antioch (where first the dignity of the Christian name arose), you had already filled Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia with the laws of the Gospel preaching. Nor, uncertain of the outcome of your works or ignorant of your own purpose, did you bring the cross of Christ to the citadels of Rome. And since both the honour of power and the glory of his passion preceded the divine preparations, he rightly said that this had been decreed beforehand by divine ordination, insofar as it had been prophesied earlier through Isaiah, that the city of Rome, the head of the world, was to be brought under the yoke of Christ through the preaching of the Apostles Peter and Paul. For he had prophesied: The lofty city he will bring low, and the foot of the poor will trample it, namely Christ, and the needy, that is, the Apostles Peter and Paul, as the holy expositors and teachers explain. The blessed teacher Ambrose also agrees with this opinion, confirming that it was instituted by God, so that in the Roman city, which holds the head of the nations, on one day and under one persecutor the princes of the Apostles should suffer, and where the head of superstition was, there the head of holiness should rest; and where the princes of the Gentiles dwelt, there the princes of the Church should remain.

units.la: Vides ergo, qui aliis obiiciebas, tenuem ... esse contextam, te nec tenuem quidem vanissimis argumentationibus texere potuisse, ... adhuc ordiretur, praecisam esse. Somniasti namque Petrum conciliariter fuisse transmissum: cum in Apostolico Concilio Petrus primus sententiam tulisse legatur: nec ipsum ab Apostolis & senioribus tunc conuenientibus Antiochiam missum, sed Barnabam & Sillam sacra Apostolorum actuum testetur historia. Ex Chrysippi aut Theophrasti te credo acumine argumenta talia mutuatum: ex ... genere illud dici potest, vt arguas Ecclesiam non vni capiti, sed omnibus pariter Apostolis esse commissam, pro eo quod hodie vsque erat Ecclesia, eorum protectione defensa. Quod sita ... nullum ordinem mansionum, nullam graduum differentiam arguamus in caelis: cum Ecclesia per singulas horas in communi commemoratione Dominum deprecetur, vt quorum merita recolis, eorum sanctae patrocinia. Ergo iam stella a stella non differet in claritate, & falsa diuersitas mansionum in caelo in Euangelio repromittitur. Illud vero qualis impudentiae? vt beatum Petrum ab Apostolis Principem constitutum sine propriae diminutione potestatis ... ex ipso constitutionis verbo Petri primatum ex Apostolis magis quam diuina institutione manasse significat: ac si coetus aliquis aut collegium Praelatus sibi praeficeret. Improbissime haereticorum, quis ista te docuit? Cum oes vere Euangelii textus Apostolorum electione, inter quos ... non vocatione, sed dignitate dictus est primus, usque ad ascensum Domini Salvatoris, Petri principatum aut promissum, aut figuratum, aut redditum eloquatur, ubi omnium cura immeditate committitur, Pasce oves meas. Quo verbo, ut beatus Chrysostomus scribit, significanter expressit, Loco mei praepositus & caput esto fratrum tuorum. Nonne haeresin tuam disertissime Nicolaus confutat in Canone dicens: Non quaelibet terrena sapientia, sed illud verbum, quo constructum est coelum & terra, per quod omnia condita sunt elementa, Romanam fundavit Ecclesiam, cuius privilegium ab ipso summo capite Ecclesiarum traditum, qui auferre conatur, hic proculdubio in haeresin labitur. Et eadem de Conciliis, a quibus quidam temere praelationem Ecclesiae Romanae concessam asseverabant, testatur beatus Pelagius dicens: Quamvis universa per orbem Catholicae instituta Ecclesia unius thalamus Christi sunt, tamen sancta Romana Ecclesia Catholica Apostolica nullis Synodiis constitutis ceteris Ecclesiis praelata est, sed Evangelica voce Domini & Salvatoris primatum obtinuit.
units.tr: You see, then, that you, who accuse others, could not weave even a thin fabric from the emptiest arguments, ... and that the thread was cut before the weaving had even begun. For you dreamed that Peter was sent out by a council, when the sacred history of the Acts of the Apostles records that Peter was the first to give judgment at the Apostolic Council, and that he was not sent to Antioch by the Apostles and elders gathered there, but Barnabas and Silas were. I believe you borrowed such arguments from the subtlety of Chrysippus or Theophrastus. It may be said that your kind of argument is this: you contend that the Church was entrusted not to one head but equally to all the Apostles, because the Church has until now been defended by their protection. Just as we do not argue that there is no order of dwelling places or difference of rank in heaven, since the Church, hour by hour in its common remembrance, prays to the Lord that, as it recalls their merits, so it may have the patronage of the saints, so there is no difference of brightness between one star and another, and the promise of different dwelling places in heaven in the Gospel is false. But what shameless impudence is this, to suppose that blessed Peter was set up as Prince of the Apostles without any diminution of his own power ... From the very wording of Peter's appointment it is clear that his primacy flowed from the Apostles rather than from divine institution, as if some company or college set a president over itself. Most wicked of heretics, who taught you this? When all the true texts of the Gospel show that Peter's primacy was promised, or prefigured, or given, while he was named first by the choice of the Apostles, among whom he was called first not by summons but by dignity, up to the ascension of the Lord and Saviour, where the care of all was committed to him at once: Feed my sheep. By this word, as blessed Chrysostom writes, he clearly expressed: Be set over my place and be the head of your brethren. Does not Nicholas refute your heresy most eloquently in the canon, saying: It was not some earthly wisdom but that Word by which heaven and earth were made, through which all the elements were created, that founded the Roman Church, whose privilege was handed down by the supreme Head of the Churches himself; whoever tries to take it away undoubtedly falls into heresy. And blessed Pelagius bears witness to the same about the councils, by which some rashly asserted that precedence had been granted to the Roman Church, saying: Although the whole Catholic Church established throughout the world is one bride of Christ, nevertheless the holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church has been set above the other Churches by no council, but has obtained the primacy by the evangelical voice of the Lord and Saviour.

units.la: Patet igitur, Apostolos non instituisse Petri primatum, sed Dominicae atque Evangelicae institutionis, quam noverant executos, illi humiliter detulisse. Sicut beatus Anacletus in Canone, Licet, inquit, omnes essent Apostoli, Petro tamen concessum est a domino, & ipsi inter se voluerunt idipsum, ut reliquis omnibus praeesset Apostolis. Notandum vero, quam fallaciter beati Hieronymi testimonium inducat, ut asserat vni ad schisma submovendum singulariter claves Ecclesiae permissas, id est, quasi haec sola fuerit divinii altitudo consilii, Petrum praeficere, ut scandala submoveret. Non illi satis est haereticum esse, nisi probatissimo omnium Catholicorum tractatorum similem notam infligat. Audi miser, quid Hieronymus sentiat, hoc nempe quod caeteri, & quod ex illius auctoritate Glossa ordinaria scribit super Matthaeum: Specialiter Petro claves concessit, ut ad unitatem nos instutaret. Ideo enim Principem Apostolorum constituit, ut Ecclesia haberet unum principalem Christi vicarium, ad quem diversa Christi membra recurrerent, si forte inter se dissentirent. Quod si diversa forent in Ecclesia capita, unitatis vincula rumperentur. Nonne & tibi videtur, & unitatis causam, & fidei convenientiam, & in vicariatu Christi plenitudinem potestatis & mystici corporis caput contra caput schismatis breui verborum serie coniunxisse? Si idcirco non sufficit, & Hieronymi de primatu Petri vis plenius nosse sententiam, ex aliis mutuare codicibus. Sed videbis in Commentariis super Matthaeum dicentem, Simonem propter fidem in petram Christum, Petri sortitum esse vocabulum: ac secundum metaphoram illi dictum, Aedificabo Ecclesiam meam: in quo manifeste primatus ipsius super totam Ecclesiam designatur. Intuere eundem scribentem ad Terentium, de vera circumcisione, & Novi Testamenti Patres Patribus veteribus comparantem, Petrum Apostolum Abrahae praeferentem, ut sicut illi generatio larga promittitur, ita huic generatio pascenda traditur, & cum ab illo iustificando procedant, in hoc iustificato fundantur. Et multa percurrens, Petrum dominici gregis Pastorem, Ecclesiae fundamentum, Apostolorum verticem clarissime profitetur. Lege rursus haeretice, quemadmodum apud Petri successorem Damasum fidem exponat: Ego, inquit, nullum primum nisi Petrum sequens, beatitudini tuae, id est, cathedrae Petri communicando consortio, super illam petram fundatam Ecclesiam scio. Quicumque extra hanc domum agnum comederit, prophanus est a lege. Iterum cum in libro Virorum illustrium tantum auctoritatis Petro attribuerit, ut a eo consummatum Evangelium esse testetur; Scripsit, inquit, Marcus Evangelium Romanis, rogatus a fratribus: quod cum Petrus audisset, probavit, & Ecclesia legendum sua auctoritate dedit. Ad quod Clementis etiam Papae inducit testimonium. Audi denique illum ad Augustinum de cap. ad Galatas differentem, tantum Petro tribuere, ut super illo, Ascendi autem secundum revelationem & expositi eis Evangelium, dicat, Paulum hisce ipsis verbis ostendere, non habuisse securitatem Evangelii praedicandi, nisi Petri & eorum, qui cum eo erant, fuisset sententia roboratum: Talia legens aut audiens de fine Catholico, define haereticorum prosecutioni tuae participationis inferre calumniam. Quae est enim societas lucis & tenebrarum, conventio Christi ad Belial, quae pars fidelis tecum, hominum perfidissime? Alterum rectius Hieronymum pro simili errore Constantiae damnatum allegare debueras, si tibi credi volebas. Nam de beatissimo viro, quod minus recte de ecclesiae institutione senserit, refugiunt aures Catholicorum audire.
units.tr: It is plain, therefore, that the Apostles did not institute Peter's primacy, but humbly yielded to it as an institution of the Lord and of the Gospel, which they knew had been carried out. So blessed Anacletus says in the canon: Although all were Apostles, yet the Lord granted the primacy to Peter, and they themselves willed among themselves that he should preside over all the other Apostles. But note how falsely he cites the testimony of blessed Jerome, to assert that the keys of the Church were given singularly to one man to remove schism, as if this alone were the purpose of the divine counsel, to set Peter over them so that he might remove scandals. It is not enough for him to be a heretic unless he also brands him with the same mark that the most approved of all Catholic writers bear. Wretched man, hear what Jerome thinks, namely what the others think, and what the Ordinary Gloss writes on Matthew from his authority: He gave the keys specially to Peter, so that he might instruct us in unity. For he appointed him Prince of the Apostles so that the Church might have one principal vicar of Christ, to whom the different members of Christ might have recourse, should they perhaps disagree among themselves. But if there were different heads in the Church, the bonds of unity would be broken. Does it not seem to you that in a short sequence of words he has joined the cause of unity, the agreement of faith, the fullness of power in Christ's vicariate, and the head of the mystical body against the head of schism? If that is not enough, and you wish to know Jerome's view of Peter's primacy more fully, borrow it from other books. But you will see him, in his Commentaries on Matthew, saying: Simon was called Peter because of his faith in Christ the rock; and by a metaphor it was said to him: I will build my Church. In this the primacy of Peter over the whole Church is plainly designated. Look also at the same writer, writing to Terentius about true circumcision, comparing the Fathers of the New Testament with the Fathers of old, and placing the Apostle Peter before Abraham: as to Abraham a large posterity was promised, so to Peter a posterity to be fed is delivered; and as they proceed from Abraham to justify, so they are founded in him who is justified. And running through many things, he most clearly professes Peter to be shepherd of the Lord's flock, foundation of the Church, summit of the Apostles. Read again, heretic, how he sets out his faith before Damasus, Peter's successor: I, he says, follow no first but Peter, and by communion with your blessedness, that is, with the chair of Peter, I know the Church is founded upon that rock. Whoever eats the lamb outside this house is profane under the law. Again, in his book On Illustrious Men, he attributed such authority to Peter that he testifies the Gospel was completed by him: Mark, he says, wrote the Gospel for the Romans at the request of the brethren; when Peter heard it, he approved it, and gave it to the Church to be read with his authority. To this he also adduces the testimony of Pope Clement. Finally, hear him, discussing in his letter to Augustine on the chapter to the Galatians, attributing so much to Peter that, on the words But I went up according to revelation and laid before them the Gospel, he says that Paul showed by these very words that he did not have security to preach the Gospel unless it had been confirmed by the judgment of Peter and of those who were with him. Reading or hearing such things from a Catholic writer, you ought not to bring against your own pursuit of heretics the charge of participation. For what fellowship has light with darkness, what agreement has Christ with Belial, what part has the faithful with you, most faithless of men? You ought rather to have cited Jerome against a similar error, condemned at Constance, if you wished to be believed. For Catholic ears shrink from hearing that this most blessed man thought less rightly about the institution of the Church.

units.la: Et quoniam beato quoque Ambrosio similem tentasti inferre calumniam, cum illum Pastorali dixisse refers, omnibus Apostolis claves vna fuisse contraditas, disce miser illum ita affirmare claves Apostolis pariter esse contraditas, ut tamen intelligat Petrum prae omnibus & pro omnibus claves regni coelorum accepisse: ut & unitas & praelatio demonstraretur in Petro. Quod ex ipsius scriptis in pluribus licet cognoscere, quibus illum fundamentum Ecclesiae, totius dominici gredis pastorem esse commemorat: cuius praelatio typice figuratur, cui navis regendi committitur, ut totius corporis Christianitatis compagem molemque contineat. Cogis nos de multis pauca proferre. Illustris ille Doctor in Commentariis super Lucam exponens eum locum, in quo Dominus in nauiculam Petri conscendisse perhibetur. Non turbatur, inquit, navis qua Petrum habet: turbatur illa qua Iudam habet. Et post pauca: Quemadmodum enim turbari poterit, cui praeratis, in quo fundamentum Ecclesiae est. Et deinde illius primatum in agnitione ac determinatione fidei attollens, ait: Denique & aliis imperatur, ut laxent retia in capturam. Soli tamen Petro dicitur, Duc in altum, hoc est, in profundum disputationum. Quid enim tam altum, quam altitudinem divinitatis videre, id est, scire Dei filium, & professionem divinae generationis assumere? Idem quoque de Apostolorum Principibus Petro & Paulo, quod emineant inter vniuersos Apostolos, & peculiari quadam virtute pcellant, satis euidens profert & omnibus notum testimonium, in quorum Martyrio Romanae Ecclesiae primatum ac singularem indicat dignitatem, uno loco illos occubuisse perhibens, ne alteri Roma diceret, atque in urbe quae principatum & caput obtinet nationum, ut illic caput quiesceret sanctitatis. Et reliqua leguntur in Canone, quae principatum Apostolicae sedis insinuant. De cuius principatus mystica in Euangelio figura alio loco sic loquitur: Est aliud piscandi genus, quo genere solum Petrum Dominus piscari iubet, dicens: Mitte hamum, & eum piscem, qui primum ascenderit, tolle. Ubi satis aperte demonstrat, per hamum intelligi iurisdictionem, qua Petrus praefuit vniuersis. Denique ut nulla tibi relinquatur tergiversandi occasio, ac fateaxis Ambrosium publice esse testatum, Petrum totius fuisse gregis pastorem, qui firmamentum sit Ecclesiae institutum, & non vnius tantum partis, sed totius Christianitatis velut mystici corporis compagem molemque continere, audi mihi huncipsum in Homilia apertius protestantem: Maiorem inquit, gratiam Petrus reperit, postquam fidem seperdidisse denegauit. Tanquam bonus enim pastor tuendum gregem accepit; ut is, qui sibi ante infirmus fuerat, fieret omnibus firmamentum, & qui interrogationis tentatione nutauerat, caeteros fidei stabilitate fundaret. Denique pro soliditate elevationis Ecclesiarum Petra dicitur, eo quod prius in nationibus fidei fundamenta posuerit, & tanquam saxum immobile totius corporis Christianitatis compagem molemque contineat. Desine haereticorum more truncata verba proferendo, tanti Praesulis calumniari sententias. Desine fidei ipsius puritati inferre calumniam: cuius omnes sententiae (beato teste Hieronimo) fidei Ecclesiae, & omnium virtutum firmae sunt columnae. Possem & aliorum sanctorum Patrum testimonia infinita congerere. Sed nimis praeposterum videretur, in re tam perspicua, quam totus orbis profitetur & noscit, quasi in recenti controversia exquirere testimonia: ut cum secundum humanas leges triginta annis praescribatur, primatus Petri post tot saecula disputatione temeraria ventiletur. At Hieronymi & Ambrosii non alia de causa subiecimus, nisi ut eorum rectam Catholicamque sententiam proferentes, ad tuae prauitatis robur de illorum auctoritate tribi non blandireris, & simpliciores quosque; eorum consideratione non falleres.
units.tr: And since you have also tried to bring a similar charge against blessed Ambrose, when you report that he said in his Pastoral Care the keys were entrusted to all the Apostles alike, learn, wretched man, that he so affirms that the keys were entrusted equally to the Apostles that he nevertheless understands that Peter received the keys of the kingdom of heaven before all and on behalf of all, so that both unity and primacy might be shown in Peter. This may be recognized from his writings in many places, where he calls Peter the foundation of the Church and shepherd of the whole Lord's flock, whose primacy is typically prefigured, to whom the ship is committed to be steered, so that it may hold together the frame and mass of the whole body of Christianity. You force us to bring forward few things out of many. That illustrious Doctor, expounding in his Commentary on Luke the passage where the Lord is said to have gone up into Peter's little boat, says: The ship which has Peter is not troubled; the ship which has Judas is troubled. And a little later: For how can that be troubled in which you are carried, in which is the foundation of the Church? And then, raising Peter's primacy in the acknowledgment and determination of the faith, he says: Finally, others are commanded to let down their nets for a catch. But to Peter alone it is said, Put out into the deep, that is, into the depth of disputations. For what is so deep as to see the depth of divinity, that is, to know the Son of God and to take up the confession of his divine generation? The same writer also, of the Princes of the Apostles, Peter and Paul, shows in a quite evident and well-known testimony that they stand out among all the Apostles and excel with a certain peculiar virtue; in their martyrdom he indicates the primacy and singular dignity of the Roman Church, saying that they died in one place, so that Rome should not say to the other, and in the city which holds the primacy and the headship of the nations, there the head of holiness might rest. And the rest is read in the canon, which insinuates the primacy of the Apostolic See. Of this primacy's mystical figure in the Gospel he speaks in another place thus: There is another kind of fishing, by which the Lord commands Peter alone to fish, saying: Cast the hook, and take up the fish which first comes up. Where he demonstrates quite plainly that by the hook is understood the jurisdiction by which Peter presided over all. Finally, so that no occasion of evasion be left to you, and that you may confess that Ambrose has openly testified that Peter was the shepherd of the whole flock, appointed as the firmament of the Church, and that he contains the frame and mass not of one part only but of the whole Christianity as of a mystical body, hear him himself in a homily declaring this more openly: Peter, he says, found greater grace after he denied that he had lost faith. For as a good shepherd he received the flock to be guarded, so that he who had been weak before should become a firmament to all, and he who had wavered under the temptation of the question should establish the others in the steadfastness of faith. Finally, for the solidity of the elevation of the Churches, he is called a rock, because he first laid the foundations of faith among the nations, and, like an immovable stone, contains the frame and mass of the whole body of Christianity. Cease, after the manner of heretics, from producing mutilated words and from slandering the opinions of so great a prelate. Cease from bringing a charge against the very purity of the faith, whose every opinion (as blessed Jerome bears witness) is the firm pillar of the faith of the Church and of all virtues. I could also heap up countless testimonies of other holy Fathers. But it would seem too absurd, in a matter so clear, which the whole world professes and knows, to seek testimonies as if in a recent controversy: as if, although by human laws a title is prescribed after thirty years, the primacy of Peter, after so many centuries, were to be tossed about in rash disputation. But I have added the words of Jerome and Ambrose for no other reason than that, by setting forth their right and Catholic opinion, you should not flatter the strength of your perversity by their authority, and that you should not deceive the simpler sort by their consideration.

units.la: Liquet igitur, te Orientalibus atque Bohemicis venenis imbutum talia protulisse, quae Petri primatum eiusque super omnem Ecclesiam principatum negarunt. Qui quidem error tam detestabilis atque grauis est, ut eos sanctus Doctor Thomas de Aquino illis haereticis comparauerit, qui Spiritum Sanctum a Patre Filioque procedere negant. Quoniam sicut CHRISTVS Dei filius Ecclesiam suam consecrat & consignat Spiritu sancto, quasi suo charactere & sigillo; ita CHRISTI vicarius suo primatu vniuersalem Ecclesiam, tanquam fidelis minister. Nec mirum quidem. Tales enim grauissimum schismatis reatum incurrunt, cuius tam immanis est culpa, ut (Augustino & Cypriano testibus) illam nec eleemosyna redimere, nec Baptismus abluere, nec pro CHRISTI nomine sanguis effusus valeat expiare. Hanc igitur tuam, quam sub verborum praestigiis contra primatum Petri declarasti sententiam, ex venenis Orientalis erroris procedentem, quidam ante te apud occiduas partes astruere conati sunt. Marsilius Patauinus & Iohannes de Iauduno, non veriti dicere, Apostolorum Principem Petrum, nec plus auctoritatis accepisse, nec pro reliquis Apostolis caput Ecclesiae diuinitus institutum. Hi quidem a Ioanne XXII. Pontifice iusto anathemate damnati sunt. Sed & Iohannem Wickleff, & sectatorem eius haereseos Iohannem Huss, eadem disseminantes magna Constantiensis Synodus condemnauit. Tu vero post damnationem eorum eandem haeresin instaurare moliris, & Catholicorum Principum auribus inculcare. Mirum profecto est, te, quorum actus imitaris, eorum exitus non perhorrescere. Quid ergo restat, nisi ut sancti illi beatissimique Pontifices excitentur, Felix atque Gelasius, haereticorum expugnatores acerrimi? quorum alter si viueret, nunc contra te ut quodam contra Achatium inclamaret: Gregorius non est factus erroris noui inuentor, sed veteris imitator, atque ideo non est necesse, ut aduersus eum noua sententia prodeat, sed vetus tantummodo renouetur. Quicunque enim in haeresin semel damnatam labitur, eius damnationi se inuolvit. Alter vero te perpetui anathematis mucrone ferit, ac diceret: Habeto cum his, quos libenter amplecteris, portionem, non cum honore & communione Catholica: nec nonetiam a fidelium numero segregatus, sublatum tibi nomen, & inimicus Christianae religionis agnosce, sancti Spiritus iudicio & Apostolica auctoritate damnatus, nunquam ab anathematis vinculis excipiendus.
units.tr: It is clear, then, that you have been steeped in Eastern and Bohemian poisons and have put forward views that deny Peter's primacy and his principate over the whole Church. This error is so detestable and grave that the holy doctor Thomas Aquinas compared those who hold it to the heretics who deny that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. For just as Christ, the Son of God, consecrates and seals his Church with the Holy Spirit, as with his own mark and seal, so the vicar of Christ, as a faithful minister, governs the universal Church by his primacy. Nor is this surprising. Such men incur the very grave guilt of schism, and its wickedness is so great that (as Augustine and Cyprian bear witness) neither almsgiving can redeem it, nor baptism wash it away, nor blood shed for the name of Christ atone for it. This opinion of yours, which you have declared against Peter's primacy under a cloak of words, springing from the poison of Eastern error, some men before you have already tried to establish in the Western parts. Marsilius of Padua and John of Jandun, not afraid to say it, held that the Prince of the Apostles, Peter, had received no greater authority, and that the headship of the Church had not been instituted by God over him in preference to the other Apostles. Indeed, these men were condemned with a just anathema by Pope John XXII. But the great Council of Constance also condemned John Wycliffe, and John Huss, a follower of his heresy, who spread the same doctrines. You, however, after their condemnation, are striving to revive the same heresy and to drum it into the ears of Catholic princes. It is truly remarkable that you, while imitating their deeds, do not dread their end. What remains, then, except that those holy and most blessed pontiffs, Felix and Gelasius, the most fierce conquerors of heretics, should be raised up? If the latter were alive, he would now cry out against you as he once did against Acacius: Gregory has not become the inventor of a new error, but the imitator of an old one, and so there is no need for a new judgment to be issued against him, but only the old one to be renewed. For whoever slips into a heresy once condemned becomes entangled in its condemnation. The former, indeed, would strike you with the sword of perpetual anathema and say: Have your portion with those whom you gladly embrace, not with the honour and communion of the Catholic Church; and, cut off even from the number of the faithful, recognise that your name has been taken away and that you are an enemy of the Christian religion, condemned by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by Apostolic authority, never to be released from the bonds of anathema.

units.la: APOLOGIA GREGORII HEIMBVRG CONTRA DETRACTIONES & blasphemias Theodoti Laelii Feltrensis Episcopi.
units.tr: APOLOGY OF GREGORY HEIMBURG AGAINST THE DETRACTIONS AND BLASPHEMIES OF THEODORUS LAELIUS, BISHOP OF FELTRE.

units.la: PVD Ciceronem in Officialibus suis duo iniustitiae genera leguntur, vnum scilicet eorum, qui inferunt, alterum eorum, qui ab his quibus infertur, dum possunt, non repulsant. Laeli Theodore, canis aduersum lupos ignaue, quid detecto clandestina fundis opprobria, me forte remorsurum suspicas si rescicam, quid tu furtim aduersum me fabricasti. Vt enim molossus pastorum amicus, & tutator gregum, per altas niues agere non desinā, qcunq; fera dabit. Actu Actu dente me petisti: vicissim attollo cornua, nec inultus flebo, tanquam puer lacessitus. Duas igitur eorum calumniatorum esse conditiones quisque facile deprehendit, quem nutantis mundi limor malignitatisque tentavit peruersitas. Quidam enim apertam leuitatem ostendere non erubescunt his, apud quos se primos omnium esse putant: qualem te Laeli esse iudico. Alii vero gravitatem simulantes, clam sunt factiosi: quales assero eos, qui te subornarunt, vanitates tuas suggerentes, ut eorum errores in te transferens retorsionis iacula pro iis excipias. Neuter vero vestrum in campum descendens palam audet occurrere.
units.tr: In Cicero's De Officiis we read of two kinds of injustice: one committed by those who inflict it, and the other by those who, though able to, do not repel it from those on whom it is inflicted. Laelius Theodorus, you are a lazy dog barking at wolves. When you are exposed, why do you pour out secret insults? Do you suspect that I will bite back if I learn what you have secretly fabricated against me? For just as a molossus, the shepherds' friend and guardian of the flocks, never stops driving off whatever beast it meets, even through deep snow, so I will drive you off. You have attacked me with your tooth, and in turn I raise my horns. I will not weep unavenged like a provoked child. Anyone who has been troubled by the fear of a tottering world or by the perversity of malice can easily see that these slanderers come in two kinds. Some do not blush to display their open levity before those whom they think are first of all. That is what I judge you to be, Laelius. Others, feigning gravity, are secretly factious. Those, I say, are the ones who put you up to it, feeding you your vanities, so that by transferring their errors onto you, you might take up the missiles of retort on their behalf. Neither of you dares to come down onto the field and confront me openly.

units.la: Primum me calumniaris blasphemiae pontificalis. Deinde Pontificem in me ritum iaculatum esse mentiris. Tertio me reum haeresis mendacissime criminaris. Haec certe propulsare in animo est, sed prius te ineptum et perplexum ostendere, qui quod in me arguis, flagitiosissime admittis, quin absque convicio, blasphemiis et contumeliis nec verbum proferis vllum. Tanta animo tuo criminandi libido incessit, ut gloriae cupido tenet eos, qui humilitatem simulantes de gloria contemnenda scribendo illis ipsis tabellis sua nomina ob gloriam inscripserunt: illico predentes sese criminum reos, quae ipsi alios accusando committunt. Sic Pseudosacerdotes, amicti pallio, pileoque operti, aliorum vitia foecundissime accusantes, intercutibus vitiis ipsi inadentes. Cum itaque vim et iniuriam propulsare, ac illatam referre, omnemque iniquitatem retorquere fas et iura sinant, et lex plane permittat, arguere mendacii eum qui alium falso criminatur; huc totius simultatis summa redit, uter utri prior iniuriam irrogaverit. Et hoc nunc tecum expostulare iuvat, de qua re sic accipe.
units.tr: First, you accuse me of blasphemy against the Pontiff. Then you lie that the Pontiff hurled a ritual curse at me. Third, you most mendaciously charge me with heresy. I certainly intend to repel these charges, but first I will show you, inept and confused as you are, that you commit most shamefully the very thing you accuse me of, and that you cannot utter a single word without slander, blasphemies and insults. Such a lust for accusing has seized your mind that it is like those who, feigning humility while writing against the contempt of glory, have inscribed their own names on those very tablets for the sake of glory. Immediately they betray themselves as guilty of the crimes they commit while accusing others. So too pseudo-priests, wrapped in cloaks and covered with caps, most copiously accuse others of their vices while being themselves smeared with hidden vices. Since right and law allow us to repel force and injury, to return the injury we have suffered, and to turn back all iniquity, and since the law plainly permits charging with lying the one who falsely accuses another, the whole sum of this quarrel comes down to this: which of us first inflicted injury on the other. It is worth pressing this point with you now, so take it as follows.

units.la: Ab Archiduce Austriae missus patruelem eius Sigismundum accessi, hortator pacis, totiusque mansuetudinis persuasor sollicitus, ne quidquam seuerius victori in victum statueret, nec fautores quondam victae partis inclementius pertractaret. Illicet mihi relatum est Cardinalem illum, quem tu laudibus effers, honorem Principis sui suggillasse, Ecclesiastica censura pro libito abusum, metallarias mineras, salinas inhiasse, et in summa statui Principis insidiatum esse. Quam coniecturam temporis suspicio exaggerabat, quo confinia illius principatus truculentus hostis invaserat, partim veronuper occuparat. Tunc ego animum meum paulisper suspendi, versans, volutans et cogitans, Cardinalem esse durum hominem et rigidum, acrem, immitem, inexorabilem, aliis persuasorem vehementem et acutum inventorem eorum, quae utrique dissidentium prodesse vel minus obesse videantur, suis tamen rebus afflictis minus consulentem, suisque motibus seu pathiis minime temperantem. Erat autem adhuc ira recens, ut non speraverim inflammata prideni pectoris restingui, animosque utrumque induratos permolliri posse. Mense continui, diem tempusque forsitan ipsum ratum leniturum iras. Cumque diutius cogitationis me fatigatio tenuisset, venit ecce familia Laurentii Blumenaw profuga, insidiis Pontificis clam elapsa, Laurentium Principis legatum apud Senas contra ius reuocandi domum vetusto iure gentium introductum nuncians ancestatum esse, et idcirco fugam adornasse: fugerit ne an comprehensus sit, parum sibi constare. Igitur ab omni spe pacis et concordiae seiectus, nil praeter refugium oppressorum habens, illud amplexus cum omni veneratione Pontificis reuerenter appellaui id est, appellandum esse persuasi. Recense iam, Laeli, si quid habes quod arguas. Missio quidem officiosa, paritio reuerentialis et obedientiaria, profecto honesta, adhortatio ac persuasio mansuetudine pietateque plenissima, remansio vero cum operarum exhibitione necessitatem habuit euidentem, etiamsi manus conserenda et gladio decertandum fuisset. Nam cuius officii susceptio honesta, etiamsi spontanea fuisset, eius impletio ineuitabilem affert necessitatem. Hoc, Laeli, iunior didicisti et in negotiorum gestione et in commodato rerum vel operarum optimo iure sanctum. Quid oro gratiae medicus referret, qui latentem morbi materiam movendo torpentem naturam excitaret, febrem provocando, tumque secedens nullum aegrotanti praeberet antidotum, dicens se perfunctum opera medicantis: aegre e contra quererentur se derelictum, ac satius se naturae sagacissimae potestati relictum esse. Rursus si quis rei militaris scientia peritus instruxisset aciem, militum ordines explicasset, praefectos in utrumque cornu constituere iussisset, primipilum pila emittere signo dato monuisset, pugna vero iam in manus, iam ad gladios, ubi Mars est atrocissimus, veniente discedat, praetendens se Imperatoris vel Ducis opera defunctum: nam si turbatis ordinibus nemo restituat, rem deficientem nemo sufficiat, labentem nullus erigat vel inclinantem sustineat, speculator alta rupe considens, vel Tiburno littus oberrans, Gnatonicus rite conclamet: Ita Pyrrhus saepe fallitavit. Nunc contra haec quid Pontifex, vel (quod ego verisimilius duco) Cardinalis tuus machinatus est, aspice. Nam qualis Pleiadum choro stridente nubes Auster exercet undas indomitas, tales ducta Cusani contra me fulminauit epistolas, quibus et me comprehendi, bona mea confiscari, ac in me velut haereticum animaduerti iussit; et haec omnia me clam ferocissimis hostibus meis proditorie demandata sunt: quasi me uno intercepto a ceruicibus suis periculum omne depulissent, suaque machinamenta in tuto collocassent. Quod hinc coniicere licet. Est mihi rus quoddam vinetis foecundum, fontium eruptione salubre, decursu insuper amnis ac rubetis littoreisque hortulis amoenum, quo me vindemiae tempore conferre solebam. Ibi me coniux operiebatur Exspectatus adueni, deliciis autumnalibus cum fructu dulcis musti potituros: iam etenim grauis Autumnus fluxerat vuis. Aestatis vero suauitatem negotiorum praefatorum functio praeoccuparat.
units.tr: Sent by the Archduke of Austria, I approached his cousin Sigismund. I came as an advocate of peace and an anxious persuader of all gentleness, to urge that the victor should decree nothing too severe against the vanquished, and should not treat the former supporters of the defeated side too harshly. At once I was told that that Cardinal whom you praise had insulted the honour of his prince, abused ecclesiastical censure at his pleasure, coveted the metal mines and salt works, and in short plotted against the prince's state. The suspicion of the moment magnified this conjecture, since a fierce enemy had invaded the borders of that principality and had in part recently seized some of them. Then I held my mind in suspense for a while, turning the matter over and thinking that the Cardinal was a hard and rigid man, sharp, harsh and inexorable, a vehement persuader of others and a subtle inventor of whatever seems to help or harm either side of the disputants, yet little concerned for his own afflicted affairs and not at all restrained in his own emotions and passions. Anger was still fresh, and I did not hope that the inflamed pride of either breast could be quenched or the two hardened minds softened. I resolved to wait several months, hoping that time itself, once settled, would soften the anger. But when the weariness of thinking had worn me down for a long while, behold, the household of Laurence Blumenau arrived, fugitives who had escaped secretly from the snares of the Pontiff. They announced that Laurence, the Prince's envoy at Siena, had been summoned home contrary to right, by an ancient custom of nations, and that he had therefore made preparations for flight, though they were not sure whether he had fled or been seized. Therefore, cast out from all hope of peace and concord, and having nothing but the refuge of the oppressed, I embraced that refuge with all reverence and appealed to the Pontiff, that is, I was persuaded that an appeal must be made. Now review, Laelius, whether you have anything to charge me with. The mission was indeed a dutiful one, my obedience reverent and obliging, surely honourable; my exhortation and persuasion were full of gentleness and piety. But my staying on, with the performance of services, was an evident necessity, even if hands had had to be joined and the matter decided by the sword. For the fulfilment of an office honourably undertaken brings an unavoidable necessity, even if it was voluntary at first. You learned this, Laelius, as a young man, that in the management of affairs and in the loan of goods or services it is held sacred by the best law. What would a physician of grace achieve who, by stirring up the hidden matter of disease, roused a sluggish nature by provoking fever, and then, withdrawing, offered the patient no antidote, saying that he had finished his work as a healer, while the sick man complained bitterly that he had been abandoned and that he would have been better left to the power of nature, the wisest of all? Again, if someone skilled in the science of war had drawn up a battle line, arranged the ranks of soldiers, ordered the commanders to be placed on either wing, and warned the chief centurion to hurl his javelins at the signal; and then, when the fight had already come to hand and to swords, where Mars rages most fiercely, he withdrew, pretending that his work as commander was finished. For if no one restores the disordered ranks, no one supplies what is failing, no one raises the fallen or supports the one who is sinking, then the scout, sitting on a high rock or wandering along the Tiburtine shore, should properly cry out, as the Gnatonic parasite would: "Thus Pyrrhus often deceived." Now look at what the Pontiff, or (as I think more likely) your Cardinal, has contrived against these things. For as the south wind stirs the untamed waves when the chorus of the Pleiades is stormy, so the letters of Cusanus thundered against me. By them he ordered me to be arrested, my goods confiscated, and me punished as if I were a heretic. All these things were treacherously committed to my fiercest enemies, secretly, as if by seizing me alone they could remove all danger from their own necks and place their machinations in safety. This may be conjectured from what follows. I have a certain estate, fertile with vines, healthful with the gushing of springs, and pleasant with the course of a stream, with brambles and little shore gardens. It was there that I used to go at vintage time. My wife was waiting for me there. I came, expected, to enjoy the delights of autumn and the fruit of sweet must, for heavy Autumn had already flowed over the grapes. The sweetness of summer had been taken up beforehand by the business I have mentioned.

units.la: Illicet mihi structæ sunt insidiæ. Fœlix & fatale negotium emersit, quod me à deliciis ad partes Rheni auocauit, simulque insidiarum molimina dissoluit. Namque (vt fieri assolet) negotium aliud ex alio partum inibi me detinuit, donec hyemis asperitas solum omne frigoribus, niuibus rigentique pruina confunderet. Mirati sunt insidiatores mei, tam breui velut puncto temporis sui a destinationis certissimæ versa esse momenta. Postquam enim horrida tempestas cœlum contraxerat, siluæque Threicio Aquilone personarent, satius duxi foco iunctis vlmis curas domi resoluere, quam stridentibus campis aut ruri incumbere glaciali; neque aliud orauì, quam vt perennia hæc mihi munera stabiliret DEVS. Erant insidiæ non satis caute creditæ, sed partim in aure rimosa depositæ, hinc effluentes meas vsque manarunt aures. Egomet mecum sic cogitaui: Insidias mihi paratas sors disturbauit: Posthæc abeuntem me negotia vexantaliena: centum per caput & circum latus saliunt quietis impedimenta: labuntur misero dies inter vota clamanti! O rus dulce, an vnquam te aspiciam, salicíis, corylis viuíbusque redimitum! O quando licebit sub alta pinu aut inter densas corylos somno vacare, & inertibus horis iucunda obliuia fouere sollicitæ vitæ! O stultas precationes meas! Nam si DEVS votis meis annuisset, insidias incidissem exitiales. Quam porro prudenter Socrates nil certum à se-peri postulandum esse monuit. Nam qui facile bona dare solet, ipse nouit precanti quid expediret. Ergo qui veris iucundi, mollis æstatis, autumnique patris dulces illecebras concedere noluit, genialis hyemis quietem propicie concessit. Iam etenim frustratis insidiatorum concinnamentis, hostes ab omni mei persecutione disterritos esse rebar, vt me velut numine diuino defensum pertinacius à modo persequi sacrilegium esse ducerent. Curas abieci, conuiuia lætus instauraui, ceu nautæ, qui per saxa & per scopulos, æstuosaiv e Syrtes varie diuque iactati, optatum tandem portum saluis attigere carinis. Tanto vero amplius gaudendum mihi esse duxi, quod expers omnis curæ tantorum hostium dolos & astutias inscius euasi. At cum insidiatores iam desperassent me personaliter comprehendere, virus iamdiu retentum passim effudere, brevia illa virulenta circumquaque dispergendo, si quem forte fortunis meis inuidentem vel auentem res meas excitare, vel aduersum me prouocare possent. Hæc tamen palam ad me, dulci fortuna plusquam Falerno bacchatum, perlata rursum commouerunt. Et quis, inquam, finis insidiarum? quid peccaui, quid commerui? Vah mihi vni tot laqueos tendi, aliud profecto agitur, aliud vero prætenditur. Repetebam ergo mecum nuper æui gesta præteriti, dum Pontifex apud Mantuam bellum in Turcos appararet, vel (si vera potius quam dictu speciosa dicenda sunt) pecuniam ex omni Germanicæ nationis statu sub prætextu belli apparandi elicere cogitaret. Cuius doli suspicionem peperit Cardinalis tui, quem Pontifex tractatui adhibuit, astutia iam dudum per Germaniam longe lateque recognita. Omni quippe succo iam pridem per Iubilæum exhausto, Cardinalis ipse, velut non missura cutem, nisi plena cruoris hirudo, tenaciter hæsit, auarior psyllo vel sanguisua. Nouis enim ac supererogatiuis indulgentiis, tosta post iecora medullas ex ossibus suxit. Verumtamen ne vana suspicione aut opinione temeraria spectatam aliis fortasse virtutem violasse criminarer, certius experimentum censui esse faciendum, an reuera esset in Pontifice Turci nedum inuadendi, sed efficaciter oppugnandi ardor, an Pontifex & Cardinales composito niterentur. Est autem modus experientiæ sumendæ non vilis, nec infimis solum, sed & summis quoque conueniens, præcipue autem audaciæ plenis viris, quem ego statim aduenientes sensi & in Pontifice & Cardinali facile eucnire posse. Ostensum est enim illis, qui rem dubiam aggredi se velle asserunt, permagnum esse negotium, magnorumque laborum ac difficultatum, & periculosæ plenum opus alere, in quo etiam aliqua nedum pusilla, sed etiam meniocris victoria explicata parum boni, parum frutus sit allatura: at ex diuerso plurimum mali res quantulumque addubitat. Id ego proceribus primo persuasis, ad Pontificem detuli, adiiciens alia plura, quæ introducendis & pabulandis exercitibus castrisque locandis, impedimentis bellicis euehendis, traiiciendis fluminibus, & receptationi militum potissime sunt prouidenda. Maxime autem illud commemoraui, quod scriptores rei militaris præcipue admonuerunt, quo pacto militum concordia foueatur. In cuius considerationis pondere præcipue versatur, Imperatorem Romanorum (qui capitis occupat locum) & Hunnorum Regem super Hungariæ regno dissidentes in gratiam reducere. Et hic labor, hoc opus, si nobilis exercitus regionibus illis concredi debeat? Neque enim Hunnorum Rex Imperialem exercitum receptet, neque enim Christi hostes oppugnet, nisi statui suo prius cauto. Et hoc idem circa plerosq; alios Imperii proceres conditio temporis adhortatur. Parum enim sunt bella foris, nisi est consilium domi: pulcherrimorum exemplorum est plena vetustas, sed ea prolixa nec satis opportuna relatu.
units.tr: Straightaway I was set upon by plots. A happy and fateful business then arose, which called me away from my pleasures to the Rhine country and at the same time broke up the schemes against me. For (as usually happens) one matter led to another and kept me there until the harshness of winter buried all the land under frost, snow and stiff rime. My would-be ambushers were astonished that the course of things, which seemed so firmly fixed, had changed in so brief a moment. For once the bristling storm had drawn the sky together and the woods were ringing with the Thracian north wind, I thought it better to settle my affairs at home by the fire, among the elms, than to bend over the windswept, icy fields in the country. I prayed for nothing else than that God would make these lasting gifts secure for me. The plots had been entrusted to a not sufficiently careful ear, and some were laid in a leaky ear, and from there they flowed out and soon reached my own ears. I reasoned with myself thus: fortune has upset the snares laid for me. Henceforth, as I go away, other people's business plagues me; a hundred hindrances to my rest leap about my head and around my sides; my days slip by while I cry out my prayers in misery! O sweet countryside, shall I ever see you again, crowned with willows, hazels and living osiers! O when shall I be allowed to rest under a tall pine or among the thick hazels, and in idle hours to cherish the pleasant forgetfulness of a troubled life! O foolish prayers of mine! For if God had granted my wishes, I would have fallen into deadly snares. How wisely Socrates warned that nothing certain should be asked of the gods. For he who is accustomed to give good things readily knows what is expedient for the one who prays. Therefore he who was unwilling to grant me the true delights of pleasant spring, soft summer and the sweet allurements of autumn, the father of fruit, graciously granted me the quiet of a mild winter. Indeed, with the schemes of my ambushers frustrated, I supposed that my enemies had been scared off from all pursuit of me; they would think it sacrilege to persecute more stubbornly one who seemed protected as by a divine power. I cast off my cares and happily renewed my feasts, like sailors who, tossed about variously and for a long time among rocks and reefs and the seething Syrtes, at last reach the longed-for harbour with their ships saved. And I thought I had all the more reason to rejoice, that, free from all care, I had escaped the tricks and cunning of so great enemies without knowing of them. But when my ambushers had now despaired of seizing me in person, they poured out the venom they had long kept back, scattering on all sides little virulent pamphlets, in case they might perhaps stir up someone who envied my fortune or who wished for my property, or might provoke him against me. Yet these things, carried openly to me, who was flushed with a fortune sweeter than Falernian wine, again stirred me. And what, I ask, is the end of these ambushes? What have I done, what have I deserved? Alas, so many snares are laid for me alone; surely one thing is being done and another is being pretended. So I recalled to myself the deeds of the past age, when the Pontiff was preparing war against the Turks at Mantua, or (if one must speak of what is true rather than what sounds fine) was planning to extract money from every estate of the German nation under the pretext of preparing war. The suspicion of this trickery arose from your Cardinal, whom the Pontiff admitted to his counsels, a cunning man whose reputation has long been known far and wide throughout Germany. For when all the juice had long since been drained out by the Jubilee, the Cardinal himself clung tenaciously, like a leech that will not let go of the skin unless it is full of blood, more greedy than a flea or a leech. For by new and supererogatory indulgences he sucked the marrow from the bones after roasting the livers. Nevertheless, lest I should wrongly accuse him, on a vain suspicion or rash opinion, of having violated a virtue perhaps esteemed by others, I judged it more certain to make an experiment: whether there really was in the Pontiff not merely a readiness to attack the Turk, but a real zeal to fight him effectively, or whether the Pontiff and the Cardinals were striving for something else under a pretence. Now there is a method of making such a trial which is not cheap, and suits not only the lowly but the highest too, especially men full of boldness; I perceived it at once on my arrival and thought it could easily be brought about in the Pontiff and the Cardinal. For it was shown to those who say they wish to undertake a doubtful enterprise that it is a very great undertaking, full of great labours and difficulties and perilous toil, in which even a small, or indeed a moderate, victory, once achieved, will bring little good and little fruit; whereas on the other hand, the outcome, however small, casts a great deal of doubt on the matter. I first persuaded the nobles of this, and then reported it to the Pontiff, adding many other points, which must chiefly be provided for: the raising and feeding of armies, the placing of camps, the moving of baggage trains for war, the crossing of rivers, and the reception of soldiers. But I chiefly recalled that point which the writers on military affairs most especially advise, by which the harmony of soldiers is fostered. The weight of this consideration rests chiefly on reconciling into harmony the Emperor of the Romans (who holds the place of head) and the King of the Huns, who are at odds over the kingdom of Hungary. And this is a labour and a task, if a noble army is to be entrusted to those regions. For the King of the Huns will neither receive the imperial army nor attack the enemies of Christ, unless first his own position is secured. And the condition of the times urges the same thing with regard to most of the other nobles of the Empire too. For wars abroad are of little use unless there is good counsel at home. Antiquity is full of most splendid examples, but they are too long and not sufficiently suitable to relate.

units.la: Nostræ autem ætatis referre libet exemplum familiare, quo inclita Elisabetha Vngariæ regina cum recolendæ memoriæ Vladislao Rege Poloniæ inducias depacisci maluit, ne priuata contentio vniuersæ Christianæ Reipublicæ pareret detrimenta. Porro si sit alicubi huius rei iudicium, etiam alia dicerem clariora hiis, quæ dixi, probaremque manifeste me suasisse, Papam vero recusasse ea, in quibus si mihi paritum esset, longe melius & honestius omnia (vt mea fert opinio) processissent. Sed verba mortuo feci, narrauì surdo fabulam. Aliud nempe animum eius sollicitauit, qui de belli administratione ne verbum quidem facere vel audire sustinuit: Sed pecuniæ per Clericos & Laicos, sed etiam Hebræos conferendæ sollicitior fuit. Cardinalis verò tuus palam censuit his omnibus post habitis in Deo spem nudam esse ponendam. Quod nil aliud est, quam rem omnem nullo consilio administrare, sed temeritati audaciaeque permittere. Non tamen adeo spem firmam in Deo reposuit, quin in exigenda pecunia remorari vellet, qui nusquam virtuti vel gratiae locum esse putat, nisi effusae affluant opes. E contra verò & proceres & ego vnatati, non esse audendum vel experiundum facinus, cuius tota salus ex etentu fortunae penderet: summi Scipionis auctoritate, eiusque disciplinae testis adprime idonei censentis, nullam esse negligentiam ignaviorem, quam eam quae violentiae Martis permittitur: neque enim sarciri, purgari vel emendari potest eiusce iactura, & accepta clade turpe est dicere, Non putaram. Haec dum ipse tacitus mente agitarem, illamque truculentam epistolam seu breue Papale legendo repeterem, qua summa crudelitas in me fortunaque meas proditorie conflata videbatur, & ne gratuita crudelitas esset, bona mea in precium concedebantur quibusque violentis, (haec sunt enim illius epistolae verba: Et bona quaecunque habet apud vos, tam mobilia quam etiam immobilia, fisco vestro applicetis, &c.) rursus ad appellationem, libertatis & innocentiae tutamen praesidiumque, aduersus furorem Pontificis scutum & clypeum, sed Mantuae iampridem euersum, animum aduerti. Cumque in illa nil impium, nil despicabile, nil contumeliosum inuenissem, mirabar quid tantam iracundiam tantumque furorem in animo Pontificis excitasset, quid commouisset bilem, ut tam felleos humores euomuerit, aut fortasse ipsa vltionis & irae satiandae dulcedo animum fragilem distenderet. Inter cogitandum autem Oratores Principum nostrorum a Caesare dimissi redierunt, omnia inibi dicta factaque referentes, maxime autem illius appellationis notam, quae contra Pontificis auaritiam & Imperatoris astutiam ad vniuersale Concilium postea interiecta fuit, recitantes. Et quia eundem ludum continuo luserat Pontisex, eandem cecinit cantilenam, videlicet machinationem eliciendae pecuniae cum suis censuris, cum Caesaris auctoritate pertinacissime prosequendo: illic pedum visa est via, illicet Pontificis detecta versutia. Haec illa haeresis Gregorii, strenuitas in repugnando, constantia in resistendo auaritiae Pontificiali, & in consulendo dirigendoque perseuerantia. Hoc sacrilegium Gregorii, libertatis fomentum & eleuamen oppressorum, ac defensio sacrorum Conciliorum, quorum auctoritas per constitutionem Mantuanam euertebatur. Haec laesae Maiestatis noxa, exigendae per Germaniam grauis collectae molimina disturbata. Hinc vulnus sub pectore Papae seruatum intumuisse, aut cicatrix obducta putruisse comperta est, ira in me Pontificis Mantuae caelata & compressa, tam crudeliter aduersus me erumpente, ut absque vlla vocatione bona mea concederet in precium crudelitatis. Cense nunc, Laeli, si quid moderationis habes, an hoc sit iudicare, an potius saeuire pro libitu. Numquid iustus fuit zelus in me, qui me in fauorem mirae nationis accendit, ut exclamarem, Vis consilii expers, & iniuriam meam retorquerem. Frustra ergo, Laeli, me criminaris (sibilans anguis) blasphemiae pontificalis: qui a Pontifice dolose petitus, persona rebusque pulsatus iniurias structas propulsaui. Assentando verò Pontifici, o vulpes ganniens, ais, illi imitari Christi, qui cum maledicetetur, non maledicebat. Si Christum imitatus ipse fuisset, nullas mihi personales aut reales struxisset insidias, neque Monachum scurram elegisset, qui vanitates eius per orbem disseminasset. Subdis Laeli procacissime, nuncupando me bestiam inter luxum epulasque sudantem. Miror si in capripedes Satyros aures acueris qui iam saliaribus dapibus habebis assuescere pontificatus. Teque bis stultem facere dico, qui Pontifex ipse Pontificum arguis coenas, summosque viros accusas, ex quibus Coruinus, quanquam Socraticis madens sermonibus, Masticum lectum vinaque promere iussit languidiora. Sed & prisci Catonis vigor legitur mero caluisse: quod lene tormentum adhibet ingenio plerunque duro. Sed ne me putes nocturno certare mero, putere diurno, nimium laeue mancoque tempore nobis exprobras voluptatem. Non est nobis suauium rerum suppetentia, nonnunquam aper Austro leui putidus, lardumue rancidum prima iratum ventrem escapacauit. Deinde Chiam vel Mareoticum, sed maris expers, me potauit sitientem. Optassem fauces obsurduisse, narelque obturatas, ne gustus vel odoratus compatérentur. Posthac rescisces singula, cum mansuescet vtrinque animus rancore iraque defaecatus. Quosdam Pontifices ais in plagam Orientis contra accusatores suos Tomos scribentes satisfecisse. Id certè valere sino, tuis Satyris tragicisve scriptis hanc apologiam obiicio. Subnectis, Pium Pontificem eloquentiae flumine manantem, omnes facile superare. Hic pol recte sapis, siquidem est sapere, summos viros assentationum laqueis infascinare. Vnde certè tibi non minima merces rei speique refulsit. Satis caute scisti vti toro. Quisquis enim Regibus uti scierit, holus fastidiet pauone rhomboque satiandus. Non cuiuis homini contingit pontificari. Sed missam faciamus ironiam. Iamdudum ego conspexi, perditissime Laeli, & nunc etiam prospicio, opes & priuatorum & dominantium quanto maiores sunt, tanto magis obtrectatores adulatoresque; ac turpium voluptatum machinatores nutrire: quo nil perniciosius gignit opulentia atque potestas. Nosti voces Sirenum & pocula Circes: quae si bibisset dux Ithacus, turpis certe vixisset & excors. Optarem ergo, Pontificę aduersus huiuscemodi blanditias aures pice obturare, quam adulationibus se sinere capi. Postea certas maledictis, homo mendacissime, donec veniam petas stylirudioris: quasi nos nitori plus quam veritati studeamus, quod mihi super omnia visum est impudentissimum. Nisi forte nitor. m (sermonis vocas verum dicere, quod si facis, profiteor me nitoris & expolitionis peritissimum esse. Nam qui meam inuenturem diligentius obseruauit, facile coniiciet mihi quanda dicendi facultatem à natura profectam inesse: quisquis studia mea considera[illegible, ~6 letters], quia vere hospes & advena sum rhetoricæ adulationis: qui etiam in Physicis, Ethicis, Metaphysicis disciplinis adolescentiam consumpsi meamque inuentam.
units.tr: I should like to cite a familiar example from our own age: the illustrious Elisabeth, Queen of Hungary, together with King Władysław of Poland, of blessed memory, preferred to make a truce rather than let a private quarrel bring harm to the whole Christian commonwealth. Moreover, if there is any judgment on this matter, I could cite other examples clearer than these, and I would show plainly that I advised this course, while the Pope refused what, if he had obeyed me, would (in my opinion) have turned out far better and more honourably in every way. But I spoke to a dead man; I told my tale to a deaf man. His mind was occupied with something else: he would not so much as say or hear a word about the conduct of the war, but was more anxious to raise money from clergy and laity, and even from the Jews. Your Cardinal openly declared that, all these other matters being set aside, bare hope in God must be placed in the first place. That amounts to nothing other than conducting the whole affair without any plan, and leaving it to recklessness and daring. Yet he did not place his hope in God so firmly that he did not want to linger over collecting the money, since he thinks that virtue and grace have no place anywhere unless wealth flows in abundance. On the other hand, the nobles and I agreed that no deed should be attempted or tried whose whole safety depended on the outcome of fortune. By the authority of the great Scipio, a witness thoroughly qualified in such matters, who judged that no negligence is more cowardly than that which is left to the violence of Mars: for such a loss cannot be made good, cleansed or repaired, and once a defeat has been received, it is shameful to say, I did not think it would happen. While I was turning these things over silently in my mind, and re-reading that savage letter, or brief, from the Pope, in which the greatest cruelty and the ruin of my fortunes seemed to be treacherously plotted, and so that the cruelty should not be without profit, my goods were put up for sale, and (for these are the words of that letter: And whatever goods you have among you, both movable and immovable, you shall apply to your treasury, etc.) I turned my attention again to the appeal, the protection and defence of liberty and innocence, the shield and buckler against the Pope's fury, though it was long since overthrown at Mantua. And when I found nothing impious, nothing contemptible, nothing insulting in it, I wondered what had stirred up so great anger and so great fury in the Pope's mind, what had roused his bile so that he vomited forth such bitter humours; or perhaps the very sweetness of revenge and of satisfying his wrath had swollen his fragile spirit. While I was pondering this, the envoys of our princes, dismissed by the Emperor, returned, reporting everything said and done there, and above all reciting the note of that appeal which was afterwards lodged, against the Pope's greed and the Emperor's craft, before a general Council. And because the Pope had been playing the same game all along, he sang the same tune, namely the scheme of extracting money by his censures, pursuing it most obstinately with the Emperor's authority: there the path was seen, and there the Pope's cunning was at once laid bare. This was the "heresy" of Gregory: his vigour in opposing, his steadfastness in resisting papal greed, and his perseverance in advising and directing. This was Gregory's "sacrilege": a fomenter of liberty and a relief of the oppressed, and a defender of the sacred Councils, whose authority was being overthrown by the Mantuan constitution. This was the injury to majesty: the schemes for exacting heavy levies throughout Germany were disrupted. Hence it was discovered that the wound kept under the Pope's breast had swollen, or that a scar, once formed, had festered; the Pope's anger against me, hidden and suppressed at Mantua, broke out so cruelly against me that without any summons he gave away my goods as the price of cruelty. Now consider, Laelius, if you have any moderation, whether this is to judge, or rather to rage at will. Was my zeal against him unjust, when it kindled me in favour of a remarkable nation, so that I cried out, Force without wisdom, and turned his injury back upon him? So, Laelius, you accuse me in vain of papal blasphemy, you hissing serpent: I, who was treacherously assailed by the Pope and struck in person and property, repelled the plots laid against me.
