But flattering the Pope, you yelping fox, you say that he imitated Christ, who, when he was cursed, did not curse back. If he had imitated Christ himself, he would not have laid personal or material traps for me, nor would he have chosen a buffoon monk to spread his follies throughout the world. You go on, Laelius, most insolently, calling me a beast sweating amid luxury and feasts. I wonder whether you will prick up your ears like goat-footed satyrs, since you are already going to become accustomed to the salt-cured banquets of the papacy. And I say that you make yourself twice a fool, when you, a Pope's man yourself, accuse the Pope's dinners and blame the greatest men, among whom Corvinus, though soaked in Socratic discourse, ordered that a Massic couch and wines of a gentler kind be brought out. Indeed, the vigour of the old Cato is said to have been warmed by undiluted wine, which is a gentle torment for a mind that is generally hard. But lest you think I am contending with wine by night and stinking of it by day, you reproach us for a pleasure too cheap and too scanty for our time. We do not have a plenty of pleasant things; sometimes a boar, foul from a gentle south wind, or rancid lard, has belched forth to our angry stomach. Then they gave me Chian wine, or Mareotic, but without sea water, to drink when I was thirsty. I should have wished my throat to have grown deaf and my nostrils stopped up, so that neither taste nor smell might suffer. Hereafter you shall learn each thing, when my spirit has grown gentle on both sides, purged of rancour and anger. You say that certain Popes satisfied their accusers by writing volumes in the Orient against them. I will certainly let that pass; against your satires or tragic writings I set this apology. You add, That the pious Pope, flowing with a river of eloquence, easily surpasses all. Here, by Pollux, you are right, since it is wisdom to ensnare great men with the nets of flattery. From this, certainly, no small reward for your purpose and hope has shone upon you. You have learned well enough how to use a couch. For whoever knows how to use kings will disdain cabbage, and be satisfied with peacock and turbot. It does not fall to every man to be a Pope. But let us drop the irony. I have long since observed, most abandoned Laelius, and I still see, that the greater the wealth and power of private men and rulers, the more they nourish detractors and flatterers, and contrivers of shameful pleasures; nothing breeds more ruin than riches and power. You know the voices of the Sirens and the cups of Circe; if the leader of Ithaca had drunk them, he would certainly have lived basely and senselessly. I would therefore wish that the Pope had stopped his ears with pitch against such flatteries, rather than letting himself be taken by adulation. Afterwards, you, most lying fellow, are sharpening your wits with abuse, until you beg pardon for a cruder style: as if we cared more for polish than for truth, which seems to me the most shameless thing of all. Unless perhaps you call the telling of the truth the polish of style; if you do, I declare that I am most skilled in polish and refinement. For whoever has observed my invention more carefully will easily conjecture that a certain facility of speech, derived from nature, is present in me; whoever considers my studies ... since I am truly a stranger and newcomer to the rhetoric of flattery: I who have also spent my youth in the disciplines of physics, ethics and metaphysics, and have made my own discovery.

units.la: Pergis in nugis, vir impudens, quasi ego mihi vtriusque iuris arrogassem instituta. Calumniator fraudulentissime, hic veritas pro me loquitur. Hæc sunt enim verba defensionis meæ: Mihi satis est didicisse ciuiles sententias, & quidquid præcipuum habet ratio vel industria, quidquid sacra traduntur vtriusque iuris instituta, hisce literis & floribus exornari posse. Hoc & tu minime inficiaberis, nisi id agas vt cum ratione insanias. Nam hæc arte, quæ à dicendi copia nomen traxit, suadentes ad legendum adhortamur, & quidquid legendo hauseris, ea ipsa arte potentius persuadebis. Apud Socratem habes Gorgiam (quem Isidorus Principem eius artis facit, Cicero vero Lysiam inuentorem vocat) ita loquentem: Sepe iam cum fratre meo, & cum alus medicis ad aliquem ægrotum ingressus, cum ille vel pharmacum potare nollet, vel secundum vrendum quæ se medico non permitteret, nec valeret medicus suadere, ego persuasi, non alia arte quam rhetorica. Rursus si aliquam urbem aduenit Rhetor & medicus, & in concione alioque cœtu inter ipsos certaretur, vter sit pro medico eligendus, Medicum quidem nusquam comparere, sed illum electum iri, qui dicendi peritiam facultate que habebit. Potentia quidem huius artis tanta & talis est. Sed quid multa; in re non dubia Hieronymum habes dicentem, beatum lob artis eius summam esse complexum, cum sublicet supra DEO disputans ipsum tanquam admonens fragilitatis humanæ naturæ tributa, secum expostulat, non æquum esse ab homine infirmo tam fortem & perseverantem exigere patientiam. Aspice hymnos nedum Prudentii, sed & illos vulgares, qui in laudem Dei vulgo decantantur: & certe videbis eria diuinas laudes floribus ipsius artis illustrari. Apud Ciceronem habes, Nil tam horridum, aut tam inculcum, quod non splendescat oratione. Et alibi è contra: tam simplex aut sincerum, quin dicendo possit... tens est vis eloquentiæ, magnum est momentum in ea, quam si à Pontifice sustulerit quabis quod laudes.
units.tr: You persist in trifles, shameless man, as if I had claimed for myself the teachings of both laws. Most deceitful slanderer, here truth speaks on my behalf. For these are the words of my defence: It is enough for me to have learned the civil opinions, and whatever is distinctive in reason or diligence, and whatever the sacred teachings of both laws hand down, can be adorned by these letters and flowers. You also will by no means deny this, unless you aim to rave with reason. For by this art, which has taken its name from the abundance of speech, we urge people persuasively to read, and whatever you have drawn in by reading, you will persuade all the more forcefully by this same art. In Socrates you have Gorgias (whom Isidore makes the prince of that art, while Cicero calls Lysias its inventor) speaking thus: Often, when I went in with my brother and other physicians to some sick man, when he would not drink the medicine, or would not allow himself to be cauterised in the way the doctor advised, and the doctor could not persuade him, I persuaded him, by no other art than rhetoric. Again, if a rhetorician and a physician arrive in some city, and there is a contest in the assembly or another gathering as to which of the two should be chosen as the physician, the physician will nowhere appear, but the one who has skill and facility in speaking will be chosen. So great and such is the power of this art. But why say more? In a matter beyond doubt you have Jerome saying that blessed Job had embraced the whole sum of this art, when, disputing with God on high, as if reminding him of the frailties of human nature, he complained to him that it was not right to require such strong and persevering patience from a weak man. Look at the hymns, not only those of Prudentius but also those common ones which are commonly sung in praise of God; and surely you will see that divine praises are illustrated by the flowers of this very art. In Cicero you have, Nothing is so rough or so unpolished that it cannot be made to shine by speech. And elsewhere, on the contrary: nothing so plain or sincere that it cannot be ... by speaking. Great is the power of eloquence, and great is its weight in it, which if the Pope had taken away from himself, he would have ...

units.la: Sed rogationem tuam, qua rogas, Vbi lege permissum caperetur, licere pœnitentiam ... ledi[illegible, ~3 letters] contraria quæstione vacuabo. Vbinam didicisti, Pontificem iustum insidiis proditoriis persecutum esse quemquam propter appellationem reuerenter cum ad se, tum ad superiorem suum, sacrum scilicet Concilium, interpositam? De quibus beatus Gregorius scribens ait, Quod quisquis ea destruere tempset, ipsum destruit. Quod & Eugenius nouissimus, ac petit ipsum Nicolaus sub bulla recognouerunt. Legisti autem Innocentium quartum Pontificem se aubitrio Concilii instituendi submisisse. Illi vero quos tu commemoras hæreseos damnatos, in fide Christi pertinaciter errauerunt, nulli Concilio sese submittentes iudicandos. Quod si nescis, & scire cupis, non est difficile Pontifices enarrare, qui culpis suis exigentibus nedum maledicta, sed depositionem, castigationem, mortem quoque meritam exceperunt. Id certe iustissimum censeo, quod in Dioscorum impium animaduersum est. Sed quid putas? Si venerabilis Leo Pontifex Dioscorum inauditum capi ac spoliari iussisset, quia à se ad Concilium Chalcedonense appellasset, nullum autem erroneum dogma seminasset, vir doctissimus & perfectus, quamadmodum tale nefas non iussisset, ita & si errore lapsus forte proripuisset, ratione tandem suspicere lapsum & errorem restituisset ac reuocasset.
units.tr: But your question, in which you ask, Where the law permits it, is repentance allowed..., I will answer with a counter-question. Where did you learn that a just Pope ever pursued anyone with treacherous snares for an appeal lodged respectfully both to himself and to his superior, namely the sacred Council? Blessed Gregory, writing about these matters, says: Whoever tries to destroy these, destroys himself. Eugenius the Last and Nicholas also acknowledged this under seal. You have read that Pope Innocent IV submitted himself to the judgment of a Council to be convened. Those whom you mention as condemned heretics stubbornly erred in the faith of Christ, and they submitted themselves to no Council to be judged. If you do not know this, and wish to know it, it is not difficult to name Popes who, because their faults demanded it, received not only curses but deposition, punishment, and even death as they deserved. I certainly think that what was done to the impious Dioscorus was most just. But what do you think? If the venerable Pope Leo had ordered Dioscorus to be seized and stripped without a hearing, because he had appealed from Leo to the Council of Chalcedon, and if Dioscorus had sown no erroneous doctrine, would that learned and perfect man not have refused to order such a crime? And if he had by chance fallen into error and slipped, would he not, reasonably, have looked up to the fallen man and restored and recalled him from his error?

units.la: Procedis longa verbositate execrando vitium scandali, quo tu me calumniaris, homo nissime: qui non cernis scandalum Pontificis, proditionem insidiosam aduersum me conflatam. Audi Socratem contra Anitum & Melitum se defendentem: Non est, inquit, inducens tam opus mihi defensione meditari, quam vobis, ne delinquentis me condemnantes. Et lex ait, Euangeliorum Codicem iudici propositum esse, vt se Deo inspectore sciat iudicare. At si Pontifici Ptolomæi bibliothecam proponas, & Demetrium Phalereum præficias, non eum reuocabis à Piccolomineum & Cortuniani consideratione. Sed Ienonem imitaris Terentianum, quem nō potuit ... &c. Nam si cæteræ vanitates pari voto successerint tibi, breui tempore rubescet vertex capitis tui, cum incedes capillo rubeo pileatus.
units.tr: You proceed with long verbosity, a detestable vice of scandal, by which you slander me, most foolish man, who do not see the scandal of the Pontiff and the treacherous plot framed against me. Hear Socrates defending himself against Anytus and Meletus: "It is not so much that I need to prepare a defence, as that you need to avoid condemning me as a wrongdoer." And the law says that the book of the Gospels is placed before the judge so that he may know that he judges with God as his overseer. But if you were to set before a Pope the library of Ptolemy and place Demetrius of Phalerum in charge of it, you would not call him back from his consideration of Piccolomini and Cortuniani. But you imitate Terentian Ienon, whom he could not... etc. For if your other vanities succeed with the same zeal, your scalp will soon turn red, when you go about with red hair under a cap.

units.la: Ritum & cerimonias consecrationis pontificalis adducis, quod inibi pronunciatur, Qui maledixerunt tibi, sit ille maledictus. Saniosò vulneri callum superducis tumidum. Vrendus certe callus & secundus est, vt purgato intus vulnere caro solidetur & pellis. Si malefacta Pontificum benefacta nuncupabimus, eosque fecerimus licentiosos, ministerium sibi commissum vertemus in tyrannidem. Audi ergo beatum Gregorium dicentem, Non oportere Prælatos adeo reuereri, vt ipsorum vitia foueamus. Quod autem Apostolus ait; Nescitis quod Princeps Sacerdotum esset, potro Saluator no maledixit colaphisantes (quod tamen nō ad Pontifices modo, sed ad cunctos milites crucifixores æque spectat) ô Læli, pcacissime, quanto conamine perurgeris, quanto flagras ardore, qui quo tendis adeo festinas, vt obuia non cernas, sed raperis per inuia, tandemq; præcipitas in scenā Comicā, personis aut inepte distribuis actus. Prospice, circumspice, retrospice, quid aliud paraueris, q; vt Gregorius personam Christi gerens, iniurias Papæ sustineat, cuius typum esse facis Annā, Caiphā, Pilatū ac Herodē. Attamē quantū ad patientiā subiiste distinctuo vel coherentitio redactam, aut perfectionis doctrina persuasam attinere videtur; hæc & mihi alia sic enodabo. Et q maximū est, q à me postulas, q nunquam ipse præstares, maledicenti benedicere, quia insidianti Pontifici virāque meæ persecutori, qui de rebus sanguine meo tudoreq; partis, delitatis in me precium statuerat appropriantis; certe summæ perfectionis opus mihi no ar- ego. rego. Nec satis exploratum habeo, si persequeretur me occidendum praebuissem, an saevitia sa- tiatus tandem man suevisset, an potius maiori ferocia strenuisset: quippe qui non contentus me perdidisse, in coniugem & liberos meos bonorum meorum ademptione saevire cupiebat. Nec enim semel ore receptus polluto sanguis gustatur manusuescere fauces. Ut ergo scias, in quo philosophantium grege meme profitear, altius ordiri iuvat intentum. Vitae Philosophia Dux, rationis in- terpres, virtutum cultrix, & expultrix vitiorum, duas partes habere perhibetur: quas qui confundit, aut minus caute secernit, labyrinthum inextricabilem texit. Hanc veteres eius professores in summa perfectione posteris tradiderunt, ut illi septem per septem urbes Graeciae dis- persi, Biantem certe Prienaeum, cum patriam eius hostis adeo pressisset, ut cuncti cives emi- grarent plaustris onusti, ipsaque liber & expeditus commigrans interrogaretur, cur nonnulliquid rerum emexisset, respondisse ferunt: Ego vero omnia mea mecum porto. Nos non sic: quiliter interpretamur, Rem in bonis esse. Milesium Thalen alterum ex ipsis septem, qui primus colicausas atque vim rerum naturalium contemplatiua ratione suspexit, tantae moderationis suisse proditum est literis, ut aureum mensam in Milesia repertam, & sapientiori Delphico de- bitam responso, ideoque sibi delatam, alteri cesserit: quo pari moderatione freto, mensa sapientum ordinem ad Solonem vicaria cessione pervenit. Vter materia est, qua patiehumilitate, qua etiam abstinentia & continentia sui, ac moderatione & paupertate summi- ri pro- vnt, quasi virtutes praeceperunt docere, quendoque docuerunt; quas neque sequeris, neque nos imitari sumus. Quid Socrates coram iudicibus capitaliter accusatus, non recte, inquit, putare, qui existimet magnam vitae mutare habendum esse ratio- nem. Quid, quod nec carceris infortunium ipsum detrectare, nec Critonis persuasio, qui corruptis custodibus in ipso carcere cum moriturus discesserit; praesertim sua, aut Simiae Thebani, aut ... Haec tamen ... aliorum pecunia aliter oblata, illum indicare potuisset virum perfectum, ut evaderet forte fortim migraret, aut latitaret? Quod tamen ... lege probatur, quae eua- torem a ... ... secernit, & captivum precio redimere finit. Odius haec erat sententia: Ego sum, qui non modo nunc, sed semper, meorum nulli parvum alteri quam rationi. Sed haec se- verissimae Philosophiae summa consilia, & praecepta salutaria, ac salubertima instituta, ad extremam tendentia perfectionem; non autem communi hominum statui, vitaeque doctrinis, cuius auctores plurimum repudiati, quandoque damnati & addicti supplicio, tanquam Reipublicae damnosi. Zenonis, Socratis, & aliorum innocentissimorum apud Graecos abundant exempla. Nam & divinus ille Plato apud Dionysium Siciliae tyrannum commanens, persectae cultor virtutis, in tale periculum incidit, ut postea Principibus Syracusanis scribens sic e- narret: Hucusque igitur mihi & philosophiae & amicis auxiliatum est: postea autem ita vixi- mus ego & Dionysius, ut ego quidem semper extra spectarem, ... quaedam eularet cupiens. Successit proinde alia, docens & inter scelleratos innoxie viuere ... quidem tolerans, ne lolium extirpando uberem segetem necet. Porro autem ... contrahentium dissimulatione praeteriens, ea demum castigans, quibus Respublicae status labefactari, aut humanae societatis commercia periclitari possent, ut Iurisconsultorum traditiones, ac praecepta Catonis & Ciceronis volunt, apud quem Diogenes & Antipater disputant, Num vir bonus vendens rem pitiosam defecer- it ea demum explicando vitia, qua legitimus sunt definita? Acrius apud Flaccum contra Antipatrum Diogenes disputat, omnem saeculi vitam morte videtur. Sed ea tam brevi responso Tullius absolvit: Aliae leges, aliter Philosophi tollunt astutia, certe cohercitionis praecepta vocans, ut verba sequentia clare demonstrant, dum dicit: Leges quantum manu tenent ... ergo Philosophia cohercitionem distinctiam non habet, habet vero doctrinae ... Ipse enim Cicero ... iustitia hominum praeclare distribuens secundum illius secundam philosophiae traditionem, Boni viri, inquit, officium est omnibus velle pro- desse, ut obesse nemini, nisi lacessitus. Hoc postremum Lactantius mordaciter inquit: O quam iustam sanctamque sententiam duorum verborum adiectione corripit. Unde haec tantorum controversia? nisi quod alter secundum philosophiam mediam, alter vero secundum perfectam doctrinam locutus est: iuste quidem & Cicero Fimbriam consularem virum laudat, volentem probatum hominem bonum virum iudicari, quum ea res infinitis virtutibus & meritis contineatur. Idem in Paradoxis nemo bonus esse potest, cui quid deest. In qua consideratione ... est & magna culpa: quamquam ... loco ... esse distorto distortius. Nam etsi peccatum ... lineam rationis, alter tamen altero plus aberrat ... vocatur. Noli ergo mihi obiectare dominum & Salvatorem nostrum Iesum Christum, consubstantialem & coaeternum patri, per quem omnia facta sunt, de caelo descendentem, in summa humilitate & huiusce mundi contemptu natum, pannis involutum, in praesepio reclinatum, Doctorem patientiae & altissimae paupertatis, nec habentem ubi caput reclinet, secundum carnem. Nec discipulos eius, quibus dixit: Omnis ex vobis, qui non renuntiat omnibus quae possidet, non potest meus esse discipulus. Hoc enim perfectionis sta- tum innuit, ipso dicente: Si vis perfectus esse, omnia quae habes, vende & da pauperibus, & habebis thesaurum in caelo. Atque illi qui aufert tibi vestimentum, & tunicam noli prohibere, & qui vult tecum in iu- dicio contendere, & tunicam tuam tollere, remitte ei & pallium. Haec si mihi esset perfectio, fortasse ne- dum re familiari adempta, sed & vitam fugere necdum indignatus essem, nisi forte Laurentium imitatus dixissem, immanissime Tyranne, &c. Apostolus quoque summae perfectionis imitator Corinthios increpans, Iam quidem, inquit, omnino delictum est in nobis, habere iudicia. Quare non magis iniuriam accipiu s fraudemque patimini? Ergo perfectus discipulus perfecti magistri perfectionem, quam verbo doctrinae persuasit, etiam exemplo vitae docuit. Hanc perfectionem si tu vel Pontifex, aut quisquam illi commanens, verbis sibi arrogat, seseque fallit, sibique falso blanditur. Vtinam mihi ad vitam ingredi Dominus concedat. Nosti, Laeli, aliud respondisse Dominum volen tiad vitam ingredi, aliam vero perfectionis legem docuisse. Vas autem electionis, Apostolorum Chrysostomo teste perfectissimus (qui Iob Apostolis praeferens, Paulum aequauit) si supererogauit, non est idcirco talis imitatio ab aliis exigenda, & per illum qui nunquam ipse praestatet. Putasne, si tempus efflagitasset, Paulusque respondisset; Nonne Christus verus Deus, cuius Euangelium praeditamus, maior est Pontifice, sed & ipso legislatore, vel Aaron sacerdote, num peccasset? Minime. Sicut nec peccauit, dum Cephae restitit in faciem, quia reprehensibilis erat. Nonne dicidisti, ea quae Spiritu Dei per quosdam singulari gratia & nutu quodam aguntur, sub humanis legib. non esse redigenda? Neque enim humana privilegia in consequentiam trahi debent. Erat autem ipse spiritu Dei plenus.
units.tr: You bring forward the rite and ceremonies of pontifical consecration, where it is pronounced: Let him who has cursed you be cursed. You lay a swollen callus over a festering wound. The callus must certainly be burned away, so that once the wound is cleansed within, flesh and skin may knit together. If we call the misdeeds of Popes good deeds, and so make them licentious, we turn the ministry committed to them into tyranny. Hear, then, blessed Gregory saying: Prelates ought not to be so revered that we cherish their vices. As for what the Apostle says, Do you not know that he was the chief of the priests?, the Saviour did not curse those who struck him with blows (a saying that applies not only to the Popes but equally to all the soldiers who crucified him). O Laelius, most acute, with what effort you are driven, with what heat you blaze! You hasten so eagerly toward your goal that you do not see the obstacles in front of you, but are carried through pathless places, and at last you plunge onto a comic stage and assign the parts to the characters foolishly. Look ahead, look around, look back: what else have you prepared, except that Gregory, bearing the person of Christ, should endure the injuries of the Pope, whose type you make Annas, Caiaphas, Pilate and Herod? Yet as far as patience is concerned, which seems to belong to a doctrine of perfection... I will explain these and other points in the same way. And the greatest thing you ask of me, which you yourself never performed, is to bless the one who curses me. The Pope, who lies in wait for me and is my persecutor, who set a price on my goods and my blood by appropriating them, certainly makes this no work of the highest perfection for me. Nor do I know for certain whether, had he pursued me, I would have offered myself to be killed, or whether, sated with cruelty, he would at last have ceased, or rather raged with still greater ferocity. For not content with having destroyed me, he wished to rage against my wife and children by taking away my possessions. Once the jaws have tasted blood from a polluted mouth, they grow accustomed to it. So that you may know in which company of philosophers I number myself, it helps to begin from a higher point. Philosophy, the guide of life, the interpreter of reason, the cultivator of virtues and the expeller of vices, is said to have two parts; whoever confuses them, or separates them less carefully, weaves an inextricable labyrinth. Its ancient professors handed this down to posterity in its highest perfection. Thus Bias of Priene, when an enemy had so pressed his homeland that all the citizens were emigrating loaded on wagons, was said to have answered, when asked, as he walked out free and unburdened, why he carried nothing of his goods with him: "I carry all my possessions with me." We do not interpret it this way; we say that everything is in one's goods. Thales of Miletus, another of the seven, who first contemplated the causes and forces of natural things by reasoned speculation, is recorded in writings to have shown such moderation that, when a golden table was found at Miletus and was owed to the wiser man of Delphi, he yielded it to another; and with the same moderation the table passed by a similar transfer to Solon. ... They taught, and sometimes taught, the virtues of patience, humility, abstinence and self-control, moderation and the highest poverty, as if they were precepts; these you neither follow nor do we try to imitate them. What did Socrates say when he was accused before the judges on a capital charge? He said that it was not right to think that one who considers that life must be exchanged for a greater good should be judged to have reasoned rightly. What of the fact that he did not refuse the misfortune of prison itself, nor the persuasion of Crito, who, having bribed the guards, offered to take him out of the prison when he was about to die, especially since Simmias of Thebes or ... Yet if, by another offer of money from others, he could have shown himself a perfect man by escaping, or fleeing secretly, or hiding? Yet the law, which separates the one who escapes ... and allows a captive to be redeemed for a price, is approved. His opinion was this: "I am one who, not only now but always, will yield to no one of mine except reason." But these are the highest counsels of the strictest philosophy, and salutary precepts and most wholesome institutions, aiming at ultimate perfection; they are not for the common condition of men or for the teaching of life. Their authors were largely rejected, sometimes condemned and handed over to execution as harmful to the commonwealth. Examples of Zeno, Socrates and other most innocent men abound among the Greeks. Divine Plato also, while staying with Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, a cultivator of perfect virtue, fell into such danger that afterwards, writing to the rulers of Syracuse, he set out the matter thus: "Up to now, then, philosophy and my friends have helped me; but afterwards Dionysius and I lived in such a way that I, indeed, always stood apart, ... wishing to ..." Another doctrine then followed, teaching that one can live innocently even among the wicked, ... tolerating some things, lest by uprooting the darnel one destroy the rich crop. Furthermore, passing over ... by the dissimulation of those who make contracts, and at last rebuking those things by which the state of the commonwealth might be shaken or the dealings of human society endangered, as the traditions of the jurists and the precepts of Cato and Cicero require, where Diogenes and Antipater dispute: whether a good man, selling a defective thing, must disclose the faults that are defined by law? Diogenes disputes more sharply against Antipater in the presence of Flaccus, and seems to take away the whole life of the age by death. But Tullius settles this with a very brief reply: other laws, other philosophers remove by cunning, calling them rules of coercion, as the following words clearly show, when he says: "Laws hold as much as they hold by hand..." Therefore philosophy does not have a distinct coercion; it does have ... teaching. For Cicero himself, distributing the justice of men admirably according to that second tradition of philosophy, says: "It is the duty of a good man to wish to be useful to all, so as to harm no one unless provoked." Lactantius bites at this last point, saying: "O what a just and holy sentence it corrupts by the addition of two words!" Whence this great controversy? Unless one speaks according to a middle philosophy, and the other according to perfect doctrine. Justly too Cicero praises the consular man Fimbria, who wished a man proved to be judged good, since that matter is contained in infinite virtues and merits. In the Paradoxes also: no one can be good who lacks something. In this consideration there is also a great fault: although ... to the line of reason, one nevertheless strays more than the other ... is called. Therefore do not object to me our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father, through whom all things were made, who came down from heaven, was born in the deepest humility and contempt of this world, wrapped in swaddling clothes, laid in a manger, the teacher of patience and of the most extreme poverty, having according to the flesh nowhere to lay his head. Nor his disciples, to whom he said: "Whoever of you does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple." For this indicates the state of perfection, as he himself says: "If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven." And to him who takes your coat, do not forbid him your tunic, and to him who wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. If this were perfection for me, perhaps I would not only have been stripped of my property but would have fled from life, and not been indignant, unless perhaps imitating Laurentius I had said: "Most savage tyrant, etc." The Apostle also, imitator of the highest perfection, rebuking the Corinthians, says: "Now indeed there is altogether a fault among you, that you have lawsuits. Why do you not rather suffer wrong and fraud?" Therefore the perfect disciple, who persuaded by the word of the doctrine of the perfect Master, also taught the perfection by the example of his life. If you, or any Pope or anyone living with him, arrogate this perfection to himself in words, he deceives himself and flatters himself falsely. May the Lord grant me to enter into life. You know, Laelius, that the Lord answered the one who wished to enter into life in another way, and taught another law of perfection. But the vessel of election, the Apostle most perfect according to Chrysostom (who placed Paul above Job and equalled him to the Apostles), if he went beyond what was required, such imitation should not be demanded of others, and through one who himself never performs it. Do you think that if the time had demanded it, and Paul had answered: "Is not Christ, the true God, whose Gospel we proclaim, greater than the Pope, and indeed greater than the lawgiver himself, or than Aaron the priest?" would he have sinned? By no means. Just as he did not sin when he withstood Cephas to his face, because he was to be reproved. Did you not say that those things which are done by some through the Spirit of God, by singular grace and a certain nod, are not to be brought under human laws? For human privileges ought not to be drawn into consequence. But he himself was full of the Spirit of God.

units.la: Habes nunc, Laeli Theodore, discretionem summae & extremae philosophiae, quae iniuriam referre vetat, seu retorquere, & alterius philosophiae, tolerantis ea, quae sunt humanae conditionis. Pergens nunc ad ea, quae lex statuit de carminibus seu libellis Fescenninis, legem Digesti iuris, quae blasphemos aut falsos obtrectatores mendacii redarguere iubet, nostin? Eam Flaccus naturae atque institutionis legem esse probat, Stertinium que (quem septem Sapientibus aequando facit octauum) haec carma sibi contra vaniloquos Musam dedisse gloriatur, ne compellaretur inultus in hunc modum comminando.
units.tr: You now have, Laelius Theodorus, the distinction between the highest and most extreme philosophy, which forbids returning an injury or repaying an insult, and the other philosophy, which tolerates what belongs to the human condition. Now turn to what the law lays down about Fescennine songs or lampoons. You know the law of the Digest which orders that blasphemous or false detractors be refuted as liars? Flaccus holds that this is the law of nature and of training. Stertinius, whom he makes the eighth of the Seven Sages, boasts that the Muse gave him these verses against loudmouths, so that he would not be attacked with threats of this kind and go unavenged.

units.la: Dixerit insanum qui me totidem audiet, atque
units.tr: Let him who hears me say as much call me mad,

units.la: Respicere ignoto discet pendentia trigo.
units.tr: And he will learn to look back at what hangs on the unknown trigo.

units.la: Nec tamen inficiabor, rebus inesse mensuram & certos denique fines, & quadamtenus prodeundem sistendumque. Sic enim composita est Fescennina licentia, quae laetis agricolarum post condita frumenta cum sociis operum pueris & coniugibus fidis, convivis alternatim opprobria fundit. Sublato autem iure nocendi, chorus obticuit. Quin etiam lex poenaque lata veterem lasciuiam vertit formidine fustis, & infamiam irrogat ei, qui ob carmen famosum condemnatus. Postremo lex capitalis sancita, cuius tu siliquas ingerens vim legis minime ponderasti. An tu famosum carmen seu libellum recte nuncupes, cuius auctor non clam, sed palam (quod tu culpas) pro sua ac Reipublicae tutela dictasse fatetur, ipse videris. De hinc ipsam legis animam, hoc est, sanctionis rationem contemplare: scilicet ne quis sibi ius dicat, neu se praeter iudicem vindicet; quin tramite legitimo & auctoritate iudiciaria prosequatur, quod sibi debetur, aut accusando praemia ferat vel denunciando: alioquin neque nocentem lacessit, nisi Reipublicae interest nocentis noscere crimen. Si in orientis aut obeuntis Solis ultimis oris, si denique in torridis Libyae arenis, aut qua pruina rigens Pontum Scythicum glaciali frigore stringit, arbiter sederet iudicare dignus & potens, an Sigismundus post Ingatum suum violatum, & tam varias iuris experiundi vias refutatas, ad sacrum Concilium nec appellasset, an Gregorius appellans idcirco haereticus iure habeatur, profecto aliquid rationis haberet. Sed cum nec rimam, neque porum aut potisma, per quae aditus ad iustitiam pateret, aperire possis; vacuatam, tene legem, cuius rationem Papa submouit. Non est hoc meum inventum, sed magnae Synodi Constantiensis excogitatum, statuentis decennio in decennium universale Concilium celebrari, ut sit quo oppressi confugiant, sitque quod Pontifex metuat ac reuereatur. Sed est vetus querela, Papam voluntate pro lege abuti. Hoc Bernardus Claraevallensis ad Eugenium scribens conqueritur, ac pie admonet; Quomodo non indecens tibi voluntate pro lege uti? & quia non ist ad quem appel-leris, potestatem exercere, negligere rationem? & caetera, quae latius exequar, cum tuis nugis candorem veritatis opponam, quam tu Lucifuga horres aspicere, in tenebris oberrans. Contritusque est laqueus tuus de Maria, Aaron, Osia, & pueris Bethleemiticis: quia neuter horum fuit provocatus, nec vitae suae per Sacerdotes insidiatum.
units.tr: Yet I will not deny that there is a measure in things, and finally fixed limits, and a certain point to go forward and to stop. For the Fescennine license was constituted in this way: after the harvest was gathered in, the farmers, merry with their fellow workers, their boys and their faithful wives, poured out insults in turn to the guests. But when the right to harm was taken away, the chorus fell silent. Indeed, a law and penalty were passed which turned the old wantonness aside by the fear of the cudgel, and inflicted infamy on the man condemned for a defamatory song. Finally a capital law was enacted, and you, piling up its details, have quite failed to weigh the force of the law. Let yourself judge whether you may rightly call a defamatory song or lampoon something whose author admits he composed it not secretly but openly (which you blame) for the protection of himself and the Commonwealth. Now consider the very soul of the law, that is, the reason for the sanction: namely, that no one should claim the right to judge for himself or avenge himself apart from the judge, but should pursue by the lawful path and through judicial authority what is owed to him, or win rewards by accusing or informing. Otherwise he does not attack a wrongdoer, unless it is in the Commonwealth's interest to know the crime of the wrongdoer. If, at the furthest shores of the rising or setting sun, or in the torrid sands of Libya, or where frost stiffens the Scythian Pontus with icy cold, a worthy and powerful arbiter were sitting in judgment, then there would certainly be some reason in asking whether Sigismund, after the violation of his safe-conduct and after so many ways of seeking justice had been refuted, had not appealed to the holy Council, and whether Gregory, appealing, is therefore to be regarded as a heretic by right. But since you cannot open up a crack, nor a pore, nor even a passage through which access to justice might lie open, hold on to a law now emptied of its reason, which the Pope has set aside. This is not my invention, but the idea of the great Council of Constance, which decreed that a general council be held every ten years, so that there would be somewhere for the oppressed to flee, and something for the Pontiff to fear and respect. But it is an old complaint that the Pope abuses his will in place of law. Bernard of Clairvaux complains of this in writing to Eugenius, and gives him a pious warning: "How is it not unseemly for you to use your will in place of law, and, because there is no one to whom you may be appealed, to exercise power and neglect reason?" And other things which I shall set out at greater length, while I oppose the candour of truth to your trifles, which you, a flight-from-the-light creature, shun to look at, wandering in darkness. Your snare has been broken by Mary, Aaron, Hosea and the boys of Bethlehem, because none of these was challenged, nor did any of them have his life plotted against by the priests.

units.la: Quod vero Papalem dignitatem ex verbis Bernardi Claraevallensis, & epistola Clementis sublimius effers, hoc ad rem nihil attinere recognoscis: quia neutrobi Papa rem seu facultates subditorum in pretium crudelitatis cuiuspiam ausus est concedere. Sed te assentandi studio illac enectum esse coniicio, teque assuefacere, ut iisdem rebus gaudeas, iisdemque doleas, quibus ipse dominaris: postremo te ita compares, ut illi quam maxime placeas. Thrasonis siquidem & Gnathonis abste non multum abluditimago. Ac ne putes, hanc fuisse Bernhardi sententiam, ut Episcopus Romanus propter suae auctoritatis amplitudinem pro libito agere possit impune, ipsum in eisdemlibris arguetem excessus eius tu vicissim audi. Verba eius, quae tu dolose truncasti, fideliter repetam, addens illa quae tu calumniose supp essisti. Inquit Bernardus ad Eugenium de consideratione libro II. Sacerdos magnus es, Summus Pontifex, Princeps Episcoporum, Tu heres Apostolorum, Tu primatu Abel, Gubernatu Noe, Patriarchatu Abraham, Ordine Melchisedech, Dignitate Aaron, Auctoritate Moyses, Iudicatu Samuel, Potestate Petrus, Unctione Christus, Tibi claues tradita, Tibi oues credita. Beatissime, Theodore, Bernhardum proferendo, quem aduersus Pontificis calumnias obiicere verebar, ne reiiceres illum velut contemplatiuum virum actiuae vitae leges horruisse. Nunc ergo lex prodeat, cuius in agendo iudicium elegisti. Eiusdem Bernhardi iaculis feriendus eris, eiusque scuto proteprægendas; Ergò huius tuæ ... [damaged by ink stains; illegible in part] ... confodere ... repudiás mentes parasti præcordiando commaculare? O vanissime Theodore, qui in Bernardis ille in vanam gloriam Eugenii blandas effudersti laudes: ac ... Pontifici liceat pro sua libidine, dominatum, imo verò tyrannidem exercere, gloriabundus exclamasti: Sacerdos magnus.
units.tr: But as for the fact that you exalt the papal dignity above the words of Bernard of Clairvaux and the letter of Clement, you acknowledge that this has nothing to do with the matter, because nowhere has the Pope dared to grant the property or goods of his subjects as the price of anyone's cruelty. But I suspect you were struck down there by the desire to flatter, and that you are accustoming yourself to rejoice in the same things and grieve over the same things by which he rules; and, finally, that you are fashioning yourself so as to please him as much as possible. Indeed, you are not much more than an image of Thraso and Gnatho. And lest you think that this was Bernard's opinion, that the Roman bishop, on account of the amplitude of his authority, might act at his pleasure with impunity, hear in turn his own rebuke of Eugenius' excesses, in the same books. I shall faithfully repeat the words which you cunningly mangled, adding those which you calumniously suppressed. Bernard says to Eugenius in the second book of On Consideration: "You are the great priest, the Supreme Pontiff, the Prince of Bishops. You are the heir of the Apostles; you have the primacy of Abel, the governance of Noah, the patriarchate of Abraham, the order of Melchizedek, the dignity of Aaron, the authority of Moses, the judgment of Samuel, the power of Peter, the anointing of Christ. To you the keys have been handed over; to you the sheep have been entrusted." Most blessed Theodorus, by bringing forward Bernard, whom I feared to set against the Pope's slanders, lest you should reject him as a contemplative man who had abhorred the laws of the active life, now let the law come forth whose judgment you have chosen in acting. By the darts of this same Bernard you will be struck, and you will be protected by his shield. Therefore ... [damaged by ink stains; illegible in part] ... to pierce ... you have prepared to stain minds with your ... O most vain Theodorus, who in your Bernard poured out flattering praises of Eugenius in vainglory! ... Let it be lawful for the Pope to exercise lordship at his own lust, nay rather tyranny, you cried out boastfully: "great priest."

units.la: Id certè Christianorum nemo negat. Sed quod tu magnum Sacerdotem hisce delinimentis cumscribis, arma crudelitatis in me acuendo, hinc contra eiusdem Bernardi dogma, ipsum iam Papam alloquentis, opponò: Facilitas, inquit, crudelitas hæc est, cuius câlidissimum occulum magnorum neminem comperi cauisse versutias. Inde enim ipsis pro nihilo magnum videtur, inde immensa frequens additio, inde prærudicia in absentes, &c. Miror quod non dixisti, Maximum quia nec quidem inficiatus essem.
units.tr: Certainly no Christian denies this. But when you surround the great priest with these flatteries, sharpening the weapons of cruelty against me, I set against this the doctrine of the same Bernard, who addresses the Pope himself: "Facility," he says, "is this cruelty, whose most cunning eye I have found no one of the great to have guarded against its tricks. For from this it seems to them nothing to be great, from this comes the frequent immense addition, from this prejudgments against the absent," and so on. I am surprised that you did not call him "greatest," for I would not even have denied it.

units.la: tus esset. Nam & omnes Episcopos magnos constat esse Sacerdotes: sicut Imperatores, Duces, tribunos, præfectos, centurionesque, magnos milites vocare solemus, quod gregarii milites ab vel arma suscipiunt, vel in ordines iubentur consistere; sicut Presbyteri (quod Seniores interpretatur) à superintendentibus (quod Episcopi dicitur) novi ritus instrumenta suscipiunt, & per limites rite distribuuntur. At quæ sit hæc magnitudo, eundem audi. Præs & singulariter. Ad quidnam regesis ...
units.tr: ... for it is well known that all bishops are called great priests, just as we are accustomed to call emperors, dukes, tribunes, prefects and centurions great soldiers, because the common soldiers either take up arms or are ordered to stand in their ranks. Likewise the presbyters (which is interpreted "elders") receive from the superintendents (who are called "bishops") the instruments of the new rite, and are duly distributed through their boundaries. But what this greatness is, hear the same man: "Presiding and singularly ... To what end do you rule ..."

units.la: bidine) consideratione. Nunquid ut de subditiis crescas? nequaquam. Sed ut ipse de te. Principem sibi te constituerunt, ... Quæ pecunia ... super eos. Beneficii vocantur. At istud de bis quæ sunt, quid ad nos? Tu id mendacii, si ... ausus esse, quam beneficia præsse intendas. Nunc ... summus Pontifex ... sus ... Pontificem, attendas pariter vilissimum cinerem, ... alioloco. Non ... laudi- tur celsitudo. Sollicitudo maior illa discrimen intendit, hac animæ propè, huic ... volumen tandem cum rubore novissimum locum tenere. Discè sarculo ... sequitur Princeps Episcoporum.
units.tr: ... (by your ... ) consideration. Is it that you may grow at the expense of subjects? By no means. But rather as he himself says of you. They have made you a prince for themselves ... "What money ... over them. They are called benefices. But what is that to us, regarding those things which are? If you have dared ... this lie, you intend benefits to be ..." Now ... the supreme Pontiff ... the Pontiff, likewise attend to the most worthless ashes, ... in another place. Not ... the height is praised. That greater anxiety brings danger, this almost to the soul, to that ... at last with blushing to hold the last place. Learn with the hoe ... follows the Prince of Bishops.

units.la: Eundem Bernardum audi contra Papas (qualis ... loquentes) plus Maiestati quam veritati ... fides omnem Ecclesiasticum zelum ferute, sola pro dignitate ... Habeo totum datur, ... Sicut nihil vel parvum, si socialiter te habere tentaveris, Absit, inquiunt, non ... tempori non congruit. Maiestatem ... Quod sublime hoc salutare dicamus, & quod gloriam redolet, hoc iustum. Omne ... ducitur inter Palatinos. Ergo principatus illius naturam vir sanctus explicavit his verbis: ante omnia Romanam, & cui Deo auctore præes, Ecclesiam matrem esse, non dominam: Te vero nos dominum Episcoporum, sed unum ex ipsis, porro fratrem diligentium Deum, & participem timentium eum. Eodem loco eundem Bernardus: Tibi urbem Romam pro Episcopio deputat dicens clerus & populus tui, ac per hoc speciali cura tenere debitor. Vbi dicit, Romam Papæ domesticam esse Ecclesiam. Ac nisi iam solius Bernardi doctrinis tecum certarem, perfacile probarem, Episcoporum Principem non decere Episcopia confundere, de omnibus disponendo, quæ sunt per Metropoles & dioceses ordinatissime distributa. Hoc beatissimus Papa Gregorius considerans noluit universalis Ecclesiæ Pontifex nuncupari.
units.tr: Hear the same Bernard against the Popes (such as ... speaking) who have cared more for majesty than for truth ... faith ... every ecclesiastical zeal ... only for dignity ... I have given the whole ... "Just as nothing, or very little, if you have tried to hold yourself in a social way: Far be it, they say, ... does not suit the time. Majesty ... Let us call this lofty and salutary, and what smells of glory, this just. Everything ... is led among the palace officials." Therefore that holy man explained the nature of that principate in these words: "Before all, the Roman Church, over which you preside by God's authority, is a mother, not a lady; but you are the lord of the bishops, yet one of them, moreover a brother of those who love God and a partaker of those who fear him." In the same place Bernard says again: "The clergy and people of Rome assign to you the city as your bishopric, and therefore you ought to hold it with special care." Where he says that Rome is the Pope's domestic church. And unless I were already contending with you on the teachings of Bernard alone, I would very easily prove that it is not fitting for the Prince of Bishops to confuse bishoprics, disposing of all things which have been most orderly distributed through the metropolitan sees and dioceses. Considering this, the most blessed Pope Gregory was unwilling to be called the Pontiff of the universal Church.

units.la: Sequitur ergo, Tu heres Apostolorum. In hac hereditate multa quidem multa, operarii vero pauci. Paternam tibi vendicato, inquit, hereditatem. Quid ... tatoris tibi assignant: quarum si tenore contenteris, curam potius hereditatis & operam, quam divitias & gloriam. aut Fernandi Regis affinitatem. Blanditur cathedra? Specula est. Inde tibi ... nomen, non dominum sonans, sed officium. Quid Petrus tibi reliquit? Quod habeo, inquit, hoc sibi dominatum & ... non est mihi, &c. ...
units.tr: It follows, then: "You are the heir of the Apostles." In this inheritance there are indeed many things, but labourers are few. "Claim for yourself, he says, the paternal inheritance. ... assigned to you by the testator. If you are content with its terms, seek the care and labour of the inheritance rather than its riches and glory." Or the alliance of King Ferdinand. "Does the chair flatter you? It is a watchtower. From it ... a name that sounds not of lordship but of office." What did Peter leave you? "What I have, he says, ... this lordship is not mine, etc." ...

units.la: habuerunt, tibi ... interdicitur dominari. Ergo tu & usurpare aude, aut dominantem Apostolum, aut Apostolicum dominum, plane ab alterutro prohiberis, si utrumque simul habere vetet, perdes utrumque. ne ex illis habearis, de quo veritas conqueritur: Ipsi regnaverunt, & non ex me: Principes extiterunt, & ego non cognovi eos. Agnosce ...
units.tr: ...they have; it is forbidden you to lord it over. So dare to usurp either the lording Apostle or the Apostolic lord. You are plainly forbidden the one by the other; if the one forbids you to have both at once, you will lose both. Do not be among those of whom the truth complains: "They reigned, but not by me; they became princes, and I did not know them." Acknowledge ...

units.la: tatem tuam in cruce Christi. Exi in agrum Domini tui, non tanquam Dominus, sed tanquam villicus.
units.tr: ...your glory in the cross of Christ. Go out into the field of your Lord, not as a lord but as a steward.

units.la: Pergis dicens, Tu primatu Abel. Si filius, si successor Abel vis haberi, ipsum imiteris. Erat enim Abel pastor, Cain autem agricola. Sacrificavit ille de primogenitis, Cain excussas obtulit spicas, f audi sacrificium, non autem amoris holocaustum. Cain ergo magis aequare videris, qui spolia Ecclesiarum in Pientiam, imo in affinitatem Fernandi prodegisti; siliquas vis Deo sacrificasti.
units.tr: You go on saying, "You are the primate of Abel." If you wish to be regarded as the son and successor of Abel, imitate him. For Abel was a shepherd, Cain a farmer. Abel sacrificed from the firstborn of his flock; Cain offered shrivelled ears of grain, not a whole burnt offering of love. So you seem rather to be the equal of Cain, you who have squandered the spoils of the churches on Pientia, indeed on the marriage alliance with Ferdinand. You wish to offer husks to God.

units.la: Num tibi quadrat hoc verbum Bernardi, quo libellum suum tertium claudit ad Eugenium: O miseranda sponsa talibus creditam Paranymphis, qui assignata cultui eius proprio retinere quasi non verentur, non amici profecto sponsi, sed emuli sunt. Rursus in quarto: Quale est quod de ... tur, qui dicunt tibi, Euge, euge. Pauperum vita in plateis diutum seminatur. Argentum ... pauperior, sed fortior. Primatum tuum certe nemo negat. At tu videris, ne iuxta parabolam ... ues habens, unicam pauperis concupiscas. Eundem Clarævallensem in tertio loquentem audi: Quid item tam ingratum tibi, quam ut totum tenens non sis contentus toto, nisi minutias quasdam atque exiguas portiones ipsius tibi credita vniversitatis, tanquam non sint tua, satagas nescio quo modo adhuc facere tuas. Erras, si ut summam, ita & solam institutam à Deo Apostolicam potestatem existimas. Si hoc sentis, dissentis ab eo, qui dixit: Non est potestas nisi à Deo ... Dei ordinationi resistit. Et si principaliter pro te facit, non tamen singulariter. Rursus, Omnium potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit. Non dixit, sublimiori. Subnectis dicens, Gubernatu Noe. Illi archa extruenda, & palas ... stegis distinguenda mandatur. Tibi corpus Christi mysticum delegatur ædificandum. Iussum exemplar, sed usus longe dispar. Quod Noe discreuit subordinando, tu confundis ... miscendo. Hoc idem Bernardus queritur in hunc modum: Monstrum factus, si manui sibi ... digitum. Tale est, sicut corpore Christi membra locus diiter, quam dispositit ipse. Nisi tu putas alium esse, qui posuit in Ecclesia quosdam Apostolos, quosdam autem Propbetas, alios vero Euangelistas, alios Doctores & Pastores, in aedificationem corporis Christi. Atque hoc corpus, quod ipse Paulus suo Apostolico figurans eloquio & capiti coaptans totum ex eo compactum, prohibet per omnem iuncturam subministrationis secundum operationem in mensuram uniuscuiusque membri, augmentum corporis faciens in aedificationem sui in charitate, non dixit, in Petro, nec in imperio.
units.tr: Does this saying of Bernard fit you, with which he closes his third book to Eugenius? "O pitiable bride, entrusted to such paranymphs, who scarcely hesitate to keep for themselves what has been assigned to her worship, are surely not friends of the bridegroom but his rivals." Again in the fourth: "What is it that ... those who say to you, 'Well done, well done'? The life of the poor is sown abroad in the streets for a long time. Silver ... poorer, but stronger. No one denies your primacy." But see that, in the words of the parable, you do not covet "the one ewe lamb of the poor man" while you have many. Hear the same Clairvaux man speaking in the third book: "What is so ungrateful to you as this, that, holding the whole, you are not content with the whole, but busy yourself, I know not how, with making your own certain small and slight portions of the universe entrusted to you, as though they were not yours. You are wrong if you think that apostolic power, instituted by God, is only the highest and sole power. If you think so, you differ from him who said, 'There is no power but of God' ... and whoever resists it resists the ordinance of God. And if it favours you as chief, it does not favour you alone. Again, 'Let every soul be subject to the higher powers.' He did not say 'the higher power.' You add, saying, 'the government of Noah.' To Noah was commanded the building of the ark and the distinguishing of the kinds of animals. To you is delegated the building of the mystical body of Christ. The pattern is commanded, but the practice is far different. What Noah distinguished by ordering, you confuse by mixing." Bernard complains of this same thing in these words: "You have become a monster, if the hand ... the finger. It is as if the members of the body of Christ were placed otherwise than he himself arranged them. Unless you think there is another who has set in the Church some apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, others teachers and pastors, for the building up of the body of Christ. And this body, which Paul himself, figuring it by his apostolic word and fitting it to the head, describes as wholly joined together through every joint of supply, according to the working in due measure of each member, making the body grow for the building up of itself in love, he did not say 'in Peter,' nor 'in empire.'"

units.la: Subsequeris dicens, Patriarchatu Abraham. Abrahae summi Patriarchae fides inprimis efferitur, quia eius virtutis opus praecipue executus est. Nam secundum rationem actuum exteriorum alios alia virtute pollere dicimus, seu praecellere in aliorum hominum comparatione. Neque nunc id agimus, quomodo virtutes pares sunt, vel connexae. Sed si quid in operibus Pontificis emicat operationis virtuosae, id si nossem, testificarer. Sed si patriarchali vel dignitati, vel auctoritati hoc tribuis, ut illi omnia singulaque licere, expedireque contenderis, fallis, & falleris, plurimumque deciperis, eodem Bernardo testante; Quod sicut Cherubin & Seraphin, ac caeteri, qui ad Archangelos & Angelos ordinantur, sub uno capite Deo, ita sub uno Pontifice summo Primates vel Patriarchae, Archiepiscopi, Episcopi, Presbyteri, &c. Quid si dicat Episcopus, Nolo esse sub Archiepiscopo. Hoc de coelo non est, nisi tu forte Angelorum quempiam dicentem audisti, Nolo sub Archangelis esse, aut ex alio quolibet inferiorum ordinum aliquem non serventem cuiquam subesse, nisi Deo. Romanus vero Patriarcha suae dispositioni cuncta reseruat.
units.tr: You follow on, saying, "by the patriarchate of Abraham." The faith of Abraham, the great patriarch, is above all extolled, because he especially carried out the work of that virtue. For we say that, in respect of outward acts, some excel by one virtue and others by another, in comparison with other men. Nor are we now considering how the virtues are equal or connected. But if anything shines forth in the works of the Pontiff as a virtuous operation, I would bear witness to it, if I knew it. But if you attribute this to the patriarchal dignity or authority, so as to contend that everything and each thing is lawful and expedient for him, you are mistaken, and you greatly deceive and are deceived, as Bernard himself bears witness: "Just as the Cherubim and Seraphim, and the rest who are ranked under the archangels and angels, are under one head, God, so under one supreme Pontiff are the primates or patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, presbyters, etc. What if a bishop says, 'I do not want to be under an archbishop'? This is not from heaven, unless perhaps you have heard some angel saying, 'I do not want to be under the archangels,' or some one of the lower orders refusing to be subject to anyone but God." The Roman patriarch, however, reserves all things to his own disposal.

units.la: Nunc quid sibi velit, Ordine Melchisedech, commemoremus, sive ille fuerit Sem filius Noe, primus post cataclysmum Deo sacrificans, sicut Abel protoplasti primogenitus, sive alius Rex Salem, qui obviam venit Abrahae regresso a caede Regum, qui interpretatur Rex iustitiae, Rex pacis; Christus certe Dominus Sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech: & ideo Aaron, ille mediator Dei & hominum, secundum humanitatem in illo figuratur. Et quia submittitur Unctione Christus, illic adiiciemus, quae hic dici a me potuissent.
units.tr: Now let us consider what it means, "after the order of Melchizedek," whether he was Shem, the son of Noah, the first after the flood to sacrifice to God, as Abel was the firstborn of the first man, or some other king of Salem who came to meet Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, whose name is interpreted "king of righteousness, king of peace." Certainly Christ is the Lord, a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek; and therefore Aaron, that mediator between God and men, is figured in him according to his humanity. And since Christ is set forth under the anointing, we shall add there what could have been said by me here.

units.la: Porro quod dixisti, Dignitate Aaron, is Moysi viro Dei, Duci Israelis, parumsse traditur cum universo ordine Leuitico. Praecepit quippe Dominus Moysi, ut post ordinationem Aaron & filiorum eius, prorsus tribus Leui ad diuini cultus ministeria ordinaretur, & consecraretur Domino, & seruirent pro Israel coram Aaron & filiis eius in tabernaculo. Hos duos ordines veteris legis fuisse, nemo tibi negat. Alios quoque novo ritu Ecclesia introduxit, quorum omnium officia caput nostrum Iesus Christus in semetipso exhibuit, & corporis suo (quod est Ecclesia) eosdem ordines instar septiformis gratiae spiritus reliquit observandos. Ergo & hunc passum unctioni Christi referuemus. Quod autem subdis Auctoritate Moysis, id eo spectat, quod idem Bernardus admonet in quarto: Tuum est vnumquemq; euocare & adscisceret tibi, exemplo Moysi, senes & iuuenes: sed senes, non tam aetate quam moribus, quos tu nosti, quia senes populi sunt, &c. Consilio non prece agendum est. Id certe quomodo seruetur, ipse iudicato. Sed pergamus ultra.
units.tr: Further, as to what you said, "by the dignity of Aaron," it is handed down that he, along with the whole Levitical order, was second to Moses, the man of God, the leader of Israel. For the Lord commanded Moses that, after the ordination of Aaron and his sons, the tribe of Levi should be set apart for the ministries of divine worship, and consecrated to the Lord, and should serve for Israel before Aaron and his sons in the tabernacle. That these two orders belonged to the old law, no one denies to you. The Church has also introduced others under the new rite, and the offices of all of these our head, Jesus Christ, displayed in himself, and he left the same orders to be observed by his body (which is the Church), like the sevenfold gift of the Spirit. So we shall refer this step, too, to the anointing of Christ. But as to what you add, "by the authority of Moses," this concerns what Bernard himself advises in the fourth book: "It is your duty to call each one and to take to yourself, after the example of Moses, elders and young men; but elders not so much by age as by character, whom you know, because they are the elders of the people, etc. It must be done by counsel, not by entreaty." How this is observed, let him judge himself. But let us go on further.

units.la: Iudicatu Samuel. Caueat ergo ne dicatur sibi, ditauimus Abraham. Sed ut cum eodem Samuele libere ad populum concionari sibi liceat: Loquimini de me coram Domino, & coram Christo eius, virum bonum cuiusquam tulerim, aut asinum; si quempiam calumniatus sum, si oppressi aliquem, si de manu cuiusquam munus accepi; & contemnam illud hodie, vobisq; restituam. His enarratis subdit Bernardus: O si daretur talium copia virorum, quales perstrinximus nunc, quid illo iucundius seculo. Nonne secunda ab aeternitate illorum tibi temporum beatitudo videretur, &c. Et nunc reduc oculos, mi Eugeni, ad eum qui nunc tua curia sicut Ecclesia est statum, & studia Prelatorum, eorum praesertim, qui in circuitu tuo sunt. Sed de his hactenus, ego palpavi non fodi parietem.
units.tr: "By the judgement of Samuel." Let him take care, then, lest it be said to him, "We have enriched Abraham." But in order that he may be free to preach to the people with the same Samuel: "Speak of me before the Lord and before his Anointed: whose ox have I taken, or whose ass; whom have I defrauded, whom have I oppressed, or from whose hand have I received a bribe, and I will despise it today and restore it to you." After recounting these things, Bernard adds: "O if there were a supply of such men as we have just described, what would be more pleasant than that age? Would not the second happiness of those times, from eternity, seem to you ... And now turn your eyes, my Eugenius, to him who is now your court, as the Church is, and to the zeal of the prelates, especially of those who are about you." But enough of these matters; I have stroked the wall, not dug into it.

units.la: Nunc sequitur, Potestate Petrus. Sed Bernardum tuum rursus audi: Tu pastor procedis deauratus, tam multa circumdatus varietate. Oues quid capiunt? si auderem dicere, demonum magis quam ouium pascua hac, &c. Scio vbi habitas, increduli & subuersores sunt tecum. Lupi, non oues sunt. Scilicet sic factitabat Petrus, sic Paulus ludebat, &c. Petrus hic est, qui nescitur processisse aliquando vel gemmis ornatus, vel sericis, non tectus auro, non vectus equo albo, nec stipatus milite, nec constrepentibus septus ministris. Absque his tamen credidit satis adimpleri posse salutare mandatum: si amas me, pasce oues meas. In hiis successisti non Petro, sed Constantino, &c. Opus fac Euangelista, & pastorum opus impleti. Dracones (inquis) me pascere & scorpiones, non oues. Propter hoc (inquam) magis aggredere eos: sed verbo, non ferro: Quid tu denuo usurpare gladium tentas, qui semel iussus es reponere in vaginam, &c. Quod sequitur de gladio bifario, id certe praetereo & ad Monarchiam Dantis Alighierii remitto, transcurrens usque illac.
units.tr: Next follows, "by the power of Peter." But hear your Bernard again: "You go forth as a shepherd, gilded, surrounded by such a multitude of finery. What do the sheep gain? If I dared to say it, these pastures are more the pastures of demons than of sheep, etc. I know where you live; there are unbelievers and subverters with you. They are wolves, not sheep. Thus Peter used to act, thus Paul played, etc. Peter is he who is not known ever to have gone forth adorned with jewels or silks, not covered in gold, not carried on a white horse, nor attended by soldiers, nor surrounded by noisy servants. Yet without these he believed the saving command could be fully carried out: 'If you love me, feed my sheep.' In these things you have succeeded not Peter but Constantine, etc. Do the work of an evangelist, and the work of a shepherd is fulfilled. 'You say,' you reply, 'that I feed dragons and scorpions, not sheep.' For this reason, I say, go more boldly against them: but with the word, not with the sword. Why do you again attempt to take up the sword, you who were once commanded to put it back into its sheath, etc.? What follows about the two-edged sword I pass over, and I refer it to the Monarchy of Dante Alighieri, passing over it at once."

units.la: Unctione Christus. Siue dixeris, chrismate unctus, seu unctione chrismatus, utrumq; tibi conceditur. Dixeris fortasse, regium nomen Christus est, sed eius regnum secundum carnem non est de hoc mundo. Eundem Bernardum lege dicentem: Non tuille de quo Propheta: Et erit omnis terra possessio eius. Christus hic est, qui possessionem sibi vendicat, & iure creationis, & merito redemptionis, & dono patris. Cui enim alteri dictum est: Postula a me, & dabo tibi gentes hereditatem tuam, & possessionem tuam terminos terrae. Possessionem & dominium cede huic. Tu curam illius habe, pars tua haec, vltra ne extendas manum tuam. Nunquid non & villa villico, & paruulus Dominus subiectus est paedagogo? Nec tamen is villa, nec iste Domini sui Dominus est. Praesis vt fidelis seruus, quem constituit Dominus super familiam suam. Nullum tibi venenum, nullum gladium plus formido, quam libidinem dominandi.
units.tr: Anointed with Christ. Whether you say anointed with chrism, or anointed with unction, both are granted to you. Perhaps you will say that Christ is named King, but that his kingdom according to the flesh is not of this world. Read the same Bernard saying: "That is not you, of whom the Prophet says: And every land shall be his possession. Christ here is he who claims possession for himself, by the right of creation, the merit of redemption, and the gift of the Father. For to whom else was it said: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession. Possession and dominion yield to him. You take care of his affairs; this is your part; do not stretch your hand further. Is not the steward also subject to the master, and the child, though lord, to the tutor? Yet neither is that steward lord, nor is this one lord of his master. You preside as a faithful servant, whom the Lord set over his household. I fear no poison, no sword, more than the lust of ruling."

units.la: Sed prosequamur illud, Tibi claues tradita. Magna est clauium significantia materialium. Clauium in conspectu rei traditio, siquidem accessus patet non impeditus, facit possessorem accipientem, si adfuit animus transferendi: alioquin custodia commendatur, quia deponere est commendare, non imperium concedere. Ut vero clauis regni coelorum non adimeret carnis fragilitatem, facultatemque peccandi. Ideo secundum eundem Bernardum, dilligentem intellige euangelizandi, ac non potestatem imperandi. Quod his verbis innuit: Non est sapiens inter vos, ait ille, qui iudicet inter fratrem & fratrem? Ad ignominiam vobis dico, contemptibiles. Qui sunt in Ecclesia, illos constituite ad iudicium. Ita secundum Apostolum indigne tibi usurpas cium vile, gradum contemptibilium. Et ne dicas Apostolum pro tempore locutum, subiicit Bernardus: Putasne haec tempora sustinerent, si hominibus litigantibus pro terrena hereditate mitte Domini respiciens. Qui me constituit iudicem super vos, &c. Nisi aliquando quispiam Apostolorum iudex fuerit hominum. Steriste denique lego Apostolos condemnandos, sedisse iudicantes non lego. Erit illud, non sunt. Bernardum tuum tibi retorqueo, meam sententiam comprimo, quia nimietatem meo iudicio damnarem ego, ut idem ait, ne assiduo coram te resonent leges Iustiniani, non Domini. Opprobrius succurrere minime vitupero, ambitionem autem praecipue condemno.
units.tr: But let us follow up that saying: "To you the keys have been given." The symbolism of material keys is great. The handing over of keys in the sight of the thing, provided access lies open and unhindered, makes the one who receives them the possessor, if there was an intention to transfer; otherwise custody is entrusted, for to deposit is to commit, not to grant rule. But so that the key of the kingdom of heaven would not remove the frailty of the flesh or the power to sin, therefore, according to the same Bernard, understand it as a key for diligent preaching of the gospel, and not as a power of commanding. He indicates this in these words: "Is there not a wise man among you, he says, who can judge between brother and brother? I say this to your shame, you who are contemptible. Those who are in the Church, appoint them to judge." So according to the Apostle you unworthily usurp for yourself the judgment seat over citizens, a base rank of the contemptible. And lest you say the Apostle spoke for the occasion, Bernard adds: "Do you think these times would endure it, if men quarrelling over an earthly inheritance were to look to the Lord's word: Who made me a judge over you? etc.? Unless perhaps one of the Apostles was ever a judge of men." Finally I read that the Apostles were to be condemned; I do not read that they sat in judgment. That will be the sense of "they are not." I turn your Bernard back upon you, and I restrain my own opinion, because I would condemn excess in my judgment, as he himself says, lest the laws of Justinian, and not of the Lord, resound constantly before you. I by no means blame coming to the aid of the disgraced, but I especially condemn ambition.

units.la: Postremo dicis, Tibi ouescredita. Siamas me, pasce oues meas, dixit Dominus, ubi Bernardus ait: Donabit lupos, sed ouibus non dominaberis. Pascendas vtique, non premendas suscepisti. Neque exploratum habes, an tunc praesto fuerint caeteri discipuli, sicut dum omnes missi in orbem. At ne Bernardum ... reediamur, eundem in tertio sic ordientem legito: Parentes tui destinati sunt, non ad aliquas regiones, ... debellaturi. Ite in orbem universum, dictum est illis. Ipsi vero vendentes tunicas suas ... eloquium, spiritum vehementem, arma potentia Dei. Quoniam peruenere victores inclitas ... non sagittae potentis arcus, &c. Et quidem in omnem terram exiuit sonus eorum, & in fines orbis terrae verba eorum. Numquid confortatus est principatus eorum. Laeli, si haec soli Cephae digne deferas, quod olim Dominus per Prophetas de omnibus praeconisauit, nouissime per filium suum dixit ad omnes. Hoc Bernardus intelligens subdisci, Tu successisti in hereditatem, non ergo soli Petro. Et nisi me intra Bernardi domum continerem, iam decerarent, an quadrans an dodrans hereditatis Christi ad Papam aut episcopos pereum, cui creditum est praeputium, an per eum qui circumcisi euangelisauit, deriuatus sit. Sed quartam vel solidum sibi deferamus, dummodo memineri mus eiusdem Bernardi dicentis: Prasis ut fidelis seruus et quid? Ut des illis escam in tempore, hoc est, ut dispenses non impetres. Recordare vocis illius: Sapientibus & insipientibus debitor sum. Ergo & insipientibus debitor es. Quae fiducia, qua conscientia Christum non offerimus tis, qui non habent? Expectamus ut fides incidat in gentes. Ar cui casu credere contigit? quomodo credent sine praedicante? Petrus ad Cornelium, Philippus ad Eunuchum missus est. Augustinus a Gregorio destinatus formam fidei tradidit Anglis, &c. An non limina Apostolorum plus iam ambitio quam devotio erat? an non vocibus eius tota die vestrum resultat palatium? an non spolis eius omnis Italica inhiat insatiabili auiditate rapacitas? Et rursus in quarto: Fuerunt ante te, qui se totos pascendis ouibus exponerent, pastoris opere & nomine gloriantes, nisi sibi reputantes indignum, nisi quod saluti omnium obesse putarent, impendebant substantiam, impendentes & semetipsos, ut is qui ait: Et ego superimpendor pro animabus vestris, ponebant quoties oportuisset sine sumptu Euangelium.
units.tr: Lastly you say, "To you the sheep have been entrusted." "If you love me, feed my sheep," said the Lord, where Bernard says: "He will give you wolves, but you shall not lord it over the sheep." You have received them to feed, not to press down. Nor do you know for certain whether the other disciples were then present, as when all were sent into the whole world. But lest we go back to Bernard, read him in the third book, beginning thus: "Your forebears were sent not to certain regions ... to wage war. Go into the whole world, it was said to them. But they, selling their tunics ... the word, a vehement spirit, the weapons of the power of God. For they came as victors to the renowned ... not the arrows of the mighty bow, etc. And indeed their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. Has their rule been strengthened?" Laelius, if you rightly transfer to Cephas alone what the Lord once proclaimed through the prophets to all, and last of all said through his Son to all, Bernard, understanding this, adds: "You have succeeded to the inheritance, therefore not to Peter alone." And unless I kept myself within Bernard's house, they would already be disputing whether a quarter or three-quarters of Christ's inheritance has passed to the Pope or to the bishops, to whom the uncircumcision was entrusted, or whether it was derived through him who preached to the circumcised. But let us grant him a quarter or the whole, provided we remember that same Bernard saying: "You preside as a faithful servant; and what then? That you give them food in due season," that is, that you dispense, not seize. Recall that saying: "I am a debtor both to the wise and to the foolish." So you are also a debtor to the foolish. What confidence, what conscience is it, that we do not offer Christ to those who lack him? We wait for faith to fall upon the nations. But by what chance does it come about that anyone believes? "How shall they believe without a preacher?" Peter was sent to Cornelius, Philip to the eunuch. Augustine, sent by Gregory, handed on the form of faith to the English, etc. Was not the threshold of the Apostles already more ambition than devotion? Does not your palace echo with his voices the whole day? Does not all Italian rapacity gape with insatiable greed for his spoils? And again in the fourth book: "There were before you those who gave themselves wholly to feeding the sheep, glorying in the work and name of shepherd; unless they thought it unworthy, unless they judged it harmful to the salvation of all, they spent their substance, spending even themselves, like him who said: And I am poured out for your souls. Whenever it was needed, they preached the Gospel without cost."

units.la: Haec super pastura pompaque pontificali ex Clarauallensi dixisse sufficiat. Me vero quoddam Concilium meminisse legisse, vbi super inuestitura Ecclesiasticorum beneficiorum Clericis restituenda, & econtra de regalia secularibus restituenda Principibus disceptabatur: quasi ... ci mores patrum praesenti Praelatorum pompae conferebantur, & quod secularia sine lictoribus & apparitoribus & ornatus luxu vix administrari possunt. Talis tandem incidit consideratio, quod sicut sponsae vel nouae nuptae primum solis ornantur ut placeant sponsis, deinde sponsi adornant ipsas, ut & coram vniuerso mundo * gloria Christi ornamentis sponsae suae resplendeat: Habeat igitur regalias, & quae duntaxat Ecclesiam fuisse * quam vidit illa ciuitatem sanctam Ierusalem nouam descendentem de coelo, a Deo paratam, velut sponsam ornatam viro suo: cum vtique nos sumus, in quos fines saeculi deuenerunt, nullam aliam expectantes praeter aduentum in gloria filii Dei. Sed neque satis parabola quadrat. Quippe apud Comicum Clitipho Cliniam zelotypia languentem solatur ex eo, quod amica eius humili veste amicta, non alieno sed proprio, vti quae sibi ornantur foeminae, sit ornata. Est ergo fornicaria sponsa, quae ornatur alteri quam Christo. In gentilitate fateor turpe reputatum esse absque ornatu sacerdotium. Nam cum tribunitiis, maxime Syllanis, factionibus nedum consulatus, sed & triumphus ac quaestura plebi cum patribus esset communicata, & (vt Liuius ait in quarto) Quaesturam namque eam non honoris ipsius sine aestimabant sed pat factus ad Consulatum ac triumphos locus nouus hominibus esse videbatur: Patres contra non pro communi catis, sed pro amissis honoribus fremere, negare, si ea ita sint, Liberos suos rendos esse, qui pulsi maiorum loco, cernentesque alios in possessione dignitatis sua, Salii Flamines qui nusquam alio quam ad sacrificandum propopulo sine imperiis ac potestatibus relinquantur. Satis palpaui, non fodi parietem. Fodiat, cuius est fodere. Ideo autem extendimus sermonem nostrum, vt intelligas quam vane linguam tuam in me acuisti,
units.tr: Let it suffice to have said this about pasture and pontifical pomp, drawn from the Clairvaux writer. I do, however, remember having read of a certain Council, where it was debated concerning the investiture of ecclesiastical benefices, to be restored to the clergy, and conversely concerning the regalia, to be restored to secular princes. As if ... the customs of the fathers were compared with the present pomp of prelates, and as if secular affairs could scarcely be administered without lictors, attendants and luxurious display. Finally this consideration arose: just as brides or newly married wives are first adorned by themselves alone, so that they may please their bridegrooms, and then the bridegrooms adorn them, so that the glory of Christ may shine in the ornaments of his bride before the whole world: let her therefore have the regalia, and those things which were merely the Church's ... which she saw, the holy city Jerusalem, new, coming down from heaven, prepared by God, adorned as a bride for her husband, since surely we are those upon whom the ends of the age have come, expecting nothing but the coming of the Son of God in glory. But neither does the parable quite fit. For in Terence, Clitipho consoles Clinia, who is languishing with jealousy, because his mistress, dressed in humble clothing, is adorned not with another's but with her own, as women adorn themselves. Therefore the bride who is adorned with anything other than Christ is a fornicating bride. I confess that among the Gentiles it was thought shameful for the priesthood to be without ornament. For when the tribunician factions, especially those of Sulla, had shared with the commons not only the consulship but also the triumph and the quaestorship with the fathers, and (as Livy says in book four) they did not regard that quaestorship as a mark of honour ... a new avenue seemed open to men towards the consulship and triumphs, the fathers, on the other hand, fumed and refused, not for the common good but for the honours they had lost, saying that if things were so their children were to be deprived, who, pushed out of the rank of their ancestors and seeing others in possession of their dignity, the Salii and Flamens, who were left nowhere else than for sacrificing to the people, without commands or powers. I have groped enough; I have not dug through the wall. Let him dig whose business it is to dig. We have extended our discourse so that you may understand how vainly you have sharpened your tongue against me.

units.la: Transgrediamur ad illam epistolam, qua dicitur, Si quis hunc (scilicet Romanum Pontificem) contristauerit, Christum quidem credidit cathedram, non recipit: & quicunque contristauerit Doctorem veritatis, peccat in Christum. Haec quidem natura & significantia verissima sunt. Nam & Rex & Princeps, omnisque potestas sublimior, auctoritatis suae virtutem per ministros expediat necesse est: quos si quis impedierit, Dei ordinationi resistit.
