Hoc nouit Appius Claudius, qui Magistratum primus suasit dictatoriae potestatis cum lictoribus praeeuntibus, dum dicit: Pulsetur cum mihi lictorem, qui sciet ius de tergo vitaque sua penes vnum illum esse, cuius Maiestatem violauerit. Ecce quod Maiestatem violat eius cuius lictorem pulsat violentus. Hoc haereticus Septimus declarauit, dum docuit eos rebelles haberi, qui Magistratus & apparitores in exercitio commissi sibi officii impediunt rebellando. Ergo qui Christi legatum in exercitio legationis suae nititur impedire, Christo rebellat. Sunt vero eius legati quibus dixit: Ite in orbem universum, & praedicate, &c. An vero te fugit, in iuribus fiscalibus concessam esse facultatem resistendi apparitori aut commentariensi, non rite personam aut res innocentis inuadenti? Et Episcopus ex interdicto unde vi recte cognenitur, si Clericum licet praetextu pontificalis officii aut iudicialis auctoritatis non rite destituit vel deiecit. Tolle ergo cauillum, improbe cauillator, & nil reliqui habebis praeter vanitatem. Quia hos Pontifici Euangelizanti aut legationem Christi exequenti non resistimus, sed percussori violento.
units.tr: Let us pass on to that letter in which it is said: "If anyone grieves this one (namely the Roman Pontiff), he has indeed not received the chair of Christ; and whoever grieves the teacher of truth sins against Christ." These things, both in their nature and their meaning, are very true. For a king and a prince, and every higher power, must needs express the strength of its authority through its ministers; whoever hinders them resists the ordinance of God. Appius Claudius knew this, who first urged the magistracy of dictatorial power with lictors going before, when he said: "Let whoever strikes my lictor know that the right over his back and his life lies with that one whose majesty he has violated." Behold, one who strikes the lictor of him whose majesty he violates is violent. The heretic Septimus declared this when he taught that those are to be held rebels who, by rebelling, hinder magistrates and attendants in the exercise of the office committed to them. Therefore whoever strives to hinder Christ's legate in the exercise of his legation rebels against Christ. Now his legates are those to whom he said: "Go into the whole world and preach," etc. Or does it escape you that, in the fiscal laws, the right is granted to resist an apparitor or a commentariensis who improperly assails the person or goods of an innocent man? And a bishop, by the interdict "unde vi," is rightly sued if he improperly deposes or expels a clergyman under pretext of pontifical office or judicial authority. Take away, therefore, your quibble, shameless quibbler, and you will have nothing left but vanity. For we do not resist those who preach to the Pontiff or carry out Christ's legation, but only the violent striker.

units.la: Sed quod de putredine scatentem in nos inuehis, omnium vilissime, hoc tibi reicimus: quoniam pus tuum induruit ardore & equitiae, ut nullo vnquam antidoto liquescat. Quia calidissimae assentationis tuae versutias etiam vsque ad Imperatoris Romani palpationem pertendere tentas: cuius ignauiam ciues mirantur & hostes, totus postremo fastidit orbis Christianus, & quisquis Imperii Romani nomen reuereretur, condolet alterum Sardanapalum hoc quondam triumphale solium occupare. Deinde profluis maledictis & conuiciis, quibus si quid vilissimo obiecero, & clauum clauo retudero, nil plus egero, quam stercora tua vicariis obruere sordibus. Satius est ergo foetores tuos sordere, quia nil affers, in quo ingenia conterere valeamus.
units.tr: But as for what you hurl at us, swarming with rot, you most worthless of men, I hand it back to you, since your pus has hardened with heat and envy so that no antidote will ever melt it. You try to stretch your hot-blooded flattery even to the fawning of the Roman Emperor, whose cowardice his citizens and enemies alike marvel at, and the whole Christian world finally holds in contempt. Anyone who respects the name of the Roman Empire grieves that another Sardanapalus should occupy this once triumphant throne. Then you pour out a stream of insults and abuse. If I answered anything so worthless with blow for blow, I would accomplish no more than covering your dung with my own filth. It is better, then, to let your stench stay as it is, since you offer nothing on which our wits could be worn down.

units.la: Ad illa pergemus, quibus contendere paras, licere Pontifici non vocatum condemnare, exemplo Moysi, qui absque praevia cognitione crimen idololatriae plurima populi strage piauit: Subsequeris de Phinees in edicti sui transgressores, de Helia in Sacerdotes Balaam, & nuncios Regis Ochoziae, de Petro, & Anania, & eius vxore Saphira, Paulo & Clinia mago. O miserum ingenium tuum, qui ex iis quae nutu Dei & gratia singulari aguntur, ad humana fragilisque opera per hominem peccatis obnoxium pro libito voluntatis suae patrata, locosducere credis exemplares, ac curuum sermone rotato tentas enthymema retorquere. Nonne iunior didicisti, humana priuilegia non esse in consequentiam trahenda? Tu vero diuinas actiones hominibus ducis communicandas. Disce nunc, ea quae spiritu Dei aguntur, nullis obnoxia legibus esse, nec mediatorem Dei & hominum Iesum Christum secundum diuinitatem, neque Sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech, neque Papam eius vicarium esse, sed secundum humanitatem quam assumpsit Deus homo factus. Si enim vna manu tot impios, quod Moysi strauisse perhibetur, ipse prosterneret, in ipso etiam sacro furore lecernens tribum innoxiam; seu precibus eius Deus petimeret eos, quos ipse censuris etiam inauditos vexauit innoxios, aut Colibum Ducem officio priuaret oculorum, iam gloriari posset omnia nutu Dei procedere. Denique surripis colloquium Moysi cum fratre praemissam ante caedem, & supprimis verba Petri, scilicet: Anania cur tentauit Sathanas cor tuum mentiri te Spiritui Sancto? quae super singulis responsa prolixa forent. Vnum te latere non sino, quod mystica Theologia ita demum est argumentativa, cum a Christo vel a sanctis Patribus inueniatur recepta. Vide nunc si nostra vel tua exempla sunt recepta.
units.tr: I will go on to those points you are trying to press, namely that a Pontiff may condemn a man who has not been summoned, on the example of Moses, who without prior examination expiated the crime of idolatry by a great slaughter of the people. You follow with Phinehas against the transgressors of his decree, Elijah against the priests of Baal and the messengers of King Ahaziah, Peter and Ananias and his wife Sapphira, and Paul and Elymas the sorcerer. O wretched wit of yours, which believes that things done by the will and singular grace of God can be brought forward as examples for human and frail works carried out by a man liable to sin at his own pleasure, and which tries to turn an awkward argument round with a twisted phrase! Have you not learned, even as a junior, that human privileges must not be drawn into precedent? You would have divine actions shared with men. Learn now that what is done by the Spirit of God is subject to no laws, and that Jesus Christ, mediator between God and men, is not the vicar of the Pope as a priest after the order of Melchizedek according to his divinity, but according to the humanity he assumed when God became man. For if with one hand he had struck down so many impious men, as Moses is said to have done, sparing in that same holy fury the innocent tribe, or if God had been moved by his prayers to spare those whom he himself had harassed with unheard-of censures, or had deprived Korah, the leader, of his eyes, then Moses could boast that everything happened by the will of God. Finally, you suppress the conversation of Moses with his brother before the slaughter, and you omit the words of Peter: "Ananias, why has Satan tempted your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit?" Each of these would call for a lengthy reply. I will not let one thing escape you: mystical theology is argumentative only when it is found accepted by Christ or by the holy Fathers. See now whether your examples or ours are accepted.

units.la: Nunc illud examinemus, quod tu vocas efficacius, egoque id reor proposite materiae propius adaptari, de Corinthio, quem absentem corpore Sathanae tamen tradidit Apostolus absque iudicii tela, ob reatus sui notorietatem, quia Corinthios non latebat incestus eius in nouercam. Non arbitreris, Laeli praesumptuose, me vasis electionis censuram in Corinthium ignorasse: sed eius exempli translationem portentosam assero, dum tete mihi texens sic licita trahis: An vero inficiari poteris, crimen tuum non fuisse notorium, qui palam criminosum & sacrilegum Sigismundum in crimina confouebas, &c. nec calumniera id non esse facti permanentis, &c. id iure factum esse contendis. Post haec deliramenta tandem eo recurris, si factum nulla possit tergiuersatione celari, neue defensio vlla competere, liceat absque cognitione praevia facinorosum damnare. Insuper adiungis, quod si quis peccat in conspectu iudicis, aliopleti debet: addere debebas hoc verbum, scilicet vt iudicii, scilicet astantibus circumseptl, vt sit par iudicialiter confitenti in quem quales sint iudicis partes, olim nostri scholaris, nunc doctoratus assumptione litura literis inducta est tuis. Nunc ad singula quaeque nostra festinat Apologia. Quid tecum Laeli contendam, qui nil omnino sapis, nec quid iudicare sit intelligis, nec quomodo vas electionis iudicarit animaduertis. Tu forte putas, neminem iudicare, nisi cui de publico sit data potestas. Iudicat sensus de sensato, & intellectus de cognito, cum phantasmata speculatur vel intuendo, aut ex intuitis eliciendo aut abstrahendo circumstantias vsque ad rem secundum se, aut discurrendo per varietatem cognoscibilium, vt de morbo medicus, ac quisque de eo in quo plurimum pollet. Apostolus absens iudicauit vt praesens. At quomodo certe intra se iudicauit, quid de Corinthio incestuoso factum esset, quando cum fratribus Corinthiis ad se venturis constitueretur, quem in spiritu vidit operantem opus sceleratum, aut forte litteris sibi fuit indicatum ad Ephesum. Non ergo tradidit, donec Corinthios congregauit. Hoc habent Apostoli verba dicentis: Ego quidem absens corpore praesens autem spiritu iam iudicaui, vt praesens. Quare? quia in spiritu vidi. Quid autem iudicauit? Scilicet eum qui hoc operatus est, in nomine Domini nostri Iesu Christi congregatis vobis, & in meo spiritu cum virtute domini Iesu,
units.tr: Now let us examine that case which you call more effective, and which I think fits the matter under discussion more closely: the Corinthian whom the Apostle, though absent in body, nevertheless handed over to Satan, without the weapons of a trial, because of the notoriety of his offence, since the Corinthians were not unaware of his incest with his stepmother. Do not suppose, presumptuous Laelius, that I am ignorant of the censure of the chosen vessel against the Corinthian. Rather, I maintain that your translation of that example is monstrous, since you weave your own web and drag in what is permitted in this way: "Can you indeed deny that your crime was not notorious, since you openly encouraged the criminal and sacrilegious Sigismund in his crimes," and so on. Nor do you claim that it is not a lasting deed, and so on; you contend that it was rightly done in law. After these ravings you finally take refuge in this: if a deed cannot be hidden by any evasion, and no defence is available, it is lawful to condemn a wrongdoer without a prior hearing. You add further that if someone sins in the sight of the judge, he ought to be condemned; you ought to have added this phrase, namely "as a judicial matter," with the bystanders standing around, so that it is equal to a judicially made confession. Of what kind the parts of a judge are, you once learned as our scholar; but now, with the assumption of your doctorate, that has been erased by the stroke of your own pen. Now our Apology hastens to answer each of your points. Why should I argue with you, Laelius, who have no sense at all, who do not understand what it is to judge, and who do not notice how the chosen vessel judged? Perhaps you think that no one judges unless public power has been given him. Sense judges the sensible, and intellect judges the known, when it contemplates phantasms either by looking at them or by drawing from what has been seen, or by abstracting the circumstances down to the thing in itself, or by ranging through the variety of knowable things, as a physician judges of a disease and each person judges of what he is most skilled in. The Apostle judged while absent just as he would have judged while present. But how did he judge within himself what was to be done about the incestuous Corinthian? He had been resolved, when the Corinthian brethren were to come to him, that he would see in spirit the wicked deed being done, or perhaps it had been reported to him in letters at Ephesus. He did not hand the man over until he had gathered the Corinthians together. The Apostle's words say this: "For I indeed, absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged, as though present." Why? Because I saw in spirit. What then did he judge? Namely, that the man who had done this, when you are gathered together in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and my spirit is with you, with the power of the Lord Jesus, should be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, and so on.

units.la: {y} Ioan. 3. Iesu, tradere huiusmodi Satanae in interitum carnis, &c. Iudicauit ergo Apostolus intra se secundum Spiritum, Sathanae vero tradidit congregatis Corinthiis fratribus, non Ephesiis aut Galatis. Alias argumentationes vacuas esse liquet. Siquidem Duci aduersus Cardinalem constituerit superesse defensionem. Id vero quanquam iam liquido compertum tibi, etiam quam vt breuius explicem, sic accipe. Cardinalis tuus sponte, libere Capitulo sup annuente, praedecessorum suorum more, Ducem Sigismundum aduocatum Ecclesiae suae recognouit, ac omnium rerum eius, cum duobus castris in Carentana sitis, eaque omnia, si quando opus esset, in auxilиis aduocati fore spopondit. Sub hac tutela impinguatus, dilatatus, Ecclesiae castra ad manus exteras transferre tentauit. Extant documenta manu sua scripta, extant qui tradiderunt, & apud quos machinatum est. Dux statui suo prouidit, illico cautione recepta securitatis status sui, omne regimen Ecclesiae apud Cardinalem libere permansit, hoc modo prouiso, ne castra sub extero dominatu redigantur. Vide num latius fuerit periculis obuiare, quam post causam vulneratam remedium quaerere. Nam (vt aiunt) suspicari de praeterito, quam ipsa experimentum capere est melius.
units.tr: John 3. Jesus: to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, and so on. The Apostle therefore judged within himself according to the Spirit, and he handed the man over to Satan when the Corinthian brethren were gathered together, not to the Ephesians or the Galatians. It is clear that your other arguments are empty. For you say that the Duke has no defence against the Cardinal. Although this is already plain to you, so that I may explain it more briefly, take it thus. Your Cardinal, of his own accord and freely, with the consent of the chapter, after the custom of his predecessors, acknowledged Duke Sigismund as advocate of his church, and promised that all his possessions, together with two castles in Carinthia, would be placed at the service of the advocate whenever it was needed. Under this protection he grew fat and expanded, and then tried to hand the castles of the Church over to foreign hands. Documents written in his own hand survive; there are men who gave evidence of it and before whom the plot was hatched. The Duke provided for his own position, and at once, having received security for his status, the whole governance of the Church remained freely with the Cardinal, on the condition that the castles should not be brought under foreign rule. See whether it was not better to meet dangers in advance than to seek a remedy after the cause has been wounded. For, as they say, it is better to suspect what has happened than to test it by experience.

units.la: Postea miserrime infatuis, quasi Princeps legibus solutus damnare valeat inauditum. Si quae scholaris didicisti, non abstersisset Doctoratus vel Pontificatus, iam promptum haberes, vbi scriptum est: Etiamsi coram Principe arrogatio habeat fieri, vocandes esse quorum interest. Hic vero de maiori praeiudicio agebatur. Dehinc caecas ineptias tuas effundis innuens, quod sicut testamentum coram Principe factum omnium testimoniorum solemnia exuperat, sic quae per Principem aguntur, legibus adeo soluta sunt, vt nec in ius vocationem requirant, tanquam a solius Principis potentia vim habeant rei iudicatae. O pauper sensus! Dic, oro, cui praeiudicatur ex omissione solemnitatis in testamento, dummodo constet, sic placuisse testatori? at cui praeiudicatur per priuilegium testamenti militaris, aut ad pias causas, vel inter liberos, aut ab intestato successores, aut in pacto mutuae successionis? aut si quis heres institutus negat a se legata relicta, deinde convictus se defendat, non esse solemniter relicta? Sed an quocunque casu etiam Principis praesentia facit narrata in testamento vim veritatis habere, sicut res iudicata? Quid si testator coram Principe dicat: Centum quae mihi debet Titius, Seio do legi, an probetur debitum? Discee pauper ingenio inter iuris solemnitatem & naturalem secernere necessitatem. Erubesce haec tua scripta doctis hominibus innotuisse. Nam licet de me male meritus sies, malem tamen errores tuos penes te retinuisses.
units.tr: Afterwards you wretchedly rave, as if a prince, released from the laws, could condemn an unheard man. If you had learned anything as a scholar, the doctorate or pontificate would not have wiped it away; you would already have at hand the passage where it is written: "Even if an adoption is to be made before a prince, those whose interest is involved must be summoned." But here it was a question of a greater prejudice. Then you pour out your blind absurdities, hinting that just as a will made before a prince surpasses all the solemnities of testimony, so what is done by a prince is so released from the laws that it does not even require a summons to court, and has the force of a thing adjudicated by the power of the prince alone. O poor sense! Tell me, I ask you, who is prejudiced by the omission of a solemnity in a will, provided it is clear that this was the testator's wish? But whom does it prejudice when a soldier's will has its privilege, or in pious bequests, or between children, or for intestate heirs, or in a pact of mutual succession? Or if an heir instituted in the will denies that legacies were left by him, and then, once convicted, defends himself by saying that they were not solemnly left? But does the mere presence of a prince, in any case at all, give the things recounted in a will the force of truth, like a thing adjudicated? What if the testator says before the prince: "The hundred which Titius owes me, I give by legacy to Seius": is the debt to be proved? Learn, poor wit, to distinguish between the solemnity of law and natural necessity. Be ashamed that these writings of yours have come to the notice of learned men. For although you have deserved ill of me, I would rather you had kept your errors to yourself.

units.la: Alias vanitates pari errore respersas mitto, hoc vnicum tibi concedens, quod vbi seditio imminet, vbi gentes & regna commouentur, licere Principi absque partium vocatione imminentia praeuenire pericula, quae interea surgerent, postea fortasse non reparabilia. Sicut apud Valerium in sapienter factis comperio, quod ciuitate clandestinis machinationibus saeuiente, Princeps eius lege de indemnatis non castigandis abrogata, comprehensis continuo sontibus & necatis, illico legem restituit. Si quis ergo Pontifex in dissensione pro Imperio Romano habita officiose interuenit, quid habet hoc commune cum causa nostra, aut etiam cum causa Maguntina, de qua Domino annuente posthac disceptabitur. Nam & de seditiosis Iustinianus nouissimo iure prouidit, vt leuiori suspicione praeuia contra notatos in crimine illo procedatur. At in omnibus his casibus tela iudicii succiditur, naturalis necessitas non violatur.
units.tr: I pass over other vanities marked by the same error, granting you only this: where sedition is threatening, where peoples and kingdoms are being stirred up, a prince may, without calling the parties, head off dangers that are gathering, which might later become irreparable. I find in Valerius, in his collection of wise deeds, that when the city was raging with secret plots, its prince repealed the law against condemning the uncondemned, seized and killed the guilty at once, and immediately restored the law. So if some Pontiff intervened in a dispute over the Roman Empire out of a sense of duty, what has this to do with our cause, or even with the Mainz cause, which, God willing, will be argued hereafter? For Justinian also provided, in his most recent law, that proceedings against those marked with the crime of sedition may be brought on lighter suspicion beforehand. But in all these cases the sword of judgment is cut down, while natural necessity is not violated.

units.la: Postremo repetitis blasphemiis, vt malignitati tuae naturae satisfacias, tandem secernis, an de crimine contra quempiam inquiratur vt damnetur, an vt declaretur poenam promulgatam incidisse: quo vltimo casu nil noui statuitur, sed tenus legis factiosus nuncia-tur. O canillator praesumptuose, num audisti Ducem Sigismundum statui suo prouidisse, ne Cardinalis dextram eius fallens alium dominum immitteret? Tales proditores Maro in VI. apud inferos prior te loco supplicii deputauit. Audiendus igitur erat Dux: quia etsi de facto constabat, de hoc erat disceptandum, num iure vel iniuria factum esset. Quod autem ad Concilium appellatum est, id argui non potest: quia ex salutaribus magnae Synodi institutis iam dies Concilii cessit, decennium effluxit: culpandus est Pontifex qui resistit. Sed dic miser, quitam patum ponsi habes; Si quis Iudex falso denunciet Titium homicidii reum, & idcirco lege Cornelia de sicariis obnoxium, an minorem fecerit iniuriam, quam si decernat eum homicidii reatum incidisse? Erras longe, si puras vllam tenere pronunciationem, sententiam vel declarationem, aut falsam publicationem, contra non vocatum vel inauditum. Num Pontifex ipse secum dissidet, qui Ducem vocauit causas dicturum, cui ad poenas comminatas procedi non debebat: at legatum Ducis iam parantem carceris comminatione disterruit, ne quid allegaret. Tibi dico, omnis cognitio causae vel rei, quae sic futura praeiudicialis, euocationem praerequirit: siue de facto constet, & quaeratur facinoris auctor, aut constet factum, & per quem, sed dubitetur iure vel iniuria; seu constet non iure factum, & disputetur de genere poenae. Sed & quandocunque de alterius praeiudicio certatur, vocandus est is qui habet interesse, etiam Principe cognoscente, quem latere possunt homines; nam factas solus Deus est, quem nullum fugit secretum.
units.tr: Finally, repeating your blasphemies, so as to satisfy the malice of your nature, you at last distinguish whether inquiry is made into a crime against someone in order to condemn him, or in order to declare that he has incurred a penalty already decreed; in the latter case, you say, nothing new is laid down, but only the law's penalty is announced, though with a factious messenger. O reckless babbler, have you not heard that Duke Sigismund provided for his own state, lest the Cardinal, deceiving his right hand, should introduce another lord? Maro, in the sixth book, placed such traitors first in the place of punishment in the underworld, and you deserve that place. The Duke therefore ought to have been heard, for although the deed itself was certain, it had to be disputed whether it was done rightly or wrongly. As for the appeal to the Council, that cannot be faulted, since by the salutary decrees of the great Synod the day of the Council has already come and a decade has passed; the Pontiff who resists is the one to be blamed. But tell me, wretch, how much weight you carry: if some judge falsely denounces Titius as a defendant in homicide, and so as liable under the Cornelian law on assassins, has he done less wrong than if he decreed that Titius had incurred the guilt of homicide? You are far wrong if you think there is any valid pronouncement, sentence or declaration, or any false publication, against a man who has not been summoned or heard. Does not the Pontiff himself contradict himself, who summoned the Duke to plead his cause, yet against whom he should not have proceeded to the threatened penalties; and yet he frightened off the Duke's envoy, who was already preparing, with a threat of prison, so that he could not plead anything? I tell you: every examination of a cause or matter which is to be prejudicial in this way requires a summons beforehand, whether the fact is certain and the author of the crime is sought, or the fact is certain and by whom it was done, but it is doubted whether it was done rightly or wrongly; or whether it is certain that it was done unlawfully and the kind of penalty is being disputed. But also, whenever a dispute concerns another's prejudice, the one who has an interest must be summoned, even when the Prince is the judge, since men can be hidden; for God alone knows the hearts, and no secret escapes Him.

units.la: De primatu Ecclesiae Romanae.
units.tr: De primatu Ecclesiae Romanae.

units.la: SEntina mendaciorum perfidissima descendens in barathrum calumniarum, quid me calumniaris quasi primatum Ecclesiae Romanae pernegem? qui scio omnibus Apostolis esse dictum: Ite in orbem, & quodcunque ligaueritis, &c. Non poteris efficere, vt verba mea sonent aliud quam vox Euangelistarum bona, praedicantium pacem. Tu vero vndecim Apostolos suppomere quaeris, vt omnem Ecclesiasticam potestatem redigas in Petrum, neque fateris coetum Apostolicum vno superiorem: qui tamen coetui paruisse pernibetur. Sacra generalia Concilia inficiatis esse fidei Christianae firmamenta, & a Christo habere potestatem in omnes Christi fideles, etiamsi Romana pontificali praefulgeant dignitate. Quod te malum rationis in hanc dementiam coniecit, vt ex meis veris & Euangelicis prolatis in falsos errores incideres? An vlla est discordia veris, semperque sibi certa cohaerent, & omne verum vero consentit. Dicis, qui solli Petro pasturam attribuis, quid est quod discipulus ille, quem diligebat Iesus, de ipsius Salutaris pectore fluenta sacra potauit: an vt intra se contineret, an vt euangelizaret? Dixerunt autem discipuli XII. in congregatione multitudinis credentium: Non est aequum nos derelinquere verbum Dei. Est autem euangelizare pascere, scilicet pabulo verbi diuini. Quid vas electionis, nuncius Iesu Christi? Non ab hominibus, neque per hominem sed per Iesum Christum & Deum patrem, &c. Sed quia utrumque errorem tuum postea falsis rationibus fucare praesumis, in processu tractatus latius confirabo, ac confusionem ordinis tui instigatus a te vestigiatim imitabor. Primo veniam habiturum fidis, si paulo altius principia repetas. Proiicis ampullas, & professus grandia turges, Quid dignum tanto feret hic promissor hiatu?
units.tr: You most treacherous sink of lies, descending into the pit of calumny, why do you slander me as though I denied the primacy of the Roman Church? I know that it was said to all the Apostles: "Go into the world, and whatever you shall bind," etc. You will not be able to make my words sound other than the good voice of the Evangelists, preaching peace. But you try to put eleven Apostles under Peter, so as to reduce all ecclesiastical power to Peter, and you do not admit that the Apostolic body was superior to him, though he is said to have obeyed that body. You deny that the holy general Councils are the foundations of the Christian faith and have their power from Christ over all Christ's faithful, even though they shine with the dignity of the Roman pontificate. What evil of reason has driven you into this madness, so that from my true and evangelical statements you fall into false errors? Or is there any discord among truths? They always cohere with themselves, and every truth agrees with truth. You say: since you assign the pasture to Peter alone, what is it that the disciple whom Jesus loved drank the sacred streams from the very breast of the Saviour: was it to keep them within himself, or to preach the gospel? The twelve disciples, moreover, said in the assembly of the multitude of believers: "It is not right that we should leave the word of God." But to evangelize is to feed, namely with the food of the divine word. What of the chosen vessel, the messenger of Jesus Christ? "Not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father," etc. But since you presume to disguise both of your errors afterwards with false arguments, I will confirm them more fully in the course of the treatise, and, prompted by the confusion of your order, I will imitate you step by step. First, you will be pardoned by the faithful if you go back to somewhat higher principles. You throw out bombast, and, professing great things, you swell up. What worthy thing will this promiser bring forth from so great a gaping?

units.la: Parturiunt montes, nascetur ridiculus mus.
units.tr: The mountains will labour, and a ridiculous mouse will be born.

units.la: Gloriaris te loqui (scire, quod nullus ignorat: Ecclesiam ab eo constitutam, cuius perfecta sunt opera, quaeque legem naturae, vt infima suminis, summa infimis, &c. Me admonEs eorum, quae didici puer, 20 scilicet elementarem mundum numerorum lege compactum. Hoc ita pueri nostri pronunciant: Omnia quae a primaeua rerum origine processerunt, sub numerorum ratione formata, &c. Deinde docetur, quod quantum vniuscuiusque elementi soliditas aut raritas alterum excedit vel ab alio superatur, tantundem alterum quantitate stringi vel distendi: rursus si vna qualitate aduersatur, altera communicatur. Dehinc aetherei mundi compagem attingis, de Angelis & Archangelis grandia, quae praefando spoponderis, exoluisse putans: quae quia postea superbius ampullaris, iam valere sino. Sed ne nos litterarum expertes aliis insinues, accipe istud Socraticum contra Callidem in Gorgia relatum. Dicunt autem Sapientes o Callides, & coelum & terram, & Deos & homines societatem & amicitiam, & ornatum & temperantiam & iustitiam continere, & hoc totum mundum nuncupant, o amice, non immunditiam. Tu autem videris non attendisse, quia aequalitas Geometrica & in Idris & in hominibus plurimum valet. Ecce quod gentilis harmoniam sensit omnium rerum compagem: neque id nostri Paedagogi nescierunt, qui nos docuerunt quod sequitur; Tu triplicis mediam naturae cuncta mouentem Connectens animam per consona membra resoluit.
units.tr: You boast that you will speak about what no one is ignorant of: that the Church was founded by him whose works are perfect, and who orders all things by natural law, the lowest by the highest and the highest by the lowest, and so on. You remind me of what I learned as a boy, namely that the elementary world is held together by the law of numbers. Our schoolboys state it this way: all things that have proceeded from the first origin of things are formed under the rule of numbers, and so on. Then it is taught that as the solidity or rarity of each element exceeds the other or is overcome by it, so much the other is drawn together or stretched out in quantity; and again, if it opposes one quality, another is shared with it. Next you touch on the structure of the ethereal world, and you talk grandly about angels and archangels, which you promised in your preface and which you think you have now paid off. But since you grow more bombastic about these things, I will let them go. Yet, lest you think you can impose on us who are unlearned in letters, take this saying of Socrates against Callicles, reported in the Gorgias: "The wise, Callicles, say that heaven and earth, gods and men, are held together by fellowship and friendship, by order, temperance and justice, and so they call this whole world by the name of order, my friend, not of disorder. But you seem not to have noticed that geometrical equality is very powerful both among the gods and among men." See, the Gentile sensed the harmony of the whole structure of things, and our own teachers were not unaware of this either, who taught us what follows: "Connecting the soul, which moves all things through the middle of the threefold nature, it loosens it through harmonious members."

units.la: Ergo si nil aliud habes, cur illud non custodisti? Compagem Ecclesiae solus Papa soluit, qui membrorum officia praefocando impedit, & oppilando suffocat, ne quis Episcoporum officium suum tute valeat explere, iunguras diliungit, confundens harmoniam, dum omnium officia solus sibi vendicat. Aufert corpori sanitatem, dum membra singula singulis officiis non finit viri. In processu dicis, Vnum in Ecclesia Principem, in quo & ex quo nemo contradicit. Si Petrum, resistit tibi Paulus: Ego enim a Domino accepi, quod & tradidi vobis, non a Petro. Et rursus: Non ab hominibus, neque per hominem, sed per Iesum Christum.
units.tr: Then if you have nothing else, why did you not keep this? The Papacy alone dissolves the structure of the Church, which by choking off the duties of the members and stifling them by blockage prevents anyone of the bishops from being able to fulfil his office properly. He pulls apart the joints, confounding the harmony, while he alone claims the duties of all for himself. He takes health from the body, while he does not allow the single members to do their own offices. In the course of your argument you say: "There is one Prince in the Church, in whom and from whom no one disagrees." If it is Peter, Paul withstands you: "For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, not from Peter." And again: "Not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ."

units.la: Pergis dicens, Non a multis vnum, sed multa ab vno. Cum a Paedagogo meo interrogarer infans, Quidnam esset numerus? respondi, Vnitatum collectio ab vno sciendens ad plura. Similiter & tempus mensura motus rerum mutabilium. Postea ab Augustino in vltimis Confessionum libris didici, esse discretionem potentiae ratiocinatiuae super rebus numerabilibus aut fluxis. Tu vero quid dicens, vix consideras, quia non inferunt quod praetendis: vt Ixnerius ait, consequentiam tollit contrarium, non inducit.
units.tr: You go on, saying: "Not many from one, but many from one." When I was a child and asked by my teacher what number was, I answered: a collection of units, proceeding from one to many. Likewise time is the measure of the motion of changeable things. Later I learned from Augustine, in the last books of the Confessions, that there is a distinction between the power of reasoning over countable or fleeting things. But you, in saying what you say, hardly consider that what you allege does not follow. As Irnerius says, a consequence removes the contrary; it does not bring it in.

units.la: Prosequeris, vt in corpore multa membra vnius capitis sumunt influxum, &c. Fatemur, sed non ita vt caput manus aut pedis vsurpet officium, reliquis scil. Episcopis nihil relinquendo.
units.tr: You go on: in the body many members receive influence from the one head, and so on. We grant it, but not so that the head seizes the office of the hand or foot, leaving nothing to the other bishops.

units.la: Sequitur, Inferiores motus primi mobilis motu gubernantur. At non Solutilo concitus igne Phaebes gelidum impedit axem, sed veterem seruant sidera pacem.
units.tr: It follows: the lower motions are governed by the motion of the first mover. "But the stars do not hinder the cold axis of the sun, stirred up by a fire that is not its own; they keep the old peace."

units.la: Sequitur, vt ex reuerentia inferiorum ad caput vna concordia fieret. Vicissim lege S. Gregorium corripientem Episcopum, quod se Vniuersalis Ecclesiae Episcopum nuncupaiet; Dicentem; Cum omnia tibi tribuis, adimis mihi, &c. Honor meus est fratrum meorum solius rigor.
units.tr: It follows: that from reverence of the lower members towards the head there might be one harmony. In turn, read St Gregory rebuking a bishop because he styled himself Bishop of the Universal Church, saying: "When you attribute everything to yourself, you take away from me... My honour is the firmness of my brothers alone."

units.la: Sequitur, In apibus vnus Rex est; & grues vnam sequuntur ordine litterario. Si attentius quae legisti, observaueris, iam scires illud de quolibet Episcopo dictum esse, vt sequitur: Scire debetis Ecclesiam in Episcopo & Episcopum in Ecclesia esse, neque inficiari debes in Ecclesia esse Romanum Pontificem, extra quam nullus salvatur. Erit igitur Ecclesia Pontifice maior, sicut coetus Apostolicus fuit maior Petro. Sed quia gloriaris in apum metaphora, quam fateor esse praecipuam, nullos quoque populos attentius Regem obseruare, quo amisso rumpitur foedus, mella diripiuntur, fauusque dissoluitur. Eum igitur humeris attollunt; & obiectant corpora bello, pro quo nec mori recusant. Sed quare, vt singula quadrent, omnes enim in commune mellificant, communiter & prolem educantes (vt ait Maro) solae communes natos, consortia testa vrbis habent, & in medium quaesita reponunt. Rex autem est operum custos; non sic etiam <bl>Pontifex</bl> Romanus, qui Piccolominibus Pientiaeque thesaurisat? Talis Rex iubetur expelli, vt rursus ait Maro:
units.tr: It follows: "Among bees there is one king, and cranes follow one leader in ordered formation." If you had observed more carefully what you have read, you would already know that this was said of any bishop, as follows: "You ought to know that the Church is in the bishop and the bishop in the Church," and you ought not to deny that the Roman Pontiff is in the Church, outside which no one is saved. The Church will therefore be greater than the Pontiff, just as the Apostolic assembly was greater than Peter. But since you boast in the metaphor of bees, which I admit is outstanding, note that no peoples observe their king more carefully, and when he is lost the bond is broken, the honey is plundered and the comb dissolves. They therefore lift him on their shoulders and expose their bodies to war for him, for whom they do not refuse to die. But why, that every detail may fit, do they all make honey in common, bringing up their offspring together (as Virgil says), and only the common-born have the common houses of the city, and they set aside what they have gathered for the common good? Is not the king the guardian of the works? Yet does not the Roman Pontiff do otherwise, who hoards up Piccolomini and the treasures of piety? Such a king is ordered to be expelled, as Virgil again says:

units.la: Deterior qui visus, cum ne prodigus obsit, Dede neci, melior vacua sine regnet in aula.
units.tr: The one who looks worse, lest the prodigal one do harm, give him to death; let the better one reign in the empty hall.

units.la: Postea calumniose praevaricaris Bernardum Claraevallensem, quasi omnem potestatem in solum Petrum innuat esse transfusam, dum dicit: Sicut Seraphin & Cherubin caeterique ordines sub uno capite, &c. Sed longe alia est mens Bernhardi, qui execrans detestandsque Praelatorum exemptiones, Eugenium sic arguit: Subtrahuntur Abbates Episcopi, Episcopi Archiepiscopi, ii Patriarchae: & sic factitando probatis vos habere plenitudinem potestatis. Honorum ac dignitatum gradus, & ordines quibusque suos seruare positi estis, &c. Tu ne denique tibi licitum censeas, suae Ecclesiam mutilare membris, confundere ordinem, perturbare terminos, quos posuerunt Patres tui? Si iustitia est ius suum cuique seruare, auferre cuiquam sua quomodo poterit conuenire? Erras, si vt summam, ita & solam institutam a Deo Apostolicam potestatem existimas, & dissentis ab eo, qui ait; Non est potestas, nisi a Deo. Proinde quod sequitur, Qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit, etsi principaliter pro te facit, non tamen singulariter. Rursus, omnu animae potestatibus sublimioribus, tanquam in multis. Non tua ergo sola potestas a Domino, sed & inferiores, &c. Monstrum facis, si manum submouens digitum facis capiti collateralem, aut in corpore Christi membra locas aliter, quam disposuit ipse. Nisi putas, alium esse qui posuit in Ecclesia quosdam Apostolos, quosdam autem Prophetas, alios Euangelistas, alios Doctores & pastores, &c. Sicut illi Cherubin & Seraphin, &c. Quod si dicat Episcopus; Nolo subesse Archiepiscopo, aut Abbas, noli obedire Episcopo, hoc de caelo non est, nisi tu forte angelorum quempiam dicentem audisti; Nolo sub Archangelo esse. Vides ergo doctrinam Bernhardi Eugenio sincere datam, quam tu impie praevaricaris, qui ex reseruationibus Ecclesiarum Cathedralium & confusione hierarchiae consequentis ad illam natus es pontificatum.
units.tr: Afterwards you wickedly distort Bernard of Clairvaux, as if he meant that all power had been transferred to Peter alone, since he says: As the Seraphim and Cherubim and the other orders are under one head, etc. But Bernard's mind is quite different: he curses and detests the exemptions of prelates, and thus argues against Eugenius: Abbots are withdrawn from bishops, bishops from archbishops, these from patriarchs; and by doing this you prove that you have the fullness of power. You have been set to keep the degrees and orders of honours and dignities, each in its place, etc. Do you finally think it permitted to you to mutilate the Church of its members, to confound the order and disturb the boundaries that your Fathers set? If justice is to keep to each his own, how can it agree that anyone should take away what is his? You are wrong if you think that the Apostolic power is instituted by God as the highest and the only one, and you dissent from him who says: "There is no power but from God." Therefore what follows, "He who resists the power resists the ordinance of God," though it chiefly favours you, does not favour you alone. Again, "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers," as to many. So your power is not the only one from the Lord, but the lower ones too, etc. You make a monster, if, by removing the hand, you make the finger a colleague of the head, or place the members of the body of Christ otherwise than he himself arranged them. Unless you think there is another who has set in the Church some apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, others teachers and pastors, etc., like those Cherubim and Seraphim, etc. But if a bishop says, "I do not want to be subject to the archbishop," or an abbot says, "Do not obey the bishop," this is not from heaven, unless perhaps you have heard some angel saying: "I do not want to be under an archangel." You see, then, Bernard's teaching given sincerely to Eugenius, which you impiously distort, you who were born to the pontificate out of the reservations of cathedral churches and the confusion of the hierarchy that follows.

units.la: Sequitur nunc illud Euangelicum, Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam. Multi calumniatores tui patres ex hoc verbo audent asserere, super solo Petro aedificatam esse Ecclesiam. Illis tuus Bernardus dissentit, vbi supra, dicens; alios Apostolos, Prophetas, Euangelistas, Doctores, Pastores ad consummationem Sanctorum, in opus ministerii, in aedificationem corporis Christi. Atque hoc corpus, quod tibi ipse Paulus hoc suo Apostolico figurans eloquio, & capiti conuenientissime adaptans, totum ex eo compactum perhibet, & connexum per omnem iuncturam subministrationis, secundum operationem in mensuram, vniuscuiusque membri augmentum corporis faciens, in aedificationem sui in charitate. Christus est ergo caput, cuius membra sumus per charitatem. Illud igitur iungas: Petra autem erat Christus indeficiens. Nam & Hieremiae dictum est a Domino: Ecce constituite super gentes & regna, vt tuellas & distruas, disperdas & dissipes, ad sices & plantes; nec tamen ideo summa rerum sibi soli collata perhibetur.
units.tr: Now comes that Gospel saying: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. Many of your slanderers, your Fathers, dare to assert from this word that the Church was built on Peter alone. Your Bernard dissents from them, in the passage above, saying: Other Apostles, Prophets, Evangelists, Teachers, Pastors, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ. And this body, which Paul himself, your Apostle, in his apostolic language representing it and most fittingly fitting it to the head, says is wholly framed from him and knit together through every joint of supply, according to the working in due measure of each member, makes increase of the body to the building up of itself in love. Christ, then, is the head, whose members we are through love. Therefore join this: But the rock was Christ, never failing. For it was also said to Jeremiah by the Lord: Behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to scatter, to build and to plant; and yet the supreme power of things is not thereby said to be given to him alone.

units.la: Sequitur, Vna est columba mea, perfecta mea, &c. vnitate fidei, & charitate Christi, non Petri, vel Pii: quibus defunctis non definit Ecclesia, neque exspirat, si duo auari certent de Papatu, vt saepe, aut Papa erret in fide, vt quandoque. Imo & Indum recte credentem in Ecclesia esse confido, ne coactio necessitatis ipsum excludat a regno Dei, quod promisit credentibus in se Dominus.
units.tr: Next comes, One is my dove, my perfect one, etc., which speaks of the unity of faith and of Christ's love, not of Peter's or Pius's. When these men die, the Church does not end or expire, even if two greedy men fight over the papacy, as they often do, or the Pope errs in faith, as he sometimes does. Indeed, I trust that an Indian who believes rightly is in the Church, and that the compulsion of necessity does not exclude him from the kingdom of God, which the Lord promised to those who believe in him.

units.la: Sequitur; Ego & Pater vnum sumus. Quis hic dubitet Iesum Christum patri consubstantialem? nec dubitatur, quin Christus ascensurus ad patrem cuncta saluti nostrae oportuna prouiderit: qui & post ascensionem & Spiritus sancti missionem Paulum ad praeputium misit, de quo differere post hoc non omittam.
units.tr: Next comes: I and the Father are one. Who here doubts that Jesus Christ is consubstantial with the Father? Nor is it doubted that Christ, about to ascend to the Father, provided for everything needful for our salvation. After his ascension and the sending of the Holy Spirit, he sent Paul to the uncircumcised, concerning whom I will not omit to speak further after this.

units.la: Redis nunc rursus ad Claraevallensem, quasi ille rem omnem soli Papae attribuat. Cogis me rem illam ab initio attingere, ne putent homines ignari, Bernhardum ipsum pompam & gloriam Eugenio persuasisse. Bernardus Claraevallensis scripsit ad Eugenium super pontificatu librum vnum, hortans eum ad Dei cultum, & contemptum mundanorum, dum dicit: Putasne haec tempora sustinerent, si hominibus pro terrenis litigantibus voce Domini responderes: Quis me constituit super vos? Et istud: Cum obsidio vrbi & barbaricus ensis imminerit, beatus Gregorius extremam & obscurissimam partem Ezechielis tam diligenter quam eleganter exposuit. Et illud: Disputationes aduocatorum magu ad subuersionem, quam inuentionem proficiunt veritati. Et illud: Timeant numinularii, nec fidant in nummis, scientes effundere quam accipere separationem. Ominatus est vir sanctus sese calumniari: idcirco telam succidit, librumque clausit hiis verbis: Atque hic sit finis istius, ne duplo te oneret minus suauis oratio, si & longa fuerit. Hoc etiam probat sequentis libri principium, quod continuo apologeticum est, tum circa prioris libri praecepta, tum circa titulum eius, quem illi iam De consideratione imposuerat. Tantus enim liuor in virum sanctum ascenderat, vt & titulus libri veniret in calumniam, quasi vir sanctus consideratione pro contemplatione nuncupasset. Huiusce defensionibus praelibaris vir sanctus ad prioris libri praecepta reuertens, ait; Non est quod blandiatur celsitudo. Disce tibi sarculo opus esse. Nam Propheta cum similiter leuaretur, audiuit, Vt euellas & dissipes, &c. Quid aliud hoc innuit, nisi cum leuaretur Propheta, sicut tu: quia similitudo differentiam notat non identitatem, &c. Tolle facium fucati honoris. Ex quo satis intelligitur Doctorem sanctum calumnias esse perpessum, qui & iam dixerat: Libens in me accipio detrahentium linguas maledicas, & venenata spicula blasphemantium. Et cum plurima scripsisset vir sanctus in execrationem deliciarum & pompae pontificalis, subdit illa: Sacerdos magnus, summus Pontifex, &c. Deinde submittit de prioritate Petri; at non ita, vt illi soli potestas sit delegata, vt superius dixi super eisdem verbis. Quid igitur in Bernardo gloriaris, qui delicias & pompas Pontificis adoras? ad quarum detestationem & omnium temporalium rerum contemptum omnes illi quatuor libri à viro sancto profecti sunt, non autem quod Eugenius prae ceteris [illegible, ~12 letters] ret, sed vt omnes Romanos Pontifices ministerii sollicitudinisque pontificalis [illegible, ~10 letters] ret, vt ipse quoque testatur. Nam cum singula quaeque ad eminentiam ipsius dignitatis [illegible, ~8 letters] tia explicuisset, admonet eum suae vilitatis, & praedecessorum suorum humilitatis, quae tu ios pie retices & supprimis, quasi vir sanctus delicias pontificales & decorationem omnium velit approbare, qui tamen contra Pontificis auaritiam scribens ait, Omnia possidens non contentaris universo, &c. vt scripsi supra, super his verbis: Tu primatu Abel. Hac igitur lege coeamus & conciliemur, Claraevallensem in omnibus vt accipias, vt ipsius Pontificis eminentiam veneremur, auaritiam vero cum Bernardo detestemur. O quid putas dicturum fuisse Bernardum, si vidisset Romanum Pontificem de minutissimis beneficiis disponentem, & hierarchicum ordinem per omnia confundentem, & suum monasterium S. Anastasii de urbe concessum in commendam? qui aegre tulit Abbatum exemtione damnans eam velut perturbationem ordinis a sanctis Patrib. praefiniti.
units.tr: You now return again to the Clairvaux writer, as if he attributed the whole matter to the Pope alone. You force me to touch on that matter from the beginning, so that ignorant people do not think that Bernard himself persuaded Eugenius of pomp and glory. Bernard of Clairvaux wrote one book to Eugenius on the papacy, urging him to the worship of God and the contempt of worldly things, when he says: Do you think these times would endure if you answered men who quarrel over earthly things with the voice of the Lord: Who has made me a judge over you? And this: When a siege threatens the city and the barbarian sword is at hand, the blessed Gregory expounded the last and most obscure part of Ezekiel as diligently as elegantly. And this: The disputations of advocates contribute to the overthrow of truth rather than to its discovery. And this: Let the money-changers fear, and let them not trust in their coins, knowing that it is a greater loss to pay out than to receive. The holy man foresaw that he would be slandered, and so he cut short the thread and closed the book with these words: Let this be the end of it, lest a less pleasing discourse burden you twice over, even if it has been long. The opening of the following book also shows this, since it is at once an apology, both concerning the precepts of the earlier book and concerning its title, which he had already given as On Consideration. For such great envy had risen against the holy man that even the title of the book was made a matter of calumny, as if the holy man had named it On Consideration instead of On Contemplation. Having touched briefly on these defences, the holy man returns to the precepts of the earlier book and says: There is no reason for your loftiness to flatter itself. Learn that you need the hoe. For when the Prophet was similarly lifted up, he heard: To pluck up and to destroy, etc. What else does this suggest, than that when the Prophet was lifted up, you were too, since a likeness marks a difference and not an identity, etc.? Take away the face of false honour. From this it is sufficiently clear that the holy teacher suffered calumnies, for he had already said: Gladly do I accept the malicious tongues of those who detract, and the poisoned darts of blasphemers. And after he had written very much in execration of the delights and pomp of the papal office, he adds these words: The great priest, the highest Pontiff, etc. Then he speaks of Peter's priority, but not in such a way that the power was delegated to him alone, as I said above on the same words. Why then do you glory in Bernard, when you admire the delights and pomp of the Pope? For the detestation of these and the contempt of all temporal things, all four of those books were produced by the holy man, not because Eugenius was preferred above others [illegible], but so that he might [illegible] all the Roman pontiffs with the care of the ministry and of the pontifical office [illegible], as he himself also testifies. For when he had explained each thing concerning the eminence of that dignity [illegible], he reminds him of his own lowliness and that of his predecessors, which you piously conceal and suppress, as if the holy man wished to approve the pontifical delights and the adornment of all things, when yet writing against the avarice of the Pope he says: Possessing everything, you are not content with the whole world, etc., as I wrote above on these words: You, Abel, the primate. Let us therefore come together and be reconciled on this condition: that you accept the Clairvaux writer in all things, that we venerate the eminence of the Pope himself, but that we detest avarice together with Bernard. O what do you think Bernard would have said, if he had seen the Roman Pontiff disposing of the smallest benefices, confusing the hierarchical order in every respect, and granting in commendam his monastery of St Anastasius in the city? He took it hard, condemning the exemption of abbots as a disturbance of order, which the holy Fathers had laid down.

units.la: Inter haec vnam admisces haeresin, dicens; In reliquos discipulos non nisi per Petrum sit derivata potestas. Hoc neque Anacletus dicit, nec magnus Leo consentit, fatentes Petro quidem omnimodam potestatem traditam, id est, nullis terminis coartatam; minime autem differentur & caeteris Apostolis claves esse traditas a Christo immediate. Dic rudis haeretice, vbi legisti, Petrum quemquam Apostolorum in Sacerdotem vel Episcopum consecrasse? Ergo disce, omnes vndecim Apostolos viva voce veritatis ordinatos: quia manuum impositio ritus est ab Apostolis introductus, postea solemnes praedicationes adiecit Ecclesia. Mathias autem non aliter legimus ordinatum, nisi quod inter duodecim annumeratus est, & spiritum Sanctum cum aliis accepit, ita vt non esset vlla manuum impositio necessaria. Atque hodie veritas est indubitata, nedum sacrum ordinem, sed & omnia Sacramenta a Christo immediate conferri. Episcoporum autem & Sacerdotum ministerii exhibitio corporalis incorporalia sacra contingere non valet, sed spiritualis collationis praebet indicium infallibile: quia non faciet Iesus irritum pactum suum vt cum minister eius officii sui ministerium in nomine eius exhibet, ipse praestat quod repromisit. Dic si speculator in colle consistere iussus, hostili exercitu inter angustias viso, signo dato monea [?] at Imperatorem, sicut pactum fuerat, isque subito impetu obruat hostem, cui actionem ... is, cui summam rerum defers? Te parem esse reor Simoni, putanti manuum impositionem Petri ac Ioannis factam super baptisatis in Samaria, qui nondum acceperant spiritum Sanctum, corporali quodam attactu id effecisse: sicut ouum quod ex cubatione gallinae vivificatur. Cui Petrus ait: Existimasti donum Dei pecunia possideri. Poenitentiam itaque age, &c. Rudis es, de sacris rudissime sentiens, alta tamen attingere audes, dum dicis, quod missio Petri & Iohannis in Samariam a Coapostolis facta non sit indicium maioritatis omnium Apostolorum ad Petrum, & dicis similem fuisse Arrii impium errorem dicentis, Spiritum Sanctum patre filioque minorem, quia mittatur ab illo.
units.tr: Among these things you mix in one heresy, saying: The power is derived to the other disciples only through Peter. Neither Anacletus says this, nor does great Leo agree, since they acknowledge that indeed the full power was handed to Peter, that is, not limited by any bounds; but by no means are the keys said to have been handed to the other Apostles immediately by Christ. Tell me, ignorant heretic, where did you read that Peter consecrated any of the Apostles as priest or bishop? Learn therefore that all eleven Apostles were ordained by the living voice of truth, since the laying on of hands is a rite introduced by the Apostles, and the Church afterwards added solemn preaching. We read that Matthias was ordained in no other way, except that he was counted among the twelve and received the Holy Spirit with the others, so that there was no laying on of hands necessary. And today it is indubitable truth that not only holy orders but all the sacraments are conferred immediately by Christ. The bodily performance of the ministry of bishops and priests cannot touch incorporeal sacred things, but it offers an infallible indication of spiritual conferral, because Jesus will not make his covenant void: when his minister exhibits the ministry of his office in his name, he himself grants what he has promised. Tell me: if a watchman, ordered to stand on a hill, sees the hostile army among the narrow passes, and by a given sign warns the Emperor, as had been agreed, and he then overwhelms the enemy with a sudden attack, to whom do you entrust the sum of affairs, the one who ... or the one who ...? I judge you to be an equal of Simon, who thought that the laying on of hands by Peter and John upon the baptized in Samaria, who had not yet received the Holy Spirit, effected this by some bodily touch, like an egg made alive by the sitting of a hen. To him Peter said: You thought that the gift of God could be possessed for money. Repent therefore, etc. You are ignorant, most ignorantly judging of sacred things, yet you dare to touch on lofty matters, when you say that the sending of Peter and John into Samaria by their fellow Apostles was not a sign of the superiority of Peter over all the Apostles, and you say that it resembled the impious error of Arius, who said: The Holy Spirit is less than the Father and the Son, because he is sent by him.

units.la: O philtrum grossum, Feltrensi populo dignum? qui generationem & genituram, spirationem & processionem aeternam, Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti putas corporalibus rebus aequari, vbi mittens ac missus, generans & genitus substantialiter absque vlla essentiae communicatione distinguantur. Sed ad textum redeamus. Ille ipse Lucas qui scripsit: Convocantes autem XII. multitudinem discipulorum, dixerunt: Non est aequum nos derelinquere verbum Dei, &c. Considerate viros ex vobis boni testimonii septem, & elegerunt Stephanum, Philippum, Prochorum, Nicanorem, Timonem, Parmenam, & Nicolaum, &c. Vides quomodo apud Hierosolymam XII. Apostoli congregaverunt Concilium, totumque Concilium elegit praedictos septem, quos constituit super hoc opus, scilicet evangelizandi verbum Dei, non autem Petrus. Ille idem Lucas subiungit, quod Stephano lapidato omnes dispersi sunt per regiones Iudaeae & Samariae, praeter Apostolos, & qui dispersi erant pertransibant evangelisantes. Philippus autem descendens in civitatem Samariam praedicabat illis Christum, intendebant autem turbae hiis, quae a Philippo dicebantur, &c. Et post pauca subdit Lucas: Cum autem audissent Apostoli, qui erant Hierosolymis, quia Samaria recepit verbum Dei, miserunt ad eos Petrum & Iohannem, &c. Ex hiis constat luce clarius, Ecclesiam Dei Stephani lapidatione dispersam, solis Apostolis manentibus congregatis, apud quos integra permansit auctoritas. Qui cum audissent Samaritas in Philippum intentos, miserunt & Petrum & Iohannem. Quid igitur calumniaris, aequiuocando missionem Philippi ac Iohannis a missione Petri, in eodem orationis contextu, praecipue autem inter Petri ac Iohannis, quasi aliter Petrus sit missus, aliter Iohannes? an quia Petrus dignitati suae derogatum esse duxisset, quiramen a solo Paulo reprehendi se sustinuit? Ita enim Galatis scribit vas electionis: Cum venisset Cephas Antiochiam, in faciem ei restiti, quia reprehensibilis erat, &c. Neque enim Petrus quidquam Paulo contulit, sed ipse contulit Petro, quod acceperat a Domino. Tu vero somnia delirans dicis, Qualiter Consiliarii mittant Regem ad bellum, quamquam Rex sit cunctorum Dominus, ita Petrus ab Apostolis Samariam missus sit, impulsis etiam amore eorum ad quos mittebatur, scilicet Samaritanorum. Vtrobique deliras phantastice. Neque enim Regii Consiliarii Regem in bellum mittere, sed consultanti Regi, an bellum indicere vel suscipere, an exercitum ducere, an alium illi praeficere expediat, adesse habent ae persuadere. Ita Xerxen fecisse legimus, cuius tanta copiae fuisse dicuntur, vt nec mare classibus, nec campestria equestrib. neq; acra telis capiendis sufficere posse, assentatores aulae suae gloriarentur, praeter vnicum qui censuit, Immoderata Regi non posse: quae vero Regi non possent, minime subsistere. Ita & cæteri Reges fecere: nisi forte quis precario regnet aut vacuo Regis nomine contenteretur, vt olim ante Faramundum Francorum Reges vidisse perhibentur. Et quia nimium inepte locutum esse comperio, existimare cogor te minime intelligere, quid Rex, quid regnum, quidue habeat dignitas & potentia regnatiua. Id ergo perstringam, quia etiam à præsenti tractatu non abhorret. Etsi omnis viuendi & agendi ritus & norma, quibus pax & tranquillitas gentium vel populorum salubriter custoditur, generali vocabulo Politia nuncupetur: tamen propter agendi varietatem, quam vel prauitas regnantium, vel ipsa dominantium improbitas, aut fati fortasse necessitas humana iudicia superans tum persuasit, tum coegit, auctores de politia scribentes illam profecto trifariam distinxerunt. Primam, quæ Principi Deo, qui omnem mundum regit, propius accedit, Monarchiam vocauerunt. Ea quidem in seipsa perfectissima est ac populis accommoda, cum heroico viro defertur. Tales quippe fuerunt, quos Græcia diuinis colit honoribus, vt & Romani Quiriuum suum ad astra tulerunt, qui tamen ob asperius ingenium à Senatu discerptus est. De his Socrates in Apologia: Nemo vnquam Reipublicæ gubernator euasit, si libere ad populum locutus sit, ac his, quæ iniuste indigneque plerunque fiunt, se opposuit. Sed necesse est ei, qui velit reuera pro iustitia pugnantem vel exiguo tempore saluum fore, priuatum degere, neque Reipublicam attingere. Tales neque hoc cœlum, neque tellus nostra gignit, quorum meminit Philosophus 3. Politicor. & Flaccus ad Ofilium: Hos vtinam inter heroas natum tellus me prima tulisset. Sed quia vnici hominis depravatione Monarchia vertitur in tyrannidem, quæ fuerat Septimi Regis ab vrbe pellendi causa, & Imperii consularis pro regno permutandi, successerit regimen optimarum, quod Aristocraticum vocatur, quia vnici hominis depravatione non adeo corrumpitur, quin ab in corruptis valeat rectificari. Hoc est, quod Cicero ab exilio reuersus commemorat, cur tribunitio furori parere & in exilium abire maluerit, quam ciuilibus armis decertare, quod alterutro Consulum incorrupto agente non dubitabat se rediturum: quem tandem omnis Italia humeris suis reportauit.
units.tr: O thick-headed fool, fit for the people of Feltre! Do you really think that generation and begetting, and the eternal spiration and procession of Father, Son and Holy Spirit, are equal to bodily things, when sending and being sent, begetting and being begotten, are distinguished in substance without any communication of the essence? But let us return to the text. That same Luke who wrote: "Then the twelve called the multitude of the disciples together and said, 'It is not right that we should leave the word of God,' etc. 'Look out among you seven men of good report,' and they chose Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas and Nicolaus,' etc. You see how the twelve Apostles at Jerusalem gathered a council, and the whole council chose the seven named, whom it appointed over this work, namely the preaching of the word of God, and not Peter. The same Luke adds that after Stephen was stoned, all were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the Apostles, and those who were scattered went about preaching the gospel. Philip, going down to the city of Samaria, preached Christ to them, and the crowds gave heed to what was said by Philip, etc. And a little later Luke adds: "Now when the Apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, etc." From this it is clearer than light that the Church of God, scattered by the stoning of Stephen, was gathered with only the Apostles remaining, among whom the full authority remained. When they heard that the Samaritans were attentive to Philip, they sent both Peter and John. Why then do you cavil, equivocating between the sending of Philip and John and the sending of Peter, within the same context of the narrative, and especially between Peter and John, as if Peter was sent in one way and John in another? Or is it because Peter thought it beneath his dignity, although he endured being rebuked by Paul alone? For the vessel of election writes thus to the Galatians: "When Cephas had come to Antioch, I withstood him to his face, because he was to be blamed, etc." Indeed Peter did not confer anything on Paul, but Paul conferred on Peter what he had received from the Lord. But you, raving in your dreams, say: "Just as counsellors send a king to war, although the king is lord of all, so Peter was sent by the Apostles to Samaria, moved also by love for those to whom he was sent, namely the Samaritans." You rave fantastically in both respects. For royal counsellors do not send the king into war, but they are present to advise the king, and to persuade him, whether it is expedient to declare or undertake war, to lead an army, or to set someone else over it. So we read that Xerxes did, of whose forces it is said that they were so great that the sea could not hold his fleets, nor the plains his cavalry, nor the rivers his water supplies, while his flatterers at court boasted; except for the one man who judged: "What is immoderate cannot be for a king; what cannot be for a king cannot stand." Other kings have done likewise, unless perhaps someone reigns by sufferance or is content with the empty name of king, as the kings of the Franks are said to have been before Pharamond. And since I find you have spoken very foolishly, I am compelled to think you do not in the least understand what a king is, what a kingdom is, or what kingly dignity and power are. I will therefore set this out, since it is not foreign to the present treatise. Although every manner and rule of living and acting by which the peace and tranquillity of nations or peoples is wholesomely preserved is called by the general name Polity, yet on account of the variety of action, which either the wickedness of rulers, or the wickedness of those in power, or perhaps the necessity of fate, exceeding human judgement, has both persuaded and compelled, writers on polity have certainly divided it into three kinds. The first, which comes nearest to God the Prince, who rules the whole world, they called Monarchy. This is indeed most perfect in itself and suited to peoples, when it is entrusted to a heroic man. Such were those whom Greece honours with divine worship, and the Romans raised their Quirinus to the stars, though he was torn to pieces by the Senate because of his harsh temper. Of these men Socrates speaks in the Apology: "No one ever became a governor of the commonwealth if he spoke freely to the people and opposed the things that are very often done unjustly and shamefully. But he who wishes to fight truly for justice must, if he is to be safe even for a short time, live as a private man and not meddle with public affairs." Neither this heaven nor our land produces such men, of whom the Philosopher makes mention in the third book of the Politics, and Flaccus to Ofilius: "Would that the first earth had borne me among such heroes!" But because, through the corruption of a single man, monarchy turns into tyranny, which was the reason for expelling the seventh king from the city and exchanging the consular empire for a kingdom, there followed the rule of the best men, which is called Aristocratic, because it is not so corrupted by the fault of one man that it cannot be set right by the uncorrupted. This is what Cicero recalls after his return from exile, explaining why he preferred to yield to the frenzy of the tribune and go into exile rather than contend with civil arms, since he did not doubt that he would return while either of the consuls acted uncorrupted; and at last all Italy carried him back on its shoulders.

units.la: Cum autem optimatibus dominandi libido incessit, Aristocratia in Oliarchiam mutata est: ad tertium genus agendi deuentum est, quod in specie Politiam vocant, in qua quilibet vicissim parricipat, id vulgo Populare vocatur, corruptum vero in tumultum vertitur, quem appellat Democratiam. In quolibet autem horum Principatuum genere, si in corrupto regimen permanserit, populi vnitas sustentatur. Ita & in Conciliis vniuersalib. etiam Papa sublato, Ecclesiæ vnitas conseruatur, & manebit vna columba formosa perfecta, sed & vnum ouile vnius pastoris æterni, Christi Domini, Sacerdotis in æternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech.
units.tr: But when the desire to rule took hold of the best men, aristocracy was changed into oligarchy, and the third kind of action was reached, which they call Polity in the specific sense, in which each in turn takes part; this is commonly called Popular, and when corrupted it turns into tumult, which he calls Democracy. However, in each kind of these principates, if the government remains in the corrupt form, the unity of the people is maintained. So also in universal Councils, even with the Pope removed, the unity of the Church is preserved, and there will remain one beautiful, perfect dove, and also one fold under one eternal Shepherd, Christ the Lord, the Priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.

units.la: Id vero, quod de amore in Samaritanos delirando somnias, nil proficit, nec inter missionem Philippi, Prochori, Nicanoris &c. ac Petri & Iohannis quidquam secernit. Vt autem intelligas, quam sit impertinens ac disparatum enthymema, quod de missione sempiterna patris & filii ad Spiritum sanctum, ac missione cœtus Apostolici ad Petrum seu quemuis Apostolorum remotissima similitudine retorques, sic accipe. Legerat Arrius: Patrem gignere filium, ipsumque genitum à Patre. Rursus, Patrem ac filium spirare Spiritum sanctum, illumque à Patre & filio procedere. Alietatem ergo discretiuam proprietatis personarum Arrius accipiens, habentem se per modum causantis & causati, ex rebus autem naturalibus productis & creatis ad Deum æternum, ad personas coæternas, & coæquales similitudine traducta, maioritatem inter illas esse putauit: minime considerans, quod in æterna generatione generans dat genito quidquid est, & quidquid habet, nil autem sibi diminuens. Similiter & spirans dat spirato vel procedenti: hoc solo dempto, quod pater filio non communicat innascibilitatem vel gignendi actiuam proprietatem, qua quidem discretione à Filio secernitur. Similique modo Pater & Filius Spiritui non communicant actiuam spirationem æternam. Has enim notiones separatas esse oportet, ne personæ confundantur. Diuina autem essentia personis singulis communicata, nec generans, nec genita, neque procedens, simplex & inefabilis eas facit esse coæquales. Ergo Pater & Filius Spiritum æterna spiratione spirantes, atque etiam nouissime in discipulos Spiritum mittentes, nihil aliud à se spirant. Nam Deum de Deo, genitum non factum confitentes, æque Deum de Deo, & lumen de lumine mitti ac procedere confiteamur oportet. Et sicut generans & genitus vnum sunt, sic mittens & missus. Nec tamen ob hoc idem seipsum gignere, mittere vel spirare dicitur, ne persona seipsam, vel essentia gignat essentiam. Non autem tic cœtus Apostolicus vnum est cum Philippo, Prochoro, Petro vel Ioanne.
units.tr: As for what you dream about his love for the Samaritans, it achieves nothing, nor does it distinguish anything between the sending of Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, etc., and that of Peter and John. But so that you may understand how irrelevant and unlike an enthymeme it is, which you twist from the eternal sending of the Father and the Son to the Holy Spirit, and from the sending of the Apostolic body to Peter or any one of the Apostles, by a most remote likeness, take it thus. Arius had read: "The Father begets the Son, and the Son is begotten by the Father." Again: "The Father and the Son breathe forth the Holy Spirit, and he proceeds from the Father and the Son." Arius, therefore, taking the distinguishing diversity of the properties of the persons, which exists in the manner of cause and effect, and transferring it by likeness from natural things produced and created to the eternal God and to the co-eternal and co-equal persons, thought there was inequality among them; not considering at all that in eternal generation the begetter gives to the begotten whatever he is and whatever he has, while diminishing nothing in himself. Likewise the breather gives to the breathed or proceeding one, except only that the Father does not communicate to the Son the unbegottenness or the active property of begetting, by which indeed he is distinguished from the Son. In the same way the Father and the Son do not communicate to the Spirit the active eternal spiration. For these notions must be kept separate, so that the persons are not confounded. But the divine essence, communicated to each of the persons, neither begetting, nor begotten, nor proceeding, makes them simple and ineffable and co-equal. Therefore the Father and the Son, breathing the Spirit by eternal spiration, and even at the last sending the Spirit to the disciples, breathe forth nothing other than themselves. For since we confess God of God, begotten not made, we must equally confess that God is sent and proceeds from God, and light from light. And as the begetter and the begotten are one, so the sender and the sent. Yet it is not on this account said that the same person begets, sends or breathes himself, lest a person beget himself or an essence beget an essence. But the Apostolic body is not one with Philip, Prochorus, Peter or John.

units.la: Pergis deinde fingendo, quasi ego innuerim Petrum ex Antiochia Romam à reliquis discipulis esse transmissum. Hoc de me (credo) fingis, vt habeas in quod conuitium habeas: neruos autem intendis, si efficere possis, vrbem Romam Petri sedem esse præcipuam, & primatum Petri ipsius vrbis Romæ principatu, quem tunc habebat vrbs ipsa confirmes. Rem satis tranquillam commouendo, plus dubitabilem reddis. Nosti communiter omnibus esse dictum: Hoc facite in meam commemorationem. Rursus: Sicut me misit Pater, & ego mitto vos. Insufflauit & dixit eis, Accipite Spiritum Sanctum, quorum remiseritis peccata, remittentur. Rursus: Euntes docete omnes gentes, &c. His quidem verbis nullus delectus personæ exprimitur, nullus orbis terræ locus cuiquam assignatur. Sed in omnem terram exiuit sonus eorum, & in fines orbis terræ vox eorum. Per reuelationem autem Pauli scimus, quod licet ipse per orbem euangelisare habebat, de quo scribitur: Hic est mihi vas electionis, vt portet nomen meum coram gentibus & Regibus, & filiis Israel, aliquo tamen respectu principalius missus ad gentes, vt de se loquutus refertur in Actis: Factum est autem re- mertensi uertenti mihi in Hierusalem, & oranti in templo, fieri me in stupore mentis, & videre illum decentem mihi: Festina & exi velociter ex Hierusalem, quoniam non recipient testimonium tuum de me. Vade, quoniam in nationes mittam te. Ipse quoque Galatis secundo scribens ait: Cum vidissent Iacobus, Petrus & Iohannes, quod creditum est mihi Euangelium praeputii, sicut Petro circumcisionis. Ac rursus: Iacobus & Cephas & Iohannes, qui videbantur columna esse, dextras dederunt mihi & Barnabæ societatis, vt nos in gentes, ipse autem in circumcisione irent Euangelium prædicandum. Quæ omnia magis innuere videntur, vrbem Romam Pauli quam Petri fuisse prouinciam, a Christo sibi non a Petro assignatam, sicut & aliam quamlibet suam functionem, vt ipse Galatis primo scribens orditur: PAVLVS Apostolus non ab hominibus neque per hominem, sed per Iesum Christum, & Deum Patrem, qui suscitauit eum a mortuis. Sed & secundo Galatis scribens se a nullo puro homine accepisse significat, dicens: Mihi enim, qui videbantur esse aliquid, nihil contulerunt, sed e contra cum vidissent, quod creditum est mihi Euangelium praeputii, sicut Petro circumcisionis. Quod enim operatus est Petro in circumcisis, operatus est mihi inter gentes. Et cum cognouissent gratiam, quae data est mihi, Iacobus & Cephas & Iohannes, dextras dederunt mihi, &c. Lucas insuper Actuum historiam clausurus, cum dixisset, Et sic venimus Romam, post pauca subiungit Apostolum Iudaeis Romae loquentem: Notum ergo fit vobis, quoniam gentibus missum est hoc salutare Dei, & ipsi audient illud. Mansit autem biennio toto in suo conductu, & suscipiebat omnes qui ingrediebantur ad eum, praedicans regnum Dei. Omnes ergo suscipiebat, licet gentibus principaliter missus est. Vt & Romanis secundo scribens profitetur: Vobis enim, inquit, dico gentibus, quamdiu quidem ego sum Apostolus gentium, ministerium meum honorificabo, si quo modo ad emulandum prouocem carnem meam. In Ecclesiis certe Germanicis decantatur: Petrus Romam Apostolorum Princeps adiit, Paulus Graciam, vbique docens gratiam. Et historiae non leues, sed extra sacrum Canonem Bibliae, & Ecclesiasticae legendae Sanctorum habent, Petrum inuenijsse Paulum Romae praedicantem. Porro etsi sciam non omnia sanctorum Apostolorum gesta sacris litteris explicata esse, attamen nimis alienum videtur, quod neque Lucas Actuum historiae scriptor, Pauloque adhaerens, ipseque Paulus de hiis, quae ambo contra Simonem Magum, aut alios Romae egerint, nullam fecerint mentionem. Neque istud sane quadrat, quod Actuum vltimo legitur, scilicet Paulum in primo eius aduentu Iudaeos allocutum, & aduentus sui caussam aperiendo dixisse: Contradicentibus autem Iudaeis coactus sum appellare Caesarem. At illi dixerunt ad eum: Nos neque litteras accepimus de te a Iudaea, neque adueniens aliquis fratrum nunciauit aut locutus est quid de te malum. Rogamus autem a te audire, quae sentimus. Nam de secta hac notum est nobis, quia vbique ei contradicitur, &c. Si ergo Petrus Paulum Romam praeuenit eundo, e contra certe Paulus Petrum praeuenit euangelizando, disputando, vel docendo, aut Petrus deliuit, aut nil relatu dignum gessit, antequam Paulus superuenit. Paulus enim non reticuisset, sicut nec reticuit ad Corinthios & Galatas scribens de Petro. Si prolixior fui, ru incitasti. Expediebat enim errorem tuum vacuare, dum dixisti: In reliquos Apostolos non nisi per Petrum a Christo deriuatam esse potestatem. Derides & illud, quod Ecclesia solemniter canit, Apostolos praesse gregi dominico. Nec tamen quidquam affers, quam quod Ecclesia illorum patrociniis adiuuari deprecatur, quorum meritra recolit.
