Non autem respondes ad hoc verbum, quo supplicat Ecclesia, Vt eisdem rectoribus gubernetur, quos operis sui vicarios contulit praesse Pastores. Non dicit Petrum vicarium, sed Apostolos vicarios constitutos. Et sic vacuata est argumentatio tua, quam subiiceis de verbis Domini ad Petrum dicentis, Pasce oues meas, vbi Glossa dicit: Cum tertio audit a Petro, se diligi, iubet pascere oues. Trina negationi redditur trina confessio, ne minus amori lingua seruiat quam timori. Dic quaeso an fortiora sint haec verba, Pasce oues meas, an ista, Hic est mihi vas electionis, vt portet nomen meum coram gentibus & Regibus, & filiis Israel. Aut rursus, quod omnibus dixit in susflans: Accipite Spiritum sanctum, quorum remiseritis peccata, remittentur eis. Atque etiam illud piissimum & supremae consolationis verbum, quo Matthaeus suum Euangelium, ad omnes quidem Apostolos diuinae vocis organo prolatum: Ecce ego vobiscum sum, omnibus diebus vsque ad consummationem seculi, &c. Hanc igitur haeresin mitte, qua dicis, reliquos Apostolos non nisi per Petrum accepisse potestatem: & prioratum Petri sic demum asseras, vt aliorum potestatem non neges. Aliter asserendo tu cum Doctoribus tuis haeresin non euades, neque Chrysostomum neque Hieronymum testes habebis, quia PAVLO minime contradicent. Alias insanias audaciae tuae more impudentissime accumulas: scilicet Euangelium S. Marci a Petro demum auctoritatem accepisse, nec Paulum habuisse securitatem Euangelii praedicandi, nisi Petri & aliorum, qui cum eo erant, fuisset sententia roboratum. Primae assertioni tuae contra dicit vox tonitrui Dei: ille scilicet, qui vidit similitudinem vultus quatuor animalium: & ille, qui dixit: Dedit quosdam quidem Apostolos, quosdam autem Prophetas, alios vero Euangelistas, &c. vt superius ex Claraeuallensi conieci super his verbis, Gubernatu Noe. Quid enim Euangelistae, si Petrus omnia? vt idem Claraeuallensis ait: Errat si v. summa, ita & solam a Deo institutam, &c. vt dixi super his verbis: Tu primatu Abel. Secundo error tuo vas electu contradicit, vt supra dixi qualiter Galatis scribens: Paulus, inquit, Apostolus non ab hominibus, neq; per hominem, &c. Ac rursus: Notum n. vobis facio Euangelium, fratres, quo euangelisatu est a me, quia non est secundum hominem: neq; n. accepi ab homine, neq; didici, sed per reuelationem Iesu Christi, &c. Ino tute tibi contradicis, afferens Euangelium Pauli, non nisi Petri & aliorum Apostolorum auctoritate fuisse roboratum. Ideo n. auctoritatem Petri non augeret, etiamsi verum esset, sed omnium Apostolorum concordiarem auctoritatem solidaret: quam ego nemiper affirmaui. Sed absit à me, ut totius orbis auctoritatem Christo praeferam, ut tu miserrime Christo derogas, quasi non sufficerit Paulo Iesu Christi auctoritas, nisi aliorum Apostolorum assensu confirmata. Disce, rudissime Christiane, à Paulo Ephesios scribente, non Episcopum Romanum solum, sed Apostolos, Prophetas, Euangelistas & Doctores datos ad consummationem Sanctorum, in opus ministerii, in aedificationem corporis Christi, donec occurramus omnes in unitate fidei. Vnitatem autem facientes in charitate, crescamus in illo per omnia, qui est caput Christus, ex quo totum corpus connexum per omnem iuncturam subministrationis. O miser, qui non aliam vnitatem quam numeralem intelligis! qui tamen audisti, nos in vnitate fidei congregatos: quae communis est Clericis & Laicis. Et beatus Petrus prima Canonii a: Cum apparuerit Princeps Pastorum, percipietis immarcescibilem gloriae coronam. Tu vero contra Apostolum scribentem fundamentum aliud ponis, praeter id quod positum est Christus Iesus. Sufficiat igitur dixisse, Petrum principaliorem fuisse constitutum: alios autem & à Christo & per Christum quoque ordinatos: ne cassa facias verba Christi, cum insufflatione ipsius & Spiritus infusione. Duos namque discipulos Euangelico testimonio legimus amoris praerogativa claruisse, quorum alter Dominum testatus ait: Tu scis Domine, quod amo te, de altero legimus, quia ipse est quem diligebat Dominus, quemque virginem elegit, & quem licet manere voluit. Cum autem divinus sicut & humanus amor amore pareretur, ut illud artis amatoriae ... Si vis amari, ama, etiam de amore Domini verificetur, quare alter Apostolorum Dominum thasse, alter à Domino diligi perhibetur? nisi forte alium cordis, alium Spiritus amorem intelligamus. Est enim cordis amor quodammodo carnalis, quod magis erga carnem Christi, & quae carne Christus gessit, cor humanum afficiat, quod repletum ad omnem de illo sermonem facile compungitur, nihil libentius audit, nihil legit studiosius, nil frequentius recolit, nil suavius meditatur. Adstat oranti aut nascentis, aut lactentis, aut docentis, aut morientis, aut resurgentis, aut ascendentis Christi sacra imago. Hanc arbitramur praecipuam invisibili Deo fuisse causam, cur vellet in carne videri, ut cunctas eorum affectiones, qui nisi carnaliter amare nescirent, ad suae carnis amorem proprie retraheret, atque ita gradatim ad amorem proveheret spiritualem. Sed qualis qualis fuerit Christi ac illorum Apostolorum amor, aetati detulit Iesus, ne adolescens & puer progressae aetatis Apostolis praeferretur in adolescentem quem dilexit, noluit conferre causam iniuriae, quod & natura semper venerabilis sunt & honorata senectus. Possem hic repetere, quae supra scripsi super his verbis, Sacerdos magnus, Summus Pontifex, &c. ni vererer prolixitatem. Sed oro praeticam Beati Petri inspicias, si sibi soli vsurpavit, quae Apostolis communiter iniuncta fuere. Non ne ante pedes Apostolorum posuerunt agrorum pretia, non Petri? & illi diiuserunt singulis? numerum quoque Apostolorum communiter supplendo, statuerunt Matthiam & Barnabam, ponentes sortes? Apostoli scilicet communiter, non Petrus singulariter. Et communiter super Euangelio disputarunt, & Pauli decisio praevaluit. Communiter quoque sententiam tulerunt, dicentes: Placuit Spiritui sancto, & nobis, absque illa praefatione Petri, memores praecepti divini. Nam ut est apud Lucam & Matthaeum, facta contentione inter eos, quis eorum esset maior &c. & rursus apud Matthaeum, Nolite vocari Rabbi, unus est enim magister vester, omnes autem vos fratres estis. Tu vero soli Petro singula defers, ut successori blandiens plura feras in pretium assentationis tuae, qui iam expertus es illud assentationis aucupium praecunctis virtutibus appreciari. Merito ergo te illis connumerabo, de quibus Apostolus scripsit Timotheo: Hoc scito, quoniam in novissimis diebus instabunt tempora periculosa, & erunt homines ipsos amantes, cupidi, elati, superbi, blasphemi, &c.
units.tr: You go on to invent things, as if I had hinted that Peter was sent from Antioch to Rome by the other disciples. I suppose you make this up about me so that you have something to rail at. What you are really aiming at, if you can manage it, is to establish that the city of Rome is Peter's principal see, and that the primacy of Peter rests on the rule of the city of Rome itself. By stirring up a matter that was quite settled, you make it more open to doubt. You know that the words Do this in remembrance of me were said to all alike. Again: As the Father has sent me, so I send you. And breathing on them he said, Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you remit, they are remitted. Again: Go and teach all nations, etc. These words express no choice of a single person, and assign no region of the world to anyone. Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. But from the revelation to Paul we know that, although he was to preach the gospel throughout the world, of whom it is written, He is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel, yet in a certain respect he was sent chiefly to the Gentiles, as he himself is reported to have said in the Acts: Factum est autem re- mertensi returning to Jerusalem, and praying in the temple, I fell into a trance and saw him saying to me: Make haste, and get you quickly out of Jerusalem, for they will not receive your testimony concerning me. Go, for I will send you far hence unto the nations. He himself also, writing to the Galatians in the second chapter, says: When James, Peter and John saw that the gospel of uncircumcision had been committed to me, as the gospel of circumcision to Peter. And again: James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision. All these things seem rather to indicate that the city of Rome was the province of Paul rather than of Peter, assigned to him by Christ and not by Peter, just as any other office of his was. So he begins his letter to the Galatians in the first chapter: Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead. And in the second letter to the Galatians he shows that he received nothing from any mere man, saying: For those who seemed to be something contributed nothing to me; but on the contrary, when they saw that the gospel of uncircumcision had been committed to me, as the gospel of circumcision to Peter. For he who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision worked also in me among the Gentiles. And when they had known the grace that was given to me, James and Cephas and John gave me the right hand, etc. Luke, moreover, closing his history of the Acts, after saying And so we came to Rome, adds a little later the words of the apostle speaking to the Jews at Rome: Be it known to you therefore, that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will hear it. He remained for two whole years in his own hired house, and received all who came in to him, preaching the kingdom of God. So he received all, although he was principally sent to the Gentiles. He also professes this to the Romans in his second letter: For I say to you Gentiles, inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry, if by any means I may provoke to emulation my flesh. In the German churches it is sung: Peter, the prince of the apostles, went to Rome; Paul went to Greece, teaching grace everywhere. And histories of no small weight, which lie outside the sacred canon of the Bible and belong to the ecclesiastical legends of the saints, relate that Peter found Paul preaching at Rome. Yet although I know that not all the deeds of the holy apostles are set out in the sacred letters, it seems very strange that neither Luke, the writer of the history of the Acts, who attended Paul, nor Paul himself, makes any mention of what both of them did at Rome against Simon Magus or others. Nor does what is read in the last chapter of the Acts agree, namely that Paul, at his first arrival, addressed the Jews and, explaining the cause of his coming, said: But when the Jews spoke against it, I was constrained to appeal to Caesar. And they said to him: We neither received letters about you from Judea, nor did any of the brethren who came here report or speak anything evil of you. But we desire to hear from you what you think. For as concerning this sect, we know that it is everywhere spoken against, etc. If therefore Peter, by going there, came before Paul to Rome, then on the other hand Paul certainly came before Peter by preaching, disputing or teaching there; either Peter was absent, or did nothing worth reporting, before Paul arrived. For Paul would not have kept silent, just as he did not keep silent when writing about Peter to the Corinthians and the Galatians. I have been rather long, but you have provoked it. For it was useful to empty your error, when you said: Power was derived from Christ to the other apostles only through Peter. You also mock what the Church sings solemnly, that the apostles preside over the Lord's flock. Yet you offer nothing except that the Church prays to be aided by the patronage of those whose merits it recalls. Nor do you answer this word by which the Church pleads that it may be governed by those same rulers whom he appointed to preside as ministers, the vicars of his work. It does not say Peter the vicar, but that the apostles were appointed as vicars. And so your argument, which you bring forward from the words of the Lord to Peter, Feed my sheep, where the gloss says: When he is asked by Peter three times whether he loves him, he bids him feed the sheep. A threefold confession answers a threefold denial, so that his tongue may serve love no less than fear, is emptied of its force. Tell me, I beg you, whether these words, Feed my sheep, are stronger than those, He is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel. Or again, what he said to all of them while breathing on them: Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them. And also that most devout word of the highest consolation, with which Matthew ends his gospel, spoken by the instrument of the divine voice to all the apostles: Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the world, etc. Therefore put away this heresy, by which you say that the other apostles received power only through Peter; and assert the priority of Peter in such a way that you do not deny the power of the others. If you assert otherwise, you will not escape heresy along with your teachers, and you will not have Chrysostom or Jerome as witnesses, since they by no means contradict Paul. You pile up other follies of your audacity in the most shameless way: namely that the gospel of Saint Mark received its authority only from Peter, and that Paul did not have the assurance of preaching the gospel unless it had been confirmed by the judgment of Peter and of the others who were with him. The voice of God's thunder contradicts your first assertion: that is, he who saw the likeness of the face of the four living creatures, and he who said: He gave some apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, etc., as I drew above from Clairvaux on these words, Noah governed. For what are the evangelists, if Peter is everything? As the same Clairvaux says: He errs if he holds the sum, and so also the one instituted by God alone, etc., as I said on these words: You, the primacy of Abel. Secondly, your chosen vessel contradicts your error, as I said above, writing to the Galatians: Paul, an apostle, not from men, nor through man, etc. And again: For I make known to you, brethren, the gospel that was preached by me, that it is not according to man; for neither did I receive it from man, nor was I taught it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ, etc. Thus you contradict yourself again, asserting that the gospel of Paul was confirmed only by the authority of Peter and the other apostles. For that would not increase the authority of Peter, even if it were true, but would strengthen the agreeing authority of all the apostles; which I have never denied. But far be it from me to set the authority of the whole world before Christ, as you, most wretchedly, derogate from Christ, as if the authority of Jesus Christ were not enough for Paul unless it were confirmed by the assent of the other apostles. Learn, most rude Christian, from Paul writing to the Ephesians, that not the Roman bishop alone, but apostles, prophets, evangelists and teachers were given for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ, until we all meet in the unity of faith. Yet making the unity in charity, we grow up in him in all things, who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, joined together through every joint of supply. O wretched man, who understand no unity but a numerical one! Yet you have heard that we are gathered in the unity of faith, which is common to clergy and laity. And blessed Peter, in his first epistle: When the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory. But you, writing against the apostle, lay another foundation besides that which is laid, Jesus Christ. It is enough therefore to have said that Peter was appointed the chief, while the others were ordained both by Christ and through Christ as well: so that you do not make void the words of Christ, along with his breathing upon them and the infusion of the Spirit. For we read in the gospel testimony of two disciples who shone with the privilege of love. One of them, bearing witness to the Lord, said: Lord, you know that I love you. Of the other we read that he is the one whom the Lord loved, whom he chose as a virgin, and whom he willed to remain. But since divine love, as well as human love, is born of love, as in that saying of the art of love, If you wish to be loved, love, and this is true also of the love of the Lord, why is one of the apostles said to love the Lord, and the other to be loved by the Lord? Unless perhaps we understand a love of the heart and a love of the Spirit as different. For the love of the heart is in a way carnal, since it moves the human heart more towards the flesh of Christ and what Christ did in the flesh; and the heart, filled with it, is easily pricked by every word about him, hears nothing more gladly, reads nothing more eagerly, recalls nothing more often, and meditates on nothing more sweetly. The holy image of Christ stands before one who prays, or who is being born, or nursing, or teaching, or dying, or rising, or ascending. We think this was the chief cause for the invisible God to wish to be seen in the flesh: so that he might draw all the affections of those who knew only how to love carnally back to the love of his own flesh, and thus gradually lift them up to spiritual love. But whatever the love of Christ and of those apostles was, Jesus yielded to their age, so that the young man and the boy should not be preferred to the apostles of advanced age in the young man whom he loved; he would not confer a cause of injury, since old age is always venerable and honoured by nature. I could repeat here what I wrote above on these words, the great priest, the chief priest, etc., were I not afraid of being too long. But I beg you to look at the practice of blessed Peter, whether he claimed for himself alone what was enjoined on the apostles in common. Did they not lay the prices of their fields at the feet of the apostles, not at Peter's? And did they distribute them to each one? Did they, in filling up the number of the apostles together, appoint Matthias and Barnabas, casting lots? The apostles, that is, acted in common, not Peter alone. And they disputed together about the gospel, and Paul's decision prevailed. They also gave judgment together, saying: It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us, without that preface of Peter's, mindful of the divine precept. For, as is found in Luke and Matthew, when a contention arose among them as to which of them was the greatest, etc.; and again in Matthew: Do not be called Rabbi; for one is your teacher, and you are all brethren. But you attribute each thing to Peter alone, flattering the successor so that you may get more in return for your flattery; you who have already learned that the pursuit of flattery is valued above all virtues. Rightly, then, I shall count you among those of whom the apostle wrote to Timothy: Know this, that in the last days perilous times will come; men will be lovers of themselves, covetous, boastful, proud, blasphemers, etc.

units.la: Mihi vero Hieronymum illum obiectas, qui Constantiae damnatus, qui de institutione Eucharistiae temere disputavit, cuius ritus usque hodie in Bohemia variatur à ritu Ecclesiae Occidentalis. Tu autem veneno contentionis penitus imbutus quacunque ineptia certare non refugis, ut supra de Arrio fecisti, cuius errorem minime cognovisti, quod ex inepta disparataque comparatione tua quisque perfacile deprehendit. Beatus vero Hieronymus contra Iovinianum I. scribens ait: Inter duodecim unus eligitur, ut capite constituto schismatis tolleretur occasio. Recensè an electus sit à Christo, an ab Apostolis sit electus. Rursus ad Euandrium scribens, cum dixisset, unum esse Praelatum, ne quisquam ad se trahens Ecclesiam, &c. ne illi soli solidam deferret auctoritatem, subiecit: Si auctoritas quaeritur, orbis maiorem urbe, &c. recte plane considerans vniversalis Ecclesiae auctoritatem ipsius Romanae Ecclesiae auctoritati praeferendam, & coetum Apostolicum Petro solo potiorem. Quia illis communiter promisit Dominus dicens: Ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem saeculi, quod nec Petro, nec alteri cuiquam ipsponditse perhibetur. Oves autem pascere iussit: Qualis sit pastura, superius satis explicui. Sed eam etiam cunctis absque limitatione commisit, Apostolis in novissimo quasi praeceptorum suorum omnibus vniuersaliter dicens: Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes. Videan minus expressterit, cum dixit Omnes gentes vniuersaliter, an cum indefinite dixit, Pasce oves meas. Et rursus ne acephalam reliquerat, adiecit; Ego vobiscum sum, &c. Ergo neque mortuo Romano Pontifice, neque etiam haeretico existente, manebit acephala, cui verum caput semper adest.
units.tr: You bring up that Jerome, who was condemned at Constance and rashly disputed about the institution of the Eucharist, whose rite to this day differs in Bohemia from the rite of the Western Church. But you, thoroughly steeped in the poison of contention, do not shrink from fighting over any trifle, as you did above concerning Arius, whose error you did not even understand, as anyone can easily see from your clumsy and mismatched comparison. Yet the blessed Jerome, writing in the first book against Jovinian, says: One is chosen from the twelve, so that once a head is established the occasion of schism may be removed. Consider whether he was chosen by Christ or chosen by the Apostles. Again, writing to Evangelus, after saying that there is one prelate, lest anyone draw the Church to himself, etc., so that solid authority would not be handed to him alone, he adds: If authority is sought, the world is greater than the city, etc. Clearly he rightly judged that the authority of the universal Church is to be preferred to the authority of the Roman Church itself, and the apostolic college to Peter alone. For the Lord promised these things to them in common, saying: I am with you all days, even to the end of the age, which is not reported to have been promised to Peter or to anyone else. He did indeed bid them feed the sheep; I have already explained sufficiently above what kind of pasture this is. But he also committed it to all of them without limitation, speaking to the Apostles collectively, as it were at the close of his precepts: Go therefore and teach all nations. Let us see whether he expressed himself less clearly when he said "all nations" collectively, or when he spoke indefinitely, "Feed my sheep." And again, so that he would not leave the Church without a head, he added: I am with you, etc. Therefore the Church will not be headless, the Roman Pontiff being dead or even being a heretic, since she always has a true head present.

units.la: Procedis ad aliam metaphoram, quod cum Apostolis dicatur, ut laxent retia in capturam, Petro dictum est, Duc in altum, hoc est, in profundum disputationum, quid enim tam altum quam altitudinem videre divinitatis, id est, scire Dei filium? O mendicatum sufficiagum! Pensa num altiora sunt haec verba, Tu es Christus filius Dei vivi, an ista, In principio erat verbum, & verbum erat apud Deum, &c. Ecce omnia æterna per verbum plusquam perfectum, velut omnis temporis expertia, piscator eloquentissimus expressit, subdens: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Mox ad præteritum perfectum migravit, dum facturam creaturarum materiæ fluitantis opus tempori subiecit, tandem dicens: Et verbum caro factum est, ut filium consubstantialem & coæternum, & ex Patre ante omnia secula genitum, ostenderet ex tempore seu in tempore incarnatum & in carne visum, ut sequitur: Et viderunt gloriam eius, gloriam quasi unigeniti a Patre. Gloria quippe Patris a credentibus, quasi vila essin filio, ab his, qui carnalibus oculis Christum in carne viderunt, quæ tunc demum perfecte videbitur ab illis, qui sempiterna fruitione satiabuntur. Videan aquila Ezechielis altius rete duxerit, qui & Trinitatem discretiuam Personarum cum unitate essentiæ præ cunctis altius explicuit. Hoc autem in quo Petri Spiritum affers, etiam mulieri datum est, & illi, quæ non spiritualis, sed corporalis ministerii sollicita, attamen hoc modo professa est: Quia tu es Christus Filius Dei vivi, qui in hunc mundum venisti. Quid vas electionis, Doctor gentium, qui antonomastice Apostolus nuncupatur, qui etiam Ecclesiasticam censuram præ cæteris clarius & potentius exercuit? ut etiam intelligas eam, quam allegasti de hamo mittendo metaphoram, & tollendo piscem qui primus ascenderit, non stringere illud, quod de iurisdictione Petri figurare tentasti. Cuius si practicam inspexeris, potius dixeris, Petrum a Paulo districtum esse, quam Paulum aut quemquam Apostolorum a Petro districtum, aut etiam talem Petri primatum, qualem tu falso adscuerasti, ut in alios Apostolos non nisi per Petrum sit deriuata potestas.
units.tr: You proceed to another metaphor: that when the Apostles are told to let down their nets for a catch, Peter was told, Put out into the deep, that is, into the depth of disputations. For what is so high as to see the height of divinity, that is, to know God's Son? O beggarly and sufficient argument! Weigh whether these words, You are Christ, the Son of the living God, are higher than those, In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, etc. Behold, the eloquent fisherman expressed all eternal things through the most perfect verb, as if free of all time, adding: All things were made by him. Soon he moved to the perfect past tense, when he subjected the making of creatures, the work of fluid matter, to time; and finally he says: And the Word was made flesh, so as to show that the Son, consubstantial and coeternal, begotten of the Father before all ages, was incarnate in time and in the flesh, and was seen in the flesh, as follows: And we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father. For the glory of the Father, which is seen by believers as in a sort of image in the Son, is seen by those who saw Christ in the flesh with carnal eyes; it will be seen perfectly only then by those who are satisfied with eternal enjoyment. Let us see how high the eagle of Ezekiel drew his net, who explained the distinct Trinity of Persons together with the unity of essence more loftily than all others. But as for what you claim about Peter's spirit in this matter, it was also given to a woman, and not one concerned with spiritual ministry but with bodily service, yet she professed it in this way: You are Christ, the Son of the living God, who came into this world. What of the chosen vessel, the teacher of the Gentiles, who is called the Apostle by preeminence, who also exercised ecclesiastical censure more clearly and powerfully than the rest? So that you may understand that the metaphor you cited about casting the hook and taking up the first fish that comes up does not bear the meaning you tried to find in it concerning Peter's jurisdiction. If you look at the practice, you would rather say that Peter was rebuked by Paul, than that Paul or any of the Apostles was rebuked by Peter, or that Peter had such a primacy as you falsely invented, so that power would be derived to the other Apostles only through Peter.

units.la: Denique replicas, quod & prius attigisti, sed nunc addis nugas, dicens de Simone Iohannis, quia Petra dicitur, eo quod prius in nationibus fidei fundamenta posuerit. Quod minime verum est, quia non Petra, sed Petrus nuncupatur. Verum quia Domini & Saluatoris nostri verbum quo dixit: Super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, tu corrumpis, ac si dixisset Dominus super hunc Petrum, aut dixisset, Tu es petra, quorum neutrum scriptura testatur; videntur autem ipsa veri & Euangelici textus verba etiam incorrupta nonnihil prioritatis innuere Petri, & a variis Doctoribus exponuntur diversimode, ergo textum Euangelii sincera fide custodientes cum Aurelio Augustino ad Hieronymum scribente dicamus: Solum eis Scripturarum libris, quæ tam Canonicæ vocantur, didici hunc honorem timoremque deferre, ut nullum earum auctorem scribendo aliquid errasse firmissime credam. At si aliquid in eis offeratur litteris, quod videatur contrarium veritati, nihil aliud quam vel mendosum esse Codicem, vel interpretem non assecutum esse, quod dictum est, vel me minime intellexisse non ambigam. Alios autem ita lego, ut quantacunque sanctitate doctrinaque prepolleant, non ideo verum putem, quod ipsi ita senserunt, sed quia probabili ratione, &c. Idem in III. de Trinitate: Noli, Lector, meis libris quasi Canonicis Scripturis inseruire, sed in illis, & quod non credis, cum inveneris, incunctanter crede, &c. Vides ergo quantam vim sibi vendicent litera auctoritate Spiritus sancti munitæ, & qualem ipsarum expositores magistrali duntaxat opinione subnixi. In quibus tamen, quia non est eorum abiicienda auctoritas, istud ponerandum reor, an a transcurrente aliquid proferatur, an propter hoc ipsum, de quo agitur, doctrina emanauerit. Plerumque, enim ita se habent ingenia humana, ut desiderio finis vel euentus assequendi media non satis fundata velut nota supponant, & intractata relinquant, ut finis principio cohærere videatur. Quod Flaccus Pisonem docens taliter enarrat: Semper ad euentum festinat, & in medias res Non secus ad notas auditorem rapit, & quæ Desperat tractata nitescere posse, relinquit: Atque ita mentitur, sic veris falsa remiscet, Primum ne medio, medium ne discrepet imo.
units.tr: Finally you repeat what you touched on before, but now you add trifles, saying that Simon son of John is called Petra because he first laid the foundations of faith among the nations. This is by no means true, for he is not named Petra but Petrus. But since you corrupt the word of our Lord and Saviour by which he said: On this rock I will build my Church, as if the Lord had said on this Peter, or had said You are a rock, neither of which Scripture attests; and since the very words of the true and Gospel text, even uncorrupted, seem to hint at some priority of Peter, and are expounded in various ways by various teachers, let us, keeping the text of the Gospel with sincere faith, say with Augustine, writing to Jerome: I have learned to show this honour and reverence only to those books of Scripture which are called canonical, so that I firmly believe that none of their authors erred in writing anything. But if anything in those letters seems contrary to the truth, I do not doubt that either the manuscript is faulty, or the translator has not grasped what was said, or I myself have not understood it. Other writers I read in such a way that, however great their holiness and learning, I do not therefore hold a thing true because they thought so, but because of probable reasoning, etc. The same in the third book on the Trinity: Do not, reader, be a slave to my books as if they were canonical Scriptures, but in them, when you find something you do not believe, believe it without hesitation, etc. You see, then, how much authority the letters claim, fortified by the authority of the Holy Spirit, and what sort of authority their expositors have, supported only by a teacher's opinion. Yet since their authority is not to be cast aside, I think this must be weighed: whether something is put forward by a passing remark, or whether the teaching itself arose for the very purpose at issue. For human minds are often so disposed that, in their desire to reach an end or outcome, they take for granted, as if known, means not sufficiently grounded, and leave them untreated, so that the end seems to cohere with the beginning. Flaccus, teaching Piso, describes this thus: He always hastens to the outcome, and snatches the hearer into the midst of things as if they were known, and leaves aside what he despairs of making shine when treated; and so he lies, and mixes false with true, so that the beginning does not clash with the middle, nor the middle with the end.

units.la: Non a sanctis viris suspicor mendacia fingi: sed cupidine finis per media rapi, & a vero labi, proprium est humanæ fragilitatis. Neque etiam hoc prætereundum reor, an scribentis animus omnis expers curæ vel pathiæ, quæ si non flectere a vero, solicitiorem tamen in alterutram partem efficere possit: an vero ex contentiosa disputatione sermo totus effluxerit. Verbi gratia, temporibus Anacleti, Marcelli, Leonis, &c. Oriens in fide Christi flagrans Antiochiam, Alexandriam, aut forte Ierosolymam Romæ præferre voluit cathedræ dignitate. Rursus Imperiali Sede Constantinopolim translata Roma noua veteri præluceret contendebat. Defensores Romanæ præeminentiæ (ut est natura contentionis) victoriæ cupiditate ad verum finem effectumq; tendentes, inter transcurrendum tamen aliquando modum excesserunt. Vt apud Platonem Socrates Gorgiam alloquitur: Puto te, ô Gorgia, in multis disputationibus iam versatum comprehendisse, non facile posse homines, cum disceptare inceperint, sic abire, ut se invicem solum doceant atque discant: sed si de aliquo contendatur, nec concedant alter alteri, graviter ferunt, certantes simul, non autem quarentes id, de quo ambigebatur, &c. Et ut Flaccusait: Gratia sic fratrum geminorum, Amphionis atque Zethi dissiliit——
units.tr: I do not suppose that lies are invented by holy men, but it is the mark of human frailty to be carried by the desire for an end through the means, and to slip from the truth. Nor do I think this should be passed over: whether the mind of the writer was free of all care or passion, which, if it could not turn him from the truth, could at least make him more anxious toward one side; or whether the whole discourse flowed out of a contentious dispute. For example, in the times of Anacletus, Marcellus, Leo, etc., the Orient, burning in the faith of Christ, wished to place Antioch, Alexandria, or perhaps Jerusalem, above Rome in the dignity of the see. Again, when the imperial seat was transferred to Constantinople, it contended that New Rome should outshine Old Rome. The defenders of Roman preeminence (as is the nature of contention), aiming at the true end and effect with a desire for victory, in passing have sometimes exceeded the proper measure. As in Plato, Socrates addresses Gorgias: I think, Gorgias, that you have now, through many disputations, understood that when men begin to dispute they cannot easily part so as to teach and learn from one another; but if they contend about something, and neither yields to the other, they take it badly, fighting with one another and not seeking what was under dispute, etc. And as Flaccus says: Thus the concord of the twin brothers, Amphion and Zethus, broke apart——

units.la: Plaut. Plura his similia adducere possem, quae in consideratione versantur, cum discordantiam Doctorum aut Scripturarum veritas enucleatur. Sed ad Euangelii textum reuertamur, scilicet Super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam. Hunc textum post varias expositiones postremo sic exponit Augustinus: Dixi in quodam loco de Apostolo Petro, quod in illo tanquam in petra aedificata sit Ecclesia, sed scio me postea saepissime sic exposuisse, quod a Domino dictum est, super hanc petram aedificabo, ut SVPER HVNC intelligeretur, quem confessus est Petrus, dicens: Tu es Christus filius Dei viui, ac si Petrus ab hac petra appellatus personam Ecclesiae figuraret, quae super hanc petram aedificatur. Non enim dictum est illi: Tu es petra, sed Tu es Petrus. Petra autem erat Christus, quem confessus Simon (sicut ei tota Ecclesia confitetur) dictus est Petrus.
units.tr: Plaut. I could adduce many similar examples, which come up for consideration whenever the disagreement of the doctors or the truth of the Scriptures is brought to light. But let us return to the text of the Gospel, namely Upon this rock I will build my church. After various interpretations, Augustine finally explains this text thus: I said in a certain place about the Apostle Peter that the Church was built upon him as upon a rock, but I know that I have very often since explained it so: that what the Lord said, "Upon this rock I will build my church," should be understood as UPON THIS, that is, upon him whom Peter confessed when he said, "You are Christ, the Son of the living God"; as if Peter, named from this rock, were representing the person of the Church, which is built upon this rock. For it was not said to him, "You are the rock," but "You are Peter." The rock, however, was Christ, whom Simon confessed, and (as the whole Church confesses to him) he was called Peter.

units.la: Risum tandem excitasti dicens: Cum secundum humanas leges triginta annis praescribatur, indignum esse, ut primatus Petri post tot secula temeraria disputatione ventiletur. Quaero a te, num Paulus cotidie praescriptionem interrupit, qui in bulla, quae litteris Pontificalibus robur omne confert, Petrum ordine actitu Christianarum tam Latinarum quam Graecarum Ecclesiarum legendi praecedit? Plurimae quoque sunt litterae Apostolicae, in quibus nulla mentio fit de Petro: nulla vero bulla Paulo vacat. Rursus dic, an praescribatur adversus illum, cui omnis iudiciaria via clauditur? Romanus autem Pontifex vniuersalem Ecclesiam congregari vetat, vbi talis interruptio efficaciam assequi potest. Neque triginta anni fluxerunt a fine Concilii Basiliensis, vbi decreta magnae Synodi Constantiensis de superioritate vniuersalium Conciliorum salubriter sancita saluberrime innouata sunt, quae decreta semper sunt in viridi obseruantia, semperque loquuntur. Nam sicut lex Codicis Iustiniani, quae damnat Arrianos, Macedonianos, Donatistas, Gazaros, Patarenos, semper est in viridi obseruantia; sic magnae Synodi decreta super maioritate generalium Conciliorum, per Concilium Basiliense innouata, & per Eugenium & Nicolaum recognita & professa, in viridi semper sunt obseruantia, ita vt contradictores eius haeretici sint declarati, nec vlla vetustatis litura vanescant.
units.tr: You have finally made us laugh by saying: "Since under human laws a prescription of thirty years is allowed, it is unworthy that the primacy of Peter should be tossed about in rash disputation after so many centuries." I ask you: does Paul interrupt the prescription every day, he who, in the bull which gives all force to papal letters, is placed before Peter in the order of reading in the Christian churches, both Latin and Greek? There are also very many apostolic letters in which no mention is made of Peter, yet no bull is without Paul. Again, tell me, does prescription run against the one to whom every judicial way is closed? The Roman Pontiff forbids a universal Church to be assembled, where such an interruption could take effect. Nor have thirty years passed since the end of the Council of Basel, where the decrees of the great Synod of Constance on the superiority of universal councils, wholesomely sanctioned, were most wholesomely renewed; these decrees have always been in green observance and always speak. For just as the law of Justinian's Code, which condemns the Arians, Macedonians, Donatists, Gazari and Patarenes, is always in green observance, so the decrees of the great Synod on the superiority of general councils, renewed by the Council of Basel and recognised and professed by Eugenius and Nicholas, are always in green observance, so that their opponents are declared heretics, and no blot of antiquity makes them vanish.

units.la: Deinde commemoras errores Orientalium ac Bohemorum, tuam haeresin palliando, qui magnae Synodi decretis falso contradicis, nec quidquam affers praeter blasphemias de pectore virulento manantes, gaudens fortasse sicut suis immunda cum quouis in coeno volutari. Wickleff Husque commemoratas Constantiae damnatos. At vero ipsius Synodi sancta decreta respuis, haeretice vilissime, poenis eius perpetuo plectendus, nisi resipiscas. Sed vt veremur, boni quidem veri vel honesti nullam habens curam, voluptate autem ac semper eo, quod dulcissimum sit, Papae Cardinalium-que aures mentemque delinis, facisque adulando vt plurimi videaris existimandus.
units.tr: Then you recall the errors of the Easterners and the Bohemians, cloaking your heresy, you who falsely contradict the decrees of the great Synod and bring forward nothing but blasphemies gushing from a venomous breast, perhaps rejoicing, as filthy swine wallow in any mire. You mention Wycliffe and Hus, condemned at Constance. But you spurn the holy decrees of that very Synod, most vile heretic, and you will be punished by its penalties forever unless you repent. But, as we fear, you who have no care for what is good, true or honourable, but only for pleasure and always for what is sweetest, soothe the ears and mind of the Pope and the cardinals with flattery, and make yourself seem, to most people, worthy of esteem.

units.la: Ad haec semel inescatus cathedra Feltrensi, spem vsurpasti capelli rubricandi. Semel autem exesa mens aerugine, & imbuta cura peculii, haud recte prospicit, neque promit opuscula cedro linenda vel digna seruari cupresso. Tuas ergo tabellas pigmentariorum trade mensis, vt tandem & vulgo fastidiosae speciebus seruandis complicentur, aut deferas in vicum vendentem thus & odores, & piper & quicquid cartis amicitur ineptis.
units.tr: Having once been lured by the see of Feltre, you have seized the hope of dyeing a hat red. But a mind once eaten away by rust and steeped in concern for money does not see clearly, nor does it bring forth little works fit to be smeared with cedar oil or kept in cypress chests. So hand your little tablets over to the apothecaries' counters, so that they may at last be folded up for wrapping spices, which the common crowd finds tiresome, or carry them off to the street where incense and perfumes are sold, and pepper, and whatever is wrapped in foolish papers.

units.la: Requiret forte quispiam, cur non pontificali tuae deferamus dignitati? Vicissim hunc ego rogo; Cur non ponderibus modulisque suis vsa est ratio? Nam qui me tuberibus offendit, verrucis est aequum ignoscat. Hac enim lege in trutina ponetur eadem.
units.tr: Someone may perhaps ask why we do not present these to your pontifical dignity? I in turn ask: why has reason not used its own weights and measures? For he who offends me with lumps should in fairness pardon warts. For by this law the same thing will be weighed in the same scales.

units.la: Xxxxxx
units.tr: Xxxxxx

units.la: INVECTIVA GREGORII HEIMBVRG VTRIVSQVE IVRIS DOCTORIS, IN REVERENDISSIMVM PATREM, DOMINVM NICOLAVM de Cusa, Sanctae Romanae Ecclesiae tituli S. Petri ad Vincula Presbyterum Cardinalem, & Episcopum Brixinensem.
units.tr: INVECTIVE OF GREGORY HEIMBURG, DOCTOR OF BOTH LAWS, AGAINST THE MOST REVEREND FATHER, LORD NICHOLAS OF CUSA, Cardinal Priest of the Holy Roman Church, of the title of St Peter in Chains, and Bishop of Brixen.

units.la: ANCER Cusa Nicolae, qui te Cardinalem Brixinensem vocas, cur non prodis in palestram? qui te Graecum & Latinum gloriaris, cur non palam pergis, ad certamen literarum? cur ficta persona & sermone composito loqueris, quem finxisti, veluti figulus, nomen vero tuum surppimis? At haec est natura libelli famosi, scilicet ab incerta ut prodeat sermo persona, an ne putas parcs tibi reddi posse vices? Proin vero si cuiuspiam aures offendantur, illi succensear, qui vitium introduxit. Dicis in fasmate, quod finxisti, Ducem Sigismundum irrite a Papa ad concilium appellasse. A concilio autem ad Papam provocasse magnum Athanasium & obtinuisse, profecto siquidem in Gymnasium procesferis, audies, qui Romani Pontifices, quaeve concilia a fide orthodoxa defecerunt. Quia etiam si ea, quae saepe legisti, memoriae tenacius commendasses, iam utique promptum haberes Papam non esse Ecclesiam illam, adversus quam portae inferi non praevalebunt. Anastasium Papam absorpsertunt portae inferi, argumento est intestinorum egestio. O dirum omen, unde gentilitas omenta nuncupauit. Caeteros Pontifices in disputationis tempus reservo, sed ex his vacuata est impugnatio tua, qua dixisti, Papam non posse suspitione notari, quippe in quem graviora crimina cadere possunt. Clarissimum virum Gregorium Heimburg, verborum venditorem vocas, qui gloriosae vocis honoraria temperatissime dimensus est. Tu vero nugas & vanitates tuas, per Germaniam disseminando, pro aere vendidisti, plusquam ducenta florenorum millia fallaciter abstrahendo, Exprobrasti sibi, quod Rex non semper vicerit. Taceo de sordibus & gratia iudicum, & caeteris quae rectum pervertunt iudicium. Te vicit, quando quidem in Sede Moguntina, expugnata haereditaris petitione, directa ex testamento, a parte tua in Rituta, tu ad Legatum Apostolicum concilio praesidentem appellasti, ac inibi vigore scedulae codicillaris, ad fideicommissariam conuolasti, nescius quod alterius electione remedii tollitur alterum: a Gregorio repulsus ruboreque confusus bellum perpetuum sacris legibus indixisti, cum desperasses in Facultate Iuris amodo praelucere posse, honestiorem causam desertioni praetendens, ad Theologiam confugisti, cuius factus abortivus, tandem Mathematicis superstitionibus, putas verae religionis sacra demonstrare. Pergis vim & insidias structas legato Ducis excusare, dicens, Laurentium procuratorem fuisse non oratorem, sed ad appellationem insinuandum missum extitisse. O iuris transfuge, quae te dementia coepit? Nonne adolescens didicisti, & per Epistolam procuratorem constitui posse? Epistolares vero literae legationem probant. Tibi dico, Cancer Cusane, quod Laurentius missus fuit, ad Papam melius informandum, quem tu variis surreptionibus obreptionibusque circumueneras, ad appellandum vero non aliter, quam in eucntum repulsionis suae, sed letargum pateris, communem illusorum mentium morbum, quod minime accidisset tibi, si ea quae adolescens didicisti, non deseruisses. Cum autem ad Theologiam confugisse glorificabaris, de Letheo bibisti, nullis Antyciris, nec ullo sanandus elleboro. Laurentium autem haereticum nominas, idcirco incapacem esse salui conductus dicere debebas, nec ius revocandi domum habere legatum, ut sic in potestate tua foret, quem velles pro libito laqueare. Num pudet vanitatis hominum vanissime, qui fidei publicae vinculum quo omnium rerum publicarum seruatur integritas, tam vana actione dissoluere putas? Quis de caetero legationis subibit functionem, si propter confictum trimen, de qua nec quicquam suspicatum est, sacrilegas habuerit formidate manus, aut quod sibi obiiciatur Dominum suum domi tenere vinctum aliquem de Clientela Cardinalis, sicut tu adversus Laurentium obiecisti? Nec minuit fidem publicam, quod Laurentius auditor est Rotae. Nam etsi longe inferius officium haberet aut superius, attamen a legationis munere non prohiberetur, nonne legisti Romanum Pontificem populi Romani gestisse legationem? Quid si Episcopus legatus esset, qui frater Papae ac illi artissimo iurisiurandi vinculo astrictus est? Transgrederis tandem ad merita causae principalis dicens, Ducem confessum esse, hostile tui persecutione, teq; diffidasse, nec tamen in literis diffidationis causam praetendisse violentiae vel repellendae vel prœueniendæ, sed agi se initiriæ postea ducem confinxisse. Putasne populum Romanum sociali iure sanctissimo belligerantem, singula quæque literis explicasse, quæ senatus censuit, dum bellum decreuit indicere? cum te postulante, Dux misisset ad te Parcifalem Caduceatorem, isque persuaderet tibi qui te iactitaueras valles quamplurimas gentibus implere, ac Ducem obruere, cum (vt eius verbis vtamur) te sibi æquare non posset; ante omnia prouidendum esse tibi, vt cum Duce redires in gratiam, aut treugas saltem inires; Interea vel differentiæ tolli, vel saltem via compromissi, congruis pactionibus Iurisarbitrio & considentium arbitratui subiici possent, vel submitti. Tu vero repudiatis viis suauissimæ pacis, neque treugas nec vllas quidem inducias depoposci voluisti. Quid restabat, nisi bellum & insidias, in quibus considebas, æquitate iustissima in te retorquere? Apud Lucanum C. Cæsar commilitones suos adhortando dixit:
units.tr: Crab of Cusa, Nicholas, you who call yourself Cardinal of Brixen, why do you not come out into the arena? You who boast that you are Greek and Latin, why do you not openly enter the contest of letters? Why do you speak through a fictitious persona and a made-up style, which you have fashioned like a potter, while suppressing your own name? But this is the nature of a defamatory pamphlet: a speech is put forward under an uncertain persona. Or do you think you can escape having your turn returned to you? Indeed, if anyone's ears are offended, let him be angry with the one who introduced the fault. In the pamphlet you have invented, you say that Duke Sigismund appealed to the Pope against the council in vain, and that the great Athanasius appealed from a council to the Pope and won. Surely, if you came into the schoolroom, you would hear which Roman pontiffs and which councils have fallen away from the orthodox faith. Indeed, even if you had committed to memory more firmly those things you have often read, you would already have ready at hand the knowledge that the Pope is not that Church against which the gates of hell shall not prevail. The gates of hell swallowed up Pope Anastasius; the evidence is the evacuation of his bowels. O dire omen, whence the Gentiles called the entrails omenta. I reserve the other pontiffs for the time of disputation. But your attack, in which you said that the Pope cannot be marked with suspicion, since very grave crimes can fall upon him, is emptied out by these examples. You call the most distinguished man Gregory Heimburg a seller of words, though he has measured out the rewards of his glorious voice with great restraint. You yourself have sold your trifles and vanities, spreading them throughout Germany, and have deceptively extracted more than two hundred thousand florins. You have reproached him for the fact that the King has not always won. I say nothing of the bribes and favouritism of judges, and the other things that pervert right judgment. He defeated you, since in the See of Mainz, when the hereditary claim derived from the will had been assaulted, you appealed on your side at Rituta to the Apostolic Legate presiding over the council, and there, by the force of a codicil, you flew to the fideicommissary court, unaware that when one remedy is chosen the other is removed. Repulsed by Gregory and confused with shame, you declared perpetual war on the sacred laws. Since you despaired of being able to shine any longer in the Faculty of Law, you pretended a more honourable reason for desertion and fled to Theology. Having turned out a miscarriage there, at last you try to demonstrate the sacred rites of true religion by mathematical superstitions. You go on to excuse the force and the snares laid by the Duke's legate, saying that Laurence was not an ambassador but a procurator, sent only to deliver the appeal. O deserter from the law, what madness has seized you? Did you not learn as a young man that a procurator can be appointed by letter? But letters of that kind prove a legation. I tell you, Crab of Cusa, that Laurence was sent to inform the Pope more fully, the Pope whom you had surrounded with various deceptions and misrepresentations. As for appealing, you did so only in the hope of reversing your own repulse, but you suffer from lethargy, the common disease of deluded minds, which would not have befallen you had you not abandoned what you learned as a young man. When you boasted that you had fled to Theology, you drank from Lethe, and no Anticyra hellebore could cure you. You call Laurence a heretic; for that reason you ought to have said he was incapable of safe-conduct, and that the legate had no right to recall him home, so that it would be in your power to snare whomever you wished at will. Are you not ashamed of your utter vanity, O most vain of men, that you think you can dissolve with such an empty act the bond of public faith, by which the integrity of all public affairs is preserved? Who will henceforth undertake the office of legation, if, because of a feigned truce, of which nothing was suspected, he must fear sacrilegious hands, or if, as you objected against Laurence, he is charged with keeping his lord confined at home, one of the clients of the Cardinal? Nor does it diminish public faith that Laurence is an auditor of the Rota. For even if he held a much lower or higher office, he would not be prevented from the function of legation. Have you not read that the Roman Pontiff himself was legate of the Roman people? What if the legate were a bishop, who is a brother of the Pope and bound to him by the closest oath? Finally you turn to the merits of the principal case, saying that the Duke confessed to having defied you by hostile pursuit, and that you were diffident, yet in the letters of defiance he did not allege any cause of violence, either to repel or to forestall it, but later, as you claim, he invented that he was acting in defence. Do you think that the Roman people, waging war under the most sacred law of alliance, explained each and every thing in letters, namely what the senate decided when it resolved to declare war? When, at your request, the Duke sent you Parzifal the herald, and he urged you, who had boasted that you would fill the valleys with very many peoples and overwhelm the Duke, since (to use his words) you could not match him, that before all things you must provide to return to favour with the Duke, or at least enter into a truce. Meanwhile the differences could be removed, or at least, by the way of a compromise, submitted by suitable agreements to the judgment of law and to the arbitration of the parties. But you, having rejected the paths of most sweet peace, did not wish to ask for a truce or any suspension of arms at all. What remained, except to turn back upon you, with most just equity, the war and the snares in which you were placed? In Lucan, Caesar, exhorting his fellow soldiers, said:

units.la: Arma tenenti Omnia dat, qui iusta negat.
units.tr: He gives everything to the man who holds arms, who denies what is just.

units.la: Vsus est Dux viribus à Deo concessis, neq; numen defuit illi.
units.tr: The Duke used the forces granted to him by God, and divine power was not wanting to him.

units.la: Pergis fingendo Ducem à te veniam petiisse. O superbissime figule, postquam rebus omnibus compositis tu despondisses, te facturum, quæcunque Duci placitura. At his similibusque blanditiis tuis, Dux allectus, te consolando dixisset, quatenus bono animo esses; posse ipsum tibi, si suæ voluntati pareres, hæc omnia variis beneficiorum in te & Ecclesiam Brixinensem collationibus abunde restaurare. Tu modo hoc veniæ postulationem nominas, hominum ingratissime, qui sic ineptus es, vt omni humano alloquio te indignum reddas, qui humanissimum principem, omnium iniuriarum obliuisci volentem, fraudulentissime calumniaris.
units.tr: You go on pretending that you sought pardon from the Duke. O most proud potter, after you had settled everything, you promised that you would do whatever would please the Duke. But the Duke, won over by these and similar flatteries of yours, would have comforted you, telling you to be of good cheer, and that he himself, if you obeyed his will, could fully restore all this to you and to the church of Brixen by various grants of benefices. Yet you call this a request for pardon, most ungrateful of men, and you are so foolish that you make yourself unworthy of every human address, when you fraudulently slander the most humane prince, who wishes to forget all injuries.

units.la: Subnectis dicens, gentes Imperatoris, compositis cum Comite Goritiæ rebus, iam dudum abiisse. Surripis autem hoc, quod Iohannes Bani de Witanitz dimidium fere comitatus Goritiæ vi raptum, tunc ab Imperatore præmium recepit, deque tam nobili & opima præda fere triumphauit. Vnde maior metus vicinis regibus, iam dissolutis castris, iniectus erat quam si agmina bellica coacta essent, nulla tamen adhuc victoria cessisset. Erant quidem adhuc in illis confiniis, tribuni, prætores, centuriones, cæteriqúe turmarum; cohortum, & cateruarum præfecti, ipseque armi ductor, Witawitz, quibus perfacile, nuper abeuntes ad castra reuocare; aut ex aliis alpinatibus & montanis, malo assuetis viris, gregariorum, iampridem abeuntium militum siue prædonum vicem numerosq; supplere, ac ordines sufficere. Tu itaq; vide, si doli tui suspitionem, tuis fictionibus sustulisti, vel potius exaggerasti.
units.tr: You add that the Emperor's troops had long since departed, once matters with the Count of Görz were settled. But you suppress the fact that John Bani de Witanitz had seized by force almost half of the county of Görz, then received a reward from the Emperor, and nearly triumphed over so noble and rich a booty. Hence greater fear was struck into the neighbouring kings, though the camps had now been broken up, than if the armies had been assembled, though no victory had yet been won. There were indeed still in those borders tribunes, praetors, centurions and the other commanders of troops, of cohorts and companies, and the leader of the arms himself, Witawitz. It would be quite easy for these to recall to camp men who had lately left, or to take from other mountain and Alpine men, used to hardship, the place of the common soldiers or robbers who had long since gone, and to fill up the ranks. So see whether you have removed suspicion of your deceit by your fictions, or rather increased it.

units.la: Gloriaris te pridie passionem Domini prædicasse, & postridie de eius resurrectione prædicaturum, despondisse. Deinde te ad Papam rediturum prænunciasse, Parcifalem quoque cui idipsum triduo ante detexeras, Duci Sigismundo significasse. Nouum certe crimen, Cancer Cusa, prætendis in Parcifalem, scilicet quia id prænuntiarit; quod tu palam proclamasti. Si quid vero illi sub taciturnitatis fiducia velut depositum commendasti; quod ipse prodiderit fidefragus; hoc pethibe, & probe respondebitur tibi.
units.tr: You boast that you preached on the day before the Lord's passion, and promised to preach on his resurrection the day after. Then you announced that you would return to the Pope, and you told Duke Sigismund that Parcifal, to whom you had revealed the same thing three days before, had done so. This is certainly a new charge, Crab of Cusa, that you bring against Parcifal, namely that he foretold it, which you yourself proclaimed openly. If, however, you entrusted something to him in confidence of silence, as a deposit, and he, faithless to his trust, betrayed it, bring that forward, and you will be answered properly.

units.la: Expurgare tentas suspicionem dolosæ machinationis iniectam tibi, ex refutatione treugarum; dicens, te semestres obtulisse treugas, in articulo mineralium, cum Dux annales postularet. Posthac tibi respondebitur, vbi tu latiori sermone, hunc pasium amplificare prætendis.
units.tr: You try to clear away the suspicion of treacherous scheming cast upon you by your refusal of truces, saying that you offered six-month truces in the matter of the mines, when the Duke demanded annual ones. You will be answered later, when you, in a longer discourse, intend to enlarge upon this point.

units.la: Gregorium gaudes falso compellare mendacissimum, homo vanissime, sagena mendaciorum insatiabilis.
units.tr: You delight in falsely calling Gregory the most lying liar, O most vain man, insatiable net of lies.

units.la: Episcopum Tridentinum, Ducem Sigismundum, Wolffgangum Neydlinger, & Parcifalem prodtionis maculanotas, dum dicis Episcopum tibi suasisse reditum; quoniam pacis viam haberet. Tu dolum suspicatus cuiasti, quod Papa scriberet Duci; te fœdus perpetuum Duci iuraturum pollicens: Idque tibi vicissim seruari postulans, Dux se obseruaturum Papæ respondit. His fretus ad castrum tuum Frauelspurg appl cauisti; quod tu sic nuncupas, mathematice sortilege, quia responsa dæmonum; quibus inibi sacrificas, Raphaelis Archangeli reuelationem confingis. In primis creditur, quod tu dolum suspicatus es, qui aliorum ingenia ex tuo metiris ingenio. Hoc etiam confiteor tibi, quod Dux respondit Papæ; seruaturum le fœdera, pacta scil. si tu quoq; seruares, quæ tu multipliciter violasti, semper enim more tuo, aliquid reticeas, sicut fecisti; cum a Papa tam exorbitantia literas & breuia surripuisti.
units.tr: You stain the Bishop of Trent, Duke Sigismund, Wolfgang Neydlinger and Parcifal with the mark of treachery, when you say that the Bishop advised you to return, since there would be a way to peace. You suspected a trick when you learned that the Pope was writing to the Duke, promising that you would swear a perpetual covenant to the Duke, and asking in return that it be kept, and the Duke replied that he would observe it towards the Pope. Relying on this, you hurried to your castle of Frauelspurg, which you, a mathematical sorcerer, call by that name because the answers of the demons, to whom you sacrifice there, are, you pretend, a revelation of the Archangel Raphael. First of all, it is believed that you suspected a trick because you measure the minds of others by your own. I also confess this to you: the Duke answered the Pope that he would keep the covenants and pacts, provided that you too kept them, which you have violated in many ways. For, as is your way, you always hold something back, as you did when you secretly took from the Pope such outrageous letters and briefs.

units.la: Procedis, dicens Wolffgingum velut caducatorem ad te venisse, ferentem literas Episcopi Tridentini Abbatis Wiltemensis, & iusiurandum Parcifalis, super securitate tua tibi supplicantem vti Brunegk proficiscereris, quo Dux ipse missurus esset; pro differentiis componendis. Tu vero miseris Camerarium tuum ad Episcopum Tridentinum; qui tum cum Duce manebat, vt rescires veritatem, cui Tridentinus tradit, se non esse traditorem, te quoque secure posse venire Brunegke. Itaque sub specie tractatus iis proditus. Omnes quippe differentiarum articulos, aiis fuisse compositos, præterquam super minera; vbi Parcifal postularit treugam annalem, tu vero semestrem dare voluisti; ne longiore mora possessionis iacturam sustineres. Itaque diu struram tibi proditionem, loco pacis expertus es. Concludis ergo, licet falso, nil insidiarum, in te præsumi posse, cum Papa ducem super obseruantia pacti fœderis, certificarit. Hæc fictio à veritate remotior est, quam Deus à Diabolo. Quid ais vanitatum gurges? Wolffgangus à Capitulo & clero Brixinensi ac vasallis & ministerialibus ipsius Ecclesiæ ad te missus est, hortator pacis, & monitor virtutum, ac persuasor tui, ne Ducem, ne totum populum omnemque statum hominum aduersus te, tuis sæue dictis provocares. Omnes quippe homines cuiuscunque status aduersum te incanduisse, tibique periculum in limite adesse præmonuit. Tu vero nemini, vix tibi ipsi fidens, Camerarium tuum usque Inspruck misisti, & Wolffgango ituro, iumentum commodasti, quem ad te missum fingis. Sed quid ad rombum, quis quemque miserit, nisi vt cuncti meminerint, te nugarum assuetum, etiam ab re vanitatibus oblectari? Sed eorsum tua verget oratio, vt fidem in te violatam vanissime persuadeas. Hoc certe renocandum est. Neque enim Tridentinus tetefellit, neque Abbas, sed ne quisquam alius præter te, qui cum Brunegke venisses, simulabas te vetera gravamina tollere, & cum Principe in gratiam redire, & quæcunque per illos rudes idiotas Gebhardum & Pollinger, quos tu præfeceras, ministerius acta essent, emendare velle. Hoc colore clerum Brixinensem lætabundum Brunegke illexisti, sperantem, iamque sibi pollicentem, quod satiatus iniuriis, quibus eos diutissime professeras, tandem pietatem ac manuetudinem in illos exercueres. Tu vero sæuitiam conduplicasti, præcipiens ne diuina peragerent; quisquis secus faceret, tu illi curam animarum abstulisti. Talibus tuis ausibus inflammata sunt omnium pectora, vt nisi Dux ipse nefarios conatus tuos modesta castigatione repressisset, profecto indomitum ac irreuocabile vulgus in te irruisset, vnusque & idem vitæ ac facultatum tuarum & furoris popularis exitus fuisset. Nunc vero salua est Brixinensis Ecclesia, tu degis superstes, & hæc omnia sine cæde, diuino quodam iudicio peracta sunt. Hæc profecto quorsum verteris, vndique quadrant; tua vero litera, sicut & reliqua omnino vita tua dissonat, nusquam sibi ipsi consentiens, sed velut sydera à terra distant, & flamma à mari, sic tua fictio à vero. Nam si fœdus contractum observassēs, sicut Papa pro te spospondérat, (tu vero violasti,) profecto Ducem propitium tibi perfacile retinuisses. Treugas vero vel inducias dare vel acceptare noluisti, teste Parcifale, quem tute mediatorem velut proscnetam postulasti. Quanta sit eius fides, si leges desuper latas relegeris, clarius agnosces.
units.tr: You go on saying that Wolfgang came to you like a herald, bringing letters from the Bishop of Trent and the Abbot of Wilten, and an oath from Parcifal, begging on your behalf for your security, that you should set out for Brunegg, where the Duke himself was to come to settle the differences. But you sent your chamberlain to the Bishop of Trent, who was then staying with the Duke, so that you might learn the truth; to him the Bishop declared that he was not a traitor, and that you too could come safely to Brunegg. Thus under the appearance of negotiation you were betrayed. Indeed, all the articles of the differences had been settled among the others, except concerning the mine, where Parcifal demanded a yearly truce, and you wished to give only a six-month one, so that you would not suffer the loss of possession by a longer delay. So you prepared a treachery for yourself and tried it in place of peace. You conclude, therefore, though falsely, that no treachery can be presumed against you, since the Pope had assured the Duke of the observance of the pact and covenant. This fiction is further from the truth than God is from the Devil. What do you say, you whirlpool of vanities? Wolfgang was sent to you by the Chapter and clergy of Brixen, and by the vassals and officials of the church itself, as a promoter of peace and a monitor of virtues, and as one to persuade you not to provoke with your fierce words the Duke, the whole people and every class of men against you. He warned you that all men of every rank had grown hot against you, and that danger was at hand on the border. But you, trusting no one, scarcely even yourself, sent your chamberlain as far as Innsbruck, and lent a beast of burden to Wolfgang, who was setting out, whom you pretend was sent to you. But what does it matter who sent whom, except that everyone should remember that you, accustomed to trifles, delight even in vanities without cause? But your speech turns in the other direction, so that you may most vainly persuade us that faith was broken with you. This must certainly be recalled. For neither the Bishop of Trent nor the Abbot deceived you, nor anyone else except yourself, who, when you came with Brunegg, pretended that you wished to remove the old grievances, to be reconciled with the Prince, and to amend whatever had been done by those rude idiots Gebhard and Pollinger, whom you had put in charge. With this pretext you enticed the joyful clergy of Brixen to Brunegg, who hoped and already promised themselves that you, sated with the injuries with which you had for so long afflicted them, would at last show piety and gentleness towards them. But you redoubled your cruelty, forbidding them to perform divine services; whoever did otherwise, you deprived of the cure of souls. By such daring acts of yours the hearts of all were so inflamed that, had the Duke himself not restrained your wicked attempts with moderate chastisement, the untamed and irrevocable crowd would certainly have rushed upon you, and there would have been one and the same end to your life and property and the popular fury. Now, however, the church of Brixen is safe, you live on, and all these things were done without bloodshed by a certain divine judgment. Indeed, these matters, wherever you turn them, fit together; but your letter, like your whole life, is discordant and nowhere agrees with itself, but, as the stars are distant from the earth and flame from the sea, so your fiction is from the truth. For if you had kept the covenant concluded, as the Pope had promised for you (but you violated it), you could certainly have kept the Duke favourably disposed towards you without difficulty. But you were unwilling to offer or accept truces or respites, as Parcifal bears witness, whom you yourself asked for as mediator, as if he were a man proscribed. How trustworthy he is, you will recognise more clearly if you read again the laws passed about him.

units.la: Porro non desinis Gregorium lacessere, quem mendacissimum falso appellas, pro eo quod primi oratores illa ipsa coram Papa non allegarunt, quæ Gregorius, vt tu figulè dicis, postea sinxit. Asseris insuper fictionem eius videri, ab his, qui ipsa mentiuntur, quibus Dux te compressit. Et quando Imperator, Comitem Gotitiæ inuasit, cuius gentes tunc emigrasse dicis, cum te Dux apud Brunegk obsidione cinxit, vel circumdedit. O miser quid insanis, cur ita gestis, vt Gregorium contra te provoces? cum tu Ducalem indignationem, sceleratis factionibus tuis, rite provocatum, & vltionis iustæ vindictam excipieres, Gregorius in Austria manebat Archiducis illius obsequiis incumbens, & hoc de mense Aprilis. De mense vero Iulii Laurentius coram Papa comparuit, allegaturus, cur aduersus Ducem ad poenas comminatas non debeat procedi; tandem repulsus appellauit. Apud quem Dux sic loquitur appellans; Non aliter quam naturali & humano iure permittitur vim vi repellentes & nostra defendentes &c. Cardinalis via facti contra nos multiplicitèr procedere parabat, castra sua rebus bellicis instruxit, subditis nostri damna inferri sustinuit ex fortis suis &c. Iactauit se vallis plurimas armigeris impleturum &c. Extant literæ manu sua scriptæ, quæ animum eius produnt: Naturalis defensio, qua vim vi repellere licet, nobis auferitur. Et infra: Postea admodum Gregorius ab Archiduce missus venit Inspruck consilium laturus duci Sigismundo. Mitte in digitos, tempora dimetiens, & errorem tuum agnosces, Gregorius tua factmata relegens exultat, velut Alcides epulans de bobus Gereonis, nec emptis, neque donatis, altero scilicet conuiciante, altero plus iubilante. Hocinsuper addit: Quod si tibi par esset benevolentia vt esset scientia, quippe qui omnium fere auctorum instituta & præcepta legisti, atque etiam audacia, quia nec pudor impedit iam gauderet, te sibi obtigisse, cuius ingenio animam atteret, sicut aurum lapidi admouetur quanto probatur, ita ipsam animam suam probaret, an recte imbuta esset. Qualiter autem migrarint gentes Imperatoris superius audisti, scilicet terris finitimis subactis, ianua vsque ad terras Ecclesiæ Brixinensis pacefacta, adeo quod vsque hodie ibi opus est maiore custodia, &c.
units.tr: Further, you do not cease to attack Gregory, whom you falsely call most lying, because the first orators did not allege before the Pope those very things which Gregory, as you, potter, say, afterwards invented. You further assert that his fiction appears from those who themselves lie, by whom the Duke has pressed you. And when the Emperor invaded the Count of Görz, whose peoples, you say, then emigrated, while the Duke besieged or surrounded you at Brunegg, O wretched man, what madness possesses you, why do you act so as to provoke Gregory against yourself? When you, by your wicked factions, were rightly provoking the Ducal indignation, and were receiving the vengeance of a just retribution, Gregory was staying in Austria, attending to the services of that Archduke, and this in the month of April. But in the month of July Laurence appeared before the Pope, to allege why proceedings should not be taken against the Duke for the threatened penalties; finally, repulsed, he appealed. Before him the Duke speaks thus, in appealing: Not otherwise than by natural and human right is it permitted to repel force with force and to defend our own, etc. The Cardinal was preparing to proceed against us in many ways by force; he fortified his castles with military supplies; he allowed damage to be inflicted on our subjects from his fortresses, etc. He boasted that he would fill many valleys with armed men, etc. There are letters extant written in his own hand, which betray his mind: The natural defence, by which it is lawful to repel force with force, is taken away from us. And below: Afterwards Gregory, sent by the Archduke, came to Innsbruck to give counsel to Duke Sigismund. Put your fingers on it, measuring the times, and you will recognise your error; Gregory, reading over your deeds, exults, like Alcides feasting on the oxen of Geryon, neither bought nor given, the one reproaching, the other rejoicing still more. He adds this besides: But if you had the goodwill to match your knowledge, since you have read the institutions and precepts of nearly all authors, and also the audacity, since shame does not hinder you, he would now rejoice that he had met you, by whose wit he wears down his soul, as gold is applied to a stone to test it, so that he might prove his own soul, whether it had been rightly instructed. But how the Emperor's peoples migrated, you have heard above: namely, after the neighbouring lands were subdued, the passage to the lands of the church of Brixen was made peaceful, so that even today greater guard is needed there, etc.

units.la: Ex his quoque responsum est petitioni tuæ, qua rogas, quomodo defendatur ab excommunicatione Dux, qui te post Brunegk euitam, & pacem proclamatam, decendio detinuit. Nescis insane, quam pie, quam benigne tecum est actum. Pax proclamata est, vt rapacium manus cohiberentur. Tu quippe nosti, quanta sit pietas viris, qui castra sequuntur. Tecum autem agebatur, quo pacto Dux & principatus eius, sub cuius aduocatia Ecclesia Brixinensis sita est, assecuraretur, ne imposterum vlla commotio fieret, sed Episcopus pro tempore ac ipsa Ecclesia suis contenti finibus communi omnium finitimorum protectione & tranquillitate gauderet. Tuque hanc viam primus inuenisti, vt castra & fortia in manibus capituli reponantur, & capitulum caueat ea talibus custodibus gubernari, qui Ecclesiæ Brixinensi ac populo illius principatus grati forent ac fideles. Hanc conditionem Dux suscepit, ne terras Ecclesiæ ambisse notaretur, neqi facinora tua, in Ecclesia reduci, darent detrimentum. Interea nonnulli dies effluxerunt, quibus tu tamen reuerenter habitus es, & quotquot voluisti de prælatis, clericis & ministerialibus accersire potuisti. O ingratissime, qui te ducem iactas & principem secularem, & iam bellica præda fuisti, quam gratiam piissimo principi rependis?
units.tr: From these points there is also an answer to your petition, in which you ask how the Duke can be defended against excommunication, since he kept you for a fortnight after Brunegk, when you were released and peace was proclaimed. You foolish man, do you not know how kindly and mercifully you were treated? Peace was proclaimed so that the hands of plunderers would be restrained. You yourself know how little mercy men show who follow armies. What was actually being arranged with you was how the Duke and his principality, under whose protection the Church of Brixen lies, could be made secure, so that no disturbance would arise in future, and so that the bishop of the time and the Church itself might be content with their own borders and enjoy the common peace and quiet of all their neighbours. You were the first to devise the plan that the castles and strongholds be placed in the hands of the chapter, and that the chapter take care that they be held by such guardians as would be pleasing and loyal to the Church of Brixen and to the people of that principality. The Duke accepted this condition, so that he would not be marked as having coveted the lands of the Church, and so that your crimes would not harm the Church once it was restored. Meanwhile several days passed, during which you were nonetheless treated with respect, and you were able to summon as many prelates, clergy and officials as you wished. O most ungrateful man, who boast of being a duke and a secular prince, and who have already been a prize of war, how do you repay such grace to a most devout prince?

units.la: Desicit.
units.tr: He breaks off.

units.la: Deficiens hactenus ad Calixti mandata confugis, quibus respondetur, comminationem non habere vim rei iudicatae. Praecepit Calixtus securitatem tibi praestari, tu dolose litteris illis inserutis talem, de qua contentus fores. Etsi hoc non aliter quam de legitime ac consueta securitate debeat intelligi, quam Dux tibi praestitit; tuam tamen calumniam assuetam veritus, a captioso praecepto prudens appellavit. Mortuus est Calixtus; Pius appellatione admissa biennium pro fatali concessit, vide, o iuris apostata, si purificata sit comminatio, iam appellationis admissione suspensa. Si vero dux ipse iam te hortatus est, quatenus auferres papales comminationes, non idcirco probatur excommunicatus. Quod vere criminaris Ducem, quod a Clericis quicquam exactionauerit, o superbissime, qui tibi praelatorum & clericorum illius dioecesis opes ac rem familiarem vsurpas, quasi omnia sint tuae ditionis, secularis praepositus Novae cellae, gratus fuit principi suo, qui in illa expeditione, qua audaciam tuam repressit, gentes suas ab omni excursione coercuit, ita ut Coloni, Censitae, emphyteutae, caeterique illius monasterii homines seculares, sed pater spiritualis, neque ipse quaeritur de duce, sub cuius protectione tranquilla fruitur securitate: Heinricus vero Magister Coquinae tuae, non se gessit pro Clerico. Passinger a populo interfectus esset, nisi dux eum redemisset. Talis disciplina fuit in schola tua, tales mores aulicorum tuorum, ut qui audacia praevaleret, is tibi fuerit acceptior.
units.tr: Failing so far, you take refuge in Calixtus's orders, to which the answer is that a threat does not have the force of a decided judgment. Calixtus ordered that safe-conduct be granted to you, but you craftily read into those letters a safe-conduct of the sort you would have been content with. Yet this ought to be understood in no other way than as the legitimate and customary safe-conduct which the Duke granted you. Fearing your usual trickery, however, he prudently appealed from the captious order. Calixtus died; Pius, when the appeal was admitted, allowed two years as the fatal term. See, you apostate from law, whether the threat has been purified, now that the admission of the appeal has suspended it. If the Duke himself has already urged you to remove the papal threats, he is not thereby proved to be excommunicated. As for your true charge that the Duke extorted something from the clergy, O most arrogant man, who claim for yourself the wealth and private property of the prelates and clergy of that diocese as if they were all under your authority: the secular provost of Neustift was pleasing to his prince, who in that campaign in which he repressed your audacity restrained his people from every raid, so that the tenants, censuary holders, emphyteutic tenants and other secular men of that monastery, but a spiritual father, enjoy a quiet security under his protection, and the Duke is not himself complained of. Henry, the Master of your Kitchen, did not conduct himself as a cleric. Passinger would have been killed by the people had the Duke not ransomed him. Such was the discipline in your school, such were the manners of your courtiers, that whoever prevailed by audacity was the more acceptable to you.
