units.la: Frustratus autem in viribus iuris ordinariis, ad plenitudinem potestatis confugis, dicens Papam posse legatos inhibere ne celebrent, etiam si nihil deliquisset populus. Vide quid loquaris, ne asseras Papam in destructionem ecclesiae, vel devorationem omnium esse constitutum. Scio enim quam plenissima est, Papae potestas; sed tu non advertis, quod Papa in literis suis non mandavit interdictum observari, ex suae potestatis plenitudine, sed quia sibi suggestum est, qualiter dux in te vim sacrilegam admiserit. His tuis falsis suggestionibus, Papa circumventus est. Ergo ad casum redacti sumus, in quo docemur non obtemperare mandatis exorbitantibus, sed Papae rescribere. Ita fecit dux catholicus. Tu vero Papam dolis tuis circumvenisti, ne veritatem audire, aut innocentiam ducis percipere vellet. Neminem vero vnquam dux coegit ad sacrificandum, vt tu singis; sed totus clerus omnisque populus sacrilegia tua, cum fornicationibus incantationibus atque infaustis nationibus tuis taliter odit, vt dicat te coniuratione omnium malignorum spirituum has partes intrasse, vt pacem perpetuam in discidium commutarets. Et qui nugis plusquam ducenta florenorum milia, de Alemania extraxisti, pat vanitate terram illam pacificam commouere, ac sedit oncs in populo excitare studuisti.
units.tr: Thwarted in the ordinary powers of law, you flee to the fullness of power, saying that the Pope can forbid legates to celebrate, even if the people have done nothing wrong. See what you are saying, lest you assert that the Pope has been appointed for the destruction or devouring of the Church. For I know how complete the power of the Pope is; but you do not notice that the Pope, in his letters, did not order the interdict to be observed out of the fullness of his power, but because it was suggested to him how the Duke had committed a sacrilegious violence against you. By these false suggestions of yours the Pope was circumvented. So we are brought to a case in which we are taught not to obey exorbitant commands, but to write back to the Pope. This is what the Catholic Duke did. You, however, circumvented the Pope with your tricks, so that he would not wish to hear the truth or perceive the innocence of the Duke. Indeed the Duke never forced anyone to sacrifice, as you pretend; rather, the whole clergy and every people hate your sacrileges, together with your fornications, incantations and unlucky dealings, to such a degree that they say you entered these parts by the conspiracy of all the evil spirits, so as to change perpetual peace into discord. And you, who drew more than two hundred thousand florins out of Germany for trifles, have tried in vain to stir that peaceful land and to incite sedition among the people.

units.la: Dehinc aggredieris argumentari, contra appellationem ducis, his locis: Si haereticus tueri se posset appellatione ad futurum concilium, interiecta, iam nulla esset fides Christiana, aliquando in quadringentis annis Concilium non fuit congregatum. Iam cursum sermone rotato torquens enthymema, quia sic argumentaris. Lis nulla quatriginta annis est trahenda. Appellatio ad futurum Concilium trahit litem annis quadringenta, ergo &c. Probatur minor propositio, quia aliquando in quadringentis amicis non fuit celebratum concilium. Profecto si annos, qui fluxerunt a Concilio Apostolorum, quando receperant Spiritum sanctum, aut quando miserunt Paulum & Iohannem in messem Domini, aut symbolum condiderunt, seu Petrum Antiochiae in cathedram collocarunt, aut vltimo convenerunt ab vno diuisi per orbem, quod etsi Lucas in Actis non meminit, est tamen in Agiographis, & ecclesia Teutonica ibidus Iulii, eius festiuam peragit memoriam, vsque ad Nicenam synodum, miseris in digitos, non redundabit summa tua neque tiecenti resultabunt anni, sed longe pauciores, quos tibi credo, vt mea liberalitate fruaris, sed haec omnia quid concludunt, nisi quod si quis a Petro, Lino, Cleto vel Clemente appellasset ad futurum Concilium, nimis prolixum fatale habuisset. Sed meminerisse legisse, quod quia ante Constantini temporanon c ac episcopis conueniendi licentia, ideo in varias haereses scissa est ecclesia. Hoc magna synodus Constantiensis intuens ait; Frequens Conciliorum celebratio agri dominici praecipua cultura est &c. Et idci co decreuit sacra concilia de decennio in decennium celebrari, ergo quadringentorum annorum prolationis praetensio inanita est. Subdis, quod si ad futurum pontificem vel Concilium rite appellaretur, eo quod successor de gestis antecessoris iudicat & quisque successor alium habet successorem, procederet in infinitum. Num de Lætheo bibisti, oblitus ne in vna eademque causa liceat tertio provocare. Dixeris fortasse, de ferri iustitiam. At omnis appellatio suspendit executionem. Non ideo defensionis facultas auferenda est, moribus introducta. Quot vidisti causas in curia Papae vsque ad tertium vel Papam vel haeredem aut successorem protelatas, nec tamen vnquam certa meta praefiniri potuit vel praescribi. Si dixeris biennium longam latis esse metam, quo lege ciuili durat instantia, quid si plus vno die? quid mensa? quid tandem semestri vel anno vtor permisso? paulatim addo vel iungo vnum, iungo iterum vnum.
units.tr: Next you set about arguing against the Duke's appeal, using these passages: If a heretic could protect himself by an appeal interposed to a future council, there would be no Christian faith left; no council has been convened in four hundred years at some time. Now you twist the argument in a whirl of words, reasoning thus: No suit should be drawn out for forty years. An appeal to a future council draws out a suit for four hundred years; therefore etc. The minor premise is proved because at some time in four hundred years no council was held. Indeed, if you count on your fingers the years that have passed from the council of the Apostles, when they received the Holy Spirit, or when they sent Paul and John into the Lord's harvest, or when they composed the creed, or when Peter set up his seat at Antioch, or when at last they gathered, divided and scattered through the world (which, although Luke does not mention it in Acts, is nonetheless in the hagiographers, and the German Church celebrates its festival on the ides of July, up to the Nicene synod), your total will not add up to four hundred years, but will be far fewer; I believe you, so that you may enjoy my generosity. But what do all these things prove, except that if anyone had appealed to a future council from Peter, Linus, Cletus or Clement, he would have had a very long fatal term? But I remember reading that because before the time of Constantine there was no permission for bishops to assemble, therefore the Church was split into various heresies. The great synod of Constance, looking at this, said: "The frequent celebration of councils is the chief cultivation of the Lord's field," etc. And for this reason the sacred councils decreed that they be celebrated from decade to decade; therefore the pretext of a four-hundred-year postponement is empty. You add that if one appealed rightly to a future pope or council, because a successor judges the acts of his predecessor, and each successor has another successor, the process would go on to infinity. Have you drunk from Lethe, forgetting that in one and the same cause it is not permitted to appeal a third time? You may perhaps say that this concerns the justice of iron. But every appeal suspends execution. The faculty of defence is not therefore to be taken away, a custom introduced by usage. How many causes have you seen in the Pope's court deferred until a third Pope, or his heir or successor? Yet no fixed limit could ever be set or prescribed for them. If you say that two years is a long limit, which the civil law sets as the duration of an instance, what if it is more than one day? What of six months? What of the permission of a year? Little by little I add one, and join one again, and join one more.

units.la: Nunc vir sacrilege atque impudice, neges Concilium supra Papam esse, quod olim aliter scripsisti. Et extant tua, tum etiam Papae scripta, in contrariam partem, qui aliter stans, alter sedens, loqueris, homo quem nil pudet vanitatis, qui sic argumentaris: Concilium Constantinense nominauit Papam Iohannem, Dominum suum, quod non fecisset, si fuisset subditus eius. O quanta insania tua, qui ex nuncupatione vrbana locos conuincere putas.
units.tr: Now, you sacrilegious and shameless man, you deny that the council is above the Pope, although formerly you wrote otherwise. Your writings survive, and also those of the Pope, on the opposite side; you speak differently standing and sitting, a man whom no vanity shames, who argues thus: The Council of Constance named Pope John "its lord"; it would not have done so if he had been its subject. O what great folly is yours, who think you can refute places by the courtesy-title of the city.

units.la: Vendica tibi dominium in Cardinales, qui te nuncupant; sua virtute dicentes, Dominus meus sanctissimus Petri, vt ipsorum abutaris benignitate, si tibi commemorem, quando incepit & inoleuit mos nuncupationis dominicæ. Quando Papæ coeperunt nominari domine domine; Quando etiam Imperatores sic appellari noluerint: Quomodo usurpatum est Papas sese pluraliter & cunctos alios singulariter nominare, quippe qui sese aliquando singulariter nuncuparint, nimium prolixus ero. Sed sufficiat tibi probatum esse, quod magna Synodus Constantiensis, sibimet nil detraxit, cum Iohannem sanctissimum dominum appellauit, quem tamen postea rite iusteq; destituit, alioquin Martinus sedem vacantem non intrasset, neque Eugenio aut is Nicolao vacuam reliquisset, qui te Cardinalem creare minime potuisset; Vide vir petulantissime, quorsum euadat tua vana superstitio, qui cauillas appellationem Ducis ad vltimum concilium interpositam esse, hoc certe non continet appellatio. Nihil enim est quod aut natura extremum inhuenerit, aut doctrina primum. Hoc etiam accipe; quod sicut Capitulum eligit episcopum, cuius assensu contrahitur spirituale matrimonium & non parum administrationis innoscitur; ita suffraganeorum assensu Archiepiscopus consecratur, nec tamen inepte, Dominus quisque suorum nuncupatur. Iudicatur etiam Archiepiscopus a Synodo prouinciali, quam tamen ipse creauit vel iudixit. Cæterum si literarum sacrarum desertor ius publicum ignoras, adea quæ moribus introducta sunt animaduerte. Regem Francorum iudicat parlamentum, Imperatorem Romanorum Palatinus Rheni, attamen vtrumque; Dominus reuerenter nuncupatur vtriusq; Procedit deinde longa quadam verbositate implicans & inuoluens, magnæ synodi quam plurima decreta iam dicens à Christo dependere, iam vero asserens supra Papam non esse, cum dicis illam tollendi schismatis causa omnia dixisse, caue dixeris; illam pro vnione assequenda dixisse vel fecisse, quod de iure non potuit. Gregorius non sustinebit, mihi paulo mitius est ingenium. Varias enim & vacillas, vt dictum sit non dictum, ratum irritum, eo tamen tendere videris, Concilium super extirpatione schismatis congregatum plurimam habeat potestatem. Oro te, Cancer Cusane, ne cancrino more resilias, sed recte perge vt cepisti, si Concilium super extirpando schismate congregatum esset, & interea surgeret hæresis, vel alter Papārum moreretur vel cederet, alter venderet Sacramenta vel aliter scandalisaret ecclesiam, nunquam patres cogerentur hoc Concilium dissoluere, & aliud pro hæresis eradicatione, vel reformatione denuo instituere? Aut cur retorto sermone tandem dicis; Et si actu concilium esset super illis congregatum, super quibus Constantiense &c. tamen non sequitur, quod concilium nondum congregatum talem haberet superioritatem; quod à Papa ad ipsum posset appellari. O bone vir, quid deliras? Nam si actu esset congregatum concilium, ridiculus esset, qui omisso principali concilio congregato, ad aliud nondum congregatum appellaret. Vide, Cancer, quam inique calumniaris Gregorium, qui dicit ex decretis magnæ synodi Concilium generale perpetuis temporibus de decennio in decennium debere celebrari. Dies cessit. Cuius est mora, tu nosti, sicut igitur ad Papam appellatio interiecta tenet sede vacante, sic ad Concilium, quia cessit dies, dissoluta est. Itaque innodatio tua, quia dicis; quod n. non est, non est supra; quia perpetua est ecclesiæ auctoritas; siue sit congregata, siue dispersa, quanquam ad opus operandum & exequendum, congregatio sit optima. Quæris tandem, quid operetur appellatio, ad futurum Concilium interiecta; etiam si rite sic appellaretur, cum non tollat sententias à iure prolatas nec suspendat effectum, quem secum trahit, sententia. In Concilio vero simplici querela introduci causa potest. De hoc vero ad hunc contenditur, an Dux poenas inciderit. Hoc coram non suspectis Dux decertare cupit, Gregorius certat & adhuc coram iudice lis est, id vero, quod Papa nulliter agit, rite contemnitur.
units.tr: You claim lordship over the cardinals who address you as "my most holy lord, the Peter," so that you may abuse their kindness. If I were to recall for you when the custom of addressing men as "lord" began and took hold, when the Popes began to be called "lord, lord," and when emperors refused to be so addressed, or how it came to be usual for the Popes to be addressed in the plural while everyone else is addressed in the singular, though the Popes themselves were sometimes addressed in the singular, I would be too long. But let it be enough for you that the great Council of Constance lost nothing of its own dignity when it called John "most holy lord." Yet it afterwards duly and justly deposed him. Otherwise Martin would not have entered the vacant see, nor would he have left it vacant for Eugenius, and Eugenius for Nicholas, who could never have made you a cardinal. See, most insolent man, where your vain superstition leads you, you who quibble that the Duke's appeal was lodged to the last council. That appeal certainly does not say this. For there is nothing that nature has found last or doctrine first. Take this as well: just as the chapter elects a bishop, and by his assent the spiritual marriage is contracted and his administration is not a little recognised, so an archbishop is consecrated with the assent of his suffragans, and yet it is not foolish for each of them to be called "lord" of his own. An archbishop is also judged by the provincial synod, which nonetheless he himself created or convened. But if you, a deserter of sacred letters, do not know public law, then notice what has been introduced by custom. The parliament judges the King of the Franks, and the Count Palatine of the Rhine judges the Emperor of the Romans, and yet both are reverently called "lord." He then proceeds with a certain long-winded verbosity, entangling and involving himself, now saying that many decrees of the great synod depend on Christ, now asserting that there is nothing above the Pope. When you say that it said everything for the sake of ending the schism, beware of saying that it said or did, for the sake of achieving union, what it could not do by right. Gregory will not put up with this; my temperament is somewhat milder. For you vary and waver, so that what was said is not said, ratified and annulled, yet you seem to tend toward this: that a council gathered for the extirpation of the schism has the greatest power. I beg you, Cusan crab, do not recoil in the manner of a crab, but proceed rightly as you began. Suppose a council were gathered to extirpate the schism, and meanwhile heresy arose, or one Pope died or resigned, while the other sold the sacraments or otherwise scandalised the Church. Would the fathers never be compelled to dissolve this council and to institute another anew for the eradication of heresy or for reform? Or why at last, with a twisted argument, do you say: "Even if a council were in fact gathered over those matters over which the Council of Constance [sat], it does not follow that a council not yet gathered would have such superiority that an appeal could be made to it from the Pope"? O good man, what are you raving about? For if a council were actually gathered, it would be ridiculous for anyone, leaving the principal council gathered, to appeal to another that is not yet gathered. See, Crab, how unjustly you calumniate Gregory, who says that by the decrees of the great synod a general council must be celebrated in perpetual times, from decade to decade. The day has passed. You know the cause of the delay. Therefore, just as an appeal lodged to the Pope holds while the see is vacant, so an appeal to the council, since the day has passed, has been dissolved. And so your entanglement, because you say, "What is not, is not above," since the authority of the Church is perpetual, whether it is gathered or scattered, although a gathering is best for doing and carrying out the work. Finally you ask what an appeal, lodged to a future council, accomplishes, even if it were rightly so lodged, since it does not annul sentences pronounced by law nor suspend the effect which a sentence carries with it. But in a simple council a complaint can be introduced as a cause. Yet this is contested with regard to this matter: whether the Duke incurred the penalties. The Duke wishes to contend this before judges who are not suspect; Gregory contends it, and the suit is still before a judge. What the Pope does without validity is rightly disregarded.

units.la: Descendis ad constitutionem sacrilegam, qua veratur ad concilium appellari. Nil autem affers probabile, nisi quod ad Ducem verba dirigens ait: Dicere non potes, quod te minus liget, quam alios Christianos, & infra subdis; Non debebas ponere os in Caelum plusquam alii: cætera quæ dicis, anilesfabulæ sunt. Tibi respondetur, quod duci opus fuit prouocare contra surreptitia poenalia mandatia; quæ tu falsis suggestionibus surripuisti, aliis forte non itidem, qui non fuere, grauati. Quibus vero grauamen impenderet, pariformia prouocarent, tam pontifices quam prælati, quibus Papa & legatus eius, decimæ triennalis impositionem comminatus est.
units.tr: You descend to the sacrilegious constitution by which it is forbidden to appeal to a council. Yet you bring forward nothing probable, except that, addressing the Duke, you say: "You cannot say that you are less bound than other Christians," and below, "You ought not to have set your mouth against heaven more than others." The rest of what you say is old wives' fables. It is answered to you that the Duke had reason to appeal against the surreptitious penal mandates, which you obtained by false suggestions, though perhaps others, who were not burdened, did not do so. But those on whom the burden would fall might appeal in the same way, both pontiffs and prelates, against whom the Pope and his legate threatened the imposition of a triennial tithe.

units.la: Quæ quidem impositio, suspecta est nugarum; propter felonium tuam veterem, quæ plusquam ducenta florenorum millia, ex Alemania suxisti, tam dulciter pollicens, nil ipsius pecuniæ ex Alemania traduci, sed inibi ad pios vsus depositam conseruari. O vtinam os tuum posuisses in caelum, atq; oculos leuasses in montes; sed in mare supia nostra dispexisti. Non ergo auxilium à Domino sperasti. Ideoq; te sol vssit per diem; cum pecuniis tuis sacrilege quæsisti. Tauferadeptus, Redenneck, Volturnum ac Iouedonum inhiasti. Nunc te urget luna per noctem, cum iustissimo Dei iudicio post fideifragium tuum, quo conuentionem Iurispublici violasti, teque exulem facete maluisti; si forte animi tui malignitatem explere posses, etiam opidis & prædiis, quibus frui poteras, te destituisti. Tu forte nuncupas os in Caelum ponere, de gestis Papæ vel eius potestate disputare. Talis quippe dicendi modus ab adulatoribus inuentus, per assentatores tandem inoleuit. At tu minor disputatio, an super bigamia per Papam ad sacerdotium valeat dispensari; & an Papa possit concedere matrimonium in certum tempus, vel vsque ad procreationem sobolis masculinæ, contrahatur. Sexcenta sunt quæ memorem si opus fiat. Nec tamen ad sacrilegium reputatur. De Deo enim disputatur, an possit producere infinitum an potentiam creandi delegare possit. Quid ergo vir bone cautaris, si quis dicat constitutionem Papæ peccare? Sunt qui dicant Papam fauore Episcopi Lucani agentis pro vi expulsiua contra Pisanos pronunciasse super turbatiua. Ac ruisum qui dicant alium Papam ex verbis Iohannis Frangapanis directae substitutionis decreuisse obligationem. Quotidie Papales, & aliae constitutiones modificantur, tum reuocantur, aliquando respuuntur. Et tu desertor iuris, abortiuae theologe, multa praetextu legationis fatuisti, ac quaerentibus aduersum te respondisti, quatenus adeant Papam desuper supplicaturi, vt sic medullam in ossibus Germaniae relictam fugendo tereres. Quae cum visa sunt, pecuniis datis tolli posse, tandem a cautioribus principibus retenta pecunia repudiata sunt ac derisa. Et haec omnia tu notas haeresim. Quid si Papa mandat solui Camerae sue mille sub poena haeresis; An recusans sic haereticus? Nequaquam. Sunt enim maleficia discreta, quae suos tenent auctores. Neque enim coeforvitium vel arborum est parricida; Nec fur est. Desine ergo conuitiari, vel audies, quod audiisse nolet.
units.tr: This imposition is itself suspect of trifling, on account of your old felony, by which you sucked more than two hundred thousand florins out of Germany, promising so sweetly that none of that money would be carried out of Germany, but would be kept there, deposited for pious uses. O, if only you had set your mouth against heaven and lifted your eyes to the mountains! But you looked down on our affairs in the sea. Therefore you did not hope for help from the Lord. Hence the sun burned you by day, when you sought money by sacrilege; you longed for Taufers, Rodeneck, Volturno and Giovedone. Now the moon presses on you by night, by the most just judgment of God, after your breach of faith, by which you violated the agreement of public law, and you preferred to make yourself an exile. If perhaps you could satisfy the malice of your mind, you also deprived yourself of towns and estates which you might have enjoyed. Perhaps you claim to set your mouth against heaven by disputing about the deeds of the Pope or his power. Indeed, this manner of speaking was invented by flatterers and at last took hold through sycophants. But you, a lesser disputant, dispute whether a dispensation for bigamy may be granted by the Pope so as to be valid for the priesthood, and whether the Pope may grant a marriage for a fixed time, or until the production of male offspring, is contracted. I could recall six hundred such questions if the need arose. Yet these are not reckoned as sacrilege. For it is disputed about God whether he can produce the infinite, and whether he can delegate the power of creating. What then, good man, are you so anxious about, if someone says that a constitution of the Pope is sinful? There are those who say that the Pope, out of favour toward the Bishop of Lucca, acting for forcible expulsion against the Pisans, pronounced on the disturbance. And again there are those who say that another Pope, from the words of John Frangipani, decreed the obligation of direct substitution. Papal and other constitutions are modified every day, sometimes revoked, sometimes rejected. And you, a deserter of law, an abortive theologian, have wasted much under the pretext of an embassy, and answered those asking against you, that they should go to the Pope to make supplication about these things, so that, by fleeing, you might wear away the marrow left in the bones of Germany. When these things seemed to be removed by the payment of money, at last the money, withheld by the more cautious princes, was rejected and mocked. And you note all these things as heresy. What if the Pope orders a thousand to be paid into his Chamber under penalty of heresy? Would one who refuses thereby be a heretic? By no means. For there are distinct wrongdoings, which have their own authors. For a worm is not a parricide of trees, nor is it a thief. Cease therefore to revile, or you will hear what you would not want to have heard.

units.la: Nunc quibus anfractibus lapsum illum vel euitare, vel erroris notam aufugere tentas, qua notaris errasse, docens, in ecclesia esse credendum. Id perstringere libet. Dicis nil referre praepositionem in appositam in citatione. Non enim, vt ais, citatus est Dux, an credat Ecclesiam, vel in Ecclesiam, quia ad symbolum remittit citatio. Tu autem non desinis procaciter errorem defendere, quod est haereticorum proprium, scilicet pertinacia. Quid dicis? Gregorium nescire inter symbola discernere? Iure suspectus haberis, quod de symbolis varie sentias. Postea subaccusas appellationem Ducis de perplexitate, quia Ducem laicum esse dicat. Gregorius autem se in ipso Duce iciolum ostendere velit. Laicus est Dux, de fide simpliciter & bene sentiens. Tu vero omnem hominem haeresi falsa criminaris, qui tuis audaciis contradicit. Nemo vero te suspectior est in fide, qui nondum purgatus es ab illa macula, quam Fratres Minores iniecerunt tibi, qui tempore Papae Nicolai articulos plurimos contra te obtulerunt, quibus de haeresi notatus, nondum autem absolutus, nequaquam purgatus es. Profecto si ladere pergis vt coepisti, talem tibi notam inuret Gregorius, quam tota reliqua vita tua eluere non poterit. Sed perge vanitates tuas prosequi, Nonne hunc legisti Versiculum?
units.tr: Now by what twists you try either to avoid that slip or to flee the mark of error, by which you are charged with having erred when you teach that one must believe in the Church. I am pleased to press this point. You say that it makes no difference whether the preposition "in" or "into" is used in the citation, since, as you say, the Duke was not cited on whether he believes in the Church, or into the Church, because the citation refers to the creed. But you do not cease to defend error stubbornly, which is the proper mark of heretics, namely obstinacy. What do you say? That Gregory does not know how to distinguish between the creeds? You are rightly held suspect, since you have various opinions about the creeds. Afterwards you accuse the Duke's appeal of obscurity, because it calls him a layman. Gregory, however, wishes to show himself simple in the Duke himself. The Duke is a layman, who thinks simply and well about the faith. But you charge every man with false heresy who opposes your audacities. Indeed no one is more suspect in the faith than you, who have not yet been cleansed of that stain which the Friars Minor fixed upon you, who in the time of Pope Nicholas presented many articles against you, by which you were marked as a heretic, and not yet absolved, you have by no means been purged. Certainly, if you go on wounding as you began, Gregory will brand you with such a mark as your whole life will not be able to wash away. But go on pursuing your vanities. Have you not read this verse?

units.la: Crede Deo, credasque Deum, plus credo valere, Vt credas in eum, quam quod ei, veleum.
units.tr: Believe God, and believe that God exists: I think it is worth more that you believe in Him than that you believe Him, or that you merely believe that He is.

units.la: Cum deliras dicens, in sanctam ecclesiam credere, quemcunq; Christianum oportere, de qua dicitur; Qui aliter credit, quam sancta mater ecclesia docet, haereticus est. O miserum ingenium tuum, qui non discernis inter credere vnam ecclesiam, aut credere cum ecclesia, vel sicut ecclesia, aut in ecclesiam. Nonne credis, vt Apostoli crediderunt. Nonne in ea fide versaris, quam diuinum Petrum Apostolum Romanis tradidisse proditum est? at non credis in ipsum, sed ipsi credis euangelizanti Christum. Nonne credis Dei genitricem Virginem? non autem idcirco credis in illam. Quod si assertioni tuae assentias; in illam ergo credas, Deos habebis infinitos. Nonne puer didicisti, fidem esse assensum ex auctoritate dicentis generatum? Deinde grandior legisti, fidem esse dictorum conuentorumq; constantiam, de imitatione Stoica, quasi fiat quod dictum est, appellata. Nostra vero fides orthodoxa, per Anthonomasiam dicitur, qua credimus & confitemur ad aeternam salutem. In qua longe diuersum est, credere aliquid esse, fore, vel fuisse; aut in illud ipsum credere. Obiectum illius assensus, qui fides aut credulitas nuncupatur, est propositio, cui per adhaesionem animi assentis: non tamen credis in ipsam: Tu credis caelum & terram, Solem & Lunam, astraque micantia a Deo creata; sed non credis in ea. In solum Deum crede, & quae ad salutem aeternam credenda sunt, quaeq; Ecclesia diffinit, crede firmissime; non autem in illam. Illa etenim in Deum credit; non autem in semetipsam, quae nec a semetipsa, sed a Spiritu sancto viuificatur. In hunc crede viuificantem, qui per os Prophetarum ecclesiam praeconisauit, qui confortans Apostolos, trophaea Christi vexit per orbem. Ecclesiam vero sic crede, vt obedias illi, ac cum illa sentias. Haec est fides Augustini scribentis ad Neophytas baptizatos dum dicit; Interrogauimus an credatis in Deum Patrem omnipotentem, & in Iesum Christum, filium eius, Et in Spiritum sanctum &c. iuxta imperium Saluatoris praecipientis; Euntes docete omnes gentes, baptizantes in nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus sancti &c. Non interrogauimus autem, vt quomodo Deum creditur, sic in sanctam ecclesiam Catholicam, quae propterea sancta & catholica est, quia recte credit in Deum; sed intelligere debetis nos dicere & dixisse vt in Ecclesia sancta conuersantes in Deum credere tis &c. Vide ergo quomodo executieris, qui fidem Christi caullas, ne tibi contingat, quod de Homero & Stesicoro narratur. Quod Socrates ne sibi contingeret, praeuenire cauit in Phaedro. Si quis vero praelatorum eius erraut, error certe non est imitandus.
units.tr: When you rave, saying that every Christian must believe in the holy Church, of which it is said, "Whoever believes otherwise than holy mother Church teaches is a heretic," what a wretched mind you have, failing to distinguish between believing in one Church, believing with the Church, believing as the Church does, and believing in the Church. Do you not believe as the Apostles believed? Do you not abide in that faith which is said to have been handed down to the Romans by the divine Apostle Peter? Yet you do not believe in him; you believe him when he preaches Christ. Do you believe in the Virgin, the Mother of God? You do not believe in her for that reason. If you agreed with your own assertion, you would then believe in her, and you would have infinitely many gods. Did you not learn as a boy that faith is assent given on the authority of one who speaks? Later, as an older student, you read that faith is the steadfastness of what is said and agreed, called by a Stoic imitation, as if what was said were done. Our orthodox faith, however, is called faith in the proper sense, by which we believe and confess for eternal salvation. In it there is a great difference between believing that something is, will be, or was, and believing in that very thing. The object of that assent which is called faith or belief is a proposition, to which we give assent by the adherence of the mind; yet you do not believe in the proposition. You believe in heaven and earth, the sun and moon, and the shining stars as created by God, but you do not believe in them. Believe in God alone, and hold most firmly what is to be believed for eternal salvation, and what the Church defines; but do not believe in the Church, for it believes in God and not in itself, since it is quickened not by itself but by the Holy Spirit. Believe in Him who quickens, who through the mouth of the prophets proclaimed the Church, who strengthened the Apostles and carried the trophies of Christ throughout the world. Believe in the Church, however, in such a way that you obey her and think with her. This is the faith of Augustine, who writes to the baptized neophytes when he says: We asked whether you believe in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ his Son, and in the Holy Spirit, etc., according to the command of the Saviour who orders, "Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit," etc. We did not ask, however, whether you believe in the holy Catholic Church in the same way as you believe in God, for the Church is holy and catholic precisely because it believes rightly in God; but you must understand that we say, and have said, that you believe in God while living in the holy Church, etc. See then how you have fared, you who spurn the faith of Christ: take care lest what is told of Homer and Stesichorus happen to you. Socrates took care to forestall this for himself in the Phaedrus. If any of your prelates has erred, that error certainly is not to be imitated.

units.la: Et ne digrediar a proposita materia, tu Papam Ecclesiae caput ministeriale decepisti, qui te pro conditione fragilitatis humanae secutus, literas emisit comminatorias. Dux fidei fragium tuum subolens, & nugas sententias tuas, ad Papam misit. Tu illum induratii, aures obturasti, obsurduit Papa contra ducem, tu Papam delinisti assentationum laqueis infscinatus ille inuolutus contra ducem incanduit, fulminauit, coruscauit, iecit grandines, & intonuit. Tu monachos, scurras vagos reperisti, qui vanitates tuas disseminarent. Dux autem posthabet horum sua seria ludo. Tu quicquid veneni quotannis aluisti euomens cum impetu, haereticos mentiris eos, qui tuis audaciis obicem ponunt. Vide si hoc est, desipere in fide, aut de authoritate ecclesiae irreuerenter aut male sentire. Sed elenchum contorsisti, sic argumentando: Christus est caput ecclesiae. Omnes autem credimus in Christum. Perge autem. Qui credit in caput ecclesiae, credit in ecclesiam, quia caput pars corporis est. Credo & de te opinor, quia si quis per Atheismum in aliis terminis tibi taxaret arguendo; Christus est verus Deus, Christus est passus, mortuus &c. Ergo Deus est mortuus. Ac rursum, Deus est deitas, ergo passa est diuinitas. Tu circulationem illam dissolueres, duas naturas vel potius substantias in Christo distinguendo, absque vlla confusione vel mixtura, in sola vnitate personae scilicet suppositalis quam nos, vt a Graecis accepimus, hypostaticam nominamus: Naturalis enim personae significatio substantiam potius dicit, quam hypostasin. Sed ex ecclesiastica locutionis vsu, venit talis acceptio, Christus igitur ex Deo patre, ante omnia secula genitus, aequalis patri secundum diuinitatem, creator est omnium, per quem omnia facta sunt; nomo vero ex Maria virgine in seculo natus, sacerdos & patris altissimi filius, non tamen duo, sed vnus est, hypostatica scilicet vnione. Nunc habes quomodo credamus in Iesum Christum. Vide si sic credatur in ecclesiam, & secerne substantiam diuinam ab humana, vt scias quomodo Christus sit creator omnium, & quomodo caput ecclesiae, & aufugies Nestoris atque Euticetis sibimet formaliter contrarios errores.
units.tr: And, not to digress from the matter at hand, you deceived the Pope, the ministerial head of the Church. Out of regard for human frailty you followed him, and he issued threatening letters. The Duke, scenting your treachery and your silly opinions, sent them to the Pope. You hardened him, you stopped his ears, and the Pope grew deaf to the Duke. You flattered the Pope, and, ensnared by the nets of your flattery, he was enveloped and flamed up against the Duke; he thundered, flashed, hurled hailstones, and roared. You found monks and wandering buffoons to spread your follies abroad. The Duke, however, puts their serious matters below his jokes. You, vomiting out with violence whatever poison you have nourished year after year, lie that those who block your audacities are heretics. See whether this is to be foolish in the faith, or to think irreverently or wrongly about the authority of the Church. But you twisted your argument with this reasoning: Christ is the head of the Church; we all believe in Christ; go on: whoever believes in the head of the Church believes in the Church, because the head is part of the body. I think you believe this too, and I judge the same of you: if someone, arguing with you in the manner of an Atheist, were to reproach you with other terms, "Christ is true God, Christ suffered, died, etc.; therefore God died"; and again, "God is deity, therefore deity suffered." You would dissolve that circle by distinguishing two natures, or rather two substances, in Christ, without any confusion or mixture, in the sole unity of the person, namely the subsistent person, which we, as we have received from the Greeks, call hypostatic; for the natural meaning of "person" signifies substance rather than hypostasis. But from the ecclesiastical usage of speech comes this understanding: Christ, therefore, begotten of God the Father before all ages, equal to the Father according to his divinity, is the creator of all things, through whom all things were made; but the same man, born in time of the Virgin Mary, priest and Son of the Most High, is not two but one, by the hypostatic union. Now you have how we believe in Jesus Christ. See whether the Church is believed in this way, and separate the divine substance from the human, so that you may know how Christ is the creator of all things and how he is the head of the Church, and you will escape the errors of Nestorius and Eutyches, which are formally contrary to each other.

units.la: Inter transcurrendum non cessas mordere Gregorium, asserentem ecclesiam esse immortalem, quia Paulus ait solum Deum immortalem. Miror quod talem obliuionis morbum incidisti, vt non memineris te didicisse, dignitates esse perpetuas; Item & perpetuam Iurisdictionem: rursum perpetuas actiones, quorum tamen quadraginta annorum spatio meta Iure clauditur. Et Gregorius auctoritatem ecclesiae perpetuam esse dicens, id loquitur, cum de iuris distinctione ecclesiae contra te certat, vbi rite vtitur vsu loquendi Iuristarum. Tu etiam more Cancri sub domo Lunae fluitans, prius allegasti, te vnionem cum duce perpetuam habere quanquam mortalis sit natura vtriusque.
units.tr: In passing, you do not cease to bite at Gregory, who asserts that the Church is immortal because Paul says that God alone is immortal. I marvel that you have fallen into such a disease of forgetfulness that you do not recall having learned that dignities are perpetual, and likewise perpetual jurisdiction, and again that actions are perpetual, although by law their limit is closed after forty years. And Gregory, saying that the authority of the Church is perpetual, speaks in this way when he contends with you about the legal distinction of the Church, and there he uses correctly the language of the lawyers. You too, like the crab floating under the house of the Moon, first alleged that you have a perpetual union with the Duke, although the nature of both is mortal.

units.la: Allegas in Capella Papae cantari, credo in ecclesiam. Vix tibi creditur, adhibe testem Sancti Sixti vel Cameracensis, quorum alter diuinarum, alter sacrarum (licet humarum) literarum peritus habetur, si vero sic canitur, profecto tale symbolum per Cameram expeditum coniicio, non per Cancellariam, vbi perspectio diligenter, & praesumptiones Iuris circa stilum aut Grammaticam in eis non militant, & quae disponuntur minus sunt trahenda in sequelam. Superaddis obseruantiam ecclesiae Graecae. O praecautissime, qui velut exhaustis Latinorum riuulis, ad Graecorum sontem recurris, propter tua Graeca vocabula, quae didicisti, quando de Concilio Basiliensi ad conuentionem Ferrariensem proditorie commigrasti. Nunc meant proscenia ludi, apud Cardinalem Cusanum sunt Dionysia Bacchi, quem foecundi calices Graecae linguae fecere disertum. An ne putas Linguam Romanam deficere in expressione fidei, eorum articulorum, quorum explicita credulitas est de necessitate salutis? Iam tu patris & matris tuorum fidem condemnares, vt Gregorium vinceres, in foro crede mihi saltares.
units.tr: You allege that I believe in the Church is sung in the Pope's Chapel. Hardly anyone believes you; bring in a witness, either the man of St. Sixtus or the man of Cambrai, of whom the first is held to be learned in divine letters and the second in sacred (though human) letters. But if it is sung in that way, I certainly conjecture that such a creed was despatched through the Chamber, not through the Chancery, where careful examination and the presumptions of law concerning style or grammar do not apply, and where what is ordained is to be drawn into consequence less. You add the observance of the Greek Church. O most cautious man, who, as if the streamlets of the Latins were drained dry, you run back to the spring of the Greeks, on account of those Greek words you learned when you treacherously migrated from the Council of Basel to the agreement at Ferrara! Now the stage-props of the play are in Cardinal Cusanus's house; they are the Dionysia of Bacchus, whom the fruitful cups of the Greek tongue have made eloquent. Or do you think the Roman language is insufficient for expressing the faith, of those articles whose explicit belief is necessary for salvation? You would now condemn the faith of your father and mother in order to defeat Gregory; believe me, you are dancing in the forum.

units.la: Subnectis iure canonico suspectum haberi, eum qui per annum fuit excommunicatus, quod de fide male sentiat. Adhuc, quid dicis? Ita demum hoc est verum, si contumax sit in causa fidei. Quid si casus tibi figurabo, vbi canon docet, potius sustinendam excommunicationem, quam quis iudici pareatur contra verum?
units.tr: You add that by canon law a man who was excommunicated for a year is to be held suspect because he thinks wrongly about the faith. Again, what do you say? That holds true only if he is obstinate in a matter of faith. What if I describe to you a case where the canon teaches that excommunication is rather to be endured than that someone should obey a judge against the truth?

units.la: Rursum repetis, censuram Papae iustificatam, quasi constet de sacrilegio ducis, iam dudum respondi, fideifragia tua & proditiones tuae compressae sunt, per Ducem, pro quibus tu compare re & te expurgare dubitas, fugitiuus Iuris, & omnis iustitiae profugus, qui non audes aliquod non suspectum subire iudicium, quod tibi iam saepe & multifarie oblatum est.
units.tr: Again you repeat that the Pope's censure was justified, as if the Duke's sacrilege were established. I have already answered long ago: your breaches of faith and your treacheries have been checked by the Duke, and for these you hesitate to clear yourself in fact, a fugitive from law and a runaway from all justice, who dare not submit to any impartial trial, though it has been offered to you many times and in many ways.

units.la: Amplius delirando dicis, quod Papa non vocatum Ducem declarare potuit, sicut Paulus excommunicauit Corinthium. Dic vbi legisti, quod ille Corinthius petierit audientiam, & Apostolus illam sibi negauerit? Putas ne si Corinthius ille venisset ad Paulum dicens, Haec mulier non est vxor mea, sed honeste cohabitat mihi, Item nunquam fuit vxor patris mei, Item aemuli mei metibi accusarunt, inquire diligentius, An vas electionis dixisset, dabo tibi carcerem pro responso. Nequaquam.
units.tr: You go on raving that the Pope could declare the Duke without first summoning him, as Paul excommunicated the Corinthian. Tell me where you read that the Corinthian asked for a hearing and Paul refused it. Do you think that if that Corinthian had come to Paul and said, "This woman is not my wife, but lives honorably with me; also she was never my father's wife; also my rivals have accused me to you; inquire more carefully," the chosen vessel would have replied, "I will give you prison as your answer"? By no means.

units.la: Iterum repetis, Ducem a te veniam petiisse, crimenq; confessum, Dux negat, Laurentius inficiatur. Procede in Palaestram, experiendo iure, & iniurias ac contumelias atque conuicia tua missa face, Hoc est officium viri, non vt Leno certare maledictis, non vt sus cum quouis in coeno volutari.
units.tr: Again you repeat that the Duke sought pardon from you and confessed the crime. The Duke denies it, and Laurentius denies it. Come into the arena, pursue your right by law, and set aside your insults, abuse and slander. This is the duty of a man: not to fight with curses like a pimp, nor to wallow in the mud like a pig.

units.la: Postremo negas ecclesiam Brixinensem fore temporaliter de limitibus comitatus Tyrolis, quia castrum Tyrolis sit feudum Ecclesiae Curiensis. Comite Tyrolis nunquam fuisse principe Mereanie dicis, qui tamen vides Mereaniam sub castro sita & obedient ecomiti Tyrolis. Vt quid insanis? Qui si memineris, quod Reges (Rex Franciae iurare dicitur genicularus in manibus Abbatis S. Dionysii, a quo regnum recognoscit) & principes, regias suas & principalium residentiarum suarum terras loca à viris ecclesiasticis agnoscar in feudum, mirari desines, nisi forte magis studeas vt non ratione insanias. Quid enim facit solanutatio nominis ipsa rerum natura & proprietate semper eadem manente? Tantum enim longinqua mutare valet vetustas, vt quæ olim Rhetia superior dicebatur, de qua scribitur, videre Rheti bene suo altibus Drusum gerentem; atque iterum; Mox graue prælium committit immanesque Rethos, auspiciis epulit secundis, ea postea Meorania, hodieque Tyrolis sit vocata, vtramque vero Rethiam adhuc vocabulum tempore Theodorici Gothi, retinentem, Rex in præfecturam concedens, superiorem illam, Vallum Italiæ vocat, cui & superior Norica est ab Oriente ac realiter victa.
units.tr: Finally you deny that the church of Brixen lies temporally within the boundaries of the county of Tyrol, because the castle of Tyrol is a fief of the church of Chur. You say that Meran was never a principality under the count of Tyrol, though you see that Meran lies below the castle and obeys the count of Tyrol. Why are you so mad? If you remember that kings (the king of France is said to swear on his knees in the hands of the abbot of Saint-Denis, from whom he holds his kingdom) and princes hold their royal and princely residences and lands as fiefs from churchmen, you will stop wondering, unless perhaps you prefer to rave without reason. For what does a change of name do, when the nature and property of things remain always the same? Antiquity can change long-standing things so much that what was once called Upper Rhaetia, of which it is written, "to see the Rhaetians well... Drusus bearing...", and again, "Soon he begins a grave battle and the fierce Rhaetians, with favorable auspices...", was afterwards called Meran and today Tyrol. Theodoric the Goth, still keeping the name Rhaetia for both, granting the upper one as a prefecture, calls it the "Wall of Italy," and upper Noricum lies to its east and is in fact conquered.

units.la: Tandem fingis te Dominum secularem vallis Eni & minerarum eius. Hæc ambis & diu celatam ambitionem detegis & aperis. Exquo plane constat, quid tua iactantia voluerit, cum te iactasti, plurimas valles armis impleturum, & omnem pacis vel treugarum oblatam tibi conditionem respuisti, confisus in Grasacorum ferocia, qui comitatum Goritiæ iam pridem populabantur partimque subegerant, vbi deficiens ad Papam confugisti, questus vim afferri. Duce autem vias iuris offerente, vt sic per legitimos tramites calumniatis detegatur iniquitas, tu fugitiue Iuris & iustitiæ ad conuicia descendis, te ducem nominas, maiestatem Sigismundi ledere, quæris. Sunt etenim Principes Austriæ velut epimetati Principes ab Imperio Romano taliter honorati, vt qui in ipsos deliquerint, in Imperatorem Romanorum deliquisse videantur: quippe apud quos plenitudo potestatis in eorum tertis, quemadmodum in Romanorum Principe constat. Vide quorsum tendat superbia tua, qui te Dominum; Ducem vero seruitorem nuncupas tuum, qui tamen auctore Archiepiscopo Salzburgense Metropolitano tuo despondisti ducem te habiturum taliter, qualiter a prædecessoribus tuis episcopis Brixinensibus habitus esset, qui omnes, cum & progenitores suos tanquam Principes vniuersales etiam per districtum ac terras ecclesiæ Brixinensis recognouerunt, paucis exceptis, quæ in ducatu Stiriæ consistunt, vbi pari modo dux & rector vniuersaliter dominatur, tenetque principatum secularem. Nescis apud inferos sedere eos, qui arma sumere impia nec veriti dominorum fallere dextras, sicut tu duci ac Principi tuo fidem violasti. Contemplare quantum distat hæc tua elatio, fastidiosis factionibus geminorum, qui manibus rescindere cœlum aggressi, superisque Iouem detrudere, regnis, quæ est figura Luciferi dicentis: ponam sedem meam ad Aquilonem & similis ero altissimo; aut eius qui turrim Babylonicam instauravit. Nonne legisti:
units.tr: Finally you pretend to be the secular lord of the valley of the Eisack and its mines. Here you reveal and expose an ambition long hidden. From this it is plainly clear what your boasting meant when you bragged that you would fill many valleys with arms, and rejected every offered condition of peace or truce, trusting in the ferocity of the Grasacs, who had long been plundering the county of Gorizia and had partly subdued it. Failing there, you fled to the Pope to complain of violence. But the Duke offered the ways of law, so that the iniquity of the calumniators might be exposed by lawful paths; you, a fugitive from law and justice, descend to abuse, and seek to injure the majesty of Sigismund by calling yourself Duke. For the princes of Austria are like epimetati, princes so honored by the Roman Empire that whoever offends them seems to have offended the Roman Emperor, since full power lies in their hands, just as it does in the Prince of the Romans. See how far your pride goes: you call yourself Lord and the Duke your servant, though under the authority of the Archbishop of Salzburg, your metropolitan, you promised to treat the Duke as your predecessors the bishops of Brixen treated him. All of them acknowledged their ancestors as universal princes, even throughout the district and lands of the church of Brixen, except a few that lie in the duchy of Styria, where in the same way the duke and ruler rules universally and holds secular princely power. You do not know that those sit in hell who take up impious arms and, not fearing, deceive the right hands of their lords, as you have broken faith with your duke and prince. Consider how far your elation is from the disdainful factions of the twins who tried to tear down heaven with their hands and thrust Jupiter from the heavens; it is also a figure of Lucifer saying, "I will set my throne in the north and be like the Most High," or of him who built the Tower of Babel. Have you not read:

units.la: Crudeles dantem Salmonea pœnas, Dum flammas Iouis & sonitus imitatur Olympi.
units.tr: Cruel men paying the penalty, Salmoneus, who imitated the flames of Jove and the thunder of Olympus.

units.la: Demens, qui necdum irritabilem principem tibi subigere putas, sola procacitate linguæ fretus, dicens fortasse melius sub infideli tyranno quam sub hoc duce viui posse. Qui vrinam Sutrinus, Nepofinus, Narniensis, Balneoreginensis, Amelienfis, aut Ortanus præsul esses, tunc demum sentires, quid amisisses. Iam Promętheus te nil sentire permittit. Iam vestis ornatus & dignitas, qua obuolutus es, & præcipue rubedo verticis, qua operiris, teipsum non sinunt de te iudicare, aliquando mitior fuisti, sed postquam irrubuit cranium capitis, veluti gruis seuitia simul acreuit tibi cum grue, & propter licentiam peccandi, maxime & insanabiliter peccasti. Arduum quippe est, vt quis in maxima peccandi licentia constitutus, recte vitam transigat. Nudus, crede mihi, iudicaberis; tunc labes animæ tuæ diu contecta cernetur conspicue. Tunc te Gnosius Rhadamanthus velut Asiaticum, quia orientalem linguam trium vocabulorum nouitate vsurpasti; vel Latinum, si ad domicilii iudicem remitteris, Minoe in insidiis succenturiato stante, iudicabit; tuq; illis transmitteris, vbi debitas subire pœnas oportet.
units.tr: Madman, who think you have not yet brought the irritable prince under your control, relying only on the boldness of your tongue, saying perhaps that it is better to live under an unfaithful tyrant than under this duke. If you were bishop of Sutri, Nepi, Narni, Bagnoregio, Amelia or Orte, you would at last feel what you had lost. Now Prometheus does not let you feel anything. Now the finery and dignity in which you are wrapped, and above all the redness of the hat with which you are covered, do not allow you to judge yourself. You were milder once, but since the crown of your head has reddened, your savagery has grown along with the crane's, like the crane's ferocity, and because of your license to sin you have sinned most incurably. For it is hard for someone placed in the greatest license to sin to live rightly. You will be judged naked, believe me; then the stain of your soul, long covered, will be seen plainly. Then Gnosian Rhadamanthus will judge you as an Asiatic, because you have usurped an eastern language with the novelty of three words; or as a Latin, if you are sent back to the judge of your domicile, with Minos standing by in reserve in the ambush. And you will be sent to those places where you ought to undergo the punishments due.

units.la: Hæc tibi rependo, gratificans tibi pro meritis, dum admonendo Ducem dixisti; conuertere ne moriaris &c. Quid enim aliud egisti, quam ex lieno contemptu, superbissime tibi clypeum sanctitatis & innocentiæ simulando assumere? si inter illecebras & blandimenta fortunæ durum aliquid expertus es, te vero delectatio præceps & inconsulta destituit. Ad cor redi, memor conditionis tuæ, Sic prosperaberis, Domino propitiante. Datum in fœlicibus castris militaribus obsidionis Viennæ Austriæ apud Sanctum Marcum, quæ via ducit ad Vngariam, Idus Augusti, Anno M. CCCCLXI.
units.tr: I repay you these things, returning thanks for your deserts, since in admonishing the Duke you said, "Turn, lest you die," and so on. For what else have you done than, out of bitter contempt, most arrogantly assume for yourself the shield of holiness and innocence by pretending? If among the allurements and flatteries of fortune you have experienced something harsh, it is delight and rash, thoughtless impulse that have abandoned you. Return to your heart, mindful of your condition. So you will prosper, with the Lord favoring you. Given in the fortunate military camp at the siege of Vienna in Austria, at Saint Mark's, which is on the road leading to Hungary, on the Ides of August, in the year 1461.

units.la: NOTATIO PETRI NVMAGEN TREVERENSIS,
units.tr: NOTATIO PETRI NUMAGEN TREVERENSIS,

units.la: Ex cuius authographo haec desumpta sunt, exarato manu eius Anno M.CCCCC.
units.tr: From whose autograph these things are taken, written out by his own hand in the year 1500.

units.la: NOta dominum Nicolaum Cardinalem de Cusa fuisse filium cuiusdam pauperis piscatoris dicti Krebsheime, quia morabatur in villa dicta Cusa ad quatuor vel quinque miliaria subtus Treuerim in littore Mosellae, quasi ex opposito oppidi et castri dicti Berrenkastel sita, agri fertilis & tam vini, quam frumenti feracis, supra quam vix virus vel duorum stadiorum distantia alia villa in eodem littore sita est, dicta Lisura: unde oriundus fuit socius dicti Cardinalis, dictus Iohannes de Lisura, doctor Iuris, cuius fratrem ego vidi. Dei is duobus extat versus multum vulgatus: Cusa, Lisura, perverterunt singula iura.
units.tr: Note that Lord Nicholas, Cardinal of Cusa, was the son of a certain poor fisherman called Krebsheim, because he lived in a village called Cusa, four or five miles below Trier on the bank of the Moselle, lying almost opposite the town and castle called Berncastel, a place of fertile land productive both of wine and of grain. Above it, at a distance of scarcely one or two stadia, lies another village on the same bank called Lisura; from there came a companion of the said Cardinal, called John of Lisura, a doctor of law, whose brother I saw. There is a couplet about them, much repeated: "Cusa and Lisura have overturned every law."

units.la: Et quia praefatus Cardinalis Cancrum in albo scuto rubentem gessit, aliasq; ex parte cognomen traxit Cancri, hinc auctor inuectiuae praefatae eum vocauit Cancrum.
units.tr: And because the aforesaid Cardinal bore a red crab on a white shield, and in part took the surname of Crab (Cancer), for this reason the author of the aforesaid invective called him Cancer.

units.la: QVAM AESTIMATIONEM PAPA PIVS ANTE PAPATVM DE CARDINALE CVSANO, ET GREGORIO HEIMBVRGIO HABVE- RIT, sequentes indicabunt Epistolae.
units.tr: What esteem Pope Pius held for Cardinal Cusanus and Gregory Heimburg before he became pope, the following letters will show.

units.la: AEneas Cardinalis, Nicolao Cardinali Sancti Petri ad vincula S. P. D. Placuit Altissimo, & domino nostro Papae Calixto per hos dies me longe immeritum, ad Cardinalatus ordinem assumere, vestro sacro coetui aggregare, scio quantum ponderis subiui, nec video quo pacto, credite mihi, dignitati satisfaciam, nisi fortasse tua Reuerendissima Paternitas ad curiam rediret. Tunc enim instructus ab ea, securus in hoc procelloso mari, navigarem. Precor igitur, si preces seruitoris audiendae sunt, vt iam demum in patriam redeas. Nam Cardinali, sola Roma patria est, etiam si apud Indos is natus fuerit; aut recusasse pileum oportuit, aut certe receptum Romae gestare, & matri omnium sedi consulere. Neque illa excusatio idonea est; Non audior recta monens. Mutantur enim tempora, & qui olim contemptui fuit, nunc praecipue honoratur. Veni igitur obscuro veni. Neque enim tua virtus est, quae inter niues & umbrosas clausa valles languescere debeat. Scio complures esse, qui te videre, audire & sequi cupiunt, inter quos me semper auditorem discipulumque obsequentem inuenies. Ex urbe Romana, die vicesimo octauo Decembris M.CCCCLVII.
units.tr: Aeneas the Cardinal to Nicholas, Cardinal of St Peter ad Vincula, greetings. It has pleased the Most High and our lord Pope Calixtus, these past days, to raise me, far unworthy, to the order of cardinals and to admit me to your sacred company. I know how great a weight I have taken on, and I see no way, believe me, of satisfying the dignity, unless perhaps your Most Reverend Paternity returns to the Curia. For then, guided by you, I would sail safely over this stormy sea. I beg therefore, if the prayers of a servant are to be heard, that you return to your homeland at last. For to a cardinal, Rome alone is the homeland, even if he was born among the Indians; he ought either to have refused the hat or certainly, having received it, to wear it at Rome and look to the see of all. Nor is that excuse fitting: "I am not heard when I give sound advice." For times change, and he who was once held in contempt is now especially honoured. Come then, come out of obscurity. For your virtue is not something that ought to languish shut away among the snows and shaded valleys. I know that there are many who wish to see, hear and follow you, among whom you will always find me as an attentive listener and disciple. From the city of Rome, on the twenty-eighth day of December 1457.

units.la: AD GREGORIVM DE HEIMBVRG.
units.tr: TO GREGORY OF HEIMBURG.

units.la: AEneas Episcopus Tergestinus Iuris consultissimo viro, Domino Gregorio Heimburgensi S P. D. Cicero cum adhuc iuuenis apud Graecos mirificam orationem habuisset, admirabantur q aderant omnes, mirisque laudibus nouum oratorem efferebant. Sentxaute quidam amantissimus patriae inter omnem laetitiam atque tripudium, solus flebat, mirati circumstantes: Quid est, inquiunt, quod te laetantibus ceteris moerore confi.it? Tum ille, omnes, inquit, Graecorum artes in Latium migrarunt, unica nobis & familiaris & carissima remanserat eloquentia, sed hanc etiam Cicero nobis abstulit atq; secum ducit. Nunquid iusta est causa lacrymarum? Sic mihi hodie de te visum est, cum in Regia de studiis quae vocant humanitatis, dissertares. Nam & Legistam & Teuthonem superabas, & Italicam redolebas oratoriamque facundiam. Sed quod fuit moerori Graeco, mihi laetitiam praebuit. Neque enim si Teutonia literis claret, quae illas tradit Italia minus habet litterarum. Sunt scientiae sicut & lumina; Qui de suo lumine accendit, & sibi retinet lucem, & accipienti tenebras aufert. Inueni apud sanctum Gallum, quod Sueuorum est oppidum, in veteri monasterio Bibliothecam peruetustam, vbi & libros reperi ornatissime conscriptos, quorum authores fuerunt Teutones. Mirabur, cur hodie nihil eloquentiae his in regionibus eluceret, sed venit in mentem apud Italos quoq; tempus fuisse, quo sepulta dicendi facultate, barbarorum insitia dominabatur. Ante centum ferme annos & antea trecentis quadringentisque non inuenies, qui per Italiam sermonem habuerit, tersum & lucidum. Sic pingendi sculpendique accidit arti, si ducentorum trecentorumque annorum aut sculpturas intueberis aut picturas, inuenies non hominum sed monstrorum portentorumque facies. Priscis vero seculis Apellem atque Zeusim, Pollicretum, Phidiam & Praxitelem, magnos fuisse comperimus. Et de statuariis quidem ipsi videmus. Et Virgilio fidem habemus dum ait: Credo equidem reliquos facient de marmore vultus,
units.tr: Aeneas, Bishop of Trieste, to the most learned jurist, Lord Gregory Heimburg, greetings. When Cicero as a young man had delivered a wonderful speech among the Greeks, all who were present marvelled and praised the new orator with remarkable acclaim. Then a certain man who loved his country most dearly, amid all the joy and rejoicing, alone wept; the bystanders, astonished, asked: "Why is it that you are overcome with grief while all the others rejoice?" Then he replied: "All the arts of the Greeks have migrated into Latium; only one, our own and most familiar and dearest eloquence, had remained to us, but now Cicero too takes it from us and carries it off with him. Is there not a just cause for tears?" So it seemed to me today about you, when you were discoursing at court on what they call the studies of humanity. For you surpassed both the lawyer and the German, and you smelled of Italian and oratorical fluency. But what was grief to the Greek has given me joy. For if Germany shines with learning, Italy, which handed it on, does not therefore have less learning. Knowledge is like light: he who kindles his lamp from his own light keeps the light for himself and takes no darkness from the one who receives it. I found at St Gall, a town of the Swabians, in an old monastery, a very ancient library, where I also found books most elegantly written, whose authors were Germans. I wondered why nothing of eloquence shone today in these regions, but it came to mind that among the Italians too there was a time when, the art of speaking buried, the ineptitude of barbarians held sway. About a hundred years ago, and before that, in the three or four hundred years earlier, you will not find anyone who spoke polished and clear language throughout Italy. So it happened to the arts of painting and sculpture: if you look at the sculptures or paintings of two or three hundred years, you will find not the faces of men but of monsters and prodigies. In earlier ages, however, we learn that Apelles and Zeuxis, Polycletus, Phidias and Praxiteles were great. Of the sculptors we ourselves indeed see the works. And we trust Virgil when he says: "I believe that others will make the likenesses from marble..."

units.la: De pictoribus vero testimonia sunt clarissimorum virorum, qui profecto minime tantis eos præconiis extulissent, si picturam non aspexissent sculpturæ vel similem vel illa pulcriorem, sed eccè iam reuixerunt sculpendi pingendiq; disciplinæ. Reuixit etiam eloquentia, & nostro quidem seculo apud Italos maxime floret. Spero idem in Teutonia futurum, si tu tuique similes continuare & ampletàti totis conatibus oratoriam detreueritis. Accepi apud Nürnbergam plebanum sancti Sebaldi, virum grauem tua permotum suasione, multis lucubrationibus historiam atq; Rhetoricam persequi. Diligo ego vos ambos, qui patriam moribus ornantes, etiam literis munire studetis. Cæterum quia de Nilo fuit hodie nobis sermo, non video quo pacto ex paradisi monte progredi possit. Paradisum namque terrestrem quam deliciarum vocant, in oriente positam volunt, atque ex Euphrate fluere, quem scriptura Tigrim appellat, quamuis & Tigris alius in Armeniæ regione caput tollat, qui Solino teste Euphraten fluuium in Persicum defert sinum. Nilus verò à monte inferioris Mauritaniæ, qui Oceano propinquat, originem habet. Sic affirmare feruntur Punici libri & Iubæ Regis scripta, si Solino credimus, & hic nunc latens, nunc apparens, diuersis argumentis deprehenditur esse, qui irrigat Ægyptum, & terminus est Africæ atq; Asiæ: Licet Lucano huius origo fluminis incognita videatur dum ait:
units.tr: Concerning the painters, there is the testimony of most distinguished men, who certainly would not have praised them with such accolades had they not looked upon paintings either similar to sculpture or more beautiful than it. But behold, now the disciplines of sculpture and painting have revived. Eloquence too has revived, and in our own age it flourishes especially among the Italians. I hope the same will happen in Germany, if you and men like you continue and strive with all your efforts to extend oratory. I have heard at Nuremberg that the parish priest of St Sebald, a serious man moved by your persuasion, pursues history and rhetoric with much study. I love you both, who adorn your country with your character and also strive to fortify it with letters. But since today our talk was about the Nile, I do not see how it can come forth from the mountain of paradise. For they hold that the earthly paradise, which they call of delights, is placed in the east and that it flows from the Euphrates, which Scripture calls the Tigris, although another Tigris rises in the region of Armenia, which, according to Solinus, carries the river Euphrates into the Persian gulf. The Nile, however, has its source in a mountain of Lower Mauretania, which approaches the Ocean. So the Punic books and the writings of King Juba are said to affirm, if we believe Solinus, and this river, now hidden, now appearing, is shown by various arguments to be the one that irrigates Egypt and is the boundary between Africa and Asia; although the origin of this river seems unknown to Lucan when he says:

units.la: Egens si quia latet nascenti conscia Nilo.
units.tr: "Needy, if there is anyone whose source is hidden from the Nile at its birth..."

units.la: Vale & quod verbis fieri debuisset, scriptis accipe. Ex nova ciuitate, pridie Calend. Februariarum.
units.tr: Farewell. What ought to have been done in words, accept in writing. From the new city, the day before the Kalends of February.

units.la: ÆNEAS SYLVIUS EPISCO- PUS SENENSIS, POSTEA PIUS PAPA SCRIBIT PETRO NOXETANO, QUOMODO GRADATIM auctus sit, & altiora conscenderit.
units.tr: Aeneas Silvius, Bishop of Siena, afterwards Pope Pius, writes to Peter of Noxeto about how he was gradually promoted and rose to higher positions.

units.la: ANNOS sex & viginti natus cum darem iuri ciuili operam, exorto bello patriam & studium coactus sum relinquere; accessi tamen grande illud Basiliense Concilium, inueniqueque gratiam in oculis patrum. Scriba in Synodo fui, & literarum abbreuiator, & vnus de duodecim viris, qui magistratus illic quasi censorius habebatur. Neque enim sine duodecim viris, ad consulendum de rebus conciliaribus quisquam admittebatur; & admissi, qui non inuenirentur idonei, his iubentibus amouebantur. Erant in Concilio quatuor conuentus, qui disputationes appellabantur, de fide, de pace, de reformatorio, de communibus præsidentes, hæ suos singulæ, singulis mensibus elegerunt. In deputatione fidei, in qua eram inscriptus, sæpe præsedi; inter collatores quoq; beneficiorum, bis sum electus. Legatus ab ipso Concilio ad complures principes missus. Cum pontificatum Amedeus Dux Sabaudiæ suscepisset Felix nuncupatus, in secretarium sum ab eo accitus. Nec diu post vocatus ad Fridericum Imperatorem, Prothonotariatus officium ab eo sum adeptus; sic Germani Secretariatum appellant. Dum legationes Cæsaris ago, vniuersam ferme Germaniam circuiui. Dissidebant Teutones cum Eugenio Maximo Pontifice. At neque illi, neque Felici obedientes, neutrales vocabantur. Concordia pluribus in conuentibus agitata est, quibus iubente Cæsare semper interfui. Bis cum tractatu pacis ad Eugenium veni, tertio nationis illius Apostolicæ sedi obedientiam attuli, Secretariatus & subdiaconatus honorem ab Eugenio, & mox illo defuncto à Nicolao suscepi, cuius conclaui, cum eligeretur, cum cæteris principum legationibus custodiæ præfui. Lapsum est postea breue tempus, in quo me Nicolaus Tergestinæ Ecclesiæ nihil tale merentem præfecit Episcopum, quadriennioque abinde decurso Senensis vrbis, vnde mihi origo est, pontificatum ad me detulit. Cæsar vero, à quo in consiliariorum ordinem susceptus essem, Neapolim me petere iussit. Quo in loco matrimonium inter ipsum Cæsarem, & Leonoram Portugaliæ regis sororem, Alphonsique neptem contrati, eandemque Imperatricem, anno post nauigio vectam è Pisis ad Imperatorem Senis agentem conduxi, cum id mihi vni committeretur. In coronatione Cæsaris, quæ Romæ celebrata est, nostri quoq; meæ partes fuerint, quippe qui me sæpius Imperatorio nomine apud Romanorum Pontificem & publicè & priuatim loquentem audiuisti. Reuerso in Germaniam legatio mihi Apostolicæ sedis per Bohemiam & omnes prouincias Austriæ Ducum commissa est. In conuentu Germanorum, qui Ratisbonæ habitus est, quo & Philippus Burgundiæ & Ludouicus Bauariæ Duces, & alii quamplures Principes & Reguli conuenerunt, de salute Christianæ rei publicæ agentes, Imperatorias vices tenui. Simili modo & in Franckfordensi Concilio, vbi & Germanos aduersus Turcos decernere bellum, dicta oratione suasimus, quamuis postea negligentia & inscitia eorum, qui cuncta sibi licere putant, Germani tepuerunt. Mortuo Nicolao Calixtum successorem eius Imperatorio nomine tanquam verum Christi vicarium cognouimus. In hisce nos honoribus, ribus. Petre versati sumus, nec tamen intelligimus cur adeo diuina pietas nostram paruitatem extulerit. Non doctrina, non vitae bonitas hoc meruit. Cognoscimus imperfectum nostrum, & nos ipsos saepe cogitantes non extollimur quidem, sed magis erubescimus & confundimur, qui pro tantis beneficiis non iumus grati: Respicimus aliquando retro, & quam multi viri nobilibus orti natalibus, virtute & doctrina praestabiles, abiecti & incogniti iacent, consideramus. Fateor quā plurimi sunt, qui opibus & honoribus antecedunt; sed multo plures sequuntur. Pluribus commiserari quam inuidere possum. Et illi quidem, qui me dignitate praecedunt, etiam virtute superant. Ergo his qui sequuntur nulla ratione sum melior. O quot viri sunt, qui non centum aureos annuos ex beneficiis ecclesiasticis haurire possunt, iuris diuini atq; humani interpretes, quorum non est mdignus corrigiam calciamenti soluere. Atque ego ignarus, hebes atq; vitiorum mole pressus, atque iniquitate circumdatus, qui aliquo beneficiolo contentus extitissem, vel minimo, iam annuos mille aureos possideo, quoque magis mirere, dum Germaniam petii, episcopatum in patria consequor. Magna haec, mi Petre, in quibus non mea solum paruitas, sed magna virtus, quiescere posset. Apud tres episcopos & totidem Cardinales dictandarum epistolarum officium exercui. Hi tres quoque pontifices maximi, secretariorum collegio me adscripserunt, Eugenius Nicolaus & Felix: quamuis hunc adulterum dixerint. Apud Caesarem non secretariatus modo, sed consiliariatus & principatus honore auctus sum. Neque ego ista fortunae imputo, quamuis nescio causam, sed ipsius rectori & dominatori omnium Deo, cuius est in quemcunque voluerit vsum vasa formare. Neque humanae corruptioni subiiciuntur quae libera sunt eiusque libertati gratias agere decet, qui dat omnibus abundanter & non improperat. An nos igitur tanta miseratione praeuenti Cardinalatum auxii expectabimus, atque hunc quoque nobis honorem deberi putabimus? Vtinam dignitati, quam consequuti sumus, pares inueniamur, & ita quod superest aeui traducamus, ne qua possit in nobis ingratitudo notari. Porro Cardinalatus fastigium maius existimamus, quam q; nostris humeris committi debeat. Vtinam ea dignatio his credatur, qui afferre illi potius, quam ab ea recipere gloriam possint. Quales nos esse nullo pacto cognoscimus, & infra. Vale ex Neapoli 9. Maii, Anno Domini M. CCCCLVI.
units.tr: At twenty-six years of age, while I was studying civil law, the war broke out and forced me to leave my homeland and my studies. Nevertheless, I went to the great Council of Basel and found favour in the eyes of the Fathers. I was a secretary at the Synod and an abbreviator of letters, and I was one of the twelve men who were regarded there as a kind of censorial magistracy. For no one was admitted to advise on conciliar business without the twelve men, and any who were admitted but were not found suitable were removed at their command. There were four committees in the Council, called deliberations: on faith, on peace, on reform, and on common matters. Each of them elected its own presidents, one for each month. I often presided over the deputation on faith, to which I had been enrolled. I was also twice elected among the collators of benefices. I was sent by the Council itself as an envoy to several princes. When Duke Amadeus of Savoy, called Felix, had assumed the papacy, he summoned me into his secretariat. Soon afterwards I was called to Emperor Frederick, and from him I obtained the office of prothonotary; the Germans call this the secretariat. While I carried out the emperor's embassies, I travelled through almost the whole of Germany. The Teutons were at odds with Pope Eugenius the Great. Yet those who were obedient neither to him nor to Felix were called neutrals. Concord was discussed in several assemblies, which I always attended at the emperor's command. Twice I came to Eugenius with proposals for peace; the third time I brought that nation's obedience to the Apostolic See. From Eugenius I received the honour of secretary and subdeacon, and soon after his death I received it from Nicholas. When a new pope was to be elected, I was put in charge of guarding the conclave together with the other princes' envoys. After that a short time passed, in which Nicholas, though I had deserved nothing of the kind, made me Bishop of the Church of Trieste. When four years had passed, the city of Siena, where I was born, offered me its bishopric. But the emperor, by whom I had been received into the order of counsellors, ordered me to go to Naples. There I arranged the marriage between the emperor himself and Leonora, sister of the king of Portugal and granddaughter of Alfonso. A year later, when this task was entrusted to me alone, I brought the empress across from Pisa by ship, and I escorted her to the emperor, who was staying at Siena. At the coronation of the emperor, celebrated at Rome, I also had my share, since you have often heard me speaking, both publicly and privately, on behalf of the emperor before the Roman Pontiff. On my return to Germany, I was entrusted with an embassy of the Apostolic See through Bohemia and all the provinces of the dukes of Austria. At the assembly of the Germans held at Regensburg, which Philip, Duke of Burgundy, Louis, Duke of Bavaria, and many other princes and petty kings attended, discussing the welfare of the Christian commonwealth, I held the imperial role. In the same way, at the Council of Frankfurt, where I urged in a speech that the Germans decree war against the Turks, the Germans nevertheless grew lukewarm afterwards, through the negligence and ignorance of those who think everything is allowed them. When Nicholas died, we recognised Callixtus as his successor, in the imperial name, as the true vicar of Christ. We have been engaged in these honours, Peter, and yet we do not understand why divine goodness has raised up our littleness so high. Neither learning nor goodness of life has earned this. We recognise our imperfection, and when I think about myself I am not indeed puffed up, but rather I blush and am confounded, because I have not been thankful enough for such great benefits. Sometimes I look back and consider how many men, noble by birth, outstanding in virtue and learning, lie cast aside and unknown. I admit that very many go before me in wealth and honours, but far more follow. I can pity many more than I can envy. Those who surpass me in rank also surpass me in virtue. So I am in no way better than those who come after me. Oh, how many men there are who cannot draw a hundred gold coins a year from ecclesiastical benefices, interpreters of divine and human law, who are not worthy to untie the strap of their shoe! And I, ignorant, dull, weighed down by the mass of my vices and surrounded by wickedness, who would have been content with some small benefice, even the least, now possess a thousand gold coins a year. And what is more astonishing, while I sought Germany, I obtain a bishopric in my homeland. These are great things, my Peter, in which not only my littleness but great virtue might rest. I have held the office of drafting letters before three bishops and as many cardinals. These three popes, the greatest of pontiffs, Eugenius, Nicholas and Felix, enrolled me in the college of secretaries, though they called the last an adulterer. With the emperor I have been honoured not only with the secretariat but with the office and dignity of counsellor and prince. I do not ascribe these things to fortune, though I do not know the cause, but to God himself, the ruler and master of all, whose right it is to shape vessels for whatever use he wills. Those things that are free are not subject to human corruption, and it is fitting to give thanks for that liberty to him who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach. Shall we then, forestalled by such great mercy, wait for the cardinalate as a help, and think this honour too is owed to us? Would that we may be found equal to the dignity we have obtained, and so spend what remains of our life that no ingratitude can be charged against us. Furthermore, we think the summit of the cardinalate is too great to be committed to our shoulders. Would that this honour might be given to those who can bring glory to it rather than receive glory from it. We know that we are by no means such men, and below. Farewell, from Naples, 9 May, in the year of the Lord 1456.

units.la: Postea factus est a Calixto III. sanctae Romanae Ecclesiae, Item sanctae Sabinae Presbyter Cardinalis, vti scribit Friderico Imperatori, vicesimo die Decembris, Anno Domini M. CCCCLVII.
units.tr: Afterwards he was made by Callixtus III. Presbyter Cardinal of the holy Roman Church, and also of Saint Sabina, as he writes to Emperor Frederick, on the twentieth day of December, in the year of the Lord 1457.

units.la: ÆNEAS SYLVIUS IN GE- STIS CONCILII BASILIENSIS DE NICO- LAO CVSANO HÆC SCRIBIT.
units.tr: Aeneas Sylvius in the Acts of the Council of Basel writes these things concerning Nicholas of Cusa.

units.la: HErcle tamen omnium Eugenianorum Nicolaus Cusanus æstimatus est, homo & priscarum literarum eruditissimus, & multarum rerum vsu perdoctus, cuius dolendum sit, tam nobile ingenium ad illa schismatis studia diuertisse, vt Legatione ad Graecos vigore falsi decreti fungeretur. Hic omne studium, omnemq; conatum in defensione Eugenii collocauerat, atque vt est versuti & callidi consilii; nunc vna, nunc alia impedimenta texebat.
units.tr: Indeed, Nicholas of Cusa was esteemed by Hercules above all the Eugenians, a man most learned in ancient literature and thoroughly versed in the experience of many matters.
