It is to be regretted that so noble a talent was turned to those studies of schism, so that he served as legate to the Greeks by virtue of a false decree. He had devoted all his zeal and every effort to the defence of Eugenius, and, being of a shrewd and crafty counsel, he now wove one obstacle, now another.

units.la: Hafdenus Codex manu Petri Numagen Treuerens. scriptus Anno 1500.
units.tr: The Hafdenus codex, written by the hand of Petrus Numagen of Trier, in the year 1500.

units.la: IOANNIS FRANCISCI PICI MIRANDVLÆ NEPOTIS, APOLOGIA PRO HIERONYMI SAVONAROLÆ VIRI PROPHETÆ Innocentia: In duas diuisa libros: Ad illustrem virum HERCVLEM ÆSTENSEM: TABVLA CAPITVLORVM PRÆSENTIS APOLOGIÆ IN DVOS LIBROS PARTITÆ. LIBER PRIMVS.
units.tr: JOHANNES FRANCISCUS PICUS MIRANDULANUS, NEPHEW, APOLOGY FOR THE INNOCENCE OF HIERONYMUS SAVONAROLA, PROPHET, DIVIDED INTO TWO BOOKS: ADDRESSED TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS MAN HERCULES OF ESTE: TABLE OF THE CHAPTERS OF THE PRESENT APOLOGY, DIVIDED INTO TWO BOOKS. BOOK ONE.

units.la: PROOEMIVM ad Illustrem virum, HERCVLEM ÆSTENSEM
units.tr: PREFACE, addressed to the illustrious man, HERCULES OF ESTE

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAP. I.

units.la: Vllum esse in terris iudicium, quod errare quandoque non possit.
units.tr: That there is no judgment on earth which can never at some time go wrong.

units.la: CAP. II. Multis modis contingere, vt excommunicationis sententia, ab Ecclesiæ Prælatis inflicta, irrita & inefficax reddatur.
units.tr: CHAP. II. That in many ways it happens that a sentence of excommunication, inflicted by the prelates of the Church, is made void and ineffective.

units.la: CAP. III. Aliquos esse ex supra memoratis casibus, quibus summorum etiam pontificum sententiæ irritæ fiunt. Inter quos est error intolerabilis: quid autem sit, & quo modo debeat intelligi, declaratur.
units.tr: CHAP. III. That there are some of the above-mentioned cases in which even the sentences of the highest pontiffs are made void. Among these is intolerable error; what it is, and how it ought to be understood, is explained.

units.la: CAP. IV. Quid deinceps agendum: item quid proprie sit excommunicatio: & de causis, ob quas infligenda est.
units.tr: CHAP. IV. What must be done next; likewise what excommunication properly is, and concerning the causes for which it is to be inflicted.

units.la: CAP. V. De obedientia subditorum erga prælatos.
units.tr: CHAP. V. Concerning the obedience of subjects towards their prelates.

units.la: CAP. VI. Notum istud dictum, Sententia pastoris, siue iusta, siue iniusta, timenda, perperam vulgo vsurpari.
units.tr: CHAP. VI. That the well-known saying, the sentence of a minister is to be feared, whether just or unjust, is commonly and wrongly used.

units.la: CAP. VII. Quomodo illud debeat intelligi.
units.tr: CHAP. VII. How that saying ought to be understood.

units.la: LIBER SECVNDVS.
units.tr: BOOK TWO.

units.la: CAP. I. Quid superiori libro actum, quid deinceps agendum. CAP. II. Causa, ob quam plerique Hieronymum Sauonarolam excommunicatum autumant. CAP. III. Ex ipsa causa, elici argumenta defensionis: & primo, quod male cognita res fuit pontifici, vtpote subdole ab iniquis suggesta. CAP. IV. Quod mandatum pontificis fuit impossibile. CAP. V. Quod mandatum pontificis exequendum non erat. CAP. VI. Quod iure rescripsit pontifici: item liquere, Sauonarolam nunquam censuram incurrisse. CAP. VII. Nec ei necessariam absolutionem, neq; ab eius communione abstinendum fuisse. CAP. VIII. Nonnulla in defensi Prophetæ laudem: Causæ quamobrem doctrinæ Christianæ assentiamur; atque insuper modus resistendi futuris persequutionibus proponitur.
units.tr: CHAP. I. What was done in the previous book, and what must be done next. CHAP. II. The cause on account of which most people think Hieronymus Savonarola was excommunicated. CHAP. III. From this very cause, arguments for his defence are drawn: and first, that the matter was poorly understood by the pontiff, as it had been craftily suggested to him by wicked men. CHAP. IV. That the pontiff's command was impossible. CHAP. V. That the pontiff's command ought not to have been obeyed. CHAP. VI. That he rightly replied to the pontiff; likewise that it is clear Savonarola never incurred the censure. CHAP. VII. That he had no need of absolution, nor should he have abstained from communion with him. CHAP. VIII. Some remarks in praise of the defended prophet: the reasons why we assent to the Christian doctrine; and moreover a manner of resisting future persecutions is proposed.

units.la: LIBER PRIMVS.
units.tr: LIBER PRIMVS.

units.la: PROOEMIVM.
units.tr: PROOEMIVM.

units.la: PVSCVLVM, de iniusta excommunicationis sententia in Hieronymi Prophetæ nostri defensionem, vt tibi Hercules Æstensis datam fidem velati ex diario relatam, iam aggredior. Effl agitasti enim, dum hac de re simul verba faceremus, vt qua coram, pro tutanda illius innocentia aduersus calumniatores attuleram, literis aliquanto
units.tr: I now undertake the little treatise on the unjust sentence of excommunication, in defence of our prophet Jerome, which I promised to you, Hercules of Este, and which I have set down from memory in the form of a diary. For you pressed me, when we were discussing this matter together, to write more fully what I had put forward before you in defence of his innocence against his calumniators.

units.la: {y} ... quanto laxius exararem. Promisi, quod nunc exoluo me facturum, & quidem tam libenter, quam videbam me unica opera, & tibi, nec non Prophetae nostro, ac veritati ipsi, debitam rem facturum: Ille, ne commentitium & subdole fictum crimen, tot praclarissima eius gesta, ad tempus aliquod obnubilaret, lucidissima quoque veritati tenebras fortasse allaturum: Tibi ne falsa haec impostura, atque praesagio, forsitan movereris. Sed & alia causa se his immiscebat, quando ansula hac duntaxat, solaque garriendi occasio relicta videbatur malevolis, bene secum actum putantibus, si fautoribus divini viri obiectare possent, defendi ab eis hominem, qui esset ab ecclesiae corpore, ceu marcidum & noxium membrum, anathematis acie resectum. Namque rationes ea, quae prophetiis iam publicatas, doctrinamque fulcirent, ab ipsomet allata magna ex parte, maledicorum rabiem compescuerant. In eandem quoque sententiam, tum Dominicus Beniuenius, tum alii plerique scripserant, modo verum astruentes, modo falso resistentes: quod etiam a nobis, & sparsim per lucubratiunculas nostras, & dicatis etiam apologeticis facilitatum est. Quare post huius calumnia dilutionem, nihil putabam residui, quod blateraret, etsi dementibus delirandi materia nunquam deest.
units.tr: ...more fully than I wrote it. I promised that I would now make good on this, and I will do so as willingly as I see that I am doing a thing owed both to you, to our prophet, and to truth itself. I do it so that this invented and craftily fabricated charge does not for a time cloud so many of his most distinguished deeds, and so that it does not perhaps bring darkness upon truth, which is itself most clear; and so that you yourself are not perhaps moved by this false imposture and forebodings. But there was another reason too: the malicious, who thought they had done well, seemed to have left only this small handle and single occasion for chatter, namely that they could reproach the supporters of the godly man that he had been defended by them, a man cut off by the blade of anathema from the body of the Church as a rotten and harmful limb. For the arguments that supported his prophecies and his doctrine, already published, had for the most part been brought forward by himself, and had restrained the rage of the slanderers. Both Dominicus Beniuenius and many others had written to the same effect, sometimes asserting the truth, sometimes resisting falsehood; and this too has been made easier by us, both scattered through our little pamphlets and in our dedicatory apologies. Therefore, after the refutation of this calumny, I thought nothing was left for them to babble about, although there is never any lack of material for madmen to rave about.

units.la: Duos igitur libros instituí. Primo generalia quaedam explicabuntur, quorum ope tam multifarie quam facile muniti, secundo deinde simus declaraturi, eum neque culpa, neque crimini confinem. Et sane, potuissem hoc efficere, cum adeo multa ab iis qui de huiusce modi negotiis tractauere, praesertim iuris pontificii interpretibus, effusa sint, tantaque diuersitate & contentione, ut nec legi quidem ab ociosissimis possint, nedum narrari ab occupatissimis. Delibavi quae mihi maturiora sunt visa, eorum more in commentando posthabito, & a crebris illis allegationibus, quae taedium & moram lectori plerunque adferunt, consulto abstinui: ratus commodius & optabilius tibi satisfactum iri, si quae ipsi subobscure, & peculiaribus quibusdam notis, idem sapius repetentes innuēs, & facile & Latine, aut saltem minus barbare, quoad fieri hac in re a me potuerit, recensere.
units.tr: I have therefore planned two books. In the first, certain general matters will be explained, by means of which we shall be armed in many ways and easily; in the second, we shall then show that he is free from both fault and crime. And indeed I could have done this, since so much has been poured out by those who have treated such affairs, especially the interpreters of papal law, and with such diversity and contention that it can hardly be read even by the most idle, much less told by the busiest. I have touched only on those points that seemed to me more mature, setting aside their manner of commentary, and I have deliberately refrained from those frequent citations which usually bring weariness and delay to the reader. I judged that it would be more convenient and more welcome to you if I set out, easily and in Latin, or at least as little barbarously as I could manage in this matter, the things that are obscure in themselves, indicating them by certain peculiar marks and repeating them often.

units.la: Eam autem praefari veniam, non tibi qui nos apprime novisti, sed apud ignotos (si nostra haec forte lecturi sunt) conuenit, nihil me unquam voluisse asserturn, nec in posterum velle, quod Ecclesia Catholica dogmatis dissonaret: cum cuius vi recte definientis decreto, semper acquiescerum me (ut Christianum hominem decet) libere profiteat, nedum sanctionibus Ecclesiae, & eius legitimorum Praesidum assentiri.
units.tr: Moreover, it is fitting to offer this apology, not to you who know us very well, but to strangers (if perhaps they read these things of ours): that I have never wished to assert anything, nor do I wish in future, that dissents from the doctrine of the Catholic Church. For I profess that I always submit freely, as a Christian man ought, to the decree of that Church's authority when it rightly defines, and still more that I assent to the sanctions of the Church and of its lawful presidents.

units.la: Rationibus igitur rem agemus, nitentes diuinis eloquiis, ac Pontificis, Imperatoriis legibus, nec non eorum interpretes, atque in primis Theologos, in testimonium citantes.
units.tr: We shall therefore treat the matter by means of reasons, relying on the divine oracles, and citing as witnesses the decrees of the Pontiffs, the imperial laws, and their interpreters, and especially the theologians.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Nullum esse in terris iudicium, quod errare quandoque non possit.
units.tr: That there is no judgment on earth which can not at some time err.

units.la: ILLVD autem commonuisse in primis expediet, solum Deum, qui a se ipso est, omninoque independens, ab omni errore, & falsitate, prorsus immunem: ab eoque utpote primaria veritate, & suprema regula quarumlibet functionum, vniuersam substantiam interdum flectere & labi, nisi eius ope fulta, & directa fuerit. Hominis namque naturam ab adolescentia pronam ad malum, cum sacrae literae docent, cum frequens testatur experientia. Sed & inter separatas mentes, quas vocamus Angelos, error olim, peccatumque; irrepsit, & ad infernas mundi partes, eorum non paruam manum praecipitem iecit. Et quanquam praeter virginem Christi matrem, quae nullum vnquam peccatum fecit, mortalium nonnulli, a peccatis eis, quae aeterno igne puniuntur, diuino beneficio exempti fuerint, non adeo tamen confirmati erant, quin quoquomodo posse a vero excidere censerentur. Sed perpaucorum etiamnum hoc priuilegium. Illi namque innumeri qui la a via gradientes, triplici offendiculo cespitant; tametsi beneficentissimi Dei assidua gratiae influxu resipiscere comoneatur.
units.tr: It will be helpful first to remind the reader that God alone, who is from himself and wholly independent, is utterly free from all error and falsehood; and that the whole of created substance, from which he is the primary truth and supreme rule of every function, may at times bend and fall unless it is supported and directed by his help. For the sacred letters teach that the nature of man is inclined to evil from youth, as frequent experience also bears witness. Moreover, among the separated minds that we call angels, error and sin once crept in, and cast a not small band of them headlong into the lower parts of the world. And although, apart from the Virgin, the mother of Christ, who never committed any sin, some mortals have by divine favour been exempted from those sins which are punished with eternal fire, they were not so confirmed as to be beyond the possibility of falling away from the truth in some way. But this privilege belongs to very few even now. For countless others, walking off the way, stumble at a threefold obstacle, although by the constant inflow of the most bountiful grace of God they are called back to repentance.

units.la: Verum, cum ecclesiam, vti sponsam, sibi Christus copulauerit, ob continuas daemonum insidias, & aperta bella, quibus, dum militat in terris assidue quatitur, decidit vt ei iudicium relinqueret, quo aut decipere aut decipi no posset, in eis maxime decernendis, quae & fidei substantiam concernerent, & ad mores pertinerent, Christianis ad beatitudinem adipiscendam necessarios. Eam namque sibi in fide & iustitia aeternum desponsandam, Osee Prophetae vaticinio cap. 2. sanxit. Merito igitur statuerunt theologi, & legum Iurisque periti, ipsam vniuersalem Ecclesiam, cum de huiusce modi causis agitur, nonnisi aequam sententiam ferre posse, Christo opem ferente; qui & ipsius fide orauit, & cum ad consummationem vsque seculi se permansurum sponsondit: quod irritum foret, nisi ad iudicium condonasset, quo repudiata falsitate, veritas eligeretur: Matthaei vltimo.
units.tr: Yet since Christ has joined the Church to himself as his bride, and since she, while she wars on earth, is constantly shaken by the continual snares of demons and open battles, he has left her a judgment by which she can neither deceive nor be deceived, especially in deciding those matters which concern the substance of the faith and pertain to the morals necessary for Christians to attain blessedness. For he pledged her to himself forever in faith and righteousness, as the prophecy of the prophet Hosea, chapter 2, declares. Therefore theologians and experts in law have rightly held that the universal Church herself, when such matters are under discussion, can give only a fair sentence, Christ bringing help; who also prayed for her faith and promised that he would remain with her until the consummation of the age. This promise would be empty unless he had granted her a judgment by which, falsehood being rejected, truth might be chosen: Matthew, last chapter.

units.la: At animaduersione dignum, loquutos nos duntaxat de fidei substantia & moribus ad salutem consequendas necessariis. Atqui id non ab re aut de nihilo dictum. Siquidem ea in reliquis errare aliquando, sententia doctorum est, atque ipsiusmet Ecclesiae consensus, vt ex epistola Innoc. III. eius nominis Pontificis manifeste indicatur, quae postea a Gregorio IX. inter decretales relata est, libro vid. V. vbi de sententia excommunicationis agitur. Ita namque scriptum legimus: Iudicium Dei, veritati quae nosfallit, neque fallitur, semper innititur: Iudicium a. Ecclesia nonnunquam opinione sequitur, quae & fallere saepe contingit & falli. Quod l. quido costare videmus, dum vi excommunicationis interdum quaepiam cum aliqua seminatori inire coforcia iubet, qui nihilominus vero apud Deum ma-trimotrimonio alteri erit adstrictus; vtpote, cum secunda nuptiali lege palam coniunctus, cum prima etiam, omnibus, qui semotis arbitris; propterea quae Ecclesia sanctionibus compelletur haerere secunda, de cuius commercio testibus idoneis apparebit. Mitto, quae multi Doctorum super huiusmodi iudiciis elucubraverint, ne superflue nimis & ambitiose factum a nobis iudices, in re admodum nota, verba prodigere.
units.tr: But it is worth noting that we have spoken only of the substance of the faith and of the morals necessary for attaining salvation. Yet this was not said without reason or for no purpose. For it is the opinion of the teachers, and the very consensus of the Church, that she may sometimes err in other matters, as is clearly indicated by the letter of Innocent III, pope of that name, which was afterwards included by Gregory IX among the decretals, in book 5, title 39, where the sentence of excommunication is treated. For we read these words there: The judgment of God always rests on truth, which neither deceives nor is deceived; the judgment of the Church often follows opinion, which it happens both to deceive and to be deceived. We see this clearly when, by force of excommunication, she sometimes orders someone to enter into a marriage with a certain woman, though he is in truth bound before God to another; for example, when he is openly joined to a second wife by a nuptial contract, while the first, with all witnesses set aside, is in secret still his wife; so that the Church, by her sanctions, is compelled to keep the second in place, whose intercourse will appear by suitable witnesses. I pass over what many of the teachers have elaborated concerning judgments of this kind, lest we, judging too much and ambitiously, pour out words superfluously on a matter that is very well known.

units.la: Porro ex his consequens fiet, reliqua & Conciliorum & Pontificis iudicia, errori ignorantiaeque subiecta: quando nec vniuersalis Ecclesia, a decipulis eiusmodi exempta est. Hinc plerique tum Theologorum, tum iuris interpretum asseverantissime voluerunt, Pontificem Concilium quoque in dirimendis controversiis hallucinari posse pro vero falsum pronunciantes: praeterea rationes afferunt exempla, quandoquidem & Ariminense & Ephesinum secundum, & Aquisgranense, aliaque non nulla aberraverunt: & summorum Pontificum alius Arrianae pravitati subscripsit, alius Idolis sacra fecit, alius aliter devia sectatus est. Quanquam sunt qui velint tam Pontifices summos, quam Concilia legitime congregata, vero semper niti, in iis diiudicandis, in quibus vniversalem Ecclesiam falli posse negauimus. Sed haec a suscepta disputatione sequestrabimus, tum quia propositae quaestionis limites praetergrederentur, tum quia & ab aliis multifariam, & a nobis etiam nonnihil in theorematis nostris, de necessitate & ordine credendi, sunt pertractata.
units.tr: Furthermore, from these things it will follow that the remaining judgments both of Councils and of the Pope are subject to error and ignorance, since not even the universal Church has been exempted from such deceptions. Hence many theologians and interpreters of law have most emphatically maintained that the Pope, and likewise a Council in settling controversies, can wander from the truth and pronounce what is false. They also bring forward reasons and examples: the Council of Rimini, the second Council of Ephesus, and that of Aachen, as well as some others, have gone astray; and one of the supreme Pontiffs subscribed to the Arian heresy, another offered sacrifice to idols, and another followed a different and erring path. Yet there are some who wish that both the supreme Pontiffs and lawfully assembled Councils always rest on truth in those matters in which we have denied that the universal Church can be deceived. But we will set these questions aside from the disputation we have undertaken, both because they would go beyond the limits of the question proposed, and because they have been treated in many ways by others, and by us too in some measure in our theses on the necessity and order of believing.

units.la: Hoc nobis sit satis, indubium apud literatos haberi, nullum esse in terris iudicium, quod errare, labi, decipi, non possit: Vt magna ex parte allusisse veritati Thebanum Cebetem cogitemus, fingentem a muliere illa, cui nomen Apaten, id est fraudem esse voluit, mortales omnes seductos atque errore & ignorantia potatos.
units.tr: Let it be enough for us that it is held beyond doubt among learned men that there is no judgment on earth which cannot err, slip, or be deceived. Thus we may think that the Theban Cebes, in large part, aimed at the truth when he feigned that the woman called Apate, that is, Deceit, had led all mortals astray and given them to drink of error and ignorance.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAP. II.

units.la: Multis modis contingere, vt excommunicationis sententia, ab Ecclesiae praelatis i- nflicta, irrita & inefficax reddatur.
units.tr: That the sentence of excommunication, inflicted by the prelates of the Church, may in many ways be made void and ineffective.

units.la: EX his facile colligi datur, eos qui ecclesiae praesunt, in absoluendis puniendisque subditis multisariam posse delinquere. Fit enim plerumque, quod a Gregorio Homilia 26. prolatum est, & a Gratiano in decretis 11. q. 3. can. plerunque repetitum, vt hic iudicu locum teneat, cuius ad locum vita minime concordat: ac proinde saepe agitur, vt vel damnet immeritos, vel alios ipse ligatus soluat; & saepe in soluendis ac ligandis subditis, sua voluntatis motus, non autem causarum merita sequatur, atque ob id ligandi soluendique potestate se priuet, mortificando animas quae non moriuntur, & viuificando quae non viuunt; qb ab Ezechiele cap. 13. legimus exprobratum: propterea Pontificio iure decretum inuenimus, multis modis contingere, poenas quae a Praelatis infliguntur inanes esse, ipsamque excommunicationis sententiam, qua nulla in ecclesia maior, irritam & inefficacem reddi. Namq; in Decretorum volumine causa 24. quaest. 1. can. audiuimus, Alexandrum eius nominis II. Pontificem, Valeriano Episcopo & martyri scripsisse legimus, ab eo qui aut haereticus aut excommunicatus fuerit, excommunicationis sententiam nequicquam in alium irrogari. Et lib. 1. Epistolarum decretalium, titulo de consuetudine, extat Innocentii Pontificis eius nominis IV. sanctio, qua edicitur, sententiam quae a iudice non suo lata fuerit, nullam obtinere firmitatem. Decreuit quoque Gregorius eius nominis IX. Archiepiscopo Bracharensi scribens, irritas esse & inanes eas excommunicationis sententias, quae a iudice violatore interdicti proruperant, vt est videre libro eius operis 5. titulo de praelatorum excessibus cap. tanta est. Vbi etiamnum Clemens III. decernit, eas non tenere sententias, quae promulgatae fuerint in subditos, ob denegatam praelatis exactionem cum Ecclesias visitant, si iuuerint personarum in Lateranensi Concilio constitutum excesserint. Eodem libro, & titulo de priuilegiis, cap. Cum ad quorundam, Innocentius III. Episcopum Lingonensem monet, excommunicationis sententiam in aliquem contra sui priuilegii tenorem nequaquam promulgandam. Ibidem tap. cum capella, Honorius III. seueritate debita eos, & episcopos castigandos pronunciat, qui eiusmodi sententias in fraudem priuilegiorum ferunt. Caeterum Gregorius IX. quem diduum citauimus, definit cap. quanto amplius, vacuam & inanem excommunicationem, quam effulminauerit is, quem constet in exequendo officio, limites eius, qp in mandatis a superiore habuerat, praetergressum; quemadmodum appare: libro 3. decretalium, titulo de praebendis & dignitatibus, cap. vltimo. Libro item 6. eiusdem operis Bonifacius VIII. eius nominis pontifex, edixit poenas eas in vanum iactari, quae ferebantur a praelatis in subditos, insinuantes inquisitoribus, vel Apostolicae sedis legatis, statum ecclesiarum, monasteriorumue, quae corrigi per eos & reformari porteret. Ex epistola quoque Innocentii III. ad Archiepiscopum Senonensem, quae 5. decretalium sita est, titulo de sententia excommunicationis, colligitur sententiam eam, quae vel post legitimam appellationem infligitur, vel intolerabilem errorem continet, viribus cassam esse. Cui Innocentius IV. in Concilio Lugdunensi adstipulatus est, quod licet videre libro 6. vbi de sententia excommunicationis pariter agitur, cap. 2. & 7. Eodem in Concilio statutum fuit, excommunicationis sententiam, in collegium non irrogandam, atque illam nihil habere virium, quam iudex tulerit in participantes cum excommunicatis, loquutione, & aliis, quibus minor excommunicatio incurritur, nisi eos prius canonice monuerit, vt liquido apparet 3. & 5. cap. eiusdem tituli. Sed & Nicolaus Abbas Panormitanus, qui plurimum in visu inter Pontificii iuris interpretes, libro Decretalium 1. titulo de censibus, cap. 6. & etiam alibi, docet excommunicationem nullam esse, cum ob causam notorie iniustam fuerit irrogata. Possem & alia commemorare, quibus huiusmodi censurae fiunt ineffica-ces.Ea ces. Ea tamen consulto praetereo, cum ne morosior quis esse videar, tum quia celebres Iuris Pontificii interpretes, eas recensent, & in promptu sunt eorum libros legentibus.
units.tr: From these things it can easily be gathered that those who preside over the Church may err in many ways when they absolve or punish their subjects. For it commonly happens, as Gregory has stated in Homily 26 and Gratian has often repeated in Decretum 11, q. 3, can. plerunque, that one who holds the place of judge does not live in harmony with his position, and so it often happens that he either condemns the undeserving or, himself bound, absolves others; and often in absolving and binding his subjects he follows the impulse of his own will rather than the merits of the causes, and by this deprives himself of the power of binding and loosing, killing souls that do not die and making alive those that do not live; which we read was rebuked by Ezekiel in chapter 13. Therefore we find it decreed in Papal law that in many ways the penalties inflicted by prelates are empty, and that the very sentence of excommunication, than which none is greater in the Church, is rendered void and ineffective. For in the Decretum, causa 24, q. 1, can. audiuimus, we read that Alexander II, bishop of that name, wrote to Valerian, bishop and martyr, that the sentence of excommunication is in vain pronounced against another by one who is either a heretic or excommunicated. And in book 1 of the Decretal Epistles, title on custom, there is a sanction of Pope Innocent IV, by which it is ordered that a sentence pronounced by a judge who is not his own has no force. Gregory IX, too, writing to the Archbishop of Braga, decreed that those sentences of excommunication are void and empty which have been issued by a judge who violates an interdict; as may be seen in book 5 of that work, under the title on the excesses of prelates, chapter "tanta est." There Clement III also decrees that those sentences do not hold which have been pronounced against subjects, because of the refusal of the payment demanded by prelates when they visit churches, if they have exceeded the limits of persons laid down in the Lateran Council. In the same book, and under the title on privileges, chapter "Cum ad quorundam," Innocent III warns the Bishop of Langres that a sentence of excommunication must by no means be pronounced against anyone contrary to the tenor of his privilege. In the same place, in chapter "cum capella", Honorius III pronounces that those who issue such sentences to the defrauding of privileges, and bishops too, are to be punished with due severity. Moreover, Gregory IX, whom we cited a little while ago, determines in chapter "quanto amplius" that an excommunication which has been hurled by one who, it is clear, has in carrying out his office overstepped the limits set on him by his superior in his commission, is empty and void; as appears in book 3 of the Decretals, title on prebends and dignities, last chapter. Likewise, in book 6 of the same work, Boniface VIII, pope of that name, ordered that those penalties are cast in vain which prelates have launched against subjects who have reported to inquisitors or to legates of the Apostolic See the condition of churches or monasteries that ought to be corrected and reformed by them. From the letter of Innocent III to the Archbishop of Sens, which stands in the fifth book of the Decretals, under the title on the sentence of excommunication, it is gathered that a sentence which is inflicted either after a lawful appeal, or which contains an intolerable error, is broken in its force. Innocent IV agreed with this in the Council of Lyons, as may be seen in book 6, where the sentence of excommunication is likewise treated, chapters 2 and 7. In the same Council it was ordained that a sentence of excommunication is not to be inflicted on a college, and that the sentence which a judge has pronounced against those who take part with the excommunicated, in speech and other things by which the lesser excommunication is incurred, has no force unless he has first canonically warned them; as is clear from chapters 3 and 5 of the same title. But also Nicolaus, the Abbot of Panormus, who is held in the highest esteem among the interpreters of Papal law, in book 1 of the Decretals, title on the censuses, chapter 6, and also elsewhere, teaches that an excommunication is null when it has been inflicted for a cause that is notoriously unjust. I could mention other things by which censures of this kind are made ineffective. I pass these over deliberately, partly lest I seem too tedious, and partly because the celebrated interpreters of Papal law recount them, and their books are at hand for those who read them.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Aliquos esse ex supra memoratis casibus, quibus summorum etiam Pontificum sententia irrita fiunt, inter quos est error intolerabilis. Et qui fit, & quomodo debeat intelligi, declaratur.
units.tr: That some of the aforementioned cases are those in which even the sentences of the supreme Pontiffs are rendered void, among which is intolerable error; and what it is and how it ought to be understood is explained.

units.la: Cum igitur omnis excommunicatio, quae in eiusmodi casibus inflicta fuerit, langueat prorsus, & vires amittas: (iudicandum enim de futuris omnibus, per ea quae iam definita sunt, ut est Gregorii eius nominis IX. Pontificis edictum, ab universali ecclesia receptum, in ipsa Decretalium Epistolarum publicatione) bene actum nobiscum fuerit, si aliquem invenerimus, quo Hieronymum Savonarolam a falsa suspitione, & calumnia vindicemus. Et quanquam hi, quos memoravimus, modi, summorum pontificum sententias non omnes retundant, aliqui tamen sunt, quibus ipsae omnino infringuntur. Et ut alios omittamus, ille qui error intolerabilis nuncupatur, nobis desumendus erit. Sed primo, quid sibi velit, quoque modo intelligendus, pro virili explicabimus. Innocentius III. ut constat 6. Decretalium, titulo de sententia excommunicationis, cap. 7. errorem intolerabilem definit in sententia patenter expressum, cum aliquid sub vi praecepti vel mandati aperte in ea continetur, quod communiter, vel in genere suo peccatum est. Consentiunt in hoc interpretes, tam hunc locum pertractantes, quam eiusdem Pontificis ad Archiepiscopum Senonensem Epistolam, quam paulo ante memoravimus. Additur ab aliquibus, quotiens quid contra ius scriptum pronunciatur, pari erroris nomine debere censeri: item dum aliquid aut turpe aut impossibile praecipitur: namque eorum quae fieri nequeunt, nullam esse obligationem tam canonicae leges, in 6. lib. Decretalium, titulo de regulis iuris, & civiles eodem titulo Digestorum volumine adstruunt: cuius operis lib. 41. titulo quod sententia sine appellatione rescindantur leg. vltima, ex Pauli Iurisconsulti auctoritate pariter decretum est, Impossibile praeceptum iudicis, nullius esse momenti. Qui etiamnum rescripsit, ab ea sententia cui pareri per rerum naturam non poterat, sine causa appellari. Sed tam remotas auctoritates consectari non est necesse, cum nobis Dei maximi & optimi clementia consertum inditumque sit, nec in peccata declinandum; nec quenquam illi efficiendo adstringi posse, quod supra suas est vires collocatum; nec turpe ullo pacto operandum: a quo tam abhorret natura, ut Aristoteles eius interpres in Ethicis censuerit optabilius esse, hac vita excedere, quam turpe quicquam operari. Ut omittam quid sacrae literae praeceperint.
units.tr: Since, therefore, every excommunication inflicted in cases of this kind is wholly enfeebled and loses its force (for all future cases must be judged by what has already been decided, as is the decree of Pope Gregory IX of that name, received by the universal Church at the publication of the Decretal Epistles themselves), we shall have done well for ourselves if we find something by which we may clear Hieronymus Savonarola of the false suspicion and calumny. And although these kinds of cases, which we have mentioned, do not all overthrow the sentences of the supreme pontiffs, there are some by which those sentences are utterly broken. And, to pass over the others, that which is called intolerable error must be taken up by us. But first we shall explain, as well as we can, what it means and how it is to be understood. Innocent III, as is well known in the sixth book of the Decretals, under the title on the sentence of excommunication, chapter 7, defines intolerable error as an error openly expressed in a sentence, when something is clearly contained in it under the force of a precept or command, which is in general, or in its own kind, a sin. The commentators agree on this, both those who treat this passage and those who treat the letter of the same Pontiff to the Archbishop of Sens, which we mentioned a little while ago. Some add that whenever something is pronounced contrary to written law, it ought to be counted under the same name of error; likewise when something either shameful or impossible is commanded: for the canon laws, in the sixth book of the Decretals under the title on the rules of law, and the civil laws under the same title in the volume of the Digest, maintain that there is no obligation to do things that cannot be done. In book 41 of that work, under the title that sentences are annulled without appeal, law last, it is likewise decreed on the authority of the jurist Paulus that a command of a judge that is impossible is of no force whatever. He also rescribed that an appeal from a sentence which, by the nature of things, could not be obeyed, is made without cause. But it is not necessary to pursue such remote authorities, since by the mercy of God, the greatest and best, we have been joined and implanted with the knowledge that we must not turn aside into sin, that no one can be bound to do what is placed beyond his powers, and that nothing shameful is to be done in any way; from which nature shrinks so much that Aristotle, his interpreter, in the Ethics judged it more desirable to depart from this life than to do anything shameful. Not to mention what the holy Scriptures have commanded.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Quid deinceps agendum: item quid proprie sit excommunicatio, & de causis ob quas infligenda est.
units.tr: What must be dealt with next: also what excommunication properly is, and the causes for which it must be inflicted.

units.la: Enimvero, priusquam ipsam defensionem aggrediamur, quod secundo libro agendum nobis est, fecisse operaepretium videbimur, si de causis ob quas ferenda est excommunicationis sententia, paucula delibemus. Et cum multifariam exorbitare praelatos monuerimus, ne inde occasio pravis nominibus contemnendi eorum praecepta daretur, de obedientia quoque nonnulla proloqui opportunum fuerit. Deinde, cum satis constet vulgatum illud dictum; Sententia pastoris sive iusta, sive iniusta fuerit, timenda est, perperam vulgo vsurpari solere, quomodo intelligi debeat, declarare pro viribus caitemur.
units.tr: Indeed, before we take up the defence itself, which we must treat in the second book, we shall think it worthwhile to set out briefly the causes for which the sentence of excommunication is to be pronounced. And since we have warned that prelates often go astray, lest an occasion be given for despising their precepts on wicked pretexts, it will be fitting to say something also about obedience. Then, since it is well established that the common saying, "The sentence of a pastor, whether just or unjust, is to be feared," is commonly and wrongly used, we shall endeavour to explain, as far as we can, how it ought to be understood.

units.la: Primum igitur, primitus exequamur. Theologorum iurisque interpretum omnium, cum veterum, tum novorum sententia est, neminem temere leuibusque de causis, anathematis mucrone feriendum: siquidem nullam atrociorem poenam ipsa excommunicatione maiori (de qua nobis in toto opere sermo, & quae proprie hac nomenclatura censetur) in Ecclesia reperiri contingit; est enim separatio ab ecclesiae communione, quo ad fructum & generalia suffragia, seu a qualibet licita communione fidelium segregatio. Quare in Agatensi concilio statutum legimus, Episcopos non debere eos qui minimis causis culpabiles essent excommunicare. Sanctum profecto decretum, & sacris literis mirifice consonans, quoniam in eis reperiri non datur, quemquam, nisi pro enormi scelere, anathemate damnatum, atque id etiam raro. Frequentior postea visus in Ecclesia, quem moleste admodum fert & damnat Ioannes Scotus Theologus insignis distinct. 19. & 25. lib. 4. sententiarum, ibi fatuam ad ferendas sententias pronitatem carpens, & maximum numerum earum, quae a iure infliguntur excommunicationum detestans. In Concilio quoque Aluernensi determinatum est, a nullo sacerdote, quemque; recte fidei hominem, pro paruis & leuibus causis, debere ab aliorum communione suspendi, praeter eas culpas, pro quibus antiqui patres arceri ab ecclesia delinquentes iusserunt: 11. q. 3. can. nemo, & can. nullus. Verum, quas ob causas id fieri solitum esset, Concilii Meldensis canone colligitur, quo promulgatum est, ab Episcoporum nemine, sine certa & manifesta peccati causa, quemq; a communione Ecclesiastica priuandum, neque sub anathemate, absque conscientia Archiepiscopi aut coepiscoporum, vllum esse ponendum, nisi canonica doceret autoritas: Cum anathema, aeternae lit mortis damnatio, neq; debeat infligi, nisi p mortali crimine atq; illis praesertim quae aliter corrigi non potuerit. Propterea credinderim a plerisq; doctoribus. in 4. Theologicarum sententiarum libri, dist. 18. & Thoma in primis Aquinate, diuini ingenii viro; binas has causas excommunicandi hóminis assignatas peccatum dignum aeterna morte, & contumaciam. Cum enim qui Ecclesiae praeest, per excommunicationis gladiū, subditos quodámodo à coelesti regno praescindat; in eos duntaxat id perpetrandū, qui indigni sunt superna patria, qua omnes qui charitatis erunt compotes donabuntur; priuabunturque, qui peccato mortali infecti fuerint. Quare quos labefactatos eo crimine constiterit, ii eiusmodi poena poterunt multari. At qui nihil atrocius ab Ecclesia erumpere potest, poenaque comparatione medicinarum propinari aegrotis debere Aristoteles 2. Ethicorum libro edisserit, quas si prudens fuerit medicus, nec violentas nec graues nisi cum necessitas postulat, exhibiturus est: Iccirco in eum etiam qui crimine morte digno obuoluntus erit, nisi idem fuerit contumax; minime adigenda, Assentit Scotus 25. distinct. mox citata, inquiens, neque à iure neque à iudice debere infligi pro quocunque peccato mortali, sed graui cui adnexa sit contumacia. Namque quamdiu paratus quispiam est audire Ecclesiam, publicanus & Ethnicus non est habendus: quandoquidem ex Christi dogmate, poena eiusmodi seruanda est extremè contumacibus.
units.tr: First, then, let us deal with the first point. It is the opinion of all theologians and jurists, both ancient and recent, that no one should be struck with the sword of anathema rashly or for slight causes. For no harsher punishment is found in the Church than excommunication in the greater sense (which is the subject of our whole work, and which is properly called by this name). It is separation from the communion of the Church, as regards its benefits and common suffrages, or the exclusion of a believer from any lawful fellowship. So we read in the Council of Agde that it was decreed that bishops should not excommunicate those who were guilty of very minor faults. That is indeed a holy decree, and wonderfully in harmony with the Holy Scriptures, since in them no one is found condemned to anathema except for an enormous crime, and even then rarely. Later it appeared more frequently in the Church, and this is what the distinguished theologian John Scotus takes very much amiss and condemns (dist. 19 and 25, book 4 of the Sentences), censuring there the foolish readiness to pronounce sentences and detesting the great number of excommunications that are imposed by law. Also in the Council of Clermont it was determined that no priest whatsoever, however orthodox, should suspend anyone from the fellowship of others for small and slight causes, apart from those faults for which the ancient Fathers ordered offenders to be shut out of the Church (11 q. 3, can. nemo, and can. nullus). But for what causes this was customarily done is gathered from the canon of the Council of Meaux, by which it was proclaimed that no bishop should deprive anyone of ecclesiastical communion without a certain and manifest cause of sin, nor place anyone under anathema without the knowledge of the archbishop or fellow bishops, unless canonical authority should teach otherwise, since anathema, the damnation of eternal death, ought not to be inflicted except for a mortal crime, and especially for those which could not be corrected in any other way. For this reason I believe that many teachers (in the 4th book of the Theological Sentences, dist. 18), and above all Thomas Aquinas, a man of divine genius, have assigned these two causes for excommunicating a man: sin worthy of eternal death, and contumacy. For since he who presides over the Church, by the sword of excommunication, in a sense cuts off his subjects from the heavenly kingdom, this ought to be done only to those who are unworthy of the heavenly fatherland, into which all who are possessed of charity will be received, and from which those who are infected with mortal sin will be excluded. Therefore those whom it is clear have been brought low by that crime may be punished with this penalty. But that nothing more severe can break out from the Church, and that punishment ought to be administered to the sick in the manner of medicines, Aristotle explains in the second book of the Ethics. A prudent physician will administer medicines that are neither violent nor severe, except when necessity requires it. Hence even against one who is entangled in a crime deserving death, the sentence should in no way be imposed, unless he is also contumacious. Scotus agrees in the 25th distinction just cited, saying that it should be imposed neither by law nor by a judge for any mortal sin whatsoever, but only for a grave sin to which contumacy is joined. For as long as anyone is ready to hear the Church, he is not to be regarded as a publican and a heathen, since by the doctrine of Christ such punishment is to be kept only for the utterly contumacious.

units.la: Qui autem contumaciae nota censeantur; tam in decretis, pluribus ex locis; quàm in Decretalibus licet deprehendere. Extat interalia Concilii Triburensis (11. quaest. 3. can. certum est.) sanctio, quae tria contumaciae genera ob quae dubio procul infligi excommunicatio poterat, recensèt: Cum videlicet, quis ad synodum canonicè vocatus, vel venire contemnit, vel si postquam illuc venerit, sacerdotalibus respuit obedire praeceptis, vel si ante finitam causam suae excommunicationem à synodo abire praesumit. Trifariam autem quispiam existimatur contumax, ad synodum iudiciumve non accedens; vt est videre 2. libro Decretalium, vbi scribitur testes lite non contestata merito admittendos, si is in quem fuit actio dirigenda, aut peremtoria citatione recepta, venire contemnit; aut seipsum malitiosè occultauit, aut impendiuit ne posset ad eum citatio peruenire. Et libro quint. eiusdem voluminis, titul. de verborum significat. cap. 23. eum contumacem iudicandum apparet, qui iussus emendare maleficium noluit.
units.tr: Which faults are regarded as contumacy may be discovered in the decrees, in many places, as well as in the Decretals. Among others there is the enactment of the Council of Tribur (11 q. 3, can. certum est), which lists three kinds of contumacy for which excommunication could undoubtedly be inflicted: namely, when someone who has been canonically summoned to a synod either refuses to come, or, having come there, refuses to obey the priestly commands, or presumes to leave the synod before the case is finished, while under excommunication from it. Moreover, someone is judged contumacious in three ways when he does not appear before a synod or court, as may be seen in the second book of the Decretals, where it is written that witnesses may rightly be admitted before the joining of issue if the person against whom the action is to be brought either refuses to come, having received a peremptory citation, or has maliciously hidden himself, or has contrived that the citation could not reach him. And in the fifth book of the same volume, title on the meaning of words, chapter 23, it appears that he is to be judged contumacious who, when ordered to make amends for a wrong, refused to do so.

units.la: CAP. V. De obedientia subditorum erga Praelatos.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. On the obedience of subjects towards prelates.

units.la: CÆTERVM, ne omnis inobedientia contumacia iudicaretur, (quoniam qui praecipienti iniuste non paret, tantum abest vt poenam mereatur, & dedecus, vt etiam gloria & praemio sit prouehendus) de obedientia subditorum erga praelatos, consequenti ordine quaepiam tractabimus. Cum ii qui aliis praesunt, quantum ad hoc attinet vice Dei fungantur in terris, omnis siquidem potestas est à Deo, Roman. 13. praeceptis eorum audire conuenit: propterea Princeps Apostolorum 2. cap. primae Epistolae inquit: Subiecti estote omni humanae creaturae propter Deum, siue Regi quasi praecellenti, siue ducibus tanquam ab eo missis. Et magister gentium Titu cap. 3. ad Titum, praecipiebat, vt quos instruendos suscepérat, admoneret principibus & potestatibus, quanquam Ethnicis, subditos esse. Neque enim, vt Thomas docet, fides Christi iustitia ordinem aufert, qua exigitur vt superioribus suis inferiores obediant: alioqui rerum humanarum status corrueret. Verum scire oportet, quatenus haec obedientia extendenda. Namque omnibus parere imperiis, nec necessarium nec consentaneum rationi. Fieri enim posset, vt vel delira, vel nocua, vel diuinae legi aduersa praeciperentur, vt rectissime scripsisse Gregorium deprehendamus, admonentem subditos, plus quam expedit non adstringi superiorum mandatis, 2. q. 7. can. admonendi: ne cum studerent plus quam necesse est hominibus subiici, compellerentur eorum vitia venerari: ni forte qui alios regunt, supra humanam naturam collocatos existimemus, variisque affectionum motibus non impelli. At dum ira inflammantur, efferuntur gaudio, diffluunt libidine, & quod est exitialius Circcis, vt sic loquar, poculis deformantur in bruta, aliosque etiam sibi similes euadere, & ratione posthabita obbrutescere procurant; ob id à viris sanctissimis, quibus Ecclesiae instruendae cura olim incubuit, edocta est posteritas, cauendum sibi ab iniquis imperiis; eorumque quibus subsunt metiendam auctoritatem, & si illud iuberis quod facere non debeas, contemnendam esse potestatem: quod Augustinus inter alios asseuerauit. Scripsit quoque Hieronymus, Pauli Epistolam ad Ephesios enarrans, subiiciendum esse domino seruum, si ea quae aduersa non essent sanctis scripturis praeciperentur: i vero mandarentur contraria, magis spiritus Domino, quam corporis obediendum. Rursus, ipsos humanarum legum gradus aduertendos Augustinus 11. q. 3. can. non semper, censet, à quibus, si diuersa manauerint iussa, maiori seruiendum: illudque semper ante oculos habendum, ne aut minis aut illecebris, hominum iussa, Dei mandatis praeponamus: quod Christianos illos milites, qui sub Iuliano Imperatore nequissimo stipendia merebant, obseruasse, tam ipse quam Ambrosius scribunt, ibidem, can. Julianus. Possent mille huiuscemodi sententiae adferri, quas breuitatis gratia dimittan, cum lumen diuini vultus super nos signatum, binas has Apostoli sententias vero veriores esse demonstret: & omnem animam potestatibus sublimioribus subditam esse, &, Deo magis quam hominibus obedire oportere: Roman. 13. & Actor. 4. & 5.
units.tr: Now, lest every disobedience be judged contumacy (since one who does not obey a command that is unjust is so far from deserving punishment and disgrace that he is even to be advanced to glory and reward), we shall treat in due order of the obedience of subjects towards prelates. Those who preside over others stand, so far as this concerns them, in the place of God on earth: for there is no power but of God, Romans 13. It is therefore fitting to hear their commands. For this reason the Prince of the Apostles, in the second chapter of his first Epistle, says: Submit yourselves to every human creature for the Lord's sake, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him. And the teacher of the Gentiles, Titus chapter 3, to Titus, ordered that those whom he had undertaken to instruct should be reminded to be subject to rulers and authorities, even though they were heathen. For, as Thomas teaches, the faith of Christ does not remove the order of justice, by which it is required that inferiors obey their superiors; otherwise the state of human affairs would collapse. But one must know how far this obedience extends. For to obey all commands is neither necessary nor consistent with reason. It may happen that things foolish, harmful, or contrary to the divine law are commanded, as we find Gregory rightly wrote, warning subjects that they should not be bound by the commands of superiors more than is fitting, 2. q. 7. can. admonendi: lest, while they strive to be subject to men more than is necessary, they be compelled to revere their vices: unless perhaps we think that those who rule others are placed above human nature and are not driven by various movements of the passions. But while they are inflamed with anger, puffed up with joy, dissolved in lust, and, what is more destructive than Circe's cups (so to speak), are transformed into beasts, they also bring it about that others become like them and, reason being set aside, grow brutish. For this reason the posterity was taught by the most holy men, to whom the care of instructing the Church once belonged, that they must beware of unjust commands, that the authority of those to whom they are subject must be measured, and that if they are ordered to do what they ought not to do, the power is to be disregarded; which Augustine among others affirmed. Jerome also wrote, expounding Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians, that a servant must submit to his master if commands are given that are not contrary to the holy Scriptures; but if contrary things are commanded, one must obey the Lord in spirit rather than in body. Again, Augustine holds that the degrees of human laws must be attended to, from which, if different commands flow, the greater must be served; and that it must always be kept before the eyes that we do not set human commands above God's commandments, either through threats or enticements. Both he and Ambrose write that the Christian soldiers who served under the most wicked Emperor Julian observed this, ibidem, can. Julianus. A thousand sayings of this kind could be cited, which for brevity's sake I omit, since the light of the divine countenance signed upon us shows that these two sayings of the Apostle are more true: that every soul is subject to the higher powers, and that we ought to obey God rather than men: Romans 13, and Acts 4 and 5.

units.la: Illud autem minime praetereundum, quod Thomas Aquinas, & doctrina & iudicio, & vitae perfectione mirabilis, multis in locis lucubrationum suarum, praesertim postrema parte secun-
units.tr: But it must by no means be passed over that Thomas Aquinas, admirable in learning, judgement, and perfection of life, taught in many places of his writings, especially in the last part of the

units.la: {y} Ex ... (marginal references in the left margin of lines 5–60 are cited in the text above and are not separately recoverable here.) secundi voluminis Theologicæ summæ, docuit, quemquam scilicet ad obediendum superiori non obligari, nisi in quibus ei subditur: propterea nec quo ad interiorem voluntatis motum, quod & Seneca voluit, nec quo ad naturam corporis, hominem homini subiici: sed in his duntaxat, quæ ad actuum rerumque humanarum dispositionem pertinent: atque in hoc etiam secundum rationem superioritatis: sicut miles duci exercitus, in his quæ spectant ad bellum: servus Domino, quo ad servilia opera exequenda: filius patri in his quæ concernunt vitæ disciplinam curamque domesticæ rei: ab eis qui in seculo degunt, spiritualibus prælatis obtemperandum, in his virtutum operibus, quæ necessario à Christianis omnibus patrari debent: illos vero qui religionum votis mancipati sunt, ipsis obnexios reddi, quantum ad illa quæ possunt ad regularem conuersationem pertinere, secundum quam subiectos se profitentur. Trifariam quoque eorum obedientiam partitus est, vt sit quæ ad salutem consequendam sufficiat; qualisea, qua necessariis, vt supra diximus, operam nauant: secunda, quæ cumulum perfectionis attingat, cuius vt omni mandato, quod liceat, obsequantur: tertia, quæ indiscreta, ob quam sine delectu passim quecunque iussa capessant, in his etiam, quæ aut diuinæ legi, aut regulæ, quam sunt professi refragantur, obedientes.
units.tr: {y} ... of the second volume of the Theological Summa, that a person is bound to obey a superior only in those matters in which he is subject to him. Hence man is not subject to man either as to the inner motion of the will, which Seneca also maintained, or as to the nature of the body, but only in those things which pertain to the ordering of acts and human affairs; and in this too according to the reason of superiority: as a soldier to the leader of an army in matters concerning war; a slave to his master in performing servile work; a son to his father in matters concerning the discipline of life and the care of domestic affairs. Those who live in the world must obey spiritual prelates in those works of virtue which all Christians must necessarily perform; but those who have been bound by the vows of religious orders are made subject to them as far as those things go which can pertain to regular life, according to which they profess themselves subject. He also divided their obedience threefold: the first, which suffices for obtaining salvation, is that by which they perform the necessary things, as we said above; the second, which reaches the height of perfection, by which they obey every command that is lawful; the third, which is indiscriminate, on account of which they undertake without distinction whatever is ordered everywhere, obeying even in those things which conflict with divine law or with the rule which they have professed.

units.la: Cæterum, memoriæ est proditum à plerisque, quod hinc forte sumpsit exordium, esse quæ supra, quæ contra, quæ præter, quæ secundum regulam præciperentur: & ei duntaxat, cuius postremo factamentio est, necessario obediendum, reliquis adstringi neminem. Namque contra eam, cum quid iubetur, non teneri præcepto, docet Decretalium Glossa, super caput 43. Tituli de Simonia, quod Innocentius ibidem & confirmat & auget. Arnoldus quoque in Summa sua, vt refert Ioannes Beetz in Sermonib. de decem præceptis, obedientiæ quempiam non obligari narrauit, nisi dum iuxta suam cuiusque viuendi normam aliquid præciperet: ab ea autem eximi, si contra mandatur, ac præsertim si vita laxior indiceretur. Ægidius item Romanus in 2. sententiarum librum distinct. 44. decernit subeundam potius mortem, quam præceptis illicitis obtemperandum, atque ipsi Pontifici, non modo contra ius diuinum, sed etiam naturale imperanti, nullo pacto parendum; nec subditos vllo modo prælatis obsequi debere, si aut quicquam eorum quæ supra diximus, aut regulā quam sunt professi aduersans, iubeantur.
units.tr: Moreover, it has been handed down by many (and perhaps this took its beginning from here) that there are commands above, against, beyond, and according to the rule, and that only to the one last mentioned must one necessarily obey, while no one is bound to the rest. For the Gloss on the Decretals, on chapter 43 of the title De Simonia, teaches that one is not bound by a precept when something contrary to it is commanded, and Innocent confirms and extends this in the same place. Arnold too, in his Summa, as Johannes Beetz reports in his Sermons on the ten commandments, related that a person is not bound to obedience except when a superior commands in accordance with each one's own norm of living; but he is exempt if something contrary is commanded, and especially if a looser life were enjoined. Likewise Giles of Rome, in the second book of the Sentences, distinction 44, decides that death is to be undergone rather than obeying illicit precepts, and that one must by no means obey even the Pontiff himself when he commands against not only divine but also natural law; nor ought subjects in any way to obey prelates if they command anything opposed to what we have said above or to the rule which they have professed.

units.la: Scribit & Innocentius super caput 42. tituli de sententia excommunicationis lib. 5. non solum mandato Papæ quod contineret hæresim, non obediendum esse, sed nec præcepto iniusto, quo vehementer præsumeretur Ecclesiæ status perturbari, vel etiam forte alia mala inde ventura: malum autem, iuxta dogma Dominici de sancto Geminiano in 7. caput de sententia excommunicationis lib. 6. quid malum: dicitur, quod tale est ex suo genere, & prima fronte malum apparet, licet aliqua latenti causa possit excusari. Pari pacto, nec præcepto iniusto, aut inhonesto, aut incommodo acquiescendum docet Decretorum Glossa, causa 11. quæst. 3. & confirmari facile potest per ea quæ à Nicolao Abbate Panormitano, super 42. caput, titulo de sentent. excommunicationis libro 5. Decretalium adferuntur: per ea item quæ legi conueniunt, vt inter alia sit iusta, honesta, atque possibilis; distinct. 4. canon, erit, quæ conditio omni mandato subaudienda est. Quemadmodum præter id quod supra docuimus colligi datur, tam ex Epistolis Alexandri & Innocentii eius nominis Pontificis III. positis lib. 2. Decretalium, titulo de iureiurando, cap. 10. & 17. quam ex Glossa, in secundum caput de voto lib. 3.
units.tr: Innocent also writes, on chapter 42 of the title de sententia excommunicationis, book 5, that one must not obey not only a mandate of the Pope which would contain heresy, but also an unjust precept by which the state of the Church would be strongly presumed to be disturbed, or perhaps other evils to come from it. "Evil," according to the teaching of Dominicus of San Geminiano on chapter 7 de sententia excommunicationis, book 6, is "what is such by its own kind and appears evil at first sight, although it may be excused by some hidden cause." In the same way, the Gloss on the Decretum, causa 11, quaestio 3, teaches that one must not acquiesce in a precept that is unjust, dishonourable, or inconvenient. This can easily be confirmed from what Nicholas, Abbot of Palermo (Panormitanus), on the 42nd chapter, title de sententia excommunicationis, book 5 of the Decretals, adduces. Also from what agrees with law: that among other things it be just, honourable, and possible; distinction 4, canon "erit", a condition which must be understood in every command. Just as, besides what we taught above, it can be gathered both from the Epistles of Alexander and of Innocent III, the Pontiff of that name, placed in book 2 of the Decretals, title de iureiurando, chapters 10 and 17, and from the Gloss on the second chapter de voto, book 3.

units.la: Dubitatum autem, tum à Theologis, tum ab interpretibus Pontificii iuris, esse tne his qui præsunt parendum, cum eorum præcepta, vtrum sint illicita, sub dubio versatur, decretumque est quamdiu ambigitur, vtrum recte sint imperata nec ne, vel charitati consonent aut aduersentur, iugum subeundum esse; cum obedientia, quæ non mediocre bonum est, digna sit præmio: nec vllum mere leuibusque de caussis perperam mandauisse quicquam existimandum. At si forte coniectura noueamur, & in sinistram partem vergat rationis libra, ab exequendo officio supersedendum, donec de iussionis vel æquitate vel iniquitate constiterit. Fieri enim facile potest, vt vel malitia propria, vel falsis suggestionibus moti qui præsident, subiectis aut quæ fieri licet prohibeant, aut non committent, aut demandent. Quare minime obeundum id officii subdito est, & quare non obtemperauit Prælato, significandum. Propterea Alexander III. eius nominis Pontifex, Rauennati Archiepiscopo scripsit, si quando ei dirigebat aliqua, quæ ipsius animum exasperare viderentur, turbari non debere; sed qualitatum negotii, pro quo scribebatur, diligenter considerando, aut mandatum reuerenter adimpleret, aut per literas, quare adimplere non posset, rationabilem causam prætenderet: cum patienter sustineret, si id minime fecisset, quod fuisset sibi praua insinuatione suggestum, vt traditur. Decretalium libro, titulo de rescriptis cap. 3. Quod pertractans Abbas Panormitanus affirmat, si quicquam obeundum cuiquam mandetur, etiam sub pœna excommunicationis, statim nisi paruerit incurrenda, & ob præcepti executionem, timetur maximum scandalum, vel de mente Principis ambigitur; licere illi ab implendo iussu sontinere se, atque rescribere. Illud etiam adiecit, si contingat vt ei præcipitur, soli notum sit in mandato contineri peccatum, tametsi princeps ex iustitia agere se credat, à nauanda opera abstinendum; nitens pro fundamento capiti 13. de restitutione spoliatorum lib. 2. Epistolarum Decretalium: vbi Innocentius III. Archidiacono Bituricensi scribit, mulierem eam, quæ conscia est se matrimonium contraxisse in gradibus consanguinitatis diuina lege prohibitis, potius excommunicationem subire debere, quam viro, ad iudicis imperium coniungi. Idem Abbas, 3. lib. super cap. 6. de Prabendis & dignitatibus, multa monet, multa docet, quibus prælatorum imperia subditos declideclinare debeat. Extat quoque Accursii Florentini Glossa, in primum Codicis Iustiniani librum, titulo, si contra ius vel utilitatem publicam, lib. 3. & in Authenticor. volumine, titulo de mandatis Principum repetita, arguens miseros Praelatos, qui metu iniquis iussis obtemperantes, veritatem minime sequuntur: cum secus agentes & Deo, & Papae magis obsequerentur.
units.tr: It has been disputed, both by theologians and by interpreters of Pontifical law, whether those who preside must be obeyed when their precepts are of doubtful lawfulness, and it has been decided that while it remains uncertain whether they have been rightly commanded or not, or whether they agree with or oppose charity, the yoke must be borne. Obedience, which is no small good, is worthy of reward, and no one should be thought to have commanded amiss for merely slight or trivial reasons. But if perhaps we are led by conjecture, and the balance of reason inclines to the wrong side, the subject should refrain from carrying out the duty until it is established whether the command is equitable or iniquitous. For it can easily happen that those who preside, moved either by their own malice or by false suggestions, forbid subjects to do what is lawful, or will not commit or entrust it to them. Therefore the subject must by no means perform that duty, and he must make clear why he did not obey the prelate. Accordingly Alexander III, Pontiff of that name, wrote to the Archbishop of Ravenna that if anything was sent to him which seemed to exasperate his mind, he should not be disturbed; rather, carefully considering the nature of the business for which he was being written to, he should either faithfully fulfil the mandate or, by letter, put forward a reasonable cause why he could not fulfil it; he should patiently bear it if he had not done what had been suggested to him by a perverse insinuation, as is related: Decretals, book, title de rescriptis, chapter 3. Discussing this, Abbot Panormitanus affirms that if anything is commanded to be done by anyone, even under pain of excommunication to be incurred at once unless he obeys, and a very great scandal is feared on account of the execution of the precept, or there is doubt about the mind of the prince, it is lawful for him to refrain from carrying out the command and to write back. He also added that if it happens, as he is ordered, that the sin contained in the mandate is known to him alone, then, although the prince believes he acts from justice, he should abstain from performing the work. He rests this on chapter 13, de restitutione spoliatorum, book 2 of the Decretal Epistles, where Innocent III writes to the Archdeacon of Bourges that a woman who is aware that she contracted marriage within degrees of consanguinity forbidden by divine law ought rather to undergo excommunication than be joined to a husband at a judge's command. The same Abbot, in book 3 on chapter 6 de praebendis et dignitatibus, admonishes and teaches many things by which subjects ought to decline the commands of prelates. There also exists the Gloss of Accursius of Florence on the first book of Justinian's Code, title si contra ius vel utilitatem publicam, book 3, and repeated in the Authenticum volume, title de mandatis principum, rebuking wretched prelates who, obeying iniquitous commands out of fear, do not follow the truth at all, whereas acting otherwise they would obey God and the Pope more.

units.la: Haec veluti in transcursu, de obedientia subditorum in Praelatos enarrasse sufficiat. Nam meo iudicio, non est quicquam adferre, cuius ope qui subest, immoderatum Praesidis imperium declinare non queat: quod autem non recensuerimus, sub quopiam eorum capitum quae memoravimus collocari possit. Illud in calce monendum, quod si aliquid mandetur quo non obligetur quispiam, neque etiam excommunicatione ob id infligta obligari. Nam si praeceptum non tenet, non tenet excommunicatio, ut docet Baldus in sextum Iustiniani Codicis librum, titulo de testamentis, libr. 2.
units.tr: These points, touched on in passing, will suffice concerning the obedience of subjects to prelates. For in my judgment there is nothing further to add by whose help one who is under authority cannot avoid the immoderate command of a superior; and whatever we have not recounted can be placed under one of the heads we have mentioned. It should be added at the end that if something is commanded from which a person is not bound, he is not bound by an excommunication inflicted on that account either. For if the precept does not hold, the excommunication does not hold either, as Baldus teaches on the sixth book of Justinian's Code, title on testaments, book 2.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Notum illud dictum, Sententia pastoris, sive iusta, sive iniusta, timenda est, perperam vulgo usurpari.
units.tr: The saying, "The sentence of a minister, whether just or unjust, is to be feared," is commonly misused.

units.la: HINC opportune explicandum occurrit, non adeo ut vulgus autumat, ab iniquis sententiis formidandum. Invaluit enim apud multitudinem consuetudo, ut maiori cum celebritate proferatur, n. quaest. 3. can. sententia: metuendam esse sententiam Pastoris, seu iusta seu iniusta fuerit; quam certum est ex duobus charitatis mandatis pendere, sicut legem & Prophetas. Atque utinam, quid pastor, quid sententia, quid iniusta, ab illis dignosceretur. Nam ut si sensu aliquo verum quod effantur, ita & aliquo fallum, explosa ignorantia, iudicarent. Primo enim satis constat, omnem excommunicationis sententiam, id enim ipsi intelligunt, timendam non esse: alioqui fatere oporteret eam quae cuipiam ob adoratum Christum infligeretur, pariter metuendam. At inquient forsitan, a pastore vllo, erumpere non posse eiusmodi facinus, nec si eruperit, sententiae appellatione dignandum. Respondebo vicissim, quantum me dubitare licet de quopiam, pastorne sit, an lupus, tantum de sententiis ipsius ambigere, cum extra controversiam sit, nullum qui vere & proprie sit pastor, oves & armenta disperdere, & feris immanibus dilaceranda committere.
units.tr: HERE it is fitting to explain that we must not fear unjust sentences, as the common people suppose. For the custom has gained ground among the multitude of quoting, with great show, n. quaest. 3. can. sententia, that the sentence of a minister is to be feared, whether it is just or unjust; which is certainly said to depend on the two commandments of charity, on which hang the Law and the Prophets. Would that they had distinguished what a minister is, what a sentence is, and what unjust means! For, as what they utter is true in one sense, so it is false in another, and once ignorance is cast out, they would judge accordingly. First, it is quite clear that every sentence of excommunication, for that is what they mean, is not to be feared. Otherwise one would have to admit that the sentence which is pronounced on anyone for worshipping Christ is equally to be feared. But they will perhaps say that no minister can commit such a crime, and that even if he did, it does not deserve the name of sentence. I reply in turn: as far as I may doubt whether someone is a minister or a wolf, I may just as well doubt his sentences, since it is beyond dispute that no one who is truly and properly a minister scatters the sheep and herds, or hands them over to be torn apart by savage beasts.

units.la: Sed cum sub ovium vestimentis, rapaces latitare lupos a Christo Deo nostro edocti sumus, eosque ex ipsorum met operibus cognoscere, consideranda esse multa crediderim, & qua pietate & prudentia decet, Praelatorum iussa examinanda. Quandoquidem, tam ignorantia iuris, quam malitia errare & labi saepe numero possunt; & propterea iniquis eorum sententiis nequaquam acquiescendum: siquidem refutare eas quandoque, nedum aut non timere, aut non recipere, consentaneum. Angelus Clavasinus in Summa sua, quindecim enumeratis modis, quibus excommunicationis sententia labefactatur, subdit in omnibus illis, sententiam nullo modo timendam esse quo ad Deum, aut quo ad Ecclesiam, si notorie de ipsorum quopiam constiterit. Et recte quidem. Si enim secundum civiles leges, non est metuendum filiis quacumque exhaeredatione, sed quae legitime facta fuerit, submoveri se a bonorum possessione contra tabulas, ut scribitur 36. libro Digest. lege 8. quanto minus nobis formidandum erit, ut iniuste vexati, aut ab aeterna haereditate, in ipsa iustitia stabilita dimoveamur; aut de matris Ecclesiae gremio, quae cultrix & nutrix est iustitiae, deturbemur? Porro excommunicationis sententia, vires ex iustitia sumit, qua destituta languet & moritur. Rursus, cum multae earum sint, quae omnium Doctorum consensu nullae appellantur, eas itidem non esse proprie ac vere colligere possumus: quod vero non est, nec vim potestatemque vllam habere, nec cuiuspiam effectus causam esse posse, adeo patet, ut probationis luce non egeat. Quod quidem suffragatur, tam Alexander de Hales, in ultima parte Theologiae summae, docens iniustam excommunicationem nequaquam nisi secundum inanem vocem, excommunicationis appellatione censendam; quam Thomas Aquinas, 18. distinctione, in quart. sententiarum libro, scribens eam excommunicationis sententiam, quae eiusmodi errorem claudit, quo nulla redditur, neque vllum effectum parere, neque excommunicationem esse. Quid? quod Gelasius Pontifex orientalibus Episcopis scribit, II. quaest. 3. can. cui est: excommunicationem iniustam ex eo curari non debere, quod nec apud Ecclesiam quisquam potest iniqua sententia gravari, ut in decretis est videre. Ubi etiam scribitur ibid. can. etsi ad tempus, aliud esse terrenam sellam, aliud tribunal coeleste; ab inferiori accipi sententiam, a superiori coronam. Item, ibid. can. illud plane: si quisquam fidelium fuerit anathematizatus iniuste, potius ei obesse qui facit, quam qui hanc patitur iniuriam. Et Salomon prius in hanc sententiam loquutus, sanxit maledictum frustra prolatum super eum venire a quo missum fuerat, Proverb. 26. Rursus Augustinus super Psalmum, quod in decretis etiam allatum est, iusto cui maledicebatur iniuste, praemium reddi censuit. Scribit praeterea Iohannes Gerson Christianissimus Theologus, in libro de Excommunicationibus & Irregularitatibus, excommunicationes iniustas, aliquando non repellere, fatuo timori asininæque patientiæ adscribendum esse. Idem in quendam Pontificis vices gerentem, peculiari tractatu inuehitur, qui in suis scriptis clausulam hanc apposuerat: Sententia nostra, etiamsi essent iniustæ, sunt tenendæ & timendæ. Glossa quoque Decretorum, super 3. quæstione causæ 11. canon. 64. asserit, posse eum iudici violenter resistere, cui constiterit sententiam iudicis iniquam esse. Et Iohannes de Baccone in 4. librum sentent. distinction. 17. quæstione & articul. 3. tradit eum qui excommunicatus fuerit ob iniustam causam, modo id sit occultum, posse omnium Ecclesiæ ordinum officio fungi.
units.tr: But since we have been taught by Christ our God that wolves lurk under sheep's clothing, and that we are to recognise them from their own works, I believe that many things must be considered, and that the commands of prelates must be examined with the piety and prudence that befit the matter. For both through ignorance of the law and through malice they can, and often do, err and fall; and therefore their unjust sentences are by no means to be acquiesced in, since it is fitting sometimes to refute them, let alone to fear or to accept them. Angelus Clavasinus, in his Summa, after listing fifteen ways by which a sentence of excommunication is weakened, adds that in all those cases the sentence is in no way to be feared, either before God or before the Church, if it is notorious that it is the case with any of them. And rightly so. For if, according to the civil laws, children are not to fear any disinheritance whatever, but only one lawfully made, so that they are removed from possession of the goods against the tablets, as it is written in 36. libro Digest. lege 8., how much less ought we to fear being unjustly harassed, or removed from the eternal inheritance which is established in justice itself, or cast out from the bosom of our mother the Church, which is the cultivator and nurse of justice? Moreover, the sentence of excommunication draws its force from justice; when justice is lacking, it languishes and dies. Again, since there are many such sentences which by the consent of all the teachers are called null, we may likewise conclude that they are not properly and truly sentences; for that which is not, has no force or power whatever, and cannot be the cause of any effect, as is so plain that it needs no proof by light of demonstration. This is supported both by Alexander of Hales, in ultima parte Theologiae summae, teaching that an unjust excommunication is by no means to be counted an excommunication except in empty words; and by Thomas Aquinas, 18. distinctione, in quart. sententiarum libro, who writes that the sentence of excommunication which is vitiated by such an error is rendered void, produces no effect, and is not an excommunication. What more? Pope Gelasius writes to the Eastern bishops, II. quaest. 3. can. cui est, that an unjust excommunication ought not to be cured on that account, since no one can be burdened by an unjust sentence even before the Church, as may be seen in the Decretals. There it is also written, ibid. can. etsi ad tempus, that the earthly seat is one thing and the heavenly tribunal another; the sentence is received from the lower, the crown from the higher. Likewise, ibid. can. illud plane: if any of the faithful has been unjustly anathematised, it is rather the one who does it who is harmed than the one who suffers this injury. And Solomon, speaking earlier to this effect, laid down that a curse uttered in vain comes upon him from whom it was sent, Proverb. 26. Again Augustine, super Psalmum, which is also cited in the Decretals, judged that a reward is to be given to the righteous man who was unjustly cursed. Moreover, John Gerson, that most Christian theologian, writes in his book in libro de Excommunicationibus & Irregularitatibus that not to reject unjust excommunications at times is to be ascribed to foolish fear and asinine patience. In a separate treatise he likewise attacks a man acting in the place of the Pope, who had added to his writings this clause: Sententia nostra, etiamsi essent iniustæ, sunt tenendæ & timendæ. The Gloss of the Decretals, super 3. quæstione causæ 11. canon. 64., also asserts that a judge may violently resist a judge when it is clear that his sentence is unjust. And John of Bacon, in 4. librum sentent. distinction. 17. quæstione & articul. 3., teaches that a person who has been excommunicated for an unjust cause may, provided the matter is kept secret, perform the duties of all the orders of the Church.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Quomodo debeat intelligi, Sententiam pastoris iustam aut iniustam timendam esse.
units.tr: How the sentence of a minister, whether just or unjust, ought to be understood as something to be feared.

units.la: OSTENDIMVS sententias excommunicationis iniustas quandoque non timendas. Nunc eas & aliquando formidandas fore, & quo modo elogium illud Gregorii intelligi debeat, pro viribili declarabimus. Quod facturis nobis, res ipsa altius repetenda est. Tripliciter sententia excommunicationis iniusta censetur à Theologis, & canonum interpretibus. Primo cum iuris prætermittitur ordo: secundo cum de prauo animo promitur: tertio cum falsa & iniqua causa pronuntiatur: prauus autem animus in causa esse non potest, vt timeri non debeat, si is in quem promulgatur aliquin sit anathemate feriendus. Iuste enim tum subditus patitur, tametsi iudex agat iniuste: posthabito quoque ordine si sententia feratur, non vsquequaque parui pendenda, nisi, ob aliquod eorum quæ supra memoravimus, viribus effœta redderetur. At propter falsam & iniquam causam, iam minime timenda est: nisi forte ob scandalum in quod inde rudes impingerent. Est enim magnopere ratio proximi habenda, quod vnicuique Deus mandauit, vt scribitur in sacris literis Ecclesiastici cap.17. abstinendumque vigili cura, ne aliquod ei offendiculum nostris operibus præbeamus. Propterea tametsi quispiam conscius sit, contra ius fasque anathemate se mulctatum; nihilominus, si aut falsitas hæc & iniquitas palam non est, & timere & obseruare eam debet, quoad veritas eluceat. Fieri tamen posset, vt oporteret statim quod esse in causa manifestare, dum inde præiudicium aliquod veritatis pullularet: tum instruendi quibus cum versaremur, & auferenda scandali suspicio, quantum ad nos attinet, & aduersus illam agere oporteret.
