Præterea Glossa Decretorum, II.q.3. can. sententia, timendam adstruit, nisi aut intolerabilem errorem continet, aut post legitimam appellationem feratur, aut pro exactionibus indebitis effulminetur. Alii metuendam dicunt, modo non sit inualida, alioqui sententiæ nomine non dignandam. Quibus autem modis id fiat, supra ex parte narrauimus. Carere quoque eius metu num debeamus, dum iuste fuerit illata nec ne, in ambiguo versatur: alioqui metu quoque dicitur carere nos posse, modo ex superbia minime contemnatur.
units.tr: We have shown that sentences of excommunication which are unjust are sometimes not to be feared. Now we shall declare, as far as we can, that they are also at times to be dreaded, and in what way that saying of Gregory ought to be understood. In doing this, the matter itself must be taken up from further back. Theologians and interpreters of the canons regard a sentence of excommunication as unjust in three ways: first, when the due order of law is set aside; second, when it is pronounced out of a wicked mind; third, when it is pronounced for a false and unjust cause. A wicked mind cannot be the cause of the sentence in such a way that it need not be feared, if the person against whom it is issued deserves to be struck with anathema in any case. For the subject suffers justly then, even though the judge acts unjustly. Likewise, if the sentence is pronounced with the order set aside, it is not to be held of little account in every respect, unless it has been rendered powerless on account of one of those things which we mentioned above. But on account of a false and unjust cause, it is by no means to be feared, except perhaps on account of the scandal into which the untaught might thereby fall. For regard for one's neighbour must be had to a great degree, as God has commanded everyone; as is written in the sacred letters, Ecclesiasticus 17, and we must take watchful care to avoid giving him any stumbling-block by our works. Therefore, although someone may be aware that he has been struck with anathema contrary to law and right, nevertheless, if the falsehood and injustice of it is not plain, he ought both to fear it and to observe it, until the truth comes to light. It could happen, however, that one must at once make known what is wrong in the cause, when some prejudice to the truth might spring from it; then we must instruct those among whom we live, and remove, so far as concerns us, the suspicion of scandal, and act against it. Moreover, the Gloss of the Decretum, II, q. 3, can. Sententia, maintains that it is to be feared, unless it contains an intolerable error, or is pronounced after a lawful appeal, or is hurled for undue exactions. Others say it is to be feared, provided it is not invalid; otherwise it is not to be counted worthy of the name of a sentence. In what ways this comes about we have explained in part above. Whether we ought to be free of fear of it, while it is uncertain whether it was justly inflicted or not, is also doubtful; otherwise it is said that we can be free of fear, provided we do not despise it out of pride.

units.la: Cæterum ex iis quæ subduntur à Gregorio, intentionis eius notitiam capimus. Siquidem vt recte ab Hilario 4. de Trinitat. libro definitum est, & in Decretalibus titulo de verborum significatione repetitum, dictorum intelligentia ex dicendi causis est assumenda. Subiecit enim statim Gregorius, ne is cui infligitur eam ex alia causa mereatur: dans intelligere, eatenus iniustam sententiam timeri debere ab aliquo, quatenus ei ambigendum, ne quopiam occulto crimine ipsa pœna dignus sit, vel tacite innuens eam quæ suapte natura iniusta esset, iustam ex contemptu reddi posse. Iniustam igitur sententiam per se metuendam nequaquam statuit: sed ob aliud quasique dixeris ex accidenti. Et in hanc sententiam loquens Petrus de Palude 18. distinct. libri quarti sententiarum, prodit excommunicationem iniustam, ratione scandali, vt supra monuimus, metuendam: sed nullo pacto ob iuris pœnam, qui sententiam irritam minime custodit, si veritati ipsi niti voluerimus.
units.tr: Moreover, from what Gregory adds we grasp the knowledge of his intention. For, as Hilary rightly defined in the fourth book of De Trinitate, and as it was repeated in the Decretals under the title de verborum significatione, the understanding of what is said must be drawn from the reasons for saying it. Gregory immediately added, lest he on whom it is inflicted deserve it on another ground, giving us to understand that an unjust sentence is to be feared by someone only so far as he must doubt lest he be worthy of that very punishment on account of some hidden crime; or tacitly hinting that a sentence which by its own nature would be unjust may become just through contempt. Therefore he by no means lays down that an unjust sentence is to be feared in itself, but on account of something else, or, as one might say, by accident. And speaking to this effect, Peter of Palude, on the eighteenth distinction of the fourth book of the Sentences, shows that an unjust excommunication is to be feared on account of scandal, as we noted above; but by no means on account of the penalty of the law, which does not hold a void sentence binding, if we are willing to stand by the truth itself.

units.la: APOLOGIÆ IOANNIS FRANCISCI PICI MIRANDVLÆ, PRO HIERONYMI SAVONAROLÆ INNOCENTIA, LIBER SECVNDVS
units.tr: APOLOGY OF GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, FOR THE INNOCENCE OF GIROLAMO SAVONAROLA, BOOK TWO

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Quid superiori libro actum, quid deinceps agendum.
units.tr: What was done in the previous book, and what remains to be done.

units.la: VNC tempus postulat, vt defensionem ipsam cominus aggrediamur. Iactis nim superiori libro doctorum sententiis, instar fundamentorum veritatis, equens est ædificium eius erigere. Ex re quippe fecisse nos credimus, de iudiciorum infirmitate inprimis pertractare, deque speciebus excommunicationis iniustæ nonnulla recensere, & quam ob causam ipsa sententia ferenda esset. De subditorum item obedientia erga prælatos, atque de timore ipsius excommunicationis iniustæ: non solum ob id quod hæc per se cognitu utilia & digna sint, verum quia his perspectis, & ad memoriam revocatis, commodius exactiusque Prophetam nostrum ab iniuria irrogatæ calumniæ, contractæque suspicionis asseremus. Namque, vt Aristoteles sapienter libro I. Physicae auscultationis monet, à communioribus exordiendum est, qui & 3. lib prima Philosophiæ docet, veritatis cognitionem, eorum quæ in dubium revocantur solutionem esse. Facilius etenim constabit, potuisse in eum perperam infligi sententiam, cum prius, & omne mortalium iudicium quandoque falli, & excommunicationes multas esse palam sit, quæ irritæ & inefficaces suapte natura reddantur.
units.tr: The time now calls for us to take up the defence itself at close quarters. For having laid down in the previous book the opinions of the learned as the foundations of the truth, it is fitting that we now raise the building upon them. We thought it appropriate, first, to treat of the weakness of judgments and to set out some kinds of unjust excommunication, and the reasons for which such a sentence ought to be pronounced; also of the obedience of subjects towards their prelates, and of the fear of unjust excommunication itself. We do this not only because these matters are in themselves useful to know and worth the trouble, but because, once they have been examined and brought back to mind, we shall more conveniently and more exactly vindicate our Prophet from the injury of the false accusation and the suspicion that has been cast upon him. For, as Aristotle wisely advises in the first book of the Physics, one must begin from the more general things; and in the third book of the First Philosophy he teaches that knowledge of the truth is the resolution of those things which are called into doubt. Indeed it will be easier to establish that a sentence could have been wrongly inflicted upon him, since it is plain that every human judgment is sometimes mistaken, and that there are many excommunications which by their very nature are void and without effect.

units.la: Demum, expeditius monstrabimus eum ab omni credita culpa alienum, & quia iure mandato rescripsit, & quia falsa ex causa vexatus est, & quia id quod nec fieri poterat, nec debebat, tanquam & rectum & facile factu, hostibus veritatis ita Pontifici maximo suggerentibus, in mandatis habuit: monstrabimus hæc inquam, postquam luce clarius ostensum iam est, & à præceptis implendis abstinere, atque rescribere vnumquemque posse, quia ea iniusta & nec ea credi erit, pœnasque nonnisi pro causa idonea, non autem commentitia & falsa, infligendas; iustisque tantum iussis, & quæ obire sit in facultate nostra, acquiescendum; nec ab omni excommunicatione, quæ iniusta sit, formidandum. Exequi ergo quod pollicitus sumus, exordiemur, si prius causam ob quam multi Prophetam nostrum excommunicatum autumarint, paucis subiecerimus.
units.tr: Finally, we shall show more readily that he was free from every alleged fault: both because he rescribed by a mandate in law, and because he was harassed on a false ground, and because he kept in his instructions, as both right and easy to do, what could neither be done nor ought to be done, while enemies of the truth were thus urging the Supreme Pontiff. We shall show these things, I say, after it has been made clearer than light that one may abstain from carrying out commands and may rescribe, since such commands are unjust and are not to be believed, and that penalties are to be inflicted only for a suitable cause, not for invented and false ones; that we must submit only to just commands and to those which lie within our power to perform, and that we need not fear every excommunication which is unjust. Therefore, to carry out what we have promised, we shall begin, if first we set out briefly the cause for which many have thought our Prophet to be excommunicated.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Causa, ob quam plerique Hieronymum Savonarolam excommunicatum autumarint.
units.tr: The cause for which many have thought Girolamo Savonarola to be excommunicated.

units.la: EPISTOLA quædam, ex eorum numero, quæ breuia vocant, sub Pontificis nomine Florentiam delata est, cuius erat summa, Hieronymum ipsum perniciosam doctrinam in ea vrbe seminasse, monitum non cessasse: ceterum præceptum ei sub pœna excommunicationis latæ sententiæ, vt conuentum sancti Marci Florentiæ situm, congregationi cuidam (quæ vocabatur Romana & Thusciæ prouincia) copularet: subditosque monerent, ei nullo pacto communicandum, sed tanquam ab Ecclesia præcisum, atque suspectum criminis hæreseos euitandum.
units.tr: A certain letter, of the kind they call briefs, was delivered to Florence in the name of the Pope. Its substance was that Girolamo himself had sown a pernicious doctrine in that city and had not ceased after being warned; and, moreover, that he had been ordered, under penalty of the excommunication latae sententiae, to join the convent of St Mark situated in Florence to a certain congregation (called the Roman and Tuscan province); and that they were to warn the subjects that on no account were they to have communion with him, but were to avoid him as cut off from the Church and suspected of the crime of heresy.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Ex ipsa causa, elici argumenta defensionis: & primo quod male cognita res fuit Pontifici, utpote subdole ab iniquis suggesta.
units.tr: From the cause itself, arguments for the defence are drawn: first, that the matter was poorly understood by the Pontiff, since it had been craftily suggested to him by wicked men.

units.la: EX sententia huius epistolae, tantum abest ut Prophetam spirituali laqueo irretitum credamus; quod etiam inde, pro tuTanda ipsius innocentia, validas rationes sumemus. Primo namque male cognita causa est Pontifici, ob quam proferri anathema veritatis hostes procurauerunt: cum tamen in eo infligendo, requiri ordinem, causaeque cognitionem, & ratio conuincit, & decretales multae, atque ipsa etiam Decretorum Glossa adstruat, causa 11. q. 3. can. 1. Quis enim ambigat aliunde quam malo zelo, & quam ignoratione causae prouenire, ut enuncietur Hieronymum Sauonarollam, qui nihil docet praeter Christi verba, falsam in animarum perniciem doctrinam seuisse? Hoc omnibus notum, qui aut illius videre scripta, aut sermones ad populum habitos audiuere; hoc vel pueri norunt, quod & hostes veritatis, quanquam ore dissimulent, pectore tamen non dissitentur: Suggesta Pontifici sunt a perfidis hominibus huiusmodi contra innocentissimum virum, nugamenta; quae credita, fecere ut in comminanda poena maturior causae disquisitio non expectaretur: quae autem falso nituntur, corruant est necesse: huiusce quippe sinistrae persuasionis gratia, prauis consiliis auscultatum est, ex re esse religionis, fratres eos qui sub Hieronymo degebant, aliis quos Reformandos dicebant copulari, idq; in ipsius arbitrio situm: qui dum de conficiendo negotio tentatus, rei, uti perniciosae abnuisset, incaluit ardor sequendi, effecitq, ut poena Pontificio mandato necteretur. Quod cum ratione duce, & patrocinante iure declinasset, nihilominus effera luporum rabies, sub ouina pelle delitescens, potens adeo fuit, ut contemptor Ecclesiasticae maiestatis insimularetur: & exorta e palatio Epistola, uti contumax anathemate percussus, & haereseos suspectus publicaretur. Vide quam paruo e fonte, mendacii ingentia falsitatis flumina eruperint. Et sane, ut dicam fateor, postquam certior factus, promulgatae huius excommunicationis, quanquam sciebam Hieronymum, & doctrina cumulatissimum, & sanctis moribus clarum, atq; inprimis obedientissimum; minime tamen credebam e loco tam celebri prodire sententiam, quae saltem verisimilitudine non fulciretur. At legens diplomatis exemplum, & primori fronte, falsae eum doctrinae insimulatum offendens, quem certius certitudine compereram nunquam vel latum quidem unguem a Catholico dogmate recessisse, causam diligentius examinandam suscepi, & praeterid quod diximus, trifariam defendi eum posse ab omni criminis suspitione deprehendimus.
units.tr: EX the sense of this letter, he is so far from being believed to have been caught in a spiritual snare that we shall also draw strong reasons from this in defence of his innocence. First, the cause was poorly understood by the Pontiff, on account of which the enemies of the truth brought about the pronouncement of anathema. Yet both reason and many decretals, and the Gloss on the Decretum itself, show that in inflicting such a penalty an order and an examination of the cause are required, causa 11. q. 3. can. 1. For who would doubt that it arises from nothing but bad zeal and ignorance of the case that it is declared that Jerome Savonarola, who teaches nothing but the words of Christ, has spread a false doctrine to the ruin of souls? This is known to all who have either read his writings or heard the sermons he preached to the people; even children know it, and the enemies of the truth, though they deny it with their mouths, do not deny it in their hearts. The suggestions made to the Pontiff against this most innocent man were the inventions of faithless men, and when they were believed, they caused a more mature inquiry into the cause not to be awaited before the penalty was threatened. But whatever rests on falsehood must necessarily collapse. For under the influence of this sinister persuasion, wicked counsels were followed: that it was a matter of religion that the brethren who lived under Jerome should be joined to others whom they called Reformandos, and that this lay in his own discretion. When he was pressed to carry out the business, he refused it as harmful to the cause, but the ardour of pursuing it grew hot and brought it about that the penalty was imposed by Pontifical command. Although he had avoided this, with reason as his guide and law as his advocate, the savage rage of wolves, hiding under a sheep's skin, was nevertheless so powerful that he was accused of despising ecclesiastical majesty; and a letter issued from the palace declared him a contumacious man, struck with anathema and suspected of heresy. See from how small a source the vast floods of lying falsehood have burst forth. And indeed, to tell the truth, I confess that when I was informed of the publication of this excommunication, although I knew Jerome to be richly endowed with learning, renowned for his holy morals, and above all most obedient, I was by no means ready to believe that a sentence had come from so famous a place which was not supported at least by some plausibility. But on reading the copy of the document, and finding at the very first glance that he was charged with false doctrine, when I had learned with greater certainty that he had never departed even the breadth of a fingernail from Catholic doctrine, I undertook to examine the cause more carefully. Besides what we have said, I found that he could be defended in three ways against every suspicion of crime.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: Quod mandatum Pontificis fuit impossibile.
units.tr: That the command of the Pontiff was impossible.

units.la: REVOCANDVM profecto in dubium non est, supra vires proprias, supraque auctoritatem agere posse neminem: & ob id poenam si mandato adiungitur in cassum proferri, nec effectum aliquem parituram. Probauimus hoc superiori libro, praeter naturae dictamen, etiam auctoritate Iuris ciuilis, & pontificii. Potuerit autem nec ne Hieronymus, vrbis illius aduena, vnico vicariatus ossicio fungens, vertere tot religiosorum fratrum voluntates, vt in id concederent, cui ex professo aduersabantur? nullus puto sapiens iudicabit. Repugnarunt namque non minus ipsi Hieronymo, vnionem illam, quae tunc proponebatur, publicis literis, uti pestiferam, detestantes; addentes se malle extrema pati, quam fratribus tam deformatis copulari: quorum tantam vesaniam narrari audiui ab iis, qui hanc mixtionem affectabant, vt motos se ad procurandum hoc negotii dicerent, ne monasteria ab ipsis habitata, quae iam speluncae latronum euaserant, penitus destruerentur. Eos autem qui secundum sanctorum Patrum decreta, & probatas ab Ecclesia Catholica sanctiones viuere eniterentur, inducere ut velint speluncas latronum habitare, & deformatis inquinatisque hominibus se immiscere, facto impossibile est. Quid ergo fuit causae, vt communis haec repugnantia in solum Hieronymum reiiceretur? At forte inquient, nihil esse tam arduum, tam difficile quod non libenter fratres reliqui Hieronymi gratia subiissent. At qui hoc fundo nixi, vana argumentatione deluduntur, cum palam sit, nec plus ditionis habere eum in ipsos, quam iura sibi permittant officii: nec, quanquam haberet, adstringi posse, vt ea vteretur. Supra enim probauimus, nullum reddi praecipienti praelato obnoxium, nisi ea ratione qua praesidet. At ipse Hieronymus Pontifici hoc in negotio non subditur, nisi quatenus ex praedicatorum ordine, & congregationis eius, quae S. Marci nominatur, praeses ad tempus est. Eatenus autem procuratam hanc ferruminationem conficere potis non est, vt dudum ostendimus. An ridiculum non iudicaretur, si aliis Fratrum Vicariis, qui de Obseruantia dicuntur (ita enim appellari consuetum) iussum foret, vt quos sub imperio haberent, eis qui conuentuales nominantur miscerent? maxime repugnantibus illis, & rem talem nequaquam se laturos protestantibus. Sane quenquam extare non puto, modo rationis capax sit, qui praeceptum id, vires & hominis & officii excedere non arbitretur.
units.tr: It is certainly beyond doubt that no one can act beyond his own powers and beyond his authority; and for that reason a penalty, if it is attached to a command, is pronounced in vain and will produce no effect. We proved this in the previous book, both by the dictate of nature and by the authority of civil and pontifical law. But could Jerome, a stranger to that city, serving only in the single office of vicar, turn the wills of so many religious brothers so that they would consent to that to which they were openly opposed? No wise man, I think, will judge that he could. For the brothers resisted Jerome no less, and in public letters they denounced that union, which was then being proposed, as pestilential; adding that they would rather suffer the worst than be joined to brothers so corrupted. I have heard from those who were pursuing this mixing that the brothers were so mad that they said they had been moved to bring about this business lest the monasteries inhabited by them, which had already turned into dens of robbers, be utterly destroyed. Yet to induce those who were striving to live according to the decrees of the holy Fathers and the sanctions approved by the Catholic Church to be willing to dwell in dens of robbers and to mix themselves with deformed and polluted men is impossible. What, then, was the reason that this common resistance was thrown back on Jerome alone? But perhaps they will say that nothing is so arduous or so difficult that the remaining brothers would not gladly have submitted to it for Jerome's sake. Yet those who rest on this foundation are deluded by empty argument, since it is plain that he had no more authority over them than the rights of his office allowed him, nor, even if he had more, could he be compelled to use it. For we have proved above that no one is bound to obey a superior who commands, except in the manner in which he presides. But Jerome himself is not subject to the Pontiff in this business, except insofar as he is for a time the president of the Order of Preachers and of that congregation which is called of St. Mark. Within that limit he is not able to bring about this joining together, as we showed a while ago. Would it not be judged ridiculous if the other vicars of the brothers, who are called of the Observance (for so they are customarily named), were ordered to mix those under their rule with those who are called Conventuals, especially when those men were resisting and protested that they would by no means tolerate such a thing? Certainly I do not think there is anyone, provided he is capable of reason, who would not judge that such a precept exceeds both the strength of the man and the bounds of his office.

units.la: Caeterum, dato etiamnum hoc atq; concesso, vt iussus facto facilis iudicetur, & qui in eis congregationibus sunt, viuant sanctissime: si fratrum tamen suorum collegio id non videatur, poteritne quisquam quod Dei solius est prærogatiua eos cogere, vt id velint & amplectantur? At si hoc supra illius facultatem, erit, qui fieri poterit, vt eosdem compellere queat, perpetua deformatorum fratrum inire consortia?
units.tr: Moreover, granting even now and conceding this, that the command would be judged easy to carry out, and that those in those congregations live most holily: if nevertheless the college of their brothers does not see fit to do so, can anyone compel them to will it and embrace it, when that prerogative belongs to God alone? But if this lies beyond his power, how could he be able to compel them to enter into lasting fellowship with deformed brothers?

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: Quod mandatum Pontificis exequendum non erat.
units.tr: That the Pontiff's command was not to be carried out.

units.la: VIdimus præceptum impleri non potuisse, nunc an sua natura esset implendum, disquiramus. Cum peruersis nos peruerti, cum sanctis fieri sanctos Dauid monet: & Christus docet à fermento Pharisæorum, quod est hypocrisis, enixe cauendum. Præterea quicumque reformandis religionibus congregationibusq; iam collapsis, & diuini amoris igne destitutis, operam dederunt, tantum abfuit, vt cum prauis & deformatis monachis, fratribusve, diuturnis commerciis implicarentur, vt etiam se ab eis sequestrarint, conarenturq; calorem pene emortuum (additis sibi pauculis, qui idem vellent, nollentque, veluti fomitibus) reparare, vt tandem fere extincta flamma reuocaretur, & solito fulgore splendesceret. Scimus hoc ducentorum annorum decursu, & eo etiam minus, à plerifque factitatum. Nisi enim à malis boni seiungerentur, pax religiosis maxime expetenda, in cassum quæreretur. Inter bonos siquidem & malos semper bellum; his argui metuentibus, & odio habentibus lucem; illis ecclesiam malignantium perosis, & cum impiis non sedentibus, quos facilius est probos corrumpere, quam contra illos ab his sanari, & integros reddi: quandoquidem pomorum aceruus, ab vnius marcidi contagio maculatur,
units.tr: We have seen that the precept could not be fulfilled; now let us inquire whether, by its own nature, it ought to be fulfilled. David warns that with the perverse we are perverted, and with the holy we become holy; and Christ teaches that we must earnestly beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Moreover, those who laboured to reform religion and congregations that had already collapsed and were destitute of the fire of divine love were so far from becoming entangled in long-standing dealings with depraved monks and brethren that they even withdrew themselves from them. They tried to restore a warmth that had almost died out (adding to themselves a few who wished the same, and who served like tinder), so that the flame, nearly extinguished, might be called back and shine with its usual brightness. We know that over the course of two hundred years, and even less, this has been done by many. For unless the good were separated from the evil, peace, which religious people most of all ought to desire, would be sought in vain. Between good and bad there is always war: the latter fear to be exposed and hate the light, while the former abhor the church of the wicked and do not sit with the impious. It is easier for the good to be corrupted than for the bad to be healed by them and made sound again; for a heap of apples is stained by the contagion of one rotten fruit:

units.la: Vuaque conspecta, liuorem ducit ab vua.
units.tr: And a grape seen spreads its envy from a grape.

units.la: Et sane, cum rei huiusce merita perpenduntur, tolerabilius malum quod ex hac mixtione paterentur qui iam reformati sunt, videretur esse infamia, quam ex deformatorum commercio contraherent: quæ quanti facienda sit, & oraculo sapientis edisserimus, qui docuit habendam curam de bono nomine,& ecclesiæ traditione, quæ contemptores eius crudeles appellauit.
units.tr: Indeed, when the merits of this matter are weighed, the disgrace that those already reformed would incur from this mixing would seem a more tolerable evil than what they would suffer from dealings with the deformed. How much this is to be valued we set out also by the saying of the wise man, who taught that care must be taken for a good name, and for the tradition of the church, which called its despisers cruel.

units.la: Quibus facile patet, & noxium esse religioni, probos improbis copulari, quod ipse Hieronymus demonstrauit peculiari Apologetico: & illud præceptum Pontificis, tametsi potuisset impleri, nihilominus non debuisse, namque iussui, qui malum claudat, obtemperare non conuenit, neque regula quam professus est quispiam, fas est moribus aduersari, quemadmodum supra probauimus, vnde errorem toleratu indignum, in mandato deprehendimus, quando id & quod factu impossibile, & quod minime honestum & salubre, sed & turpe & nocuum esse complecteretur.
units.tr: From these things it is easily clear both that it is harmful to religion to join the upright to the wicked, as Jerome himself demonstrated in his special Apology, and that the Pontiff's precept, although it could have been carried out, nevertheless ought not to have been. For it is not fitting to obey a command that shuts out evil, nor is it lawful to go against the rule that anyone has professed; hence, as we have shown above, we find in the mandate an error unworthy of toleration, since it embraced both something impossible to do and something by no means honourable and wholesome, but rather shameful and harmful.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Quod iure rescripsit Pontifici: Item liquere eum nunquam censuram incurrisse.
units.tr: That he rightly rescinded the Pontiff's order, and that it is clear he never incurred the censure.

units.la: SEd veritatis hostes criminatoresque, potiori etiam in loco constituo. Do eis gratis, nullaq; extorquente ratione, pro comperto non haberi, quod duobus superioribus capitibus manifestauimus. Experiamur, an alia via possimus Prophetam nostrum de faucibus obloquentiū eripere. Quanto enim particularius acta eius negotii examinauerimus, tanto colliquebit apertius abs re prorsus fuisse, in eum quicquam esse adstructum. Recepto namque diplomate, quo pœnam statim incurrendam, nisi pareret mandato, Pontifex minabatur, (hoc est nisi congregationem, quæ sancti Marci dicitur, cui præerat, illi quam Thusciæ & Romanæ prouinciæ vocabant conglutinaret) Rescripsit eiusmodi vnionem, subdola mente à quibusdam Pontifici oblatam, cum in ea, simul & se persequi conarentur (quem ex suscepta asserendæ veritatis causa acerrimo odio insectabantur) & rem perniciosam serere, qua scandalum exoriretur: Confectoque libello, cuius ante meminimus, dedit etiam epistolas, quibus significabat eam quam procurabant ferruminationem, tam diuino honori contrariam, quam animarum saluti pestilentem: demum ab eo peti, quod præstare non poterat: consensu etenim vniuersorum fratrum opus fore: rogarentur ipsi: consentientibus enim repugnare non posse: compellere inuitos & contra nitentes, sui arbitrii & facultatis non esse.
units.tr: But I will place the enemies and accusers of the truth in a stronger position still. I grant them freely, and without forcing any argument, that what we showed in the two preceding chapters is not accepted as established. Let us test whether by another way we can snatch our Prophet from the jaws of his detractors. For the more closely we examine the particulars of that affair, the more clearly it will become plain that nothing at all was brought against him in this matter. He received the decree in which the Pontiff threatened that a penalty would be incurred at once unless he obeyed the order, that is, unless he joined together the congregation called of St Mark, over which he presided, with the one which they called the province of Tuscany and Rome. He wrote back that such a union, offered to the Pontiff by certain men with a crafty intent, was not to be made, since in it they would at the same time attempt to persecute him (whom they hated most bitterly for his undertaking of the cause of asserting the truth) and to sow a ruinous thing from which a scandal would arise. Having composed the little book which we mentioned before, he also gave letters in which he declared that the fusion they were pressing for was as contrary to the honour of God as it was deadly to the salvation of souls. Finally he was asked to do what he could not do: the union, they said, would need the consent of all the brothers; let them be asked themselves, for those who consent cannot resist, and to compel the unwilling and those who strive against it is not within one's power or authority.

units.la: Quæ cum ita sint, quis retiocabit in dubium, virum hunc ab omni culpa insimulati criminis immunem? Siquidem supra cum de obedientia egeremus, multis modis ostendimus, licere subditis à prælati mandatis, quæ excommunicationem annexam gererent, abstinere, atque rescribere. Hoc clamant iura, hoc eorum interpretes asseruantissime volunt, monentque secundam iussionē expectandam, si aut de mente Principis ambigatur, aut in exequendo præcepto, scandalum, malique aliquid formidetur. Et præter ea quæ ibi allata sunt, in eandem sententiam loquitur Baldus, in Iustiniani Principii Codicem, titulo de Vsuris: & Petrus de Ancharano, Consilio 235. docet cum res aliter se habet, quam scribentis mens præsupponat, supersedendum esse, licet mandato excommunicationis latæ sententiæ poena misceatur. At perfidi homines mandari aliud Hieronymo non procurarunt, scientes ei qui iure à primo belli insultu se defenderat, secundo etiam & tertio non defutura propugnacula: sed epistolam extorserunt, cuius vi possent ostendere, rudibus ipsius negotii, iusta quem poena multatum, quam & caruisse iustitia, & viribus, & illi quicquam non obfuisse, iam arbitror comprehendi: patrocinante quippe ratione, & suffragantibus legibus rescripsit: quod sit, ut irrogemus, nulli eum aut culpae aut poenae subfuisse; modo cum epistola nihil aliud colligatur, quam eum ob inobedientiam censura damnatum, & parte alia, iuste iureque non obediuisse a nobis monstratum sit. Quare omnis excommunicationis scrupulus & suspicio, cum omni metu prorsus eliminanda est.
units.tr: Since these things stand thus, who will hesitate to doubt that this man is free of all fault of the crime with which he has been charged? For when we treated of obedience above, we showed in many ways that subjects may refrain from the commands of a prelate which carry an attached excommunication, and may write back in reply. The laws cry out this, and their interpreters most strongly maintain it, and they advise that a second command be awaited if either the intention of the Prince is in doubt, or a scandal and some evil is feared in carrying out the precept. Besides those things which were brought forward there, Baldus speaks to the same effect in his commentary on the Code of the Emperor Justinian, under the title On Usury; and Peter of Ancarano, in Consilium 235, teaches that when the matter stands otherwise than the mind of the writer presupposed, one must hold off, even though the penalty of excommunication latae sententiae is mixed into the command. But these faithless men did not manage to make Jerome into anything else, knowing that for him, who had defended himself rightfully against the first onslaught of the war, bulwarks would not be lacking against a second and a third attack. Instead they wrung out a letter by whose force they could show, to those unskilled in the affair itself, that he had been punished with a just penalty; yet I think it is now clear that he lacked justice and strength, and that nothing of this harmed him. For, with reason pleading for him and the laws supporting him, he wrote back; so that we conclude that he was subject to no fault or penalty at all, since nothing else can be gathered from the letter than that he was condemned by censure for disobedience, and it has been shown by us that on the other side he rightly and justly did not obey. Therefore every scruple and suspicion of excommunication, together with all fear, must be entirely removed.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Neque ei necessariam absolutionem, neque ab eius communione abstinendum esse.
units.tr: That no necessary absolution is due to him, nor must one abstain from his communion.

units.la: AB his consequens est declarare; nullam ei necessariam absolutionem fore, nec ab illius communione vllo pacto abstinendum esse: Et sane, quanquam reverentia Apostolicae sedis, sententiam ipsam petierit aboleri, id tamen quantum ad se attinet minime oportuit, ut ex verbis Gelasii Pontificis, in libro decretorum, satis abunde docemur. Postquam enim scripsit ad Episcopos Orientales, eam sententiam quae iniusta esset, ex eo curari non debere, ex quo nec apud Deum, nec eius ecclesiam nemo poterat iniqua sententia gravari. haec subdit 11. q. 3. can. cui est: Ita ergo ea se absolui non debet, qua se nullatenus percipit obligatum. Cui mirifice consentit ratio, nam solutione ibi opus non fore manifestum est, ubi non est nodus & ligamentum. Eos autem non alligari qui sunt insontes Divus Hieronymus censet: nec Augustinus dissentit, docens iniusta vincula ab iustitia disrumpi: quae alibi quoque (ibidem, can. quomodo, can. ridiculum & can. quid obest) testatus est non obesse homini, quod ex illa tabula velit eum delere humana ignorantia, si de libro viventium non deleat iniqua conscientia. Praeterea, Iohannes Gerso in libello de excommunicationibus & irregularitatibus, affirmat multis in casibus, quos enumerat, nequaquam ligari eum qui a quopiam aut Theologo, aut Iuris interprete responsum habuerit, sententiam in se iactatam tenendam, timendamue non esse; praesertim dum habita fuerit ratio, ne ignari simplicesque offendantur. illum ab ortu naturæ, donati visus miraculo peclarum, quem Iudæi maledicentes, ob Christi nomè ab eo suspectum, eliminauerunt? Et nihilominus satis constat legem Moysi non adeo emortuâ, quin & seruari posset, & deberet, quam etiam ipse Iesus seruandam præcipiebat, inquiens, (Matt.23.) Super cathedram Moysi sederunt Scribæ & Pharisæi: Omnia ergo quecunque dixerint vobis seruate & facite: secundum opera vero eorum nolite facere: dans intelligere, nullo pacto eorum vitam, quæ mala erat, trahi in exemplum debere: Attamen doctrinam seruandam, si eos aperte non contingeret à vero deuiare, tum eis nullo pacto acquiescendum, nec ab iniustis excommunicationibus metuendum, vt in suscipiendo quem illuminauerat cæco, faciendum monstrauit. Et alibi, cum palam discipulis edixit, prædixitque futurum, vt absque synagogis fierent: Ioan. 9. & 16.
units.tr: From this it follows that we must declare that there will be no necessary absolution for him, and that one must in no way abstain from his communion. Indeed, although out of reverence for the Apostolic See he asked that the sentence itself be annulled, this was by no means necessary so far as he himself was concerned, as we are taught abundantly enough by the words of Pope Gelasius in the book of decrees. For after he wrote to the Eastern bishops that a sentence which was unjust ought not to be cured by that very fact, since no one could be weighed down by an unjust sentence either before God or his Church, he adds these words (11 q. 3, can. cui est): "Therefore he ought not to be absolved from that by which he perceives that he is in no way bound." Reason agrees wonderfully with this, for it is plain that there is no need of loosing where there is no knot or bond. Blessed Jerome holds that those who are innocent are not bound, and Augustine does not disagree, teaching that unjust bonds are broken by justice. He also testifies elsewhere (in the same place, can. quomodo, can. ridiculum and can. quid obest) that it does not harm a man if human ignorance wishes to blot him out of that tablet, provided an unjust conscience does not blot him out of the book of the living. Moreover, John Gerson, in his little book on excommunications and irregularities, affirms that in many cases which he enumerates, one who has received an answer from some theologian or jurist is in no way bound, and should neither hold nor fear a sentence thrown against him, especially when account has been taken lest the ignorant and simple be offended. That man, blind from his birth and renowned for the miracle of restored sight, whom the cursing Jews cast out because he was suspected of confessing the name of Christ? And yet it is quite certain that the law of Moses was not so dead that it could not, and should not, be kept, and Jesus himself commanded that it be kept, saying (Matt.23.): "The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat. Therefore all things whatsoever they bid you, these observe and do; but do not do according to their works." Thereby he gave us to understand that by no means should their life, which was evil, be taken as an example; yet the doctrine was to be kept, so long as they did not openly stray from the truth. Then by no means should one acquiesce in them, nor fear unjust excommunications, as he showed to be done when he received the man whom he had illuminated though he was blind. And elsewhere, when he openly told his disciples and foretold that they would be made to live outside the synagogues (John 9 and 16.).

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: Nonnulla in defensi Prophetæ laudem, & causa quamobrem doctrina Christiana assentiamur afferuntur; atque insuper modus resistendi futuris persequutionibus proponitur.
units.tr: Several arguments are offered in praise of the defended Prophet and for the reason why we assent to Christian doctrine; and in addition a method of resisting future persecutions is proposed.

units.la: OBea quæ attulimus, innocentiam vii i Prophetæ tibi arbitror manifestam, atque etiam his qui opusculum hoc legerint, si qui tamen futuri sint, qui verum defecata sceleribus vita vestigauerint. Plerumque enim quorumpiam mens adeo malitia obtenebratur, vt qui suapte natura, vel in cotrouersiarum crepusculo veritatem exquisite cernerent, quandoque interdiu, soleque meridiano illucescente, errorum nebulis caligent: quos erroris sui causam sibi non aliis adscribere decet: quandoquidem, demptis impedimentis, lux etiam ad eos peruaderet: scriptum quippe est in sacris literis, Exortum est in tenebris lumen rectis corde, & alibi, Quam bonus Israel Deus, iis qui recto sunt corde? Quare, si diuino lumini non obstiterint, hæc puto satis superque futura: sin autem & claudere oculos, & obdere auribus ceras maluerint, quæcunque aut dicta vnquam, in veritatis huiusce probationem, aut in posterum dicenda, in cassum, quantum ad eos spectat, proferentur; scripta tamen erunt ad fideles confirmandos, atque ad prauorum versutias & detegendas, & impugnandas.
units.tr: From what we have set out, I think the innocence of this man, the Prophet, is clear to you, and also to those who will read this little work, if there are any who will examine with a pure life, free of wickedness, what is true. For often the mind of some people is so darkened by malice that they, who by their nature could discern the truth carefully even in the twilight of controversies, sometimes walk in the mists of error in broad daylight, with the midday sun shining. They ought not to ascribe the cause of their error to others, since, with the hindrances removed, the light would reach even them. For it is written in the sacred letters: Light has risen in the darkness for the upright in heart, and elsewhere: How good God is to Israel, to those who are upright in heart. Therefore, if they do not stand in the way of the divine light, I think these things will be more than enough. But if they prefer to close their eyes and stop their ears with wax, then whatever has ever been said, or will be said in future, to prove this truth will be offered in vain as far as they are concerned. Nevertheless, these things will be written to strengthen the faithful, and to uncover and to refute the cunning of the wicked.

units.la: Sed cum hæc simulachra sint belli, pugnæq; ludicræ, atrocis comparatione præli, quod ei pro Christo ineundum est (siquidem futurum sibi prædixit certamen ingens, de quo omnino sit triumphaturus; sed aduersus duplicem potentiam, sapientiam, atque malitiam instructa prius acie dimicandum) paratos in stationibus stare conuenit eos, qui vitam istam deserere, quam veritatem malūt; atque armis confertos, bellicisque instrumentis stipatos, classici sonum expectare. Hæ profecto militum copiæ, quibus exercitus mendacii profligabitur; hæ bellicæ machinæ, quarum vi falsitatis & tepidorum mœnia corruent: pensare Prophetam ipsum (quatum humani fert infirmitas) Iesum Dominum imitara, eaque insistere semita, quæ fuerit priorum Prophetarum, & martyrum calcata vestigiis, diuini honoris ardentissimum, salutis animarum sitibundum, intrepidum præterea, atq; omnis pauoris expertem: nihil profecto in eius vita, quod à probata illa quam professus est viuendi norma, deliret: nihil in doctrina, præter veritatem fidei, puritatem Christiani ritus, rerum futurarum prænotiones, quæ adeo constanter tenet, prædicat, & asseuerat, vt ipsa Roma, Italiaque pene vniuersa, ab incepto reuocare illum procurans, nequicquam laborauerit: eundemque sæpenumero aggressa modo cæsim truncare, modo punctim confodere, viribus cassæ fuerint. Vnde cerni, nisi exoculatis datum est, huc Dei ministrum, rerum futurarum præconem, Christianæ fidei & promulgatorem & propugnatorem, eorumque omnium, qui ad supernam Hierusalem suspirant peritissimum ducem.
units.tr: But since these are only the images of war and a sort of sportive fight, compared with the savage battle which he must join for Christ (for he foretold that a great struggle lay ahead, in which he was certainly to triumph; yet he must fight against a twofold power, that of wisdom and that of malice, with his battle line drawn up beforehand), it is fitting that those stand ready at their posts who prefer to forsake this life rather than the truth, and that, bunched together in arms and crowded with weapons of war, they await the sound of the trumpet. These are indeed the troops of soldiers by which the army of falsehood will be routed; these are the siege engines by whose power the walls of falsehood and of the lukewarm will fall. The Prophet himself (as far as human weakness allows) weighs himself against the example of Jesus the Lord, and treads that path which was trodden by the earlier Prophets and martyrs: burning with zeal for the divine honour, thirsting for the salvation of souls, moreover fearless and free from all dread. Certainly nothing in his life departs from that approved rule of living which he professed. Nothing in his teaching, apart from the truth of the faith, the purity of the Christian rite, and his foreknowledge of future events, which he holds, preaches and asserts so constantly, is open to fault. For this reason Rome itself, and nearly all of Italy, have laboured in vain, seeking to call him back from his undertaking; and they have often attacked him, now trying to cut him down with blows, now to pierce him with thrusts, but their efforts have been in vain. From this it can be seen, unless one is blind, that here is a minister of God, a herald of future events, a proclaimer and defender of the Christian faith, and the most skilled leader of all those who long for the heavenly Jerusalem.

units.la: Tria olim mecum ipse cogitans, fidem Christi doctrinamq; & gignere & augere sum contemplatus; lumé superne demissum, quo ea intueamur, ad quæ cernenda in limitibus nostræ naturæ iam infectæ derelicti cæcutiremus: efficacissimas rationes ex effectibus desumptas: miracula atque prodigia in testimonium allata. Quæ omnia, rei ipsius Hieronymi adeo conueniunt, adeo quadrant, vt ipsum simul & Christi sectatorem, & eius doctrinæ fidem deprehendas interpretem. Lumen quippe cœlitus demissum in causa est, cur illi assentiamur, quandoquidem statim à plerisque subscribi ei videmus, nulla ratione percepta, nullo viso prodigio, meræ narrationi acquiescentibus, qui tamen & prudentia cumulati, & doctrina referti: nonnullos contra protinus refragari, nec rationum molibus cedere, nec prodigiis flecti. Quales autem sunt & quantæ rationes adstipulentur, cum aliunde, tum ex Domini Beniuieni doctissimi & integerrimi viri lucubrationibus huic muneri dedicatis, colligere licet. Prodigia vero cum multa, tum magna dignissimorum hominum relatum, prædicationes illius, & vitæ rectitudinem roborare, extollereque, factus sum certior. A me ipso id perpetratum ab eo vidi, quod vi naturæ fieri, nullo pacto posse iudicaui: & plerisque mecum, quibus explorata naturæ potestas, eandem sententiam tulerunt: vt tibi olim me narrasse memini.
units.tr: Once, pondering three things in my own mind, I considered how the faith and doctrine of Christ both give birth to and increase: the light sent down from above by which we see those things which, were it not for it, we would be left blind in the bounds of our nature, now corrupted; the most effective arguments drawn from its effects; and the miracles and prodigies brought forward as testimony. All of these agree so closely with the case of Hieronymus himself, and fit so exactly, that you find him at once a follower of Christ and an interpreter of the faith of his teaching. For the light sent down from heaven is the reason why we assent to him, since we see that many subscribe to him at once, without any reason perceived or any prodigy seen, merely acquiescing in the account, and yet are endowed with prudence and full of learning; while on the other hand some straightway contradict him, yielding neither to the masses of arguments nor bending to prodigies. What sort of arguments these are, and how great, may be gathered both from elsewhere and from the writings of the most learned and upright man, Lord Beniveni, dedicated to this task. I have been made certain that many prodigies, and great ones, have been reported by most worthy men, confirming and exalting his preaching and the uprightness of his life. I myself have seen him perform what, by the power of nature, I judged could in no way be done; and many with me, to whom the power of nature was well known, have given the same opinion, as I remember telling you once.

units.la: Hæc & similia vero, vt dici solet, veriora, quæque nec diffusius tractata, nec exactius (vtpote, qui tibi & mihi eius viri amicis & domesticis scribo) habere ad manum oportet: quibus & bellare possimus, & vincere. Eam enim doctrinam, quæ Christianæ omni ex parte sit consona, imo simillima, imo eadem (licet aliquanto particularius, pro temporum conditione explicata) vti lucidissimum iubar effulgens, huic nostræ tempestati (qua rerum potiuntur vitia, virtutes in vniuersum exulant, refriguit charitas, deiecta est spes, fides elanguit) eam inquam doctrinam, quæ omnibus his damnum adferre occepit, Deique maximi & optimi prouidentia, atque clementia, vniuerso iam or-
units.tr: These and similar things, to use the common saying, are rather the truer, and they ought to be at hand, not treated more widely or more exactly (since I write to you and to me, friends and intimates of that man), so that we may both fight and conquer by them. For that doctrine, which is in every part consistent with Christianity, indeed most like it, indeed the same (though explained somewhat more particularly, as the condition of the times required), shining forth like the brightest light, has begun to bring harm to all these things in this our storm, in which vices hold sway, virtues in general are banished, charity has grown cold, hope has been cast down, and faith has grown faint. That doctrine, I say, which has begun to bring harm to all these things, and which, by the providence and clemency of the greatest and best God, has now been shown to the whole world,

units.la: bi monstrata (vt eius deturpata facies, depositis larualibus simulachris, sed ad ipsam effingens veluti exemplar, veram induat speciem) non sequi, non magnificare, non extollere, omnique conatu tueri, non sani esse hominis, non sanus iuret Orestes.
units.tr: (so that its disfigured face, with the masks laid aside, takes on its true appearance, as if shaping itself upon its very model) not to follow it, not to honour it, not to exalt it, and not to defend it with every effort, is the mark of no sane man; not even Orestes, if sane, would swear to it.

units.la: BERNARDI LAVRETI TI IC. EXCELLENTISSIMI, ET PRIMI PRÆSIDIS THOLOSÆ.
units.tr: Bernard Lauret, jurisconsult, most excellent First President of Toulouse.

units.la: TRACTATVS CONTINENS CASVS, IN QVIBVS IVDEX SECVLARIS potest manus in personas Clericorum sine metu excom- municationes imponere. SVMMARIA
units.tr: A TREATISE CONTAINING THE CASES IN WHICH A SECULAR JUDGE MAY LAY HANDS ON THE PERSONS OF CLERICS WITHOUT FEAR OF EXCOMMUNICATION. SUMMARY

units.la: 1. Iurisdictiones distincta debent esse. Iurisdictio Ecclesiastica temporali maior censetur.
units.tr: 1. Jurisdictions ought to be kept distinct. Ecclesiastical jurisdiction is held to be greater than temporal jurisdiction.

units.la: 2. Leges sacros canones imitari non pudet. Iurisdictio una alii non debet esse impedimento.
units.tr: 2. Laws are not ashamed to imitate the sacred canons. One jurisdiction should not be an obstacle to another.

units.la: 3. Laici in clericos nullum iurisdictionis actum exercere possunt.
units.tr: 3. Laymen can exercise no act of jurisdiction against clerics.

units.la: 4. Laicus in clericum iurisdictionem habet in causa reconuentionis & feudali.
units.tr: 4. A layman has jurisdiction over a cleric in a counterclaim and in a feudal cause.

units.la: 5. Clerici a laicorum potestate exempti sunt summi Dei auctoritate.
units.tr: 5. Clerics are exempt from the power of laymen by the authority of almighty God.

units.la: 6. Iudices seculares nullam in clericos iurisdictionem exercere possunt.
units.tr: 6. Secular judges can exercise no jurisdiction over clerics.

units.la: 7. Percutiens clericum in septem casibus excommunicationem non incurrit.
units.tr: 7. One who strikes a cleric does not incur excommunication in seven cases.

units.la: 8. Iudex secularis sex casibus clericum coercere potest.
units.tr: 8. A secular judge can restrain a cleric in six cases.

units.la: 9. Clericus per iudicem secularem puniri potest, si sauis & enormibus se immiscuerit.
units.tr: 9. A cleric can be punished by a secular judge if he has meddled in serious and gross matters.

units.la: 10. Clericum militarem habitum gerentem percutiens non efficitur excommunicatus.
units.tr: 10. One who strikes a cleric wearing military dress does not become excommunicate.

units.la: 11. Clericus vitam turpem ducens, trina per annum facta monitione, omni priuilegio clericali spoliatur.
units.tr: 11. A cleric who leads a shameful life, after three warnings given over a year, is stripped of all clerical privilege.

units.la: 12. Cardinales ad celebrandum Romani Episcopi electionem possunt includi per dominos temporales.
units.tr: 12. Cardinals may be shut in by temporal lords for the purpose of electing the Roman Bishop.

units.la: 13. Curialis effectus clericus per secularem iudicem, ad curiam reuocari potest.
units.tr: 13. A cleric who has become a court official may be recalled to the court by a secular judge.

units.la: 14. Clericus attentans aliquid in iurisdictionis temporalis praeiudicium, potest per iudicem secularem coerceri.
units.tr: 14. A cleric who attempts anything to the prejudice of temporal jurisdiction may be restrained by a secular judge.

units.la: 15. Iurisdictio Ecclesiastica iuste defendi debet, non tamen iniuste.
units.tr: 15. Ecclesiastical jurisdiction ought to be defended justly, but not unjustly.

units.la: 16. Executio multa pecuniaria non contra personam clerici, aut in bonis Ecclesiasticis fieri debet, sed in bonis suis temporalibus.
units.tr: 16. Enforcement of a fine must not be made against the person of a cleric or upon ecclesiastical goods, but upon his own temporal goods.

units.la: 17. Iudex secularis de possessorio causa seu reiecclesiastica potest cognoscere.
units.tr: 17. A secular judge may take cognizance of a case of possession, or of a matter that is ecclesiastical in name only.

units.la: 18. Episcopi olim territorio carentes suas non exequebantur sententias.
units.tr: 18. Bishops who formerly lacked territory did not carry out their sentences.

units.la: 19. Iudex secularis sex casibus clericum tapere & carceri mancipare potest.
units.tr: 19. A secular judge can seize a cleric and commit him to prison in six cases.

units.la: 20. Iudex secularis clericum in flagranti crimine comprehensum per viginti horas detinere potest.
units.tr: 20. A secular judge can detain for twenty hours a cleric caught in the act of a crime.

units.la: 21. Creditor potest debitorem clericum de fuga suspectum capere.
units.tr: 21. A creditor may seize a cleric debtor whom he suspects of flight.

units.la: 22. Verbum Dei non debet adulterari, nec de Deo est aliquid falsi etiam in eius laudem afferendum, quod plerique faciunt mandata ipsius negligentes, vt suas stabiliant adinuentiones.
units.tr: 22. The Word of God must not be corrupted, nor should anything false be asserted about God even in his praise, as many do when they neglect his commands in order to establish their own inventions.

units.la: QVoniam frequenter intuebor modernis temporibus clericos capi, distringi, & plerumq; iudicari a temporalibus iudicibus siue magistratibus, igitur vigilanti studio inuestigare curaui totis viribus, an & quando hoc sit eis licitum, sc. laicis imponere manus in personas clericorum sine metu excommunicationis atque offensa diuini iudicii.
units.tr: Since I frequently observe in modern times that clerics are seized, harassed, and for the most part tried by temporal judges or magistrates, I have therefore taken care, with vigilant study and all my strength, to investigate whether and when it is lawful for laymen to lay hands on the persons of clerics without fear of excommunication and offence against divine judgment.

units.la: 1 Primitus est praesupponendum, quod iurisdictiones sunt distinctae, in aut.que.oport.episc.& cler. col.1.circa princ. iuncto ca.nouit, de iud.ext. cum concordant iurisdictio tamen ecclesiastica maior est & excellentior temporali, in cap.solita, de maiorit. & obed.
units.tr: 1 First, it must be presupposed that jurisdictions are distinct: in aut. que. oport. episc. & cler. col. 1, circa princ., joined with cap. nouit, de iud. ext., since they agree. Nevertheless, ecclesiastical jurisdiction is greater and more excellent than temporal jurisdiction: in cap. solita, de maiorit. & obed.

units.la: 2 Ideo dicit Imperator, quod leges non dedignantur sacros canones imitari, in aut. vt clericus apud propr.episc.§.penult.col.6.ca.clerici, de iud. & ca.cum secundum, de sec.nupt. Qua de re una iurisdictio non debet aliam impedire, vt d.ca.nouit, de iudic.iuncta l.consulta dinalia.C.de testam. imo potius una aliam iuuare debet, vt 24.quaest.2.Dominus, iuncta l.sin.circa princ. de re milit.l.12.C. & ibi de hoc per Lucam de Penn. De quo etiam egregie loquitur Guil.de Monte Lauduno in ca.1.circ.sin.de foro compet.in cleric. & est textus in ca.1. de offic.ordin.
units.tr: 2 Therefore the Emperor says that the laws do not disdain to imitate the sacred canons: in aut. ut clericus apud propr. episc. § penult., col. 6; ca. clerici, de iud.; and ca. cum secundum, de sec. nupt. For this reason one jurisdiction ought not to hinder another: d. ca. nouit, de iudic., joined with l. consulta dinalia, C. de testam. Indeed, rather, one ought to help another: 24 quaest. 2, Dominus, joined with l. sin., circa princ., de re milit.; l. 12, C., and there on this point by Lucas de Penna. Guillelmus de Monte Lauduno also speaks admirably of this in ca. 1, circ. sin., de foro compet. in cleric., and there is a text in ca. 1, de offic. ordin.

units.la: Vnde hæc est regula, quod laici in clericos nullam habent iurisdictionem, nec in criminalibus, vt in cap. at. si clerici, & in cap. cum non ab homine, extra de iudic. & in cap. 1. & 2. 11. q. 1. cum concordan. nec etiam in causa pecuniaria ex criminali descendente, vt notat Ioan. 32. distinct. cap. ad hec, & in ca. Adrianus, 63. distinct. Item Bernard. & Hostien. in cap. decernimus, de iudic. & in cap. 2. de foro compet. Et ibid. hoc tenet Ioan. Andreas. Idem not. in cap. 1. de cleric. coniug. lib. 1. Nec in causa mere ciuili, in ca. non licet. 3. q. 6. & est hoc expeditum in cap. 1. & 2. 11. qu. 1. & in cap. qualiter & quando de iudic. quod tenent Hostien. & Ioan. Andr. in c. clerici, de iudic. de quo etiam in cap. quod clericis, de foro compet. & in cap. verum, eo tit. per Ioan. Andr. Ita etiam notat Hugo 11. q. 1. c. clericum, & in cap. allegato unico, de cleric. coniug. libr. 6. facit optime capit. seculares, de foro compet. libr. 6. cum concord. ibi signatis, vbi est hodie declaratum.
units.tr: Hence this is the rule: laymen have no jurisdiction over clerics, neither in criminal matters, as in cap. at. si clerici, & in cap. cum non ab homine, extra de iudic. and in cap. 1. & 2. 11. q. 1., with agreeing passages; nor even in a pecuniary cause arising from a criminal one, as John notes, 32 distinct., cap. ad hec, and in ca. Adrianus, 63 distinct. Likewise Bernard and Hostiensis, in cap. decernimus, de iudic. and in cap. 2, de foro compet. And there John Andreas holds the same. The same is noted in cap. 1, de cleric. coniug., lib. 1. Nor in a purely civil matter, in ca. non licet, 3 q. 6; and this is settled in cap. 1. & 2., 11 qu. 1, & in cap. qualiter & quando de iudic., which Hostiensis and John Andreas hold in c. clerici, de iudic. On this point also in cap. quod clericis, de foro compet. & in cap. verum, eo tit., by John Andreas. So also Hugo notes 11 q. 1, c. clericum, and in cap. allegato unico, de cleric. coniug., libr. 6. The chapter seculares, de foro compet., libr. 6, agrees very well, with the concordant passages marked there, where the matter is now declared.

units.la: In hoc tamen vltimo membro dicunt nostri maiores; excipi duos casus: Primus casus est in causa reconuentionis: Secundus casus est in causa feudali, licet de hoc sint opiniones contrariæ: tamen Innoc. hoc tenet in capit. verum, de foro compet. dicens, quod si in causa feudali Dominus clericum vasallum distringat, vel alias repellat, non incidit in canonem, &c. de quo plene disputat Henric. Bohic. in capi. a. at si clerici, de iudic. hæc tamen iura prædicta sunt familiaria, unde probatio est familiaris, vt dicit Ioan. in cap patet 11. q. 3. quando vnus Papa alium Papam inducit in testem, vt recitat Ioan. 1. Romani principes, de iureiur. in Clemen. super verbo, Bonifacius, hoc tamen non obstante nullus fidelis abnegare debet istorum iurium & similium auctoritatem. Absit enim dicere, vt Scriptura mentiatur, deci. tert. quæstion. 5. quid ergo, &c.
units.tr: In this last member, however, our elders say that two cases are excepted. The first case is a counterclaim. The second case is a feudal cause, although opinions on this are contrary. Nevertheless Innocent holds this in capit. verum, de foro compet., saying that if in a feudal cause a lord distrains a cleric who is his vassal, or otherwise repels him, he does not fall under the canon, etc. Henricus Bohic disputes this fully in capi. a. at si clerici, de iudic. These aforesaid laws, however, are commonplace, and so the proof is commonplace, as John says in cap. patet, 11 q. 3, when one pope brings in another pope as a witness, as John recounts in 1. Romani principes, de iureiur., in Clement., under the word Bonifacius. Nevertheless, despite this, no faithful person ought to deny the authority of these laws and similar ones. Far be it to say that Scripture lies: dec. tert., quaest. 5, quid ergo, etc.

units.la: Præterea prædicta probantur non solum authoribus iuris canonici, imo & authoribus iuris diuini, & etiam ciuilis. Quoniam clerici sunt exempti a potestate laicorum authoritate summi Dei omnium rerum conditoris, prout legitur in cap. cum ad verum, & cap. duo sunt, & cap. Imperator 16. distin. secundum Guil. de Monte Lauduno in cap. 1. de offic. ordin. in Clem. de quo plane per Innoc. in cap. si quis, de maiorit. & obed. Et plenius per ipsum in cap. licet, de foro compet. vbi plene ipse Innoc. disserit de iurisdictione ecclesiastica, & de illius origine & progressu. De libertatibus vero & priuilegiis a Deo & a principibus concessis ipsi ecclesiæ & personis & bonis clericorum eleganter ponit Innoc. in cap. nouerit, de sent. excommunic. extra, vbi de hoc remitto causa breuitatis. Vnde veritas testatur sacri eloquii dicens: Nolite tangere Christos meos, & in prophetis meis nolite malignari. Vlterius prædicta probantur auctoritate iuris ciuilis, in auth. statuimus, Cod. de episcop. & cleric. vbi ad literam patet, quod iudices temporales nullam habent iurisdictionem nec in criminalibus nec in ciuilibus in personis clericorum.
units.tr: Moreover, the aforesaid points are proved not only by the authors of canon law, but also by the authors of divine law and of civil law. For clerics are exempt from the power of laymen by the authority of almighty God, the Creator of all things, as is read in cap. cum ad verum, & cap. duo sunt, & cap. Imperator, 16 distin., according to Guillelmus de Monte Lauduno in cap. 1, de offic. ordin., in Clem. On this Innocent plainly speaks in cap. si quis, de maiorit. & obed. and more fully through him in cap. licet, de foro compet., where Innocent himself discourses fully on ecclesiastical jurisdiction and on its origin and progress. On the liberties and privileges granted to the Church itself and to the persons and goods of clerics by God and by princes, Innocent sets this out elegantly in cap. nouerit, de sent. excommunic., extra, where I refer the reader on this point for the sake of brevity. Hence the truth of sacred speech bears witness, saying: Nolite tangere Christos meos, et in prophetis meis nolite malignari [Touch not my anointed, and do my prophets no harm]. Further, the aforesaid points are proved by the authority of civil law, in auth. statuimus, Cod. de episcop. & cleric., where it is plain from the letter that temporal judges have no jurisdiction, either in criminal or in civil matters, over the persons of clerics.

units.la: Per quam authoritatem dicunt ibi doctores, & præcipue Bald. quod omnia alia iura ciuilia, quæ dicebant laicos habere aliquam iurisdictionem in clericos, sunt correcta per illam auth. vt l. nullum. C. de testib. & l. abditos, C. de episcopor. aud. cum simil. tractant Hostien. & Ioan. Andr. in ca. rerum, de foro. compet. Omnis tamen diffinitio in iure periculosa est; parum est enim quin subuerti possit, l. omnis diffinitio ff. de regul. iur. Ideo libet casus a prædictis exceptos hic enumerare. Ea de re subiiciam septem casus, in quibus verberans clericum non incidit in sententiam excommunicationis. Et sex, in quibus clerici distringuntur per seculares iudices. Et alios sex, in quibus laici capiunt clericos absque metu excommunicationis. Quos casus recollegi ex variis passibus iuris, & diuersorum doctorum conclusionibus.
units.tr: By this authority the doctors there say, and especially Baldus, that all the other civil laws which seemed to grant laymen some jurisdiction over clerics are corrected by that authority: auth. ut l. nullum, C. de testib. and l. abditos, C. de episcopor. aud. Hostiensis and John Andreas treat the same in ca. rerum, de foro compet. Yet every definition in law is dangerous; there is hardly one that could not be overturned: l. omnis definitio, ff. de regul. iur. Therefore I am pleased to list here the cases excepted from the aforesaid rules. For this reason I shall set down seven cases in which one who strikes a cleric does not incur the sentence of excommunication, six in which clerics are restrained by secular judges, and six more in which laymen take clerics without fear of excommunication. I have gathered these cases from various passages of law and from the conclusions of various doctors.

units.la: Sunt igitur septem casus, in quibus quis percutiendo clericum non incidit in sententiam excommunicationis, quos enumerat Innoc. in cap. non dubium de sent. excommunic. Primus est, cum bono zelo causa correctionis quis clericum verberat, vt pater, mater, magister, & prælatus, vt in capit. 1. de sent. excommun. & ibi de hoc per Henri. de Bohic. Secundus est, si cum iocosa leuitate, vt in c. 1. & ibi per Henr. in 2. di. Tertius est cum quis inuenerit clericum turpiter agentem cum vxore, sorore & matre, de quo in cap. si vero, de sentent. excommunicat. in 2. distinction. per Henric. Quartus, si vim vi repellat, vt in e. ca. si vero, & ibi de hoc per Henr. in 1. dist. Quintus, si ignorauit eum esse clericum, in cap. si vero 2. & ibi de hoc per Henr. in 1. dist. Sextus, si inuenerit clericum apostatam, scilicet non deferendo habitum & tonsuram clericalem, post trinam monitionem, vel si sæuis & enormibus se immisceat, sine habitu & tonsura clericalibus, sine monitione, de quo tamen latius inferius dicam. Septimus & vltimus, cum clericus se prorsus transfert ad actus contrarios clericatui, vt quando efficitur miles, se immiscendo sæuis & enormibus, vt quando bigamus efficitur. Et etiam de his dicam in sequenti.
units.tr: There are therefore seven cases in which a person who strikes a cleric does not incur the sentence of excommunication, as Innocent lists them in cap. non dubium de sent. excommunic. (1) The first is when someone, with good intent and for the purpose of correction, strikes a cleric, as a father, mother, teacher or prelate may do, vt in capit. 1. de sent. excommun. and on this see Henry of Bohic there. (2) The second is when it is done with playful levity, vt in c. 1. and see Henry there in 2 dist. (3) The third is when someone finds a cleric acting shamefully with a wife, sister or mother, on which see in cap. si vero, de sentent. excommunicat. and Henry in the 2nd distinction. (4) The fourth is when someone repels force with force, in e. ca. si vero, and on this see Henry in the 1st distinction. (5) The fifth is when he did not know that the man was a cleric, in cap. si vero 2. and on this see Henry in the 1st distinction. (6) The sixth is when he finds a cleric who is an apostate, that is, one who does not wear the clerical habit and tonsure, after three warnings; or when a cleric engages in savage and outrageous acts without the clerical habit and tonsure, with no warning given. I will say more about this below. (7) The seventh and last is when a cleric wholly turns to acts contrary to the clerical state, as when he becomes a soldier by engaging in savage and outrageous acts, or when he becomes a bigamist. I will discuss these too in what follows.

units.la: Præterea & secundo reperio sex casus, in quibus iudex secularis vel temporalis coercere potest clericum. Primus est, quando clericus incorrigibilis est, & est degradatus & traditus brachio seculari, in cap. cum non ab homine, cum concord. suis, de iudic. Et intelligo, quod sit degradatus iuxta formam c. degradato, de pæn. lib. 6. Casus autem in quibus clericus traditur brachio seculari, enumerantur per gloss. in cap. ad abolendam, extra de hære. Secundus casus est, vbicunque ecclesiastica potestas deficit, iuxta ea quæ notantur in cap. Princeps 32. q. 5. in cap. filius 16. qu. 7. vbi dicit textus, quod metropolitano dissipante bona ecclesiæ, adeatur Regia dignitas, & ibid. per Glos. vide etiam per Lucam de Penn. in l. si coloni. C. de agric. & censit. lib. 11. Tertius, quando per ecclesiam inuocatur brachium seculare, in l. 1. cum ibi notat. de offic. ordin.
units.tr: Furthermore, and secondly, I find six cases in which a secular or temporal judge may restrain a cleric. (1) The first is when a cleric is incorrigible, has been degraded and handed over to the secular arm, in cap. cum non ab homine, cum concord. suis, de iudic. and I understand that he has been degraded according to the form of c. degradato, de pæn. lib. 6. The cases in which a cleric is handed over to the secular arm are listed in gloss. in cap. ad abolendam, extra de hære. (2) The second case is wherever ecclesiastical power fails, in accordance with what is noted in cap. Princeps 32. q. 5. and in cap. filius 16. qu. 7. where the text says that when a metropolitan squanders the goods of the Church, recourse is to be had to the royal authority, and see there the gloss; see also Luca de Penna in l. si coloni. C. de agric. & censit. lib. 11. (3) The third is when the secular arm is invoked by the Church, in l. 1. cum ibi notat. de offic. ordin.

units.la: Quartus, vbicunque clericus se immiscet sæuis & enormibus, in cap. ex parte 3. de priuil. iuncto c. perpendimus, & cap. cum non ab homine, de sentent. excommun. vbi de hoc, de quo latissime per Henr. in cap. vt fame, de sentent. excommun. & in cap. ex literis, in 3. distinction. extra de vi. & bone. cler. vbi inter cætera legitur, quod si clericus facit contra statutum clericale, assumendo malitiam, immiscendo se sævis & turpibus, vel apostatando ab ordine clericali pariter enormia committendo sine laicali monitione, exuitur omni privilegio clericali.
units.tr: (4) The fourth is wherever a cleric engages in savage and outrageous acts, in cap. ex parte 3. de priuil. joined with c. perpendimus, and cap. cum non ab homine, de sentent. excommun. On this, very fully, see Henry in cap. vt fame, de sentent. excommun. and in cap. ex literis, in 3. distinction. extra de vi. & bone. cler. where, among other things, it is read that if a cleric acts against the clerical statute, by taking up malice, engaging in savage and base acts, or by apostasy from the clerical order while committing outrages equally, without secular warning, he is stripped of every clerical privilege.

units.la: Hoc idem tenet Innoc. in ca. in audientia, de sent. excomm. qui textus dicit, quod clericus assumens habitum militarem, si tertio monitus non desistat, si capitur seu percutitur per tales laicos, non sunt tales laici excommunicati. Innoc. tamen supplet super verbo, moniti, subaudi, maxime. Et nota, quod ille textus non dicit, quod se sævis & enormibus immisceat, sed solum quod habitum militarem assumpserit. Sed in ca. 1. de apostat. Innoc dicit, quod ad hoc, quod privilegium perdat clericale, duo requiruntur, sc. quod se transferat ad habitum militarem; & quod sæva & enormia committat.
units.tr: Innocent holds the same in ca. in audientia, de sent. excomm. That text says that if a cleric who has taken up the military habit does not desist after a third warning, and is seized or struck by such laymen, those laymen are not excommunicated. Innocent, however, supplies a word after moniti, namely maxime. Note also that this text does not say that the cleric engages in savage and outrageous acts, only that he has taken up the military habit. But in ca. 1. de apostat. Innocent says that to lose the clerical privilege two things are required: that he has turned to the military habit, and that he commits savage and outrageous acts.

units.la: Si autem clericus vitam turpem ducat, ut quando est publicus ioculator, buffo, seu goliardus, tunc sive sit in sacris, sive non, post annum ipso iure, vel etiam intra annum, trina tamen monitione præcedente, perpetuo exuitur omni privilegio clericali, in ca. unico, de vi. & honest. cleric. li. 6. Si vero alias turpem clericus exerceat vitam, ut carnificum, macellariorum vel tabernariorum personaliter, tamē post trinam monitionem, post terminum competentem arbitrio monentis præfixum, si sit coniugatus, omnino; si non sit coniugatus, in rebus. Et tunc si omnino incedat in habitu laicali, etiam in persona privilegium clericale, quamdiu in præmissis insistit, amittit, ut in Clem. 1. de vi. & bone. cler. in Clem.
units.tr: If, however, a cleric leads a shameful life, as when he is a public jester, buffoon or goliard, then, whether he is in holy orders or not, after a year by the law itself, or even within the year, but with a threefold warning preceding, he is stripped of every clerical privilege for ever, in ca. unico, de vi. & honest. cleric. li. 6. If, on the other hand, a cleric pursues some other shameful occupation in person, such as that of executioner, butcher or tavern-keeper, then after a threefold warning and after a suitable period fixed at the discretion of the one warning him, he loses the privilege entirely if he is married, but only as to property if he is not married. And if he then goes about wholly in lay dress, he loses the clerical privilege even as a person for as long as he persists in these things, ut in Clem. 1. de vi. & bone. cler. in Clem.

units.la: Quintus est in casus, c. vbi maius periculum, de elect. li. 6. iuncto ca. ne Romani, eo tit. in Clem. vbi domini temporales possunt de facto includere Dominos Cardinales ad celebrandam electionem summi Pontificis. Sed quando hoc faciunt Domini temporales ex commissione vel concessione summi Pontificis, à quo in hoc casu prædictis Dominis temporalibus attribuitur talis potestas, dico quod laicus ex commissione vel delegatione Papæ potest clericos non solum civiliter, quinimo criminaliter coercere secundum Ioan. qui hoc notat 32. dist. ca. ad hoc, & in ca. Adrianus 63. Idem tenet Henric. Bohic post Bernar. Ho. Innoc. & Ioan. Andr. ca. al. at si clerici, de iudic. Et per hoc (ut opinor) excusantur ossiciarii nostri Regis Francorum, qui Rex in his multa habet privilegia Apostolica & plures præeminentias, adeo, quod officiarii sui capiunt clericos, & detinent sine metu excommunicationis, sed eos corporaliter non puniunt, sed bene pecuniariter in casibus privilegiatis, ut infra dicetur.
units.tr: (5) The fifth case is in c. vbi maius periculum, de elect. li. 6. joined with ca. ne Romani, eo tit. in Clem. where temporal lords may in fact shut up the Lord Cardinals to celebrate the election of the supreme Pontiff. But when temporal lords do this by commission or concession of the supreme Pontiff, by whom such power is granted to those temporal lords in this case, I say that a layman, by commission or delegation of the Pope, may restrain clerics not only civilly but also criminally, according to John, who notes this in 32. dist. ca. ad hoc, and in ca. Adrianus 63. Henry of Bohic holds the same after Bernard, Innocent and John Andreae, ca. al. at si clerici, de iudic. By this (as I think) our officials of the King of the French are excused, since the King has many apostolic privileges and several pre-eminences in these matters, so that his officials seize and detain clerics without fear of excommunication, though they do not punish them in person, but do fine them in privileged cases, as will be said below.

units.la: Sextus & ultimus casus est in l. si quis curialis, de episcop. & cleric. C. vbi curialis, si clericetur, potest per temporalem iudicem, etiam per manus iniectionem ad curiam revocari, & vide ibi Bald. Et potest huius esse ratio, quando vbi aliqua sunt in cognitione & iurisdictione ex naturæ causæ iudicii temporalis, potest cognitio seu iurisdictio exerceri per temporalem iudicem in clericum, ut in ca. verum, de foro compet. & in capitu ex transmissa, eo titul. quæ loquuntur in feudo, & in cap. caterum, de iudic. Unde si clericus resistat, tunc iudici seculari potest de facto repelli, & eius persona potest de facto a feudo exui sine metu excommunicationis, secundum Innoc. in ca. verum, & ex hoc practicamus quotidie, quod in causis, quæ pertinent temporalibus de iure vel privilegio, ut in casibus quos dicimus privilegiatos in hoc Regno.
units.tr: (6) The sixth and last case is in l. si quis curialis, de episcop. & cleric. C. where, if a town councillor (curialis) is made a cleric, he can be recalled to the court by the temporal judge, even by laying hands on him; see Baldus there. The reason for this may be that where some matters belong, by the nature of the case, to the cognizance and jurisdiction of a temporal judge, cognizance or jurisdiction may be exercised over a cleric by the temporal judge, as in ca. verum, de foro compet. and in the chapter ex transmissa, eo titul. which speak of a fief, and in cap. caterum, de iudic. Hence, if a cleric resists, he may be actually repelled by the secular judge, and his person may actually be stripped of a fief without fear of excommunication, according to Innocent in ca. verum. And from this we daily practise, in causes that belong to temporal matters by right or privilege, as in the cases we call privileged in this Kingdom.

units.la: Vel quando clerici aliquid attentant in præiudicium temporalis iurisdictionis, profecto temporales possunt coercere clericos resistentes, & merito; quādo quilibet potest tueri suam iurisdictionem, etiam pœnali iudicio, ut in l. unica, in princ. ff. si quis ius di. non obtemper. & notat Innoc. in ca. 1. de offic. deleg. Quo casu iudex potest etiam non subditos coercere, iuxta ca. Romana, de pœnis lib. 6. & not. plene Innocent. in d.c. 1. de off. deleg.
