Et ob id iudices temporales in dictis casibus clericos multant, nec propter hoc puto eos incidere in sententiam excommunicationis, nec facere contra libertatem ecclesiasticam, quæ licet sit fovenda & amplianda, non tamen quod aliis ius suum auferatur, arg. ca. ex tenore, de foro compet. non enim debet apponi laqueus fauore ecclesiarum, ut in ca. mulieri, de iureiur. & ibi sunt concordant.
units.tr: Or when clerics undertake something to the prejudice of temporal jurisdiction, the temporal authorities may indeed restrain resisting clerics, and rightly so, since anyone may defend his own jurisdiction, even by penal judgment, as in in l. unica, in princ. ff. si quis ius di. non obtemper. and Innocent notes it in ca. 1. de offic. deleg. In that case a judge may also restrain even those who are not his subjects, according to ca. Romana, de pœnis lib. 6. and Innocent notes it fully in d.c. 1. de off. deleg. For this reason temporal judges in the said cases fine clerics, and I do not think that for this reason they incur the sentence of excommunication, nor that they act against ecclesiastical liberty, which, though it is to be cherished and extended, must not nevertheless take away another's right, arg. ca. ex tenore, de foro compet. for a snare ought not to be set in favour of the churches, as in ca. mulieri, de iureiur. and the passages there agree.

units.la: Iurisdictio enim ecclesiæ semper tueri debet ob Dei reverentiam, sc. iuste, sed nullatenus iniuste, ut dicitur de causa pupillari in l. quoties, Nec vtiq. ff. de administr. tutor. Ex quibus opinor, quod iudices seculares contra personas ecclesiasticas iurisdictionem exercentes debito modo vtiq; non excedunt, & maxime, quando hoc faciunt ex privilegio iuris vel Papæ, aut saltem ipso Papa sciente & tolerante, ad quod bene faciunt notata in cap. quoniam, de vita & honestate clericor. per Innoc. in cap. 1. de treug. & pace, & vide quæ posui ibidem satis late post Innoc.
units.tr: For the jurisdiction of the Church ought always to be defended out of reverence for God, that is, justly, but never unjustly, as is said in the case of a ward in l. quoties, Nec vtiq. ff. de administr. tutor. From this I think that secular judges who exercise jurisdiction against ecclesiastical persons certainly do not exceed the proper limits, especially when they do so by privilege of law or of the Pope, or at least with the Pope himself knowing and tolerating it. On this point the notes in cap. quoniam, de vita & honestate clericor. are good, as is Innocent in cap. 1. de treug. & pace, and see what I have set out there at sufficient length after Innocent.

units.la: Verum est tamen protunc executio huiusmodi multæ pecuniariæ non fiet contra personam clerici, nec in bonis ecclesiasticis, quæ non subiiciuntur iudici temporali, sed bene fiet executio in bonis eorum temporalib. immobilib. tamē cum mobilia sequantur personam, iuxta l. si captivum. §. expulsus. ff. de captiv. & postlim. reversi. & not. Dyn. in l. etiam, § patronus de bon. li. & plene Oldr. de Ponte de Laude, consil. 59. & consil. 17. Fiet igitur executio in bonis immobilibus, seu in rerum temporalitate, si quam habeant, cum talia bona temporalia subiiciuntur iurisdictioni Regum & aliorum temporalium dominorum, ut in cap. quo iure 8. distinct. & ita seruamus.
units.tr: It is true, however, that in such a case execution of the pecuniary fine will not be made against the person of the cleric, nor on ecclesiastical goods, which are not subject to a temporal judge. But execution will well be made on his temporal immovable goods, although movables follow the person, according to l. si captivum. §. expulsus. ff. de captiv. & postlim. reversi. and the note of Dynus in l. etiam, § patronus de bon. li. and fully Oldradus de Ponte Laude, consil. 59. & consil. 17. Execution will therefore be made on immovable goods, or on whatever temporal property they have, since such temporal goods are subject to the jurisdiction of kings and of other temporal lords, as in cap. quo iure 8. distinct. and so we observe it.

units.la: Præterea iudices temporales in Regno Franciæ cognoscunt de possessorio causæ seu rei ecclesiasticæ, quando possessorium rei ecclesiasticæ seu beneficialis est quid temporale, & non spirituale, secundum Innoc. in ca. cum dilecti, de elect. licet quidam in hoc contra. Sed Bernar. videtur hoc astruere, in ca. literis, de iur. calum. quia possessio habet plurimum facti, & propterea de ea potest iudex temporalis cognoscere, ac etiam in rebus spiritualib. seu ecclesiasticis, secundum Bernar. in l. potest pupil. ff. de auto. tutor. & in l. Titia. ff. soluto matri. & melius in l. quoties, de iud. C. & Ioan. Andr. in c. tuam, ext. de ordin. cognit. & Paul. de Lea in cap. 1. de vsu. in Clem. qui dicunt, quod quando agitur de quæstione facti incidentis in materia ecclesiastica, iudex temporalis cognoscere potest. Vnde secundum iura antiqua Episcopi non habebant territorium, & ideo non exequebantur sententias suas: sed iudices temporales suas exequebantur, secundum Cyn. & Bald. in l. episcop. C. de episcop. audient. Et propterea licet cognitio dotis pertineat ad ecclesiam, vt in cap. 1. & 2. de donat. inter vir. & vxor. tamen in quantum requiritur in ea executio facti, illa fiet per iudicem secularem, & non per ecclesiasticum, secundum Innoc. in ca. significasti, de offic. delegat. secundum vnum intellectum. Et ex hoc dicemus inuentarium bonorum temporalium clericorum debere fieri per iudices temporales, quando illa subiiciuntur temporalibus, vt in ca. quo iure 8. distinct. superius alleg.
units.tr: Moreover, temporal judges in the Kingdom of France take cognizance of the possessory suit concerning an ecclesiastical matter, when the possession of an ecclesiastical or beneficial thing is something temporal and not spiritual, according to Innocent in cap. cum dilecti, de elect. although some argue against this. But Bernard seems to maintain it in cap. literis, de iur. calum. because possession has largely the character of fact, and therefore a temporal judge can take cognizance of it, and even in spiritual or ecclesiastical matters, according to Bernard in l. potest pupil. ff. de auto. tutor. and in l. Titia. ff. soluto matri. and more fully in l. quoties, de iud. C. and John Andrew in c. tuam, ext. de ordin. cognit. and Paul of Lea in cap. 1. de vsu. in Clem. who say that when a question of fact arising in an ecclesiastical matter is at issue, a temporal judge can take cognizance of it. Hence, according to the ancient laws, bishops had no territory, and therefore did not execute their sentences; rather temporal judges executed them, according to Cynus and Baldus in l. episcop. C. de episcop. audient. And therefore, although cognizance of dowry belongs to the Church, as in cap. 1. & 2. de donat. inter vir. & vxor. yet insofar as the execution of fact is required in it, that execution will be made by the secular judge and not by the ecclesiastical one, according to Innocent in ca. significasti, de offic. delegat. on one interpretation. From this we shall also say that the inventory of the temporal goods of clerics ought to be made by temporal judges, when those goods are subject to temporal authority, as in cap. quo iure 8. distinct. cited above.

units.la: Postremo reperio alios sex casus, in quibus iudex temporalis sine metu excommunicationis potest capere clericum & incarcerare. Primus est in casibus praedictis, in quibus potest fieri punitio seu coertio personae, quando cui licet, quod maius est, &c. Secundus de mandato iudicis Ecclesiastici ipsorum malefactorum ad fines remittendi, in cap. vniuersitatis, & cap. vt fama, de sent. excom. & ita tenent Archi. & Ioan. Andr. in ca. si clerici, eo tit. li. 6. Tertius, quando iudex laicus videt clericum ad alterius iniuriam praeparatum, & non adest Praelatus suus, si ipsum clericum alias compescere non potest, nam tunc potest eum sine metu excommunicationis ligare vel incarcerare, secundum Innoc. qui hoc notat in ca. si vero. de sent. excom. quem sequitur Lucas de Penn. in l. generali, de decurion. lib. 10. C.
units.tr: Finally, I find six other cases in which a temporal judge may, without fear of excommunication, arrest a cleric and imprison him. The first is in the cases mentioned above, in which punishment or restraint of the person can be carried out, when cui licet, quod maius est, etc. The second is on the mandate of an ecclesiastical judge, to remit the malefactors for the purpose of punishment, in cap. vniuersitatis, & cap. vt fama, de sent. excom. and so Archidiaconus and John Andrew hold in ca. si clerici, eo tit. li. 6. The third is when a lay judge sees a cleric prepared to do harm to another, and his own prelate is not present, and he cannot otherwise restrain that cleric; for then he may bind or imprison him without fear of excommunication, according to Innocent, who notes this in ca. si vero. de sent. excom. whom Lucas de Penna follows in l. generali, de decurion. lib. 10. C.

units.la: Quartus, quando iudex secularis reperit clericum in flagranti crimine, quem potest per viginti horas detinere, secundum Bernar. & Ioan. Andr. Hosti. tamen contra in ca. vt fame, de sent. excomm. & Gau. & Guil. de Monte Laudun. in ca. 1. de offic. ordinan. in Clem. Quos sequitur Henr. Bohic. in ca. cum non ab homine, de iudic. Archi. tamen in ca. presbyt. 81. dist. Luc. de Penn. post eum in d. l. generali, sequitur opinionem primam, quae videtur esse consuetudine approbata. Quintus casus est, quando maritus inuenit clericum adulterantem cum vxore sua, secundum Hosti. & Henr. Bohic. d. ca. si vero, de sent. excomm. Cui autem pertinet vel incumbit probatio clericatus, & coram quo, est hodie declaratum, in cap. si iudex laicus, de sent. excomm. lib. 6.
units.tr: The fourth is when a secular judge finds a cleric in the act of a crime, whom he may hold for twenty hours, according to Bernard and John Andrew. Hostiensis, however, holds the contrary in ca. vt fame, de sent. excomm. and Gaucelm and William de Monte Laudun in ca. 1. de offic. ordinan. in Clem. whom Henry Bohic follows in ca. cum non ab homine, de iudic. Archidiaconus, however, in ca. presbyt. 81. dist. Lucas de Penna after him in the said l. generali follows the first opinion, which seems to have been approved by custom. The fifth case is when a husband finds a cleric committing adultery with his wife, according to Hostiensis and Henry Bohic on the said ca. si vero, de sent. excomm. On whom the burden of proving clerical status falls, and before whom, has now been declared in cap. si iudex laicus, de sent. excomm. lib. 6.

units.la: Sextus & vltimus casus est, vbi timetur de fuga debitoris etiam clerici, quoniam creditor potest tunc debitorem capere, iuxta terminos Lait praetor. §. si debitorem. ff. quae in fraud. cred. alie. sunt. vt restit. & hoc absque metu excommunicationis, vt singulariter ponit Ioan. Andr. in Nouella, & Innoc. in cap. vt fame, de sent. excom. & ibi de hoc.
units.tr: The sixth and last case is where there is fear of the flight of a debtor, even a cleric, since the creditor may then arrest the debtor, according to the terms of the Praetor's edict in Lait praetor. §. si debitorem. ff. quae in fraud. cred. alie. sunt. vt restit. and this without fear of excommunication, as John Andrew singularly lays down in the Novella, and Innocent in cap. vt fame, de sent. excom. and there on this matter.

units.la: Haec vero citra praeiudicium potestatis, iurisdictionis & libertatis ecclesiae perstrinxisse sufficiat, quibus nullatenus derogare intendo, sed solum pro tuenda veritate iustitiae praedicta gratificari praesumpsi. Non enim debemus esse adulterantes verbum Dei, vetante Apostolo, 2. Cor. ca. 2. vnde non solum de ecclesia, sed etiam de Deo valde perhorrendum est, aliquid falsi astruere, etiamsi ad eius laudem videatur pertinere, vt scribit Magister Sententiarum, & ad Cor. 15. subiungens, quod non minori sed maiori fortassis scelere, si in Deo laudatur falsitas, quam vituperatur veritas, quod est tenaci animo commendandum, & perpetuo menti tenendum. Omnia tamen submittendo correctioni & determinationi sanctae matris ecclesiae. Nam sicut errare vel minus sapere communis est infirmitas: sic & in errore persistere praecipuum est horrendae iniquitatis. Deo gratias. Bernardus Laurenti utriusque iuris Doctor.
units.tr: These things, set out without prejudice to the power, jurisdiction and liberty of the Church, may suffice; I intend to derogate from none of them, but have presumed to set forth the foregoing only in order to defend the truth of justice. For we ought not to be adulterating the word of God, as the Apostle forbids, 2 Cor. ch. 2. Hence it is most dreadful not only with respect to the Church but also with respect to God to assert anything false, even if it seems to pertain to his praise, as the Master of the Sentences writes, commenting on 1 Cor. 15, adding that it is perhaps no less but rather greater wickedness if falsehood is praised in God than if truth is disparaged; this is to be commended to a tenacious mind and kept perpetually in memory. Nevertheless, I submit all things to the correction and determination of holy mother Church. For, as to err or to know less is a common weakness, so to persist in error is the chief mark of dreadful iniquity. Thanks be to God. Bernard Laurenti, Doctor of both laws.

units.la: ARTICVLI PROPOSITI, DELIBERATI ET CONCLVSI IN CONCILIO ECCLESIAE GALLICANAE, congregato mense Septembri anno Domini M. DX. in civitate Turonensi, auctoritate Christianiss- imi Regis D. Ludouici XII.
units.tr: Articles proposed, deliberated and concluded in the Council of the Gallican Church, convened in the month of September in the year of the Lord 1510, in the city of Tours, by the authority of the most Christian King, Lord Louis XII.

units.la: I. AN liceat Papae bellum inferre Principibus temporalibus, in terris quae non sunt de patrimonio vel dominio Ecclesiae, &c.
units.tr: I. Whether it is lawful for the Pope to make war upon temporal princes, in lands which are not part of the patrimony or dominion of the Church, etc.

units.la: Conclusum fuit vnanimiter per Concilium, Papam non posse, nec debere.
units.tr: It was concluded unanimously by the Council that the Pope neither may nor ought to do so.

units.la: II. AN liceat Principi defendenti se & sua, non solum propulsare armis eiusmodi iniuriam, sed etiam inuadere terras ecclesiae possessas a Papa notorio hoste suo; non tamen ea intentione vt illas retineat, sed tantum vt impediat, ne per eas Papa illefortior & potentior sit ad offendendum dictum Principem & suos.
units.tr: II. Whether it is lawful for a prince, defending himself and his own, not only to repel such an injury by arms, but also to invade lands of the Church held by the Pope, his notorious enemy; not, however, with the intention of keeping them, but only so that the Pope may not be made stronger and more powerful through them for attacking the said prince and his people.

units.la: Conclusum est per Concilium Principem tunc posse sub conditionibus & qualitatibus in Articulo propositis.
units.tr: It was concluded by the Council that the prince may do so under the conditions and qualifications set out in the article.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: AN ob tale odium notorium & aggressionem iniustam, liceat tali Principi subtrahere se ab obedientia huiusmodi Pontificis, attento etiam quod Pontifex concitauit alios quosdam Principes & communitates, imo & tentauit cogere ad inuadendas terras & dominia eiusdem principis, qui potius beneuolentia sedis Apostolicæ dignus fuit.
units.tr: Whether, on account of such notorious hatred and unjust aggression, it is lawful for such a prince to withdraw himself from the obedience of such a Pontiff, especially since the Pontiff has stirred up certain other princes and communities, and even attempted to compel them to invade the lands and dominions of this same prince, who rather deserved the goodwill of the Apostolic See.

units.la: Conclusum est per concilium, Principem posse ab obedientia Papæ subducere ac subtrahere: non tamen in totum & indistincte, sed pro tuitione tantum ac defensione iurium suorum temporalium.
units.tr: It was concluded by the Council that the prince may withdraw and withhold himself from the obedience of the Pope; yet not wholly and indiscriminately, but only for the protection and defence of his temporal rights.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: TAli subtractione licite facta, quid agendum sit, tum Principi ipsi ac subditis eius, tum etiam Prælatis & Ecclesiasticis personis regni sui in rebus de quibus ad sedem Apostolicam antea recurri solebat.
units.tr: Once such a withdrawal has been lawfully made, what is to be done, both by the prince himself and his subjects, and also by the prelates and ecclesiastical persons of his realm, in matters for which they were previously accustomed to have recourse to the Apostolic See.

units.la: Conclusum est per Concilium, seruandum esse ius commune antiquum, & Pragmaticam sanctionem Regni, ex decretis sacrosancti Concilii Basiliensis desumptam.
units.tr: It was concluded by the Council that the ancient common law is to be observed, and the Pragmatic Sanction of the kingdom, drawn from the decrees of the sacred Council of Basel.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: AN liceat huiusmodi Principi Christiano armis tueri ac defendere alium Principem sibi confœderatum, & cuius protectionem legitime suscepit, &c.
units.tr: Whether it is lawful for such a Christian prince to protect and defend by arms another prince allied to him, whose protection he has lawfully undertaken, etc.

units.la: Conclusum fuit per Concilium, licere.
units.tr: It was concluded by the Council that it is lawful.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: SI quod ius talis Pontifex ad se pertinere contendat, vt patrimonii sanctæ Ecclesiæ Romanæ partem: contra Princeps Imperii, iuris sui esse dicat, & de ea controuersia paratus sit & offerat stare arbitrio vel iudicio bonorum virorum per compromissum prout de iure: an eo casu liceat Pontifici absque alia causæ cognitione, bellum inferre dicto Principi: & si fecerit, an liceat Principi armis resistere, & aliis etiam Principibus in huiusmodi dissidio ei adesse, eumque defendere: maxime illis qui ei cognatione vel affinitate coniuncti sunt, cum etiam per centum annos proximos, Ecclesia Romana in eius iuris controuersi possessione non fuerit.
units.tr: If such a Pontiff claims some right belonging to him, as part of the patrimony of the holy Roman Church, while the prince of the Empire says it is his own right, and is ready to submit this disputed matter to the arbitration or judgment of good men by compromise, as is lawful: in that case, may the Pontiff make war upon the said prince without any other examination of the cause? And if he does so, may the prince resist by arms, and may other princes also come to his aid in such a dispute and defend him, especially those who are joined to him by blood or marriage, since for the last hundred years the Roman Church has not been in possession of the disputed right?

units.la: Conclusum est per Concilium, licere Principi hoc casu resistere de facto, & aliis ei adesse in iure suo tuendo.
units.tr: It was concluded by the Council that in this case the prince may resist in fact, and others may come to his aid in defending his right.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: QVid si Papa nolit acceptare quod Princeps iuridice & honeste offert, sed contra, non obseruato iuris ordine, contra talem Principem pronunciet sententiam aliquam, an ei obtemperandum sit, maxime cum non est integrum ac tutum tali Principi ad sedem Romanam ire vel mittere, & ius suum via iuris ciuilis, & rationibus defendere.
units.tr: What if the Pope refuses to accept what the prince offers in a lawful and honourable way, but on the contrary, without observing the order of law, pronounces some sentence against such a prince: is it to be obeyed, especially since it is neither safe nor possible for such a prince to go or send to the Roman See, and to defend his right by the way of civil law and by reasons?

units.la: Conclusum est per Concilium, non teneri talem Principem parere tali sententia.
units.tr: It was concluded by the Council that such a prince is not bound to obey such a sentence.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: SI Pontifex iniuste, ordine iuris non seruato, procedens de facto, & manu armata, pronunciet ac publicet aliquas Censuras contra Principes sibi resistentes eorumque subditos & confœderatos, an ei parendum sit, & quod remedium adhibendum.
units.tr: If the Pontiff, proceeding unjustly, without observing the order of law, proceeds in fact with an armed hand, and pronounces and publishes certain censures against princes resisting him and their subjects and allies, is he to be obeyed, and what remedy is to be applied?

units.la: Conclusum est vnanimiter per Concilium, talem sententiam nullam esse, nec de iure vel alio quocunque modo ligare.
units.tr: It was concluded unanimously by the Council that such a sentence is null, and does not bind by law or in any other way.

units.la: Visum est tamen Concilio, ante omnia, mittendos ab Ecclesia Gallicana legatos ad D. Papam Iulium, qui fraterna charitate, & secundum Euangelicam correctionem, eum admoneant, vt à coeptis desistere velit, pacemque & concordiam Principum amplecti. Quod si nolit legatos in hoc audire, interpelletur de conuocando Concilio libero, iuxta sacrosancti Basiliensis decreta, & hoc facto responsoque eius accepto prouidebitur prout ius erit.
units.tr: Yet it seemed good to the Council that, before all else, legates should be sent by the Gallican Church to Pope Julius, who, with brotherly charity and according to the Gospel correction, should admonish him to be willing to desist from his undertakings and to embrace peace and concord among the princes. But if he is unwilling to hear the legates in this, he should be petitioned concerning the convoking of a free Council, according to the decrees of the sacred Council of Basel; and when this has been done and his answer received, provision will be made as the law allows.

units.la: APOLOGIAE SACRI PISANI CONCILII CELEBRATI
units.tr: APOLOGY OF THE HOLY PISAN COUNCIL CONVENED

units.la: Anno Domini M. D. XI.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1511.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: 1. Vmilitas, Constantia, & veritas, tres sunt dotes Christi atq; ecclesiae eius sponsa.
units.tr: 1. Humility, constancy, and truth are the three gifts of Christ and of his bride, the Church.

units.la: 2. Iulius II. duas acerbissimas euulgauit literas Apostolicas, quae causam praebuerunt huis Apologiae.
units.tr: 2. Julius II issued two most bitter apostolic letters, which gave occasion to this Apology.

units.la: 3. Humilis & modesta responsio Patrum Pisanorum ad eos qui consilium dederunt Iulio II. ut Concilium Lateranense indiceret, & censuris Patres Pisanos percelleret.
units.tr: 3. A humble and moderate reply of the Pisan Fathers to those who advised Julius II to summon the Lateran Council and to strike the Pisan Fathers with censures.

units.la: 4. Depulsio quatuordecim conuitiorum Patribus Pisanis obiectorum.
units.tr: 4. Refutation of the fourteen reproaches objected to the Pisan Fathers.

units.la: 5. Summa capita rerum, quae Patribus Pisanis à Iulio II. obiiciebantur, & earum dilutio.
units.tr: 5. The main heads of the charges which Julius II brought against the Pisan Fathers, and their refutation.

units.la: 6. Patres Pisani nunquam affectarunt dignitatem Pontificiam, sed aristocraticam moderationem, qua Christus primatum S. sedis Apostolicae temperauit, retinere voluerunt.
units.tr: 6. The Pisan Fathers never aimed at papal dignity, but wished to keep the aristocratic moderation by which Christ tempered the primacy of the Holy Apostolic See.

units.la: 7. Cardinales Pisani, à Curia Romana decesserunt, eo quod nedum in sententiis liberi, sed nec in vita quidem tuti erant, quando Apostolicae praeceptiones notorium continent periculum, audiri quidem sed non impleri debent.
units.tr: 7. The Pisan cardinals withdrew from the Roman Curia, because they were not only free in their opinions but not even safe in their lives; when apostolic commands carry a notorious danger, they ought to be heard but not obeyed.

units.la: 8. Memorati Cardinales recesserunt cum manu militari, ut se à periculo & insidiis episcopi Concordiens. eximerent.
units.tr: 8. The said cardinals withdrew under military escort, so that they might free themselves from the danger and snares of the bishop of Concordia.

units.la: 9. Patres fatentur se aliqua dissimulasse, ut fraudes & dolos episcopi Concordiensis vitarent.
units.tr: 9. The Fathers confess that they dissembled some matters, so as to avoid the frauds and tricks of the bishop of Concordia.

units.la: 10. Responsio ad obiectionem duorum Cardinalium, qui dicebant falsum esse se assensum praebuisse convocationi Pisana Synodi.
units.tr: 10. Reply to the objection of two cardinals, who said it was false that they had given their assent to the convocation of the Synod of Pisa.

units.la: 11. Omnes Canones, quibus docetur Papam debere Concilia generalia convocare, intelligi debent regulariter & ordinarie: nam extraordinarie & in certis casibus congregari possunt absque Papa.
units.tr: 11. All the canons which teach that the Pope ought to convene general councils must be understood as regular and ordinary; for in extraordinary cases and in certain circumstances councils may assemble without the Pope.

units.la: 12. Indictio Concilii Pisani, quatuor firmissimis principiis nititur, praecepto sci. ecclesiae, voto, ac iuramento Papae & Cardinalium, nec non etiam ad vitandum grauissimum & intolerabile scandalum.
units.tr: 12. The indiction of the Council of Pisa rests on four most firm principles: the precept of the Church, the vow and oath of the Pope and cardinals, and also the need to avoid a most grave and intolerable scandal.

units.la: 13. Praeceptum ducitur ex sessione 39. Concilii Constantiensis: dilutio obiectionum contra hoc praeceptum.
units.tr: 13. The precept is derived from the thirty-ninth session of the Council of Constance; refutation of the objections against this precept.

units.la: 14. Depulsio eorum quae obiiciebantur, ad votum & iuramentum Papae excusandum.
units.tr: 14. Answer to the points that were objected, in order to excuse the vow and oath of the Pope.

units.la: 15. Quo casu concedatur alicui mora purgatio & de legibus ad eam requisitis: sero mora purgatur, cum ius ad alios devolutum est.
units.tr: 15. In what case a delay may be granted to someone for purgation, and the laws required for it: a purgation delayed too long is made when the right has passed to others.

units.la: 16. Iulius II. armatus Concilium Romae indixit, non tam studio liberi Concilii habendi, quam impediendi ne haberetur, & ne de ecclesia reformanda ageretur.
units.tr: 20. Julius II, under arms, summoned a council at Rome, not so much from zeal for holding a free council as from a wish to prevent one being held, and to prevent the reform of the Church from being discussed.

units.la: 17. Cardinales qui Pisanam Synodum indixerunt, quamdiu Romae degerunt, non ausi sunt mentionem facere habendi Concilii, propter notissimam Iulii II. violentiam.
units.tr: 17. The cardinals who summoned the Synod of Pisa, as long as they stayed in Rome, did not dare to mention holding a council, on account of the notorious violence of Julius II.

units.la: 18. Vtrum Papa in causa propria Concilium debeat convocare: frustra alicuius auctoritas contra semetipsum expectatur: & utrum Ioannes XXIII. Concilium Constantiense contra semetipsum indixerit.
units.tr: 18. Whether the Pope ought to convene a council in his own cause: it is vain to look for anyone's authority against himself; and whether John XXIII convened the Council of Constance against himself.

units.la: 19. Dilutio obiectionum contra temporis brevitatem, & quodnam tempus olim Patribus ecclesiae primitiua ut convenirent ad Concilium praescriberetur.
units.tr: 19. Refutation of the objections against the brevity of the time, and what time was formerly prescribed to the Fathers of the primitive Church for assembling in council.

units.la: 20. Ciuitatem Pisanam maxime idoneam esse habendo Concilio generali: & de numero Praelatorum qui interfuerunt primo Concilio Pisano, ad extinguendam schisma.
units.tr: 20. That the city of Pisa is most suitable for holding a general council; and concerning the number of prelates who took part in the first Council of Pisa, for ending the schism.

units.la: 21. Ab eo tempore quo Romani Pontifices habuerunt arces atque armatas custodias, Roma non fuit idonea habendis Conciliis: nam Spiritus sanctus non afflat nisi liberas mentes: Unde cum Iulius II. exercitum habeat instructissimum, Roma non est tutus locus iis qui de ecclesia reformanda libere loqui vellent.
units.tr: 21. From the time when the Roman Pontiffs held fortresses and armed guards, Rome has not been fit for holding councils: for the Holy Spirit breathes only on free minds. Hence, since Julius II has a most well-equipped army, Rome is not a safe place for those who wished to speak freely about reforming the Church.

units.la: 22. De censuris irrogatis contra Patres Pisanos: & necessitate liberi Concilii habendi, ad spiritum ecclesiae retinendum, & disciplinam ecclesiasticam vindicandam.
units.tr: 22. On the censures imposed against the Pisan Fathers, and on the necessity of holding a free council, to preserve the spirit of the Church and to vindicate ecclesiastical discipline.

units.la: THEOLOGICI VATIS ET SACRI IVRECONSVLTI DOMINI Zachariae Ferrerii, Subasiensis Abbatis Epigramma.
units.tr: EPIGRAM OF THE THEOLOGIAN-POET AND SACRED LAWYER, LORD ZACHARIAS FERRERIUS, ABBOT OF SUBASIO.

units.la: Quisquis auet sancta de religione doceri, Non pede praecipiti curritet istud opus. Sint testitudinei gressus, sit odora Lycisca Vis, oculi Lyncis, Palladis ingenium. Ponderet ingentes in paruo Codice sensus, Relegat, & fructus colliget innumeros. Tollitur ambigui quicquid contingere possit Contra Pisani foedera Concilii. Iam pateat quanto diuini robore iuris Fundamenta loces, culmina, tecta, gradus. Sermo benignus adest, & summa modestia linguae, Probra, Simultates, pagina docta fugit. Dat sine verborum phaleris praeguantia dicta Et sine nugarum syrmate, vera parit.
units.tr: Whoever wishes to be taught about sacred religion, let him not run at this work with headlong haste. Let his steps be tortoise-slow, let him have the keen nose of a hound, the eyes of a lynx, the wit of Pallas. Let him weigh the great meanings in this small volume, read it through, and gather its countless fruits. Whatever could be doubtful is removed by it, against the treaties of the Pisan Council. Now let it be clear by how much strength of divine law you lay its foundations, heights, roofs, and steps. A gentle speech is present, and the utmost moderation of tongue; it shuns insults, hostilities, and learned pages. Without the trappings of words it offers weighty sayings, and without the fringe of trifles it brings forth truths.

units.la: APOLOGIA SACRI PI- SANI CONCILII.
units.tr: Apology of the Holy Council of Pisa

units.la: REVERENDISSIMI IN CHRISTO PATRES ET DOMINI S. R. E. Cardinales simul cum aliis secunda Pisana Synodi indictoribus, qui alias de mense Maii anni praesentis, Concilium generale vniuersalis Ecclesia iuxta illius praeceptum & necessitatem Pisis tenendum indixerunt, & conuocarunt cum aliis Principibus, Prelatis, & Potentatibus, sibi adhaerere, pro Dei causa, volentibus, ad futuram rei memoriam.
units.tr: The most reverend fathers in Christ and lords, the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, together with the other instigators of the second Synod of Pisa, who in May of this present year called and convened a general Council of the universal Church, to be held at Pisa in accordance with its command and need, and who, together with other princes, prelates and potentates who wish to adhere to them for the cause of God, send this for the memory of the matter in future.

units.la: REATOR & redemptor noster Christus Dominus, qui est via, veritas & vita, & qui ad hoc natum esse & in mundum venisse se asserit, vt testimonium perhiberet veritati, & in quo non est inuentum mendacium, nec inuentus est dolus in ore eius, ipse se mitem appellat & humilem, ac vere etiam fuisse constantem & fortem, ad mortem vsque acerbissimam pro veritate asserenda testatur, adeo vt omnis Christi actio humano potissimum generi imitabilis veritas sit & constans & humilis, veritatemque ipsam illius magister non aliter custodiri recte posse doceat, quam constantia & humilitate: altera ne nos terror a vero deiiciat: altera ne nos excellentia & firmitas veritatis extollat, & in magnis & mirabilibus super nos efferri nos faciat, vnde tria haec pretiosa monilia sponsae suae, non habenti maculam nec rugam, Ecclesiae videl. suae sanctae catholicae, cuius fideles omnes merito aut numero mystica membra sumus, praecipue seruanda reliquit, vt in fundamento domus suae quam perennis dicebat sanctitudo, & cuius decorem prae omnibus dilexerat, tanquam sapiens architectus triplicem hunc angularem lapidem reponeret, cui innixa omnis structura firma subsisteret, & sanctum Dei templum redderet gloriosum. Vnde apud Ioannem ait, Qui ex veritate est, audit vocem meam. Et alibi, Qui sequitur me, tollat crucem suam & sequatur me. Et rursum, Discite a me, quia mitis sum & humilis corde.
units.tr: Our Creator and Redeemer, Christ the Lord, who is the way, the truth and the life, and who declares that he was born for this purpose and came into the world to bear witness to the truth, and in whom no lie was found, nor was guile found in his mouth, calls himself meek and humble. He also testifies that he was truly constant and strong, even to the most bitter death, in asserting the truth. So every action of Christ is a truth that the human race can most of all imitate, a constant and humble truth. And as its teacher he teaches that the truth itself cannot rightly be guarded except by constancy and humility: the one so that terror does not drive us from the truth, the other so that the excellence and firmness of the truth do not lift us up and make us raise ourselves above others in great and wonderful things. Hence he left these three precious jewels especially to be preserved by his bride, the Church, which has no spot or wrinkle, that is, his holy catholic Church, of which all the faithful are rightly, or by number, mystical members. He did this so that, like a wise architect, he might set this threefold corner stone in the foundation of his house, which he called everlasting holiness and whose beauty he had loved above all others. On it every firm structure would rest and stand, and he would make the holy temple of God glorious. Hence he says in John, "He who is of the truth hears my voice." And elsewhere, "Whoever follows me, let him take up his cross and follow me." And again, "Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart."

units.la: 2 Nnper autem quum non sine graui moerore, & mentis amaritudine vago relatu acceperimus sub nomine sanctissimi D.N. Iulii Papae II. (nonnullorum vt creditur suggestione, qui magis loqui quaerunt sibi placentia, quam fidelium quietem & pacem) disseminatas esse per vniuersam Ecclesiam duas epistolas apostolicas: alteram quā dicunt Concilii, in qua in dictores secundi Pisani Concilii grauioribus increpationibus & immeritis appellationibus obiurgat, indictionemque ipsam annullat & reuocat, aliudque Concilium Romae instaurat, alteram monitorii, in qua nonnullos ex dictis indictoribus, vt a prosecutione Pisanae synodi abstineat, & in vrbe Roma personas suas sub breui quodam praestituto termino exhibeant, sub grauissimis censuris & poenis monet & citat.
units.tr: 2 Recently, however, we have received by vague report, not without grave sorrow and bitterness of mind, that under the name of our most holy lord, Pope Julius II (at the suggestion, as is believed, of some men who seek to say what pleases them rather than what brings the quiet and peace of the faithful), two apostolic letters have been spread throughout the whole Church. One they call a letter of the Council, in which he rebukes the instigators of the second Synod of Pisa with heavy reproaches and undeserved names, annuls and revokes the convocation itself, and sets up another Council at Rome. The other is a monitory, in which he warns and summons some of the said instigators, under the most grave censures and penalties, to abstain from pursuing the Synod of Pisa and to present themselves in person in the city of Rome within a short fixed period.

units.la: 3 Nos cum illius auxilio, qui in Euangelio assistentiam suam ante reges & praesides pollicetur professoribus veritatis, vniti omnes eodem corde & ore, non vt literae illae nos disiungere satagebant, sed iuxta Apostolum alter alterius onera portantes, vt quae communi consilio pro bono ecclesiae edeximus, communi voto tueamur, curabimus pro Dei causa vna communi epistola duarum illarum capitibus constanti & humili veritate satisfacere, vt pro viribus sermo noster Christianae disciplinae conueniat. Respondebimus itaque in omni patientia & mansuetudine non ad singula epistolarum, quae sunt pene innumera, & si discuterentur omnia responsalis epistolae modum excederent, nec ipsi Principi directe respondere mens est, quamuis in factis propriis & personalibus signanter legali contentione suscitata, scriptis eius reniti possit & debeat. Nam & alina Balaam pro veritatis custodia, domino suo intrepide contradixit, & nos non serui modo, sed & filii, & fratres, liberi sumus, qua libertate iuxta Apostolum Christus nos liberauit, parisq; cum Paulo in hoc iurisdictionis, qui Petro quia immemoresset in obseruatione legalium tertii Hierosolymitani Concilii, in faciem restitit, & tamen culpa Petri (vtpote in gratia confirmati) leuis fuisse creditur. Sed cum verba illarum epistolarum tam aspera & grauia, ex tam leui causa simplicis nostrae admonitionis concilii mentis principis adscribi nodebeant (nam & hominum sicut & apum reges fortioribus aculeis carere debere omnis philosophia praedicat) non ipsi itaque, sed consultoribus, aut ordinatoribus literarū, qui grauius peccatum habent, prout dominus Pontio praesidi dixerat, respondebitur: nec omnibus consultoribus: quum verisimile sit antiquiores & vere necessarios, & qui in causis cardinaliū iuxta Apostolicas iuratas constitutiones & capitula iustiorem vocem habent, talia non potuisse consulere. Illis ergo ordinatoribus, quandoq; in prima, interdum in tertia persona vtcunque respondendo, ordinem philosophorum seruabimus, qui primo nomina, inde res solent perscrutari: nam & sermocinales scientiae tempore reales procedunt, in rebus autem obiectis ipsarum literarum ordini pro posse insistemus.
units.tr: 3 We, with the help of him who in the Gospel promises his assistance before kings and governors to the professors of truth, united in one heart and mouth, and not as those letters tried to divide us but, according to the Apostle, bearing one another's burdens, will take care, for the cause of God, to answer the heads of those two letters in one common letter, with a constant and humble truth, and so, as far as we can, to make our speech fit Christian discipline. We will therefore reply with all patience and gentleness. We will not answer each of the letters, which are almost countless, and if all were discussed the reply would exceed its proper measure. Nor is it our intention to reply directly to the Prince himself, although in his own and personal matters, especially those raised by legal dispute, he can and ought to be resisted in writing. For Balaam too fearlessly contradicted his lord in defence of the truth. And we are not only servants but also sons and brothers, free; with this liberty, according to the Apostle, Christ has made us free. In this matter we are like Paul, who withstood Peter to his face because he had neglected the observance of the legal decrees of the third Council of Jerusalem; yet Peter's fault, since he was confirmed in grace, is believed to have been slight. But since the words of those letters are so harsh and grave, they should not be ascribed to the mind of the prince for such a slight cause as our simple admonition of the Council. (Every philosophy declares that kings, like the kings of bees among men, ought to lack the stronger stings.) So we will reply not to him himself, but to his advisers or to the drafters of the letters, who have the graver sin, just as the Lord said to the governor Pontius. Nor will we reply to all the advisers, since it is likely that the older and truly necessary ones, who according to the sworn Apostolic constitutions and chapters have the more authoritative voice in causes concerning cardinals, could not have advised such things. So, to those drafters, responding sometimes in the first person and sometimes in the third, however it turns out, we will follow the order of the philosophers, who usually examine first the names and then the things. For the sciences of discourse also proceed at times from words to realities, and in the matters raised we will keep to the order of the letters as far as we can.

units.la: 4 Ordinatores itaque immemores doctrinae Domini, qui apud Matthaeum statuit, Quicunque dixerit fratri suo Raccha, reus erit iudicio, & qui dixerit Fatue, reus erit gehennae ignis: pro leui tamen concilii admonitione supra modum excandescentes, non modo incerto conuitio aliquo, aut fatuos modo patres Pisanae synodi nuncupant? sed insana Ecclesiae membra, Acephalos, locustas, nomine tamen Cardinales,
units.tr: 4 The drafters, then, forgetting the teaching of the Lord, who in Matthew laid down, "Whoever says to his brother, 'Raca,' shall be liable to judgment, and whoever says, 'Fool,' shall be liable to the fire of hell," yet flaring up beyond measure over a slight admonition of the Council, do not only call the fathers of the Synod of Pisa by some vague insult, or merely "fools," but insane members of the Church, Acephali, locusts, though named Cardinals,

units.la: lis, les, schismaticos, Iudaos, filios tenebrarum, synagogam Sathana, ecclesiam malignantium schismaticam, atque etiam conuenticulum Dathan, & Abiron, Acatium & Dioscorum, & caetera id genus iniuriarum, plenis titulis appellant, aliumque ex partibus aurigam, & clauium moderatorem per calumniam pungunt, & coram vniuersa ecclesia, quod eius splendori & spiritualitati studeant, criminantur. Et quamuis Christus Dominus beatitudinem repromittat iis, qui propter nomen suum ab hominibus maledicuntur, & persecutionem patiuntur, vnde & Apostoli ibant gaudentes a conspectu Concilii, quoniam digni habiti sunt pro nomine Iesu contumeliam pati, & Petrus beatos appellat propter Dominum exprobratos, & in iis omnib. Psalmista possint dicere gaudentes quoniam propter te Domine sustinuimus opprobrium, & existimati sumus, sicut oues occisionis; & illi excusationem & vltionem remittere, qui ait, Mihi vindicam & ego retribuam; Quia tamen haec improperio plurimum improportionata sunt Patrum meritis, qui summis laudibus, quod culturae agri Dominici omni conatu intendunt, esse extollendi, & non solum eos tangunt, sed subinte lligendo plures alios comprehendunt: attendentesque Augustini dictum esse, non licere silentium viris sanctis dum reprehenduntur, in iis aquibus vitam suam longe abesse sciunt, & dicere, sufficit nobis recta ante Deum conscientia, si aestimationem hominum impudenter & crudeliter contemnunt; Conscientia enim nobis necessaria est, Fama autem proximo, de qua Sapiens, Crudelis est qui famam negligit, & alibi, fama bona impinguat ossa, ideo attendentes dictum Apostoli ad Colossenses, Qui iniuriam facit, pati expectet. Verbum illud Senecae ordinatoribus iis (quibus inuiti) rependunt, incerta conuitia ab iis plurimum irrogari qui iis abundent: Aristotelisq; sermo fuit, qualis vnusquisque est, talia facit aut dicit, nempe quatuordecim illae graues appellationes nullo commercio Patres istos contingunt.
units.tr: schismatics, Jews, sons of darkness, a synagogue of Satan, a malignant schismatic church, and also a conventicle of Dathan and Abiram, Acacius and Dioscorus, and other injuries of that kind they name with full titles. By calumny they also sting the others as charioteer and keeper of the keys, and before the whole Church they accuse them of striving after its splendour and spirituality. Although Christ the Lord promises blessedness to those who are reviled by men and suffer persecution for his name's sake, and although the Apostles went rejoicing from the presence of the Council, because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus, and Peter calls blessed those who are reproached for the Lord, and in all these things the Psalmist can say, "Rejoicing that for your sake, O Lord, we bear reproach, and are counted as sheep for the slaughter," and leaves vindication and vengeance to him who says, "Vengeance is mine, and I will repay," still, these reproaches are very ill-suited to the merits of the Fathers, who with every effort strive to be extolled with the highest praise for their cultivation of the Lord's field. They touch not only them but, by implication, take in many others. Considering Augustine's saying that holy men may not keep silent while they are reproached in matters from which they know their lives are far removed, and that it is enough for us to have a right conscience before God if they shamelessly and cruelly despise the esteem of men ("For conscience is necessary to us, but reputation to our neighbour," of which the Wise Man says, "Cruel is he who neglects a good name," and elsewhere, "A good name fattens the bones"), therefore, considering the Apostle's saying to the Colossians, "He who does injury, let him await the suffering," we return to those drafters, against their will, the word of Seneca: "Uncertain insults are very much heaped on by those who abound in them." And the saying of Aristotle was, "Whatever each one is, such things he does or says." Clearly, those fourteen grave names touch those Fathers not at all.

units.la: Quid enim cum membris insanis Ecclesiae qui sola causa sanitatis & puritatis suae tam studiose & per tot pericula congregatur? Quid cum acephalis? qui Christum pientissime colunt, quem iuxta Apostolum, dedit Deus caput super omnem ecclesiam, & vicarium suum ministeriale ecclesiae caput iusta obedientia venerantur & honorant? Quid locustas? magna apud Deum & ecclesiam animalia oculis plena, & spiritum Dei habentia, nisi quod humilitate cordis parua & modica mancipia Deo, & vicario suo ad ecclesiae splendorem cum effectu se offerunt; quare ergo Cardinales maximo fructu, & principes reales ecclesiae illius gratia ad omnia expositi pericula, solide se ostendunt? Quid cum schismate, iis qui ecclesiae veram vnionem, & ipsius veneranda praecepta seruant? & vota ac iuramenta sua Deo pro viribus reddunt? In quo Iudaeos referunt, qui Christi & sponsae honorem tam seriose deposcunt, tritumque sacrorum Conciliorum, quo fides firmata & purgata est, tam assidue effla gitant. Anne libri Constantiensis synodi tanquam Iudaeorum explodendi sunt, a quibus salus omnis ecclesiae maxime pendet? In quo filii tenebrarum, lucem ecclesiae requirentes? In quo synagogam Sathanae, vel ecclesiam malignantium, aut schismaticam conuenticulam referunt? qui innouationem sanctam ecclesiae, iuxta irrefragabilem & infallibilem Synodorum veritatem curant? Caueant ne haec aliorum obduratio, & vetustatis criminosae obseruatio & defensio, potius synagogam illam veterem referat, quam Dominus & verbis, & funiculis purgare conatus est. In quo Dathan & Abyron effigiantur patres? Numquid Pontificatum petierunt, vel auferre cui Dominus dedit, moliti sunt? Absit, Parentalii insidias, praeparent & mensas & monopolia, vt Pontificatu fruantur, Patres hi apud quos timor Domini sanctus permanet, & qui nouerunt tales ingressus absq; resignatione & restitutione desperatum aeternae salutis statum continere, obedientia contenti sunt, non praesidatu ambiunt, istis potissimum artibus asse quendum. Dum corpus ecclesiae bene valeat simul cum capite suo (cui plurimum studet) potius membra esse volunt, quam caput infectum. Quid sibi videtur hoc sub specie timoris schismatis, prius schisma incipere, & sub timore ne proripiatur primatus ecclesiae tyrannidem exercere, & malis illum artibus aucupari? Quid horum patrum humilitas & temperantia cofine habet cum Achatio & Dioscoro? qui violentia Concilia diripiebant, & suorum temporum patres ad subscribendum synodales epistolas gladiis super patrum capita vibratis, compellebant. Iubeat hic Dominus quiescere, nec enim sine amaritudine haec referri possunt. Filii sunt patres hi S.R.E. & sanctissimi D.N. quibus detrahere nullo modo cogitant, dum ecclesia reformata in libero vno generali concilio, honoretur, & dum sanctitas sua filios recognoscat. Sed quid aurigam & moderatore cosultores hi patrem alium calumniantur? qui aetate & sapientia minor est omnibus, & qui de se humilia semper concepit: & docendum se non sequendum patribus aliis pro Dei causa semper exhibuit. Nec ista tamen exprobratio aut aemulationis occasio charitatem patrum Dei honore fundatam quoquo modo turbatura est, Aurigam habeat patres Christum Dominum qui eorum est currus & auriga, per quem currum & splendorem ecclesiae comprehendant. Nec tamen qui plantat est aliquid, nec qui rigat, sed qui incrementum dat Deus: qui plantat autem & qui rigat apud eos, vnum sunt, quia in eis est cor vnum, & anima vna in Domino, & iuxta Domini & aurigae nostri Iesu Christi testamentu, Qui maior est inter eos, tanquam ministrator obedit, & qui primus est, tanquam seruus absq; elatione obsequitur. Sed haec grauia & ampullosa verba epistolarum consultores satis damnant, & aperta luce ostendunt, qua libertate Patres apud primam sedem vtantur. Si namq; contra liberos, & absentes, ac mediocri honore & fauore existimatos Cardinales, splendoremque ecclesiae petentes, pro simplici admonitione tot conuitia intorquentur; quid cum aliis non liberis & quodammodo aridis a Principum & populorum fauore fieri existimandum est, si tantillum praesidi non conueniant: Cessent ergo verba quae odia generant & charitatem vulnerant. Illis tamen omnib. improperiis facile dimittimus, si in patientia nostra & mansuetudine pacem reformationis Ecclesiae nanciscamur. Sed iam ad res transeamus: nec enim quum de rebus constat magnam vim in verbis faciendam esse docet Ambros. Resitaque patribus obiectas suo ordine transigamus.
units.tr: What, then, of the diseased members of the Church, who gather so eagerly, and through so many dangers, for the sole cause of its health and purity? What of the acephali, who worship Christ most devoutly, whom God, as the Apostle says, gave as head over the whole Church, and who honour and venerate with due obedience his ministerial vicar as the Church's head? What of the locusts, great creatures before God and the Church, full of eyes and having the Spirit of God, except that in humility of heart they offer themselves as small and modest servants of God and his vicar, to the splendour of the Church and with effect? Why then do the Cardinals, to their great credit, and the royal princes, expose themselves to every danger for the sake of that Church and show themselves steadfast? What of the schismatics, who keep the true union of the Church and its venerable precepts, and pay their vows and oaths to God as far as they are able? In this they resemble the Jews, who so earnestly demand the honour of Christ and his bride, and who so constantly cry out the well-worn [formula] of the sacred Councils, by which the faith was confirmed and purified. Must the books of the Council of Constance be hissed off the stage like those of the Jews, when all the salvation of the Church depends chiefly on them? In this are they sons of darkness, seeking the light of the Church? In this do they represent the synagogue of Satan, or the church of the malignant, or a schismatic little conventicle, who take care of the holy renewal of the Church according to the irrefragable and infallible truth of the Synods? Let them beware lest this obstinacy of others, and this observance and defence of a criminal antiquity, rather represent that old synagogue which the Lord tried to purge both with words and with cords. Are the Fathers here depicted as Dathan and Abiram? Did they seek the papacy, or plot to take away what the Lord has given? Far from it! These Fathers, in whom the holy fear of the Lord remains, and who know that entrance by such means, without resignation and restitution, keeps the state of eternal salvation in despair, are content with obedience; they do not court the presidency, nor do they seek it by those arts, and they do not lay snares through kinsmen, nor prepare both tables and monopolies, so that they may enjoy the papacy. While the body of the Church is in good health, together with its head (which they study most diligently), they would rather be members than a diseased head. What does it mean, under the appearance of fear of schism, to begin schism first, and, under fear lest the primacy of the Church be snatched away, to exercise tyranny and to angle for it by evil arts? What do the humility and temperance of these Fathers have in common with Achatius and Dioscorus, who seized councils by violence and compelled the Fathers of their own time to subscribe synodal letters, with swords brandished over the Fathers' heads? Let the Lord bid this be silent, for these things cannot be recounted without bitterness. These Fathers are sons of the Holy Roman Church and of our most holy Lord, whom they in no way think of disparaging, while the Church, reformed in a free and general council, is honoured, and while his holiness acknowledges them as sons. But why do these advisers of the ordinators slander another father, the charioteer and governor, who is younger than all in age and wisdom, who has always conceived of himself humbly, and who has always shown himself to be one to be taught, not one to be followed, by the other Fathers for the cause of God? Yet this reproach, or occasion of rivalry, shall in no way disturb the charity of the Fathers, founded on the honour of God. Let the Fathers have Christ the Lord as their charioteer, who is their chariot and charioteer, through whom they may comprehend both the chariot and the splendour of the Church. Nor is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase; and he who plants and he who waters among them are one, because in them there is one heart and one soul in the Lord, and according to the testament of our Lord and charioteer Jesus Christ, he who is greatest among them obeys as a servant, and he who is first serves without arrogance. But the ordinators' advisers condemn these grave and bombastic words enough, and by plain light show with what freedom the Fathers speak before the first see. For if, for simple admonition, so many reproaches are hurled against Cardinals who are free, absent, esteemed with moderate honour and favour, and who seek the splendour of the Church, what must be thought will happen with others who are not free and are in some way dried up, lacking the favour of princes and peoples, if they do not meet with even a little help? Let therefore those words cease which breed hatred and wound charity. Yet we shall easily set aside all these reproaches, if, by our patience and gentleness, we obtain the peace of a reformed Church. But now let us come to the matter itself: for when the facts are established, Ambrose teaches that not much weight should be put on words. Let us therefore take up the objections made against the Fathers in their proper order.

units.la: Obiiciunt ordinatores quadrupliciter. Primo, quinq; contra personas patrum: quod illicentiati recesserunt, quod mendacio usi, quod falsitate, quod usurpatione Pontificalis dignitatis. Secundo ad quatuor fundamenta iurisdictionis Patrum respondent; praeceptum videl. ecclesiae, & iuramentum & votum proprium dato impedimento non obstare: Negligentiam Pontificis aut Cardinalium nullam esse, & moram purgari posse: in causa quoq; propria ad solum Romanum Pontificem indictionem Concilii spectare: quod etiam ex Constantiensi Concilio deducere nituntur. Tertio, contra indictionem Pisanam triplicem obiiciunt defectum, iurisdictionis videl. temporis, & loci. Ultimo, indictione Romana tria inducunt, scil. Concilii necessitatem propter multa, habilitatem loci Romani, & securitatem per salvos conductus. Ad quatuordecim haec opposita multis verbis in prima epistola comprehensa sub clypeo veritatis constantis & humilis cum omni charitate atque modestia respondent Patres, imo & respondebit Omnipotens, cuius sunt spiritu congregati. Et tu Domine vim patimur, responde pro nobis causam sponsae tuae iuvare nitentibus.
units.tr: The ordinators object in four ways. First, against the persons of the Fathers: that they departed without licence, that they used falsehood, that they used deceit, and that they usurped the papal dignity. Second, they reply to the four foundations of the Fathers' jurisdiction: namely, that the command of the Church, the oath, and their own vow do not stand in the way when there is an impediment; that the negligence of the Pope or of the Cardinals is not a bar, and that delay can be purged; and that in their own cause the calling of a Council belongs to the Roman Pontiff alone, which they also try to deduce from the Council of Constance. Third, against the Council of Pisa's calling, they object a threefold defect: of jurisdiction, of time, and of place. Lastly, against the Roman calling they bring forward three things: the necessity of a Council because of many matters, the suitability of the Roman place, and the security given by safe-conducts. The Fathers answer these objections, set forth at length in the first letter, under the shield of a steadfast and humble truth, with all charity and modesty; and indeed the Almighty will answer, by whose Spirit they are gathered. And you, Lord, we suffer violence; answer for us, you who strive to help the cause of your bride.

units.la: Et primum, iuxta clarissimorum sapientum sententiam confitebimur Apostolicam sedem, Romanam ecclesiam, & Apostolicum primatum ex Christi & Petri ordinatione corpus unum mysticum esse, & politiam unicam supremam, & primam spiritualem constituere, cui sicut primae & omnium mensurae, potestas omnis spiritualis & temporalis tenetur obtemperare. Eam tamen Dominus propter humanam fragilitatem ne labi contingat, quum in spiritualib. & aeternis lapsus plurimum gravis sit, & quum ex illa universa penderent, mixtam & compositam esse voluit, ex monarchia in Papa ad praecepta & exsequutionem; & Aristocratia, in optimatum principatu in senatu Cardinalium, pro consilio & providentia, ut haec mixtio in Romano primatu semper actu maneret, & altera potestas, alteram, ne labatur, iuvaret, & pertinentia ad primatum (qualia sunt maiora & ardua ecclesiae negotia) altera minime explicaret: quod satis constare potest, si Veteris & Novi Testam. paginam, & quae de iis potestatibus ibi leguntur copulatiue (prout decet) & non disiunctiue accipimus, & lectione historiae Damasi & Concilio Stephani Papae ac dictis Innocentii III. Ipsi quoque actus Apostoliciistius gubernationis concessionem experimento actuali interpretantes, id satis insinuant, in quibus Petrum sine Apostolis aut eorum necessario consilio, nullum arduum in ecclesia negotium legimus admisisse: qui tamen a Deo fuit Dominici praecepti constans & diligens observator, ut si illum Dominus solum & in solidum ecclesiae regimen tenere voluisset, & non permisisset Apostolos convocare Concilium, sicut in secundo Hierosolymitano Concilio, (& tunc non pro causa fidei, sed pro administratione temporalium) factum legimus: Et in tertio diffinitionem illam magnam legalis, cuius tenore verborum forma diffinitionis aliis Conciliis praescribitur Jacobo & aliis Apostol. non reliquisset. Sic ergo quae meliora sunt in utraque gubernatione: in mystico Romanae ecclesiae corpore & politia iuncta inveniemus. Monarchiae enim ordine & executione excedit aristocratiam, & ab illa exceditur prudentia & consilio, plus enim vident plures oculi quam unus, ut in politicis Aristoteles refert. Accepit ergo a Domino mixtus hic Romanus primatus quod in utraque, simplici politia supereminet: A Monarchia quidem ordinem, praeceptionem & exsecutionem vnitam: Ab Aristocratia providentiam solidam & efficax Concilium. Quae mixta gubernatio, meliorem & securiorem in fragilitate humana reddit primam illam spiritualem politiam, ut Monarchia illa solum imperet & exequatur, quae suo & communi optimatum consilio in maioribus decreta essent. Quod etiam specialib. & priuatis constitutionibus & iuratis capitulis semper Pontifices cum Cardinalibus promittunt & vouet, maxime in vim istius primae institutionis Papatus & Cardinalatus. Haec ergo domina nostra sancta Romana ecclesia quando iis artibus quibus coepit, progressum habuit, plurimum apud Deum & homines in religione, doctrina, veneratione, ac temporali dominio creuit, nihilque sibi plus nocuit, quam cum aliquando Monarchia Aristocratiam non audit. Hinc fere mala omnia quae ecclesiam contristant, prouenerunt, quae quamuis multa hodie sint, ea tamen Patres Pisanae synodi minime intenduit reuelare. Si qua vero contra forsan temperare referrent, protestantur non ad aliquorum calumniam vel iniuriam id se facturos, sed solum iure moderatae defensionis suae & intra tutelae terminos coactos induxisse. Ex his ergo non est difficile videre quam aperte primae illae increpationes contra patrum personas irrogatae excludantur.
units.tr: And first, following the opinion of the most distinguished wise men, we shall confess that the Apostolic See, the Roman Church and the Apostolic primacy, by the ordinance of Christ and Peter, are one mystical body and one supreme and first spiritual polity, to which every spiritual and temporal power, as to the first and measure of all, is bound to render obedience. Yet the Lord, because of human frailty, so that it might not come to a fall (since a fall in spiritual and eternal matters is very grievous, and since all things depend on it), willed that it be mixed and compounded: from monarchy, in the Pope, for command and execution; and from aristocracy, in the principate of the best men, in the senate of Cardinals, for counsel and foresight; so that this mixture should always remain in action in the Roman primacy, and that the one power should help the other lest it totter, and that the one should not wholly unfold the matters pertaining to the primacy (such as the greater and more arduous affairs of the Church). This can be sufficiently established if we take the pages of the Old and New Testament, and what is read there about these powers, conjunctively (as is fitting) and not disjunctively; and by reading the history of Damasus and the Council of Pope Stephen, and the sayings of Innocent III. Interpreting also the actual practice of that apostolic government by experience, they sufficiently hint at this, in which we read that Peter admitted no arduous matter in the Church without the Apostles or their necessary counsel; he who was nonetheless, by God's grace, a steadfast and diligent observer of the Lord's precept. For if the Lord had wished him alone, and wholly, to hold the government of the Church, and had not permitted the Apostles to convene a Council, as we read was done at the second Council of Jerusalem (and then not for a matter of faith, but for the administration of temporal affairs), and at the third he would not have left to James and the other Apostles that great definition of the law, by whose wording the form of a definition is prescribed to other Councils. Thus, in either form of government, we shall find what is better united in the mystical body and polity of the Roman Church. For monarchy surpasses aristocracy in order and execution, and is surpassed by it in prudence and counsel; for, as Aristotle reports in the Politics, more eyes see more than one. The mixed Roman primacy, therefore, has received from the Lord what excels in both the simple forms of government: from monarchy, a united order, command and execution; from aristocracy, a solid and effective council. This mixed government makes that first spiritual polity better and safer in human frailty, so that the monarchy should only command and execute what has been decreed in major matters by its own and the common counsel of the best men. The Pontiffs, together with the Cardinals, have always promised and vowed this as well, in special and private constitutions and sworn capitularies, especially by virtue of the first institution of the Papacy and the Cardinalate. Therefore this mistress of ours, the holy Roman Church, when it advanced by the same arts by which it began, grew greatly before God and men in religion, teaching, veneration and temporal dominion; and nothing has harmed it more than when at times the monarchy would not hear the aristocracy. From this almost all the evils that sadden the Church have arisen; and although these are many today, the Fathers of the Synod of Pisa have by no means intended to reveal them. If, on the contrary, they should bring forward something perhaps more moderate, they protest that they do not do so to slander or injure anyone, but only that they have been driven to it by the right of a moderate defence, and within the bounds of protection. From these things, therefore, it is not difficult to see how plainly those first accusations against the persons of the Fathers are excluded.

units.la: Arguunt Ordinatores quod illicentiati a Romano Pontifice recesserunt Patres. Nec attendunt admittatur ne hodie eorum consilium in arduis ecclesiae rebus ut necessarium, vel ut nec quidem voluntarium ut plurimum ad facta, & non ad agenda vocantur Patres, vbi si sanum consilium liberum & verum, procul a blanditiis (ut tenentur & voverunt Patres) profertur, in odia, comminationes, offensiones, & mala omnia quotidiano & graui experimento (quod dolentissime referunt) certi certo incidunt. Quae eorum recta consilia, & nullae aliae causae (quum continuato obsequio & indefesso Romanae ecclesiam, & illius caput semper venerati sint) infensos eos Praesidi reddiderunt: ut iam nedum liberi in sententiis, sed nec in vita quidem tuti satis esse possent. Consulentes itaque animi libertati, & vitae securitati, ac spiritualitati ecclesiae, secesserunt tantisper a Curia, sicut & Dauid a Saule secessit, & Iacob a fratre Esau, & inde a Laban socero fugit, quoad tuti forent, & libertatem ac spiritualitatem ecclesiae in vna sancta illius congregatione, iuxta ecclesiae praecepta, & sua vota ac iuramenta vindicarent, & quod Dominus in Euangelio praecepit, Dic ecclesiae, quantum cum Deo possent, efficaci-
units.tr: The Ordinators argue that the Fathers withdrew from the Roman Pontiff without licence. They do not consider whether, in the arduous affairs of the Church today, the Fathers' counsel is admitted as necessary, or even as voluntary. For the Fathers are for the most part summoned to ratify deeds, not to take action. Where sound, free and true counsel is offered, far from flattery (as the Fathers are bound and have vowed to offer it), they certainly fall, as they most sorrowfully report, into hatred, threats, offences and every kind of evil, by daily and grievous experience. Their upright counsels, and no other causes, have made them hostile to the President, although they have always venerated the Roman Church and its head with continual obedience and unwearying devotion. So now they could be safe not merely free in their opinions, but not even secure in their lives. Therefore, caring for the freedom of their minds, the security of their lives and the spirituality of the Church, they withdrew for a time from the Curia, just as David withdrew from Saul, Jacob from his brother Esau, and fled from his father-in-law Laban, until they might be safe and might defend the freedom and spirituality of the Church in that one holy congregation, according to the precepts of the Church and their own vows and oaths, and might do, as far as they could with God, what the Lord commanded in the Gospel: "Tell the Church," and so forth, effectively.

units.la: ter ver præstarent. Quod plures patres minóri de causa aliis temporibus fecerunt, & qui illicentiati à Gregorio. XII. olim ad Pisanum primum Concilium recesserunt Patres plurimum ab omnibus commendati sunt. Sed decuisset consultores hoc consulto tacuisse, quum Princeps cuius scribunt nomine, à tribus summis Pontificibus, quorum tempore Cardinalatus eius claudebatur, & ab vlimo tandem per decem annos continuos illicentiatus aberrauerit, nihil tamen inde contra se aut alios absentes dominos actum fuisse grauius senserunt, quale contra innocentes in praesentia agitur. Nec ipsi Patres Pisani, qui tunc Romae erant, talia vnquam contra eos qui haec agunt probauerunt, aut asserierunt. Petierunt tamen Patres ex Florentia licentiam manendi extra curiam, pro sui securitate, & spiritualitate Ecclesiae, cum omni moderatione & humilitate, pro quibus in praesentia veniam deprecari, nihil esset aliud, quam vincula & carceres postulasse, manserunque & manent hactenus Patres in optima sanctissimi D. N. obedientia. Nisi quid iuxta Canonicas sanctiones, quado Apostolicae praeceptiones periculum notorium continent (spiritualis vel corporalis vitae aut turbationis, vel decolorationis status vniuersalis Ecclesiae, auditi quidem possunt, admitti tamen vel impleri non debent, sed ab eis licitum est prouocare.
units.tr: Many Fathers have done this at other times on lesser grounds, and those who withdrew without licence from Gregory XII to the first Council of Pisa were greatly commended by all. But the consultors ought to have kept quiet about this, since the Prince in whose name they write was, by three supreme Pontiffs during whose time his cardinalate was shut, and at last by the final one for ten continuous years absent without licence, yet they did not feel that anything more severe had been done thereby against him or against other absent lords, such as is now being done against the innocent in the present. Nor did the Pisan Fathers themselves, who were then at Rome, ever approve or assert such things against those who now act thus. Yet the Fathers asked from Florence leave to remain outside the Curia, for their own safety and the spirituality of the Church, with all moderation and humility. To beg pardon for this now would be nothing other than to have asked for chains and prisons. And the Fathers have remained, and still remain, in the best obedience to our most holy Lord. Unless, according to the canonical sanctions, when apostolic precepts contain a notorious danger (to spiritual or bodily life, or a disturbance, or a discolouring of the state of the universal Church), such precepts may indeed be heard, but ought not to be admitted or carried out; instead it is lawful to appeal from them.

units.la: Minus officit quod dicunt armatos recessisse, Nempe nec ita se habet, vt referrent, thoracem induti abiisse, Bona venia cum habitu Cardinalium & armis Christianae militiae, (quae secundum Apostolum carnalia non sunt, sed spiritualia) potentia tamen in domino, contra munitiones oes carnales palam & publice cum omni apparatu & reputatione bonorum Praelatorum progressi sunt ex Florentia, & toto itinere ad Papiam: Ex Pisa tamen vsq; Lucam parua & necessaria tantum manu militari comitante, defensionis suae tantum gratia (quae licitum facit armorum vsum profecti sunt intelligentes Concordiensem aut discordiensem Episcopum, & aliquos tales consultores mari & terra multas gentes & insidias ad intercipiendos Patres in via dispositisse, quod in effectu satis constat, quae tamen omnia diuina gratia sunt.
units.tr: It does less harm that they say the Fathers withdrew armed. Indeed it is not so as they report, that they went off wearing breastplates. With due respect, they went forth from Florence, and along the whole road to Pavia, in the dress of Cardinals and with the arms of Christian warfare (which, according to the Apostle, are not carnal but spiritual), yet mighty in the Lord to pull down every carnal stronghold, openly and publicly, with all the equipage and esteem befitting good Prelates. From Pisa, however, as far as Lucca, they travelled accompanied only by a small and necessary military escort, for the sake of their defence alone (which makes the use of arms lawful). They set out understanding that the Bishop of Concordia, or Discordia, and certain such consultors had arranged, by land and sea, many peoples and snares to intercept the Fathers on the road. This in effect is quite certain. Yet all these things were overcome by divine grace.

units.la: Quod tertio de mendacio arguunt. Concordiensi videlicet Episcopo Florentiae obtulisse patres reditum, & ex Papia et petiisse dolose literis venia vtrumque, non ita se habet. Et quando bono dolo euitatur iniquitas, non multum inconuenit. Nam & Dauid apud regem Geth vt viueret, se insanum simulauit: Et patres, vt illius Concordiensis fugerent dolos, qui exploraturus eorum secreta venerat, non dissitentur se aliqua etiam dissimulasse, prout dominus apud Lucam finxit se longius ire, Salomon quoque ad eruendam veritatem finxit se puerum filium meretricis medium velle scindere. Scripta vero ex Papia non de venia, sed de animi aduersantis mitigando furore processerunt, & vt interim necessaria conducerent indicendo Concilio.
units.tr: As to the third point, they accuse the Fathers of lying, namely in saying that they offered the Bishop of Concordia at Florence a return, and that from Pavia they sought pardon for both by letter by deceit. This is not so. And when iniquity is avoided by a good stratagem, there is little harm. For David too feigned madness before the king of Gath that he might live. And the Fathers, that they might escape the snares of that Bishop of Concordia who had come to spy out their secrets, do not deny that they also dissembled somewhat, just as the Lord in Luke pretended to go farther. Solomon too pretended that he was willing to cut in two the child of the harlot, in order to bring out the truth. The letters from Pavia, however, proceeded not about pardon but about calming the fury of a hostile mind, and so that meanwhile they might secure what was necessary by summoning a Council.

units.la: Quod quarto loco consultores maiori verbum efficacia obiiciunt de falsitate, ex hoc ipso refellitur, quandoquidem ad Concilii solidam indictionem pauciores sufficerent. Patres tresq; efficaciter illam explerent, causis tam vrgentib. compulsi & vnit, de quib. in schedulis indictionis constat. Et plures qui in edicto asseruntur Patres, praesentes fuerunt, vel per instrumenta aut per literas, vel nuntios assensterunt Concilio, & iis modis omnibus assensus & mandata praestari posse, iuris indubitati est. Et ille vnus Pater qui praetenditur publice coram Notario protestatus mandatum huiusmodi non dedisse, per testes tamen conuincitur promissionem & assensum nuntiis & literis praestitisse Concilio & omnib. virib. suis & impensis illi opem laturum fuisse pollicitu, & quū tres Patres id referat, plus illis quā vni credi debet, & quū indictio & conuocatio facta sit omni meliori modo quo fieri pot valet conuocatio ex illorum personis qui conuocare potuerunt de commissariis Principū & eorū verissimis mandatis per instrumenta Notariorū & literas ratificatorias satis eorū acta loquuntur, Cessent ergo ordinatores falso inniti, q tantopere aliis expbrant.
units.tr: As to the fourth point, where the consultors object with greater emphasis the charge of falsehood regarding the efficacy of the word, this is refuted by the very fact that fewer would suffice for the solid indiction of a Council. Three Fathers would effectively carry it out, being compelled and united by such urgent causes, as is clear from the schedules of the indiction. And several who are named in the edict as Fathers were present, or assented to the Council by instruments, or by letters, or by messengers; and that assent and mandates can be given in all these ways is a matter of undoubted law. And that one Father who is alleged to have publicly protested before a notary that he had not given such a mandate is nevertheless convicted by witnesses of having given promise and assent to the Council by messengers and letters, and of having pledged to bring it aid with all his strength and expense. And since three Fathers report this, more credit should be given to them than to one. And since the indiction and convocation was made in the best manner possible, the convocation is valid, by those persons who could convoke, from the commissioners of the Princes and their most true mandates, by notarial instruments and letters of ratification; their acts speak sufficiently. Let the Ordinators therefore cease to rest on falsehood, which they so greatly cast in the teeth of others.

units.la: Quod quinto increpant, vsurpasse Patres dignitatem Pontificiā, ridiculum omnino est, nec satis fuit aequum consultoribus, ita assentiari Romano Pontifici, vt quacunque & omnimodam generalis Concilii congregationem sua auctoritate indigere persuaserint: Nempe si tempora nascentis Ecclesiae perspexerimus, Apostoli, qui & Cardinales, Concilia generalia saepius indicerunt, vt apertum est videre per omne Apostolicorum actu historiā: inde annales Ecclesiae & imperii legentibus perspicuum est, imperatores generales synodos nonnunquam conuocasse, q multis in locis decretorum satis liquet. Postmodū vero, aucta & honorata Ecclesia, summi Pontifices regulam statuerunt & quidem iustissimam, ne sine Apostolicae sedis consensu generalia Concilia ediceretur. Caput n. pro vniuerso corpore loqui solet. Quod distinctio 17. decretorum, quasi per totū, regulariter explicat, quumq; conciliares causae vt plurimum spirituales & sponsi Ecclesiae, à spirituali primo capite vocari Synodū decet. Ea tamē regula exceptiones habet tā fere communes, quā sit ipsa regula, antiquas sc. & modernas. Antiqua siquidem vna est, in casu quo existente Ecclesiae necessitate vel praecepto, aut iuramento Pontificis de cōcilo congregando praecedente, ipse tamen conuocare contemnit. In quo (vt sapientes referunt) indicendius primo ad Collegium Cardinalium deferatur: & si qui erunt negligentes, ad diligentes tanquam ad saniorem partem, esto minore, & illis omnib. negligentib. ad Imperatore devoluitur. Secunda et antiqua exceptio regulae fuit. Nisi de Pontificis haeresi, cito secreta vel haeresisfuspitione agendu sit. Quo casu Synodu conuocari absq; eius auctoritate à Cardinalib. vel eis non curantibus, ab aliis Ecclesiae Praelatis, aut ab Imperatore, vel Principibus, & et tūc ad Pontificis electionem, indubitati iuris est. Tertia etiam antiqua exceptio, Nisi de casu Papae in crimine graui, notorio inoriigibili, & scandalizate ageretur, tunc etiam sapientum iudicio absq; eo posset synodus conuocari, quod verisimile sit reū tergi-uersauersaturū esse iudiciū. In eo tamen casu an conuocata synodus Pontificem possit eiicere, vel ratum corrigere, & commonere auctoribusq; statutis etiam iuratis astringere, sapientes varii sunt. Signanter li dicta incorrigibilitas ex habitu tantum vel duratione sit. Nempe si cū defensione criminis foret perinde ac hæresis haberetur. Magna tamen Constantiensis synodus in Spiritu sancto legitime congregata, modernis temporib. dubitationes oes antiquorū, & opiniones varias excludendo, & diffiniendo, addidit in tribus casibus, hæresis videlicet, aut schismatis, vel notorii scandalizantis incorrigibilis criminis, conuocatā synodum eiectionem Pontificum facere posse.
