Quod & ipsa factis cōprobauit: Ioannem n. XXIII. propter crimina notoria scādalizantia, ac Benedictū XIII. propter schisma, absq; vllo genere hæresis proprie depositit, & superioritate Concilii in tribus causis, fidei, schismatis, & vniuersalis reformationis, super omnia membra Ecclesiæ, et supra Pontificem, longa & matura primum habita disceptatione, in duab. sessionibus diffinuit. Quare omnis alia disputatio, nisi in alia synodo diffinitio hæc corrigatur, subricenda est. Et synodus illa generalis & magna semper fuit habita, auctoritate videlicet Pontificis in rei veritate indubitati congregata: Duo enim alii contendentes de Pontificatu per synodum Pisanam præcedentem iure exauctorati fuerant & omnis alia obedientia exinde minime legalis erat, auctoritate quoque collegii & Imperatoris, imo & ipsius Papæ ac omnium fere Cardinalium, & multorum, Prælatorum præsentia, cum summa auctoritate magnificentissime incœpta fuit, ac deinde ante illius conclusionem, omnis alia quæcunque obedientia, vtcunque de papatu contendentium, & Pontifex ipse Martinus V. vnicus aliis reiectis electus, synodum ipsam Constantiensem & eius decreta approbauerunt, & admiserunt, & tanquam sanctissimam & Ecclesiæ summe necessariam, vtpote quæ tam perniciosum schisma exclusit, & futura extirpate docuit, venerati sunt. Attendat nunc consultores si Patres vsurparunt iurisdictionem alienā: Nemo namq; inuadit vel præsumit, quin in casu iure sibi liceat: quomodo aut licuerit vel intelligetur, ex literis & schedulis indictionis satis cōstabit, vel suo tempore (si pax non dabitur) magis innotescet. 12 Secundo loco respondent ordinatores ad fundamenta quatuor iurisdictionis Patrū, præceptum videlicet, votū, iuramentum, scandalū, q; simul cum negligentia Papæ & Cardinaliū in quolibet istorū constituūt Patres idoneos Cōcilii indictores, ac si quadrato agmine arguerēt patres, præceptū est, votū est, iuramentū est indicendi Concilii, & tempus effluxum est; scandalū quoq; proprium papæ est, quod solo Concilio sedari potest & debet: In omnibus tamen iis negligens quoq; altera pars collegii: Ergo ista portio Patrum libera & diligens, est apta indictioni Concilii. 13 Vbi dicant primo ordinatores præceptum illud vniuersalis Ecclesiæ in 39. sessione Constantiensis Concilii, in decreto q; incipit frequens de Conciliis generalib. singulis decennius celebrandis solemnissime edicto, ab octoginta fere annis seruatum nō fuisse, & si fuisset, ex causa bellorū licere Papæ illud transgredi, sicut & fecit Eugenius IV. quinimo dicūt stante quolibet legitimo impedimento locum nō habere, Respōsio in magno periculo constituerēt Pontificē simul & Ecclesiam Dei. Attendant ergo ordinatores decretū hoc statum vniuersalis Ecclesiæ reipicere, & sine Concilio ad libitū vnius hominis mutari non posse, quinimo expressè tenor ipsius decreti hoc Papæ inhibet, & Basileæ (et cum illis Eugenius adhæret,) diffinierunt decretū hoc ad fidem pertinere. Nō ergo quolibet impedimēto (nō voluntario ad minus) decretū tā necessariū reiiciendū & suspendendū est. Qui tamē Martinus V. & Eugenius IV. soleniter satis fecerunt in Concilis Senensi & Basileensi, nisi q; postea super loco cōuentionis orientalis Ecclesiæ differentia aliqua intercessit inter patres Basileæ & Eugenii, in qua tamē Eugenius offerebat acceptare pro nouo loco Concilii, quemcunq; locū Basiliensis in Italia delegissent, & in eo omnem iurisdictionem & libertatem illis permittebat. Sola tamen hæc translatio Cōcilii Basiliēsis ad Ferrariam & inde Florentiam sine consensu synodi constituit Eugenium in maximo periculo, Nisi quod nonnulla, q; nūc subricentur, Basiliensēs in diuisione cōstituerunt: & aliquorū membrorū Cōcilii decessus, & recessus re synodi maxime attriuit. Vnde Eugenius simul cū sancto ingressu suo, & vitæ perspicua probitate, profusaq; liberalitate, periculum illius animosæ translationis euasit: non fuit tamē decretum illud Constantiense per aliquam synodum aut aliquem Pontificem sublatum aut moderatū; quinimo nec potuit nec debuit moderari, nisi in simili generali Concilio: & transgressiones illæ quę referuntur prædecessorū Pontificum, qui Concilia deinde tanto tempore nō seruatūr, potius damnari oporteret, quam pro clypeo defensionis inducere, & huiusmodi excusatione peccatorum acceptare. Scriptum est n. Non adiiciās peccatum supra peccatum. Et alibi, Non minus ardebunt qui cum multis ardebunt. Et Gregorius dixit, Tanto sunt graviora peccata quanto diutius infœlicem animam detinent alligatam. Tēpus vero q; interpellat pro homine, iam diu constituit in mora Pontifices. Deinde non constat quibus legitimis impedimentis tam salubre opus sub hoc Pontificatu fuerit impedimentum. Nam bella quæ in principio inter duos magnos Reges in Italia vigebant, Dei virtute breui sopita sunt, & quasi pax Octauiana, illis pacatis, orbi est reddita. Cur ergo tūc præceptum Ecclesiæ non est admissum? Quare votum & iuramentum non persolutum? Si vero deinde bella in Italia surrexerunt, voluntaria potius fuerunt, poterantque iustius suspendi, quam Ecclesiæ vniuersalis congregatio, in qua bellis sedandis & confirmandæ paci Christianæ, belloq; contra crucis inimicos disponendo, ac reformationi Ecclesiæ ipsiusque recuperandis iuribus, tutius & securius fuisset cōsultū. Omnia namq; prius consilio quā armis experiri sapientem decere. Comicus ille dicebat. Sed quomodo ordinatores vocis propriæ non meminerint in hac excusatione Concilii, non satis videmus. Contradicunt enim sibi ipsis, & voces propDas ignorant, excusantes enim Concilium, a bellis argumentantur. Deinde Romanum suum Concilium instituentes, ad sedanda bella præcipue ratiocinantur, eamq; magnam causam fore ordinandæ vnius pacificę synodi omnes admittunt, nullaq; re magis posse religionem Christi pacari, & contra infideles armari, quam vna sancta vniuersali congregatione Christianorum, communis est omnium animorum conceptus, vbi Spiritus sanctus, qui auctor est vnionis & charitatis & vniuersa Concilia dirigit, ita Christianos inuicem in vera concordia & confœderatione coniunget, vt omnile illud vnum & plenum, quod Christus in Euangelio constituere pollicetur, & Angelus in Apocalypsi futurum Ioanni reuelauit, pro cuius reuelationis gratitudine Ioannes ipse ad pedes Angeli corruit, breui colligendum sub vnius sanctæ synodi directione, & diuino fauore speremus.
units.tr: As for their fifth charge, that the Fathers usurped papal authority, it is wholly ridiculous. The consultors ought not to have agreed so readily with the Roman Pontiff that a general council needs his authority for every assembly whatsoever. If we look at the early days of the Church, the Apostles, who were also its Cardinals, often convened general councils, as is plain to see throughout the whole history of the Apostolic acts. The annals of the Church and the Empire also make clear to readers that emperors sometimes convened general synods, as the decrees show in many places. Later, when the Church had grown and been honoured, the supreme Pontiffs laid down a rule, and a very just one, that general councils should not be summoned without the consent of the Apostolic See. For the head usually speaks for the whole body. Distinction 17 of the Decretals explains this rule as applying throughout. Since conciliar matters are for the most part spiritual, and the spouse of the Church ought to be summoned to a synod by its spiritual head first. Yet that rule has exceptions, nearly as many as the rule itself, both ancient and modern. One ancient exception is this: when there is a necessity of the Church or a command, or a previous oath of the Pontiff to convene a council, and yet he refuses to convene it. In that case, as the wise report, the summons should first be referred to the College of Cardinals; and if any of them are negligent, it passes to the diligent as the sounder part, even if they are the smaller number, and if all of them are negligent, it devolves upon the Emperor. A second ancient exception to the rule was this: when the matter concerns the heresy of the Pontiff, or a suspicion of heresy that must be dealt with at once. In that case it is an indisputable right that a synod may be convened without his authority, by the Cardinals, or, if they do not care, by other prelates of the Church, or by the Emperor or the princes, and then for the election of a Pontiff. A third ancient exception: when the case concerns a Pope guilty of a grave, notorious and incorrigible crime that gives scandal, then, in the judgement of the wise, a synod may be convened even without his authority, because it is likely that the accused would evade judgement. In that case, however, the wise differ on whether the synod so convened may cast out the Pontiff, or correct and admonish him, and bind him by statutes, even sworn ones. The incorrigibility in question is to be understood as arising only from habit or duration; that is, if he were to defend the crime, it would be regarded in the same way as heresy. Yet the great Council of Constance, lawfully gathered in the Holy Spirit, in modern times, excluding and defining all the doubts and varying opinions of the ancients, added that in three cases, namely heresy, or schism, or an incorrigible crime giving notorious scandal, a council so convened may depose the Pontiff. This the council itself confirmed by its acts. For it deposed John XXIII for notorious scandalous crimes, and Benedict XIII for schism, without any kind of heresy properly so called. And after long and mature debate, it first decided in two sessions the superiority of the Council over all members of the Church, and over the Pontiff, in three matters: faith, schism, and universal reform. Therefore every other dispute must be disregarded unless this decision is corrected in another synod. And that synod was always held to be a general and great one, being indeed convened by the authority of the Pontiff, beyond doubt in fact. For the two rival claimants to the papacy had been lawfully deposed by the preceding Synod of Pisa, and every other obedience thereafter was by no means lawful. It was begun with the highest authority and most magnificently, both by the authority of the College and of the Emperor, and indeed with the presence of the Pope himself, of nearly all the Cardinals, and of many prelates. Then, before its conclusion, every other obedience whatsoever, from whichever of the contenders for the papacy, was set aside, and Pope Martin V, elected alone, approved and admitted the Council of Constance and its decrees, and venerated them as most holy and most necessary to the Church, since it had cut off so pernicious a schism and taught how to root out future ones. Let the consultors now consider whether the Fathers usurped another's jurisdiction. For no one invades or presumes upon what is not lawfully his in such a case. How and whether it was lawful, or how it will be understood, will be made sufficiently clear from the letters and papers of the summons, or in its own time (if peace is not given) it will become more evident. 12 Second, the organisers respond to the four foundations of the Fathers' jurisdiction: namely precept, vow, oath, and scandal, which together with the negligence of the Pope and the Cardinals in each of these make the Fathers suitable convenors of a council. It is as if they argued with a drawn-up battle line: there is a precept, there is a vow, there is an oath to convene a council, and the time has passed; and the scandal too belongs peculiarly to the Pope, and can be calmed only by a council and ought to be. In all these matters, however, the other part of the college is negligent too. Therefore this portion of the Fathers, free and diligent, is fit to convene the council. 13 Here the organisers should first say that the universal precept in the thirty-ninth session of the Council of Constance, in the decree beginning Frequens, solemnly ordaining that general councils be celebrated every ten years, was not observed for nearly eighty years, and that even if it had been, the Pope could lawfully break it because of wars. They even say that it has no force whenever some lawful hindrance exists. Answer: this would place the Pope and the Church of God in great danger at once. Let the organisers consider that this decree concerns the state of the universal Church, and cannot be changed without a council at the pleasure of one man. Indeed the very wording of the decree expressly forbids the Pope to do so, and the Council of Basel (and Eugenius, with them, adheres) defined that this decree pertains to faith. Therefore a decree so necessary must not be rejected or suspended on account of any hindrance, at least not a voluntary one. Yet Martin V and Eugenius IV did sufficiently comply solemnly with it in the councils of Siena and Basel, except that afterwards some disagreement arose between the Fathers of Basel and Eugenius about the place of the council of the Eastern Church. In that dispute Eugenius offered to accept as a new venue for the council whatever place in Italy the Basel fathers should choose, and in it he granted them full jurisdiction and freedom. Yet this transfer of the Council of Basel to Ferrara and then to Florence, made without the consent of the synod, alone placed Eugenius in the greatest danger. Certain matters, which are now passed over, the Basel fathers had settled in their division; and the departure and withdrawal of some members had greatly weakened the synod. Hence Eugenius, together with his holy entrance, his clearly proven probity of life, and his lavish generosity, escaped the danger of that bold transfer. Yet that Constance decree was never repealed or moderated by any synod or any Pontiff. Indeed it neither could nor ought to be moderated, except by a similar general council. And those transgressions of earlier Pontiffs, who for so long a time did not observe the councils, ought rather to be condemned than brought forward as a shield of defence and accepted as an excuse for their sins. For it is written: "Do not add sin to sin." And elsewhere: "They will burn no less who burn with many." And Gregory said: "Sins are the heavier the longer they hold the unhappy soul bound." Moreover, the time that pleads on behalf of man has long since placed the Pontiffs in delay. Furthermore, it is not clear by what lawful hindrances so salutary a work was impeded under this Pontificate. For the wars which at the beginning raged in Italy between two great kings were quickly quieted by God's power, and as if the Augustan peace, with them pacified, was restored to the world. Why, then, was the Church's precept not then observed? Why was the vow and oath not fulfilled? And if wars afterwards arose in Italy, they were rather voluntary, and could more justly have been suspended than the gathering of the universal Church, in which, for quelling wars, confirming Christian peace, arranging war against the enemies of the cross, and reforming the Church and recovering its rights, it would have been safer and more secure to consult. For "a wise man ought to try everything by counsel before arms," as that comic poet said. But how the organisers have not remembered this proper saying in their excuse for the Council, we do not well see. For they contradict themselves and do not know their own words: in excusing the Council they argue from wars. Then, in establishing their Roman council, they reason chiefly to quell wars, and all admit that this would be the great reason for ordaining one peaceful synod. And nothing, all agree, can calm the religion of Christ or arm it against the infidels more than one holy universal gathering of Christians, a common concept of all minds, where the Holy Spirit, who is the author of unity and charity and directs all councils, will join Christians to one another in true concord and confederation. Thus we hope, under the direction of one holy synod and by divine favour, to gather soon that one and full fold which Christ promised to constitute in the Gospel, and which the Angel revealed would come to John in the Apocalypse, for the gratitude of which revelation John himself fell at the Angel's feet.

units.la: 14 Quod vero de voto & iuramento consultores referunt, pari bellorum impedimento ad illa seruanda Pontificē non teneri, tā leuis cuiusio est, vt nō diuinis mō vinculis, qualia illa magna sunt, ita vt maiora esse non possent, responsio sufficiens & accommodata non videatur: sed nec simplici verborum obligationi, aut leuibus aranearū telis a sticitis hominibus excusabilis minime valida censeri possit. Quis nempe voluntarius bellis, esto fortasse iustis, tā solemnia vincula, voti, & iuramenti in melior. actionib. disrumperet? Docuit namq; Paulus non esse facienda mala vt inde veniant bona: & Salomon in proverbiis, quinā magna hominū asseuerat, per Deū vouere, & inde vota detrectare. Reuerentia namq; Deo & fides hominib. hinc apertissime violatur & frangitur. Quæ tamen prophetā regius minime frangere desiderans dicebat, Reddā tibi vota mea, quā dixerunt labia mea, & quæ locutum est os meum in tribulatione mea, & cæteros admonens, ait, Vouete & reddite domino Deo vestro.
units.tr: 14 As for the consultors' claim that the Pope is not bound to keep his vow and oath when war stands in the way, that answer seems neither sufficient nor fitting. It is so trivial that it does not match bonds of divine weight, such as these great ones are, which could hardly be greater. Nor can it be held valid even for a simple verbal promise, or accepted as an excuse for sensible men, since it rests on flimsy spiders' webs. Who, indeed, would willingly break such solemn bonds of vow and oath for the sake of wars, perhaps even just ones, or for some better undertaking? Paul taught that evil must not be done so that good may come of it (Rom. 3). Solomon in the Proverbs warns that it is a snare for a man to vow rashly to God and afterwards to retract his vows (Prov. 20). For reverence toward God and faith among men are most plainly violated and broken by this. The royal prophet, unwilling to break such vows, said: "I will pay You my vows, which my lips uttered and my mouth spoke in my trouble" (Ps. 66), and admonishing others he says: "Vow and pay to the Lord your God" (Ps. 76).

units.la: Quumq; Deus magnus omnipotens, voto suo & iuramento indissolubiliter astringi se asseruat vt in voto & iuramento Domini & Abrahā, Isaac, & Iacob, de multiplicando semine suo sicut arenas maris & stellas cœli, & benedictione gentium in eo, scriptura sacra saepius meminit Pontificē ergo summū eius vicarium, voto suo & iuramento præ aliis strictissime teneri, dum materia voti & iuramenti de genere bonorū sit, indubitatū esse debet. Signater cū ipse sit à Deo immediatus, magisterq; fidei, & veritatis doctor, diuinæ reuerentiæ & fidei hominū seruandæ super omnes astringitur. Quare, vota sua aut iuramenta, nisi maxime in noxā vergat soluere aut cōmutare nec debet, nec potest, aut aliis vt id secū faciant, cōmittere. Etsi iuxta Salomonē nulla digna est cōparatio continentis animæ, & inde votū religionis, cui studiū continentiæ annectitur, cōmutare minime posse sapientes nonnulli voluerunt. Quæ cōparatio esse pōt cōtinentis & reformatæ Ecclesiæ, quū cōmuniora & publica meliora & diuiniora sint, secundū philosophos? In congregatione aut vniuersalis Ecclesiæ potissimū huic cōtinentiæ & reformationi Ecclesiæ in fide, vnione, & moribus attenditur. Quis ergo tam modico obstaculo tā magnum bonū irritabit? Meminisse debuissent ordinatores Iephreillius intentissimi ac fortissimi iudicis Israel, quē Paulus inter sanctos aunumerat, qui ne votū, quo Deo vouerat, violaret, vnicę et filię saluti, non pepercit. Et non tā leui impedimento, quam facile excludi potuit tam magnū bonū blandientes & fallentes excusarent, præcipue si tenore voti & iuramenti considerare vellent, quam solemne & publicum, Deo, virginibus Apostolorū, & omnib. sanctis ac hominib. factum legitur, etiam per viam contractus, vt timere legentes debeant, quanto plus frangentes? Signanter attenta execratione pœnarum etiam temporalium, quibus se vouentes & iurantes obligant, vt Pontifex si quæ vouet & iurat non reddiderit, tāquam scandalizator & perturbator Ecclesiæ & totius Christianitatis habeatur: quæ vero pœna publicæ Ecclesiam scandalizantibus debeatur, Dominus apud Matthæum, de eiectione & appensione molæ asinariæ & maris demersione, apertissime docuit.
units.tr: Since the great and almighty God declares that He binds Himself indissolubly by His vow and oath, as in the vow and oath of the Lord to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to multiply their seed like the sand of the sea and the stars of heaven, and to bless the nations in it, Holy Scripture often recalls this. It must therefore be beyond doubt that the Pope, as the supreme vicar of God, is bound by his vow and oath more strictly than others, since the matter of the vow and oath is of a good kind. Especially since he is immediately from God, the teacher of faith and the doctor of truth, he is bound beyond all others to preserve reverence toward God and faith among men. Therefore he neither ought nor is able to dissolve or change his vows or oaths, unless the harm is very great, nor may he commit this to others to do on his behalf. Although, according to Solomon, no comparison is worthy of a continent soul, and some wise men held that a vow of religion, to which the pursuit of continence is joined, cannot be changed, what comparison can there be with a continent and reformed Church, since common and public goods are, according to the philosophers, better and more divine? In a gathering of the universal Church, above all, attention is paid to this continence and to the reformation of the Church in faith, unity and morals. Who, then, would overturn so great a good for so slight an obstacle? The organizers ought to have remembered Jephthah, the most resolute and courageous judge of Israel, whom Paul counts among the saints (Heb. 11), who did not spare his only daughter so that he would not break the vow he had made to God. And they ought not to have excused a great good, which could easily have been brought about, by such a slight hindrance, flattering and deceiving themselves, especially if they had wished to consider how solemn and public the vow and oath were, made to God, to the virgins, to the Apostles, to all the saints and to men, and how it is read to have been made even by way of a contract, so that readers ought to fear all the more if those who break them. Especially, weighing the curse of penalties, even temporal ones, by which those who vow and swear bind themselves, if the Pope does not fulfil what he vows and swears, he is to be regarded as a scandalizer and disturber of the Church and of all Christendom. What penalty is owed to those who scandalize the public Church the Lord taught most plainly in Matthew, concerning the millstone hung round the neck and the drowning in the sea (Matt. 18).

units.la: Cardinalib. quoq; in euentum non redditionis voti & iuramenti Pontifex facultā concedit generale Concilii conuocandi: Cuius sententiæ & determinationi se sponte submisit, & vltra hoc Cardinales vouerunt & iurauerunt huic promissioni nullo vnquā tempore contrauenire; quinimo si pontifici contrauenienti assenserunt, fructibus capellii, & beneficiorum suorum, alia sententia non expectata, priuati censeantur. Viderint ordinatores si tam triplicatus nodus tam breui sua solutione rumpatur. Attendant quoque, vbi Concilio impedimentum opponi debeat, priusquam lege contractu & iuramento Pontifice promisisse nullum vnquam nisi euidentissimum allegare, & quod tale iudicatum sit ad minus à duabus partibus dominorum Cardinalium per suffragia balotarum. Viderint si tale fuerit quod inducitur, & si huiusmodi diligentia iudicii præcesserit.
units.tr: Likewise, in the event that the Pope does not fulfil his vow and oath, he grants the cardinals the power to summon a general council. He voluntarily submitted himself to their judgment and decision. Moreover, the cardinals vowed and swore that they would never at any time act against this promise; indeed, if they consented to a Pope acting against it, they should be deemed deprived of the fruits of their chapter and benefices, without any other sentence being awaited. Let the organizers see whether so triple a knot can be broken by so brief a solution. Let them also consider where an obstacle to the council ought to be raised: before they allege, on the basis of law, contract and oath which the Pope has promised, nothing except what is most evident, and that this has been judged to be such by at least two parts of the lords cardinals by the votes of ballots. Let them see whether what is brought forward is of such a kind, and whether such diligence of judgment has preceded.

units.la: Addunt quoque ipsi consultores votum & iuramentum in solo conscientiæ foro versari, immemores Apostolicæ doctrinæ, quæ finem contentionis hominum & causarum iuramentum esse constituit, quo voto solemni & iuramento Patres etiam contentiose potuerunt. Pontificem de Concilio admouere. Hæc autem diximus, quia ordinatores forum conscientiæ non videntur existimasse, quamtamen Pontifex à Deo immediatus, plusquam hominum contentiones vereri tenetur.
units.tr: The consultors also add that vow and oath belong only to the forum of conscience, forgetting the apostolic teaching which set an oath as the end of men's strife and disputes. By this solemn vow and oath the Fathers too could have bound the Pope to a council, even in contentious matters. We have said this because the organizers do not seem to have considered the forum of conscience, although the Pope, being immediately from God, is bound to reverence more than the disputes of men.

units.la: 15 Insuper legalius adiunguūt ordinatores ex æquitate Canonica nō posse Pōtifici denegari purgationē morę, si Concilium distulit conuocare. Vtinā hac vna sola probabiliori excusatione sine tot iniuriis & contumeliis, absque tam grauibus censuris, quæ tamen debuerant esse mitiores & medicinæ non tam vltimæ exterminationes Consultores isti vsq; à tot scriptis liberassent, & cum eius iocundius egissent Patres. Sed nec ista excusatio solida est: Nempe fundamentū purgationis morę sola æquitas est, atq; adeo vt nisi bonum vel æquum suadeat, purgationem lex non admittat, præcedenteq; tam diutina notoriaq; summi Pontificis & Reuerendissimorum dominorū Cardinalium illi adhærentium negligētia Concilii congregandi, ius ad illos qui Pisanum Concilium indixerūt, ipso facto iuris ministerio devolutum est. Ergo cui bonū æquū ne videri possit in eorū quiquibus quæsitum sit ius præiudicium, purgationem q; admittere. Stat enim vulgaris iuris regula citra alterius præiudicium legalia beneficia interpretanda esse. Nec est in purgationis mora materia, quia quam apud omnes recte sentientes antiquitas, veritas, aut frequentius, quare iure ad alios devolutum, seram esse morae purgationem. Existimauerunt enim iuris prudentes, vbi ius alterius quæsitum sit, radicib. quasi in alieno adactis, non facile posse convelli. Quod tamen maxime absq; vllahabitatione procedit, vbi res integra non sit: quemadmodum in causa nostro prorsus dubio non est, postquam iure in se translato vtentes patres Pisanæ synodi, Concilio indicendo præcesserunt, & præuenerunt. Præterea, qui moram purgare volunt, ita agere debent, ne quid contra id quod offerunt iure obiici possit. Indicio vero Romani Concilii notorio loci vitio liberat, Romanum vt latius suo loco prosequemur, nec nos, nec innumerabiles alii tutò esse locum consulendi, statim endiq; vera, & necessaria pro Ecclesia, hodie arbitramur. Itaq; liquidò constat purgationis argumentum nullo iure subsistere: Et rursum, Si de causa capitis esset in synodo agendum, quum alienis iuris sit talis indicio non conueniet capiti moram purgare: Ad rem tamen vero summi Pontificis negligentiam, magno verborum apparatu, magnisq; eloquentiæ vinculo consultorib. elaboratum cernimus. Quo fit vt quæ proponuntur, quamquam pulchra, commentitia tamen & ficta satis appareant. Intelleximus nempe summum Pontificem, dum Cardinalatus officio fungeretur, sæpius Alpes transiisse, & maria traiectisse, nouum tamen atque inauditum patribus esse generalis Concilii indictione perquisierit aut tractauerit. Ergo Pontifex creatus orator ob obedientiæ suæ certum aliquid de tenendo Concilio proposuerit, aut innuuerit. Pater quoq; ille cui legatione Germanica sponte oblata nunc immerito exprobrat, quam tamen ad gloriam suæ sanctitatis nullo suo commodo, sed laboribus & impensis innumeris administrauit, de pace quidem Christiana, & infidelium bello, commissiones pulchras accepisse se asserit. De congregando tamen Concilio, nec verbum quidem, imo tunc aliquando & alias sæpius, ab ipso moderate propositum reticit animadvertit.
units.tr: 15 Furthermore, the organizers add, from canonical equity, that a plea of delay cannot be denied to the Pope if the council has put off its convocation. Would that these consultors, with this one more probable excuse alone, without so many injuries and insults, and without such grave censures, which ought to have been milder and more like a remedy than final extermination, had freed themselves from so many writings, and had dealt more pleasantly with the Fathers. But this excuse too is not sound. The sole foundation of a plea of delay is equity; and so, unless it suggests a good or fair result, the law does not admit a plea of delay. Moreover, given the so long and notorious negligence of the supreme Pontiff and of the most reverend lords cardinals who adhered to him in convoking a council, the right to call one passed by the very operation of law to those who summoned the Council of Pisa. Therefore, how can it seem good or fair to admit a plea of delay in favour of those who have had a right of prejudice acquired against them? For the common rule of law stands that legal benefits are to be interpreted without prejudice to another. Nor is there matter for a plea of delay, since, as all who think rightly admit, antiquity, truth, or rather frequency, shows that a plea of delay is late when the right has passed to others. For jurists have held that where another's right has been acquired, once it has taken root, as it were, in what is not one's own, it cannot easily be torn up. This holds especially where the matter is not still open: as in our case, which is entirely beyond doubt, since the fathers of the Synod of Pisa, using the right transferred to themselves, went before and anticipated the summoning of the council. Moreover, those who wish to plead delay must act so that nothing can be objected to them on the law concerning what they offer. But the notorious defect of place in the Roman council frees the council from that defect; we, and countless others, think that it is not safe, even today, to consult that place, as we shall pursue more fully in its own place, nor are the true and necessary things for the Church to be sought there. Thus it is clearly established that the argument from delay rests on no law. And again, if a matter of capital cause were to be treated in the synod, since it belongs to another's right, it would not be fitting for such a judgment to lay a plea of delay against the head. Yet we see that the consultors have worked out, with a great display of words and a strong bond of eloquence, the Pope's negligence in the matter of truth. The result is that what they put forward, although beautiful, appears sufficiently fabricated and feigned. We understand, indeed, that the supreme Pontiff, while he discharged the office of cardinal, often crossed the Alps and sailed the seas, yet he sought or treated the convocation of a general council with the Fathers as something new and unheard of. Therefore, the Pope, created orator on account of his obedience, proposed or hinted at something certain about holding a council. That Father too, to whom the German legation was voluntarily offered, whom they now unjustly reproach, and whom he administered, not for his own advantage but for the glory of his holiness, at the cost of countless labours and expenses, asserts that he received fine commissions concerning Christian peace and the war against the infidels. Yet concerning the convocation of a council not even a word, nay, he notes that at times and often otherwise the matter was moderately proposed by him and passed over in silence.

units.la: 16 Sed quorsum tam longam de Concilii desiderio consultores texerunt historiam? Tam ardebat, cur desiderio reb. ipsis Pontifex pacificus satisfacere neglexit? Consultores suunt nihil esse antiquius, quam propositum mente retentum nihil operari, nec apud Deum & homines præstare, vbi quò adest exequutionis occasio, non exercetur. Nam præ bella, satis superq; est dictum: Nonautem Romani Concilii indictio, propositum celebrandæ synodi vero non explicarunt, nam nisi Pisana prouocatio præcessisset, non creditur fuisse illa Romana attemprata, nec tam vtilla, tenearur, quam vt alia fiangatur: (quod verò Dominus) cogitata suspicatur. Sed negligentia Pontificis ostendat, illa dominus Cardinalium adhærentium nota esse debebat, quò de adhærentibus sapientes idem iudicium fecerunt. Ipsi quoq; non ignari præcepti & necessitatis notoriæ, veritq; & iuramenti sui immemores, ad quid moueri iterum debuissent? Sciebant partes quocunq; verteret Pontifex, illi adhæsuros, & par periculum admonitionis eorum in præsentia, ac Pontificis fuisse. Iam vero Pontifice & illis per literas edictis patrum admonitis, Concilium generale & liberum (ad quæ tenentur, & quale universalis Ecclesiæ esse debet) videntur refugere, domumque iam vallatam aurib. & exercitibus, & non aliam pro loco Concilii vel aliquid deligere. 17 Quod vero de negligentia nostra in proponendo Concilio, quò apud Romanum Pontificem attemus, nobis retruditur, admittimus: quum aperte libertate careremus, non ausus tunc Pontificem irritare, atque hoc verius negligentiam excusat. Liberi tamen & absentes, statim cogitauimus præcepto Ecclesiæ, voto & iuramento nostris facere satis. Ista hæc occasio liberius & securius loquendi in præsentia Romani Pontificis (quam nos iam absentia nostra dandus dominus Reverendissimis Cardinalibus nunc in Curia degentibus) nobis per alios dominos (quum eramus de corpore Curiæ) fuisset exhibita, cum effectu omni conatu curauissemus Pisis, aut alio loco tuto, Concilium generale indici & teneri, & contra Patres hæc admonentes non ita insurgere, nec eorum literas mordere, & laniare, Petrum imitati, qui literas Pauli, quib. eum gravius de Concilio arguebat, suis canonicis Epistolis non reprehendisse, sed confirmasse, atque commendasse cognoscimus. 18 Addunt quoq; litterarum ordinatores, etiam in causa propria ad Rom. Pontificem indictio Concilii spectare. Quib. vno verbo (vt prædiximus) respondebitur, eo videlicet nomine (summo Pontifici banditos: Nunquam n. si vera hæc esset sententia, contra Pontifices Concilia pararentur, quandoquidem iuris præsumptione coniunctibus contra se auctoritas frustra expectatur, nullusque bene sentiens ab hac sententia creditur recessisse: nec ad rem pertinet quod de Ioanne XXIII. ad nos vt Iudæos cohuincendos ex propria (vt dicunt) Scriptura non absque calumnia obiicitur. Nam si recte Constantiensis Concilii & a considera mus, eiusq; non vt Iudæi falsam & perversam, sed veram & congruam, vt veri Christiani & spirituales viri interpretationem accommodemus, nusquam compertum erit ad causam aduersus te tractandam Ioannem XXIII. Concilium Constantiæ indixisse, sed ad reformationem & pacem Ecclesiæ, quæ in Pisano Concilio Alexander V. infecta reliquerat instituisse, prout ex bulla conuocationis Concilii Constantiensis data Lege de anno quinto pontificatus Ioannis, satis constat. Congregata vero synodo proeca causa ad cuius congregationem auctoritatem Pontificiam regulariter, vel aliorum in calibus (supra positis necessariam esse confiremur, Postmodum, ipsa synodus congregata, per seipsam à Domino auctoritate habet in Ecclesia plenariam, in tribus quidem causis, quibus diffinitor superio Pontifice plenissime disponendi, & determinandi; ordinarie et sine Pontifice (In aliis vero causis Pontificis, nisi cum Pontifice aut suis legatis necessitate tamen cogente, vel sede vacante, etiam sine eis omnia plc bia plenaria concludendi & explicandi. Quare Ioanne 23. post secundâ sessione Constantiensem à Concilio dissimulato habitu fugiente, & Ecclesiâ deserente, Synodus ipsa iâ actu congregata, Christi Domini principalis Ecclesiæ capitis auctoritate, & suâ ordinariâ cōtra illū quasi turbantē synodū & Ecclesiâ scandalizantem procedere incepit, nullâ ipsius Ioannis novâ auctoritate expectata. Non ergo synodus contra Ioannē processit auctoritate Ioannis, sed suâ & verius Domini dicentis, Dic Ecclesiæ. Necistorū consultorū argumentatio procedit, dicentium auctoritate Ioan. Constantiensem synodū collectam esse in eâq; causam contra eundem Pontificem actâ. Ergo ad Concilium contra Papam congregandū ipsius Pontificis auctoritas est necessaria. Satis n. leue est iaculum, quo multitudo reiiciuntur, & nisi tu vinci aut percuti velis minimè ferit. Dicimus n. ad primam propositionem, Ioannem indixisse Constantiensem synodū non contra se; & ad secundam, processisse synodum tunc non Ioannis auctoritate, sed suâ ordinariâ postquā actu congregata. Secundo, argumentatio non bene discurrit, dato quod Ioan. contra se principaliter indixisset Concilium, quod minimè verum est. Posito tamen casu, sic procederetur; Ioan. XXIII. de industriâ aduersus le Concilium indixit; Ergo ad causam contra Pontificem requiritur Pontificis auctoritas. Argumentatio nō procedit, vitio fallaciæ accidentis. Potest n. maior annis auctore Prætore prædium vendere, verumq; erit Prætoris auctoritatem tunc intervenisse, nec tamen verum erit Prætoris auctoritatem necessariam esse quum sine Prætore maior vendere potuisset.
units.tr: 16 But why have the advisers woven such a long history of the desire for a council? If the peace-loving Pontiff was so eager for it, why did he neglect to satisfy that desire in fact? The advisers say that nothing is more worthless than a purpose kept in the mind, which achieves nothing and counts for nothing before God and men when the opportunity to carry it out is present and it is not acted upon. As for the wars, enough has been said. Nor have they explained the summoning of a Roman council, or the purpose of truly holding a synod. For unless the Pisan summons had gone before, it is not believed that the Roman attempt would have been made, nor would it have been so useful as to be needed in place of another. (What the Lord suspects was thought out.) But the Pontiff's negligence shows that these matters ought to have been known to the adhering Cardinals, so that wise men judged the same about the adherents. They themselves, not ignorant of the precept and of the notorious necessity, and forgetful of their truth and their oath, why should they have been moved again? They knew that wherever the Pontiff turned, they would cling to him, and that the danger of their admonition was equal in their presence and in the Pontiff's. Now, with the Pontiff and his men warned by letters and edicts from the Fathers, they seem to shun a general and free council (which they are bound to hold, and which the universal Church ought to be), and to have fortified the house with ears and armies, and not to choose any other place for the council or anything else. 17 As to what is thrown back at us, that we were negligent in proposing a council to the Roman Pontiff, we admit it. Since we openly lacked liberty, we did not dare then to provoke the Pontiff, and this more truly excuses the negligence. Yet free and absent as we are, we immediately resolved to satisfy the Church's precept, our vow and our oath. This occasion for speaking more freely and safely in the presence of the Roman Pontiff (which we, now absent, were given through other lords, the most reverend Cardinals now living at the Curia, since we were of the Curia's body) we would have used to the full, striving with every effort to have a general council summoned and held at Pisa or some other safe place. We would not then have risen up against the Fathers who give these admonitions, nor bitten and torn their letters, imitating Peter. We know that Peter did not rebuke Paul's letters, in which Paul argued more gravely about the council, but confirmed and commended them in his canonical epistles. 18 They add also that the orderers of letters hold that, even in a cause of one's own, the indiction of a council belongs to the Roman Pontiff. This may be answered in one word, as we said before: namely, that under that name the Supreme Pontiff is outlawed. For if this opinion were true, councils would never be prepared against Pontiffs, since by the presumption of law authority is vainly expected from those who are joined against themselves, and no well-minded person is believed to have departed from this opinion. Nor does it bear on the matter what is objected to us, not without calumny, about John XXIII, that we are to be convicted, as the Jews are, from his own Scripture (as they say). For if we rightly consider the Council of Constance, and apply its interpretation not as Jews would, falsely and perversely, but as true Christians and spiritual men would, truly and fittingly, it will nowhere be found that John XXIII summoned the Council of Constance to handle a cause against you. He established it for the reformation and peace of the Church, which Alexander V had left unfinished at the Council of Pisa, as is clear enough from the bull convoking the Council of Constance, given in the fifth year of John's pontificate. Indeed, when a synod has been assembled for a cause, we confess that papal authority is ordinarily necessary for its assembly, or that of others in the cases set out above. Afterwards, the synod once assembled has from the Lord, through itself, full authority in the Church. In three causes it is defined that the synod, above the Pope, has the fullest power to dispose and determine, ordinarily and without the Pope. In other causes, with the Pope or his legates, or when necessity compels, or the see is vacant, even without them, it has full power to conclude and settle all matters. Therefore, after the second session at Constance, John XXIII, disguised, fled from the council and deserted the Church. The synod itself, already actually assembled, by the authority of Christ the Lord, the principal head of the Church, and by its own ordinary authority, began to proceed against him as one who was disturbing the synod and scandalising the Church, no new authority from John himself being awaited. Therefore the synod did not proceed against John by John's authority, but by its own, and more truly by the Lord's word, Tell it to the Church. Nor does the argument of these advisers hold, who say that the Council of Constance was gathered by John's authority and that a cause against the same Pontiff was tried in it. Therefore the Pontiff's own authority is necessary for convening a council against the Pope. A dart of that kind is light enough to throw back a crowd, but unless you wish to be conquered or struck, it does not wound. For to the first proposition we say that John did not summon the Council of Constance against himself; and to the second, that the synod then proceeded not by John's authority but by its own ordinary authority, once it was actually assembled. Second, the argument does not run well, even granting that John had summoned the council chiefly against himself, which is by no means true. Yet, supposing the case, it would proceed thus: John XXIII deliberately summoned a council against himself; therefore for a cause against the Pope the Pope's authority is required. The argument does not hold, because of the fallacy of accident. A man over age may sell his estate with the praetor's authority, and it will be true that the praetor's authority then intervened, yet it will not be true that the praetor's authority is necessary, since without the praetor he could have sold it.

units.la: 19. Absolutimus secundæ petitionis singulas oppositiones; tertiâ obiectiua portionem, contra Pisanâ indictione attingere res admonet, & quod prior loci huiusmodi obiectio abunde supra evacuata sit (ostendimus n. clarissime, ius indicendi Concilii apud Patres fuisse) reliquū est ut cætera subiiciamus. Inuehunt consultores, cōtra tēporis breuitatē exquisita quadā diligentia dies cōputantes, magnoq; verborum fastu vehementiq; apparatu exclamant, poterunt ne venturi necessaria exquisisse? Poterūt ne Principes accedere, volètes statue sui securitati cōsuluisse? Poterunt ne & reliqua? Sed nō tanta cū fiducia prorupissent, si semotis, quib. vera iudicia corrūpuntur, animorū passionib. tetum veritati potius quā assentationib. & blandimentis studuissent. Nā præter id q à iure nullus certus terminus huiusmodi indictionib. præfixus est, atq; ideo pro rerū, locorum, & temporum contingentiâ arbitrarium relinquitur. Cui dubium etiamsi determinatū tempus statutum esset, ex causa tamen restringi posse q omni iure euidenter esset, si & ipsi cōsultores id probant. Nā quum annum dicant assuetum esse terminum ad tantā rem inciendam, illud tamen ne cuiquā (vt dicunt) calumniandi causa daretur, ad nouē menses restringunt. Hic attendant consultores si licuit propter vei borum calumnias, quā dicunt antiquissimum & vsitatum terminū, arctare; cur propter realia & actualia magna Ecclesiæ scandala præsentia, & quæ timebantur breui: futura, quibusq; aliter quā per Concilium occurri nō poterat, terminus nō esset abbreuiandus; quæ autē hæc sint quāuis iactis nō orbi Patres crediderint, ea tamē nondum illorum mentis est in specie reuelare, si quo modo pax Ecclesiæ cum eius reformatione, vel cum hac māsuetudine haberi possit. Nēpe quando Cōcilia in pace non existentib. actu scandalis ad futuras reformationes cōgregabantur; quando & Ecclesia Orientalis cōueniebat, vnius anni terminus cōgregandi Concilii præscribebatur: sed nunc quum scandalis præsentib. citissime prouidendū sit, cōgregari illa celerius oportet. Signāter quum solus ille Latinorum Europæ angulus excitari debeat, vocandiq; omnes, duorū mensium spatio cōuenire Pisas possint, si ad extinguendū incēdium Ecclesiæ, & rē Dei diligenter curandā animentur. Quodq; superiores patres nostri vno pene anno notū facere orbi Christiano nō poterāt, nunc tabellariorū celeritate, & impressorū summa diligentia, litteris & schedulis imprimendis, vno fere mense tantumdem conficì potest: Et boni ac prudētis medici officium esse debet, vbi morbus inualescit, nulla tēporis habita ratione præsto occurrere, ne dum tēporum superstitione sequimur, ante tēpus, infoelix æger opprimatur. Et quāuis breuior terminus ad excitandam diligentiam edicto Patrum præfixus sit, mentis tamen suæ superfuit, ne quid præcipitâret ageretur, sed in omnib. quorum dilatio euidenter periculosa non sit, mature procedere, omnesq; necessarios etiam diutissime expectare, quorum auxilio & consilio tam sanctū opus iuuari posse censerent. Nec n, suæ prudentiæ iuxta sapientis verbum, inniti voluerunt Patres; sed in Domino (à quo omnis sapientia est) primum confidunt, mox in consiliis bene in causa Dei sententium, non leue præsidium reponunt.
units.tr: 19 We have dealt with each objection to the second petition. The third objection concerns the Pisan indiction, and it reminds us to touch on it. Since the earlier objection of this kind was already sufficiently answered above (for we showed very clearly that the right of summoning a council belonged to the Fathers), what remains is to add the rest. The advisers rail against the brevity of the time, counting the days with a certain exquisite care, and cry out with great show of words and vehement display: "Could the coming men have sought out what was necessary? Could the princes come, wishing to have provided for their own security? Could the rest come too?" But they would not have burst out with such confidence if, with the passions of mind set aside, by which true judgments are corrupted, they had sought the truth above flattery and cajolery. For apart from the fact that by law no fixed term is prescribed for summonses of this kind, the matter is therefore left to be decided according to the circumstances of things, places and times. Who doubts that, even if a fixed time had been set, it could evidently be shortened for cause by every right? The advisers themselves admit this. For while they say that a year is the customary term for summoning so great a matter, yet, so that this should not be given to anyone (as they say) for the sake of calumny, they cut it down to nine months. Here let the advisers consider: if it was allowed to shorten the term, which they call most ancient and customary, because of the calumnies of words, why should the term not be shortened because of the present and actual great scandals of the Church, which were feared to be soon to come, and which could be met in no other way than by a council? What these are, although the Fathers have not thrown them to the world, it is not yet their purpose to reveal in detail, if the peace of the Church, together with its reformation, or with this gentleness, can be had in any way. Indeed, when councils were gathered for future reformations while there were no actual scandals and the peace held, a term of one year for gathering the council was prescribed. But now, since the present scandals must be provided for as quickly as possible, it is right that they be gathered more speedily. Especially since only that corner of Latin Europe needs to be stirred and everyone summoned, they could assemble at Pisa within a space of two months, if they were moved to put out the fire of the Church and to care diligently for the work of God. And what our older fathers could not make known to the Christian world in almost a year, can now be accomplished in nearly a month by the speed of couriers and the great diligence of printers in printing letters and broadsheets. And it is the duty of a good and wise physician, when the disease gains strength, to meet it at once without regard for time, lest, through superstition about times, the unhappy patient be overwhelmed before the time. And although a shorter term was fixed by the Fathers' edict to rouse diligence, yet it was in their mind that nothing should be done rashly, but that in all matters whose delay is not evidently dangerous, they should proceed maturely and wait long even for all the necessary persons, whose help and counsel they thought could aid so holy a work. For the Fathers, according to the word of the wise man, did not wish to lean on their own prudence; rather, they trust first in the Lord, from whom all wisdom comes, and then place no slight reliance on counsels that judge rightly in the cause of God.

units.la: 20. Loci vero obiectio fragilis est, & paucis verbis refelleda. Pisana ciuitas generale alias Concilii recepit, à nouē Cardinalib. indictum tēpore Gregorii XII. Pontificis alias religiosissimi & prudentissimi, nisi q Cardinales illi, q Pontifex capitula cœlaruis iurata seruare renuit, ab eo discesserunt, & Pisis Concilium indixerunt: quo (tātā est vt veritatis) cōcursus incredibilis Christianorum omnium breui coiuit, vt celeriter collecta synodus magno hominum numero, sapientum, multas alias diuersis temporib. à Pontificib. cōgregatas superauerit. Nā, vt in illius gestis habetur, XXIII. Cardinales: tres patriarchæ principales, oratores Principū orbis in magno numero & insigni apparatu Pisis cōuenerunt: Archiepiscopi et X. Episcopi LXXI. electi V I. Abbates LXXV. aliorū Episcoporū procuratores LXXVI. Abbatū L V. oratores solenes vniuersitatū XII. studiorū generalium: Magister generalis hospitalis Hierosolymitani, Rhodiēsis, Priores generales IV. ordinum Mendicantium: Procuratores ciuitatū & capitulorū Ecclesiarum cathedraliū LXX. Magistri in Theologia supra cētum: Doctores iuris sive CCCC. Qui omnes diligenter Dei tractātes, exauctoratis duob. de Papatu cōtendentib. Alexandrū V. doctissimū & prudentissimum tissimum Pontifice eligentes, multa bona in Ecclesia Dei constituerunt gloriose illi magna synodo Constantiensi, in qua fine ultimo executionis accepit omnis iniqua de Pontificatu tam diuturna contentio. Synodus ergo tam solemnis Pisis habita, admonet si & alterius capax civitas illa erit: Civitas est ad hoc sua natura non parum accommoda coeli temperie, & agri fertilitate, & aedificiorum frequentia & magnitudine, mari exposita, Arno insignis navigabili, & piscoso, intersluente, civitatibus & oppidis ditissimis vicina, nec non insulis omnium rerum feracissimis in medio quasi Italiae sita. Urbsque (tametsi proximis annis bello vexata est) biennio tamen iam fere respiravit, & pro magna parte reparata & aucta est. Nec non excelsa respublica Florentina omnium diligentissima, quod de est reparatione domorum & villarum simul cum Pisanis civib. promidere citissime curat: & in bellum quod in Etruria timebatur, transactione Florentium, & Senensium, & longioris constitutionem pace, divino favore sublatum est. Sed quando Pisae alia statione non probaretur, quae potius sceleris est ita causa esset qua vera, conveniamus per Dei pietatem de loco idoneo ad omnibus tuto: ablitis ut loci contentio, nisi ex aliis culpa provenerit, sanctissimum hoc opus perturbare dicatur.
units.tr: 20. The objection based on the place is weak, and it can be answered in a few words. The city of Pisa once received a general council, convened by nine cardinals in the time of Pope Gregory XII, a pontiff otherwise most pious and prudent, when those cardinals withdrew from him because he refused to keep the oaths he had sworn in the conclave, and they called a council at Pisa. By the grace of God, an incredible crowd of Christians gathered there in a short time, so that the synod, quickly assembled, surpassed in the great number of its men, and in their wisdom, the many councils that popes had convened at various times. For, as is recorded in its acts, there came to Pisa twenty-three cardinals, three principal patriarchs, and envoys of the princes of the world in great number and with notable splendour; seventy-one archbishops and bishops, and six elected; seventy-five abbots, and seventy-six proctors of other bishops; fifty-five abbots' envoys; twelve solemn envoys of the universities of the general studies; the general master of the Hospitallers of Jerusalem and of Rhodes; four general priors of the mendicant orders; seventy proctors of cities and cathedral chapters; more than one hundred masters of theology; and four hundred doctors of law. All of them, attending diligently to the affairs of God, deposed the two contenders for the papacy and elected Alexander V, a most learned and prudent pontiff. They established many good things in the Church of God, and in that glorious great synod at Constance, the whole unjust contention over the papacy, which had lasted so long, at last came to its final conclusion. This synod, so solemnly held at Pisa, shows that the same city would be capable of another. The city is by its nature not a little suited to this: its climate and fertile land, its many and large buildings, its position on the sea, its navigable and fish-rich river Arno flowing through it, its nearness to very rich cities and towns, and the islands, most fruitful in all things, make it lie almost in the middle of Italy. And the city, although it was harassed by war in recent years, has for nearly two years now recovered its breath and been largely repaired and enlarged. Moreover, the noble Florentine republic, the most diligent of all, takes great care to provide with the citizens of Pisa for the rebuilding of houses and villas as quickly as possible; and the war that was feared in Tuscany has been removed, by the favour of God, through the agreement of the Florentines and the Sienese and a longer-lasting peace. But since Pisa would not be approved on any other ground, and since the cause of this would be a bad one, and the cause that is true is this, let us agree, by the goodness of God, on a place suitable and safe for all; and let it not be said that a dispute over the place, unless it arises from some other fault, disturbs this most holy work.

units.la: 21. Sed iam res admonet ad postremam optiorum literarum partem, in qua Concilii Romanicorum Pisanum indictionem attinet, properare. Imprimis, duplice in Ecclesia universali synodum erigere gravissima haeresis nota esset, contra articulum unam sanctam & Apostolicam Ecclesiam. Quumque Pisana synodus superioris rationibus subsistat, Altare alterum erigit & duplicitur Ecclesiam constituit, non sane a consultoribus est recte provisum. Fuit haec nostra practica Eugenii IV, alias per nullum Pontificem cogitata, nisi per Hieroboam, qui altare instituit contra Hierusalem: Constantius quoque duplex Concilium universale simul statuit Arimini, videlicet & Nicomediae, quorum errant utrumque. Deinde quod consultores verbis ornatioribus dicunt, Pontificem ad indictionem Concilii inclinari, neminem putari sibi posse illud Hieremiae, non ascendistis ex adverso, nec opposuistis vas pro domo Israel, quod tamen Hieremiae dictum non fuit, sed Ezechielis 6. 13. eadem Patres induxit ratio, ut in Pisanae synodi mentionem praevenissent. Fatemur ergo omnes quae Pontifex afferxit invocandae synodi generalis subesse necessitatem, atque utrinque perinde in ceteris conveniremus. Apud Lateranum autem ubi verius quae Pisis aedificiorum ruinae expectantur, infamisque atque pestilens aura obstat, tutum esse nunc conveniendi locum ad vere & salubriter Ecclesiae consulendum, absit ut concedamus. Latere insidiarum non parum in Lateranum suspicamur, proinde ut notorie & manifeste suspectum, capitibusque nostris perniciosum ac formidabile iis potissimum temporibus, aliis insistentes protestationibus vehementissime & constantissime denuo requisamus: ipsis quidem consultoribus aptissimum & tutissimum locum firmiter admittimus: equitum n. peditumque copiam illic habet instructissima, arces munitissimas, classem non procul paratam, urbem deinde ipsam, populos finitimos bello & armis assuetos, suo nutu pendentes, assuetosque capitaneos pro Pontificis voluntate, Cardinales & Praelatos parui pendere, & iam illic Cardinales hoc timore coacti, non vera, sed blandientis consulturi sunt. Verum, Pisanae synodi indictoribus, caeterisque quib. Concilio adesse convenit, nullus profecto hominum est hodie illum insidiosissimum, periculosissimumque, vel iureiurando protinus non affirmet, nec toto in orbe quidquam adeo notum esse scimus, quo hoc notius manifestiusque non sit, maximoque salutis Patrum discrimine accessus in urbe hodie ab omnibus teneretur. Quare, molesta esse non debet isthaec recusatio: Quis n. vel elegantissime Clemens V. inquit, ad indicegradi & feroci exercitus stipatum facile venerit? Quis auderet vel qua ratione teneretur illi se vltroneum offerre, & eorum se sinu reponere, quorum non temere violentia timeatur? hoc n. de iure timetur, de more vitatur, refugit ratio, abhorret natura, nec ad iustissimum animorum Patrum terrorem tollendum aut minuendum ampla illa verba salui conductus a Pontifice oblati proficiunt, promissioque benigne & charitatiue suscipiendi atque tractandi. Quae n. solemnior unquam fides & promissio, quae illa capitulorum conclavis et per viam contractus omni voto & iuramento valida, & alias per Apostolicas literas data, cogitari potest & debet? quo vero pacto seruata sit, creationes Cardinalium & eorum libertas minime seruata ostendant? Sed admittamus q; speremus sanctitatem suam hanc promissionem integra mente seruare velle, ut nec odio, nec iracundiae censura sit, quomodo tamen (Absit sanctitati suae indignatio) ex praeteritis actionibus animi Patrum securi esse poterunt? homines etenim sunt summi Pontifices, & duodecim horas esse diei Dominus meminit? Quis tamen eos ab innumeris summo Pontifici assistentibus, quis a pluribus hominum, quorum copia in Curia esse solet, iniuriis, & violentiis securos reddet? admonent intolerabiles iniuriae, admonent immanissimae violentiae, admonent inauditae & nefandissimae caedes, quas nonnulli Patres Curiae sequentes perpessi sunt. Ipse deinde ne logius (ut aiunt) exempla peramus Pontifex summus, dum in minoribus ageret, quantum in salvi conductus esse, abunde docuit. Stultissimum n. esse sapiens dicebat, libertate & vita ut pelle mortua bellue, id est cum membrana salui conductus, comutare. Quodq; ipse ita constanter tanto tempore aliis non credidit, difficillimum erit ut aliis sibi credatur, quod sententia ratione sane non caret. Nam & Innocent. III. docet, non teneri quempiam cum litteris salui conductus sese aduersanti credere. Pontifices quoque superiores, postquam exercitus, armatasque custodias & arces Romae tenuerunt, & nisi alia libertas Senatus restituatur, & modus alius vivendi gubernandi a Pontificib. in urbe seruetur, nemo est qui eum locum nunc ad hanc Ecclesiam libertate idoneum aptumque in fluctiae S. Spiritus, qui communiter liberas mentes in Concilio implet, diiudicare possit. Quare postquam loci exceptio omni iure & ratione legitima reddita, postquam salui conductus oblatio iustissimum metu in viros
units.tr: 21. But now the matter urges us to hasten to the last part of your letter, which concerns the Roman council's convocation at Pisa. First, to set up a double synod in the universal Church would be a most grave mark of heresy, against the article unam sanctam & Apostolicam Ecclesiam. And since the Pisan synod stands on the reasons given above, it erects another altar and makes the Church double; the advisers have certainly not provided wisely in this. This practice of ours under Eugenius IV was never contrived by any other pope, except by Jeroboam, who set up an altar against Jerusalem. Constantius too established two universal councils at once, at Arminium and at Nicomedia, and both were in error. Then, what the advisers say in more ornate words, that the pope is inclined to convene a council, and that no one thinks he can apply to himself that saying of Jeremiah, non ascendistis ex adverso, nec opposuistis vas pro domo Israel, is not a saying of Jeremiah at all, but of Ezekiel 6. 13. The same reasoning led the Fathers to anticipate the mention of the Pisan synod. We therefore all confess that the necessity of calling a general synod, which the pope has asserted, lies upon us, and on this we would agree on all other points as well. But that the Lateran, where the ruins of the Pisan buildings are expected to be more real, and a foul and pestilential air stands in the way, is now a safe place to meet for the true and wholesome good of the Church, we will by no means concede. We suspect no small plot against us in the Lateran; being notoriously and manifestly suspect, and dangerous and frightening to our heads especially in these times, we again demand, insisting on other protests most vehemently and most steadfastly, that it be avoided. For the advisers themselves, we firmly admit that it is a most suitable and safest place: there it has a most well-equipped supply of horsemen and foot soldiers, most strongly fortified citadels, a fleet not far off at hand, and the city itself, with neighbouring peoples accustomed to war and arms, hanging on his nod, and captains accustomed to act at the pope's will, and to think little of cardinals and prelates; and already the cardinals there, compelled by this fear, will give not true but flattering counsel. But truly, to the instigators of the Pisan synod and to the others who ought to attend the council, there is surely no one in the world today who would not swear at once that that place is most treacherous and most dangerous; nor do we know anything in the whole world so well known, or more manifest than this, and today access to the city is held by everyone at the greatest peril to the safety of the Fathers. Wherefore this refusal ought not to be taken amiss: for, as the most elegant Clement V said, who would easily come to a council surrounded by a fierce army? Who would dare, or on what ground would he consent, to offer himself of his own accord and place himself in the bosom of those whose violence is not lightly feared? For this is feared by right, avoided by custom, shunned by reason, abhorred by nature; and to remove or lessen the terror of the most just minds of the Fathers, those ample words of a safe-conduct offered by the pope do not avail, nor does the promise of a kind and charitable reception and treatment. For what more solemn faith and promise could ever be thought of, or ought to be, than that of the capitulations of the conclave, valid by every vow and oath and by way of contract, and given at other times by apostolic letters? But how it has been kept, the creation of cardinals and their scarcely preserved freedom show. But let us grant that we hope his holiness wishes to keep this promise with a sincere mind, so that there is no censure from hatred or anger; yet how, (far be it from his holiness to take offence), can the minds of the Fathers be secure from his past actions? For popes are men, and the Lord reminds us that the day has twelve hours. Yet who will make them secure from the countless attendants of the supreme pontiff, and from the many men, whose numbers are usually at the Curia, and from injuries and violence? Intolerable injuries warn us, most savage violence warns us, unheard-of and most wicked slaughters warn us, which some of the Fathers who followed the Curia have suffered. Then, that we may not go further afield (as they say) for examples, the supreme pontiff himself, when he was acting in smaller matters, has amply shown how much a safe-conduct is worth. For the wise man used to say that it is most foolish to exchange liberty and life, like a beast's skin when dead, that is, for the parchment of a safe-conduct. And since he himself would not for so long trust others so constantly, it will be most difficult for others to trust him, which opinion is certainly not without reason. For Innocent III also teaches that no one is bound to trust a man who opposes him, even with letters of safe-conduct. Earlier popes too, after they held the army, armed guards and citadels of Rome, and unless the freedom of the Senate is restored and another way of living and governing is kept by the popes in the city, there is no one who can judge that place, now, to be suitable and fit for this Church's liberty, for the breath of the Holy Spirit, which commonly fills free minds in a council. Wherefore, since the objection to the place has been answered by every right and lawful reason, and since the offer of a safe-conduct does not remove the most just fear falling upon the men, nor by right nor by reason is it set aside. Let the advisers, for God's sake, omit this same mention of the Lateran place. For by this difficulty of place and danger they present no slight suspicion, that it is not so much dear to them that the synod be held at the Lateran...

units.la: { } ornament In vitos constantes cadentem, nec iure nec ratione submouet; Omittant pro Deo eandem consultores Laterani loci mentionem. Suspicionem n. nō leuem eam hac loci difficultate & discrimine præbent, non tam eis cordi esse apud Lateranā synodum teneri, quam ne Pisis aut alibi teneatur, impedire. Quod si (vt diximus) Pisanā ciuitatem non probant (quam tamen optimam, omnibusq; tutam & idoneam putauimus, credimusq;) alterius idonei atq; omnib. tuti loci oblationem non negamus; quinimo & antea per litteras & nuntios nostros obtulimus, & nunc harū tenore rursus offerre non cessamus, vt intelligat vniuersa Ecclesia, sciant omnes Principes, cunctiq; fideles, non ad contentionē aut turbationem, minusq; ad perniciosissimum schisma (vt obiicitur) excitandum, sed ad quietē & pacē inducendam, ad animarū salute procurandā, ad splendorem Ecclesiæ iuuandum, ad expeditionē contra infideles promouendā, vinculis præcepti & iuramenti motos Patres Pisanæ synodi curam subiisse. Quod post quā hac ratione & mente processisse omnipotens creator & redemptor noster intelligis, aperta namq; tibi sunt hominū corda omniū omnesq; cogitationes clare intelligis occurro diuinæ prouidentiæ tuæ munere, occurre quæsumus prius quā in flammam surgat paratū incendiū, & quod humana diligentia, mortaliq; studio fieri non potest, fac vt cœlestis gratiā dono consequamur, & pacifica vniuersali ac libera congregatione Ecclesiæ, pro vera eius reformatione, quā tot laboribus quærimus, tam spiritualiter quam temporaliter in vnum conuenientes perfruamur.
units.tr: ornament In vitos constantes cadentem, nec iure nec ratione submouet; Let the counsellors of the Lateran place, for God's sake, omit that same mention of the place. For by this difficulty and danger of the place they give no slight suspicion that it is not so much their concern that the synod be held at the Lateran as that it not be held at Pisa or anywhere else. But if (as we have said) they do not approve the city of Pisa (which we nonetheless have thought, and still believe, to be most excellent, safe for all and suitable), we do not refuse to offer another suitable place, safe for all. Indeed we have already offered this before, through our letters and messengers, and now by the tenor of these letters we do not cease to offer it again. Let the whole Church understand, and let all princes and all the faithful know, that the Fathers of the Synod of Pisa, moved by the bonds of precept and oath, undertook this charge not to stir up contention or disturbance, still less the most pernicious schism (as is objected), but to bring about quiet and peace, to procure the salvation of souls, to aid the splendour of the Church, and to promote the expedition against the infidels. Since our almighty Creator and Redeemer understands that this was undertaken with this reasoning and intention, for the hearts of all men lie open to him and he clearly understands all their thoughts, we beseech you, by the gift of your divine providence, come to meet us before the ready fire rises into flame. What human diligence and mortal effort cannot accomplish, let us obtain by heavenly grace, so that, gathered together as one in a peaceful, universal and free assembly of the Church for its true reformation, which we seek with so many labours, we may enjoy it both spiritually and temporally.

units.la: 22. Hæc sunt, quæ pro refellendis iis quæ priores literæ continebant adducenda censuimus; omissis ne modū excedamus, aliis quā plurimis quib. ad iura nostra tuēda abundamus. Super est, vt quantū posteriores monitorii literæ æquitatis habeant, quam breuissime videcamus, maior n. earū vis ex superioribus sublata cernitur: In illis tamen satis liquet cōtumeliose admodum consultores aduersum Patres egisse, illosq; maximis ac pene inauditis iniuriis & contumeliis, iniquisq; censuris & pœnis pro nulla aut leui culpa afficere voluisse, quos nunc laudant & extollunt, nunc vituperant & cruciant, ad instar militū præsidis, q Christū salutantes, dicentesq; illi auē, mox arundine pcutiebant. Nēpe fortuna quadā consultores literis illas monitorii ex duab. aliis Pontificū literis apertissimo furto verborū contexerunt: ex altera videl. Nicolai IV. bulla q incipit, Cœlestis altitudo potentiæ, & ad aue quodāmodo pertinuisse videtur: & altera Eugenii quoq; IV. incipiente, Multa sanctorum exempla, quæ colaphos & arundinē concernit; In quib. monitorii literis, sic ex prædictis latrocinio aperto subtractis non solū patres grauissime sunt lacessiti, verū & Pontifices ipsi, quorū verbis & doctrinis literæ illæ subsistunt quum ipsorū menti Pontificū euidenter obstent, nō mediocriter iniuriari videntur. Sublimem n. illā Cardinalium laudationem, quam Nicol. ad effectum partitionis patrimonii, S.R.E. inter Papā & Senatum induxit, ad maledictionem & priuationē Cardinalium repetita esse dē verbis præfatione retorquent, quam tamē Nicol. Pontifex sapientissimus nisi in Concilio generali aut calib. vrgentioribus maturioriq; iudicio nunquam excogitasset. Similiterq; congesta quædam grauissima comitia & maledicta, quib. Eugenius suo monitorio contra Felicē Amedeum & illius electores, post priuationē de se factam & Amedei electionē, cumulatissime inuehitur; eadē maledicta, eisdemq; terminis, eodemq; more propositionis consistorialis, pro simplici Patrum admonitione Concilii, perperam & inconsulte profundunt: quæ tamen Eugenius pro simili causa minime vnquā usus fuisset attentare. Immemores ergo consultores clementiæ & æquitatis Dei & superiorū Pontificum q proponunt & offerunt omni feritate & crudelitate aduersum Patres intemperatissime debacchantur, inconsideratos medicos imitati, qui apud Hippocratem sanam medicinā alicui morbo legentes, morbis aliis improportionate distribuunt. Inducunt et atroces quosdā vespilones, fiscos in senatu proponentes, & ad tumultū quasi viuētes Patres inducere satagentes, Carrosum quendā & Cuccinū, nomina ipso pene horrenda sono, ac si hominum carnes dilaniaturi & cocturi accessissent, quorum os vanitate & dolos locutum est: quum responsa priorum literarum istis adaptari possint, nisi nouiter deductis respondere non cogimur. Inter alia tamen visum est istis addere de contentionib. Patrū Florentiæ initis, quas pleno ore iniquas appellant, sicut febricitantis lingua omne dulce amarū iudicat. Nēpe, conuentiones illæ libertati sacri Senatus, splendori & spiritualitati Ecclesiæ, & iuriū suorū conseruationi vnice innituntur, quarū scripta si pferantur, non possunt à sapientib. nisi summe commendari. Pro illis tamen, consulentium feritas, Notarium vnum rogarū, qui bona fide nihil mali suspicās, quū ad Apostolicā Curiā negotia sua tractaturus accessisset, in tetrimū carcere detrusit, & grauissime torsit: quæ euidens est coniectura rancoris & odii contra Patres. Nā si cliēntem pacificū & innocuū: quod testimonio veritatis astitit à patronis suis rogatus, tam efferate torserunt, quid cogitandū erit de odio cōtra Patres? Quare omnis verborū promissio ab illorū odiis qui parcere nesciunt, Patres iure tutari minime potest. Verū consultores ipsi, qui tam copiosē, tam frequenter officia quib. Cardinales summo Pontifici tenentur explicauerunt, debuissent, si recte vterentur consilio, quibus et Pontifex illis teneatur, admonuisse, ne in tam notorie excedentē prolabetetur offensam. Summus namque Pontifex præcipuo quodā vinculo charitatis & clementiæ sacrum Senatum & illius membra debuit respexisse, cuius peculiari quodāmodo caput, pater, & frater est, quæ omnia sunt dilectionis summæ, & charitatis nomina, non certe euersionis & odii. Caputn. quod vigilat & prospicit, & laborat pro membris, nunquā illa odio habet, quinimo gratulatur, quum membra ipsius languorem aliquem admoneret & curaret. Pater ergo & frater summæ charitatis appellationes sunt pastor Ecclesiæ & vicarii Dei, qui alias recte Pontifex nuncupatur, non feritatē & tyrannidē prætendunt, summam charitatem & clementiā. Cōmissurus namq; Dominus Petro curā pastoralē & primatum Ecclesiæ, non semel, sed tertio ei dixit, Simon Ioannis & diligis me plus iis, Pasce oves meas: & rursus vicariatus Dei omnem charitate & clementiā præ se fert, quum illum referat, de quo scribitur, Deus charitas est, & cui proprium est misereri semper & parcere, & miserationes eius super omnia opera eius: qua vero charitate cum patrib. litteris istis agatur, satis ex illis perspicuum est, pro admonitione Concilii, quā ex iustis summis causis patres conceperunt, imo illis dominus inspirauit, acerrimas censuras, interdicta, auferendarum dignitatum, beneficiorum poenas cōsultores minantur. Hæccine, respondeat hoc loco Carrosus & Cuccinus in graui illa de nobis querela pietatē tantā præ se ferētes, pietatis sunt argumenta? Hæccine boni pastoris & vicarii Dei officia? sunt ne hæc munera quib. pater, & frater charitatē suam explicant. Et quum hic respónderint, mox si placet obiiciant, an sicut æquū est bene valenti capiti membra obsequi, ita æquissimum sit eisdē, si laboraret, auxilio potius prodesse quā obsequio placere. Respondeant deniq; quanto aduersus eos fieri postulare nt, qui scelestissimum aliquod porrexissent; si aduersus procurantes per necessaria sanctissimamq; Ecclesiæ reformationem tot tantasq; poenas poposcerunt. Intelligit ergo vniuersus orbis, vident docti, indocti, cœci etiam manibus tangunt, de bono opere Patres lapidari, nullamq; ob rem aliam insensum illis summum Pontificē, nisi quod Deo magis quam hominib. obedire maluerint: Quæ res fiduciam & magnam aduersus omnem vim securitatem illis præbitura est. Iamq; Spiritus S. (quo auctore coeperunt) Pontificē ipsum, qui hactenus ad Concilia durior videbatur, quum admonitione Pisanæ synodi a patrib. præuenti se sensit continuo maximā Concilii cōuocandi necessitatem subesse profitetur, atq; Lateranum protinus indicit. Inde qui antea penitus dissentiebant, nunc de loco tantum dissentire videntur. Iniungitur tamen Patrib. per consultores, vt Romam breui quodam termino accedant, & a prosequutione Pisanæ synodi abstineant, præceptione altera corpus, animā altera occidere satagentes. Nam Romæ dieb. istis absq; notorio vitæ discrimine (vt est dictum) manere non possunt, a Concilii prosequutione, ratione præcepti, voti, & iuramenti ac scandali, sine interitu salutis æternæ cessare non valent, & iuxta Canonicas sanctiones & aperta Innocentii IV. doctrina (vt prædiximus) quoniā Apostolica præcepta notorie continent, vtriusq; vel alterius vitæ periculum aut decolorationem, vel turbationem status vniuersalis Ecclesiæ, vel vnde multa mala verisimiliter futura timerent, audienda quidē sunt, sed minime admittenda, quinimo ab eis prouocandum esse debeat, quam doctrinam imitati olim patres primæ Pisanæ synodi, quib. Gregor. XII. sub grauissimis censuris præcipiebat vt a prosequutione synodi cessarent, minime obtempetarunt, sed prouocatione præcedente synodum sanctissime tenuerunt, quod sapientes omnes & patres Constantiæ laudauerunt; censurasq; Apostolicas, contra illos fulminatas, quamuis semper timendas, in hoc tamen casu minime obseruandas esse approbauerunt; quam tamen apud Pisanos patres non starent adhuc determinationes synodi Constantiensis de superioritate Concilii, nec præceptum de congregando Concilio singulis decenniis, nec statutum aut practicatum, impedimenta præstita Conciliis per quoscunq; suspicionem hæresis continerent: ac si prætenderent velle corrigibilitatem criminum tueri & defendere: Quæ crimina potissimum capitis in Concilio moderantur, & ea potissimum ratione quod Cōcilia impediebant, Ioan. XXII. & Benedict. XIII. Constantiæ sunt exauctorati. Quare ergo tam efferate consultores prosequentur Patres secundæ Pisanæ synodi? quū primi de hoc fuerint laudati, nec isti sicut illi statim prima conuocatione Concilii Pontifici obedientiam subtraxerint. Patres namq; moderni in bona Iulii II. Pōtificis maximi obedientia manent, & manere volunt vt est dictum.
