Nisi consultores causam schismati per aliquas priuationes obtulerint, periculis tamen notoriis corporis & animæ seclusis, & esto quod præuentione Patrum, & tam iustis causis synodus Pisana aperte subsistat: vt tamen obedire clarius videantur Patres, dum Pontifex censuras & poenas auferat, vel suspendat, parati quoq; erunt suspendere aut prorogare synodi Pisanæ prosequutionē, dum statim de loco libero & tuto extra Ecclesiæ Romanæ iurisdictionē conue niatur, in quo et, vt claudantur ora detrahentium Patrib. quod eiectioni Pontificis præcipue studeant, quod tamen alienissimum ab illis fuit, possent in tale euentum suspensionis censuratū & actualis assignati loci neutralis liberi cōtentari Patres, si in alis dissensio nō sit titulum præfigi & assignari Concilii concordandi ad reformationes futuras, & extinguendas hæreses, pacē Christianorum promouendā, & bellum contra infideles dirigendum, vt de iis solum, & dissidentibus quæstionum fidei, quæ in Ecclesia indecisæ manerent, in Concilio tractentur, & re Bononiensem, & Ferrariensem omnimode Concilio remittere, vt quæ ibi determinabuntur, efficaciter & solide per omnes Principes obseruari permittantur, & iureiurando statuantur: ita vt sine Christiani sanguinis effusione, sine priuationib. & turbationib. Ecclesiæ, ista medicina Concilii tam desiderata, Ecclesia ipsam absq; magna anxietate purget & sanet, pacemq; Christianorum cōtinear, & expeditionē contra infideles recte & rite promoueat: quod supplicib. votis Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum enixe omnes oramus, & vt sanctissimo D. N. vicario suo, hanc mentē cōcordiæ loci simul & pietatis & clementiæ inspiret. Quod si (quod absit) Pontifex renuerit (quum locus Romanus hodie Cōcilio libero nō sit aptus) euidentissimum erit vniuersæ Ecclesiæ omne Concilium prorsus illum recusare, in eumq; euentum, prout de iure, Pisis aut alio loco, quo transferetur Concilium vniuersale liberum, prosequemur. Quare rogamus per viscera Domini Dei nostri
units.tr: 22. These are the points we have thought it right to bring forward in answer to what the earlier letters contained. We have left out many others, which we could have used to defend our rights, so that we do not go beyond due measure. It remains to see, as briefly as possible, how much fairness the later admonitory letters have, for their force is seen to be largely removed by what has gone before. Still, it is clear enough from them that the advisers have acted very insultingly against the Fathers, and have wished to punish them with the greatest and almost unheard-of injuries and insults, with unjust censures and penalties, for no fault or a slight one. These are the men they now praise and exalt, now denounce and torment, like the soldiers of the governor who greeted Christ, saying "Hail," and then straightway struck him with a reed. By some lucky chance the advisers wove these admonitory letters, by a plainly obvious theft of words, out of two other papal letters: namely, the bull of Nicholas IV that begins Caelestis altitudo potentiae, which seems in a way to belong to the "Hail," and the letter of Eugenius IV that begins Multa sanctorum exempla, which concerns the blows and the reed. In these admonitory letters, with the foregoing material taken away in open theft, not only have the Fathers been most severely assailed, but the Popes themselves, on whose words and teachings those letters rest, seem to have been injured no little, since they plainly stand in the way of the Popes' own purpose. For that lofty praise of the Cardinals, which Nicholas introduced when he dealt with dividing the patrimony of the Holy Roman Church between the Pope and the Senate, they twist into a curse and deprivation of the Cardinals, repeating it in the very words of its preamble; yet Nicholas, the most wise Pope, would never have devised it except in a general council or in other more pressing matters and with more mature judgment. Likewise, certain very grave accusations and curses, heaped together, with which Eugenius in his admonition against Felix Amadeus and his electors, after the deprivation pronounced against them and the election of Amadeus, rails most copiously, these same curses, in the same terms and the same manner of consistorial proposal, they rashly and carelessly pour out against the Fathers as a simple admonition of the Council; and yet Eugenius, in a similar case, never once presumed to attempt this. Forgetful, therefore, of the mercy and fairness of God and of the earlier Popes, whom they put forward and hold up, the advisers rage against the Fathers with every savagery and cruelty, like ill-advised physicians whom Hippocrates describes, who, reading a sound remedy for one disease, distribute it inappropriately among other diseases. They also bring forward certain atrocious gravediggers, proposing confiscations in the Senate, and striving to bring in the Fathers as if they were still alive and in an uproar; a certain Carrosus and Cuccinus, names almost dreadful in sound, as though they had come to tear and cook men's flesh, whose mouths have spoken vanity and deceit. Since the answers to the earlier letters could be fitted to these men, we are not obliged to reply except to what has been newly brought forward. Among other things, however, they thought fit to add a complaint about the agreements entered into by the Fathers at Florence, which they call unjust with full mouth, just as the tongue of a feverish man judges every sweet thing bitter. Indeed, those agreements rest solely on the liberty of the sacred Senate, the splendour and spirituality of the Church, and the preservation of its rights; if their writings were produced, they could not be praised by wise men except in the highest terms. Yet in return for these things the savagery of the advisers has thrust into a most foul prison one notary, who had come to the Apostolic Curia to conduct his business in good faith, suspecting no harm, and has tortured him most severely; which is clear evidence of their rancour and hatred against the Fathers. For if they have tortured so cruelly a peaceable and harmless client, who had stood by the testimony of truth when asked by his patrons, what must we think of their hatred against the Fathers? Wherefore no promise of words can rightly protect the Fathers from the hatreds of men who do not know how to spare. But the advisers themselves, who have so fully and so often explained the duties to which the Cardinals are bound toward the supreme Pontiff, ought, if they used sound counsel, to have admonished him to what duties the Pontiff himself is bound, lest he slip into an offence so notoriously exceeding bounds. For the supreme Pontiff, by a special bond of charity and clemency, ought to have regarded the sacred Senate and its members, of whom he is in a peculiar way the head, father and brother; all of which are names of supreme love and charity, certainly not of overthrow and hatred. The head, which watches over and looks out for and labours for the members, never hates them; rather it rejoices when the members admonish and cure some weakness of theirs. Therefore "father" and "brother," names of the highest charity, and "shepherd of the Church" and "vicar of God," by which the Pontiff is rightly called, do not put forward ferocity and tyranny, but the highest charity and clemency. When the Lord was about to entrust to Peter the pastoral care and primacy of the Church, He said to him not once but three times, "Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these? Feed my sheep." And again, the vicariate of God displays all charity and clemency, since it refers to Him of whom it is written, "God is love," and whose property it is always to show mercy and to spare, "and his tender mercies are over all his works." How the case is being handled with the Fathers by these letters is clear enough from them: for the admonition of the Council, which the Fathers conceived from just and very weighty causes, indeed which the Lord inspired in them, the advisers threaten the most bitter censures, interdicts, penalties of removal from offices and benefices. Let Carrosus and Cuccinus answer here: are these the proofs of piety, which they display in their grave complaint against us? Are these the duties of a good shepherd and vicar of God? Are these the services by which a father and brother show their love? And when they have answered here, let them then, if they please, object: as it is fair for the members to obey a head in good health, so it would be most fair for the head, if it were ailing, to help the members rather than to demand their obedience. Finally, let them answer how severely they would demand that men be dealt with who had committed some most wicked crime, when they have called for so many and such great penalties against those who promote the necessary and most holy reformation of the Church. Therefore the whole world understands; the learned and the unlearned see it; even the blind touch it with their hands: the Fathers are being stoned for a good work, and the supreme Pontiff is incensed against them for no other reason than that they chose to obey God rather than men. This will give them confidence and great security against every violence. And now the Holy Spirit (by whose authority they began), when the Pontiff himself, who until now had seemed harder toward councils, was anticipated by the Fathers through the admonition of the Synod of Pisa, feels at once that there is the greatest necessity to call a Council, professes this, and forthwith appoints the Lateran. From this point, those who before were entirely at odds now seem to differ only about the place. Yet the advisers order the Fathers to come to Rome within a certain short term and to cease from pursuing the Synod of Pisa, one party striving to kill the body by one precept and the soul by another. For they cannot remain in Rome in those days without notorious danger to life (as has been said); they cannot cease from pursuing the Council, by reason of precept, vow and oath, and of scandal, without the loss of eternal salvation. And according to the canonical sanctions and the plain teaching of Innocent IV (as we have said above), since the apostolic precepts notoriously contain that if there is danger to either life or body, or disturbance or disruption of the state of the universal Church, or if many evils are reasonably feared to follow from it, such commands are indeed to be heard, but by no means admitted; nay, one ought to appeal against them. Following this teaching, the Fathers of the first Synod of Pisa, to whom Gregory XII commanded under the gravest censures that they cease from pursuing the Synod, did not obey, but by a prior appeal held fast most sanctely to the Synod; and all the wise men and the Fathers of Constance praised this, and approved that the apostolic censures hurled against those men, though always to be feared, were in this case by no means to be observed. Nor, indeed, did the determinations of the Synod of Constance on the superiority of the Council, nor the precept about convoking a Council every ten years, nor any statute or practice, stand in the way of the Fathers of Pisa; nor did any impediments placed in the way of councils by whomsoever, which involve suspicion of heresy, or as if they pretended to wish to protect and defend the correction of crimes: crimes which chiefly are punished by capital sentence in a Council, and chiefly for the reason that they obstructed councils; for this reason John XXII and Benedict XIII were deposed at Constance. Why, then, do the advisers pursue the Fathers of the second Synod of Pisa so savagely, since the first Fathers were praised for this, and these men did not, like those, withdraw obedience from the Pontiff at once upon the first convocation of a Council? For the Fathers of today remain, and wish to remain, in the good obedience of the supreme Pontiff Julius II, as has been said. Unless the advisers have put the cause of the schism forward by some deprivations, while the notorious dangers to body and soul are set aside; and even if the Synod of Pisa stands openly, by the anticipation of the Fathers and for such just causes, yet, so that the Fathers may appear to obey more clearly, while the Pontiff removes or suspends censures and penalties, they will also be ready to suspend or postpone the pursuit of the Synod of Pisa, provided that at once they meet in a free and safe place outside the jurisdiction of the Roman Church, and in such an event the Fathers could be content with the suspension of the censures and a neutral free place actually assigned, so that also the mouths of those who slander the Fathers may be closed, since they especially strive for the expulsion of the Pontiff, which yet was most alien to them. If there is no dissension in other matters, a title may be prescribed and assigned for the Council, to the effect that it will meet for the reconciliation of the Church for future reformations, for extinguishing heresies, for promoting peace among Christians, and for directing war against the infidels; so that only those matters of faith which remain undecided in the Church, and those who dissent about them, are treated in the Council; and that the affair of Bologna and Ferrara is entirely remitted to the Council, so that whatever is determined there may be permitted to be observed efficiently and firmly by all princes, and be established by oath; so that without the shedding of Christian blood, without deprivations and disturbances of the Church, this remedy of a Council, so much desired, may cleanse and heal the Church itself without great anxiety, may maintain the peace of Christians, and may rightly and duly promote the expedition against the infidels. This we all earnestly beseech the Lord our Jesus Christ with suppliant prayers, and that He may inspire our most holy lord, His vicar, with this mind of concord, of place, and at the same time of piety and clemency. But if (which God forbid) the Pontiff refuse, since the Roman place today is not suited to a free Council, it will be most evident to the whole Church that he rejects every Council altogether; and in that event, as is lawful, we shall proceed at Pisa, or elsewhere to which the universal free Council is transferred. Wherefore we ask, through the bowels of the Lord our God,

units.la: Concil. Pis. hostri Sanctissimum D. N. omnesque S.R.E. Cardinales, Principes, & Prælatos, vt in hac nostra sancta, imo Dei intentione consentiant, ne ritus sacrorum Conciliorum, quo bona omnia in Ecclesia fundamenta sunt, prorsus aboleant. Considerétq; Principes, spiritu Ecclesiæ obliteratione Conciliorum quotidie magis ac magis extingui, quale reformatis religionibus contingeret, si capitula sua triennalia vel annalia non seruarent, Concilia namque generalia, libertatem Ecclesiæ, spiritualitatemque & pacem continerent, literasque alerent, & fouerent, aceuidentissime & efficacissime fidei exaltationem in partibus, quas infideles Christianis derinent, promouerent. Quare Principes omnes imo & vniuersi fideles assurgite, adeste, fauete vniuersali Ecclesiæ, pro qua Dominus sanguinem suum fudit, intra quam nos omnes saluari firmissime credimus, & proillius pace, non pro vnius hominis obliquabilis quiete laborate. Nempe ex hac duplici indíctione Concilii, nostra videlicet, quæ iure præuenit, quæ subsequuta & sanctissimi D.N. quum duplex Concilium vniuersale simul teneri non posset, qui contra articulum esset, vnam sanctam: Si non consurgeret vnius Concilii liberæ œruti œcumenici congregatio, exprobrabimur oes à Principibus, lapidabimur à populis quod splendori sponsæ Domini obiicem tam notorie oppoluerimus. Cuius tamen culpæ Patres Pisani immunes esse voluut, quum nullis laboriis & periculis, ad tam sanctum opus vere & realiter cum pace perficiendum pepercerint.
units.tr: Concil. Pis. We beseech our most holy Lord and all the Cardinals, Princes and Prelates of the Holy Roman Church, that in this our holy, or rather God's, purpose they consent, lest they utterly abolish the rite of the sacred Councils, on which all good things in the Church are founded. Let the Princes also consider that the spirit of the Church is extinguished more and more every day by the disregard of Councils, as happens in the reformed religions when they do not keep their triennial or annual chapters. For general Councils maintain the liberty, spirituality and peace of the Church, nourish and cherish letters, and most evidently and effectively promote the exaltation of the faith in those parts which the infidels tear from the Christians. Therefore, all you Princes and all the faithful, rise up, come to help and favour the universal Church, for which the Lord shed his blood, within which we firmly believe all of us are saved, and labour for her peace, not for the easily disturbed quiet of one man. Indeed, from this double summons of a Council, namely ours, which came first by right, and the later one of our most holy Lord, since a double universal Council could not be held at the same time, which would be contrary to the article "one holy" (Church), if the free and lawful gathering of one ecumenical Council did not arise, we shall all be reproached by the Princes and stoned by the peoples, because we have so notoriously set an obstacle before the splendour of the Lord's bride. Yet the Pisan Fathers wish to be free of this guilt, since they have spared no labours and dangers to bring about truly and really, in peace, so holy a work.

units.la: Deniq;, quum incerti simus quantum apud summum Pontificem voces nostræ valituræ sint dubiumq; nobis sit an quæ aduersus nos comminatur, cū effectu perficiat, vt res nostra rutius procedat, licet aperti iuris sit hoc casu Concilii vniuersalis Ecclesiæ irritas & nullas esse censuras & pœnas prohibituas; constetque talia, si quando aduersus eos propositæ fuissent, maiores nostros minime exist imasse, imo & contemptisse: sicut Patres antiquos Pianos fecisse vulgarum est, quos vniuersa Ecclesia commendauit: ad cautelam tamen abundantem, maioremq; Apostolicæ sedis reuerentiam, protestationibus, prouocationibus, & appellationibus nostris sæpius interpositis adhærentes, easque pro expressis & ad verbum repetitis haberi volentes comminationes, pœnas, censuras, priuationes, inhabilitationes, interdicta omnia denique in nostrum, fautorumque nostrorum omnium quoquo modo nobiscum sentientium attentata, & attentanda, inania, irrita, & nulla profitemur & protestamur, sicut in primis est dictum. Et quatenus aliqua sint (quod non fatemur) harum tenore iniquissima & iniustissima dicimus, atque ad actu indictum sacri Concilium Pisanum, aut quo transferetur tenendum, omnesque alios ad quos iure prouocandum & appellandum sit, prouocamus, & appellamus, Ad laudem & gloriam Redemptoris & Domini nostri Iesu Christi, ac immaculatæ sponsæ suæ Catholicæ vniuersalis ecclesiæ splendorem & exaltationem.
units.tr: Finally, since we are uncertain how far our voices will avail with the supreme Pontiff, and it is doubtful to us whether what he threatens against us will be carried out, so that our cause may proceed more quickly: although it is clearly the law in this case that the censures and penalties prohibited by a universal Council of the Church are void and null, and it is agreed that our forefathers did not at all fear such things, if they were ever proposed against them, but rather despised them, just as it is commonly known that the ancient Fathers of Pisa did, whom the whole Church commended; nevertheless, for abundant caution and the greater reverence due to the Apostolic See, adhering to our protestations, provocations and appeals, often interposed, and wishing the threats, penalties, censures, deprivations, disqualifications and all interdicts whatever, attempted or to be attempted against us and all our supporters who think with us in any way, to be held as expressed and repeated word for word, we profess and protest that they are empty, void and null, as has been said at the outset. And insofar as some of them are (which we do not admit), we declare them most iniquitous and most unjust, and we provoke and appeal to the sacred Council of Pisa, now convened, or to whatever place it is transferred, and to all others to whom it is right to provoke and appeal, to the praise and glory of our Redeemer and Lord Jesus Christ, and to the splendour and exaltation of his spotless bride, the Catholic universal Church.

units.la: Datum in Borgo Sancti Domini, nullius diœcesis prope Parmam Die XXVII. Septembris, Anno Domini millesimo quingentesimo vndecimo, Pontificatus Sanctissimi Domini nostri Iulii Papæ II. anno octauo.
units.tr: Given at Borgo San Donnino, a place in no diocese, near Parma, on the 27th day of September, in the year of our Lord 1511, in the eighth year of the pontificate of our most holy Lord Pope Julius II.

units.la: PRæmissis vero Pisas qui in Kalend. Septemb. nomine patrum qui comparerent procuratoribus. Et quæ in Apologia offeruntur Iustissima pacis & Concilii fœdera sanctissimo Domino nostro penitus renuente, reuerendissimi Domini Cardinales, reuerendi Archiepiscopi, Episcopi, Abbates, Regii Prælatorumque & vniuersitatum procuratores consiliares cum celeberrimis diuini & humani iuris doctoribus in copioso numero Pisanam ciuitatem cœlestibus auspiciis ingressi Kalend. Nouemb. supra scripti anni ipsum sacrum Pisanum Concilium in Spiritu sancto deuotissime inchoarunt.
units.tr: Indeed, after these matters, procurators of those Fathers who were to appear at Pisa on the first of September, the most reverend Lord Cardinals, the reverend Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, royal Prelates and procurators and counsellors of universities, with the most famous doctors of divine and human law in great numbers, entered the city of Pisa under heavenly auspices, and on the first of November of the year written above, they most devoutly began the sacred Council of Pisa in the Holy Spirit, our most holy Lord having utterly refused the most just terms of peace and Council offered in the Apology.

units.la: EX DECRETIS PRIMÆ SESSIONIS SACRI PISANI Concilii moderni.
units.tr: FROM THE DECREES OF THE FIRST SESSION OF THE RECENT SACRED COUNCIL OF PISA.

units.la: SAcrosancta synodus Pisana in Spiritu sancto legitime congregata generale Concilium faciens, & vniuersalem Ecclesiam repræsentans omnibus modo, via, iure & forma, quibus nel us potest & debet, decernit, ordinat, diffinit & declarat omnia & singula tam per dominum Papam quam alios quosuis prætextu conuocationis dicti Concilii Pisani dependentiumque, & Connexorum acta & agenda, attentata, & attentanda siue per indicta aliasue censuras & priuationes, seu inhabilitationes (etiam consistoriales) de personis dominorum Cardinalium, dignitatibus, Ecclesiis, monasteriis & beneficiis, siue pensionibus, ac iuribus, siue aliter quomodocunque, in præiudicium dictæ sacræ synodi omniumque & singulorum eiusdem indictorum, fautorum & auxiliatorum, & quouis modo adhærentium, & quandocumque adhæsurorum, nulla, irrita & inania fuisse ac fore: Illisq; vti notorie nullis, irritis, & erroneis nullatenus deferendum. Nam & Vrbanus Pontifex rescripsit, quod Dominus & Apostoli, vel patres sancti statuerunt, debet Romanus Pontisex ad animam vsque & sanguinem confirmare: alioquin non sententiam daresed errare, comminatur: Quæ tamen quatenus de facto processerunt, vel postmodum processerint, ex nunc cassat, irritat, revocat, & annullat.
units.tr: The most holy synod of Pisa, lawfully gathered in the Holy Spirit, making a general Council and representing the universal Church, decrees, ordains, defines and declares, by every means, way, right and form by which it can and ought, that all and each of the acts and proceedings, attempted or to be attempted, whether by the lord Pope or by any others under whatever pretext of the convocation of the said Council of Pisa and of matters dependent upon and connected with it, whether by indictions or other censures and deprivations, or disqualifications (even consistorial) concerning the persons of the lord Cardinals, dignities, churches, monasteries and benefices, whether pensions, rights, or in any other way whatever, to the prejudice of the said holy synod and of all and each of its indicters, supporters and helpers, and of all those adhering in any way, and of those who shall adhere at any time, have been and will be null, void and empty; and that they are by no means to be given any heed as manifestly null, void and erroneous. For also Urban the Pontiff wrote that what the Lord and the Apostles or holy Fathers have decreed, the Roman Pontiff ought to confirm even to the soul and blood, otherwise he threatens that he would not be giving a judgment but going astray. Yet, insofar as these things have proceeded in fact, or shall proceed afterwards, they now quash, annul, revoke and cancel them.

units.la: EPISTOLA
units.tr: EPISTLE

units.la: EPISTOLA EIVSDEM SYNODI AD SERENISSIMVM ROMANO- RVM ELECTVM IMPERATOREM.
units.tr: EPISTLE OF THE SAME SYNOD TO THE MOST SERENE ELECTED EMPEROR OF THE ROMANS.

units.la: Sacrosancta generalis Synodus Pisana in Spiritu sancto legitime congregata generale Concilium faciens: & vniversalem Ecclesiam representans charissimo Ecclesiae filio & aduocato serenissimo domino Maximiliano Electo Romanorum Imperatori semper Augusto salutem & omnipotentis Dei benedictionem.
units.tr: The most holy general Synod of Pisa, lawfully gathered in the Holy Spirit, making a general Council and representing the universal Church, sends greeting and the blessing of almighty God to its most beloved son of the Church and advocate, the most serene lord Maximilian, elected Emperor of the Romans, always Augustus.

units.la: QVONIAM concussis parietib. disiectisq; columnis consequens est vt omnis aedificii moles protinus corruat: neque sine totali corporis iactura corruptio membrorum sequatur: cauere diligenter oportet omnem Rempublicam omnemq; vniuersitatem, non modo vt ipsa intacta illibataq; custodiatur, verum etiam ne membra (praesertim precipua, vt praestantia) vim & iniuriam sentiant. Nuper igitur quum illatum ad nos fuerit breuis cuiusdam sanctissimi D. Iulii Papae secundi exemplum, quo tum maiestati tuae, tum caeteris regibus & Christianis principibus cum magno quasi gaudio (ac si egregium & praeclarum aliquod peregisset) notum facit venerabiles in Christo patres B. de Caruajal Episcopum Sabinensis. Sanctae Crucis G. Episcopum Praeneatinum Narbonen. F. tit. Sanctorum Nerei & Archillei ac R. de prie. tit. Sanctae Sabinae Presbyteros S.R.E. Cardinales galero Cardinalatus, honore, titulis, insignibus, voce etiam activa atque passiva, Patriarchalibus quoque, Metropolitanis, & aliis quibus praesunt Ecclesiis primasse: caeteraque quae in breui ipso continentur, iniqua quidem & immania, ipsoque auditu & lectione horrenda & detestanda: cerro quodam iracundia (ne deterius dicamus) spiritu fulminasse: mirati fuimus primum nouum sententiae genus (si sententia nomine dignum est) quod tam irrationabiliter tanquam perperam & contra omnem usum est. Ac licet multa ante eiusmodi occurrerent quae qualem se habere consueuerit summus Pontifex duin iracundia subditur, plane admonebant: vix tamen eo usque prolapsurum Sanctissimum Patrem credidissemus. Verum postquam ita res successit quemadmodum tum re ipsa notorium, etiam ipsius Pontificis publicatione manifestissimum effectum est, quasi instar eorum qui in exteriores tenebras deuenerunt, non satis sit grauissime trasse, nisi & erratu, quod omni studio celare debet ...
units.tr: Since, when walls are shaken and columns thrown down, it follows that the whole mass of the building collapses at once, and the corruption of the members cannot follow without the loss of the whole body, every commonwealth and every community ought carefully to take care, not only that it be preserved intact and unharmed, but also that its members, especially the chief and most distinguished ones, do not feel violence and injury. Lately, therefore, when there was brought to us a short copy of a certain letter of the most holy lord Pope Julius II, by which he makes known to your majesty and to the other kings and Christian princes (as if he had accomplished something outstanding and distinguished, and with great joy) that the venerable fathers in Christ, B. de Carvajal, bishop of Sabina; G., bishop of Santa Croce, of Praeneste, of Narbonne; F., of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus; and R. de Prie, of the title of Santa Sabina, cardinal presbyters of the Holy Roman Church, have been stripped of the cardinal's hat, honour, titles, insignia, and even of active and passive voice, and also of the patriarchal, metropolitan and other primacies over the churches they preside over; and other matters contained in the same brief, unjust indeed and monstrous, and horrible and detestable even to hear and read, as if he had thundered them out in a kind of spirit of anger (not to say worse): we were first astonished at this new kind of sentence (if it deserves the name of sentence), which is so unreasonable, as though it were wrongly and against all custom. And although many things had occurred earlier which plainly warned us what state the supreme Pontiff is wont to be in while he is given over to anger, yet we would scarcely have believed that the most holy Father would fall so far. But since matters have turned out as they are, as is notorious from the facts themselves and most manifest from the Pontiff's own publication, as if like those who have fallen into outer darkness, it is not enough to have gone very far astray, unless he also seeks, with every effort he ought to conceal, to pursue the error as though he were already openly making it plain, that nothing is dearer to him than, as Julius Caesar once celebrated a triumph over subdued enemies, so he may someday triumph over enemies and the ruined Church of God, that is, over her good members (which God forbid)...

units.la: Dat. Pisis in generali Congregatione nostra, die XII. Nouembris, Anno Domini M.D.XI.
units.tr: Given at Pisa, in our general congregation, on the 12th day of November, in the year of our Lord 1511.

units.la: Per Palladium Bellonem Decium, Sacri Pisani Concilii moderni Calcographum.
units.tr: By Palladius Bellonus Decius, printer of the present sacred Council of Pisa.

units.la: CONSILIVM CLI. PHILIPPI DECII IVRIS- CONSVLTI CLARISSIMI, HABITVM PRO ECCLESIAE AVCTORITATE, ANNO M.D.XI.
units.tr: The Consilium of the most illustrious jurist Philip Decius, given on behalf of the authority of the Church, in the year 1511.

units.la: SVMMARIVM.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: I. VERITAS omnibus praeferenda est.
units.tr: I. Truth is to be preferred above all things.

units.la: II. Papa an accusare possit, si incorrigibilis sit in crimine.
units.tr: II. Whether the Pope can be accused if he is incorrigible in crime.

units.la: III. Contumacia non dicitur proprie haeresis, sed large modo.
units.tr: III. Contumacy is not properly called heresy, but only in a broad sense.

units.la: IV. Haeresis proprie dicitur in duobus tantum casibus.
units.tr: IV. Heresy is properly said to occur in only two cases.

units.la: V. Quinque de causis Papa iudicari potest. VI. Episcopus potest removeri ab Ecclesia particulari ut scandalum evitetur. VII. Ratione scandali generaliter a communibus regulis receditur. VIII. Iudicibus aliquid extraiudicialiter facientibus armata manu resisti potest. IX. Papa non potest turbare statum Ecclesiae. X. Privilegia locum habere non possunt ubi aliquod grande scandalum resultat. XI. In rebus ad mores & politiam Ecclesiae spectantibus, credendum est potius Canonistis quam Theologis. XII. Solutio rationum contrariarum. XIII. Duobus in casibus Papa accusari potest in Concilio. XIV. Licet exceptio firmet regulam, non tamen videtur illam ampliare. XV. Simoniacus & schismaticus largo modo dicuntur haeretici. XVI. Non valet argumentum a delicto quod fit in omittendo, ad delictum quod fit in committendo. XVII. An Papa qui post suam creationem iurauit, & voluit infra biennium celebrare Concilium, obligetur ex visa sacramenti sui. XVIII. Duplex vinculum potentiae ligat. XIX. Princeps contractu obligatus, absoluta potestate contravenire non potest obligationi. XX. Nemo absolui potest a iuramento, nisi iuramentum exortum aut illicitum est. XXI. Iuri repugnat naturali ut quis seipsum absolute possit. XXII. Certis in casibus, Concilium generale Papam iudicare potest. XXIII. Cuiusnam sit congregare Concilium contra Papam. XXIV. An minor pars Cardinalium, pro congregatione Concilii generalis, maiorem partem requirere possit. XXV. Vbi agitur de interesse Papae, eius aut Cardinalium, qui ei adhaerent auctoritas, in congregatione Concilii minime requiritur. XXVI. Vbi agitur de interesse Ecclesiae particularis, si Prelatus sit negligens, potestas agendi ad Capitulum devolvitur.
units.tr: V. The Pope can be judged for five reasons. VI. A bishop can be removed from a particular Church to avoid scandal. VII. On account of scandal, one departs in general from the common rules. VIII. Judges who act outside the judicial process may be resisted by armed force. IX. The Pope cannot disturb the state of the Church. X. Privileges cannot have effect where some great scandal would result. XI. In matters concerning the morals and polity of the Church, one should believe the canonists rather than the theologians. XII. Solution of the opposing arguments. XIII. In two cases the Pope can be accused in a Council. XIV. Although an exception confirms the rule, it does not seem to extend it. XV. A simoniac and a schismatic are called heretics in a broad sense. XVI. An argument from a fault committed by omission does not hold good for a fault committed by commission. XVII. Whether a Pope who swore after his creation, and wished to hold a Council within two years, is bound by the force of his sacred oath. XVIII. A double bond binds the power. XIX. A prince bound by contract cannot, with absolute power, act against the obligation. XX. No one can be absolved from an oath unless the oath arose unlawfully or is unlawful. XXI. It is contrary to natural law that anyone should be able to absolve himself absolutely. XXII. In certain cases a general Council can judge the Pope. XXIII. To whom belongs the calling of a Council against the Pope. XXIV. Whether a smaller part of the Cardinals may require a majority for the convening of a general Council. XXV. Where the interest of the Pope, or of his Cardinals who adhere to him, is at stake, their authority is in no way required for the convening of a Council. XXVI. Where the interest of a particular Church is at stake, if the prelate is negligent, the power of acting devolves upon the Chapter.

units.la: XXVII. Propter scandalum euitandum Concilium generale potest congregari sine Papa auctoritate.
units.tr: XXVII. To avoid scandal, a general Council can be convened without the authority of the Pope.

units.la: XXVIII. Ius Colegii in uno solo redigi potest, quare duo aut tres Cardinales Pisanum Concilium indicere potuerunt.
units.tr: XXVIII. The right of the College can be reduced to one person alone, which is why two or three Cardinals were able to summon the Council of Pisa.

units.la: DIuino implorato praesidio, rnaximi ponderis est praesentis casus materia, in qua admoneri me tacite sentio, officii mei non esse hanc prouinciam contra summum Pontificem suscipere, cuius antecessor Innocentius VIII. proprio motu me eius & Apostolicæ sedis Capellanum, Rotaeque auditorem constituit. Requisitus tamen nomine Christianissimi Regis nostri, ab his qui pro regia Maiestate Mediolani imperiū moderantur & regunt (cū ipsa regia Maiestas de me optime merita sit, q; in patria maxima a cū dignitate me reuocauit, & amplissimū stipendiū, q; mihi Paduae a Venetis praestabatur, vltra o es qui hactenus in iure Canonico legerint, non solū cōseruauit sed auxit) non potuissem tale onus mihi iniunctū, absq; maxima ingratitudinis nota recusare. I. Praesertim cum maxima modestia requisitus fuerim, vt dicam pro Veritate & iustitia quod mihi videtur. Quo casu et ambobus existentib. superioribus. vt de communib. amicis legitur, sanctum est praehonorare veritatem: Nam qui veritatem sequitur, Deum sequitur, 11. quaest. 3. in Can. quisquis, & potius debet quodlibet scandalum tolerari, quam quod veritas relinquatur, Vt dicitur in ca. quus scandalizauerit, de Regul. iuris. Et pro veritate melius est pati supplicium, quam pro adulatione beneficium 11. quaest. 3. in Can. nemo peritorum. Et ideo hanc disputationem pro veritate summus Pontifex aequo animo pati debet, praesertim, qui ia non de his quae in facto consistunt sed solum de iure verba factarus sum, & sermo noster duntaxat in disputatione iuris versabitur; & in facto de tanto Pontifice praesumendum est pro eius integritate & sanctimonia, quem apex tantae dignitatis extollit, vt dicitur in Can. non nos 40. dist. Iuridice itaq; propositam quaestione aggredior, in qua vt distincte procedamus ex themate breuiter ppositio p vera resolutione, quatuor elici possunt quaest.
units.tr: Having implored divine help, the matter of the present case is of the greatest weight. In it I sense that I am tacitly warned that it is not my duty to take up this task against the supreme Pontiff, whose predecessor Innocent VIII, on his own initiative, appointed me his chaplain and that of the Apostolic See, and auditor of the Rota. Nevertheless, I was asked in the name of our most Christian King, by those who govern and rule the empire at Milan on behalf of the royal Majesty (since the royal Majesty has deserved very well of me, having recalled me to my homeland with the greatest dignity and having not only preserved but increased the most generous salary which the Venetians paid me at Padua, above all those who have hitherto lectured in canon law), I could not refuse this burden laid upon me without the greatest mark of ingratitude. I. Especially since I was asked with the greatest modesty to say what seems to me true and just. In this case, with both superiors existing, as is read of common friends, it is holy to honour truth above all: For whoever follows truth, follows God, 11 q. 3, in can. quisquis, and rather any scandal ought to be tolerated than that truth be abandoned, as it is said in ca. Quus scandalizaverit, de Regulis iuris. And for the sake of truth it is better to suffer punishment than to receive a benefit for flattery, 11 q. 3, in can. nemo peritorum. Therefore the supreme Pontiff ought to bear this disputation calmly for the sake of truth, especially since I am not speaking about matters that consist in fact, but only about law, and our discourse will turn solely on a disputation of law; and in fact concerning so great a Pontiff, one must presume his integrity and sanctity, which the summit of so great a dignity exalts, as it is said in can. non nos, dist. 40. Therefore I approach the question proposed in legal form, in which, that we may proceed distinctly, from the theme, four questions can be drawn out by a brief proposition and true resolution.

units.la: Prima erit, an Papa accusari possit si incorrigibilis sit in crimine, pro quo religio Christiana scandalum patiatur.
units.tr: The first will be whether the Pope can be accused if he is incorrigible in a crime by which the Christian religion suffers scandal.

units.la: Secunda, an Papa efficaciter obligetur ad illud quod cum voto & iuramento promisit, ita quod seipsum absoluere non possit.
units.tr: The second, whether the Pope is effectually bound to that which he promised with a vow and an oath, such that he cannot absolve himself from it.

units.la: Tertia quaestio erit, an in dictis & similibus casibus Concilium generale sit iudex contra Papam.
units.tr: The third question will be whether, in the said and similar cases, a general Council is a judge against the Pope.

units.la: Quarta erit de modo & forma congregandi Concilium in dictis casibus.
units.tr: The fourth will concern the manner and form of convening a Council in the said cases.

units.la: II. Circa primum dubium, videbatur primo motu quod Papa tali casu accusari non posset. Et ita quamplures esse non ambigo qui pares summi pontificis suscipèrent & tuerentur, ex eo q; legitur in Can. aliorum. 9. quaest. 3. Aliorum hominum causas Deus voluit per homines terminare, sed sedu ipsum Praesule, suo sine quaest. reseruauit iudicio, & qui Dei iudicio reseruatur, ab humano iudicio iudicari non potest, Can quorundam 23. dist. Et idem dicitur in Can. Nemo, in Can. facta, in Can. Cuncta per mundum, 9. q. 3. Ex quibus & similib. iuribus, Glossa in Can. si quis pecunia, 79. dist. infert, quod si de crimine contra Papam obiecto disceptatur, ipse non cogitur alicuius stare iudicio; sed excipere potest Dominus est qui me iudicat. Et ideo Glossa in dicto Can. nemo, 9. q. 3. per illum textum ibi ab omni, Clero, arguit, q; & Concilio Papa iudicare non possit. Itè Glossa in Can. mandatū, 2. q. 5. Et ad hoc videtur textus in Can. Cœcilia, §. hinc et, in verb. Symmachus Papa, 17. dist. vbi cū Symmachus Papa apud Concilium de haeresi accusatus fuisset, patres cōcilii residētes ibi dixerūt Symmachus quātū ad hominem respicit, sit immunis & liberi eius causa tota Dei iudicio reseruamus. Et hoc idē pbatur 21. dist. Can. nunc autē. vbi Marcellinū vrbis Romae Episcopū accusatū de haeresi, ex eo q; à paganis cōpulsus idolis sacrificasset, Cōciliū noluit iudicare, sed ipsi Marcellino Papae dixit, Tuo ore iudica causam tuā, non nostro iudicio, prima sedes non iudicabitur à quoquā. Et ideo Hostiensis in in ca. propositum, de concess. praeben. dicit, q; si Papa iacet in peccato, admoneri potest iuxta regulam Euangelii, cui subiicitur quantū ad primam partē, dum dicitur: Si peccauerit in te frater tuus, corripe eum inter te & ipsum, vt habetur in ca. nouit, de iudiciis. & 2. q. 1. in Can. si peccauerit, in principio. Quantum vero ad aliam partem regulae quae dicit, quod si non audierit ecclesiam. Hostiensis dicit, quod non habet locum in summo Pontifice, quia ipse ab Ecclesia militante iudicari non potest per iura supraallegata: unde illa verba ut Ecclesiae, intelliguntur in summo Pontifice de Ecclesia triumphante & caelesti. Et notat Abbas in ca. nouit, charta antepenult. vers. secūdo ca hoc quaero, de iudic. nec praedictis videtur obstare Glossa, in Can. si Papa, 40. dist. quae in terminis dicit, q; Papa accusari potest de crimine notorio in quo incorrigibilis sit & inde scandalizetur Ecclesia: quia Theologi dicunt illā non esse veram: & ita concludunt Aug. de Anchona, Petrus de Palude, & Antoninus Archiep. Florentinus, qui illos refert & sequitur in tertia parte eius summa, in tit. 20. chart. 4 §. 3. incipiente quaeritur utrū Papa. Et in tit. 23. c. 2. §. 6. in fine: & moueretur ratione satis colorata & apparenti, quia glossa in dicto Can. si Papa, adducit rationē quae non est vera, dum inquit, quod tali casu Papa accusari potest, quia est in contumacia ex quo non vult corrigi, & talis contumacia dicitur haeresis 81. dist. Can. si qui sunt presbyteri, 33. distinct. Can. sin. q; incipit Nullus Pro haeresi aut Papa accusari potest, vt est casus in dicto Can. si Papa: Ergo videtur quod tali casu accusari possit. Sed dicunt ipsi q; praedicta ratio in qua dictum glossae fundatur, nō est vera, quia textus in dicto Can. si Papa, de haeresi, proprie dicta intelligitur, p errore fixo eorū q; sūt fidei.
units.tr: II. Concerning the first doubt, it seemed at first impulse that the Pope could not be accused in such a case. And I do not doubt that many would take up and defend the cause of the supreme Pontiff on this ground, from what is read in can. aliorum, 9 q. 3: God wished the causes of other men to be ended by men, but he reserved the Prelate himself, his own, to his judgment; and whoever is reserved to the judgment of God cannot be judged by human judgment, can. quorundam, dist. 23. And the same is said in can. Nemo, in can. facta, in can. Cuncta per mundum, 9 q. 3. From these and similar laws, the Gloss on can. si quis pecunia, dist. 79, infers that if a dispute arises concerning a crime objected against the Pope, he is not compelled to stand to the judgment of anyone, but may plead: It is the Lord who judges me. And therefore the Gloss on the said can. nemo, 9 q. 3, through that text there, from all the clergy, argues that the Pope cannot be judged even by a Council. Likewise the Gloss on can. mandatum, 2 q. 5. And to this the text in can. Caecilia, §. hinc et, under the word Symmachus Papa, 17 dist. seems to point, where, when Pope Symmachus had been accused of heresy before a Council, the fathers sitting in the council said: As far as the man is concerned, let Symmachus be free and immune; we reserve his whole cause to the judgment of God. And the same is proved in dist. 21, can. nunc autem, where the bishop of the city of Rome, Marcellinus, accused of heresy because, compelled by the pagans, he had sacrificed to idols, the Council was unwilling to judge, but said to Pope Marcellinus himself: Judge your own cause by your own mouth, not by our judgment; the first see shall not be judged by anyone. And therefore Hostiensis, in ca. propositum, de concessione praebendae, says that if the Pope lies in sin, he can be admonished according to the rule of the Gospel, to which he is subject as far as the first part is concerned, when it is said: If your brother sins against you, correct him between you and him alone, as is found in ca. nouit, de iudiciis, and 2 q. 1, in can. si peccaverit, at the beginning. But as far as the other part of the rule is concerned, which says: But if he will not hear the Church, Hostiensis says that this has no place in the supreme Pontiff, because he cannot be judged by the militant Church, by the laws cited above; whence those words tell it to the Church are understood in the supreme Pontiff of the triumphant and heavenly Church. And the Abbot notes this in ca. nouit, charta antepenult., verse secundo, ca. hoc quaero, de iudiciis. Nor does the Gloss in can. si Papa, 40 dist., which in its terms says that the Pope can be accused of a notorious crime in which he is incorrigible and by which the Church is scandalized, seem to stand in the way of these matters: for the theologians say that this is not true; and so Augustinus de Ancona, Petrus de Palude, and Antoninus, Archbishop of Florence, conclude, who report and follow them in the third part of his Summa, in title 20, chart. 4, §. 3, beginning "It is asked whether the Pope", and in title 23, c. 2, §. 6, at the end. And one might be moved by a reason that is fairly plausible and apparent, because the gloss in the said can. si Papa adduces a reason which is not true, when it says that in such a case the Pope can be accused because he is in contumacy, since he does not wish to be corrected, and such contumacy is called heresy, 81 dist., can. si qui sunt presbyteri, and 33 dist., can. sin., which begins Nullus. Therefore, for heresy or the Pope, an accusation can be brought, as is the case in the said can. si Papa. Therefore it seems that in such a case he can be accused. But they themselves say that the aforesaid reason, on which the gloss's statement is founded, is not true, because the text in the said can. si Papa is understood of heresy properly so called, through a fixed error of those who hold the faith.

units.la: III. Cōtumacia vero non dicitur proprie haeresis sed largo modo & improprie: Et ideo secundū eos glossa non est vera, & idē dicit Card. in dicto Can. si Papa, & S. Thomas, vt refert ibi Card. Alex Et ad hoc facit, quia et Simonia dicitur haeresis 1. q. 1. Can. quisquis, in Can. eos qui: & notatur per glossam in ca. firmissime, de haeret. Et similiter schisma haeresis dicitur, 24 q. 3. Can. inter haeresin. Et pluribus aliis casib. dicitur haeresis, vt glossa prosequitur 23. q. 4. Can. illi qui, §. quia vero, & dicto cap firmissime.
units.tr: III. Contumacy, however, is not properly called heresy but is so called in a broad and improper sense. Therefore, according to them, the gloss is not true, and the Cardinal says the same on the said Can. si Papa, as does St Thomas, as the Cardinal Alexander reports there. And this agrees, because simony is also called heresy (1. q. 1. Can. quisquis, in Can. eos qui), and it is noted by the gloss on ca. firmissime, de haeret. Likewise schism is called heresy (24 q. 3. Can. inter haeresin). And by many other cases it is called heresy, as the gloss goes on to show (23 q. 4. Can. illi qui, §. quia vero, and the said cap. firmissime).

units.la: IV. Sed proprie hæresis dicitur solum in duobus casibus, quando quis aliter sentit de articulis fidei quam Romana Ecclesia, 24. q. 1. in Can. hæc est fides: & quando quis male sentit de Sacramentis Ecclesiæ in c. ad abolendam, de hær. in princ. Et ita Abb. post Hostiensem & alios concludit in d. c. firmissimè, de hær. Et ideo dicitur de hæresi in dict. Can. si Papa, intelligitur proprie, qa verba legis propriè intelliguntur, vt notat. Bart. in l. ita vulneratus ff. ad l. Aquiliam: & quia loquitur in materia exorbitanti contra regulam qstrictè debet interpretari, l. si vero §. de viro ff. sol. mat. in reg. ea qua de reg. iur. in 6. & ita in terminis tenet gl. in Can. si quis episcopus, 79. dist. Unde concludedum videtur, qd Papa p tali crimine, licet incorrigibilis sit, non possit p hæretico accusari. Similiter non videtur qd pro ipso crimine notorio & scandaloso accusari possit, quia hoc iure cautum non reperitur, ergo non est dicendum, c. illa, ne sede vacante, c. is qui, de sent. excom. in 6. nota. in l. illam Cod. de Collatio. Et hoc comprobatur per text. in d. Can. si Papa, vbi regula ponitur qd Papa non potest ab alio iudicari: & excipitur causa hæresis: unde exceptio illa facta de hæresi, videtur confirmare regulam in omnibus aliis casib. non exceptuatis, 32. q. 7. in Can. Dominus, c. 2. in sin. de Coniugis leprof. & not. Bart. in l. quæsitum, §. denique ff. de fundo instruct. & text. in d. Can. si Papa, videtur loqui in delicto scandaloso, dum dicit qd propter eius delictum, innumerabiles populos secum in præcipitium ducit, & tamen tali casu ibi dicitur qd à nemine iudicari potest: & sic ibi videtur text. contra glos. in d. Can. si Papa: & ex his opinio Theologorum suaderi posse videbatur.
units.tr: IV. But heresy is properly said to occur only in two cases: when someone thinks differently about the articles of faith from the Roman Church (24 q. 1. in Can. haec est fides); and when someone thinks wrongly about the sacraments of the Church (c. ad abolendam, de haer. in princ.). And so Abbas, following Hostiensis and others, concludes on the said cap. firmissime, de haer. Hence when the said Can. si Papa speaks of heresy, it is to be understood properly, because the words of a law are properly understood, as Bartolus notes on l. ita vulneratus ff. ad l. Aquiliam; and because it deals with a matter that departs from the rule, it must be interpreted strictly (l. si vero §. de viro ff. sol. matr.; reg. ea quae de reg. iur. in 6.); and the gloss on Can. si quis episcopus, 79 dist., holds this expressly in these terms. Whence it seems to follow that the Pope, although incorrigible, cannot be accused of heresy for such a crime. Likewise it does not seem that he can be accused for the notorious and scandalous crime itself, because no law is found that provides this; therefore it should not be said (c. illa, ne sede vacante; c. is qui, de sent. excom. in 6; nota in l. illam Cod. de collatione). And this is confirmed by the text in the said Can. si Papa, where the rule is laid down that the Pope cannot be judged by anyone, and an exception is made for the cause of heresy; so that this exception, made for heresy, seems to confirm the rule in all other cases not excepted (32 q. 7. in Can. Dominus; c. 2 in fin. de coniugis leprosis; and note Bartolus on l. quaesitum, §. denique ff. de fundo instructo). And the text of the said Can. si Papa seems to speak of a scandalous offence, since it says that by his crime he leads countless peoples with him into the abyss, and yet in such a case it is said there that he can be judged by no one; and so there the text seems to be against the gloss on the said Can. si Papa. From these points it seemed that the opinion of the theologians could be persuaded.

units.la: V. Sed s. dictis non obstantibus, & similib. q adduci possent, contrarium de iure esse arbitror, saltem in aliquib. casib. in quib. communiter Doctores tenent qd Papa ab alio iudicari possit. Primus est in hæresi, in quo omnes Doctores conveniunt qd accusari possit, vt expresse dicitur in d. Can. si Papa, ibi, à nemine est iudicandus nisi deprehendatur à fide deuius: & merito, quia nullum peccatum est grauius hæresi, 22. q. 2. Can. primum, in princ. 32. q. 7. Can. quid in omnib. & quia admodum perniciosum est, si vera fides q in toto populo Christiano requiritur, in capite non reperiatur, vt dicitur 61. dist. Can. miramur. Et ideo Papa hæreticus in eo qd hereticus est, minor est quolibet Catholico, vt dicit glos. in Can. Achatius 24. q. 1. in verb. in hæresin. Secundus casus, qn Papa sponte Concilio se subijceret, nam isto casu et clarum est, qd à Concilio iudicari potest, 2. q. 7. in Can. nos si incompetenter, in princ. Et ita sæpenumero multi Pontifices fecerunt expurgando eorum innocentiam de criminibus p quib. infamati fuerunt. Sic Damasus Pontifex Rom. infamatus de adulterio, coram XLII. Episcopis se purgauit, vt dicitur in dict. Can. nos si incompetenter, §. pen. Sic & Sixtus fecit cum à quodam Basso iniuste persequeretur, vt habetur 2. q. 5. in Can. mandastis. Sic de Leone legitur eadem causa & quæstione in Can. audituri: Sic & Petrus Apost. vt Gratian. refert, 2. q. 7. in Can. Pet. Sic & Gregor. vt in Can. si quis super, eadem causa & quæstione. Et recte isti, & benefecerunt vt humilitatem ostenderent, qua nihil est in summo Pontifice splendidius, vt dicit tex. Can. d. contra morem: & quia expedit qd à criminum suspicione liberetur, qn mala fama de Pontifice in lucem prodierit, ne infirmorum corda percutiantur, & Pontificis ministerium, vituperetur vt legitur 2. q. 5. in Can. si mala fama. Et ad hoc plura iura Roman. adducit in Consi. 522. Beatissimus. Et ex isto secundo casu, Abb. infert in disputatione: Episcopus & quidam Rector, in solutione secundi dubii, qd à Papa appellari potest ad Concilium qn Papa consentit. Tertius casus est qn Papa confitetur peccata eius confessori, qa illi subiicitur, isto tres casus ponit gl. in Can. nemo, 9. q. 3. Quartus est casus, qn esset schisma inter duo contendentes de Papatu, vt sentit gl. in Can. si 69 dist. & not. Cardinalis in Consi. 150. quæstitum sæpe fuit. in 1. dubio. Abb. in c. quia diligenti, & colu. 1. de elect. Et de istis casib. no agitur in casu propositio, ideo in his vlterius non insisto.
units.tr: V. Yet, notwithstanding what has been said and similar arguments that could be brought forward, I hold that the contrary is the law, at least in some cases in which the Doctors commonly hold that the Pope can be judged by another. The first is heresy, on which all the Doctors agree that he can be accused, as is expressly said in the said Can. si Papa: "he is to be judged by no one unless he is found to have deviated from the faith." And rightly so, because no sin is graver than heresy (22 q. 2. Can. primum, in princ.; 32 q. 7. Can. quid in omnibus); and because it is very harmful if the true faith, which is required in the whole Christian people, is not found in the head (61 dist. Can. miramur). And so the heretical Pope, in that he is a heretic, is less than any Catholic, as the gloss on Can. Achatius, 24 q. 1, in the words "in heresin," says. The second case is when the Pope submits himself voluntarily to a Council, for in this case it is clear that he can be judged by the Council (2 q. 7. in Can. nos si incompetenter, in princ.). And so very often many Pontifices have done this, clearing their innocence of the crimes by which they were defamed. Thus Damasus, Pope of Rome, defamed of adultery, purged himself before forty-two bishops, as is said in the said Can. nos si incompetenter, §. pen. So also Sixtus did when he was unjustly persecuted by a certain Bassus, as is found in 2 q. 5. in Can. mandastis. So too of Leo it is read, in the same cause and question, in Can. audituri. So also Peter the Apostle, as Gratian reports (2 q. 7. in Can. Petrus). So also Gregory, as in Can. si quis super, the same cause and question. And these men acted rightly and did well, to show their humility, than which nothing is more splendid in the supreme Pontiff, as the text of Can. contra morem says; and because it is fitting that he be freed from the suspicion of crime when an ill report of the Pontiff has come to light, lest the hearts of the weak be struck and the ministry of the Pontiff be disparaged, as is read in 2 q. 5. in Can. si mala fama. And to this he brings forward many Roman laws in Consilium 522, Beatissimus. And from this second case Abbas infers, in the disputation: the bishop and a certain rector, in the solution of the second doubt, that an appeal can be made from the Pope to a Council when the Pope consents. The third case is when the Pope confesses his sins to his confessor, because he is subject to him; the gloss on Can. nemo, 9 q. 3, sets out these three cases. The fourth case is when there would be a schism between two contenders for the papacy, as the gloss on Can. si, 69 dist., thinks; and the Cardinal's note in Consilium 150, quaesitum saepe fuit, in the first doubt; Abbas on c. quia diligenti, and col. 1, de elect. But since these cases are not the subject of the case proposed, I do not dwell on them further here.

units.la: Est quintus casus in quo difficultas consistit, videlicet qn Papa incorrigibilis sit in aliquo notorio delicto, p quo Ecclesia scandalizatur. & tali casu gl. in terminis in d. Can. si Papa, tenet qd Papa accusari possit. Et de illa gl. maximum factum fuit fundamentum contra Eugenium 6. in Concilio Basiliensi: & illa gl. communiter tenetur per omnes, vt dicit Abb. in c. significasti de electione. Et in d. disputatione, Episcop. & quidam Rector in sin. secundi dub. j, vbi inquit qd totus mundus approbat illam gl. & idem Abb. in c. proposuit colu fi. de concess. præben. & in c. cum venissent, col. 4. de iud. & illam gl. plurib. rationib. comprobat Rom. in consil. 123 q d. scutiendae est. Primo qd Papa, qui in notorio crimine persistit & non vult corrigi incidit in suspicionem hæresis 38. dist. in Can. si. 81. dist. in Can. si qui sunt, & in c. sin. de pæn. Sed p hæresi Papa accusari potest, d. Can. si Papa. Ergo & p tali crimine, & fuit ista ratio glossæ, in d. Can. si Papa.
units.tr: There is a fifth case, in which the difficulty lies: namely, when the Pope is incorrigible in some notorious offence by which the Church is scandalized. And in such a case the gloss, in these very terms on the said Can. si Papa, holds that the Pope can be accused. And upon that gloss the greatest foundation was laid against Eugenius IV at the Council of Basel; and that gloss is commonly held by all, as Abbas says on c. significasti de electione. And in the said disputation the bishop and a certain rector, at the end of the second doubt, where they say that the whole world approves that gloss; and the same Abbas on c. proposuit, col. fin., de concess. praeben., and on c. cum venissent, col. 4, de iud.; and Romanus in Consilium 123, Quaeq d. scutiendae est, proves that gloss by many reasons. First, because the Pope who persists in a notorious crime and does not wish to be corrected falls under suspicion of heresy (38 dist. in Can. si; 81 dist. in Can. si qui sunt; and in c. sin. de poen.). But a Pope can be accused of heresy (said Can. si Papa). Therefore also for such a crime; and this was the reasoning of the gloss on the said Can. si Papa.

units.la: VI. Secundo, quia remouetur Episcopus ab Ecclesia particulari vt scandalum tollatur, vt notat. Innoc. in c. cum oridem, de renu. idem à fortiori videtur dicendum in summo Pontifice, in quo est periculum vniuersalis Ecclesiæ. Tertio per auctoritatem Euangelij, si oculus tuus aut pes scandalizaverit te, de quo tex. eleganter loquitur in Can. illud sane, 24. q. 3. expedit enim vt vnus homo moriatur p populo ne tota gens pereat: Ergo Papa incorrigibilis moriatur ciuiliter, ne tota Ecclesia pereat: qa Papa positus ad gubernationem populorum non debet esse ruina illorum, vt tex. dicit 11. q. 3. in Can. ita corporis: Nam tot mortib. dignus est, quod exempla perditionis ad populos suos transmittit, Can. pra ipse, 11. q. 3. Quarto qa Papa posit est vt vitia extirpet, excessus corrigat, & mores reformet, vt habet in pæn. Clem. vers. quia et: & ideo hac ratione Zacharias priuare potuit Childericum Regem Franciæ regno: qa ex suo regimine, vniuerso regno scandala imminebat, 15. q. 6. in Can. alio, cum gl. Pari ratione Concilium potest Papam deponere, cum super eo in tali casu habeat potestatem, vt latius Roman. concludit in consil. 5. allegato, & hoc idem tenet Bald. in cap. olim, col. sin. circa finem in verf. idem dicit, de rescript. vbi refert Hugutionem in Can. si duo forte, 79. dist. & postremo concludit, quod Papa potest remoueri propter notorium crimen & enorme. Et hoc coprobatur quia delicto notorio Papae & Praelatorum, facile transit in exemplum subditorum, & scandalum generatur mentib. laicorum dicentium, vbi est Deus clericorum? vt dicitur in c. Magna de voto. Vnde in tali delicto scandaloso videt quod accusari possit: qua videm, quod licet Papae regulariter obediendum sit, etiamsi praeceptum graue & intolerabile videat, 19. dist. Can. in memoria & 100. dist. Can. contra morem, tamen vbi scandalum imminet, non est Papae obediendum, vt not. Innoc. in c. inquisitioni, de sent. excom. circa fine: vbi inquit non esse obediendum Papae, quod ex tali praecepto praesumeretur statum Ecclesiae perturbari, vel forte alia mala ventura esse, quia tunc obedientes peccant, cum debeant futura mala praecaeere & non inuare, vt formaliter Innocentius dicit, quae sequitur ibi Hostien. & Ioan. Andr. Pet. de Perus. Ant. de But. & Abb. & Cardin. in Consil. 147. videtur circa finem, & in Consil. 150. quaesitum fuit, in fine. Abb. in c. si quando, de rescript. in c. cum teneamur, de Praeb. Et propter hoc Abb. in d. c. inquisitioni, excusat Cardinales qui recesserant a Gregorio XII. ratione scandali quod imminebat, vt citati sub poena excommunicationis non teneantur comparere. Ita ergo videtur in proposito dicendum, quod licet regulariter a nemine Papa debeat iudicari, tamen ista regula limitari debet, & non habere locum quando Papa in crimine scandaloso reperitur.
units.tr: VI. Secondly, a bishop is removed from a particular church so that scandal may be taken away, as Innocent notes in c. cum oridem, de renun. The same should be said all the more of the supreme Pontiff, in whom lies the danger to the whole universal Church. Thirdly, by the authority of the Gospel: "If your eye or your foot causes you to stumble" (Matth. 5), on which the text speaks finely in Can. illud sane, 24 q. 3: "it is expedient that one man die for the people, lest the whole nation perish." Therefore an incorrigible Pope should die civilly, lest the whole Church perish; for a Pope set over the government of peoples ought not to be the ruin of them, as the text says in 11 q. 3, Can. ita corporis: "he deserves many deaths, since he transmits examples of perdition to his peoples," Can. prae ipse, 11 q. 3. Fourthly, because the Pope is set in place to root out vices, correct excesses and reform morals, as is contained in pæn. Clem. vers. quia et. For this reason Zacharias could deprive Childeric, King of the Franks, of his kingdom, because scandals threatened the whole kingdom from his rule, 15 q. 6, Can. alio, with the gloss. By the same reasoning a Council can depose the Pope, since in such a case it has power over him, as Romanus concludes more fully in the consilium 5 cited; and Bald. holds the same in cap. olim, col. sin., near the end, in the words idem dicit, de rescript., where he cites Hugutio in Can. si duo forte, 79. dist.. Finally he concludes that the Pope can be removed on account of a notorious and enormous crime. This is confirmed, because from a notorious offence of the Pope and prelates the example readily passes to subjects, and scandal is produced in the minds of laymen, who say "where is the God of the clergy?", as is said in c. Magna de voto. Hence in such a scandalous offence it is seen that he can be accused. For although as a rule the Pope must be obeyed even if a command seems grievous and intolerable (19. dist. Can. in memoria and 100. dist. Can. contra morem), yet where scandal threatens, the Pope is not to be obeyed, as Innocent notes in c. inquisitioni, de sent. excom. near the end. There he says that the Pope is not to be obeyed when from such a command it is presumed that the state of the Church would be disturbed, or perhaps other evils would follow, because then those who obey sin, since they ought to foresee future evils and not bring them about, as Innocent formally says. What follows there is in Hostiensis, John Andreae, Peter of Perugia, Antonius de Butrio, the Abbot and the Cardinal, in Consil. 147, see near the end, and in Consil. 150, the question was raised at the end. Abb. in c. si quando, de rescript. in c. cum teneamur, de Praeb. And for this reason the Abbot, in d. c. inquisitioni, excuses the Cardinals who had withdrawn from Gregory XII on account of the scandal that threatened, so that those cited under penalty of excommunication need not appear. So it seems that in the present case it must be said that, although as a rule the Pope may be judged by no one, this rule must be limited and must not apply when the Pope is found guilty of a scandalous crime.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Na ratione scandali generaliter a communib. regulis recedit, vt ex plurib. probat Rom. iu. si vero § de viro, in 7. fallentia ff. sol. matrim. facit text. in cap. cum teneamur, de praeb. in cap. nihil cum scandalo, de praescript. & in cap. tua de Cle. aegro. & in cap. quia circa, de consang. & affinit. cum similibus, vt tradunt moderni in dicto cap. nihil, de praescript. Ad idem facit textus in Can. presbyteros, in Can. peruenit 65. dist. in Can. de bis vero 50. dist. & 23. q. 3. Can. 1. § 1. Et ideo bene consonata quod si scandalum aliter remoueri non potest, quod Papa accusari possit.
units.tr: For on account of scandal he generally departs from the common rules, as Romanus proves from many sources: iu. si vero § de viro, in 7. fallentia ff. sol. matrim. The text is to the same effect: in cap. cum teneamur, de praeb. in cap. nihil cum scandalo, de praescript. and in cap. tua de Cle. aegro. and in cap. quia circa, de consang. and affinit. with similar passages, as the moderns teach in the said cap. nihil, de praescript. The texts in Can. presbyteros, in Can. peruenit 65. dist. in Can. de bis vero 50. dist. and 23. q. 3. Can. 1. § 1 point the same way. Therefore it is rightly agreed that, if scandal cannot otherwise be removed, the Pope may be accused.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: IX. Et si aliter diceretur, esset magnum absurdum, quia esset in potestate Papae suis malis moribus Ecclesiae statum turbare, & Ecclesia destruere, si resisti sibi non posset: quod nullo modo dicendum est pro dicta. Nam iura quae dicunt quod Papa non potest turbare statum Ecclesiae, vt per gl. 8 q. 1. in Can. apostolica, in Can. per principalem, 9 q. 3. & in c. literas, de restit. spol. in ver. non potest, cum similibus quae parum operantur. Si Papa non posset accusari, & a Concilio iudicari: quia parum esset iura condere, nisi essent constituti magistratus qui illa exequerentur l. 2. § post orig. nem. ff. de Origine iuris.
units.tr: IX. And if it were otherwise said, it would be a great absurdity, for it would be in the Pope's power, by his evil morals, to disturb the state of the Church and destroy the Church, if he could not be resisted. This must by no means be said. For the laws which say that the Pope cannot disturb the state of the Church (as in the gloss on 8 q. 1, Can. apostolica; in Can. per principalem, 9 q. 3; and in c. literas, de restit. spol., in the word non potest, with similar passages) would accomplish little. If the Pope could not be accused and judged by a Council, it would be pointless to enact laws unless there were magistrates appointed to carry them out: l. 2. § post orig. nem. ff. de Origine iuris.

units.la: X. Et hoc ideo confirmatur, quia priuilegium illud datum summo Pontifici, vt ab alio iudicari non possit, non videtur habere locum in isto casu, in quo maximum detrimentum Ecclesiae & fidelibus resultaret. Arg. c. [?] de deci: vbi priuilegium restringitur, vt non habeat locum quin scandalum resultaret: facit textus in l. ex facto, in princip. ff. de vul. & pup. & ad idem facit quia in tali priuilegio mens & intentio concedentis attenditur, dicta l. ex facto vbi Bald. in notabil. & Innocentius in c. cum Ecclesiastica, de excep. intentio aut concedentis non videtur fuisse quod voluerit priuilegiare personam Papae, stante scandalo in praeiudicium Ecclesiae, cum ipsi Ecclesiae plus tribuendum sit quam personae Papae, vt in simili dicitur, quod maior fauor praestatur loco, quam personae, in cap. ne aliqui, & glossa sin de priuil. in 6. ad idem glossa in cap. sin. in verbo dignitatibus, de rescript. in 6 in cap. ad nostram, in gl. 1. in fine de confir. util. Et ita ex omnibus s. dictis corroborata est conclusio glossae, in dict. Can si Papa. & plurimum etiam confirmabitur ex his quae inferius dicam, respondendo ad allegata supra in contrarium.
units.tr: X. This is confirmed further, because that privilege granted to the supreme Pontiff, that he may not be judged by another, does not seem to apply in this case, in which the greatest harm would result to the Church and to the faithful. Argument from c. [?] de deci, where a privilege is restricted so that it does not apply where scandal would result. The text in l. ex facto, in princip. ff. de vul. & pup. is to the same effect. And to the same purpose: in such a privilege the mind and intention of the granter is what counts (the said l. ex facto, where Bald. is noted, and Innocent in c. cum Ecclesiastica, de excep.). The intention of the granter does not seem to have been that he wished to privilege the person of the Pope when scandal threatens to the prejudice of the Church, since more should be given to the Church itself than to the person of the Pope. As it is said in a similar case, greater favour is shown to a place than to a person: in cap. ne aliqui, & glossa sin de priuil. in 6. To the same effect the gloss in cap. sin., in the word dignitatibus, de rescript. in 6 in cap. ad nostram, in gl. 1 at the end de confir. util. And so the conclusion of the gloss in the said Can. si Papa is strengthened by all the things said above, and it will be confirmed even more by what I shall say below in reply to the arguments adduced above to the contrary.

units.la: XI. Et nobis sufficit quod opinio d. gl. communiter approbata sit a Doctorib. iuris Canonici, vt ex s. dictis colligitur. Nec curandum est quod Theologi aliter dicant, quia in ista materia magis standum est Doctorib. Canonum, quam in Theologiae Magistris, quia hic non agitur de articulis fidei, sed de morib. & integritate vitae, quo casu magis credendum est peritissimo. Canonum, prout est in Matrimonio, in voto, in Decimis, in Usuris, quia ista respiciunt morale philosophia, vt late tradit Pet. de Anch. in disputatione incipiete, Antiquus & moderni tempor ib. quae refert sequitur Ioan. de Ana. in c. in ciuitate, in 4 char. de Vsur. Alex. in consil. 1. col. 6. lib. 2. Et ex his habetur responsio generalis ad omnia allegata s. in contrarium.
units.tr: XI. And it is enough for us that the opinion of the gloss, commonly approved by the teachers of canon law, is as is gathered from what has been said. Nor need we worry that the theologians say otherwise, for in this matter one must rather abide by the teachers of the Canons than by the masters of theology, since what is at issue here is not articles of faith but morals and the integrity of life; in such a case one must rather trust the most skilled in the Canons, as is the case in matrimony, in vows, in tithes, and in usury, since these matters belong to moral philosophy. Peter of Ancarano treats this at length in the disputation beginning "Antiquus & moderni tempor ib.", which John of Anania follows in his commentary on the chapter "in ciuitate", in the fourth gloss on usury; Alexander in consilium 1, column 6, book 2. And from these points a general answer is had to all the authorities cited above on the other side.

units.la: XII. Ad maiorem tamen declarationem specialiter ad omnia respondetur. Primo, ergo non obstat quod dicitur in Can. aliorum. 9 q. 3. cum similib. quaestionib. allegatis in contrarium quia procedunt regulariter, & talis regula limitat non procedere in quibusdam casib. s. dictis, & praesertim in haeresi per text. in d. Can. si Papa. Non obstant quaedam iura, in quibus etiam de haeresi Concilium noluit iudicare Symmachum Papam, nec Marcellinum, quia primo de Symmacho (secundum glossam ibi in verbo immunis dicto Canone Concilia, paragraph. hunc etiam, in verbo Symmachus Papa calumniose. calumniose accusatus fuit, & constabat Concilio de calumnia, ideo absolutus fuit: & licet tex. dicat causa synmachi Dei inducto reseruatur, ita placuit pnunciare Concilio, qa non constabat de crimine, & de occultis Ecclesia nō iudicat 32.q.5. in Can.si.n.31.dist.in cano.erubescant & in 2.q.5 in Can.consuluisti. Si enim crimen haeresis probatum fuisset. Concilio iudicare potuisset, vt probatur in dict Can.si Papa. Nā vana fuisset congregatio Cōcilij, si potestate iudicandi non habuisset. Secūdo de Marcelliro non fuit iudicatus vt haereticus, quia paratus erat se corrigere, quo casu non debet pro haeretico reputari, si Papa velit se corrigere, secundū gl.in dict. Can.si Papa, in verbo a fide. Facit textus in c. ad abolendam, de haeret. 24.q.3. Can. dixit Apostolus. Et gloss. 2. in Can. nec licuit, 17. distinct & gloss. 24.q.1. in Can. hoc est fides. Secundo respondetur q Marcellinus cōpulsus idolis sacrificauit, unde per hoc non dicitur haereticus licet peccauerit, vt dicitur depoenit. distin.1. in Can. potest fieri. in glo.2. & idem glo.sin.9.q.3. in Can.non solum Et in haeresi omnes ita tenent. Unde nō est in hoc laborandum. Non obstat q dicit Hostiensis in dict. c.propositum, q illa verba d.c Ecclesia intelliguntur in summo Pontifice de Ecclesia triumphanti, & non de Ecclesia militanti, quia illud verum est regulariter, sed fallit in quibusdam casib. supradictis, & pserrim in haeresi, & crimine scandaloso. Et ita Abb. in terminis dicit in dict. c.propositum, colum.sin vbi inquit dictum Hostiensis procedere in delicto occulto, p quo non scandalizatur Ecclesia: secus si notorium sit & scandalosum delictum, quia tunc tota regula Euangelica habet locum in summo Pontifice, cum p tali crimine accusari possit, vt voluit singulariter glosa in dict. Can.si Papa, 40. distinct. Et ad s. dicta omnia etiam aliter & late respondet Rom. in Consil. 5.3. allegato. Non obstat successiue q cōtra illam tenet Theologi, quia nobis sufficit q approbata sit per Magistros & Doctores Canonum, quorum auctoritas in casu isto praevalet vt dictum fuit: Nō obstat q ratio glosse, in dict. Can.si Papa, non videtur vera, quia in tali casu non dicitur proprie haeresis, & text. in dict. Can.si Papa, de haeresi proprie intelligitur, vt s. in contrarium late dictum fuit.
units.tr: XII. For a fuller explanation, however, I reply specifically to each point. First, what is said in Can. aliorum, 9 q. 3, together with similar questions cited to the contrary, is no obstacle, because those texts state a general rule, and such a rule is limited so that it does not apply in certain cases, namely those already mentioned, and especially in heresy, according to the text in the said Can. si Papa. Nor do certain laws stand in the way, in which the Council was unwilling to judge Pope Symmachus or Marcellinus. For, first, concerning Symmachus (according to the gloss there, on the word immunis, in the said canon Concilia, paragraph hunc etiam, on the words Symmachus Papa calumniose), he was accused calumniously, and it was established to the Council that the charge was a calumny, so he was acquitted. Although the text says "the cause of Symmachus is reserved to God," the Council decided to pronounce thus because the crime was not established, and the Church does not judge hidden matters (32 q. 5, Can. si; 31 dist., Can. erubescant; and 2 q. 5, Can. consuluisti). For if the crime of heresy had been proved, the Council could have judged, as is shown in the said Can. si Papa; the gathering of the Council would have been pointless if it had no power to judge. Second, Marcellinus was not judged as a heretic, because he was ready to correct himself, and in that case he should not be regarded as a heretic if the Pope is willing to correct himself, according to the gloss in the said Can. si Papa, on the words a fide. The text in c. ad abolendam, de haeret., and 24 q. 3, Can. dixit Apostolus, supports this, as do the gloss 2 in Can. nec licuit, dist. 17, and the gloss on 24 q. 1, Can. hoc est fides. Secondly, it is answered that Marcellinus, being compelled, sacrificed to idols; hence he is not called a heretic by this, although he sinned, as is said in de poenit., dist. 1, Can. potest fieri, gloss 2, and in the same gloss on 9 q. 3, Can. non solum. And all hold this in the case of heresy, so there is no need to labour over this point. It is no obstacle that Hostiensis, in the said c. propositum, says those words, d. c. Ecclesia, are to be understood of the supreme Pontiff as referring to the Church triumphant and not the Church militant, because that is true as a rule, but it fails in the cases mentioned above, especially in heresy and in a scandalous crime. Abbas says the same in terms in the said c. propositum, col. (sin.), where he states that the opinion of Hostiensis applies to a hidden offence by which the Church is not scandalised; otherwise, if the offence is notorious and scandalous, the whole evangelical rule applies to the supreme Pontiff, since he can be accused of such a crime, as the gloss in the said Can. si Papa, dist. 40, specially wished. Roman, in his cited Consilium 5.3, also answers all the said objections otherwise and at length. It is further no obstacle that the Theologians hold the contrary, because it is enough for us that the view is approved by the Masters and Doctors of the Canons, whose authority in this case prevails, as was said. It is no obstacle that the reasoning of the gloss in the said Can. si Papa does not seem true, because in such a case it is not properly called heresy; for the text in the said Can. si Papa is understood of heresy properly, as was said at length above to the contrary.

units.la: XIII. Quia pro responsione & intellectu dict. glos. aduertendum est q gl. ibi in dict. Can. si Papa ponit duos casus, in quib. Papa accusari potest. Primus est in haeresi, vt ibi expresse dicitur:
units.tr: XIII. Because, for the answer and the understanding of the said gloss, it must be noted that the gloss there, in the said Can. si Papa, sets out two cases in which a Pope can be accused. The first is heresy, as is there expressly said:

units.la: Secundus est in alio delicto notorio & scandaloso, in quo Papa in corrigibilis sit: Illa enim incorrigibilitas seu contumacia dicitur haeresis secundum glos. ibi, & tali casu non requirit q sit haeresis proprie, quia tunc secundus casus reduceretur ad primum de haeresi.
